column36: Aging, neurofunctional reorganization and communication abilities
column37: This research program is about how the brain reorganizes itself to support the preservation of communication abilities during successful aging. The components of communication that will be studied are important for everyday life as they include the ability to use and process the meanings of words, to understand narratives and to understand the non-literal meanings of utterances such as indirect requests. Using the most powerful neuroimaging technologies -- including functional magnetic resonance and optical imaging -- this study will allow to describe the patterns of neural networks for communication associated with successful aging. At the same time, the impact of education and the relationship with cognitive abilities will be explored. Overall, this program will allow us to identify the optimal functional reorganization that sustains successful communication with increased age as well as the most suitable rehabilitation strategies for elderly who have to live with communication deficits due to a brain lesion.

column36: Effectiveness of a consumer-targeted pharmacist-led educational intervention to reduce inappropriate prescriptions
column37: As Canadians age, the probability of suffering from different medical conditions and having to take many medications increases. As the number of medications increases, so too does the risk of side effects. Some medications pose greater risks than others. For example, some medications can cause a person to fall, have trouble with their memory, or lead to hospital emergency room visits for low blood sugar. When medications are prescribed for which safer alternatives exist, it is called "inappropriate prescribing". National specialist consensus panels regularly publish lists of inappropriate drugs that pose an elevated risk of adverse effects, yet unfortunately inappropriate prescribing persists. As many as 1 in 4 Canadian seniors on public drug programs consume one or more inappropriate medications. Our project proposes a novel intervention whereby pharmacists provide educational materials to both seniors and their primary care providers on the risks of taking inappropriate prescriptions. Recommendations to change inappropriate prescriptions to safer alternatives are provided. Forty-six community pharmacies in Quebec will help us recruit 400 of clients to this project. We hope to show that empowered patients can play a role in helping health professionals reduce inappropriate prescriptions and increase medication safety in the elderly.

column36: The Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) Health Outcomes Team (COHORT)
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), also known as emphysema or chronic bronchitis, is the third leading cause of death worldwide. In Canada, it affects an estimated one in four adults aged 35 and older and is the most common cause of chronic disease hospital admission and readmission. My goal is to improve the health of the substantial number of Canadians affected by COPD and reduce its burden on our health care system. I am an internationally known health services researcher and a practicing respirologist who has published high impact studies in the world's most prestigious peer review medical journals. I have received close to 17 million dollars in peer-reviewed funding as principal and co-investigator. I will conduct my research using unique population data sources-including clinical databases and electronic medical records-and innovative techniques to examine the real world experiences of people with COPD. My success will be assured through excellent mentorship, an outstanding research environment and by working with an engaged network of clinicians, decision makers and stakeholders to ensure my results are immediately relevant and applied in improving clinical care and developing health policy. Over the next five years, the following four objectives will drive my research and knowledge translation agenda: 1. Create new knowledge that improves clinical care and policy for people with COPD, 2. Identify and fill gaps in quality, evidence-based COPD care, 3. Ensure my research results are translated into improvements in COPD clinical care and policy and ultimately contribute to improved health and a strengthened health care system, and 4. Train and mentor the next generation of respiratory disease researchers and knowledge translation specialists. Achieving my objectives will lead to substantial and sustainable improvements in care for Canadians with COPD, improving their health and reducing strain on our already overburdened health care system.

column36: Muscle-bone interactions in Canadians: a national, population-based study
column37: Osteoporosis is a common bone disorder that can affect people of any age, even children. The role of muscle as a determinant of bone health is increasingly recognized, but factors influencing muscle-bone interactions across the lifespan have not been investigated in detail. Overall Objective: In this study we will elucidate determinants of muscle-bone interactions in Canadians from 6 to 79 years of age. Study Design: The Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) is a fully operational program for determining health indicators the Canadian population that is led by Statistics Canada. Statistics Canada has agreed to our proposal to collect data on musculoskeletal health in a population-based sample of 10,000 Canadians from 6 to 79 years of age. Participants will undergo peripheral quantitative computed tomography to assess muscle and bone characteristics at the lower leg, muscle function tests, as well as biomarkers of bone metabolism. The aims are (1) to develop reference data for key musculoskeletal parameters; (2) to assess the muscle-bone relationship in healthy subjects and (3) to assess the effect of common obesity on the muscle-bone relationship. Statistics Canada has agreed to contribute $5,700,000 to this project. Clinical Importance: These studies will improve tools to study muscle-bone interactions and identify factors that can be targeted for interventions. As CHMS makes raw data of all studies available to the Canadian scientific community, the present project establishes a research platform that can be accessed by multiple investigators in Canada.

column36: Developing, Implementing and Evaluating a Model for Youth Mental Health Service Transformation: ACCESS*- Canada *ACCESS: Adolescent / young adult Connections to Community-driven, Early, Strengths-based and stigma-free Services
column37: Over 75% of mental disorders begin in early adolescence or young adulthood. When untreated, mental disorders can have serious negative consequences for youth, cause immense suffering for youth and families, and have high costs to society. Outcomes for most mental disorders have remained generally poor for many years. It is estimated that only 20-25% of youth with mental health challenges in Canada receive help. A major reason for this are inadequacies in the manner in which mental health services are provided to youth. Current services often do not offer "best-practice" treatments in a readily accessible way. Other obstacles include long wait times and difficulties encountered in navigating a complicated mental health care system. Also, traditional mental health services often do not sufficiently engage youth, resulting in high drop-out rates. ACCESS is a network including youth, families, mental health clinicians, researchers, policy makers and community members. Our goal is to conduct an in-depth, innovative transformation in the way youth are cared for by mental health services in the "real world", and to evaluate what worked. At sites across Canada, this transformation will target urban, rural and Aboriginal youth, and vulnerable populations including youth who are homeless, under youth protection or in contact with the criminal justice system. Our major aims are: -To identify more youth in need, sooner, through improved mental health awareness, well-publicized means of entry, open referral and rapid response (within 72 hours) -To offer the youth appropriate, optimal care with seamless navigation through various services -To create cultures of care that feature youth-friendly treatment, an optimistic tone, sustained youth and family participation at all levels, shared decision making and improved work/educational outcomes -A final important goal will be to sustain the positive changes in mental health services that produce better outcomes for our youth

column36: Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) is a national study of adult development and aging that includes 50,000 individuals between the ages of 45 and 85 from across Canada to be followed over 20 years. The ultimate aim of the CLSA is to find ways to improve the health of Canadians by better understanding the processes and dimensions of aging. Over the past 5 years, the CLSA research team has planned and implemented the study and recruited more than 38,000 of the 50,000 participants who have completed baseline assessments including telephone interviews, face-to-face interviews, as well as visits to specially designed data collection sites. The data provided by the 20,000 individuals who completed telephone interviews are now ready for release to researchers, who meet the CLSA requirements for access and are approved through a formal evaluation process. All 50,000 individuals will have completed their baseline assessment by the spring of 2015. The first follow up of the CLSA participants is scheduled to begin in the early summer of 2015 taking place 3 years after the baseline assessments. As part of the follow up participants will undergo repeat assessments and will be asked to complete additional components that have been selected based on recommendations from expert researchers to enhance the information collected and expand the science of the study. In this application, we are requesting funds to enable the CLSA team to plan and complete the first follow up and to plan and begin the second follow up. The need for information collected over time to inform decisions and design interventions and policies to improve the health and well-being of today and tomorrows seniors is widely recognized by researchers, and federal, provincial, and territorial governments. The CLSA was conceived to fill this information gap and to provide solid evidence to inform health and social care policies in Canada.

column36: The Hippo pathway as a regulator of ovarian follicle development
column37: Oocytes develop and mature in the ovary within structures called follicles. Follicles are recruited from a reserve and grow under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) produced by the pituitary gland. Once terminally developed, the follicle ruptures to release the (now mature) oocyte at the moment of ovulation. Ovulation itself is triggered by a second pituitary hormone, luteinizing hormone (LH), which also causes the reorganization of the ovulated follicle into a new glandular tissue termed the corpus luteum, which secretes the large amounts of progesterone necessary for the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy. Whereas we have long known FSH and LH to be major players in ovarian follicle development, how exactly they exert their effects remains incompletely understood. Ourselves and others have recently found that a signaling pathway called Hippo is inactivated during FSH-mediated follicle growth, but is rapidly activated during LH-mediate ovulation/luteinization, suggesting that FSH and LH exert their effects, at least in part, via Hippo signaling. This proposal will seek to confirm these preliminary results, in part by studying mice that lack the Hippo pathway genes Yap, Taz, Lats1 and Lats2, in which we expect defects in FSH- and LH-mediated ovarian processes. We will also study the mechanisms whereby Hippo transmits biological signals, and identify the genes that it regulates. Together, our studies will uncover new information regarding how FSH and LH act, and about the biological roles of Hippo signaling in the ovary. This research should also provide new insight into fertility disorders such as ovulatory failure and luteal insufficiency.

We now know that the immature brain is extremely fragile, especially during the last few weeks of pregnancy when there is a period of rapid brain maturation. Using novel brain scanning techniques, we showed that newborns with heart defects have slower brain development before their surgeries - suggesting that heart defects affect brain development before birth. Furthermore, we recently demonstrated that in the last 3 months of pregnancy, fetuses with heart defects have reduced amounts of oxygen being delivered to the brain. The fundamental premise of this proposal is that, in fetuses with heart defects, reduced amounts of oxygen delivered to the brain interfere with normal brain maturation. Furthermore, we believe that if the limitation in brain oxygenation persists after birth, the brain does not recover, and motor and cognitive skills do not develop normally. We propose the use of heart and brain imaging to measure brain oxygen delivery in two serious and common heart defects at several time points: from fetal life, through the newborn period, and into infancy. We aim to characterize how delivery of oxygen to the brain impacts: 1) brain maturation, and 2) the development of thinking, language, behaviour, and motor skills. We will be able to examine how improvements in brain oxygen delivery brought about by heart surgery can improve brain maturation and developmental function in childhood.

The goal of the present research project is to identify transcription factors regulating Leydig cell development and function. To do so, different but complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches will be used. column37: One in four infants are born with low amounts of vitamin D stored in their body. This study is designed to test whether improving vitamin D status quickly after birth helps infants to build muscle and to normalize growth. Vitamin D supplementation is a modifiable factor that is already recommended for all term born infants. Knowing how much is needed in infants born with low stores has not been tested in a controlled manner in Canada.

column36: Mechanisms of breast cancer metastasis: Understanding the roles and molecular functions of the RTK AXL
column37: The most important clinical factor associated with poor survival during breast cancer progression is the appearance of metastases. It is such secondary tumors, often far away from the initial breast tumor, that threaten the life of afflicted women. Our research program aims at uncovering the molecular mechanisms that facilitate both the escape of cancer cells from the breast tumor and their ability to enter blood vessels to ultimately travel to secondary tumor soil where they can grow as metastasis. We focus here on a protein named AXL that is found at the surface of both the cancer cells and the tumor blood vessels. The presence of AXL in human breast tumors correlates with the formation of metastases. Here, we first study the progression of breast cancer in a mouse model of breast cancer where AXL is deleted. Second, we use sophisticated protein analyses methods to detect the large number of proteins engaged by AXL to promote cell invasion. The function of the modulated proteins will be analyzed in molecular details. Finally, we used gene signatures of aggressive cancer cells lacking AXL expression to identify candidate anti-metastatic drugs that we will test in vitro and in vivo. Globally, this project aims to develop strategies to interfere with AXL function in metastatic breast cancer cells with the ultimate objective of moving toward the identification of anti-metastatic strategies.

column36: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Neurophotonics
column37: Psychiatric disorders represent a major public health problem, accruing enormous socioeconomic costs. The available treatments remain largely insufficient. Advances in the field are impaired by the lack of proper tools to conduct adequate biological measurements to guide diagnosis and treatment. This is particularly critical given evidence that early treatment of psychiatric disorders, before the onset of debilitating symptoms, leads to significantly improved clinical outcomes.The CERC in Neurophotonics proposes to fill this gap by developing and exploiting advanced photonics technologies to probe brain cells and tissue function non-invasively with high spatial and temporal resolution. The aim is to identify novel biomarkers of psychiatric diseases; in particular, to identify in children within affected families, early biomarkers reflecting a high risk of later developing psychiatric diseases.Optical technology developments that will be pursued include:1) Coherent imaging techniques, such as digital holography quantitative phase microscopy (DH-QPM), to study the structure and dynamics of cells at nanoscale levels (protein content, nanoscale membrane fluctuations, water movements). DH-QPM will be combined with other imaging and spectroscopic approaches (fluorescence, Coherent Anti-Stokes-Raman Scattering, High Harmonics) for multimodal optical interrogation of cells and tissue.2) Incoherent imaging methods will also be developed including multi-fiber, miniaturized optical probes (optiprobes) to extract spatia-temporally resolved reflectance spectra in small tissue volumes. This will yield structural and functional (neurovascular/neurometabolic) information for in vivo biopsies performed during cognitive tasks with previously inaccessible temporal resolution.Diagnostic potential will be validated using different paradigms:A) in vivo measurements in brain tissue to explore pathophysiological mechanisms inanimal models reproducing certain features of psychiatric disorders;B) non-invasive photonics-based structural/functional measurements in volunteers, psychiatric patients (e.g., schizophrenia and bipolar disorders) and high risk children during cognitive tasks and neurophysiological tests;C) in vitro measurements to study the structure, dynamics, metabolism and stress response of neural cells generated from volunteer- and patient-derived stem cells.The proposed research offers extraordinary translational perspectives for personalized medicine for the prevention and treatment of psychiatric diseases.

column37: The primary care system in Newfoundland & Labrador today looks much the same as it did 20 years ago, but the need for more comprehensive care among the residents of NL has been steadily increasing. The province is facing high rates of chronic diseases like diabetes, and a large proportion of the population is approaching retirement age. To give patients across the province full access to the best possible primary care, we must change our current system into one where teams of healthcare professionals work with each other and with their patients to achieve better health. The Primary Healthcare Research and Integration to Improve Health System Efficiency (PRIIME) Network brings researchers, clinicians and policymakers in the province together with patients and their families to find ways to improve the way primary healthcare is delivered in our communities. PRIIME has significant expertise in health systems research, experience in using technology to improve care, an appreciation for the unique challenges faced by our rural and remote communities, and a dedication to pursue research outcomes that matter to patients. With the commitment of key decision-makers across NL, PRIIME has an opportunity to support major changes to the primary care system that will provide better care for patients from birth to death, particularly complex patients whose needs haven't always been met. The Network's leadership is dedicated to finding new ways to care for patients in community-based primary care while making efficient use of limited resources. PRIIME will look at changes to primary care that have worked in other parts of Canada, such as care teams that include doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other allied health practitioners working together to support their complex patients. The goal is to build a sustainable system of community-based primary health care in a way that will meet the needs and improve the health of Newfoundlanders and Labradorians.

column37: Infections caused by respiratory viruses and herpes viruses are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality among Canadians. For instance, influenza viruses affect 1 of 6 Canadians each winter and cause approximately 30 000 hospitalizations and 3 000 deaths annually. In addition, the incidence of genital herpes has increased by 30% over the past 20 years. In the next 7 years, Dr Guy Boivin proposes an ambitious research program to better understand these viral diseases using relevant laboratory and animal models and to develop/evaluate novel therapeutic and preventive approaches. The second theme involves the characterization of antiviral drug resistance mechanisms as well as the development of innovative antiviral and immune-based therapeutic strategies. The third theme consists in developing/improving a series of vaccines based on new routes of immunization (mucosal, intradermal), powerful adjuvants and recombinant attenuated viral strains. The research program of Dr Boivin will be significant at many levels for the Canadian population. First, his work on drug-resistant viruses and development of new antivirals and immunomodulatory compounds will result in improved health care towards patients with respiratory and herpes virus infections. Also, his research on new vaccines and viral transmission could have a major impact on public health policies and pandemic preparedness.

column36: The role of the immune system in obesity related insulin resistance and metabolic disease
column37: Obesity is associated with a metabolic syndrome characterized by high fat and sugar in the blood, and is linked to type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. Obesity associated metabolic disease is a major health concern, affecting more than 20% of Canadian adults, with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes alone affecting at least 10 million Canadians, and costing our healthcare system more than $10 billion. Despite this burden on Canadians, the underlying mechanisms of disease are poorly understood. The Winer lab and others have shown that low levels of inflammation lies at the core of metabolic disease. When people become obese, inflammation blocks the body's ability to respond well to insulin, called insulin resistance (prediabetes), and this process leads to high blood fatty acids and sugar, triggering type 2 diabetes and liver disease. The Winer lab has identified inflammation in the fat surrounding internal organs as a major cause of insulin resistance. In particular, fatty tissues in obese mice and people contain high amounts of white blood cells, including T and B cells that cause inflammation. These cells produce inflammatory molecules called cytokines, which cause insulin resistance. The identification of immune cells in fat controlling metabolic disease is considered as one of the "breakthroughs of the decade" in metabolic research. The goal of the research program is to build on this work, and investigate how the immune system drives insulin resistance in fat and in other organs like the liver and gut. The lab will also understand how insulin affects immune system function. The program will utilize the latest in high resolution and robotic equipment, mouse models, and metabolic assessment, with aim to translate findings in humans. This program may lead to new ways to prevent, diagnose, and treat diabetes. Moreover, it is only through study of the immune system will vaccines with the ability to prevent diabetes altogether become a future reality.

column37: In the absence of treatment, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 34 million people worldwide. The proposed research program will put us a step closer towards HIV eradication by extending these observations and generating better molecules to expose vulnerable parts of Env. Information generated by my research program will also be valuable in the current worldwide efforts aimed at developing an HIV-1 vaccine.

column36: Inherited susceptibility to cancer: from gene discovery to mechanisms to clinical applications
column37: Cancer is a common disease which is typically the result of genetic changes that lead to aberrant growth and behaviour of affected cells, which then produce tumours which can spread throughout the body. Some individuals are at higher risk for cancer because of a family history of the disease. In these families, critical genetic alterations are inherited from one generation to the next in cancer predisposition genes. A better understanding of these predisposing genetic changes is not only useful to help the individuals who are mutation carriers, but it also improves our general understanding of how cancers develop in everyone else in the population by better understanding which genes are involved and how. The work performed in our laboratory for the past 20 years has focused on the study of inherited cancers in high risk families. This work led us to identify a number of new cancer susceptibility genes where genetic alterations can cause disease. In addition, we have also identified very specific changes, referred to as founder mutations, which are observed at higher frequency in our local Quebec populations. There are several reasons to continue this important work. 1) The discovery of novel cancer susceptibility genes / mutations provides at risk patients with surveillance and prevention options for their cancers. This can improve the odds for patients to survive their cancer and can also improve their psychological well-being by giving them a measure of control over their disease. 2) The establishment of population-specific screening panels provides cost effective avenues for genetic screening tailored to local populations, making screening more financially accessible to the health care system providing this service locally. 3) Identification of mutations can allow physicians to choose more effective treatment options for some cancers by using targeted treatments based on the molecular profile of the patients and the tumours they harbour.

column36: Harnessing chemical biology to control pathogenic bacteria and regulate the gut microbiota
column37: Bacteria have the ability to either harm or help us. Harm comes from pathogenic bacteria that can cause infections. Help comes from beneficial bacteria, such as those that live in the human gut, that help to digest food and prevent infection. To eliminate harmful bacteria and promote the growth of beneficial bacteria, we must first study the underlying chemistry and biology that controls their growth and function. The proposed research program will study bacterial chemistry and biology in two ways: 1) we are developing new antibiotics against bacteria that cause infections; and 2) we are studying the biochemical pathways that enable beneficial bacteria to survive in the human gut. A brief summary of both components is provided below. The first part of the proposed research program aims to develop antibiotics to treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics are chemicals that specifically kill bacteria. Since the discovery of antibiotics, these chemicals have become essential medicines to prevent and cure infections. A key challenge for using antibiotics, however, is the emergence of drug-resistance, where bacteria acquire the ability to survive despite the presence of the antibiotic. We are developing new antibiotics to treat antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The second part of the proposed research program aims to understand how certain bacteria survive in the human gut. Babies are born with a sterile gut, and gradually acquire a complex community of bacteria through interaction with the environment. These gut bacteria help digest food and prevent infections by pathogenic bacteria. Many diseases are caused by 'microbial imbalance,' where the composition of bacteria and other microorganisms in the gut deviates from normal. We will investigate how the underlying chemistry and biology enable certain bacterial species to survive in the human gut. This knowledge could ultimately enable the development of probiotic and nutritional supplements to prevent and treat disease.

column36: Enteric neural and glial control of gastrointestinal function in health and inflammatory disease.
column37: The function of your digestive system is key to good health. During digestion food moves from the stomach to the small intestine, where absorption of nutrients occurs, and finally to the colon for elimination. Movement of food through the intestines requires precise control. Not only does the gut move and digest food, but while doing so it must protect the rest of the body from ingested pathogens and from the microbes that live in its lumen. These microbes are essential for health, but must remain in the intestine or they can cause harm. Thus the gut has a dual role: digestion and defense. Digestion and defense are sufficiently complex that a "brain" is required to regulate and control them. This brain in the gut is called the enteric nervous system (ENS). The ENS is composed of nerves and specialized cells called enteric glial cells. Enteric glial cells were originally thought to be passive support cells, but through my research we know that nerves and glial cells actively communicate with each other by releasing chemical messengers. This bi-directional nerve-glial communication is important for the ENS to control the movement of food through the gut and for defense. Alterations in chemical communication in the ENS appears to be responsible for many of the symptoms of gastrointestinal disease. The vision of my research program is to discover new ways to alleviate the symptoms of gut disorders through studies of enteric nerve-glial communication. I will study the movements of the gut in the normal state and establish how nerves and glial cells communicate to regulate them. I will build on this information to find new ways to correct the abnormal gut movements that occur in disease. I will also focus on how microbes in the gut influence the neural and glial regulation of gut functions in health and disease. My ultimate goal is to develop better treatments for debilitating conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and irritable bowel syndrome.

column37: The current proposal is founded on the discovery of a new approach for the treatment of autoimmune disease (occurring when the white blood cells of our immune system mistakenly recognize and attack natural components of our own tissues). Traditionally, vaccines have been used to expand white blood cells affording protection against viruses, bacteria or cancer, or to delete white blood cells causing autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes (T1D) and multiple sclerosis (MS). We have developed a new type of 'vaccine' based on nanotechnology (using particles thousands of times smaller than the size of normal white blood cell) that can stop anti-self immune responses by selectively expanding what we call 'autoregulatory' white blood cells. These 'autoregulatory' white blood cells put the brakes on the disease-causing autoimmune attack, by inhibiting the activation of all the disease-causing white blood cells, resulting in their complete suppression. As a result, these nanomedicines can blunt highly complex autoimmune responses in mice, including T1D, MS, primary biliary cirrhosis and arthritis, without causing generalized suppression of the immune system. Importantly, we have established that human disease-relevant nanomedicines can effectively trigger the expansion of human autoregulatory white blood cells in 'humanized' mice (mice carrying white blood cells from patients), indicating that this approach is applicable to humans. Here, we will dissect the cellular origin of the disease-suppressor cell type triggered by our nanomedicines, as well as the mechanisms and the downstream cellular targets through which it suppresses disease. Furthermore, we will use mice 'humanized' with white blood cells from T1D patients to select the corresponding drug candidates for clinical development. We anticipate that these studies will open new lines of inquiry in immunity and autoimmunity and will propel a promising new therapeutic avenue for autoimmunity to the clinic.

Our goal is to fully describe the molecular mechanisms through which PCSK9 acts and to use this knowledge to develop more effective and better-targeted drugs against PCSK9. 2-The engineered PC7 inactivation in mice results in much reduced anxiety, depression and emotional fear. In humans, lower PC7 levels are also associated with a more efficient iron metabolism, higher levels of the good cholesterol high density lipoprotein (HDL) and lower levels of the bad triglycerides. We will study the biology of PC7 in mice and humans and develop PC7 inhibitors that should find new therapeutic clinical applications for the above indications.

column36: Muscarinic cholinergic modulation of cognition in primates
column37: Changes in normal cognition are a characteristic feature of schizophrenia. These problems can be seen in a reduced attention span, difficulties to memorize things, poor judgment skills, and in difficulties to plan and prioritize everyday life. Although our current drugs are quite successful in treating hallucinations and delusions, they largely fail in treating these cognitive deficits. Told to look away from a flash of light, they are unable to resist the automatic urge to glance at the stimulus. Subjects without the disorder can override the impulse. We will focus on drugs that act on muscarinic acetylcholine receptors which have been proposed as a novel way to treat cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. We will record the activity of individual brain cells in different areas in trained monkeys, manipulate their activity through the application of drugs that act on different muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and measure brain-wide changes in activity and communication using functional imaging techniques. My goal is to understand the role of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in cognition from the level of single brain cells to the communication in the entire brain. By understanding how brain areas interact and how certain drugs can improve cognitive processes, we hope to identify drugs that will improve the cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

column37: Circulating in the blood is a myriad of cells with different functions that are critical for our health, including red blood cells that carry oxygen, platelets that help to stop bleeding and immune cells that fight off infections and cancers. These circulating blood cells are not immortal, but rather are constantly being renewed by a continuous repetition of the process that led to their initial specialization. In this complex process, banks of genes are turned on and off in precursor cells to "steer" their differentiation toward one specialized cell type or another. This occurs primarily through the action of proteins called transcription factors, which reside in the cell nucleus and can regulate the activity of thousands of genes simultaneously. Not surprisingly, mistakes sometimes occur in this complex process and can lead to a number of very serious diseases. My own research has focused on identifying the critical components in normal blood cell differentiation and in characterizing the molecular defects that lead, in particular, to bleeding disorders and blood-borne cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma. Over 20 years ago, I co-discovered two transcription factors (Gfi1 and Gfi1b) and was the first to determine the role of Gfi1 in blood diseases including leukemia. More recently, I discovered the role of another transcription factor and co-factor of Gfi1, called Miz-1, in blood cell formation and leukemia. My goal is to understand how key blood formation processes are controlled on a molecular level and how deficiencies in these processes that lead to diseases can be fixed. Over the next few years, we will bring together clinical expertise and the most advanced biomedical research techniques to address two blood cancers: acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) as well as inherited platelet disorders (IPD) that lead to blood clotting problems.

column36: Dissecting synaptic mechanisms in sensory processing, motivation, and development.
column37: Understanding the brain is one of the greatest scientific puzzles of our time. This enormous challenge requires a long-term strategy that spans multiple disciplines and leverages diverse approaches ranging from basic science to applied clinical research. A key component of this collective effort is the use of model systems with brains far smaller than our own. Unraveling the principles of how these simpler brains develop and operate to encode and decode information is a critical step in the more complex task of understanding the human brain, and how we can repair it when it no longer functions properly. My research program is focused on discovering fundamental principles of how the brain processes taste information and translates it into feeding behavior. I study this problem in fruit flies because the relative simplicity of the fly brain, combined with a wealth of available genetic and optical tools, allows us to probe neural circuit function with higher resolution and more complete coverage than is currently possible in mammalian systems. My proposed Foundation research program is built on three complementary objectives: 1) To uncover the neural circuit mechanisms driving integration of different tastes. 2) To delineate the mechanisms underlying hunger-dependent changes in taste perception. 3) To discover important new genes involved in brain development. Understanding how taste drives animals to consume calorie-dense foods will lead to new strategies in the fight against overconsumption and obesity. Uncovering specific mechanisms that affect insect taste sensitivity and feeding behavior will also aid in developing tools to control devastating human insect-borne diseases, such as malaria. Finally, discovering genes with novel roles in brain development will provide possible new targets for drugs to treat or prevent neurodevelopmental disorders like autism and intellectual disability.

column36: Thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self
column37: Self/nonself discrimination by T lymphocytes is a fundamental requirement of life in vertebrates and is implicated in most fatal diseases in humans. Indeed, i) nonself recognition is essential for elimination of microbes and cancer cells, while ii) immune responses against self antigens cause classic autoimmune diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis) and are instrumental in chronic inflammatory diseases, hypertension and atherosclerosis. T lymphocytes learn how to distinguish self from nonself in the thymus. Importantly, the thymus ages more rapidly than all other organs, and by the age of 45 y, 75% of the thymus is lost in humans. Thymus senescence decreases the ability to recognize new antigens and responsiveness to vaccines, and increases the risk of infection, cancer and autoimmune diseases in ageing people. Hence, it is a sobering thought that our understanding of the molecular composition of the immune self is very rudimentary and that we do not understand the mechanisms of thymic involution. Accordingly, the two main themes of my research program are thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self. My specific objectives are i) to discover the molecular composition of the immune self, ii) to uncover how the immune self is perturbed in cancer cells, iii) to understand the rules governing T lymphocyte education in the thymus, and iv) to find a strategy to rejuvenate the thymus. Answers to these questions will be instrumental in i) treating thymus atrophy, the most common cause of immune deficiency in humans, ii) understanding the molecular bases of self-tolerance and enabling molecular evidence-based treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, and iii) discovering cancer-specific antigens that can be used as personalized vaccines for cancer treatment.

column36: Defining critical pathways for neuronal loss and dysfunction in Parkinsons disease and stroke
column37: Stroke and Parkinson's disease are devastating neurological disorders with devastating personal, social, and economic consequences. Stroke affects 15 million people a year worldwide and is the third leading cause of death. Parkinson's disease, a movement disorder, affects 10 million people worldwide and is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. We now realize that there are incredibly sophisticated processes that govern the death of brain cells in these conditions. Our work is focused on understanding these complex processes and blocking the signals that lead to death thereby eliminating or reducing the brain injury in these conditions. While seemingly simple in concept, this strategy is incredibly difficult. For example, multiple signals likely control the death process, some of which work in parallel to control the long-term survival of brain cells. Also, how/whether manipulation of these signals ultimately lead to a proper functioning brain circuit is unclear. Finally, because it is difficult to actually work in humans to manipulate these signals, the development and use of appropriate animal models of study are critical. Our research program takes all these complex issues into consideration to systematically work through the issues that are impeding effective therapeutic strategies to treat stroke and PD. We have exciting and novel insights into the complex network of events that occur in a brain damaged by stroke or in PD. We will critically test whether these signals effectively lead to improved brain circuitry and animal behavior in these diseases. Together with a team of researchers and clinicians, we are working to define the appropriate strategies to treat these devastating neurological conditions. Our work is central to this important effort.

column36: Dietary Flaxseed as a Nutritional Intervention for Cardiovascular Disease
column37: High blood pressure (hypertension) is an important silent killer that can cause heart attacks and stroke. Not only is hypertension a deadly disease, it also cost $76 B last year in the US alone. Current drugs used to control hypertension are costly, can induce unwanted side-effects and they are not always effective in controlling blood pressure (BP) in all hypertensive patients. Having a food that will control BP represents a less expensive intervention than drugs. We have recently completed a major tightly controlled trial in which patients with peripheral arterial disease were supplemented daily for one year with flaxseed in their diet. Patients who entered the trial with high BP were the most affected by dietary flaxseed and systolic BP decreased by 15 mm Hg, an effect comparable to most hypertensive drugs available today. This decline in BP would lower the incidence of heart attacks and strokes by more than 50%. In the Foundation grant, we will continue our research with an on-going CIHR clinical trial to determine if flaxseed will lower BP in patients with high BP but without secondary disease. We will also study if flaxseed can delay or reduce the need for anti-hypertensive drugs. In a separate line of study in animal models, we will also examine the potential for dietary flaxseed to reduce damage to the heart after a heart attack has occurred. The mechanisms responsible for the anti-hypertensive action of flaxseed as well as its effects on heart protection from heart attacks will be studied. Providing low cost alternatives to drug therapy that can be used alone or in conjunction with medication has enormous appeal for the Canadian health care system. Even more importantly, this low cost alternative to expensive medication for high BP represents an appealing choice for third world countries and poor communities everywhere that cannot afford the drugs they need to lower BP and protect themselves from heart attacks and strokes.

column36: Quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Human Brain: Technical Innovation and Application to Neurological Disorders
column37: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides unparalleled insight into human disease. Through continued technical innovation, we will further its utility by advancing image acquisition, quantitative analysis, and physics knowledge. Our novel brain MRI methods will be applied to stroke patients, where current MRI protocols are insufficient for accurate diagnosis in some patient subgroups (e.g. transient ischemic attack, wake up strokes). These MRI methods will also provide insight into typical brain development with age, a process important for 'normal' cognitive and behavioural maturation that may also provide clues about vulnerability to neurological or psychiatric disorders. In addition, advanced MRI will capture the lifelong impact that prenatal exposure to neurotoxins (e.g. alcohol) can have on the brain and its development. The outcomes of this research are: (i) Technical Innovation of Brain MRI - advanced quantitative MRI methods with higher spatial resolution and greater specificity to metabolic and microstructural changes in brain. (ii) Better MRI Diagnosis of Stroke - improved lesion detection in cases where clinical symptoms suggest stroke but conventional MRI lacks sufficient image resolution to confirm diagnosis, stroke onset time estimation to allow treatment for patients who wake with symptoms, and the discovery of the mechanisms behind the sensitivity of MRI for stroke. (iii) MRI Insights into Brain Development - identification of new aspects of typical brain development in healthy individuals over the lifespan, and detection of otherwise "invisible" brain injury underlying cognitive deficits in fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). Brain imaging innovations have the potential to detect disease processes earlier, guide individualized treatment strategies, track rehabilitation, achieve better patient outcomes, enhance quality of life, yield insight into disease mechanisms, and provide evidence to support key public health policies.

column36: Ultra-high field Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Brain Structure and Function in Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Canada's multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence rate is amongst the highest in the world at 240 per 100,000 population, for reasons we don't understand. Fortunately, there are drugs that can reduce the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease, but these drugs are very expensive. The lifetime cost of these drugs for a single MS patient is about $1 million. If we could come up with a way to decide when, and what dose of drug to deliver to each patient, we could save the health care system billions of dollars. The goal of our research program is to develop and use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods to inform such decisions, by measuring biomarkers of the disease. MRI has been used for many years as part of the diagnosis of MS. However normal MRI findings have not correlated well with clinical symptoms and have not demonstrated significant ability to predict the course of the disease. This may be related to the fact that conventional MRI visualizes only some of the lesions and damage seen by pathologists in brain slices. Ultra-high magnetic field MRI systems have the potential to be more sensitive to the microscopic changes in tissue properties that occur as MS begins and progresses. MRI machines at such magnetic field strengths are undergoing approvals for clinical diagnostic use. Using a 7 Tesla (140,000 times the earth's magnetic field) human MRI system, we will develop MRI techniques that can characterize MS in patients on a microscopic scale. This could lead to earlier diagnosis of MS, and therefore the ability to intervene sooner with drug treatments. Earlier intervention results in better patient outcomes and lower treatment costs

column36: Molecular and Genetic basis of heart development and disease
column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 1-5% of the population and represents the largest class of birth defects. It is the leading cause of death in infants during the first year of life. It is also an independent risk factor for premature onset of adult cardiovascular disease including degenerative valve disease, myocardial infarction and sudden death. It is well established that CHD is a heritable trait, i.e. it 'runs in the family'. However, its transmission does not follow simple Mendelian inheritance and is influenced by other genetic as well as environmental factors. Despite great advances over the past decade, the genes responsible for the majority of human CHD remain unknown. A better understanding of the genes required for normal heart development will immensely advance our understanding and detection of CHD. It will also improve care for individuals with CHD and help prevent cardiovascular complications. During the past decade, our lab has proudly contributed to this area thru our discovery and characterization of several genes essential for normal heart development such as GATA4 and GATA5. Alterations in these genes are associated with several types of human CHD, including bicuspid aortic valve, atrial and ventricular septal defects as well as rhythm abnormalities. Using our unique tools and animal models of human disease, we wish to pursue our studies aimed at understanding the genetics of normal and abnormal heart development. We will also use our animal models to gain a better understanding of how cardiac birth defects make the heart more vulnerable to other cardiovascular problems. Such knowledge will help design therapies for prevention and treatment that are presently unavailable. The results of our research will continue to impact diagnosis and care of individuals with heart disease or with a family history of the disease.

column36: A Rapid Analytics Platform for Influenza Vaccine Evaluation and Translational Research
column37: Influenza remains a major cause of death and illness in Canada and globally. "Seasonal" flu vaccines remain the mainstay of flu control, but their field effectiveness, especially among the sick and elderly who need them the most, is questionable. Newer expensive vaccines with limited data have mushroomed raising the cost and complexity of vaccine programs. Flu vaccine effectiveness (VE) is influenced by vaccine potency and uptake; viral strain, infectivity and virulence and by host characteristics; factors that often vary by season, product and population. Progress towards developing better vaccines has been hampered by dogma, and over-reliance on poorly validated immune correlates, paucity of clinical trials due to ethical/practical constraints and fragmentary reductionist approaches to post-licensure evaluation. Flu VE cannot be understood using one-off studies limited to specific seasons, populations and outcomes, and interpreted in isolation of viral and host characteristics. Our challenge is to design effective & sustainable strategies of continually and comprehensively evaluating conventional and novel flu vaccines and understanding their complex interactions with viral, host & environmental factors. I envision a safe and effective societal response to both seasonal epidemics and& pandemics. To this end, I propose to further develop our rapid analytics platform built on a continually updated comprehensive data warehouse and use it to address knowledge gaps, guide decision-making and develop new vaccine research methods. This research program will create methods and tools to create data warehouses and automate rapid analysis of their data which can be shared with other provinces and to develop an integrated rich data to facilitate research and quality improvement initiatives. The program will also provide excellent opportunities for training new researchers & knowledge users.

column36: Wearable technology to assist with hand and finger function
column37: Many conditions, including stroke and cerebral palsy, may impair the use of the hand. My program focuses on developing an innovative technology to assist individuals whose finger function either can or cannot be recovered. column36: The biology and clinical significance of the tumour microenvironment in B cell lymphomas
column37: Lymphoid cancers are the fifth most frequent cancer in humans, affect patients of all ages, and despite generally effective treatments, a significant number of patients still die of their disease. Our studies will be very important for physicians and patients as our research will develop clinical tests that provide information about the individual prognosis of lymphoma patient and will help developing new drugs and personalized treatments. Ultimately, these treatment improvements will lead to higher cure rates and fewer side effects for patients suffering from malignant lymphomas.

column36: Tuberculosis: From Genomics to Control
column37: As a doctor and a scientist, I ask why many people are exposed to the bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but only a minority develop the disease tuberculosis (TB). To understand these variable outcomes, I have established CIHR-funded programs of research that study the spread of this bacterium (epidemiology) and the fundamental biology of the disease (looking from both the perspective of the bacterium and that of the human host). The present application brings together three themes of TB research that share conceptual and methodologic synergies. In molecular epidemiology work (theme 1), our group makes a DNA 'fingerprint' of bacteria to track chains of transmission. This information, integrated with Public Health data, will define better ways to intervene with antibiotics in settings with drug sensitive and multidrug resistant settings. In bacteria-based studies (theme 2), our group compares the bacteria that causes TB with related bacteria that live in the environment and do not cause a contagious disease. These studies will uncover bacterial targets to neutralize in a new vaccine. In host-based studies (theme 3), our group studies how a part of the immune system, called innate immunity, recognizes Mycobacterium tuberculosis and how this translates into effective control of the infection. These studies will define host responses to be enhanced by a new vaccine. Together, these studies, carried out at the level of human populations and within a laboratory setting, will identify critical bacterial- and human-determinants of disease. I am one of very few TB researchers in the world who has the necessary training and a track record of success to lead this combination of studies. The information gained will drive the best application of existing antibiotics, to better control TB, and inform the development of a new vaccine, to eliminate TB.

column36: Insomnia: Research Innovations to Optimize Treatment Outcome in Primary Care
column37: Sleep problems are among the most common health complaints, with insomnia affecting 20% of adults at least occasionally and 10% on a chronic basis. Insomnia is characterized by difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep associated with distress and impairments of daytime functioning. Chronic insomnia produces significant psychological (increased risks of depression), physical (increased risk of hypertension), and economic burdens (reduced productivity and increased absenteeism). Despite some recent progress in insomnia research, there are still some major gaps in understanding and treating this sleep disorder. First, little is known about its risk factors and long-term consequences. Secondly, although chronic sleep disturbances are often associated with co-existing medical and psychiatric conditions, the specific role of psychological and biological factors in insomnia is still poorly understood. Thirdly, despite its high prevalence, insomnia often remains untreated and when treatment is initiated, it is usually limited to prescribed or over-the-counter drugs. Long-term use of sleep medications is often problematic due to their adverse effects and risks of tolerance and dependency. Behavioural therapies for insomnia are effective and well accepted by patients, yet they are not readily available and are infrequently used in practice. The main objectives of this research proposal are to: a) document the natural history, risk factors, and long-term health consequences of insomnia; b) develop more efficient and cost-effective therapies; and c) examine how we can make these interventions more accessible to those who need it (i.e., patients and health care practitioners). This research program is likely to have practical implications by producing new knowledge that will improve our understanding of insomnia and how best to treat it in clinical practice, hence reducing the individual and societal burden of this important public health problem.

column36: Uncovering Pathways to Recovery and Optimizing Treatment for Child and Adolescent Victims of Sexual Abuse
column37: Child sexual abuse (CSA) is an important public health problem with recent estimates showing that one in five women and one in ten men report being sexually abused before the age of 18. CSA is associated with an increased risk for mental health disorders, alcohol and drug abuse, criminality and suicide as well as adverse physical health symptoms. The inter-generational transmission of CSA and the link with later traumas (e.g. victimization in the context of romantic relationships) underscore the need for early identification and implementation of efficient strategies to break the cycle of violence. The proposed research program aims to address current gaps in the scientific literature concerning the mechanisms linking CSA and mental health outcomes. Our program will also test the incremental value of relying on a tailored approach to foster recovery in all victims of CSA, compared to the 'one-size-fits-all' current approach. The objectives are to: 1) disentangle the diversity of mental health profiles in victims of CSA and identify key predictors (e.g. emotion regulation) that contribute prospectively to health outcomes; and 2) implement and assess the effectiveness of a modular approach based on the most renowned evidence-based therapy to treat CSA victims (Trauma Focused-Cognitive Behavioral Therapy - TF-CBT). This research program will contribute to knowledge on theoretical models of recovery in children and youth. Documentation of the consequences of CSA will provide crucial information to health planning agencies in terms of needed services. The program will also offer a unique opportunity to implement a personalized, patient-centered approach to treatment for CSA children and youth in Canada. Such an approach could be associated with a substantial reduction in health costs and significantly reduce the risks of morbidity among this vulnerable population.

column36: Maximizing Safety and Efficiency in Managing Vascular Emergencies
column37: This application focuses on research to improve care for emergency department (ED) patients with vascular emergencies. My program includes: 1) Implementing the Ottawa SAH Rule to identify headache patients at risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH); 2) Developing the Canadian TIA Score to identify transient ischemic attack (TIA) patients at risk for subsequent stroke; 3) Conducting trials for recent-onset atrial fibrillation (RAF); and 4) Optimizing and measuring knowledge translation (KT) for each condition. We developed the Canadian TIA Score, to determine the impending stroke risk. This study will test the Canadian TIA Score in 5,000 new TIA patients to confirm it is accurate to identify patients' risk of stroke within 7 days. The Canadian TIA Score will improve patient outcomes through the efficient use of existing resources. RAF results in a rapid heart rate, requiring urgent treatment to restore normal heart rhythm. RAF is the most common rhythm disorder managed in the ED. No studies have been conducted comparing an electrical shock (Shock Only) or drugs followed by shock (Drug-Shock). Our trial compares these two strategies for conversion to normal rhythm. Given a consistent failure to translate new and existing research into clinical and public health practice, this research program will measure the KT implementation of The Ottawa SAH Rule, The Canadian TIA Score and clinical practice guidelines for RAF and acute headache (including all causes of headache). This research will build the science of KT in acute settings and optimize uptake of new evidence from our research program.

column36: Promoting Reflexive Family Physical Activity: A test of Habit and Identity Formation
column37: Regular physical activity (PA) has enormous health benefits. Among children and adolescents, PA protects against metabolic syndrome, low bone density, depression, and obesity, and forms the behavioral patterns necessary to foster health benefits across the life course. Unfortunately, very few Canadians engage in enough PA to reap its health benefits. There is a clear need to promote PA within the family unit yet interventions focused on the family have been scarce and have had negligible impact. My research career has focused on the theoretical underpinnings of family-level PA and the application of these factors to PA promotion. Much of the past research on family-based PA has focused on increasing the knowledge base of PA's benefits in an attempt to raise intentions to act. My research has shown that most parents already agree that regular PA is important for them and their children but have difficulty following through on supportive PA intentions. My team's ongoing and recently completed research trials have examined how to promote the factors that bind good intentions to behaviour. The primary objectives of this foundation grant will be to expand upon these prior results by promoting two potentially important factors that have not received enough research attention. One of these factors is parental support habits (trial 1) and the other is parental support identity (subsequent trial 2). The key outcome in these trials will be child PA (measured objectively through a monitoring device). My team will compare whether a habit/identity promotion program focused on parental support of PA can improve child PA beyond basic education and goal-setting over six months. Participants will be families with at least one child between 6 and 12 years old who is not active. All of this research has the potential to be directly applied to national promotion campaigns and physical activity programs for families and contribute to long-term economic health outcomes of Canadians.

column36: The pancreatic islet in human health and diabetes
column37: I am a world-leading expert on the insulin producing pancreatic islets of Langerhans. My work focuses on understanding the cellular mechanisms that control insulin secretion, and how these process is impaired in type 2 diabetes (T2D). The insulin-producing pancreatic islets of Langerhans are central to nearly all forms of diabetes, since these are destroyed through autoimmunity in type 1 diabetes (T1D; ~10% of cases) and are dysfunctional in T2D (~80% of cases). The result is an impaired regulation of metabolism that leads to an increased risk of stroke, heart disease, kidney failure, blindness, and amputation. Diabetes affects nearly 3 million Canadians and costs our healthcare system $17 billion annually. My group is ideally positioned address key questions about insulin secretion in clinically relevant tissue samples from patients with and without diabetes. To achieve this I have established a human pancreas tissue program, allowing us to study clinically relevant tissue from organ donors with and without diabetes. My group combines this with molecular, imaging, and cell physiological approaches to study: biochemical connections linking cellular metabolism with insulin secretion; the organization of insulin release at the cell membrane; and processes that underlie insulin secretory dysfunction in human T2D islets and animal models of diabetes. My lab is making important inroads in these areas, leading to a better understanding of insulin secretory function in health and diabetes. This work is informing drug development and testing through partnerships with industry, and providing new insights into how secretory dysfunction in T2D may be reversed.

column36: Immune Regulation during Chronic Disease
column37: Persistent viral infections are a global health concern, with over 500 million people infected with HIV and hepatitis B and C viruses. A major cause of morbidity and mortality during these persistent infections is the co-infections and cancers they foster. Strategies to enhance immune activity to clear these persistent viral infections or prevent co-infection/cancer have so far been unsuccessful largely because they cannot adequately rehabilitate the dysfunctional host immune response. The proposed experiments will define critical immune dysfunctions during persistent infection and develop immune redirecting therapies to eliminate persistent viruses and the co-diseases that arise during them. Further, many of the same pathways that suppress immunity during persistent viral infections, are also being identified to inhibit the immune response from eliminating many cancers. We will translate the mechanisms of immunosuppression we uncover in the persistent virus infection into cancer to identify conserved mechanisms of immunosuppression and targets for therapeutic intervention. Ultimately, we propose a unifying principle of immunosuppression in chronic diseases and that by understanding the underlying roots of immunosuppression it will be possible to target these pathways at their core to cure multiple chronic diseases. The mechanisms and paradigms we reveal will have the potential to lead to new strategies to treat disease.

column37: Infections caused by new emerging bacterial and viral pathogens, or by common microbes that have become drug resistant, and that we are exposed to in the nosocomial or community settings or during travel abroad, remain a serious threat to the health of Canadians. column36: Materials and Mechanisms for Understanding and Controlling Hemorrhage
column37: Uncontrolled bleeding is a leading cause of death in Canada and worldwide, particularly in young healthy adults. While there are a range of therapies for stopping blood flow, they are still ineffective in the most severe cases of hemorrhage. My research program aims to develop new therapeutics that can be used in severe bleeding, by exploring novel mechanisms that could explain why current therapeutics are ineffective in these scenarios. Specifically, we will investigate three possible approaches; 1) Improve the penetration of blood clotting agents to wounds using delivery vehicles that can move against blood flow, which otherwise washes away factors that promote clotting, 2) Increase the ability of platelets to induce clotting, as these cell are first-wave responders that naturally help blood clot, and 3) Increase the strength by which blood clots adhere to injured blood vessels. Each strategy is based on biochemical insights and drug delivery techniques that my lab has already developed, and the research program will focus on applying these techniques to understanding and treating severe bleeding. My lab is uniquely poised to address this issue due to our extensive experience in both blood biochemistry and biomedical engineering, as well as the extensive support we have received from clinicians and the industry, which will allow us to translate laboratory findings into the clinic. The short-term goal of this program is to identify limiting factors that prevent the successful treatment of severe bleeding with current therapeutics, and then use these insights to develop novel technologies that enhance blood clotting. In the long-term, this program will lead to new clinical tools for treating severe bleeding, and has the potential to reduce death and related complications from uncontrolled bleeding in Canada and abroad.

column37: Rationale and Goals: Life-threatening infections (LTIs) remain leading causes of global illness and death especially for children and pregnant women in low-resource settings. The goals of our translational research program are: (1) to characterize the mechanisms underlying LTIs; and (2) to develop new triage tools and treatments to prevent death and brain injury in survivors. While malaria is the primary model used, the findings have broad implications for other LTIs and causes of adverse birth outcomes. Given Canada's leadership role in global maternal-child health, these goals are directly relevant to both Canadian and global health priorities. Specific Research Aims and Impact: i. Next generation diagnostics: Our research is contributing to the next generation of rapid triage and diagnostic tests that will not only diagnose infection but will also determine how severe the infection is and help predict outcome. This approach could enable personalized medicine rapidly, inexpensively and at point-of-care. ii. Novel therapies to prevent death and brain injury: Despite potent antimicrobials and supportive care, fatality rates for LTIs remain high and survivors often have brain injury. Our research has identified new interventions that are in human trials to improve survival and prevent brain injury in severe malaria. These studies have broad implications for many LTIs. iii. Improving pregnancy outcomes: Preventing poor birth outcomes is a global health priority; but we know relatively little about how and why they happen. Our studies have addressed important knowledge gaps and have identified new potential interventions to improve pregnancy outcomes and to prevent brain injury in offspring. Outcomes: Our research will help to identify new tools and treatments for LTIs that are appropriate for use in low resource settings. These advances have the potential to change global policy and practice for LTIs in maternal-child health.

column36: Informing health care policy makers on health care financing and sustainability
column37: The Canadian population is aging and chronic diseases are becoming more common, leading to increasing health care costs and demand for system-wide change to improve sustainability. In a recent international study of 11 peer countries, Canada's health care system ranked 10th. I am a physician who links clinical medicine with research and health policy. I hold a Research Chair in Health Economics and my research program informs health care sustainability across a variety of areas such as measuring the impact of new treatments or strategies on patient outcomes and health care costs. Research deliverables will empower government decision-making to improve health system sustainability, quality of care, equitable access and efficiency. column36: Chromosome instability and synthetic lethality in yeast and cancer
column37: Effective cancer therapy exploits specific biological differences between cancer cells and normal cells. Cancer cells often have defects that reduce the efficiency of chromosome transmission. Indeed, mutations in cancer cells that cause chromosome instability (CIN) are now widely recognized to be an important driver in cancer initiation and progression. These CIN mutations also represent tumour specific genetic vulnerabilities that could be exploited in developing new cancer treatments. Because the same building blocks are used to construct organisms as diverse as yeast, worms, and humans, "model organisms" provide powerful experimental tools for investigating the mechanistic basis of disease and for developing potential therapeutic interventions. The goals of our work are to understand the mechanisms of chromosome transmission at the levels of genes, pathways, and networks using yeast and the nematode worm as models, and to directly relate our studies to cancer and the development of new cancer therapies. Using yeast genetic techniques, in particular, global synthetic lethality analysis, we will identify yeast genes, and the corresponding human gene counterparts, that define potential therapeutic targets for selective killing of cancer cells relative to normal cells. We will use yeast to rapidly test millions of possible combinations of tumour-associated defects, drug targets, and chemotherapeutic agents to identify effective combinations, and will prioritize them for further testing in tumour cell cultures. The results of our proposed research will provide a basic understanding of the mechanisms of normal chromosome transmission, and of the corresponding defects associated with cancer pathology. Our results will also lead to the identification of new drug targets and will enable the identification of new small molecule inhibitors and combination therapies that could be used for the selective killing of cancer cells in patients.

column37: Most Canadians are proud that their health care system provides services on the basis of need rather than ability to pay. His research in this proposed CIHR-funded program includes studies on the affordability of prescription drugs, the impact of drug plan deductibles, evaluations of policy changes enacted by governments, and the impact of changes in HIV treatment regimes. column36: Molecular regulation of muscle stem cell function in regenerative myogenesis
column37: I am interested in understanding the mechanisms that control stem cell function and applying this knowledge to improve health. Our studies are focused on muscle stem cells and how they function in the growth and repair of skeletal muscle. The research is critical for developing novel treatments for many muscle-wasting diseases, for example Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). Our studies have already transformed our understanding of the mechanisms that control muscle stem cell function and have led to the development of a protein called Wnt7a as a novel therapy. First, we will investigate the mechanism by which Wnt7a stimulates muscle regeneration and test therapeutic strategies to treat muscle-wasting disease. The experiments will direct the development of Wnt7a as a drug and clinical trials will be conducted with Wnt7a in the near future. Second, we will define the mechanisms that regulate the division of muscle stem cells as this is a central control point that governs regeneration efficiency. We will investigate these control mechanisms with the longer-term goal of identifying targets and hence drugs that could be used to stimulate muscle stem cell function. Third, we will map the regulatory networks of proteins called transcription factors that control the expression of genes in muscle stem cells from healthy versus diseased tissue. This information is key to understanding how these stem cells function. Finally, we will identify new drugs capable of stimulating muscle stems cells to enhance muscle regeneration. In parallel, we will validate our findings on human muscle stem cells to transition our therapeutic strategies into the clinic. In conclusion, the research will advance our knowledge of stem cell function and lead to novel treatments for diseases involving wasting of skeletal muscle. Importantly, this work will improve the health of patients, and also benefit the families and care givers that are affected by these devastating diseases.

column36: Bridging the Gap in Paediatric Traumatic Brain Injury: Environmental, biological and clinical markers associated with preschool concussion and TBI
column37: Concussions and other traumatic brain injuries are a frequent cause of death and disability in youth, and children under the age of 6 are at particularly high risk. Older children with brain injuries often suffer serious mental, psychological, social, and behaviour problems. Even mild injuries have the potential to cause lasting problems in children because of subtle changes in how the brain works. Recently, international teams have been working to better understand the course of recovery in children with concussion or brain injury; however, children under 6 have generally been excluded from this research. This is extremely problematic because of the high prevalence of brain injuries in toddlers and preschoolers and because they are particularly vulnerable to the effects of brain injury. Indeed, injury to the brain disrupts normal development and critically affects acquisition of new knowledge and skills. Currently, we know very little about the consequence of brain injuries in young children, or what initial signs and symptoms might help us predict development in later years. This research program will investigate the functioning of young children after they sustain brain injuries and determine how we can predict their outcomes. We will also determine whether functional problems are associated with changes in the integrity of the brain or particular genetic predispositions. The results will help us to better understand how problems develop after brain injuries in the youngest and most vulnerable age group. In turn, these findings will lead to the development of clear guidelines for doctors and health practitioners to follow when treating young children after a concussion or brain injury. We will also be able to quickly identify preschoolers who are at-risk for problems after brain injury and provide them and their families with the resources needed to prevent problems before they occur and to foster their development and quality of life.
