column36: Characterizing molecular determinants of autoimmune disease
column37: This research proposal is aimed at developing new understanding of autoimmune disease pathogenesis that will drive the development of novel markers and treatments to improve diagnosis, management and health outcomes. These goals will be achieved using two distinct, but complementary approaches. As one approach, we will focus on two autoimmune diseases, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC), for which cause is unknown, treatment often ineffective and prevention or cure not possible. We will define the genetic and molecular pathways that cause these conditions, capitalizing on our access to large RA and PBC patient populations and new knowledge that provides important clues as to the genetic changes conferring risk for each disease. We will use newly-developed technologies and analytic methods to pinpoint the genetic variants most relevant to disease and establish how these variants alter gene/protein function to trigger autoimmunity. We will also study the effects of these gene variants on disease progression and treatment responses in our patient populations. The second thrust of this proposal builds on our derivation of mice carrying specific genetic changes associated with development of autoimmune disease. Because we know the altered gene/protein that causes disease in these animals, we can explore and thereby characterize the molecular pathways whereby these gene/protein changes induce disease. Such studies provide unique opportunity to identify new targets for drug therapy and to explore the potential for such therapies to ameliorate disease. Via these strategies, this research will identify the gene variants that cause and influence outcome of two prototypical autoimmune diseases and elucidate the mechanistic pathways that link such variants to disease. This new knowledge will illuminate novel biomarkers and more effective therapies that will alleviate the enormous medical and socioeconomic burden imposed by autoimmune diseases.

column36: Evolutionary approaches to treat and evade antibiotic resistant pathogenic bacteria
column37: Bacterial infections are major threats to human health. In the last century, antibiotics have served as our arsenals to fight bacterial infections. However, unfortunately, bacteria have since evolved resistance against virtually all known antibiotics, in several cases only a few years after a new antibiotic was introduced. We therefore urgently need to develop novel strategies if we are to prevent the spread of antibiotic resistance, and to discover sustainable antibiotic reagents (i.e. for which resistance cannot easily evolve). I envision that I will lead the field to pioneer new antibiotic strategies to improve our healthcare system by employing "evolutionary approaches" to predict and prevent the evolution of antibiotic resistance. First, I will establish a platform to examine evolutionary potential and limit of antibiotic resistance using experimental evolution in the laboratory. Second, using laboratory evolution and engineering, I will generate novel anti-virulence reagents, e.g. enzymes to degrade cell-to-cell signaling molecules and therefore inhibit biofilm formation. Targeting such molecules is a potentially sustainable antibiotic strategy as it is unlikely that bacteria can easily evolve resistance. My research program will create powerful new approaches and tools to combat multi-drug resistant pathogenic bacteria. My strong expertise in laboratory evolution and engineering, and established collaborations with structural biologists, microbiologists and computational biologists will enable me to effectively tackle this challenge. My CIHR Foundation program will lead us to the development of novel antibiotic strategies and reagents to battle against antibiotic-resistant pathogenic bacteria.

column36: Effective Knowledge Translation Strategies for Enhancing Impact and Improving Outcomes in Infant Pain
column37: Understanding how to prevent and treat pain in hospitalized infants is critical for healthy behaviour and brain development. Although there has been significant research generating new knowledge on infant pain treatments, research results are not effectively or efficiently translated into practice and infants do not optimally benefit from them. Therefore, the overarching aim is to develop a comprehensive research program that both generates new research evidence on effective pain treatments and identifies effective strategies for implementing research results and changing health care professionals' practice. Specifically, the research goals are (a) to generate new knowledge on the effectiveness and safety of repeated use of an evidence-based pain treatment (sucrose) and the effect on infant development and (b) to facilitate knowledge translation (KT) by (i) developing, implementing and evaluating a novel, web-based knowledge implementation infant pain resource (ImPaC) to stimulate practice change across the full spectrum of Canadian infant care hospital settings and (ii) determining the factors in the work environment that influence KT, clinical pain practices and change. The overarching goal is to enhance health care professionals' prevention and treatment of pain in hospitalized infants for improved individual (less pain and consequences of pain for the infant) and health care system outcomes. Ultimately, this program of research will address how the integration of newly generated research evidence and effective KT strategies will impact and enhance infant health outcomes in a variety of practice settings to inform future clinical, research and policy agendas.

column36: Towards new therapeutics through manipulation of glyco-enzymes
column37: The surfaces of every cell in the human body are coated with specific sugars. These play several roles, principally providing a way for the cell to interact with other cells and their components. Invading bacteria and viruses also use these sugars as an entry point, thus an understanding of these interactions and of how the specific sugars are built and degraded, can lead to new therapeutics. An example is the influenza virus drug Tamiflu, which blocks the critical viral enzyme that cuts a sugar off our cell surfaces and allows the virus to spread. Our recent research has shown that some of the enzymes used by disease-causing bacteria and parasites in order to infect human cells are unlike any enzymes present in human cells. This allows us to design and synthesize new classes of drug to either specifically block these enzymes, as with Tamiflu, or to liberate toxins specifically within the invader. Using such approaches, in collaboration with microbiologists, we shall develop new strategies for treatment of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, as well as the parasites that cause Chagas disease in South America. In a second part of our work we shall use enzymes to modify these cell surface sugars for a variety of applications. In one case we use enzymes to cut specific sugars off the surface of red blood cells, thereby changing their blood type from A or B (or AB) to the "universal donor" Type O. Using an approach that mimics the process of natural evolution, but accelerates it, we shall engineer these enzymes to speed them up for clinical use. This work should greatly improve our supply of blood for transfusions. In a second case we shall use enzymes to improve the performance of increasingly important protein-based drugs such as antibodies and growth factors. Most such proteins have sugars on their surface that play important roles. We shall engineer enzymes to add sugars in a highly controlled manner, yielding drugs of improved performance.

column36: Towards a better understanding of Influenza Vaccination: Lessons from the Hutterite Community
column37: The primary goal of my research program is to advance knowledge about the prevention and management of influenza. I will achieve this goal by undertaking analyses using banked specimens and data from randomized trials that I have conducted the Hutterite community, conducting a longitudinal study in this community, and conduct two randomized controlled trials. The primary objectives of my research program are to gain a comprehensive understanding of the impact of the annual administration of influenza vaccine on the prevention of influenza and its complications. The proposed Foundation Grant builds on a research program that I have developed over the past 15 years on the prevention of influenza and other respiratory infections, largely on studies conducted in the Hutterite community. The specific study aims focus on influenza vaccination. The effect of prior year (s) vaccination on current year vaccine protection is uncertain. The effect of repeated live attenuated influenza vaccination (LAIV) in children is uncertain, where vaccine efficacy (VE) may decline. The impact on herd protection of such repeated vaccination in children is unknown. Although theories have been proposed to explain year to year variability in influenza VE, these have not tested in long-term epidemiologic studies. Identification of clinically useful biomarkers to predict infection, the effect of influenza vaccination on preventing pneumococcal infection in children, the effect of influenza vaccine on reducing myocardial infarction and stroke, and therapy with the anti-viral medication oseltamivir to reduce influenza complications will be assessed. My research program will provide clear results to these questions. Given that > 500 million people receive influenza vaccine annually, this research will have major implications both in Canada and globally.

column36: Using Neuroimaging in Schizophrenia to Predict Outcome and Enhance Treatment Reponse
column37: There are currently no approved treatments for negative symptoms (lack of motivation, poor word production, and minimal social interaction) and cognitive impairments (difficulties with organization, planning, remembering) in people with schizophrenia. Negative symptoms and cognitive impairments are the major sources of functional disability for people with schizophrenia, and are often life-long. Therefore, new treatments are desperately needed. Identifying the brain circuits responsible for these deficits will accelerate treatment development. For negative symptoms, we will perform advanced brain imaging at the first episode of illness, to confirm the disrupted brain circuitry underlying these deficits, and test who will develop these deficits over time. These approaches will guide early intervention efforts for these debilitating symptoms. For cognitive impairment, we will utilize the infrastructure of an already funded brain stimulation clinical trial aiming to improve cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. In the new work proposed, we will test a neuroimaging approach based an individual's functional brain connectivity that allows us to best position the brain stimulation coil, and compare it to the current standard. Overall, our studies will improve the quality of life for people with schizophrenia, by enhancing existing treatment efforts, or setting the stage for new treatment efforts for the major sources of functional disability in this disorder.

column36: Discovery and engineering of ice-binding proteins for health applications.
column37: Some organisms resist freezing to below -30 C, but quickly die if ice forms in the body. Other organisms actively promote freezing at -2 C and can tolerate freezing and thawing with minimal damage. My CIHR-funded research program has discovered ice-binding proteins that control these processes. They include antifreeze proteins that stop the growth of ice and protect animals and their organs, tissues and cells from freezing; as well as ice recrystallization inhibitors used by freeze-tolerant organisms to lessen the damage that occurs on freezing and thawing. Here we will apply these ice-binding proteins to cool organs well below 0 C so that they can be kept for longer and hence increase the supply of organs for transplant. We will also use these proteins to improve the recovery of frozen blood and stem cells for transfusions. In addition, we will engineer improvements to the ice-binding proteins that will give them greater activity and potency for these human health applications.

column36: Beyond Structured Administrative Data (BEST DATA)
column37: To monitor how our health care system functions, researchers use data routinely collected through public services, such as bills from physician visits, hospital discharge information, and social data from non-health services. Analyzing these records allows us to examine factors that influence the health of Canadians and how we use public services. Until now, researchers have performed these analyses using structured data (such as spreadsheets) that can be easily plugged into statistical programs. However, with the development of new analysis techniques, there is great potential to conduct more in-depth research using unstructured data, such as clinical notes from electronic medical records (EMR). Big data analytics can be used to analyze free text (i.e. natural language). This proposal will employ these new techniques to analyze free text in the health and social data at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy (MCHP). Big data analytics will allow us to answer broader research questions that will help to improve clinical practice. For example, Canadians sometimes receive unnecessary medications (antibiotics), and undergo unnecessary tests like back x-rays. By developing the tools to analyze clinician's notes (free text) in EMRs, we can examine why these events occur and better understand the role of patients in decision making. Using the extensive person-level data available at MCHP, we will follow patient exposure to antibiotics over time while considering travel history and other contributing factors. Thus, the inclusion of free text analysis adds an additional dimension to our understanding of antibiotic resistance and will help to curb this growing problem. This research will advance the science of population level data analysis to a new level, adding depth to the research questions we can answer, and supporting the development of evidence-based policy.

column36: Neurovascular and neuroimmune interplay in retinal vasculopathies
column37: Loss of eyesight is the most feared ailment in North America after cancer. The part of the eye that senses visuals scenes and transmits them to the brain is a structure rich in nerve cells and blood vessels called the retina. This structure is biochemically part of the brain. In debilitating diseases of the retina such as the sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity and age-related macular degeneration, the degeneration of blood vessels precipitates loss of nerve cell function. These retinopathies are the leading causes blindness in the industrial world and account for over 25 million cases of compromised vision in North America. The degeneration of blood vessels in the retina prevents nutrient and oxygen delivery and leads to a constellation of biochemical changes that deregulate cellular function. While the body attempts to repair and restore blood vessels, there are a number of yet unknown factors that hinder reparative vessel growth and consequently aggravate the loss of nerve cell function. Current treatment paradigms are largely inefficient and focus on destroying diseased blood vessels instead of repairing those that provide oxygen and essential nutrients. An attractive alternative approach would be to regenerate functional vessels into zones of the retina where vessels were damaged. In this proposal we outline a therapeutic strategy that would restore healthy blood vessels to the retina in retinopathies. This approach will help design new medications and be achieved by molecularly altering the response of retinal nerve cells to vascular injury.

column36: Targeting the dynamics and genomics of clonal evolution in cancer patients
column37: Cancers evolve over time and the gene mutations driving them can change. A major bottleneck in the treatment of epithelial cancers is a lack of diverse therapeutic / treatment options. This is especially relevant in cancer, as tumours are able to evolve/adapt to "escape" from single-agent treatment (similar to what occurs in antibiotic-resistant bacteria, where a combination of drugs is required to treat the infection); breast cancers often develop drug resistance so that their tumors recur, and mutational evolution likely underlies this event. It is critical to identify new options/approaches to target tumours that have become drug-resistant, as a result of mutational evolution. We know that clonal complexity - the so called "cellular superbug" phenomenon, is associated with instability in the tumour's genetic sequence (driven by the inability of DNA to repair itself). We hypothesize that specific sections of the genome, with unique DNA structures may be targetable through directed approaches, and plan to explore novel approaches that target structural vulnerabilities within the human genome. By combining chemical genomics of DNA targeting with genetic technologies to uncover conditional genetic interactions and methods for measuring clonal structure, we expect to derive a completely new mechanistic approach to targeting genomically unstable epithelial cancers. Our studies have the potential to answer specific questions about how breast cancer arises, progresses, and becomes resistant to treatment. These findings will have a global impact within the cancer research community, allowing the design of improved and more effective therapies. In short, the practical application of cancer cell genetics will become a reality in the clinic -- representing a significant step forward in direct translational benefits for patients.

column36: Epigenetic Approaches to Enhance Cancer Immunotherapy and to Target Cancer Initiating Cells
column37: The premise of Cancer Immunotherapy is to stimulate the patient's immune system to attack the tumour cells. Recent progress in cancer immunotherapy protocols has led to a transformation in the treatment of several types of solid tumours. However, the majority of Colorectal Cancer (CRC) patients do not respond to immunotherapy, suggesting the need to combine immunotherapies with other anti-tumour strategies. Unfortunately, chemotherapy - the mainstay of cancer treatment for over 40 years - is immunosuppressive and not suitable for combination with immunotherapy. On the other hand, the new class of therapeutics called epigenetic therapies hold great potential for enhancing anti-tumour immune response and for use in combination with immunotherapy. We have found that DNA demethylating drugs can activate immunogenic signals in cancer cells, specifically those that engage the interferon and antiviral pathways. We will investigate how this process happens and how it can be used to increase the tumour cell immunogenicity and to improve the immune response against the tumour. Another major barrier in effectively treating CRC arises from the emergence of resistance to current standard of care. The source of therapeutic resistance is due to a rare group of cells within the tumour called cancer-initiating cells (CICs, also known as cancer stem cells) that are responsible for the continued tumour self-renewal. These CICs are highly resistant to chemo- and radiation therapy. Evidence from mouse models of cancer and human clinical trials indicates anti-cancer therapies select for and increase the number of CICs in tumours, which explain why tumours tend to be more resistant following the initial rounds of therapy. We have found that DNA demethylating agents can target colorectal CICs. We will explore a strategy of targeting CICs using epigenetic therapy and how it can be used to avoid tumour recurrence with the ultimate aim of curing this disease.

column36: Assembly, trafficking and functional selectivity of G protein-coupled receptors; from molecular mechanisms to therapeutic discovery
column37: Many hormones and transmitters have their biological effects by modulating the activity of receptors located at the surface of cells. Among these, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) represent the largest family of protein involved in transferring information from the outside to the inside of the cells. With more than 800 members, GPCR control many distinct physiological functions such as neurotransmission, cardiac contraction, vascular tone, endocrine secretion, metabolism, etc.... As a consequence, they represent privileged targets for the development of drugs for many distinct clinical indications. It is estimated that more than 30% of the current prescription drugs act through GPCR. Yet, only a limited fraction of the therapeutic potential of GPCR has been exploited to date. Many receptors with important roles have not yet been targeted and new developments in molecular pharmacology and structural biology offer new opportunities for the development of drugs with greater therapeutic efficacies and less undesirable effects. In particular, new tools allowing to unravel their structures and to monitor their signaling activities with unprecedented sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution open the perspective of developing new drugs based on an intimate understanding of their mode of action at the molecular level. Therefore, the present proposal aims at further understanding the molecular mechanisms controlling GPCR activity, with the intention of identifying novel processes that could be pharmacologically targeted for therapeutic purposes. The studies proposed also include the search for new chemical entities that will serve as tools to better probe receptor functions and could represent interesting lead candidates for the development of new drugs classes for unmet clinical needs.

column36: Vaccination & screening for control sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and STI-related cancers
column37: Sexually transmitted infections (STI) are a major public health concern among Canadians. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common STI, so much so that 3/4 people will get this infection at least once. This is concerning because certain HPV types cause cervical, anal, and oral cancers. Rates of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis have risen for more than a decade. HIV infections continue and the effects of STIs are worse among people living with HIV. STIs are more commonly diagnosed among gay men with HIV than the general population. Women and men with HIV are many times more likely to get a cancer caused by HPV compared to people without HIV. Our vision is to gather the highest quality evidence to help Canadians choose the best vaccination & screening strategies to prevent and control STIs and STI-related cancers among Canadians at risk, especially those living with HIV. The newest HPV vaccines could prevent 90% of cancers caused by these viruses and are effective and safe, including in people with HIV. The negative consequences of STIs can be largely avoided by testing more often and getting treated right away. This not only improves patient health but prevents passing on the infection to partners. Screening for early signs of cancers caused by HPV, such as Pap tests for women, can ensure proper follow-up to prevent cancer development. Solutions will specifically address communities that may be harder to reach due to stigma and poverty. First, we will find out why people do or do not get vaccinated or tested for STIs and cancers caused by HPV. Next we will test new ways to offer vaccination & screening to see which are most effective and practical. Finally, we will follow our progress over the long term to ensure that chosen strategies protect the health of Canadians for years to come. Globally, 1 million people acquire an STI each day. Thus lessons learned may also assist international efforts to end STI epidemics, complications & deaths.

column36: Program of Research on Outcomes, Treatment, and Evaluation of Care in the Spectrum of HF (PROTECT HF)
column37: Heart failure is a major reason for hospital admission. Most patients with heart failure will seek care in the emergency department because they experience shortness of breath. The hospital is an important setting for the care of heart failure patients, and many patients are hospitalized. In our prior work, we found that the quality of care for patients who seek care in the emergency department could be improved, and we developed mathematical tools to help doctors make better decisions about admitting or discharging patients who present acutely with heart failure. In this study, we will continue our work on improving care of patients with heart failure in the emergency department by evaluating the benefits of our tools when used in 'real time' in a clinical trial. We will also expand our work by examining further along the pathway of care of heart failure patients. Specifically, we will identify how care can be improved for patients who are hospitalized on the ward. column36: Developmental Pathways to Health and Disease: Fetal Programming and Protection
column37: My research program integrates discovery, translational and clinical research with a goal of optimizing fetal health and preventing the negative life-long consequences of early adversity. column36: Living Kidney Donation: Improving Safety, Access, and Outcomes
column37: Kidney Failure: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Living Kidney Donation: It is safe for a living person who is healthy to donate one of their kidneys. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often volunteer to donate one of their kidneys. With advances in transplantation, the donor and recipient do not have to be related or be of the same gender, race, or age. Canada and other countries are looking for ways to safely increase living kidney donation. Barriers to Living Kidney Donation: Unfortunately, many patients who would benefit from a kidney transplant do not receive one. There are many reasons for this. Doctors do not always talk to their patients about transplantation. Patients are often uncomfortable discussing living kidney donation with family and friends. Many people do not realize that it is safe to donate a kidney; some are told they are too old to donate despite new research showing it is safe if they are healthy. As well, donor evaluation often takes a year to complete (when it should only take 3 months). A long evaluation process has negative consequences for both donors and recipients. Safely Increasing Living Kidney Donation: My research team is working with living kidney donors and transplant programs to develop and test solutions to overcome barriers to living kidney donation. As well, we are studying a large group of living kidney donors over many decades to confirm long-term safety. Information from our studies will enable more patients with kidney failure to safely receive transplants, and will help candidates make informed decisions about becoming living kidney donors.

column36: New Resources for Chemical Genomics and Metabolomics in Biomedicine
column37: Small molecule compounds such as drugs, nutrients and pollutants affect our health in many ways. Nutrients are needed to sustain life, drugs are needed to cure us of illnesses, while pollutants can kill us. Millions of these compounds exist. The complete collection of these compounds is called the "metabolome" -- derived from the word metabolite (a substance produced by metabolism). The study of how the metabolome affects us is called metabolomics. While metabolomics is a relatively new field, scientists have been collecting detailed information about metabolites for ~100 years. Unfortunately, most of this data is scattered in millions of textbooks and journal articles. The lack of centralized databases or electronic resources for metabolomics means that we still know very little about the chemical universe around us. We don't know how many metabolites there are, we struggle to identify or measure them, we don't know where they come from, we can't tell if they are good or bad and we rarely know how they act on our cells or modify our genes. My long-term research goal is to develop the resources needed to address these problems. Using advanced methods in information technology and analytical chemistry, my lab has created a number of databases and software tools that are helping to answer some of these questions. Our plan is to greatly improve these resources by using the latest techniques in artificial intelligence. By using computers to automatically identify and harvest vast amounts of data from the literature and learn from that data, it should be possible to develop far better resources that will allow us to better characterize, predict and exploit the chemical universe around us. This work will not only revolutionize metabolomics, it will greatly accelerate the discovery of new drugs, identify the underlying chemical causes of diseases, enable improved diagnostics and help predict those at risk of developing diseases such as cancer, heart disease and diabetes.

column37: Severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression, tends to develop in late adolescence. Once the illness is established, available treatments cannot cure it. Families Overcoming Risks and Building Opportunities for Well-being (FORBOW) tests a novel type of pre-emptive early intervention that aims to prevent severe mental illness. We test the effects of the intervention by comparing those who were offered SWELL against those who were not offered the intervention. We also want to find out whether a genetic test may help select individuals who are most likely to benefit from the intervention. Our vision is to provide timely personalized interventions to maximize the benefits for mental health of the next generation.

The goals of my Foundation program are to gain greater understanding on how these novel genes drive the malignancy of lung or pancreatic cancers, and to develop new agents targeting some of these genes for improving the diagnosis and treatment of these two deadly cancers.

column36: Discovery and characterization of alternative splicing regulatory networks with critical roles in development and disease
column37: We have shown that almost all human genes encode multiple protein products through a process known as alternative splicing. Each gene is transcribed into an RNA copy that contains coding and non-coding segments. RNA splicing joins the coding segments into a contiguous messenger RNA that can be translated into a functional protein product. Alternative splicing occurs when the coding segments are spliced in different combinations such that a single gene can produce multiple RNA and protein products. This process greatly diversifies the regulatory and functional capacity of genes, resulting in biological complexity. Alternative splicing is frequently disrupted by mutations that cause or contribute to human diseases and disorders. Moreover, some disease mutations can affect entire programs of alternative splicing by targeting the factors that regulate this process. However, we currently know nothing about the specific functions of most individual protein variants generated by alternative splicing, nor how these variants, when mis-regulated, contribute to human diseases. These questions represent key challenges for future biomedical research and form the main goals of this proposal. We will draw on our world-leading expertise in the areas of alternative splicing, functional genomics, and proteomics, to provide the first large-scale map of splice variant function in the context of both normal physiology and human disease. We will systematically dissect the regulatory pathways that control functionally important and disease-associated splicing events. Finally, we will use information generated by our project to develop new therapeutic strategies for correcting altered splicing programs that underlie human diseases and disorders, focusing on autism. Our research will yield unprecedented new insight into the multitasking functions of our genes, and it will further facilitate the development of a new generation of splicing-directed therapeutics.

My research will show how glia respond to brain diseases and traumatic damage and how they aid in recovery. The major cause of patient mortality after stroke or brain injury is brain swelling called brain edema. We have found a new pathway allowing chloride to enter nerve cells that leads to increased water entry into neurons. We will determine how to block chloride entry and brain swelling in nerve cells and we will investigate the contributions of glia to the control of chloride entry into neurons and brain swelling. The goal is to discover the triggers that cause brain swelling and how therapeutic compounds could block brain edema to reduce brain damage and patient mortality. One type of glia, called microglia are the immune cells of the brain and respond to infections and to damage by repairing surrounding tissue and removing debris. Sometimes however microglia can themselves cause damage and brain impairment. We will determine the factors that cause microglia to switch from protecting the brain to releasing factors to cause damage or impair brain function. This will guide us in developing drugs to prevent microglia-induced damage. The brain is the most metabolically active region of the body and requires a constant supply of oxygen and glucose (sugar) via the blood via processes regulated by astrocytes, another glial cell. Experiments will be undertaken to carefully determine the conditions under which astrocytes regulate neuronal activity and cerebral blood flow in normal brains and in conditions of neurodegeneration such as Alzheimer's. This work will guide the development of new therapies to maintain brain health.

column36: Mapping the resting brain: A new frontier for studying neurovascular physiology and age-related brain diseases
column37: Aging, often accompanied by brain and cognitive decline, is an enormous challenge for the Canadian health system. In the past decade, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized the study of the aging brain. However, tasks or invasive challenges have traditionally been required to assess brain function. Resting-state brain mapping, which came on the scene two decades ago, does not require tasks or challenges, is particularly well suited to the elderly and patients, and has revealed age- and disease-related brain-network changes. However, despite heavy worldwide investment in resting-state fMRI, the resulting data are difficult to interpret and limited in utility. My research is dedicated to achieving a fundamental biological understanding of resting fMRI data, and to expanding current resting brain mapping techniques into a family of patient-friendly methods that provide useful assessments of brain health. Such techniques, which do not yet exist, will be important for healthy aging, as well as dementia and late-life depression. My work will lead to a paradigm shift in the global effort for large-scale information gathering in order to understand aging, eventually leading to the identification of viable therapeutic targets against Alzheimer's disease and other age-related brain diseases.

column36: FROM PROTEOLYTIC NETWORKS TO HUMAN BIOLOGY AND DISEASE: Protease regulation of signal transduction in chronic inflammatory diseases
column37: Chronic inflammatory diseases like periodontitis, arthritis and lupus affect 82% of Canadians and for the 1/2000 Canadians with immunodeficiencies, untreatable infections are imminent threats as drug resistance rises. These diseases commonly involve loss of disease-fighting defense proteins. I discovered that defense proteins are lost after they are cut by white blood cell immune proteases. In immunodeficiencies, inherited genetic defects reduce defense proteins in white blood cells. These crucial discoveries were possible by my innovative and highly advanced techniques known as degradomics. Degradomics is a method of uniquely identifying the cut ends of proteins by selectively purifying them from the rest of the protein. As cuts are formed only during active disease, these segments are highly valuable as disease markers to develop new clinical tests. By detecting and treating earlier, inflammatory diseases are easier to manage before disease worsens, and thus reduce long-term disability. Also, as part of the international Human Proteome Project consortium, I am using degradomics to identify the natural ends of all human proteins. This will allow us to characterize the functions of normal vs. diseased proteins and hence reveal new disease mechanisms. I will now use degradomics to generate clinically relevant knowledge on how proteases damage disease-fighting defense systems in human inflammatory and immunodeficiency diseases. I will obtain human tissues discarded in treatment, e.g. inflamed gum from wisdom teeth extractions, and study white blood cells from patients. As defense proteins are alike in many diseases, my results will be broadly applicable. This knowledge will translate to develop new drugs to combat inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. From identifying cut protein ends in these diseases, I will reveal the damaging proteases that can be targeted with new drugs to improve health of Canadians and thereby ensuring sustainable health care costs.

column36: Design for Better Health: User-Centred Design and Evaluation of Interactive Media for Health Education, Communication and Decision-Making
column37: This research is about helping people make decisions about their health. I want to help people make decisions that (1) are informed by the best available medical evidence and (2) reflect what matters to the person or people affected by the decision. This can be hard to do. One reason it's hard is that it can be difficult to make sense of medical statistics. The statistics may not be very clear, people may not feel confident interpreting statistics, and different ways of presenting statistics feel different. For example, being told you have a 1% chance of having a side effect can feel different than being told you have a 99% chance of everything being fine. Doctors and other health care professionals are influenced by different ways of presenting statistics, too. Even when people understand the statistics, it can still be hard to deal with tradeoffs. Many health decisions require people to choose between competing priorities. For example, people may have to choose between maximizing their quality of life or their length of life. I have figured out ways to address these challenges by designing interactive web applications that help people better understand complicated statistics, sort out what matters to them in tradeoffs, and make decisions by putting medical evidence together with what's important to them. However, there is still work to do. In this research project, I aim to develop new web and mobile tools to help more people make their best health decisions. My team includes patients, doctors, nurses, and others to make sure I take everyone's ideas into account. I will use advanced testing methods to make sure that the tools I develop are helpful and easy to use. Once I am confident that they help people, I will implement my tools in patient portals connected to electronic health records. This will help people across Canada get the information and tools they need to make the best possible health decisions for themselves and their families.

column36: Using artificial pancreas closed-loop systems for the treatment of type 1 diabetes
column37: In healthy individuals, blood sugar levels are tightly controlled by 2 hormones: insulin and glucagon. Secretion of insulin, a vital hormone to reduce blood sugar, is lost in type 1 diabetes (T1D). Thus, patients with T1D are treated by insulin therapy using multiple daily injections or insulin pump. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is frequent in T1D individuals and can lead to malaise, convulsions and death. In case of hypoglycemia, patients might need glucagon, a key hormone to raise blood glucose. Our team has developed a wearable artificial pancreas (WAP) that regulates sugar levels for patients with T1D. The WAP is composed of three components: continuous glucose sensor (to measure blood sugar changes), infusion pumps (to provide insulin with or without glucagon) and an intelligent dosing method that links the sensor with the pump to implement dose changes with the pump based on the blood sugar fluctuations. Two configurations of the WAP have been developed: one that infuses insulin and another that infuses insulin and glucagon. Completed trials demonstrate that, compared to conventional pump therapy, both WAP versions increase the time that sugar levels remain within recommended targets and reduce hypoglycemic risk. The objectives of this application are: 1) to improve daytime sugar control after meal & during exercise, two remaining challenging situations; 2) to conduct clinical trials in 2 key populations: patients with a reduced perception of hypoglycemia and children with T1D; 3) to perform a 6-month trial with the WAP targeting A1c improvement (marker of diabetes control & risk of complication) and severe hypoglycemia. The WAP has a great potential to improve patients' quality of life, reduce the risk of complication (e.g. blindness, kidney failure), prevent hypoglycemia (malaise), provide confidence for physical activities and meals as well as alleviate the burden of diabetes for families and healthcare providers.

column36: Mitochondrial targeting as a novel therapeutic approach to human disease: a translational program
column37: One of the major ways that normal cells can get sick is when their fuel's supply to demand balance is disrupted. The "power plants" that regulate the handling of fuel (oxygen, sugars, lipids) in the cell are organelles called mitochondria. We now know that there is mitochondrial dysfunction in many common diseases (like diabetes or cancer for example) but also in more rare but deadly diseases like pulmonary hypertension, where the blood vessels of the lungs are gradually destroyed leading to shortness of breath and premature death. There are no effective treatments that prolong the life of patients with pulmonary hypertension, similar to cancer. Here we propose to perform studies in order to understand better how the mitochondria dysfunction leads to pulmonary hypertension. We have drugs that can normalize mitochondrial function and we will test to see whether they may become therapies for pulmonary hypertension. We will use animal models and human organs that we receive at the time of transplant surgery. We also plan to test some of these drugs to actual patients in order to answer the critical questions that exist before testing them in large groups of patients to prove that they help without harm. The breadth and depth of our work provides a superb training environment in which to train future doctors and scientists to discover novel therapies for deadly human diseases. Our previous success in this field of research and the strong support from our institution and our collaborators make us confident that we will succeed to actually improve the lives of patients in addition to advancing our scientific knowledge.

column36: Increasing safe mobility of older Canadian pedestrians and drivers
column37: I will develop solutions to enable seniors to walk with less chance of falling and to drive safely. The ability to continue walking and driving safely is key to staying independent. Falls and accidents not only cause pain and cost but the resulting need for assistance with mobility creates a burden on family at home and may result in earlier admission to an institution. One component of my research will focus on opportunities to prevent falls by reducing environmental causes. We have provided evidence supporting changes to the Building Code of Canada to make stairs safer. That work will be extended to include standards for handrails on stairs, pathways and ramps as well as grab bars in bathrooms. In addition, many seniors are injured because of falls on ice. Fear of walking outside in winter causes many people to reduce their outings and their exercise. We will continue developing tests to guide consumers in the selection of safer footwear that will dramatically increase safety when walking on slippery surfaces. In parallel with walking research, I will focus on safer driving. One of the most devastating moments is being told that you can no longer drive safely and your keys are being taken away. As we grow older we need our cars more than ever because our walking is more limited, particularly in winter. Yet, our driving abilities may be challenged by vision or cognitive problems. It is neither safe nor practical to subject older people with, for example, dementia to challenging highway driving tests across all weather conditions. This research will focus on the ability to create realistic and valid driver testing using an advanced driving simulator. One of the main questions to be answered is whether such tests could be used to support a program of customized driving licenses. Such a program could limit driving for an individual, for example, to local streets in daylight where that person can be demonstrated to be safe rather than banning driving outright.

column36: Using the eye movement system to study brain function and dysfunction
column37: One of the most pressing challenges in neuroscience is to understand how human perception, memory, and action, become dysfunctional with neurological and psychiatric disease. We use eye movements, and pupil dilation systems to study intact and impaired sensory, motor, and cognitive processes, employing behavioural testing, neuroimaging, neurophysiology and computational modeling. Our approach has the potential to revolutionize not only our understanding of the brain, but also the diagnosis and rehabilitation of patients with brain disorders and development of animal models for therapeutic drug testing. We study non-human primates (NHPs) and compare recordings from single neurons in crucial regions of the cerebral cortex and brainstem to determine how active vision is both coordinated and controlled. NHPs have similar sensory, motor, and cognitive systems as humans, thus the knowledge gained from detailed neurophysiological and behavioural experiments can be used to search for behavioural biomarkers in neurological and psychiatric patient groups. Knowledge gained from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now guiding a reverse translational effort: we are using our knowledge of patient pathology to generate and study a form of AD in NHPs. Because there has been great difficulty translating therapies that work in rodents to the specific human disease condition, shifting to NHPs with a brain similar to humans is crucial. In AD there is a build-up of toxic molecules in the brain called amyloid-beta oligomers (ABOs). We have shown that injection of these ABOs into the NHP brain leads to similar brain pathology as found in AD patients. We are now examining if there are changes in behaviour and cognition, and if so, how therapeutics can prevent or reverse those changes. The expected outcome of the proposed studies is the identification of a strategy that could slow AD progression and/or interrupt the onset of AD.

column36: Discrete dynamic complexes and phase-separated states of disordered proteins in neurobiology
column37: Proteins are the molecular machines that perform most biological functions. Some proteins have stable structure but others, called intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), are highly flexible. Disorder is very abundant in brain proteins, particularly those associated with neurological diseases, as flexibility is advantageous for protein interactions, which are essential for regulating key biological processes. We have pioneered studies of disordered proteins and their interactions, leading the development of methodology to study them and defining a new paradigm for protein binding that relies on dynamic interactions. Our studies of disordered proteins have been published in major journals (including Nature, Molecular Cell, PNAS, EMBO) and have led to 164 invitations to speak at conferences and universities, as well as 32 invitations to write review articles. Our work has changed the way proteins interactions are viewed, including those between two, multiple or even huge numbers of protein molecules, which can come together in a process called phase-separation to form liquid droplets involved in organizing the cell. Brain function is poorly understood and there are no effective drugs for major neurological disorders, such as autism, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The previously dominant static view of protein binding has hindered progress and we propose that our perspective focusing on the role of dynamic interactions of disordered proteins will fundamentally change the understanding of brain function. We will apply our considerable expertise and powerful methods to key disordered proteins involved in brain function and their interactions. We hypothesize that loss of regulation and rigidification of dynamic complexes of these disordered proteins leads to pathology in the brain. We will test this hypothesis and glean information to enable novel therapeutics for a variety of neurological diseases.

column37: Cancer is promoted by increased amounts of eIF4E, a protein that I discovered in 1978. The main role of eIF4E is to promote protein synthesis, which is a process that controls how much proteins are made, and is critical for cells to proliferate. It is now well established that eIF4E is present at high levels in many types of human cancer and may serve as a prognostic tumor marker. Moreover, eIF4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) antagonize eIF4E activity, and act as tumor inhibitors. I, together with my research team, have not only discovered these proteins but have determined how they function and have defined their importance in many physiological and pathological conditions. Learning and memory is dependent on many of these proteins and mutant mice in which initiation of protein synthesis is enhanced demonstrate improvement in memory as compared to control mice. More recently, we discovered that eIF4E and 4E-BPs play important roles in causing an autism-like disease, and showed that by manipulating eIF4E activity we can reverse many abnormalities in mouse models of autism. We also demonstrated that eIF4E and 4E-BPs regulate circadian rhythms or an organism's "internal biological clock". The overarching research theme of my laboratory is the study of the mechanisms by which gene expression is controlled at the level of protein synthesis in health and disease. We will strive to discover drugs, in collaboration with pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, to treat diseases that are caused by dysregulated protein synthesis including cancer, autism, Fragile X syndrome, and metabolic disorders.

column36: Decoding gene regulation
column37: The goal of this research is to understand how human genes are regulated. The human genome consists of 3 billion bases, only 1% of which encodes protein-this is the proportion to which the "genetic code" applies. A much larger fraction - up to 10% by some estimates - functions to regulate the protein-coding genes. The details of how regulatory DNA works are still opaque, and how it is read by DNA binding proteins has been called the "second genetic code" - the next frontier in human genetics. We aim to crack this second code by studying the proteins that bind DNA, how they work together, and what they do to turn genes on and off, on a global level. The results of our research will enable us to make sense of how genes work normally, how they are impacted by common genetic variants, and how disease-causing mutations influence genetic regulatory programs.

Although molecularly distinct, these core pathways interact extensively and this crosstalk plays a key role in ensuring normal cell function under varying conditions. Failure in an individual pathway or in the way the pathways crosstalk, can lead to serious diseases such as cancer. My overall objective is to uncover the fundamental biology behind cell signalling and communication and to apply advanced, multidimensional screening approaches to identify novel protein targets and candidate drugs. The goal is to translate our findings so that they can be further developed as potential therapeutics to restore normal communication in diseased cells.

column36: Lipid nanomedicines for health and disease
column37: Current drugs suffer from two major limitations. First, they go everywhere in the body and only a small proportion arrives at a disease site such as a cancerous tumour. This results in toxic "side effects" due the effects of the drug on healthy tissue, as well as limited potency. Second, most drugs used today are "small molecules" that are small enough to penetrate into cells in the body to affect disease. The ability to use larger "genetic" drugs based on RNA and DNA to enable genetic therapies would have revolutionary consequences. Such drugs use natural regulatory processes in the body to treat disease leading to new potential treatments for most human diseases. The goal of this project is to develop "smart" nanomedicines that target small molecule drugs more accurately to disease sites and that enable genetic drugs to be used as therapeutics. These smart nanomedicines consist of the drug encapsulated into a nanoparticle that is administered by intravenous injection. These nanoparticles have dimensions of 100 nm or less, approximately 100 times smaller than a cell in the body. They are therefore able to permeate through most tissues and can be readily accumulated by most cells in the body. Specific goals of the project are to: 1) Development of triggered release lipid nanoparticle (LNP) systems to release therapeutic concentrations of small molecule drugs at sites of disease; 2) Development of LNP systems to extend applications of genetic drugs to extra-hepatic tissues; 3) Development of LNP systems containing genetic drugs that are not immunogenic; 4) Demonstrate efficacy of LNP systems in animal models of osteoporosis, diabetes, inflammation, neurological disorders, prostate cancer and leukemia. This research program builds on a strong record in drug development, as well as a well-established interdisciplinary network of collaborators in academia and industry.

column36: When Treatments Harm: Building Better Systems and Enhancing Research Capacity to Reduce Adverse Drug Events
column37: Medications have transformed the lives of Canadians who suffer from painful or debilitating illnesses. However, medications may also cause harm. As medication use rises, so does the incidence of adverse drug events-harmful and unintended events related to medication use. Today, adverse drug events cause 1.7M annual emergency department visits in Canada, and are a leading cause of hospital admissions. Identifying and treating patients with adverse drug events is not easy. Healthcare providers often unknowingly re-expose patients to medications that previously caused harm. This is because we misdiagnose 40% of adverse drug events, and lack effective ways of communicating information about these events between care providers even after the diagnosis is made. For example: "I saw a diabetic who was discharged from hospital recently, where he was admitted for hypoglycemia [low blood sugar] due to glyburide [a blood sugar lowering drug]. The physician asked him to stop the glyburide, and gave him a prescription for gliclazide, a drug with a lower risk of causing hypoglycemia. But the patient presented here comatose with an even lower blood sugar. When I looked at the patient's blister pack I discovered that both glyburide and gliclazide had been dispensed. The patient had been given a discharge prescription for gliclazide, but no note was made to discontinue glyburide, and neither the GP [general practitioner] nor the community pharmacist were aware of what had happened." Hospital pharmacist, 2012. To address this gap, I aim to develop, evaluate and implement innovative solutions to help healthcare providers diagnose and treat patients with adverse drug events, and prevent harmful re-exposure. My team plans to create the first adverse drug event surveillance program in Canada, improve the quality of data on adverse drug event outcomes, and create a new resource for health professionals to study safer prescribing, optimize medication use and improve health outcomes.

column36: Evaluating and Understanding the Impact of Tobacco Control Policies of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in a Rapidly Changing Global Tobacco Market: The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation Project
column37: This century, 1 billion people will die from tobacco use. The 2003 WHO treaty, the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) obligates 180 countries (90% of the world's population) to implement policies to reduce global tobacco use. If fully implemented, the FCTC would be the greatest disease prevention initiative in history. But FCTC implementation has been slow, weakened by tobacco industry influence. The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation (ITC) Project is a global research program addressing the urgent need for strong evidence about FCTC policy impact by (1) evaluating FCTC policies, (2) understanding determinants of tobacco use vs. quitting, (3) identifying differences in global FCTC policy impact. The ITC research team of >100 tobacco control experts has conducted cutting edge evaluation studies of FCTC policies in 22 countries, home to >70% of the world's tobacco users. ITC has consistently reported evidence used globally to strengthen tobacco policies that improve population health (www.itcproject.org). Since its start 13 years ago, ITC data have been used to strengthen tobacco control policies in many countries, including Canada. We propose to continue this global project by: 1) continuing our rigorous evaluation of FCTC policies, focusing on regions where the tobacco industry is increasing its attention (e.g., Asia, Africa, Middle East); 2) expand ITC to evaluate new leading-edge policies (e.g., plain packaging, additive bans), 3) conduct the first-ever international cohort study of e-cigarettes to answer critical questions about their impact on tobacco use; and 4) strengthen dissemination efforts to bring our evidence to governments to support stronger tobacco control globally. ITC has advanced science, improved population health initiatives, and built strong collaborations with governments and health communities globally. We will strengthen our efforts to use science to combat the world's leading preventable cause of death and disease.

column36: Development epidemiology: identifying evidence-based interventions for improving population health and promoting health equity
column37: There is abundant evidence that social conditions impact health. However, our ability to improve population health and reduce health inequalities is limited: we do not yet understand well enough how public policies and programs can be used to influence these social determinants of health. Rigorously assessing the impact of interventions, from national policies to smaller-scale programs, has become an active area of inquiry in social sciences such as economics, but less so in epidemiology. This research program will fill this gap by systematically identifying and evaluating evidence-based interventions that can improve population health and promote health equity in a global context. Countries are constantly designing and implementing policies and programs. By systematically grouping countries together and carefully analyzing comparable similarities or differences in implementation and outcomes, we can achieve a far better understanding of what public policies and programs really make a difference to the health of individuals. As the world moves towards the new Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 2015, there is as a new set of targets to meet that will improve health and reduce health inequality worldwide, and an outstanding window of opportunity to generate new evidence to meet them. This program focuses particularly on policies related to socioeconomic status, health services, public health, and the environment, and identifies the effects on the health-related SDGs of different policy variations across nations (Aim 1); within nations that have substantial policy variation at the provincial or state level (Aim 2); and in terms of their cost-effectiveness (Aim 3). The program will develop partnerships with policymakers, non-governmental organizations, and intergovernmental institutions to develop relevant research questions and ensure that research results inform the development of effective policies and programs on the ground.

column36: Structures and Functions of Megaenzymes
column37: Very many clinically-used therapeutics are produced naturally by earth's flora and fauna. They are often made in microbes by huge enzymes called nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) and polyketide synthases (PKSs). Examples include daptomycin, used against MRSA superbugs; viomycin, used to treat multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; actinomycin D, used to fight cancers like Wilms tumor; cyclosporin, which was widely used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants and can also inhibit the hepatitis C virus; and penicillin. A frequent target of natural compounds is another megaenzyme, the ribosome. The ribosome makes proteins in all cells. Inhibiting the ribosome in bacterial cells can kill bacteria and cure infections. The goal of this research is to expand our knowledge of how megaenzymes make important natural drugs and how megaenzyme-made drugs act on the ribosome. Using biochemistry and biophysics, we will analyze NRPSs and PKSs and capture 3D pictures of them at different points in the process of making natural products. We will also capture 3D pictures of natural products bound to and inhibiting the ribosome. This enables us to answer a range of questions, elucidating the details of how building blocks are chemically assembled into the antibiotics, explaining the large rearrangements NRPSs need to perform to create drugs and revealing new ways that natural drugs work against the ribosome. Megaenzymes hold a vast potential to produce new drugs. Because NRPSs and PKSs are divided into segments, with each segment adding one building block to the drug, we can alter the order of segments and the specific types of segment to produce variants of the drug product. For some drugs, we will visualize what each building block is doing to the ribosome. Our studies can help us learn how best to rearrange NRPS segments to make millions of new compounds, to better kill antibiotic resistant bacteria and also to fight other challenges to human health like viruses and cancer.

column37: The rising rate of obesity poses the biggest challenge to our health care system, such that obesity is complicated with many other comorbidities. I have the unique expertise to address this problem as we employ techniques that can address changes at the synaptic, circuitry and behavioral level in lean and obese animals.

column37: The primary goal of my research is to understand how brain circuits form during early development and how mutations and errors give rise to dysfunctional circuits that underlie common neurodevelopmental disorders such as Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) and Epilepsy. The distinctive feature of our research approach is the development of multi-disciplinary and highly innovative imaging tools that combine electrophysiology, genetics and technology development in microscope design to see brain neural network activity and growth. In addition to the development of these tools, I also developed a leading model of vertebrate brain circuit formation by taking advantage of the unique development features of the albino Xenopus tadpole. Specifically, the external development and transparency of the embryos allows us to directly image brain circuit formation in live animals. Another example of our novel approach involves labeling individual brain neurons using single-cell electroporation, a technique I invented to tag neurons and control their gene expression so that we can image 3D growth in real time using ultrafast microscopes constructed in my lab. Our research has demonstrated that neural activity in response to external stimuli guides neuronal growth and connectivity in a manner that allows for self-organization and optimization in processing the input encountered during development. Our findings on brain circuit formation have provided important insight into the origins of ASD where a large proportion of associated gene mutations disrupt the function of synaptic proteins. We also created single-cell models of ASD to express mutant genes in order to test alterations in growth, synapse formation and encoding. In parallel, we study Epilepsy to test whether seizures hijack activity-driven growth events. Once we understand how normal and dysfunctional brain circuits are formed, we will develop and evaluate new interventions for preventative and corrective treatments.

column36: Pannexin 1 in swelling-induced neuronal death
column37: Brain swelling is a major cause of mortality following insults such as stroke and traumatic brain injury. This condition is often caused by an underlying swelling of neurons in the brain, leading to cell death. We currently have limited capacity to replace these neurons, and therefore must devise strategies to reduce the swelling-induced cell death. Recent evidence suggests that an ion channel protein, called Panx1, is involved in this process. Ion channels act essentially as conduits between cells and the external environment. These proteins pass important signalling molecules to co-ordinate cellular responses, such as cell growth, movement, or death. In this project, I will test whether Panx1 conduits promote cell death following neuronal swelling. I will also examine the mechanisms through which Panx1 channels are activated during neuronal swelling. Early experiments indicate that harmful molecules known as reactive oxygen species, which are created within swollen cells, might play a role in this Panx1 activation and neuron death. Reactive oxygen species cause damage to all cellular components, including proteins. Therefore I will also examine whether these molecules activate Panx1 conduits by modifying parts of the protein structure. This work contributes to unraveling the complex and still largely unknown mechanisms underlying neuronal swelling and death, and will guide future studies on therapeutic interventions for brain edema and neuronal death.

column36: Treatment of paediatric anxiety disorders using reconsolidation update mechanisms: implications of executive functioning
column37: Paediatric anxiety disorders are frequent, can be extremely impairing and may lead to increased risks for adult anxiety disorders. Exposure-based therapies (including cognitive behavioural therapy [CBT]) are the first-line treatment for paediatric anxiety disorders. However, some children do not adequately benefit from treatment, and some experience a relapse of symptoms following treatment cessation. There is clearly scope to enhance the efficacy and durability of exposure therapy in paediatric anxiety disorders. The reconsolidation update mechanism suggests that following initial encoding, a memory is stored, but does not necessarily remain stable. When the memory is reactivated, it becomes labile and sensitive to change for a window of time. New information presented during this window can disrupt the reconsolidation of this memory, updating the original memory trace with new information. Augmentation of the fear memory may improve the maintenance of treatment gains following exposure therapy, because the memory can be modified and replaced with a less anxiety-evoking one. column36: Leukodystrophy: A Translational Research Program
column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of rare genetic diseases affecting previously healthy children and leading to progressive disabilities and death over months to years. Unfortunately, no curative treatment is available. It is estimated that 30-50% of patients remain without a precise diagnosis despite multiple tests. The first step to discover a treatment is to understand the causes of the diseases and therefore, to identify the causal genes. Leukodystrophies are characterized by abnormal white matter (myelin) of the brain. Myelin is responsible for the insulation of brain cells (neurons), allowing fast electric conduction in the nervous system. Leukodystrophies are classified as hypomyelinating (lack of myelin formation) and non-hypomyelinating (abnormal myelin maintenance) based on features seen in brain scans. My research program focuses on hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, and more specifically on one disorder called POLR3-related or 4H leukodystrophy. Children with this disease develop progressive difficulties to walk, talk, swallow and see (myopia). 4H is caused by mutations in 3 genes that are important for survival of the cells. Using 4H as my primary disease of interest, my comprehensive research program aims at describing these diseases, including their evolution over time and their impact on patients and their families, finding causal genes and explaining how mutations lead to disease (pathophysiology) in order to improve medical care for the patients and families, find new treatments and prepare for the upcoming clinical trials.

column36: Towards the use of Epigenetic Therapy as a Primer for Cancer Immunotherapy
column37: The main premise of Cancer Immunotherapy is to stimulate the patient's immune system to attack the malignant tumour cells. column36: Targeting Epigenetic Mechanisms in Prostate Cancer
column37: Prostate Cancer (PCa) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men in Canada. Although cure can be accomplished when the cancer is detected at its early stages, there is currently no curative treatment when the cancer has metastasized, a phenomenon that is accompanied by the appearance of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). The major clinical challenges in PCa are thus the lack of biomarkers that can distinguish early stage, indonent from more aggressive forms of PCa, and the lack of effective treatment for the CRPC. PCa is one the most heritable disease, and more than one hundred genetic variants have been found to increase the risk of PCa -cumulatively explaining 33% of the familial risk for PCa. Understanding of how the genetic variants predispose PCa provides opportunities to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. A few of the risk genetic variants affect genes that translate into protein, but the majority of them don't. About 1.5% of the human genome encodes protein-coding genes, and about 70% encodes genes that do not translate into protein, which are named as noncoding RNAs. Noncoding RNAs function through epigenetic regulation. Unlike genetics that is irreversible, epigenetics can be reversed by various approaches. Through computational analysis, we have identified sixty noncoding RNAs affected by more than half of the genetic variants in PCa. We propose to further investigate how these genetic variants affect noncoding RNAs, and through what epigenetic mechanisms these noncoding RNAs promote PCa development and progression. Finally, we will target these epigenetic mechanisms to improve the treatment of PCa. By revealing the functional nature of specific genetic variants our proposed research may identify specific genetic and lncRNA biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This will favor personalized/precision medicine where therapies are tailored to the unique genetic identity of each patient.

We will then determine whether key differences identified in our models identify subsets of human tumors with distinct clinical outcomes. These studies will expand our understanding of factors underlying the development of tumor heterogeneity and also provide preclinical models to test novel therapeutic strategies potentially revealed by our studies. The knowledge generated by this research will aid identification of molecular markers that can reproducibly identify human PDAC subtypes with distinct therapeutic responses and clinical outcomes.

column36: Integrating innovative interventions promoting social participation to foster health in aging Canadians
column37: Social participation, which involves activities that meet fundamental needs for interactions and self-actualization, is seriously challenged in aging and a major intervention target. Although included in health orientations, few social participation interventions are implemented in Canada. Our recent research demonstrated the feasibility and positive impact of clinical interventions in increasing seniors' functional autonomy, social participation and quality of life. However, to reach a substantial number of seniors, population interventions are also needed. Over the next five years, we will continue to develop, implement and evaluate clinical and population interventions targeting the social participation of older adults. Specifically, we will evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of two clinical interventions with older adults from pilot communities: the Personalized citizen assistance for social participation (APIC; Obj.1) and the Lifestyle Redesign(R) (Obj.2), in helping community organizations and clinicians target social participation. In parallel, one population intervention, the Index of Social Participation Potential (IPPS), will be developed, implemented and evaluated (Obj.3) to guide municipal stakeholders in identifying policies, services and structures that best foster social participation among seniors. Development of the IPPS will be enriched by exploring how age-friendly key components foster positive health, social participation and health equity of aging adults across Canada (Obj.4). These innovations, i.e. APIC, Lifestyle Redesign(R) and IPPS, will be optimized and integrated in one multicomponent intervention, implemented and evaluated in other communities (Obj.5). Our preliminary results suggest that this multicomponent intervention will foster social participation in aging. Since most chronic diseases can be prevented or delayed by an active lifestyle, our results point to one of the most promising avenues to live longer and better.

column36: Developmental Coordination Disorder: Integrating Brain Imaging and Rehabilitation to Improve Outcomes
column37: Developmental coordination disorder (DCD) is a common condition that affects 5-6% of school-aged children, or 1-2 children in every Canadian classroom. Children with DCD find it hard to learn motor skills and perform everyday activities, such as getting dressed, tying shoelaces, using a fork and knife, printing, riding a bicycle, or playing sports. Children with DCD often feel lonely, depressed or anxious, and may have low self-esteem and problems with peers. They also tend to avoid physical and social activities, which further affects their friendships. DCD is a life-long condition that affects school performance, vocational choices, and leisure activities. Up to 50% of children with DCD will also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which further compounds the difficulties that these children face in daily life. We do not know what causes DCD, but we think there are differences in brain development and brain function in children with DCD compared to typical children. Our previous studies have shown that children with DCD use different brain areas to perform and learn motor skills compared to typically-developing children. Having a better understanding of other brain differences will help to explain why children with DCD struggle to learn motor skills. We can then determine if we can change the brain and improve motor skills through rehabilitation. In this study, we will use MRI to compare images of children's brains to accomplish two goals: (1) determine how the brain differs in children with DCD and children with DCD+ADHD compared to typically-developing children; (2) determine if rehabilitation can change the brain and improve motor function of children with DCD+/-ADHD. This study is the first of its kind and will advance our understanding of DCD and hopefully improve outcomes of affected children. Findings will provide evidence for current treatment approaches or offer insight into developing alternate interventions.

column36: Developing Adequate Protein and Energy Recommendations for the Prevention and Treatment of Sarcopenia in Cancer
column37: Two out of five Canadians will develop cancer in their lifetimes. People with cancer lose significant amounts of muscle mass due to the disease itself or its treatment. These include physical disability, frailty, extended hospitalization, infectious complications, poorer quality of life, cancer progression and shorter survival. Eating an adequate amount of protein and energy is essential to sustain muscle mass but our current nutritional recommendations are not specific to people with cancer, and have not been developed based on scientific evidence. By improving principles of optimal nutrition intervention to counteract sarcopenia, we will improve well-being and survival, ultimately reducing the burden on Canada's health care system.

column37: Adverse events (AEs) occur in 2.9% to 16.6% of all acute care hospitalizations and are responsible for 44,000 to 98,000 deaths each year. An important prerequisite to answer these important questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals is to have access to accurate measures of AE occurrence. For this reason, a fourth objective of this program of research is to pursue the development and the validation of such measures.

column36: The Molecular Mechanisms that Regulate Immunological 'Exhaustion' in Chronic conditions
column37: A certain immune cell type, killer T cells, play an important role in controlling chronic infections such as HIV and cancer. These immune checkpoints' inhibitors jump-start a patient's immune system to recognize and kill infected cells and tumors. They are game-changers for chronic infections and cancer. Using immune checkpoints' inhibitor therapy is revolutionizing cancer treatment by manipulating a person's immune system to fight their infected cells and cancer cells. I aim to understand how killer T cells become dysfunctional in the context of HIV and cancer in order to develop novel immunotherapy drugs. I will identify and develop novel immunotherapy approaches to target these immune checkpoints to allow killer T cells to stay protective and kill infected cells and cancer cells.
