column36: Understanding the generation and protective functions of broadly-neutralizing humoral immune responses against influenza A virus
column37: Influenza virus is one of the top ten leading causes of death in Canada, and remains one of the gravest threats to global public health due to its propensity to cause pandemics. To combat seasonal influenza epidemics, massive annual vaccination programs are carried out at tremendous expense to the healthcare system. The ability of influenza virus to cause seasonal epidemics is conferred by its capacity to rapidly evolve in order to escape pre-existing immunity. This in turn necessitates that influenza virus vaccines be reformulated on a nearly annual basis. Frequently, the strains of influenza virus that actually circulate do not perfectly resemble the strains included in the vaccine. Due to the exquisitely strain-specific immunity that current vaccines elicit, vaccine efficacy can suffer substantially when imperfect matches occur. More importantly, current vaccines offer little to no protection against the emergence of a novel influenza virus pandemic. Therefore, there is a tremendous need to develop new influenza virus vaccines capable of inducing broad and long-lasting protection. The recent discovery of broadly-neutralizing antibodies that bind to the stalk domain of hemagglutinin has raised the hope that development of a "universal" influenza virus vaccine may be within reach. While many studies have addressed how these antibodies function in isolation, little is known about the way that broadly-neutralizing antibodies are generated and function in the context of the polyclonal responses that are naturally elicited by vaccination and infection. Our studies will define the mechanisms that govern the generation and function of broadly-neutralizing antibodies in the context of the polyclonal response to infection and vaccination. The knowledge gained from these studies will be used to advance the development of "universal" influenza virus vaccines and therapeutics which have the potential to substantially reduce the global burden of influenza-related illnesses.

column36: Comprehending epigenomic changes in gene dysregulation and cancer using machine learning
column37: To diagnose and treat a broad range of patients using sequence data, we must understand how genomic and epigenomic differences lead to changes in gene regulation and phenotype. Changes in gene regulation often underlie the mechanism of genetic disorders and cancer. These changes can arise from variation in genomic DNA sequence. They can also come from alterations in epigenomic properties, such as DNA methylation, chromatin packaging, histone modifications, or 3D chromosome conformation. New sequencing technology reveals a forest of genomic and epigenomic variation, but we are hindered by insufficient understanding of the variation's consequences. As a result, we can apply these data to diagnosis or personalized drug therapy only in limited cases. My research program addresses this gap in knowledge to understand interactions between genome, epigenome, and phenotype in human cancers. My program applies a systematic framework to create and validate predictive models of (1) how genetic variants cause epigenomic changes, and (2) the effect of epigenomic changes on gene regulation and phenotype. First, we start with data from collaborators or public resources, using cancer cell lines and cancer patient primary tissue. Second, we develop machine learning models of how a genomic or epigenomic input leads to an epigenomic or phenotypic output. Third, we perturb input data and predict changes in output. Fourth, we validate predictions with targeted experiments. Our research will yield better understanding of the impact of epigenomic changes in cancer. It will also deliver new software and annotations to help biologists and clinicians assess changes in the noncoding sequence and epigenome of cancer patients.

column36: Cell surface signaling microdomains in heath and disease
column37: Tumours are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists by several changes they exhibit compared to normal cells. Some of these changes involve alteration in the abundance and function of a family of proteins called receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) within tumour cells. These changes in the function of RTKs are required for tumours to grow and spread in the body. Obtaining a better understanding of how a cell controls RTKs (and related proteins) has the potential to provide new ways to treat tumours and prevent cancer spreading. One member of the RTK family of particular interest is named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). Much has been learned about how EGFR functions to control the behaviour and growth of cells, mostly by identifying the other proteins in a cell required for EGFR to do this. However, much like knowing the name of dancers does not tell us much about the dance that they will perform, we need to know more than the identify of proteins that work with EGFR to control cell growth and spread: we need to understand their choreography. In molecular terms, we need to understand the organization of EGFR and other key proteins in space and time. We have recently discovered that EGFR signals must be organized in structures called clathrin-coated signaling microdomains to control cell growth and movement. Using advanced microscopy that allow us to 'see' the movement of EGFR and other key proteins (dancers), we aim to understand how these clathrin-coated signaling microdomains work in normal cells and how they are disrupted in cancer cells. Understanding how these structures control the "dance" of EGFR required to dictate cell growth and movement has the potential to allow the development of new therapies aimed at changing the "beat" to control how RTKs drive tumour growth and spreading. Hence, our research aims to help uncover novel strategies to treat certain types of cancer that are difficult to treat with existing therapies.

column36: Preventing Injecting by Modifying Existing Responses (PRIMER)
column37: Injection drug use remains a primary source of HIV transmission globally, and people who inject drugs (PWID) have been shown to play a key role in the initiation of others into injecting. However, no interventions to prevent injecting initiation are proven effective. Importantly, ongoing exposure to injecting increases the risk that street youth and other 'at-risk' populations might initiate injecting, and data suggest that the majority of non-injectors are initiated into injecting by PWID. Reducing the exposure of street youth to injecting is therefore likely to reduce their risk of initiation into injection. This multicountry, mixed methods project will therefore investigate whether a range of interventions and factors that influence injecting among PWID (opioid substitution therapy, supervised injection facilities, stable housing, incarceration environments, public injecting, and gender) may also influence the risk that they initiate others into injecting. This study will seek to: 1) determine how often PWID initiate others into injecting; 2) assess factors potentially influencing the risk that PWID initiate others into injecting; 3) investigate drug scene roles (i.e., drug dealer) that increase the risk that PWID might initiate others into injecting; and 4) test the impact of an existing structural or biomedical intervention on the risk that PWID will initiate others into injecting. To accomplish this, we will conduct a multi-site study of 3,050 PWID across North America and France employing quantitative and qualitative data from five separate ongoing observational studies of PWID (San Diego, STAHR; Tijuana, El Cuete; Vancouver, VIDUS/ARYS; Toronto, HHiT, Bordeaux/Marseille/Paris, COSINUS). This project is the first study to investigate structural approaches to reducing HIV risk by preventing injecting initiation. This novel approach addresses a major gap in HIV prevention programming.

column36: Stiffness as a novel biomarker and therapeutic target for kidney fibrosis
column37: Scarring is a major cause of organ failure, accounting for up to 50% of all deaths in the developed world. In the kidney, scarring is the final common pathway of damage activated by nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. If left unchecked, kidney scarring can lead to kidney failure, an increasingly common, costly, and life-threatening condition requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival. Unfortunately, clinicians have no safe and effective ways to diagnose or treat kidney scarring currently. Following injury and especially with scarring, organs stiffen. My lab has been working on ways to take advantage of this knowledge to better diagnose and treat kidney scarring, to identify those patients at highest risk for kidney failure and to treat these individuals with new anti-scarring treatments. In the first set of studies described in this application, we will take advantage of our discovery: (1) that fibroblasts, the main producers of kidney scar tissue, can sense stiffening after injury, and (2) that this stiffening makes them more sensitive to pro-scarring stimuli. We will explore how fibroblasts sense kidney stiffening, to develop new treatments that block the ability of fibroblasts to recognize that stiffening is occurring, and therefore that shut off the scarring process. In the second set of studies, we will take advantage of our recent development of new MRI techniques that can image the stiffness of a kidney without needles or surgery. Our goal is to test: (1) whether MRI measures of kidney stiffness are accurate, (2) whether they correlate with kidney scar measurements as determined by gold standard analysis of kidney biopsies, and (3) whether they predict if kidney function will decline. Given the importance of scarring to kidney disease, our expectation is that these studies, through improving the care of kidney scarring, will ultimately improve the lives of patients with kidney disease.

column36: MOM-LINC: Mechanisms, Outcomes, and Mobilization of maternally-Led Interventions for Newborn Care
column37: Mothers have been crucial to infant survival and well-being through time, yet now they are minimally involved in critical care settings. The aim of this program of research is to improve the way that healthcare is delivered to infants requiring intensive care by enhancing maternal and family active contribution to their child's care. More specifically, the research focuses on three areas. The first is how maternally led interventions can improve outcomes in at-risk newborns related to stress, pain and neurodevelopment. The second is to understand the mechanisms that underlie immediate effectiveness and potential protective longer lasting outcomes of these interventions. The third area focuses on ways to improve the uptake of these interventions by both parents and health care providers. Within this research focus, there are two inter-related content areas: skin-to-skin contact as a pain relieving strategy and breastfeeding in neonatal populations. column36: Improving Outcomes in Frail Older Adults with Cardiovascular Disease
column37: The aging population has redefined the field of heart disease from single-system disease-oriented care to multi-faceted patient-oriented care. Frailty is a syndrome seen mainly in older adults that is central to the patient-oriented care model as it reflects the individual patient's reserves and resiliency to stressful events such as surgery. My research has shown that frail patients suffer a 3-fold increase in death, complications, and poor recovery of physical function after heart surgery and other invasive heart procedures. However, existing tools to measure frailty are limited by low specificity in hospitalized patients and ambiguity about their actionable ramifications - this is a critical barrier that has stifled the advancement of treatment strategies. The solution that I am proposing is to use a different marker to measure frailty, one that has the potential to be treated in clinical practice, namely - sarcopenia. Sarcopenia, "the biological substrate of frailty", is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Various criteria exist to define it, some using special scales and others using bone density scanners, but these have not been adequately assessed in patients with heart disease who may have issues such as fluid retention that can cause inaccurate measurements. Thus, I will compare the accuracy and prognostic value of various criteria to determine how we should optimally diagnose sarcopenia in patients with heart disease. Then, I will identify patients who are referred for heart surgery and have low muscle mass and strength (sarcopenia) to test a targeted treatment - a specialized protein supplement beverage - which was designed to stimulate muscle building in older adults, and, I hypothesize, will improve their recovery of physical function and other outcomes after the heart surgery procedure.

column37: In the pancreas, alpha-cells release glucagon (which causes blood sugar to go up) and beta-cells release insulin (which causes blood sugar to go down). column37: Most pharmacological principles used in psychiatry have been discovered by serendipity in the 1950s and 60s. column36: Optimizing the delivery of HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis with Text Messaging Services and Nursing Support
column37: HIV Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is an HIV prevention modality where uninfected persons take 28 days of antiretroviral medications (ARVs) shortly after an HIV exposure to minimize the risk of acquiring HIV. PEP is highly efficacious and is considered the standard of care on medical and ethical grounds. Unfortunately, implementation challenges have limited its clinical and public health impact in Canada. At present, access to PEP is inconsistent and the quality of care varies nationwide. We seek to address two major issues with PEP delivery: First, retention in care after nPEP initiation is a major challenge as only 50% of our patients complete follow-up at the required 3-4 month time point. Mobile phone-based text messaging may offer a simple, innovative solution to address this problem. The 'WelTel' text messaging platform has proven been to improve health outcomes in prior randomized controlled trials but has never been studied in nPEP. Second, the costs associated with nPEP are high, in part because care is usually provided by specialist physicians. However, nPEP patients could readily be followed by trained nurses, since it is administered according to strict protocols and because most patients are healthy. Nurses in public health clinics are ideally suited to this role, being experienced with sexual health and available in health units nationwide.. We propose a pragmatic randomized controlled trial using a 2x2 factorial design to determine whether the proportion of nPEP patients that successfully complete follow-up: a) is higher among those receiving mobile phone-based text messaging support via WelTel than among those receiving standard care; and b) is non-inferior among those receiving care from a sexual health clinic nurse compared to those receiving hospital-based physician care. Our data will provide important information on how to strengthen retention in care and reduce costs to the healthcare system for PEP delivery.

column36: From genetic diversity to genomic instability: in vivo characterization of the deubiquitinase OTUB1 in B-cells
column37: Our DNA carries the information required for the growth/maintenance of life. Problematically, environmental agents or pollutants can jeopardize its integrity and generate DNA lesions. If not repaired, these lesions can lead to mutations and the development of cancer and immunodeficiencies. We are particularly interested in one type of DNA lesions, called DNA double-strand break (DSB). DSB is a highly dangerous DNA lesion with unexpectedly beneficial applications. B-cells use DSBs during an infection to produce high affinity antibodies that eliminate the intruders. This process, named antibody diversification, carries however the risk of deleterious chromosomal rearrangements that favor the development of malignancies, including lymphoma, leukemia and multiple myeloma. Thus, it is imperative that we fully understand how DSBs are regulated to elicit a functional immune response while preserving DNA integrity and limiting cancer development. Ubiquitin, a small regulatory protein, plays a major role in DSB signaling/repair. Several ubiquitylation events catalyzed by E3 ubiquitin ligases take place during the DSB response and have been implicated in antibody diversification. However, less is known about the importance of deubiquitylation events, the process of cleavage of ubiquitin, in B-cells. We are particularly interested in a specific deubiquitinase named OTUB1, which has been previously linked to the DSB response. We are currently characterizing the role of OTUB1 in B-cell biology and the emergence of B-cell malignancies in vivo using an Otub1 knockout mouse model. Understanding OTUB1 functions in vivo will provide insight into B cell biology and carcinogenesis. It may also provide a rationale for the development of therapeutic approaches targeting OTUB1. This work will have broader implication for immunology and cancer biology due to the central role of DSB repair in these fields

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma affect over 6M Canadians. These chronic diseases are typically progressive, debilitating and punctuated by sudden, worsening of symptoms or "lung attack" requiring immediate medical care and hospital admission. COPD and asthma lung attacks account for the vast majority of Canadian hospital admissions and represent a staggering burden that is under-appreciated. The enormity of this becomes apparent by recognizing that in 2008-2011, 1 in 4 Ontario hospital beds was occupied by a COPD patient, equivalent to filling 250 of the 1000 hospitals in Canada with COPD patients alone. On a broader level, the availability of thousands of gene knockouts in C. elegans will provide a powerful resource to study a range of basic problems in developmental biology. The impact of this project will be to open up new avenues of discovery on gene function. The C. elegans Gene Knockout Facility at the University of British Columbia is part of an International Consortium and is recognized worldwide as a leader for C. elegans genetics and genomic studies. column36: Testing existing and new therapeutic interventions in a novel animal model of acute Spot Positive intracranial hemorrhage
column37: There is no effective treatment for bleeding into the brain or ICH. While we cannot do anything about the initial ICH, expansion of a bleed is the most important cause of bad outcome in ICH. We first described the Spot Sign which, when seen in ICH, strongly predicts expansion. We developed clinical trials (that are ongoing) selecting patients for treatment with drugs that stop bleeding based on the presence or absence of the Spot sign. There is evidence now however to suggest that this approach is flawed as the Spot sign represents varying rates of ICH expansion rather than an all-or-none situation. In other words, some Spot positive bleeding may be so quick that no medical treatment will be effective while others so slow that no treatment is needed because no meaningful expansion will occur. The problem is that current studies will not tell us what rates of bleeding are responsive to existing medicines and will likely fail because we did not consider the rate of bleeding. We have therefore developed a unique animal model that most closely mimics the Spot positive bleeding that occurs in humans. By aiming ultrasound beams from outside the head to specific brain regions we are able to damage the walls of small vessels causing them to rupture. By controlling the power of the ultrasound delivered we can adjust the rate of bleeding by targeting different vessel sizes. We propose using this model to test existing (medicines) and new (new medicines, using ultrasound to stop bleeding and surgical) ways to minimize expansion of bleeds based on the rate of bleeding associated with Spot positive bleeds. Once the ranges of bleeding rates responsive to our proposed medicines and novel treatments are established we can test these in humans using existing imaging sequences that measure rates of bleeding. By selecting patients based on these measures we can tailor treatment to the particular rate of bleeding ensuring better outcomes, less dependency and lower cost to society

column36: Structural composition and regulation of electrical synapses in the CNS
column37: Numerous neurotransmitters are used by nerve cells in the brain to communicate with each other at chemical synapses. However, over the past 15 years, surprising discoveries by us and others have shown that another mode of neuronal communication mediated by electrical synapses is also prevalent in the mammalian central nervous system. These synapses are critical for information processing related to cognitive, sensory and motor functions of the brain. Such synapses are formed by structures called gap junctions that are located at close appositions between neurons, and are composed of the gap junction-forming protein connexin36 as well as a growing list of accessory proteins. Our work shows that these structures are complex, with many protein components supporting their assembly, maintenance and neurotransmission functions. Identification of those components and their functions is essential for understanding the normal operation of electrical synapses and how their malfunction could contribute to brain disorders. With our past and more recent discoveries of some of their key protein components (ZO-1, MUPP1, AF6, cingulin, N-cadherin, nectin-1, alpha-catenins and beta-catenin, SynGAP1), we aim to determine how these proteins are organized and regulate electrical synapses. Our finding of the protein SynGAP1 at these synapses is particularly intriguing, because it is already known to be important for regulating communication at chemical synapses and may be equally important at electrical synapses. Further, mutations in the gene coding for this protein were recently found to cause significant intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy in people. We expect that our work will reveal entirely new concepts on cellular mechanisms that govern the activities of electrical synapses, which will ultimately be important for considerations of how these synapses could potentially malfunction and contribute to neurological disorders.

In the past decade, our research, as well as the work of many others, has identified key elements of the immune system that sense and respond to incoming viruses. Recently we have demonstrated that a host factor called Nrf2 plays a key role during infection and inhibits the antiviral response. The known functions of Nrf2 do not explain these observations, and it is of great importance to expand our knowledge regarding the negative controls of host immunity. The goal of this project is thus to investigate the role that Nrf2 plays in enhancing viral infections, and discover how it does so. We will also examine the potential of inhibiting this suppressive pathway in the hopes of enhancing protection against Vesicular Stomatitis Virus and Herpes simplex virus 1 pathologies. Lastly, we will determine if Nrf2 can be exploited by reducing cancer cell resistance to oncolytic viral therapy. Understanding these virus-host interactions will provide important insights concerning virus infection and disease, and this project will develop novel antiviral and anticancer therapeutic options for patients.

column37: Malaria is one of the greatest threats to human health today. Globally, there are approximately 200 million cases per year, resulting in approximately 600,000 deaths, the majority of which are small children. Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite transmitted from mosquitoes to human hosts. Once inside the host, the parasite invades red blood cells to consume nutrients from the host in order to develop and multiply. The treatment, control, and eradication of malaria have long been impeded by the ability of the parasite to rapidly develop resistance to antimalarial drugs. Therefore, it is imperative to develop new drugs that act through molecular mechanisms distinct from existing drugs to control the disease and combat the spread of drug resistance. Due to the complex biochemical interactions between the drug, parasite, and human host, identification of the molecular target of potential antimalarial drugs is an enormous challenge requiring years of intense research. An emerging approach for identifying the molecular target of antimalarials is to sequence the genome of parasites that have developed drug resistance in order to identify the responsible genetic mutations. This project aims to develop a new technology to isolate these drug-resistant parasites in order to sequence their genome to rapidly identify the molecular target of antimalarial drugs. This work leverages a recent discovery made by our research team that found all antimalarial drugs dramatically reduce the deformability of infected red blood cells, which aids the clearance of the infected cells from the host. Using this characteristic, our technology will separate infected red blood cells based on mechanical deformability in order to isolate cells drug-resistant parasites from those containing drug-sensitive parasites. Once separated, we will then sequence the genome of mutated parasites in order to identify the molecular target of potential antimalarial drugs.

column36: Characterization of the proteostasis decline upon aging
column37: Aging is a complex process characterized by a progressive decline of the ability of tissues to retain their functional integrity. At the cellular level, aging has been associated to a reduced capacity to maintain the integrity of the proteome (which is the ensemble of proteins present in the cell). This decline has been associated to the accumulation and aggregation (i.e., clumping) of several proteins in age-related pathologies like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's and prion diseases. In this project, we will specifically identify which proteins become misshapen and tend to clump in brain tissues of aging mice. Our hypothesis is that clumping proteins share similar characteristics that make them more susceptible. We will employ a computational approach to identify these features and thereby rationalize why the identified proteins are more affected upon aging. This study will lead to unique and novel fundamental knowledge that could potentially reveal how proteostasis (i.e., maintenance of a balanced proteome) is affected upon aging, and provide a first glimpse of how the cell landscape is affected when things "start to go wrong". With the current ageing society, it becomes critical that we address this knowledge gap, and identify biomarkers related to cellular aging. These age-related biomarkers could be used in the future to guide studies aiming at delaying cellular aging and stop the progression of age-related diseases.

column36: Cell Response and Wound Healing Through Electrical Stimulation Mediated by Conductive Scaffold
column37: Electrical activity commonly exists in our body. It transfers information through nerve and activates our muscles. So there are cells that are sensitive to electricity and are responsive to electrical stimulation. Based on this, we have been studying how to use electricity to change cell activities in order to help the repair of wound. Instead of using metals to conduct electricity, we use conductive polymers. Conductive polymers are manmade organic materials that allow electricity to pass. The advantages of using conductive polymers but metals are that polymers are more like natural tissues such as in softness and elasticity. Polymers also do not get corrosion that may produce metal ions toxic to cells. Organic materials can also be degraded. In previous years we have successfully produced three categories of conductive polymers, the composite with biodegradable polymers and the composites with biostable or biodegradable textiles. We grow human cells on such polymers and then connect electricity to the polymers. In such a way the cells are exposed to electricity. We found that under some types of electrical stimulation, human cells become more active, growth faster, move faster, and produce chemicals and proteins that accelerate the repair of wound. We have presented our results in about 30 scientific articles and many scientific conferences, which makes our group the international leader in this research field. In the next five years, we will expand our research to look at the mechanisms about how electricity affects cells, and to develop protocols to find out how the electrically activated cells can heal the wound in animals. We will use our electrical stimulation model to study the interactions between the cells that made up our skin and blood vessel. Our project combines material science, electrical engineering and biosciences, providing an excellent environment to train students.

column37: Thousands of dental and orthopedic implants are placed each year to address the ravages of bone degenerative diseases such as osteoporosis, osteoarthristis, osteonecrosis and periodontal disease. column37: Recent clinical trials have convincingly demonstrated that immunotherapy with anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can induce impressive clinical responses in children and adult patients with refractory B cell acute lymphocytic leukemia. We have recently found that a fragment (peptide) of the WT1 protein is presented on the leukemia cell's surface by another protein called the HLA class II molecule. It is already known that acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) cells often express the WT1 protein and HLA class II molecules. We hope that this study will lay the groundwork to use our innovative CAR T cells targeting the WT1 peptide/class II complex in the clinic to treat patients with AML in the near future.

column36: Therapeutic strategies for improvement of airway epithelial repair by targeting CFTR defect and bacterial infection in cystic fibrosis patients
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF), the most common genetic disease among Caucasians, is due to mutations in the gene coding for a protein called CFTR. Although CF affects many organs, the progressive lung damage due to bacterial infections remains the first cause of mortality in CF patients. Several years ago, we thus decided to devote our efforts to identify novel therapeutic strategies to promote lung repair in CF patients. We first discovered that the capability of airways to repair after injury is less efficient in CF patients than in healthy subjects, due to both the CFTR dysfunction and the presence of infections. Our work also unveiled that CFTR rescue with new compounds called correctors significantly enhances airway repair, but this CFTR rescue and repair improvement are dampened by bacteria. Importantly, we have new data supporting that lung repair could be improved by targeting products released by bacteria and using combinations of CFTR modulators. Using both airway cells and bacteria collected from CF patients, our aim is now to dissect the mechanisms whereby CFTR and infection regulate epithelial repair. Then, we will precisely define the bacterial products responsible for the deleterious effect of infection on airway repair and CFTR rescue. Finally, our aim is to evaluate the most effective strategy, with CFTR modulators and compounds interfering with bacteria, to reach the highest level of CFTR rescue and CF airway repair improvement, despite the presence of infection. Our project will allow better understanding of the contribution of the CFTR defect and bacterial infection in the failure of the CF airway to repair after injury. Our data will also give novel insights to predict the efficiency of CFTR correctors in the presence of infection and to define the best strategy to improve lung repair in infected CF patients.

column36: Regulation of muscle satellite cell self-renewal and differentiation by CCAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein beta: Implications in disease pathogenesis.
column37: Skeletal muscle has a remarkable ability to repair itself after injury or exercise, a feature that can be attributed to resident stem cells called satellite cells. After injury, satellite cells begin to divide to produce daughter cells. Of these, the majority will mature into myocytes that can fuse to one another or to damaged muscle fibers to initiate repair. The remaining daughter cells remain as satellite cells, ensuring that the muscle retains its capacity to repair over the lifespan of the organism. Understanding, on a molecular level, what makes a cell decide to mature or to remain a stem cell can help understand how disease arises in muscle and can help us develop better stem cell-based therapies. My laboratory has discovered that the protein C/EBPbeta regulates entry into myogenesis, promotes stem cell marker expression, and is necessary for maintaining the satellite cell population. In the absence of C/EBPbeta, satellite cells precociously differentiate and don't self-renew, resulting in bigger muscle fibers and a smaller stem cell population that cannot support muscle repair long term. In healthy muscle, C/EBPbeta can be found in satellite cells but once these cells become activated to repair muscle, C/EBPbeta levels drop but reappear at the late stages of new fiber formation. C/EBPbeta is misexpressed in skeletal muscle in cachexia and during aging where muscle wasting occurs. While we know that C/EBPbeta is important to prevent satellite cell maturation, it is unclear how C/EBPbeta regulates self-renewal or what its function is in new myofibers. The proposal will concentrate on answering these questions with the ultimate goal of understanding how C/EBPbeta contributes to muscle disease, and how this can be converted into novel therapies for muscle wasting.

column36: Epigenetic Mechanisms in Chronic Pain
column37: The Canadian Pain Society estimates that one in five Canadians suffer from chronic pain, costing up to $60 billion a year in health care and lost productivity. One reason that chronic pain is resistant to treatment is that it is associated with long term biological changes that are difficult to reverse, including pathological changes in gene expression in the brain. Very little is known about how pain-related changes in gene expression are regulated. We hypothesize that they are controlled by chemical changes to the genes referred to as epigenetic modifications. Epigenetic changes can occur in response to the environment or to injury and act as a memory, altering gene expression for decades. We have previously demonstrated that chronic pain results in widespread epigenetic changes in the brain. In this study we propose to use a rodent model of chronic pain to determine the role of epigenetically-regulated genes in chronic pain and if we can target these mechanisms for the treatment of chronic pain. The research team represents a partnership between pain researchers and epigenetic experts coming together to study chronic pain in a new way. Improved understanding of the role of epigenomic modulation in chronic pain could have significant impact on the quality of life for millions of individuals currently suffering from chronic pain.

column37: Parasitic Helminths (PHs) are major human pathogens. They include the giant roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides as well as whipworms and hookworms. PHs infect over 2 billion people worldwide causing tens of thousands of deaths per year and widespread sickness. PHs are thus a major global health problem and, while there are a few available drugs, resistance is rapidly emerging and there is therefore a great need for new drugs. How can we treat PHs? To do this effectively, we must kill the infecting PH without harming the human host. This means that we need to exploit crucial differences in the biology of humans and PHs. One key possibility lies in the way that humans and PHs make energy. For much of their life cycle, PHs make energy in the same way that humans do. However, when PHs are inside the human body, there is little oxygen available for them - under these conditions, they make energy using an unusual pathway, the FR/RQ pathway, that is completely absent from humans. Drugs that block FR/RQ would thus be ideal anti-PH treatments. No such drugs exist since almost all the simple living systems in which drug screens are done (e.g. yeast, mammalian cells) do not have FR/RQ and so one cannot find FR/RQ inhibitors in these models. The nematode worm C.elegans is different - it has an intact FR/RQ pathway and is easy to grow and study in the lab. We have established conditions in which we can rapidly assay FR/RQ activity in C.elegans. We have also built a novel drug screening pipeline which allows us to screen thousands of drugs per day to find drugs that block FR/RQ. column36: Driving disease: Molecular mechanisms of apicomplexan parasite motility
column37: Parasitic infections pose a major threat to global human health. Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium falciparum, the causative agents of toxoplasmosis and severe malaria, respectively, are particularly important due to their widespread distribution and disease outcomes. Toxoplasmosis is highly prevalent in the developed world and is a leading cause of food-borne illness related deaths in the United States. Toxoplasma infections can lead to a variety of disease outcomes and, if congenitally transmitted, can result in abortion, neonatal death and fetal abnormalities. Children that survive prenatal infection are likely to suffer significantly reduced quality of life with neurological deficiencies such as mental retardation. Nearly 3.4 billion people live in at risk zones for malaria resulting in more than 200 million clinical cases and half a million deaths per year, 85% of which are young children. Given the clear impact of these parasitic diseases on human health and the current challenges in effectively controlling them, novel treatments are desperately needed. To establish infection and cause disease, these parasites must invade the individual cells of a host. To accomplish this, they rely on a sophisticated motility system driven by a unique molecular "motor". However, very little is known about the inner workings of this motor and thus the overall process of parasite motility is poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we will use cutting edge biophysical and biochemical techniques to dissect the motor complex. These studies will provide crucial insight into how these globally devastating pathogens invade host cells, which we will, in turn, leverage to identify novel targeted therapies.

column36: The structural basis of plasmid segregation by bacterial actins
column37: In addition to their chromosomes, bacteria possess small pieces of DNA called plasmids. Plasmids play a vital role in human health and disease because they encode genes for antibiotic resistance, virulence machinery, pathways to digest unusual substances and synthesize toxins. With this project we focus on plasmid segregation systems driven by bacterial actin, a distant relative of the cytoskeletal filament actin of eukaryotic cells. To understand the molecular mechanism that drives plasmid segregation, we will integrate cutting-edge structural and biochemical approaches aimed at bridging single molecules to macromolecular assemblies in the cell. Understanding how the machinery of plasmid segregation works at the molecular level and within the cell will provide opportunities to effectively disrupt the process in drug-resistant pathogenic bacteria.

column36: Investigating the role of eIF2beta in translation reprogramming in cancer
column37: mRNA translation is a process during which proteins are synthesized by translation machinery based on the information stored in messenger RNAs (mRNAs). Abnormal mRNA translation is common in cancer. Alterations in mRNA translation provide proteins necessary for neoplastic transformation (a process during which normal cells become malignant), as well as tumor progression and dissemination. However, understanding of the role of translation in cancer remains incomplete. This hampers development of therapeutic strategies to target translation machinery in cancer. The mammalian/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is considered to be the major pathway that controls mRNA translation in response to changes in the cellular environment. mTOR function is elevated in the vast majority of cancers. Through CIHR funded research, we demonstrated that mTOR together with CK2, another regulatory cellular protein implicated in numerous malignancies, activates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2) by phosphorylating its eIF2B subunit. eIF2 is a pivotal translation regulator that has a crucial role to deliver the very first transfer RNA carrying amino acid methionine (initiator tRNA) during the initiation step of translation. Activation of eIF2 constitutes a previously unrecognized way of how mTOR may stimulate mRNA translation. Persistent eIF2B phosphorylation leads to increased protein synthesis, proliferation (increase in cell number) and neoplastic growth, which are all characteristics of cancer cells. column36: Pre-Existing Immunity Prior to Heparin Exposure Increases Susceptibility for Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
column37: Platelets are small cells in the blood that help control bleeding. Heparin is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used in major surgeries, such as heart surgery, and to manage heart attacks and strokes. Patients receiving heparin may have an allergic-type reaction called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Patients with HIT have low platelets (thrombocytopenia) and can develop severe clotting (gelling of blood so it no longer flows) causing loss of limbs, heart attacks, stroke and even death. So this drug (heparin), which usually helps patients, can actually cause more strokes and heart attacks in some people. HIT is a serious problem because it causes catastrophic effects in patients. The problem starts because some people develop attack proteins (antibodies) when they are given heparin. Some of these dangerous HIT antibodies attack platelets. However, other antibodies look the same but do not attack platelets. Testing if people have HIT is a major problem because most tests cannot tell the difference between the dangerous antibodies and the antibodies that do not cause HIT. Our first goal will be to find ways to determine ahead of time who will react to heparin and who will not. If we know that a patient will react to heparin, then the doctor can avoid its use. Our second goal is to understand why some patients develop HIT while others do not. We will study specific cells in patients to see if there is a change during HIT compared to the ones that do not have HIT during major heart surgery. Our group has the knowledge and the equipment to carry out all planned experiments. We are a HIT testing centre for many hospitals across Canada and we are located in an area that specializes in both heart- and blood-diseases providing us with ongoing access to patients with HIT. Once we understand why some patients get HIT and others do not, we will be able to provide better tests and better patient care while avoiding the disease.

column36: AMPK regulation of macrophage cholesterol metabolism in atherosclerosis
column37: Heart disease is a condition that affects millions of Canadians and costs the Canadian healthcare system almost 21 billion dollars annually. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of cholesterol and immune cells in the lining of the arteries (atherosclerotic plaque) and is a leading cause of heart attack and stroke. In addition to risk factors such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, the way that our body handles the build up of cholesterol in the arteries is critically important. Specialized immune cells called macrophages are able to take up and store excess cholesterol, protecting the artery wall in the process. These macrophages have specialized pathways to then transfer the cholesterol they scavenge to the circulating lipoprotein "HDL", which then carries the cholesterol to the liver, where it can be safely removed (this is why HDL-cholesterol is called the "good" cholesterol). This is known as reverse cholesterol transport. However, when this process is overwhelmed, cholesterol builds in macrophages, turning them into foam cells and causing atherosclerosis to progress. We have discovered that an important metabolic regulator called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), activates reverse cholesterol transport in macrophages, but the mechanisms involved are still unknown. The objectives of this proposal are to determine how AMPK causes this beneficial removal of cholesterol from macrophage foam cells and to test if this is enough to slow or prevent atherosclerosis. We will use genetically engineered mice that are lacking the AMPK gene, as well as therapeutic compounds that specifically activate AMPK to test our hypotheses. The goal of our research is to investigate and uncover novel mechanisms that contribute to atherosclerosis and heart disease in the hopes of developing more effective prevention and therapeutic strategies.

column36: HIV antiretroviral exposure in early pregnancy - assessing the impact on progesterone mediated decidual development and function.
column37: It is now recommended that all HIV-positive (HIV+) women take HIV medications during their pregnancy. In Canada, most HIV+ women begin HIV medications before they become pregnant or early in pregnancy. Taking HIV medications reduces the risk of HIV transmission to the baby to almost zero. However, these medications have side effects: they have been associated with a higher risk of having a miscarriage, a preterm birth, and a low birth weight baby. We don't fully understand how HIV medications cause these side effects, or which HIV medications have the fewest side effects when taken during pregnancy. Our lab discovered that some HIV medications cause the levels of progesterone, the "pregnancy hormone", to decrease in HIV+ pregnant women. Progesterone is very important in maintaining pregnancy by helping form the placenta, an organ shared by the mother and the fetus. In particular, the maternal side of the placenta, called the decidua, relies on progesterone to form properly. If progesterone levels are lowered by HIV medications, the decidua may not form properly, possibly affecting the success of the pregnancy. To examine this possibility, we will investigate how different HIV medications affect the formation and function of the decidua. We will use a test-tube model and an experimental model of pregnancy to test how HIV medications affect the growth of blood vessels in the decidua, an important developmental process to ensure that enough maternal blood is available to provide oxygen and food to the fetus. We will also use advanced imaging techniques to compare decidua blood vessels in HIV+ pregnant women on HIV medications with those from uninfected women. Finally, we will test whether supplementing with progesterone will reverse the effects of HIV medications on the decidua. Our findings will inform the selection of safer HIV medications to use in pregnancy and help identify therapies to use in combination with HIV medications to improve pregnancy outcome.

column36: Fetal Origin of Endocrine Dysfunction: The Plasticizer Model
column37: Reduced testosterone has been linked to obesity, cardiovascular diseases, erectile dysfunction and infertility. Adrenal dysfunction can lead to changes in blood pressure. Phthalate esters are used as plasticizers to add softness and flexibility to polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastics, used for a wide variety of products, including personal care products, toys, food wrappings, medical devices, and building and household products. DEHP is the most commonly used phthalate in industry. Because it is not covalently bound to the PVC polymer, it leaches into the environment and comes into contact with humans mainly through dermal exposure, oral ingestion, and inhalation. Active metabolites of DEHP are found in humans of all ages, from fetus to adulthood, and have been shown to decrease fetal testosterone production in animals. In men, there is an inverse correlation between DEHP metabolites and circulating androgen levels. In rats, fetal DEHP exposure results in reduced circulating testosterone and aldosterone levels in the adult offspring, affecting blood pressure and adipose tissue function. Recently, a new plasticizer DINCH has been introduced to replace DEHP in medical devices, toys and food packaging. Based upon preliminary data we hypothesize that in utero exposure to low doses of DEHP as well as DINCH leads to changes in testicular and adrenal function in the adult offspring, and that the altered endocrine physiology results in increased vulnerability to additional exposures to drugs and pollutants. We propose to determine the endocrine and metabolic changes occurring in adult males following in utero exposure to relevant doses of plasticizers, and to identify the mechanisms underlying long-term effects on androgen and adrenal steroids. It is critical to determine whether plasticizer exposure could be a risk factor in the origin of reproductive and metabolic disorders and identify targets for the potential pharmacological reversal of their detrimental effects.

column37: Steroid hormones are critical for the maintenance of the organism's homeostasis, adaptability to the environment, developmental and reproductive functions. Changes in the rate of steroid formation in response to genetic defects, metabolic disorders, and/or drug or environmental exposures can result in life-altering diseases. Reduced testosterone has been linked to infertility, erectile dysfunction, obesity, osteoporosis and cardiovascular diseases. Adrenal cortisol synthesis is involved in stress-response and adaptation; changes in adrenal aldosterone production can lead to changes in blood pressure and thus cardiovascular diseases. Adrenocortical tumors produce excessive amounts of cortisol, and androgen and ovarian tumors produce androgen and estrogen, all leading to endocrine disorders and potentially to pathological conditions. Changes in circulating steroids in peripheral tissues and brain have been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders. The adrenals, gonads and placenta form steroids from cholesterol. The steroids exert their functions throughout the body. Other tissues, including brain, adipose, prostate, and skin can also form steroids that fulfill local needs. For over 50 years, steroid levels have been as indicators used to diagnose various diseases, e.g. Cushing's syndrome, Addison's disease, congential adrenal hypeplasia, hypogonadism, precocious puberty, etc, and steroids have served as drugs for the treatment of endocrine, reproductive and metabolic disorders. These conditions span from early development to aging. Despite the widespread use, and abuse, of steroids, there are major gaps in our knowledge of the mechanisms regulating their production, and the effects of hormones and drugs on their synthesis and function. The goal of this project is to understand the mechanisms underlying steroid hormone biosynthesis and regulation, and thus pave the way for the development of novel pharmacological strategies to control steroid formation.

This reduces the overall inflammation in the lesion, protects against the loss of additional neurons and increases the overall rate of neurological recovery. Our goal is to advance the CD11d antibody strategy for use in human SCI or TBI clinical trials. column36: The collaborative ideal in Canadian healthcare delivery: Its rise, practice and future
column37: Collaboration is widely touted as a solution to healthcare's challenges, from fatal errors to escalating costs. Canadian governments, institutions of higher education and hospitals have acted on this rhetoric, and invested time, money and personnel resources to improve collaborative practice. Decades after the initial calls to improve care delivery through collaboration, the literature connecting these investments with positive patient care outcomes remains exceedingly sparse and inconclusive. We know that failures of collaboration and communication often harm patients, but educating providers for collaborative practice has proven to be very difficult, and rarely leads to improved patient care. The goal of this project is to draw on historical and social scientific evidence to transform how we teach healthcare professionals to collaborate. In contrast with the pre-existing literature, we see collaboration as a social construction: an idea that was championed by individuals and organizations who successfully integrated it into education and policy. This new framing will help us reach two related aims. First, it will make the development of the idea of collaboration visible through a historical case study. Second, it will allow us to document the impact of the rise of collaboration as a solution on current patient care practices. Providers will be interviewed about their views on collaborative healthcare delivery, on how collaboration has changed practices in their work environments, and on how education for collaboration could be improved. column36: Prohibitin: a circulating mitokine involved in the Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Syndrome.
column37: Patients with pulmonary hypertension (PHT; high blood pressure in the lungs) have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. These cells proliferate like cancer cells and create an obstruction of the vessels, making it difficult for the blood to go through. Their right chamber of the heart fails as it has to pump against increased pressure, causing many symptoms like shortness of breath, poor exercise capacity, and eventually death. They also have evidence of inflammation in their blood, similar to patients suffering from infections. Although we know that this inflammation is detrimental to the blood vessels and the heart, we do not know its cause in PHT. Finally, evidence of insulin resistance has been found in patients with PHT like in diabetic patients, and again without known cause. All these organs have something in common: they display the same abnormal way to produce energy (metabolism). We therefore hypothesized that factors circulating in the whole body could be responsible for this overall aberrant metabolism seen in organs otherwise unconnected. We were particularly interested in Prohibitin (PHB), a circulating factor that has been found increased in the serum of patients with cancer, another disease with multi-organ metabolism abnormalities. We propose to study the role of circulating PHB in PHT. We will determine 1) whether PHB levels are increased in the blood of humans and animal models of PHT; 2) the potential of PHB to change arterial cells' metabolism, proliferation and survival, and to induce PHT in animals; 4) the mechanisms by which circulating PHB acts; 5) whether the inhibition of these mechanisms improve PHT in human cells and animals. If this is proven to be true in humans, it will have a tremendous impact on our knowledge regarding how PHT starts and progresses and may reveal new ways to treat the disease.

column36: Lymphatic vessel function in atherosclerosis
column37: High blood cholesterol is an important risk factor of cardiovascular disease such as atherosclerosis. High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is called ''good cholesterol'' because it transports cholesterol away from tissues, such as the blood vessel walls, carrying cholesterol through the blood circulation for eventual excretion into intestines. Unfortunately, the clinical outcomes aiming at increasing levels of circulating HDL (or "good cholesterol") have not been as successful as expected, suggesting that raising HDL may not lead to an increased cholesterol clearance capacity or prevention of coronary heart disease. Expressed differently, more cargo ships (cholesterol transporter) leaving from the harbour docks (blood vessel wall), have not led to more merchandise delivered (cholesterol clearance). Thus, a better understanding of the cholesterol clearance process has become necessary to efficiently modulate the progression of atherosclerosis. In this regard, we provided unprecedented insight into the path that cholesterol trapped in peripheral tissues takes during cholesterol mobilization for eventual excretion (Martel, JCI 2013). We demonstrated that cholesterol (merchandise) gets out of tissues (harbour docks) and reaches the bloodstream (sea) by first entering so-called lymphatic vessels (canals). As the lymphatic system - lymph, from Latin lympha, meaning water - generally governs the transport of macromolecules from the tissues to the blood and, accordingly, peripheral lymph contains cholesterol transporters (HDL), a role in cholesterol transport seemed logical. Therefore, we view that improvement of the delivery efficiency would rely on enhancing the navigation conditions, instead of the number of cargo ships per se. The main objective of our emerging research team aims to understand the mechanisms connecting abnormal lymphatic function and atherosclerosis progression, to ultimately lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets.

column37: Inherited retinal degenerative diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders that are a major cause of blindness in Canada and the developed world. They are typically characterized by progressive loss in vision resulting from mutations in genes encoding proteins essential for the survival of rod and cone photoreceptor cells. Stargardt macular degeneration (STGD1) linked to mutations in the membrane transporter ABCA4 is the most common monogenic inherited retinal degenerative disease. Affected individuals typically experience loss in central vision in their first decade of life often progressing to total blindness in later years. Mutations in ABCA4 are also associated with other severe retinal diseases including retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration. My lab has shown that ABCA4 functions in the removal of vitamin A derivatives known as retinoids that are produced as part of the visual process. Disease-associated mutations cause a loss in the ability of ABCA4 to remove retinoids. As a result toxic retinoid compounds accumulate causing photoreceptor cell death and a loss in vision. The goal of this research is to further understand the molecular structure and function of ABCA4 and determine how mutations in this protein cause a loss in vision. This information together with our expertise in retinal degenerative diseases will be used to design and develop novel pharmaceutical agents (drugs) as promising treatments for STGD1. This research will increase our knowledge of the visual system and retinal degenerative diseases and lead to therapeutic treatments that will improve the health care and quality of life of individuals with STGD1 and related diseases, and reduce their economic burden on society. Our research program will also train graduate students and postdocs for future careers in basic science and translational medicine and produce new intellectual property and commercialization that will benefit Canada.

column36: Characterization and cytoskeletal regulation of nucleocytoplasmic traffic and expression of mechanosensitive transcription factors. Relevance to organ fibrosis.
column37: Organ fibrosis or progressive scarring of vital organs such as kidney, lung liver and heart is a failed healing attempt in response to chronic injury. Fibrosis is the final common pathway leading to organ failure in many common diseases including diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis and substance abuse. It is a striking but lesser known fact that fibrosis is a major component of mortality, being responsible for 45% of all deaths in the Western World. Despite its paramount medical importance, fibrosis has no cure; currently there are no means to stop or reverse the disease process and the only temporary hope is organ replacement therapy. It is therefore critically important to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the initiation and progression of organ fibrosis. Fibrosis-associated changes are brought about by altered gene expression in various cells. This is due to chemical and mechanical injury-induced activation of transcription factors. These factors need to travel to the cell's nucleus where they turn on target genes. However we do not understand how this process happens and how it can be inhibited or exploited to lessen fibrosis. Our previous work shows that cellular stress induces robust remodeling of the cell's skeleton (cytoskeleton), which may be a key regulator of the nuclear traffic of transcription factors. Therefore, the overall aim of my research is to understand the molecular and cell biological mechanisms underlying the general and cytoskeletal regulation of fibrosis-inducing transcription factors. We will use this knowledge to develop new antifibrotic molecular therapies, such as antifibrotic viruses to halt or reverse fibrosis. To achieve these goals we will create a new molecular toolkit to study and alter the traffic of transcription factors. In summary, these studies will provide fundamental insight into a new area of cell biology, and use the acquired knowledge to combat a common, currently incurable disease.

column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), or blood forming cells, are found in the adult bone marrow, where they are essential for the continuous generation of circulating blood cells, including the cells of the immune system. Their function is normally tightly regulated, and the different types of blood cells are being produced in balanced quantities. In a situation of stress, such as an acute infection, HSCs become activated and they will multiply and change the proportions of the different blood cells being produced with the goal to better respond to the infection and eliminate the infectious agent. Once the infection is resolved, the HSCs will go back to their normal, dormant state. However, it is not known what happens to the HSCs when the infectious agent cannot be eliminated. Some chronic infections lead to bone marrow failure, or the loss of new blood cell production, which can be fatal. There is very little information on how this happens or how it could be prevented. The goal of our research therefore is to better understand how HSCs react during chronic infections using two well-established mouse models. We also propose that the infectious agents (virus or parasite) may actually use the HSCs to escape the immune response by inducing the HSCs to produce one type of blood cell over another. After the completion of our studies we expect to have sufficient new information to identify new targets to treat and hopefully cure chronic viral or parasitic infections.

column37: Cardiac arrhythmias are life-threatening conditions whereby the heart beats irregularly and blood flow to the brain can be temporarily restricted. This can lead to fainting or, in worse cases, to sudden death. Knowing which type of arrhythmia someone has is absolutely key to adjust the lifestyle appropriately and to receive the proper treatment. Many arrhythmias have a clear genetic cause, and typically certain genes are linked to very specific types of arrhythmia. We know that mutations in specific genes can lead to cardiac mutations, but in most cases we don't know how. We simply know that 'somehow a mutation in gene X or Y triggers this or that particular arrhythmia'. In this project, we wish to solve this problem, by investigating the direct mechanisms of individual mutations. In particular, we will investigate several mutations in a gene known as 'CALM'. These mutations have been found in various patients worldwide that have cardiac arrhythmias. Surprisingly, depending on the exact mutation within the CALM gene, the arrhythmia is different. We wish to pinpoint exactly how each mutation works, and how it affects the electrical properties of the heart. Almost every gene in our DNA forms a code to make protein. Ultimately, it is the protein, and not the gene, that plays the actual role in our bodies. A mutation in a gene thus leads to a slightly different protein, which could then result in differences large enough to cause a serious disorder. One problem is that proteins are so small that they are hard to visualize via regular microscopy. We therefore use a highly advanced technique, known as 'X-ray crystallography', whereby we can easily see differences smaller than a 10-billionth of a meter. Here we will compare normal and diseased forms of the protein encoded by the CALM gene. This will yield important insights into the exact mechanism of the disease.

column36: Metabolic Adaptations During Breast Cancer Metastasis
column37: The ability of breast cancer cells to spread from the primary tumor to distant sites in the body, a process called metastasis, is the most deadly aspect of this disease. Recent research has focused on how cancer cells meet the energy and building block requirements needed for rapid primary tumor growth. We demonstrate that breast cancer cells increasingly rely on glycolytic metabolism as they progress from being tumorigenic to becoming highly metastatic. We hypothesize that in order for breast cancer cells to successfully metastasize, several metabolic adaptations must occur which engage different pathways in the cell. We will also address whether breast cancer cells can stimulate the production of such pro-tumorigenic metabolites from liver cells, which feed back to the tumor cells themselves. We have also identified metabolic regulators within breast cancer cells that may be targeted to reduce breast cancer metastases to the liver. Thus, this project will investigate the utility of targeting altered cancer cell metabolism as a means to impair metastasis.

column37: During pregnancy, disruption of the supply of oxygen to the baby is a common cause of injury and death. Early delivery is a treatment option, but this must be weighed against the risks of premature birth such as infection and poor organ development. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a versatile non-invasive technology which offers unprecedented possibilities for evaluating the fetal circulation. Thus, the goal of our proposal is to develop fast, motion insensitive MRI methods to reliably measure fetal blood flow and oxygen supply. This will enable scanning earlier in pregnancy, when the fetus can move more easily, and reduce the length of fetal MRI examinations. The first aims of this proposal are the technical development of fast, three-dimensional (3D) fetal MRI. These methods will provide 3D images of the fetal anatomy, blood flow, and oxygen content of blood. Initial development will be done using computer simulations and testing in non-pregnant adult volunteers. The methods will then be applied to healthy and at-risk pregnancies. column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) likely result from deregulated immune responses to the indigenous microorganisms that reside within the intestine, collectively termed the microbiota, in genetically susceptible hosts. column36: Imaging Tools for Quick and Appropriate Triage of Stroke Patients
column37: Stroke, mainly caused by a blood clot blocking a brain artery, is the leading cause of morbidity in the developed world. Removing the clot quickly saves at-risk brain tissue, improving the patient's chance of a good outcome. A current clinical method for removing blood clots is giving a drug that dissolves clot (clot-buster); however, this method only works 15-25% of the time for larger clots, and may cause bleeding into the brain in some patients. A more recent method of clot removal is to pull it out mechanically using a catheter inserted through an artery in the groin. This technique has a much higher success rate, but is only available at large hospitals and requires a talented surgeon. This procedure is therefore not available in community hospitals. When treating a patient with stroke, a community physician therefore needs to know if the clot in the patient's brain blood vessel dissolves quickly with the clot-busting drug or will the patient need to be sent to a larger hospital where the clot could be pulled out with a catheter? The community physician has to make decisions on treatment and transfer fast as every minute counts with stroke treatment. On the other hand, decisions have to be appropriate and correct, as otherwise some patients may be harmed while others who do not need the catheter-based procedure may be transferred unnecessarily to the bigger hospital. Moreover, the community physician sees a small number of patients with stroke each year and therefore lacks expertise in interpreting brain scans and making these decisions. To address this gap in expertise between large hospitals and community hospitals, we propose to develop an automated imaging-based triaging decision support tool that can help community physicians make clinical decisions on triage of patients with acute ischemic stroke at any time of the day or night quickly and correctly. We will automate many important imaging concepts we have developed until now for this purpose.

column36: Investigation of the role of HIV-Envelope specific antibody dependent innate immune cell functionality in HIV control.
column37: Antibody (Ab) molecules have an Fab region, which binds antigen specifically and an Fc region, which binds to various Fc receptors (FcR) on many types of innate immune cells. Fc-FcR interactions can activate FcR+ innate immune cells and induce anti-viral activity. Which FcR an Ab Fc region binds and the strength of the binding interaction depends on the Ab immunoglobulin class, the amino acid sequence of the Fc domain and the composition of added sugars (i.e. Fc biophysical features). These Fc features in turn determine which innate immune cells are activated for functions that can kill or clear pathogens (i.e. function). The pattern of HIV-specific Ab Fc functions and features differs in recipients of protective versus non protective HIV vaccines. Remarkably, the rare subset of HIV infected individuals, known as Elite Controllers (ECs) have patterns of Fc functions and features that differ from those seen in progressors suggesting that Ab dependent anti-HIV activity can control HIV. The proposal will investigate this hypothesis by considering the degree of HIV control as measured by HIV viral load (VL) and cellular HIV reservoir size and how these correlate with Fc dependent parameters. HIV+ ECs and those starting treatment in acute infection (AT) can achieve similarly low HIV viral loads and HIV reservoirs unlike those left untreated or who start treatment late in infection. But AT loose HIV control when treatment is stopped. We will investigate whether and which patterns of HIV-specific Ab Fc parameters distinguish EC from AT. The goal will be to better understand the link between Ab dependent activity and HIV control. The field of Ab therapeutics is developing ways to deliver and engineer Abs having desirable characteristics for particular disease outcomes. The information learned from this project will characterize the Ab Fc parameters that support HIV control thus potentially providing a benchmark for therapeutic Ab design for control of HIV infection.

column36: Elucidation of the molecular mechanisms governing currently untargeted RAS effector pathways towards novel therapeutic approaches for the most refractory human cancers
column37: Cancers are driven by abnormal changes to the genetic material of various cell types in the human body. These changes frequently result in the production of mutated proteins, or an overproduction of proteins, leading to unregulated cell growth. The protein RAS has long been recognized as a key driver of human cancers with fully 30% having mutations in RAS genes, and significantly more showing high activity of associated pathways. RAS has thus been a vitally important target for drug development, but efforts have so far proven unsuccessful. Indeed, a lack of effective therapies for RAS-driven cancers is the major reason why lung, colon, and pancreatic cancers remain the most refractory to available treatments. Improved technological approaches, however, should allow a better understanding of mutant RAS and its associated proteins, and have massively revitalized interest in developing RAS-targeted therapeutics. I have developed new methods to study RAS function, and its connections with other proteins in cells. Targeting such associations is finally proving effective in treating some cancers, yet important relationships between RAS and some partners remain completely unstudied. This includes proteins that regulate the ability of cells to move, linked to metastasis, and proteins that lead to self-directed cell death, which I believe could be exploited as a novel cancer therapy. I use leading-edge techniques such as NMR spectroscopy and X-Ray crystallography to gain insight to the structure of proteins at a molecular level, and complement these data with studies in human cells to observe how mutations lead to cellular transformation. I propose to identify and characterize new therapeutic targets in the RAS pathway, and these efforts will be complemented by the drug discovery capabilities at IRIC. These studies are highly significance to many patients, particularly those with currently untreatable cancers such as pancreatic adenocarcinomas and lung NSCLCs.

column37: End-stage kidney failure (ESKF) is common (41 931 Canadians in 2013), increasing (by 35% since 2004) and costly (>$1.3 billion/yr). A major challenge in transplantation is how to optimize anti-rejection therapy to balance the risk of rejection from under-immunosuppression against the risk of infections/cancer from over-immunosuppression. In the 1st year post-transplant, 30% patients have rejection of which 2/3 is not detected by clinical markers. We showed that urine CXCL10 detects rejection better than standard-of-care tests. Urine CCL2, CXCL10 & CXCL9 also predict late kidney transplant outcomes. Thus a secondary goal is to independently validate their performance. Early prognostic markers may be useful to identify patients at high risk of losing their transplants so they may undergo more intensive therapy and avoid minimization/withdrawal of their anti-rejection medications. This trial is the first of its kind to evaluate the impact of an early rejection marker on transplant outcomes. These new urine tests may be used to personalize medicine and improve patient and transplant outcomes. Finally, strategies that improve transplant outcomes may result in long-term health care savings.

column36: The impact of perturbations in T cell migration on the spatio-temporal dynamics of CD4 T cell homeostasis and effector cell differentiation
column37: In our global society, many of us travel to and from work, fly between cities, or even set up residence somewhere new. Along the way, we might bump into others, exchange information, and learn new things that inform our behaviour. Hence, what we learn during our travels can have a dramatic impact on our lives. T lymphocytes have a similarly cosmopolitan lifestyle within the body. The job of T cells in the immune system - to detect and stop the replication of a pathogen or cancer cell as quickly as possible - makes it essential for them to commute continuously between the blood and secondary lymphoid organs. Within lymphoid organs, T cells make critical interactions with other cells that dictate their function and fate. During infections, such interactions can license them to enter tissues and even set up residence there, protecting from reinfection. To understand the implications of the jet-setting behaviour of T cells on their function, we use advanced microscopy to track their movements within tissues in real time. This approach enables us to investigate a number of important questions. How do the interactions T cells make with other cells keep them alive? Why do pathogens or gene defects that prevent migration lead paradoxically both to severe immune deficiencies and to immune-mediated disease? In the long-term, answers to these questions will contribute to the design of better therapies for immunological diseases, such as allergy and autoimmunity, and allow us to harness the function of T cells to improve our ability to treat or prevent infections, from Ebola virus to HIV and beyond.

column36: The Influence of Acute Bouts of Aerobic Exercise on Neuroplasticity and Motor Learning after Stroke
column37: Recovery from stroke is most often incomplete and requires large amounts of practice that are expensive and often not feasible. Because of this it is important to develop new ways to speed learning after stroke. One approach that is promising is to prepare or "prime" the brain for learning by pairing exercise with skilled practice of movement tasks. Past work showed that pairing single sessions of exercise with skilled motor practice enhances learning. Our work demonstrated that the short bout of exercise primes or prepares the brain for learning by lessening inhibition which then facilitates brain plasticity. However this intervention has only been tested in healthy controls. Further, at this time we have only tested single sessions that pair a short bout of priming exercise with skilled practice. As such we do not know what the effect of multiple sessions that pair priming exercise with skilled practice would be on motor learning. The present study is designed to test the effects of priming exercise on motor learning as an intervention that is designed to enhance motor learning after stroke. This is important as such an intervention could be used to enhance the effects of rehabilitation after stroke. In total we will test two main aims: 1)We will determine if the effect of priming exercise is to lessen inhibition in the brain after stroke. 2)We will deliver repeated sessions of priming exercise paired with skilled motor practice to see if compared to a group who rests before motor practice, the exercise group shows greater learning. Our data will illustrate a new way by which learning could be enhanced after stroke. Exercise could easily be incorporated into rehabilitation settings. As such our findings can be rapidly translated to the clinical setting to promote the recovery of Canadians with stroke.

column37: How is it that 10-15% of school children end up with mental health problems? We know that most of these children showed early signs in preschool, and many risk factors were evident in the perinatal period. Some suggest that the challenges of having to rapidly adapt to a more structured and demanding environment such as formal school will be very stressful for vulnerable children, depending on the support they will receive from family and school environments. Further, a mismatch between child and environment could not only worsen symptoms to the status of disorders, but also spill over into additional problems.
