Taking all of this into account would allow prevention science to be informed about opportunities to intervene between pregnancy and grade 2. column37: COMPASS is the world's largest and most comprehensive longitudinal school-based primary prevention project. The purpose of this proposal is to extend COMPASS for an additional 5 years (2017-2021). Each year, COMPASS collects longitudinal data from ~45,000 grade 9 to 12 students attending 89 secondary schools in Ontario and Alberta. The purpose is to evaluate how ongoing real-world changes in programs, policies, or built environment resources within or surrounding schools are related to changes in youth risk factors [tobacco use (including e-cigarettes), obesity, poor diet, physical inactivity, screen time, alcohol use, marijuana use, bullying] over time. First, maintaining this internationally unique study is critical as it is just now starting to provide sufficient waves of longitudinal data to generate scientifically robust evidence of what programs or policies work over time to help prevent chronic disease related behaviour among youth. Second, by building on the existing research infrastructure, we are saving valuable prevention resources, especially when COMPASS is the only study that can: -evaluate the 100's of changes that occur in COMPASS schools annually, -evaluate the impact of emerging provincial prevention initiatives (e.g., the Healthy Kids Community Challenge or the Smoke-free Ontario Strategy), or -explore how changes to federal policies (e.g., the potential legalization of marijuana in Canada or changes to e-cigarette product regulations) impact youth behaviour over time.

column36: Promoting neurovascular recovery following focal ischemic stroke
column37: In the healthy brain, neurons, glia, and vessels work in concert so that blood flow adjusts in proportion to the level of neuronal activity. In stroke, a blockage of a major artery results in a sharp decline in blood flow, damaging the neurons and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. If the blood clot is dissolved rapidly, a complete recovery is possible. However, because the currently available treatments are safe and effective only when applied rapidly following the stroke onset, only ~10% of patients receive them; most suffer significant disabilities, and up to a third are institutionalized. Uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes needed for full recovery of brain function is a major factor preventing the development of more widely applicable therapies. It has become clear that recovery is strongly affected by changes that occur in the neurons, glia and blood vessels in the peri-infarct zone, the impaired, but potentially salvageable brain region surrounding the site of stroke. Using advanced imaging in live rats, we will track the function of peri-infarct neurons, glia, and vessels in the weeks following stroke. We will treat the animals with specific drugs, delivered directly to the perilesional tissue, to raise the activity of the surviving neurons while providing them with increased metabolic support, so as to bolster the remapping of lost function to these neurons. We will develop these interventions first in the young rats and then tailor them to the middle-aged rats suffering from metabolic syndrome (e.g. high cholesterol, diabetes) that are common in humans and known to impede stroke recovery. These experiments will establish the ways by which brain functioning can be affected in the chronic stage of stroke so as to improve recovery. The insights obtained will spur the development of new treatments that are effective in the chronic stage following stroke and thus stand to benefit the vast majority of patients.

column36: Cannabis smoking and psychotic experiences in adolescents: A longitudinal brain Imaging study
column37: Cannabis smoking increases the risk for psychosis. Although the effects are small at the population level, growing evidence indicates that they are large in those with premorbid vulnerabilities and those who initiate cannabis use in early adolescence. What remain unclear are the biological mechanisms involved. Important clues are provided by the core characteristics of schizophrenia. Indeed, schizophrenia is associated with aberrant emotion processing, a disturbed sense of self and deficits in working memory. In schizophrenia patients and young adults at risk for psychosis, functional imaging studies show that the neural pathways underlying these functions are impaired. Notably, cannabis smoking impairs these brain networks, indicating that there is a significant overlap between the neural effects of cannabis and the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Despite this, no functional imaging study has examined the neural effects of cannabis smoking in psychosis-prone adolescents. Here, we propose to perform a 3-year longitudinal neuroimaging study examining the neural effects of cannabis smoking in psychosis-prone adolescents using tasks assessing emotional processing, self-reflection and executive function. We hypothesize that "at risk" adolescents will have impairments in the targeted neural pathways, which will be further impaired by the growth in cannabis use during adolescence. The project will be embedded in an ongoing 5-year clinical study involving 3850 adolescents, providing the unique opportunity to recruit an uncommon though vulnerable group of teenagers. The current study will shed new light on the mechanisms underlying the cannabis-psychosis association. Such inquiry is of the utmost importance given that cannabis use is highly prevalent in Canada and schizophrenia is one of the top 10 causes of disability. column36: Contribution of circulating microRNAs to the etiology of vascular disease
column37: Heart diseases (including atherosclerosis) are a major cause of death and debilitation in Canada. Atherosclerosis results from blocked blood flow to the heart muscle due to the thickening of the vessel wall by the growth of a plaque, which mostly contains inflammatory white blood cells. During the early stages of disease, the cells lining blood vessels (endothelial cells) send signals to inflammatory cells in the blood to enter the wall of the blood vessel. In advanced stages plaques can burst, resulting in heart attack or stroke. It would benefit patients if we had a better way to diagnose heart disease at early stages and if we could determine the best treatment for a particular patient. This may be achieved by measuring biomarkers, which indicate aspects of the disease that are not easily seen by a doctor. It has been found that small nucleic acids known as microRNAs are found in the blood and the level of particular microRNAs may be useful as biomarkers for heart disease. We have found that endothelial cells secrete microRNAs into the blood, which can be taken up by inflammatory white blood cells. This microRNA uptake decreases the ability of monocytes to enter the vessel wall and produce plaques. Our proposal will test whether this communication between endothelial cells and inflammatory cells is disrupted during the development of heart disease. We will also measure differences in the types of microRNAs that are transferred between these cells during disease. While certain types of microRNAs are beneficial in health, the microRNAs present during heart disease may have damaging effects and actually promote atherosclerosis. Finally, we will develop methods to deliver helpful microRNAs to inflammatory cells to prevent these cells from forming an atherosclerotic plaque. Our studies will provide important new insight into the diagnosis and treatment of heart disease.

column36: Predicting the impact of mutations in intrinsically disordered regions
column37: Current "personalized medicine" projects are identifying all the mutations in every patient, and we need to know which of those mutations are likely to cause diseases. About 1/5 of known disease mutations occur in enigmatic protein regions known as intrinsically disordered regions. When we discover new mutations in disordered regions, we currently can't tell which are harmful (drivers of disease) and which ones are benign (bystanders). Evolutionary analysis can point to biological function because functional sequences are preferentially preserved during evolution. If mutations in disordered regions disrupt features of disordered regions that have been preserved over evolutionary time, we predict that these are more likely to affect function and cause disease. Based on this principle, we propose to develop new bioinformatics to better predict the impact of mutations in disordered regions. To understand why disrupting the conserved features is harmful, we will test the impact of engineered mutations in yeast cells, because they are simpler and easier to study than human cells. In the end, we hope to develop better methods to predict the impact of mutations in disordered regions, and also understand why the mutations in these regions lead to disease.

column36: Role of TDAG51 in vascular calcification associated with chronic renal disease
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the major cause of death in patients suffering from chronic kidney disease (CKD). column36: Interfering with HIV persistence in CD4+ T cells during antiretroviral therapy
column37: HIV/AIDS continues to impact the health of millions of people worldwide. Advances in the treatment of HIV infection have dramatically reduced the death rate from AIDS and improved the quality of life of many HIV-infected patients. Despite this unquestioned success, effective therapy does not eradicate HIV and requires life-long adherence. In addition, the possible long-term toxicity associated with antiretroviral therapy (ART), resistance, stigma and cost all contribute to the necessity of finding a cure. In infected individuals taking ART, HIV persists in a small number of cells that can survive for the lifetime of the infected host. This pool of persistently infected cells, usually referred as the "reservoir for HIV infection", is the main barrier to HIV eradication. The overarching goal of this project is to develop therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing the size of the reservoir, with the ultimate objective of finding a cure for HIV infection. Multiple gaps still exist in our understanding of the basic mechanisms involved in the maintenance of the HIV reservoir. We propose to identify the cells in which HIV persists in the blood and tissues (such as the gut) of HIV-infected individuals taking ART. We will isolate the cells carrying HIV from these anatomical reservoirs. This will allow us to characterize the mechanisms by which HIV is able to persist in these cells. We will then test the ability of several drugs at interfering with HIV persistence in these cells and identify combinations that will lead to the death of the reservoir cells. Our goal is to identify a combination of drugs that can eliminate all latently infected cells in HIV-infected individuals. The results from these studies will constitute the basis for the design of a clinical trial aimed at eradicating HIV.

column36: Preclinical approach to improve testing of immuno-oncology combination therapies for early or late stage metastatic disease
column37: The proposed Project Scheme has two major complementary aims. One is designed to leverage what is the most promising development in cancer therapy since the discovery of chemotherapy: the impact of new drugs which harness the body's immune system ability to fight cancer. The other is to develop improved mouse cancer models to better predict the clinical impact of immune therapy drugs when used in combination with other selected therapies to treat early or late stage distant metastatic disease. These other therapies are antiangiogenic drugs which target a tumor's blood supply, or chemotherapy given in a less toxic, continuous low dose ('metronomic') manner. The overall rationale is twofold. First, while the clinical impact of new immune therapies is remarkable, only a minor subset of patients (eg. 10-15%) derive dramatic benefits. So strategies are needed to improve these figures, e.g. to combine immunotherapy drugs creating 'cocktails' with different anti-cancer drugs - especially those where there is a sound underlying rationale. Second, initial assessment of new therapies is almost always done in mice - usually by treating localized 'primary' tumors - an approach historically poor in predicting what later happens in patients with distant metastatic disease. Dr. Kerbel's lab instead has focused on the development of postsurgical models of metastatic disease of different cancers to model "adjuvant" antiangiogenic drug or chemotherapy treatment of either early stage or advanced metastatic disease. His results have helped contribute to the initiation of phase II and III clinical trials, a number of which have now shown positive results. However, the models - which have been distributed to numerous investigators around the world - involve growth of human tumors in immune suppressed mice. This does not allow testing of immune therapy. So the next step is to develop a similar resource using immune competent mice for studying promising combination based immunotherapies.

column36: Understanding and harnessing the therapeutic potential of VISTA: a PD-1-like negative immune checkpoint regulator
column37: Activating or dampening immune responses are events that are triggered by the binding of co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory molecular partners expressed on T cells, antigen-presenting cells and cancer cells. The uncontrolled activation of immune responses can manifest itself as inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease. In contrast, the suppression of immune responses directed at tumor cells reflects the fact that such cells are perceived as being normal cells by presenting a complement of "self antigens", allowing cancer cells to growth in an uncontrolled fashion. Altering the interaction of co-inhibitory molecules with their respective ligands [immune checkpoint pairs such as PD-1:PD-L1 and CD200:CD200R1] can be used to re-tune immune responses. For instance, clinical trials have recently demonstrated that blocking the binding of PD-1 to PD-L1 with either anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies represents a powerful way of restoring immune responses for treating late stage patients with melanoma and other cancers. Dampening inflammatory responses can also be achieved by using for instance CD200Fc or agonists of its receptor CD200R1 present on immune cells. We have found that VISTA, a newly identified immune checkpoint regulator, can be engineered to act as a powerful anti-inflammatory agent. Here, we propose to identify VISTA's receptor on T cells and cancer cells. Another aim is to evaluate the anti-inflammatory properties of our designed VISTA homolog in several mouse models of inflammation. Finally, we also plan to generate VISTA blockers that will be evaluated in tumor models as agents able to restore immune responses against tumor cells. This proposal will open-up a new area of research in immunotherapy leading to tailored VISTA-blocking agents to treat cancer patients as well as VISTA-like molecules to reduce inflammatory responses in patients with acute and chronic inflammatory diseases.

column36: Oscillatory mechanisms of sensorimotor integration
column37: Vision is of primary importance to humans, and yet we only see things clearly when we look directly at them. We therefore need to move our eyes to gather information about our surroundings. Although we are mostly unaware of these eye movements, they occur with great frequency - most people make around three eye movements per second. Interestingly, these eye movements occur at regular intervals, as if the eyes are following a rhythm. Moreover, the rhythmic nature of eye movements appears to be related to rhythmic electrical signals in the brain, which oscillate at particular frequencies. In this research, we will determine how oscillating activity in the brain is related to the rhythms of visual exploration during eye movements. We will use this oscillating activity as a means of studying key brain circuits responsible for vision and its interaction with other functions, such as memory and attention. Because these functions are known to be impaired in certain mental disorders, we will develop animal models to pinpoint the precise nature of these impairments, with the goal of informing future diagnostic and treatment protocols.

column36: The Health Effects of Prenatal Maternal Stress from the 1998 Quebec Ice Storm
column37: Background. Many studies show that a major stress in pregnancy has negative effects on the unborn child's cognitive and health outcomes. However, those studies have a variety of weaknesses, mostly because researchers cannot randomly assign pregnant women to experience stress. But disasters can. We began Project Ice Storm soon after freezing rain in January 1998 knocked out power in southern Quebec for >3 million people. We recruited women who had been pregnant during the storm and assessed their stress levels. Over the past 17 years we have observed persistent effects of that stress on their children's cognitive development, metabolic, immune and mental health. Although Project Ice Storm shows strong effects of stress in pregnancy, we cannot make conclusions about effects of the storm on the population because we have no unaffected control group, our participants are mostly upper class, and the sample size is relatively small. Objectives. Our goal is to determine the magnitude of the effects of the ice storm on the health of the unborn children from the hardest hit region. We will then estimate the economic impact of the storm on the province's children who were born in 1998. Methods. We will compare population data from three Quebec regions: one that was hard hit by the ice storm, and two others that were untouched. Health outcomes will be compared between youth born in 1998 and those born in the 3 years before and 3 years after 1998. We will obtain data on birth outcomes, health diagnoses and prescriptions, and educational testing from provincial administrative data. Importance. Although the US public health and safety agencies have procedures for protecting pregnant women during disasters, Canada does not. This study will provide the Canadian evidence needed to lobby for greater recognition of pregnant women and their unborn children as vulnerable populations during disasters, and justify providing specific care that will protect their unborn children.

Finally, we will determine how inflammation changes with time and disease progression in blood and cerebrospinal fluid of people at high risk of developing the disease, such as individuals with a family history of AD and Down syndrome sufferers. column36: The unrecognized importance of smooth muscle foam cells in atherosclerosis development and treatment
column37: Heart attacks and strokes are caused by a buildup of fats, including cholesterol, as well as inflammation in arteries. This buildup is known as atherosclerosis. These diseases are the leading cause of death and decreased quality of life in Canada and worldwide, as well as an enormous economic burden on the healthcare system. Until now it was assumed that most of the cholesterol that builds up in coronary and other arteries occurs in a type of white blood cell called macrophages. However, recently while studying human hearts donated by people having a heart transplant, we discovered that the majority of cells that accumulate excess cholesterol in human coronary arteries are actually smooth muscle cells. These cells were already known to be the main cell type in the 'plaques' that build up in arteries, but their importance as the main place cholesterol deposits had never been recognized until now. This information provides a whole new way of looking at how atherosclerosis develops, and how to design new treatments to reduce the death-toll and poor quality of life it causes. The goals of this research are to understand: 1) the exact contribution of smooth muscle cells to total cholesterol overload in plaques; 2) whether mouse models used to study atherosclerosis have the same buildup of cholesterol in smooth muscle cells as humans and are therefore good models to study this problem; 3) what the reasons are for the loss of a key cholesterol exporter that we also discovered in the plaque smooth muscle cells; and 4) how to overcome this cholesterol accumulation problem in these cells, either by increasing this exporter or by bypassing it to get the cholesterol out of the cells. Our recent findings are groundbreaking, and the results of this further research stand to revolutionize how we prevent heart disease and stroke, for the benefit of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: Translation reading frame selection directed by a viral internal ribosome entry site
column37: All viruses go through an important stage during their life cycle called translation where viral proteins are synthesized from a viral RNA. Some viruses such as poliovirus and Hepatitis C virus use a translation mechanism called an Internal Ribosome Entry Site or IRES for expressing their proteins. This IRES mechanism is not only important for viruses but also for cellular genes, including those involved in cancer. Therefore, elucidating IRES mechanisms is crucial for understanding a fundamental process of gene expression. Currently, IRES mechanisms are poorly understood. To gain insight, we will characterize a novel IRES mechanism found in an insect virus, called the Cricket Paralysis virus. Using biochemical techniques, we will identify how this IRES interacts with and hijacks the host cell's machinery. Furthermore, we found that this IRES can direct translation of two overlapping genes thus producing a hidden viral protein. We will explore how this novel mechanism increases the coding capacity of a viral genome (recoding) using a combination of biochemical, molecular and virological approaches. Numerous viruses such as HIV and coronavirus (i.e. SARS) use recoding mechanisms to expand coding capacity. Thus, this proposal will not only shed light into the biochemical mechanisms underlying this novel viral IRES recoding mechanism but also provide a unique and powerful model for understanding how other viral IRES and recoding mechanisms work. Understanding these fundamental mechanisms are important for human health; it provides a framework for understanding viruses that infect humans and gains useful knowledge that may reveal novel targets for antiviral therapy.

column36: From Birth to Adulthood: The Risk and Protective Factors Leading to Mental Health Problems (MHPs) in a Representative Population Sample.
column37: While physical illnesses account for most of the social and economical burden among adults, Mental Health Problems (MHPs) are the first cause of disability among youths (18-25 years). Youth with MHPs such as substance abuse, antisocial behaviour, and depression are at high risk for school failure, unemployment and continued mental health problems. Our goal is to generate knowledge to improve the prevention of the heavy social, personal and economic burden of MHPs. Research on MHPs indicates that many MHPs have roots early in life and persist across the lifespan. Therefore, risk factors for MHPs should be studied from early childhood onwards. In addition, although poverty or coercive parenting are important risk factors for MHPs, most children exposed to such risks do not develop MHPs. Finally, some children benefit from receiving psychosocial services to prevent MHPs, while others do not. To better understand the interplay between risk factors and improve the effectiveness of preventive efforts, we need to understand the sequence of risk factors for adult MHPs as they unfold between birth and adulthood, as well as the reasons for the wide variations in responses to risks or services. Our objectives are to identify 1) which risk factors for adult MHPs emerge at which point in time, and how they co-develop over the life course, 2) for whom environmental factors are more likely to lead to MHPs, and 3) for whom the use of childhood psychosocial services can be most beneficial. In order to do so, we will assess MHPs at age 20 years (2017) in a uniquely well-documented Canadian population-based cohort (n=1979) assessed repeatedly since birth. Importance. This research will provide information on 'for whom' childhood risk factors lead to MHPs and 'for whom' psychosocial services are most beneficial. Because this project will collect reliable and clinically relevant data on MHPs in a Canadian cohort studied extensively since birth, the return on investment will be high.

column36: Hypertensive heart disease is regulated by distinct cardiac macrophage lineages controlled by the Renin-Angiotensin System
column37: High blood pressure causes hypertensive heart disease, which is one of the 10 leading causes of death worldwide despite significant investment in medical therapies. In animal studies, our group has made two important new findings that may help explain how the heart is injured by hypertension. First, we have shown that during hypertensive episodes, there is a rapid increase in the number of immune cells called macrophages in the heart. Importantly, this increase is made up of two types of macrophages. 1) Traditional macrophages produced from the bone marrow enter the heart from the blood and 2) Importantly, we have discovered macrophages that first entered the heart during embryonic development, and their progeny continue live within the heart of adults - this MF group also increases in number. The heart then becomes stiff and fibrotic, causing symptoms of heart failure. If all macrophages are removed, fibrosis is improved, however at the same time, heart contraction can be impaired leading to severe heart failure and death. We believe recruited macrophages that enter the heart cause damage, while embryonic derived cardiac macrophages are protective. Our second major finding is that we have shown that certain neurohormones control both macrophage types, and if we manipulate these neurohormonal pathways, we can decrease influx of macrophages that cause tissue damage, and promote growth of macrophages that prevent hypertensive heart disease. Our research will determine the exact role of individual macrophage types during hypertension, and how they are controlled by neurohormonal pathways ACE2 / AngII.

column36: Control of ER-mitochondria contacts and mitophagy by the Gp78 ubiquitin ligase: Role in tumor progression
column37: Select breast cancers and certain other cancers are difficult to treat, resulting in devastating prognostic outcomes. Autocrine motility factor (AMF) and its receptor, Gp78 (also known as AMFR), are linked to malignancy in various cancers. However, Gp78 has recently been shown to prevent cancer formation. Gp78 is found both at the cell surface, where it binds and internalizes AMF from outside the cell, and inside the cell in the endoplasmic reticulum, where it targets proteins for degradation. Our work has defined novel mechanisms by which Gp78 and AMF control interaction of the endoplasmic reticulum with mitochondria, the energy producing organelle of the cell. These interactions control the movement and destruction of mitochondria and limit the production by damaged mitochondria of toxic chemicals that contribute to cancer progression. Further, interaction between ER and mitochondria play important roles in cell death. We propose that by preventing Gp78 proximity to mitochondria, AMF controls whether or not Gp78 prevents cancer formation. We will now study how AMF controls Gp78 localization to the mitochondria-associated ER and how it impacts Gp78 function in breast and other cancers, i.e. whether Gp78 prevents tumor formation or rather drives tumor malignancy. Our proposed mechanism of AMF control of Gp78 function in the endoplasmic reticulum is quite novel and suggests that targeting AMF outside the cell will induce Gp78 tumor suppressor activity. Once validated, these studies will lead to the development of specific therapeutics to prevent AMF control of Gp78. We expect our knowledge translation approach will enable new mechanistic understandings leading to new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to better treat these potentially terminal cancers and provide better prognoses for cancer patients.

column36: Deciphering the mechanisms underlying synaptic dysfunction at the neuromuscular junction in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder caused by progressive dysfunction, and later death, of motoneurons innervating skeletal muscle fibers. MNs are the part of the nervous system that control muscles involved in movements such as walking and breathing. They do so because they physically contact muscles where they signal them to contract by releasing a chemical at a site on the muscle known as the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). As the disease progresses, connections between the nervous system and muscles become fewer causing the muscle to become progressively weaker to a point where they are paralyzed. Patients usually succumb to ALS within 2-3 years of diagnosis as a result of an inability to control respiratory functions such as coughing and breathing. There is no cure for ALS and treatment options are limited. ALS occurs sporadically, with no known cause, in 90% of the cases. The other 10% are caused by genetic mutations. Despite this diversity, one of the shared features of the disease is the progressive withdrawal of the motoneurons from the NMJ prior to cell death. This withdrawal speeds up the rate of paralysis and contributes to MN death. This proposal will examine why motoneurons withdraw from the NMJ in ALS. We will combine mouse genetics with electrophysiological, anatomical, biochemical and behavioral techniques to examine whether a group of proteins known BMPs are involved in stabilizing the NMJ in mice (similar proteins are well known to stabilize the NMJ in fruit flies). Furthermore, we will examine how BMPs are misregulated in ALS mice in order to determine how this misregulation affects disease progression. Ultimately, we believe that results will provide a foundation of knowledge to later develop pharmacological interventions that will stabilize the connections between motoneurons and muscle in ALS and thus improve muscle strength and quality of life for those living with the disease.

column36: Study of pathogenesis and reversibility of central and peripheral airway remodeling in an equine model of asthma
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic inflammatory disease of the respiratory tract worldwide, and 5-10% of patients are severely affected and poorly responsive to current medications. Among those, patients with neutrophilic lung inflammation represent a major health concern has they require high healthcare costs due to the severity of the disease and the poor response to therapy. The severity of asthma is considered to be a consequence of ongoing damage (remodeling) to the lungs. However, currently, the causes, functional consequences, and the possible reversibility of remodeling remain poorly characterized. This is primarily due to ethical considerations limiting lung biopsies in patients, particularly of the peripheral airways, due to their invasiveness. Thus, the study of airway remodeling in animal models of asthma is critical in better understanding the disease and developing effective therapy. The aim of the proposed research program is to investigate the contribution of neutrophilic inflammation to airway remodeling of the central and peripheral asthmatic airways, and their response to therapy with macrolides, a class of antibiotics that has been used to treat neutrophilic asthma, due to their anti-inflammatory properties. Horses, similarly to humans, spontaneously develop a condition (equine asthma) that has most of the clinical, functional, and remodeling features of human asthma. Using this unique animal disease, combined with cell culture, a novel tissue engineered 3D bronchus, and decellularized asthmatic and healthy airways, we will investigate the cells and the signaling pathways contributing to airway remodeling and response to therapy in the asthmatic lung. The proposed research will substantially advance knowledge of the role of neutrophils in asthma, the signaling pathways contributing to the airway remodeling in neutrophilic asthma, and the efficacy of macrolides at controlling airway neutrophilic inflammation and reversing remodeling.

column36: Targeting Triple Negative Breast Cancer: Role of KISS1R
column37: Breast cancer, the most common cancer among Canadian women killed 5000 women last year. In particular, triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) represents 15-20% of all breast cancers that occurs commonly in younger women (<50 yrs of age). TNBC remains the most difficult subtype of breast cancer to treat. TNBC tumors are defined by a lack of estrogen receptor (ERalpha), progesterone receptor and human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2, aka ErbB2) and so TNBC patients do not benefit from drugs used to treat other breast cancer subtypes, that target hormone receptors or HER2. TNBC patients have poor prognosis and are typically high grade and metastatic. Additionally, drug resistance to chemotherapeutics is a major problem in TNBC. Thus, an urgent need remains to identify new molecular targets for effective treatment in TNBC. We have found that in TNBC cells, kisspeptins (KPs) promote TNBC cell invasion. KPs are blood-borne secreted peptides that signal upon binding receptor proteins called KISS1R, that are highly expressed in TNBC cells, compared to normal breast cells. We found that the gene that codes for KPs (called KISS1) is highly expressed in TNBC primary tumors. The proposed work will determine whether plasma KP levels increase in TNBC patients compared to healthy patients, thus potentially identifying a prognostic biomarker for disease progression. We will determine whether KISS1R protein levels are higher in TNBC primary tumors, compared to normal breast. Our new data indicates that KISS1R signaling confers drug resistance to chemotherapeutics. Using various models (cells, pre-clinical animal and clinical samples), we will determine whether targeting KISS1R inhibits metastasis and drug resistance, and the underlying mechanisms by which this occurs. Thus, our 'bench to bedside' studies may identify KISS1R as a novel anti-cancer drug, targeting of which will inhibit metastasis and improve the effectiveness of chemotherapy that TNBC patients currently receive.

column36: Cerebral cortical neural mechanisms for feedback vs feedforward contributions to motor skill learning
column37: When our arm is perturbed by an external force or obstacle during a movement, the brain possesses neural circuits that rapidly detect the error and make a corrective adjustment to complete the movement as intended. This is called feedback control. If the same perturbation occurs repeatedly, the brain gradually learns to anticipate the effect of the perturbation and adjusts the motor command for the next movement to reduce its effect. This is called predictive feedforward control. Similarly, when we try to learn a new motor skill, we make many mistakes at first but gradually reduce our errors as our skill improves. Motor control theory had long proposed that the errors sensed by feedback circuits were used to "teach" the feedforward neural circuits that plan and execute movements what to learn and how, but the feedback circuits did not change. As the feedforward circuits changed, errors decreased and the motor system increasingly functioned in feedforward mode. However, a recent study found that both feedback and feedforward circuits change while subjects learn to compensate for external force fields; they collaborate as partners during both motor learning and skilled performance, rather than only as teacher and student. This project studies the neural mechanisms in motor cortical areas of non-human primates that play a key role in detecting and correcting errors while learning a new skill, and cause adaptive changes both in the feedback and feedforward circuits to permit skilled motor performance. A better understanding of how the cortical motor system learns new skills will help in the development of new rehabilitation procedures for patients with motor control deficits. It will also lead to improved design of neuroprosthetic controllers that use neural signals about desired movements recorded in the brains of paralyzed patients to control robotic devices, thereby greatly improving their independence and quality of life.

column36: Zika virus biology, diagnostics and therapeutic approaches
column37: Zika virus (ZV) is an emerging pathogen that is transmitted by mosquitoes. Until recently, circulation of this virus was limited to Africa and Asia. However, in 2015, a large ZV outbreak occurred in Brazil followed by rapid spreading throughout South and Central America reaching Mexico by years end. Infections can be subclinical but often flu-like symptoms, conjunctivitis, arthralgia and neurological disorders (Guillain-Barre syndrome) can also occur. In addition, the virus may cross the placenta to infect the brains of fetuses resulting in severe neurological damage, microcephaly and death. Indeed, during the ZV outbreak in Brazil, a 2700% increase in cases of microcephaly was observed. Currently, the Centers for Disease Control is advising pregnant women not travel to 22 Latin American countries including Brazil. With millions of new ZV infections and thousands of babies being born with microcephaly, there is an urgent need for effective therapeutics and vaccines. As outbreaks were relatively rare until recently, research on ZV has been limited and no molecular tools or animal models exist to study this virus. We will develop the necessary reagents and models to study ZV. In turn, these tools will be used to screen for and design therapeutic molecules that block transmission of the virus.

column36: Cancer target discovery and validation in the stromal phospho-proteome
column37: Every year, worldwide and in Canada, lung cancer kills more men and women than any other cancer. Lung cancer cells in tumours can only grow and survive when supported by surrounding "stroma" cells. column36: Understanding and exploiting lysine polyphosphorylation as a new post-translational modification regulating cell growth
column37: Background: Essential processes in our cells are controlled by molecules called proteins, which are comprised of individual building blocks called amino acids. These can be modified by chemicals in the cell in different ways that tell a protein what to do and when to do it. We can think of these modifications as sets of instructions. For example, instructions might tell a protein to promote cell growth or, in other circumstances, to repair damaged DNA. Project Goals: The overarching goal of this project is to determine the function of a brand new and poorly understood chemical modification called polyphosphorylation. As their name suggests, polyphosphates are long chains of individual molecules called phosphates, which cells use in a number of metabolic processes to keep us healthy. A recent study made the surprising but fascinating observation that these chains can be attached to amino acids in proteins to regulate their functions. Our own work suggests that they serve as instructions to a set of proteins that are essential for cell growth. Project Objectives: In this project we will first determine if polyphosphorylation is an important regulator of cell growth using a combination of directed experiments and cutting-edge genetic analyses. We will then use novel protein analysis tools to determine how polyphosphate chains instruct proteins on what to do. Project Outputs: The major outputs of the project will be the identification of new targets and pathways regulated by polyphosphorylation, and mechanistic insights on how polyphosphorylation impacts protein localization, stability and interaction with other constituents of the cell. Health Impact: Since cell growth is required for tumour formation, understanding polyphosphorylation will afford us new opportunities to treat cancer. Our long-term vision is to re-establish control over processes gone awry in cancer cells by artificially modulating the length of polyphosphate chains on modified proteins.

column36: Primitive cardiac macrophages and their reparative role following ischemic injury
column37: Heart attacks represent the leading cause of death worldwide, including in Canada. The immune system plays a major role in both the initial injury that occurs after a heart attack, but also how the heart repairs itself after injury. One critical problem in the field is that we do not know what exact immune cells reside in heart, nor do we understand what their role is after a heart attack. We have found that the heart contains multiple new immune cell subsets called macrophages, which have never been discovered before. For the last 50 years, scientists have always thought immune cells in the body are produced from stem cells in the bone marrow. Our new work has shown that some immune cells called macrophages come from very early during embryonic development prior to birth, and those primitive macrophages continue to live in the heart into adulthood. Alternatively, other heart macrophages are constantly replaced from the bone marrow. Our preliminary results suggest these different macrophage types possess different functions, where primitive macrophages improve tissue healing while the bone marrow macrophages promote tissue damage. We will specifically test if primitive embryonic macrophages promote tissue repair following a heart attack in animal studies.

column36: Functional and evolutionary dissection of vascular endothelial cell responses to Inflammation
column37: The cardiovascular system is composed of a network of arteries, veins and capillaries. These blood vessels deliver oxygen and nutrients to the body and are the main communication channel that connects the heart, the brain and other vital organs. The cells that form their inner lining, known as endothelial cells (ECs), are vital to maintain health. They can detect danger signals in the blood. When they do, they become inflamed. For example, ECs react to infection and to risk factors for cardiovascular disease such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol. In fact, one of the root causes of cardiovascular disease is EC inflammation. Inflammation results in build up of plaque in arteries of the heart, a disease known as atherosclerosis. When plaques rupture, blood clots can form and block the flow of blood to the heart and brain, resulting in heart attack and stroke, respectively. During the inflammatory response the cell orchestrates the expression of a network of genes. To identify and inform people who have genetic risk factors for cardiovascular disease, we need to find the DNA sequences that control when, where and how much of these genes are made by ECs in response to inflammation. In this project, we will find the DNA sequences that control inflammatory genes in ECs obtained from the hearts of humans and other species. In order to catch regulatory DNA in action, we will treat these ECs with substances that cause inflammation. A necessary second objective of this study is to find the regulatory DNA that is the most important for disease. To do this we will look for regulatory DNA in ECs that is activated in a mouse that rapidly develops heart disease (atherosclerosis) when fed a high cholesterol diet. Finding regulatory regions that are activated by heart disease in the mouse will help us find the regions of DNA that are important for human atherosclerosis and other diseases involving cardiovascular inflammation.

column36: Chromosome 16q, a Cancer Suppressor Chromosome Arm
column37: Patients with estrogen receptor positive (ER+) breast cancer (BC), including those with lobular tumors, show a relatively good prognosis on the five-year horizon. However, unlike triple negative breast cancer (estrogen receptor negative, progesterone receptor negative and Her2 negative, aka TNBC), which is typically either lethal or cured within five years, ER+ BCs can progress and recur decades after what appeared to be successful treatment. Over the past 35 years, a great deal of effort, and resources, has been spent on identification of genetic alterations that cause ER+ BC. This has led to the discovery of specific growth promoting "oncogenes" that are mutated or amplified in up to 30 or 40% of cases. In addition, a number of "tumor suppressor genes" (TSG) have been identified, whereby both chromosomal copies of these genes are destroyed in some ER+ tumors. The oncogenes and TSG are relatively easy to define and study. Consequently, the vast majority of genetic, cell biological and biochemical analyses have been focused of these genes. Unfortunately, the eight hundred pound gorilla in the room, gains and losses of entire chromosome arms in BC, has been ignored for a lack of tools to approach it. Indeed, almost 100% of estrogen receptor positive breast cancers have lost one copy of chromosome 16q. Nobody knows why this happens, if this represents an important driver of tumor formation and progression, or if this feature can be exploited by targeted therapy. We have combined the two most frequently mutated genes in human lobular breast cancer to generate the first mouse model for this disease. More recently, we have used state-of-the-art CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing technology to generate a mouse model for 16q loss that can now be applied to define how this event might drive ER+ BC formation (including both lobular and ductal forms) and to find drugs to kill tumors with only one copy of chromosome 16q.

column36: Early prediction of bone erosiveness in rheumatoid arthritis using miRNAs
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a lifelong inflammatory condition that affects most joints, with chronic pain and swelling leading to joint damage with bone destruction and disability. Medication serves to control the inflammation, but existing treatments cannot totally prevent the long-term bone destruction. The objective of our project is to identify novel biomarkers predicting joint damage in RA; these biomarkers will facilitate fast, non-invasive, accurate, and early detection of high-risk patients as well as the development of new drugs and individualized treatment for RA. MicroRNAs regulate various genes and play a role in the pathogenesis of many diseases, including RA. Their level will be measured in osteoclasts (the cells responsible for bone destruction) and blood of the patients at the onset of arthritis. All patients will be followed up for 30 months and bone erosion will be evaluated in hand and foot X-ray images. We will assess the relationship between microRNA levels in osteoclasts at disease onset and the bone destruction rate in RA, as well as the correlation with their serum levels a more convenient tissue for clinical diagnostics. Our team includes three rheumatologists with long-established expertise in bone biology and RA and experts in epigenetics and biostatistics, who position us favorably for a successful outcome of the proposed project. Even within a single disease such as RA, patients markedly differ in their clinical course and outcomes. Establishing an individual's prognosis could allow physicians to identify patients at risk of bone destruction and to promptly initiate an aggressive (and more targeted) therapeutic strategy to prevent devastating damage to joints and the resulting disability.

column36: Regulation of Antigen-Specific Memory CD4+ T Cell Response in Leishmaniasis
column37: Human leishmaniasis are a complex spectrum of diseases affecting over 12 million people with an estimated 350 million people at risk of becoming infected globally. The effects of the disease range from small self-healing skin ulcers and lesions to large disfiguring scars or even death, depending on the species of Leishmania involved. Despite this significant health and societal burden, there is currently no effective vaccine against the disease. Worse still, the existing treatments either cause major side effects or are only effective in specific circumstances. The lack of effective vaccine is mostly attributed to the poor understanding of factors that regulate the development, maintenance and loss of secondary immunity. Interestingly, humans and animals that recover from infection remain immune for life, suggesting that memory cells able to protect against secondary infection develop following recovery from primary infection. Using reverse immunology and proteomics techniques, we identified a highly conserved protein that provides striking protection in vaccinated mice. With the help of collaborators around the globe, we demonstrated this protein also induces strong immune response in human patients. These studies subsequently led to the development of first Leishmania-specific reagent called tetramers, which is capable of identifying Leishmania-specific T cells at single cell level over an entire course of infection. It also helped to show that majority of the immune response is directed towards this protein. This unique reagent helped us to generate transgenic mice whose T cells all express receptor for this particular protein. We are now poised to use these animals to address fundamental questions regarding the factors that regulate antigen-specific memory response in leishmaniasis. Understanding these factors is critical to developing effective vaccine and vaccination strategies against leishmaniasis.

column36: Modulation of HIV provirus expression to eliminate latently infected cells
column37: Contrary to common belief, AIDS and HIV infection remains a significant problem for society. Decades of extensive research has produced combinations of drugs that can stop growth of the virus and suppress the disease we call AIDS. But, unfortunately, these drugs are only a short-term solution, because they do not cure the infection, and they are unaffordable for most infected people, particularly in the developing world. People living with HIV, taking these current drugs, still have the virus in their body because they have cells wherein the virus is hiding, known as latency, and consequently must continue their medication throughout the remainder of their lives. Unfortunately, many people become intolerant towards treatment after some time, and also strains of HIV are beginning to emerge that are resistant to the current drugs. Consequently, in order to prevent a resurgence of an uncontrollable HIV/AIDS epidemic it is necessary that new treatments be developed that can eliminate latent virus from patients on therapy. The research we describe in this proposal is designed to develop new classes of drugs that can completely eliminate HIV from infected people, with the goal of ultimately providing a cure for AIDS.

column36: High throughput culturing, phenotyping, sequencing and bioprospecting of the human microbiome
column37: The human body is colonized by a diverse community of microorganisms (mostly bacteria but also fungi and viruses) - the human microbiome. In some ways we are more them than us with more bacterial cells than our own and 100-1000 more bacterial genes than human genes. We know that the microbiome is critical for health and an imbalance in the microbiome is associated with gastrointestinal diseases, asthma, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and even psychological disorders such as anxiety and depression. Most studies of the microbiome rely on DNA sequencing and it is a widely held belief that most of the human microbiome is not readily cultured in the laboratory. We have challenged that dogma and established methods that allow growth of almost all of the human microbiome. Our results reveal more complexity is obtained by culturing than by sequencing alone. We propose that to fully exploit the biological potential of the microbiome and to validate hypotheses generated from culture-independent studies, we need to develop robust and high throughput methods for culturing and characterizing the microbiome and that is the focus of this proposal. Here we propose to expand our efforts to develop comprehensive strain and sequence libraries of the human microbiome as a resource for the research community and to explore our cultures collections for the discovery of novel antibiotics, immunomodulators, and probiotics.

column37: Health practitioners around the world are fighting a losing battle against multi-drug resistant strains of bacteria that are the leading cause of hospital-acquired infections. Since these mechanisms are required for the bacteria to survive within the host, the lipoproteins have become important targets for the development of vaccines and antibiotics. Information on the lipoprotein export apparatus will aid in the development of novel antibiotics and vaccines. Through these objectives, we will help specifically eradicate these pathogenic bacteria and aid in the global crisis of infections caused by multi-drug resistant strains of bacteria.

column36: Correction of brain triglyceride metabolism in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Clinical trials for Alzheimer's disease (AD) have thus far not succeeded, highlighting an urgent need to better understand how this disease develops. Over the past 5 years, our research program has been focused on identifying the missing links that determine AD progression. In a recently published discovery that received extensive international media attention, we reported that the post-mortem brains of Alzheimer patients exhibit a striking accumulation of triglycerides (stores of fatty acids) on the brain's internal ventricular surface. Using a mouse model of AD, where brains can be analyzed during disease progression, we found that these triglyceride accumulations developed before defects in learning and memory, that they are produced by the AD brain itself, and that one of their consequences is suppression of the brain's stem cell systems. Since brain stem cells participate in functions such as learning, memory, emotion, and general brain maintenance, disruption of brain stem cell activity represents a previously unsuspected mechanism contributing to cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's. This project investigates the therapeutic potential of correcting defects in how the AD brain processes triglycerides. We will use an array of novel animal-based experiments to gain insight into why these triglyceride accumulations happen, whether these accumulations are modifiable by lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise, and whether preventing their occurrence is beneficial in Alzheimer's. Answering these questions may reveal new treatment strategies for this devastating disease.

column36: Understanding the function of DIXDC1 in normal and abnormal brain development
column37: The establishment of neuronal connections, called synapses, is a major milestone in human brain development that is necessary for cognitive processes such as learning, memory and motor function. Synapses are specialized connections that allow nerve cells (neurons) to communicate. Abnormalities in their structure and function underlie neurodevelopmental disorders (eg. Autism Spectrum Disorder [ASD]) and psychiatric disease (eg. Bipolar Disorder and Schizophrenia). These disorders negatively impact the daily lives of affected individuals, causing an economical and social burden, but due to a poor understanding of their biological mechanisms, there are no cures. This underscores the need to better understand how abnormal brain development causes disease. There is strong emerging evidence that molecules belonging to a class called Wingless (Wnt) signaling in the brain play a significant role in disease. Furthermore, there are multiple lines of evidence (human genetic studies, animal models and medications used in the clinic) that indicate disrupting Wnt signaling causes profound synaptic defects and ASD-like pathologies. This suggests studying Wnt signaling molecules may reveal new mechanisms underlying disease pathophysiology. In this study, we examine a new candidate molecule named Dix domain containing 1 (DIXDC1) to determine its role in neuronal growth, synaptic development and ASD pathophysiology. This project will examine DIXDC's role as a new molecular player in synaptic function, and explore a novel signaling pathway regulating DIXDC1 function. Importantly, we have discovered new ASD-linked mutations in DIXDC1 using next-generation sequencing, and we will examine how these human mutations cause brain dysfunction. Together, our experiments will provide new information that will help us understand how Wnt signaling molecules are involved in normal synaptic development, and how their disease-associated abnormalities leads to ASD pathological consequences.

column36: Understanding and treating neurological phenotypes in the 15q13.3 microdeletion syndrome
column37: Neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders (NDDs) are characterized by impairments of personal, social, academic, or occupational functioning. There are no treatments that reverse these impairments, highlighting the need to understand their biological aetiologies. One important discovery is that genetic risk factors are associated with these disorders. Therefore, by studying these genetic factors using model systems, we can better understand how risk genes cause abnormal brain development. In the current grant, we are studying a strong genetic risk factor where individuals are missing a piece of chromosome 15 (a microdeletion) and can have autism, schizophrenia, epilepsy or developmental delay. We have assembled a research team who will use different biological model systems (mouse models, human and mouse brain imaging, cultured human brain cells, genetic sequencing and bioinformatics) to study the chromosome 15 microdeletion. Our approach will also shed light on the factors that contribute to the different clinical symptoms associated with this syndrome. This will lead to better disease classification, closer monitoring of patient symptoms depending on their genetic diagnosis, and possibly early invention. Our preliminary results demonstrate the success of using a multidisciplinary approach. We have discovered a novel target gene in this deletion that is responsible for most of the neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities in our mouse model. Our team has the appropriate scientific and clinical experience to generate new information that will help clinicians manage patients with a chromosome 15 microdeletion. Our approach will not only be successful for this microdeletion, but will serve as a model to study other, similar, poorly characterized genetic lesions.

column36: Mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contacts and cristae dynamics in health and disease
column37: Metabolic flexibility is a key feature of cellular function; it consists in switching back and forth between glucose and fat oxidation, matching the energetic and biosynthetic needs of the cell to the type and amount of nutrients that are available. For the cell, the ability to adapt to metabolic shifts means survival; but for the mitochondrion, which is the powerplant of the cell, this consists in adapting to periodic shifts in carbon combustion rates and to switches between alternative fuels according to nutrients availability. The goal of our research program is to understand how mitochondria secure metabolic flexibility to the cell. The function of the mitochondrion depends on its unique ultrastructure: the cristae and the MERCs, which are the sites of contact with another organelle, the endoplasmic reticulum. Recently, we published a paper in PNAS, the prestigious journal of the US National Academy of Sciences, showing that the cristae and the MERCs change in shape, number, size, and thickness every time that the hepatic metabolism switches gear (which is something that happens after a meal or upon feeling hungry). This study gave us the idea is that when metabolism shifts, a nutrients-sensing pathway instructs mitochondria to adapt their functional output to the needs of the cell by activating a molecular mechanism that simultaneously changes cristae and MERCs structure, which, together, control mitochondrial bioenergetics. In other words, we hypothesize that changes in the organelle's ultrastructure are behind its ability to secure metabolic flexibility to the cell, and failure to do so is central to the development of metabolic syndromes and diseases. To address this model we shall: 1) identify the nutrients-sensing pathway that activates MERCs and cristae remodeling in vivo; 2) reveal the mechanisms governing mitochondrial ultrastructure remodeling during metabolic shifts; 3) link MERCs and cristae dynamics to liver physiology and disease

column36: Colonic Goblet Cells: Active Players in Host Defense and Mucosal Protection?
column37: The cells that line our intestines have many functions, including making and releasing mucus. Mucus is made up of proteins that are covered with sugars, and it creates a thick and slimy layer that coats the whole inner surface of our intestines. The mucus layer is our "first line of defense" against food and water-borne disease causing bacteria - such as the dangerous "Hamburger disease" causing E. coli bacteria that cause bloody diarrhea and kidney failure. To inflict disease, these bacteria have to move across the mucus layer and enter the body. We propose that intestinal mucus plays an active role in determining whether dangerous bacteria can infect their hosts. We have found that during infection, intestinal cells make more mucus and they also increase the content of certain sugars found on the mucus. This led us to predict that these mucus changes may (a) protect the host by pushing the bacteria away from the intestinal lining, and/or (b) the mucus may provide additional nutrients (the sugars) for the dangerous bacteria, reducing their need to invade and damage the intestine to obtain food. In this project, we will investigate the role of mucus, by studying how the immune system causes these changes in the mucus. We will also study what parts of the mucus layer are most important in providing protection, and what happens to dangerous bacteria when the mucus layer is missing. We will also test whether changing the ability of the E. coli bacteria to use sugars as food, or changing the availability of these sugars affects how much damage the bacteria cause to the intestine. This project addresses an understudied, yet critical aspect of intestinal defense and will test if modifying the levels of sugars in mucus offers a new way to fight dangerous gut infections by targeting bacterial pathogen nutrition.

column36: Prevention of primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation; a bench to bedside approach
column37: Lung transplant patients are at risk of developing injury immediately after surgery-a condition called primary graft dysfunction. Patients with this condition are also at greater risk of poorer long term health. Unfortunately, there are no drug treatments available to combat primary graft dysfunction, even though researchers have found some potential therapies in scientific lab settings. The main reason why these findings have not been tried in humans is a lack of a pre-clinical model that would most closely mimic and predict treatment in these patients. Our research team will use a pre-clinical model that will let us test new drug therapies before using them in the patient clinic. We are also the developers of a new technology called Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion, where we can keep donor lungs at normal body temperature and provide it with oxygen and nutrients while outside of the body. This allows the surgeon to carefully inspect the health of the working lung before transplant. This technology also allows us to apply drug therapies before transplant, in an attempt to improve donor lung health. We will work with CSL Behring, a world-class drug company, who will support our project. We will investigate the use of two experimental drugs: alpha-1-antitrypsin and delta-V1-1 delivered with gold nanoparticles. We have previously shown in cell and small animal models that these two drugs helped to prevent primary graft dysfunction. Together, we will develop a new way to bring safe drug therapies to the patient bedside, and help future researchers develop more therapies using our pre-clinical model. Outcomes will lead to a future clinical trial in further testing these drugs for hospital use. Reducing lung injury after transplant will result in better long-term health and a much less chance of death in lung transplant patients. Importantly, we will help to improve Canada's reputation as a leader in innovative clinical health care research.

column36: PTP Alpha in Normal and Tumor Cell Motility
column37: One of the biggest challenges in cancer treatment is preventing metastasis, the process by which cells from a tumor spread to other sites in the body and form secondary tumors that cause most cancer deaths. Tumor cells have acquired special properties that allow them to spread; notably the ability to invade tissues. Developing treatments to prevent cancer cell spreading requires better understanding of the mechanisms that enable this invasive ability. Cancer cell invasion is mediated by cell structures called invadopodia. These organized structures protrude from the cell body and produce enzymes that degrade the surroundings, clearing a path for the tumor cell to move. Growing knowledge of the molecular regulation and biology of invadopodia has been informed by research into similar but clearly distinct cell structures that regulate normal cell movement. In normal cells, related but non-invasive structures called focal adhesions (FAs) control interactions with their surroundings and cell migration. We discovered that a molecule called PTPa is present in FAs and plays key roles in the molecular communication that regulates FA function and normal cell movement. In our proposed research we will identify interactions between PTPa and other FA molecules, and elucidate how the outcomes of these interactions control cell movement. In parallel, we will investigate the roles of PTPa in cancer cell invadopodia, using breast and colorectal cancer cell lines as models. Our findings suggest that PTPa is involved in regulating the formation of these structures. We will investigate this, and determine if PTPa is required for invasive activity of invadopodia and how PTPa co-ordinates with other molecules to control this. Our research will provide new knowledge of the molecular connections and functions of PTPa that promote normal cell movement and tumor cell invasion. This will increase opportunities to develop targeted molecular therapies to combat cancer metastasis.

column37: DNA double-strand breaks are breaks in individual chromosomes that can arise as a result of metabolism (breathing oxygen) and from environmental sources. These breaks are commonly repaired by one of two mechanisms termed non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination. These two types of repair differ in a very important way. column36: Novel strategies for treating respiratory muscle failure in muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a fatal disease in which most muscles, including the diaphragm and other breathing muscles, are progressively destroyed and replaced by scar tissue. We plan to evaluate whether interventions that affect the function of macrophages, which are by far the most abundant inflammatory cells in DMD muscles, are effective in treating the disease. This will include testing a new drug called drug cenicriviroc, which blocks receptors that are very important in attracting harmful macrophages during early disease. We are entering an era of what has been called "personalized" medicine. One practical application of personalized medicine can be summarized as "Giving the right drug to the right patient at the right time". Unfortunately, the current drug management of DMD is based on a "one size fits all" approach. Therefore, in addition to assessing the effectiveness of these drugs, we will also try to identify new blood tests called "biomarkers" that help to predict which drug works best at a given stage of the disease. The majority of outcomes in our studies will be determined in the diaphragm because it is the most severely affected skeletal muscle in our mouse model of DMD with respect to fibrosis and muscle weakness, and it most closely resembles what is found in human patients. We will also do preliminary exploratory studies of our biomarkers by taking blood samples from DMD patients in our clinic. The risk of the medications we are studying is low relative to their potential benefit and especially compared to the major adverse effects associated with the current standard treatment (corticosteroids). All of these drugs could be rapidly moved to the clinic for use in DMD patients if our studies are successful.

column36: Thermostatted proteins that control bacterial biofilm development in response to body heat
column37: Biofilms are slime-covered communities of microbes that stick to each other and to surfaces. This prevalent form of microbial life accounts for many chronic infections that defeat the immune system and are highly resistant to antibiotics. My work seeks to understand a process called signal transduction. All living cells use this process to sense external stimuli and trigger a chain of chemical events inside the cell, resulting in physiological adaptation to the environment. This project centers on signal transduction that coordinates biofilm growth. In many bacteria, biofilm signal transduction depends on a key intracellular molecule, cyclic diguanylate (c-di-GMP). I study c-di-GMP in the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This organism infects medical devices, the urinary tract and burn wounds. It also forms biofilms in the lungs of people suffering from cystic fibrosis (CF), causing life-threatening infections that can last for years. Nearly 4,000 Canadians suffer from CF. While a lot is known about how enzymes "make and break" c-di-GMP, little is known about the environmental stimuli that activate and inhibit these enzymes. This is a key research area because bacteria must use c-di-GMP signaling to sense and respond to host stimuli to build biofilms. C-di-GMP is a promising therapeutic target because it is absent in mammals. My lab has discovered that some isolates of P. aeruginosa have a protein that makes c-di-GMP in response to body heat. My 5-year project aims to understand - at a molecular and biophysical level - how this protein functions as a thermosensor and modulates virulence. Bioinformatics predict that this thermosensing protein is widespread among pathogens. My vision is that this research will guide the design of inhibitors targeting heat-sensing proteins that bacteria use to cause infection. Finally, I propose that these heat-sensing proteins can be reverse-engineered, enabling the design of thermally-activated proteins for biotechnology.

column37: Despite remarkable strides made by the research community, over 45% of Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer during their life and about 30% will die from complications arising from it. The most common type of cancers are the squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), which are associated with high risk of metastasis, chronic pain, organ failure, wasting and death. Current SCC treatments are poor and broadly toxic, killing the dividing cells not only of the tumor but also of healthy tissues. A major impediment to developing more selective therapies is the incomplete knowledge of the constellation of genes that fuels tumor growth. Comprehensive sequencing techniques have elucidated the genetic alterations associated with SCCs. Now, the biggest challenge is to weed out circumstantial bystander mutations and identify the diver mutations that trigger tumor growth and metastasis. Secondly, we have to identify novel drug targets for a given cancer and build faithful pre-clinical models to devise novel therapeutic strategies. However, conventional methods to achieve these goals are tedious, too costly and take several years. We have therefore developed a unique technique to analyze the role of hundreds of genes in cancer development within a single mouse within a couple of weeks. We produce highly concentrated viruses specifically designed to destroy or activate candidate cancer genes. Using ultrasound imaging, we then inject these viruses into the sac of a living mouse embryo, where the viruses infect the surface cells that cover the tiny embryo. This enables us to manipulate genes in the tissues most commonly affected by SCCs such as the skin, cervix, lung, oral cavity or esophagus and to analyze tumor development once the mice are born. The overreaching goal is to conduct a series of comprehensive screens to identify the genes that cause SCCs initiation, progression and metastasis, and to elucidate the genes required for tumor growth - the quest for a tumor's Achilles' heel.

column37: Adult stem and progenitor cells play fundamental roles in tissue homeostasis, renewal and regeneration, and when these cells become dysfunctional, they likely increase the pace of aging. column37: Alcohol misuse remains a major public health problem in emerging adults (age 18-25) in Canada. Although many emerging adults 'mature out' of alcohol misuse over time, others exhibit persistently high levels of problem drinking and the process of maturing out is not well understood. Integrating psychology and economics, the field of behavioural economics (BE) is increasingly used to study alcohol misuse and is highly relevant to maturing out. These are alcohol demand and proportionate alcohol-related reinforcement, two different strategies for measuring how much a person values alcohol. These indices may predict maturing out of alcohol misuse over time, but no longitudinal studies have been conducted to date. This study will systematically test the hypothesis that these BE measures will predict changes in alcohol misuse during the transition to adulthood. The study has two primary aims. The first primary aim is to predict changes in alcohol misuse from age 22-25 using the novel BE measures, both individually and in the context of established risk factors. The second primary aim is to examine mechanistic interrelationships among these variables. This includes examining whether the BE variables cause changes in alcohol misuse over time or, alternatively, whether their influence is caused by the established risk factors. In addition, the study will examine whether there are systematic differences in the predictive relationships based on biological sex, university student status, and the use of other substances. For exploratory purposes, the study will also identify the most salient periods of change and psychosocial factors that increase or decrease the value of alcohol. Taken together, the study proposes to leverage recent advances in BE to substantially increase the understanding of maturing out of alcohol misuse.

column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide, suffering from a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis and a paucity of effective drugs available to treat advanced tumours. Despite a greater understanding of the genetic basis of lung cancer development, discovery of new therapeutics has been slow as the activities of genes implicated in this disease are difficult to inhibit while new agents targeting lung cancer cells have been ineffective due to drug resistance. Therefore, new strategies are urgently needed to develop effective therapeutic strategies for lung cancer patient therapy that yield robust responses and improve long-term survival rates. The idea is that the reason these genes are not activated in lung tumours is because they were incompatible with cancer growth. When we engineered lung cancer cells to have activation of both of these genes, we found that the cancer cells died in robust fashion. The goal of this proposal is to understand why co-activation of these two genes kills cancer cells and determine whether drugs that can mimic this scenario offer an effective way of inhibiting lung tumour growth. We also aim to test candidate drugs in mice that develop lung cancer to gain insight regarding their potential use in the treatment of human patients. Thus, this work will offer true progress towards developing new agents for the treatment of lung cancer, ultimately leading to improved survival rates for patients.

column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major public health issue that continues to rise coincident with increased longevity and the obesity, diabetes and hypertension epidemic, and ~3 million Canadians are already living with this devastating illness. Presently, dialysis and transplantation are the only forms of treatment for advanced kidney disease, and these approaches are associated with considerable morbidity, mortality and healthcare costs. Despite the burden of disease, the molecular and cellular basis of CKD is poorly understood, limiting opportunities for development of new therapies. Fundamental discoveries over the past decade have highlighted the key role of the podocyte in the pathogenesis and progression of CKD. These cells are a crucial component of the glomerular blood filtration barrier, and their function is closely tied to their unique morphology. Podocytes extend a series of interdigitating actin-based foot processes that are bridged by specialized signaling junctions known as slit diaphragms (SD). One of the earliest features of kidney disease is remodeling of podocyte foot processes and collapse of the actin cytoskeleton, resulting in disrupted filtration and proteinuria. Our lab provided some of the first evidence that signaling from the SD directly regulates foot process morphology, and we have since validated the importance of such signaling in podocyte injury and repair. These discoveries provide a molecular foothold to help understand the basis of podocyte function, and the underlying hypothesis of our research program is that perturbations in SD signaling are the initiating cause of podocyte injury progressing to CKD. Leveraging a series of novel mutant mouse models and complementary cell-based tools, the goal of this proposal is to identify molecular and cellular processes that are coordinated by the central SD protein nephrin. Our long-term objective is to translate this knowledge to the bedside to identify new podocyte-specific therapies.
