column36: Bacteremia Antibiotic Length Actually Needed for Clinical Effectiveness (BALANCE): A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial
column37: Bloodstream infections are a common and serious problem, affecting 15% of critically ill patients, increasing length of hospital stay by 2-3 weeks, adding $25,000-40,000 in excess hospital costs, and tripling the risk of death. At the same time, antibiotic overuse is also a common and serious problem, in that 30-50% of antibiotic use is unnecessary or inappropriate, and results in avoidable drug side effects such as kidney failure, Clostridium difficile infection, increased costs, and spiraling antibiotic resistance rates. The greatest contributor to antibiotic overuse is excessive treatment duration. Shorter duration antibiotic treatment (= 7 days) is as effective as longer duration treatment for ear infections, bladder infections, and pneumonia, but this question has not been directly studied in the setting of bloodstream infection. Our team's systematic review of the medical literature, national survey of Canadian infectious diseases and critical care physicians, and multicentre retrospective study (N=1202) all support the need for a randomized controlled trial comparing shorter (7 days) versus longer (14 days) antibiotic treatment for bloodstream infections. Our CIHR-funded multicenter BALANCE Pilot trial, has established the feasibility of this trial design, with excellent recruitment rates, and adherence to treatment duration protocols. In this proposal for the main BALANCE trial, we will definitively determine whether 7 days of treatment is associated with non-inferior survival rates as compared to 14 days of treatment. By defining the duration of treatment for bloodstream infections, our research program will help maximize the clinical cure of individual patients, while minimizing their risk of drug side effects, C. difficile, and antibiotic resistance. Since this intervention would require no new technology, and would reduce (rather than increase) health care costs, it would offer immediate benefits to patients and the healthcare system.

column36: Systemic immunity: the missing link between gut microbiome and asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways currently affecting more than 300 million people worldwide. It is now the most common childhood disease in Western countries. Asthma has a genetic component, but genetics offers only a partial explanation for the dramatic rise in prevalence over the last five decades. Accumulating evidence points to environmental factors as key contributors. One such factor is the microbiome, the collection of microorganisms that inhabit our body. Using stool samples collected from children enrolled in the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) Study, we recently demonstrated a connection between gut microbiome alterations in the first 100 days of life and an increased risk to develop asthma. We also found that low levels of specific intestinal bacteria in asthmatic children are linked to low levels of microbial products (metabolites) known to regulate essential immune functions. However, the immune status of those children was not determined, and the mechanisms by which an altered microbiome and metabolites functionally link to asthma is unknown. Based on the role of the immune system in asthma, we hypothesize that specific changes in the gut microbiome contribute to the development of childhood asthma by producing metabolites that modulate the host immune response. We will test this hypothesis as follows. First, we will leverage the CHILD cohort to study the immune and metabolic signatures that correlate with clinical asthma. Second, we will determine the interrelationships among the infant gut microbiome, microbial metabolites, immune system status, and asthma. Third, we will validate those interrelationships in a mouse model of asthma. This project will provide important new understanding of how asthma develops, and it will identify ways that we might prevent or treat asthma, potentially using probiotics.

column36: Vaginal Surgery for the Pelvic Floor: A Randomized Trial of Synthetic Mesh Versus Synthetic Sutures
column37: More than 4 million women in Canada suffer from pelvic floor diseases. Pelvic floor muscles, nerves and ligaments can tear and stretch, mainly from vaginal deliveries of babies and aging. They affect women's ability to lead normal lives, be physically active and enjoy normal sexual relations. Many become depressed and isolated. Surgery for prolapse often fails and symptoms come back. Surgeons thought that plastic permanent mesh behind the vagina would offer a more durable repair. Unfortunately, mesh kits were commercialized without much study. This technique is not perfect because it can tension the vagina too much and can still cause pain and return of prolapse. We know, from successful surgeries with slings for urine incontinence, and from other small studies, that vaginal mesh is safe if introduced in small amounts, deep in the pelvis, without tension. Therefore, we propose to study 2 surgeries for vaginal repair of prolapse, using small mesh arms versus permanent sutures. We think that surgery with mesh may be more durable than surgery with sutures, but we cannot know for sure until we perform our study. Women will be randomly assigned to one of the two surgeries and followed for 2 years. We will study women's opinion of how the surgery worked for their prolapse, their other pelvic symptoms, pelvic exam and their sexual health. We hope to solve the controversy about vaginal mesh for prolapse and investigate a new procedure that may be a better, more durable option for women with prolapse.

column37: Leishmaniasis is one of the 17 neglected tropical diseases impacting over 1 billion of the world's poorest populations. As a follow-up of previous studies in my lab, our research program aims at investigating timely questions on how this intracellular pathogen regulates gene expression inside macrophages to ensure its survival and to establish disease. Outputs from this research program could lead to the identification of promising targets for the development of novel therapeutic and preventive strategies against this important human pathogen, hence impacting the health sector and foresee Canada as a main contributor to global health efforts. column36: The physiological role of the axo-myelinic synapse
column37: Multiple sclerosis, stroke and spinal cord injury are common and devastating human disorders. The central nervous system is composed of two different types of tissue: gray matter, which comprises the nerve cell bodies, and white matter, which represents the nerve fibers connecting nerve cells to each other. Nerve fibers in the brains of mammals are highly specialized, being very thin (to pack millions of fibers into a small volume) and wrapped by an insulating fatty material called myelin to prevent short circuits. How this all-important myelin is damaged in human neurological disorders, and how the nerve fiber tells the myelin to start wrapping and insulating it, remain mysteries. This ongoing project has focused on chemical communication between axons (nerve fibers) and their myelin sheaths. We discovered that axons signal their myelin sheaths using chemical transmitters in a way that is very similar to how nerve cells communicate: through a chemical "synapse". This new axon-myelin synapse causes damage to myelin when excessively activated, and may be the first step in myelin loss in MS for instance. This project will explore the purpose of this axon-myelin synapse: why do axons need to talk to their myelin sheaths? What might myelin do for its axon when it senses a lot of electrical traffic traveling down the axon? We propose that myelin supports its axon by physically transferring material essential for the axon's long term survival. A breakdown of this communication and transfer may underlie diverse diseases such as MS, cerebral palsy and even psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.

column37: Cancer is a devastating disease defined by genetic changes that activate proteins supporting cell growth, or are inhibitory of cell death. Our second aim will assess candidate druggability and involves the development of therapeutic antibodies, which are engineered versions of naturally occurring human proteins that can be trained to bind and inhibit cancer targets. column36: Direct lymphocyte-mediated antimicrobial mechanisms
column37: Infections, particularly those that affect patients with compromised immunity are among the most pressing challenges for mankind. It is not clear how we will defend ourselves against these ever increasing microbial invaders. The answer may lie in studies of the immune system. With this goal in mind, Dr. Mody's laboratory has been studying a class of cells that was originally identified because of their ability to kill tumor cells and virus-infected cells. Because of their ability to be toxic to, and kill cells, they are called cytotoxic lymphocytes. Because this finding is so new, the mechanisms of recognition of the microbe, mechanisms of activation of the microbicidal lymphocytes and the killing mechanisms have not been well worked out. Moreover, recent studies from Dr. Mody's laboratory demonstrate that this lymphocyte-mediated microbicidal response is defective in HIV-infected patients, but has the potential to be restored. It is the goal of this proposal to study the normal and defective mechanisms with the purpose of providing new therapies for these challenging infections.

column36: Engineering a broadly cross-protective vaccine that confers sterilizing immunity against Haemophilus influenzae.
column37: Haemophilus influenzae is responsible for a substantial proportion of respiratory infections in humans, including ear infections, sinus infections and pneumonia, as well as invasive infections such as meningitis. This bacterium lives in the human upper respiratory tract, not in other animals or in the environment. While most bacteria cannot live in human tissues because there is no free iron, which is essential for life, H. influenzae binds and removes iron from the iron transport protein in human blood, transferrin (Tf). Because this is an essential process, and because the Tf binding proteins (Tbps) must be accessible at the bacterial surface, these receptor proteins are ideal targets for vaccination to produce antibodies that protect against infection. In contrast to other H. influenzae vaccine targets, the Tbps are shared by both groups of pathogenic H. influenzae for which vaccines are needed. This means that a single Tbp-based vaccine could protect against both the respiratory tract and invasive infections. Moreover, we have recently demonstrated that Tbp-based vaccines prevent bacterial colonization of respiratory tissues, so that they provide 'sterilizing' immunity that should ultimately allow elimination of the bacteria rather than just protecting against clinical disease caused by infection. The purpose of this project is to apply our established approaches to understand the structure, function and sequence diversity of H. influenzae Tbps and then use protein engineering to create vaccine antigens that are capable of preventing colonization by all known strains of H. influenzae. Then, our novel, integrated vaccine design and evaluation pipeline approach, which includes the use of a 'humanized' mouse model for colonization, will be used to confirm how well the engineered antigens work and refine the composition of engineered antigens to produce a safe, effective and broadly protective vaccine.

To target these vectors into the brain, we will use focused ultrasound in order to make affected brain areas more permeable to the gene vectors.. Following the treatment, we will assess the extent of behavioural and pathological improvements. Our optimal expectation is that there will be a reduction in the movement impairments and the less a-syn accumulation in animals that received both the ultrasound and gene therapy.

column36: Regulation of retromer in health and disease
column37: Every cell is like a busy city: it has to coordinate information flow, perform thousands of different tasks, and move materials, like fats and proteins, to where they are needed. Like cities, cells have a complex internal transportation system that controls traffic. This system works well most of the time, but can get disrupted, and persistent disruptions can cause dysfunction and disease. This project focuses on an important part of this cellular transportation system called "retromer". Problems with retromer cause neurological disorders such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, but to develop effective treatments for these conditions, we first need to understand the fundamental causes of disease. Many of the traffic signals and pathways linked to human disease are also found in yeast, a simple one-celled organism. Studying retromer in yeast allows us to use different genome-wide technologies to uncover pathways and machinery on a very large scale and allows us to make discoveries that would be difficult or impossible in complex organisms. In fact, retromer was first discovered in yeast, and many important discoveries about retromer are still being made in this cell system. Recently, we discovered that a family of "VPS9-like" proteins regulates retromer assembly in yeast. One of these proteins, called "VARP", was also found to be important for retromer function in human cells. This gives us the unparalleled opportunity to use yeast to study VARP and establish exactly how it regulates retromer. Once we have made discoveries in yeast, we can transfer this knowledge to the study of cells from mice or humans to test if increasing VARP function can overcome the retromer defects seen in Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease. In the longer term, our research is expected to identify new drug targets that will help in the development of new treatments for these neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Chronic stress, synaptic remodelling and neuroendocrine adaptation
column37: Chronic stress is a strong risk factor for serious mental illnesses including major depression and many other disorders in mood and cognition. These stress-related disorders are now the fastest growing category of disability insurance claims in Canada, costing an estimated $31 billion each year in lost productivity, and billions more in direct medical costs. Despite its tremendous impact on our health and society, we know surprisingly little about how stress leads to mental illness. This lack of knowledge is a major obstacle in the search for better treatments and prevention of stress-related disorders. An emerging view is that neuroplasticity is important for successful coping with stress, and that severe stress disturbs this process and leads to stress-related disorders. We hypothesize that neuroplastic mechanisms are important for fine-tuning the levels of stress hormones (i.e. corticosteroids) during chronic stress. This project will use an animal model of chronic stress to first study the neuroplasticity that occurs when the animal adapts to chronic stress. We will then investigate how this adaptation to chronic stress fails when the animal receives a more severe form of stress that causes dysregulation of the hormonal stress response. Using state-of-the-art techniques that enable us to study communication between neural cells at high temporal and spatial resolutions, we have conducted a pilot study, which has found stress-induced plasticity within a brain area that regulates the hormonal stress response. We seek to further investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which this plasticity becomes dysregulated during severe chronic stress. These experiments will identify specific brain mechanisms for stress adaptation, promising targets for future therapeutics and prevention of stress-related disorders. This project will also provide outstanding opportunities for trainees to be immersed in this emerging field along with sophisticated technologies.

column36: Impact of rewarming on the brain health of cooled neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
column37: Birth asphyxia due to lack of oxygen at birth is the leading cause of death in term newborns. Half of survivors fail to fully develop their language and motor skills and may present epilepsy later in life, which pose significant burdens on patients, families and society. The current practice is to cool these newborns for the first three days of life to protect their brain. Yet, studies on asphyxiated animals showed that rapid rewarming after cooling can abolish or reduce benefits of cooling. Remarkably, no systematic studies investigated the reaction of human brain to rewarming. We demonstrated, using non-invasive bedside brain monitoring, that asphyxiated newborns may experience worsening of their brain activity and seizures on rewarming. Moreover, we developed non-invasive bedside tools that detect insufficient brain oxygen consumption in these neonates during cooling. We think that brain oxygen consumption abnormalities precede neurological deterioration on rewarming. In this study, we propose to use sophisticated methods of analysis and state-of-the-art brain imaging tools to study how rewarming affects brain health in cooled asphyxiated neonates. We will evaluate whether brain oxygen consumption abnormalities contribute to the worsening of brain activity and seizures on rewarming. We will also study whether these measures are related to abnormal findings on advanced magnetic resonance brain images, and predict increased risks of epilepsy and abnormal development. Hence, asphyxiated newborns will be closely followed through cooling and rewarming phases using non-invasive bedside brain imaging tools. They will continue to be followed through infancy and their development will be evaluated at 18 months of age. This study will help understand how rewarming affects the brain of asphyxiated newborns. It will allow the development of new interventions to protect the brain of neonates at high risk of adverse neurological outcomes.

column37: Background: Current treatment of low rectal cancer (LRC) is chemotherapy and radiotherapy (CRT) followed by surgery and involves creating a permanent colostomy (bag). The benefit is that patients with LRC may be able to safely avoid surgery and a permanent colostomy, thus leading to an improved quality of life. While physicians across Canada would like to offer NOM to patients with LRC, they do not feel comfortable doing so unless there is a standardized clinical protocol so that patients are properly informed of the risks and benefits and the outcomes are collected and measured in a standardized way. Methods: Patients with LRC who have achieved a cCR following CRT will be invited to participate. Patients who participate will undergo active follow up with regular clinical visits, physical exam, endoscopy and imaging assessments at regular intervals for 2 years to assess for tumour re-growth or spread to the liver and lungs. The primary outcome will be the rate of local re-growth. The NOM approach will be considered safe if the rate of tumour re-growth is <10%. This study is of high priority to patients and strongly supports patient-centred care. Our Patient & Family Advisory Council that consists of 30 patients with rectal cancer and family members across Canada indicated that this study is a research priority and expressed interest in being involved in this study.

column37: It has been 53 years since the introduction of dopamine replacement therapy for Parkinson disease (PD). It remains the gold standard of clinical care but does not stop disease progression. The goals of the studies proposed in our application are to: 1) identify how these two genes act in an integrated response to protect the body and brain from infection; and 2) test a new understanding of PD development. There is growing recognition of the role of inflammation and the immune system in PD and related neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's. These studies will inform current drug trials (note, LRRK2 is the lead therapeutic molecule for PD) and have the possibility to open an entirely new field of targets for drug discovery that are rooted in the immune response. column36: Anatomy of leptin sensing
column37: Obesity is a major health threat due to its strong association with diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and cancer. As obesity has reached pandemic proportions interventional strategies are urgently needed. Obesity is based on an excessive increase in the body's fat mass. Key to fat mass regulation is the hormone leptin, which is produced by the fat cells and in order to keep a constant body weight, circulating leptin acts on brain areas that control feeding to trigger a reduction in food intake. While the weight lowering effect of leptin has been known since its discovery some 20 years ago, we still do not know where and how leptin enters the brain to exert its weight lowering effect. However, understanding of this process is important as obesity is usually associated with leptin resistance, i.e., while circulating leptin levels increase in proportion with fat mass, leptin seemingly looses its ability to reduce appetite in obese individuals. We have recently discovered a novel structure within the nerve cells that respond to leptin. We found that this structure, a specific bulbous enlargement in the nerve cell's filaments, to be typically located close to blood vessels and it could thus serve a sensing function for circulating leptin. We wish to study this structure in much greater detail, to establish if and how it senses leptin. We want to determine if the leptin resistance associated with mouse models of obesity is due to a selective functional impairment or degeneration of the bulbous structure we discovered. Elucidating its functional role in the context of body weight control, may critically help to develop targeted therapeutic interventions aimed at 're-sensitizing' the brain to leptin, which would lead to reduced food intake and thus weight loss.

The production of steroid hormone is thus a meticulously regulated process to ensure accurate amount are produced. In the testis, the main steroidogenic cells are the Leydig cells. Steroid hormone synthesis in these cells is mainly regulated by the pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH). In Leydig cells, LH will triggers activation of proteins called kinases that modify other proteins which ultimately leads to alteration in the expression of genes involved in steroid hormone synthesis. Novel kinases were recently identified in our lab that have opposing effects on steroid hormone production; CAMKI enhances it while AMPK decreases it. The opposing action of CAMKI and AMPK allows for a fine regulation of the steroid synthesis process thus preventing detrimental overproduction or insufficiency. On the other hand, very little is known about the proteins that are targeted by CAMKI and AMPK. The goal of the present project is to identify the proteins targeted by CAMKI and AMPK and to determine their roles in steroid hormone production. A better characterization of these CAMKI and AMPK target proteins could lead to novel treatments for numerous hormone-dependent pathologies.

column36: Antigen-specific functional properties and molecular profiling of autoreactive T-cells in individuals at risk for type 1 diabetes.
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease, resulting from the destruction of the insulin-producing beta- cells in the pancreas by the T-cells of the immune system. In recent years we have discovered over forty places in the genome, where genetic variants inherited from the individual's parents determine the probability that the individual will develop T1D. Normally, T-cells whose receptor recognizes parts of self either die or become inactive thanks to a variety of successive roadblocks, collectively assuring immune self-tolerance. Autoimmunity happens when a small number of T-cells evade these roadblocks and multiply to reach numbers sufficient to do the autoimmune damage. In the past few years, we have discovered a large number of places in the human genome that contain genetic variants, inherited from an individual's parents that can weaken self-tolerance. Self-tolerance is assured by the regulatory T-cells, a subset of the immune system that protect normal tissues while the rest of the T-cells attack bacteria and viruses. The delicate balance between defense from microbes and "collateral damage" to one's own body parts is occasionally broken by rogue T-cells or by a weakening of the regulatory cells. Until recently, distinguishing between these two categories of cells was difficult. Thanks to the discovery of novel markers by Dr. Piccirillo, this distinction can now be made and the cells can be separated and studied. We now wish to use this breakthrough to study whether the progression from antibody positivity to T1D is due to an overactive immune system or to weakening of the regulatory component. Moreover, we have also the technology to separate T-cells that are directed against insulin, from other cells that do their normal job in fighting infection. This powerful combination of methodologies will allow us to isolate the cells directly involved in the development of T1D and study them with the powerful genome-wide methodologies of the CAG.

column37: Advances in transplantation of human insulin producing tissue (islets) have established the proof-of-concept for this therapy to emerge as a treatment for patients with type 1 diabetes. The hope for a cure from islet replacement is, however lessened by the decline in insulin independence rates seen in clinical islet transplantation. This decline is currently not fully understood, but likely involves reduced islet survival and immune rejection. Strategies to maximize survival of the transplanted islets and reduce the immune response are likely to have a major impact in enhancing long-term clinical outcomes. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) reside in many tissues such as bone marrow and have shown potential as a regenerative medicine therapy for many degenerative diseases and immune disorders. Notably, with Edmonton's Clinical Islet Transplant program, along with Korbutt's $26 million stem cell facility for the clinical grade production of cells for diabetes therapy, this team is well positioned to rapidly transfer findings to clinical trials.

column36: One size does not fit all: Tailoring exercise prescription for brain health based on BDNF polymorphism
column37: The size of Canadian population aged 65 and older is growing, so will the number of individuals with dementia. Exercise is a viable dementia prevention strategy. To maximize the utility of exercise (e.g., by providing personalized exercise recommendations), it is vital to determine factors that influence its effectiveness. Exercise type and a person's genotype are factors that require further investigation. There are 2 main types of exercise, aerobic training (AT) and strength training (ST). Both have benefits for brain health, but do so using different biological pathways. Specifically, AT appears to largely rely on the release of a particular protein called brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). In contrast, ST is not BDNF-dependent, but relies on another protein. Understanding how both AT and ST benefit the brain is important because in ~35% of the population, there is an alteration within the BDNF gene that results in less secretion of BDNF. Thus, we believe this BDNF gene variant may determine the degree of benefit an individual will receive from AT. Specifically, we speculate that persons with this BDNF gene variant will not experience the same degree of brain health gains from AT as those without this gene variant. Thus, for individuals with this BDNF gene variant, ST may be the more appropriate form of exercise training to promote brain health. For our research, we will examine how this BDNF gene variant may modify the degree of brain health benefits from 6 months of 3 times per week AT or ST, in older adults at risk for dementia. Our study is critical to understanding how genes may influence the cognitive response to different types of exercise training. Given the immense health and financial burden imposed by dementia, our proposed study could have major impact in Canada and internationally as the results will contribute to evidence-based, personalized exercise recommendations for dementia prevention.

column37: Permanent hearing loss affects 2-4 per 1000 children and usually interferes with typical language acquisition. Newborn hearing screening has been implemented worldwide to give children with hearing loss a better start in life. column36: Development of magnetic tumor killing nanoparticles to breakthrough the blood-brain barrier
column37: Normal brain function requires a highly regulated and controlled environment. The brain capillaries that form the blood-brain barrier (BBB) have a special role in maintaining the proper brain environment. However, for many brain related diseases and disorders, the limited BBB permeability of drugs presents a substantial obstacle to effective treatment. This is certainly the case for glioblastomas, the most commonly occurring brain tumor in adults. Our project builds on our previous work establishing an approach for delivery of magnetic nanoparticles across the BBB. In the present study, we examine the use of magnetic nanoparticles as drug carriers to increase drug delivery to the brain and improve the treatment of brain tumors. The specific aims of this research project are to examine the influence of nanoparticle shape, and surface chemistry to hone in on the optimal magnetic nanoparticle composition for enhanced BBB penetration. Based on our previous studies, we believe non-spherical shaped nanoparticles will provide better BBB penetration and better magnetic targeting properties. These magnetic nanoparticles will be evaluated for delivery of drug and therapeutic response in a series of patient derived glioblastoma cells. Those nanoparticles with the best response in cell culture will be examined for effectiveness in an animal model of glioblastoma. In addition, the effects of the magnetic nanoparticles on normal cellular function in the brain will be examined. The ultimate goal of these studies is to provide a new method for the safe and effective treatment of brain tumors and potentially other brain related diseases.

column36: Restoring binocular vision in amblyopia by through engagement of stimulus-specific adaptive compensatory mechanisms
column37: Amblyopia is characterized by the loss or attenuation of vision in one eye despite the eye being normal and healthy. Currently, most approaches to understanding amblyopia treat this disorder as one where all vision in the amblyopic eye is suppressed. This idea holds insofar as it describes the main symptoms of amblyopia, but it does not explain the many ways in which vision in the amblyopic eye is integrated with that of the dominant eye. For example, peripheral vision is largely unaffected in amblyopia, as is vision for more blurred patterns or moving patterns. We propose a different paradigm for understanding amblyopia--we propose that amblyopia involves the selective integration of information from the two eyes, a process we call adaptive compensation. The process is adaptive because it requires suppression to be modulated by the specific stimuli present in a given scene, and compensatory because it seeks to make up for vision lost in the amblyopic eye. The adaptive compensatory model explains many features of amblyopia and makes important predictions as to how vision in amblyopia can be improved through training.

column36: Microvascular injury and blood-brain barrier dysfunction as novel biomarkers and targets for treatment in traumatic brain injury
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability around the world. While long-term neurological and cognitive complications and disability are a major concern,to this date there are no means to accurately predict such complications nor therapies for their prevention. An emerging consensus points to the critical importance of including new means for the identification of brain pathological events in order to allow efficient prevention. In this proposal we address this unmet need by investigating traumatic microvascular injury (TMI), an established but understudied TBI pathology with a potential as a candidate diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is a prominent feature of TMI and often obtained in animal TBI models as well as in human pathological specimens. The BBB is a unique structural and functional barrier allowing the normal function of the nervous system. Our previous studies confirmed a direct role for BBB pathology in inducing brain dysfunction and damage. The goals of this research are (1) to test a new imaging approach to detect, localize, and track BBB pathology in animal models of TBI; (2) to test new therapeutics that target TMI and follow BBB pathology; and (3) implement a similar imaging approach in humans to evaluate the prevalence and spatio-temporal dynamics of BBB pathology in human subjects after acute TBI. We strongly believe that the proposed pre-clinical and translational approach will result in the first objective,quantitative and reliable diagnostic approach for the identification of TMI.

column36: Ketone-Mediated Epigenetic Modulation of Mitochondrial Function in Epileptic Brain
column37: Epilepsy is a common neurological problem affecting approximately 1% of the general population. While current medical treatments are effective in two-thirds of patients, there are associated short-term and long-term side-effects of drugs that pose potentially serious health risks. Moreover, the remaining third of patients with epilepsy continue to have seizures that impair quality of life and increase the risk of brain damage and even sudden unexpected death. Hence, there is an urgent need to identify new treatments that can both increase effectiveness, but also minimize undesired side-effects. A remarkable non-drug treatment for difficult-to-control epilepsy is the ketogenic diet, a high-fat and low-carbohydrate regimen that often works when medications fail. While we do not yet fully understand how this diet works, there is increasing evidence that ketone bodies - chemicals produced by the liver as a result of this diet - may be critical players. Specifically, we hypothesize that ketone bodies produce beneficial changes within the energy factories of cells (called "mitochondria") that prevent both seizures and cell death. Our preliminary studies indicate that ketone bodies increase the activity of a specific enzyme family known Sirt3 (i.e., sirtuin 3) and that these enzymes alter the chemical structure of an important protein within the mitochondria called cyclophilin D (or CypD) which helps determine whether cells live or die. The major goal of the proposed studies is to identify the precise mechanism of how ketone bodies produce anti-seizure effects, and in so doing highlight novel targets within mitochondria that can be exploited for the development of better treatments for medically intractable epilepsy. Specific experiments will be conducted to show that the hypothesized mechanism is relevant to multiple types of epilepsy in laboratory models, a necessary step before new treatments emerging from this research can be tested in humans.

column36: Regulation of Neutrophil (PMN) Inflammatory Function by Caspase-8 Phosphorylation
column37: With the widespread availability of antibiotics to kill bacteria, and of intensive care units (ICUs) to support patients with otherwise life-threatening vital organ failure, the major threat to survival for critically ill patients is the adverse effects of the immune response to infection; this deleterious host defense process is called sepsis. Circulating white blood cells called neutrophils (PMNs) play a key role in both the initial response to infection and in the lethal organ injury that results from that response. PMN activity - both beneficial and detrimental - is critically impacted by the capacity of the PMN to undergo cellular suicide through a process called apoptosis. My laboratory has found that the ability of the PMN to undergo apoptosis is regulated by subtle and inducible changes in caspase-8, the enzyme responsible for initiating apoptosis. The simple addition of a phosphate molecule to caspase-8 transforms its function from pro-to anti-apoptotic, and results in the activation of pro-survival and pro-inflammatory mechanisms in the PMN. Our work seeks to understand how this process, known as phosphorylation, is regulated, and how it might be targeted to improve the survival of patients with sepsis. We will first determine the role played by caspase-8 phosphorylation in the initial response of PMN to bacteria and their products. We will then study the mechanisms that support or block the phosphorylation of caspase-8. Finally we will determine how these changes impact key elements of PMN function. Our studies will use PMN from critically ill septic patients to understand mechanisms, and experimental models in zebrafish and mice to study the consequences of modifying the caspase-8 phosphorylation state. In aggregate they will both shed light on a novel mechanism involved in the regulation of inflammation, and provide a rational basis for treatments for sepsis based on accelerating the resolution of inflammation.

column37: Protein molecules are what are created when genetic information is translated into a real world molecular actor that can affect change within a cell. Too much or too little of a protein can harm a cell and lead to diseases such as cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, or autism spectrum disorders. Unfortunately, little is known about how the production of proteins within a cell changes over time and in response to external factors. For example, when a brain cell learns something new, how does the production of specific proteins change? How fast does this happen? Where in the cell does this happen? These experiments will give us unprecedented insight into the inner workings of the most important and final step when a gene is translated into action. Accomplishing this will allow us to understand what happens when protein production goes wrong in a disease state, and what the outcome for the cell is. This will give researchers more accurate targets and knowledge for interventions and therapies for these diseases.

column36: Carotid body potentiation in sleep apnea: identification of novel causes and solutions
column37: Sleep apnea is a serious respiratory disease affecting millions of Canadians. Medical devices for the treatment of sleep apnea continue to improve. However, the ability to comply with device-based treatments over long periods remains mixed. Sensory organs in the neck, the carotid bodies, are likely critical to the pathology of sleep apnea. When breathing is insufficient to supply enough oxygen to the body, these organs tell the brain to increase breathing and deliver more blood to tissues; when the reverse is true, they tell the brain to reduce or stop breathing. Usually, oxygen and carbon dioxide are tightly regulated, but in sleep apnea the carotid bodies become sensitized. This leads to exaggerated breathing responses to changes in oxygenation, destabilizing breathing and causing high blood pressure. Important questions regarding the treatment of sleep apnea patients are thus, why are the carotid bodies sensitized, and how can this be reversed? This proposal addresses both questions with the aim to identify novel and/or repurpose existing drugs to treat sleep apnea. Our preliminary data identify novel mechanisms of carotid body sensitization caused by fluctuating oxygenation and signalling molecules resulting from inflammation, both associated with respiratory disease. In addition, our data suggest that the effects of these mechanisms on carotid body activity can be reversed by somatostatin. This is significant because somatostatin analogues are already approved for treatment of acromegaly, circumventing the most expensive and time-consuming drug development stages. We propose to confirm the above data, investigate receptors involved, and test if somatostatin analogues can be used to treat sleep apnea. This project will help us understand carotid body function and its involvement in respiratory disease. Importantly, this project will also test feasibility of repurposing clinically-approved somatostatin analogues while identifying new targets for drug discovery.

column36: A genome-wide search for exonic variants affecting translational efficiency
column37: Susceptibility or resistance to most common diseases is determined by the type of genes we inherit in our parent's DNA. The DNA is 99.9% identical between any two unrelated individuals and it is the 0.1% that determines differences between individuals. These inherited small variants modify the DNA, the blueprint that determines how our body is built and how it functions. The DNA encodes proteins, the building blocks of the body. The variants sometimes change the protein itself but, more often, what varies among individuals is how much of the protein will be expressed, when and under what stimulus. This is done in many cases by modulating transcription of DNA into RNA. RNA carries the DNA instructions to the ribosomes, the cell's protein-production factory. In 1997, our lab discovered one of the first such effects, of a variant of the insulin gene in type 1 diabetes and now thousands of such effects are known. A much less-well studied level at which genetic variants can determine protein production is the translation of RNA variants into protein. Proteins are much harder to study than RNA but we have developed a method that quantifies how much RNA is associated with ribosomes as an indirect but powerful way of identify proteins whose production is affected by variants in the RNA sequence, and validated it in a small number of subjects. We now propose to apply this method to a much larger sample of individuals to discover all common variants that affect association of RNA with ribosomes. The method will then be validated by using targeted protein quantification using targeted methods of modern proteomics. Significance: Thousands of variants are known to affect susceptibility to various diseases but, to translate this into understanding of disease and therapeutic targets, we need to define the mechanism of the genetic effect.

The establishment of this project, with the CIHR support, will potentially improve outcomes for over one million Canadians affected by cardiac arrhythmias, as well as reduce health care costs and increase industry and job opportunities in Canada.

column36: A New Mechanism Regulating Synapse Function in the Brain
column37: The day to day function of the nervous system depends on the ability of nerve cells to communicate with each other. Neuron-to-neuron communication is possible through synapses, highly specialized structures that allow transfer of information from one cell to another. Synapses are constantly changing and they are dramatically altered in neurodegenerative diseases. A long-term focus of my research program is to understand how synapses are formed, how they change and how they can be maintained in the aging and injured brain. We recently discovered that a family of proteins named netrins is essential for synapse formation during development. Importantly, we also found that netrins are made in the adult brain and play a crucial role regulating memory. Exciting new studies in humans have identified mutations in the genes encoding netrins and netrin receptors in individuals affected by Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings open up the possibility of recovering neuronal function, learning and memory through the modulation of netrin activity. A major roadblock towards this goal is that very little is known about how netrins work in the adult nervous system. To gain an in-depth understanding of how netrins promote synapse function and modulate communication between neurons in the aging and diseased brain, we will identify the consequences of genetic deletion of netrin-1 from neurons in the mouse brain. We will determine if neuronal activity regulates the function of netrin at synapses, and investigate the contribution of these mechanisms to deficits associated with early stages of Alzheimer's disease. My laboratory has developed experimental tools and animal models that place us in a unique position to make groundbreaking discoveries. The proposed studies will create new knowledge of how synapses are maintained and modified and will identify therapeutic targets to prevent loss of function in aging and disease.

column36: Investigate The Role Of mRNP Structure In Translation And RNA Metabolism
column37: In all living organisms, the genetic information stored in DNA is copied into mRNA molecules before translated into proteins, the functional molecules the perform most cellular functions. The flow of information from DNA to RNA and proteins is termed the gene expression pathway and regulating the expression of its genes is an essential task for all cells. Mis-regulation, for instance by mutations in factors acting along the gene expression pathway, results in various pathologies, including cancer predisposition, development and progression and a multitude of neurological disorders. RNA has a central molecule of this process, and consists of a copy of an DNA sequence, forming a long polymer of several hundreds to several thousand nucleotides in length. However, RNA does not exist as a linear molecule but is packaged into a 3D assembly with the help of proteins that bind to RNA. The structural organization of the RNA-protein complexes influences many aspects of what happens with an RNA in cells, including whether an RNA is translated into proteins. For example, the two extremities for an RNA have to be in close proximity to allow translation. Inhibiting this interaction inhibits translation of many RNAs and reduces cell growth, and drugs interfering with this process are used as anti-cancer drugs. Understanding how the cell assures the communication between different regions of these long RNA molecules, however is not understood. Furthermore, in general, we completely lack understanding on the structural organization of the RNA polymer. In this project, we will determine how mRNA molecules are organized and how the binding of proteins to the RNA changes the 3D organization of mRNA molecules. This will reveal important insight into the role of mRNP conformation in regulating translation, sensitivity to anti-cancer drugs and RNA metabolism in general, which, in turn, will allow the development of better tools for diagnosis and treatment.

column37: Studies have shown that radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes following mastectomy and radiotherapy to regional nodes after breast conserving surgery reduces the risk of recurrence and breast cancer mortality in women with node positive breast cancer. column36: Regulation of TGF-beta action in chondrocytes: signaling via ALK1 versus ALK5 pathways
column37: Arthritis refers to several related conditions that affect joints, causing pain, inflammation and swelling. Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and occurs when there is damage in and around the joints, which the body cannot repair. Currently there is no cure for OA and its progression significantly affects an individual's quality of life. OA affects nearly 4.6 million Canadians and is expected to increase to about 7.5 million by 2036. Despite much research effort, the causes and factors involved in OA are not fully understood. Transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta is a protein made in many tissues of the body and there is ample evidence to indicate that its abnormal action in cartilage is involved in the OA disease process. Our research has shown that TGF-beta can have both beneficial and harmful effects on cartilage cells (chondrocytes) depending on the type of "receptor" it uses. In particular, we have shown that TGF-beta will promote healthy cartilage by acting through one type of chondrocytes receptor (known as ALK5) but gives rise to OA-like features when acting through another receptor (ALK1). We have also shown that certain molecules such as TGF-beta co-receptors can influence whether TGF-beta acts through ALK5 or ALK1 receptor. Thus we will examine the role of two co-receptors called endoglin and CD109 in regulating the activity of ALK5 and ALK1. Our goal will be to unravel the mechanism involved in the abnormal action of TGF-beta in chondrocytes and to manipulate the activity of proteins (such as ALK1 and co-receptors) to regulate TGF-beta action, in order to promote cartilage repair. The experiments will be performed using cell and animal models of OA. We expect that findings from the proposed research may lead to the development of innovative therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this debilitating disease.

column36: Characterization of the TGFbeta microRNAome - implications for new biomarkers and therapeutic targets in human cancer
column37: Proteins are synthesized as a result of gene expression and play a critical role in maintaining normal cell function. When expression of proteins is deregulated, diseases such as cancer can arise. We focus on the action of microRNAs (miRNAs), which are micromolecules naturally synthesized by the body and capable of regulating the production of a large proportion of proteins. MicroRNAs are interesting because given the nature of their structure, they are easy to synthesize in a laboratory setting and non-toxic to cells, hence offer a valuable therapeutic option. TGFB is a growth factor capable of promoting or inhibiting critical miRNAs. Indeed, we found that when we expose a cell to TGFB, the expression of these miRNAs changes, and that as a consequence, the expression pattern of proteins within the cell will also change. Interestingly, TGFB can prevent the formation of tumors in healthy cells and early cancers, and promote metastasis (i.e. cancer dissemination) in more advanced cancer cases. With our current research, we want to identify the miRNAs that are regulated by TGFB, and investigate how modulating their expression affects tumor suppression and progression. With our newly acquired knowledge, we will determine if the abundance of our identified miRNAs is of relevance in differentiating between normal versus tumor tissue and between different types of tumors, and if they can be an indication of prognosis or response to treatment. Furthermore, we will investigate their ability to refrain tumor development, growth, and dissemination in live organisms.

column37: Sleep and wake follows a 24hr rhythm, which is controlled by an internal timing system, the circadian clock. We have now identified the timer that generates these rhythms and it critically relies on the brain chemical dopamine, which is known to promote arousal. column36: Resolution of inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity in DLBCL using mass cytometry
column37: Recent work has shown that patients with cancer often have tumors that are composed of several different types of cancer cells, each with a slightly different set of genetic mutations. This variability, or "heterogeneity", means that successful therapy must target not just one, but perhaps several different cancers at the same time. We will use this information to develop a new, cost-effective, same-day test that can be provided to each and every patient and will help doctors to better understand what sort of tumor is present, if and how well the patient's immune system is responding, and what the best treatment options may be.

column36: Adult neurogenesis and delay-based decision making
column37: We are continually faced with choices and must consider the benefits associated with making one particular choice over another. However, we do not always choose the most beneficial option if the payout is very hard to obtain or if we are unsure about its availability. Another cost to consider is the time required to benefit from our actions. Often is it advantageous to forego something that immediately satisfying and wait for something better. For example, despite the short-term pleasure of consuming junk food, we may instead opt for healthy food knowing that the long-term benefits will be greater. Many disorders, such as schizophrenia, depression, drug addiction and Alzheimer's disease are associated with impulsive preference for immediate rewards. We are interested in the possibility that newborn neurons that are added to the adult brain could reduce impulsivity and promote preference for delayed, advantageous rewards. New neurons are continually added to the brain of all animals, including humans. They are largely added to the hippocampus, and they contribute to hippocampal functions in memory but their exact role remains unclear. Current evidence indicates that the hippocampus is important for mentally recreating past experiences and for creating mental representations of possible future experiences. The hippocampus may reduce impulsivity by enabling individuals to envision possible future experiences and choose the behaviors that lead to long-term beneficial outcomes. However, a role for new neurons in impulsivity has never been investigated. To test this role for new neurons we will block neurogenesis in rats and assess their ability to choose a large delayed reward over a small immediate reward. We will also examine how learning to choose delayed rewards activates circuits of new neurons, to see if their functions are different from older neurons. These findings will be important for developing new treatments for disorders of impulsive decision-making.

column37: Rationale: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is one of the most common and debilitating injuries to the knee and many injured patients go on to develop post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA). Follow up assessment of ACL injured individuals and healthy controls will provide the means to identify how these measures interact and clarify the mechanisms of early PTOA progression. column36: Circuit computations of the cortical system for spatial cognition and memory
column37: Many psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases including Dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, and Schizophrenia are characterized by reduced size, metabolic activity, and physiology of hippocampal brain circuits and result in severe memory impairments. These disorders and diseases cause far-reaching negative personal and economic burdens on individuals and their caregivers. Efforts are therefore needed to understand the fundamental principles of how the hippocampal memory systems works in order to guide efforts to restore its function in disease. The set of research aims in this Project Scheme Grant will use state-of-the-art technologies to monitor and control brain activity in freely behaving animals to identify how neuronal circuits in mammalian memory system function. Two key aspects of memory which are often impaired in disease include the ability to recall the location and temporal order of events in our lives. The aims of this grant focus on how the brain's memory system generates representations of space and time in the brain. Animals will perform various behaviors during these recordings, from simple foraging behavior to solving spatial memory tasks. For each experiment, we will use a transgenic mouse and viral strategy to selectively express photo-activated of non endogenous ligand-activated channels in select neuronal populations (i.e. cell type, or specific circuit projection). column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, affecting nearly 50% of Canadians over 80 years of age. With the aging of the population, the prevalence of dementia is expected to increase dramatically, generating major social and economic costs. Amyloid PET imaging has helped establish that vascular risk factors can increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease via pathways that directly related to amyloid pathology. The current research proposal will explore mechanisms by which vascular factors may increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease. More specifically we propose a series of experiments to explore mechanisms by which genetic (e.g. ApoE and other genes related to both Alzheimer's disease and vascular health) and lifestyle risk factors (e.g. hypertension and diet) may impact brain change and memory deficits. This study will be conducted in cognitively normal and mildly impaired individuals with a family history of Alzheimer's disease. The overall goal is to identify new preventive strategies that may delay the onset of Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: etiology involving troponin mutations
column37: Familial hypertrophy cardiomyopathy (FHC) is a congenital heart disease which causes the walls of the heart to thicken (hypertrophy) and disrupts the organization of the heart's contractile machinery. Even though numerous genetic defects (mutations) have been associated with FHC, the underlying cause is not understood. As a result of this disease the heart restructures itself not just on a gross level that can be seen by echocardiography but also on a microscopic level, often resulting in irregularities in contraction and electrical disturbances (arrhythmias). We will explore one of the major hypotheses as to the cause of FHC by making mutations in the molecules (troponin C) which sense the signal (calcium concentration inside the heart cells) that serves as the coupling between cardiac excitation (as seen on an ECG) and contraction. We believe that mutations in the troponin complex which is made up of three protein including troponin C which are associated FHC alter the manner in which molecule interacts with calcium and we will test this hypothesis. We will address the idea that sudden cardiac death in patients with FHC is due to factors which increase the risk for SCD and precede the development of hypertrophy. The work will be undertaken at many different levels of organization from a detailed structural analysis of the thin filament which houses the troponin molecule, all the way to comprehensive studies on possible changes in the structure and function of the heart that occur as a result of the mutations engineered into this molecule. We believe that because sudden cardiac death is often the first symptom of abnormality for these individuals, it is critical to understanding the underlying cause of this disease.

column36: Studies on novel immune-surveillance mechanisms underlying cancer elimination
column37: Cancer is a devastating disease and is the number one killer in Canada. The immune system is the body's primary defence against cancer and is tasked with the elimination of tumour cells. During the emergence of cancerous cells, they can undergo mutations altering their genetic code and enabling the cells to divide rapidly. These cells form the primary tumour that grows in one location of the body and can be medically treated. However, newly formed tumour cells may acquire further mutations that mask them from the immune system. This immunoevasive phenotype allows them to covertly enter the blood and lymph vessels and travel to distant organs. This type of cancer is classified as metastatic upon the successful colonization of these alternative sites in the body. Metastatic cancer is considered the final stage of the disease, and survival of patients with this form of cancer is significantly reduced due to the difficulty of treatment. Recently, researchers have discovered methods that can predict the turning point in cancer where the disease moves from the primary to the metastatic form; by examining the gene mutations that are present in the patient's tumour cells. We have conducted studies on metastatic tumours and have identified a key gene that is involved in metastatic progression. This gene controls the recruitment and activation of a newly described type of white blood cell and our data implies that this novel cell type plays an unidentified role in immunity to cancer cells. This observation has been validated in prostate and kidney cancer patients. Through the use of mouse studies, we will further validate the ability of this gene and the new type of white blood cells it induces, to reduce tumour burden and prevent metastasis. These novel and exciting discoveries will be explored as entirely new immunotherapies for cancer patients and could prevent metastasis.

column36: Transfusion in traumatic brain injury (TSiTBI Trial)
column37: The incidence of anemia (a decrease in the quantity or quality of red blood cells) is frequent among critically ill patients. Because red blood cells, through the molecules of hemoglobin, are oxygen carriers, a decrease in the availability of oxygen to the different organs is often to fear. In patients with traumatic brain injury, mechanisms regulating oxygen delivery to the brain are affected by the injury. The development of anemia may thus potentially worsen lesions to the brain and blood transfusion may correct anemia. However, clinicians are currently restricting the use of blood transfusion in traumatic brain injury making inferences with non brain-injured populations. Few evidence-based data help clinicians treating patients with traumatic brain injury to determine what minimal red blood cell levels (hemoglobin levels) can be tolerated before a blood transfusion is required. This project aims to conduct a pan-canadian multicenter clinical trial to compare a liberal transfusion strategy (transfusion when the red blood cell levels are not too low with the objective to keep it high) to a restrictive transfusion strategy (transfusion when red blood cell levels are low with the objective to keep it low). We believe that liberal transfusion strategy will allow better oxygen delivery to the brain, prevent secondary cerebral lesions and will improve long-term outcomes. This project is part of a vast research program aiming to identify when and under what circumstances should we give red blood cells following traumatic brain injury.

column37: Adolescence is a sensitive period for engagement in health-risk behaviors (e.g., substance use, physical inactivity, poor nutrition, risky sexual activity), which can have life-long repercussions. This project assesses the prominent Dual Systems model of adolescent brain development, which suggests that adolescent sensitivity to health-risk behaviors is due to the asynchrony between an early maturing reward-seeking system (likely due to puberty) and a slower maturing impulse control system. Participants will include 600 boys and girls (ages 8-13 at Year 1) who will be followed for 5 years. Participants will complete an annual self-report survey and a three-year lab component. This project will provide 1) an integrated investigation of the development of youth health-risk behaviors, 2) evidence-based support (or lack of support) for the Dual Systems Model of adolescent brain development and its implications for youth vulnerabilities and opportunities, 3) annual updates of precipitating factors that impact on on health-risk behaviors and brain reactivity over time that are best to target in prevention/intervention programs, such as activities that enhance impulse control and positive lifestyle choices, and 4) a timely and widespread application of findings given the strong team of researchers, partners, and integrated knowledge translation strategies.

column36: New statistical methods for cohort studies of adverse effects of medications
column37: The number of medications available to treat various health problems increases steadily. Most new drugs help improve patients' health, their quality of life and life expectancy, but some may have important unintended side effects while other may be less effective than existing, often less expensive, 'older' medications. Thus, an accurate assessment and comparison of the safety and effectiveness of alternative medications has become one of the primary objectives for both public health agencies and patients' organizations. Accordingly, considerable resources are invested in research attempting to link data on the use of specific medications with both intended and unintended health outcomes. In Canada, such research endeavors are largely facilitated by the existence, in several provinces, of large, administrative databases that contain complete information on both health outcomes and prescriptions received by individual subjects. However, to draw scientifically valid and rigorous conclusions from the analyses of population-based studies of drug safety or effectiveness, we have to address several methodological challenges. For example, patients prescribed a new drug may be more likely to have a more advanced disease and additional risk factors than those not given any drug or prescribed a less expensive older drug. If not accounted for, such differences in the characteristics of drug users may lead to biased results and incorrect conclusions. In addition, differences in the treatment duration and dose of drugs used by different patients, possibly due to treatment non-adherence, may also affect the accuracy of the results. We propose several new statistical methods that will address the above challenges and will permit more accurate assessments of the safety and effectiveness of different drugs used by Canadians. Our new methods may also help designing more rational treatment regimens, to maximize health benefits while reducing the risks of serious adverse events.

column36: Characterization of the genes and gene regulatory mechanisms that control motor neuron stability and neurotransmission in a Drosophila model.
column37: How neurons maintain structural and physiological stability of synapses (contact points) is poorly understood, even though synaptic degeneration is an established hallmark of most neurological disorders. An important clue has come from work in the fruit fly, Drosophila, which revealed that bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) secreted from muscle activate BMP signaling in motor neurons. Loss of BMP signaling (or BMP regulated gene expression) in motor neurons severely destabilizes synaptic morphology and reduces neurotransmission. Follow up work confirmed that BMPs play the same role in mammalian motor neurons, and disrupted BMP signaling has become implicated in motor neuron diseases such as ALS. It is now clear that BMP signaling controls a battery of novel genes required for morphological and physiological stability of motor neuron synapses (and other synapses) from Drosophila to humans. Most of these genes have not been identified. Our preliminary data has taken the first important step by identifying all BMP regulated genes in fly neurons (by RNAseq). With these in hand, this project can now address two, important knowledge gaps: 1) How does BMP signaling control those genes' expression? We will determine which transcription factors, resident in motor neurons, enable the BMP pathway to control gene expression in motor neurons. 2) What is the function of those genes? We will determine the function of ~100 of these novel genes that we postulate play novel conserved roles in synaptic stability of morphology and neurotransmission in humans. We address these questions in Drosophila. The mechanisms under examination are extremely well conserved from Drosophila to humans, and Drosophila offers the only genetic toolset able to complete these goals in 5 years. As this project will reveal how a novel gene network is regulated and deployed to control synaptic stability, our work will revolutionize our ability to combat synaptic degeneration in neurological disorder

column36: Epigenetic Signatures of Successful Aging
column37: Aging is a complex process that involves a host of physiological changes. Approximately 25% of the variation in human lifespan is attributed to genetics, with the remainder proposed as being associated with life style or environmental exposure. Epigenetics is the study of how experiences can "get under the skin" by acting as a mediator between environmental influences and genetics. DNA methylation is the most well studied epigenetic mark, and has the potential to influence how certain genes are turned on or off in association with environmental or life styles exposures, such as stress or smoking. We aim to assess DNA methylation in the longevity population of Costa Rica, the Nicoya Peninsula, to characterize an epigenetic blueprint of healthy aging. Our preliminary pilot study results suggest that age-related DNA methylation trends are different in high longevity populations when compared to individuals from adjacent control regions. We propose to expand our sample size in Nicoya, and investigate two other longevity populations: Sardinia, Italy and Ikaria Greece. We then propose to compare these findings with the DNA methylation profiles of Canadians from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. The characterization of biological aging will not only aid in understanding the etiology of age-related disease but will contribute to eventually extending the number of healthy and mobile years Canadians spend in old age.

column36: Individual differences in autobiographical memory: cognitive, behavioural, and neural correlates and their relationship to aging
column37: The notion that people differ with respect to memory abilities is accepted in the general public. Recently, people with extreme profiles of memory abilities have been discovered. Individuals with highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) have an uncanny ability to access details from personal past events regardless of the nature or importance of the event. Individuals with severely deficient autobiographical memory (SDAM) have normal learning and memory for factual information, but do not recollect details of personal events at all. These extreme memory syndromes may reflect the ends of a normal continuum of memory abilities that would be expected based on introspection and comparison with others. Yet when studying memory, researchers calculate averages across groups of people, ignoring such individual differences. In this research, we will contrast groups of individuals with HSAM and SDAM to better understand the nature of their memory function. We will test specific hypotheses regarding memory abilities and their relationship to brain structure and function that will shed light on the entire range of memory ability, not just the extremes. We will also examine how individual differences in autobiographical memory play out with aging. Memory impairment is among the commonest cognitive complaints in aging and is considered a cardinal sign of neurodegenerative disease, such as Alzheimer's disease. Yet no one has examined how such complaints and abilities relate to individual differences in autobiographical memory. It may be that individuals with high or low autobiographical memory abilities have differential susceptibility to aging and neurodegenerative effects. This research will contribute to the creation of new memory assessment tools that will be important to diagnosis and intervention in individuals with memory changes due to aging or age-related disorders.

column36: Refugee integration and long-term health outcomes in Canada
column37: Canada provides protection to refugees from overseas through two different programs. In one, the government selects and supports refugees for the first year of settlement: government assisted refugees (GARs). In the other, support is provided by volunteer groups: private sponsored refugees (PSRs). Private sponsorship is unique to Canada but is of increasing interest internationally. Yet, despite resettling a third of refugees as PSRs, there is little research comparing GAR and PSR effectiveness in supporting the integration of refugees into society. Resettled refugees have poorer health than host populations. Studies show that social integration affects wellness but we do not have much research examining how the experiences of settlement and integration contribute to the long-term health of refugees. Refugees face unique challenges prior to migration, including exposure to trauma, prolonged uncertainty, hazardous living conditions, and disrupted education trajectories. In the short-term, security, less hazardous living conditions, and access to health services result in improvements in resettled refugees' health. However, research with other immigrant groups in Canada shows that in the long term, health and well-being are affected by newcomers' sense of inclusion, respect and belonging in their new country. Thus, early improvements in refugee health may be followed by deterioration if social integration is not successful. This pan-Canadian study will compare how GAR and PSR resettlement programs support long-term social integration pathways for refugees and the impact of these pathways on physical and mental health. We will collect data from adult resettled refugees arriving between 2015 and 2017 in 3 of Canada's largest refugee resettlement provinces: British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec. By understanding what leads to successful outcomes we can improve refugee settlement services and policies, and ultimately the health and well-being of refugees.

column37: The immune system plays an important role in discriminating between molecules that are foreign, such as those in bacteria and viruses, and molecules that are normal parts of the body (self). Foreign molecules are attacked while self-molecules are normally left unharmed. We believe that Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (lupus) results from defects in the immune system that lead to abnormal activation of cells that react to self-molecules, resulting in production of autoantibodies that attack the body's organs. In the immune system two classes of cells, T and B cells, act in concert to mount an immune response. In many strains of mice that develop lupus, B cell functional abnormalities play a central role in the pathogenesis of disease. In our previous work, we found several B cell functional abnormalities in human lupus, consistent with this possibility. In addition, we found that lupus patients had increased proportions of B cells in their blood that had features suggesting that they were specific for self-molecules. These blood changes result in part from the presence of inflammatory molecules in the blood of lupus patients that alter B cell function. However genetic factors are also proposed to play an important role in the development of lupus, and a number of genes that promote lupus are predicted to alter B cell function. In this grant we will examine how genetic factors and pro-inflammatory molecules perturb B cell function to promote production of autoantibodies. This will be done by examining genetically manipulated mice with changes that mimic those seen with lupus genes and mice with high levels of the pro-inflammatory factors similar to those seen in lupus patients. We will also investigate the impact of these changes and factors on human B cell function. Identification of the underlying causes for the altered B cell function and production of autoantibodies in lupus will allow us to develop better therapies for this condition.

column37: Proper brain function relies on a precise balance of excitatory and inhibitory information exchanged between nerve cells. Inhibitory nerve cells play a special role in this balance by modulating the electrical activities of other nerve cells and coordinating the activities of brain networks. Defects in the development or function of inhibitory nerve cells are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders such as epilepsies, schizophrenia and autisms. The root causes and long-term consequences of inhibitory dysfunction in the developing brain are unknown. This research proposal investigates how inhibitory nerve cells develop and establish an excitatory-inhibitory balance, and how defects in these events cause brain circuit dysfunction and behavioral deficits. Using this knowledge, we can learn how excitatory/inhibitory imbalances cause neurodevelopmental disorders, and offer better treatments and therapeutic options to restore this balance in brain function.

column37: Forty percent of patients that require dialysis for kidney failure die within three years mostly due to heart disease. In patients without kidney disease, spironlactone reduces heart scarring which reduces heart related deaths and hospitalizations. Kidney failure appears to trigger progressive changes in the heart that lead to heart scarring and ultimately heart related deaths. It therefore makes sense that spironolactone will help patients with kidney failure. Although spironolactone is promising, there are no large studies to tell us if it helps patients live longer or better lives. In addition, current dialysis does not effectively clear all toxins from the blood the way natural kidneys do. Some of the molecules that are not cleared build up and can affect the blood vessels and the heart. A new type of dialysis filter, the Theranova, effectively clears many of these potential toxins. However, it is not clear if removing these toxins will improve patient's lives or if there are potential negative consequences. We will perform a large study in several countries that will give physicians and patients the information they need to determine if spironolactone or the Theranova reduces heart related deaths and hospitalizations and/or reduce the symptoms of dialysis. We call this study the Aldosterone antagonism and enhanced Clearance for Health Improvement EValuation in End-stage renal disease (ACHIEVE).
