column36: Analysis of the Anabolic Activity of Hormones Regulating Skeletal Metabolism
column37: One of the most common causes of disability and death during aging is metabolic bone disease, which includes osteoporosis, bone disease due to cancer, hyperparathyroidism, and osteomalacia. We are studying three major hormones, parathyroid hormone (PTH), PTH related peptide (PTHrP), and vitamin D which regulate normal bone metabolism, but can also contribute to the development and progression of metabolic bone disease. Calcium itself can act as a hormone by interacting with a calcium sensing receptor (CaSR), which has been identified in several tissues including parathyroid (which produces PTH), kidney and bone. Activation of CaSR can lower PTH and CaSR activators, called calcimimetics have been developed to control hyperparathyroidism. Although continuously high levels of blood PTH, as occur in hyperparathyroidism, can destroy (resorb) bone (producing "catabolic" effects), in contrast, intermittent PTH administration forms bone (an "anabolic" effect) and is therefore used in osteoporosis therapy. Vitamin D has also been reported to have both anabolic and catabolic effects on bone but the precise mechanism is also unclear. Wnt is a growth factor which is a potent stimulator of bone formation, and can be inhibited by a bone-derived protein called sclerostin. Our goal is to understand how PTH, PTHrP and vitamin D exert their anabolic effects on bone. We will use genetically modified mouse models to examine the ways PTH and PTHrP act to form bone, determine if CaSR activation can influence the anabolic effects of PTH on bone, and determine if vitamin D stimulates bone by interacting with sclerostin. These studies should improve our understanding of how these hormones influence bone, and how to develop improved anabolic therapies for important diseases of the skeleton.

column36: Determining the role of histone modifications in mediating transcriptional consistency in beta-cells and in diabetes pathogenesis
column37: During the development of type 2 diabetes immune cell induced inflammation and metabolic stress induce insulin secreting beta-cells to lose their normal functionality. In part this is because the beta-cells have reduced levels or critical genes that help maintain them as fully functional cells. Restoring the levels of these critical genes can restore beta-cell functionality and is a possible therapeutic approach to treating type 2 diabetes. Despite this the mechanisms by which the levels of these factors become reduced in beta-cells during T2D progression is not clear. Our recent data shows that the structure of the chromatin around these genes plays a key role in regulating their expression, which dictates the levels they are present in in the cell. Specifically, we have found a unique type of modification that can occur to the chromatin can help reduce the variability of a genes expression in different cells, as genes with these modifications have reduced cell to cell variability than genes that do not have it. However, we find that in patients with T2D genes with these modifications become just as variably expressed as genes without these modifications. This not only results in an overall reduction in the levels of these genes in the beta-cells of T2D patients, but also means that some beta-cells exist in these patients with much lower levels than the average. We believe these cells become highly dysfunctional, and are a critical component of how T2D progresses. In this work we intend to determine how age and T2D increase transcriptional variability in beta-cells in both mouse models and in humans. We will assess whether these factors directly affect the chromatin modifications we believe control gene expression variability, and generate mouse models to understand the role these modifications play in maintaining normal gene expression. This work stands to generate significant novel insight into T2D progression, and may implicate novel therapeutic approaches.

column36: Dissecting NF1 signaling in melanoma
column37: Unlike the majority of cancers where the rate of newly diagnosed cases and deaths are declining, melanoma rates have been increasing significantly in both men and women. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in Canada, and in 2015, melanoma was responsible for 70% of skin cancer-related deaths. Much progress has been made in the development of treatment options for melanoma patients based on basic science discoveries. For example, from focused gene sequencing studies, we know melanoma is caused by mutations in two genes, BRAF and NRAS, that lead to uncontrolled growth of melanocytes in about 70% of patients. These findings led to the development of targeted therapies, so-called "smart drugs", designed against BRAF and targeting NRAS in an indirect way. Unfortunately, many patients that are given these "smart drugs" eventually develop resistance. Furthermore, targeted therapy options for patients that lack BRAF and NRAS mutations are limited. In contrast, other immune-based therapy that harness the power of a patient's immune system have shown incredible clinical utility for melanoma patients. However, over 50% of melanoma patients do not have durable long-term responses to immune therapy. It is still unclear why some patients respond to immune therapy and why others do not. With the advent of next generation sequencing technology, we recently gained the ability to sequence all genes in many melanoma patient samples. Our studies revealed half of patients that lack mutations in BRAF and NRAS possess mutations in a gene called NF1. However, it is still unclear how we can use this information in the clinic to treat patients. Our preliminary work suggests that NF1 regulates components of the immune system that may have implications for immune therapy response. The goal of this project is to understand how NF1 promotes melanoma and modulates the response to immune therapy, as well as to develop novel therapeutic strategies to treat this melanoma subtype.

column36: Molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern the development of cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM)
column37: Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCM, also referred to as Cavernous Angiomas) are dilations that form mainly in the blood vessels of the brain. CCM are surprisingly common, with roughly 0.5% (1 in 200) of the population having at least one such lesion. CCM result in leaky vessels that can lead to symptoms ranging from a mild headache to seizure and even hemorrhagic stroke. A CCM diagnosis can only be achieved at present via detailed MRI, something a patient would not have until the symptoms have become very severe. The only "treatment" available at present is surgical removal of CCM, however in severe cases lesions are either not accessible to surgery or they are too numerous to remove. Because CCM are diagnosed late, we do not understand how they first arise and then develop to full-blown leaky lesions. This knowledge is critical to designing therapies that can prevent worsening or new development of CCM in patients or people from at-risk families. To address this, we will use complementary approaches in roundworm (C. elegans) and vertebrate (zebrafish) animal models to dissect the events that lead to CCM. C. elegans is a genetic powerhouse, which has been used to discover many genetic pathways that regulate human development and disease, notably cancer. Zebrafish have a brain vasculature much like our own, and as their embryos are transparent, we can use microscopy to watch the vasculature at high resolution as disease develops in real time. Using C. elegans and zebrafish, we will uncover the key players in CCM disease progression, identify what goes wrong in vascular cells in CCM, and examine the ability of different interventions to stop CCM onset and progression. This will lay the foundation for future clinical work aimed at preventing severe neurological damage in patients suffering from CCM.

column36: Reactivation of occult hepadnaviral infection and hepatitis in the woodchuck model of hepatitis B
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) belongs to the most deadly human microbes. It causes life-threatening liver diseases, such as chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis and liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). More than 2 billion people (~1/3 of global population) show evidence of HBV infection, while 240-370 million have symptomatic chronic hepatitis B of which up to one million die annually. In Canada, ~270,000 individuals have chronic hepatitis B. We discovered that, in addition to symptomatic infection, HBV in humans and woodchuck hepatitis virus (WHV) in woodchucks cause asymptomatic (occult) chronic infection that can also culminate in development of HCC. This occult infection under certain conditions, like immunosuppression or anti-cancer therapy, can reactivate and cause sever hepatitis, liver failure and death. The mechanisms of this reactivation are unknown. Because HBV infects only humans and higher primates and the caused liver disease cannot be studied in cultured cells, the use of an appropriate animal model is essential. We developed a unique research facility at Memorial University in which woodchucks susceptible to WHV infection are studied. We also devised models of occult HBV infection in woodchucks. In this study, we want to reactivate occult infection in woodchucks by commonly used drugs, such as dexamethasone (corticosteroid) and a drug against rheumatoid arthritis and B cell lymphoma. We want to identify factors that predispose to development of severe hepatitis in occult infection and molecular mechanisms involved. By doing so, we can learn how to predict if reactivation may occur and what to do to prevent it. Also, the preclinical model for testing of new drugs for their HBV reactivation abilities will be established. In addition, we will learn about mechanisms of reactivation of other silent (latent) viral infections which complicate current treatments.

column36: Improving Clinical Decision Making for Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects 1 in 10 Canadian adults, and can lead to kidney failure requiring dialysis. In most cases, CKD remains stable, and can be safely managed by a family doctor. However, for some patients, it can progress quickly and needs specialist care. In 2011, we developed an equation that accurately identifies patients at the highest risk of progression. We are now proposing national studies that will test how our equation can be integrated in patient care. First, we want family doctors to use the equation to talk to their patients about their risk of kidney failure and how to reduce it. Doctors will use the equation to determine whether a patient needs to see a kidney specialist or not. Second, we want kidney specialists to use the equation to plan for dialysis or transplantation, but only for patients at the highest risk of kidney failure. These studies will help ensure patients are involved in making health care decisions with their doctor and will help provide clinical care specific to each patient. In the next 5 years, these studies will transform care for CKD in Canada and beyond our borders.

column37: Bipolar disorder is a severe psychiatric illness that runs in families and onsets in adolescence - a critical time of brain and emotional development. Bipolar disorder is likely the result of a number of susceptibility genes triggered by exposure to multiple social, psychological, and biological risk factors. At the end of this study, we will be able to develop a predictive model - a first of its kind - that will estimate the likelihood and timing of illness in individuals with variable sets of risk factors. We will also collect saliva and blood samples for future studies of changes in gene activity associated with risk exposure and illness onset. This information will improve identification of individuals at familial risk who are most likely to develop mood disorders and advance the development of specific innovative preventative and early intervention approaches. Ultimately, this work will result in a major leap forward in understanding genetically-mediated causal pathways leading to bipolar disorder and help to change the trajectory of this illness through informing strategies to prevent onset and progression.

column36: Small nucleolar RNAs as regulators of gene expression
column37: Small RNAs form several large families of biomolecules emerging as essential regulators of fundamental cellular processes. While miRNAs, a large family of cytoplasmic small RNAs regulating transcript stability on widespread levels, have been extensively characterized, nuclear small RNAs are also emerging as fundamental regulators performing varied roles. The conserved family of small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a group of such nuclear small RNAs. SnoRNAs have been well-characterized as guiding the chemical modification of ribosomal RNAs, an important step in ribosome biogenesis and ultimately in protein synthesis. However, over the past 5 years, many independent reports have identified specific snoRNAs as involved in diverse other functions ranging from the maturation of pre-messenger RNAs to the response to stress in the cytoplasm. By analysis of deep-sequencing datasets of small RNAs of several human cell lines, we identified groups of snoRNAs differing in terms of their protein binding preferences and terminal sequences, suggesting they could play different regulatory roles in the cell. In light of these recent findings, we propose to characterise specific families and subgroups of small RNAs and to define their role in the regulation of essential nuclear processes, using computational and experimental methods. Many small RNAs display significantly deregulated expression in cancer and a subset have been shown to play an important role in cancer development and maintenance. This study will shed light on a large group of nuclear regulators of gene expression that have been generally ignored in this role, significantly increasing our understanding of the multi-layered regulation of gene expression.

column36: Telephone-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Post-Operative Bariatric Surgery Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Bariatric (weight loss) surgery is the most effective treatment for extreme obesity, but surgery does not treat underlying psychological and behavioural issues. Implications: If Tele-CBT is found to improve bariatric surgery outcomes, it could become the standard of care in Canadian bariatric surgery programs and beyond, and be routinely offered to patients who cannot feasibly attend CBT sessions due to physical or practical barriers.

column36: Consequences of ultraviolet light-induced aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling on intestinal immunity
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) affect 1 in 150 Canadians, one of the highest incidences worldwide. The AhR is abundant in several organs, including the gut, and is implicated in protection against IBD. The capacity of the AhR to be activated by molecules of dietary and environmental origin may be key to its protective actions in IBD. We have compelling evidence that molecules produced in skin by moderate UV exposure activate the AhR in several peripheral organs including the gut and influence immune signaling. We will also study the effects of activation of the AhR on microbial components of the gut. Our working hypotheses are that (i) moderate UV exposure produces molecules that act to reinforce immune signaling by the AhR in peripheral organs, and (ii) that AhR signaling induced by cutaneous UV exposure influences the microbial composition of the intestine. column36: Transient disruption of blood-testis barrier for efficient delivery of spermatogonial stem cells to their niches: Toward a novel fertility restoration strategy for boys with cancer
column37: Recent research progress has made many types of cancer curable. This development led to a new situation where the post-cancer quality of life became a significant concern for cancer patients. Preservation of the ability to have children draws a particular interest in the patients, and their partners and families. For male patients, the only approach to protect their fertility is currently sperm banking. This approach, however, is not applicable to boys before puberty. Thus, childhood cancer patients face a significant risk of infertility, long before they are ready to make decisions about childbearing and household formation, which also places burdens on their parents. An emerging concept of therapeutic approach to this problem is based on sperm-making stem cells. These cells continuously produce millions of sperm everyday throughout life after puberty. Although sperm production is not fully functional in prepubertal boys, these sperm-producing stem cells do exist from the time of birth. Thus, these cells can be harvested and freeze-stored before cancer therapy, and transplanted back to the patients afterwards when they are ready to form a family. Our research aims at improving the efficiency of transplanting these cells toward making our novel approach a clinical reality.

column36: Activation of Pyruvate Kinase M2 as a Novel Therapy for Chemotherapy-Induced Cardiotoxicity
column37: Chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity (CIC) is a very common complication of many anti-cancer agents and although cancer therapies maybe suppressing tumor growth, these patients begin to develop heart failure. Therefore, a better understanding of the signalling pathways involved in CIC are desperately needed, as there are currently no therapies that prevent the onset of this condition and most patients eventually die of either cancer or heart failure. One of the challenges in designing appropriate therapies to prevent CIC is selectively protecting the heart without preventing the benefits of cancer therapies against tumors. An intriguing difference between the heart and the tumor environments are the levels of oxygen (the molecule we breathe and required for life). The heart is present in an area of high oxygen levels, while the tumor can survive in areas of low oxygen. Therefore, screening for oxygen-sensitive proteins that may be induced by CIC agents in the heart may provide targetable therapies that are selective to the heart, without interfering with the anti-cancer effects of promising cancer therapies in the tumor. We have identified a candidate oxygen-sensitive protein called pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) that is induced in the heart by CIC agents. Intriguingly, drugs that activate PKM2 has previously been shown to suppress tumor growth, however, PKM2 function in the heart remains elusive. We show that activating PKM2 in the heart, where oxygen levels are high protects against CIC, but maintains and in some cases even enhances cancer therapy-mediated regression of the tumor, where oxygen levels are low. The therapeutic implications of this project may provide drug discovery platforms that could directly prevent CIC, which are desperately needed, but may also be applicable to other metabolic pathologies, including other forms of heart failure, cancer and diabetes.

column36: Mechanism of Ribosomal RNA Gene Silencing and Its Roles in Pluripotency and Cancer
column37: Building the cell's protein factories is a complex job involving many hundreds of components and takes up much of a cell's efforts to grow. For cancers to grow, they must find ways to make more of these protein factories than surrounding normal tissues. So, if we could find ways to limit the manufacture the protein factories, known as ribosomes, we could control cancer. In fact, we have recently demonstrated that targeting the genes that make the RNAs of the ribosome kills cancer cells while leaving normal cells untouched. Several "tumour suppressor" proteins prevent cancer by doing just this. For example, the ARF and TP53 tumour suppressors are very important in limiting ribosome production and either or both are inactivated in 80% of cancers. We recently discovered that highly proliferative cancer cells show an unusual "epigenetic silencing" of the Ribosomal RNA genes. Epigenetic silencing is one means by which genes are selectively inactivated to establish different tissues such as skin, bone, blood, intestine, etc. We found that silencing of the Ribosomal RNA genes is lost in some cancer cells and closely resembles the situation in the embryonic stem cells that will create all the different tissues of the body. We discovered some years ago that the ARF tumour suppressor regulates a protein called TTF1. This protein is known to determine epigenetic silencing of the Ribosomal RNA genes. We hypothesize that the changes in ribosomal RNA gene silencing may allow pre-cancerous cells to grow rapidly, but more importantly cause the type of chromosome rearrangements that lead to full-blown cancer. Our lab. is trying to understand how this happens in the hope of discovering novel and more effective ways of treating cancer.

column37: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is characterized by weakening of the abdominal aortic vessel wall and the formation of blood-filled, balloon-like bulges. Rupture of these bulges can cause severe internal bleeding, leading to a collapse of the circulatory system and ultimately death. 50-85% of patients with ruptured AAA die before reaching the hospital, yet management of disease remains limited to surveillance and surgical intervention. AAA is characterized by accumulation of white blood cells in the aortic wall, however, the molecular and cellular processes that cause this inflammation are incompletely understood. Our research will focus on macrophages, a white blood cell that drives AAA formation. We will utilize a comprehensive approach that includes novel, clinically relevant preclinical models and state of the art technology. Knowledge generated through our research will guide the development of novel treatment strategies to prevent and, possibly, cure established disease.

column36: Structural and Functional MRI Assessment of Treatment Response in Early Cystic Fibrosis Lung Disease
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common genetic disorder affecting children and young adults in Canada. While life expectancy for CF patients has improved in recent decades, recurrent and persistent infections are major causes of lung function decline that ultimately lead to death. New treatments are becoming available that can slow the long term rate of decline in lung function. However, conventional breathing tests often look normal in young patients with early CF lung disease and cannot be used reliably to determine if the treatment is working. Therefore, the medical community needs tests that can better assess the lungs of young CF patients, especially to follow the effects of treatment. A picture taken of the lungs, or medical imaging test, would allow doctors to see and properly treat the lungs of children with CF at an early stage, before disease is severe. X-ray imaging is one such approach but is generally not able to measure the effects of CF treatments and also involves unwanted radiation, a particular concern for repeated scans in younger patients. In this proposal, we will investigate a novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique called xenon-MRI (Xe-MRI). Xe-MRI provides clear pictures inside of the lungs and involves no radiation so can be used repeatedly in children. Xe-MRI has been used successfully to diagnose several lung diseases but has not yet been investigated for monitoring lung disease treatment in children with CF. We will test the ability of Xe-MRI to detect improvements following treatment of early CF lung disease, not demonstrated by conventional breathing tests. By showing that Xe-MRI is useful for detecting and following the treatment of early CF lung disease, this test could also be used for the development of new improved treatments for children with CF in future. Furthermore, this test would likely also be useful for assessing other lung diseases such as asthma.

column36: Perineuronal nets in medial prefrontal cortex: roles in the pathophysiology associated with schizophrenia
column37: According to the Canadian Mental Health Association, 20% of Canadians will experience mental illness at some points during their lives. Schizophrenia is one mental illness that is particularly costly given its typical onset in early adulthood and persistence throughout life. Research supports the hypothesis that changes in brain circuits including those in areas of the cerebral cortex are involved in schizophrenia. However, how activity within and among these brain areas is altered is not well understood. Recent evidence suggests that reduced expression of perineuronal nets, structures in the tissue around cells that ensheath certain kinds of neurons, may contribute to brain dysfunction. The present proposal explores this connection using rodent models. Our series of experiments will assess the expression of perineuronal nets over the course of development in a well characterized rat model of maternal immune activation. Maternal immune activation (i.e. serious illness during pregnancy) is a risk factor for the development of schizophrenia in children, and this model results in behaviour in rat offspring consistent with schizophrenia. We have collected exciting preliminary data suggesting that perineuronal nets are reduced in the prefrontal cortex of offspring exposed to maternal immune activation while in utero. These changes are restricted to adulthood when the expression of perineuronal nets normally peaks and the symptoms of schizophrenia are expressed. In the second phase of the project, we will assess the effects of degrading perineuronal nets in prefrontal cortex using behavioural, electrophysiological, and imaging techniques. The long-term implications of this study may contribute to both new therapeutic strategies combatting the symptoms of schizophrenia, as well as interventions that prevent the loss of perineuronal nets following adverse events during development.

column36: Molecular underpinnings of pharmacology associated with G-Protein-Coupled Receptor Activation
column37: 40% of pharmaceuticals target G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a class of membrane proteins which regulate vision, sensory- and neurotransmitter-mediated response, inflammation, and signalling across cell membranes. GPCRs are often imagined as molecular switches whose intracellular topology is primed for activation upon binding of a ligand to an extracellular drug pocket. The adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) is a prototypical GPCR and one of the most important drug targets in inflammation, cancer, sickle cell disease, diabetes, and brain disorders such as Parkinson's disease. Activation mechanisms and drug response of A2AR can be understood using a spectroscopic technique called NMR which allows us to "visualize" inactive states, intermediates, and specific active states all at once. Thus, the effect of a new drug or lead compound can be immediately understood in terms of the distribution of states that result and are seen by NMR. We also present new ways of studying GPCR activation by NMR of either the ligand, the receptor, allosteric species such as metals, or the G protein binding protein. Armed with this new methodology we plan to advance our understanding of many nuances of A2AR activation and add to our arsenal of drug discovery methods in this important Parkinson's target.

column36: Targeting molecular scaffolds for the treatment of obesity and metabolic disease
column37: As a risk factor for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, obesity has been steadily increasing in society at alarming rates. Approximately 25% of Canadians are either over-weight or obese. Anti-obesity therapies have varying degrees of effectiveness, but no therapies actually target fat cells, which are key in the development of obesity. Fat cells, or adipocytes, grow through a complicated roadmap of signals that need precise direction. It is currently not known what are the proteins in fat cells that direct these signals needed for fat cell growth, but specialized proteins called molecular scaffolds could be the key players. One type of molecular scaffolds are 14-3-3 proteins, which we previously found to control the growth of fat cells in mice. We previously studied one member of 14-3-3 proteins, 14-3-3zeta, and mice that were genetically modified to have no 14-3-3zeta in all cells had less fat than normal mice. When mice were made to have more 14-3-3zeta in every cell, they actually gained more weight when fed food high in fat. It has been found that fat samples from obese individuals have higher levels of 14-3-3zeta. Combined with our mouse data, this raises the question of whether having more 14-3-3zeta in fat cells is enough to promote the development of obesity. Therefore, the aim of this proposal is to see if 14-3-3zeta can be a suitable target in the fat cell for treating obesity. This will be tested in mice that do not have 14-3-3zeta in their fat cells and to see if this protects them from developing obesity. Studies will also try to understand what 14-3-3zeta does in a fat cell and also if new drugs can be developed to block the actions of 14-3-3zeta in fat cells. Collectively, these studies will examine if 14-3-3zeta can be a suitable drug target to treat obesity, which continues to grow at alarming rates throughout the world.

column36: Discovery, validation, and pre-clinical development of novel strategies to prevent anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.
column37: Background: A staggering 42% of childhood cancer patients develop disabling/life-threatening adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Anthracyclines are widely used for the treatment of ~70% of adult and childhood cancers. However, anthracyclines cause serious heart damage in 5-16% of patients, resulting in death or life-long disability. Currently prevention is limited to reducing the dose of anthracyclines or using a second drug to protect the heart, dexrazoxane. However, dose reduction reduces anti-cancer effectiveness and dexrazoxane is restricted to adult patients with advanced cancer receiving high anthracycline doses, and dexrazoxane is not approved for use in pediatric patients due to risks of secondary cancers. Our goal is to prevent anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We identified that the RARG gene is related to anthracycline-cardiotoxicity in a large children's cancer study (Nat Gen, 2015). Building upon these findings, we will pursue two prevention strategies: 1. Develop a novel cardioprotectant that disrupts the RARG pathway. We will screen a panel of targeted drugs in a human cardiac cells, followed by evaluation in well-established animal models of anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We have now demonstrated proof-of-principle for 2 drugs exhibiting up to 95% cardioprotection in cultured cardiac cells and these were more effective than dexrazoxane. 2. Identify new genetic risk factors to pre-emptively identify patients at higher risk of anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We have collected DNA from a large group of adult patients for high-throughput genomic analyses. We will combine pediatric and adult studies to improve the study. Validated factors will be incorporated into a predictive test and explored as additional candidates for strategy #1. Expected Outcomes: A new safe and effective anthracycline-cardioprotectant will be primed for clinical evaluation in patients. New genetic risk factors will be transitioned to a clinical testing program.

column36: Mechanisms of insulin resistance in podocytes and diabetic nephropathy
column37: Clinically evident kidney failure eventually develops in patients with type 1 (T1D) and type 2 (T2D) diabetes, and continues to progress despite receiving intensified glycemic control and renal protective drugs. Moreover, up to now, we have only a diffuse understanding of why some diabetic patients develop nephropathy whereas other patients never progress to dialysis. Elevated glucose and saturated fat (FFA) levels may cause local factor changes affecting podocyte survival, an important vascular cell in kidney, which are not easily reversed. I made a very interesting finding on a potential target called SHP-1 that is elevated with high glucose concentrations in diabetic kidney of rodent animals. SHP-1 is a member of the protein tyrosine phosphatase family that downregulates the activity of important growth factors such as insulin, VEGF and nephrin, which are crucial for podocyte survival and function. Interestingly, insulin resistance caused by FFA is triggered by the activation of the protein kinase C (PKC)-alpha. Thus, unwanted abnormalities of renal podocyte function causing insulin resistance in T1D and T2D can be regulated by the activation of two independent pathways: SHP-1 and PKC-alpha. The aim of the present proposal will characterize and explore the role of SHP-1 and PKC-alpha activation producing biological abnormalities such as podocyte death and insulin resistance. To accomplish this aim, we will use several methods to specifically manipulate the protein expression level of SHP-1 and PKC-alpha in podocyte cell line and evaluate their impact on insulin and nephrin actions. Moreover, I will use genetically modified tissue specific mice of SHP-1 to characterize its cellular mechanisms implicated in diabetic nephropathy using a T1D and T2D mouse models. We believe that this proposal will help us better understand the mechanisms underlying renal cell dysfunction related to kidney failure in T1D and T2D.

column36: Neural circuitry for detection of texture boundaries
column37: Our rich and effortless perception of the complex mixtures of objects and surfaces comprising our everyday world is one of the most remarkable achievements of the human brain. A key early step in the required neural processing is separation of the retinal image into regions corresponding to distinct surfaces of different objects. In natural images we can effortlessly perform such "figure-ground segmentation" of borders defined by differences in a variety of local image properties, for example differences in luminance, colour, contrast, or texture. This segmentation process necessarily precedes higher-level visual functions such as object recognition, and is fundamentally important to normal visual perception. Analysis of complex visual patterns begins in the early visual cortex, areas V1 and V2. The responses of single neurons in these cortical areas are highly specific, or "tuned", to particular kinds of visual stimuli. An understanding of the nature of stimulus selectivity of these neurons forms a critical basis of our current understanding of human visual perception. This research program has three specific objectives: to evaluate and extend our recently discovered model of the neural circuitry for detecting luminance and texture boundaries in early visual cortex; to explore whether there might be two different kinds of such neural processing; and to examine the relationship to detection of colour boundaries. The outcomes of this work will yield fundamental, health-related knowledge that may facilitate the future design of diagnostic tests and therapies for visual disorders.

column36: Microparticles in Diabetes
column37: People with diabetes are far more likely to suffer a heart attack than nondiabetics. Diabetes causes changes to the blood vessels and this is believed to responsible for the increased risk of heart attacks and stroke. This project seeks to expand our understanding of how diabetes causes damage to the blood vessels. Microparticles are tiny pieces of cells that are released from dying cells in the body. Recently it has been found that the levels of microparticles in the blood are increased significantly in diabetes. Increased microparticles can predict a risk of a heart attack or death due to heart problems. The goal of this project is to determine how microparticles are formed in diabetes and how they may cause damage to blood vessels. We anticipate that by understanding the proteins carried by microparticles and the signaling that microparticles activate in diabetes we will be able to develop new drug treatments that can be used to reduce risk of heart and kidney problems in diabetes.

column36: Functional organization of the human brain for colour and form vision: from LGN to extrastriate cortex.
column37: The understanding of human colour vision is a challenge that has interested scientists for over 300 years. The core of the problem is to understand how the spectral differences across the visual scene in the physical world are translated by the brain into the neural signals that represent the wide array of colours that we see in our perceptual world; in other words, how the human brain sees in colour. It is well known that there are two major subdivisions in the human visual system. The dorsal pathway is dedicated to visual guidance of our actions and motion through the visual world, whereas the ventral pathway encodes what we see in terms of the shapes and objects in the visual scene. In this proposal I investigate the role of the ventral pathway in the encoding of form and colour. I aim to identify which pathways and brain areas are used to encode colour as compared to the achromatic (black & white) components of the visual image, and how colour, form and shape analyses are combined within the brain. The research uses the latest techniques, including fMRI of the human brain and brain stimulation (TMS), to identify how the brain regions and pathways are functionally organized to deconstruct the visual image and then reform it into global percepts, enabling us to see the coloured version of the visual world that we so easily take for granted.

column36: Efficacy and Safety of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in patients with mild vascular cognitive impairment
column37: Despite promising leads, to date clinical trials of medications to halt or reverse dementia have failed. Consequently, treatment interventions for dementia are now focusing on those with cognitive problems who are at high risk of progressing, to intervene before there is irreversible damage to the brain. Cognitive problems are common in patients with heart disease and those who experience cognitive difficulties are more likely to develop dementia. While exercise can help many people maintain cognition, many people do not achieve cognitive benefits. Our research has provided the first evidence that oxidative stress may limit the benefits of exercise on brain function and cognition. Recent research suggests that reducing oxidative damage in the brain may possibly be an effective way to prevent the brain changes that lead to the cognitive deficits and functional impairment in dementia. N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a widely available and safe supplement, has powerful antioxidant effects, which may be beneficial to boost cognition. This study will test whether the antioxidant supplement NAC is safe and effective to improve cognition in patients with heart disease who show early memory problems, known as vascular cognitive impairment-no dementia (VCIND). In the current study, patients will be randomized to NAC supplements or placebo orally for 24 weeks while participating in a supervised exercise program. Standardized neuropsychological testing will be used to compare cognitive performance between the placebo and NAC groups. We will use new techniques to accurately measure the amount of oxidative stress damage in blood and evaluate whether the treatment is more efficacious in individuals with certain brain characteristics on MRI scans. If positive, these results will be important for the design of a longer term trial to investigate whether NAC can delay the onset of dementia.

column36: Sleep and circadian rhythms in men and women
column37: Women are up to twice as likely to suffer from insomnia as men. For a similar sleep schedule, we find that young adult women's circadian clock causes them to fall asleep and wake up earlier than men. These results in naturally cycling women are helping us understand why women are more likely than men to wake up earlier in the morning and feel tired after a night's sleep. After menopause, the risk of sleep disturbances increases substantially and affect 25-50% of women. Yet, almost nothing is known about the changes that occur with the circadian system regulating sleep and waking during menopause. In the present study, we propose to recruit postmenopausal women, aged 45 and older. From this group, 14 will be healthy sleepers and 14 will suffer from chronic insomnia. Each participant will be studied twice in time isolation for 3 consecutive days. During each visit, they will undergo a special procedure of multiple naps designed to test how their circadian clock controls sleep, waking, and mood. Saliva samples will be collected in order to assess internal biological time by measuring their content in the hormones cortisol and melatonin. Sleep will be recorded during naps and performance will be tested during waking episodes. Results will be compared between healthy sleepers and insomniacs in order to clarify how the circadian clock and melatonin affect sleep and waking in postmenopausal women. The present study will help understand the role the circadian system plays in the greater female susceptibility to sleep-wake disturbances. Future studies will pursue similar questions in men.

column37: The term "liver disease" comprises over 100 types of disorders. However, the most common form of chronic liver disease is Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), which affects an estimated 30-46% of the population in the US. In Canada, over 2,000 deaths per year are due to liver disease and a further 1,700 deaths from liver cancer. As in the US, obesity is the leading cause of liver disease, with over-exposure to common chemicals or medications and viral infections such as hepatitis, being major contributors. Regardless of the initiating factor, chronic liver disease can cause permanent liver damage and scarring that will progress to cirrhosis, poor liver function and eventually may advance to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Currently, there is no cure for cirrhosis. Treatment focuses on slowing progression and minimizing complications, such as portal hypertension. When it is no longer possible to manage the complications, a liver transplant is required, but demand for transplants far exceeds available donor tissue. Recent advances in the differentiation of human pluripotent cells (hPSCs) into hepatocytes has excited researchers by providing a potential source of cells for liver transplants, drug testing and bioartificial liver devices. However, current methods of growing liver from hPSCs do not yet result in fully functional cells. Thus, methods to improve donor tissue expansion or the derivation of liver tissue from hPSCs require a better understanding of the factors that promote and maintain liver cells proliferation and differentiation. column37: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is the second most common hematological malignancy in Canada. Our goal is to determine at what level these pathways are dysregulated, thereby contributing to the heterogeneity and aggressiveness of MM. Understanding DSB repair pathways in MM will provide targets for the treatment of this pathology. It may also provide novel biomarkers to predict the risk of relapse/refractory MM.

column37: Understanding how cells grow and divide is a fundamental question in biology. For example, in both humans and fruit flies similar genes regulate growth and mutations in these genes often lead to cancer. These similarities allow us to use the fruit fly as a simple, yet powerful genetic system to study what genes and molecules controls growth. We made the striking discovery that overproduction of a single molecule, called transfer RNA, can accelerate growth and increase body size in fruit flies. Transfer RNA plays a critical role in the synthesis all of the proteins and enzymes in a cell, including those essential for growth. Our goal in this grant is to understand how the production of tRNA is controlled and how increase in the production of transfer RNA can drive growth. Abnormal production of transfer RNA is often seen in cancer cells, therefore our work in fruit flies may provide clues to help us understand the runaway growth that makes this disease so devastating.

column37: Our cells are constantly subjected to stress that can damage their genetic material and cause mutations. Mutations can lead to the development of diseases such as cancer. Our work will help us understand how the modification of RPA and other proteins by PRP19 and additional PRP19-like proteins called ubiquitin ligases allows our cells to protect their DNA. We will thus examine how PRP19 works with other proteins to remove the toxic DNA lesions that may appear when cells replicate their genetic material. This new information will improve our understanding of the complex pathways that protect our DNA and guide us in the elaboration of novel strategies that will improve the efficiency of current anti-cancer treatments.

column36: Imaging of cerebral vascular adaptation following traumatic brain injury
column37: The blood vessels that supply the brain with oxygen and nutrients form a complex and highly organized network whose proper functioning is essential for our survival. Disease or injury to the brain may damage this network and disrupt the transport of blood and the mechanisms that regulate how much oxygen and nutrients are delivered. As the brain recovers from injury, new blood vessels are added, others are removed, and existing blood vessels may change in dimensions or even move. How these changes occur is poorly understood yet is thought to be essential to recovering healthy brain function. The goal of this project is to understand this adaptation process for the purpose of developing better methods to monitor and promote recovery following brain injury. Our research strategy is to use experimental mice that receive an injury to the part of the brain that is responsible for controlling movement. Advanced 3D optical microscopy methods will be used to directly observe the changing blood vessel network following injury. Magnetic resonance imaging will be used to assess how blood is being distributed within the brain and the capacity of the brain to elevate blood flow when needed. A subset of the mice will undertake voluntary exercise to evaluate whether this improves recovery. We will use these observations to identify beneficial patterns of blood vessel remodelling following traumatic brain injury and to assess when and if exercise can be used to promote recovery. Finally, we will evaluate a new ultrasound diagnostic technique in the mice to monitor changes in how blood is supplied. Together these findings could lead both to better methods to promote recovery following brain injury and to new diagnostic methods that could be used clinically to monitor the progress of treatment.

column37: Attention Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common childhood psychiatric condition,which often persists into adolescence. In adolescence ADHD is associated with poor academic, social, and emotional functioning, other psychiatric problems, substance abuse, and antisocial behaviour. Although medication effectively reduces symptoms such as hyperactivity and inattention, it does not directly address academic, social, emotional, and behavioural problems. Overcoming these would require building skills in organization, time management, problem solving, emotional modulation, stress management and interpersonal rapport. Yet, psychosocial treatments targeting such skills in adolescents with ADHD have been little studied and are scarce in the community. The proposed study will evaluate cognitive behavioural and skills training therapy (CBT+S) for adolescents with ADHD. Adolescents will be randomly assigned to 14 sessions of either manualized group CBT+S or manualized supportive group therapy (SGT, control condition). An additional treatment-as-usual group will be evaluated to control for repeated measurements. CBT+S will focus on skill acquisition in common problem areas for adolescents with ADHD, such as organization and time management, distractibility, impulsivity, and social skills. A coach will call each participant twice a week to help practice the learned skills. Parallel groups will be provided for parents of CBT+S and SGT participants focusing on education, support and sharing experiences. If CBT+S proves to benefit adolescents with ADHD, it can be made widely available to these adolescents in the community. This would help them improve their academic, social, and emotional functioning and ultimately their long term outcomes.

column37: A growth restricted fetus is more likely to be born premature or with birth defects and is at increased risk for adverse neonatal, childhood and adult health outcomes. column37: Clinical Issue: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a debilitating mental disorder affecting young adults. SZ symptoms include early social isolation, cognitive decline prior to episodes of auditory hallucinations, false beliefs and associated anxiety and depression. Current treatments targeting the dopaminergic system remedy psychosis but not other schizophrenia symptoms. The goal is to identify therapeutic targets dysregulated early in the disease process to provide better outcomes for SZ. We have recently discovered a new mouse model of SZ in which the phosphatase enzyme PTP1B is hyperactive in the brain. We also found that in two other commonly used experimentally induced mouse models of SZ this enzyme activity is increased in the affected brain regions. Our previous work showed that hyperactivity of this enzyme disrupts the function of important glutamate receptors on neurons. This can lead to malfunction of dopaminergic circuitry and cause psychosis in humans. Moreover, we reported that hyperactivity of this enzyme also impairs the production of one of the body's own cannabis-like substances (endogenous cannabinoid). Since cannabinoids control how much neurotransmitters are released from neurons, this would further lead to aberrant neuronal activity. Dysregulated levels of cannabinoids in the serum and the cerebrospinal fluid are observed in SZ patients. Our hypothesis is that elevated PTP1B activity is the central mechanism that accounts for functional deficits in the SZ brain. We will test whether targeting this enzyme with a selective inhibitor called Trodusquemine will ameliorate SZ symptoms in two preclinical mouse models. Significance: In Canada, about 1% of the population (~350,000) has SZ. Successful validation of targeting PTP1B to improve SZ in preclinical mouse models can rapidly move to clinical trials since Trodusquemine has already undergone phase 1 clinical trials to treat obesity.

column37: Each year more than 28,000 Canadians are treated surgically for lower back pain. Many of these cases require instrumentation with pedicle screws, which requires some form of X-ray imaging like fluoroscopy or intra-operative CT thus exposing patients and operating room personnel to significant amounts of harmful radiation. This project will adapt and clinically test a new intra-operative ultrasound-based navigation system that is an inexpensive, radiation-free alternative to intra-operative X-ray imaging. This novel technology allows for precise identification of the bony surface of the vertebrae without exposing the spine by merging the pre-operative CT and intra-operative ultrasound images. Such 3D renditions of the spine improve patient-to-image registration facilitating image-guided spine surgery. The novel system will be validated as a safe, accurate, and novel method for intraoperative guidance to perform instrumented lumbar spinal fusion and decompressions. The immediate benefits of this system compared to current standard intraoperative X-ray-based imaging technology are: 1) Elimination of all intraoperative radiation exposure to patient and operating room personnel 2) Real-time navigation at every level of the spine with intuitive visualization. 3) Increased accessibility (in terms of lower costs, smaller footprint, less cumbersome) of navigated spine surgery for all surgeons. 4) Decreased operating room time and thus decreased morbidity of spine surgery. 5) Improved accuracy of navigation through better registration. 6) Decreased numbers of malpositioned screws and consequently, reduced numbers of revision surgeries. And finally, 7) unlimited levels of fusion may be performed with the novel navigation method. This is of particular importance in scoliosis cases where current technology only captures 5 to 6 segments at a time and dose constraints limits the number of X-ray based images.

column36: Developmental origins of childhood obesity: tracking the causal epigenetic changes programming adiposity in children
column37: Obesity now affects up to 1 in 5 children in Canada. Obese children are more likely to stay obese as adults and this has profound impacts on their long-term health. Indeed, obesity increases risk to develop diabetes and heart diseases among many other diseases. Events during pregnancy are suspected to play a role in 'programming' whether a child develops obesity, but we still do not know much about the mechanisms involved. Scientific and medical observations strongly suggest that "epigenetic" factors are important. The term epigenetics refers to chemical modifications of the genes that act as a change in the software reading the genetic information (hardware). Maternal conditions - such as diabetes in pregnancy - influence the environment in which the foetus develops. The environment of the foetus in the womb can affect the epigenetic marks with profound effects on the reading and expression of the genetic information throughout life. Such long-term changes involving genes implicated in weight control will have an impact on the risk to develop obesity and related chronic diseases. For this reason, the so-called epigenetic mechanisms have a real potential to explain why some unfavourable environment within the womb affecting foetal development during pregnancy may predispose newborns to develop obesity early in their life as well as diabetes and heart disease later on. Our primary objective is to identify epigenetic marks observed at birth that predict which child will become obese. Then, we will determine which specific pregnancy events, whether maternal obesity or diabetes during pregnancy, cause these epigenetic changes. Finally, the impact of these epigenetic changes on gene expression levels will be assessed. Our study will help to understand the biological mechanisms linking epigenetic events occurring during pregnancy and the increased risk for children to develop obesity.

column36: Rescue of microvasculature enhances repair in muscle degenerative disorders
column37: Rationale: Progressive degeneration characterizes muscle disorders (e.g. Duchenne muscular dystrophy [DMD]) and age- or disease-related declines in muscle mass/function. Poor blood flow (ischemia), inflammation and fibrosis are profound in these diseases, generating an environment that prevents muscle repair. New strategies must improve this environment to impact the lives of patients. A promising approach that is believed may improve the muscle environment uses vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to improve blood flow. However, contrary to this approach, our group has now demonstrated in a preclinical mouse model of DMD that delivery of VEGF is not sufficient to reduce ischemia, and in fact increases muscle inflammation and fibrosis! Our hypothesis is that the vasculature in DMD is abnormal. Thus, our overarching objective is to rescue abnormal vasculature in DMD by administering a factor that stabilizes it, Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1). Specific Aims: 1.To characterize abnormal vasculature in detail, in (a) preclinical mouse models of DMD and (b) skeletal muscle tissue samples from DMD patients. These data will allow us to critically identify a window of opportunity to intervene with delivery of Ang-1 as a therapeutic. 2. To provide laboratory-based proof of concept in DMD mice for the administration of Ang-1 to improve muscle repair. 3. To develop a novel, targeted Ang-1 delivery approach that will allow for the precise regulation of Ang-1 delivery that will be essential for future clinical use in patients. Significance: Without an approach to improve the muscle environment, and prevent/reduce ischemia/inflammation/fibrosis, it is unlikely that the benefits of therapeutics for muscle regenerative disorders can ever be fully realized. Our vascular-targeted strategy will reduce medical costs, prolong ambulation and longevity, and improve quality of life for patients not only affected by muscle degeneration, but perhaps by any vascular defect.

column36: The role of RhoA/mDia1 pathway in salt-sensitive hypertension
column37: Hypertension is the prevalent treatable risk factor contributing to cardiovascular diseases, which remain the most common cause of death in industrialized countries taking the lives of over one million people every year in the U.S. alone. In Canada, over 20% of adults are diagnosed with hypertension, and an estimated 9 in 10 people who live an average lifespan will develop the condition in their lifetime. Excessive dietary salt intake is strongly correlated with cardiovascular diseases such as myocardial infarction and stroke, and is regarded as a major contributing factor to hypertension. While the link between salt and hypertension is well established, the mechanisms by which high salt intake leads to increased blood pressure remain unclear. Consumption of salt in a meal increases the levels of salt (sodium) in the blood, causing activation of specialized brain cells that release a hormone called vasopressin. Vasopressin leads to retention of water in the kidney in order to decrease blood sodium levels back to normal. Vasopressin also affects blood vessels causing them to constrict. These effects of vasopressin can lead to the elevation of blood pressure. Our hypothesis is that chronic exposure to excessive amounts of salt causes a hyperactivation of vasopressin-secreting brain cells. These cells have a specialized cellular skeleton that determine their shape (just like the shape of the body is determined by its skeleton). This cellular skeleton becomes denser and stiffer when the cells are chronically exposed to high salt levels. As a result, the cells become overly activated and secrete excessive amounts of vasopressin, leading to a sustained blood pressure increase and hypertension. We propose to study the mechanisms by which high salt causes the modification of cellular skeleton in the brain cells thereby leading to hypertension.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an incurable, severely debilitating disease with suboptimal therapy and no cure. Canada has the highest incidence of MS in the world with 291 cases per 100,000 people. MS is most commonly diagnosed in young adults and patients suffer progressive and irreversible damage to the brain. The root causes and risk factors for MS are still unknown. As such, current therapies are limited to treating symptoms, rather than the root cause. Other incurable diseases that lead to progressive loss of quality of life, and death, include the occupational respiratory diseases; which are caused by breathing in toxic materials such as asbestos and silica. These diseases commonly affect our firefighters, miners and military personnel. MS and occupational respiratory diseases are caused by chronic inflammation of the brain and lung respectively. Although the brain and lung have very different functions in the body, they share some common features during inflammation. One common feature is that the inflammatory protein IL-1 is made by cells locally and leads to excessive inflammation and tissue damage. It is well known that if we limit IL-1, we can protect from MS and occupational respiratory diseases; but we don't fully understand how and why IL-1 is made. We have exciting new evidence to suggest that a recently found digestive protein in immune cells triggers the release of IL-1 in both the brain and lung. Mice that don't have this protein are protected from experimental models of MS and respiratory disease caused by silica. Interestingly, this protein was recently identified by other scientists as being a possible risk factor for MS. Our research will determine how this protein brings about IL-1 release and inflammation in the brain and lung. This will allow scientists and doctors to better understand how chronic inflammation develops and potentially formulate new strategies to treat diseases such as MS and occupational respiratory disease.

column36: Targeting brain inflammation and its resolution. Omega-3 fatty acids, omega-6 fatty acids or both?
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases are a relatively broad class of neurological disorders, however, recent evidence suggests that dietary n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), commonly found in fish, may be of benefit in preventing or treating these diseases, including Alzheimer's Disease. One common link between neurodegenerative disorders is that they have a neuroinflammatory component. It is well established that n-3 PUFA are anti-inflammatory in the periphery, but whether or not they are also anti-inflammatory within the brain is unknown. It is thought that one way omega-3 might be beneficial in the brain is by interfering with omega-6 fatty acid metabolism. We have developed diets that can lower or increase omega-6s. By combining these approaches we will be able figure out if it is the omega-3s, the omega-6s or both. This is very important as, currently, diets are very high in omega-6 fatty acids and, thus, there is a lot of room to decrease them. The objective of the current proposal is to test if n-3 PUFA are anti-inflammatory within the mouse brain and to evaluate the mechanisms by which they accomplish this. We have established a mouse model of neuroinflammation to test this hypothesis and our preliminary results strongly suggest that docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is protective against neuroinflammation. Having a better understanding whether increasing omega-3 fatty acids and or decreasing omega-6 fatty acids can protect us from the neuroinflammation associated with Alzheimer's disease could lead to new therapies for prevention.

column36: Role of the Type 2 Ryanodine Receptor in Familial Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and a huge burden on health care globally. Despite worldwide efforts, all clinical trials on AD to date have failed. These disappointing findings demonstrate that our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of AD is far from complete, and that novel and effective treatments for AD are urgently needed. It is thought that the accumulation of amyloid-B (AB) in the brain is a primary driver of AD. However, an unresolved question is what causes the accumulation of AB. An increasing body of evidence indicates that alterations in intracellular Ca handling occur in AD long before the appearance of AB plaques. We recently discovered that genetically suppressing the activity of ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2) dramatically reduces AB level and blocks memory impairment in a mouse model of AD. This exciting finding indicates that RyR2 plays a major role in AD pathogenesis. The goals of this project are to determine RyR2's contributions to AD pathogenesis and to develop novel RyR2-targeted treatments for AD. To achieve these goals, we will determine the role of RyR2 in AB accumulation, neuron loss, and memory impairment in AD mice. We will define how genetically suppressing or enhancing RyR2 activity affects Ca regulation in AD neurons. Further, we will establish if pharmacological RyR2 inhibition suppresses AD pathology. We have developed the necessary tools and obtained key preliminary data demonstrating the feasibility of our approaches. We expect to reveal for the first time direct evidence that RyR2 plays a major role in AD pathology. We also expect to reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanism underlying abnormal Ca regulation in AD and identify the first RyR2-targeted potential treatment for AD. These proposed studies will advance health-related knowledge and improve health outcomes by uncovering novel fundamental mechanisms and developing novel treatments for AD.

column36: Health service redesign in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside: A linked, observational cohort design for comprehensive evaluation
column37: Every year, one in five Canadians experiences a mental health or addiction problem, with an estimated cost of $51 billion annually. While such patients commonly have multiple health and social service needs, Canada's healthcare sectors typically run in silos, posing immense challenges to continuity of care. In 2017, following years of consultation with patients, local care providers and provincial stakeholders, Vancouver Coastal Health (VCH) will embark upon a comprehensive redesign of health services delivered within the city's impoverished downtown Eastside (DTES) neighbourhood. Over the next 5 years, the DTES Second Generation Strategy (2GS) will roll out coordinated policy changes aimed to integrate over 50 different service to provide better-coordinated care. Our study uniquely offers the best possible empirical basis to assess the impact of DTES-2G. Using cutting-edge econometric and epidemiological techniques, we propose a multidimensional health services research platform focusing on access to care, quality of health care delivery, and costs during the implementation of the DTES-2GS. Data will come from long-running observational cohort studies of >3000 people who use drugs in Vancouver that is linked to various health administrative data. As healthcare quality itself is multidimensional, we consider measures of unmet need for health services, clinical outcomes, patient-reported outcome measures, measures of clinical process and health system responsiveness. Finally, we will measure expenditure related to the redesign to help identify the optimal allocation of available resources for DTES-2GS. Working closely with VCH staff and local groups, our findings will inform DTES-2GS policy change as the systemic redesign occurs, while also providing relevant evidence for other urban jurisdictions contending with similar problems in Canada and beyond.

column36: A new Argonaute-2 binding protein with key roles in neural crest cells
column37: Neurocristopathies form a specific group of rare genetic diseases that result from problems with neural crest cells - a specific type of stem cells that migrate extensively from the neural tube (the central nervous system primordium) during embryogenesis. Such characteristics allow neural crest cells to colonize several regions of the developing embryo and generate a wide array of cell types such as peripheral neurons and glia, pigment cells, craniofacial bone cells as well as specific cell subsets of the heart, inner ear and thymus. Because of the large number of neural crest cell derivatives, distinct structures/cell types (isolated or in combination) are affected in each neurocristopathy. The most important issue in this research field is that the underlying genetic cause and associated pathogenic mechanism of most cases of neurocristopathy are poorly understood. To address this problem, we use the mouse as a model organism and take advantage of the state-of-the-art methods of genomic modifications and analyses. Such studies are complemented by more classical techniques of molecular and cellular biology. Importantly, through established collaborations with researchers working in a clinical setting, we also validate our findings in children affected by the studied neurocristopathy. Notably, this work allowed us to identify a new gene for which the mutation can cause CHARGE syndrome - a neurocristopathy with a very complex clinical presentation and which can be fatal for many young children. The main objective of the current project is to understand the function of this new gene (Fam172a) in both normal and pathological conditions. This work is expected to significantly improve the way children suffering from CHARGE syndrome - as well as their families - are currently being taken care of.

column36: Tau: a novel target to prevent early neuronal dysfunction and death in glaucoma.
column37: Sight is essential for humans to gather critical information about their surroundings. The fear of going blind has been reported to be more powerful than that of having cancer or heart disease. Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, affecting >60 million people worldwide. There is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the death of retinal ganglion cells, the neurons that convey visual information from the retina to the brain. High intraocular pressure is the most significant risk factor for developing the disease, but the mechanisms by which ocular hypertension damages retinal ganglion cells are unknown. A major roadblock towards developing effective therapeutics for glaucoma is that very little is known about the early pathological alterations that lead to retinal ganglion cell dysfunction and death. Our recent work has identified a new and intriguing role for tau, a microtubule binding protein implicated in Alzheimer's disease, in ganglion cell neurodegeneration. We showed that tau undergoes substantial alterations early in glaucoma including abnormal phosphorylation, aggregation and missorting. In this application, we will determine the role of tau in the earliest pathological changes in glaucoma, namely retinal ganglion cell dendrite retraction and anterograde axonal transport impairment. This project is unique and timely because it will provide new insight into the molecular mechanisms that govern glaucoma pathogenesis, and it will serve as a springboard to identify new therapeutic targets and potential diagnostic tools for this blinding disease.

column36: Studying microbial load and antibiotic resistance genes in source and drinking water from First Nation Reserves
column37: Data from the past two decades indicate that approximately 1 in 5 First Nation communities in Canada are under a drinking water advisory at any given time. Most of the drinking water advisories are due to microbial contaminants. Many First Nations homes rely on cisterns (water-holding tanks) for home storage of drinking water and Canadian experts identified in 2013 the urgent need for science research on these systems. In a pilot study carried out by us in a First Nation community, we found significant numbers of coliforms, E. coli, and also antibiotic resistance genes drinking water supply. In this project, we will expand our study to four different communities and compare piped and cistern water distribution systems using state-of-the-art analytical chemistry and molecular biology methods to provide for detailed water quality measurements. Water samples collected along distribution pathways will be analyzed on a seasonal basis for chlorine concentrations, the presence of coliforms (indicator of fecal contamination), total microbial community, and also for the presence of antibiotic resistance genes. In addition, an alternative in-house water treatment technology will be tested. This Project Grant application is a research collaboration between academic researchers, First Nations leaders, and four First Nations communities. These researchers have collaborated in preliminary studies (2014) that led to the development of the proposed research plan that will improve the drinking water quality in the participating communities and in other First Nations. Safe drinking water will not only improve the health of individuals and families in First Nations communities but will also result in reduced heath-care costs for Canada. It will also provide for greater opportunities for First Nation socio-economic development since most businesses require clean water.

column36: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy: Seizure induced brainstem hypoxia
column37: People with epilepsy often die suddenly and unexpectedly. In fact they are 27 times more likely to do so compared with the general population. This unfortunate occurrence is called Sudden Unexpected Death in EPilepsy (SUDEP) and it is the leading cause of death in persons with epilepsy. SUDEP most often occurs where an individual with a history of epilepsy is found dead with evidence of a prior seizure. From the few studies on patients in a hospital setting, that would have died if not for medical intervention; we know that SUDEP is ultimately caused by failure to breathe either during a seizure or very soon after a seizure ends followed quickly by heart failure. What we don't know is what causes the failure to breathe. My laboratory has recently discovered a period of severely low oxygen levels (hypoxia) during and following a seizure. The hypoxia is found only in brain regions involved in the seizure and is severe enough to cause behavioural dysfunction. I hypothesize that SUDEP occurs when seizures invade the breathing centers in the brainstem and local tissue oxygen falls below a critical level impairing the function of those areas which leads to breathing failure and death. We will first determine the relationship between seizure activity and local oxygen levels in brain breathing centers on breathing behaviour. To do this we will use an implantable device that continuously measures the absolute levels of oxygen in awake behaving mice. We will next determine more drugs that can prevent seizure-induced hypoxia. We have previously identified two kinds of drugs that prevent the seizure-induced blood vessel constriction and low oxygen levels. We will use these to determine the effect of preventing the seizure-induced hypoxic period on mouse breathing and survival. We believe that SUDEP is preventable and that the knowledge generated by these proposed studies will ultimately save lives.

column36: Genetic mechanisms of arterial calcification
column37: Calcification of the heart's (coronary) arteries occurs as a result of atherosclerosis and increases the risk of dying. Normally, the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the artery wall release calcium but also produce specialized proteins that bind to calcium and prevent calcification of the arteries by promoting calcium removal by macrophages. Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is heritable and common genetic variants on chromosome 9 (at 9p21.3) increase the susceptibility to atherosclerosis and accelerate CAC through an unknown mechanism. We compared human arterial SMCs with 0, 1 or 2 copies of the 9p21.3 risk variants and found that the most differently expressed gene is statherin, a tiny protein known to block calcification in the saliva but not previously tied to this function in SMCs. SMCs with 2 copies of the risk variants expressed almost no statherin, were susceptible to calcification in culture, and could be rescued from calcification by over-expressed statherin. Importantly, we detect statherin in the blood and find lower levels in patients with atherosclerosis and CAC. Our hypothesis is that loss of statherin is the reason 9p21.3 risk variants accelerate CAC. We propose 3 Aims: 1) We will confirm in patients with coronary artery disease that coronary calcification is tied to lower active (phosphorylated ) or higher inactive (dephosphorylated) plasma levels of statherin. 2) We will determine how statherin affects calcium crystal uptake and inflammation of macrophages. 3) We will use a transgenic mouse expressing an active form of human statherin to reverse arterial calcification caused by atherosclerosis or by a genetic defect. Significance: 75% of the world population carries the 9p21.3 risk variants. Therapy targeting statherin to block progression of arterial calcification could reduce mortality in many people.

column36: Non-invasive monitoring of liver cancer recurrence following surgery using circulating tumour DNA sequencing
column37: Liver cancer is a highly fatal cancer with an overall cure rate of approximately 10% and a prevalence that is the second-fastest growing in Canada. column36: Immune Regulation of Placental Development and Function During Normal and Pathological Pregnancy.
column37: Preeclampsia is a serious and prevalent disease of pregnancy. It is clinically diagnosed by severe, sudden-onset high blood pressure and blood vessel damage that can lead to organ dysfunction and death in pregnant women. Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal and infant illness and death in Canada and worldwide, with up to 76,000 maternal and 500,000 infant deaths attributed to the disease globally, and there is no known cure. The major cause of preeclampsia is defective development of the placenta, which is the organ that embeds itself into the mother's uterus and is responsible for nourishing the baby throughout pregnancy. We know little about why the placenta does not develop properly in these pregnancies. Without this knowledge, devising better management strategies and interventions is not possible. Therefore, the objective of this research is to determine underlying factors that cause placental maldevelopment during early pregnancy. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that abnormal behaviour of a unique subset of highly abundant uterine immune cells has a causative role in disrupting placental development. In this project, we will determine how aberrant activity of these uterine immune cells leads to placental dysfunction and affects fetal health. We will also examine whether the absence of these immune cells can improve placental and fetal health. Collectively, this project will test the applicability of targeting uterine immune cells to improve placental development, and will form a foundation by which we can decrease or prevent the incidence of preeclampsia.
