column36: Establishing chloride intracellular channel CLIC1 as a therapeutic target for pediatric brain tumor
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The conventional treatment that combines surgery, irradiation and chemotherapy is highly toxic to normal brain cells and produces life-long side effects such as lowered intelligence, early aging, and increased chance to develop other cancer. Therefore, identifying the molecules that fuel aggressive MB growth but are largely dispensable for normal cells is key to develop cancer-specific therapy. Ions, such as potassium and chloride, are essential constituents of human cells. Ion channel proteins form tiny pores to control ion to move in or out of cells. The movement of ions can change the electrical and physical properties of the cells, which control many biological processes including tumor growth. We recently found a potassium channel named EAG2 that is required for MB growth but not normal brain development. We discovered an old drug as a novel EAG2 blocker and found that the drug had strong efficacy in a human MB patient. Therefore, we pioneer in identifying ion channels as novel regulators for brain tumor and developing channel-targeted therapy. In order to effectively treat MB, a combinatorial therapy, in which multiple tumor-specific molecules are targeted, is necessary. We found that a chloride-permeating channel named CLIC1 is abnormally accumulated in MB cells, and inhibiting CLIC1 slowed MB growth in mice. We hypothesize that CLIC1 as a novel regulator of MB can be blocked to suppress tumor growth. We will reveal the tumor stage in which CLIC1 is required for MB growth and define the mechanism by which CLIC1 regulates MB, knowing which will instruct the logical designing of a CLIC1-targeted therapy. Completing these studies will solidify our research program, which is based on a unique scientific niche in brain tumor therapeutics by targeting ion channels. We will innovate cancer therapy by targeting ion channels to treat the devastating brain tumors.

column36: Single-cell characterization of viral transcription- and translation-competent HIV and SIV reservoirs
column37: A vaccine against HIV is crucially required worldwide to limit the spread of this virus. The major HIV-infected (HIV+) cell population, a type of white blood cells known as CD4 T cells, comes in multiple different "flavours", each with different functions. In order to develop a vaccine that can teach the immune system how to target and kill HIV+ cells, scientists must first understand which flavors of CD4 T cells are infected. However, currently available technologies have made it difficult to visualize these HIV+ cells in great detail. Previous work has relied on looking at the relative numbers of HIV+ cells in different populations, rather than the individual HIV+ cells, or studying HIV infection using cells and viruses grown in the lab. The interactions between these "in vitro" cells and viruses may be very different to the events occurring within a HIV-positive individual. To address this important issue, we have developed a novel assay that, for the first time, allows very rare HIV+ cells to be visualized at a single-cell level. We will perform in-depth analysis of individual HIV+ cells from the blood of patients who are infected with HIV. We will also use an animal model of HIV, SIV in non-human primates (monkeys), to image the infected cells in important tissues and organs. This will provide researchers with a highly detailed picture of HIV+ cells and guide development of a vaccine. In addition to a vaccine, a cure is required to treat those individuals that are HIV-positive. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is not a cure for HIV; as long as a patient takes their medication the virus is forced into hiding, but it can reappear when ART is stopped. Specialized drugs (known as latency reversing agents or LRAs) have been developed to kick the virus out of its hiding place. We will investigate how different flavors of CD4 T cells respond to LRAs, and use this knowledge to inform studies working towards a cure for HIV.

column36: An optogenetic approach for rewiring thalamocortical circuits to restore function after stroke
column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult disability in North America, often robbing its victims of the ability to perform even the most basic sensory-motor tasks (dressing, eating, brushing teeth, driving) that we take for granted in daily life. Since many patients fail to recover adequately with existing treatment options, there is a great need to develop a deeper understanding of what happens to sensory circuits after stroke and use this knowledge to develop new treatments that will maximize recovery. One brain region that plays a crucial role in processing sensory information is the thalamus. After stroke, it is thought that the connections from this region are either damaged or are dysfunctional thereby disrupting how our brain processes sensory information. Surprisingly little is known about what happens to these connections after stroke and to what extent can they recover normal function. The first goal of this research project will be to use imaging technologies to assess the structure and functionality of thalamic connections after stroke. Since our preliminary data suggest that stroke does indeed make these connections less excitable, we will then use a powerful new experimental approach to promote the excitability of these connections. This approach involves genetically modifying cells to make them more excitable by expressing proteins (derived from algae) that can be activated by light (called "optogenetics"). We will then determine the impact of optogenetic stimulation on neural circuit rewiring and recovery of sensorimotor function. And finally, since we have pilot data proving the feasibility and utility of this experimental stroke therapy, we will explore what molecular mechanisms mediate its beneficial effects. Ultimately, the proposed project will generate critical foundational data regarding the effects of stroke on sensory circuits and will test a new therapeutic approach to improve recovery of sensori-motor function in a rodent model of stroke.

column36: Characterization and modification of Bordetella lipid A

column37: Colds are the main cause of asthma attacks in preschoolers, an age group with the highest rate of visits to the emergency room because of asthma. In this 7-month randomized controlled trial, children aged 1-5 years with asthma attacks triggered mostly by colds, will receive a high dose of vitamin D or a placebo every 3 months during their usual clinic visit. They will also take a daily dose of vitamin D. This study will test whether if children receiving vitamin D have less severe and less frequent asthma attacks compared with the placebo. The study will also document the safety profile of this strategy. Vitamin D may prove an effective means to prevent moderate and severe asthma attacks triggered by colds in young children. If positive, results of this study may offer an effective means to prevent asthma triggered by colds in young children.

column36: Personalized medicine from theory to health practice: making dynamic treatment regimes more accessible
column37: Personalized medicine provides treatment decisions tailored to each individual patient, maximizing the chance of the best possible health outcomes. Dynamic treatment regimes formalize this idea. These are sequences of rules which, based on a patient's medical history, suggest which treatment to prescribe at particular times to give patients the best results. A 'regime' can be as simple as giving one drug to men and another to women, or a long list of options that update over the treatment of a lengthy illness. There are, however, many unanswered questions in this area, and this project will address some of most importance to health researchers studying the treatment of long-term conditions. The project will cover three areas. One will consider different definitions of the 'best' outcome for a group of patients. Usually, we pick treatment rules that give a population the best overall average result, but sometimes we may want something else. For example, in a health setting we care about avoiding especially bad outcomes (such as death, or major complications), and so might prioritize this above all else. How to do so requires further study. A second topic will look at assumptions researchers must make to carry out analyses, studying the impact of these assumptions and how to check if they're met. A final aim is to compare some of the more popular methods for finding the best treatment decisions. There are a number of methods available, with 'better' ones often more difficult to use. This last area will aim to identify when simpler methods can compete with more complex ones in practice. All new methods developed will be made available through software. With a focus on real-world, practical concerns, this project will make dynamic treatment regimes far more accessible and useful. In turn, this will further the study and understanding of personalized medicine, leading to better health outcomes for society as a whole.

column36: The Epinephrine Randomized Optimal Versus Current Dose (EpiROC) Canada Trial
column37: Each year in Canada, there are over 40,000 people who collapse from cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest is a sudden stoppage of the heart. This life threatening problem is treated by paramedics with CPR, shocks and drugs, including the routine use of adrenaline. The worldwide standard dose of adrenaline is 1mg every 3 to 5 minutes with no total limit. Although the standard dose of adrenaline can help restart the heart, half of these patients die in the hospital from irreversible brain injury and brain death. Despite decades of use, there is no proof that the standard dose of adrenaline is effective at improving survival out of the hospital and there is growing evidence suggesting that the standard dose of adrenaline may be harmful to the brain, particularly with higher total doses. Adrenaline increases blood flow to the heart to improve its chances to restart but when more than 2mg total of adrenaline is used, there is decreased blood flow to the brain leading to brain injury and brain death. We believe and would like to test how effective are low (optimal) doses (up to 2mg total) of adrenaline compared to the current standard doses (no total limit). We also want to test whether the low dose of adrenaline is better than nothing (placebo). We will test these three treatments in a large group of patients treated in an existing world-class Canadian out-of-hospital resuscitation research network called the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) consisting of central and southern Ontario, and all of British Columbia. This will be the first clinical trial to test the effects of low dose adrenaline, the standard dose of adrenaline, and placebo in cardiac arrest. This research may improve patient survival and brain function after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, and change the way in which cardiac arrest is treated worldwide.

column37: Most women in rural Manitoba First Nations communities travel to tertiary centres to deliver their babies. Having support during pregnancy, delivery and postpartum can alleviate some of these poor health outcomes. Doula care is about supporting women during labour and birth and has shown considerable efficacy with women from marginalized groups or transcultural climates. This research will examine how an Indigenous doula program can address poor health and social outcomes for First Nations women who travel for birth. This project involves four First Nations communities in Manitoba with the Manitoba Indigenous Doulas Initiative (MIDI), university researchers (University of Winnipeg/Manitoba), and First Nation's researchers (First Nations Health and Social Secretariat of Manitoba/Nanaandawawegimeg). Women will receive the care of her community doula up until she temporarily relocates to the referral centre at which time she will come under the care of her urban doula who will also provide care during the birth. Once the women has given birth and she returns to her community, the community doula will take over care. Throughout the care from her two-doula team, a variety of health measurements will be taken. The four participating communities are the largest First Nations communities in the province and we will recruit 15% of the expectant mothers for a total of 240 women.

In this proposal we will use our LAM-like cell lines and our 3D lung tissue like culture system to tease apart why Rapamycin only slows down LAM but does not stop it and to explore why mutations in TSC2 predispose a woman LAM more than mutations in TSC1. In addition, we will perform a drug screen of nearly 1300 FDA-approved drugs to identify drugs that can work alone or in concert with Rapamycin to preferentially kill LAM cells or to stop their production of MMPs, which destroy the lungs of LAM patients. In addition, since we are using both male and female cells, we may learn why LAM only strikes women.

column36: Deciphering the transcriptional control of cytoprotective responses to identify new therapeutic targets
column37: All of our body's cells have systems, collectively called "cytoprotective factors", that protect the cell's components from damage. These factors help maintain cell health, and thus help prevent many diseases, such as neurodegenerative disease (e.g. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, etc). However, when erroneously activated, cytoprotective factors also allow cancer cells to thrive and to resist treatment with chemotherapies. In cancer, disrupting hyperactive cytoprotective systems is therefore a potential therapeutic approach. Our research focuses on the 'Mediator', a molecular machine that is required to read and transcribe genetic information. Mediator is present in all organisms from yeast cells to humans. This means we can study it in animals like roundworms to make new discoveries that can help improve human health. In my lab, we use the tiny worm called Caenorhabditis elegans to study how Mediator works in cells. We discovered that one particular Mediator protein acts like a cytoprotective factors: it helps cells remove foreign substances like drugs and toxins, and making whole animals resistant to such stress. Moreover, this protein interacts with others that are known to help cancers become drug resistant. Therefore, targeting this one Mediator protein could be a new cancer treatment. However, we do not yet know how this works at the level of molecules, which prevents us from targeting this specific protein to improve human health. Our goal is to determine how this Mediator protein works, thus laying the foundation for developing new Mediator-targeting cancer drugs.

column36: In vivo two-photon imaging of cell type-specific reorganization of inhibitory circuits during motor learning in awake and behaving mice.
column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult disability and the third leading cause of death in Canada. In addition to having potentially devastating effects on quality of life, stroke is estimated to cost the Canadian economy more than $3.6 billion a year in treatment, physician services, hospital costs, lost wages, and decreased productivity (Statistics Canada, 2012). The primary motor cortex in the brain is responsible for voluntary movement. It has also been proposed to be one of the sites for motor memory formation and storage, also known as motor representations. Therefore, when the motor cortex is damaged following a stroke, we lose the ability to execute movements that were formerly part of normal daily life. One hypothesis to achieve true recovery is to re-initiate motor learning in the brain and establish new representation to replace the destroyed ones (Murphy and Corbett, 2009). Hence, a determination of the basic molecular mechanisms underlying motor learning will enhance our understanding of post-traumatic rehabilitation in brain injury and disease. Our lab has developed a novel forelimb lever-press task for head-fixed mice, permitting us to perform chronic two-photon imaging and follow learning-related dynamic changes among various neuron subtypes in the motor cortex of behaving mice over weeks of training. Here, we propose a series of experiments employing in vivo two-photon imaging combined with the lever-press task to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying learning-driven inhibitory neural circuit modifications essential for the structural and functional plasticity with motor memory formation in the awake brain. By deciphering the basic mechanisms underlying motor movement acquisition in normal heathy brains, our work will have immense potential to understand dysfunction in circuits altered by stroke and aid in the development of novel therapeutic targets for stroke recovery and other brain injuries impairing motor function

column36: Identification of HP1a as a key regulator and a novel therapeutic target for neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is a currently incurable, lethal subtype of prostate cancer that can develop from the disease following prolonged hormonal therapy. Unfortunately, there are few treatment options available for NEPC and new therapeutic targets and more effective treatments are urgently needed to improve its management. A state-of-the-art pre-clinical model of NEPC, developed in our group, is giving us unprecedented levels of accuracy in monitoring how NEPC progresses. Using this model and advanced gene and gene expression analyses, we have observed that elevated expression of HP1a, a gene not previously reported to be involved NEPC, is correlated with NEPC development. In our pilot study, these findings were further validated in clinical samples. Furthermore, we also observed increased HP1a is an early event during NEPC development and a reduction in HP1a expression was found to lead to inhibition of cancer cell growth. These results suggest HP1a may play an important role in NEPC development. In the proposed study, we hypothesize that 1) HP1a impacts multiple aspects of cancer biology and is functionally important in NEPC development; 2) reduced HP1a expression in cancer cells will significantly suppress NEPC growth; and 3) reagent targeting HP1a can be used as a novel therapy to treat NEPC. The ultimate goals of this project are to have a better understanding of the function of HP1a in NEPC and to produce potential therapeutics designed to target HP1a and hence suppress NEPC development. When successful, this study will improve our understanding of mechanisms underlying the development of NEPC and also provide new insights for the personalized treatment strategy for prostate cancer patients. Identification of novel therapeutic agents in this study will lead to more effective therapy and better quality of life of prostate cancer patients.

column36: The lungs as HIV reservoirs: Interplay between disrupted respiratory immunity and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
column37: AIDS remains one of the world's most serious health challenges. Globally, 35 million people are living with HIV including 75,000 in Canada. Despite intense efforts to cure HIV, HIV reservoirs are a main barrier to eradication. A reservoir refers to a place (either a cell type or anatomical compartment) where HIV "hides" from the immune system. The lungs have many features which make them ideal reservoirs for HIV, and HIV has been detected within the lungs of individuals even after several years of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Having HIV within the lungs is associated with several imbalances in chemicals affecting interaction and communication between cells. Furthermore, as people with HIV are living longer due to the success of HAART, they are suffering from more chronic diseases associated with aging, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is the 3rd leading cause of death in the general population in North America. People living with HIV show signs of COPD more often than people without HIV (20-60% vs. 7%). Like in the lungs of people living with HIV, people with COPD have disturbances in lung immune cells. Furthermore, it is possible that having HIV within cells changes genetic material within the cells (ribonucleic acid or "RNA" and deoxyribonucleic acid or "DNA") and influences cell functions, making lungs more susceptible to develop COPD. We plan to study the interaction between immune cells and HIV reservoir size in the lungs of people living with HIV, both with and without COPD. We also plan to study the genetic characteristics of lung cells in relation to the amount of HIV they contain. These findings are important for understanding how HIV may contribute to chronic lung disease such as COPD. Ultimately, these findings are important for the development of strategies to reduce chronic diseases associated with HIV infection and improve quality of life.

column36: A new approach to preserving female fertility
column37: A woman's fertility declines sharply beginning at about 35 years of age. In large part, this is due to a decrease in the quality of her oocytes, meaning in their ability to give rise to a healthy baby. Although scientists have identified specific defects in oocytes of reproductively aged women, we do not understand when or how these defects arise. If we knew why oocyte quality decreases as women age, we might be able to prevent this process and preserve her fertility. Our preliminary experiments suggest that the problem originates not in the oocyte itself, but in its interaction with cells of the follicle that provide essential nourishment to the oocyte as it grows. Our objective is to discover why interaction becomes disrupted. This will allow us to develop methods to maintain this essential interaction, so that the follicle cells can properly nourish the oocyte. We hope that our results will help not only women who delay childbearing but also those who suffer impaired fertility as a reult of disease or environmental agents.

column36: Impacts of City-Wide Bicycle Infrastructure Investment on Population Health & Health Equity
column37: Governments are making major investments in transit, cycling, and walking infrastructure to alleviate the pressures of traffic congestion, car pollutant emissions, and population growth. These changes may have lasting impacts on population health. However, these endeavours are costly and require strong political will. There is a need for evidence to identify the policies and programs most likely to impact on health behaviours, and which population groups are most impacted ('how much' and 'for whom'). The City of Victoria, together with province, have committed $9M to build a connected network of cycling facilities that separate bicycles from motor vehicles. This is an unprecedented opportunity to study the impact of building a city-wide network designed to attract people of all ages and abilities to cycling in a mid-sized Canadian city. We will assess impacts of this intervention on population health, comparing Victoria with two other mid-sized cities. We will assess active transportation and safety-related outcomes, using data collected through population surveys before, during, and after the intervention. We will map the access to cycling facilities, and changes in safety impacts, especially within disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Finally, we will calculate the health-related economic benefits of cycling. The outcomes of this project will be: preliminary evidence on whether investment in an 'all ages and abilities' network can induce a shift in travel behaviour and safety, both overall and across population groups; evidence on the impact in terms of access to cycling routes and safety; and an economic assessment of the health-related benefits, which can be used to contextualize the investment. We will provide actionable evidence to guide decision making on public investment in active transportation, in study cities as well as the many other North American cities facing growing transportation and population health challenges.

column36: Novel signaling mechanisms leading to pain in irritable bowel syndrome
column37: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is characterized by abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. It is extremely common, affecting over 10% of the adult population in North America and exerts a tremendous societal impact. For example, it is among the most common reasons for workplace absenteeism and in Canada, costs over $1B annually for diagnosis alone. Despite this, the mechanisms that underlie IBS remain poorly understood and as a result, the available treatments are not very effective. The most debilitating symptom is abdominal pain, and we have evidence that inflammatory mediators in the gut, known as proteases, can activate pain-sensing nerves in the gut and intensify the IBS patient's pain. Our previous studies and preliminary data have revealed that: 1) in IBS patients, multiple proteases are released and trigger sustained activation of pain-sensing visceral nerves; 2) changing the diet of IBS patients can alter the activation of inflammatory cells called mast cells (an important source of gut proteases); and 3) in germ-free mice inoculated with the microbiome of IBS patients, we can recapitulate the increased pain signaling and protease activity when we feed these mice diets comparable to those in humans. Based on these findings, we believe that multiple proteases lead to sustained pain signaling in IBS and that dietary factors sustain this abnormal neuronal activation. Using human biopsies in animal IBS models, we will define the protease profile released in response to changes in diet, and examine if the microbiome of a given patient influences the degree of protease-induced pain. We will also investigate how these proteases, once triggered, can sustain excitation of gut pain-sensing nerves and determine whether protease signaling is amplified by other mast cell mediators, such as histamine. Together, our work will clarify how proteases trigger and prolong pain signaling and in doing so, identify novel targets for treating IBS pain.

column36: Control of Breathing during Sleep: Brainstem Mechanisms of Respiratory Control
column37: Approximately one in four Canadians is affected by significant sleep problems that can diminish their health, alertness, safety and quality of life. The most common and serious of the sleep disorders have impairments of breathing as their root cause. One example is sleep apnea, which affects up to 20% of adults and is thought to be involved in some cases of sudden unexplained death in infancy. Sleep apnea is defined as cessation of breathing during sleep, and is typically caused by closure of the air passage in the throat in sleep due to relaxation of those breathing muscles (e.g., the tongue) whose activity normally keeps this air passage open. Episodes of breathing cessation in sleep can occur hundreds of times per night, each resulting in temporary suffocation that causes major sleep disruption. Understanding the brain mechanisms causing sleep apnea is important because of the adverse medical, societal and economic costs of this common disorder, such as increased strokes, angina and heart attacks, debilitating daytime sleepiness, increased traffic and work-related accidents, impaired work performance and decreased quality of life. Our research will identify the brain mechanisms that cause changes in breathing across wakefulness and sleep. Research will also identify how commonly used prescription and non-prescription sedating drugs (such as anesthetics, sleeping tablets, painkillers and alcohol) can also depress breathing and the waking-up responses to respiratory distress. This information will identify common mechanisms causing the prevalent problems of sleep and sedation-induced depression of breathing, and will guide pharmacological approaches aimed at preventing or reinstating breathing when it is depressed or fails.

column36: Regulation of the hepatic fibrogenic response by Suppressor of cytokine signaling (SOCS) proteins
column37: The liver is constantly exposed to toxic chemicals from food and medication that cause inflammation. Normally, the liver is able to fend off these insults and repair itself quite rapidly. However, when the onslaught is chronic, for example, during chronic alcohol abuse or infection by hepatitis viruses, the inflammation persists and outpaces the normal repair process. This results in persistent liver damage, leading to a condition known as liver fibrosis, which can progress towards cirrhosis, wherein the vital liver functions are compromised and often leads to liver cancer. Liver cancer ranks as the fifth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related death. Most liver cancer patients die within one year due to late diagnosis and lack of effective treatment. While the liver cancer is difficult to treat, early detection of fibrosis and development of anti-fibrotic interventions could prevent the advancement of disease and its progression towards cancer. Inflammation in general is mediated by a group of proteins called 'inflammatory cytokines', which have a normal function as long as their activity is controlled. This is achieved by a variety of mechanisms, of which the control exerted by a family of proteins called 'Suppressor of cytokine signaling' appears to be very important. This is supported by data from human patients who do not express the SOCS1 protein in the liver, and from our own studies using mice lacking SOCS1. We propose to use this mouse models to gain a better understanding of how SOCS1 regulates liver fibrosis. This knowledge could lead to development of new therapeutic approaches to treat liver fibrosis, and thus diminish patient suffering and healthcare burden from cirrhosis and liver cancer.

column36: In vivo interrogation and control of genetically-identified somatosensory neurons in neuropathic pain pathways
column37: Chronic pain affects as many as 1 in 5 people worldwide. As the population ages and modern medicine allows people to survive serious illness, the number of people affected by chronic pain is expected to rise to 1 in 3. Chronic pain can be debilitating, isolating, dehumanizing, and all too frequently, abuse of opioid painkillers can turn deadly (see the current crisis of fentanyl overdoses). Developing new tools to study pain and develop new avenues for analgesia is critical. Previous approaches to activate pain pathways used chemical, thermal, mechanical, or electrical stimulation. These stimuli lack spatial and/or temporal control and often involve invasive procedures. Our goal is to design novel genetic tools that ensure highly precise control on the activity of peripheral pain pathways, and therefore pain perception. Our data provide evidence that optical analgesia can be achieved in freely moving rodents without noxious stimuli or injury. Our approach relies on transgenic mice expressing light-sensitive proteins (opsins) into a specific group of genetically-identified sensory neurons called nociceptors. When exposed to light, light-sensitive proteins are activated, triggering or inhibiting the propagation of electric signals from the periphery to the brain, where pain is perceived. In this project, we propose the development of preclinical models in which pain can be modulated and remotely controlled without any tissue damage. The high sensitivity and specificity of our approach resulted in measurable behavioral responses of the transgenic transducer-expressing mice, following exposure to activators (nociception) or inhibitors (analgesia). Opto/chemogenetic stimulation or inhibition of the sensory pathways in vivo will allow us to investigate the critical role of specific neuronal populations in peripheral pain circuits, facilitating the development of analgesic drugs and gene therapy for the treatment of chronic pain.

column36: Dendritic mechanisms for cortical associations in layer 5 pyramidal neurons from a mouse model of Fragile X syndrome.
column37: Fragile X mental retardation syndrome (FXS) is the most common known cause of autism. Studies in the mouse model of FXS (Fmr1-KO mice) have demonstrated defects in the cerebral cortex at cellular and circuit levels. A key function of the cerebral cortex is its ability to associate external sensory information with an internal representation of the world in order to make predictions about the future. One particular type of cortical neuron, the layer 5 (L5) pyramidal neuron, is believed to be the main associative neuron integrating sensory inputs in their proximal dendrites (dendrite=the receptive surface) with contextual information at their distal dendrites. Recently, it has been shown in Fmr1-KO mice that the distal dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons have an enhanced summation of excitatory inputs, while in our preliminary data we show that proximal dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons from Fmr1-KO mice have a diminished summation of excitatory inputs. Hence, we hypothesize that these cellular impairments can lead to an underrepresentation of sensory information and an overrepresentation of contextual information, which alter the firing and encoding of information of L5 pyramidal neurons from Fmr1-KO mice. Hence, we will examine synaptic transmission and integration of excitatory inputs in proximal and distal dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons from control and Fmr1-KO mice, and study the functional consequences that these defects have in the association of sensory and contextual information in the Fmr1-KO mice. Lastly, we will uncover the specific mechanisms responsible for the altered synaptic integration found in the distal and proximal dendrites of Fmr1-KO L5 pyramidal neurons. To perform this work we will use cutting edge imaging, genetic, and electrophysiological tools. Our prediction is that these defects will affect the encoding of information in single neurons and the circuit they reside on; representing one of the mayor cortical defects associated with FXS.

Dr. Penuela will use a number of different mouse and human tissues and cells to assess if these Panx1 channels are acting to promote cancer progression. About 15 years ago, the pannexin family of proteins that forms channels on the surface of human cells for communication was first discovered. We and others have found that these channels, when present at low levels are important in releasing and ingesting small molecules that tell cells how to behave. In mice, we found that these channels are extremely abundant in aggressive melanoma cells, suggesting that they give melanomas a survival benefit enhancing their ability to grow, migrate and enter other organs ultimately causing death. In this proposal we will explore the expression of Pannexin 1 in human melanoma biopsies from different stages of disease progression. We will evaluate the susceptibility of mouse models that are lacking Panx1 to develop tumours after inoculation with melanoma cells. Finally, we will use mouse models to determine how Panx1 causes tumor cells to grow and move to form metastasis, and we will test several chemicals and new compounds that have been shown to block Panx1 channels, as potential new therapies to be used in the fight against malignant melanoma.

column36: Gait as a clinical marker to predict progression to dementia syndromes in MCI
column37: A decrease in walking speed (gait slowing) is a common problem in older persons that is frequently overlooked; however, it is a strong predictor of future cognitive disability, and adverse events. Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a transitional state between normal cognition and mild dementia, although not all older individuals with MCI will progress to dementia. A recent Canadian consensus on dementia called for better characterization of MCI emphasizing the need to identify potential clinical, imaging, and biological changes that may serve as predictors of further dementia. To date, the predictors identified are difficult to apply in clinics. However, since an association between gait slowing and dementia has been established, gait itself might be able to serve as a clinical predictor. This study will build upon the previous Gait & Brain Study, which has demonstrated that a greater slowing on walking speed under a dual-task condition (e.g., walking while talking) is associated with accelerated cognitive decline in MCI. We will also look for physical changes in the brain that are associated with slowed gait speed under a dual-task condition. We hypothesize that a high dual-task cost in older people with MCI will predict future progression to dementia. Furthermore, we will test combinations of dual-task test with clinically available variables to improve prediction. If our hypothesis is confirmed, conducting practical walking assessment in clinics may help detect who will eventually progress to dementia. We believe that combining simple gait testing with available clinical information (age, sex, and cognitive testing) will improve dementia prediction in MCI. A better detection of those with MCI who will progress to dementia will help the Canadian health system optimize available resources by identifying who may benefit from additional testing, and help implement early strategies and interventions to improve quality of life.

column36: MicroRNA-218s and their regulated signaling networks in placental development and preeclampsia
column37: Preeclampsia (PE) is a major disorder of human pregnancy, characterized by high blood pressure and presence of proteins in the urine. PE is not only the leading cause of maternal death and still birth, but also affects the health of mothers and children later in their lives. The cause of PE is not well understood; however, insufficient invasion of placental cells into the uterus and subsequent failure to modify uterine blood vessels is thought to be the initial event of PE. This results in insufficient blood supplies to the placenta, causing an abnormal secretion of factors from the placenta into the blood to affect the functions of cells lining the blood vessels, known as endothelial cells. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that have important roles in controlling the levels of proteins being made in cells. We have recently discovered that miR-218 levels are lower in placentas of PE patients than those of healthy women. Our preliminary data showed that miR-218 has potent effects in promoting invasion of placental cells to the uterus and to dilate the maternal blood vessels. We also found that miR-218 may regulate the function of endothelial cells. These novel findings suggest that miR-218 plays important roles in maintaining the proper development of the placenta and that insufficient production of miR-218 in the placenta contributes to the development of PE. The major objectives of this grant are to further investigate the role of miR-218 in placenta development; to identify which key molecules are regulated by miR-218; and to determine how abnormal production of miR-218 may lead to PE. We will use cells derived from placenta, placental organ culture and placenta/uterus co-culture systems, as well as endothelial cells, to study the functions of miR-218 and the key molecules regulated by miR-218. The proposed research will improve the understanding of PE and may reveal novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets for this disorder.

column36: Functional and Molecular Characterization of Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts in High Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer
column37: High grade serous ovarian cancer is a highly aggressive and lethal cancer. Our project is focused on gaining a better understanding of the biology of the different types of cells present within ovarian cancers in the hopes that doing so will lead to identification of new therapies. In addition to the cancer cells, tumors contain normal cells from the body called fibroblasts. We believe that fibroblasts provide an environment that promotes the survival of the cancer cells, as well as promoting other cancer properties such as the ability to spread to other parts of the body. It is possible that by blocking the interactions between fibroblasts and cancer cells, we may be able to interfere with cancer progression. The major goal of this application is to understand how fibroblasts support the growth of ovarian cancer, and to develop ways to interfere with that support. We have already developed methods to separate out the fibroblasts and cancer cells from patient tumors and have analyzed them to determine what genes each cell type is expressing. From this we have generated a list of possible mechanisms for how the fibroblasts are functioning. In this project, we will test whether blocking fibroblast-cancer cell interactions can slow down or stop tumor progression, allowing us to develop new strategies to treat ovarian cancer patients in the future.

column36: Dissecting early and progressive leukemogenic impairments in the hematopoietic hierarchy and function using pre-leukemic inherited bone marrow failure syndromes as human disease models
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a blood cancer with a bleak outlook despite treatment with intensive chemotherapy and bone marrow (BM) transplant. Tools for early detection and prevention are desperately needed. Yet, it is unknown how AML evolves because patients is generally not tested before they become ill. The purpose of this study is to decipher how BM progresses from a non-leukemic state to leukemia, while discovering BM defects in patients with high leukemia risk, namely, inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFSs). Fanconi anemia (FA) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) are IBMFSs that start with deficient formation of blood cells in the BM during childhood and progress to pre-leukemia (early signs of cancer), which, if untreated, culminate in AML. Patients with FA and SDS die from either low blood counts (causing infections and bleeding) or leukemia or from the treatments' side effects. Since patients with FA and SDS annually undergo BM testing to check if they develop leukemia, samples for research can be obtained from consenting patients before, during pre-leukemia and overt leukemia. Such samples provide a unique opportunity to study how leukemia develops and identify early changes in BM that indicate treatment. In this study we will analyze BM cells from patients with SDS and FA at three stages: no-leukemia, pre-leukemia and leukemia. We will identify BM cells that grow fast (like leukemia cells), discover genetic mutations that indicate early leukemia and determine why early leukemic cells grow in excess. Last, we will use specially prepared cells from IBMFS patients called pluripotent stem cells as a model to insert mutations that we identify and study which mutations turn the cells leukemic. The results of our study can be used for early detection and prevention of leukemia in IBMFSs, and for discovery of drugs that correct the early damage. The principles learned will likely apply to other cancers, though the specific defects may vary.

column37: Effective treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) usually emphasize a behavioural approach called Exposure and Response Prevention. In this treatment, patients are encouraged to face their fears repeatedly and for extended periods of time, with the help and support of a caring therapist. Although this is an approach that has been shown to work, many patients find the treatment to be difficult; some even refuse the treatment, or drop out before improvements are seen. We have been working to develop an alternate approach which is just as effective as Exposure and Response Prevention, but which we think will be much more acceptable to those who seek help for their OCD. This study will compare the traditional behavioural approach, with our newer cognitively-based approach. We expect that the two treatments will both reduce the symptoms and distress of people with OCD, but that our newer cognitive therapy will have fewer people who refuse or drop out of the treatment, and will be rated as more acceptable. This research will have important implications not only for those struggling with OCD, but also for other anxiety-related problems where behavioural approaches are typically recommended, including posttraumatic stress disorder, social anxiety disorder, and other problems.

column36: Quantitative electroencephalography in rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep: an early marker of cholinergic neurodegeneration in mild cognitive impairment
column37: The prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia is increasing at a rapid pace. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent cause of dementia. The Alzheimer Society of Canada states that 747,000 Canadians had AD in 2011 and that the current estimated costs of dementia for Canada is around $33 billion annually. The degenerative process leading to AD is believed to start decades before the onset of dementia. This long and progressive period is called mild cognitive impairment (MCI) but not all individuals with MCI will develop AD. The identification of earlier markers to detect which MCI individuals will progress to AD is urgently needed for the development and assessment of preventive and therapeutic strategies. Up to now, promising markers measuring brain activity have been identified in awake patients. We propose that rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep is a more sensitive state than wakefulness to detect early neurodegeneration in MCI patients. Indeed, during REM sleep, the activity of the acetylcholine system, which is affected early in MCI, is not masked by other systems that are active during wakefulness. The goal of this project is to predict, in individuals with MCI, those who will develop AD three years later by studying REM sleep characteristics. We will also validate that REM sleep is linked to the integrity of the cholinergic system using brain imaging. If our hypotheses are confirmed, REM sleep characteristics have the potential to become a reliable non-invasive and low-cost tool to help identify MCI individuals at high risk of progressing to AD and test the efficacy of preventive treatments.

column37: Thrombosis- clotting of the blood in blood vessels- is the leading cause of death in Canada and in the Developed society. Blood clot formation in arteries (blood supply vessels) is a major cause of majority of heart attacks and stroke. Blood clot in veins (venous thromboembolism (VTE)) is the third leading cause of death in world after heart attacks and stroke, and is one of the leading cause of death in patients with cancer. Current treatment of these diseases includes the use of drugs which can prevent platelet (a type of blood cell) activation and aggregation, and the use of anticoagulants (blood thinners). However, none of these therapies are perfect due to inherent bleeding side effects associated. Importantly, none of these treatments target the fundamental cause of pathological thrombosis in veins and arteries. Recent studies discovered that biomolecules such as polyphosphate released by platelets and extracellular nucleic acids released by the damaged or activated cells in the blood vessels initiate blood coagulation and cause pathological thrombosis. Thus, in this proposal we are developing novel molecules that can directly neutralize the activity of these potent thrombus generating polyanionic biomolecules by selectively binding them and forming a complex thereby preventing the thrombus formation. This novel drug molecules will also have no or minimal bleeding side effects unlike the current drugs used in the management of thrombosis. This research is based on a recent discovery of a patented novel class of dendritic polymeric inhibitors in our laboratory. This novel therapeutic approach will change the way clinicians treat the patients suffering from blood clot problems and will save the lives of millions of people, and improve their quality of life.

column37: The role of bacterial communities throughout the body in health and disease is being widely studied. This research will lead to a deeper understanding of the potential role of the maternal bacterial community on the infant gut bacterial community.

column37: Many proteins expressed by cancer cells are modified with carbohydrate chains. However, we have recently discovered that VAR2CSA also binds a similar placental-like CS structure broadly present in human cancer. It is therefore tempting to speculate that tumors re-express placental-type CS to accommodate these important cellular processes. In this project we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind CS reconfigurations in human prostate and bladder cancer, and establish the role of these CS modifications in tumor cell growth and survival. Our work will provide new insight into the regulation and function of cancer-associated carbohydrates, essential for developing effective therapeutic strategies targeting human cancer.

column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rhythm disorder that causes one out of six strokes. Prevention of strokes in AF is achieved through the use of blood thinners such as coumadin. These patients will be treated in the usual manner except for this small procedure which has been shown to be quite safe. Having successfully recruited 2300 participants into the trial supported by multiple seed and bridge grants, we now seek full funding to complete recruitment to the full 4,700 participants required to know if left atrial appendage closure works. The LAAOS III trial will determine if closing the left atrial appendage can reduce stroke and other complications in addition to usual therapy. A positive study will change the way heart surgery is performed on patients with AF and result in a large reduction in the number of strokes in Canada. column36: Opposite roles of MYCN and YAP in cancer initiation
column37: Retinoblastoma is a rare childhood cancer of the eye. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a common and very lethal adult tumor caused by smoking. It kills more people than any other cancer. These cancers have much in common, including frequent loss of the RB tumor suppressor gene. Dissecting other shared features that drive these cancers will illuminate new strategies to prevent and treat both diseases. Retinoblastoma arises from cone photoreceptors in the embryonic retina, the cells we use to detect colour. They are hypersensitive to RB loss because they have naturally high levels of MYC, a pro-cancer protein. Why do they need such a dangerous protein? We discovered that MYC is potent at forcing cells to become cones. Cones make other pro-cancer proteins, so by driving this cell fate, MYC inadvertently facilitates tumor formation. Remarkably, we find that MYC also promotes formation of the lung cells that give rise to SCLC. MYC regulates gene expression, so we will identify the targets it controls that promote formation of the tumor-prone cell types in retina and lung. In related work, we discovered that the YAP protein blocks retinoblastoma and SCLC. This is also surprising, because in many other tumor types YAP drives cancer. Our data suggests that YAP impairs retinoblastoma by inhibiting cone formation (and so MYC production). Here, we will examine more closely whether YAP does this in the embryonic human retina, and whether it also blocks the formation of the cells that give rise to SCLC in the lung. YAP is switched off in retinoblastoma and SCLC, so reactivating this gene could be a potent new therapy. To test this idea we will ask if inducing YAP blocks SCLC progression in the mouse lung. If it does, this result would justify extensive efforts to identify drugs that reactivate the silent YAP gene in RB-deficient cancers. SCLC treatment has changed little in decades, but our insights offer hope for new therapies.

column36: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage - Red Blood Cell Transfusion and Outcome (SAHaRA):A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is the result of a burst artery in the brain. It affects young people (40-60 years), nearly half of whom will die, and a third will have permanent disability. Managing patients with aSAH is challenging because the recovering brain is very sensitive and at great risk of further injury (like new strokes) from a lack of blood flow. This risk period can last days to weeks. This may be made worse by having low blood levels (that is red blood cells called anemia), which is very common in these patients. With this study we aim to answer the question: does keeping blood levels higher with transfusion help these patients or just expose them to transfusions unnecessarily? The best way to answer a clinical question is with a controlled and well-conducted clinical trial. With our SAHaRA pilot trial we have shown our ability to conduct such a trial. In the trial we propose here, we aim to prove that maintaining a higher hemoglobin (blood) levels in the first 21 days following aSAH will result in less death and better outcomes 12 months after their aSAH. We will compare higher blood levels to the usual care of allowing blood levels to drop before considering transfusion. We will also assess the effect of these 2 treatment options several other outcomes. These include the effect on complications like stroke, time in an intensive care unit and hospital and on quality of life. column37: Insomnia is a frequent problem in the general population and is associated with physical and mental health problems. It is still difficult to treat insomnia. Indeed, sleeping pills have side effects and tend to lose efficacy over time in many people with insomnia. Psychological treatment for insomnia - called cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-I) - is effective in a majority of people with insomnia, even in the long term, but requires access to qualified therapists. In addition, up to 40% people will still have insomnia symptoms after treatment. In order to provide the treatment option that is the most likely to work for each specific person, it is important to be able to predict which individuals will respond better to CBT-I. Brain electrical signals measured with electroencephalography (EEG) during sleep (particularly a type of brain signal called sleep spindle) tend to vary from one person to another, but remain stable from one night to the other in a specific person; for this reason, they are considered as a 'trait', i.e. a fingerprint characterizing a specific individual. Some of our preliminary work shows that insomniacs with less sleep spindles tend to benefit less from CBT-I treatment. This means that sleep spindle could be used to predict if people will be likely to have their sleep improved after CBT-I before it is used. In this project, we now wish to confirm these results on a larger group of insomniacs, using more detailed measures of sleep spindles. We also wish to define reference values of sleep spindles - adjusted for age and sex - that will allow identifying insomniacs likely to respond to CBT-I. The findings from this research will allow evaluating if a brain electrical measure such as spindles can be used to predict the efficacy of the recommended first-line treatment option for insomnia, and can thus be used as a tool to guide which treatment to recommend in a specific person.

column37: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) affects 5-6% of school-aged children and is characterized by difficulties in activities of daily living. These children are of normal intelligence but show slow and inaccurate gross and/or fine motor movements. Without intervention, the deficits continue into adulthood in the majority of cases. This population is at high risk to develop anxiety, depression, and obesity; these children are at generally increased risk for physical and mental health problems because DCD affects children's ability to interact socially. One of the core deficits in DCD is poor motor timing. Rhythms and timing are fundamental to biological organisms. In humans, breathing, heart beats, walking, and perceiving speech and music rely on the ability to extract timing regularities in auditory signals and/or to produce regular movements. Remediation treatments for DCD have focused on movement therapies. However, recent work from our group and others on understanding how time and rhythm information is processed in the brain shows that the perception of auditory rhythms is accomplished through interactions between auditory and motor (movement) areas of the brain. Simply hearing an auditory rhythm sets up oscillatory brain rhythms we can measure with electroencephalography (EEG) involving both auditory and motor regions. Thus, we hypothesized, and pilot data corroborated, that children with DCD also show timing deficits in the perception of sounds. The research program aims to (1) understand these auditory perceptual deficits in DCD from both a brain and behavioural perspective and (2) investigate benefits of adding auditory rhythmic cuing to existing movement-training therapies to improve outcomes. The research is significant in furthering our understanding of sensorimotor timing deficits underlying DCD and applying this knowledge to improve treatment programs.

The prevalence of Ras genetic lesions is especially high in pancreatic (>90%), colorectal (50%), and lung (30%) cancers. We therefore propose to synthesize larger molecules, named macrocyclic peptides, designed to interact over an extended surface while retaining drug-like properties. It can be expected that compounds emerging from these approaches will form the ground of effective treatments for many common cancers bearing activating Ras mutations.

column37: The liver carries out many vital functions such as metabolism of dietary nutrients, storage of vitamins and iron, synthesis of blood proteins and formation of bile. Besides, the liver purifies blood to prevent toxic substances from reaching other vital organs. Hepatocytes, which are the main cell type in the liver, detoxify and eliminate toxic substances that enter blood. During this process, hepatocytes may get injured and undergo death, which prompts adjacent normal cells to proliferate regenerate a functional liver mass. However, repeated/persistent assaults (e.g., alcohol abuse, hepatitis virus infection) induce chronic inflammation and liver 'fibrosis', leading to 'cirrhosis' - characterized by replacement of loss of liver tissue with fibrous tissue, resulting in reduced liver functions. In livers with cirrhosis, hepatocytes undergo recurrent proliferation to restore liver functions. This causes the formation of liver nodules, within which cells accumulate genetic lesions and may become cancerous. While liver failure caused by cirrhosis ranks among the top 10 causes of death in the western world, liver cancer remains the 3rd leading cause of cancer death. Understanding the molecular basis of abnormal hepatocyte proliferation following liver injury is essential to develop more efficient treatments for liver cancer. The key mediators of hepatocyte proliferation are cytokines and growth factors. Normally, their actions are tightly controlled by diverse mechanisms, one of which is mediated by the 'Suppressor Of Cytokine Signaling' (SOCS) family of proteins. The genes coding for SOCS1 and SOCS3 proteins are frequently inactivated in liver cancer biopsies, indicating that they play important roles in preventing hepatocytes from becoming cancerous. Our goal is to understand how these SOCS proteins function in the liver using mouse models of liver cancer so that this knowledge could be used to develop rational strategies to treat liver cancer.

column37: The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) and the Functional Annotation Of Mouse (FANTOM) consortiums reported that there are far more transcripts than initially anticipated. The existence of the large number of noncoding transcripts has been disregarded as junk DNA and transcript noises for some time, but increasing evidence suggests that a significant part of such noncoding transcripts are in fact functionally active RNA molecules. Importantly, the biological function of noncoding RNAs is thus primarily determined by their structure and their interactions with protein partners. Among these non-coding RNAs are riboswitches, which are structured elements typically found in the 5' untranslated regions of mRNAs. Riboswitches regulate gene expression by altering their structure upon binding to small cellular metabolites. As a result, it is imperative to employ novel high-resolution methods to characterize RNA structures under conditions closer to the in vivo context, most preferably allowing to study the structure of nascent transcripts. A major goal of our research is to unravel the molecular mechanisms by which riboswitches perform ligand binding during their transcription (i.e., co-transcriptionally) to control gene expression. Our research could be used to design novel general antimicrobial drugs based on riboswitch ligand analogs, which would be selectively toxic to bacteria carrying these RNAs. The knowledge obtained from this research will also be generally applicable to study more complex systems, such as long non-coding RNAs associated to cardiovascular diseases and several types of cancer.

column36: Molecular Therapeutic Targeting of Malignant Gliomas
column37: Malignant gliomas are highly aggressive cancers with a survival expectancy of less than 2 years despite surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Over the past 30 years, limited progress has been made in treating this aggressive cancer despite our increased understanding of the molecular genetics and basic biology of these tumours. Intrinsic resistance mechanisms of these cancer cells in the GC prevent chemotherapy and radiation therapy from being effective. In addition, malignant gliomas are characterized by highly invasive cells which are not rapidly dividing but are capable of migrating a considerable distance away from the central core in a zone of infiltration (ZOI). These invading glioma cells are somewhat protected by an intact blood brain barrier (BBB) which prevents chemotherapy from effectively reaching the ZOI. We will focus on metabolically reprogramming glioma cells in the GC to reduce their proliferation, and to inhibit glioma cells from following pro-survival pathways in response to cellular stresses such as hypoxia, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. In addition, we will target the invading glioma cells in the ZOI using novel inhibitors of cell invasion, and magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound to break down the BBB around the GC to facilitate contact of these inhibitors with the invading glioma cells. We expect that simultaneous precision targeting of the GC and ZOI with potent drugs and advanced delivery strategies will provide therapeutic and survival benefit to patients suffering from this lethal cancer.

Expanding our patient cohort, we will also carefully study and compare the human retinal disease to ensure we can translate this therapy to patients. If successful, this will be the first targeted therapy for PBD and address a devastating feature, blindness. column36: What is the cause of chromosome segregation error in the mammalian preimplantation embryo?
column37: The health of the newly fertilised embryo is an important determinant of fertility. One problem commonly experienced by women undergoing fertility treatments is that the early embryo has cells with the wrong number of chromosomes - termed 'aneuploid' cells. Embryos with aneuploid cells are considered unlikely to give rise to a healthy baby. Indeed, many clinics use the presence of aneuploid cells to discard bad-quality embryos rather than transfer them back to the patient. The presence of aneuploid cells in the early embryo indicates that errors have taken place during chromosome segregation - the process of sharing the chromosomes between the daughter cells at the time of cell division. However, despite the clear importance in human fertility, the cause of these chromosome segregation errors in early embryos is unknown. Our laboratory specialises in the use of state-of-the-art imaging approaches to observe and investigate the process of chromosome segregation, and we have developed an assortment of techniques for observing these processes in embryos. Here we will perform some of the first examinations of how chromosome segregation works in the early mammalian embryo, and try to understand why this process goes wrong so often. Most of our experiments will use mouse embryos, with some experiments using human embryos that can no longer be used for treatments. This work will shed light upon the causes of chromosome mis-segregation in the embryo, helping to explain the problems experienced by many fertility patients, and we hope that our experiments will directly lead to improved methods for selecting embryos for transfer to patients in the clinic.

column36: The role of TRPV1 receptors in the pathogenesis of febrile seizures- links to respiration and inflammation
column37: Febrile seizures are the most common seizure disorder to affect children who are at a high risk of developing intractable epilepsy. The mechanisms of febrile seizures are unknown which has limited the development of prophylactic treatments. There is strong evidence supporting that febrile seizures occur when children have fever-induced increases in breathing associated with an infection that leads to respiratory alkalosis and subsequent decreased seizure thresholds. Indeed, shifts in acid-base balance are well recognized to alter brain function such that alkalosis leads to hyperexcitability and decreased seizure thresholds, and acidosis producing the opposite effect. Given this link between fever, respiration and febrile seizures, it is important to determine the precise mechanisms by which fever leads to increases in breathing and subsequent respiratory alkalosis. Transient receptor potential vanilloid type 1 receptors (TRPV1) are heat sensitive receptors that play an important role in thermoregulation and responses to inflammation. Importantly, TRPV1 has been localized in the vagus nerve which is a key driver of the fever-induced increases in breathing linked to respiratory alkalosis. The overall goal of this proposal is to test, in an inflammation-based model of febrile seizures established in my laboratory, the link between TRPV1, inflammation and fever-induced increases in breathing accounting for respiratory alkalosis and consequent increased risk of febrile seizures. The results of this study will provide a molecular target upon which, currently unavailable, prophylactic treatments for febrile seizures can be developed and made available for use in clinical practice.

column36: Molecular Rules in Brain Cell Microcircuits in Health and Disease
column37: Maintaining the balance between excitation and inhibition is a fundamental attribute of brain function that is necessary for information processing and higher functions, such as affect and cognition. The maintenance of this balance occurs through the constant fine-tuning of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission on multiple time scales, from milliseconds to weeks and months. Much has been learned about short-term functional adaptations (seconds to hours) at the cell contact level; however how the different cell types of brain microcircuits synchronize their functions on longer time-scales (weeks to months) to maintain optimal function, while allowing plasticity, is less well-known. Our data suggest a predominant role for inhibitory cells in mediating adaptive changes during brain aging. We and others show similar inhibitory changes, albeit out of synchrony or exaggerated, in the context of depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Hence we predict that (1) changes in gene function, specifically in inhibitory neurons, maintain long-term adaptations during life-long brain aging, and that (2) changes in the same cell-dependent gene programs occur in several brain disorders. Using molecular biology and computational methods, we will test this hypothesis directly in the human post-mortem brain, using samples from midlife and older subjects. Similar approaches will be used in rodent models to investigate mechanisms and conservation of processes across species. We will then determine the extent of changes in the same cells and pathways in the context of diseases, using human samples from bipolar depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's patients. This novel dimensional approach across species, lifespan and brain disorders has the potential to reveal the molecular mechanisms and rules that govern long-term homeostatic processes across the main cell types of brain cell microcircuits in health and brain diseases.

column36: The Role of Kidney Injury Molecule-1 in Renal Transplantation
column37: Kidney transplantation is the ideal treatment for patients with end-stage kidney disease. Despite better drugs to suppress the immune system, however, the long-term survival of the transplants remains suboptimal. Damage of the kidney due to the lack of blood flow during organ procurement and cold storage before transplantation (ischemia-reperfusion injury, or IRI) is believed to be a major contributor to the limited lifespan of transplants. The tissue injury is further compounded by rejection episodes in the transplanted kidney. There is also growing evidence to suggest that IRI may interact with immune factors worsening graft injury. Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) is a protein produced by native and donor kidneys following injury. Using mice genetically engineered to be deficient in KIM-1, we previously showed that KIM-1 protects the native kidneys of mice from tissue damage and kidney dysfunction following IRI. Paradoxically, however, KIM-1 can also promote chronic kidney disease and scarring. Whether KIM-1 protects or is harmful in transplanted kidneys is unknown. In this project, we will use a mouse model of transplantation to help determine if KIM-1 in the transplanted kidney can protect it from tissue damage from IRI as well as from acute rejection, or whether KIM-1 leads to long-term scarring and premature graft loss. We will also test the therapeutic potential of a new molecule called AIM, which we have shown can protect native kidneys from the damaging effects of IRI via a KIM-1 dependent pathway, in improving the lifespan of transplanted organs. The findings from our proposed studies will advance our understanding of why transplanted kidneys fail prematurely, and help us to develop new potential treatments to prolong their lifespan.

column36: Cocaine Addiction: Epigenetic Studies in Living and Postmortem Brain
column37: The overarching goal of this research is to understand how interactions between inherited genes and early drug use can affect vulnerability to addictions. We are starting with the study of addictions because understanding better the causes of addiction could help us develop effective treatment and prevention strategies. And the need for new treatments is urgent. Substance use is associated with economic costs greater than all other psychiatric disorders combined, and the present research is expected to identify critical genes, enzymes, and brain pathways that could serve as important therapeutic targets. column37: Microtubules (MTs) are protein polymers that form a cable-like network of transport super-highway to move important cargoes around inside a cell. One of these cargoes is our chromosomes, the genetic material that makes us what we are. It turns out that these cables need to grow and shrink all the time to perform their functions such as capturing and transporting chromosomes, especially when cells are dividing. A clinically proven strategy to stop cancer cell proliferation is to perturb the growing and shrinking dynamics of MT polymers. In fact, MT-targeting drugs are among the most successful chemotherapeutic agents currently used in the clinics. However, their success is hindered by adverse side effects and the development of drug resistance in cancer patients. To address these shortcomings, we propose to further exploit this proven approach through an alternative route - by targeting the protein enzymes that control the MT polymers. Using a high-throughput screening approach, our lab has already identified chemical agents that modulate these MT modifying enzymes. Importantly, these agents exert a potent growth suppressive effect on cancer cells, but seem to spare non-cancer cells. However, the precise molecular mechanism how these molecules work is still not known. In the proposed project, we aim to use modern cutting-edge technologies to understand the following: 1) How these chemical agents affect the MT-regulating enzymes at the molecular level; 2) how this in turn affects cancer cell proliferation; and 3) how to improve the specificity and efficacy of this new class of potential chemotherapeutics. Our ultimate goal is to validate this new strategy in order to develop the next generation anti-cancer drugs.

column37: Human papillomaviruses (HPV) infect undifferentiated stem cells of our skin. column36: On the road to promoting mobility and health after driving cessation among older adults
column37: Mobility is a broad concept that can be understood as the ability to move oneself within environments that include one's residence and neighbourhood. This study will follow individuals for an additional 4 years in order to observe more cases of driving cessation. This study will identify factors that promote health among older adults after driving cessation and will be used to develop interventions and policies to facilitate a healthy transition to non-driving.

column36: Optimizing the Curative Treatment for High Risk Prostate Cancer: Combining Advanced Imaging, Trans-perineal Mapping Biopsies, and Dual Air Kerma Strength LDR Brachytherapy Implants to Minimize Radiation Dose to Normal Tissues
column37: Radiotherapy plus hormonal treatment is the recommended form of treatment for men with high risk prostate cancer. column37: Stem cell transplantation to prevent amputation in patients with critical limb ischemia (CLI) is under intense investigation. column36: Exploring structure-function relationships between dietary fibre and the gut microbiome: Towards predicting and personalizing nutritional strategies.
column37: Being overweight significantly increases risk for numerous diseases that have been linked to the microbial populations that inhabit our gastrointestinal tract. The exact role of the gut microbiota in human health appears to depend partially on diet. A diet high in fat can trigger inflammation when harmful molecules are produced by gut bacteria and taken up into the body. On the other hand, gut bacteria can ferment dietary fibre to produce short-chain fatty acids, molecules that have anti-inflammatory properties. However, we do not yet understand all the consequences of microbial fibre fermentation in the gut to healthy functioning of an individual. We also do not know how individual differences in types of bacteria that compose each person's gut microbial community influence how we can ferment different chemical types of dietary fibre. With such knowledge at hand, it would be possible to adjust an individual's diet based on the configuration of the microbes in our digestive tract. We propose to systematically investigate the interactions between fiber chemistry, the genetic make-up of the gut microbiota, and metabolic and immunological measures of health in overweight and mildly obese people. We will also look for links between different types of dietary fibre and the composition and function of each person's gut microbiota. This will allow us to test whether microbiome patterns in individuals predict the effects of the fibre. To achieve this, we will begin with an exploratory nutritional trial that compares the effects of three types of fermentable dietary fibre with the effects of non-fermentable cellulose. We will measure how fibre type and microbiota composition and function affect specific health outcomes such as reduced inflammation. This new knowledge can be used to improve dietary strategies for preventing obesity, develop strategies to modulate a person's gut microbiota for better health outcomes, and lay groundwork for personalized human nutrition.

column37: Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH) is a disease characterized by aberrant mineralization of soft connective tissues in the spine. column36: Symptom screening and early palliative care in patients with advanced cancer: a randomized trial
column37: Palliative care is defined as care by a team of specialists that increases quality of life (QOL) for patients with a life-threatening illness. Four large randomized controlled trials showed that when patients with advanced cancer were referred early to specialized palliative care teams, they had improved QOL and greater satisfaction with their cancer care. Although it is known that patients with the most severe physical and psychological symptoms have the greatest need for palliative care, these patients are often not referred to palliative care teams. Therefore, it has been suggested that there should be a triage system to identify patients who have the greatest need. Our research team has developed a system that identifies patients with high symptom burden in order to offer them access to the palliative care team. This system, which uses information patients already report about their symptoms at each oncology clinic appointment, is called STEP (Symptom screening with Targeted Early Palliative care). We propose to run a trial at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre and Kingston General Hospital comparing STEP with regular symptom screening in oncology clinics. Patients are eligible to participate if they have advanced cancer and a life expectancy of at least 6 months. Consenting patients will be assigned randomly (by chance) either to receive STEP or to follow routine symptom screening. Patients in both groups complete symptom screening on computers in the waiting room of oncology clinics. For patients in the STEP group, if one or more of their symptom ratings are higher than the defined cut-off, a nurse will be alerted to call them to offer an appointment in the palliative care clinic for assessment and follow-up. All patients will complete questionnaires measuring outcomes of QOL, depression, symptom control and satisfaction with care at recruitment, 2, 4 and 6 months. We will measure the impact of STEP on these outcomes, compared to screening alone.
