column37: The image of the 'therapeutic missile' commonly used to present targeted drug delivery agents emphasizes precision, control, and efficiency. For the next evolution of cancer treatment, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a great representative of this concept. ADCs home to tumor cells with exquisite precision and control. However, upon landing on tumor cells, ADCs lose their precision, control, and efficiency for effectively delivering and accumulating the drugs inside the cell. ADCs travel in an intracellular route that is controlled by the cancer cell that transports ADC back outside the cell or respond in ways that kick the delivered drugs out. Without the drugs reaching effective cellular concentrations, cancer cells are able to resist and survive and patients soon relapse and die. We will develop ADCs that take control of their intracellular travel by incorporating our new Canadian technology (ACCUM) that mimics how viruses travel inside the cell. ACCUM attaches easily to ADCs enabling them to take control of their travel, which consists of a more efficient route to deliver their drugs. The result is that ACCUM-empowered ADCs are able to deliver their drugs with better efficiency inside target cancer cells than current ADCs. The increased accumulation has resulted in more effective cancer cell killing. The goal of this project is to further mature this technology for use in patients with invasive bladder cancer (IBC) - a worldwide problem without any life saving medications. We performed a clinical study and discovered a target (IL-5Ra) for IBC and developed rodent models that mimics the growth of human IL-5Ra-IBC. The research experiments designed in this proposal are to optimize conditions for clinical translation by optimizing ACCUM-ADC formulation and IBC cell killing. We will then determine the tumor killing effectiveness in our rodent models. This research will place Canada in an ADC leadership role and provide effective treatment for IBC.

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) - commonly referred to as chronic bronchitis or emphysema - is a progressive and debilitating disorder of the lungs. Typically, COPD is characterised by persistent inflammation of the lungs leading to difficulty in breathing and, ultimately, premature death. An acute attack of COPD, known as an exacerbation, describes a rapid worsening of a patient's disease above normal day-to-day variability. Such attacks can be life threatening, are one of the leading cause of hospitalizations in North America and have a detrimental impact on ease of breathing and quality of life. It is believed by many investigators that LABAs protect against exacerbations by opening the airway passages. However, recent research from our laboratory suggests that the beneficial effects of LABAs may also be due to their ability to switch-on a variety of genes in the lungs that, together, suppress inflammation, improve breathing and reduce the severity of attacks. We will also conduct a clinical study to measure the effect of a LABA on gene expression changes in the lungs of patients with COPD to confirm results obtained with isolated cells. We believe this research is important because acute attacks of COPD are associated with a considerable risk of death. The work proposed here should improve our understanding of how LABAs benefit patients with COPD and identify novel genes that could be exploited therapeutically.

column37: About six million Canadians are now at the age of 65 or older. For these people, their age is inevitably a major risk factor for contracting cardiovascular diseases. column37: Scar formation following injury to skin is a common, unwanted outcome of the wound healing process. The goal of this study is to investigate the function of specific genes that have been associated with doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity. By understanding if these genes directly impact the response to doxorubicin, and what biological mechanisms are involved, we could potentially use these genes as genetic tests to predict which patients are most likely to develop cardiotoxicity from this drug. We will study the role of these genes in heart cells generated from human stem cells. My lab has recently described a new way of studying doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity using such stem cell - derived heart cells. We will introduce the specific gene variants of interest using a state-of-the-art gene editing technology called CRISPR. We will compare heart cells with or without these gene variants to determine how they respond to doxorubicin. We will also isolate stem cells from the blood of patients that have suffered from doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity, turn these stem cells into heart cells, and study how they respond to the drug, in the presence or absence of the specific gene variants. If we can identify the patients at highest risk of drug-induced heart damage, we could take steps to prevent or mitigate this devastating adverse drug reaction. Ultimately these efforts will result in safer and more effective drugs and will allow Canadians to stay healthier and experience fewer side effects.

A better understanding of this particular source of hedonic reactions will provide a framework for a more general understanding the neural underpinnings of pleasure. Insights gained from these kinds of circuit analyses have already been used in the development of highly specific therapeutic interventions designed to improve the lives of patients afflicted by mental illness.

column36: Stimulating Functional Networks to Enhance Stroke Recovery
column37: Currently ~400,000 Canadians live with the after effects of stroke and stroke is the number one cause of disability. Despite often not having a full recovery from stroke, most people will have a remarkable improvement in function in the absence of any therapy. The problem is that this only occurs in the first few months after a stroke. This fact suggests that the brain has the ability to temporarily heal itself "naturally" through repairing and rebuilding connections between the cells in the brain called neurons. During recovery from a stroke regions of the brain reorganizing on their own. This suggests that we can enhance stroke recovery by stimulating new, active group of neurons. New treatments are being tested in patients that aim to strengthen the formation of new sets of neurons by stimulating the brain. These treatments appear promising yet only some patients get better. One reason why stimulation therapy may not always work is that we do not know which particular neurons need to be stimulated. This project will identify which neurons reorganize naturally during recovery and test if stimulating these neurons can improve recovery. Our work will be performed in animal models of strokes since there is no non-surgical method that allows us to manipulate or visualize individual neurons after a stroke in humans. We will determine which specific neurons participate in recovery from stroke and identify the timeline of brain reorganization following stroke. We are well suited to accomplish this task using special mice that allow us to 1) label and visualize individual neurons to see what neurons are active at any given time and 2) stimulate neurons in a live animal that is performing a behavior task. Thus, this fundamental study will not only shed light on the underlying mechanisms of stroke recovery, but also allow us to design better treatments for stroke recovery, so survivors will struggle less with disability and enjoy a better quality of life.

column36: Viral Control of Autophagy to Reprogram the Host Cell Secretome
column37: Viruses are incredible tools that teach us how our cells work. In my lab, we study the virus, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). This virus causes a rare skin cancer called Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). My lab is interested in how this virus changes cells that comprise blood vessels, called endothelial cells, to make them secrete proteins that are called inflammatory cytokines, that promote the cancer KS. I have discovered that KSHV targets granules called processing bodies (PBs) that play an important role in controlling inflammatory cytokine production (Corcoran et al. 2015 PLoS Path. 11:e1004597). My lab now has exciting new evidence that connects the disappearance of PBs to the process of autophagy, which literally means 'self-eating'. Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that permits cells to survive the stress of starvation by promoting the degradation and recycling of a variety of cellular structures, thereby providing essential cellular building blocks and energy for survival. Autophagy has also been shown to regulate inflammatory cytokine production; however how this occurs is not clear in most cases. My compelling preliminary evidence connects autophagy increases with the disassembly of PBs and increased inflammatory cytokine production. This is the first evidence suggesting the coordinated regulation of autophagy and PBs controls inflammation in our cells. Impact and Significance: My lab has made a fundamental discovery about how inflammatory cytokine expression is regulated. Inflammatory cytokines are aberrantly produced in many disorders in addition to KS, such as rheumatoid arthritis and many other cancers. Increasing our knowledge of how autophagy and PBs are functionally linked will help develop new treatments to limit inflammation in many situations.

column36: Mobilizing a land-based culturally appropriate active living intervention among Indigenous youth
column37: The benefits of physical activity (PA) are far-reaching, and individuals with high PA have better mental, physical and emotional health. However, our population is more inactive than ever and to tackle this health issue it is important to act early, especially in populations that are most vulnerable. In Canada, one of the most marginalized groups is Indigenous youth. Even though they are Canada's fastest growing group, Indigenous youth have poorer health outcomes than others. As PA's benefits are numerous, we propose to develop sustainable ways to improve PA in Indigenous youth and thus, ultimately increase their chances of leading a healthy life. We have devised an intervention that is not only culturally appropriate, but also novel. In our 5 year intervention we will invite youth from our partnering communities to spend 5 days/year at a tipi camp. In this tipi camp we will teach youth to take advantage of living on the land, and combine this approach with introducing them to active arts-based theatre games. We have done a similar tipi camp in the past and observed that being in the tipi camp improved not only their PA, but also their mental health and overall wellbeing. After the tipi camp we will follow up with active arts-based programs through the schools of these youth. We will assess their PA and overall wellbeing in three different seasons every year throughout the intervention period. We aim to demonstrate that this novel intervention will allow Indigenous youth to lead a healthier, active life. We believe that if we generate evidence that establishes the importance of culturally appropriate active living, it will change the current state of affairs, where Indigenous youth are left to fend for themselves. We ultimately aim to show that this is an effective and economical approach to address a wide range of health issues in Indigenous youth.

column36: Lipid homeostasis regulation by brain glucagon signalling
column37: Background: A key feature of diabetes and obesity is an abnormal level of fats ("lipids") in the blood. High blood levels of lipids made by the liver increase the risk of damaging bodily systems that serve to maintain our metabolism. Thus, it is important to discover and understand mechanisms that affect how lipid production and balance is controlled by our bodies and work towards the goal of lowering lipid levels in the blood, to reduce the risks of health problems associated with an imbalance in metabolism. Objective: Our research aims to unveil novel actions of glucagon, in the brain, that alters whole-body balance of lipid levels. Research project: We will test how glucagon, a hormone made and found in the body, is used by the brain to control liver lipid production, and consequently lipid levels in the blood. We will assess the action of glucagon in the brain under normal conditions and in obesity (from high calorie feeding) and in diabetes. We hypothesize that the brain, by specific pathways controlled by this hormone, alters lipid production and output by the liver. Hence, glucagon action in the brain will affect blood lipid levels. We hypothesize that nutrient excess impairs glucagon's action in the brain, which contributes to an over-production of lipids by the liver. Hence, targeting this defect will help restore blood lipid levels in conditions of obesity and diabetes. Impact: Insights gained from the proposed research will reveal new pathways and mechanisms to regulate blood lipid levels. The research will advance our current understanding of how glucagon affects lipid metabolism, not just by its known effects on tissues like the liver, but also by its novel actions in the brain. These findings will reveal putative new targets, which can help lower blood lipid levels in diabetes and obesity, and thus improve the quality of life of people affected by these conditions. This also helps to reduce the collateral effects on health care and spending.

In addition to testing clinical outcomes, part of the project will focus on understanding how oxytocin improves psychotherapy outcomes (does it improve the relationship between the therapist and patient?), and whether some people may benefit from this dual treatment more than others (does oxytocin augmentation benefit patients with poor interpersonal functioning or adverse childhood experiences?). However, the studies supporting this recommendation are of low quality and may have led to biased conclusions. Specifically, existing studies include only people who eventually started dialysis, as opposed to the vast majority of CKD population not yet treated with dialysis and whose family doctors must decide whether to refer to a kidney specialist, and when. In addition, the observation in existing studies that longer pre-dialysis nephrology care leads to better patient outcomes following dialysis start could be explained by the fact that people who have rapidly progressive kidney disease tend to require dialysis sooner making the length of pre-dialysis care is shorter. These people tend to be sicker and are therefore more likely to have poor health outcomes. In contrast, people who are healthy and have kidney disease that progresses more slowly tend to be followed for a longer time in pre-dialysis clinics. It is unclear if longer pre-dialysis care is a marker for a healthier patient, or if the care provided in pre-dialysis clinics leads to improved patient outcomes. The proposed research will take these factors into account and leverage detailed Alberta provincial data sources to assess the impact of timing of referral to kidney specialist services on kidney failure, hospitalization and death in people with CKD. Given the large patient population, the widespread practice of early referral and limited health care resources, this unique work is expected to provide high-quality evidence to inform referral guidelines and health policy, identify areas of clinical focus to improve outcomes, and stimulate future research.

column36: Neuroprotective effects of upper extremity skilled learning in people with multiple sclerosis

Learning a skill produces positive changes in brain tissue, such as myelin. To investigate the effects of practicing a skill, individuals will perform an at home-based therapy that requires goal-directed hand use. We believe encouraging individuals to learn motor skills will improve brain and hand function in people with MS.

column36: Making accurate depression screening and assessment a reality for Canadians: using individual patient data meta-analysis to personalize risk estimates
column37: Major depression is a mood disorder that has a negative impact on quality of life. Depression screening, which involves using short questionnaires to identify people who may have unrecognized depression, has been suggested as a way to improve the detection, management, and treatment of depression. Depression screening is recommended in the United States and in certain medical guidelines in Canada (e.g., stroke guidelines), but is not currently recommended in Canada's main primary health care guidelines due to concerns that screening tools do not accurately distinguish between patients with and without depression. Only approximately 20-40% of patients identified as depressed by current screening tools truly have depression. In my project, I will combine original patient data from published depression screening studies to create a very large database that can be used to determine more accurate ways to assess and appropriately identify patients with depression. My project will allow us to determine the probability that a specific patient is depressed by considering the patient's individual depression score along with specific characteristics, such as age, sex, and medical diagnosis, which are associated with depression. This method will be more accurate than current procedures that only classify patients as "likely" or "not likely" depressed. To implement my findings, I will develop a free online calculator that allows healthcare professionals to use the results of my research with actual patients in practice. This project will improve the effectiveness of depression screening, which depends on accurate screening questionnaires. In collaboration with Canadian guideline-makers, findings from my project will be applied in hospitals and health clinics to facilitate effective depression screening programs, improve the management of depression, and set Canada apart as a leader in depression research and practice.

column36: Analysis of breast cancer REaCT (Rethinking Clinical Trials) data
column37: Telomeres are sections of DNA found at the ends of our chromosomes. Telomerase is an essential component of the makeup of our genetic information. It helps to assemble and protect our DNA in our telomeres from damage. Since telomerase possesses such a critical role for our cell's health and make-up, it's dysfunction can result in devastating effects to our well-being. Cancer is a disease characterized by the rapid and uncontrolled division of cells. As a cell begins to become cancerous, it divides more often, and its telomeres become very short. If its telomeres get too short, the cell may die. However, these cells can escape death by making more telomerase, which prevents the telomeres from getting even shorter. Cancer cells contain active telomerase to enable them to become 'immortal' and continue dividing uncontrollably. When compared to normal healthy cells in our body, the levels of telomerase are greatly increased in cancer cells. This observation, which is found to be true for a wide number of different cancer types, can be exploited to develop new cancer therapies which specifically target the out-of-control telomerase. If telomerase activity was switched off in cancer cells, their telomeres would shorten until they reached a 'critical length'. This would, prevent the cancer cells from dividing uncontrollably to form tumours. Further research into the different processes which control telomerase levels and activity, once identified, can be exploited as targets for cancer therapy. Based on these findings, compounds can be developed which specifically target this out-of-control cellular process, and tested on human cancer cells to determine their efficacy in slowing the progression of cancer.

column36: Assembly of inhibitory circuits in the normal and premature cerebellum
column37: The brain depends on connections of nerve cells. These connections can be excitatory or inhibitory and the balance between the two is essential for brain function. Abnormal development of inhibitory nerve cells and their connections plays an important part in many disorders including epilepsy and autism. Babies born prematurely or who do not get enough oxygen at birth are more likely to develop these problems - possibly because their inhibitory circuits are not formed correctly. In this project, I am looking at a group of inhibitory nerve cells that are born later in pregnancy - beginning around the time babies can survive outside the womb. I will identify the events that help the cells become the correct type of nerve cell and form the right connections. I will also see how injury around the time of birth (low oxygen, infection) affects the normal development of these cells. Finally, I will see if treatments during and immediately after injury can help damaged brains regain their normal wiring. The knowledge from this work will help us learn how inhibitory connections form in the brain and how premature birth and damage can affect this wiring. In the future, this can be used to change treatment of premature infants and to offer preventative strategies for serious pediatric neurological disorders.

column36: Help Seeking Behaviours, Access to Care and Suicide among Rural and Urban Populations in Ontario, Canada
column37: Previous research has indicated that those living in rural areas may have increased risk of suicide compared to their urban counterparts and research from the United States suggests that those living in rural areas are less likely to seek help from mental health care professionals prior to suicide. Factors that are associated with rurality and that may predict these help seeking behaviours will also be examined such as travel time to the nearest mental health service centre and nearest general health service centre, having a family physician, and prevalence of health professionals in the nearest town. This study will be completed using health services data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Research. We hypothesize that lower rates of help seeking will be associated with increasing distance to nearest hospital or mental health services centre, lower prevalence of mental health care professionals and other health professionals and lack of primary care physician. This research contributes new knowledge because previous research comparing suicide rates in Canada is based on 1996 data and does not evaluate health care service utilization prior to suicide.(1) Additionally, help seeking prior to suicide attempts have not yet been compared in an urban versus rural setting. This research is important because rural populations are vulnerable and historic trends suggest increased risk of suicide.(2, 3) My background growing up in a rural setting living and working on a farm, previous epidemiological research involving rural populations, my undergraduate degree in Psychology and my experiences as a suicide phone line volunteer are reasons why I am an ideal candidate to conduct this research.

column37: HIV medications are getting better but for many HIV-infected Canadians taking their lifelong medication is a serious challenge. Current HIV care insufficiently addresses this. Dr. Lebouche's research program centers on the development and testing of a new measure, a questionnaire about factors that patients believe make it hard for them to take their HIV medication. It aims to ensure that care is more patient-centered and responsive to these factors. This measure will be filled out on an electronic tablet prior to patients' regular clinic visits and scores will be shared with their doctor so that any difficulties can be discussed and addressed. Dr. Lebouche is consulting with both patients and HIV doctors to create this measure to ensure that it is relevant to them and he has several clinical trials planned to evaluate it. This research program puts the patient's perspective at the top of research priorities and is an ideal context to mentor trainees and new investigators in patient-oriented research and in the conduct of innovative clinical trials. With this Chair, Dr. Lebouche will recruit talented trainees with a range of academic backgrounds to create qualified researchers in these areas. His research and mentorship programs are set to not only innovate HIV care but to increase the pool of investigators committed to engaging patients and other concerned groups in health research.

column36: Improving Medication PRescribing for Ontario's Vulnerable Elderly High Cost Healthcare Users (IMPROVE-HCU)
column37: High cost healthcare users (HCUs) are a small group of patients that use a disproportionate healthcare resources compared to the average patient. In 2011, 5% of Ontarians used 65% ($19.8 billion) of total measurable public healthcare expenditures. Most HCUs are seniors with multiple chronic conditions taking multiple medications. With costs expected to double in 20 years, the current approach to HCUs has been deemed unsustainable by leading economists and there is an urgent need to design interventions to improve their health outcomes and costs. Our proposed research program seeks to better understand the impact of prescribing quality and drug use in senior HCUs. It is currently unknown whether HCUs are using optimal drugs and whether savings can be found through more cost-effective drug use. In Study 1, we will be using health administrative databases to investigate the current quality of prescribing and drug use in senior HCUs. We will be using the STOPP-START screening tool to look for potentially inappropriate prescribing that should have been stopped or started based on high quality scientific evidence. We will also explore the cost-savings if the government adopted a policy known as "reference-based pricing" for select high cost drugs with cheaper, equally effective alternatives. In Study 2, we will test the feasibility of conducting a large randomized trial to test the effectiveness of a new strategy to optimize drugs for hospitalized seniors HCUs to reduce their risk of death, re-hospitalization and healthcare costs. This project will demonstrate the impact of optimizing medications for Canada's high need, high cost seniors. It is the first of its kind internationally and it will help clinicians, hospitals and government develop new strategies to address the healthcare sustainability crisis. If only 10% of HCU expenses could be avoided or delayed, an additional $1.7 billion would be available in Ontario alone to fund better care for these seniors.

column36: Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies (CEMT)
column37: The term epigenome refers to chemical modifications of DNA and proteins that control the structure and regulation of the "genome", a term referring to all the DNA within our cells. In contrast to the genome, which changes very little if at all over the course of an individual's life, the epigenome is dynamic and changes during normal development, aging, disease challenges and in response to various external stimuli. Such epigenome changes can result in significant differences in how genes, and thus how cells, behave. Thus, an understanding of the epigenome and how it works in different cell types is critically important to understanding many aspects of human health and disease. The Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies (CEMT) has established a track record of leadership in the International Human Epigenomic Consortium; in the generation of reference epigenomes from a broad spectrum of normal and diseased human cell types; in the development and testing of technology for broader future applications; and in making such technology rapidly available to Canadian scientists. The CEMT is designed as an integrated unit composed of internationally leading biologists and clinicians with specialized access to, and knowledge of, the normal and diseased cell types we will analyze. The collaborative team effort described herein will transform our understanding of the relationship between the dynamic nature of the epigenome and how genes are turned on and turned off, and lay the foundation for larger studies to revolutionize our understanding of the role played by the epigenome in health and diseases, and from there how to more effectively manage the health of our populations.

By building a map of genetic and epigenetic regulation in these syndromes we will identify key genes and pathways that impact on human cognition, speech and behaviour. Dr.MacVicar will continue to investigate why neurons die in response to Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) and ischemic stroke, and how neurons and the surrounding support cells called glia, communicate in the healthy and diseased brain. Aberrant neuron-glia communication contributes to neuroinflammation, synaptic disruption and neurodegeneration. This research will reveal the ways by which neurons die in response to trauma, and how the normal communication between neurons and glia goes awry. These discoveries will allow us to develop novel and efficacious treatments to debilitating and intractable brain conditions.

Donald Redelmeier proposes to apply the fundamentals of decision science using the methods of clinical epidemiology to explore driver error and life-threatening traffic crashes. This provides the impetus for my goals to understand the structural basis of protein kinase and UPS enzyme function and to develop new therapeutics.

column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. It is incurable, with average patient survival of about 13 months even with aggressive therapeutic regimens. A main reason for therapeutic failure is that not all cells in a tumor are identical, but some cells are uniquely responsible for tumor growth and recurrence after therapy. We call these "cancer stem cells." We found that cancer stem cells package their DNA is a very specific manner. We will identify ways of targeting this vulnerability to eliminate the cancer stem cells with next generation therapeutics, thereby preventing tumor recurrence.

Type 1 diabetes is a chronic disease that is treated with life-long insulin replacement therapy using injections or portable pump. However, most patients do not currently achieve glucose targets and at risk of long-term complications. The focus of my research is to develop an electro-mechanical artificial pancreas that automatically regulates sugar levels for patients with type 1 diabetes. Short-term clinical trials have shown promising results, and we are currently optimizing the system design and conducting long-term trials. The artificial pancreas has a great potential to revolutionize diabetes care and patients safety.

column37: The health and economic burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is increasing rapidly worldwide and falls disproportionally on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where almost 75% of the global deaths from NCDs occur. column36: Enhancing the Effects of Written Exposure for Generalized Anxiety Disorder via Imagery Training
column37: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a highly prevalent, chronic, and difficult-to-treat condition characterized by excessive worry and anxiety. Research has shown that people with GAD avoid thinking about feared situations in a clear way in an attempt to keep anxiety and other uncomfortable emotions at bay. However, this avoidance is actually counterproductive because it intensifies worry and anxiety. Past research has shown that an intervention called written exposure (WE) improves worry. In WE, people counteract their avoidance by fully imagining and processing clear, vivid thoughts of their worst fear coming true. This is accomplished by writing repeatedly and concretely about their worst fear. This study will examine a way to optimize the WE intervention; specifically, whether the addition of an imagery-training (IT) phase can further enhance WE's beneficial effects. Research in other clinical populations has shown that those who have better imagery abilities show larger symptom improvements within exposure-based treatments. For individuals with GAD, imagery ability may be even more important because these individuals report difficulties generating vivid images of their worst fears. Individuals with GAD will be assigned to one of two conditions: (1) WE with imagery training or (2) WE without imagery training. Both conditions will engage in 20-minute WE sessions on 3 consecutive days, but participants in the IT condition will also receive a 15-minute imagery training each day prior to engaging in WE. During IT, individuals will be trained to engage in imagery through different exercises. We hypothesize that the addition of imagery training to WE will lead to greater improvements in GAD symptoms, worry and worry-related difficulties than WE without imagery training. WE has considerable promise as a brief, inexpensive treatment for Canadians with GAD and the proposed experiment examines a novel enhancement of it.

column36: Canadian Frailty Network - Technology Evaluation in the Elderly Network (TVN)
column37: Canadian Frailty Network (CFN) is Canada's Networks of Centres of Excellence (NCE) focussed on frailty, a common yet under-recognized health state associated with functional decline, chronic illness, multiple health problems, cognitive impairment and poorer health outcomes in late life. Recognizing the growing prevalence of frailty and the dearth of research evidence to address the complex care needs of frail elderly Canadians, in 2012 NCE awarded CFN (Technology Evaluation in the Elderly Network) a funding mandate to improve the care of frail elderly Canadians and their families within the Canadian healthcare system through the development, rigorous evaluation and ethically-guided implementation of evidence-informed care strategies and practices. The burden of frailty in Canada is steadily growing. Today, approximately 25% of seniors over age 65 and 50% past 85 - over one million Canadians - are medically frail. These individuals are at higher risk for poor health outcomes, adverse events and mortality than would be expected based on their age alone. Frail elderly Canadians are over-represented in all sectors of the healthcare system including primary care, community and residential care, acute care and end-of-life care, and frailty is associated with increased healthcare resource consumption. In 10 years, based on population growth it is estimated that well over two million Canadians will be living with frailty and this growing population is both under-recognized and under-serviced, challenging the healthcare system to improve the quality and quantity of care delivered.

column36: Primary Integrated Health Care Innovation Network Coordinating Office
column37: In recent years, health systems in Canada and other countries have been exploring how to better assist people with complex needs, who account for a large share of system costs, but receive fragmented care. Integrating primary care providers, specialists, and community services is a key strategy for improving their experiences and outcomes. The Canadian Institute for Health Research (CIHR) Strategy for Patient Oriented Research (SPOR) has funded the Primary and Integrated Health Care Innovations Network (PIHCIN) of networks in 11 provinces and territories to address this issue, each co-led by a researcher, clinician, and policymaker. They have supported 4 rounds of funding of new approaches to primary and integrated care, as well as several cross-provincial policy comparisons. There is a Network Leadership Council (NLC) with representation from each network, but there is no structure to engage with national and international partners or coordinate pan-Canadian evaluation initiatives. This proposal describes a Coordinating Office that will act as a secretariat for the NLC, facilitate information exchange internally and externally, set and report on common performance measures, and engage with national and international groups to support transformation of health systems to improve care for people with complex needs. It will do this through information sharing across networks with a shared database of operational documents, a platform for video conferencing, and a website. It will help organize symposia to disseminate new knowledge emerging from the networks and mentor junior researchers in primary and integrated care. It will also raise funds to grow and sustain these efforts. The overall goal of the Coordinating Office is to work with provincial networks, national, and international partners to promote a learning health system to help people with complex needs, and promote the spread and scale of successful primary and integrated health care innovations across Canada.

column36: Mitigating cisplatin-induced ototoxicity in childhood cancer treatment through applied pharmacogenomics
column37: Advances in the treatment of childhood cancer have successfully increased the 5-year survival rate to almost 80%. While this is a dramatic improvement over the 1960s survival rate, it comes at the cost of causing poor long-term health outcomes for the majority of children treated with chemotherapy. Studies that follow childhood cancer survivors into adulthood clearly show that children receiving chemotherapy suffer serious health complications that include major organ and sensory toxicities. These toxicities, known as adverse drug reactions (ADRs), can also occur soon after the completion of chemotherapy, or even during treatment resulting in the withdrawal of life-saving cancer drugs. For example, cisplatin is the chemotherapy of choice for treating solid tumours in children including brain, liver, bone and germ cell cancers. Unfortunately over half of treated children will permanently lose their hearing after receiving cisplatin, which severely impairs a child's ability to develop language skills, social skills and self-confidence. We now know that genetic differences between children can influence whether hearing loss, or other ADRs will develop from chemotherapy treatment. Pharmacogenomics is the study of how genetic variation influences drug response and this understanding can open the door to developing tools to predict and prevent the occurrence of ADRs. We have now completed the first stage of a comprehensive pharmacogenomic study in Canadian patients that has identified a new pathway involved in cisplatin-induced hearing loss. This project will capitalize on this discovery and explore its application towards developing predictive biomarkers and preventative treatments to reduce the occurrence of cisplatin-induced hearing loss in childhood cancer patients.

column36: TRajectories Of healthy life using Public Health and primary care Interventions in Canada: The TROPHIC Trial
column37: The "Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD)" hypothesis suggests that a healthy growth and development in pregnancy and early childhood is critical for optimal health and lifetime wellbeing. Yet, Canada's children are falling behind. Nearly 1 in 3 Canadian children are overweight or obese, 1 in 4 is not developmentally ready for school, and 1 in 5 has a mental health problem. Early interventions can improve child health and development. Our study will evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention on child obesity and broader indicators of child development. Our trial, TROPHIC (TRajectories Of healthy life using Public Health and primary care Interventions in Canada), will take a 'cumulative-impact' approach, designed to improve health behaviours and reduce modifiable risk factors across the entire early child developmental period. TROPHIC will randomise pregnancy-planning women to evaluate a 4-phase intervention, from preconceptually all the way through early childhood. Its innovative design will enable the collection of family-level data, by including fathers/partners preconceptionally, and following more than one child within the family. TROPHIC comprises of a pan-Canadian team of 48 established investigators, from 21 institutions, across 6 provinces with proven expertise to successfully undertake this Healthy Life Trajectories initiative (HeLTI) project. The proposed project is aligned with the international HeLTI studies. TROPHIC capitalizes on efficient study recruitment and data collection methods, using existing research initiatives, such as TARGet Kids! The planned linkage of TROPHIC data to provincial administrative health datasets will enable longitudinal follow-up of children past age 5 years. We will leverage existing structures in public health and primary care to recruit participants, and then deliver interventions, if proven effective, to enable scalability at provincial and national levels.

column36: Disease-modifying Drug Safety and Effectiveness in Multiple Sclerosis [DRUMS]
column37: The goal of our research is to determine how safe and effective the drugs used to treat multiple sclerosis (MS) are when used in the real world. Canada has some of the world's highest rates of MS. This chronic disease of the brain and spinal cord often affects young adults and there is no known cure. In the last two decades, over 10 different drugs have been approved to treat people with MS. These drugs are very expensive and can require regular injections as well as frequent blood tests to monitor safety (side effects). We know how well these drugs work in the short-term, but only against certain aspects of MS. In the real world, people with MS may take these drugs for many years but we do not yet understand all their possible benefits and side effects. There have been few studies as large as ours investigating such a range of possible side effects, including cancer, stroke and infections. We will also look at whether the MS drugs have benefits which are often hard to measure, such as MS disability and fewer hospital or doctors' visits. Our research brings together medical data collected for over 2 decades within multiple large health databases in several Canada provinces. No study as large or as comprehensive as ours has ever been done. Our team approach enables findings to be directly relevant to Canadians, including people in poorer communities or those with co-existing medical conditions, who are often excluded from studies. Our research will be independent from the pharmaceutical industry, the manufacturers of MS drugs. This important research will help develop a framework in which to evaluate the benefits and side effects of both the current and future new drugs for MS across Canada. Our study findings will provide much needed information to help treatment-related decision making for both patients and doctors. Ultimately our study findings will directly benefit the outcomes related to treatment and health-related quality of life of people living with MS.

column36: Host microbe interactions in health and disease
column37: Humans have evolved with microbes. Although a subset of microbes have long been known to cause infectious diseases, there is growing appreciation of the critical role they play in health and chronic diseases. This new development also opens up powerful opportunities to find new ways of treating diseases and improving health outcomes. To this end, my lab has been studying how Salmonella and pathogenic E. coli cause diarrhea and related diseases, using new techniques to gain a much more comprehensive understanding of these diseases. Moreover, we have found that normal microbial inhabitants of the gut - the microbiome - can be used to inhibit these pathogens, thus we are pursuing these as potential therapeutics. We have also shown that certain early life microbes can affect the risk of asthma, and these are being explored as potential asthma preventatives. This work is being expanded to related food allergies, especially in the context of very early life gut microbes. A novel mouse model has been developed for malnutrition and an associated intestinal disease (environmental enteropathy). This model will allow us to gain a better understanding of these worldwide problems, as well as to test new products that can then be used to prevent these diseases. Recently, we have begun to explore the gut-brain axis in the context of microbes affecting brain function in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's/dementia. Exciting preliminary data indicate that the microbiomes in these patients are different, and we have new experiments planned to mechanistically probe this initial finding. Important next steps include the development of clinical tools that can be used to decrease these brain diseases. I am proposing a compelling and ambitious program to study these host-microbe interactions. Collectively, this research has significant potential to impact on many major Canadian health issues, including intestinal infections, asthma and allergies, malnutrition and degenerative brain diseases.

column36: Transcriptional control of cancer metabolism
column37: Cancer cells need specific nutrients and to transform these nutrients using specific biochemical pathways to generate enough energy and building blocks to sustain their growth and rapid division. My research program is centered on understanding how cancer cells adapt their metabolism to favor their proliferation and resistance to therapeutic intervention. More precisely, our team is investigating changes in the expression of specialized genes that modify the metabolic program of cancer cells. These changes in gene expression often result from the aberrant activity of proteins known as transcription factors. The normal function of transcription factors is to respond to cellular needs by modulating gene expression so that the cells have the necessary tools to perform their normal activities during the development and lifespan of the organism. However, cancer cells highjack transcription factors to promote tumour growth and their metastasis to distant organs. The abnormal action of transcription factors in cancer is best-exemplified by a class of proteins known as nuclear receptors, which include the estrogen and androgen receptors that promote the growth of breast and prostate cancer, respectively. In recent years, my research program has been focused on studying the roles played by nuclear receptors and other transcription factors in regulating energy metabolism, notably how cancer cells differentially process nutrients such as amino acids, sugars and lipids to fuel their growth. Our goals are to find differences between the action of transcription factors in normal and cancer cells and to exploit these differences to induce metabolic vulnerabilities in tumours, thus making them more responsive to anti-cancer drugs. The ultimate outcome of this program should be improvement in the treatment and quality of life of cancer patients.

column36: Novel Type 1 Cannabinoid Receptor Allosteric Modulators
column37: The type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) is present at high levels throughout the brain and other parts of the body. CB1R is activated by the body's own cannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol), synthetic cannabinoids, and cannabinoids from marijuana (e.g. THC and cannabidiol). CB1R is considered a potential target for the regulation of appetite and the treatment of addiction, pain, spasticity in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, epilepsy, post-traumatic stress disorder, and anxiety. Despite its potential as a therapeutic target, we are still learning how the many naturally occurring and synthetic cannabinoids that exist affect CB1R and how CB1R in turn produces distinct effects in the body. To this end, new compounds known as allosteric modulators are being developed that can increase or decrease CB1R's response to the body's cannabinoids, but lack intrinsic activity and will not, therefore, produce the intoxicating effects associated with other cannabinoids. The goals of my research are: (1) to develop allosteric modulators of CB1R that alter the body's response to its own cannabinoids, (2) test those modulators in animal models, and (3) to apply the knowledge gained from goals 1 and 2 to specific disease states where cannabinoids might be therapeutically beneficial. This research project will provide insight into the mechanisms of CB1R activity, important considerations for the use of cannabinoids as a medicine, and lead to the development of new drug compounds.

column37: Oral health research contributes significantly to improvement of oral health status of Canadians. Improvements in oral health research, in turn, can largely benefit from increased networking of those involved, from patients to oral care providers, from basic science researchers to manufacturers of products for oral health, and from government institutions to the general population and their needs.1-6 This was recognized by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) and the Institute of Musculoskeletal Health and Arthritis (IHMA) through a consultation process, which identified the relatively weak state oral health research finds itself in.7,8 The oral health research community comprises a broad range of research expertise across Canada but remains a small group and so is vulnerable despite the excellence of Canadian oral health researchers. Therefore, the funding support of CIHR-IHMA through a catalyst grant led in 2012 to the creation of the Network for Canadian Oral Health Research (NCOHR), which has demonstrated over the years its capacity to initiate, support, sustain and advance oral health research networking to impact the health of Canadians. The initial funding period (2012-2017) has allowed NCOHR to establish leadership in the creation of a national oral health network by enhancing the convergence of disciplines through the combination of basic and clinical sciences, engineering and patient needs resulting in the development of increased collaboration, new knowledge, discoveries and innovations. Indeed, interdisciplinary collaboration is the cornerstone of NCOHR. However, there is still work that needs to be done in order to improve the state of oral health research in Canada and to build a more fulsome national oral health research ecosystem. This new proposal will take advantage of the transformative and integrated university-hospital-patients-stakeholder-industry framework of NCOHR to shape the future of oral health research. column36: A foundation grant for bridging the mutation and interactome landscapes of the eukaryotic cell
column37: Every two individuals are genetically different due to mutations inherited from their parents or new mutations that have accumulated during their lifetime. Most of these mutations have no noticeable consequences. Yet, a small number have strong effects and lead to inherited diseases and somatic ones, such as cancers. Some healthy individuals can tolerate the complete loss of genes, while others develop diseases in response to these mutations. The difference between benign and harmful mutations comes from the organization of the cellular machinery and the interaction between this organization and the thousands of mutations that make everyone unique. For instance, the human genome contains hundreds of genes with multiple copies and having these backup copies could be a strong determinant of the resilience of the cell to otherwise harmful mutations. Here we propose an innovative research program that will elucidate these mechanisms of resilience and sensitivity to mutations of the eukaryotic cell. Our approach will involve cutting edge technologies in genome sequencing, high-throughput screening, genome editing and bioinformatics to determine what are the effects of disease and non-disease mutations directly on the inner organization of the cell. Our discoveries will shed light on the mechanisms of resilience and fragility to mutations in addition to providing mechanistic details on how human disease mutations alter the inner cell machinery. This will lead to more powerful approaches for the prediction of disease susceptibility and outcome from genome sequences, as well as to the development of knowledge-guided drug development.

column36: Physical Activity and Cancer Outcomes: Generating Practice-Changing Evidence
column37: My research program focuses on physical activity (PA) in cancer patients. Specifically, I am interested in how PA may help cancer patients prepare for treatments, cope with treatments, recover after treatments, and improve long-term survival. The long term goal of my research program is to reduce the negative impact of cancer by ensuring that all cancer patients have access to high quality exercise programs. Research has shown that PA improves fitness and quality of life in cancer survivors but clinical practice has not really changed. I have argued that the chances of PA being offered in clinical oncology practice would be greatly increased if PA was shown to improve survival. The overall aim of my proposed research program is to find out if PA can actually improve survival in cancer patients. I am proposing to study this question with 5 projects including: (a) the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Study, which is the first study examining the associations between objective PA, fitness, and breast cancer survival in 1,500 newly diagnosed breast cancer patients, (b) the Colon Health and Life-Long Exercise Change (CHALLENGE) Trial, which is the first experimental study examining the effects of a 3 year exercise program on survival in 962 colon cancer patients, (c) the Intense Exercise for Survival (INTERVAL) Trial, which is the first experimental study examining the effects of a 2 year exercise program on survival in 866 patients with advanced prostate cancer, and (d) 2 smaller studies in rectal cancer patients receiving combined chemoradiation therapy and prostate cancer patients receiving no treatments. PA is a low cost, low risk intervention that improves fitness and quality of life in cancer survivors but it has not been put into practice to help cancer patients. If PA can be shown to improve cancer survival, it would likely be offered to all cancer patients in Canada and around the world as part of their standard care.

column36: Replication stress and pulmonary hypertension: Role for checkpoint kinase 1
column37: Patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. Like cancer cells, PAH cells are characterized by exaggerated capacity to multiplicate and resistance to death resulting in a progressive narrowing or obstruction of the vessels. Indeed, if the blood vessels tighten up, making the space for the passage of blood narrower, it takes greater pressure to get the same amount of blood through to its destination. The heart has to work harder to pump blood through those arteries. The heart progressively fails causing shortness of breath and poor exercise capacity, which rapidly culminate in death. In spite of recent progress in our understanding of the mechanisms involved in this disease, no substantial modification of the rapid progression and fatal course of this disease has been achieved, leaving lung transplantation as the only treatment in end-stage PAH. Therefore, the identification of new therapeutic targets is a pressing need. Although exposed to stressful conditions that jeopardize their survival, PAH cells continue to multiplicate indicating that these cells have developed adaptive protective response allowing them to survive. Nevertheless, the factors implicated in this pathological protective response remains largely unknown. In the present proposal, we hypothesize that a factor called CHK1 known to confer resistance to harmful stress conditions is overexpressed in PAH cells leading to the development of PAH. To test the validity of our hypothesis, we will 1) determine whether CHK1 is increased in PAH cells and contributes to PAH cells' anomalies; 2) decorticate the mechanisms by which CHK1 acts; and 3) assess whether inhibition of CHK1 improve PAH in animal models.

column36: Human Fungal Infections - Targeting host-pathogen interactions to develop novel antifungal therapies
column37: Fungal infections are common and devastating in patients whose immune systems do not work properly or those with long-term lung disease. Our research program seeks to understand at a molecular level how molds and other fungi can cause human disease. We have identified two types of sugars made by fungi such as the mold Aspergillus that allow them to attach to human tissues and invade our lungs. We have developed new therapies that target these sugars in order to develop new therapies to treat or prevent these infections. These therapies include proteins that can be used to break down these sugars during infection, and vaccines that boost the response of our immune system against fungi. These strategies have already shown promise in animal studies. In the coming years we will refine and optimize these therapies and continue our discovery research to identify new sugar molecules that fungi use to cause human disease. Identifying these new sugars will provide us with new targets for our antifungal development pipeline. These studies will both improve our understanding of how fungi cause human disease, and provide us with new weapons in the fight against these devastating infections.

column36: Harnessing Neuron-Astrocyte Communication for Promoting Brain Health
column37: A common feature in nearly all brain disorders and diseases is a breakdown in brain homeostasis. Key to brain homeostasis are highly specialized cells called astrocytes. Astrocytes play fundamental roles in brain function including controlling extracellular ion and neurotransmitter levels, brain energetics, and cerebrovasculature. Astrocytes perform diverse functions through their complex molecular, functional, structural properties. However, the mechanisms that create and sustain differences among astrocytes that allow them to fulfill unique physiological roles in the brain remain poorly understood. We discovered a completely new mechanism involving neurons for making different types of astrocytes in the brain. Communication between neurons and astrocytes enables astrocytes to produce key molecules including neurotransmitter transporters and receptors, adhesion molecules, potassium channels, and water channels. Thus, neurons in the mature brain control astrocytes to ensure that astrocytes acquire and maintain specialized properties that are precisely tuned to associated brain circuits. In this grant, we will determine how different astrocytes are created and maintained in the brain to support neuronal health and circuit function and identify how the properties of astrocytes can be harnessed to mitigate brain disorders and diseases.

column36: Integrated Nanotechnology and Biomedical Sciences Laboratory
column37: Many researchers are developing drugs for the treatment of cancer. These drugs are administered in to the body and they kill cancer cells as well as healthy cells because the drug can go all over the body. This leads to excruciating side effects. Nanotechnology involves the use and design of structures, particles, or materials that have at least one dimensions smaller than 100 nm. Many researchers and companies are developing strategies to package drugs into a nanotechnology that can be further engineered to target and release the drug at the cancer cells in the body. The successful achievement of this would lead to increased therapeutic outcome and reduce side effects. The Chan group's research showed that 7 out of 1000 administered nanotechnology can target the solid tumour, 3 out of 100,000 can reach the cancer cells, and only 2 out of 100 cancer cells will be targeted by the nanotechnology. Thus, the delivery efficiency to each of the cancer components is low because the body is a hostile environment with biological traps such as the liver that removes the nanotechnology and prevents them from targeting cancer cells. With the funding from the CIHR Foundation grant, the Chan lab is aiming to solve the problem of delivery for nanotechnology. This will be achieved by studying how the nanotechnology interacts with each of the biological traps. These studies will allow us to develop a blueprint to build a nanotechnology that can escape them and identify strategies to increase the delivery efficiency to greater than 10% in the solid tumour. We will finally correlate the delivery efficiency with therapeutic outcome and side effects. Beyond seven-years, we will examine the optimized strategy derived from this study in human patients. column36: Dissecting the function and mechanisms of the Mediator Kinase module
column37: The control of gene expression is key to all cellular processes. One universal player in this regulation is the Mediator complex. Mediator plays a central role in the regulation of gene expression acting as a bridge between the so-called general transcription factors (involved in the regulation of all genes) and the gene-specific transcription factors. Mediator is frequently mutated or present in abnormal level in many cancers and genetic diseases. Mediator contains a built-in regulator, an enzyme that adds phosphate groups on Mediator and other proteins, allowing for fine tuning its activity. This regulator module (called CKM) within Mediator is the most frequently Mediator component affected in cancers. Because it is an enzyme, the activity of CKM is in principle "drug-able" but before this can be achieved, a better understanding of how it works is required. In this project, we will use the power of budding yeast as a model system to dissect the mechanisms and function of CKM. This knowledge will leverage our capacity to mine strategies to re-equilibrate Mediator activity in diseases.

column36: Elucidating novel mechanisms of extracellular nucleic acid recognition, internalization, trafficking and signaling: implications for infection, inflammation and autoimmunity.
column37: Extracellular or circulating nucleic acids derived from infected or damaged cells can be of virus or self origin. Once recognized and taken up by healthy cells, these nucleic acids rapidly and potently lead to the production of cytokines, including interferon. While interferon is important to protect against infections and cancer, inappropriate interferon responses lead to a variety of diseases, including autoimmunity. While class A scavenger receptors (SRAs) are required for binding and internalization of circulating nucleic acids, little is known about how individual SRA family members carry out these functions. Surprisingly, little is also understood about the cellular trafficking or localization of different nucleic acid species following uptake by SRAs. We have uncovered several unexplained anomalies in how different forms and lengths of nucleic acids traffic within cells and induce interferon following uptake by SRAs. In this grant, we will study the internalization, trafficking and signaling of various forms and lengths of nucleic acids to understand the mechanisms of how they activate cytokines such as interferon. Given that interferon can either prevent disease or cause disease, depending on its regulation, understanding basic mechanisms of interferon production in response to circulating nucleic acids is of critical importance.

column36: Beyond diarrhea, to disability and death: uncovering the hidden health consequences of foodborne infections
column37: Each year, over 4 million Canadians develop a new infection because of the food they eat; short term symptoms, like diarrhea, alone result in 2.5 million days of work missed, and $400 million in health care and other costs. And although these infections can have serious consequences, including miscarriage, arthritis, kidney failure, and death, just how many Canadians go on to experience such consequences, and what this costs our healthcare system, is unknown. Without this knowledge, policy makers struggle to protect Canadians, unable to adequately argue for sufficient investments to make food safer, and clinicians do not have the evidence they need to avert such serious consequences in their patients. Previously, the approach required to accurately determine the serious consequences of foodborne infections across the population was lacking. Now, with decades of population-wide electronic health records, including sufficient details on foodborne infections, we are finally able to address this issue. The province of BC is uniquely positioned to support this novel work. BC's rich collection of health records allows us to seamlessly explore the various medical consequences experienced by everyone in BC who tests positive for a foodborne infection. Thus, we will conduct a longitudinal cohort study, across the population of BC, determining what fraction of people develop serious consequences following a foodborne infection, what this costs the health system, and what risks infected Canadians face (e.g., of miscarriage, death), regardless of whether or not they are already vulnerable (e.g., young, old, pregnant). This work will uncover the real risks faced by the >4 million Canadians infected from food each year. This knowledge will allow provincial and national policy makers to invest in making food safer, and physicians to better diagnose and treat patients, which will ultimately prevent foodborne infections, and their serious consequences, among Canadians.

column36: Post-translational protein arginylation in skeletal muscles
column37: Muscle contraction is a basic function of life, responsible for body movements, hear beating, breathing, to cite a few. Contraction is regulated by a variety of processes, including biochemical pathways that may change the way muscles work. Such changes may improve or inhibit contractions, and may eventually lead to weakness and muscular diseases, such a muscle dystrophies. The goal of this proposal is to investigate one regulatory mechanism called arginylation, a process by which muscle proteins receive arginine (Arg) from tRNA. We have pilot data showing that arginylation is a strong regulator of muscle contraction, and that lack of arginylation leads to muscle weakness and dystrophy. We will use novel and accurate methods that include sub-cellular structures and single molecules isolated from muscles to test the mechanism by which arginylation regulates muscle contraction. We will also test the effects of potential treatments for muscle dystrophy caused by lack of arginylation. This research will provide information that is needed for the understanding of the basic mechanisms of muscle contraction in health and disease, and may have implications for everyday life.

column36: Epithelial alpha-v-beta-6 integrin: critical regulator of periodontal inflammation
column37: A large segment of the adult population suffers from periodontal diseases (PDs) that can result in loss of teeth, a financial burden, and potentially contribute to many systemic conditions. The pathogenesis of PDs is a complex process in which intricate subgingival bacterial biofilm induces inflammation that leads to tissue degradation and bone loss. In health, junctional epithelium (JE) links the gingiva to the tooth enamel, creating a seal and preventing bacteria from entering the gingival tissue. In PD, bone loss develops around the teeth with periodontal pockets and the JE transforms into pocket epithelium (PE). However, it is not clear how JE/PE participates in the regulation of periodontal inflammation. In the inflammatory infiltrate, the outcome of the cytokine response is regulated by the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that are countered by anti-inflammatory cytokines. These cytokines need to be activated for biological function. An integrin known as alpha-v-beta-6 can activate them. Mutations in this integrin cause PD in mice and humans. We have shown that JE constitutively expresses this integrin and these anti-inflammatory cytokines. In PD, the expression of this integrin in PE is strongly downregulated, resulting in "acquired integrin deficiency." This integrin-mediated cytokine activation in JE appears to be crucial for the maintenance of periodontal health and preventing systemic inflammation. The factors leading to the downregulation of this integrin expression in PE cells are not known. In the present proposal, we will determine the mechanisms through which this integrin expression is downregulated in JE/PE in periodontal disease and how this integrin "deficiency" regulates cytokine expression in epithelial cells. The long-term goal is to determine the molecular mechanism of periodontal inflammation and use this information for preventive therapies.

column36: TEMPO-2 - A randomized controlled trial of TNK-tPA versus standard of care for minor ischemic stroke with proven occlusion.
column37: Most minor strokes are due to lack of blood getting to a part of the brain. When this occurs, patients get sudden loss of function in that region of the brain. This might mean inability to move a limb or inability to speak. In the luckiest case, this dysfunction resolves rapidly by itself and we call it a transient ischemic attack (TIA). If less lucky, the disability persists due to a minor stroke. Minor stroke and TIA account for about 50% of all strokes in Canada. Most physicians think that patients with minor stroke or TIA do not need aggressive treatment with clot busting drugs because the risk of bleeding in the brain is greater than any benefit. However, we believe that this judgment is incorrect. We have shown that minor stroke and TIA patients with evidence of a blocked blood vessel on a brain scan are at a very high risk of being left disabled with conservative treatment. This subgroup of patients can benefit from aggressive therapy with clot-busting drugs. The usual clot-busting drug usually used in Stroke is called tPA. A newer drug used in patients with heart attack called TNK works faster and is safer than tPA. In the TEMPO-2 clinical trial, we will determine if TNK, given as a single dose, is better than usual care for patients with minor stroke with a proven blocked artery. Patients will have a 50:50 chance (i.e. like the toss of a coin) of getting either treatment or usual care. Patients will be assessed 3 months after the event for evidence of disability. If this study shows that the clot busting medicine should be used in minor stroke and TIA with blocked blood vessels then this will change care of patients throughout the world.

column36: The VANISH2 Trial: Ventricular Tachycardia Antiarrhythmics or Ablation in Structural Heart Disease 2
column37: Background: The VANISH2 trial is designed to determine the best treatment for people who have life-threatening abnormalities of heart rhythm. Heart attacks leave scars in the heart muscle. The scars can interfere with the normal signaling within the heart that controls the heart beat. In some cases, the interference can cause a very dangerous abnormal heart rhythm known as ventricular tachycardia (VT). This rhythm is the most common cause of sudden death in Canada. When patients are at high risk for recurrences of VT, a defibrillator (ICD) can be implanted which can shock the heart back to normal rhythm from a cardiac arrest. These devices are life-saving but do not prevent the abnormal rhythm, they just provide a rescue when it occurs. In order to prevent dangerous arrhythmias, doctors use strong rhythm control drugs or a procedure called catheter ablation. An ablation is performed by advancing wires through the blood vessels into the heart, using X-rays and other imaging to see where they are and the short circuits within the scar can then be identified and interrupted (ablated). Neither the drugs nor the ablation procedure work perfectly and both carry risk. This trial is designed to determine which treatment is the best. Study design: Patients who have had heart attacks and develop VT will be randomly allocated (50:50) to be treated either with rhythm control drugs or catheter ablation. All patients will receive an implanted defibrillator. We will enroll a total of 366 patients and follow them for at least 2 years to see which group does the best with respect to recurrent abnormal heart rhythms and survival. Expected Outcomes: This trial will determine whether the best treatment for VT is heart rhythm drugs or catheter ablation. This evidence will permit more optimal treatment for many thousands of patients worldwide.

column36: Adequate intake of choline in pregnancy may be critical for MTHFD1 synthetase deficiency, a common genetic variant in folate metabolism
column37: Folate and choline are important nutrients required to support healthy pregnancies. Inadequate intake of these nutrients before and during pregnancy can increase the risk of birth defects and other pregnancy complications. Folate is a critical vitamin that provides the building blocks for DNA (e.g. purines) and methyl groups for a host of biosynthetic reactions. Choline is required to produce important components of cell membranes, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Choline becomes even more important when folate metabolism is disturbed, because it replaces folate for certain functions. Although most Canadian women are aware of the importance of folate and reach the recommended intakes due to folate fortification programs and use of folate supplements, 85-90% do not have adequate choline intakes. Gene variants in folate metabolism, such as MTHFD1 R653Q, may also increase risk for neural tube defects, heart defects and other pregnancy complications. About 20% of Canadians have the QQ genotype, which we have shown to impair MTHFD1 function and decrease purine synthesis. Some studies have suggested that QQ women are more sensitive to low choline intake. Our goal is to determine whether inadequate choline contributes to the reproductive complications associated with the 653QQ genotype, and whether supplementation with choline or choline metabolites can overcome the effect of the genetic defect. We will examine human placentas from women with the 653RR and QQ genotypes with high and low folate intakes to assess the effects of diet and genotype on choline metabolism. We will use our mouse model for the variant to determine if low choline diets impair embryonic development and see if different types of choline supplements improve pregnancy outcomes. Our research will highlight a neglected aspect of nutrition during pregnancy and lay the groundwork for personalized dietary recommendations based on R653Q genotype to prevent reproductive complications.

column36: Improving responsiveness across the continuum of kidney health care in rural and remote Manitoba First Nation communities (I-KHealth)
column37: Manitoba First Nations (MFNs) have the highest documented prevalence and the second highest incidence of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in Canada. Those living in rural/remote locations and requiring care experience significant barriers. Although preventable, nephrologists heard FN patients, especially from "renal families" (where other members have chronic kidney disease, CKD/ESKD), report that ESKD is inevitable. These statements likely reflect limited opportunities for maintaining health in the face of barriers including racism, perpetuating risk factors and undermining prevention efforts. This partnership-based program of research brings together community-based researchers from the Nanaandawewigamig Diabetes Integration Program (hereafter DIP, a part of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs), FN patients with lived experience of renal disease, University of Manitoba (UM) university-based researchers and members of the MRP (nephrologists, nurses, dietitian, social worker). We propose a 5 year program of research with 2 broad objectives: 1. To improve access to effective PC-based care for patients identified at being at low and medium risk of CKD; and 2. To expand the number of dialysis modalities available to FNs through the development of a FN-centric assisted PD model (APD), developed in partnership with FN communities. ESKD/CKD continues to fundamentally impact the lives of Indigenous patients, their families and communities. Despite repeated reviews and the implementation of a range of renal service plans, access to dialysis (in varied forms) in Manitoba rural and remote communities, including MFN communities, remains poor and still results in family dislocation. The critical questions outlined in this application remain unanswered, and stand to make a significant impact on primary care, treatment options and outcomes.

column36: Targeting Key Autophagy Proteins/Pathways for Treatment of Human Leukemia
column37: Blood cancer (leukemia) is common, with ~55,000 cases expected in the United States and Canada in 2017. The National Cancer Institute (US) calculated an overall 5-year survival rate of 56% for various blood cancers. This is because drug resistance and relapse pose significant challenges. Life-long treatment is required, with potential side-effects and a high cost. Blood cancer cells generally respond to drug therapy at the onset, but the drugs lose their effectiveness after 6-12 months. We and others have discovered that this is mainly due to the inability of current therapies to eradicate blood cancer stem cells, which maintain the potential for relapse. There is thus an urgent need to develop new therapies that specifically target blood cancer stem cells so that these cells can be eliminated, leading to a cure. We have found that ATG4B, a novel drug target and key driver in autophagy, displays abnormal activity in blood cancer stem cells, particularly in drug-resistant patients. However, there is currently no drug that blocks autophagy in a specific and potent way, nor any related drugs for autophagy inhibition that are approved as therapeutics. We have identified several promising new drugs that specifically target ATG4B in blood cancer stem cells. Combining these with current anti-cancer drugs more effectively inhibits blood cancer stem cell growth in culture than single drug treatment; this treatment strategy also doesn't have side-effects on normal blood stem cells. This study will thus investigate if this combination therapy will more effectively eradicate blood cancer stem cells obtained from drug-resistant patients, using our established animal cancer models. This will provide ultimate proof-of-concept for the development of more effective therapies with fewer side effects than currently used therapies. More immediate economic benefits are also expected from the commercialization and drug development that will be fuelled by this research.
