column36: Understanding Schwann cell heterogeneity for improved nerve repair
column37: Traumatic injuries to nerve and other disorders affecting nerve (called neuropathies) are common conditions, resulting in severe paralysis, sensory loss and pain in many Canadians. Techniques to repair nerve injuries to date allow some recovery of function, but most patients continue to have significant neurological dysfunction and debilitating pain. We propose a cell-based therapy to improve outcomes. The adult skin, which can be obtained from patients with minimal side-effects, contains unique stem cells (skin-derived precursors, or SKPs) that can be differentiated into a repair type of cell that normally provides support to nerve cells. This cell, called a Schwann cell, supports nerve cell axons, along with providing insulating myelin and growth factors, which helps axons regenerate following injury. We have already developed techniques to rapidly generate skin Schwann cells (SCs) from human skin, and have preliminary data on their ability to repair nerve and to produce some myelin. In this proposal, we aim to optimize SCs for repair potential and then validate their effect after delivery in a rodent nerve injury model. The optimization of SCs will include approaches to genetically re-program cells and the use of advanced cell identification and sorting techniques to isolate and then expand cells that are most potent for repair. We will deliver the optimized SCs via an approved for human use nerve guidance conduit, leveraging state-of-the-art innovation from a partner company, to examine the functionality of these cells in nerve injury and repair in rodents. We have put together a dynamic team with expertise in nerve surgery and repair (Midha), stem cell biology (Biernaskie) and neural development and genetic reprogramming (Schuurmans) and have some promising preliminary results. This research has the potential to improve the way in how nerve injury is managed, thereby positively impacting the health and well-being of many Canadians.

column36: Control of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling by clathrin signalosomes
column37: Tumours are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists by several changes they exhibit compared to normal cells. Some of these changes involve alteration in the abundance and function of proteins found on the outer surface of the tumour cells. These changes in the function of cell surface proteins are required for tumours to grow and spread throughout in the body (metastasis). Hence, obtaining a better understanding of how cells control the function of proteins found on their outer surface has the potential to provide new ways to treat cancer. One of the types of cell surface proteins altered in cancer cells is hormone receptors, in particular one named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). EGFR signals to cells to grow and migrate and when uncontrolled, these traits can lead to cancer and metastasis. The cell surface is like that of a soccer-ball in that it is made up of "patches". As the hexagonal patches on a soccer ball are of different colours, the "patches" on the outer surface of a cell, termed microdomains, also have unique properties. We have discovered that a particular type of microdomain on the cell surface, called a clathrin signalosome, determines how a cell responds to certain hormones. The hormone receptor EGFR is found within the clathrin signalosomes on the surface of a cell, yet how clathrin signalosomes control hormone receptors such as EGFR remains a mystery. To uncover how clathrin signalosomes control the function of EGFR and thus cancer progression, we will use several different approaches including advanced microscopy of cells engineered to contain fluorescent versions of specific key proteins, allowing us to "see" EGFR within microdomains. This research will reveal how clathrin signalosomes work within healthy and cancerous cells to control EGFR function. Since alterations in the normal function of EGFR cause cancer cells to grow and metastasize, this work may reveal new ways to treat various types of cancer

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating form of dementia characterized by memory loss and accumulation of amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles. Developing effective therapies relies on uncovering common mechanisms that underlie memory loss and AD pathology. Finally, we will validate H2A.Z as a target in human AD brains, and use human cell lines to directly test the ability of H2A.Z to reverse AD pathology. The use of multiple H2A.Z regulators allows us to test several promising new targets as potential AD therapies, with the potential to simultaneously reverse memory deficits and the underlying plaques and tangles through a novel category of histone proteins.

column37: In retinal degenerative diseases, the progressive loss of the light-sensing photoreceptor cells eventually leads to blindness. Cell-based therapies are generating excitement for the treatment of retinal degeneration, as they offer the potential to restore vision. But this approach still faces major challenges. Photoreceptor cells are highly specialized neurons and generating them from stem cells remains inefficient. While some improvement was made in recent years to increase rod photoreceptor production from various populations of stem cells, the generation of a large number of cone photoreceptors, essential for daylight vision, remains a challenge. Our hypothesis to explain this limited success is that current protocols do not take into consideration the intrinsic identity of stem cell-derived progenitors. As in normal retinal development, we believe that stem cell-derived retinal progenitors have an intrinsic temporal identity that restricts their competence to generate specific populations of cell types produced during a given time window. Cone photoreceptors, for example, are produced at early stages during retinal development, whereas rod photoreceptors are produced late. Understanding how progenitors change over time to switch from cone-producing phase to a rod-producing phase is essential towards improving cell replacement protocols. We posit that manipulating the temporal identity of stem cell-derived retinal progenitors will increase cone production, which could be used for grafting or disease modelling. We will test this idea using human embryonic stem cell-derived retinal progenitors and provide mechanistic insights on how temporal identity is regulated in retinal progenitors during retinal development using mouse models. We will also test whether temporal factors can be used to reprogram retinal glial cells into photoreceptors, which would bypass the need for costly stem cell culture and grafting by stimulating endogenous regeneration.

column37: In our intestine, there is a large cohort of microbes, including bacteria and fungi. Their presence is important for our immune system development. In germ-free mice (no microbes in the gut), lymph nodes in the host are small and incapable of mounting efficient responses against invading pathogens. For many years, we know this dependence of our immune system on those "microbial guests", but no molecular understanding was available. We previously found that a group of resident fungi called Candida tropicalis is critical for the peripheral lymph node maturation. The presence of these fungi in our gut microbiota drives a group of retinoic acid-producing dendritic cells (a type of immune cells) to leave the gut and come the growing lymph nodes, where they stimulate the structural development. They do so by inducing a particular set of molecules, PNAd, at the entry portal of lymph nodes. Interestingly, in the early weeks, lymphocytes entering those sites are educated to return to the gut to build the defense there first. This makes sense as the microbial burden is the heaviest in the gastrointestinal tract after birth. To follow up on those findings, we plan to study what types of fungal productions are driving these cells to leave the gut, and how these dendritic cells change the chemotaxis molecule expression in the peripheral lymph nodes. We also wish to study whether the homing of lymphocytes from the peripheral lymph nodes is critical to the initial gut immune homeostasis in the neonates. These questions are critical for us to comprehensively understand the interplays between our microbiota and the health of our immune system.

column36: ROS metabolism and mitochondrial function in the aging process and in age-dependent diseases.
column37: Most diseases that threaten Canadians, including cancer, heart disease, metabolic diseases, and neurodegenerative disease (such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease) are associated with age: they are much more likely in older individuals. Our goal is to understand the role that free radicals (also called reactive oxygen species (ROS)) play in the overall process of aging and in age-dependent diseases. Free radicals are chemically reactive molecules, which means that they can potentially damage cellular constituents. However, we have discovered that, rather than causing aging, the important role of free radicals as regulators of cell function contributes to longevity by helping cells and organisms to react to, and combat, various stresses. On the other hand, in aging individuals, the production and removal of these free radicals becomes much less well-balanced. It is in this situation that free radicals can be produced in excess, thus leading to damage to cells and promoting the development of disease. We are studying the role of free radicals in both situations, beneficial in young individuals and potentially deleterious old individuals, in order to learn both to harness their beneficial properties and protect from their deleterious effects.

column36: A ONE Health approach for the prevention of MERS-CoV
column37: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a newly emerged pathogen that causes severe respiratory disease in humans. To date, more than a third (35%) of people infected do not survive. MERS-CoV is thought to be passed from dromedary camels to humans. Contact with dromedary camels is a frequent factor in initial human cases. These primary humans cases have subsequently caused large outbreaks of MERS-CoV, typically in hospitals. This has resulted in the temporary closure of healthcare facilities in order to control the spread of MERS-CoV. Here we propose to design a vaccine that stops transmission of MERS-CoV in camels, and as result transmission to humans as well. The vaccine we are designing is based on one that is already used in dromedary camels for the prevention of camelpox. This vaccine, called Ducapox, is a weakened version of the virus that causes camelpox in camels. We have introduced the gene that encodes the spike protein from MERS-CoV into this virus and propose to use this approach to demonstrate that this vaccine can prevent infection alpaca with MERS-CoV. Then, using assays that measure various components of the immune response to infection and vaccination we will determine what immune response results in protection from infection with MERS-CoV. From our previous work we know that alpacas are protected from re-infection and thus we can compare and contrast the immune response from experimental infection to the immune response to vaccination. Here we propose that an agricultural vaccine for camels can prevent infection and transmission of MERS-CoV in camels to halt MERS-CoV infections in humans.

column36: Generalized anxiety disorder in older adults : Efficacy of a self-help treatment guided by trained lay providers
column37: Few older adults receive treatment for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) despite a high prevalence in this population and significant associated health care costs. Although older adults generally prefer psychotherapy to medication for help with anxiety, face-to-face psychotherapy is difficult to access for many of them. Psychological guided self-help (GSH), which patients use by themselves at home under the supervision of a licensed mental health provider (e.g., psychologist), has been shown to be effective. However, the capacity of our health care system to respond adequately to the mental health needs of seniors has been questioned and cost-effective solutions are required. Because the therapist's role in GSH is limited to supporting the patient, it is conceivable that this role could be assumed by trained and supervised lay providers (LP) instead of licensed providers. If this approach is effective, it could help provide many older adults with much needed mental health treatment at a lower cost. The main objective of this project is to evaluate the effectiveness of GSH guided by LP for GAD in older adults. Participants will be assigned randomly to an experimental group, which will receive treatment immediately, or to a control group whose treatment will be delayed. Data will be obtained through clinician evaluations and self-assessment questionnaires. They will include socio-demographic characteristics, symptoms of GAD, variables related to anxiety, such as depression and sleep difficulties, and participants' perception of treatment. Data collection will take place at different times: before treatment begins, after treatment ends, and at 6 and 12 months after the end of treatment. The efficacy of GSH will be established by comparing the change in the two groups on the main variables. We will also identify the characteristics of patients associated with improvement during treatment and document their perception of treatment.

column36: Minimizing Lung Injury during Mechanical Ventilation
column37: Over 90,000 Canadians each year become critically ill and need a life-support device called a mechanical ventilator; this forces oxygen into the lungs through a breathing tube, and helps the patient to breathe. While mechanical ventilation saves lives there is also a serious price: forcing air into the lungs causes additional lung damage that can lead to disability or death. The current grant application builds on two novel findings in my laboratory. First, our laboratory reported that an old-fashioned 'Iron Lung' could be applied to the outside of the abdomen (not the chest) in conjunction with conventional mechanical ventilation; the effect was to selectively open up the lower parts of the lung without over-stretching (and injuring) the upper lung regions. We will understand how this works, and then by knowing which patients might benefit, will rapidly move to test the approach in volunteers and then in patients. If successful, this would represent a fundamental advance in mechanical ventilation. Second, briefly disconnecting a ventilator, a common occurrence to carry out routine patient care, can result in rapid deflation of the lung. This was traditionally thought to be without consequence. However, using laboratory models we have discovered that this may cause significant harm, and have preliminary data explaining how and where in the lung this harm occurs. We will determine the exact mechanisms and then determine if this occurs in patients, and devise approaches to its prevention. These two complementary lines of research will make mechanical ventilation safer (and more effective) and if successful, will save the lives of many critically ill patients.

column36: Characterizing RecQ helicase Sgs1 in maintaining genomic stability during aging
column37: Cancer and aging are seemingly distinct events. However, similar changes in the ability of our cells to respond to environmental challenges are observed in both aging and cancer. For example, damage to DNA, our hereditary material, accumulates in both cancer cells and older cells. Normally, when DNA becomes damaged, pathways become activated to repair the damage. These repair pathways are known to become disrupted in cancer and now some pathway components are proving to be effective targets in particular types of cancer therapy. In older cells, DNA damage accumulates, however the underlying reason for this is not known. To date, most work in cancer research has been performed in young cells, young model organisms or in human cancer cell lines. Since most cancers occur in older individuals, we believe that it will be much more relevant to study DNA repair during aging, especially since there is very little known about how these processes might change or contribute to cancer development. Confounding issues certainly arise with age, but at the cellular level, where cancer and aging biologically converge, pathways that protect our DNA from mutations clearly need to be studied in cells that have aged. My lab uses the model organism budding yeast. Over the past 60 years, work in yeast has provided a foundation of knowledge critical for understanding the molecular events leading to cancer in humans. Since yeast cells are well characterized regarding DNA repair and they also age, they represent a powerful model for rapidly asking how age is related to DNA repair. Thus, characterizing DNA repair in old yeast cells will provide important clues for why DNA repair efficiency decreases and cancer increases exponentially with age in our population.

column37: Getting research results into everyday health care practice and policies is a long and painstaking process. The field of Knowledge Translation (KT) has emerged and is expanding in attempt to speed up this process. One approach, called integrated KT, includes the users of research throughout the research process. The goal of integrated KT is to produce more relevant research that is more likely to be used. Although it is a popular approach, there is little data on the effects of integrated KT. This project will examine how integrated KT has been conducted and evaluated with key research user groups: people who have experience living with a health condition, health professionals, and health research funders. We will conduct a comprehensive review of existing integrated KT research, survey and interview researchers and research users who have received integrated KT grants, and make recommendations for conducting, reporting, and evaluating integrated KT projects. The long term goal of this project is to improve the health of people across Canada by ensuring the latest research is quickly incorporate into everyday health care practice and policies.

column36: Airway Epithelial Cell ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) Transporter C4 in Lung Health and Disease
column37: Everyday we breathe in over 10000 liters of air just to survive. For some of us, breathing in air presents no problems. For over 3 million Canadians with lung diseases, breathing in air can lead to lung "attacks" that make it difficult to breathe, require hospitalization, and in the most severe cases, death. The air that we breathe in daily can contain substances like air pollution, allergens, cigarette smoke, fungi, bacteria, and viruses. Studies have shown that exposure to these substances can lead to lung "attacks" in those with lung diseases, but it remains a mystery as to how this happens. Our research group studies how exposure to inhaled substances can lead to inflammation in the lungs and how this leads to lung "attacks". We are studying how inflammation "leaks" out of different cells in the lung in response to inhaled substances, leading to a spread of inflammation that can grow bigger and bigger if left unchecked. We propose that plugging the "leaks" can prevent inflammation from spreading, preventing lung "attacks", and saving lives. Our experiments are designed to study a specific "leak" that is important in inflammation, determine how this "leak" is different in healthy and diseased patients, investigate how genetic differences contribute to this "leak", and to make safe drugs that can plug the "leak". Collectively our studies will increase our understanding of how inhaled substances can trigger lung "attacks" and also provide a unique new strategy for treating individuals that suffer from lung diseases.

column36: Quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Pulmonary Edema: Application in Acute Heart Failure
column37: Heart failure (HF) affects over half a million Canadians and growing. Acute HF is a leading cause of hospitalization (>65 years) and 20-30% of these patients die with 6 months, with a cost of billions of dollars a year. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (water in the lungs) is a key symptom of HF (a result of poor heart function) and is a major cause of shortness of breath. Treating edema is the primary treatment in acute HF. However, pulmonary edema is most commonly assessed with qualitative tests like a stethoscope and/or chest X-ray. There is a widely recognized need for safe tests that can quantify the amount of water in the lungs in patients with pulmonary edema, particularly for the evaluation of existing and newly developed treatments. We propose that magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an ideal teat for assessment of pulmonary edema (the source of MRI signal is water). We will develop new fast MRI methods to make lung water maps. The aims of our proposed research program are to first to develop new MRI methods that will allow fast and accurate images of the amount of water in the lungs. We will use these methods determine normal values for MRI lung water density. These values are need in order to identify which patients have elevated lung water. Second, we will study heart failure patients admitted to hospital for acute HF, who are treated primarily for their pulmonary edema. We will measure the change in lung water with standard hospital therapy (e.g. diuretic). We will show that we can directly measure the amount of water removed with therapy, and thus show that MRI is a good test to study new drugs. Finally, we will determine the relationship between elevated lung water and subsequent events, such as emergency room visits, hospitalization or death. We will show that elevated lung water will predict these events. This is important as we will be able to identify which patients need to managed more aggressively, to help avoid these future events.

column36: Structure-function relationship of peptidoglycan O-acetyltransferase, a potential new antivirulence target to combat AMR
column37: Ensuring the mechanical strength of their cell walls is essential to the viability of bacteria. This strength to the wall is conferred by a continuous (macro)molecule unique to bacteria called peptidoglycan which completely encases the cell. Given the importance of the peptidoglycan layer for bacterial survival, it is not surprising that higher eukaryotes have exploited this "Achilles heel" to combat infections. However, pathogenic bacteria have adapted to this response by chemically modifying their peptidoglycan thereby preventing its disruption. One such modification is O-acetylation. In the absence of this modification, pathogenic bacteria become extremely susceptible to host innate immune factors, particularly to the peptidoglycan-lytic enzyme called lysozyme. Additionally, this O-acetylation serves to control peptidoglycan metabolism within a bacterium by blocking the function of endogenous lytic enzymes essential for cell growth and division. Consequently, bacteria require the activity of an enzyme (named Ape) to remove blocking acetyl groups when required to permit continued PG metabolism. Inhibition of Ape prevents further growth of bacteria that require the enzyme (eg., Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and its activity is essential for survival of Neisseria meningitidis in animal models. The research plan that we propose builds on our findings to date on the specificity and structure-function relationships of the enzymes involved in both adding and removing this O-acetylation. Experiments involving biochemical, kinetic, and structural characterisations are designed to better inform the search/development of strong inhibitors of these enzymes that my represent leads to new antibacterials.

column36: Children's Street Crossing Behaviours and Pedestrian Injury Risk
column37: Unintentional injury is the leading cause of death for Canadian children 1-19 years. For elementary-school children, motor vehicle pedestrian injury is the key issue. The proposed research will address this issue by studying how children cross streets and identifying risk factors for injury. Although both environmental factors and child attributes are implicated in pedestrian injuries, few studies have explored interactive effects of these factors (e.g., Do child attributes elevate injury risk only under certain traffic conditions?). Also, research has been limited by the challenge of how to measure children's crossing behaviors in traffic without elevating risk of injury. This research will address these issues in an innovative way -- using a Virtual Reality pedestrian environment to study how children cross streets in highly realistic traffic conditions that can be completely controlled. The overall goals are to determine: (1) how individual-difference attributes interact with contextual factors (built environment features, traffic conditions) to influence children's risk of injury when crossing streets and (2) if these relations differ by child sex or age group (e.g., Can attention differences explain why boys and younger children are at highest risk for pedestrian injuries?). The knowledge gained from this research can inform: city planning about traffic flow and road design; school policies about crossing guards and guidelines about safe school routes; guidelines for parents about children's readiness to cross unsupervised; and the development of behavioral training systems to teach children safer crossing skills.

column37: Blood vessels in a healthy adult are stable and do not change very much. When diseases affect blood vessels, the cells that are contained in blood vessels can change. If we are correct, we will be able to test the idea that using drugs that act at these specific sites, rather than everywhere in the cell, we will have fewer side-effects than are seen in drugs that target these events everywhere in the cell. column37: Depression is a debilitating mental disorder affecting over 350 million people globally and is associated with high personal and socioeconomic burden. Efficacy of classical antidepressant medications, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants is compromised by extended delays to achieve therapeutic efficacy. Sadly, 50% of patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) do not obtain remission with traditional antidepressants. One of the most exciting discoveries in neuropharmacology in two decades is that a single intravenous infusion of ketamine has robust, rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in individuals with TRD lasting up to 1-2 weeks. Not surprisingly, this discovery has inspired great interest in identifying the underlying molecular mechanisms. Ketamine blocks the NMDA class of glutamate receptors, consistent with dysfunctions within the glutamatergic system and dysregulation of synaptic plasticity in the pathophysiology of depression. Systematic investigations of ketamine's effects on in vivo synaptic plasticity in animal models of depression, as well as direct contribution of synaptic plasticity changes to ketamine's antidepressant effects, are key to understanding the mechanisms by which ketamine and other candidate drugs achieve their unique effects. Proposed experiments will utilize a genetic model of depression (Wistar-Kyoto WKY rat). In preliminary experiments we observed weakness in synaptic plasticity that was rescued by ketamine. Therefore, we hypothesize that impaired synaptic plasticity in WKY rats causes depression-like deficits in motivation, cognition, and social interaction. Furthermore, we propose that restitution of synaptic plasticity is a crucial mediator of the antidepressant response to ketamine. Novel candidate compounds will be screened using the WKY model of TRD.

column36: Mechanisms of Genome Instability
column37: Before a cell can grow and divide it must duplicate its DNA. Mistakes during the copying of the DNA can lead to the kinds of changes that are frequently seen in cancerous cells (mutations, for example). These changes are important for cancer development, progression, and treatment, but there is little information about how they arise. Understanding how changes to the DNA arise could lead to improvements in cancer detection and treatment, and is also relevant to ageing, where mistakes in the DNA happen more often. We will study how proteins help copy the DNA, how proteins prevent mistakes during the copying of the DNA, and will apply this knowledge to discover new ways to prevent the kinds of mistakes that can lead to human diseases, including cancers.

column36: Predictors of poor health and functional recovery following road trauma: An emergency department inception cohort study.
column37: BACKGROUND: Each year in Canada, road trauma causes over 2,000 deaths and 10,000 serious injuries. Disability after an injury is a major public health concern, but the long term health outcome after road trauma is poorly investigated and based mostly on outdated research that does not reflect modern vehicle safety features or modern medical treatment, and largely ignored cyclists and pedestrians. In addition, there is almost no research that helps healthcare providers know which patients are most likely to have a bad outcome following a crash - making it difficult to provide them with the care they require. It is important for policy makers to know the healthcare costs and lost productivity that results from road trauma, but this information has not been well studied. Our study will provide this missing information. METHODS: We will interview patients who visit an emergency department after a car crash. The interview will ask about their general health before the crash, the injuries they had from the crash, and other details of the crash. We will interview them again at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months after the crash to find out about problems they had since the crash. The follow-up interview will ask about pain, ability to go about their usual activities, whether they have returned to work, and about the medical care they required after the crash. STUDY FINDINGS and IMPORTANCE: Our study will help doctors and nurses know how quickly people recover from their injuries and which patients are likely to have long term health problems after a car crash. We will also describe how much medical treatment these patients require and how much work they miss. This information will also help policy makers make informed decisions on how much money and resources to devote to crash prevention or to treatment programs for crash victims.

column36: Mutational mechanisms of pancreatic cancer development
column37: A diagnosis of pancreatic cancer is often fatal. This deadly tumour is highly aggressive, metastasizes rapidly in patients, and is resistant to nearly all forms of cancer therapy. This disease is expected to be the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the coming decade. Improving clinical outcomes has proven to be stubbornly difficult in pancreatic cancer and highlight an urgent need for scientific advances. This deadly disease often strikes "out of nowhere," and the cancer is usually inoperable by the time the patient experiences symptoms. The cause of pancreatic cancer's frequent appearance at an advanced stage has long been a medical mystery. Using whole genome sequencing, our group reconstructed the history of pancreatic cancer development in 150 independent tumours. Unexpectedly, we found that many of the important genetic events that cause this cancer actually occur 'all at once', similar to the idea of the 'big-bang". These results provide fresh insights into how these tumours develop and help to explain why this disease is so aggressive. These 'big-bang' type events, which are so frequent in pancreatic cancer, are rare in cancers that are not as aggressive. This leads us to believe that they play an important role in the biology of pancreatic cancer. Our goal is to evaluate the impact of these 'big-bang' events on pancreatic cancer development. Overall, we plan to determine if these events are the actual cause this cancer, how they influence metastasis, and therapy resistance. By better understanding the biology of this lethal tumour, we hope to eventually design more effective therapies to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Role of cerebrovascular abnormalities in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorders.
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) alter the child's development, affecting motor skills and social interactions. Genetic anomalies (mutations) have been identified as possible origins for ASD, leading for instance to delays in the maturation of neurons. About 1% to 2% of children worldwide have been diagnosed with ASD, but the causes of ASD remain enigmatic. Brain maturation heavily depends on a steady supply of oxygen and nutrients from the blood stream. As such, key vascular features ensure proper brain maturation: the growth of blood vessels, the maintenance of blood vessel permeability, and the regulation of blood flow. Early life impairments in these vascular features will alter the normal course of brain development. Very few studies have investigated the possible contribution of vascular deficits to this group of disorders. Several studies suggested a link between ASD and altered cerebral blood flow, and a recent postmortem study using brains of young ASD patients suggested a possible impairment in the formation of brain blood vessels. But these observations have not been thoroughly verified, nor tested in a robust animal model of the disease. As a result, involvement of the brain vasculature to the onset and/or progression of ASD remains to be elucidated. We propose to address this gap of knowledge by thoroughly investigating 1) the health of the brain vasculature in a genetically-engineered animal model of ASD, and 2) the consequences on neuronal development when only brain blood vessels (not neurons) are affected by a known, ASD-associated mutation. Our goal is to test novel questions: How do blood vessels develop in the ASD brain? What role(s) do vascular deficits play in the progression of ASD? Our research program proposes a new angle to ASD research, providing novel insight into the involvement of brain blood vessels in ASD. Identification of new players in ASD pathogenesis is essential to the develop new therapeutic strategies.

column36: Impact of the organophosphate ester flame retardants found in the Canadian environment on the reproductive system
column37: As part of our everyday lives we are exposed to a wide variety of chemicals derived from consumer products, such as foam, electronic equipment and plastics. Most of these chemicals are present at very low concentrations. However, exposure to even low doses of substances that disrupt hormones can exert important biological effects. In particular, exposures to endocrine disrupting chemicals are suspected of contributing to the declines in human fertility reported from the developed world. In the past decade governments across the world have regulated the production, uses and importation of specific environmental chemicals that have been shown to disrupt hormone actions. As a consequence, alternative chemicals have entered the market to fill the "gaps". However, there is often little information on the extent to which we are exposed to these replacements or on their health impacts. Our research will focus on a major group of such chemicals, the organophosphate esters (OPEs), that is in rapidly increasing use. We will test the hypothesis that exposure to these compounds is associated with adverse effects on the male and/or female reproductive systems. Cells with key endocrine functions will be used to identify genes and pathways that are disrupted by OPEs and may serve as biomarkers of their effects on fertility. Using an animal model we will elucidate the effects of exposure to the mixture of OPEs found in Canadian house dust on male and female fertility. Finally, we will assess the association of human OPE body burden with female and male infertility. These studies will enhance our understanding of the health consequences of exposure to a family of widely used chemicals for which we currently have very limited data. In addition, we expect that they will contribute to the development of policies to ensure the identification of alternative chemicals that are safer and have a reduced environmental impact prior to their use as replacements.

column36: Reducing the burden of bleeding and cardiovascular complications of bleeding
column37: Cardiovascular disease, which includes coronary heart disease and stroke, affects more than 1 million Canadians and 300 million persons worldwide, and results in 18 million death each year. One of the most effective and widely used approaches to prevent cardiovascular disease is antithrombotic treatment (e.g., aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, newer direct acting oral anticoagulants) that prevent potentially harmful blood clots from forming at the site of atherosclerotic plaques. The most important side-effect of these treatments is bleeding. The importance of bleeding has been vastly under-rated. We paid little attention to bleeding, thinking that for the most part this was easily treatable, and much less important than heart attack and stroke. We now know that bleeding is not only common, affecting thousands of Canadians with cardiovascular disease each year, but is also a powerful risk factor for heart attack and stroke, the very events that these treatments aim to prevent. My research program focuses on determining why persons with cardiovascular disease develop bleeding, and why those who bleed are at such high risk of attack and stroke after bleeding. Having identified the risk factors and mechanisms, my subsequent studies will evaluate whether targeted interventions can prevent cardiovascular events and mortality related to bleeding.

column36: Molecular and physiological understanding of the protein tyrosine phosphatome towards clinical applications.
column37: For the past 25 years, my laboratory focused on elucidating the function of a family of genes named "protein tyrosine phosphatases" (PTPs). The PTP family contains 107 different genes in humans that control a plethora of normal cell functions. PTPs have one common property: to remove a phosphate molecule added to specific tyrosine residues present in many cellular proteins, which confer, or deny, various properties to proteins. Our main purpose is to understand PTP function and to transfer this knowledge into common scientific knowledge and towards clinical applications. Herein we propose three experimental sections. Section 1 is a continuation of our recent work on PTPN1(also known as PTP1B) and PTPN2 (also known as TC-PTP) in characterizing their roles in the immune system. We plan to examine their function in a type of immune cells named "T-cell ". These comprise several subsets of T-cell with different function that kill tumor cells and maintain surveillance against cancer cells. Our proposal is to use small molecule inhibitor of PTPs to reactivate patients T- cells or improve the novel cancer immunotherapeutic approaches of CAR-T cells. Section 2 is pursuing a new system of proteins (the PRL-CNNM proteins) that we first reported in 2014. Involved in the supplies of magnesium to all higher organisms, PRL PTPs are upregulated in almost all cancers to sustain growth and invasion. By understanding their roles and preventing their binding to CNNMs, we intend to develop a novel class of anti- cancer drugs. Finally, section 3 has for objective to explore further this large and relatively still unknown gene family. Our previous data showed that most PTPs are involved in the immune system. We plan to assess the function of each one of the entire gene family towards inhibiting or activating the immune system response against cancer. We are confident that this program will contribute original and important scientific advances and novel clinical applications.

column36: Decoding the DNA double-strand break repair pathways: from mechanistic insights to human genome instability diseases
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of mortality in Canada representing 30% of all deaths. One in 2.3 individual will get cancer and 1 in ~3.8 will die from it, incurring $1.16 trillion in direct cost worldwide in 2010. Genomic instability is a common feature of tumor cells and is thought to represent a basic mechanism to acquire the several genetic alterations required during the neoplastic process. Double-strand breaks (DSBs), the most lethal kind of DNA lesions, can be repaired by two pathways; homologous recombination (HR) or non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). The choice between NHEJ and HR involves an intricate network of resection enzymes whose interplay and hierarchy remain largely unexplored. It is becoming increasing clear that not only failure, but also misuse, of these pathways can trigger genomic instability leading to cancer, the biggest killer in Canada. Paradoxically, defects in the DSB pathways provide weaknesses that can be exploited to design new targeted cancer therapies. The DSB repair machinery can thus be seen as a double-edged sword in cancer protection and treatment, making the understanding of its regulatory mechanisms of crucial importance in the cancer research field. This proposal aims to obtain a comprehensive view of the functions of HR enzymes. By funding this Foundation Program, it will ensure that the mechanisms of these enzymes are defined. Furthermore, using novel inhibitors discovered by our group, we will inhibit the functions of these enzymes to target the vulnerabilities of cancer cells to improve patient care.

column36: Needles without tears: Inoculating children against pain and fear
column37: Not just a poke, needle pain and related fear are in fact major health concerns. All Canadian children undergo painful needle procedures; hospitalized children undergo multiple procedures daily. Pain causes unnecessary suffering, fear, procedure complications (e.g., fainting, failed procedures), and avoidance behaviours. An alarming 20% of unvaccinated 6- 18-year-old children (herein called youth) refuse vaccination due to fear of needle-related pain. This leaves them at risk of acquiring and spreading disease. My vision is to make children all over the world healthier by improving their experiences during needle procedures which will increase needle procedure acceptance. In previous work, I led the creation of a Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG) to address pain and fear and documented gaps for youth. The current project has been developed with key user groups to address these gaps using real-world solutions. Over 7 years, I will build on my successes with my CIHR-funded Help ELiminate Pain in Kids & Adults (HELPinKids&Adults) team to address key unanswered questions. Specifically, to help close the pain care gap for youth, I will: 1) identify best practices for injection techniques, 2) implement and evaluate a novel tool/game developed by youth teaching youth how to reduce pain, fear and fainting, and 3) create both an updated CPG that incorporates this new evidence and a national plan to facilitate integration into healthcare systems. I expect improvements in patient-prioritized outcomes (pain, fear, fainting and needle procedure acceptance); I estimate a 5% absolute increase in school-based vaccine uptake alone. Long-term, I expect improved health outcomes and health cost savings due to improved compliance and efficiency. Importantly, this research program engages youth and other stakeholders to address youth's most pressing concern about healthcare - the needle - and fulfills our ethical obligation to first, do no harm.

column36: Mechanochemical signalling in embryonic wound repair
column37: An outstanding question in biology is how cells coordinate their behaviours. Cells coordinate their movements to sculpt, repair, or invade tissues. A common feature of collective cell movements in development, repair, and disease is the reorganization of the cytoskeleton, the network or proteins that cells use to generate mechanical forces. However, the mechanisms that promote cytoskeletal redistribution during collective cell migration are not understood. We found that highly reactive, oxygen-containing molecules (reactive oxygen species) are critical for cytoskeletal rearrangements during collective cell movement. In addition, we and others showed that cytoskeletal proteins can be regulated by the mechanical forces sustained by cells in living animals. We will use the process of epidermal wound repair in fruit fly embryos to model collective cell movements and establish the basic molecular and physical mechanisms of cytoskeletal reorganization during collective cell migration. Fruit fly embryos are transparent, allowing visualization of coordinated cell movements with high spatial and temporal detail; they are easy to manipulate genetically, and also with drugs and lasers; and over 75% of the genes involved in human disease exist in fruit flies. We will apply advanced microscopy and image analysis to track the distribution of molecules in living embryos; mathematical modelling to develop hypotheses about how changes in chemical or mechanical signals may affect cytoskeletal protein dynamics and cell behaviour; and pharmacological, genetic and biophysical manipulations to test modelling predictions and determine the molecular pathways by which reactive oxygen species and mechanical forces affect cytoskeletal dynamics. Our results will reveal the mechanochemical signals that coordinate cell movements, and will enable subsequent efforts to manipulate cell migration for tissue engineering or cancer research applications.

column36: Molecular regulation of neocortical circuit formation in a model for neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), such as hydrocephaly, lissencephaly, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and intellectual disability affect up to 1 in 8 children born and represent a significant challenge to the health care system and resources available to Canadian families. In Ontario alone, an estimated 300,000 children are diagnosed with developmental disorders of the brain, while ASD alone occurs at a high frequency of 1/88, and is associated with a lifetime cost per individual of $5.5 million. NDDs are thought to arise from abnormal brain formation in the fetus. Yet the underlying genetic and cellular mechanisms remain largely unknown and treatment options are extremely limited. One of the key brain regions involved in NDDs is the neocortex. Its formation relies on the production of a diverse set of neuronal populations and their organization into specific networks important for cognition. Understanding what controls the differentiation and migration of neurons is crucial as alterations in brain anatomy are seen in patients with a range of psychiatric illnesses. We have identified a novel regulator of neocortical organization that when mutated in the mouse gives rise to several hallmarks of developmental disorders of the human brain, including the abnormal formation of neural circuits, enlarged ventricular spaces, reduced axonal growth, and an abnormal accumulation of cells near the ventricles. We propose to study use this mouse model to advance our knowledge of the cellular and molecular processes that contribute to the formation of the neocortex and its connections to regions of the brain important for emotion and cognition. In so doing we will identify diagnostic events and therapeutic strategies for addressing developmental disorders of the brain.

column36: The Pain Squad+ Smartphone App To Support Real-Time Pain Management for Adolescents with Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Pain negatively affects the quality of life (QOL) of adolescents with cancer (AWC), slows cancer recovery, and results in negative long-term health effects. Pain is also significant cost to the healthcare system and families. To address this problem, our team has developed and used a phased-approach to test a smartphone-based app, called Pain Squad+. Using this app AWC report the pain they have and the app provides AWC with advice on how to treat this pain based on an algorithm our team developed. An email is also sent to a nurse if an AWC reports severe pain 3 times in a row. The nurse then contacts the AWC to assist in treating pain. This project will test the effect of the Pain Squad+ app, with and without nurse help, on treating pain and other pain-related health issues and managing costs associated with pain care, when compared to AWC not using the app. We will enroll 222 AWC recruited from 9 Canadian pediatric oncology care centres into a 3-group randomized controlled trial. AWC in the experimental groups will be asked to use Pain Squad+ for 8 weeks (with or without nurse involvement) and all groups will complete pain-related outcome measures at baseline, 2-, 4-, 8-, and 16-weeks. The primary study outcome will be pain intensity. The secondary study outcomes will be (a) pain interference; (b) QOL; (c) pain self-efficacy; and (d) cost effectiveness and utility. We will use established statistical methods to analyze the health and cost data we collect over the course of this study. A real-time and cost effective way to address the problem of pain in AWC is needed. Pain Squad+ can improve pain treatment and QOL for AWC as well as decrease costs incurred by families and the healthcare system. If effective, the Pain Squad+ as a model of technology-assisted care may represent a way to improve the QOL for a range of Canadian patients by treating a variety of physical and psychological symptoms the moment they occur.

column36: Asthmatic phenotyping by microfluidic assessment of shortening velocity and contractile force of airway smooth muscle cells obtained from biopsies
column37: Two million people suffer from uncontrolled asthma in Canada. Asthma is a respiratory disease characterized by breathing difficulty caused by excessive airway narrowing. This narrowing is the result of contraction of the smooth muscle (SM) in the airway wall. While many asthmatics have increased airway SM mass, which may explain excessive airway narrowing, others do not. Thus, these latter cases may suffer from increased contractile capacity of individual SM cells. We have shown that in the horse with heaves, an animal model of asthma, the rate at which airway SM shortens is increased whereas airway SM of horses under remission exhibits an increase in stress and stiffness. Thus, we hypothesize that different subtypes of asthma are characterized by differences in airway SM contractile properties. We propose to develop a "lab on a chip" device for measuring these contractile properties from SM cells acquired by biopsy from people with asthma. Goal: To identify asthma subtypes by measuring the rate of shortening and the contractile force of airway SM from biopsies of human asthmatics and controls. Approach: Airway SM cells from biopsies will be isolated and injected into a device that we will develop from two layers of silicone, each containing a network of micro-channels. Cells will flow into separate lanes and get sucked to the floor of the lanes, which is made up of micro-pillars of known stiffness with perpendicular channels, attached to a low-pressure source, in between them. The immobilized cells will be exposed to contractile or relaxing solutions and bending of the micropillars by the contracting cells will allow measurement of the contractile force, while a sudden release of the cells will allow measurement of the rate of shortening. Significance: This study will enable differential diagnoses of asthma subtypes based on airway SM contractility, directly contributing to more effective, personalized treatments.

column36: Scaling up shared decision making for patient-centred care
column37: Most Canadians wish to stay at home in their old age, but to still have access to healthcare. With new medical technologies (such as alarm bracelets), more and more seniors can stay at home for longer and receive care from home care teams. But seniors living at home often face difficult decisions, such as "Who will look after me when I can't look after myself any more, or if I have dementia?" or "Should I move to a nursing home, or stay here?" For the caregiver, the decision may be "Can I continue to care for my loved one at home?" When more than one option is possible, home care teams can help seniors and their families who are making these hard decisions by giving them the information they need and asking about their values and preferences. This way, seniors and their caregivers can know more about their choices and choose options that reflect what is important to them. We call this 'shared decision making', and it has been shown to improve patient experiences (less disappointment, anxiety or regret) and better use of healthcare dollars. More and more, seniors will be making such decisions in consultation with their home care teams. Over the years we have developed tools and training programs to help home care teams support seniors and their caregivers in making the decision about whether a senior who is no longer independent should stay at home with more help, or move to a nursing home. However, most of our research has been at the regional level. Too many pilot projects that could benefit far more people stay hidden at the local level. So we plan to scale up the tools, programs and systems that seem to work well for one decision and one region. We will adapt and apply them to home care in other places across Canada and to other difficult decisions, so that more seniors and their caregivers benefit from shared decision making and can make decisions together that are better for their health, their pocket, and their quality of life.

column37: Cilia are hair-like structures attached to the surface of almost all cells in the human body. Understanding the architecture of this complex nano-machine will provide opportunities to effectively diagnose and treat cilia-related diseases. Here, the proposed research uses multidisciplinary approaches to elucidate the three-dimensional structure of the cilium. The research outcome will ultimately lead to the mechanistic understanding of cilia related diseases and potential solutions for overcoming their effects to the cell.

column36: Molecular Targeting of Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Bone Marrow Regeneration
column37: Cancer has become a major healthcare issue for Canada, and is now the leading cause of death in our country. 1 in 2 Canadians may be afflicted with cancer, and 1 in 4 Canadians are expected to die from it. Although progress in therapy has been made in many cancers, such as breast and prostate, treatment options for other cancers remain stagnant. This is exemplified by acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a type of blood cancer where dysfunctional leukemic cells take over the blood system. Disease burden can initially be reduced by lowering the leukemic cell numbers (called remission) with chemotherapy, but the disease usually comes back within 2 years (called relapse). When AML relapses, the option is to re-treat the cancer with the same chemotherapy but at a higher dose, and for longer. Unfortunately, the disease usually becomes resistant to treatment and can no longer be controlled. However, the exact reason for AML relapse and resistance to chemotherapy remains unclear. Our program group in Hamilton, Ottawa and London has now identified rare leukemic cells that: a) survive chemotherapy and b) regrow to give rise to relapsed disease. Detailed tests on these unique cells revealed that before they regenerate AML disease, they begin to express leukemia-specific proteins that give them a growth advantage in the bone marrow space where they live. Furthermore, we have revealed that the bone marrow space itself changes to support leukemia, and is directly affected by chemotherapy. Available drugs can inhibit some changes in the bone, and our early findings indicate these drugs can reduce relapse when combined with chemotherapy. Our team of physicians, biochemists and stem cell biologists will define and test a series of new drugs that target proteins that inhibit surviving leukemic cells and change the bone marrow environment that will prevent relapse before it occurs, and activate normal blood stem cells to combat leukemia in patients in the next 7 years of support.

column36: Systematically mapping functional human sequence variation and context-dependent protein interactions
column37: There are few cases where we fully understand how DNA sequence variants impact gene function, and how these changes propagate through networks of molecular and cellular interactions to yield human disease. My team is developing genomic technology to address two distinct goals to improve our understanding of genetic disease: 1) Mapping sequence-function relationships to identify human DNA sequence variants affecting their gene product; and 2) Mapping the downstream network of macromolecular interactions, including their dynamics and context-dependence, to better understand how the connection from genotype to phenotype is mediated. Towards the first goal, we developed a hybrid experimental/computational platform for deep mutational scanning (DMS), in which the functional effects of missense variants are exhaustively mapped in specific target human disease genes. These maps have already been validated for two human disease genes: calmodulin and cystathionine beta-synthase, with the former map already in clinical use. We will continue improving the DMS technology: extending it to human cell models and experimentally detecting the impact of both intronic and exonic variation on splicing and gene function, and applying it to ~100 human disease genes over the next 7 years (approximately 2% of the ~4000 annotated human disease genes). Towards the second goal, we developed a 'barcode-fusion genetics' (BFG) strategy, enabling two reagent libraries to be coupled so that all reagent pairs are tracked via combined ('fused') barcodes. This allows efficient mapping of protein interactions under different environments and genetic backgrounds. We recently developed a prototype method, 'messenger BFG', in which fused barcodes are transcribed, sensing interaction dynamics on the time scale of minutes. We will continue developing this approach, adapting it to human cell-based protein interaction assays, and applying it at proteome scale to both human and yeast proteomes.

column37: Patients with cancer often experience noticeable weight loss, which can start prior to diagnosis and which rapidly increases when the disease reaches an advanced stage. This wasting, known as cachexia, is causes patients to become weak, frail and increasingly dependent on others for daily tasks and self care. Wasting also has important medical implications. Patients with wasting show very poor ability to tolerate cancer treatments and are sometimes forced to stop chemotherapy early due to severe side effects. There are no approved treatments for cancer-associated wasting. While all of the reasons for this are unclear, we may simply know too little about how body weight is controlled in people with cancer to be able to succeed. My vision is to discover new ways to alleviate cancer associated wasting. I developed a highly successful and internationally acclaimed research team in this area, which is unrivalled in its capacity to make key strides forward so that we can alleviate the suffering associated with this condition. 1. I will develop standardized criteria for diagnosis and early detection, so that every patient with risk of developing wasting can be identified as early as possible. 2. I will work to reveal the diverse factors which lead to wasting, so that we can provide a personalized and specific treatment approach to each patient. 3. I will also develop personalized chemotherapy dosing to limit toxicity in patients with wasting, allowing them to complete and benefit from their treatment plan. 4. I will continue to catalyze research partnerships to rapidly advance basic and clinical research and multiply the productivity of this unique Canadian-led effort.

column36: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy to Improve Patient Outcomes Following Internal Fixation of Extremity Fractures: A Randomized Controlled Trial (SPOC-CBT)
column37: Each year, over 12 million individuals in North America sustain a fracture of the extremity, many of which are managed operatively. However, outcomes are variable and many patients continue to experience persistent pain and disability at one-year after surgery. In a recent trial of patients with open extremity fractures, 67% of patients reported moderate to severe pain and 38% reported pain that interfered at least moderately with daily activities at one year. Data from the same trial demonstrated that patients' beliefs about recovery soon after surgery were the most powerful predictor of recovery. These findings contribute to a growing body of literature documenting the importance of psychological factors in predicting outcomes following surgery; however, to date, there are no approaches used in practice to identify, and treat, patients with psychological factors that place them at risk for poor outcomes. A large, high quality trial is needed to establish whether psychotherapy targeting unhelpful illness beliefs is effective in improving physical functioning and reducing pain after surgical fracture repair. We propose a multi-centre randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effect of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) versus usual care in 1,500 patients with operatively managed extremity fractures and at high risk of poor outcome due to unhelpful illness beliefs. This trial will evaluate the effect of CBT on the proportion of patients who experience persistent post-surgical pain and pain that interferes with daily activities, as well as its effect on physical and mental functioning and return to pre-injury function over one year after surgery. Targeting and modifying unhelpful beliefs through CBT may provide an effective strategy to improve outcomes among high-risk trauma patients.

column36: Modeling antibody diversification processes through Cas9-mediated mutagenesis
column37: The immune system plays a major role in protecting humans from bacteria, viruses, and toxins (known as antigens). One of the ways that the immune system accomplishes this is by producing antibodies that bind to and neutralize these antigens. Antibodies are small molecules made by B cells. Each B cell makes only one type of antibody which will bind to only one antigen. By changing the antibody stalk, the properties of the antibody are changed. For example, IgM antibodies can be changed to IgG antibodies which can be used by macrophages to engulf bacteria that are coated by these antibodies, or to IgA antibodies that can be secreted into mucosal tissue and neutralize pathogens in the lung or the gut. Changing the antibody class is accomplished by the class switch recombination process, and the key enzyme that initiates this process is called AID. However, much needs to be learned about this process. In this grant proposal, we plan determine the types of mutations and the enzymes that are required by AID to induce class switch recombination. In addition, since AID has been shown to induce chromosomal translocations that are central to the development of lymphomas, this proposal will also examine the types of mutations and enzymes involved in the development of these cancer-causing events. Hence, the proposed work will allow us to determine how an effective antibody response is generated against pathogens, and will also characterize molecular pathways that play important roles in cancer development. This new information will in turn influence vaccine development or the generation of therapeutic agents that target lymphomas.

column36: Host cell protein substrates of enterovirus proteases
column37: Enterovirus infections are associated with several acute and chronic diseases worldwide and in Canada. Most enterovirus infections are cleared by the immune system, however, infection by certain enteroviral species and strains can be more severe. Poliovirus is the most well-known member which causes paralytic poliomyelitis. The non-poliovirus members are more common such as rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, and coxsackievirus and EV71, which are associated with more debilitating diseases such as viral myocarditis, Type I diabetes, and hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and in rare cases, meningitits. Although enteroviruses have been studied for several decades, the molecular basis of infection and the pathogenic mechanisms leading to disease are still poorly understood. One of the signature properties of enteroviruses is that the virus expresses a protein, called a protease, which cleaves host proteins in the cell to facilitate virus infection. Currently, the extent of host proteins targeted by the viral protease is not known. In this study, we will utilize a novel unbiased proteomics approach to comprehensively identify all of the targets of the proteases from coxsackievirus. Unlike other methods, this new approach is sensitive and can identify the location of the cleavage site on the target protein. The identification of novel targets will provide a catalog of the host processes that viruses affect. Importantly, the knowledge gained will allow us to identify new targets for antiviral therapy. The development of this strategy can be exploited to identify the repertoire of host targets of proteases from other viruses.

column36: Identifying Autosomal Recessive Genes for Intellectual Disability
column37: The program goals are to identify new genes for intellectual disability (ID), focusing mainly on autosomal recessive (AR) causes, to deduce their functions, to direct findings back to the clinic, and to identify therapeutic opportunities. The vast majority with ID currently receive no molecular diagnosis-a shortcoming that significantly impacts health and lifespan. Knowing the causative gene benefits through diagnosis, care and treatment, overall health and lifespan, and counselling and planning for families. AR forms of ID are believed to account for a large proportion of affected individuals, and are the main genetic cause of ID in countries where within-family marriage (consanguinity) is common. However, attempts to map the genes responsible have been poorly explored. Mapping genes for autosomal recessive disorders can be performed with great efficiency in consanguineous families with multiple affected individuals (MPX) using microarray genotyping combined with next generation DNA sequencing approaches. We have completed studies of 192 MPX consanguineous non-syndromic ID families and identified 38 new genes. We aim to continue with >300 additional MPX, and >100 single affected (SPX) families (or proband/mother/father trios) from countries where consanguinity is common. We aim to identify causative genes/mutations in these families, using a combination of genotyping and next generation sequencing. Genes identified in consanguineous families are also relevant to outbred populations, thus we plan to survey the genes identified in >2500 ID patients from Canada. Our studies to date have already had an impact on diagnosis, and the proposed work will add significantly to this legacy. The results will also help illuminate the pathophysiology, facilitating the development of treatments. Understanding the genetics of these diseases will improve diagnosis and treatment in the long term.

column36: PTCHD1 in autism and cognition: from function to phenotype
column37: Truncating mutations in the X-linked gene PTCHD1 have been shown to cause autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or intellectual disability (ID). While the link between gene and disease is very strong, our understanding of what PTCHD1 does is very weak. Initial suggestions for a role in the Hedgehog/Smoothened signalling pathway now look likely to be incorrect. The project outlined here aims to explore the function of PTCHD1, its role in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD and ID, and its relationship to ASD/ID gene networks. This will be done through three main aims: 1. studying the function of the protein, what molecules does it interact with and how; 2. how disruption of PTCHD1 leads to neurodevelopmental disorders, using studies of knockout mice and zebrafish; 3. refining the phenotype- what clinical features are shared by patients with disrupted PTCHD1, and how does this relate to the protein's function, and the phenotypes observed in the mice and zebrafish. For our zebrafish studies, we also aim to look for larval phenotypes that may then be used for high-throughput screening for therapeutic molecules. We have assembled a multi-disciplinary team with expertise across four diverse areas- namely protein function, animal neurobehaviour, molecular genetics, and clinical genetics- who have the background, experience, and motivation, to perform the proposed work, as well as promising preliminary data, that together will lead to high-impact discoveries.

column36: Thrombosis and Thrombocytopenia: Novel mechanisms and treatments
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that aggregate and are responsible for bleeding arrest (hemostasis) at sites of injury. They are also key targets in many diseases. High platelet activity may result in heart attack and stroke (thrombosis), which are leading causes of death worldwide, while low platelet number may cause severe bleeding and miscarriages (thrombocytopenia). Our goal is to elucidate underlying mechanisms of these diseases and develop novel therapeutics. Platelet surface integrin alphaIIb beta3, is traditionally thought to exclusively bind fibrinogen (Fg)/VWF and mediate cross-linking of platelets (aggregation) during hemostasis/thrombosis. My discovery of Fg/VWF-independent thrombosis, proved that unidentified proteins ("X" ligands) bind beta3 integrin to support platelet aggregation. However, these ligands and their role in thrombosis still need to be delineated. We will use chemically engineered beads coupled with alphaIIb beta3 to pull down with high purity unidentified plasma and platelet proteins that bind alphaIIb beta3 (GPIIbIIIa). Specific alphaIIb beta3-protein interactions will be measured and the roles of new ligands in platelet biology, thrombosis and hemostasis will be studied using platelet function assays. We expect these ligands may affect both facets of platelets (activation and inhibition) and may be targeted to control many diseases. Immune-mediated thrombocytopenias involve targeting of self- or non-self (e.g. fetal)-platelet antigens by antibodies leading to platelet destruction known as autoimmune (ITP) and fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT), respectively. We have shown antibodies targeting different platelet surface receptors (i.e. GPIIbIIIa vs. GPIbalpha) can lead to very different disease outcomes and response to treatment. We will continue to explore these differences between the anti-GPIIbIIIa and GPIbalpha immune response in ITP and FNAIT to enhance treatment efficacy.

column36: The Development and Genetics of the Face

column36: Unraveling sensory coding dysfunctions that underlie chronic pain
column37: Intractable pain continues to be the single most common cause of disability that impairs quality of life. Unfortunately, current pain treatments rarely achieve complete pain control, and are often associated with disabling side effects. This is concerning, since persistent untreated pain is associated with several brain disorders, including cognitive deficits, anxiety, depression and addiction. New approaches are needed to address this public health issue. To address this medical problem, the objective of my research program is to elucidate how the nervous system processes pain signals and how this is disrupted in chronic pain syndromes. For example, what makes a normal touch be misinterpreted by the brain as signalling pain? To gain these new insights, we design and use advanced light-based technologies to view and control both healthy and diseased brain circuits; develop new tools to analyse data from physiological, cellular and molecular studies, and develop computer-based approaches to model brain functioning to address issues that are not easy to tackle experimentally. This combination of novel approaches has allowed us to identify new therapeutic targets and develop new drugs that have potential to reverse abnormal pain. We will continue to refine our drug discovery strategies so that we can ultimately help bring relief to those suffering from chronic pain.

column36: Synaptic Plasticity and Dysfunction in the Brain
column37: The development of the brain is an enormously complex task that requires the formation and refinement of trillions of connections between billions of brain cells (neurons). These connections, known as synapses, are critical for all brain functions. They control our movement and senses; they regulate our emotions and decisions. They make us who we are. Dysfunctions in the development or function of synapses are thought to be central to many brain disorders including intellectual disability, schizophrenia, autism, Alzheimer's disease and addiction. If we are to develop targeted therapeutic and behavioral interventions for brain disorders, then studying the fundamental mechanisms of how synapses form and function is crucial. The overarching goal of my lab is to elucidate specific cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying synapse formation and function, and then use this information to probe synaptic dysfunctions that contribute to diseases of the brain. In order to develop a comprehensive understanding of synapses and to modify synapse function at the molecular level, we use rodent models. Mice and rats share similar genes with humans, have related brain structures (including synapses), and can learn and remember simple tasks. My work will identify and manipulate specific molecular targets that are essential for proper synapse development and brain function. This will result in a better understanding of which disruptions in synaptic function lead to brain disorders, and set the stage for refined approaches that can be leveraged to develop new therapeutics for restoring brain function and cognition. Collectively, my work will address: the molecular and cellular mechanisms of how we learn and remember; how disrupting proper synaptic communication in the brain can lead to brain disorders; and whether improving synaptic function later in life might be a therapeutic target for restoring cognitive and functional abilities.

column37: My objective is to improve the efficacy and safety of blood and marrow transplantation (BMT), and, ultimately, to expand its clinical applications. Our ability to get rid of cGvHD is limited by our inability to predict when it will of will not happen and which medical approaches will work best to treat it. One way to decrease cGvHD is to have better blood tests or biomarkers that cane be used to assist in guiding medical care. Our group at BC Children's Hospital is the only one worldwide to work on cGvHD biomarkers for children and we are close to have tests that will help to minimize this serious disease in the next few years. With our work we hope to use cGvHD biomarkers to personalize therapy, develop new therapies, and expand its use of BMT.

column36: The Regulation of Alternative Splicing in Dopaminergic and Serotonergic Neurons
column37: Information from our genes flows from DNA to messenger RNA, an intermediate that will ultimately carry instructions to produce proteins, the principal building blocks for our cellular machinery. In multi-cellular animals, a phenomenon known as alternative messenger RNA splicing provides the capacity to encode multiple proteins from single genes, diversifying our repertoire of protein building blocks. Differential usage of alternative splicing has served as a mechanism contributing to customizing the functions of individual brain cells. However, the rules by which different cells of the nervous system utilize alternative splicing to contribute to their unique functions is unclear. This proposal will aim to better understand the rules used to create these differences in two important types of brain cells that secrete dopamine and serotonin, chemicals that can alter brain states. Dysfunction of these cells can lead to neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease and depression. Thus, in addition to providing fundamental insights into the inner workings of specific brain cells in animals, our work has the potential to shed light on how these mechanisms can go awry in diseases of the nervous system.

To circumvent this concern, here we propose to take advantage of a basic biological concept called "Synthetic Dosage Lethality", where cancer cells overexpressing genes like PLK1 could be killed, when another gene is turned "OFF". In other words, rather than directly inhibiting genes like PLK1, we have developed a method that can query every single gene in the genome, in a span of four weeks, and identify those target genes whose loss-of-function can selectively kill PLK1-overexpressing cancer cells. Using this approach, we will execute our investigation in colon cancer cells as it ranks third in morbidity among all other malignancies. In addition, our lab is fully equipped with all the tools and reagents required to test the effect of the target genes that we identify in this cancer. Thus the successful completion of our project has the potential to identify several new druggable targets for colon cancer treatment. Our findings are expected to trigger the development of novel targeted therapies that would improve the survival of colon cancer patients.
