column36: Molecular mechanisms underlying the clinical efficacy of inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist combination therapies in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease, characterised by intermittent airways constriction and occurs in up to 10% of individuals. Regular inhaled glucocorticoids are clinically referred to as inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and dampen lung inflammation to control mild to moderate asthma. However, more severe disease and asthma exacerbations are poorly controlled by ICS and clinical guidelines recommend the addition of a long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist (LABA). These drugs enhance the effectiveness of the ICS to a level that is not achieved by increasing the glucocorticoid dose. The glucocorticoid receptor (GR), the protein target by which glucocorticoids act, is responsible for modulating gene expression to mediate beneficial effects in asthma. In the context of LABA, combinatorial effects between glucocorticoid and LABA-activated pathways result in enhanced clinical effectiveness of ICS/LABA therapies. However, the mechanistic basis, and the genes modulated, are not established and therefore cannot be selectively targeted. The current proposal will elucidate mechanisms underlying this clinically important effect. In this context, it is salient that the pharmaceutical sector is currently testing novel drugs that activate GR in ways that are different to conventional glucocorticoids. These compounds enhance some aspects of GR function relative to other activities. While, the objective is to improve the clinical efficacy of GR-based therapies, it is important to stress that we do not know which aspects of GR function are most important for synergy with LABA. There is therefore a risk of failing to identify novel GR ligands that most effectively synergise with LABAs. This will preclude maximising benefit from future combination therapies. The current project addresses this key knowledge gap by identifying mechanisms of GR action that are important for synergy with LABA. Such data will help guide the discovery of improved combination treatments for asthma.

column36: The Role of Small Airways Disease Heterogeneity in Asthma
column37: Asthma is not just a Canadian health issue but a serious world-wide public health problem, with an estimated 235 million people suffering with asthma. To date clinical trials have established that treatment with bronchodilators and inhaled steroids can relieve patient symptoms but these treatments are unable to reverse the disease process. Asthma patients have difficulty breathing as their airways - the tubes that carry air in and out of the lung - become partially scared. This is caused by the structural cells that line the airway tubes which respond to allergen exposure by promoting inflammation and thickening of the airways, termed fibrosis. The goal of our study is to identify the disease drivers that cause airway fibrosis in asthma patients and to identify new therapies to prevent the disease. Our work leverages a unique set of donated human lungs which will be analyzed with new computed tomography (CT) scanning methods to understand how the physical damage and airway fibrosis occurs throughout the asthmatic lung. We will then use lung cells isolated from the patients with asthma to test if the disease-drivers we identify can be modulated with new or existing therapies. This research will allow better understanding of airway fibrosis in asthma, and should lead to improved measures to help Canadians with asthma experience less disease symptoms.

column37: Sexual health is an integral part of physical and mental health, quality of life, and healthy relationships. Sexual arousal and desire problems, however, affect up to one third of women, yet approved treatments do not yet exist. One impediment to effective treatment is poor understanding of how sexual difficulties develop in women. Recently, scientists have reconceptualized sexual desire as being triggered by sexual cues and emerging from sexual arousal, instead of a drive, like hunger, that motivates people to seek out sex. This new model of sexual response more accurately captures women's experiences and may better characterize women's sexual difficulties, but it has not been scientifically tested. Understanding the relationships between sexual arousal and desire will create gender-specific knowledge about women's sexuality and about the causes of women's sexual difficulties, will have direct implications for identifying risk factors for sexual arousal and desire problems, will inform treatment decisions, and will decrease the burden of sexual difficulties and its negative impacts for Canadian women.

column36: Beyond Transparency in Pharmaceutical Research and Regulation
column37: Making pharmaceutical safety and effectiveness evidence transparent, i.e. accessible, to physicians, researchers, healthcare payers, and ultimately patients is an essential but elusive goal. Consider the drug rofecoxib (Vioxx). It was approved in Canada and elsewhere in 1999 for treating arthritis only to be withdrawn from markets in 2004, before which thousands of patients who took Vioxx are estimated to have suffered cardiac arrest and death. Regulatory officials had prior knowledge of this safety risk but kept it confidential on the grounds that information was the drug manufacturer's property. Following Vioxx and similar cases a variety of new laws and policies were put into place to increase the transparency of pharmaceutical evidence and regulators' decision-making. Most recently, Parliament enacted Bill C-17, "Vanessa's Law", arming Health Canada with several new powers, including the ability to make drug safety and effectiveness information more transparent. However, meaningful improvements in transparency have been slow to arrive; changing the real world practices of regulators and clinical researchers, much less industry, remains a huge challenge. Working with Health Canada and other key knowledge users we will determine: i) how pharmaceutical data can be made more transparent to researchers; ii) what procedural, social, and political factors constrain Health Canada's ability to enforce greater transparency; and iii) how the regulator can communicate and collaborate with key actors such as clinical researchers, research institutions, funding agencies to improve pharmaceutical transparency. With expertise in law, medicine, epidemiology, anthropology, political science, and bioethics, our multidisciplinary team is uniquely positioned to identify and help overcome barriers to pharmaceutical transparency for the benefit of Canadians.

column37: Concussion and brain injury are recognized as a major health issue for Canadians. This problem may be especially severe in pediatric populations where brain injury could have life long implications and since children are more likely than adults to have persistent symptoms. We need better tools to quantify concussion. We have data indicating that regional brain communication may be impaired in brain injury and that we can detect the injury with a portable brain imaging system based on light. This method, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) detects changes in hemoglobin oxygenation as a marker of brain activity. Regions with similar frequency oscillations are thought to be in communication with each other. These fluctuations can be quantified using an analysis called coherence. We have published data, and a new pilot study, showing that coherence is reduced between regions in patients with long term symptoms. This project will collect data on a cohort (75) of mTBI patients over 3 months and compare with controls as well as people with other injuries (to control for pain and other confounding factors). We will determine if measurements at an early point can be used to predict outcome. We will show how these data relate to specific types of cognitive and functional symptoms. We will expand our knowledge of whether damage to regional brain communication is a common problem. The group is the only one in the world with the pilot data, the team and the patient population needed for such a study. This study will provide definitive information on whether this fNIRS protocol could be used for concussion monitoring-in what could be a transformative study.

column37: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as high blood sugar that is first recognized during pregnancy. It is a common condition affecting up to 14% of pregnant women. This study will help to shed light on the early changes in the body that lead to the development of diabetes in young women of childbearing age (who represent the segment of the Canadian population that has had the largest increase in diabetes in recent years). column37: Conditions during pregnancy can have long-term effects on the health of mothers and babies. Pregnant women who have high blood pressure and their urine contains protein are said to suffer from pre-eclampsia. Our proposed studies are important because, if exercise and anti-inflammatories reduce the risk of disease in pregnant women and their children, this could lay the groundwork for to new treatments to prevent heart disease.

PI3Kalpha(a) is an interesting molecule as it is involved in both, heart physiology and cancer development, but it plays opposing roles in these two scenarios. In the heart, PI3Ka is required for healthy function, whereas in cancer, its inhibition has become the most effective treatment in anti-cancer therapies. As such, several drugs have been developed that directly/indirectly target PI3Ka. As a result, cancer patients who receive these drugs show promising improvements in tumor growth regression and recovery from cancer, but a significant fraction of them end up with heart failure. While the adverse effects of the anti-cancer drugs on the heart and the vasculature are now well established, the molecular mechanism underlying these unfortunate side-effects have not been yet determined. Our research to date has identified PI3Ka, an enzyme that mediates various cellular responses (growth, death, proliferation) as the key player. We have generated genetic mouse models that lack PI3Ka in specific cells (cardiomyocytes in heart; endothelial cells in vessels). We have also obtained the pharmacological inhibitor of PI3Ka, BYL719, currently in clinical trial for anti-cancer therapies. We will use our genetic models, and the pharmacological inhibitor of PI3Ka, in combination with models of heart disease, and other conventional anti-cancer drugs to reveal the central role of PI3Ka in the cardiovascular toxicities associated with anti-cancer treatments. We will take a comprehensive approach which will include animal disease models, functional assessment of heart and arteries, electrical activity of the heart, and detailed molecular/cellular analyses. We will also use the cancer patient registry in Alberta to determine the connection between the type of anti-cancer treatment/drugs that patients receive and the severity of cardiac and vascular complication

column36: A pragmatic registry-based randomized trial of drug tapering in rheumatoid arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects up to 1% of the adult population and causes fatigue, joint pain, swelling and a reduced quality of life. Fortunately, the treatment for rheumatoid arthritis has advanced, and most patients can now have their disease effectively controlled with medications. After a patient's disease has been successfully treated and controlled, the usual practice is to continue with these medications for life. Emerging evidence suggests some patients may be able to successfully reduce medication once their disease is under control, but this evidence has important limitations, and more clinical trials are needed. In this grant, we will conduct a clinical trial to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a patient-centered approach for treatment reduction in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The study will be embedded within an ongoing national study of over 2000 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. From this study, we will identify patients whose disease has been well controlled for at least 6 months and ask if they would like to participate. Interested patients will be randomized to either usual care or a structured but flexible approach to reduce treatment in a shared decision with their physician. Treatment outcomes, including both benefits (ability to successfully reduce treatment) and harms (disease flares) will be compared over 18 months. Alongside these outcomes, we will also measure patient preferences for the benefits and harms, and other outcomes to evaluate the impact on healthcare costs. The data generated will provide real-world data on a patient-centered approach to treatment reduction in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, a common chronic disease with high drug costs.

column36: Role of lysosomal enzymes cathepsins B and D in neuronal vulnerability: potential implications in Alzheimer's disease pathology
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a brain disease characterized by a gradual loss of memory, followed by deterioration of higher cognitive functions such as language, calculation and judgement. The pathological features associated with AD brain include the loss of nerve cells in selected regions along with abnormal deposits of certain molecules such as amyloid beta (Ab) peptide and tau protein in structures called plaques and tangles, respectively. The brain regions which are severely affected in AD are hippocampus and cortex, whereas certain other regions such as cerebellum and striatum are relatively spared. It is believed that accumulation of Ab peptide can trigger the loss of nerve cells, but why only selected cells die in AD brains remain unclear. There is evidence that leakage of lysosomal enzymes called cathepsins B and D from their storage sites is markedly increased in nerve cells before they die in AD brains, but the role of these enzymes in the death of these cells is not fully understood. In a series of experiments, we will first establish the significance of the leakage of cathepsins in Ab-induced death of nerve cells grown in Petri dishes and the underlying cause of leakage of these enzymes from their storage sites. In parallel, we will measure the levels and activity of these enzymes in affected as well as unaffected regions of genetically modified animal models of AD and in post-mortem human AD brain samples. Subsequently, we will determine whether nanoparticles that have been shown to restore leakage of cathepsins can protect nerve cells against Ab-mediated toxicity in Petri dishes and in animal models of AD. This study will establish the role of cathepsins in the selective loss of nerve cells in AD brains. Additionally, these results could lead to identification of new molecular targets for the early diagnosis and/or development of new therapeutic opportunities such as nanoparticles in preventing the loss of nerve cells in AD brains

column36: Follicle-stimulating hormone regulation of bone physiology and pathophysiology
column37: Osteoporosis is a common and debilitating disorder of bone fragility in aging populations, which is associated with increased fracture rates. In women, the incidence of osteoporosis increases markedly following menopause. As estrogen promotes bone health, it is the postmenopausal loss of estrogen that is usually linked to osteoporosis. Indeed, many therapies target the estrogen receptor to prevent or treat postmenopausal osteoporosis. Recent observations over the past decade challenge this current dogma, attributing bone loss to the actions of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary gland. Estrogen and FSH levels in the bloodstream are tightly linked as FSH stimulates the ovaries to make estrogen. When estrogen levels fall at menopause, FSH levels rise, ostensibly to stimulate more estrogen production. However, the ovaries lack the ability to produce estrogen at this stage of life. Therefore, postmenopausal women have both low estrogen and high FSH, and some researchers have recently argued that it is the elevated FSH that is driving bone loss. In support of their view, they identified receptors for FSH on osteoclast cells in the bone. The normal function of osteoclasts is to degrade bone and FSH has been argued to increase osteoclast activity, and therefore bone loss. As a result of these observations, efforts are being made to develop inhibitors of FSH to treat bone loss in postmenopausal women. This new approach is highly controversial as many investigators question whether previous studies on FSH in bone physiology were correctly interpreted. Here, we propose to resolve this controversy using mouse models unique to our research team. The results of our work will definitely establish whether or not FSH regulates bone.

column37: Ischemic heart disease leading to myocardial infarction (MI, heart attack) is a leading cause of death worldwide. Studies using broad approaches to reduce inflammation fail to show clinical effectiveness because they act on both beneficial and deleterious immune pathways involved in infarct healing. Specific targets are needed instead. We recently showed that the circadian system is an important mechanism regulating immunocyte recruitment to infarcted myocardium. However, direct targeting of the circadian mechanism to reduce reperfusion injury and benefit treatment of clinically relevant mI/R has not yet been pursued, in large part because we lacked the pharmacology to do so. In this grant we will investigate direct pharmacological targeting of the circadian mechanism factor REV-ERB to reduce reperfusion injury and benefit healing after mI/R in murine models. We will use genetic circadian models to investigate the specificity of this approach. We will also demonstrate that this strategy is vital using a pre-clinical model and state-of-the-art imaging relevant to humans. This is a unique and direct pharmacological approach to limit infarct expansion and remodelling after mI/R, can be given alongside conventional therapies, and is effective for improving outcomes.

column36: Cortical contributions to visually-guided locomotion in the cat
column37: This project is designed to determine the contribution of one part of the cerebral cortex, known to be involved in the planning of voluntary movements (the premotor cortex) to the planning of visually-guided gait modifications. While locomotion is sometimes thought of as a relatively automatic behavior in which the major function is to produce rhythmical, alternating movements of the limbs, it is actually a highly complex activity requiring cognitive and voluntary control under natural circumstances. On uneven terrain, for example, decisions have to be made about where to make the next step and frequently one plans a sequence of steps to avoid an obstacle. Walking in the street, one must decide how to walk around objects and people and how and when to step on and off a curb. Even indoors, one must navigate the furniture and objects on the floor. These behaviours require processing of visual information about the environment and a means to integrate this information with the immediate and long-term locomotor goals of the subject and the state of the limbs at the time of making the decision (e.g. which limb is in stance and which in swing and how do I adjust gait to most efficiently. or quickly, step over that obstacle). In the current project, I intend to test the hypothesis that the premotor cortex contributes to several essential aspects of goal-directed locomotion, including: decision processes that determine which limb will step over an obstacle; determining the parameters of the gait modification (trajectory and/or muscle activation patterns); and in more complex circumstances determining the sequence of steps required to clear a series of obstacles (e.g. a boulder field on a walking trail).

column36: Combining bedside neuroimaging monitoring and clinical markers to enhance developmental screening in preterm infants born 29-36 weeks of gestational age
column37: Every year in Canada, 27,000 babies are born preterm between 29 and 36 weeks of gestational age. About a third will have developmental delay at 2 years. It is important to identify infants with developmental delay sooner rather than later so intervention to improve child development can be started as early as possible to maximise benefits. However, developmental delay is difficult to recognize for primary care physicians. Yet, specialized developmental follow-up for all is not cost-efficient. Therefore, the challenge is to target preterm infants at higher risk of developmental delay who will benefit the most from assessment and intervention by a specialized team. We propose a new developmental screening protocol that combines non-invasive clinical markers that reflect brain health from birth to 18 months to identify preterm infants at higher risk of developmental delay. To do so, we will recruit 235 infants born 29-36 weeks of gestational age at Sainte-Justine Hospital neonatal intensive care unit (Montreal, QC). These infants will go through our protocol which includes bedside measures of the brain level of oxygen, blood flow and electrical activity, physical neurological examination and parental questionnaires on child's developmental skills during infancy. These measures along with information on medical complications and socio-economic status will be used to predict whether the child has developmental delay at 2 years. This new developmental screening protocol will enhance the quality and efficiency of developmental follow-up for preterm children.

column36: Functional Roles and Therapeutic Potentials of Invariant NKT Cells in Sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening illness caused by a disproportionate host response to microbes. It is characterized by early, severe inflammation followed by impaired immunity to opportunistic infections. Successful treatment of sepsis may thus require a two-step approach, namely to prevent excessive inflammation in the early phase and to boost antimicrobial immunity in the later phase. Natural killer T (NKT) cells are a tiny but powerful subset of lymphocytes with a unique ability to recognize glycolipids (molecules composed of sugar and fat). Promptly after activation, NKT cells secrete large quantities of soluble molecules called cytokines that mediate cell-to-cell communications in the immune system. Importantly, NKT cells can be manipulated to produce cytokines that either promote or suppress inflammation. The proposed research will follow 4 Specific Objectives. Objective 1 will test how NKT cell depletion in mouse models of sepsis may affect host responses, morbidity and mortality. In Objective 2, we will use glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells in a "two-hit" experimental model that simulates early and late phases of sepsis. Mice will be treated sequentially with anti- and pro-inflammatory glycolipids in the above phases, respectively, and will be evaluated for their ability to clear secondary infections. In Objective 3, we will generate mice that harbor either the entire human immune system or human NKT cells. "Humanized" mice will be rendered septic and treated with glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells. In Objective 4, we will obtain blood samples from septic patients shortly after presentation and shortly after resolution of their symptoms. Immune cells will be isolated, exposed to NKT cell stimuli and subjected to functional analyses. Collectively, the proposed studies will reveal the role of mouse and human NKT cells in sepsis, and also importantly hold the promise of introducing new and effective treatments for this dangerous and potentially fatal illness.

column37: Recent research progress has made many types of cancer curable. This development led to a new situation where the post-cancer quality of life became a significant concern for cancer patients. Preservation of the ability to have children draws a particular interest in the patients, and their partners and families. For male patients, the only approach to protect their fertility is currently sperm banking. This approach, however, is not applicable to boys before puberty. Thus, childhood cancer patients face a significant risk of infertility, long before they are ready to make decisions about childbearing and household formation, which also places burdens on their parents. An emerging concept of therapeutic approach to this problem is based on sperm-making stem cells. These cells continuously produce millions of sperm everyday throughout life after puberty. Thus, these cells can be harvested and freeze-stored before cancer therapy, and transplanted back to the patients afterwards when they are ready to form a family. This scheme has been feasible and routinely operational in mice; yet, research on sperm-producing stem cells in humans has seen only a very limited extent of progress. The proposed research addresses the key elements that have been the obstacle to the advancement of our knowledge about sperm-producing stem cells in humans and technical development for their clinical use - what are the cells' markers and how can we amplify these cells?

column37: Opioids are commonly used medications for pain but have very high liability for misuse and addiction. There are also street opioids such heroin and the deadly fentanyl and carfentanil. column37: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics has become a global medical concern as shown by recent reports on the rise of highly drug resistant bacterial strains. Although this resistance was predictable, research to identify new antibiotics or cellular drug target has dropped drastically. Furthermore, many of the most commonly used and often last resort antibiotics have debilitating side effects. In stark contrast, we now appreciate that microbes in human microbiomes play crucial roles in maintaining good health. It is now clear that commensal bacteria in the intestine of mammals accomplish many beneficial functions. Although symbiotic bacteria and mammals have co-evolved and adapted to each other, the ecological niche offered by the host is plagued with environmental insults, to which the bacteria need to adapt rapidly and continuously. In response to stressful environment, bacteria express small regulatory RNAs to coordinate gene expression and adapt to various stress. Our recent work with small regulatory RNAs strongly suggest there is a large amount of unknown yet significant RNA-RNA interactions within bacterial cells. These interactions might regulate virulence and pathogenicity as well as antibiotic resistance. We will map the global RNA-RNA interactions quantitatively within the model bacterium E. coli as well as the major human pathogen Salmonella. Concurrently with this long-term goal, we will investigate the most promising RNA-RNA interactions to establish novel mechanisms of gene expression. We already have established the extended interactome of a few specific sRNAs in E. coli using a novel approach that we developed in the lab. Deciphering the most critical RNA-based regulations (including sRNA-mRNA, mRNA-mRNA, tRNA-mRNA), in bacterial cells. New RNA-RNA interactions are creating specific targets to test novel RNA-based therapies for medical doctors, pharmaceutical companies and drug developers.

column36: Unconventional NMDA Receptor Signalling in Neocortical Plasticity
column37: Few would probably dispute that one of the most important functions of the brain is learning and memory. If you open up any modern neuroscience textbook, you will learn that NMDA receptors are critical for memory formation in the brain. It is therefore perhaps not so surprising that these receptors have been implicated in devastating neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. In recent years, however, its become clear that our understanding of NMDA receptors is incomplete. For example, they are sometimes located on transmitting instead of receiving side of neuronal connections, where they cannot function according to the standard textbook view on how learning in the brain operates. Furthermore, they sometimes signal metabotropically, i.e. in the absence of depolarising neuronal activation, which completely changes how neuroscientists think about their function. This proposal will explore tow unorthodox modes of NMDA receptor signalling: on the transmitting side, and metabotropically. This is a virtual blank on the map, and must be understood to treat major neurological pathologies such as Alzheimer's and epilepsy.

column36: Quantitative ultrasound techniques for diagnosis of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
column37: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is the most common liver disease in Western countries, due in large part to its association with type 2 diabetes and obesity. The more advanced form of this disease is known as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). If left untreated, NASH can evolve to cirrhosis, the late stage of fibrosis. Once cirrhosis is established, patients are at increased risk of developing gastrointestinal bleeding, liver cancer and liver failure that may require transplantation. Fatty liver disease is difficult to diagnose because symptoms can be vague. In some cases, the liver may already be damaged without any symptoms. Furthermore, blood tests cannot be used to definitely establish a clear diagnosis. A liver biopsy is currently needed to diagnose the severity of fatty liver disease but this is usually not indicated in asymptomatic patients. This procedure requires the insertion of a needle inside the liver to remove a small piece of tissue for examination under microscope. Ultrasound is optimum for screening patients with or without symptoms because it is a safe and widely available technology to scan the whole liver. Members of our team have developed advanced ultrasound techniques that provide unique information not possible with state-of-the-art techniques. Unlike liver biopsy, these techniques would be applicable even in asymptomatic patients because it is non-invasive. This research proposal proposes a novel approach for diagnosis of NASH and will be the first study to measure individual components of NASH (fat, inflammation and fibrosis) with quantitative ultrasound (QUS) scores. This study is timely because NASH is the second leading cause of liver transplantation in North America and is predicted to become the leading indication in the near future.

column36: Targeting vulnerabilities in SMARCA4-deficient lung cancers
column37: Cancer is a heterogeneous disease. Distinct subtypes of cancers from the same primary site of origin can be defined by their unique molecular pathological features. Consequently, cancer therapy is shifting towards strategies aimed at genes specific to each patient, where mutated cancer-causing genes in tumors are targeted by highly selective inhibitors. These drugs are often very effective and have minimal side effects as normal tissues do not harbor the cancer-causing mutations, which are being targeted. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer and is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in Canada. NSCLC consists of different subtypes characterized by distinct cancer-causing mutations. For subtypes with mutations activating genes such as EGFR (10-35%) or ALK (3-7%), there are potent drugs that target these activated gene products and have significantly improved patient survival. In contrast, 10-37 % of NSCLCs are deficient in SMARCA4, a known tumor suppressor gene lost in many cancer types and which to this date remains undruggable. Therefore, effective treatment of these patients remains an unmet clinical challenge. In this proposal, we will first exploit a molecular weakness of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs. We have previously uncovered a vulnerability of SMARCA4 loss in an ovarian cancer subtype, which can be targeted using an FDA-approved drug originally developed for treating breast cancers. To extend our findings to NSCLCs, we will use a variety of model systems, including cell culture, mouse preclinical cancer models, and tumor samples from lung cancer patients. Independently, we will use powerful genetic tools to identify novel vulnerabilities of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs that can be exploited therapeutically. Our goal is to provide potential treatment strategies to treat SMARCA4-deficient NSCLCs and provide a clinical benefit for cancer patients.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Our immune system changes as we age. As an example, we begin to produce more of some kinds of white blood cells (monocytes and neutrophils) and less of others (B and T cells). Since monocytes and neutrophils are required to protect us from infection, you might think that this would protect older adults from infections, but what actually happens is that these cells don't mature properly and enter into the bloodstream prematurely. These immature monocytes don't help fight infection but actually make some infections worse. Furthermore, these immature monocytes produce a lot of inflammation which also has a negative impact on our health as we age. The purpose of this proposal is to determine why we start to produce more monocytes as we get older, to determine why these monocytes do not mature properly and to identify ways in which we might be able to restore this process. To do this we will collect blood from young and older adults and assess how maturity decreases with age and determine whether this immaturity correlates with levels of inflammation. Specifically we believe that a molecule called TNF might be involved because when we aged mice that did not have TNF, they did not have any changes in the development or function of their monocytes with age. To determine if this is the case in humans, we have collected samples from humans who are undergoing anti-TNF therapy. We predict that when their TNF is high, their monocytes will be less mature and when their TNF goes down due to their therapy, their monocytes will become normal. We will use our unique colony of old mice (18-22 mo), including old mice that don't make TNF (called TNF knockout mice) to determine which cells make this TNF. The long-term goal of this project is to find novel ways to keep us healthier as we get older. Because monocytes protect us from infections but can also contribute to diseases that increase with age (e.g. cardiovascular disease), we hope these findings will have broad applications.

column36: Inference-Based Cognitive Therapy versus Exposure and Response Prevention for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A 16-Session Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a highly disabling psychiatric illness, characterized by obsessional thoughts that cause patients to perform time-consuming and distressing compulsive rituals. Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is a first-line psychological treatment of choice, which requires patients to face their fears by being exposed to feared stimuli. ERP has been shown to reduce symptoms among those who comply with treatment. However, there is still a significant portion of patients that do not improve, especially those who firmly believe their obsessions are realistic and reasonable (i.e. OCD with Overvalued Ideation). Also, a large proportion of patients refuse the treatment or drop out during treatment due to the distress provoked by ERP. That leaves at most 3-4 out of 10 people with OCD who benefit from ERP, and even then, residual symptoms often remain, or symptoms eventually reappear after treatment. One evidence-based approach to the treatment of OCD, termed inference-based cognitive therapy (IBCT) has been shown to be as effective as ERP with the potential to overcome the limitations of ERP. Since IBCT is a cognitive approach, the treatment does not require exposure to feared stimuli and likely more tolerable for patients with OCD. Also, there is evidence that IBCT is more effective than ERP for those with overvalued ideation, since it directly targets the distorted reasoning that is responsible for the intensity and persistence of the obsession. The current study aims to directly compare ERP with this promising evidence-based cognitive therapy, which is expected to be significantly more effective for those with overvalued ideation, as well as significantly more tolerable with lower rates of treatment refusal, drop-out and higher treatment satisfaction. The project is designed to maximize potential beneficial health outcomes and offer a new evidence-based treatment option for the large proportion of patients unable to benefit from ERP.

column37: Phosphate and vitamin D are critical for many physiological functions including skeletal development, mineral balance, energy metabolism, and proper nerve and muscle function. Findings arising from this work will help uncover previously unrecognized targets and strategies for the treatment of patients with these genetic disorders.

column36: Novel therapies to augment neurological benefits of cellular therapies for traumatic spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a leading cause of permanent neurological disabilities affecting over 2.5 million individuals worldwide. In Canada, there are over 86,000 patients who are afflicted with lifelong consequences of SCI with approximately 4,200 new cases each year. The lifetime medical cost of each SCI patient is estimated at 1.6 to 3 million dollars. Thus, SCI has a profound impact on patients, their caregivers, and the healthcare system. Extensive research by our group and others show that transplantation of neural stem cells offers tremendous possibility for SCI repair. To this end, we have discovered new therapeutic targets with the potential to harness the regenerative capacity of neural stem cells for repairing the injured spinal cord. We have identified that formation of a glia scar around the lesion and increased production of inhibitory molecules in the scar limit the benefits of neural stem cell transplantation. We show that inhibiting these factors facilitates the longterm survival of stem cells and their abilities for tissue regeneration. We are currently investigating several aspects of these strategies and importantly their potential in improving functional recovery in an animal model that clinically reflects human SCI. Our goal is to develop effective regenerative medicine strategies for improving the quality of life in SCI patients.

column37: Vitamin A is an essential part of our diet and is used by the body in many ways, including vision, immunity and reproduction. The liver acts as a warehouse for vitamin A: storing it and releasing it for use in other parts of the body. Vitamin A is also important in maintaining liver health, and it has been suggested that a disruption in this role promotes the development of liver disease. Alcohol abuse is a major cause of preventable death and gives rise to a significant disease burden in Canada. The main organ affected by drinking too much alcohol is the liver, with a well-described disease response ranging from fat accumulation (steatosis), to inflammation (hepatitis), scarring (fibrosis and cirrhosis) and ultimately liver failure. According to the Canadian Liver Foundation, approximately 1 in 12 Canadians drink heavily, and thousands of Canadians die every year because of alcoholic liver disease, making it a national research priority. Moreover, heavy drinking rates are double for First Nations people living on Reserves, representing a population at increased risk of alcohol-related disease. The research described in this proposal aims to establish that alcohol disturbs the way vitamin A works in the liver, contributing to hepatic disease. Through a series of complementary experiments, we will determine the mechanism through which alcohol disturbs vitamin A function at two points in the disease process: 1) the initial step of fat accumulation, and 2) the formation of scar tissue, representing the worsening of liver disease. This research will provide a better understanding of how alcohol causes liver disease by disrupting vitamin A function. The new knowledge generated by this research may be translated into improved care for heavy drinkers at risk of alcoholic liver disease by providing ways to prevent its formation, or stop it from worsening. This knowledge will also provide new insight into how altered vitamin A function contributes to other human diseases.

column36: Structural Basis of Cyclic Nucleotide Signal Translation and Inhibition
column37: Pancreatic, endocrine and cardiac tumours as well as intellectual disabilities and abnormal bone growth in children are caused by defective reading of the signal transmitted within cells by a messenger molecule called cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). Furthermore, a closely related molecule, cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), plays a critical role in the replication of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. The goals of this project are to study two proteins that bind to cAMP and cGMP, i.e. the cAMP-dependent protein kinase A in mammals (PKA) and cGMP-dependent protein kinase G in P. falciparum (pfPKG), and to: (a) elucidate the structural and dynamical changes caused by inherited mutations that lead to incorrect translation of the cAMP signal and diseases such as cancer and developmental defects; (b) to understand how to suppress the signals carried by the cAMP and cGMP cyclic nucleotides to improve current cancer and malaria treatments. We will use nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to investigate how modified molecules that resemble cAMP and cGMP, and which may serve as future cancer and malaria drugs, interact with PKA and pfPKG, respectively. Their effects on these proteins are currently poorly understood at the structural and dynamical level, and NMR has only recently been used to investigate these interactions at atomic resolution. NMR will reveal the structural and dynamical changes in PKA and pfPKG caused by cAMP and cGMP analogs, respectively, as needed to fully understand how to modulate these proteins' activities. NMR is also ideally suited to unveil how disease-causing inherited mutations alter the physiological interactions of PKA with cAMP. Elucidating the structural and dynamical changes caused by disease-related mutations and modified cyclic nucleotides will help understand the molecular origins of multiple tumours and pediatric disorders, and will also facilitate the design of improved cancer and malaria drugs.

column37: In Canada, breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer in women accounting for 26% of all newly diagnosed cancers. Novel combinations of existing therapies offer an exciting opportunity to enhance the killing of BC cells while at the same time avoiding the development of resistance to therapies, which can occur rapidly when treating patients with a single agent. This nanoparticle therapy will also be combined with targeted radiotherapy to offer an exciting combination-based approach for the treatment of recurrent breast cancer in the chest wall.

column36: Understanding Class I MHC Receptor Control of Natural Killer Cell Memory
column37: Adaptive immune memory is one of the most powerful weapons the body has to fight infections. It is how vaccines work: the immune system sees harmful, foreign matter, and T and B cells remember it so that the immune response is stronger and faster the next time that target is encountered. Surprisingly, natural killer cells, a cousin to the T cell, can also remember these targets, in a process we do not yet understand. We have previously demonstrated that this natural killer memory relies on a specific natural killer cell protein called Ly49I. This proposed research seeks to better understand what Ly49I does that allows memory in these cells, and to identify which other proteins and which helper cells contribute to natural killer memory. Understanding natural killer cell memory is exciting because it works through different mechanisms than T cell memory, so learning how this memory works will open a whole new field of study in immunology. It is also exciting because natural killer cells are experts at killing cancer, so understanding their memory could lead to novel cancer vaccines and therapies designed to prevent the recurrence of a dormant cancer.

column37: First Nations peoples in Canada have more challenges with their lung health compared to non-First Nations people. We know that cigarette smoking causes COPD, but there is much less known about the effects of household, historical/community/cultural, and work-related factors on the burden of COPD in First Nations people. This project is a new partnership between UBC, Carrier Sekani Family Services and eleven partner Nations. This study is unique in being able to address the individual, community, and historical risks of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. The goal of this study is to better understand the burden of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. Aim 1: Estimate how many people have COPD and how many people have not been diagnosed. Aim 2: Find out if there is a link between inhaled pollutants (from household, work-related, and historical/community/cultural sources) and: 1) symptoms; 2) blocked airflow; and 3) health care use. We will collect detailed measures of lung function, symptoms, self-reported current & past exposure to lung irritants, and health care use. We will also collect indoor air quality measures from homes and community buildings. With the study results, communities will be able to better plan for health services, and create prevention strategies to reduce the chance of First Nations people developing COPD in the future.

column36: The role of victimization in adolescents' sexual health: A longitudinal study
column37: Exposure to victimization in childhood and adolescence is a widespread social and health issue in Canada. In a representative sample of more than 23,000 Canadians aged 18 years and older, the rate of child sexual abuse, physical abuse, or exposure to domestic violence was found to be 32%. Victimization is associated with a host of negative short- and long-term mental and physical health consequences, such as internalizing and externalizing problems, post-traumatic stress disorder, substance abuse, chronic pain and sexual revictimization. Although several studies have examined the consequences of childhood and adolescent victimization, progress in this area is hampered by important methodological limitations, such as the use of clinical samples, cross-sectional designs, and adult retrospective reports of victimization. Further, very little work has focused on sexuality, beyond sexual risk-taking. The proposed longitudinal study will overcome prior methodological limitations by examining the effect of different types of victimization assessed at age 14 on the sexual health of adolescents aged 14-17 over a three-year period. In their high school classrooms, 4,000 community participants will complete standardized measures at baseline as well as one and two years later. We hypothesize that victimization assessed at Time 1 will significantly predict worse sexual health outcomes at two- and three-year follow-ups. Our interdisciplinary team of psychologists, sexologists and physicians specialized in victimization, adolescence, and sexuality is well positioned to carry out the proposed research, which has direct implications for the health of Canadians. Findings will generate novel longitudinal data concerning the relationship between childhood and adolescent victimization and sexual health, and will contribute to the identification of factors to be targeted in prevention and intervention programs aimed at improving adolescents' sexual health.

column36: Deciphering the mechanisms of synaptic dysfunction in a genetic model of spinal muscular atrophy
column37: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease characterized by death of motoneurons innervating skeletal muscle fibers. In SMA, connections between nerve cells and muscles at specialized sites called synapses become fewer causing the muscle to become progressively weaker. We will further characterize how SMN deficiency causes synaptic defects at the cellular and molecular level. This proposed research will enhance our understanding of synaptic pathology in SMA and provide important insights to later develop pharmacological interventions that will stabilize synaptic connections and motor function in SMA.

column36: Sexual pain in endometriosis: role of somatic mutations and local neurogenesis
column37: Endometriosis affects 1 in 10 women of reproductive-age. It is defined as tissue from inside the uterus growing in other parts of the body, such as on or near other pelvic organs such as the ovary and colon. Half of women with endometriosis experience sexual pain: specifically deep dyspareunia, defined as pelvic pain with deep penetration during sexual activity. In our recent research, we identified new genetic and molecular pathways by which endometriosis may cause pain with sexual intercourse. Sexual pain in endometriosis is associated with a subtype of endometriosis known as deep infiltrating endometriosis, in which endometriosis invades pelvic organs and forms adhesions. We recently reported the existence of somatic (non-inherited) gene mutations, such as in the KRAS gene, in this type of endometriosis. These mutations may be responsible for the invasive qualities of this type of endometriosis and thus sexual pain. We also have found evidence that sexual pain in endometriosis is associated with increased nerve density around endometriosis. This nerve growth in turn may be under the influence of nerve growth factor and an immune factor known as interleukin-1b (IL-1b). In this proposal, we will validate our findings in a prospective data registry and accompanying tissue bank for endometriosis. Using this large prospective dataset, we will test whether the KRAS (or other gene) mutations are associated with deep infiltrating endometriosis and thus sexual pain. Similarly, we will test whether nerve growth factor and IL-1b are associated with nerve growth around endometriosis and thus sexual pain. We will also develop a new mouse model of endometriosis. In the future we will use this model to test new drugs for endometriosis, which either target the gene mutations, or block nerve growth factor or IL-1b. In 5-10 years of grant end, we propose a clinical trial of the most promising drug, with the aim of providing a new treatment for this common condition.

column36: STandard versus Accelerated initiation of Renal Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury (STARRT-AKI): A Multi-Centre, Randomized, Controlled Trial
column37: Background: Sick patients receiving care in the intensive care unit (ICU) commonly develop acute injury to their kidneys. This sudden loss of kidney function predisposes these patients to the accumulation of fluid and blood toxins and often leads to death. Acute kidney injury often prompts clinicians to start dialysis therapy, which involves passing a patient's blood through a specialized filter to remove excess fluid and metabolic waste. However, the right time to start dialysis is not clearly known to clinicians. Starting dialysis early or proactively can help better control fluid and blood toxin levels and may lead to a lower risk of death. On the other hand, dialysis has side effects and is expensive and if early dialysis does not improve patient outcomes, it may be best to only start it when the patient gets much sicker and the clinician does not believe there is any other choice. Aims: This study will establish which one of two strategies for starting dialysis (accelerated/early vs. standard) in ICU patients with acute kidney injury leads to a lower risk of death and non-recovery of kidney function and which approach is more cost-effective. Design: This study is an international, multicentre, randomized clinical trial comparing early vs. standard start of dialysis in 2866 critically ill ICU patients with acute kidney injury. Significance: The study will guide clinical practice and inform policy on when to start dialysis in ICU patients with acute kidney injury. The trial has enrolled 970 participants (34% target) from active 90 sites across 10 countries and has fostered extraordinary collaboration with endorsement from critical care trials groups and medical organizations around the world. These funds will enable us to complete recruitment and perform a rigorous cost comparison of these two approaches to starting dialysis in ICU patients.

column36: Impact of low testosterone on cardiac structure/function in aging
column37: Heart disease increases with age in men and women as sex hormone levels fall. Since a women's risk of heart disease goes up after menopause, there has been a lot of interest in the idea that estrogen influences heart disease. However, it is now clear that testosterone decreases with age not only during "manopause" in men, but in women too. Marketing campaigns focused on the benefits of testosterone have led to an increase in the use of testosterone supplements in older people. This is important, because low testosterone increases the risk of diseases like heart failure, where the heart cannot pump blood very well, but high testosterone can be harmful too. We discovered that age decreases the ability of male hearts to contract by changing the ability of heart cells to regulate internal calcium. Some calcium is needed for the heart to contract, but the balance needs to be right. When calcium is disrupted it can lead to diseases like heart failure. There is still a great deal more to know about how testosterone affects the heart. We plan to look at how long term exposure to low testosterone changes contraction in whole hearts and affects contractions and calcium levels in individual heart cells in males and females. We will start to look at effects in middle age (1 year old mice) and follow them until they reach 2 years of age, which is about 85 human years. We will also treat male and female mice with testosterone to find out if testosterone therapy is beneficial or harmful and if this depends on the dose used. This research project will help us understand the links between testosterone, aging and heart disease. It will help us recognize whether testosterone supplementation is good or bad in vulnerable older people with heart diseases.

column36: The role of circ-Itga9 in cardiac remodeling
column37: Cardiac diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries. Over time, as hearts age or become senescent, adverse remodelling that is initially beneficial, progressively leads to reduced cardiac functioning. Our research aims to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie this remodeling and repair. Circular RNAs are closed continuous loops of RNA that were recently detected in eukaryotic cells, and may affect cell physiology through a variety of mechanisms. We can also use the reverse approach to silence circular RNA expression, and observe the changes in function. Using these approaches, in conjunction with standard experimental models, we can better understand the function of circular RNAs in cardiac diseases. There are two unique aspects to our proposed study. Firstly, we are among the first to produce a stable expression construct allowing long-term studies of circular RNAs. The second unique approach is our inhibitor system that is designed to block the function of individual circular RNAs in cell and animal models. These allow us to specifically study individual circular RNAs, and better understand any causal relationships. Our proposed experiments will help us explore the regulatory roles of circular RNAs in both cardiac aging and other cellular repair contexts. The agents developed may be used as tools in understanding the role of circular RNAs in heart development, aging, disease-associated injury and tissue regeneration. With these approaches, we hope to design therapies to intervene against the adverse remodeling associated with age-related heart disease.

column36: Cellular mechanisms of sensorimotor integration
column37: Our sensory experience of the world remains stable and predictable, even as we move through our environment and interact with it in complex ways. This is because our brains are somehow able to seamlessly integrate action and perception. Before our muscles even move, our brain is predicting the consequences of those actions on what we see, hear, and feel. This is why, for example, it is nearly impossible to tickle yourself--your brain is ready for the sensation and actively filters out the "ticklishness." When the brain systems that perform functions like this fail, the consequences can range from motion sickness and vertigo to the kinds of hallucinations and delusions that characterize schizophrenia. How the integration of sensory input and behaviour happens is only partly understood. To understand what events happen in individual nerve cells during integration, we are studying this process in a tiny roundworm. Despite its simplicity, it has to solve the same action-perception problems we do in order to successfully interpret and navigate in its environemnt. This same simplicity means that we can study molecular events, signaling between nerve cells, and behaviour all at the same time in an intact animal. Because all animals share the same fundamental biology at this level, what we learn will help us understand what happens in both healthy and dysfunctional brains to allow action and perception to work together.

column36: Epigenetic regulation of repeat expression by RB and EZH2 in cancer
column37: Cancer cells possess a number of features that distinguish them from the normal cells in our bodies. This grant application is focused on studying the remnants of ancient infections that leave behind foreign DNA sequences called repeats. Their expression can be uniquely misregulated in cancer, creating a feature that distinguishes cancer cells from surrounding normal cells. In most cases these repeat sequences are sufficiently altered that they no longer generate viruses or cause new diseases. However, some pieces of these DNA sequences can be expressed and this leads to two major outcomes for host cells. The first is that expressing these sequences creates the opportunity for repeat sequences to move to a new location in the cell nucleus. This is called transposition and it is potentially damaging to the cell as it can alter the expression and function of the cell's normal genes at its new location. From a cancer perspective this can be the source of changes in DNA sequence (mutations) that cause the disease. While this is bad, the second consequence of expressing repeat sequences is that it can lead the host cell to appear as though it has been infected. This can trigger an immune response in which our natural defence system will kill the 'infected' cell. Thus these repeat sequences are an attractive means to recruit our natural defences to help fight cancer. This grant proposal will study repetitive sequences with the aim of using this information to design more effective ways to kill cancer cells.

column36: Nicotine mechanisms contributing to tobacco smoking
column37: The societal costs of tobacco smoking are immense, with around 37,000 deaths each year due to smoking in Canada alone. Current quitting aids are of little help. Although nicotine clearly plays an important role in tobacco addiction, we have no clear idea what that role is. Oddly, when nicotine is tested in pure form, divorced from tobacco, it turns out to be a remarkably weak reinforcer (please note: in this context, a reinforcer is basically a reward). For example, neither human subjects nor animals will typically work hard to obtain injections of the drug. In this respect, nicotine is not in the same league as cocaine, amphetamine or heroin. There are, however, several less conventional ways by which nicotine could make tobacco addictive. For a start, nicotine has the ability to make other rewarding stimuli more powerfully rewarding (the so-called reinforcer-enhancing effect), which could, for example, allow nicotine to boost the effects of other addictive chemicals lurking in tobacco smoke. The proposed research will use animal models in order to better understand the addictive actions of nicotine. Unfortunately, much animal research has been done using excessively high doses of nicotine that do not translate readily to tobacco smoking; I propose to rectify this. We will investigate how nicotine exerts its reinforcer-enhancing effect (for example: is this an action of nicotine directly in the brain, and if so which types of nicotine receptor targets are involved?). We will also study whether nicotine's rewarding effects can "rub off" onto sensory cues through frequent association. We are also interested in finding ways to alleviate the unpleasant effects of nicotine withdrawal, which are often a barrier to quitting smoking. Overall, this research will deepen our understanding of the behavioural and chemical basis for tobacco addiction, which in turn should uncover new approaches to possible treatment.

column36: Early growth response 1 and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating condition that results in cognitive impairment, loss of executive functions and dementia. It is estimated that 47 million people world-wide suffer from dementia. In Canada alone, 564 000 people have dementia with 25 000 people dying as a result each year, creating an annual financial burden of $10.4 billion. In 15 years, this number is projected to double. Currently no disease modifying therapy is available and treatment of AD remains symptomatic.Tangles and plaques are the two characteristic lesions found in the brains of AD patients. Tangles are found inside the nerve cells and are formed by the abnormal hyperphosphorylation of tau protein (containing more phosphates that normal). Hyperphosphorylated tau is unable to provide mechanical support to neurons. Plaques are found outside of the nerve cells and interfere with cell communication, trigger inflammation and promote cell demise. Plaques are formed from a peptide called beta amyloid by the actions of two enzymes: beta secretase-1 (BACE-1) and gamma secretes. Studies have determined that BACE-1 is somehow over activated in the AD brain, leading to excess production of beta amyloid. What activates BACE-1 and how tau becomes hyperphosphorylated in AD patients had remained mystery Several researchers found that Early growth response 1 (Egr-1) protein was significantly elevated in the autopsied brains of AD patients. Recently, we showed that Egr-1 promotes tau hyperphosphorylation and activates BACE-1 in mouse brain. Very recently, we demonstrated that inhibition of Egr-1 in the hippocampus reduces levels of both hyperphosphorylated tau and beta amyloid and improves learning and memory in mouse model of AD. Our data indicate that Egr-1 is a potential therapeutic target for AD. More recently, we have designed a peptide derived from a physiological inhibitor of Egr-1 to treat AD. In this project, we wish to test the efficacy of this peptide in two mouse models of AD.

column37: The biological function and disease-causing malfunction of proteins are underpinned by their structures and interactions with themselves and other biomolecules. Despite tremendous progress in past decades, the basic driving forces of protein conformational changes are not well understood, limiting the application of biophysical knowledge of disease-related proteins in therapeutics development. The need for a deeper physical understanding is especially acute for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) that lack a stable structure. Comprising ~30% of the proteome, IDPs are prominently involved in cellular regulation, a role facilitated by IDPs' ability to perform dynamic, multi-site recognition of other biomolecules. Malfunctioning of IDPs causes numerous diseases, notably various forms of cancer and neurological degeneration. A remarkable recent discovery is that liquid-liquid phase-separated IDPs -- like oil droplets in water -- are a major component of functional compartments in the cell. However, the biophysical basis of individual and collective IDP properties remains mostly undeciphered. The proposed research builds on the fundamental advances we have recently made, particularly in understanding how IDP phase separation depends on their amino acid sequences. Harnessing the unique interdisciplinary expertise of our own research group as well as those of our collaborators, we endeavour to expand significantly our fundamental physico-chemical knowledge of biomolecular organization and recognition for the novel multi-site interactions and liquid-liquid phase behaviours of IDPs. Results of our investigation will enable advances in understanding disease processes and ultimately to developing new therapies.

column36: Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Cohort Study
column37: With improvements in early detection and treatment, survival rates for breast cancer have improved. Unfortunately, breast cancer treatments can cause both short and long term physical and psychological side effects. More specifically, breast cancer survivors are at a higher risk for breast cancer recurrence, second cancers, heart disease, weight gain, bone loss, fatigue, anxiety and depression. Previous research has shown that regular physical activity can improve the physical and psychological function of breast cancer survivors, help manage some short term side effects of treatment and reduce the risk of having a recurrence. However, this research has not been adopted into regular oncology practice because specific exercise advice cannot be provided regarding the type and volume of exercise necessary for improving quality of life and survival of breast cancer survivors. We initiated the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer cohort study in 2011 with a CIHR Team Grant. The aim is to determine if physical activity can help breast cancer survivors manage the side effects of treatments, enhance quality of life, reduce their risk of disease recurrence and improve survival. Study participants are asked to complete questionnaires, undergo tests for physical fitness tests and lymphedema (swelling in the arms), have their body composition measured (body fat, lean mass, bone density), give a fasting blood sample and wear devices that objectively measure their physical activity and sedentary behavior (time spent sitting) at breast cancer diagnosis and again at 1, 3, and 5 years. They are then followed for breast cancer outcomes. To date, we have recruited 75% of our cohort of 1500 and are now seeking funding to complete the recruitment and follow-up of all participants. A better understanding of precisely how physical activity and physical fitness affect breast cancer recurrence and survival will lead to improvements in exercise recommendations for breast cancer survivors.

column36: Role of CLEC12B+ macrophages in the pathogenesis of vitiligo and melanoma
column37: For the past 17 years, my laboratory has been studying skin diseases caused by abnormalities of melanocytes, the cells that produce melanin pigment that protects our skin from the harmful effects of ultraviolet light in the sun. More than 50 million people worldwide develop a severe disfiguring disease called vitiligo, which is caused by patchy loss of normal skin color due to death of melanocytes. In addition, more than 300 thousand of people develop melanoma each year in the world, which is caused by the opposite change in the melanocytes, i.e. uncontrolled multiplication of cancerous melanocytes. The exact mechanisms leading to the opposite fates of melanocytes in these two diseases are unclear. There is an urgent need to develop better therapies for vitiligo and melanoma. My laboratory recently found a new type of innate immune cells in the surroundings of the melanocytes in the skin, the CLEC12B+ macrophages. These cells are important participants of the immune response to pathogens attacking our skin, such as bacteria, allergens and viruses. They are also required for stopping the immune responses when the pathogens are eliminated, so that the immunologic balance is restored, tissue injuries are repaired, and damaged cells are replenished. My lab found that in vitiligo, there is a shortage of these cells, where as in melanoma, there is an excess. In culture dishes, these macrophages secrete growth factors that can enhance melanocyte survival, but suppress professional killer cells, such as the natural killer cells and killer lymphocytes. Therefore, I speculate that deficiency of these macrophages is the reason for vitiligo development, and that over population of these cells have the opposite effect, that is, unchecked growth of the melanoma cells. In this project, I will test these hypotheses using cultured cells in petri dishes and in animal models. The results generated will help develop more effective therapies for vitiligo and melanoma.

column37: What do we know about this topic? Cancer patients, adults and children, are greatly distressed by vomiting due to chemotherapy. Vomiting due to chemotherapy is completely prevented in most adults with cancer by giving medicines called antiemetics. Antiemetics are much less effective in children. Even when recommended antiemetics are given to children receiving chemotherapy, about half still vomit. Bone marrow transplant is the only curative therapy available for some children. The second will receive standard antiemetics plus placebo. Children will take olanzapine or placebo on each day they receive chemotherapy and for 4 days after. Children or their parents will record when children vomit. Using a special tool, older children will also tell us how nauseated they are. We will monitor and question children and parents to see if children have side effects. Why is this study important? This study will tell us if olanzapine reduces vomiting in children receiving chemotherapy for bone marrow transplant and the side effects that these children experience. Our findings will influence the care of children undergoing bone marrow transplant and receiving chemotherapy in Canada and elsewhere. We hope to improve the health and the quality of life of these vulnerable children.

column36: Repurposing slow-release oral morphine as new oral alternative for the treatment of opioid use disorder
column37: While reversing overdoses with medications like naloxone is a cornerstone of the response to the opioid public health emergency, preventing overdoses through the development of effective treatments for opioid use disorder (OUD) is critical to addressing this epidemic. Unfortunately, in Canada, there are only two proven life-saving treatments: buprenorphine/naloxone (BNX) and methadone. However, these medications have limitations and are not acceptable for many individuals, resulting in a substantial proportion of individuals who remained untreated and at immediate risk of overdose, death and other negative outcomes. Small European studies suggest that slow-release oral morphine (SROM) may be another potentially effective treatment that is better tolerated, and is associated with greater patient satisfaction and reductions in craving compared to methadone. The goal of the proposed research is to build on these encouraging results and rigorously evaluate the relative effectiveness, safety and acceptability of SROM and methadone in real-life clinical settings in Canada. To that end, we will enrol approximately 200 adults with OUD, who are currently exposed to fentanyl, and who have tried but not benefited from treatment with BNX. Eligible participants will be randomized to receive either methadone or SROM for approximately six months, using a double-blind design where neither participants nor their physicians will know which medication they are receiving. Findings from this study will greatly increase our knowledge of the relative benefits of different treatment alternatives for OUD, and how each of them may suit different individuals' needs. Importantly, from a health policy perspective, positive results confirming SROM clinical utility could present significant potential to increase access to an additional form of evidence-based treatment for OUD in Canada, with potential to be scaled up rapidly given that SROM is already available as an inexpensive generic drug.

column36: Targeting perinodal adipose tissue for lymphedema therapy
column37: Lymphedema is a condition of uncontrolled fluid accumulation and tissue swelling that affects ~140 million people worldwide. Lymphedema can cause discomfort, immobility and organ dysfunction. Edematous tissue in lymphedema presents a high risk of infection. The major cause of lymphedema in the world is lymphatic filariasis. In Canada, the major cause of lymphedema is the damage to the lymphatic vessels and LNs associated with cancer and cancer therapies, which impacts almost all of the cancer types that involve cancer spread via the lymphatic vessels. Infection and obesity are the major risk factors of lymphedema in cancer survivors: 38-89% of breast cancer patients will eventually develop lymphedema. Currently, there is no cure for lymphedema, mainly due to the lack of mechanistic understanding of its development. Some lymphedema patients exhibit significant body disfigurement and need life long intervention with compression garments, which cause a huge psycho-social and economic impact on these patients. The lack of knowledge regarding the regulation of lymph flow has been the barrier for the disease prevention or treatment. Lymphatic vessels maintain fluid balance and transport tissue waste, pathogens and cells to lymph nodes for protection by the immune system. In the lymph node, lymph flow direction determines the time, the location and the cell types that antigens will encounter after immune stimulation. Lymph nodes are typically surrounded by fat tissue and I have found that this perinodal fat may partially compensate for the immune protection function when lymph flow via lymphatic vessels is compromised. In this study, I will determine how fat tissue around the LN participates in fluid balance and combating bacterial infection when lymphatic vessel function is compromised. Our work aims to target perinodal adipose tissue in order to develop potential therapeutic methods to reduce edema and improve host immune protection.

column37: Everyone is aware of the impact heart attacks have on peoples quality of life, and ultimately that death due to heart failure is an all too common event. This is particularly true in people who have obesity and/or diabetes. We now understand much about the complexity of the heart, its structure and how it functions. This has also allowed researchers to identify things which change in the heart before a heart attack to cause this event. The changes which occur even after heart attack that cause failure of the heart are also now quite well characterized. You may see these changes referred to as "cardiac remodeling". Basically, they involve: 1. changes in the ability of the heart to use nutrients to produce energy (energy production becomes less efficient). 2. change in the size of the heart (the size of heart cells initially increases). 3. change in the number of heart cells decreases (normally these 'muscular' cells work together to cause contraction: less number of cells means less force) and 4. a change in the balance between elasticity and stiffness of the beating heart (mainly due to changes in the 'scaffold' that normally supports the heart). column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common disabling neurodegenerative disorder, affecting an increasing number of Canadians, for which we have no cure. column37: The world is facing an unprecedented level of migration due to violence and persecution with many countries struggling to develop best models for resettling refugees. We have involved provincial and federal policymakers, as well as community organizations and private citizens in the conduct of the project so that our analyses are relevant and communicated to those who can act on the results. column36: Developing a culture-specific model of resilience against substance use among Canada's on-reserve Indigenous youth
column37: The cultural strengths of Canada's Indigenous communities are prominent in the midst of centuries of devastating colonization. Moreover, evidence shows that cultural connectedness inspires well-being among Indigenous youth. However, adolescence is a time fraught with uncertainty about one's identity and opportunities to drink and smoke. The objective of our project is to leverage the inherent strengths of Indigenous culture to develop a model of resilience. We aim to use a two-eyed seeing approach, in which both Indigenous and Western perspectives are used to identify factors that protect Indigenous youth from substance use. Further, we aim to translate knowledge learned back to Indigenous community youth using the traditional method of storytelling. To reach these aims, we propose a five-year study that will focus on adolescents in one Northern Quebec Indigenous community. This will be a three stage project. Stage 1 will be community listening. The research team and community members will come together to define culture and community context, and how these relate to youth substance use. Stage 2 will be an empirical study. In a school-based study, potential predictors of substance use will be assessed over a three-year period as adolescents progress through secondary school. This will permit the unique opportunity to track culturally- (community-) relevant protective factors of substance use as they unfold across formative years. Stage 3 will focus on knowledge translation and communicating what is learned back to the community. The findings will be shaped into stories of resilience that are told by community members. A compilation of storytelling will be filmed, and DVDs and an online version produced. These will be the property of the community and distributed through varied platforms, such as community events and youth programs. To summarize, this research aims to illustrate the process and product of using two-eyed seeing to address a compelling health issue.
