column36: Targeted Therapies for Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
column37: Finding new therapies for rare diseases is an urgent need in Canada. Our research program seeks to develop effective and safe treatments for patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a devastating lung disease that causes destruction and failure of the lungs. LAM is caused by cancer-like abnormalities arising in cells (LAM cells) with genetic mutations in the 'tuberous sclerosis complex-2' (TSC2) gene. LAM also develops in ~1/3 of patients with 'tuberous sclerosis complex' (TSC), an inherited disease of mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 gene that affect ~1 in 6000 Canadians, and leads to tumours in multiple body locations. Key roadblocks in finding new treatments for LAM include the inability to grow and study LAM cells from patients, and a poor understanding of how loss of TSC2 gene function contribute to their cancer-like properties. In pilot studies, we identified the hormone 'urotensin' as a potential target for therapy that is particularly active in LAM cells. At the same time, we used stem cell technology to engineer a 'test tube' model that closely resembles LAM cells from patients, and that can be used to discover potential therapies. In Part 1 of this project, we will to use these LAM-like cells to understand the cellular mechanism(s) by which urotensin activity is altered in LAM cells, and how urotensin contributes to their cancer-like properties. Once these patients become resistant to treatment, very few options are available to them. It is generally believed that resistance to drug treatment in leukemia patients is acquired through a process that entails the progressive modification of leukemic cells such that they acquire novel properties allowing them to escape drug treatment. However, the mechanism(s) through which leukemic cells acquire resistance while being subjected to drug treatment is unclear. In this application, we propose to fully characterize the mechanism through which OGT mediates resistance. For this purpose, we will use a variety of molecular and cellular techniques as well as unique in vivo models of disease. Successful completion of this proposal is expected to identify new therapeutic targets that could be used to prevent and/or treat relapse in leukemia patients.

column36: Characterization of HR-Killer1 and identification of small molecules for cancer therapy and enhanced gene editing using CRISPR/Cas9-based DNA repair strategies
column37: Inherited diseases arise from mutations in our genes, and similarly genetic mutations underlie the development of a variety of cancers. These mutations arise from DNA damage that is repaired incorrectly in our cells, and ironically radiation or drugs that damage DNA are the most common form of cancer therapy. Thus, if you can manipulate DNA repair you can also enhance DNA damage in cancer cells as a means of therapy. In 2013, scientists discovered that you could efficiently edit DNA in human cells using a system from bacteria called CRISPR (clustered regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats). CRISPR represents a primitive immune system found in many species of bacteria, which provides them with the ability to "fight" viruses by cutting the viral DNA into pieces. This cutting activity is provided by the CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), which uses small guide RNAs (gRNAs) to pair with and target DNA molecules for cleavage. CRISPR/Cas9 can be applied to genome editing by using the DNA cutting activity to repair damaged genes, or to insert new genes; and for this advance, CRISPR/Cas9 was named "Breakthrough of the Year" by Science Magazine in 2015. Using a novel assay based on CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing we have identified a new small molecule inhibitor of DNA repair called HRK1, which we will characterize as a potential new cancer therapy. In addition, we have partnered with the Centre for Drug Research and Development (Vancouver B.C.) to screen for both enhancers and inhibitors of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing. Enhancers of CRISPR/Cas9 can be used to improve the efficiency of gene editing; whereas inhibitors will likely block DNA repair, and thus can be used to sensitize cancers to radiation and chemotherapy. Ultimately, the compounds we identify and characterize will provide new therapeutics for cancer and agents to enhance the efficiency of gene therapy.

column37: In 2018, Canada will become only the second country to legalize recreational cannabis use. A cohort of youth and young adults (aged 16 to 30) will be recruited at 'baseline'- prior to the implementation of legalization in Canada- and at 12-, 24-, and 36-month 'post-implementation'. Representative samples will be recruited from each of three study conditions: Canada (n=10,000; 1,000 in each province), 'US Illegal' states (n=10,000), and 'US Legal' states (n=10,000). Analyses will examine national-level changes in Canada over time compared to 'US Legal' and 'US Illegal' states, as well as between provinces to examine differences in policy implementation. Overall, the proposed research will provide a rigorous design for evaluating the impact of national-level cannabis legislation in Canada using 'within-country' and 'between-country' controls over time. column36: The impact of lesion location on contralesional plasticity and its role in motor recovery after ischemic brain injury
column37: Stroke can damage different regions of the brain. After the injury, patients often suffer the loss of functions of the hand. Time and rehabilitation can provide some recovery of function but it is usually incomplete. Better treatments are necessary, but to achieve this we need to understand the mechanisms involved in recovery. Some imaging studies report that after a stroke, the unaffected regions of the brain change their activity during recovery. This suggests that these spared areas could be involved in recovery. However, the way they can do so remains unclear. This is particularly a problem for the areas in the hemisphere opposite to the lesion, the contralesional hemisphere. Some studies suggest that this hemisphere helps the recovery while others show it hinders recovery, and this appears to be influenced by the location of the lesion. The broad goal of our project is to understand how lesion location affects changes in contralesional areas and, as a result, the role these areas undertake in recovery. To address these questions, we use monkeys because their motor areas are similar to the ones in humans. In different groups of animals, we will provoke lesions similar in sizes but destroying progressively more brain regions involved in the control of hand movements. During the recovery, we will record the activity of the neurons in the contralesional hemisphere and study how it changes. After the animal has completed its spontaneous recovery (without any treatment), we will use drugs to inactivate each contralesional area. This will reveal the new role the contralesional areas undertook for recovery of the paretic hand after different types of lesion. Finally, we will inject anatomical tracers and study the rewiring of connections of the contralesional areas. Our experiments will greatly increase our understanding of the mechanisms that allow contralesional areas to take a good or bad role in recovery and how the location of lesion affects these processes

column36: Investigating the contribution of Shank3 in Alzheimer's disease
column37: More than 740,000 Canadians are living with Alzheimer disease (AD) or related dementia, a number expected to double by 2031. Compared to other prevalent diseases, the absence of effective treatments for AD is shocking. It is of prime importance for AD patients, their loved ones and the society as a whole, that we rapidly develop new therapeutic strategies. To achieve that aim, the identification of new relevant drug targets is the key. My laboratory has always been trying to understand why neurons fail to communicate in AD and whether it is caused by loss of proteins located in "synapses", where neurons interconnect with each other. My specific interest in one of those synapse proteins, Shank3, started when I learned 5 years ago that the child of one of my close friend had mental retardation due to a lack of this protein. I could witness with my own eyes the consequence of a loss of 50% of this protein on a child's capacity to learn and memorize. If lacking Shank3 has such an effect on a child, could it do the same in AD? We then found that there is almost 50% less Shank3 in the brain of AD patients. Since we know that children born missing 50% of the gene coding for Shank3 display extensive cognitive impairments, it seems likely that a comparable loss of Shank3 protein in AD may contribute to symptoms. To test that hypothesis, we thus propose to determine whether the consequences of shutting down half of Shank3 in animal models leads to signs and symptoms similar to AD. In summary, the proposed experiments in animal models will establish whether (i) Shank3 deactivation causes or aggravates behavioral, functional and biochemical markers of AD, (ii) it is possible with 3 selected treatments to reverse the deleterious effects of a Shank3 loss. The ultimate goal is to find out whether Shank3 could be a suitable target to develop new treatments for AD.

We have used a strategy that focuses on the French Canadians of Quebec, a study population known for its contribution to medical genetics. This proposal describes our strategy for identifying and characterizing our most promising candidate genes. Understanding the role of new cancer risk genes to hereditary ovarian cancer will advance knowledge of its causation. Also, such genes have the strongest potential as genetic biomarkers that could be useful for developing ovarian cancer prevention and management strategies. In the long-term our research has the potential to impact policies for medical genetic testing for identifying women at increased risk for ovarian cancer for which the overall survival is less than 30% and where few treatment options are currently available.

column37: Accurate detection and diagnosis of breast cancer remains a major problem in today's society. Even when something suspicious is diagnosed and breast surgery is decided upon, the success of surgery depends on the doctor's ability to accurately identify (and remove!) all cancer regions within the surrounding healthy breast tissue. Unfortunately, some tumor is often left behind (as it does not look very different from healthy tissue), and surgery must be repeated at a later time. A promising new method to definitively address this issue uses a technique called mass spectrometry (MS). It is very sensitive and accurate at distinguishing tumors, but also slow. Here we propose to use polarized light imaging ("polarimetry") to get a rapid overview of the exposed breast tissue, identifying potential cancer regions that will benefit from targeted MS diagnosis. Polarimetry is indeed well suited for this task -- it is fast, robust, able to image large tissue regions, and yields useful information for directing MS. The unique combined polarimetry-guided MS instrument will draw upon the strengths of the two technologies and should prove useful as a rapid, accurate and practical method to improve the success of breast cancer surgery.

column37: Narcolepsy is a disorder characterized by excessive sleepiness: patients fall asleep during the day without being able to resist the urge to sleep. Narcolepsy is often accompanied by sudden episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotions and termed cataplexy. Research in the past decade demonstrated that daytime sleepiness in narcoleptic patients who present cataplexy is related to a lack of a substance in the brain called hypocretin. However, some patients with narcolepsy never experience episodes of cataplexy. Furthermore, other patients presenting daytime sleepiness and no cataplexy closely resemble narcoleptic patients, but they tend to sleep for longer durations during the night and during daytime naps, without feeling refreshed after naps. This disorder is called idiopathic hypersomnia. No consistent lack of hypocretin has been observed in narcolepsy without cataplexy and idiopathic hypersomnia, and the brain abnormalities responsible for sleepiness in these disorders are poorly understood. This lack of knowledge considerably limits the possibility of developing optimal treatments. In the absence of more effective interventions, many patients with idiopathic hypersomnia or narcolepsy are dramatically affected by severe daytime sleepiness, which causes threatening risks of accidents, and impairs productivity and quality of life. Our objective is to analyze complementary modalities of brain imaging in patients with narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia. This will allow us to identify brain regions and networks that are affected by these disorders, and will thus help us clarify the distinct brain mechanisms of daytime sleepiness in these different conditions. Understanding the brain regions and networks responsible for the disruption of daytime functioning in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia will be critical for developing new treatments, which will target the brain mechanisms specifically involved in each of these disabling disorders.

column36: Role of the insula in refractory epilepsy
column37: The insula, the fifth lobe of the brain, is a complex structure hidden by the frontal, temporal and parietal brain lobes. Despite important advances in the comprehension of frontal, temporal and parietal epilepsies, insular epilepsy remains to date a relatively neglected disease. Our group is among the few in the world to have expertise in the diagnosis and treatment of insular epilepsy. By systematically recording insular activity directly during epilepsy investigations, our group showed that a significant portion of patients suspected with other forms of epilepsy actually suffer from insular seizures. In addition, we showed that failure to recognize insular seizures can lead to wrong selection of surgical targets and dramatic epilepsy surgery failures. The main issue faced by clinicians is that they don't recognize or poorly understand insular epilepsy, thus they cannot diagnose it efficiently. In this proposal, we tackle this important challenge by addressing the following questions: 1) What are the clinical symptoms or combinations of symptoms the are highly suggestive of insular epilepsy? 2) What is the value of modern brain imaging techniques for detecting insular epilepsy, 3) How does the insula interact with other regions of the brain to generate seizures? 4) Do neural interactions between the insula and other brain regions bear predictive factors regarding the chances of success of epilepsy surgeries? Ultimately, we expect the knowledge gathered during the proposed research to bring the clinical management of insular epilepsy patients to the level reached for other forms of epilepsy. By providing clinicians with efficient tools for understanding and diagnosing insular epilepsy, in addition to uncovering new factors for insular epilepsy surgery success, better surgical outcomes will be achieved.

column37: The ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) is responsible for recycling damaged or excess cellular proteins, and plays a variety of critical roles in normal cellular physiology. Deregulation of the UPS has been implicated in many human diseases, including cancer, cachexia and Parkinson's disease. However, we still know surprisingly little about: (i) the stable binding partners and specific substrates of individual E3 ubiquitin ligases, the UPS components that target specific subsets of proteins for destruction; (ii) how E3 protein-protein interactions are altered in response to common disease-associated mutations, and; (iii) the linear amino acid motifs (or "degrons") recognized by individual human E3s. We now have the tools and technology to address all three of these questions. Here, I propose to conduct the first large-scale, integrated study of the 69 member human F-Box E3 ligase family.

column36: Functional crosstalk between TRPML3 and BK in autophagy induction and pathogen defense
column37: Bacterial infections are the most common medical conditions, resulting in considerable economic and public health burdens and substantially affect the life quality of afflicted individuals. Patients suffering from bacterial infections are commonly treated with antibiotics. However, these treatments can result in the development of antibiotic resistance. Therefore, alternative therapies are needed. Vertebrate cells use the cell-autonomous defense programs to monitor infection and to evoke counter responses. Autophagy, the self-eating process for balancing sources of energy at critical times in development and in response to nutrient stress, represents an important innate defense mechanism for control of intracellular pathogens. A common measure for clearing intracellular pathogens involves detection followed by sequestration of pathogen in the autophagosome, a de-novo-generated membrane-bound compartment, which is promptly shuttled to the endolysosome where pathogens are degraded. Because our preliminary data have suggested that two endolysosomal membrane ion channels, BK and TRPML3 regulate autophagosome formation, we hypothesize that TRPML3 and BK increase pathogen clearance by increasing autophagy. We also predict that chemicals promoting TRPML3 and BK activity may combat bacterial infection. To test the hypothesis, we have collaborated with multidisciplinary teams of medical specialists in the fields of autophagy and microbial pathogenesis. We have also collected substantial preliminary data, acquired experience with the proposed work and have been equipped with all the necessary knowledge, space, equipment, techniques and materials that allow us to complete the proposed work. We believe that our study will not only provide important information regarding the role of TRPML3 and BK in autophagy regulation, but also lead to new therapeutic strategies combating many bacterial infections, i.e. developing drugs targeting TRPML3 or BK.

column36: Novel interactive roles of cAMP/cGMP in synaptic plasticity, learning and memory
column37: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of learning and memory is essential for designing effective therapies for brain disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. The proposal aims to study the role of critical neuronal signals mediated by cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP (cAMP/cGMP). We will utilize our newly established techniques that allow for their rapid and independent manipulation by light. Brain synapses undergo long-lasting changes in the strength of communication known as synaptic plasticity, which is the accepted cellular mechanism for learning and memory. Signalling via cAMP and cGMP are deemed important for the process, yet, the detailed nature of their regulation at (e.g. time course, response size and interactions) remains obscure owing to a lack of precise methods and tools. To decipher the roles of cAMP/cGMP, I will apply our newly established technologies to light-dependently control their levels in a location-specific manner by the use of advanced microscopy and engineered light-sensitive proteins. Utilizing these technologies, we will reveal how cAMP and cGMP interact to control synaptic function, plasticity and cognitive performance. The proposed research and light-sensitive technologies will advance our knowledge of brain function and provide an in-depth understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying brain function in health and disease. The work is directly relevant to understanding and treating brain disorders that affect cognitive function, including Alzheimer's disease. The expected outcomes include the development of novel optical technologies and valuable tools to elucidate the role of signalling cascades in broad research fields. cAMP, cGMP and other signals to be studied are used by all cells in the body and hence the work has applications to a wide range of medical conditions. The new knowledge will form the basis for development of novel strategies for patients afflicted with devastating brain disorders.

column36: Regulation of T cell central tolerance by non-apoptotic mechanisms
column37: Protection against pathogen infections and cancers is provided by the immune system. However, the immune system is responsible for the development of autoimmunity in genetically susceptible individuals. A white blood cell type critical for both immune protection and induction of autoimmunity is the T cell. During their development, T cells undergo rigorous selection processes in the thymus in an attempt to enrich the body with protective T cells and limit the presence of potentially harmful T cells. Much attention has been focused on the physical removal of T cells that recognize one's own healthy cells during development through a cell death mechanism. However, it is becoming clear that the ability of T cells to recognize one's own cells results in the generation of T cell populations that can protect against damage. Furthermore, we have evidence that, as opposed to the physical elimination of potentially harmful T cells, functional inactivation of these T cells is a more potent way to prevent autoimmunity. We propose to investigate the important events that regulate the development of protective T cell populations and to determine the relative importance of, and key molecules involved in, the functional inactivation of potentially harmful T cells during their development. Information generated from our experiments will provide valuable information into how the body normally avoids autoimmunity and will also generate insight into treatment options and therapeutics for cancer immunotherapy, chronic infections and organ transplantation.

column36: Central nervous system mechanisms underlying the effects of exercise therapy on chronic low back pain .
column37: It is estimated that approximately 20% of the Canadian population is currently suffering from chronic pain. Amongst the different chronic pain syndromes, chronic low back pain (CLBP) is by far the most prevalent, and the one responsible for the most years lived with disability. Alas, we still have a limited understanding of the factors contributing to pain chronicity. Consequently, most current treatments only have modest effects on CLBP. However, in recent years, evidence has mounted to support the effectiveness of physical exercise as a treatment for CLBP. Unfortunately, we know very little of the physiological mechanisms underlying the impact of exercise therapy on CLBP. Indeed, because the backs of most CLBP patients (~85%) do not show any particular signs of pathology explaining the persistence of the pain, it has been proposed that CLBP may be principally maintained or amplified by the central nervous system (CNS, i.e. brain and spinal cord). The objective of the proposed project will therefore be to investigate the CNS mediators of the effects of exercise therapy on CLBP. More specifically, we hypothesize that physical exercise will reverse the stress-related central inflammation and hippocampal atrophy associated with CLBP. In order to test this hypothesis, 100 patients with CLBP and 100 age-matched controls will be tested before and after a 16-week long physical exercise intervention (3 x 1 hour of high intensity aerobic and muscular exercise per week). Blood draws will be taken to measure circulating levels of pro- and anti- inflammatory molecules, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) will be used to measure the volume and connectivity of several brain structures, including the hippocampus. Finally, half of the participants will start the study with a 16-week long period without exercise training in order to control for time and other non-specific effects of exercise therapy.

column36: Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a novel factor regulates hyperphagia and obesity associated with atypical antipsychotics
column37: Severe mental disorders such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder affect more than 2% of the Canadian population, especially youth. Atypical antipsychotics (AAPs) are the first-line medications for treating these diseases, while they are often associated with severe metabolic side-effects (insulin resistance and diabetes) and heart disease. Increasing evidence is accumulating that metabolic abnormalities play a crucial role in the development of heart disease. Thus, studying the molecular mechanisms through which AAPs induce metabolic dysfunction and their effects on heart metabolism are essential to understanding the development of heart disease following AAP treatment. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a pro-inflammatory factor, well known to be involved in inflammation and also to play a role in regulating metabolism. Our preliminary data indicate that schizophrenic patients following treatments of AAPs for 2 months have increased plasma MIF. MIF plays a crucial role in the development of metabolic dysfunction induced by a classical AAP, olanzapine. Thus, we will use olanzapine as a representative atypical drug to explore the possible mechanisms of MIF in AAP induced metabolic dysfunction. Our research will include multiple techniques related to basic medicine and molecular biology. I hope to develop a novel strategy to inhibit metabolic side effects and heart disease during atypical antipsychotic treatment. We believe that MIF inhibitors will improve the clinical psychiatric treatment with atypical antipsychotics. Based on the results of these experiments, in our future studies, we are planning to extend the use of MIF inhibitors to clinical practice by collaborating with Dr. Donghong Cui in Shanghai Mental Health Center, China. We would then explore the pharmaceutical possibility of making a combined MIF inhibitor and AAP therapy.

column37: The protection of the airway lining is extremely important since it is a single cell layer thick and its integrity allows for oxygen exchange. Immune responses to infectious microbes and to innocuous environmental agents like pollen have to be balanced to clear serious challenges yet not over react to harmless ones. This balance in immune responses depends on several immune mediators called "cytokines". Several cell types can make cytokines but one relatively new immune cell type called innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) have been found to play important roles in recovering from infections by initiating repair but are also capable of triggering allergic reactions that can lead to asthma. We work on a cytokine receptor molecule, CD127 or IL-7Ralpha that is a known surface protein on ILCs. We know it has diverse roles in other immune cells that display it but its unknown what its exact role in ILCs is. We will determine that using selective gene targeted mouse models, gene profiling and large immune profiling approaches in 2 models of airway diseases: asthma and influenza. We expect that this study will shed light on how CD127 signals direct ILC development and function and how this is changed in the diseases above. This will allow identification of better targets to treat such diseases.

column36: Discovery and development of VISTA antagonists that restore antitumor immunity
column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) represent a new class of typically antibody-based agents that restores the body's natural immune response directed at cancer cells. They do so by blocking signals, often sent by cancer cells to immune cells to dampen immune responses directed at them. ICIs thus allow for the release of tumor-directed immune responses. These blocking agents, namely anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibodies, have led to impressive clinical results in patients with advanced melanoma and lung cancer, particularly when combined together or with other established cancer therapies. However, these treatments only prolong patient survival in certain types of cancers. One key reason is that our immune system has evolved many checkpoints to control its responses directed at infections or to dampen them to avoid self-immunity. One key checkpoint pathway that works in parallel with PD-1 and PD-L1 involves a molecule called VISTA. We propose to develop VISTA inhibitors since the expression of this molecule has recently been shown to increase on both immune and cancer cells of prostate cancer patients that do not respond to anti-CTLA-4 therapy. This finding indicates that tumor cells are evading recognition from immune responses by de-activating immune cells such as T cells through their VISTA pathway. We propose to develop and test several classes of VISTA inhibitors that will work with approved ICIs to restore immunity towards tumors.

column36: What will it take to decrease the burden of the HIV and STI epidemics among MSM in British Columbia, Canada? A sexual network modeling analysis, combining syndemic theory, to evaluate the impact of behavioural and biomedical interventions for HIV and STI prevention
column37: Gay, bisexual, two-spirited and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are disproportionally affected by the HIV epidemic in high-resource countries. Since 2004, in British Columbia (BC), the proportion of new diagnoses among MSM have plateaued, while those of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), especially syphilis, have been rapidly increasing, consistent with a substantial level of condomless anal intercourse. Today, there are three powerful strategies available to prevent HIV infection among MSM, including: the use of condoms, treatment as prevention (TasP), and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). In this 5-year study, our key contribution will be to develop a new methodology to forecast the consequences and benefits of emerging programs and policies for HIV and STI prevention among MSM prior to their implementation. This methodology will provide a deep understanding of the heterogeneity in sexual practices within MSM networks over time, enabling a more accurate assessment of the impact of different interventions targeting these networks. The proposed analyses accounts for the role of key factors affecting HIV and STI transmission among MSM, including demographic (e.g., age, income level), psychosocial (e.g., substance abuse, history of partner violence, childhood sexual abuse), and health-related factors (e.g., health status). Our ability to confidentially link administrative databases of all people diagnosed with HIV and at risk of acquiring HIV in BC, and assess surveillance testing data, makes this one of the first interdisciplinary research studies of how co-occurring STIs and risk behaviour are fuelling the HIV epidemic within MSM sexual networks. Importantly, this study will provide highly relevant new information for decision makers to inform resource prioritization and policies as they address the future impact of HIV, STIs and utilization of healthcare resources by HIV infected MSM in BC, Canada and internationally.

column36: Role of HSP90-alpha in preserving immunoprivilege of allogenic mesenchymal stem cells in the ischemic heart
column37: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Canada. Unfortunately, there are no effective therapies available that can provide permanent solution to the problem. Identifying, new research approaches that can offer permanent therapies for this disease are needed. Patients with heart disease require constant long-term treatment and care. Therefore, it imposes a significant economic burden on Canadian healthcare system. The strategy of transplanting stem cells into damaged heart has emerged as a novel therapy for the treatment of heart disease as stem cells have the ability to transform into heart cells and replace dead cardiac cells. Bone marrow derived allogeneic (unrelated donor) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from young healthy donors have emerged as ideal candidates for cardiac repair, because these cells have the ability to suppress the host immune system and survive in the heart after transplantation. Moreover, there are no ethical issues involved with these cells. However, recent reviews of animal studies and initial clinical trials reported that allogeneic MSCs were rejected by host immune system that impaired the benefits of allogeneic MSCs mediated therapy. Therefore, understanding the cell signaling pathways that regulate transplanted stem cell survival/rejection in the heart will help in developing new therapeutic agents that could prevent stem cell rejection and enhance the benefits of stem cell therapy. The objectives of current proposal are to study the mechanisms of transplanted stem cell rejection and to find out the strategies to increase post-transplantation survival in the heart. The outcome of this research will help in interpreting the results of ongoing allogeneic mesenchymal stem cell based clinical trials, and to carefully design future trials. The long-term objectives of this research are directed toward improving the quality of life of patients with heart disease using stem cell therapy.

column36: HEARTBiT: A novel multi-marker blood test for management of acute cardiac allograft rejection
column37: Heart transplantation is a life saving therapy for people with end stage heart failure. Acute rejection, a process where the immune system recognizes the transplanted heart as foreign and mounts a response against it, remains a clinical problem despite improvements in immunosuppressive drugs. Acute rejection occurs in 20-30% of patients within the first 3 months post-transplant, and is currently detected by highly invasive heart tissue biopsies that happen 12-15 times in the first year post-transplant. Replacing the biopsy with a simple blood test is of utmost value to patients and will reduce healthcare costs. The goal of our project is to develop a new blood test to monitor heart transplant rejection. Advances in biotechnology have enabled simultaneous measurement of many molecules (e.g., proteins, nucleic acids) in blood, driving the development of new diagnostics. Our team is a leader in using computational tools to combine information from numerous biological molecules and clinical data to generate "biomarker panels" that are more powerful than existing diagnostic tests. Our sophisticated analytic methods has recently derived HEARTBiT, a promising test of acute rejection comprising 9 RNA biomarkers, from the measurement of 30,000 blood molecules in 150 Canadian heart transplant patients. Our objective is to study a custom-built HEARTBiT test in a setting and on a technology that enable clinical adoption. We will evaluate the new test on 400 new patients from 5 North American transplant centres. We will also track patients' HEARTBiT scores over time to help predict future rejection, and explore use of proteins and micoRNAs to improve HEARTBiT. Our work will provide the basis for a future clinical trial. The significance of this work rests in that it will provide a tool to identify acute cardiac rejection in a fast, accurate, cost-effective and minimally invasive manner, allowing for facile long-term monitoring and therapy tailoring for heart transplant patients.

column36: How does frailty influence the risk and expression of dementia in Alzheimer disease?
column37: Dementia is a clinical syndrome in which impaired memory and thinking interferes with a person's daily life. The most common cause of dementia is mixed Alzheimer disease (AD) / vascular dementia. AD can be diagnosed clinically when someone is alive and, after death, by brain autopsy. Even so, not everyone who meets the autopsy diagnostic criteria for AD actually has dementia in life. Despite some study, why this discrepancy exists is still unclear. We plan to address it by looking at how overall health affects brain function. To do this, we must measure health problems, which we quantify with a frailty index. The frailty index counts the number of health problems that an individual has accumulated. Frailty increases the risk for many age-related illnesses (including heart disease, hip fracture and dementia). Now we want to know if this helps explain why brain autopsy findings alone do not account for the clinical features of dementia. We hypothesize that the frailer a person is, even though it is more likely that they will have cognitive impairment, this will be less clearly related to their brain autopsy findings. We will use data from two large, community-based, autopsy series in older people (Chicago USA; Cambridge UK). The people in those studies generously agreed to have their memory and thinking tested every 1-2 years and to donate their brains after they had died. These extremely valuable studies are well suited to what we plan to do. Our research team includes physicians who study both dementia in people and AD in brains, as well as scientists skilled in data analysis. We have team members at varying levels of their careers, from PhD student to established professor. Understanding how frailty affects brain function can improve our understanding of how dementia arises, and how it can be treated and even prevented.

column36: Viral determinants of natural human cytomegalovirus transmission
column37: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection causes birth defects in >2 per 1,000 births worldwide. As such, a vaccine to prevent CMV infection is needed. Most people in the world acquire CMV during early childhood from CMV in breast milk, saliva or urine. Children are often infected with CMV by their mothers, but mothers are frequently also infected by children, and interrupting the cycle of transmission between mothers and children is the key to reducing the enormous global health burden from CMV. Our study will guide the development of a CMV vaccine by characterizing the specific viral variants and modes of transmission between mothers and children. We have shown that only one or very few individual viruses that are able to successfully establish infection, which we call transmitted/founder (T/F) viruses. We are able to capture CMV transmission events between mothers and children, and determine the precise time of infection. Because CMV is highly genetically variable, we can use next-generation sequencing (NGS) to distinguish viruses from different individuals, as well as between compartments (e.g., breast milk, saliva, or urine) in the same individual. Thus, we are able to determine the exact source of a CMV infection. We can also measure the number of viruses present, and sequence of the entire genome of T/F viruses that initiate CMV infection. We will enroll a prospective cohort of 100 pregnant Kenyan women and their children, and collect samples of breast milk, saliva, urine, and blood to measure CMV viral loads and sequence the T/F viruses that infect infants and mothers. Our project will be conducted in Nairobi, Kenya, where our team has worked for >20 years on maternal-child viral infections, and brings together experts in epidemiology, virology, genomics, and mathematical modeling. This work will be invaluable for defining optimal CMV vaccine targets and evaluating vaccine strategies to prevent the transmission and morbidity of CMV.

column36: Identification of therapeutic targets for pediatric acute megakaryoblastic leukemia
column37: In Canada, nearly one quarter of childhood cancers are leukemias. Encouragingly, many of these pediatric leukemias are now treatable with a variety of anti-cancer drugs. Nonetheless, leukemia still accounts for an alarming ~25% of cancer-related deaths in children. One of the most aggressive forms of leukemia is known as "acute megakaryoblastic leukemia" (abbreviated as AMKL), and the particular form of AMKL we are focusing on responds very poorly to current treatments. Indeed, 80% of afflicted children succumb to this type of AMKL within 5 years after diagnosis. In view of this shocking statistic, we have assembled a diverse team of investigators spanning fundamental science and clinical expertise with the common goal of identifying novel treatments for this aggressive and often fatal form of pediatric AMKL. Importantly, we have developed a unique way to study human AMKL in mice. Our team will exploit this new "mouse model" along with cancer cells taken from human patients and cutting edge scientific methods, to approach an important challenge in childhood leukemia research. The proposed studies have great potential to not only identify effective drugs for combating pediatric AMKL, but may also lead to new treatment options for other types of leukemia and blood disorders.

column36: Enhancing ovarian cancer immunogenicity by increasing antitumoral responses using engineered oncolytic vaccines
column37: Cancer immunotherapy is a revolutionary approach based on methods that stimulate the immune responses in our body to kill the cancer cells. Immune cells called cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) specifically recognize cancer cells to eliminate them. However, when a tumor is established, cancer cells use several mechanisms that dampen the immune system. Growing tumors establish an immunosuppressive microenvironment that renders CTLs dysfunctional. Tumors also escape from immune recognition by their ability to decrease the expression of proteins in their cell surface called major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I). In this project, we propose to combine different approaches in cancer immunotherapy to efficiently target and eliminate tumor cells. First, oncolytic virus (OV) are able to specifically replicate and kill tumor cells directly but also by stimulating CTL responses. Second, OV can be modified to make them express proteins that will empower immune cells sitting in the tumor niche. Using OV modified to express the proteins IL-15 and IL-21, tumor cells will produce a more supportive environment for CTLs to execute their killing capacities and generate a long-lasting protection against tumor cells. Third, MHC-I proteins can be increased on tumor cells by delivering NLRC5, a master protein that promotes the expression of MHC-I and other related proteins to increase tumor cell visibility towards CTLs. We have developed an infected cell vaccine (ICV) platform using tumor cells infected with the OV Maraba MG1 modified to express IL-15 and IL-21. The ICV-IL15+IL21 expressing NLRC5 will be used as a vaccine to stimulate the activation of antitumoral CTLs. Focusing on ovarian cancer, a cancer that is in dire need of more effective treatments, the combination of these three approaches should result in a treatment that generates robust CTL responses and stimulates the formation of memory that will confer long-lasting protection against relapse.

column36: Pannexin1 mediation of stroke recovery responses: Sex and sex steroid influences
column37: Pannexin 1 (Panx1) is a protein found in the membrane of various cell types, including neurons, to assist in the passage or communication of very small molecules. Ischemic injuries that deprive neurons of oxygen and glucose (e.g. stroke) can enhance the activity of Panx1 to promote cell death (apoptosis). Men and women often show differences in stroke severity to suggest a potential role for the gonadal steroid hormones, estradiol and testosterone. Because Panx1 can mediate apoptosis and inflammatory signaling responses in injured neurons, we reason that it may come to explain sex differences in stroke outcome responses. Indeed, in our brain stroke model we have evidence to show that either the loss of the Panx1 gene or its pharmacological blockade significantly reduce the amount of neuronal damage in female, but not in male mice. This striking difference underscores Panx1 as an important focal point for unmasking underlying gonadal hormone and cellular mechanisms mediating sexual dimorphisms in stroke severity, as we propose to examine in the current application. The findings of this grant promise to provide novel frameworks for sex- and age-dependent differences in stroke vulnerability and rescue.

column36: Development, evaluation and implementation of genetic clustering methods for the real-time molecular surveillance of HIV outbreaks
column37: Immediate access to combination antiretroviral therapy not only drastically reduces HIV-related morbidity and mortality in people living with HIV, but also has public health benefits because it significantly reduces transmission. The global effort to eradicate the HIV pandemic has thus turned to issues of implementation: e.g., to reach populations at the greatest risk of HIV transmission for focused deployment for HIV testing and prevention resources. A person's HIV population rapidly accumulates new mutations within months of infection to become genetically unique. This means that clusters of infectious that remain very genetically similar may indicate a recent outbreak of virus transmission. Because HIV sequences are already routinely collected as standard-of-care, these large treatment databases are perpetually accumulating at clinical and research centres around the world. There is now tremendous interest in making secondary use of these databases to support public health efforts by detecting transmission outbreaks in "near real-time". We were responsible for building the world's first real-time cluster monitoring system for the HIV treatment database in British Columbia, Canada. However, HIV genetic clustering methods have seldom been examined rigorously. We recently discovered that current methods are severely biased to detect "clusters of diagnosis" - populations who tend to be diagnosed sooner post-infection than others - and fail to detect the clusters of transmission intended to be foci for public health efforts. We propose to: (1) develop a fundamentally new approach to HIV genetic clustering that focuses on transmission rates; (2) evaluate clustering methods using detailed simulation models and the retrospective analysis of treatment databases, and; (3) develop an open-source implementation toolkit and evaluate knowledge translation issues in building real-time systems in Uganda and Malaysia.

column36: Modulating peri-ischemic neuronal hyperexcitability
column37: In the healthy brain, neuronal functioning depends on continual tuning of blood flow in proportion to the level of local neuronal activity. A blockage of a major artery during stroke results in a sharp decline in blood flow, killing the neurons and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. Despite the availability of treatments for clot dissolution in the acute and rehabilitation regimens in the chronic stage, most patients suffer significant long-term disabilities and up to a third are institutionalized. Development of more effective therapies is hindered by the uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes required for complete recovery. Recent evidence suggests that the activity of the neurons in the peri-infarct zone, the damaged but potentially salvageable brain region surrounding the site of stroke, greatly influences recovery. Using advanced imaging techniques in rats, we will monitor the function of peri-infarct neurons in the hours following stroke induction. We will inject the brains of these rats with viruses that carry specific membrane channels to allow us to modulate the activity of peri-infarct neurons non-invasively, by illuminating them with light of specific wavelength. These finely controlled experiments will allow us to determine activity levels of these neurons that minimize short- and long-term functional deficits. We will then attempt to achieve comparable activity profiles by tuning the dose of locally delivered novel anti-convulsant medication. These experiments will establish the ways by which brain functioning can be affected early post stroke so as to improve neuronal function. The insights gained will guide the development of next generation, non-invasive treatments that can be readily combined with current therapies to enhance recovery from ischemic stroke.

column36: Gestational exposure to chemicals related to hydraulic fracturing in Northeastern British Columbia, and their endocrine disrupting potential
column37: In 2016, we conducted a pilot study that evaluated exposure to environmental contaminants (toxicants) in 29 pregnant women living in Northeastern British Columbia. This region is characterized by intense natural gas exploitation by hydraulic fracturing known to release contaminants in the environment. We found that exposure to a toxic solvent (benzene) in these women was four times higher than in the Canadian population; in Indigenous women, exposure to this solvent was six times higher. Exposure to toxic heavy metals was also high. This is concerning because exposure to these contaminants during pregnancy could alter fetal development. column36: Targeting of a mobile genetic element into the genome using budding yeast as a model system
column37: Mobile genetic elements are regions of DNA that copy and paste themselves into a genome. More than half of the human genome is full of repetitive elements and movement of these elements can result in cancers as well as other disorders. The elements that move in the human genome are called retrotransposons. We use the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S. cerevisiae) and the Ty1 retrotransposon, which is present in 32 copies in the yeast genome, as a model system. The yeast Ty1 retrotransposon is similar in structure and life cycle to retroviruses such as the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1), which results in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Studies of the Ty1 retrotransposon have already been important for elucidating the fundamental mechanisms of how retrotransposons/retroviruses replicate and enter the genome. In this research proposal, we will study the precise mechanism of how the Ty1 retrotransposon is pasted into a specific region of the genome. The highly conserved Ty1 integrase protein is necessary for pasting the retrotransposon into the genome but needs the help of host cellular proteins to accomplish genome entry. We will uncover which host proteins interact with Ty1 integrase and how this interaction results in targeting to a region of the genome. Because Ty1 integrase is conserved with retroviral integrases, and many yeast proteins are conserved with mammalian proteins, the knowledge we gain from our research can be applied to human cells and ultimately health care. Our fundamental research using a model organism is critical for understanding how disruptions can occur in the human genome.

column36: Early intensive leg exercise to improve walking in children with spastic diplegia from encephalopathy of prematurity
column37: Children born prematurely are at risk of brain injury that can result in cerebral palsy, most often affecting the both legs. Current treatment is largely passive, including leg braces, repeated injection of a paralyzing agent (botulinum toxin) in muscles that are abnormally active, and surgery as deformities occur. Active, physical therapy for weak muscles is infrequent, occurring twice a month or less. Yet, recent work in mammals show that early brain injury can be alleviated by intensive exercise therapy, but only while the animal is very young. Building on our success with early, intensive therapy for children with perinatal (around birth) stroke, we will apply intensive therapy for the legs in children with cerebral palsy involving both legs. Children (8 mo - 3 yr old) will be randomly assigned to start treatment immediately or delay treatment for 6 months. The delay period controls for improvement without treatment. The children in the Delay Group will also receive the same treatment after the delay period. The therapy will be guided by physical therapists and centred on play. Measures will be taken before, during and after the delay and treatment periods. Measures will include clinical scores of motor development, proficiency of walking, participation at home, and physiological measures of motor and sensory function. All children will be followed until they turn 4 yr old, to determine if there are long term benefits. The cost-effectiveness of the intervention will be evaluated by a health economist. We anticipate that like the children with perinatal stroke, early intensive exercise will improve mobility, facilitate earlier and better walking, and that the effects will be enduring.

column36: Vitamin K as a positive modulator of cognition in cardiovascular disease: mechanistic studies of its vascular actions
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is highly prevalent amongst Canadians and represents an important risk factor for late-life cognitive impairment (i.e. learning, memory) and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease. Conditions such as atherosclerosis (ATX) and hypertension (HT) have been linked to arterial stiffness, alterations in cerebral blood flow, and decreased brain perfusion. Initially discovered for its role in blood coagulation, vitamin K (VK) has recently emerged as an important nutrient for vascular health and brain function. In the vasculature, VK is beneficial through the actions of proteins which act as calcium inhibitor. In brain, VK is widely present and participates in the activation of a number of proteins involved in blood flow, vessel integrity, and brain cell activity. Moreover, VK has been shown to modulate cognition in both animals and humans, notably during aging. In studies by our group, feeding rats a high VK diet throughout their lives was associated with better learning and memory functions in late-life. The overreaching goal of this proposal is to provide evidence for the beneficial effect of enhanced VK status on cognition in the context of CVD and characterize its mechanism of action. Our specific aim will be to determine, using two rodent models, the potential of VK to mitigate cognitive impairment through an amelioration of the vasculature, cerebral blood flow, brain oxygenation, and brain structure integrity. Animals will be fed various levels of dietary VK and will be investigated at different life stages. Experiments will include multidisciplinary approaches including imagery studies. The proposed studies will be amongst the very few to integrate state-of-the-art imaging technology to investigate the role of a nutrient in rodent brain, and will expand the importance of VK to the context of CVD. Importantly, they will help plan future intervention studies in this group of patients who could largely benefit from this nutrient.

column37: Gut diseases have a huge impact on the Canadian health care system cost. Indeed, Canada has among the highest rates of intestinal inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) in the world with approximately 233 thousands of people that were living with it in 2012. With the use of novel biological systems derived from mice and human tumours, we expect to discover the biological relevance of HNF4A interaction with WNT. This research will allow the discovery of alternative ways of improving therapeutically targeting strategies against gut diseases.

column36: Pharmacological chaperones that bind F508del-CFTR and their mechanisms of action
column37: Proteins are string-like molecules that play many vital roles in the human body. They are made up of about 20 different building blocks called amino acids, which are in a particular sequence that enables the string to fold up into its correct 3 dimensional structure. When the sequence is changed due to a genetic mutation, the protein may not fold up correctly and cause disease. Misfolded proteins are often mislocalized and degraded, but if they can reach their normal cellular location they are still functional. This is what happens in cystic fibrosis, in which the misfolded protein is called CFTR. Drugs that correct the localization and function of CFTR have been developed, but they provide only a small benefit for most patients and better drugs are needed. We have identified new compounds that bind directly to CFTR and correct it's trafficking, but to improve them we need to answer questions such as "Where do they bind? Do different drugs bind at different sites? How do they work to trigger correction? Which combination of these correctors gives the most therapeutic benefit? These questions will be addressed in this grant proposal with a view to developing better therapies for protein trafficking diseases.

column36: The Functional Improvement Trajectories After Surgery (FIT After Surgery) Study: A Multicentre Prospective Cohort Study to Evaluate the Incidence, Trajectories, Risk Factors, Impact and Healthcare Costs Related to Significant New Disability after Major Elective Surgery
column37: About 190 million people have surgery every year in developed countries. Many of them are older and have pre-existing health problems, such as heart disease. A good understanding of their risks with surgery is critical. Such information guides patients and healthcare teams on which operation is the best option, and helps identify people who need help to recover well after surgery. At present, doctors simply tell patients about their risks of death or complications within 30 days after surgery. This practice is problematic. Few patients (less than 3%) die shortly after surgery, but many more (30-40%) have major complications that lead to long-term health problems, such as heart disease or stroke. These problems can cause significant disability such that, even months afterwards, some patients can no longer take care of themselves, live in their own home, or work. Thus, understanding how often and why major disability occurs after surgery is important, especially since most people want to both survive surgery and function well. We will therefore conduct the FIT After Surgery Study to understand the risks, underlying reasons and impact of significant new disability in people who are aged 65 years or more, and having major surgery. The study will include 2000 patients having major surgery at 10 hospitals across Canada. Using special interviews and tests, participants will be followed for 1 year after surgery to find out if they develop a significant new disability. We will measure the risk and impact of significant new disability after surgery, and identify which types of patients, operations and complications are likely to lead to disability. Our study will help patients to make better-informed decisions about having surgery, and help identify patients needing help to recover after surgery. It will also identify which complications research and quality improvement must focus on. The FIT After Surgery study will thus improve the care of surgical patients worldwide.

column36: The influence of microglia on the developing hypothalamus
column37: The human hypothalamus is only about the size of an almond and yet, it is very important to our survival. Indeed, the hypothalamus is essential for regulating key physiologies such as when to eat, sleep, drink, reproduce, shiver, and even love. To control these physiologies, the hypothalamus acts as a thermostat, first by sensing cues and then eliciting a response via its many neurons. Interestingly, even during embryonic development, the hypothalamus is still responsive to its environment. Microglia are another type of sensing cell in the brain but instead of responding to external cues, microglia respond to internal ones. For example, microglia are tasked with detecting injury and trying to repair it, as well as identifying unnecessary debris (e.g., dying cells) and clearing them away. Recent studies are starting to show that microglia also influence fetal brain development. Our own work has demonstrated a unique role for microglia in the developing hypothalamus. We have discovered that microglia in the embryonic hypothalamus are particularly activated, clustering around a discrete niche of the dorsal third ventricle. We showed that hypothalamic microglia interact with progenitors and can influence normal developmental programs. Consistent with these findings, elimination of microglia during gestation caused newborn pups to be born obese, strongly supporting a role for microglia in hypothalamic development. From these data and others, we hypothesize that microglia communicate with hypothalamic RGCs to influence development, particularly tanycytes. In this proposal, we will test the intriguing notion that cells whose primary purpose is to sense insults (e.g., microglia) are used to establish the key brain region essential to sensing homeostatic cues throughout life.

column37: The adult brain contains several populations of neural stem cells. In addition to the "active" neural stem cells, which participate in processes such as learning and memory and ongoing replacement of cells in certain brain regions, there also appear to be several types of "quiescent" neural stem cells, whose biological functions remain poorly understood. We believe that these quiescent neural stem cells can be harnessed to enhance the brain's intrinsic self-repair capacity during neurodegenerative diseases and following injury. Our laboratory has recently developed an experimental strategy that allows us for the first time to directly study and manipulate one of the adult brain's quiescent neural stem cell populations. In this research proposal, we take advantage of this strategy to determine what the normal functions of these cells are, how their quiescence is controlled, and how they can be activated during normal aging and in Alzheimer's disease. Our experiments will be carried out using innovative and powerful animal models, which will provide us with fundamental new insights into how stem cells are regulated in the adult brain and can be re-activated under pathological conditions. It is our hope that this will accelerate the development of therapeutic approaches for using the brain's own stem cell system in order to promote brain health and repair.

column36: Randomized Controlled Trial of an Electronic Patient Decision Aid (PDA) for Antidepressant Medication Use in Pregnancy
column37: Major depressive disorder is a debilitating and often chronic mental illness that affects 1 in 5 women over the lifespan. When depression is not treated effectively during pregnancy, the mother's and her child's health is at risk. Antidepressant medications are a mainstay of treatment for women whose depression is severe, or not adequately responsive to psychotherapy. Yet, it is very hard to determine when risks for relapse/ongoing depression definitely outweigh the small, but still uncertain risks of antidepressants. So, treatment decisions regarding antidepressant use in pregnancy must be guided not only by evidence about harms and benefits, but also by: (1) how a woman values the potential benefits and harms of the treatment options; (2) which option she prefers; and (3) the extent to which she wants to be involved in the treatment decision. Women have significant difficulty making this decision, but want to be active in decision-making. We designed an interactive electronic PDA to help women with depression make decisions about whether or not to use antidepressant medication in pregnancy, and successfully pilot-tested it with women across Canada. We now propose a randomized controlled trial to determine the efficacy of the online PDA in women with depression who are pregnancy-planning or in the early stages of pregnancy and facing decisions about use of antidepressants in pregnancy. column37: Outbreaks of emerging viral diseases are increasing at an alarming rate and are a worldwide concern. A notable example of emerging viruses is the Ebola virus that causes severe hemorrhagic fevers in humans and non-human primates with lethality rates that can reach 90% and against which there is currently no antiviral therapy. The threat of unpredictable outbreaks emphasizes the need for the development of therapeutic drugs against Ebola virus. However, fundamental to developing new drugs is the elucidation of the different steps of the life cycle of the virus, such as the discovery of host proteins essential for infection that can be targeted to block virus spread. We have previously identified the receptor of the Ebola virus, the protein Niemann-Pick C1, which resides in late endocytic vesicles. This discovery allowed us to propose a model of infection by which the Ebola virus attaches to the cell surface, is internalized, and is trafficked to intracellular vesicles containing essential host factors such as the Ebola virus receptor triggering entry and delivery of the viral genetic material into the host cell. The requirement of multiple host proteins for viral entry offers several targets for pharmacological inhibition. A promising target includes a protein complex involved in the turnover of endosomal phosphoinositides. Genetic manipulation and chemical inhibition of the complex activity lead to efficient block in Ebola virus infection, suggesting that these proteins and endosomal phosphoinositides are critical for infection. Here, we propose to investigate their roles of in viral trafficking and entry using genetic and chemical biology approaches. The ultimate goal of the proposed research program is the development of urgently needed antiviral therapies against Ebola virus for Canadians and worldwide.

column37: Epilepsy is a serious neurological disorder. About 54,000 Canadians have seizures that cannot be controlled by anti-seizure drugs. In these cases, the only available strategy is removal of the brain area generating seizures, called the seizure onset zone. However, seizure cure is <50% due to incomplete identification and removal of this area. We will use an established technique called Computerized Tomography Perfusion (CTP) to better identify and remove the entire seizure onset zone and improve post-surgical outcome. In routine clinical practice, the seizure onset zone is located by electroencephalographic recordings of seizures or single photon emission computerized tomography measures of blood flow during a seizure. However, these techniques have limited spatial resolution or are very labour-intensive and costly. Recently, we showed that seizures are followed by highly significant post-seizure blood flow reductions at the seizure onset zone lasting up to 1 hour that can be precisely measured using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These exciting findings suggest that the area of post-seizure hypoperfusion may be a novel seizure onset zone marker and better target for epilepsy surgery. Measuring post-seizure blood in clinical practice is hampered by difficulty in obtaining MRI scans within 1 hr. We will therefore measure post-seizure blood flow reductions in 150 patients using CTP as CT scanners are rapidly accessible. We will determine if CTP can better detect the full extent of the seizure onset zone compared to conventional methods (Aim 1) and if it can better predict post-surgical freedom (Aim 2). Our project is directly applicable to health care as we will determine if post-seizure hypoperfusion can better identify the full extent of the seizure onset zone and predict post-surgical outcome. Our study will ultimately allow clinicians to use this measure to direct surgery and improve surgical cure rates since CT scanners are widely available across Canada.

column36: Exploring the role of environmental factors in neuronal aging
column37: Our bodies are inhabited by thousands of bacteria. These bacteria (collectively referred to as the microbiota) are not passive inhabitants, but instead play important roles in metabolism, development of the immune system, and protection against pathogens. In addition to these roles, alterations in the bacterial makeup of the microbiota have been observed in a number of diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases. However, these studies are correlative, demonstrating alterations in already diseased patients; they do not demonstrate a causal role in disease development and do not identify specific factors that contribute to disease. Further investigation is required to determine if, and how, alterations in the microbiota contribute to the development of these diseases. To this end, we are focusing on the potential role of microbiota in influencing neurodegeneration. Our goal is to identify possible interventions that will slow the decline in neuronal function that occurs with age. The development of treatments and interventions designed to target the microbiota requires the identification of specific bacterial factors that influence disease state and an understanding of how these factors work. To accomplish this, an experimental system is needed that allows alteration of the microbiota and where genetic differences between individuals does not exist. We use a small nematode (worm), C. elegans for this purpose. Using these animals, we are able to easily generate large populations (millions) of genetically identical animals for analysis. We will determine the influence of hundreds of bacterial strains isolated from humans, on neurodegeneration using C. elegans models of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases. Using the bacteria that differentially influence neurodegeneration, we will identify specific molecules produced by these bacteria and examine changes in the expression of genes that occur in response to these factors.

column36: Characterizing the pathophysiological roles of secretory microRNAs in multiple sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic brain disease with an unknown cause or cure. At present, the drugs used for treating MS patients target the immune system and have very little effect on preventing disease progression and neurodegeneration. While cells of the immune system play a significant role in MS, we must uncover novel strategies that both protect the brain and promote repair following injury. Such strategies would not only benefit MS, but other neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer's, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and ALS. MS is a highly complex disease that involves significant cross-talk between cells of the brain and immune system. Unfortunately, many of the drugs that selectively target molecules involved in this cross-talk are ineffective in most neuroinflammatory conditions, including MS. While these drugs are clinically effective for treating several other immune-mediated diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis, we now acknowledge that cell-to-cell communication is much more complex in the inflamed brain and requires further study. Our research focuses on a newly discovered method of cell-to-cell communication that occurs via exosomes, which are small enclosed biological structures that have been implicated in inflammation and neurodegeneration. Exosomes can be detected in all bodily fluids and may have the potential to be used as disease biomarkers and/or targets of drug therapy. In MS, we hypothesize that exosomes deliver molecules called microRNAs that help to mediate inflammation, neurodegeneration, and brain repair. This research will provide a detailed characterization of the microRNAs within exosomes and identify how they can directly impact key genes and biological pathways that are implicated in MS. In the future, the ability to alter microRNA profiles within exosomes may lead to an exciting therapeutic avenue to explore in MS and other brain diseases.

column37: North America's overdose crisis has significantly impacted British Columbia (BC), leading to the declaration of a public health emergency in 2016. Research has demonstrated that gendered power relations shape women's exposure to drug-related risks and harms. However, the relationship between gender and overdose remains poorly understood. Effective overdose-related interventions for highly-impacted subgroups of women (e.g., Indigenous women; transgender women) also must be informed by better understandings of the social experiences of women who use drugs. This 4-year study aims to generate evidence to strengthen interventions and strategies to decrease overdose-related harms, including death, among women who use drugs through an examination of the socio-structural forces shaping overdose risk, women's access to and experiences with overdose-related interventions, and the perspectives of drug-using women on potential strategies to improving overdose-related interventions and outcomes. Our innovative research aims to tackle key enduring knowledge gaps surrounding overdose-related risks and harms to women who use drugs, and to translate research evidence into practical improvements, informing the ethical delivery of effective policies, programs, and practices in BC, across North America and globally.

column36: Of Worm and Man: Using C. elegans to uncover genetic modifiers for rare human disorders
column37: High-throughput sequencing has accelerated the pace at which gene-disease associations are established. However, we need to start addressing the next challenge: why two individuals with the same rare disease-causing variant may have different clinical presentation of the disease? Genetic modifiers are factors that can either alleviate or exacerbate the severity of the disease-causing variants. Identification of such modifiers provides important information about the biological functions of human disease genes and mechanistic role they play in the development of the disease. This in turn allows for better disease outcome prediction, planned prevention protocols and development of targeted treatments. Complexity of human biology makes it difficult to address this challenge effectively; however, fundamental aspects of human disease had been in past and will be in future efficiently addressed through analysis of orthologous genes using experimentally tractable model organisms. The goal of my research is to combine powers of unbiased mutagen-induced modifier screens using Caenorhabditis elegans model and whole genome sequencing (WGS) in order to accelerate discovery of new disease-associated genes, modifiers of known disease-associated genes and potential Orphan drug targets. To reach these goals, I will: (1) isolate modifiers by performing forward genetic screens on orthologous genes implicated in human rare disorders; (2) identify molecular basis of modifiers using WGS, state-of-the-art bioinformatics and molecular genetics techniques, and (3) characterize the phenotypes and mode of action of the genetic modifiers. This research is of high importance as it will establish C. elegans as a model organism for systematic high-throughput heritable genetic modifier screens with high potential for direct impact on diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of rare diseases, in particular the ones with no treatment options (currently >95% of rare diseases).

column36: Regulation and impact of productive AID targeting during antibody responses.
column37: Antibodies are a major component of the human immune system. A large repertoire of specialized cells named B-lymphocytes, each producing a different antibody, are constantly renewed to be able to detect any of innumerable and constantly evolving pathogens. The initial recognition of a pathogen, by the antibody on the surface of a B-lymphocyte, signals the onset of changes in the genes encoding the antibody, which will allow improving its affinity and effectivity to eliminate the infection. Most vaccination strategies rely on stimulating the B-lymphocytes that produce antibodies against known pathogens so that they expand and undergo the AID-mediated antibody improvements before any exposure to the actual pathogen. The genetic mechanisms that shape the antibodies and mediate immunity are initiated by an enzyme named AID. As a side effect of changing the antibody genes, AID can also cause collateral genetic damage. This can predispose to cancer or negatively affect the B-lymphocyte's ability to multiply, which is critical for the process of generating a protective response. column36: Practice patterns among early-career primary care physicians and workforce planning implications: a mixed methods study
column37: There are more family doctors in Canada then ever. Yet, patients still have trouble finding a family doctor and getting an appointment when they need one. Changes in how much family doctors work and what services they provide (for example, choosing to practice with a clinical specialty, in a walk-in clinic, or providing care in hospital, rather than traditional family medicine), may help explain the gap between the number of doctors and patient access to primary care. It is widely speculated that new primary care doctors are practicing differently than previous generations. We know there have always been differences between doctors starting their careers and those who are already established, but we do not know if these differences are actually growing. This project will use information from qualitative interviews with doctors, surveys of doctors, and data routinely collected as part of health care delivery in British Columbia, Ontario, and Nova Scotia to achieve several related objectives. First, we will use survey data and interviews to explore plans for practice among doctors training in family medicine and the choices they make as they start out in practice. We want to understand what values and preferences, including the type work, lifestyle, and financial considerations, shape plans and choices. Second, we will use health care data to compare practice patterns among new and established doctors. We will determine if any changes over time are unique to the most recent generation of family doctors, or if there have been changes over time across all family doctors. Finally, we will examine how opportunities available to doctors in each province align with their preferences. We will reach out to doctors and policymakers to explore what other opportunities might be chosen, if available, and consider what policy changes may be needed to make sure that patients can access the services they need.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases are the number one killer in Canada. The current therapy for preventing and treating atherosclerosis (stiffening and blocking of arteries) uses statins to reduce levels of LDL (bad) cholesterol in the blood. Given that more than 50,000 strokes and 75,000 heart attacks occur in Canada every year, the need for new cardiovascular therapies is clear and urgent. Recently, we found that the protein MMP14 reduces the levels of a protein called the LDL receptor that is critical for clearing LDL cholesterol from the blood. Blocking the action of MMP14 increases levels of the LDL receptor and reduces LDL cholesterol in blood. In this project we will characterize MMP14 and determine how it works when it reduces levels of the LDL receptor. This basic knowledge will open up new opportunities for blocking MMP14 and reducing LDL cholesterol in blood.
