column36: Molecular Basis of Quebec Platelet Disorder
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that help control bleeding. Our team is studying an inherited disorder called Quebec platelet disorder (QPD) that alters platelets and causes serious bleeding. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD including its genetic cause. In Canada, about 1:200,000 Quebecers has QPD and each person with QPD has a 50:50 chance of passing on QPD each of their children. QPD causes bleeding because it increases a clot busting enzyme called urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA). Persons with QPD have very high levels of uPA in platelets but not in other cells - we are trying to find out why. QPD is caused by a "duplication mutation" which means that a person with QPD an extra copy of the uPA gene and nearby DNA. In QPD cells that make platelets, uPA production is >100 times normal, which is far more than expected for having one extra uPA gene. Additionally, the overproduction of uPA occurs only in QPD cells that make platelets. We explored why and found that QPD duplicates a gene enhancer ("turn on switch") for vinculin (the next gene) - this switch is active only in cells that make platelets. QPD puts the extra copy of this switch right front of the uPA gene. We suspect this is why the gene for uPA becomes turned on too much in QPD cells that make platelets. We will use special methods, including "chromatic conformation capture methods" to test this "swtich" and if it is the reason that the uPA gene in is switched on in QPD cells that make platelets. We will also use special methods to alter genes to test if we can correct the problem in QPD cells that make platelets. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD. We have exciting new information and the technical skills that are needed to study what causes QPD. The study will give us important new information on how genes are controlled when the body makes platelets and how this is changed by QPD. The study will give us new insights on what causes platelet disorders

column36: A novel role for the breast cancer 1 protein (BRCA1) in prenatal protection against oxidative DNA damage, embryotoxicity and abnormal postnatal brain function
column37: The breast cancer 1 (BRCA1) protein is known to protect against breast cancer. However, we have discovered that during pregnancy BRCA1 also protects fetal mice from DNA damage that can cause birth defects and disorders in brain function after birth. The DNA damage is caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are normal forms of activated oxygen essential for fetal development. However, when the fetus lacks proteins like BRCA1 that prevent and repair DNA damage, or when ROS production is enhanced by drugs like alcohol (ethanol, EtOH), the damage accumulates and causes abnormal fetal development. The developmental disorders in BRCA1-deficient mice may be relevant to children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), and the exacerbated disorders with fetal EtOH exposure may be relevant to children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). To elucidate the role of BRCA1 in these disorders, we have developed a genetically altered mouse model lacking only 1 of their 2 copies (+/-) of the Brca1 gene, with a small decrease in BRCA1 protein. The progeny exhibit increased DNA damage and postnatal learning and memory deficits, which are worsened by a single low-level fetal EtOH exposure. We will use this mouse model to determine how both normal and EtOH-enhanced ROS levels and prenatal DNA damage cause birth defects and postnatal behavioural differences, and how BRCA1 protects the fetus from DNA damage. Our studies will establish a biological role for BRCA1 beyond cancer, in protecting the developing fetus from normal and chemically-enhanced ROS levels. This developmentally protective role of BRCA1 is likely important, since both copies of the Brca1 gene must be lost to increase the risk of cancer, whereas the loss of only 1 copy increases the risk of developmental disorders. Our results may identify new mechanisms and risk factors relevant to ASD and FASD, which could help in developing novel predictive and therapeutic strategies for high-risk pregnancies.

column36: Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT): A pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial of a gender-sensitized weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for men who are overweight or obese
column37: About 40% of Canadian men are overweight and another 20% are obese. Approximately 70% of men's staggering health care costs (estimated at $36.9 billion annually) could be prevented if men improved their lifestyles (i.e., got active, ate better, and lost weight); however, few men engage in lifestyle change. The apparent reluctance of men to engage in healthy lifestyle programs may reflect the fact that men with excess weight tend to be less aware or concerned than women about their overweight status. Research has shown that programs situated in a sporting context, where men have a strong sense of affiliation as a fan, are effective and lead to high satisfaction among men. Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT) is adapted from Football Fans in Training and our own HealtheSteps lifestyle prescription program. Hockey FIT is a 12-month (3-month active phase and 9-month maintenance phase) weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for middle-aged, overweight/obese male hockey fans, delivered by trained coaches in collaboration with teams in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL). Across the CHL, there are 52 teams spanning small to large urban centres, located throughout Canada. In the proposed study, 32 sites (affiliated with major junior hockey teams and local YMCA facilities) will be randomly assigned to either the intervention (Hockey FIT program) or comparator (wait-list control). At each site, 40 male hockey fans at-risk for chronic diseases will be recruited to take part in the study. Sites assigned to the comparator will offer the Hockey FIT program to their enrolled male hockey fans after 12 months. Through the Hockey FIT program, our study aims to promote weight loss, increase physical activity levels, and improve other health measures through a cost-effective solution that is acceptable and appealing to men who are overweight or obese. Indeed, findings from our pilot study indicate that Hockey FIT has the potential to achieve these goals.

column36: The effects of reward cues on risky decision making: the role of dopamine and relevance to addiction
column37: In addicted people, exposure to things like drug paraphernalia (known as contextual cues) is believed to trigger cravings, drug use and relapse. Exactly how cues promote such outcomes remains poorly understood. One possibility is that cues influence decision-making and tip the scales in favor of the maladaptive addictive behaviour, making it seem more appealing and worthwhile. Our work in both rats and humans suggests that adding sensory reward cues - similar to the lights and sounds in gambling settings - results in riskier and more disadvantageous choice on gambling-like task. In rats, these effects of cues are dependent on the neurotransmitter dopamine. Our goals are: 1) to study whether problem gamblers are particularly susceptible to risk-promoting effects of sensory reward cues - which are abundant in gambling settings; 2) investigate whether dopamine contributes to cue-driven risky choice in healthy humans and problem gamblers, and dopamine system's responsiveness to cues might be associated with problem gambling. To address these aims, we will use positron emission tomography to look at dopamine levels during decision-making in the presence versus in the absence of sensory reward cues. We will do this in a group of healthy participants and a group of problem gamblers. We expect to find that decisions of problem gamblers will be more influenced by cues than those of healthy participants. We also expect that the presence of cues will result in greater elevation in dopamine levels for problem gamblers than healthy controls.

column36: Understanding molecular control of lipid metabolism in brain aging
column37: While perturbed lipid metabolism has been implicated as a risk factor for aging-related neurological degeneration, it remains unknown how the perturbed lipid metabolism arises during the aging process. Importantly, bioactive lipids have been shown as controllers to regulate neural stem cell function that plays an essential role in learning and memory by producing adult-born neurons. To this end, we are interested in understanding molecular mechanisms that control lipid metabolism to regulate neural stem cell function in the context of aging brain with the long term goal of identifying the molecular target for drug discovery to treat aging-associated cognitive decline. Recently, we discovered a signaling-induced molecular pathway that is required to maintain homeostatic neurogenesis and new memory formation during normal aging. This molecular pathway involves the direct phosphorylation of CBP, a histone acetyltransferase, by atypical protein kinase C (aPKC). We recently identified that monoacylglycerol lipase (Mgll), an enzyme that converts endocannabinoid (2-AG) into arachidonic acid, is a downstream target of the aPKC-CBP pathway. Importantly, we observe that the attenuation of the aPKC-CBP pathway causes upregulation of Mgll expression occurring in both normal and Alzheimer's Disease aging brain of animal models. Thus, we hypothesize that deregulation of the aPKC-CBP pathway in brain aging impairs lipid composition and adult neurogenesis that culminate in the cognitive decline, a phenotype associated with brain aging. Together, our experiments will provide important new information regarding regulation of lipid metabolism and provide fundamental knowledge towards the development of therapeutic strategies fighting against the aging process.

column37: Functional connections between nerve cells (called synapses) are essential to establish the architecture of the nervous system. The modification of synapses is thought to be one of the mechanisms by which learning and memory occur. It has been known for decades that cannabis consumption has a profound influence on learning and memory and that maternal marijuana smoking during perinatal period causes cognitive and social deficits that last in the adulthood of the offspring. For the moment, we do not know if these effects are mediated by the classic CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors or by other receptors such as the GPR55. Therefore, the main objective of this project is to identify the contribution and the mechanisms by which GPR55, and its ligands modulate the synapse number. The identification of a fundamental molecular mechanism regulating the connections between nerve cells will provide important insight into normal brain function and learning process. Furthermore, it will probably permit the discovery of new pharmacological targets and the development of innovative therapeutic strategies aiming at treating congenital or neurodegenerative diseases. This project is timely because Canadians are among the highest consumers of cannabis in the World and its consumption might be on the rise when it will be legalized in 2018. Moreover, the GPR55 system is the target of several compounds in the pipelines of pharmaceutical companies (Sativex(THC+CBD), Epidiolex, and GWP42003(CBD)). column37: 'To approach, or not to approach?' Many situations in life induce a state of motivational conflict in us as to whether we should approach a seemingly attractive proposition or stimulus (e.g.,highly calorific chocolate cake), or whether we should avoid the very same stimulus as it may have negative consequences (e.g, weight gain). Very little is known about how the mammalian brain regulates this fundamental process of decision making that can potentially go awry in psychological disorders such as addiction, in which the 'approach' tendency takes predominant control, and others such anxiety, which involve heightened 'avoidance' tendencies. Using both rodent and human subjects, the proposed project will provide evidence that the hippocampus, a brain region more known for its importance in mnemonic processes, and its connection with other areas in the brain that are known to be important in motivational processes, comprise neural circuits that is crucial in approach-avoidance conflict resolution. This will offer a new perspective on the role of the hippocampus in decision-making processes, a capacity that is currently thought to be predominantly mediated by the medial prefrontal cortex. Furthering our understanding of the neural basis of approach avoidance conflict resolution, and the identification of differential neural pathways for the control of approach/avoidance behaviour has the potential to create new therapeutic avenues for psychological disorders in which 'approach' or 'avoidance' tendencies are aberrantly dominant.

column36: Development of Viral Sensitizing Antibody Drug Conjugate and Oncolytic virus Combination Regimens for the Treatment of Breast Cancer
column37: Oncolytic viruses are safe viruses engineered to specifically infect and kill cancer cells, and can also stimulate the immune system to recognize tumors. Although they have the potential to treat a broad range of malignancies, the inconsistency of treatment response remains a major challenge and poor infection of tumors is a recognized issue. We have pioneered the development of small molecules that we termed "viral sensitizers" that are able to sensitize tumors to viral infection and potentiate the activity of oncolytic viruses. However, for these molecules to act at maximum efficacy, they currently need to be injected directly into the tumor, which is often not possible. column37: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a devastating genetic disorder of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. The gene most commonly involved in RP is rhodopsin, which produces a protein that detects light. There are large quantities of rhodopsin protein in the light-sensitive rod photoreceptor cells of the retina. Mutations in the rhodopsin gene result in death of rods. However, it is unclear how rhodopsin mutations kill rods. It is proposed that because rods make so much rhodopsin, even subtle rhodopsin defects can result in drastic consequences. We pioneered the use of genetically modified Xenopus laevis frog tadpoles to study this problem. It is easy to make numerous types of genetic changes (e.g., different disease-causing mutations) in this animal to reproduce and compare different forms of the disease. We demonstrated that there are different types of rhodopsin mutations that kill rods in various ways. Two of these ways kill rods faster if the animals are exposed to light. Although the two light-exacerbated mechanisms are caused by mutations in the same gene, and although to an ophthalmologist, patients with these mutations appear to have the same disease, we find that these are actually two very distinct forms of RP that respond differently to treatment. In fact, certain treatments that benefit one form of RP actually worsen the other form. This has important implications for patient treatment: genetic testing will be necessary to test treatments and establish which treatments to use. We propose experiments that will help us understand how these mutations kill rod cells and key ways these mechanisms differ. Our new knowledge of the underlying cell death mechanisms, the unique genetic aspects of the system, and technical advances in manipulating the X. laevis genome will be of value to the scientific community and patients who suffer from RP.

column37: Retinal degenerative diseases are genetic disorders of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. Retinitis pigmentosa is a disorder causing death of rod photoreceptors, while other retinal degenerations affect both rods and cones, or primarily cones. Rods and cones are the light sensitive cells of the retina. They are named for the shapes of their light sensitive outer segment organelles, which are modified non-motile cilia. The outer segments contain a highly organized stack of non-contiguous (rods) or contiguous (cones) disk-shaped membranes that contain very high concentrations of the G-protein coupled receptor rhodopsin. The exact mechanism by which these disks form is unclear. However, it is clear that defects in biosynthesis of both the disks themselves, and disk components such as rhodopsin, are responsible for inherited human retinal disease. Disk biosynthesis is proposed to involve the proteins prcad-21 and prominin-1 which form a complex that may be involved in a step such as disk evagination or sealing. We propose to examine the roles of prcad-21 and prominin-1 in disk formation using X. laevis and D. Rerio (frog and fish) knockout animal models, in combination with our newly developed assays for disk membrane synthesis. We will also use transgenic and knockout X. laevis and novel transgene tools to examine the biosynthesis and quality control of the disk component rhodopsin, including the role rhodopsin codon usage in biosynthesis, the roles of different degradation pathways in rhodopsin quality control, and roles of glycosylation and chromophore binding on regulating pathway use.

column36: How Approaches to Care Shape the Pathways of Older Adult Home Care Clients
column37: Home care is increasingly looked to as a means of strengthening the healthcare system by addressing wait lists for residential long term care and supporting older adults to age in place. Although provincial home care policies claim a commitment to "client-centered" approaches to care, there is variation in who delivers home care services, what services are available and for how long, and what the supports are for family/friend caregivers. Regional differences in approaches to care make it difficult to assess the appropriateness of the goals of home care policies, and know if everything is being done that could be done to support clients, caregivers, home support workers and the system in achieving the best possible outcomes. Our multi-method project analyzes how approaches to care shape client pathways within, and potentially out of, the home care system in 2 provinces with similar population size but different service delivery models (Nova Scotia and Manitoba). Our overarching research question is: How do approaches to care shape older adult home care client pathways through the home care system? We will construct typical scenarios of a person's movement over time, by analyzing client data between 2011-2017. We will then interview care groups of clients, caregivers, and care providers at 3 points in time in an 18 month period to understand individual experiences. To gain a systems level understanding, we will examine how regional policies organize approaches to care by analyzing interviews with policy makers and sector representatives, and policy and practice documents. This will create research evidence that can be used to improve home care clients' experiences, and inform care practices, while taking into account individual, provider and system perspectives. We will work with our partners and knowledge users to develop workshops and webinars to share our findings and to support informed decision making at all levels of care.

column37: Asthma is the most common chronic respiratory disease, characterized by inflammation in the lungs and narrowing of the airways, which makes it difficult to breathe. Nearly 3 million Canadians suffer from asthma. The direct and indirect cost related to asthma in Canada is around $2.2 billion annually. Nearly 10% of patients do not respond to available steroid therapies and have severe uncontrolled asthma. These patients represent the major burden of asthma and associated healthcare costs. Moreover, commonly used steroid therapies can increase the risk of lung infections, which results in worsening of asthma. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new therapies that can control asthma, without compromising a patient's ability to resolve infections. This study focuses on new molecules known as innate defence regulator (IDR) peptides, which are designed from natural molecules that play a critical role in the immune response. IDR peptides can control both inflammation and infection in the lung, with the potential to overcome side effects associated with current therapies. We have shown that IDR peptides improve breathing capacity in an animal model of asthma, and can control cellular processes linked to steroid unresponsiveness. This project is aimed at the development of IDR peptides as a new therapy for asthma. In this project, we will identify the changes that occur in lung cells after they are treated with IDR peptides. We will also study the biological effects of IDR peptides in the control of lung inflammation and fibrosis, in a mouse model of asthma. The results from these studies will allow us to identify new drug targets with the potential to alleviate unresponsiveness to steroid therapies, a condition for which there is currently no effective treatment. This project will directly support the development of a new IDR peptide-based therapy for asthma, which will have the added benefit of countering steroid-refractory asthma and controlling lung infections

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disorder that results in degeneration of the brain which leads to severe memory impairments. This is a devastating disease producing personal and societal costs that are immeasurable and growing as the "baby boomers" age. The common and central feature of AD is amyloid deposition, of which the major component is the amyloid beta peptide (Abeta). As new clinical trials focus on the initial stages of the disease, early diagnosis is now more important than ever. There is growing evidence from human neuroimaging that the preclinical stage of AD is associated with profound functional alterations of specific brain network. Recent studies using transgenic mice model of AD have shown that some brain cells become highly active in the early stages of AD when the animal exhibit normal learning and memory. In the later stages of AD, neurons become less active with an accompanying decline in animals cognitive abilities. Although the relationship between altered neuronal activity, neural network abnormalities and the behavioral consequences are less known, it is fundamentally important to understand these early brain changes as they provide a target for therapeutic interventions early in the progression of the disease before significant and irreversible brain damage occurs. In particular, this work will provide new understanding of how pathogenic forms of Abeta contribute to neuronal activity and network dysfunction and behavioral & cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease. Our hypothesis is that cellular hyperactivity in the early stages of AD is a key driver of changes in the brain that ultimately lead to the descent into dementia. The proposed work will provide evidence of where in the brain and when these changes occur, the cause of these brain changes, and a target for treatments that could halt or slow devastating effects of AD from occurring.

column36: Does traffic-related air pollution reduce the effectiveness of corticosteroids in asthma treatment?
column37: We are all routinely exposed to air pollution derived from transport and power generation, or occupationally in industries that underpin the Canadian economy (forestry, mining, oil & gas), with many Canadians exposed to unacceptable levels. The Government of Canada notes "air pollution costs Canadians and the Canadian economy billions of dollars per year". Much of these costs derive from pollution-induced worsening of respiratory diseases, including asthma (which affects 1 in 10 Canadians at a cost of nearly $3 billion annually). The primary medications for controlling asthma are inhaled corticosteroids, which reduce the inflammation that increases airways muscle contraction, mucus and, consequentially, difficulty breathing. The current proposal will validate and build on our early results and, additionally, elucidate the underlying mechanisms therein. To do this, we will conduct a novel, controlled crossover trial of diesel exhaust (DE) and an inhaled corticosteroid in mild asthmatics. We will collect lung samples and assess how air pollution may alter the expression of genes and proteins in the lung. In parallel, we will grow lung epithelial cells and use them to examine mechanisms underlying the effects of air pollution on corticosteroid responsiveness and determine the effectiveness of interventions. This study has the potential to enhance both prevention and therapy for Canadian asthmatics. Our results can inform physician practices and drive regulatory policies to protect vulnerable groups. Additionally, understanding how the effects of corticosteroids on lung gene expression are modified by air pollution could lead to the development of improved medications for the millions of Canadians suffering from airways disease.

column36: Function of Flaviviridae viral RNAs in the host cell nucleus
column37: Pathogenic RNA viruses of the Flaviviridae family include Zika (ZIKV), West Nile (WNV), Dengue (DV), and Hepatitis C (HCV). ZIKV outbreaks are occurring in more than 80 countries and in 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. DV is endemic in at least 100 countries and WHO estimates that nearly 400 million infections occur yearly, while HCV causes serious liver damage with more than 170 million individuals infected worldwide. A central tenant of Flaviviridae virus biology, and one that guides therapeutic strategies, is that the virus production cycle occurs within the cytoplasm of host cells. However, we recently discovered that the RNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV shuttle in and out of the host cell nucleus. The movement of ZIKV and HCV RNA genomes through the host nucleus has not been explored in the literature, and the functional importance of nuclear viral RNAs remains completely unknown. Critically, altering the transport of ZIKV and HCV RNAs through the nucleus negatively impacts virus production, pointing to a crucial, yet uncharacterized, role for the nucleus in Flaviviridae biology. We hypothesize that the vRNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV enter the host nucleus to (1) engage nuclear pathways that aid in virus production and (2) to regulate host cell gene expression including activition of cell defence mechanisms. We expect that our research will produce new knowledge, technologies, and methodologies that will establish an area of research with pan-Flaviviridae therapeutic opportunities.

column37: Cilia, the antenna-shaped structures found on most human cells, have recently emerged as major hotspots for genetic diseases called ciliopathies. Over 30 different ciliopathies, caused by mutations in nearly 200 genes, are currently known. Defects in the functions of cilia, which play critical roles in physiology and development, result in many clinical ailments. These include blindness, polycystic kidney disease, morbid obesity, skeletal anomalies and brain defects. Since 2003, my group has made seminal contributions to the understanding of cilia and ciliopathies. In particular, we were the first to link a multi-organ genetic disorder, Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), to defective cilia function. We discovered that several components (proteins) implicated in BBS specifically function in a process termed intraflagellar transport (IFT), which is responsible for the formation and functions of cilia. We also identified and uncovered the functions of novel IFT-associated proteins, all of which are now associated with ciliopathies. The central goal of our research proposal is to establish an experimental system in which we can decipher or 'model' the mechanisms by which different patient ciliopathy mutations cause IFT and ciliary defects. To further enhance our ability to understand how patient mutations affect IFT, we will conduct genetic, cell biology and biochemistry experiments to shed new insights into the functions and regulation of the IFT system. We will accomplish these goals by taking advantage of innovative resources and experimental tools that are either not available for, or not easily applicable to, other researchers using mammalian (e.g., human cells) or vertebrate (e.g., zebrafish) model systems. Collectively, our findings will help unravel fundamental mechanisms of cilia formation and function, and importantly, provide molecular diagnostic tools necessary to understand how IFT mutations can lead to an important and growing class of human disorders.

column36: Reducing HIV target cells in the female genital tract: Determining the mechanism of inducing immune quiescence.
column37: The two basic elements of successful Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) transmission are a viable virus and a susceptible target host cell. Activated immune cells are more susceptible to HIV infection than resting cells and, once infected, they produce up to 1000 times more virus. It is known that inflammation brings activated HIV target cells to the site of irritation. Most of biomedical prevention approaches focus on either keeping HIV away (condom use) or neutralizing it once it is present in the genital tract (antiviral drugs, microbicides, vaccines). However, what has not been a focus of HIV prevention efforts, is trying to limit the availability of susceptible HIV-target cells at the genital tract. We conducted a pilot study to determine if a common anti-inflammatory drug acetylsalicylic acid (ASA or Aspirin) could decrease inflammation among low-risk Kenya women. The results showed ASA reduced the number of HIV target cells in the female genital tract by 35%. In this current study, we build on those finding using detailed molecular studies to determine the molecular mechanism(s) involved in ASA's effect on the recruitment of HIV target cells in the genital tract. We will also determine if daily administration of ASA will reduce HIV target cells numbers at the genital tract Kenyan female sex workers who are at high risk of acquiring HIV. We will also determine which dose of ASA is most effective, the duration of the effect and whether there are any side-effects on the vaginal microbiome. The long-term goal of this study is to provide a novel HIV-prevention approach that is both readily available and non-stigmatizing. If we can demonstrate that ASA is able to reduce HIV target cells among women at high risk of acquiring HIV, then we will be one step closer to a much needed novel HIV prevention.

column37: Stroke is the 3rd leading cause of death and is a leading cause of long-term disability in Canada, with the risk of stroke doubling every 10 years after the age of 55. The Canadian Stroke Network's Burden of Ischemic Stroke (BURST) study has calculated that 50,000 new strokes occur each year. This leads to health-care costs in excess of $2.5 billion. For the most part there is not much we can do to treat or prevent strokes at this time other than encourage patients to develop good lifestyle habits that promote cardiovascular health. The clot-busting drug tPA is used to treat patients who have a large stroke and results in very favorable outcomes. However, the vast majority of strokes are "covert" strokes with no obvious clinical presentation. The cumulative impact of these strokes leads to substantial, irreversible neuronal damage. Our research aims to characterize a new mechanism by which we can protect the brain against these stroke events. In this proposal, we set out a series of experiments to characterize a potential new avenue for stroke therapy. Our preliminary results show that administration of drug that increases brain glycine, called NFPS, leads to a dramatic decrease in stroke size. In our proposed experiments, we will elucidate the molecular mechanism that underlies this phenomenon and also determine the therapeutic window of NFPS as a stroke treatment. NFPS is well tolerated in the clinic and our discovery will open up new avenues for treatment using a drug that is readily available. This will greatly improve the health of Canadians and lessen the economic costs associated with stroke recovery.

column36: Dissecting the neural and behavioural mechanisms of persistent behavioural change
column37: Reducing or eliminating problem behaviours is a critical component to every-day healthy functioning and to the successful treatment of clinical conditions such as drug and food addiction or anxiety disorders. Reduction in unwanted behaviours can be achieved through extinction training. This training consists of the presentation of cues for biologically significant events in the absence of those events. In the laboratory this training is used to better understand the behavioural and neural mechanisms that regulate extinction learning and its diminutive effect on behavior. In the clinical setting, extinction-based therapies such as abstinence or cue exposure, are used to help patients eliminate behaviours that define their psychopathologies. However, the success of extinction-based training strongly depends on the generalizability of this learning to new contexts, across long temporal intervals or upon experience with motivationally or emotionally charged events. This proposal seeks to develop novel, long-lasting and generalizable behavioural routes via which reduction in unwanted behaviour can be achieved. This will be done using two distinct paradigms, which drive extinction learning via two ways: by manipulating outcome delivery (omission of an expected outcome) or by manipulating outcome expectation (generating an inflated expectation of an outcome). We will use these two paradigms to uncover the general or common neural mechanisms of this learning by studying how the brain processes extinction in a variety of settings real-time, and what neural circuits are causally involved in regulating this learning. Our ultimate goal is to use behaviour and neuroscience to develop novel routes that support lasting reduction of unwanted behavior from bench to beside.

column37: Worldwide, 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men over 50 years of age will experience osteoporotic fractures. Current osteoporosis treatments have various shortcomings such as poor bone quality and several skeletal and non-skeletal side effects. Therefore major investments have been made into the development of more effective drugs that are less prone to side effects. Due to efforts of ourselves and many others it has been discovered that bone-degrading cathepsin K (CatK) is a highly suitable drug target whose inhibition led to increased bone quality and reduced fracture rates in clinical osteoporosis trials. Although there is little doubt about the validity of CatK as a drug target, none of the CatK inhibitors have been approved because of various safety concerns. Based on our research, this might be due to the multifunctional character of the enzyme, where total inhibition leads to the observed side effects. However, the osteoporosis relevant activity of this enzyme is limited to its potent collagenase activity, which should be selectively blocked. Based on our previous studies on the mechanism of collagen degradation by CatK, we have developed a strategy to specifically block the collagen-degrading activity without affecting other biologically important actions of this protease. We termed this novel and innovative type of drugs "ectosteric inhibitors" and our proposed project is aimed at characterizing these substrate-specific drugs at their molecular, cellular and in vivo levels of action and efficacy as anti-resorptives. We have identified compounds that have a similar bone-preserving potency in cell assays and in an osteoporosis mouse model similar to the most advanced clinically evaluated CatK inhibitor without affecting non-bone-related pathways. column36: Phylodynamics of HIV within hosts
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infects different parts of the body and types of cells, including cells that play an important role in our immune system. Furthermore, an infected cell can become "latent" so that it does not produce new copies of the virus, making it essentially invisible to the immune system and drug treatments, only to become reactivated months or years afterwards. The existence of these reservoirs of latently infected cells is a key reason why it is so difficult to cure an HIV infection. HIV also evolves rapidly because it makes many mistakes when copying its own genome. This rapid evolution makes it possible to infer how different copies of a virus from the same patient are related. These evolutionary relationships are usually represented by a tree or "phylogeny". Phylodynamics is a new interdisciplinary field where the shape of a phylogeny is used to reconstruct how an epidemic has spread through a human population. Methods from phylodynamics have already made enormous impacts on our understanding of HIV, influenza A virus, and the recent Ebolavirus outbreak in West Africa. Our proposal is a completely novel application of phylodynamic methods to examine the proliferation of HIV within patients. We will extend techniques from pattern recognition being developed in our lab to enable computers to extract information about HIV latency and its spread among different populations of cells from the shapes of phylogenetic trees. The key expected benefits of the proposed research are to inform the development of HIV cure strategies by reconstructing how the virus spreads among different cell types and tissues, and their respective characteristics as potential latent reservoirs.

column36: Enabling Multi-site,Tailored Feedback Interventions to Reduce Low-Value Test Ordering in Critical Care: A Systematic Approach
column37: Laboratory testing of patient blood samples is one of the highest volume activities in health care, but between 20-30% of tests ordered are thought to be low-value or entirely unnecessary. This leads to three major problems: 1) wasted spending on unnecessary tests that could be used for other healthcare purposes 2) increased health risks (e.g. blood loss causing anemia that can be particularly dangerous for the highly vulnerable patients in critical care), and 3) risk of false positive results that lead to further unnecessary testing that can be costly, anxiety-provoking, and invasive. Reducing low-value testing is often difficult, particularly in team-based settings like critical care. A potentially effective strategy is Audit and Feedback, where providers' own practice data (e.g. the number of a specific lab tests ordered over the past month) is provided back to them to spur change. Our overall goal is to develop, test and deliver feedback strategies to reduce low-value test ordering in critical care, a highly complex and team-based environment that is one of the heaviest users of laboratory testing. Our team combines 1) lab testing data, infrastructure, and expertise from the Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association (EORLA), the body responsible for all 13 million annual in-hospital lab tests in Eastern Ontario; 2) world-leading expertise in feedback and healthcare professional behavior change, and 3) critical care clinical expertise from a range of critical care units in Eastern Ontario. This project will 1) develop tools to help organizations identify low-value tests and design feedback strategies to reduce their use; 2) design tailored feedback strategies for several critical care sites, and 3) evaluate the effectiveness of these feedback strategies. This work will enable better test ordering practice, help improve efficiency of a major component of modern health care, and reduce the need for patients to be put at risk by unnecessary testing.

column36: Changing the patient-PCP dialogue: fostering trust through joint clinical decision making
column37: A patient visits their doctor with a set of symptoms hoping for a diagnostic test, a prescription, or a diagnosis. Yet, sometimes doing nothing is better. Unnecessary interventions needlessly expose the patient to harms, lengthen the wait for other patients in need of tests or therapy, and burden the health system with avoidable costs. The challenge is how to have doctor-patient conversations about clinical decisions about tests and procedures in a way that is patient-focused and maintains trust. To change the conversation, we need a better understanding of the doctor-patient interaction. We need to understand how doctors build trust with their patients, and do these strategies change if the doctor feels that the patient before them might face barriers in accessing health services. This is very important when faced with suggestions that "doing more" (tests, procedures) is not necessarily better. We need to understand how different groups of patients perceive their doctor visits, including how these might affect Metis patients compared to other Manitobans. In theory, all Manitobans, including the Metis, have equal access to the health care system, but the reality is quite varied and different. Some, by virtue of education, income, race, gender, language, and other issues might have trouble accessing health services and have poorer health outcomes. It is important to understand if there are aspects of initiatives promoting "more isn't better" that might harm some Manitoba patients, like the Metis, because of their already poorer health status. Equally important, unless the expectations of patients who are able to access the health system are met about what they need to feel assured they are getting the best care, trust in doctor recommendations may be compromised. Using interviews with doctors and focus groups with Metis and other Manitobans in Winnipeg, Brandon and Winkler, we focus on common reasons bringing patients to visit their doctor: pain or infection.

column36: Regulation of the PCSK9 binding interaction with LDL receptor
column37: Hypercholesterolemia is associated with increased incidence of heart disease, specifically due to increased blood levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL), the so-called "bad cholesterol". LDL removal from blood requires the LDL receptor, a cell surface protein that latches onto circulating LDL particles and mediates their uptake into cells. PCSK9 is a protein in blood that also binds to the LDL receptor, but this binding causes the LDL receptor to be degraded inside cells. PCSK9 may have evolved to help maintain a balance between cell surface LDL receptor levels and production of lipoproteins by the liver, but this function is detrimental with a modern high-fat and high-cholesterol diet. We recently discovered that PCSK9 also binds to LDL particles themselves, with LDL-bound PCSK9 being less active against the LDL receptor. The project will determine how LDL binding affects the structure and function of PCSK9 and how these changes lower PCSK9's ability to bind to LDL receptors. Our aim is identify regions in the PCSK9 molecule that are necessary for its function in the blood. These protein regions would in turn represent targets for therapeutic inhibition of PCSK9-mediated LDL receptor degradation in the treatment and prevention of hypercholesterolemia.

column36: Functional Dissection of Germline Small RNA Pathways
column37: Patterns of gene expression distinguish different cell types (i.e. brain, hair, and muscle cells express different sets of genes to make them different from each other). Misregulated gene expression can lead to developmental disorders, infertility, cancer, and other diseases, thus there are many cellular safety mechanisms that regulate the process. One key mechanism for controlling gene expression involves sRNA pathways that can act in different cellular compartments and at several steps in the process of turning a gene on or off. Small RNA pathways play key gene regulatory roles in a variety of organisms, and rely on conserved Argonaute effector proteins, which utilize sRNAs to provide sequence-specific identification of target genes. Our research focuses on understanding how sRNA pathways regulate gene expression in the nuclei of cells known as germ cells (sperm and egg). The nucleus is where the process of gene expression initiates, and sRNA activities in the nucleus are currently poorly understood, especially in animals. Our studies focus on understanding the molecular mechanisms by which sRNA pathways impact chromatin (how chromosomes are packaged), using the nematode, C. elegans, as a powerful model system, and applying integrated genetic, genomic, molecular and cell biology approaches. Uncovering the molecular mechanisms of sRNA-mediated gene regulation in germ cell nuclei reveals a deeper understanding of basic cellular functions that contribute to development, differentiation, fertility and disease, and provides a more precise means to manipulate gene expression, leading to more effective sRNA-based therapeutics and laboratory techniques.

column36: Role of alternative polyadenylation in Ras-driven cancers
column37: Cancer is a disease of genes, which are blueprints for proteins that carry out the work of cells. Genes make proteins through an intermediate template called messenger RNA (mRNA). Proto-oncogenes can be thought of as gas pedals that drive cell proliferation. Mutations that convert proto-oncogenes into oncogenes push the "pedal to the metal", causing cells to over proliferate and form tumours. Oncogenes drive cell proliferation in simple organisms like worms by same mechanisms as they function in humans. Despite sequencing thousands of cancer genomes we still lack an understanding of how oncogenes drive tumour growth. Taking advantage of the powerful gene manipulation techniques of the tiny worm C. elegans we found that an oncogene called Ras cooperates with insulin signalling to promote tumour growth, which is also conserved in human tumour cells. We show that Ras requires an intact insulin pathway to sustain its oncogenic activity, and that this is achieved by dictating where messenger RNA tails are placed. These tails have sections where specific molecules can bind and put the brakes on to prevent its translation into protein. Cancer cells produce too much protein, which is required to fuel their rapid growth. We hypothesize that inhibiting insulin signalling promotes the formation mRNAs with longer tails containing sites to apply the brakes on activated oncogenes, and suppress tumour formation. To understand how this works we will combine the powerful gene manipulation technologies available in C. elegans, human cells, and mice. By exploiting these models we hope to identify new drug targets that can prevent abnormal tumour cell growth in humans.

column36: Novel targeted therapeutics against leukemia stem cells
column37: The goal of this project is to identify drugs that can target the rare cells that cause treatment failure in leukemia - leukemic stem cells (LSCs). We propose to examine these 12 compounds in depth and determine how well they work against multiple leukemia samples, what exactly they do, and how safe they are. Our efforts to understand their mechanisms of action and their effectiveness in primary leukemic cells will yield novel insight into the unique functioning of LSCs. This increase in our knowledge of LSC and leukemia biology will in turn enable additional gains in prognosis, therapy and prevention.

column37: In the heart, muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium from the internal calcium stores through the calcium release channel, called the ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2). The objective of this research proposal is to explore the mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment of heart dysfunction associated with LOF RyR2 mutations. To achieve this goal, we propose to identify and characterize LOF RyR2 mutations and their associated heart defects, to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms of their actions, and to develop novel diagnostic tests and therapeutic strategies for RyR2 LOF mutation associated diseases. column36: Stem cell related genesis and maintenance of glioblastoma
column37: Brain cancers, particularly glioblastomas (GBM), are amongst the worst human cancers. The 5-year survival is <10%, effectively rendering patients with this diagnosis to a death sentence. Patients are desperate for better treatments. A major barrier to finding better treatments has been a poor understanding of the mechanisms of brain tumor initiation and growth. My research group found that GBM growth was dependent on a few cells in the tumour that have stem cell properties, these cells lie at the root of GBM growth and are also resistant to conventional therapies. We have found that human GBM stem cells depend on the Sox2 gene, which is a master gene of stem cells. These findings suggest that the Sox2+ normal stem cells in the brain may be the cells that give rise to glioblastoma, but how, when, and why they do is not known. In this proposal, we will study the role of the brain's normal Sox2 expressing cells in the genesis and growth of glioblastoma, using experimental approaches that cannot be performed with human cells, by creating tumours in the brains of mice. We will test whether normal Sox2+ neural stem cells in the mouse give rise to experimental glioblastomas and how activation or suppression of the growth activity of these cells affects the emergence of glioblastoma. We will also determine if the growth of these tumors, and their therapeutic resistance depends on subpopulations of Sox2+ cells. These studies will complement and extend knowledge derived in research of human cells by allowing us to study all stages of glioblastoma, from the earliest tumors to full-blown cancers both pre- and post-treatment. We cannot easily get access to the first steps of the disease, nor some of its worst forms, so this work in mice will fulfill areas of unmet need in the research of this cancer. We will then use these models to test preventative measures and to develop more effective therapies.

column37: Hydatidiform mole is an aberrant human pregnancy with no embryo that has fascinated scientists in all civilizations since its description by Hippocrates more than 2000 years ago. I, together with my team, identified a major gene, NLRP7, responsible for a rare form of recurrent moles and have made significant contribution to its current understanding. Because of the contribution of my group, patients with recurrent moles are now tested for NLRP7 and those with recessive mutations counselled that their defect lies in their oocytes and that they can have normal pregnancies and live births from ovum donation. Our most recent and important finding is that the root of this disease in patients with NLRP7 mutations stems from the placenta because it did not complete its full differentiation and that is why it keeps proliferating. This proposal aims at delineating the extent of the undifferentiated state of the placenta of recurrent moles from patients with recessive NLRP7 mutations, investigating whether the identified markers are involved in the malignant degeneration of sporadic moles, and demonstrating the roles of these markers in conferring tumorigenesis. In this application, I am seeking the CIHR support to start understanding the molecular basis of the malignant component of moles and help the most fragile patients with this condition.

column36: Synaptic, cellular and molecular mechanisms of depression susceptibility
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and existing antidepressant therapies have limited efficacy. It is well known that chronic stress can lead to depression, yet not all those who encounter stress will become depressed. Understanding what makes some people especially vulnerable to depression is essential for developing proper treatment and for possibly even preventing the disorder. Stress experienced in early life is one factor known to increase risk for depression but key questions remain unanswered. What are the enduring changes in brain function that are induced by early life stress to mediate life-long susceptibility to depression? Can neural signatures of aberrant brain function be detected before depression is observed? To answer these questions, we will employ a multi-disciplinary approach integrating advanced neuroscience techniques with robust mouse models to probe the enduring effects of early life experience on neuronal activity and the underlying changes in gene expression in a key brain circuit implicated in depression, the ventral hippocampus projection to the nucleus accumbens. We will use ex vivo measurements of neuronal connectivity, in vivo imaging of neuronal activity and post-mortem assays of genome-wide gene expression to examine how maternal separation in mice, a form of early life stress, shapes neuronal function and gene networks in the ventral-hippocampus to nucleus accumbens circuit to increase susceptibility to chronic stress in adulthood. Elucidating both the alterations in brain circuit function and the underlying gene networks that render an individual susceptible to depression will provide the knowledge necessary to develop treatments to treat and even prevent depression. This research will open the door to new interventions to regulate brain activity to mitigate susceptibility before depression emerges, reducing the enormous societal costs and improving the lives of millions of Canadians struggling with depression

column36: Lipophagy in Reverse Cholesterol Transport
column37: Atherosclerosis, a form of heart disease caused by the build-up of cholesterol deposits in the artery wall, is responsible for one in five deaths in Canada. Meanwhile, existing cholesterol-lowering drugs are only partially effective at reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. New therapies are urgently needed to combat this deadly disease. Our research team is looking for new ways to improve the removal of cholesterol from atherosclerotic plaques, stop the plaques from growing bigger, and possibly even reduce their size. We are testing whether increasing a process in cells called "autophagy"-which breaks down lipids and exports them-could achieve this. Autophagy plays a key role in recycling toxic elements from cells and promotes cell survival during periods of cell stress. Through autophagy, cellular components are delivered to organelles called lysosomes (the waste disposal system of the cell), which digest unwanted materials. Our research has already shown that autophagy can also engulf and digest cholesterol that has accumulated in the artery wall. This process helps remove cholesterol, through a process called 'reverse cholesterol transport' providing an entirely new therapeutic target to reverse atherosclerosis. Specifically, this proposal seeks to determine the role of autophagy in digesting accumulated lipid in various cell types found in atherosclerotic plaques (macrophages, vascular smooth muscle cells), and to compare the relative importance of the autophagy pathway in these cells for reverse cholesterol transport and atherosclerosis regression. By shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms of lipid autophagy, our research team hopes to identify pathway components that can be targeted and manipulated to treat heart disease. We are also looking for new targets for developing drugs that can increase cholesterol breakdown and export by cells in the artery wall.

column36: Deciphering the role of DCIR in HIV-1 pathogenesis
column37: Several studies have shown that early or pre-exposure treatments help prevent HIV-1 infection and the consequent destruction of the immune system which is then able to regain some control over the infection. In link with these observations, identification of new targets for HIV-1 involved in the first stages of infection remains the best option to eradicate HIV-1 infection. Dendritic cells (DCs) are the first immune cells which recognize HIV-1 in mucosal tissue. The initial interaction between HIV-1 and DCs occurs through attachment factors and we have identified the dendritic cell immunoreceptor (DCIR) as a key receptor. The binding of HIV-1 to DCIR allows the virus to be internalized, to escape the mounting of an immune response and to be transported to the lymphoid organs, where it gains entry into CD4 expressing T cells (CD4TL) by cell-to-cell transmission from DCs. Subsequent virus replication causes severe and irreversible depletion of CD4TL, bereaving the infected person of an efficient immune response against HIV-1. We are now interested in a possible role of DCIR in the early step of infection that appear to interfere with and ultimately compromise the immune response to HIV-1. We propose to test this hypothesis in vitro and in vivo using well-characterized cell models and humanized mouse models. We hope this novel approach will constitute a springboard for the development of new innovative therapeutic strategies against HIV-1 by blocking HIV-1 binding to DCs via DCIR without affecting the specific immune responses.

column36: Roles of Alkali Cation/Proton Exchangers in Organellar Function and Neurodevelopmental Disorders
column37: The human brain has one of the highest rates of consumption of biochemical fuel (i.e., glucose) needed to sustain neuronal electrical activity. This in turn produces significant levels of metabolic ionic byproducts, such as protons (acid), bicarbonate and phosphates (bases) that must be effectively buffered, recycled for other purposes, or removed in order to maintain a suitable acid-base (pH) milieu for optimal brain function. Abnormal disturbances in brain pH balance are associated with the progression of various pathophysiological conditions, including newborn asphyxia, stroke, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and neuropsychiatric disorders - debilitating conditions that have an enormous human and economic impact on society. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that control brain pH levels are not fully understood. This project examines the roles of one major class of pH-regulating ion transport proteins called alkali cation/proton exchangers (i.e., SLC9A gene family), with a specific focus on the SLC9A6 transporter that is located in mobile membrane-bound vesicles located inside most brain cell types. Recent studies have identified mutations in SLC9A6 that cause an increasing diagnosed form of severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and autistic behaviour called Christianson Syndrome. We have isolated the SLC9A6 gene and are currently studying the effects the mutations have on neuronal function. We hypothesize that these defects impair the proper pH and functioning of vesicles that carry neurotransmitter receptors and other proteins to synapses of neurons, which in turn affects brain electrical activity and function. This assumption will be tested using a range of molecular, cellular, genetic and electrophysiological techniques in cultured cells and mouse animal models; thereby shedding new insights into the contributions of SLC9A6 to human health and disease, and identification of efficacious strategies for disease treatment.

column37: No therapy can yet rid the body of HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, thus requiring life-long adherence to drugs. column36: MR-Guided Management of Occlusive Peripheral Arterial Disease
column37: Occlusive peripheral arterial disease occurs when blockages in blood vessels limit the blood supply to the leg. This disease is widespread and represents a major societal burden. Approximately 20% of those over the age of 59 years suffer from this disease, which results in over 160,000 limb amputations being performed per year in the US alone. Our goal over the next 5 years is to extend the role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to increase the success rates in patients who can have this disease treated using minimally invasive percutaneous techniques using catheters and wires advanced through blood vessels. X-ray fluoroscopy, the imaging modality that is currently used to guide percutaneous procedures, has relatively poor soft tissue contrast. This makes it difficult to visualize blockages and to ensure that a revascularization device stays within the vessel during the procedure. This limits success rates and restricts minimally invasive treatment to short blockages in large arteries (which occur much less frequently than long occlusions further down the leg). Other treatment options include bypass surgery, which has substantial associated risk, and medical therapy, which has been shown to have limited effectiveness. MRI, unlike x-ray, has excellent soft-tissue contrast and with MRI it is possible to develop a detailed picture of blocked vessels and downstream tissue that can greatly aid in guiding revascularization procedures. Through a program of technical developments we plan to advance methods which will improve revascularization of blocked blood vessels. We anticipate this will facilitate less invasive treatment in a significant population that would ordinarily be subjected to more invasive surgery or to less effective treatments.

column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting more than 1% of the Canadian population. Key deliverables include (a) statistical methods to identify atrophy patterns and at-risk patients, and (b) computational methods to infer spreading patterns and predict future atrophy. column37: In Canada, hunger jeopardizes the health and well-being of one out of eight households. Donations of food banks are a well-known attempt to resolve the problem, but not everyone agrees on their benefit. Some think they are part of the problem, because they undermine the movement to adopt policies to fight against poverty. Others see them rather as a bridge to other community services that help people pull through. Who is right? For now, there is insufficient scientific data available to settle the matter. column36: Regulation of stem cell proliferation in the C. elegans germ line
column37: Stem cells provide the source material for development, tissue maintenance and wound repair. They are able to provide these functions because of their unique ability to both self-renew and differentiate. Self-renewal, or the ability to make new stem cells, ensures that a stem cell population is maintained. Differentiation is the process by which these cells form the desired tissue. A balance must be maintained between self-renewal and differentiation in order for stem cells to function properly. If there is too much self-renewal, a tumour may form instead of the desired tissue. If there is too much differentiation, the stem cell population will become depleted, preventing the desired tissue from being formed in the future. We study the genetic and molecular mechanisms that control the balance between self-renewal and differentiation. As a model, we use the germ line of the small nematode worm, C. elegans. This model is one of the best-understood stem cell systems due to the vast array of investigative tools that are available. We have identified a number of genes that, when mutated, cause the balance between self-renewal and differentiation to become compromised. By studying how these genes function, we will determine the molecular mechanisms involved in regulating stem cell behaviour. Importantly, each of the genes we have identified have similar genes in humans, which are also thought to be involved in regulating stem cell proliferation; therefore, our analysis will be directly applicable to understanding human stem cell behaviour. We are also taking the next step in understanding stem cell behaviour by identifying the proteins that are enriched in stem cells. Through this exquisitely sensitive stem cell system, we will determine the proteins that provide stem cells with their unique characteristics. Understanding how specific factors regulate stem cell behaviour will bring us closer to realizing their full therapeutic potential.

column37: Brain arteriovenous malformations (BAVMs) are a tangle of large, abnormal blood vessels within the brain. The resulting high blood flow can cause these blood vessel malformations to rupture and bleed, which may lead to severe illness or even death. BAVMs are a leading cause of bleeding in the brains of children and young adults. The main reason to treat a BAVM is to prevent a rupture. Treatment of BAVMs with surgery or radiation carries significant risk, and is both invasive as well as costly. There are currently no drugs available to treat this disorder and the cause of BAVMs is not known. We have identified spontaneous, non-inherited genetic mutations in a gene called KRAS in the majority of BAVM patients. These mutations occur in the cells that line blood vessels within BAVMs, but do not occur elsewhere in the patient. The KRAS gene codes for a protein that serves as an ON-OFF switch in blood vessel cells. When the KRAS gene is mutated, blood vessel cells are stuck in the 'ON' state and think that they are receiving cell growth and migration signals, even when they are not. In this proposal, we first aim to identify the defective genes in BAVMs that do not have mutations in KRAS, and second to understand how KRAS mutations influence the formation of BAVMs. To do this, we will introduce mutations in KRAS in blood vessel cells of mice and zebrafish; both common animal models to study blood vessel development and disease. In addition to testing whether these animals develop BAVMs, we will also use drugs to block cellular signalling pathways downstream of the 'ON' switch to determine whether we can treat BAVMs in these animal models. This may help us to discover drugs that could be used to treat this disorder in humans.

column36: Contributions of the Ventral Auditory Cortical Pathway to Auditory Cognition
column37: Auditory categorization enables listeners to efficiently identify and respond to auditory stimuli. It is a computational process in which auditory stimuli are classified and grouped into sound categories based on their acoustic features, perceptual representations, or other types of information. For example, when we hear the word "fundable" from different speakers, we can categorize the sex of each speaker based on the pitch of the speaker's voice. On the other hand, to analyze the linguistic content transmitted by speech stimuli, we ignore the unique pitch, timbre etc. of each speaker's voice and categorize it into the distinct word category "fundable". Despite an important literature on the neuronal mechanisms of auditory categorization, many issues remain unknown or have yet to be fully elucidated. First, no studies have identified the sites in the brain that contain the information needed to create categorical representations. Second, and relatedly, there is not a clear understanding of distinct contributions of different brain regions to different types of auditory categorization. Finally, although our world is inherently multisensory, it is not known the degree to which the ventral auditory pathway contributes to multisensory categorization. The accomplish these goals, we combine high-density recordings within and across brain regions, rigorous and quantitative behavioral studies, and causal manipulations in rhesus monkeys to address these issues and identify the mechanisms underlying auditory categorization. These studies will provide important insights into hearing dysfunction and hearing perception. This understanding is crucial for guiding the development of more effective clinical approaches to alleviating hearing difficulties in complex acoustic environments- difficulties which are common in the elderly, the hearing impaired, and in individuals with cochlear implants or certain developmental disorders.

column37: Clostridium difficile (C.diff) is the leading cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea in the developed world. This opportunistic bacterium is a major problem in hospitals for three main reasons. The first is that C.diff is able to form highly resilient spores outside of the body that are difficult to eradicate from hospital settings. The second is that C.diff disease is triggered by antibiotics, which deplete most of the normal healthy gut bacteria, with the exception of antibiotic-resistant C.diff itself. Third, C.diff produces toxins in the gut that cause tissue damage leading diarrhea and in some cases death. Recent studies have shown that the so-called "good bacteria" in the gut (often referred to as the microbiota) also play an important role in C.diff disease. Indeed, it has been shown that a subset of bile acids produced in the gut are chemically modified by certain gut bacteria into molecules that prevent C.diff growth. We recently uncovered an entirely new role for the chemically modified bile acids - as direct inhibitors of the gut-damaging toxins. We hypothesize that in addition to modulating bacterial growth that modified bile acids play a role in preventing toxin-induced damage in healthy carriers of C.difficile. Further characterization of this new pathway will help define the specific molecules responsible for this protection and guide development of anti-toxin molecules to prevent the symptoms of disease in patients suffering a C.diff infection.

column36: Bridging Place and Social Spaces: Building Healthful Relationships Towards Indigenous Food Sovereignty in Southwestern Ontario
column37: Traditional foods harvested locally contribute to the wellbeing of Indigenous peoples. Store-bought foods tend to be processed, while foods harvested from the land are more nutritious. In Canada, research on traditional foods has mainly taken place in the north. Southern communities also experience limited food and land access. In southwestern Ontario, Indigenous communities have expressed an interest in eating more local foods. An organization in the community of Six Nations offers programming to increase food access on reserve. Urban Indigenous families and youth who frequently relocate to cities for work or school are also in need of support to reinforce these important relationships. To build on local initiatives and investigate barriers identified in this region, a participatory research project is proposed. Study objectives are to address traditional food access and knowledge barriers by profiling community examples, while exploring innovative land-based education and practices across generations. Working with a diverse set of partners on reserve, in cities, and campus, the study will be community-based and use Photovoice methodology to capture sources and stories of traditional foods in the community of Six Nations, and the nearby urban environments. Participants will take pictures where foods are harvested, hunted, or shared. Photographs will become the objects of interviews to collect stories behind the images. Distributing study results will involve Elders, parents and youth in sharing circles and the development of workshops in urban centres and out on the land. The photographs and digital stories will be displayed at local events to advocate for the continued building of relationships in support of land-based initiatives and knowledge transfer. Sharing practices, increasing food knowledge and access through increased social supports will contribute towards the health and wellbeing of individuals, Nations and Territories.

column37: Social interactions are essential to our mental health and their deficits are hallmark symptoms of many brain disorders, including autism, intellectual disability, depression and schizophrenia, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. column36: Type IV pilins - multifunctional subunits of bacterial virulence factors
column37: Many bacterial pathogens use hair-like filaments called type IV pili (T4P) as mini grappling hooks to stick to their hosts and rapidly spread. T4P are thus potential targets for new antimicrobial therapies such as vaccines. Each filament is made of thousands of small lollipop-shaped proteins called pilins. The "stick" of the lollipop is very conserved and has a number of important functions. It stores pilins in the cytoplasmic membrane; forms the inner core of the pilus; and acts as a recognition domain for sensor proteins that monitor pilin inventories, so more are made only if needed. We will investigate how these monitoring systems recognize pilins, so we can fool them into shutting down even if there aren't enough pilins available. In contrast, the "lollipop" part of a pilin is diverse, making it harder to design a vaccine that will cover all possible "flavours". We are trying to understand the causes and consequences of pilin diversity, to inform the design of new treatments. We study Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), a pathogen designated by the World Health Organization as a critical priority for new therapies due to its high level of resistance to antibiotics. We searched thousands of Pa DNA sequences to find all of its pilin flavours, and constructed a panel of different pilins in a common genetic background. This unique and expandable resource will allow us to ask how the immune system "sees" different pilins - when is recognition lost? We think that diversity arises from attempts to escape from viruses that stick to the pili. Changing a pilin's sequence or hiding it with sugars blocks attachment. Remarkably, some viruses can bind to very different pilins, suggesting they see a non-obvious common feature. We will characterize how those viruses interact with diverse pilins. They are of interest as therapeutics, as they can kill multidrug resistant bacteria. Together, this work will give us an unprecedented understanding of how pilus diversity is shaped.

column36: Base Excision Repair in Cancer- New Mechanisms, Dependencies and Vulnerabilities
column37: Cancer develops following increased alterations within DNA, which are usually repaired by complex groups of proteins involved in DNA repair. Defects in one or more DNA repair mechanisms cause the accumulation of changes in DNA, called mutations, that increase the possibility that certain cells become tumorigenic. Paradoxically, once cancer cells emerge they are acutely dependent on certain DNA repair mechanisms, even more so than normal cells, because they proliferate rapidly and their metabolism generates highly reactive DNA-damaging molecules. Hence, to survive cancer cells must adapt by increasing their capacity to repair specific types of DNA damage. As a by-product of this adaptation, cancer cells become more resistant to therapies that cause DNA damage, such as chemotherapy and radiation. We have discovered one strategy that cancer cells use to augment their DNA repair capability. They can increase the expression of proteins that stimulate the activity of DNA repair enzymes. In contrast to DNA repair enzymes, these accessory proteins are not essential to normal cells under physiological conditions, but are required by cancer cells. This provides a therapeutic window to develop new drugs targeting accessory proteins to which cancer cells have become addicted to. Our characterization of the CUT domain family of proteins has established a paradigm in this field. We now have identified a novel accessory factor that stimulates a different DNA repair enzyme. In the current project, we will characterize the activity of this accessory protein, determine which cancers are dependent on it and demonstrate why cancer cells die without it whereas normal cells can survive. We will develop biochemical tests that are amenable to high-throughput screening in order to identify small molecules that inhibit the accessory protein. These studies are expected to target multiple cancers and eventually to provide new mechanisms to treat cancer.

column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, but can be successfully treated if diagnosed early. We propose to leverage our team expertise and develop a novel diagnostic test-"EBUS-Chek"-which will reduce the need for an on-site cytopathologist and enable all lung cancer clinics with the ability to provide high quality lung cancer patient care. This unique pairing of a biosensing approach with EBUS-TBNA will be able to significantly reduce the bronchoscopic burden that lung cancer patients face and, at the same time, enable all hospitals with a low-cost, highly accurate lung cancer diagnostic tool.

Building on preliminary success, we will now test this intervention's effectiveness in a randomized trial. This involves comparing outcomes of the Y-BEAT intervention to usual treatment. If Y-BEAT is shown to improve employment, school, and health outcomes, we expect to reach thousands of youth by subsequently sharing the program with health and social agencies nationwide.

column36: Health, Prevention, and Policy Environments (HAPPEN): Investigating Policy-Maker and Public Knowledge, Attitudes, and Beliefs about the Effectiveness of Healthy Public Policies
column37: Healthy public policies are key strategies for supporting health. While some places have policies that make the healthy choice easier, those policies vary widely. There is little research that helps coordinate policy adoption across places. We need to know which policy options (e.g., taxes, education, etc) are the most acceptable to, and highest priority for, policymakers and the general public. The HeAlth, Prevention, and Policy ENvironments (HAPPEN) project will address this critical gap. Our team will study the knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs of policymakers and the public about policies related to preventing chronic disease and promoting mental health. We have done 5 surveys focused on chronic disease prevention (2009-2016) of the public and policymakers across Canada. Now, we propose to: i) use research and practice expertise to add mental health and substance misuse policies to that survey; and, ii) repeat the survey for two more years (2019 and 2021) in AB and MB to identify trends in policy priorities and to build on other work in those provinces. We will conduct email and phone surveys with school, workplace, municipal, and provincial policymakers and the general public. HAPPEN's research-practice team will gather and share policy evidence and develop practitioner resources. Our past surveys helped partners to act on policy opportunities, evaluate policies, and target advocacy efforts (e.g., smoke-free vehicles, school food strategies). Currently, there is no other survey that asks both policymakers and the public about policies related to chronic disease, mental health and substance misuse. We will share our data to help NGOs and others act on the most promising policies and focus policymakers' attention on policies with strong public support. HAPPEN will create new and much needed evidence on trends in policy priorities over time and place, enhancing policy action and evaluation in Canada.
