column36: Regulation of an ion channel complex in Fragile X syndrome
column37: Fragile X Syndrome is the greatest inherited cause of intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorder worldwide and yet has no cure. Fragile X occurs at a rate of 1 in 4000 males and 1 in 6000 females, and 1 in ~200 females are carriers that could pass this disorder onto children. The Fragile X mutation leads to the loss of "Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein" (FMRP). Previous work has shown that FMRP regulates the translation of numerous proteins needed to maintain normal synaptic function and plasticity. Because Fragile X is known to reduce synaptic plasticity in cerebellum, we use the mouse cerebellar mossy fiber-granule cell pathway as a model to explore the basis for synaptic abnormalities in Fragile X. Our preliminary data reveal that FMRP binds to an ion channel complex between calcium and potassium channels (Cav3-Kv4) that potentiates the mossy fiber EPSP and increases granule cell excitability via an ERK kinase pathway. We find that FMRP knockout mice completely lack mossy fiber potentiation and associated changes in granule cell excitability. Importantly, intracellular infusion of an active FMRP fragment into granule cells of FMRP knockout mice in vitro restores Cav3-Kv4 function and potentiation of excitability. In addition, an FMRP fragment attached to a tat peptide to facilitate passage across cell membranes rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier and enters cerebellar granule cells after injection into the bloodstream, opening the door to reintroducing FMRP in live animals. These exciting results provide important steps to understanding a new role for FMRP in controlling a membrane ion channel complex that sets cell excitability, and to assess tat-FMRP as a therapeutic strategy to reduce abnormal behaviour in Fragile X Syndrome.

column36: Dissecting RNA binding protein-directed control of hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Blood stem cells, because of their ability to remake all blood cell types as well as regenerate themselves, hold the key to a healthy immune system and have lifesaving potential for the treatments of a range of blood cancers and immune disorders. Despite their promise, the lack of understanding of the mechanics that control these specialized cell types has prevented their widespread use, depriving many patients of a potentially curative therapy for their disease. Our work aims to uncover proteins that are required for blood stem cells to carry out regeneration and to perform experiments that will shed light on how they operate. While in the past, much research has focused on defining the molecular players that work on the DNA of these blood stem cells to make their RNA intermediate, we have new evidence that how this RNA intermediate is changed to impact the final step of protein production is of major importance to the regenerative capacity of blood stem cells. Our study will focus on systematically identifying and understanding the players that act on RNA in these rare and clinically valuable cell types in the hopes that we can capitalize on them and on this previously underappreciated layer of control to promote blood stem cell-based regeneration.

column36: Neurochemical and behavioural characterisation of a novel Dopamine Transporter Deficiency Syndrome mouse model.
column37: Dopamine transmission in the brain is a tightly regulated process, and alterations in dopamine signaling result in several disease with enormous human and economic burden, including schizophrenia, ADHD, Bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease and dyskinesias. One of the key regulators of dopamine transmission is the plasma membrane dopamine transporter, DAT, which transports released dopamine back into the neuron. In addition to the above prevalent diseases, there is also a rare, fatal disease caused by mutations in the dopamine transporter, called dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. We hypothesize that several disease states could be corrected by increasing the protein levels of the dopamine transporter. Drugs that increase dopamine transporter activity could potentially treat conditions such as such as dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. We have worked to identify drugs that would increase the levels and activity of the dopamine transporter, and have discovered that the prescribed drug bupropion increases dopamine transporter levels and activity. Recently, we generated a transgenic mouse model of dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. Our proposed research is designed to uncover the pathophysiology of this by studying these new transgenic animals. Also, we will measure whether bupropion will be able to have therapeutic effect in this new mouse model. Positive results from our studies could be quickly translated into the clinic, since bupropion is already an approved drug and used in humans.

column36: Mechanism of Microtubule assembly by CKAP2
column37: When cells divide, the DNA in form of chromosomes is pulled into the two new daughter cells. The machinery, that exerts the force necessary for separating the chromosomes and is made out of tiny flexible tubes that we call microtubules. Microtubules have to form and grow very quickly and precisely during cell division. They have to be very stable and very dynamic at the same time and constantly be replenished. To make these microtubules, help them grow, stabilize them and ultimately break them apart again, cells use an army of proteins, called MAPs (microtubule-associated proteins). While we know some MAPs, the large majority of these proteins is still not well characterized or completely unknown. We are investigating a MAP that makes new microtubules and helps them grow extremely fast. The same MAP is involved in causing several types of cancer as well as making these cancers more aggressive. We will attempt to solve how this protein makes microtubules grow, how it is involved in building the machinery that divides chromosomes, why cell division is not working well when the protein is misregulated, and how that can cause cancer. In addition, we will solve the structure of that protein bound to microtubules, which might help developing new anti-cancer drugs.

column36: DCIS-Precise: A Genomics-Driven Model for Predicting DCIS Response to Radiation
column37: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast cancer but some DCIS will progress to invasive breast cancer. DCIS is not life-threatening but women with DCIS require treatment to lower their risk of developing invasive breast cancer. Most women with DCIS receive breast-conserving surgery and whole breast radiation treatment (RT) which is proven to lower the risk of recurrent disease including invasive breast cancer. Our inability to identify which women benefit from radiation results in unnecessary treatment of many women who will not benefit from radiation and inadequate treatment of women with aggressive but radiation-resistant DCIS who will develop recurrence despite receiving radiation. Genomic biomarkers that predict chemotherapy benefit have revolutionized the treatment of breast cancer, but predictors of radiation benefit are unknown. The goal of this study is to develop a biomarker assay that predicts RT benefit in DCIS. This will help reduce unnecessary RT in women who have a low risk of recurrence. However, it will also identify those with aggressive DCIS who will respond (benefit) from radiation and identify those who have radiation-resistant disease in whom alternate interventions are needed to lower their future risk of breast cancer. To accomplish this goal we have established 3 cohorts of DCIS. The Sunnybrook institutional cohort will be used for genomic profiling and assay (termed DCIS RT assay) development. The Ontario population-based DCIS cohort and the Swedish DCIS clinical trial cohort will be used as two independent cohorts for validation of the novel assay. We will also create a nomogram which will help provide women with more accurate estimates of the risks/benefits of RT. We have assembled an international team of experts with a proven track record who have the expertise to accomplish this goal and improvement the management of DCIS by reducing over-treatment and reducing the future burden of invasive cancer worldwide.

column36: Mechanisms of action of antiestrogens: towards improved treatment of relapse in ER+ breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer death among Canadian women. Estrogens contribute to breast tumorigenesis by acting via a specific effector, estrogen receptor alpha (ER), present in 2/3 breast tumors. Inhibition of estrogenic action is achieved for therapeutic purpose via different drugs that have distinct mechanisms of action, collectively known as hormonal therapies. However, resistance occurs in 30-50% of breast cancer patients treated with hormonal therapies. The mechanisms of action of antiestrogens, a class of drugs frequently used for both first and second line hormonal treatment of ER+ breast cancer, are still not fully understood, preventing their optimal use in patients relapsing after hormonal therapies. The Mader lab has uncovered novel mechanisms of action for antiestrogens that explain the spectrum of clinical profiles displayed by this class of molecules, and has characterized the impact of different antiestrogens in models of resistance to hormonal treatments due to different genetic changes in the estrogen receptor. The current application will further characterize aspects of the mechanisms of action of antiestrogens that remain poorly understood, such as the proteins that cooperate with the estrogen receptor to lead to resistance to these agents. The team will also investigate novel therapeutic combinations that would increase response in progressing patients by suppressing estrogen signalling more efficiently.

column36: Regulation of proteostasis by glycosylation of nucleocytoplasmic proteins.
column37: The cells of all organisms need to adapt to changes in their environment. One mechanism enabling adaptation to environmental changes, including variation in nutrient availability and cellular stressors such as heat, is the ability of cells to tune their levels of specific proteins. This process, known as proteostasis, is of great interest to researchers because it is now well recognized that disruptions in proteostasis contribute to various diseases including various neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson and Alzheimer disease. Further, proteostasis appears to become slowly impaired in processes such as aging. One mechanism that has emerged as a regulator of proteostasis is the modification of a set of proteins, found on the inside of cells, with specialized sugar units. We have recently uncovered that this sugar modification regulates the stability of proteins right at the moment of their creation and extending on to when they are found in large protein complexes that fulfill essential roles in the cell. Because this sugar modification is abundant within cells and depends on the amount of available nutrients, we aim to understand the scope of this modification and its impact on the broad set of sugar modified proteins. We further aim to evaluate the locations of sugar modification and to then determine which of these are physiological important for cell function. These data will help guide more targeted strategies to manipulate this promising but poorly understood pathway that has already delivered compounds into clinical trials.

column36: Frailty assessment for older adults at points of care: Validating the electronic comprehensive geriatric assessment / frailty index (eFI-CGA)
column37: Frailty is characterized by loss of biological reserves across multiple organ systems resulting in an increased risk of death and other adverse outcomes. Mounting evidence suggests frailty may be modifiable and can be prevented and sometimes even reversed. Frailty guidelines recommend the early identification of frailty in "at risk" seniors to address modifiable variables. The Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is a well-established clinical tool used to determine older adults' medical, psychological, and functional capabilities. It provides key baseline data for identifying degrees of risk and establishing individual care plans. A deficit accumulation based frailty index can be calculated using CGA items (FI-CGA). Key to care planning, the FI-CGA precisely measures the level of frailty. Performing a CGA and calculating an FI-CGA typically requires extra work for front-line clinicians. Electronic healthcare tools offer a more time efficient, cost-effective alternative. In partnership with the world's experts in frailty, our team conducted a pilot study to develop an electronic CGA in the Electronic Medical Records system and to automate the simultaneous calculation of an eFI-CGA in primary care and family medicine. The EMR allows widespread use across the healthcare system, making an eCGA and eFI-CGA an example of how to provide efficient care for older adults. This project aims to establish the reliability and validity of the eFI-CGA for widespread use in the management of older adults (e.g. identifying at-risk individuals and monitoring frailty changes in relation to short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes). Determining the eFI-CGA to be a reliable and valid measurement of frailty may help healthcare providers make more meaningful and comprehensive healthcare decisions; improve patients' clinical outcomes and self-management competence; reducing costly hospital admissions and prolonged stays by providing a better chance to address frailty at an early stage.

column36: The Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database: Expanded tools for molecular surveillance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the environment, agriculture, and clinic
column37: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is among the most pressing public health crises of the 21st Century as bacteria are evolving drug resistance faster than we can discover new drugs. Once treatable infectious diseases now include nearly untreatable strains. In addition, many of the 'miracles' of modern medicine, such as chemotherapy or routine surgery, are under threat due to a degraded ability to control secondary infection. Discovery of new antimicrobials is furthermore at an all-time low, making stewardship of our current antimicrobial arsenal critical. Yet, we have recently seen emergence of very serious threats to our last two 'drugs of last resort' - carbapenem effectiveness has been undermined by emergence of NDM-1 in 2006 and colistin effectiveness by emergence of MCR-1, first reported in November 2015. As such, while there is an urgent need to re-boot the drug discovery process for antimicrobials, we have an increasing need for better data for clinical practice, antimicrobial stewardship, and public health policy. In both a Canadian and global perspective, we need to know which resistance genes are prevalent, which genes are moving around, and which pose a threat. This Project Scheme proposal is focused on the accurate detection of resistome (the complement of resistance genes and mutations) and subsequent accurate prediction of antibiogram (the range of antimicrobial resistance and susceptibility) from raw DNA sequencing data. Building upon our successful Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database, we propose development and application of AMR gene detection models, high resolution prediction of resistance phenotype, and powerful prediction of molecular epidemiological context to push AMR genomic surveillance beyond its current state. Our key scientific objective is to supersede the current paradigm of basic sequence similarity detection tools with intelligent systems for DNA sequencing based molecular epidemiology of infectious pathogens.

column36: Nuclear Receptor Signaling in High-Fat Diet and Glucocorticoid-Induced Metabolic Disease
column37: Metabolic diseases, including diabetes and obesity, are reaching epidemic levels in the Western world. Chronic activation of the glucocorticoid receptor signaling pathway by stress hormones can contribute to diabetes and metabolic dysfunction. Diabetes is characterized by elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia) caused by the body's inability to properly secrete insulin and/or respond to increasing insulin levels. A high-fat diet and long-term therapeutic use of glucocorticoid drugs can cause obesity and type 2 diabetes. These negative effects are due in part to the glucose production pathway being strongly induced by glucocorticoid drugs in the liver and by the increased delivery of glucose precursors from other tissues, such as fat. We have a strong interest in understanding the molecular connections between high-fat diet, stress hormones (glucocorticoids) and the ultimate response obtained in tissues such as the liver and adipose tissue. We have identified a new protein called ARGLU1 that is important for transmitting the stress hormone signals to the liver to increase glucose production and does not appear to impact the role of glucocorticoids on the immune system. In this proposal, we will assess the importance of high-fat diet and glucocorticoid drugs on metabolism using in vivo mouse models that have ARGLU1 deleted from either the liver or the fat tissue. We will use new proteomic and sequencing technologies to uncover the different signaling mechanisms involved, and in the process, identify new determinants of glucocorticoid specificity. This project has high public relevance because it will allow us to identify new drug targets to benefit patients with metabolic disease and potentially identify pathways that can be targeted to allow safer glucocorticoid drug use for the future.

column36: Regulation of Hipk protein kinases by nutrient sensing mechanisms
column37: We study "Hipk" proteins and their regulation of cell and organ growth. Hipks are found in many species including humans and fruit flies. Research in flies provides a powerful and rapid way to use genetics to manipulate development and cellular growth. We generated a new type of fly strain that has too much Hipk protein. These flies have tumors, and their organs and limbs overgrow dramatically. We are very interested in how cells normally can keep Hipk proteins under control, so that they don't cause such effects. We used genetic tricks to find other proteins that are required for Hipk to be so potent. When we remove either of these two proteins (called 'OGT' and 'Siks') the flies no longer get tumors or malformed limbs. This tells us that these two proteins help Hipk trigger overgrowth. OGT and Siks are both interesting proteins because they help a cell sense how many nutrients are available to it. So when there is a lot of food (like sugar) OGT and Siks have roles in the cell that are different than during times of starvation. We propose to study in detail exactly how these two proteins can control Hipk activity, and also to learn how Hipk is influenced by nutrients. This is important because a number of studies have shown that cancer cells are more aggressive and grow faster in high nutrient conditions, and we think Hipks may be contributing to this. Since OGT and Siks both promote Hipk activity, we think that there are counteracting proteins that work to put the brakes on Hipk, preventing it from hijacking the cell's normal control of growth. Therefore, we plan to find other proteins that might be involved in controlling both fly and human Hipk proteins. All together, these studies will give us new information about how cells control their growth and how this process gets disrupted in cases of development and disease, and how these might be linked to diet and nutrition.

column36: Opportunities for Moving More and Sitting Less: Exploring a Whole School Approach to Improve Children's 24-Hour Movement Patterns
column37: Physical activity (PA) participation, limited sedentary behaviour (SB), and sufficient sleep are associated with numerous positive health and academic outcomes. The Canadian 24-hour movement guidelines encourage a daily balance; yet, only 9% of Canadian children meet the recommended 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous PA per day. Further, only 24% of Canadian children and youth meet the guideline of no more than two hours of recreational screen time per day, and 31% of children are sleep-deprived. These behaviours are interactive, such that screen time can disrupt sleep and displace PA, while lack of sleep can reduce PA and is linked to increased screen time. Schools are an ideal setting for recalibrating children's health behaviours, yet research has not examined the independent and relative contributions of school day segments (PE, breaks, instructional time) as well as contextual and regional factors (e.g., school schedules, urban/rural) influencing these behaviours within the 24-hour context. The proposed research aims to improve children's ability to meet the 24-hour movement guidelines by identifying school day opportunities for increasing PA and reducing SB, and then implementing feasible theory-based and context-specific strategies with a meaningful impact on children's behaviour. We will use a collaborative whole-school approach that engages key community stakeholders (parents, teachers, administrators, health promoters, students). Specifically, we will longitudinally measure 24-hour activity patterns and mental health of children in Grades 1-8 in NE and SW Ontario over a 3-year period, while assessing stakeholders' perceptions of children's PA, SB, and sleep patterns. This data will help inform and evaluate intervention strategies. Our research addresses important gaps related to children's PA, SB, sleep, and the importance of theory- and school-based strategies on children's 24-hour activity patterns.

column36: White matter plasticity in brain synchronisation and memory
column37: Our brain connections are insulated with a fatty white substance called myelin. Across the entire brain this insulation is called white matter. White matter helps in sending messages in the brain and the growth of new white matter - or white matter plasticity - is thought to be very important in brain communication. Disrupted white matter plasticity occurs in many brain disorders and can cause difficulties in thinking. Despite this problem, it is not yet known how white matter plasticity has an impact on the brain communication that produces learning and memory. It is important to know this because understanding these links can help us in creating and testing new treatments for brain disorders. In this proposal we will ask whether white matter plasticity helps in remembering through fine-tuning brain communication. To answer this question we will study: (a) children and adolescents who have memory impairment and disrupted white matter growth because of their treatment for a brain tumour, (b) mice whose genes have been edited to disturb white matter plasticity, and (c) computer simulations of brain function. Using neuroimaging we will measure the growth of white matter and brain activation during a memory task in children and adolescents who were treated with cranial radiation for brain tumours and healthy children. In mice we will measure the impact of genetically disrupting white matter plasticity on the growth of new myelin, brain communication, and memory. Using computer simulations we will model the impact of disturbing white matter plasticity on brain activation. By studying children with white matter injury, mice where we can genetically modify white matter plasticity, and computer models - all at the same time - we can decode the role of white matter plasticity in brain communication and remembering. Through this work we can identify people with brain disorders who are at-risk for long-term learning problems and develop treatments to help them.

column36: The HeLiX Trial: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Tranexamic Acid Versus Placebo to Reduce Perioperative Blood Transfusion in Patients Undergoing Liver Resection
column37: Liver resection is the optimal treatment for patients with liver tumors. Despite improvements in preoperative imaging and evaluation of liver functional reserve, intraoperative blood loss remains a major risk factor for postoperative complications and long-term survival. In Canada, TXA is rarely used in patients undergoing liver surgery. This grant will support a multicentre, blinded, definitive RCT examining the impact of TXA on blood transfusion and long-term survival in patients undergoing liver resection.

column36: The role of episodic, declarative, and spatial memory systems in the planning and control of real-world action tasks
column37: The ability to skillfully interact with objects is critical in most daily tasks and, therefore, impairments to this ability, which often occur following stroke or neurological disease, are particularly devastating. To date research on object manipulation has focused on simple object lifting movements. However, real-world action tasks, such as making a cup of tea or preparing a meal, involve interacting with multiple objects as they are lifted, moved about in space, and lifted again. Skilled performance of such tasks requires keeping track of the weights of the objects based on their appearance and, especially when handling similar looking objects, their location. Thus, not only do manipulation tasks require declarative and spatial memory resources, involved in encoding the properties (e.g., weight) and locations of objects, they engage an 'episodic-like' memory that, as the task unfolds, links object weights to particular locations at particular points in time. This raises the provocative idea that medial temporal lobe (MTL) structures, which have been implicated in episodic, declarative and spatial memory, are engaged in object manipulation tasks. The broad objective of this research project is to investigate, using advanced neuroimaging methods, the role of MTL structures in the planning and control of object manipulation tasks. Motivated by extremely promising initial results, the proposed experiments will test a series of highly novel hypotheses about how MTL structures encode and combine information about object weights and locations during manipulation tasks.

Our recent data show that the regulation of this pathway controls inflammation in a mouse model of IBD and that the blockade of the nucleotide receptor P2Y6 expressed at the luminal surface of the intestine fully prevents inflammation in this model. column36: The cellular mechanisms underlying sensory motile ciliopathies
column37: The cells lining the airway have tiny hair-like structures named motile (or moving) cilia. We plan to study how this novel cilium might cause lung disease. This research is highly innovative because it applies basic new imaging technologies, capable of visualizing molecules in cells more clearly than ever before, to better understand an important clinical problem. column36: Brain networks and neurocognitive aging
column37: As we grow older we continue to gain a wealth of knowledge and experience across many life domains. This vast store of knowledge and lived experience can be accessed to support decision making, problem solving, and reasoning, all essential functions for performing activities of everyday life. At the same time, some cognitive abilities which allow us to function in novel or changing situations decline with age. This suggests that if our knowledge and experience is not a 'good fit' with the problem we're confronting or the decision we're making, then bringing this information to the table might not help, and could even harm our ability to make decisions or solve problems. Unfortunately, our understanding of how to effectively harness this repertoire of knowledge and experience to aid cognitive functioning in later life remains limited. Interestingly, changes in the brain that occur with aging seem to reflect this pattern of age-related cognitive changes. Communication between brain regions involved in accessing our stored knowledge, and those involved in applying it in novel situations, increases with age. This suggests that older adults may rely on increased communication flow between these brain regions to gain access and use past knowledge to support cognitive functioning. In the proposed research we investigate this possibility using brain imaging and cognitive testing. We are interested in discovering whether age-related changes in communication patterns between these brain regions are associated with cognitive abilities in later life. Our goal is to understand what factors may help older adults to take advantage of these brain changes, and to maximally leverage their knowledge and life experience to support functioning in everyday life.

column36: Investigating drug therapies for inherited and acquired long QT syndrome using iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and zebrafish whole hearts as translational models
column37: Each heart beat is generated by a co-ordinated wave of electrical excitation that spreads across the heart muscle. Each wave causes the muscle to contract and pump blood in the circulation. The waves have to be tightly controlled so that the heart beats in a normal rhythmic manner. Changes in the electrical activity and the spread of excitation can lead to a heart attack. The electrical activity is controlled by proteins in the membranes of the heart cells that form channels. Failure of these channels to work properly is associated with abnormal heart rhythm, heart attack and sudden death. Dysfunction can result from an inherited gene mutation, or as a side effect of other drugs. We propose to test the ability of new drugs to activate these channels to overcome the dysfunction. To study this, we will use two strategies. Firstly, we will use heart cells, beating in a dish, which carry one of the gene mutations or are exposed to a drug that causes channel dysfunction. Secondly, we will use whole hearts taken from zebrafish, which despite their size difference, have electrical properties that are similar to human hearts. In both cases, we will measure the electrical activity of the cells or hearts and investigate how well the new activator drugs are able to restore normal function. Our aim is to identify novel drugs that could be used to prevent abnormal heart rhythm.

column36: Role of Pexophagy in Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders
column37: Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorder (PBD) is a group of rare genetic diseases affecting children. Presently there is no cure for this devastating disease. PBD is caused by the lack of a cellular compartment (organelle) called Peroxisomes, which is required to break down fats and toxins. Like all organelles, peroxisome numbers are maintained for optimal cell function by being continuously formed and broken down. We find that a conserved cellular process called autophagy breaks down peroxisomes. Recently we made a novel discovery that suggests that for most PBD patients, the lack of peroxisomes in their cells is not due to the inability of their cells to form them, but rather their inability to prevent the breakdown or degradation of peroxisomes by autophagy. To develop possible treatment that target peroxisome degradation, we propose to study the molecular mechanisms that governs peroxisomes degradation. Using advanced cell imaging and genetic approaches, we will determine the mechanisms that control peroxisome turnover. Such knowledge is required to develop treatments that can improve peroxisome numbers in PBD, which will not only prolong the life of those suffering with this disease, but also positively affect the quality of life of both patients and their families.

column36: Role of VPS33B-VPS16B in platelet granule formation
column37: Each drop of blood contains over a million platelets. These tiny cells patrol the bloodstream, and when they encounter cuts they initiate clotting to stop bleeding. Disease processes can also trigger the platelet clotting response, such as inflammation and rupture or atherosclerotic plaques. This can produce clots (thrombi) that cause heart attacks, strokes and other internal damage. Platelets also contribute to wound healing and immunity, and to plaque development and the spread and growth of cancers. The wide-ranging impacts of platelets on health and disease are linked to their ability release an assortment of proteins that are packed in structures called a-granules. These granules originate in megakaryocytes, large cells found in the bone marrow that can each shed thousands of platelets into the bloodstream. My group has identified several proteins required for a-granule development, including VPS33B and VPS16B. This research project will determine how these proteins and the complex they form, VPS33B-16B, control the early stages of a-granule development. We will employ approaches and techniques where my research group has gained internationally-recognized expertise, such as microscopy imaging and the development of animal and cell model systems. We will also work with local experts in advanced techniques such as molecular structure determination. The results of this project will advance understanding of platelet biology, which will assist efforts to control the negative impacts of platelets on health and enhance their positive roles. We will also open up new avenues of research, and since the proteins we are studying influence other processes besides a-granule development, our findings will be relevant to many aspects of cell biology, health and disease.

column36: Targeting the genital microbiota to reduce HIV susceptibility in African/Caribbean women
column37: The HIV epidemic disproportionately affects African, Caribbean and other Black (ACB) women. An important determinant of a woman's risk of acquiring HIV after an exposure during sex is the presence of inflammation in the genital tract, and although sexually transmitted infections (STIs) can cause inflammation, the types of bacteria present in the vagina even without an STI (called the vaginal microbiome) can too. A microbiome that has low numbers of bacteria called "lactobacilli", and instead has a range of other bacteria, is associated with more inflammation - and sometimes causes symptoms and is diagnosed as a condition called bacterial vaginosis (BV). Unfortunately, both this type of microbiome and BV itself are more common in ACB women. While it seems that treating BV should reduce HIV risk, we recently made the unexpected finding it increased some genital immune factors that enhance HIV risk. Furthermore, we saw that the types of lactobacilli that tend to be more common in ACB women (Lactobacillus iners) caused more inflammation than a different species (called Lactobacillus crispatus). This suggests that it may not be enough to simply treat BV, but that it may be necessary to restore an L. crispatus-predominant vaginal microbiome. To test this we propose three main aims: 1) A much more detailed clinical study of BV treatment in Toronto ACB women with BV will help us to really understand the impact on genital immune factors that increase HIV risk. 2) To assess the effect of these different bacteria on genital cells in the test tube. This allows us to exclude the possible effects of other genital bacteria, recent sex and so on. 3) A long-term collaborator at UCSF is running a clinical trial of an L. crispatus probiotic, and he is storing genital swabs. This will let us compare immune changes after BV treatment in women who restore an L. iners-predominant microbiome vs. one with L. crispatus, and also the potential impact of this new probiotic.

column36: Heptose-containing metabolites in Neisseria gonorrhoeae immune evasion and immunopathogenesis
column37: Neisseria gonorrhoeae has re-emerged as a global public health concern as it now causes nearly 100 million new infections each year and isolates have emerged that are resistant to all clinically-relevant antibiotics, prompting the US Center for Disease Control to name it as one of three 'urgent' microbial threats. The success of this organism is attributable in part to its capacity to colonize the female genital tract without obvious clinical manifestation, allowing it to persist undetected as it is spread to sexual partners. Consistent with this, N. gonorrhoeae does not express factors with overt virulent potential, but instead exhibits a lifestyle intent on avoiding and actively subverting immune detection. In this context, disease arises when the innate immune system eventually recognizes and responds to the infection with an overzealous neutrophil-based inflammatory response that damages the mucosal tissues. However, inexplicable in this context, this innate response does not lead to an adaptive immune response, so infected individuals remain susceptible to re-infection by even closely-related strains. This research project aims to understand the fine balance between immunity and immunopathogenesis in the context of N. gonorrhoeae infection, with a specific focus on the contribution of a bacterial-derived metabolite that we have recently discovered to have both immune modulatory and immune stimulatory properties.

column36: Enhancing immunotherapy with ultrasound stimulated bubbles
column37: Immunotherapies in cancer are used to help kick-start the body's natural defences to attack tumours. They are showing highly promising results in many cancer patients, while in others the effect is unfortunately limited, temporary or nonexistent. It is becoming increasingly clear that to broaden the impact of immunotherapies they will generally have to be combined with other therapies. In the case of a major class of immunotherapies- checkpoint inhibitors- a primary approach is to combine with therapies that can make tumour more 'hot' from an immune perspective. In recent work we have shown for the first time that when FUS is combined with microbubbles it can improve the tumour killing effects of a major checkpoint inhibitor. This project has the overall goal of investigating the mechanism of how this happens and how best to harness and control this effect. The work will be carried out in tumours that are located in the liver, as these affect a large number of patients and can benefit from locally applied treatments. The project is divided into three parts. In the first part we will use a cutting edge custom microscope to look directly at the effects of our FUS exposures on blood vessels in a specialized tumour model. This will tell us how vessels are affected, how to hone in on the appropriate settings, and what types of signals to 'listen' to from the bubbles when this is happening. Using this information, we will then use a custom MRI guided FUS system to create a control method for exposing realistic tumour models located in mouse livers. This will involve using the bubble signals as feedback to control the exposures. Finally we will investigate the therapeutic effects of using this method coupled with an immunotherapy in a realistic liver tumour model. The end result with be a validated new method to potentiate immunotherapy, which has the potential to impact the treatment of a large patient population.

column36: Glucose Lowering in T2DM: Mechanism of Action of Dipeptidyl Peptidase 4 Inhibitors
column37: We are looking into dipeptidyl peptidase 4, an enzyme, and its role in inactivating hormones that could have important implications for the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2DM). We eat for energy, and sugar is a main source of energy for the body. When we eat, sugars are absorbed into the blood stream, but these molecules are toxic to blood vessels if they stay in circulation for long periods of time. They are removed by the action of insulin, which is secreted from the pancreas rapidly in response to food. T2DM occurs when the pancreas does not secrete enough insulin or the cells no longer listen to the signal from insulin. When glucose remains in the blood stream, over time complications like cardiovascular disease can occur. Elevated blood glucose can be corrected by inhibiting an enzyme called DPP4, which acts like a pair of scissors, cleaving proteins and inactivating them. One of the proteins it inactivates is a messenger carrying signals from the human gut to the pancreas that releases insulin and lowers blood glucose levels. By understanding where DPP4 cleaves this messenger, we can make a molecular map indicating which cells we need to target to allow the messenger to get its signal through. The molecular map will allow us to leverage what occurs normally in our bodies to improve what are known as combination treatments for diabetes. Currently, over 25% of Canadians live with T2DM or pre-T2DM. This amounts to over 11 million people, highlighting the need for new therapies.

column36: Relative deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase in arterial smooth muscle cells as a novel target for atherosclerosis treatment and prevention
column37: Background/Importance: Atherosclerosis or "hardening of the arteries" is the leading cause of death in Canada and worldwide. Accumulation of harmful cholesterol from LDL particles in blood vessels is the key reason for formation of the blockages or "plaques" that lead to heart attacks and strokes. A key enzyme called lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) is necessary to break down the cholesterol molecules from LDL so that cells can excrete this cholesterol and reduce the size of plaques. Goals/Research Aims: We recently reported that the type of cells accumulating the most cholesterol in arteries are smooth muscle cells (SMCs), not macrophages, a type of white blood cell attracted into the artery due to damage and inflammation, as long believed. While studying the reason SMCs accumulate the most cholesterol, we have made the original observation that they have a relatively low amount of LAL when compared to macrophages. We therefore want to test the possibility that low LAL in SMCs is the main reason these cells do not excrete their excess cholesterol, and that increasing the amount of LAL in SMCs is a novel way to reduce atherosclerosis. Approaches: To address this question we will 1) examine whether giving cells back LAL helps them to turn on the cholesterol removal pathway, 2) study human coronary arteries and aortas to confirm that SMCs in the plaques have low levels of LAL, 3) study whether mice, which also show most cholesterol in SMCs in the artery plaque, also have reduced LAL in SMCs and whether extra LAL corrects their ability to excrete cholesterol, and 4) study whether mice that have an increase in LAL specifically in their artery SMCs show less plaque development and increased ability to remove existing plaque. Expected Outcomes: Based on our strong initial data we expect these studies to show that low levels of LAL in artery SMCs is a major cause of plaque formation, and that supplementing LAL in the SMCs is a novel way to reduce heart attacks and strokes.

column36: Priming Notch-activated basal like breast cancer for immune checkpoint blockade
column37: Genes that control normal breast growth can also be involved in the development of breast cancer. For example, genes called "Notch" control breast development but when active at the wrong time and place, can lead to breast cancer. Our group has previously shown that patients, whose breast cancers have abnormal Notch, have very aggressive disease and poor survival rates. We have recently discovered that Notch helps breast cancer grow by causing the release of special proteins called "cytokines" from tumor cells. Cytokines act as beacons to attract immune cells to the tumor. Against expectations, some of these immune cells actually help the tumor grow and spread. Scientists have known for decades that cytokines encourage the onset of diseases like arthritis and kidney disease. For this reason effective drugs that destroy cytokines (anti-cytokine drugs) have been developed. Based on our work, these drugs may be useful to fight breast cancers that depend on Notch. We predict that cancers with abnormal Notch, high levels of certain cytokines, and large numbers of specific immune cells will be the best candidates for anti-cytokine treatment, but the details need to be learned. In this project anti-cytokine drugs will be tested in mice that develop breast cancer. This project will provide evidence that breast cancer patients can be effectively treated with anti-cytokines. Repurposing these drugs for cancer could rapidly bring them into the cancer clinic, reducing time and cost and saving the lives of patients who previously had few options.

column36: Evaluation of a group education program to improve the transition from pediatric to adult care for emerging adults with type 1 diabetes
column37: Emerging adulthood, the transition period between childhood and adulthood, is a life stage that is challenging even for those without medical illness. For those with diabetes they must additionally learn to take responsibility for their own health. At this time, emerging adults (ages 18-30 years old) also move from pediatric to adult medical healthcare systems. This transition period places them at risk for disengaging from the healthcare system, only to return with diabetes-related complications. Despite the recognized importance of transition care, the medical literature on this topic is limited. At this moment, we know little about how to provide transition care services to emerging adults with diabetes. We propose to examine group education visits as an alternative and potentially cost-effective approach. Such visits have the potential to enhance peer-to-peer support. We will study if group education visits better prepare emerging adults for adult care and reduces their risk of complications as compared to usual care. We will conduct a prospective, randomized, allocation-concealed, single blind controlled trial of adolescents with diabetes (ages 17 years +/- 3 months) followed at one of the two university hospital-based pediatric diabetes clinics in Montreal. Interventions will occur over 12-months. Follow-up will be to 24 months from enrollment. Visits in the active arm will consist of a group education visits (every 3 months) followed by an individual appointment with the patient's diabetes physician. The group session, facilitated by a diabetes nurse educator, will be a patient-driven discussion on topics relevant to adolescents with diabetes. Patients in the control arm, will have in parallel, individual appointments with their diabetes physician as per usual care. Ultimately, our study can serve as a foundational step in guiding the development of transition care services across all childhood-onset chronic diseases.

column36: The Canadian ADNI BraIn Donation and Neuropathology Network (CABIN) - Optimizing Canadian Participation in the Neuropathology Program of ADNI
column37: Canadian sites have been active in the Alzheimer Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) since its inception. ADNI is a major study to track the progression of Alzheimer Disease (AD), devise tests to use as outcomes for potential interventions, and to develop accurate means of risk assessment for AD. Currently, there are Canadian ADNI centres in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, and London Ontario. ADNI has a neuropathology component to obtain brain autopsies in any of the >1000 participants who succumb to their illness. Unfortunately, Canadian sites have provided few brain autopsies in ADNI. Our relatively poor performance here reflects the lack of a national program and infrastructure for research brain donation and tissue banking at the Canadian sites. In contrast, brain donation programs and academic neuropathology cores are present in all U.S. centres. In this grant we are proposing to establish the infrastructure necessary to maximize the brain autopsies for the ADNI program in Canada; referred to here as the Canadian ADNI BraIn bank Network (i.e. CABIN). The coordinating centre for CABIN will be under direction of Dr. Ian Mackenzie (University of British Colombia), an internationally recognized neuropathology expert in dementia. He will work with a team of dementia neuropathologists and clinicians, at the respective Canadian ADNI centres. Not only will CABIN provide brain samples for ADNI, but it will establish the organization, planning, oversight, personnel and physical infrastructure needed to promote brain donations for other ongoing and future dementia research programs in Canada. The creation of this infrastructure will be transformative to the ability to study the causes of these diseases in Canada.

column36: The Frequency of Screening and SBT Technique Trial: The FAST Trial (North American Weaning Collaborative)
column37: Background: The sickest patients who are admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) often require assistance with their breathing. When patients start to get better, they gradually do more of the breathing and the machine does less-this is called weaning. Although ventilator use saves lives, the longer it is used, the more complications can occur. Clinicians aim to wean patients from ventilators in a timely and safe manner. In most ICUs, patients are screened (looked at) once per day to see if they are ready to undergo a weaning test (using a variety of techniques) to see if the breathing tube can be removed. Screening more than once per day may allow more weaning tests to be conducted. Knowing the best way to do a weaning test is important because some methods may better determine who can have the breathing tube removed safely. At present, we don't know the best way to wean patients from ventilators. Patients: Adults in North American ICUs who are on ventilators for at least 24 hours and who can take breaths on their own. Interventions: Patients in our study will receive one type of screening and one type of weaning test at random. In the 'once daily' screening groups, clinicians will screen patients each morning. In the 'two or more times daily screening' groups, patients will be screened in the morning, afternoon, and whenever else clinicians wish to screen. When screening criteria are met, patients will undergo one of two weaning tests with low ventilator support or no support. Outcomes: The main outcome of this study will be the time for patients to be successfully removed from the ventilator - an outcome important to patients, families, and clinicians. Relevance: For patients, this study will clarify the best way to remove them from ventilators in a timely and safe manner. For clinicians and our health care systems, this study holds promise to improve patient outcomes and change how care is delivered in North American ICUs.

column36: Giving Voice to Mothers; Measuring access to high quality, respectful maternity care in Canada
column37: Person-centred care values the preferences and cultures of patients, supports informed decision-making, and is linked to improved outcomes and reduced healthcare costs. By contrast, lack of involvement in decision-making and mistreatment during the course of pregnancy and birth can lead to several adverse outcomes, including impacts on mental health and parenting success. In Canada very little is known about whether childbearing women are encouraged to lead decisions about their care, if they feel pressured or coerced into accepting interventions or tests, or if they feel their preferences for care are respected by care providers. Patients who experience mental illness, poverty, lifestyle, immigrant status, or other vulnerabilities during pregnancy may face barriers to access to their preferred modes of care. Our team includes consumers, researchers, clinician leaders and community partners. We will use a community-led process to design a study that focuses on the World Health Organization standards for high quality, respectful maternity care: "safe, effective, equitable and person-centred care". Using a patient-designed survey instrument we will examine experience and outcomes of maternity care across diverse communities in Canada. Our previous studies, Changing Childbirth in BC and Giving Voice to Mothers: US, used best practices for patient-oriented research. We will recruit a broad sample of people who had care during a pregnancy in the last 5 years, using community networks, social media, and Survey Cafes at locations where members from targeted communities access services, with peer assistance for data-entry. We will support communities to interpret results and tell the story to clinicians, hospitals, and government. Our study will raise awareness about options and rights in maternity care, improve health professional education, and lead to data-driven policies to improve health outcomes and to lower costs associated with the quality of maternity care.

column36: PRICE 2: A phase 3 randomized controlled trial of phlebotomy resulting in controlled hypovolemia to prevent blood loss in major hepatic resections
column37: The need for major liver surgery is growing rapidly. Despite improvements in techniques, these operations continue to carry a significant risk of hemorrhage and blood transfusion. Hypovolemic phlebotomy represents a simple, cheap, safe, and underreported intervention to decrease blood loss and transfusion in liver surgery. Blood transfusion is known to pose significant risk for patients. This technique involves the removal of blood from a patient prior to cutting the liver. It is thought that this approach decreases the blood pressure within the liver, which may lead to less bleeding while it is being cut. The patient's own blood is given back once the liver has been cut. As a result, it is thought that this technique decreases the need for blood transfusion. This grant proposes a clinical trial to test whether hypovolemic phlebotomy is in fact effective at reducing the need for blood transfusion in major liver surgery. Patients from three Canadian liver surgery hospitals will be randomly assigned to receiving surgery using the usual technique or using hypovolemic phlebotomy. After surgery, patients will be followed for 30 days and the number of patients requiring blood transfusions will be compared between the two study groups. If successful, this study will lead to the saving of large amounts of altruistically donated blood and will have a major impact upon all future liver surgeries worldwide.

column36: Adapting and scaling-up "Peer Navigators" to targeted populations of street-involved youth in Canada and Kenya to increase linkage to HIV prevention, testing, and treatment
column37: Today, the people most at risk of HIV are those who are vulnerable, marginalized, and living in difficult situations. One such group is homeless youth. We already know that homeless youth are driven to the streets by poverty, family dysfunction, and child abuse and neglect. The circumstances of their lives once on the street involve many challenges including poverty, substance abuse and addiction, mental health issues, and vulnerability to sexual violence and trafficking; all of which raise their risk of acquiring and dying from HIV since they are also hard to engage in HIV care and treatment. We also know that homeless youth in Canada's cities are more likely to come from marginalized communities, including lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, queer, Two-Spirited and other Indigenous youth. Almost no research exists to guide HIV and other health service providers in successfully engaging with and caring for these extremely vulnerable populations. We are proposing a Peer Navigator (PN) program to engage homeless youth in Canada and western Kenya in HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. The PN model is based on the idea that peers-people who have themselves experienced youth homelessness and live with or are at-risk of HIV-intimately understand the challenges facing other homeless youth in a way that no researcher or healthcare worker can. As a result, peers are uniquely able to guide, connect, refer, and educate, and accompany homeless youth through the process of HIV prevention, testing and treatment.This project has three objectives:1) Adapt the Peer Navigator Model to three Canadian and two Kenyan sites: Toronto, London, Montreal, Kitale, and Huruma. 2) Describe and evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and ethics of the PN program among homeless youth, community, and stakeholders. 3) Evaluate the equitability (reach, uptake) and sustainability (cost, impact, uptake) of the PN program across the implementation sites.

column36: Scaling up PrEP for HIV Prevention: Optimizing strategies for targeting and delivering PrEP to MSM in British Columbia and Ontario
column37: Gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) account for over half of new HIV infections in Canada each year. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is an effective, safe and acceptable HIV prevention option among MSM, and holds great promise for reversing the course of the epidemic. However, for PrEP to achieve its full public health potential, two challenges must be overcome. First, PrEP must be targeted to those at highest HIV risk. Evidence suggests that having certain bacterial sexually transmitted infections or scoring highly on a validated risk index are particularly strong predictors of subsequent HIV. Since public health units routinely generate these data through daily activities, personnel could readily build such PrEP targeting strategies onto existing healthcare encounters. Second, more providers are needed within the healthcare system to deliver PrEP at scale. Engaging primary care providers, sexual health clinics nurses and PrEP-specific clinics in PrEP delivery may relieve the bottleneck of having too few specialists. Our experienced, multidisciplinary team in British Columbia and Ontario will implement and study the scale-up of these targeting and delivery strategies. Public health units and PrEP delivery sites in 5 cities will routinize a cascade of steps including identifying MSM with these criteria, offering PrEP services, linking patients to care, and ultimately initiating and retaining them on PrEP over time. Our research team will document how well the cascade is operationalized, tabulate healthcare costs, analyze qualitative and quantitative data on barriers and facilitators, and provide ongoing feedback to program implementers to inform how they modify programs. By synthesizing findings in mathematical models of HIV transmission we will determine the optimal strategies for targeting and delivering PrEP to MSM that maximize infections averted for the least additional cost, across a range of social, health systems and epidemic contexts.

column36: Addressing sexual- and drug-related HIV risk among young gay, bisexual and other MSM
column37: In BC and many other contexts, there are increasing concerns that HIV and other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs) diagnoses (e.g., chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are accumulating among young gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) at higher rates than previous generations. Our team's level of interaction and integration will be high, and we have designed our research approach, governance structure and scale up activities to facilitate this approach to collaboration. column36: Understanding contextual factors to effectively and equitably scale up GetCheckedOnline to diverse populations and geographic settings
column37: Digital health services are thought to be cost-effective and improve access particularly in rural areas, despite limited evidence and challenges to their implementation. We need to examine the "rhetoric and reality" of these services, and understand what external factors influence their success or failure. GetCheckedOnline (GCO) is an effective program developed by the BC Centre for Disease Control to reduce barriers in accessing testing for sexually transmitted infections and blood borne infections (STBBI). Research from the Vancouver pilot phase of GCO has found the service to be acceptable and effective in reaching people with barriers to accessing testing. Our initial analysis of GCO's scale-up to other urban, suburban and rural communities in two regional health authorities (RHA) in BC has found differences from Vancouver and between expansion sites (e.g., in the proportions of first-time testers). Further scale-up in BC is planned to other RHA, and eventually to other parts of Canada. However, further adaptation of GCO may be needed to reach other populations facing barriers to STBBI testing. Our team's overall goal is produce research which leads to the best implementation and maximum effectiveness of GCO for multiple populations affected by STBBI, and that informs further scale-up in BC and potentially in other parts of Canada. We do this in order to reduce barriers to accessing testing, leading to earlier diagnosis and linkage to care for STBBI in Canada. Our research approach uses an implementation science framework to: (1) understand what works, for whom, during scale-up; (2) adapt the intervention for better impact in minority language communities, men sex workers, and people who inject drugs; (3) assess the feasibility of implementation in a different health care system (Toronto); and (4) describe external factors influencing GCO implementation and whether access is improved equitably across populations who use it.

column37: Canada is experiencing a public health emergency related to medical (prescription) opioids and, in some regions, illicitly produced opioids (e.g., fentanyl, heroin). Services are being expanded in many jurisdictions, but progress is slow and only patchworks of public health interventions and treatment services are currently in place across the country. Without scaling up evidence-based programs in different regions and among different populations, the individual and population burden of opioid use will continue to be high. This proposal was written in response to CIHR's Request for Applications to the Canadian Research Initiative on Substance Misuse (CRISM) network for a directed grant addressing the opioid emergency (https://tinyurl.com/y9sgx64x). CRISM is a unique CIHR funded national research network of researchers, system managers, people with lived experience, and decision-makers. Its purpose is to conduct research and support knowledge translation to enhance delivery of evidence-based interventions for substance misuse.CRISM will develop and execute a program in four thematic areas that have high potential for reducing the individual and population burden of opioid use: (1) scaling up public health interventions (i.e., safer consumption services and naloxone delivery); (2) optimizing opioid use disorder treatments (i.e., oral and injectable opioid pharmacotherapy); (3) improving the evidence base for withdrawal management, psychosocial and recovery-based treatment options; and (4) collaboratively developing new intervention approaches to meet the needs of high-risk target populations. The proposed implementation science program will be developed purposively, capitalizing on service innovations that are rapidly being deployed at the regional level; strategically, by developing effective longer-term working relationships with groups disproportionately affected by the opioid emergency; and collaboratively, through a structured process to engage CRISM member expertise and people with lived experience of opioid problems. The overall aim is to inform and support the implementation of an improved national intervention continuum to address this complex health challenge.

column37: Advances in human genomics are revolutionizing the field of medicine by supporting the development of treatments that are specifically tailored to individual patients. column36: Cortico-Cortical Communication and Processing
column37: The brain is often conceived of as modules that process particular bits of information. Like all computers, brain modules also have to communicate with each other. Many of the interactions between brain areas are not even just for communication--they are modulatory, meaning that the interactions serve to change the level or type of activity in a given part of the brain. Understanding the nature of these interactions will have direct implications for models of brain function and for designing effective neuro-rehabilitation strategies.

column37: My research addresses how early life stress affects adult behavior, which has critical health implications in humans. Because this relationship between stress, brain development, and behaviour exists in all animals, it likely relies on evolutionarily ancient mechanisms. column36: The Endocannabinoid System in Glucocorticoid-Induced Metabolic Outcomes: A Focus on Genetic Variants of Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase
column37: Chronic stress, with the coordinated rise in stress hormones known as glucocorticoids (GCs, cortisol in humans), is a major risk factor for obesity. Evidence suggests that GC actions underlie the effects of chronic stress on energy balance. Yet the relationship between stress, GCs, and energy balance is highly complex. For example when confronted with stress, some individuals gain weight, whereas others lose weight. It is believed that an individual's response to stress and GCs is moderated by genetic variants. Nevertheless, genetic risk factors at the interface between energy balance and stress regulation remain elusive. In humans, there is a common genetic variant in the gene for fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), present in ~38% of Europeans. This genetic variant (C385A) reduces levels of FAAH. This reduction in FAAH ultimately affects the endocannabinoid system since FAAH breaks down the endocannabinoid ligand anandamide. Indeed anandamide regulates energy balance and the stress response. Importantly, the low-expressing FAAH variant (A-allele carriers) has been associated with improved stress coping and increased rates of obesity in humans. Thus, the FAAH variant is positioned to moderate stress-induced metabolic outcomes. The proposed project will be the first to examine whether genetic variants of FAAH predict individual susceptibility to obesity in response to chronic GC exposure. We will employ a mouse model, which recapitulates the common human mutation in the FAAH gene (C385A), to investigate the effects of differential FAAH expression (between C- and A-allele carriers) on feeding and energy expenditure. This project has the potential to establish a molecular link between energy balance and stress, and help to explain why diverging metabolic outcomes arise when confronted with stress. Together, the outcomes of these studies may have implications for obesity prevention, via lifestyle modification (stress reduction) in genetically susceptible individuals.

column37: Mental illnesses like anxiety and depression affect more than 20% of the Canadian population, and lead to an economic burden at the population level of an estimated $51 billion per year. A common risk factor for these conditions is adversity or abuse during early life. Interestingly, even during prenatal development, exposure to stress or adversity in the mother can be transferred to the fetus brain, and subsequently can permanently affect how the stress hormone system is regulated. Given the prevalence of mental illnesses and the role of stress in causing them, it is imperative to learn more about the biological mechanisms involved and the system components where intervention is possible. Some progress has been made in elucidating the neurobiology of stress, but many questions cannot be addressed with current tools, which include animal models and 2-dimensional human cell culture systems. This proposal aims to establish 3-dimensional culture systems called cerebral organoids or "mini-brains" - stem-cell derived tissues that mimic the human brain - as research models for developmental psychiatric disturbances. Stress will be simulated in these cerebral organoids by manipulating the main hormone associated to stress, cortisol. Molecular mechanisms will be investigated comparing 'stressed' and 'unstressed' conditions in cerebral organoids by studying specialized cells types. This is important, because the human brain is very complex, and very different processes occur from cell to adjacent cell (i.e. neurons, etc.). Comparing findings from this model to evidence from brains of individuals who experienced severe adversity during early childhood and subsequently suffered from depression in adulthood, will allow placement of our findings into the clinical context. The outcomes from this research have the potential to expedite identification of at-risk populations, and even guide development of intervention strategies.

column36: "Through the veil": Revealing Mysteries of San Rock Art
column37: Rock art is one of the most ancient expressions of the human mind, and is found across the world, ranging from the Late Pleistocene to the present day. It raises several questions: When was it first produced? How was it made? Who created it? In this project, such questions are intended to be answered for San rock art, also called Later Stone Age (LSA) rock art, one of the longest traditions in the world. Thanks to detailed interpretative work using the extensive San ethnographic studies available, the meaning of LSA rock art is well known. In contrast, little is understood about how the paint itself was made or what it was made from, while the age of these paintings also remains mostly unknown. However, this information is critical to interpreting rock art and apprehending the changes in the art and, by extension, societal and spiritual changes among the San groups that may have occurred when they were in contact with sedentary populations and then Europeans. We aim first at studying San rock art: its representations, the techniques used by the artists, the provenance of raw materials, and detailing its changes through time. Second, we seek to explore changes in San spirituality and to assess whether they are linked to societal changes. To deal with these questions, San rock art will be characterised and dated and the same will also be done for portable art and objects with traces of pigments such as grindstones. This will be the first time that such comparisons are considered in the study of San rock art, though they are crucially needed to assess whether societal changes are linked to changes in the art. The main strength of this project is its interdisciplinary aspect, as it combines chemistry, geology, geochemistry, archaeology, material culture, and the history of art. All of these complementary fields are linked together to give new insights into the San groups, well-known by their art, but still mysterious in their beliefs and aspects of daily life

column36: Spatiotemporal resolution of the contributions of pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms to synapse-specific transmission variability and synaptic plasticity
column37: Activity-dependent changes of synaptic efficacy are the cellular basis of learning and memory. Synaptic plasticity bidirectionally modifies synaptic strength by enhancing or depressing transmission, effected through a complexity of mechanisms that act pre- and postsynaptically, over different time scales, and in response to different stimuli. Despite decades of intensive research, the fundamental question of how changes in synaptic efficacy are ultimately expressed during plasticity remains to be unequivocally answered; that is, to what extent and over what timescales do plasticity events modify respectively presynaptic neurotransmitter release and the number or function of postsynaptic receptors? This outstanding question represents a fundamental gap in our knowledge about how synaptic plasticity is evoked to modify the function of neuronal networks controlling behaviour. The rapid and dynamic regulation of AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPAR) surface mobility constitutes a major mechanism underlying synaptic plasticity. However, it is also apparent that the recruitment or removal of AMPARs by exo- and endocytotic mechanisms postsynaptically, and changes in neurotransmitter release probability presynaptically, are also involved in synaptic modulation during plasticity. Here, I propose to use a multi-level approach combining electrophysiology, genetically-encoded optical reporters, innovative molecular tools to control AMPAR trafficking, and state-of-the-art super-resolution imaging approaches to determine how the dynamics of AMPAR surface mobility postsynaptically, and synaptic vesicle release presynaptically, define the functional properties of synaptic transmission during both basal and plastic states. This work will shed new light on the fundamental mechanisms of synaptic transmission, plasticity and specificity, and advance our knowledge of the etiology of numerous psychiatric, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders that are linked to AMPAR dysregulation.

column36: YOUTH WELLBEING IN CHINA AND CENTRAL AMERICA:IMPLEMENTATION OF AN INTEGRATED PREVENTION AND INTERVENTION PROGRAM
column37: High rates of mental illness and addiction (often associated with self-harm) have been reported in China and Central America. Stigma, poor mental health knowledge, and limited awareness and/or accessibility to health services lead to low help-seeking, further compounding the problem. Thus, there is an urgent need for strategies to promote mental health knowledge to enable early identification and treatment and to improve help-seeking behaviour. The aim of this 5-year project is to implement and evaluate a multi-level, integrated mental health education, screening, and intervention program to improve functioning and well-being in youth in China, Honduras and El Salvador. About 5000 students in China, 2000 students in Honduras and 2000 students in El Salvador will be recruited. Participants will receive a 12-week mental wellness and leadership program (MWL) online (at universities) or in class (at vocational/technical schools). Curriculum topics will include mental health education (illness and stigma, help-seeking, stress management), social responsibility (prejudice, violence, gender-based violence), and leadership (values, skills). Students will be assessed on psychosocial function (e.g.distress, coping, stress, academic performance) and physiological measures of stress (saliva and hair cortisol) before and after MWL completion. An open-access phone app will be created to screen for emotional difficulties and addictive behaviours and will be available to MWL and non-MWL students. Those students who screen positive for significant emotional difficulties, as well as those with depression, anxiety and/or addictive behaviours who are referred by health professionals, will receive one of two forms of an 8-week internetbased cognitive-behavioural therapy (iCBT) program. The iCBT emotional well-being program will target mood and anxiety symptoms, and the iCBT addictions program will target substance abuse (including alcohol and tobacco) and problematic internet use. Students will be assessed on symptom and functional improvement as well as on physiological measures of stress before and after program completion. This project offers the opportunity to implement and evaluate the broad benefits of a novel integrated prevention and psychological intervention program for youth in culturally differing regions. The program will be adapted and incorporated into existing postsecondary institutions in the three countries with measurement of cross-cultural acceptability, efficacy, fidelity of implementation, and sustainability. It is proposed that the project will improve the mental wellness of transitional youth with good sustainability in two distinct global regions, and furthermore, it offers an opportunity to objectively evaluate to cost and benefit of this implementation.

column36: Implementation research: community intervention to prevent repeated suicide attempts in Ningxia China and Nunavut Canada
column37: BACKGROUND: Suicide is the most serious outcome of a variety of mental illnesses, including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, eating disorders and substance abuse. Reducing suicide mortality is an important objective of the World Health Organization's 2013-2020 Global Mental Health Action Plan and the United Nation's 2015-2030 Sustainable Development Goals. A prior suicide attempt is the most important risk factor for death by suicide, but regular brief community follow-up after an attempt can prevent repeated suicidal behavior. AIMS: This 5-year implementation science project will develop methods for adapting the WH0 SUPRE-MISS intervention for suicide attempters in parallel projects in Ningxia, China, and among Inuit in Nunavut, Canada. These methods for adapting SUPRE-MISS will then be promulgated in Inuit and other indigenous populations, other parts of China, other low- and middle-income countries, and other low-resourced settings in high-income countries. METHODS: PHASE 1. Conduct focus groups with local stakeholders to identify local factors that need to be considered when developing a location-specific version of SUPRE-MISS that provides a brief educational intervention about suicide prevention to individuals who have recently made a suicide attempt and periodic social support and access to emergency services to these highrisk individuals. PHASE 2. Pilot-test the adapted intervention in a small number of settings for one year. PHASE 3. Revise and then scale-up the intervention to more settings for 30 months and continuously collect outcome measures, process measures, and resource utilization measures (for cost-effectiveness assessment). PHASE 4. Conduct post-intervention focus groups with stakeholders to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the intervention. Integrate these qualitative results with the quantitative results (e.g., rates of repeated suicidal behavior) to prepare a report on the process of implementing the SUPRE-MISS intervention in low-resource settings. Work with administrators and policy makers in China, Nunavut, and other locations to develop policies that will widely promulgate the use of this approach to suicide prevention. FEASIBILITY: A strong multidisciplinary team with extensive experience in suicide prevention in the target communities has been assembled and the active support of local administrators and policy makers who can provide practical support for the project and develop policies to promote its results has been obtained. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: This project will develop methods that can be widely disseminated to help achieve the United Nation's ambitious goal of reducing suicide mortality by 1/3 by 2030. Combining findings from parallel projects in a low-middle-income country with those from a low-resource setting in a high-income country will provide a unique case example of how implementation science can be used to address complex mental health problems in different low-resource settings.
