column36: Enhanced Measurement-Based Care Effectiveness for Depression (EMBED): A Canada-China Implementation Project
column37: Depression affects 300+ million people globally and is now the leading cause of disability and burden of disease worldwide. In China, the National Mental Health Work Plan 2015-20 specifies improving the ability of healthcare facilities to identify depression and increase the treatment rate by 50%. Measurement-based care (MBC) - the routine use of validated outcomes such as the PHQ-9 depression questionnaire to guide clinical decision-making - is a simple evidence-based practice (EBP) that may help meet these objectives. However, there is still a significant care gap in the implementation of MBC in China and elsewhere. In Canada, we have adopted the concept of enhanced MBC (eMBC), in which technology can engage both patients & physicians in using MBC; eMBC enhancements include web and mobile app tools for patients to track their own progress with the PHQ-9, and an evidence-based, lowcost, low-intensity psychological treatment (guided self-management with telephone coaches) that has embedded patient measurement and feedback to physicians. EMBED: a Canada-China implementation project, proposes to develop a novel EBP implementation strategy by adapting, implementing and evaluating eMBC in diverse community mental health clinics in Shanghai, modeled on programs implemented in Canada. EMBED addresses 4 broad aims: 1) identify contextual enablers & barriers to MBC implementation; 2) explore physicianand patient-level factors as mediators for an EBP implementation; 3) provide clinical & health economic outcomes to establish effectiveness of eMBC; and 4) build knowledge & capacity for scale up of eMBC in China and beyond. Our hypothesis is that physician & patient factors that are barriers for implementation of standard MBC will be enablers for implementation of eMBC. To achieve these aims, we will first conduct a Situation Analysis to determine the key barriers & enablers for MBC implementation in Shanghai. We will adapt a Canadian eMBC program for the Chinese context, then will use a hybrid implementation-effectiveness design (an adaptive cluster randomized evaluation) to compare eMBC with standard MBC implementation in 12 community clinics, 240 physicians, and 1200 patients. We hypothesize that eMBC implementation will lead to superior implementation, patient and costeffectiveness outcomes, compared to standard MBC. EMBED will advance the international literature on MBC broadly by focusing on the understudied role of patients in implementation of MBC. column36: Linking Hearts: Advancing Mental Health Care of University Students Through Interdisciplinary Collaboration (in Jinan)
column37: Young people are vulnerable to the onset of mental illness. Research shows that delayed treatment of mental illness leads to negative outcomes. In China, prevalence of depression among university students is as high as 20 to 30%. However, 9 out of 10 people diagnosed with a mental disorder never sought mental health care. Stigma and low mental health literacy are among the most important help-seeking barriers. Further, mental health services, largely at specialized hospitals only, are overstretched, while community and informal levels of care are underdeveloped. To address this, the study will examine the implementation of an evidence-based intervention, Acceptance and Commitment to Empowerment - Linking Youth and 'Xin' (hearts) (ACE-LYNX), to: (1) decrease stigma (attitude), (2) increase mental health literacy (knowledge), and (3) promote individual well-being (outcomes) and the collective capacity to collaborate (action) to promote mental health and form an integrative network of care for students. ACE-LYNX consists of two components: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a mindfulness-based cognitive-behavioral intervention, and Group Empowerment Psychoeducation (GEP), psychoeducation integrated with principles of equity, empowerment, and social justice. The study will take place in three regions of Jinan, Shandong, China. We will engage one hospital and two universities in each region. We will begin with an assessment of contexts, consisting of a university student survey (n= 600), student focus groups (n=144), and stakeholder and professional focus groups (n=144). The data will inform intervention adaptation. Using a train-the-trainer model, we will train 90 interdisciplinary professionals to become ACE-LYNX-Pro Champions. They will in turn train the "2nd generation" ACELYNX- Pro Champions (n=270) and students to become ACE-LYNX Student Champions(n=360) with a lay version of the intervention. All champions will form a collaborative integrated mental health care network supported by a community of practice through a Learning Management System and Weixin (WeChat). The champions will be followed over 6 months for their outreach and health promotional activities, including using Weixin to form a Student Mental Health Virtual Network. The RE-AIM framework will be used to examine Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance/Sustainability of ACE-LYNX and the integrated network. Psychometric measures will track the intervention's impact on attitude (CAMI), knowledge (MAKS), empowerment (Bulls-Eye, monthly activity logs), and mental health outcomes (DASS-21, AAQ-II), while service volumes and Social Network Analysis will be used to examine the functioning of the real and virtual networks. We will apply an Integrated Knowledge Translation framework to engage key stakeholders throughout the study to ensure maximal impact and dissemination with the aim of system transformation at the micro, meso, and macro levels.

column36: Shared Care for ADHD in Children and Youth: Merging the Canadian and Chinese Experiences
column37: In the context of modern China, children experience a tremendous pressure to perform at high levels. This stressful environment is associated with depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation and attempts in adolescence. Children with a diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are highly inattentive, restless, impulsive, and therefore at high risk, despite a normal intellectual potential. ADHD is easy to diagnose and treat, but difficult to diagnose and treat well. The treatment effects are dependent on the quality of care and on the coordination of different interventions, planned according to individual needs. The first main barrier to treatment is the shortage of qualified clinicians. In response, our main strategy will be to implement a shared care between general practitioners (GPs) and specialists. The second barrier is the lack of training in GPs. We will implement a focused ADHD training targeted to the needs of GPs. A third barrier is the lack referral process. We will implement stepped care in which the patient is treated at the most appropriate level of care, depending on complexity or outcome. We will adapt the Canadian shared care model for ADHD to the Chinese context. To test its flexibility, it will be implemented within the pediatric care system in two districts of Shanghai and within the mental health care system in one district of Beijing. We will first assess how ADHD guidelines are used, and the existing collaboration between GPs and specialists. After a Consensus Conference, we will implement a shared care pathway and we will produce actionable findings in a formative evaluation to improve implementation. At the end of the setup phase, we will assess the use of guidelines, the deviation from the intended protocol, how its members evaluate the care process, examine the effectiveness with regard to ADHD outcome, and functioning of the pathway, in terms of patient flow and timing. Once the shared care model is functionally implemented, we will scale up the care system horizontally by linking it progressively with schools selected randomly in the target districts. Using already established collaborations with the educational psychologists, we will first survey the knowledge and perceived needs of teacher, then implement a screening strategy for ADHD problems in the schools, as well as web-based effective strategies to educate parents and teachers about ADHD and mitigate its impact. We will assess the effectiveness of the intervention, and how it changes the perception of ADHD and the help-seeking process, as well as the rate of referrals into the shared care system. These two steps will allow defining the scalable unit that could be used in further implementation of the model. A costeffectiveness analysis is integrated in the project in order to support its scalability. Beyond ADHD, this shared care model will be able to respond to various mental health treatment challenges, both in children and adults.

column36: Screening and management of perinatal depression within primary care
column37: Depression during pregnancy and after an infant's birth is more common in China than in high-income countries and can harm the mother, infant, and family. Chinese women's mental health needs are unmet given lack of investment in mental health, unequal distribution of mental health services, and few specialized healthcare providers to support mental health issues. Our goal is to create an effective perinatal depression screening and management (PDSM) program that will be sustainable within the maternal and child healthcare system in China. Our implementation strategy is guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and RE-AIM (Reach x Efficacy, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance) and includes 2 Phases: (1) Pilot in Ma'anshan City, Anhui Province during which we will, through stakeholder engagement, adapt current evidence and test the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted screening guidelines and psychosocial intervention (internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy; iCBT) by healthcare providers and women. We will use mixed-methods to (a) identify and evaluate various implementation strategies (e.g., individual, organizational) to promote uptake of the screening guidelines and iCBT; (b) evaluate acceptability (i.e., knowledge, attitudes, and behavior) before and after implementation of guidelines and iCBT; (c) evaluate reach by determining the degree to which the population that is eligible to benefit from the program actually received it; (d) evaluate treatment fidelity by determining the extent to which the screening guidelines and iCBT was implemented as designed by monitoring adherence, dosage of delivery (i.e., the number of weeks completed), and program quality. (2) Scale-up to Hefei (capital and largest city), Bengbu (mid-sized urban city), and Fuyang (urban city) adapting the screening guidelines and iCBT based on Phase 1, and using steps (a)-(d) to promote uptake. Our monitoring and evaluation plan includes evaluating impact, effectiveness, and quality (i.e., public health impact) in both the Pilot and Scale-up phases. Our project is jointly supported by Chinese and Canadian researcher, focuses on implementation research related to depression, an affective disorder that will become the second leading cause of disease by 2010. It also, addresses women's mental health during pregnancy and following birth when vulnerability to depression is intensified, and promotes uptake screening which promotes use of mental health service and iCBT a psychosocial self-administered intervention with support from a trained mental health care provider that promotes reduction in depressive symptoms. Our study will enable integration of PDSM into the maternal and child healthcare system with flexible guidelines that considers context, ensures mental healthcare is personalized and responsive to Chinese women's needs, and promotes implementation outcomes of acceptability, reach, and fidelity.

column36: Standardizing the treatment, prevention, and management of depression in China: a multi-disciplinary approach
column37: Depression is a common mental disorder affecting approximately 350 million people worldwide and representing the third leading contributor to the global disease burden (World Health Organization [WHO], 2012). However, much of the literature on the depression derives from studies conducted in Western Europe and North America. Consequently, there is a need for novel depression research in low- and middle-income countries, including China. In China, depression is highly prevalent but is not treated in existing community mental health programs, limiting many residents' access to mental health care and contributing to the large treatment gap. Currently, mental health care for depression exists at urban mental health centres; additionally, there is a lack of integration between primary and mental health care and the absence of mental health training for primary care physicians. Collectively, these factors hinder access to mental health care in rural and urban areas, and across communities of various socioeconomic backgrounds, languages and dialects. Thus, the development of community mental health prevention and treatment programs for depression would increase access to mental health care for residents of China in both rural and urban areas. Additional barriers that contribute to the treatment gap include culturally ingrained negativistic attitudes towards mental disorders that contribute to social- and self-stigma, and lack of education about mental disorders and their treatment. Consequently, our research endeavors, involving coordination between Canada and China, are as follows: (1) to help develop community-based mental health services for the early identification of individuals with depressive symptoms and prevention of clinical depression, (2) to improve access to mental health care and the management of patients with depression in community- and hospital-based settings, and (3) to establish international psychosocial networks or systems to monitor the quality of care. In addition, we aim to implement prevention and intervention strategies that address the aforementioned barriers to improve the quality of depression management and increase willingness to seek mental health care. Studies have reported that screening individuals with depressive symptoms and the subsequent provision of psychological therapy to prevent the onset of clinical depression is a cost-effective intervention, compared to treatment after depression onset. If depression prevention strategies become a standard part of mental health services, unnecessary suffering due to depression will be greatly reduced.

column36: Assessing the effectiveness of an online intervention addressing barriers to skin cancer screening behaviours among middle-aged men: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Melanoma can be a deadly disease when diagnosed at an advanced stage, but survival rates are > 98% when detected early and treated. Melanoma often develops with a visible, preclinical phase, hence there are opportunities for early detection via visually inspecting the skin. Skin self-examination (SSE) followed by physician-led clinical skin examination (CSE) are effective means to detect early signs of melanoma1. Middle-age men are often diagnosed with more advanced melanoma, have worse prognosis, and face higher mortality compared to women in the same age groups and younger men. Melanoma early detection interventions targeting men's SSE and CSE behaviours are sparse, primarily because male gender and older age are not generally regarded as risk factors for melanoma. Yet, approximately 60% of all deaths from melanoma occur in men of 50 years of age or older [SEER database; 2013]. Most available melanoma prevention interventions targeting SSE and CSE utilize an in-person educational model, which is time and resource-intensive, and potentially less amenable to men. There is an urgent need for low-cost, effective (evidence-based), and easily accessible interventions targeting middle-age men's SSE and CSE, as part of the overall effort to decrease melanoma-related mortality in this population.

column36: Contribution to neuroinflammation of immunometabolic reprogramming of resident microglia and infiltrating macrophages
column37: Macrophages are tissue-resident cells that fulfill homeostatic functions, notably in the central nervous system. Following assault, they become activated and secrete mediators that lead to a local inflammation (neuroinflammation). Moreover, large numbers of infiltrating macrophages exert inflammatory effects that contribute to neuroinflammation. Even though resident and infiltrating macrophages may have differing immunological functions and roles, these are dependent on their metabolism (a phenomenon called immunometabolism). As such, metabolic reprogramming can modulate macrophage functions, and subsequently their role, including their inflammatory activities and participation in the development of disease. While controlled inflammation is required to resolve an assault and repair damage, its exacerbation can result in permanent damage and debilitating disabilities. Indeed, exacerbated neuroinflammation is responsible for numerous life-threatening diseases whose burden on human health in Canada is extensive. However, information regarding the contribution to neuroinflammation of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming remains largely unknown. Consequently, the goal of this project is to study this contribution using a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Firstly, the metabolic processes of resident and infiltrating macrophages modulated during neuroinflammation, in comparison with homeostasis, will be identified. Thereafter the role of this reprogramming on the immunological functions of macrophages will be evaluated using cells isolated from mice deficient for key metabolic pathways and/or specific checkpoints previously identified. Finally, the contribution of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming to neuroinflammation and the development of and outcome of disease will be assessed using these same deficient mice. In summary, this project aims to dissect the contribution to neuroinflammation of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming

column36: Developing resilience to obesogenic food environments through food literacy
column37: More Canadians now die from diseases caused by poor diet than from smoking-related illnesses, and diets low in fruit and vegetable intake cost Canadians 3.3 billion dollars a year. The food environment profoundly influences diet and is associated with diseases such as obesity and diabetes. This environment has evolved so that children and adolescents are constantly fed cues to consume unhealthy foods. Food literacy is the foundation of healthy dietary practices and provides youth with an opportunity to build resilience to unhealthy food environments. Food literacy will equip youth with the abilities, knowledge and self-efficacy to make healthy food choices, which will reduce risk for diseases and decrease healthcare costs. This research will strengthen Health Canada's healthy eating strategy to improve healthy eating and protect vulnerable populations by understanding how to improve food literacy and make healthy dietary choices in unhealthy food environments.

column36: Beyond Function: Exploring Participation in Life Roles in People with COPD
column37: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a lung condition that makes it hard for people to breathe. Treatment for people with COPD usually focuses on helping them walk for longer and manage their breathing problems. A patient's ability to participate in life roles by visiting with friends and taking care of loved ones is another important part of health. Unfortunately, this is an area not often considered in people with COPD. In fact, people with COPD often say they feel alone and like they have lost their identity. In order to find ways to increase participation in people with COPD we need to start by finding an accurate and valid tool to measure it. Objective: We will test the ability of a questionnaire to measure participation in COPD. We will also see if our usual treatment has any effect on participation. Method: One hundred people with COPD in Toronto and Hamilton will complete a few questionnaires and physical tests. We will ask some of those people to complete the questionnaire a second time within one week. People with COPD who are starting a rehabilitation program will complete the participation questionnaire and some related tests at the beginning and end of their programs. This will tell us if the participation questionnaire measures what it should, if it can detect any change in participation that happens with rehabilitation and if there is meaningful change in participation during the program. Importance: This will be the first study to show the measurement abilities of this questionnaire in people with COPD. It will also be the first study to show if the usual treatment for people with COPD does anything to change participation. These projects will help us develop new treatments to increase participation in people with COPD. Being able to participate in life roles is important to patients so this will have a positive impact on their lives.

column36: The proteomic and metabolomic characterization of clear cell ovarian carcinoma: towards better management strategies
column37: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death for women from cancers, with about 25,000 women diagnosed in North America each year. Ovarian cancer is divided into subtypes based on molecular characteristics and clinical outcome. Although we have understood ovarian cancer as many diseases, the treatment has remained the same for the past 30 years for all subtypes - untargeted platinum-based chemotherapy. Clear cell ovarian cancer (CCOC) is the second most common subtype of ovarian cancer affecting many women. At late stage, it is more aggressive and resistant to current chemotherapy compared to other subtypes. Although deadly, CCOC is still not well understood and lacks effective targeted therapy. Existing molecular and genomic studies suggest that it is a metabolically driven malignancy, but its metabolic profile has not yet been studied. This research will be the first characterization of a large cohort of clinical cases of CCOC using protein expression in conjunction with global metabolite profiling. Understanding of the altered metabolism in CCOC will revolutionize the ovarian cancer research community and provide strong foundations on which to build further discoveries. Most importantly, we hope that identifying targetable metabolic pathways will guide the development of more effective therapies to help patients with this deadly disease.

column36: Developing An Unconscious Neural-Reinforcement Therapy for Common Fears
column37: Can 'hardwired' fear responses, e.g. for spiders and snakes, be reprogramed unconsciously in the human brain? Currently, exposure therapy is amongst the most effective treatments for anxiety disorders, but this intervention is subjectively aversive to patients, and rates of premature attrition have been reported to be as high as 70%. We developed a fully unconscious method to bypass the unpleasantness in conscious exposure using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) neurofeedback. Using this method, the similarity between the current brain activity and the brain representation of a feared object is computed in real-time and fed back to participants. Over the course of multiple trials, participants learn to generate brain patterns increasingly similar to the pattern of the feared object. I have previously shown that this intervention leads to a decrease in physiological fear responses without exposing patients to feared objects. Despite these promising findings, we could not observe long-lasting changes in fear reports probably because we did not have the technology to target all the relevant brain regions. Now, recent developments in machine learning allow to target whole-brain representations, which might be necessary to achieve clinically significant changes. I will conduct a randomized control trial with patients diagnosed with 2 specific animal phobias. In a double-blind fMRI neurofeedback protocol, participants will be trained to activate the whole-brain neural representation of one of the two feared animals, while the second animal will act as a control. We hope to observe a specific decrease in clinical symptoms, physiological fear responses and behavioural avoidance of real animals, for at least 6-8 months. Combining our unique unconscious fMRI method with in-scanner virtual reality may eventually extend our approach to other forms of fear, and particularly to post-traumatic stress disorders, which still present a considerable therapeutic challenge

column36: Planned missing data designs for health research
column37: Missing data can create significant problems for researchers throughout the health sciences. Missing data arise when participants drop out of a study before completing it, as in longitudinal studies when people move away or become too busy to continue in a study, or when participants skip questions on a survey or parts of a test, because they are bored, or tired, or do not want to answer sensitive or difficult questions. Traditional statistical analysis methods are designed to be used with complete data, so researchers often delete whole cases (participants) who have missing data points. This practice, however, frequently leads to biased results. As such, unplanned missingness can be a serious problem for research generalization. Planned missingness, on the other hand, has tremendous (and for the most part unrealized) potential. With new statistical methods that produce unbiased results, planned missing data designs are an efficient way to manage cost, improve data quality, and reduce participant fatigue and practice effects. To date, however, there is little guidance for researchers on how to design such studies: how to choose the variables which will have missing values, what percent of data should be missing, how large a sample is needed, and to what extent the model will be able to detect meaningful effects. The present proposal aims to provide comprehensive guidance to researchers for using planned missing research designs in longitudinal research. The results will educate researchers on when, how, and why to use planned missing elements in their research designs. Planned missing data designs will increase the validity, generalizability, and cost-effectiveness of applied health research.

Heureusement, il est possible d'agir efficacement pour reduire l'isolement social des aines et les aider a s'integrer plus facilement dans la communaute. column36: Depression as a gut feeling: The gut microbiome as a mediating factor in the dysregulation of the gut-vagus-brain epigenome in the context of depression.
column37: We live our lives engaged in a biochemical conversation with trillions of intestinal microbes. It is known that this gut 'microbiota' can modulate the intestines, and that neurons in our intestines can 'talk' to neurons in our brain along the vagus nerve, as part of a larger bidirectional signaling system called the gut-brain axis. Recent research has suggested that microbial signals can be transmitted up the gut-brain axis to modulate mood, and may be a factor in the development of mental illnesses, such as depression. However, the exact mechanisms by which the gut microbiome alters gut-brain signaling and depression risk are still unclear. Depression is strongly associated with disrupted stress response pathways. Gene regulatory processes known collectively as epigenetic mechanisms have been shown to be key mediators in this disruption. Interestingly, gut bacteria produce many of the chemicals that epigenetic processes require, and changes in the levels of these chemicals in mice have been associated with specific epigenetic changes in host cells. Thus, the gut microbiome may be an important epigenetic modulator. In addition, some of the gut microbiota-associated mood alterations disappear in animals if the vagus nerve is severed, suggesting that some moods begin in the gut. I therefore hypothesize that gut microbiome mediated epigenetic processes increase depression risk in humans by altering the gut-vagal-brain axis. My PhD project will identify depression-associated changes in epigenetic regulators in the gut microbiomes of depressed people who died by suicide, and clinically depressed populations. I will test whether specific gut microbe species predict the epigenetic changes in neurons along a gut-vagal-brain pathway. As the first investigation of the gut-microbiome-brain epigenome, this project will further our understanding of microbial-host interactions, which may be a factor in multiple other diseases and an important target for future intervention

column36: Prospective, population-based studies of antimalarials and their impact on vision loss, quality-of-life, disease activity, and mortality in patients with rheumatic disease
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and lupus are forms of inflammatory arthritis that affect at least 1 of every 100 Canadians, mainly females. Immune dysfunction leads to organ and joint damage, disability, work loss, pain, fatigue and early mortality. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), an anti-malarial drug, is also a long-term treatment for lupus and RA that improves survival. Though effective, low cost, and generally safe, one serious adverse effect of HCQ is irreversible retinopathy (damage to the back of the eye) that can lead to vision loss and blindness. Retinopathy was thought to be rare (<2% of long-term HCQ users), but in a recent study using more sensitive screening tests, many more were affected (7.5%). As a result, guidelines now call for HCQ users to have these new, more sensitive eye tests every year, to diagnose it earlier. But much is unknown about the risk of retinopathy, risk factors, and impact of earlier diagnosis on patients' vision, survival and quality-of-life. For example, detecting more cases of mild retinopathy (which may not progress) could simply increase patients' anxiety. To fill these gaps, we will use electronic healthcare data (without names or identifying information) to follow ~3,000 people with lupus and RA who have used HCQ for at least 5 years. We will use new statistical methods to estimate of the risk of retinopathy (overall, and with HCQ different doses), and risk factors, which may include female sex, increased age, kidney disease, and using higher doses of HCQ. We will also study its progression over time - we expect severe cases of retinopathy will progress to vision loss, but milder cases will not. Finally, we will also see what happens when patients stop HCQ, or reduce the dose. While that may help prevent vision loss, risk of death may increase alongside. Our findings will help clinicians and patients make more informed treatment decisions to reduce their chances of vision loss, while optimising their survival and quality-of-life

column36: Cesarean delivery rates and perinatal outcomes in Canada and Sweden: Identifying targets for safely reducing the cesarean deliveries
column37: The rate of cesarean delivery (CD) in Canada has increased from 17.6% in 1995 to 27.9% in 2015. High rates of CD are potentially responsible for unnecessary utilization of health resources as well as maternal and neonatal harm. The reasons for the increase in CD rates are multifactorial and not well understood. Recent data suggests that CD rates below 20% are possible, safe, and compatible with optimal health outcomes for mothers and their newborns. For instance, Sweden has had a stable, relatively low CD rate for years (16.4% in 2003 and 17.4% in 2015), along with low rates of maternal and perinatal adverse outcomes. However, direct comparisons of CD rates between populations tends to be compromised by differences in obstetric profiles and risk factors for adverse perinatal outcomes. Furthermore, there is an implied presumption that any increase in CD rates represents an adverse change which needs to be remedied. The alternative perspective on this issue is that any increase in CD rates needs to be set against potential improvements in maternal, fetal and infant health. Increases in CD rates that occur concomitantly with declines in maternal, fetal and infant adverse outcomes may potentially justify higher CD rates. Therefore, this research aims to use retrospective cohort studies with data from Canada and Sweden to 1) identify subpopulations of women responsible for the variation in CD rates between Canada and Sweden, 2) contrast these populations using analyses that incorporate important between-country differences in risk factors for CD, such as maternal age, pre-pregnancy body-mass-index and weight gain in pregnancy, and 3) evaluate differences in CD rates in Canada and Sweden within the context of maternal, fetal and infant morbidity and mortality. These issues have yet to be addressed in the extant literature and hence represent critical knowledge gaps for women, clinicians, public health policy-makers, and related stakeholders.

column37: Cerebral microvascular disease (CMD) is a disease that affects the small blood vessels in the brain and impairs their ability to properly supply nutrients to the brain. column36: Longitudinal analysis of incubation of cue-induced craving in individuals with cocaine use disorder: An event-related potential study
column37: One of the main challenges in the treatment of drug addiction is the high risk of relapse that can happen very early at the beginning of the abstinence period. The relapse phenomenon is accompanied by an experience of a strong urge to use drugs called craving, which can be triggered by a re-exposure to cues and contexts previously associated with drug use. Studies have shown a phenomenon called incubation of craving, which is an increase of craving in the first months after stopping the use of drugs, such as cocaine. However, these studies used self-reported methods to qualify craving, a subjective method that may be biased. Moreover, no human studies have attempted to monitor the evolution of craving over a long period of time. Therefore, this project aims at objectively evaluating how the incubation of craving evolves over a period of one year in cocaine-addicted adults. Two hundred and ten subjects will be assessed using an electroencephalographic method called event-related potentials, which measures brain activity in response to images. In this case, neutral images and images associated with cocaine use will be presented. Brain reactivity to the images as measured by a specific component of event-related potentials will be compared at different times following the beginning of abstinence (3, 6, 9, and 12 months). Finally, this study will increase our knowledge about the fluctuation of craving over time and its involvement in relapse. This project will specifically inform clinicians about the risk factors for relapse at specific moments during the abstinence period, which may also guide the development of new interventions and prevention tools in order to reduce the chances of relapse.

column36: Epigenomic characterization of early mouse intestinal cancers
column37: It is now widely recognized that while cancer is a genetic disorder, epigenetics plays a significant role in cancer progression. Epigenetics describes a set of modifications that are placed on DNA and can alter the message of the DNA sequence. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the fourth leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide, and arises as the result of genetic and epigenetic abnormalities within the cells of the intestine. This proposal directly tests some of the DNA methylation observations that were detected in primary human cancers by use of an innovative reporter. This fluorescence signal allows us for the first time to visualize cells that have undergone the earliest genetic changes in the path to cancer. In summary, we aim to identify those DNA methylation changes that are essential for the earliest stages of CRC. We anticipate that the findings from this study will have a lasting impact on the understanding of colorectal cancer initiation, will inform new biomarkers of early colorectal cancer and identify new therapeutic vulnerabilities. As these epigenetic DNA modifications are reversible, we have the potential to manipulate them with drugs for the ultimate goal of tumour suppression.

column37: Mood instability, defined as an emotional dysregulation, mood swings, or emotional impulsiveness, is a common feature of mood and anxiety disorders. column36: The role of ontologically distinct cardiac macrophage subsets in ischemic injury
column37: Heart failure is a leading cause of hospitalization and mortality in Canada and world-wide. A common initiating factor in the development of heart failure is adverse cardiac remodeling due to acute/chronic inflammation following myocardial infarction (MI). Understanding the role innate immune cells play in the initial inflammation and subsequent reparative response following injury is of critical importance. Recent observations from our group have identified a heterogeneous population of cardiac resident macrophages (MFs) which play important roles in tissue injury/repair dependent on their ontological origin. In contrast to the prevailing theory that all cardiac MFs are derived from blood monocytes we have definitively shown that cardiac MFs have two distinct origins. The majority of cardiac MFs are embryonically derived (EmbryoD-MFs) while the remainder are monocyte-derived, produced by bone-marrow hematopoietic stem cells (HscD-MF). Importantly, our preliminary data suggests MF origin drives MF function, with embryonic-derived subsets being responsible for tissue repair, while HscD-MFs promote inflammation, which may lead to pathological repair. Together, this provides a novel framework to study cardiac MF populations which we predict will have distinct and opposing roles following MI. The overall goal of this study is to define the distinct roles of EmbryoD-MFs and HscD-MFs for the first time, in order to exploit novel ontogeny-guided therapies that prevent MF-driven tissue damage while simultaneously promoting MF-driven cardiac tissue repair.

column36: Long-term behavior of tailings dams after closure: implications for dam safety risk management
column37: The mining process produces slurry wastes known as tailings, which are stored in containment structures called tailings dams. Following mine closures, tailings dams are subject to natural forces, such as erosion, as the dam transitions into a landform that is compatible with the natural landscape. This poses a significant problem as tailings dams are designed to be safe during the mine's active life, which is much shorter than the lifespan of the dam. Failure of these structures can result in catastrophic consequences to the public and the environment as the tailings may escape the dam resulting in extensive environmental contamination and even fatalities. To prevent failure of these large structures after mining, their long-term behavior must be understood and incorporated into the original design. Unfortunately, there is currently little information available regarding how these structures age over time. This is problematic as there are thousands of tailings dams worldwide, many of which are located in the vicinity of urban centers. The objective of the proposed research is to describe the long-term behavior of tailings dams following mine closure to aid in risk management. The proposed research involves three main stages. First, a fault tree will be developed to visually illustrate the causes, effects, and consequences of different failure modes based on a detailed case study review of multiple tailings dams. Second, the failure modes identified in the first stage will be analyzed and modelled over time. The model will be evaluated using tailings dam case studies. Third, a risk assessment tool will be developed based on the probability and consequences of failure for tailings structures post-closure. This is expected to improve the design of tailings dams which will reduce the probability of failure and the release of tailings to the environment. Consequently, this research is expected to improve public safety and aid in environmental protection.

column37: My research investigates recent political efforts by cities to confront global challenges. It examines the rise of "city-networks" as a response to a range of transnational issues from natural disasters and health pandemics to nuclear proliferation and terrorism. Specifically, it examines the efforts of two city-networks, the C40 City Climate Leadership Group and the Strong Cities Network, which address climate change and violent extremism respectively. It examines why and how these city-networks emerged and the strategies they employ when attempting to influence global politics. It further asks about the conditions under which these networks are successful in achieving their policy objectives. In addition to improving our understanding of how cities are meeting the challenges of climate change and violent extremism, this examination provides insight into the changing nature of the global political order. Are cities in these networks becoming more influential, in the sense that they are writing new rules and commanding legitimacy in these issue areas? And if cities are making rules and influencing global politics beyond the state, what does this mean for our traditional system of international authority? By analyzing how contemporary global politics is functioning, we can better understand which political strategies are effective and which are not, and with that knowledge, learn more about how to overcome political gridlock on pressing global issues.

column36: Etude des modulations de l'expression des genes et de l'epissage des ARNm cellulaires dans le cadre d'une infection par differents Flavivirus: le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune et le virus Zika
column37: Les Flavivirus, tel que le virus Zika, le virus du Nil occidental, et le virus de la fievre jaune, sont des virus transmis par les moustiques auxquels plusieurs milliards de personnes sont exposees au niveau mondial. Ces virus sont etroitement apparentes, mais ils causent des maladies distinctes. De facon generale, tous les Flavivirus peuvent infecter le systeme nerveux et causer des inflammations du cerveau. Par contre, seulement certains Flavivirus, dont le virus de la fievre jaune, peuvent causer des fievres hemorragiques. De plus, le virus Zika est le seul Flavivirus associe au developpement de microcephalie, soit une croissance anormalement faible du cerveau chez le foetus, lorsque la mere est infectee durant la grossesse. Il est connu que les virus deregulent un grand nombre de processus cellulaires de l'hote dans le but de favoriser l'infection. Par contre, les mecanismes par lesquels les virus causent ces changements restent a etre elucides. Dans cette etude, nous investiguons l'infection de cellules avec trois differents Flavivirus, soit le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune, et le virus Zika, dans le but de comprendre comment ces virus interagissent avec l'hote. En effectuant les infections dans les memes conditions, il est egalement possible de comparer les differents virus et leurs effets sur les cellules, en plus de determiner des deregulations communes aux trois virus ainsi que des deregulations uniques a chaque virus. Ces resultats permettront de mieux comprendre comment ces virus affectent l'hote et pourquoi ils causent des maladies differentes.

column36: Quantifying the drivers of animal migration - an integrative approach
column37: Migration is the seasonal movement of animals between two distinct ranges, and is a strategy used by a variety of species worldwide to maximize reproductive success. Migration is critical for populations to thrive in changing environments. Despite this, it is among the most threatened processes on the planet, with declines in migratory behaviour attributed to climate change and habitat loss. We know little about what shapes individual differences in migratory behaviour and the relative roles of genetics, physiology (e.g., body condition), and environmental heterogeneity in shaping migration in a changing landscape. My objective is to develop a complete understanding of migration by untangling the effects of environmental conditions, physiology, and genetics on this fundamental process. Using data collected from three migratory species: moose, mule deer, and mountain goat, I will measure individual variation in migratory behaviour within each species and test multiple hypotheses about the drivers of migration. Using recent advances in technology, I will screen the DNA of all three species to determine if the same genes that control migratory behaviour are shared across species. I predict that while environmental factors will be the main factor controlling migration across species, the remaining variation in behaviour can be explained by a few genes of large effect that are shared across all three species. My project takes an original approach to understanding the drivers of migration behaviour and combines ideas and techniques from multiple disciplines in biology, including ecology, genetics, and physiology. My results will contribute to the understanding of migration behaviours in three species that are important for food security, tourism, and culture in Canada, and whose populations are at risk as their migration routes become threatened due to climate change and habitat loss.

column36: Enhancing and Expanding the "Know Your Status" Initiative in on-reserve Indigenous Communities in Saskatchewan: A Community-engaged Intervention to Increase Diagnosis, Linkage to Care and Prevention of HIV, HCV and STBBIs
column37: First Nations people living on-reserve in Saskatchewan have the highest rates of HIV infection in Canada, with an incidence approximately 7.3-times higher than the national average. They also have the least access to care and to life saving antiretroviral therapy. To address this need, a comprehensive on-reserve HIV testing and treatment initiative called "Know Your Status" (KYS) was launched in 2011. KYS is a community-designed and community-managed program based on partnerships and collaborations between First Nations communities and care providers. Key components of KYS include: community involvement and leadership, education, prevention, specialized nursing support, support for mental health and addictions, lab testing and accessible and culturally-safe clinical management that meets clients where they are located. Culturally supportive services, such as mentorship from Elders and traditional teachings, are also integrated within the program. Thus far, KYS has been primarily implemented to care for HIV and sexually transmitted infections on a few on-reserve communities. However, there is a need to expand the program to include hepatitis C testing, linkage and treatment, as a result of similarly high on-reserve rates. The research team, in close partnership with First Nation communities, intends to refine, adapt, and expand the KYS intervention to communities with the greatest need. Traditional experimental designs to evaluate the KYS initiative cannot be used for various reasons. Instead, the team will use practical, though rigorous, methods to evaluate the effectiveness, acceptability and sustainability of the expanded KYS program, while ensuring that community needs are met. First Nations leaders and communities, policy makers and other physicians will be engaged throughout the project to build community and provincial capacity to treat on-reserve HIV and hepatitis C, and to ensure program sustainability for years to come.

column36: Evaluating Innovative Health Care Solutions to Improve Outcomes for Persons with Type 1 Diabetes using a Novel Electronic Data Repository
column37: Living with type 1 diabetes (T1D) is challenging in many ways. People with T1D are expected to fit self-management and regular clinic appointments into busy lives, balancing short- and long-term risks of low and high blood sugar levels. Our research aims to improve the lives of people with T1D by testing an innovative health system intervention to help patients achieve better diabetes control in a way that places less burden on individuals and is more patient-oriented. Specifically, the intervention will involve electronic delivery of health care and related support services to people living with T1D in addition to usual care, including 1) frequent, brief virtual visits with their diabetes care team to share and discuss blood sugar patterns, diabetes self-management, coping strategies, personalized goals and action plans and 2) structured online educational courses, tools and supports. Virtual visits will use videoconferencing technology that can be securely accessed free of charge from any personal device (PC, tablet, smart phone). We will test the intervention's impact on diabetes control, patient-reported experiences and outcomes, and heath care use and costs. The intervention will be tailored to two age groups: young adults 17-24 years of age and adults 25 years of age and older. It will enable "high frequency, low touch" care to patients with poorer diabetes control and at times in their lives when they are at high risk for diabetes complications. This approach will allow patients to receive more education and support than is feasible in traditional health care models based solely on in-person clinic visits, in a way that is more seamless (fewer disruptions to daily life) and tailored to individual needs (by offering an array of online educational classes, tools and resources) based on stage of life. We hypothesize that the intervention will improve diabetes control, patient experience and access to self-management education and support for patients with T1D.

column36: The development, implementation, and evaluation of a transdiagnostic group intervention for First Nations children.
column37: Wait-lists for mental health services in First Nations' communities often make services inadequate to meet community needs. The use of transdiagnostic treatments could serve to reduce these wait-times by allowing individuals who are experiencing a wide array of difficulties (e.g., depression, anxiety, substance use) to receive services that address underlying symptoms at the same time. These treatments also provide a new framework for evidence based culturally appropriate services within First Nations' communities by incorporating strategies that align with cultural values. Working in collaboration with a community based organization serving First Nations communities in North Western Ontario, a skill based transdiagnostic group intervention will be developed and implemented. This treatment will target community specific needs through consultation with organizational staff and community members. Culturally appropriate skills, concepts, and examples will be identified and integrated into the treatment. This is the first project to adapt and assess the effectiveness of a transdiagnostic mental health treatment for First Nations children. Following an initial pilot group of the treatment, approximately 50 children aged 7-12 years will complete a revised version. It is anticipated that these group interventions will reduce difficulties in emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, behavioural avoidance, and self-care of the children while developing positive coping strategies.

column36: ACHRU Community Partnership Program for Diabetes Self-Management for Older Adults - Canada
column37: Living with diabetes and other chronic (ongoing) conditions is common in older adults. These individuals have poorer health and higher use of health services compared to older adults with diabetes alone. Programs that help older adults self-manage their diabetes and other health conditions benefit both individuals and the healthcare system. The McMaster University Aging, Community and Health Research Unit developed and tested a new patient-centered, community-based program to improve the delivery and outcomes of care for older adults with diabetes and other chronic conditions. This 6-month program was developed in partnership with patients, caregivers, primary and community care providers and researchers. The program is delivered by nurses, dietitians and community providers. It involves in-home visits by nurses and dietitians, monthly group wellness sessions at community centers, and monthly team meetings. Wellness sessions include exercise, education, shared meals, and social support. Caregivers are invited to be active participants along with patients. The program was successfully implemented in Ontario and Alberta. Participants who received the program had better quality of life, self-management, and mental health at no additional cost compared to those receiving usual care. To determine how the program can best help people, more testing is needed with different communities and groups of people. We will partner with primary healthcare teams (e.g., family doctors' offices) in three provinces to adapt and test the program in a variety of real-world settings. We will assess how to best put this program into practice and measure outcomes important to patients and caregivers so study results are relevant to them. Study findings will guide the development of a plan for expanding the program to reach and benefit more older adults with diabetes and other chronic health conditions. Patients and caregivers will be involved as key partners in all aspects of the research.

column36: SPIDER-NET, A Structured Process Informed by Data, Evidence and Research-Network: An approach to support primary care practices in optimizing the management of patients with complex needs
column37: Health care costs are increasing quickly. About half is spent on a small number of people with complex health problems. We need to address this. Built on a successful model for improving care by working together, the Structured Process Informed by Data, Evidence and Research (SPIDER) contains 3 parts: 1) Build teams with family physicians, nurses, pharmacists, medical staff and patients. These teams will learn together, from each other and from experts about improving quality in practice; 2) Use information from Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) to discover what the issues in each practice are, and decide together what could be done; and 3) Start making the practice changes that were agreed to with the help of coaches. Repeatedly test, measure and improve care. We will test SPIDER to see if it helps older patients taking many medications (polypharmacy), some of which may not be necessary or may even be harmful. More drugs often mean more side effects and this is even worse as people age. The risks of side effects like confusion, dizziness and falls increases in elders. Older patients taking ten or more medications are especially complex and high risk; we can do better for them. We expect SPIDER to help family doctors and their teams deliver better care by reviewing and reducing riskier drugs for these patients. We will test SPIDER in seven centres, in five provinces. We expect that it will improve patients' quality of life and their heath; it may also save money by reducing the number of times people are admitted to hospital. Our team is made up of experts and leaders in quality improvement, audit and feedback, pharmacists, physicians, patients and researchers. All of us have experience in the parts that make up SPIDER, so we are able to do this; we will now work together to improve care for elders in our communities by reducing and improving medications, to support their health and help them reach their goals for quality of life.

column36: Screening for Poverty And Related social determinants and intervening to improve Knowledge of and links to resources (SPARK) Study
column37: The social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions and processes at an individual, family, neighbourhood, community and societal level that impact on health. Numerous studies have confirmed the central role that SDOH play in creating and maintaining health inequities. While much is known about SDOH, we lack the individual-level data necessary to target interventions, and lack rigorously evaluated interventions to meet social needs in health settings. Sociodemographic data collected at the individual level, paired with interventions to meet social needs when identified, could address this problem. Further, robust sociodemographic data linked to electronic medical records (EMRs) can support quality improvement and new care pathways at the organizational level, planning and resource allocation at the system level, and advance research on health inequities. The SPARK Study is a cluster randomized controlled trial that will rigorously evaluate a "modest" versus "intensive" intervention to help address poverty when identified. While the primary outcome of this intervention is change in income attributable to the poverty intervention, we will capture data on additional impacts, including linkage to community resources, psychological stress and quality of life. column36: Personalized Risk Assessment for Prevention and Early Detection of Breast Cancer: Integration and Implementation
column37: Breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. A woman faces a one in eight chance of developing the disease in her lifetime. Currently, women aged 50 to 74 are recommended to have a mammogram every 2 to 3 years. To maximize the benefits and reduce harms, women should be screened based on their personal risk of the disease. More precise risk assessment combining data on genomic profiling and other BC risk factors has the potential to markedly increase the proportion of identifiable high risk women. This project will provide evidence that can significantly expand the benefits of current age-based population screening programs by supporting the transition to a risk-based approach. It will also improve counseling of women with a family history of BC who are seen in cancer genetic clinics. Earlier detection of BC will allow more cancers to be detected while they are still small and curable, which in turn will save lives and bring significant health and socio-economic benefits. By studying very large cohorts of women using high throughput genomic technologies together with statistical and epidemiological methods, this project will develop a validated multi-gene panel test including genetic variants reliably associated with BC risk. This will enable individualized risk assessment and improve the counseling process by health care providers for women with and without a known BC family history. To support a framework for future implementation of a risk-based screening approach, a large population-based cohort will be assembled to evaluate the acceptability and feasibility of using a new comprehensive risk prediction web tool and a genomic profiling test within the existing health care system. The cohort will be followed to determine behavioural, psychosocial and clinical outcomes. Policies will be developed to address the socio-ethical and legal challenges for women, health professionals and decision makers associated with implementing risk-based breast screening. By providing this evidence, this project will change breast screening practice and ensure better use of human and financial resources. Women will face less invasive BC treatment with fewer complications and improved quality of life and survival, thereby reducing both the clinical and economic burden for a large proportion of Canadian women.

column36: Reducing the global burden of infectious diseases through precision population health
column37: The global rise in the prevalence of antibiotic resistant bacteria is a problem so serious that it threatens all modern medicine. We have already reached the point where half of the common bacteria that cause infections are resistant to our front-line drugs. Moreover, new superbugs have emerged that cannot be cured with any drug. Once these multiple-drug resistant organisms take hold in our healthcare setting, many of the benefits of modern medicine, including hip replacement surgery, chemotherapy, and organ transplant, will become too risky due to the chances of acquiring a deadly infection. Finding an immediate solution to this global health crisis is our moral imperative to ensure that future generations will benefit from modern medical practices. One of the primary reasons for the increasing levels of antibiotic resistance is the one-size-fits-all approach we take to treating infections, which encourages the over use of these drugs. The one-size-fits-all approach also causes unnecessary sickness and deaths. Different strains of bacteria can be dramatically different in the risks they pose to our health. However, we do not consider these risks when treating infections because of technological limitations. To solve this problem, we have assembled an international team of infectious disease experts, microbiologists, database experts, and analytical chemistry experts to develop a new approach to treating infections. Our solution is to 1) identify every significant biochemical trait that is found in the most dangerous bacteria, 2) create an automated analytical system and database for predicting the potential risks posed by each individual infection, and 3) implement a new Precisions Infection Management (PIM) strategy that will allow clinicians to match each patient to the exact level of antibiotic therapy necessary to cure infections without unnecessarily selecting for antibiotic resistant bacteria. PIM will reduce overall antibiotic use and may preserve the lifespan of our critical front-line drugs. In addition, it will help ensure people suffering from dangerous bacterial infections (e.g. "flesh-eating" strains) get aggressive therapy faster. Likewise, PIM will ensure that people infected with non-dangerous strains receive milder therapies and minimize the risks of medical complications (e.g. kidney failure). PIM allows these significant health improvements without increasing costs to our healthcare system: we predict that PIM will actually save money because of the reduced time people will need to spend in the hospital, and more importantly, it will save lives.

column36: Care4Rare Canada: Harnessing multi-omics to deliver innovative diagnostic care for rare genetic diseases in Canada (C4R-SOLVE)
column37: There are about 7,000 rare genetic diseases (RDs) that affect more than one million Canadians. RDs have a devastating impact on Canadians: two-thirds cause significant disability, threequarters affect children, more than half lead to early death, and almost all have no treatment. The cause of more than one-third of the 7000 RDs is currently unknown. Care4Rare Canada Consortium leads the world by using genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) to identify the genetic cause of RDs. However, more than one third of patients seen each year in Canada with a suspected RD remain undiagnosed and can spend years visiting specialists and undergoing unnecessary testing to explain their disease. Contributing to this gap in care is that genomic sequencing is not available as a clinical test anywhere in Canada. Thus, building on the success of Care4Rare, the goal of the C4R-SOLVE project is to identify the genetic cause for the remaining unsolved RDs while making genomic sequencing available as a clinical diagnostic test in Canada. To understand the remaining unsolved RDs, C4R-SOLVE will explore new sequencing technologies and improve data sharing world-wide, enabling the discovery of new causes of RDs. To improve access to clinical diagnostic testing, C4R-SOLVE will work with provincial ministries of health to determine the best way to include genomic sequencing as a clinical test to diagnose RDs. By achieving its goal, the C4R-SOLVE project will more than double our ability to diagnose this one third of RD patients, while building the infrastructure and tools needed to improve RD diagnosis around the world. An accurate diagnosis will benefit patients and their families as a genetic diagnosis leads to optimized care, improved family wellbeing, and new disease insights. Further, optimal delivery of clinical genomic sequencing has the potential save at least $28M per year, benefiting the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Silent Genomes: Reducing health care disparities and improving diagnostic success for children with genetic diseases from Indigenous populations.
column37: Indigenous populations face unique health challenges, inequities, and barriers to healthcare in Canada and around the world. As such, they typically have poorer health outcomes than do non-Indigenous groups. While genomics (the study of the complete set of human genes) has advanced health care by allowing medical treatments to be tailored to the specific needs of individual patients ('precision medicine'), this 'genomics revolution' is also contributing to health inequities. In particular, compared to what is becoming routinely available to other Canadians, Indigenous populations often have little or no access to genomic technologies and the research that drives them. This has created a 'genomic divide', a key component of which is the lack of background genetic variation data for Indigenous populations. This prevents accurate diagnosis because the reference data are needed when multi-gene and exome (entire genome) testing panels are used. Notably, these genomics resources are silent with respect to First Nations (FN), Inuit and Metis peoples (collectively our Canadian Indigenous populations). Silent Genomes will address the genomic divide by reducing access barriers to diagnosis of genetic disease in Indigenous children. With our First Nations, Inuit and Metis partners we will: 1) Establish processes, through an Indigenous lens, for safe governance of biological samples and genome data in the Silent Genomes project, which will lead to broader policy. 2) Address barriers to accessing genetic/genomic health care and bring genomic testing to at least 200 Indigenous children with suspected genetic disorders. 3) Develop an Indigenous Background Variant Library (IBVL) of genetic variation from a diverse group of 1500 FN Canadians and assess improvement in diagnosis for referred children. 4) Assess effectiveness of the IBVL to lower health care costs and plan for long term use of IBVL for Canadian Indigenous children and adults needing genetic/genomic health care.

column36: PEGASUS-2 - PErsonalized Genomics for prenatal Abnormalities Screening USing maternal blood : Towards First Tier Screening and Beyond
column37: The discovery that DNA of fetal origin is present in maternal blood during pregnancy has led to a new genomics-based maternal blood test called non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS), which is very reliable at screening for Down syndrome. Currently, public healthcare systems pay for this expensive NIPS test only as a second-tier screening for women who have first screened positive on less costly and less accurate biochemical and ultrasound tests. Hence, only after an initial screen has delivered a positive result is NIPS currently used to help women participating in prenatal screening programs avoid a diagnostic amniocentesis. If NIPS were used as the entry-level test for Down syndrome screening, it would benefit women by providing a higher chance of detecting an affected pregnancy and a lower chance of providing a false positive result. It would also enable women to have their final diagnostic result sooner than the current standard of care permits. As well, because NIPS can also detect other fetal chromosome anomalies, its use could enable screening for more conditions. This project aims to provide highquality evidence to inform decisions by health care organisations about using first-tier NIPS to replace traditional screening tests for Down syndrome, and potentially to screen for other fetal chromosome anomalies. We will compare the current screening approach of second-tier NIPS with the use of first-tier NIPS in a large cohort of pregnant women. We will also study the costeffectiveness of expanding screening to other conditions, and the ethical, social and legal implications of doing so. As well, we will provide strategies for scaling up shared decision making processes between couples and their health care practitioners. Finally, we will further develop the NIPS technology to lower its costs, expand the detection of other anomalies, and ensure the quality control of clinical-grade NIPS testing in Canada and worldwide. While taking into account the values informing couples' decisions about participation in prenatal screening, this project will enable publicly funded access to a promising genomics technology for all pregnant women in Canada. Further, it will ensure that couples have access to web-based tools to help their decision making, and that all health care professionals are trained in shared decision making for prenatal screening.

column36: Tackling Childhood Brain Cancer at the root to improve survival and quality of life
column37: One in every 285 children will suffer from a cancer before the age of 15 years. While overall survival and quality of life for child survivors have improved substantially over the last 3 decades for cancers of the blood (leukemia), brain cancers are still lethal and disabling. For some aggressive forms of brain cancer barely 10% of children and young adults survive 3 years after diagnosis, despite enormous efforts and costs to families and to the health care system. Those who do survive often have severe disabilities resulting from their treatment (which can include surgery, radiation therapy to the brain and the use of toxic drugs), with consequent limitations to their social and professional lives. Through previous research our team discovered that many paediatric brain tumours are driven by mutations in genes essential for regulating the development and growth of all body tissues, but which have specific roles in brain development. These findings have enabled more accurate diagnosis of the specific subtype of each paediatric brain tumour, and partly explain why these cancers are unresponsive to existing treatments. This new research aims to fast-track the use of targeted therapies against some of the mutated proteins, while continuing to identify new therapeutic targets for children whose tumours do not yet have a clear molecular diagnosis. We will do this using novel ways of interrogating the genome on the single cell level, determining how the genome is rearranged in childhood cancers, and identifying specific vulnerabilities of the cancer cell compared to the normal cell from which it originated. We will validate proposed therapies in reliable models and accelerate translation to the bedside through our network of care providers. As well, we will assess how to assign children rapidly to a personalised treatment strategy early in the disease course, based on the molecular diagnosis of each tumour. These goals will be pursued by engaging relevant stakeholders and developing an innovative business model enabling drug discovery even for rare disease sub-types. Our project promises to improve survival and quality of life for all children and young adults with brain tumours. By leading to more efficient drugs tailored to specific patients, it will enable health care providers to increase success in treating children with brain tumours, while also decreasing the burden of survivorship on patients, their families and Canada's health care system.

column36: Precision Medicine CanPREVENT AMR: Applying Precision Medicine Technologies in Canada to Prevent Antibody Mediated Rejection and Premature Kidney Transplant Loss
column37: Chronic kidney disease affects 1 in 10 Canadians with estimated costs of over $2 billion/year. Transplantation is the treatment of choice for those whose kidneys fail: it improves survival (>85% vs <50% at 5yr), optimizes quality of life (85% vs 70% of normal) and decreases health-care costs ($15,000 vs $55,000/yr) compared with dialysis. But severe graft rejection (known as "antibody-mediated" rejection or AMR) occurs in up to 30% of transplant patients causing premature graft loss, return to dialysis, and early death. We will develop a program to prevent AMR and promote lifetime survival of the transplanted kidney. Our program will employ genetic technologies to: (a) reduce the risk of rejection through better donor-patient matching; (b) monitor the immune response after transplant to predict AMR; (c) enable personalized treatment with powerful drugs to prevent rejection while avoiding infection or cancer; and (d) study the legal, ethical, societal and economic considerations of introducing these strategies into clinical practice to improve quality of life and reduce health-care costs. The program builds on our highly successful national transplant program coordinated through the Canadian Blood Services (CBS) and links 16 major transplant programs, 9 leading universities, and 14 provincial transplant organizations and laboratories. It is led by an experienced Canadian and international team of genome experts, transplant immunologists, clinical scientists, legal scholars, ethicists, and health economists, working collaboratively with patients, members of the public, health providers, provincial health organizations, national coordinating bodies and commercial partners. Our program seeks to reduce the frequency of AMR by at least 50%, with the expected benefits from preventing rejection commencing quickly and increasing annually due to increased survival of transplanted kidneys. Approximately 500 Canadian patients lose their graft every year, and return to dialysis results in a 4-fold increase in the risk of death, decreased quality-of-life and incremental costs of up to $1 million per patient over their remaining life years. The benefits of this program will consequently occur at three levels: (a) the patient and family, with a gain in survival and quality of life, reduced caregiver burden, and personal health expenditures; (b) the healthcare system, with reduced dialysis care and re-transplant needs; (c) and society, due to increased workforce productivity and decreased kidney management costs.

column36: Genomic and Outcomes Databank for Pharmacogenomic and Implementation Studies (GoPGx)
column37: The vision of Go-PGx is to save lives and improve the quality of life for patients through the prevention of serious adverse drug reactions (ADRs) - often called 'side effects'. The treatment of childhood cancer is particularly impacted by ADRs. ADRs in children are 3-fold more likely to be life-threatening and a staggering 75% of childhood cancer patients develop chronic health conditions and 42% develop disabling or life-threatening ADRs from cancer treatment. It is increasingly evident that genetic differences in patients affect one's likelihood of experiencing an ADR - studying the variability in response to medication is called pharmacogenomics (PGx). Go-PGx is an integrated pipeline of innovative research and the development of tools to facilitate these findings (usually referred to as knowledge translation) into clinical practice by implementing lab tests to predict a patient's likelihood of suffering from an ADR in pediatric cancer treatment. Go-PGx builds upon over 14 years of experience in studying ADRs with research collaborators integrated in 10 pediatric hospitals across Canada. We have collected over 6,125 DNA samples and have corresponding reports of medication use and ADR outcomes recorded in a clinical database. We will build upon this with four linked research activities: (1) We will make new research discoveries of genetic susceptibility to ADRs and (2) develop tools to educate and inform physicians and patients beginning with a prioritized focus on five severe pediatric oncology ADRs. We will generate a comprehensive ADR database of linked clinical and genetic information to provide an accessible resource for to help researchers around the world. (3) At the same time, we will start providing PGx testing in 10 pediatric oncology centers across Canada, (4) while studying important components to the uptake of ADR screening in the health care system, such as understanding what the barriers and facilitators are to making this kind of testing successful; what the perceptions of clinicians, patients and families are to this kind of testing; and understanding the economic implications of introducing this kind of testing into clinical practice across Canada. Go-PGx wants to provide this much-needed access to pharmacogenomic testing in pediatric oncology and lay the foundation for accessible pharmacogenomic testing in Canada.

column36: Deciphering the genome biology of relapsed lymphoid cancers to improve patient management
column37: Collectively, lymphoid cancers are the 5th most common cancers in men and women and affect patients of all ages. In Canada alone, 16,000 patients are newly diagnosed, and 6,000 patients will die of the disease each year. The mortality of the disease is almost exclusively linked to disease relapse when the current standard of care fails to cure the cancer. Therefore, successful treatment and symptom control of relapsed disease represents the single most important need for patients suffering from lymphoid cancers. Unfortunately, the causes of treatment failure are mostly unknown and, as a consequence, no clinical tests are available to inform on the individual prognosis of patients, likely treatment outcomes of salvage therapy, and to guide physicians and patient to use alternative therapeutic choices, such as small molecule drugs or modern immunotherapy. Moreover, treatment relapse and associated treatment cost is a major burden for the health care system with over $315 million attributed to relapsed disease in Canada alone. This means that often times expensive, but ineffective treatments are applied without guidance by adequate clinical testing. In this project, we will focus on the most common forms of lymphoid cancer, namely follicular lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia that together account for approximately two thirds of all lymphoid cancers. The main goals of our research are to develop clinical tests, alongside modern treatments available at relapse, to improve patient outcomes, quality of life, and to make tests widely available in the Canadian, publicly funded health care system. We will achieve these goals by applying state-of-the-art sequencing of patient biopsies taken at the time point of clinical relapse, performing detailed economic analyses, and engaging patients into joint decision making with their treating physicians. Our project will provide novel clinical tests in diagnostic laboratories, access to cutting-edge scientific progress, produce decision aids for patients, and help policy makers in the process of implementing personalized treatment approaches into the health care system.
