column36: LARGE SCALE GE3LS PROJECT: GenCOUNSEL: OPTIMIZATION OF GENETIC COUNSELLING FOR CLINICAL IMPLEMENTATION OF GENOME-WIDE SEQUENCING
column37: Genome-wide sequencing (GWS) is a powerful new genetic test that analyzes a person's entire genetic make-up to diagnose the cause of genetic disorders. GWS generates unique genetic counselling issues, as it may diagnose disorders or disease risk factors that are unrelated to the original reason for testing. In addition, it can generate complex results that are difficult for nonexpert health providers to interpret. Currently, this technology is not routinely available in Canada, but because of its diagnostic capability, GWS will soon be available for most Canadian patients who need it. This means that many more families will be considering GWS as a test option, further increasing the demand for genetic counselling. Genetic counsellors are specialist healthcare providers with the expertise to lead the integration of genomics into patient care across all areas of medicine. They represent the "front line" of medical genetics. By providing education, emotional and decisional support to patients and families, guiding them to make informed decisions regarding genetic testing, they help prevent inappropriate decision making that can have devastating health and /or emotional consequences for patients and families. In Canada, there is limited access to genetic counselling. Factors such as cost of time and travel, language and cultural barriers exist for many Canadians. Furthermore, the lack of legal recognition of genetic counsellors in Canada means they work primarily in clinical genetics units at academic centres, rather than in the community. GenCOUNSEL, led by international researchers in genetic counselling, genomics, ethics, health services implementation and health economics will determine the most effective socio-ethical, clinical, legal and economic methods to provide genetic counselling with clinical GWS implementation. GenCOUNSEL aims to: understand the current and future need for genetic counsellors, investigate and develop best practices for delivery of genetic counselling, improve access to genetic counselling, in particular for underserved patient populations, and develop a framework for the legal recognition of genetic counsellors. These activities will result in increased access, patient satisfaction, and cost-efficiency through provision of effective and professional genetic counselling for all Canadians who need it.

column37: Simplistic representations of our genome usually display genes on a linear DNA string. However, the genome complexity is much greater. Therefore, we are moving our global understanding of gene regulation from single-gene to gene communities-based approaches. Our main goal is to integrate the information provided by the gene communities to better understand normal and disease development.

Methylmercury in hair will used as an alternate to estimate exposure to methylmercury. Foods in the diet that contribute to contaminant exposure will be reviewed by the community research team to address how contaminant exposure could be reduced without adversely impacting the cultural and nutritional importance of these foods.

column36: Can nutrition care be optimized within an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol for colorectal cancer patients? The effect of pre-operative N-3 fatty acid supplementation on surgical outcomes
column37: Cancer is one of the diseases most commonly associated with malnutrition. Surgery is a main treatment for cancer. When surgical patients also have malnutrition it takes them longer to recover, they stay longer in the hospital and cost the health system more. Specialized surgical programs known as Enhance Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) help to minimize the negative effects of malnutrition with standardized nutrition care protocols. ERAS programs screen patients for malnutrition before surgery, but there are no specific nutrition therapies offered before surgery to treat specific nutrition problems. Muscle depletion and the development of fatty muscle are specific nutrition problems caused by malnutrition. These muscle abnormalities can be detected using computed tomography (CT) images and may be treated with a specific nutrition intervention such as N-3 fatty acids, which are found in fish oil capsules. The aims of this study are to: 1) teach registered dietitians to identify patients with muscle abnormalities using CT and 2) determine if pre-surgical supplementation with N-3 fatty acids (fish oil) will treat muscle abnormalities resulting in a shorter hospital stay. This study will contribute to the optimization of nutrition care in ERAS programs..

column37: The development of medications to safely promote B-cell replication would be ground-breaking for the treatment of all forms of diabetes. GABA, a neurotransmitter, was shown to facilitate B-cell regeneration in mice. However, GABA exerts unspecific effects, mainly due to the activation of its various receptors, leading to cellular events unrelated to proliferation. Specific positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of GABA offer increased specificity and are currently in clinical use. I hypothesize that GABAA-R PAM will increase B-cell mass in both normal mice and those with experimental diabetes (prediabetes and type 2 diabetes [T2D]), being more effective than GABA itself. Repurposing GABAA-R PAMs to treat diabetes is theoretically appealing due to their safety profile and potential to enhance the ability of GABA to promote B-cell replication. Part 1 of the study will focus on the PAM-mediated effect(s) on B-cell proliferation. Pancreatic islet expansion and B-cell regeneration will be evaluated in mice treated with GABAA-R PAMs. To explore the potential use of PAM drugs as an anti-diabetic tool, prediabetic and T2D mice models will be used; thereafter, B-cell proliferation and islet mass will be assessed. I will also verify whether hyperglycemia and glucose intolerance was corrected with PAM administration. Part 2 will focus on the functional and mechanistic effect(s) of PAMs on B-cell function and expansion. I will measure insulin release, insulin granules and the gene levels of proinsulin and preproinsulin in mice and human islets. The mechanism of PAM-mediated B-cell expansion will also be rigorously assessed through a variety of ex vitro experiments. In the end, I will determine the PAMs' 1) effectiveness to expand B-cell mass; 2) ability to correct hyperglycemia in prediabetes and T2D; and 3) functional and mechanistic effect(s) on mouse and human pancreatic B-cells. This study could usher in a new class of drugs for diabetes treatment.

column36: Ontario Healthcare Implementation Laboratory: A Learning Health System Approach that Leverages Data to Improve Quality in Primary Care
column37: When clinicians do not have the supports in place to help them follow best practices, patients may not reliably receive the ideal tests and treatments. As a result, they are less likely to achieve the best possible health outcomes. Providing clinicians with data on how often they follow best practices helps improve healthcare quality. This strategy is known as 'audit and feedback' and it can play an important role in directing the efforts of clinicians to improve in areas where improvement is most needed to make sure that patients have the best possible outcomes. Our team is working with provincial organizations using audit and feedback and additional supports to help primary care providers like family doctors improve patient care and outcomes in two important areas: opioid prescribing and antibiotic prescribing. Our patient partners and other stakeholders have endorsed these areas as high-priority for action. Our innovative trials will test how audit and feedback can help primary care practices improve in these areas. Conducting experiments in each area will help us learn about how to better deliver evidence-based, patient-centred primary care across a range of acute and chronic conditions. Patients will be involved in governance and will be on steering committees at every level of this research. Patients will also help co-design interventions (including educational materials that primary care providers can share with their patients). By providing education and orientation to our patient and researcher partners and evaluating our patient engagement strategy, we will build capacity in patient engagement and patient oriented research in innovative trials and implementation science. Our partnerships with provincial health care organizations will help us achieve large-scale impact during this project and beyond, ensuring the results of this research will benefit large numbers of patients.

column36: CoMFORT (Cow's Milk Fat Obesity pRevention Trial)
column37: Childhood obesity is a looming healthcare crisis with 1 in 3 Canadian children now living with overweight or obesity. The long term consequences of childhood obesity include increased risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and stroke which reduce quality of life and longevity. Cardiovascular disease currently costs Canada's health systems $7 billion annually and is forecasted to triple in the next 30 years. Since 1992 Health Canada has recommended that children older than 2 years consume reduced fat milk (i.e. 1% milk fat) rather than whole milk (3.25% milk fat) to prevent childhood obesity. Unfortunately, childhood obesity has tripled since then and whole cow's milk intake has halved leading many to wonder whether the reduction in whole milk consumption is leading to childhood obesity. New research from our group and others supports that reduced milk fat intake early in life may be promoting rather than preventing childhood obesity. Although several biological mechanisms have been proposed, the leading theory is that children may feel more 'full' after consuming whole milk and less likely to seek calories from unhealthy foods. This innovative clinical trial will compare the effect of primary healthcare recommendation for whole milk (intervention) vs. reduced fat milk (control) in early childhood in optimizing childhood growth development and nutrition at 4-5 years of age. We will use new cohort trial methods leveraging Canada's largest childhood cohort study (TARGet Kids!) to conduct this trial which will minimize cost and maximize feasibility. This trial must be conducted now to ensure that primary healthcare providers are delivering the correct nutritional recommendation and to protect the next generation of Canada's children from the long term consequences of childhood obesity.

column36: De-implementing low value care: a research program of the Choosing Wisely Canada Implementation Research Network
column37: Up to 30% of tests and treatments given to patients are not needed. This can lead to significant inconvenience and harms for these patients without any benefit. It also wastes money for patients and the health system. Choosing Wisely Canada (CWC) is engaging patients and health professionals to fix this problem. CWC has made 280 recommendations about tests and treatments that should be avoided in certain situations. But these are still happening because it is not an easy thing to change health care processes. Implementation science aims to understand the underlying reasons for health care processes and to develop and test potential solutions to improve them. This project links CWC, patient and health system partners in three provinces with leading Canadian implementation scientists to develop and test solutions for two important topics: x-rays/CT/MRI scans that are not needed for patients with low-risk back pain; and pre-operative tests that are not needed for patients having low-risk surgery. In each province, we will do preliminary studies to make sure we fully understand the different reasons for unnecessary care. Then we will develop targeted solutions using insights from behavioural and system science that support both health professionals and patients to make informed decisions about whether these tests are needed. We will test these solutions in experiments. Some health organisations (either family practices for low back pain imaging or hospitals for pre-operative testing) will receive the solution and some will not. We will determine who gets the solution using an approach similar to flipping a coin to ensure that health organisations that receive or do not receive the solution are similar. We are working with the Canadian Institute of Health Information to use the data already collected routinely to measure whether the solution worked. If our solutions work, we will engage our partners to spread and scale them across Canada.

column37: Some patients who have multiple long-term health conditions have significant challenges in accessing needed services despite available primary care and social services resources. Patient navigation programs may help those with complex health conditions improve their care and outcomes and if delivered by community health workers (CHWs) who have close community ties, these programs have the potential to reduce barriers to care and increase access to coordinated, person-centred care. The University of Calgary's ENCOMPASS program aims to improve the care and health outcomes for high-risk patients by linking patients with chronic disease with a CHW to help them navigate the health system, facilitate communication between patients and providers, improve patients' understanding of their conditions and treatment plans, and support patients in their self-management. In Canada, patient navigation programs have not been well studied or broadly implemented in patients with chronic disease, making a comprehensive evaluation of ENCOMPASS important. This program has great potential to improve care for patients with chronic diseases in Alberta's primary care system. A key element of ENCOMPASS is that patients have been involved in all stages from planning, to pilot testing, to implementation. Given the increasing popularity of patient navigation/CHW programs in other Canadian provinces as well as in the United States, the results of the proposed research will have value outside Alberta.

column36: Canadian Adaptive Platform Trial in Intensive Care (CAPTIC) Program
column37: More than 250,000 Canadians are admitted to an ICU each year. While most survive, the mortality rate of 10% remains high, and survivors often experience severe long term disability and a reduced quality of life. Improved ICU care has come largely from using available treatments more effectively, than from the development of new drugs. But the questions are many, and available funding is limited. We will introduce a new model of a clinical trial - the platform trial - to Canada. Platform trials study several different questions at a time and use adaptive techniques to increase the odds that patients in the trial receive the interventions that are performing better. They are potentially more efficient and cost-effective than traditional trials, but they are new and untested. We will assemble groups of key stakeholders - patients, clinicians, researchers, and policy-makers - to study the opportunities and threats of the platform trial model. We will recruit 300 patients to an ongoing international platform trial that is building pandemic research capacity. We will use these experiences to design a Canadian platform to support the research activities of the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group - the oldest and most productive ICU research group in the world. The insights gained, and the research capacity created, will affirm Canadian research leadership in critical care, and lead to better patient outcomes in a learning health care system.

column36: Reducing Diabetic Foot Complications through a Multidisciplinary Chiropodist Based Intervention
column37: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is a major complication of diabetes and can be a significant physical, social, financial and emotional burden. About 25% of persons with diabetes develop DFUs. If poorly managed, DFUs can lead to amputations, 1 of the 2 most feared complications of diabetes. The risk of DFUs can be reduced with simple preventative measures yet DFUs and DFU relapses have not declined as there is no high-quality data supporting proactive DFU treatment. Chiropodists are experts at managing foot disorders. A small study linked chiropodist care with markedly less leg amputations in people with diabetes and on dialysis. This led us to think that an intensive, structured, chiropodist-led strategy will lower amputation-related hospitalizations in those with diabetes and their need for medical, social and financial resources. In consultation with persons with diabetes, amputees and representatives from health agencies, and diabetes and DFU professional groups, we designed a novel trial to study if chiropodist care will lower amputation-related hospitalizations in those with diabetes undergoing dialysis since this group is deemed to have the greatest need and is one that administrators are most likely to effect change in funding allocation and health care systems delivery. Our study will include 2200 participants from 40 sites in Ontario, Alberta and Manitoba. The 2-year study will record amputation-related hospitalizations, deaths, cost effectiveness and perceived quality of life. Our committee includes persons with diabetes, amputees, chiropodists, a nurse, a family doctor and specialists. We have trial experts, a health care economist and statisticians who will assist in data interpretation, and individuals in the government and professional groups who will provide guidance on rolling out the findings (if positive) into clinical practice. Finally, the trainees will receive hands on experience to enrich their expertise as they carve out their career paths.

column36: Regulation of gonadotropin action by Slit/Robo signaling in the mammalian ovary
column37: Oocytes develop and mature in the ovary within structures called follicles. Follicles are recruited from a reserve and grow under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) produced by the pituitary gland. Once terminally developed, the follicle ruptures to release the (now mature) oocyte at the moment of ovulation. Ovulation itself is triggered by a second pituitary hormone, luteinizing hormone (LH), which also causes the reorganization of the ovulated follicle into a new glandular tissue termed the corpus luteum, which secretes the large amounts of progesterone necessary for the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy. Whereas we have long known FSH and LH to be major players in ovarian follicle development, how exactly they exert their effects remains incompletely understood. Ourselves and others have shown that a class of secreted signaling molecules called SLITs, along with their receptors called ROBOs, are expressed in the ovary in a pattern suggesting their involvement in follicle development. Our preliminary data indicate that, when follicle cells are treated in vitro with SLIT ligand, gonadotropin signaling and action is suppressed. This proposal will seek to confirm these preliminary results, in part by studying mice that lack Slit1, Slit2, Robo1 and Robo2, which we expect to be hyperfertile due to augmented FSH- and LH-mediated signaling processes. We will also study the molecular mechanisms whereby Slit/Robo and gonadotropin signaling interact. Together, our studies will uncover new information regarding how FSH and LH act, and about the biological roles of Slit/Robo signaling in the ovary. Importantly, this research may also identify new and valuable pharmacologic targets that could be exploited in the clinical context, in fields of application as wide-ranging as the treatment of fertility disorders, contraception, and recovery of fertility following chemotherapy.

column36: Cortical Plasticity Following Deafness
column37: In Canada, hearing loss is the most common sensory disability in adults and deafness is the most common congenital sensory abnormality in children. A 2006 Australian study estimated that costs to that nation's economy from hearing loss amounted to $10.6 billion per year. On a per capita basis, this translates to a Canadian equivalent of almost $18-billion annually. Although we hear with our brains little is known about what occurs to the brain as a consequence of deafness. In this proposal we will be studying what happens inside the brain following the onset of deafness shortly after birth or in adulthood. Specifically, we will be studying the regions of the brain that normally process sounds in hearing individuals. To do this we will examine deafness in an animal model. This approach will permit us to examine the activity of individual neurons, to examine changes in brain circuitry and activity, and to examine how changes in the brain affect perception and behavior. If the part of the brain that normally processes hearing is not receiving sound, then what is it doing? Is it processing visual information? Is it processing information concerning touch? If it is processing sight, then it may very well help explain the increased visual abilities of deaf humans. Changes in the brain such as this are known as "plastic" changes, or simply "plasticity". These changes are also called "compensatory" because they help the subject enhance their ability to use their remaining senses. Therefore, the goal of this study is to examine the natural plasticity of the brain. Knowing how the brain responds to changes in its inputs in this way will help us develop appropriate therapeutic strategies to help increase brain plasticity and help patients to overcome conditions such as deafness and blindness.

column36: Correlates of Healthy Aging in Geriatric HIV: CHANGE HIV STUDY
column37: The population of persons living with HIV (PLWH) is aging due to effective HIV therapy and new infections occurring in older individuals. Much needs to be learned about what it means to age with HIV. Although organ diseases (like heart and brain) are increased in PLWH, aging is more complex and health evaluations must consider the impact of these conditions on a person's ability to function well. We propose to bring together this new interdisciplinary team and the CHANGE HIV (Correlates of Healthy aging in Geriatric HIV) STUDY. We will invite men and women living with HIV >65 years of age from primary care and hospital HIV clinics in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver to join. At regular clinic visits we will add tests of physical, cognitive, mental, social function and quality of life and collect data on external factors like housing, behaviors and stigma that might influence health. We will analyze the way the factors interact to identify the ones that contribute most to healthy aging well if these differ by sex or gender. From the data, we will calculate a healthy aging score that can inform care and research by assessing a person's overall health status and track changes with time or therapy. The knowledge gained will inform interventions and strategies to improve healthy aging and help us know which ones are the most important, feasible and acceptable to those aging with HIV. Our data can be used to advocate for changes to health and social policies and appropriate allocation of resources for services for aging PLWH. A program strength is to train and stimulate new academic and community investigators building future research capacity in HIV and aging. Community members will be meaningfully involved in all stages ensures our research is feasible, ethical and relevant and supports the development of knowledge that is useful to key. Our learning's will advance understanding of aging in PLWH and ultimately lead to improved clinical and community practice and policy.

column36: Healthy Living for HIV-exposed Uninfected Children - cognitive, behavioural, neuroimaging and animal studies to assess the impact of in utero exposure to HIV and antiretrovirals.
column37: The use of HIV medications in pregnancy has enabled a radical reduction in the rate of vertical HIV transmission. As a consequence, there is now a large and growing number of HIV-exposed uninfected children (HEU)-children born to women living with HIV that are not HIV infected. While most HEU children are in good health, some studies suggest that these children may experience developmental delays compared to their peers, including learning difficulties, issues with their memory, and behavioural problems. We know that the environment the child is exposed to during pregnancy (the in utero environment) can influence their long-term health. However, we don't know how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment and whether these changes affect the long-term health of HEU children. Our team will investigate how exposure to HIV and various HIV medications during pregnancy affects brain development and mental health in HEU children. We will perform cognitive and behavioural tests and brain imaging studies in a cohort of HEU and HIV unexposed children of similar age and background. We will examine correlations between their brain anatomy and behavioural and cognitive performance. We will measure various factors in the cord blood of these children (collected at the time of birth) to better understand how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment. We will perform similar tests in a mouse model where we can directly compare different HIV medications, examine how they affect brain development and behaviour of the pups, and design and test therapies that will improve outcomes. Our duty to HEU children does not stop with the prevention of HIV infection. We must understand how HIV and HIV medications alter the in utero environment and influence long-term health, so we can optimize HIV treatment in pregnancy and ensure the best health outcomes for HEU children.

column37: Scientists have made extraordinary advances in understanding and treating HIV infection over the past 20 years. Even with antiretroviral therapy, HIV-1 is still able to infect and damage the nervous system. This continues to be a major problem for people who are living with HIV/AIDS. The main problems when HIV-1 infects a person's nervous system are difficulties in thinking and persistent pain from damaged nerves. These problems are part of a condition called NeuroHIV. They diminish a person's quality of life, impair their sleep, reduce their ability to hold a job, affect their mood and isolate them socially. Over the past 5 years, our team has defined how often these problems occur and their severity. We have also discovered new disease processes and used that knowledge to develop and test new approaches to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. For example, we uncovered new biological markers for people who have cognitive problems and pain from NeuroHIV. We found new possible treatments for these cognitive problems and pain, and we are testing those treatments in clinical trials. We have also identified specific sex and gender factors that make some people with NeuroHIV more vulnerable to thinking problems and pain from damaged nerves. NeuroHIV causes other problems that need research. These problems are linked to sex and gender diversity, and to how aging affects people with NeuroHIV. Our team of researchers from different areas of science and health will map basic pathways in the biology of NeuroHIV. Discovering these pathways can help us to analyze symptoms and risk factors for NeuroHIV. Understanding the pathways will also lead to new ways to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. Part of our work will be to build broader community knowledge of NeuroHIV and its related problems.

column37: Older people living with HIV worry about their memory, and with good reason. A third or more have problems with thinking or concentration, despite good control of their HIV infection. Rates of depression, anxiety and poor motivation are also high. Separately or together, these brain health problems affect function and quality of life. The causes of brain health symptoms in HIV are not fully understood, and we don't know whether brain health inevitably worsens over time. Our team has developed new ways to assess these problems in the clinic, identified the factors that relate to poor brain health in a large on-going cohort study, and provided preliminary information about whether these symptoms can be treated. Here, we build on this foundation to meet three broad aims: (1) Understand the factors that lead to poor brain health, focusing on viral, cerebrovascular, and social contributors; (2) Empower people living with HIV and the clinicians who care for them with practical tools to assess brain health and personalize treatment; (3) Act to help people living with HIV improve brain health through lifestyle changes. We will extend the existing cohort study to provide crucial information about whether brain health worsens over longer follow-up. column36: SEARCH (active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare) & PREVENT (Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team)
column37: The debilitating and lethal consequences of severe adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are a striking failure of modern medicine. The consequences for patients who experience severe ADRs are catastrophic. In Canada, there are an estimated 200,000 severe ADRs, claiming 10,000-22,000 lives, and costing $14-18 billion each year. To tackle this complex problem requires a multi-faceted collaborative linking of scientists, clinicians and regulators sharing complementary expertise in an environment that promotes teamwork. The Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) Active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare (SEARCH) initiative was first funded in 2011, with the overarching goal of conducting active surveillance to identify important drug risks, reduce the occurrence of severe ADRs and improve drug safety in Canadians. In close collaboration with the Drug Safety and Effectiveness (DSEN) Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team (PREVENT) the work of SEARCH is strengthened through the discovery of pharmacogenomics biomarkers - that is understanding the genetic variation between patients that affects their individual drug response. This inter-individual variation acts as key predictors of ADRs for many drugs in clinical use today. Our team will build on its broad experience in active surveillance methods, pharmacogenomics expertise and its established network of ADR surveillance clinicians in Canadian health centres. These surveillance clinicians are located at 13 pediatric academic health centers and 13 adult academic health centers and their role is to identify and report ADRs, and collect DNA and the detailed clinical information that is needed to evaluate potential drug risks. This will allow SEARCH & PREVENT to continue active surveillance in areas of importance to the CIHR Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network, Health Canada and other pertinent stakeholders.

column36: Rhinovirus induced modulation of epithelial phenotype in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic airway disease that affects 300 million people worldwide. Although all children get multiple infections with human rhinovirus (HRV - the "common cold virus") in early life, only a subset get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, and are far more likely to develop asthma by age 6. It is not clear why only some children get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, but the interaction of HRV and development of allergies may play a role. Human airway epithelial cells (HAE) are the main site of HRV infection and it is thought that HRV affects asthma by changing HAE biology. The characteristic features (phenotype) of HAE are altered in asthma, and these altered HAE interact with nearby structural and immune cells to help cause asthma. Despite the central role of HAE in regulating airway diseases, the effects of HRV infection on HAE phenotype have not been well characterized. We have found that HRV infection of HAE from normal people causes transient changes in cell biology. In this proposal, we will fully characterize the effects of HRV on epithelial phenotype and will define the mechanisms by which HRV causes these changes. We will determine if repeated infections with HRV cause greater effects in HAE than a single infection. In addition, we will test the idea that HRV infections (single or repeated) in the setting of an "allergic" environment produce more profound alterations in HAE that mimic the phenotype seen in asthma. We will compare HAE from asthmatic children to those from normal children to see if they have greater responses to HRV. Finally, we will experimentally infect normal and asthmatic volunteers with HRV to test the idea that HAE in asthmatic patients show greater response to HRV in vivo. By understanding how HRV infections alter epithelial responses, alone and in an allergic setting, we may be able to develop ways to prevent or reduce the effects of HRV in asthma in order to improve the well-being of patients with asthma.

column36: The functions of mammalian TRAPP complexes and their role in disease
column37: The Transport Protein Particle (TRAPP) complexes were first discovered in yeast. Subsequent work identified related, conserved complexes in humans. These complexes function in moving proteins between various intracellular compartments within a cell. Although they share a core of common proteins, there are unique proteins that are associated with the core to form the various complexes (three complexes in yeast, two in higher eukaryotes). While the functions of the complexes in yeast are better understood, the functions of the mammalian complexes are less clear. In addition, several of the subunits that associate with the complex in humans have been shown to have functions independent of the complex. Furthermore, recent work has led to the identification of individuals that have mutations in TRAPP proteins. Curiously, these individuals all have different phenotypes depending on which TRAPP protein is mutated. Thus, understanding the functions of the mammalian TRAPP proteins and their role in disease is a necessary next step in our understanding of these complexes. This present application seeks to understand the functions of two specific subunits called C11 and C2L. In order to facilitate this work, we are developing a simplified in vitro assay that reconstitutes transport in the secretory pathway. We will use wild type TRAPP complexes as well as complexes harboring mutations in the aforementioned proteins to assess their ability to reconstitute membrane traffic in this pathway. The results of these studies will provide insight into specific human disorders that are linked to TRAPP mutations and will allow clinicians to more quickly assess new disorders that may be linked to these complexes.

column37: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin in biphasic manner, an initial peak phase (~15 min) followed by a sustained phase (several hours), to ensure continuous assimilation of circulating nutrients into tissues. In type-2 diabetes, both phases are perturbed resulting in deficient insulin release causing hyperglycemia. Half of initial peak phase is attributed to secretory granules (SGs) predocked on calcium channels (Cav1.2/1.3) on the plasma membrane where calcium influx induces SG fusion to release insulin. Newcomer SGs (NSG) are a newly discovered SG population that account for the entire sustained phase and half of first-phase secretion. We discovered the SNARE (syntaxin-3, VAMP8) and associated proteins responsible for NSG fusion; but unlike predocked SGs, little else is known about the NSG secretory machinery. Our first hypothesis (Aim 1) is that NSGs specifically land on and undergo fusion at a new set of calcium channels (Cav2.1/2.3) which bind syntaxin-3. An undefined reserve pool must exist to continually replenish NSGs after depletion from stimulated release. We found potassium channel (Kv2.1) clusters on plasma membrane that bind NSG-syntaxin-3. Our second hypothesis (Aim 2) is that syntaxin-3/Kv2.1 clusters form complexes that serve as an accessible reserve pool for NSGs to park prior to their relocation to adjacent calcium channels. This provides a unique architecture that couples the reserve pool (Kv2.1 clusters) of SGs to SG release sites (Cav), a process that has long eluded previous investigation. This work has broad application to many endocrine cells that exhibit sustained secretion required to meet varying metabolic needs. Insights into these novel fundamental steps of secretion are a basis for development of treatment strategies to improve secretion. As proof, we will express (with virus) Cav and Kv2.1 into pancreatic islets of diabetic humans (in vitro) and rats (in vivo) to improve the deficient insulin secretion and restore glucose homeostasis.

column37: There is a strong association between chronic inflammation, and the risk of developing cancer. One of the most prevalent examples of chronic inflammation is obesity, which affects over 1/3 of adults in Canada/USA. Inevitably, obesity now rivals smoking as the #1 preventable risk factor for cancer. Obesity is associated with higher incidence of breast cancer metastasis (i.e. cancer spread), particularly to liver and lung. Of particular interest is lung metastasis, given the high frequency of breast cancer progression to this site in patients, and the association between obesity and multiple lung-inflammatory conditions (e.g. asthma). These are significant findings because the lung is one of the most frequent sites of metastasis, which causes death in patients. The objective of this study is to provide a translational framework for understanding how overweight/obesity affects breast cancer metastasis, with the goal of identifying blood-based prognostic markers and new therapies. This could improve treatment methods for a large proportion of breast cancer patients, and contribute to a broader understanding of the relationship between the immune system and cancer. We hypothesize that breast cancer progresses differently in obese patients compared to lean patients, and therefore, obese patients will require different treatment considerations.

column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. We will conduct a randomized controlled trial which evaluates the effectiveness of daily symptom screening by children seen in hospital daily for 5 days and feedback of symptom reports to healthcare providers with links to guidelines for symptom management. Participants in the control arm will receive the standard of care in which symptom screening with feedback is not performed. We will include English-speaking children and adolescents 8-18 years of age expected to be in hospital daily for 5 days. The primary endpoint will be the day 5 total SSPedi score which ranges from 0 to 60 (higher means more bothersome symptoms). We plan to enroll 345 children across 7 Canadian institutions over 4 years. This research will enable children to report symptoms and will help providers know how to manage symptoms using the best available evidence. Ultimately, SPARK implementation will lead to better symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column37: Antibiotic resistance is rising to dangerously high levels in all parts of the world, compromising our ability to treat infectious diseases, as well as undermining many other advances in health and medicine. The phenomenon threatens our ability to treat common infections, resulting in prolonged illness, disability, and death. The epidemic of resistant bacteria challenges the scientific community to urgently identify novel antibiotics and discover new antimicrobial targets. One attractive target in Gram-negative bacteria consists in the critical bacterial envelope and the conserved molecular machines involved in its biogenesis. Particularly, the current proposal will focus on the Translocation and Assembly Module (TAM) promoting secretion of virulence factors in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in hospital-acquired infections associated with multidrug-resistant phenotype. This CIHR project grant proposes to dissect the structure-function relationship of this protein assembly module in order to generate health-related knowledge. Our molecular and structural biology approaches will provide critical insights into the molecular mechanism of TAM, thus guiding downstream developments of small molecule inhibitors interfering with TAM functions and bacterial pathogenesis.

column36: Characterization of quality control pathways that target cytosolic misfolded proteins with missense mutations for proteasome degradation
column37: Gene mutations that cause diseases often do so by causing misfolding and degradation of the mutant proteins. Protein misfolding occurs when a protein does not attain its so-called native structure, which is reached when the protein is properly folded to perform its function in the cell. Our goal is to better understand how mutant proteins that misfold are recognized by elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system. The ubiquitin proteasome system consists of groups of enzymes that first mark proteins targeted for degradation by attaching to them a small protein tag called ubiquitin. These ubiquitin-tagged proteins are then recognized by the proteasome, which eliminates them from the cell. Our main hypothesis is there are several degradation paths for different groups of proteins that misfold due to mutations. To test this idea, we will analyze using different cell-based assays a large panel of mutations that have been associated to genetic disorders or diseases. More specifically, we will focus on missense mutations that induce the change of single amino acids. First, we will identify which mutated cytosolic proteins are degraded by the ubiquitin proteasome system from a large panel of known disease-associated mutations. We will then determine which known elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system target these misfolded mutant proteins. A major question is how E3 enzymes that attach ubiquitin recognize misfolded proteins. To address this question, we will employ the identified mutant proteins as model substrates to better identify which regions or domains on E3 enzymes recognize the misfolded proteins. Finally, we will set up a screen to identify novel genes involved in targeting misfolded proteins for degradation. By better understanding how misfolded proteins are triaged within the cell, we will gain fundamental knowledge of disease mechanisms, leading to potential novel therapeutic approaches.

column36: Stress, Brain and Neurodevelopment in Children Born Preterm
column37: In Canada, as in other high resource countries, preterm birth (<37 weeks gestation) is the most important cause of disability. Among children born preterm >50% show significant developmental problems (cognitive, attention, behaviour, social, motor, academic) impacting family and society. While abnormal brain development is evident in these vulnerable children, persisting to adulthood, little is known about why some preterm children do well and others decline, even when born in the same gestational age range. Early stress impacts brain structure and function. Children born very preterm (<32 weeks gestation) are exposed to pain-related stress of medical and nursing procedures (~10 per day) during weeks to months in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Our research has shown that this neonatal pain/stress is associated with altered brain development and stress hormone (cortisol) regulation, beyond clinical factors related to premature birth. The goal of this project is to determine in a longitudinal prospective study of children born very preterm (24-32 weeks) how the developing brain and stress systems may affect the pattern of cognitive and behavioral outcomes across ages 1.5, 3, 4.5 and 8 years, the role of parenting, and whether effects differ by sex. Understanding factors that explain the wide variation in neurodevelopmental outcomes in children born preterm, and that promote stress regulation and brain recovery in children born very preterm will provide critical underpinnings for developing interventions to optimize long-term neurodevelopment in this fragile population.

column36: How is anxiety represented in the anterior cingulate cortex?
column37: Many psychiatric conditions have an anxiety component but it is not clear how anxiety develops at a neural level. The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) plays a critical role in anxiety and anxiety-based disorders. We have studied the behavior of ACC neurons and networks and have developed a theory about how they may create anxiety. The activity in groups of ACC neurons form patterns that represent the events the animal experiences. We discovered unique patterns that arise in anticipation of unpleasant, threatening events. These patterns may act on other brain regions, to influence autonomic arousal and create a sensation of anxiety that in turn affects ongoing thought or action. The present proposal seeks to better understand the patterns in ACC neurons that represent anticipated threats and to test possible ways to weaken these patterns and in turn, reduce anxiety.

column36: Targeting Exercise Activated Pathways to Counter the Side Effects of Antipsychotic Drugs
column37: Antipsychotic drugs are used to treat a number of conditions including schizophrenia, anxiety and bipolar disorders and their use has increased dramatically over the past decade. Unfortunately, these drugs have harmful metabolic side effects such as weight gain and rapid increases in blood sugar with each dose of drug. Together these effects increase the risk for developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. In recent work, we have shown that a single session of exercise prior to treatment with antipsychotics completely protected against the acute increase in blood sugar. Although exercise adherence is poor in individuals taking anti-psychotic drugs we have been using exercise as a model to identify pathways which could be targeted to reduce the metabolic side effects of these drugs. Based on preliminary data from our laboratory we have shown that the activation of an energy-sensing enzyme called AMPK confers the same protection against anti-psychotic metabolic side effects as exercise. The purpose of this project is to examine the effects of AMPK in protecting against the acute and long-term metabolic side effects of antipsychotic drugs and to determine if AMPK mediates the beneficial effects of exercise. The data generated from these studies will provide insight into new approaches that could be used to lessen the metabolic consequences of antipsychotic drugs and could shed insight into the mechanisms mediating the protective effects of exercise.

column36: Multi-centre Temporal Ultrasound Image Analysis for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer diagnosed in Canadian men, with about 25,000 new cases per year. The gold standard for PCa diagnosis and prognosis is ultrasound (US)-guided needle biopsy with pathologic grading. The biopsy procedure is not patient specific; rather, it involves taking "blind" biopsy cores, leading to frequent re-biopsy or over diagnosis of insignificant cancer. There is an acute need for patient-specific targeting techniques that have higher chance of detecting early aggressive PCa. Aggressive PCa must be diagnosed early and accurately to appropriately treat patients at higher risk of morbidity and mortality. Meanwhile, it is critical to balance against over-treatment of indolent PCa, of which is more appropriately managed using an active surveillance approach. The best biopsy technique today is to localize PCa with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and use its fusion with US to improve the detection rate of aggressive PCa. However, this method alone is not able to accurately differentiate indolent PCa and cannot reliably detect small lesions of aggressive PCa. In this project, we propose a turnkey technology, where subtle variations of backscattered US signals from a tissue location over a short time span, i.e., temporal enhanced US, are used to detect physical properties of the underlying tissue using a machine-learning framework. Our objective is to establish the efficacy of this technology in identifying clinically significant PCa in real-time US, so that accurate biopsy targeting is achieved. In a series of clinical studies, we will develop and deploy this technology across multiple institutions. This technology is expected to positively and rapidly benefit the lives of all patients suffering from PCa. Collaboration with leading investigators in Canada and USA will create an effective environment for leading international development of next generation cancer diagnosis imaging tools.

column36: Role of autophagy dysregulation in pancreatitis caused by alcohol and glucagon-like peptide
column37: Acute pancreatitis (AP) causes high morbidity and mortality, and at considerable financial costs to health care in Canada. The most common cause of AP is alcohol, affecting 10% of alcoholics. There is still no effective specific treatment directed at the pathogenesis of alcoholic AP in part because the postulated disease mechanisms could not be directly tested on human pancreatic tissue. Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, which potentiate glucose-mediated insulin secretion, is the new panacea for treating diabetes; now a multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical market. However, GLP-1 drug treatments exhibited six-fold increase in AP, the basis is totally unknown. Our overarching hypothesis is that alcohol and GLP-1 drugs can cause perturbations in autophagy, the cellular 'self-eating' process that normally gets rid of cellular garbage. Autophagy involves a series of vesicle formations that involve distinct SNARE proteins (Aim 1), which when pathologically activated (alcohol - Aim 2, GLP-1 - Aim 3), causes inadvertent protease activation (instead of physiologic degradation) which can damage and destroy acinar cells (i.e. AP). To mechanistically address these conditions in a clinically-relevant manner, we've developed the method of preparing fresh human pancreatic slices to assess autophagy processes and how their perturbations contribute to acinar cell injury. We will assess whether manipulation of autophagy SNAREs expression in rat pancreas can modify alcohol- and GLP-1-mediated pancreatic injury. This work may identify novel treatments for AP and impact current diabetes management in patients taking GLP-1 drugs.

column36: Equity in Mental Health Care for Children and Youth
column37: Mental health problems and suicide are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality for children and youth. Yet access to mental health care for children is an ongoing challenge. The principle of equity in access to healthcare is reflected in the Canada Health Act. However, equity in access to MH care is ill-defined and has rarely been examined in relation to child/youth mental health services (CYMHS). The current study will conduct a systematic review of how equity has been evaluated with respect to MH care for children and youth. Equity can be defined as equal access to services. Within Ontario and across Canada, specialized MH and psychiatric services for children and youth are delivered mainly through publicly-funded agencies and psychiatrists. Private providers (psychologists and social workers) also play a role; we have little information on the role that private providers play in the systems that care for this population. The present study will also examine the distribution of publicly-funded agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers, and the extent to which sociodemographic factors (e.g., family income) are related to the distribution of child and youth MH services. If the distribution of agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers varies by regions, this would likely result in inequity in access to care for individuals in regions with fewer agencies/providers. Second, if the distribution of agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers varies by region as a function of sociodemographic factors, it would also reflect inequities in access to care. Identification of inequity is the first step to addressing those inequities and ultimately improving the systems in place to care for children and youth with mental health problems.

column36: Functional and genetic susceptibility to progressive cryptococcal pneumonia
column37: Cryptococcus neoformans is an environmental fungus found throughout the world that causes serious disease of the lungs and brain in over one million humans each year. This pathogen is capable of infecting healthy humans and is particularly dangerous for those with weakened immune defences. Interestingly, only a minority of all individuals that are exposed to Cryptococcus neoformans will become ill. We believe that humans have natural differences that influence their susceptibility to severe cryptococcal infection and their response to treatment; however, we lack a firm understanding of the basic mechanisms that control these processes. Precise knowledge of host immune defense would be extremely valuable for diagnosis, prediction and monitoring of disease progression, and personalized therapy of cryptococcal infection. To identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control the development of severe cryptococcal disease, we use a mouse model of infection that closely resembles the human disease. We will apply cutting edge technology to analyze the function of lung cells, tissues, and organs and determine how the underlying cellular pathways and genes influence immunity. The knowledge we derive through this project will be translated into improved prevention and clinical management of serious human fungal infections.

column36: Understanding mutagenic replication-transcription conflicts in cancer-initiation
column37: Mutations in DNA are a driving force in cancer initiation, progression and therapy resistance. Some mutations arise from normal functions involving DNA. These functions include copying DNA during cell division, and transcribing DNA into RNA messages that control the production of proteins in the cell. These two independent processes, termed DNA replication and transcription, must occur at the same time on the same DNA, and therefore they can interfere with one another. We now know that these replication-transcription conflicts are a potential source of DNA damage and mutations and are thought to be influenced by breast cancer susceptibility genes. This proposal will clearly define new roles for breast cancer tumour suppressor genes in preventing replication-transcription conflicts, and survey the prevalence of such conflicts in normal cells from individuals with elevated 5-year risk for breast cancer and in early and late stage breast cancer samples. Our hope is to find new ways to selectively eliminate breast cancer cells experiencing high levels of replication-transcription collisions.

column36: The impact of nuclear G protein signalling in health and disease

column36: Establishing the importance of diet and insulin resistance in modulating immune function in obesity
column37: Obesity is associated with several risk factors (for example, high blood sugar, poor insulin response and inflammation) that increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Obesity is also associated with abnormalities in the immune system and an increased risk of infection. Specific components of the diet such as high dietary intake of fat and sugar influence not only the development of obesity but also the immune system. Therefore, it is still unclear if the immune dysfunction associated with obesity in human are attributable to 1- the excess of body fat per se and/or 2- the metabolic complications also often associated with obesity such as elevated blood glucose and/or 3- the overall poor diet quality of an individual. We are proposing a study where we will characterize, in controlled feeding conditions, the functionality of the immune system by investigating a panel of makers of the immune system (inflammation in the blood and the response of immune cells). At the end of a 4-week feeding period where participants will all consume the same standardized diet, we will compare the immune system of three groups of adults with obesity: a. obesity with normal blood glucose concentrations; b. obesity with marginally elevated blood glucose concentrations; and c. obesity with T2DM. All groups will be matched for age, sex and body mass index, and compared to a group of healthy normal weight subjects. By comparing these four groups, we will be able to gain an understanding of the immune complications associated with obesity alone (e.g. excess of body fat per se) and the association of blood sugar and diet in modulating these immune complications. This is essential to subsequently identify dietary interventions to counteract the immune dysfunctions associated with obesity.

column36: Mechanisms of REM sleep behaviour disorder
column37: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) affects 2-6% of the elderly population and is characterized by excessive movement during REM sleep. These movements are typically so violent that they result in patient injuries, which often require medical attention. However, the most alarming aspect of RBD is that 80-90% of patients eventually develop a brain disease like Parkinson's disease or dementia after being diagnosed with RBD. During healthy REM sleep, most of the body's muscles are paralyzed. However, in RBD muscle paralysis is lost, which causes RBD patients to actively move during REM sleep. Because RBD is tightly associated with brain degeneration and this degeneration begins in brain regions that cause REM sleep paralysis, it is hypothesized that RBD is caused by degeneration of the brain regions that control REM sleep paralysis. However, it still remains unclear which cells in the brainstem control REM sleep paralysis and if damage to these cell circuits underlies RBD. This medical research will be of importance to Canadians because it identifies the brain mechanisms that cause healthy REM sleep and it determines if degeneration of these regions causes RBD.

The regulation of protein stability by this pathway is critical in the molecular basis of carcinogenesis, as it is involved in the regulation of cell growth and preventing abnormal accumulation of proteins. Additionally, ubiquitin modification of target proteins signals many cellular processes other than proteolysis that are also important for the development of cancer. Deregulation of ubiquitin ligases, which are proteins involved in many biological processes including protein degradation, results in uncontrolled proliferation, genomic instability and cancer. Attempts to develop general protein degradation inhibitors for cancer therapy have been questioned because it is highly toxic, and could results in long-term effects from the accumulation of misfolded proteins that is the hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, there is great interests in identifying specific proteins involved in this process that could be targeted instead. We identified UBBP4, a gene encoding novel ubiquitins that could be involved in such specific ubiquitination of proteins. The main goal of studying ubiquitin and ubiquitin ligases is to develop drugs that specifically target these enzymes. Thus, it is crucial to identify the substrates of these ubiquitin ligases and understand their cellular functions. We will be using different innovative approaches to identify the proteins modified by UBBP4, as well as functional role for this new modification. The results obtained from the experiments proposed in this application will allow us to better understand the molecular mechanisms regulated by ubiquitin.

column36: Putting Social Citizenship into Practice: Reducing Stigma and Promoting Social Inclusion of People with Dementia
column37: PURPOSE: The purpose of this four-year study is to learn how communities can reduce stigma and promote social inclusion of people living with dementia. We are creating a team of academic researchers, people with dementia, and community partners who will work together, using the approach of "participatory action research", to meet two goals: (1) create a useful definition of "social citizenship" based on the experiences and opinions of people with dementia; and (2) show how this definition can provide practical guidance for communities to reduce stigma and promote social inclusion of people with dementia. METHODS: An action group of people with dementia will be the centre of a team that includes academic researchers and community partners. To meet the first goal, the action group will direct the team on gathering in-depth information from different groups of people in the community who are living with dementia. Methods will include focus groups, workshops, interviews, and observation. The information will be analysed to create a framework defining the concept of social citizenship and identifying ways to respect citizenship. To meet the second goal, the research team will use this framework with direction from the action group to identify, apply, and assess strategies communities can use to support social citizenship for people living with dementia. Information about the process and impact of these strategies will be gathered and analysed. IMPACT: Study outcomes will include a set of practical guidelines to provide direction for communities to reduce stigma and promote social inclusion of the growing numbers of people with dementia. We expect this to shape policy and decision-making at organizational and municipal levels. Including people with dementia in a full participatory role as co-researchers is groundbreaking in Canada, so we also expect study results to be influential for health and social care planning, and for further research.

column36: Integrated phylogenetic, molecular and functional analyses of the within-host latent HIV reservoir
column37: Thanks to the advent of combination antiretroviral therapies, HIV infection is now considered a chronically manageable condition. These drugs however do not completely eliminate HIV from the body; as such, an HIV cure is actively being pursued. HIV is able to persist in the body because the virus establishes "latent HIV reservoirs", long-lived cells that harbor a dormant copy of the HIV genome within them. HIV can persist for decades within these cells, but the virus may reactivate at any time to produce infectious particles. It is for this reason that HIV therapy needs to be maintained for life. Establishment of latent HIV reservoirs is a continuous process that begins shortly after infection. Moreover, HIV is continually evolving within a given host. Thus, by the time an individual reaches chronic infection, their latent HIV reservoir is expected to comprise a genetically diverse pool of viral sequences that constitute a "fossil record" of HIV evolution in that individual. Importantly, latently-infected cells are likely to differ in key respects including their ability to reactivate to produce infectious HIV particles and their susceptibility to recognition by the immune system. Methods to study HIV reservoir diversity and to identify key characteristics that associate with reservoir reactivation would greatly aid efforts towards an HIV cure. Our interdisciplinary team, comprising molecular biology, bioinformatics, and clinical experts, has developed an innovative genetics-based method for determining when a given HIV sequence "went dormant" within a host. We now seek to apply our method to address foundational gaps in our understanding of HIV persistence. We believe that our integrated approach will provide a versatile and potentially transformative addition to the growing armamentarium of tools in HIV cure research, towards the ultimate goal of developing strategies for HIV reservoir elimination.

Also, no system is in place to identify and address barriers and facilitators to the implementation of high quality care for this new service. This study, beginning just as this new practice is first adopted in Canada, proposes to identify and address the factors necessary to ensure high quality, accessible provision of medical abortion services by Nurse Practitioners throughout Canada.

column36: Unravelling the contribution to the hypoxic ventilatory response of purinergic and glial signalling in the preBotzinger Complex
column37: The mammalian brain depends on a constant supply of oxygen to meet its energy needs. If this supply fails for even a few minutes permanent brain damage or death can result. A host of adaptive responses have evolved to protect brain oxygen. Prominent among these is the biphasic hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) in which a fall in blood oxygen (hypoxia) supplying the brain triggers an initial increase in breathing. If this increase does not restore oxygen levels, breathing falls in what is called the secondary hypoxic respiratory depression. Release of the excitatory neurochemical ATP in breathing centers of the brain helps maintain the increased breathing. However, this ATP is degraded to adenosine; brain hypoxia also causes widespread release of adenosine. Adenosine causes widespread depression of neuronal activity. This depression is highly adaptive in most brain regions because it reduces metabolic demand and hypoxic brain injury. However, depression of breathing is highly maladaptive because it is only through increases in breathing that oxygen levels can be restored. The net result is that the initial hypoxia-induced increase in breathing is followed by a secondary depression that is potentially fatal in premature infants who suffer from apnea of prematurity; it is also problematic in adults with sleep-disordered breathing where repeated, cyclic falls in oxygen exacerbate cardiovascular disease. Thus, there is great clinical interest in understanding the mechanisms underlying the HVR. The interaction between ATP excitation and adenosine inhibition of breathing is emerging as key in determining the magnitude of the hypoxic depression. The aim of this proposal is to use rodent models to determine the factors that control the balance between the excitatory actions of ATP and inhibitory actions of adenosine during hypoxia and develop strategies to shift the balance in favor of excitation to counteract the life-threatening hypoxic respiratory depression.

column37: Cancers are caused by mutations and genetic alterations. Usually these enzymes act for our benefit and use their activity to alter the DNA sequence of viruses to make the viral DNA nonfunctional. This research is focused on the internal origins of these mutations caused by a specific family of enzymes, called the APOBEC3 enzymes. column36: Genetic instability of the haploid male germ cells
column37: Genetic diversity is provided by de novo transmittable mutations and it is now known that most new mutations are male- driven. During the formation of spermatozoa, the final steps involves a major change in the way DNA is packaged and we demonstrated that this is accompanied by the formation of transient DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in spermatids of both human and mouse pointing to an evolutionary-conserved mechanism. These DSBs arise in haploid cells where there is a single set of chromosome. The repair process cannot therefore proceed using the homologous chromosome as template as in normal somatic cells and must rather rely on a end-joining process. These end-joining repair processes are less reliable and known to induce DNA deletions and insertions. Our hypothesis is that mutations can therefore be induced when the DSBs are repaired in the subsequent steps of the spermatid's differentiation process. Our goal is therefore to confirm whether this process is indeed genetically unstable and if specific regions are involved in the ethiology of genetic diseases since our first screen suggest that neurodevelopmental genes are targeted with high significance. DSBs are also observed during yeast gamete formation emphasizing the conserved nature of this transition and providing a powerful genetic tool to decipher the DSBs mechanism. These investigations may confirm the discovery of a novel mechanism contributing to genetic diversity, evolution and possibly to neurodevelopment disorders such as autism.

column36: Amylin Receptor: A potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease and diabetes mellitus, two of the most serious public health concerns of our times share many commonalities. In Alzheimer's disease, abnormal deposition of a protein in the brain referred to as amyloid is linked to destruction and death of brain cells involved in learning and memory. In a similar manner, the presence of another protein, human amylin, discovered in the pancreas of diabetic patients, renders insulin-producing cells dysfunctional. Work from our laboratory has shown that both amyloid and amylin exert their damaging effects on cells through the same receptor or "keyhole". We have therefore been working with compounds, which block the amylin receptor/keyhole in the brain, and thus can protect brain cells from toxic effects of amyloid. More recently, we have used such amylin receptor blocking drugs to improve the memory and learning deficits in mice, which are genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's disease. In this project, we plan to #1) genetically reduce the amylin receptor (keyhole) in Alzheimer mice thus preventing the amyloid from damaging brain cells, and in the process delay or prevent the development of Alzheimer-like symptoms, #2) develop compounds that can easily penetrate the brains of Alzheimer's mice, block the amylin receptor/keyhole and thus alleviate the memory problems. At present there is no treatment for AD other than for its symptoms. Studies such as those contained in this proposal may identify newer therapies based on protecting nerve cells from the deleterious effects of amyloid-beta in the brains of AD patients and thus slowing or preventing the disease altogether.

column37: Sepsis (ie. blood poisoning) is triggered by harmful microorganisms or their toxins in the blood or tissues. These harmful agents can cause a vicious cycle of blood clot formation and inflammation, which may lead to multiple organ failure and death even after the microorganisms have been cleared with antibiotics. In Canada, there are approximately 90,000 patients with sepsis each year. Of these, 30% to 50% of these patients will die. Many anti-sepsis drugs have been tested in humans, but all of these clinical studies have failed. This suggests that some fundamental knowledge is lacking in our current understanding of why sepsis kills patients. In recent years, neutrophils (a type of white blood cells) have been shown to release web-like structures (called NETs) to capture and kill microorganisms. NETs consist of DNA, histones, and neutrophils enzymes. However, NETs can also cause collateral damage to the body. We have previously shown that the DNA and histone components of NETs can trigger blood clotting and prevent blood breakdown. We have also shown that high levels of DNA in the blood of septic patients is a strong predictor of death. In a mouse model of sepsis, injection of DNAse (an enzyme that breaks down DNA) results in improved organ function and improved survival rates. In the current proposal, we plan to further study how DNA and histones triggers blood clots and inflammation in sepsis. We will perform studies of blood cells and blood molecules in test tubes. By comparing blood samples from septic and non-septic ICU patients, we can identify the precise biological pathways that lead to high levels of DNA in septic patients. We will also perform studies in a mouse model of sepsis to see if removal of DNA and/or histones from the blood can improve survival in septic mice. Our research thus has the potential to identify new anti-sepsis strategies that will improve the lives of septic patients.

column37: Streptococcus pneumonia (the pneumococcus) is a bacterium that often lives in the nose and throats of humans. This relationship is most often benign but this microorganism is also an accomplished disease-causing germ that can cause mild ailments, such as earaches, to lethal illnesses like pneumonia, blood poisoning, and infections of the brain and central nervous system. There are effective vaccines and medicines (antibiotics) to treat infections caused by the pneumococcus; however, this germ is constantly adapting to avoid both of these medical interventions. The importance of S. pneumoniae as a disease-causing germ dictates intense research efforts be directed to understand how it causes infections with the aim of using this knowledge to guide new treatment strategies. The human body has large amounts of carbohydrates with complex structures, termed glycans, displayed on the surface of cells and coating the surfaces of tissues (e.g. mucous). Remarkably, the pneumococcus relies on its ability to attack these glycans to colonize humans and ultimately cause disease. Our research is aimed at determining how this happens. What glycans does the germ attack? What pneumococcal factors do this? What is the outcome of destroying a host sugar? Armed with the fundamental insight from examining these questions we plan to develop and study molecules that can be used to prevent S. pneumoniae from attacking host glycans; such molecules are proving useful as research tools but may also provide a platform for developing new treatments to combat S. pneumoniae infections.

column36: Replication of guanine-rich DNA
column37: The broad goal of the research proposed here is to improve our understanding of how DNA, the hereditary information that determines the development and functioning of all living organisms, is maintained over a human lifetime. Specifically, I propose to focus on the replication of DNA that is enriched for guanine, one of the four DNA bases, in normal development and genome instability. The proposed research is a logical extension of earlier, published work from my laboratory. Following studies on the purification and self-renewal of blood forming stem cells, we focused on the role of telomeres, the normal ends of chromosomes, in normal and malignant cell proliferation. This work led us to studies of the pathways that ensure proper replication of the guanine (G)-rich DNA. In the course of this work, we discovered several genes including DOG-1 (FANCJ) and RTEL that are required for replication of G-rich DNA. Interestingly, both these genes encode for proteins with helicase activity: that is they are capable of unwinding secondary DNA structures of G-rich DNA, called guanine quadruplex (G4) structures. Recently we found that the Bloom helicase protein, deficient in patients with the cancer-prone Bloom syndrome, is required to suppress recombination at G-rich DNA. Here we propose further studies on the pathways required to resolve G4 structures and faithfully replicate Grich DNA at telomeres and at genes. The goal of these studies is to better understand the nature of the lesions that cause problems during replication of G-rich DNA and the pathways that different cells have available to solve such problems. Our studies will generate new knowledge about DNA replication and DNA repair and pathways that prevent genome instability. A better understanding of these pathways has broad potential for our understanding of normal development and aging as well specific disorders linked to DNA repair defects including specific types of cancer.

column36: Mechanisms of long-term change to neuronal activity and secretion
column37: My research focuses on nerve cells from the brain. I am interested in how the bio-electrical properties of nerve cells are controlled. These properties are governed by minute holes in nerve cells called channel proteins, which pass ions (like calcium, sodium or potassium) in and out of the cell. Because ions are charged, their movement through channels results in the flow of electrical current. Nerve cells harness currents to receive sensations, code information, and signal other nerve cells, muscles, or glands. Signalling involves the release of either small chemicals or specialized proteins, termed neuro-peptides, from a nerve cell. My objective is to examine how nerve cells use channels in a coordinated fashion to release neuro-peptides and initiate behaviour. Taking a reductionist approach, I employ the brain of a sea snail, called Aplysia, which has large and identifiable nerve cells. In particular, I study the bag cells, which are motivational cells that evoke reproduction, a behaviour essential to all animals. My work concerns how, after only a very short stimulus, the action of certain channels allows these nerves cells to respond with a prolonged episode of neuro-peptide release to trigger reproduction. I will investigate the mechanisms that allow channels to remain open for lengthy time periods. This includes interactions with structures inside the bag cells, known as mitochondria, which normally act as an energy source, but in this case regulate channel function. Long-term responses are found in nerve cells from many animals, and are essential for handling sensory information, learning, movement, and controlling drinking, eating, ovulation, birth, or breast feeding. Thus, my findings will apply to processes such as perception, memory, and fundamental behaviours. Furthermore, because the channels permit a nerve cell to be active on its own, there may be implications for epilepsy, where bio-electrical properties are inappropriately adjusted.
