column36: Behavioural profile matching: A precision medicine approach to concussion rehabilitation
column37: Concussions are very common. Although many people recover well from concussion, at least 1 in 5 will have persistent symptoms and difficulties with daily activities. How people cope with their symptoms following concussion powerfully influences their recovery. We have recently identified two unhelpful coping styles following a concussion - (1) avoidance, where people perceive activity as unnecessarily dangerous and take great care to avoid overexertion, and (2) endurance, where people engage in high levels of activity despite worsening symptoms until they "crash," requiring recuperative rest. These same unhelpful coping styles are seen in other health conditions, such as chronic pain. We believe that individuals who engage in avoidance behaviour benefit from a different type of concussion treatment than those who engage in endurance behaviour. If our belief is true, the current one-size-fits-all approach is not likely to work for everyone who suffers a concussion. We will evaluate whether assigning individuals to a specific treatment tailored to their coping style is practical, acceptable, and beneficial for their recovery. In the proposed study, patients will be recruited from concussion clinics and offered one of two treatment programs based on random assignment (like a coin toss). Both programs will be delivered by an occupational therapist and psychologist over eight weeks, using a videoconference system. We expect that the majority of patients who we approach will choose to join the study and that most of them will attend regularly, do their therapy assignments, and complete a final assessment. We will also check that the therapists are providing the treatments as outlined in a treatment manual. The information collected in this study will inform the development for a larger trial involving additional clinics across Canada, so that we can learn more definitively whether our matching approach can speed up recovery and reduce the burden of concussion.

column36: Ecological Momentary Assessment of Simultaneous Cannabis and Alcohol Use
column37: Cannabis and alcohol are widely used among young adults in Canada and both substances are often used at the same time. Rates of simultaneous use of alcohol and cannabis may increase as a result of legalization and increased access to cannabis in Canada. Combining cannabis with alcohol can increase risk for harms such as psychological and physical symptoms, social problems, and risk for substance use disorders. However, little is currently known about real-time patterns of simultaneous use of cannabis and alcohol, or how these contribute to risk for harms above and beyond using either substance alone. This study will use real-time mobile data collection to examine patterns of simultaneous cannabis and alcohol use in individuals' daily lives. Young adults who regularly use cannabis and alcohol will be asked to track their use of both substances using a smartphone app for three, 21-day periods spaced 6 months apart. On mornings following alcohol and/or cannabis use, participants will complete measures of substance use consequences. Data will be used to examine patterns of simultaneous use, including the frequency of co-use, the overall quantity of each substance used, and the temporal ordering of each substance (e.g., cannabis before alcohol or vice versa). Contextual influences on simultaneous use and the subjective effects of combining cannabis with alcohol will also be investigated. Further, the unique risks of combining cannabis and alcohol (e.g., risky behaviours, hangovers) will be examined relative to the use of either substance alone. Finally, changes in patterns of simultaneous use will be examined over a one-year period in relation to health outcomes such as symptoms of substance use disorders. The findings will improve our understanding of the unique health risks of cannabis and alcohol co-use, which will have direct implications for public health policies as cannabis becomes legal in Canada.

column36: Quantifying Brown Adipose Tissue Thermogenesis in Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Brown fat is the only organ able to burn energy to directly produce heat. This tissue allows small animals to live in cold environments without having to rely on muscle shivering. Brown fat is present in adults and can be seen using 'positron emission tomography' imaging (or 'PET imaging') with injection of a radioactive sugar label (or 'sugar tracer') that is taken up by brown fat when it is activated upon cold exposure. PET imaging with a sugar tracer is currently the standard method to measure brown fat. We have found that brown fat in adults burns energy mostly by utilizing its own fat content. We have demonstrated that PET imaging with a sugar tracer underestimates the total contribution of brown fat to energy expenditure, especially in people with type 2 diabetes. The contribution of brown fat to energy balance cannot be precisely determined using the current methods we have. As brown fat is currently viewed as a promising target for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes, it is essential to quantify its role in energy expenditure in people without and with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes. We propose here to develop and validate new methods to quantify brown fat energy expenditure by measuring its own fat utilization with a combination of PET imaging with a novel fat tracer and magnetic resonance imaging techniques. We will apply these novel techniques during cold exposure and stimulation with a drug known to activate brown fat in people. Our laboratory has made outstanding contributions to the field of brown fat research through the imaging innovations we made and our integrated approach to the study of energy metabolism directly in people. This project will lead to new standard methods to measure brown fat energy expenditure and will provide essential knowledge on brown fat as a target to prevent and treat obesity and type 2 diabetes.

column36: PARP inhibition in PAH: A Phase 1 clinical trial
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a progressive condition characterized by the chronic elevation of pulmonary artery (PA) pressure leading to failure of the heart. In spite of recent advances in approved therapies, PAH remains a serious disease with significant mortality. In contrast to the earlier belief that contraction of pulmonary vessels played a key role in PAH, it is now established that excessive proliferation of the cells within the pulmonary artery wall is a pivotal component of pulmonary vascular obliteration, a currently irreversible feature of PAH for which available pharmacotherapies have no/limited efficacy. In recently years, it has become increasingly appreciated that, contrary to normal cells, these cells are exposed to stressful conditions, jeopardizing their survival. To deal with these insults, these cells have developed pathways, allowing them to survive and proliferate and leading to intense remodelling of pulmonary vessels. Central to these strategies are the activation of the mechanisms that repair DNA. We recently documented that pharmacological inhibition of PARP1, the most important mechanism involved in DNA repair, reverses PAH in human cells and animal models of PAH. Very recently, Olaparib, an orally available PARP1 inhibitor, was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in treating cancers and was approved by Health Canada for the treatment of ovarian cancer. The time is thus right to translate our findings in human PAH. This proposal addresses a very novel and promising therapeutic avenue to treat and is one of the first step of personalized medicine in PAH. We propose an early phase clinical trial to determine whether: 1) PARP1 inhibition with olaparib is safe and effective; 2) patients' genes can predict the efficacy and the side effect profile of olaparib in adult patients with symptomatic PAH.

column36: Systematic Analysis of Post-transcriptional Regulatory Mechanisms and Functions in Drosophila
column37: DNA is copied into messenger RNAs (mRNAs), which in turn encode proteins. For most of the second half of the 20th Century it was thought that the regulation of which proteins are made in any particular cell of the body or stage of development is at the level of transcription (production of mRNA from DNA). However, it has become clear in the last decade that a great deal of this regulation occurs post-transcriptionally via control of mRNA stability, localization within the cell and/or in the translation of the mRNA into protein. These processes are regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which together with their bound mRNAs and other associated proteins, regulate these processes. In order to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms of post-transcriptional control and how the compendium of proteins in each cell type is assembled, we will use the powerful model organism, the fruit fly Drosophila, to systematically identify the mRNAs bound to each of 68 RBPs in the early embryo together with other associated RNAs and proteins. We will use experimental and computational methods to identify the binding sites for each of these 68 RBPs. Finally, we will assess the molecular functions of these binding sites in control of the post-transcriptional processes listed above. Together these studies will provide the first insights into how the 'post-transcriptional code' is read out as the compendium of proteins present in a cell. Given that RBPs and their binding sites tend to be highly evolutionarily conserved and that 90% of the closely related human RBPs have been associated with a variety of diseases, our results will lead directly to insights into the components and functions of post-transcriptional processes in other organisms, including humans.

column37: Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable illness and death in Canada; using precision medicine genomics approaches we plan to personalize smoking cessation treatment choices. In this proposal, we seek to identify genetic factors that influence the nicotine metabolite ratio (NMR), a measure of nicotine inactivation that predicts treatment outcomes in multiple smoking cessation clinical trials. NMR is also associated with the amount smoked, dependence, reactivity to smoking cues, risk for lung cancer, and many other smoking-related behaviours; in general, faster nicotine metabolizers (higher NMR) smoke more, are more dependent, have lower quit rates, and a higher risk for lung cancer, compared to slower metabolizers. Up to 80% of NMR variability between smokers is due to genetics, however only a small fraction of this genetic variation is known. While NMR itself could be used clinically to personalize smoking cessation, this is not yet possible because measuring NMR requires sophisticated techniques; there are no commercially available NMR kits and NMR is not routinely measured. In contrast, DNA, from which genetic information can be determined, is more easily collected. Thus, using genetics to better understand NMR, and how NMR is related to smoking and illness, we will enhance quitting and reduce tobacco-related illness and death. Our goal is to sequence (i.e. read) the major nicotine inactivation gene in ~1,000 smokers to identify specific variants affecting NMR. We also have data from 9 smoking cessation clinical trials, where >5,000 smokers with NMR will be examined for the variants identified in our sequencing analyses. We will then study how these variants functionally influence NMR, smoking behaviours, and cessation outcomes using this unparalleled clinical resource. Through these analyses, we will improve our ability to genetically tailor treatment, which will ultimately improve smoking cessation rates and the mortality associated with smoking.

column37: Gastrointestinal infections by Salmonella and related enteropathogenic bacteria can lead to severe diarrheal disease and accordingly present a serious human health problem. This cell invasion process requires the expression of a large set of genes encoded on a 40 kb chromosomal DNA segment called Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1). The control of SPI-1 gene expression is complex involving a positive feed-forward cascade that includes several different transcription factors. We recently discovered that the insertion sequence IS200 encodes small regulatory RNAs (tad-sRNA for short) that contribute to SPI-1 gene expression. Part of the current proposal is focused on defining what genes in SPI-1 tad-sRNAs regulate and how this regulation occurs. Further investigation into the scope of tad-sRNA gene regulation in Salmonella led to the discovery that tad-sRNAs also regulate the expression of genes required for cysteine biosynthesis. As cysteine biosynthesis plays an important role in oxidative stress response and Salmonella needs to mount an aggressive oxidative stress response to propagate in certain cell types, we will test the possibility that tad-sRNA regulation of cysteine biosynthesis contributes to Salmonella pathogenicity. Finally, we will determine if host gene regulation by tad-sRNAs is a widespread phenomenon in bacteria. Overall, we expect results from this proposal to provide valuable new information in three important biomedical areas including: (1) how bacterial pathogenicity is controlled; (2) how the expression of a component of central metabolism (cysteine biosynthesis) is regulated and (3) why insertion sequences are stably maintained in bacterial genomes - notably insertion sequences can make major contributions to the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

column36: Role of beta-PIX and CdGAP in the pathogenesis of proteinuria
column37: Leakage of proteins into urine (proteinuria) is a hallmark of many kidney diseases. When you have a lot of proteinuria, you are more likely to progress to kidney failure. This is why it is important to find effective treatments to stop proteinuria. Current treatments are non-specific with a lot of undesired side effects and not always effective. What is blocking the discovery of specific and effective treatments is the fact that we do not know how proteinuria develops. Normal kidneys have a barrier function that allows the passage of water and waste products into the urine while retaining proteins that are essential for body function. In the kidney, cells called podocytes are maintaining this barrier function. When podocytes are injured, this causes proteinuria. The proposed research will define what is happening in podocytes when they are injured. Our recent research identified that in proteinuric kidney diseases, the molecule called Rac1 is activated in podocytes and this makes podocytes to malfunction. When the Rac1 activation is persistent, eventually podocytes are lost in the urine and that leads to kidney failure. Thus, blocking Rac1 is a promising treatment strategy for proteinuria. However, Rac1 is expressed in all the cells in the body and blocking Rac1 itself will likely harm the body. Instead, we have identified two proteins, called beta-PIX and CdGAP that regulate Rac1 in podocytes. We will study how these proteins work in podocytes and establish if they could be good therapeutic targets. The results of the research will make us understand how proteinuria occurs and allow the development of a better therapeutic approach.

column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease which can cause inflammation and damage to any part of the body. It affects 1:2000 people, women nine times more frequently than men, usually during the most productive time of their lives. Consequently, there is a significant social and economic cost associated with it. Involvement of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) by SLE results in a variety of neurological and psychiatric problems. Frequently, there is disturbance of normal cognitive function (e.g. the ability to think clearly, remember recent and past events and organize everyday tasks) which is called cognitive dysfunction ("lupus fog"). It is one of the least understood features of the illness despite its negative impact on daily function and quality of life. Dr. Hanly, who has conducted several research projects in this area, plans a study with experts in neuropsychology and neuroimaging to learn more about why lupus patients suffer from cognitive dysfunction. Patients attending the Lupus clinic at the Queen Elizabeth II Health Sciences Center in Halifax will be invited to undergo clinical testing for cognitive dysfunction. On the same day, brain imaging studies using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) will be performed to assess information flow through brain networks, something that is required for normal cognitive functioning. The function of the blood-brain-barrier, a structure the protects the brain by controlling which components of the blood diffuse into the brain, will also be assessed. The proposed studies have not previously been done in SLE and should provide new information on why lupus patients have cognitive difficulties. The results should lead to improvements in the diagnosis and treatment of this distressing condition. The investigators are well established researchers, who bring diverse and complementary skills to address this important area of clinical need for SLE patients.

column36: Molecular mechanisms underlying a mitochondria-to-nucleus signaling pathway that promotes longevity
column37: As the population of Canada ages, there is an increasingly urgent need to understand the aging process. Currently, there are almost 6 million Canadians over the age of 65, which is more than 15% of the total population. In addition to the general decline in health that occurs with age, aging is the greatest risk factor for the development of many diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular disease and some forms of cancer. Nonetheless, the role of aging in these diseases remains undefined, and the aging process is poorly understood. By advancing our understanding of the aging process, we believe that the knowledge obtained may not only be used to promote healthy aging but also to treat age-onset diseases. Our research has shown that a mild increase in the levels of reactive oxygen species (also known as free radicals) specifically in the energy-generating part of the cell called the mitochondria can increase lifespan. Our initial studies into the underlying mechanisms suggest that the increase in longevity results from a signal that is transmitted from the mitochondria to the nucleus to change gene expression. The current proposal will define the mechanisms by which changes in the mitochondria can extend the longevity of the whole organism. Our long-term goal is to translate these findings in order to improve human health span, the number of years that an individual remains healthy. Accordingly, this research has the potential to improve the quality of life of older Canadians and to decrease health care spending.

column36: Iron and inflammatory regulation of hepcidin: implications for anemias and infectious diseases
column37: Iron is an essential nutrient but also a potential biohazard; therefore, its metabolism is tightly controlled. Most of body iron is utilized within red blood cells for oxygen transport to tissues. Aged red blood cells are cleared by tissue macrophages, which liberate iron and recycle it to the bloodstream for new erythropoiesis. Iron efflux from macrophages and other cells is inhibited by hepcidin, a liver-derived hormone. The expression of hepcidin is primarily regulated by iron, inflammatory and erythropoietic cues. Genetic defects in hepcidin pathways cause hemochromatosis, a disease of iron overload. Pathological suppression of hepcidin also occurs in anemias with ineffective erythropoiesis, such as beta thalassemia, and contributes to iron overload. During infection, inflammatory induction of hepcidin triggers iron sequestration from the bloodstream to macrophages. This is considered a protective response by reducing iron availability to invading bacteria but may favor growth of intracellular pathogens. Prolonged inflammatory induction of hepcidin reduces iron availability for erythropoiesis and contributes to the anemia of inflammation, the most common cause of anemia among hospitalized patients. Targeting hepcidin pathways offers new therapeutic opportunities for iron-related disorders. However, the development of hepcidin-based therapeutics requires a better understanding of mechanisms underlying hepcidin regulation. Herein, we hypothesize that the pathways for hepcidin regulation by iron and inflammatory signals are interconnected and affect the development of anemias and the outcome of intracellular infections. We propose experiments with mouse models of iron metabolism, anemia of inflammation, beta thalassemia and infection with the intracellular Leishmania parasite to investigate basic mechanisms, which is essential for the development of new pharmacological interventions.

column36: Dietary manipulation of gut microbiota to mitigate early-life antibiotic associated obesity
column37: Antibiotics are life-saving drugs that have considerably reduced the rates of human death and disease and were thought to have minimal long-term adverse effects. However, recent research suggests that when antibiotics are given in early life, either to pregnant mothers or to infants, intestinal bacteria can be disrupted and result in increased risk of obesity and asthma in later life. Intestinal bacteria are less stable in early life and therefore susceptible to their environment including antibiotics but also diet. Prebiotics are non-digestible food ingredients like fiber that selectively feed health promoting bacteria in the gut. Their intake is associated with lower body weight and fat mass, improved glucose control and reduced inflammation. Given the current epidemic of childhood obesity and the high prevalence of infant antibiotic exposure, research is needed to develop strategies to reduce obesity risk, especially when early life antibiotic treatment cannot be avoided. Given that prebiotics positively modify intestinal bacteria, there is the potential that consuming them at the same time as antibiotics could provide protection. Two situations that are highly relevant to real life will be examined. The first experiment will examine whether giving prebiotics (inulin and oligofructose) to pregnant rats at the same time that they receive antibiotics will reduce the risk of obesity in their offspring. The second experiment will examine whether giving prebiotics to very young rats at the same time as antibiotics will reduce their risk of developing obesity later in life. Fecal transplant studies will help us determine the direct role of intestinal bacteria in providing protection with prebiotics. This work will provide important insight into whether prebiotics can reverse some of the metabolic risk of early life antibiotic exposure. Overall, this work has the potential to identify a novel therapy for reducing the burden of obesity and improving longterm health.

column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia in the elderly. column36: Evaluation of Diagnostic Testing for Primary Aldosteronism
column37: Hypertension affects >6 million Canadians and is a leading cause of heart attacks, strokes, and death. 1 in 4 of people with hypertension have uncontrolled high blood pressure despite taking multiple drugs. This is called resistant hypertension, and is often due to unrecognized and untreated causes of elevated blood pressure. One of the most common causes of resistant hypertension is primary aldosteronism (PA), a condition where the adrenal glands make an excessive amount of a hormone called aldosterone, leading to high blood pressure. PA is important to recognize because highly effective treatment is available. However, PA is challenging to diagnose. The current process for diagnosing PA is lengthy and expensive. The first step involves a screening blood test. Patients with positive screens are sent for costly "confirmatory" testing. Further invasive testing and definitive treatment are offered to those confirmed to have the diagnosis. However, the usefulness of confirmatory testing is unclear. It is uncertain how often "normal" or "abnormal" results correspond with the truth. It is unresolved whether confirmatory testing is needed, or whether it merely adds an unnecessary step to an already complicated diagnostic pathway. In an effort to better understand the role of confirmatory testing for people with resistant hypertension, we propose to evaluate the performance of confirmatory testing compared to an established gold-standard. Individuals suspected of having PA will receive confirmatory testing and definitive treatment. The outcomes will be compared to determine how many people with PA are misclassified with confirmatory testing. We will examine for potential differences in responses between women and men. column37: Regenerative medicine is a branch of translational research aiming to replace, engineer or regenerate human cells, tissues and organs to re-establish normal function. Since this entire process occurs naturally during the repair of tissues by the activation of adult stem cells after injury, the knowledge gained from their study will accelerate regenerative medicine. The remarkable capacity of tissue regeneration is illustrated by the activity of the muscle stem cell, which is normally a rare cell resting within muscle, but is rapidly activated in response to injury to expand a population of muscle cells needed for repair. These diseases, including muscular dystrophies and muscle wasting associated with cancer or aging, are associated with a decline in stem cell function. The central dogma of molecular biology states that DNA makes proteins through an RNA intermediate. We focus on mechanisms that regulate the final step, the 'translation' of RNA to protein (otherwise known as protein synthesis), a previously underappreciated aspect of gene regulation that is readily targetable by pharmacological strategies. column36: New Quantitative MRI for Human Stroke
column37: Stroke is a very common cause of death and disability in Canada. Imaging is used to determine the type and location of the stroke, and to follow its evolution. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is increasingly used in stroke follow-up, since it is sensitive to subtle tissue changes. However, current stroke MRI has limitations and could be even more useful. We plan to develop and test new MRI methods for stroke. The base of our new methods builds on technical MRI areas where we have already made major advances and are recognized leaders. The new MRI methods will yield accurate measurements of tissue properties, and are thus quantitative methods. We expect to create new MRI for stroke to measure key tissue changes including iron and volume changes in hemorrhage, size and evolution of microbleeds, tissue decay rates, and tissue and vein oxygenation. These measures will be tested against current standards in patient research studies using a dedicated research MRI centre. Each measure opens new windows into the study of stroke evolution and future response to therapy. To gain entry into clinical MRI protocols, the methods must be very fast or make use of current clinical MRI techniques in new ways. Methods that require no extra scan time will also be tested in our local MRI clinic. This research involves an MRI physicist, two stroke neurologists, and a neuroradiologist. The end result of this research will be new MRI methods that can provide greater insight into stroke and have the potential to change future use of clinical MRI for stroke follow-up.

column37: BACKGROUND: Platelets are small cells that circulate in blood. They form a plug to prevent bleeding in case of injury in the blood vessel. Platelets then take on a role in wound healing. Platelets can discharge many proteins around the wound, including growth factors that help the vessel grow new cells to close the wound. Surprisingly, platelets also contain brain growth factors, which they also discharge when they respond to injury. There is 100 times more brain growth factors released by platelets than from brain cells. However, what brain growth factors do in the blood vessels remains unknown. WHAT WE HAVE DONE: We have isolated platelets from the blood of healthy volunteers to study their ability to release a specific brain growth factor named the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). We have found that platelets release large amounts of BDNF, as well as its parent molecule proBDNF. We have also found that both BDNF and proBDNF are able to stimulate platelets to stick together, form a clot and release more of their cargo. We do not know how BDNF and proBDNF act on platelets or on blood vessels. WHAT WE WILL DO: We will identify which pathways BDNF and proBDNF use to induce clot formation. We will block different pathways to determine which ones are the most important. We will pinpoint which receptors (locks) respond to BDNF and proBDNF (keys). Taken together, these experiments will allow us to understand the biology of brain growth factors outside the brain. POTENTIAL BENEFITS: By better understanding how platelets respond to brain growth factors, we will be able to encourage platelet to release of their useful cargoes and help vessels heal. This might be particularly important in the vessels that nourish the brain, where damaged blood vessels could lead to stroke and dementia. Platelets may be a new avenue of treatment for these crippling diseases.

column37: Adolescence is a time of rapid brain maturation that is partly influenced by sex hormones. We are currently using magnetic resonance imaging to assess the influence of sex hormones on brain structure. This project will take us one step further and use state-of-the-art functional magnetic resonance imaging techniques to better understand the influence of sex hormones on brain function. Specifically, we will examine how brain functioning of transgender adolescents, who strongly experience themselves as the opposite gender, differs from that of typically developing adolescents. Because sex hormone therapy directly influences the sex hormones that are already in the body, this project will provide insight regarding how sex hormones affect the functioning of the adolescent brain. Our research will also examine a very popular biological explanation of transgenderism, namely, that brain function is shifted in the direction of the other sex. column36: Elucidating the role of the Alzheimer risk factor CD2AP in brain capillary endothelial cells & vascular functions
column37: The human brain requires adequate blood flow to perform its many functions. A complex network of arteries, capillaries and veins called the cerebrovasculature direct important nutrients throughout the brain. In structure, this network can be described as resembling the many branches in a tree. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating brain disorder and the most common form of dementia in the elderly. An estimated 60-90 % of AD patients have cerebrovasculature abnormalities; this means that their brains fail to receive all the necessary nutrients from the blood. Individuals with diabetes and hypertension have an even higher risk of developing AD. It is thought that these diseases directly damage the cerebrovasculature. Unfortunately, we still do not understand why the cerebrovasculature fails to do its job in AD. Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels and they are surrounded by endothelial cells. Together with other cells called pericytes and astrocyte endfeet, brain capillary endothelial cells form the blood-brain-barrier. This barrier is vital: It oversees the exchanges between the brain and blood, and controls brain vascular functions. CD2AP is a protein that we have found to be highly enriched in the cerebrovasculature, particularly in brain capillary endothelial cells. Genetic studies show that abnormalities in this protein contribute to AD. Levels of CD2AP are also altered in patients who died with AD. Our research studies will investigate the roles of CD2AP in brain capillary endothelial cells, as well as its contribution to the blood-brain-barrier and how it functions. We intend to shed new light on the causes of AD, particularly on the associated vascular defects. This new health knowledge will serve to develop treatment of the impaired cerebrovasculature in AD patients.

column36: Integrated muscle protein turnover and mechanisms underpinning muscle loss in healthy and sarcopenic older men and women
column37: As we age we lose muscle and strength. This phenomenon is known as sarcopenia and it, like osteopenia is to osteoporosis, is a precursor to significant health problems. In the case of osteopenia and osteoporosis we know that one's risk for fracture increases. However, with sarcopenia there is no corresponding sarcoporosis, but instead we begin to lose strength and muscle function. Eventually the loss of muscle function can become so bad that we lose the ability to conduct activities of daily living and tasks such as getting into and out of chair are significantly compromised. People with more advanced muscle and strength loss are at high risk for the development of full disability, which oftentimes leads to full time institutionalized care. Nonetheless, we know that eating an appropriate amount of protein, containing the right amount of amino acids (the building blocks of protein), can help in preserving muscle mass. We also know, based on previous work from our group that the protein needs of older persons are higher, likely by 50% or more, than those of young persons. Regrettably, this evidence is not incorporated into professional practice. In fact, advice to consume less protein, particularly from high quality animal proteins may be, if followed, unwittingly resulting in accelerating muscle loss in older persons. Thus, the aim of this project is to combine two highly innovative methodologies using what are know as stable isotopes (non-radioactive isotopes) to determine just how much protein older men and women need to maintain their muscles. We are studying men and women separately since there are important sex-based differences. Importantly, we will focus on how much protein their muscles need to slow muscle loss as they age. We will also study older men and women who have sarcopenia to see what has happened in their muscle that led to them developing sarcopenia.

column37: A toxic childhood environment including physical, sexual, and emotional abuse, exposure to violence and crime in the home or neighbourhood, severe household dysfunction such as substance abuse, serious mental illness, separation from parents and family, severe neglect, material disadvantage or homelessness, and natural disasters, serious illnesses, accidents or injuries has been linked to many adult physical health issues and disease as well as other negative outcomes including poor school performance, mental disorder, criminality, substance abuse, and general life instability.[1-3] Collectively referred to as adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), recent reviews have found strong links between an accumulation of these experiences and adult cardiovascular disease (CVD).[4-11] It is largely perceived that child abuse, neglect and severe household dysfunction and other ACEs are rare occurrences and their effect on the overall health of the population is minimal. Instead, they direct future research to focus on the interaction between psychosocial factors and physiological systems. column37: Mitral valve role is to prevent the blood going backward as the heart pumps forward. In many cardiac diseases, the heart enlarges and becomes too big relatively to the valve size. Because we want to study conditions similar to what happens in human, we will work with sheep since their heart is of similar size and shape compared with human heart. We will create heart attacks in the animals; one group will be treated with cyproheptadine, and another group will not be treated. We have tested this drug in sheep before and we know it is well tolerated. column37: The cerebellum ("little brain") is a highly folded brain structure that communicates tightly with the cerebrum ("big brain"). While it was traditionally thought that the cerebellum was only important in the coordination of movement, research over the last 30 years has made clear that it is involved in a much wider range of functions, including memory, attention, emotion, and social cognition. Potentially, we should be able to detect disrupted organization using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technology that allows researchers and clinicians to observe neural activity in the whole brain in awake humans. Despite the great promise of this approach, it has proven difficult to pinpoint specific cerebellar deficits. One obstacle is that we currently do not have a full understanding of the functional organization of the healthy cerebellum or of the normal communication between cerebrum and cerebellum. The goal of the project is therefore to develop a comprehensive functional map of the human cerebellum and of cerebro-cerebellar connections in healthy adults. Moreover, the project will develop a simple and time-efficient procedure for measuring this functional organization within a single individual. Having such an instrument will allow researchers to more easily detect abnormalities of cerebellar function in psychiatric and developmental disorders. Ultimately, the research project will contribute to our ability to predict disorders such as schizophrenia, dyslexia and autism to evaluate the outcome of novel treatments.

column37: The human gut is normally filled with 'good' bacteria that help us digest our food. They also help defend us from 'bad' bacteria that cause food poisoning. This work will identify the molecular determinants that control creatine-dependent energy expenditure and will examine the role of these new molecules in regulating thermogenesis and providing protection from obesity. The proposed research has tremendous potential to discover new molecules that can be exploited therapeutically to combat obesity. Importantly, thermogenic brown fat has been found in humans, and so understanding how to activate this tissue has direct implications toward human health and well-being. The findings that come out of this proposal hold promise for improving the health of individuals and the population.

The emergency doctor will collect information about the risks of having a brain bleed and will follow a protocol for ordering a head scan. We will follow each patient for 6 weeks, to determine whether they are diagnosed with bleeding in the brain or not. We will use this information to develop a simple and safe test designed to guide emergency head scanning and improve the quality of care offered to seniors.

column36: Role of enteroviral infection in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a devastating disease marked by the deterioration of nerve cells that control muscles, leading to paralysis and ultimately death. ALS afflicts approximately 30,000 people in North America; however, there is currently no cure for this disease. ALS can be genetically inherited or can occur sporadically in people without any apparent history of the disorder in their family. The cause(s) of sporadic ALS remain(s) unknown. Infection with enteroviruses, a family of RNA viruses that include poliovirus, coxsackievirus, enterovirus-A71, and enterovirus-D68, has been proposed as a possible factor because they can target muscle-controlling nerve cells and polio survivors have been reported to experience new weakening in muscles that were previously affected by viral infection. However, definitive evidence of the role of enteroviruses in sporadic ALS is lacking. We recently made an exciting discovery that enteroviral infection results in the hallmark molecular and pathological features of ALS. In the present project, we will examine whether enteroviral infection induces ALS-like symptoms in normal mice and/or accelerates disease onset and progression in mice that are genetically susceptible. We will also test whether application of anti-enterovirus drugs can lessen the development of ALS. Moreover, we will investigate the possible mechanisms involved, with an emphasis on the RNA metabolic pathway, the host disposal system for damaged proteins and organelles, and the spreading mechanisms of ALS. We expect that the results of this project will not only uncover a potentially powerful new factor that contributes to the development of ALS, but also will allow for the development of novel forms of treatments for ALS.

column36: Molecular, Cellular, and Subunit-dependent Regulation of Voltage-Gated Calcium Channels
column37: The human heart continuously beat over a person's lifetime at a regular pace (more than 2 billion heartbeats in a 70-year lifespan). For the heart to function properly, its upper (atria) and lower (ventricle) chambers must fill with and pump blood in an organized manner. This is achieved through an intricate network of electrical signals. Electrical signals are propagated through specialized proteins called ion channels. Each ion channel must fulfill a very specific function to ensure that the electrical impulse is transmitted normally. By bringing in the cell the calcium ions necessary for the heart contraction (beating), the L-type calcium channel is one of most important proteins for the heart function. Change in the function of the channel will affect the amount of calcium ions coming in the cell. Excess calcium ions in the cell trigger a series of maladaptive reactions that could ultimately result in fatal heart failure. It is therefore paramount to understand how calcium ions transit through the ion channel. L-type calcium channels are made from multiple proteins or subunits that ensure the controlled passage of calcium ions from the circulation to the cardiac cell. This project investigates the role of the "Cavalpha2delta1" subunit in bringing in calcium in the cell. Too many calcium ions will kill the cell and not enough calcium ions will make beating impossible. We are identifying the hotspots of the "Cavalpha2delta1" protein that are critical for incoming calcium ions under normal physiological conditions. We are further investigating the variations in the expression of "Cavalpha2delta1" in pathological settings, using rat models of heart failure. We use molecular tools that label regions of "Cavalpha2delta1" and we track their role by measuring the electrical activity of the protein. This knowledge will provide valuable insight into future gene and pharmacological therapies to target the active sites and design improved calcium channel blockers.

column36: Evaluation of a Smartphone Based Intervention for Improving Food Literacy, Food Purchasing, and Diet Quality Among Youth in Urban, Suburban, and Rural Environments
column37: Research shows that poor diet is linked to diseases such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer. Adolescence is a critical time to promote healthy diets because lifelong eating habits begin in childhood and diet quality tends to decline sharply around age 14. Smartphone 'apps' may provide a major opportunity for resolving this public health issue because they are increasingly popular and they have the capacity to deliver individually targeted information and activities. Our team is proposing to undertake a research project to make use of an existing smartphone app called SmartAPPetite to provide high school youth (13-18 years) with healthy food information, including nutrition tips, recipes, and directions to nearby healthy food retailers. Our Primary Objective is to assess whether this app is effective at changing knowledge of healthy food and healthy eating behaviours among youth in a full range of urban, suburban and rural settings across Southwestern Ontario. We will monitor progress in three ways. First, participation with the app will be tracked using web analytics software. Second, surveys including dietary recall and food behaviour questionnaires will be administered online to all participants before and after they use the app for a 12-week period. Third, we will conduct focus groups with participants to gain insight into their experiences using the app to enhance the product for future versions. We will also be considering how low-income youth and youth at risk for health issues (e.g. diabetes or obesity) benefit from using the app. This will provide a model on how to use smartphone technology for promoting healthier diets and behaviours.

column36: ICOS signaling in T cell tolerance and gut homeostasis
column37: Our immune system works under two major rules: i) recognize and destroy pathogens ii) do not harm body's own cells. Failure of the first rule causes immunodeficiency whereas breach of the second rule leads to autoimmune diseases. White blood cells termed "T cells" play important roles in enforcing these rules. To perform this duty, T cells are guided by a group of cell surface sensors including "ICOS (inducible costimulator)". Highlighting the importance of ICOS in promoting immunity, humans lacking ICOS suffer from severe immunodeficiency repeatedly coming down to infections. However, some patients are affected by both immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. It has been puzzling how the lack of ICOS increases the chance of autoimmune attack in patients whose ability to fight pathogens is weakened. Using genetically modified mouse models, Dr. Suh's research team began to understand why: on one hand, ICOS supports "helper T cells" that facilitate immune responses against pathogens; on the other hand, it promotes a particular subset of "regulatory T cells" whose role is to stop autoimmune T cells from erroneously attacking body's own cells. Building up on these observations, Dr. Suh's team will elucidate what biochemical events ICOS evokes inside T cells and how those change T cells' behavior ultimately leading to immune disorders. This study will not only advance basic T cell biology but also help devise new ways to treat immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases.

column36: The Influence of Selenium on Human Arsenic Metabolism and Transport Pathways
column37: Hundreds of millions of people world-wide are exposed to the natural element arsenic in their drinking water. This has resulted in a global public health crisis because arsenic causes cancer in humans. In Canada, arsenic "hot-spots" naturally exist with levels in well water potentially exceeding acceptable levels. As a waste product of industry (especially mining), arsenic is also a serious Canadian concern. While reducing human exposure to arsenic should be a major priority, evidence suggests that humans are susceptible to arsenic-induced disease for decades following cessation of chronic exposure. Furthermore, in many regions, removing exposure is not economically feasible. Thus, strategies for the treatment and prevention of As-induced disease, in addition to exposure reduction, are necessary. Selenium is an essential trace element which is toxic in excess. Selenium reduces the toxic effects of arsenic in laboratory animals by increasing its elimination from the body. Low blood selenium levels in humans chronically exposed to arsenic have been associated with increased risk for arsenic-induced disease. Clinical trials for testing the ability of selenium tablets or selenium-enriched diets to prevent arsenic-induced disease have been initiated in arsenic-endemic regions. The study of how selenium modifies the toxicity of arsenic in human tissues has been largely ignored. Furthermore, selenium comes in many different chemical forms and the best form for supplementation and prevention of arsenic-induced disease is not known. The overall goal of this research is to understand the influence of different forms of selenium on arsenic metabolism and transport in human liver and red blood cells. Ultimately, this information is critical for optimizing human selenium supplementation and for the prevention and treatment of arsenic-induced disease.

column36: Influence of visual and proprioceptive feedback during voluntary motor actions
column37: A basketball player must make split second decisions on how to avoid her opponent as she drives for the net. Even if the opponent bumps into her, skilled players rapidly make adjustments to score the basket. This ability to move and interact in a complex world is a key aspect of voluntary control. The present proposal will apply mechanical disturbances (small bumps to the arm) and/or visual disturbances (shift a cursor representing hand position) and observe how monkeys generate motor corrections under a range of behavioural contexts. Critically, we will also record in primary motor cortex (M1), a key region involved in voluntary control, to understand how it supports rapid motor corrections. The first project will modify specific features of the environment (target shape or presence of obstacles) to observe how neural activity in M1 of monkeys and corresponding motor corrections change based on these features of the environment. Preliminary observations highlight how M1 responses to a visual disturbance increase when the monkey must generate a more vigorous correction to attain a small target as compared to a large target. Our second project addresses the fact that we can use different types of feedback (visual or proprioceptive feedback of the limb) to make motor corrections. The question is how do you combine these different types of feedback. We use mathematical models that consider features of sensory feedback (noise and transmission times) to predict how each sensory signal should contribute to online control. Preliminary data highlight how feedback from the limb has a much more powerful influence on motor corrections than vision. Examination of the pattern in M1 of activity associated with different types of sensory feedback highlight that these sources of sensory feedback are broadly distributed across this motor region. The results will provide important properties on brain circuits control that support our ability to move and interact in the world.

column36: Characterization of the immunologic events that lead to development of Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Disease
column37: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic Sclerosis, and Sjogren's Disease, are all Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases (SARD). These conditions share many clinical, immune, and genetic features, including high blood levels of antibodies that react against the nucleus of the patient's own cells, called anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA). These antibodies can be seen in SARD patients many years before development of symptoms. Although this finding suggests that it may be possible to identify people that are going to develop SARD prior to the onset of symptoms, high levels of autoantibodies can also be seen in healthy people who will never develop SARD. Because the SARD conditions at disease onset can already be associated with extensive inflammation and damage of various organs, the ability to identify people at high risk of developing SARD prior to the onset of organ damage would improve the prognosis of these conditions. However, to do this we need to have blood tests that accurately identify those individuals who will develop clinical disease and a better knowledge of what immune pathways would be best to target with drug treatment. In previous work, we identified several immune changes that are seen in individuals with ANAs who have no SARD symptoms or insufficient symptoms to make a diagnosis, and compared them with patients with new onset SARD. This has led us to propose a model for the critical immune events that lead to SARD development. In this study we seek to further develop this model and to determine whether it accurately predicts the individuals with a positive ANA test who will progress to clinical SARD. This will allow us to develop a biomarker panel that more accurately predicts individuals who are at high risk of developing SARD and to determine the best treatment to prevent and/or delay disease onset.

column37: Glaucoma is an age-related visual disorder that affects the lives of 2% of the population aged over 40 years and up to 5% of those aged over 70 years. column36: Impact of temporary lesions of frontoparietal cortex on feedback processing during voluntary motor actions
column37: We take for granted our ability to perform simple daily activities such as reaching for a cup of coffee. Impressively, if we are accidentally bumped while reaching we automatically make swift and agile corrections to reach and grasp the cup. These motor corrections require the brain to quickly process sensory information about the body and the world around us, and convert this information into patterns of muscle activity to attain the goal. While cerebral cortex has been known to be involved in planning voluntary motor actions, recent studies suggest cerebral cortex may play a more prominent role in processing sensory feedback from the limb during voluntary movements. In Project 1, we will directly test this idea by transiently reducing neural activity (by cooling the cortical surface) in one of two key cortical regions in monkeys and quantifying how motor corrections to unexpected disturbances of the contralateral arm are altered during voluntary motor actions. Our preliminary data demonstrate that inhibiting neural activity in one of two brain regions, dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) or parietal area 5 (A5), alters the ability of the animal to generate motor corrections, demonstrating their causal role in feedback control of the arm. We develop mathematical models that highlight the patterns of errors associated with each cortical region are similar to that expected if PMd is involved in generating motor commands, and A5 is involved in sensory processing for online control. In Project 2, we will explore whether these cortical areas also influence feedback corrections with the ipsilateral arm by observing how cooling of PMd and A5 bilaterally or unilaterally impact motor corrections to unexpected limb disturbances. This work provides important new knowledge on the role of cerebral cortex in voluntary control that will guide our ongoing clinical studies quantifying motor impairments associated with various brain injuries and diseases.

column36: Understanding and managing the limits of physiological tolerance in heat vulnerable individuals during rest and physical activity
column37: Canada is entering unchartered territory as it experiences record high temperatures. However, our understanding of the effects of heat exposure on vulnerable Canadians remains incomplete, limiting our ability to make evidence-based decisions on the best strategies to implement to protect the most vulnerable. Recently, we showed that the body's response to heat is impaired in healthy adults as young as 40 years. This impairment is worse in older adults and in those with even well-controlled diabetes. In these individuals, heat tolerance is reduced as the body is unable to cool itself via the evaporation of sweat, placing them at increased risk of heat-induced illnesses or death. Further, we showed that commonly recommended exposure limits such as the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists Threshold Limit Values (TLV(R)) to manage the health and safety of individuals during exercise in the heat do not protect middle-aged and older adults from potentially dangerous increases in body heat storage and therefore core temperature. Our project will build on this work by using our air calorimeter (a device to accurately measure the heat dissipated and stored by the body) to assess how the presence of hypertension in older adults, with and without type 2 diabetes, may affect the body's ability to lose heat. Using this gold-standard method we will define the heat thresholds where age- and disease-related impairments in the body's capacity to dissipate can lead to dangerous increases in the amount of heat stored in the body (and therefore core temperature) during simulated exposures to hot weather conditions at rest and during exercise. Our project findings will enable 1) the identification of age- and disease-specific 'high risk' weather and exercise conditions, and 2) the development of short-term (heat advisories, work/exercise exposure limits, etc.) and long-term (heat adaptation strategies) heat protection measures to safeguard health during hot weather.

column36: Population-based longitudinal cohort study of femoroacetabular impingement of the hip using magnetic resonance imaging outcomes
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis. Hip OA on x-ray occurs in 19.6% of adults over age 50 and 14.3% of people over the age of 60 have hip pain. Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a condition where a bony bump in the hip region leads to pressure on different tissues in the hip. This is thought to be exacerbated by physical activity. FAI can be identified on x-rays. It has been proposed that FAI is the single most common cause of hip OA. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the only modality that can assess different joint tissues in detail, including cartilage and bone, and can detect early stage OA, often decades before it shows up on x-ray. With novel techniques, such as contrast-enhanced MRI of cartilage, we can see damage in cartilage even earlier. We have previously recruited a randomly selected cohort of 182 people with and without FAI, with and without hip pain. Subjects were evaluated in detail at baseline with questionnaires, including a life-time physical activity questionnaire, x-rays, MRI, contrast-enhanced MRI and blood/urine samples for future biomarker analysis. We propose to reevaluate this cohort 6 years after baseline. The objectives of this study are to determine whether 1) those with FAI, compared to those without, are at increased risk of worsening of cartilage damage and early hip OA on MRI; 2) physical activity is a risk factor for early hip OA on MRI and whether this risk is exacerbated with FAI; 3) biomarkers predict early hip OA. This study is unique. For the first time, in such a well-defined cohort, we will determine the risk of FAI and of physical activity on early hip OA. Our results will be generalizable to the population at large. Understanding the role that these factors play in the development of hip OA over time is a key step in future prevention strategies, to improve treatment of this disabling condition and thereby reduce the burden and health care costs of this disease in Canada and world-wide.

column37: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), also referred to as Axial Spondyloarthritis, imposes immense burdens on Canadians with this disease in terms of function and quality of life. The chronic pain, stiffness, and fatigue of this condition leads not only to a symptomatic burden but left unchecked the chronic inflammation can lead to total fusion of the spine and marked disability as a result. Despite advances in symptomatic treatments there is no cure at present and no treatment which reliably prevents spinal fusion over time. Recent insights into the genetic and immune basis of AS have revealed that the inflammation in the joints is accompanied by chronic inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. Our research focusses on identifying factors which lead to activation of these white blood cells in the gut and their subsequent migration to the joints. We will analyze both the unique pattern of white blood cells migrating between gut and joint in order to define what distinctive aspects of the immune response account for the inflammatory attack on tissues. We will also define the genetic signature of the white blood cells which are activated in AS and which maintain the inflammation in the joints. The outcome of our research can have significant impact on the treatment and diagnosis of patients with AS. First, identifying the molecules which direct white blood cells from the gut to the joint sets the stage for novel treatments to block such cell traffic. Secondly, identifying receptors on the critical white blood cells opens the possibility of identifying what activates these cells and what innovative approaches could interrupt the activation of these inflammatory cells. Finally, the addition of genetic profiling of T cells to currently known risk factors could contribute to earlier diagnosis of AS.

column37: Transgender (trans) persons are those whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth. This project builds on our success in Trans PULSE Ontario (2005-2014), a trans health study that documented major inequalities and changed social and health care policies. Trans PULSE Canada aims to describe and compare health outcomes and access to care for trans people across provinces/territories and within four priority population subgroups: those who are Indigenous, sex workers, immigrants, and/or those who identify as gender non-binary. All Canadian residents 16 and older whose gender identity does not match their sex assigned at birth will be eligible to complete a 'long form' survey or, if unwilling or unable, to choose a 'short form'. Both will span all content areas, with the short form prioritizing key items. The survey (in English or French) will be accessed online or on paper, and can be completed by phone with an interpreter in another language if needed. In ten cities, peer workers will also visit community organizations with electronic tablets, collecting data from trans people who are homeless, street-involved, and/or sex workers. Trans PULSE Canada uses a CBR approach, with a trans-majority research team, an Indigenous Leadership Group, and Priority Population Consultation Teams. The project is led by a pan-Canadian team of academic, community, service provider, and policy partners, and uses an integrated and responsive knowledge translation process.

column36: Uncovering the structural basis for the mechanical properties of elastin
column37: The proper function of many human tissues, such as major arteries, lungs, and skin, depends on their capacity for elastic extension and recoil. The protein called elastin is responsible for these vital properties, and defects in the elastic matrix formed by elastin lead to various cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases. In addition, biological techniques have made it possible to generate artificial materials with mechanical properties resembling those of human elastin, with important potential applications as biomaterials for tissue repair and drug delivery. However, to understand the role of elastin in health and disease and to design useful materials with tuneable mechanical properties, we must first understand how elasticity is controlled at the molecular level. In this project, we will use a combination of computer simulations, NMR spectroscopy, and other biophysical approaches to uncover the molecular basis for the mechanical properties of elastin. We have developed simplified model systems that encapsulate the key properties of the entire protein and enable us for the first time to obtain detailed information about how this protein imparts critical mechanical properties to elastic tissues. In particular, we will investigate how the molecular structure of elastin controls extensibility and elastic recoil (how spring-like these materials are), resilience (how much heat is dissipated in every stretching and recoil cycle), and stress relaxation (how much energy it takes to keep them extended). This work will provide critical insight into the factors underlying susceptibility to highly-prevalent vascular diseases such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and aneurysms. Ultimately, this insight will also guide the rational design of biomimetic materials of high significance to the health and well-being of Canadians, with potential for use in artificial skin for burn victims, vascular grafts for heart patients, or in scaffolds for growth of artificial tissues and organs.

column36: Validation of the human geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase (hGGPPS) as a therapeutic target for cancer chemotherapy and design of pre-clinical candidates for the treatment of multiple myeloma
column37: The human enzyme geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase (hGGPPS) is responsible for the biosynthesis of the metabolite geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), which plays an important role in activating proteins involved in cancer progression. Recent biochemical studies have indicated that hGGPPS plays a leading role in the physiology of cancers that are resistant to most of the current chemotherapeutic drugs. A landmark trial in Multiple Myeloma (MM) showed improved overall survival in patients treated with the drug zoledronic acid, which blocks the production of the natural starting material required by hGGPPS to produce its metabolite GGPP. At the present time, clinically validated drugs that bind to hGGPPS are not available and consequently, the potential clinical value of this target is still unclear. There are very few exploratory compounds reported that inhibit hGGPPS, however, none of these molecules have yet been shown to have the appropriate biopharmaceutical properties to be useful in investigating the role of this enzyme in the progression of cancer. Therefore, the goal of our research is to develop inhibitors of hGGPPS that have good biopharmaceutical properties and consequently, can be used to properly validate this enzyme as a therapeutic target. We designed compounds with superior pharmaceutical properties to those previously reported in the literature that inhibit hGGPPS and induce cell-death to MM and other types of cancer cells without causing toxicity to healthy bone marrow and other healthy cells.

column36: The socioeconomic health gradient in the life course in Canada
column37: It is well known that social position strongly determines health status among adults. Less clear, though, is whether social position also influences healthy aging: do better educated individuals manage to enter old age healthier and to slow down the aging process? Another, related question, is to know whether this social advantage always exists or can be stronger or weaker depending on time and place. Reliable and definitive answers to these questions are nowhere to be found (not only in Canada, internationally), due to methodological and data issues. In this project, we will take advantage of two types of data available in Canada to produce a reliable answer to these two questions, thus contributing to international knowledge and to policy discussions on healthy aging in Canada.

column36: A Pre-Clinical Research for Treatment of Prematurity and BronchoPulmonary Dysplasia through Intracrinology
column37: Treatments related to preterm birth and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) exert important financial constraints on the healthcare system. BPD is a disease arising as a consequence of preterm birth affecting lung structures. The subject of this research is based on the essential role of sex steroids in lung development. Many cells, not involved in sexual characteristics, use a sex steroid precursor (SSP) from blood to produce sex steroids specifically for themselves. DHEA, an important human SSP, is produced at high levels by the placenta late in gestation in such a way that most of the babies born preterm are deprived of this high level of SSP. We have shown recently in the mouse that the production of androgens within the lung from a blood SSP is essential to normal lung development of males and females and also reduces lung damages observed upon laboratory-induced BPD. Our hypothesis is that administration of SSP to preterm neonates will reduce morbidity associated with preterm birth and will reduce the severity of BPD. To test this hypothesis, SSP will be administered to preterm mice with and without laboratory-induced BPD consisting in a 3-day exposure of preterm newborns to a 80% oxygen atmosphere. The proposed research is a proof-of-concept aiming to demonstrate in a mouse model that SSP replacement therapy reduces preterm morbidity and reduces the severity of experimental BPD. SSP replacement therapy is a potential therapeutic avenue using an already available drug that may be rapidly tested in clinic settings.

column36: Functional and clinical characterization of PALMD calcific aortic valve stenosis risk locus
column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is the most common valvular heart disease. Although we can make a diagnosis of CAVS quite early we cannot treat this disorder with a medication. A 'wait and see approach' is used and when patients have a symptomatic severe CAVS they are referred for an open heart surgery. It is worth to point out that surgery is invasive and is associated with potential complications. Hence, the development of a medical therapy that would stop the disease process when diagnosed would obviate the need of a surgery. However, before we can develop novel medical therapies for CAVS further research is necessary in order to understand the molecular underpinnings of the disease process. We recently identified that a gene variant controlling the PALMD gene was involved in increasing the susceptibility to develop CAVS. We have identified that individuals that are carrier of this gene variant have less expression of PALMD in their aortic valves and ongoing work suggest that PALMD is an important regulator of valvular cellular function. A decreased level of PALMD promotes the thickening of the aortic valve. We will in the next several years investigate the role of PALMD during CAVS and we will also assess a novel therapy based on increasing PALMD level that we recently developed.

column36: Workplace exposures and prostate cancer: analysis and reporting on a Canadian population-based study
column37: Each year, more than 21,000 Canadian men are diagnosed with prostate cancer. Because its causes have not yet been identified, ways to prevent it remain unknown. There is compelling evidence that the environment plays a role in the development of this cancer. Several chemicals are themselves carcinogens or act as hormone modulators, and could be at play. The workplace is a preferential window for studying environmental chemicals. Most workplace chemicals eventually find their way into the general environment so studying them bear relevance to the population at large. However, there has been very little research based on strong methodological protocols in this area. Benefiting from the support of several Canadian funding agencies, the largest and most comprehensive study ever conducted on workplace risk factors for prostate cancer was initiated in Montreal in 2002. Some 4,000 men were recruited and interviewed to elicit information on a wide range of sociodemographic, lifestyle and medical factors. Lifetime work histories, representing 15,727 detailed job descriptions, were collected and translated into exposure to hundreds of specific chemical agents. Using state-of-the art methodological approaches, we assembled an unparalleled occupational database enabling to study the role that lifetime exposure to occupational chemicals, night work and physical activity/inactivity play in prostate cancer development. The coding of this colossal occupational component was completed in 2015, but funding available could not support its analysis. CIHR funding is sought at this time to leverage this large effort and investment, to support the primary data analysis and dissemination of findings on 19 sub-groups of environmental exposures assessed in the workplace. Workplace research is a major driver of environmental protection. Study findings will serve as important evidence for establishing preventive measures against prostate cancer in Canada, and elsewhere in the world.

column36: Neurocognitive effects of osteocalcin in type 2 diabetes
column37: As they age, people with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) suffer a faster decline in memory and thinking abilities, allowing dementia to set in on average 2 years earlier than in people without T2DM. As people live longer with T2DM, strategies to protect the brain from the debilitating and costly cognitive complications of T2DM are urgently needed. Current medications for T2DM improve blood sugar control, but they do not fully correct the hormone changes seen in T2DM. New evidence suggests that lower levels of a particular hormone released from bone during exercise, osteocalcin, is associated with brain changes and thinking abilities in older people. This hormone is 35% lower in people with T2DM, but it remains to be seen whether it can explain the deficits in memory that commonly occur in T2DM. We aim to show that lower levels of osteocalcin in the blood predict poorer memory and thinking abilities in people with T2DM. We also aim to show that the benefits of a 6 month exercise program are limited in T2DM by low osteocalcin levels. We will follow people with T2DM as they undertake either 6 months of exercise or an education intervention, to see if exercise increases osteocalcin levels. We will also compare the exercising T2DM group to a control group without T2DM of similar age, gender and body weight undertaking the same exercise intervention to see if people with T2DM can attain the same increases in osteocalcin and cognition when they exercise as people without T2DM. Overall, this study will determine if the body uses osteocalcin to protect against cognitive decline, and if T2DM blocks these benefits. The study will determine whether the osteocalcin system could be targeted with new drugs to prevent cognitive decline in people with T2DM.

column36: Bioengineering a finger joint replacement
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a disease of joints which are composed of soft tissue (cartilage) covering the ends of bones. It is the most common type of arthritis in Canada, and finger OA affects 10% of women and 7% of men. In the absence of disease modifying treatments, current therapeutic modalities are aimed at reducing pain. These treatments alleviate symptoms but do not inhibit the processes that result in the changes characteristic of this disease. Failure of these treatments usually culminates in joint replacement surgery. Current studies reporting outcomes of artificial finger joint replacements have highlighted the high rate of failure and lack of efficacy in restoring hand function by such implants. We have developed an alternative biological approach to joint repair that involves formation of a personalized biological replacement designed for secure fixation by bone ingrowth while presenting a surface lined by cartilage that will mimic the native joint form. In time as the bone substitute component degrades and is replaced by natural tissues (bone), this replacement part will allow for complete joint regeneration to desired form and function. The goal of this research proposal is to develop and evaluate a biologic small joint replacement in a pre-clinical animal model. The goal is to design a finger joint replacement that can be used to resurface a joint in the hand or wrist affected by either osteoarthritis or any inflammatory arthritis such as psoriatic or rheumatoid arthritis. With the results obtained from the proposed studies it will be possible to progress towards translating our approach into a clinical treatment for people with hand arthritis.

column36: Premature carotid atherosclerosis evolution and plaque vulnerability assessed by quantitative ultrasound biomarkers in HIV-infected individuals
column37: Atherosclerosis development is multifactorial and involves the accumulation of lipids within the artery wall. At the early development stages of the disease, the cross-sectional area of the artery is not modified as only an inward vessel wall thickening is observed. With more advanced progression of the disease, partial and total artery blockage may occur thus impacting the flow of oxygen and nutrients to downstream organs. An occluding artery is known in the medical field as a stenosis, whereas the thickening of the artery wall at the origin of this flow obstruction or stenosis is labeled a plaque or an atherosclerotic plaque. Carotid arteries are particularly prone to atherosclerosis and the rupture of a plaque by mechanical stresses (due to the blood pressure and cyclic pulsation of the artery) can lead to the formation of a blood clot, its migration within the arterial system of the brain, leading to a subsequent stroke. Although knowledge on characteristics defining carotid plaques at risk has advanced, predicting rupture is very challenging. A few imaging methods have been developed for this objective, namely magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray computed tomography, positron emission tomography and ultrasound imaging. These technologies provide imaging biomarkers of risk but none of them aim imaging biomechanical stresses at the origin of plaque rupture. We developed a method that can directly image the deformation of the artery wall likely contributing to the initiation of plaque rupture. We are also developing quantitative ultrasound imaging methods to study plaque structural characteristics. The objective of our proposal is to further develop these methods to provide a computer platform to process ultrasound images and extract these new mechanical and tissue biomarkers for clinical evaluation of HIV patients at higher risk of atherosclerosis evolution and stroke.
