column36: The everyday experiences of minorities in the health professions: 'Strange faces in the hallways'
column37: Researchers, educators and professional bodies have argued that we need greater presence of underrepresented minority groups in the health professions to meet the needs of changing populations. Evidence shows minority health care professionals are more likely to work with marginalized populations, and minority patients are more likely to seek care from them, and be satisfied with that care. While numbers of minorities have slowly risen in the health professions, there are still significant problems of recruitment and retention. Little is known about the day-to-day experiences of minority individuals who do enter the health professions, experiences which may shape where and how they practice, how long they stay in the profession and the extent to which they may be able to fulfill the potential for reducing health inequities. This qualitative study will ask: How do members of minority groups experience working within the health professions in Canada? Thirty to 35 professionals will be interviewed from each of three health professions that differ in history, social status and degree of autonomy: medicine, nursing and occupational therapy. They will be from groups marginalized by race and ethnicity, Indigeneity, class, disability, and/or sexual/gender identity. Interviews will inquire about experiences of belonging and marginality, 'invisible work' such as deciding about disclosures, and strengths such as social networks, community relationships, values and beliefs, and connection with patients. This research will illuminate potential losses if efforts to increase diversity are not accompanied by efforts to reduce marginalization within the professions. It may inform the recruitment and retention of skilled health professionals, highlighting the resources minority group members bring to the professions as well as challenges they face. Ultimately, the results may help ensure that efforts to diversify health care reach their full potential.

column36: Cryobiology of Cardiomyocytes and Engineered Living Cardiac Tissue
column37: Heart failure occurs when damaged heart muscle cells cannot pump enough blood and is the cause of over 30% of deaths worldwide. Heart muscle cells, called cardiomyocytes, have almost no ability to replace themselves. Promising treatments involve replacing dead cardiomyocytes with live cardiomyocytes, either as cells or as engineered (lab-grown) tissues. Co-Investigator Radisic's group has developed a new type of tissue from cardiomyocytes, called "Biowires". These can be used as a substitute for heart muscle tissue in research, for example, to test how well new heart drugs work or to test whether other drugs are toxic to heart tissues, a major reason for drug recall. A critical obstacle to the use of cardiomyocytes and Biowires is the inability to store them and keep them alive until needed. Cryopreservation uses temperatures as low as that of liquid nitrogen (-196 C) to preserve biological materials and is the only way to store mammalian (including human) cells and tissues long term. Cryopreservation is used routinely in medicine; cryopreserved stem cells are used to treat blood disorders and cryopreserved heart valves to replace faulty valves (heart valves are not made of cardiomyocytes). Despite the need for cardiomyocytes, there has been no comprehensive research on cryopreserving them. This study will develop procedures to cryopreserve heart muscle cells and engineered heart tissues in such a way that live and functioning cells are recovered when thawed. Principal Investigators Elliott and McGann will use their cryobiology and cryopreservation expertise to carry out the first comprehensive cryobiological study of cardiomyocytes with the outcome of making cardiac cells and tissues available on demand. This collaboration between Canada's leading cryobiology centre at the University of Alberta and Canada's leading tissue-engineering centre at the University of Toronto will advance Canada's international reputation in regenerative medicine and biotechnology.

column36: Pre-dementia at-risk states: a longitudinal study of cognition and neuroimaging biomarkers in Mild Behavioural Impairment (PARADIGM)
column37: Early detection of dementia is essential to implement preventative interventions and optimize treatment. The current approach to detection is to identify overt impairment in memory and thinking as a marker of dementia. However, the vast majority of treatments at this stage have not been successful, with the explanation that disease course is too advanced by the time cognitive impairment is recognized. A new approach to detecting dementia risk earlier involves assessing the emergence of changes in behaviour or personality in later life as potential indicators of brain dysfunction leading to dementia. A neurobehavioural syndrome called Mild Behavioural Impairment (MBI) has been described by an Alzheimer's Association consensus group, which identifies later-life onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS- eg. changes in behaviour or personality, onset of apathy or social disinhibition) as a high-risk group for developing dementia. For some, NPS may be the earliest manifestation of dementia, first noticed by family members and caregivers. Often, these changes in behaviour and personality are attributed to a psychiatric illness, and the connection to dementia is not appreciated. Further, the neuroanatomy of these symptoms is poorly understood. We will recruit people with MBI and perform brain scans and cognitive testing, at baseline and at 2 year follow up. We will compare brain scans in these patients to those collected in other studies funded by Brain Canada and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research to determine the neural signatures of MBI. We will also compare the rates of cognitive decline in MBI to those without MBI, and progression to dementia. This study will help identify symptoms for early diagnosis of dementia and potential targets for early treatment. It will also help us understand the importance of monitoring for emerging changes in personality and behaviour in older adults, as a cost-effective method for identifying people with a high risk of dementia.

column36: Intracrine endothelin signalling in heart cells
column37: Enlargement and stiffening of the heart occurs when the heart is continuously exposed to conditions such as elevated blood pressure and/or increases in the amount of certain molecules, such as hormones, in the blood. Certain factors, including endothelin, also stimulate the heart to enlarge, or hypertrophy, by acting on cardiomyocytes - the muscle cells of the heart. In addition, fibroblasts, another type cell in the heart, become activated, increase in number, and make the walls of the heart stiffer and less able to relax. Relaxation of the heart with each heartbeat is essential for the heart to fill with blood for the next contraction. We are investigating how endothelin, a naturally occurring regulatory protein, is involved in fibroblast activation and cardiomyocyte enlargement. If the underlying cause for these processes (e.g., increased endothelin release, high blood pressure) continue to be present, a point is reached where the heart can no longer function properly. column36: Characterizing cerebral thrombus composition with Phase-based MRI
column37: In Canada, over 50,000 people suffer a stroke every year. Of those, 85% are ischemic - i.e. caused by a clot that blocks an artery in the brain. Not all clots are the same, and studies have shown that knowing the composition of the clot can help doctors plan the best therapy. For example, some clots can be removed to restart blood-flow and thereby improve patient outcome. Clot composition can also help to infer the source of the clot (i.e. did it come from the heart or break off from a large artery); this is important to determine the best post-stroke treatment to prevent a second stroke. Unfortunately, there are no current methods that can be used to determine clot composition in stroke patients. We have developed a fast new MRI method that that - for the first time - can create different types of images, which are sensitive to the different components of stroke-causing clot (i.e. red blood cells, platelets, fibrin, lipid, calcifications). We plan to determine the relationship of the different MRI parameters and clot composition by first imaging clot samples that have been removed from patients with a stroke (as part of treatment) and correlating these images against histological measures of composition. We will then image patients who have suffered a stroke and still have the thrombus in their brain vessels. Using a combination of MRI parameters we will be able for the first time to distinguish between strokes caused by clots that have come from the heart versus clots that have broken off from a large artery. Knowledge of the source will enable doctors to more appropriately treat patients who have a clot from a cardiac source (usually related to irregular heart rhythm) earlier by giving blood thinners, that results in preventing repeat strokes. Ultimately, our new method can also be used in the emergency department, to determine the best treatment option for each patient's stroke.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease in which the insulating sheath that surrounds nerve cells of the brain and spinal cord begins to degrade. These efforts will help identify drug targets, and may also help generate tools with which we can better predict disease progression.

column36: Precision diagnostics in childhood diabetes; therapeutic implications
column37: Our research aims to address the problem of certain uncommon forms of diabetes that are often incorrectly diagnosed and, as a consequence, prescribed a treatment that is not the best for the specific patient. There are different causes of diabetes but, in children, the most common form is type 1 diabetes (T1D) that results from autoimmune destruction of the beta cells in the pancreas that produce insulin. Insulin by injections or by pump is the only treatment. Type 2 diabetes, due to obesity and sedentary life, can rarely be seen in teenagers but in a non-obese individual under the age of 18, a high blood sugar is automatically diagnosed as T1D and treated with insulin injections. This is correct in most cases but about 1% of children diagnosed as T1D have uncommon genetic forms of diabetes. These patients have the same symptoms as T1D and are clinically indistinguishable from T1D but they have intact beta cells that only need some "help" and can be treated with pills. We propose that the percentage of these cases is higher than 1%, because we have evidence that not all genes whose mutations cause these uncommon forms have been discovered. In our cross-country collaboration, we will test 5,000 Canadian children and we will select about 1,000 who are the best candidates for a whole exome sequencing, a state-of-the-art technology that allows a thorough examination of all 18,000 known human genes. With the new genes that we will discover, we expect that the total number of such cases will be considerably more than 1%. The number of cases is small, but across Canada there are as many as 3,000 or more patients that can benefit from this life-changing diagnosis. More important than pills vs. injections is that the pills allow much better control of the blood sugar that helps prevent the long-term complications of diabetes (blindness, kidney failure, amputations)

column36: Process Evaluation of the SuDDICU trial: An international randomized cluster crossover trial of the impact of a preventative antibiotic regimen (SDD) on patient outcome and antibiotic resistance within intensive care
column37: To understand if treatments such as drugs or procedures effect patient outcomes (e.g. symptoms, quality of life, survival), medical researchers conduct studies comparing outcomes of patients that receive the treatment to outcomes of patients that do not. However, because many treatments are complex (involve multiple parts and/or people), it can be difficult to understand the meaning of study results due to local differences influencing the way the treatment being studied was introduced and delivered. A process evaluation is a type of study that occurs alongside the main study and enables understanding of factors influencing how a treatment was introduced and maintained over the duration of a study as well as how much of the treatment was delivered as planned. We will conduct a process evaluation of a multi-centre study studying if a regimen of antibiotics (drugs that kill bugs) given to prevent rather than treat an infection to critically ill adults during admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) reduces death, antibiotic usage, and antibiotic resistance rates (drug is no longer effective for a certain infection) - The SuDDICU study. We will conduct surveys, interviews, audits, and observe practice in ICUs taking part in the trial to understand: (1) how the treatment was introduced at each ICU and maintained over time; (2) if the treatment was delivered as planned; and (3) what this information can tell us to understand the results of the main trial. Our process evaluation will enable us to better understand if these preventative antibiotics saves lives and reduces antibiotic usage as well as the impact on antibiotic resistance. It also will give us information about whether we could expect the same findings if we introduced the intervention into other ICUs after the study and how best to do this.

column36: Alberta oil sands development: impact on reproductive health
column37: The oil sands in Northern Alberta have undergone intense development over the past decade. There are widely opposing views of the industry with oil sands supporters highlighting the significant economic benefits for Canadians, and critics raising concerns regarding environmental and human health impacts of oil sands development. The people who are most affected by the oil sands industry are the First Nations communities living in the Peace-Athabasca Delta. Elders and community members are concerned that chemicals produced from oil sands activity are contaminating the water supply and harming the health of wildlife and humans. One of the major areas of concern is related to reproductive health. Oil and gas contaminants have the potential to impact fertility of Indigenous men, women and children as well as the unborn generations. In addition, reduced reproductive success in wildlife means population declines which impact the cultural, economic and social well-being of Indigenous communities through the erosion of the trust they have in their natural environment, and as a consequence, impacts on their ability to harvest and consume traditional foods. The goal of this project is to determine the impact of chemicals from oil sands activity on reproduction in mink, a culturally and economically significant species. These results will also provide insight about the effects of these chemicals on human reproductive health.

column36: Neural and Molecular Basis of Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression
column37: Opioid medications are widely used in pain management, but present the side-effect of respiratory depression that can be lethal with overdose. Opioid drugs induce sedation, i.e. loss of consciousness, and considerably reduce breathing. When overdosed, opioids can shut down the nervous system, completely stop breathing, induce severe hypoxemia and patients may eventually die. The current epidemic of opioid overdoses is resulting in over 2,500 in Canada according to the Public Health Agency of Canada. Opioid drugs are responsible for thousands of emergency visits every year, causing a severe health and financial burden. Nevertheless, opioids remain the pharmacological cornerstone of modern pain therapy and there are currently no treatments to prevent respiratory depression by opioids without reducing their analgesic properties. The current opioid antagonist naloxone is very effective at blocking mu -opioid receptors, i.e. the receptors that mediate respiratory depression by opioid drugs, but it also blocks opioid analgesia so it cannot be used as a preventive treatment. The development of new therapies has been hindered by a lack of knowledge about how opioid medications alter brain activity and what mechanisms underlie respiratory depression by opioids. This research program proposes to identify the mechanisms underlying respiratory depression by opioids and to find new therapeutic solutions to prevent it. Without a preventive treatment to reduce the severity of respiratory depression, opioid medications will continue to present severe health issues and the death toll associated with opioid drugs will continue to rise.

column36: Stress Hydrocortisone in Pediatric Septic Shock (The SHIPSS trial)
column37: Septic shock accounts for up to 8% of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admissions worldwide, carries significant morbidity and has a mortality rate between 5% and 40% depending on the geographic region in which it occurs. Mainstays of treatment involve antibiotics, fluids and medications to improve blood pressure. However, the high morbidity and mortality of pediatric septic shock have led physicians to consider corticosteroids for unstable patients since corticosteroids are inexpensive and widely available. However, although the use of corticosteroids for septic shock has been widely debated for over 40 years, there is no clear evidence for or against this practice. Some pediatric studies have reported an improvement in blood pressure and organ function with corticosteroids while other studies have suggested an increase in blood sugar and the inability to fight infection. We therefore plan to conduct a randomized controlled trial to determine if hydrocortisone (a corticosteroid) compared to placebo improves outcomes (as measured by mortality and quality of life) in children with septic shock. This study will enroll 1032 patients in 30 centres across Canada and the US. Eligible children will include those from age 1 month to 17 years, with a severe infection and need for medications to support their blood pressure. We will exclude patients that have a known reason for receiving corticosteroids, who have malaria or a fungal infection and those who do not wish to participate. We will also assess organ function, potential side effects and healthcare costs in the hydrocortisone and placebo groups. Our study will be the first pediatric septic shock trial that is large enough to assess the potential benefits of corticosteroids and the first trial to assess the effect of a treatment for septic shock on quality of life. The results of this study will provide evidence on which to base recommendations for corticosteroid administration in pediatric septic shock.

column36: The physiology of adult neural stem cells
column37: Since the beginning of the 19th century, the adult brain was considered as an organ deprived of any regenerating capacity. This dogma was, however, shaken by the discovery of neural stem cells in certain regions of the adult human brain and their ability to produce new neurons. This discovery raised an exciting possibility of using endogenous brain regenerative capacity to cure brain damage and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, although promising, the use of neural stem cells to heal these devastating diseases is far from reach. The main reason for this is that endogenous neural stem cells in the human brain are found in their quiescent "dormant" state and in order to induce brain regenerative capacity we need to understand what are the signals and mechanisms that control the transition of stem cells from their quiescent to proliferative states. In this project using mouse models, advanced imaging and genetic tools, in vivo monitoring of stem cells activity, and pharmacological interventions we will study intrinsic mechanisms underlying maintenance of quiescent state and their entry into the proliferative phase. Our study will allow better understanding of the mechanisms that maintain stem cells quiescence and control their proliferation. This, in turn, will provide new strategies to increase neurogenesis and "turn on" brain regenerative capacity to heal devastating neurodegenerative diseases and brain trauma.

column36: Targeting RIPK3 as a key regulator in the development of SLE
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that affects approximately one in every 1000 Canadians, and can result in life-long suffering and premature death. Individuals with SLE develop an immune response against their own cells, but it is not known how or why this abnormal immune response arises. Treatment of SLE often involves broad suppression of the immune response, with consequences for the patient's resistance to infection. A better understanding of how SLE arises will lead to more selective drugs that target the specific biological processes that cause SLE. The aim of the proposed research is to investigate how SLE originates. Using an animal model of SLE developed by us, we identified an important protein called "RIPK3". RIPK3 regulates cell death and inflammation, and is essential for the development of SLE in our animal model. In this study, we will determine whether RIPK3-dependent effects on cell death or inflammation, or both, are responsible for murine SLE. Moreover, we will ask whether RIPK3-dependent cell death is increased in cells from SLE patients, and, if so, how the patient's immune system responds to dying cells. For our murine model, we will use mice that are deficient in either cell death or inflammation processes regulated by RIPK3 to identify which of these processes is required for initiating SLE. We will then use drugs (pharmacologic agents) to specifically block these RIPK3-dependent processes. Our research in animal models will provide proof that targeting RIPK3-dependent mechanisms may lead to the prevention or improvement of SLE. Our findings with human cells will indicate whether RIPK3-dependent cell death is important in human SLE. In summary, our proposed research has the potential to generate a novel innovation that can impact both knowledge about SLE and patient care. An improved understanding of SLE will ultimately result in better treatment and prevention of this chronic and debilitating disease.

column36: The Hsp70 chaperone system and protein quality control
column37: Age-related diseases are a growing medical challenge for an aging population. These include neurodegenerative diseases which have no known cure, such as Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and which are characterized by the accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates. Normally folded proteins can become damaged by mutation or stress, leading to misfolding and aggregation. The chaperone proteins are critical cellular defenses against aggregation. They bind misfolded proteins to promote folding, or help remove permanently damaged proteins by degradation. Nevertheless, damaged proteins build up during aging and are thought to overwhelm the chaperones. Hsp70 is one of the most important chaperones, as it has key roles in protein folding and prevention of aggregation. The different functions of Hsp70 are determined by its regulatory co-chaperone proteins. Recently, another role of Hsp70 was found, in the solubilization of proteins out of aggregates. We propose that disaggregation of proteins is an important pathway for their degradation by proteasomes, which may have an advantage over the slower degradation of aggregates by autophagy. We will examine Hsp70-mediated disaggregation using purified proteins and in live cells, to determine its biochemical mechanisms. A focus will be the co-chaperones and chaperones required for disaggregation. Next, we will address the importance of disaggregation and proteasomal degradation in models of ALS, caused by mutations in the SOD1 protein leading to its aggregation. We will then address other cellular proteins that are at risk of aggregation when the Hsp70 system is impaired. Post-translational modifications on Hsp70 that regulate its function under different stress conditions will be identified. Our project will explore how Hsp70 acts and fails in protein aggregation diseases, and the possibility of enhancing its function towards future therapies.

column36: Pol II and its R-loops in the control of rDNA and genome stability
column37: The human body is composed of trillions of cells, the longevity of which is dependent on the balance between forces that promote or stall growth. On one hand, early cell stalling is known as senescence and it can lead to premature cellular aging if kept unchecked. On the other hand, uncontrolled cell growth can lead to cancer. Critical to the cell's ability to strike the right balance between growth and senescence are highly repetitive DNA regions known as ribosomal DNA (rDNA) repeats. These rDNA repeats harbour genes from which molecules known as ribosomal RNA (rRNA) are produced. rRNA production is critical to general protein production and cell growth. In contrast, DNA damage at rDNA repeats can lead to premature senescence. How cells strike the right balance between the impact of rDNA repeats on growth and senescence remains unclear. Here, we pursue new findings suggesting that a new protein complex localizes to poorly understood spacers located between rDNA units in order to optimize protein production and growth while limiting DNA damage and cell senescence. We have two main objectives. First, we wish to decipher the rDNA-regulatory role of this complex at rDNA in order to reveal new mechanisms that are critical to the regulation of growth and senescence in human cells. Second, we will exploit the new knowledge of this mechanism to preferentially induce early senescence and limit tumorigenic potential in breast cancer cells. Overall, this work will uncover key health-related knowledge pertaining to the balance between cell growth and senescence while revealing how it can be exploited to combat deadly human diseases.

column36: Oriented cell division in prostate stem cell homeostasis and cancer
column37: Prostate cancer is one of the most common and most deadly cancers in males. Over the years, research has mostly focused on the identification of treatments against advanced forms of prostate cancer. In this grant proposal, we rather aim to understand the cellular environment that promote cancer initiation, to eventually devise preventative treatments aimed at maintaining a healthy prostate tissue organization. Such approach is not currently available for prostate cancer. Our recent results in mouse models show that when the cells of the prostate divide in the plane of the tissue (horizontal), they maintain a proper tissue architecture made of one layer of basal cells and one layer of luminal cells. However, when the cells divide vertically, they create an aberrant layer of cells that lose their polarity, proliferate more and harbor stem/progenitor cell characteristics. We believe that this cellular environment promotes the birth and growth of tumor initiating cells. Here, we will study how cells defective in the orientation of cell divisions generate this abnormal cell population and will identify new regulators that promote vertical divisions. We will also generate cancer initiating cells (single cells missing the tumor suppressor Pten) and identify the detailed characteristics in the cellular environments that promote their growth. We expect the normal prostate epithelium to suppress cancer initiation but the aberrant depolarized cell populations to promote it. We will corroborate our results in premalignant human tissues obtained from our clinical collaborators and link these results to disease outcome. Together these results will greatly advance our understanding of oriented cell division and the maintenance of tissue architecture. More importantly, it will identify the characteristics of premalignant lesions that are associated with cancer initiation and progression. These results will be critical to develop interventions aimed at preventing prostate cancer.

column36: Neuroimaging Prodromal Neurodegeneration in Synucleinopathy
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) have a long prodromal interval, meaning that symptoms have started but the disease is not yet fully developed. This interval is key to developing new preventative treatments, because they can be used at a stage when they are most likely to work. Studying prodromal PD and DLB was limited until the discovery that >80% of people with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), a disorder in which people act out their dreams at night, actually have prodromal PD/DLB. This means that studying people with iRBD gives a rare opportunity to directly observe the earliest stages of disease. Although routine clinical scans in PD/DLB are normal, there have been major recent developments. PET and SPECT scanning can find loss of the dopamine system which underlies motor parkinsonism. We have developed a new PET scan of the cholinergic system, to help understand cognitive loss. Also, there are new MRI scan techniques with exciting potential to identify early PD/DLB. We will recruit 40 iRBD patients and 20 controls. They will have a comprehensive clinical prodromal marker assessment as part of our ongoing cohort study (our center has the largest cohort of iRBD patients in the world). All patients will have three different brain scans: a cholinergic PET scan, a dopaminergic PET scan, and an MRI scan that includes three new markers of prodromal PD/DLB. We will follow patients each year, to see the scans predict development of disease over time. column37: Parkinson disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder in the developed world. Although several drugs are available to alleviate some of the symptoms of PD (such as tremor or stiffness), we sorely lack medications which slow the destruction of nerve cells in the affected brain regions. Two abnormalities observed in the PD brain which are thought to contribute to nerve cell damage in this disease are 1) the excessive accumulation of iron and 2) injury to mitochondria, the cells' power generators. Our laboratory has collected evidence that both of these abnormalities may be caused by an enzyme called heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) which is overactive in the brains of PD patients. We recently created a mouse model that mimics the increased brain HO-1 seen in individuals with PD. In the current proposal, we will document the deleterious effects of this excessive HO-1 on the structure and chemistry of the brain and the behaviour of the animals. We will then try to cure other experimental models of PD with a new drug we are developing that blocks the action of HO-1. If successful, this study may herald a novel and rational approach to the prevention of brain cell loss in PD and provide fresh hope to sufferers of this debilitating condition.

column36: Characterization of the TBC1D2 family of Rab GAPs in endosome trafficking
column37: Eukaryotic cells are defined in part by the presence of membrane bound organelles. Proteins and lipids are transported between these organelles on small membrane vesicles along specific routes. Cells interact with their environment via secretion of proteins and the uptake of proteins via the secretory and endocytic pathways, respectively. Therefore, these membrane trafficking pathways are essential for regulating the milieu of cell surface proteins that are involved in cell signaling (communication), nutrient uptake and regulation of cell physiology, and defense against pathogens. Defects in these pathways lead to a myriad of diseases, including lysosome storage disorders and are thought to greatly contribute to a host of neurodegenerative diseases. Using the genetically tractable model organism, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, we have identified and characterized an important regulator of endosome trafficking. Humans have two related proteins. The objective of this research project is to understand the molecular mechanisms that regulate these endosomal proteins in nematodes and humans. This will be a first step toward determining if these regulators might be suitable targets for manipulation of endosome trafficking in humans to correct diseases that result from defects in these pathways.

column36: Kir Channel Regulation by Membrane Lipids: An Enabler of Hemodynamic Sensing in the Cerebral Circulation
column37: Brain arteries control how much blood is delivered to nerve cells. To ensure the right amount of blood is delivered, cells in the artery alter their electrical activity using "ion channels". As their name suggests, ion channels allow sodium, chloride, potassium and calcium to move across a membrane and there are many different types. One, called the inward rectifying K+ (KIR) channel is unique as it breaks away from expectations, leading us to raise key questions. Is KIR a simple channel or is it regulated in a way we haven't defined? What is the function of this unique channel and what impact does disease have on it? We propose that KIR channels in brain blood vessels are regulated by plasma membrane lipids. Specific lipids allow KIR channels to sense blood pressure and flow and when cholesterol rises, this channel is compromised. Goal, Aims: We will examine KIR channels in brain blood vessels and determine the chemical agents and stimuli which control them. There are three aims and they include: 1)Defining whether membrane lipids regulate KIR. 2)Defining whether blood pressure/flow regulate KIR. 3)Defining whether high cholesterol impairs KIR. Methods, Expertise: We will test ideas in cells and brain blood vessels from rats, genetically altered mice and humans. We will use computer models, measure the electrical activity of isolated cells, see how vessel size changes and quantify brain perfusion. Our work is supported by a network of collaborators. Impact: This grant challenges the idea that KIR is a boring background channel. We argue that KIR is uniquely regulated by membrane lipids, enabling them to sense blood pressure/flow, the dominant factors setting vessel size and tissue perfusion. We incorporate Knowledge Translation by working with neurosurgeons who provide brain arteries so that we can validate our ideas in humans. We also use animal models of high cholesterol to see whether this lipid impairs KIR and consequently blood vessel size.

column36: Investigating the role of repeated low-dose infections in Chlamydia pathogenesis.
column37: Chlamydia is the leading cause of sexually transmitted bacterial infections and the most common cause of infectious blindness worldwide. Rates of Chlamydia infection are increasing steadily worldwide, including in Canada and the US. Despite this demonstrated and growing impact on human health, there is currently no vaccine against Chlamydia. A key component of vaccine research is to have reliable animal models that can mimic closely human infection and disease processes. The symptoms of Chlamydia infection are often subtle or absent. As most people are unaware of their infection until they are tested or develop complications such as infertility, Chlamydia infections are commonly transmitted between sex partners in a series of repeated low-dose infections (RLDIs). However, conventional mouse models use a single high-dose of infection. Importantly, Chlamydia infection in mice, but not humans, protects against reinfection, raising a question as to whether we are using an appropriate animal model for studying Chlamydia and for vaccine research. My laboratory has recently developed a new mouse model of RLDIs to mimic closely the nature of infections in humans. We have acquired multiple lines of evidence to show that a single high-dose infection and RLDIs induce different types of immune responses and degrees of tissue damage, with the most severe tissue damage occurring with RLDIs. The proposed research will use this newly developed RLDIs mouse model to investigate the immune responses and immunological mechanisms involved in each step of the disease. The results of this research will advance greatly our understanding of the Chlamydia-induced disease process. Our study has a strong potential to translate the design and evaluation of vaccines and novel therapies from animal model to humans. Our work can also be applied to understanding other infectious diseases.

L'acces adapte demande des changements de pratique importants pour les professionnels. Pour repondre a cet objectif, plusieurs strategies de recherche seront utilisees dont une enquete par questionnaire aupres de tous les GMFU au Quebec (n=47), de meme qu'une etude de cas multiples contrastes (n=4). Des entrevues semi-dirigees avec des professionnels, des groupes de discussion avec des patients seront realisees de meme qu'une mesure des effets via les dossiers medicaux eelectroniques.

column36: Self-Regulation in the Offspring of Women Enrolled in an RCT Assessing the Effectiveness of a Nutrition+Exercise Intervention for Healthy Gestational Weight Gain
column37: Optimal self-regulation, the ability to set limits and manage one's own emotions, attention, and behaviour is vital to health and success in life. Since the building blocks of self-regulation begin to develop at conception, maternal health problems, dietary imbalances, and physical inactivity during pregnancy can lead to self-regulation difficulties in offspring. Many Canadian women consume an unhealthy diet and/or fail to get enough exercise during pregnancy. It is not surprising then that up to 40% of women enter pregnancy overweight and that even more (up to 75%) gain too much weight during pregnancy. Despite these facts, no studies in humans have examined if interventions that optimize maternal diet and exercise during pregnancy can improve the emotional and/or behavioural functioning of their children. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a study that will follow the offspring of the 250 women that will be enrolled in an ongoing study of a nutrition+exercise intervention in pregnant women. The nutrition component of this intervention consists of an individualized nutrition plan that is tailored to women's needs, as well as educational sessions with a dietitian. Our exercise intervention involves women engaging in a structured and monitored walking program. In this study, half of the women will receive our nutrition+exercise program and the other half will get treatment as usual from their healthcare providers. The main objective of this study is to determine if fetal exposure to our maternal intervention leads to improved self-regulation in offspring at 48 months of age compared to women who receive usual pregnancy care. If we are able to show that offspring self-regulation can be improved via our structured and monitored nutrition+exercise program during pregnancy, it could be used to prevent or reduce the severity of behavioural, emotional, and cognitive problems in children early in life.

column37: Leishmaniasis is a parasitic infection affecting millions of individuals worldwide, including our soldiers in the Middle-East, and is responsible for thousands of human deaths yearly. My laboratory studies how this insect-transmitted infection can hijack our immune response and progress in human causing skin lesion and enlargement of liver and spleen. For example, we found that this microscopic parasite can concentrate several virulence factors within small vesicles named exosomes. Once released from the parasite within the gut of the insect vector they are transmitted together to the host during the insect blood meal. These vesicles were found to be critical for the parasite to effectively invade the mammalian host. Experiments proposed in my research project will permit to understand how Leishmania and its released vesicles can modulate our immune system by interacting with specific surface receptors of the immune cells. We suspect that this interaction will send biochemical messages involved in the control of their protective functions. Collectively, knowledge stemming from our investigation should concur to the development of new diagnostic, vaccine and prophylactic to fight this important infectious agent.

column36: Molecular characterization of VHL-HIF axis in cancer
column37: Oxygen homeostasis or balance is a vital organizing principle for human development and physiology. A universal response to compromised oxygen availability involves a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which accumulates during low oxygen levels or hypoxia to trigger the expression of numerous genes including those that promote new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), anaerobic metabolism, and the production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells to facilitate adaptation and survival in hypoxia. We and others have shown that von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumour suppressor protein targets HIF for oxygen-dependent degradation. Mutations in VHL cause VHL disease, characterized by the development of tumours in multiple organs including the kidney, as well as a chronic condition called polycythemia where patients produce too many red blood cells. Notably, kidney cancer remains to be the leading cause of both morbidity and mortality for VHL patients. More recently, mutations in HIF have been reported to cause certain types of cancers also observed in VHL patients as well as polycythemia, revealing a new class of HIF-driven disease. However, it remains unclear what drives the metastatic process of kidney cancer and why certain HIF mutations cause cancer while other HIF mutations cause polycythemia. This proposal, based on our promising preliminary data, aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying these mysteries with important clinical implications.

Early life is also marked by the maturation of select brain circuits which are implicated in mental illness and are particularly sensitive to stress. column36: Crystalloid FLUID Choices for Resuscitation of Hospitalized Patients: A Pragmatic Comparative Effectiveness Trial (FLUID)
column37: Patients who are acutely ill and admitted to a hospital will likely receive salt fluids to help improve blood pressure, and maintain vital organs (ex: heart and kidney) and the circulatory system. Two salt fluids most commonly used for these purposes are normal saline and Ringer's lactate. Both salt fluids have been used for several decades. Until recently, it was thought the fluids are essentially equivalent other than some minor differences related to the concentration of salt components and buffers that are contained to reduce acid in the blood. Normal saline is the dominant fluid used and contains more sodium and chloride than Ringer's lactate. In contrast to normal saline, Ringer's lactate contains a buffer as well as a small amount of potassium and calcium. Recent data suggests that salt fluids that contain less chloride like Ringer's lactate, may cause less acid in the blood, and less kidney failure and death. But Ringer's is more expensive than saline and previous studies have been small or had weak designs. To answer this question with confidence, it requires many patients to be recruited into the trial from many hospitals, using a process of randomization. Such a large sample size is required when the expected differences in study outcomes between the two fluids are small. Our research team will conduct a novel pragmatic randomized trial in 16 hospitals where each hospital stocks exclusively one type of fluid for 3 months and then switches to stocking the other fluid for another 3 months. We will determine if Ringer's lactate versus normal saline reduces death and re-admissions to hospital, emergency department visits, need for dialysis, surgical re-operation or re-intubation, and discharge to a facility other than home. Our team will also conduct a costing analysis. The information gained from FLUID will have a significant impact on fluid therapy practise and is relevant to patients, clinicians, and the Health Care System.

column36: Microglia response to chronic sleep restriction
column37: Chronically insufficient sleep is common in our society and is increasingly recognized as a cause of health and safety problems with significant economic costs. We only have a limited understanding of the mechanisms underlying the health and cognitive impairments associated with chronic sleep loss. It is crucial to develop improved strategies to deal with these negative consequences by understanding the mechanisms underlying impaired health due to chronic sleep loss. Towards this goal, we have developed a rat model of chronic sleep restriction. Our recent findings show that 4 days of insufficient sleep activates microglia (immune cells in the brain) and that this activation persists for at least one week following sleep loss. We propose to use this model to examine the mechanisms underlying the effects of chronic sleep loss, with a focus on the role, if any, of microglia. As there can be sex differences, we will use both male and female rats. To examine whether microglia activation is involved in the changes in sleep patterns observed during chronic sleep restriction, microglia will be inhibited using an antibiotic that blocks microglia functions, and sleep patterns will be recorded. We will also assess the response of microglia to chronic sleep loss and examine the anatomical relationship between microglia and neurons involved in sleep regulation after chronic sleep loss. In addition, we will determine whether chronic sleep loss sensitizes microglia to produce an exaggerated immune response in the brain to inflammatory stimuli that are subsequently administered. Insights gained from the proposed research could have significant health and economic impacts since sleep is so important, yet so often sacrificed for other activities. Ultimately, the proposed research will help us develop innovative strategies for coping with the negative impacts of reduced sleep and help reduce the adverse impacts of chronic sleep loss on the health of both men and women.

column36: Hormone therapy induces reprogramming to drive aggressive prostate cancer
column37: Targeting the androgen receptor (AR) has been the cornerstone of treatment for men suffering from prostate cancer, essentially starving tumors of the fuel they need to grow and survive. However, these therapies have been a double-edged sword; undoubtedly they have benefited survival, but in nearly 25% of patients the tumors eventually come back even stronger and more aggressive than before. For these men who progress to this deadly form of prostate cancer called Neuroendocrine Prostate Cancer (NEPC), the only treatment option is a highly toxic chemotherapy however the survival is only measured in months. Our research is focused on deciphering how prostate tumors treated with AR-directed therapy evolve into NEPC. Toward this end, we discovered a protein called BRN2 that is essential for the growth and survival of NEPC. Moreover, we have developed drugs that can inhibit BRN2 and display potential to inhibit NEPC progression. The current proposal outlines the following strategies: - Understand BRN2's role in structural changes in the genome and how that causes treatment resistance as well as this transformation to NEPC. - Test our first-in-field BRN2 inhibitors on human patient derived NEPC tumors that are grown in mice. - Test the efficacy of the BRN2 inhibitors in combination with current AR inhibitors. column36: Novel therapeutic targeting for cognitive deficits in depression and aging
column37: Cognitive deficits, including impaired attention, learning, memory and problem solving, occur in the majority of depressed patients and are a hallmark of normal aging. They greatly reduce the quality of life for affected individuals and their family, and significantly impact the health care system and society's productivity. Notably, cognitive deficits are not treated, and in some cases are negatively affected by current drugs, and persist in periods of remission. In normal aging and depression, we previously reported biological changes affecting a subtype of brain cells that provide chemical inhibition, namely somatostatin (SST)-positive GABA neurons. Preclinical rodent models confirm the alterations in SST-neurons and support a causal role in cognitive deficits. SST-neurons signal through a5-GABA-A receptors (a5-GABAA-R), suggesting that augmenting brain inhibition through a5-GABAA-R may have pro-cognitive effects. Over the last 10+ years we and colleagues have developed and optimized a series of compounds that activate a5-GABAA-Rs and that display drug-like properties and therapeutic efficacy in mouse models of cognitive deficits in depression and during aging. A patent application was submitted and conversations are on-going with biotech companies. Here we will select the best candidate among our optimized leads, based on drug-like profile and therapeutic efficacy (Aim 1). We will then complete studies under regulatory guidelines to submit a new drug application to health care regulatory institutions (Aim 2). Finally, we will develop in parallel a non-invasive neurophysiological tool to measure brain inhibition in human subjects (Aim 3). This tool will be used to stratify patients based on pathological severity, and to facilitate subsequent clinical trials. Industry partnership will be sought throughout the project. At completion, this project will deliver the first potential cognitive enhancer drug and a companion diagnostic tool to test it in humans.

column36: Apoptotic control of urinary tract morphogenesis by the IAP pathway
column37: In recent years, we have shown that proteins called LAR-family phosphatases are necessary for the normal maturation of the connection between the ureter and the bladder. When these genes are inactivated in the mouse, urine is produced but the obstruction between the ureter and the bladder prevents it from reaching the bladder, which results in severe renal damage. We found that this defect occurs because a group of cells should be eliminated to allow for the ureter-bladder connection but in mouse embryos mutant for the phosphatases, these cell are not eliminated correctly. Hence, LAR-family phosphatases are necessary for a form of cellular suicide called programmed cell death (or apoptosis). We have now identified that LAR phosphatases regulate cell death through Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (IAPs) and obtained evidence that this pathway may be also be involved in malformations of the urogenital system. In this proposal, we layout our plan to elucidate precisely how LAR-phosphatases, tyrosine kinases and IAPs regulate apoptosis. We will explore the role of dead cell removal in tissue formation and will further determine whether the regulators of programmed cell death we identified in the mouse are responsible for developmental defects in humans. For this, we established a collaboration with a pediatric nephrologist who collected the DNA from patients suffering from ureter-bladder connection problems. Using this DNA we found that some of these patients seem to carry mutations in the programmed cell death pathway we identified. We will characterize further these mutations and validate them in mouse models. In addition to shed light on the newly identified link between LAR-phosphatases and programmed cell death, these results will impact our understanding of renal malformations in newborns and help physicians determine the best course of action to ureter-bladder connection defects with the least stress and invasive procedures for children.

column36: Improving Access to Specialist Care through eConsult for Patients Living with Chronic Pain
column37: One in five Canadians suffers from chronic pain, a debilitating condition that requires prompt access to care for effective treatment. Individuals with chronic pain report the lowest health-related quality of life among all patients with chronic conditions. Unfortunately, these patients often wait months or even years for treatment, causing anxiety and reducing their capacity to participate in daily activities. Innovative solutions are needed to provide these individuals with prompt access to the care they need. One such innovation is the Champlain BASE (TM) eConsult service, which allows primary care providers and specialists to communicate electronically. By providing a channel for primary care providers to contact specialists with questions about their patients' care and receive a quick reply-often in as little as two days-eConsult can improve access to specialist advice for chronic pain patients. Since its launch in 2009, eConsult has shown its ability to improve access to specialist advice. This includes chronic pain specialists, who feature among the 109 specialty groups the service offers. Building on our past success, we are now proposing to expand the eConsult chronic pain services in three provinces: Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec. We will begin by looking at the unique needs of patients in each province and adjusting the service to best address them. Next, we will launch the service in select regions within each province and identify any challenges we face. Lastly, we will expand the services provincially, measure their outcomes on patients' care, and create a series of communication tools that can be used by others looking to launch eConsult in their own regions. Our team includes experts in eConsult and chronic pain care, as well as patient partners who will review the entire process and have a say in how the project is run. Together, we will work to ensure that all patients have quick access to high quality chronic pain care.

column36: Organization of the Cerebellum
column37: The majority of neurons (up to 85%) in the brain are found in the cerebellum. The cerebellum integrates information from various sensory systems and is involved in numerous processes including motor control, learning and cognition. How the cerebellum organizes information from the various senses is still poorly understood. The cerebellum has a unique organization: some neurochemicals are expressed as "stripes" throughout the cerebellum. The most thoroughly studied of these neurochemicals is the enzyme aldolase C, also known as zebrin. Although the exact role of zebrin is not clear, it is expressed in the same way in all vertebrate species studied, indicating that it is essential for cerebellar function. The organization is such that there are stripes of neurons that express zebrin alternating with stripes of cells that do not express zebrin. The goal of the proposed research is to understand how these stripes relate to function and processing of information in the cerebellum. We use a part of the cerebellum known as the vestibulocerebellum as a model. This is an area where visual, vestibular and spinal information is integrated in order to control eye movements, posture, locomotion, and balance. To understand how information is organized with respect to the zebrin stripes, we will determine how the visual, vestibular, and spinal connections are associated with particular zebrin stripes in the vestibulocerebellum. Moreover, we will record from neurons in particular zebrin stripes to determine the nature of sensory processing within each stripe. These studies will provide basic information about the principles of fundamental sensory organization in the cerebellum. This is critical for understanding diseases of the vestibulocerebellum that cause disturbances of visuo-motor behaviour (e.g., oscillopsia, oculomotor abnormalities, vertigo), and diseases that affect the cerebellum in general such as Wernicke's encephalopathy, Alzheimer's disease and autism.

column36: Dissecting mechanisms by which Excitatory Amino Acid Transporters (EAATs) contribute to CNS function and neurological diseases
column37: The brain has two main cell types - neurons and glia - and interactions between them are crucial for many processes involved in brain development and information processing. For example, their two-way communication regulates the number and types of cells that are produced, and influences how neurons communicate chemically with one another at their sites of contact called synapses. There is still much to learn about the interactions between neurons and different types of glia. We are particularly interested in how glia use Excitatory Amino Acid Transporters EAATs) to take up important chemical transmitters like glutamate from synapses, and to act as channels for the passage of chloride ions in and out of cells. Defects of EAATs are a common feature of a variety of disorders such as ataxia, stroke, epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases. Historically there has been a dearth of tools to study and manipulate glial subtypes in the laboratory. We have spent several years generating and collecting such tools, and we have launched new approaches to study neuron-glial interactions. In particular we are using a genetically tractable model organism, the fruit fly, because it has a simple yet sophisticated brain and central nervous system (CNS) in which neurons and glia perform many of the same functions they do in humans. It is also easy to study how the CNS controls behaviors like movement and sleep. The fruit fly has two EAATs that predominate in two distinct subtypes of glia. In this proposal we are specifically addressing the following questions: What is the role of the EAAT1 chloride channel? How do mutations of the EAAT1 cause episodic ataxia? How is EAAT2 different from EAAT1, and what is the role of EAAT2 in controlling sleep?

column36: Molecular based approach for discovery and improved outcome for children and young adults with low grade glioma
column37: Brain tumors are the most common cause of death and long term disability in children, and adolescent/young adults (AYA). Low grade gliomas (LGG) are the most common brain cancer in this age group. Childhood and adult LGG have very different biology and patient outcomes. Most children with LGG have excellent survival rates but have suffered from long term sequelae of over-aggressive therapy. This has led to new treatment strategies (targeted therapies with use of oral pills) and rarely using aggressive surgery and radiation. In contrast, adult LGG typically transform to high grade glioma resulting in very poor outcome even with aggressive therapy. Importantly, some AYA LGG behave like childhood LGG and unfortunately get unnecessary toxic treatments. Similarly, some childhood LGG behave as adult LGG and die from their tumor. Figuring out which is which is still an extensive research gap. To address this issue, we established the LGG taskforce, which includes major pediatric centers in Canada, US and adult centers in Toronto. Our group played a key role in uncovering many of the common mutations in childhood and adult LGG. Based on these data we plan to use novel genomic diagnostic tools to find all the mutations driving childhood and AYA LGG. We will use new tools to detect these mutations in blood and other body fluids thus avoiding the need for surgery to diagnose and monitor response to LGG. We will then the right new therapy to fit the right mutation. Finally, we will treat these children and AYA with targeted therapies which will replace the current toxic surgery and chemo-radiation approaches. Completion of this project will transform our way of treating these children and young adults to improve survival rates for these patients. This study can serve as a model for other cancers in this vulnerable age group.

column36: Academic health centers in Canada: Prospects and challenges for learning health systems
column37: Health care organizations are being criticized for their low ability to adapt and improve at a sufficient pace to meet patients' needs and expectations. Recently, a new form of organization, namely Academic Health Centers (AHC), have emerged with promises of being incubators for innovation. Hence, bringing together three core components of education, research and delivery of care, these organizations are supposed to continuously improve their practices. These promised are also rooted in the digital revolution that is underway, where electronic data open new doors for learning about the actual outcomes of care. In Canada, huge investments have been made to create AHCs, but little is known on their actual ability to support innovation. This is where this project will make a contribution: by analysing what are the ingredients for AHC to become incubator for innovations in the Canadian health systems and ultimately to improve care. Our research is structured around three phases: 1) An exploratory study throughout all 17 AHC in Canada will be conducted to identify key innovations, and essential ingredients for their emergence and scaling up. Documents analysis on innovations, as well as interviews with CEO and key stakeholders will be performed. 2) Case studies will be conducted in purposefully selected sites to understand dynamics of innovation within these organizations. Various sources of data (e.g. internal reports, interview with key informants) will be used to analyze in-depth processes of innovation and their relationship with organizational and policy contexts. This phase will allow for the elaboration of critical pathways and identification of key ingredients for innovation in AHC. 3) These pathways and ingredients will be validated through a consensus with experts from Canada and other jurisdictions using a Delphi method. It will culminate in recommendations for policy makers and managers to increase the value proposition of AHC in Canada.

column36: Frailty rehabilitation: A community-based program to promote healthy aging
column37: Frailty is an important clinical state that contributes to falls, hospitalization, institutionalization and death. When an individual simultaneously has many health problems, a frailty "tipping point" may be triggered by even a minor stressful event such as adding a new drug or urinary tract infection. Our research suggests that approximately 23% of Canadians over age 65 are frail, and by age 85 this estimate increases to over 40%. As we learn more about frailty and its consequences, there is an urgent need to develop community-based interventions that will prevent or delay frailty in older adults. Our proposed study will examine if frailty rehabilitation program is an effective community-based intervention to promote healthy aging. We will recruit 324 frail community-dwelling older adults (aged 70+) into three groups: Group 1: will receive twice-weekly socialization program Group 2: will receive twice-weekly group exercise program Group 3: will receive the multimodal frailty rehabilitation program including twice-weekly group exercise, and additional frailty management (nutrition assessment and medication review plus protein supplementation, as needed). We will examine how effective frailty rehabilitation is by tracking changes in physical function and frailty status at 0, 6 and 12-months. We will also examine healthcare by tracking emergency department visits, hospitalization and institutionalization for 1-year after the intervention. Results of this study will help us to understand the best ways to keep older adults healthy, independent, and active for as long as possible. Our research team are international leaders with expertise in healthy aging, rehabilitation, geriatric and family medicine.

column36: Nanodelivery systems for targeted inhibition of DNA repair in the treatment of unresectable lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the second most common cancer in both men and women and the number one cause of cancer related death in North America. Lung cancer is rarely detected at the early stages of disease because symptoms tend to be mild and non-specific. When diagnosed, 60-75% of patients have advanced disease and are considered incurable. For the large group of patients with advanced disease, survival is only 12-15 months after treatment. Therefore, even a small improvement in treatment, is significant for these patients. Lung cancer treatment is based on damaging the DNA of cancer cells with chemotherapy and radiation. Many patients do not benefit from this treatment because their tumors have strong DNA repair systems. Our aim in this project is to develop new drugs that can block DNA repair in lung cancer but do not affect normal cells, so that the toxic effects of DNA repair inhibition is not observed in normal cells. We have already found "hit" molecules that block specific DNA repair pathways in human lung cancer cells through chemistry and modelling of their interactions with the DNA repair pathways. The newly developed "hit"s were shown to be effective in killing cancer cells of specific genetic defects (known as PTEN deficiency, which is reported in up to 70 % of lung cancer cases) in petri dish or in animals. In addition, the "hit" inhibitors of DNA repair were found to sensitise cancer cells to DNA damaging chemo and radio therapy. In this proposal, we will develop nano-carriers with specific signal molecules on their surfaces that bind to lung tumor cells but not to normal cells. These nano-carriers will direct the inhibitors of DNA repair to lung tumors, so that their activity can be enhanced,. They will also reduce drug exposure to normal cells so that their toxic side effects are reduced at the same time.

column36: When Expertise Collides: Using Experience-Based Co-Design to Enhance Care Experiences for Children with Medical Complexity in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit
column37: The goal of this project is to improve care for hospitalized medically fragile children and their families. The care of these children is a high priority for our health care system because of their growing numbers, and the challenges their care poses for families and health care professionals. To improve care, we will partner with parents and children with medically complex conditions admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), and critical care health providers. Our approach places the experiences of parents and children at the heart of efforts to improve care. We will video/audio-record interviews with children and their parents to collect their stories of PICU care. Seeing and hearing these stories firsthand is a powerful mechanism to help others understand the lived experiences of these children and families. We will produce a 30-minute film of the highlights of those families' PICU experiences and use it to inspire groups of children, parents and health care professionals (doctors, nurses, and others involved in their PICU care) who will work together to design ways to enhance PICU care. We will then make changes necessary to improve PICU care for children with medically complex conditions and their families. This approach is called Experience-Based Co-Design (EBCD), and it places the family's experience at the centre of the design process. Lastly our team will explore and evaluate peoples' experiences with EBCD, and whether or not this approach contributes to lasting improvements in PICU care. Our team will work with parent and professional stakeholders to share the study findings broadly, and influence care across the country.

column36: The influence of heme on the gut microbiota and colon carcinogenesis
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 2nd most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canada, with an average of 72 Canadians being diagnosed with CRC every day. A link between red meat consumption and the development of CRC has been documented by many studies, and has been partially attributed to the presence of heme in the red meat. Heme, an essential part of the protein hemoglobin, is an iron-containing molecule that serves to bind oxygen. An important role in the development of CRC has also been attributed to the gut microbiota, the complex community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that live in the digestive tract. Because bacteria compete for iron, an essential metal indispensable for their growth, and not all bacteria are equipped with the necessary tools to capture and utilize heme iron, we think that heme may change the gut microbiota composition by promoting the growth of certain bacteria over others and cause a bacterial imbalance (dysbiosis). We have generated preliminary results suggesting that dietary heme induces dysbiosis, aggravates inflammation of the colon (colitis, as seen in Inflammatory Bowel Disease), and promotes CRC development in rodents. The overall goal of our research is to determine the role and the mechanisms by which dietary heme modulates the gut microbial composition. In addition, we will test different strategies based on natural and engineered probiotics to reverse the non-beneficial effects of heme-induced microbiota shifts. The high incidence of CRC in Canada compared to other countries has increased the need for preventive measurements, for which it is critical to understand contributing mechanisms. This project will further our understanding of the link between heme, microbiota, and CRC, and how to reverse gut microbiota imbalances (dysbiosis), opening novel avenues for CRC prevention. This project builds on our team's unique expertise in iron metabolism, microbiology, and bioengineering as well as specialist platforms in the institute.

column36: Cholinergic influence in aging and brain pathology
column37: Canada faces significant aging of its population as the proportion of adults 65 years of age or older increases more rapidly than all other age groups. Since the incidence and prevalence of dementing disorders such as Alzheimer's disease increase with advancing age, the number of persons with dementia is expected to increase as the Canadian population grows older. Degeneration of a group of brain cells that release the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, named cholinergic neurons, is a key feature in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and correlates with pathology and dementia. Importantly, ACh signaling seems to be important to modulate inflammation as well as aging of cells however, the molecular mechanisms are not completely understood. Our goals in this proposal are to determine how cholinergic neurons influence brain inflammation and cellular senescence and to investigate different alternatives to bypass cholinergic failure and improve brain inflammation. Importantly, results from these studies are highly translational and could reach the clinic in a foreseeable future.

column36: Studying inflammatory bowel disease etiology: a life course approach
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease is a chronic disease of the gut. It affects digestion and absorption of food, and elimination of waste. Its causes are unknown. After many studies, researchers have only been able to identify a few risk factors with certainty. They include family history of the disease and cigarette smoking. The causes of this disease are still unknown, but some researchers think that certain times in life could be more critical for the development of the disease. Our goal is to clarify the causes of disease, and identify which ones could be targeted by prevention program. We will study medical, lifestyle, and psychosocial factors from the time of birth until adult years. We will determine if they are linked to the development of the disease. These factors are for example: prematurity, breastfeeding, antibiotic use, diet, smoking, stress. We will also study carefully when these factors occur during a person's life. For this research, we will use a cohort of about 400,000 persons born between 1970 and 1974, in the province of Quebec, Canada. We created this cohort for a previous study by linking together some provincial administrative databases. Data on medical services and hospitalizations for inflammatory bowel disease were obtained until 2014 and will be used to determine who is affected by the disease. Then, we will ask about 2600 persons of the cohort to complete a web survey to obtain additional information. Among the participants, we will compare persons who have the disease to those who do not, and evaluate what are the key moments throughout their lives when these factors could increase the risk of the disease. This research will help understanding which factors increase the risk of inflammatory bowel disease by detecting if there are certain times in a person's life that are especially important. We will produce crucial information to establish prevention programs.

column36: Home to Stay: An integrated monitoring system using a mobile app to help reduce readmissions following colorectal surgery
column37: Background: Colorectal surgery includes surgery for colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease and other benign diseases such as diverticulitis. In Canada, approximately 21,000 colorectal surgeries are performed each year. Patients undergoing colorectal surgery face high rates of unplanned hospital visits including readmission to hospital and Emergency Room (ER) visits. These unplanned hospital visits lead to significant distress and anxiety for patients and increased health care costs. Research Aims: The goal is to evaluate the use of an integrated discharge monitoring system with a mobile application (app) to support colorectal surgery patients at home following discharge from hospital. Methods: The study will include 3 hospitals across Canada. Patients will be assigned to either a control group or intervention group. Control group patients will receive standard follow up care after going home following surgery. Intervention group patients will be enrolled in an integrated discharge monitoring system using an app to monitor their progress at home following discharge after surgery. The main outcomes are to measure the number of patients with unplanned hospital visits within 30 days of discharge following surgery, the quality of patient recovery and confidence managing one's own health care. Patients are eligible if they are being discharge home after having elective colorectal surgery, are 18 years or older and speak and understand English or French. At the end of the study, the outcomes between the control group and intervention group will be compared to look for important differences. Expected Outcomes: It is expected that the results of this study will show that the integrated discharge monitoring system will lead to a significant improvement in the quality of patient recovery and self-confidence with one's own health care, as well as significantly reduce the number of unplanned hospital visits for patients undergoing colorectal surgery in Canada.

column36: Developing evidence-based recommendations to prevent falls and improve safety during bathing transfers
column37: Bathrooms are common locations of slips and falls for older adults, with a significant number of injuries occurring in tubs or showers. Grab bars, bathmats and other assistive devices can improve safety when used during bathing, and are commonly recommended by healthcare professionals to help those with mobility limitations to safely enter and exit tubs and showers. Current clinical recommendations for bathing safety equipment are not based on evidence of their effectiveness for fall prevention, but rather on clinical experience and client perceptions of safety and ease of use. Proactive installation of grab bars has also been recommended to reduce fall risk in non-clinical populations (who also experience high rates of slip and falls in bathrooms), but information is lacking on where these should be installed to maximize effectiveness. With focus on aging and disability, this study will take a comprehensive approach to understanding and improving the safety of bathing transfers using rigorous laboratory evaluation of current and innovative practices to determine effectiveness of bathroom assistive devices for fall prevention. This important research is actively sought by two main stakeholders: clinicians who advise on bathroom safety and advisory members for building codes currently debating whether bathroom grab bars should be mandatory in newly-built homes. The former group seeks biomechanical evidence to guide client recommendations on the comparative effectiveness of bathroom safety devices. The latter group requires evidence to inform deliberations on the expected costs and benefits of requiring grab bars to be installed in home bathrooms. Our team will work with leading clinicians and policy makers to provide an evidence base to inform clinical practice and building code development. Preventing falls through improved evidence-based environmental design is of paramount importance to the health of Canadians and to support aging-in-place strategies.

column36: Cancer Therapy exploiting Conditional Synthetic Lethality based on Genotoxic Stress levels
column37: Because cancer cells have lost checkpoints that healthy cells have, they have increased levels of DNA damage. This DNA damage causes particular problems during replication, when cells make a copy of their DNA. (When a cell divides, both cells should have a complete set of the DNA.) Cancer cells therefore have higher stress levels than healthy cells and they rely on certain remaining pathways to survive this stress. An important signaling pathway after replication stress is initiated by a protein called ATR. Another important signaling protein is Wee1. Our unpublished studies indicate that cancer cells strongly rely on these two proteins to survive, and inhibiting the function of Wee1 or ATR by selective drugs is harmful to the cancer cells. But if both, ATR and Wee1, are inhibited, the cancer cell killing is stronger than one would expect from just an additive effect of each drug alone. We call this "Synergy". This promises to get a much better therapy response with a novel treatment combining the two drugs. Furthermore we see the synergistic killing in cancer cells at doses well tolerated by healthy cells. This is important to avoid side effects which are due to killing of healthy cells. In our preclinical studies, using human cancers grown in mice, we will test the combination treatment targeting ATR and Wee1 for the ability to inhibit tumour growth and prevent metastasis. column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive type of blood cancer that kills over 1,000 people every year in Canada. column37: Schizophrenia is associated with long-lasting health, social and financial burden for patients, families, caregivers and society. column37: Maintaining independence in our communities is a priority to ensure healthy, active and meaningful lives for our growing senior population and persons with disability. While home environments can be easily adapted to changes in one's unique needs, an overhaul of shared public spaces within our cities would require leadership and policy change from our governments - a challenge to implement unless sufficient evidence is provided. In outdoor spaces, pedestrian street crossing is a particularly challenging task for many older adults and persons with impairments. This is due in part to the physical design of the intersection and/or signaling features.
