The objective of our research is to understand and address current barriers to safety and accessibility at pedestrian street crossings, with a specific emphasis on winter travel. Focus groups with different user groups representing older adults, and persons with mobility, visual and hearing deficits, will be conducted to identify current barriers to accessibility and safety at intersections. We will then present innovative solutions to address the identified features of concern, to be constructed and evaluated in our simulation winter lab. In this manner, we will be able to uniquely evaluate the impact of each modified feature of the intersection individually and as part of a "whole" design. Our results will define a new standard for pedestrian crossings, addressing barriers to community mobility in winter. Our team will work with cities and policy makers to inform transportation standards and propose changes that reflect more suitable intersection designs for Canada's four-season climate. This project will discover genes causing lupus kidney disease. column37: Living cells are divided into specialized compartments called organelles. Typically, membranes form a selective barrier between organelles and the cytoplasm, such that each compartment can maintain a distinct biochemical composition that is tailored to its function. By concentrating substrates and isolating reactions, membrane-bound organelles increase the rate and efficiency of cellular metabolism. However, cells also contain organelles that are not enclosed by membranes. With no physical barrier, molecules can freely exchange between these compartments and the surrounding cytoplasm or nucleoplasm. Recent progress has focused on the composition and assembly of membraneless organelles, but their function remains poorly understood. The proposed research aims to establish how the unusual structure of membraneless organelles impacts their function. To answer this question, we will use quantitative imaging to visualize the nucleolus in the model organism C. elegans. The nucleolus is a membraneless organelle that produces ribosomes, molecular machines that a cell needs to grow. Indeed, cancer cells, which experience uncontrolled growth, have enlarged and hyperactive nucleoli. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that links neurodegenerative disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's disease, to changes in the fluidity and activity of stress granules and other membraneless organelles. Thus, understanding the relationship between the fluidity and activity of the nucleolus in the worm has the potential to advance the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of human disease.

column36: Dynamic molecular and cellular mechanisms driving epithelial cell ingression
column37: Most cells that give rise to cancer in the skin, breast, lung, colon or many other organs have a common feature: they are epithelial cells. Epithelial cells have to lose their characteristic cell shape either partially or completely to initiate tumor formation or invade other organs to form metastases. This process is called epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and is a key step in cancer progression. We will study EMT in a novel unique model to gain insight into cancer formation that will ultimately help to diagnose and combat cancer. Epithelial cells are held together by a molecular glue called adherens junctions. These structures prevent epithelial cells from excess proliferation to form tumors or from migration to other organs to form metastases. It has been established that the loss of adherens junctions occurs during EMTs and is a key early step in promoting cancer. We have established a model in which the loss of adherens junctions during EMTs can be investigated with unprecedented clarity, and is analyzed with computational tools that reveal details of the process that have not been seen before. The application of state-of-the-art live imaging approaches has greatly advanced our understanding of how cell change shape and molecules control cell behavior in recent years. EMTs occur in cancer but also in normal development, and the underlying mechanisms are believed to be essentially the same. Cells in the fruit fly embryo that give rise to the nervous system undergoes an EMT-like process in a context that is uniquely accessible to advanced live imaging methods. Fruit flies are a proven model in cancer research; combining the powerful genetic and molecular tools available in the fly with our state-of-the-art imaging capabilities, and the ongoing development of computational tools for image analysis will give us novel insights into a core process in cancer progression.

column36: Mapping the Anatomy of Decision-Making
column37: We make decisions, large and small, every single day. When we choose food from the grocery store shelves, or mark our X in the ballot box, what is happening in our brains? How do we make the best choices when faced with many options, which may vary in many ways? Understanding which regions of the brain are critical for making decisions, and exactly how they contribute to this complex process, is important for understanding why decisions sometimes go wrong. Why do people with psychiatric or neurological illnesses, such as dementia or schizophrenia, often show poor judgment? Why do even healthy people choose the cake when they are supposed to be dieting, or the cigarette when they mean to quit smoking? This project studies the basic components of human decision-making, focusing on the contributions of specific parts of the frontal lobes, and how these regions interact with the rest of the brain. We will work with people with focal brain injury, testing which regions and circuits are critical for normal decision-making. This work will shed light on the brain mechanisms that allow us to find the best option in a crowded decision landscape and help us understand how emotional and motivational influences colour how we see the world around us. It will yield new ways to understand clinical symptoms like low motivation and poor judgment, opening the door to better tests of these abilities, and better approaches to treat or prevent impairments in these domains.

column36: Epidural stimulation to neurorehabilitate the sympathetic nervous system and improve cardiovascular health after spinal cord injury
column37: The sympathetic nervous system regulates a number of critical physiological functions. Spinal cord damage leads to severe sympathetic dysfunctions, including a loss of blood pressure control. The loss of blood pressure control underlies the #1 cause of death in people with spinal cord injury, which is cardiovascular disease. The clinical options for managing these life-threatening swings in blood pressure are limited. While drugs can be used to increase or decrease blood pressure, the slow and long-lasting effects obviate effective management of the rapid changes in blood pressure occurring after spinal cord injury. Over the past decade, electrical stimulation of the spinal cord has shown remarkable promise for improving voluntary movement after injury by restoring nervous system connections. We will use novel electronic device, that when implanted onto the spinal cord, can specifically target neural circuits responsible for cardiovascular and blood pressure control. Here, we propose to harness this intervention to neurorehabilitate sympathetic control of blood pressure after spinal cord injury. Moreover, we will deploy a judicious combination of cutting-edge scientific methods to identify the mechanisms underlying the immediate and long-term effects of this intervention, with an emphasis on the health of the cardiovascular system and the rehabilitation of normal circuits with in the sympathetic nervous system. Our ultimate objective is to establish a novel non-pharmacological therapy to rehabilitate sympathetic function after spinal cord injury that will prevent blood pressure instability, improve heart and blood vessel health, and thus enhance and extend the lives of people living with this condition.

column36: Suppression of regulatory B cells by neutrophils in a model of multiple sclerosis
column37: B cells contribute to multiple sclerosis (MS) and other autoimmune diseases in a variety of ways (e.g. by producing antibodies); depleting them improves clinical outcomes. However, current treatments deplete most B cells, including regulatory B cells (Bregs) with beneficial anti-inflammatory properties. Studying Bregs could lead to more specific and safer therapies. In preliminary work, we found compelling evidence that another type of blood cells, the neutrophil, acts as a brake on a novel subset of Bregs expressing the protein Foxp3. This was observed in a new B cell-dependent form of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), an improved mouse model for MS. In this project, our general goals are to: 1) determine the nature, anatomical distribution and function of these Foxp3+ Bregs; and 2) elucidate how neutrophils suppress their development. Our hypothesis is that Foxp3+ Bregs develop in lymph nodes, then migrate to the nervous system and restrain inflammation (e.g. via anti-inflammatory molecules); however, neutrophils counteract these Bregs by inhibiting their development via proinflammatory mediators, thereby promoting EAE. To test this, we will use state-of-the-art techniques to: 1) clarify the nature and fate of Foxp3+ Bregs in two forms of EAE; 2) validate that neutrophils suppress the development of Foxp3+ Bregs and elucidate the underlying mechanism; and 3) determine the ability of Foxp3+ Bregs to attenuate EAE when altered by genetic manipulations or when transplanted into EAE mice. Results will be confirmed in human. This project will unveil the existence of a neutrophil-Breg connection of great clinical relevance. For example, this connection offers a mechanism by which neutrophils may contribute to MS without entering the brain. This project will also help to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic strategies (e.g. anti-inflammatory drugs, autologous transplantation of Bregs) for MS and other immune conditions.

column36: Contribution of Dioxin-Like Chemicals to Beta Cell Death and Dysfunction in Diabetes
column37: Diabetes prevalence is rising at an alarming rate, yet the factors that trigger disease onset and drive disease progression are still poorly understood. Generally, diabetes is caused by a deficiency in insulin-secreting beta cells, which are located throughout the pancreas in endocrine clusters called 'islets'. There is mounting evidence that exposure to environmental chemicals is linked to increased diabetes risk, but the effects of pollutants on beta cells are only beginning to emerge. Our project will investigate the contribution of environmental pollutants to beta cell death and dysfunction during diabetes. We will first examine the impact of a specific pollutant called 'TCDD' in mouse models of diabetes to determine: a) whether mice with long-term TCDD exposure are more susceptible to an environment that promotes diabetes than non-exposed mice (controls), and b) whether pre-diabetic mice are more sensitive to TCDD exposure than healthy mice. Since TCDD is the most potent member of the 'dioxin' family, it serves as a useful model for the ~400 'dioxin-like' chemicals in the environment. Therefore, we will also examine how a variety of related dioxin-like chemicals impact human beta cell function and survival. Finally, we will measure the concentration of environmental pollutants in human islets from organ donors, and determine if pollutant exposure is linked to beta cell health or diabetes incidence. If we identify environmental chemicals that are associated with pancreatic beta cell death or dysfunction in human tissues, then subsequent studies will explore the role of chronic exposure to these predicted beta cell toxins in diabetic mouse models. Overall, this important work will inform the clinical community and policy makers about priority chemicals of concern for diabetes risk.

column36: Investigating mechanisms of in vivo variability in spindle assembly checkpoint strength
column37: Uncontrolled cell division forms the basis for all cancers. Consequently, most anti-cancer drugs block the cell cycle, with many specifically targeting mitosis (e.g. Taxol). Variable drug efficiency is a major obstacle in the development of robust cancer therapies. It is not known why cancer cell responses vary, but underlying differences in core mitotic processes may contribute. Proper cell division is also vital to maintain the function of many adult tissues, allowing adult stem cells to sustain normal tissue turnover and to promote tissue regeneration following damage. A decline in stem cell function has been linked to a range of age-related pathologies, including organ failure and the development of cancer. A significant gap in our understanding of mitosis derives from the lack of model systems to study cells dividing within their native environment. Consequently, we know very little about how mitosis occurs within specific cell types, within the complex physiological environment of a living organism. Importantly, mitosis in both adult stem cells and tumor cells will be influenced by these in vivo factors. The goal of this proposal is to investigate how mitosis occurs in vivo and to uncover how key aspects of mitotic regulation are affected by cell fate and broader physiological factors. We use a small nematode worm (C. elegans) as a model system, which permits live-imaging studies of mitosis within intact living animals that are challenging in mammalian models and not possible in human subjects. As many C. elegans genes perform conserved functions in humans and several major mitotic proteins were discovered in C. elegans, it is highly likely that the mechanisms uncovered in my lab will be important for mitosis in human cells. Understanding how mitosis occurs in vivo will fill a major gap in our understanding of the cell biology of mitosis and inform the development of new, more effective drugs designed to improve adult stem cell function or to treat cancer.

column36: Predicting Seizure Responsiveness to Neuromodulation Using Connectomic Profiling
column37: Epilepsy is the most common serious neurological condition that affects children. Active epilepsy interferes with normal childhood development, leading to disability and diminished quality-of-life. One-third of children will continue to have seizures despite the best available medications and therefore surgical treatments are increasingly utilized to reduce seizure frequency and mitigate the burden of the illness. For the most severely affected children, vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) offers hope of seizure control. An electrical nerve stimulator is attached to the vagus nerve at the neck and an implanted battery delivers continuous electrical stimulation that ascends to the brain, rendering the brain less susceptible to seizures. At present, however, only a minority of children implanted with VNS achieve meaningful reduction in seizures. There are no pre-operative means to identify those who will and will not respond to treatment. This lack of knowledge unnecessarily subjects some children to the risks of surgery and also deprives others, who would be better candidates from potential benefit. Because of the high cost of VNS, this also imposes a significant burden on the Canadian healthcare system. Using multiple, complementary advanced neuroimaging techniques, we will study how the connectivity of the brain circuits that mediate the effects of VNS differ between those who do and do not respond to treatment and compare them to typically-developing children. Findings from these multiple modalities will be used to train a machine learning algorithm to prospectively predict whether or not a child is likely to respond to VNS. For children and their families, these findings will mean less uncertainty about surgical outcomes. For healthcare providers, this will provide the means to deliver the correct treatment to the right child. For the Canadian healthcare system, this will translate into better allocation of limited healthcare resources.

column37: Background: Obesity and the linked cardiovascular risk factors are common in youth, and are associated with health problems later in life. If effective, wide dissemination on a population scale through simple electronic channels will facilitate improved cardiovascular risk profiles for any family with access to a smartphone.

column36: Overcoming chemotherapy-resistance in triple-negative breast cancer
column37: Over 20,000 Canadian women are diagnosed and more than 5,000 die each year from Breast cancer (BCa). BCa is subdivided into at least five different subtypes. Some BCa patients benefit from targeted therapies. However, those with Triple-Negative BCa (TNBC) can only be treated with chemotherapy, which fails to cure most patients with metastatic disease due to the development of chemotherapy-resistant tumours within a few years of treatment. Hence, there is an urgent need to understand how resistance develops to find better therapies against TNBC. We and others showed that resistance to drug treatment across different cancer types relies on "cosmetic" changes to the DNA, known as "epigenetics". In parallel, we recently developed over 40 new drugs preventing cosmetic changes. Finally, we created preclinical models of chemotherapy resistance in TNBC derived from patients' tumours. Hence, we now have the means to identify and to drug the cosmetic changes to the DNA arising in chemotherapy-resistant TNBC using the most relevant preclinical models to work towards finding a cure against this deadly disease. From this project, we expect to identify the epigenetic basis for chemotherapy resistance, to uncover new means to treat chemotherapy-resistant TNBC and to demonstrate their efficacy in preclinical trial settings using patient tumour derived models. Together, this should identify new effective strategies to eradicate TNBC. This application builds upon the complementary expertise of Dr. Lupien, Senior Scientist and expert in epigenetics and drug resistance in breast cancer; Dr. Arrowsmith, Senior Scientist leading the epigenetic drugs design; Dr. Cescon, a Breast Medical Oncologist expert facilitating the incorporation of research discoveries to the clinic and improve breast cancer treatment. Together, these investigators have made impactful discoveries in breast cancer and now propose a research program poised to significantly improve the care of TNBC patients.

column36: PRecision medicine for IMproving the diagnosis of pediatric appendicitis in the Emergency Department (PRIMED)
column37: Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in children. Early, accurate diagnosis is important to decrease the risk of serious complications such as rupture of the appendix, severe infection and death. Basic blood and imaging tests are currently used to diagnose appendicitis. However these tests lack accuracy and availability, are time-consuming, painful and potentially harmful (radiation) resulting in significant differences in the way doctors diagnose children with appendicitis in Emergency Departments (ED) across Canada. Precision Medicine uses next-generation laboratory testing of molecules (biomarkers) to find distinct patterns (bio-profiles), that act like a fingerprint; they pick out a specific disease amongst similar illnesses. We have found that bio-profiles can identify which abdominal pain is caused by appendicitis, and determine how severe the illness is. The goal of this study is to evaluate the accuracy of these bio-profiles in children across age, sex, and geographic location and to compare them to currently used investigations. This study will be performed at 10 pediatric EDs across Canada. We will include children aged 0-17 years with suspected appendicitis. Blood and urine will be tested for biomarkers (metabolites, proteins and metals) using advanced technologies (nuclear magnetic resonance, mass-spectrometry, multi-plex assays). Clinical data will be collected from the health record. Using multivariate statistics we will determine the bio-profiles that best identify children with appendicitis and compare their accuracy to those of current appendicitis investigations. Our study will result in bio-profiles that can accurately identify children with appendicitis. These bio-profiles can be made into point-of-care (POC) technologies that can be used at the bedside. Rapid, accurate, accessible, economic POC tests can improve efficiency in the ED, access to diagnostic tests, therapeutic decision making and patient outcomes and satisfaction.

column36: The effects of adjunctive transcranial direct current stimulation on treatment adherence in schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a psychiatric illness that affects approximately 1% of the world's population. Medication adherence is critically important to the treatment of SCZ. Non-adherence occurs in up to 60% of patients with SCZ with more than 80% of non-adherent patients discontinuing their medication by 6 months. Medication non-adherence is not only associated with worsening symptoms, but also increased rates of hospitalization, and suicide. A principle predictor of medication nonadherence in patients with SCZ is impaired insight, described as having partial or lack of conscious awareness of one's illness, its symptoms, and need for treatment. Currently, there are no established treatment options to improve insight and medication adherence in patients with SCZ. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a non-invasive device that applies a weak current to the brain. Evidence is accumulating to support tDCS as an efficacious treatment for SCZ, including a recent study by our group indicating that tDCS improves insight into psychosis. The proposed study employs a novel approach to investigate the effects of adjunctive tDCS on antipsychotic medication adherence. Participants will receive twice-daily tDCS for 10 days (20 sessions). Brain scans will be performed before and after 10 days of tDCS. Antipsychotic drug adherence will be assessed monthly based primarily on pill-count, and secondarily, plasma level concentrations and clinician-judgement. The results of this study will provide support for the use of this safe device in out-patient and ambulatory settings as an adjunctive treatment to antipsychotic medication. If proven effective, this intervention would have the potential to improve individual's capacity for illness recognition and engagement in treatment, undoubtedly having a significant impact on the well-being of patients and their families.

column36: Genomics of Aortic Stenosis - an International Collaboration
column37: Aortic valve disease is the most common form of heart valve disease in the developed world and a major burden to society. With the ageing of the Canadian population, aortic valve disease is expected to become increasingly common. Currently, over 2.5 million individuals in North America have aortic stenosis, which is a narrowing of the aortic valve, the main valve of the heart, and leads to symptoms of heart failure and sometimes death. Despite the major importance of this disease worldwide, there are currently no medical treatments to prevent the development of aortic stenosis. The lack of preventative treatments stems in large part to a poor understanding of the causes of this disease. Using cutting-edge genetic technologies, we plan to build on our recent genetic discovery linking an unusual type of cholesterol to this disease. In this proposed project, we will scan the entire genome of several thousand individuals with and without aortic stenosis to try to pinpoint regions in the DNA that may predispose to the development of this disease. This may provide clues for why certain people develop this disease. We hope to use these clues to identify currently available drugs that could be useful to treat this disease. Using this strategy, we have already identified one potential new therapy that we will be tested soon to evaluate whether this can stop the disease process. If successful, our program would be notable in several ways. First, it will represent the largest study of this type worldwide. Second, we expect to glean major insights into the biology of aortic stenosis that may help us identify a treatment. Ultimately, a new treatment for aortic stenosis would significantly impact the cardiovascular health of many individuals in Canada and throughout the world.

column36: Quantity of Opioids for Acute Pain and Limit Unused Medication (OPUM study)
column37: Opioids (morphine and morphine-like substances) are often prescribed to patients to manage pain after an emergency department visit. In the past 20 years, opioid prescriptions have risen sharply, accompanied by a significant rise in opioid misuse (e.g., recreational or non-medical use, potentially leading to addiction or overdose). One explanation for this crisis is the availability and easy access of leftover opioid pills in Canadian homes, allowing family members (including children) and friends to take them for reasons other than pain relief. Canada has no recommendations for the dosage, duration, or quantity of opioids that physicians should prescribe to manage acute pain at home. Physicians are therefore left guessing as to how much to prescribe when a patient with a condition like a fracture or renal colic is discharged from the emergency department. Our preliminary study showed that two-thirds of the pills from the initial opioid prescription to treat acute pain actually remained unused and were therefore available for potential misuse. We propose to determine how many opioid pills are consumed by patients who suffer from acute pain as they recover at home. We will ask 2,560 patients (from 6 Canadian hospitals) to record their pain medication consumption in a 14-day diary. We will also determine, their pain intensity level, whether or not they had new opioid prescriptions, and health services revisits. In case of missing information, patients will be contacted by phone at 2 weeks. The overall aim is to help emergency department physicians prescribe the right number of pills in order to manage patients' pain and at the same time reduce substantially leftovers available for potential misuse.

column36: Using A Novel Virtual Reality Training Paradigm to Treat Negative Symptoms in Early Schizophrenia
column37: Negative symptoms, including the loss of motivation and reduced emotional expression, have emerged as highly prevalent and critical symptoms in schizophrenia. Among these, the loss of motivation is a key contributor to the enduring functional disability affected individuals experience. Despite advances in treatment, there are no effective treatments for these motivation deficits, which ultimately hinders recovery for individuals with schizophrenia. To address this critical unmet therapeutic need, this study aims to investigate the use of virtual reality motivation training to treat these motivation deficits early in the course of schizophrenia. We anticipate the results of this study will provide the first evidence supporting the efficacy of this virtual reality treatment for individuals with schizophrenia, both in terms of improving motivation and community functioning, as well as the brain circuitry that supports motivated behaviour.

column36: A comprehensive study of the natural history of ARSACS: An essential step towards clinical trial readiness and evidence-based interventions
column37: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) is a rare neurological disorder presents worldwide, with the highest prevalence in the Saguenay - Lac-St-Jean region. It is difficult to conduct study on rare diseases given the small number of patients in each country. Only few scientific papers are available to help develop evidence-based rehabilitation interventions or give meaningful information on the natural course of the disease so the physician can better inform the patient and his/her family about the prognosis and offer timely interventions. Our research group is currently building a unique dataset on impairments present and their progression over time (2013 -) in ARSACS. However, the small number of patients has limited our capacity to predict and explain participation restrictions found in this population such as lost of employment and decreased ability to walk. The proposed research aims to assess all major impairments (cognitive impairments, physical limitations and participation restrictions) on a large cohort of ARSACS patients (n = 100) over a 3-year period (two measurement times) to characterize their progression over time, and to try to determine which aspect of the disease has the main impact on the social participation of the patients. The selection of tools to assess these impairments is based on our previous studies where the validity (does the tool assess what it is supposed to assess?) and reliability (is the measure stable over time?) have been determined in the ARSACS population, which strengthens the confidence to obtain relevant data at the end of the project. The final purpose is to give to healthcare professionals the fundamental information necessary to plan a better medical follow-up for the patients. Also, all data to be acquired in this study will provide the scientific foundation to build robust clinical trial protocols in a near future.

column37: Our team made up of First Nations knowledge holders and researchers in Canada that have come together over the past year two years to discuss advances in biological health research and how they may be relevant to First Nations health. column36: The role of muscle pyruvate kinase 2 (Pkm2) in cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac repair.
column37: Heart failure occurs when the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the demands of the body. In the adult, the heart is not able to repair itself to any significant degree. As such, after a heart attack, the damage to the heart is permanent with a loss of heart muscle cells. While the heart attempts to repair itself, it is unable to replace the lost heart muscle cells. The medications that we use can only slow this chain of events and over time the function of the heart becomes worse and patients die. We wish to find ways to help the heart heal itself by allowing it to renew and replace the lost heart muscle cells. This type of research is not only of scientific importance but can have an impact on a large number of Canadians who have heart attacks and develop a failing heart. The heart muscle cells need a lot of energy to function properly and allow the heart to act as a pump. When the heart fails, there are major changes that occur in the source and amount of energy that is generated in the heart muscle cells. This is controlled by a family of molecules called muscle pyruvate kinase (Pkm). In the cancer field, specific Pkm's have been shown to also control how cancer cells multiply and produce more of themselves. How this happens has still not been clearly defined. Interestingly, the observations that have been made in the cancer field can also be seen in the heart. More specifically, if we change the amount of the Pkm protein produced, the heart is protected from the damage that occurs during a heart attack and the heart actually repairs itself by replacing heart muscle cells through a process called proliferation. Therefore, we wish to work in this exciting area of research to define the mechanisms that are responsible for repair in the heart after it is injured. This work will allow us to develop new drugs and provide the foundation to do clinical trials in the future.

column36: Pharmacologic and RNAi Screens for Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 foci modulators; towards Novel DM1 therapeutic approaches
column37: Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 (DM1) is the most common form of adult muscular dystrophy affecting as many as 1 in 500 people in some regions of Quebec. DM1 can manifest in infancy, in old age or at any stage in between affecting all systems in the body including eyes, heart, brain and muscle (myotonia). Infants with DM1 often do not survive due to weak lungs and insufficient breathing; those who survive are usually affected by intellectual delay. Cells from DM1 patients when studied under the microscope reveal bright spots known as RNA foci. These foci are products of the mutated DM1 gene; in addition to helping make the diagnosis of the DM1, it is believed that these bodies interfere with normal cell function and are thus involved in causing the disease itself; the foci are in this sense a therapeutic target. When these aggregates are broken apart, proper cellular function is often restored, making "foci busters" good candidates for DM1 therapy. We shall therefore treat DM1 patient cells with thousands of compounds, including hundreds of currently used FDA-approved medications and using automated microscopy looking for reduction of these aggregates. Similarly we will interfere with 1000's of genes in the body and look for similar impact. Importantly we will use muscle cells from DM1 patient to do this test. Drugs and genes which reduce the number and or size of aggregates will be next tested in a mouse genetically engineered to have DM1 which display signs similar to that seen in humans. We will compare untreated and drug-treated mice to determine if the medications improved their DM1 signs. If treated animals show improved signs; this information could be used as the basis for a clinical trial. Using medications which are already in use for other conditions is advantageous as it by-passes the significant time required for safety and efficacy testing of newly developed drugs, saving both time and money.

column36: Development of cancer therapies targeting Myc with cell penetrating b-HLH-LZ domains
column37: Cancer arises because cells in our body acquire the potential of multiplying almost indefinitely. Contrary to healthy cells in the rest of the body, cancer cells become addicted to the cellular deregulations caused by the activation of oncogenes and/or by the inactivation of tumor suppressors. One of these deregulations, which occurs in almost all cancers, is the accumulation of a protein called c-Myc. One tumor suppressor that is inactivated in many cancers is called Max. Interestingly, Max is able to interact with c-Myc and help it to perform non-oncogenic functions. However, inactivating modification in Max contributes to the oncogenic potential of c-Myc. On the other hand, the introduction of normal Max or mimics in cancer cells can kill them. In this proposal, we will test if we can cure cancer in mice using Max and another molecule that can mimic its functions. More precisely, we propose to perform complex studies that will evaluate the drug-like properties and the mode of action of Max and one mimic. We have highly encouraging preliminary results that support their therapeutic potential. Upon completion of our research objectives, we will have completed most of the work necessary to warrant clinical studies in human. Considering that c-Myc plays a role in almost all types of cancers, our research could lead to the development of a revolutionary cancer therapy.

column36: An integrative brain health model for the individual prediction of cognitive decline
column37: The concept of "brain health" has been proposed to capture the relationship between the state of the brain and cognitive fitness. We propose to model this brain health by looking at various elements of neuronal health. We further wish to link brain health to cognition, in the context of healthy aging and probable Alzheimer's disease. We wish to test the hypothesis that as brain health declines, so does cognition. This type of integrative work is missing in the field, and we feel confident, using large scale databases and state of the art mathematical modelling and machine learning approaches, that we can produce a model which will predict decline years ahead of diagnostic. This would provide individuals with sufficient time to take measures to improve their general health and lifestyle in order to maintain brain health and cognition.

column36: Investigating the impact of cigarette smoke on antibody responses in the respiratory tract mucosa
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a life-threatening lung disease. It is a major cause of suffering and death in Canada and places a large burden on our healthcare system. It is estimated by the World Health Organization that COPD will be the third leading cause of death in the world by 2030. Despite this, COPD is among the most overlooked chronic diseases in Canada. Cigarette smoking and exposure to second-hand smoke are the main causes of COPD. Alarmingly, strategies to promote smoking cessation will not improve the burden of COPD over the next decades, as the benefit of decreased smoking rates in recent years is offset by the aging population and high smoking rates in the past. We urgently need better medication for this serious health problem, as current therapies are not very effective and mostly aimed at relieving symptoms. Smokers and patients with COPD suffer from repeated lung infections. The objective of our research is to investigate whether cigarette smoking impairs the ability to fight bacterial infections because of a weakened immune system. To do this, we will investigate immune function in smokers and patients with COPD, as well as experimental models of cigarette smoke exposure. The goal of our research is to understand how smoking damages the immune system and how to rebuild protective immunity against harmful bacteria. To accomplish this goal, we have assembled a team of world experts in clinical research, immunology, microbiology, and virology to tackle this challenging health problem. By pursuing this research, we will gain a better understanding of the harmful effects of cigarette smoke on the immune system. Our goal is to develop novel drugs to restore immune function in patients with COPD. Our experimental approach is innovative, as we aim to prevent infections rather than deal with the often irreversible damage caused by infections.

column36: Elucidating the Role of CSB in the Maintenance of Genomic Stability
column37: On a daily basis, our DNA, the genetic material that determines who we are and how we function, is under constant insult by chemicals and radiation found in the food we eat and in the environment we live. Fortunately cells in our body have evolved a number of mechanisms to ensure that damaged DNA is repaired promptly and properly so that the integrity of our DNA is maintained. One of these repair mechanisms is specifically evolved to repair DNA in which breaks occur in both strands (double strand breaks). DNA double strand breaks are extremely deleterious and if not repaired properly, they can lead to loss or deregulation of genes that help prevent cancer. As we age or in some genetic conditions, this break repair mechanism is altered or weakened, favoring the development of cancer. In addition, cancer can also arise from a disruption in the maintenance of telomeres, specialized structures found at the ends of our chromosomes. Understanding how DNA double strand breaks are repaired and how telomeres are maintained will be crucial to finding solutions to eradicate cancer or to slow down cancer progression. The proposed research aims to elucidate the role of CSB, a protein recently uncovered to play a role in DSB repair and telomere maintenance, in cancer cells. The knowledge gained from this proposed research will not only deepen our understanding of these two processes but also lay the foundation for future exploration of CSB as a target in cancer therapeutics.

column36: Effectiveness of Interventions in Early Daycare to Prevent Disruptive Behaviours in Children of Low-Income Neighbourhoods (I-CARE): A 2x2 Factorial Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial.
column37: Disruptive behaviour problems (DBPs) violate social norms and generate high costs to society. Adults with DBPs have problems ranging from mental health issues to substance abuse, spousal abuse, depression, and suicide. Disruptive behaviours begin in early childhood. Toddlers do not know how to express and meet their needs, so they may kick, hit, scream, and fight. As they grow older, they learn more acceptable ways to obtain what they want and disruptive behaviours fade away. Studies in the USA in the 1960s-80s show that child care-based interventions with parental support have long-term positive impacts in low-income neighbourhoods. In Canada today, where healthcare is universally available and daycare use is common, the same conditions do not necessarily apply. We need information on which interventions work best for low-income families in real-life situations and which are the most cost-effective. For example, parenting skills interventions are 3 times more expensive than daycare-based programs. Daycares are essentially preschools where parents send their children during working hours. We will conduct a trial comparing 3 different programs to reduce disruptive behaviour in 2-4-year-olds in daycare. We will enrol 80 daycares, i.e. about 1280 toddlers. Daycares will be randomly selected to receive one of the following: 1) training of educators to improve social skills in daycare; 2) at-home training for parents of the most disruptive children; 3) daycare and home-based training; and 4) a control group with daycare services as usual. Daycares will be chosen from low-income areas in Greater Montreal and Sherbrooke (Quebec). The program will last 2 years and then be evaluated. A biobank of saliva and hair samples will also be kept and analysed to test markers of disruptive behaviour and to measure improvement. Results will help decision-makers set up evidence-based best practice programs that are both useful and cost-effective and can be applied on a larger scale

column36: The Surgical Safety Checklist Revisited: Redevelopment of a Point-of-Care Tool to Improve Surgical Safety
column37: Goal: To improve the current surgical safety checklist tool used to decrease complications after surgery Background: Health care errors, including preventable surgical complications, are a tremendous burden to patients and health care systems internationally. The surgical safety checklist was created by the World Health Organization to improve surgical outcomes and decrease morbidity and mortality after surgery. The checklist held significant promise. It performed well in a pilot study but has had variable success in real-life settings. We aim to develop a new point-of-care surgical safety tool and implementation strategy that will reduce surgical complications in Canada and other high-income countries. Methods: This study was developed with integrated stakeholder involvement and will build on our previous and ongoing studies. The first stage will use surveys and interviews of surgical team members to explore aspects that makes surgical safety tools succeed or fail within specific centers. We will explore, in detailed interviews, the strategies developed by successful centers to improve surgical safety. In our second stage, our international team of researchers, knowledge-users and stakeholders will use the information from our previous studies as well as, surveys and interviews to create a new point-of care surgical safety tool. In the third and final stage, we will deploy this tool in three Canadian centers to examine its acceptability to users and its success in improving surgical processes that decrease complications. Expertise: Our team is partnered with the Canadian Patient Safety Institute and includes international research experts in surgical safety research as well as stakeholders and knowledge-users.

column36: Sex-specific investigations of Parkinson's disease mouse models: application for gonadal drugs repurposing.
column37: Both the prevalence and the incidence of Parkinson's disease (PD) are well documented to be higher in men than in women and these sex differences could be due to effects of the circulating sex hormones. Most PD patients experience gastrointestinal dysfunctions often preceding motor dysfunctions. PD might originate in the peripheral nervous system spreading later to the brain. Drugs for PD only improve motor symptoms: no drug is yet available to limit disease progression. It is thus important to identify pharmacological agents that would interfere with peripheral dysfunctions before spreading to the brain. This project will investigate two drugs to target the gut-brain axis for PD therapy: 1) dutasteride that inhibits the enzyme 5alpha-reductase already approved to treat prostate hyperplasia and 2) raloxifene that selectively modulates estrogen receptors already approved to treat post-menopausal osteoporosis. We have shown that these drugs possess anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties in a male toxin-induced mouse model of PD. We hypothesize that these drugs will have an effect as well in male than female mice but to a different extent. We will also start investigating the sex difference in an alpha-synuclein mouse model of PD with the hypothesis that alpha-synuclein accumulation is less in females due to estrogen neuroprotection. Our objectives are to evaluate A) the pharmacological properties of dutasteride and raloxifene in an early peripheral model of neurotoxin-induced PD with male and female mice to determine the contribution to the disease of male and female hormones, B) investigate the sex differences in alpha-synuclein accumulation in alpha-synuclein genetically modified intact and gonadectomised mice and C) investigate mechanisms implicated in cells. This project will validate novel indications for two drugs already approved for human administration to accelerate their use by PD patients. This project has high translational potential.

column36: The COMPASS Mental Health Module - A System to Improve Youth Mental Health Trajectories in Schools
column37: The prevention and early identification of mental illness, and promotion of mental health, are leading national and provincial priorities. Youth represent a key target population for such efforts since the onset of 70% of all mental illnesses occurs before age 18, impacting 1 in 5 young Canadians. Schools are recognized as an ideal context for equitably addressing mental health, as almost all youth attend for 25 hours a week. Assisting schools in providing mental health resources is a priority, yet limited evidence exists on how to effectively intervene. In response, our team received CIHR funding to develop and test a new tool to determine the real-world effectiveness of school-based mental health interventions - the COMPASS mental health module (MH-M). The tool is designed to be integrated within the COMPASS system - the world's largest and most comprehensive longitudinal school-based research platform. The 9-year CIHR-Health Canada funded COMPASS study (2012-21) annually collects data from 70,000+ grade 9-12 students attending 100+ secondary schools in Ontario, Alberta, Quebec, British Columbia, and Nunavut. Using our CIHR bridge funding, we incorporated the MH-M into the 2017/18 wave of the COMPASS study to collect one-year of baseline data. The goal of this project is to support the continued implementation of the MH-M for three additional years (2018/19-2020/21), providing up to four years of longitudinal data from the students and schools participating in the COMPASS host study, in order to build capacity and provide infrastructure for the continual improvement of youth mental health and the ability of schools and partners to support students. This study will allow collection of the ongoing data necessary to evaluate how the myriads of changes that occur in schools annually impact youth mental health over time, enabling evaluation of mental health programs being implemented, and building the evidence base of what interventions work among which populations.

column36: The role of state-dependent neural correlations in population coding and behavior
column37: As you are reading this text, neurons in your brain coordinate their activities, thereby enabling you to correctly perceive and interpret the visual input forming on your retina. Our senses play a primordial role in enabling us to interact with our environment on our day to day lives. This is however not the case for a significant portion of the population suffering from sensory disorders. In fact, Autism spectrum disorders are associated with symptoms indicating impaired sensory processing. Growing evidence shows that perception of the sensory environment relies on the coordinated firing of large groups of neurons within our brain: this is known as population coding. What complicates our understanding of population coding is that the neural activities are not independent of one another but are rather related (i.e., "correlated"). Neural correlations have been observed across multiple brain areas but how they impact coding remains largely controversial. This is in part due to the fact that they change depending on sensory input as well as the brain's internal state (e.g., attention). The primary goal of this research project is to understand the functional role of neural correlations in sensory coding. Our preliminary data shows that correlations can vary dynamically as a function of behaviorally relevant stimulus attributes, thereby providing information. Our project aims at understanding the nature of the underlying mechanisms. This research will provide key knowledge into how neural populations can encode sensory input, which in turn will lead to better understanding of how changes in brain architecture can lead to pathologies and better treatment options for patients.

column37: Dengue is increasing in its global presence with an estimated 4 billion people at-risk of infection in at least 128 countries. column36: Using resting-state fMRI prospectively to predict the optimal stimulation site and improve treatment outcomes for rTMS in major depression
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is among the most common and disabling illnesses in Canada. Although many treatments are available, finding the right one is a slow, trial-and-error process. Furthermore, 1/3 of MDD patients do not improve on medications or therapy (treatment-resistant depression, TRD). Currently, there is no routinely available brain scan to diagnose depression, or to select the best treatment in TRD. We recently helped develop a method to scan TRD patients and classify their depression into 1 of 4 'biotypes', based on their brain activity patterns on MRI. For treatment, since medications and therapy have already failed, we can instead directly stimulate the areas with abnormal activity, using a brain-stimulation technology called repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). rTMS is safe, non-invasive, and already Health Canada-approved for TRD. However, current rTMS practice is usually to stimulate the same area in everyone, and current success rates are modest, at 20-30%. Yet some 'biotypes' of MDD have shown rTMS response rates of 60-80%, suggesting that much better outcomes are possible with a personalized approach. In a world-first trial of its type, we will use the MRI 'biotypes' to personalize the rTMS target in each TRD patient, aiming to improve rTMS success rates up to two-fold. Our project will perform a randomized clinical trial comparing treatment outcomes for rTMS targeting two different brain areas, in 280 people with TRD. 1/2 will get rTMS targeted by their 'biotype'; 1/2 will get rTMS of the opposite area. The results will show whether using the biotypes can improve the response and remission rates for rTMS in TRD. If successful, the study will be the first ever to demonstrate effective MRI biotype-guided treatment selection in TRD, and could be the first to achieve remission in a majority of TRD patients using biotype-guided rTMS.

column37: Human autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most frequent hereditary disorder, afflicting 1 in 500 individuals. ADPKD is a severe condition with major impact on health and accounts for ~10% of all cases of end stage renal disease in Canada and worldwide. It is characterized by development of multiple renal cysts that can be detected in childhood, and grow in number and size over time, completely destroying the kidneys. Other organs are also frequently affected like liver, brain, and heart. Presently, progression of ADPKD is unstoppable: kidneys become non-functional and patients die if they have no access to hemodialysis or kidney transplant. A therapeutic strategy for ADPKD that could prevent or even delay renal destruction by a factor of 2- to 3-fold, would minimize cystic disease, improve quality of life and prolong very significantly lifespan. This research project aims at understanding the cellular and molecular mechanism(s) that lead to ADPKD. The PKD1 gene is responsible for ~85% of ADPKD cases. We study the molecular pathology associated with defective PKD1 gene in the mouse, the best experimental system. Our laboratory developed novel genetically modified Pkd1 mouse models that reproduce typical kidney symptoms of ADPKD. We will investigate the mechanism(s) of cyst formation and expansion with Pkd1 models. Cyst expansion is governed by proliferation and fluid secretion under the control of ion-fluid channels as KCNN4. We will test whether KCNN4 is the major channel responsible for cyst expansion by complementary genetic and pharmacologic approaches. We will also dissect the cellular and molecular mechanisms of KCNN4 in ADPKD pathology. Significantly, a KCNN4 specific inhibitor has been developed and tested in sickle cell disease clinical trials. We hope to repurpose this drug for ADPKD and delay renal destruction as prevention if not cure, and even be valuable to target at large, other renal cystic diseases.

column36: Rapid correction of vitamin D deficiency in pediatric critical illness: A phase III multicentre randomized controlled trial
column37: Vitamin D plays an important role in calcium balance, heart and lung health, inflammation, infection prevention, and muscle strength. Due to these roles, it has been suggested that critically ill patients with low levels might have higher rates of death and worse long term health. We believe that identifying critically ill children with vitamin D deficiency and then restoring vitamin D levels quickly could represent a safe, easy and inexpensive means of reducing patient illness, preventing death and improving quality of life. This application seeks funding for a clinical trial that will determine whether rapid normalization of vitamin D deficiency improves survival and health-related quality of life following critical illness. The project is designed as a multicentre trial in ten Canadian Pediatric Intensive Care Units. Critically ill children who agree to participate (consent given by caregivers) will have their blood vitamin D level measured, and those who are deficient will be randomized to receive a single dose of either high dose vitamin D3 or placebo (no drug). Study participants assigned to the high dose vitamin D arm will receive 10000 IU/kg of enteral cholecalciferol (up to a maximum of 400000 IU). We have tested this dose in a pilot trial, and no patient experienced serious adverse events related to vitamin D administration. Patients will be followed for 90 days to determine whether they survived and had a significant change in their health and quality of life. Vitamin D deficiency is a common problem not only among critically ill Canadian children, but in PICUs worldwide. In addition to being applicable in Canada, our study protocol has been designed to be generalizable and meaningful to critically ill children worldwide.

column36: Revolutionizing the treatment of neonatal short bowel syndrome by novel therapeutic approaches to intestinal growth
column37: Babies depend on the small bowel or gut to absorb nutrition. Some babies, especially those that are born preterm, can be born with a short gut, or have a surgical emergency after birth that causes the short bowel syndrome (SBS). These babies cannot stay healthy or grow without intravenous nutrition, called parenteral nutrition (PN) and PN at home or in hospital is very expensive. SBS is rare, but truly devastating. In the recent past, one third of babies with SBS died or needed an intestinal transplant. In Canada, two-thirds of intestinal transplants are due to neonatal SBS. To avoid death or transplant the babies must be able to stop PN. This is called adaptation, where the intestine grows and functions better. Babies can spend months or years failing to adapt and still die. The cost of medical care for the babies is more than 1.6 million US$ in the first 5 years of their life. From 2012-2016, we were funded by CIHR to develop a new baby model of SBS in piglets and to test a new therapy to help the gut adapt, using glucagon like peptide-2 (GLP-2). Our piglet model compared to all other models is the most like the severe SBS that babies develop. It has only been studied here, as our team includes a surgeon who also operates on the babies with SBS. We found GLP-2 did help the gut to adapt, but not to grow. When we added another treatment, epidermal growth factor, the gut finally grew. We want to now study insulin like growth factor-1, as we believe it will be even better than epidermal growth factor. We think that combining together these three treatments will be the very best way for the gut to grow, so that babies could stop the PN much more quickly. This will make a huge difference to the babies, to their families and will also reduce health care costs. It is exciting that GLP-2 is now being studied in children. This makes now the right time to do this study for babies with SBS in Canada.

column36: Medical Innovation and the Patient Consumer: Explaining the Rise of Minimally Invasive Surgery
column37: In the last thirty years, modern surgery has undergone a major revolution. Open operations have largely been replaced by an alternative: minimally invasive surgery (MIS). In MIS, surgeons insert laparoscopic visualization devices and other miniaturized surgical tools through small incisions to the abdomen. In the late 1980s and early 90s, in the space of less than five years, MIS became the technique of choice among general surgeons in North America and Europe. This rapid uptake has been widely explained as a patient-driven revolution, in which the "patient consumer" was a major player. However, we do not know, for instance, how patients actually influenced surgical therapy, especially in countries with predominantly public healthcare systems. Focusing on Canada and the USA, our proposed project asks, among other things, how exactly patients put pressure upon surgeons, how they communicate with one another to voice approval or express dissent. Answering these types of questions will help in understanding and defining the role of the patient-consumerism in modern healthcare. This history will provide a comparative analysis of patient consumerism at the end of the twentieth century, looking at its various manifestations and its limitations. The proposed project will thus be a major contribution to the still little explored history of MIS as an important and ever-evolving technology in modern surgery, and, more generally, to the history of technological innovation in modern medicine with its technical, scientific, social and cultural aspects. At the same time, it will help understand the changing role of patients in shaping modern medicine and its technologies. Its results will thus provide a better basis for future policy decisions about supporting and guiding technical innovation health care in accordance with the demands of the population.

column36: Model-based impact evaluation of pre-exposure prophylaxis on HIV transmission among men who have sex with men in Montreal
column37: Over the last decade, the number of HIV diagnoses among men who have sex with men (MSM) has failed to decline in Quebec despite the public health response. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) - taking a daily antiretroviral pill - can prevent HIV acquisition among those who do not have HIV but are at risk of getting it. Studies suggest that PrEP could decrease an HIV acquisition risk by 86% among MSM and possibly by 100% among those adherent. In comparison, using a condom during anal sex reduces infection rates by 70%. Starting in 2013, PrEP has been recommended by the Quebec government and the province was the first to reimburse the drug using public funds. Preliminary data suggests that 15% of MSM in Montreal have used PrEP in 2016. Understanding the impact of PrEP on the HIV epidemic at the population level is important. Clinical studies only consider the individual benefits of PrEP and not the long-term population-level benefits of averting chains of transmission. Evaluating the population-level impact of Quebec's PrEP program on HIV transmission is challenging as there is no appropriate comparison group. Further, PrEP could increase transmission of other sexually transmitted infections if it leads to lower condom use. Mathematical modeling - computer simulations of epidemics - can be used to tease-out the impact of PrEP. Specifically, we will: 1) Estimate the uptake of PrEP and characterize users' risk profile in Montreal. 2) Evaluate the population-level impact of PrEP interventions on HIV transmission. 3) Examine the reasons for PrEP interventions' success or failure in reducing HIV incidence. 4) Assess the impact of PrEP on gonorrhea incidence. Quebec is the only Canadian province where PrEP is an important component of the HIV response. By drawing on the expertise of our research team, this model-based impact evaluation provides a unique opportunity to optimize PrEP delivery and inform HIV prevention programs in Canada.

column36: Novel determinants of CMG DNA helicase activity and their impact on Primordial Dwarfism
column37: Human genes are encoded on long DNA molecules that act as instruction manuals. Each 'manual' is organized as a helix made of two matching DNA strands, on which information is inscribed. Every time a cell divides, this script needs to be faithfully duplicated. This requires the two DNA strands to be separated and copied to generate a new set of instruction manuals, one for each of the two new cells. We study how a specialized "molecular motor" separates the two DNA strands when cells divide. This motor is called the 'CMG helicase', and gets its name from the ability to unwind the two strands of the DNA double helix. DNA cannot be copied unless the two DNA strands are first separated. The CMG helicase is therefore required for human life, and its functions allow multicellular organisms to grow as cells multiply. Our group recently identified rare defects in the CMG helicase that cause dwarfism. Our preliminary results suggest that these defects have a profound effect on the cell's ability to multiply. We therefore hypothesize that defects in the CMG helicase cause dwarfism by preventing cells from copying DNA in a timely manner, thereby diminishing their ability to multiply which leads to short stature. We have assembled a team with specialized expertise that will determine how and why defects in the CMG helicase cause short stature. Our team is the first to reconstruct DNA unwinding by the human CMG helicase in the context of these defects. Our cellular, biophysical, and biochemical studies will provide conclusive results explaining why defects in the CMG helicase have such profound effects on growth. It may also lead to the design of new therapies and diagnostic tests for children born with CMG helicase defects and dwarfism.

column37: Brain tumors represent the leading cause of childhood cancer mortality, due to their highly aggressive and often incurable nature. Medulloblastoma (MB), the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, is defined by four molecular subgroups (Wnt, Shh, Group 3, Group 4) based on gene expression profiles. Clinically, Wnt MB patients who have high activity of a developmental signaling pathway called Wnt, have the most favorable prognosis with a >95% 5-year survivorship. By contrast, non-Wnt MB patients are characterized by metastatic disease, increased rates of recurrence, and intermediate-poor overall survivorship. Given that Wnt MBs represent the only subgroup in which metastasis is not indicative of a poor prognosis, it has been suggested that Wnt signaling may contribute to their remarkable response to therapy. Given the excellent clinical outcome in Wnt-driven MB, we aim to convert treatment-resistant Group 3 and 4 MBs into ostensibly benign tumors by activation of Wnt signaling. Our preliminary results show that the non-Wnt MB cells have reduced growth when they are treated with Wnt activators. By using animal models, we found that Wnt-activated cells have decreased tumorigenicity. In the current work we aim to understand the mechanism by which the Wnt pathway can be modulated for therapy of poor prognosis MBs. We also aim to identify novel Wnt activators through genetic screens using CRISPR technology. Ultimately, this work will lead to increasing our molecular understanding of treatment-refractory MB, and identify new therapeutic targets for MB patients who still die from relapse.

column36: Aging in Autism Spectrum Disorders: Changes in Brain Structure and Function

column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is increasing at an alarming rate in Canada. Disproportionally affected are Canada's Indigenous Peoples. The Oji-Cree linguistic group that lives in Central Canada experiences up to 5X higher rates and much earlier onset of T2D compared to the general Canadian population. This gene variant not only strongly associates with T2D in the Oji-Cree sub-population, but also strongly associates with a younger age-of-onset of T2D. Despite being discovered almost 2 decades ago, we currently do not understand how this gene variant affects the insulin-secreting beta cells leading to increased risk for T2D development. column36: The nature of pelvic floor muscle involvement in dyspareunia

Although some believe that the deeper layer of the PFMs is also implicated in vulvodynia, findings have been less consistent. However, studies to date have been small, have carried a large risk of bias, and have not considered the potential confounding factors of pain and anxiety during testing. column36: Engineering therapeutics for the treatment of anemia in oncology patients
column37: Anemia (a low number of red blood cells or low amount of hemoglobin in blood) affects many cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, leading to fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath and other symptoms, which severely reduce the patients' quality of life. Cancer-related anemia is also associated with shorter survival times. While treating anemia with the hormone erythropoietin (EPO) has been highly successful, the use of EPO in cancer-related anemia is sometimes considered unsafe since it also encourages tumor growth. Previous research has shown that the desired response to EPO (red blood cell production) likely occurs via a different mechanism than the undesired tumor-promoting effects. That is, the stimulation of red blood cell production depends on a cell surface receptor called EPOR, while tumor-stimulating effects depend on other cell surface receptors unrelated to EPOR. These observations suggest that the development of molecules capable of stimulating only the desirable EPOR-dependent responses may provide novel avenues for a more effective treatment of cancer-related anemia. We have developed a rapid and efficient method to engineer protein variants of EPO and antibodies that attach to EPOR. This involves searching through large collections of EPO-like variants or antibodies for molecules that attach to EPOR and stimulate its activity. The effect of these novel molecules on EPOR activation is assessed in cultured cells and screened in cultured tumor cells to identify molecules that do not stimulate tumor growth. The proposed project builds on current knowledge from available anemia treatments by creating novel, improved molecules that will stimulate production of red blood cells via an EPO-dependent mechanism, but unlike natural EPO, they will not stimulate other pathways that lead to undesired side effects. Therefore, this project has the potential to greatly improve the quality of life and survival for cancer patients.

column36: Effect of maternal vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy and lactation on offspring bone mass, body composition and muscle strength in early childhood: follow-up of a randomized controlled trial cohort.
column37: Optimal child development requires healthy bone and muscle growth, starting in the womb. Bone health and body composition (i.e. amount of fat vs. non-fat tissue) may also influence the risks of osteoporosis, obesity and heart disease in later life. Vitamin D is an essential nutrient that contributes to the formation of bones and muscles. Yet, it remains unknown if the amount of vitamin D a woman consumes during her pregnancy and while breastfeeding affects the growth of her child's bones and muscles. In collaboration with researchers in Bangladesh, our Canadian research team has recently completed a study of vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy and breastfeeding in 1300 women. Participants were assigned to 1 of 5 groups. Each group received different doses of vitamin D or placebo (no vitamin D) during pregnancy and up to 6 months after delivery. Children have been followed up to 2 years of age. We aim to conduct a longer-term follow-up study of a sample of 600 children at 4 years of age. In this new study, we will use state-of-the-art equipment to test the possible effects of vitamin D in pregnancy and breastfeeding on children's bones, their body composition and the strength of their muscles, which are important markers of child development. We will also collect information about each child's dietary intake that may affect bone and muscle health in childhood. The study is being conducted in Bangladesh because of its high rates of vitamin D deficiency. However, the results will be relevant in Canada, where many pregnant and breastfeeding women are at risk of vitamin D deficiency due to factors such as dark skin pigmentation, avoidance of vitamin D-fortified dairy products, as well as a lack of "sunshine vitamin D" because of Canada's northern latitude. The study will provide new information that will contribute to evidence-based guidelines for vitamin D intake in pregnant and breastfeeding women, thereby helping to improve long-term maternal and child health.

column36: Characterization of the Relationship Between Innate Immune Activation and Intestinal Stem Cell Homeostasis.
column37: Our gastrointestinal tract establishes a physical barrier that allows essential nutrients to enter circulation, and keeps harmful microbes at bay. This barrier is maintained throughout our lives by a population of stem cells that grow and replace dead or dying cells at the gut surface. If stem cells fail to divide at an adequate rate, gut barriers break down, and noxious molecules breach the animal interior. In contrast, excess stem cell growth often disturbs gut architecture. In many cases, prolonged overgrowth of stem cells enables the development of intestinal tumors. For example, in inflammatory bowel disease, persistent activation of immune responses to gut bacteria drives excess growth of stem cells. The subsequent disruptions to intestinal function negatively impact quality of life, and elevate the risk of colorectal cancer in patients by approximately twenty-fold. Researchers in my group generated a transgenic fly that allows us to experimentally mimic the immune-dependent growth of stem cells. We showed that persistent immune responses to gut bacteria caused a rapid expansion of stem cells and a harmful loss of gut organization. In follow-up work, we identified the bacteria responsible for immune-dependent overgrowth of stem cells. We showed that immune responses to the bacterial cell wall interrupts conventional growth programs, and fuels the disorganized expansion of stem cells. In this project, we will determine the exact effects of immune activity on gut stem cell growth and determine how bacteria modify these responses. Flies are excellent models for this work, as the biological blueprint for gut formation and function was established very early in animal evolution. Thus, work in flies provides important insights into critical aspects of human gut biology.

column36: Molecular and Functional Characterization of Childhood Ependymoma
column37: Ependymoma is a major cause of childhood cancer related morbidity and mortality. Current therapies are limited to aggressive surgeries and external beam irradiation, which is effective in only 50% of cases, while resulting in significant lifelong neurocognitive sequelae in survivors. At relapse, the only therapies available are repeat surgery and radiation, where less than 10% of cases can be salvaged, while adding to the plethora of long-term side effects. As such new therapies and an enhanced understanding of this tumor are urgently required. Currently we treat all patients with the same treatment, but we don't know if all patients with a specific type of ependymoma called supratentorial ependymoma all have the same type of tumour or if they are different. Using samples from a trans-Canadian clinical trial of relapsed ependymoma which I am leading, we will try to understand what leads to relapse and how to prevent it. Overall this proposal has the potential to significantly advance our knowledge of a lethal and understudied cancer.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of long-term nervous system protection
column37: While mental decline and the onset of neurodegenerative diseases are strongly dependent on age, the mechanisms that trigger these conditions are largely unknown. The goal of this project is to understand how brain cells, after birth, are protected lifelong from post-natal growth and maturation, and from the wear and tear of everyday life, with the major goal of uncovering strategies to counteract brain decline and neurodegenerative disorders that manifest during adulthood. We predict that this research strategy will open up novel and powerful advances into our understanding of the long-term protection of the nervous system. Ultimately, these studies are expected to speed up future research in mammalian systems, where genetic approaches to identify genes regulating neuronal maintenance are still quite complicated. The proposed studies in C. elegans are expected to establish a strong foundation to elucidate the molecular and cellular mechanisms of neuronal maintenance, at the single-neuron, circuit, and circuit output (behavior) levels. We expect that our findings will foster the study of novel molecular mechanisms that control neuronal decline, which will dramatically enhance our understanding of the molecular codes used by neurons to actively protect neuronal function despite developmental, mechanical, and environmental challenges. We expect that our research will have fundamental implications for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases and the development of approaches to ameliorate the consequences of adult-onset neurological conditions, thus improving the quality of human life.

column36: Finding the molecular drivers of calcific aortic valve stenosis
column37: The human heart consists of four chambers that contract in a repeated, rhythmic and synchronized manner to pump blood in the body. The heart also has four valves that ensure that blood flow goes only in one direction. One of these valves is called the aortic valve. The aortic valve lies between the main heart chamber (left ventricle) and the aorta, which is the largest artery that distributes blood to all parts of the body. Calcification of the aortic valve, or more specifically aortic stenosis, is the most frequent heart valve disease and the third leading cause of heart disease in adults. The incidence increases with age, and with the current shift toward an older population, it is becoming a major societal and economic burden. There is currently no medical treatment available other than surgery to replace the diseased native valve by a prosthetic heart valve. It is thus urgent to understand the causes of the disease at the most fundamental levels in order to elucidate new therapeutic options. Many factors are predicted to cause the disease and an important genetic predisposition was demonstrated. However, only a small number of studies have tried to identify the susceptibility genes. In this research program, we plan to expand this work using a series of complementary genomic approaches. This program will take advantage of the large volume of clinical and biological materials that we have collected during the last few years to study patients with aortic stenosis. The most modern genomics and bioinformatics approaches will be used to find new therapeutic targets to treat this condition. Data collected in this proposal will serve for many years and strengthen our research program which ultimately, aims at finding a cure for aortic stenosis. Overall, this proposal will increase our understanding of the disease processes, which will lead to innovative therapeutic strategies to treat this life-threatening and frequent disease.

column36: Mitochondrial quality control during hemorrhagic shock: positive impact of remote ischemic conditioning.
column37: Traumatic injury is a major cause of death and disability among the civilian population. One of the major causes for these outcomes is loss of blood related to the injury. Patients either die due to massive blood loss or they survive but suffer from the morbid effects of the injury. Blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock, contributes to these effects by injuring cells, leading to poor function of entire organs. One important way that shock exerts this effect is by causing dysfunction of mitochondria, the main source of energy in cells. Our group has recently demonstrated that a simple intervention, performed by applying a tourniquet to an extremity, and cycling it on and off, so called "Remote Ischemic Conditioning (RIC)" can protect against cellular and organ damage. Our preliminary studies indicate that RIC might exert these effects by improving mitochondrial quality. The purpose of our studies is to examine the effect of shock on mitochondrial quality and understand how RIC might lessen the detrimental effect of hemorrhagic shock on their function. Together, these studies will elucidate potentially novel therapeutic targets aimed at improving outcomes in people sustaining traumatic injury.
