column36: Delineating the Mechanisms Underlying Nitric Oxide Induced Muscle Wasting During Cachexia
column37: Cachexia is a debilitating syndrome characterized by uncontrollable body weight loss that arises in patients with pro-inflammatory conditions, such as cancer. Numerous pathophysiological events have been associated with cachexia, including anorexia, liver dysfunction, fat tissue depletion, and, notably, loss of skeletal muscle mass. Loss of muscle mass during cachexia leads to weakness, lower quality of life, and is associated with reduce response to disease treatment. While our understanding of how cachexia is initiated is still incomplete, it is well established that chronically elevated proinflammatory hormones, also known as cytokines, are a primary driver of the condition. However, therapies against these cytokines have proven ineffective, indicating that no one inflammatory hormone is the primary driver of this syndrome. This highlights the need to identify common downstream pathways that are induced in affected tissues for targeted therapeutics. Recently, impairment of mitochondrial function and metabolic aberrations in muscle have been associated with the cachectic phenotype. However, the intra-cellular mechanisms leading to this dysfunction remain elusive. We have acquired preliminary data suggesting that elevated nitric oxide (NO) levels produced from inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) during cytokine exposure is a primary cause of mitochondrial impairment in skeletal muscle. In past studies, we also showed that iNOS/NO is a key mediator of the cachectic phenotype by affecting the expression of factors, such as MyoD, which are required for muscle formation. Thus, we propose to study in this grant how NO production from iNOS alters metabolic function and the expression of factors such as MyoD in muscles exposed to cachectic stimuli, as well as the impact of these changes on muscle function. In doing so, we hope to increase our understanding of how cytokines induce atrophy and dysfunction in muscle and identify novel targets for therapeutic development.

column36: Reversal of atrial substrate to prevent atrial fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an abnormal heart rhythm that comes from the upper chambers of the heart. Atrial fibrillation causes the main pumping chambers of the heart to beat in an irregular and sometimes very rapid fashion. Some people with atrial fibrillation feel completely well. Others feel unwell, with palpitations, a feeling of shortness of breath, reduced exercise ability, lightheadedness or chest pain. Atrial fibrillation is not usually a dangerous rhythm but can cause you to feel unwell and can reduce your quality of life. If atrial fibrillation causes significant symptoms, catheter ablation is often used to try to prevent it from coming back. Catheter ablation involves putting special wires up through the veins of the legs to record the electrical signals of the heart and to cauterize the areas of the heart that cause this abnormal rhythm. The cure rate is between 50 and 70%. There may be ways to improve this cure rate significantly, reducing the need for second and third procedures for this problem with treatment of risk factors and exercise. With each procedure, the risks for major and minor complications is up to 6%, with a risk of death of 1 in 1000. Objective: We propose to determine if a combined home-based exercise and risk factor treatment reduces the recurrence of atrial fibrillation after a catheter ablation procedure for atrial fibrillation. Methods: This objective will be accomplished by performing a clinical trial whereby patients with persistent AF who will be undergoing catheter ablation to treat their AF will be randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: 1) aggressive risk factor treatment versus 2) standard therapy. There will be 670 patients required for the entire study. This is the first trial to study the effects of exercise in combination with risk factor treatment on atrial fibrillation in a randomized fashion.

column37: Exosomes are extracellular vesicles that are released from living cells under a variety of circumstances. In this proposal we seek to manipulate and engineer these vesicles to carry anti-viral cargo, utilizing altered cellular systems to generate biocompatible exosomal therapeutics that contain small ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules called microRNAs. column36: Healing Hearts Together: Evaluating a couples-based intervention to improve health outcomes
column37: The quality of interpersonal relationships has a significant impact on emotional and physical health. Relationship quality, which is how satisfied people are in their relationship, predicts health outcomes for cardiac patients. Couple distress is related to high blood pressure, elevated heart rate, and the development of coronary artery disease. In contrast, supportive relationships can protect the heart and help patients follow medical advice. In addition to the patient, partners often experience psychological distress. As such, it is essential that the partner be involved in the care after a cardiac event. Despite the strong connection between relationship quality and heart health, few interventions include the partner. This is a problem because most patients are in relationships and the partner can be an important source of support. Our team has developed an 8-week relationship-enhancement program for couples facing heart disease called "Healing Hearts Together" or HHT. The main objective of our study is to determine whether the HHT program helps cardiac patients and their partners improve the quality of their relationship more than patients receiving standard usual care. We will also study whether the program has a greater effect on blood pressure and other stress responses, mental health, quality of life, heart health behaviors, and cardiac risk factors and outcomes. Participants will be 304 patients who experienced a recent cardiac event (such as a heart attack) and their partners. They will complete questionnaires and get physical measures taken (such as blood work and weight) before and after the HHT intervention as well as 4 months later. We will also track how often they have heart symptoms or problems for one year. We expect greater reductions in couple distress, improved behavioural and emotional functioning, and better heart health among patients attending the HHT program as compared to usual care.

column36: Poxvirus replication and recombination as drivers of genome evolution
column37: Poxviruses are big DNA viruses that infect many different creatures including humans. The most well known is variola virus, which causes smallpox, and the poxvirus most commonly studied in laboratories is vaccinia virus. Forty years ago vaccinia virus was used as a vaccine to eradicate smallpox. Although no longer commonly used for that original purpose, recombinant forms of vaccinia virus are still used to vaccinate against other diseases like malaria. More complex genetic modifications have also been introduced into vaccinia with the goal of producing forms of virus that will selectively kill cancer cells. These are called "oncolytic" viruses. My laboratory has a long history of studying the linked processes of poxvirus replication and genetic recombination. (Replication makes copies of the virus, recombination rearranges the DNA in a virus genome.) Our basic research has produced a popular commercial recombination-based cloning technology ("InFusion"), contracts to help develop smallpox antivirals and new vaccines, an oncolytic virus targeted for Phase I trials in 2019, and a new method for producing recombinant poxviruses from "scratch" using synthetic DNA. All of these translational activities require an understanding of how poxviruses recombine DNA and all are enhanced if we can optimize the rapid production of properly assembled recombinants. To this end we plan to study three aspects of poxvirus replication and recombination. First, we'd like to gain a better understanding of how the cell in which vaccinia replicates affects production of recombinant viruses. Second, we've discovered a new way of making synthetic recombinant viruses and will use it study how virus genomes are constructed. Third, our new technology also provides a tool for exploring how smallpox vaccines might have evolved over time from a horsepox virus-like ancestor. This will provide ways to improve the safety of these vaccines and other vaccinia-based biotherapeutics.

column36: Exposure to Environmental Contaminants and Immune Function in South African Children
column37: Despite important gains over the last decades, infectious diseases continue to account for almost half of the global burden of disease in sub-Saharan Africa. Factors such as inadequate sanitation, difficult access to clean water, deficient health care systems and incomplete vaccine coverage are important determinants of infectious disease occurrence, accumulating evidence suggests that exposure to environmental immunotoxicants may play a role. DDT and pyrethroid insecticides are commonly used as part of Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) programs, resulting in high exposure to children. Residents of IRS areas often use solid fuels such as wood and other biomass, which causes high exposure to household air pollution (HAP). Experimental in vitro and in vivo studies suggest that postnatal exposure to DDT, pyrethroids and HAP may inhibit immune response to vaccines and trigger allergic airway diseases. However, few human studies have investigated the question and no study has evaluated the combined effect of insecticides and HAP. The objective of this proposal is to characterize postnatal exposure to DDT, pyrethroid insecticides and PM2.5, and to determine whether exposure to these contaminants impact the immune system among highly-exposed South African children. Specifically, we aim to: 1. Characterize the levels, sources and determinants of exposure to DDT/E, pyrethroid insecticides and PM2.5 in rural South African children. 2. Determine whether exposure to DDT/E, pyrethroid insecticides and/or PM2.5 is associated with altered immunity between ages 6.5 and 8 years. We will determine whether 3. column36: Imaging synaptic density in schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a psychiatric illness with a significant burden for patients, their families, and the society. However, the reasons why some people develop schizophrenia remain poorly understood. It typically develops during late adolescence and early adulthood, the stage when the brain is rapidly maturing. As the brain becomes mature it identifies connections between brain cells that are not being used and removes them, a process called "pruning". This process leads to an efficient adult brain. A reduced count of brain cell bodies and extensions has been observed in post-mortem tissue from patients with schizophrenia. This is believed to result from an excessive pruning leading to distorted thought processes and odd behaviour as observed in patients. However, it has not been possible to quantify brain cell bodies and their extensions in living humans until now. Recently, a novel radioactive dye ([11C]UCB-J) has been developed to image brain cell extensions using a positron emission tomography (PET) camera. In this study, PET will be used to quantify brain cell extensions in the cerebral cortex in healthy volunteers and patients with schizophrenia. Information on changes in brain cell extensions as well as brain volume, behaviour and cognition will be collected, and interactions between them explored. The results of this study will help us understand the underlying causes of schizophrenia. This proposal is anticipated to provide the first proof for a reduction of brain cell extensions in schizophrenia in living humans needed to inform future studies in order to detect the disease at an earlier stage and for identification of disease mechanisms that will help target mental health interventions.

column36: The role of the RNase G3BP1 in Senescence
column37: Aged individuals are characterized by an increase in the number of cells that undergo growth arrest, a phenomenon known as replicative senescence. It is believed that the onset of diseases in the aged population is mediated in part by the increased accumulation of these senescent cells. The conversion of DNA into proteins requires the synthesis of an intermediate template molecule called RNA. Several proteins regulate the export of RNA out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm where it is converted into proteins. The research done in my laboratory focuses on such a protein, named G3BP1 that also regulates the longevity of RNA molecules. Although the identity of genes that mediate scenescene is well defined, very little is know as to how they are regulated during this process. Since our data suggest that G3BP1mediates the induction of scenescence, we hypothesize that it does so by regulating the expression of RNAs involved in this phenotype. The purpose of this study is to assess this possibility and to further verify the role of G3BP1 partners or the implication of modifications of the G3BP1 protein on replicative scenescene. We therefore aim to establish the pathways and mechanisms by which G3BP1 is involved in replicative scenescence.

column36: Ross for Valve replacement in AduLts (REVIVAL) trial
column37: Heart valves help control blood flow through the heart and, if diseased, may need to be replaced. After having a heart valve replaced, patients have a higher risk of death than people who have not had a valve replaced. In young adult patients, replacing the aortic heart valve with a mechanical valve halves their life-span compared to other people their age. Mechanical valves tend to form blood clots so they need long-term blood thinners that increase risk of bleeding and lower quality of life. Animal tissue valves reduce clotting and bleeding risks but wear out sooner and shorten patient life-span. An operation, called the Ross procedure, replaces a patient's diseased aortic valve with his/her own pulmonary valve and uses a donor valve in the pulmonary position which receives less stress than the aortic valve. The Ross procedure aims to improve valve durability with less clotting, avoiding use of blood thinners. Patients and physicians need a large, high-quality study comparing the Ross procedure and standard valve replacement to know if either approach is better. We will perform a 3-year feasibility study in seven sites, in Canada and abroad, to test the study design and ability to do a larger, conclusive study comparing the impact of the Ross procedure to standard valve replacement on survival without valve-related life-threatening complications. Patients will be randomized, like flipping a coin, to receive the Ross or standard valve surgery. The goals are 1) to evaluate if we can recruit 6 patients per site per year, 2) to test if the assigned procedure is performed in over 90% of study patients, and 3) to see how many mechanical vs. tissue valves are used in the standard valve group. Patients eligible but not enrolled in the trial will be asked if we can collect some data on how they do after their surgery. If we show the study is feasible, we will request funds for the full study and will include the feasibility patients in the full study.

column36: The Intensive Care Unit Resident Scheduling (InCURS) trial: A cluster RCT of 16 and 24 hour schedules in Canadian ICUs
column37: Many patients, doctors and others worry that tired doctors provide worse patient care, may not learn well and become burnt-out. In response to these concerns, some countries changed their laws to limit work-hours for doctors in training ('residents'). In Canada, most residents work six or seven 24-30h shifts each month. A recent Canadian report ordered by Health Canada said that making good decisions about resident work-hour rules was " significantly limited by quality evidence, especially evidence directly attributable to the Canadian context." Creating this evidence is the main goal of our research. Our pilot study in 2 intensive care units (ICU) found that shorter shifts may be worse for patients, and for residents were more tiring than expected but improved wellbeing. Learning was not assessed. Previous studies on resident work-hours report similar findings: conflicting effects for patients, benefits for resident wellbeing, inconsistent and under-studied effects on learning. Overall, these results are not conclusive and confirm the need for a larger study. The current study will provide high-quality Canadian evidence. We will compare two common ICU schedules used in Canada: resident shifts of 16h and 24h. ICU patients are very sick, there is little margin for error: they need doctors who know them well and are thinking clearly. We will measure the effects of each schedule on patients and residents. For patients, we will study mortality rates and harm caused by care in ICU. For residents, we will study their learning about managing common illnesses in ICU, do basic ICU procedures, and communicate with families. Resident wellbeing measures will include sleepiness, other fatigue symptoms, and burnout. We need to study both resident and patient outcomes so that Canadians can understand trade-offs linked to changing schedules. With this knowledge, Canadians can expect safer care for today's patients and better-trained doctors for the patients of tomorrow.

column36: Regulation of microtubule motors in organelle transport
column37: Motor proteins move along microtubule tracks to transport mRNA, proteins, organelles, and other cargoes in the cell. Two motor proteins, kinesin and dynein, are responsible for long-range transport. Kinesins move towards the cell periphery while dynein moves towards the cell center. These motors coordinate to transport cargoes in both directions along microtubules and enable navigation through the dense and crowded cellular environment. Defects in transport cause neurodegenerative and developmental disorders. For example, mutations in kinesin-1 and dynein result in the neurodegenerative diseases Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia and Charcot-Marie Tooth disease, and impaired transport is a hallmark of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, and Huntington's disease. While studies over the past two decades have identified the motor proteins that drive transport and how they generate movement, the mechanisms that regulate kinesin and dynein to control the direction of transport remain unclear. We hypothesize the scaffolding molecules that recruit motor proteins to cargoes play an important role in controlling their activity. We will employ powerful microscopy techniques that allow us to image single motor proteins with nanometer precision and measure the forces they exert to understand how motor proteins are turned on and off in the cell.

column37: Parenting typically-developing children is one of our most challenging roles; parenting children with developmental disabilities is known to take a considerable toll on parents' physical and mental health and wellbeing. It is obvious that promoting parent wellbeing is important for the best outcomes for all children, especially those facing life-long challenges. To date we have little understanding, and no direct evidence, about whether it is possible to prevent the physical and mental health impacts on parents when they have a child with an impairment, which in turn will benefit their children. In the 21st century there have been some significant advances in how we think about 'health' and about 'family-centred services'. The time is ripe for a major exploration of the impact of these workshops - collectively referred to as ENVISAGE (ENabling VISions And Growing Expectations) - on a host of parent-reported outcomes. Outcomes will be assessed before the workshops, at the end of the 5 weekly sessions, and at 3, 6 and 12 months after the ENVISAGE program. We expect that this program will have an important short-term effect on parent outcomes, and provide powerful evidence for a large-scale randomized trial that will then include measures of children's outcomes as well as parent wellbeing. If the program is demonstrated to 'work' over a 2-year period it can be further developed and made available across the world.

column36: The prevalence and impact of intensive diabetes treatment in older adults
column37: With increasing age, diabetes is more common. In Canada, 1 in 4 people over the age of 75 have diabetes. While lowering glucose levels is the goal of treatment, aggressive diabetes management increases the risk of low blood sugars, hypoglycemia. In older adults, hypoglycemia is associated with devastating health consequences, including death. As a result, guidelines recommend relaxing glycemic targets in older adults. However, studies show that more than half of older people with diabetes are over treated and at high risk of hypoglycemia. In Canada, very little research has studied patterns in diabetes management and risk of overtreatment in this population. Given the potential risks of overtreatment, our study will provide much needed information for creating strategies that optimize the care of older adults with diabetes. The goal of this study is to explore patterns of diabetes management in older adults in Ontario in order to identify evidence and risk factors for overtreatment. To do so, we will use Ontario health care databases and identify all individuals over the age of 75 who have diabetes. First, we will evaluate the proportion of older patients in Ontario who are overtreated based on medication use and average blood sugar levels and identify risk factors for overtreatment. Second, we will evaluate rates of emergency room visits, hospitalizations and death between older adults with evidence of overtreatment and those without. Lastly, we will assess the impact of 2013 Diabetes Canada guidelines for frail older adults on trends in glycemic control before and after their publication. This research is important because of the number of older adults with diabetes is steadily increasing, and older adults are particularly vulnerable to overtreatment and hypoglycemia. Our study will provide evidence of risk factors associated with overtreatment and therefore help researchers and policy makers identify ways in which to improve care for older adults with diabetes

column36: Determining structure-based mechanisms for the roles of RAD51 paralogs in DNA repair
column37: The 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was shared between Paul Modrich, Tomas Lindahl, and Aziz Sancar, who pioneered research into mechanisms of DNA repair. DNA repair is essential for the recognition and subsequent repair of damaged or aberrant DNA molecules. This is a critical process for cellular health as it prevents genome instability, which is the accumulation of mutations or DNA rearrangements within the genome. The importance of understanding molecular mechanisms of how DNA repair maintains genome stability is important for human health, as genome instability is a hallmark of both cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. Indeed, inherited mutations in DNA repair genes can lead to severe human diseases, such as Fanconi anemia and Ataxia telangiectasia, or can result in cancer predisposition. However, once cancer has formed the DNA repair defects that are often specific to the cancer cell can be a good thing. Recent clinical approaches have shown that a class of drugs called PARP inhibitors, which specifically kill cancer cells by targeting their DNA repair defect, can be used to treat advanced ovarian cancer. These PARP inhibitors target defects in the DNA repair pathway called homologous recombination repair. Homologous recombination repair is involved in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks that are one of the most toxic forms of DNA damage as both strands of the DNA double-helix are broken, which can lead to their separation and loss of genetic information or large rearrangements of DNA within the genome. The goals of this project are to understand the molecular mechanisms of how homologous recombination repair works to accurately fix these double-stranded DNA breaks. This will help us understand how this essential process works, how it protects against cancer, how cancer or other disease states arise when this pathway is defective, and how we can target this pathway for future advanced cancer therapies.

column36: PROphylaxis for venous ThromboEmbolism in Severe Traumatic brain injury (PROTEST): a Double-blind Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Severe traumatic brain injury is common, potentially lethal, and can result in severe and irreversible disability. It is also often associated with potentially life-threatening complications during the early period following the injury, when patients are critically ill and receiving life support. One of these complications is the development of clots in the legs and the lungs because the patients are not moving. Injectable clot prevention medications (anticoagulants) can help prevent these clots from forming, but there is a risk that these may increase the risk of progression of brain bleeding early after the injury. Currently, there is debate about the best timing to start these medications: as soon as possible during the first week after the brain injury, or waiting until at least 7 days after the brain injury. This study will help doctors determine which of these two approaches is better: early use of the medications to reduce the risk of clot, versus withholding these medications until one week after the brain injury to reduce the risk of bleeding. Both of these options have competing risks and benefits. This study will involve 11 of the largest major Canadian Trauma hospitals, and will provide valuable information to help improve outcomes for these critically ill patients.

column36: Peripheral and central chemoreceptor reflex regulation of sympathetic activity in heart failure patients with and without sleep apnea
column37: When the heart fails to pump normally, the brain releases into the bloodstream more of a molecule called noradrenaline (NA). NA increases heart rate, retains salt and water and constricts blood vessels. At first, more NA improves heart function but over time this muscle weakens and can no longer pump enough blood to the kidney and muscles. This condition is called "heart failure" (HF). For older Canadians, HF is the most common cause of hospitalization and a major cause of premature death. Our research aims to learn what it is about HF that causes more NA to be released from sympathetic nerves. Specialized blood oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors become very sensitive in about 50% of HF patients who then breathe more vigorously if blood O2 is low or blood CO2 is high. This ventilation then brings O2 or CO2 back to normal. However, these O2/CO2 sensors also connect to brain areas controlling NA. We think that: i) if these O2/CO2 sensors are more sensitive they will tell the sympathetic nerves to release more NA and ii) that HF patients with the most overactive O2/CO2 sensors will have highest nerve firing. Sleep apnea (SA), where breathing stops often during sleep, causes blood O2 to fall and CO2 to increase. As it turns out, about 50% of HF patients have SA and the sympathetic nerves of HF patients with SA fire more often to release NA than nerves of those without SA. However, not known is if this is because their O2/CO2 sensors are more active. This Project will determine: i) if O2 or CO2 sensors are more active in those HF patients with SA; ii) if this causes more sympathetic firing during blood O2 or CO2 changes that mimic SA; and iii) if more active O2/CO2 sensors contribute to high nerve firing even when SA patients wake up and apnea stops. We are confident that these experiments will discover 1 or more causes of high NA in HF and that this in turn will stimulate new ways of identifying and treating this important cause of suffering and death.

column36: Comparing the neural basis of memory integration in humans and mice.
column37: Over 1 million Canadians suffer from dementia. This disease costs our economy over $10 billion annually and robs patients of their precious memories. With no effective treatment available, these costs will only increase as our population ages. The best strategy to halt this epidemic is to first understand how the healthy brain supports memory. Traditionally, one of two methods is used: (1) high-precision neuroscience techniques in rodents, inferring that humans share the same basic mechanisms; or (2) non-invasive neuroimaging in humans, inferring neural mechanisms from indirect measurements. Both approaches, though, merely assume equivalence; combining the strengths of rodent and human neuroscience methods in a single, integrated effort is needed to uncover how memories are stored-or lost-in humans. We have assembled a team of experts in both methods to conduct parallel studies in humans and mice. We will leverage recent technical advances to 'decode' the structure of navigation memories, essentially reading a map of real-world space directly from both the rodent and human brain. We will also determine if both species build these mental maps through the same neurobiological mechanisms by applying the same physiologically-relevant manipulation to each. Specifically, in mice, we recently uncovered that memories formed close in time are more likely to be represented by the same neurons because their persistent excitability links experiences in memory. We will manipulate the time separating related learning sessions where humans or mice become familiar with digital/real environments, allowing us to determine whether memory for these environments are integrated within the human and mouse brain via similar persistent neural excitability mechanisms. By directly combining findings across species, our approach builds the foundation for further translational investigations into the basis of age and disease-related memory impairments.

column37: Indigenous youth are facing major mental health predicaments. Inuit youth are particularly at risk and show a high prevalence of suicide. The system struggles to offer proper services for these youth, not only because of insufficient resources but also because of major communication, collaboration, training and structural issues. Communities of Practice (CoP) have shown to have positive impacts on professional development, peer support, collaboration, effectiveness and innovation. Recent research concluded on the importance of implementing a CoP in Inuit contexts to improve quality of care in youth mental health (YMH). A CoP brings together people sharing a common professional practice, to exchange and learn from one another, to support and inspire one another. This project aims at evaluating the implementation of a CoP in YMH/wellness in Nunavik (land of Inuit communities of Quebec). This CoP will provide face-to-face and online activities to YMH/wellness first line workers (community workers, social workers, educators, health workers). The project aims at providing an innovative contribution to the health system aligned with CIHR priorities of Indigenous Peoples' Health and of Mental Health and respecting Inuit knowledge/values/culture. This will be a participatory research project using qualitative and quantitative methods and will involve key stakeholders in the identification, design and conducting phases of the project. Participants are YMH/wellness workers members of the CoP. Data will be collected at the start of the CoP, and at 8, 16 and 24 months later. The research team includes researchers and knowledge-users (Inuit and non-Inuit) with extensive expertise in CoPs, collaborative YMH care, mixed-method research, participatory research, and Inuit knowledge, values, and culture. Apart from contributing to the implementation of a YMH CoP in Nunavik, project results are likely to inform similar initiatives in Indigenous contexts in Canada and internationally.

column36: Germline and Environmental Determinants of Somatic Tumour DNA Methylation in Localized, Non-Indolent Prostate Cancer
column37: While most newly diagnosed prostate cancers are curable, some men will have their cancer return after treatment, often within 1-2 years. These men need more aggressive treatment to prevent the cancer from spreading and threatening their lives. Unfortunately, doctors cannot accurately distinguish curable from aggressive cancer, and better tools are urgently needed to tailor treatments for individual men. This would result in fewer men being treated for non-life threatening cancers, reducing unnecessary side effects such as sexual dysfunction and incontinence, and would allow more aggressive treatment for men who require it, increasing the number of cancers that are ultimately cured. We propose to lead an international effort to profile a type of chemical modification of DNA, known as methylation, taken from 600 prostate cancers. Methylation is involved in turning genes off, and the pattern of methylation in a given cancer may be an important factor in distinguishing between curable and aggressive disease. Thus, we will identify methylation patterns present in life-threatening prostate cancer but not in curable disease. We will then test whether environmental factors such exposure to pesticides and socio-economic status can cause changes in DNA methylation, giving rise to aggressive prostate cancer, and test if inherited DNA mutations influence methylation and aggression. Finally, we will study the economic impact of using DNA methylation patterns in the prostate cancer clinic to identify life-threatening prostate cancer. At the conclusion of our study, we will have developed a DNA methylation test that accurately identifies men who are at the highest risk of aggressive, life-threatening prostate cancer. We will also determine how our test is affected by a man's exposure to common environmental factors and by the man's family history. Finally, we will have produced the evidence necessary to implement our DNA methylation test in the prostate cancer clinic.

column36: Multifactorial control of mRNA stability during the Drosophila maternal-to-zygotic transition
column37: The growth and development of all multi-celled organisms-including humans-requires that cells within the body adopt specialized functions. Cell specialization involves the presence of different proteins in different cell types (e.g. muscle proteins in muscle cells, liver proteins in liver cells, etc.). Cells produce individual proteins using specific signals known as mRNAs in a process called translation. We are studying one strategy that is employed to control which proteins are present in any particular cell. In this strategy, the production of a protein can be blocked by destroying the corresponding mRNA via mRNA degradation. The decision to degrade an mRNA is controlled by proteins-called RNA-binding proteins (RBPs)-that bind mRNAs. The work in this proposal is aimed at understanding how RBP function is controlled. These types of mechanisms function throughout the life span of all multi-celled organisms and play particularly prominent roles during the earliest stages of development. We are using a simple organism-the fruit fly-to study how RBPs are controlled during the earliest stages of the organism's life. Since there are many similarities between how flies and humans grow and develop, our work is applicable to humans.

column36: Exploiting tumour innate immunity for sensitization of ovarian tumours to PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade immunotherapy
column37: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) leads to over 16,000 deaths in north American women each year. Approximately 87% of EOC cases are diagnosed at late stages of the disease with a 10-year survival rate of a mere 15%. Late diagnosis and poor response to currently used chemotherapy are the major problems in management of EOC. Due to its complex nature, ovarian cancer has not yet benefited from the newer immunotherapies that lead to durable outcomes in a small proportion of other cancer types. Our previous investigations evaluating immune biomarkers, in tumour specimens obtained from the ovarian cancer patient tissue biobanks, revealed that high levels of a key immune response related protein called Signal Transducer and activator of transcription (STAT1) and high numbers of the anti-tumour white blood cells, called the CD8 T cells, are present in tumours from patients who survive longer and respond better to chemotherapy. Given the impact of cancer cell genetic make up in antitumour immunity, we aim to fully characterize the links between the key genetic features and the corresponding anti-tumour immune responses. We hypothesize that these associations can be used in combination as biomarkers to predict patient response and guide personalized treatment approaches. We will conduct a detailed evaluation of patient tumour samples to confirm these correlations for use as a test to classify patients as sensitive or resistant for personalized immunotherapy. To increase patient response chemotherapy we also aim to establish the potential of novel immune stimulatory therapy called the "Stimulator of Interferon genes, agonist" that boosts anti-tumour immune responses and can be combined with chemotherapy. Findings will lead to significant improvements in survival of ovarian cancer patients.

column36: Electroencephalography Guidance of Anesthesia to Alleviate Geriatric Syndromes (ENGAGES-CANADA) Study in Cardiac Surgery Patients: a Pragmatic, Randomized Clinical Trial
column37: Delirium is the most common complication in patients over 60 years of age after cardiac surgery (up to 57%). Patients suffering from postoperative delirium will also be at increased risk of traumatic falls, longer intensive care unit and hospital stay, psychiatric crisis, hospital re-admission, degradation toward dementia and death. Postoperative delirium has a high emotional cost on families and on the health care system with an average of $60,000 per capita and per year. Despite the importance of postoperative delirium, no single approach has proven effective to prevent it. Our group found that excessively deep general anesthesia supresses the electrical activity of the brain and is associated with more postoperative delirium and even death. Some evidence suggests, without clearly proving, that purposefully avoiding excessively deep general anesthesia can protect from postoperative delirium. The ENGAGES-CANADA study proposes to address this question by comparing the effect of two ways of managing cardiac anesthesia on the reduction of the occurrence of post-operative delirium. One way will be to give general anesthesia for cardiac surgery according to the actual standards of practice. The other way will be to observe brain electrical activity and avoid excessively deep anesthesia by altering the amount of anesthesia to keep patients asleep without suppressing brain electrical activity. We will also measure psychiatric and cognitive factors for up to a year to understand how they relate to the depth of anesthesia and to delirium. Postoperative delirium after cardiac surgery is so detrimental to patients and costly to the health care system that even a small reduction in it's occurrence would have a large positive impact. The ENGAGES-CANADA study could make a major contribution to the care of older cardiac surgery patients at risk of delirium and its consequences, reduce caregivers suffering and anxiety, and reduce the costs to the health care system.

column36: ProNGF and Neurodegeneration in Aging and Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease is a major medical and socioeconomic problem for the world's aging population. However, there are large gaps in our understanding of its basic biology. One of those gaps concerns nerve growth factor, a small but essential protein found in the brain and nervous system that regulates cell-cell communication, neuronal function and survival, and repair after injury. We were one of the first labs to demonstrate that its protein precursor, called proNGF, is the predominant form in the brain and that it has biological activity. In the healthy brain, proNGF is taken up by neurons that need it and transported to the cell body. In Alzheimer's disease, proNGF is not taken up and accumulates, and this accumulation causes neurodegeneration and correlates with cognitive decline. The mechanisms causing abnormal proNGF accumulation are not well understood. In this application we propose to study the mechanisms by which proNGF is transported within the particular neurons that are vulnerable in aging and Alzheimer's disease and that are crucial for learning and memory. Our proposed research will use novel cell culture approaches and mouse models of aging and Alzheimer's disease to study the roles of receptor loss and defective proNGF transport in neurodegeneration, and how aging and Alzheimer's pathology compromise proNGF transport. The overall goal of our research is to prevent cognitive decline. Understanding how proNGF is transported within the cell and how that transport is compromised is relevant to the molecular mechanisms of cognitive decline in aging and Alzheimer's disease. This project will provide new understanding and new targets for therapeutic intervention for neurodegenerative disease and aging and may allow us to restore degenerating neurons and their connections. This knowledge will thereby promote advances in health care for older Canadians.

column36: Metabolic control of innate immunity and cell death
column37: The interaction between the immune system and its metabolic environment is an important determinant of immune cell function. Upon activation, inflammatory leukocytes shift their metabolism to aerobic glycolysis to meet their biosynthetic and functional needs e.g. enhanced production of inflammatory mediators. While the mechanisms underlying this metabolic reprogramming are emerging, little is known on how metabolic alterations translate into distinct immunological phenotypes and functions. The innate immune system is our first line of defense against microbial invasion, tissue injury and cellular transformation. Among its arsenals are evolutionary conserved sensors of 'danger' signals, highly expressed in myeloid cells that defend the organism from pathogens and noxious insults by inducing protective responses such as inflammation and cell death. The proposed research project explores how the activation of innate immunity contributes to myeloid cell metabolic reprogramming and reciprocally how metabolic adaptations molecularly regulate myeloid cell functions in inflammatory diseases and tumorigenesis. We focus on the Hexosamine Biosynthetic Pathway, a nutrient sensor fueled by glucose and glutamine and explore a) its role in the survival, activation and function of myeloid cells; and b) its targets in inflammation and cell death regulation.

column36: Novel therapeutic and delivery strategies for age-related macular degeneration
column37: We study a particularly prevalent disease, known as age-related macular degeneration. The macula is the centre portion of the retina, a thin layer of cells and tissue at the back of the eye. The cells which degenerate and die in the macula are called 'cones', a type of photoreceptors responsible for high acuity colour vision. Without these cones, individuals lose their central vision, and they can no longer read, drive or navigate in the environment. Mechanistically, photoreceptors of the eye respond to light, convert this light information into electrical signals and transmit these signals through the retinal layers to the optic nerve, a bundle of about a million of nerve fibres, which connects different parts of the brain, ending in the visual cortex. The brain converts the information collected by the photoreceptors of the eye to create vision. The loss of photoreceptors in the retina is a devastating event because without them we cannot see, and these cells cannot be replaced naturally. Millions of people worldwide have eye diseases in which their photoreceptors die, resulting in vision loss and blindness. For the next five years, our goal is to generate new gene and cell-based therapies to replace these lost photoreceptors. We will also address the challenge of therapeutic access to the retina. The retina is protected by a blood-retinal-barrier, which impedes the delivery of therapeutics when they are administered in the bloodstream. We will test the efficacy of using ultrasound waves to transiently permeate this barrier so that therapies injected into the blood can pass through the barrier and enter the retina. Such an approach has already been used in the brain, and we have preliminary evidence that it will work in the retina. The data obtained through this research will inform on the best strategy to pursue for translation to human patients affected by age-related macular degeneration.

column36: Air Pollution, Indoor Temperature, and Health Impacts of the Beijing Coal Ban and Heating Stove Replacement
column37: Air pollution is a leading public health problem. Over 400 million Chinese homes burn coal to meet their indoor space heating needs, leading to high levels of air pollution and health impacts in adults and children. Coal burning in China also contributes to poor air quality and mercury contamination in Canada. China recently announced a new policy that bans coal use in the greater-Beijing region and offers a subsidy for transitioning to a new clean heating technology. Our primary objective is to assess whether the coal ban and new clean heating technology will impact air pollution and indoor temperature or the health of people who live in homes impacted by the policy. This study will provide data that will help policy makers to implement household heating programs that reduce air pollution and its health impacts but also keep homes sufficiently warm. Our results will also help Canada to monitor its progress in meeting environmental goals on mercury. We will work with researchers and members of government and civil society in China and Canada to communicate our findings. We will provide regular updates and reports, and hold annual meetings to review our findings and discuss any identified barriers to the policies achieving their intended results.

column36: Transition to parenthood: realistic sleep-related expectations as a protective factor for mothers' and fathers' mental health
column37: The transition to parenthood is a challenging time of life. Postnatal mental health problems have major consequences in infants and parents. Among the different factors associated with mental health, postnatal sleep disruption was shown to be associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms in both others and fathers. However, although new parents are frequently sleep-deprived, not all of them develop mental health problems. Consequently, there is a need to identify protective factors for parents' mental health. While there is a lot of information circulating about sleep in early infancy, advice is too often contradictory, leading to unrealistic expectations in parents. In general, unrealistic expectations have been identified as a factor inhibiting the transition to parenthood. Therefore, we propose that realistic parental sleep-related expectations will have a protective influence on parental mental health. The main objective of this research program is to better understand the association between infant's sleep patterns, parental sleep duration and quality, sleep-related expectations and mental health. We propose that realistic sleep-related expectations have a protective role for parental mental health. First-time mothers and fathers will be recruited during pregnancy. Sleep measures (infant and parents), depressive and anxiety symptoms (parents) and sleep-related expectations (parents) will be measured during pregnancy, at 3 months postpartum, and at 6 months postpartum. Given the importance of sleep in new parents, this project is of great importance to knowledge dissemination. It will help us to identify new protective factors during the transition to parenthood and contribute positively to health care services provided to expectant and new parents. Incorporating both mothers' and fathers' point of view will advance knowledge in the field of transition to parenthood, and will promote optimal parental mental health and healthier development in infants.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of autophagy in skeletal muscle homeostasis
column37: Skeletal muscle is a critical organ that is responsible for many functions in the body, including providing body support and mobility. As well, skeletal muscle is an important organ for metabolism, as an organ of energy storage and an important source of energy particularly during exercise and fasting. With aging there is a decline in muscle mass that contributes to frailty and overall decline in body function. Thus it is critical to understand the molecular mechanisms that determine age-related decline in muscle mass and function. We have a novel experimental mouse model in which we observe an accelerated age-dependent decline in muscle mass and function. We thus believe this mouse model as a powerful experimental tool to identify mechanisms that are involved in age-related muscle abnormalities which will provide new therapeutic avenues to combat against age-related decline in muscle function. Autophagy is a process in which cells under stress preserves itself through degrading and using one's own cell components for its survival. This is a critical process that is important in many cells in the body to maintain health with aging. UVRAG is a newly discovered gene that is involved in the process of autophagy. We have recently found that UVRAG is critically important for autophagy in muscle. We have generated a new experimental mouse model in which muscle that are deficient in UVRAG have accelerated age-related decline in muscle mass. We wish to comprehensively understand the role of UVRAG in muscle which will provide new therapies to fight against age-related decline in muscle mass. Overall these findings will help in maintaining health while combatting against age-related frailty.

column36: Uncovering how the female germline eliminates deleterious mitochondrial DNA mutations
column37: We inherit a small number of essential genes, called mitochondrial genes, only from our mothers. Given their fundamental importance, mothers have evolved mechanisms to ensure they pass good, mutant free copies of these genes to their children. Without such mechanisms, we would not exist. Exactly, how mothers do this remains unknown. In this proposal, we seek to understand how these selection mechanisms work. Even though mothers do their best to make sure we start with good mitochondrial genes, mutations inevitably arise in them as we age. This causes disease in people, most often neurological, affecting on the order of 1 in 4,300. By understanding how mothers prevent bad mitochondrial genes from being inherited, we aim to develop strategies to eliminate these bad mutations and the diseases they cause as we age.

column36: Brain imaging of sport concussion: mapping recovery relative to pre-injury structure and function
column37: Concussions are a growing health concern, with over 4 million occurring annually in sport and recreation in North America. These injuries are associated with impairments in thinking (confusion, feeling "slow"), emotion (anger, depression) and physical function (dizziness, nausea). Currently, medical clearance (a "clean bill of health") is based on resolution of symptoms and tests comparing their thinking ability before and after injury. These assessments do not directly measure the severity of brain injury. This is a concern, as athletes are at risk for significantly worse outcomes if they are re-injured before brain recovery is complete. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a versatile tool that can measure aspects of brain anatomy, function and blood flow. However, at present, it has seen limited use in medical assessment of concussion. One major limitation is that we do not know how the brain has changed, relative to "pre-injury" brain structure and function, making it difficult to determine when the brain has fully recovered from injury. In this project, we propose to use advanced MRI techniques to scan a large group of university athletes without concussion. For athletes in this group that go on to receive a concussion, we will perform scanning at key time-points in the recovery process, including early injury (<5 days), time of medical clearance, and 1 month after clearance. This will allow us to visualize brain changes in concussed athletes, relative to their "normal" uninjured brain, and to determine if the brain has recovered or is still healing at the time of medical clearance to return to play. This research will provide novel information about the brain's recovery from injury. It may be used to develop safer guidelines for concussion management, and in the future, will lay the groundwork to develop better measures of brain health and recovery.

column36: Circadian epigenomic biomarkers for predicting bipolar disorder in high-risk youth
column37: The Mental Health Commission of Canada has estimated the cost of mood disorders to be $50B/year, with a dramatic rise expected in the near future. Therefore, uncovering disease mechanisms and risk factors is of great importance as well as of scientific interest. A major priority is the identification of personalized disease signatures that promise a customized approach to predicting disease risks, prognosis, and to facilitate early and targeted interventions. Bipolar disorder (BPD) is a debilitating mood disorder that affects around 2.5-4% of the general population, with peak age of onset between 15-25 years old. Family history is the single most robust risk factor, yet there are no individual-specific predictors for BPD. Substantial evidence points to a strong association between an abnormal circadian rhythm and BPD. Circadian rhythmicity allows living organisms on earth to adapt to cyclical day and night changes. There are also studies that highlight the role of epigenetic factors (gene regulating "switches") in BPD. We recently discovered that epigenetic switches oscillate in a circadian fashion. This led us to a new theory that daily changes in epigenetic profiles gradually accumulate mistakes and become major risk factors that disturb brain function and result in BPD. In this project, we propose a unique study of youths with high-risk of BPD. We will look at changes in epigenetic signatures prior to a crucial developmental time-frame for BPD susceptibility. Our goal is to identify molecular signatures that can be used for precise prediction of BPD, long before the onset of the disease. There is evidence that circadian epigenomes play a role in cancer, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease. Principles developed in this project can be used in future circadian studies of other diseases. Linking individual molecular circadian changes with specific pathologies can create the foundation for new diagnostic and therapeutic tools in precision medicine.

column36: SOX9-Dependent Transcriptional Networks in Heart Valve Development
column37: Congenital heart defects are observed in 0.9% of newborns and are responsible for an estimated 10% of all stillbirths. Abnormal development of heart valves and septa occurs in 20-30% of cardiac malformations. Current research suggests that valve disease in adults can arise from underlying congenital defects. Since valve disease, resulting in failure of valve leaflets to close properly, affects over 3% of the population in North America, improvements in managing of valve disorders can have a major health impact. A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying congenital valve defects will provide options to correct valve disorders in children and provide opportunities to reverse valve disease in adults. Our laboratory is interested in the mechanisms through which genes are regulated in heart valve development, using the mouse embryo as our model. Our work has focused on a protein, called SOX9, which regulates how genes are turned on and off in cells. In heart valves, SOX9 is required for normal development but how it does this is unknown. Our hypothesis is that SOX9 controls cascades of genes that dynamically change at different stages during valve development. We believe that SOX9 functions are dependent on the expression of proteins, called co-factors, that function with SOX9 to control genes. To address this hypothesis, we are using whole genome sequencing methods to identify all of the genes that are regulated by SOX9 in mouse embryonic valves throughout development. In our first aim, we will examine how SOX9 regulates DNA structure. In the second aim, we will look at how co-factors interact with SOX9 to regulated gene expression in embryonic valves. In the third aim, we will examine how many cell types are present in embryonic valves. By providing insight into the normal biology of valves development, our work may identify new targets that can be developed for therapeutic applications in valve repair strategies.

column36: hs cTn - Optimizing the Diagnosis of Acute Myocardial Infarction/Injury in Women (CODE-MI)
column37: Women with heart disease are under-diagnosed, under-treated, and have worse outcomes than men. Among young women (<55 years) with a heart attack, the risk of death is 2X higher than among men of the same age. With the introduction of a more sensitive diagnostic test - high sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn), it has become apparent that using a single level (cut-point) to identify patients with a heart attack disadvantages women. Hs-cTn is a biomarker, or protein, released into the blood when the heart is damaged during heart attack. Women produce lower amounts of this biomarker when they have a heart attack than men. We believe that by using a lower cut-point for hs-cTn in women, we will identify more women who have had damage to their hearts, and this will allow us to provide better care, leading to better outcomes for these women. The study will be conducted in 26 emergency departments (EDs) across Canada. Every site will start using the standard single cut-point to identify patients with heart attack or heart damage. Randomly, they will be asked to change practice in their hospitals by using a lower cut-point for women; the cut-point for men will remain unchanged. At the end of the study, every ED will be using the lower cut-point in women. We will then determine what impact this change has had on additional diagnostic testing, like referral to cardiology for an x-ray of the heart, stress testing, etc. We will also determine if there has been a change in outcomes as a result of this change. Specifically, we will determine if, after the introduction of a lower cut-point, women are more likely to received appropriate care and are less likely to die, present to hospital with a heart attack, stroke, heart failure, or the need for urgent revascularization (procedures to open clogged arteries) within a year of discharge from the hospital. We believe this simple change in health care delivery will improve the care and outcomes of women with suspected heart disease.

column36: Impact of maternal pertussis immunization on pregnancy outcome and child health
column37: Pertussis (also known as whooping cough) is a highly contagious infectious illness that mainly affects the lungs. The highest risk of severe pertussis illness occurs in babies under the age of two months, and can lead to breathing difficulties, hospitalization, and even death. In order to prevent these early cases, women are sometimes vaccinated against pertussis during their pregnancy, which provides protection to the babies before they are fully vaccinated themselves in the early months of life. However, even in countries where pertussis vaccination is recommended and provided for free, not all pregnant women become vaccinated possibly due to ongoing concern about the benefits and safety of vaccination during pregnancy for their children. As there is limited information on possible benefits or concerns of pertussis vaccination during pregnancy on longer-term health, our study will examine important health outcomes among children up to six years of age. Our findings will provide valuable information to pregnant women and their families, as well as to health care providers working to ensure that mothers and their children are in the best possible health.

column36: A Community-Based Family Treatment Program for Children with Epilepsy: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain characterized by recurrent seizures. There is increasing evidence about the impact of epilepsy beyond seizures, finding that children and their parents commonly have mental health problems (such as anxiety and depression) and poor quality of life. Although we know that these problems often co-occur with epilepsy, they still go unrecognized in many and thus remain under-treated. Unfortunately, little has been done to provide more comprehensive care. The goal of the proposed study is to target this unmet healthcare need by providing children with epilepsy and their parents with an innovative, low-cost, community-based program to improve quality of life and reduce the burden of mental health problems. This program, Making Mindfulness Matter (M3), is an 8-week parent and child program that incorporates mindful awareness, social-emotional learning skills, neuroscience, and positive psychology. It is modelled after the school-based program, MindUP , to be provided in the community and to include a parent component. MindUP has been shown to improve depressive symptoms, perspective taking, emotional control, optimism, cognitive control and reduce stress. Our objectives are to 1) evaluate the feasibility of implementing the M3 program for children with epilepsy and their parents, and 2) evaluate the effect of M3 on children's and parents' quality of life, as well as on their overall mental-health and well-being. We will recruit children with epilepsy (aged 4 - 10 years) and their parents, and randomly assign them to the M3 program or to a control condition. This experiment will provide the first results assessing a low-cost support program that may be easily delivered by non-medical staff in the community and directly target the unmet mental health and well-being needs of children with epilepsy and their parents.

column36: Implementing culturally appropriate, evidence-based, and community-driven interventions to improve maternal health among Indigenous women in Northern Canada
column37: Indigenous women in Canada's north can face healthcare challenges including limited access to affordable healthy food, inadequate social supports and difficulty accessing maternal healthcare services which may complicate maternal and neonatal health care and outcomes. A healthy start from conception to a child's second birthday is important for a mother and her child, and it has a lasting impact on the well-being of individuals, families, and entire communities.On average, Indigenous women become mothers at a younger age than non-Indigenous women, and Indigenous women of childbearing age may feel overwhelmed with the limited availability of healthcare services and supports. Healthcare professionals and decision makers in the Northwest Territories and the communities of Fort Good Hope, Yellowknife and Inuvik, requested that Dr. Sharma and her team work with community members and health professionals to develop and evaluate culturally appropriate evidence based programs to improve maternal health. The communities will work with the team to document the availability of, utilization of, and experiences with maternal healthcare services during pregnancy through one-on-one interviews with Indigenous women who are currently pregnant or have given birth in the previous 3 years. The team will also talk with key informants to identify barriers to, and opportunities for, improving maternal health outcomes. The findings will be shared with the communities who will then identify community specific priority areas. Based on the findings, a series of educational materials, including videos will be developed covering topics such as maintaining a healthy lifestyle during pregnancy, seeking maternal health supports, and what to expect when travelling to another community to receive care. This project will guide personal health practices and healthcare services with Indigenous women in the Canadian north and inform maternal healthcare policies.

column36: Examining the longitudinal associations between neighbourhood socioeconomic position and the built environment on future health throughout the life course: Data from a large multigenerational cohort study
column37: Half of all Canadian adults will experience a major chronic illness such as cardiovascular disease or cancer. While the risk of these illnesses has been higher in men compared to women in the past, the gap is narrowing. Those of lower socioeconomic position (SEP) are at greater risk. The risk starts early in life and continues across the lifespan. Differences in the built environment features (such as the distance to nearby parks), are believed to be the connection. However, as health is also passed down generations, it's unclear how much the environment also explains health. In order to separate out the environment from biology, both need to be measured at the same time across generations. With the recent advancements in technology, conducting a study that can assess both at the same time is finally possible. This proposal uses data from three generations of 4000 families (>10,000 people) with 35 years of data. This project will be able to test whether risk from the environment differs (1) between generations, (2) based on age, (3) between men and women. How these differences may also change over time will also be tested. Study findings will identify some of the root causes of health differences. Results may help show how healthcare providers and city planners can reduce health inequality

column36: Hypoxia in tumour-draining lymph nodes as an indication of immune activation and immunotherapy response
column37: Over the past several years, a new treatment option called immunotherapy, which stimulates the patient's own immune system to kill cancer cells, has been approved to treat several different cancer types. Tumours generally survive by evading attack from the immune system, and immunotherapy works best in patients with tumours that are more easily detected by the immune system. While immunotherapy can produce outstanding responses in 10-20% of patients with some tumour types, many tumours are harder for the immune system to recognize as harmful, and immunotherapy works in only a small fraction of patients with these cancers. A critical unmet need in immunotherapy research is a reliable way to predict which patients will benefit from this promising treatment option. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped organs located throughout the body, where immune responses to bacteria, viruses, and cancers develop. We have discovered that when a tumour is recognized by the immune system, nearby lymph nodes display regions of low oxygen (hypoxia) and we predict that cancer patients with hypoxic regions in their lymph nodes will benefit the most from immunotherapy. In this proposal, we will test whether the oxygen levels in lymph nodes can predict responses to immunotherapies currently used in the clinic. We will also determine how this low oxygen environment affects the ability of the immune system to kill cancer cells, and we will analyze the oxygenation status of lymph node samples from patients with breast cancer. This proposal will lay the foundation for future clinical studies to help oncologists direct immunotherapies to patients that are most likely to benefit from this remarkably effective therapy.

column36: Identification of molecular events enabling vacuole escape of Shigella: an avenue toward novel therapeutic strategies
column37: Infectious diseases are still among the most frequent causes of deaths. Fortunately, antibiotics save millions of lives every year. However, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), antibiotic resistance is a major threat to public health. The rapid spread of antibacterial resistance highlights the need to globally combat this problem. Compounding things, the pace of novel antibiotic discovery has plummeted to a level not seen since the 1940's. Thus, the discovery of novel antibiotics is critical. This project aims to identify novel anti-infective agents that will replace classic and failing antibiotics. Our research focuses on bacterial pathogens that intimately interact with human tissue because current antibiotics do not specifically target these. The focus of this proposal is the bacterium Shigella, which on a global scale is responsible for hundred of millions infections each year. The outcome for roughly 1 million of these cases is death. According to the WHO, Shigella is one of the bacteria for which novel antibiotics are urgently needed. Shigella is a pathogen that lives within human intestinal cells. Normally, human cells can recognize intracellular bacteria and destroy them, however Shigella is capable of evading detection and destruction. This project will identify the mechanisms used by Shigella to hijack human cellular factors. This deeper understanding of Shigella pathogenesis will facilitate the design of novel therapeutics stimulating the host defense and inhibiting Shigella hijacking mechanisms. Because of their specificity, these novel therapeutic strategies will be less prone to resistance than classical antibiotics. As a result, this work will impact both Canadian and global communities, and translation of the acquired knowledge to new treatments will open the door to collaboration between basic scientists and clinicians.

column36: Sex and Gender-related Differences in Access to Care for Premature ACS: Does the Health Care System Matter?
column37: Women still struggle to achieve high-quality equitable cardiovascular care. Recently, there has been growing attention to young women (=55 years) with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), who experience worse recoveries and higher mortality compared with similar aged men. Moreover, the rising incidence of ACS in young is of immediate concern. Despite recent advancements in understanding premature ACS outcomes, important questions remain. Access to high-quality care which may differ across health care systems (private/public) could explain the suboptimal care and poorer outcomes in young women post-ACS. Gender-related factors (e.g. socioeconomic status) have been associated with poorer access to timely cardiac procedures among women, independent of sex. The impact of sex and gender on access to care along the continuum of care for premature ACS, including how it varies across health care systems requires further investigation. Accordingly, our objective is to examine sex differences in the trajectory of access to care from pre-ACS to post-ACS setting among young patients and whether gender-related factors are associated with access to care. We hypothesize that female sex and gender-related factors traditionally ascribed to women are associated with poorer access to care in young and the magnitude of such disparities depends on health care system. To test this, we will merge data on two largest prospective cohorts of young patients with premature ACS to date: GENESIS-PRAXY and VIRGO studies. A sex and gender-based approach to address the unmet health care needs of premature ACS is much needed. It will help identify factors for targeted interventions aimed at improving women's access to high-quality health care. Merging these cohorts across 4 countries (US, Canada, Spain, Switzerland) will provide an opportunity for high-impact international research on sex and gender differences on access to care and for accessing the generalizability of results across health care systems.

column36: Unravelling the role of primary cilia in the control of male fertility
column37: Because more than 30% of male infertility cases are of unknown origin, it is crucial to identify the molecular factors controlling the male reproductive system. The epididymis is a long tubule located downstream of the testis in charge of the acquisition of sperm fertilizing ability. It is therefore an exquisite model for studying sequential events that transform an immature sperm cell into a fully motile and fertile spermatozoon. Recently, primary cilia have been found associated with epithelial cells of the epididymis. These organelles are unique antennae that emerge on the surface of cells and are mediators of many signaling pathways involved in differentiation, proliferation and cell migration. In Human, primary cilia dysfunctions are associated with a broad spectrum of defects, including male infertility, that are commonly referred to ciliopathies. Since primary cilia are essential to maintain the physiological functions of most organs, our research project aims at unravelling the role of primary cilia in epididymis development and homeostasis. This innovative project combines complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches on cell lines and mouse models. Considering the importance of epididymal functions in the control of sperm fertilizing abilities, carrying out this research will help decipher the cellular functions that may be impaired in some cases of male infertility.

column36: Deciphering the function and mechanism of long noncoding RNAs in lung cancer
column37: Non-small cell lung carcinoma is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide with activation of KRAS signaling being one of the most prevalent oncogenic events. Current efforts to understand the genetic and molecular interactions contributing to KRAS-induced tumors have focused mostly on protein coding genes, leaving the noncoding genome vastly under-explored. We now know that a large fraction of the genome is transcribed and generates thousands of long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) that do not encode proteins. Accumulating evidence point to lncRNAs as risk factors frequently dysregulated or mutated in a variety of human cancers. Amongst the few lncRNAs that have been characterized, some were found to affect processes relevant to transformation, such as proliferation and genomic stability. Yet, most studies have been limited to cell line-based assays or remain correlative. Thus, whether lncRNAs contribute to the formation or progression of lung cancer in vivo and how they may affect oncogenic pathways such as KRAS still remains poorly characterized. Recently, downregulation of the lncRNA Tug1 was found to correlate with poor prognosis in human non-small cell lung carcinoma. Our preliminary experiments indicate that loss of Tug1 collaborates with activated KRAS signaling to promote cellular transformation. Using genetically engineered mouse models, we propose to characterize the putative tumor suppressor function of Tug1 in vivo and determine which pathways involved in cellular transformation are affected. We will also decipher its mechanism of action in KRAS-induced lung cancer and use xenograft models to determine whether its function is conserved in human. This project will uncover novel lncRNA-based mechanisms contributing to the formation and progression of lung cancer in vivo. It will also provide potential new therapeutic avenues by revealing new aspects of KRAS signaling, one of the most frequently activated pathway in lung cancer.

column36: A Primary Care Online Appointment Scheduling Platform for Emergency Departments: Improving the Care Transition between Emergency and Primary Care
column37: With the aging of the population the number of people living with chronic diseases is going to go up dramatically. When these patients have flares of their disease, they go to the ER. After treatment in the ER, many of these patients could go home to their own beds (instead of being admitted to hospital), IF reliable, timely outpatient followup care was available. Unfortunately, there is no real 'system' of care between ERs and family doctor (FD) offices; in fact, patients themselves constitute the current system, arranging their own followup care. For older patients in particular, this can be challenging, and they are the people at the greatest risk of poor outcomes. To solve this dilemma the PI conducted a CIHR-funded meeting of leaders from the government, hospitals, and FD offices. They chose an online FD appointment system as the best solution to this problem. ERs can login and give patients being discharged from the ER an appointment at their FD's office in real-time, before they leave the ER (24h/day). Because the emergency doctor knows when the patient is going to be seen next, he or she feels safe discharging the patient (rather than admitting them to hospital), and the patient doesn't have to call the FD office, nor try to explain the diagnosis and importance of follow-up care to the office receptionist. We have 3 ER test sites, and we will engage FD offices in the surrounding areas to upload several open appointments per week to the online system. We have created a similar scheduling system at our hospital using hospital clinics. If early followup is improved for patients at these ERs, we can use the techniques learned in this project to efficiently roll-out to all of Ontario's EDs and FD offices, and eventually to all of Canada. Our partners at eHealth and Ontario government will help us do this. We believe that we can dramatically improve continuity of care for ER patients, resulting in less deaths, hospitalizations, and return ER visits for them.
