column37: The United Nations, the World Health Organization, and the Public Health Agency of Canada have each declared the rise in drug resistant infections to be a global threat to health due to the rapid increase in resistance and decline of new drug development. Combatting resistance is an international priority but surveillance of drug resistant infections is challenging due to the large number of bacteria, antibiotics, and laboratories involved, combined with suboptimal reporting mechanisms. In most jurisdictions, current surveillance systems rely on manually completed surveys submitted voluntarily by hospitals, meaning that the system is slow, labour intensive, prone to bias, and unable to measure the resistance in long-term care and outpatient settings. The COMBAT-AMR project will use the newly developed Ontario Laboratory Information System (OLIS) which is an electronic compilation of all patient test results from all laboratories in the province. Using OLIS, we will identify antibiotic resistance from the summary reports of all clinical microbiology culture specimens in the province. By linking OLIS to Ontario population databases, we will be able determine the total extent to which antimicrobial resistant infections contribute to hospitalization and death in Ontario by creating the Clinical Antibiotic Resistance Index (CARI). The CARI will be broken down by bacterium, region, healthcare sector, patient characteristics such as age and sex, and time, thereby revealing important bacteria and population subgroups where antibiotic resistance is of primary concern. The CARI will be the first index that accounts for the importance of antimicrobial resistance from the patients' perspective and will provide crucial evidence to inform clinical decisions and government policy for combatting resistance.

column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in Canadian women. The majority of breast tumors at primary diagnosis are positive for the estrogen receptor ERa. These types of breast tumors generally have a better prognosis and respond well to antihormone therapy. While this treatment is beneficial for the majority of patients, some of them still develop locally recurrent or metastatic disease. Breast cancers called "triple negative" (TNBC), which represent nearly 15% of breast cancers, are generally very aggressive, present a risk of higher recurrence and development of metastasis. Since TNBC cannot be treated with conventional breast cancer antihormonal-based or trastuzumab-based treatments, it is of the utmost importance to develop effective new treatments by defining new therapeutic targets in TNBC. In this research project, we are particularly interested in 1) elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which LRH-1 controls TNBC cells progression and metastasis; and (2) confirming the LRH-1 as a potential therapeutic target in TNBC. We will use genomic approaches and molecular and cellular biology techniques that will help to reveal the functions of LRH-1 and to evaluate its potential as therapeutic target. The results obtained from these studies should lead to new insight that will be directly relevant to the understanding, treatment and prevention of breast cancer.

column36: Peers4Wellness: Indigenous Approaches to Wellness Support and Research for Indigenous Women with HIV and HCV in British Columbia and Saskatchewan
column37: Peers4Wellness is an Indigenous research study, which is peer-led and community-driven. It is focused on Indigenous women (cis-and trans-gendered) who have lived experience with HIV and/or hepatitis C (HCV). Our goal is to help these women with their HIV/HCV wellness and health care needs by developing Indigenous-grounded supportive care. In Canada, the rates of HIV and HCV, respectively, are 3 and 5 times higher among Indigenous people, and Indigenous women in particular, than non-Indigenous people. Yet, Indigenous people have lower HIV/HCV health care utilization than non-Indigenous people. This pattern is a result of the barriers which Indigenous people experience when accessing HIV/HCV care, including the lack of Indigenous ways of wellness and health care. Peer navigation programs, which train peers as support health workers, are shown to help people with their health and getting health care. These programs are not widely used for HIV and are almost lacking for HCV. Importantly, existing peer navigation programs do not have systematic, explicit and robust approaches to address the unique needs of Indigenous people. Because peer navigation is a promising approach to better health care, this study is focused on extending the scope of research and practice on peer navigation to include HCV and Indigenous people, particularly Indigenous women. This study will develop a wise practice peer navigation toolkit for providing culturally safe and responsive supportive care to improve the engagement and retention of Indigenous people in HIV/HCV care. Peer navigation will serve as a springboard to further develop Indigenous models for supportive HIV/HCV care. This study's current focus is Indigenous women in two priority provinces: British Columbia and Saskatchewan. The model will be gender and context adaptable. We expect that the implementation of this innovative model will improve HIV/HCV outcomes for Indigenous people in Canada, and Indigenous women in particular.

column36: A Paper-based Microfluidic Platform for Automated Point-of-Care Diagnosis of Laryngopharyngeal Reflux
column37: Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), also known as "silent reflux", is the back flow of gastric juice into larynx and pharynx, and affects 20-60% of population in developed countries. Rapid quantification of the digestive enzyme, pepsin, in saliva or laryngeal surface secretion could allow accurate diagnosis and thus effective treatment of LPR. Currently, only lateral flow strip based tests are available for pepsin tests at the point of care (POC), which is limited in detection accuracy and sensitivity. This project aims to develop a novel paper-based microfluidic platform for rapid and accurate detection of LPR protein markers in an automated "sample-in-answer-out" fashion. The platform can perform multiplexed enzyme-linked immunosorbent arrays (ELISAs) of pepsin and two other LPR markers on a paper-based microfluidic chip, and automatically regulate the transport of reagent solutions on the chip, and accurately quantify colorimetric readout signals of the assays. It will be integrated into a handheld device, and does not require human intervention during operation. We will study the correlation of concentrations of LPR biomarkers in saliva and laryngeal surface secretion with conventional diagnostic outputs in individuals with and without LPR, and confirm the most relevant biomarkers for LPR diagnosis. We will evaluate the effectiveness of our microfluidic platform using patient samples, and compare it with the standard laboratory ELISA tests. This project will lead to the next generation of POC diagnostic technology for LPR with high sensitivity, which will facilitate doctors to identify LPR patients without going through time-consuming laboratory tests and thus improve the life quality of the large population of LPR patients.

column36: Understanding dermal progenitor cell biology towards improved skin wound healing.
column37: More than 14 million severe skin wounds (burns, trauma, ulcers) are treated each year in North America. The consequence is chronic pain, immobility, disfigurement and in many cases infection leading to further medical complication or death, particularly in the elderly. The annual societal cost of wound care in Canada alone is estimated at $4 billion. One of the primary reasons that wounds do not heal is due to an inability to regrow healthy dermis and a tendency to form fibrous scar tissue. The dermis provides essential nutrients and mechanical support to the overlying epidermis and skin appendages (hair follicles, glands, nerves, blood vessels) embedded within it. Strategies to regrow new functional dermis and its appendages are desperately needed to reduce health care costs and to restore quality of life after skin injury, particularly in the elderly. An attractive approach is to stimulate stem cells that reside in adult skin. Our preliminary studies identified two different populations of dermal stem cells that are activated in response to injury and are recruited into skin wounds where they typically form scar. However, under some circumstances, these same cells can become regenerative, rather than scar-forming, even initiating formation of new hair follicles and healthy fat cells within the wound. Thus, enhancing dermal stem/ cell function could limit formation of scar and improve skin healing. To realize this clinical potential, we will: 1) Characterize the signals within the wound that drive regenerative versus scar-forming stem cell responses 2) Identify mechanisms to effectively stimulate and recruit dermal stem cells after injury 3) Determine how old age changes dermal stem cell response to injury. Our goal is to identify drug targets that could be used to modulate dermal stem cell response after injury in order to improve the quality of wound healing, thereby improving functional outcomes for Canadians suffering severe skin injury or disease.

column36: Developing a transdiagnostic group intervention for First Nations children and youth
column37: Wait-lists for mental health services in First Nations' communities often make services inadequate to meet community needs. This treatment will target community specific needs through consultation with organizational staff and community members. This is the first project to adapt and assess the effectiveness of a transdiagnostic mental health treatment for First Nations children. An initial pilot group of the treatment with approximately 8 children aged 7-12 years will be implemented, after which the adjusted full treatment protocol will be implemented with 5 groups of 8-10 children (N = ~50). It is anticipated that these group interventions will reduce difficulties in emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, behavioural avoidance, and self-care of the children while developing positive coping strategies.

column36: Gene Therapy to Prevent Blindness in Patients with Congenital Aniridia
column37: Aniridia is a rare eye disorder caused by half the normal amount of the protein paired box gene 6 (PAX6). It affects both sexes and is not known to be influenced by gender. Individuals with aniridia are typically born with low vision, and because there is no effective treatment, subsequently lose all vision. Thus, there is a therapeutic window available to prevent vision loss. This application will take advantage of recent advances in the fields of both traditional gene therapy and CRISPR gene therapy. Traditional "augmentation" gene therapy methods allow us to directly increase the amount of missing protein in affected cells to treat disease. CRISPR gene therapy allows us to modify DNA in affected cells to alter the behavior of the cells and treat disease. The broad goal of this proposal is to develop a gene therapy to treat patients with aniridia and to engage with the aniridia patient community. We hypothesize that using both traditional gene therapy and CRISPR gene therapy we can increase the amount of PAX6 protein and improve eye function in a mouse model of aniridia. We will also undertake a patient engagement initiative, which will include an analysis of Canadian policies on gene sequencing, characterization of patient motivators and barriers to gene sequencing, and generate a fact sheet regarding sequencing for aniridia. This work builds on Dr. Simpson's expertise in both mouse models and aniridia, and Dr. Robillard's expertise in patient engagement. By the end of the proposal, we will have completed the preclinical work in mouse and positioned the therapy for commercial investment. In addition, we will have given the tools we developed to not-for-profit companies for world-wide availability to researchers. Finally, we will have disseminated a fact sheet illuminating issues surrounding patient engagement in future clinical trials.

column36: Epigenetic changes affecting muscle stem cell function in the aging population
column37: Building and maintaining our muscle mass is an ongoing battle between the stem cell-based processes that build muscle, and the degenerative processes that cause muscle loss. In our youth, stem cells have the upper hand in the battle where they make muscle faster than it is broken down. This allows for growth and increased strength in young healthy individuals. Unfortunately, as we age our stem cells get worn down and become less efficient at building new muscle. This allows the degenerative processes to get an edge in the battle leading to the loss of 1% of our muscle mass each year after the age of 40. Evidence in mice suggest that epigenetic processes contribute to age-related decline in stem cell function that leads to muscle loss. As epigenetic processes are reversible, this suggests that we may be able to find ways to extend the functional lifespan of our muscle stem cells to prevent muscle loss as we get older. In this project, we will use the latest technologies in the study of epigenetics to identify the changes taking place in muscle stem cells of aging humans. From these studies, we expect to identify specific factors we can target therapeutically to help ensure that our aging population is able to enjoy mobility and good quality of life while reducing the costs on our health care system.

column36: Epigenetic reorganization and differentiation of glioblastoma
column37: Brain cancers, particularly glioblastomas (GBM), are amongst the worst human cancers. The 5-year survival is <10%, effectively rendering patients with this diagnosis to a death sentence. Patients are desperate for better treatments. The Dirks group found that GBM growth was dependent on a few cells in the tumour that have stem cell properties, these cells lie at the root of GBM growth and are also resistant to conventional therapies. Reminiscent of normal stem cells, these specialized GBM cells divide to replenish themselves (a process called self-renewal) and can generate more mature cell types that lose the ability to sustain tumour growth, through the process of differentiation. We have recently identified that GBM stem cells have a unique packaging of their DNA, or "epigenetic state", that facilitates self-renewal and blocks maturation. We also found that about half of GBM patient tumors have GBM stem cells (GSCs) that can be more easily coaxed into a much more mature state, by activation of a gene ("ASCL1") that normally controls brain cell maturation into functioning nerve cells (neurons) during development. ASCL1-expressing GSCs can be treated with drugs causing them to turn into cells that resemble mature brain neurons, meaning they lose ability to divide and stop the tumour from growing. Key to this transition is a reorganization of the epigenetic state from one that is pro-self-renewing to one that is pro-differentiating. In this program, we will investigate the balance between epigenetic states of self renewal and differentiation in GBM. We will explore the potential for epigenetic reorganization and differentiation-based therapy for GBM by testing clinic-ready pro-differentiation drugs, testing novel classes of compounds that modify epigenetic states, and by using-editing technologies to discover new ways of differentiating GSCs. This project will usher in a completely new area of GBM research, which could have massive impact for patients.

column36: Early detection of cancer in high-risk patients through profiling of circulating tumour DNA
column37: Across Canada, 1 in 10 cancers occur in people with an inherited strong family risk of cancer (hereditary cancer syndrome: HCS). These families have multiple members affected with similar cancers, often at a younger age. When a family member with cancer is detected with an inherited faulty version of a gene, some healthy relatives will also share the faulty gene. These cancer "previvors" often refer to themselves as a ticking cancer time bomb. As such, they often enroll in intensive cancer surveillance programs that include colonoscopy, mammogram, and magnetic resonance imaging. These programs are costly ($94.5M/year in Ontario alone), not personalized and do not detect all potential cancers. As a result, many patients show up with late-stage cancer or cancer of an organ that is not screened. Lifetime treatment costs are substantial (Ontario averages are $76,000 for breast, $58,000 for ovarian and $70,000 for colorectal cancer), and often with poor outcome as 40% of cancer patients die within 5 years. The key to preventing these tragedies is early detection of disease. Circulating tumour DNA analysis is a promising method for detecting DNA from cancer cells in the blood. We will develop this method to detect early signs of cancer in previvors, people with HCS but not yet a cancer diagnosis. This will enable prediction of cancer onset so that patients and their doctors can make decisions to treat or prevent their cancers. We will recruit HCS patients from across Canada to provide blood samples before and after they develop cancer. In parallel, we will build a test to detect early stage disease, and work with provincial health authorities to determine cost-effectiveness. Doctors and their patients will help us establish recommendations for use in the broader health care system. Lessons learned from our project can be extended to cancer screening programs for all Canadians.

column36: The Longitudinal Study of Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) in Patients with Advanced Cancer
column37: There have been enormous changes in Canada over the past decade in public attitudes about medical care at the end-of-life. Palliative care has become much more accessible and medical assistance in dying (MAiD) was legalized in June 2016. Since that time, over 2000 Canadians have received assisted death, of whom more than 60% had advanced cancer. The physical, psychological and social factors that lead to the desire for death and requests for MAiD, and the stability of this desire over time has not been studied in countries where MAiD is legally available. This study will identify patient, disease and treatment-related factors that drive the desire for death and for MAiD in patients with advanced cancer. We will study whether these factors can predict the desire for death and for MAID and will compare results with our Will to Live (WTL) study in advanced cancer that was completed 10 years ago. We now propose a five year study that will assess 1000 patients at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (PM) from diagnosis of advanced cancer to death. We will collect survey information and interview patients every six months on: (1) the desire for death and attitudes and desire for MAiD; (2) psychological and physical suffering and quality of life; (3) social support; (4) communication with health care providers about MAiD; (5) psychosocial and palliative care treatments; and (6) advance care planning. We will collect information from the UHN MAiD database on MAiD approval and completions, and reasons for not receiving MAiD. The findings from this study will help healthcare providers have conversations about MAiD and the desire for death with patients, guide legal changes being considered to permit MAiD as an advanced directive, and inform health systems to ensure appropriate access to MAiD and to alternative supportive treatments for patients with advanced cancer.

column36: Molecular and biomechanical studies of bacterial-vascular adhesion mechanisms and their contributions to Lyme disease
column37: Blood-borne spread of bacteria via the cardiovascular system (dissemination) is responsible for most death due to bacterial infection. A key dissemination step is bacterial adhesion to the cells lining blood vessels (endothelial cells), which permits bacteria to slow down and escape from the bloodstream to infect new tissues. Bacterial interaction with blood vessels is challenging due to the force generated by flowing blood. Defining the physical mechanisms allowing bacteria to stick to blood vessel surfaces under flow is crucial for understanding how bacteria disseminate, and may lead to the development of strategies for slowing or preventing bacterial dissemination. However, the vascular adhesion mechanisms of most pathogens are largely unknown. The bacterium that causes Lyme disease, Borrelia burgdorferi, is a highly invasive pathogen that disseminates to most organs and tissues. Blood vessel and flow properties vary widely in different tissues and organs, generating unique, postal code-like conditions in each vascular bed that affect how bacteria disseminate to these tissues. Since B. burgdorferi disseminates to many tissues this pathogen may produce many adhesion molecules facilitating vascular interactions under diverse conditions. Vascular interaction mechanisms are better-understood for B. burgdorferi than most other pathogens, largely because we and collaborators have developed powerful methods to study dissemination in living mice and artificial systems mimicking blood vessels. We have identified several Borrelia, endothelial cell and blood molecules contributing to B. burgdorferi-endothelial interactions, although many molecules and mechanisms supporting B. burgdorferi dissemination to different tissues remain unknown. These studies will examine the repertoire of molecules and mechanisms supporting Borrelia dissemination to diverse tissues, and will provide the groundwork for exploring dissemination mechanisms of other bacterial pathogens.

column36: Coordination of inhibition and excitation underlying neural computations
column37: Nerve cells in the brain communicate with each other via chemical synapses. Generally, each nerve cell releases either an excitatory or an inhibitory neurotransmitter onto its postsynaptic partner. Excitatory neurotransmitters activate postsynaptic neurons, increasing the probability that they fire action potentials; while inhibitory neurotransmitters do the opposite. The efficiency of most computations rely on 'balanced' excitation/inhibition (E/I), where on the gross scale these opposing forces are always in competition. It is the fine imbalances in E/I that in fact controls the level of neural activity. Despite its central importance, measuring the fine balance between E and I is not easy. This is inhibitory and excitatory inputs are made throughout the neurons dendritic tree, where they interact. Current methods do not allow us to easily measure electrical activity in the dendritic trees. Instead, electrodes are usually placed at the soma, which collects the average I/E throughout the dendritic tree. While, results from such measurements have provided a framework for understanding E/I balance, the lack of insights of how E/I interacts in the dendritic tree strongly limits our understanding how neural computations occur in the brain. In this proposal, we aim to understanding how E/ I shape a specific computation that underlies our ability to compute the direction of moving objects, performed by neural circuit that lies at the back of the eye, in the retina. Our experiments will use a multidisciplinary approach including molecular, electrophysiological and two-photon Ca2+ imaging techniques, which allow us to view synaptic activity throughout the intricate dendritic trees of neurons. We hypothesize that the E/I is finely modulated in space and in time, which enables the circuit to compute direction with speed and extreme precision. This allows us to accurately perceive the direction of rapidly moving objects, which of course, is crucial for our survival.

column36: GCN5-directed acetylation of YY1 regulates the expression of dystrophin and associated proteins
column37: Muscular dystrophy is a life-threatening muscular disorder, to which there is no cure. Part of the difficulty in treating this disorder is the fact that this is a genetic disease that affects key proteins that maintain muscle integrity. The purpose of this study is to better understand the regulation of structural proteins by further exploring the robust effect of GCN5 on the expression of dystrophin and other important structural proteins in muscle. GCN5 is a protein known to modify other proteins through a process called acetylation. During this process GCN5 adds an acetyl group to specific proteins in order to alter their function. While examining mice that specifically lack the expression of GCN5 in muscle we unexpectedly found a reduction in gene and protein expression of dystrophin. Upon further examination we found that these mice exhibited similar phenotypes to mice with muscular dystrophy, called mdx mice. column37: Many mental illnesses begin before age 18 and can have devastating effects throughout life. Spit for Science 2 (S2) continues the work of the Spit for Science (S1) by using alternative approaches to identify risk genes for childhood-mental illness. To understand the genetics of mental illness in youth, we will recruit 30,000 children and adolescents from the Ontario Science Centre. They will provide DNA via spit, mental health trait information and complete an executive function cognitive task (Stop-Signal Task). Environmental risk data will be extracted from postal codes. Combining S2 and S1 data will create the largest pediatric mental health genetic sample in Canada providing sufficient statistical power to identify genetic signals. We will use a range of cutting-edge genetic methods to identify and validate genetic risk variants for these traits, understand which genetic risk are unique and shared across traits and disorders and test gene by environment interactions. We hope to identify novel genes involved in childhood mental illness which could potentially lead to early detection, better treatments and improved treatment-outcomes for Canadian youth.

column36: Microfiltration of Circulating and Disseminated Tumor Cells in Ovarian Cancer: From Monitoring Therapeutic Response Towards Predicting Disease Outcome
column37: Circulating and disseminated tumor cells (CTCs, DTCs) that dissociate from the primary tumor, can be found, respectively, in blood and ascites of ovarian cancer patients, and could be used to monitor the response to therapy, and help track the tumor state. CTCs and DTCs are very rare and present in low numbers, and isolating them has been a great challenge and has prevented using them more broadly for cancer disease management. As CTC isolation technologies have progressed, subpopulations of CTCs with various metastatic potentials have been identified. Very recently, aggregates of CTCs, callled CTC clusters, have been discovered, and they were found to have an approx. 50 times higher metastatic potential. Our team developed a microfiltration system which we believe outperforms other CTC isolation systems as when we analyzed a small ovarian cancer patient cohort in a pilot study, we observed CTCs and clusters in every patient, whereas previously they were only rarely found. Our method is also simple to use, potentially low cost if mass produced, and hence could be adopted for clinical use in the future. Here, we propose to use our microfiltration system to monitor the response to therapy in ovarian cancer patients by taking blood and ascites before surgery, after surgery, and at different time points during chemotherapy. We will isolate CTCs, DTCs and clusters, and analyze the number of cells and clusters, their morphology, and different molecular markers that are expressed and which have been linked to cancer metastasis and resistance to therapy. This study will validate our technology in a clinical context, and provide insight into the mechanisms of tumor response and resistance to therapy in ovarian cancer. It will set the foundation for future studies to help stratify patients and establish disease prognostics, and perhaps identify groups that might benefit from targeted, precision therapies, both for ovarian and other cancers.

column37: A family of approx. 800 different G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in our cell membranes controls most of our physiology by sensing hormones, neurotransmitters and chemical signals, which result in the modulation of signaling pathways. More than a third of current prescription drugs target GPCRs. The adenosine A2A receptor is a prototypical GPCR and an important drug target for a wide spectrum of diseases including oncologic, inflammatory, Parkinson's and cardiovascular diseases. GPCRs can adopt different shapes (conformations), of which only active conformations couple to G proteins and modulate intracellular signaling. Detailed molecular insight into receptor shape changes and G protein coupling will provide new avenues for pharmaceutical intervention. How G proteins are activated by adenosine A2A receptors and modulate intracellular signaling can be uncovered with paramagnetic resonance techniques like EPR and DEER spectroscopy, where small labels are covalently attached to the individual proteins which allow us to "visualize" GPCR conformations. The effect of pharmaceuticals on the A2A receptor and its subsequent interaction with intra-cellular binding partners, like G proteins, can be interrogated using the labels as environmentally sensitive antennas. Measuring distances between two labels attached to a protein allows the "visualization" of conformational changes. Our research centre is the sole facility in Canada for these vital and complex spectroscopic techniques, allowing us to monitor the responses of pharmaceutical compounds on the dynamic interplay between A2A receptor and G proteins. We wish to enhance our understanding of A2A receptor-mediated G protein activation to improve our still limited knowledge about this crucial drug target and GPCRs in general.

column37: The innate immune system protects us from pathogenic bacteria, viruses, and cancer, and also helps to maintain normal tissue function at mucosal barriers, such as the skin, gut, and lungs. Natural killer (NK) cells are a subset of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) that possess cytotoxic/killer cell function and can detect/eliminate infected, cancer, and transplanted cells. How NK cells perform these functions requires understanding of the molecules they use to sense what is harmless or dangerous, and how these molecules assist in the decision to ignore a healthy cell, or respond to a diseased cell. We have identified a receptor-ligand family (NKR-P1:Clr) that contributes to NK cell recognition at the molecular level. Some NKR-P1 receptors are inhibitory, so normal cells display "self" Clr ligands to prevent NK cell responses ("healthy-self"), while infected cells lose Clr expression and are killed by NK cells ("missing-self"). This supports a role for NKR-P1:Clr interactions in fighting cancer and infectious disease. However, malignant cancer cells and viral pathogens can evolve ways to subvert innate immunity and become pathogenic, including abnormal display of self ligands, or the evolution of decoy proteins or surrogate "non-self" ligands, respectively. In addition, activating NKR-P1 receptors can recognize some of these abnormal proteins and directly activate NK cells ("induced-self"). We propose to advance our understanding of innate immunity by studying how NK cells use receptors to see "self" ligands, and how viruses use immune evasion proteins to subvert NK detection. Detailed knowledge about how pathogens evade normal immunity, specifically details about how structure-function relationships evolve between host and pathogen, will ultimately lead to advanced therapies in cancer treatment and control of infectious disease, in turn supporting our immune defences to cancer and infection.

column37: Since April 2016, British Columbia (BC) has been in a state of public health emergency due to opioid-related overdoses and deaths, in which Indigenous people have been disproportionately affected. Responding to the opioid crisis has been a top priority for the FNHA since the start of BC's opioid crisis. Harm reduction is an effective way to reduce stigma and harms associated with opioid use and other licit and illicit drugs. An Indigenous approach to health research and health care service delivery is critically needed to develop effective practices for Indigenous Peoples in Canada. However, an Indigenous approach to harm reduction for opioid use has not been studied extensively, and there is limited literature on community-based harm reduction practices for First Nations in Canada. The main objectives of this project are to: 1) synthesize current Indigenous approaches to harm reduction for opioid use using a Western scoping review that includes Indigenous storytelling methods, 2) refine and/or implement and measure Indigenous harm reduction interventions in all five health regions in BC, and 3) develop an Indigenized harm reduction model for opioid use. First Nation communities will lead the research with the support and guidance of project team members as needed. A multidisciplinary research team with experience exploring substance use, mental health and wellness, and harm reduction will work together to implement this five-year project. Results will be used to improve harm reduction initiatives and better support Indigenous people who use opioids, ultimately informing the FNHA's health programs and services and other harm reduction initiatives across Canada.

column36: Canadian Donation and Transplantation Research Program (CDTRP): Maximizing benefits through national infrastructure and sustainability planning
column37: Transplantation is used much more broadly to treat diseases than most Canadians realize. No longer is it restricted to people with organ failure. Instead, it is poised to become the preferred treatment for many chronic diseases and blood cancers. Nonetheless, challenges remain, such as the 50% transplant failure rate and the risk of complications and cancer from immunosuppressive medication. Even though 90% of Canadians want to be organ donors, few succeed: nationally, there are only around 750 deceased donors per year. As a result, only 33% of Canadians on waitlists receive transplants. The others wait-or die waiting. In 2013, the Canadian National Transplant Research Program (CNTRP) was created to increase the number and quality of transplants in Canada by uniting the donation, solid organ transplant and bone marrow transplant research communities. Building on CNTRP's success, in the renamed Canadian Donation and Transplant Research Program (CDTRP), we are now restructuring the projects into broader themes that will forge new collaborations, strengthen existing ideas and create new ones, and lead to innovations that maintain our position as a global leader in donation and transplantation research. We are also shifting from centralized funding to supporting research through grant competitions funded by partners according to their priorities. Our program infrastructure will support research, training and knowledge transfer, and will catalyze collaborations across disciplines, stakeholders and researchers nationwide (and beyond) to advance research in donation and transplantation, and promote equity and diversity in these fields. This grant will allow us to transition towards a more self-sustaining national network in which we can achieve our long-term vision: that Canada fulfills every donation opportunity and realizes the full potential of transplantation as a cure for many chronic diseases and blood cancers.

column36: Modelling the cardiovascular health impacts of urban policies in Accra, Ghana
column37: Cities can promote or harm the health of the populations that live within them. In low-income settings, especially those in Africa and Asia, urban dwellers are exposed to many things, including household and community air pollution and noise pollution. The increasing prevalence of these health-harming exposures, as well as the rise of urban populations, has contributed to the increasing burden of cardiovascular diseases and mortality in many low and middle-income settings. However, cities can also use the powers and assets available to them to create healthy environments by creating and implementing health-promoting policies and regulations that affect urban form and services (e.g., transportation, housing, energy). My PhD research is part of a larger multi-country research program that is comparing the trade-offs and health benefits of different pathways for urban development. My PhD research will use innovative machine learning, statistical, and epidemiological, techniques to measure and characterize the spatial patterns of environmental exposures in Accra, Ghana, and simulate the impacts of different policy scenarios on levels of blood pressure and body-mass index. Policy scenario's, such as increasing bus rapid transit (BRT) options, subsidizing cleaner household cooking fuels, banning the import of old, diesel fuel, cars, or improving housing quality in slums, will be refined and amended with local stakeholders in Accra through in-country workshops and meetings. The data I will use will be from emerging (e.g., satellite images), existing (e.g., publicly available population-based surveys), or new (e.g., I will collect on the ground noise-pollution measurements) sources. My research will provide researchers, urban planners, and public health experts in Ghana with the tools and information to make informed decisions on the potential cardiovascular health benefits of changes to urban environments and services.

column36: Soft Robotic Diaphragmatic Assist Device for the Treatment of Mechanical Respiratory Failure
column37: The diaphragm is the large, dome-shaped muscle responsible for breathing. Diaphragm failure occurs in a variety of conditions including phrenic nerve injury, congenital diaphragmatic hernias (CDH), and many degenerative neuromuscular diseases. In phrenic nerve injury, the diaphragm doesn't properly contract because it isn't receiving the proper signals, and in patients with CDH and muscular dystrophies, the muscle lacks the ability to contract properly. Regardless of cause, diaphragm failure ultimately causes the patient to struggle to breathe. The constant struggle to breathe can cause chronically low oxygen, muscle fatigue and even respiratory failure. When these cases are severe, patients often got on a noninvasive ventilator, which involves a face mask that covers the nose and mouth and forces air into the lungs. Because noninvasive ventilation options hinder freedom of movement, speaking, and eating, noninvasive ventilation is generally only used overnight during sleep, which only provides temporary relief for fatigued respiratory muscles. We propose the development of an "implantable ventilator" that would help push the diaphragm into a normal breathing motion. This device would allow the patient to go about their life freely, unhindered by bulky face masks. This ventilator can be operated at all hours of the day, providing the therapeutic effect of proper ventilation around-the-clock. Our proposed device is inspired by our previous work on a soft robotic heart sleeve developed for heart failure. Similar to a blood pressure cuff, the heart sleeve was wrapped around the heart and when inflated, the sleeve would squeeze the heart. An external control box automatically inflated and deflated the device in time with the normal heart beat, aiding the hearts failing pumping ability. Using a similar technology, we plan to use soft robotic technology to create a device that pushes the diaphragm into its normal motion, allowing patients to breathe properly again.

column36: Caracteriser les mecanismes des anticorps anti-HLA qui perturbent l'hemostase endotheliale et menent au dommage glomerulaire chez les transplantes renaux en rejet humoral.
column37: Depuis vingt ans, il y a eu des progres considerables en greffe renale. De nouveaux agents immunosuppresseurs ont diminue considerablement le taux de rejet dans la premiere annee suivant une transplantation. Or, la survie a long terme n'a pas autant augmente, en partie en raison du rejet tardif, en particulier celui cause par les anticorps contre le greffon. Le specialiste en transplantation est confronte a un probleme lorsqu'il traite ce type de rejet : s'il n'y a pas assez d'immunosuppresseurs il y aura un rejet tandis qu'une trop grande quantite expose le patient aux infections et cancers. Pour gagner le combat contre ce rejet, il faut comprendre comment il se developpe dans le greffon et elucider les composantes immunitaires impliquees. Dans certains cas, les anticorps produisent des dommages en promouvant la coagulation dans les capillaires du greffon. Pour d'autres, des anticorps specifiques attirent des lymphocytes T CD8+, pour endommager la greffe. Finalement, dans certains patients, le rejet, que nous croyons du aux anticorps, serait cause par des cellules sanguines specialisees appelees monocytes, que nous savons activees lors des rejets. L'objectif de notre projet est de dechiffrer les differentes sequences d'evenements par lesquelles les anticorps peuvent endommager le greffon. Dans le laboratoire, nous utilisons des cellules reproduisant les micro-vaisseaux presents dans le compartiment renal, le glomerule. En utilisant ce modele pour etudier les cellules immunitaires, nous esperons atteindre notre objectif et esperons que ces connaissances aideront au developpement de protocoles efficaces et securitaires pour traiter le rejet et augmenter l'esperance de vie chez les greffes renaux.

column36: Assessing and improving the use of online information about child development, health and well-being by parents with low socioeconomic standards and their children
column37: RATIONALE Low education low income parents (parents with low socioeconomic status, hereafter SES) usually have a low level of literacy and health status. This study is born from a partnership between online information provider, 'Naitre et grandir' (N&G) and researchers who developed the Information Assessment Method questionnaire (IAM). N&G produces a website and a newsletter providing free, independent and trustworthy information about child development, health and well-being, to parents of 0-8-year old children. N&G is funded by the Chagnon Foundation which seeks to reduce poverty. The IAM allows parents to evaluate N&G information and provide feedback to N&G editors. High quality online consumer information improves health, quality of life, and participation in healthcare, for low SES parents. However, our previous work shows that low SES parents underuse N&G and IAM. Yet, it is these very parents who are more likely to report decreased worries and increased confidence as outcomes of using N&G information. Thus, our previous work clearly indicates a need to improve N&G and IAM. METHODS I will conduct my study in three phases. Phase 1. I will interview 30 low SES parents to identify barriers and facilitators to using N&G information and to interacting with N&G editors via IAM. We will use Phase 1 findings to implement a new version: the IAM+N&G+. Phase 2. I will compare the use of the original (IAM/N&G) and new (IAM+N&G+) versions. Phase 3. I will interview 30 parents to understand what outcomes they experienced after using N&G+. IMPACT Results will directly benefit low SES parents and children. In addition, results will lead to develop a free toolkit for all Web editors that will help improve health interventions to better support and empower low SES parents. AboutKidsHealth (information providers at SickKids Hospital in Toronto) will be the first other resource to implement our results.

column36: Masters Athlete Screening Study (MASS): Evaluation of Pre-participation Screening and Cardiovascular Risk in Masters Athletes
column37: Middle-aged individuals are exercising more and living longer. Underlying coronary artery disease is the primary cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in Masters athletes (> 35 years) with symptoms preceding the event in only 12-36% of cases. The risk of SCD during vigorous exercise is transiently increased in those with underlying heart disease. Pre-participation screening (PPS) can detect heart disease and prevent SCD but the optimal screening method is undefined. The Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire for Everyone (PAR-Q+) and the AHA Pre-participation Questionnaire are currently used; however, a more comprehensive risk assessment is needed. The percentage of Masters athletes that undergo current recommendations to detect heart disease is modest with the primary driver for a healthcare provider to refer an athlete for PPS is increasing age and participation in long distance events, rather than the presence of traditional risk factors. Our pilot study in 286 Masters athletes suggests that they are not immune to cardiovascular risk and 12% have significant heart disease. This present study will assess the prevalence of heart disease and risk in 800 Masters athletes. We will follow the cohort for five years to determine the incidence of, and the most effective tool for detecting significant heart disease. Study participants diagnosed with heart disease will be invited to participate in a psychological impact evaluation survey to determine the impact of a heart diagnosis through PPS to ensure optimal support in those diagnosed. This research will guide physicians and sporting organizations to determine which athletes are at risk and how to screen to prevent SCD and ensure safe sport participation. This will be the first prospective, longitudinal, large-scale (800 athletes) study in Canada examining cardiovascular risk, incidence of heart disease and examination of comprehensive screening tools in recreational and competitive athletes.

column36: Motives for Desired or Compliant Sex for Young Adult Women with BPD Symptomology
column37: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a prevalent and serious mental illness. Symptoms of BPD include intense and rapid mood swings, unstable relationships, and engagement in self-harm or suicidal behaviors. Effective psychotherapeutic treatments for BPD have been developed, such as dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). There is still, however, much room for improvement when it comes to alleviating key interpersonal problems in BPD. Therapeutic interventions that increase self-compassion (reacting to one's own suffering with kindness and understanding) may improve the treatment of these interpersonal difficulties. This study will evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of adding self-compassion training to DBT skills groups and will explore whether the added self-compassion training impacts interpersonal functioning. Participants diagnosed with BPD will be randomized to complete either thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training, or thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training modified to include self-compassion training. Feasibility and acceptability of the programs will be assessed post-treatment and compared between the two groups. Outcome variables, including interpersonal functioning, will be measured pre-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and at follow-up thirteen weeks later. It is anticipated that there will not be differences in acceptability and feasibility between groups, and participants that receive self-compassion training will show greater improvement in interpersonal functioning. This research will determine whether self-compassion training is a potentially useful addition to evidence-based care for BPD. Furthermore, this research has the potential to reduce the significant personal suffering and healthcare toll of BPD by informing improvements in treatment.

column36: Exercise Response: Is Irisin a Novel Factor that Explains the Metabolic Adaptation?
column37: Over the past few years, the prevalence of obesity and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) has drastically increased, and is expected to continue to rise. This is unfortunate, as it has led to extreme costs to our health care system. Exercise has been recognized as a first line of treatment to prevent and manage these two chronic conditions; but, not everyone benefits from exercise in the same way. For example, some individuals may lose weight from an exercise program, while others who participated in the same program will not see any results. A number of factors may lead to this variation, including a hormone released from your muscles during exercise, called irisin. Irisin is a recently discovered hormone that has the potential to provide a multitude of health benefits for individuals living with obesity and T2D. However, as irisin is novel, it is not clearly understood how different forms of exercise (intensity or duration) impact the typical health outcomes usually observed with exercise. First, our study will investigate whether irisin is released at a greater extent during high intensity aerobic exercise (e.g.: vigorous bike ride) compared to moderate intensity aerobic exercise (e.g.: jogging) in adults living with obesity. Second, we will study the release of irisin in a group of individuals who did not get any health benefits from a 12-week exercise program. Then, we will see if they get exercise benefits after an additional, more challenging, exercise program that lasts 12 more weeks. This will tell us what form of exercise best stimulates irisin release and whether these changes are related to meaningful clinical outcomes in individuals living with diabetes/pre-diabetes. Results of this study will be of great importance for health research, as they will provide a better understanding of the link between irisin, exercise, and health outcomes. Furthermore, they will provide us with further insight regarding the right amount of exercise needed to optimize health benefits.

column36: Breastfeeding and medically high-risk pregnancy: A mixed methods approach to examining feeding intentions, experiences, support, and outcomes
column37: Optimal breastfeeding protects women and infants against numerous acute and chronic diseases, yet three quarters of Canadian mothers do not meet the global recommendation of exclusive breastfeeding from birth to six months. In Canada, approximately one in four pregnant women have high-risk medical complications, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, placental disorders, or pre-existing medical conditions. These women are less likely to plan to breastfeed, to begin breastfeeding after birth, and to continue exclusive breastfeeding until six months compared to women without medical complications. This is worrisome because a high-risk pregnancy often leads to the delivery of a preterm or sick infant, and breastfeeding plays an important role in protecting the survival and health of these newborns. Unfortunately, explanations for suboptimal breastfeeding behaviours among women with high-risk pregnancies are lacking which makes it impossible to effectively address this problem. This research will examine the prenatal breastfeeding goals of women with high-risk pregnancies and the reasons behind these goals. We will track whether mothers begin and continue breastfeeding, as well as explore their postpartum breastfeeding experiences including the type and quality of supports that they access. Finally, we will identify what factors positively or negatively influence the achievement of breastfeeding goals among mothers, which may include demographic or social characteristics, maternal medical complications, delivery outcomes, and breastfeeding experiences. We can use these findings to collaborate with health professionals and decision makers in developing education and support services that are sensitive and responsive to the breastfeeding needs of women with high-risk pregnancies. Ultimately, this research will be instrumental in improving the number of high-risk women and their infants who receive the diverse and lifelong health benefits of breastfeeding.

column36: Explorer l'efficacite de la therapie cognitive-comportementale du trouble panique chez les patients qui presentent une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique comorbide
column37: Le TP est un trouble anxieux entrainant de severes limitations dans le fonctionnement quotidien et une importante detresse psychologique, en plus d'etre associe a un risque suicidaire accru et a une forte utilisation des services medicaux. Lorsqu'il est present en comorbidite avec une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique, le trouble panique peut etre associe a une augmentation du risque de mortalite ou d'evenement cardiaque. De plus, la presence d'un trouble panique peut nuire au traitement et a l'evolution de la maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique, notamment parce que ce trouble est associe a l'adoption d'habitudes de vie nefastes, a un evitement de l'activite physique et a une faible adhesion aux traitements medicaux. Le traitement de premier recours pour le trouble panique est la therapie cognitive-comportementale, mais des adaptations pourraient y etre necessaires afin de tenir compte de la presence d'une condition cardiaque. De plus, l'efficacite de la therapie cognitive-comportementale n'a pas encore ete demontree chez ces patients. Ainsi, compte tenu de l'impact potentiellement majeur du trouble panique sur l'evolution de la maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique, il est essentiel de determiner si la therapie cognitive-comportementale est efficace dans cette population. Ainsi, le present projet de recherche a pour objectif principal d'evaluer l'efficacite d'une therapie cognitive-comportementale adaptee aux particularites des patients qui souffrent egalement d'une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique pour traiter le trouble panique. Il vise egalement a documenter l'impact du traitement sur la qualite de vie, l'adhesion aux traitements, la detresse psychologique et l'utilisation des services medicaux. Ce projet de recherche a donc le potentiel de contribuer significativement a l'amelioration de la sante globale et de la qualite de vie des individus souffrant a la fois d'un trouble panique et d'une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique.

column36: Circulating tumor DNA as a predictive biomarker in metastatic bladder cancer
column37: Metastatic bladder cancer is a lethal and under-studied disease. Chemotherapy has historically been the most effective treatment for metastatic disease, but long-term survival is rare. Exciting new treatment options have recently emerged, however, responses to these new therapies are highly variable and we lack a reliable method of predicting who the responders will be. Therefore, efforts are underway to develop tools to determine the ideal therapy for each individual based on their tumor's molecular features. My research aims to develop a blood-based test for identifying genetic changes (mutations) present in metastatic bladder tumors. This test relies on the fact that when cancer cells die they often shed their DNA into the circulating bloodstream (known as circulating tumor DNA, ctDNA). We can therefore use ctDNA to evaluate the mutations in metastatic cancers that correspond to treatment response or resistance. In my preliminary research, I found that most patients with metastatic bladder cancer can have their tumors analyzed in this manner. Importantly, my initial work showed that it was feasible for patients to have real-time testing of their cancer's molecular features, without the need for invasive tissue biopsy - which is often impractical, costly and can cause significant patient morbidity. In this project, I will identify mutations in the ctDNA of hundreds of Canadians with metastatic bladder cancer, and determine which mutations predict a patient's subsequent response to treatment. Success with my project will help explain why some metastatic bladder cancers are intrinsically responsive or resistant to the most commonly used therapies. Furthermore, I will have developed a clinically-practical framework (requiring only a blood sample) that may ultimately help guide rational therapy selection in advanced bladder cancer.

column36: A National Research Network on Lyme Disease
column37: Lyme Disease (LD) is an emerging microbial threat and new approaches are required to help contain this risk to human health. LD is caused by the bacterial pathogen, B. burgdorferi that is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick. LD is of increasingly urgent concern in Canada; between 2009-2016 there was a 700% increase in the number of reported cases. Additionally, areas of Canada that were once considered to be at low-risk are transitioning to high risk as tick populations become further established due to climate change. Further research is necessary to address the many critical knowledge gaps that exist in Canada. We will establish the Canadian Lyme Disease Research Network (CLyDRN) which is composed of researchers, clinicians, patients, community members and other stakeholders with the ultimate vision of reducing the impact of LD on the health of Canadians. We will accomplish this vision by creating foundational resources and spearheading new research initiatives. This includes the creation of Canada's first repository for tissue samples from LD patients and an associated clinical database that will include detailed patient information. We will also develop national research capacity and support training of new LD researchers. These resources will support research initiatives in four areas: 1)Develop and evaluate new diagnostic tools and methods, 2)Identify preventive measures, interventions, and population health approaches to decrease risk of occurrence of LD, 3)Determine the burden and natural history of disease, clinical management and risk factors and 4)Attend to the contextual complexity through patient and community engagement, training and integrated KT research. Our Network will mobilize and build LD-specific capacity and training opportunities, improve clinical science and practice, provide best evidence in testing and patient care, improve patient outcomes and inform policy.

column36: BEhaviors, Therapies, TEchnologies and hypoglycemic Risk in Type 1 diabetes: The BETTER study
column37: Type 1 diabetes requires that patients inject themselves insulin to control the level of sugar in their blood because their pancreas cannot do it anymore. A consequence of this treatment is low blood sugar episodes. This is named hypoglycemia. Severe hypoglycemia has the potential to cause accidents, injuries, coma, and death. Patients voiced a need for better strategies to reduce those episodes. This is the focus of the BETTER program. In this program, we will test an online educational strategy to help patients who are wearing an insulin pump or are wearing a monitor to know in real time their blood sugar, to optimise their use of these devices. It will also include a peer-to-peer forum discussion to further offer social support. The program will be built in partnership with patients. It will be tested across the province of Quebec among adolescents and adults. We hypothesize that this program will help patients reduce hypoglycemia episodes. To recruit patients for this trial, we will first build a registry of patients. From this registry, we will know who is using the devices and who is having the most hypoglycemic episodes. Patients will answer questionnaires annually part of the registry. In this questionnaire they will have to report hypoglycemia, answer to questions on fear of hypoglycemia, if they feel their hypoglycemia, etc. We will also carry out small trials to improve effectiveness of the wearable device measuring blood glucose in real time, to test new strategies to correct a low blood sugar episode, to obtain the point of view of caregivers for helping during serious episodes and finally, to test an artificial pancreas system in a specific condition in which it may be harder for the system to prevent or correct a low blood sugar episode. All these trials will increase our knowledge on hypoglycemia, how to prevent and treat those episodes.

column36: Canadian Autoimmunity Standardization Core (CAN-ASC)
column37: To stay healthy, we need to have an immune system that works properly: it needs to attack foreign cells, but leave our own cells alone. If our immune system attacks our cells, it causes an illness called an autoimmune disease. There are many types of autoimmune disease, including type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, celiac disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. Two million Canadians of all ages live with an autoimmune disease. Researchers and healthcare professionals are working hard to find new and better ways to treat these lifelong diseases. But we face the challenge that there is not a consistent set of established 'recipes' (called standard operating procedures, or SOPs) for the ways that researchers collect, process, and analyze samples to make discoveries or test new treatments. Here, we have brought together a Canada-wide group of experts to create the Canadian Autoimmunity Standardization Core (CAN-ASC), which will develop SOPs for the most important tests and methods that are needed by the researchers who study autoimmune diseases. We will work together and with our colleagues to produce and test the SOPs. Then we will make the SOPs available via the web and train researchers and students to use them. In this way, we will ensure that Canadian researchers have ideal methods to study what causes autoimmunity in humans and to develop new treatments that can restore normal immune system function.

column36: Disability Prevention and Rehabilitation
column37: Musculoskeletal pain and mental health disorders are the two leading causes of disability worldwide. Despite large societal investments in the treatment of musculoskeletal pain and mental health disorders, the prevalence of resulting disabilities, continues to grow significantly. One reason for this epidemic is that musculoskeletal pain and mental health disorders often co-exist in individuals, yet research has not considered their shared etiology and prognosis. The CRC research program proposes a novel approach to conceptualizing disability related to the shared etiology and prognosis of musculoskeletal pain and mental health disorders to inform the development of prevention and rehabilitation interventions for disability.

My research aims to better understand the link between obesity and diabetes to reduce the burden of obesity and its metabolic complications. column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is the most common acute leukemia in adults. The majority of AML patients respond to toxic chemotherapy initially, but due to therapy resistant relapses, the 5-year overall survival is below 50%, and below 20% for patients >60 years. There is an intense medical need for new therapeutic options. The major hurdle in identifying an effective AML drug is that it must be capable of entering blood producing organs like bone marrow to efficiently kill leukemic cells. We have developed a molecule, which targets STAT%, an important driver of blood cancers. The compound exhibits potent killing of AML cells while not killing normal cells and most importantly, penetrates bone marrow. We seek to optimize the drug and conduct trials in animal models of AM to identify an advanced preclinical candidate for treatment of AML.

column36: EpiBrain: Epigenetic effects of B-vitamins on brain health throughout life: scientific substantiation and translation of evidence for health-improvement strategies
column37: Low or imbalanced dietary intake of B-vitamins such as folate and vitamin B12 may have adverse effects on brain development in early life and brain function in later life. Human studies show that improved folate status of mums during pregnancy is associated with better cognition in the child, whilst optimal folate and related B-vitamin status may prevent cognitive decline in older adults. The biological basis explaining these relationships could involve B-vitamin-driven regulation of genes involved in brain development and function. A better understanding of the mechanisms linking relevant B-vitamins and gene-controlling mechanisms with brain health at critical stages of the lifecycle is necessary to support evidence-based health improvement strategies. With a team of interdisciplinary researchers from Canada, the UK and Spain, we propose to investigate the linkage between nutrition and brain function across the lifespan, and to study the genetic basis to explain these relationships. We will access existing data and blood samples, and conduct new genetic analysis of existing, well-characterized studies in pregnancy and older adults, in Canada and in Europe. This project will lead to improved understanding of the role of B vitamins and their genetic effects in relation to brain function in childhood and older age, with expected results anticipated to provide scientific substantiation to support nutritional strategies for sustaining better brain health through the lifespan.

column37: A person's environment - including their diet - can affect the activity levels of some of their genes. These "epigenetic" changes have recently emerged as a possible way by which early life exposures and experiences can leave behind a biological signature that influences lifelong health. DNA methylation, a commonly studied epigenetic mark that affects gene regulation, has been studied in a variety of contexts in human populations, such as aging, cancer, and disease. One area that has been lacking is an understanding of how early-life nutritional exposures and subsequent epigenetic changes may lead to metabolic adaptations and affect disease risk across the full life course. We propose to fill this gap by examining epigenetic changes in relation to maternal and infant nutrition-related factors and subsequent risk factors for metabolic health and disease. We can then build on these findings in order to identify molecular mechanisms through which nutrition-related specific DNA methylation changes lead to developmental adaptations.

column37: Background: Many cutting-edge therapies rely on manipulating the adaptive immune system, which has evolved a vast diversity (repertoire) of immune receptors to recognize and remove pathogens and cancer cells. The sequence-data sets characterizing this Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (i.e., AIRR-seq data) have the potential to revolutionize vaccine research and the development of therapies against autoimmune diseases and cancer; however, AIRR-seq data are typically stored and curated by individual labs, using a variety of tools and technologies. Sharing these data in a common way across disease studies, labs, and institutions around the world will improve our ability to recognize patterns in basic research and clinical trials, and increase our confidence in these patterns. The existing iReceptor Platform uses community-developed standards to facilitate sharing of AIRR-seq data by enabling queries across a system of distributed data repositories. These improvements will reduce the social and economic burden of these diseases, advance Canada's leadership role in immunotherapy, and contribute to improved patient care worldwide.

column37: One of health care's largest outstanding issues is that many patients do not respond to treatment or are harmed by a treatment. The project builds on existing databases and infrastructural resources, including Europe's largest controlled access database - EGA - and a worldwide collection of human genome datasets, including major cohort studies in Canada. This project will also incorporate important outreach and training initiatives, and address particular ethical, legal and social issues associated with this federated data analysis. This work will address key gaps in the development of the personalised medicine vision described in the ICPerMed Action Plan and by CIHR. column36: EUCAN-Connect: A federated FAIR platform enabling large-scale analysis of high-value cohort data connecting Europe and Canada in personalized health
column37: Rapid progress in information and biotechnologies offers the promise of better, personalized health strategies using rich phenotypic, environmental and molecular (omics) profiles of every individual. To capitalize on this great promise, the key challenge is to relate these profiles to health and disease while accounting for high diversity in individuals, populations and environments. Both Europe and Canada have long-term investments in population-based prospective cohort studies providing essential longitudinal data. These data must be analyzed in unison to reach statistical power, however, presently cohort data repositories are scattered, hard to search and integrate, and data protection and governance rules discourage central pooling. EUCAN-Connect will enable large-scale integrated cohort data analysis for personalized and preventive healthcare across EU and Canada. This will be based on an open, scalable data platform for cohorts, researchers and networks, incorporating FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) for optimal reuse of existing data, and building on maturing federated technologies, with sensitive data kept locally and only results being shared and integrated, in line with key data governance guidelines. Widespread uptake will be promoted via beyond state-of-the-art research in close collaboration with leading cohort networks, focused on early-life origins of cardio-metabolic, developmental, musculoskeletal and respiratory health and disease impacting human life course. To address challenges of sustainability and curation, we will deliver innovative solutions for distributed, low-cost data harvesting and preservation, community curation/harmonization, privacy protection, open source bioinformatics toolbox development, and international governance. EUCAN-Connect platform and collaborations will be coordinated through BBMRI-ERIC (EU) and Maelstrom Research (Canada) to sustain long-term benefits to science and citizens worldwide.

column37: EU-CAN-SHARE builds on existing infrastructures and partnerships to develop a sustainable model for the storage, curation, and analyses of the complex data sets collected by infectious disease (ID)-related cohorts. We develop data architecture and governance that link biobanks to data repositories to facilitate equitable use, collaborative, cross-domain analyses, and replicability. The team leverages partnerships with multicentre ID cohorts in the global South, and connects EU investments in OMICS infrastructures with Canadian expertise on pipeline and workflow development, biostatistical methods, and ethical and governance issues related to the establishment of repositories for CE&HDL data in resource-limited settings. Drawing from best practice and governance elaborated for similar initiatives, the repository will employ a federated model where a tiered permission system and cohort-specific hubs facilitate cohorts' analysis of their own data, cross-cohort analyses, and connections with the open science community within a clearly elaborated legal, ethical, and equitable framework. The cloud-based platform will provide analytic tools and computational power to facilitate cross-domain, collaborative analyses that inform personalized medicine approaches to diagnostic, treatment, and vaccine development in ID-focused international cohorts.

column37: Personalised medicine approaches are highly needed in the domain of cardiology, as cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the major contributors to mortality and morbidity worldwide. To date, cardiovascular research has been conducted by interrogating biomedical data in single cohorts, but these are often limited to specific populations, geographical areas, or data type. These challenges call for integrated multi-cohort approaches to allow researchers to investigate established and emerging markers within and across heterogeneous populations. In Canada, CVD research has been at the forefront of multi-cohort approaches through the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) (MUHC, McGill, McMaster, ICES). The CAHHM exploited Canadian know-how in legal data (McGill) and in harmonisation and integration (MUHC) to create a centralised longitudinal super-cohort from 8 Canadian cohorts for enhanced data sharing in cardiovascular research. However, infrastructures and models to facilitate integrated sharing of information and data between Canadian and European cohorts are missing. The euCanSHare project proposes to leverage, extend and integrate two complimentary initiatives in Canada (CAHHM) and Europe (BiomarCaRE) to develop a robust ecosystem for enhanced data sharing, integration and exploitation in CVD research. In this way, existing Canadian and European tools will be put on a Common IT platform developed within euCanSHare, and will offer extensive services and functionalities. Comparative analysis of legal frameworks in Canada and Europe will be led by experts from Canada (McGill) to inform the shared automation of such services. The integrated cloud-based collection of technologies, policies and standardised procedures will reduce the cost of research, allowing efficient data management at scale across international projects.

column36: Canadian "Rare Diseases: Models and Mechanisms" (RDMM) Network
column37: Thousands of rare genetic diseases (RDs) affect one million Canadians, mostly children, and cause significant disability, lead to early death, and almost all have no treatment. Genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) has transformed our ability to identify gene mutations that cause RDs, but we understand very little about the impact of those genes and mutations on biology and health. As a result, we don't know how to treat most of these devastating diseases. Studying gene mutations in model organisms (such as yeast, worm, fly, fish, and mouse) provides important information about how mutations cause disease and can identify potential therapies. However, geneticists discovering genes that cause RD do not usually conduct research in model organisms, and model organism scientists are not usually aware of genes being discovered by geneticists. Thus, in 2014 we established the Canadian 'Rare Diseases: Models and Mechanisms' Network ('The RDMM Network') to a) connect geneticists discovering RD genes with model organism scientists able to study that gene and b) provide small grants to support collaborative research. The RDMM Network has engaged these communities, made connections for 72 RD genes, and funded 79 projects. Our research has already led to original scientific publications, successful large-scale grants, and identified two life-changing therapies. These results are very promising, and we want to expand the impact and reach of the RDMM Network. To do so we will: - Further engage the clinical and model organism communities - Enable connections when model organism expertise is not available in the country where the gene was discovered, by linking similar networks around the world - Support more projects by partnering with Canadian organizations interested in co-funding research. Building on our experience running the RDMM Network, we will support more than 50 collaborative projects to generate new knowledge that will improve the care of Canadians with RD.

column36: Disability, Employment, and Public Policies Initiative
column37: Employment is an important channel through which individuals develop self-esteem, consolidate their social network, and secure sufficient income for retirement. Yet, it remains widely acknowledged that persons with disabilities lag seriously in employment. According to Statistics Canada, the employment rate of people with disabilities was twenty percentage points lower and their unemployment rate five percentage points higher. Women and those aged 35 and above seem particularly vulnerable.In 2001, 40% of women with disabilities aged of 15-64 years were part of the Canadian workforce, compared to 69% of women without disabilities in the same age category (Statistics Canada, 2012). Aging of the Canadian population will add further challenges to public services and programs. Data on the prevalence of disabilities are clear - rates of disability for Canadians 65 years or older are double those of the population at large, and the prevalence of disabilities increases with age for almost all types of disabilities. The later suggests that the socioeconomic impacts of disabilities will likely grow in the future as the Canadian population continues aging. This proposal contains an interdisciplinary research program aimed at developing economic policies to help persons with disabilities. Our research program covers policies to foster job search, job retention and promotion, and facilitate transition from the labor market to retirement. Our research program recognizes that existing data sources (survey and administrative data)are necessary yet insufficient to estimate econometric models capturing the complex realities facing persons with disabilities. Persons with disabilities may for example have pessimistic views of their chances on the labor market and withhold effort to search for jobs and get promoted. They may also fail to understand the complexities of public programs and their fiscal incidences.
