column36: TYDE: Transitioning Youth with Disabilities and Employment
column37: Article 27 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) recognizes "the right of persons with disabilities to work on an equal basis with others... in a work environment that is open, inclusive and accessible to persons with disabilities," and compels "State Parties to safeguard and promote the realization of the right to work." In Canada, people with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to employment with only 49% of individuals with disabilities reporting work (Statistics Canada, 2012). The employment situation for people with intellectual disability (ID) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is significantly worse; working age individuals represent the most unemployed and underemployed citizens in Canada. According to the Canadian Survey on Disability (2012), only 22.3% of persons with ID or ASD indicated some kind of employment, and, when employed, these individuals received low wages, worked few hours, and often worked in segregated settings; further, when ID/ASD research considers sex/gender, females fare worse than their male counterparts. In spite of this, work is an aspiration for people with ID or ASD and is a key mechanism for social inclusion.The BC Transitioning Youth with Disabilities and Employment Project -- "The TYDE Project" -- aims to improve employment outcomes for transitioning youth ages 14 - 18 with ID or ASD in British Columbia through early interventions that target youth and their parents with particular attention paid to gender in the design, implementation and assessment of this research and knowledge mobilization (KM). Research consistently supports that intervening early when young adolescent girls and boys with ID or ASD are transitioning from school to adult life translates to positive employment outcomes. Further, research demonstrates that 1) experiences with inclusive education, 2) positive parental expectations for employment and/or post-secondary education, 3) greater levels of self-determination among transitioning youth with ID or ASD, and, 4) early work experience are predictive of higher employment outcomes. These four domains underpin our research and KM program. Through this partnership, we will:1. Develop and test The TYDE Transitioning Youth to Employment Tool; an online interactive learning environment designed to enhance employment outcomes for youth with ID or ASD by increasing youth pre-employment skills, increasing youth self-determination, and improving parental/caregiver knowledge and expectations for fostering their youth's future employment experiences.

column36: Healthy Professional/Knowledge Workers: Examining the Gendered Nature of Mental Health Issues, Leaves of Absence & Return to Work Experiences from a Comparative Perspective
column37: Mental Health (MH) related leave accounts for nearly 30 per cent of short- and long-term disability claims, yet many suffer in silence. The combined effects of absenteeism and presenteeism due to MH issues has been estimated to account for more than $6 billion in lost productivity costs.(6) Given their knowledge service role, these presenteeism and absenteeism can be uniquely challenging for professional workers. Indeed the negative consequences extend not only affect relations with co-workers and employers, but, with the broader public in terms of accessibility to and quality of services. Negotiating leaves of absence and return to work can be particularly difficult when potentially stigmatizing MH issues are involved and when work culture and structure constitute insurmountable barriers. Although MH-related presenteeism and absenteeism are areas of growing concern for professional/knowledge workers, they are seriously understudied, particularly from a comparative perspective. The role gender plays is also conspicuously absent as an explicit focus. Addressing absenteeism and presenteeism across a range of workers, we ask: - What are the mental health experiences of professional/knowledge workers causing them to take or contemplate taking a leave of absence from work? - What are the key factors causing them to leave work -- with a focus on personal, family and work context -- and which of these factors are most influential in fostering their return to work? - Which of these key factors prevent others experiencing mental health issues from taking a leave?Reflecting an explicit gender perspective, we will examine how the barriers, facilitators and experience of contemplating and negotiating leaves of absence and return to work are gendered at the level of the worker and their profession. We also ask what interventions can mediate these gendered experiences.Our Partnership will be the first interdisciplinary, collaborative, comparative research initiative investigating and addressing the gendered experiences of MH, LoA and RTW for regulated professional/knowledge workers. We bring together academic researchers, worker representatives, unions, professional associations, employers, service providers, insurers, policy-makers, and other stakeholders across the following domains: 1) healthcare, including dentists, midwives, nurses and physicians; 2) education, including professors and teachers; and 3) accountants. In addition to cutting across sectors, these groups of workers also differ by work context and gender composition. We take an explicit gender perspective in the collection and interpretation of the data gathered, which we will augment with a broader intersectionality lens and life course approach. A mixed methods approachPage 2 will capture the complexity of the issues, involving qualitative data -- documents, observations and interviews with the range of stakeholders -- augmented with quantitative data from available administrative and newly developed survey datasets. These components will inform targeted case studies and evaluations of ongoing interventions drawing upon the input from our participating stakeholders. Comparing across knowledge worker groups, locations and using mixed-methods allow us to address the complexity of the phenomena for a truly ground-breaking research program. We will integrate our partners throughout the entire research process beginning with co-developing the research foci, accessing existing and collecting new data, interpreting the findings, and translating the knowledge into more effective and equitable leave of absence and return to work policies, practices and programs. We will contribute to the development, implementation, and scale-up of evidence-based and gender-responsive interventions.

column36: Policy and practice in return to work after work injury: Challenging circumstances and innovative solutions
column37: A fundamental purpose of workers' compensation (WC) law and policy is to help people return to work after injury, to which end it creates regulatory economic drivers as incentives. However, our pilot studies, focusing on some of the most vulnerable categories of workers, suggest that such drivers often become the new purpose of the process, pre-empting the original purpose of the law. We have gathered together a multi-disciplinary team of 14 academics, 18 partners and over 20 trainees to address the overarching policy question: How can we get back to the purpose of the legislation and promote sustainable return to work (RTW) for all workers injured or made ill because of work? We focus in particular on the effectiveness of current policies as applied to three overlapping categories of potentially vulnerable workers: the precariously employed, the geographically mobile and low wage earners in Quebec, Ontario, and the Maritime Provinces. We are interested in workers suffering from either physical or mental health problems attributable to the workplace and in the roles of unions and workplaces in supporting RTW in light of the policy frameworks applicable. The proposal seeks funding for 7 research programs (A-G), to examine the scope and effectiveness of regulated RTW policies and the application of those protections to three categories of workers in particular: 1) those injured while working in non-standard employment (defined) or 2) while engaging in employment-related geographic mobility or 3) full time low wage earners. When possible we will include both unionized and non-unionized workers within the purview of our research, and partners have been chosen accordingly. Programs A-G build on our pilot projects while adding new dimensions(role of workplaces and immigration issues): A: Classic legal analysis of rules governing injured workers' rights to support for sustainable return to pre-injury employment or to the broader labour market, looking specifically at WC, occupational health and safety and human rights law; qualitative studies in B Ontario and C Quebec to document experiences of workers injured while precariously employed who attempt to return to pre-injury employment or return to the labour market. D: a mixed methods study to document experiences of mobile workers injured while working outside their home province who attempt to return to pre-injury employment or the broader labour market. E will develop tools for workplaces and unions to assist them with RTW of workers with physical or mental health problems. F focuses on immigration issues and the temporary foreign worker program as related to RTW in Ontario and Quebec. G will synthesize the results from the six research programs, to develop recommendations for policy makers and workplace actors as to types of regulatory and policy protections, and workplace practices, that work for promoting sustainable RTW for the working populations targeted by this project. All of our studies include a gender lens, seeking to ensure that academics and partners understand how policies and practices apply to men andwomen. This approach will include a consideration of work-family balance issues, at the time of determination of suitable post-injury employment, but also consideration of the segmented labour market, and the disproportionate presence of women in part time, temporary, and low wage employment. Partners supporting this application, include governmental agencies representing the interests of employers, workers, and the protection of public health and NGOs. Their participation in research design and knowledge mobilisation will strengthen the research program and facilitate recruitment of new partners while providing economic support ($957,209) for our activities.

column36: Mobilizing a Caregiver-Friendly Workplace Standard: A Partnership Approach
column37: INTRODUCTION: There are more than 5.6 million employees in Canada with adult/elder care responsibilities and 35% of them are simultaneously employed (2012). Lack of workplace support can result in carer-employees (CEs) leaving the workforce, and/or missed work days, or early retirements which can impact employers in terms of reduced productivity and avoidable costs due to a range of HR issues, such as turnover and absenteeism. Given the gendered nature of both family caregiving and the labour sector, it is incumbent upon workplaces to implement gender-sensitive caregiver-friendly workplace practices (CFWPs) to appropriately accommodate CEs whilst sustaining efficiencies in the workplace. Doing so enhances work-life balance, workforce retention, and reduces health costs. The Healthy, Productive Workplace -- Partnership Development Grant (HPW-PDG) allowed McMaster University to partner with the Canadian Standards Association, among others, to create a bilingual Caregiver Inclusive and Accommodating Workplace Organizations Standard for Canadian workplaces. This HPW-Partnership Grant (PG) will mobilize uptake of the Standard in Canada and abroad, while accruing evidence on the Standard's broader health and economic impacts.GOALS: In partnership with: (i) academic researchers; (ii) a range of diverse, committed partners - representing academia, government, non-government/non-profit, private business/service providers, and labour, and; (iii) collaborators representing various industries, the proposed partnership will disseminate and mobilize the Standard across Canada and the world. We will deliver a sex and gender-sensitive program of research to assist CEs, human resource professionals, unions, workers associations, government organizations, and a variety of employers, to implement the successful uptake of the Standard. RESEARCH PROGRAM: Led by Dr. Allison Williams, a CIHR Research Chair in Gender, Work and Health, and the Sex and Gender Champion for the PG, the proposed research program will be executed by a geographically representative group of invited partners and collaborators, together with world-class academic researchers with unmatched expertise in this field. In addition to the internationalization of the Standard (Project 1), where the Canadian Standards Association will follow a specific standards protocol, an international comparative review of CFWPs will be undertaken to provide a baseline for the global uptake. Carers Canada will lead Project 2, which includes a rigorous program of knowledge mobilization and evaluation. Project 3 involves a qualitative assessment of experts, recruited from the Conference Board of Canada, to diagnose readiness to support CEs in Canadian organizations. The results of Project 3 will inform a feasibility study (Project 4), which will be realized in partnership with Habanero Consulting Inc. Working with a host of partners representing precarious workers and cultural minority groups, Projects 5 and 6 will realize the Standard's cultural competency/ safety. RESEARCH OUTCOMES: This proposed research project, which includes a robust knowledge mobilization program, will support new thinking and behavior that will lead to improvements in the economic, social, cultural and intellectual well-being in Canada and internationally. Research capacity will be built, with 29 trainees and 2 emerging scholars integrated in all aspects of the research, governance and partnership. New knowledge about CFWPs will be generated, providing the evidence needed for continued uptake of the Standard, and informing curricula in business management/HR -- both of which will ensure ongoing sustainability of the Standard as a significant intervention in improving healthy, productive workplaces in Canada and abroad.

column36: Accommodating and Communicating about Episodic Disabilities (ACED): A partnership to deliver workplace tools and resources to sustain the employment of people with chronic, episodic conditions
column37: Central to this initiative is that many physical and mental health conditions cause episodic disability. Episodic disabilities are intermittent, often unpredictable, and may be largely invisible to others until symptoms are severe. Examples are depression, anxiety, multiple sclerosis, Crohn's, colitis and arthritis. Taken together, they are among the most common and costly chronic conditions in Canada. The nature of episodic conditions creates unique challenges for workplace disability management, particularly in implementing privacy and duty to accommodate policies. Objectives: The aim of this partnership is to enhance the work sustainability of Canadians with chronic, episodic mental and physical health conditions through the development of easily accessed, evidence-based tools, resources and training that protects privacy and facilitates communication and accommodation planning among workers, supervisors and others in the workplace. Objectives are: 1) consolidate and enhance existing evidence for toolkit development; 2) develop new evidence-informed resources, including a communication decision-making tool, interactive job analysis and accommodation planning tool, and skills training workshops for supervisors and HR/disability managers; 3) pilot test and evaluate the toolkit in diverse workplaces, including conducting cost analyses; 4) expand the evidence base to include greater attention to sex/gender, age/life course, diverse employment contexts and episodic conditions; 5) develop new researcher capacity in disability studies; 6) build new workplace partnerships for testing and dissemination.Methods: We will use a theory-driven, integrated evaluation approach that comprises researchers, partners and other stakeholders to develop and evaluate the toolkit and that follows a recommended four-stage life cycle: 1) evaluation of needs; 2) toolkit development and initial implementation; 3) mature implementation; 4) outcome and economic evaluation and dissemination. Partners: Our identification of team members is strategic and adds value compared to an approach that focuses on a single health condition or type of workplace. Research team members have expertise in psychology, economics, health sciences, ergonomics, public health, and knowledge translation. Partners are five national health charities of conditions often causing episodic disabilities and four workplace focused partners. They are: the Canadian Mental Health Association, Crohn's & Colitis Canada, Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada, Realize, The Arthritis Society, the Institute for Work & Health, the Great-West Life Centre for Mental Health in theWorkplace, Mindful Employer Canada, and the Ontario Ministry of Labour. All partners have a mandate to improve the inclusiveness of work and the employment participation of workers with episodic disabilities. They are at the forefront of progressive thinking about workplace disability policies and practices and/or are leaders in creating innovative tools and resources. Outcomes: Our partnership will produce important scholarly and social benefits, including: new tools, resources and skills training applicable to a range of episodic conditions and contexts; providing new trainees and a cadre of early career investigators with research and leadership experience in disability studies; greater understanding of the personal, social and economic value of addressing the workplace needs of individuals with chronic, episodic disabilities; knowledge mobilization and dissemination plans that will result in a lasting legacy of our partnership.

column36: Partners for enhancing healthy and productive work for young men and women with disabilities
column37: Maintaining a healthy workforce is a priority for employers, workers and policy makers. Of the 1.5 million working age Canadians with a disability, 411,000 are unemployed but want to work and their disabilities do not prevent them from doing so [1-2]. There are nearly 200,000 Canadian young adults aged 15-25 who have a disability, representing a substantial untapped pool of capable future workers [1]. Despite the strong business case for hiring people with disabilities, their employment rates are consistently half or less compared to people without disabilities [3-4]. Workplace accommodations can optimize disabled workers' labour participation [5-6]. However, despite the benefits of accommodations, employers struggle with how to accommodate employees with disabilities and the types of accommodations that will facilitate employment [7]. Although many people with a disability could benefit from accommodations, only a small proportion of workers disclose their need for accommodations due to fear of discrimination or job loss [8-9]. Little is known about the experiences of disability disclosure and workplace accommodations among young people who attempt to enter and remain in the workforce. It is critical to identify effective disclosure strategies and workplace accommodation processes because they can improve quality of life and job performance [10].This grant is linked to the "Insight" and "Connection" programs and is designed to connect academics and knowledge user partners to increase the multi-directional flow of knowledge. This five-year CIHR-SSHRC partnership grant in "Healthy and Productive Work" will allow us to develop an interdisciplinary partnership and co-create knowledge to develop, implement and evaluate the following evidence-informed, gender-responsive solutions to enhance healthy and inclusive labour force participation of youth with disabilities. OBJECTIVES: (1) to develop evidence on disability disclosure and workplace accommodations that help youth with disabilities to enter, remain healthy and productive in the workplace; (2) to implement and evaluate evidence-informed, gender-responsive solutions for effective implementation, evaluation, and scaling up of interventions (i.e., toolkits, simulations, mentoring) that enable productive work among youth with disabilities; (3) to build capacity for measuring and demonstrating the broader health and socio-economic impacts of these interventions; (4) to expand the evidence base and research capacity regarding the integration of sex and gender-based analysis with respect to healthy and productive work; and (5) to enhance inter-disciplinary partnerships through the Inclusive Youth Employment Research Coalition through inter-disciplinary collaborations between researchers and knowledge users while building capacityof the next generation of researchers. We will develop a cross-sector partnership of academics, employers, youth with disabilities and knowledge users to understand how best to provide workplace accommodations. To enable knowledge generation through engagement with these partners, the partnership also includes leading Canadian academics with expertise in child disabilities, workplace accommodations, gender, diversity, and human resources management. These individuals are committed to advancing our understanding of workplace accommodations and improving employment opportunities for young people with disabilities. KEY DELIVERABLES: The project deliverables involve the following: three toolkits; (2) interactive bi-monthly webinars and 5 workshops; (3) interactive project website; (4) infographics, policy briefs, videos; (5) publications / presentations; and (6) development of an Inclusive Youth Employment Research Coalition.

column36: Cultural Agility in Northern BC's Healthcare System: Increasing Indigenous Employment Participation and Responsiveness to Indigenous Well-Being
column37: Building on a 2016 SSHRC Partnership Development Grant (FILE #890-2016-3038) in primary partnership w/ Northern Health (NH) and the First Nations Health Authority (FNHA), the broadest goal of this 2018-2023 Partnership Grant is: to improve health sector employment environments, and the delivery of healthcare services, in Northern BC (and beyond) by researching, implementing, and evidencing "culturally agile" healthcare services especially by using community-informed decolonizing critical humanities and social science methods and methodologies. Culturally agile healthcare services in BC would: 1) support (especially Indigenous) people from northern and rural places to join and stay in healthcare employment professions and 2) ensure the healthcare system is safer for all Indigenous peoples, including employees. This goal was honed over 17 months in consultation w/ 20+ community organizations across Northern BC and in close partnership w/ NH and FNHA.Delivery of healthcare services in BC is uniquely complex: in 2005, BC First Nations (FN), the Province of BC, and the Government of Canada signed a Transformative Change Accord, agreeing to work together to "...restore, revitalize and strengthen [the health of] First Nations and their communities and families [and] to eliminate the gap in standards of living w/ other British Columbians...". This resulted, in part, in the FNHA, the first province-wide health authority of its kind in Canada. In 2013, the FNHA assumed programs, services, and responsibilities formerly handled by Health Canada's First Nations Inuit Health Branch -- Pacific Region: the FNHA's vision is to transform the health and well-being of BC's First Nations and Aboriginal people by dramatically changing healthcare for the better. The FNHA works closely w/ other Health Authorities, including NH, which, w/ over 35% of the FN population in BC, serves the highest proportion of FN people in BC. With more than 8000 employees, NH is one of the largest employers in northern BC.Indigenous people live w/ multiple health barriers, including chronic illnesses and poor mental health, w/ Indigenous women facing increased barriers. Fostering Indigenous participation in the healthcare labour force, especially as it is demonstrated to increase the health of ALL Indigenous peoples in a service delivery area, is an urgent and dynamically emerging concern. Conversations between NH and Aboriginal Health Improvement Committees (AHICs -- who are tasked w/ collaboratively addressing local challenges that manifest first at a systems level based on relationships w/ communities) established a critical need to address issues such a racism and cultural safety within NH. These conversations established needs for new tools and interventions, which are 'beyond tables and numbers' and instead'speak to the heart' and 'incorporate Indigenous ways of knowing and being'. Our Partnership Grant (PG) will extend established partnerships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous multi-sectoral and interdisciplinary stakeholders across Northern BC. We align specifically w/ SSHRC's 'future challenge area' in addressing how experiences and aspirations of Indigenous Peoples are essential in building a successful shared future healthcare workforce in Northern BC. Our team (representing Indigenous and non-Indigenous stakeholders, social and medical/health scientists, along w/ humanities scholars and health employers) will work together in developing new ways of educating and strengthening a culturally safe & agile northern healthcare workforce for tomorrow by focusing on ways decolonizing community-informed social sciences and humanities approaches to knowledge production and dissemination might be mobilized to inform or develop healthcare delivery.

column36: Transforming Nurses' Work Environments Through a Strengths-Based Leadership and Management Training Program
column37: CHALLENGES: The current healthcare system is fragmented, depersonalized, disease-centric, and costly. Patients and families often feel powerless, disconnected, and voiceless, as do the nurses who care for them. Nurses report that dissatisfaction with the work environment is sufficient to make them want to leave nursing. Nurses often experience systemic sex and gender discrimination expressed in bullying, verbal abuse, and devaluing of their contributions, impacting their physical and mental health. What is needed is a paradigm shift from the current deficit-based management approach to a strength-based approach. Strengths-Based Nursing (SB-N/C) is both a philosophy and value driven-approach to guide the actions of clinicians, leaders, and managers. SB-N/C enhances, develops, and works with peoples' existing and potential strengths to bring out the best in the person and to contain, minimize, and/or circumvent what is not working. This shift requires re-training clinical managers and leaders to work through a strengths-based lens to build communities of caring and create safe workplaces for nurses ensuring that nurses can then provide safe, quality care to patients and families. GOALS & OBJECTIVES: The overall objective is to transform nurses' work-life environments from deficit-focused to strengths-focused through developing leaders/managers who are guided by a strengths-based approach to improve their health and productivity. To achieve this, we will refine a Strengths-Based-Leadership and Management (SB-L/M) Integrated Training Program for clinical leaders and managers with 3 components: 1- create and use innovative, multi-media teaching materials for story-sharing and sharing circles; 2- refine a 12-module course that integrates the best practice of healthcare with a SB-N/C approach paying attention to sex and gender issues in the workplace; 3- develop mentorship with situated coaching to ensure implementation and sustainability. Using a mixed-methods design, we will evaluate the processes and impact of this program on clinical leaders/managers, point-of-care nurses, and quality of patient/family care. PARTNERSHIP: To accomplish the objectives requires a multi-disciplinary Partnership. Partners continuing from Stage 1 (PDG) are: McGill University, Ingram School of Nursing, the birthplace of SB-N/C and SB-L/M; Concordia University's Center of Oral History and Digital Storytelling, with considerable expertise in multi-media story-sharing, collecting and analyzing oral histories and their impact on bringing about social change; and two clinical hospitals in Toronto, SickKids and Holland-Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital. Both hospitals have robust family-centred care, a developmental approach underpinning their pediatric care, and a commitment to SB-N/C in their strategic plans. Added to Stage 2 (PG) are: Two newclinical partners in Quebec, the Jewish General Hospital, Department of Nursing and CIUSSS-Ouest-de-L'Ile-de-Montreal, both of whom are committed to SB-N/C and strengthening their nurse-managers who directly supervise point-of-care nurses; the Canadian Nurses Association, the national voice of Canadian nursing profession that advocates on policy and legislation; and Concordia University's John Molson School of Business, bringing their experience and expertise in teaching operations, management skills, and in evaluation of the program. Our team continues collaboration with an award-winning visual anthropologist, and a knowledgeable scholar in sex and gender issues. Ultimately, this Partnership will contribute to a deeper understanding of the factors that create improvements to or obstacles in nurses' work-life environments, so that we can then inform policy and legislation at local, national, and international levels.

column36: Neuroimmune guidance cues, MicroRNAs & Inflammatory responses: Sex differences in cardiovascular diseases (MISs-CVD)
column37: Atherosclerotic vascular disease continues to be a leader of morbidity and mortality. Although sex hormones are known to play a role in this lipid- and inflammatory-driven disease, the underlying mechanisms are largely unclear. Neuroimmune guidance cues (NGCs) are key regulators of cell movement and positioning, and have emerged as significant players in inflammation. We have previously reported a role for Netrin-1 on macrophage emigration from plaques as well as key regulation of lipid metabolism by microRNA (miRNA)-33. Recently, we have uncovered sex-biased miRNAs targeting NGCs and hypothesize that these miRNAs provide missing mechanistic links in the endothelial-monocyte interactions and macrophage retention in the vascular wall during atherosclerosis in women vs men. We now seek to fully characterize the clinically relevant sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs in monocytes, plasma and aorta specimens from healthy subject and patients with atherosclerosis. We will also use primary endothelial cells and assess direct interactions between the sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs and unravel the functional impact of promising miRNAs on endothelial permeability, monocyte and macrophage trafficking and atherosclerosis using an innovative 3D vessel-on-a-chip platform and in vivo mouse models. This ambitious interdisciplinary project requires combined expertise of molecular cell biology, bioinformatics and physiology to provide crucial understanding of the gender differences in atherosclerosis and may provide novel gender specific therapeutic avenues to combat atherogenesis in both men and women.

column36: Unravelling proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) mechanisms in calcific aortic valve disease: from aortic valve sclerosis to stenosis
column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is a fatal pathology that affects 2-3% of the population. Yet, drug therapies are ineffective, leaving the urgency to fully characterize the aetiology of aortic valve calcification (AVC) to develop innovative therapies. Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) binds to and targets the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). It was recently shown that individuals with loss-of-function genetic variant at the PCSK9 gene have low levels of atherogenic lipoprotein concentrations (LDL and Lipoprotein(a)) and reduced risk of coronary heart disease and CAVS. However, the mechanisms through which altered PCSK9 activity could protect against or cause CAVS is lacking. Our preliminary data suggest that PCSK9 plays an active role in CAVS. We will, therefore, determine whether PCSK9 is a causal risk factor for CAVS using genetic epidemiology. Further, we will shed light on the molecular underpinnings through which PCSK9 causes CAVS in humans using state-of-the-art in vivo as well as in vitro models in combination with next-generation sequencing. As a complementary and potential pre-clinical model, we will determine the role of PCSK9 in the development of aortic valve calcification in mice. The overarching aim of this research program is to provide the required biological evidence using a highly translational approach to support PCSK9 as a therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of patients with CAVS.

column36: Identification of converging Molecular Pathways Across Chromatinopathies as Targets for Therapy: IMPACT
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a large and heterogeneous group of disorders. Many NDD risk genes are involved in modification of DNA structure and conformation otherwise known as "chromatin". The end result is that these genes control the production of RNA by a process known as "transcription" which impacts its "translation" into protein in nerve cells. In this proposal we study five distinct NDDs that are grouped together as chromatinopathies: Kabuki, Kleefstra, Gabriele-de Vries, Helsmoortel-Van der Aa, and a syndromic type of Autism Syndrome Disorder. They are caused respectively by mutations in KMT2D, EHMT1, YY1, ADNP and CHD8, which are involved in regulation of chromatin and ultimately transcription. These syndromes share overlapping clinical features, are interconnected by the molecular role of the causative genes, which are further connected by molecular partners. We hypothesize that mutations in these five genes give rise to unique as well as common downstream effects in gene transcription and translation. In brief, we will generate stem cells with mutations in the 5 genes using a method called gene editing; differentiate them into nerve cells to study functional effects on neural connectivity and network circuitry; explore the underlying molecular mechanisms using sequencing approaches that assess chromatin states, RNA transcription and protein translation; and integrate these findings to validate common molecular targets that disrupt neural network activity in NDD. Therefore, the IMPACT collaborative project (featuring labs in Europe and Canada) will reveal common converging disease mechanisms as attractive targets for therapeutic intervention. The development of such knowledge-based therapeutic interventions across individual NDDs can potentially be useful for designing interventions suitable for multiple related rare neurodevelopmental disorders.

column36: Impact of Early life MetaBolic and psychosocial strEss on susceptibility to mental Disorders; from converging epigenetic signatures to novel targets for therapeutic intervention
column37: Each year 38.2% of the EU population suffers from a mental disorder. Extensive research on the biology of stress now shows that healthy development can be derailed by excessive or prolonged activation of stress response systems in the body and brain during fetal life. Such toxic stress can have damaging effects on learning, behavior, and mental health across the lifespan. The consortium has been built to integrate basic researchers and clinicians to work on two very relevant cohorts (offspring of obese or stressed mothers) that will be here combined in a very innovative way to ask specific questions on mental health risk factors and their potential prevention. One main concept is that maternal obesity during prenatal life can trigger similar responses to maternal stress, altering developmental trajectories and increasing the risk for mental health at adulthood. It is hypothesized that maternal stress might be accompanied by inappropriate nutrition patterns which could synergize in activating stress-response systems in the developing organism. These adverse experiences can increase the likelihood of developmental delays and later health problems, including heart disease, diabetes, and depression. This consortium will assess whether common biological signals characterise early exposure to metabolic and psychological stress, affecting the long-term expression of genes involved in brain as well as immune-metabolic function, triggering mental disorders. A special emphasis will be given to long lasting epigenetic modifications, which could alter context- and time-dependent expression of genes relevant for brain function as well as peripheral biomarkers indices of immune-metabolic function that might be used in the clinic for disease prevention and health promotion during pregnancy. The Canadian team will be responsible for mapping epigenetic modifications in human blood and brain samples.

column36: Co-designing dementia diagnosis and post-diagnostic care (COGNISANCE)
column37: Despite many national guidelines for diagnosis and management of dementia, persons diagnosed with dementia and their family care partners are often dissatisfied with the diagnostic process, and receive limited post-diagnostic support. Our aims are to co-design and deliver in partnership with people with dementia, family care partners and health care professionals, toolkits and campaigns to improve the dementia diagnostic process and post-diagnostic support in Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, the UK and Poland; and to evaluate the campaigns. Work packages will: (1) explore through surveys and focus groups current experiences, barriers and facilitators to dementia diagnosis and post-diagnosis support from the perspectives of persons with dementia, care partners and health care professionals; (2) develop internationally-applicable toolkits supporting guideline implementation for the at-risk public and health care professionals; (3) devise and deliver campaigns to produce behavioural change using the aforementioned toolkits in selected regions; (4) evaluate the campaigns using the RE-AIM framework including measuring impact on the diagnosis, post-diagnosis experiences, and practitioner attitudes and behaviour; (5) develop an implementation playbook outlining how to deliver similar campaigns in other countries COGNISANCE will provide a new internationally adaptable set of recommendations and toolkits for persons with dementia, care partners, and health care practitioners on how to make the diagnostic process and post-diagnostic care as positive an experience as possible, and a playbook to assist other countries with implementing their own change campaigns.

column36: Correlation radio-pathologique dans la maladie d'Alzheimer : Identification precoce par IRM pre-mortem
column37: La maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) est une maladie degenerative qui, au vu du vieillissement croissant de la population, verra son incidence multipliee, entrainant d'importantes consequences socioeconomiques pour les patients, les proches aidants ainsi que la societe. Le diagnostic n'est invoque qu'a un stade avance de son evolution etant donne l'apparition tardive des premiers symptomes. Les dommages irreversibles au cerveau sont alors considerables et s'accumulent deja depuis plusieurs annees. De nouveaux outils sont donc imperatifs afin d'identifier les individus a risque de developper la MA avant que celle-ci ne se manifeste, permettant d'agir plus rapidement et d'en minimiser les impacts. L'imagerie par resonance magnetique (IRM) est une technique d'imagerie sans effet nefaste pour la sante qui pourrait potentiellement repondre a ce besoin. Dans le cadre de ce projet, je me concentrerai sur la capacite de l'IRM a detecter les changements structuraux causes par les lesions pathologiques de la MA et de ses comorbidites, avec une attention particuliere pour la proteine tau. Cette proteine s'accumule de facon anormale dans le cerveau des individus atteints de la maladie et semble etre fortement associee a la perte de volume cerebral observee chez ces patients. Je creerai egalement un outil pour evaluer la presence et la severite des changements cerebrovasculaires associes au vieillissement. Il est attendu que les mesures de surfaces, de volumes et d'epaisseurs des structures du cerveau permettront de detecter la presence et predire la distribution regionale des depots de proteines et des lesions vasculaires qui, pour l'instant, ne peuvent etre objectivees qu'au moment de l'autopsie. Ce projet novateur entrainera des retombees importantes, notamment en permettant aux cliniciens de poser un diagnostic precoce et d'intervenir rapidement, en plus de faciliter la recherche de nouveaux medicaments capables de ralentir ou meme guerir la maladie.

column36: Scaling up the Family Carer Decision Support Intervention: A Transnational Effectiveness-Implementation Evaluation
column37: Dementia is increasing across the world. The effect of the disease on families, caregivers and communities is an important global public health challenge. Family carers of dementia patients often make end-of-life decisions for their family members. But, they do not know if these decisions are what their family member would want. Also, staff at care homes do not have the skills and information to speak with family members about end-of-life care decisions. Both of these experiences can put the person living with dementia at-risk for care that they would not want. This project will try to reduce the uncertainty towards end-of-life decision making. It will do this by using a tool called the Family Carer Decision Support (FCDS) intervention. The tool will tell family members about the options for end-of-life care for a person living with advanced dementia. This tool has been used in a study in Northern Ireland. In Northern Ireland, it helped families to make decisions about goals of care at the end-of-life. When this tool was used, family members were happier with the care given to their family member. The goal of this study is to use the tool in homes within different countries and determine if it is helpful for family members to make decisions. When the tool is used in different countries, it will encourage the use of the tool across the world. It will also encourage families to make end-of-life care decisions. This new information about the tool will also help set-up guidelines for the tool's use.

column36: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell dysfunction linked to schizophrenia: from mechanisms towards new therapeutic strategies (project coordinator: Dr. Maria Cecilia Angulo, project acronym: OPCphrenia)
column37: Schizophrenia is a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder affecting 0.5% of the world population. Symptoms include hallucinations, delusions as well as impaired cognition, attention and social interactions. The underlying brain pathology is abnormal function of a particular type of neuron, the fast-spiking inhibitory interneuron. Recent findings also implicate the abnormal integrity of myelin, a fatty substance that coats nerve cell projections and is essential for efficient neuronal signal propagation. Myelin is produced solely by oligodendrocytes, a non-neuronal cell type in the brain. Schizophrenia patient studies suggest myelination impairments could be a critical determinant of the disease. Yet, the mechanisms linking oligodendrocyte lineage cell dysfunction to schizophrenia are unknown. Our team has discovered unique properties of interneuron myelination and critical forms of communication between interneurons and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs). Given their intrinsic regenerative capacity as the cell type responsible for generating oligodendrocytes in the adult brain, OPCs represent a potential therapeutic target for enhancing the repair of myelin deficiencies in schizophrenia. Notably, we recently discovered that OPCs derived from genetically-identified familial schizophrenia patients have impaired function and defective myelination potential. Thus, we propose that schizophrenia is likely to be, at least in part, an OPC disease ("OPCphrenia"), arising from aberrant interneuron-OPC communication. In this proposal, we will dissect interneuron-OPC communication and investigate potential therapeutic rescue strategies for aberrant schizophrenia-related OPC dysfunction by re-balancing the levels of interneuron-secreted factors. We will leverage novel methodological advances, mouse genetics, and human patient samples to advance the understanding of schizophrenia pathophysiology and identify new molecular targets for future therapeutic intervention.

column36: Integrated Parkinson Care Networks: addressing complex care in Parkinson disease in contemporary society
column37: Parkinson disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that affects 80,000 Canadians and is expected to double by 2030 worldwide. Care needs are complex. The traditional model of care delivery centred in the physician has strains and limitations. Care Integration has the potential to improve patient quality of life by tailoring the care approach, facilitating the navigation of the patient and caregiver in the complex map of care resources available in the hospital and the community. Informed by the Ontario-developed Framework for Chronic Disease Prevention and Management, we have developed an Integrated Parkinson's disease Care Network in Canada with a significant attention to the participation of patient and care partners in the design of the proposed solutions. Following this model, we are now poised to develop it in other countries partnering with seven reference Parkinson's European centers. We will start by assessing 1) What are the views and needs of people with Parkinson's and care partners in a care delivery model based at home and the community, and 2) How can the implementation of a care delivery model based at home/community be successful in different social geographies and health-economical contexts. We will also develop a novel integrated solution of health technologies to optimize complex care delivery in PD using a patient-center approach throughout its entire development. This solution, the PD virtual coach, will be a powerful tool for empowerment of patients for self-management. Using the knowledge gathered during the early project activities, we will test the real-life feasibility of a patient-centred multi-national integrated care delivery model to set the foundations of its dissemination into national healthcare systems. iCARE-PD care delivery model has the potential to improve the lives of patients with PD and potentially with other neurodegenerative disorders, with optimal use of taxpayer money across a vast geography in Europe and Canada.

column37: Atypical brain connectivity is a major contributor to the pathophysiology of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) including Autism spectrum disorders (ASD). Our proposal builds upon these observations to test the exciting hypothesis that TAO2 is a molecular hub in synapse function and ASD.

column37: Autism, characterized by highly-variable qualitative impairments in social interaction and communication skills, is a poorly understood disorder. In this proposal, we will analyze a form of autism that is caused by mutations in a single gene called ADNP. The utility of this assay will permit the assessment of the potential contribution of somatic mutations of ADNP, and other genes, to autism. column36: Multi-scale exploration of autoantibodies against synaptic receptors
column37: Psychotic disorders (PDs) encompassing schizophrenia and bipolar disorders, are major health problems worldwide. Growing evidence suggest that these major psychoses have a neurodevelopmental component involving in particular synaptic imbalance mostly between glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurotransmitter systems. However, due to their complexity our understanding of PDs remains limited. It is well-established that several converging factors are involved in these complex PDs, among which immune status, including autoimmunity, are particularly relevant. A role for autoimmune dysfunction in PDs, reported in schizophrenia almost a century ago, is supported by specific autoimmune responses to selfantigens identified in particular in PD. The importance of autoimmunity in major psychosis has been strongly reinforced as a number of syndromes characterized by global encephalopathy and by more focal psychiatric symptoms was found to result from autoimmune dysfunction, caused by anti-neuronal antibodies that alter synaptic transmission, such as NMDARAb in encephalitis. Thus, the role of the autoimmunity against neuronal receptor targets in the pathogenesis of PDs has gained tremendous support over the last years and urgently requires multidisciplinary in-depth investigations to unravel the molecular mechanisms underlying psychosis and offer new therapeutic strategies. We identified that almost 20% of patients diagnosed with schizophrenia are seropositive for these autoantibodies, opening therapeutical options for these patients. Here, we plan to tackle such a major challenge in a unique, complementary and synergistic consortium of clinical and basic research experts, who strongly contributed to our current understanding of autoimmunity in brain disorders. Our objective is to uncover how NMDAR-Ab underliesPDs in seropositive NMDAR-Ab patients, using a unique and multi-scale combination of experimental approaches, from pre-clinical experiments to clinical exploration.

column36: A novel paradigm for effective and safer treatment of schizophrenia: biased (ant)agonists with a characterized polypharmacological profile
column37: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a severe disease affecting 1-2% of the population. Current treatment is associated to side effects such as motor coordination problems, a feeling of the mind slowing down, abnormal electrical activity in the brain, altered heart rhythm, among many others. In addition, a high percentage of patients do not respond (30%) or only partially (additional 30%) to treatment. There is therefore a real need for developing better drugs. The drugs currently used to treat SZ are antipsychotics that act primarily through receptors that belong to a large family of proteins, the G protein-coupled receptors. They are present at the surface of neurons where they recognize and transduce the information of neurotransmitters. One of the main target of antipsychotic drugs is a receptor binding serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood control. However, these drugs are not fully selective and they also act on closely related receptors, the monoamine receptors, resulting in a polypharmacological profile. However, the relative contribution of each receptor to the beneficial and undesired effects is poorly understood. Moreover, each of these receptors control multiple cellular signaling cascades that are differentially regulated by distinct drugs. This phenomenon of 'biased signalling' is an important aspect of drug action. We therefore propose to develop chemical probes with defined biased and polypharmacology profiles to interrogate which signalling activities are responsible for alleviating the different SZ symptoms and which ones underlie the various side effects. For this purpose, we assembled an international team of experts with complementary know-how in computational and medicinal chemistry, molecular pharmacology and cell signalling as well as animal model of SZ. In addition to provide highly original insights into the mode of action of antipsychotics, these studies should open the way to the design of better and safer therapeutics for the treatment of SZ.

column37: ALS is the most common motor neuron disease. It is characterized by the death of motor neurons (MNs) in the brain and spinal cord. In this regard, the present application seeks to develop and validate previously unavailable experimental model systems to study ALS pathophysiology based on both neuronal and glial cells derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) obtained from ALS patients or non-ALS controls. This project involves academic partners with solid expertise in ALS, iPSC technology and high-throughput ("omics") approaches. This unique combined international discovery effort will allow the assessment of the roles played by energy metabolism and immune pathways in ALS pathogenesis and their potential as therapeutic targets. Achieving these objectives will lead to new advances into the study of ALS pathophysiology and will contribute to the emerging field of ALS disease modeling based on disease-relevant human iPSC-derived cells. column36: Violence against women migrants and refugees: Analysing causes and effective policy response
column37: Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) is a major infringement of women's human rights, and an obstacle to sustainable development as set out in the SDGs. SGBV against migrant and refugee women is widespread, but often remains invisible and under-analysed both in academic research and policy-making. This research will take an intersectional approach to understand SGBV in the context of migration, analysing the ways in which discriminations and inequalities based on gender, race, nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity and age, interact to make certain women more vulnerable to SGBV and less able to access support and services for survivors than others. SGBV may be exacerbated by policies aiming to restrict migration, or to increase control of borders, which can push women into adopting dangerous routes to arrive in their country of destination. Conflict and the risks of migration may also render women vulnerable to trafficking and sexual exploitation. Conditions of reception, and policies for integration in receiving countries may also lead to increased risk of SGBV for migrant and refugee women. But these women are not just "victims", and their strategies and agency should also be explored. In sum while we know that female migrants and refugees are particularly exposed to violence we lack a systematic understanding of the underlying dynamics that (re)produce patterns of violence. It is this gap that the research seeks to fill in order to make policy recommendations for reducing these women's vulnerability to SGBV and increasing their access to services.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibres in the wall of arteries. Atherosclerotic plaques develop slowly over time. They gradually encroach onto the interior of blood vessels, and only become symptomatic when a blood vessel is obstructed by 70% or more. A more serious situation arises when the atherosclerotic plaque ruptures suddenly. This happens because the contents of the plaque include fatty deposits that provide poor resistance to daily wear and tear. If a large fatty deposit is accompanied by a thin cap (the cap forms a protective fibrous layer between the atherosclerotic plaque and the interior of the blood vessel), the risk of rupture is enhanced. When a rupture occurs, the contents of the atherosclerotic plaque are exposed to the blood flowing in the vessel, leading to the formation of a blood clot within the vessel. This may completely and suddenly block the vessel, causing heart attack or stroke. Our proposed research will investigate a new treatment option that would reinforce the plaque cap, rendering plaques less susceptible to rupture, based on molecules that influence protein synthesis within cells.

Morphine and its derivatives bind and activate at least three subtypes of G protein-coupled receptors, the mu (MOP), delta (DOP) and kappa (KOP) opioid receptors. Although these three receptor subtypes possess analgesic properties, the actions of the majority of opioids used clinically target MOP. In contrast to the latter, activation of DOP leads to few unwanted effects. Under normal conditions (i.e. in healthy animals), the analgesic potency of delta selective agonists is lower than that of morphine. In recent years, however, it has been shown that under certain conditions, the activation of DOP can counter the painful sensations with an efficacy close to morphine. In my laboratory we are interested in studying the mechanisms regulating the trafficking of DOP toward the plasma membrane of nociceptive neurons under conditions of chronic pain. A better understanding of these mechanisms could help develop strategies to increase the effectiveness of pain therapies and thus improve the quality of life of patients.

column37: Vulnerable populations that experience social precarity tend to have a chronic SUD and require long-term services that are adapted to their complex care needs. column36: Targeting potassium channel to disrupt the cellular hierarchy and suppress malignant growth of pediatric brain tumor
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The conventional treatment, which combines surgery, irradiation and chemotherapy, is toxic to normal brain cells and produces life-long side effects such as lowered intelligence, early aging, and increased chance to develop other cancer. Therefore, identifying the molecules that fuel aggressive MB growth but are dispensable for normal cells is key to develop cancer-specific therapy. Ions, such as potassium and chloride, are essential constituents of human cell. Ion channel proteins form tiny pores to control ion to move in or out of cell. The movement of ions can change the electrical and physical properties of the cells, which control biological processes including tumor growth. We recently found that potassium channel Eag2 is required for MB growth, discovered a drug as a novel Eag2 blocker, and showed that the drug had marked anti-MB efficacy in mice and a MB patient. Therefore, we pioneer in identifying ion channels as novel regulators for MB and developing ion channel-targeting therapy. Brain tumor-initiating cells (BTICs) are rare cells that generate multiple tumor cell types to fuel the malignant brain tumor growth. Since BTICs are insensitive to irradiation and conventional chemotherapy, they are the roots for tumor initiation and recurrence. While Eag2 regulates the growth of non-BTICs, our unpublished study identified that potassium channel Kcnb2 is present in MB BTICs. We discovered that genetic deletion of Kcnb2 reduced the number of BTICs and suppressed MB growth, but it did not overtly alter the normal development of mice. We propose to define the mechanism by which Kcnb2 regulates BTICs and MB growth, and determine the therapeutic efficacy of combining Kcnb2 inhibition and conventional therapy. By completing our studies, we will uncover the unrealized potential of targeting ion channels to treat brain cancer by attacking the root of brain tumor growth and recurrence.

column36: Unitization: a strategy to circumvent memory deficits in aging and amnesia.
column37: Memory is the repository of our personal histories and stored knowledge, and it is essential to planning our futures and maintaining a sense of self. By 2036, almost a quarter of Canadians will be aged 65 and older, and many will experience memory decline. As memory declines, other cognitive functions are affected, as are daily activities. To support our aging population we must develop simple, cost-effective cognitive strategies to alleviate age-related memory declines. We recently discovered that a cognitive strategy, unitization, supports memory function in older adults and even in cases of amnesia who have severe impairments in memory. Through unitization, information about multiple items is represented as a single unit through an interaction between new and existing knowledge. In order to ultimately use unitization more widely to improve cognition in memory-impaired individuals, we must first understand what level of cognitive and neural function is needed for the strategy to be successfully used. We will use neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies to examine the cognitive functions and brain regions that correlate with the successful use of unitization. This will allow us to predict which people would be most likely to benefit from unitization. Additionally, we will examine if unitization can support inference, a cognitive function that relies on memory. The ability to infer information beyond what is directly observed is essential to daily living, as it plays a role in problem solving and in guiding behavior in social interactions. Successful use of unitization to alleviate impairments in inference will show how unitization has broad potential to support declining cognition, allowing older adults to maintain their independence and quality of life for longer.

column37: Nowadays, treatment of respiratory insufficiency by mechanical respiratory support is delivered non-invasively whenever possible. A nasal mask or small nasal cannulae are used to avoid the complications related to the traditional albeit more invasive placement of a tube deep into the trachea (wind pipe). The air mechanically insufflated at positive pressure into the nasal passages and the throat however does not always flows freely into the lungs. Our research program uses preterm lambs to understand the interplay between non-invasive respiratory support, laryngeal and esophageal function in preterm infants. Our team is internationally recognized for having a unique capacity to perform such animal model studies. The expected results ultimately will assist the clinician in selecting the optimal respiratory support for premature infants.

column36: Structural analysis of mycobacterial oxidative phosphorylation and targeting it to treat tuberculosis
column37: Cells use oxygen to convert chemical energy from diverse sources into the universal energy currency ATP before use. This process, called oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos), is performed by a series of large molecular machines that reside in cell membranes. In OxPhos, electrons stripped from fuel molecules ("oxidation") are passed between several of the molecular machines (Complexes I, II, III, and IV) with oxygen serving as the final electron acceptor, reducing it to water. During electron transfer Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from one side of the membrane to the other, establishing a chemical and electrical proton gradient. A final machine, known as ATP synthase, allows protons back across the membrane, using the energy released to make ATP. While example atomic-resolution structures have now been determined for all OxPhos complexes it is still not clear how electron transfer is coupled to the proton pumping that powers aerobic life. Understanding OxPhos has important biomedical implications. Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the organism Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a leading causes of death worldwide and an important health issue in Canada's indigenous populations. The breakthrough TB drug bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase. Mycobacterial Complexes III and IV form an unusual supercomplex (CIII2CIV2) with a dramatically different structure than the human Complexes III and IV. This structure is both unique and essential, making it an attractive target for developing TB drugs. We will determine structures for CIII2CIV2 and ATP synthase from mycobacteria. The unique CIII2CIV2, which carries out two thirds of the electron transfer pathway in a self contained stable assembly, provides a valuable tool for understanding universal principles of electron transfer. Structures of CIII2CIV2 and mycobacterial ATP synthase in complex with approved and candidate antimycobacterial drugs will provide key insights into how these drugs work and can be improved.

column37: Malaria is one of the world's most common infectious diseases, with approximately 274 million cases each year and 400 000 deaths, and thus represents one of the most devastating global public health problems. The lack of an effective vaccine, the emergence of resistance to first-line drugs like artemisinines, combined with the small number of suitable new drugs against the malaria parasite demonstrate the urgent need for the development and implementation of novel intervention strategies in the form of drugs, vector control measures and an effective vaccine. Indeed, it is expected that if the trend in malaria prevalence stays on its current upwards course, the death rate could double in the next twenty years. Invasion of a red blood cell by Plasmodium falciparum parasites is an essential step in the malaria lifecycle and host response to parasite antigens are an important component of human malarial immunity. Consequently, the molecular players involved in erythrocyte invasion are key targets for both therapeutic and vaccine-based strategies to block parasite development. Several of these invasion proteins are stored in the apical complex of the parasite, a structure containing secretory organelles called dense granules, micronemes and rhoptries, and are released at different times during invasion. Because of its essential role, interfering with the generation of the apical complex represents a very attractive target for the design of a new kind of antimalarial. Our studies will focus on trying to understand how the parasite directs proteins to the different structures of the apical complex. Understanding this complex process will likely provide a wealth of new targets for the development of strategies to block apical complex generation and preventing malaria pathogenesis.

column36: The discovery of new antibiotics derived from inhibitors of sporulation
column37: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, sepsis and various kinds of infection that result from surgery or in patients whose immune system is compromised by chemotherapy. They are therefore at the front line of virtually all aspects of modern medicine. The efficacy of these incredible drugs, mostly discovered during the period from 1940-60, is being rapidly eroded through the antibiotic resistance. As a result, new antibiotics are desperately needed if we are to sustain our current standard of care. But the classical approaches to antibiotics discovery are not working all that well. The reason for this is that all of the available molecules in the world have been tested for the inhibition of growth of pathogens. New approaches are therefore desperately needed. We have discovered that the filamentous bacteria of the genus Streptomyces provide a fascinating alternative approach. Because these bacteria are filamentous in structure, they use many elements of the core molecular machinery (cell wall biosynthesis, cell division, chromosome segregation etc) differently than rod shaped or coccoid bacteria - which include almost all of the pathogens. Many processes which are essential for viability in pathogenic bacteria are employed primarily for sporulation in the streptomycetes. Our hypothesis therefore, is that screening for inhibitors of sporulation in Streptomyces has the potential to reveal novel inhibitors of these core processes and that these inhibitors might be developed as antibiotics against "conventional" bacteria. We have tested this hypothesis and thereby discovered three novel antibiotics: EN-7, Min-1 and Fil-1. In this project we will further develop these compounds in the hopes that we can provide valuable leads for fighting infectious disease.

column36: Molecular control of neural stem cell fate decisions
column37: The neocortex is the region of the brain where higher cognitive functioning occurs, allowing us to perceive stimuli in the environment and have conscious thought. The original dogma was that new neurons could not be generated after embryonic development since there were no stem cells to replace lost neurons. However, more recent studies have identified a pool of neural stem cells that reside in the adult brain. Moreover, it has been found that these stem cells are first born in the embryonic period, persisting in an inactive state until adulthood. We have been studying how neural stem cells decide to be inactive, or divide and differentiate into neurons in the embryonic brain. These studies have focused on proneural genes, which we found mark a pool of slow-dividing neural stem cells in the embryo and adult. We now try to understand how the proneural genes control whether neural stem cells remain inactive, divide or differentiate. We have three aims in this study. In the first aim we examine how slow-dividing stem cells that express these proneural genes respond to a brain injury, and trace their embryonic progeny. In the second aim, we ask how these proneural genes can be manipulated to induce neural stem cells to produce new neurons in development and after brain injury. In the third aim, we begin to model the roles of these proneural genes in a primate system, using monkey tissue and generating brain organoids from human cells as a surrogate model system. These studies are important because re-invigoration of these dormant stem cells by manipulating the proneural genes may aid brain repair.

column37: Some 20% of youth have mental health/addiction (MHA) disorders, and adolescence is an optimal time to intervene. Yet, youth are challenged to access effective services in a timely way. However, these efforts are advancing in the absence of rigorous research data demonstrating effectiveness. The study will randomly assign 450 youth to receive either hospital-based care or ICCT services to compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the two service pathways for youth with MHA challenges. We have already successfully recruited 112 youth into the study as of August 2018 and have progressed to five hospitals now actively recruiting participants. As provincial, national, and international efforts to implement ICCT-type models of care advance under significant public and private investment, it is critical that robust data be collected to examine their effectiveness. By providing rapid access to integrated, collaborative care geared to youth needs and preferences in youth-friendly community settings, this project is expected to substantially improve the mental health of this population, making Ontario a leader in innovative systems of care.

column36: Repairing the brain of sick newborns: From bench to bedside
column37: At birth, some babies experienced a condition called asphyxia, which means that their brain and other organs did not receive enough blood and/or oxygen. This life-threatening condition accounts for 23% of all babies' deaths around the world, and often leads to cerebral palsy and trouble with learning and functioning in everyday life. At this time, no treatment is available to repair the brain damage in these babies. Sildenafil (Viagra(R)) already is given safely to babies suffering from increased blood pressure in their lungs for other reasons than asphyxia at birth. Our recent studies in an animal model of asphyxia at birth suggested that sildenafil may improve the damage to the brain. Also, our recent pilot study with human babies showed that it is feasible to give sildenafil to babies who suffer from asphyxia at birth. We hypothesize that (1) sildenafil can repair the damage to a baby's brain by stimulating the growth of new nerve cells and decreasing brain swelling; and that (2) sildenafil can be safely increased up to 6 mg/kg/day in these babies and may improve how their brain and heart/lungs work. We will use a rat model of asphyxia at birth to study the mechanisms involved in repairing the brain after it is damaged. We also will determine the optimal dose of sildenafil that can be given to human babies who suffered from asphyxia at birth to improve their brain, heart, and lungs. This project will enable us to understand the repair mechanisms involved in the damaged baby's brain after asphyxia at birth and to determine whether sildenafil is a promising treatment for repairing this damage. This project may provide new solutions for these babies to reduce the consequences of asphyxia at birth and improve their future life. Thus, it may help many families around the world who are dealing with this devastating condition.

column36: Role of ELKS1 and Rab17 in Differential Antigen Sorting and MHC II Trafficking Following Efferocytosis and Phagocytosis
column37: Our immune system has the incredible ability to launch immune responses which target specific molecular signatures within pathogens. However, this highly specific targeting requires careful control over which molecules are targeted, as the accidental targeting of a self-molecule can lead to debilitating diseases in which a patient's immune system destroys their own body. Our immune systems have multiple levels of control, each intended to ensure that responses against pathogens are strongly activated, while those against harmless agents - e.g. the billions of cells that our bodies turn-over daily - are suppressed. We have recently discovered a previously unknown pathway which allows immune cells to "decide" whether the molecules from recently encountered objects are processed in a way which allows for them to be presented to the immune system, versus processing them in a way which avoids presentation and thus prevents activation of the immune system. In this grant we will further explore this pathway, to determine how it functions and its role in mediating the activation of the immune system.

column36: Gender Outcomes INternational Group: to Further Well-being Development (GOING-FWD)
column37: Background: Beyond biological sex, gender is increasingly recognized as a pivotal determinant of health. However, there are no standardized gender measurements. We hypothesize that gender-related factors and their effect will vary substantially between countries and diseases. Aims: The overarching aims of this large Consortium are to integrate sex and gender dimensions in applied health research, to evaluate their impact on clinical cost-sensitive outcomes and patients reported outcomes related to quality of life in noncommunicable diseases including cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease, chronic kidney disease and neurological disease. We also aim to construct innovative ways to disseminate the application of gender measurement towards personalized approaches to chronic disease prevention, diagnosis and treatment. Methods: With a five-country transatlantic network comprised of 30 investigators, we will benchmark innovative solutions to measure gender in retrospective cohorts. Based on consensus, we will develop a framework to identify gender-related factors, as well as cost-sensitive and patients reported outcomes and measure their associations in 32 accessible cohorts of patients affected by cardiovascular, chronic kidney and neurological diseases and metabolic syndrome. Large database analysis and when appropriate machine learning approaches will allow the derivation of pan and within country disease specific gender scores which will be validated through e-Health and m-Health applications in prospective disease groups. Educational modules will be developed to promote awareness, implementation and dissemination. Innovation: As a five-country multidisciplinary Consortium with access to granular large databases, we are uniquely positioned to harness an innovative methodology that will provide a framework to close gender gaps in chronic disease management and promote knowledge transfer in the scientific community and clinical practice.

column36: Evolving gender differences in health & care across cohorts
column37: The inevitability of physical and functional decline is not uniform with ageing. Unlike the biological impact of time, social and individual circumstances (eg wealth, access to resources, social capital) are malleable via public policies. Limited research suggests their effect on health is entwined with sex/gender. Understanding social determinants and what health outcomes older adults view as central to ageing successfully despite chronic disease is essential to fostering health equality. For example, explaining the gender paradox in health (despite being poorer than men women live longer albeit reporting more suffering) could inform policies to equalize underlying social differentials. FUTUREGEN will examine current and future social circumstances that contribute to sex/gender inequalities in the health of older adults and their uneven access to care-giving/receiving. We will 1) develop research methods and measures that incorporate the complexity of individual roles and affiliations (eg within the category 'women' lies the variability of access to resources, autonomy at home and work, social support, early life adversity, etc.) 2) apply these novel methods to analysing comparable European and Canadian datasets that better embed cultural norms than does single country data & 3) obtain older people's definitions of healthy and successful ageing through qualitative research. All steps will be integrated in a back and forth manner and reviewed and challenged by an international expert Sounding Board. Our international research team brings awareness of the impact of different cultural milieux on health (ie a varied set of cultural eyes to interpret findings) as well as the intellectual and methodological richness of multiple disciplines (social sciences, economics, medicine). In addition to scholarly papers and policy advice we will deliver a manual & two workshops for young academics on methods for studying the depth and breadth of sex/gender and health equality.

column36: Microglia and cognitive impairments in offspring exposed to gestational diabetes mellitus
column37: Maternal diabetes is the most common complication in pregnancy affecting up to 18% of pregnancies. Maternal diabetes increases offspring risk for developing various health problems. Population studies have demonstrated that maternal diabetes increases offspring risk to have learning and memory deficits, and behavioral issues. Maternal diabetes is associated with elevated inflammation status, which can be detrimental for the developing brain. We propose that fetal brain immune cells, which role is to protect brain from pathogens and toxins, are chronically activated and their responses are subverted and become toxic leading to reduced neuronal connections. Our study will identify the role of brain immune cells and the mechanism by how they can impair brain cells function. We will also assess whether maternal gestational diabetes differentially affects male and female offspring. Our ultimate goal is to identify targets for drug development and promote healthy brain development and, thus prevent cognitive impairments in children of mothers with gestational diabetes.
