column36: Targeting Cell Cycle Checkpoints in Glioma
column37: Glioblastoma multiforme is an aggressive brain cancer of which there are currently no effective treatment options. Glioblastoma cells have very rapid mutation rates and the tumour itself is comprised of a mix of different cells with differing capabilities of driving tumour recurrence. Research has shown that only a small population of cells (called Brain Tumour Initiating Cells; BTICs) within the tumour are the most deadly, but these cells are also insensitive to available therapies. The Porter lab has found a protein, called Spy1 that is important in the expansion of the BTIC population. Spy1 is highly expressed in patients with glioblastoma, and early pre-clinical data suggests that targeting its mechanism may make an exciting therapy for these patients. This project will determine how the Spy1 protein is involved in driving these BTICs to divide and it will test the potential of targeting Spy1 for treatment of this aggressive form of cancer.

column36: Transcriptional control of disease modifiers for the treatment of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common form of inherited skeletal muscle disorders. There is no cure, and DMD leads to a debilitating loss of skeletal muscle mass with a limited life expectancy. Standard treatment regimens are associated with significant side effects and only target the symptoms of the disease and not the underlying causes. Despite the lack of functional dystrophin being a common feature of DMD, there is great variability in disease progression due to the differential presence of other proteins which contribute to the severity of the disease. We will explore the potential of a revolutionary genome engineering technology called CRISPR/Cas9 to modulate protein expression of disease modifiers associated with DMD. Specifically, we will use the technology in cell and animal models to increase the expression of utrophin - a structural protein that can compensate for the loss of dystrophin. Also, we will design strategies to decrease expression of osteopontin - a protein known to enhance the severity of DMD. This research will provide the necessary evidence base to support further exploratory studies in using CRISPR/Cas9 as a new treatment option for patients with muscular dystrophies.

column36: Hearts in Rhythm Organization (HiRO): Improving detection and treatment of inherited heart rhythm disorders to prevent sudden death
column37: Inherited heart rhythm disorders include Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. These conditions affect 150,000 Canadians and are the major cause of sudden cardiac death in the young. Early diagnosis of these disorders can provide the most effective care, including personalized exercise restriction, personalized medications and more appropriate use of implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) to regulate heart rhythms. These conditions pose a high risk for cardiac arrest and sudden death, and new methods for identifying those at risk are urgently needed. The primary goal of this research is to develop more effective methods for predicting who are at greatest risk of a serious cardiac event. To do this, we will use healthcare data collected from participants in the Hearts in Rhythm Organization (HiRO) research database. This includes inherited heart rhythm disorder patients from 19 specialized adult and pediatric clinics across Canada. Our additional goal is to create a patient-oriented research program that addresses the current and future needs of these patients, their families and their communities. In the long-term, we expect this research to result in improved screening practices to better identify at-risk patients and individualize their treatment to prevent and decrease the tragedy of sudden cardiac death. Involving patients in the research process will ensure that we are addressing issues that are most pertinent to their well-being. We envision that this will improve communication between the healthcare provider and patients, so that patients are well informed about their condition and ensuring that they can take an active role in managing their health and improve their quality of life.

column36: Non-invasive multi-omics urinary biomarkers to guide prostate cancer management
column37: Men with early prostate cancer can elect to be treated aggressively with surgery or radiation (with a risk of side effects), or be watched under an "Active Surveillance" regimen (AS). Although we have shown that the likelihood of prostate cancer spreading when being watched on AS is quite low, it is not zero, as some men will progress to having more aggressive disease, needing even more aggressive treatment with a lower chance of success. In addition, AS requires invasive biopsies which have a chance of serious side effects including infection. This is why a non-invasive test is needed that will help us determine upfront which men are more likely to need treatment so we can offer it right away. In this research, we are looking at factors secreted into the urine ('biomarkers') by the prostate gland, that we believe can identify men on AS that actually have aggressive cancer. We will use one of the largest and most mature AS populations in the world to try to answer these questions. Ultimately we hope to prove our urine biomarkers will provide an effective non-invasive way to differentiate those men with early disease that can be watched from those with higher grade disease that should be treated. This personalized approach will improve the long term survival and quality of life of men diagnosed with prostate cancer.

column36: Identifying Key Prescribing CASCADes in the Elderly: A Transnational Initiative on Drug Safety
column37: Prescribing cascades occur when a health care provider misinterprets the side effect of a drug as a new medical condition and prescribes a second, potentially unnecessary, harmful drug to address the side effect. Identifying prescribing cascades represents an important, actionable, strategy to improve the health of older adults. Adverse events are generally more common in women than in men. To inform tailored interventions, there is a need to understand potential sex and gender differences in how cascades develop and are managed. In this transnational study, an interdisciplinary team of experts in sex, gender, and ageing will respond to this critical gap by applying a sex and gender lens to complementary health data from four countries. Specifically we plan to evaluate whether men and women develop prescribing cascades in the same way, and if there are differences in how they present with adverse event(s) from a prescribing cascade. We will use administrative and clinical data on older adults to calculate sex-stratified prevalence rates for three prescribing cascades prioritized by our collaborating partners. We will also interview prescribers, patients, and caregivers to explore how socially constructed gender roles contribute to the experience, presentation, and management of prescribing cascades. Findings will improve our understanding of how adverse drug events are different between older women and men and inform the development and dissemination of tailored knowledge translation products to reduce the frequency and impact of prescribing cascades.

column36: Risky decision making as a cause, consequence and treatment target for addiction.
column37: Whether someone is dependent on a chemical substance like cocaine, or has developed a behavioural addiction such as gambling disorder, the maladaptive choice to pursue the addiction at the expense of other goals lies at the heart of the problem. Indeed, individuals with an addiction disorder, or who later develop problems with addiction, score poorly on laboratory-based decision-making tests such as the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT) that involve the weighing of costs and benefits. One hypothesis is that decision-making impairments may be compounded as the addiction develops because of the way in which addictive drugs, and also engagement in addictive behaviours, affect brain function, biasing the decision-making process in favour of the addiction. Choosing to abstain from the addictive substance or behaviour then becomes really hard. We have successfully developed an animal model of cost/benefit decision making based on the IGT: the rat Gambling Task (rGT). On both human and animal tests, subjects must choose between four different options, each of which is associated with different amounts of potential reward and loss. By avoiding high-risk, high-reward options, subjects can maximise gains. Most rats develop this optimal strategy, although some animals instead favour the risky options. These risk-preferring rats are uniquely and adversely affected by taking cocaine: their decision making gets worse and they show increased drug-seeking in withdrawal indicative of greater relapse risk. Adding sound and light cues when the rats win on this gambling task significantly increases the proportion of rats biased towards the risky options. We now want to use this model to understand why the addition of these "bells and whistles" potentiates risky choice and addiction vulnerability, and harness that knowledge to pilot potential therapies for addiction.

column36: IMproved Personalized medicine through machine LEarning in MENTal disorders
column37: Psychotic disorders are severe mental illnesses with early onset, frequently chronic course and often lifelong impairment. As a consequence, they cause an enormous healthcare burden, costing close to Euro100 billion annually in Europe alone. The biology of these illnesses is insufficiently understood and no objective tools exist to aid in diagnosis or treatment selection. This leads to long periods of inadequate and ineffective treatment, significantly limiting the opportunity for achieving more optimal clinical outcomes. To address this, IMPLEMENT will develop a translational research framework that identifies biomarkers for treatment-relevant stratification of the most severe psychotic disorder, schizophrenia. Building on known candidates, IMPLEMENT will use advanced machine learning on high-dimensional multi-OMICS and brain scans to identify illness-associated profiles indexing patient subgroups. Using big data approaches (n > 60,000), IMPLEMENT will explore the impact of genetic risk and neurodevelopmental processes on the formation of biological subgroups and use clinical studies of conventional antipsychotic treatment and innovative treatment approaches to tune subgroup profiles towards clinical utility. The IMPLEMENT framework will incorporate preclinical validation to leverage neurobiological understanding and optimize biological subgroup profiles. The clinical utility of these profiles will be validated in independent clinical samples and prospectively recruited subjects. IMPLEMENT will integrate these efforts with ICT development, to optimize the use of high-dimensional datasets across diverse repositories, to optimally harmonize data for personalized medicine investigations and safeguard patient privacy. Overall, IMPLEMENT will provide the basis for biologically-informed personalized medicine approaches in schizophrenia, addressing an enormous unmet medical need in an area of medicine in which currently no robust clinical stratification tools exist.

column36: Engineering of a probiotic bacterium for precise microbiome editing
column37: We propose to develop a safe-to-use, efficient and programmable conjugative probiotic (COP) as a highly innovative tool to precisely edit the microbiome and fight multidrug resistant pathogens. The E. coli Nissle 1917 probiotic strain, which has previously been shown to be clinically safe, is used as the COP chassis for our experiments. COP bacteria also include potent bacterial conjugation machineries for high-efficiency delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 systems into the microbiota. The CRISPR-Cas9 system can easily be programmed to cleave DNA simply by providing custom guide RNA (gRNA) spacer sequences that match the desired target sites. Targeting DNA sequences located in a bacterial chromosome leads to cell death by compromising genome integrity. The CRISPR-Cas9 system can also cure cells from plasmids carrying antibiotic resistance or virulence genes, thereby "disarming" potentially dangerous bacteria by restoring susceptibility to antibiotics. Unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics, the COP system is designed to be highly specific, with selectivity conferred by carefully chosen CRISPR-Cas9 target sequences and tuning of the host range through the selection of appropriate COP conjugative machineries. This new technology would also constitute a powerful microbiome manipulation tool for fundamental research, and to progressively advance towards clinical applications. Once established, this innovative method could have a significant impact on medicine by eventually offering a new tool to treat dysbiosis or as an alternative to antimicrobials for the prevention or treatment of many infectious diseases.

column36: Individualizing the hemodialysis access strategy: addressing knowledge gaps to promote shared decision-making
column37: Hemodialysis requires a reliable method of connecting the patient to the blood-purification machine, called vascular access. The two most common forms of vascular access are catheters and fistulas. A catheter is a plastic tube inserted into a vein in the neck; a fistula is a vein surgically connected to an artery in the arm that is accessed by needles. Many expert committees consider fistulas the preferred form of vascular access and actively promote them. However, these recommendations are based on studies that may have overestimated the benefits of fistulas and underestimated the potential risks associated with procedures required to achieve and maintain fistula patency. We do not have sufficient data to provide patients with enough information to allow them to make an informed decision about pursuing a fistula creation attempt or using a hemodialysis catheter without attempting a fistula. We cannot offer decision support to promote shared decision-making because we do not know patient, caregiver and healthcare provider decision needs. We will study people who start hemodialysis with a catheter in six large renal programs in Canada. We will follow participants from the start of hemodialysis to determine the benefits and harms associated with attempting fistula creation, and whether they vary with sex, age or presence of disease conditions. We will also assess decision needs of patients and caregivers, and healthcare providers. This project will leverage multicenter, high-quality data describing vascular access procedures and our expertise in this area of research. We will provide important data on potential benefits and possible harms of attempting or avoiding fistulas and will identify the attributes of hemodialysis access-related decisions that are important to patients and caregivers, and healthcare providers in order to inform the design of a tool to support decision-making about the vascular access for hemodialysis.

column36: Mapping anti-mitochondrial antibodies in systemic lupus erythematosus
column37: Mitochondria are structures inside living cells essential to life. Mitochondria have their own genetic material called DNA and a membrane with the only source of cardiolipin in humans. If released outside their protective cell into the blood circulation, they may be recognized as foreign by our immune system and cause confusion in our immune response. We observed that the number of mitochondria outside of cells in the plasma of persons with lupus was significantly higher than in controls and that free mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) was abnormally high. As persons with lupus develop antibodies to several self-antigens and, interestingly to the mitochondrial cardiolipin, we looked at whether the immune system reacted to mitochondria in lupus. For this, we reviewed the literature on known anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) and we developed a new system to detect newly described AMA. column36: Rational antiepileptic drug selection by combining gene network and ICT analysis (RAISE-GENIC)
column37: Epilepsy is a common disease affecting >70 million people worldwide. Patients with epilepsy suffer from recurrent seizures that lead to injuries, death, social stigma as well as job and driving restrictions. Epilepsy is treated with anti-seizure drugs with the aim to stop the seizures. Although many anti-seizure drugs are available, we are currently unable to predict which drug works best in a particular patient. Therefore, we must select the drugs based on trial and error. Unfortunately, though, using this approach typically means that less than one in two patients become seizure free with the first drug, which then leads to a cycle of selecting another drug, testing its anti-seizure effects for several weeks or months before another drug can be tried. It would revolutionize epilepsy treatment if we were able to predict the anti-seizure drug with the highest likelihood of success in an individual patient (personalized medicine). We aim to achieve this by combining two strategies. The first strategy examines human brain cells which are generated from skin cells of adult donors. These cells are treated with four different anti-seizure drugs (carbamazepine, valproate, lacosamide, levetiracetam) and we will investigate how specific genes respond to being exposed to these drugs. We will then look at available genetic data from 1382 patients and examine if changes in these genes correlate with a drugs's ability to stop seizures. The second approach will perform a "big data analysis" incorporating details on the patient's epilepsy, genetic data, brain wave signals and brain imaging to predict treatment effect. Using these large sources of complementary data, we will develop tools to help doctors and patients predict the effect of the different anti-seizure drugs. Subsequently, we will test in an independent cohort of 100 patients if the tool correctly predicts the best anti-seizure drug. Finally, we will prepare a clinical study to establish the tool in clinical practice.

column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 1 in 100 live births and is the leading cause of neonatal deaths related to birth defects. Children with complex CHD account for a disproportionately large healthcare burden in society. To find the missing cause of CHD, we will use whole genome sequencing (WGS) which allows exploration of the entire genome to find gene defects that cause CHD and determine if and how these gene defects predict severity of disease and outcomes. Canadian, Dutch and German partners have established a consortium that leverages DNA samples from population biorepositories to create the largest cohort of CHD for WGS. We will sequence over 1500 children and adults with TOF/TGA. Preliminary data has identified novel causes of CHD not previously reported e.g. defects in new genes, defects in multiple genes, and defects outside of genes in regions that control gene expression. Thus WGS will help unravel the genetic architecture of CHD in a way not previously possible. We will use this information to determine if type and number of gene defects predicts which patients will have a mild versus severe phenotype. This information can then be used to advise families about chances of having another affected child and potentially reduce this risk by pre-implantation genetic diagnosis. It can also inform which patients should undergo fetal interventions that prevent the heart disease from progressing to severe forms. Together, this can help to reduce the burden of CHD and to improve outcomes in this vulnerable population.

column36: Functional Genomics of Neurodegenerative Diseases: Defining Molecular Pathogenesis and Targets for Biomarkers and Personalised Therapies
column37: Neurodegenerative dementias are the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, affecting >24 million people at a cost of >US$172 billion annually. Despite a lot of effort, apart from a handful of mildly effective symptomatic treatments there are no proven ways of stopping these diseases. This proposal addresses takes an innovative approach to develop therapies that address this unmet need. The program is built upon our recent success in identifying genes that carry DNA variants that increase risk of dementia. We have noticed that these genes cluster into functional groups ("cellular pathways"). Two of the largest clusters are of particular interest. One cluster regulates the function of brain inflammatory cells (microglia), which search the brain for damaged cells and aggregated proteins. Another function of these cells is to prune unwanted nerve connections (synapses). The other cluster contains proteins that can change their conformation in order to facilitate key cellular functions (such as making proteins in synapses that are crucial for memory, or regulating the function of microglial cells). Because these clusters contain multiple different genes with DNA sequence changes that increase risk of dementia, it is clear that these clusters govern pathways that are very important in causing synaptic damage leading to dementia. A vital clue is that some of the genes in these pathways also contain variants that actually protect the patient from developing clinical disease. This clearly suggests that mimicking the effect of these protective genetic variants could be a way of preventing/slowing the progression of these diseases. The current program will therefore develop a better understanding of the components in these disease causing pathways, understand how they are regulated, and identify specific components that could be used as molecular targets for treatments that would make the pathway function normally.

column36: Personalization of Long term Treatment in Bipolar Disorder
column37: We propose a set of studies to improve the selection of long term treatment for bipolar disorder. Bipolar disorder is a severe psychiatric condition characterized by periods of mania and depression as well as by changes in brain structure and function. People with bipolar disorder have high rates of disability and are at risk of suicide if not receiving proper treatment. Long term treatment with mood stabilizing medications is the cornerstone of the disease management. However, even the most effective treatment, lithium, is effective in less than one third of all patients. To select among several available treatment options, clinicians rely on trial-and-error: different medications are given for months at a time until an effective one is found. Finding clinical and biological markers associated with good treatment response is expected to shorten this otherwise lengthy and inefficient process. To find such markers, we have established a partnership of specialized clinical programs and expert molecular-genetic laboratories. Our proposal combines novel techniques of studies of nerve cells produced from induced pluripotent stem cells and analyses of factors regulating functions of various genes (epigenetic factors). The project has three related aims: Aim 1: Confirmation of genetic predictors of response to lithium found in a study recently conducted by several of us. Aim 2: Testing the hypothesis of differences in epigenetic regulations between responders and non-responders to lithium and integrating these findings with the genetic results in Aim 1. Aim 3: Characterization of neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of patients with bipolar disorder responsive and non-responsive to lithium. Our results will 1) inform future studies of treatment response, and 2) contribute to developments of personalized clinical management of bipolar disorder.

column36: Testing a conceptual model of adjustment and compliance in couples seeking fertility treatment
column37: Infertility is a growing public health issue, affecting 12-16% of Canadian couples. Although advances in assisted reproductive technologies now allow more couples to become parents, treatment is strenuous, has limited success rates, and can disrupt both partners' psychological, relationship, and sexual adjustment. Hence, despite a favourable prognosis, 20-30% of couples choose to end treatment before achieving birth. Yet, fundamental knowledge about compliance with fertility treatment is still lacking. The most common reasons for dropout are physical and psychological burden of treatment and relationship strain. Research in this area, however, suffers from important flaws, including the use of retrospective designs and the use of general descriptors to identify causes of discontinuation. Evidence about the predictors of non-compliance is also scare. This 2-year prospective study will examine predictors of treatment non-compliance in both partners of 350 couples seeking fertility treatment. Patient, treatment, and clinic factors, as well as psychological, relational and sexual strain are expected to predict treatment discontinuation. This study will 1) provide novel prospective data about factors associated with treatment burden and discontinuation in couples seeking fertility treatment, 2) help identify barriers to treatment compliance, 3) help inform the development of interventions to guide couples through their decisional process, and 4) highlight clinical factors that could be modified to promote better patient care, prevent undue treatment termination, and improve cumulative pregnancy rates.

column36: Integrative Personal Omics Profiles in Glioblastoma Recurrence and Therapy Resistance
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the most aggressive brain tumors with a grim prognosis and median survival times of less than 15 months. Despite multimodal therapy, including surgical resection and radio-chemotherapy, recurrence is inevitable. However, time to recurrence is an individual parameter in patients and depends on genetic factors and on clinical parameters such as extent of resection. In recurrent GBM, repeated surgery can substantially prolong the lifespan if recurrent tumors are detected at early stages. Until now, recurrence monitoring is based on radiologic imaging but suffers from limited sensitivity and confounding effects. Therefore, circulating "liquid biopsy" markers predicting the time-window of recurrence are an unmet clinical need. We propose to use a spectrum of "Omics" methods to dissect the individual parameters that determine recurrence and therapy resistance in GBM. We will use a retrospective cohort of 100 patients clinically fully annotated GBM primary and recurrent samples. Abundance-based biomarkers associated with time-to-recurrence and therapy resistance will be obtained by analyzing extracellular vesicles (EVs) with respect to proteolytic fragments (mass-spectrometry based), protease actvitivies, and miRNA content. In addition, a full NGS analysis will be performed to characterise recurrent tumors in each individual patient to combine all "Omics" with clinical and imaging data. From these analyses, we propose to identify personalised easy-to-access biopsy markers so that investigation of pre- and post-surgery blood samples (at time of initial surgery) allows to faithfully discern tumor-originating molecules through their decreased abundance in post-surgery samples. We further hypothesize that multimodal monitoring, e.g. combining imaging data with molecular markers allows to establish a molecular signature of GBM recurrence which is particularly powerful for reliable prediction of GBM recurrence in a prospective patient cohort.

column36: Impact of Protein Nutrition in Critically-ill Patients
column37: Critically-ill patients admitted to the intensive care unit undergo inflammation and tissue damage, which contribute to ongoing organ malfunction. Studies indicate that increased dietary protein, or protein building blocks (amino acids), may improve their health outcomes. In agreement, studies in clinical and laboratory research studies indicate that the administration of amino acids can prevent protein breakdown. Controversy arises, however, from a number of clinical trials that failed to show an overall benefit for early nutrition in the critically-ill. This may be because the trials did not focus on protein therapy, nor did they use biological measurements to discriminate between patients who responded to nutritional therapy and those who did not. Here, we propose that the intravenous supplementation of amino acids in critically-ill patients can improve protein metabolism, and that this is associated with biological signatures ('biomarkers') that identify the patients who will most likely benefit. Our team is in a unique position to measure protein metabolism and biomarkers using state-of-the-art technologies that can be translated to clinical practice. The discovery and development of biomarkers of nutritional response is a critical step towards a larger clinical trial to establish protein nutrition as an effective therapy in the critically-ill.

column36: Pharmacological Characterization of eNOS-based Platelet Subpopulations

By the end of our studies we expect to have established that the two platelet subtypes differ in their response to antiplatelet drugs and that heart attack patients with an elevated ratio of non-NO-producing to NO-producing platelets may not fully respond to current anti-platelet therapy. These basic and translational studies of platelet biology have the potential to significantly impact the health of Canadians by better predicting risk and extent of clot formation. Lastly, these studies have the potential to inform personal anti-platelet therapy, and to potentially inform the future development of more effective anti-platelet drugs.

column36: Novel Mechanisms of Leishmania Pathogenesis
column37: Leishmaniases are a group of infectious diseases caused by parasites that infect 12 million people worldwide with 1.3 million new cases every year. Like many neglected diseases, leishmaniasis is primarily endemic to developing nations and thus presents additional socioeconomic burdens to already impoverished people. Leishmania donovani-the focus of this project-causes visceral leishmaniasis with severe morbidity and mortality. There are no effective vaccines and current treatments have limited efficacy and significant toxicities. The mechanisms that enable intracellular pathogens such as leishmania to chronically infect macrophages -pivotal cells of the innate immune system- are a focus of intense interest. Research is proposed here to investigate two novel mechanisms of leishmania pathogenesis. The first mechanism relates to investigate the roles of small, non-coding RNAs (snRNAs) in immunity to intracellular infection. These snRNAs are found in both animals and plants and some viruses and are well conserved and recognized as a vital component of genetic regulation. snRNAs have been implicated in stress, cancer, infection and innate immunity. Our hypothesis is that leishmania uses small RNA-based effector mechanisms to establish chronic infection. Research relevant to the second novel mechanism of pathogenesis relates to exploitation of host cell signaling pathway-PI3K-Akt in particular- by leishmania to create an environment which is permissive to survive inside the host. Our hypothesis is that PI3K functions as a master regulator of innate immunity to leishmania and promotes chronic infection. We will study the molecular mechanism of PI3K-Akt regulation by leishmania. This research will greatly improve the current understanding of leishmania biology and pathogenesis, and has the potential to aid in the discovery and development of novel therapeutics and vaccines to both treat and prevent leishmania infection and disease.

L'etude proposee constitue une deuxieme phase d'une recherche presentement en cours dans sept milieux cliniques quebecois, le projet AMONT. Le but de la nouvelle etude proposee consiste a mieux comprendre les parcours residentiels des personnes dans les trois premieres annees apres leur premier contact avec les services de sante mentale. Ultimement, nous esperons pouvoir identifier des facteurs individuels ou presents dans les services qui ont un impact important sur les conditions de logement des personnes ayant un trouble mental. column37: Cancer is a deadly disease. Despite decades of research, cancer remains the leading cause of death worldwide. As early detection and treatment can greatly improve patient outcomes, better diagnostic and therapeutic agents are urgently needed. One method physicians used to diagnose cancers is by giving patients an imaging scan called positron emission tomography. Patients receive a small dose of a radioactive agent, which selectively targets tumours and sends a signal to a detector to pinpoint their location. These imaging agents can be easily modified to carry a more potent radioactive element to kill cancer cells for therapeutic applications. While radioactive imaging/therapeutic agents designed for various cancers have been developed, these existing agents are encumbered by severe limitations. The most common problem is their high accumulation in kidneys. The high accumulation leads to very bright signal coming from kidneys, overshadows nearby small tumours, and makes it harder to detect tumours adjacent to kidneys. Similarly, the high accumulation of the radioactive agents can result in severe damage to kidneys. The goal of this proposed research is to develop a general strategy to minimize accumulation of radioactive imaging and therapeutic agents in kidneys. Most importantly, this strategy is expected to have very broad applicability, and can be used to reduce the high kidney accumulation of most of the previously reported radioactive imaging and therapeutic agents, and facilitate their clinical translation. The success of this research will generate more sensitive imaging agents for cancer detection and more efficacious therapeutic agents with minimized toxicity to kidneys. Overall, the success of this proposed research will significantly improve the diagnosis and prognosis of cancer patients in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Itch is a common features of various cancers, while cancer cells actively secrete factors promoting neuronal infiltration of tumors. column36: Deciphering the role of the newly uncovered dopaminergic pathways to brainstem locomotor circuits in mammals: from cell to behaviour.
column37: Brainstem cells generate the walking command sent to the spinal cord to activate the leg muscles. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine cells die in the brain, resulting in walking deficits. Classically, the connection between dopamine and brainstem cells is considered as solely indirect and to involve intermediary brain regions. However, direct connections between dopaminergic and brainstem cells were recently uncovered. These direct connections promote locomotion in basal vertebrates. In mammals, such connections could play a key role in locomotor control as well. In Parkinson's disease, the loss of such direct connections could be involved in the walking deficits. However, we still do not know the functional role of such direct connections in mammals. Our goal is to identify in mice the locomotor role of the direct connections between dopaminergic cells and brainstem cells. The brainstem cells targeted by the dopaminergic cells will be identified using high-resolution examination of brain anatomy, where the different cells will appear in different colors. Using in vivo optogenetics, we will determine whether turning on these direct dopaminergic connections is sufficient to initiate or speed up locomotion. Using in vivo chemogenetics, we will determine whether turning off these dopaminergic connections impairs gait or stop locomotion. Finally, the cellular mechanisms through which dopamine controls brainstem cells will be identified using patch-clamp electrodes able to detect the electric currents underlying brain cell activities. The proposed project will provide important new knowledge on the mechanisms through which the walking commands are controlled by dopamine in the brain. This knowledge is essential to understand why the walking commands are impaired by the loss of dopaminergic cells in Parkinson's disease. This will allow us to propose new strategies to improve locomotor function in Parkinson's disease and other locomotor disorders.

column36: Harnessing the power of Monocytes/Macrophages in Intestinal Immunity to Candidiasis
column37: Invasive fungal infections affect more than 2 million people worldwide annually, and result in death for more than half of these patients. In a healthy immune system, a hormone called GM-CSF activates antifungal defenses to protect against fungal infection. One molecule that controls GM-CSF, called CARD9, appears to be highly important, because humans that have mutations that interfere with the function of CARD9 spontaneously develop life-threatening invasive fungal infections, including of the brain. Although the roles of GM-CSF and of CARD9 in protecting against fungal infections are therefore clear, HOW they protect specific organs is not understood. We believe that these molecules do so by preventing fungus in the gut from escaping into the body. When GM-CSF or CARD9 are malfunctioning, we hypothesize that macrophages in the gut are defective, which allows the fungi normally residing in the gut to escape from the gut tissue and then into specific circulating cells (called monocytes), that then carry the hidden fungus to specific organs, like the brain, leading to life threatening disease. My research aims to understand how GM-CSF and CARD9 enable monocytes and macrophages to combat fungal infections at the level of the gut, blood and brain. I will use innovative cutting-edge techniques to investigate these processes, in whole mice and in cells. This exciting research will provide important and new insights into organ- and cell-specific immunity to fungal infections, opening the door to developing new ways to treat these devastating infections.

column36: Understanding the contribution of the peripheral nervous system to central neuropathic pain
column37: Chronic pain can develop in patients with the disease Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Because the central nervous system (spinal cord and brain) is affected in disease like MS-this type of chronic pain is referred to as 'central neuropathic pain' (CNP). CNP affects nearly half of the people with MS and is incredibly distressing. Currently there is no effective treatment for CNP. Finding a treatment that can target the spinal cord or brain directly can be very challenging and comes with the risk of unwanted side effects. On the other hand, the 'peripheral nervous system' (the nerves and cells that reside outside of the spinal cord and brain but communicate with them) is much easier to target, is often more amenable to treatment and is the focus of our proposed research. Our research to date has revealed that sensory neurons which reside in a structure of the peripheral nervous system known as the 'dorsal root ganglion' become stressed when disease affects the spinal cord and brain. Stressed sensory neurons can begin to send inappropriate signals into the central nervous system and we hypothesize that this is a major factor that establishes CNP in diseases like MS. Our studies will examine this at a variety of levels. First, we aim to understand the specific changes that arise in a stressed sensory neuron that can cause it to function inappropriately. We will then examine several novel therapeutic strategies aimed at relieving the stress on the neurons and determine if this will restore normal function and relieve CNP.

column36: Structural biological studies of antibiotic resistance mechanisms
column37: In 2014, the World Health Organization labeled antibiotic resistance a "global threat" that requires urgent action. This message has been reinforced by many reports including a UK report, which predicts that if no steps are made to curtail antibiotic resistance, an extra 10 million people a year worldwide will die by 2050. The media has captured the essence of this report with the sound bite "Superbugs to kill 'more than cancer' by 2050". The present situation is indeed alarming in that there are no antibiotics to which bacteria have not developed resistance and many bacteria have multiple resistance mechanisms, making infections caused by superbugs nearly impossible to cure. Aggravating the situation is the fact that for economic reasons, the pharmaceutical industry has largely abandoned new antibiotic drug development. To address this pressing healthcare threat, a multi-pronged approach is required. Most importantly, in addition to curtailing the indiscriminate and unnecessary usage of antibiotics, one crucial aspect to pursue is to study the mechanisms by which bacteria resist the effects of antibiotics and exploit this information for the development of new antibiotic therapies that are less impacted by such resistance mechanisms. Therefore, we will examine in atomic detail how superbugs are resistant to two different classes of antibiotics. We know that these bacteria have dedicated enzymes that detoxify many antibiotics, and the research will reveal how this is exactly achieved. We will than take these insights and explore how we can slightly alter the antibiotics by chemical means so that they can no longer be detoxified, while still retaining their antibiotic properties. Complementary, we will also examine if we can prevent the bacterial enzymes from detoxifying the antibiotics in the first place, using a blocking strategy. Either avenue should provide us with new and much needed solutions for treating infections caused by superbugs.

column37: Les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) sont la cause la plus frequente de deces dans le monde occidental et representent un defit pour la recherche et la medecine moderne. Les MCV sont les manifestations cliniques de l'atherosclerose qui correspond au depot de cholesterol, sous forme de plaque, dans les parois des arteres pouvant causer leur obstruction. La rupture de la plaque atherosclerotique est impliquee dans approximativement 70% d'infarctus fatal du myocarde et/ou de mort subite. Meme si les techniques actuelles de diagnostic de MCV permettent d'evaluer l'etendue de la plaque atherosclerotique et le niveau de stenose arteriel, elles ne permettent pas d'evaluer avec precision la stabilite de la plaque. La stabilite de la plaque atherosclerotique depend fortement du niveau d'inflammation a l'interieur de la plaque. Les resultats de plusieurs travaux suggerent que l'huile d'olive, en reduisant l'inflammation systemique, permet d'augmenter la stabilite de la plaque atherosclerotique. Cependant, il n'existe pas de donnees concernant l'effet de l'huile d'olive sur l'inflammation arterielle qui reste le meilleur marqueur de la fragilite de la plaque. L'imagerie par tomographie d'emission par positrons (TEP) est une technique utilisee en clinique pour, a la fois quantifier l'inflammation au sein de la plaque atherosclerotique mais aussi pour suivre l'effet d'interventions ciblant de ce type d'inflammation. Cependant, le probleme d'accessibilite a ce type d'imagerie et les couts eleves qui lui sont associes limitent son utilisation.

column36: Ultrasound-Mediated Drug Delivery to the Spinal Cord
column37: The brain and spinal cord have protective barriers that regulate their environment. While these barriers are beneficial in healthy individuals, in patients with brain or spinal cord disorders, these barriers prevent drugs from reaching their target. This work will investigate the use of ultrasound to temporarily open the barrier between the blood vessels and spinal cord in order to deliver drugs more efficiently. Medical ultrasound (US) has many potential therapeutic applications, one of which is facilitating drug delivery in the brain by temporarily opening the barrier between the blood and the brain. This is accomplished when the US interacts with micro-sized gas spheres that are injected in the blood stream and causes them to vibrate, stimulating the blood vessels walls. By focusing the US energy to a small volume, this effect can be directed to specific sites without impacting the surrounding tissue. In the brain, a number of anti-cancer agents have been delivered in preclinical studies using this method and have shown improved effects in combating tumors. In preliminary studies, this technique has also been used to open the barrier to the spinal cord, and recently a positive therapeutic effect was seen in an animal model. We hypothesize that US-based drug delivery can safely increase the therapeutic efficacy of drugs delivered to the spinal cord. In rats, we will examine the effects of ultrasound on the spinal cord, develop methods to safely control the treatment exposures, and test this method as a treatment for spinal cord tumors.Using benchtop measurements and experiments in a large animal model we will also investigate how the human spinal geometry will impact treatment monitoring and control techniques. If this study is successful it could lead to a noninvasive treatment option for patients with spinal cord disease and encourage the investigation of new drug interventions for these conditions.

column37: Systemic sclerosis (SSc), or scleroderma, is a rare, chronic, autoimmune connective tissue disease. Support groups are an important resource for people rare diseases, including SSc, and most support groups are led by people with the disease. Many SSc patients, however, cannot access support groups, and many existing groups are not sustainable due to factors that could be addressed by training peer leaders. We will enroll and randomize 178 patient support group leaders to receive the SSLED Program or to a wait-list control arm and compare outcomes, including self-efficacy, burden, and health outcomes following the 3-month SSLED training and 3 months later. column36: Advancing the methodological frontiers of adaptive treatment strategies
column37: While our current understanding of how well biomedical treatments work is based on population averages, the average effect of a treatment across a population may not be a good indicator of whether or not to recommend a particular treatment for an individual patient. This is because individual patients may respond differently to the same treatment due to their unique combinations of factors such as pre-existing health conditions, genetics, environmental factors, and lifestyle choices. Moreover, a patient may respond differently to the same treatment over time, e.g. as he/she ages. These two types of variability (between individuals and within a single individual over time) motivate the need for targeted treatment plans in which patient care is improved by using information on an individual's changing health status to adapt treatment recommendations accordingly. Examples include the management of chronic conditions, treatments that require frequent adjustments, or clinical decisions based on events such as remissions or intolerable side effects of a drug therapy. This approach, known as precision medicine, relies on "adaptive treatment strategies" where treatment plans account for between and within individual differences over time. The goal is to help physicians deliver the best treatment for each patient each time a treatment decision is made. These strategies provide answers to questions like "If a patient has not responded to an antidepressant, should the dose of that drug be increased, or should a new drug be prescribed?" While the concept of adaptive treatment strategies has existed for more than 2 decades, new statistical methods and tools are needed to gain maximum insight from contemporary "big data" datasets and to accommodate new treatments that have been developed . My research goals for the next 7 years are to advance statistical theory and develop the needed methods and tools for answering clinically relevant questions related to HIV and mental health.

column36: Frailty and the Kidney Transplant Wait List
column37: Many people with advanced kidney disease will benefit from a kidney transplant. Some people are not eligible because they are have health conditions that put them at a high risk of dying before receiving a transplant or high risk of deteriorating health after a transplant. Deciding who is able to receive a transplant involves a detailed evaluation of a person's health and a review by transplant specialists. Some people with kidney disease who are being considered for a kidney transplant have difficulties in their health, mobility or function that put them at a risk for a shortened lifespan. This is often referred to as frailty. Currently, we do not know how being frail might affect the health of those who are waiting for a kidney transplant. Knowing this information could be helpful in a number of ways. It would provide transplant specialists with information to allow them to make an informed, objective decision about whether patients should be put on the wait list and not rely solely on their clinical impression. It would also provide a more complete picture of a person's overall health in addition to the tests that are currently used to better inform patients who are deciding about being put on the wait list. In this study, we aim to examine what happens to people who are frail and wait listed for a kidney transplant compared with those who are not frail. We will use several different tools to assess frailty. We will follow patients to see if they die or are removed from the wait list before they can receive a transplant in addition to a number of other important outcomes such as being admitted to hospital or changes in their quality of life. We hope that the results of this study may lead to better allocation of kidney transplant organs and a more objective method of evaluating eligibility for the wait list.

column36: Studying telomeres maintenance by telomerase using live cell imaging
column37: In order to properly grow and divide, normal cells must maintain the integrity of their genome. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and are essential to maintain their stability. Telomere shortening leads to genomic instability and favors the rise of cancers. In most eukaryotes, telomerase is a specialized enzyme used to elongate telomeres. Most of our knowledge on telomerase relies on the detection of its activity in large populations of cells. However, little is known about the behavior of telomerase in single cells, as it acts on a single telomere. For this purpose, we developed an assay to image both telomerase molecules and telomere in single living cells, using the budding yeast as a model organism. Using this approach, the events leading to the recruitment of telomerase at a single short telomere will be studied in real time, in single cells. We will particularly focus on the role of sister telomeres cohesion during telomerase recruitment at short telomeres. We will explore how telomerase is regulated in a telomere-specific manner by focusing especially on its interaction with telomeric repeat-containing noncoding RNA (TERRA). Finally, we will use live cell imaging to study the dynamics of telomerase molecules and their recruitment at telomeres in living human cancer cells. Identifying the pathways involved in the regulation of telomerase and telomeres will help understand how tumors arise and develop into cancer, and also reveal new potential targets for cancer therapy.

column36: Ski is a negative regulator of cardiac fibrosis
column37: Patients surviving a heart attack or those with hypertension develop chronic heart disease. These patients make too much collagen in their heart muscle, wherein non-muscle cells called myofibroblasts secrete excessive collagens, which stiffens the heart. Most of the "glue" (extracellular matrix) between muscle cells in healthy hearts is made of tough collagen proteins. Too much collagen leads to cardiac fibrosis which results in weak muscle contraction and relaxation. Despite this, there is currently no treatment for cardiac fibrosis, nor are there any specific cardiac drugs approved to fix cardiac fibrosis. In recent years, we have found a new protein called Ski. Ski turns off this over-deposition of matrix, in diseased heart cells. Further, we have made progress of how Ski actually achieves this positive change. We are now poised to extend our understanding of how Ski corrects cardiac fibrosis. We discovered that Ski is able to deactivate cells that cause fibrosis, and this is associated with normal control of the extracellular matrix; but our also work shows that Ski somehow is redirected and lost in heart failure. So, we hypothesize that loss of Ski's function in sick hearts may contribute to cardiac fibrosis and speed up the onset of heart disease - our experiments will test this hypothesis directly in mice wherein we specifically turn off Ski in cells making extracellular matrix. Finally we hypothesize that Ski turns off the function of special proteins that normally promote fibrosis in sick hearts. Experiments designed to answer this will show the mechanism of Ski's beneficial effects. Thus we will tease out and develop our understanding of how Ski protein influences the progression of cardiac fibrosis, and how this work will allow us to design new Ski-based therapies to treat cardiac fibrosis, for the prevention of heart failure.

column36: Harnessing neuroinflammation to develop new treatments for multiple sclerosis and glioblastoma
column37: In response to insults, the body launches an immune response to eradicate the threat and instigate tissue repair. Unfortunately, chronic excessive inflammation leads to tissue damage while dampened immune responses may favor the development of tumors. My research programs are centered on inflammation within the brain and spinal cord, termed neuroinflammation. I focus my research activities on multiple sclerosis (MS) and glioblastoma (the most malignant and deadly form of brain tumor), where MS exhibits chronic neuroinflammation that destroys cells within the brain and spinal cord, and glioblastoma has suppressed immunity that allows brain tumor cells to escape detection and being killed. Indeed, brain tumor cells change the nature of immune cells and exploit them for cancer growth. My research programs thus seek to: 1) stop immune cells from going into the brain and spinal cord to inflict injury in MS, and neutralize the injury that immune cells can produce within the brain/spinal cord; 2) understand and harness the beneficial aspects of the immune system to facilitate the repair of myelin, particularly in aging subjects where the newly formed myelin can protect nerve fibers and thus slow the progression of disability in MS; and 3) rejuvenate the compromised immune system in glioblastoma in order that immune cells can perform their evolutionary function of fighting threats and eliminate the brain tumor. Thus, rather than considering MS and glioblastoma as distinct entities that should not be researched together, I have taken the unique approach of removing the silos from these diseases to study them together. By understanding why they lie on opposite ends of a spectrum, the lessons and drugs acquired in MS can be used to inform and treat glioblastoma, and vice versa. Thus, the overall research seeks to acquire new knowledge and enable recovery from devastating MS and glioblastoma.

column36: Cognitive Control and Vulnerability to Major Depressive Disorder
column37: Depression is a highly recurrent disorder, underscoring the need to identify risk factors for relapse. Cognitive control involves a set of cognitive processes that allow selective processing of information, which includes inhibiting irrelevant information, shifting from one task to another, and updating working memory. People with depression have difficulty exerting cognitive control over emotional information, and these cognitive difficulties are associated with functional and occupational impairment. People who have recovered from depression do not exhibit cognitive control dysfunction. However, negative mood or stress may activate depressive cognitive processes, such that during periods of mood decline, previously depressed people have difficulty controlling the processing of emotional information, thereby increasing risk of prolonged negative mood and relapse to depression. The objectives of this study are to evaluate the hypotheses that: 1) previously depressed people will show impairments in cognitive control over emotional information when in a negative mood state compared to a baseline mood state; and 2) mood-induced impairments in cognitive control will predict relapse to depression. A sample of currently, remitted, and never depressed individuals will complete computer tasks to assess the primary components of cognitive control: inhibition, set-shifting, and updating. Tasks will be administered in a baseline mood state in one study session and after a negative mood induction in a second session, which will allow us to evaluate cognitive processing in response to negative mood. Remitted depressed participants will enter a 1-year follow-up period during which they will be assessed every 2 weeks for depression. This study will test a novel cognitive risk factor for the recurrence of depression, which can help us to identify people who are most at risk of relapse, and develop targeted treatment approaches to reduce this risk.

column36: Cytoneme-mediated growth signalling in Drosophila
column37: The growth of embryonic tissues is controlled by "growth factors" that are produced by discrete populations of cells, move through the tissues, and stimulate cells at a distance to grow and divide. In many cases, the movement of these factors has been shown to occur via long thin cellular projections called cytonemes that connect signal-sending cells and target cells. We have been characterizing a protein called Slik that promotes the growth of tissues in the fruit fly embryo, a powerful model system for genetic studies of this process. In preliminary experiments we found that Slik activity is to be controlled by a recently identified complex of proteins in cells called STRIPAK, that Slik protein is found in cytonemes, and that the STRIPAK complex is important for cytoneme formation. We are proposing to characterize the molecular details of how STRIPAK regulates Slik, and to determine what role both play in signaling through cytonemes in cultured cells and in fly embryos. Slik and STRIPAK complex proteins are also present in humans. We expect that our finding in flies will provide much-needed insights into the role these proteins are likely to play in cell-cell signaling in humans, both during normal physiology and in disease.

column37: According to the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one the largest threats to public health and economic growth. Recently, the WHO for the first time divided pathogens into three categories according to the urgency of need for new antibiotics: critical, high and medium priority. The most critical group of all includes multidrug resistant bacteria that pose a particular threat in hospitals, nursing homes, and among patients whose care requires devices such as ventilators and blood catheters. They include Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas and various Enterobacteriaceae that cause severe and often deadly infections such as bloodstream infections and pneumonia. Despite significant investments by industry and academia into antibiotic discovery and development over the past decades, no new antibiotic class with novel mode(s) of action to fight these pathogens has been approved in half a century. The reasons for this failure have been identified and are caused by the inability of current compounds to penetrate into bacteria (low permeability) and their likelihood of being pumped out (efflux). To overcome this bottleneck in antibacterial drug discovery, we plan to develop helper molecules (adjuvants) designed to enhance membrane permeability, reduce efflux of antibiotics and prevent or delay resistance development against these pathogens. The overall goal of this proposal is to identify optimized helper molecules capable of rescuing antibiotics from resistance in animal models of infection against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens and to understand their mode of actions.

column36: Regulation of cerebral blood flow in obstructive sleep apnea
column37: In healthy humans, brain blood flow is influenced by changes in the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the circulating blood. However, the brain's important ability to regulate its blood flow is impaired in disease processes such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). People who have OSA stop breathing intermittently throughout the night, resulting in repeated episodes of low oxygen and high carbon dioxide in the blood. Because of these repeated episodes, the ability of the brain vessels to regulate blood flow becomes impaired. This impairment can lead to hypertension and stroke. The mechanisms that regulate brain blood flow in health, and how these mechanisms become impaired with disease, is poorly understood. It is thought that nitric oxide (NO) plays a major role in regulating blood flow in several vascular beds, including the brain. In a first study, we will determine, in an experimental human model of intermittent hypoxia during sleep, the effects of intermittent hypoxia on the regulation of brain blood flow and the role of changes in brain blood flow on the stability of breathing. In a second study, we will determine the extent to which the brain blood flow response to low oxygen is altered in a broad range of patients with moderate to severe OSA. Finally, our research will determine if the brain blood flow impairments observed in untreated OSA patients can be corrected after treatment with night-time continuous positive airway pressure. This work may help us better understand conditions such as hypertension, OSA, stroke and aging, in which endothelium-dependent relaxation (i.e., relaxation of cells that line brain blood vessels) by NO is impaired. Our research will provide useful information about how well treatment for OSA reverses brain blood flow impairments that may lead to stroke. Ultimately, this will translate into improved health and disease prevention for Canadians.

column37: The aim of this project is to provide important insights into sensory feedback mechanisms that regulate the locomotor activity and how these mechanisms are affected during aging. We plan to reach this aim by using a combination of mouse genetics, in vivo electrophysiology, and behavioral observations. From research over a century, it has been established that locomotor activity is controlled by a set of interconnected spinal interneurons, referred to as "central pattern generator" (CPG). Sensory feedback has been shown to be important in aiding CPG function, so that the locomotor activity is always appropriate to the environmental need. Moreover, walking in the natural environment is typically unpredictably variable, making sensory feedback necessary for functional locomotion. However, the capability to cope with unpredicted changes in the environment during walking gets compromised with advancing age. This leads to increased incidences of injuries related to falls in elderly people adding to costs to health care. Therefore, understanding the sensory feedback mechanisms that control locomotor activity and how these mechanisms change during aging can help elderly patients to regain the walking ability compromised by disease or aging. Therefore, the data emerging from this project will provide important insights that will be crucial for clinical research to help patients with compromised walking ability not only due to aging, but also to diseases or injuries.

column36: Innovations in Assessment and Management of Musculoskeletal Injury, Pain and Arthritis
column37: Health conditions and injuries that involve bones, muscles and joints affect 11 million Canadians, causing pain, mobility limitations and work restrictions. Many of these problems can be managed with physical treatments, exercise, activity changes and work accommodation. For others, surgery is required. Patients have difficulty getting timely access to all of these services. Patients prefer to work with health professionals who can offer evidence-based treatment, but also want to spend less time in clinics. While technology may offer an alternative way of providing such treatment programs, we do not know if these approaches can improve access or outcomes. This research will develop and test new ways of treating broken bones where patients can access treatment education, home exercises, self-management and remote supervision using technology or apps. Wearable or mobile sensors, video and web-based education platforms will be used to enhance current treatment approaches. We will work with patients to find the best design and delivery methods based on personal and fracture characteristics. We will focus on treatment programs that restore hand function and prevent future fractures and chronic pain. Other programs will be developed to manage shoulder pain. These programs will prevent and manage early shoulder injuries that can occur at work, and help people recover from shoulder surgery (shoulder tendon repair or shoulder joint replacement). The impact of these new interventions on pain, mobility and work outcomes will be compared to what is achieved with current treatments. We will adapt interventions for different people considering different risks, job demands, levels of difficulty, and personal factors so that we can tailor treatment programs. This program will involve patients, firefighters, health care providers, engineers and scientists to co-create new interventions and test them. This will lead to new solutions for disabling bone and joint problems.

column36: Sex-dependent effects of early life stress on the development of the basolateral amygdala-prefrontal cortex circuit for fear conditioning
column37: Early life stress (ELS) in the form of parental abuse or neglect has a significant impact on brain development and increases vulnerability to stress-related pathologies such as mood and emotionality disorders. One particular brain circuitry is essential for fear conditioning and anxiety in both humans and rodents: this circuitry links the amygdala, a structure important for the generation of fear and anxiety and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a structure important for cognition and evaluation of threats. Since connections between the amygdala and the mPFC primarily mature postnatally in humans and rodents, this pathway is thus extremely vulnerable to environmental stressors encountered in infancy. In this project, we will investigate how sex and an early environmental challenge that approximates maternal neglect will shape the formation and activity of the amygdala-mPFC circuit in the developing brain and influence adult emotionality in the long-term.

column36: An International Multiphase Program of Research to Develop and Implement a Patient-Reported Outcome Measure for Gender-Affirming Treatments (GENDER-Q)
column37: Hormones and gender-affirming surgery provided to transgender and gender diverse people can dramatically change how the face, body and genitals look and function. However, a critical barrier to measuring outcomes for such gender-affirming healthcare is the lack of a patient-reported outcome measure (PRO). This Foundation award would be used to cover the development of a PRO for gender-affirming treatment (GENDER-Q) and its implementation into clinical practice. The GENDER-Q will provide a comprehensive set of independently functioning scales that cover concepts such as appearance, body image, physical, sexual and psychosocial function. Phase 1 (underway) is an international qualitative study. Trans men and women aged 16 years and older who are seeking or have had hormonal or surgical treatments are being invited to take part in an interview. Recruitment is taking place in Canada, USA, Denmark and the Netherlands. Interviews are recorded, transcribed and coded. From the analysis, a conceptual framework will be formally defined that covers outcomes of importance. We will also create a pool of items that will inform the development of scales. Scales will be refined through cognitive patient interviews and expert input. In Phase 2, preliminary scales will be administered to a large international sample of transgender people. The modern psychometric method of Rasch Measurement Theory analysis will be employed to shorten and define the measurement properties for each scale. At this stage the GENDER-Q will be ready for use. Phase 3 involves studies to examine responsiveness to change for a range of gender-affirming treatments. Phase 4 involves implementing the GENDER-Q into clinical practice for use in patient care. Once developed, the GENDER-Q will be made available to researchers, providers, administrators and payers around the world to collect meaningful, valid and reliable data on important transgender-specific patient-centered outcomes.

column36: Development of a therapeutic modality to treat GM2 gangliosidoses
column37: Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff Disease (also knows as the GM2 gangliosidoses) are inherited neurodegenerative diseases that result from genetic mutations that inactivate an enzyme known as HexA. HexA is a protein in our cells that degrades GM2-ganglioside (GM2), a molecule found primarily on neurons of the central and peripheral nervous system. HexA degrades GM2, and if it is not active, GM2 rapidly accumulates and causes severe neurological disease. The rate of GM2 accumulation depends on how severely the genetic mutations impact HexA activity. Totally inactive HexA leads to rapid GM2 accumulation and death by 1-4 years of age; whereas, mutations that allow for some residual HexA activity (1-10% of normal), GM2 accumulation is slowed and disease progression is delayed. While still neurologically debilitating, these late-onset forms of the disease may not significantly impact lifespan. Importantly, HexA activity as low as 10% can prevent, and possibly reverse, GM2 accumulation and the associated neurodegeneration. We hypothesize that a therapy for infantile and late-onset forms of GM2 gangliosidosis is achievable by supplementing patients with active Hex enzyme (i.e. enzyme replacement therapy), and in late-onset cases, combing enzyme replacement with drugs known to boost residual Hex activity to bring the total Hex activity above the critical 10% activity threshold. We have recently engineered HexA to markedly improve its stability and function for enzyme replacement therapy. We now propose to use the engineered enzyme, known as HexM, to develop an enzyme replacement therapy that will be evaluated in mouse models of GM2 gangliosidosis in combination with a drug known to rescue residual HexA activity in cells. Our approach holds promise to reduce GM2 accumulation and reverse the progression of this debilitating family of neurological diseases.

column36: Regulation of chaperone-mediated proteostasis by STI1
column37: Proteins need help to attain their three dimensional structure and their abnormal folding is linked to many neurodegenerative diseases. To help nerve cells deal with abnormally folded proteins and other types of cellular stresses during aging, organisms evolved a set of chaperone and co-chaperone proteins that are present from yeast to humans. Chaperones such as Hsp70 and Hsp90 bind to proteins to help them to stabilize a given conformation; these proteins are known as "clients" of chaperones. A protein named Stress-inducible phosphoprotein I or STI1 interacts with Hsp70 and Hsp90 and it is critical to regulate the activity of the chaperone network. We find that decreased levels of STI1 in mice affects proteins that are stabilized by Hsp70/Hsp90 and causes age-dependent degeneration of neurons. Our experiments also show that certain proteins involved in neurodegenerative diseases are stabilized by STI1, and that STI1 can protect against toxic effects of these proteins by moonlighting outside cells. Our proposed research will investigate whether increasing STI1 levels may protect against age-dependent neurodegeneration and the abnormal folding of alpha-synuclein, a protein that is critical in Parkinson's disease. This work may provide new ways to help neurons to become resilient to stress and to deal with misfolded proteins that can cause neurodegeneration.

column36: The role of chronic stress and sleep reactivity in the persistence of insomnia over time.
column37: While many individuals experience transient sleep disturbances, about 9% of the Canadian population suffers from chronic insomnia. Although stress is recognized as a common cause for the onset of insomnia, the role of chronic stress in the maintenance of insomnia over time is less well understood. One reason is that there are individual differences in stress reactivity; that is, some people experience stronger bodily responses to stress than others. This means that some individuals are more vulnerable to experience insomnia in response to stress than others. Furthermore, most of the past studies have not examined the types of stressors that are chronic in nature. Moreover, some studies suggest that not only can stress lead to poor sleep, but poor sleep is also associated with increased stress. To better understand the role of chronic stress in insomnia, we will follow a group of insomniacs who will receive a psychological treatment for insomnia. At the beginning of the study, insomniacs will complete assessments of chronic stress, stress reactivity, and current insomnia symptoms. Then, the participants will be assigned to either a cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia or to a waiting period. Changes in insomnia and chronic stress will be assessed after treatment as well as 12 months later. This study will allow us to examine whether chronic stress is related to changes in insomnia over time, whether insomnia treatment reduces chronic stress, and whether individuals with high stress reactivity are more susceptible to the impact of chronic stress on sleep. Our overall goal is to identify a subgroup of insomniacs more susceptible to the impact of chronic stress on insomnia that may benefit from treatment targeting stress reactivity.

column36: Rewiring the Metabolic Ecosystem to Improve Cellular Immunotherapy
column37: A major paradigm shift is taking place in the field of cancer treatment. This type of treatment is called immunotherapy where it is now possible to harness the immune system to fight cancer. One type of immunotherapy called chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy involves engineering natural immune cells, known as T cells, to recognize and eliminate cancer cells. Several recent clinical trials have reported exciting successes, whereby certain types of hard to treat and late-stage white blood cell cancers such as leukemia, CAR-T therapy can lead to long-lasting tumor elimination several months after treatment. Despite the promise of CAR-T therapy, this treatment has only been successful in certain types of leukemias and not in the vast majority of other solid tumors like ovarian cancer. The major goal of this CIHR Project Grant is to define the barriers that limit the effectiveness of T cells that are produced for CAR-T treatments. Using our teams expertise, we will study the metabolic features of ovarian tumors and decipher ways in which tumor metabolism impacts the function of CAR-T cells. With this information, we will use sophisticated genetic-engineering technologies to produce highly effective CAR-T cells that can overcome the barriers that are typically found in ovarian tumors.

At present, it is not known how mucus secretion in the gut is regulation by the protein secretion complex in goblet cells. In this study our goal is to identify the protein binding partners that interact in goblet cells to control mucus secretion basally and in response to chemical induced colitis and pathogen stimulation that enhance mucus secretion to protect the epithelium from damage. We will extent the study to quantify if defects in the mucus secretion machinery exists in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). In IBD, mucus is severely altered that predisposes the gut to pathogen damage. A major goal in IBD treatment is mucosal healing where mucus is at the center stage in this process. Our studies will define a mechanistic role on how mucus secretion is defective that will inform us on new treatment regimes in treating IBD and infectious colitis.

column36: Optimized coding of natural self-motion by single and neural populations in early vestibular pathways: implications for perception and behaviour.
column37: As we move about in our environment during regular everyday activities (e.g., walking to work), we constantly rely on signals sent from our inner ear to our brain. Indeed, vestibular afferents there are activated by head movements (e.g., rotating the head from side to side). Their signals are then processed by the brain, which gives us our sense of balance and perception of our body's orientation in space. Unfortunately, patients suffering from vestibular disorders experience dizziness, imbalance, and an increased risk of falls - all symptoms that profoundly impair quality of life, which imposes a substantial burden on the economy in the form of increased medical costs, work-related absenteeism, and reduced productivity. Unfortunately, almost all previous studies of vestibular processing have used low amplitude sinusoidal head movements that have nothing to do with the signals experience during our everyday lives (e.g., when walking). Here we will instead investigate how single and multiple vestibular neurons encode self-motion signals experienced naturally. Our results will yield new knowledge that will revolutionize our understanding of how the brain processes vestibular input that is experienced during natural everyday activities (e.g., walking), which will yield better treatment options for patients suffering from vestibular disorders.
