column36: Prefrontal-subcortical network mechanisms underlying risky decision making.
column37: Impairments in decision making entailing cost/benefit evaluations about risks and rewards have been observed in a number of disorders such as schizophrenia, depression and drug addiction. The cognitive dysfunction associated with these disorders are thought to be due in part to dysfunction in pathways linking the frontal lobes to subcortical systems and neurochemical imbalances in brain dopamine levels. However, is unclear how these different brain systems work in concert to regulate different aspects of risk/reward decision making. We intend to clarify these issues using animal models of "gambling" behaviour. We will combine conventional pharmacological approaches with cutting-edge techniques that can manipulate brain pathways with exquisite temporal and cellular precision to elucidate precisely when and how distinct neural networks are engaged during different phases of the decision process to promote adaptive vs maladaptive decisions. These studies will provide important new information about how different brain circuits interact to solve these types of risk/reward decision making problems. Furthermore, the information provided by these studies may yield important insight into the brain dysfunction that underlies impairments in this form of cognition associated with a number of psychiatric disorders.

column36: Linking biomechanical and imaging outcomes to better understand the effects of running on knee joint health
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects more than 16% of Canadian adults and results in more than $27.5 billion in annual economic burden. The knee is the most commonly affected joint, and people with knee OA report chronic pain, physical dysfunction, and reduced quality of life. Maintaining an active lifestyle is advocated for all patients with knee OA. Recreational running (jogging) is enjoyed by millions of Canadians as an inexpensive and effective means to remain physically active. However, many former runners have stopped running upon receiving a diagnosis of knee OA, and many current runners would stop running if they were to receive a similar diagnosis. Further, many people choose not to take up running in order to protect their knees. These beliefs are based on a fear of causing joint damage and/or speeding up disease progression. This not only has a negative effect on quality of life and overall well-being, but results in dramatic decreases in physical activity levels. Unfortunately, these decisions are not based on scientific evidence, as no data can definitively dictate whether running is damaging (or not) for joint health. Our research will shed new light on the safety of running for knee joint health. We will be the first to directly assess the immediate changes in cartilage following a single bout of running in people with and without knee OA, as well as the first to compare running biomechanics (patterns) between these two groups in order to determine if the knee joint functions differently during running in the presence of OA. In addition to providing better clinical advice, based on evidence, to people with knee OA who wish to continue running, this study will provide fundamental knowledge of the role of high impact activities such as running on cartilage health. This information can be used to refine strategies such as running modification that can help to prevent the onset of knee OA for many physically-active individuals.

column36: Determining The Architecture Of Genetic Disease: Statistical Methods and Applications
column37: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) affects children and is caused by the gene CFTR. Many different changes (i.e. mutations) in CFTR can cause disease, and an effective medicine for 4% of individuals with one type of CFTR mutation is now available. However, recent efforts to identify drugs for other mutations have resulted in more modest improvements; and the majority of individuals with CF have no approved CFTR-targeting medicine. Alternative drugs that could lead to better outcomes are needed. CF affects the normal functioning of several organs resulting in co-morbidities and progressive lung disease which ultimately leads to premature death. Not every individual with CF has an equally severe course of disease. For example, only 15% are born with intestinal obstruction and there is significant variability in lung disease across patients. These differences are due to other genes, called modifier genes. Designing modifier-targeting medicines could be an effective strategy to treat CF, independent of the CFTR mutation. We are leaders in modifier gene research, and we have identified several that influence CF disease severity. For one modifier, we have learned how it influences different CF-affected organs and how it works in concert with CFTR; we have recently partnered with industry to develop a therapy targeting this modifier. The other modifiers have been much more difficult to study because, until now, we have not had the genetic information necessary. In this foundation grant we are proposing to identify the changes in the modifier genes that could impact CF disease severity using new genome sequencing technologies. We are developing statistical models that can combine the genetic changes we identify with experimental data, paving the way towards more modifier-targeting medicines. We are ensuring broad impact by developing computer software for other researchers to use and we are applying the methods ourselves to studies in epilepsy.

column36: An evaluation of patient reported outcomes, patterns of symptoms severity, survival and healthcare costs for neuroendocrine tumours (NETs).
column37: Neuronendocrine tumors (NETs) are one of the fastest growing cancers. They can arise in any organ, but most commonly in the stomach, intestine, pancreas, and lungs. They are slow growing tumors that can secrete hormones creating debilitating symptoms. Over 50% of patients will present with metastases that are incurable, but can be managed for a prolonged time. However, the optimal sequence of therapy is unknown and NETs lack standardized care. Furthermore, NETs have been reported to be uniquely tied to neuropsychological diseases (due to hormonal activity), but there is no evidence to guide patient support and address those special needs. Combining prolonged survival with active disease and hormonal production, and heterogeneous care, NETs can seriously impact patients' quality of life and experience, as well as healthcare resources utilization. Our study aims to use healthcare data collected from a cohort of NETs patients in Ontario, as well as speak directly with patients, caregivers, and physicians, to understand variation in clinical, patient-centred, and economic outcomes, and set priorities in improving NETs care. We will pay careful attention to the cancer care provided to patients who may be vulnerable to experiencing worse outcomes, such as the elderly, those with a mental illness, and those living in rural communities. This study will combine newly available province-wide data sources, including a patient-reported symptom screening tool and a novel Cancer Costing Algorithm. We will conduct a systematic analysis of clinical, economic, and patient-reported outcomes for NETs in Ontario (2004-2017). We will engage a group of patients, caregivers, healthcare providers, and policy-makers to interact with the research team and provide ongoing feedback on the project, and how to identify strategies to incorporate the information derived from the analysis into clinical practice.

column36: Characterization of a novel cofactor for tissue factor (TF) that enhances its pro-thrombotic and pro-inflammatory activities.
column37: Our bodies have systems in the blood that co-ordinately respond to injuries: the blood clotting system controls bleeding, and the immune system removes damaged cells and infection. If these systems are out of balance due to genetic or environmental factors, bleeding may persist or too much clotting may occur; infections may spread or too much inflammation may cause organ damage. Such imbalances are manifest as disease (e.g. heart disease, stroke, venous thrombosis, atherosclerosis, haemophilia). A major trigger of these systems is a protein called Tissue Factor (TF). TF is made by cells wrapped around blood vessels. With an injury, TF is exposed to the blood and initiates clot formation and turns on the immune system. TF has partner proteins that assemble and function in complex ways that are incompletely understood, yet important to understand. Indeed, such information will help in designing treatments to correct imbalances that may cause disease. We recently uncovered a protein, CD248, that interacts with TF and increases its clotting activity. Mice that lack CD248 are resistant to the formation of excess blood clots. The mice are also protected against inflammatory disease. Our findings are important, as they may point to the development of drugs that reduce CD248 to treat or prevent several diseases. This proposal aims to better understand how CD248 works. We will figure out which CD248-producing cells are important by using mice that do or do not have CD248 in different cells. The mice will be challenged by inducing blood clots and inflammation to replicate what happens in humans. We expect that reducing CD248 in one or the other cell, will be protective. In other experiments, we will figure out how CD248 participates with TF and its partners in controlling blood clotting and inflammation. We hope our results will yield new information for the design of better therapies for patients who otherwise suffer from immune and/or clotting & bleeding disorders.

column36: Elimination of senescent vascular endothelial cells delays atherogenesis in mice
column37: During aging, the human mortality rate rises exponentially as a result of a loss of normal organ functions. Of those, age-related cardiovascular diseases are of particular clinical concern because they represent 50% of premature deaths. By 2030, 1 billion individuals are projected to be over 65 years old. Today, 38% of people age 40 to 60 years, and 83% of those over 85 years have cardiovascular diseases. The main cause of premature death is atherosclerosis, plaques of fat (atheroma) that form with time in the arteries and eventually clog them, preventing blood flow to the organs, the heart being the first target. In this project, we propose that the inner layer of cells in the main arteries, the endothelium, becomes senescent with age, a process that could favour the development of the atheroma. Indeed, senescent cells accumulate and produce factors responsible for inflammation that contribute to change the structure of the vessel wall. This deleterious inflammatory environment could also affect the organ cells, promoting their senescence and therefore the dysfunction of the organ with time. We have discovered in old patients with cardiovascular diseases a protein produced by these senescent endothelial cells. We now have preliminary data showing that if we inactivate this protein in mice with atheroma, it improves the function of the arteries, it reduces the amount of senescent endothelial cells in the aorta, it decreases the level of inflammation in the aorta and reduces the growth rate of the atheroma plaque formation in the aorta. In addition, it increases health-span, that is, increases median mouse lifespan. We almost know nothing about the impact of senescence of endothelial cells on vascular function. Our aim is to demonstrate that by eliminating these senescent vascular cells, atheroma plaque growth will be reduced and this will maintain an adequate blood flow to the organ to maintain their function with age.

column36: The on-going conflict between APOBEC3 immune factors and HIV-1 Vif
column37: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 (HIV-1) causes the disease of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). There are currently estimated to be 37 million people worldwide living with HIV/AIDS. When HIV-1 infects a person, there are many barriers that the virus must overcome to establish a long-term infection that results in AIDS. However, HIV-1 can overcome these barriers in most people because it produces many different proteins that specifically inhibit the function of proteins in the human immune system. We study a specific interaction between the HIV protein called Vif and the APOBEC3 family of human immune system proteins. The HIV Vif protein causes APOBEC3 proteins to become unstable in cells so that they cannot do their job as well to inhibit replication of HIV. However, they are not completely purged from HIV infected cells and there is evidence of their suppressive action in HIV+ individuals. APOBEC3 proteins are able to restrict the replication of HIV by mutating its genetic information so that the virus can no longer produce the proteins that it needs to function. We have recently identified some of the ways in which APOBEC3 proteins can overcome HIV Vif suppression and are conducting research to understand this better so that we can develop new therapies for HIV based on releasing this natural anti-HIV activity of our immune system. We hope that a new therapy based on APOBEC3 activity would have less toxicity associated with life-long use in comparison to current antivirals since current HIV+ people can live 50 years or more after diagnosis, but often suffer significant co-morbidities

column36: The role of striatal clock genes in depression and anxiety-like behaviors
column37: The striatum is a brain region, strongly linked with the neocortex, that mediates fundamental behaviors related to motor control, cognition, motivation, reward processing and emotion regulation. Dysfunction within the striatum contributes to neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders including addiction, depression, and anxiety. Recent work from our laboratory has shown that the striatum exhibits synchronized rhythms in genes that produce circadian (i.e., daily) rhythms in striatal neurons. Increasingly, studies point to the involvement of circadian clock genes in pathologies related to striatal dysfunction, including depression and anxiety. Currently, the contribution of disrupted striatal clock gene expression to these disorders is poorly understood. We will use genetic manipulation and molecular, electrophysiological, and behavioral methods to study the effects of targeted deletion of core clock genes, Bmal1 and Per2 from striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), which make up approximately 95% of the entire neuronal population of the striatum, and which have been implicated in a range of behaviors and pathological conditions. In preliminary work, we generated and validated mouse lines in which Bmal1 or Per2 is deleted from MSNs. Using these novel mouse lines, as well as virus injections to selectively delete clock genes from striatal subregions and different MSNs types in adult male and female mice, we will determine how deletion of core clock genes from MSNs affects performance on a range of behavioral tests to assess how disruption of striatal circadian rhythms result in changes in depression and anxiety-like behaviors. Studying the consequences of targeted clock gene manipulations within the striatum provides a powerful approach to determine the role of striatal clock genes in normal behavior, as well as the involvement of these genes in mechanisms of striatal-dependent disease states.

column36: Manipulating the neuroimmune response to promote spinal cord repair
column37: Over four million individuals are afflicted by different types of spinal cord injury (SCI). One of the consequences of SCI is the loss of neural tissue at the site of injury. This results in an inflammatory response characterized by the entry of immune cells that are essential for the clearance of cellular debris. It has been assumed that during this process the inflammatory response may also contribute to secondary bystander damage in the spinal cord, causing the death of neighbouring neurons and myelin-producing cells called oligodendrocytes. As a consequence of this, both lesion volume and demyelination increase with time. Because of the inability of the human spinal cord to repair itself, damages sustained after injury often lead to permanent functional deficits for which no cure is currently available. Among the factors that mediate neuroinflammation are molecules normally found within cells that get released upon cell lysis. These intracellular host molecules, called danger signals or alarmins, include the inflammatory protein interleukin (IL)-1 alpha and nucleotides. IL-1 alpha and nucleotides are normally sequestrated inside cells, where they participate in gene expression regulation. However, when released after cell damage and death, they become powerful activators of neuroinflammation. We recently discovered that in addition to its role in inflammation, IL-1 alpha can act on oligodendrocytes to reduce their expression of genes coding for cell survival. Our results also revealed that nucleotides, as well as possibly other alarmins, stimulate microglia to form a rim between infiltrating immune cells and reactive astrocytes, a response that we called the 'microglial scar' and which we believe plays a key role in regulating axon regeneration and plasticity. The main goal of this research proposal is to identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in these responses and to utilize this knowledge to promote spinal cord repair after injury.

column36: Molecular basis of PPM1A controlled macrophage apoptosis in tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB), a contagious respiratory disease of the lung caused by inhaling the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is responsible for over 2 million deaths each year, establishing it as one of the leading causes of infectious disease-related deaths worldwide. Inhaled Mtb are engulfed by special cells in the lung called macrophages, which normally kill invading bacteria. However, Mtb reprograms host macrophages to deprive their killing ability, allowing the bacteria to remain hidden from the immune response and protected from drug therapy while inside these cells. Host-directed therapy, which targets host cell proteins rather than the bacteria itself offers a promising alternative treatment for TB as this strategy will circumvent development of antibiotic resistance and the need for drugs to penetrate the impermeable Mtb cell wall. We have identified PPM1A as critical host protein produced by macrophages that is exploited by Mtb to shut down the killing function of these immune cells. In this proposal, we will (1) elucidate the mechanisms regulating PPM1A expression during Mtb infection, and (2) characterize PPM1A associated signaling proteins that allow the bacteria to survive inside the cell. These approaches will identify and characterize key host proteins involved in the PPM1A signaling pathway that could be targeted for host-directed TB therapy. Finally, we will (3) examine the feasibility of targeting PPM1A to restore and improve the ability of macrophages to kill Mtb in vivo. This research will advance host-directed therapies aimed at eliminating TB.

This study aims to understand the role of this circular RNA in heart transplantation. We will investigate the effect of this circular RNA on immune cells in vitro using cell culture system. We will then investigate the effect of this circular RNA in vivo on preventing immune rejection in heart transplantation using a mouse transplantation model. Finally we will investigate how this circular RNA functions. The proposed study will provide better understanding of this RNA and its role in heart transplantation. It will also help in the development of new treatments for prevent allograft rejection.

column36: Brain oscillations in the dynamic pain connectome
column37: Pain is a major public health issue and societal problem that affects millions of Canadians (more than those with heart disease, cancer, and diabetes combined), costs >$43B annually and is difficult to treat when chronic because it is not well understood. We developed a concept called the Dynamic Pain Connectome (DPC) that emphasizes the flexibility of connections between brain networks that are involved in the processing and modulation of pain, attention and salience. The DPC has only been studied with functional MRI, whose signals arise from slow blood flow changes that indirectly relate to activity in neurons. To understand the timing of communication in the DPC, an approach like magnetoencephalograhy (MEG) is needed because it measures fast brain signals every millisecond and directly reflects neuronal activity. The brain uses temporal codes to represent perception. Neurons in the brain have spontaneous (ongoing) activity that provides a baseline from which responses to a given situation can arise and so contributes to behavioural responsivity and sensitivity. Neuronal firing pattern signatures on millisecond timescales characterize brain regions, and aberrant firing patterns can reflect pathology in disease states. Temporal dynamics in the DPC may code for chronic pain and for sensing, processing, modulation, and response to pain. Thus, the goal of this project is to measure DPC regional activity on a fine temporal scale with MEG to characterize the DPC in health and chronic pain conditions. Characterizing MEG activity in the DPC will provide 1) fundamental knowledge of regional activity and how it reflects individual pain sensitivity, 2) a framework to characterize communication between brain regions in the DPC, and 3) insight into aberrant activity that characterizes chronic pain. In the future, methods that stimulate the brain could be developed to normalize aberrant activity in the DPC as a strategy to manage chronic pain.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada, and although advances in treatment options have improved the overall survival for early stage CRCs, ~50% of individuals are still diagnosed with late stage disease that is often incurable. The development of highly specific, anti-cancer treatments is a significant research challenge; however, recent efforts suggest that exploiting the mutated genes and abnormal pathways that drive cancer development may hold tremendous clinical potential. Accordingly, greater insight into the mutated genes and abnormal pathways driving CRC formation is needed so that new treatment strategies and drug options can be developed that exploit them. Mutations in specific genes cause genome instability, which is an early step in the development of most CRCs. Genome instability often leads to abnormal numbers of chromosomes (structural elements that contain the DNA or genes) that further promote cancer development. We believe that to create new, effective chemotherapeutic options requires a deeper understanding of the abnormal genes and pathways driving CRC formation. In this regard, emerging data have identified a gene (USP22) that we suspect is a driver of CRC. Data from patient samples shows that USP22 is altered in ~50% of CRCs, while our pilot studies show that reduced expression causes genome instability and is associated with changes in chromosome numbers, which collectively suggest that abnormal expression may play a key role in CRC. To explore this possibility, we will employ newly generated and disease relevant models along with leading-edge genetic and cell biology techniques to gain unprecedented insight into USP22 and its role in CRC development. We will exploit this information to identify novel drug targets and lead chemotherapeutics that we will test in pre-clinical studies to ideally and ultimately deliver new therapeutic options to individuals diagnosed with CRC.

column36: Genomics of antimicrobial resistance and drug/target discovery
column37: Pathogens and their human hosts are locked in an evolutionary arms race. Humans are fighting back with better drugs, but the pathogens adapt to evolve drug resistance. As a result, the medicines become ineffective and infections persist in the body, increasing the risk of spread to others. We have entered in an era of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a phenomenon of serious public health concern. If nothing is done by 2050 it will have cost $100 trillion and 10M people/yr are expected to die. Our research program will address this issue. We propose to investigate at the whole genome level how a microorganism becomes resistant. In order to achieve this we will conduct high throughput sequencing of resistant microorganisms. We will complement these data with a series of powerful chemogenomic screens developed in the laboratory. These screens are niched and complementary, offering a holistic view of AMR. The output data will be integrated using bioinformatics pipeline to generate a complete map of genes/mutations necessary to achieve resistance. The role of these mutations will each be evaluated experimentally. This knowledge will be used to implement new diagnostics approaches using machine learning. It will also lead to novel drug targets against new promising drug candidates and to novel more effective treatments of infectious diseases.

The exploration, validation and testing of these therapies in clinical trials, their approval by regulators, and the necessary articulation of novel approaches with established clinical practices raise, however, a number of major organizational, regulatory, and sociotechnical issues, which in turn call for innovative solutions. The purpose of our project is to provide an analytical understanding of this intricate process, based on a detailed empirical investigation of the aforementioned initiatives. Our analysis of clinical research will provide the grounds for exploring these issues and thus offer both oncologists and healthcare analysts implements with which to better frame genomic medicine initiatives.

column36: Non-suicidal self-injury among youth: Perspectives of youth who self-harm, their families and service providers
column37: Self-harm among youth is a major public health concern. Usually first occurring in early adolescence, it is estimated that 18% of youth engage in self-harming behaviours at some point in their lives. These may include cutting, self-hitting, pinching, scratching, burning, minor overdosing and interfering with wound healing. Recent media reports reinforce that self-harming provokes a great deal of suffering among youth and their families, who struggle to access appropriate care. Likewise, service providers find it difficult to treat youth who self-harm. While self-harming can have a significant impact on a youth's life, it is poorly understood. Before we can develop effective services and supports, we first need to gain an understanding of self-harm from the perspectives of youth who self-harm and their families as well as service providers who support them. The aim of this study is to increase our understanding of the experiences and needs of youth who self-harm and their families. This information is essential in order to design better services and supports for this population. Youth with a history of engaging in self-harming behaviours and their families will be interviewed. Youth will take part in art-based activities that will help them reflect on and express their experiences of self-harm. Healthcare and social service providers and school counsellors will also be interviewed. This study will engage youth who self-harm, their families and service providers and provide them an opportunity to more fully articulate their experiences and develop a shared vision of care for those affected, whose voices are virtually absent in healthcare research and practice. In framing self-harm through the lived experience of multiple perspectives, increased insight on self-harm will result. This study is a necessary initial step of a first of its kind research program aimed at advancing patient-oriented service delivery and outcomes for youth who self-harm.

column36: Taking the "idiopathic" out of scoliosis: from biology and genetics to non-invasive therapies
column37: Idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a poorly understood disorder characterized by rotational spine deformity that typically arises during adolescence in otherwise healthy individuals. AIS afflicts 4% of children worldwide and in severe cases (predominantly females) can produce chronic back pain, disfigurement and functional disability. First described by Hippocrates, scoliosis is the oldest birth defect known to humankind. Historically, AIS was thought to result from defects in bone or cartilage development. However, despite decades of intense research, the causes of AIS remain unknown and, as a result, treatment options are limited to archaic measures like prolonged bracing and/or invasive corrective surgery. Our poor understanding of AIS stems largely from a lack of appropriate animal models. Human upright posture, with head-to-toe spine compression, contributes greatly to scoliosis progression. However, most lab animals walk on four legs and the structure, center of gravity, and biomechanical loading of their spines differ radically from humans. Fish, however, experience head-to-tail spinal loads generated by swimming forward through water. The zebrafish, in particular, has emerged as a powerful animal for studying human birth defects and disease, and my lab has pioneered the use of zebrafish for modeling human AIS. Remarkably, we discovered an "inside-out" cause of AIS - where defects in the movement of fluid through ventricles of the brain and spinal cord ultimately cause spine curvature. We have even identified non-invasive pharmaceutical therapies that might block scoliosis. Here, we apply our unique zebrafish models to define the full range of mechanisms driving scoliosis, and to identify genetic causes of human disease. We screen for more powerful drugs that block scoliosis, and translate our findings towards clinical applications. Proposed studies thus hold tremendous potential to improve the lives of Canadians diagnosed with AIS and related spine deformities.

column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic disease affecting 10-15% of Canada's population. It causes severe pain and disability, and is the leading cause of joint replacement surgery. Healthcare service planning does not currently consider patient preferences and its impact on health interventions. This could lead to the introduction of programs that patients do not use, which is a waste of system resources. The explicit consideration of evidence from patient-preferences in assessing uptake of health services and the impact on wait times, patient outcomes and costs is essential to inform the design of effective patient-centered health services delivery. In previous work by our team, we built a simulation model that captures OA patient flows, healthcare resource use and costs. We will measure individual patient preferences, and incorporate these into the simulation model. Then, we will use it evaluate how patient outcomes and system performance will be altered when new health interventions are implemented, taking into account how many patients would choose those interventions. We will look at two different policies aimed at addressing wait times for surgery. The first is a referral management policy which would give patients information about wait times for different surgeons, and allows them to choose their preferred surgeon or the surgeon with the shortest wait time. The second policy offers patients the choice of an evidence-based conservative medical management program. Our study will look at whether patients would take up this alternative program and how this varies by characteristics of the program such as its cost. Depending on patient choices, both policies may shorten overall wait times, improve outcomes and reduce costs. Our team of OA clinicians, decision makers, researchers, patients and analysts has the expertise and engagement to ensure our research is clinically meaningful and is translated into patient-centred policy and practice.

column36: Perineuronal nets-mediated regulation of spinal nociceptive circuits
column37: In the nervous system, neurons and glial cells are embedded within a network of molecules called the extracellular matrix (ECM). The ECM components provide structural support, regulate synapse formation and function, and modulate neuronal excitability. In the brain, the ECM restricts neuroplasticity; thus, enzymatic digestion of the ECM enhances acquisition of memories and promotes cognitive flexibility and extinction. In the pain pathway, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), the major ECM-digesting enzymes, are activated in neuropathic pain conditions to promote mechanical hypersensitivity. However, it remains unknown whether this remodelling of the spinal cord ECM contributes to pathological changes in dorsal horn nociceptive circuits and pain hypersensitivity. We hypothesize that, similar to cognitive functions, the ECM restrains spinal plasticity and its remodelling facilitates the sensitization of nociceptive circuits. One of the major forms of the ECM found in the nervous system is perineuronal nets (PNNs). PNNs are densely packed network of the ECM located around cell bodies and proximal dendrites, predominantly enwrapping a subset of inhibitory interneurons. Inhibitory neurons have been shown to suppress nociceptive circuits' activation in the dorsal horn. Interestingly, digestion of PNNs around inhibitory neurons decreases their inhibitory activity. This raises the hypothesis that the digestion of PNNs in neuropathic pain sensitizes spinal cord central circuits by decreasing the activity of the inhibitory neurons. We will study the remodeling of spinal PNNs in neuropathic and inflammatory pain, and examine whether the degradation of PNNs surrounding inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord contributes to hyperexcitability. In summary, we will test the intriguing hypothesis that the ECM in the spinal cord restricts neuroplasticity, and that the remodeling of the ECM in neuropathic pain conditions contributes to the hypersensitivity.

column36: Optimizing hospital-to-home transitional care to promote functioning in older persons with dementia in rural communities
column37: During and after a hospital stay, older people with dementia are at risk of losing the ability to function independently in everyday activities like getting up and dressing themselves. If they do not get back to functioning independently within one month of coming home, they are unlikely to ever do so. Transitional care refers to the healthcare services people receive to ensure their needs continue to be met as they move from hospital to home. Most transitional care studies excluded older people with dementia and their families and did not focus on helping people get back to functioning in everyday activities. In addition, the few studies that focused on functioning excluded rural communities. These exclusions have resulted in gaps in knowledge to guide practice and policy for this population. This study will address these gaps. We reviewed the research literature and found six practical care strategies that are likely to be helpful. In this study, we will invite older people with dementia who were discharged from hospital and their families in rural areas in Ontario and Nova Scotia to tell us what they think about the care strategies. We will ask them if the care strategies fit their needs and how to improve the care strategies so that they better fit their needs. Then, we will bring these care strategies forward to healthcare providers who give transitional care in rural Ontario and Nova Scotia. We will invite the healthcare providers to tell us what they think about the care strategies, what they would need to provide them, and how to adjust their delivery so that healthcare providers can help older people with dementia and their families learn about the care strategies and participate in them. We will use the results to refine the care strategies so that they become part of transitional care in rural areas and help older people with dementia and their families learn how to promote functioning at home after a hospital stay.

column37: Children with complex care needs and conditions (CCNC) are those with chronic physical and developmental disabilities who require multiple services. As such, family well-being can be greatly impacted. Grounded on the premise of providing families periodic relief from ongoing extraordinary caregiving responsibilities, respite care has been shown to have many benefits, including reduced fatigue and stress for parents as well as increased independence, functioning and social participation for children. However, demand for respite care continues to exceed supply. Families experience issues with availability, affordability and accessibility. Current models of respite care need to be reshaped to become more accessible and effective for families of children with CCNC. The goal of this study is to provide evidence to inform the design of a new model of respite care that can respond to the diverse and changing needs of families of children with CCNC in Manitoba (MB). Families of children with CCNC will also take part in the photovoice process, which will involve them taking photos to document their experiences. Short-term, a new model of respite care for families of children with CCNC in MB will emerge so that respite care may be responsive and integrative. This work is foundational for future studies to test the effectiveness of a new respite model in MB. Long-term, what is learned from the implementation and testing of the MB model may be used to inform respite care policy nationally and internationally to improve outcomes for children with CCNC.

column36: Cellular Drivers of Skeletal Muscle Aging
column37: Global gains in life expectancy allow current generations to enjoy many extra healthy and active years. However, aging is also associated with a higher incidence of disease, which severely affects the quality of life and increases pressure on healthcare systems. Declining skeletal muscle (SkM) mass and function coupled with a reduced tissue healing capacity is one of the main drivers of loss of independence in the elderly. SkM tissue is highly complex and composed of a wide range of different cell types. Up to date, it remains unclear which cell types in SkM are most susceptible to aging and how age-induced dysfunction in these cellular compartments affects the maintenance and healing capacity of the tissue. Here we propose to model the impact of aging on the different cell populations in SkM using a range of novel and innovative mouse models. These models allow us to induce accelerated aging restricted to certain cell populations in SkM so that we can interrogate effects on tissue composition, function and regeneration. For the first time, this approach will allow us to identify the cell populations that represent the main "drivers" of SkM aging. We also propose to investigate a novel cell-therapy based approach that can restore the youthful function of cellular compartments involved in muscle aging. Lastly, we will evaluate the systemic application of growth factors controlling driver cell function for therapeutic efficiency in rejuvenating SkM tissue in aged mice. Our work will not only provide fundamental insights into the biology of SkM tissue but will also lay the foundation for the development of much needed therapeutic interventions for SkM aging and its associated pathologies.

column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) is an emerging mosquito-borne pathogen that is a significant global health concern. column36: Longitudinal Monitoring for Quality of Care at the End of Life in Nursing Homes
column37: Nursing homes are important sites of care for people who can no longer live safely in their own homes. The majority of people who enter a nursing home will die there, meaning that nursing homes should be experts in providing quality end of life care; yet, nursing home residents at the end of life often receive aggressive treatments that provide little benefit (such as use of certain medications or physical restraints) and they frequently suffer from distressing yet treatable symptoms (such as pain or shortness of breath). Accurately measuring and monitoring such care practices and distressing symptoms is important to reduce their occurrence and improve quality end of life care in nursing homes. Most provinces mandate the use of a clinical assessment tool called the Resident Assessment Instrument - Minimum Data Set 2.0 (RAI-MDS 2.0), which is regularly used to monitor overall quality; however, the tool is not regularly used to monitor quality of care at the end of life, specifically. In this research project, we will partner with care staff, decision makers, and nursing home residents and their families to study the modifiable symptoms and inappropriate care practices experienced by residents in Canadian nursing homes during the last year of life. Together with our partners, we will identify priority symptoms and practices for quality monitoring and will use RAI-MDS 2.0 data to develop quality measures for these priorities. The goal is to develop a new set of quality measures that can be used by different groups (including residents and their families, nursing home administrators and staff, and decision makers) to understand the quality of care at end of life provided in nursing homes and identify opportunities for improvement.

column37: The secret to cure human disease is to understand how the cell, the fundamental building block of the human body, functions. We simply cannot fix what we do not understand and the key to understanding cellular behavior is determining how the static information stored within genes is converted into visible effects. Recently my lab has shown that by and large, the amount and type of gene-output, i.e. the amount and type of proteins made, depend on the nature of a certain part of the coding tape dedicated to this synthesis. The coding tape is called RNA and it contains in fact non-coding fragments, or introns, that interrupt the code of protein synthesis. These non-coding fragments need to be removed in order for the tape to work, a process called splicing. Dysregulation of splicing is the hallmark of many human diseases including cancer. Indeed, our work indicates that introns play an important role in improving cell fitness under stress and that variation in splicing patterns promotes the survival of cancer cells. However, we know very little about why introns were first inserted in the coding tape nor do we understand the signaling pathways leading to the removal of a specific intron at a given time. Understanding the function of introns and the mechanisms of normal and alternative splicing represents a key challenge for future biomedical research, the discovery of biomarkers and therapy development. We will draw on our world-leading expertise in RNA biology and yeast genetics to generate the first global assessment of intron function on an organismal scale and annotate factors that modify splicing in human diseases.

column37: Heart diseases remain the first cause of mortality in the world. In Canada, it affects 1.4 million people, taking more than 50,000 lives per year in the country. Half of this mortality is due to heart failure, a progressive deterioration of cardiac contraction. The other half occurs suddenly (Sudden Cardiac Death, SCD) owing to ventricular tachycardias (VTs), abrupt accelerations of heart rate which precede cardiac arrest and death. Most victims of SCD were not identified as high risk individuals and could not be protected by specific drug treatments or implantable medical device (defibrillator). This unacceptable situation is the direct consequence of our poor understanding of what exactly triggers VTs. Our research addresses this issue. A majority of VTs is associated with structural heart disease (virtually any disease of the heart), and about 40% of VTs arise as complications of heart attack (myocardial infarction; MI). The origin of VTs is attributed to abnormal electric signals from the cells (Pcells) that compose the "electric wires" of the heart. Experimental animal models showed that electric properties of these "wires" are affected after MI due to an abnormal elevations of calcium (Ca2+) in Pcells. The first goal of the project is to identify abnormal proteins responsible for these Ca2+ elevations in Pcells after MI. The second goal is to understand how cell death in the cardiac wall during MI affects these proteins in Pcells. Experiments will be conducted on Pcells of pig heart. Advanced technical approaches including predicting abnormal Ca2+ activity in Pcells by a computer program will be implemented to identify the "triggers" of the process leading to SCD. The project is anticipated to provide clinically measurable indicators of the risk of VT and to identify new avenues for (so far nonexistent) specific treatments of patients at risk of SCD. The impact of MI will be investigated in males and females to evaluate the sex-differences in the risk of SCD.

column37: Excess body weight is a serious concern for many women of reproductive age. Being overweight or obese has several potential effects on the health of mother and baby, especially because of higher rates of complications like gestational diabetes, high blood pressure and spontaneous pregnancy loss. These effects may be related to an effect of excess body weight on the very earliest developmental events, such as the development of the placenta. The placenta is the essential link between the mother and developing baby, so if it does not form properly, there can be severe consequences. My proposal aims to examine the effects of obesity in altering the cell make-up of the fetal-maternal environment in early human pregnancy. We hypothesize that the state of obesity alters the local makeup and function of maternal and fetal cells leading to impaired placenta function. To achieve these aims, we will directly compare placenta and uterine tissues obtained from obese and non- obese women in the first trimester of pregnancy, and findings from human clinical specimens will be mechanistically examined using an obesity mouse model. I will compare cellular, molecular and genetic characteristics of the two groups by measuring blood chemistry, cellular composition (maternal and fetal), cell function and gene expression. The proposed studies will establish if there are inherent differences in the cell biology of placentas from obese women compared to non-obese women. I anticipate that there will be differences in fetal-maternal cellular composition between these groups of women. These changes in the local placental-uterine environment are predicted to modify placental function, in part by altering gene expression. Results from these experiments will lay the groundwork for future studies aiming to define the role of obesity in the development of pregnancy-related disorders.

column37: Even though asthma is a disease of the lungs, people with asthma have an increased risk for cardiovascular disease such as heart attack and stroke. During asthma attacks, the risk for cardiovascular problems is especially high. The cardiovascular risk is also higher in older people and in women with asthma. It is not known why asthmatics have a higher cardiovascular risk and we aim to investigate this. Inflammation and poor function of the blood vessels are two risk factors for cardiovascular disease. We will study how an asthma attack affects inflammation in the lungs, the spill-over to the rest of the body and the blood vessel function. We will also test whether an 8 week rehabilitation program involving exercise is effective at decreasing the inflammation and preventing impaired blood vessel function after an induced asthma attack. This will be done in older asthmatics as they appear to be at the highest cardiovascular risk, and more often have difficulties in controlling their asthma. With this research we will understand more about how asthma and cardiovascular disease are linked and find out whether exercise is an effective way to improve cardiovascular risk and asthma control.

column37: The right ventricle is one of four chambers in the heart. It is responsible for pumping blood from the heart to the lungs, where the blood is replenished with oxygen. If the muscle of the right ventricle by changing either its structure or its functioning is not pumping as efficiently as it should be, right ventricular failure and premature death occur. This can be caused by a number of conditions, including high blood pressure in the lungs. Indeed, due to high blood pressure, the right ventricle has to work harder, that means over time that the right ventricle thickens and weakens because of the extra work it does. Although right ventricular failure is a common, costly and fatal condition, its diagnosis is suboptimal and no cure exists. In the present research proposal, we hypothesize that a molecule called H19 is specifically increased in the right ventricle of human patients with high blood pressure and animal models causing failure of the latter and that its detection in blood can serve as a tool in diagnosis and monitoring the disease. In addition, we propose that inhibition of H19 could be a new and promising avenue to improve the function of diseased right ventricle and thus help patients to live longer. We expect that the knowledge gained from the proposed project will provide new ways to treat the disease.

column36: Revisiting the Mitochondria-Associated Membrane: Redox Controls Tethers
column37: The control of cellular energy production is an area of intense investigation. The reason for this interest is that many devastating diseases, such as cancer, diabetes or various brain dysfunctions are now recognized as "metabolic diseases". This designation means that these diseases result from defects in the metabolic, chemical reactions that generate energy from "respiration" or breakdown of sugar within the cells of our organs. Because of this insight, cell biologists today investigate the mechanisms that control cellular me-tabolism with the aim to tweak or rescue the balance of cellular energy production in disease. Our laboratory works on an intracellular membrane structure that controls cellular metabolism. This struc-ture is called the mitochondria-associated membrane (MAM). The MAM is a very small site inside our cells where multiple "biomembranes" attach to each other. At the MAM, calcium- and chemical-based signals turn on respiration when energy becomes scarce. If this crosstalk is disrupted, energy production is shifted towards the breakdown of sugar, and this is a known signature of cancer. We have discovered a mechanism that allows the MAM to control cellular energy production. The MAM activates this mechanism when cells are stressed. Under this condition, a protein assembly forms that chemically modifies the MAM structure. We will investigate what is needed to form this assembly and how the proteins that make up the MAM react to these chemical modifications. We will then determine what our discoveries mean for metabolism in cancer tissue. Using cell culture models and tumor growth in animals, we will explore pharmacological strategies to control the MAM structure. The new insight we gain will explain how metabolic changes allow tumors to speed up growth and how this property may be eventually harnessed to control cancer.

column37: Although advancements in therapies to treat cardiovascular disease have reduced the number of deaths of patients with heart disease, these treatments/interventions have ultimately increased the number of people who eventually go on to develop another clinical condition called heart failure. Simply stated, clinical heart failure is a condition that is defined by poor heart function that prevents the heart from pumping enough blood to the rest of the body for proper organ function. As a result, heart failure patients have a very poor quality of life. Although heart failure is often a "chronic" condition, the chances of dying at one year following diagnosis are between 20-30%, even with our most state-of-the-art treatments. Due to the short life expectancy and poor quality of life of the heart failure patient, the increasing amount of people developing heart failure is a major medical concern. A long-standing concept in heart failure is that the failing heart has defects in specific processes that allow the heart to generate enough energy to function normally. Since scientists already know that the failing heart is starved for energy, a new approach to treating heart failure may reside in improving the ability of the heart to use fuels appropriately and thus restore the amount of energy being produced by the heart. The proposed research will investigate what processes involved in energy production are decreased in the failing heart, and will determine if normalizing these processes can improve the function of the heart. We will use this information to develop novel approaches to treating heart failure. Given the accumulating information regarding the occurrence and poor health outcomes associated with heart failure, there is need to identify additional treatment options for this condition in a large and growing population of Canadians.

column37: Pain is a key feature of arthritis, a disease of the joint and a leading cause of disability in both young and old. Despite recent advances in treating joint inflammation, and the widespread use of pain medications by arthritis patients, adequate pain control is an ongoing and challenging health care problem. Joint pain is poorly understood: some individuals with severe joint damage report little pain, while paradoxically others with seemingly minor joint damage, complain of debilitating pain. This disconnect suggests joint damage somehow influences arthritis pain, possibly by "filtering" the sensation of pain at some level in our body before reaching our brain. This proposal examines how arthritis pain impacts immune cells (microglia) in the spinal cord to mediate pain sensations between the joint and the brain. Although microglia reside within the confines of the blood brain barrier (a protective barrier that normally shields the brain), the injured joint can somehow communicate with these cells. In preliminary studies, we discovered that joint injury activates a specific molecule (the pannexin-1 channel) in microglia located in the region of the spinal cord associated with joint pain sensation. We also discovered that blocking pannexin-1 substantially reduces pain in this experimental arthritis model. Microglia, working as an amplifier at the level of the spinal cord, may influence how joint damage signals chronic pain to the brain. Understanding why and how arthritis pain occurs will enable us to develop new health care strategies to prevent or treat pain in patients with chronic joint disease.

Medical costs related to BPD are among the highest for all childhood diseases, being second only to asthma. Preventing disease due to prematurity is therefore of critical importance to the health of Canadians. Another molecule regulated by ROCK is TSP-1, which our work suggests is critical to interruption of normal lung development. Importantly, we will allow rats to grow into adults to see whether benefits of targeting ROCK and TSP-1 are long-lasting. Our group is uniquely equipped with the facilities and expertise to perform the experiments that are proposed. In particular, ours is the only group possessing the ability to perform precise measurements of lung structure using a technique called "unbiased stereology". Collectively, these experiments represent a critical step toward the translation of novel drugs targeting molecules implicated in BPD, which could represent a breakthrough in our ability to improve health outcomes among Canadians who were born premature.

column37: Lung disease is an important clinical problem and our group has a proven track record of translating laboratory advances into clinical use. Acute and chronic lung diseases remain major healthcare burdens, and are expected to increase with an aging population. For patients with end-stage lung disease, lung transplantation is often the only life-saving option, despite significant associated risks of mortality and morbidity due to graft rejection and infection. Regenerative medicine approaches, while exciting in their potential, remain limited by an inadequate supply of appropriate cell types required for therapeutic benefit. For both autologous and allogeneic cell-based therapeutic applications, the potential benefit of the therapy is critically dependent on the efficacy of donor cells which declines with age. This is particularly important an elderly population as many of the most challenging lung diseases affect older individuals. To avoid all the issues of rejection, it will be required to utilize 'rejuvenated' cells derived from the patient's own aged cells. We have been working to develop a conceptual approach called transient reprogramming. We have shown that initiating the reprogramming process but NOT ALLOWING it to continue to the full pluripotent state (which would result in induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells), leads to a cell type we have called an induced Progenitor-Like (iPL) cell, whose proliferation and differentiation can be controlled. These iPL cells are powerful therapeutic products and we have been investigating their potential in the lung. Herein we propose to test the hypothesis that (1) transient expression of reprogramming factors generates 'rejuvenated' iPL cells from aged lung alveolar epithelial cells. And (2) these 'rejuvenated' iPL cells can be used in cell-based regenerative medicine applications, specifically for the amelioration of Pulmonary Fibrosis.

column36: Gender inequalities in adolescent mental health in Canada
column37: During early childhood, boys and girls have similar mental health experiences. By adolescence, gaps start to appear for mental health outcomes. Anxiety and depression are diagnosed more commonly among girls, while for boys risk-taking behaviours and fatal outcomes such as suicide pose greater risks. These are examples of "gender-based mental health inequalities", and we want to focus here on the deep reasons why they exist. Using survey data and young people's own stories, we want to understand: (1) how individual behaviours and social processes (such as use of social media, available peer and adult supports, and risk-taking) contribute to mental health inequalities between adolescent boys and girls; (2) how differences in mental health between boys and girls are shaped by gendered differences in their social backgrounds. We will bring together new analyses of health survey data with information from a series of interviews with young Canadians. Integration of all study findings will provide new evidence about factors that effect mental health among groups of adolescents, inform interventions, and enrich the evidence base for health policy. This project is especially timely because the mental health of Canadian adolescents, as well as gender-based inequalities, have emerged as two very pressing social challenges in our country.

column36: Mechanisms of neuronal and vascular impairments in ischemic retinopathies
column37: Ischemic retinopathies are a group of ocular diseases, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), responsible for major vision deficits. According to the International Diabetes Federation, 382 millions of people suffer of diabetes in the world. DR is a severe complication of diabetes that can lead to blindness. One estimates that DR is one of the most prevalent ocular diseases impairing vision in the working population. The number of DR patients is expected to dramatically increase in the next decades by the World Health Organization. Current therapies are not sufficient to stop the disease or can cause severe side-effects. The search for new therapeutic approaches to fight ischemic retinopathies such as DR is therefore a public health priority. Clinical signs of DR retinae consist of abnormal blood vessel morphologies and bleeding in the eyes. Moreover, aberrant proliferation of blood vessels and retinal edema dramatically worsen vision in 50% of type 1 patients and in 10% of type 2 patients after 15 years. Retinal neuron dysfunction is a direct consequence of ensuing ischemic damage. Indeed, the ability of retinal neurons to repair after injury is very poor. In this project, the potential implication of a new molecule will be investigated in neuronal and blood vessel dysfunctions using retinal ischemia animal models, in vivo. In the current research proposal, it is suggested that this molecule disturbs blood supply of the eye and alters the neurological processing of the visual information by the eye. Developing a new treatment targeting this molecule may stabilize blood supply of the eye and may restore the visual function of the eye in DR patients.

column36: Advanced multi-modal imaging to monitor progressive joint adaptation in the knee following an acute ligament injury
column37: The role of subchondral bone in the knee following an acute injury is not well understood, yet there are significant changes in all the joint tissues that lead to a high likelihood of developing post-traumatic osteoarthritis (OA) in the long-term. While much of the focus has been on the degeneration of cartilage, largely because in knee OA cartilage wear is associated with disease severity, it is well known that other tissues in the joint are also affected. Bone, which has been associated with knee pain, is a particularly dynamic tissue in terms of adaptation due to physiological and mechanical stimuli, both of which are present in an acutely injured knee. However, the ability to monitor bone changes has been hampered by a lack of sensitive technology to assess 3D changes, in particular the microarchitectural features that lead to functional changes of the tissue. Our lab has developed a new technique that allows longitudinal assessment of knee bone microarchitecture following an acute knee injury, and this allows unprecedented insight into the adaptive processes. Preliminary work has shown significant changes to subchondral bone microarchitecture that are associated with concurrent cartilage adaptation following a rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament of the knee. Our goal in this study is to establish the time course of bone, ligament and cartilage changes following an acute ligament injury of the knee, both before and after reconstructive surgery. These novel longitudinal data, based on multi-modal imaging techniques, will provide insight into the early tissue changes of a knee injury that are likely associated with the long-term debilitating development of knee OA. This information will form a basis to develop future interventions and improved surgical practices that can lead to better long-term outcomes. Key to our approach is the advanced imaging technologies we have developed to simultaneously measure bone and cartilage in injured patients over time.

column36: GAL-7-specific nanobodies for treatment of triple-negative breast cancer
column37: The immune system plays a key role in fighting cancer. Unfortunately, cancer cells release a number of factors that neutralize the activity of cancer-killing immune cells. Galectin-7 is a small protein that is produced and released at abnormally high levels by breast cancer cells. Binding of galectin-7 on the surface of immune T cells induce cell death, favoring the development of an immunosuppressive environment within the tumor. In this work, we propose to validate the commercial potential of the first galectin-7-specific drug for the treatment of patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Among all subtypes of breast cancer, TNBC has the fewest therapeutic options due to the lack of well-defined molecular target(s). TNBCs account for 10-20% of all cases of breast carcinoma and have a 5-year mortality rate of 30%. Because they do not express significant levels of progesterone receptor (PR), estrogen receptor (ER), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), they are not responsive to hormonal intervention or to HER2-targeted therapy. TNBC is thus a biologically aggressive disease that is particularly difficult to treat.

column36: Irnisursiriartutuq nunaringngitamini (birthing outside the community): Childbirth evacuation, perinatal mental health, and postnatal health outcomes of Nunavimmiut mothers and their infants
column37: In Nunavik, Inuit women with medically high-risk pregnancies are sent to Montreal for childbirth. Childbirth evacuation may affect maternal-infant health through maternal mental health pathways. The study will 1) explore whether and how childbirth evacuation affects prenatal stress and antepartum depression; 2) examine the associations among antepartum depression, postpartum depression, and infant growth/development; 3) validate the EPDS-Inuktitut, a cross-culturally adapted questionnaire that screens for perinatal depression; and 4) implement a knowledge transfer plan with community members and organizations to raise awareness of perinatal depression, promote healthy pregnancies, and increase support for childbirth evacuees and their families. In this mixed method, longitudinal observational study. Eligible women will be enrolled in the study upon their arrival in Montreal and will be followed through childbirth and up to 12 months postpartum in Nunavik. Our target sample size is 334 women over 5 years. Using a participatory framework, a Steering Committee consisting of representatives of key Inuit health and social service organizations, an Inuk Elder, and an Inuk spiritual leader is involved in all stages of the study. Community engagement activities include annual community open houses in four Nunavik villages and quarterly meetings of a women's advisory group (Inuit midwife trainees and mothers). The researchers are experts in maternal-infant health, maternal-fetal medicine, Inuit health services, and Indigenous mental health. Expected products include a validated perinatal depression screening tool specifically for Inuit; Elder-led videos and community radio programming on traditional Inuit childbirth practices and healthy pregnancy; annual community open houses in Nunavik; journal articles; conference presentations; infographics; and a report for community organizations and government agencies.

column36: Epithelial-specific role of SOCS1 in prevention of intestinal inflammation
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a common inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) typified by recurring episodes of inflammation and tissue injury in the mucosal layers of the colon. The SOCS1 protein is an inhibitor of cytokine signaling affecting intestinal inflammation in a cell-specific manner, but its role in the intestinal epithelial cells (IEC) is unknown. This research team previously showed that mice with Socs1 gene deletion in IECs (Socs1dIEC) develop fatal UC at about seven months of age. Comparison of Socs1dIEC mice who displayed UC with those younger having no clinical sign of intestinal disease support a model whereby SOCS1 deficit in IECs may trigger UC by causing IEC secretory defects. This would lead to aberrant mucosal immune response to commensal bacterial invasion, where IEC hypersensitivity to death-inducing molecules produced by pathogenic immune cells may account for erosion of the colon epithelium. To tackle these postulates, we will define IEC-microbial-immune dynamic changes in the intestine of Socs1dIEC mouse cohorts (paired with WT littermates) featuring discrete disease evolution by performing functional, histologic and biochemical analyses. We will test whether disruption of the intestinal barrier integrity, bacterial invasion or mucosal infiltration of specific immune cell subsets cause UC or affect its evolution in Socs1dIEC mice. We will define IEC-intrinsic SOCS1 molecular pathways by global profiling changes in protein and gene abundance in IECs driven by SOCS1-deficiency, while SOCS1-regulated biological processes in mouse intestinal organoid culture systems. The cause of IBD is unknown but their pathogenesis is linked with aberrant immune response to the commensal microbiota. Insights of the mechanisms by which SOCS1 in IECs limits colitis may shed light on novel causes of IBD and identify cell targets for designing tailored new therapies to fight these diseases. Thus, our work would impact future diagnosis or treatments for IBD patients.

column36: Improving Health Economic Evaluation: Better Measures of Work Productivity Losses due to Illness in Canada
column37: Societal and health care resources are limited. Stakeholders such as policy makers, insurers, and employers need to make decisions on how to best allocate funding to different health care interventions such as new drugs. Health economic evaluation is a tool commonly used to inform these funding decisions. In economic evaluations, the costs of an intervention are compared to its benefits. Productivity losses for some diseases are substantial and even greater than their direct healthcare costs (e.g., physician, hospital and drug costs). Therefore, productivity loss due to illness is an important cost component that should be considered in economic evaluations from a societal perspective. The impact of illness on work productivity is usually measured in terms of three components: job loss, absenteeism (absence from work) and presenteeism (reduced performance and productivity while working). Currently, only a few population-based studies in other countries, and none in Canada, have comprehensively measured work productivity losses due to illness. Consequently, economic evaluations largely do not incorporate appropriately estimated productivity losses. The goal of our research is to improve the quality of economic evaluations by providing better productivity loss estimates. Specifically, using a population-based survey conducted by Statistics Canada, we will measure and value productivity losses among different chronic diseases, compare two different methods of measuring presenteeism, and identify the factors other than health (e.g., lifestyle and work-related characteristics) that may affect productivity. This study will enhance our understanding of the burden of specific diseases in terms of work productivity losses. The information generated can be used in other economic evaluation studies to improve the accuracy of their productivity loss estimates. When funding for health care interventions is based on better economic evaluations, society will directly benefit.

column36: BRCA1-induced pro-inflammatory signaling associated with ovarian cancer predisposition
column37: Ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in Canadian women and is the most lethal cancer of the female reproductive tract. Unfortunately, there are no reliable tests for early detection of the disease, and symptoms that might alert a woman to seek medical treatment at an early disease stage are easily dismissed as being due to minor ailments. Women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer are at very high risk of developing ovarian cancer, with much of this risk being due to a mutation within the breast cancer susceptibility gene BRCA1. Studies indicate that the most common and lethal form of ovarian cancer arises from cells lining the fallopian tube, and women with BRCA1 mutations often have their ovaries and fallopian tubes removed to reduce their risk of the disease. The fallopian tube is a structure that carries the egg cell to the uterus following its release from the ovary. We have identified molecular differences in the cells lining fallopian tubes from women with BRCA1 mutations relative to those from control patients, that could contribute to cancer development. Besides genetic risks, other risk factors for ovarian cancer suggest that factors associated with a lifetime of ovulatory events may contribute to predisposition to ovarian/fallopian tube cancer. Our studies are targeted at providing an understanding of how ovulation and BRCA1 mutations can predispose to ovarian cancer. It is hoped that this work will identify potential molecules that are likely to participate in turning cells within the fallopian tube to cancer cells, and ultimately lead to non-surgical ways to prevent ovarian cancer in women who are at an elevated risk.

column36: Control of B cell metabolism by the PI3K pathway: applications for autoimmunity
column37: The immune system is critical to human health. In order to develop vaccines and treatments for diseases where the immune system malfunctions (such as autoimmunity, inflammatory diseases or immunodeficiency), we need to better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing immune responses. Our research deals with the arm of the immune system responsible for producing antibodies, which are specialized proteins that bind to microorganisms and target them for destruction by the immune system. Antibodies are secreted into the blood and mucosal surfaces by cells called B lymphocytes. B lymphocytes express receptor proteins on their cell surface which allow them to sense the presence of foreign invaders, damaged cells and tissues, and other activated immune cells. Signals from these receptors trigger activation of individual B lymphocytes to divide, producing more copies of themselves, and mature into antibody secreting factories. Cell surface receptors deliver signals to the interior of the cell through signal transduction proteins which in turn activate enzymes that reprogram cellular metabolism to carry out either protective or damaging activities of these cells. Our research aims to define the molecular signaling pathways that regulate the activities of B lymphocytes during normal immune responses or abnormal autoimmune responses. Our work is identifying new molecular pathways that can be targeted to shut down B cells and treat autoimmune disease.

column36: Disentangling the intricate functions of the RNA polymerase II CTD
column37: Transcription is the very first step in gene expression. It consists in producing a messenger molecule (the messenger RNA) that provides instructions for the synthesis of the protein encoded by a given gene. Transcription is tightly regulated as it is in large part dictating which proteins are produced by a given cell. Regulating transcription is therefore key for processes such as cellular differentiation and homeostasis. Inappropriate transcription can have catastrophic consequences such as emergence of cancer cells. Transcription of protein-encoding genes is executed by an enzyme called RNA polymerase II. This enzyme contains a unique domain called CTD. The CTD acts as a connector that allows coherent organization of the different enzymatic reactions required to produce a functional messenger RNA, and hence a functional protein. This application aims at understanding the molecular mechanisms allowing the CTD to achieve its connecting function.

column36: White adipose tissue LDL receptors and omega-3 as modulators of the risk for type 2 diabetes
column37: Every 3 minutes a new case of diabetes is diagnosed in Canada, mostly type 2 diabetes (T2D). Diabetes increases the risk of having many other disease, such as heart disease, and about 65-80% of diabetic patients die from heart disease and stroke. T2D and heart disease develop because many risk factors such as aging, obesity and unhealthy lifestyle accumulate over years leading to their onset. Lowering blood LDL, commonly known as "bad cholesterol", is protective against heart disease. However human studies over the past 10 years have shown that the lower is blood LDL, the higher is the chance of developing T2D. This phenomena is happening whether blood LDL is lowered by widely used drugs against heart disease (statins), or by being born with certain genes, some of which are very common (~80% of people have them). The reason why lowering blood LDL is associated with higher risk for diabetes and how to naturally treat them with nutrients is unknown. We believe that blood LDL is low in some people because more LDL is entering into their tissues. We were the first to show that when LDL enters into human fat tissue it induces multiple defects that lead to its dysfunction. Fat tissue dysfunction induces the accumulation of risk factors for T2D. On the other hand, omega-3 is a unique type of fat that is found mostly in fish oil. We also were the first to show that omega-3 can directly treat the same defects that are induced by LDL entry into fat tissue. Thus the aim from this study is to establish in 48 overweight and obese subjects with normal plasma LDL; 1) if people with higher LDL entry into fat tissue have higher risk for T2D, and 2) if 6-month supplementation of omega-3 from fish oil can treat these people reducing their risk for T2D. This study is original and important as it aims to understand and treat a new risk factor for T2D using an inexpensive and widely accessible nutraceutical. It will help prevent T2D in large proportion of Canadians.

column36: Defining the mechanism of ALDH1A3 in breast cancer for the identification of novel therapeutic targets
column37: To treat breast cancer patients more effectively, we need to better understand why cancer spreads and comes back years later after treatment. Breast tumors are made up of different cancer cells. Among them, cancer stem cells (CSCs) have the greatest potential to form new tumors, are very hard to kill and can cause cancer to come back. My lab is investigating these CSCs and the mechanisms that cause cancer to spread. Our long-term goal is to identify new targets for drugs that kill CSCs and stop the spread of cancer. This should decrease the chance the cancer will return. Previously, we found that breast CSCs make an enzyme called aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A3 (ALDH1A3) that promotes tumor growth and the spread of cancer. Patients with higher levels of this enzyme in their tumors are less likely to survive in the long term. We have new data showing that ALDH1A3 promotes breast cancer growth and spread by producing other factors. First, we found a new ALDH1A3-induced molecule (a long non-coding RNA) that is linked to breast cancer growth and CSCs, with potential as a drug target to treat breast cancer. Second, we found that ALDH1A3 increases the production of plasmin; a cell component that helps cancer cells spread by breaking down surrounding structures.
