column36: The Endocannabinoid System in Borderline Personality Disorder: Relationships to Fluctuations in Anger and Comorbid Psychiatric Conditions
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a common and serious psychiatric illness that places a heavy burden on affected individuals, their families, and healthcare systems. Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), or the intentional destruction of bodily tissue, is a hallmark of BPD. High levels of anger often precede NSSI and are a potent risk factor for continued self-harm. We previously discovered that fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), a component of the brain endocannabinoid system that dampens neural signaling, is elevated in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) of BPD assessed using positron emission tomography, a state-of-the-art brain imaging technique. We also found that PFC FAAH levels were correlated with a measure of anger in BPD. The present proposal seeks to understand whether high levels of FAAH in BPD can change in response to psychosocial interventions that treat anger and other clinical symptoms of BPD, such as NSSI. We are also interested in pursuing whether FAAH levels are increased in clinical disorders related to BPD, such as major depressive episodes (MDEs). Thus, we will also test FAAH binding in MDEs. We predict that we will find higher levels of FAAH in MDEs, because there are clinical similarities between BPD and MDEs. Finally, we will measure whether FAAH levels are increased in BPD+MDE compared with MDE alone to discover whether FAAH is elevated even further in comorbid conditions. These series of experiments will help discern whether FAAH is malleable to change, especially in relation to core features of BPD. They will also uncover whether similar disorders have the same pathology; if so, results would provide an impetus for developing new treatments that could ameliorate multiple psychiatric conditions. Ultimately, we hope to decrease the clinical burden associated with BPD, including anger, and reduce NSSI that contributes to the exceedingly high morbidity and mortality associated with BPD.

column36: A genome-wide association study of dysanapsis
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airflow limitation (inability to empty the lungs), and is a major public health problem in Canada and globally. Smoking is the best known COPD risk factor, and reducing smoking is essential to public health. There are, however, some inconvenient truths about COPD that we must confront if we want to meaningfully lower the public health burden of COPD. First, smoking rates in several countries have declined by 50% over the past 5 decades (including Canada), but the corresponding COPD mortality is not declining. Second, one-quarter of COPD occurs in never-smokers (27% in Canada). Third, only a minority of lifetime smokers develop COPD. As COPD mortality continues to increase, understanding major determinants of COPD susceptibility and progression beyond smoking is critical. A growing body of evidence suggests that dysanapsis is a major contributor to COPD. Dysanapsis refers to the disproportionate scaling of airway-to-lung dimensions. Since airway dimensions determine airflow resistance, disproportionate scaling of airway-to-lung dimensions (dysanapsis) may contribute to airflow limitation. We recently developed and validated a computed tomography (CT) measure of dysanapsis. This dysanapsis measure explains more airflow limitation than all traditional COPD risk factors including smoking. Furthermore, our dysanapsis measure was strongly associated with the COPD Genetic Risk Score - a composite genetic score based on 97 known COPD genes, suggesting that genetic pathways contribute to dysanapsis. Unraveling the mechanisms of dysanapsis - a major contributor to COPD on par with smoking - is essential in order to develop early life interventions to promote healthy lungs for life. We propose a genome-wide association study of CT-measured dysanapsis among older adults, and testing whether these polymorphisms predict airflow limitation and respiratory events in children.

column36: Stopping Syphilis Transmission in Arctic communities through Rapid Diagnostic Testing (STAR study)
column37: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with serious health consequences if left untreated, including transmission to unborn children. This may result in death or serious complications. In several parts of the Arctic, syphilis has emerged in the last few years and continues unabated. Identifying and treating cases promptly is critical to preventing transmission. The remoteness of most villages and lack of specialized diagnostic labs however, makes timely access to diagnostics difficult. Reliance on testing in distant labs leads to delays of typically 6-19 days between screening and treatment. This delay may contribute to continued transmission within sexual networks and between communities. Reducing this delay is therefore a key priority in Arctic communities. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) intended to screen for syphilis, have been developed and used successfully in several counties. Syphilis RDTs are designed to be used without additional equipment and by individuals with minimal training to inform treatment decisions within the same visit thereby eliminating delays to treatment. To stop disease transmission and overcome obstacles to timely treatment, we will evaluate the use of RDTs in parallel with current standard lab-based testing. Unlike traditional testing, the RDTs will be used directly in affected communities and provide results in minutes, allowing for immediate initiation of treatment to help stop transmission. We will estimate the number of cases averted by early treatment of infectious syphilis, and model the impact of rapid testing on syphilis transmission. Our research aims to provide robust evidence for both the benefit and lack-of-harm from much needed interventions to control of syphilis transmission in remote Arctic communities. As such, this work aims to fill gaps in both knowledge and implementation using innovative evidence-based solutions for an ongoing public health emergency that can be readily solved.

column36: Chemokine-mediated control of anti-tumor immunity in DNA-repair deficient colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer afflicting Canadians. Cancer cells arise when the body's own cells become mutated to the point that they develop independence from the body's normal growth control mechanisms. In many cases, mutations in a gene mean that it cannot function normally. Mutations in many different types of genes can lead to colorectal cancer and some of the most common mutations change the ability of a cell to keep its DNA healthy. When this happens, cancer cells cannot repair damage to their genes and so even more faulty and abnormal-looking proteins build up inside of them. The body possesses a natural defense (the immune system) that detects and attacks foreign looking cells such as bacteria and viruses. While this system expertly recognizes and destroys infecting microbes, it consistently fails to recognize mutated cancer cells as dangerous despite their high content of abnormal proteins. Scientists are still trying to understand why this is the case and how we can help the immune system "see" cancer cells as foreign. In the proposed project, we will investigate whether there is any association between the failure of a cancer cell to maintain healthy DNA and how easily it can be detected by the immune system. We are interested in doing this because it is relatively easy with current technology to look at a colon cancer sample and determine if it has mutations that disable DNA monitoring but it is difficult to find out how visible a particular cancer is to the immune system. If we do find such an association, it would be possible for doctors to screen a patient's tumor sample for such mutations in DNA monitoring genes and use this information to better determine a patient's prognosis and optimal treatment strategy. This research will also help us develop a better understanding of why the immune system is blind to most colorectal cancer cells and help us develop new treatments that can boost natural cancer detection.

column36: The impact of the in utero environment on the developing human brain: Longitudinal investigations of epigenetic mechanisms in monozygotic twins from birth to adolescence
column37: Many studies have shown that what happens to a fetus in the womb (so-called in utero environment) influences the way the brain develops. Studies in animals have shown that undesirable factors during a mother's pregnancy (e.g. malnutrition, stress exposure) can influence the way her baby's genes are expressed through "DNA methylation", a process in which genes are marked with a chemical coating. This alters the development of certain brain regions and may have later consequences for the way the child will develop emotionally, socially and cognitively. In the proposed project, we will study whether this is also the case in humans. To accomplish this, we have followed the behaviour and family environment of genetically identical twins since birth. We have also collected DNA regularly in the first 2 years of life. They will now undergo a brain scan (called MRI) at 4 years old in order to measure the size of certain brain regions and the connections between them. While these twins have the same genes, their prenatal environment can be different, leading to differences in birth weight, which are related to health differences later in life. We expect that differences in birth weight will be related to differences in the size of certain brain regions and the connections between them. We will assess DNA methylation across the genome and in specific genes that affect serotonin, a brain chemical important for early brain development, as well as for regulation of emotions and cognition. We will determine whether DNA methylation in the first years of life is a process through which the in utero environment can influence a child's brain development. We hope that this study will improve our understanding of the specific role of stressors during pregnancy on brain development and psychological problems later in life. Results should eventually lead to a better understanding of possible early ways to foster optimal brain development and prevent health problems.

column37: Advances in technology have only recently allowed a systematic and comprehensive exploration of the genetic basis of cancer. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) is a global collaborative effort that has identified many of the key genomic changes in over 30 types of cancer. The publicly available TCGA datasets help the cancer research community improve the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer. This wealth of information has allowed cancer researchers to subdivide tumors into two major classes: tumors primarily arising and progressing from mutations in specific genes, and those from the gain or loss of DNA referred to as somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs). column36: Muscarinic receptor antagonism as a novel mechanism for sensory nerve repair
column37: Objective Diabetic sensory neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by loss of nerve fibers in the skin. Both diseases cause significant pain and eventually lead to sensory loss. The impact of these diseases on human health is enormously damaging and there are no therapies. Our recent work has uncovered an endogenous signaling pathway in neurons that negatively modulates nerve fiber growth of sensory neurons. The neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, is produced by sensory neurons and skin cells and activates the muscarinic receptor. Inhibiting the function of the receptor in sensory neurons using selective drugs or by genetically removing the gene significantly increases nerve fiber growth. We propose a "cholinergic constraint hypothesis" describing a role for acetylcholine in restricting growth of nerves within the skin. The general objectives are: a) To suppress the muscarinic receptor pathway to repair nerve endings damaged by diabetes or anti-cancer agents. b) To determine the mechanism whereby receptor blockade enhances nerve growth with a focus on a role in control of calcium signaling and mitochondrial function. Impact statement The proposed studies have a strong translational potential if successful. Our work with topical delivery of muscarinic blocking drugs (already FDA-approved for another indication) has progressed to a point where one small phase 2 clinical trial is complete and additional studies are envisaged for early 2019 for treatment of diabetic neuropathy. A company, WinSanTor, Inc., has been set up and will oversee delivery of this plan. This proposal, if funded, will enable the work to broaden in scope and permit this therapeutic approach to be performed in a wide range of distal dying back neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Regulation of bone remodeling by transglutaminases
column37: Osteoporosis is a disease that is characterized by low bone mass, bone fragility and increased prevalence of fractures. Osteoporosis hinders the life of over to 2 million Canadians and fractures cause loss of mobility, increased pain and dramatically compromised quality of life. The cost of treating osteoporosis related fractures and immobility is over 2 billion dollars each year and it is predicted that these numbers will keep increasing as Canadian population ages. The causes for osteoporosis can be linked to genetics, nutrition, medication, and it can occur at any time during life of both men and women. Bone mass is maintained by bone cells that renew bone in cycles of bone tissue removal and new bone formation. In osteoporosis, this cycle does not function properly and is tilted towards bone removal which leads to total decrease in bone mass and weakened bones. We have discovered that transglutaminase-enzymes are important regulators of bone tissue removal. Mice lacking transglutaminases develop osteoporosis, because bone cells do not function properly and produce biochemical that increase bone removal. In this proposal, we further explore how transglutaminases can cause the loss of bone mass and we will test if they can be targeted in osteoporosis in mice to correct the bone removal-formation balance. Our aims are to examine mechanisms how transglutaminases work inside bone cells and to test chemical inhibitors of transglutaminases as therapeutics in osteoporotic mice. From this work, we hope to understand how human bone tissue is formed and removed and how bone cell activity could be modulated in osteoporosis to maintain optimal bone formation activity and bone mass throughout life.

column36: Evaluation of a peer-led eHealth wheelchair skills training program: Training to Enhance Adaptation and Management for Wheelchair users (TEAM Wheel)
column37: Mobility impairment is the third most common disability; nearly 300,000 Canadians use a wheelchair or scooter because their disability makes walking difficult. Many Canadians receive their wheelchair while in hospital and must learn to contend with the social and environmental challenges of use when they return home. Because of shorter hospital stays and reduced access to outpatient rehabilitation services, wheelchair users often receive little training in how to operate and manage their mobility device. Without the appropriate skills, wheelchair users can experience health declines, diminished physical activity, and restricted participation in activities of life. The impact of reduced independence can have social and financial costs for the individual, their caregivers, and the health care system. Training to Enhance Adaptation and Management for Wheelchair users (TEAM Wheel) is a novel intervention designed to address this important transition to wheelchair use. The program features two innovative elements. First, it is delivered by a peer trainer (an experienced wheelchair user) who can relate to wheelchair mobility issues and offer insight into wheelchair management. Second, a computer tablet is provided to participants with a custom wheelchair skills training program to learn and practice at home. With over 150 video demonstrations and training activities, participants can practice at their own convenience in any location they choose. The peer trainer monitors the home training program and provides input when required. The aim of this project is to translate the TEAM Wheel program from English into French and then evaluate the benefits of the program with individuals in three provinces transitioning to wheelchair use. We will compare the TEAM Wheel program to services currently provided and evaluate its impact on participation in activities of life; confidence and skill with wheelchair use; mobility in the community; and quality of life.

column37: Herpesviruses include the common human pathogens, herpes simplex virus (HSV) types 1 and 2, and varicella zoster virus. Herpesviruses cause lifelong infections and once an individual is infected there is no cure. HSV-2, the focus of this proposal, is the main cause of HSV genital infections, devastating neonatal infections, and is fueling the epidemic transmission of HIV in Africa. It is estimated that roughly 500 million people are infected with HSV-2. While antiviral drugs are available to treat some herpesvirus infections, the emergence of drug resistant viruses is a serious problem. The initial stages of herpesvirus assembly take place in the cell nucleus where virus DNA is replicated and packaged into a protein shell called a capsid. DNA-containing capsids must exit the nucleus into the cell cytoplasm where final steps in virus assembly take place. This process is referred to as nuclear egress. During the past funding period we identified two new viral molecules, pUL16 and pUL21, that are required for nuclear egress and discovered that a third viral molecule previously known to be involved in nuclear egress, pUs3, has a unique and unexpected activity. We hypothesize that pUL16, pUL21 and pUs3 act sequentially in the nuclear egress of HSV-2 capsids. The goals of the experiments described in this proposal are to understand the mechanisms by which pUL21 and pUs3 function to promote HSV-2 assembly. These studies are expected to reveal vulnerabilities that may be exploited for the treatment of HSV-2 disease.

column36: International food policy study: Evaluating the impact of food labelling, marketing, and fiscal nutrition policies.
column37: Poor diet quality is a leading cause of non-communicable disease, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. In Canada, the prevalence of obesity continues to increase, while few Canadians meet dietary recommendations. An increasing number of countries are implementing national-level food policies in an effort to modify the food environment. Canada has announced several new regulations, including mandatory front-of-package 'warnings' and comprehensive restrictions on food marketing to children, and is actively considering fiscal measures to reduce sugary drink intake. Other countries are also implementing novel policies, including the UK's sugary drink tax and alternative approaches to food labelling. The primary objective of the proposed study is to evaluate the impact of three national-level policies: food labelling, restrictions on food marketing, and fiscal measures to reduce sugar intake. The International Policy Evaluation Study (IFPS) is a prospective cohort study of 16,000 adults, including 4,000 adults in each of four countries: Canada, USA, Australia, and the United Kingdom. The IFPS survey and 24-hour dietary recalls will be conducted annually over a 5-year period to evaluate the impact of the national-level policies implemented in the four countries between 2019 and 2024. The IFPS survey includes modules for a range of dietary measures, including food purchasing, and food security, as well as modules for each of the three policy domains of primary focus: food marketing, food labelling, and sugary drink taxes. 24-hour dietary recalls will be linked with the survey data to examine population-level changes in dietary intake. Overall, the study would provide a rigorous 'quasi-experimental' design to evaluate national nutrition policies implemented in Canada, USA, Australia, and the UK using 'within-country' and 'between-country' controls over time. The findings have the potential to directly inform policy in Canada and globally.

column36: Rationalizing Genetic Referral Practices in Pediatric Oncology: An eHealth Decision-Support Tool for Identifying Cancer Predisposition Syndromes
column37: Cancer predisposition syndromes are genetic diseases that increase the risk of developing one or more cancers over a lifetime. More than 10% of children who are diagnosed with cancer have and underlying cancer predisposition syndrome. Cancer predisposition syndromes are very difficult to recognize in children with over 125 currently known types. These patients need to be referred to Genetics in order to make the diagnosis. Our team has developed an eHealth decision-support tool, called MIPOGG (McGill Interactive Pediatric OncoGenetic Guidelines), that helps doctors recognize their patients with cancer who need to be referred to Genetics because they are at increased risk of having a cancer predisposition syndrome. This study aims to evaluate the performance of MIPOGG in detecting children with and without a cancer predisposition syndrome in a large childhood cancer patient population as well as to determine MIPOGG's costs and effects compared with other existing cancer predisposition syndrome detection strategies. When a cancer predisposition syndrome is diagnosed, doctors can initiate tumor surveillance protocols and sometimes change the treatment of their patients' in order to improve their quality of life and chances of survival. All children and families should have an equal chance at being identified with a cancer predisposition syndrome, independently of where they live and by whom they are treated. MIPOGG is a simple and accessible clinical decision-support tool made for doctors, benefitting pediatric oncology patients and their families.

column36: Dissecting the role of TRAF1 in regulating linear ubiquitination and the impact on inflammatory diseases
column37: Excessive inflammation is the root cause of many debilitating human diseases, including heart disease, autoimmune diseases and cancer. Therefore, it's essential to identify and understand the mechanisms that keep inflammation in check. We recently reported a novel role of TRAF1, a signaling adapter protein, in controlling inflammation. We showed that people with a genetic variation in their TRAF1 make less TRAF1 protein, which loosens the "brakes" on their inflammatory cells and increases their risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis. However, therapies targeting TRAF1 in inflammatory and autoimmune diseases is complicated because TRAF1 plays additional, often opposing, roles in other immune pathways. Therefore, this proposal aims at dissecting the disparate TRAF1 functions, by identifying the sites of TRAF1 interaction with these pathways, and mutating them to affect one pathway at a time. This allows us to design therapies targeting specific TRAF1 functions that provides favorable therapeutic outcome for the aforementioned diseases.

column36: Improving diagnosis and prognosis in acute brain injury: a multimodal imaging approach
column37: Advances in life-saving medical technology have dramatically increased survival rates for patients after severe brain injury. The recovery and continued care of these individuals often require extensive stays in intensive care units (ICUs), where critical treatment decisions are made to maximize the likelihood of recovering consciousness and cognitive function. These decisions are typically based on unreliable behavioural responses, rather than on objective and quantifiable indicators. We propose a transformative research program that combines cutting edge functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), advanced electroencephalography (EEG), and time-resolved functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to dramatically improve diagnosis and prognosis in the ICU. We will use fMRI to map residual cognitive function and to look for evidence of covert awareness in patients who clinically appear to be comatose. We will develop novel EEG methods to detect and quantify these residual capabilities at the bedside, addressing many of the challenges and risks associated with performing fMRI in this vulnerable population. When covert awareness is detected, we will use fNIRS to communicate with these patients, allowing them to convey information about their condition, and their wishes, to families and care staff. This program of work will have significant direct impact on the assessment and clinical care of patients in the ICU, inform medical ethics and legal discussions (in terms of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies), and drive efforts to develop interventions to facilitate recovery and quality of life after serious brain injury.

column36: Functional characterization of genomic DNA elements regulating epigenetic silencing
column37: As all cells contain the same genes, the ability to shut off genes is essential if an organism is to have different cell types. Understanding how genes are shut off is challenging, but silencing of one of the X chromosomes in females is an excellent model with which to study this fundamental process. Males only have one X chromosome (and a sex-determining Y chromosome), while females have two. To avoid a double dose of the almost one thousand genes on the X chromosome, mechanisms have evolved to silence one of the female X chromosomes. The initial silencing event, which occurs very early in development, is random but once an X is silenced, that status is maintained in all progeny cells. Silencing is not always complete, about 20 percent of the genes on the 'silent' X chromosome still show expression - we call them escapees. When an escapee contributes to a medical condition, there can be differences between men and women. Because silencing takes place very early in development, much research is done using mouse embryonic stem cells. Fewer genes are expressed from the silent mouse X chromosome than the silent human X chromosome. Therefore, we examine human escapees that are integrated onto the mouse X chromosome in mouse embryonic stem cells. We have recently shown that 200 kilobase pairs of DNA around a human escapee contains the DNA elements that tell the gene to not be silenced - even on a mouse X chromosome where the equivalent mouse gene is silenced! In the work we propose here we will identify the important factors by reducing the region containing these DNA sequences. We will also examine additional escapees, including ones that differ between individuals. Overall this work will help us understand how genes are silenced, and how the X chromosome contributes to sex differences.

column36: Risk of Retinal Toxicity in Patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Rheumatoid Arthritis on Long-term Hydroxychloroquine Therapy
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are diseases of the immune system that affect many parts of the body (e.g., joints, heart, eyes, skin), dramatically altering quality of life, and can result in other medical complications and untimely death. A drug called hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is commonly used to treat SLE and RA. Many studies have highlighted benefits of HCQ, including less severe disease, fewer complications (e.g., blood clots, problems with pregnancy or kidneys), and longer life. Stopping HCQ can lead to episodes of more severe disease. Also, because HCQ is safe and inexpensive, this drug is now also being studied as a method to prevent RA in people who are at risk. Although HCQ is typically safe and easy to take, a serious long-term side-effect is eye damage that could cause blindness. Although it was previously thought that there was a very small risk of vision damage, a recent study showed that the risk may be greater. However, the way that study was designed may have overestimated the risk. Therefore, it is important to now determine the 'real risk' using state-of-the-art eye testing equipment. Given the benefits and common use of HCQ, it is critical that the real risk be determined and findings shared with doctors and patients so that patients receive the best and safest care, and the health care system can use its dollars wisely.

column36: The role of dedifferentiated Schwann cells in non-healing skin wounds
column37: The incidence of chronic (non-healing) wounds is rising in Canada, yet there is no effective therapeutic approach to treat chronic wounds. To this end, we identified a novel mechanism that regulates both skin and nerve repair which relies on a particular cell type that is associated with small nerves in the skin (cutaneous nerves): Schwann cells. We uncovered that skin damage "activates" cutaneous Schwann cells, inducing them to transform into a stem cell-like state (termed dedifferentiated Schwann cells, or DSCs). It is these DSCs that function to promote skin wound healing, and do so by encouraging other skin cells (dermal cells) to divide. Additionally, these DSCs also promote the repair of skin nerves following injury. These findings suggest that DSCs are imperative to multiple facets of skin/nerve biology and represent a novel experimental therapy target, potentially useful in the treatment of both chronic wounds and peripheral neuropathy. We will test if DSCs or the factors they produce have therapeutic potential for chronic wounds. Using a pre-diabetic rodent model which displays poor wound healing, we will either transplant DSCs or known factors they produce into the wounds of these mice and assess if they are able to rescue the defects in wound healing capacity. This work will define a novel linkage between peripheral neuropathy and impaired wound healing, which are hallmarks of many chronic conditions including diabetes. Therefore, these experiments have broad therapeutic potential and represent the first steps in developing novel therapeutic strategies for many chronic skin conditions.

column36: Targeting metastatic disease of triple negative breast cancer with an immunogenic cancer vaccine
column37: This project will establish the most effective way to use a cancer vaccine to treat a very aggressive type of breast cancer, called triple negative breast cancer. For some patients with this disease who are diagnosed very early and who respond to traditional therapy such as chemotherapy, their disease may be cured. Unfortunately, the majority of patients with this type of breast cancer progress very quickly and do not respond to chemotherapy. For these poor outcome patients, there are very limited treatment options. We will create a cancer cell vaccine prepared from the patient's own breast cancer cells taken out at the time of their surgery. These cancer cells will be infected with a cancer killing virus, called an oncolytic virus to make them better targets for the body's own immune system. We will measure the body's immune response to this vaccine, using breast cancer cells and mouse models of surgery and breast cancer. Importantly, we will measure the effectiveness of this cancer vaccine to prevent aggressive breast cancer from coming back after surgery. The results of these studies will provide the critical information needed to design a clinical trial to test personalized breast cancer vaccines in poor outcome triple negative breast cancer patients.

column36: Untangling tau contribution to cognitive impairments in Huntington's disease.
column37: Tau is a protein present mainly in brain cells. Tau helps maintain cell structure due to its presence in the cellular internal skeleton, however, in many disorders of the central nervous system, tau forms into clumps and impairs neuronal function. This is particularly well described in Alzheimer's disease, but other disorders, such as Huntington's disease (HD) - a genetic disorder of the brain - were only recently found to have detrimental changes in tau. The presence of tau clumps in multiple nervous system disorders presenting with cognitive decline suggests that the abnormal tau may contribute to this aspect of disease. Further evidence of this relationship, at least in HD, comes from studies demonstrating that different forms of the gene leading to the production of tau, correlate with cognitive decline and its severity in patients. By further investigating tau pathology in HD patients and by decreasing tau levels in HD mice, we aim to gain a more complete understanding of the contribution of tau to cognitive decline in patients. We anticipate that this information can lead to the design of a tau-targeted therapy to improve cognition for HD patients.

column36: Deletion of the Ste20-like kinase SLK in HER2+ breast cancers activates an alternate Akt-Sox10 pathway
column37: HER2 is overexpressed in about 30% of all breast cancer and is associated with a poor prognosis. We have identified a protein termed SLK that is required for cell growth, motility and invasion. We have genetically deleted this protein in a mouse model of HER2+ breast cancer. Surprisingly, deletion of SLK enhanced tumor growth in a HER2+ model, suggesting that the targeting of one system results in the activation of compensatory mechanisms allowing tumor progression. We have identified the genetic basis for this compensation. We find that SLK deletion leads to the activation of another gene called SOX10, often expressed in triple negative breast cancer. Activation of SOX10 in HER2+ mice leads to the activation of genes associated with more aggressive cancers. We will test the double deletion of SLK and SOX10 on HER2+ breast cancer development and progression. We predict that a double deletion will markedly impair cancer development and could pave the way for the use of combination therapy targeting both SLK and SOX10 to suppress HER2 breast cancer progression.

column36: Interventions research in homelessness, housing, and health
column37: Homelessness is a serious problem, with more than 235,000 Canadians experiencing homelessness each year. People who are homeless suffer from high rates of physical and mental illness, and they often need specialized services and supports to obtain stable housing and improve their life situation. This research program will study innovative interventions to help Canadians who are homeless to achieve better health and well-being, and ultimately to end homelessness itself. This research program has three main goals. The first goal is to improve the ability of housing and support programs known as "Housing First" to end homelessness and improve well-being for people who have been chronically homeless. The second goal is to develop a new program that will help homeless young people between the ages of 14-25 to get stable housing, move forward, and lay the foundation for success in their lives. The third goal is to develop an intervention that will help homeless people who have recently been in the hospital to connect to services, have a better recovery, and stay out of the hospital. This research program will improve the health and well-being of Canadians experiencing homelessness and enhance the ability of our health care and social service systems to meet their needs. In doing so, this program will help make Canada a healthier society for all.

column36: The role of Nox5 in hypertension-associated renal injury
column37: High blood pressure is the 2nd leading cause of kidney disease. We are investigating how high blood pressure through an abnormal level of oxygen based molecules, called oxidative stress, damages the kidney and its ability to function normally. In particular, we have identified an enzyme, called Nox5, that contributes to oxidative stress in the kidney. We propose that Nox5, when its levels are increased in high blood pressure, contributes to the ongoing elevation in blood pressure and causes damage to the kidney. As such, we believe that Nox5 could become a target for future drugs that would help prevent or treat hypertension associated kidney disease.

column36: Characterizing Dopamine D2 and D3 Receptor Binding in Treatment Resistant Depression
column37: It is estimated that 30% of individuals with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) do not significantly improve with antidepressant medication, accounting for over 1 million Canadians in their lifetime. Treatment resistant depression (TRD), defined as a failure of at least two antidepressant trials for the current episode, results in almost double the health-associated costs and a greater likelihood of occupational disability, causing significant economic and personal burden. Importantly, there are few treatment strategies to target TRD and we do not have a comprehensive understanding of what processes in the brain cause it. Preliminary evidence from our group suggests there is an impairment in the dopamine system that plays an important role in processing rewarding stimuli. Deficits in this system are associated with loss of pleasure, one of the core symptoms of depression that is more prevalent in those with TRD. How the dopamine system functions in TRD compared to non-resistant patients and the full extent of the impairment is unclear. Consequently, more comprehensive evaluation of the dopamine system is necessary to determine if it is a relevant avenue for the development of new therapeutics. The goal of this study is to characterize the dopamine system in the brain within patients with TRD, non-resistant MDD and healthy controls. Three groups of participants aged 25-55 will be recruited: 15 unmedicated MDD, 15 unmedicated TRD, and 15 healthy controls. The TRD and MDD groups will have depression of moderate severity with no presence of bipolarity, psychosis or substance abuse. Healthy controls will have no lifetime psychiatric history. Imaging of the dopamine system will be done using two positron emission tomography (PET) scans to determine impairment across the whole brain. Results of this study will represent the first comprehensive assessment of dopamine in the brain among resistant and non-resistant MDD patients.

column36: Mono-ADP-ribosylation by TIPARP regulates AHR biology and dioxin toxicity
column37: Dioxins and related chemicals are a class of persistent environmental pollutants that, despite their tight regulation, still contaminate the global environment. Laboratory animals exposed to dioxins show a range of toxic responses including fatty liver, reproductive problems and weight loss leading to a lethal wasting syndrome. Although the toxic effects of dioxins in humans seem to be less severe, dioxin exposure has been linked to reproductive disorders, metabolic syndrome and increased cancer risk. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) is the signalling protein that is responsible for mediating the toxic effects of dioxins. More recently, however, the importance of AHR signalling in inflammation, intestinal immunity and overall gut health has led to the development of therapeutic agents that target AHR for the treatment of a variety of human diseases, including colitis, multiple sclerosis, arthritis and cancer. Despite extensive research efforts, our understanding of the normal biological roles of AHR and of how dioxins cause their wide variety of toxic effects remain poorly understood. We have found that another protein called TCDD-inducible poly-ADP-ribose polymerase (TIPARP) turns off AHR signalling, and it may therefore represent another key regulator of both the toxic and beneficial actions of the activated AHR. Our laboratory uses molecular and cell biology techniques combined with unique animal models to determine the role of the AHR-TIPARP signaling axis in either the toxicity or the beneficial effects of dioxin-like and other food-derived chemicals. By better understanding the function of TIPARP and its role in AHR action our research may lead to the development of new strategies to treat human disease, and allow for better prediction of both the health risks and the benefits associated with exposure to various chemicals that activate AHR.

column36: Functional pharmacogenomics of cancer : from mechanisms to personalized therapy
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death and nearly 1 in 2 Canadians is expected to develop cancer in its lifetime. Our research program focuses on prostate cancer (PCa), the most common cancer in Canadian men, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), the most diagnosed leukemia in Canadian adults. The progression of these cancers varies widely and is difficult to predict. Early determination of drug susceptibility is also a challenge that remains to be addressed to define which patients will respond to treatment, and which ones will not respond or develop resistance to treatment. One of our goals is to develop new tools to improve prediction of cancer progression and response to treatment using a simple blood draw, which can be easily incorporated in the clinic. Teaming up with clinicians-scientists, we focus on addressing which metabolites such as hormones and their pathways may serve as markers to help predict progression, and whether targeting these pathways can prevent or delay progression. This approach is applied to PCa, a cancer that is well known to be driven by hormones, but also to CLL, for which we have evidence that hormones significantly impact cancer aggressiveness, with a clear difference between men and women. At the tumor level, we want to understand how a key metabolic pathway related to hormones, oncogenic molecules and cancer therapeutics is linked to progression and also to a new mode of multidrug resistance. This pathway could be targeted to prevent/delay progression and restore drug sensitivity. By this mean we want to identify cancer cell weaknesses that could be exploited by novel therapies. Our research program offers high translational potential. We anticipate that it will provide new tools to help decision-making process, offer mechanistic insights and relevant drug targets. This knowledge will lead to the development of more effective strategies to identify and treat high-risk CLL and PCa patients and ultimately improve their survival.

column36: Improving palliative care in the home and community: Building CAPACITI (Community Access to PAlliative Care via Interprofessional primary care Teams Intervention)
column37: Palliative care is care that emphasizes quality-of-life rather than curative treatment for patients with advanced illness. Particularly home-based palliative care is important because 80% of patients want to die at home, yet 65% die in hospital. Strong evidence shows home-based palliative care-delivered by physicians working in primary care teams-reduces pain and symptoms, improves quality-of-life, and reduces health care costs. Yet <10% of patients get access to home-based palliative care by family physicians in the last year of life. Improving access to home-based palliative care can improve patient and system outcomes. However, we lack interventions that build capacity among primary care teams to deliver home-base palliative care. To address this, we propose an intervention called CAPACITI (Community Access to PAlliative Care via Interprofessional Teams Intervention). CAPACITI is a 1-year palliative care training and coaching program for primary care teams. Over monthly sessions and bi-weekly calls, it integrates 4 components: clinical education for early identification and communication; evidence-based tools for symptom management and care pathways; practice supports for team collaboration and system coordination; and high-facilitation and expert coaching for adaptation to local context. Our study will evaluate outcomes in 53 primary care teams in Ontario before vs. after implementation of CAPACITI, using a phased approach that compares intervention teams to control teams who have yet to start CAPACITI. The outcomes are access to home-based palliative care, team knowledge and collaboration, and patient-caregiver satisfaction. Our team has tested, evaluated and refined elements of CAPACITI, demonstrating its effectiveness on small numbers of primary care teams. We are ready to test CAPACITI on a provincial scale. Ultimately this study's results will strengthen the primary care system and increase access to home-based palliative care for patients across Canada.

column36: Integrating cognitive-behavioural therapy for social anxiety disorder with HIV risk reduction counselling for HIV-negative gay and bisexual men who are at high risk for HIV: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Given the continued high HIV prevalence rates among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in North American cities, there is a critical need for HIV prevention programs that meet the needs of this population. Social anxiety - anxiety about being evaluated in interpersonal and performance situations - is a risk factor for condomless anal sex (CAS), the main HIV transmission route among MSM. Social anxiety may increase substance use in sexual situations, which is also linked to increased CAS. Following this logic, treating social anxiety using cognitive behavioural therapy, an evidence-based social anxiety treatment, may also reduce HIV risk behaviour. This study will evaluate a new HIV prevention intervention designed to reduce HIV risk, social anxiety, and problematic substance use among MSM. We will randomly assign 176 participants to receive either this new intervention ("Sexual Confidence") or applied relaxation, which is an empirically-supported behavior therapy for social anxiety disorder that does not address substance use problems or risks for contracting HIV or sexually transmitted infections. Participants will be eligible for the trial if they self-identify as a man aged 18-65, and report HIV-negative status, symptoms of social anxiety disorder, substance use within 2 hours before or during sexual activity, and CAS with a man who was not known to be HIV-negative. This study will be the first in Canada to evaluate a combined cognitive behavioural therapy and HIV prevention program for HIV-negative MSM using a randomized controlled trial. This therapy, if found to be efficacious, will allow mental health clinicians to not only treat social anxiety and substance use problems but also to reduce the risk of contracting HIV in their higher-risk clients. The potential contribution of this research to advancing effective HIV prevention programming for gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men is therefore substantial.

column36: Improving the identification and treatment of young adults with heart disease: the Study to Avoid cardioVascular Events in British Columbia (SAVE BC)
column37: Heart disease risk is strongly influenced by genetics, particularly when it occurs at a young age. As a consequence, when one individual develops heart disease under the age of 55 years, his or her first degree relatives (siblings, children and parents) are at substantially increased risk of also developing heart disease. Current approaches to identify patients at risk for heart disease focuses largely on older adults, and thus fails to identify most of the cases of early onset heart disease. We have devised a study, called SAVE BC (Study to Avoid Vascular Events in British Columbia), to identify individuals with early onset heart disease (which we define as men less than 50 and women less than 55 years), and then to systematically identify the affected individual's first degree relatives, and use state-of-the-art screening approaches to predict their risk of developing disease. Where appropriate, these family members will be offered preventative therapies to reduce their risk. The goals of this proposal are to assess the ability of this screening approach to identify individuals at risk of heart disease who are eligible for preventative therapy. We will also study the clinical and genetic risk factors for early onset heart disease in Canada, and work with patients and health care providers to improve family based screening. This work is expected to improve the dedications of Canadians at risk for early onset heart disease and to lower the burden of this disease in Canada.

column37: An American Heart Association Scientific Statement positioned bipolar disorder (BD) as a Tier II-Moderate Risk condition that predisposes youth to early development of heart disease. Cognition will be measured using a computerized touch-screen program. We predict that the health of small blood vessels will differ across the different study groups: small blood vessel health will be worst in BD, intermediate in offspring of parents with BD and offspring of parents with heart-related conditions, and best in healthy teens. column36: Locus coeruleus NE modulation in learning and Alzheimer's disease
column37: The beginnings of Alzheimer's Disease occur in a group of cells in the brainstem that produce noradrenaline. This group is called the locus coeruleus. The first brain changes in humans appear quite early as production of abnormal tau protein by these cells. The abnormal tau spreads from locus coeruleus along memory pathways until reaching the cortex and becoming tangles. Abnormal tau in locus coeruleus cells occurs early in our lives and is seen in most by age 30, but its effects are not noticeable and spread occurs over decades. We need to detect and prevent these early events. Our evidence suggests distinguishing between very similar patterns is helped by the locus coeruleus. We will test this idea by producing abnormal human tau in rat locus coeruleus cells and testing similar odor discrimination ability. We know the locus coeruleus is activated by new, and by stressful, experiences. Importantly, it is activated differently by these two experiences. We think novel experience activation will slow abnormal brain changes, while stress will increase their rate and extent. We will activate rat locus coeruleus cells containing abnormal tau to mimic either novel and enriched or stressful experience. We predict the spread of abnormal tau along memory pathways will be fast with stress patterns and slow, or prevented by, novelty patterns that can promote learning and memory. Locus coeruleus may be a two-edged sword in Alzheimer's Disease acting either to diminish or accelerate the later likelihood of Alzheimer's Disease appearing. We will identify activity patterns that decrease, or increase, the spread of the earliest brain changes and we will relate their occurrence to pattern discrimination ability to provide new ideas for detecting early locus coeruleus changes and for designing lifestyles to prevent the spread and expression of abnormality, thus stopping later Alzheimer's Disease.

column36: Understanding cancer burden and outcomes for Canadians living with intellectual and developmental disabilities
column37: Not all Canadians have the same cancer risk, receive the same quality of healthcare after a cancer diagnosis, or have the same prognosis. This may be the result of many things including how much money someone has, their education, where they live, or discrimination within the healthcare system that causes people to be treated differently, regardless of how sick they are. Although cancer is a leading cause of death for Canadians living with intellectual disabilities and developmental disabilities (IDD), they may be less likely to receive high quality cancer treatment compared to other Canadians. Because people living with IDD are more likely to live in vulnerable circumstances (such as those described above), this may impact how quickly their cancer is diagnosed, their access to life-saving treatment and result in worse outcomes. The goal of this project is to determine whether or not Canadians living with IDD are more likely than Canadians who do not have IDD to be 1) diagnosed with cancer; 2) diagnosed with incurable cancer; 3) not receive the right cancer treatment; and 4) to die of their cancer. To achieve our goal, our team of cancer and IDD researchers and clinicians will perform simultaneous research studies of breast, colorectal, and cancer patients living in Manitoba and Ontario. This will be done by using data routinely collected during encounters with provincial health, social, and education systems. Analyses will be conducted within each respective province. This study will provide the first Canadian research describing cancer outcomes for people with IDD. Without this information, people with IDD may not receive the best care for their cancer, causing unnecessary harm. This study will highlight ways to improve the quality of care provided. We will work with our policy partners to ensure this information is usable and informative to the care of underserved cancer populations.

column36: Alpha particle-labeled antibody-drug radioconjugates for radiotherapy of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC)
column37: Metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is the second leading cause of death from cancer. At initial diagnosis almost half of patients have advanced disease and fewer than 10% live for more than five years. Surgery is the most effective treatment for controlling further spread, although local recurrence rates can range from 36-88%. A protein called epidermal growth factor receptor I (EGFR) has been shown to be increased in up to 80% of mCRC. Available drugs that target this protein are not effective. Another problem with treating patients with EGFR positive mCRC is that the current method for patient selection is less than optimal. Our goal is to develop more effective therapeutic and imaging agents that will improve the care of mCRC Radioimmunotherapy (i.e.radiolabeled antibodies ) have shown some promise in treating mCRC. However, current strategies have often given suboptimal results since all studies have focused on beta emitting radiation, which is less potent and tends to be toxic to adjacent healthy cells. In contrast, radioimmunotherapy strategies based on alpha particles, such as 225Ac, are up to 1000-fold more effective. Firstly, we propose to develop a set of novel therapeutic compounds which will be based on an antibody nimotuzumab (an antibody that specifically binds to EGFR protein on the cancer cell), linked to two other anticancer agents namely a drug and an alpha particle (actinium-225: 225Ac). The approach will be tested in cells and in mice bearing colorectal cancers. Secondly, we will develop an antibody imaging agent 89Zr-FABH that can be used together with PET/CT to more accurately diagnose and evaluate response to the new treatments against colorectal cancer. We anticipate that these strategies will be more effective than current treatment approaches for colorectal cancer and can be beneficial to other cancer types that express this protein - annually about 1 million new cases of EGFR-positive cancers are reported in North America.

column37: Memory B cells are pivotal to the establishment and maintenance of protection from re-encountered pathogens, both in the context of natural infection and vaccination. Following activation memory B cells divide and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells more rapidly than naive B cells. The importance of pathogen-specific antibodies is emphasized by observations illustrating that neutralizing antibody responses are an important component of most successful vaccines. The Fc Receptor-Like (FCRL) family of cell surface receptors is preferentially expressed on B lineage cells. Among these, FCRL4 family member is expressed only on a subpopulation of memory B cells that are functionally impaired in chronic infectious diseases like HIV. In previous work, we could demonstrate the strong regulatory activity of FCRL4 on memory B cells. Furthermore, we determined that antibodies encoded by FCRL4+ memory B cells preferentially detect commensal microbiota. In this research proposal we will investigate the antibodies to known antigens from vaccinations that are encoded by FCRL4+ and FCRL4- memory B cells. We will determine the factors that lead to the generation of FCRL4-bearing memory B cells and we will investigate the characteristics antibody secreting plasma cells derived from FCRL4+ and FCRL4- memory B cells. The results from this study will provide deeper understanding of functionally distinct memory B cell populations and their plasma cell progeny. Ultimately, this information will be important in vaccine design efforts aiming to elicit long lasting protective antibody titres to pathogens to which presently no effective vaccines are available.

column36: Myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF) and serum response factor (SRF) are constituents and key regulators of the primary cilium
column37: The primary cilium is an important chemical and mechanical antenna of practically every cell in the body. This organelle, once thought to be vestigial, is a major organizer of differentiation, cell growth and proliferation. The paramount importance of the cilium became obvious with the recognition that errors in the genes that encode cilium proteins cause serious and ultimately often lethal hereditary diseases, so called ciliopathies. The most common of these is polycystic kidney disease, but mutation in ciliary proteins lead to a set of other syndromes too, with wide-ranging symptoms including impaired mental function due to malformation of the nervous system, blindness, left-right side inversion, bone deformities, obesity as well as liver, heart and other kidney diseases. Moreover, acquired (non-inherited) abnormalities in the cilium contribute to cancer and chronic scarring of tissues (fibrosis). While complex machineries control both the assembly and the disassembly of the cilium and coordinate these evens with cell division, the underlying molecular mechanisms are not well understood. Our proposal stems from our discovery that two proteins, myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF) and serum response factor (SRF) regulate cilium assembly and disassembly. These factors, controlled by the cell's skeleton, can drive genes, some of which are necessary for cilium maintenance. However, in addition to their gene-regulating (transcriptional) effect, we found that MRTF and SRF are also part of the cilium itself. These recognitions open a new way to affect the cilium. Using a variety of cell and molecular biology techniques, we propose to uncover how these proteins contribute to the normal structure and function of the primary cilium, and how they might be involved in serious ciliopathies and cancer-related cilium defects. Understanding these processes will lead to fundamental insights necessary for correcting cilium errors.

column37: In Canada, most health research is focused on a disease or deficit end-point, whether designing, testing or implementing interventions, treatments or preventive measures. The focus of this Indigenous knowledge development project is on wellness - promoting, maintaining and re-gaining wellness, by itself, or in the context of a variety of conditions or life circumstances that First Nations, Inuit and Metis peoples may find themselves. There is much Indigenous health and wellness knowledge/wisdom that has yet to be re-awakened, and in fact, cannot be well-supported in our current colonized structures and conceptualizations. To do so will take the development and re-development of roles and processes within community. It is within this context that we see Indigenous community as being the primary research leader, with the academy and the health system as being knowledge users. We propose a network of Indigenous health knowledge development centres. These centres will be grounded in the land and in culture, with land-based Indigenous research methodologies a critical component of the network. Using a health determinants approach and working with communities of Indigenous people including Elders, Knowledge Holders, youth, researchers and health workers, we will explore what makes Indigenous people well, what keeps them well, and how Indigenous wellness can be achieved or re-gained and maintained through practices and interventions based on traditional and western knowledge. Through meaningful engagement between academic centres and Indigenous communities, our network of knowledge development centres will increase and build on our understanding of wellness. In the words of the Elder: "Let's research ourselves back to life."

column36: Creating a Living Knowledge Translation Agenda to Improve the Delivery of Evidence-based Care in Adult Critical Care Medicine
column37: Healthcare systems need to more consistently incorporate findings from research into patient care. With the amount of research in the current medical literature, and limited resources available to apply this research, some research findings should be given higher priority over others. This is especially important for patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) where multiple expensive, potentially risky tests, and treatments are used to save lives. In a review of ICU research, we identified 14 medical practices that high-quality research suggests are beneficial among ICU patients, and 21 practices that are of no benefit. Decision-makers for ICUs in Alberta have asked us to use this list of 35 ICU practices to develop a method that can both determine from within a list of current research which ICU care practices should be given greater priority for use or removal from patient care, and allows for annual updating of the list by being responsive to new research. We plan to do this in 4 connected steps, guided by a governing group consisting of patients, researchers, and healthcare providers. First, we will develop a method that enables our review of ICU research to be continuously updated in response to new research. Second, using electronic health data, we will determine predicted outcomes and costs associated with changes in use of each practice. Third, we will survey a national group of healthcare providers and former ICU patients and their family members to rank priorities for practice change. Fourth, we will present the results of steps 1-3 to decision-makers in Alberta to determine which patient care practices will be targets for practice change in Alberta ICUs. This work is important because it will help improve care in ICUs, and potentially contribute to future improvements in other areas of healthcare through development of a strong, widely applicable, sustainable approach for incorporating high-quality science into the care of patients admitted to ICUs.

column36: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) for intestinal decolonization of multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogens
column37: Antimicrobial resistance is a global threat to public health. The Canadian government recently made antimicrobial resistance a nationwide health priority (Antimicrobial Resistance and Use in Canada: A Federal Framework for Action). Kidney transplant patients are at especially high-risk of developing infections caused by multidrug-resistant bacteria, so-called 'super-bugs'. These drug-resistant infections are hard to treat, result in longer hospital stays, and lead to more deaths and higher medical costs. The source of these 'super-bugs' is often the patient's own gut, where they can remain until escaping to cause infection. Current approaches to eliminating resistant bacteria from the gut do not work very well and can sometimes lead to an increase in resistant bacteria. Emerging evidence suggests that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), otherwise known as a 'poop' transplant, may be an effective and innovative approach to eradicating multidrug-resistant bacteria from the gut before they can cause infection. FMT involves the infusion of fully screened, healthy donor stool into a patient. FMT is already known to be a safe and effective way to remove Clostridium difficile, a cause of hospital-associated diarrhea, from infected patients. In this randomized controlled trial, we will test the efficacy of FMT via enema to eliminate highly resistant bacteria from the intestinal tract of kidney transplant patients. We will also examine (1) FMT safety; (2) how long patients remain decolonized; (3) if there are fewer infections after FMT; and (4) how FMT might work. Our research team has obtained all the necessary ethics and Health Canada approvals and started study recruitment. Ideally, FMT donor feces will be replaced by a well-defined community of bacteria that is just as effective as FMT. Vedanta Biosciences, our industry partner, will work with us to develop a transformative microbial therapy to prevent carriage and infection by highly drug-resistant 'super-bugs'.

column36: Discovery of non-coding driver mutations and pathways in thousands of whole cancer genomes using gene regulatory and long-range chromatin interactions
column37: Cancer is a genetic disease however most cancers are not inherited but are instead caused by random mutations in individuals' DNA over time. While most such mutations are harmless, a minority called cancer driver mutations (drivers) affect critical genes and cause unlimited cell growth and other cancerous properties. To understand cancer biology and develop therapies, we need to deeply characterize drivers. As drivers are known to affect the same DNA region more frequently than expected by chance alone, we can find drivers statistically by analysing many cancer genomes and millions of mutations. While earlier studies only mapped the small fraction (<2%) of the human genome that produces proteins, recent DNA sequencing tools map entire genomes. As such whole-genome sequencing datasets are only becoming available recently, little is known about drivers in the entire genome. We will build the largest dataset of whole cancer genomes by combining all available studies of this kind, using statistical and machine-learning tools we and others developed. We will study different cancer types and also combine all data to find drivers that are rare but important in many cancer types. We will focus on the least-studied part of the genome outside of protein-coding genes. As genes often act together in cancer, we will find additional drivers by grouping biologically related genes. We will conduct modern genetic experiments using CRISPR with cancer cell lines and confirm top-ranking candidates as true drivers of cancer by measuring cell growth, motility and other oncogenic properties. We will produce a reliable catalogue of cancer drivers supported by validation experiments of our best findings at project completion. The catalogue will increase understanding of cancer biology and ultimately improve therapies. Some drivers may be applicable as biomarkers to diagnose cancer and predict response to chemotherapies.

column36: Role of miR-299a in regulating diabetic kidney disease
column37: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure, leading to scarring of the filtering units of the kidneys. Patients with diabetes have high glucose levels in their blood. High glucose causes kidney cells called mesangial cells to make scar proteins. These scar proteins accumulate in the filtering units of the kidneys and prevent them from functioning properly. Our previous studies showed that absence of the protein caveolin-1 from kidney cells and from kidneys protected against scarring due to diabetes. In diabetic kidneys and kidney cells exposed to high glucose, micro RNA 299a-5p is increased, and blocking it prevents cells from making scar proteins. Drugs which block other molecules like micro RNA-299a-5p have already been successfully used in patients. If our studies show that blocking micro RNA-299a-5p prevents or improves diabetic kidney disease, this will give us a new treatment to test in patients with kidney disease due to diabetes.

column37: Our research focuses on the most common arrhythmia affecting humans. This arrhythmia is known as atrial fibrillation (AF). column37: Intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICUAW) describes muscle weakness that develops in some people who have been admitted to an ICU with a serious illness. We found that muscle stem (satellite) cells are lost, implying the muscle is unable to regenerate. We have identified some molecular regulators, known as microRNAs (miRs), are likely to play a causative role. In this study we propose to determine the mechanism by which our candidate factors impair muscle regeneration and growth and determine if we can in turn, impact muscle regeneration and growth by modulating our candidate factors in cell culture models and patients with ICUAW. The significance and strength of this proposal lies in its potential translatability to the clinical setting. By generating totally novel insights into sustained muscle wasting and potential therapeutic target identification, this will allow us to develop various approaches aimed at limiting loss of, and/or enhancing growth of muscle in individuals with sustained ICUAW.

column36: Non-canonical role of initiator caspases in colorectal cancer
column37: The body relies on a particular cell death program called apoptosis to eliminate defective cells. This program involves the sequential activation of a distinct set of caspases, which are enzymes that cleave and thereby inactivate hundreds of proteins necessary for cell survival. A fundamental trait of cancer cells is their inherent or acquired resistance to apoptosis. This cancer feature often accounts for chemotherapeutic failure and is associated with enhanced tumorigenesis and metastasis. At the molecular level, resistance to apoptosis usually involves a block of death signal transmission from the initiator to the executioner caspases, the latter of which is responsible for killing the cell. As such, a direct consequence of resistance to apoptosis is that tumor cells can uniquely sustain the activity of initiator caspases by avoiding the killing effects of the others. Results from our recent study support the hypothesis that substrate products of initiator caspases contribute to enhancing tumorigenic and metastatic features of apoptosis-resistant cancer cells. The proposed project seeks to validate this postulate by designing a method for detecting the activity of initiator caspases and their cleaved substrates as biomarkers of colorectal cancer progression, by identifying proteins cleaved by initiator caspases in apoptosis-resistant cancer cells, and by verifying the tumorigenic and metastatic properties of these identified substrates in colorectal cancer cell models. Experimental validation of our hypothesis would offer a ground-breaking paradigm shift in the current understanding of the roles of caspases in cell death and when tumor cells become resistant to apoptosis. Notably, our work could lead to the development of new biomarkers and innovative therapies to overcome clinical resistance to several types of current clinically used cancer-death-based chemotherapies.

column36: Targeting AMPK to treat muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) are the most prevalent muscular dystrophies in children and adults in Canada and worldwide. There are no cures, thus the health- and life-limiting nature of these disorders is, at present, inevitable. We know that when a protein in our muscles called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is turned on, it has some benefit in reducing the severity of DMD and DM1 in animals engineered to have these disorders. The use of better compounds to activate AMPK, those that are safe, effective, and able to be taken orally, would greatly increase their clinical impact and translation into human DMD and DM1 patients. Here we will employ new approaches to examine the effectiveness of targeting AMPK for the treatment of muscular dystrophy. Specifically, the purpose of this project is to investigate whether stimulation of AMPK with practical, next-generation compounds improves the health of mice with DMD and DM1, which would provide a better outlook for applicability in human muscular dystrophy patients. We will focus on the ability of the AMPK-activating drugs to restore the proper structure and function of dystrophic skeletal muscles, as well as explore the underlying molecular mechanisms of their action. There is no better time than the present to perform these studies since these drugs are also currently in clinical trials for treating epidemics such as diabetes and metabolic disease. This proposal is designed to reveal critical information about the therapeutic potential of a new class of AMPK-stimulating compounds, which may ultimately improve the quality and quantity of life of Canadians.

column36: Towards the micro-elimination of hepatitis C virus among Canadian provincial prison inmates: The effectiveness of patient navigation on treatment uptake
column37: The prevalence of chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is approximately 40-fold higher among provincial prison inmates compared to the Canadian population. Left untreated, there is ongoing risk of transmission within prisons and to the community at large upon release. Treatment of prisoners for HCV could substantially reduce prevalent and incident infections. However, due to short sentences in provincial prisons, inmates are often released prior to treatment completion, making linkage to HCV care upon release essential. Currently, less than 1% of inmates link to care following release. Patient navigation, whereby a peer typically assists patients in completing a health care goal, may have a role in linking inmates to HCV care following release. However, no research has yet to be done on different models of patient navigation for inmates. While linkage to care is the rate-limiting step in the HCV cascade of care for released inmates, linkage in the absence of treatment uptake will fail to achieve the goal of HCV micro-elimination, underscoring treatment uptake as the most meaningful clinical outcome. This study will assess two models of patient navigation, a transitional and a tailored model, on HCV treatment uptake. The tailored model will be designed following one-to-one qualitative interviews with inmates and an expert review of providers and inmates. Both models will be implemented and evaluated on treatment uptake, the primary outcome measure, as well as linkage to care, the secondary outcome measure. The goal will be to capitalize on the existing infrastructure and partnerships that are currently in place at Bordeaux prison to conduct this study. The findings of this study will be critical in developing optimal models of patient navigation for scale up in other provincial prisons, ensuring that we are one step closer towards to the "micro-elimination" of HCV among one of the most important sub-populations fueling the current epidemic in Canada.

column37: Despite enormous advances in prevention, diagnosis and management over the past few decades, heart disease remains the leading cause of death and disability in western societies. column37: Infertility affects around 15% of couples of reproductive age, and about half of the infertility is associated with male partner. To date, intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is a common clinical practice as an assisted reproductive technology (ART) procedure to achieve fertilization in vitro. Despite the relatively high fertilization rate of ICSI, the latter is a more expensive and invasive treatment compared to the standard in vitro fertilization (IVF) and the intrauterine insemination (IUI) procedures. There has been increasing reports on the association of increased genetic anomalies and birth defects in ICSI concepti. This may be due partly to damages to gamete chromosomes caused by the invasive ICSI procedure. To encourage the use of the less invasive standard IVF and IUI for male infertility treatment, there is need to improve the fertilization rate of standard IVF and IUI. Functionally, does oviductin enhance sperm fertilizing ability and what is the mechanism that regulates the functional property of oviductin? Clinically, will supplementation of culture medium with oviductin enhance fertilization as measured by in vitro functional assays? The ultimate goal is to improve the health service use of IVF and IUI procedures involving couples with male infertility indications in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Child abuse and neglect is a serious public health concern not only in North America but worldwide. In Ontario, child neglect is the second most common form of substantiated maltreatment among cases investigated by child welfare, with an incidence rate of 24%. SafeCare(R) is an evidence-based, in-home parenting program that specifically addresses child neglect for young families (newborn-5 years) involved in child welfare. Following a previous CIHR grant in which we successfully implemented SafeCare across 6 Ontario child welfare agencies, we are now seeking funds to evaluate the program in greater detail across child welfare agencies that are diverse in terms of size (urban, rural), location (northern, southern Ontario), and culture (Indigenous families). For the evaluation, we will gather information from both children and caregivers prior to the SafeCare program and at various time points following program completion. We will use various data collection methods (questionnaires, testing, child welfare data) to examine three research questions: 1) Does the program work differently for families and if so, what factors are associated with better outcomes over time? 2) How does SafeCare work in terms of mechanisms of change (parental improvements in emotion regulation)? and 3) Does participation in SafeCare decrease rates of re-entry into child welfare? The current project not only has the potential to impact the health of individual children and families but it also has population health implications. Specifically, child neglect is expensive from a community point of view (medical care, out-of-home placement, poor educational outcomes) and once established, it tends to remain persistent. By evaluating SafeCare outcomes over a long-term basis and better understanding the ways in which it works, child welfare may continue to invest in this evidence-based program and make refinements to improve its effectiveness
