column37: Liver disease has a significant impact on the Canadian population affecting more than 8 million Canadians. Muscle wasting and hepatic encephalopathy (HE; complex neuropsychiatric disorder) are serious complications of chronic liver disease (CLD; cirrhosis) affecting 80% of patients. These complications increase hospital admissions and mortality, hence adding to the already significant economic burden on health care systems. Liver transplantation, the only curative treatment for CLD, is a limiting therapeutic option due to a shortage of available livers. Therefore, development of alternative therapeutic strategies to prevent complications and prolong survival until a liver becomes available for transplantation is crucial. Inflammation and ammonia are major factors implicated in the development of HE. Muscle wasting may predispose to the development of HE since the muscle plays a vital compensatory role in ammonia detoxification. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1alpha) and brain-derived neurotrophic fator (BDNF) are factors implicated in the regulation of muscle mass. We hypothesize that ammonia and inflammation-induced PGC-1alpha downregulation in cirrhosis adversely leads to muscle mass loss (through decreased BDNF) and, consequently, to HE, which are attenuated with exercise training and omega-3 fatty acids supplementation. We will use in vitro, in vivo model systems and cirrhotic patients to verify our hypothesis. Results of this study will clarify the role of PGC-1alpha/BNDF in the pathogenesis of cirrhosis-related muscle mass loss and HE. Finally, as the pathophysiological mechanisms are identified, insights for efficient therapeutic strategies will be uncovered, not only to improve the quality of life of cirrhotic patients while waiting for a healthy liver, but also to lead to a better outcome following liver transplantation.

column36: Characterizing a Process of Stress-Inducible Protein Aggregation
column37: Proteins are the building blocks of life and are essential to all basic cellular and organismal pathways (e.g. survival, growth and replication). Once made, a protein is carefully folded to generate a functional molecule, which "floats" around the cell and associates with DNA, RNA or other molecules to accomplish important tasks. Under harsh or stressful environmental conditions (e.g., high fever and oxygen-deprivation) proteins can change shape and clump together, inactivating themselves and turning off certain cellular pathways. This natural process is similar to hibernation, as it allows the cell to save energy and ensure survival. Once favourable conditions are restored, the cell can wake up by dissolving the aggregates, re-fold the proteins and re-activate the important machinery. In this study we will investigate the mechanisms controlling protein aggregation. Here, we plan to: 1) identify the sensing and control molecules that regulate protein clumping and 2) examine the cellular pathways that are shutdown under distinct environmental settings, thereby creating a basic understanding of how cells recognize and tailor their responses to different harmful stressors. It is also interesting to note that abnormal protein clumping is seen in many neurodegenerative disorders (i.e., Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases). Therefore, we suspect that dysregulation of this natural pathway may be associated with these debilitating conditions.

column36: Reverse engineering working memory circuits in the primate brain: Implications for the study of memory deficits.
column37: Working memory (WM), the ability to maintain and manipulate information for short time periods, is one of the main pillars of human and animal cognition. WM is deeply impaired in mental diseases such as Alzheimer and Schizophrenia. There is no effective treatment for WM deficits in humans, partly because we have a poor understanding of the mechanisms underlying WM function in the human brain. Studies in non-human primates have revealed that the persistent activity of neurons in the lateral prefrontal cortex encodes the features and location of remembered objects. Thus, it has been proposed that persistent activity in this area supports WM coding in the brain. The mechanisms by which persistent activity encoding WM arises remain a matter of debate. In this proposal, we will conduct a series of experiments in behaving non-human primates using behavioral, electrophysiological and anatomical/histological techniques in order to clarify these and other related issues. We will: first, contrast two main mechanisms by which persistent activity may arise, network dynamics vs intrinsic cell properties, second, identify the features of cortical microcircuits that allow persistent activity to emerge in association areas of the primate neocortex; third, investigate whether and how persistent activity encodes the content of WM in naturalistic environments simulated via virtual reality; and finally, we will test predictions of how Ketamine, a recreational drug that block NMDA receptors and interfere with synaptic transmission, produces specific changes in neural activity and WM deficits. Our results will provide a mechanistic understanding of the mechanisms underlying WM function in the primate brain. They will pave the road to our understanding of WM impairments during mental disease and the search for effective treatment solutions.

column37: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is a disorder of heart muscle and heart rhythm that is passed on in families. ARVC occurs in 1 in 2500 persons, but is responsible for 11% of sudden cardiac deaths (SCD) in adults (under 65), 22% of athletes and up to 25% of children. The average age at death is 40 years, and so it contributes even more to SCD when measured in years of potential life lost. SCD is exceeded only by all cancer in this measure. ARVC is hard to detect, and many tests are needed to identify people with the disease. These tests still miss disease in almost 1/3 of people assessed. Genetic testing also missed most people with disease. There are some similarities between ARVC and blistering diseases of the skin, which can bee caused by either gene changes or antibodies. We therefore looked for antibodies in ARVC, and found one antibody that detects 98% of people with disease. The objectives of our study are: 1.) identify whether anti-DSG2 antibody will be accurate in a large study of patients, and identify persons even before disease can be detected through other tests. 2.) evaluate whether antibody level predicts severity and risk of disease. 3.) Use this test to help find new ARVC genes. To study these objectives, we are collecting information and blood samples from many subjects with ARVC, by working with other large expert groups including the Toronto General Hospital, the Canadian ARVC Registry, Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, Zurich, Poland and China. These will provide us with 2600 samples and data including groups patients with definite disease, 'pre-clinical' disease and high-risk disease. These groups will let us address each of our objectives above. We will measure antibody using standard research and clinical methods. For comparison, we have access to blood samples from large groups of normal individuals over a broad range of ages and both sexes. Our study is unique in studying a novel sensitive and specific marker of ARVC.

column36: PCSK9, a novel contributor to the development of castration resistant prostate cancer
column37: Prostate cancer is the most common male malignancy in Canada. The disease affects one in six men and is the second leading cause of cancer-associated deaths in Canadian men. Mortality is mainly caused by disease progression on the standard of care: androgen deprivation therapy. Since the 1940s, androgen deprivation is the first line therapy used in patients with advanced prostate cancer. This treatment temporarily stops prostate cancer growth. However, resistant tumors in the form of castration resistant prostate cancers (CRPCs) always arise, and are lethal. CRPC is the dominant cause of prostate cancer death. Understanding what causes CRPC development is critical to offer patients the best medical care. Our group has recently found a protein that promotes CRPC development. The expression of this protein is increased in prostate cancers metastasized to the bone. Bone is the major site of prostate cancer metastasis; prostate cancers metastatic to bone are the dominant source of CRPC. Furthermore, we found that prostate cancers with higher levels of this protein are likely to progress to CRPC. Importantly, using mouse models for human CRPC, we have shown that by increasing the level of this protein expression alone is sufficient to convert castration-sensitive prostate cancer cells to cells resistant to castration. Collectively, our research suggests this protein being an important contributor to CRPC development in human prostate cancer. In this project, we will thoroughly examine this protein's contributions to the progression of castration resistant prostate cancers using human prostate cancer cell lines, mouse models for CRPC, and patients' tumor tissues. We will also determine whether by reducing this protein expression will prevent or reduce CRPC development. This research will reveal a new factor that enhances CRPC development. This knowledge will pave the way to develop new means of diagnosis and new treatments in patients with advanced prostate cancer.

column37: Excess fat (cholesterol) deposits in our blood vessels can lead to heart disease. The blood vessel wall is made up of special proteins that contain sugar molecules with sticky regions that specifically attach and trap the cholesterol-carrying particles circulating in our blood. Current treatments aim to reduce the amount of cholesterol (e.g LDL or bad cholesterol) in the blood stream. There is currently no drug (available or under research) that can specifically target the blood vessels to reduce the accumulation of cholesterol. We have collaborated with the Centre for Molecular Immunology in Cuba, that are experts in developing vaccine like drugs. They have recently developed a compound (antibody) called 'chP3R99' that has two fold action: (i) It specifically binds to the sugar chains which prevents the cholesterol from attaching to blood vessels (ii) This antibody has vaccine-like properties, which means it does not have to be injected repeatedly to maintain its effect. Once injected it can continue to produce similar antibodies and reduce the overall cost of the therapy. Diabetes increases the risk for heart disease. There are two types of bad forms of cholesterol in our blood (i) Traditional bad cholesterol (LDL) produced from the liver and (ii) 'Remnant' cholesterol, derived from diet and secreted by the intestine. During diabetes, remnant cholesterol is often increased while the LDL cholesterol can remain normal. Therefore the aim of this project is to determine if the novel antibody 'chP3R99' can reduce the accumulation of remnant cholesterol as well as LDL cholesterol in blood vessels of animal models that have diabetes. We also have a collaboration with a cardiologist who can provide us with donor (discarded) human blood vessels and other tissues. We propose to use donor blood vessels to circulate remnant cholesterol with/without the antibody chP3R99 to assess the extent that we can reduce cholesterol build up in human tissue.

column37: Diabetes and pre-diabetes are metabolic disorders affecting more than 15% of the world's population. The prevalence of these disorders is currently increasing mainly due to the increasingly sedentary lifestyles associated with rising obesity rates and aging of the population. Because diabetes and pre-diabetes are so closely associated with major health problems such as high blood pressure, high blood lipids and cardiovascular disease (CVD), they have a tremendous impact on the health-care costs of our society. Significant efforts should therefore be dedicated to tackling this problem from a societal perspective. Although elevated blood lipid levels observed in diabetes and pre-diabetes have largely been attributed to overproduction by the liver, recent studies by our group have indicated that the small intestine also contributes significantly to elevated blood lipid levels. Recent studies provide strong support for the beneficial role of dietary monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) for primary cardiovascular prevention. New data also suggest that MUFAs from olive oil may exert beneficial effects on CVD risk by reducing intestinal lipid production, but no studies have examined this issue in patients with diabetes or pre-diabetes. This study will allow us to investigate whether substitution of canola oil rich in MUFAs for saturated fats could reduce intestinal lipid production in patients with pre-diabetes. We will also examine the impact of MUFAs on the expression of the major genes involved in the regulation of intestinal lipid metabolism. The identification of therapeutic strategies using non-pharmacologic agents such as MUFAs is likely to lead to significant advances in our attempts to reduce CVD risk in this vulnerable population.

Our research involves residents, family and staff in all research activities. We make sure that their voices are heard to learn from them. Together, we build our tools to help improve resident and family experience with living and dying in LTC. We evaluate how our work is developing and let the residents, families and staff know what is happening through LTC visits and meetings. Our research team regularly meets with national leaders across organizations, communities, and disciplines to exchange ideas. By exploring what happens within each LTC site, we will make accessible online tools that meet the needs of diverse groups across Canada. Our research has the potential for widespread use across sectors. As a result, we will support improvements in health-related knowledge and health system and health care.

column37: Heart disease is the primary cause of death in the western world. Cardiac fibrosis is a stiffening of the heart caused by many forms of heart disease. Aim 2: we will test existing drugs (angiotensin II inhibitors - ACEi/ARB) that have shown beneficial effects on fibrosis for their ability to reduce scleraxis levels, and show that these drugs lose their efficacy when excessive scleraxis is made. Aim 3: using mouse models, we will demonstrate that deleting the scleraxis gene reverses heart fibrosis even when the disease is well-established. Aim 4: we will test the ability of a novel scleraxis mutant, developed in our lab, to interfere with normal scleraxis in the heart in order to reduce fibrosis. These results will reveal new details of how scleraxis causes cardiac fibrosis, will provide crucial supporting evidence for the eventual adoption of ACEi/ARB as treatments for this condition, and will demonstrate the efficacy of our scleraxis mutant as a potential new treatment for fibrosis.

column36: Comprehensive mapping and evolutionary dynamics of the mutational landscape of antimicrobial resistance
column37: We are surrounded by bacteria that could potentially cause harmful infections. However, we have been able to keep them at bay because of antibiotics. Indeed, advances in medicine, such as chemotherapy, surgery, and treatment of chronic diseases, crucially depend on our ability to control infections with antibiotics. But this has been compromised by the evolution of bacterial strains with mutations that make them resistant to antibiotics. The classic approach to antibiotic resistance is to discover new drugs. But this may not be enough. We also need to conserve the efficacy and maximize the duration of the usefulness of both current and future antibiotics. Antibiotic resistance will always arise, but if we are able to predict how they evolve, we could potentially delay their emergence. To predict bacterial evolution, we need to know what types of mutations can arise in the bacteria and how much resistance level they confer. Moreover, since multiple co-existing mutations can compete amongst themselves for evolutionary dominance, we also need to track the history of the bacterial population. This project proposes an interdisciplinary approach that brings together concepts from biochemistry, microbiology, and evolutionary biology. We will use state-of-the-art experimental techniques in protein engineering to determine the fitness effects of several thousands of mutations in 3 proteins that are crucial antibiotic targets. Then, by performing lab evolution using robotics and microfluidics, we will determine the survival probability of these mutations. We also developed a novel genetic tool that uniquely barcodes each cell in an evolving bacterial community. This enables us to track at high resolution the lineage and history of the bacterial population as resistance emerges. Ultimately, uncovering how bacteria evolve resistance could lead to novel regimens for optimal drug use that may delay antibiotic resistance and thus help preserve our ability to fight infections.

column36: Metabolic disorders of pregnancy and early-onset disease risk in the offspring: role of adipose tissue expandability
column37: Babies born to mothers who were obese or diabetic during pregnancy are more likely to develop risk factors for cardiovascular disease before they reach adulthood. Given that these metabolic disorders have become the most common complications of pregnancy, they have likely contributed significantly to the current epidemic of early-onset cardiovascular risk among Canadian youth. We have developed novel mouse models of maternal metabolic dysfunction that allow us to identify the developmental perturbations underlying later-life risk and understand how these perturbations impact health at the level of the cell, organ and organ system. Our data suggest that early-onset cardiovascular risk results from a perturbation in the development of fat tissue during fetal life that impairs its ability to expand after birth. Expansion of fat tissue to buffer excess energy plays a critical role in maintaining cardiovascular health under conditions of high caloric intake. Fat tissue has a defined limit of expansion, which is eventually reached as an individual gains weight. Recent studies in obese humans reveal that a failure in fat tissue expansion precipitates the onset of obesity-associated cardiovascular disease. Therefore, we will test the hypothesis that early-onset cardiovascular risk in offspring born to mothers with metabolic dysfunction during pregnancy results from accelerated fat cell maturation leading to a premature limitation in fat expansion. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) promote cardiovascular health by regulating fat cell expansion. Several clinical trials have demonstrated PUFA supplementation to be safe in human infants; however, their utility in optimizing long-term cardiovascular health in infants born to obese or diabetic mothers is currently unknown. Thus, we will determine if early-life PUFA supplementation prevents the development of cardiovascular risk factors in babies born to pregnancies complicated by maternal metabolic dysfunction.

column36: The role of the Inhibitors of Apoptosis (IAPs) in health and disease
column37: Twenty-three years ago, my research group discovered a novel family of mammalian genes, which we called the inhibitors of apoptosis (or IAPs) due to their similarity with viral genes that regulate a process of cell death known as apoptosis. The IAPs not only control how cells die under stress but also have critical roles in cell division and in cell signalling. Moreover, they are especially important for the function of the immune system. The dysregulation of the IAPs are associated with a range of diseases, from cancer to neurodegeneration to infection. Indeed, drugs that target key IAPs, known as Smac mimetics (SMCs) are in clinical trials for the treatment of various cancers and infectious diseases. The inactivation of the IAPs by SMCs renders cancer cells quite sensitive to death triggers produced by the immune system. Remarkably, normal cells do not die when treated with SMCs. We have recently shown that SMCs can complement a new class of revolutionary anti-cancer drugs, called cancer immunotherapy. The combination of SMCs and cancer immunotherapy cures mice of cancer and this research has now led to the initiation of human clinical trials for cancer in 2017-18. My research program studies how the IAPs control life and death decisions at the cellular level and how the IAPs modulate immunity to enhance the activity of immunotherapies. In the span of two decades, we have gone from gene discovery and the creation of a whole new field of study, to the clinical investigation of novel drug classes and approaches that are expected to yield insights into disease and therapy.

column36: Economic impact of falls prevention interventions: We know the "value", but what about the "value for money"?
column37: RATIONALE: Falls have a substantial impact on the quality of life, morbidity, and mortality of older adults, and are costly for our healthcare system. Many falls prevention interventions have proven to be effective. With constrained healthcare resources, the most effective intervention is not always cost-effective, and we are often faced with determining whether an intervention is truly worth the resources it requires. Therefore, in addition to answering the question "does the intervention work?", decision- and policy-makers must also answer the 'value for money' question, "is it cost-effective?". OBJECTIVE: Members of our team previously conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis on falls prevention interventions. This project will examine the cost-effectiveness of effective falls prevention interventions identified through our previous work. Our findings will help identify falls prevention interventions that are not only effective but also cost-effective. METHODS: We will develop a health economics model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of each falls prevention intervention from the perspective of public healthcare payers, using data from our previous work and published literature. We will explore factors that influence the interventions' cost-effectiveness and conduct subgroup analyses by factors such as history of falls. IMPACT: Information on the cost-effectiveness of falls prevention interventions will assist policy-makers to make informed decisions on which intervention they should fund and implement. Our findings will provide evidence on both the value for money and budget impact of falls prevention interventions to decision-makers who fund these interventions and to those who are considering their implementation, namely our colleagues from Department of Medicine at the University of Toronto, Alberta Health Services, the Regional Geriatrics Program of Toronto, Osteoporosis Canada, and the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care.

column36: Improving the specificity of CRISPR/Cas9 using chemically-modified guide RNAs
column37: Thousands of human genetic diseases ranging from cystic fibrosis to muscular dystrophy are caused by a mutation in a single known gene. Yet, despite extensive effort, we have been unable to identify conventional pharmaceuticals to treat many of them. However, modern-day gene editing technology could revolutionize the treatment of these diseases by allowing researchers to permanently correct the underlying genetic mutations causing these diseases. For example, a recently described system called CRISPR/Cas9 can be used to precisely delete, insert, or edit genetic information (DNA) in cell and animal models. In the future, this system could also be applied to the treatment of many of the human diseases listed above by replacing the defective copy of a gene with a correct copy. However, there still remains several hurdles that must be overcome to translate this technology to the clinic. The greatest of these challenges is imperfect specificity. While these tools alter the sequence at the correct target location the majority of the time, they also occasionally alter the genetic information at off-target locations. Unintended DNA cleavage or editing could have detrimental consequences in humans and could give rise to diseases such as cancer. This project proposes to dramatically improve the precision of CRISPR/Cas9, making it safer for eventual human applications. My lab has recently uncovered a way to decrease off-target DNA cutting by CRISPR/Cas9 by over 10,000-fold. This project will broaden and extend our findings to enable precise cleavage of any gene using CRISPR/Cas9. In addition, we will apply our findings to not only Cas9 DNA cutting, but also to optimizing the precision of safer gene editing technology that has recently been invented. Ultimately, we hope to partner with a biotechnology company to advance the development of safer, next-generation gene editing technology for humans.

column36: Developing radioimmunotherapy of osteosarcoma using comparative oncology approach
column37: Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common primary malignant bone tumor and the fifth most common primary malignancy among adolescents and young adults. Unfortunately, overall survival is approximately 70%, with no meaningful improvement realized in over 20 years. Patients with metastatic disease to the lungs and to the bone generally have poor outcomes, with an overall survival of less than 40% and 20%, respectively. In addition, OS demonstrates sweeping genetic variability from one tumor to the next which makes it challenging to pursue conventional targeting approaches. In our previous studies we have found out that a protein called Insulin Growth Factor Receptor Type 2 (IGF2R) is consistently expressed on all OS cell lines, including the ones derived from patients. When targeting the experimental OS tumors in mice with the mouse antibodies to the IGF2R protein, which were carrying the radioactive "payload" capable of destroying tumor cells, we observed considerable slowing down of tumor growth without side effects. However, to move this encouraging approach into the clinical trials, we need two things: make human antibodies to IGF2R which would allow to treat patients multiple times without side effects from the immune system, and to test these antibodies in the animals with the tumors comparable to human ones. It turns to be that OS is one of the most widespread cancers in companion dogs, it very closely resembles human OS, and treatments for dogs are very limited. Thus, our hypothesis is that we will be able to create highly IGF2R-specific human antibodies which would effectively target OS tumor cells in companion dogs with OS and deliver curative tumoricidal doses of radioactivity to the tumors without toxicity to normal organs. If successful, this project will generate the antibodies and the data needed to move this approach into the clinical trials in patients with OS, and, as added benefit, will create the treatment for companion dogs with OS.

column36: HIV-1's hold on host cell vesicular trafficking and metabolism and the impact on pathogenesis, latency and treatment
column37: Over 40 million people worldwide are infected by HIV-1 and it still represents a major health and economic problem worldwide. HIV-1 infection has devastating effects on the immune system resulting in diminishing levels of T cells, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and death. As of mid-2016, there is still no cure or vaccine. Nevertheless, over forty anti-HIV- 1 drugs are available to infected individuals and make HIV-1 infection a chronic and manageable disease since these drugs suppress circulating virus to undetectable levels, allaying many of the pathological effects on the immune system. The pathologies are largely due to the impact of the virus' ability to hijack the host cell. In this work, we uncover HIV-1's ability to commandeer a central regulator of the host cell metabolism (the mammalian target of rapamycin, mTOR) and the host's vesicular trafficking machinery. These two machineries impact on the host at several points including how proteins are synthesized, and how the cell clears cellular debris and derives energy sources, especially when nutrients are lacking or when cells are submitted to stress or pathogen insult. The latter process, called autophagy, represents an important degradative process that maintains cell homeostasis. It recycles cellular components under nutrient deprivation in order to decrease the cell's energy needs. Interestingly, autophagy is also a key component in the defense against pathogens and consequently, viruses, including HIV-1, have evolved to manipulate autophagy to their advantage. In this grant request, we propose to examine the consequences of HIV-1- mediated modulation of mTOR, lysosomal trafficking and autophagy. Biochemistry, the latest gene editing and quantitative microscopy techniques will be used to measure the metabolic consequences of HIV-1 infection in clinically relevant HIV-1 infected CD4+ T cells and macrophages and during latent infection. Targeting these processes may effectively suppress HIV-1.

column36: Structural biology of innate immune proteins
column37: Innate immunity is an ancient system of host defense that predates the adaptive immune system and is conserved in almost all multicellular organisms from insects to mammals. Innate immunity relies on a set of protein receptors that are strategically expressed in cells that are likely to encounter pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, early on in an infection. The interaction of these receptors with components from the pathogen, propagates a signal into the cell that leads to changes in gene expression and accompanying responses by the host that work to eliminate the pathogen. Pathogens try to counteract immunity to gain an advantage by for example injecting toxic proteins into the host. It is necessary to understand the molecular of both of these processes to help develop better therapeutics against infection. This research proposal aims to elucidate the atomic level details for host-pathogen interactions on both sides of interface: 1) IFIT host defence proteins that fend of viral infection and 2) Bacterial effector proteins called YopJ acetyltransferases, which are enzymes that bacteria deliver into the host to subvert the immune response. Understanding the molecular details of how these proteins engage their respective target molecules to enhance or undermine the immune response is an important step towards the development of therapeutic drugs in diseases like cancer and autoimmune disorders, as well as several infectious and inflammatory diseases.

column36: A new model to study the role of intestinal inflammation as a driver of Parkinson's Disease development
column37: In recent years, more and more evidence has accumulated in support of the idea that the gut and the bacteria within it can influence susceptibility to a wide range of diseases, including ones not classically thought of as intestinal diseases. We have recently shown, in a mouse model with a mutation in a Parkinson's Disease-associated gene, that Parkinson's Disease symptoms develop only after infection with bacteria that cause intestinal inflammation and short-term diarrheal disease. For example, people suffering from inflammatory bowel disease are much more likely to develop Parkinson's Disease. Our discovery now provides us with a unique system to investigate exactly how events in the intestine can influence the development of Parkinson's Disease. Using this model we can now study in more detail the specifics of how intestinal bacteria are involved in this process, which of the intestinal responses to the infection are important, and how the signals in the gut get relayed to the brain. We anticipate that our studies may lead to the new ways to detect or prevent Parkinson's Disease early on in its development and before any of the motor symptoms occur.

column36: The McMaster Cohort of Extremely Low Birth Weight Survivors in the Fifth Decade of Life: Physical, Neuropsychiatric, and Socioeconomic Outcomes
column37: With advances in neonatal care, more of the 21,000 babies born in Canada each year at extremely low birth weight (ELBW; less than 1000 g at birth) are surviving. Individuals born extremely preterm face a range of difficulties, affecting their vision, breathing, motor coordination, metabolic, cardiovascular and kidney function, attention, mood, and social integration. These problems do not appear to resolve in adulthood. ELBW survivors are also at greater risk than adults born at normal birth weight (NBW; more than 2500 g at birth) for health-threatening chronic diseases such as hypertension and diabetes at a relatively young age. The McMaster University Cohort is the oldest-known cohort of ELBW survivors in the world. They are now entering their 40s, a life stage that requires active management to maintain physical and psychological health. However, the long-term physical and psychological consequences of being born extremely preterm are unknown and of critical importance. The first goal of the proposed study is to assess the physical, mental, economic, and social challenges faced by ELBW survivors at middle age. This will determine the current health status of ELBW survivors, and also establish valuable benchmarks against which to compare future age-related risks for disease and cognitive decline. Some factors (e.g., differences in brain structure and metabolic regulation) are likely to continue to impact preterm health as the cohort ages, but others may be modifiable. Therefore, the second goal of this study is to identify resilience factors that will modify ELBW outcomes beyond middle age. These factors will provide potential targets for interventions to promote long-term good health and optimal aging in ELBW survivors.

column36: Cardiovascular effects of GLP-1(28-36): focus on heart failure.
column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) including heart failure (HF) are leading causes of death & disability worldwide, and are particular problematic for patients with diabetes. With diabetes approaching epidemic proportions, our need to prevent and treat CVD & HF in these vulnerable groups is pressing. However, unlike the success of reducing CVD by lowering blood pressure or cholesterol, treating diabetes had not translated into reductions in CVD, possibly due to the unwanted side-effects of older diabetes drugs. Our work has identified a new class of diabetes drugs based on the structure of the gut protein 'glucagon-like peptide' (GLP-1) as holding promise for preventing and reducing CVD in animal models. Importantly, our findings have been validated in large clinical trials of diabetic subjects treated with GLP-1 analogs. However, these agents appear not to benefit patients with HF, which may be due to their unwanted effect of increasing heart rate by activating the heart's pacemaker. We have discovered a cleavage fragment of GLP-1, namely GLP-1(28-36), with as much heart protection as GLP-1, without heart rate effects. We propose to test if this peptide can prevent HF in a mouse model. Our approach includes treating heart-injured mice with GLP-1(28-36) vs. control (scrambled) peptide, before and after HF has developed. As we believe our peptide works by changing the heart's 'fuel' (from fatty acid to glucose) we will identify which fuel is being used in mice with HF by measuring the metabolism of isolated heart vessel cells and whole intact working hearts, before & after HF, and in the presence & absence of our peptide & controls. By using genetically engineered mice that lack the enzyme-target of GLP-1(28-36), or lack the ability to generate GLP-1(28-36) from GLP-1, we will also be able to figure out how important this new drug pathway is in HF. Together, we believe these experiments will define a new application (HF) for a very promising new therapeutic molecule.

column36: Understanding the burden and health system impact of loneliness and social isolation in older adults in Canada
column37: Feeling lonely or being socially isolated puts older adults at risk of dying sooner, and may lead to increased use of health system resources. Many older adults report loneliness and social isolation, especially women, due to major life transitions that accompany aging including declining health and/or losing a spouse, relatives and friends. As countries like Canada move towards "super-aged" status, tackling loneliness and social isolation has become an important priority. Whether strategies to address loneliness and social isolation could also alleviate demands on the health system is unclear, but an important question. Prior studies of the relationship between loneliness, social isolation and health use have found mixed results, which may be due to important limitations. We can overcome these problems in Canada with the availability of unique population-level data. Our goals are to measure the burden of loneliness and social isolation in older adults and their impact on the health system, and to see whether there are important differences between women and men. We will use Canada's most comprehensive health survey data (Canadian Community Health Survey) linked with health encounters captured by our universal health care system. These data will allow us to identify vulnerable groups of older adults who are more likely to be lonely or isolated. We will measure the impact of isolation on the health system by comparing patterns of health system use (e.g. medication dispensing, home care, primary care and emergency department visits, hospitalization, long-term care, and death) in older adults who are lonely or socially isolated to their socially engaged peers. We will engage a diverse group of stakeholders across sectors so that our findings are useful to those who can action them, and to form a partnership that can propose community-based solutions. Our research will help communities and the health system improve the health of our aging population.

column36: Sex differences in the risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism: testing an epigenetic hypothesis
column37: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a blood clot that forms in a vein. VTE is a common, lethal, costly, yet treatable condition. There are effective drugs to prevent VTE but they increase the risk of bleeding. Our team has long-term interest in understanding what causes VTE, and how to prevent and treat VTE. We argue that we need to understand how DNA and the way it is packaged and 'read' (i.e. the epigenetic 'code') leads to disease in order to better prevent and manage VTE. The epigenetic code is the intermediate player linking a person's environment and his/her genetic make up. An individual's sex is an important variable on how the genetic and epigenetic codes impact a person's risk to VTE, and how he or she responds to treatment. In particular, we are intrigued by the fact that men and women have a similar risk of developing a first VTE, but men have more than twice the risk of a subsequent VTE after a 'blood thinner' drug treatment is stopped. We propose that sex-specific epigenetic marks underlie the protective effects against subsequent VTE observed in women after treatment with a 'blood thinner'. We will analyze patients' blood samples, biological and clinical data, and perform lab experiments, to understand the biology behind sex differences in the response to VTE treatment. This will be the basis of new tests that will ultimately improve the standard of care received by men and women after a first VTE event. Given the importance and the risk of using 'blood thinners' to manage patients following a VTE, being able to predict who will benefit the most from such drugs and who can safely discontinue their use after initial treatment are of major importance in caring for these patients. This will also inform on novel intervention targets that could reverse the risk of VTE.

column36: Using a novel class of effectors to probe fundamental mechanisms of intracellular disease.
column37: The incidence of the severe pneumonia that Legionella causes (Legionnaires' disease) is inexplicably on the rise - and deadly outbreaks have occurred in Toronto, Quebec City, and Calgary. Legionella can be isolated from the water systems of approximately 1 in 8 homes - and our aging population and aging infrastructure are only increasing the risk to health. Legionella pneumophila is the leading cause of waterborne outbreaks in the US, where it is estimated to cost over $400 million in direct hospitalization costs per year. Given worldwide incidence and trends, a similar relative impact on Canadian health is likely, if not as well quantified. Defining the molecular mechanisms by which Legionella replicates in our water and causes disease is essential to understanding and responding to these alarming trends. A central pillar of molecular pathogenesis is that bacteria inject proteins (effectors) into the host cell in order to modulate host proteins. We have recently uncovered a functionally novel class of effectors in Legionella pneumophila: "metaeffectors" (or "effectors of effectors") that target other effectors rather than host proteins. Metaeffectors are a gamechanger in the study of effector biology - they fundamentally change the way in which we study these important proteins and provide powerful connections to known biology from which we can build outwards from. In this proposal, we will leverage our discovery of metaeffectors to learn how effectors are regulated once inside the host cell. We will build outward from experimental beachheads of known biology to discover new aspects of the host-pathogen interface. Emerging data suggest that metaeffectors are a common feature of bacterial pathogens - meaning that we can no longer afford to overlook this biology. In addition to understanding Legionella metaeffectors, one key deliverable from this work is the establishment of a set of tools and approaches that will be broadly applicable to these other pathogens.

column37: Intractable, pathological pain is the single most common cause of disability, affecting more than 20% of the population world-wide. Enhanced or abnormal pain sensations that typify chronic pain can arise from cellular changes in sensory processing pathways in the spinal cord. In our previous work, we've observed that the cellular changes that occur during the development of persistent pain in the spinal cord are strikingly similar to the changes that occur in the brain during memory formation. Specifically, we have drawn a parallel between the cellular processes in the brain that allow memories to be updated or strengthened, and the processes that are initiated by ongoing activation of pain-sensitive cells in the spinal cord. The process of recalling a memory destabilizes the cellular memory trace, providing a window of opportunity for the strengthening or weakening of the memory. Similarly, we observed that the cellular 'memory' trace in the spinal cord that contributes to pathological pain sensation can also be destabilized by sensory input to the spinal cord. Through this research program, we seek to investigate the mechanisms by which ongoing sensory input can reverse the cellular changes underlying the misprocessing of painful sensory input in the spinal cord. We will identify the exact conditions of activity that enable the destabilization of the memory trace and use these findings to reverse pathological sensory processing in animal models of pain. These data will reveal new approaches for the reversal of pathological pain and provide detailed insight into the role of aberrant spinal activity in various causes of pathological pain.

column36: Genetic drivers of medulloblastoma metastasis
column37: Medulloblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer that most often affects children and adolescents. Current multimodal treatment comprising chemotherapy, surgery and radiation cures about ~70% of the patients. Neurosurgeons remove the tumor in the brain - the so called 'primary tumor' - very easily, however in some patients the tumor can spread (metastasize) to form cancer in other areas of the brain different from the original location. Very often these metastases present in the form of a layer of tumor cells that covers regions of the brain hardly accessible by surgery. As a consequence, medulloblastoma metastases are usually inoperable and patients that have metastases have a very low chance of survival. The therapies that work on the primary tumors are ineffective on the metastases for unknown reasons. In fact, despite metastases represent a major clinical challenge, almost no effort has been directed toward understanding the mechanisms of metastatic spread of medulloblastoma tumor cells. In this proposal we will use a new model of medulloblastoma metastasis based on human cells grown in mice. This approach will allow us to reproduce the life cycle of medulloblastoma in a mouse model, by the way of treating the tumor bearing mice with surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy with the same protocols used in paediatric medulloblastoma patients. Some medulloblastomas will metastasize, just like human cancers do, and then we will be able to directly compare the genetic mutations of the primary tumors and the metastases by using next-generation sequencing techniques. By direct comparison of pre-therapy and post-therapy metastases we will gain key knowledge into the mechanism of metastatic dissemination of medulloblastoma, and identify new potential targets for treatment.

column36: Toking 9 to 5? Examining the impact of cannabis legalization on workplace cannabis use and perceptions among Canadian workers
column37: On October 17, 2018, cannabis use for non-medical purposes will be legalized in Canada. Canadian researchers have recommended a number of indicators that need to be monitored in order to understand the impact of this major policy change on public health and safety. Yet absent from consideration is how legalization may impact use before and at work. Given the important role of work in the lives of Canadians, there is the potential for cannabis use to spill over to the workplace after legalization, which could have occupational health and safety consequences. We recently conducted a survey of 2,014 workers across Canada from a wide range of industries and occupations to better understand current (pre-legalization) workplace use patterns and perceptions. Preliminary findings suggest some workers engage in potentially risky workplace use and demonstrate problematic perceptions of the risks of using cannabis in the workplace. The results justify the need to monitor these patterns following legalization. Through this study, we will continue to collect information from this group of workers to determine whether legalization is associated with changes in workplace use and related perceptions and norms. We will also increase the study sample to ensure we accurately estimate the extent of workplace cannabis use and better understand workplace cannabis use patterns among workers in safety-sensitive occupations, who are at highest risk for safety consequences of workplace use. We will survey 4,000 workers at one, two, and three years after legalization and explore whether differences in trends exist across segments of the labour market. We will also examine how perceptions and norms may influence future cannabis use and vice versa. This project will provide information to understand the short-term effects of legalization on the workplace and help to inform development of policies, practices, and prevention initiatives to ensure lower risk use among Canadian workers.

column37: Among the most common causes of death by heart failure are diseases of the heart muscle, or cardiomyopathies. The most common of these is dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), which affects as many as 1 in every 250 people. In DCM, the heart's chambers become enlarged, and the heart muscle stretches and thins, eventually reaching a point where the heart can no longer function. Right now we do not know what causes DCM in about 70% of people who have it. These people are only diagnosed with DCM after their hearts have lost function. The goal of this research is to understand the events that occur before the heart loses function, and how DCM initiation is regulated. This new information is needed to diagnose DCM early enough to reduce the number of people who die of heart failure. My laboratory established a mouse, unique to our lab, whose heart loses function just like people with DCM, and dies of fulminant heart failure. Using this mouse, we discovered that, before it loses function, the heart changes the way it produces energy. We also identified a protein that controls this change in energy production, called Tbx15. We will now study our mouse and samples from the hearts of people with DCM to define the early events that lead to loss of heart function, and to find out how Tbx15 controls DCM. The knowledge we gain from this work can be used to find ways to diagnose DCM before the heart loses function and mitigate the devastating effects of heart failure.

column37: More than 10% of births are premature, and premature birth kills more Canadian children than any other cause. Babies delivered prematurely have increased risk for both short- and long-term negative health consequences. There is currently no screening method to identify which pregnancies will deliver early. A method to detect pregnancies with a high risk of premature birth is needed to improve health outcomes for both the mother and baby. During pregnancy, a fetus develops an organ called the placenta, which connects it to the mother and delivers nutrients from mother to fetus. DNA from the placenta circulates in the mother's blood, along with the mother's DNA. Many studies have used the sequence of circulating DNA to predict pregnancy complications. In this study, we will look at the chemical changes found between circulating DNA of healthy pregnancies and pregnancies involving premature birth. Specifically, we will look at DNA methylation, a kind of chemical change known to affect which genes are active in different human tissues. We will identify changes in DNA methylation that can determine pregnancies with a high risk of premature birth. Since the test only uses DNA in the mother's blood, we can do this with a non-invasive blood test with little additional risk to the pregnancy. As such, findings from this study can be easily applied to current pregnancy care. This study will result in a noninvasive blood test that can detect pregnancies with increased risk of premature delivery. Use of this test will lead to changes in pregnancy care to try to prevent premature birth. This will lead to better long-term health for both mother and child. It will also decrease the need for the extreme medical care often used on premature infants. Improved health outcomes with decreased interventions will reduce costs to the Canadian health care system.

column36: Defining the Natural History and Predictors of Disease Progression in Mild Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy: A Longitudinal Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study
column37: Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy (DCM) is a common disorder which occurs when progressive age-related changes affecting the bones and discs in the neck lead to compression of the spinal cord, resulting in symptoms of hand weakness, walking difficulties and loss of bladder control. Patients with DCM are classified according to the severity of symptoms as either mild, moderate or severe. Given their significant disability, it is recommended that moderate and severe patients undergo spine surgery to help improve symptoms. In comparison, mild patients (most common type of DCM) experience much less disability; however, an unpredictable proportion of these patients (30-60%) will develop worsening symptoms without surgery, with the remaining fraction remaining stable or improving over time. Ideally, doctors would have a clear understanding of which mild patients are likely to deteriorate such that this fraction could be offered surgery to prevent worsening, while those likely to remain stable or improve could be closely monitored without surgery. Unfortunately, current studies do not provide such information. As a result, doctors have little to guide them when counseling mild DCM patients and making treatment recommendations. To facilitate improvements in understanding and care, 236 mild DCM patients treated without surgery will be enrolled at four Canadian hospitals and followed closely for up to 5 years, observing for changes in clinical status. At the outset, all patients will undergo comprehensive testing including hand function and walking assessments as well as MRI scans. At study completion, using statistics, we will identify which patient information predicts a higher likelihood of clinical deterioration. This information will then be used to help doctors customize treatment plans, with those patients calculated to be at high risk of future deterioration given a recommendation of surgery.

column37: Despite greater understanding and improved management, epilepsy continues to be a major problem in childhood. Early life epilepsy often does not response to the best medical treatment and results in serious long-term consequences. To date, the mechanism and no specific treatments for early life epilepsy are not well understood. Since 1936, the prevailing view of seizures has been "The harmony of the symphony orchestra has become a single note (William Lennox, 1936)". However, given that neurons in the brain are known to be heterogeneous, these neurons may show very different activities during early life seizures. Thus, for precise understanding early life epilepsy at the cellular level, it is crucial to selectively label neurons with different activities during seizures and analyze their specific nature in detail. c-fos, an immediate early gene, has been extensively used as a marker for neuronal activation induced by numerous kinds of stimulations, including seizures. We have bred c-Fos-GFP/c-Fos-tTA mice that express green fluorescent protein in activated neurons. Identification of live hippocampal neurons that were active during early life seizures has never been done before. We have found unique physiological alterations that occur only in selectively activated neurons in early life seizures. Here, we hypothesize that the selectively activated neurons have crucial roles in early life epilepsy. We will determine whether these selectively activated neurons appear to be the key cellular targets mediating seizure-induced neural network alterations and long-term cognitive consequences. We will also probe the potential to reverse early-life epilepsy and associated long-term cognitive deficits by precisely suppressing the activity of these neurons. column37: Despite progress in recent years, maternal mortality rates remain unacceptably high with the majority of maternal deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and resulting from causes for which proven interventions exist but are not optimally implemented. Effective implementation requires that barriers and facilitators to implementation are identified and addressed using theory-informed, evidence-based implementation strategies adapted to the relevant political and cultural context. Our goal is to develop and evaluate an inexpensive tool-kit designed for use by non-experts to support effective implementation planning and execution. Our group includes implementation scientists, maternal health content experts, and stakeholders including front line clinicians, researchers, and policy makers based in participating LMICs. Prior work conducted by our group found a high degree of commonality among barriers and facilitators to implementation across a range of LMICs and clinical areas, as well as unique barriers and facilitators requiring specific attention. Based on a comprehensive literature review, our prior research and our experience in conducting implementation planning workshops with LMIC stakeholders, we will develop and usability test a novel tool-kit, designed to facilitate assessment of barriers and facilitators to implementation and mapping of barriers and facilitators to theory-informed evidence-based implementation strategies. The tool-kit will be pilot tested in 2 LMICs with varying levels of in-country implementation experience and barrier/facilitator distributions within a locally identified maternal health implementation priority with the ultimate goal of improving maternal health outcomes.

column36: Parallel Radiofrequency Transmission MRI Applied to Deep Brain Stimulation
column37: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is increasingly used to treat the symptoms of many brain conditions. Neurosurgery is performed to implant metal electrodes into targets deep within the brain; then, a small device is also implanted underneath the skin, in the upper chest, to send electrical signals to the brain to achieve the DBS treatment effect. DBS patients need short-term and long-term follow-up to make sure that the electrodes are implanted correctly, to check for side effects, and to make sure that the electrodes continue to work well. Also, DBS patients develop other health problems throughout life. For their ongoing healthcare management, it is highly desirable for DBS patients to be able to have magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) exams. MRI is the main medical imaging method for examining diseases of the brain and spinal cord, and of other soft tissues in the body. MRI is also a very flexible, non-invasive way to measure both brain anatomy and function, and so it is highly desirable to use MRI as a tool in research studies of DBS patients. Such research will help to unravel how DBS actually works, towards improving DBS devices for even better treatments. Presently, however, extremely few DBS patients are receiving MRI exams after their devices are implanted, and MRI research studies of DBS patients are at a very early stage. This is because of a major safety concern: brain tissue near the DBS implant can be permanently damaged from heating during MRI. This grant proposal investigates a promising MRI method called "parallel radiofrequency transmission (PTX)" for its ability to suppress these heating effects. The optimal PTX conditions that minimize heating will be determined, and practical methods will be developed so that safe and comprehensive PTX MRI becomes viable for DBS patients. Ultimately this work will lay the groundwork for improved healthcare for DBS patients, and for safe research MRI studies to improve understanding of DBS mechanisms.

column36: Neuropathic pain through misregulated excitability and abnormal neural coding
column37: The nervous system encodes information using pulses of electricity known as spikes. Our perception of sensory input relies on spike-based neural codes. If neurons generate too many or too few spikes, our sensory experience can be profoundly altered. This is what occurs in neuropathic pain. Neuropathic pain is a form of chronic pain that results from damage to the nervous system. When damaged, neurons often become hyperexcitable, which is to say that they generate too many spikes in response to a given input, or start responding to weaker inputs. The primary sensory neurons responsible for sensing stimuli applied to the skin and relaying that information to the central nervous system are especially prone to becoming hyperexcitable. But precisely how that hyperexcitability develops, and how it disrupts sensation, remain poorly understood. Neuron excitability is controlled by ion channels. Changes in specific ion channels have been linked to neuropathic pain. But any one type of ion channel rarely changes in isolation; in fact, a pathological change in one ion channel may trigger other types of ion channels to undergo compensatory changes that offset effects of the primary change on excitability. I predict that hyperexcitability occurs when compensation fails. My proposed research will explore changes in gene regulation to decipher exactly how and why compensation fails. This will help identify new ways in which drugs can be used to restore regulation and reverse hyperexcitability. We will also explore how changes in the excitability of different types of sensory neurons affect the pattern of neurons activated by different types of stimuli, and how changes in neuron activation patterns ultimately impact perception. With this information, we hope to use a patient's sensory symptoms to identify the underlying pattern of sensory neuron hyperexcitability, and that information will, in turn, be used to choose the best therapy.

column37: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is complicated by high failure rates in young active individuals, which is associated with worse outcomes and higher rates of osteoarthritis (OA). Therefore, strategies to reduce ACLR failure are imperative. Traditionally, surgeons believed that the different tendons used to rebuild the torn ACL, did not impact failure. Specifically, a bone patella tendon bone (BPTB) graft was thought to be just as good as a hamstring tendon (HT) graft. Recent reviews, however, suggest BPTB provides better stability albeit with greater complications at the site of the donor tendon. Moreover, the quadriceps tendon (QT) is now being used to build ACL grafts, with claims of similar stability as the BPTB graft without the same complications. In addition, rebuilding the ligaments associated with rotational stability of the knee such as lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) at the same time as the ACLR may provide even greater overall stability; however, LET may contribute to increased knee OA. Despite its importance, there has not been a good study to prove whether one graft is better at reducing failure and minimizing donor site complications. Furthermore, no study has determined whether the addition of a LET helps to reduce failure. Research Questions: Is there a graft type +/- LET that offers a greater reduction in rate of failure, better functional performance, and rate of return-to-sport at two years following ACLR? Which graft type +/- LET offers the lowest complication rates? Do females do better with a particular graft type? Methods: Adding to our recent study comparing 624 patients who underwent ACLR using HT (+/- LET), this is an international, multi-centre, RCT that will assign 1200 patients to ACLR using QT (+/- LET) or BPTB (+/- LET) (n=1800). Expected Results: This study will determine the best graft choice for young patients at-risk of ACLR failure which will ultimately lead to positive effects on activity and QOL.

column36: Cognitive assays of hippocampal dysfunction in Parkinson's Disease
column37: In addition to physical symptoms, people with Parkinson's disease often experience cognitive decline with the progression of their illness and as a side-effect of therapies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS). There is marked heterogeneity in the rate and degree of cognitive decline across individuals, and therefore identifying predictors of poor cognitive outcome is a key research priority. Recent data suggest that alterations in brain regions such as the hippocampus are potentially strong predictors of cognitive decline in PD and DBS. This has not been corroborated using cognitive tasks that are sensitive and specific indicators of hippocampal function. Tests such as word list recall, used in standard clinical practice, lack specificity because they are impacted strongly by the type of executive deficits that are common in PD. Standardized clinical recognition memory tasks have lower executive demands, but they lack sensitivity as they do not tap core hippocampal operations that have been identified in experimental research. Our research aims to overcome these limitations by applying the latest cognitive neuroscience methods to the study of memory in PD. We will identify novel memory tasks that are minimally influenced by executive abilities, are sensitive to hippocampal integrity, and are accurate predictors of cognitive decline with disease progression and after DBS. Importantly, we expect to identify and validate memory assays of hippocampal integrity in PD that can be readily integrated into clinical practice. Our results will greatly improve understanding of memory deficits in PD and of cognitive side-effects of DBS. Critically, we believe our research will enhance our ability to predict cognitive decline in individual patients, and will contribute to future cognitive intervention research in PD.

column36: OSMR Regulation of Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
column37: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adult with a median survival rate of only 16 months after the disease diagnosis. The present standard of care includes maximal surgical removal of the tumors followed by standard treatment with radiation and chemotherapy. Unfortunately, these current treatments are ineffective in prolonging life and alleviating patient suffering. There is an urgent need to develop new and more effective treatment modalities for glioblastoma patients. Although multiple genetic mutations have been implicated as oncogenic (tumor-causing) genes in glioblastoma, the EGFRvIII gene is one of the major drivers of the GBM oncogenesis. Therefore, strategies to block the activities of EGFRvIII is a promising area in glioblastoma research. Problematically, despite intense research, therapies against EGFRvIII alone have not led to clinically significant outcome or improved prognosis. Our recent discoveries that EGFRvIII acts in tandem with another gene called OSMR to drive glioblastoma tumorigenesis, suggests that inhibition of OSMR either alone or as a combination therapy suppresses these tumors. Here, we will first define the mechanisms through which OSMR promotes tumor growth. Second, we will use patient derived models of glioblastoma to establish that OSMR is a viable drug target for these patients. We predict that inhibition of OSMR in combination with EGFRvIII will be an effective therapeutic strategy to treat these deadly tumors.

column36: Synchrony and reset of fast brain oscillations for perception and speech encoding
column37: When we interact with our environment, we interpret what we see, hear, and feel effortless. We can separate the image of a person from the background, although colours and textures may be very similar. We can listen to the voice of a speaker when concurrently other people are talking. How the brain combines sensory details into a meaningful object is still unknown. One concept is that neurons that are rhythmically active, we say they oscillate at a certain frequency, help to solve the problem of binding. Neurons, representing sensory information, oscillate in synchrony and communicate with each other. Thus the sensory information is combined into an object. Such fast synchronous oscillations last for about 200 ms, which is time enough for conscious perception of an object and forming a memory. In this project, we are using MEG for recording brain oscillations while participants listen to speech sounds. In recent years, we developed experimental techniques and data analysis methods to study how neural oscillations change their state of synchrony, which we term a phase reset. We will study how the phase resets of neural oscillations relate to the syllable structure of speech. The results will give us new insights into the brain function of perception and how speech is encoded in the brain. Knowing the details about the brain mechanism of perceptual binding will help us to explain what is going wrong when people cannot understand what they hear or misinterpret what they see. Varies disorders and deterioration of brain function can be explained with reduced ability of binding information in the correct way. The underlying cause seems to be disruptions of rhythmic brain activity.

column36: Targeting Relapsed Metastatic Neuroblastoma
column37: Neuroblastoma (NB) is the 3rd most common pediatric cancer, but the most frequent cause of death in children with cancer with a survival rate < 40%. Localized tumors (usually in the abdomen) are curable. However, for children with NB that has spread, over 50% relapse, usually with metastases to bone, bone marrow, and/or brain. When NB recurs it often initially responds to chemotherapy, but over time and with multiple recurrences NB becomes increasingly resistant and ultimately most patients die. Most NB cells and animal models do not get metastases like our patients, and there are no effective drugs for metastases. Thus, to identify novel therapies, we have (1) amassed a collection of NB cells isolated from patients' metastatic tumors and (2) developed a new mouse model for NB that spreads to the bone, bone marrow, and the brain. We have used a technique called 'in vivo selection' to select increasingly more aggressive "hypermetastatic" NB cells. When injected into our mice these "hypermetastatic" cells give the mice metastases in their bones and brains much earlier than the original cells. Using this model, we have identified genes, pathways, and drug targets for metastatic NB. We will generate additional models with different mutations commonly found in patients with the most aggressive relapses. We propose to use state of the art techniques to identify small groups of difficult to detect cells (clones) that spread from the primary tumor to form metastases. We will also use a technique called phosphoproteomics to identify "protein fingerprints" of the metastatic cells to give us clues to better treatments that can reverse this fingerprint to that of a primary tumor that cannot spread. We have a track record for translating drug discoveries from the lab to NB clinical trials. Our multi-faceted approach will lead to identification of new drugs to use in clinical trials for patients with NB metastatic recurrences in the bone, bone marrow brain.

column36: Mechanism and function of mitochondrial derived vesicle transport to peroxisomes.
column37: The cell is a highly ordered and compartmentalized place with intracellular organelles carrying protein, lipid and signals throughout the cell. In addition to these carriers, there are two important compartments in the cell that perform a host of essential biochemical reactions, mitochondria and peroxisomes. Mitochondria are primarily known as the "energy powerhouse" of the cell, recycling sugar, protein and fat into cellular energy. However, there are many other reactions that occur in mitochondria and a host of these reactions rely on a second, smaller organelle called the peroxisomes to complete the chain reaction and build, or degrade, the final product. For example, the breakdown of very long chain fatty acids occurs first in peroxisomes, and the resulting shorter chain lipids are then transferred to mitochondria to be burned as energy. Without peroxisomes this cannot occur and the very long chain fatty acids are highly toxic, causing cell death and disease. In other cases enzymes in each organelle work sequentially to build new molecules, like bile acids in liver, or unique protective lipids called plasmalogen in the brain. The extent of the relationship between mitochondria and peroxisomes is so high that they share a number of common proteins, and we have shown that there is a direct, vesicle based delivery of protein and lipid from mitochondria to peroxisomes both in steady state, and for the formation of newly born peroxisomes. This proposal aims to understand how and why this type of vesicle transport exists in health and disease. There are many devastating diseases, both rare and more common, where peroxisomes or mitochondria are dysfunctional and we are currently without any therapy to treat them. By understanding the molecular basis of the integration between these two organelles we can contribute to the strategic design of new therapies to target disease.

column36: Regulating the dynamic cycling of palmitate on proteins
column37: Proteins are essential for all processes in our cells. Some proteins can be modified by the repeated addition and removal of a fatty molecule called palmitate. This process, termed the "palmitoylation cycle", helps direct these proteins to parts of the cell where they are needed to carry out their roles. One target of palmitoylation is NRAS, which is a protein that can promote the development of cancers such as leukemia and melanoma. By interrupting the NRAS palmitoylation cycle, we may be able to block the growth of cancer cells. We understand quite a lot about how palmitate is added to proteins, but much less about how it is removed. Until recently, researchers had identified only two enzymes - known as APT1 and APT2 - that can remove palmitate from proteins. My lab showed that APT1 and APT2 are not needed to remove palmitate from NRAS or from a brain protein called PSD95. Instead we discovered another enzyme called ABHD17 that does remove palmitate from NRAS. A drug against ABHD17 might stop the cancer-causing activity of NRAS by blocking its palmitoylation cycle. Before we try to develop such a drug, we first need to find out if ABHD17 acts on other proteins in cells and, if so, which ones. We also want to understand what makes ABHD17 specific for some proteins but not others, and how its action on NRAS is controlled. Cells have three different types of ABHD17 enzymes, so it will also be important to know if we can target just one form of the enzyme, or if we need to inhibit all three. This project will help establish if ABHD17 is a good target for future drug development. If so, the longer-term challenge will be to develop specific chemicals that inhibit ABHD17 activity and test if they can treat cancers such as leukemia and melanoma.

Project aims: The aims of this project are to: 1) determine accuracy of GP ASD diagnosis compared to an expert team assessment; 2) to determine child features associated with accurate diagnosis by GPs. Possible features include: child's age; sex; cultural background; ASD severity; developmental delays; and having a sibling with ASD. Methods: We will recruit 30 GPs from across Ontario, as well as 300 of their patients (10 per GP) who have been referred with possible ASD. The GP will complete their assessment and decide on a diagnosis, but will not tell the family. The ASD expert team, consisting of a developmental paediatrician and a psychologist, will also perform a diagnostic assessment without knowing the GP's opinion. The ASD expert team will inform the family of their diagnostic opinion. We will determine the diagnostic agreement between the two assessments. We will then determine which of the child's characteristics (age, sex, cultural background, ASD severity, developmental delays, having a sibling with ASD) predict agreement in diagnosis. Expected Results: Results from this study will determine whether GPs can independently and accurately diagnose ASD. Future activities include refinement of educational workshops for GPs on ASD diagnosis and development of pathways to identify which children can be diagnosed in a community setting.

column37: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is caused by prenatal exposure to alcohol, and affects 4% of individuals in Canada. Key features of FASD are learning, growth and behaviour problems, and most people with FASD (>90%) also have mental health problems. Depression and anxiety are among the most common. However, treatments for depression and anxiety are much less likely to be effective in individuals with FASD. This is, in part, because we do not understand the brain differences in youth FASD, and how these underlie symptoms of anxiety and depression. A better knowledge of brain development in children and youth with FASD, and how the brain is related to mental health symptoms, would enable us to target treatments to the right time, place, and individual. We will recruit youth with FASD and unexposed controls aged 7-15 years in Calgary and Edmonton. Using longitudinal neuroimaging and mental health assessments, we will (1) measure patterns of brain development in children and youth with FASD, (2) test whether brain abnormalities underlie the increased risk of depression and anxiety in youth with FASD, and (3) evaluate baseline brain factors that predict mental health outcomes in these children and youth. We will use structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine brain connectivity, and caregiver and child reports of mental health symptoms to measure anxiety and depression. Measurements will be done at baseline, and again two years later. This study will provide new knowledge of brain alterations that underlie anxiety and depression in children and youth with FASD, and identify predictors of mental health outcomes. column36: STAT6-dependent control of innate immunity as a target for therapeutic intervention in asthma
column37: Both the incidence and severity of asthma have been increasing steadily over the last 2-3 decades. Although asthma in childhood is more prominent in boys, this sex difference changes around the time of puberty, when asthma prevalence declines in men and rises in women. We have developed a model of allergic lung inflammation where we deliver (directly to the lungs) a cytokine called IL-33, which is implicated in asthma onset. Our data show that adult mice treated with this cytokine develop 'acute' inflammation in the lung within days that is similar in many aspects to the inflammation found in asthmatics with established disease. We have found that females have much greater responses than males. We have also developed a combined viral infection-asthma model that mimics studies showing that, in children, there is an association between some viral infections, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and asthma development. RSV infection increases IL-33 levels in the lung, particularly in young mice, and thus we believe responses in the lung driven by RSV infection are similar to those caused by IL-33. As part of our ongoing studies, we are characterizing an inhibitor we developed called STAT6-IP. Our data show that STAT6-IP reduces some of the inflammatory responses in the lung caused by IL-33 delivery in adults or RSV infection in young mice. Our goals are now to define which responses promote asthma onset, including disease that develops as a consequence of prior RSV infection. We will define how these responses differ in males and females and we will define how they are modulated by STAT6-IP, recognizing that STAT6-IP may provide protection by targeting different responses in males and females. We believe these preclinical studies may provide a foundation to reduce the induction of asthma in both men and women.
