column36: Microvascular Blood Flow Regulation and Insulin Resistance in an Animal Model of Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a growing public health concern affecting over 3 million Canadians. The risk of cardiovascular disease is substantially higher in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), including increased risk of heart attack, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease. T2D causes the loss of the ability of pancreatic cells to produce sufficient insulin and the development of persistent high blood sugar. Excess glucose in the blood can damage blood vessels, further exacerbating factors that impair the body's ability to respond to insulin and clear glucose. These factors include vascular surface area, distance between capillaries and skeletal muscle, and the distribution of blood flow. We aim to examine how changes in capillary network structure, and defects in microvascular blood flow regulation contribute to impaired glucose uptake in T2D. Our approach uses an animal model that recreates the insulin resistance of T2D, combined with obesity, to replicate the conditions observed in human disease. Using microscopy we can then to look at capillaries, the smallest blood vessels in the body, and specialized software to measure blood flow in living muscle tissue. The predictable progression of T2D in our animal model makes it ideal to study microvascular changes similar to that which would be observed in humans. The data collected will also be integrated into a mathematical model of glucose and insulin transport to further our understanding of insulin resistance. Quantifying how T2D impacts microvascular function and structure in our animal model furthers our understanding of the progression of T2D in humans due to the similar physiology and physical properties of our vascular systems. This study will be the first to study oxygen mediated blood flow regulation and the impact of insulin on blood flow distribution in capillaries which informs our understanding of exercise intolerance in T2D as well as how insulin resistance is linked to microvascular factors.

column36: Genomics-based radiosensitization for HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the aerodigestive tract
column37: Squamous cell carcinomas of the aerodigestive tract that are not associated with the human papillomavirus (HPV-negative SCC) are locally aggressive and treatment resistant cancers with only ~50% local control despite aggressive management. A backbone of definitive treatment includes high-dose radiotherapy (RT) in combination platinum-based chemotherapy (i.e., chemoradiotherapy); this regimen only cures a subset of patients and causes significant toxicities, highlighting the dire need for improved treatment approaches. Despite known differences in radiosensitivity between individual tumours, molecular biomarkers of treatment sensitivity are not available, so clinicians continue to employ a one-size-fits-all approach. Aside from platinum-based chemotherapy, alternative systemic agents have not been systematically profiled for their radiosensitization potential due to the lack of robust and pragmatic preclinical pipelines needed to assess the large number of candidate drugs. We hypothesize that the efficacy of RT could be substantially improved by a more personalized medicine approach, in which the delivery of radiosensitizing drugs is tailored to each patient based on molecular features of their tumour in order to maximize the curative potential while limiting side effects. Our objective is to enable genomics-based precision medicine for HPV-negative SCCs of the aerodigestive tract. To achieve this, will evaluate promising drug-RT combinations that have the potential to specifically benefit subsets of patients based on molecular features of their tumours. We will also explore novel biomarkers that can be tested in future studies. By the end of this project, we will have a set of drugs and biomarker tests that can be further evaluated in prospective early phase clinical trials. Thus, our project will lead to new frontiers in personalized treatment of HPV-negative SCC and will usher the Precision Medicine era into the field of radiation oncology.

column36: Mechanisms and implications of fast turnover in the DNA replication machinery of bacteria
column37: Cells originate from other cells. A crucial part of this process requires them to inherit their DNA to the next generation. This task is accomplished by an elegant multicomponent protein machine, called the replisome. Even though the basic underlying chemical reactions are understood, the question of how this machine works remains unanswered. Since the initial description of the replisome in bacteria, it was thought that a tight physical association among its components allowed them to act as a single unit. As such, the replisome could function uninterrupted from the time it starts copying the long chromosomal DNA, to the point it finishes it, one hour later! Making an analogy, it would be like typing at a rate of 1,000 letters per second for an hour-period without making any mistakes. Not to mention that mistakes, prolonged pauses, or the permanent inability of the writer to continue, can cause complete loss of the text - and for the cell, its death. Recent data from my lab shows instead that most replisome components participate in the process in pulses that last for few seconds - in the analogy, a new writer would seat in front of the keyboard every few hundreds of words. As this discovery was unexpected in the field, its molecular causes and consequences for the cell are yet unknown. Understanding these aspects is the aim of this proposal. As DNA replication in bacteria is a factor in the spread of antibiotic resistance and a potential target for antibiotics, the outcome of our work may help in the development of new strategies to counter the current antibiotic resistance crisis.

column36: Preimplantation et implantation d'un programme de prevention de l'agression sexuelle pour les etudiantes en milieu universitaire : Les milieux sont-ils prets et le programme est-il efficace lorsque plusieurs facteurs de risque sont presents?
column37: L'agression sexuelle des femmes adultes au Canada en 2009 a entraine des couts de plus de 4,8 milliards en frais medicaux et autres couts associes. Si rien ne change, 1 femme sur 4 sera agressee sexuellement, ou vivra une tentative d'agression, durant ses etudes universitaires. Ces experiences ont des consequences negatives immediates et a long terme sur la sante mentale et physique. Une equipe de chercheurs canadiens a mis au point un programme visant a diminuer le risque de subir une agression sexuelle pour les etudiantes universitaires, que l'on nomme EAAA. Le programme a demontre son efficacite et permet de reduire l'agression sexuelle de 46% et les tentatives d'agression sexuelle de 63% pour les femmes l'ayant recu en comparaison a celles ne l'ayant pas recu. La recherche proposee constitue la prochaine etape logique qui permettra de determiner si les milieux universitaires sont prets a l'offrir et a verifier s'il est efficace lorsqu'offert en milieu naturel et aupres de toutes les etudiantes, meme celles presentant des niveaux de risque de subir de la violence sexuelle qui sont plus eleves que la moyenne. La formation et la supervision sera transferee aux professionnels des campus universitaires, qui offriront ensuite le programme EAAA a leurs etudiantes. Les professionnels et les etudiantes participeront a la recherche visant a identifier les conditions necessaires a son implantation et a examiner l'efficacite du programme dans ce contexte, notamment s'il demeure efficace en presence de plusieurs facteurs de risque de violence sexuelle (handicap, maltraitance durant l'enfance, minorite de genre et sexuelle, etc.). En plus d'etre diffuses a d'autres chercheurs par des conferences et publications, les resultats seront partages avec divers intervenants en prevention de la violence sexuelle, etudiants et decideurs des milieux impliques dans un atelier deliberatif qui permettra de determiner les conditions d'implantation du programme dans d'autres universites.

column36: Analyse economique de la prevention et controle des infections nosocomiales au Quebec: AnePCI
column37: Les infections nosocomiales (INs) constituent l'un des principaux accidents de soins de sante evitables. A l'instar de tous les pays du monde, le Quebec est particulierement affecte par les INs. Pour faire face a ce probleme persistant, le ministere de la sante et des services sociaux du Quebec (MSSS) de l'epoque avait mis en place en 2004, un programme obligatoire de prevention et controle des INs (programme PCI) dans les etablissements hospitaliers du Quebec. Dans son plan d'action 2015-2020 sur la prevention et le controle des INs pour une prestation securitaire des soins de sante au Quebec, le MSSS indique dans sa cible 22 vouloir evaluer l'implantation, les couts, les effets et le retour sur investissement du programme PCI dans les etablissements de sante de soins de courte duree. Le present projet s'inscrit dans la meme perspective et se presente comme la premiere recherche d'envergure dans la province du Quebec au Canada en matiere d'evaluation de l'efficience du programme PCI. Il a pour objectif principal d'evaluer l'efficience d'un programme de prevention et controle des INs a travers l'analyse economique des pratiques cliniques exemplaires associees. Trois objectifs specifiques seront poursuivis : i) Evaluer le cout des pratiques cliniques associees a la prevention et controle des INs au Quebec; ii) Evaluer le fardeau economique attribuable aux INs ; iii) Examiner la rentabilite de la prevention et controle des INs en comparant le cout d'implantation et les couts des infections. Cette recherche produira des evidences empiriques sur l'efficience du programme PCI au Quebec, et au Canada. Il permettrait a tous les acteurs du systeme de soins de sante de prendre conscience des gains economiques potentiels attribuables a la PCI. Il contribuera au renforcement de son implantation, a l'amelioration de son suivi et surtout a la sensibilisation de tous les acteurs de la sante sur l'importance de la prevention des infections.

column37: More than 200,000 older Canadians have major surgery each year; 40% live with frailty. This is important for a number of reasons. First, older people represent well over half of all people having major surgery in Canada. Second, older people with frailty face a greater than two times higher risk of having a major complication, developing a new disability, or dying after surgery than older people without frailty. Strategies and treatments to decrease the risks faced by older people with frailty having surgery are urgently needed but have not been widely developed or studied. The strongest findings suggest that exercise before surgery may improve older people's ability to walk and stand after surgery and lower rates of complications. Unfortunately, these findings are limited by a number of factors: 1) studies have been small and conducted in single hospitals, which means that we don't know if these findings are widely applicable; 2) existing studies have many flaws which could invalidate their findings; 3) outcomes measured in these studies have not been patient-reported or patient-centered, whereas we know that patient-reported outcomes are key to ensuring that research directly influences care in a way that matters to patients; and 4) most exercise interventions have been very resource-intensive, which can limit people's access to exercise, especially if they have trouble getting around or don't live near the hospital. Therefore, to help improve outcomes after surgery in a meaningful way for the growing number of older Canadians with frailty, we propose to study a home-based exercise program compared to the type of care that people usually receive. Using a randomized trial design performed across eleven different hospitals we will evaluate whether participating in this home-based exercise program, which we already know can be performed by older people with frailty, leads to lower levels of patient-reported disability and complication rates after surgery.

column36: Treatment of Anxiety in Children and youth with Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder affecting almost 1.5% of youth (children and adolescents) in North America. Youth with ASD present with social difficulties and repetitive behavior, but also with a variety of other conditions including anxiety, ADHD, intellectual disability, neurological, immune and gastrointestinal differences. Anxiety affects up to 84% of youth with ASD, interfering with daily living skills and family and peer relationships. Data suggest that untreated childhood anxiety often leads to long-term mental health disability. In typically developing youth with anxiety, evidence supports the use of cognitive behavioral therapies, medications, and more recently, their combination. Although there is early evidence for adapted cognitive behavioral treatment for high-functioning youth with ASD and anxiety, no randomized controlled trials have evaluated medications for anxiety in this population, despite common use. The goal of this research is to collect pilot data on the effects of sertraline, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, in reducing anxiety in youth with ASD, in order to inform the design of a follow-up pivotal clinical trial. We will recruit youth with ASD who experience clinically significant symptoms of anxiety. Participants will be randomized to sertraline or placebo for 16 weeks. We will measure the effect of the medication on anxiety severity and quality of life. The role of biological markers such as autonomic nervous system function an d blood serotonin levels will also be explored. Given the frequency of debilitating levels of anxiety in youth with ASD, and how little is known about treatment response to medication in these youth, this research is critical for its potential to inform clinical practice across Canada and beyond.

column37: Voluntary movement of muscles in humans requires electric signalling down the nerves: beginning at the spinal cord and ending at muscles that help us speak, eat, breathe and move. This process is impaired in neuromuscular diseases (NMDs), which are associated with progressive muscle weakness, disability and early death. Until recently, most NMDs were very difficult to diagnose and considered untreatable. Fortunately, genomics (deciphering a person's genetic code to understand the mutation responsible for a particular disease) has transformed our ability to diagnose and treat these devastating disorders. My research program studies gene mutations responsible for NMDs to provide a diagnosis, understand disease progression, and test new therapies. My program focuses on two types of NMDs: congenital myasthenia syndromes (CMS) and myotonic dystrophy (DM1). I will use a combination of genomics, molecular biology, animal models, and clinical trials to improve their diagnosis and treatment. Specifically, I will: 1.Use genomics to identify the genetic causes of CMS while discovering new disease genes. I will provide a genetic diagnosis for at least 300 families with CMS while discovering at least 20 novel genes. 2.Use genomics, molecular biology, and animal models to understand how genetic mutations cause NMD in order to guide treatment and identify new therapies. I will reveal the genetic mechanisms of 20 new NMD genes, discover 5 new therapies, and study 7 therapies (4 re-purposed, 3 new) in animal models. 3.Build an 'Ottawa River' cohort of 250 families with DM1 and use patient samples to study biomarkers. I will identify 10 biomarkers to indicate which patients will be most responsive to therapy and another 5 to measure treatment response in clinical trials. 4.Conduct clinical trials to test new NMD therapies for CMS and DM1 using novel and repurposed drugs. This research will improve the diagnosis and treatment of NMDs and grow Canada's international leadership.

column37: The efficiency and safety of radiotherapy, in which ionizing radiation is used to kill cancer cells, rests largely on our ability to determine the amount of radiation (or radiation dose) delivered to a tumor and nearby healthy tissue. Well-established methods exist to do this when the source of radiation lies outside the patient. However, if the radiation source is inside the patient, for example as a radioactive atom delivered into a cancer cell, then the situation is more complex. In such cases, we require information on where radioactive atoms are found in the cell and of how and where their radiation travels once it is emitted. This latter can be achieved through computer simulations that follow step-by-step the slowing down of the emitted radiation. Since low energy electrons are the most numerous of the species emitted and/or generated by the radioactive atoms, the computer simulations require information on how these electrons travel in the cell and what kinds of damage they can do. This project will measure how low energy electrons interact with cellular biomolecules using a range of experimental techniques we have developed. This basic quantitative information will be included in new computer models of radiation damage to more accurately calculate radiation dose delivered to patients in such novel types of radiotherapy.

column36: Obesity exacerbates ammonia-induced neurological dysfunction in cirrhosis
column37: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE), characterized by cognitive, psychiatric and motor disturbances, is a devastating complication of liver disease. With as much as 80% of patients with cirrhosis suffering from HE, the burden of HE is immense considering its wide-ranging effects on the patients, family and society. Ammonia is believed to be the major factor involved in the pathogenesis of HE. Cirrhosis causes an increase in blood ammonia (hyperammonemia) which leads to increased neurotoxic levels of ammonia in the brain. Obesity has become a major worldwide health problem. As a result, the number of patients with liver disease due to fatty-liver is rising and is becoming the leading cause of cirrhosis. Obesity has been demonstrated to induce cognitive changes but it is not clear how obesity impact HE. Our project proposes to study the effect of ammonia and obesity alone as well as together on neurological dysfunction. This will be studied using complimentary rat models of cirrhosis and obesity and closely looking at the impact of fatty acids, adipokines and ammonia on the blood-brain barrier. In addition, lipids can infiltrate into muscle (myosteatosis) which can impact the muscle's capacity to remove ammonia. Therefore, obesity can directly (via the blood brain barrier) or indirectly (by inhibiting ammonia clearance in the muscle) affect the brain, leading to a higher risk of developing HE. Cognitive impairment due to obese cirrhosis will be a challenging population of patients to treat as neurological dysfunction may develop due to either hyperammonemia and/or obesity. To date, treatment strategies remain an unmet clinical need in this population of patients. Therefore, the results from this project will provide valuable insights on the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment in patients with obesity-induced cirrhosis and lead to new management strategies for these patients.

column37: Sexual arousal, desire, and pleasure are integral parts of the human condition, hardwired within our brains and bodies, yet molded by our experiences. Sexual activity is important for overall health and well-being, and numerous studies have shown the positive effects of a healthy and satisfying sex life as well as the detrimental effects of sexual dysfunctions. Distressing sexual dysfunctions occur in approximately 7 to 42% of premenopausal women for periods of time that are either lifelong or situational, of which the most common are sexual desire and orgasm disorders. Decreases in sexual arousal and desire also occur in a majority of postmenopausal women as ovarian function wanes. In the past 15 years, predictive preclinical rat models have been generated in my laboratory, including models of arousal from vaginal and clitoral engorgement, full and partial sexual solicitations as models of sexual desire, and models of orgasm from clitoral stimulation and copulation that occurs at a preferred rate for each female under her control. The proposed experiments will examine several potential pharmacotherapies currently in clinical trials, along with experientially-based therapies, to complete the validation of the behavioral models and to use them to assess neurochemical, epigenetic, and molecular mechanisms of onset and therapeutic efficacy. It is hypothesized that amelioration of sexual arousal and/or desire disorders will depend on one of two common mechanisms: the activation of one or more excitatory brain neurochemical pathways, including dopamine, noradrenaline, along with important reward induced by pleasurable opioid activation, or the inhibition of inhibitory pathways driven largely by serotonin. The goal of this project is to generate a neurochemical model of different female sexual dysfunctions that can be used to create rational pharmacotherapies or examine as causal mechanisms in conjunction with behavioral endpoints in experientially-based interventions.

column37: Increasing the function and number of insulin-secreting cells is critical to the treatment of type 2 diabetes. It has been known for some time however that insulin-secreting cells are very variable in their response to glucose. Advanced single cell techniques have more recently confirmed an underling genetic variability suggesting that any treatment directed to increase the number of insulin secreting cells in the treatment of type 2 diabetes would be relatively ineffective (i.e. work on only a subset of the cells). A major goal therefore would be to determine the root cause of the variability and thus reveal mechanisms to increase the efficacy of any treatment. The majority of evidence suggests the variability of insulin-secreting cells stems from aging and how it changes the way cells metabolize glucose. Our lab has unique expertise in using imaging methods to measure the metabolism of individual cells. More recently we created a unique imaging sensor for a molecule (termed 'NADPH') critically required for proliferation and survival. We now aim to use our expertise and unique tool to look for differences in the way individual cells metabolize glucose and to reveal whether metabolic stress exacerbates whether a specific population is more / less responsive to glucose. These studies will have two aims: 1) Determine whether metabolic stress can cause insulin secreting cells to grow in number. 2) Determine how NADPH production is varied across many different insulin-secreting cells at different stages of the cell-cycle. These studies will use advanced live cell imaging of cells, isolated tissues (mouse and human), and living organisms. This wide span of models is necessary to develop our technology, and confirm the uniformity of our results across species. Overall, these studies will explore the root cause of the high variability of insulin-secreting beta-cells to determine whether this variability is a potential target for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.

column36: Transcriptional memory and plasticity in embryonic stem cells
column37: A kidney cell functions differently from a skin cell despite the fact that all the cells in one organism share the same DNA. This is because not all of the genes encoded within the DNA are active in the cells. Instead, cells can turn on just those genes that are specific to how that cell type works. One way that cells can regulate their genes is by using proteins called transcription factors and chromatin modifiers that can bind to DNA to turn nearby genes on and off. We study these processes using embryonic stem cells, a specialized cell type that can maintain its identity indefinitely while having the capacity to differentiate into all cell types of the body. When embryonic stem cells divide to form new embryonic stem cells to maintain its identity, the DNA is condensed and gene activity is turned off. However, each dividing cell also has to 'remember' the program of genes that specifies its identity. After division, how do the new embryonic stem cells know which genes to turn on and which ones to keep off? On the other hand, when embryonic stem cells differentiate into a new cell type, this transcriptional memory needs to be wiped clean, and a new transcription program needs to be established. How do differentiating embryonic stem cells achieve this complex process? These questions will be addressed in my proposed research project.

column37: Average human body weight has been on a steady rise over the past 25 years. This global obesity epidemic has led to an increased burden of heart disease and diabetes, and, as we are learning in the last several years, a rise in incidence, severity and poor outcome of many human cancers. Recent clinical trials have revealed that more than one third of current breast cancer patients are overweight or obese. Breast cancer is more difficult to treat in these patients and they are more likely to die from their disease when compared to women of normal weight. While a number of social initiatives are aiming to slow down the increase in obesity amongst the general population, it is becoming clear that direct therapeutic interventions are needed to counter cancer in the obese. One of the consequences of obesity is an increase in the body levels of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood sugar metabolism. Ample evidence indicates that breast cancer cells find ways to use insulin as a spark-plug to support their growth. Research from our laboratory over the last several years is uncovering ways by which insulin may be contributing to breast cancer development and progression. Our team has discovered an aspect of insulin function in cancer that may be amenable to therapies. Here, we are proposing a comprehensive set of experiments, to be conducted in cancer cells, and mice as model animals, to gain a full understanding of this new mechanism of insulin function. Moreover, by analysis of the data from several already completed breast cancer clinical trials, we will chart a path towards clinical application of our findings in the treatment of breast cancer in the obese. Our goal is to use the already existing therapeutics and repurpose them for the treatment of obesity-associated breast cancers, considerably accelerating the applicability of our findings in the clinic. The realization of our program would have a major impact on breast cancer treatment and cure.

column36: Targeting the long term effects of maternal psychosocial disorders on preterm birth and childhood morbidity
column37: Mental health problems in mothers may affect the health of their children as they grow. Mental health conditions in mothers may affect the way they care for their children, increasing the risk of preventable health problems. More and more studies show that women with poor mental health have a greater risk of delivering preterm. Preterm birth, or birth before 37 weeks of pregnancy, increases a child's chance of having health problems later in life. However, it is not clear if poor mental health in mothers has a direct impact on childhood health, or if it interacts with preterm birth to increase the vulnerability of children to later health problems. This project aims to determine what maternal mental health problems could be targeted early in the lives of mothers to prevent future diseases in their children, especially if they were born preterm. We will use a dataset containing hospital data for all newborns in Quebec, Canada between 2006 and 2016 and will track infants over time. We will identify mothers with mental health conditions before or during pregnancy. We will follow infants for up to 11 years after birth and identify those who were born preterm and those hospitalized later in childhood. We will determine the association of maternal mental health conditions with the risk of preterm birth and childhood diseases, and how preterm birth influences the relationship between maternal mental health problems and childhood diseases. This project will generate new knowledge by identifying maternal mental health problems associated with preterm birth and later childhood diseases. We will find what mental health conditions could be targeted early in life to prevent later adverse outcomes in children. The data will help physicians improve their care of vulnerable mothers and infants, and will influence prevention and care guidelines.

column36: Microglial regulation of cocaine self-administration in rats
column37: Drug addiction is a chronic and debilitating disorder that has an immense social and financial impact on individuals and society. Substance abuse accounts for the highest number of preventable illnesses and deaths each year in Canada and places a significant social and financial toll on individuals, families and society. In 2006, the estimated cost of substance abuse in Canada was estimated to be $39.8 billion, with illegal drugs accounting for $8.2 billion. More recent Canadian health surveys have suggested that 1 in 10 Canadians report symptoms consistent with alcohol or illicit drug dependence, and 1-2% of the population report cocaine use. Despite our understanding of the primary molecular action of drugs of abuse, our comprehension of the modifications of neural circuitry underlying addiction remains far from complete. Drugs of abuse are believed to elicit changes in neural circuits that ultimately manifest themselves in a variety of self-destructive behaviors. Emerging evidence indicates that changes of glutamatergic synapses in key reward structures is critical for functional changes of neurons in addiction; however, the various molecular mechanisms involved are only partly understood. Inflammation is an observed part of the response to drugs of abuse, but its role in addiction is not defined. The pro-inflammatory cytokine Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF) is a key player in the inflammatory response, and can directly regulate synaptic function. Here we investigate how TNF modifies circuit properties in reward relevant parts of the brain in a model of drug self-administration. We then investigate how engaging TNF signaling from microglia can alter the motivation to acquire drug in animals trained to chronically administration cocaine.

column36: Using C.elegans to understand how the GAR-3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor modulates other signaling pathways
column37: The human nervous system is bewilderingly complex. There are over 100 billion nerve cells, but this is just the start of the complexity. The key properties of the nervous system - eg how we respond to stimuli or coordinate our movement - come not from single nerve cells but from the ways they connect with eachother and there are over a trillion such connections in the brain. This raises key challenges. We can understand how cells divide or make energy by studying single cells in a dish, but we cannot understand how the nervous system works by studying a single nerve cell - we need to know how they are connected and how they talk to each other. Rather than study the complex human nervous system, we turn to a simpler nervous system. The nematode worm C.elegans has just over 300 nerve cells - crucially, every connection between them is known and it is the best characterised nervous system of any animal. We study how perturbing the nervous system either with drugs or with genetic mutations affects worm movement. To do this, we built a system for measuring worm movement in a very rapid way - this system is unique to our group. This lets us examine many thousands of mutant worms to look for changes in movement. Crucially, we can use combinations of drugs, or combinations of mutants to look for examples where one pathway appears to affect another, showing cross-talk. We used this system to discover a new crosstalk between nerve signaling pathways. One signal rapidly affects movement, while a second signal slowly shut this down again. Now we want to understand exactly how this cross talk works. Do these pathways affect eachother in the same nerve cells or does one nerve cell talk to another? What are the genes involved? If we understand how these pathways interact in worms, we may be able to regulate them in humans, where they play key roles in multiple disorders of the nervous system.

column36: Investigating the role of E2F family proteins in ploidy control
column37: My overall research goal is to study how mutations in human cancers change the characteristics of normal cells to become like cancer cells. Specifically, I am interested in a family of genes called E2F whose function is abnormally activated in virtually all types of cancers. In my lab, we use fruit flies as a model system to better understand the function of E2F. More than 100 years of fruit fly research has helped scientists to develop sophisticated genetic tools and techniques allowing investigation of various aspects of E2F that are difficult to study in mice. Abnormality in the copy number of the genome is one of the common features of cancer cells. In particular, polyploidy, meaning multiple copies of the genome, can lead to gain or loss of specific chromosomes that can favour cancer development. The fruit fly is an ideal system to study ploidy control since many tissues increase size and mass through polyploidy. We used a modern gene-editing tool called CRISPR/Cas9 and discovered a variant form of E2F in flies that is specifically needed for this process. The goal of this proposal is to use the fruit fly as a model system to investigate the role of E2F in ploidy control. Given the prevalence of E2F deregulation in cancer, our study may reveal a previously unappreciated role of E2F in ploidy regulation during cancer development.

column36: Regulation of skeletal muscle function by PINK-1-Parkin mitophagy pathway
column37: Sepsis is a leading cause of death in the intensive care units and is responsible for ten thousand deaths in Canada each year. Skeletal muscle dysfunction manifested as fiber atrophy and weakness is a primary clinical observation in critically ill septic patients during the acute phase of sepsis . Long-term ramifications of limb muscle weakness include functional impairment and poor quality of life. Sepsis-induced skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness are associated with accumulation of damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria (the main source of cellular energy). In normal skeletal muscles, dysfunctional mitochondria are selectively recycled through the autophagy pathway, a process known as mitophagy. In this process, autophagosomes recognize dysfunctional mitochondria primarily through the PINK1-Parkin pathway. This process is inhibited by a protein called P53 which retains Parkin in the cytosol. The main aim of this proposal is to evaluate the therapeutic potentials of enhancing mitophagy by overexpressing Parkin and PINK1 selectively in skeletal muscles or by inhibiting p53 on mitochondrial function, atrophy and depressed contractility in two models of sepsis in mice. To achieve this aim, we have assembled an experienced team of leading investigators in the field of muscle research, Hussain, and Gouspillou, who have extensive expertise in skeletal muscle disease, mitochondrial function, proteolysis, and autophagy and have produced many papers linking mitochondrial injury to skeletal muscle dysfunction in catabolic conditions. Overexpression of Parkin and PINK1 will be achieved by injection of adeno-associated viruses in limb muscles and these muscles will be examined under control and septic conditions. P53 inhibition will be achieved by using mice defective in muscle p53 or by using a pharmacological p53 inhibitor. Mitochondrial function and morphology as well as muscle fiber size and contractile performance will be evaluated in both control and septic mice.

column36: PRMT6 as a novel therapeutic target for breast cancer
column37: Although therapies for breast cancer have been improving, it remains a very common problem that patients develop a resistance to their therapy. When this happens there are unfortunately very few alternatives available to clinicians to help those patients and this usually means that the chances of surviving the cancer are greatly reduced. We are working on a new strategy that could help to make a drug that is currently used in the clinic (so we know it is safe) work for breast cancer. Specifically, we are focusing on a cancer drug named Velcade, which works really well for cancers of blood origin, but has proven significantly less efficient at killing other cancers, including breast cancer tumours. Our lab is working towards gaining a better understanding of the role(s) of a protein modification, called 'arginine methylation'. This modification of proteins is a 'flag' that is added to certain proteins in our cells. This mark in turn can change how the protein will work, and can even confer new functions to it. This work has led to the discovery that arginine methylation is somehow involved in the way that Velcade works to kill cancer cells, and in turn, that tinkering with this modification in breast cancer cells using various strategies can in fact make them more sensitive to this drug. We thus propose in the current project to assess the feasibility of a novel strategy to sensitize breast cancer cells to the chemotherapeutic drug Velcade. The proposed research will first aim to assess the relative whether our strategy works in all types of breast cancer or just in a specific subtype. We will also pursue experiments to gain a better understanding of how blocking arginine methylation can make Velcade work better in breast cancer cells. Finally, we will use mouse models of breast cancer to determine whether our strategy can also work in the context of a whole animal. This project could enable the development of alternative therapies for patients developing resistance.

column36: Reducing HIV-related Stigma in School Children in Northern Uganda: A Multi-level Arts-based Population Health Intervention
column37: Over 2.6 million children aged 0-15 years are living with HIV globally, with the majority living in low and middle income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa (1). Stigma associated with HIV is recognized as a key global problem due to its harmful health and social impacts which are particularly pronounced for children. Children living with HIV experience stigma among their peers at school. Previous research with this population in Uganda showed that stigma comes in the form of verbal and physical abuse from teachers and peers (bullying), leading to social isolation, school drop-out, depression and feelings of suicide. Little information is known about how to reduce this HIV-related stigma. Efforts to help these stigmatized children to live a healthy and vibrant life are of tremendous importance. Our proposed study addresses the need to reduce stigma in school-going (10-18 years) children by utilizing an arts-based program in twelve rural schools in the Omoro District of Northern Uganda (Acholi people). Traditional Northern Ugandan storytelling, proverbs, and songs whose messages and moral teachings demonstrate what society expects of children and transfer these teachings from Elder to child, form the foundation of the arts-based intervention. These traditional activities will help to instill the Acholi's long-held values and beliefs that promote peace and conflict resolution. Additionally, this intervention will create an opportunity to revitalize and sustain intergenerational knowledge transfer that has been diminished due to the impact of the civil war. Utilizing traditional knowledge as an arts-based program could provide an effective context-specific intervention to improve knowledge, attitudes, and behaviour of these children as well as a strategy to change policy at the school level and impact the broader community.

column36: Physical regulation of chromatin during development
column37: Appropriate control over gene activation is essential to many biological processes including embryonic development. Current models of gene control invoke biochemical molecules that unfold DNA/protein strands called chromatin to allow for the activation of genes contained therein. One largely unexplored possibility is that physical force can directly unravel chromatin to control gene activation. Our laboratories developed tools that allow us to test for this possibility in the mouse embyo. We will first use our transgenic force sensors to measure how much force (in pico-Newtons) is normally applied to chromatin that contains a group of Hox genes that control limb development. We will then manipulate how much force is transmitted to chromatin in the developing limb using a nano-scale magnetic bead system that we developed to test the degree to which force directly influences Hox gene activation. By using these biophysical methods in mutant embryos, we will determine whether known molecular regulators of chromatin folding act in part by modulating force transmission to chromatin. This project bridges biochemical and physical mechanisms of genetic control and will be useful to understand numerous biological and disease processes in greater depth.

column37: Rhabdoid brain tumours, also celled ATRTs, are the most common malignant brain tumours in children less than 3 years old. These highly aggressive tumours were historically considered incureable. Use of more intensive therapies over the last 15 years has improved the survival of children with ATRTs, however, only 40-50% of children will survive in the long term. Group 1 AT/RTs generally respond very well to current chemotherapy regimens, while the Group 2A and 2B AT/RTs do not do as well. Preliminary studies in our lab suggest that the composition of group 2A and 2B tumours differ from that of Group 1 AT/RTs. Specifically, our studies suggest that infiltration of cells by immune and other normal cell types are distinct features of group 2A and 2B AT/RTs. We propose that these differences within tumours or intra-tumoral heterogeneity is the underlying basis for the different clinical behaviour of AT?RTs In this grant we propose to use novel genomic tools that will allow us to dissect the composition of the different sub-types of human AT/RTs. Identification of the specific composition of different sub-types of AT/RTs will allow us to exploit novel therapies directed at tumour promoting normal cells including immune cells.

column36: Evaluating eye-movement and brain imaging indicators that predict dementia in healthy older adults
column37: Early detection of dementia is important for effective treatment of the disease. However, no test is sufficiently reliable in the detection of dementia prior to symptom onset. Our research is currently focused on non-invasive tests that can identify those who are at-risk for dementia. In our recent research, we have used brain imaging to measure brain structures in community- dwelling older adults without a dementia diagnosis. We have identified a target brain measure that was correlated with very subtle cognitive issues in a group of older adults who did not notice memory problems in their everyday lives. We further identified a novel eye-tracking measure that is related to brain volume in the regions that are affected by early dementia. These brain and eye-tracking measures may indicate the earliest markers of cognitive decline, which may predict dementia in otherwise healthy older adults. Funding of the current grant application will allow for the expansion of this study, including follow-up testing of these individuals three years later. We will additionally test a second, larger cohort, at two timepoints separated by three years, which will triple the original sample size and allow for the investigation of sex differences. Genetic markers, identified by previous dementia research, will also be collected from all participants to help interpret the observed cognitive and brain changes. We expect that the brain and cognitive measures associated with cognitive decline will be impacted by genetic risk factors. This research will allow scientists and clinicians to make better predictions about who will go on to develop dementia and allow for more effective treatment. Moreover, the brain and eye-tracking tools developed by this research can be used to evaluate treatment efficacy in clinical trials of dementia interventions.

column36: Active surveillance or surgery for primary management of very low risk papillary thyroid cancer: How often are the long-term disease management goals achieved?
column37: Treatment of low risk cancers that are detected early must be balanced with the possible risks of negative effects of therapy. Low risk cancers are those that cause no symptoms and are highly unlikely to become life-threatening. A traditional approach in managing low risk solid tumors is surgery with the intent to cure the cancer. An alternative approach to reduce potential overtreatment of low risk cancers that may never cause harm, is to consider close monitoring, with the intent to perform curative surgery if there is evidence of disease progression; this approach is referred to as active surveillance (AS). AS may reduce the risk of treatment-related complications and associated potential quality of life impairment, in individuals whose disease is unlikely to progress. Very low risk papillary thyroid cancer (VL-PTC) is defined as papillary thyroid cancer that is smaller than 2 cm in maximum diameter, which has not spread outside the gland. In this prospective multi-centre long-term follow-up study, we will determine how often disease management goals are met in patients with VL-PTC who choose AS or surgery, respectively. The disease management of goals will be defined as follows for respective groups: active surveillance group - survival without thyroid surgery (in absence of significant growth of the primary tumor or development of metastatic disease), and for the surgical arm - an excellent response to therapy (analogous to cure), as defined by current clinical practice guidelines. Our study will also compare the following outcomes in AS and surgical groups: quality of life, psychological distress, quality of life, rate of requirement for long-term thyroid hormone treatment, and healthcare resource utilization. We will also conduct an in-depth qualitative analysis of the experiences of a subgroup of study participants in the AS and surgical groups. This study will inform disease management options for future VL-PTC patients.

We will then use this important information to significantly improve chronic pain delivery in Ontario in ways that are sensitive to the needs and experiences of these patients. We hope that these improvements should ultimately help improve the health of all Canadians and also help future researchers be able to collaborate with a more diverse range of patients in their studies. column36: Preserving synaptic function following gene-silencing therapy in Huntington disease: mechanisms and specificity requirements
column37: Huntington disease (HD) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by debilitating motor, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms. HD has been described as having symptoms of ALS, Alzheimer's disease and Schizophrenia at the same time. There is no cure for HD; however, great excitement lies ahead in the potential of so-called "gene-silencing drugs." Unlike the majority of brain disorders, HD has a known cause. A protein known as the huntingtin protein is found in everybody's brain, and appears to be important for the health of our brain cells. The huntingtin protein exists in two forms; one good, one bad. In individuals without HD, there is no bad huntingtin and plenty of good huntingtin. In HD, the good huntingtin is reduced and the bad huntingtin is present, resulting in the slow death of brain cells. As a result of this known cause, drugs can be developed that decrease the brain's production of huntingtin. Gene-silencing drugs do just this. However, one potential roadblock to successful HD treatment is the fact that many gene-silencing drugs are not specific for bad or good huntingtin, and will therefore reduce both the good and the bad. Reducing bad huntingtin will likely help delay or even prevent HD symptoms; however, we have no idea how the long-term reduction of good huntingtin affects the brain. Clinical trials with gene-silencing drugs are already underway, making it extremely important to prioritize basic research into studying the consequences of reducing good huntingtin. In the proposed research, we will use a variety of strategies to understand how good huntingtin reductions can alter the way our brain cells communicate with each other, and whether gene-silencing drugs that are specific for the bad protein should be used exclusively for the treatment of HD. Our research will help to make more informed decisions on which drugs should be administered to those suffering from this devastating disease.

column36: Cam type femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a cause of hip pain in the young adult and a precursor to osteoarthritis (OA)
column37: An abnormally formed hip joint (cam deformity) is a major cause of osteoarthritis (OA). Individuals may not experience any symptoms until OA is severe due to extensive cartilage loss and changes in underlying bone. A series of studies showed that the cam can lead to the development of OA if left untreated, thus strongly suggesting a causal relationship. Currently, the cam that causes pain is surgically removed to relieve the pain and treat the associated cartilage damage. Recent studies have demonstrated that surgical treatment leads to bone and cartilage changes that were related to improved function and reduced pain. As an extension of our original work, this study will allow us to gain a better understanding of the relationship between cartilage and bone changes. We will examine adults in the disease state that require surgical correction and compare to age-matched controls. We will look at the impact of surgical intervention through joint-specific biomarkers of OA, specifically the PET-MRI and blood biomarkers, which will allow us to simultaneously query cartilage and bone activity. We propose that the use of PET-MRI will give more sensitive and hip-specific information about the joint health compared to the blood biomarkers in patients with symptomatic cam morphology. Patients will undergo motion analysis and 3D modeling to help us better understand the disease process during the performance of specific activities and define joint contact mechanics as they relate to the PET-MRI imaging, validating a biomarker for early joint degeneration. This diagnostic tool will be extremely useful for younger individuals with a cam deformity who have not yet developed symptoms. In the future we could use this to detect early degeneration in adolescents to prevent and mitigate development of OA later on. This will also help us develop activity guidelines for people with smaller cam deformities in order to avoid surgery and prevent degeneration.

column36: The Prevention of Group B Streptococcal (GBS) disease in infants
column37: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease is a life-threatening bacterial infection that is the leading cause of blood and brain infections in newborns. Despite advances in treatment, many infants with GBS disease die from the infection. Of the babies who survive, up to half suffer long-term effects, including deafness, mild to severe delays in mental function, or paralysis of all four limbs. The highest risk of GBS disease occurs in the first week of life when the infection is acquired from the baby's mother during birth. In order to prevent these early cases, women are screened when they are 35-37 weeks pregnant to see if GBS bacteria are present. Antibiotics are given to all women who are found to have the bacteria, plus women who go into labour prematurely. This reduces cases in the first week of life, but misses some cases and does not prevent cases in older babies. Treating the mother with antibiotics is risky if she has allergies, and might harm the baby by killing beneficial bacteria. The solution may be a vaccine that would be given to women during pregnancy to prevent GBS in the baby. Although vaccines are quite advanced in development, we need to know more about the impact of GBS on babies and the effectiveness of the current screen-and-treat strategy to understand whether a vaccine will be better at preventing cases and reducing healthcare costs. Our study aims to fill the evidence gap by linking information about all pregnant women who give birth in Ontario with health care information about their baby to understand how many babies get sick with GBS disease. Our results will show how well our current strategy is working, how much it costs and how this compares with the potential benefits and costs of a vaccine. In this way we can find out the best way to protect Canadian children from this devastating infection.

column36: Novel insights into TGFbeta superfamily regulation of follicle-stimulating hormone synthesis
column37: Reproduction is controlled by a hormonal feedback system called the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The hypothalamus of the brain produces and secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which reaches the pituitary gland. The pituitary sits at the base of the brain and, in response to GnRH, produces two additional hormones called luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). LH and FSH travel via the bloodstream to the ovaries in women and testicles in men where they stimulate fundamental aspects of reproductive physiology. In women, the two hormones stimulate growth and ovulation of egg-containing structures called follicles. They also stimulate production of hormones such estrogen and inhibin. In men, LH stimulates testosterone production. Together with FSH, this testosterone controls sperm production. FSH also stimulates inhibin production. Steroid hormones, like estrogen and testosterone, travel back to the brain, where they suppress GnRH secretion. This leads to decreases in LH and FSH secretion. In contrast, inhibins travel to the pituitary where they suppress FSH without affecting LH. Inhibins are thought to produce their actions by blocking the activity of yet another hormone called activin. Activins are thought to be made by the pituitary and stimulate FSH production. In contrast, research from our lab suggests that hormones like activins, but not activins themselves, stimulate FSH and are blocked by inhibins. Moreover, our work shows that our current conceptions of how inhibins suppress FSH are either incorrect or incomplete. In this application, we propose to identify the activin-like hormone that stimulates FSH as well as the mechanisms through which inhibins block this hormone. The result of this work will redefine our understanding of basic mechanisms of reproductive hormone control. Moreover, we may identify a new approach to treat human infertility.

column36: Centrosome-cilium biogenesis and function in human cells.
column37: Centrosomes are cellular structures composed of a centriole pair surrounded by an ordered matrix of proteins, collectively referred to as pericentriolar material. Centrosomes play a key role in mitotic spindle assembly and therefore need to duplicate once and only once per cell cycle so that two centrosomes are present during mitosis, each centrosome organizing one of the two spindle poles. Without a normal complement of centrosomes, chromosomes would not segregate properly to each daughter cell, giving rise to aneuploidy, a condition that can cause cancer. Centrioles also template the formation of cilia and flagella, cellular "antennas" that play a prominent role during human development. When cilia or flagella are defective, this can lead to polycystic kidney disease and infertility. The work proposed in this application will use protein identification tools to discover novel proteins that localize to centrosome and cilia. To study these proteins, our laboratory will use cutting-edge microscopy in both live and fixed cells in combination with genome-editing tools like CRISPR and biochemical approaches to pinpoint the exact role of these proteins in cilia and/or centrosome assembly and function. More specifically, our research program will investigate the cellular mechanisms that ensure cells have the correct number of centrosomes, through the tight control of centriole duplication and decipher how cilia assemble, disassemble and receive signal from outside the cell. Moreover, we will investigate non-conventional functions for centrosome proteins in the regulation of cell motility and proteostasis, a process by which cells control the level of proteins they contain which can go awry in cancer and Huntington's disease. Ultimately, our goal is to determine if the novel proteins identified contribute to the establishment of centrosome-related diseases, including neurological disorders and cancer.

column36: Integrative genomics and functional analyses to uncover the molecular mechanisms involved in bicuspid aortic valve disease
column37: The aortic valve is one of the four valves present in a human heart that ensure that blood flows only in one direction. A normal aortic valve is composed of three leaflets. A problem during heart development can lead to a valve with only two leaflets, a condition called bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). It is the most common congenital heart defect in adults. It has a prevalence as high as 2% in the general population. It is associated with a significant increase in the risk of obstruction and calcification of the aortic valve, a condition that can lead to severe cardiac disease and death. There is currently no medical treatment for this condition, only surgical treatment is available. BAV is present in as much as 50% of cases of patients requiring surgery for obstruction of the aortic valve. It is therefore a serious medical condition with an important societal and economic burden. BAV can be found in many individuals from the same family, suggesting that is has a strong genetic component. The genetic mechanisms responsible for this condition are however largely unknown, with only a few genes identified so far. This project proposes to integrate genomic data from different sources to identify the mechanisms involved in BAV and obstruction of the aortic valve. We will use blood and heart tissue samples from patients who had cardiac surgery to obtain genomic data in cases of BAV. We will compare this data to individuals with a normally formed but obstructed aortic valve and individuals with a normal aortic valve. We will use recent bioinformatics tools to integrate this large amount of data. We will also make experiments directly on cardiac cells and tissue to confirm the findings. We plan to identify the genetic mechanisms involved in BAV and how they differ from obstruction of normally formed aortic valve. This could lead to the development of new treatments for obstruction of the aortic valve.

column36: Function and therapeutic potential of SUV420H2 in neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: Treatment-resistant neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is a currently incurable, lethal subtype of prostate cancer that usually develops following prolonged hormonal therapy. The only treatment option for NEPC is a highly toxic chemotherapy, which provides only limited survival benefits. Therefore, more effective treatments are urgently needed to improve the management of NEPC. Our current research goal is to understand how NEPC develops and progresses and pave the road to develop new therapy for the disease treatment. Toward this end, our group has developed a panel of state-of-the-art pre-clinical models of NEPC, which are giving us unprecedented levels of accuracy in monitoring how NEPC progresses. Using these models and advanced gene expression analyses, we for the first time discovered a protein named SUV420H2 that plays an important role in NEPC development. We observed the increased expression of SUV420H2 in our models and clinical NEPC samples. Furthermore, we demonstrated the increased SUV420H2 expression can functionally promote NEPC development while its decreased expression inhibited NEPC cell growth. In the proposed study, we are aiming to further confirm the function of SUV420H2 in NEPC, understand how it causes NEPC development and aggressiveness and test the effect of the SUV420H2 inhibitor alone and in combination with current chemotherapy on NEPC. This study will improve our understanding of the development and progression of NEPC and provide new insights into the targeted treatment strategy for NEPC patients. The future development of novel therapeutic agents based on this study will lead to more effective therapy and better quality of life for prostate cancer patients.

column36: Redefining Human Liver Disease Using Single Cell RNA Transcriptomics
column37: The human liver is critical to our health, but we do not really understand how it responds to disease. As a result, many diseases of the liver lead to terminal scarring and liver failure that can only be treated by transplanting a new liver into the patient. Liver transplantation is effective, but the liver grafts can be rejected by the recipient immune system and the drugs used to prevent rejection have serious side effects. We want to identify new drugs that can prevent liver graft rejection and liver disease, but up until now it has been very hard to study the cells that make up the human liver. This is because it is difficult to get samples of human livers and because it is hard to isolate the cells that form its structure. Five years ago we modified our liver transplant procedure so that we now routinely obtain samples from liver donors; using this source of liver tissue we have developed ways to isolate and study the cells that make up the organ. In this grant we are proposing to use an exciting new technology, single cell RNA sequencing, to study each cell from the liver and generate a map of the genes expressed in each individual cell. This powerful technology will allow us to describe exactly what cells are in the human liver and how they react to disease. We will use this information to identify drugs that can target and treat the cells that are important for disease. We will use this technology to describe the human liver in both health and disease: we will focus first on describing the cellular composition of transplanted livers that are undergoing rejection. In this way, we can identify new drugs to treat liver graft rejection which will improve post-transplantation outcomes and patient quality of life.

column36: The 'Cholesteryl ester transfer protein' in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia. We now understand that the first changes in the brain occur as early as 15-30 years before symptoms of Alzheimer's disease become evident. Therefore, new strategies are needed to both prevent and treat Alzheimer's disease. At the molecular level, protein fragments called amyloid-beta are produced in the brain and form the characteristic pathology that defines Alzheimer's disease. They thus constitute a specific marker of Alzheimer's disease. The goal of our research program is to identify molecular processes that have not been investigated before to stop Alzheimer's disease at early stages. Alzheimer's disease patients often suffer from hardening of blood vessels (atherosclerosis). Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis share the same risk factors, including high cholesterol levels in the blood, high blood pressure, and type II diabetes. There is a blood protein contributing to high levels of "bad" cholesterol called CETP. Blockers of CETP activity have been developed for the treatment of cardiovascular disease including atherosclerosis and myocardial infarct and have been tested in clinical trials. Interestingly, several genetic studies showed an association of CETP variants with maintenance of good brain functioning during aging. Some studies even implied that CETP variants may protect from Alzheimer's disease. However, CETP has never been investigated in relation to Alzheimer's disease on a molecular level. Results from our laboratory indicate that CETP has a strong impact on amyloid-beta formation. With the data generated in this project, we aim to able to initiate clinical trials to investigate if CETP blockers may be effective in preventing or treating Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Antiretroviral-based HIV prevention and its impact on sexual risk behaviours and HIV/STIs among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men: Engage Cohort Study
column37: In Canada, half of new HIV cases continue to be among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM). GbMSM are also more affected by sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as syphilis. Antiretroviral (ARV)-based HIV prevention, such as Treatment as Prevention (TasP; screening, ARV treatment and care retention) for HIV-positive individuals and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV-negative individuals, is changing how we think about preventing HIV and other STIs among gbMSM. The use of these new prevention strategies is expected to vary greatly across Canada because of differing provincial policies affecting availability and access. Also, ARV-based HIV prevention may lead to unforeseen effects such as less condom use and more STIs. The Engage Cohort Study will investigate trends in the use of ARV-based HIV prevention by following 1489 HIV-positive and high-risk HIV-negative gbMSM in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal. Participants will do study visits (questionnaire and HIV/STI screening) every 6 months for three years. The study aims to 1) measure trends in the use of ARV-based HIV prevention, psychosocial-behavioural factors (e.g., experiences of discrimination, substance use, etc.), condom-use, STIs, and HIV and 2) examine relationships between ARV-based HIV prevention and various sexual health outcomes (e.g., occurrence of STIs). Also, because some groups of gbMSM (e.g., transmen) may have unique experiences of ARV-based HIV prevention, interviews will be done in each city to better understand their realities. The experienced study team will work with community engagement committees and knowledge users in each city to ensure the study is conducted appropriately and that study results are communicated properly. Doing the Engage Cohort Study now, as ARV-based HIV prevention becomes more available, is an important opportunity to learn how best to use these new prevention strategies in controlling HIV and STI epidemics among gbMSM in Canada.

column36: Using deep learning to estimate breast cancer recurrence scores from histopathology images
column37: Breast cancer is not a single disease and there are many different sub-types. It is important to understand what kind of cancer an individual patient has before deciding on treatment. A group from Google have shown that a computer can detect cancer cells more accurately than a pathologist and another group has shown that it is possible to predict the results from an expansive genomic test using a simple tissue slide image. Other work has demonstrated that using information from images can improve the accuracy of genetic tests. We also know which patients went on to have a recurrence of cancer. We propose to train deep learning algorithms to use the lower cost, more readily available image data to predict whether a particular cancer will lead to recurrence. We will compare the accuracy of these algorithms with the genetic tests. Our aim is to develop a tool for identifying high and low-risk cancers so that an individual patient can be offered the best course of therapy for them.

column37: Identifying the genetic cause of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) sufficiently early in life can be beneficial in several ways; e.g., early interventions may improve outcomes and allow a timely start of appropriate educational supports. column36: Architecture and chemical modulation of genetic networks
column37: Complex networks of interacting genes and proteins control all aspects of human biology and are perturbed in genetic disorders, cancer, diabetes, infection, autoimmunity, neurological dysfunction and literally every other disease state. The overarching challenge in biomedical research is thus to understand how these interconnected networks govern cellular behaviour in both health and disease. This research program will exploit leading edge genome-scale technologies to systematically map biological networks in human cells. In particular, we will use genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic screens and sensitive protein mass spectrometry techniques to probe the cellular networks that control the growth and division of normal and cancer cells. The complexity of these measurements will require the development of databases, software tools and computational models to track and predict network responses. To exploit this knowledge for therapeutic benefit, chemicals that alter cellular networks will be identified and combined to specifically control network outputs and thereby provide a more precise means of treating disease. In parallel, the effects of thousands of different drugs, toxins and industrial chemicals will be investigated using CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic screens to understand how these compounds act on human cells. To address a serious shortfall in the drug discovery pipeline, an innovative synthetic biology strategy will be used to create massive collections of natural product-like compounds that will be screened in ultra-high throughput and low-cost formats. These novel screening technologies will allow us to identify novel modulators of network activity and will be focused on targets in infectious disease and cancer. The combined systems biology, chemical biology and synthetic biology approaches we propose will help underpin a long-term framework that will transform our understanding and treatment of disease.

column36: Electrical stimulation prior to nerve transection and surgical repair promotes nerve regeneration and functional recovery in a manner exceeding a conditioning lesion
column37: Peripheral nerve injury is common, especially among young, working individuals. Unfortunately, with current treatments, nerve regeneration following severe injury is often poor. A major reason is the very slow rate of regrowth, at 0.5-1 mm/day. Through animal studies, there is strong evidence that a conditioning lesion (CL), in which a nerve is deliberately damaged before the actual nerve injury, increases the speed of axon regeneration up to 3 mm/day. Faster regeneration increases the likelihood of functional motor and sensory recovery, therefore this accelerated nerve regeneration is extremely important. CL, however, cannot be applied to patients because it is not ethically acceptable or clinically feasible to subject patients to an additional surgery to crush a nerve. As such, another method of conditioning that does not require injuring the nerve is needed. A recent study showed brief electrical stimulation (ES) administered prior to injury increased the speed of regeneration of sensory neurons grown in culture. This opens the possibility that conditioning ES may be an clinically feasible alternative to CL. This treatment would be particularly applicable to nerve transfer surgeries in which a healthy nerve is cut and rerouted to a damaged nerve in order to reinnervate a muscle. These increasingly common elective procedures are pre-planned so they are ideally suited for conditioning ES. Our goal is to systemically evaluate the effects and mechanisms of conditioning ES on nerve regeneration and functional recovery in a rat model. We will concurrently perform a pilot clinical trial to ensure a seamless bidirectional translation between the bench and the bedside.

column37: Depression is a serious and recurrent chronic disorder that affects 5-8% of children. column37: Hardening of the arteries leads to heart disease and stroke, and therefore, is a major health burden for Canadians. Cholesterol is a fat and does not, by itself, dissolve in the watery environment of the blood. Instead, it is carried in the blood packaged in specialized structures called lipoproteins. Two types of lipoproteins that have the most influence on hardening of the arteries, and therefore heart disease and stroke, are LDL (the bad cholesterol) and HDL (the good cholesterol). High levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood support the development of hardening of the arteries and treatment efforts have been aimed at reducing LDL cholesterol. On the other hand, high levels of HDL cholesterol counteract hardening of the arteries because HDL both prevents and reverses cholesterol build up in the arteries. Treatments centered on HDL have so far been aimed at increasing HDL levels, without regarding HDL function. This application is aimed at understanding the role of a novel cellular factor, PDZK1, in mediating beneficial functions of HDL in cells within atherosclerotic plaques, which can both halt the development and even reverse the growth of the plaques. We will carry out our studies using laboratory mice engineered to develop atherosclerosis when fed a fatty diet. Moreover, these mice are engineered to lack or express PDZK1 in specific tissues which will allow us to tease apart how it protects against atherosclerosis and its role in protection brought about by HDL. Understanding how HDL brings about reversal or "regression" of atherosclerosis will pave the way to identifying new pathways that can be potential targets for treatment.

The outcome of our experiments will be evidence testing the causal role for circulating protein biomarkers in the risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic fracture. This information will be helpful to patients and their clinicians because it can help to identify people at risk of fractures. It can also be helpful to identify critical control points in osteoporosis development, which can be targeted through pharmacotherapies.

column37: Cannabis is a plant that is commonly referred to as marijuana. Cannabis has been used for medicinal purposes for thousands of years. Cannabinoids are believed to be why cannabis has therapeutic properties for many diseases- including autoimmune and chronic inflammatory conditions (asthma), pain and lung infections. These chemicals may work by affecting how the immune system functions. For example, THC and CBD can cause an immune cell in the body- called a T cell- to switch its armour. THC and CBD make a T cell become regulatory (as in regulates the disease to help make it better) and not pathogenic (disease-causing). In this research project, we will test whether cannabis alters the immune response to protect against infection. We will also provide answers as to whether there are long term health consequences of inhaling cannabis on a regular basis. Given the paucity of information on the long term consequences of cannabis smoke, together with the increasing use of pure cannabinoids for medical purposes, we are in a unique position to provide novel mechanistic evidence on the health impact of cannabis.

column37: My team is one of the world's leading multidisciplinary health research group in the field of obesity. Over 30 years ago, with the use of computed tomography (CT), I began measuring the inner fat located in the abdomen (commonly called visceral fat). My team was the first to report that an excessive amount of visceral fat is related to major health problems such as diabetes and heart disease. We also found that fat underneath the skin (subcutaneous fat) was much less dangerous to health. Since then, the notion that visceral fat (visceral obesity) is dangerous to health has been widely accepted by scientists worldwide. Recently, we found that visceral obesity was also associated with too much fat stored in normally lean tissues such as the liver, the heart, and muscles. For instance, although excess liver fat is a major cause of liver failure and transplantation, its link with visceral obesity and lifestyle habits is not considered by clinicians and patients. The central theme of my program grant application is that when we are exposed to a "toxic lifestyle" (sedentary habits and poor diet), those who put on a certain amount of subcutaneous fat remain relatively healthy, while individuals who store fat in their inner organs become viscerally obese and develop chronic diseases. This notion has major clinical and public health consequences and represents a conceptual shift as the risk of overweight/obesity is largely estimated by the assessment of excess body weight without distinguishing where the fat is stored. Globally, the research program that I propose aims at a better understanding of how we store fat in various regions of the body, how genetic factors play a role (visceral obesity runs in families) and how this can be affected by our lifestyle habits. I will also remain committed to medical and lay public education as my research program is relevant to the health of millions of Canadians.

column37: Shoulder fractures are increasingly common in older adults, and result in considerable limitations in function and quality of life. Unfortunately, the best way to treat shoulder fractures is currently one of the most debated areas of orthopaedics. Existing clinical studies comparing various methods of surgical and non-surgical management have reported conflicting results. These studies have had limited numbers of patients, involved single centres, and used inconsistent treatment methods and inclusion/exclusion criteria. Therefore, there is insufficient evidence supporting any one treatment type, and a poor understanding of what factors influence the outcomes that are important to patients, making decisions regarding treatment difficult. We propose to establish DECIPHER, the first nation-wide, multi-centre observational study with 744 fully characterized patients with the ultimate goal of determining what specific factors influence patient important outcomes. Additionally, we will answer important research questions concerning treatment and rehabilitation strategies. Patients 50 and older with shoulder fractures will be recruited from 17 centres across Canada.
