column36: Significance of S100A10 (p11) in breast cancer tumor progression
column37: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. The high incidence of deaths linked to this cancer is due to spreading (metastasis) of the cancer to organs such as lungs and bones. Cancer cell spreading is assisted by a protein called plasmin which chews other proteins surrounding the tumor cells thereby making the way for the cancer cells to move from the tumor site to distant organs. Plasmin is produced from a blood protein called, plasminogen, by the action of proteins located on the surface of the cancer cells. One such protein, S100A10 (p11), binds plasminogen on the cell surface and speeds up plasmin formation. In our initial studies, we observed that breast tumors and metastasis to the lung are dramatically reduced in mice engineered not to make p11 (p11- null). Moreover, we have shown, by analyzing breast cancer patient tumor samples, that patients with low p11 levels in their breast tissue have a better rate of survival than patients with high p11 levels. In the current project, we will investigate how p11 affects tumor growth and metastasis in breast cancer using a well-established breast cancer mouse model that is known to mimic human breast cancer, the PyMT mouse model. We will determine if the plasmin generated by p11 is important for the ability of the cancer cells to develop tumors, leave the tumor site and/or grow in other tissues. We will determine if the reduction in tumor growth seen when cancer cells cannot produce p11 is due to decreased cancer cell growth or increased cancer cell death. We will also determine if p11 produced by the other cells in the tumor that support cancer cell development and growth are important or necessary for tumor growth and metastasis. Identifying the mechanisms by which p11 contributes to tumor growth and metastasis will facilitate the development of new therapies to block tumor growth and metastasis by specifically targeting p11.

column37: Despite marked reductions in infant mortality over the past several decades, the rates of adverse birth outcomes such as premature birth, a key determinant of infant mortality and morbidity, have remained the same or even increased over the same period in many countries. Pregnancy and birth outcomes are not only good measures of current population health but can also predict future health of the population, because health in early life predicts health later in life. Therefore, achieving socioeconomic equity in pregnancy outcomes is an important public health goal. However, existing scientific evidence on socioeconomic and ethno-cultural disparities in pregnancy and birth outcomes in Canada is limited, owing to the lack of detailed socioeconomic and ethno-cultural background information in routinely collected birth and death data. This will allow us to systematically examine the most recent patterns of perinatal health across social, racial/ethnic, and cultural groups, and importantly, disparity patterns over the past 20 years in Canada as a whole and across provinces. This work has not previously been possible in Canada.

column36: A randomized controlled trial of individualized yoga to reduce fatigue in hospitalized children receiving intensive chemotherapy
column37: Fatigue or tiredness is a major problem in children and adolescents receiving intensive treatment for cancer and undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). While exercise is good for reducing fatigue, these patients are often too sick to participate in regular exercise sessions. A unique intervention that combines exercise and relaxation is yoga. We previously performed 2 feasibility studies of yoga in children admitted to the hospital receiving very intensive chemotherapy or HSCT and found that our program of yoga is doable. We also found children and their parents like the program. This is a randomized controlled trial which will determine if a 3 week program of yoga is associated with less fatigue, better quality of life and less pain mediation use compared to the control intervention of iPad games, music, movies or books. Yoga sessions will be conducted once a day during the regular work week and will be led by a trained yoga teacher. In the control arm, the yoga teacher will visit once a day and will offer children games, music, movies or books on an iPad. Fatigue and quality of life will be measured by the parent at baseline, on day 10 and on day 21. We plan to enroll 210 subjects total at 4 centers in Canada and the United States over 4 years. Yoga has the potential to improve the health of children who are at the highest risk of poor quality of life. This trial is an important step in a program of research designed to improve quality of life for children with cancer and HSCT.

column37: In the past decade, we have witnessed a burst of knowledge about cellular processes that are deregulated in human cancer cells. One such biological process is the regulation of protein stability by ubiquitin, a small protein that is assembled to other proteins (so-called "ubiquitination") and signals for their destruction or functional changes. Among several protein families involved in this process, ubiquitin ligases (~600 in human) have attracted increasing attention as anti-cancer targets, as they catalyze the attachment of ubiquitin and therefore determine the specificity of ubiquitination. In particular, the HECT family members (28 in human) are deemed as promising targets due to the availability of an active site and other biochemical properties. However, existing inhibitory molecules of HECT ligases fall short in terms of potency, selectivity, and generally have had limited utility in probing unknown HECT mechanisms. To tackle this problem, we have used protein design and engineering approaches to systematically develop protein modulators for HECT ligases. We showed that the synthetic molecules could bind HECT ligases tightly on places other than the active site and were able to compromise or enhance their biological function. In this proposal, we will generate potent and specific non-active site inhibitors of selected oncogenic HECT ligases and validate their function in human cells. Additional biochemical and cellular analyses will provide information on molecular mechanisms by which HECT ligases function and further aid the design of chemical inhibitors as drug leads. In summary, this work will generate unique probes to understand and manipulate HECT ligases in normal and cancerous cells and will provide novel routes for cancer therapy.

column37: Coronary artery disease is the number one killer globally and will remain so for the next 20 years. We will then use high quality, population-level data to develop mathematical formulas to calculate a patient's risk of developing this outcome, using the characteristics of the patient as input variables. These formulas will be made freely available to patients, families, caregivers and clinicians over a web-based app to provide personalized risk estimates, to enhance the shared decision-making process and to place patients back at the center of the care they receive.

column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rhythm disorder that causes one out of six strokes. Prevention of strokes in AF is achieved through the use of blood thinners such as coumadin. This structure is easily accessible for removal during open heart surgery, and has been a target of interest for stroke prevention. However, there is currently no definitive evidence that removing it prevents strokes. The LAAOS III trial randomly (like the flip of a coin) assigned patients with AF undergoing heart surgery for other reasons to have their left atrial appendage closed or not closed. These patients are treated in the usual manner except for this small procedure which has been shown to be quite safe. Having successfully recruited 4700 participants into the trial supported by multiple grants, we now seek funding to complete long-term follow-up of the 4,700 participants required to know if left atrial appendage closure works. The LAAOS III trial will determine if closing the left atrial appendage can reduce stroke and other complications in addition to usual therapy. A positive study will change the way heart surgery is performed on patients with AF and result in a large reduction in the number of strokes in Canada. Further, it will promote further research into this approach that could be applied beyond AF patients undergoing heart surgery.

column37: Traumatic spinal cord injuries (SCIs) have devastating long-term physical, social, and financial impacts on patients and their families. Currently, there are no effective regenerative therapies available for nearly one million North Americans living with SCI. Damage to the spinal cord results in the loss of cells critical for sending signals from the brain to the rest of the body. Without these signals, the ability to perform everyday activities such as walking, grasping and controlling bowel/bladder function is lost resulting in debilitating impairments such as para/quadriplegia, reduced breathing capacity, immune system dysfunction and death. To overcome these issues, I have developed novel human NPCs that have been specifically engineered to repair the spinal cord. This proposal focuses on mechanistically understanding how these novel engineered cells replace those lost through injury and how they promote recovery. Additionally, this proposal aims to determine how these cells can be further optimized to maximise recovery. I believe these novel engineered human cells will result in the restoration of function following SCI by promoting the formation of new spinal cord cells whilst repairing other cells damaged by the injury. I expect that by the end of the grant my research will result in the generation of a viable living cell therapy for SCI.

column36: Understanding Cellular Response to Stress: Role of DEAD Box 1
column37: The cells in our body are routinely exposed to different types of stress, such as agents that damage DNA, and 'environmental' stressors that affect the function of cells. Environmental stressors include agents that induce reactive oxygen species which can damage cells. Importantly, the presence of excessive reactive oxygen species in brain neurons has been associated with a number of neurodegenerative diseases. DEAD box proteins are RNA unwinding proteins whose main role is to alter the structure of RNA, thereby affecting the amount and types of proteins expressed in cells. We are working on a DEAD box gene called DEAD Box 1, or DDX1, originally identified in my lab. Over the last few years, we have shown that DDX1 helps to repair a type of DNA damage called 'double strand breaks'. We have also shown that DDX1 is important for the resolution of stress caused by agents that induce reactive oxygen species. Intriguingly, we have recently discovered that DDX1 interacts with DNA repair proteins (such as ATM) associated with neurodegeneration. Mutations in the ATM gene are the underlying cause of ataxia telangiectasia, an inherited neurodegenerative disease that affects children and adults. Our combined research findings have led us to hypothesize that DDX1 helps to resolve stress in neurons. Thus, we propose that inability of DDX1 to carry out its normal function keeps cells in a state of stress, a condition that leads to premature cell death in neurons. The goal of this proposal is to determine how DDX1 resolves stress with a focus on understanding DDX1's mechanism of action in cells that are defective in ATM, as well as in neuronal cells. Thus, we will use cells from patients with ataxia telangiectasia and neuronal cells to examine the molecules that DDX1 interacts with under normal versus stress conditions. Our long term goal is to determine whether DDX1 and its partners could be used to either prevent or slow down neuronal cell death in susceptible individuals.

column36: Defining mechanisms of PI4P-dependent transport during secretory granule biogenesis
column37: Each of our cells is like a busy city, with fleets of trucks that pick up and deliver cargo to specific destinations. Instead of street signs, the drivers of these vehicles find the correct address by reading signals provided by lipids, which are fatty molecules present in cellular membranes. Different membranous structures (organelles) within each cell contain different lipids. If the correct lipid signals are not present, cellular materials can be delivered to the wrong destination or wind up in the trash. We are studying an enzyme, PI4KII, that makes an important lipid called PI4P. PI4P is found at the Golgi, which is an organelle devoted to transport of cargo (proteins) to many destinations in the cell. PI4P is also found at membrane contact sites, where it helps transfer other lipids such as cholesterol between organelles. A small amount of PI4P is found on endosomal tubules, which retrieve proteins and send them back to the Golgi. Our experiments ask how PI4KII and PI4P act at these organelles to help form the storage depots (secretory granules) that house hormones, digest enzymes and other biologically active molecules in the cell. To understand how secretory granules form, we developed the fruit fly salivary gland as a model system. This allows us to take advantage of powerful genetics and microscopy techniques available in the fly to study the role of PI4P in this process. So far, we discovered that endosomal tubules and cholesterol help drive secretory granule maturation. The proposed experiments will enable us to understand how PI4KII and PI4P control these transport pathways. Our findings will have application to human diseases that result from defects in secretory granule formation.

column36: Improving Indigenous cultural safety in Ontario's cancer screening programs
column37: While historically uncommon, today, cancer is common and has a greater impact on Ontario Indigenous populations. Cancer Care Ontario (CCO), Ontario's provincial cancer agency, runs the screening programs for breast, colorectal and cervical cancer. Screening catches cancers early, at a stage when they are more likely to be treatable. Indigenous persons in Ontario are screened less often in Ontario than the general population. In prior work, we learned that a generally poor Indigenous experience of cancer screening (racism during health care encounters, problems with CCO's mailed invitations to be screened (did not receive or difficulties understanding) and poor support for screening participants) might lead to lower participation. To address these gaps, we will do 3 linked projects with the overall objective of improving Indigenous peoples' experience of cancer screening in Ontario. First, we will examine Indigenous cultural safety (CS) at CCO. CS is defined as quality care for people of diverse ethnicities. CS emphasizes respecting cultural differences, demands empathy and self-reflection, and is attentive to empowering the care recipient. We will develop a CS Assessment tool then use it to interview CCO leaders and employees about their values, beliefs, and experiences of Indigenous CS and their opinion of CCO's commitment to these issues. Second, we will work with First Nations, Inuit and Metis partners separately to develop CS and implementable communication strategies and materials using established health communication principles. Third, we will collaboratively develop a CS shared decision making (SDM) strategy with Indigenous partners. SDM is a process where patients work with clinicians or peers to make health care decisions based on science as well as their values and preferences. Findings from these 3 projects will inform recommendations for change in Ontario's cancer screening programs so as to improve Indigenous persons' experiences with cancer screening.

column36: Community-driven Helicobacter pylori genomics investigation of the disproportionate H. pylori-associated disease burden among northern Indigenous Canadians
column37: Northern Indigenous communities view H. pylori infection as a health research priority because of its link to stomach cancer, which occurs more frequently in northern Canada than on average across the nation. Compared to southern Canadians, this infection is diagnosed more often in northern Indigenous Canadians, in whom it also causes more severe disease and is more difficult to cure. This proposal was developed in partnership with Northwest Territories (NT) and Yukon (YT) communities that seek research aimed at explaining why this common infection causes a disproportionate health burden in their region. The Canadian North Helicobacter pylori (CANHelp) Working Group conducts community-driven research on H. pylori infection, with projects in 4 NT and 5 YT communities. We propose to conduct a genomic analysis of H. pylori bacteria cultured from stomach biopsies of 274 community project participants. Genomic studies examine an organism's genome (its full set of genes). We will describe features of genomes of the H. pylori strains that infect residents of participating communities and investigate whether these genomic features determine how H. pylori infection impacts stomach health among participants. Our proposed research aims to: describe genomic features of H. pylori strains and how they are distributed across NT and YT communities; examine the relatedness of H. pylori strains within household, families, and communities; and estimate associations of genomic features with disease severity. The CANHelp Working Group has a unique collection of H. pylori isolated from northern Indigenous communities, along with clinical outcome data. It is one of few population-based collections of H. pylori in the world. Thus, the proposed research has the potential to advance knowledge of H. pylori genomics in human populations while furthering community-driven biomedical research that addresses priorities of Indigenous Canadian communities.

column36: Determining the etiologies of age-related clonal hematopoiesis (ARCH), a new biomarker of cancer and cardiovascular disease development: focus on the roles of inflammation and genetic predisposition.
column37: Aging is associated with the acquisition of small changes (mutations) in the genes of blood cells called Age-Related Clonal Hematopoiesis (ARCH). It seems benign as people have no abnormalities in their blood counts. However, ARCH is associated with a 10-fold increased risk of developing a blood cancer, and it also doubles the risk of having a heart disease. In this application, we seek to clarify the cause of ARCH and to find a way to prevent its deleterious impact on health. Our previous work suggests that there are two major factors influencing ARCH: inflammation and genetic predisposition. The Hopital Maisonneuve-Rosemont (HMR) group, led by Dr. Busque, has 20 years' experience in the field of ARCH. To undertake the proposed study, it will be joined by world leaders in the field of cardiology (Dr. Tardif) and epidemiogenetics (Dr. Dube) from the Montreal Heart Institute (MHI). We will first evaluate the role of inflammation in ARCH by using a previously established cohort of over 5000 subjects. We will correlate deep sequencing data (determining ARCH) and blood levels of the C-reactive protein (a reliable biomarker of inflammation). Secondly, we will investigate if inflammation is related to bacterial translocation coming from the gut's microbiota (germs), as we have previously shown in mice. Thirdly, we will evaluate if an anti-inflammatory treatment (colchicine) impacts ARCH development and patient outcome in the context of an ongoing randomized clinical trial called COLCOT. Fourthly, we will search for a genetic predisposition to ARCH using an already recruited cohort comprised of 311 families. If our study hypotheses hold true, we will be in positon to identify subjects at risk of ARCH early in life and hopefully curb the emergence and/or clinical impacts of cardiovascular disease and cancer through anti-inflammatory intervention. Our work is ultimately intended to promote healthy aging, one of the most important societal objectives of the present time

column37: An estimated 35,000 people die from bone metastases each year in Canada, and skeletal complications before death cause considerable suffering and morbidity. Bone metastases are currently treated with anti-resorptive agents such as the potent bisphosphonate zoledronate or Denosumab (Xgeva). Unfortunately, this is not a cure and the number of patients experiencing skeletal complications is reduced by only 40% with no survival benefit, which exemplifies the need for improving the efficacy of such therapy. A lack of vitamin D has been linked to several types of cancer including breast cancer and the majority of breast cancer patients who have a recurrence will develop cancer spread to the skeleton. Active forms of vitamin D have anti-cancer properties but have not been effective when administered in humans. Significant side effects limit their use at high doses that can lead to hypercalcemia (elevation of blood calcium) with severe consequences such as tissue calcification and heart arrhythmias. Our goals are to understand how vitamin D may be beneficial to patients with bone metastasis, and to develop improved vitamin D therapies with minimal side effects by enhancing the local activity of vitamin D in the bone microenvironment to prevent its systemic effects and hypercalcemia-related complications. These novel therapies will be combined with currently approved anti-resorptive therapies such as bisphosphonates and Denosumab to treat/prevent bone metastasis in breast cancer patients. Overall, we propose to develop pre-clinical models that will serve as proofs of principle for therapeutic intervention in breast cancer spreading to the skeleton.

column37: Blood vessels in the brain form a barrier that protects the brain from toxic components of the blood. After the onset of stroke, this barrier is rapidly disrupted and this leads to secondary clinical consequences and poor prognosis. Following stroke, there is considerable interest in preventing the break-down of this barrier between blood and brain. Indeed, maintaining this blood barrier can prevent future damages of the brain and enhance function recovery. The major goal of this application is to demonstrate the role of a protein on blood brain barrier maintenance. We identified a protein from the liver that is involved in the maintenance of the blood brain barrier and can prevent barrier opening following stroke. The liver is known to affect brain health however, to our knowledge no liver-secreted protein was shown to protect the maintenance of the blood barrier. Thus, this application will contribute to our understanding of how the liver can influence brain health, which is important in many conditions (e.g. Stroke, MS). To demonstrate the role of this liver-protein we will use a new imaging technique as well as multiple behavioral assessments.

column36: Evaluating the renoprotective effect of acetaminophen in pediatric severe falciparum malaria: A randomized controlled trial.
column37: Acute kidney injury (AKI) complicating critical illness is an important problem, contributing to an estimated 1.7 million deaths annually. The burden of AKI care is estimated to cost US1.72 billion per year. Treatment is limited to dialysis which is resource intensive and frequently unavailable in resource-limited settings. Therefore, preventing AKI is a critical step in reducing mortality. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) has the potential to reduce AKI caused by hemoglobin (released from red blood cells) and myoglobin (released from muscle cells). Hemoglobin and myoglobin cause oxidative damage and this is a common mechanism of AKI seen in various conditions including sepsis, malaria and crush injuries. Acetaminophen has been shown to inhibit oxidative stress and reduce kidney dysfunction in pre-clinical models and to reduce hemoglobin-mediated oxidative stress in patients post-cardiac surgery and in patients with sepsis. Our recent randomized controlled trial in adults with severe malaria showed that acetaminophen improved kidney function and reduced the odds of developing AKI. Since children bear the major burden of malaria, it is now crucial to test this protective effect in African children where AKI affects up to 45% of patients. The ultimate goal is to assess the role of acetaminophen as a renoprotective adjunctive therapy in severe malaria. The hypothesis is that acetaminophen will reduce kidney dysfunction by inhibiting hemoglobin-mediated oxidative damage. We propose a randomized controlled trial of adjunctive acetaminophen in African children with severe malaria. If the trial is positive, our results would change management of severe malaria globally. It could be rapidly scalable as acetaminophen is inexpensive, safe and widely used. Our findings will also have broad implications for other major causes of hemoprotein-mediated AKI including crush injury and sepsis, which directly impact thousands of Canadians.

column36: Regulation of chromosome architecture by SMC complexes in health and disease
column37: Any mistake in the repair or transmission of our genetic material is sufficient to generate genome instability, one of the most potent stimulator of cancer development. The overall objective of this proposal is to understand how living organisms promote effective maintenance and repair of their chromosomal DNA during cell division. To achieve this objective, we focus our work on a family of proteins known as the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) proteins. Our interest in this family of proteins comes from the fact that they are known as central gatekeepers of genome stability, and mutations affecting these proteins are associated with tumorigenesis and other severe developmental disorders in humans. The main aim of our work is to uncover how the SMC proteins recognizes normal and damaged DNA during cell division. Then, we aim to reveal how cells regulate the behavior of the SMC proteins when they suffer DNA damage. Ultimately, our work will have a major positive impact on human health by revealing new cellular mechanisms critical for cancer development and by identifying new genetic vulnerabilities that could be used for cancer treatment.

column36: Apo(a):apoB100 interactions as key determinants of Lp(a) biosynthesis
column37: Lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) is a fat/protein complex that circulates in blood. High concentrations of Lp(a) in the blood place individuals at a higher risk of having a heart attack or stroke. Lp(a) consists of a lipoprotein particle identical to low density lipoprotein (LDL) as well as an additional protein called apolipoprotein(a) (apo(a)). It is apo(a) that is thought to be responsible for the unique effects of Lp(a) in the body. Lp(a) can promote a process called atherosclerosis, which involves deposition of fatty material and overactive inflammation in the artery wall and which is ultimately the cause of the blood clots that form in arteries to cause heart attacks and strokes. Although concentrations of Lp(a) are thought to be determined mainly by genetic factors (i.e. are largely inherited), this does not explain all the variability that is observed. Furthermore, very little is known about how apo(a) production by the liver and assembly of Lp(a) from its component parts are controlled. Interestingly, some drugs have been shown to lower Lp(a) levels, although how they work in this context is unknown. In this project, we will demonstrate the importance of two factors that we believe are key regulators of Lp(a) production by the liver. The first is interactions between the two proteins that make up Lp(a) - apo(a) and apoB100 - within the cell itself. The second is a series of proteins and drugs that may regulate apo(a) and/or apoB100 production and therefore Lp(a) secretion from liver cells. We will study the molecular mechanisms by which these two factors regulate Lp(a) synthesis in the liver, and will look for evidence of their action in human subjects. Our findings will indicate new targets for drug development to lower Lp(a) concentrations.

column36: Therapeutic potential of bloodless oxygenated perfusion of donor kidneys for prolonged storage and protection for transplantation
column37: Kidney failure among Canadians has tripled over the past 20 years. Transplantation improves the quality of life and survival of patients at a much lower cost than dialysis. However, only 40% of patients receive functional kidneys due to a lack of living organ donors. To increase the number of kidneys available for transplantation, surgeons are accepting organs from deceased donors. These kidneys are commonly stored at 4C without oxygen. While this method can increase storage times, it does not properly preserve kidneys as the organs can suffer injuries from a lack of oxygen as well as cold temperature. Moreover, these conditions are not conducive to apply any drugs to prevent damage even when they are available. Therefore, we need to develop a new method to preserve donated kidneys that address these issues. To this end, we used pig kidneys to resemble human kidneys donated from dead donors. We showed that perfusing pig kidneys with oxygenated blood at 22C (near room temperature) instead of storing them in static cold conditions improved their preservation. However, the lack of availability of type-matched blood and the potential presence of infectious agents can limit the use of blood in the clinic. Thus, our objective is to study the effects of a bloodless oxygen carrying perfusion liquid on storing human donor kidneys for long periods of time (16 hours) at room temperature. We will also evaluate if certain drugs can maximize the preservation of these organs. Our main goal is to properly preserve kidneys coming from dead donors, to extend their lifetime after transplantation and to improve the quality of life of patients while reducing the cost of transplantation worldwide.

column36: The INITIATE Study: Initiating nicotine dependence treatment for smokers admitted to emergency departments
column37: Tobacco-related illnesses cost the healthcare system millions each year. Quitting smoking improves smoking-related outcomes, like the onset or management of heart disease, stroke, lung diseases, and several cancers. There are ~16 million visits to Canadian emergency departments (ED) each year; an estimated 3-4 million involve smokers. Effective quit smoking interventions exist, but are underutilized. Given the realities of the ED environment, interventions need to be simple. Considering that stopping smoking improves health outcomes, that tobacco-use is an important cause of preventable ED-use, and the volume of smokers, Canadian EDs are a missed opportunity in the initiation of quit smoking support. The INITIATE study aims to test the effect of a tobacco treatment intervention initiated in hospital EDs that includes a behavioural incentive and proactive follow-up support, on long-term smoking abstinence, health and healthcare utilization. This will be a 6-site, prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial. Individuals will be randomly allocated to either the Quit Card intervention (QCI, n=604) or usual care (UC) condition (n=604). The CCI group will receive: a "Quit Card" (a gift card worth $600 that can be used to buy nicotine replacement therapies at any pharmacy); a self-help booklet; and, enrolment in tailored telephone follow-up support. The UC will receive a brochure for a local smoking cessation program. The primary outcome will be 26-week prolonged smoking abstinence, bio-chemically validated through expired carbon monoxide measurement. Secondary outcomes will include 4, 52, and 104 week smoking status and all-cause and smoking-related health and health services outcomes. We hypothesize that intervention participants will have higher abstinence rates, improved health outcomes, and decreased healthcare utilization.

column37: Fibrillin-1 is a protein in the connective tissue of many organs, including blood vessels and bone. Abnormalities in the fibrillin-1 gene cause various disorders which lead to severe and continuously developing clinical complications. Examples of this include various forms of Marfan syndrome, stiff skin syndrome, dominant Weill-Marchesani syndrome, acromicric and geleophysic dysplasias, familial tall stature, ectopia lentis, among others. It is estimated that about 1 in 3,000-5,000 individuals suffer from one of these disorders, resulting in high levels of physical and mental distress for patients and families, in addition to immense costs for the health care system. Marfan syndrome is the most frequent disorder in this group. We have recently found that the molecular interaction of fibrillin-1 with connective tissue cells controls a group of important regulatory molecules, the so-called microRNAs. These are molecules within cells that determine which proteins are produced. We also found that some of these microRNAs are dysregulated in a Marfan syndrome mouse model. The current proposal aims to determine how fibrillin-1 regulates different microRNAs under physiological conditions, and to identify some that can be exploited therapeutically in the long term in Marfan syndrome. We will use cell culture and genetically modified mice affected with Marfan syndrome as model systems. We will identify microRNAs and the genes they control in normal and in the disease situation, and define their function in relation to fibrillin-1. Since microRNAs are very small molecules, they can be potentially used for therapeutic approaches. In this context, we will explore whether inhibition or elevation of some microRNAs in mice leads to an improvement of the typical disease symptoms in blood vessels and bone. The identification of microRNAs in the pathogenesis of Marfan syndrome has the potential to open new avenues for novel treatment strategies for the affected patients.

column36: Evaluation, optimization and validation of structural and functional MRI-based parcellation of the cerebral cortex
column37: The human brain can be modeled as a network of brain areas (network nodes) with anatomical connections (links between the nodes) that transfer information between brain areas. In order to understand the function of the healthy human brain and the development of neurological diseases, it is essential to correctly delineate distinct brain areas. Structural and functional MRI are non-invasive imaging methods that hold the potential to identify relevant brain areas. However, MRI and functional MRI-based delineation of brain areas have neither been thoroughly validated nor optimized. We propose to apply non-invasive structural and functional MRI methods in an animal model, followed by the evaluation and optimization of methods for delineating brain areas. column36: Paving the Way for ICD-11 Adoption to Advance Health Information
column37: The World Health Organization (WHO) routinely collects global information on causes of death and diseases/conditions using a system called the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Since its original release in 1893, ICD has evolved to become the standard by which global, national, and local health information systems and databases support population health and healthcare performance monitoring. These, in turn, facilitate surveillance, healthcare planning and research. To support advancement of medical science in disease specification and new conditions, the WHO regularly updates the ICD. It is currently preparing the 11th version (ICD-11; released June 2018, implementation planned for 2023/24), which will track 40,000 additional clinical concepts over ICD-10 (1989) and integrate new features such as richer descriptions of diseases/conditions, the tracking of disease severity and progression, and disease clustering. This new version is poised to catalyze the advancement of health and medical sciences, the identification of optimal clinical care pathways, and evidence-based decision-making. Research is required to explore and understand the extensive ICD-11 adoption challenges faced by healthcare systems worldwide, and to develop the methods, technologies and approaches needed to overcome these challenges. This is the goal of the proposed research program. Dr. Hude Quan is the Director of the WHO Collaborating Centre in Classification, Terminology and Standards at the University of Calgary and a world leader in ICD health data science and methodology. CIHR funding will enable global ICD-11 preparedness and adoption, and advance Canadian and global health information research and practice. Thomson Reuters has identified him as one of the world's most highly cited researchers. Collaborators include the WHO, Health Canada, the Public Health Agency of Canada, Statistics Canada and the Canadian Institute for Health Information.

column36: Hematopoietic stem cell aging
column37: Blood stem cells create all the cells in the circulating blood system, and are also able to generate new stem cells. As an individual gets older, their blood stem cells do not replenish themselves as well. The stem cells also tend to become more of one type of white blood cell while not producing as many immune cells. This combination leads to more inflammation and inflammation-related diseases and less ability to fight infections. microRNAs are small molecules that regulate the function of genes. A single microRNA can regulate the function of many genes. We have found that one of these microRNAs, called miR-146a, decreases with age. Loss of miR-146a results in blood stem cells that do not function as well and resemble the aging stem cell. In part this is because miR-146a regulates genes that drive inflammation. Loss of this microRNA results in continued low level inflammation that we predict results in aging. In this grant, we will examine how miR-146a affects blood stem cell aging with a focus on the inflammatory molecules that it regulates in both mouse and human models. We will also determine whether we can reverse the poor function of old blood stem cells by replenishing miR-146a or blocking inflammation. Because the blood system produces many inflammation-related cells and molecules, and because blood travels all over the body, it is likely that by reversing the aging of blood stem cells that we might also help to reduce the impact of aging on other systems such as the heart and brain.

column37: Over the past 50 years, care for children born with heart defects or congenital heart disease (CHD) has focused on surgical repair with unquestionable success. Although heart surgery enables >95% of children to survive to adulthood, many will experience a slow decline in heart function. Heart failure is now the leading cause of death in the CHD population affecting patients at a much younger age than their counterparts with acquired heart disease. Failure of the right heart pumping chamber (the right ventricle or RV) is a recurring theme in long-term outcome studies in CHD and is an important driver of HF. In contrast to the left heart pumping chamber (the left ventricle or [LV]), contemporary management guidelines highlight the absence of evidence to support medical therapy for right heart failure. In the absence of recognized treatments to address right heart failure, there is a desperate need to answer the following: (1) What causes scarring of the right heart muscle? (2) Can we identify new drugs to treat scarring of the right heart muscle? (3) Can we improve our prediction tools (serum and imaging biomarkers) to identify those at risk of deterioration secondary to right heart muscle scarring? (4) Do novel therapies for CHD apply to other forms of acquired RV failure? In this study, we address each of these critical questions through focused study of right heart failure in adults with extreme heart dilation due to a leaking pulmonary valve in the setting of a CHD defect called "tetralogy of Fallot". We anticipate that early detection of heart muscle scarring and early treatment may transform care through prevention of late right heart failure. Finally, new insights into the diagnosis and therapy of right heart failure to emerge from this study may inform care for other populations with non-congenital forms of right or left heart dysfunction.

column36: Elucidating the role of CD33 in regulating microglia
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative disease. Despite the enormous efforts, we still do not understand the origins of AD. This lack of knowledge translates to the inability to effectively treat patients suffering from the plethora of pathologies associated with the disease, let alone a preventative. Keys to better understanding AD and developing new treatment strategies may lie in genetic factors that correlate with AD-susceptibility, which have much to teach us about brain homeostasis. Of particular interest are genetic factors related to genes expressed in immune cells of the brain called microglia. Microglia play many roles in the brain with the most well characterized being the removal of unwanted matter. This removal is an orchestrated event with specific receptors on microglia that guide this process known as phagocytosis. Curiously, several of the recently-emerging genetic factors correlating with AD-susceptibility are receptors in microglia that regulate phagocytosis. Accordingly, it has been proposed that an altered phagocytic ability by microglia could be a key element in AD-susceptibility. However, due to the complex role(s) played by microglia in AD, there are still many unanswered questions. One of the aforementioned genetic factors is CD33, a receptor on microglia that is a sugar-binding lectin. Two different versions (alleles) of CD33 are present in the human population with the rare allele correlating with protection from AD. It is of great interest to discover precisely how this protective controls microglia compared to the common risk allele of CD33. This project aims to elucidates the roles for these CD33 alleles by studying them in the context of a mouse model of AD and their divergent abilities to regulate microglia.

column36: Effects of Cannabidiol on Cellular and Mitochondrial Metabolism: Implications for the Epileptic Brain
column37: Public and scientific interest in marijuana (or cannabis)-derived products for treatment resistant epilepsy has increased exponentially in recent years. Specifically, cannabidiol (CBD) has been used by a growing number of patients in mostly unregulated ways due to immediate accessibility of commercial artisanal forms. Recent clinical studies indicate that pharmaceutical grade CBD is effective in pediatric patients with treatment-resistant epilepsy (i.e., those with Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes), but how this compound works remains a mystery. Given the mounting use of CBD and other cannabinoids, it is vitally important to understand the mechanisms of action, as this knowledge is necessary for uncovering new medications with greater clinical efficacy and improved tolerability. Recently, we have identified a novel target inside brain mitochondria (the specialized structures that generate energy molecules) that is affected directly by CBD. Specifically, we found that CBD blocks a chloride channel on the inner membrane of mitochondria, and that this action affects the metabolic function of mitochondria as well as the neuron itself. The overall goal of our research project is to study the effects of CBD on the mitochondrial chloride channel, and to determine whether this action contributes to seizure control in two animal models of epilepsy (one that models Dravet syndrome). Further, we will examine the effects of CBD on various aspects of cellular metabolism and mitochondrial function, and in validated tests of cognition (learning/memory) and behavior. Importantly, these experiments are designed to establish safe and effective dose and concentration ranges for CBD. Our team possesses the necessary expertise in molecular neuropharmacology to successfully implement the proposed studies. With the explosive growth of cannabis and cannabinoid use, especially in Canada, the research described herein is both timely and clinically relevant.

column36: Role of CD109 in regulating cellular signaling and responses in skin and oral squamous cell carcinoma cells
column37: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is one of the most prevalent types of malignancy and its incidence continues to increase globally. The fatal consequences of cancer are due to the spreading (metastasis) of cancer cells from the original tumor site to other organs of the body. Despite intensive research efforts, there has been limited success in blocking recurrence and metastasis that occurs in a significant proportion of these patients. Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) is a growth factor that is important for normal development and maintenance of healthy tissues. TGF-beta normally acts as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting the growth of cells but switches to a tumor promoter during cancer progression by making cells more invasive and metastatic. We have identified a cell surface protein named CD109 and found that it acts as a strong inhibitor of TGF-beta actions. Emerging evidence indicates that CD109 levels are increased in skin and oral SCC, and premalignant lesions in the oral cavity that highly express CD109 show a greater risk to progress to SCC. In addition, studies indicate that CD109 not only inhibits TGF-beta but may also activate other tumor promoting (oncogenic) pathways including those initiated by proteins known as EGFR and Jak/Stat3. The proposed research will determine whether CD109 promotes skin and oral SCC progression and metastasis in experimental models and establish the mechanisms that mediate the CD109's actions. The findings from the proposed studies is anticipated to lead to the development of novel CD109-based molecules for the treatment of skin and oral SCC.

column36: Short, medium, and long term effectiveness of interdisciplinary teams and other primary care reforms in Ontario
column37: Better access to primary care results in better patient health, fewer visits to emergency departments, and fewer hospital stays leading to lower health system costs. Therefore, health care policy makers across the country and internationally have focused on improving quality and increasing patient access to primary care in order to achieve these outcomes. In Canada, Ontario has implemented the greatest number of changes to primary care delivery but the models they introduced were focused on two key areas: how physicians are paid and the introduction of multidisciplinary teams. Despite more than doubling spending on primary care between 2006 and 2009 to accommodate these changes, there is only very limited evidence telling us whether they have translated into better health or cost savings. The goal of this project is to study the short, medium, and long term effectiveness of the models that were introduced in Ontario over the last 15 years. We are looking to determine which models resulted in changes to the cost of delivering primary care and the total cost of caring for each patient. Multi-disciplinary teams were introduced in part to offload some of the work done by physicians and give that work to other practitioners, so we will also determine whether family physicians were able to care for more patients because of this. Finally, we will also compare the different models of primary care for health outcomes (mortality) and health service utilization (emergency department visits and hospitalizations). Many other provinces are now considering or piloting reforms similar to the ones introduced in Ontario. The results of this study will help Ontario to plan the future of their primary care, and will help other provinces choose the most cost effective changes to introduce.

column36: Extracellular vesicle-based therapy for atrial fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent and persistent heart rhythm disorder worldwide. AF occurs when electrical coordination of the top two chambers of the heart (the atria) becomes disorganized and chaotic. AF afflicts almost 350,000 Canadians and accounts for over 200,000 hospitalizations every year. In 80% of patients, AF significantly impacts daily quality of life causing dizziness, palpitations and syncope. Although not life threatening itself, AF increases the risk of blood clots and the risk of debilitating stroke by five fold. Treatment strategies for AF are limited. Drug therapy is non-specific, often ineffective with significant side effects. While catheter ablation has received much attention, success rates varies and this invasive approach has the potential for rare, but serious, complications. These realities rationalize a new focus on developing novel biological therapies to prevent AF and reverse the biological causes of AF. In this study, we explore the ability of cardioprotective extracellular vesicles to reduce atrial fibrosis causative for AF. Extracelullar vesicles are small membrane-bound signaling "packets" secreted by all cells. Extracelullar vesicles from blood and heart stem cells reduce scar sizes after heart attacks. Our preliminary data has shown extracelullar vesicles also reduce scar formation in the atria of the heart by re-programming connective tissue cells (fibroblasts) to a pro-healing, non-scar, fate. The ability of extracelullar vesicles to reduce atrial fibrillation will be investigated using our rat model of atrial fibrillation to see if injecting extracelullar vesicles can prevent the development of AF. If successful, this study will provide a new way to reduce AF beyond simply destroying tissue (ablation) or imperfect suppression using potentially toxic drugs.

column36: Preventing the progression of Alzheimer's disease pathology by targeting the effects of lifestyle factors and personality traits.
column37: There are over half a million Canadians living with dementia, the leading cause being Alzheimer's disease (AD). Amyloid and tau are the pathological hallmarks of AD. They start to accumulate between one and two decades before memory impairment. We know that the apolipoprotein (APOE) 4 allele, the main genetic risk factor for AD, influences amyloid and tau accumulation. It is unclear if other factors, such as lifestyle factors (e.g. education and cognitive activity) or personality traits (e.g. optimism and neuroticism), can also modify amyloid and tau accumulation and/or if these factors can buffer the deleterious effect of APOE4 on AD pathology accumulation. Lifestyle and personality traits are of interest because they are modifiable (particularly lifestyle) and, therefore, could be prime targets for prevention efforts. The first objective of this proposal is to determine the lifestyle factors and personality traits that are associated with amyloid and tau burden in cognitively normal older adults at risk of developing AD dementia. The second objective is to determine if some lifestyle/personality factors can counteract the negative effects of APOE4 on AD pathology accumulation. Finally, we want to test if the lifestyle/personality factors can delay the clinical onset of the disease by buffering the negative impact of AD pathology on cognition. Finally, we will test if the factors influencing AD pathology differ between men and women, since we know that women are at increased risk of developing AD dementia. This work will be done in collaboration with the PREVENT-AD, a cohort of almost 400 cognitively normal or very mildly impaired older adults who have a parental history of AD-like dementia. It will focus on 120 individuals that did a brain scan to quantify amyloid and tau in vivo. This multidisciplinary study will give insights about new, sex-specific prevention strategies.

column36: Reversal of Adipose Fibrosis by Intermittent Fasting and VEGF
column37: White fat plays an important role in energy balance and metabolic health. In response to diet and temperature, white fat undergoes rapid remodelling, such as "browning" in order to consume more energy. This remodeling is critical to adapt to different nutritional and environmental conditions. In obese and aged fat, unhealthy remodeling results in inflammation, low oxygen supply, and tissue stiffness (fibrosis). This process, called fat fibrosis, is directly linked with age-associated metabolic disorders, such as fatty liver disease and type 2 diabetes. Unfortunately, there are no promising therapies available for this crucial condition. Thus, understanding the fundamentals of fat fibrotic process is very important to develop proper therapeutic and preventive measures. Our research previously reported that intermittent fasting - a periodic diet restriction regimen - improves metabolism by promoting healthy fat remodelling, such as browning of white fat, via production of fat-derived vascular endothelial growth factor (fat-VEGF). Recently, our group discovered that aged fat contains unhealthy fat stem cells, which could be the source of fat fibrosis. Interestingly, our preliminary study found that intermittent fasting can prevent and even reverse this unhealthy remodelling of the fat tissue, generating a good and healthy fat, likely through the action of fat-VEGF. In this research proposal, we will study the pathway of how intermittent fasting can halt unhealthy fat remodelling, and whether these effects are mediated through fat-VEGF's action on fat stem cells. We will use genetically modified mouse models, advanced molecular visualization techniques, gene expression assays and single cell analysis systems. Our study will shed light on the potential implication of dietary intervention and fat-VEGF for the treatment and prevention of abnormal fat remodelling associated with age-related obesity and metabolic diseases.

column36: Randomized comparison of the Outcome of single versus Multiple Arterial grafts: ROMA Trial - The Definitive Phase
column37: Coronary artery bypass surgery is an operation to improve the circulation of the heart where healthy blood vessels from the patients are used to go around blockages caused by hardening of the arteries, like a detour (bypass). Leg veins (saphenous veins) are used for most of the bypasses. Survival, prevention of further heart attacks and relief of angina are improved following coronary surgery when a chest wall artery (left internal thoracic artery) is used for one of the bypasses rather than using leg veins for all the bypasses. This is the most commonly performed coronary bypass operation. It has also been assumed that patients with an otherwise long anticipated life expectancy who receive a second chest wall artery (right internal thoracic artery) or an artery from the arm (radial artery) have better cardiac outcomes than following the standard operation. Yet this viewpoint is largely based on scientifically weak evidence, rather than randomized clinical trials. ROMA is an international, multicentre randomized clinical trial of 4300 patients with extended follow-up designed to address whether the use of two or more bypass grafts using arteries from the chest wall or the arm improves outcomes compared to the standard operation late after coronary surgery. The pilot phase of the study of 430 patients is currently underway with CIHR funding to determine the viability of the project prior to commitment to the full study. As of July 31, 2018, 380 patients have been enrolled - we predict that the pilot phase will be completed in October 2018. The pilot phase is on target in terms of the timelines and the stated pilot phase objectives and strongly supports the viability of the project. This submission is to fund the definitive phase of the study, i.e. complete the total study enrollment and extend the patient follow-up (up to 7 years) to determine with confidence if the multiple arterial grafting approach is better for patients.

column37: Mechanical ventilation is the most common form of life support and is required by most patients who receive treatment in intensive care units. Although mechanical ventilation is essential in such situations, it can induce weakness of the respiratory muscles which may lead to prolonged dependence on the ventilator. Prolonged dependence on mechanical ventilation is associated with worse patient outcomes and high cost to the healthcare system. Pressure support ventilation (PSV) is the most frequently used mode of ventilation for assisting breathing of patients during the recovery phase of acute respiratory failure. Proportional assist ventilation (PAV) is a newer method of mechanical ventilation which delivers assistance to breathe in proportion to the patient's effort. This method may preserve respiratory muscle function while supporting the patient's need for respiratory assistance. Several studies have shown short term advantages of PAV over PSV, including improved patient-ventilator synchronization, improved adaptability to changes in patient effort, and improved sleep quality. There are no studies showing superiority of either method for clinically important outcomes. In our study, we will compare PAV to PSV using a randomized controlled trial. Our study is designed to demonstrate that PAV results in a reduction of time on mechanical ventilation of at least 1.5 days. This will be an important result for patients and potentially produce large cost savings for the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Pathophysiology and treatment of adult somnambulism
column37: Despite almost 5 decades of clinical and laboratory investigations of sleep disorders, relatively little is known about the mechanisms which give rise to sleepwalking (somnambulism) and even less about how to effectively treat the disorder. Sleepwalking occurs in 4% to 17% of children and is far more common in adults (approximately 4%) than commonly acknowledged. Patients suffering from this sleep disorder often consult due to a history of aggressive and/or injurious behaviour during sleep. In a significant number of cases, patients report having suffered serious injuries (e.g., contusions, fractures to limbs, rib cage, multiple lacerations) and/or having attacked a bed partner during an episode. Establishing a correct diagnosis and adequately treating sleepwalking is vital for the patient's health as well as in light of the growing number of medico-legal cases of sleep-related violence. In most centers, the benzodiazepinic drug clonazepam is used for treatment. A significant proportion of clinicians, however, are reluctant to prescribe daily doses of benzodiazepines over long periods of time due to concerns about drug habituation and potentially harmful consequences of long-term usage. Moreover, many sleepwalkers do not respond to this medication or present side effects. Numerous descriptive studies suggest that hypnosis can be effective in the long-term management of sleepwalking. The first aim of the proposed research is to evaluate the treatment effects of hypnosis on sleepwalking frequency and intensity. A second aim of the proposed research is to elucidate our understanding of sleepwalking by recording sleepwalkers' brain activity during sleep both before and after a period sleep deprivation. Taken together, these studies should a) lead us to a better understanding of why some people suffer from sleepwalking, b) help identify neurobiological markers of the disorder, and c) guide future clinical treatments.

column36: Our Counts, Our Future: Building Applied and Self-Determined First Nations, Inuit and Metis Health and Well-Being Information Systems in Urban Homelands
column37: First Nations, Inuit, and Metis (FNIM) peoples living in Canadian cities are not being "counted in". The systems that collect information about population size, health, illness, healthcare use, and living conditions either exclude or don't correctly recognize Indigenous peoples living in cities. This is a big problem since the majority of Indigenous peoples now live in cities and Indigenous peoples experience a high burden health and social challenges that doesn't improve with urban residence. A new approach to gathering FNIM health information in cities is needed. The goal of this research program is to develop, share, test and apply new models and methods to gather this information. We will do this by working together with FNIM and allied health and health information organizations at the national, regional, and city levels. We will also work to train more people who have advanced skills to do this work. Working together at a national level we will develop and share new models and standards for urban FNIM health information. At the regional level we will design and test training workshops. At the city level we will continue to build better urban FNIM datasets using some specialized methods we have developed over the past 10 years. These methods use social networks to find FNIM peoples living in cities who are otherwise hidden in the regular information systems. In this research program we will test out these methods in Winnipeg, which will be the first time that we have tested them outside of Ontario. To do this work we have gathered together a team of over 50 FNIM organizational partners and researchers from across Canada and around the world. This research program has the potential to change the way that FNIM living in cities are counted, ensuring that in the future every FNIM person is counted in, regardless of where they live. This new information will in turn improve health services for FNIM in cities, making them more effective and efficient.

column36: BRD4 Inhibition in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: a Phase 2 Clinical Trial
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive condition characterized by the chronic elevation of pulmonary artery (PA) pressure leading to failure of the heart. In spite of recent advances in approved therapies, PAH remains a serious disease with significant mortality. In contrast to the earlier belief that contraction of pulmonary vessels played a key role in PAH, it is now established that excessive proliferation of the cells within the pulmonary artery wall is a pivotal component of pulmonary vascular obliteration, a currently irreversible feature of PAH for which available pharmacotherapies have no/limited efficacy. In recent years, it has become increasingly appreciated that, in addition to rare mutations in genes, changes in their expression in the absence of changes in their structure (i.e. epigenetics) largely contributes to this phenomenon in PAH. Changes in gene expression influence numerous functions of the cells. We recently documented that by regulating genes known to be deregulated in PAH, Bromodomain-containing Protein-4 (BRD4) largely contributes to excessive cell proliferation and pulmonary vascular obliteration in PAH. More importantly, we observed that the pharmacological inhibition of BRD4, reverses PAH in human cells and animal models of PAH. Very recently, apabetalone, an orally available BRD4inhibitor, was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in treating cancers vascular cell proliferation leading to other types of vascular obliteration such as coronary artery disease. The time is thus right to translate our findings in human PAH. This proposal addresses a very novel and promising therapeutic avenue to treat and is one of the first steps of personalized medicine in PAH. We propose an early phase clinical trial to determine whether: BRD4 inhibition with apabetalone is safe and effective and; patients' characteristics can predict response to therapy in adult patients with symptomatic PAH.

column36: DNA Methylation and Mediation of Risk Factors for Chronic Facial Pain
column37: About 5 to 10% of Canadians live with chronic pain in their mouth, jaws and face (called orofacial pain) caused by temporomandibular disorder (or TMD, meaning issues with your jaw or the muscles that control it). TMD's cause is unknown and there are no specific molecular markers for TMD to help diagnose, predict or treat it. While TMD has some inherited genetic components that are passed on through families, how are genes work can be modulated by environmental factors such as exposure to stress, inflammation, diet, and medication. One way that environmental factors alter how our genes work is by adding 'marks' to the DNA through a process called methylation. We will study blood and tissue samples provided by healthy people and people with TMD, as well as people with other chronic pain conditions. All samples will be examined for genome-wide methylation patterns. These studies will allow us to identify how methylation patterns affect TMD, who will get TMD and who will not, and whose TMD will persist over time. In addition, by comparing to samples from other types of chronic pain, we will identify methylation patterns in people that are common to TMD and other chronic pain conditions. Ultimately this will help us understand more about how the environment affects a person's genetics in terms of their risk of TMD and how better to predict, diagnose, and ultimately treat or prevent painful TMD.

column36: Targeting the epigenetic state of refractory and relapsing acute myeloid leukemia
column37: In 2013, according to the Canadian Cancer Society, 1315 patients in Canada were diagnosed with the blood cancer acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and 1047 died of the disease. AML is the most common adult blood cancer and one of the most deadly forms of cancer. Unfortunately, these numbers have not changed much in the last 30 plus years. This is due primarily because only minor changes to therapy have occurred over this time period. About 40 year ago, an innovative chemotherapy known as induction therapy was introduced as the frontline treatment for AML patients. While some modest improvements have been made to induction therapy, new innovative therapeutic approaches are necessary to make substantive improvements to the survival of AML patients. In contrast to the "one size fits all" induction therapy, we propose to implement a "precision medicine" strategy to treat AML patients. To implement precision medicine in AML, we need to identify different sub-classes of AML, identify which patients fit a particular subclass, develop targeted therapies for these sub-classes of AML and treat the patients accordingly. In this proposal, we will focus on the "epigenetic state" of AML because these states can be reversed. Recently, we demonstrated in mice that we can reverse the epigenetic state of a group of AML patients who are resistant to induction therapy. This group of patients are known as "refractory" AML patients. In this proposal, we aim to determine how different drugs reverse the epigenetic state of this group of refractory AML patients and perform additional experiments to enable us to file for a precision medicine clinical trial in this group of AML patients. We will also develop the tools to treat other groups of refractory and relapse AML patients. These tools include methods to identify these patients at diagnosis and novel drugs to treat these normally drug resistant AML cells.

column36: MGMT promoter methylated breast cancer: An opportunity for a targeted treatment with alkylating agent temozolomide in combination with existing breast cancer therapeutics.
column37: Breast cancer (BC) is responsible for 25% of all female cancer diagnoses annually, affects 1 in 8 women, and is the 2nd leading cause of cancer death among Canadian women. Temozolomide (TMZ) is a well-tolerated oral chemotherapy used to treat brain cancers and its efficacy is linked to down regulation of a protein named MGMT. MGMT is involved in the the repair of DNA damage and is expressed in normal human cells; however, in cancer cells the modification (methylation) of the MGMT gene promoter leads to down regulation of the MGMT protein. MGMT when present, repairs the damage caused by TMZ promoting cancer survival and when absent allows cellular death. Down regulation of MGMT has been consistently noted in certain subtypes of BC, and we hypothesize that TMZ may be a novel, targeted, therapeutic option that can be combined with other DNA targeting therapies such as PARP inhibition in patients whose tumors apriori fail to express MGMT.

column37: Type 2 diabetes and obesity disproportionately affect Indigenous children in Canada. During the last 2 years as a Pathways 2 Implementation Research Team we expanded from 5 communities in Manitoba and to 13 communities across 4 provinces in Canada. Using a participatory action model, guided by the teachings of elders, knowledge keepers and youth on our team, we will build on the successes of the past 2 years to (1) explore a novel pathway through which IYMP can reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes in youth, through the Indigenous concept of Mino-pimatisiwin/bimaadiziwin "living in a god way", (2) deepen the reach of IYMP within existing communities, (3) explore relational models of rippling IYMP to new communities, and (4) study the process of moving IYMP from a university-based program to a sustainable community-led organization. This information will provide information and infrastructure to support rippling of other wellness promoting community-based programs across Canada.

column37: Since 1990, the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network (CTN) has supported a thriving community of researchers and stakeholders who collaborate to produce impactful clinical research in HIV. Seen through the lens of the World Health Organization's 'cascade of care', the CTN recognizes that HIV prevention, testing, ART initiation, adherence and treatment success are all influenced by several factors such as social stigma, discrimination and other barriers. These priorities are underpinned by the prospect for a cure and the quest to understand and eliminate viral reservoirs. The CTN proposes a renewed scientific vision for 2019-2024 through a National and Strategic Research Agenda for HIV research in Canada. column36: IMPACTT: A Microbiome Research Core based on Integrated Microbiome Platforms for Advancing Causation Testing and Translation
column37: Our body surfaces, including the gut, mouth, skin, and lung are colonized by trillions of microbes. This colonization is a dynamic process that begins primarily at birth and is heavily influenced by environmental factors, including mode of birth, diet, antibiotic use, hygiene and health status. Alterations in microbial communities are associated with a number of diseases, such as allergy, autoimmunity, autism, and obesity. However, association is not the same as causation. Changes in the microbiome could lead to disease, occur as a result of disease, or both. Therefore, researchers must now clearly define microbial function and identify the molecular mechanisms by which the microbiome interacts with the human host to influence health. Such functional studies will facilitate the design of new approaches for disease treatment and prevention. We will establish a Microbiome Research Core based on Integrated Microbiome Platforms for Advancing Causation Testing and Translation (IMPACTT). IMPACTT is a multi-centre collaboration to provide expertise and sharing of resources to foster and standardize microbiome research across Canada. The new gnotobiotic facility at the University of Calgary will form the basis for the study of complex functional interactions between the microbiome and the host. It will allow for precise control of all colonizing microbes to identify mechanistic links between the microbiome and the host. IMPACTT will also facilitate microbiome studies in human cohorts by providing expertise for study design, sample collection, and computational analysis. IMPACTT will establish and maintain a large repository of microbes, with genetic and metabolic information, available to microbiome researchers across Canada to enable functional microbiome studies. Finally, we will also develop a platform to discover links between microbial genes, proteins, and metabolism with microbial function, and then further link this to human health and disease.

Dr. Cygler will examine roles of effectors in bacterial infections. Iron-Sulfur cofactors are essential components of many cellular proteins. column36: Antibiotic Treatment of Staphylococcus aureus in Stable Patients with CF (ASAP-CF)
column37: Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is among the most common life-limiting genetic disorders in Canada, with more than 4000 people living with this disease. The primary cause of death in CF is respiratory failure from chronic infection of the lung. In CF care, it is routine practice to monitor the sputum for bacterial infection. The most common bacterium isolated in the airways of children with CF is methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Antibiotics are a mainstay of treatment in CF, and are of clear benefit when people with CF have increased pulmonary symptoms (cough, increased sputum etc). However, there is controversy in the CF community over whether we should treat people who are clinically well, but have bacteria in their airways. Part of this uncertainty has arisen from the fact that traditional pulmonary function measures are often not sensitive enough to detect subtle improvements in lung function following treatment in mild CF lung disease. The forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) is the most commonly used pulmonary function test in CF but is a poor marker of early lung disease. The lung clearance index (LCI) is a new marker that has been shown to be a more sensitive measure of early CF lung disease. In this study, we will use LCI and other outcomes measures to assess the effect of antibiotic treatment in clinically stable children with CF who have MSSA growing in their sputum. Question: Does treatment with three weeks of oral cephalexin (a common antibiotic used in CF care) result in an improvement in the lung function of children with CF who are symptomatically stable, but have MSSA growing in their sputum? Study Design: This is a randomised trial, comparing placebo to cephalexin. Children will receive a blinded medication for 3 weeks. We will use LCI, FEV1 and clinical symptoms to measure response. Hypothesis: Compared to placebo, a 3 week course of cepahalexin will result in an improvement in lung function in this population.

column37: This research involves Indigenous Peoples. Emerging infectious diseases represent an increasing threat to wildlife and to the people who depend on wildlife for food security, economic opportunity, and cultural practices. However, the role of disease in wildlife declines can be difficult to identify because health surveillance of wildlife populations is challenging and the impact of disease can be overshadowed by the cumulative effects of multiple stressors. In the Arctic, climate change is facilitating the emergence and spread of novel parasites while putting stress on wildlife that are adapted to a cold climate. Wildlife health surveillance in such a vast and remote area is a huge challenge, making timely detection of disease and population impacts an impossibility for scientists. However, a wealth of knowledge exists in local communities that are intimately connected to the land through a long and continuous history of subsistence use of natural resources. Connecting with local and Indigenous knowledge on wildlife health can address data gaps, while simultaneously increasing local relevance of scientific research and promoting co-management of natural resources. This project will elucidate how disease may act synergistically with other stressors to contribute to wildlife declines by developing and integrating ecological models with scientific, local, and Indigenous knowledge on wildlife health and abundance. I will focus on caribou, which are a highly valued species in Canada, particularly for Indigenous cultures, but have experienced widespread declines in recent decades. The outcomes will provide new theory in wildlife disease ecology, address the knowledge gap around how health interacts with other stressors to influence caribou population dynamics, and guide effective conservation and co-management efforts for caribou.

column36: Reducing the burden of antimicrobial resistance via rapid diagnosis of urinary tract infections
column37: Antibiotics are a critical part of modern medicine. In addition to treating infections, they are necessary for many medical procedures including: joint replacement, organ transplant, and some types of cancer therapy. Unfortunately, bacteria are developing resistance to all of our antibiotics. If we do not stop this problem, Canadian life expectancy will eventually be 20 years shorter. This project will help preserve our antibiotics by eliminating one source of antibiotic resistance: slow diagnostic tests for urinary tract infections. Currently, it takes 2-4 days for labs to identify bacteria and find which drug will be most effective. Since waiting this long to treat infections poses a serious health risk, clinicians must prescribe drugs using their best guess as to which pathogen is causing an infection. This circumstance encourages the overuse of antibiotics-up to half of all antibiotic prescriptions have no benefit. Fortunately, we have found a promising solution. Our MicroUDxTM system can detect bacteria in urine and find the best antibiotic in under 4 hours. This is fast enough that clinicians can wait for laboratory test results to help guide their prescriptions. The best antibiotic therapy can then be called in to the patient's pharmacy the same day. This solution will significantly reduce the inappropriate use of antibiotics and will extend the service life of our existing drugs. In addition, the MicroUDxTM will save thousands of people who are currently being given the wrong drug. These patients are at a much higher risk of developing urosepsis, a life-threatening condition that can occur if infections are not treated quickly. Thus, the MicroUDxTM is an exciting step forward because it fights antibiotic resistant organisms and prevents people from dying as a result of slow diagnostics. This grant provides the critical support for transitioning this diagnostic technology into the real world.
