column36: The Cortical Activation of Dynamic Balance Recovery Post-stroke using fNIRS
column37: Effectiveness of stroke rehabilitation is important; there are about 62,000 strokes in Canada every year and more than 400,000 people living with long-term disability from stroke(1). These numbers are expected to double in the next 20 years(1). Stroke survivors say that regaining walking ability is a top priority; but, reduced balance often limits community levels of mobility(2). Today's stroke rehabilitation treatment decisions are guided by observing physical limitations to balance and walking, and not by brain measures. Differences in how much balance recovery someone achieves likely stems from the brain's ability to recover after stroke. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is an imaging technology that can help us understand how the brain recovers balance after stroke, and may help identify those people who will benefit from an exercise intervention. fNIRS is special in that it can be used while people are moving in tasks like standing and balancing. At this point, it is not known whether a recording with fNIRS can give us a brain activity profile that can predict who will improve their balance, prior to starting an exercise intervention. So, the goals of our randomized clinical trial, is to test which regions of the brain and how they interact, produce high levels of balance recovery with the Fitness And Mobility Exercise (FAME) program for stroke(3). If we can find a fNIRS brain activity profile, instead of treating patients based on physical limitations, we will identify which individuals benefit from an exercise program like FAME. Given that stroke damages the brain, involving brain measures to guide treatment decisions could increase effectiveness of stroke rehabilitation. column36: The cellular ecosystem of Hodgkin lymphoma: novel insight through single cell genomics and imaging mass cytometry
column37: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is a cancer derived from white blood cells and typically occurs in young adults under the age of 30. Despite the fact that most patients can be cured with chemotherapy, 30% still experience relapse and eventually succumb to their disease. There is now increasing evidence that not only tumour cells, but also normal immune cells surrounding them ("tumour microenvironment, TME"), are of importance for tumour development and growth. Cancer cells influence the composition of their TME in many ways, resulting in a disabled immune response. Our project aims to reveal how changes in the genetic material of the tumour cells associate with the spatial arrangement and functional properties of immune cells in the TME. We propose to comprehensively characterize patients' biopsies using two novel technologies from the respective fields of cancer genomics and cancer imaging: Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) and single cell sequencing (scRNAseq and scWGS). IMC takes advantage of detecting and visualizing over 40 different protein markers to label cell types at the same time in the spatial context. Single cell genomics uncovers changes in the genetic material of cancer cells on the individual cell level. Our proposed studies will bring to bear, for the first time, single cell sequencing techniques to study cHL - allowing direct measurement of how genomic alterations in the malignant cells of cHL influence the composition and architecture of the TME. Our study will change the current paradigm of biological studies in cHL as we will establish comprehensive and integrative views on how different cell types in the cancer interact and form cellular 'ecosystems'. Our approach and technical solutions will generate new knowledge that will be the foundation for better diagnostic testing. Moreover, it will lead to novel and refined immunotherapies that alter anti-tumour immune responses and result in higher cure rates and less toxic treatments for patients.

column36: Designing Highly Porous Drug-Impregnated Polymer Scaffolds Using Pressurized Gas Expanded Liquids for the Treatment of Lung Fibrosis and Wound Infections
column37: Highly porous materials offer significant advantages in many biomedical applications based on their extremely high surface areas. In particular, for the delivery of drugs with low water solubility, the high surface area provided by highly porous scaffolds offers unique opportunities for enhancing drug loading thus improving the efficacy of drug therapy. However, most strategies used to prepare such scaffolds are extremely slow and/or require the use of solvents or other additives that can cause issues when the material is used in the body. Our knowledge user Ceapro (a Edmonton-based biotechnology company) has recently developed a high-throughput and rapid processing technology called pressurized gas expanded liquids (PGX) that overcomes these challenges in addition to offering exceptional control over both the macroscopic size of the materials generated (from large continuous networks to microscale particles) as well as the size of the internal pores. We have also, in partnership, developed methods to (1) convert these biopolymer networks to hydrogels by post-processing the polymer scaffolds and/or performing gelation and PGX processing simultaneously and (2) load multiple drugs via a simple and residual solvent-free process. In this proposed project, we aim to exploit these advantages to address key challenges in treating lung fibrosis and infected wounds. For lung fibrosis, the potential to create a highly porous microparticle delivery vehicles loaded with drug would improve the efficacy of inhalation-based therapy; in addition, one of the key biopolymers produced by Ceapro (beta-glucan) provides desirable cell targeting effects. For wound healing, the capacity of the scaffolds to absorb exudate and load tunable mixtures of drugs offers benefits for delivering synergistic drug combinations to treat antibiotic-resistant infections. Together, this work will leverage a patented Canadian technology (PGX) to address key and emerging health challenges for Canadians.

column36: Early integration of palliative care in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
column37: Research has shown that early palliative care (PC) is not only associated with improved quality of life (QOL) but also with improved survival in some patients with cancer. Palliative care can provide an additional layer of support to patients and caregivers and help patients live as well as they can for as long as they can. In spite of the proven benefits of the integration of PC in oncology, it has been well established that patients with blood cancers and those undergoing bone marrow or blood stem cell transplant do not routinely receive PC and that end-of-life quality measures are typically worse in patients with blood cancers compared to those with solid tumours. Bone marrow and blood stem cell transplantation are associated with high symptom burden and the potential for serious complications, many of which may be persistent and distressing to patients and their family caregivers. There is an urgent need to proactively address suffering throughout bone marrow or blood stem cell transplant, even before treatment starts, so that patients and caregivers are not inevitably waiting for symptoms to arise before they can be addressed and to optimize QOL for patients undergoing transplant and their caregivers. The purpose of this study is to investigate the impact of early PC integration, in the outpatient setting, for patients undergoing bone marrow or blood stem cell transplantation. Patients and their caregivers will meet with a palliative care nurse practitioner prior to their transplant as well as at various time points following transplant. Validated questionnaires will be utilized to assess patients' symptoms, quality of life, distress and mood; caregivers will also be asked to complete validated questionnaires to assess quality of life, distress and mood. It is hoped that the integration of PC will help improve the experience of bone marrow or blood stem cell transplantation for patients as well as for their caregivers.

column36: A multimodal seizure detection artificial intelligence-based smart wear
column37: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological condition that affects as many as 1 in every 100 Canadians. With the ageing of the population, the prevalence and incidence of epilepsy among the elderly is greater than any other age group due to the increasing number brain insults. The first line of treatment consists of long-term drug therapy but more than a third of patients are said to be drug-resistant and continue to suffer from disabling seizures. Due to their unpredictable nature, uncontrolled seizures represent a major personal handicap and source of worriment for patients (risks of injury and death). In addition, persistent seizures constitute a considerable public health burden due to high use of health care resources, high number of disability days or unemployment, and low annual income. For these patients, accurate and rapid detection of seizures could significantly improve their care. Indeed, a system capable of detecting seizures could alert family members, caretakers or medical personnel to intervene in a timely fashion to limit the risk of injuries and death. Hence, the main objective of this project is to develop a user-friendly artificial intelligence-based seizure detection system based on non-invasive multimodal physiological signals obtained through smart wearable devices. Social, ethical, environmental, economic, and legal implications will be taken into account to ensure a smooth and rapid translation to patients with epilepsy. Potential applications are numerous for the benefit of patients (reducing anxiety and enhancing self- confidence), caretakers (evaluation and surveillance), and the healthcare system (reducing associated costs).

column36: Effects of Puberty Blockers on Brain Function in Adolescents Experiencing Gender Dysphoria: A Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
column37: Transgender adolescents strongly experience themselves as another gender. A popular explanation of brain development in transgender individuals is that it is shifted in the direction of the experienced gender rather than the birth gender. Transgender adolescents are often recommended puberty blockers (and potentially cross-sex hormones at a later stage) as part of their therapy. Puberty blockers delay the start of puberty, including development of secondary sex characteristics. Surprisingly, even though puberty blockers are widely used to help transgender adolescents go through gender transition, their impact on brain function during this critical stage of brain development is largely unknown. This project will use state-of-the-art functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) techniques and behavioural-cognitive experiments to examine transgender adolescents' brain function. First, brain function will be assessed prior to puberty blockers to test whether transgender adolescents' brain development is more similar to the experienced gender (Objective 1). Then, 6-10 months after starting puberty blocker treatment, their brain function will be re-examined to evaluate impacts of puberty blockers (Objective 2). At each time point, comparisons will be made to a group of non-transgender (i.e., "cisgender") adolescents, whose birth and experienced gender align. Given that adolescence is a time of rapid brain maturation that is influenced by hormones, this project will provide critical insights into transgender brain function and how it might be influenced by current standard-of-care hormonal treatments. This project's findings will elucidate important scientific and clinical insights into transgender development and the potential impacts of hormone therapy on brain function during treatment.

column37: Smoking is the leading cause of preventable illness and death in North America. Unfortunately, treating tobacco addiction is difficult. A majority of smokers who attempt to quit relapse, even when using smoking cessation aids. A better understanding of the factors that impact responses to smoking cessation aids may help with the development of more effective cessation strategies, which could help more people to quit. This could reduce the harms (eg. stroke, heart disease, cancer, death) of long-term smoking. The goal of this research is to examine how individual genetic and psychological differences influence laboratory measures of smoking relapse (ability to delay cigarette smoking and number of cigarettes smoked) following the use of two types of smoking cessation aids: nicotine replacement therapy and very low nicotine content cigarettes. Breaking down nicotine more quickly (higher NMR) is associated with heavier smoking and greater difficulty quitting. Psychological differences will be measured by giving participants different instructions about the nicotine content of smoking cessation aids. Previous research shows that being told that a product contains nicotine is effective in reducing cigarette craving, regardless of whether or not the product actually contains nicotine. This will be the first study to examine the combined impact of genetic and psychological differences on responses to smoking cessation aids. Results of this research could help show how biological and psychological factors impact the effectiveness of smoking cessation aids. This knowledge could help with development of new smoking cessation strategies that are more effective in helping people to quit.

column36: The role of Rap1 GTPase in coordinating cell adhesion and cytoskeletal rearrangement during epithelial wound healing
column37: Cells move collectively to drive many fundamental physiological and pathophysiological processes. For example, collective cell migration during development ensures the proper formation of different tissues. On the other hand, cancer metastasis occurs when cancer cells migrate together away from a tumour. In all cases, the mechanisms by which cells coordinate their movement are still unclear. Generally, cells interact with each other through cell adhesions, which link cells to each other and their environment, and the cytoskeleton, which provides structure and a means for generating contractility. In this project, I will use the Drosophila embryo to study collective cell migration during wound healing, which is a process conserved across species. Post-wounding, cells at the exposed edge simultaneously rearrange their adhesions and cytoskeleton to facilitate rapid, scarless repair, but it is unclear what mediates this response. I hypothesize that the GTPase Rap1 drives both reorganization of adhesions and the cytoskeleton to mount a collective cell response to wounding. Rap1 has been demonstrated in different contexts to respond to mechanical cues, affect distribution of cell adhesion proteins, and interact with cytoskeletal organizers. I will first track Rap1 localization and activity during wound repair and the effect of removing Rap1 on wound closure dynamics using timelapse confocal microscopy and image processing to determine the role of Rap1. Then, I will quantify the effect of Rap1 activity on the localization and dynamics of adhesive and cytoskeletal structures during wound repair. Finally, I will test the sensitivity of Rap1 activation to mechanical load exerted by the cytoskeleton and across cell-cell adhesions. My findings will elucidate how mechanical and molecular signals are integrated to coordinate cell movements via dynamic regulation of adhesions and the cytoskeleton, contributing to the overall understanding of collective cell migration.

column36: Electroconvulsive Therapy: Analysis of its Safety and Efficacy
column37: Depression affects about 20% of the population in their lifetime and is now the leading cause of illness burden worldwide. It is usually treated with either medications or psychotherapy but a substantial number of people do not respond to these treatments. In this case, a treatment known as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) may be offered. ECT uses electricity delivered under anesthesia to induce a generalized seizure, which is thought to be safe and effective for depression. Numerous clinical trials of ECT have shown it to be effective in treating depression and reducing suicidal thoughts. Furthermore, recent work using administrative health data from Ontario found extremely low rates of adverse medical events (AME) - similar to low-risk outpatient surgeries. Despite this, <1% of depressed individuals receive ECT which may be due to lack of knowledge about ECT's relationship with patient-relevant outcomes for AME (death or hospitalization) and suicide (attempted or completed). We do not currently know the specific contribution of ECT to either of these outcomes as individuals with depression have higher rates for both. Determining the specific contribution of ECT to suicide or AME requires comparing large groups of individuals who receive ECT to a group of similar individuals who do not receive ECT. While there have been previous studies comparing individuals receiving ECT to those not, these have been limited by differences between groups and were conducted in a single location. Therefore, our goal is to compare depressed individuals who receive ECT to a closely matched group of individuals who do not receive ECT using data from the province of Ontario. We hypothesize individuals who receive ECT will have a slightly increased risk of AME (due to the anesthesia required for ECT) but reduced risk of suicide (due to the effectiveness of ECT for treating depression). We believe this knowledge will improve patients' ability to make effective decisions regarding ECT.

column37: Late-life depression affects approximately 20% of older adults in Canada, though the rates can be as high as 40% in hospitals. Chronic, or treatment-resistant late-life depression (TRLLD) escalates the risk for both Alzheimer's and vascular dementia by as much as 33%. As Canada's population ages, the increasing number of older adults suffering from dementia represents a massive drain on social and healthcare resources. Lifestyle factors such as exercise, education, challenging jobs and learning a second language are collectively known as cognitive reserve (CR) and extend the amount of time a person can cope with Alzheimer's-related degeneration. Two brain circuits involved in cognitive ability and memory are both decimated by TRLLD and dementia, while CR actively strengthens brain regions involved in these functions. Does having higher CR allow people with TRLLD to recover faster and perhaps avert the conversion to dementia? In the present study, we will assess the impact of CR on cognitive ability and memory in older adults with TRLLD at first visit and across time through the course of novel drug treatments. We predict that higher CR accrued over the lifetime will strengthen brain circuits involved in cognitive ability thus allowing these individuals to better resist the devastating effects of TRLLD. Additionally, novel work from our group shows that patient subgroups can be identified using optimal combinations of brain imaging and behavioral data. These subgroups likely represent more biologically plausible groupings than clinical labels afford. We propose to use this technique to identify subgroups of individuals with TRLLD and varying amounts of CR. People with higher CR should respond to novel treatments faster and have a lower risk of converting to dementia. Conversely, these findings also represent a novel way to identify those individuals most at risk of converting to dementia which will allow for intervention far in advance of cognitive impairment.

column36: Investigating the lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3) exhaustion marker and its associated defects in invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) immune cell function in HIV infection
column37: Background: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a global health issue, with 36.9 million HIV-infected people in 2018. HIV exhausts the infected person's immune system to the point where it cannot properly fight infections. Despite treatment with anti-HIV drugs to stop virus replication, immune system exhaustion still occurs. Understanding how to reverse this exhaustion is critical in enhancing long-term well-being of HIV-infected people. We have shown that a protein, lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3), inhibits immune cells from functioning in HIV infection. LAG-3 is like the handbrake of a car. If you leave the handbrake on while driving, the car will never reach its full-speed. So, with LAG-3 present, the immune system cannot reach its full potential and fight infections. Our lab has shown there is more LAG-3 on immune cells called invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells of HIV-infected people. iNKT cells are essential to a strong immune response; if iNKT cells do not function properly due to LAG-3, the immune system cannot work optimally to protect individuals. Hypothesis: I will determine if by blocking LAG-3, we will remove its handbrake-effect, allowing iNKT cells to work properly, helping to restore the immune system in HIV-infected people. My project is highly feasible and future applications are very relevant, as the goal is to provide data to ultimately move the LAG-3 exhaustion marker blockade into HIV treatment clinical trials. If successful, this opens doors to transformative approaches in HIV therapy.

column36: Development of a Magnetic Resonance guided High Intensity Focused Ultrasound Therapy Platform for Perinatal Applications
column37: Congenital abnormalities are complications of pregnancy that can lead to heart failure of the baby and loss of pregnancy. These are diagnosed by ultrasound and can be treated if the risk of fetal death outweighs the risk of surgery. Current therapies all involve minimally invasive access into the uterus and comes with a risk of preterm birth. Magnetic resonance guided high intensity focused ultrasound (MRgHIFU) is a noninvasive therapy that is clinically approved in Canada for thermal ablation of uterine fibroids, and bone metastasis. MRgHIFU transmits ultrasound energy from a transducer located inside a dedicated MRI table that is below the patient, and focuses that energy into the body, producing a thermal lesion as small as a rice kernel. This focus is steered to cover a large treatment volume without repositioning the patient. Since the absorbed energy is nonionizing and incisionless, the risk of infection and long-term side effects are minimal, making it an ideal modality for fetal interventions. However, in the approved devices the energy source is located in configurations that are not adapted for a pregnant mother, and this is not amenable to a safe and ergonomically feasible treatment. The objective of this project is to develop a new modular MRgHIFU robotic platform that brings a HIFU transducer to a patient inside an MRI scanner in a configuration that provides a novel, safe and noninvasive therapy technology for some of our most vulnerable pediatric patients.

column36: Utilizing high resolution physiological data and artificial intelligence to develop a pediatric cardiac arrest prediction tool for integration into bedside clinical practice
column37: Critically ill children are at risk of cardio-pulmonary arrest (CPA). These devastating events occur 300-700 times per year in Canadian pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) and are associated with high mortality (45 to 85%), disability and higher costs of care. Effective management of CPA requires immediate reaction from clinicians. However, changes in a patient's state that precede the CPA are subtle. If these were appreciated, interventions would be possible, potentially preventing CPA and the associated poor outcomes and costs. The objective of this project is to use artificial intelligence to develop and implement a tool to predict CPA in critically ill children. We have been collecting and storing continuous physiologic signals in our PICU since April 2013. We have undertaken preliminary work using machine learning to analyze these data in patients who suffered a CPA. Our results indicate that earlier prediction of CPA is possible. We will use funding from this grant to: 1) Further validate, train and test the model predicting CPA, utilizing multidisciplinary expertise in a team that includes clinicians, engineers, computer scientists, and 2) Translate the model to the bedside using a visualization platform and implementation plan developed with human factors engineers and ethicists. This project is part of the new field of predictive, personalized medicine, and is associated with novel ethical dilemmas related to communicating the significance of predictions to patients and their families, which we will explore and define. An accurate model for CPA will save the lives of critically ill Canadian children and reduce the burden associated with these events. Its development will create opportunities for Canadian researchers to extend predictive modelling and redefine the healthcare team. This initiative will reduce healthcare costs, and positions Canada as a leader in using artificial intelligence to solve crucial healthcare problems.

column37: The prevalence of problem gambling (PG) among low income persons in Canada is up to 9 times higher than within the general population. PG is associated with other health and social needs such as homelessness, disability, substance use and mental illness. There is a lack of services available to provide PG care either as a standalone service or as part of an integrated care approach. Previous work by our team identified self-management as an important element of treatment, including the potential of technology in self-managed care. In response, a team of experts is co-developing a free and first-of-its-kind Smartphone/web app to help persons in vulnerable populations self-manage their PG and other complex needs. By collecting client information the app will be able to detect potential crisis situations and push supportive content to the user, such as an option to connect with social supports, a reminder of a PG-related goal or other resources such as self-help materials, gambling facts and motivational quotes. The app will be introduced to clients within the context of existing PG programming/case management as a way to encourage uptake, and then used by clients independently to self-manage post-treatment. It is expected that the technology will facilitate client self-management, improve client outcomes relating to PG and other complex needs and enhance client-provider communication. Lastly, we will work with commercial, service and technical partners towards delivery of a robust and fully substantiated product, with high quality data to support use of the app within target populations and more generally in those affected by problem gambling. There is ample opportunity for the app to be commercialized and incorporated into the Canadian healthcare and social service systems and applied to the treatment and self-management of PG and related health/social problems; a necessity in a sparse treatment environment marked by long wait lists.

column36: Evaluation of an Online Tool to Reduce Unnecessary Antibiotic Prescribing Among General Practitioners
column37: Infections are rapidly becoming resistant to the antibiotics we use to treat them. These resistant infections are responsible for a growing number of deaths and place a tremendous strain on the healthcare system. The World Health Organization has called this issue "one of the biggest threats to global health, food security, and development today." And yet, few new antibiotics are being developed, making it critical to safeguard the efficacy of existing antibiotics. The overuse of antibiotics is recognized as the leading causing of antibiotic resistance, as these medications are often prescribed unnecessarily. While campaigns to improve antibiotic prescribing practices in hospitals have been effective, progress has been slower outside of hospitals, where the vast majority of antibiotics in Canada are prescribed, mainly by family doctors. OPEN Stewardship is an international collaboration to implement a simple, web-based tool to empower family doctors make the right decision about when to prescribe antibiotics and which antibiotics to prescribe. OPEN Stewardship works by providing automated feedback to doctors on their prescribing practices and comparing them to an anonymous sample of their peers. The tool assists doctors by connecting them to information about local guidelines and antibiotic resistance rates and allows the exchange of relevant information. The first phase of the study will test the tool with family doctors in Toronto and Southern Israel. My role will be to develop and apply the statistical methods to analyze how the tool changes each doctor's prescribing practices. The way we use antibiotics is unsustainable and threatens our ability to treat deadly infections. OPEN Stewardship empowers doctors to make the best antibiotic prescribing decisions and has the potential to become an important tool in the fight against antibiotic resistance. As a standardized, low-cost tool, OPEN Stewardship offers a global solution to a global problem.

column36: Combining genome-wide CRISPR screens and microfluidics to discover genetic regulators during the differentiation pathway towards transplantable hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Stem cells have the ability to become nearly any cell type in the human body. Therefore, they have tremendous potential to be used in the treatment of disease. For example, stem cells can be used to generate healthy blood and bone cells for cancer patients. Currently this is done using bone marrow transplants. However, there are outstanding issues with this treatment. These include difficulties finding a suitable donor and complications such as rejection of the new cells, infection, or reoccurrence of the disease. In fact, nearly 30% of transplant patients die within one year of the treatment. My research aims to provide a better alternative -- turning a patient's own skin cells into stem cells and then blood. This would eliminate the need for a donor and reduce the likelihood of complications resulting in death. To do this I am leveraging a new gene-editing tool, called CRISPR, to search for genes that control the differentiation of stem cells. I am also engineering a platform based on micro-scale fluidic chips which can sort billions of cells using magnetic nanoparticles. This platform allows the search to cover more of the human genome, take less time and be less expensive. This approach has the additional potential to treat other diseases by identifying genes that could tell stem cells to become heart or brain cells.

column36: Vaccine effectiveness against persistent human papillomavirus infection in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal
column37: Gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are recommended to get the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. Most Canadian provinces have introduced publicly funded HPV vaccination programs for boys and high-risk males such as MSM, but we do not know how well the HPV vaccine works in these populations outside of a clinical setting. MSM have higher rates of HPV-associated diseases like anal cancer compared to the general population. In part, this is because they have higher rates of HIV. Based on clinical studies, we know that the HPV vaccine protects against infection about 75-78% of the time in healthy MSM who have had relatively few lifetime sex partners. However, less information is known about how this translates to vaccine protection in a real-life setting or in higher risk groups, such as those who have multiple sex partners or prior HPV infection or in those living with HIV. My PhD will study how well the HPV vaccine protects against ongoing HPV infection in MSM over a one-year period. I will estimate the percent of MSM infected with HPV at the beginning of the study and 12 months after enrollment; identify patient characteristics, such as sexual behaviours or HIV status, associated with infection; and measure the amount of protection from HPV vaccine. I will use data from a community-based study of MSM aged 16-30 years in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal known as Engage-HPV. At each study visit, men answered questions about their sexual health, including self-reported HPV vaccination status. They were also asked to self-collect oral and anal specimens for HPV testing. This research will fill an important knowledge gap about ongoing HPV infection in this population and will provide a real-world measure of HPV vaccine effectiveness. My findings will help evaluate targeted HPV vaccination programs recently implemented in three Canadian cities with large populations of MSM and contribute to the design of optimal HPV prevention strategies.

column36: Differentiating Suicide Attempters From Suicidal Ideators: A Multimodal Investigation of Impulsivity
column37: Suicide is a public health epidemic. The World Health Organization estimates that suicide is attempted every 1-2 seconds. Though extensive resources are invested in suicide prevention, our ability to predict suicide attempt is only marginally better than chance. Addressing the root of this problem requires that we answer why some people only contemplate suicide while others actually attempt it. To do so, the ideation-to-action framework offers a novel approach to suicide research that emphasizes the importance of separately understanding the origin of suicidal thoughts (i.e., ideation) and the transition from thoughts to suicide attempt (i.e., action). Within this framework, difficulty with impulse control is a risk factor that has been linked to suicide attempt but is poorly understood. Impulse control is a complex process with numerous constituent parts that have not been concurrently analyzed within the context of suicide. In my proposed research, I will apply the ideation-to-action framework to determine which aspects of impulse control differentiate people who have attempted suicide from those who have only contemplated it. I will investigate this research question using multiple measures of impulse control (i.e., personality traits, cognition, and neural systems) in patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD), a group of people that frequently think about suicide, often have a history of suicide attempt, and are highly impulsive. Future public health strategies to prevent suicide require that we discriminate between suicidal thought and suicide attempt to better focus prevention efforts and improve risk assessment tools for health care professionals. Thus, this research informs these efforts by contributing to a comprehensive risk profile of suicide attempt and inviting the exploration of specific treatment and intervention targets related to impulse control.

column36: Defining the pre-leukemic stem cell state through transcriptional and epigenetic interrogation at single cell resolution
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia is a deadly blood cancer with only 1 in 3 patients surviving 3 years beyond diagnosis. Most AML patients are diagnosed only after they present with acute complications of bone marrow failure, highlighting the importance of early detection and intervention. I will then examine these networks to identify targets that we can exploit therapeutically in order to eliminate the pre-leukemic stem cells while sparing healthy blood stem cells. The results from this study will inform efforts to understand and target pre-leukemia and bring us closer to introducing early detection and intervention into the clinic towards preventing this devastating disease.

column36: Probing T-Cell Response in a Hypoxic Pancreatic Tumour Microenvironment using TRACER
column37: Pancreatic cancer is set to surpass breast cancer as the third leading cause of cancer deaths in Canada. Currently, only 7% of patients with pancreatic cancer will survive five years after diagnosis. The disease is often diagnosed too late for surgery, and it is generally resistant to chemotherapy and radiation. As such, new treatment options are desperately needed. Immunotherapy - treatments which recruit a patient's immune system to eliminate cancer cells - has been successful for some cancers but has fallen short in pancreatic cancer. This is partly because pancreatic cancer actively suppresses the immune system, preventing it from killing cancer cells. Investigating the interaction between the immune system and cancer cells using traditional 2D or living animal models has not yielded effective ways to solve this problem. Now, a 3D platform developed by our lab called "Tumour Roll for Analysis of Cellular Environment" - TRACER - is creating new opportunities to study these interactions. TRACER is an engineered 3D tumour model. Cells are grown on a paper strip wrapped around a metal cylinder to create a tumour in a dish that is similar to what would be in a patient. Unlike in a patient, TRACER can be unrolled to look inside the tumour to examine cell interactions up-close. This allows us to understand why immune cells are not functioning properly. Using TRACER, we will create tumours using patients' cells to investigate cellular interactions and identify molecules in the environment that affect the immune system. We will then engineer immune cells to function in the tumour environment and kill cancer cells. In knowing which engineered cells are successful, we can highlight the gene and protein targets which may be important to enhancing immunotherapy in pancreatic cancer and pass these targets along to those developing new drugs. In doing so, we will potentially create treatments that improve the quality of life and survival of pancreatic cancer patients.

column36: Conceptualizing Learning Health Systems from an Indigenous Perspective: A Multiple Case Study in Northwest Territories
column37: This research involves Indigenous Peoples. If you go to the doctor with a problem and the doctor tells you there is nothing wrong, you might feel rejected and misunderstood. Maybe in your community there is no other doctor to go to, so next time you are ill you decide not to go to the doctor at all, making things worse. Unfortunately, this situation is common in many parts of Canada. Our health care system assumes disease is the cause of illness. However, there is more than one way to understand health. This study will help to build a health care system that learns from our different understandings, and constantly improves to provide better care. Many Indigenous peoples do not see health as an absence of disease, but as the result of good relationships with their family, community, environment, and spirit. The differences between these beliefs and the beliefs of our health care system mean that Indigenous patients often receive unhelpful, and even harmful, care. One idea is to build "learning health systems" that continuously improve care by learning from a variety of information sources, including patients. To improve care for Indigenous patients, learning health systems must know what to learn, how, and from whom. This research will take place from 2019 to 2022 in Northwest Territories, where 51% of the population is Indigenous. We will use sharing circles and interviews with Indigenous Elders and communities to find answers to two questions. First, in the eyes of Indigenous community members, what is a learning health system? Second, in what ways can a health system learn from the Indigenous communities it serves? These questions have not been studied before. Our results will indicate how the Northwest Territories health system can improve care for Indigenous patients, but will also benefit places across Canada and the world that have many cultural groups with different beliefs about health.

column36: Genomic and Pathological Consequences of Obesity on Prostate Cancer
column37: More than 1 in 3 Canadians are living with obesity and half will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetimes. Obesity increases the risk of prostate cancer, and in particular aggressive disease that is not cured by standard treatment. It is still unclear what influences obesity is playing on prostate cancer risk and aggression. My project seeks to answer this question by applying new DNA sequencing techniques and state-of-the-art machine learning to study the prostate tumours of obese and non-obese men. In each cell, the information that passes down from parents to child is encoded in the DNA. Some genes (pieces of DNA) that are passed down increase a person's risk for obesity or cancer, and during a person's lifetime genetic changes can make cells turn cancerous. My first question is: Compared to non-obese men, do obese men carry unique genetic changes in their cancers, or do they have changes that are more frequently found in aggressive cancers? Second: What patterns in inherited genes are shared between people who have high risks for both obesity and prostate cancer? Finally: How different do tumour cells appear in men with and without obesity? I will link these questions to clinical outcomes to understand their importance to prevention and patient care. The answers to these questions are critical for better predicting outcomes of patients with both obesity and prostate cancer, for helping doctors make better treatment decisions, and for more cost-effective diagnosis through microscopes. This study will be the first to look at the relationship between obesity and the genetic features of prostate cancer. By understanding how and why prostate cancer differs in obese men, scientists can better understand how prostate cancers develop and how to better match obese patients to the targeted therapy most likely to cure their disease. This research will be vital for improving the care and treatment of thousands of Canadians affected by both obesity and prostate cancer.

column36: Evaluating the Impact of Multi-Site Drug Checking Services on Overdose Risk in Toronto, Ontario During a National Opioid Overdose Crisis
column37: Opioid overdose is a primary public health concern in Canada. There is growing evidence that the rising number of overdose deaths is related in large part to the presence of highly potent opioids, such as fentanyl, in street drugs. Against the backdrop of a national opioid overdose crisis, drug checking services (DCS) have emerged as part of a comprehensive approach to preventing overdose deaths with Health Canada committing to approve and fund pilot projects providing DCS at supervised consumptions sites, including in Toronto, Ontario. Available throughout Europe since the 1990s, DCS provide people who use drugs with information on what is in their street drugs and how strong they are. This information can allow for more educated choices about drug use and enable people who use drugs to avoid consuming lethal amounts of toxic substances. Since DCS in Europe have traditionally targeted people who use drugs recreationally in nightlife settings, little is known about whether DCS can prevent overdose deaths among a high-risk population. column36: Seasonal Transmission Dynamics of Influenza and Avian Influenza in Bangladesh: identifying pandemic risk and opportunities for control
column37: Influenza viruses are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Avian influenza viruses in particular have generated global health concern because of their ability to cause severe disease in humans. Avian strains are also capable of combining with human strains, which allows new influenza viruses to evolve. The emergence of a new influenza virus with improved human-to-human transmission is of concern because it could cause the next global pandemic. The public health risks posed by avian influenza are particularly high in Bangladesh, where high population densities and expanding poultry production industries are bringing humans and animals in closer contact. Despite these risks, there is limited understanding of the seasonal transmission patterns of influenza in human and poultry populations in Bangladesh. To address this research gap, my PhD aims to evaluate human and avian influenza transmission to better understand risk of pandemic emergence and opportunities for control in Dhaka, Bangladesh. This project will bring together routinely collected datasets from laboratories, hospitals, and veterinary programmes in Bangladesh. Using these data, I will implement innovative statistical, mathematical, and epidemiological techniques to characterize the seasonal patterns of influenza in human and poultry populations, as well as simulate the impact of influenza control strategies. Plausible control strategies, such as human vaccination, poultry vaccination, and improved biosecurity practices, will be defined in collaboration with stakeholders in Dhaka, through local workshops and meetings. This work will provide researchers and public health experts in Bangladesh with novel tools to make informed and actionable decisions to control potential influenza threats and support human and animal well-being.

column36: A population health- and policy-based evaluation of cannabis legalization in Canada: The effect of recent federal policy change on cannabis and alcohol use and related substance use disorders
column37: Canada will legalize the sale and possession of cannabis in October 2018, marking a foundational shift in national substance use policy as cannabis joins alcohol as a legal psychoactive drug. Research studying recent events in the United States has shown that cannabis legalization has led to increased cannabis use and cannabis use disorders; however, the simultaneous effect on alcohol use and alcohol use disorders is not clear. It is important to study these two now-legal substances in parallel as alcohol is used more widely and is responsible for greater health harms than cannabis in Canada. This program of research, completed as a collaboration between the Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and the National Drug Research Institute (Australia), will evaluate the effect of cannabis legalization on alcohol and cannabis use and associated mental health disorders. Will cannabis legalization lead to an increase in the prevalence of use of cannabis and alcohol among Canadians? Will Canadians experience higher rates of alcohol use disorders and cannabis use disorders after legalization? Or may Canadians substitute cannabis use for alcohol use and therefore experience fewer negative health consequences overall? Changes in prevalence and patterns of cannabis and alcohol use resulting from legalization will be studied using Canadian survey sources. Health records will be analyzed to estimate the rate of cannabis use and alcohol use disorders, for a period before and after legalization. Time series methods will then be employed to study the unique effect of legalization, using Australian states as control groups where legalization did not take place. This proposed research will provide answers to important questions regarding recent substance use policy change in Canada. The results will be both relevant and timely, providing critical information to policymakers in Canada, Australia and around the world regarding the health impacts of cannabis legalization.

column37: Almost 37 millions of people are living with HIV (PLWH) worldwide, including 75,000 in Canada. HIV infection is characterized by a progressive destruction of the overall immune defenses. Actual HIV treatments help PLWH to live almost as long as people who are not infected by HIV. However, the virus persists and hides within their body and exhausts their immune system. Recently, a population of human immune cells, called "regulatory T-cells" (Treg) has been identified to contribute in cancer and chronic viral illnesses progression. Specifically, we aim to understand (1) what is the status of Th17/Treg balance in PLWH with different clinical outcomes; (2) what are the metabolic mechanisms involved in Th17/Treg balance during HIV infection; and, (3) how Tregs contribute in HIV persistence and the immuno-deficiency. In this regard, our laboratories will use different well-established experiments on biological specimens from PLWH with different clinical and therapeutic outcomes. This research will help to develop new therapeutic approaches aimed at modulating deleterious functions of Tregs. Targeting of Tregs with appropriate immuno-therapeutic interventions in PLWH, could lead to a better immune recovery and might help to find an HIV cure.

column36: Targeting mRNA translation to effectively treat metastatic breast cancer
column37: Current treatments for metastatic breast cancer are ineffective for disease that has spread (metastasized) to other organs. Moreover, while new immunotherapies are promising for other cancer types, their effect in breast cancer is limited. Therefore, when laboratory scientists uncover promising new leads, it is imperative to determine how they can be applied to benefit patients. We and others have shown that new drugs blocking this do not affect the production of all proteins equally, but selectively inhibit proteins needed for the aggressive behavior of breast cancer cells. We have also shown that these drugs can unleash immune responses suppressed by tumor cells, potentially stimulating the immune system to attack metastatic breast cancer. In this project, we will test these drugs in sophisticated models of metastatic breast cancer and bring them to the clinic for phase I trials in breast cancer patients. Our team unites world-leading Canadian fundamental and translational scientists with breast cancer clinical trials experts. We will identify all proteins whose production is altered by these drugs, identify responsive breast cancer subtypes and therapeutic combinations that allow us to maximize their effects, and determine whether their immunity-enhancing actions can be harnessed to further increase their effectiveness. column36: Survival of the fittest: cell competition in cancer progression
column37: Despite decades of research and development of diagnostic technology, cancer is still often diagnosed based on relatively large abnormalities in the tissue - growths, lumps, or bumps visible to the naked eye. The size of the smallest detectable tumor is still approximately a billion cells. Furthermore, it is often only possible to detect cancer cells that have spread from the initial tumor site to distant organs at late stages, when the cancer has progressed past the point of being curable. Thus, being able to identify cancer cells at very early stages and low numbers could enable identification of molecules to mark cancerous and pre-cancerous cells, and lead to development of therapies to kill cancer cells before the cancer spreads. One potential way to identify cancer cells at early stages is by discovering novel mechanisms cancer cells use to promote their own growth and survival. Cell competition is a process by which faster growing ("winner") cells kill the slower growing ("loser") cells around them, in order to enable their own growth. Although cell competition is known to be important for animal development and for maintaining tissue health, it has not been extensively studied in cancer in animals. I will use a zebrafish model of melanoma to investigate if cancer cells use cell competition to promote their own growth by killing the cells around them. I will transplant melanoma cells into transparent fish and use cutting-edge live, whole-animal microscopy to investigate if tumors cause the death of the surrounding normal cells. In parallel, I will induce cell competition in tumors by upregulating the cancer-promoting gene Myc, and perform a drug screen to identify molecules that inhibit competition and tumor growth, to provide insight into signaling pathways that could be driving cell competition in cancer. These studies will detail molecules that promote cancer progression, and describe potential targets for development of drugs to block cancer spreading.

column36: Predicting response to cognitive behavioural therapy for major depressive disorder

column37: Concussion is a major public health concern. Despite increased recognition of the serious health impacts of concussion, the number of injuries is rising. Feedback will allow the child/youth to immediately adjust activity level to prevent symptom exacerbation and longer recovery time.

column36: Investigating the Neural Basis of Social Cognition in Autism Spectrum Disorders
column37: Impaired social functioning is a central feature of Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs); however, few treatments are available. There is evidence that two networks in the brain are important for social functioning: one for understanding the actions and basic emotions of others (mirror neuron system), and another for understanding that others can have thoughts and feelings that differ from one's own (theory of mind). Social functioning deficits are also central to schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs), and healthy controls (HCs) exhibit a wide range of social functioning. These two networks have been shown to exist along a continuum in ASDs, SSDs and HCs; thus, studying these populations together has the potential to reveal patterns of brain-behaviour relationships that cut across these diagnoses and that underlie social functioning. In the proposed study, we will evaluate how brain structure is related to brain function, and how both are related to social functioning. To achieve this, we will use two types of brain imaging: one to examine structural connections between these networks, and another to examine brain activity in these networks (while performing a task that activates them). We will relate both these brain measures to behavioural and clinical assessments of social functioning. We hypothesize that altered brain structure will result in impaired brain function, and consequently poor social functioning. We also expect that greater usage of the theory of mind network will be associated with better social functioning, whereas greater usage of the mirror neuron network will be associated with worse social functioning. By characterizing brain structure-function-behaviour relations in and between each network, we are taking a critical step towards identifying targets for novel treatments to improve social functioning. Improvements in social functioning will ameliorate the quality of life of individuals with ASD and their families, and benefit Canada economically.

column37: Opioid overdose has caused more deaths in Canada than seen at the peak of the HIV epidemic in the 1990s. National planning requires evidence about which implementation strategies are effective in different settings. This study is the first of its kind in North America. Together, we will identify factors supporting or hindering implementation in British Columbia and Canada. We will then test the effectiveness of different implementation strategies in different settings. Some of these strategies will include education, changing policy and improving communication networks. Effective implementation will mean better access to these life-saving interventions. column36: Cognitive function in a sleep clinic cohort of patients with obstructive sleep apnea
column37: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic medical condition where patients stop breathing during sleep due to recurrent collapse of their upper airway, causing low oxygen levels (called "hypoxemia") and disturbed sleep. OSA can lead to trouble with memory, concentration and decision making (termed "cognitive impairment") in some, but not all, patients. Similarly, treatment of OSA improves cognitive functioning in some, but not all, patients. Though hypoxemia and sleep disruption are the most likely mechanisms whereby OSA leads to cognitive impairment, the size of this effect may be modified by co-existing factors such as age, gender, sleepiness, cognitive reserve (the brain's ability to resist damage), genetics, other health conditions and medications. Also, how much these factors impact the benefits of treating OSA is not known. Thus, the objectives of this study are to 1) determine the prevalence and severity of cognitive impairment in OSA before, and after, treatment, and 2) identify patient traits (termed "biomarkers") that can help predict which patients are at the greatest risk for cognitive impairment and who may benefit the most from OSA treatment. Adults with suspected OSA will be recruited from 5 academic sleep centres in Calgary, Saskatoon, Vancouver, Montreal and Quebec City. Patients will complete sleep and medical questionnaires and undergo cognitive testing (tests of memory and decision making) at study entry and 3 years later. All patients diagnosed with OSA will be offered the gold-standard treatment of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and their adherence to this therapy will be monitored. Blood samples will be taken at study entry for genetic analyses. The prevalence of cognitive impairment and its link to hypoxemia and disturbed sleep will be determined at study entry and 3 years later, while controlling for age, gender, sleepiness, cognitive reserve, genetics, other health conditions and medications, and adherence to CPAP treatment.

Further, this work will show that improvements in hand and arm function are maximized when targets are tailored to the individual. Ultimately, this research will advance rehabilitation and recovery after stroke, leading to improved daily function and better quality of life for Canadians living with stroke.

column37: While the 5-year survival rates for children with cancer continue to improve, the major problem of drug-related side effects remains. column36: Genetic Characterization of the Latent HIV Reservoir Towards its Immune-mediated Elimination
column37: HIV infection, while manageable with antiretroviral drugs, cannot be cured, leaving 37 million persons globally vulnerable to the long-term health effects and stigma associated with this condition. Current antiretroviral drugs cannot cure HIV because of the presence of a subset of immune cells that, after infection, enter a state of "hibernation" or latency. Latently HIV-infected cells are invisible to the immune system and can persist in the body for years or even decades. Furthermore, a subset of these cells is capable of reactivating at a future date to produce infectious HIV. We refer to the total pool of hibernating viruses as "the latent HIV reservoir", and to the latter subset as the "inducible, replication competent" fraction. Curing HIV will require us to eliminate the latter, but multiple challenges remain. First, since HIV continually mutates during untreated infection, an individual's pool of hibernating viruses is likely to be genetically diverse. In addition, some hibernating viral strains would harbor mutations that, upon reactivation, would render them resistant to host immune responses. Achieving a better understanding of latent HIV reservoir genetic composition and responsiveness to immune-mediated elimination, and the extent to which these features vary between individuals, is critical for designing HIV cure strategies. Using a unique cohort for whom longitudinal historic bio-specimens are available, we will investigate the genetic characteristics of both the total and inducible, replication competent pool of hibernating viruses in each individual. In doing so, we will identify viral targets that remain susceptible to recognition by the immune system in a "personalized" manner. Finally, we will test whether these "personalized" targets can better stimulate an individual's immune cells to kill latently infected cells in vitro, compared to standard targets. Results will help scientists design therapeutic strategies towards achieving an HIV cure.

column36: Psychiatric phenotypes in chronic traumatic encephalopathy
column37: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive, psychiatric, and motor symptoms, and is caused by repetitive head impacts such as those seen in athletes of contact sports and military veterans. column36: Investigating how ribosome heterogeneity guides cell fate specification of human embryonic stem cells into cardiac cell lineages
column37: The regulation of protein production is critical to maintain cellular homeostasis. When disrupted, this can result in devastating human disease. The cellular machinery used to produce proteins, termed ribosomes, has traditionally been viewed as a universal machine that is similar between organisms and cell types. Interestingly, mutations in core ribosome proteins lead to devastating congenital birth defects (e.g. neural crest defects) and stem cell defects (e.g. Diamond Blackfan Anemia), suggesting that specific proteins are required for proper development and cellular maintenance. Indeed, specialized ribosomes have been found to drive synthesis of specific proteins in key pathways of tissue development. As well, this level of specialization has recently been found to be augmented by auxiliary proteins that bind to the ribosome to effect its function; however, the role of these ribosome-associated proteins in human health and disease remains largely unknown. Here, we aim to fill this gap in knowledge by characterizing ribosome-associated proteins and their functions during stem cell differentiation. Specifically, we hypothesize that proteins bound to the ribosome are crucial in directing cell fate decisions of human embryonic stem cells down cardiac cell lineages. To study this, we will combine state-of-the-art methodologies including high-throughput ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry to fully understand the repertoire of ribosome-associated proteins during cardiac cell development and their cognate regulatory targets. Moreover, we will use gene editing technology to further understand their specific functional roles in cellular protein synthesis and eventually use animal models to assess their impacts on disease.

column36: Evaluating gender-sensitive interventions for people who use drugs in the context of British Columbia's opioid overdose crisis
column37: Overdose death rates have increased dramatically in Canada in recent years, largely driven by contamination of the drug supply with illicitly manufactured synthetic opioids such as fentanyl. The overdose crisis has been hardest felt in British Columbia (BC), which declared a public health emergency in 2016. Strategies to address the overdose crisis have therefore become an urgent public health priority. Previous research and evidence have shown that gender plays a key role in shaping contexts of drug use (e.g., within sex work or intimate partnerships) and access to treatment and harm reduction services. Women access treatment with more severe substance-related profiles relative to men (e.g., physical/sexual violence and trauma), yet few services are women-specific. New Vancouver Coastal Health guidelines highlight grave gaps in supports and prevention for marginalized women, and several new models of care are being rolled out (e.g., women-only supervised consumption rooms). Clinical interventions to address the overdose crisis and expand access to evidence-based treatments in BC include randomized clinical trials (RCTs) on the efficacy of opioid agonist therapies (OAT), slow-release oral morphine (SROM), and psychedelic-assisted therapy. However, the gender-related impacts of these interventions remain poorly understood and under investigated. The proposed research will evaluate the impacts of 'naturally occurring' and clinical interventions (i.e., through prospective methods and RCTs) to address the overdose crisis using a gendered lens, to identify gender differences in treatment outcomes and barriers to accessing services. This project also aims to widely disseminate findings to support scale-up of gender-sensitive substance use programs and policies, and inform directions for future research. It is hoped that this research will make important contributions to optimizing gender-specific treatment and care for people who use drugs in Canada and internationally.

column36: Regulation of axonal damage signaling by the dileucine zipper kinase, DLK
column37: A fundamental feature of nervous system function is communication between neurons, which is carried out via communication cables, called axons. Damage to axons in the central nervous system (CNS) often leads to debilitating paralysis, and defects in axons are associated with neuropathology and death in neurodegenerative diseases. In contrast, axon injury in the mammalian peripheral nervous system (PNS) is usually not debilitating, since mechanisms exist to stimulate regrowth of damaged axons and to repair damaged circuits. My work studies the mechanisms of an enzyme that detects defects in axons, and regulates dual responses of new axonal growth in the PNS, and death of neurons in the CNS. Understanding the activation mechanisms of this enzyme will help in strategies to stimulate repair after spinal cord injury and stroke, and to inhibit pathology in neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's Disease. My goal is to understand how this enzyme, a dileucine zipper kinase named DLK, becomes activated in damaged axons. I have developed a new injury paradigm in the model organism Drosophila for introducing axonal damage to specific locations in branched axons while monitoring DLK activation. My data indicate that injury location is important for DLK activation mechanism: injuries to synaptic branches that leave at least one synaptic connection intact fail to activate DLK signaling. In the proposed project, I will use my new injury assay to: (Aim 1) test the hypothesis that functional synaptic communication at spared presynaptic terminals restrains DLK signaling, and (Aim 2) test whether the E3 ubiquitin ligase Hiw, which promotes the destruction of DLK protein, regulates DLK at intact synaptic terminals. This work will shed light on how neurons detect axonal damage which is important for understanding the mechanisms of repair and degeneration in the nervous system.

column37: Shared decision making (SDM) is considered the best approach for making health decisions. In pediatrics, SDM occurs when the healthcare team, parents, and children exchange information and work together as partners to decide the best treatment plan for the child. SDM helps parents and children participate in decision making, feel more confident about the decision that was made, and can improve the child's health. Unfortunately, SDM is rarely used in pediatric clinical settings. The goal of my research is to improve the use of SDM in pediatric clinical practice. To do this, I am developing a SDM program that will include education, training, clinical tools, and expert support for healthcare teams, parents, and children. To ensure the SDM program works, we must test it using advanced research methods. Although very informative, these methods are resource and time intensive. To avoid waste, it is often necessary to 'pilot' the methods using a smaller-scale experiment that will identify and provide an opportunity to fix problems before doing the larger experiment. Therefore, I am proposing to pilot advanced research methods for evaluating how well the SDM program works in pediatric clinical practice. We will ask healthcare teams, parents and children to participate in the study. The results will provide valuable information about recruiting people to our study, collecting data, and whether the program is likely to improve child and parent decision making experiences. We will use this information to run a larger experiment that will provide a definitive answer about whether our program improves the use of shared decision making in pediatric clinical practice.

column37: En raison de la prevalence alarmante, l'interet scientifique et celui du public a l'egard des effets des commotions ne cesse de grandir, ce qui en fait l'une des questions de sante publique les plus actuelles et debattues. Toute discussion des effets a long terme mene inevitablement a l'encephalopathie traumatique chronique (ETC), une maladie neurodegenerative qui ne peut etre diagnostiquee qu'a l'autopsie et pour laquelle les medias etablissent un lien de cause a effet entre l'exposition aux coups repetes a la tete et le developpement de cette maladie. Cependant, il est trop precoce d'affirmer un lien de causalite en raison de lacunes scientifiques importantes. Il a ete demontre que les patients atteints d'ETC partagent des symptomes similaires avec d'autres maladies neurodegeneratives, telle la maladie d'Alzheimer, ce qui complexifie l'etablissement d'un diagnostic clinique et la comprehension des mecanismes pathologiques. Le present projet propose une etude longitudinale des changements anormaux du cerveau qui pourraient etre impliques dans le declin cognitif anormal chez les athletes commotionnes. Grace a l'avancement fulgurant de la qualite des examens de neuroimagerie, il sera possible de deceler des particularites biologiques du cerveau commotionne nous permettant de predire le declin cognitif d'anciennes athletes commotionnees. Les connaissances qui seront acquises en definissant la signature biologique des effets a long terme des commotions faciliteront l'identification des athletes a risque de souffrir de neurodegenerescence. De plus, les resultats permettront d'identifier des pistes de traitement precoce pour retarder la progression de la maladie avant que ne s'installent des changements irreversibles au cerveau tout en ameliorant la qualite de vie d'athletes commotionnes qui souffrent en silence.

column36: Suicidalite chez les jeunes atteints d'un premier episode psychotique : trajectoires d'evolution et facteurs associes.
column37: Le suicide est un grave probleme de sante publique representant une cause importante de mortalite. Plus de 5 % des individus atteints d'un trouble psychotique meurent par suicide (Melle & Barrett, 2014). Au cours des premiers stades de la psychose, le risque suicidaire est 60 % plus eleve qu'au cours des stades subsequents (Bornheimer, 2018). La psychose est caracterisee par une alteration du contact avec la realite, des hallucinations et des idees delirantes (Abdel-Baki, Lalonde, & Gingras, 2016). Peu d'etudes ont evalue de facon approfondie les facteurs de risque de la suicidalite. De plus, aucune etude quebecoise ou canadienne n'a etudie ce phenomene chez les jeunes atteints d'un premier episode psychotique (PEP). Objectifs : Les objectifs sont de decrire la frequence des differents types de suicidalite (idees suicidaires, tentatives de suicide et suicide complete), d'identifier les facteurs de risque de la suicidalite, de determiner les trajectoires d'augmentation, de maintien ou de diminution de la suicidalite sur une periode de cinq ans chez les jeunes atteints d'un PEP et d'explorer les predicteurs de ces trajectoires. Methode : Cette etude a lieu dans deux services d'intervention precoce en psychose en milieu urbain a Montreal (Quebec). L'echantillon est compose de 567 Jeunes souffrants d'un PEP ayant ete suivis par ces services pendant une periode de cinq ans. Les donnees sociodemographiques, les symptomes, la suicidalite, le fonctionnement global, la consommation d'alcool et de drogues, les traumatismes vecus pendant l'enfance et le diagnostic des participants sont consideres pour mieux comprendre les facteurs associes aux trajectoires de la suicidalite. Retombees : Le projet permettra de mieux soutenir les jeunes atteints d'un PEP qui sont a risque de passage a l'acte suicidaire en developpant de meilleurs outils pour predire le suicide et en mettant en place des strategies preventives specifiques a cette population.

column36: Targeting M3R's internalization to treat Asthma and COPD
column37: Asthma and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) are obstructive lung disorders affecting about 435 million individuals worldwide in which the symptoms of difficulty of breathing derived from the obstruction of the airways. In both respiratory disorders, this obstruction of the airways involves the activation of the muscarinic receptor M3 (M3R) leading to the contraction of the airway smooth muscle that compress the airways. Nevertheless, the current drugs blocking the M3R upregulate, paradoxically, their expression over time leading to negative side effects, such as an aggravation of airway hyperresponsiveness, a characteristic feature of asthma correlating with the symptoms. This project evaluates a new avenue to target M3R which avoids these side effects by inducing the receptor downregulation. M3R is a member of the large family of transmembrane proteins called G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). In a situation of over-activation, GPCRs downregulate their activity, a phenomenon called desensitization. Previously, we demonstrated, in vivo, that desensitization of the M3R has potential clinical benefits such as reversing the airway hyperresponsiveness in a murine model of asthma. This project aims to develop a compound that inducing exclusively the molecular pathways leading to the M3R's desensitization to treat asthma and COPD. For this purpose, firstly, the molecular pathways of contraction and desensitization will be characterized in tissue and cell-based models with molecular biology methods. Secondly, the actual compounds known to interact with the M3R will be screens to find some with a capacity to induce the desensitization of the receptor. Thirdly, these compounds will be chemically optimized, and their potential clinical benefits will be confirmed in murine models of asthma.

column36: In silico elucidation and functional characterization of human intestinal microbiota enzymes targeting host-derived carbohydrates
column37: Within the human intestinal tract reside an enormous consortium of bacterial species. Although a full picture of human-bacteria interactions is still emerging, it is clear that these microbes play important roles in human health, as patients suffering from gastrointestinal diseases typically posses fewer species than healthy individuals. One critical responsibility of intestinal bacteria is digestion of the elaborate array of complex carbohydrates from dietary sources, which largely remain untouched by human enzymes. Bacterial carbohydrate digestion ultimately yields short-chain fatty acid end products which collectively benefit their human host. Short-chain fatty acids serve as a main energy source for epithelial cells in the colon, have anti-tumorigenic and anti-inflammatory properties and reduce the incidence of type II diabetes and obesity. In addition to dietary polysaccharides, some bacteria digest polysaccharides produced by human cells. These processes are important for in how bacteria colonize the gut and regulate the immune system throughout life. Recent advancements have allowed us to grow the complete human intestinal microbiome within mixed communities in the lab. This has resulted in increased bacterial DNA yields and richer DNA sequence datasets. The goal of this research is to use computational approaches to search through DNA sequences and identify novel genes involved in degradation of human-derived polysaccharides. From there, we will identify which organism it is derived from, and purify the enzyme it encodes. Biochemical experiments on these enzymes will elucidate their precise substrates. Insights from this research may be important for the development of therapeutic strategies and preventative measures favouring the proliferation of beneficial bacterial species important for intestinal wellbeing.

column36: Modifying Aspergillomarasmine A to Improve Metallo-Beta-Lactamase Inhibition and the Efficacy of Carbapenem Antibiotics
column37: The global spread of antibiotic resistance continues to challenge clinicians and threaten the lives of infected patients. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaciae (CRE), which include the pathogenic bacteria Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are a major public health concern. This is because of the high mortality rates associated with these bacterial infections and their ability to rapidly spread from person to person. CRE are resistant to last-resort antibiotics known as carbapenems, because they produce metallo-beta-lactamases (MBL) which break these drugs down. Therefore, the development of new countermeasures are sorely needed to mitigate the threat of CRE. A promising solution to this problem is the identification of antibiotic adjuvants, which are non-antibiotic compounds that block antibiotic resistance. An example of one such compound is aspergillomarasmine A (AMA), as it inhibits the activity of MBLs and rescues carbapenems from degradation. column36: Exploring the biological and behavioural causes of sarcopenia through large biobanks and Mendelian randomization analyses
column37: At approximately the fifth decade of life humans start losing muscle mass and strength (i.e., sarcopenia). Importantly, sarcopenia is associated with a number of negative health outcomes including fracture risk, cardiovascular disease, and all-cause mortality. Thus, understanding, preventing, and reversing sarcopenia would substantially improve public health. Accordingly, the present research project proposal is designed to identify the biological and behavioural causes of sarcopenia. Using large datasets generated from the Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology Study and the UK Biobank, we will explore the behavioural (e.g., diet and physical activity) and biological (e.g., proteins measured in the blood) factors that may mediate sarcopenia. Our findings will establish behavioural factors that mediate sarcopenia, which will encourage healthcare professionals to advocate for them as preventative medicine. In addition, by identifying a biomarker for sarcopenia we will provide healthcare professionals and researchers with a feasible assessment tool and an outcome to target for intervention. We hypothesize this project will considerably improve our understanding of sarcopenia and will be a strong contribution towards the goal of preventing, reversing, and eliminating sarcopenia altogether.

column36: Investigating the effect of physical activity on executive functions and health in adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: Executive functions (EF) are brain-based processes that are necessary for controlling goal-directed behaviours, and are related to several physical and mental health outcomes.
