This work will include a series of studies to test both the immediate and long-term effects of physical activity on EF and health in this population. Results from initial lab-based studies will inform modifications to existing clinical and community physical activity programs, and the effectiveness of these modified programs will also be evaluated. Specifically, I will examine the immediate effect of different types of physical activity on changes in EF in adolescents with NDD. These results will inform a study exploring the long-term effect of physical activity on EF and health outcomes. Finally, in collaboration with existing clinical and community partners, modifications will be made to inclusive physical activity programs in order to target improvements in EF and health outcomes for adolescents with NDD, and the effect of these modifications will be tested in comparison to unmodified programs. These will be among the first studies to systematically test the effect of physical activity on EF and health outcomes in adolescents with NDD through a series of efficacy and effectiveness trials. It is anticipated that the results will contribute to the development of evidence-based physical activity programming for this at-risk population, which will have numerous implications across the sectors of health, education, and recreation.

column36: Elucidating the microstructural and genetic risk architecture of major adolescent-onset psychiatric disorders in early life
column37: One in five Canadians are affected by mental illness, with a high proportion of these individuals experiencing their first symptoms in adolescence. This dynamic and critical time period in the lifespan of an individual holds key milestones in the development of white matter "highways" in the brain, and offers a unique and informative target to study alongside genetic information. This project will provide an important neurobiological framework to assess psychiatric risk in early life that represents a significant departure from the classical definitions of psychiatric disorders, with the hope of re-routing current treatment plans to better meet the needs of patients and their families.

column36: Understanding the preconception health of women with disabilities in Ontario: Service user and provider perspectives
column37: Being healthy before pregnancy is vital, as preconception health (PCH) impacts maternal and infant outcomes. However, half of pregnancies are unplanned and improving health at the first prenatal visit is too late to prevent poor outcomes. Women with disabilities (WWD) represent about 10% of women of reproductive age and are becoming pregnant at similar rates to women without disabilities; yet, there is little research on the PCH of WWD in Canada. Attending to the PCH of WWD is important, as WWD experience physical and psychological health disparities that put them at increased risk for poor PCH. Further, compared to women without disability, WWD have lower rates of contraception use and experience higher rates of unplanned pregnancy, short spacing between pregnancies, and sexual violence. Using qualitative methods, this study aims to (1) understand the PCH of WWD in Ontario, (2) explore how social, health, and health care factors may impact the PCH of WWD, and (3) identify how knowledge of barriers to care and risks for poor PCH outcomes can be used to improve care for WWD. Women from three disability subgroups (physical, sensory, intellectual and developmental) and health care providers will be interviewed. Analysis will explore similarities and differences across disability subgroups, as well as compare WWD and health care providers' responses, to identify key PCH health needs of WWD, what might be contributing to PCH disparities among WWD, and which interventions may be most effective. This study will be one of the first to explore similarities and differences across disability groups from the perspective of both WWD and care providers. This study will have important implications for reducing health disparities among WWD; it will inform the development of interventions to improve the PCH of WWD, which may in turn contribute to better outcomes for WWD and their infants.

column36: What comes next? Uptake of cancer risk reduction strategies by women who receive inconclusive results from BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing
column37: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the 2nd leading cause of cancer death for women in Canada. 20% of familial forms of breast cancer are due to genetic mutations, most commonly in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. When a risk-increasing mutation is identified in these genes, women are eligible for risk reduction strategies such as yearly breast cancer screening with MRI and mammography and/or preventive surgery. However, many women who are tested do not receive a definitive result as to whether they carry a genetic predisposition to cancer; instead, many receive inconclusive results (a mutation with uncertain cancer risk is identified or no BRCA mutation is identified but a mutation may exist in an untested gene). For these women, cancer risk is harder to predict. Although no previous studies have shown a benefit to risk-reduction strategies for women with inconclusive results, current guidelines are vague about the need for further treatment. It is, therefore, likely that recommendations made to these women vary by treating physician. The goal of this study is to examine how frequently women who receive inconclusive results from BRCA testing undertake risk reducing strategies. Specifically, we will use a unique data platform that brings together genetic testing and health care utilization information for close to 17,000 women who underwent BRCA testing in Ontario from 2007 to 2016. We will determine factors that influence the use of screening and preventive surgery, including the role of an inconclusive test result. In examining how often these strategies are used, we will identify targets for patients and healthcare provider education around genetic test interpretation and risk reduction. As direct-to-consumer genetic testing becomes more readily available, accurate genetic test interpretation will be increasingly important as both patients and physicians will be faced with the challenge of how to manage an inconclusive genetic test result.

column36: Brain connectivity and cognitive control in children with Tourette syndrome: the impact of comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
column37: Tourette syndrome (TS) is a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one phonic tic. TS patients often faces various comorbid disorders, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). For a child with TS, having comorbid ADHD comes with a lot of complications, such as more inhibitory deficits and increased impulsivity. Our project aims to assess the brain function of children with TS and/or ADHD. We want to identify markers that would facilitate an earlier diagnosis of these conditions. An earlier diagnosis would enable treatment strategies to be put in place more quickly. For instance, earlier treatment of ADHD symptoms could prevent the development of several behavioral problems in adulthood. To evaluate the brain function of these children, we will use electroencephalography, which records the electrical activity of the brain. We will evaluate the connections between some regions of the brain during different conditions. We will first use a cognitive control task. Cognitive control is very important in TS patients because it allows them to control their tics in certain situations and for short periods. In addition, we will evaluate brain function directly while children with TS are voluntarily attempting to suppress their tics. We expect that having both TS and ADHD will have a negative impact on cognitive control. This should also be reflected in brain function, which should differ between children with TS, those with ADHD, and those with both TS and ADHD.

column36: Population-Level Effects of Pregnancy Complications on Maternal and Offspring Mortality
column37: Pregnancy complications, including hypertension and diabetes during pregnancy, occur in 1-8% of pregnancies and are associated with serious outcomes in mothers and infants. Previous studies have shown that women with more than 2 complications and/or consecutive pregnancies affected by pregnancy complications are at higher risk of a negative outcome. Additionally, women with pregnancy complications have been found to have a higher risk of heart disease. New research suggests that these complications may also impact the long-term health of children. There is therefore a need to understand how pregnancy complications effect the risk of death in women and their children and how the risk of death differs within and between pregnancies. There is also a need to find new risk factors that will identify women and children at increased risk of death. This project will use 46,474 women enrolled in the Collaborative Perinatal Project from 1959-1965 across the United States. Children of women enrolled in this study will also be used. We will examine the effect of pregnancy complications on the risk of all-cause and cause-specific death among women and children and how this effect differs within and between pregnancies. A predictive model will be subsequently developed to identify factors prior to or during pregnancy that predict future risk of death in women and children. This study will provide a better understanding of the impact of pregnancy complications on the risk of death in women and children. The findings of this work will also help to isolate risk factors that can identify women and children at highest risk. This work has the potential to improve the long-term health outcomes of mothers and children through the early detection and management of risk factors.

column36: Eukaryotic Elongation Factor-2 Kinase (eEF2K) as a new therapeutic target in pediatric brain cancer
column37: More than 600,000 people in North America die from cancer each year. Within the scope of people affected by this disease, brain cancer is the most common pediatric solid cancer, devastating the lives of more than 4,600 children and their families every year. Aggressive brain surgery and radiation are the treatments currently available for children. However, these therapies are often ineffective and cause serious side effects on the developing brain, such as permanent seizures and learning disabilities. Thus, more specific and less damaging therapies are urgently needed. Cancers grow very quickly and need high quantities of nutrients. However, increased nutrient supply to the cancer is not always possible for the human body. When cancer cells do not have enough nutrients to grow, they find ways to compensate for this. Our laboratory team at the BC Cancer Agency recently made a significant discovery: a small protein called eEF2K helps cancer to survive when it has no nutrients. Pediatric brain tumors produce a very high amount of this protein. In addition, children with tumors that produce excessive eEF2K protein usually die earlier than children with tumors that do not produce the protein. We are convinced that by blocking the function of the eEF2K protein, we can starve tumors to death. To test our idea, we will work with cells derived from childhood brain tumors such as medulloblastoma. We will first study if cells lacking the eEF2K protein grow slower under starvation conditions, compared to cells that have the protein. We will then grow these cells in mice and look at the same effect. If our assumption is confirmed, we will try a drug that blocks eEF2K to determine if it can kill tumor cells. No specific and effective therapy for children with brain tumors is currently available. Our study is crucial not only in understanding how eEF2K affects pediatric brain tumors, but also in finding new possible therapies for children affected by this destructing disease.

column36: Elucidating the role of prefrontal cortex GABAergic interneuron subtypes in the enduring effects of adolescent cannabis exposure using electrophysiological and behavioral approaches
column37: Adolescence is a dynamic period characterized by maturation of higher-order cognitive functions, including decision-making and working memory, to their adult levels. It can also be a period of increased risk-taking, during which some individuals commence use of drugs such as cannabis. Several of the biological changes that support adolescent maturation of complex behavior occur within a brain region called the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Given the extended development of PFC, it is particularly vulnerable to the deleterious effects of drug-taking during adolescence, which may have lasting consequences on cognition and increase risk for psychiatric disorders including schizophrenia. Indeed, past research has shown that cannabis exposure, particularly during the early adolescent period, leads to enduring changes in cognitive and emotional processes that stem from PFC functional changes. In particular, certain PFC cells that release the inhibitory neurochemical GABA undergo physiological maturation during adolescence that is disrupted by drug exposure. PFC GABA cells are also impacted in schizophrenia, and may represent the cellular mechanism by which cannabis exposure increases the risk of developing the disorder. This proposal is aimed at identifying the cellular players that underlie the long-lasting effects of cannabis use during adolescence within PFC. It uses electrophysiological approaches to examine how cannabis exposure affects the function of particular types of PFC GABA cells, including how they process input from other brain regions, coupled with behavioral approaches probing how these alterations may be implicated in cognitive changes relevant to psychiatric disorders. These insights into impacts of cannabis may be particularly valuable given its recent legalization and possible increased accessibility for adolescents. Furthermore, the work has the potential to identify new intervention targets for schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders.

column36: Elucidating the mechanisms driving formation and maintenance of healthy heart valves
column37: Heart valves are important structures that promote optimal circulation within the body. Heart valve disease affects about 2.5% of the Canadian population, and can cause debilitating health issues or mortality. Identifying the genes involved in heart valve formation or valve dysfunction will give insight into the underlying cause of heart valve disease. My proposed work uses zebrafish as a model to study valve development and disease, with the aim of potentially applying our findings in a clinical setting and identifying genetic targets for diagnosis and therapeutic treatments. My first aim is to characterize the development of valve interstitial cells (VICs), which are crucial specialized cells that maintain valve strength and flexibility. I am particularly interested in studying the roles of three molecules - Nfatc1, Notch and Wnt - all of which have been linked to heart valve defects. By genetically altering their expression, I can examine the effects on VIC development and valve function. Furthermore, I propose to identify targets of Nfatc1, a molecule whose function is to regulate genes that control cellular behaviours. In patients, drugs inhibiting Nfatc1 alleviate heart problems, but have strong off-target effects. Finding Nfatc1 targets has the potential to yield more specialized therapies for treating valve dysfunction. My second aim is to study the molecular anomalies that manifest in valve disease progression. A molecular aberration found in diseased valves is abnormal overactivation of the Wnt pathway. I propose to examine the effects of increasing Wnt in normal VICs, and perform a large scale screen to identify the misregulated molecules. In particular, I am interested in whether Wnt overactivation induces pro-inflammation effects that cause excessive immune response and valve pathogenesis. In the long term, I aim to establish an assay for compounds that can alleviate inflammatory response causing symptoms of valve disease.

column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, incurable disease with painful symptoms including joint stiffness and swelling affecting more than 300 000 Canadians. We are studying how these proteins interact, and how the FcRn could predispose people to develop RA, when they possess a variation in a gene that encodes for a specific Fcgamma receptor, the FcgammaR3a. We will test whether a new medication that blocks the FcRn can be beneficial in mice which have been genetically engineered to have the FcgammaR3a variation and predisposed to RA. These studies will help us understand basic biological mechanisms involving the FcRn and FcgammaR3a, which will help us understand why people with the FcgammaR3a variation develop rheumatoid arthritis or other autoimmune diseases. Our research may lead to personalized medical treatments for rheumatoid arthritis, which will depend on a person's genetics.

column36: Using eHealth Technology to Drive Shared Decision-Making in Asthma Care
column37: Asthma affects 7.8% of Canadians, leads to serious respiratory symptoms, and could cost our health system $4.2 billion per year by 2030. Health-related smartphone apps can provide patients with personalized health information anytime and anywhere, allowing them to better manage diseases like asthma. Health providers can also benefit from electronic tools to improve the efficiency and quality of asthma care. Together, patients and health care providers could use a smartphone app to engage in discussions about asthma medication choices. We previously built the Electronic Asthma Management System (eAMS). The system required patients to complete a questionnaire about their asthma on a tablet device in the waiting room and this information was processed and transmitted to their doctor's computer. Our pilot study of this tool showed that it does improve care, however less than one third of patients completed the tablet questionnaire. We are now improving the system by developing and testing an asthma care app that will: 1) allow patients to complete the questionnaire on their own devices; and 2) provide a tool that will help patients and doctors to make shared decisions about medication choices. We will integrate this app with the eAMS such that both systems share all data. This study aims to test the updated system to see if and how patients and doctors actually use it, if they are satisfied with it, and how it affects the care that they receive. If successful, our unique approach may be a model for the design of similar technologies for the care of other chronic diseases. Ultimately, we will seek to implement our app and asthma care system across Canada to improve not only the way that healthcare is delivered, but also the everyday health of Canada's 2.4 million asthma sufferers.

column36: Assessing the effectiveness of a structured exercise program on exercise- and disease-related outcomes in a long-term lifestyle intervention study for the secondary prevention of heart disease.
column37: Cardiovascular disease affects the heart and major blood vessels and is the second leading cause of death in Canada. Lifestyle behaviours account for the majority of cardiovascular disease risk. Consuming a diet rich in plant-based foods decreases disease risk factors, namely cholesterol and inflammation. Regular exercise also mitigates disease risk; however, some evidence suggests that women may not respond to exercise the same way as men. Moreover, whether the long-term combination of an established diet for cholesterol reduction, called the Portfolio Diet, and exercise training enhances health improvements in adults with cardiovascular disease is unknown. The purpose of our ongoing, multi-centre, three year, randomized clinical trial is to investigate the combined effects of the Portfolio Diet and structured exercise training on health markers in adults with cardiovascular disease. We hypothesize that consuming a Portfolio Diet will enhance improvements in body composition (reduced fat and increased muscle mass), disease risk biomarkers (lower cholesterol and inflammation) and fitness following regular exercise training. To investigate this, we will recruit a large sample of 200 adults with cardiovascular disease. Participants will be randomized to receive either i) food from the Portfolio Diet and a monitored exercise program; ii) food from the Portfolio Diet and advice on healthy exercise habits; iii) advice on healthy eating and a monitored exercise program; and iv) advice on both healthy eating and exercise habits. We will compare health changes across the four groups and between men and women. The major goal of this project is to provide evidence-based recommendations for long-term, feasible, lifestyle modification strategies for improving cardiovascular disease risk. Importantly, this research will also increase our knowledge about the influence of sex on lifestyle behaviour-induced improvements on the secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

column36: WNT signaling in the postnatal brain: roles for Interferon Regulatory Factor 2 Binding Protein-Like in development and neuronal maintenance.
column37: We have recently identified IRF2BPL as a novel human disease gene causing a progressive and severe neurodegenerative disorder. Patients are born normal, but at age ~3-5 years, begin falling, develop seizures and eventually become immobile before the age of 10. Brain imaging in older patients shows progressive brain atrophy. Neuronal loss of IRF2BPL in fruit flies results in gradual neurodegeneration and behavioral defects reminiscent of the human condition. The function of IRF2BPL is very poorly understood across species. My preliminary data indicates that IRF2BPL can inhibit WNT signaling in vivo, a critical biological pathway conserved in animals with well-established roles in development including the brain. However, a role for WNT signaling in the mature brain and neurodegenerative disorders is currently ill defined. A cell based study suggested that IRF2BPL reduces WNT signaling activity by ubiquitinating beta-catenin, a core WNT activator. I hypothesize that IRF2BPL inhibits WNT signaling and that loss of IRF2BPL should result in excess WNT signaling in the postnatal brain. In this proposal, I will: 1) Determine the functional consequences of increased WNT signaling in mature brains and determine if IRF2BPL loss of function ectopically activates WNT signaling in vivo. 2) Determine if IRF2BPL targets beta-catenin or other proteins implicated in WNT signaling in flies, mice and human cells. 3) Generate and characterize Irf2bpl knockout mice and assess if WNT signaling is affected. I will also use these mice to model the human disease as they may serve as a therapeutic testing platform. Mechanistic insight into a role for WNT, which is highly therapeutically targetable as drugs have been developed to reduce WNT signaling, and IRF2BPL in the postnatal brain will deepen our understanding of both neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Sustained engagement in HIV care: Novel approaches to identify and evaluate the impact of socioeconomic disparities
column37: HIV remains a global public health threat, with 37 million people living with HIV (PLWH). Advancements in HIV therapy have transformed the clinical landscape increasing life expectancies and reducing new HIV infections. But benefits rest on the lifetime commitment of PLWH to adhere to treatments. Over the last 20 years, the proportion of patients virally suppressed- and therefore those with controlled infections- has risen from 25% to over 80% in the United States (US). Although encouraging, progress is uneven and falls short of global targets. Race continues to play a differentiating role in the inequality of HIV infections. African Americans make up more than half of new cases while only representing 14% of the US population. Moreover, even in cities with universal health care coverage such as San Francisco, where overall ~85% of PLWH are virally suppressed, that number plummets to 30% among those marginally housed and homeless. Worldwide, people who fare poorly in HIV care have little or no access to care, face stigma and encounter socio-structural barriers. Socioeconomic status and race have been shown to predict health outcomes. But research on this topic has not optimally captured the multi-dimensional ways in which disparities interact and how this leads to adverse health outcomes for PLWH. For example, low income is often the consequence of mental illness, substance abuse, limited education. Even though each of these factors has been shown to be associated with poor health outcomes, the extent to which these factors intersect to create underlying expressions of socioeconomic deprivation remains to be explored. Identifying and understanding the consequences of disparities is the first step in addressing inequalities through targeted interventions and health policies. Results from this research will characterize and evaluate the role of socioeconomic drivers of HIV care engagement, which will ultimately play a critical role in ending the HIV epidemic.

column36: Investigating host susceptibility factors and a pathobiont in Crohn's disease-like intestinal inflammation
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of Crohn's disease (CD) in the world. This chronic inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract significantly reduces the quality of life for the 130 000 Canadians living with CD as they experience symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and fatigue. While the composition of bacteria in the gut is severely altered in CD patients, it is unclear whether this is secondary to intestinal inflammation or plays a causal role in the disease. Moreover, it is unclear whether a specific bacterium can trigger disease in genetically susceptible individuals. A major limitation in understanding the causes of CD is the lack of experimental models that address these factors. Intriguingly, we found that the deficiency of genes involved in bacteria detection and killing triggers spontaneous intestinal inflammation in mice that resembles CD pathology. Furthermore, development of disease in the genetically susceptible host required the presence of Mucispirillum schaedleri (Mucispirillum), a bacterium that inhabits the colon of normal mice. The current proposal focuses on identifying the processes by which bacteria sensing and Mucispirillum accumulation causes CD-like pathology. This work provides important insights into the causes of CD and offers the possibility of targeting specific-disease causing bacterium as an innovative strategy to treat the CD.

column36: Prospective study of psychosocial predictors and outcomes of breast cancer surgery among women with unilateral breast cancer.
column37: When a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer, the standard of care for surgery is to remove any evidence of disease on the affected breast. However, more and more women are choosing to remove both breasts. This overtreatment has placed increased financial and resource burden on the Canadian healthcare system. In addition, women treated with bilateral mastectomies have an increased risk of post-surgical complications. There is significant interest in finding out why this phenomenon is occurring but research has so far focused on administrative and clinical reasons behind why more women are choosing to remove both breasts. It seems intuitive that psychosocial reasons are playing a major role behind this decision process but this has not been adequately studied. The goal of our studies is to understand why women choose the surgery that they do for their breast cancer, including those who choose to remove both breasts. We will also determine satisfaction and health-related quality of life after such surgeries and compare by surgical procedure (lumpectomy versus removing one breast versus removing both breasts). Women with breast cancer will be recruited at three major hospital centers in Toronto, Ontario (Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, Toronto General Hospital and Women's College Hospital). Baseline information regarding patients and their breast cancer will be collected. We will use validated psychosocial questionnaires and instruments to measure our outcomes of interest, including cancer worry, cancer-related distress, body image, quality of life, decision satisfaction and decision regret. By performing these studies, we hope to understand the psychosocial reasons behind why more women are choosing to remove both breasts when they are diagnosed with breast cancer. In doing so, we may be better able to counsel women with newly-diagnosed breast cancer, with the hopes of not having to overtreat them and lessen the burden on the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Cellular and Molecular Basis for Impaired Autonomic Nervous System Regulation of the Sinoatrial Node in Diabetes Mellitus
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a growing epidemic health issue that is associated with many severe cardiovascular complications that ultimately result in death in as many as 65% of diabetic patients. Included amongst these are cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, which results in an inability to properly regulate heart rate. My objective is to determine how and why abnormal heart rate regulation occurs in diabetic patients. Heart rate is determined by specialized 'pacemaker cells' in a region of the heart called the sinoatrial node (the natural pacemaker present in everyone's heart). Although often attributed to damage to the nerves innervating the sinoatrial node, our work demonstrates that improper regulation of heart rate in diabetes is also associated with abnormal sinoatrial node function, independently of the nerves. This represents an important new way of looking at cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. My proposed studies will greatly advance our understanding of abnormal heart rate regulation in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. This will be accomplished using a range of powerful experimental approaches in intact diabetic mice, as well as in isolated hearts and isolated cells from the sinoatrial node. Our laboratory is one of only a handful worldwide that can study the sinoatrial node in mice, which uniquely positions us carry out these highly important studies. The ultimate goal of our work is to identify new therapeutic targets for cardiovascular disease in diabetics.

column36: TSMS Optimization of Developmental Trajectories in Preschoolers with Stroke (TOTS): Parent-directed, home-based, non-invasive neurostimulation for infants and toddlers with perinatal stroke and hemiparetic cerebral palsy
column37: Stroke in the newborn affects 10,000 Canadian children and is the primary cause of lifelong weakness on one side, a form of cerebral palsy. Evidence-based physical interventions for children with newborn stroke are limited and are often initiated after two years of age. This time period falls beyond the most critical window of opportunity to capitalize on the remarkable ability of the developing brain to change. Early therapies targeting activity of the affected arm have the potential to drive brain development toward better lifelong function. Home therapy may be ideal, but methods to effectively engage and empower families and optimize outcomes are yet to be established. Non-invasive brain stimulation technologies have been shown to augment therapy in older children affected by newborn stroke. While existing technologies are not feasible for small children in the home, a new simple, portable and inexpensive static stimulation has effects that may enhance motor therapy. We propose a clinical trial to establish the safety, feasibility and possible efficacy of combining transcranial static magnetic stimulation with home-based movement therapy to improve motor function in infants and toddlers with newborn stroke. We will enrol 24 children aged 6 to 48 months. Families will complete a six-month home-based goal directed program, with random assignment to either active or placebo stimulation during therapy. Changes in activity levels, motor skill performance, individualized goal achievement, and family well-being will be assessed before, following, and 6-months after the intervention. For the first time, this study brings together non-invasive brain stimulation and early intervention in young children with newborn stroke. Caregivers are directly engaged and empowered to improve their child's motor function. This early, personalized, family-centred, patient-oriented approach has the potential to benefit many of the millions of children globally affected by cerebral palsy.

column36: Measuring and Valuing Health Benefits for Economic Evaluations in Breast Cancer: Development and Validation of a Scoring Algorithm for the BREAST-Q Utility Scale (BREAST-QU)
column37: Explicit rationing attempts to battle fiscal debt and increasing demand for healthcare were the focus of 2018 Ontario provincial elections. While rationing is one of the options to curb health care costs, it slowly disinherits us from the core principles of the Canada Health Act. An alternative solution is to base budget allocation decisions on "value" of healthcare interventions (cost vs. outcome). Quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) is the preferred metric for valuing health outcomes in terms of quality of life (QOL). Once cost per QALY is determined, service with the lowest cost per QALY is chosen. Traditionally, generic preference-based measures (PBM) have been used to calculate QALYs. However, they do not include concerns unique to breast cancer patients (body image, appearance, sexual) and hence lack sensitivity. The BREAST-Q is a widely used and validated breast cancer-specific QOL instrument, but it cannot be used to calculate QALYs. Hence, a descriptive classification system, the BREAST-Q Utility (BREAST-QU), was developed from BREAST-Q using patient interviews and input from an international team of experts. My postdoctoral research will advance this work by generating a scoring algorithm (i.e., preference weights for health states defined by BREAST-QU). A representative sample of the general population and women with breast cancer will be asked to participate in choice-based tasks (discrete choice experiment and best-worst scaling) to identify their preferences for various breast cancer health states. The responses will be analyzed using advanced statistical techniques, resulting in scoring algorithm for the BREAST-QU. The reliability, validity, and responsiveness of BREAST-QU will be assessed. The use of BREAST-QU in clinical practice, economic evaluation and policy-making will be promoted through publications, presentations, and professional networks; ultimately resulting in "biggest bang for the buck" in breast cancer and improved population health.

column36: Identifying clinically-relevant circulating protein biomarkers for osteoporosis
column37: Osteoporosis is an aging-related skeletal disease and a major cause of morbidity and mortality. While therapies currently exist to prevent fractures, current risk stratification algorithms fail to identify the majority of people who fracture. Thus, a major clinical goal in osteoporosis is to identify individuals at risk. Our objective is to improve fracture screening programs by identifying clinically relevant circulating biomarkers for osteoporosis and incorporate them in the risk stratification algorithms. We will first use Mendelian randomization (MR) to high-throughput screen circulating proteins using available proteomic GWAS studies in our large cohort of individuals with osteoporosis phenotypes from UK Biobank and the international GEFOS consortium. We will then validate our prioritized biomarkers in well-characterized cohorts (CaMos and Rotterdam) with rich phenotypic information, by measuring protein levels using validated ELISA based assays. Eventually, we will combine the biomarkers with the strongest prediction power with traditional fracture prediction algorithm (FRAX) and our newly developed polygenic risk score via machine learning, in order to provide clinically-relevant fracture risk stratification. We have already generated preliminary data from 83 candidate biomarkers that associate with fracture and bone mineral density, a major risk factor for osteoporosis, which were identified from 922 proteins. We have prioritized RSPO3 as a novel, functionally relevant biomarker for osteoporosis and the validation process is currently underway. We plan to increase the number of proteins tested to identify additional circulating biomarkers that strongly associated with the risk of fracture, in order to provide targets for clinical interventions and to effectively identify high-risk individuals for more effectively tailored preventive therapy.

column36: CryoEM analysis of the structural dynamics of mitochondrial Complex I during catalysis
column37: Complex I is a large protein found in the energy producing compartments of cells. Complex I is essential for life, performing the first step in a series of chemical reactions that eventually lead to the production of ATP, the chemical energy currency of living cells and is a potential drug target for a number of diseases, including diabetes and cancer. In addition, it is a significant producer of reactive oxygen species, molecules that cause damage to components of the cell and can lead to cell death. The production of reactive oxygen species by Complex I is particularly problematic after tissues are resupplied with oxygenated blood following a period when the supply of oxygenated blood was blocked, such as during a heart attack, stroke, or surgery. During this sort of injury, Complex I transitions between an operative and inoperative state and its structure changes. Importantly, these states are thought to be related to how Complex I carries out its function and its roll in tissue damage through the production of reactive oxygen species. The relationship between structural changes in Complex I and its function remains unknown. In this project, I will use state-of-the-art electron microscopy techniques available at SickKids to determine the structure of mammalian Complex I as it performs its chemical reactions. These experiments will allow me to determine how changes in its structure relate to its function, and will reveal how Complex I operates on a molecular level. This knowledge will help provide a framework for the design of therapeutics to protect against the injury to tissues that occur in heart attack and stroke, and to treat diabetes and cancer. Thus, this project has the potential to improve human health, in particular in relation to cardiovascular disease.

column36: Modeling the long-term contribution of incarceration and of prison-based prevention strategies to drug-related harms among people who inject drugs
column37: Drug use is criminalized at various degrees globally. Incarceration and the period post-release can increase risk for HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections and overdose among people who inject drugs (PWID). Thus, over time, incarceration is likely to be "responsible" for a significant proportion of the total new cases of these health-harms among PWID. Yet, no study has attempted to estimate its potential contribution over time. In addition, access to prison-based strategies such as opioid agonist treatment, needle and syringe provision and naloxone kits, with continuation upon release, can prevent the occurrence of these health harms but no study has yet estimated their potential long-term prevention benefit. This study seeks to address these gaps using mathematical modeling. This technique enables the forecasting of the future burden of an epidemic and of the potential impact of introducing an intervention on its course. Such modelling outputs are widely used by policy-makers to inform their decisions regarding the control of diseases. Given that different global settings have distinct incarceration levels and distinct realistic scenarios of future scale-up of prevention strategies within prisons, these simulations must be tailored to specific settings. In this study, we will carry out the simulations in two distinct settings, Montreal, Canada and Nairobi and Mombasa, Kenya. For each setting, the model parameters will be informed by data collected through two studies (HEPCO, Montreal and TLC-IDU, Nairobi and Mombasa, Kenya). Altogether, this study has the potential to provide estimates on the extent to which incarceration may be fueling HIV and HCV transmission and overdose among PWID, and the necessary scale-up levels of prison-based prevention interventions to achieve meaningful reductions in these health harms over time. In the long-run, findings could inform appropriate public health and policy changes to reduce the burden of HIV, HCV and overdose.

column36: Informing high-resolution functional MRI through modeling microvascular dynamics
column37: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is the most widely used technique for measuring dynamic neuronal activity across the whole brain with no harmful effects, making it an invaluable tool for human neuroscience. FMRI measurements are based on tracking focal changes in blood flow and oxygenation that occur during brain activity to meet energetic demand. Because fMRI is, therefore, an indirect measure of neuronal activity, the confidence with which changes in neuronal activity can be inferred is limited. The hypothesis of this study is that a more complete picture of the blood vessels in the brain, and how they react to brain activity, will help us to better interpret the fMRI signals. New evidence from microscopy studies in rodents indicates that the control of blood flow in response to neuronal activity is far more precise than previously believed, suggesting that fMRI has the potential to be a reliable marker of neuronal activity if measured and interpreted correctly. However, it is challenging to translate these findings to humans since the organization of rodent blood vessels is markedly different from ours. This project will create a 3D reconstruction of the blood vessel network-down to the smallest capillaries-from human brain specimens, from which a model of how the vessels react to neuronal firing to control blood delivery will be generated-and from this, how the fMRI signals change in response to brain activity. To ensure accuracy, the model will be validated against high-resolution human fMRI data acquired on an ultra-high magnetic field strength MRI scanner. This bottom-up approach will provide a crucial missing link between measured fMRI signals and the detailed underlying physiology, helping to better understand fMRI signals and improve our ability to accurately measure brain function.

column36: Growth trajectories of children with autism spectrum disorder: Latent class growth model analysis using two sources of primary care data
column37: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may be at high risk of obesity because of restricted diet with a preference for processed foods, low levels of physical activity participation, excessive screen time, and use of medications that may contribute to weight gain. Previous scientific work has suggested that obesity risk in children with ASD might be seen early, with unhealthy weight gain between 2 to 5 years of age. As ASD now affects about 1 in 68 individuals, results will be important to a large group of Canadian children. I will explore weight trajectories in ASD, using two sources of data: (1) the Applied Research Group for Kids (TARGet Kids!), which collects rich early childhood data from paediatricians' and family doctors' offices, and (2) the Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database (EMRALD(R)), which contains electronic medical record data from family doctors in Ontario. Using statistical methods, I will see how weight trajectories in children with ASD compare to weight trajectories in children without ASD. If the ASD group shows unhealthy weight trajectories (for example, early development of obesity), the time when growth becomes abnormal will be explored. In addition, I will identify what nutritional, behavioural and medical factors are linked with abnormal weight trajectories in ASD. We know that addressing obesity is important, because unhealthy weight is associated with negative impacts on health, quality of life, and use of health services. We also know that children with ASD likely need different types of intervention for obesity than typically developing children. Results of my work will help in preventing and treating obesity specifically in children with ASD, thereby making an important contribution to improving the health of Canadian children.

column36: Dissecting tissue-resident memory T cell heterogeneity in human tissues
column37: Despite the extraordinary advances in medicine over the last few decades, infectious disease remains among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Our understanding of how protective immune responses can be generated and augmented by vaccines or immunotherapies are therefore of prime importance for improving human health. Recent studies have identified a heterogeneous population of non-circulating memory T cells, known as tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), that are distributed in mucosal/barrier sites and are essential in mediating protective immunity during infection and after vaccination. However, due to the difficulty of studying immune cells directly in human tissues, basic questions of how TRM function and how they differ across multiple tissues within the same individual remain unanswered. My research will utilize a unique human tissue resource in which multiple mucosal and lymphoid organs are obtained from research-consented organ donors in order to dissect the similarities and differences between TRM subsets across tissue sites. I will use a combination of cutting-edge techniques including high-dimensional immune profiling, multi-parameter imaging, and single cell transcriptomic approaches to generate a "human atlas" of TRM phenotype and function throughout the human body. With this investigation, my objective is to define and characterize TRM identity and function using a one-of-a-kind tissue resource that allows unprecedented access to study human tissue immunity. Understanding how TRM function in humans is central to the design of new vaccines and immunotherapies aimed at boosting tissue immunity, with the ultimate goal reducing deaths from infectious disease.

column37: To address the need for therapies that eliminate HIV infection, we propose development of a new method to deliver non-viral genome editing enzymes to the immune cells within the body to render them resistant to the virus. The specialized genome editing enzymes we develop will be targeted specifically to immune cells at the front lines of HIV infection, turning off genes required for HIV infectivity and eliminating the need for continued antiretroviral therapy. column37: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are specialized stem cells (SCs) that give rise to the blood and immune cells. First HSCs emerge during the embryogenesis. These new HSCs have a higher ability for proliferation and differentiation into different cell types than the adult HSCs, suggesting that their environment influences their fate. Previous studies showed that SCs reside in small niche environment. Such environments provide a special setting for cell-cell communication, extracellular matrix construction, and control of signalling between the cells. Yet, genes/pathways and expression profile of individual cells within the human embryonic HSCs niches remain poorly understood. Our current inability to generate bona fide human HSCs from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) suggests that these HSCs derived in vitro may have different gene expression profile than the ones developed in embryos due to different stem cell niche environments. Studying these niche environments was difficult until the recent development of the Fluorescent In Situ Sequencing (FISSEQ) by the Church lab. FISSEQ enables single-cell transcriptome sequencing of fixed, intact tissue samples. Subsequent development of a modified version of FISSEQ called targeted FISSEQ (tFISSEQ) allows detection of small RNAs and even proteins by FISSEQ. These technologies, for the very first time, enable us to evaluate the gene expression landscape of SCs and all other cells in the SCs niche, in the context of their native spatial environment. Human PSCs-derived teratoma engrafted in immunodeficient mice, develops HSCs that possess good repopulation ability in secondary recipient mice. This could be a faithful model that represents at least in part the heamogenic emergence process in the embryo. Using tFISSEQ to obtain spatial expression landscape of proteins and miRNAs in the teratoma and PSC-to-HSCs in vitro models will finally shed light on the key effectors and pathways in heamogenic development in human embryos.

column37: Just like humans, mycobacteria, such as the species that cause tuberculosis (TB) and leprosy, need oxygen to live. This combination of essentiality and uniqueness make these systems vulnerable to drugs designed to treat mycobacterial infections. Indeed, the breakthrough drug bedaquiline (also known as Sirturo, produced by Janssen Pharmaceutica), which was the first new TB therapeutic in 40 years when it was approved in 2012, targets the process of using oxygen to burn fuel and provide cells with energy. We will use the technique of electron cryomicroscopy (cryoEM) to reveal, at near-atomic resolution, how candidate drugs target an essential component of the cellular respiration system in mycobacteria, known as the respiratory supercomplex. These structures will provide information on how drugs can be improved, through a process known as structure-based drug design. We will also perform high-throughput experiments, known as screens, to find new candidate drugs and use our structural studies to guide the improvement of these molecules into useful therapeutics. Together, these studies will help us and our collaborators to lay the foundation for a new generation of drugs to combat the constant threat of mycobacterial drug resistance.

column37: Health professionals often work in silos. If any health information is communicated, the most common formats are paper or fax. Separate Delphi processes will be conducted to refine the lists of information needs and components, and to prioritize by value added to the eLCP for 'patient and family' and 'health professional' views. column36: Investigating the role of APJ heterodimers in pain modulation
column37: A large number of currently prescribed drugs target G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). These transmembrane proteins form the most important protein family present at the cell surface. GPCRs are involved in transducing a signal from the surrounding cellular environment into intracellular activity. Drugs targeting the same binding pocket as the endogenous ligand may have an activity similar to that of the ligand (agonist), or may block its effect (antagonists). Prescribed drugs often have side effects that could be due to a lack of specificity of these molecules. Traditionally, GPCR signaling was conceptualized with monomeric receptors, however, it is now accepted that some GPCRs are able to associate with others to form heteromeric complexes. The close relationship maintained by two GPCRs in a dimeric complex could influence the intracellular signaling events triggered by each. In this study, we propose to evaluate the activity of dimers formed by the apelin receptor and the neurotensin NTS1 receptor, or the apelin receptor and the kappa-opioid receptor. These three GPCRs are known to have powerful analgesic properties, thus we would like to evaluate the role played by these heterodimeric complexes in pain modulation. A better understanding of the role of heterodimeric complexes involving the apelin receptor would allow the development of new molecules specifically targeting these GPCR dimers. Such drugs would be more efficient, more specific, and therefore, have fewer side effects.

column36: Identifying the neuronal activity of adult born neurons in the dentate gyrus that support behavioural pattern separation.
column37: Until as recently as the 1990s it was assumed that in the adult brain cells die, but are never born. This was shown to be incorrect: in some regions of the brain - and of interest to us, the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus - new cells are born. Evidence increasingly suggests that these adult born neurons (ABNs) are essential for hippocampal function; specifically, in the formation of distinct representations of similar inputs, a mechanism known as pattern separation (PS). Abnormalities in adult neurogenesis, and consequent PS impairments, were then linked to several neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases, such as Parkinsons, Alzheimer's, Huntingtons disease and schizophrenia. Although we know about ABNs involvement in PS, we know almost nothing about how ABNs operate at the network level to support it. This is in part because determining the answer to this question is difficult: it requires recording from multiple, sparsely-organized neurons along with precise and well-controlled assessment of a subtle aspect of cognition. To do so, we proposed to use Miniscopes, that allow us to visualize the activity of large populations of neurons during behavior, in combination with genetically targeted expression of a calcium indicator to ABNs in the DG. By combining cutting-edge technology in calcium imaging with precise assessment of behavioral PS we are confident that we can determine how ABNs supports PS hippocampal processing at the network and behavioral levels. Because of the paucity of information on the role of ABNs in cognition, using precise molecular and behavioural tools to discover clear evidence of this relationship along with underlying mechanism will be high-impact and transformative; understanding the basis of this process will help us to develop new tools for an early diagnosis of different disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease or dementias, and will unveil new targets for intervention in neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases.

column36: Investigating the role of cellular metabolism in effector T cell responses and T cell exhaustion
column37: T cells play a crucial role in the immune response against infections and cancer. Over the course of an immune response, T cells engage various metabolic pathways to meet the energetic demands of expansion and development of their effector functions. The proposed research aims to characterize the metabolic pathways used by T cells during both functional and dysregulated immune responses. The different strains of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus are ideal to study T cell metabolism. The Armstrong strain induces a normal T cell response in mice. In contrast, infection of mice with the Clone-13 strain leads to T cell "exhaustion", a term used to describe T cells that are dysfunctional. Exhausted T cells, which are often associated with chronic infections as well as cancer, are characterized by their reduced proliferation and poor effector functions. Taken together, these infection models serve as great tools to study cellular metabolism in T cells during both normal and dysregulated immune responses. Recent studies suggest that exhausted T cells have altered cellular metabolism. The unique immune and metabolic environment linked with chronic infections and cancer triggers metabolic adaptation in exhausted T cells to promote survival in these stressful conditions. Our research therefore aims to characterize and compare the metabolic demands of functional and exhausted T cells. In addition, our work will determine the impact of immune checkpoint therapy, which is used to reverse T cell exhaustion to treat cancer, on T cell metabolism. Finally, by performing a large-scale screen of metabolic genes in T cells, our research seeks to identify novel metabolic pathways that regulate T cell function and exhaustion. Overall, the findings of this study will lead to a better understanding of how metabolism regulates T cell function and may potentially uncover novel strategies to increase the effectiveness of T cell-based therapies by modulating cellular metabolism.

column36: Reducing patient boarding practices and impact on patient mortality by using optimization and machine learning methodologies that account for the heterogeneity of individual patients
column37: Critically ill patients, requiring timely and specialized treatment, are subject to substantial delays before admission into intensive care units (ICUs) due to patient overcrowding and the lack of staffed ICU beds. Patient "boarding" has become a common strategy for hospitals to provide care for patients despite bed allocation problems in the ICU and involves caring for patients in alternative locations, such as emergency departments, until an ICU bed is available. However, these alternative locations are generally neither trained for, nor designed to treat critically ill patients, compromising the quality of care provided. As such, patient boarding and delays in ICU admission significantly increases increase patient mortality The development of optimization and simulation tools have been promising towards reducing the number of boarded patients and delays to admission but rarely account for differences between each individual patient. By assessing patients at an individual level, hospitals may more accurately measure the impact of delays to ICU admission on patient survival. The goal of my proposed research is to develop a novel optimization model, integrated with machine learning algorithms, that accounts for the heterogeneity of individual patients to reduce boarding practices and patient mortality. To do this, I will estimate the difference in survival between boarded and nonboarded patients based on individual patient demographics and disease characteristics, and operating information from hospitals. I will then develop an optimization model to optimize decisions regarding patient boarding, bed capacity, and staffing to maximize the predicted survival of each patient. The novel combination of predictive and optimization methodologies will allow hospitals to minimize the effects of patient boarding, reduce and eliminate boarding practices, and ultimately increase patient survival.

column36: Generation of Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Left Ventricular Cardiomyocytes for the Treatment of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
column37: The normal human heart has two pumping chambers: the right ventricle and left ventricle. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs (low-pressure system), whereas the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body (high-pressure system). Some children are born without a left ventricle, a malformation called hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). To survive, these children must undergo surgery to connect the right ventricle to the rest of the body. However, the right ventricle, which is designed to pump blood into a low-pressure system, is often unable to sustain the high pressure of the rest of the body, and gradually starts failing, leading to heart failure and death. Unfortunately, we currently have no drugs to treat this type of heart failure. The goal of our project is to develop a novel therapy for HLHS using human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). These cells are unique in that they can give rise to all the cell types in the body. Our lab has previously designed a protocol to generate heart muscle cells - called cardiomyocytes - from hPSCs. However, all cardiomyocytes are not identical, and there are significant differences between cardiomyocytes in the right versus left ventricle. We hypothesize that cardiomyocytes from the left ventricle are better suited to sustain high pressure and that transplanting left ventricular cardiomyocytes into a pressure-overloaded right ventricle could prevent heart failure. The aims of our proposal are to 1) understand the molecular differences between right and left ventricle cardiomyocytes; 2) elaborate a protocol to make left ventricle cardiomyocytes from hPSCs; 3) transplant left ventricle cardiomyocytes into pigs with a pressure-overloaded right ventricle to see if these cells can prevent failure. If successful, this project could transform the care of children with HLHS. This would have a profound impact on our healthcare system, as HLHS has become the largest driver of cost in pediatric cardiovascular care.

column36: Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) as a Crucial Regulatory Cytokine and Therapeutic Target in Ankylosing Spondylitis
column37: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common form of spine arthritis which causes bones in the spine to fuse together, making the spine rigid and leading to severe low back pain (LBP). The main characteristics in AS are inflammation and abnormal new bone formation. Despite biomedical advancements in suppressing joint inflammation, there is no effective treatment to slow down the bone formation. The exact mechanism that links inflammation and spinal bone fusion remains unknown. Therefore, finding the key regulators that control both inflammation and bone formation is critical in AS. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a molecule plays pivotal roles in inflammation which is also reported as a potential regulator for bone formation. However, the roles of MIF in AS have never been explored. We recently discovered that the expression of MIF is remarkably higher in blood obtained from AS patients compared to healthy individuals. We also determined that MIF has a great potential as a disease progression marker in the prediction of spinal bone fusion. In my preliminary data using a well-established mouse model of AS, I found that the expression of MIF in the both serum and tissue are remarkably higher in mice with AS compared to healthy mice. Mice with enhanced MIF expression clearly showed AS clinical features including severe arthritis and new bone formation in spine and ankle joints. In contrast, MIF deficient mice or MIF suppression with specific blockers dramatically prevented the AS clinical features. I also determined the cell groups that substantially produce MIF in AS disease conditions. Interestingly, injection of these cells into a MIF deficient healthy mouse led to AS clinical features, whereas blocking the function of these cells also blocked the AS clinical features. This proposal aims to comprehensively confirm my pilot studies on the role of MIF in AS disease-onset and progression, and establish MIF as a new therapeutic target in AS.

column36: Identification of novel vulnerabilities and therapeutic strategies for breast cancers with acquired resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors
column37: Improvements in the early detection and drug treatments for breast cancer have led to increased rates of survival and cure. However, metastatic breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body remain incurable and represent a major challenge. The recent development of a new targeted treatments called CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) have substantially improved the ability to control disease in the most common form of metastatic breast cancer. Unfortunately, this therapy does not provide a cure. Despite the initial response to the treatment, resistance to CDK4/6i eventually develops and tumors continue to grow. Since the tumors evolve during this process, finding new strategies for breast cancers that acquire resistance to CDK4/6i is an imperative for improving survival rates. To address this health challenge, I will use cutting edge laboratory tools identify the factors which the drug-resistant breast tumors rely on to survive and grow. Then, blocking the function of these genes by using specific targeted drugs will allow us to tackle the tumor cell vulnerabilities, and develop new approaches to improve the survival of these patients. My discoveries could be tested through clinical trials, and linked to specific markers to permit "personalized" treatment in this setting. The findings from this project have the potential to be rapidly integrated into the clinical management of patients and to ultimately improve breast cancer survival.

column36: The Impact of Exposure to Dolutegravir and other HIV Antiretrovirals during Pregnancy: Risks Associated with Neural Tube Defects and Impaired Metabolism
column37: The majority of people living with HIV are women of childbearing age. Dolutegravir (DTG) and other integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTI) are commonly used antiretrovirals (ARVs) in people living with HIV, including pregnant women. While these ARVs are very good at preventing transmission of HIV from mother to child, the secondary effects of ARVs, which include maternal metabolic perturbations and negative effects on early fetal development remain a concern. Higher incidence of neural tube defects (NTD) in women living with HIV receiving DTG from conception was reported by an ongoing NIH-funded observational study in Botswana. These findings highlight the urgent need to improve our understanding of the underlying pathophysiology associated with DTG exposure in pregnancy. Maternal obesity and diabetes are recognised risk factors for NTD. DTG has been associated with hyperglycemia and metabolic complications are common side-effects of ARVs. In this study we will investigate the impact of exposure to DTG and other INSTIs during pregnancy on maternal metabolic health and fetal development - focusing on NTD - using a mouse model. We will examine whether DTG exposure affects maternal liver function and glucose metabolism. We will study the effect of DTG exposure on insulin-responsive tissues and examine the effects on insulin production and activity. Our study will help to determine if DTG exposure increases the risk for NTD and if this risk extends to other INSTIs. We will identify potential biomarkers of NTD in DTG exposed pregnancies, and mechanistically assess biological pathways contributing to NTD, specifically metabolic dysregulation. Our study will address critical knowledge gaps in our understanding of the pathobiology of NTD in the context of ARV use in pregnancy, establish a rational basis for further evaluation of effective interventions, and help inform regimen selection in pregnancy.

column37: Epilepsy is a neurological disease where the brain experiences seizures repeatedly over a life-time. Seizures are debilitating states of abnormal and widespread firing of neurons in the brain. Their impact on an individual's life is significant. Given their largely unpredictable nature, epilepsy patients may lose their ability to drive and work in certain jobs, thus suffering from a loss of independence. Furthermore, about half of all epilepsy cases cannot be managed by medication alone. Currently, the only solution for these 'medication-resistant' patients is invasive surgery to excise the region of the brain causing the seizures. I am interested in seizures because they appear to be the result of a "final common pathway" that develops across a myriad of neurological disorders including genetic disorders, stroke, brain tumors, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's. This begs the question, what is this mechanistic "final common pathway", that allows the brain to transition unpredictably to the abnormal neuronal firing seen during seizures? Our hypothesis is that epilepsy develops in the brain when populations of neurons lose their ability to efficiently parse incoming inputs into their various parts, known as de-correlation. When these neurons are not able to sufficiently de-correlate incoming inputs from other brain regions, they begin to fire in a hyper-synchronous manner that defines seizure activity. Our lab's vision is to develop a neuro-electronics platform, precisely analogous to a computer chip, that can be implanted into the brain. This computer chip will have the ability to detect the transition of the brain into the abnormal seizure state and provide electrical stimulation to prevent the seizure from fully taking form. Such a device would routinely stop seizures in a patient's brain without them even knowing it. My doctoral studies will contribute to the development of this device by providing mechanistic insights into seizures and epilepsy.

column36: Overcoming Obstacles in Cancer Nanomedicine Delivery using a Versatile In Situ Ultrasound-Triggered Microbubble-to-Nanoparticle Conversion
column37: Difficult-to-treat solid tumours have long been a problem for the cancer research community. While modern advances in nanomedicine have created smart drugs that are designed to specifically target different cancers, the improvement they provide is limited by the amount of drug that can infiltrate the complex tumour environment relative to normal, healthy tissue. The development of a delivery system that could load drugs and be selectively triggered to release them into the tumour would revolutionize drug design for some of the deadliest cancers. In 2015, researchers discovered that specially designed contrast agents called microbubbles could be converted into stable nanostructures using a particular type of ultrasound. While microbubbles themselves must remain in the blood vessels, these smaller structures have the potential to leave the circulation and enter their surrounding environment. This opens up the possibility of loading a microbubble with therapeutic nanoparticles and initiating the conversion at a tumour boundary, enhancing local delivery at the tumour site. Because the delivery platform would not depend on the drug itself, it could be used to deliver all types of nanoagents in a versatile and consistent manner. This would open new doors for those designing cancer drugs, allowing for researchers to use more specialized nanomedicines at lower doses and with fewer systemic side-effects. This tool and its accompanying shift in the mindset of drug development is necessary in order to produce the next wave of therapies that will help us fight the most lethal cancers.

column36: Sniffing around the Issue: investigating the relationship between solvent use and HIV risk
column37: HIV disproportionally affects the indigenous peoples of Canada with an incident rate 3.5 times higher than the national average and is associated with social-health factors such as poverty. Solvent use, the inhaling of substances to get a psychoactive effect, among street-involved individuals in Winnipeg is considerably higher than the population average. As HIV risk and solvent use are both associated with poverty, understanding how they interact with each other is an important question. Inflammation is a major biological risk factor for contracting HIV. Since solvent use is believed to cause inflammation, it may contribute to HIV acquisition risk and disease progression. However, there is a little information about the effect of solvent use on the immune system generally or HIV susceptibility specifically. Following consultations with the community, and in conjunction with our community partner Sunshine House, I conducted a pilot study of 14 HIV- solvent users and 13 community matched controls. When I analyzed their blood, I found that solvent users exhibited higher levels of immune activation. To confirm and extend this observation, we will enroll 100 Individuals with and without HIV who are or are not solvent users. We will perform studies to determine if solvent users have more inflammation than matched non-solvent users and if HIV positive individuals are at greater risk for faster HIV-disease progression. We will assess the impact of solvent use on: bacteria access to the blood, markers of inflammation and the functioning of the immune system. Understanding the effects of solvent use on the immune system and the potential impact on HIV risk and diseases progression is an important step in improving the health of this underserved community.

column36: So Far From Denendeh
column37: I am a Dene woman who was removed from Denendeh before I was born. I am a member of the Deninu Kue First Nation in Northwest Territories. I am an image-based storyteller. I come from generations of translators but I do not speak my language. My translation takes place in a different capacity. I am a translator of images. I situate Dene concepts of wellness in digital images I paint and I extract story from them. In my thesis, I will use Dene land-based systems of knowledge and image-based storytelling as my methodology). Specifically, I will use the arts-based approach of digital painting whereby I will paint images and extract stories to draw out Indigenous experience and perspectives about disability. Paintings give me the ability to confront the colonial indignities my family have suffered while simultaneously illuminating our resilience as Indigenous people. It is important to be truthful about the brutality of colonialism, yet I must honor our strength, spirit and resilience in my thesis. My objective in this thesis is to explore the disabling effects of colonialism by reflecting on and contrasting: (1) my journey as an Indigenous person who has been diagnosed with a disability (i.e., a learning disability) and (2) the journey of my father as an Indigenous person who was diagnosed with a disability (i.e. a mobility impairment caused by polio). I will use arts-based Indigenous research methods to compare our journeys in terms of our educational/academic and healthcare/clinical experiences as 'disabled' individuals. I will also explore the role of healing and 'rehabilitation' in addressing our disabilities and the disabling effects of the academic and healthcare structures. Both were extremely harmful; there was no healing to take place in the academy or through clinical methods of rehabilitation. We rejected colonial constructed identities. Rather, I will explore how rehabilitation took place through reclamation of culture.

column36: Integrating Indigenous Ways of Knowing into overdose responses for urban Indigenous people who use drugs
column37: The overdose epidemic remains one of the most pressing public health issues in Canada. In British Columba (BC), Indigenous people who use drugs (IPWUD) have been disproportionally affected by the overdose crisis. Further, it has become clear that overdose epidemic patterns are different among IPWUD. For example, while non-Indigenous men are overdosing at greater rates than non-Indigenous women, Indigenous women remain disproportionately impacted by the overdose crisis, and are experiencing non-fatal overdoses and overdose deaths at rates similar to Indigenous men. Diverse models of overdose-focused interventions are now being implemented in jurisdictions such as Vancouver's Downtown Eastside neighbourhood. However, research to date has failed to examine the overdose risk environment surrounding IPWUD living off reserve in inner cities. Given the ongoing harms experienced by off-reserve IPWUD, research is urgently needed to improve overdose-focused harm reduction and substance use programs for this population. This study addresses this gap by using ethnographic approaches that center Indigenous knowledges and ways of knowing to examine how social-structural and environmental conditions shape access to and outcomes from overdose-focused harm reduction and substance use treatment programs among IPWUD. Findings from this study will contribute to the overdose response for IPWUD by identifying policy and programmatic changes to improve the public health benefits of overdose response services.

column36: Prognostic Value of a Prospective, Longitudinal Evaluation of Body Composition in Patients with Cirrhosis Evaluated for Liver Transplantation
column37: Two main body compartments, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (fat), exhibit independent functions. Patients with liver cirrhosis frequently experience body composition abnormalities including loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat but not visceral fat (around internal organs). Liver cirrhosis, characterized by liver failure and replacement of normal tissue by scarring is the main indication for liver transplantation. These body composition abnormalities are associated with higher risk of complications such as infections, longer recovery after surgeries, and higher probability of death. The aim of this study is to evaluate muscle and subcutaneous fat abnormalities in relation to adverse outcomes both before and after liver transplantation. Muscle and fat amount and condition will be assessed using high resolution image-based techniques (computed tomography) at 6-month intervals in cirrhotic patients being evaluated for liver transplantation. During liver transplantation surgery, a small biopsy of muscle and fat will be obtained for analysis of cell types and signals. This information will establish the real burden of body composition abnormalities and their behavior in patients with cirrhosis over time to improve the prediction of outcomes, identify potential targets for treatment, and facilitate development of clinical trials for these conditions.

column36: Can Blending Together Traditional and Western Knowledge Improve Diabetes and Obesity Health Outcomes in Urban Indigenous Communities?
column37: Indigenous peoples in Canada suffer from significantly higher rates of diabetes and obesity, resulting in reduced quality of life. Health, government and community organizations often lack Traditional Knowledge and community ownership, required to decrease healthcare gaps and burden of disease. Site-specific, culturally safe, and locally-informed interventions will be co-developed/implemented/evaluated within the six FC/MC partner sites. Indigenous methodologies will be used to acknowledge and honour Indigenous knowledge, traditions, and protocols. Two sites will be offered to join a sub-study exploring the effects/outcomes of the community interventions on diabetes and obesity clinical variables (blood glucose, HbA1c, blood pressure, and waist circumference). One to two community interventions will be implemented at each site per year over three years. Diabetes and obesity clinical variables will be measured before, after, and one month following each intervention in the sub-study sites. The goal of the overall project is to reduce diabetes and obesity health inequities in Indigenous communities. Ultimately, the knowledge gained from this project will support change in diabetes and obesity policy, research, and practice in urban Indigenous communities and health systems, and to ultimately improve wellness.
