column36: Regulation of male fertility by peroxiredoxin 6
column37: Infertility is an important human health problem that affects about 16% of couples worldwide; half of these cases can be traced to men. The diagnosis and treatment of this health problem is difficult because in 37-58% of cases the causes are not known. Infertile men often have high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in their semen. These molecules are normally produced by the cell; but when they are present in high amounts, they become toxic. As men age, spermatogenesis is affected resulting in the production of fewer spermatozoa; these spermatozoa show impaired function. Because of professional and/or work priorities, men are planning to have children around or after their 40s. This deliberated delay may impact negatively on their success to achieve fatherhood or could be the cause of transmitting defects to their children. Spermatozoa, as other cell types, can cope with certain levels of ROS by removing those with antioxidants. However, if the antioxidant amount is low and or the production of ROS is too high, then toxic effects can be observed in the sperm. This proposal is focused on the 1-Cys peroxiredoxin (PRDX6), the unique member of the PRDX family of antioxidant enzymes with peroxidase and calcium-independent phospholipase A2 activities and its role in the protection of the male reproductive tract against the toxic effect of high levels of ROS. Spermatozoa from infertile men have low levels of PRDX6 and mice lacking PRDX6 are subfertile and unable to fertilize oocyte and produce embryos in vitro. Furthermore, these abnormal reproductive outcomes worsen as the mice age. Understanding the role of PRDX6 in spermatozoa under physiological conditions will allow us to seek for therapeutic strategies to keep the levels of ROS at desirable physiological levels in infertile young and aging men seeking fatherhood.

column37: Sleep disruption increases throughout the course of pregnancy and has recently been shown to be involved in pregnancy complications. In particular, sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) occurs in ~30% of pregnant women by the third trimester. SDB consists of snoring and breathing pauses during sleep, leading to fragmented or disrupted sleep and decreases in oxygen levels during sleep. SDB during pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure, diabetes and delivering infants with low birth weight. However, studies are needed to determine if SDB in pregnancy has any adverse long-term effects on child health. The proposed research project will evaluate the association between SDB during pregnancy on a variety of child health outcomes, including cardiometabolic health (obesity, diabetes risk, high blood pressure), behavioural problems, and SDB risk in the child. An existing pregnancy cohort (~2,500 women) with completed assessments of SDB during the third trimester of pregnancy will be used. We will invite participants from Montreal and Quebec City who are part of this cohort to have their children (at age 8-10 years old) to complete one follow-up study visit for assessments of child health outcomes. Measurements for obesity, blood pressure and insulin resistance will be taken. Children will also be assessed for disturbances in breathing, which often remain undiagnosed. Sleep studies in the laboratory will be performed in children in order to monitor oxygen levels and episodes where breathing is stopped (i.e., apneas). The results of this study may have important implications for identifying and treating SDB in pregnancy in order to ultimately improve the health and development of affected children.

column36: Are epileptic seizures linked to memory-like neural pattern sequences?
column37: Reflex epilepsy is defined as epilepsy syndrome in which known stimuli evoke seizures. For example, reflex seizures in some patients may be elicited by flickering lights, certain sounds, specific odors or activities. However, in a vast majority of epileptic patients, seizures do not have identifiable triggers and are classified as spontaneous. Here, we ask whether spontaneous seizures might also have identifiable triggers that are generated internally in the brain, i.e.: they are result of specific 'thoughts'. For example, we propose that 'memory' of specific events or places could be an internal trigger of seizures. To study this, in rats, we will induce seizures in specific spatial locations. We hypothesise that, when a rat will have a spontaneous seizure, even in different location or during rest in a home-cage, the brain activity before seizure will be similar as in the place where seizures were initially induced. This project will give us better understanding of mechanisms generating seizures, which could help to prevent seizures from happening. For instance, as the last goal of this project we will test multiple therapeutic strategies. We will monitor continuously brain activity, and if 'memory pattern' triggering seizure are detected, we will deliver electric stimulation to the brain to disturb this pattern and so prevent the seizure. Our team has proven excellent track record in long-term monitoring of brain activity in normal and epileptic rats, and also in memory research. Thus, we are in unique position to investigate 'memory-like' triggers of spontaneous seizures, and to use this knowledge to test novel therapeutic strategies in epilepsy.

column37: While all cells of an organism have essentially the same genetic sequence, their genome, the addition of chemical modifications directly on DNA, such as methylation, can influence what genes are expressed or silenced in different cell types. During germline development, the process by which mature eggs and sperm are produced, DNA marks are first erased in the developing embryo and then re-established according to the sex of the embryo. During the formation of mature eggs, the establishment of DNA methylation patterns occurs after birth and is guided by gene expression: the body of expressed genes acquires DNA methylation. Some of these maternal marks are responsible for the expression of certain genes, called imprinted genes, only from the un-methylated paternal copy in the embryo. Imprinted genes play important roles in the regulation of embryonic growth and are linked to several human imprinting disorders. We recently showed that some of the egg's gene expression and DNA methylation are controlled by repetitive retroviral-like sequences in human and mouse. We hypothesize that these repetitive sequences, which are highly divergent between species, have contributed to the evolution of new imprinted genes. In this project, we will first study the functions of human genes expressed only from their paternal copy in the placenta, a key organ controlling embryonic growth. We will also study the molecular mechanism whereby retroviral-like sequences are implicated in the acquisition of DNA marks in the egg, using new mouse models. These studies, aimed at confirming our hypothesis, will yield new fundamental knowledge of processes required for normal development and associated with a number of inborn diseases in humans. They will directly test a new evolutionary function for retroviral-like sequences and provide critical functional data on human placental genes that might have been selected for imprinted expression because of their importance in regulating embryonic growth.

column36: Protein acyltransferase mediated S-palmitoylation and its Importance in Innate Immunity and Lipid Metabolism.
column37: Most of the essential processes within our cells are carried out by molecules called 'proteins'. Proteins are made from a specific combination of building blocks termed amino acids. In the simplest case, proteins are a combination of the standard 20 amino acid alphabet. However, to achieve enhanced diversity beyond the 20 amino acids, some of these building blocks can be chemically modified. These modifications can act as an 'on-off' switch, a signal to control protein localization or as a way of marking old proteins for recycling. The goal of this proposal is to understand a poorly studied modification termed S-palmitoylation. This modification involves attaching a 16 carbon long fat to a particular amino acid. Because 16 carbon fats are hydrophobic (doesn't like being in water) this modification can target proteins to cellular compartments delineated by other fatty molecules. The human cells contain 24 enzymes that perform this modification yet little is known about these enzymes, and only a few of their targets have been identified. We have found that one of these enzymes modifies proteins critical for detecting bacteria and alerting the immune system. We have found that patients with defects in this chemical modification are prone to disorders such as Crohn's disease. In another example, we find that S-palmitoylation is critical for the liver to metabolize fats and defects may cause fatty liver disease and liver cancer. Overall, the primary outcome of this grant will be to characterize these new targets of S-palmitoylation and identify the enzymes responsible for the modification. We will also gain insight into how this modification impacts the localization and function of proteins essential for the immune system and in metabolism. Understanding this level of regulation within the cell may allow for the development of treatments to reverse or bypass the defects seen in patients with these specific immune disorders and fatty liver disease or liver cancer.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in Canada. When detected early, survival rates for CRC are dramatically increased and symptoms are substantially reduced. Colonoscopy is the standard for CRC screening in "high risk" adults (with a personal or family history of CRC and/or certain inherited syndromes). However, a tool or that can accurately predict the risk of CRC development among those who are considered "average risk" can be used to target certain individuals for earlier or more intensive screening. Only a handful of tools for risk prediction of colorectal polyps (common precursors of CRC) currently exist and solely include demographic, clinical and lifestyle factors. In this project, we will develop a colorectal polyp risk prediction model that improves upon existing tools by incorporating biomarkers from circulating blood. We will use two existing databases of consenting participants undergoing colonoscopy from two colorectal cancer screening centres in Calgary, AB and Toronto, ON, who provided blood samples and completed questionnaires on their lifestyle, diet and physical activity. We will select 400 individuals who had advanced polyps (cases) and 400 individuals who were polyp-free (controls) at the time of colonoscopy. We will examine relationships between biomarkers and advanced polyps and will expand a risk prediction model for advanced polyps using information blood biomarkers in addition to questionnaire data. Polyps are one of the earliest stages in CRC progression and their identification and removal can prevent CRC development. Risk prediction models that combine demographic, clinical and lifestyle factors, in addition to biological blood markers, may provide a unique opportunity to increase the effectiveness of CRC screening among "average risk" adults.

column36: Regulation of germinal center B cell function during antibody responses
column37: Immunity to many infections and the efficacy of vaccination depend on producing sufficient and highly specific antibodies. The quality of the antibodies produced in response to infection or immunization improves with time, by a process that requires that the antibody-producing immune cells, or B-lymphocytes, undergo a complex set of genetic and functional changes. These changes take place in special structures named germinal centers, within lymphoid organs like the spleen or lymph nodes. Inside germinal centers, the B lymphocytes multiply and randomly change the information of the genes encoding the antibody molecules. This generates a repertoire of related B lymphocytes that are triaged according to the quality of the antibody they produce. Those that make the best antibodies survive and transform into another type of cell, which produces large amounts of antibody. This process to confer immunity can be compromised, causing immunodeficiency, or improved to boost vaccination. We have identified an enzyme that is essential for the formation and function of germinal centers and thereby for the antibody response. Preliminary data shows that this enzyme is required to maintain the organization and cellular composition of the germinal centers. We posit that this enzyme regulates the proliferation, movement, and metabolism of B lymphocytes to maintain the complex dynamics of the germinal center. Using mouse models and diverse molecular, biochemical and cellular techniques, we will define the mechanisms whereby this enzyme underpins the antibody response. This project will reveal novel mechanisms regulation the antibody response that can be exploited in the clinic to improve immunity.

column36: Calcitriol-dependent and independent regulation of calcium and bone metabolism during pregnancy, lactation, and fetal/neonatal development
column37: Adaptations during reproduction ensure adequate delivery of calcium and phosphate. During pregnancy, intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption double, whereas during lactation, the skeleton is preferentially resorbed. After weaning, intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and bone formation increase, and the maternal skeleton is restored. During fetal development, the placenta actively pumps minerals to facilitate skeletal growth and mineralization, while in the neonate, the intestines use passive mechanisms to upregulate intestinal mineral absorption. The known calcium and phosphate regulating hormones are not required for these adaptations to be invoked. Overall significance: understanding normal mineral and skeletal physiology during these time periods, and the pathophysiology of relevant disorders, will increase our ability to optimally treat these conditions. We may also identify novel regulators, which in turn may lead to new approaches to treating disorders of mineral and bone metabolism. Our goals of this proposal are to clarify the role of calcitriol (active vitamin D) in the mother during reproductive cycles and in the fetus and early neonate. Our hypotheses are that a) maternal calcitriol rather than offspring calcitriol influences fetal and early neonatal development; b) catabolism of calcitriol has important effects on mineral homeostasis during reproductive cycles as well as fetal and neonatal development; and c) factors other than calcitriol upregulate intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption during pregnancy, lactation and post-weaning. Four specific aims address these goals and hypotheses, by assessing: 1. whether maternal calcitriol deficiency has lasting effects on neonatal skeletal metabolism 2. how loss of catabolism of calcitriol alters maternal or fetal mineral homeostasis 3. whether Pdia3 mediates actions of calcitriol on the placenta 4. to identify regulators of intestinal mineral absorption during pregnancy and lactation

column37: Low back pain affects 50% of Canadians with direct medical costs of 6-12 billion annually. Its major cause, intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration, often needs surgical interventions at advanced disease stages. Existing treatment options include spine fusion, total disc replacement, repair of nucleus pulposus (NP; a substructure of IVD). Whereas spine fusion causes degeneration in adjacent spinal segments and total disc replacement involves complicated surgery and high failure rates, repair of the total or partial NP is appealing because it can minimize tissue removal and reduce surgical and post-surgical complications. However, the NP repair has long limited by extrusion or subsidence of the implants that are poorly integrated with adjacent tissues in the disc. It is due to the poor adhesion property of the implants like hydrogels and their limited ability to integrate with the body. We recently developed bioinspired hydrogel adhesives that can achieve superior tissue-adhesion performance on various wet dynamic tissues. We also established a tissue-engineering strategy of NP cell delivery to prompt IVD healing. The advances highlight an unprecedented opportunity for NP repair by combining the novel adhesives and cell delivery strategies. We hypothesize that this strategy could enable immediate and long-term integration of the implants with the body by tissue adhesion and cell activities, potentially transforming the IVD repair. This project includes four Aims: (1) Benchmarking mechanical properties of IVD; (2) Developing injectable biodegradable tough IVD glues; (3) Engineering the IVD glues with optimal viscoelastic and cell-adhesion properties; (4) Functional analysis with a whole disc culture model with bioreactors. This project will greatly advance the science of IVD biomechanics and biology, overcome limitations of existing NP implants, improve surgical outcomes of NP repair and quality of life of millions of Canadians living with low back pain.

column37: One reason that blood cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are so difficult to cure is that current therapies are targeted against the bulk of the blood cancer cells but somehow miss the leukemia stem cells (LSCs) that contribute significantly to disease relapse after treatment. These LSCs can evade therapy and give rise to disease relapse because they are stuck in an aberrant stem cell state that continues to fuel new rounds of disease. This project deals with the transcription factors of the ZEB and SNAI families and how when their expression is increased in AML they can alter epigenetic control factors that lead to LSC disease causing state. Here we will show that if you decrease ZEB and SNAI or get rid of them completely in blood cancer stem cells then the epigenetic factors that they interact with will no longer drive the LSC state and the cancer cells will become easier to target. column36: Electron cryo-microscopy of fatty acid biosynthesis
column37: Fatty acids are the building blocks of membranes that define our cells. In mammals and fungi, synthesis of these molecules are regulated by large and multi-protein complexes including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FAS). ACC and FAS complexes contain all necessary components to carry out the multi-step synthesis of fatty acid. These proteins have important implication to human health. Cancer cells become addicted and dependent on increased fatty acid synthesis relative to normal cells as they need to replenish their membranes due to rapid cell growth and division. On the other hand fungal ACC and FAS are important drug targets to combat infection, specially in immune compromised patients. Additionally, fatty acid synthesis is an important drug target in lipid metabolic disorders such as diabetes. We will used electron cryomicroscopy to visualize ACC and FAS during fatty acid synthesis and to investigate how current inhibitors interact with these complexes. New and effective inhibitors of this class of enzymes are desperately needed for treatment in cancers such as breast, liver, and prostate tumors and combating fungal infections. Our work will elucidate the structure of each step of fatty acid synthesis, opening an important window into the inner workings of these mega enzymes.

column36: Identifying vascular targets to treat cerebral small vessel disease
column37: The arteries that enter the brain are approximately one centimeter wide. These arteries branch into smaller vessels, called arterioles. The branching is repeated until the vessels are many times smaller in width. It is at this small level that vessels supply brain tissue with the oxygen and nutrients required for regular function. A brain disease that targets these small vessels is called "small vessel disease" (SVD). In SVD the blood flow through vessels in the brain is impaired or restricted. We see signs of SVD on pictures collected during medical imaging, namely Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Older people, above 55 years old are more likely to have SVD than younger people. This is important because in Canada there are more people living in their senior years than people younger than 15 years old. Older people are also more likely to have a stroke: a blockage of blood flow in the brain. An estimated 1 in 5 strokes is caused by SVD. As we learn more about SVD in the human brain we will be in a better position to prevent old age impairments. This project seeks to discover new ways to visualize and understand SVD. Our approach is to develop "dynamic" and "functional" images using an MRI scanner. We will study how the brain's arterioles pulsate with each heartbeat and how the vessels react to a stimulus that causes them to expand, known as vasodilation. It is important to observe change over time and over the course of therapy. Therefore, we propose to gather these images and other assessments at the beginning of the study and after 12-weeks of aerobic exercise training. There is strong evidence that exercise is good for all the blood vessels in the body, including the brain, as it causes the blood vessels to dilate and increase the amount of blood flowing. This research can help us identify ways to treat and observe SVD.

column36: SynoPlate - Human physiology on demand
column37: As the spending on drug development increases over the past 20 years, the number of drugs approved annually has, in fact, declined. column37: Abdominal pain is a debilitating and distressing symptom for many patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). This microbe is markedly reduced in IBD patients, and we theorise that the loss of this analgesic bacterium contributes to pain in IBD. We have also found that gut microbes from IBD patients can produce pain-causing substances. We also will explore how what changes in the microbiota of IBD patients to lead to worsening pain. Our work will reveal the role that a dysfunctional microbiota plays in IBD-related pain and, more importantly, lay the groundwork for a novel microbial therapy that is more effective and safer than existing opioid pain medications.

column37: Cardiovascular disease was responsible for 20 million deaths in 2015. Lifestyle factors (e.g. dietary habits and physical activity) are very important to define risk for these diseases. Some individuals are more vulnerable than others to develop these conditions, either due to their genetic background or because they were exposed to poor health or stress during their early life. A key hormone that is involved in this process is insulin, produced by the pancreas and responsible for controlling the use of glucose by the cells. Insulin also acts on the brain and influences our behavioral reactivity to the environment, modifying food preferences, decision-making, mood and cognition. The question of this project is if we can identify individuals vulnerable for cardiovascular and metabolic diseases very early in life, before they even develop these conditions. column37: Patients with Li Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) have a mutation in a gene called TP53 in every cell in their bodies, which puts them at much greater risk for developing cancers early in life and throughout their lifetime. Malkin and Shlien have been studying a large number of LFS patients and have identified the most common specific mutations in TP53, the history of cancers in these patients and the secondary mutations that may contribute to cancer development. We can screen these fish early in development for signs that their TP53 gene is not functional and introduce additional mutations found in LFS patient tumours. We can then use these young fish to screen for drugs that restore normal TP53 and observe if cancers are prevented. By demonstrating that these responses in zebrafish are conserved in patient samples, we aim to improve the outcome for these children.

column37: Humans are continuously exposed to fungi that can potentially cause disease or allergic reactions. For example, the pathogenic fungus Cryptococcus neoformans causes life-threatening meningitis in people with defective immune systems. The global impact of this fungal pathogen is dramatically illustrated by the fact that it is responsible ~15% of deaths in patients with Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS). C. neoformans is therefore a major threat to the ~37 million people suffering from AIDS worldwide. Alarmingly, a related species, Cryptococcus gattii, has emerged as a primary pathogen with the ability to cause meningitis in people with healthy immune systems. The disease caused by C. gattii is particularly relevant to the health of Canadians because the fungus has caused a disease outbreak in British Columbia. The long-term goal of our research project is to acquire knowledge that will lead to new strategies to prevent and/or effectively treat the infections caused by fungal pathogens such as C. neoformans and C. gattii. In particular, we are working to acquire a detailed understanding of the weapons that fungi deploy to attack people, and to use our new knowledge in strategies to treat fungal diseases. In our current project, we will determine how C. neoformans builds protective structures to shield itself from our immune defences. We plan to use the latest technologies in genetics, biochemistry and cell biology to complete our objectives. The new knowledge we obtain may lead to therapies that enhance the ability of our immune defences to control disease by preventing the fungus from protecting itself during infection. These studies will extend our exciting recent discoveries of candidate drugs that inhibit the growth of C. neoformans in culture. In summary, our project will provide advanced knowledge into the ways that fungal pathogens cause infections in humans, and support the discovery and application of new methods to treat fungal diseases.

column36: Investigating the functions of the pluripotency factor SOX2 within the mammalian suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN): implications for circadian timekeeping, SCN clock development, and mood disorders
column37: We live in a 24-hour world where our daily activities are organized around the day-night cycle. Many of us wake up, eat our meals, go to work, and sleep at approximately the same time every day. Our internal organs behave in a similar fashion, changing their activities over the course of 24 hours. These bodily rhythms, or so-called "circadian" rhythms, are the result of an internal clock in the brain, called the SCN (short for suprachiasmatic nucleus), that keeps track of the time of day and communicates that information to the rest of the body. However, many aspects of modern life are at odds with the workings of this internal timekeeping system. Rotating shift work, traveling across time zones and even "sleeping in" on weekends can lead to misalignment between our internal clock and the outside world. A misaligned or perturbed clock can have serious health consequences, such as increasing the risk of becoming overweight or developing diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, breast and prostate cancer, major depression, and Alzheimer's disease. Another major risk factor for many of these pathologies is aging, which is associated with a worsening in the performance of the SCN. By restoring or bolstering its performance and improving circadian rhythms, we may be able to treat or ameliorate various diseases, promote healthy aging, and enhance physical and mental health. The objective of this proposal is to identify and understand the genes responsible for the optimal performance of the SCN. We have found a gene called SOX2 that appears to be necessary for maintaining normal circadian rhythms. We will use various approaches, including mouse models where the Sox2 gene is "knocked out" in the SCN, to determine its roles in circadian timekeeping. Through our work, we will acquire new insights into how the SCN is regulated, knowledge that may be leveraged for the development of therapeutic and health-promoting strategies that target our internal clock.

column36: The role of NOD1 in obesity-associated diabetes
column37: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by impaired response of the body's tissues to insulin and impaired production of insulin from pancreatic beta cells. Obesity is associated with type 2 diabetes. In obesity, excess fat in tissues causes formation of damaging products that generate low-grade inflammation. Such inflammation in tissues that respond to insulin and tissues that produce insulin impairs their function, thus causing diabetes. However, anti-inflammatory treatment of diabetes has been only partially effective so far, we believe because it is not targeted towards the sensors of the fat-derived toxic products that initiate such low-grade inflammation. Our objective is to single out specific sensor(s) that participate in obesity-associated diabetes and are activated by fat-derived products. NOD1 is a sensor candidate because it is located inside cells and induces low-grade inflammation. Indeed, we have shown that NOD1 deficiency protects against high fat diet-induced diabetes in mice. However, we do not know whether NOD1 is activated by fat-derived products or by bacterial products, since high fat diet can increase intestinal absorption of bacterial products. Our preliminary data show that fat impairs the response to insulin and the secretion to insulin via NOD1, independently of gut bacteria, and thus implicate fat-derived products. We hypothesize that fat-derived products are recognized by NOD1 which brings about low-grade inflammation resulting in diabetes. In the present proposal we will feed a high fat diet to mice that have or do not have gut bacteria. We will also give fat directly into a vein, thus bypassing the gut. We will study mice that lack NOD1 in the whole body or in specific tissues that are responsible for the response to insulin and the production of insulin. Finally, we will explore the possibility of inhibiting NOD1 action as a treatment of type 2 diabetes.

Paradoxically, calpain can either promote or inhibit cell death in response to different toxic challenges, including many therapeutic drugs currently used to treat cancers. The reasons for this relate to the many different roles of calpain, and the context in which it becomes engaged. We have developed genetic models to explore calpain functions, and we are using them to identify specific therapeutic challenges where calpain inhibition will enhance their ability to kill cancer cells. This leads to our hypothesis that calpain inhibition will make some cancer drugs more effective when used in combination. We propose to develop biosensors to add in the identification of calpain inhibitors suitable for clinical use, and to identify specific cancer therapeutics that can be made more effective by combining them with calpain inhibitors.

column37: The number of Canadians living with more than one health problem is increasing due to longer lifespan, rising obesity and physical inactivity. Among the most common conditions are knee osteoarthritis (OA) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which often co-exist. As many as 50% of people with DM also have OA; 1 in 6 with OA also have T2DM. Unfortunately, people with knee OA who also have T2DM are less likely to get treatment for their OA. Without a diagnosis and treatment, people with knee OA manage their pain by avoiding activities, like walking, that aggravate the pain. This contributes to physical inactivity, which increases risk for T2DM complications. Better treatment of knee OA in people with T2DM has potential to improve both OA and T2DM outcomes. Research shows that peoples' beliefs about OA as unimportant 'normal aging', fear of weight bearing on a painful joint, and limitations in physician's time and level of comfort diagnosing and managing OA, especially in patients who also have T2DM, are major barriers to OA care and have been inadequately addressed. The goal of our research is to develop and pilot-test a multi-component intervention to address these barriers to knee OA care in people with T2DM. In Aim 1, we will use interviews with patients and providers (family physicians, endocrinologists, physical therapists and diabetes nurse educators) to identify strategies to overcome these barriers and assess their usability in a primary care and diabetes clinic setting. Through a process of trial and review, the intervention will be revised to improve its likelihood of working. In Aim 2, we will assess the acceptability, feasibility and potential impact of the intervention on OA and diabetes in a randomized, controlled trial. Findings will be used to inform the design and conduct of a clinical trial evaluating the benefits and costs of the strategy on patient outcomes for OA and T2DM.

column36: Evaluating inhibitors of CSPG synthesis in models of spinal cord injury
column37: Other than general medical support, there are currently no therapies to treat spinal cord injury. Chondroitinase has been shown by many laboratories to produce significant benefits to recovery from spinal cord injury in a variety of animal species and in a variety of injuries. Chondroitinase works in all these models because it is an enzyme that degrades a family of molecules called chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs). CSPGs form part of the normal extracellular matrix in the mature nervous system and serve to limit nerve growth after the nervous system has wired itself correctly. After spinal cord injury CSPG levels increase. Reducing CSPG levels using Chondroitinase allows for increased nerve sprouting (a process called neuroplasticity) and better recovery. The positive effects of chondroitinase on recovery from spinal cord injury in animals has been known for about 20 years yet it has not been translated to the clinic because as a large bacterial enzyme it faces many problems for drug delivery in humans. Delivery of chondroitinase in spinal cord injured animals by injecting the enzyme directly into the spinal cord poses safety problems for humans as does the engineering of chondroitinase expressing viruses. The majority of drugs in medical use today are small molecules. Because of a long history of use in the pharmaceutical industry there is a well-known pathway for moving small molecules from preclinical to clinical studies. Thus an ideal solution to the problem of translating chondroitinase to the clinic is to develop one or more small molecules that reduce CSPG levels in the injured spinal cord. Using two clinically relevant models we will evaluate and compare 3 small molecule inhibitors of CSPG synthesis for their effects on recovery after spinal cord injury in rats.

column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects 1 in 140 Canadians. It is caused by inflammation along the gastrointestinal (GI) tract that can lead to symptoms including abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. There are two main types of IBD, Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). In CD, GI inflammation can lead to a very serious complication called fibrosis. Fibrosis occurs because repeated cycles of inflammation and healing cause scarring that prevents the intestine from working properly and can even cause intestinal blockages. 1 in 3 people with CD develop fibrosis within 10 years of diagnosis and require surgery to remove the diseased bowel. The use of new biological therapies has revolutionized treatment for intestinal inflammation in CD but has not reduced the number of people, who go on to develop fibrosis. It may be that small amounts of subclinical inflammation are enough to kick start the development of fibrosis. Unfortunately, we do not have any drugs to prevent of treat intestinal fibrosis. My laboratory has developed a mouse model that mimics key features of CD, including intestinal fibrosis. Mice that are missing an enzyme called "SHIP" develop CD-like intestinal inflammation and fibrosis. We have also found that some people with CD have very low SHIP levels and those people have more severe disease and require more surgeries. Using two mouse models, we will identify key proteins that drive intestinal fibrosis. We will target those proteins to see if we can reduce intestinal fibrosis in mice. We will also examine SHIP and fibrosis-inducing proteins in blood and biopsy specimens from people with CD, who have intestinal fibrosis. This is exciting because there is already a drug on the market (idelalisib) that can be used to target one of the fibrosis-inducing proteins that we have identified. Our research could be rapidly translated into a 'first-in-kind' therapy to treat fibrosis in people with CD.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of oncogene-induced senescence
column37: Cellular senescence is a tumor suppressor mechanism that plays a dual role in biology. The acute senescent response to cancer-causing stimuli is beneficial since it helps to prevent tumors by halting cell proliferation and stimulating immune-mediated clearance of stressed cells. However, senescent cells that accumulate in tissues with age contribute to chronic inflammation and aging. It is thus clear that understanding molecular and cellular mechanisms that control cellular senescence will open the way for the successful identification of compounds that can be used to treat both cancer and age-related diseases. The overall goal of the proposal is to gain critical insights into the mechanisms of cellular senescence, identify new tumor suppressors that mediate the process and oncogenic mechanisms that allow cancer cell to bypass it. The latter can be targets to develop novel anti-cancer therapies.

column36: The role of natriuretic peptides in sinoatrial node dysfunction and atrial fibrillation in hypertensive heart disease
column37: Each and every heartbeat is initiated by a natural pacemaker in our hearts called the sinoatrial node. Normal sinus node function leads to proper activation of the atria (the upper chambers of the heart). This sequence of events ensures our heart rate is normal and that the heart is properly able to pump blood to our bodies. Common forms of cardiovascular disease, including hypertension (high blood pressure) and heart failure result in serious damage to the sinoatrial node and the atria leading to arrhythmias (irregular, abnormal patterns in the heartbeat) such as sinoatrial node dysfunction and atrial fibrillation. Although sinoatrial node dysfunction and atrial fibrillation are very common in hypertension very little is known about why this happens our how they can be treated. Currently, people with sinoatrial node disease have to get an artificial pacemaker, which is costly and has a number of serious limitations. Similarly, current atrial fibrillation treatments are often not effective. My laboratory is one of only a few worldwide with the expertise to study the sinoatrial node (and the atria) in mice, including at the cellular and molecular level. This is critical because it enables us to make use of genetically altered mice in our experiments. We have discovered that a family of protective hormones, called natriuretic peptides, can protect against sinoatrial node disease and atrial fibrillation in mouse models of hypertension. Natriuretic peptide effects are complex because there are several forms of these hormones and they can cause their effects in a number of different ways. Our proposed experiments will help us understand the complex effects of natriuretic peptides in the diseased heart. Our ultimate goal is to use this information to generate new synthetic natriuretic peptides that are designed to enhance the beneficial effects of these hormones for the treatment and prevention of sinoatrial node disease and atrial fibrillation.

column36: Visual and cognitive development in preemies: the role of neonatal hypoglycemia
column37: Neonatal hypoglycemia is characterized by low blood glucose level in the first days after birth. It has been associated with brain injury affecting preferentially cerebral areas in charge of vision. Therefore, newborns who suffered from neonatal hypoglycemia are at higher risk to present visual problems and developmental impairments including visual perception and visuospatial abilities. A major risk factor for neonatal hypoglycemia is premature birth, with one third of neonates born prematurely presenting low blood glucose level. Preterm infants are also at higher risk for visual and intellectual difficulties as well as brain abnormalities compared to babies born at term. Yet, the impact of neonatal hypoglycemia on the development of babies born prematurely and on their vulnerable brain has not been specifically studied. Therefore, the main goal of this project is to characterize the relationship between neonatal hypoglycemia and brain, visual and intellectual development in preemies. We will use three methodologies: 1) the electroencephalogram (EEG), to appreciate brain activity related to visual perception; 2) the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a brain imaging technique allowing to identify brain injuries; and 3) behavioral assessments, to measure intellectual and visuospatial abilities. We will recruit 120 neonates born preterm between 28 and less than 34 weeks of gestation. We expect that one third of them will present neonatal hypoglycemia. All participants will undergo a MRI in the first week after birth and at term equivalent age. Patients will then be enrolled in a 3-year study that will include EEG and behavioral assessments at 3, 12, 24 and 36 months of age. This study will provide a better understanding of the role of neonatal hypoglycemia on cerebral, visual and intellectual development in preemies. It will improve our ability to identify preterm infants at-risk of developmental delay and provide them with better individualized patient care.

column36: Translation regulation and lysosome expansion in immune function
column37: Macrophages and dendritic cells engulf microbes in order to remove these from our bodies. Once engulfed, the pathogen is sequestered within a new organelle called a phagosome, which matures into a digestive phagolysosome by fusing with lysosomes. Lysosomes are organelles that host digestive enzymes. These cells are also known as antigen-presenting cells (APCs) because they have a critical role in processing and presenting antigenic peptides, microbe fragments formed during digestion. Presentation of antigens activates T cells, which train the immune system to make antibodies against a specific microbe. Thus, antigen presentation and T cell priming are essential steps during vaccination. In resting APCs, lysosomes are vesicular. Yet, APC exposure to bacterial molecules transforms lysosomes into an expanded tubular network. We discovered that expansion of the lysosome system helps APCs take up more extracellular cargo, which seems to improve antigen presentation. We also found that lysosome expansion is driven by rapid activation of cellular machines that convert genetic information in the form of mRNA into proteins, a process called translation. In this project, we will precisely determine which pathways responsible for up-regulating translation are important for lysosome expansion and antigen presentation. We will apply a systems-biology approach to obtain a global understanding of how translation drives APC maturation. Lastly, we will identify adjuvants that remodel the lysosome system and if this is important for their immuno-potentiation. Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to improve their efficacy and efficiency. Ultimately, this project uses a multi-disciplinary approach to examine how fundamental processes of information transfer within cells are used to adapt APC function to promote adaptive immunity. This knowledge may then provide tools to help boost the innate immune system and/or produce better and safer vaccines.

column36: Integrin Alpha8 is a novel mediator of T lymphocyte migration across the CNS barriers
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) with high prevalence in young adults. The clinical symptoms of MS are the result of self-targeting immune cells migrating across the brain and spinal cord blood vessels into the CNS, where they cause destruction to the myelin insulation surrounding the nerve cells (a process that does not occur in healthy individuals). Cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) on immune cells are essential mediators of immune cell migration across blood vessels. While current MS therapies are able to decrease the number of relapses, none are able to completely prevent or halt disease progression, and many carry severe risks resulting from immune suppression. Thus, identifying novel, specific targets to prevent harmful immune cells from entering the CNS is a major therapeutic goal to prevent MS disease activity and progression. My lab has identified a novel CAM, integrin alpha8 (alpha8), on a harmful subset of immune cells in MS. The binding partner of alpha8, nephronectin, is found on the CNS blood vessels, suggesting that it might facilitate the entry of alpha8-bearing immune cells into the brain and spinal cord. The goals of our research are (1) to study the presence of alpha8 on various harmful immune cells and its binding partner nephronectin on the CNS blood vessels; (2) investigate which stage(s) of immune cell migration alpha8 is critical for; (3) study whether alpha8 blockade prevents the pathogenic immune cells from crossing the CNS blood vessels, thereby preventing disease activity and progression in various animal models of MS and (4) determine whether alpha8 is an effective biomarker of disease activity and response to treatment in MS. A better understanding of the mechanisms by which harmful immune cells enter the CNS in MS is critical for the development of new therapies that prevent CNS damage and therefore ward off or inhibit disease progression.

column36: MET signalling in bone and fracture healing
column37: Delays in fracture repair causing non-union are a significant Canadian health problem. Around 10% of all long bone fractures heal with delay, despite better surgical techniques. Therefore, new therapeutic options are needed. We discovered MET receptor gene mutations that prolong receptor activity cause osteofibrous dysplasia (OFD). A complication of OFD is tibial fracture non-union due to abnormal bone cells function. Surprisingly little is known about the role of MET in fracture repair. We have subsequently found elevated MET expression in a subset of human fracture non-union tissue. The identification of MET mutations which cause non-healing tibial fractures, indicates an unrecognized role for MET in fracture repair. We have created a mouse carrying an OFD mutation and the mouse cells show similar changes to patient cells. Long bone fracture repair is also delayed in these mice. We propose that MET signaling influences bone stem cell differentiation, and MET over-expression causes abnormal bone repair, OFD and at least a subset of fracture non-union. To test this hypothesis, we propose: 1. To define the effect of MET expression in human fracture repair and bone cells. 2. To define the role of MET in osteoblast and osteoclast signalling. 3. To determine the effect of gain-of-function MET mutations on bone repair. We plan to define the role MET plays in fracture repair and bone cell differentiation. We further determine if low oxygen levels contribute to delayed fracture healing in our animal model and test the response of bone healing to MET inhibitors. Significance: This is the first study to define the role of MET in fracture repair. Through studying how MET influences bone repair, we ultimately wish to develop new therapies augmenting bone repair. Our strategy has immense clinical relevance for our aging population and burgeoning epidemic of fragility fractures

column36: Calcium Sensing Receptor (CaSR) Signaling in the Thick Ascending Limb (TAL): Delineating the Pathways Perturbed in Kidney Stone Formers
column37: Kidney stones are common, painful and expensive to treat. The most common risk factor for kidney stones is peeing too much calcium. The primary goal of this proposal is to understand why some individuals pee too much calcium, thereby increasing their risk for a kidney stone. To do this we are examining the cause of a rare disease in a child who as part of her disease pees too much calcium. We have found that she has a mutation in a gene called FAM111A. Our preliminary work tells us that this gene when made into a protein, regulates how much of the cell sensor for calcium is present. Specifically it decreases the amount of this receptor, known as the calcium sensing receptor (CaSR), in special kidney cells. When it is mutated, i.e. not functional, there is too much of this receptor at the surface and it tells the kidney to pee more calcium. We are going to examine how this is occurring in cells and make an animal model of her disease to test new treatments on. The other aspect of this work is to determine how the CaSR signals in a specific part of the kidney (the thick ascending limb, TAL) to prevent calcium from getting back into the blood and therefore ending up in the urine. We have created a model system that senses this signalling and will tease out the specific signals that activate this. We will also directly look at this signalling in TALs we have dissected and kept alive via a technique called renal tubular microperfusion. We are one of only a few laboratories in the world that can do this. Together these studies will provide much needed new information about what causes people to pee too much calcium and therefore potential drug targets for the treatment of persons with kidney stones.

column36: Screening for Occult Malignancy in Patients with Unprovoked Venous Thromboembolism: a Randomized Controlled Trial using 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Computed Tomography. SOME-2 Trial
column37: Blood clots in leg veins (deep vein thrombosis) or lung arteries (pulmonary embolism) that happen for no reason are both called "unprovoked venous thromboembolism" . These unexplained blood clots can be the first manifestation of cancer. Current data suggest that after the occurrence of a first unexplained blood clot, approximately 5% of the patients will be diagnosed with cancer in the following year. In patients older than 50, this rate reaches 7%. Unfortunately, all types of cancers can be found and whether systematic cancer screening should be performed has remained controversial: extensive cancer testing may find more cancers but is potentially uncomfortable and harmful for patients. Markedly, two recent studies demonstrated that the number or cancer diagnosed or missed after an extensive screening approach was not different to the numbers observed after a limited screening approach (medical history, physical examination, basic blood work and chest X-ray). However, focusing workup in patients older than 50 could greatly improve the performance of extending cancer screening strategies. A PET scan, is a non-invasive whole body imaging test performed to find out many cancers at once. It combines computed tomography (CT) with functional imaging using sugar. It is routinely used for the diagnosis, staging and restaging of various cancers in oncology. Previous studies showed promising performances in finding an unknown cancer at the time of an unexplained blood clot by using PET scan. Our research question is whether a PET scan misses less cancers than a limited cancer screening plan in patients aged 50 years or more who are diagnosed with a first unexplained blood clot. We hope our study will also help in identifying more curable cancers when PET scan is performed and that a negative PET scan means that the patient has a risk of subsequent cancer similar to the general population.

column36: Regulation of ventricular remodeling by a circular RNA circ-Slc8a1
column37: Heart diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries. Over time, as hearts age or become senescent, adverse remodelling that is initially beneficial, progressively leads to reduced heart functioning. Our research aims to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie this remodeling and repair. Circular RNAs are closed continuous loops of RNA that were recently detected in eukaryotic cells, and may affect cell physiology through a variety of mechanisms. Our RNA sequencing results revealed that the circular RNA circSlc8A1 is tightly associated with heart diseases. We hypothesize that circular RNAs may regulate cellular ageing and tissue repair by binding to protein regulators of heart fibrosis. To test this, we will modify the two cell types in the heart, namely cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts, so that they express more of the circular RNAs in question. We can also use the reverse approach to silence circular RNA expression, and observe the changes in function. Using these approaches, in conjunction with standard experimental models, we can better understand the function of circular RNAs in heart diseases. There are two unique aspects to our proposed study. Firstly, we are among the first to produce a stable expression system allowing long-term studies. The second unique approach is our inhibitor system that is designed to block the function of individual circular RNAs in cell and animal models. These allow us to specifically study individual circular RNAs, and better understand any causal relationships. Our proposed experiments will help us explore the regulatory roles of circular RNAs in both heart aging and other cellular repair contexts. The agents developed may be used as tools in understanding the role of circular RNAs in heart development, aging, disease-associated injury and tissue regeneration. With these approaches, we hope to design therapies to intervene against the adverse remodeling associated with age-related heart disease.

Healthy cells precisely replicate their DNA (in the form of chromosomes) and then ensure one copy of each chromosome is inhertited by each daughter cell by the end of cell division. In cancer cells, chromosome inheritance is frequently defective, leading cells to receive too many chromosomes or too few. These mistakes arise from defects in the mitotic spindle, which forms at the start of mitosis to collect and separate the chromosomes. The proposed studies will very likely lead to the development of novel targeted therapies for EOC. Since the Wnt/ B-catenin pathway is involved in the development of many types of cancers, the small molecular inhibitors we develop will be useful for targeting a wide range of cancers.

column36: Intra-arterial chilled saline and external cooling to treat severe ischemic stroke
column37: Stroke affects over 62,000 Canadians each year. Most cases result from a blood clot that impairs blood flow to part of the brain. Brain damage occurs when this ischemia is severe or prolonged, and that leads to behavioral and cognitive deficits or even death. There are clinically approved pharmacological and mechanical therapies to remove clots, which when done quickly can rescue brain tissue and improve outcome. Sadly, some do not benefit from clot removal. Those patients are left with life-long disability. We will use rats to model those patients with severe stroke who receive modest to no benefit from clot removal, as these patients desperately need additional treatments. We will test a combination of hypothermia therapies that should reduce brain injury and improve behavioral outcome. The first involves infusing intra-arterial cold saline (20C) into the ischemic brain for 20 min at the time blood flow is restored (clot removal time in patients). This should improve blood flow and attenuate injury. Second, we will test whether adding external head cooling (e.g., brain temperature at 35C for up to a day) will further lessen brain damage. These therapies have many beneficial effects, such as reducing brain swelling, and we expect that they will improve outcome after this severe stroke. However, while these cooling therapies work in certain animal models and settings, existing studies were quite limited in scope, and there was little done to evaluate combination treatments against severe stroke. Thus, we will test these therapies using translationally rigorous, clinically relevant endpoints and experimental design features (e.g., high statistical power, use of hypertensive animals, and comparisons of aged male and female animals). Our goals are to identify the best hypothermia therapy to inform upcoming clinical trials on therapeutic cooling, and to further improve our mechanistic knowledge of these treatments.

column37: More than half a million Canadians live with bipolar disorder (BD), a long-term and potentially disabling mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings from depression to mania. Suicide rates are disturbingly high - up to 15% of people with BD will end their own lives. This evidence paints a bleak picture. Our research network - the Collaborative RESearch Team to study psychosocial issues in BD (CREST.BD) - uses a pioneering participatory approach in which researchers, healthcare providers and, critically, people who live with BD work collectively to conduct BD research, and to move research results into action. The app will addresses some of the most pressing real-world problems that people with BD currently face when using online technologies. First, it will take advantage of advances in online technologies to provide a secure and safe interface where the user is in control of their own health data. Second, it will empower the user to combine and learn from different forms of online self-management or self-care data (for example, medication use, sleep quality, mood variability, activity levels) in one place. Third, it will be co-designed with diverse (for example, people with different gender identities, or of different ethnic or cultural backgrounds) people with bipolar disorder. At the same time, Bipolar Bridges will provide a new way for researchers to assess the relationship between self-management and quality of life outcomes in diverse people with BD.

column36: Cryobiology and Cryopreservation of Corneal Endothelial Monolayers
column37: Cryobiology is the study of the effects of extremely low temperatures on living systems. A major application is the low-temperature storage (cryopreservation, for example in liquid nitrogen at -196 C) of cells and tissues to be distributed for transplantation to treat injury and disease. While many cell types have been successfully cryopreserved and used clinically for decades, some cells and the vast majority of tissues present significant hurdles for cryopreservation. For example, a widely transplanted tissue is the cornea, the clear tissue of the eye through which people see. The endothelial monolayer is the delicate layer of cells on the inner surface of the cornea that is critical to its transparency, and is the functional element that needs to be replaced in the majority of corneal transplants. Corneal endothelial monolayers cannot be adequately cryopreserved using current techniques without considerable cell loss. For this reason, currently corneal endothelial monolayer transplants (85% of all cornea transplants) must use fresh tissue, leading to tissue wastage and inequities in distribution. In addition, lab-grown corneal endothelial monolayers are poised to meet transplant needs despite donor shortage, but will require cryopreservation for widespread distribution. We are developing procedures to cryopreserve both lab-grown and natural corneal endothelial monolayers. As cellular therapies and transplant of both natural and engineered tissue are increasingly used in modern medicine, there is an urgent need for effective cryopreservation strategies. The objective of the proposed research is to combine advanced engineering modeling, cryobiological expertise, and biological experimentation to develop key understanding of identified issues in cell and tissue cryopreservation with immediate application to corneal endothelial monolayers. Proposed experiments will use cultured cells, discarded pig eyeballs, and non-transplantable donated human corneas.

column37: Occupational asthma (OA) is the most common chronic occupational respiratory diseases in industrialized countries and second most common in developing countries. Diagnosing OA is challenging due to delayed referral by general practitioners, or specialists' failure to take proper diagnostic steps. The procedures are complex and time-consuming; it could be several months before a diagnosis is established. Often times, patients did not complete the process, especially those who live in distant places. Moreover, specific inhalation challenge (SIC) as the reference test is only available in a few specialized centres worldwide. These problems inspired researchers at the Hopital du Sacre-Coeur de Montreal to develop model consisted of information from clinical interview as well as objective tests other than SIC (i.e. non-SIC based model) for diagnosing OA. Four objectives are proposed in this project: to develop non-SIC-based diagnostic models for OA induced by low-molecular weight (LMW) agents (mostly chemical agents, e.g. isocyanates, red cedar) in Quebec data and validate them in Poland data (Objective#1); to evaluate the clinical value of both HMW- and LMW-induced OA models in places where SIC is routinely done (Objective #2) and in places where SIC is not available or routinely done (Objective #3); and finally for knowledge transfer, the OA models will be transformed into calculators ("OccAs-Calc") and made available in Web and mobile versions (Objective#4). Our model has a potential to be implemented as one-visit diagnostic procedure for patients coming to a work-related asthma center. OccAs-calc will facilitate the implementation of the models in occupational health practice in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Depressive disorders are common and debilitating conditions affecting about 20% of people in North America within their lifetime. Despite some effective treatments, roughly one third of depressive patients are treatment-resistant. It is well known that responses to life-stressful events are extremely different from one individual to another. When facing the same situation, a job-loss, the passing from a closely-related, a car accident..... one person could become severely depressed whereas the next one will not. Our research proposal will focus on the identification of the mechanisms that are implicated in these differential responses, what makes us resilient or vulnerable facing stressful events. Too little noradrenaline render all the mice vulnerable to chronic stress, whereas increasing the noradrenergic transmission in a very specific brain area will transform vulnerable mice into resilient mice. Finally, we will identify precisely the mechanisms and the receptor subtypes that are put in play in this control. All together, this research should allow identifying vulnerability or resistant factors in human facing depression, but also the development of original antidepressant therapies.

column37: Preventing the transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) during unprotected heterosexual intercourse is an international concern. Women face unique challenges in preventing transmission. Women are biologically two times more likely than men to become infected because after sexual intercourse, semen remains within the female genital tract for prolonged periods of time, increasing exposure to HIV. Currently, the best option for women to protect themselves is pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or condom use, a solution that is not always available or socially accepted. The scaffolds are designed to be simple to use without the assistance of a healthcare professional, and scaffold replacement is infrequent (once every 30 days as opposed to daily applications using vaginal gels). From a sociocultural perspective, this technology is designed to increase user adherence - a major factor that can hinder the effectiveness of HIV prevention strategies. This novel technology may provide a significant breakthrough for addressing the challenges associated with HIV transmission and infection for women.

column37: Myelin is a fatty substance that coats nerve projections for efficient signal propagation. When myelin is damaged, demyelination disorders occur leading to neurological impairments in vision, movement and/or cognition. Demyelination occurs in Multiple Sclerosis (MS), which is known as "Canada's disease" because the country has one of the highest rates in the world with an estimated 100,000 patients. MS is caused by abnormal activity of the immune system whereby the body's own immune cells damage myelin and myelin-producing cells, oligodendrocytes, in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). Current MS treatments are disease-modifying drugs that target inflammation and aid patients with relapse-remitting MS, in which episodes of neurological dysfunction are followed by remission. Yet, they are ineffective for progressive MS, which usually evolves from the relapsing stage and involves a continual worsening of the disease with no improvement. Effective treatments for this type of MS would require central nervous system regeneration and remyelination (restoration of myelin). Remyelination can be achieved by forming oligodendrocytes from oligodendrocyte precursor cells in the human central nervous system. However, this process is highly inefficient in MS patients. I discovered that a specific type of neurons (inhibitory neurons) secrete an immunological molecule, called fractalkine, that acts directly on the oligodendrocyte precursor cells in the developing mouse brain and promotes oligodendrocyte formation. This effect could form the basis of much needed future MS therapies. This proposal will determine whether fractalkine regulates remyelination and regeneration in the adult central nervous system using mouse demyelination models. We will determine if fractalkine a) enhances oligodendrocyte formation from precursor cells and subsequent remyelination; and b) modulates interactions between precursors and neighbouring brain immune cells called microglia.

column37: Low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability, is one of the most common reasons for visiting a family doctor, and costs the Canadian health care system between $6 and $12 billion a year. A growing population that is increasing in age and experiencing more chronic health concerns is making it difficult for family doctors to meet the multiple needs of patients. One way to support doctors is to build a team of healthcare providers to help address the needs of patients. Physiotherapists provide evidence-based management for LBP. If physiotherapists are integrated within primary care teams and people with LBP are able to see the physiotherapist at their first visit for LBP, they may get a more focused LBP assessment and experience improved outcomes. This new model of care also has the potential to reduce workload on family doctors and reduce unnecessary diagnostic imaging and specialist referrals that are common in LBP. The proposed study will determine the effectiveness of integrating physiotherapists within family doctor's offices for patients with LBP. column36: Folic acid supplementation in children with sickle cell disease: A double-blind randomized crossover trial
column37: Sickle cell disease is a blood disorder that is passed down from parents to their children. People with sickle cell disease cannot make healthy red blood cells and have an increased risk of illness and death. Folate is a B-vitamin needed to make proteins in our body and to help proteins function in our body. Sickle cell disease causes children to have higher folate needs than healthy children. Currently, children with sickle cell disease take 1-6 mg/day of folic acid (the man-made form of folate). However, even the lowest recommended dose of 1 mg/d folic acid provides six times more folate than is recommended for healthy children aged 1-3 years. There is growing concern that high amounts of synthetic folic acid may be harmful in the long term, as it may interfere with how natural folate works in the body, and it is associated with an increased risk of some types of cancers. We will study the effectiveness and potential risk of folic acid supplementation in 36 children (2-19 years of age) with sickle cell disease who are attending BC Children's Hospital. Children will receive 1 mg/d folic acid or a placebo for 12 weeks. After a 12-week washout period (no supplements), the treatments will be reversed. Blood samples will be collected at baseline and after 12 weeks of each treatment. We will measure several different forms of folate in the blood, hemoglobin, vitamins B12 and B6, and other clinical outcomes (anemia and pain crises) in children. Our study will be the first-step towards determining if the recommendation for high-dose folic acid supplementation in children with sickle cell disease requires re-evaluation. Our overall goal is to improve the nutritional status and clinical care of Canadian children with sickle cell disease.

column37: Contractility and synchronicity of the heartbeat requires resilient mechanical and electric coupling to maintain the functional and structural stability of the heart. Anchoring cell-cell junctions are particularly critical as they provide stability to cardiac myocytes in the face of severe stress by mechanically anchoring cells during cardiac systolic and diastolic cycles. In myocytes, these cell junctions are primarily localized at the longitudinal end of the cell in a stair-like profile, forming a structure classified as the intercalated disc (ICD). At the molecular level, the ICD is a highly organized triad of junctions between cardiac myocytes, including adhesive and communicating macromolecular complexes containing anchoring junctions (desmosomes and fascia adherens junctions) and communicating junctions (gap junctions). We are studying how this region is formed and maintained in cardiac myocytes

This research will provide useful information on factors that can modify the course of MHPs in a critical period of life such as transitioning from adolescence into adulthood. column36: Understanding the impact of smoking cessation treatment on health and healthcare service use among smokers in Ontario
column37: Healthcare service use and costs of current of smokers are higher than those of non-smokers. This fact highlights the healthcare burden that results from smoking and suggests benefits of interventions that decrease smoking prevalence. There are evidence-based treatments that can help smokers quit. Studies of such treatments are usually judged only on how effective they are in helping smokers achieve full abstinence at a particular time point. This narrow focus does not reflect the variation in cessation trajectories of smokers who lapse and relapse during a quit attempt, employ a reduce-to-quit strategy, or seek to reduce, but not quit, smoking. Nor does it speak to the ultimate reason for funding large-scale interventions: improving the health of smokers and avoiding the healthcare burden associated with treating continuing smokers. The Smoking Treatment for Ontario Patients program is a publicly-funded smoking cessation treatment program accessed by 25,000 smokers per year in over 300 health care organizations. Treatment is individually tailored, and within a one year episode of care, there is no set number or frequency of clinical care visits. Evaluation is currently limited to survey questions answered by a portion of patients, which, in the context of a relapsing remitting condition, provide a slim understanding of the effects of receiving smoking cessation treatment. Healthcare use data provide an objective means by which to determine effects. We will use a database of patients who received STOP smoking cessation treatments, a population-based comparison group of smokers who did not receive STOP smoking cessation treatments, and population-based healthcare databases (e.g. physician billings, emergency room and hospital visits) to compare health and healthcare use between groups of smokers. This information can be used to help inform debates concerning how to best implement smoking cessation services within the publicly funded healthcare system in Ontario.

column36: Defining the role of DEPTOR in the regulation of brown adipose tissue development/function and evaluation of its impact on systemic metabolism.

In response to cold, activation of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) rapidly turns on oxidative metabolism and heat production in BAT. Until recently, BAT was thought to be present and active only in small mammals and human newborns. Over the last years, several groups confirmed the existence of BAT in adult humans. Interestingly, BAT activation is reduced in obese and type 2 diabetic individuals. Moreover, studies show inverse relationships between BAT activity, diabetes and glycemia. These results suggest that BAT may be exploited to dissipate energy excess and improve metabolic homeostasis. Unfortunately, the precise mechanisms regulating BAT development, recruitment and function are still incompletely characterized. Over the last years, we and other have discovered that the mTOR signaling pathway plays key roles in BAT. The loss of mTOR signaling severely impairs BAT development/function and impairs systemic glucose and lipid metabolism. Here we propose a research project whose objective is to define whether modulating the action of mTOR through one of its well-established modulator (DEPTOR) could represent a viable approach to promote BAT development and function and improve systemic metabolism. We believe that our work has the potential to provide additional knowledge to generate new options to improve metabolism and enhance human health.

column36: Situating Suicide Risk: An inquiry into the production of the lives and afterlives of neurobiological vulnerability
column37: With at least 3900 Canadians lost to suicide each year, identifying the factors thought to lead to suicide risk is a top priority of scientific researchers and clinicians. Recently, neuroscience researchers identified biomarkers that they believe reflect suicide risk acquired over the life course as a result of specific negative experiences. These experiences include child abuse, which is thought to lead to measurable neurobiological changes that have durable and tangible effects. Researchers argue that these "embodied" forms of vulnerability are associated with the development of personality traits directly related to increased risk of suicidal behaviour. In this project we ask: what understandings of suicide risk are emerging in specific forms of scientific and psychiatric research? How do emerging notions of vulnerability overlap or not? We will examine the extent to which studies of biomarkers for suicide risk might change people's understandings of choice, risk, and volition as well as beliefs about appropriate management of suicide risk if it comes to be understood as "in the brain". Drawing on a unique, long-term engagement with a team of clinical and molecular researchers, this project traces intersecting notions of psychiatric vulnerability within the fields of developmental research, neuroscience, and environmental epigenetics. Based on qualitative interviews and ethnographic research, this empirically grounded study focuses on three intersections: (1) of the lab and the clinic, (2) of epigenetics and neuroanatomical studies, and (3) of prospective cohort studies and retrospectively produced models of neuropsychiatric risk. This project will offer a clarifying role of the specific nature of risk emerging at each of these intersections along with the implications of these risk models for addressing psychiatric conditions and suffering in the 21st century, at the crossroads of different sciences, experiences of suffering, and health care.

column37: Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental illness affecting approximately 1% of the world population. It is one of the leading causes of long-term disability, costing the Canadian health care system approximately $7 billion per year in medical care and lost productivity. One of the major obstacles in developing new therapeutics for schizophrenia is a lack of understanding of the cellular basis of the disease. Studies with schizophrenia brains consistently show deficits in inhibitory neurons in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Despite this important link, little is known about how such dysfunctional inhibitory neurons contribute to schizophrenia and whether one can rescue behavioural impairments by restoring the neuron dysfunction. The proposed experiments are aimed at addressing this knowledge gap. We will first study the changes in the important characteristics of inhibitory neurons (known as CCK-GABA cells) in well-established mouse models of schizophrenia. Next, using light-mediated neuron silencing and imaging, we will demonstrate its causal contribution to cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia and determine how their activity dynamically change during working memory task. Lastly, we will explore the therapeutic benefit of activating inhibitory neurons as a treatment of behavioural impairments. To this end, we have established a highly selective genetic method called the intersectional approach. This innovative tool allows us to examine systemically the core features of specific inhibitory neuron subtypes and manipulate their activity in freely behaving animals. The proposed research is an essential step for identifying pathophysiologically-based targets for novel therapeutic interventions for schizophrenia. If successful, it will lead to a better understanding of how distinct cortical interneuron subtypes contribute to schizophrenia and reveal novel treatment strategies that aim at correcting the underlying neural circuit deficits.

column36: Using real-world data to simulate the effects of efficient referral strategies on wait times for elective surgery in Canada
column37: Surgical care in Canada is in crisis. Wait times for elective surgery can be long. Lack of hospital beds frequently causes cancellations or delays in surgery. We still rely on old systems to coordinate care for people having surgery. The way we provide surgical care must be reimagined so that we can continue to provide high-quality health care for Canadians in the future. Transforming surgical care for the future requires a number of innovations. We need better ways of getting people to surgery with shorter wait times, and we need sensible policies to guide how we organize surgery within the health system.
