column36: Occupational health, safety and labour rights among street and indoor sex workers in the context of evolving laws and policing: Ethnographic and qualitative participatory-action research
column37: Prohibitive sex work legislation and restrictive policing strategies have consistently been shown to endanger the health and safety of sex workers both in Canada and globally. Despite this, in December 2014 the former Canadian government implemented new legislation to regulate sex work, termed the Protection of Communities and Exploited Persons Act (PCEPA). The PCEPA criminalizes the purchase of sex and anyone who commercially profits from the proceeds of sex work (e.g., receptionists, security personnel, drivers etc.). Emerging research from Canada now suggests that end-demand approaches such as the PCEPA may recreate the harms of previous punitive approaches, while introducing new restrictions that put sex workers and sex industry actors such third parties (e.g. receptionists, security personnel etc.) in precarious legal positions. The proposed 5-year participatory-action research project aims to evaluate how evolving laws and policies regulating sex work (PCEPA, municipal licensing, policing appoarches, venue-based regulations) shape occupational health (e.g. experiences of physical and sexual violence, negotiation of safer sex practices) and safety (e.g. working conditions, access to workplace protections and labour rights) in the sex industry in Metro Vancouver. This new longitudinal research project will be well positioned to inform sex work law reform efforts, strategic litigation and the development, evaluation and implementation of sex work environment interventions at the municipal-level (e.g. enforcement policies, safe workplace standards for the sex industry, licensing regimes) and community-level (e.g. sex worker tools for safer workplace standards, potential for labour organization, collectivization of workers).

column36: Transformer les modeles actuels pour favoriser la securisation culturelle des soins offerts aux patients autochtones: Co-developpement d'un nouveau modele d'intervenant avec trois communautes atikamekw
column37: Les systemes de sante sont penses et organises par les groupes majoritaires et dominants des societes. Pour cette raison, le systeme de sante ne repond pas toujours aux besoins des groupes culturellement minoritaires, tels que les populations autochtones (Premieres Nations, Inuits, Metis). Des soins mal adaptes culturellement peuvent augmenter les inegalites de sante que ces groupes experimentent. La securisation culturelle est une approche qui vise a transformer les soins pour mieux repondre aux besoins et respecter la culture des patients issus de groupes culturels minoritaires comme les Autochtones. Ce projet de recherche est mene en partenariat respectueux avec la Nation Atikamekw, repartie au sein de trois communautes (Manawan, d'Opitciwan et de Wemotaci) au Quebec. Il vise a repenser la facon de donner des soins aux patients autochtones a l'exterieur de leur communaute, en creant un nouveau type d'intervenant pour la securisation culturelle qui puisse integrer les savoirs, les valeurs et les traditions de la culture atikamekw a l'interieur de notre systeme de sante occidental. D'abord, nous co-developperons un nouveau modele d'intervenant en nous basant a la fois sur les connaissances de la litterature scientifique mais aussi sur les valeurs, les pratiques de guerison et les perspectives de la sante atikamekw. Ensuite, nous organiserons un forum avec plusieurs acteurs des trois communautes pour leur presenter ce modele et evaluer s'il est acceptable pour tous. Puis, nous co-developperons un cadre de competences et une formation pour les futurs intervenants, ainsi que des ententes de collaboration avec des organisations de sante. Enfin, nous co-developperons, avec un groupe de patients atikamekws, une echelle pour evaluer la securisation culturelle, qui puisse servir a mesurer les effets de l'intervention. Ce projet participatif reconnait le role central des populations autochtones dans le developpement de solutions pertinentes pour ameliorer leur sante.

column36: Spit for Science 2 Autism Spectrum Project: Harnessing the Power of Population-Based Samples for Gene x Environment Studies
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can have devastating effects throughout life. Genetic factors play an important role in ASD but the specific genes are still unclear. Spit for Science 2 - Autism Spectrum Project continues the work of the original Spit for Science by using alternative approaches to identify risk genes for ASD. Most studies focus on clinical diagnoses, which are complex and vary considerably from person to person. We are studying behavioural (e.g., social communication) and cognitive traits (executive functions - how you control behaviour to reach your goals) strongly linked to the disorders and that cut across disorders. Patients are considered to be at the extreme of these traits but these traits vary widely in the population (excellent to poor social communication). We also can leverage leading Canadian expertise in using Postal Codes to map environmental factors like air pollution and psychosocial disadvantage so we can examine how genetic factors might interact with environmental factors to impact risk for ASD. To understand the genetics of mental illness in youth, we will recruit a large sample of children and adolescents (30,000) from the Ontario Science Centre. These children will provide DNA via spit, Postal Codes and trait information related ASD and other related disorders, and complete cognitive task (Stop-Signal Task) that measures different aspects of executive function. We will use a range of cutting-edge gene by environment and genetic methods to identify genetic risk variants for these traits, validate them in clinical samples and understand which genetic risk are unique and shared across traits and disorders. We hope to identify novel genes involved in childhood mental illness which could potentially lead to early detection, better treatments and improved treatment-outcomes for Canadian youth.

column36: Integrating community-based recruitment with data linkage to inform and enhance scale-up of hepatitis C treatment among people who inject drugs: A pan-Canadian 'virtual' cohort study
column37: Roughly 250,000 Canadians live with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, a major cause of liver cirrhosis, cancer, and transplantation that places a significant burden on infected individuals and the health system. People who inject drugs (PWID) are the principal group at risk of this blood-borne infection. Recent advances in curative treatment present an opportunity to drastically reduce HCV transmission in the absence of a vaccine. However, even a universally effective treatment cannot cure people who remain undiagnosed and untreated, and the public health impact of new medications will rely on linking and retaining infected individuals in appropriate healthcare. For PWID, a range of conditions (discrimination, stigma, a lack of insurance or stable housing, and difficulty navigating the health system) can hinder access to necessary services, and many individuals are lost along the 'cascade of care' connecting HCV testing, treatment, and cure. This study seeks to improve our understanding of the accessibility of HCV care and treatment for diverse groups of people with a history of injecting drug use, including Indigenous people and women who inject drugs. In partnership with community-based organisations across Canada, we will recruit current or former PWID and provide on-the-spot hepatitis C testing, with counselling and clinical referral for those testing positive. Participants will complete a short questionnaire to collect information on their background, medical history, and perspectives on barriers to healthcare. We will then request permission to follow their healthcare utilisation and medical outcomes "virtually" through records routinely collected and stored in administrative databases during clinic, hospital, laboratory, and pharmacy visits for the next five years. Altogether, the study aims to identify modifiable barriers and facilitators to care and guide evidence-based public health interventions and policy in the new landscape of HCV therapy.

column36: Serotonin and alcohol: therapeutic possibilities and neurobiological mechanisms
column37: Alcohol use disorders have detrimental effects on health and society. The neurotransmitter serotonin has been linked to aspects of alcohol use, and is a therapeutic target for several disorders. The main goal of this work is to use animal models to understand the role of serotonin in modulating multiple aspects of alcohol use. We have three main aims. Firstly, using a pharmacological approach we will explore the potential for drugs interacting with serotonin to modulate different aspects of alcohol use, including reinforcement, relapse, dependence and impulsivity. Two drugs that interact with serotonin in different ways are pimavanserin and lorcaserin. They are used to treat Parkinson's disease and obesity, respectively. However, based on their pharmacological actions we predict that they may be useful for treating addiction. We will produce a comprehensive behavioural analysis of the effects of pimavanserin and lorcaserin on multiple aspects of alcohol use and addiction, including measures of alcohol reinforcement (self-administration), binge-drinking, reinstatement of alcohol seeking and alcohol-induced impulsivity. To look at possible sex differences and the impact of past alcohol use, these studies will be done in non-dependent as well as alcohol-dependent male and female animals. Secondly, we will examine underlying mechanisms mediating effects of pimavanserin and lorcaserin on alcohol use. This will be done by measuring changes in brain activity following exposure to alcohol with and without pimavanserin and lorcaserin. We will also assess how lorcaserin and pimavanserin alter alcohol-induced changes in dopamine release, since this neurotransmitter is the one most closely linked to reward-related behaviours. Finally we will determine where in the brain these drugs act to produce their effects. The significance of this work is that it may lead to the testing of clinically used drugs, pimavanserin and lorcaserin, for treating alcohol abuse and addiction.

column36: Prevention of preterm birth (PTB) and fetal inflammation (FI): the pharmacology and toxicology of targeting interleukin (IL)6 with HSJ633, a small peptide allosteric IL6 receptor antagonist
column37: Preterm birth (PTB) and fetal inflammation (FI) are the major perinatal causes of mortality in children <5 years and of life-long morbidity. These are caused by maternal inflammation or infection and can lead to the arrest of fetal organ development and death. A key mediator for these events is interleukin (IL)6. We have synthesized a very specific allosteric peptide antagonist to the IL6 receptor, HSJ633 (sequence: VRKFQNSPA), that is highly effective in preliminary experiments in blocking PTB and FI due to infectious stimulants. We hypothesize that HSJ633 is a safe and efficacious therapeutic for preventing PTB and FI. Our objective is to understand better the pharmacology and toxicology of HSJ633. We will use sophisticated methodology to discern how HSJ633 selectively blocks molecular and cellular mechanisms of the IL6 receptor and specifically the STAT3 intracellular signaling pathway. Next, we will test whether HSJ633 antagonizes IL6 actions in human fetal membranes to prove that it works in humans. Then, we will continue testing various doses HSJ633 in mouse models to determine its optimal dosage. To demonstrate it is pharmacologically superior, we will compare it to the established monoclonal antibody antagonist to IL6, Tocilizumab (TOC), which is FDA approved for rheumatoid arthritis. To demonstrate its safety, we will test the toxicology of HSJ633 in two generations of mice to show that fetal exposure does not impair offspring growth and reproduction. An exhaustive examination of fetal organs will be made. Last, we will test the efficacy of HSJ633 in a chronically inflamed pregnant mouse model using low dose LPS to ascertain whether it blocks FI. Together these tests will confirm that IL6 is a key target for blocking PTB and FI, that HSJ633 is effective and safe, and is a therapeutic that should undergo more rigorous testing for its clinical and commercial potential.

column36: Anticoagulation for stroke prevention in patients with recent episodes of perioperative atrial fibrillation after noncardiac surgery - The ASPIRE-AF pilot study
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) during or after surgery (i.e. perioperative AF) is very common after surgery. Approximately 3% of patients are diagnosed with perioperative AF within 30 days of a surgical procedure not including open heart surgery (i.e. noncardiac surgery. Patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery have a high risk of stroke. For patients who develop AF outside of the surgical setting, there is strong evidence that blood thinners ('anticoagulants') are beneficial in lowering the risk of stroke. This suggests that patients with perioperative AF may benefit from an anticoagulant. However, whether these medications are also effective and safe in patients with perioperative AF is currently unclear. The aim of this proposal is to assess the feasibility of a randomized clinical trial of an anticoagulant versus usual clinical care in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. We will perform a randomized clinical pilot study of an anticoagulant versus usual care in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. Patients will be assigned by chance (randomized) to a blood thinner (oral anticoagulant) or usual care. For this pilot study, we will include 100 patients to test the feasibility of our trial. Patient have at least 1 confirmed episode of perioperative AF, be in normal sinus rhythm at the time of randomization, and have some additional risk factors for stroke. Patients will be followed at 1 month, 6 months and then every 6 months up to a maximum of 24 months. We will consider this pilot study to be successful if we can recruit 100 patients at an average recruitment rate of 1 patient per centre per month. In summary, this research proposal will inform the feasibility of a large clinical trial to determine the ability of blood thinners to prevent stroke in patients with perioperative AF.

column36: Mechanisms of Leishmania dissemination and transit in the mammalian host following vector transmission
column37: Many infectious diseases are initiated following pathogen deposition into the skin by an insect vector but subsequently cause systemic disease. These diseases include Malaria, Lyme's Disease, Zika and West Nile virus disease and Leishmaniasis. These infections represent a current and growing global health problem, accounting for 17% of the human global infectious disease burden. Increasing or altered geographical distribution of insect vectors due to climate change and increased migration, travel and urbanization of human populations is exposing larger numbers of people to vector transmitted infections. In Canada, the spread of West Nile virus disease and Lyme's disease emphasizes the need for institutions to meet the challenge of vector-transmitted infections in a changing world. A major factor contributing to the manner in which these infections cause disease is their ability to move around the body after deposition into the skin by an insect bite. Understanding how vector transmitted infections disseminate out of the skin and subsequently move around the body is understudied, and how various treatment options influence this dissemination is almost completely unknown. This new knowledge is especially relevant to prophylactic vaccination against disseminating vector transmitted pathogens, where, despite old assumptions that the skin stage of infection is transient and somehow less important than subsequent systemic stages, the early expression of immunity at the dermal site of vector inoculation may be essential for vaccine efficacy. We aim to define and understand how pathogens leave the skin and move around the body in order to develop therapies or strategies to prevent this from happening, thereby reducing the burden of disease caused by vector transmitted disseminating infections.

We expect that these measures will allow MRI to play a role in diagnosing and staging PD for clinical trials and, also, in clinical practice.

column36: Examining patient partner and advisor roles in the Canadian health system: a mixed-methods policy analysis
column37: Patients and family caregivers are contributing to an ever-widening array of roles and activities as part of the growing patient engagement movement. Findings from these research phases will be used to generate an in-depth understanding of the patient advisor/partner role and its prospects for contributing to health system decision making and policy in Canada. column36: Getting to the heart of hard-to-treat cancers: Anti-CD133 theranostics for molecular imaging and treatment of GBM
column37: A fundamental reason why many cancer treatments fail to provide long-term patient survival is the presence of specialized cancer cells that resist standard radiation and drug therapies. These resilient cells, often referred to as cancer stem cells or tumour initiating cells, can cause the regrowth of a tumour or result in the spread of cancer throughout the body after treatments have been completed. It is possible for antibodies to be created that target surface molecules that are unique to tumour initiating cells, and to use those antibodies to deliver radioactive compounds directly to those cells. One type of radioactive compound can mark the cells so they can be seen on imaging scanners, creating a non-invasive means of detecting highly resistant cancers. A different but complementary radioactive compound can also be used to kill the cancer stem cells with exquisite potency and selectivity. For the latter, a specific type of radiation will be used, which is highly effective at killing cancer cells but will only penetrate a distance of 1 or 2 cells, reducing damage to nearby normal tissue. There is no known resistance mechanism by cancer cells to this type of radiation, and this radiotherapy has the added benefit that it can enhance the ability of the patient's own immune system to attack tumour cells. Consequently, this antibody-targeted radiotherapy against tumour initiating cells represents a viable and new approach for treating highly-resistant tumours. Thus, a novel antibody-targeted radiotherapy will be developed and evaluated for its ability to treat glioblastoma: a form of brain cancer, where the prognosis is poor and there are no effective therapies. The proposed research involves a multidisciplinary team that will develop and validate the new therapy, and in doing so will advance both new diagnostic and treatment options for brain cancer, for early use in clinical trials.

column36: A novel approach to studying the function of the Batten disease protein CLN5
column37: Mutations in CLN5 cause neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) commonly known as Batten disease. This devastating neurological disorder is linked to mutations in 13 genetically distinct genes. NCL affects all ages and ethnicities, is the most common form of childhood neurodegeneration, and is particularly prevalent in certain regions of Canada. Unfortunately, the precise functions of many of the NCL proteins are not known. Understanding a protein's function is central to being able to devise ways to target it therapeutically. Since mutations in NCL proteins result in nearly identical clinical phenotypes, they are thought to participate in the same biological pathway. Thus, studying the function of any one NCL protein is highly likely to enhance our knowledge of the neurodegenerative process, knowledge that can then be applied to all subtypes of the disease. The proposed research will study the localization and function of the CLN5 protein in the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, which has emerged as an excellent model system for studying a variety of human neurological disorders, and is one of the only model organisms that contains the CLN5 gene. We will then perform a small molecule drug screen to identify compounds that suppress the effects of CLN5-deficiency in Dictyostelium and human cells to advance targeted therapy development for this currently untreatable disease. Finally, we will translate CLN5-deficiency phenotypes revealed in Dictyostelium to human cell models to enhance our understanding of NCL pathology. Recent genetic advances show a strong overlap of NCL with later onset forms of neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and frontotemporal dementia. Thus, this work has the potential to provide fresh new insight into the mechanisms underlying other forms of neurodegeneration, which is of paramount importance considering the aging Canadian population.

column36: Establishing an International Core Outcome Set for Clinical Trials of Interventions for Venous Thromboembolism in Adults (VTE-COS)
column37: Blood clots in the veins (called venous thromboembolism or VTE) are common and affect up to 70,000 Canadians per year. This condition can be fatal if a blood clot in the leg or arm travels to the lungs. Treatment mostly relies on anticoagulants (blood thinners), which are very effective but involve risks and inconvenience for patients. Clinical trials are vital for determining the effectiveness of new treatments. Researchers measure outcomes that they believe are important for decision-making. Two problems that we have identified in clinical trials of VTE treatment are: 1) inconsistent measurement of outcomes, and 2) they may not be measuring all outcomes that are important, especially to patients but also to other stakeholders such as policy makers. The development of "core outcome sets" is gaining popularity as a strategy to address these problems. They are an agreed upon collection of standardized outcomes that should be measured and reported for a condition. A variety of perspectives are required to create a useful core outcome set. CanVECTOR, a national VTE research network, plans to involve researchers, clinicians, patients and other stakeholders to decide together on the best outcomes for VTE studies. We will seek input from international groups to develop a core outcome set that is applicable worldwide. Our project has several steps: 1) Review VTE studies to create a comprehensive list of outcomes; 2) Hold small group sessions with patients to identify outcomes that are meaningful to them; 3) Survey a large group of clinicians, researchers, patients and policy makers to prioritize the list of outcomes; 4) Hold a consensus meeting with representatives of each group to decide on the final core outcome set; and 5) Introduce and promote the core outcome set to Canadian and International researchers and stakeholders in our Canadian and global networks.

column37: Background and Importance: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in youth (MDD-Y) is a common and recurrent mood disorder, affecting 7-18% of young people. MDD-Y has severe impacts on psychosocial development, family and school functioning, long-term health outcomes, and increases risk of death by suicide. While effective treatment is available, half of affected youth experience relapse or recurrence, hence there is a real need for early detection of mood deterioration to prevent repeating MDD-Y episodes. Goal(s) / Research Aims: The project's main aim is to develop and validate a computer prediction system for MDD-Y relapse and recurrence. Secondary aims include: computerized prediction of when relapse/recurrence will happen, and grouping patterns of illness and recovery over time. Methods / Approaches Expertise: Overall, the study will be four years and participants will be 12-21 years old and will need to have MDD. Mobile phone use is on the rise in youth and gives objective, nearly invisible research data collection. We will collect six kinds of measures: 1) wearable wrist actigraph device and mobile phone sensor data; 2) mobile phone-based assessments in daily life; 3) speech sound data; 4) facial behavior; 5) Electronic Medical Records (EMR) data and 6) routine clinical ratings. Wearable, mobile phone sensor and assessment, speech, face, rating scale and EMR text data will be integrated. Statistical computer programs will be used for analysis and our research group has experience with those methods. We will use the computer programs to develop new insights and support better understanding of the course of MDD over time. Expected Outcomes: Our results will set the stage for a more definitive clinical study - a "clinical trial". A non-invasive, accurate way to predict MDD-Y relapse and recurrence will be a major preventative advance. Moreover, our project will empower youth by actively involving them in the tracking and care of their mental health.

column37: Intraocular neovascular diseases are the leading causes of vision loss in the industrial world, affecting millions of people worldwide. The development and maturation of a functional vascular network are critical to ensuring appropriate oxygen and nutrient supply of every tissue and cell in the body. In the eye, newly formed blood vessels are composed of endothelial tubes that are highly unstable and require further maturation to prevent vascular leakage. Transforming growth factor b (TGFb) signaling is essential for vessel maturation and integrity. Our preliminary results show that neonatal inhibition of non-canonical TGFb signaling induces retinal vascular malformations and bleeding in mouse, mimicking some aspects of ROP. The current proposal aims to identify new TGFb signaling mechanisms controlling pathological vascularization. For the first time, we want to identify cell polarity protein PAR6A function in TGFb-mediated EC proliferation and vessel integrity. Therefore, we will characterize a new signaling pathway regulating pathological EC proliferation and vascular leakage. Understanding these mechanisms will provide novel avenues for the therapy of ocular and brain vascular diseases.

column36: Righting wrongs: Developing appropriate follow-up for mercury-related deficits and disorders in Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek (also known as Grassy Narrows First Nation)
column37: The Grassy Narrows First Nation has been exposed to very high concentrations of mercury from freshwater fish consumption, following the release of over 9 tons of mercury into their waters in the 1960's. We have created a unique, merged database with historic longitudinal mercury biomarker data (blood, hair and cord blood), collected in Grassy Narrows between 1970 and 1997. A total of 176 persons from Grassy Narrows will undergo a general medical examination, a neurological examination and neuropsychological and neurophysiological tests. Persons who require further follow-up, including psychological assessment, will be referred. Blood will be sampled and analyzed for specific nutrients and disease indicators. The results, coupled to integrated knowledge translation and exchange, will allow us to: (i) develop a comprehensive and appropriate protocols for diagnosis of mercury poisoning; (ii) identify early signs and symptoms of mercury poisoning; (iii) propose adequate rehabilitative follow-up and care; (iv) alleviate some of the harmful consequences.

column36: An intervention study of prenatal air pollution exposure and its impacts on cardiometabolic and respiratory health in children
column37: Globally over 380 million individuals under the age of 19 are overweight or obese, including 41 million children under age five. Among other effects, excess weight in childhood is linked with reduced lung function and chronic disease in adulthood. Most previous research on children has focused on diet and physical activity, but given the rising prevalence and potential for lifelong impacts it is important to identify other risk factors. Moreover, most interventions have targeted school-aged children, but the risk of overweight/obesity may be "programmed" early in life so there is a need for prevention at earlier stages of development. There is evidence that air pollution exposure during pregnancy may cause the fetus to undergo changes that affect health later in life. Air pollution is the most widespread environmental risk factor - nearly 90% of the world's population breathes air that is considered unhealthy - so developmental effects from prenatal exposure could have major public health implications for generations to come. Unfortunately, the few studies conducted to date have had important limitations and have not evaluated the potential for exposure interventions during pregnancy to reduce the risks of overweight/obesity or impaired lung function in childhood. Portable indoor air cleaners represent a promising intervention because they are relatively inexpensive and reduce concentrations indoors, where individuals spend the majority of time. In our ongoing CIHR-funded birth cohort study in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia - one of the world's most polluted cities - we randomly allocated pregnant participants to an intervention or control group, with participants in the intervention group operating air cleaners in their homes during pregnancy. We propose to extend follow-up of children in this cohort to assess the impacts of prenatal air pollution on growth and development and to evaluate the potential for a simple intervention to reduce those impacts.

column36: Treating advanced retinal degeneration - rebuilding multiple co-dependent retinal layers with stem cells
column37: Despite dozens of clinical trials, and countless animal trials, to regenerate the retina with stem cell transplants, none have solved the challenge successfully. This is because the retina has many layers, and all layers are necessary in order to permanently restore vision in patients with advanced retinal degeneration - ~1 million patients in Canada and >50 million worldwide. This results in a staggering amount of suffering and considerable global economic burden of 1/3rd of a trillion dollars (USD) annually for age-related macular degeneration alone. The millions of patients that suffer from advanced, diabetes-related or inherited, retinal degeneration add to these costs. Current stem-cell suspension transplants can only replace a single retinal layer. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplants can delay further degeneration, but they cannot replace dead photoreceptors. Photoreceptor transplants can restore vision, but only briefly since the diseased RPE cannot maintain the new photoreceptor graft. Current scaffold- or sheet-based transplants can be multi-layered. However, they provide limited retinal coverage, result in higher levels of surgical trauma than suspension injection, can form inappropriate graft structure, and can cause additional cell death - in many cases, scaffolds harm the layer they were designed to regenerate. Given this, there is considerable need for simple and safe replacement of multiple retinal layers. Here, we propose to develop a new technology that organizes subretinal graft (including RPE and photoreceptors) into correct orientation and layering with wide coverage. In the future, this therapeutic will be administered using standard surgical techniques and infrastructure and will offer tangible hope for those suffering from vision loss due to retinal degeneration.

column36: Role of extrasynaptic GABA in the recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury.
column37: This proposal explores a fundamentally new mechanism for regulating nerve conduction in the spinal cord, with far reaching implications to understanding normal sensorimotor control and opening new therapeutic opportunities for restoring locomotion after spinal cord injury (SCI). While the primary inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord is GABA, we have discovered that GABA seems to have a paradoxical excitatory action on conduction in sensory axons, which likely generalizes to other types of axons. That is, our recent finding that extrasynaptic GABA receptors are adjacent to the sodium channels in sensory axons has led us to the idea that sodium spike transmission in sensory axons is facilitated by these GABA receptors, by virtue of their long-lasting depolarizing excitatory actions (termed PAD). To test this idea we will record from inside fine branches of sensory axons in the spinal cord of mice while activating the neuronal circuits that provide GABA to the axons, using genetically modified mice that allow light activation and visualization of specific GABA neurons, and also traditional nerve stimulation protocols known to evoke PAD. We will also make recordings from motoneurons in mice and single motor units in humans to further confirm that activating these GABA neurons (and PAD, indirectly with nerve stimulation in humans) increases sensory transmission to motoneurons, and also to demonstrate the relevance of the animal studies to humans. Finally, we will repeat these studies in mice and humans with SCI, and explore whether excess extrasynaptic GABA contributes to motor disorders. Our preliminary results suggest that drugs that selectively block extrasynaptic GABA receptors inhibit spasms and markedly improve walking after SCI. These drugs lack the negative sedative side effects of other drugs used in SCI, and are already being tested by other laboratories in human stroke patients, and thus now hold considerable promise for treating SCI.

column37: Six million Canadians are at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D). Without lifestyle changes, one-third of these Canadians will develop T2D within 3-5 years. Therefore, self-compassion (SC) would be an asset for people at risk for T2D who face the challenge of increasing their PA in the midst of a health threat. People at risk for T2D will learn about their T2D risk and strategies to increase their PA, which represents the recommended information that people at risk for T2D should receive. In addition to this, some participants, but not all, will be taught to be self-compassionate in relation to their T2D risk and their efforts to increase their PA. We expect that people who receive the additional training about how to be self-compassionate will engage in more PA than people who do not and they will do so because of SC's positive effect on aspects of self-management - adaptive reactions and a tendency to use strong self-management skills. This study is important for health promotion because it allows us to determine if we can improve how we currently help people prevent T2D through engaging in PA.

column36: Drivers of oligodendrocyte precursor cell dysfunction in the origin and maintenance of oligodendroglioma
column37: Oligodendrocytes are cells in the brain that make myelin to help nerve cells send signals to each another. Oligodendrogliomas are malignant brain tumours composed of cells resembling early immature oligodendrocytes. Recently, the gene CIC has been found to be mutated in most oligodendrogliomas, and this change is suspected to be important in how oligodendrogliomas arise and how they behave. But what CIC does, and why oligodendrogliomas may arise when this gene is altered remain unknown. Recently, using a mouse model in which we genetically deleted CIC, we showed that CIC loss increases the proliferation of the very earliest and most primitive of cells in the brain, the neural stem cells. Loss of CIC also biases the stem cells to start to become early oligodendrocytes. Interestingly, however, these increased early oligodendrocytes appear to be trapped in a proliferative immature state and do not progress to form non-dividing myelin-generating cells. These as-yet-undescribed functions for CIC are important to understand, as cancer is not only a problem of overproduction of stem-like cells but also a problem of their survival and failed maturation. We hypothesize that CIC functions as a key tumour suppressor in oligodendrogliomas through its regulation of neural stem cell and oligodendrocyte precursor proliferation, and its requirement for progression to mature oligodendrocytes - thus leading to an excess of cells that form a tumour when CIC is lost. Our project aims to: 1) Gain a comprehensive view of OPC differentiation and population dynamics regulated by CIC 2) Determine the contribution of CIC-ETV5 to cell cycle control in OPCs and ODG 3) Identify molecular mechanisms by which the CIC-ETV5 axis maintains malignancy in ODG Our work will shed light on the biology of a poorly understood brain tumour, has the potential to reveal new functions of for this recently identified gene, and may point to new therapeutic strategies for brain tumours.

column37: About 2% of the population is born with a biscupid aortic valve, which has only two cusps rather than the normal three. The aortas of these patients commonly balloon due to breakdown of the blood vessel wall. This can cause the aorta to split, which is usually fatal. Why patients with biscupid valves are particularly prone to aortic ballooning is unknown. It may be due to their underlying genetics or it may be due to disrupted blood flow patterns through their bicuspid valve, which cause the blood to drag on the wall of the aorta in ways it shouldn't. Most likely, both factors are at play, but it is important to dissect the contributions of each so that medical and surgical plans can take them into account. Some mice without the protective effects of CNP had bicuspid aortic valves and worse aortic ballooning than mice with tricuspid valves, just as in humans. The advantage of our mice is that they all have the same genetics and therefore the differences in ballooning are due only to the "bad" blood flow that occurs with a bicuspid valve. Using this mouse and a new imaging method we developed, we will determine which proteins and molecular pathways are disrupted by abnormal blood flow to lead to ballooning. Based on our mouse model, we will also specifically test the role of CNP in protecting against aortic ballooning. First we will test in the lab whether patterns of blood flow that are associated with aortic ballooning reduce the amount of CNP in the aorta, leading to ballooning. Second, we will examine normal and ballooned aortas removed from patients at surgery to determine whether there is less CNP in ballooned aortas and in women, which is something we have seen in heart valves. Together, these studies may lead to new targets for the treatment and diagnosis of aortic ballooning in patients with bicuspid valves.

Upon consent, patients will be assessed for the occurrence of POD while in hospital, and followed up to evaluate their cognitive performance at 1 year. We expect to have up to 4,500 patients from 20 countries wordwide. POD is a major problem that is very distressing for patients and their families, and consumes substantial resources. column37: The world is facing the highest numbers of forcibly displaced people and refugees ever seen. The United Nations High Commission for Refugees says that about 69 million people have been forced to flee from their homes because of war, famine, persecution, natural disasters and other crises. column36: A unique model to assess the oral transfer of dietary microRNAs
column37: MicroRNAs modulate ~60% of our genes and are important to our health, as deregulation of microRNA levels has been associated with a panoply of major human diseases, including cancer. Intriguingly, all the plant and animal species composing our diet contain "dietary" microRNAs that we ingest on a daily basis. A long-standing belief is that microRNAs contained in foods do not resist the chemical and biochemical conditions of digestion, and are readily degraded. This dogma, however, was shaken by a provocative study suggesting that a plant microRNA could be absorbed orally and detected in the circulation and organs of mice. Subsequent studies and analyses failed to appease this controversy, due mainly to intrinsic limitations related to the conservation of microRNA sequences between species. Seven years later, whether microRNAs can be transferred orally remains highly debated and controversial. To address most of these limitations, we established a partnership with a major biotechnology firm to set up a unique experimental approach based on the use of milk produced by transgenic (TG) cows. This milk contains endogenously expressed, TG microRNA sequences inexistent in the species under study. Its comparison to the milk of wild-type (WT) cows of the same lineage will allow us to fully assess cow's milk microRNA bioavailability with little to no bias. Preliminary analyses of TG cow's milk revealed the abundance of TG microRNAs and their association with extracellular vesicles formed of a lipid bilayer, coated with proteins and containing the microRNA effector protein Argonaute 2. This unique packaging, offering "triple" protection, may explain that 7-14% of TG microRNAs resisted simulated human digestion and could reach the colon of mice fed by gavage. Our proposal is expected to settle the controversy surrounding the oral transfer of dietary microRNAs and establish the basis for the formulation of a safe and reliable vehicle for the delivery of therapeutic RNAs.

column37: With few exceptions, surgery remains the most effective treatment for patients with solid tumors. However, the trauma of undergoing surgery invariably leads to a weakened immune system which contributes to the likelihood of the tumour reappearing and spreading throughout the patient's body. Natural killer (NK) cells, as their name suggests, are proficient at surveying the body and destroying any cancer cells that appear before they can develop into solid tumours. Although the importance of NK cells in controlling tumour growth is well recognized, my research has shown that surgery dramatically impairs their ability to recognize and respond to tumour cells. Unfortunately, there is no current strategy for addressing the suppression in NK cell activity which occurs following surgery and new approaches targeting this critical stage may hold the potential for improving patient outcomes. We have recently shown that following surgery a large number highly immune suppressive cells are released from the bone marrow and that strategies that prevent their interaction with NK cells can have beneficial effects in animal models. Therefore, we believe that targeting these myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in patients may provide an effective approach for reversing the immune suppressive effects of surgery. To accomplish this goal we have attempted to identify ways of targeting the MDSC population that arises following surgery. These efforts have revealed a distinct identifier present only on MDSCs which we propose can be used to deliver a drug to inhibit their suppressive activity ultimately restoring normal NK cell activity. The current proposal seeks to answer whether this strategy would be safe and effective prior to use in cancer surgery patients. Considering that over 65,000 Canadians undergo tumour removal surgery each year, we believe this research has the potential to benefit a significant number of Canadians and cancer patients throughout the world.

column37: Humans are living longer than ever before, but it is often with age-related illnesses. We will also test if aging can be reversed in a novel yeast model of a human premature aging disease called Progeria. Progeria causes children to age normally, but at an 8-fold accelerated rate. We will also use the Progeria model to discover novel conserved pathways that reverse the effects of aging. Our team, composed of researchers with broad expertise in aging at the molecular, cellular and organismal levels, will identify ways to improve health during aging, such that the quality of life humans live will benefit.

column37: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, both red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and anemia are associated with an increased risk for morbidity and mortality; and the point at which the risks associated with anemia and transfusion are balanced remains undefined. To address this, we will conduct the TRICS IV study, which is a multi-center open-label randomized controlled trial of a restrictive versus liberal transfusion strategy in high risk patients under 65 years of age having cardiac surgery, using a superiority trial design. The study will incorporate an innovative pragmatic and adaptive design. The results from TRICS IV will provide definitive evidence to determine whether a liberal strategy is better than a restrictive one in younger patients. Irrespective of the results, such information is likely to be of high impact for transfusion practice in cardiac surgery around the world, with significant potential implications for all patients undergoing surgical procedures.

column37: All cells contain two main compartments, the inner nucleus, which contains all of our genetic material, and the cytoplasm where much of this material is converted into proteins. column37: INTRODUCTION: There is a pressing need to develop safer and more effective methods of treating movement disorders of the brain, such as Parkinson's Disease. column36: Genomic and Epigenomic Characterization of Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
column37: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is a hereditary disease that affects 1 in 3,500 individuals and results in the development of multiple tumours outside the skull that are called peripheral nerve sheath tumours (PNSTs). Although a large number of these PNST tumours are benign, they cause significant morbidities such as physical disfigurement, neurological defects and pain. The malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours (MPNSTs) are a malignant subtype with poor prognosis. Recently, a novel method of diagnosis was proposed by pathologist for a specific subtype of neurofibroma called atypical neurofibromatosis neoplasm of unknown biological significance (ANNUBP), which is characterized by aggressive features. This subtype is likely to become a malignant tumour and pose a major clinical challenge, as the biological reason for this transformation into a malignant tumour is not known. Preliminary data from our laboratory has uncovered specific modifications in the DNA of majority of ANNUBPs, which is a finding not observed in other benign neurofibroma types. We hypothesize that ANNUBPs have specific genomic features that increase the risk of malignant transformation. The goal of our research proposal is to characterize the molecular alterations in both malignant and benign PNSTs and identify potential therapeutic methods. This will allow future research to target the critical mutated genes with specific drugs that may be already available for other tumor types. Ultimately, any new findings will be tested in cells and mice with PNSTs to confirm their functional role in tumor development and malignancy. The genomic analysis proposed in this study would establish distinct signatures in PNSTs that would potentially predict malignant transformation and enable identification of patient-specific therapies.

column36: Les parcours d'utilisation des ressources alimentaires et l'insecurite alimentaire chez les beneficiaires de l'aide alimentaire : Une analyse longitudinale
column37: L'insecurite alimentaire (IA), ou l'acces restreint ou incertain a une quantite suffisante d'aliments de bonne qualite est un probleme de sante publique au Canada, touchant 12 % des menages canadiens. Des resultats d'etudes scientifiques montrent une correlation entre l'acces limite aux ressources alimentaires (RA) et l'IA. Tres peu d'etudes longitudinales ont examine cette relation, et aucune etude a ce jour n'a examine les parcours d'utilisation des RA et leurs liens avec l'IA, en region. Cette etude vise a identifier les liens entre les parcours d'utilisation des RA est l'IA aupres de 400 nouveaux participants (18-63 ans) d'interventions communautaires en securite alimentaire (ICSA). Nous allons 1) caracteriser en profondeur l'acces aux RA en Estrie, 2) estimer la direction et la taille de l'association entre l'acces aux RA et l'IA chez nouveaux usagers d'ICSA, 3) analyser les liens entre les parcours d'utilisation des RA et l'IA apres 2 ans. Nous menerons une etude en milieu naturel adoptant un devis mixte comprenant multiples donnees qualitatives (entrevues semi-dirigees et documents administratifs) et quantitatives a partir d'une etude longitudinale plus large (IRSC PH1-391312). Nous utiliserons les donnees de 400 nouveaux participants aux ICSA de l'Estrie, interviewes trois fois en face a face entre 2018 et 2020, car dans cette region, les acteurs locaux institutionnels et communautaires sont en train de developper un reseau de coordination en matiere de securite alimentaire, ce qui nous permettra de mieux comprendre les parcours d'utilisation des RA pour repondre aux objectifs 2 et 3. Des analyses descriptives, bivariees, multivariees et multiniveaux seront effectuees. Les resultats de cette etude vont aider les acteurs en sante publique a comprendre l'influence des parcours d'utilisation sur l'IA et serviront de base pour le developpement d'une reponse a l'IA plus efficace.

column36: Development and impact of a knowledge translation intervention for the primary health care management of shoulder pain
column37: Shoulder pain is highly prevalent in the adult population. Patients suffering from shoulder pain usually consult in primary health care and the initial management plan for shoulder pain needs to be optimized to prevent delays in access to health care professionals, prevent chronic pain and disability for patients and avoid overuse of medical imaging, medication and reference to specialists. The objectives of the present project are therefore to: 1- develop a KT intervention for the diagnosis and management of shoulder pain by primary health care (PHC) clinicians; 2- assess the impact of the intervention a. in terms of imaging prescription and reference to specialists and other professionals; b. confidence and knowledge of the primary health care clinicians 3- evaluate the perception of the PHC clinicians of the gap in their practice in the management of patients with shoulder pain and the barriers and facilitators to the implementation of the KT intervention. A decision aid tool and a workshop will be created based on literature review and guidelines from a clinical practice guideline created by our team. PHC clinicians will receive the intervention and participate in focus groups and will be compared to PHC clinicians from other primary care groups not receiving the intervention. Statistical analyses will be performed to determine if the KT intervention reduce the rate of imagery prescription and reference to specialist and to evaluate the change in confidence and knowledge of the primary care physicians. Qualitative analysis will be performed to determine the gap in practice and barriers and facilitators to the implementation of the intervention. This KT intervention can improve quality of life and access to healthcare for patients suffering from shoulder pain by optimizing the management of shoulder pain in primary health care.

column36: Investigating the role of the complement cascade in NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic plasticity during hippocampus development.
column37: Synapses are the primary sites of communication between neurons within the brain, and are capable of undergoing a process known as synaptic plasticity, in which synaptic connections are added or remove to mediate learning and memory. It has become evident from numerous studies that the dysfunction and aberrant elimination of synapses is a critical process underlying the etiology of a number of neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and schizophrenia. The immune cells of the brain, known as microglia, engulf excess 'weak' synapses to refine the connectivity patterns of the brain during development. In mouse models of AD and schizophrenia, it has been found that microglia become abnormally active and that gene mutations found to be risk factors for AD and schizophrenia are microglia-specific. This evidence suggests that microglia play an important role in the pathological synaptic loss seen in multiple neurological disorders. Therefore, a better understanding of how this process occurs normally during development provides the basis for knowing how it goes wrong in a number of disorders. Though it is known that brain activity plays a role in this process of synapse removal during development, the exact activity patterns and molecules involved are unexplored. Therefore, my project aims to elucidate the types of neuronal activity and molecules involved by examining the types of synaptic plasticity during development that can recruit microglia to synapses to eat them. The knowledge gained from my project will contribute to a better understanding of the role of microglia in synaptic plasticity in the healthy brain and how this process can go awry in disease.

column36: Hands-Up: An exercise, nutrition, and falls prevention program
column37: People aged 50-65 diagnosed with osteoporosis feel too young to have the disease. They need to learn how to modify their lifestyle to minimize the chances of fractures. Osteoporosis is a bone disease that increases the risk of fractures. In this age group, a wrist fracture is usually the first sign of osteoporosis. Fracture risk increases if they are not taught to exercise, eat properly, and identify fall risk factors early in their diagnosis. Some studies have looked at interventions for osteoporosis in women over the age of 65, but by this age they have likely already had a spine fracture. No studies have addressed the early-onset osteoporosis age group, intervening before spine fractures occur. I will develop an exercise, nutrition, and falls prevention education program to improve the strength, balance and knowledge of people aged 50-65 who had an osteoporotic wrist fracture. I will use this treatment approach and determine if it is more effective than the usual way of treating people with wrist fractures, determining if this is a better strategy for managing osteoporosis. I will have two groups of patients. First, those, over six weeks, receive twice weekly classes that include exercise and education. Here the focus is on bone health and fracture prevention. The control will receive usual physical therapy and the educational materials at the end of their study participation. The treatment will be randomly allocated to 74 men and women between the ages of 50-65 years of age who are 6-10 weeks post-fracture. The outcomes on both groups will be assessed and compared. I will focus on hand function, balance, fall hazard detection, and a bone health behaviour checklist. Using these outcomes, I can determine which treatment approach works best. Osteoporosis affects one in three women and one in five men, making this an important study to improve the lives of a lot of people. The risk of osteoporosis fractures increases with age, making early interventions critical.

column36: Parental Prevention of Newborn Pain: Evaluation of an eHealth Learning Platform on Parent-Led Management of Infant Procedural Pain
column37: Newborn babies routinely require painful procedures to ensure they are healthy. Sadly, despite known ways to relieve their pain, many do not receive any form of treatment. Untreated pain can affect how these babies feel and react to later pain, how their brains grow and impact development. Research has found many ways that parents can reduce their baby's pain, such as breastfeeding. With today's technological advancements, there is growing evidence that printed educational materials are often set aside and parents now turn to websites on the Internet to search for health information. Since websites are not always accurate, it is important for care areas to meet parents informational needs by offering user-friendly, evidence-based education. However, no studies have examined if parental confidence and capacity to manage their baby's pain is influenced by the method of education. The proposed study will be conducted in three phases. 1) Adapt an existing eHealth learning program to target parents of healthy term babies. This program aims to educate parents on all aspects of newborn pain care during procedures. 2) Parents will test and provide an assessment of ease of use and acceptability of the adapted program. 3) Determine if the eHealth learning program helps parents learn demonstrated by their increased knowledge, confidence and participation in pain management and reduced newborn pain. This study will recruit 140 participants anticipated to give birth to a healthy full-term baby. At a prenatal appointment, these parents will be randomized to receive either 1) the adapted program or 2) standard care. After the birth of their baby, we will evaluate the impact of the eHealth learning program on parental knowledge and confidence in pain care, the frequency of parent-led pain care interventions, and parental usage of the learning materials.

column36: Hemiarthroplasty versus total hip arthroplasty for femoral neck fracture: propensity-score matched cohort study and census of Orthopaedic Surgeons in Ontario
column37: Approximately 30,000 Canadians suffer a hip fracture per year, and this number is expected to increase with an aging population. Patients aged 60 years and older with a displaced femoral neck fracture (representing >30% of all hip fractures) are typically treated with one of two prosthetic implants: a total hip replacement or a partial hip replacement. Several trials suggest that total hip replacement is superior to partial hip replacement, since it is associated with less pain and fewer complications; however, there are important differences between patients recruited in these trials and the average patient who has a hip fracture. The latter tends to be older, frailer, and have multiple health conditions that puts him/her at higher risk of complications. Population-level research suggests that patients treated with total hip replacement are having more complications than expected from trial data. Also, there is significant variation in treatment type based on surgeon training and geographic location. This project has two parts. The first set of objectives involves the use of healthcare administrative data to look at the outcomes (death, complications, pain, functional status, and ministry healthcare costs) of all Ontario patients aged 60 years and older treated with each type of prosthetic implant for hip fracture. For the second part, we will explore reasons for the existing variation in care by conducting a census of Orthopaedic Surgeons across Ontario. This research will allow us to understand why there are individual-level and system-level differences in the care of older patients with hip fractures. This is the first step to changing medical practice and improving the care we provide to patients with hip fractures. This work will help clinicians decide which surgical treatment is most effective for patients with displaced femoral neck fractures outside the trial setting.

column36: In-solution targeted capture for sequencing of antibiotic resistance genes
column37: Antibiotic resistance mechanisms are rapidly spreading amongst bacteria globally, limiting current antibiotic treatment options. An accurate and rapid method to profile antibiotic resistance genes in various environments including the human gastrointestinal tract is needed to increase our understanding of antibiotic resistance, the changes that affect resistance, and ultimately improve targeting antibiotic use. Current methods for detecting resistance are not time- nor cost-effective. In a bacterial genome, antibiotic resistance determinants represent a small proportion of all the genetic content; therefore a method that is targeted and specifically captures resistance-conferring genes will revolutionize the study of antibiotic resistance. This project aims to develop and optimize an enrichment approach by designing capture probes that are specific to a set of resistance gene sequences. DNA isolated from multi-drug resistant clinical pathogens was investigated through this approach and sequenced. Across various bacteria, more than 80% of the sequencing data was determined to belong to antibiotic resistance genes. A method will be optimized to identify antibiotic resistance sequences from bacteria in the human gastrointestinal tract and applied to samples from patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy. The goal of this project is to provide a cost-effective and timely approach to understand the factors that select for antibiotic resistance. As a potential method for surveillance in environments where resistance determinants are likely to spread, this technique can help to prepare physicians for impending antibiotic-resistant outbreaks, improve the prudent use of antibiotics, and prevent further selection for antibiotic resistance. Along with a better understanding of the connection between the presence of individual genes and antibiotic susceptibility, this method can be developed into a diagnostic to improve human health and ultimately prevent a post-antibiotic era.

column36: Defining the consequences associated with early embryonic alcohol exposure and investigate the impact of a nutritional preventive intervention.
column37: In Canada, about 2-3% of children are born with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD) because of prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE). FASD are the most common cause of brain damage before birth and the leading cause of nonhereditary neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). About 40% of pregnancies are unplanned, consequently many women inadvertently subject their embryos to PAE during early pregnancy. With this project, we aim to investigate the adverse effect of a PAE during the first week of pregnancy on the future baby and get a better comprehension of the epigenetic mechanisms underlying those adverse consequences. Epigenetic modifications are chemical modifications associated to genes that provide the means by which genes can be turned on or off at specific times. These modifications provide a link between the environment and gene function. Early embryonic development is critical for the rest of the pregnancy. During that period, cells divide and grow under a specific program, dictated by major changes of epigenetic modifications. We hypothesis that irregularities occurring during the organisation of this program may increase the vulnerability of the central nervous system to NDDs development later in life. Since alcohol can alter the epigenetic landscape, which is heavily reworked in the early embryo, we believe that embryonic epigenetic disruption caused by alcohol could alter the normal developmental program of the central nervous system and lead to FASD. We aim also to determine the therapeutic potential of a preventive diet enrich in methyl donor groups to counteract the adverse effect of early PAE on the embryo development. Altogether, our finding will deepen understanding on the epigenetics mechanisms underlying the adverse consequences of an early PAE on embryo and nervous system development. Moreover, this project could lead to novel information and tools to promote earlier diagnosis, better treatment, and optimal outcomes for children affected of FASD.

column37: La demence et la dysfonction cognitive se manifestent par des troubles affectant la memoire. Avec le vieillissement de la population, ces troubles cognitifs auront de serieuses repercussions pour les personnes atteintes, les familles qui s'en occupent et le systeme des soins de sante. L'inflammation et l'oxydation sont des reactions dans l'organisme associees au vieillissement et au developpement de la demence. Ainsi, des concentrations sanguines elevees de facteurs d'inflammation comme la proteine C-reactive (CRP) et l'interleukine-6 (IL-6) de meme que le raccourcissement des telomeres, des structures qui protegent nos cellules de l'oxydation et de l'inflammation, pourraient etre relies a un risque plus eleve de demence. Par ailleurs, certains stresseurs au travail ont ete associes a des concentrations elevees de CRP et d'IL-6 et a un raccourcissement des telomeres. Il serait alors possible que ces stresseurs au travail jouent un role dans le developpement de la demence via l'effet intermediaire des facteurs d'inflammation et d'oxydation. Le present projet de recherche vise a evaluer : 1) l'association entre trois facteurs d'inflammation et d'oxydation (CRP, IL-6 et telomeres) et la dysfonction cognitive; et 2) le role intermediaire de ces facteurs sanguins dans la relation entre les stresseurs au travail et la dysfonction cognitive. Ces objectifs seront realises a partir d'une etude importante constituee de plus de 9 000 Canadiens suivis depuis 22 ans. Les resultats de ce projet de recherche contribueront a identifier des facteurs qui precedent le diagnostic de troubles cognitifs comme la dysfonction cognitive. Les stresseurs au travail etant frequents, il serait possible d'intervenir eventuellement dans les milieux de travail pour ralentir le developpement de troubles cognitifs plus severes comme la demence. Cette etude permettra d'obtenir des informations qui serviront aux connaissances pour un vieillissement actif et satisfaisant.

column36: The Role of Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase (iNOS) in Promoting Cytokine-Induced Cachexia
column37: Historically overlooked, cachexia is a debilitating illness that currently has no available treatments. Cachexia develops in patients suffering from inflammatory diseases such as cancer and is marked by uncontrolled and involuntary muscle and fat loss. The muscle loss within cachectic patients is believed to be the predominant cause of its pathology leading to dramatic decreases in patient quality of life. Cancer patients suffering from cachexia are also significantly less responsive to their treatments and have much higher mortality rates. As a result, this draining disease that almost doubles the durations of hospitalization for patients, not only places a serious financial burden on patients' families, but also on the health care system. Due to its significant impacts on patient wellbeing and its economic burden, there is a strong need to develop treatments for cachexia. Currently it is believed that cachexia is caused by the elevation of several inflammatory factors that are made during our body's response to overlying diseases. The fundamental mechanisms induced by these factors, which drive the negative symptoms of cachexia are poorly understood. Due to the complex nature of the disease, all previous attempts to treat it have failed; therefore, further investigations into the main drivers of its pathology may uncover more efficacious treatment strategies. An accumulating body of evidence suggests that the enzyme inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is a primary promoter of cachexia. iNOS has been observed to target and disrupt factors involved in metabolism within muscle cells, and the programs required for muscle formation, integrity, and activity. We believe that revealing the targets of iNOS could unveil potential drug targets to help alleviate this disease.

column36: Understanding and improving the quality of melanoma diagnosis in Ontario: A population-based study
column37: The incidence rate of melanoma is rising in Canada and other economically developed countries. There is a wide range of survival expectancies depending on the thickness at which the melanoma is diagnosed, with thick melanomas having 5-year survival rates of only 56% (compared to ~100% for thin lesions). We plan to assess whether differences exist between advanced and non-advanced patients according to factors such as the diagnostic process and its length, patients' usual use of healthcare, patient characteristics and health status, and the melanoma-related resources in their community (e.g. dermatologist supply). This study will be conducted using electronic health data for the province of Ontario linked to our clinical population database containing detailed information on patient's melanoma characteristics. column36: Understanding the timing, mechanism and recovery of brain injury in complex congenital heart disease (CHD)
column37: Structural heart defects in newborn babies, termed congenital heart disease (CHD), are the most common birth defect. Babies with CHD often go on to develop neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), which limit their quality of life. Unsurprisingly, MRI of CHD babies show brain abnormalities, with white matter (tracts of the brain which allow brain regions to communicate) often implicated. The link between an abnormal heart, its action on the developing brain, and the subsequent abnormalities seen on MRI are poorly understood. Current consensus is that CHD results in the developing brain receiving less oxygen than normal. How this results in brain injuries remains to be seen. To address the link between CHD and subsequent brain injuries, and to determine whether increased oxygen protects the newborn brain, I will examine CHD-related laboratory mice using advanced imaging techniques developed at our lab. Mice share common developmental features with humans, all while allowing for short studies due to their rapid development and for invasive procedures not possible in humans. I will first establish a mouse model of CHD by creating a heart specific defect through surgical manipulation. Next, I will image the brain and label its cells to identify the underlying cellular events responsible for brain injury in CHD. I predict that the lack of oxygen will affect brain regions containing cell types that are vulnerable to oxygen deficits. Additionally, I will investigate whether these abnormalities can be reduced by increasing oxygen delivery to the mother. I hypothesize that increased oxygen will have a protective effect on the brain, and that both brain MRI and cellular imaging will show a recovery back to normal. NDDs cost Ontario approximately $2 million / person over their lifetime. A successful outcome of this study promises a reduction in the prevalence of NDDs due to CHD, lower healthcare costs, and more importantly, a better quality of life for individuals with CHD.

column36: Valve Choice in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease
column37: Heart disease is the most common cause of death in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Affecting three million Canadians, CKD can progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) when patients require dialysis. Valvular heart disease is found in over 30% of patients with ESRD and diagnosed at a rate four to five times higher than the general population. As a result, a large proportion of patients with ESRD need valve replacement surgery to relieve symptoms and prevent permanent heart damage. Native valves can be replaced with a mechanical or bioprosthetic valve, each with their own advantages and disadvantages. Mechanical valves are more durable, but require life-long blood thinning medication (i.e. warfarin) to prevent clot formation on the valve and other parts of the body. In addition to challenges of medication adherence, blood thinning medication is associated with increased risk of bleeding. Bioprosthetic valves, made with tissue, avoid life-long blood thinning medication and its complications, but are less durable and require a complex reoperation long-term. Currently, there is a lack of research to support choosing either valve in patients with ESRD, contributing to variable clinical practice amongst physicians. Using various types of studies, we will 1) Describe the quality of current research. 2) Describe the preferences of patients and physicians for different prosthetic valves. 3) Evaluate outcomes of patients with ESRD who previously received either valve, using advanced statistics. 4) Evaluate outcomes of valve surgery in patients in earlier stages of CKD. These studies will evaluate the best valve given current body of scientific evidence, and contribute new evidence that improves on the shortcomings of past research. The evidence gained from these studies will inform a randomized control trial in this patient population. Ultimately, we hope to improve the decision making and outcomes of patients with CKD who require valve replacement surgery.

column36: Modelling the regulatory networks that govern mRNA stability and their implication in cancer
column37: Gene expression is the process by which deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)'s genetic instructions are used to synthesize gene products. Genes are read by the cell to produce ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules, which carry their genetic information. Gene expression is often de-regulated in diseases such as cancer, as many genes have either increased or decreased expression compared to normal cells, leading to their abnormal behavior. However, the specific mechanisms that lead to these changes are mostly unknown. Identifying these processes would allow us to better understand the underlying mechanisms of cancer progression and to develop potential therapeutic approaches to reverse it. The goal of my research project is to investigate the regulation of RNA stability, one of the least characterized aspects of gene expression regulation in cancer. The stability of individual RNAs determines their lifespan, which in turn determines the amount of gene products they will be able to generate. However, the genes that have altered stability in cancer and the factors responsible for these changes are still unknown. I am developing new computational tools to systematically analyze genomics data, with the aim of identifying the specific factors responsible for the changes in RNA stability observed in cancer. Identifying these mechanisms will improve our understanding of gene expression regulation and provide new insights into the causes of gene expression changes in cancer, pointing to new therapeutic approaches.

column36: CRISPR-mediated engineering of autophagy-deficient human T lymphocytes for CAR-T cell immunotherapy
column37: Fighting cancer is no easy task. Our immune system has the ability to detect and eradicate cancer cells, but these cells use a wide variety of mechanisms to evade or impair our immune surveillance. Hence restoring and strengthening our immune system is a promising approach to fight back diverse tumours. CAR-T cell immunotherapy, a promising treatment, consists of collecting patient's immune T cells and genetically reprogramming them to specifically target and destroy cancer cells. The engineered T cells are then administered to cancer patients to eradicate the malignant cells. This new treatment showed impressive results against blood cancers. However, treating solid tumours remains a difficult challenge for the scientific community and many hurdles need to be overcome before this therapy is accessible to all. During immune cells reprogramming, a new gene coding for a receptor called CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) is incorporated in the patient's immune cells. This CAR receptor will recognize cancer cells and trigger the immune response. Even if these CAR-T cells are effective against cancer cells in the bloodstream, they don't persist in solid tumours. This lack of activity is attributed to the low amount of nutrients and oxygen near the tumour, which activates a pathway called autophagy. Preliminary results showed that autophagy-deficient mice had a significantly enhanced anti-tumour activity against prostate and breast cancer cells. We hypothesize that autophagy-deficient CAR-T cells will have an increased lifespan and anti-tumour activity in solid tumours. This project aims at using a molecular scissor called CRISPR-Cas9 to simultaneously target and inactivate a gene essential for autophagy and insert the CAR receptor. By modifying the CAR specificity, it will be possible to generate CAR-T cells targeting a wide array of cancer. I will develop a safe, rapid and efficient method to generate powerful CAR-T cells against a variety of cancer cells.

column37: Around 30,000 Canadians are diagnosed with post-stroke aphasia each year. Aphasia is an acquired language disorder that occurs after brain injury and leads to significant consequences, such as social isolation and depression. The principal symptom is a difficulty finding words, called anomia. Anomia is present in the majority of persons with aphasia (PWA). Recovery from aphasia is dependent on brain plasticity (BP) mechanisms; the brain's ability to adapt and remodel throughout life, especially after an injury such as stroke leading to aphasia. This project proposes to study the recovery of the capacity to find words, and the brain's changes that support this recovery. To do so, we study the effects of two therapies, one based on the sounds of the words and the other based on the meaning of the words. We will recruit PWA who suffer from anomia, and assign them randomly to each therapy. It is expected that both of these therapies will lead to improvements in the ability to find words, but that the strategies used will differ. Also, by using functional magnetic resonance imaging, we aim to identify the areas in the brain where activity is essential to achieve recovery. The identification of these mechanisms of recovery following language therapy will allow optimizing the chances of recovery of people with aphasia by predicting the most effective therapy to trigger BP and recovery. The final purpose of this work is to deliver aphasia therapy guidelines that will maximize each person's recovery according to their stroke recovery and symptoms. The impact of this research on the health and quality of life of PWA lies in its potential to maximize recovery from aphasia, thus preventing depression and isolation that occurs when PWA do not improve their communication abilities.

column36: Engaging Families as Advisors in Child Health Organizations in Ontario, Canada
column37: There is growing momentum for involving patients and families in treatment decisions, health research, health service delivery, and health policy development across the world. column36: Predicting the Impact of Somatic Structural Variation in Cancer Whole Genomes
column37: Cancer is driven by mutations in the genome that accumulate over the course of lifetime. Some of these mutations are harmful and drive the progression of cancer while others are tolerated without damage to cells and tissues. To distinguish between these mutations, we look for patterns of mutational recurrence across a population, determine whether they are present in the healthy population and design strategies to predict their impact on biological function based on established knowledge.
