column36: Characterization and Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA in Liquid Biopsy for Cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death in Canada and technologies to detect and monitor the disease are sorely needed. Currently, this is done through frequent tissue biopsy, but this is unpractical and challenging if the tumor is too small. Alternatively, cancer mutational targets can be found in the blood and saliva of cancer patients in a concept called liquid biopsy. Recently, the fragment lengths of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has been shown to differ amongst cancer and healthy patients which can explain why current DNA detection technologies such as digital droplet PCR have difficulty finding tumor DNA in biofluids. Electric field-induced release and measurement (EFIRM) technology, however, can detect these tumor fragments accurately in plasma and saliva samples from lung cancer patients. We hypothesize that a combination of shorter circulating tumor DNA and EFIRM's mechanics may explain the detection performance in biofluids. This proposal has three fundamental goals to scientifically underpin the performance of EFIRM liquid biopsy. Firstly, we will isolate DNA from plasma and saliva samples from lung cancer patients to study various characteristics, one being length. Secondly, we will examine and describe how DNA capturing probe design and density impact EFIRM's ability to locate tumor DNA in biofluids. Thirdly, we will use EFIRM to demonstrate a proof of concept of liquid biopsy by measuring the changes of tumor DNA in the saliva and blood samples of lung cancer patients throughout their cancer treatment. The impact of this study is multi-factorial. Learning about tumor DNA characteristic will provide new biological information about these tumor biomarker targets. Understanding EFIRM fundamental mechanics will reveal the scientific rationale of its performance. Third, we will introduce a tool which can reliably monitor and adjust drug selection in patients undergoing cancer therapy.

column36: Implementing effective community health worker programs to address health disparities among the urban poor in low- and middle-income countries
column37: By 2050, 80% of the world's urban population will live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with the urban poor experiencing stark health inequities. Innovative strategies are needed to meet the health needs of the growing urban poor. In light of health worker shortages and resource constraints in LMICs, this research seeks to understand how community health worker (CHW) programs - which have been predominantly implemented in rural contexts - can be effectively applied in urban settings. CHWs are lay persons who are briefly trained in specific health tasks, but do not hold formal professional medical certificates. Past experience demonstrates that 'proven' primary health care innovations designed for rural communities are not always well-suited to urban contexts. In urban contexts where community cohesion, safety, employment, and other factors differ significantly from rural settings, CHW program features require adaptation. This research will explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when adapting the CHW model to the urban context, with the intention of providing practical recommendations for the design and implementation of urban-specific programs. A scoping review of urban, LMIC-based, CHW programs will be conducted to synthesize the little evidence available. Interviews with LMIC-based program managers will document lessons on how CHW program design and implementation can respond to urban contexts and challenges. Finally, a case study in Colombia will investigate whether a newly piloted role for CHWs (conducting follow-up home visits for patients with chronic diseases) improves CHW job satisfaction and accountability - two important elements for effective and sustainable urban programming. This study is the first to synthesize evidence from urban CHW programs and generate cross-cutting implementation lessons. The findings will contribute to theory-building and serve as a resource for developing future research and guidelines.

column36: The Effect of Developmental Odour Exposure on the Development of the Olfactory System, Eating Habits, and Metabolic Health
column37: The World Health Organization estimates that 340 million people under 19 are overweight or obese. This is troubling as childhood obesity is the strongest predictor of lifelong obesity, a major health burden worldwide. Strong evidence from the past decade indicates that a strong predictor for childhood obesity is nutritional quality during pregnancy. Maternal diets high in fats and calories correlate strongly with overeating in children, predisposing them to a lifetime of obesity. Separately, the olfactory system has been increasingly shown to influence the metabolic health of individuals. Enhancement or elimination of the olfactory system within mice alters their metabolic health and weight, without changing eating habits. Within humans, the olfactory system has been shown to be sensitive to metabolic hormones, including insulin. As well, a decline in olfactory ability is associated with many metabolic diseases. Currently, there is very little information on how maternal diet alters the development of the olfactory system, and its subsequent effects on metabolic health. Therefore, my project will aim to understand how fat-related odors in the maternal diet alter the olfactory system of the developing child, and if that has lifelong consequences on metabolic health. Pregnant mice will be fed specially designed food enriched in odours common to high-fat foods, but containing identical nutrition. I will then measure the olfactory development, eating habits, and metabolic health of the offspring mice. I will use analytical chemistry, molecular biology, and systems neuroscience approaches to determine possible mechanisms contributing to any changes found. Information from this project will help determine whether the olfactory system may contribute to the modern prevalence of overeating, obesity, and metabolic disease. Additionally, the project aims to begin studying more nuanced aspects of maternal nutrition and its effects on childhood and lifelong metabolic health.

column36: Endogenous retroelements as novel immune escape mechanisms in human cancers
column37: Immunotherapy has drastically changed the landscape of cancer treatment. By retargeting the body's own immune system towards a tumour, immunotherapy has proved effective where more traditional therapies have failed. However, tumours have developed sophisticated mechanisms to evade the anti-tumour immune response, thus rendering such immunotherapies ineffective. The advent of next-generation sequencing technologies has highlighted the importance of the non-coding genome in health and disease. A significant proportion of these non-coding genes comprise endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), remnants of ancient viral infections that have since become a part of human DNA. Given their viral origins, these genes have retained their capacity to modulate immune responses. As ERVs and other retroelements are globally deregulated in cancer cells, we propose that they may promote the immune evasive capacity of tumours. Our preliminary analysis of gene expression patterns from 964 cancer patients comprising 31 tumour types has uncovered a novel subset of immune genes that may be regulated by ERVs and other retroelements. My preliminary findings show a novel mechanism by which a retroelement drives expression of alternative soluble form of PD-L1, a molecule that inhibits antitumour immune responses and is thus a key immunotherapeutic target. We propose that this retroelement-derived PD-L1 may affect patient response to immunotherapy, which we will test using in vitro and in vivo models as well as screening patient samples. We aim to uncover diverse mechanisms by which ERVs can contribute to resistance to immunotherapy as well as potential novel therapeutic targets.

column36: Studies of the structure, function and regulation of the ATR-ATRIP complex
column37: The complete and accurate replication of the genetic information in our DNA prior to each cycle of cell division is critical to our health and survival. Changes to the integrity of our genome can result from ongoing intracellular and environmental sources of DNA damage that, if left unrepaired, could disrupt key cellular processes. Importantly, such damage is often a barrier to the completion of DNA replication, a phenomenon known as replication stress. Human cells have mechanisms of preserving genomic integrity during replication that are controlled by a protein called ATR (short for 'ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related'). ATR sits atop a signaling network known as the DNA damage response that detects, signals and resolves DNA damage and replication stress. Upon recognition of aberrant DNA structures, ATR binds to DNA near affected sites where it gets "turned on" by interaction with other signaling molecules. ATR proceeds to coordinate a number of processes required for repairing the damage and restarting the replication process. This study will address two important aspects of ATR function at the molecular level: its ability to bind to damaged DNA, and how it becomes activated in response to damage. In recent years, ATR has been proposed as a potential anti-cancer drug target for a number of reasons. Cancer cells are prone to replication stress and thus highly reliant on ATR for their survival. The DNA repair capacity of ATR signaling mediates resistance to chemotherapy, a mainstay of cancer treatment whose efficacy is dependent on the ability to cause lethal amounts of DNA damage. Taken together, pharmacological inhibition of ATR can be effective on two fronts: by targeting an essential process on which cancer cells depend, and sensitizing the cells to existing chemotherapeutic agents. A better mechanistic understanding of ATR will allow for the rational design of new drugs and open up new cancer treatment options.

column36: Unlocking HIV-1 Env Towards a Cure
column37: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected more than 77 million people since the beginning of the epidemic. In the absence of treatment, HIV causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 35.4 million people worldwide. column37: The number of new HIV infections each year continues to remain unacceptably high. Just as cancer therapy attacks with multiple drugs, we will employ a combination of biomedical approaches that blocks HIV infections in different ways. Firstly, will be to use anti-HIV drugs that work by blocking the ability of the virus to replicate. Our mid-term studies will use a laboratory mouse with a human immune system to determine the mechanism of how ASA affects the migration of HIV target cells and we perform HIV infection studies to directly test is ASA can reduce HIV infection. This proposal will determine if our "Combination HIV Prevention" approach is more effective thereby providing women with more options for protecting themselves.

column36: Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise 2.0: Targeting the interplay between myeloid cells and CD4+ T-cells for HIV cure
column37: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in decreasing mortality for HIV-infected individuals, ART has not cured HIV/AIDS. The failure to eradicate HIV infection during ART stems from the virus' ability to persist in the body in multiple cell types and tissues. Without lifetime therapy, the virus quickly rebounds resulting in accelerated morbidity and mortality. The most commonly studied form of persistence is in memory CD4+ T-cells (CD4+ Tm-cells) that are harboring virus out of view of drugs or from the immune system. However, evidence indicates that other long-lived cells, known as myeloid cells, might contribute to HIV persistence. Cells that allow virus persistence are called viral reservoirs (VRs) and represent the main barrier to an HIV cure. While much is known about HIV persistence, many puzzles remain about the source of persistent HIV, the mechanisms underlying the establishment and persistence of VRs, particularly in CD4+ Tm-cells, and the ways to eliminate VRs. The Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise 2.0 (CanCURE 2.0), a team of leading Canadian HIV researchers, proposes an integrated and innovative research program informed by new knowledge in the field and new findings generated under CanCURE 1.0 (2014-2019) to: 1) Define the role and impact of long-lived self-renewing tissue-resident myeloid cells called macrophages in HIV persistence during ART; 2) Conduct detailed mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the critical role played by myeloid cells in the establishment and persistence of VR in CD4+ Tm-cells; 3) Identify new therapeutic strategies to tackle HIV persistence that capitalize on these discoveries and pursue the preclinical and clinical development of therapeutic interventions aimed at targeting VRs initiated under CanCURE 1.0. These studies are all aimed at finding new effective approaches to curing HIV infection in humans by eliminating persistent HIV infection from VRs in ART-treated patients.

column37: The war against HIV/AIDS is not yet over. Although anti-viral drug cocktails have changed HIV/AIDS to a chronic manageable disease, people living with HIV infection still have an increased risk of drug side effects, heart, kidney, and brain diseases, as well as cancer. In addition, living with HIV infection is associated with stigma. Thus, a cure for HIV infection is needed. A main obstacle to cure is the presence of a persistent reservoir of HIV infected cells in the body, where our current drugs cannot reach. Our project proposes harnessing the immune system, in particular, a cell called a 'killer T cell' to eradicate the remaining reservoir in order to cure the infection. In order to do this, we will first extensively characterize the genetic signatures of the remaining virus hiding in the reservoir from blood samples from persons living with HIV. We will then design a number of strategies, where we can mobilize a person's killer cells to be able to eliminate their remaining viruses. We will use a 'personalized' approach by studying each person's own viruses and their own immune systems. We will also borrow from a recent revolution in the cancer field, to improve the killer cells to kill HIV infected cells better and more efficiently, by using new genetic engineering techniques. All of our work will be done in the test tube or in pre-clinical models as a preparation to design clinical trials to cure HIV infection.follow

column36: Encouraging Informed Decisions about Cannabis Use in Pregnancy: Educational Needs of Women and Prenatal Care Providers
column37: Recreational use of cannabis has been legal in Canada since 2018; Medical use has been legal since 2001. More and more Canadians are choosing to use cannabis for both recreational and medical reasons. Some women use cannabis during pregnancy and breastfeeding, especially if they were regular users before pregnancy. There is evidence that using cannabis during pregnancy may cause babies to be born early, have low birth weight, and have some impairments in the way their brain develops. However, the medical evidence on this is uncertain and some studies have found no association with cannabis use and these negative outcomes. For women who are only occasional users, this may be a good enough reason not to use cannabis at all during pregnancy and breastfeeding. However, there are many reasons that other women may struggle with abstaining from cannabis use during pregnancy. Some may not understand the potential harms. Others who used cannabis to treat certain conditions before pregnancy may wish to continue this use. Some may choose to use cannabis as a way to stop using other, more harmful substances like opioids. Others may start to use cannabis during pregnancy in order to treat their morning sickness. Because of the stigmatization of cannabis use in pregnancy, women may not feel comfortable talking with their health care providers about this. Health care providers may be uncertain what advice to offer, since the evidence about cannabis is so undeveloped, and many women have compelling reasons to use. This research considers the question of cannabis in pregnancy from the perspective of the pregnant woman, and from the perspective of the prenatal health care provider counselling this woman. It considers existing clinical evidence and creates new ethical, social evidence to formulate advice for pregnant women, creating educational aids for women and health care providers to facilitate discussions about using cannabis during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

column36: Total liquid ventilation for bronchopulmonary dysplasia prevention in a model of extreme preterm lamb
column37: Modern medical care allows for more extremely preterm-born babies to survive. These patients have immature lungs that tend to collapse and render breathing extremely difficult. Despite efforts to avoid mechanical ventilation, most of these babies will require such support in the first few days of life. The use of a gas ventilator to ensure their survival generates inflammation that damages the lungs. Unfortunately, most babies born before the 25th week of pregnancy that survive will develop chronic pulmonary disease, called bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Altered lung function and neurological development are now clearly associated with this chronic lung disease developed after a preterm birth. Total liquid ventilation, where the lungs are filled and then ventilated with a liquid called perfluorocarbon, has been proven to lower inflammation induced by ventilation and could be useful to prevent lung damage. A ventilator developed by our INOLIVENT team at the 'Universite de Sherbrooke' now allows for the precise control of liquid ventilation parameters. We can thus now refine liquid ventilation techniques in order to use this advanced respiratory support on the premature infant to reduce lung damage and potentially prevent bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Our multidisciplinary team has already put in place the techniques to assess the effect of different liquid ventilation strategies on the heart and lung and to evaluate the inflammatory response using a term lamb model. The aim of the current project is to use a preterm lamb model to evaluate the clinical potential of total liquid ventilation to limit lung inflammation induced by mechanical ventilation when compared to conventional gas ventilation.

column37: Each year, approximately 7,600 adolescents and young adults (AYAs; aged 15-39 years) are diagnosed with cancer in Canada. These individuals fall between childhood and adult cancer care programs, and have complex needs because they were diagnosed with cancer during critical developmental, social, and reproductive years. A primary concern among AYAs with cancer is fertility. Because more women are having children later in life, many AYA patients will not have had a child when they are diagnosed with cancer. Previous research has found that cancer therapies can lead to high-risk pregnancies or infertility, and thus the possibility of having future children after cancer is uncertain for these survivors. To date, limited information is available to guide women and doctors about pregnancy after cancer at a young age. In this study, we will look at the impact of cancer on subsequent pregnancy complications and outcomes. Using a Canadian cohort of AYA cancer survivors, we will assess: 1.the rate of abortions, stillbirths, and live births, 2.the degree of complications in mothers and newborns, and 3.whether risks of these complications and outcomes change with time from diagnosis or treatment period. These points will also be explored using more detailed data from Alberta to establish the effect of radiotherapy and chemotherapy treatment, and develop recommendations for doctors. For all outcomes, we will compare AYA cancer survivors to the general population so that the results can be translated easily and clearly. The results of this study will add to the current understanding of pregnancy after cancer by providing evidence to support a hands-on approach to fertility counselling at diagnosis, as well as greater monitoring of pregnancies and deliveries in this vulnerable group.

column36: Identifying premorbid environmental and neural markers of risk for first lifetime onsets of depressive and anxiety disorders in high-risk youth.
column37: Depression and anxiety are common, disabling, and typically first occur in adolescence. Once a person has had one episode of these illnesses, they are at increased risk for subsequent episodes, and often have a poorer prognosis for treatment. We know that a lack of parental care places youth at risk for depression and anxiety. Despite this, there is relatively little knowledge about brain factors that might put youth at risk for the first lifetime occurrence of depression or anxiety. There is also little knowledge of how parenting influences the development over time of brain functioning that is linked to adolescents' risk for depression and anxiety. The first goal of this study is to examine whether brain functioning in regions that govern how individuals process emotions as well as rewards predicts the whether or not high-risk youth develop an episode of depression or anxiety for the first time in their life. We will also examine whether low parental care predicts the development over time in functioning in these ostensible neural markers of risk for depression and anxiety. Participants will be adolescents with least one parent with a history of depression or anxiety, but who have not experienced such an episode themselves. Thus, this will be a sample of youth at high risk for depression and anxiety but who have yet to develop either. Participants and at least one parent will complete measures of depression and anxiety and parental care towards the adolescent, and the adolescent will complete brain scans, at baseline and again 18 months later. We expect aberrant functioning in emotion and reward processing circuitry to predict the first lifetime onsets of depressive and anxiety disorders by follow-up. We also expect a lack of parental care to predict aberrant development of functioning in these circuits.

column36: Evaluating, refining and bringing to scale the endogenous health-promoting attributes of alternative food networks to address diabetes mellitus and hypertension among Ecuadorian farmers
column37: In Ecuador, rural people, and particularly rural Indigenous people are disproportionately affected by both nutrient inadequacies as well as overweight and obesity. This double burden of malnutrition magnifies their risk of developing diet-related chronic diseases such as diabetes mellitus (DM) and hypertension (Hyp). In parallel, many rural Indigenous people in Ecuador have organized around alternative food networks (AFNs) such as farmers' markets to seek more sustainable livelihoods. These local AFNs support food environments and practices that hold strong potential to prevent DM and Hyp among participating farmers. For example, AFNs have been demonstrated to promote food literacy, favor consumption of fruits, vegetables and whole grains, and to place income in women's hands; these, in turn have all been associated with healthier nutritional status and reduced risk of diet-related chronic disease. Our research aims to evaluate specific AFN attributes for their measurable contribution to DM and Hyp prevention in order to leverage the most effective attributes for a stronger and broader positive impact. To do so, we will use validated instruments for assessing diet and physiological risk factors among AFN farming households and a comparison group of non-AFN neighbouring farmers, and we will use participatory qualitative research to determine the most effective implementation strategy for translating research findings into practice. Our implementing partners run an ongoing intervention for managing communication and knowledge-sharing among an estimated 132 Ecuadorian AFNs, positioning them as the cornerstone for streamlining research findings into practice. Through the implementation of our research findings, we expect to provide strategic and practical guidance for integrating health-sensitive attributes into the regular practices of AFNs as they continue to replicate and evolve in Ecuador and elsewhere.

column36: The role of age of cannabis use onset in the developmental pathways leading to substance use problems by early adulthood: key mediators and moderators.
column37: One in three Canadian youth in the 16-25 years of age group are active cannabis users, with statistics showing that trends in cannabis use (CU) are rising. This is worrying as some studies have shown that CU during adolescence is associated with higher risk for adult cannabis and other substance use disorders. However, it is still unclear whether starting CU earlier in adolescence puts youth at higher risk of developing later substance use problems after accounting for early risk factors or different patterns of substance use. We also don't know what individual and environmental factors place boys and girls who initiate cannabis use during adolescence at higher risk of developing later substance use problems. Thus, the present project aims to examine (1) whether the association between CU initiation and later substance use problems remain when considering important environmental and individual factors; (2) whether the association between early CU initiation and later substance use problems can be explained by CU profiles (how much one uses, how frequently, etc.) and individual and environmental characteristics, and (3) whether the effect between age of initiation and later substance use problems differ for different CU profiles, and individual and environmental factors. For this, we will build on two ongoing longitudinal studies, in which participants were followed from age 5 months to 18/19 years, and we will collect detailed information on their cannabis use and other substance use, mental health, and the youth's environment at 23 and 25 years. This study could provide much needed information about how individual and environmental factors work together to increase the risk of developing substance use problems, potentially helping guide policy and prevention for those more likely to develop substance use problems by early adulthood.

column36: Placental Par Polarity Complex in the Pathogenesis of Preeclampsia
column37: Proper placental function is essential for the health of the fetus and mother during pregnancy. Placental dysfunction, which is when cells in the placenta do not form or function properly, is a characteristic of the common pregnancy complications preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction. Importantly, these complications significantly affect the lifelong health of mothers and their babies. The cell that forms the surface of the placenta, the syncytiotrophoblast (ST), is particularly important in the development of placental dysfunction. Unfortunately, there are large gaps in our knowledge about basic ways that the ST functions. This hampers our ability to understand how we could correct ST function in placental dysfunction in order to treat both mothers and their babies. Here we will examine how the ST establishes and maintains the separated arrangement of proteins and cellular components between the "top" and "bottom" side of the cell. This is known as cell polarity, and it is important for cellular function to allow for delivery of nutrients and waste between the mother and the fetus. We will examine the role of the Par polarity complex, a group of proteins known to control cell polarity that have not been studied in the placenta. The Par complex also controls the arrangement of the cytoskeleton, endocytosis, and response to inflammation. These are critical processes that maintain ST function and are disrupted in placental dysfunction, but how these processes are carried out in ST are mostly unknown. Therefore, these studies will increase our knowledge about fundamental aspects of ST cell biology. The knowledge we gain will help us to understand the unique ways in which the ST functions and in the future will lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets to treat placental dysfunction and improve outcomes for both mothers and their children.

column36: A prospective study evaluating complement activation among pregnant patients with obstetrical antiphospholipid syndrome
column37: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disease that can lead to blood clots (thrombosis) or complications in pregnancy such as pregnancy loss, pre-eclampsia or intrauterine growth restriction because of placental insufficiency. The cause of APS is poorly understood, and there is a high rate of pregnancy loss despite standard blood thinner injections and aspirin given during pregnancy. The complement system is a network of proteins and is an important part of the immune system. There is growing evidence that changes to the complement system may play a central role in what causes APS. By better understanding complement activation and which complement proteins are abnormal in pregnant patients with APS, we can research targeted therapies to improve pregnancy outcomes for women with APS. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have recently developed a blood test (the modified Ham test) that can detect complement activation in patients. They have already shown that there is complement activation in a related pregnancy complication called HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), and that complement activation was present before any clinical evidence of HELLP syndrome started. The aim of our study is to assess if there is complement activation in pregnant patients with APS using the modified Ham test and other complement studies, compared to healthy pregnant women, and if this is related to pregnancy complications. We will also test if there are genetic mutations in complement genes. We will follow pregnant patients with and without APS throughout pregnancy. We will test for complement activation with monthly blood tests until the third trimester, and then every 2 weeks until delivery. By collecting this information over time, we will determine if there is an association with the development of pregnancy complications, and if we can identify changes in complement before those complications happen.

column36: Value for money: A mixed methods study to investigate the impact of funding expanded midwifery care models in Canada
column37: Birth is costly. About 10% of the money that Canadian health care systems spend on hospitals are to pay for the costs of giving birth or being born in a hospital. Canadian research suggests that midwives can provide birth care at lower cost while still ensuring good health outcomes. Midwives help lower costs because they are less likely to use costly interventions, the people they care for leave hospital earlier, and they attend some births at home. Until recently, almost all Canadian midwives work in models that involve providing prenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum care to every person they care for. The way midwives have been paid has limited the ways in which midwives can work within Canadian health care systems. Our research will take advantage of a natural experiment that involves funding midwives in Ontario to work in new models of care, providing a wider range of services, and working in settings that they have not previously worked in. Programs funded by this initiative include a new hospital-based, midwifery-led birthing unit, and programs that target people who are at risk of poor access to health care and poor health outcomes. Our goal is to understand the value for money that has been achieved through this new funding. Our project will involve three parts. One, we will analyse the costs of the new alongside midwifery unit to learn whether the new funding supports a lower cost model of hospital-based midwifery care for births. Two, we will interview patients, health care providers, administrators, and policy-makers to identify what they see to be the value of the new funding and the programs it funds. This will help us to understand the impact of the funding from different perspectives. Third, we will develop a framework that can be used to examine the costs and cost savings of programs that target people who are at risk of poor access to health care and poor health outcomes, and we will use this framework to evaluate the costs of one of these programs.

column36: Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network Methods and Applications Group in Indirect Comparisons (DSEN MAGIC) Team
column37: In this proposal, we outline the composition, purpose, and future growth of the Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR) Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) Methods and Applications Group for Indirect Comparisons (MAGIC) Team. The MAGIC team includes health methodologists and research scientists from universities and research centers across Canada, with internationally recognized expertise in knowledge synthesis, biostatistics, safety and effectiveness research, knowledge translation, sex and gender analysis, and health economics. The goal of MAGIC is to apply innovative research methods to produce trusted, timely, unbiased and clear evidence that inform policy decisions on post-market drug safety and effectiveness. Over the past 8 years, MAGIC has conducted 35 research projects for DSEN knowledge users (KUs) including Health Canada, Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH), and provincial/territorial ministries of health, while mentoring 23 trainees and delivering evidence-based KT products. MAGIC remains firmly focused on its primary objective to enhance Canadian pharmacovigilance, the healthcare system, and the health of all Canadians by continuing to generate rigorous knowledge synthesis products for DSEN, including all types of reviews and analyses, and primary data collection, as needed, to best inform DSEN's KUs and meet their evidence needs. MAGIC aims to use our research findings to influence capacity-building and health research methods across Canada, and globally. Our capacity-building and networking strategies will allow our trainees and new investigators to develop skills in this rapidly evolving field and will contribute to the creation of highly qualified personnel in Canada who will continue to work in academic, industry or policy fields on post-market drug safety and effectiveness.

column36: Optimizing preterm delivery time: brain health & neurodevelopmental outcomes
column37: Preterm birth is a leading cause of still birth and childhood disabilities in Canada. With advances in medical care, the number of babies being born early has increased significantly. Much of this change is related to medical decision making, where babies are delivered early to minimize birth complications. For fetuses who are restricted in their growth, typically due to a failing placenta, early delivery can prevent serious illness and death. However, placental failure causes decreased oxygen supply to the brain and places fetuses at high risk for brain injury and cerebral palsy. Presently, doctors lack tools to determine when the fetal brain is at greatest risk for injury and which babies need to be delivered early. Developing sensitive medical imaging tools that can predict brain injury in growth restricted babies are needed to inform delivery time and promote healthy outcomes. Presently, the decision to deliver a baby who is growth restricted is largely based on ultrasound. While this technology is inexpensive and can be done at the patient's bedside it can only provide limited measurements about blood flow to the fetal brain. Altered blood flow patterns reflect blood being directed away from major organs in order to protect the brain. Ultrasound may only be able to detect injury when it is too late, when there is a risk that brain damage has already occurred. An alternative to using ultrasound is MRI, which can monitor brain regions vulnerable to injury. The long-term goal of this research program is to address this critical need for obstetricians to use better methods to monitor growth restricted babies at risk for brain injury while still inside the womb, to improve newborn brain health and prevent developmental difficulties in learning and motor skills. Presently, no therapies or interventions are available for growth restricted fetuses, so the focus on prevention of neonatal brain injury is key to improving outcomes in this vulnerable population.

column36: Learning from and enhancing Community Capacity for Climate Change and Food Security (C4FS) action in the NWT
column37: The food systems of Indigenous peoples in the Northwest Territories (NWT) are based on the harvesting of country foods, and form the foundation of spiritual, cultural, physical, and mental well-being for individuals and communities. There is a dual food system in communities in the NWT, with country foods complemented by market foods. The lack of fresh and affordable market foods compounded by changes in country food access and availability fuels alarming rates of food insecurity throughout the NWT. There are documented impacts of climate change for Indigenous peoples' food systems, including: access to, and availability of traditional food species and, changes in harvesting practices (including harvester safety concerns). Understanding climate change impacts and identifying local adaptations in the food systems of Indigenous communities in the NWT is critical for the health and sustainability of communities, the environment and land. The proposed research aims to learn from and enhance community capacity to address place-based priorities to inform climate change and food security action locally, regionally, and territorially. The approach includes cross-cutting themes of Traditional Knowledge, Governance, Youth, and Sex and Gender, and is grounded in Participatory Action Research (PAR). Our multidisciplinary team will work closely with community partners in six case study communities in four regions in the NWT to understand the potential of local actions, and to scale-out and scale-up learning. This research will promote community action and self-determination of local food systems in communities in the NWT and ultimately improve health outcomes. The knowledge gathered, and shared across multiples levels (locally, regionally, territorially, government decision-makers/ knowledge users) will facilitate development of more effective programs and policies to address food security and climate change in the NWT.

column36: Niqivut Silalu Asijjipalliajuq: "Our Food and Climate Change" Program
column37: The most dramatic and fastest climate change is occurring in Inuit Nunangat, which has led to decreased ice thickness and extent, later ice freeze-up and early ice break-up, and changing snow conditions. These changing environmental conditions impact local wildlife and vegetation that are important for Inuit diet. These changing conditions also impact the ability of Inuit to access, prepare, and consume country foods (local foods). Climate change impacts on country foods have important implications for Inuit health and wellbeing. The Niqivut Silalu Asijjipalliajuq ("Our Food and Climate Change") research program addresses a significant gap in research. The research program will promote adaptive capacity among Inuit by enhancing local capacity to detect and respond to food-related climate-health outcomes; and evaluate opportunities for food-related climate change adaptation polices, programs, and actions. The program has 2 research themes: -Research Theme 1: Strengthen Inuit food sovereignty for climate change adaptation. -Research Theme 2: Share Inuit knowledge to support climate change adaptation. -Cross-cutting Research Themes: The importance of Inuit knowledge (IK) in research; Inuit health, nutrition, and wellness; climate change adaptation; and gender. Four intensive research projects span these themes: Project 1: Stories about Country Food Preparation; Project 2: Stories to Inform Reintroduction of Food Sources; Project 3: Stories of Food for Health and Healing; and Project 4: Sharing Stories and Inuit Self-Determination in Research. This is a Nunavut-led research program. Our Nunavummiut-led approach will offer best practice guidance for other initiatives; will create leaders with expertise in climate change, country food, and Inuit health; and demonstrate the importance of Inuit knowledge and Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit for adaptation, enabling communities to manage the food-related health effects of climate change.

column36: The food and beverage industry's sponsorship of junior sports clubs in Canada: its extent, nature and potential effect on child and adolescent health
column37: "Unhealthy food marketing has been shown to promote poor dietary behaviors and obesity among children. The sponsorship of sports clubs is one type of marketing to which children and youth are exposed. Evidence from abroad suggests that this promotional technique, which allows for extended and repeated exposure to marketing, is frequently used to promote unhealthy foods. To date, no research has documented the extent and nature of food company sponsorship of sports clubs in Canada. Furthermore, little research has specifically examined the potential impact of this activity on the health of children and youth. The purpose of this study is to determine the frequency and healthfulness of food company sponsorship of junior sports clubs in Canada and to examine its potential effect on the dietary behaviors of children and youth. To do so, this study will identify junior sports clubs for the 8 most popular sports among children and youth in 4 cities located across Canada. Focus groups will be held with children and youth to explore their perceptions and attitudes toward food company sponsorship and sponsoring companies, and whether sponsorship influences their food purchasing or requesting behaviors. This law, however, will not prohibit food company sponsorship of children's sports nor will it protect adolescents over age 12 from unhealthy food marketing. A review of this legislation is scheduled for 2025. During this review, the law will be evaluated, and its scope may be expanded should evidence support such action. Considering this window of opportunity, this research will provide critical evidence needed to consider the restriction of food company sponsorship targeting children and the extension of protections to adolescents."

column36: Canadian Epigenetics, Environment and Health Research Consortium Network Phase II
column37: The DNA that makes up the genome (the collection of all the DNA in your cell) is tagged with various chemical marks that are attached either directly to the DNA or to its packaging proteins. These marks, collectively called the epigenome, act as a kind of molecular mark-up language that tells the cell's proteins which genes to turn 'on' and which to turn 'off'. Unlike the genome, which remains largely the same throughout life, the epigenome changes with age, in response to environmental influences, and in many types of disease. As the bridge between environmental exposures and peoples' genomes, the epigenome harbours enormous promise to understand normal development and disorders arising throughout a person's lifespan. Our accelerated ability to 'read' these epigenetic marks is revealing their disruption in most diseases; however, the rapid rate of the emergence of new scientific methodologies coupled with the increasing desire of researchers to incorporate epigenetics into new studies highlights the urgent need for a nationally coordinated approach. The CEEHRC Network Phase II aims to continue to address this gap by developing and strengthening collaborations between basic and applied scientists, clinicians, bioinformaticians, statisticians, and experts in drug development. We seek to address the bench-to-bedside gulf in epigenetics research in Canada, to harness improved understanding of epigenetic mechanisms and the potential improve patient outcomes by altering epigenetic states associated with disease.

column36: Development, Implementation and Evaluation of an Innovative Integrated Supportive Care Pathway by Primary Care across Alberta
column37: Caring for patients with advanced-stage diseases is a growing challenge in Canada. Care is uncoordinated with high rates of hospitalization, and aggressive use of treatments towards the end of life, despite limited benefit. Care often does not reflect patients' preferences and is associated with poor outcomes and quality of life. Integrated community- and home-based care aligned with patients' preferences is essential to improving patient outcomes. The use of clinical pathways is effective in integrating care and optimizing patient outcomes. The implementation of a Conservative Kidney Management (CKM) pathway across Alberta for patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) who were unlikely to benefit from dialysis has improved symptoms, increased patient satisfaction, and reduced costs for these patients. This study aims to build on the success of the CKM Pathway by adapting and spreading the Pathway to include patients with advanced cancer and heart, lung, and liver failure. This newly co-designed interactive, on-line Supportive Care Pathway will have health care provider and patient portals to navigate the pathway and access patient education resources, interactive decision aids, and management strategies appropriate for an individual's needs and preferences. This Supportive Care Pathway will be implemented within primary care clinics across Alberta. The effect of the Pathway on patient outcomes and quality of life will be evaluated along with its cost effectiveness. We anticipate high uptake of the Pathway resulting in care that is more consistent with patients' preferences, improved patient outcomes, greater satisfaction with care, and reduced costs across the health system. We anticipate that health care providers will have greater satisfaction with the care they provide using the Pathway. This project will set a benchmark nationally and internationally and will serve as a model for pathway development for patients with advanced-stage diseases.

column36: Implementing ActionADE to Transform Medication Safety
column37: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are unintended and harmful events resulting from medications. They are an enormous burden to patients, families and the health system, causing 276,000 emergency department visits, and 100,000 admissions in BC each year. Unfortunately, healthcare providers commonly re-expose patients to the same medications as ones that previously caused harm resulting in repeat ADEs. This happens because there are no effective health information technologies to ensure that ADEs are documented and shared between providers in a patient's circle of care. We have designed a software application called ActionADE that allows frontline care providers to document ADEs, and communicate this information between one another and across health sectors (for example, from hospitals to community pharmacies). We have partnered with the Ministry of Health, Vancouver Coastal Health, Lower Mainland Pharmacy Services and the College of Pharmacists of BC to integrate ActionADE with PharmaNet, BC's drug information system, and with community pharmacy information systems. This will allow care providers to share information with one another about ADEs to prevent their recurrence. After completing ActionADE's integration with other health information systems, we will implement ActionADE in acute care hospitals in Vancouver Costal Health. We will then evaluate whether ActionADE can prevent re-exposures to harmful medications, and improve patient and health system outcomes in a randomized trial. We will complete an economic evaluation to assess ActionADE's cost effectiveness. ActionADE has the potential to advance the quadruple aims of enhancing patient care, improving population health, improving health system sustainability, and improving the work of care providers. If beneficial, we plan to scale ActionADE to other health sectors in BC, including to other hospitals, long-term care, physician offices, and to rural and remote locations to transform medication safety for all.

column36: Integrating clinical data systems to improve the capacity, performance, and value of Manitoba's healthcare system
column37: Manitoba has many computerized health databases but they are largely disconnected from one another. 'Data-fragmentation' limits the capacity of the health system, and leads to inefficiencies in the delivery of healthcare. Partnering with Manitoba's Ministry of Health (Manitoba Health, Seniors and Active Living), we propose the creation of a scalable and sustainable integrated health data platform that connects the many Provincial Health databases. To show the value and expansion potential of such an integrated/connected health platform, we will complete three innovative demonstration projects, each of which will address one of Manitoba's stated health priorities. The first demonstration trial (TRACTION) will show how an integrated data platform can enable the conduct of large clinical trials that will inform best practice. The trial will also show how an inexpensive drug can reduce blood transfusion and costs associated with blood transfusion. The second innovative demonstration trial (Home First) will show how, using integrated data to target at-risk populations, assisted home dialysis will improve patient outcomes and decrease costs to the healthcare system. The third demonstration trial (CAPTAIN) will show how an integrated health data platform can improve the cancer journey for patients newly diagnosed with cancer. Each innovative clinical trial has been developed with multiple stakeholders including patients. A portion of the economic benefits derived from each trial will be used to conduct further studies that will expand the capabilities of the integrated data platform while addressing Provincial health priorities. The creation of an integrated Health data platform will be a transformative undertaking for Manitoba. The integrated data platform will increase Manitoba's ability to make evidence-informed health decisions, help improve patient-centred outcomes, and will promote the sustainability of our healthcare system.

column36: SurgeCon: An Emergency Department Surge Management Platform
column37: Canadian emergency departments (ED) have some of the longest wait times compared to many other first world countries. Extreme waits mean patients will be in pain or discomfort for hours before being seen which can cause serious harm. To address this healthcare system challenge and improve patient experiences, we propose SurgeCon, a quality improvement initiative to reduce ED wait times. SurgeCon includes an electronic Health component, a training program for ED staff, and a series of quality improvement initiatives. SurgeCon provides ED staff with different tasks to complete to improve efficiency based on real-time information (E.g. bed availability, average wait times, available resources, etc.). We tested SurgeCon in a rural hospital ED and found it reduced the average wait time from 104 minutes to 42 minutes, the total time spent in the ED from 199 minutes to 134 minutes, and the proportion of patients who left the ED without being seen by a doctor from 12.1% to 4.6%. This application aims to determine whether these results can be reproduced in other hospitals. To keep the study relevant to patient priorities, patients selected the outcomes that the team should measure (wait times, patient satisfaction, etc.). To ensure our solution results in positive change that addresses these priorities, we have partnered with Eastern Health (EH), the largest regional health authority in Newfoundland and Labrador (NL). EH is responsible for both rural and urban hospitals, reflecting the diversity of hospitals across the rest of Canada. Using an innovative study design, we will measure SurgeCon's effect on ED wait times and patient experience through a patient survey. At the same time, we will determine the cost of implementation and the departmental factors which result in improved ED performance. Working closely with EH as a collaborator and testing SurgeCon in rural and urban EDs will prepare it for future use by other health regions in NL and across Canada.

column36: Feast Centre for Indigenous STBBI Research
column37: The current political and social realities of Indigenous life in Canada (i.e., higher rates of sexually-transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs), ongoing colonization, the need for health policy and programs responsive to Indigenous world views, etc.) requires thoughtful attention to Indigenous health research that effect positive social change. Let by a team of Indigenous community and scholars, the goal of the centre is to use Indigenous knowledge to shape future STBBI research. Drawing community-based research, and Indigenous and decolonizing approaches to doing research, the following objectives are proposed: (1) support STBBI research that uses Indigenous knowledge to reduce STBBIs in Indigenous communities; (2) support communities, investigators, and trainees through mentorship programs, Learning Institutes, writing retreats, and conference participation; and (3) to focus on interventions and the use of knowledge produced in research to inform health policy and programs. column36: Wuniska! Indigenous Centre on HIV/HCV/STBBI Inequities
column37: Wuniska is a Cree and Saulteaux word that means wake up, arise. It's a concept filled with optimism for the new day, which we greet with renewed energy and passion. It's a verb, reflecting that as Indigenous people, our knowledge is action-oriented. It is also known as Waniska (spelling variation) and Waanishka (Metis). Wuniska describes the Saskatchewan Health Authority Patient/Family Advisory Committee for HIV/AIDS, and is a tribute to people with lived experience of HIV. The HIV and HCV incidence rates in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba rank among the highest in Canada. In both provinces, Indigenous people bear the burden of these infections with rates 2-6 times the provincial rates. There exists a critical need for a regional Indigenous-led HIV/HepC/STBBI research centre, grounded in Indigenous philosophies and methodologies. Research on HIV and HCV among Indigenous communities has largely ignored the social, colonial and historical context of HIV-related health problems and the inequitable access to screening, diagnosis, treatment, care and social supports. Furthermore, the research is predominantly led by non-Indigenous researchers, and historically by researchers from outside the SK/MB region. Wuniska will address these gaps by building approaches grounded in Indigenous philosophies and methodologies, and employing the concept of Two-eyed Seeing to take advantage of the best of Indigenous and Western capabilities. Via the centre, we will build innovative land-and culture-based research, develop infrastructure to support Indigenous communities and academics, and train the next generation of Indigenous scholars, practitioners and community members to develop innovative HIV research projects in these geographically connected territories. The Wuniska Centre is led by Indigenous PIs and strong Allies, bringing unique partnerships with Indigenous entities regionally, nationally and globally.

column36: Metabolic therapy of heart failure: which role for B vitamins?
column37: Heart failure (HF) is a complex disease resulting from the incapacity of the heart to effectively contract and unfortunately this pathology is a major leading cause of mortality. There is therefore an urging need to find new therapeutic options to slow down the course of this pathology and reduce the mortality rate. The failing heart might be defined as "an engine out of fuel" where the power station of the cell, named mitochondria, is dysfunctional and where the fuel, namely nutrients, replenishing this power station is not correctly used. Moreover, the calcium, important for this contractility process, is also misused in the failing heart, which again affects heart function. All these disregulated events are closely linked to disease progression. In this regard, efforts are undertaken to fix this power station in HF and propose as a metabolic therapy of HF. We are building on complementarity expertise of all members of the Consortium to validate the relevance of using a metabolic therapy using a cocktail of B vitamins, either alone or in combination with current drugs used to treat HF, first in experimental animal models of HF as a proof-of concept. To achieve our aims, the efficiency of such treatment will be evaluated with animal survival rate, and as secondary outcomes we will examine i) in vivo and ex vivo heart function, ii) mitochondrial function, iii) how nutrients needed for an optimal function of mitochondria are used, in other terms metabolized, by the heart, and iv) how the calcium used to promote contractility is processed by cardiac cells. Through this Consortium, we are confident to validate and propose a relevant metabolic therapy for HF that will correct both the energetic deficiency and the defect in contractility of the heart. This will be ultimately of significant clinical relevance to offer alternative or add-on therapy improving the survival of HF patients.

column36: Inflammation and Metabolism in Pulmonary Hypertension are Linked to skewed chromosome X Inactivation: new therapeutic optiONS
column37: Patients with pulmonary hypertension (PHT; high blood pressure in the lungs) have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. These cells proliferate like cancer cells and create an obstruction of the vessels, making it difficult for the blood to go through. They also have evidence of inflammation in their blood, similar to patients suffering from infections. Finally, in patients with PHT several organs display the same abnormal way to produce energy (metabolism). PHT occurs more often in women than in men and it's an area of ongoing research. Women have 2 chromosome x, and one is normally inactivated to equal gene expression of men that have one X and one Y chromosome. In some diseases like cancer, the inactivated chromosome X is re-activated, resulting in increased expression of genes located on the chromosome X. We hypothesized that this phenomenon also occur in women with PHT. We will study the state of activation of the chromosome x in 30 women with PHT compared to 30 healthy control women, as well as in animal models. We will study the mechanisms responsible for chromosome X reactivation and test whether we can reverse it in cells in culture, lung slices and animal models, using specific inhibitors of factors influencing chromosome X reactivation.

column36: Gut-brain interactions modulate immune response in hypertensive heart disease
column37: Pathogenesis of adverse cardiovascular remodelling in hypertension (HTN) has been extensively investigated. However, the intricate interactions established among different organ systems participating in the process hinder therapeutic advancement. Aberration of the compositions or functions of the gut microbes (dysbiosis) is strongly associated with HTN. However, it is still unclear whether it plays a causative or supportive role, or simply a bystander of HTN and related cardiovascular dysfunction. (1) We aim to address this question through interventions altering microbiome profiles i.e. faecal transplantation or antibiotics treatment. Next, to provide mechanistic insight of dysbiosis-HTN relationship, we will focus our investigation on microbiota crosstalk with the nervous and immune systems. We plan to exploit single-cell whole genome profiling (2) to elucidate the response of diverse immune cell subsets residing in the gut and the spleen to dysbiosis and to address whether immune-modulating function of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) is altered. Moreover, employing a series of multidisciplinary approaches including novel genetic tool, optogenetics, and live imaging (3) we aim to elucidate the neural circuit that communicates microbiota signal from the gut and address how the central nervous system (CNS) can, vice versa, influence the gut barrier function. Finally, (4) we will identify bioactive metabolites with the potential to modulate ANS and dysregulated Immune response, and prevent maladaptive cardiac remodelling in HTN.

column36: Interdisciplinary Canadian Collaborative ME Research Network
column37: Myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME), also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), is a complex chronic multi-systemic disease whose etiology remains poorly understood. It is characterized by unexplained long-term fatigue and post-exertional malaise. Of note, women are more often affected than men although little is known about this sex difference. It is estimated that ME may affect over 600,000 Canadians. ME is life-altering and for its more severe forms can be life-threatening. There is growing recognition that ME is a serious disease rooted in fundamental metabolic dysfunctions that impair energy production, immune functions and physiological response to exertion. We are proposing the creation of a national interdisciplinary collaborative ME research network that will carry-out a patient-centered research program, from discovery to implementation, with the ultimate goal of finding the cause(s) and possible treatments for ME. The complexity of unresolved questions around ME require the coordinated efforts of Canadian and international experts and a wide range of stakeholders. By leveraging our collective knowledge, important health data and pockets of innovation, we will contribute to initiate the transformation of ME research landscape in Canada, and to improve the health of Canadians living with ME.

column36: Co-designing a Patient and Family Caregiver-Oriented Transitions in Care Bundle
column37: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are very sick. When a patient leaves the ICU they may have a change in their health that is new to them and their family members, such as new medical problems or new medications. When a patient leaves an ICU they can move to another part of the hospital or go home. Moving from the ICU to other parts of the hospital can be confusing and stressful for a patient and family because there will be new doctors and nurses and it will look and work differently than the ICU. The only people who remain the same when a patient moves from the ICU are the patient and their family. It makes sense that patients and their family should be at the center of their care as they move from across the healthcare system. The goal of this study is to build a tool that puts the patient and their family at the center and in control of their care. The tool will help family caregivers be involved in the patient's care while they are in the ICU. This tool will teach patients and families about the care a patient got in the ICU, the care the patient needs after the ICU, and medical problems the patient may still have. This tool will encourage patients and their families to reach out to other patients and families for peer support. This tool will improve communication between patients, families, doctors and nurses. These actions will put the patient and their family in control of their care. Once built, this tool will make the care that a patient receives better and more adapted to that patient's needs. The tool will also help patients have better recoveries from their sickness. This tool will be made with and used by patients, families, doctors and nurses. This will make sure the tool is easy to understand and useful for all patients and their families. When patients and families have more knowledge, are involved in the patient's care and can communicate with patients, families, nurses and caregivers, they are put in in control of their care.

column36: CONnecting and Coordinating an Enhanced Network for TRansitions In Care (CONCENTRIC): A New Model for Spinal Cord Injury Care in Alberta
column37: Transition in care (TiC) refers to the complicated processes that help coordinate the continuation of services as people experience changes in their health, care needs and where they receive care. Poor coordination of TiC can cause additional health issues, causing more problems such as trips to the emergency department and/or being re-admitted to the hospital. This is very expensive for the patient, their family, and the health care system, and can lead to more health concerns. When someone has a lifelong condition, they have multiple TiC because their needs change over time. A good example of this are those who have a spinal cord injury (SCI). In Alberta, the provincial SCI community (patients, clinicians, decision makers, community partners, researchers) has been working together since 2016, and has agreed that improving TiC for persons with SCI is most important, knowing that other groups with lifelong conditions face similar challenges. Our provincial research team plans to carry out a 4 year project that will create and test a new model for TiC which will be part of a larger provincial "hub and spokes system". The "hub" sites are Calgary and Edmonton (where the SCI specialty services are) and the "spoke" sites will be Lethbridge and Slave Lake, since many patients are discharged there from the hubs. We will measure the impact this new model has on patient health, experiences and well-being, the use of health care services and associated costs. In fact, early analysis by the Alberta Health Services showed that reducing emergency department visits by persons with SCI by 11% we will save $1M per year! column36: RECOVER Program: A Care Continuum after Critical Illness
column37: Critical illness is a catastrophic life event for the patient and their family. Over 250,000 Canadians are admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) each year. These admissions cost 0.2% of the Gross Domestic Product, or $4 billion annually. Most of these patients will require mechanical ventilation to assist with breathing and more than 10% will die. Those who survive have substantial morbidity, disability, impaired quality of life and increased healthcare utilization. As well, family caregivers experience new mood disorders that compromise their health and well-being. There is no systematic care pathway for these vulnerable patients and their caregivers to meet these complex health needs. This problem must be addressed with high priority. The CIHR-funded, multi-phase RECOVER Program was initiated in 2007 to establish an innovative longitudinal care pathway for patients and families after critical illness. RECOVER Program: Phase I (published in 2016) contributed a comprehensive description of multimorbidities sustained by patients and their families, a longitudinal needs assessment and disability risk stratification to inform rehabilitation and post ICU care. RECOVER Program: Phase II was developed from this foundational work in collaboration with our patient and family engagement group. The current CIHR proposal evaluates the feasibility of an early entry, risk-stratified, inpatient rehabilitation and concurrent mental health program to mitigate care transitions and an evaluation of barriers to establishing RECOVER in three other provinces. Insights gleaned from this work will further the development of the RECOVER Program and its goal to establish a national practice standard for an integrated and seamless continuum of patient-and family-centred care after critical illness.

column36: Facilitating transitions and access across the pregnancy continuum of care - A Health System Intervention for Indigenous Women Living in Northern Manitoba
column37: Pregnancy is a time of transition. Women and families transition from pregnancy, to birth, to post pregnancy care. Each transition requires a connection to various health care providers, from a nurse, physician or midwife, sometimes to a specialist, and from care in an office setting, to hospital care for birth, and back home. In northern Manitoba one of every three pregnant women does not receive adequate care in pregnancy. Indigenous women and children experience the greatest health inequities in this region and in Canada more broadly. These inequities are compounded by transitions between health care systems. The federal government provides health care in First Nations communities, however, for specialized services and birth, women need to transition to the provincial health care system. Many barriers including, travel, transportation issues, financial constraints, poor communication, different providers, and weak referral links are encountered through those transitions. For many, relocating for care and birth away from home is characterized by insecurity, strange surroundings, and isolation from family. A pregnancy collective impact network of service providers, families and community members led by a patient navigator is proposed to assist with access to care, navigation of complex system transitions, and to improve linkages between the services and across systems. Culturally safe care and promotion of shared-decision making between patients and providers are foundational and will be supported through training. It is not enough to facilitate access and navigation, services need to be inclusive and respectful of Indigenous beliefs and issues faced by Indigenous peoples. Shared-decision making promotes effective participation in care. These strategies are expected to increase use of care, decrease low birth weight and premature birth, increase breastfeeding, increase use of well-child care and vaccination rates, and improve patient experiences.

column36: ED to EPI: Using SMS (Text) Messaging to Improve the Transition from the Emergency Department to Early Psychosis Intervention for Young People with Psychosis
column37: Psychosis, a syndrome characterized by loss of touch with reality, is a disabling and life-threatening condition that typically starts in adolescence and young adulthood, a time of life associated with gaps in mental health service use. Despite the availability of effective treatment through early psychosis intervention (EPI) programs, around half of youth do not access these services. Even when youth with psychosis present in crisis to the emergency department (ED), rates of follow-up care are poor, in large part related to young people not attending EPI services when they are referred. The goal of this study is to improve transitions from the ED to evidence-based EPI services for youth with psychosis using a short message service (SMS) text messaging intervention. We will recruit 186 youth aged 16-29 referred by the ED for consultation in EPI services for a pragmatic randomized-controlled trial of 2-way SMS reminders, psychoeducation and check-ins, with the aim of improving rate of attendance at the consultation appointment. We will review participants' charts and link with provincial health data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences to examine additional and longer-term indicators of service engagement and the effect of health equity factors such as gender and race/ethnicity. We will also perform cost-effectiveness analysis of the intervention and use qualitative methods to explore young people's perspectives on the intervention. The project will engage patient and family representatives, early career researchers and trainees, as well as key team members to champion spread of the intervention to other EPI programs and youth mental health services. Establishing evidence that a low-cost, easily implemented strategy improves transitions from the ED to EPI programs can result in more young people with psychosis getting appropriate treatment earlier, leading to improved long-term trajectories.

column36: A Virtual Transition Intervention For Children and Adults Transitioning To Home Ventilation in Ontario: A Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: The number of people that use a ventilator (a machine that supports breathing) at home is increasing in Canada and around the world. These individuals have complex health problems, require a lot of care and they use the healthcare system often. Unfortunately, the care for individuals using mechanical ventilators isn't coordinated which results in frequent visits to the hospital and stress on the patient and family. Virtual care is a way to improve healthcare for individuals using ventilators. Virtual care is a good idea for individuals using ventilators because it can bring "the right people with the right expertise at the right time" into the homes of these complex patients. A newly developed virtual care platform called aTouchAway (TM) is now developed. It is sophisticated enough to meet the needs of individuals using ventilators and their care needs. This study will test a virtual care intervention using the aTouchAway (TM) platform for children and adults newly going home with ventilators in Ontario, Canada. We are studying the effect on the following: visits to the Emergency Department, patient and families' experience and if they like using it, the costs on the healthcare system and healthcare provider time and if they like using the intervention. We have worked closely with individuals using ventilators at home and their families to design this study and make sure the results are important to them. Our study is testing a promising virtual care intervention for individuals newly going home with ventilators. Our results will help to improve the quality of life for individuals using ventilators at home by making their healthcare better.

column36: Neurosurgical Transition e-Program (Neuro-STEP): Pilot evaluation of an e-Health program to improve the transition of neurosurgical patients from remote locations to specialist neurosurgical care, across life's trajectory from pediatric to adult, and through dynamic changes in acute or chronic health states.
column37: Currently, long wait-times for patients to see a specialist are a big problem. Often, the patient does not know much about the latest status of their referral, causing anxiety. For neurosurgery patients any delay in seeing a specialist can result in worse outcomes. In addition, having a neurosurgical problem in general can be quite worrisome for many. Some people travel from long distances to see a neurosurgeon. Others are neurosurgery patients who have been used to the pediatric setting and now have to transition to an adult hospital. Finally, after having had a neurosurgical operation, an individual could either be going home, a local hospital, or to rehabilitation. In either scenario, it is helpful to have real-time information customized to the specific person, diagnosis, and state of health. As technology improves, it is important to use it safely and effectively to handle many of these challenges. The Neurosurgery Division at the Toronto Western Hospital has teamed up with Akinox, an e-Health company specializing in technology for health, along with patients to develop an internet-based application to fix this problem. Our application will make sure that all referrals are standardized. This means that people who do not need to see a neurosurgeon don't make an extra trip and those who do, can have an effective visit. It will also show the user the latest status of their referral. Depending on the diagnosis and stage of care, each user (patient) will receive updates on upcoming appointments and get directed to appropriate resources to help them better understand their diagnosis. This will better prepare patients for taking charge of their own care. We plan to evaluate how effective our application is by collecting data on patient satisfaction, wait-times, referring physician satisfaction, and costs. We hope that this application will help improve our challenges so that one day it can be made available to all healthcare providers and patients across Canada.

column36: The Digital Bridge: Using technology to support patient-centred transitions from hospital to home
column37: Older adults who live with multiple chronic conditions are more likely to experience frequent admissions and discharges from hospital. These transitions are often challenging and leave people at risk of readmission. Appropriate, timely and person-centred communication across all health care providers involved in transitions (in and out of hospital) as well as with patients and their families is critical to ensure a smooth and effective transition process. Digital health technologies can play an important role in improving person-centred communication across clinical settings and clinicians. This project will develop and test a Digital Bridge by connecting communication technologies already in use in hospital and primary care/community settings to improve communication between providers in hospital and in primary care, patients and family caregivers from admission to 6 months post-discharge. We will engage with all the technology users to co-design the Digital Bridge, ensuring that how we connect the existing technologies and adopt them into practice will meet the needs of providers, patients and their caregivers. Next our hospital partners will adopt the technology into general medicine and rehabilitation services in hospital systems in Toronto (Sinai Health System) and Mississauga (Trillium Health Partners). We will evaluate the Digital Bridge through a pre-post pragmatic trial, assessing impact on patient experience (quality of transition), patient outcomes (quality of life), transition processes (provider communication and teamwork), and system costs (economic evaluation). This project adopts an implementation science lens, allowing us to collect qualitative data on enablers and barriers to adopting the Digital Bridge to help inform development of a scale and spread strategy.
