column36: Keeping in Touch (KiT) with Young Adults as They Transition Through Type 1 Diabetes Care
column37: For young adults living with type 1 diabetes moving from pediatric to adult care can be overwhelming because many feel unprepared and find it difficult to make a meaningful connection with the new adult team. It is also challenging for young adults to balance their diabetes self-care with other competing priorities such as education, social activities, and work putting them at risk for life-threatening complications and poor diabetes control. We know that many young people find it challenging to attend diabetes clinics and that we can improve the connectedness between young people and their pediatric and adult diabetes teams. Our study aims to improve the lives of young adults as they move from pediatric to adult care using a mobile electronic Health application that will engage patients and providers. For patients it will 1) provide personalized young adult-friendly transition resources such as videos and tip sheets based on what patients tell us they are interested in, 2) deliver an introduction to the new adult diabetes team, and 3) provide incentives for filling out questionnaires about patient experience and outcome measures. For providers it will 1) let providers know if a patient they referred to adult care has not had a visit with that adult provider within 6 months or if they have had a diabetes-related admission or emergency department visit, 2) show them how their patients are doing in comparison to other patients in the study and according to best practice standards. We will evaluate the impact of this intervention on patient-reported experience and outcome measures such as diabetes control, quality of life and diabetes empowerment as well as use and cost of healthcare services. If this eHealth intervention is successful, it will be an important building block of a system that can connect important health information between pediatric and adult care, share it with patients and providers, and improve transition outcomes and experiences.

column36: Digitizing Stepped Mental Health Care: A Pragmatic Trial
column37: Access to mental health care in Canada is considerably delayed compared to other countries; a finding which is due, in part, to an under supply of services and long wait lists.This study will evaluate a new mental health care service model called Stepped Care 2.0 at 15 sites in Newfoundland and 15 sites in Nova Scotia. We expect the new approach, along with the new technology, will have the potential to improve the quality of care, reduce wait times and increase access to care, especially for people living in remote areas and those whose changing life circumstances require a more flexible kind of care tailored to their unique challenges. This new approach to care includes a wider range of treatment options, including psychiatric care, individual and group counselling, online treatment programs with built in professional support, self-help resources and peer support. The management system will make it easy to tell quickly when treatment is working well or when a transition in care is required. The program will also allow patients to be more involved in care planning and decision making. Training will be provided to care providers to use the new system. Changes will be made to the program as we learn what does and does not work. This attention to continuous improvement is expected to empower patients to be more resourceful and to encourage providers to be more innovative and flexible. We also expect that programming will be available to more people without increasing costs. In other words, we expect this approach to care to be more efficient, effective and sustainable. Finally, with a team of researchers, patients, providers and other stakeholders representing every province, it will be possible to implement across the country any of the new programming that proves effective.

column36: The Impact of an Innovative eHealth Transition Intervention on Self-Management Skills Among Young Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
column37: There have been major advances in the care of children born with heart defects ("congenital heart disease"- CHD) over the past 3 decades. Now over 90% of children with CHD reach adulthood. However, adolescent and young adult "survivors" are at risk of further heart problems. Unfortunately, most have very little understanding of their CHD and they lack confidence communicating with doctors and nurses about their heart. Over half do not attend specialized adult CHD clinics after graduating from their children's hospital, despite being advised to do so. This increases the risk that new heart problems, which may develop in early adulthood, will be discovered too late. Transition is the planned movement of adolescents with lifelong health conditions from child to adult healthcare. The Canadian Pediatric Society and other organizations have published guidelines about how children's hospitals should help adolescents prepare for the move to adult healthcare. Nurse-led programs to help with transition are effective but time-consuming, expensive, and not easily accessible to adolescents living in rural communities. However, smartphone apps are widely accessible and may be helpful in providing important transition information and coping strategies to adolescents as they enter adult health care. The objective of this research is to determine whether a transition app is better than a nurse-led transition intervention in preparing adolescents (age 16-17) with CHD to take on responsibility for their healthcare (self-management). We will enroll 188 participants across 5 children's hospitals. Each participant will randomly (like the flip of a coin) be assigned to either receive the transition app or the nurse-led transition intervention. We will also determine if the transition app results in better knowledge of their heart condition, greater self-efficacy, timelier first appointments in the adult health care system, and cost savings relative to the nurse-led transition program.

column36: A multidimensional single-cell approach to understand muscle dystrophy
column37: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) and LAMA2-related Muscular Dystrophy (LAMA2 MD) are rare and devastating genetic disease of childhood manifested by progressive skeletal muscle wasting and ultimately death. In both diseases, muscle undergoes constant cycles of degeneration-regeneration exacerbated by intrinsic muscle stem cell (MuSC) dysfunction and their impaired ability to support long-term regeneration. The overall goal of the project is to use a combination of single-cell transcriptomics (RNA-sequencing) and proteomics (mass cytometry, CyTOF) to define the cellular composition of diseased muscle tissues at the single-cell resolution. We will delineate the different cell populations that pre-exist and arise during disease progression and classify the novel cellular subsets involved in this process. This data, in combination with genetic lineage tracing will allow reconstruction of the MuSC lineage hierarchy. We will further characterize cellular subpopulations associated with human muscle dystrophies by performing 3-Dimensional intact-tissue RNA sequencing on patient biopsies The unbiased elucidation of the cellular events underlying the different steps of muscle disease progression at the single-cell level represents crucial missing information, which will push forward our current knowledge on muscle dystrophies. Ultimately, our goal is to develop new biomarkers and eventually new pharmacological approaches to enhance therapy by stimulating intrinsic muscle tissue repair and capitalize on our single cell expertise to uncover disease-related subsets in human biopsies.

column36: Defining and Targeting Autoimmune Liver Disease
column37: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC), a liver autoimmune disease, affects 0.5-1 adults and 0.2 children in 100,000 per year. As a result of the destruction of liver cells during PSC, eventually, many PSC patients will require a liver transplant. The immune system is critical to our health, but much of what is known about the human immune system is derived from animal studies. Since less than 10% of new therapies make it to the clinic, it is critical to develop a better understanding of the human immune system and new models that better predict therapeutic outcomes in humans. A major obstacle to understanding the human immune system is gaining access to healthy human tissues. The surgical team at the Multi-Organ Transplant centre in Toronto modified its liver transplant procedure, which now requires the removal of a small piece of the healthy liver. Using this tissue, we have established a method for isolating the fragile cells from the human liver. Using a new revolutionary technique, single cell RNA sequencing, we generated RNA expression profiles for individual cells obtained from five donated livers. The expression profiles were used to put together the first ever map of the cells that make up the human liver. Using the human healthy liver as a reference, we will generate similar maps from discarded healthy pediatric livers and in both pediatric and adult patients afflicted with PSC. These new maps of PSC patient livers will help identify the immune cells in the liver that contribute and advance PSC pathogenesis. Using these maps, we will address questions about the role of sex (PSC is more prevalent in men) and underlying differences in PSC in children (fast vs. slow progression) vs. PSC in adults. With this knowledge, we aim to identify potential cellular targets and effective therapies for the treatment of autoimmune liver disease.

column36: For Improving diagnostics and grasping the disease mechanisms of rare hypomagnesemia in patients with CNNM2 mutations
column37: Low blood magnesium (hypomagnesemia) is a common electrolyte disorder that causes fatigue, muscle cramps, and arrhythmias. The CNNM2 gene encodes a protein that is responsible for the transport of magnesium in the kidney, the primary organ responsible for maintaining magnesium balance through urinary excretion. Our collaborators have previously described patient mutations in the CNNM2 gene that are causative of hypomagnesemia and that the activity of CNNM2 may be directly dependent on its interaction with other factors. Therefore, in this multidisciplinary grant proposal, my group plans to specifically address the question of which factors can interact with CNNM2. We will use various biochemical approaches to identify such partners and how they affect CNNM2 function, including its magnesium transport ability in kidney cells. We believe that uncovering the determinants of CNNM2 function will provide us with a landscape of the physiological mechanism by which CNNM2 regulates magnesium levels. This information would then be employed to investigate potential changes in CNNM2 function induced by the patient mutations, guide future therapeutic development, and provide other means to mitigate the severity of CNNM2 associated diseases.

column36: Evaluating Burden of Care for Caregivers of Children with Intestinal Failure on Long-Term Parenteral Nutrition
column37: Intestinal failure (IF) is a complex medical condition resulting in malabsorption of fluids and nutrients that requires partial or total parenteral nutrition (PN) support to sustain growth and hydration. I Pediatric intestinal failure (PIF) is caused by short bowel syndrome (SBS), dysmotility disorders and mucosal enteropathies. IF is often further compounded by additional nutritional, infectious and metabolic complications. With improved survival rates, more patients are receiving intensive management within the home setting that includes PN, enteral nutrition therapy, medications, as well as, devices such as feeding tubes, stomas and central venous catheters. Few studies have discussed the impact of highly specialized medical care on caregivers as most pediatric IF patients are unable to provide their own care due to their young age at diagnosis. Caring for a child with IF on home PN requires significant training and continued hypervigilence for years and potentially life long. Anecdotally, parents report significant strain on finances, relationships and individual/family functioning. Families also receive minimal, if any, home care support as they are considered fully trained to provide the care required and do not qualify for most resources. Currently, there are no publications on the burden of care for caregivers of children on home PN. The goal of this research project is to determine the effects of caring for a child with intestinal failure on long-term PN on the caregivers. Through the evaluation of their quality of life, informal care and sleep we can better understand the burden of care on the caregivers, including overall mental and physical well-being, financial and social. Further evaluation of what supports they currently have access to and what gaps exist will allow us to advocate for resources and supports in the areas that families need them to preserve this valuable commodity.

column36: A Cross-Study Data Analytic Approach to Identifying Neuroanatomical Signatures of Anxiety in Neurodevelopmental Disorders
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are a common class of disorders characterized by impairment of the development of the central nervous system. Such disorders often co-occur with additional psychiatric conditions that have a negative impact on the quality of life of patients. In particular, anxiety is a comorbidity that is not well understood in this sub-population. No established treatment pathways exist by which clinicians can aid children and youth with neurodevelopmental disorders who also suffer from anxiety. The identification and development of potentially effective novel treatments calls for a deeper understanding of the neuroscience that underlies this comorbidity. As a first step towards teasing out the neurobiology underlying the condition, data from neuroimaging studies can be used to discern which brain regions play a role in anxiety within the context of NDDs. To that end, I plan to analyze the data from three separate preclinical and clinical neuroimaging studies of neurodevelopmental disorders with the goal of identifying a convergent neuroanatomical signature of comorbid anxiety. A preliminary analysis of data from one of the studies has hinted at the potential implication of a number of structures, including the cerebellum, hippocampus and amygdala. The neuroanatomical signature identified following the analysis of all three data sets can ultimately be used as the basis for subsequent inquiries into the underlying neurobiological mechanisms.

column36: Improving internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy: Including insomnia treatment in transdiagnostic therapy for anxiety and depression to maximize patient benefit.
column37: One in five Canadians will meet criteria for an anxiety or depression disorder in their lifetime. Anxiety and depression can be debilitating and these disorders produce a large economic cost and present significant challenges for our health care systems. Cognitive behavioural therapy has been shown to produce long-lasting reductions in anxiety and depression symptoms, but patients face significant barriers to accessing face-to-face psychotherapy, such as high costs, long travel distances, and scheduling difficulties. New transdiagnostic programs eliminate many barriers by offering therapy online and have been shown to reduce symptoms by 50% on average; however, one quarter of patients do not complete treatment and another quarter do not report significant benefit. To improve treatment outcomes for these clients, I examined the primary concerns reported by previous patients who received anxiety and depression therapy. The most common concern, reported by 75% of patients, was sleep disruption. Sleep problems are known to play a role in the development of depression. In fact, research shows that insomnia often precedes a depressive episode. Insomnia appears to play such an important role in depression that online treatments that only address insomnia produce reductions in depression symptoms. Despite this evidence, transdiagnostic therapies for anxiety and depression do not focus on sleep. I propose that a new sleep-enhanced transdiagnostic protocol be developed and then tested in a randomized trial. The sleep-enhanced program is expected to produce greater reductions in symptoms and could also increase completion rates. The improved program will then be available to the public through the Online Therapy Unit, which provides free therapy online to over 1000 patients in Saskatchewan each year. Results will be published in order to inform other practitioners of internet-delivered therapy about the importance of sleep in treatment for anxiety and depression.

column36: Development of CAR-T cells targeting WT1 peptide presented by HLA class II molecules
column37: Immunotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that strengthens body's immune system against cancer cells. Among various forms of immunotherapy, adoptive T cell therapy is a promising and well-established approach. It involves isolation of immune cells from patients, especially T cells, which are then genetically modified to express tumor-specific receptors prior to re-infusion back into patients. For instance, T cells can be engineered to express tumor-specific CAR (chimeric antigen receptor). Importantly, CAR-T cell therapy has been shown to induce remarkable clinical responses in some patients with leukemia. WT1 (Wilms Tumour 1) is a protein which is over-expressed in tumour cells compared to normal cells. Strategies targeting WT1-expressing tumour cells have been developed; however, so far these strategies can only be applied to certain subsets of patients with compatible gene types. Here, we aim to develop WT1-specific CAR-T cell therapy which targets WT1 protein in an unique manner in order to target WT1-expressing tumour cells from patients with a variety of gene types. In addition, our strategy can also be applied to other tumour-related proteins, hence it can benefit numerous patients with different types of cancer.

column36: Modelisation des atteintes neurologiques dans la dystrophie myotonique de type 1 de forme congenitale a l'aide d'organoides de cerveau
column37: La dystrophie myotonique de type 1 (DM1) est une maladie genetique provoquant entre autres une faiblesse musculaire et une difficulte a relacher le muscle apres une contraction. Alors que la DM1 apparait generalement au debut de la vingtaine, il existe une forme congenitale de la maladie qui entraine des symptomes plus graves et donne lieu a des bebes mous a la naissance. Ceux-ci developpent egalement un retard mental severe dont la cause n'est pas encore connue. Recemment, de nouvelles methodes ont permis de produire en laboratoire des organoides de cerveau. Ces ebauches d'organe reproduisent en partie la composition cellulaire et la structure du cerveau. Nous pensons que ce modele permettra de comprendre l'effet de la DM1 sur le developpement embryonnaire du cerveau. Notre objectif est de comparer des organoides de cerveau derives d'individus normaux et de patients ayant la forme congenitale ou adulte de la DM1. Pour ce faire, nous allons prelever des biopsies de peau afin d'obtenir des cellules dans lesquelles nous injecterons a l'aide de virus inactives des genes associes au stade embryonnaire. Cela aura pour effet de << reprogrammer >> genetiquement ces cellules afin qu'elles redeviennent souches et qu'elles aient la capacite de de se differencier en n'importe quelle cellule des trois feuillets embryonnaires. Lorsque ces cellules reprogrammees seront placees dans un cocktail induisant la differenciation en neurone et qu'elles seront enrobees dans un gel leur permettant de se developper dans l'espace 3-D, elles formeront un organoide de cerveau. Nous regarderons s'il y a une difference au niveau de la proliferation et de la migration des cellules souches neuronales dans les organoides avec la forme congenitale de la DM1. Enfin, nous verifierons s'il est possible de corriger le gene mute dans la DM1 avec une technologie d'edition de genome appelee CRISPR-Cas9. Ce projet pourrait permettre de developper de nouvelles therapies pour la DM1 de forme congenitale.

column36: Unveiling the role of glutamate in dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome
column37: Dopamine transmission in the brain is a tightly regulated process, and alterations in dopamine signaling result in several disease with enormous human and economic burden, including schizophrenia, ADHD, Bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease and dyskinesias. One of the key regulators of dopamine transmission is the plasma membrane dopamine transporter, DAT, which transports released dopamine back into the neuron. In addition to the above prevalent diseases, there is also a rare, fatal disease caused by mutations in the dopamine transporter, called dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. We have developed several models to study dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome and in this study we will be assessing the effects of various drug treatments on these models to see if they can have beneficial effects. We hypothesize that manipulating neurotransmitters in the brain could improve some of the sympotms associated with dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. Positive results from our studies could be quickly translated into the clinic, since the drugs that we will be testing are already an approved and used in humans.

column36: PROSPAX: an integrated multimodal progression chart in spastic ataxias
column37: Spastic ataxias (SPAX) present an expanding group of >100 rare degenerative diseases with joined damage of cerebellum and corticospinal tract (CST). While rapid genetic stratification facilitates current development of molecular therapies, effective trial-planning for SPAX is hampered by a lack of valid outcome measures and natural history studies. Uniting all major European ataxia and spastic paraplegia networks, PROSPAX will establish a paradigmatic IRDiRC-guided integrated trial-ready model of disease progression and mechanistic evolution in SPAX, which will allow to track and understand selective as well as overlapping dysfunction of the cerebellum and CST. In a 2-year transatlantic natural history study we will validate clinician- and patient-reported, digital and molecular outcomes. In addition, PROSPAX will improve on existing and develop new outcome parameters that show superior sensitivity to change. These include a clinical SPAX composite score, a smartphone mHealth toolbox combining wearable sensors with app-based patient-entered outcomes, and multimodal MRI radiomics with an innovative machine learning approach for multisite MRI analysis. Single-cell multi-omic studies in mouse will identify shared pathways and vulnerabilities between cerebellar and corticospinal neurons and will unravel new molecular biomarkers. By example of the two most common recessive SPAX (SPG7, ARSACS) PROSPAX will create a paradigmatic trial-readiness pathway for charting disease progression and multimodal outcome measures that will be applicable to many of the >100 SPAX diseases alike.

column37: Genetic defects may cause congenital disfigurements of the face which may have profound effects on the appearance of the person leading to psychological complications. More importantly, these anomalies have serious effects on vital body functions, such as feeding and breathing. Our group has studied a form of abnormal facial development caused by mutations in matrix Gla protein (MGP) gene. MGP is produced in the cartilage and its absence leads to cartilage calcification. More specifically, we observe abnormal calcification of the nasal cartilage and cartilaginous joints in the head and calcification of the trachea of mice lacking MGP. In the current study, we will examine the structural features in MGP, which are necessary for its function and use gene therapy to correct the head and face problems in MGP-deficient mice. This knowledge will be very useful to prevent some forms of facial abnormalities in humans with genetic defects causing abnormal cartilage calcification.

column36: A K-mer Based Approach for Institutional AMR Surveillance, Transmission Monitoring, and Rapid Diagnostics
column37: Antibiotic resistant organisms (AROs) have become increasingly difficult to treat, with rising morbidity and mortality worldwide. Healthcare institutions are often the epicenter for outbreaks of these antibiotic resistant organisms, and are also windows into their circulation within the broader community. Transmission of antibiotic resistant organisms within hospitals is under appreciated. Moreover, identification of linked strains that may be causing occult outbreaks is often not systematically performed. Genomic approaches can provide a better understanding of within-hospital transmission of AROs, which can be used to guide infection control practices. Some institutions have augmented their ARO surveillance with whole genome sequencing, but this is both expensive and time consuming, making it unsuitable for routine use. However, new approaches that use k-mer based algorithms along with genomic reference databases can provide rapid evaluation of pathogen lineage and potential for linked transmission. These same approaches can also be used to provide important rapid diagnostic information about the likelihood of resistance to a given antibiotic. While there is much potential in these approaches, they need to be formally evaluated across care settings and geography before they can be trialled in the clinical setting. Here we propose a multi-continental prospective evaluation of the performance of a k-mer based approach for institutional surveillance of common multidrug resistant Gram-negative pathogens as well rapid prediction of antibiotic resistance patterns.

column36: Multi-level integrative 'omics to identify biomarkers in a Schizophrenia and other major psychoses. Jeremie Poschmann. Muliobio
column37: We will leverage a unique, large patient cohort selected based on molecular and clinical characteristics, combined with advanced molecular profiling and computational analysis to identify and then validate clinically useful biomarkers predictive of major psychosis. Our goal is to leverage a multi-level, interdisciplinary approach and simultaneously monitor serum protein levels, promising molecular phenotypes including gene expression and epigenetics, cellular immune phenotypes known to be altered during major psychosis while precisely controlling for immune cell population variation. We will use integrative computational analyses and machine learning methods to define a novel and unique set of BM predictive of major psychosis. This will enable us to compare for the first time: (i) longitudinal patient information reaching until childhood trauma, (ii) polygenic risk scores, (iii) cellular phenotypes including the variation in immune cell populations and their response to stimuli, (iii) molecular phenotypes such miRNA expression, whole transcriptome analysis and epigenomic analysis, together (iv) with serum protein investigation based on BM candidates from psychosis literature. The project is organized into four objectives. This project unites clinical neuroscientists, genomics scientists, cell biologists and immunologists each employing cutting edge methods in their own respective field. This collaboration highlights the different layers of investigations. Notably, it integrates patient phenotypic time courses assessed by our clinical scientists, immune cell phenotypes as determined by our immunologist, molecular phenotype information investigated by genomics scientists combined with machine learning approaches and integrative analysis by computational scientists.

column37: The discovery of antimicrobial agents was one of the great triumphs of the 20th century. The sobering news is that antibiotic resistance was part of the process as well. If nothing is done by 2050, AMR will cost $100 trillion with 10M people/year expected to die (https://amr-review.org). Factors driving AMR extend beyond human healthcare with implications in agriculture and the environment (the One Health approach). New and improved approaches for tackling AMR include better surveillance; rational drug use, different business model for generating antibiotics, innovation at all levels and most importantly a global approach. This transnational team grant proposal is tasked to apply new machine learning approaches for modeling AMR for faster diagnosis, better surveillance and prediction of resistance emergence. Specifically, we will develop machine learning implementation that can orient the selection of treatments by assessing the level of resistance, provide rational for the generation of novel antibiotics, and assist in the surveillance of human and livestock AMR around the globe. To achieve this, we have assembled a transnational team (Canada, China, Finland, France) with complementary skills with demonstrated expertise in machine learning applied to both genomics and metabolomics and AMR domain experts. Our transnational team has all the elements to be highly impactful and to continue collaborating well past the JPIAMR funding. Our complementarity of expertise will help us tackle the challenges ahead and ensure our continued success.

column36: Develop a multi-disciplinary approach for the personalized prenatal diagnostic and antepartum feto-maternal risk evaluation for twin pregnancies.
column37: The frequency of twin pregnancies has risen globally due to increased use of assisted conception and increasing maternal age. Twin pregnancies have 5-9 times higher frequencies of fetal chromosomal and structural abnormalities, often deliver preterm, and have high prevalence of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), preeclampsia (PE), and intrauterine growth restriction compared to singletons. Twins have unique complications such as the twin-to twin transfusion syndrome in monochorionic (MC) twins. Consequently, more twins are born prematurely, suffer from low birth weight, require admission to newborn intensive care units, and are at greater risk of developing motor and cognitive disorders and cerebral palsy in later life. These impose a huge burden on individuals, families, and societies. We aim to develop a multi-marker, personalized, prenatal diagnostic model to predict feto-maternal complications in twin pregnancies. A multi-national network will recruit a statistically powered cohort of 1,200 twins and follow them through pregnancy until delivery using biochemical, endocrine, imaging, immunologic and cell free DNA (cfDNA) parameters to modify a priori risks. Initial cohorts (Prof Maymon, Israel), demonstrated good prediction of Down syndrome, PE, and GDM using ultrasound and serum markers. We will use these markers and evaluate structural and chromosomal abnormalities [developed by Prof Kagan (Tubingen, Germany)], standardised imaging for MC twins [Prof's Brown and Miron (McGill, Canada)], and endocrine, sonographic, and biophysical markers [Prof Borrell (Barcelona, Spain), and Dr Geipel (Bonn, Germany)]. Prof Nicolaides (London, UK) will contribute his twin cohort data. Prof. Cuckle (Israel) will perform modelling using this large dataset to identify risk stratification algorithms for twins, offering personalized, preventive clinical care pathways for feto-maternal disorders. This would enable a paradigm shift in prenatal personalized care for twin pregnancy.

column36: IDx: An exploration of regulatory, corporate, relational, and technical barriers to uptake of diagnostics in the fight against AMR
column37: Greater availability of fast and accurate diagnostics for infections would greatly reduce the over-prescription of antibiotics and slow the growth of antibiotic resistance which limits treatment options. It would also help prescribe the right drug at the right time, thus reducing suffering and increasing survival. However, despite advances in technology, few useful diagnostics for bacterial infections have come to market and we are seeing a downward trend in innovation. This study proposes to identify the key barriers that remain once a new diagnostic has been developed, looking at recent technological advances that ultimately failed to be authorized, adopted, or able to change prescribing. It will also look at technologies that have helped in the fight against antimicrobial resistance. Are there any features or particularities that seem to have improved their chance of success? Lessons from the failures and few successes will be used to assess chances for products in the pipeline, examining how regulation, reimbursement, technology transfer, and organizational characteristics might be improved to make them succeed within the clinical setting. The work will focus on each of these themes in developed world settings but also use them as a lens (in addition to diagnostic technical characteristics) to examine determinants of uptake in rural parts of South Africa, which are to some extent a proxy for LMIC.

column37: The behavioral variant of frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) is a common cause of early-onset dementia (before age 65) with a lot of different variations in underlying pathology, genetics, and natural course. It therefore demands a customized approach to predict individual prognosis and develop personalized treatments. BvFTD is often mistaken for a primary psychiatric disorder (PPD), causing substantial diagnostic delay up to 6 years in average. Therefore, the most time critical clinical challenge is how to differentiate early bvFTD (in majority non-genetic) from late-onset psychiatric disorders that may mimic FTD, in order to deliver relevant interventions and treatments. All members of our multidisciplinary consortium have a strong track record in bvFTD research. We selected the most promising results of our ongoing research, including neuropsychological and social cognitive markers; neuroimaging- based classifiers; cerebrospinal fluid and serum biomarkers; and genetic makers. In this project, we will combined cohorts from all sites to examine and validate the above-mentioned markers (discovery cohort). This includes a large number of autopsy confirmed cases. We will then validate these markers in a deeply phenotyped prospective multi-national cohort that we will collect over the next 3 years. We will use advanced statistics to create the best diagnostic and prognostic models for bvFTD and PPD. Our project will contribute towards an early and accurate bvFTD identification, that is crucial for trial enrollment, whereas on the other hand early PPD identification will lead to the appropriate psychiatric treatments.

column36: Stratification of presymptomatic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: the development of novel imaging biomarkers. Jean-Francois Pradat - STRATALS
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Charcot's disease, is a severe neurodegenerative disease occurring between the ages of 50 and 70 years. It causes progressive paralysis of the limbs as well as muscles of speech and swallowing. There is no effective treatment and death occurs by respiratory failure after 3 to 5 years. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop new treatments, a limit being the extreme variability of the disease in its causes (there are hereditary and non-familial forms) and its clinical presentations. It is thus essential to characterize these different forms, in order to propose a personalized treatment. Importantly, a pre-symptomatic period is now well characterized in individuals who carry a mutation responsible for familial forms of ALS, and who have not yet developed the disease. Recent developments in gene therapy, which are currently evaluated in symptomatic patients, open for the first time the possibility to prevent the disease. To achieve this goal, we need to develop new tools that will allow us to characterize this pre-symptomatic phase and to monitor the effect of these new therapies as well. For example, new imaging methods with magnetic resonance imaging now offers the possibility of knowing when the first lesions begin and how they evolve over time. In this study, we plan to develop new imaging tools and outcome metrics that will allow even finer analysis of the changes occurring in the nervous system, especially in the spinal cord, which is the main site of abnormalities. We will apply these methods to individuals carrying a mutation causing ALS, whether they are pre-symptomatic or symptomatic, and will monitor their evolution over time. Thanks to this project we will be able to better predict the evolution of this devastating disease, and to design the clinical trials with drugs under development for future therapies

column37: Bloodstream infections (BSI) are annually responsible of hundred thousand estimated deaths worldwide. The time frame for identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing of the causative agent(s) of BSI directly impact the delay in the administration of appropriate antimicrobial therapy and, consequently, the clinical outcome of patients. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry revolutionized routine microbial identification by drastically shortening the delay of the identification (ID). There is however no consensus on a universal and affordable tool for shortening the characterization of putative antibiotic resistance mechanisms. Within a 5-year time horizon, this project, called IDAREMS (Determination of concomitant IDentification and Antibiotic REsistance profile of bacteria in one hour with an adaptive targeted single Mass Spectrometry analysis), should lead to the marketing of a disruptive IDAREMS tool for clinical diagnosis of BSI based on a new patented targeted proteomics technique named Scout-MRM, carried out by tandem mass spectrometry (MS). The innovation lies in the ability of concomitantly identifying a pathogen and profiling its phenotype of antibiotic resistance mechanisms directly from an aliquot of positive blood culture in less than one hour. The IDAREMS project is structured over three main work packages: WP1) the development by partner 1 (France) of a prototype assay for concomitant identification and rapid diagnostics of antimicrobial resistance in Gram-negative bacteria using a limited number of antibiotic-resistant bacterial isolates provided by partner 2 (France), partner 3 (Poland), partner 4 (Thailand), and partner 5 (Canada); WP2) the validation of the assay through blind testing of new clinical strains provided by the same partners; WP3) technician training and deployment of the validated assay in the respective partner's clinical platforms.

column36: Preparing the Canadian health care system to meet the needs of older adults with combined vision and hearing impairments and their caregivers
column37: Dual Sensory Impairment (DSI), also referred to as age-related deafblindness, is the combined loss of vision and hearing that results in a condition that is more complex and disabling than hearing or vision loss alone. Older adults with DSI often present with severe communication challenges and experience barriers in access to healthcare. Invariably, healthcare professionals also face challenges while screening, clinical assessments and delivering interventions due to associated communication difficulties and possible age-related cognitive decline. Two percent of the world population is estimated to have DSI. With the rapid increase in our ageing trends, over 500,000 to 1 million Canadians are expected to experience DSI by 2036. To address the problem in time, we need to prepare our healthcare system to provide optimal care for those aging with DSI in Canada. Using an appreciative inquiry approach, I aim to understand the challenges associated while accessing or providing care to older adults with DSI, in a phase-wise manner wherein each study will inform the next. In study 1, I plan to conduct a systematic review to synthesize evidence on existing and emergent strategies to provide optimal care to older adults with DSI. I will collect data from older adults with DSI and their caregivers (study 2), healthcare professionals (study 3), and policymakers or healthcare administrators (study 4) to develop a holistic understanding of what can be done to provide optimal care to older adults with DSI. The study will be guided by the World Report on Ageing and Health (2015), the Institut Nazareth et Louis-Braille (research priorities) and the Universite de Montreal Action Plan for Research, Discovery, Creation, and Innovation (2017-2021) on Aging. Findings will inform future service design, healthcare workforce development, and policy changes by providing recommendations and an action plan required to meet the needs of the rising population of older adults with DSI.

column37: In Northern British Columbia, a region rich in natural resources, there has been a rapid expansion of resource extraction projects across the region in recent years. column37: There are over 14,000 survivors of childhood and adolescent cancer in Ontario. Unfortunately, the treatments used to cure their cancer in childhood leads to a high risk for severe health conditions during adulthood, including the development of new cancers and heart problems. These are called "late effects" of cancer treatment. My main fellowship project will involve developing a health-system-wide, evidence-based program to identify adult survivors of childhood cancer at highest risk of these late effects and provide them (and their primary care providers) with the information they need to prevent or mitigate their impact. Presently, most adult survivors of childhood cancer do not complete recommended tests to screen for late effects. This leads to missed opportunities to take early action to stay healthy. Working with survivors, clinicians, and health-system partners, we will design a province-wide intervention to deliver personalized reminders and supports. We will engage survivors and their doctors to ensure the planned strategy is user-centred while incorporating the science of behaviour change. By the end of this project, we will be prepared to work with our provincial partners on implementing and evaluating a province-wide scale-up of the intervention. This fellowship will enhance my academic training, and expand my skills using patient engagement and patient-centred methods in the design and delivery of health care, as well as my capacity to conduct applied research in partnership with health system organizations. The training from the fellowship project, in combination with network building and leadership skills, will give me a strong foundation to begin a career of developing innovative solutions to challenges facing the health care system.

column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes paralysis which affects the person's ability to feed, bathe, or dress themselves and affects their ability to move about their home/community. The complexity of SCI care in the health system is reflected in the number of health care professionals involved in the rehabilitation process (doctors, nurses, physical and occupational therapists, social workers, and psychologists). Although delivery of rehabilitation is interprofessional, clinicians tend to work alone, and often do not know have time for continuing education and do not understand the impact of their practice on health system efficiency. Thus, strategies to integrate clinical expertise and improve the quality of rehabilitation services across the health system are needed. This application aims to support the development of a continuing education model for SCI rehabilitation for clinicians. The first phase of this fellowship will identify and synthesize current successful models of continuing education used in other health conditions. The second phase will use the products of phase one to inform the creation of a continuing education model specific to SCI rehabilitation providers. This project is the result of a partnership between the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation (ONF) and the University Health Network allowing knowledge produced in an academic setting to be incorporated into the partner organization's processes. We envision creating a platform for interprofessional groups of clinicians to share their expertise and identify the best pathway of care for SCI rehabilitation. This fellowship will support the creation of a continuing education model. The model will enable the initiatives of ONF related to advancing the SCI Quality Consortium (i.e. measuring and improving quality of SCI rehabilitation care in Ontario) and the Care Pathways (i.e. appropriate care for people with motor vehicle injuries), to achieve ONF's mandate of improved access to quality care across Ontario.

column36: Investing wisely: using economic modelling to optimize public health strategies to reduce harm from alcohol, tobacco and cannabis and optimize benefits in British Columbia
column37: Substance use costs British Columbia $4.9 billion in 2014, of which 70% was due to alcohol and tobacco. These estimates include costs related to the use of health care resources, productivity losses, criminal justice, and other direct costs such as accidents, research and prevention. Broader societal costs not included in these estimates relate to inequities, marginalization and hindered social development. This project aims to develop a model to evaluate the economic and social impact of legal substance use harm prevention in British Columbia. Evidence on economic consequences and how public health programs can minimize costs and harms from substance use is important for policy makers, who need to consider the health system priorities against efficiency, scalability and sustainability of interventions. The challenges to developing comprehensive economic evaluations in public health are well known. In the area of substance use, these pertain to the multitude of the socioeconomic determinants that influence use - such as employment, income, social exclusion, and hopelessness - and the difficulty of measuring broader benefits including family wellbeing, community development and equity gains. This fellowship will facilitate collaboration between knowledge users and academics with the aim of optimizing investment in the area of alcohol, tobacco and cannabis harm prevention in BC. It will provide the Ministry of Health with tools to implement efficient priority setting that aligns with the institution's values and development goals. This will be achieved through important methodological advances to allow evaluations to account for the broader societal impact of preventing harm from legal substance use in BC. As a result, this fellowship will sustain future research in health economics with an increased ability to respond to policy makers' needs when it comes to priority setting.

column36: Early Mechanistic Biomarkers for late Epilepsy and long-term Brain Injury Outcome Jens P. Dreier EBio2
column37: Stroke and traumatic brain injuries (TBI) in humans are common causes of mortality and impose a poor quality of life on the affected individuals and their families. Life-saving treatments after brain injuries improved patients' survival but long-term severe complications, such as motor and cognitive disabilities and epilepsy, still lack preventive treatments. Our studies indicate that specific structural and functional alterations involving neurons, glia and brain vessels underlie the progressive evolution of brain injuries and contribute to the late onset of epilepsy. The unmet need for early identification of these pathologic events in injured patients with clinically applicable approaches is the basis for the current project. Our ultimate goal is to improve current treatment interventions in brain-injured patients by discovering mechanism-driven biomarkers that will permit early preventive treatments for neurological complications. Through a combination approach based on improved and novel analyses of electrophysiological signals, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and selected blood molecules, we will search for common fingerprints of brain network dysfunctions reflecting disease progression using (1) our existing database of brain-injured patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage who underwent intensive neuromonitoring, serial MRI scans, blood collection, and were evaluated for epilepsy after 3 years, and (2) clinically relevant animal models of brain injury that are associated with late epilepsy development and allow neuromonitoring in a similar manner as in the ICU. We envision that monitoring of post-injury brain dynamics will allow us to develop biomarkers that identify patients at high-risk for developing a disease progressive course and epilepsy, thus permitting novel treatments to be applied timely following the concept of Personalized Medicine.

column36: Biomarkers of ANTidepressant RESponse : early indicators and novel targets
column37: Antidepressants (AD) are for now, the best treatment we have for major depression (MDD) a severe mental disorder. AD are one of the most commonly prescribed drugs in the western hemisphere, however their trial-and error nature combined with unwanted side-effects, leave a lot to be desired. More than 60% of patients suffering from MDD fail to respond to the first AD they are prescribed. For those that respond, full response is only observed after several weeks of treatment, and, in case of failure it can take too long a time before alternative options are explored. To be able to predict clinical response at an early-stage of AD treatment is an important aim for the clinician and the potential impact for patients suffering from MDD and for the health system is very high. However, up to date there are no early biomarkers that could help therapeutic decision while this is already true in cancer and other fields of medicine. We recently described the involvement of ELK1 in depression, particularly how ELK1 gene expression in blood may help follow treatment response and will further characterize ELK1 and related genes, and other regulators of cell machinery associated with early clinical improvement. First we aim to identify peripheral "early post-treatment biomarkers" in a novel multicentre human cohort of patients with MDE. Then, we want to validate "early post-treatment biomarkers" in animal models of depression, in the blood. Last, we want to explore the plausibility of our blood biomarkers by studying our biomarkers in the brain. We will focus our analysis on both long and small RNA, by using cutting-edge approaches. These results will constitute the necessary first step to develop new biomarkers predictive of AD response. Such biomarkers, would reduce time to change medication and help avoid unnecessary side effects for patients, inform therapeutic decisions and reduce stress for clinicians, and reduce personal and public health costs.

column37: Predictive risk algorithms for chronic disease are used by organizations like Public Health Ontario (PHO) for population health surveillance, examining the contribution of risk factors to disease, and assessing the impact of prevention strategies. Vast amounts of population health data are now available and able to support a wide range of "big data" approaches for chronic disease risk prediction. Population health has traditionally used simple risk prediction methods, however, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are ideally suited to enhancing population risk prediction tools. To date, however, evidence on risk prediction using these methods for population health applications is limited and it is unclear how AI approaches could be used to benefit health protection, promotion, prevention and health equity. The objectives of the proposed program of work are to: 1) develop an AI strategy for PHO, the host organization; 2) develop two new risk prediction models for dementia and multiple chronic disease using AI methods; and 3) support public health units in building AI capacity. It is important for Canada to build capacity for AI, as there is significant potential for these methods to support population health surveillance and disease prevention.

column36: Systematic analysis of the molecular mechanisms of leukocyte entry into the pancreas. MRC NPA Adrian Liston
column37: Lymphocytes, also known as white blood cells, defend the body against microbes, viruses and cancer by circulating throughout the body. Aside from lymphoid tissues (spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow, etc), a small number of lymphocytes can be found in all other tissues, including the pancreas. Entry of lymphocytes in tissues such as the brain, the eyes, the muscles or the pancreas is regulated by specific proteins and processes. Aberrant or facilitated entry of lymphocytes into these non-lymphoid tissues can lead to severe immune pathologies. Notably, lymphocyte infiltrates in the pancreas have been documented in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Blocking immune cell entry in the pancreas would certainly provide therapeutic benefit to diabetes patients. Our overall objective is to identify the proteins that allow both normal and aberrant lymphocyte infiltration in the pancreas. We will use two complementary non-targeted approach to identify key pathways facilitating lymphocyte entry into pancreatic tissue. First, by a novel molecular biology approach, namely ProCode, we will test the role of over 200 proteins in inhibiting or facilitating lymphocyte entry in the pancreas. Second, we will screen over 200 strains of mice from the Collaborative Cross and determine which of these mice present with more or less lymphocytes in the pancreas. As the genome of the Collaborative Cross mice is known, this unbiased approach will reveal genes that influence lymphocyte entry in the pancreas. Altogether, these complementary approaches will unravel the specific molecular pathways that need to be targeted to prevent lymphocyte entry in pancreatic tissue.

These data have led to the premise that the target of rapamycin a protein denoted mTOR may provide the female heart greater resistance to damage. Therefore, the present grant proposal will attempt to identify the signaling events that regulate mTOR activity, and elucidate that targets of mTOR that provide the female heart greater resistance to damage after a heart attack.

column36: The regulation of Cell-Matrix Adhesion in mouse development and tissue homeostasis
column37: Integrins are the main molecules in the human body that link cells to the extracellular matrix (ECM), a mixture of complex sugars and proteins that forms the base upon which tissues are built. Integrins are very important for many processes and disruptions in integrin function are associated with a large array of disease processes in humans. We are interested in understanding the mechanisms by which integrin carry out their diverse functions as this will give us crucial insight into many disease processes. To understand how integrins carry out so many diverse functions we are focusing on how they are regulated, that is, how they are switched on and off at certain times. Our proposal presents experiments that seek to understand how integrins are regulated and how this regulation contributes to tissue formation and repair. We propose to use mice containing mutations that up or down regulate integrin based adhesion to see how integrin regulation contributes to diverse processes. in particular we will focus on integrin's role in fibroblasts, specialised cells that are important for tissue repair, melanocytes which are the cells that give skin its pigmentation, and platelets, which are responsible for blood clotting. Results of this study will shed important light on how integrins are controlled during human development and tissue maintenance, and also provide insight into how dysregulation of integrin function leads to disease.

column36: Contribution of the NKG2D pathway to multiple sclerosis
column37: Several studies showed that the immune system contributes to the development of multiple sclerosis (MS). Normally, the immune system defends the body against foreign elements. However, in the case of MS, the immune system attacks the protective sheath surrounding our neurons, called myelin and impairs several essential functions of brain cells. Our team investigates how immune cells hurt brain cells of MS patients. Stressed brain cells can put on their surface alert molecules that are subsequently detected by white blood cells carrying a receptor called NKG2D. The NKG2D-bearing immune cells can recognize and kill cells carrying these alert molecules. We observed that white blood cells from MS patients carry a greater amount of NKG2D compared to those from healthy donors. We will investigate whether these immune cells from MS patients can cause more damage to brain cells. We also observed that some human neurons but also other cells called astrocytes (which are important to maintain neurons' health), express these alert molecules. Our project will evaluate whether blocking the detection by immune cells via NKG2D could prevent harmful attack on neurons and astrocytes. We will also evaluate whether neurons and astrocytes carry these alert molecules in postmortem brains from MS patients.

column36: Prognostic and Therapeutic Utility of Human Antigen R (HuR) in Fibrosis
column37: Pulmonary fibrosis occurs when the lung becomes scarred and stiffened, leading to death from respiratory failure. The average survival of an individual with pulmonary fibrosis is only 3-5 years, worse than many types of cancer. One of the reasons is that it is very hard to diagnose pulmonary fibrosis. Furthermore, there is no biomarker that tells if you have pulmonary fibrosis. Although the cause of pulmonary fibrosis is not known, risk factors include genetic susceptibility and cigarette smoke. There is no cure for pulmonary fibrosis and remarkably few effective therapies. This research will investigate a novel protein- called human antigen R (HuR)- that has never been studied in pulmonary fibrosis. However, HuR may control protein expression associated with pulmonary fibrosis that leads to respiratory failure. Based on what we know about HuR in cancer, we predict that HuR will promote pulmonary fibrosis when it does not behave in a normal fashion. Some things that cause HuR to behave improperly include cigarette smoke and radiation- risk factors for pulmonary fibrosis. The localization of HuR within a cell shows that someone with cancer will progress very rapidly. It is not known where HuR is found in the lung in fibrosis conditions, but we predict that in a person with pulmonary fibrosis, HuR levels and location in the lung may be very different compared to someone without the disease. Determining this may be one way to tell who has the disease and who does not. Finally, inhibiting HuR with a drug would be one way to prevent its function from being irregular. Using animal models of fibrosis, biological samples from individuals with IPF as well as cell and molecular biology techniques, we will test the therapeutic and prognostic utility of HuR in pulmonary fibrosis. In essence, HuR represents an unexplored and innovative pathway that will ultimately serving as a catalyst for future experiments to explore novel drugs and the utility of HuR as a biomarker.

column36: Targeting global programs of gene expression to promote axon regeneration
column37: Numerous neurological conditions and traumatic injuries disrupt connections between nerve in the adult mammalian central nervous system (CNS). Damaged CNS neurons have a limited capacity to repair themselves leading to motor, sensory and cognitive impairments. Promoting axon regeneration could support neurological recovery from a variety of conditions and serve as an adjunct for cellular transplantation approaches. There are currently no approved treatments to stimulate CNS axon regeneration. An exciting advance in the CNS regeneration field is that specific changes in gene expression in injured neurons can trigger extensive axon regeneration; however therapeutic translation of these findings is limited by off-target effects associated with these particular genes. An alternative attractive strategy to positively regulate the repair of injured neurons is through targetting a family of molecules called miRNAs that affect the expression of many genes simultaneusly and may thus have robust effects on axon regeneration. We are using a combination of cell based and animal models to identify miRNAs with robust axon regeneration promoting activity and are identifying the molecular targets of these miRNA that may be therapeutically targeted to promote axon regeneration following injury.

column36: Preventing pathological protein spread in Huntington's disease: relevance to pathology and treatment.
column37: To date, the problem in Huntington's Disease (HD) has been thought to result from a genetic mutation which leads to the production of an abnormal protein - called mutant huntingtin - within brain cells. Over time, this protein causes the cells to slowly stop working and die. In recent years, new evidence has emerged which suggests that other factors may also contribute to the death of these nerve cells but these factors were thought to be of only minor significance for the disease. However, we found that this may not be the case as we detected the abnormal mutant huntingtin protein in healthy transplanted tissue implanted in the brains of affected individuals. This indicates that mutant huntingtin had spread and entered the implanted healthy graft tissue. These findings have been repeated in both cell and animal models and it is now accepted that mutant huntingtin can be transported between cells. We now seek to explore how mutant huntingtin spread relates to disease presentation and how prevention or reduction of this spread by vaccines could diminish disease burden. If true, the theory that we propose would both improve our understanding of what goes wrong in HD and, more importantly, potentially lead to new treatment options.

column36: Prenatal exposure to chemicals in plastics can cause epigenetic variation in genes associated with neurodevelopment in girls and boys
column37: The healthy development of children is very sensitive to exposure to environmental chemicals during pregnancy. Prenatal exposure to chemicals in plastics, specifically phthalates, is substantial due to their widespread use in food packaging, household cleaners, cosmetics and personal care products. Phthalates can cross the placenta and affect the activity of genes critical for brain development. This in turn could influence the development of children's thinking and reasoning abilities and behaviour. Prenatal exposure to phthalates has been associated with adverse effects on children's development, including lower levels of intelligence, poorer motor and language skills and a higher risk for autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. The effect of phthalates on genes is poorly understood and may be different for girls and boys. This could explain the greater proportion of boys who are diagnosed with developmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Our team is comprised of researchers with expertise in child development, epigenetics, environmental toxicology and public health. We will use already collected data on mother's prenatal exposure to phthalate chemicals and children's cognitive, motor and behavioural outcomes at 2, 3-4 and 5-9 years of age. This data comes from two studies that recruited women during pregnancy, one in Canada and the other in Australia. These studies have biobanked DNA samples that will be used to identify genes that change due to phthalate exposure. We will investigate the relationship between these genes and intelligence, language and motor skills, and behaviour in girls and boys. Our results could be used to update recommendations on exposure to chemicals in plastics during pregnancy. They could also be used to design interventions to prevent or reverse the potential negative effects of exposure to these plastic chemicals on children's brains and behaviour.

column36: A role for the regulator of purine biosynthesis at the host-pathogen interface
column37: The bacterium Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most common causes of human infections. These infections range from mild (minor wound infections and carbuncles, for example) to more serious, and often fatal illnesses (e.g. endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septicemia, and toxic shock syndrome). S. aureus is also the most common source of hospital-acquired infections and is frequently found as the cause of surgical wound and indwelling medical device infections. However, efforts to control this bacterium with antibiotics are becoming increasingly difficult due to its multi-drug resistance. This research is centred around a new discovery in my laboratory that has profound implications on the pathogenic potential of S. aureus. We have discovered that mutations in a regulator of purine biosynthesis, as yet uncharacterized in S. aureus, occur in response to stress. These mutations lead to upregulation of proteins on the S. aureus cell surface that bind fibronectin, a host protein. The upregulation of fibronectin-binding proteins results in bacterial cell clumping, massive aggregation in the presence of fibronectin and, during systemic infection of rodents, occlusion of the vasculature resulting in a hypervirulent S. aureus phenotype. The goal of this research is to characterize these mutants and identify targets that when perturbed curtail virulence. Our studies will provide novel information on how serious human pathogens, like S. aureus, have the potential to cause such a wide array of infections, or severity of infection. It is envisioned that uncovering these essential processes will lead to the rational design of successful next-generation drugs and therapeutic strategies to treat patients suffering from S. aureus infection.

column37: In Canada, approximately 1.6 million people suffer from cardiovascular diseases, and someone dies from these diseases every 7 minutes. The heart is made of different cell types that work together to generate a heart beat. These cells share a common mechanism to handle cellular stress in response to unfavorable conditions, but the outcome of the stress coping strategy depends on the type of heart cell. A condition called cardiac fibrosis results from malfunction of the cell stress coping response, which eventually results in heart failure. We found that long-term stress coping response in cardiomyocytes, (the cells responsible for contraction and relaxation of the heart) and in cardiac fibroblasts (the cells responsible for repairing damage to heart tissue) is instrumental to development of cardiac fibrosis. We will apply the new knowledge generated to guide therapeutic interventions that can prevent or treat the development of heart disease in humans.

column36: Sensory processing impairments in autism
column37: Sensory processing disruptions are common in autism spectrum and some other neuro-developmental disorders. Sensory input is the sole neural input into the brain; in this context, it is debated to what extent changes in sensory processing throughout development is a root cause for brain alterations resulting in autism symptoms. At the very least, sensory processing pathways in the brain might be affected by the disorder in the same way as other brain areas. On a positive note, sensory processing pathways are highly conserved, well described, and relatively easily accessible - they therefore offer a unique window of opportunity for translational studies on sensory processing disruptions and their impact on brain development and function using an animal model. From our previous work we learned two important things: 1) increased reactivity to sound is NOT necessarily due to increased sound sensitivity, as it is often wrongly interpreted in kids with developmental disorders and 2) early disruptions in sensory processing lead to compensatory changes that might be the real problem for the developing brain. We here propose a study in an excellent animal model showing the exact same sensory symptoms as observed in kids with autism, in order to further understand how these compensatory mechanisms work and how we can avoid or reverse them. The animal model will also allow to test the efficacy of early intervention either with drugs or occupational therapy in order to avoid these detrimental compensatory changes induced by sensory processing disruptions. Our results will have a huge impact on clinical assessments and intervention for all people with autism and other disorders that are associated with altered sensory processing, e.g. schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive disorder, or Tourett's syndrome.

column36: Development of a peptide-based membrane mimetic for solution studies in membrane protein research.
column37: Membrane proteins are a vital component of cells. Until recently, membrane proteins were not studied as extensively as cytosolic proteins. This is due to the propensity of membrane proteins to aggregate outside a membrane environment during their isolation using detergents. Therefore, in recent years, several membrane mimics have been developed in order to facilitate interrogation of membrane proteins by rigorous biophysical and analytical techniques. However, stabilization of membrane proteins in these mimetic remains laborious, costly and difficult to perform. To overcome these limitations, our laboratory has developed a simple method to stabilize membrane proteins in aqueous solution. Called the "peptidisc", the method uses multiple copies of a unique peptide that wraps around membrane proteins to make them feel like they never left the membrane environment. The end result is membrane proteins that are perfectly stable, soluble and free of detergent effects. The peptidisc technology will allow us to better study membrane proteins, yielding a better understanding of their structure and activity, which ones associates and how they interact in the cell and with their environment. Since the peptidisc approach is both simple and easy to apply, more membrane proteins can now also be included in high-throughput searches for new drugs that target medical conditions.

column36: CETP Inhibition as a novel treatment to remove pathogen lipids and improve survival in sepsis
column37: Sepsis, or the severe inflammation in response to an infection, is one of the leading causes of death of Canadians in the hospital. Sepsis occurs when the immune system is activated by lipid molecules from invading bacteria. These "pathogen-associated lipids", or PALs, are transported through the bloodstream by lipoproteins, the same particles that also transport cholesterol. Of the different lipoprotein particles, HDL (also called the "good cholesterol") plays a particularly important role in transporting PALs. HDL levels are known to drop acutely during sepsis, and we have recently shown that the degree of drop in HDL during sepsis is a very strong predictor of whether or not a patient will survive sepsis, with a lower HDL level predicting a worse outcome. How and why HDL levels drop during sepsis is unknown. The major goal of this project is to investigate genetic mechanisms that determine HDL levels in sepsis. We have discovered a gene, called CETP, that appears to play a very important role in determining HDL levels during sepsis, and thereby contributes to whether or not a patient will survive the episode of sepsis. The goals of this proposal are to explore whether inhibition of CETP may represent a new treatment strategy for sepsis. To do this, we will use an existing drug that inhibits CETP to examine its effects in mouse models of sepsis. We will also investigate the role of genetic variation in HDL-related genes on HDL levels and survival from sepsis in large population cohorts. This research will provide new insight into the important role of HDL and CETP in sepsis. The results of this research could lead to new ways to treat sepsis, for example by altering the function of CETP. Ultimately these results will improve the health of Canadians by leading to new approaches to treat sepsis, one of the leading causes of death in Canada.

column36: Allosteric Modulation of the Urotensin Receptor with Small-Molecule Peptide Mimics
column37: The urotensin II receptor (UT) plays important roles in the heart, kidneys, pancreas, adrenal gland, and central nervous system. The receptor is known to bind to two endogenous cyclic peptide ligands: urotensin II (UII) and urotensin II-related peptide (URP). These ligands and the parent receptor have been implicated in heart disease, metabolic syndrome, and kidney failure. For example, in the cardiovascular system, UII acts as a potent endothelium independent vasoconstrictor and endothelium-dependent vasodilator; however, in disease states, this constriction-dilation equilibrium is disrupted. Their specific influences on UT have been difficult to decipher due to a dearth in molecules that can selectively block the activity of UII and URP; however, it is suspected that their functional selectivity leads to differential participation in specific cardiovascular disease pathology. Our collaborative research has identified novel small-molecule receptor modulators that can differentiate the effects of UII and URP. Di- and triazepin-2-one peptide mimics have been conceived based on the side chain orientations and backbone conformation of a biologically relevant tripeptide motif common to both endogenous urotensin receptor (UT) ligands. Contingent on structure the diand triazepin-2-ones can modulate selectively and differentially the contractile effects of UII and URP ex vivo. Considering the importance of UT and its ligands in cardiovascular diseases, these modulators offer unique potential for dissecting the different biological pathways mediated by UII and URP in normal physiology and during disease pathology. A plan is proposed for improving ligand potency to develop probes and ideally therapeutics to treat cardiovascular diseases by an interdisciplinary approach featuring organic synthesis, in vitro and ex vivo screening, and animal models of atherosclerosis.

column36: Audit & Feedback Module Targeting Low-Value Clinical Practices in Injury Care: an Economic Evaluation
column37: In Canada, injury leads to more potential years of life lost and to greater costs than heart and stroke diseases combined. Furthermore, more than 50% of patients hospitalised following injury do not receive optimal care, 20% of injury deaths are estimated to be preventable and significant variations in injury mortality and morbidity have been observed across trauma centers in Canada, the UK, Australia and the USA. Over the past decades, emphasis on adherence to evidence-based processes of care (rewards for doing more) and rapid innovation in imaging and therapeutic techniques has led to an exponential rise in unnecessary tests and procedures. Whole body CT scan for minor trauma is just one example. Low-value clinical practices, defined as "the common use of a particular intervention when the benefits don't justify the potential harm or cost" consume up to 30% of healthcare budgets. They expose patients to physical and psychological adverse events and put enormous pressure on healthcare budgets, thereby threatening accessible, universal health care. According the Canadian Institute for Health Information, 1 in 4 Canadians were recommended a test or treatment that they did not feel was necessary in 2015. column36: Ferroptosis-mediated damage in Chronic EAE: implications for Progressive MS
column37: There are limited treatments options for progressive MS, with only one approved drug. Unlike relapsing-remitting MS, progressive MS is not responsive to anti-inflammatory drugs. This suggests that progressive MS is not mainly an inflammatory disease but could be a neurodegenerative disease caused by 'oxidative stress'. 'Ferroptosis' is a newly discovered form of oxidative stress, triggered by excess iron which causes damage to lipids (or fats) found in cells. Ferroptosis can cause damage to myelin which is rich in lipids. It can also cause damage to cells in the brain that produce myelin as well as to nerve cells (neurodegeneration). We have preliminary evidence from a mouse model of MS called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) that ferroptosis occurs in a chronic form of EAE (CH-EAE), which models aspects of progressive MS. Once ferroptosis starts, it can take off like "wildfire in the hot, dry summer". The good news is, that there are drugs that can "quench this fire" and stop damage to lipids. We already have evidence that certain biomarkers of ferroptosis are produced more highly in CH-EAE. We propose to treat CH-EAE mice with a drug that blocks ferroptosis. We have preliminary evidence that such treatment works. We will confirm this by assessing if this treatment improves weakness and paralysis in these mice and also analyze improvement in pathology. We also plan to study a combination-treatment with a ferroptosis inhibitor and an iron chelator to block ferroptosis-mediated damage to lipids, and other iron-mediated damage to proteins and DNA. We hope this will act like a "one-two punch" to stop progression. In addition, we will also assess various ferroptosis biomarkers in human MS brain autopsy samples of secondary progressive and primary progressive MS. This work could open the way for the development of novel therapies for progressive forms of MS for which there is currently no effective treatment.

column36: Immunogenic wheat protein metabolism by gut bacteria.
column37: Celiac disease is a common food sensitivity triggered by gluten in cereals like wheat, rye and barley and its incidence is rising at an alarming rate. The reasons for this are not fully understood but suggestions are that they relate to changes in the composition or function of gut microbes. We discovered that some pathogens present in the gut use gluten and other non-gluten proteins, as a source of food, but this digestion is partial and generates peptides that cause more inflammation in celiac disease patients. Thus, the metabolic activity of certain bacteria within the gut could increase the chances to develop wheat sensitivity and targeting this function could prevent or treat it. The proposal will study the capacity to digest wheat proteins by the microbe community that resides in the upper gut of celiac patients or controls without the disease. We will then apply these communities to mouse models that express celiac risk genes, and thus are relevant to human disease, to study the inflammation induced. The gluten-free diet is the only available therapy for celiac disease, but it is difficult to follow, expensive and not always effective. The knowledge learned here will guide us in identifying groups of bacteria with optimal capacity to detoxify wheat proteins to prevent or treat food sensitivities, such as celiac disease.
