column36: Optimizing patient adherence to stroke rehabilitation treatment: a telerehabilitation trial
column37: Stroke impacts nearly 400,000 Canadians annually. Three quarters of stroke survivors will live with minor to severe impairments or disabilities; which require rehabilitation care representing >$3.6 billion for the Canadian economy. Enhancing stroke rehabilitation care delivery can reduce those costs while optimizing patient outcomes and allowing patients to return home earlier following the stroke event. Strong evidence supports initiating rehabilitation as soon as the patient's medical status has stabilized; however, the need to travel to access rehabilitation, the lack of interprofessional communication among service providers, and the failure to engage the patient/families in the decision making process, limit access to optimal services. This intervention will entail participants receiving rehabilitation care through remote, live treatment sessions with an interdisciplinary group of clinicians (called telerehabilitation). The aim of this application is to evaluate whether telerehabilitation could provide patients who have had stroke the opportunity to return home safely after their acute hospital stay, encourage patient (and family) engagement in rehabilitation care, and overcome challenges of access to interprofessional rehabilitation care. The process of care, clinical outcomes and costs will be captured for 296 patients, half of whom will be offered telerehabilitation. Through qualitative interviews, the research team will uncover and describe contextual factors (both personal and environmental) that will facilitate the delivery of stroke rehabilitation care using a telerehabilitation platform (for whom and how does it work). Given stark contrasts between the Canadian stroke care recommendations and actual rehabilitation practice, and little robust data to support change, this study represents a unique, highly relevant, and innovative opportunity to minimize gaps in both knowledge and practice.

column36: Targeting Translational Control in Retinal Ganglion Cell Degeneration
column37: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, afflicting over 70 million people, and nearly one in ten elderly Canadians. Although glaucoma is often associated with increased eye pressure, it is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the death of retinal ganglion cell neurons to compromise vision. Yet we still do not understand the molecular mechanisms that drive this damage, and there are no neuroprotective treatments. In studying the degenerative process we have identified a gene family, the MNKs, that function to influence protein production in retinal ganglion cells. However, this process has not been previously linked to ganglion cell death or glaucoma. Based on our preliminary evidence we propose that the actions of MNKs have an important role in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. Our research program will generate new insights into how changes in this mechanism contributes to retinal damage, and provide proof of principle for targeting this process as a new therapeutic strategy.

column36: Circadian regulation of host-pathogen interactions in vector-borne parasitic infections
column37: Vector-borne diseases (e.g. parasites or other pathogens transmitted to humans by insects) are major public health concerns for billions of people in tropical and subtropical regions. Of utmost importance, with global warming, the spreading of these vector-borne infections is predicted to reach temperate latitudes within the next decades. Recent research has shown that immune responses, including against pathogens, vary across the day-night cycle and are controlled by biological clocks located in most tissues, including immune cells. Very little research has been performed on the influence of circadian clocks on parasitic infections or any other vector-transmitted diseases. We propose that vector-borne parasitic infections represent ideal models to study circadian regulation of host-pathogen interactions. As a model for the study of circadian rhythms in parasitic infections, we study leishmaniasis, a debilitating and often mortal human disease affecting millions of individuals in tropical and subtropical areas. It is caused by infection by the parasite Leishmania sps., which is transferred by sandflies that are active at dusk and dawn. We previously found that the magnitude of Leishmania infection vary according to the time of day at which the host meets the parasite. We will now aim to determine the mechanisms involved in this circadian rhythm and the involvement of immune cell clocks in controlling the infection, and on the other hand, the effect of the parasitic infection on the circadian rhythms of the host. A better understanding of the timed regulation of host-parasite interactions will allow developing better prophylactic and therapeutic strategies to fight off these vector-borne diseases.

column36: Polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase: its role in DNA strand break repair and a potential therapeutic target to enhance radio- and chemotherapy
column37: A problem frequently encountered in cancer therapy is that of tumour cell resistance to therapeutic agents, so that although the majority of cells in a tumour will be destroyed, a small fraction will survive, and have the potential to metastasize. At present our ability to predict tumour response to treatment or diminish the resistance to radiation or drugs is very limited. Such methods are only likely to be developed when we have a clearer understanding, at the molecular level, of how cells respond to these agents. For many of these agents, DNA is considered to be the main target leading to cell death. It is known that cells have the capacity to repair much of this damage. Uncovering all the enzymes responsible for repair and learning how they operate is still a major task. This proposal focuses on a particular type of damage, DNA strand breaks, and on the role of a particular enzyme, polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), in carrying out the repair of these lesions. We intend to learn how PNKP interacts with other proteins required to mend strand breaks and if it plays an important role in making cells resistant to a variety of anti-cancer drugs. Almost all cancer cells lack specific proteins called tumour suppressor proteins. We have recently found that cells that have lost specific tumour suppressors either die or become very weak if PNKP is also lost. This is a process called synthetic lethality and it presents an opportunity to target cancer cells rather than normal cells. In order to make full use of this opportunity we will investigate the mechanism(s) responsible for synthetic lethality involving loss of PNKP.

column36: Physiological and pathophysiological roles of renal intercalated cells
column37: Kidneys in our bodies regulate how much and which waste products are eliminated in the urine. Key cells in this process are called intercalated cells, which regulate blood acid-base balance and urinary acidification. Our preliminary results show that kAE1 interacts with another protein called claudin-4, and that altering one or the other results in the disease symptoms. In this funding period, we will dissect the relationship between these 2 proteins, verify our findings in vivo and alter their functional and physical interaction using drugs or genetic engineering as a lead towards development of therapeutic approaches to not only treat dRTA patients but also patients with chronic kidney disease.

column36: Elucidating the role of the IL-1 system in the pathogenesis of CNS autoimmunity
column37: This project is at the crossroads of neuroscience and immunology. It aims at understanding the role of the cytokine interleukin (IL)-1B, a molecule that allows immune cells to communicate with each other, in multiple sclerosis (MS). Because of the availability of transgenic mouse lines lacking key molecules of this signalling system or having fluorescently labeled neurons, glia and immune cells, we have decided to focus our work on an animal model of MS called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Up to now, these transgenic animals have allowed us to demonstrate that IL-1B has early detrimental effects, causing loss of neurons and their projections (termed axons), myelin sheaths and neurological function. Our results show that the negative effects of IL-1B are mediated by a subclass of innate immune cells called neutrophils and macrophages, and involve stimulation of the IL-1 receptor (IL-1R1) present at the surface of certain veins draining the central nervous system (CNS). More specifically, we showed that IL-1B production by innate immune cells is a critical step for their mobilization inside the CNS. Furthermore, we found that the subsequent activation of IL-1R1 signaling in CNS blood vessels induces a communication loop that drives neuroinflammation and the recruitment of autoaggressive (termed effector) lymphocytes into the CNS, eventually leading to immune attacks and demyelination. In this grant proposal, we aim at identifying the exact molecules involved in the production of IL-1 by both subclasses of innate immune cells involved. Since IL-1 can influence many types of immune and CNS cells (e.g. blood vessels, neurons, T lymphocytes, etc.), we also want to better understand their interplay in the attack phase. Finally, we want to determine whether we can use anti-IL-1 therapies (many are currently approved for arthritis) or downstream molecules to prevent EAE development and/or progression and to offer an additional therapy for MS patients.

column36: Mechanisms by which hyperinsulinemia promotes pancreatic cancer
column37: High levels of the hormone insulin are a cardinal feature of obesity and early type 2 diabetes, and are induced by unhealthy 'Western diets' high in sugar and fat. It has been suggested that excess insulin contributes to cancer initiation and/or progression, but this has never been tested directly in a way that can address cause and effect. Over the past 5 years, we tested for the first time the hypothesis high levels of insulin play a causal role in pancreatic cancer initiation using new mouse models. Remarkably, our data show a clear reduction in the early stages of pancreatic cancer in the mice that with only a relatively modest reduction in insulin. We now want to know how excess insulin has this cancer promoting effect. Specifically, we want to know whether the effects of insulin are direct on the cancer cells, or indirect by altering something else in the body or the cells that are nearby to the tumours. These studies have the potential to further clarify the known links between insulin and many forms of cancer, as well as uncover the exact mechanisms by which excess insulin influences cancer risk. Our findings will have major implications for both cancer prevention via nutrition/lifestyle modification and for cancer treatment by inhibition of insulin signalling in tumours.

column36: Determining the role of the nuclear basket protein Mlp1/TPR in mRNA homeostasis
column37: Regulating the expression of its genes is an essential task for any living organism. In eukaryotic cells, a membrane impermeable to large molecules separates the site where the genetic information is stored (the nucleus) from the site where the information is translated into protein (cytoplasm), the functional molecules executing all cellular processes. After the genetic information stored in the DNA is copied into a messenger molecule, called RNA, RNA has to exit the nucleus and reach the cytoplasm to get translated. The only path to reach the site of protein synthesis is through the nuclear pore complex (NPC), large macromolecular complexes embedded in the nuclear membrane. In this project, we will use different molecular biology, genetic, proteomic and microscopy based approaches to study the mechanism by which the nuclear basket, a substructure of the NPC, regulates the transport of some RNAs, but not all RNAs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Understanding this process is important to gain a better understanding of many diseases, as mutations in the proteins involved in this process have been found mutated in patients suffering from various diseases such as cancer or Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).

column36: The implication of the adaptive arm of the integrated stress response in KRAS lung cancer.
column37: Mutations in KRAS gene are found in deadly forms of cancer like colorectal, lung and pancreatic cancers. In lung cancer, 30% of adenocarcinomas possess mutations in KRAS gene, which render this type of cancer refractory to anti-tumor therapies. Mutant KRAS gene produces a protein that has the capacity to reprogram the functions of normal cells and establish stressful conditions that disrupt normal proliferation. Under these conditions, cells employ mechanisms that help them survive and adapt to stress. However, these adaptive mechanisms act in favor of mutant KRAS to maintain the abnormal proliferation and cause cancer. We have identified that adaptation of cells to the function of mutant KRAS requires a protein known as eIF2. In stressed cells, eIF2 is modified by a process named phosphorylation, which reorganizes key cellular functions to promote the expression of genes and synthesis of proteins that further enhance the oncogenic function of mutant KRAS. In this proposal, we investigate the mechanisms utilized by eIF2 to promote the formation of lung cancer through the action of mutant KRAS. We employ mice, which have been genetically engineered for the disruption of eIF2 function, to examine the effects of eIF2 inhibition on the formation of lung tumors containing mutant KRAS. Also, we will examine the function of proteins that assist eIF2 in the development of lung cancer through the action of mutant KRAS. Moreover, we will test the effects of newly developed eIF2 inhibitory drugs to assess their anti-tumor effects on lung cancer in mice. Our work reveals new mechanisms of lung cancer formation by mutant KRAS, which will help the design of better approaches to treat one of the deadliest forms of cancer like lung cancer.

column37: The vision of the Artificial Intelligence for Public Health (AI4PH) Summer Institute is to enable participants to apply AI innovations in public health research with a health equity focus. Our goal is to develop, deliver, and disseminate a comprehensive set of resources for teaching how artificial intelligence (AI), including the subfield of machine learning (ML), can be applied to address important public health problems while explicitly prioritizing health equity. column36: High needs, high cost patients: A precision public health approach to improve lives and system sustainability
column37: Research has shown that 5% of health care users account for 65% of health care costs. These 'high-needs, high cost' patients are a diverse group with varying medical, social, and behavioural needs. Further, there is no single model of care that can provide all the services required by this patient population and the interventions that have been developed are often complex and require adaptation to the local setting. This has left decision makers struggling to implement effective strategies to improve care while curbing health care spending in this high-risk group. As costs continue to rise, there is a desperate need to move beyond simply describing high cost patients and start highlighting actionable policy options by breaking this problem down into more manageable pieces. To do this, we have partnered with Alberta Health Services - Strategic Clinical Networks to create a roadmap to help decision makers effectively identify the right intervention for the right population at the right time. Using a 3-pronged phased approach we will: (1) Use population-level linked data sources to develop a classification scheme to identify the common sub-types of high cost patients; (2) Complete an environmental scan and scoping review to identify promising care models for one prioritized high cost sub-group (determined by our knowledge users); (3) Provide key stakeholders with this evidence and discuss the full range of factors that influence the policy making process (e.g. financial constraints, values, beliefs, etc.) with the goal of identifying areas for action based on local context. This roadmap will provide decision makers with clearer pathways to program delivery based on available evidence and is a necessary step to improve care and address concerns of system sustainability posed by this high-risk group. It will also drive research forward in this priority area within Canada.

column37: Enlargement of the heart is one of the most common causes of heart failure in Canada. Once cardiac failure develops, the condition is irreversible and is associated with a very high death rate. Fifty percent of patients whose heart failure has progressed to include shortness of breath without physical activity do not survive beyond one year. As the heart becomes enlarged, it also disrupts the production of small lipid molecules that control the heart function, causing further damage and increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. The heart enlargement reduces the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules called epoxyeicosatrienoic acids and increases the production of cardiotoxic molecules called hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid. While most patients can be treated with drug therapy, these treatments have side effects and are not effective in all patients. The objectives of our work are to control and prevent enlargement of the heart to improve treatment options for patients and reduce mortality. By increasing the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules (epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) and inhibiting the production of cardiotoxic molecules (hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid) in the heart, we can prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. Our research will identify the molecules that are responsible for the enlargement of the heart and heart failure. In addition, we will test new chemicals that are known to increase the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules and inhibit the production of cardiotoxic molecules in the heart. This will prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. This research will help to diminish health care costs, as well as to design strategies that improve treatment of heart failure.

column37: Although several breast cancers are responsive to targeted therapies and/or chemotherapy, even today, a significant number of women will either never respond to these therapies or unfortunately experience relapse. A significant barrier to long term survival in these women stems from the fact that breast cancers are highly heterogeneous. Moreover, breast cancer cells are under constant environmental stress as a result of limiting nutrient and/or oxygen availability, leading to the development of adaptive responses that allows them to withstand these environmental insults. Unfortunately, many times these adaptations lead to permanent changes in breast cancer cells, even when the stress response is removed. In this grant, we will explore how these intra-tumoral genetic differences influence breast tumor evolution in response to microenvironmental stress stimuli, leading to the emergence of increasing aggressive breast cancers. column37: Patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. Like cancer cells, PAH cells are characterized by exaggerated capacity to multiplicate and resistance to death resulting in a progressive narrowing or obstruction of the vessels. Indeed, if the blood vessels tighten up, making the sapce for the passage of blood narrower, it takes greater pressure to get the same amount of blood through to its destination. The heart has to work harder to pump blood through those arteries. The heart progressively fails causing shortness of breath and poor exercise capacity, which rapidly culminate in death. In spite of recent progress in our understanding of the mechanisms involved in this disease, no substantial modification of the rapid progression and fatal course of this disease has been achieved, leaving lung transplantation as the only treatment in end-stage PAH. Therefore, the identification of new therapeutic targets is a pressing need. Although exposed to stressful conditions that jeopardize their survival, PAH cells continue to multiplicate indicating that these cells have developed adaptive protective response allowing them to survive. Nevertheless, the factors implicated in this pathological protective response remains largely unknown. In the present proposal, we hypothesize that a factor called MTH1 known to confer resistance to harmful stress conditions is overexpressed in PAH cells leading to the development of PAH. To test the validity of our hypothesis, we will 1) determine whether MTH1 is increased in PAH cells and contributes to PAH cells' anormalies; 2) decorticate the mechanisms by which MTH1 acts; and 3) assess whether inhibition of MTH1 improve PAH in animal models.

column36: Targeting mailed nicotine patch distribution interventions to rural regions of Canada: Randomized controlled trial
column37: Quitting smoking is the most effective way of reducing the risk of cancer. One way of helping people stop smoking is to provide them with free Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT; e.g., nicotine patch), such as when NRT is sent to people by postal mail as part of a mass distribution initiative. Our previous research indicated that the impact of the mailed NRT intervention on increasing quit rates in rural areas may be substantial. The current research project seeks to confirm this finding and to understand the social determinants of health driving these anticipated large effects. This information is essential in order to target limited health resources to regions that are most in need, and who are likely to experience the greatest benefit. Telephone numbers will be randomly selected from across rural regions of Canada in order to recruit adult smokers interested in completing a smoking survey and willing to be interviewed again in 6 months. The survey will ask participants about their smoking history, demographic characteristics, and a hypothetical question: would they be interested in receiving the nicotine patch if this were provided to them free of charge? Half of the smokers interested in receiving nicotine patches will be selected by chance and offered the NRT package. The other half of smokers will not be offered the nicotine patches until after the 6-month follow-up interview. In addition, the municipality where each participant lives will be identified and participant data will be linked to relevant municipal characteristics (e.g., smoking rates, availability of health services). Characteristics of the participants and the municipalities in which they live will be used to explain why the nicotine patch intervention has a larger impact in some rural regions compared to others. Finally, comparisons will be made with our existing urban study sample in order to shed further light on why the impact of the NRT intervention may be so large in rural settings.

column37: Pancreatic beta cells make and release insulin, the hormone controlling blood glucose in humans. When people develop diabetes, it may be because their beta cells are producing less or no insulin, or possibly the cells have died after trying to produce too much insulin for too long a period of time. A protein called PERK is essential for beta cells to produce sufficient amounts of active insulin and importantly, humans who carry a PERK protein that does not work develop diabetes early in life. We recently found that mice lacking a protein called Nck1 have powerful beta cells that make and release more insulin than those of normal mice, without any signs of cell fatigue. We discovered that Nck1 normally interacts with and decreases PERK activity, inhibiting PERK's beneficial effects on beta cells to produce insulin and survive stress. Our goal is to produce robust human beta cells by preventing the Nck1 and PERK interaction. For this, we will decrease levels of Nck1 in pancreatic beta cells to minimize its interaction with PERK. We will then test whether these strategies improve the production of active insulin and protect against diabetes-related stresses. Given that PERK is important for healthy beta cells, our discovery that the Nck1/PERK interaction controls insulin production AND beta cell survival in the face of stress is promising. We propose that weakening this interaction could serve many purposes toward treating diabetes, including improving the function and health of beta cells in the body and those destined for transplantation.

column36: The midline thalamus and anxiety
column37: A large number of Canadians suffer from anxiety disorders. Unfortunately, the treatments available to them are limited by their inconsistent effectiveness, side effects and abuse potential. Anxiety is a complicated emotional state that involves a rather poorly understood interconnected network of brain regions that serve to evaluate the potential risks and benefits available to people and animals. It is hypothesized that perturbations in this distributed network can lead to an overemphasis of risks resulting in anxiety. A logical approach for developing new treatments for anxiety disorders is to get a better understanding of how different regions of the brain function together to produce excessive anxiety. Towards this goal, our laboratory has identified the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) as a potentially key node in the neural network that mediates anxiety. In fact, the PVT is of special interest for understanding the neural mechanisms of anxiety because it is connected with many of the key regions of the brain identified as being part of the neural network that controls anxiety levels. In this application, we propose to apply innovative techniques that combine viral vectors and biological engineering tools to identify and precisely control the neural circuits by which the PVT modulates anxiety-like behaviors in a rodent model of stress-induced anxiety. This research will give us a better understanding of how the thalamus interacts with other brain regions to control anxiety in a way that could lead to new and more effective treatments for anxiety disorders.

column36: The role of interleukin-1 beta in preterm birth diagnosis and treatment
column37: Preterm birth (PTB) occurs in >10% of all births, and fetal inflammation (FI) in at least 40% of PTBs. Both are major causes of child death <5 years and of life-long morbidity. PTB and FI are unmet medical needs without effective diagnostics or therapeutics. Fortunately, Olson and Chemtob have each independently developed a diagnostic and therapeutic, respectively, that are complementary since the former is stimulated by the upstream mediator of PTB and FI, interleukin-1b, or IL1b, and the latter blocks IL1b action. Olson's diagnostic, the Leukocyte Migration Assay (LMA), uses white blood cells collected from pregnant women who are at risk of PTB or FI. By counting the number of cells that migrate to a stimulus extracted from the placental membranes, we can predict with precision women who will deliver within 7 days. Chemtob has designed a small peptide drug, rytvela, that blocks the action of IL1b and stops leukocyte migration in the LMA. We predict that IL1b stimulates PTB & FI in the pregnant mouse, that this is diagnosed by the LMA, and that rytvela is able to block PTB & FI and protect the fetus for normal birth, growth and development. We will perform three tests. In the first, we will stimulate PTB & FI in pregnant mice with powerful activators of silent or infectious inflammation. Then we will determine whether the LMA diagnoses PTB & FI and whether rytvela blocks these and restores maternal and fetal health. In the second, we will use a very low dose of IL1b to create a chronic fetal inflammation model without PTB. Again we will test whether the LMA detects this FI and whether rytvela improves fetal outcomes. In the last aim, we will study the chemotactic attraction molecules called chemokines stimulated by IL1b in human placental membranes to identify those key for attracting leukocytes at PTB. We will also identify how leukocytes are activated by IL1b and the key chemokines. This information will lead to human trials for a new diagnostic and therapeutic.

column36: Regulation of thymic selection thresholds and their role in establishing T cell function
column37: T cells are a type of white blood cell that collaborates with other cells of the immune system to identify and remove infectious agents and also abnormal cells. It has long been thought that T cells not yet exposed to infectious agents, thus named 'naive' T cells, are a homogeneous population all with the same potential to contribute different specialized skills to an immune response. However, it is becoming increasingly clear that naive T cells vary in pre-existing biases for certain skills prior to their deployment during an immune response. Indeed, subtle differences in the amount of a particular molecule, named CD5, found on the surface of T cells appears to mark cells with distinct functions before they respond. We do not yet understand how this functional skewing is established and maintained while they remain in reserve. T cells are trained in an organ called the thymus, where they learn to distinguish healthy cells from those expressing foreign or mutated proteins. The strength of interactions T cells make with other cells during this training period generates a naive T cell population with different levels of CD5. We propose that this thymic training period imprints individual T cells with latent skills only revealed once they participate in fighting an infection. Here we will study this imprinting process, and also investigate how the training program differs in newborns and adults, causing important changes in T cell responses to infection with age.

column37: In the past 20 years there has been a rapid growth in the number of persons living with cognitive impairment or dementia in the community. Similarly, retirement homes have grown in prominence as a way of providing care for those who can no longer live independently. Both of these groups are prone to nutrition problems; poor food intake and weight loss are associated with several adverse outcomes such as falls and hospitalizations, as well as the progression of dementia. Determining which older adults are at nutrition risk will allow the health care system to target interventions and start early treatment that can improve their overall health and independence. Yet, nutrition screening tools specific to these groups are unavailable. SCREEN is a questionnaire that was created in Canada and is used worldwide to measure nutrition risk. However, SCREEN was not tested in those with cognitive impairment or living in retirement residences. The proposed study will determine if SCREEN is valid for use with these two groups of community-living seniors. Persons living with cognitive impairment (and their family member) and persons living in retirement homes will be recruited. Participants (~ 600) will complete SCREEN and other health measures and a dietitian will determine the nutrition risk of the participant based on an assessment. SCREEN results will be compared to this assessment to determine if it adequately represents nutrition risk. Availability of a feasible nutrition risk tool that can be used with all community-living seniors, including those with dementia and/or living in retirement homes will promote screening in family doctors' offices, retirement homes and other clinics, which is currently absent. Early identification of nutrition problems will promote the development and use of preventative services to improve senior health, potentially delaying or avoiding frailty and increased use of healthcare services by these vulnerable older adults.

column36: Characterizing the human mitochondrial processing peptidase in neurodegenerative disease
column37: Neurodegenerative disorders have become one of the most critical health issues, as the world's aging population increases and treatments remain scarce. For most of these disorders, current treatments serve solely as "symptomatic band-aids" given too late in the disease progression. As such, there exists a desperate need to study these disorders from unique avenues to reveal novel points of regulation and other potential drug targets. In our bodies, mitochondria have been typically labelled as the "energy generators" of our cells, however, their importance in the brain and their implications in neurodegenerative disorders have become increasingly apparent over the last 10 years. Today, biologists acknowledge the existence of an intimate link between mitochondrial dysfunction and neurodegeneration. This project will investigate this link through the lens of one specific, overlooked molecular player: the mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP). Recently, mutations in both MPP and its interactors have been implicated in Parkinson's disease and certain ataxias, yet their underlying mechanisms and neuronal consequences remain uncharacterized. Our work will serve to answer a few key questions: how does MPP contribute to these disorders? Can we study these interactions to design neuroprotective drugs? Our work will lay the foundation for a drug design platform targeting MPP whose effect will be two-fold: first, it will allow us to design research tools for studying basic mitochondrial mechanisms, and second, it will propel the development of therapeutics against MPP-linked neurodegenerative disorders. Our results will also provide new biochemical models to reveal how key mitochondrial functions exert such a unique effect in our brains. Globally, this project will foster collaboration with scientists across the world, and will be directly impactful to researchers, clinicians, and those suffering from neurodegenerative disease alike.

column37: Children with medical complexity refer to those who experience a variety of complex chronic health conditions which impact their daily life. While we expect this population of children to be small in numbers, they require a large amount of health care resources to manage their medical conditions. Many of these children are discharged from hospital to be cared for in their home communities by their families and a range of interdisciplinary care providers. This transfer of responsibility highlights the need to adequately support the complex medical, social, and financial needs of these families. Unfortunately, there is a disconnect between our current health care system and the needs of these children and their families. Thus, this proposed research will focus on examining and describing the population of children with medical complexity who live in the Canadian Maritimes to develop practice and policy recommendations. column36: Longitudinal implications of adverse childhood experiences on cardiovascular health and function, inflammation, and cardiovascular reactivity to postural stress
column37: Childhood cardiovascular (CV) health is a key factor that influences risk of adult CV disease. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), a term encompassing abuse, severe household dysfunction, and other toxic childhood events, are shown to contribute towards increased health risks such as adult CV disease. Once perceived as rare occurrences and their overall effect minimal, recent studies have reported Canadian prevalence estimates of childhood abuse at 32%. As CV disease is a leading cause of death in Canada, the potential implications of ACEs are more significant than initially believed, yet how ACEs amplify the risk for CV disease later in life remains unclear. Researchers hypothesize ACEs "get under the skin" and alter neuro-immune pathways which further stress the CV system and contribute towards adverse responses to stress. In fact, there is evidence of altered acute stress responses in individuals with ACEs for both psychosocial and mild postural stress although the latter is unexplored in young adults. The link between postural stress and ACEs is also evident in late life and older adults with greater early life stress reported fainting more often, suggesting a link between CV regulatory processes and ACEs. I propose to conduct a longitudinal study investigating the effects of ACEs on changes in CV health in a sample of ~550 young adults whom completed CV testing in our lab 10 years prior as children. Additionally, I will implement a postural challenge designed to detect altered CV response in these young adults. I anticipate ACEs will be associated with increased inflammation, arterial stiffening, and decreases in cardiac function over time. Moreover, that individuals with ACEs will demonstrate a blunted CV response to postural stress. Results of my studies will help explain why ACEs amplify CV disease risk and the pathways involved.

column36: Etude de la contribution de la kinase WNK1 a la guerison des plaies corneennes in vitro et in vivo
column37: La cornee est une structure transparente qui forme la couche externe de l'oeil. Sa localisation anatomique superficielle la rend particulierement vulnerable aux forces abrasives et aux traumatismes. Ces dommages peuvent mener a des deficiences visuelles importantes, telles que la perte de la vision. A la suite d'une lesion, differents mecanismes sont enclenches afin de permettre aux cellules de restaurer la surface corneenne lesee et de reorganiser les cellules des couches sous-jacentes. Une meilleure comprehension de ces mecanismes pourrait permettre d'ameliorer les traitements existants, qui, pour la plupart, ne permettent pas une guerison rapide et adequate de la cornee et ne previennent pas contre les recidives. Au laboratoire, nous utilisons un modele de cornees humaines reconstruites par genie tissulaire (hCRs) afin d'etudier les mecanismes impliques dans la guerison des plaies corneennes. Des travaux anterieurs realises en utilisant ce modele ont demontre que l'expression de certains genes et l'activite de certaines proteines etaient differentiellement regulees durant la guerison des plaies corneennes. C'est le cas de WNK1, qui est en fait la proteine la plus fortement activee durant la guerison des plaies corneennes. En raison de son statut d'activation particulierement eleve, nous soulevons l'hypothese que WNK1 joue un role important durant le processus de guerison des plaies corneennes. Nos objectifs de recherche sont donc d'etudier la contribution de WNK1 a la guerison des plaies corneennes en utilisant des modeles in vitro (hCRs et modele en culture monocouche) et in vivo chez le lapin. Les resultats de ce projet permettront d'ameliorer nos connaissances sur les mecanismes cellulaires et moleculaires impliques dans la guerison des plaies corneennes et pourraient aussi mener a des progres cliniques dans le domaine des lesions corneennes grace a l'identification de nouvelles cibles therapeutiques.

column37: L'enzyme "mitogen-activated protein kinase " (MAPK) p38 est connue depuis plus de 15 ans comme etant necessaire au maintien des fonctions normales du coeur tout en contribuant paradoxalement au developpement de pathologies cardiaques. En debut d'etudes graduees, j'ai identifie par une approche novatrice la "serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3 " (SRSF3) parmi les proteines interagissant avec la MAPK p38 active. Notre decouverte inattendue demontre que p38 module, chez les cardiomyocytes (cellules contractiles du coeur) en culture, l'epissage alternatif exerce par SRSF3 sur des ARNm reconnus pour etre modifies en insuffisance cardiaque. Est-ce que l'interaction fonctionnelle entre ces deux proteines est benefique ou nefaste dans le processus de developpement des cardiomyopathies cardiaques? Afin de repondre a cette question importante, nous voulons elucider le role de la proteine SRSF3 et les mecanismes regulant son action dans le coeur. Pour ce faire, je retirerai specifiquement le gene encodant la proteine SRSF3 chez les cardiomyocytes de souris par une approche dites d'invalidation conditionnelle. Dans un contexte de stress pathologique cause par la TAC, un modele mimant l'insuffisance cardiaque, nous evaluerons differents parametres cardiaques et analyserons l'etat des ARNm au niveau de leur expression et de leurs evenements d'epissage alternatif par sequencage a haut-debit. L'interaction p38-SRSF3 sera aussi exploree plus en details par une technique d'immunofluorescence sur des coupes de tissus fixes (isPLA) provenant de coeurs ex vivo stresses par une ischemie reconnue pour activer p38. Sur ces memes echantillons, nous identifierons les sites de SRSF3 phosphoryles par la kinase p38 en utilisant la spectrometrie de masse apres avoir isole SRSF3. Reveler ce nouveau mecanisme de regulation est essentiel pour mieux saisir la fonction complexe de p38 lors de l'insuffisance cardiaque.

column37: During the past few decades, the rate of obesity has tripled worldwide. column37: Antibiotics and other antimicrobial agents are central for the treatment of microbial infections. However, the indiscriminate use of these agents has led to the development of high rates of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in various microorganisms, rendering many drugs useless. Today, AMR is emerging as a global public health threat, killing an estimated 700,000 people annually. Recently, 'metagenomics', or techniques that can profile microbes as a community, rather than as a single species, are emerging as a powerful tool for AMR surveillance and public health risk assessment that dramatically increases the speed of diagnosis and epidemiological investigations. Although advances have been made in AMR research, current methods are still limited and cannot be used by public health due to the lack of understanding of AMR genes that have the ability to spread between pathogens and harmless bacteria. Furthermore, better tools are needed for rapid AMR predictions from metagenomics data. To address this, I will conduct a comprehensive analysis of AMR gene mobility in the context of different antimicrobial properties, e.g. drug classes. I will also contribute to the development of an AMR metagenomics predictor, as part of a nationwide effort, and apply it to study temporal and spatial AMR gene prevalence in freshwater microbiomes impacted by agriculture/urbanization. Taken together, my research aims to significantly strengthen the effectiveness of public health AMR risk assessment, improving the ability of the public health system to monitor and respond to AMR and infectious disease outbreak threats.

column36: Identifying and characterizing pathogen-associated, conserved hypothetical proteins with potential novel roles in virulence, from over 8000 bacterial genomes
column37: The vast expansion of DNA data now enables large-scale comparisons of thousands of bacterial genomes to elucidate the distinction in gene/protein composition between pathogens (disease-causing microbes) and non-pathogens. Proteins found exclusively in pathogens are thought to more likely to play a role in disease processes. To date, 19556 pathogen-associated proteins have been identified in over 8000 bacterial genomes. Of these, less than 14% have defined functions in literature. The remaining majority are hypothetical proteins, with no validated existence or function, of which some are present in multiple bacterial genera/families. The subset of uncharacterized proteins found only in disease-causing bacteria in multiple families, but not in bacteria thought not to cause disease in these same families, are of particular interest and provide an underexplored avenue to study the mechanism of infections of important pathogens, leading to potential new anti-virulence therapies. I will develop a more sophisticated computational approach to identify and then functionally characterize hypothetical proteins found exclusively in pathogens that are not found in closely related non-pathogens. I will characterize them in datasets of microbes associated with disease outbreaks data and evaluate their mutation rates to identify those that are being selected for. Finally, I will validate the functional predictions of the proteins through laboratory testing in an infection model. The outcome of my work will provide insight into the functional importance of previously undefined proteins, potentially identifying their potential roles in the mechanisms of infection. The research output will potentially generate novel anti-infective drug target candidates and protein markers for tracking infectious disease transmission, offering novel insights into disease pathogenesis.

column36: Evaluation of Dynamic Axis Optimization for Ablative Radiotherapy
column37: Radiation dose reduction to healthy tissue is a primary objective when treating cancerous disease. Conventional radiotherapy is delivered using a medical linear accelerator (LINAC) that rotates 360 degrees around a patient laying stationary on a treatment couch. The couch can translate and rotate for initial alignment, however literature has shown that rotating it dynamically during treatment offered geometries where greater sparing of healthy brain tissue was possible. The goal of this research is to build on the dynamic algorithm that currently exists for brain treatments, to make it applicable to any site in the body. The main limitation when treating other anatomies with this technique is due to changing "collision zones". A collision zone is defined as a location in the treatment room where the LINAC gantry and couch would physically collide, halting treatment. Treatments to patient extremities (head, feet, or hands) have less collision zones, compared to centralized anatomies. To decrease the collision zones in a centralized treatment (e.g. - breast), the couch could also be dynamically translated laterally and vertically. If this movement is accounted for in the current algorithm, better sparing of healthy tissues (e.g. - heart, for breast treatments) could be realized. These new patient specific collision zones will be tested using human-like phantoms. Phantoms will have radiation sensitive detectors embedded within so new treatments can be delivered in a research setting to compare with the current standard. Successful implementation of this research will allow for widespread adoption of dynamic techniques, by addressing critical needs in the field to reduce dose to healthy tissues and improve long-term patient quality of life. Furthermore, this technique aims to promote dose reductions without requiring completely new radiotherapy infrastructures, and could serve as a foundation for fully automated treatment planning.

column36: Are cognitive deficits in Parkinson's disease associated with dopaminergic dysfunction
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is typically known for its motor symptoms, however progressive cognitive decline is a common complication of the disease, with over 60% of PD patients impaired in one or more cognitive domains. Cognitive decline contributes to significant impairments, resulting in a poorer quality of life and higher levels of care dependency. Despite its significance, the neural basis cognitive decline in PD is poorly understood. PD motor progression has been well characterized by the loss of the neurotransmitter dopamine in the brain due to the death of dopamine-producing cells in the brain. New research suggests the loss of dopamine may also play a role in the cognitive decline of PD as well. A better understanding of the neural mechanisms involved in PD cognitive decline is an important prerequisite for improved therapeutic strategies. The proposed study will look at how dopamine regulation is affected in PD patients both with and without cognitive decline. Using a neuroimaging technique called positron emission tomography (PET), we will visualize the dopamine receptors in the brains of PD patients in vivo using a radiotracer that binds preferentially to one common type of dopamine receptor called the D2 receptor. Whole-brain network dysfunction of this dopamine receptor may have a role in cognitive decline and we will use graph theory analysis to investigate in vivo D2 communication patterns in the brains of PD patients. Uncovering the pathological mechanisms involved in PD cognitive decline can have many benefits, such as 1) finding an early indicator of cognitive decline 2) discovering new treatment options for present PD patients and 3) possible new development of future preventative measures to slow the progression into PD dementia. Additionally, validation of this approach will allow for the use of network analysis tools for a wider range of neurotransmitters to measure dysfunctional brain activation patterns in other neurotransmitter systems.

When a parent has physical and cognitive disabilities following traumatic injuries, congenital or degenerative disorders, the challenges associated with parenting are even more important. Despite the increasing number of parents with disabilities, the needs regarding infant parenting have to date received scarce attention in research. A comprehensive understanding of those families' needs is crucial to offer prompt and personalized support aiming to foster their social participation along with their baby's safety and optimal development. In collaboration with a pioneer Canadian clinic offering parenting rehabilitation services, this novel clinical-research project aims to explore the unmet needs of these individuals. To do so, the state of knowledge regarding infant parenting with disabilities will be examined using a scoping review, along with a grey literature review to examine the current resources and rehabilitation services available for this clientele. At the core of this project, interviews with parents with physical and cognitive disabilities and in-home assessments of their everyday parenting tasks will be conducted to fully grasp their needs. Additional interviews with significant family members and expert health care professionals will complete the identification of priority needs for safe parenting. Finally, focus groups will be held with parents with disabilities, clinicians, national and international researchers, community organizations and policy makers to collectively problem solve how to best respond to the reported family needs. Such work will provide needed knowledge to better understand the needs for autonomous, meaningful and safe parenting.

column36: Neural and Psychological Markers of Dysregulated Emotion and Treatment Response in Children with Disruptive Behaviours
column37: Childhood Disruptive Behaviour Disorders (DBD) have onset early in development and are a robust predictor of chronic and severe mental illness in adolescence and adulthood. Although high prevalence, referral-rates, and negative outcomes signal great need, current treatment approaches are inadequate, with recent data estimating that approximately 25 - 40% of children continue to experience clinically significant symptoms and behavioral and emotional dysregulation following treatment completion. Emerging research suggests that heterogeneity (i.e., diversity) in the factors that contribute to a child's DBD, including their neurobiology and clinical dimensions such as emotion dysregulation, are important factors that may influence treatment effectiveness. Novel approaches that distill heterogeneity are necessary to improve treatment precision and outcomes. My proposed doctoral dissertation consists of three studies with the overall objective of identifying biomarkers of emotion dysregulation in children with DBD to inform novel targets for intervention. These studies include, 1) a systematic review to identify and classify neural correlates of emotion dysregulation in children with DBD. 2) Analysing existing data from an ongoing neuroimaging study to identify biomarkers (i.e., brain structure) of emotion dysregulation in children with DBD. 3) A randomized and controlled micro-trial (RCT) to test whether treatment non-responders benefit from a brief intervention that targets their emotion regulation and distress tolerance skills. These studies will pave the way for novel assessment practices and treatment innovation by bridging and integrating biological, psychological, and clinical perspectives.

column36: Caracterisation des variables nutritionnelles et hormonales durant la grossesse: associations avec le profil metabolique.
column37: Problematique : La grossesse est caracterisee par des variations hormonales qui entrainent, des le 1er trimestre, de nombreux changements chez la mere. La litterature demeure cependant pauvre et incoherente quant aux variations dans les facteurs alimentaires et hormonaux tout au long de la grossesse et quant a leur impact sur la sante de la mere et celle de son enfant. Objectifs : Caracteriser et etudier les liens, a chaque trimestre, entre les variables alimentaires, hormonales et metaboliques durant la grossesse. Methodologie : A chaque trimestre, les apports alimentaires de 106 femmes enceintes seront evalues via 3 rappels de 24h Web. L'epaisseur des tissus adipeux sera mesuree par echographie au 1er trimestre, tandis que les hormones de regulation de la prise alimentaire seront mesures, a chaque trimestre, a la suite d'un repas-test effectue chez 20 des 106 participantes. Des marqueurs metaboliques tels que le gain de poids, la glycemie a jeun, le marqueur inflammatoire interleukine-6 et le statut en vitamine D seront aussi mesures et mis en association avec les variables alimentaires et hormonales. Impact potentiel : Les femmes enceintes representent une sous population vulnerable pour qui l'alimentation a un impact considerable. De plus, un nombre grandissant de femmes debutent aujourd'hui leur grossesse avec un surpoids, suggerant des habitudes alimentaires inadequates et augmentant leur risque de complications perinatales, tel que la preeclampsie et le diabete gestationnel. L'analyse des spheres nutritionnelle, hormonale et metabolique entrainera une meilleure comprehension des determinants de la sante durant la periode perinatale, ce qui contribuera a l'amelioration de la prise en charge des femmes a risque de complications. L'avancement des connaissances dans ce domaine precis servira egalement de base pour des etudes d'intervention visant a optimiser la sante des femmes enceintes et des generations futures.

column36: Self-Compassion among people undergoing cardiac surgery: associations with physical activity, other health behaviors and health outcomes.
column37: Heart surgeries are being performed on people who are not engaging in enough health behaviours (HBs; physical activity); low engagement increases the risk of poor health outcomes after surgery. People with cardiovascular disease (CVD) may not engage in enough HBs because they face barriers (e.g., fear of exercise). Self-regulation, a form of behavioral control, is important for behavior change because it helps find solutions to barriers. Self-regulation of HBs is hard for people who have had heart surgery because they must self-regulate while dealing with the barriers of living with CVD. These negative emotional experiences can negatively affect an individuals' ability to self-regulate HBs. Self-compassion (SC), extending support to oneself in difficult times, may help people self-regulate their HBs after heart surgery. No research has examined SC in the context of CVD. I will determine whether SC relates to HB engagement and health outcomes after surgery, negatively relates to negative emotions, and if people are open to SC while recovering from heart surgery. This information may help researchers develop interventions to reduce the number of complications that occur after surgery. I plan to take a two-study approach; the first study will follow participants before heart surgery to a year after surgery and the second study will involve interviewing a sub-sample of participants through the recovery period. Participants will be asked to provide information on HB participation, health outcomes, negative emotions, and their ability to manage their health goals. Twenty participants will be asked to participate in the interview process to explore their openness to SC. This will be the first study to look at SC in the context of CVD. This research will examine ways that SC may help people participate in HBs (decrease negative emotions, improve self-regulatory ability). It will also acknowledge whether people are open to SC when having and recovering from heart surgery.

column36: The Clinical Utility of Genomic Sequencing in Hereditary Cancer Syndrome Care: A Prospective, Mixed-Methods Cohort Study
column37: Genetic tests are used to identify patients who have inherited diseases. For patients who are diagnosed with cancer, genetic testing can be used to see if they have an inherited genetic mutation that caused their cancer. Patients with inherited cancer mutations have a hereditary cancer syndrome and have a high risk to develop more cancers over their lifetime. Once they are found to have a hereditary cancer syndrome from genetic testing, doctors will place patients in advanced cancer screening programs and refer to them to specialists to help reduce their risk to develop cancer or detect it earlier. Although genetic testing for cancer patients has advanced in recent years, it is still only able to look at a few genes at a time. Because of this, most patients who have testing to determine if they have a hereditary cancer syndrome receive a negative result, meaning that no genetic mutation was found. These patients are not eligible for advanced screening programs and do not benefit from genetic testing. However, a new genetic test called genomic sequencing may help to change this. Unlike other genetic tests, genomic sequencing can analyze all of the genes in the human body . Therefore, it is more likely than current genetic tests to find a mutation in patients who have a hereditary cancer syndrome. This means that more patients will become eligible for cancer screening and other procedures to reduce their risk. However, genomic sequencing is a new test, and so information on its benefits for patients is limited. This study will aim to evaluate the benefits of genomic sequencing for cancer patients by determining the number of patients who are found to have a cancer mutation and the number of patients who have changes in their cancer screening and management. Our study will give important information to doctors who may wish to use this test if it is shown to improve patient care.

column36: Interpretable Deep Learning to Unlock the Potential of Clinical RNA Sequencing for Precision Oncology Research
column37: When a patient fails standard cancer therapy, the oncologist is faced with the conundrum of selecting one of dozens of treatments. Present clinical trials are investigating whether DNA sequencing of tumors can inform the choice of treatment, but for 50+% of patients, none of the mutations found provide information predictive of treatment response. What could supply greater predictive value is gene expression profiling, which gives insights into which processes are active inside a given cell type. For cancer cells grown in a petri dish, the additional information of gene expression has been shown to be more informative than only DNA sequencing for predicting drug response. We want to translate these positive results into the clinic, to help patients for which DNA sequencing cannot inform the optimal treatment. In this project, we will use advances in Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence to build a computer system helping oncologists interpret this gene expression data. Using 50,000 human expression profiles, we will teach the system to map gene expression onto measures of biological pathways and processes activity. we will then focus on 13 drugs tested in a pan-Canadian clinical trial, building human-interpretable models to predict response to these drugs from my pathway measures. Looking retrospectively at patient data, we will validate the prediction accuracy of our models. Finally, for validated models, we will automate the system to make predictions for future patients. Outcomes of this study include: 1) buildings models that select patients who will respond to these 13 drugs, 2) strengthening the rationale for transcriptomic profiling to help guide cancer treatment, and 3) proof-of-concept for intelligent computer systems that can guide cancer care.

column36: A Preoperative Virtual Reality Simulation of Surgery to Reduce Perioperative Psychiatric Sequelae
column37: Mental health difficulties such as anxiety and distress are commonly experienced before and after surgery. For some, surgery may be traumatic and can cause symptoms of posttraumatic stress. Given that elective surgeries are scheduled in advanced, this provides a unique opportunity for preventative interventions to target poor mental health outcomes. The primary objective of this research is to scientifically evaluate the effectiveness of a virtual reality (VR) simulation prior to surgery on mental health outcomes. This simulation is informed by the military literature on pre-deployment interventions, and will mirror the pre-surgical experience for patients, from arrival at the hospital up until anesthetic induction in the operating room. A series of two study methodologies will evaluate the primary objective of this research: (1) a randomized controlled trial will assess whether a novel VR pre-surgical simulation of surgery, compared to treatment as usual, can help reduce mental health difficulties throughout the surgical period and (2) qualitative interviews will examine a subset of participants' perceptions of this intervention and the impact it had on their experience throughout the surgical period. I hypothesize that individuals who participate in the VR simulation of surgery will experience fewer mental health difficulties before and after surgery compared to individuals who do not participate in the intervention. This research will help health providers understand whether and how a pre-surgical VR simulation of surgery is effective in reducing mental health difficulties throughout the surgical period. If results support the effectiveness of this intervention, this research will inform future larger replication studies and studies evaluating whether this intervention can also improve physical health outcomes throughout the surgical period. Ultimately, results of this research may inform changes to standard of care throughout the surgical period.

column36: Vulnerability of GLUT4 Translocation During Insulin Resistance: A Focus on Rab GTPases
column37: Glucose (sugar) is the main source of fuel for most tissues in the body. After a meal, dietary glucose enters the blood stream and causes glucose levels to rise. The pancreas senses this increase in blood glucose and dispatches insulin into the circulation to instruct the skeletal muscle to extract glucose from the blood. In healthy muscle cells, insulin binds to the insulin receptor and tells the muscle to put more glucose transporters (GLUT4) on the surface of each cell. This increase in glucose transporters allows more glucose to enter the muscle, where it is stored and eventually used for energy. This process of increasing surface GLUT4 transporters is called GLUT4 translocation and involves a complex network of signalling events. During Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), the skeletal muscle does not respond to insulin (called insulin resistance) and fails to increase surface GLUT4 levels, causing chronic hyperglycemia (high blood sugar). Yet, our knowledge of how and why GLUT4 translocation fails during insulin resistance is unknown. The major goal of this research is to identify and study, at the molecular level, which elements of GLUT4 translocation dysfunction during insulin resistance and thereby contribute to impaired skeletal muscle glucose disposal. Identifying these mechanisms could generate unique avenues for therapeutic intervention targeting the muscle in T2D.

column37: Le cancer de la prostate touche environ 21 300 hommes au Canada par annee, il est le troisieme plus mortel des cancers. Les methodes de detection actuelles sont le toucher rectal et/ou une prise de sang pour doser une molecule, soit l'antigene prostatique specifique (APS). Ces tests ont le desavantage de souvent indiquer des resultats << faux positif >>, cela signifie que le test de depistage est positif, donc la presence du cancer, mais le test de confirmation, plus specifique mais aussi plus invasif et incommodant par des prelevements de tissus au niveau de la prostate indique qu'il n'y a aucun cancer. Une autre problematique concerne l'identification des tumeurs benignes et les malignes, cela entraine une difficulte a evaluer si une intervention medicale est reellement necessaire pour le bien du patient. Un des projets de recherche mene dans le laboratoire du Pr Robert Day est la mise au point d'un test de depistage du cancer de la prostate par la decouverte de nouvelles molecules, soit des biomarqueurs specifiques a la proteine PACE4 qui est surexprimee chez les patients atteints du cancer de la prostate. Dans les etudes anterieures, PACE4 s'est averee etre une cible therapeutique interessante pour freiner la multiplication des cellules cancereuses, et ce particulierement au niveau de la prostate. En utilisant des molecules dont la presence serait modifiee selon la quantite de PACE4 presente chez les patients, il serait envisageable de suivre le traitement developpe au laboratoire qui permet d'inactiver la PACE4. La decouverte de ces biomarqueurs permettrait de reduire le nombre de biopsies, mais aussi de differencier les tumeurs benignes des tumeurs malignes. Ce serait une precieuse aide pour predire quels patients sont predisposes a recidiver. Cela permettrait de suivre avec une plus grande vigilance l'evolution du cancer en fonction du traitement de ces patients, d'appliquer une medecine personnalisee et d'eviter des interventions inutiles.

column36: Discovering novel antimicrobials against intracellular pathogens
column37: There is an urgent need to identify new treatments for multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. The continuous evolution of resistance has rendered many of our frequently prescribed and last-resort antibiotics ineffective, yet very little progress has been made to identify suitable alternatives. Overcoming this global health crisis will require remarkable innovation in antibiotic discovery, to search for drugs that kill bacteria in unique ways. To meet this demand, I propose to screen for small molecules that selectively target and inhibit intracellular bacteria such as Salmonella Typhimurium. Traditional antibiotic discovery efforts have not focused on intracellular pathogens, which reside within host cells during infection and are therefore difficult to eradicate. Our lab has previously established a platform in which to measure antimicrobial activity in the intracellular environment. We now aim to apply this technique to identify new leads for antibiotics that target a highly invasive, multidrug-resistant strain of Salmonella (ST313). ST313 is a distinct, human-adapted lineage of Salmonella, and is capable of causing life-threatening systemic disease. In my proposed research project, I aim to (1) characterize the genetic requirements for intracellular growth of ST313 using RNA-sequencing, (2) identify novel compounds with antibacterial activity against ST313 grown in human macrophages, and (3) determine the mechanism of action of any lead antimicrobial compounds and test for their activity in an animal model of Salmonella infection. This proposed research will help us to unravel the genetic basis of bacterial survival within host cells, while also identifying new treatment alternatives for complicated and recurrent intracellular infections.

column36: Exploring Pathways to Sexual and Reproductive Health in a Cohort Study with Northern and Indigenous Youth in the Northwest Territories, Canada
column37: THE ISSUE: Indigenous and Northern youth experience sexual and mental health disparities in the Northwest Territories (NWT). Contexts of historical and ongoing racism, disconnection from culture and land, and intergenerational trauma contribute to these health disparities. Our past CIHR-funded research demonstrated the potential of Fostering Open eXpression among Youth (FOXY) and Strengths, Masculinities & Sexual Health (SMASH). FOXY and SMASH are arts-based, culturally grounded, strengths-focused and Indigenous-led sexual health programs to improve sexual health among Northern and Indigenous youth. We also found age, gender and sexual orientation differences in FOXY and SMASH outcomes, pointing to the need for mixed-methods research to further explore and address health needs and priorities of diverse youth in the NWT. OUR IDEA: We will first conduct qualitative research to understand how and why FOXY and SMASH work for improving sexual and reproductive health (SRH), for whom, and in what circumstance. We will then adapt FOXY and SMASH, and conduct a longitudinal cohort study with Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT to explore trajectories of health and resilience. (1) We will work with a youth advisory board, youth, parents and Elders using human centred design approaches and community engagement to identify how to better meet the needs of youth. (2) We will conduct FOXY and SMASH school-based workshops, with a pre-and post test, 6-month, 12 month and 18-month follow-up surveys. We will explore social ecological factors associated with SRH and resilience trajectories. (3) Interconnected knowledge mobilization. IMPACT: We will gather and integrate multiple knowledge sources to refine sexual health programs to better meet the needs of Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT, and evaluate the long term effects of participating in arts-based sexual health programs. We fill knowledge gaps of resilience and wellbeing among Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT.

column36: 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 as a modulator of human adipose tissue function and distribution
column37: Excess accumulation of fat inside the abdomen, termed visceral obesity, is generally predominant in men but it is also found in women. The presence of those large visceral fat stores has been closely linked to metabolic abnormalities which lead to diabetes and heart disease. Would it be possible to reduce fat storage in adipose tissue located inside the abdominal cavity and favor accumulation of fat tissues located under the skin, or subcutaneous fat? If so, this could delay the onset of diseases in individuals with abdominal obesity. Our main postulate is that this can be done by changing the amount of hormone dihydrotestosterone specifically in visceral fat. We have evidence that adipose tissues can generate a portion of their own dihydrotestosterone from other hormones such as adrenal androgen precursors or testosterone and also inactivate this hormone. We wish to prove that blocking the enzyme responsible for dihydrotestosterone inactivation will change the availability of the hormone in each fat compartment and will direct excess dietary lipids away from the visceral fat stores. To reach this goal, we will use cultures of adipose cells or explants obtained from various fat compartments in men and women. We will prove that the enzyme involved in dihydrotestosterone inactivation plays a significant role in the modulation of fat distribution patterns in humans by studying its impact on adipose tissue, its hormonal regulation and its genetic variation. We postulate that studying androgen inactivation in fat will contribute to identify new targets for the remodeling of adipose tissue distribution in humans.

column37: Arthritic degeneration of the spine is a natural part of human aging, affecting 51% of adults, and is the most common cause of reversible spinal cord injury in people over 55 years. The results from surgical treatment can vary and we believe could be substantially improved through rehabilitation therapy during recovery. Our overall goal is to improve the outcomes and quality of life for people that undergo surgery for degenerative spinal cord compression in the neck. We have previously used advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measurements in the brain to show how the brain adapts and changes after neck surgery. In this project, we will combine a rigorous platform of clinical care spanning preoperative evaluation, surgery, and rehabilitation with state-of-the art imaging techniques to demonstrate how rehabilitative therapy can accelerate and predict recovery of neurological function and improve quality of life in patients by triggering brain recruitment and plasticity. Using hand function as a proxy of neurological recovery, we will evaluate how the brain and spinal cord respond in two groups of patients; those receiving rehabilitation and those receiving the standard of care after spine surgery, and correlate functional outcome with changes measured by advanced imaging. Upon completion of this project we will have established a disease specific rehabilitation program that could redefine the current standard of care.

column37: Globally, nurses are the largest regulated healthcare profession providing all levels of care to patients within health systems. The deployment of various nursing roles (registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, etc) within healthcare settings is determined by using one of many nurse staffing models. These nurse staffing models range from all registered nurses (who hold a baccalaureate degree) to a mix of differentially educated nurses and aides. Cost of providing care and availability of specific nursing roles often drive decision-making about which model to use. Many systematic reviews have been used to examine the relationships between specific nursing skill mix models and a variety of specific or general health outcomes for patients (e.g. mortality, adverse events, health education, length of stay, health care costs etc.), with inconclusive or contradictory results. Given economic, quality, and contextual factors that confound the impact of individual staffing models, the approach to determining which nursing skill mix model to use is considerably more complex than a simple formula or ratio of nurses to patients needing care. By conducting a realist review and evaluation, we will determine in what contexts and through which mechanisms, certain nurse staffing models produce better health system, staff and patient outcomes. These results will allow us to produce Recommendations for Policy and Practice: Nurse Staffing Principles and Guidelines with our health system decision-makers and collaborators from four countries that will guide decision-making on the deployment of nursing roles across a variety of healthcare contexts to achieve better healthcare outcomes.

column36: Genetics and epigenetics of sex differences in placental and fetal development
column37: Many differences between males and females arise between conception and birth. As the main regulator of fetal growth and development is the placenta, many of these differences arise because male and female placentas are not equivalent. Male and female placentas differ in their sex chromosome complement, XX vs XY; This leads to sex-chromosome gene expression differences that cause downstream effects on the remainder of the genome. The degree to which male and female placentas differ from each other can also be affected by exposures to fetal and maternal androgens and by genetic variation affecting the expression of key hormones. As such, the effect of sex on the non-sex chromosomes is not discrete, but exists on more of a continuum. Data from DNA methylation, a chemical modification to DNA that is associated with gene expression, has already been collected on over 1000 placentas. Our goal is to identify sex-influenced DNA methylation within the placenta, identify the factors that affect this measurement, and determine if the sex-related differentiation of the placenta is associated with perinatal outcomes such and fetal birth weight and gestational age at birth. This work is important to understand the early events that set males and females on different health trajectories at birth.

column36: Hybrids and commonalities of thiotemplate enzymes
column37: Many of the drugs and medicines that we rely on today are natural products, made by the earth's flora. Important classes of these compounds are made in fungi and bacteria by massive enzymes called nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) and polyketide synthases (PKSs), or by fusions of these enzymes (PKS-NRPSs). They synthesize all sorts of antibiotics, which can kill dangerous fungi and bacteria, as well as compounds to help us fight off viral infections and cancers. For example, these compounds include viomycin, an antibiotic used for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; cyclosporin, which has been widely used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants and can inhibit hepatitis virus C replication; and the familiar antibiotic penicillin. The goal of this research is to expand our knowledge of NRPSs, PKSs, and NRPS-PKSs and the mechanisms they employ to synthesize important drugs. We will use biochemistry and biophysics, including techniques known as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy, to capture three-dimensional pictures of an NRPS or PKS at different points in the process of making these natural products. We will answer questions ranging from how, in a natural hybrid fusion of one kind of enzyme (PKS) and the other (NRPS), the separate parts can function together, to how a domain normally found in a PKS has adapted to work in an NRPS, to how the last step of synthesis, common to both NRPSs and PKSs, releases the molecule in its proper, active form. These enzymes have excellent potential to produce new therapeutics. They are divided into segments called modules, where each module adds one building block to form the product. If we have enough knowledge of the enzymes, we should be able to switch around the order of the modules to produce variants of the current therapeutics. Our studies can help understand how to make new compounds which may be able to fight antibiotic resistant bacteria, viruses and cancer.
