column37: In general, women have a higher risk of adverse drug reactions than men. This is believed to be because women may present higher blood concentrations of drugs than men when they are given a specific dose of a medication. Yet, the exact reasons for these differences are unknown. This is partly because the inclusion of women in studies during the development of new drugs is generally limited. Thus, doses used in clinical studies, and eventually in the "real world", are largely based on information collected in men. Many mechanisms have been proposed to explain the differences in drug concentrations between women and men. For example, women have a lower body weight and kidney function, which should lead to higher drug concentrations. Another potential mechanism that has not been widely studied is that genetic variations could have different effects between women and men. We propose to conduct a comprehensive study in 10 000 participants from a large study to identify if individual characteristics, such as weight and age, as well as genetic variations in genes implicated in the absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination of drugs, influence the concentrations and dosing of 48 drugs commonly used by Canadians. The goal of this project is to identify these factors and determine how they can be used to more closely tailor drug selection and treatment in patients.

column37: Recent research indicates a high prevalence of co-occurring addiction, mental and physical illness in people living in homelessness or precarious housing such as single room occupancy hotels. The standardized mortality rate is over eight times higher than a Canadian sample matched for age and gender. Nearly half of people studied have a neurological illness, three-quarters a mental illness. These illnesses, especially if untreated, may accelerate aging, result in considerable secondary disability, and contribute to early mortality. The present proposal seeks to investigate risk factors for co-occurring illness, and perform detailed clinical evaluations of outcomes, using magnetic resonance imaging and neuropsychological testing. We will also investigate possible protective factors. Social networks are smaller than expected, but do contribute to behaviour and could be a source of strength. There is also a range of types of housing and support available. Although duration of time spent living in an impoverished neighbourhood contributes to cognitive decline, we will investigate the possibility that more recent, better supported housing can ameliorate some of these effects. Through neurological, cognitive, and brain imaging studies, we will learn how these risk and protect factors act on the brain, and in turn, the consequences for memory and movement disorders. The results will help identify targets for early intervention to prevent disability, and aid rehabilitation.

column37: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a three-dimensional deformity affecting the orientation and position of the vertebrae, intervertebral disk and spine in space. AIS affects between 2- 3% of the population with young adolescent female being affected more commonly. Risk factors for progression include female gender, curve magnitude and location, skeletal maturity and growth velocity. However, these risk factors have been shown to be inconsistent in predicting curve progression which remains a constant challenge for the treating physician. The aim of this study is to evaluate the global risk of scoliotic curve progression based on local three-dimensional vertebral and pelvic indices. Over the past 7 years, we have developed a predictive model of the final Cobb angle in AIS based on 3D spinal parameters. This analysis was based on a prospective cohort of 172 patients that were enrolled upon their initial visit and followed until maturity. This predictive model, based on multiple linear regression, has a determination coefficient (prediction) of 0.64. The proposed new study aims at testing a new refine model by measuring the agreement between prediction of the outcome from the new model and the traditional Cobb angle measurement at maturity in a large multicentre study. To test our hypotheses, we propose a multicenter prospective study evaluating these local 3D vertebral measurements of the scoliotic deformity and with a quality of life instrument over a period of 5 years with the inclusion of 8 high volume sites. A total of 816 patients will be enrolled in the study.

column36: Metabolic and Metagenomic effects of repopulation of the intestinal microbiome in patients with severe unexplained atherosclerosis
column37: Some patients have severe disease of the arteries (atherosclerosis) even though they do not have the usual risk factors such as high cholesterol levels, smoking, or diabetes. Such patients are at very high risk, and some are resistant to usual therapy such as drugs that lower blood cholesterol levels. We reported in 2018 that such patients have significantly higher blood levels of toxic chemicals that are produced by intestinal bacteria from meat and egg yolks, whereas people who are the opposite of them - those with severe risk factors and normal arteries, so "protected" from atherosclerosis - have significantly lower blood levels of those toxic chemicals (metabolites). This indicates that their intestinal bacteria are different. It is possible to replace the intestinal bacteria with bacteria from other patients; this is called intestinal repopulation (or fecal transplantation); it is now routine for treatment of an infection called Clostridium difficile, and has also been used to treat ulcerative colitis and fatty liver disease. Members of our team have done this in recent years. We propose a novel approach to treating atherosclerosis, to reduce the risk of strokes and heart attacks. We propose to do intestinal repopulation in patients with unexplained atherosclerosis, using capsules of freeze-dried stool of "protected" patients in order to identify which bacteria are responsible for improvement in the blood levels of the toxic metabolites. This will allow us to design capsules of combinations of cultured bacteria to treat atherosclerosis. Members of our team have done this successfully with Clostridium difficile infection.That approach is much better than using stool donors, because the intestinal bacterial tend to revert to the baseline state, and it is very difficult to sustain stool donors. Once those capsules are developed, we plan to study their effects on progression of atherosclerosis in patients with unexplained atherosclerosis in a followup study.

column36: Decolonizing childbirth with Nunavik Inuit women transferred to high-risk hospitals for childbirth: a co-designed pilot intervention
column37: BACKGROUND Inuit women in Canada carry a disproportionate burden of poor health, with higher rates of maternal mortality and negative birth outcomes. Some 14% of Inuit women in Nunavik (Inuit territory in Quebec) travel to tertiary southern hospitals for specialized obstetric care (a process known as fly-out births). Fly-out births are linked to adverse health outcomes for Inuit women, their families and communities. This participatory research supports culturally safe Inuit childbirth, and will co-design pilot interventions with Inuit stakeholders and their care providers, to inform the decolonization of obstetric care in Quebec tertiary hospitals. METHODS The study engages Nunavik-based Inuit women, their families and community members, as well as perinatal healthcare providers and policy makers in Nunavik and Montreal. With each group, a series of group fuzzy cognitive mapping sessions will explore experiences with fly-out childbirth and perspectives of decolonization in obstetric care. Individual and household questionnaires will document the frequency of these findings. Stakeholders will co-design an intervention through deliberative dialogue and community meetings. Recommendations will be shared with obstetrical staff of a Montreal tertiary hospital. A follow-up survey will measure quantitative changes in birth outcomes, patient satisfaction, and decolonizing care practices. An integrated knowledge translation and exchange strategy engages stakeholders in cognitive mapping sessions, and co-design interventions in deliberative dialogue. DISCUSSION Evacuation for childbirth aims to reduce health disparities faced by Inuit women, yet it is inadvertently associated with adverse health outcomes. Affirming Inuit values of childbirth and engaging Inuit voices in service delivery improvement can support culturally safe care. The protocol and instruments developed may have wider relevance for rural Inuit across Canada.

column37: Heart disease is a broad health concern for all post industrial societies. A consistent feature to the many variants of cardiac illness is the inappropriate enlargement of heart muscle, commonly referred to as pathologic cardiac hypertrophy. This variant of heart disease is also a common step in the transition to heart failure, an illness with limited treatments and a poor prognosis. The heart also grows in a beneficial way, termed physiologic hypertrophy, a form of growth that is observed with exercise training and pregnancy. Physiologic hypertrophy can also counter the pathologic form of growth and slow the transition to overt heart failure. Although these forms of heart muscle growth result in very distinct outcomes, work from our laboratory suggests that the same biochemical pathway is critical for both forms of hypertrophy. In fact, our observations suggest that pathologic hypertrophy may simple be the result of 'turning on' this pathway for longer periods of time. In our current research application, we will focus on understanding how this biochemical pathway promotes physiologic vs pathologic hypertrophy, and whether this pathway stimulates the unique protein activity for each condition. We anticipate, that the information obtained from these experiments will identify proteins that can be targeted to mitigate the onset of pathologic hypertrophy and/or promote the beneficial form of cardiac growth.

column36: Reprogramming HSCs to generate protective trained immunity against TB
column37: Ever since German scientist Robert Koch first discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) to be the infectious agent of tuberculosis in 1882, it has defied efforts by scientists to prevent or cure the disease. The presence of Mtb DNA in ancient Egyptian mummies (dated 1550- 1080 BC) suggests a long-standing evolutionary relationship between this bacterium and humans. Despite the world-wide application of BCG vaccination and other anti-Mtb interventions, Mtb remains one of the deadliest human pathogens killing annually two million people. Eight to ten million new cases of active tuberculosis occur each year due in large part to asymptomatic people chronically infected with Mtb. The ability of Mtb to persist in individuals with apparently normal immune systems implies that Mtb has developed strategies to avoid, evade, and even subvert our host defense system. Considering Mtb also desires to be a "residence" of the bone marrow, which is home to stem cells that produce all immune cells, Mtb potentially hijack the control centre of the immune response. Although we know a great deal about the immune response to Mtb in the lung, our understanding of BM immunity to Mtb is extremely limited. The tropism of Mtb for the bone marrow may also explain why it is an incredibly successful pathogen, as the vast majority of our efforts have been dedicated to controlling its growth in the lung while the root of the disease is seeded in the bone marrow. Thus the major objective of this proposal is to define the cellular and molecular signatures involved in HSC activation/function during infection with virulent strains of Mtb or vaccine with the ultimate goal of developing a roadmap of protective versus detrimental immunity to this devastating disease.

column36: Targeting the eicosanoid/macrophage axis to enhance host defense against influenza virus infection
column37: Despite the world-wide application of vaccination and other anti-viral interventions, influenza infection remains a persistent threat to human health. The 1918 "Spanish" influenza pandemic killed approximately 40 million people in just one year. Similar to human infection, mouse models of the highly pathogenic 1918 strains have revealed that excessive inflammatory responses lead to lung injury/dysfunction and mortality. Therefore, understanding the severe pathology associated with highly virulent influenza viruses is a matter of urgency as further underscored by the recent pandemic of H1N1 influenza A. In fact, most influenza related deaths result from an unregulated host immune response to the virus rather than the cytopathic effects of the virus itself. Thus, it can be argued that the influenza virus is not the main threat; rather, it is the host's own immune-inflammatory response that jeopardizes host survival. How the immune system becomes dysregulated to the point of causing such massive immunopathology is currently not well understood. In this application, we aim to identify the molecular mechanisms involved in influenza virus induced pulmonary injury that will allow us to develop novel host-directed therapeutic strategies against influenza virus infection.

column36: Fluids in Septic Shock (FISSH): a randomized controlled trial.
column37: Severe infection can lead to many complications within the human body including low blood pressure, which is called septic shock. Rates of death for those with septic shock can be as high as 40%. The main treatments for septic shock are intravenous antibiotics and intravenous (IV) fluids. There are many different intravenous fluids available for doctors to use. Each one of these fluids has potential advantages as well as potential disadvantages. Some preliminary and limited research in the field has suggested that one specific electrolyte, called chloride, may be harmful when given to patients in high concentrations. Some intravenous fluids have higher concentrations of chloride than others. One high chloride fluid, called Normal Saline, remains the most widely used intravenous fluid worldwide. It is unlikely that clinical practice will change until a large-scale study examining outcomes that are important to patients is performed. The investigators plan to study the impact of giving patients with septic shock intravenous fluids with either a high chloride concentration or a low chloride concentration. If there is benefit seen using low chloride concentration fluids this would be easy to initiate across the world leading to a dramatic and relatively inexpensive improvement in patient care.

column36: Pilot RCT study to assess feasibility of "supra-marginal" surgical resection of malignant glioma (G-SUMIT: Glioma Supra Marginal Incision Trial)
column37: Majority of neurosurgeons agree that removing more tissue of malignant brain tumor will lead to better survival. This is a small study to show ability to perform larger study testing best surgical principle in terms of extent of malignant brain tumor removal. It will mainly look at the ability to enrol and collect complete data on a pre-specified number of patients, while following their response in terms of controlling tumor recurrence and documenting any added risk to patient as the result of surgical complications. As this is small-scale study, it only has power to test the ability to collect enough patients, perform study accurately, and collect results. The result of this study is important to help to better design a larger similar study to answer a common clinical question in management of patients with aggressive brain cancer. column36: Emotion regulation and treatment-based change in children with neurodevelopmental disorders: A diffusion spectrum imaging tractography study
column37: Between 40 - 70% of children with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) such as autism, ADHD and specific learning disorder experience complex emotional problems. Few accessible treatment options are available and current approaches are limited by their focus on one diagnostic category despite frequent overlap of symptoms across disorders; currently over a third of children with NDDs are non-responsive to cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Emotion regulation - a child's ability to appropriately adapt the intensity of their behaviour - may play a critical role as a moderator of treatment efficacy, modulating symptom expression across a range of emotional difficulties and diagnoses. Additionally, research has identified shared brain-based impairments between groups of children with autism and ADHD, but not OCD, suggesting that these impairments may be common across only the first two disorders. Currently, no research exists using advanced neuroimaging techniques to investigate common neural targets for emotion regulation and treatment-based change in children with NDDs. Further, females are severely underrepresented in clinical pediatric neuroimaging research, limiting the generalizability of current findings. This study has three aims: First, using diffusion spectrum imaging, to identify shared neural biomarkers predicting response to emotion-focused CBT for children with NDDs. Second, to examine the relationship between parent and child-reported emotion regulation and transdiagnostic biomarkers of treatment change; and third, to evaluate findings according to a biological sex and gender-based lens. Greater understanding of the biomarkers related to emotion regulation and treatment responsiveness is critical to ensure a greater number of youth with NDDs are able to access quality care that effectively meets their needs; ultimately, results of this study have the potential to reduce the significant relational and economic costs associated with ineffective treatment.

column36: Testing the Efficacy of an Online Self-Help Treatment for Alcohol Misuse and Emotional Problems in Young Adult Manitobans: A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
column37: Nearly half of individuals who struggle with alcohol use also experience emotional problems (i.e., depression and anxiety), especially in Manitoba. The combination of these challenges can have devastating consequences such as more severe symptoms of each disorder, disease, and early death. These combined difficulties also place a financial burden on the healthcare system. The highest rates of these problems are seen among young adults, especially those living in Northern and remote communities. This is concerning as there are often barriers to accessing health services in these areas (e.g., stigma, lack of resources, distance). Considering the high co-occurrence between alcohol use and emotional problems, there is a critical need to develop accessible, cost-effective, self-guided treatments in order to reach the thousands of struggling Manitobans. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to examine the benefits of an online, integrated (i.e., treatment for alcohol use and emotional problems together), self-guided program. Currently, for young adults, no intervention like this exists in Canada that targets the full spectrum of negative emotions (i.e., depression and anxiety). A total of 214 young adults experiencing issues with alcohol use and depression and/or anxiety will be recruited through the treatment website. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either an 8-week online intervention (i.e., integrated cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing) or to the control group (i.e., education about mental health). This research stands to provide a user-friendly, cost-effective, and feasible option in order to improve the mental health of young adults struggling in the community.

column36: Monitoring food security with Indigenous Batwa in a changing climate
column37: Indigenous communities in many countries are often more food insecure compared to their non-Indigenous counterparts. Climate change is further threatening Indigenous food security by reducing access to traditional foods. As the impacts of climate change are projected to intensify over the coming decades, adaptation efforts that reduce vulnerability of Indigenous food systems to climate change are urgently needed. Community-based monitoring is considered a promising strategy to improve monitoring of, and local adaptation, to environmental change. Yet, its application towards food security, particularly Indigenous food security, is limited. The goal of my research is to better understand the process of community-based monitoring as well as enhance existing monitoring systems for Indigenous Batwa food security under a changing climate. The project involves reviewing the literature on community-based monitoring as well as engaging Batwa and other community partners in Uganda to identify priorities in community-based monitoring, develop indicators of food security and climate change, design data collection procedures, and evaluate the process of this collaboration. The project builds on expertise and partnerships of a larger food security and climate change research project in Uganda. Overall, my research aims to improve the capacity of Batwa and other community partners in Uganda to adapt food systems to climate change, along with advance tools to monitor Indigenous food security under a changing climate.

column36: Advancing the Science of Knowledge Translation: Measuring Context
column37: Context is important to the success of interventions aimed to promote use of best available research evidence by healthcare providers in clinical practice. Context refers broadly to social, physical, structural, political, and relational influences on society, organizations, groups, and individuals. Context differs between settings (e.g., between units within hospitals) and changes over time. As a result, context assessment is essential to the design and delivery of interventions to increase the use of research evidence in healthcare. However, information about how to best measure context is lacking. Our previous research focused on obtaining a well-developed and clearly articulated definition of context and resulted in the development of a comprehensive framework (Implementation in CONtext (ICON)) of context domains, defining attributes and their features. Now that we have conceptual clarity on context, the purpose of this project is to advance its measurement. The study will be conducted in two phases. In Phase 1, we will conduct a living systematic review to identify and evaluate measures of context used in knowledge translation and quality improvement studies in any healthcare setting. In Phase 2, using our systematic review findings, we will develop a dynamic publicly accessible resource centre for context measurement in knowledge translation. Central to this resource will be a publicly accessible, interactive web-based repository of the context measures identified. In addition to containing an interactive repository of context measures, the resource centre will provide: 1) access to high-quality context measures; 2) micro-profiles of context measures tailored to users' needs; 3) a decision support tool to aid individuals in selecting context measures appropriate for use in their setting and their specific project; and 4) a research agenda on areas of context measurement where future development, research and/or testing are needed.

column36: Regulating chromatin landscape and organization with non-coding RNAs
column37: Recent technological advances have led to a number of important discoveries. Amongst these is the realization that the better part of our genome is read at one time or another to produce RNA molecules that do not encode proteins. Given that the biological function of most of these "non-coding RNA" transcripts is unknown, they currently fall into different categories based mainly on their size and the site from which they are produced in the genome. The "long non-coding RNAs" (lncRNAs) are one such class of molecules. The biological relevance of many lncRNAs has been demonstrated, with family members even considered as promising therapeutic or prognostic tools. Yet, how they regulate gene expression is very poorly understood. In this project, we suggest using four lncRNAs as discovery tools to identify and characterize new mechanisms used by this family of molecules to control gene expression. These lncRNAs are encoded within the HOXA gene cluster and have been linked to human cancers. We previous showed that one of them, HOTAIRM1, regulates the expression of HOXA genes both by regulating what binds and shapes the DNA encoding them. Our preliminary data indicates that HOTAIRM1 regulates many other genes across the genome. To better understand their biological function, we will first identify new gene targets genome-wide. We will investigate how they regulate genome folding and spatial organization using state-of-the-art technologies that yield three-dimensional maps of our genome at very high resolution. This information will then be used to characterize the molecular mechanisms used by the HOXA-encoded lncRNAs to regulate gene expression, and test our hypothesis that given lncRNAs can use different molecular mechanisms to modulate gene expression depending on the DNA context and/or target gene.

column37: NODAL is a protein that is normally in stem cells but that re-emerges in cancer, where it promotes cancer progression and metastasis. If successful, we will have developed a new drug to be tested in ovarian cancer patients.

column36: Pannexin-1 Opening in Neurons: Mechanisms of Intrinsic Neuroprotection
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in Canada. When the blood supply to the brain is disrupted, either regionally or globally, the nerve cells can rapidly malfunction and die. Neuronal death during stroke has several characteristic features, including loss of the cell's electrical activity and the formation of blebs in their processes (dendrites). Interestingly, nerve cells that reside outside the core of the stroke damage show blebbing in their dendritic regions that cross into the core, but may ultimately survive the insult. Here we propose that the molecular machinery responsible for bleb formation functions in a protective role. This is achieved by isolation of damaging signals (calcium) from spreading to the rest of the cell. We propose that by understanding how these traditionally damaging structures (blebs) form and potentially protect the nerve cells will form a basis for exploiting them in the future to reduce brain damage and improve recovery after stroke.

column36: Elucidation of bromodomain functions within SWI/SNF complexes
column37: The effective structural regulation and utilization of a cell's genetic material is essential to its fitness. Unsurprisingly, it is now clear that epigenetic regulators, proteins that organize and regulate the accessibility of the genetic material, are commonly altered in human diseases, including cancer. Notably, the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes are among the most commonly mutated protein complexes in human cancers, with ~20% of patients possessing at least one affected subunit. Intriguingly, SWI/SNF complexes contain a high density of bromodomains, conserved protein domains responsible for binding acetylated lysine residues, suggesting that they may have important functions in these complexes. In recent years, bromodomains have become actionable therapeutic targets, with the development of numerous small molecule inhibitors that effectively and specifically block their function. Clinical trials investigating these innovative inhibitors are ongoing in Canada and elsewhere. Unfortunately, fundamental understanding of the functions of the ten bromodomains incorporated in SWI/SNF complex components is still lacking. This project aims to provide this knowledge by employing state-of-the-art tools to identify the cellular targets of SWI/SNF bromodomains, examine how they engage these targets, and determine the functions of these interactions. This will aid in predicting the molecular consequences of specific mutations within SWI/SNF complex components, support the ongoing development of novel bromodomain inhibitors, and further our understanding of the regulatory processes controlling a cell's genomic material.

column36: Cognitive organization of maltreatment memories as a key moderator of the association between child maltreatment and mental health in early adulthood
column37: Child maltreatment (CM) refers to any act of commission or omission by a parent or other caregiver that results in intended or unintended harm such as physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, or neglect. One out of three adults have experienced CM in Canada. It is estimated to account for around a quarter of all mental disorders in adulthood and to cost more than 100 billion dollars each year. Despite these dramatic consequences, little has been done to better understand how CM can keep hindering mental health in adulthood, decades after the abuse. While memories for trauma (e.g., car accident) have been more investigated, CM memories have received much less attention. In addition, existing treatments for distressing memories in general have typically focused on increasing the processing of the distressing memory, but not on facilitating its integration into broader memory structure. Our past work shows that such integration of negative memories is key to mental health and prevents the negative memories to continuously hinder mental health over time. For the first time in memory or child maltreatment research, we seek to determine whether the level of integration in the memory system of accessible memories of past maltreatment could explain the association between CM and mental health in adulthood. We will follow adult CM victims and a control matched sample during three years. We will investigate whether increases or decreases of symptoms over time can be predicted by a weaker or greater integration of CM memories in the memory system, respectively. The present large-scale study is likely to lead to better prevention programs to victims of CM by devoting more attention to the cognitive organization of their CM memories, and to adaptation of existing treatments that could specifically target CM memories and their cognitive organization. Altogether, the expected findings should considerably contribute to reduce the dramatic economic cost of CM in the society.

column37: It is now predicted that 90% of cancer-related deaths are due to the formation of metastases rather than from the primary tumour. For example, breast cancer has the tendency to metastasize to the bones, liver and lungs whereas sarcomas and colon cancer tend to almost exclusively spread to the lungs and liver respectively. This proposal builds from the discovery that there are specific endothelial receptors that act as 'zip codes' to mediate the recruitment of both innate immune cells and metastatic cancer cells into the liver and lungs. In this proposal we will address some very important questions related to cancer metastasis, a major unmet clinical need in cancer control. Using a series of biochemical, genetic, pharmacological, intravital imaging and in vivo pre-clinical approaches we will determine the molecular means that cancer cells are recruited to specific organs? Second, we will determine how the recruitment of innate immune cells into the tumor microenvironment impact metastatic growth in specific organs? Third, determine if there are specific ways to harness these steps in the metastatic process for therapeutic gain?

column36: A population-level linked data study of the long-term developmental impacts of prenatal antidepressant exposure
column37: Each year, approximately 13% of North American women experience depression and/or anxiety during pregnancy and a third are treated with an antidepressant that alters levels of serotonin, a key neurotransmitter during fetal brain development. We know that these antidepressant cross the placenta and the fetal blood brain barrier, leading to critical unanswered questions about the long-term developmental effects associated with prenatal antidepressant exposure. Over the past 18 years our research has examined women treated with SRI antidepressants during pregnancy. We have studied development and behavior in infants, children and adolescents of depressed mothers and reported novel findings showing that in utero SRI exposure is associated with altered brain development in infancy and behavioral disturbances, such as increased anxiety in young children. While population-level data have the advantage of large sample sizes, the level of detail regarding educational and behavioral outcomes across childhood has generally been limited. There is an urgent need to study long-term outcomes using objective non-categorical behavioral and educational data. These data are now available in British Columbia. Thus we aim to use these population-based administrative datasets to assess whether maternal mood during pregnancy and/or its treatment with an SRI antidepressant is associated with an increased risk for delayed language and cogonitive development during childhood, as well as social and emotional development and wellbeing during early (age 5) and middle childhood (age 9). We will assemble a population-based cohort including all children born in British Columbia between 2000 and 2012 and follow them until 2016. We will include individual-level behavioral, education and health data on children in kindergarten and at Grade 4 to assess their well-being and development. Our research results will be used to minimize the incidence of adverse outcomes for mothers and their children.

column36: Diagnosis of Aggressive Prostate Cancer Using Key Features of Raman Spectroscopy
column37: The diagnosis of prostate cancer, the most frequent cancer among Canadian men, is fraught with recurrent difficulties in establishing the aggressiveness of the disease (prognosis). Indeed, with a wide spectrum of possible therapeutic options, the prognosis of prostate cancer has to be well-defined in order to better individualize that treatment. Accordingly, using a laser-based molecular characterization method (Raman spectroscopy), we previously identified key features of a marker of prostate cancer aggressiveness, intraductal carcinoma of the prostate. In this project, we first aim to verify how each of these key feature can be used clinically to improve the identification of this aggressive variant of prostate cancer. To do this, we will use a special type of Raman spectroscopy, which is based on the targeted evaluation of one key feature at the time. In parallel, since Raman spectroscopy features involves many underlying molecules, we aim at exploring which of these molecules are responsible for the modifications we observed using the laser-based method. To do this, we will use mass spectrometry, a technique which allows to identify specific molecules according partly to their weight. Overall, this study will not only provide a comprehensive understanding of our previous results, but it will in parallel establish a clinically applicable method and provide a unique opportunity to identify new potential diagnostic and/or therapeutic biomarkers of prostate cancer.

column36: Symptom Screening Linked to Care Pathways for Children with Cancer: a Cluster Randomized Trial
column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. To address these gaps, we developed the Symptom Screening in Pediatrics Tool (SSPedi) for children receiving cancer treatments. We also created evidence-based guidelines to help providers know how to manage symptoms. To bring identification and management of symptoms together, we created a web-based application called Supportive care Prioritization, Assessment and Recommendations for Kids (SPARK). To evaluate SPARK, we plan to randomize 20 institutions. In intervention institutions, we will prompt children newly diagnosed with cancer to complete symptom screening three times weekly for 8 weeks. Reports will be emailed to the primary healthcare team. We will also create care pathways that help clinicians know how to best manage symptoms. Participants in control sites will receive the standard of care. We will not facilitate symptom screening with feedback or create care pathways. We will enroll English and Spanish-speaking children 8-18 years of age with a new diagnosis of cancer and a plan for treatment. The primary endpoint will be the week 8 total SSPedi score (ranges from 0-60; higher means worse symptoms). We plan to enroll 444 children across 20 US institutions. This study is proposed for US sites because we are conducting a CIHR-funded randomized trial evaluating 5 consecutive days of symptom screening and feedback among hospitalized pediatric cancer patients in 7 Canadian sites. These studies cannot be conducted at the same site. This study will test an innovative application to improve symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column36: Implication of neutrophil extracellular traps in the efficacy of bladder-sparing therapy in muscle invasive bladder cancer
column37: Radical cystectomy remains the standard of care for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). This surgery entails complete removal of the bladder and surrounding organs, leading to a serious impact on the quality of life (QoL) of patients and associated with a 5-year overall survival of only 50 %. Radiation therapy (RT), which preserves the bladder, would be a more appropriate treatment modality if we could improve efficacy, as lack of local control remains problematic. As part from its direct tumor cell killing potential, there is increasing evidence that RT also leads to significant alterations in the tumor microenvironment, which inflammation being one of the most important factors modulating radiation responsiveness of tumors. During the acute phase of inflammation, neutrophils are one of the first-line responders of inflammatory cells to migrate towards the site of inflammation. Recently, it has been shown neutrophils can exhibit dual behaviors and are increasingly being seen as important players in cancer progression. Neutrophils can expel DNA studded with various proteins to form web-like structures known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NET), which has been shown to be associated with tumor progression and metastasis. Our preliminary findings strongly indicate NET are implicated in radioresistance. Determining the NET-related molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying response to radiation will have direct clinical relevance to better select patients who will benefit most from bladder preservation therapy. The novel approach of the proposal herein can bring transformative changes in developing novel strategies in bladder cancer (BC) therapy as it has the potential to transfer from the bench to the patient, an unquestionably, positive impact on survival and quality of life of MIBC patients.

column36: Microbial Causes of Ulcerative Colitis: Looking Outside the Involved Region
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic disease affecting the gut with limited treatments and significant risk of needing surgery to remove the large bowel (colon). It is very concerning that we still don't know what causes UC, especially since it is becoming more common, particularly in children in Canada. Microbes (mostly bacteria) are different in UC but we don't know if they cause the disease or are changed because of the inflammation found in UC. We have recently shown that children with UC have different bacteria in the healthy-appearing small bowel; we have also developed and just published a new method to isolate bacteria that might be virulent (disease causing) by utilizing the patient's immune system to trap bacteria and identified how they might do this. The next step is to combine these findings and find bacteria that might be causing or at least driving damage in UC. To do this we will also take advantage of some of the basic and unexplained features of UC: 1. It only involves the colon; 2. It is a continuous disease; 3. The appendix seems to have an important (but not understood) role. This study will build on these interesting observations to test our hypothesis that bacteria (and molecules/products they make) from unaffected areas travel down the bowel and cause the damage seen in UC. We will test this by collecting samples from different parts of the bowel in children just diagnosed with UC during a colonoscopy test. Three large Canadian centers, that are already working together through a funded National Network, will collect samples during colonoscopy to identify these bacteria. We will find the bacteria that travel down to the sick areas and identify those that can penetrate and injure the bowel and those that activate the immune system. We will then confirm that these bacteria indeed cause damage using cell models and germ-free mice. This will help explain what causes UC and will direct new therapies.

column36: The roles of betaine and its mitochondrial synthesis in oocyte and preimplantation embryo health
column37: There is strong evidence that the mother's nutrition, health, and environment during the earliest stages of pregnancy immediately after conception can significantly affect the health of the embryo and the fetus and placenta into which it develops. Also, the treatment of human infertility by assisted reproduction technologies (ART), in which multiple eggs are obtained from women, fertilized, and cultured for an extended period before being transferred into the uterus, has been very effective and produced millions of babies, but there is increasing evidence that how eggs and very early embryos are handled during ART can damage eggs before fertilization and can cause health problems in the fetus, placenta, and offspring. In this work, we will be investigating mechanisms that may be important in preventing such problems. We are focusing on a molecule called betaine, which is a modified form of the common amino acid glycine. Betaine is supplied in the diet, for example by wheat germ, spinach, and shellfish. It can also be synthesized in the body from the vitamin, choline. We have previously found that betaine has important roles in mammalian eggs and very early embryos. One function is to control cell size, which turns out to be particularly critical for early embryo health. Another role is in supplying the molecules needed for controlling gene activity in later embryos, just before they implant in the uterus. We also have new evidence that betaine is also involved in the normal function of mitochondria, which are the part of the cell that makes energy, in eggs. How betaine is supplied to the egg and embryo, where it comes from, and the consequences of its dysregulation, are still poorly understood. We hope to show that creating the conditions in which these mechanisms can function normally in eggs and very early embryos will produce healthy eggs and embryos.

column36: Perivascular fibroblasts in maintaining blood vessel integrity
column37: Blood vessels are essential to sustain life in humans. Defects in blood vessels can result in serious consequences, such as hemorrhage, tissue ischemia, and stroke. The conventional view is that interactions between endothelial cells, the inner layer of the blood vessel, and surrounding vessel support cells known as mural cells help keep the blood vessel as a stable tube. Loss of these cells result in fragile vessels prone to damage. We will determine where these perivascular fibroblasts come from during embryo development and how they help stabilize blood vessels. column36: The regulation of mRNA translation by the Nucleoporin RanBP2/Nup358
column37: To express a gene, its DNA must copied into mRNA in the nucleus. This mRNA is then packaged into complexes that contain proteins and known as messenger ribonucleoproteins (mRNPs). These mRNPs are then ferried across the nuclear pore to reach the cytoplasm where they are used by ribosomes to make new proteins. These proteins are functional molecules that impact the development, physiology and homeostasis of the organism. We have uncovered a key step in the gene expression pathway. We have shown that the protein RanBP2, which is part of the nuclear pore, is required for the efficient production of secretory proteins, likely by modifying how mRNAs are packaged into mRNPs. This mRNP maturation event likely impacts how many mRNAs are translated into proteins. Mutations in RanBP2 are associated to Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy 1 (ANE1), a condition where otherwise normal individuals overproduce cytokines in response to influenza infections. This leads to seizures, coma and a high rate of mortality. Four separate dominant point mutations in RanBP2 have been linked to this disease. In cells that lack RanBP2 or that have mutations that impair its ability to modify other proteins, we find that the cytokine interleukin 6 (IL6) is over-expressed, indicating that RanBP2 likely alters the mRNP that contains the mRNA that is used to make IL6 protein. In this proposal we outline our plans to determine the molecular mechanisms by which RanBP2 regulates mRNP maturation. We have also been in contact with families afflicted by ANE1 and we plan to use epithelial nasal swabs and white blood cells (monocytes) from these patients to understand how mutations in RanBP2 alters cytokine production in normal conditions and after viral infection. Our work will not only provide key insights into the pathology of ANE1, but will also provide a deeper understanding of how RanBP2 regulates the expression of cytokines and other secretory proteins.

column36: Hypoxia mimicry for enhancing peripheral nerve regeneration
column37: In the absence of sufficient oxygen (i.e. during hypoxia), cells die. When oxygen levels are low but not lethal, cells can cope by changing how they metabolize nutrients: they use alternate mechanisms that do not depend so heavily on oxygen, and at the same time increase the capacity for oxygen to be delivered (increasing the number of red blood cells and blood vessels, for example). Interestingly, these mechanisms are also partially engaged when nerves are injured, as they are in 2-3% of all injuries to any part of the body. Nerve injury leads to loss of function (sensation and movement, for example), as well as to neuropathic pain, most frequently described as unpleasant burning, electric shock-like, or crushing sensations. Often these consequences of nerve injury fail to resolve, prompting us to ask whether artificially engaging the hypoxia response can improve peripheral nerve regeneration and reduce neuropathic pain. Our cells "know" how much oxygen is present by virtue of oxygen-sensing proteins called PHDs. There are three of these: PHD1, 2 and 3. When these proteins are blocked with a drug (DMOG), or genetically silenced, cells are "tricked" into behaving as they would under hypoxia. We will use DMOG and PHD-deficient mice to ask whether and how mimicking hypoxia can improve recovery, including preventing neuropathic pain, following nerve injury.

column37: Duchennes's Muscular Dystrophy is a disease of muscle that affects approximately 1 in 3500 boys. column36: Chromatin context of somatic mutations delineate oncogenic drivers in triple-negative breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is a collection of different types of cancer. One of these, known as triple-negative breast cancer, comprises approximately 20% of breast cancers diagnosed each year. It is highly aggressive and the only standard-of-care therapy offered to patients is chemotherapy, which unfortunately fails in over 40% of patients. This leads to disease progression and death. Hence, new approaches are required to treat and cure triple-negative breast cancer patients. To address this need for new therapy we propose to identify what drives growth of triple-negative breast cancer. In the last year, scientists identified thousands of mutations that populate the genome of triple-negative breast cancer, but unlike other types of breast cancer, the "drivers" are not easy to identity due to the diversity of mutations across patients. We argue that the heterogeneity of mutations underlies their convergence toward common targets. We developed in recent years two methods to identify drivers of cancer development based on convergence of mutations towards genes or proteins. Here, we propose to apply these methods to mine mutations found in triple-negative breast cancer and find the drivers of growth. My approaches contrast with standard strategies in the field by comprehensively analyzing each mutation based on the normal function of the DNA sequence they alter, inclusive of genes and the remaining 98% of DNA sequences found in each cancer cell. My ultimate goal is to identify drivers of oncogenesis, based on the genetics of tumours taking into account their epigenetic context, and use this information to precisely find targets for drug treatment against triple-negative breast cancer. Overall, this proposal is at the forefront of personalized cancer medicine and offers a unique opportunity to accelerate the translation of research discoveries into improved clinical care.

column36: Prognostic Biomarkers and Novel Therapies for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Patients
column37: Patients with head and neck cancer have a 50% 5-year survival. Patients are treated with surgery, and may also receive radiation therapy, or combined radiation and chemotherapy. These therapies are very toxic and can have long-term negative side effects. The needs for these patients include: 1) A better way to identify which patients are in need of more aggressive therapy; 2) More effective therapies for those patients with the most aggressive and life-threatening disease. We have been acquiring tumor tissues from HNSCC patients for many years and implanting them into mice with a defective immune system. 2/3 of these samples successfully grow in the mice ("engraft") and they grow at varying rates: some form a 1 cm mass within a short time (<8 weeks; rapid engrafters); others grow more slowly and can take up to 6 months to form a 1 cm mass; and still others fail to grow at all. Our proposal is focused on using these results to identify new therapies, in particular for those patients that have the most aggressive disease. We will do this by: 1) Identifying the genetic differences between patients in the three categories (rapid engrafters, slow engrafters, and non-engrafters); 2) Using the genetic information to identify drugs predicted to target the genetic profile of rapid engrafters. Any drug candidates that we identify can be tested for their efficacy against aggressive, rapidly growing tumors in the engrafted mice. This project will result in "biomarkers", which can be used to predict which patients have the most aggressive form of the disease and thus adjust their therapies appropriately, and also in new candidate therapies for these patients.

column36: Inflammation and LDL transcytosis - implications for early atherosclerosis
column37: Atherosclerosis leads to heart attacks and strokes and is a leading cause of death in Canada. The first step in the disease is the build-up of the bad cholesterol, LDL, in the wall of blood vessels. Specifically, LDL builds up under the innermost layer of arteries, called the endothelium. How the LDL gets under the endothelium is very poorly understood. We have discovered ways to study this process, which is known as LDL transcytosis. We now wish to learn how a big risk factor for heart disease - inflammation - affects LDL transcytosis. We suspect that inflammation causes more LDL transcytosis to occur, accelerating the build-up of cholesterol in the artery wall. Understanding how this happens will help us develop ways to prevent or treat it. If we can prevent cholesterol from accumulating in the blood vessel wall, we will prevent heart disease and stroke. We will use sophisticated microscopes to study the process by which cholesterol builds up under the special cells that line blood vessels, known as endothelium. We will identify the specific molecules that regulate this build-up, especially under conditions of inflammation. We will also prove that our findings from cells hold true in mice, which are the typical animals used in studies of atherosclerosis. We will compare our findings using cells from men as well as women to determine if there is a sex-based difference. We are the only lab in Canada to study this process of transcytosis, by which the bad cholesterol (LDL) gets under endothelial cells. We therefore have the potential to make huge advances in this field of research.

column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is one of nine neurological diseases caused by DNA expansion in genes. This disease affects 1 in 7000 Canadians, is progressive and fatal, and has no direct treatment. The result of this DNA expansion is a long tract of glutamine amino acids that alter the function of the protein, leading to disease. This data allowed us to formulate a fundamental new idea of how this diseases are triggered, which has important implications for more common degenerative brain diseases for which half the Canadian population is at risk over age 65. The excitement from this work is that we have a new drug lead, with industry development, aset of pathways well understood by cancer research and a potential list of drugs that may be effective in these diseases. column36: The Role of Intramuscular Immune Cell Infiltrations in Tumor and Age Related Muscle Wasting
column37: Muscle wasting that occurs with cancer is known as cachexia and with aging is called sarcopenia. Cachexia and sarcopenia are important healthcare issues. Cachexia affects the majority of patients with late stage malignancy, and is thought to contribute to one third of cancer deaths, while sarcopenia is associated with falls, disability, and mortality in the elderly, and costs as high as 1.5% of our total healthcare expenditure. Despite these significant features, cachexia and sarcopenia are relatively understudied entities with poor understanding of their pathophysiology. One common link that could explain how these conditions occur is the immune system. Our research focuses on the idea that both tumors and an aging body release factors that activate some cells of the immune system which, in turn, release other signals that cause muscles to shrink. Our preliminary data suggest that the immune cell at the "heart" of this process is the myeloid derived suppressor cell (MDSC). These cells rapidly rise during cancer, and steadily rise during aging. Using mice with cachexia caused by tumors, and sarcopenia of old age, we have identified subsets of these MDSCs infiltrating hearts and skeletal muscle. On depletion of these cells during mouse models of cancer, we can eliminate muscle wasting, even though the cancer remains. In this grant, we will characterize the nature of the MDSCs infiltrating the hearts and skeletal muscles during cachexia and sarcopenia, and their role in these processes using functional assays and state of the art technologies, including single cell sequencing. Next, we will determine which factors support the generation and activation of these cells. Finally, we determine the mechanisms by which these cells cause muscles to shrink in cachexia and sarcopenia. Understanding how these immune cells tell the heart and muscles to shrink can help us to prevent or revert these processes and improve the lives of people with muscle wasting from age or cancer.

It is increasingly recognized that insulin in the blood also affects the brain. For example, insulin is under clinical trial in Alzheimer's disease, because studies show it improves memory. The BBB is mainly composed of highly active cells called "endothelial cells", which basically control everything that goes in the brain or that goes out. Although small quantities of insulin are generated in the brain, the vast majority is produced by the pancreas and secreted in the bloodstream. Therefore, to interact with brain cells, blood insulin must first interact with the BBB. Surprisingly enough, how exactly insulin interacts with the BBB remains relatively unknown. Although it is clear that insulin must interact with its receptor located on the BBB, we don't know much of what happens next. The purpose of the present grant application is to better understand how blood insulin (i) is transported into the brain, (ii) stimulates BBB endothelial cells to carry metabolic information into the brain, (iii) changes brain function and behavior. We expect that answering these questions will be extremely useful for treating not only diabetes, but also Alzheimer's disease. For example, we recently found that neurotoxic amyloid peptides are washed out of the brain into the bloodstream within minutes after an injection of insulin, suggesting that insulin-related mechanisms can be used to treat this terrible disease. In summary, we hope that the present proposal will contribute to develop new drugs that will benefit both diabetes and Alzheimer's disease patients.

column36: Predicting and preventing brain injury in the antenatal period
column37: An insufficient supply of oxygen and nutrients to the developing fetus impairs normal growth and risks causing lasting and serious injury to the body organs that have the highest consumption of oxygen, especially the developing brain. Growth restriction of this kind affects 5% of pregnancies in Canada and is particularly difficult to diagnose near the end of pregnancy because of limitations of current diagnostic ultrasound methods. Our proposal is to develop a new diagnostic imaging procedure for reliable use late in pregnancy that could aid in identifying these fetuses that have insufficient oxygen and are at risk of either brain injury or death. We will make use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a specialized measurement protocol called BOLD to assess the health of a fetus. While many of the technical aspects of making BOLD measurements have already been established in pregnant women, it is presently not known how to interpret these data to identify fetuses at risk. We propose to overcome this challenge by using experimental mice under controlled conditions to learn specific signatures of fetal distress that could be applied in human pregnancies. Our research strategy makes use of pregnant mice where pregnancy continues too long, such that the needs of the fetus exceed the available supply of oxygen and nutrients. By taking advantage of advances in genetic engineering in mice, specialized 3D optical imaging methods to visualize the smallest of blood vessels, and computational methods that will relate the distribution of oxygen among the fetal organs to BOLD signal, we proposed to gain a clear understanding of how to use this MRI technology to identify fetuses at risk from brain injury. We will also evaluate this approach for guiding an intervention to protect the fetus from brain injury. This work will open a new avenue for anticipating and preventing brain injury that will be translated into improved clinical outcomes.

column36: Mechanisms regulating contribution of pericytes to brain repair after stroke
column37: Stroke constitutes a major cause of death and disability of the adults in Canada, imposing considerable burden on society and economy. Currently, no efficient therapy exists. The cerebral blood vessels form with the nerve cells a functional interface that enables proper brain functioning. The interface comprises multifunctional perivascular cells located between nerve cells and vessels, called pericytes. Emerging reports are suggesting that pericytes contribute to brain repair after stroke by giving rise to other brain cell types, namely nerve and vascular cells. Our findings suggest that the reparative potential of pericytes is regulated by low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms, which are induced after stroke due to blood interruption. Our findings suggest as well that targeting pericytes using pharmacological and cell-based approaches stimulates brain regeneration. The project will dissect how low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms regulate the intrinsic capacity of pericytes to convert to other cells types to compensate for the lost brain tissue. Furthermore, the project will explore novel therapeutic interventions to promote recovery by exploiting the reparative capabilities of pericytes. To achieve these objectives, clinically relevant animal stroke models in which low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms are genetically modified in pericytes will be used. Furthermore, novel cell transplantation approach will be applied by delivering into the brain via the intranasal cavity pericytes modified to convert to nerve and vascular cells. The expected results will provide new fundamental insights into how low-oxygen sensitive mechanisms regulate the reparative capabilities of pericytes, and will highlight new cell-based therapeutic avenues for stroke that can be safely used in patients.

column36: Disc degeneration, back pain and obesity: PPARdelta as a potential therapeutic target
column37: Back pain is the most common cause of disability worldwide, affecting over 80% of Canadians. Though the specific causes of back pain are not well understood, it is often associated with degeneration of intervertebral discs, the cartilaginous structures that anchor adjacent vertebrae along the spine. The exact cause of disc degeneration is unclear, but it is associated clinically with risk factors including age, sex, obesity and genetic variants. The health care and socio-economic burden resulting from the exceptionally high prevalence of disc degeneration and back pain requires research focused on better understanding the biological processes that regulate disease initiation in order to identify potential therapeutic targets. Our recent work has identified a potential novel treatment strategy, by identifying a role for a specific class of proteins called nuclear receptors in intervertebral disc disease. These proteins are metabolic regulators that might explain the link between obesity and disc degeneration. Using genetically modified mice we showed that when the nuclear receptor PPARdelta is removed from the intervertebral disc, mice are protected from disc degeneration. In this grant, we propose to further investigate the role of nuclear receptor activity in the intervertebral disc, using existing genetically modified mice and model systems. We will characterize how loss of PPARdelta alters age-associated and or diet-induced disc degeneration in mouse models. These studies will measure markers of degeneration in disc tissues, as well as pain related behavior in the mice. We will also use isolated mouse and human disc tissues to investigate if drug compounds that activate or block this pathway can be used to alter the health of disc tissues. These studies will determine if modulation of nuclear receptor proteins is a strategy to treat disc degeneration.

column37: Traditional chemo- and radiation-therapy, though often effective, has serious side and long-term effects, particularly for children, who face significant life-long health problems and increased risk for secondary cancers. We need to develop new "targeted therapies" that selectively attack cancer cells and leave healthy organs untouched. Targeted therapies are drugs that interfere with a specific molecule, the 'target', in the cancer cell to block its growth or kill it. The most specific targets are 'abnormal' proteins created by mutation or fusion between two genes. These abnormal proteins are found only in cancer cells, and are distinguishable from normal proteins. But they are also rare. Therefore, most targeted therapies are directed at proteins that occur in both healthy and cancer cells, and so they cause side effects. When they are uncoiled, proteins are a long chain of amino acids that have a start and an end, called the termini. The process called proteolysis cuts the protein apart, creating fragments that have different termini. We have shown that we can identify and quantify these termini in healthy and unhealthy cells, and we could show that in cancer proteolysis creates new termini not found in healthy cells. We found that there are more differences between termini than between the proteins. We now propose to study bone marrow biopsies from children with leukemia to identify cancer specific termini that have the potential to work as drug target. In addition, we will test blood and spinal fluid from these children. If we can find the other part of the protein, that has been cleaved off and released from the cancer cell, we may be able to use this fragment as very specific marker, not only for leukemia in general, but for the presence of the specific drug target. We will also investigate the mechanisms leading to the cleavage that generates the terminus and fragment. Our work will help to develop therapies that target only cancer cells.

The brain synthesizes and secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which controls production of two pituitary gland hormones, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). The answers to these questions will greatly advance our understanding of the hormonal control of reproduction, but may also identify potential treatments for human infertility disorders, including polycystic ovarian syndrome.

column36: Novel Roles for Iron Regulatory Protein 1
column37: Life on earth without iron is nearly impossible. Iron is important for many functions in our body, and probably best known for its role in transporting oxygen, allowing us to breathe. Inhaled oxygen is bound by iron, which sits at the centre of a special molecule called heme. The heme molecule itself is docked to a larger structure called hemoglobin, and together, they deliver oxygen to where it is needed via the bloodstream. These heme groups are also important for other processes in our cells, including the removal of harmful substances and the production of steroid hormones, like the famous testosterone. The King-Jones lab uses the fruit fly as a model to study undiscovered aspects of iron biology. When they studied steroid hormone-producing cells, they discovered that these cells have very high levels of iron and heme. Importantly, King-Jones and colleagues learned that they can take advantage of this system to learn new things about how humans regulate their iron "balance sheet". Since both too much and too little iron can cause severe diseases in humans, it is essential that we learn more about how iron handled in our bodies, and how this is regulated. Using a range of genetic tricks, King-Jones and colleagues have recently discovered more than 20 genes with unexpected roles in regulating and balancing appropriate iron levels. Three of these genes shed new light on how the so-called "Iron Regulatory Protein 1" (IRP1) works. Researchers have studied IRP1 for more than 30 years, and know that IRP1 is very important for our health. The new findings in the King-Jones lab show that our current ideas about how IRP1 controls proper iron balance in cells are remarkably incomplete. The study of these new, unexpected aspects of iron regulation helps us to understand better diseases that are caused by too much or too little iron.

column36: Injury Risk to Youth Skateboarders in Skateparks
column37: Skateboarding is gaining in popularity. In fact, estimates show a growth rate exceeding that of any other sport and reaching 166% yearly. With increasing growth of the sport, there has been a dramatic increase in the popularity of skateparks (SP). Municipalities are building SP to move skateboarders away from traffic, to motivate more outdoor play activities in an effort to improve health, and in response to demands from youth and parents for safe-play resources for skateboarders. Unfortunately, the increase in SPs is paralleled by an increase in injuries. In fact, in every instance that it has been studied in Canada and elsewhere, injuries post-SP openings have significantly exceeded pre-SP injury rates, resulting in significant increased health care costs. Unlike playgrounds, for which there are voluntary safety standards to reduce injury risk, SP can be built with any features - there are no safety guidelines (mandatory or voluntary). The proposed research addresses this child safety issue. The objectives will be achieved by completing two studies that capitalize on a feasibility pilot project already completed by the team. Study 1 will be an observational study of the usage patterns shown by youth (two age groups) on an outdoor SP so we can determine to what extent different features are used and the differential rate of falls for different maneuvers (tricks, typical usage) performed on those features. These findings will be used to develop a "Guidelines for Safer Design of Skateparks" manual. In Study 2 we will conduct focus group interviews with youth skateboarders, including those who have experienced a fracture on the SP, to understand their perspectives on our findings and suggestions for solutions. These findings will be used to develop a "Guide for Safer Skateboarding for Youth" which will highlight the risk behaviors that increase risk of injuries. These studies can inform future efforts to prevent injuries to youth who skateboard on skateparks.

column36: Computer vision for daily monitoring of gait instability to detect an increased risk of falling.
column37: People living in long-term care are at a high risk of falls and the negative consequences of falls, including injury or death. Falls are sometimes preceded by a change in physical functioning, and may be prevented if clinicians were alerted to this change. Available clinical assessments for measuring falls risk are of limited value because they have difficulty detecting changes in falls risk over time. We have identified a marker of unstable gait that is associated with an imminent fall in older adults. We measure this marker using video cameras that record short videos of people as they walk naturally down the corridor of their long-term care home. These videos are then processed using advances in artificial intelligence to identify joint locations and extract measurements of gait instability. On a daily basis, this system can collect information about stability when walking, and this information can then be used to identify worsening in gait stability that occur in the weeks before a fall. The aim of this project is to establish whether video-measured gait instability is a predictor of an imminent fall. Towards this aim, we will collect daily information about gait instability from people living in a long-term care home over several years. We will confirm that changes in gait instability are associated with falls. We will identify factors that are associated with worsening gait instability over time. Finally, we will develop dynamic falls risk models that incorporate clinical falls risk factors and daily measurements of gait instability, to predict someone's risk of falling over the next week or month.

column36: Food Security and Climate Change in Subarctic Canada: Challenges and Opportunities
column37: Indigenous Knowledge is a body of knowledge and beliefs transmitted orally, being both cumulative and dynamic. When there is more than one way of knowing, all ways should be used to contribute to a more complete understanding of complex issues -- such as, food security and climate change in subarctic Canada -- so that future decisions are better informed, and actions taken, more appropriate. Food security exists when people have access to safe, nutritionally adequate, and culturally appropriate food required for a healthy life. Taking into account that subarctic Canada is being disproportionately impacted by climate warming, there are challenges associated with climate change, such as, the changing of migratory patterns of waterfowl and the overpopulation of geese. However, the warming climate also offers opportunities for the growth of fruits and vegetables under ambient conditions in northern Canada. Our research will evaluate the scaled-up version of the Sharing-the-Harvest initiative in subarctic Canada. To evaluate the initiative, we will use both quantitative and qualitative methods. We are trying to identify the key elements of this harmonized land-based program of traditional pursuits (e.g. goose harvesting) and non-traditional activities (e.g. sustainable agriculture) that promotes health and wellness, in the context of food security and climate change. Our long-term goal is to develop a best practices framework to help inform existing and future land-based initiatives. The proposed study will provide Indigenous communities, health care professionals, and policy makers with new information on health and wellness, with respect to land-based initiatives, in the context of food security and climate change.

column36: Defining the peroxisome-lipid signaling network in innate immunity.
column37: Organisms need an efficient and tightly controlled immune system to defend against infections and cancer. Recently, scientists discovered that immune cells change their "font of energy" and the way they use and transform it (metabolism) to augment the fight against an immune challenge. Peroxisomes are structures found in every cell that control important processes in metabolism. We found that peroxisomes are central regulators of an organism's immune system. Peroxisomes in immune cells are important for producing and managing molecules like "fats" and hydrogen peroxide that are needed to turn on or off immune responses such as the engulfment of invading microbes or cancer cells. Our discovery added a previously unknown contributor to the growing number of cellular "players" that control the immune response. Knowing how the immune responses function is quintessential to understand the mechanisms of diseases of immune disorders and to find new and more effective cures. We use the fruit fly as a model system in our studies to dissect the mechanisms of diseases. We use the fruit fly because their genes can be easily manipulated and they have basic cellular processes, including aspects of immune defense, that are similar to those in humans. Thus, studies in fruit fly can help us to quickly define the mechanisms by which peroxisomes function during systemic immune responses and then transfer our discovery to human health. Our research program aims to define 1) how peroxisomes contribute to changing metabolism in immune cells to activate their "defense mode' during microbial challenge; 2) how immune cells use "fats" to control an organism's way to fight an infection; and 3) how conserved in mammals are the mechanisms and pathways found in fruit flies, so that we can exploit peroxisomes as a disease marker for immune disorders and as therapeutic targets for new and more efficient drugs to treat patients with immune deficiency, autoimmune disease and cancer.

column36: Understanding what pretangle tau does to neurons and testing potential damage control by an anti-cis-ptau treatment
column37: New evidence from human brains reveals that the earliest sign of the possible development of Alzheimer's Disease is the appearance of a protein called pretangle tau in brainstem neurons even at young ages. In older brains one of the major signs of Alzheimer's Disease is tau tangles and this pretangle tau is its precursor. Over years pretangle tau spreads from the brainstem neurons to other neurons, finally appearing in most of the brain's cortical neurons in advanced Alzheimer's Disease. We have used gene insertion techniques to put pretangle human tau into rat brainstem neurons. In this experimental model, the human pretangle material spreads from brainstem neurons to other brain areas over time as has been described in humans. Pretangle tau rats also develop odor discrimination problems later in life as reported in humans who are likely to go on to experience more severe memory loss. Inserting pretangle tau in the brainstem neurons of middle aged rats produces worse effects. In a shorter time they begin to lose neurons and have severe learning problems. Now we want to know how pretangle tau changes neurons at first and over time. We will look at the brainstem neurons where Alzheimer's Disease begins and at the cortical neurons needed for olfactory discrimination and for life memories. We will use electrophysiology and genetic methods to learn how pretangles change neuron function over time and we will try to identify therapies by which negative changes can be prevented. We will also test the hypothesis that pretangle tau changes its structure in a small way before it becomes toxic to neurons and that preventing this change in pretangle tau structure can prevent the bad effects of pretangles and prevent the development of Alzheimer's Disease.

column36: Role of transcription factor NFAT5 in viral myocarditis: a novel strategy for therapy
column37: In North America and globally, heart disease is still the leading cause of death. Viral myocarditis (damage of heart muscle cells by viral infection) is an infectious heart disease. Coxsackie-virus is a very common cause of myocarditis, particularly in children and people < 40 years old. This disease can often lead to heart failure and sudden unexpected death. Currently, there is no effective treatment or vaccine available. To develop a treatment, it is essential to first understand how the virus destroys the heart muscle cells during infection. In our early experiments to identify the genes damaged by viral infection, we found that a gene called NFAT5 may be of importance. The NFAT5 gene is initially known to be protective to our body through study of kidney disease. However, its role in the heart is not known. We found that NFAT5 can protect the heart by enhancing production of protective proteins against coxsackie-virus infection. However, we further found that NFAT5 protein is damaged by viral infection (i.e., the virus cuts the NFAT5 protein into 2 fragments); this damage decreases the ability of heart cells to defend against infection, leading to increased viral growth and heart muscle cell injury. To better understand this mechanism, we will grow mouse heart muscle cells in Petri dishes and replace the full-length NFAT5 gene with NFAT5-fragments in these cells to mimic the viral infection. The anti-viral activities of the cells containing the full-length NFAT5 gene will be compared to those cells that have the NFAT5 fragments. We will also do a similar experiment using genetically modified mice. These studies will help us confirm that virus-caused damage of the NFAT5 gene can increase viral multiplication and lead to heart muscle cell death. Based on these results, we will have a better understanding on why viral infection can cause heart disease and how we can prevent and treat this disease by enhancing NFAT5 protein production in our body.
