column36: Neurosteroid regulation of executive function
column37: Steroid hormones are very powerful, and they have widespread and profound effects on human health and behaviour. Steroid hormones are critical for the brain to develop and function normally, and they also play important roles in psychiatric and neurological diseases. The brain is generally considered a recipient of blood-borne steroids from peripheral organs, such as the gonads and adrenal glands, but the brain can also locally synthesize its own steroids (neurosteroids). My recent studies discovered that a key circuit within the brain, the mesocorticolimbic dopamine system, locally synthesizes testosterone and contains receptors for testosterone. This circuit regulates higher order cognition and executive function, including decision making and behavioural flexibility. This project aims to understand how neurosteroids affect the mesocorticolimbic system, dopamine signaling, and executive function. In particular, the research will use cutting-edge techniques to map neurosteroids in this circuit and will use pharmacological and genetic tools to dissect the roles of gonadal and neural steroids in executive function. This project will improve our understanding of how steroid hormones act on the brain, including the prefrontal cortex, to impact higher order cognitive processes. Such knowledge will help in the design of novel hormone treatments for psychiatric and neurological diseases, including those that are characterized by deficits in executive function.

column36: Kinesin motor protein dynamics and mitotic mechanisms in Candida albicans
column37: Fungi are significant and increasing mediators of pathogenesis; causing serious challenges medically and economically. Candida albicans is the most prevalent cause of fungal infections in people, and can cause life-threatening systemic infections if our immune defenses are compromised. A battery of fitness attributes promote the pathogenicity and drug resistance of this fungus, most of which arise by rapid generation of genetic diversity within a population in response to stressful growth conditions, such as exposure to antifungal drugs, as a means of adaptation. Research has shown that aneuploidy (an abnormal number of chromosomes) accounts for much of this diversity, and that this condition often arises from changes in components of the chromosome segregation machinery. Our findings indicate that some of these changes could be induced or enabled by kinesin motor proteins that regulate the structure of the cell's chromosome segregation apparatus - 'the mitotic spindle'. By addressing central questions about how kinesins control the assembly and function of the mitotic spindle, and how they integrate spindle function with cell division, we will provide insight into an important mutational process generating chromosome aberrations in fungal genomes that lead to drug resistance.

column36: Improving treatment for GRIN disorders
column37: GRIN disorders are caused by mutations in the GRIN genes, which carry the instructions to make NMDA receptors. When children are born with these mutations, they have intellectual disability and often have other symptoms like movement disorders, loss of muscle tone, developmental delays, and seizures. Some patients are able to attend school, while others are non-verbal and must use a wheelchair. We want to understand the reasons why some patients have a milder phenotype than other patients. We also want to determine what the best treatment strategy should be. GRIN disorder is a new diagnosis that has only been made possible because of genome sequencing, and the long-term prognosis and best treatments are still not known. Therefore, we will use mouse models that harbor patient disease-causing mutations, and will study the phenotypes of these mice and test a number of therapeutic interventions. In Specific Aim 1, we study NMDA receptor biochemistry and function in model animals. In Specific Aim 2, we assess behavioural phenotypes to determine whether the severity of phenotypes parallels that of the patients. In Specific Aim 3, we test treatments for their ability to improve neurological impairments caused by mutations in GRIN genes.

column36: Novel treatment to establish spatial hearing in children who are deaf
column37: Over 1 in 1000 children have permanent hearing loss and need early treatment and therapy to help them develop speech and language. We showed that many children hear better with two rather than one hearing device but that they still have a very hard time listening. Normally, the auditory system combines information from our two ears together seamlessly to help us hear each sound around us and to know where each sound is coming from. This "spatial" hearing is very important because this is how we sense the world in all directions around us and how we pick out and focus on one sound at a time to listen to. The problem is that children with hearing loss are not developing spatial hearing properly. We want to fix this by making sure that two hearing aids or two cochlear implants work well together like two normal hearing ears do. We use responses from the auditory brainstem to tell us when sound from both ears is best matched and then reset the devices to send sound in this new way for >100 children with hearing loss (>50 using two hearing aids and >50 using two cochlear implants). We ask each child to use the new device settings for 12 months. After the first 6 months, we measure changes in responses from the auditory system and the children's ability to hear from both ears. Sound localization therapy in half of the group begins at this time. After 12 months, we test whether children can better hear where sound is located and better understand spoken words in a noisy room. We also do the same tests in >100 similar children with hearing loss and >50 children with normal hearing so that we know how well the treatments have worked and how close these children with hearing loss have come to listening normally. We are known around the world for showing that it is important to give children hearing in both ears. We now have to correct the gaps in present treatment so that they can make the best use of their hearing devices to develop the spatial hearing they need.

column36: Altered vitamin A homeostasis and retinoic acid signaling in the development of congenital diaphragmatic hernia
column37: A newborn baby's first breath is driven by the contraction of the diaphragm, a muscle we all use unconsciously thousands of time every day to aid breathing. Try to imagine what happens if the diaphragm does not form properly during pregnancy. If a hole forms in the growing diaphragm, the liver can grow up into the developing baby's chest and prevent the lungs from growing. At birth, their incomplete diaphragm and crushed lungs mean these babies have a very difficult time breathing and they require intensive care - many will not survive the first week of life. Mercifully uncommon, this birth defect is called Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH), and its cause is unknown. The research proposed in this application is intended to answer questions surrounding the cause of CDH, and hopefully improve the health outcomes for these critically ill babies. Vitamin A is an essential part of the diet, while it is widely known for its role in vision, it is also an extremely important signaling molecule with many different roles in the body. This proposal's specific research question is uniquely focused on how problems with vitamin A signaling in the developing diaphragm may cause CDH. We aim to address this question in three novel ways: 1) develop an animal (mouse) model of CDH caused by specifically blocking how vitamin A signals in the growing diaphragm, 2) determine how important a mother's vitamin A status and intake is for susceptibility to CDH in an animal model, and 3) better understand how vitamin A signaling controls specific genes that have been associated with clinical cases of CDH. While we are using experimental models to answer our research questions, our work is guided by clinical observations. This 'bedside to bench' approach means our research is informed by actual cases of CDH, with the ultimate goal of taking new knowledge generated by our research back to the clinic to improve the outcomes of CDH.

column36: Perennial Policy Issues in Directly-Funded Home Care in Canada: An Intersectional, Qualitative Study to enhance Social and Health Outcomes
column37: The organization and delivery of quality home care services for long-term care needs associated with aging and disability is one of today's greatest health policy challenges. Directly-funded (DF) home care provides government funds to individuals to arrange assistance with the activities of daily living. DF, also referred to as 'self-managed' home care, may relieve the strain on home care systems and is expanding across Canada. While promising, emerging evidence suggests DF home care may exacerbate health inequities when scaled up. Our research team proposes the question: How can DF home care programs be designed to enhance social and health outcomes for diverse home care clients, informal supports, and care workers in Canadian contexts? We hone in on three perennial policy issues - that is, areas in which consensus has not been reached and that present challenges to equitable service delivery. First, we consider the role of home care agencies in DF service delivery. The role of non-profit and for-profit home care agencies is unclear and there may be health equity implications compared to a 'hire-your-neighbour' approach historically endorsed in DF programs. Secondly, we consider the implications of expanding DF to a larger portion of home care users in contrast to focusing on specific groups of people. Finally, we explore how to best adapt DF for rural contexts. Framed with the concepts of intersectionality and health equity, our 5-year study will take place in four provinces (Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Newfoundland & Labrador). We will use a variety of qualitative methods, including an environmental scan, focus groups, key informant and lived-experience interviews, and content and discourse analysis. Our study aims to generate insights about how DF can most equitably serve users, their families and supports, and workers.

column36: Effects of added sucrose on hormones, neural circuits, and behaviour
column37: Sugars such as sucrose (table sugar) are extremely common in the diet, in Canada and across the world. The World Health Organization advises that added sugars should make up 5% or less of daily calories for adults, and even less for children under 2 years. However, in Canada, adults and children often greatly exceed these recommendations. Of particular concern, added sugars during early development might have major and long-lasting effects on hormones, neural circuits, and behaviour. This project will use an animal model to experimentally determine how maternal consumption of sucrose during pregnancy and lactation affects the offspring. This project will examine the long-lasting effects on adult offspring, including important hormones, brain chemicals, and behaviours. Overall, this project will help us understand how maternal diet "programs" hormones, the brain reward system, and sugar-seeking behaviour in the offspring. The results will have important implications for the health of Canadians because very little is known about how added sugars affect brain circuits.

column36: The Muscarinic Hypothesis of Schizophrenia: A [18F]-FP-TZTP PET Study
column37: Acetylcholine is a natural chemical in the brain that carries signals between brain neurons. It is released by one set of neurons, called cholinergic neurons, and attaches to muscarinic and nicotinic 'receptors' on other sets of neurons. This is known as the cholinergic system. There are several types of nicotinic and muscarinic receptors (e.g. M1, M2, M3, M4, and M5). Changes in acetycholine levels and a reduction in the number of muscarinic receptors are thought to contribute to the symptoms of schizophrenia. Many medications, including common over-the-counter medications like diphenhydramine (aka Benadryl), act on muscarinic receptors. They can produce symptoms similar to that of schizophrenia when taken at toxic doses, such as confusion and hallucinations. However, little research has focused on the role of muscarinic receptors in schizophrenia. The M2 receptor is thought to control the release of acetylcholine in the striatum, a part of the brain directly related to the symptoms of schizophrenia. M2 is the first muscarinic receptor that can be studied independent of the others using the brain imaging technique PET (Positron Emission Tomography). With the discovery of a compound the binds preferentially to M2 receptors, it is now possible to measure their amount and location within the brain. The current study therefore seeks to quantify the amount of M2 receptors in patients with schizophrenia. To do this we will: (1) compare 20 patients with good response to antipsychotic treatment with 20 healthy controls matched for age, sex, and smoking status, and (2) determine the statistical relationship between the symptoms of schizophrenia and the quantity of M2 receptors. The results of this study may lead to a new diagnostic marker for schizophrenia, increase our understanding of the pathophysiology of the disease, and provide a new target for treatment.

column36: A Randomized Clinical Trial of At-Home Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) for Depression in Pregnancy
column37: Major depression affects up to 10% of pregnant women. Untreated or undertreated, it can have negative and long-lasting effects on a pregnant woman and her developing child. Standard depression treatments such as psychotherapy and medication are not ideal in pregnancy. Psychotherapies require time to take effect, and work less well for severe depression. Antidepressant drugs can improve symptoms in weeks, but there are concerns, not unfounded, about their safety for the fetus, limiting desire for use by patients and physicians. There is evidence that as few as 20% of pregnant women with depression receive adequate care for their illness. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is an effective localized brain stimulation treatment for depression that changes brain activity specifically in the area of the brain targeting depression, so it poses no theoretical risk to a developing fetus. The tDCS equipment is affordable and portable, and women can be trained in its use for self-administration at-home. So, if it is shown to be safe and effective, there is significant potential for it to be widely used. In our pilot study, pregnant women's views of tDCS were very positive, and there was no evidence of impact on the developing fetus. Furthermore, women receiving tDCS had fewer depressive symptoms after 3 weeks of treatment than women receiving a placebo treatment - and after delivery, they had a lower risk of remaining depressed postpartum. We now propose a large trial to definitively evaluate tDCS as a treatment for depression in pregnancy, recruiting over 150 women, and following them and their children to evaluate the impact of tDCS on maternal and child health during pregnancy and until 1 year postpartum. We expect that this trial will provide evidence for a strategy around treatment of depression in pregnancy that could reach a large number of women in Canada and beyond, and promote positive health outcomes in this vulnerable maternal-child population.

column36: Adult Mental and Social Health Outcomes of Peer Victimization: The Role of Neural and Physiological Responses to Social Challenges and Stress
column37: In Canada, up to a third of girls and boys are bullied by their peers. Depression symptoms are the most frequently reported consequence for bullying victims. For some, these negative consequences persist into young adulthood and beyond. Chronic peer victimization in school also increases the risk of revictimization in other contexts (e.g., in college, at work or in dating relationships) later in life. Adverse experiences such as peer victimization are thought to trigger lasting changes in how our brain works and the way our body responds to stress. However, the extent to which these neural and physiological responses are involved in explaining the long-term effects of peer victimization on mental and social health problems in emerging adulthood is still poorly understood. Equally important is the identification of factors that can protect against disrupted neural and physiological responses and long-term health problems in adulthood. To address these issues, we will use a genetically informed design involving 425 twin pairs who were regularly followed since birth until age 20. We propose to build on this rich data set with a new data collection in young adulthood (age 25) to examine participants' brain reactivity as well as their cardiac and hormonal responses during exposure to socially challenging and stressful lab tasks. Current depression symptoms as well as current victimization experiences and social support will also be assessed. An overarching aim will be to investigate possible sex- and gender-related differences in these associations. This research project will contribute to our understanding of how the well-known differences in depression and victimization rates between adult women and men develop. It will also offer important information about protective factors that can be used by health professionals to promote a healthy transition to adulthood for female and male victims of school bullying.

column36: Dissecting the role of the claustrum in anxiety
column37: Mood and anxiety disorders are the number one class of mental illness in Canada. Understanding the connections in the brain that support normal and abnormal anxiety remains a high priority for basic and translational biomedical research. Neural activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays a vital role in managing anxiety levels, and brain regions connected to the PFC have been shown to contribute to the generation of anxiety. The claustrum is a small subcortical nucleus that receives input from other anxiety related brain regions and sends axonal outputs to the PFC. Therefore, the claustrum is positioned to participate in the generation or modulation of anxiety. Due to technical difficulties associated with measuring and manipulating neural activity in this small nucleus, its role in anxiety-related behaviors has not been systematically investigated. We have devised a strategy to specifically measure and manipulate neural activity in claustrum neurons projecting to the PFC. This grant proposal outlines a series of experiments that will determine how neural activity in the claustrum participates in generating or modulating anxiety in mice. The results will provide insight into the function of this previously overlooked brain region and determine its role in anxiety processing. Treatments for anxiety-related disorders will benefit from the basic neurobiological knowledge generated through this project, as the claustrum presents a new brain structure that can be targeted by novel anxiolytic pharmacological agents.

column36: Sex Matters: Understanding Sex Differences in Exercise Efficacy on Brain Health in Mild Cognitive Impairment
column37: Developing dementia is one of the greatest fears of aging. In fact, many fear it more than cancer. Unfortunately, it is estimated that the number of individuals with dementia will only rapidly increase over the next few decades. Thus, the societal value of identifying and developing effective intervention strategies against dementia cannot be overstated. Exercise is a promising strategy for dementia prevention. However, a large degree of variation exists in the observed benefit of exercise on cognition in older adults. Data suggest that older women's thinking abilities and brains may benefit more than older men from exercise. Yet, no intervention study to date have been designed to specifically and comprehensively examine this possible sex difference. Dedicated examination of this possible sex difference is needed because there are more Canadian women with dementia than men, while more men may be at risk for dementia than women. In this proposed study, we will study whether biological sex (i.e., female versus male) alters the impact of exercise on cognitive function in older adults who are at risk for dementia (i.e., mild cognitive impairment). Older adults with mild cognitive impairment represent an ideal target population for intervention strategies, as the preservation of their cognitive function will likely maintain and prolong their ability to live independently and with quality. We will also study how exercise improves cognitive function and whether the "how" is different between older women and older men. The health and financial burden imposed by dementia is immense. Our proposed study could have major impact in Canada and internationally by advancing our ability to use "exercise as medicine" in a specific manner for older women and older men to promote healthy cognitive aging and prevent dementia.

column37: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a genetic condition characterized by marked elevation in the blood of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C, the "bad" cholesterol). FH affects 1 in 250 Canadians, making it among the most common genetic disorders in humans and one of the most common causes of premature cardiovascular disease and death. We expect approximately 140,000 cases in Canada. FH is under-recognized and under-treated world-wide and in Canada, more than 85% of cases are undiagnosed. New approaches to identify and diagnose these patients are urgently needed. Genetic testing for FH is widely endorsed internationally, but is not widely available in Canada. National registries of FH play a key role in increasing the detection of patients with FH and improving management and outcomes. We created the FH Canada National Registry (www.FHCanada.net), which recruits patients with FH from 19 academic medical centers and many clinics across the country; as of July 2019, we have recruited over 4400 patients. Our hypotheses are that a personalized approach to diagnosis and risk prediction will increase the identification of patients with FH in Canada, and that a coordinated national registry will facilitate access to appropriate therapies, and reduce the burden of premature cardiovascular disease and death in Canadians with FH. The specific objectives of this proposal are: 1) Predict ASCVD risk in patients with FH using a specific risk algorithm and genetic diagnosis. We will also examine the 10-year survival in our cohort. 2) Identify the patient-specific barriers to care, especially the patient's sex and gender through an innovative questionnaire. We will then determine if knowledge of the genetic diagnosis has an impact on the intensity of statin treatment, adherence to medication and compliance with current guidelines. 3) We will implement change through performance indicators collected through the FHCanada registry and a process of feedback to physicians.

column36: Does the use of higher versus lower oxygen concentration improve neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18-24 months in very low birthweight infants? - The HiLo-Trial
column37: Preterm birth, or birth before 37 weeks gestation, is increasingly common, occurring in 8% of pregnancies in Canada. Preterm birth is associated with many health complications, particularly when the birth happens before 29 weeks gestation. At this gestational age, the lungs are not fully developed and it is not uncommon for infants to have problems breathing at the time of birth. One complication that can arise is when an infant stops breathing and needs to be resuscitated. When preterm babies need to be resuscitated doctors must take special care because of the small infant size and the immaturity of the brain and lungs. Oxygen is used to resuscitate babies who need it, but unfortunately there is disagreement about the best oxygen concentration to use. Oxygen concentration is important because both too much and too little oxygen can cause brain injury. Our research aims to fill this knowledge gap by participating in an international clinical trial to compare the effects of resuscitating babies less than 29 weeks gestational age with either a low oxygen concentration or a high oxygen concentration. The oxygen concentrations have been selected using the best available knowledge. During the first 12 months of the clinical trial we will treat all babies less than 29 weeks gestation who need resuscitation with the oxygen concentration we are randomly assigned. After 12 months we will reassess and then in the next 12 months we will treat babies using the other oxygen concentration. After the trial we will determine whether the babies resuscitated with lower oxygen or those resuscitated with higher oxygen have better survival and long-term health outcomes. Our research fills a critical knowledge gap in the care of extremely preterm babies and will impact their survival both here in Canada and internationally.

column36: Regulation of SLC43A3 expression and function, and its impact on 6-mercaptopurine cytotoxicity and resistance in the treatment of leukemia
column37: 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP) is used in combination with other drugs to treat acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL). It is well known that not all patients respond to this drug to the same degree, with the therapeutic success rate declining with patient age. To be effective, 6-MP must gain access to the inside of the target leukemia cells. Therapeutic effectiveness as well as the severity of the 'off-target' side-effects of these drugs can thus be influenced by the activity of the 'transporters' in the cell membrane that 6-MP uses to get into the cells. Until recently, the identity of the transporters for 6-MP was unknown. This has now changed with the identification of a protein called ENBT1, encoded by the gene SLC43A3, which we propose to be the primary mechanism by which 6-MP gets into leukemia cells. We will determine how this novel protein transports 6-MP and assess other potential drug interactions. We will also use animal and isolated cell models to see whether blockade of this transport protein leads to reduced effectiveness of 6-MP and/or changes to its side-effect profile. We will also examine ways in which the number of these transporters can be increased in leukemia cells to make 6- MP even more effective. Finally, we will obtain blood and bone marrow samples from patients suffering from leukaemia and examine these for their level of SLC43A3 activity, and then correlate this information with the responsiveness of these patients to 6-MP. Understanding how this novel transport protein influences the therapeutic activity of 6-MP drugs will allow new clinical protocols to be developed to guide drug choice and enhance treatment of leukaemia.

column36: Endocannabinoid Regulation of Stress Responsive Neural Circuits
column37: The endocannabinoid (eCB) system--the biological system through which THC from cannabis exerts its effects on the bran and body through-- is widely recognized as an important regulator of the stress response. Impairments in eCB signaling both produce activation of stress responses in and of itself, and potentiates the effects of stress exposure, while elevations in eCB signaling are well established to dampen many aspects of the stress response. While there is ample evidence, from rodents to humans, which demonstrates that eCB signaling is an important stress regulatory system, there a notable knowledge gaps regarding where in the brain eCB signaling acts to dampen stress responses. The primary goal of the current proposal will be to determine the mechanisms and processes within the brain by which eCB signaling dampens stress responses. Given that many pharmaceutical companies are developing drugs which target the eCB system as novel treatment approaches to treating stress-related psychiatric illnesses, such as anxiety disorders and post-traumatic stress disorder, understanding how eCB signaling regulates how stress impacts the brain is of significant importance. This proposal will determine the brain sites of action, and neural circuits influenced by eCB signaling, to develop a roadmap of the anti-stress effects of eCB signaling. This research will focus on the amygdala, a brain region important for threat detection and the generation of an anxiety state following stress exposure, as well as the hypothalamus, which coordinates the release of stress hormones after exposure to a challenge. Ultimately these data may be coupled to circuit-specific neuroimaging studies in humans to determine which stress-related illnesses may be particularly benefited by drugs which boost eCB signaling.

column36: Rewiring diabetic axons: rescue, regrowth and repurposing insulin
column37: Over half of all persons with diabetes mellitus, either type 1 or 2, develop polyneuropathy, or nerve damage. This entails loss of sensation in their skin, first in the feet then other areas of the body. Polyneuropathy develops because of progressive damage to sensory neurons that supply this sensation. Not only is there loss of sensation but also pain, with loss of balance and failure to recognize injury. Diabetic polyneuropathy predisposes people toward skin ulceration and amputation. There is no proven treatment in humans to arrest or reverse this chronic damage. The Zochodne laboratory is working on new ways to rescue sensory neurons from degeneration. This involves understanding why neuron branches, or axons for example in the skin, degenerate and disappear and fail to regenerate. These events may, surprisingly, also involve insulin, an action unrelated to its glucose lowering role. Here the Zochodne laboratory proposes to study and manipulate molecules that determine if axons can be rescued and regenerated in diabetes. The work involves finding molecules that support neurons from diabetic mice (culture studies) and applying these possible treatments to mice with experimental diabetes, including long term chronic disease, who show neuropathy similar to that experienced by humans. Preliminary work in the laboratory indicates that new approaches including insulin itself, or sensitizing its receptors so that it can be more effective, can slow degeneration and prompt regeneration of axons.These actions of insulin do not depend on its blood glucose lowering role. The laboratory plans to analyze how insulin supports nerves and how related and newer molecules may help.

column37: Over 125 million pregnancies annually are at risk of complications from malaria that threaten the life of the mother and fetus. A vaccine to protect pregnant women from malaria is urgently needed and can save an estimated 10,000 mothers and 200,000 newborns from death, particularly in Africa. Currently, vaccines are under development that target a specific protein made by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum when it infects the placenta. Women who are immunized with this protein will form antibodies that should protect them from placental infection. However, this approach is not likely to be highly effective since the parasite has the ability to produce different forms of the protein and hide from the vaccine. We made the unexpected discovery that women in Colombia have some natural protection from malaria in pregnancy. As we examined this further, we found that women who had been exposed to a different species of malaria found in Colombia called Plasmodium vivax were protected against falciparum malaria, the main species that endangers pregnant women. We already discovered one protein from P. vivax that contains a segment that can induce antibodies to protect against falciparum malaria in pregnancy. In this project we will generate different synthetic versions of this segment and pursue these as vaccine candidates against falciparum placental malaria. We will measure how these candidates induce protective antibodies in pre-clinical studies of mice, in preparation for future vaccine trials in humans. The ultimate goal is to exploit these findings to develop an alternative approach to a vaccine to protect pregnant women from malaria.

column36: Non-classical mechanisms for leukocyte recruitment in the lungs: therapeutic targets for attenuating acute lung injury
column37: The innate immune system plays a critical component of initial host defense. The recruitment of immune cells to sites of infection, immune reaction or injury is complex and requires a multistep adhesion cascade between the leukocytes (white blood cells) and the endothelial cells that line the vasculature. The classic paradigm for leukocyte recruitment involves the adhesive tethering, rolling followed by firm adhesion on the activated vasculature wall and involves the timely activation of the integrin and selectin families of adhesion receptors. Although this paradigm does hold true for a number of organs there is an increasing number of exceptions including the liver and lung microvasculature where the integrins and selectins play a small role if any. We and others have contributed to an evolving paradigm change in the identification of new organ-specific inflammatory molecules that mediate leukocyte activation and recruitment in different organs. Herein, we provide evidence that a specific molecule known as DPEP1 acts as a physical adhesion receptor for a specific type of white blood cell called neutrophils within the liver and lung blood vessels after stimulation with a bacterial component known as LPS. DPEP1 represents the first major adhesion receptor identified on lung endothelium. We propose that DPEP1 be added to the growing list of non-classical adhesion molecules, and accordingly represents a novel target for anti-inflammatory therapy for diseases of the lungs where acute and chronic inflammation is involved in the pathogenesis.

column37: In Canada, 8% of all babies are born prematurely. To survive, they need help with breathing either with high oxygen and/or a machine such as respirator. However, both high oxygen and respirator can damage babies' lungs. To decrease lung injury, we use less invasive machine called continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or place them on Humidified Heated High Air Flow via Nasal Cannula (HHFNC). Feeding by mouth is also a big challenge for premature babies. When very small, they are fed via a tube placed in their stomach through mouth or nose. Usually, babies are ready to take small milk volumes by mouth after 32 wk of gestation (full-term = 40 wk). Health care providers worry that if babies are breast or bottle-fed while on CPAP machine or on HHFNC, they might inhale milk in their lungs, which could make them very sick. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that it is safe to breast/bottle-feed babies while they are needing help with breathing. In this research proposal, we will extend our studies from pilot to a larger number of babies to examine if it is, indeed, safe to feed them orally while they are being helped via CPAP or HHFNC. We will use our feeding protocol known as Safe Individualized Nipple-feeding Competence protocol, where we increase oral feeds starting at only 5% of the total volume and gradually increase it to full breast/bottle intake. We plan to record and analyze cardiac and respiratory responses, and blood oxygen levels as the babies progress through increasing volumes of oral feeding while still on CPAP or HHFNC. We believe that starting smaller oral volumes of feeds and gradually increasing them, 1) the infants will learn to coordinate breathing and feeding skills leading to early discharge home, 2) less home-tube feeding, 3) improved overall development, 4) promote parent-baby interaction and 5) reduce health care costs. Our study has the potential to change the current way how we manage respiratory care in premature infants.

column36: Unraveling the molecular basis of novel forms of hypomyelinating leukodystrophies
column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of genetic diseases affecting previously healthy children, leading to progressive disabilities and death over months to years. Unfortunately, no curative treatment is available for most of these children, a situation only exacerbated by the fact that an estimated 20-30% of patients remain without a precise diagnosis despite extensive clinical testing. Finding the cause of these diseases, the erroneous gene, is the first step towards finding a cure. Leukodystrophies are characterized by abnormalities in the white matter of the brain, whose main component, the myelin, is needed to insulate brain cells (neurons), protect them, and allow fast electrical conduction necessary in the nervous system. Leukodystrophies are classified as hypomyelinating (lack of myelin formation) and non-hypomyelinating (unhealthy myelin) based on distinguishing features seen in brain scans. This research project focuses on identifying new genes that cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and understanding how errors in these genes lead to disease. Children with these errors in these genes develop progressive difficulties that affect their walking, talking, swallowing, and reduce their quality of life. This project will allow patients and their families to have a proper diagnosis, one of the most important tools to obtain proper genetic counselling and make family-planning decisions, as well as open the door for the discovery of treatments.

column36: Using data to guide population health management: A comprehensive evaluation of analytic approaches for population segmentation
column37: The goal of segmentation is to separate the population intro groups according to health status and health care needs so that the health system can manage care in a way that best matches those needs with different strategies. Experts use different ways to form these meaningful groups including based on expert-opinion of groups of conditions, as well data-driven approaches based on health billing data, and to a lesser extent models that predict future health need. Managing the population using these approaches would be very useful for managing a health system for a population within a province or in Canada. However, despite the enthusiasm, there remains some significant gaps that prevent these approaches from being used. Firstly, very few of these methods are validated or tested in populations before they are planned for use. For example, although approaches have been applied to the Canadian data, they have not been done with the intention of integrating for population health management and testing with leaders that work in the health system. This has significant implications on the way health services and resources are managed and affect both costs and health outcomes. The second major gap is that most of these models focus on how people already use health care already, which limits the characteristics that need is based, particularly missing characteristics that are not available in traditional health care utilization data such as socioeconomic status or ethnicity. This limits the ability to plan care for different groups in the population. The final gap is that very few health system administrators know what to do with the outputs of these models to inform the way our health system is run. By rigorously testing existing and new approaches to segmentation and by studying the impact in a decision-making organization, this grant will result in the important opportunity to better use data to inform health system management.

column36: Endothelial cell genetics and blood pressure regulation
column37: Hypertension, or high blood pressure, affects >1 billion people in the World and is a major risk factor for several vascular diseases, including stroke, heart attack and heart failure. Endothelial cells, which form the inner layer of blood vessels, actively module the vascular tone by secreting vasoactive molecules. In this project, we will use human genetic and functional genomic approaches to identify the genes that control how endothelial cells influence blood pressure in humans. This project will lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms that lead to hypertension, and might guide to the development of better therapies.

column36: Mobilizing early management of mental health complications after mild traumatic brain injury (M4)
column37: People who sustain a concussion (also known as a mild traumatic brain injury) often develop mental health problems such as depression and anxiety. Mental health problems can make concussion symptoms worse and magnify difficulties with daily activities. Best practice guidelines recommend that family doctors routinely screen for mental health problems after concussion and if present, start treatment or refer to a mental health specialist. Unfortunately, this does not happen in the majority of cases. Depression and anxiety are frequently missed, and treatment is delayed. Drawing on theories of behaviour change, we have developed a strategy for supporting family doctors to implement mental health screening and early treatment after concussion. Patients will learn about the study when they attend a local Emergency Department. After leaving the Emergency Department, they will complete standardized questionnaires that screen for depression and anxiety. The screening test results will be shared with their family doctor, along with advice from best practice guidelines about which mental health treatments are most likely to work. A portion of the patients in the study will also receive written education about the significance of mental health problems after concussion and a decision-aid to help them discuss treatment options with their family doctor. For comparison, some doctors and patients will not receive any screening test results or specific recommendations. The study findings should help us understand how to ensure that the 250,000 Canadians a year who get a concussion will be checked for mental health problems, and directed to an effective treatment without delay.

column36: Optimizing audit and feedback: Personalizing delivery according to team differences
column37: Health systems around the world continue to invest in generating and analyzing routinely generated clinical data for research and quality improvement in Canada. Performance feedback initiatives have emerged as an increasingly popular strategy to utilize this data to support individual performance improvement, presenting substantial promise for improving the quality of healthcare delivery. The science of performance feedback is growing rapidly in order to identify how best to design and deliver these initiatives to maximize their impact. Much of this work has focused on design features and characteristics of individual recipient; however the reality is the majority of healthcare providers deliver care in team-based environments. This work will explore differences in team culture, learning, beliefs about feedback, and readiness to change to understand how they contribute to variations in the quality of patient care. We will identify which aspects of individual and team differences might need to be addressed in order to successfully improve individual performance. Results will provide actionable insights for an emerging performance feedback initiative in a hospital setting (the GEMINI program) while advancing the broader scientific understanding about how best to implement data-driven performance feedback for physicians working in team environments.

column36: Investigating the structure and function of the human autophagy regulator EPG5
column37: Autophagy is an essential "junk removal" system used by all cells in our bodies to package large objects such as cellular organelles and protein aggregates and deliver these packages to the "cellular incinerator" the lysosome for breakdown. Malfunction of autophagy affects the normal balance between production and breakdown and has been shown to lead to a wide range of human diseases from neurodegeneration, cancer, to infectious diseases. To determine how autophagy is disrupted in the disease state, our laboratory is trying to obtain a comprehensive understanding of how autophagy operates at the molecular level through studying the dedicated protein machinery that coordinates this multi-step process. This project grant application focuses on EPG5, a recently identified component of this machinery that makes sure packages containing the "junk" are correctly delivered to lysosome for breakdown. Furthermore, mutation to EPG5 causes a serious genetic disease called Vici syndrome characterized by incomplete development of the brain and immunodeficiency. Using advanced molecular visualization methods including single-particle electron microscopy (EM) and X-ray crystallography, we will capture the overall shape or detailed molecular structure of this protein. The acquired structural information, together with results from other complementary biochemical and cell-based experiments that we will conduct, will enable us to determine the molecular bases of how EPG5 recognizes the junk packages and the lysosome, and generate mechanistic insights into EPG5's role in autophagy. In the long term, our research will pave the way for the development of autophagy-targeted therapeutics for treating different human diseases, and improve the quality of life of the large number of Canadians suffering from these disorders.

column36: Drugging Beta Arrestin Signaling Interfaces
column37: G protein coupled receptors (GPCR) are the main target of existing pharmacological agents.These receptors signal via coupling mechanisms involving either g-proteins or beta arrestins-mediated mechanisms. Previous research by our group has identified a lithium sensitive beta arrestin mediated cell signaling mechanism for the dopamine D2 receptor, a GPCR targeted by psycho-active drugs. Activation of D2R leads to the formation of a protein complex comprising the kinase Akt and beta arrestin 2. This complex is involved in the regulation of mood. We have identified the sequences of beta arrestin 2 that are responsible for its interaction with Akt. Furthermore disruption of this interaction, using cell permeable peptides, exert biochemical and behavioral lithium-mimetic effects in animal models of mania. This suggests that targeting beta arrestin 2 interfaces with signaling proteins may constitute a viable new strategy for drug development. We propose to resolve the structure of the beta arrestin 2/Akt protein complex and to establish if this complex is a desirable target for drug development. This information will be used in the future for the rational design of a new class of compounds selectively disrupting this modality of cell signaling.

column36: Non-Inferiority Trial Comparing Online and On-site Cognitive Behaviour Therapy in Major Depressive Disorder
column37: Mental health disorders, Canada's most expensive chronic health problem (for patients and the health system) are increasing in incidence. column36: The role of fatty liver in the epidemic of advanced chronic liver disease among people living with HIV
column37: Nowadays, people living with HIV live longer thanks to the widespread use of antiretroviral treatment (ART). As a direct consequence, they develop aging-related conditions such as diabetes, obesity, hypercholesterolemia. These are risk factors for fatty liver, the most frequent liver disease in Canada, affecting 25% of the general population. Our data indicate that fatty liver is particularly frequent in Canadians living with HIV, affecting up to 48% of patients. This excess is likely due to additional risk factors for liver damage, including ART needed for the whole life and inflammation caused by HIV. However, it is not known if fatty liver evolves to more advanced stages of liver disease and liver failure in HIV+ persons and who is at higher risk for these important complications. As a consequence, HIV+ patients are excluded from global clinical trials of new medications to treat fatty liver. Our team has championed the non-invasive method Fibroscan equipped with a special software for the quantification of fat in the liver (controlled attenuation parameter, CAP). This patient-friendly test can accurately and safely diagnose fatty liver with no need for liver biopsy, which can be painful and has complications. We will follow 968 HIV+ patients from 4 major HIV clinical centres with Fibroscan with CAP for 4 years. We will determine how many patients with fatty liver develop advanced stages of liver disease and liver failure. We will also study the contribution of important risk factors for advanced liver disease, such as ART, obesity, insulin resistance, sex. These factors will be used to develop a risk score aimed at identify HIV+ persons at higher risk for these important complications. Our ultimate aim is to determine the impact of fatty liver on advanced liver disease in HIV+ patients in order to advocate for their inclusion in new clinical trials for fatty liver and for clinical strategies to identify those at high risk of developing advanced liver disease.

column36: C-reactive Protein Modulation of Inflammation Underlying Acute Coronary Artery Disease
column37: Inflammation plays a fundamental role in mediating all stages of atherosclerosis ("hardening" of the blood vessels), including acute coronary artery disease (CAD) and stroke, the leading causes of death in Canada and the Western world. C-reactive protein (CRP) is a biomarker of inflammation. However, its role in the development of CAD is still incompletely understood for CRP possesses biological properties that can either promote or dampen inflammation. Previous research from our and other laboratories suggest that the pro-inflammatory actions of CRP, which is present in our blood, are "hidden" and will be expressed only following structural changes. Thus, understanding how structural changes affect the biological activities of CRP is critical for defining its role in CAD. We hypothesize that oxidative stress, a common features of inflammation, results in structural changes (oxCRP) that will unlock the pro-inflammatory activities of CRP. We will investigate how oxCRP is generated by activated white blood cells and characterize its effects on platelets, white blood cells and endothelial cells (the cells lining the blood vessels inside) as activation of these cells trigger heart attack. We will also explore whether treatment with anti-inflammatory lipids (that are produced inside our body and promote healing) can prevent formation of oxCRP and/or inhibit its deleterious actions. We will employ a combination of cutting-edge biochemical, molecular and cell biology techniques to address these questions using isolated human cells, mouse models and archived human atherosclerotic coronary artery samples. We anticipate that by understanding how oxCRP regulates inflammation, our research will identify novel therapeutic targets for reducing inflammation and promoting healing within the coronary arteries, ultimately reducing the health burden of acute CAD.

column36: Mechanisms of neuronal demise via a-Syn mislocalization in neurodegenerative diseases
column37: Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia and related disorders all have one feature in common: an abnormally accumulated protein called alpha-synuclein (a-syn). Though two decades of research have provided insight into how a-syn accumulates in cells, very little is known about how and why it is toxic to the cell. This has consequently slowed therapeutic development, largely due to a paucity in animal models. Specifically, the question of why a normally abundant brain-resident protein becomes toxic over time remains enigmatic. Work from our lab and others has suggested that the toxic misplacement, or mislocalization of a-syn to the nucleus is a contributor to the pathogenic process. As a result, our lab recently made new mouse models to study: 1) what factors cause a-syn to mislocalize, and 2) whether constitutively forcing a-syn into the nucleus causes features reminiscent of PD in mice. In the first case, we found that a-syn interacts with another Parkinson's related protein called Synaptojanin 1 (Synj1), and that disruption of this interaction results in features reminiscent of early PD. In the second mouse line, we found that we were able to target a-syn to the cell's nucleus and that these mice, even at an early age, begin to exhibit motor deficits. Building on this foundational data, this proposal aims to look at the interplay between both proteins and will capitalize on this genetic interaction to: 1) Determine the contribution of the a-syn-Synj1 protein interaction to PD in mice and humans; and 2) Generate novel preclinical mouse models of this disease that can be used for pharmacological testing down the line. At the end of this study, we will be able place the toxicity of nuclear a-syn as a key facet of disease, creating new opportunities for therapeutic intervention for individuals suffering from this terrible disorder.

column36: Fate, function and high-dimensional analyses of monocyte-derived macrophages in viral cardiomyopathy
column37: We have found that the heart contains multiple novel macrophage / dendritic cell subsets, which have never been discovered before. For last 50 years, scientists have always thought immune cells in the body are produced from stem cells in the bone marrow. Our new work has shown that some macrophages come from very early during embryonic development prior to birth, and those primitive macrophages continue to live in the heart into adulthood. Alternatively, other heart macrophages and dendritic cells are constantly replaced through a bone marrow dependent process. If you remove all macrophages in mice during viral infection, those mice will die, but we do not know which cell types are required for resistance to viral infection. We will now determine which immune cells clear virus and protect heart function, and which contribute to injury of the heart during infection. The work will be done in mice that develop heart disease following viral infection. For the first time, we will generate mice that lack individual immune macrophages so that we can determine the role of each subset in response viral cardiac infection. Prior to our recent work, it was not known which exact immune subsets live within the heart, which is itself a major innovation. Now that we clearly understand that these different cell types exist, and how to delete one subset, but leave untouched the others, we have the ability to understand the role (whether protective or damaging), each subset plays following viral infection. Since the tools and understanding to address these questions were not present prior to our work, we will be the first to ask these questions in setting of viral heart disease.

column36: Melanoma Margins Trial II - A Phase III, Multi-centre Randomized Controlled Trial Investigating 1cm v 2cm Wide Surgical Excision Margins for AJCC stage II Primary Cutaneous Melanoma (MelMarT-II)
column37: The incidence of melanoma is increasing worldwide. In 2019, 7800 Canadians will be diagnosed and 1300 will die from melanoma. Wide local excision (WLE) around the primary melanoma and a sentinel lymph node biopsy is standard treatment. The thickness (or depth) of the melanoma determines the extent of the WLE. Randomized trials to date have progressively confirmed the safety and effectiveness of reduced margins, but there is no randomized evidence comparing 1 versus 2cm margins for patients with clinical stage II melanoma. In Canada, this trial would affect 20% of all patients with melanoma or 1400 patients per year. With the current lack of randomized data, international guidelines suggest WLE margins of 1-3cm around a stage II melanoma. Such surgery results in a defect of 3-8cm (a result of a 1-3cm margin on either side of the melanoma which itself can be 1-2cm). In certain parts of the body where the skin is tight or there is less excess skin (e.g. mid-lower forearm, upper back or lower leg), this defect may need more extensive surgery such as a skin graft/skin flap to close the skin. Wider margins can increase morbidity, hospitalization rates, and recovery time and delay adjuvant systemic therapy. Patient groups emphasized the importance of minimizing disfigurement with surgery, wound discomfort, and time away from work, which may occur with narrower margins of excision. In a published pilot trial that compared 1cm vs 2cm margins and assessed feasibility for a larger trial, more patients in the 2cm margin group required complex reconstruction and had increased wound/skin breakdown. This melanoma margins trial is an international collaboration addressing the critical surgical question determined by national and international melanoma clinicians and Cochrane reviewers. It has strong support from patient advocacy groups in both Canada and worldwide, it is feasible, and results will potentially change current standard of care for stage II melanoma to a 1cm WLE.

column36: Atlantic Canada Together Enhancing Acute Stroke Treatment (ACTEAST): Improving Access and Efficiency of Treatment
column37: Stroke is a devastating disease, as the leading cause of severe physical disability. Ischemic stroke is the most common form of stroke; and is treatable with medical treatment and a new minimally invasive surgical procedure. These treatments can transform lives, but minutes matter for improving outcomes. The research objectives are focused on increasing the proportion of ischemic stroke patients receiving treatment, and improving the efficiency of treatment. We will carry out this work across all of the Atlantic provinces. In Canada, healthcare is administered within provincial boundaries; this presents a particular challenge in Atlantic Canada due to small populations and the lack of locally available medical specialists. We aim to overcome these care barriers to ensure that all stroke patients have access to efficient treatment based on their clinical presentation, not on system restrictions. We will employ an Improvement Collaborative intervention. It has been used successfully in health care to implement improvements across multiple hospitals. This intervention uses the Model for Improvement adopted from Industrial Engineering, which employs alternating face-to-face workshops and action periods to test and implement changes at local hospitals. The workshops involve sharing information with hospital teams and facilitation of cross-site learning. Additionally, operations research in simulation will be employed to ensure that the health system can adequately support the changes. This research presents many challenges such as cross-provincial access and a novel trial design; however, the potential benefit for patients experiencing ischemic stroke is profound. It is anticipated that 10-20% of ischemic stroke patients will have improved outcomes, which means that up to 550 more patients each year in Atlantic Canada can return to their homes with no or little disability, and utilize much less rehabilitation and long-term care services.

column36: When Rare Becomes Common: The impact of the AnkB p.S646F variant on heart disease in a Northern BC First Nation
column37: In the Gitxsan First Nation of Northern British Columbia, we recently identified a change in a gene called ANK2 linking a variety of heart conditions in families affected with long QT syndrome (LQTS). We are long-standing research partners (15 years) with the Gitxsan community and have enrolled >800 participants in studies addressing a high rate of LQTS. Although most people in the community with LQTS have a common genetic change causing LQTS type 1 (KCNQ1 p.V205M), not all families with LQTS have that change. Importantly, the discovery of the new gene change (AnkB p.S646F) identifies the underlying cause of LQTS type 4 in several people without the p.V205M change. We have also found that this gene may have effects beyond LQTS, such as on heart structure. Notably, in these families the gene change may contribute to infants with heart disease (congenital heart malformations) and heart muscle disease in adults (cardiomyopathy). Our study proposes to explore further the presence of the p.S646F variant in the population, and the role in heart disease throughout the life course. Clinical management strategies will be based on evidence learned from the clinical and population studies. We will also carry out laboratory studies in heart cells from mice to determine the effects of the gene change at the level of the cell, and how they may lead to heart development and heart muscle disease. Our team combines strong expertise in the local Indigenous context, clinical genetics, cardiology, and cell biology and builds from our preliminary results to provide a full understanding of the range of heart disease caused by this gene change. This study will contribute to a broader understanding of how the ANK2 gene contributes not only to LQTS in some people, but also other types of common heart disease.

column36: Back to the future: fast and accurate identification of shared genomic segments for disease gene mapping using population-based linkage analysis to take advantage of founder effects
column37: Genetic studies of many diseases have focused on families with multiple affected individuals. Now that most of these families have a genetic cause identified for their disease, there still remain many people with disease who have no known affected relatives, but in whom we also expect genetics to play an important role. Given the high frequency of genetic variations in the genome, it is difficult to pinpoint the genetic cause(s) in such people. This limits the application of risk prediction, since until we identify the specific genetic cause(s) in a person, we cannot offer specific therapy and prevention. Here we will take advantage of a long-known, but little used phenomenon, whereby some people with the same disease share the identical genetic cause. In addition, because they have inherited that variant from the same ancestor, they also share many other genetic variants in the region around the variant. This offers an exciting opportunity to identify such variants that contribute to disease by identifying cryptically related individuals, by identifying the segments of their genomes that they share, even if we do not know that they are closely related. This endeavor is now possible with datasets containing millions of people. We will achieve this by using statistical methods combined with fast computer algorithms on high-resolution genomic data, across hundreds of thousands of individuals. The specific segments shared by individuals with the same disease help identify the genetic variants that contribute to disease risk, that may have been missed by standard approaches. We will use these approaches to search across millions of pairs of individuals in a fast and accurate fashion to achieve this. We will use a number of methods to speed up the method, to allow it to work on high density genetic data from millions of individuals. Once the genetic cause(s) for disease in each individual are known, this can enable efforts to prevent disease or treat it early.

column36: Ectopic reactivation of normally silenced germ cell programs contributes to genomic instability, carcinogenesis and cancer progression in Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas (CTCL).
column37: Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (CTCL) is the most common lymphoma of the skin. Despite recent advances, this lymphoma remains difficult to diagnose (time to diagnosis ~6 years) because it mimics other common skin rashes such as eczema and psoriasis. It is also not possible to predict which patients with early stage CTCL will progress to advanced stages. Furthermore, advanced CTCL remains difficult to treat with a median survival of only 2-4 years. Hence, new diagnostic/prognostic markers and novel therapeutic targets are urgently needed to aid the medical management of this cancer. We showed that a number of programs that are usually only present in germline tissues (testis/ovaries) are abnormally re-expressed in CTCL. We are proposing to study how reactivation of these genes/programs (e.g., LINE-1 retrotransposition, cancer testis/meiosis regulatory genes) arises contributing to genomic instability, CTCL cancer development and progression. Since these programs are usually not expressed in healthy somatic tissues, their upregulation could be used as a diagnostic marker. Also, since these genes likely promote cancer progression, their expression in early stages may serve as a harbinger for an aggressive disease requiring systemic therapy. Finally, activity of several of these genes is likely central to cancer cell division/survival and, hence, targeting them may lead to novel therapies for CTCL patients. In the proposed grant we will study expression/activation patterns for these genes, their regulation and molecular function in CTCL, determine how they could be used as novel diagnostic/prognostic markers and exploited as therapeutic targets. This project will produce a reliable set of markers that will help shorten the time to diagnosis and help distinguish CTCL from other benign skin rashes; select prognostic markers that will identify early stage patients requiring aggressive therapies and define how these important genes/proteins could be targeted to treat CTCL.

column36: Studying development and function of human atrioventricular node cells for biological pacemaker applications
column37: The human heart rate is controlled by two specialized pacemaker tissues known as the sinoatrial node and the atrioventricular node. The sinoatrial node initiates electrical signals that drive the heartbeat. The atrioventricular node propagates these electrical signals from the upper heart chambers to the bottom heart chambers, which activates their contraction and results in pumping of blood through the body. Failure of either pacemaker causes life threatening slow heartbeat and needs to be treated by implantation of an electronic pacemaker. Approximately 21,000 Canadians receive an electronic pacemaker every year, a number that is steadily increasing with an aging population. Electronic pacemakers do represent and effective treatment, but they are associated with a relatively high complication rate (~16%) mostly caused by lead infection. Additional downsides of electronic pacemakers are the need for surgical battery replacement every 5-10 years and the limited adoption to growth requiring surgical refitting of the pacemaker leads resulting in an even higher risk for pediatric patients. The ability to replace the failing pacemaker tissue with functional pacemaker cells generated from stem cells represents an attractive alternative that could overcome these disadvantages. We have previously been successful in generating sinoatrial node pacemaker cells form stem cells and have shown that these cells can function as a biological pacemaker in a small animal model. The studies outlined in this application aim to identify methods to generate atrioventricular node pacemaker cells from stem cells and to test their ability to function as a conduction bridge between the upper and lower heart chambers in an animal model of conduction failure of the atrioventricular node. These studies will pave the way towards clinical application of stem cell-derived pacemaker cells to establish improved treatment options for patients with heart rhythm disorders.

column36: Deficience intellectuelle et maltraitance chez les enfants: Examen des facteurs et des consequences associes et influence des services medicaux, sociaux et de readaptation recus
column37: Les enfants presentant une deficience intellectuelle sont quatre fois plus a risque de subir de la maltraitance durant l'enfance que les autres enfants. Tres peu de connaissances sont disponibles sur les facteurs de risque et les consequences de la maltraitance propres aux enfants presentant une deficience intellectuelle. En outre, le role des services recus par les enfants maltraites presentant une deficience intellectuelle sur l'attenuation des risques ou des consequences est inconnu. Ce projet de recherche vise a 1) identifier les facteurs associes au risque de maltraitance des enfants presentant une deficience intellectuelle; 2) evaluer les consequences de la maltraitance sur leur developpement et leur adaptation; 3) etudier le role de trois types de services (medicaux, de protection et de readaptation) sur le developpement ou l'intensite des consequences. Ce projet de recherche combinera les informations obtenues par trois banques de donnees : celle des directions de la protection de l'enfance du Quebec, celle du Regime d'assurance maladie du Quebec et celle des centres quebecois de readaptation en deficience intellectuelle. Une collecte de donnees aupres de familles permettra de documenter les facteurs familiaux et les consequences cliniques qui ne sont pas des diagnostics medicaux. Quatre groupes d'enfants seront compares: avec ou sans maltraitance et avec ou sans deficience intellectuelle. Les analyses isoleront ainsi les facteurs, consequences et services associes a la combinaison de la maltraitance et de la deficience intellectuelle des enfants. Cette recherche permettra d'identifier des pistes pour la prevention du risque de maltraitance des enfants presentant une deficience intellectuelle et des ajustements possibles, le cas echeant, dans la prestation de services medicaux et psychosociaux pour leur sante, leur protection, leur developpement et leur adaptation.

column36: The role of ROCK1 cleavage during apoptosis in liver homeostasis and cancer
column37: The process of apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, allows for the removal of damaged or redundant cells from a tissue without triggering inflammatory responses. During apoptotic cell death, dying cells undergo a number of characteristic changes shape, including rapid contraction, membrane blebbing, destruction of the integrity of the nucleus, and the release of small cell fragments called apoptotic bodies. Apoptotic cell death is markedly different from necrotic cell death, in which there is loss of cell membrane integrity and the release of cellular contents leading to inflammation. In 2001, we discovered the mechanism that drives the dramatic morphological changes which occur during apoptotic cell death. Caspase cleavage of the ROCK1 kinase results in the release of a constitutively-active protein fragment that promotes actin-myosin contraction, which provides force that powers cell contraction, membrane blebbing, nuclear disintegration and apoptotic body formation. By mutating a single amino acid in the ROCK1 caspase cleavage site in a genetically-modified (GM) mouse model, normal kinase activity was not affected, but ROCK1 cleavage and activation during apoptotic cell death were blocked. In a chemically-induced model of liver cancer, there were fewer primary and metastatic tumors in ROCK1 mutant mice relative to wild-type mice. In ROCK1 mutant liver tumors, there were immunological profiles consistent with those associated with better outcomes and recurrence free survival in human liver cancer patients. These results suggest that altering the pattern of ROCK1-mediated morphological changes during apoptotic cell death helps the immune system to fight cancer more effectively. An implication of these findings is that treatment with ROCK inhibitors converts immunologically "cold" tumors into "hot" tumors that would enable the immune system to more effectively suppress tumor growth and spread, and which could improve chemotherapeutic responses.

column36: The roles of MICAL1 and protein oxidation in cell signalling and cancer
column37: The MICAL1 enzyme produces the reactive oxygen species molecule H2O2, and is expressed at higher than normal levels in a variety of cancer types, including breast, liver, kidney, pancreas, skin and brain/central nervous system cancers. To determine how MICAL1 contributes to cancer, we blocked its expression and observed significant effects on protein oxidation, cell migration, survival and tumour growth in a mouse breast cancer model. Together, these observations reveal a major role of MICAL1 in cancer, indicating that MICAL1 is a potential cancer drug target due to its role as a critically important signalling linker. Building on our experience and knowledge of signal transduction pathways in cancer, particularly in examining how protein oxidation influences cancer cell motility, we will determine how the MICAL1 protein contributes to cancer growth via targeted protein oxidation. We hypothesize that: (1) MICAL1 responds to upstream signals by changing its specific activity, leading to the oxidation of target proteins to affect their functions; (2) MICAL1-induced protein oxidations contribute to cancer growth, invasion and metastasis; (3) MICAL1 is a novel potential cancer drug target. By characterizing how MICAL1-induced protein oxidation affects cellular functions, we will address a significant knowledge gap regarding protein oxidation as a fundamentally important protein modification. These studies will uncover fundamental new knowledge about the role of regulated and targeted protein oxidation in signal transduction pathways, and will determine whether MICAL1 is a critically important signal transduction intermediary, and thus a novel cancer drug target.

column36: An application of Super-Imposition by Translation And Rotation (SITAR) modelling to population-level child height trajectories of children aged 0-5 years using data from 145 Demographic Health Surveys (DHS) from 64 countries between 2000 and 2018
column37: Reducing the burden of child growth faltering and malnutrition is a prioritized global public health target that is represented within the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the WHO global targets for 2025 and includes Canada where obesity is a major public health challenge. Specifically, the SDG's goals 2 and 3 relate to improved nutrition, good health and well-being. The Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are a rich source of data that records population-representative health information and includes indicators of child growth and malnutrition in low and middle-income countries. Typically, height and weight data is standardized by sex and age of the child based on the WHO child growth standards as the reference population. The availability of multiple waves of DHS data for each country provides an opportunity to study these secular trends in height and weight that have occurred within and between countries. We propose to use DHS data collected between 2000 and 2018 from 64 countries (145 surveys) to adapt an applied model, previously used to characterize adolescent growth, to describe child growth trajectories with the aim of quantifying changes in growth at a population level in the following domains: absolute growth, rate of growth, and timing of growth. We will use a methodology of growth curve analysis that summarizes the entire growth trajectory into these three biologically meaningful parameters related to growth. The methodology fits a single mean curve to all data and estimates differences in growth for each survey data relative to the estimated mean derived from using all the data. We will then use these parameters estimated for each survey, and separately for boys and girls, to explore associations between attained size and other target national and global indicators used to evaluate whether a country is on track to achieving international targets such as reducing the burden of child growth faltering and malnutrition.

column36: Growth and empowerment measure adapted for the Indigenous in Quebec - utility evaluation for psychiatric measurement and intervention
column37: Indigenous peoples have among the highest rates of psychiatric disorders and suicide. Good quality psychiatric treatment should confirm cultural safety not only in remote areas but also in urban centers where 60% of Indigenous of Canada live. The traumatic history of colonization makes help seeking and acceptance of western psychiatric treatment harder among these populations. In psychiatry, screening for symptoms or evaluating recovery is often done using symptom scales. The patient is expected to respond to questions about how often he/she has certain symptoms. However, the Indigenous view of mental wellbeing may not fit well with this approach. In our work with Indigenous community members and stakeholders working with these populations, we selected and translated the scale Growth and Empowerment Measure (GEM). Although the GEM was originally developed in Australian Aboriginals, the Inuit and Mohawk in Quebec found that the GEM measures critical aspects of their mental wellbeing more respectfully and accurately than measures that focus on symptoms. The GEM captures both positive and negative ends of factors supporting wellbeing; it uses visual elements and does not ask to quantify emotions. However, it has not been developed nor validated for clinical use. We believe that use of the adapted GEM can contribute to mental health promotion / prevention as well as to improve psychiatric services by giving helpers useful tools for discussion. We want to see if integrating the GEM in existing services can help create a bridge to improve communication between the Indigenous cultural perspective of the patient and the biomedical view of health care personnel. We also want to see whether GEM can be used to screen for psychiatric disorders, monitor symptom severity and track treatment outcomes. Eventually, we plan to develop interventions that can be guided by information from the GEM, such as eHealth interventions for remote communities with limited mental health services.
