column36: Dissecting the homeostatic mechanisms that regulate adult stem cell proliferation
column37: Age is still considered as the greatest cancer risk factor, but according to recent evidence, it could actually be the total number of divisions stem cells execute over a lifetime that really is the greatest risk factor. Indeed, combined with a natural selection favouring enhanced growth and survival abilities, the stochastic accumulation of genetic and epigenetic errors, which mainly occur during cell division, inevitably tends to transform our stem cells into cancer cells as they divide over the course of our lives. Most of our differentiated cells, in contrast, have limited division potentials, such that the risk that they progressively transform to initiate tumorigenesis is much smaller. Thus, this emerging theory essentially claims that the longer we live, the more our stem cells divide, the more they accumulate changes and can progress towards unscheduled growth and eventually, tumorigenesis. The eventual transformation of a stem cell into a cancer cell requires escaping from the in vivo mechanisms that keep stem cell proliferation under control. Indeed, when stem cells are taken outside of animals and cultured in vitro (in the absence of these in vivo control mechanisms), they readily proliferate to form a tumour. To understand the initial transformation steps that may underlie stem cell-based tumorigenesis, we therefore need to define those in vivo mechanisms that limit stem cell proliferation. One such mechanism ensures stem cells only divide when the tissue they serve needs new differentiated cells. Homeostatic stem cell regulation is conserved and its localized properties may offer potential means to influence individual stem cell population activities by drugs in vivo, which could greatly impact our medical strategies in regenerative medicine, and cancer prevention/treatment. We recently established a powerful model system in C. elegans in which we plan to efficiently elucidate how homeostatic stem cell regulation is locally achieved in vivo.

column36: Kwiis hen niip - Change: Change for emergency care services in rural and remote Indigenous communities in British Columbia.
column37: The health care system has failed the Indigenous peoples of Canada; a history of abuse and mistreatment has left many communities with higher rates of disease, suicide, and shorter lifespans. Many communities are far from hospital. There are stories of medical emergencies that face stormy weather, no available boats or helicopters, unavailable responders with first aid training, no cell service, and missing medical supplies. This project, Kwiis hen niip, the Nuu-chah-nulth term for 'change', aims to be a small part of reconciliation to help change some of these glaring inequities. Teamwork is key to solving these complex problems. Our research project brings communities, researchers, government, and health service organizations together to design and evaluate solutions that address problems head on. The research will focus on four Nuu chah nulth communities living on the west coast of Vancouver Island. We have found that government and organizations have many excellent ideas to address the gaps in emergency care; however, these services are uncoordinated and scattered and often not co-developed with Indigenous communities. Our research aims to bring community voices and experience together with service providers and feature indigenous research methods to create and evaluate innovative solutions to improve emergency care. The project team is careful not to fall into colonialistic patterns that interfere with the right to self-determination (to have control of their own lives). We have had several meetings with community members. The project has been met with enthusiasm overlaying a deep frustration that these inequities even exist in. Distinct themes have emerged: first responder support and training, transport, communications, and community readiness. Partner organizations involved will help to improve these essential components of emergency response in an effort to have a holistic model of emergency care with targeted solutions to community-defined challenges.

column36: The Effects of In Utero and Neonatal Wildfire Smoke Exposure on Birth Outcomes and Health in Early Life
column37: The 2017 and 2018 wildfire seasons were the worst in the history of British Columbia (BC). In both seasons, more than 1.2 million hectares of land were burned, and approximately 200 million tons of wildfire smoke were emitted. Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations were elevated throughout the province for several weeks. A small number of studies conducted in other regions suggest that such extreme smoke-related PM2.5 exposures may affect unborn and newborn infants, but no studies have been conducted in Canada. This project will take advantage of the extreme 2017 and 2018 wildfire seasons and the milder 2016 and 2019 wildfire seasons to investigate how wildfire smoke exposure affects birth outcomes and risk of diseases in the first year of life. Specifically, all BC infants who were in the womb or born during the summers of 2016-2019 (approximately 200,000 in total) will be grouped into those with low, moderate, or high wildfire smoke exposure using an existing PM2.5 model. Birth outcomes and adverse health outcomes in the first year of life will then be compared across the three groups using administrative databases. The birth outcomes will include stillbirths, birth defects, preterm births, term low birth weight, small for gestational age, and full-term birth weight. The adverse health outcomes will include non-accidental deaths, respiratory diseases, congenital heart defects not identified at birth, ear infections, and antibiotic prescriptions. Based on previous literature we hypothesize that infants who were more exposed to wildfire smoke will have worse birth outcomes and higher risks of adverse health outcomes in the first year of life when compared with infants who were less exposed. This project will provide important new knowledge to better understand the health impacts of wildfire smoke for pregnant women and newborn infants and will inform public health and medical practitioners to better prepare for future wildfire events.

column36: Examining the influence of a school travel planning intervention on children's travel behaviour, physical activity, and exposure to pollution around their schools
column37: In the past, children mostly walked or biked to school. However, in the last two decades we have seen a worrisome decline in the share of children using these active modes of transportation to get to school. Active school travel contributes to children's overall physical activity. Given that stemming increasing chronic disease rates is a priority in the Canadian healthcare system, we propose an innovative school-based transportation intervention to build lifelong healthy physical activity habits. A partnership in the St. Thomas-Elgin, Middlesex-London, and Oxford region runs a School Travel Planning (STP) program, which encourages children to use active school travel. We propose to leverage this existing STP program that uses a combination of engineering changes to school neighbourhoods to make it easier to use active modes, education to increase knowledge on how to be safe using active travel, encouragement of active travel, and enforcement to ensure people traveling through the neighbourhood follow the laws of the road. This project will examine how the STP program can improve active school travel, physical activity levels, and reduce air pollution around schools. Students and parents from grades 4-6 at 24 schools will be involved in this study. Twelve schools will receive the intervention, while the other twelve will be used as control schools. The project will use air pollution monitors, parent and child surveys, Global Positioning System tracking devices, physical activity trackers, and self-reported trip diaries to collect data. We will compare changes over time in travel mode choice, physical activity levels, and air pollution between intervention and control schools. We hypothesize that students attending schools involved in the STP program will use more active travel modes, be more active, and have better air quality around school. This research will contribute to improving the effectiveness of STP programs for improving child health across Canada.

column36: Actin regulation of ciliogenesis: unraveling novel mechanisms of human ciliopathies caused by mutations in the PCP effector genes
column37: Some very severe human developmental disorders are caused by dysfunction of the microscopic hair-like structure (primary cilium). Primary cilium projects from most cells in the human body and acts like a "GPS- antenna" to survey the environment outside cells and transduce this information into inside the cell so that the cells can adjust their shape, movement and proliferation and other functions during organ development. It is therefore not surprising that defects in primary cilia lead to a wide-range of congenital abnormalities affecting brain, heart, skeleton, and kidneys. Ciliopathies are incurable and may cause fetal death, considerable morbidity after birth or reduced longevity. Investigation of the functions of the genes mutated in humans is crucial if we want to find a cure for ciliopathies. We focus on a specific group of genes (Fuzzy, Inturned and Wdpcp), termed PCP effectors. Mutations in these 3 genes are associated with various human ciliopathies which feature facial and rib defects, neural tube defects, and cystic kidneys. Mouse mutants for these genes have severe malformations which resemble features of humans with PCP effector gene mutations. Using cells and mice bearing mutations of the Fuzzy as our main experimental model, we will try to identify and explain the mechanisms through which loss of Fuzzy (and its molecular partners, Inturned and Wdpcp) disturbs generation of cilia and distorts the cilial signals that are so crucial for normal development. Based on our studies, we hope to offer novel therapeutic strategy for the severe human developmental defects caused by the mutation in the PCP effector genes and, likely, other ciliopathies.

column36: Novel hyperbranched polyglycerol-derived biliary excretable osmotic agents for peritoneal dialysis - preclinical evaluation
column37: People who lose their kidney function require either dialysis or a kidney transplant to keep them alive. Given the lack of enough kidney donors available for transplantation, 80% of patients have to use dialysis which acts as an artificial kidney to remove waste from the body. There are two forms of dialysis: hemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD). In PD, a special PD fluid is infused in the abdomen to filter out the waste and water through the stomach lining called the peritoneal membrane, while HD uses a machine in the hospital attached to the patient's blood system to clean up the blood. But PD has many advantages over HD: PD can be administered independently by patients in their homes, and patients on PD do better when they receive a kidney transplant and can be less careful about their dietary restraints. These factors greatly improve the quality-of-life of PD patients and also PD costs tens of thousands of dollars less per patient/year resulting in reduced healthcare costs. Currently, glucose (sugar) is commonly used in the PD fluid in order to remove the waste and water through the peritoneal membrane, but sugar causes many long-term problems for PD patients; it scars the peritoneal lining and eventually patients are unable to receive PD. Furthermore, too much sugar can cause diseases such as diabetes or more challenging in the control of diabetes. Our research group has designed a new "non-sugar" polymer to substitute glucose in the PD fluid. Our results demonstrate that this novel polymer is safer and more efficacious than the conventional glucose-based PD fluid in many different experiments. We are continuing to test the safety and efficacy this exciting new polymer in long-term studies that better approximate the human condition. We are a multidisciplinary team of medical doctors, scientists and drug development experts working together to develop a new PD fluid that will help many people with chronic kidney disease in Canada and around the world.

column36: Investigation of CSF1 hematopoietic niches in atherosclerosis
column37: A quarter of all deaths in Canada are caused by complications associated with cardiovascular disease. The main cause of vascular disease is atherosclerosis, or build-up of plaque in the arteries. Atherosclerosis is an inflammatory disease in which white blood cells, including monocytes and macrophages (MO), accumulate progressively in the expanding arterial wall. Once in atherosclerotic plaques, monocytes/MO ingest lipoproteins and become lipid-loaded foam cells, a key culprit in atherosclerosis and its complications. As atherosclerosis develops, monocytes and MO increase in number in several tissues including the blood, bone marrow, spleen, and developing plaques in the arteries. These tissue micro-environments or niches maintain monocyte/MO and coordinate their function by producing factors that act directly on them. Identification of the cells within these niches and the mechanisms by which they regulate monocytes/MO affords the opportunity to better understand inflammation and identify new targets for therapy. Our preliminary data shows that monocytes and MO accumulate near either arterial or venous blood vessels, depending on the tissues in which they reside. Based on these observations, we propose that in atherosclerosis, harmful monocyte/MO responses are regulated within perivascular niches. To test our hypothesis, we will use sophisticated animal models of atherosclerosis in which macrophage colony stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) - a key factor required for maintenance of monocytes/MO - is preferentially deleted in specific cell types. Using state-of-the-art immunological methods, including flow cytometry and single cell RNA sequencing, we will determine how specific niche components affect inflammation as atherosclerosis develops. We anticipate that information gained from the proposed studies will provide mechanistic information and a rationale for new therapeutic approaches targeting monocyte/MO niche biology in atherosclerotic disease.

column36: Using advanced imaging techniques to demonstrate hippocampal subfield pathology and predict surgical outcome in temporal lobe epilepsy
column37: One third of patients with epilepsy are unable to control their seizures with medication. For these patients, surgery can cure their epilepsy if the area in the brain that the seizures start from can be identified and removed. However, among patients who undergo this brain surgery, seizures recur in 50% of patients. Given this poor success rate, better tools are needed to select patients for surgery and predict their outcomes. We have developed a new MRI method that provides far superior resolution (8x) compared to standard MRI, and shows promise in uncovering important information about brain structure that may predict seizure outcomes in these patients. The ultimate goal of this proposal is to develop new advanced MRI techniques that will allow doctors and patients to make more informed decisions about whether brain surgery is the right option for them and if it is likely to cure their epilepsy.

column36: Targeted immunotherapy for the treatment of brain cancer
column37: A promising class of drugs has recently emerged that recruits the patient's own immune system to fight cancer, fulfilling a long-held belief that 'immunotherapy' can help in the treatment of cancer. The drugs called "immune checkpoint inhibitors", or ICIs, are significantly extending the life of patients with advanced stages of cancer, such as melanoma, a disease once thought to be incurable. ICIs are poised to improve survival rates for many other forms of cancer. However, these drugs have significant side effects and there remains much room for improvement. I recently discovered that a family of experimental drugs called Smac mimetics, which have been proven safe in Phase I/II cancer trials, can also make use of the immune system to dramatically increase the effectiveness of ICIs in animal models of cancer. I discovered that the combination of Smac mimetics with ICIs can cure mice with glioblastoma, a highly fatal brain cancer seen in adults and children. In this proposal, I seek to understand the broad-based nature of this combination and to decipher the ways that Smac mimetics improve the activity of ICIs against glioblastoma. These studies will improve our understanding of this specific deadly brain cancer and help justify the initiation of combination trials using Smac mimetics and ICIs for cancer patients who are in dire need of more effective therapies.

column36: Development of a personalized medicine approach to corticosteroid treatment in IgA nephropathy
column37: IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is an autoimmune disease that causes kidney failure, affecting 8,000 Canadians annually. Currently, corticosteroid treatment is used to decrease disease progression in patients with high amounts of protein in their urine. However, this treatment is suboptimal as there is a high risk of serious and life-threatening side effects and this "one size fits all" approach results in a large number of patients that are unnecessarily treated, don't respond, or are inappropriately denied treatment. Targeting treatment at those more likely to respond and who are at higher risk of disease progression has not previously been possible because there was no way to determine in which patients the disease is likely to progress. We recently led an international collaboration that developed the IgAN Prediction Tool, the first tool in the world that can successfully identify patients likely to have progressive IgAN disease, and created a globally unique dataset. The proposed project will expand on this work by developing a personalized corticosteroid treatment approach optimized for each patient, an approach that will be a world first. We will use our dataset to develop a new tool that can identify patients more likely to respond to treatment. It will be validated using an external dataset from an international randomized trial. We will then develop a model that can be applied to each patient to determine the optimal treatment decision. The model will account for the risks and benefits of corticosteroids, and each patient's risk of disease progression and likelihood of responding to treatment. The results of this project will be converted into a prototype of a mobile-app for doctors and a web-based platform for patients.

column36: Increasing access to community-based task-oriented exercise programs through healthcare-recreation partnerships to improve function for people with balance and mobility limitations: A multi-site randomized controlled trial
column37: The ability to balance and walk is key to doing everyday activities like getting dressed, preparing meals, and getting out of the house to do shopping and social activities. When everyday activities are limited, costly homecare services may be needed, or a family member or friend has to help and has less time to do things important to them. Functional exercise programs that involve practising everyday movements, like standing up and sitting down, stepping, and walking, have been shown to improve balance and walking in people with chronic conditions like stroke, and arthritis. If these programs were widely available in local recreation centres, more people could benefit. We have shown that physical therapists can: 1) train fitness instructors how to teach these programs to people with balance and walking problems; and 2) help keep the program safe and beneficial by visiting classes and giving feedback to instructors. We call this a healthcare-recreation partnership. Functional exercise programs for people with balance and walking problems are more costly to run than usual fitness classes because more instructors are needed to supervise. We need evidence showing these programs help improve everyday function so that we can advocate for financial support. In this study, adults who have balance and walking problems will participate in a 12-week functional group exercise program at a local community centre right away, or six months later. A physical therapist will train the fitness instructors, visit classes, and answer questions by email/phone. We will evaluate the effect of the program on ability to perform everyday activities, quality of life, balance, leg strength, walking, cognition, mood, and caregiver assistance/mental health. Each participant will complete three evaluations: before the exercise program and 3, and 6 months later. Increasing everyday function is expected to support caregivers, and help people live independently in the community for longer.

column36: BootleBlast, a movement tracking video game for home-based motor therapy - Navigating gaps to market readiness
column37: Background/Rationale. Many children experience challenges in motor skills that impact well-being. Therapies can help, but can be costly and difficult to access. We worked with children, parents and clinicians to co-create a video game, BootleBlast, for home practice of motor skills. Using the Microsoft Kinect, BootleBlast tracks movements and manipulation of real-life objects. Research shows that children can improve motor skills by playing BootleBlast at home. Aims. Our goal is to increase commercial viability of BootleBlast by: (1) Reducing the need for specialized/expensive hardware. (2) Conducting real-world testing to identify barriers to home use. Research Plan. Two new versions of BootleBlast will be tested with tracking enabled by (1) a low-cost, combined computer-depth sensor-camera, or (2) simple webcams. We will test usability and how well actions are captured within the game with 12 children of diverse abilities. Second, we will test BootleBlast for 15 weeks in home settings with 60 children with diverse diagnoses affecting motor skills, including developmental coordination disorder (affects 1 in 16 children). We will assess feasibility (e.g. independent home setup, ability to set and meet self-directed play time targets), enablers/barriers to use, and perceived value. User experience will inform product strategy, training and resource development. Commercialization Plan. BootleBlast will be marketed first to rehabilitation hospitals/clinics, and then to families in Canada and the US. Commercialization activities will include disseminating research evidence, pre-market preparation (e.g. establish partnerships, market research), and product launch (e.g. spread awareness, generate buy-in). Impact. BootleBlast offers children, families, and clinicians an innovative tool to promote function, playfulness, and well-being. It address practical healthcare funding and accessibility issues. This project will enhance Canada's burgeoning digital health sector.

column36: Functional dissection of the serotoninergic system in normal and pathological conditions.
column37: One of the most conspicuous characteristics of any organism is its ability to react to salient stimuli with an appropriate behavioral response that maximizes survival and minimizes threatening or unpleasant events. In mammals, emotions have been proposed as the evolutionary strategy to detect changes, either internally or from the environment, to organize proper behavioral responses. When negative events occur, such as stress, processing of these signals in the brain becomes inappropriate and leads to cognitive and behavioral deficits characteristic of mood disorders. The implication of serotonin in the control of emotions and action selection have been widely described. Its role in mood control is also well-recognized, as exemplified by the fact that pharmacological antidepressants are based on the modulation of serotonin in the brain. However, because of the complexity of serotoninergic neural pathways in the brain, the main role of serotonin in the control of emotion, cognition and behavior is still elusive. In this research proposal, we will use innovative approaches to measure and manipulate, in real-time and freely moving mice, specific serotoninergic neural pathways. When combined with different behavioral tests commonly used with mice, these approaches will allow us to precisely dissect how serotoninergic neural pathways in the brain process emotions to organize proper behavioral responses. We will also perform electrophysiological recordings at these serotoninergic pathways from normal and depressed mice to reveal cellular and molecular dysfunctions underlying cognitive and behavioral deficits associated with mood disorders. In the long term, our work will lead in the development of new therapeutic approaches to ultimately help people suffering from mood disorders.

column36: Targeting lysophosphatidate (LPA) signaling to improve therapeutic outcomes for breast cancer patients
column37: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (RT) are an essential treatment for eliminating cancer cells. These treatments often fail and the tumour spreads to other organs. Also, a common side effect of RT is scarring. About 60% of breast cancer patients have tumours removed surgically (lumpectomy). They are then treated with 16 daily doses of RT to the remaining breast. This causes inflammation and production of a compound called LPA. Repeating the RT amplifies this effect. LPA protects cancer cells from being killed by RT and it is also responsible for scarring, which occurs in 28% of breast cancer patients. Scarring causes pain, distress and shrinkage of the breast, which in severe cases requires cosmetic correction. We discovered that an anti-inflammatory agent (dexamethasone) blocks the effects of LPA. This decreases scarring in the breast and underlying lungs, which are damaged by collateral radiation. Dexamethasone could be used to improve the outcomes of patients from RT, but we will study other anti-inflammatory agents that have fewer side effects. These include a new drug that blocks LPA formation. This compound halts the progression of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis where scarring develops in the absence of RT. Compounds, which are designed to block the effects of LPA, have never been used in cancer treatments. This provides an ideal opportunity to improve the outcomes of breast cancer patients from RT and chemotherapy. To translate our work into clinical practice, we will perform the first studies on how breast cancer patients treated with RT activate the effects of LPA. We predict that those patients who show the highest and longest LPA responses will be the ones to develop fibrosis. This work will lay the foundations for designing a clinical trial where we will test if blocking the effects of LPA prevents long-term fibrosis. This work can be extended to other cancers where RT produces such severe scarring that its use is restricted.

column36: The Maritime Community Health and Housing Initiative: Investigating the Impact of Public Housing Interventions on Mental Health and Healthcare Use in Low-Income Households in New Brunswick
column37: Income and housing are pervasive social determinants of health. New Brunswick is experiencing a low-income epidemic. New Brunswick's low-income rate is significantly higher than the overall rate of low-income in Canada. Rent geared-to-income ("public") housing provides low-income households with more affordable accommodations. In theory, subsidized rents should provide greater access to residual income, which can improve health outcomes. However, to date, little is known about the health and wellbeing of tenants who reside in public housing. This is especially problematic for New Brunswick, a province with a rural landscape and low population density, whose inhabitants also experience challenges with mental health, income inequality, social exclusion, and lengthy waitlists for primary care physicians. This study addresses a large gap in knowledge of the contributions of housing to health. Public housing applicants will be systematically surveyed on their mental health at baseline and again at 6 month intervals as they wait for and are housed in public housing. Additionally, participants' housing dates will be linked to a provincial administrative database using health card numbers. This database contains the Discharge Abstracts Database (DAD) will be used to compare healthcare use for a period of 18 months pre and post-move. Healthcare use is operationalized in the DAD as visits to primary health providers, walk-in clinics, and hospitalizations. Knowledge of housing and health is sparse in Canada and this study provides crucial information on the contribution of housing to health. This study will provide stakeholders with a wealth of health information on a population that is historically under-researched, underserved and unhealthy.

column36: Mechanisms involved in triggering the rapid and sustained antidepressant effects of ketamine
column37: Depression is now the leading cause of ill health and disability worldwide. There remain three important unmet needs in the treatment of depression. Specifically, there is urgency for medications with faster therapeutic action, a requirement for higher rates of recovery and effective strategies to maintain the antidepressant response for patients with major depressive disorder. With existing treatments, one third of patients remains ill even after several treatment trials and are designated as treatment-resistant. Among patients who do respond, all existing antidepressant treatments have a delayed action of several weeks and can stop working after few months. Strikingly, low doses of ketamine can produce a rapid antidepressant effect (within 24 hours) in a significant number of patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD). This antidepressant effect however, dissipates within one week. The first goal of this project is to compare the mechanisms involved in the rapid and more delayed antidepressant effects induced, respectively, by ketamine and a treatment that combines two existing medications (combination of escitalopram and aripiprazole), also known to be efficacious in TRD. The second goal is to understand why the antidepressant effects of ketamine are not sustained and lead to patient relapse. The third goal is to determine the brain adaptations that occur with repeated ketamine administration that can maintain its antidepressant effects, as was shown in our clinical study. Understanding the mechanisms underlying the rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine, their transient nature, and how they can be maintained, will inform design of new treatment strategies aimed at inducing rapid and sustained antidepressant response.

column36: Unravelling the complex process of synuclein seeding and propagation with human stem cell derived models
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 2% of the worldwide population. Classical hallmarks of this disorder are a progressive loss of cells from the brain, and an accumulation of protein clumps termed Lewy bodies (LBs). LBs are observed early in the development of PD, and imaging studies have shown that these LBs can move throughout the brain ultimately leading to a loss of cells within the brains of PD patients. The predominant component of these clumps is alpha-synuclein (alpha-syn), with recent studies identifying a new disease-causing mechanism by which alpha-syn can move from cell to cell, acting as a template to seed new clumps. Thus, preventing the spread of these toxic alpha-syn seeds represents an attractive therapeutic approach. However, to date much is still unknown about how these inclusions form and move around within the brain using animal models. To move away from animal models, and to understand better how alpha-syn acts, we are proposing to use cells present within the human brain to gain insight into the mechanisms behind this devastating human disease. For making these cells from the brain, we will take advantage of new stem cell technology, in which we can form stem cells from a person's skin or blood. column37: Nearly all life forms on earth require iron to survive. Iron is important for many functions in our body, and probably best known for its role in transporting oxygen, allowing us to breathe. Once oxygen is taken up through the lung, it is transferred to an iron atom that sits at the centre of a special molecule called heme. The heme molecule itself is docked to a larger structure called hemoglobin, and together, they deliver oxygen to where it is needed via the bloodstream. These heme groups are also important for other processes in our cells, including the removal of harmful substances and the production of steroid hormones, like the famous testosterone. The King-Jones lab uses the fruit fly as a model to study undiscovered aspects of iron biology. For instance, they discovered that steroid hormone-producing cells have a high demand for iron and heme. Importantly, King-Jones and colleagues realized that they can take advantage of these cells to learn new things about how humans regulate their iron "balance sheet". Since both too much and too little iron can cause severe diseases in humans, it is essential that we learn more about how iron handled in our bodies, and how this is regulated. Using a range of genetic tricks, King-Jones and colleagues have recently discovered more than 20 genes with unexpected roles in regulating and balancing appropriate iron levels. The proposal focuses on the so-called "Iron Regulatory Protein 1" (IRP1) and how it regulates genes important for the safe handling of iron. The King-Jones lab has shown that IRP1 regulates more genes than previously thought and that this occurs by new, unexpected mechanisms. The study of these new, unexpected aspects of iron biology will improve our understanding of diseases that are caused by too much or too little iron.

column36: Modeling the Transition to Cocaine Addiction in Rats
column37: Drug addiction is amongst the leading preventable causes of death and illness in the world. In Canada, cocaine is now the most used illicit drug. Drug addiction is involved in the death of one in five people, and addiction costs Canadians nearly $40 billion per year. Over half of people addicted to cocaine seek treatment, but the prevalence of cocaine addiction has not decreased over time. This is in part because there are no approved medications to treat cocaine addiction. To develop new medications, we need to understand how initial cocaine use changes the brain, psychological function and behaviour to promote the transition from casual drug use to addiction. Animal models are on the front lines to achieve this, because laboratory animals can show the characteristic behavioural features of addiction. This in turn allows researchers to study how drugs change the brain to produce these features. Currently, the most widely used procedure to study cocaine addiction in laboratory animals involves allowing them to self-administer cocaine continuously for several hours a day. However, an alternative model has recently been developed, that might better capture the intermittent-rather than continuous-pattern of cocaine use in humans. This new model also appears especially effective in producing addiction-like features in animals. Our goal here is to directly compare and contrast these two models of addiction. We will also focus on cocaine-induced changes in i) the actions of the chemical messenger dopamine, which mediates motivation for rewards, and ii) neuronal activity in brain circuits involving a brain region called the prefrontal cortex, which mediates judgement and self-regulation. We expect that our findings will be critical in helping researchers make informed decisions about how to model addiction-like features in laboratory animals. This in turn will be important in determining directions for new anti-addiction medications in people.

column36: Chronotherapy of Non-Steroidal Anti Inflammatory Drugs could enhance bone fracture recovery
column37: Bone fractures are extremely painful, and unfortunately, the drugs available to relieve this pain are problematic. Tylenol (paracetamol) is not strong enough, opioids can cause addiction, and Advil (ibuprofen) can delay healing. This project is focused on finding a simple and inexpensive solution for this problem. Pain intensity and our ability to heal varies throughout the day due to an internal day-and night rhythm that regulates our body. According to this rhythm healing and recovery happens mainly when we are sleeping while pain and inflammation are most intense when we are awake. Accordingly, this project will investigate the effect of timing the dose of Advil with the body day-night rhythm in order to maximize the benefits of the drug while minimizing its side effects. This project can improve the way we manage bone fractures with Advil and it can also provide an extremely useful tool against the current opioid epidemic.

column36: Targeting specific domains of AMPA glutamate receptors in synaptic and cognitive impairments in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia and imposes enormous social and financial burden on affected individuals and our society, but no effective treatment or cure is currently available. A hallmark pathology of AD is the accumulation of amyloid plaques in the brain mainly composed of amyloid peptides, but how these peptides lead to neuronal loss and cognitive impairments remains unclear. Recent studies indicate that AD begins with changes at the synapse, the key site of neuronal communication and plasticity, and that synaptic deficits are the best correlates of cognitive impairments. Therefore, elucidating how amyloid peptides cause synaptic and cognitive dysfunction is essential for the understanding and treatment of the disease. The overall objective of this project is to unravel the molecular mechanisms by which amyloid peptides cause synaptic and memory deficits. We will focus on AMPA receptors (AMPARs) because they are the principal mediator of excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for synaptic plasticity widely accepted as the cellular basis for memory formation. We have developed several superior mouse models with changes in specific subunits and regions of AMPARs and shown that these mice are differentially altered in different forms of synaptic plasticity as well as in synaptic impairments induced by amyloid peptides. These results lead to a hypothesis that different subunits/regions of AMPARs differentially contribute to synaptic and cognitive impairments in AD. We will use a multidisciplinary approach and a combination of cutting-edge techniques to address this hypothesis. This project will reveal novel molecular mechanisms by which amyloid peptides cause neuronal and cognitive deficits in AD and provide highly specific therapeutic targets to treat this devastating disease.

column37: Metabolic disorders are a huge and growing clinical and financial burden in the world. Economic progress has generated a global epidemic in obesity that is in turn producing an epidemic of diabetes along with its long-term complications of cardiovascular diseases, renal failure, blindness, cancer and dementia. Medical progress has converted many previous life threatening diseases into chronic disorders. These chronic disorders (e.g. congestive heart failure, COPD, kidney insufficiency, diabetes, HIV, some forms of cancer) are often complicated by muscle atrophy which leads to weakness, impaired physical function and decreased survival. My laboratory has been exploring the role of the ubiquitin system in metabolism. The ubiquitin system functions in cells by regulating in a precise manner, the degradation of specific proteins in the cell. We have found an enzyme in the ubiquitin system called USP19 that when inactivated in mice protects them from obesity and diabetes on a high fat diet as well as from muscle wasting due to many catabolic conditions such as nutritional insufficiency, glucocorticoid treatment and muscular inactivity. In this project, we propose to understand at a molecular level how USP19 exerts these functions in order to better direct drug development on this enzyme which is currently underway.

column36: Selective Brain Hypothermia via Intranasal Cooling to Limit Brain Injury Post Cardiac Arrest
column37: There are 40,000 cardiac arrests each year in Canada. Less than 10% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients survive to hospital discharge. Nearly 50% of survivors suffer from brain damage and only 3% to 7% are able to live independently after the event. Brain injury among survivors represents an enormous burden on patients, their families, and health care resources. The current American Heart Association guidelines on post-resuscitation care recommend cooling the whole body hence the brain to protect it from the damaging effects of cardiac arrest. Hurdles in the clinical application of cooling are: first, whole body cooling instead of cooling the brain only can trigger complications including abnormal blood clotting and new heart attack; second, to limit these deleterious effects of whole body cooling, only mild hypothermia, in which the body is cooled to 36oC has been used in clinical settings, whereas enhanced brain protection may be achieved by selectively cooling the brain quickly to below 36oC; third, there does not exist simple, effective and non-invasive method to selectively cool the brain below 36oC that can be readily applied in hospitals. We propose to develop a simple means to cool down the brain by blowing cold air, generated from compressed air, into the nostrils. This would cool down the nasal cavity which in turn would chill warm blood coming into the nasal cavity on its way to the brain. In initial testing of the method with normal pigs, we have shown that the method can selectively cool the pig brain to 34oC within 40 minutes and maintain this temperature for 6 hours before rewarming slowly over 3 hours back to normal temperature while leaving the body at normal temperature throughout this period. Before we can try this method on patients, we have to show that the method is safe to use in a large animal model, for example, pigs which have similar physiology to humans. We also have to show that the method is able to protect the brain.

column36: Examining a digital health approach for advancing schizophrenia illness self-management and provider engagement
column37: The effective treatment of schizophrenia is very challenging due to a number of factors. These include issues such as poor engagement with treatment plans and care providers, limited contacts with providers due to under-resourced health services, and the challenges inherent to schizophrenia symptoms. These findings will lay the groundwork for a larger program of research and software development that will (i) validate the technology across multiple sites and, (ii) catalyze engagement with healthcare systems and caregiver networks to scale out access to this promising resource.

column36: Formation of an islet regenerative niche using human mesenchymal stem cell secreted signals
column37: Background Diabetes results from the destruction of insulin producing beta cells within pancreatic islets leaving patients unable to control blood glucose levels. Even with modern insulin therapy, the majority of diabetes patients will develop severe health complications including heart attack and stroke. Diabetes is a global epidemic that currently affects >450 million people worldwide. Thus, the development of strategies to replace or regenerate lost beta cells is under intense investigation for the treatment of diabetes. Experimental Platforms Our lab has pioneered the use of bone marrow-derived stem cells to stimulate islet regeneration after transplantation. Using human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSC) as potent 'biofactories' for the production of proteins with islet regenerative functions, we have discovered new methods to generate a concentrated mixture of proteins that reverse the symptoms of diabetes after direct injection into the pancreas of mice. By effectively bypassing the need for cellular transplantation, understanding how these proteins 'help the pancreas heal itself' remains the key to improving regenerative therapies for diabetes. Hypothesis We predict that exposure to proteins secreted by hMSC will stimulate new islet formation in the damaged pancreas and will improve human islet survival and function after transplantation. Objectives 1. We will discover of multiple hMSC-secreted proteins that collectively stimulate new islet formation. 2. We will expose isolated human islets to hMSC-secreted proteins to improve human islet survival and function after implantation into mice with autoimmune diabetes. 3. We will inject hMSC-secreted proteins into specialized mice that permit the identification of beta cell precursors that form new pancreatic islets. Impact These experiments will contribute to the advancement of 'cell-free' regenerative medicine treatments to cure diabetes.

In 2014, therapy for hepatitis C has underwent a major shift, with the introduction of Direct Acting Antivirals (DAAs). These drugs are a major advancement in treatment as they have been shown to have cure rates >95%. Although the DAAs are a major shift in treatment, they have placed a massive burden on the healthcare system, due to the high price of these drugs of each treatment costing over $80,000 a person. DAAs quickly became one of the highest costing drugs for public payers- with national spending over $2 billion, one of the single largest drug spends of all-time. Because of the high price, initial listing of was highly restrictive limited to only to those with advanced disease. In 2017, the pan-Canadian pharmaceutical alliance lead a national negotiations that broaden access to the medications. The negotiation were informed by economic models that helped find a good value for these new treatments. These models were largely informed by only clinical trial evidence. Based on this pan-Canadian approach, these drugs were made available on most provincial public drug program formularies, making them available on general formularies across most provinces. This change allowed easier access to treatments. It is unknown if the expanded listing of these curative agents has been a good investment. These drugs will have future re-negotiations on price. It is important that the upcoming negotiations and decisions related to these drugs be informed with information that comes from the real-world evidence to tell us how well the drugs worked in the Canadian setting.

column36: Constructing large-scale computational models of the healthy aging brain.
column37: The way our brain processes information changes throughout life. This is partly because of changes in our brain's structure and function with maturation and experience. column36: Improving pain education across entry-level physiotherapy programs in Canada: An integrated knowledge translation study
column37: One out of every five Canadians lives with chronic pain. A common problem reported by people living with pain is that their health providers do not have the required understanding and skills to provide them with effective care. This can result in misunderstanding, stigma, uncontrolled symptoms and prolonged disability. National strategies to address these problems focus on resolving important inconsistencies in how health providers are initially trained to manage pain. However, in order to make training programs more consistent and better aligned with research, we need to know more about the causes and consequences of these inconsistencies. This research aims to resolve these gaps in our understanding within the context of Canadian physiotherapy (PT) training programs. People living with pain, PT students and recent graduates, PT educators and PT program directors will all help lead and implement this project. We will interview faculty members in PT programs across the country; create a new assessment tool to evaluate PT students' knowledge and skills in pain management; and run the first nation-wide assessment to determine effectiveness of PT training programs in preparing PTs to manage pain. One of the innovative aspects of this project is that people living with pain will help create the assessment tool that will be used to determine whether PTs are adequately prepared to manage pain. Importantly, this assessment tool will include both written and practical components. The practical component of this assessment will be particularly useful in establishing the communication and interpersonal skills that are essential to effective pain management. Therefore, one of the important contributions of this work is that people living with pain will have the chance to shape the standards by which future health providers will be evaluated, thus ensuring they have the required knowledge and skills to provide effective care for the millions of Canadians suffering from pain.

column36: Understanding and Optimizing Opioid Use in Long Term Care.
column37: Many older adults residing in long-term care facilities (or nursing homes), including those without cancer, live with daily pain. This is often because of arthritis or related bone or joint conditions. For many residents, this pain may be poorly recognized or treated leading to lower quality of life and worse health outcomes. An important focus of the work is to examine whether different pain treatments (including opioids) are being used in ways that enhance residents' quality of life while lowering their risks of medication side effects. Research findings will be used to support care guidelines and interventions to improve pain detection and management in long-term care and ultimately, the quality of life and health of vulnerable older women and men residing in these care settings.

To date, no research has measured the extent, nature and impact of food company sponsorship of sports clubs in Canada nor has any research examined the financial impact of sponsorship on children's access to sports. The perceptions of parents and sports club officials regarding this activity and its restriction are also unknown. The purpose of this study is to determine the frequency and healthfulness of food company sponsorship of junior sports clubs in Canada, to examine its potential effects on the dietary behaviors of youth and to understand the perceptions of parents and sport club officials regarding this activity. To do so, this study will identify junior sports clubs for the 8 most popular sports among youth (5-17 years) in 7 cities in Ontario and 7 in Quebec. Sports club officials will be interviewed over the phone to identify all food company sponsors and to determine how much funding and other benefits they receive from food company sponsorship. The attitudes of parents and sports club officials regarding food company sponsorship and its restriction will also be assessed using surveys and individual interviews. Finally, surveys and focus groups will be conducted with youth to determine whether sponsorship influences their food purchasing or dietary behaviors and to understand their attitudes toward food sponsors. This research will help inform Canadian policies aimed at protecting children from unhealthy food marketing and improving their diet and health.

column36: PRECEDE: Preconception risk factors and Cardiometabolic health in Early childhood
column37: Cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes are major public health priorities. More than 1 in 3 Canadian children have factors that put them at risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, including overweight and obesity, unhealthy lifestyle behaviours, and abnormal measures of blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose. The first 1000 days, including the period before pregnancy (called 'preconception') represents an important period in which maternal and paternal physical health, mental health, lifestyle behaviours, and family functioning may impact the growth and development of children. However, a critical gap in knowledge exists on the role of these preconception maternal and paternal risk factors. A study that begins in preconception and follows families through to child health outcomes beyond birth does not currently exist. We will invite pregnancy-planning parents who have a child already participating in the largest ongoing study of children in the primary care practice setting in Canada called TARGet Kids!. We will collect data on weight, mental health, lifestyle behaviours, and family functioning in 1180 mothers and fathers who are planning a pregnancy in the next year. We will measure how these factors are related to their child's health at 2 years of age. Child health outcomes will include weight, blood pressure, blood cholesterol, blood sugar and health behaviours like physical activity, sleep, and nutrition. This study is important because prior research has shown that young children who had higher weight, cholesterol, blood pressure and blood sugar had higher weight, heart-health and diabetes risk as they became adults. Therefore this study will help us understand which factors parents may modify before they are pregnant in order to help reduce heart-health and diabetes risk factors in early childhood and beyond. This study will be among the first in the world to help answer these important questions.

column36: Probing molecular and mechanical signals that shape blood vessel growth
column37: Vascular malformations are very common in humans and include arteriovenous malformations (connections of arteries and veins directly), capillary malformations (dilated, disorganized vessels with abnormally fast or slow circulation) and vascular tumors such as hemangioma. Rasa1 is a gene that causes capillary and arteriovenous malformations (CM-AVM) when mutated in humans and was one of the first vascular malformation genes identified. In the past 5 years we have found that many human vascular malformations and tumors are caused by mutations in genes that function in a pathway related to Rasa1. Surprisingly, benign malformations and vascular tumors can be caused by mutations in the same genes; we do not understand why some are benign and some malignant. Also, the only treatments currently available are not based on scientific evidence but are 'best guesses. Our goals in this project are to identify mechanisms and possible therapeutics for vascular malformations, focusing on Rasa1. We will study this gene in an animal model where Rasa1 is lost. We will test its role in the blood vessel wall and identify small molecules that improve malformations.

column36: The Artificial Placenta
column37: Preterm birth remains the leading cause of death in children under the age of 5 worldwide. Despite advances in the technology used in neonatal intensive care practice, complications due to the damage of immature organs resulting from premature exposure to life outside the womb are common and often lead to ongoing health issues throughout life. The creation of an artificial environment that imitates the mother's womb and protects the fetus from injury while also promoting normal growth and development may be a solution for extremely preterm infants. In collaboration with the leading US research group working in this field, we have shown in an animal model that it is possible to create such an environment using a fluid-filled bag and an oxygenator circuit connected to the umbilical cord which acts as an artificial placenta. However, our preliminary experiments indicate that commercially available oxygenator technology designed for term infants undergoing cardiac surgery are unlikely to be appropriate for use in the extremely preterm human infants that are the target population for this research. The current research proposal aims to collect information about critical elements of the human placenta at the lower limits of viability that are needed to design an artificial placenta that faithfully reproduces the cardiovascular function of the real placenta. We will use this information to design and test custom made oxygenators for use as an artificial placenta in a realistic animal model of the extremely preterm human infant. Our laboratory is the first to attempt this kind of research in Canada and the work described in this proposal would represent an important step towards bringing this technology to our human patients.

column36: Implementation and Evaluation of an Indigenous-Specific Managed Alcohol Program for the Homeless Indigenous Population in Calgary, AB and Victoria, BC
column37: Indigenous peoples are disproportionately represented in the homeless population, while homeless individuals with substance dependency are an extremely vulnerable population susceptible to violence, victimization, premature death, poor health, social exclusion, marginalization and a vicious cycle of hospitalization, emergency shelter use, and incarceration. A lack of trauma-informed, culturally competent, culturally safe and Indigenous harm reduction services available for the homeless Indigenous population that struggle with severe alcohol use results in continued oppression while dismissing the importance of Indigenous epistemologies of healing. With the guidance of an Elder Advisory Circle and continued engagement with Elders, Knowledge Keepers and Indigenous community partners, the goal of this project is to implement and evaluate a managed alcohol program (MAP) that supports homeless Indigenous peoples living in Calgary and Victoria who struggle with severe alcohol use disorder. Research suggests MAPs are associated with tremendous positive outcomes including significant reductions in detox admissions, hospital visits, and police run-ins, while participants experience a better quality of life, gain better access to primary healthcare services and are more likely to retain their housing. This study will utilize a mixed-methods, community-based participatory approach that engages the Indigenous community, focuses on the priorities identified during engagement sessions, and seeks to improve the health outcomes of the homeless Indigenous population. It is anticipated results from this study will demonstrate a significant social return on investment and improve the health and well-being of the homeless Indigenous population while producing valuable outcomes that shape policy and best practices for culturally appropriate population health interventions.

column36: Le lavage uterin au salin physiologique comme traitement de l'infertilite inexpliquee: un essai clinique randomise a double insu
column37: L'infertilite atteint un couple canadien sur six. Dans plus du quart des cas, aucune cause n'est mise en evidence, c'est ce qu'on appelle l'infertilite inexpliquee. Malheureusement, les traitements indiques se limitent alors a la fecondation in vitro qui est associee a des effets secondaires et des couts importants. L'evaluation de la permeabilite tubaire est essentielle au diagnostic de l'infertilite inexpliquee afin d'exclure une obstruction des trompes uterines. Dans le mois suivant le test de la permeabilite tubaire, des etudes ont rapporte une augmentation des grossesses et naissances vivantes. En effet, il semble que le lavage uterin engendre lors de cette evaluation pourrait s'averer therapeutique. Un nombre croissant de donnees probantes, tant en recherche experimentale que clinique, suggere que certains cas d'infertilite pourraient etre causes par des facteurs mecaniques ou immunologiques au niveau de la cavite uterine empechant la fecondation. Ces facteurs seraient contres par la realisation du lavage uterin. L'etude proposee consiste en un essai clinique randomise evaluant l'efficacite du lavage uterin a l'aide d'une solution d'eau saline en pre-ovulatoire comme traitement de l'infertilite inexpliquee. Un tel traitement constituerait une avancee importante dans le domaine, puisqu'en comparaison avec les traitements actuellement disponibles, le lavage uterin pourrait s'averer une avenue therapeutique beaucoup moins invasive et couteuse.

column36: VISION Cardiac Surgery - ECG Evaluation Sub-Study
column37: Each year, more than 30,000 Canadians undergo cardiac surgery. Myocardial infarction, known commonly as a heart attack, is a frequent major cardiac complication after any type of heart surgery. Diagnosing a heart attack after open-heart surgery is challenging: the classic symptoms of chest pain and shortness of breath are commonly masked by painkillers or can be confused with post-operative discomfort. The markers of heart damage in the blood (troponins) are always elevated after heart surgery due to the intervention on the heart during the surgery. The electrocardiogram (ECG), which traces the heart's electrical activity, is a test often used in the diagnosis of myocardial infarction. However, its value after heart surgery is unclear because manipulating the heart, as done during heart surgery, can cause ECG changes making it difficult for physicians to know if a heart attack has occurred. We are conducting a study, called the Vascular events In Surgery patIents cOhort evaluatioN (VISION) Cardiac Surgery study, at 23 hospitals in 11 countries and we have almost completed recruitment of 15,000 patients who have had cardiac surgery. Information about these patients, including their medical history, type of heart surgery, and how well they recovered was collected. We measured troponins and collected ECGs before and after surgery for all patients. All patients were followed for one year after surgery. For this proposed study, experts will review the ECGs for all patients, both before and after their heart surgery, for signs of heart injury or damage. This will determine whether ECG changes increase the ability of physicians to diagnose a heart attack after heart surgery and whether physicians can predict which patients may die due to this complication.

column36: Interactions between PV interneurons and neuromodulators in cognition relevant to schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a neuropsychiatric disease that leads to a range of debilitating symptoms. Psychotic symptoms can be treated reasonably well, but few treatments exist for impairments in cognition including attention, working memory and cognitive flexibility. These impairments have a major impact on patients'-and their carers'-quality of life. To develop new treatments, we need to understand the brain changes underlying these cognitive impairments. Considerable research indicates that schizophrenia involves 1. dysfunction in a specific type of brain cell called a 'parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneuron' and 2. abnormal function of neuromodulators-molecules that modulate the activity of brain cells-such as dopamine and acetylcholine. Both types of dysfunction are linked with cognitive impairments. Although work is being done separately in these two areas, little is known about what these two types of brain dysfunction have to do with each other. For example, does the neuromodulator dysfunction cause or worsen the PV interneuron dysfunction? Is the interaction itself important for schizophrenia, or do the two types of dysfunction affect cognition in different ways? Recent, powerful technological developments in mice have now made this critical area of investigation possible. We will use novel, light-based techniques to observe PV interneuron and neuromodulator activity and to manipulate PV interneuron activity. This will be done while the mice engage in ipad-based cognitive tests that are identical to those used in humans, so that the findings can be more successfully translated to patients. These studies will lead to a better understanding of how brain changes lead to cognitive difficulties in schizophrenia, and how to better treat the debilitating symptoms of this devastating disease.

column36: Semaglutide in comorbid obesity and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders for metformin non-responders: a double-blind randomized control trial
column37: Almost one in every two patients with schizophrenia (SCZ) are obese and patients die 15-20 years earlier than the general population from heart disease. Medications called antipsychotics are needed to treat SCZ, but they cause a lot of weight gain. Weight gain is associated with poorer quality of life, barriers to social engagement, worse medication adherence, and poorer brain function. However, available treatments for managing obesity and related problems are not adequate. A drug called metformin has support from research studies to help treat weight gain in SCZ. However, it is effective in only about 20% of people, and doctors don't know what to use next. Newer treatments for diabetes and obesity such as a class called "glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists" (GLP-1RAs) can potentially help. Semaglutide is a newer, well-tolerated GLP-1RA, also found to have excellent weight-loss effects. We plan to study SCZ patients who suffer from obesity and don't lose weight on metformin, to see if adding semaglutide can help with body weight reduction and other risk factors for heart disease. Patients will first be treated with metformin for 4 months, and those who don't lose at least 5% of their body weight will enter a second study phase. At the start of this phase, they will be assigned to a weekly injection of semaglutide or placebo ("dummy"), which will be added to metformin. Participants have an equal chance of receiving semaglutide or the placebo. Neither patients, or study personnel know if placebo or semaglutide is being given. Over the next 6 months, participants will undergo body weight measurements, measures of blood sugar metabolism, an MRI scan to measure body fat changes, and tests of brain function to see if these improve with semaglutide. The goal of this study is to help develop logical and effective care pathways that can reduce the huge disparities in cardiovascular-related health that burden people already suffering with severe mental illness.

column36: Cellular responses to protein misfolding in a yeast model of aging
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is neurodegenerative disease affecting one in every 7,000 Canadians. HD occurs due to expansion of CAG repeats in the Huntingtin gene, which increases the number of polyglutamine (polyQ) repeats and tendency of the Huntingtin protein to misfold and aggregate in cells. There is currently no effective treatment available to either cure or slow the disease progression in humans. Importantly, the mechanisms that link accumulation of misfolded proteins to polyQ toxicity remain elusive. Our previous recent work has established a strong correlation between polyQ toxicity and dysregulation of transcription. This project is therefore aimed at understanding the mechanisms by which toxic polyQ expansions affect the regulation of gene expression. To address this, we employ a powerful yeast model of HD to model the genetic basis of transcriptional dysregulation in HD and identified key signaling molecules capable of reducing misfolded protein accumulation and promoting mHtt cell survival. Due to the increasing incidence of protein misfolding diseases in our aging population, our work will contribute to our understanding the role of regulators of transcription not only in HD but also in other human diseases.

column36: The Costs and Benefits of Transitioning from ICD-10-CA to ICD-11 in Canada
column37: Global surveillance and monitoring of disease requires the most current and comprehensive system to track and improve the health of individuals worldwide. The International Classification of Disease (ICD) is a system used worldwide to code disease diagnoses. Currently, Canada uses the 10th version of ICD to code health information. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recently released the 11th version of ICD (ICD-11), which offers updated diagnoses codes that reflect changes in society and medicine (e.g. opioid overdose and gaming addictions codes), and user-friendly electronic coding tools. ICD-11 will include 55,000 codes compared to that of ICD-10-CA (14,400). However, urgent questions have arisen about the costs and benefits of transitioning to a new classification system from decision-makers and health information management across Canada. The proposed study aims to provide evidence to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, to support the ICD-11 transition in Canada. To do this, we will create a cost and benefit framework, an online calculator tool, and provide the corresponding projections, for the ICD-11 transition in Canada. Our team is ideally positioned to conduct this work. The University of Calgary is a WHO Collaborating Centre on Classification, Terminologies and Standards that has been instrumental in testing and improving ICD-11. Further, we have established lasting relationships with the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) and the Canadian Health Information Management Association (CHIMA), both key stakeholders in overseeing Canadian coded health data and adoption of ICD-11. This project will provide critical information for countries worldwide to make a decision on ICD-11 adoption and will create an opportunity to elucidate the benefits and prepare for the challenges of transition (e.g. training and technology).

column36: Neurovascular adaptations driving stress-induced depression vs resilience
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disabilities worldwide and will affect 1 out of 5 individuals in their lifetime. Antidepressant treatments are not effective for 30-50% of patients, only 30% completely remit and do not suffer from another depressive episode, suggesting that current therapies do not address important biological mechanisms involved. Depression is more prevalent and recurrent in patients affected by cardiovascular diseases and stroke and, conversely, depressed individuals are more at risk to develop these pathologies, indicating that vascular dysfunction may contribute to the development of depression. We showed that chronic social stress induces blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage in male mice, promoting depressive behaviors. Chronic stress is depression's main risk factor and the BBB is an active barrier preventing harmful circulating signals to penetrate the healthy brain. Here we propose to investigate if stress-induced loss of BBB integrity is occurring in a sex- and region-specific manner. We hypothesize that BBB integrity may be affected in different brain regions in females explaining sex-specific symptoms. We will also define critical time points and evaluate if vulnerability to depression can be predicted by testing BBB integrity before stress exposure. Effects of chronic stress on BBB-astrocyte interface will be characterized as well. Astrocytes are part of the neurovascular unit and maintain BBB integrity in the healthy brain. Finally, we will test prevention strategies to promote neurovascular health and stress resilience. The strength of our approach is a reverse translational strategy that consists in studying stress responses in mice to unravel novel biological mechanisms underlying depression in humans. Depression is more prevalent in women and correlated with reported stress levels in daily life. It is imperative to explore stress-induced vascular maladaptive responses to develop innovative therapeutic strategies.

column36: How does chemotherapy to treat childhood cancer affect brain development?
column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood cancer, with 300 new cases per year in Canada. Fortunately, current chemotherapy treatments for ALL are remarkably successful: 90% of children diagnosed with ALL will be cured. About half of these children, however, experience problems with thinking speed, attention and memory, leading to limitations in school, work or social settings, and ultimately reducing quality of life. Before we can design a strategy to improve outcomes for children, we need to understand how these problems occur. Many of the drugs used in modern chemotherapy treatments have the potential to affect brain development. In previous work, we treated mice with individual ALL chemotherapy agents and identified the three that most altered the structure of the brain. We propose a three-part research program to determine how these three agents act on the brain during ALL treatment. In the first aim, we will focus on two of the agents that - surprisingly - do not penetrate the brain. We will measure immune and hormone changes induced by chemotherapy and determine if they are responsible for affecting the brain. In the second aim, we will manipulate the identified immune and hormone changes to see if we can rescue brain development. In the third aim, we will focus on the third chemotherapy agent which does enter the brain. We will determine whether selected drugs and/or nutrition supplements can limit toxicity, promote healthy metabolism, and restore brain development. Outcomes will be evaluated based on brain structure and behaviour. Our results will help us to understand how chemotherapy interrupts brain development during ALL treatment. Such an understanding is a critical step in designing strategies to improve brain function and quality of life for future childhood cancer survivors.

column36: Overcoming resistance to antidepressant treatment
column37: Major depression strikes 1 in 6 people and is twice as prevalent in women. In Canada, it is the second leading cause of disability. Depressed people have a greater risk of anxiety, suicide and cardiovascular diseases. Since reduced serotonin often leads to depression, first-line antidepressant drugs like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) work to increase serotonin in the brain. However, these drugs take many weeks to work and produce long-term recovery from depression in only 30% of patients. Our goal is to understand why some patients do not respond to SSRIs and find the best way to treat these patients. We focused on an important receptor for serotonin, the serotonin-1A autoreceptor. It is a strong inhibitor of the serotonin system. Human depressed patients who do not respond to SSRI treatment often have too many serotonin-1A autoreceptors. To model this genetic problem in mice, we knocked out a key genetic inhibitor of the receptor. These knockout mice have increased serotonin-1A autoreceptors and reduced serotonin. They have increased anxiety and depression traits and do not respond to SSRI treatment. Our research will compare male and female knockout mice to test how we can overcome this SSRI resistance using brain stimulation or other kinds of antidepressant drugs. In particular, we will overcome inhibition of the serotonin system using new therapies, including optogenetics to directly stimulate serotonin remodeling. Like depressed patients, our knockout mice show changes in activity in specific brain areas. Using optogenetics, we can to stimulate serotonin in specific brain areas whose activity is abnormal. These studies will guide brain stimulation approaches for treating depression. We will also test antidepressants that target different systems than serotonin in our SSRI-resistant mice. These studies could inform better treatment options in depressed patients who do not recovery when treated with SSRIs.

column36: Functional Studies of Coding Variants in Polycomb Repressive Complex Found in Humans
column37: DNA sequencing has ushered in a "Golden Age" of disease discovery. The causes of many rare genetic diseases have been found, and the genetic contributions to common diseases are also being solved very quickly. However, digging through multiple human genomes has unearthed thousands of new DNA variants, and often it isn't obvious which ones are the disease-causing mutations that affect health, and which other ones have no health effects. Our lab focuses on rare mutations that cause human overgrowth. Overgrowth syndromes cause tall stature, large head size and medical problems such as obesity, cancer, autism and intellectual disability. Having discovered the overgrowth syndromes that are caused by rare mutations in the "PRC2" group of proteins, we're now trying to understand exactly which DNA variants in PRC2 cause overgrowth and which ones don't. We have also found that some PRC2 mutations cause other medical problems, such as muscle fatigue and even stunted growth (i.e. the opposite of overgrowth). In this project we seek to recruit people who have rare DNA variants in PRC2 members, so we can follow them over time and find out what medical problems they have (if any). Because the human PRC2 genes each have an analogous gene that does pretty much the same thing in fruit flies, we plan to engineer our human mutations into experimental fruit flies. In this way we can figure out which of our variants are true mutations that produce a non-working protein, and which variants produce a protein that works well enough to allow normal function. By taking advantage of the wealth of molecular techniques that exist for fruit flies, we can quickly find out which human variants are likely to be benign with no effects on health, and which human variants are likely to be disease-causing mutations. The data from our study will help diagnostic labs sort out the small number of disease-causing PRC2 variants from the larger number of benign DNA variants in the PRC2 proteins.
