column36: Predicting weight loss and metabolic improvements after bariatric surgery through a novel genetic and epigenetic score.
column37: Obesity is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and type 2 diabetes. However, the obesity trait is highly variable from one individual to another. Genetics and epigenetic factors may contribute to this inter-individual variability. In the past decades, several international research efforts we were part of have taken on the challenge of decoding the genome and epigenome sequences associated with obesity and its related metabolic complications. However, most of these diseases are influenced by several genes each having only a small effect on its own. Polygenic approaches dealing with mass genetic and epigenetic data access more of the variance of these traits and can better predict individual risks of obesity and its metabolic complications, and more importantly treatment success. Weight loss and metabolic improvements after an anti-obesity surgery are highly variable and remain a poorly studied phenomenon. Time and efforts must be devoted to the identification of determinants of this large inter-individual variability in order to direct the patient to the treatment option with the greatest chance of success. We then propose to find a genetic/epigenetic set of determinants of body weight loss and metabolic recovery after bariatric surgery that may be used to develop applications to target the best surgical options for a patient. The specific aims are: Specific Aim 1: To derive a polygenic risk score (PRS) associated to the progression of weight loss and metabolic outcomes after a bariatric surgery. Specific Aim 2: To assess the potential of a blood DNA methylation risk score (MRS) to predict body weight loss and metabolic improvements after a bariatric surgery. Specific Aim 3: To test whether a combination of genetic and epigenetic determinants can better predict post-bariatric surgery outcomes than either a PRS or a MRS individually. These high-potential, new research avenues merit further investigation.

column36: Photoacoustics as a novel kidney fibrosis imaging tool
column37: 1 in 10 Canadians has kidney disease, many of whom will progress to kidney failure, a condition that leads to impaired quality of life, higher mortality, and costs of up to $100,000/pt/year. Although kidney transplantation offers hope for such patients, donor kidneys are in short supply, with patients now waiting up to 8 years for a transplant. As such, kidneys from sicker donors are frequently used, despite the fact that they are often already scarred, a process that can reduce their lifespan. While scarred kidneys are still useable, they are best transplanted into older patients, rather than younger people who need longer lasting kidneys. Importantly, scarring affects not only donor kidneys, but also drives the progression of nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. The only way to measure scarring currently is via looking at the kidney under a microscope. In animals, this is done by taking the kidneys out. As such, serial testing can not be performed, resulting in the needless use of many animals. In humans, scarring is assessed by biopsy, an invasive procedure that samples < 1% of one kidney and can cause bleeding. Unlike biopsy, ultrasound non-invasively images the entire kidney. Our goal is to test whether ultrasound can measure scarring in rodent and human kidneys. In rodents, we will test if through-the-skin ultrasound can track kidney scarring as it progresses (Aim 1). In human studies, we will test whether our ultrasound technique can image scarring of ex vivo donor kidneys (Aim 2). If successful, our studies could have major applications for preclinical research, by allowing easy tracking of scarring in the same animal over time. Moreover, as kidneys are removed from donors prior to transplant, our work could aid in how donor kidneys are matched to recipients, to maximize the benefit for all patients. Taken together, we expect that our results could have potentially transformative effects for the study and management of kidney scarring.

column36: Post-transcriptional regulation of functionally significant gene sets during neurodevelopment of Rett syndrome
column37: Genes function by making RNA that is then "translated" into proteins. We study the neurodevelopmental disorder Rett syndrome (RTT) which is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene. We discovered that the MECP2 gene makes RNA in human stem cells but it is not stable and is actively degraded. The ability to translate MECP2 RNA into MECP2 protein is also inhibited in stem cells and activated in nerve cells by the binding of two competing factors. These layers of RNA regulation ensure that stem cells do not make too much MECP2 protein until they mature into nerve cells, and we predict that many additional genes are subject to similar mechanisms of RNA regulation. Using RNA sequencing technologies, our preliminary experiments obtained a dataset to calculate the stability of all RNAs in these cells, and discovered a defect in protein degradation in RTT. Our overall goal is to comprehensively understand RNA regulation in human stem cells as they develop into nerve cells, and use this information to find proteins that are perturbed in RTT and which alter nerve cell function. AIM 1 will explore translational regulation of genes that control protein stability, and will identify the proteins that escape degradation and accumulate in RTT nerve cells. AIM 2 will identify global changes in RNA stability that occur as stem cells mature into healthy or RTT nerve cells. The underlying mechanisms controlling RNA stability will also be defined, and the impact on protein levels assessed in RTT nerve cells. The expected outcomes will be the elucidation of RNA regulation of genes in healthy and RTT nerve cells that can be applied to unveil perturbed proteins that are candidates for future drug development.

column36: Identifying the biological basis of GWAS hits for plasma triglyceride response to an omega-3 fatty acid supplementation.
column37: Diet is a major aspect of the environment that can be targeted in preventing cardiometabolic diseases. However, the effect of dietary changes on the cardiometabolic risk profile differs significantly between individuals. In a nutritional intervention, we have observed the hypotriglyceridemic effect of omega-3 fatty acids of marine origine in the entire cohort. However, the plasma triglyceride response was highly heterogeneous with 28.8% of individuals being considered as non-responders since no decrease in plasma triglyceride levels was observed after the supplementation despite compliance to the protocol. These results suggest that intrinsic characteristics of study participants such as genetic factors are likely to influence the plasma lipid response to diet. Accordingly, we have shown that genetic variations within genes modulated by omega-3 fatty acids explain, at least partly, the heterogeneity of the plasma triglyceride response to omega-3 fatty acids. We performed a genome wide association study and identified loci with significant differences in allele frequency between responders and non-responders to the omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. In the present research program, we wish to pursue the identification of genetic factors explaining the heterogeneity of the plasma TG response by increasing the density of genetic markers in the loci previously identified and to demonstrate the potential functional significance of these polymorphisms.

column36: A multicentre, double blind, randomized trial comparing lyophilized fecal filtrate to lyophilized stool in treating recurrent Clostridiodes difficile infection
column37: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI), the most common bowel infection in the hospital setting, is usually triggered by antibiotics. The treatment for CDI is with another antibiotic called vancomycin. After treatment, the chance of CDI coming back is about 20% after the initial episode, increasing to at least 60% after the 3rd episode. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), or stool transplant, is the most effective therapy for recurrent CDI (RCDI). The success rate is 80-90%. However, we don't know how it works. Recently there were 2 cases of mutli-drug resistant organism (MDRO) transmitted through FMT, resulting in one death. Both patients were immunosuppressed and their donor was not tested for MDRO. Furthermore, we do not know if there are long-term effects. For example, studies in mice have shown that obesity can be transferred with FMT, thus raising the possibility that other conditions such as autoimmune diseases and cancer could potentially be transferred with FMT. Therefore, safer and targeted therapy is needed, but we need to understand how FMT works first. The assumption is that transferring healthy gut bacteria from a donor to a patient corrects the disrupted gut bacterial community, but there may be more to this. A recent study showed despite removing live bacteria from donor stool, 5 RCDI patients were still successfully treated. This brings into question whether components in the stool other than live bacteria may be crucial. We believe that live bacteria may not be necessary for FMT to work. In this proposal, we will compare two forms of FMT: one with live bacteria and one without. Both formulations will be freeze-dried and put into pills. By removing live bacteria from the equation, this study will conclusively show whether other components within stool are enough to reshape the bacterial community in the gut. The results will lay foundation for future effort in developing more targeted RCDI treatment.

column36: Deciphering the role of the Yin Yang1 (YY1) transcription factor to understand pleuropulmonary blastoma
column37: Pediatric lung cancers are rare but diverse. Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is the most common pediatric primary lung cancer. It arises during fetal life and occurs in children under 7 years of age. PPB results from the progression of abnormal lung cysts to an aggressive sarcoma with poor survival. It is crucial to correctly recognize PPB early since it is the most curable stage. We produced a mutant mouse line devoid of YY1 function in lung epithelium. YY1 is a transcription factor essential for normal and cancer development. The mutation causes lung cysts as those seen in PPB patients at early stage. Accordingly, less YY1 protein is detected in PPB patients. PPB is associated with mutations in DICER1, an enzyme important for the production of microRNAs. microRNAs negatively control gene expression. How DICER1 and microRNAs act in PPB remains ill-defined. Our data suggested that the low YY1 protein levels detected in PPB are due to abnormal microRNAs caused by the DICER1 mutations. We also showed that the Yy1 mutation in mice affects the expression of key regulators of lung formation and that similar changes are seen in PPB patients. These data led us to hypothesize that reduced expression of YY1 participates in PPB pathogenesis by perturbing the expression of key regulators of lung development. Our objective is to elucidate the role of YY1 in PPB based on our knowledge of the mechanisms of action fulfilled by YY1 during lung formation. We propose to: (1) determine the role of microRNAs in YY1 expression, (2) identify the gene networks controlled by YY1 during lung formation, and (3) test if modulating the levels of YY1 effectors can rescue the cystic lung phenotype of mutant mice. Characterizing the YY1-driven basic mechanisms by which lung development occurs is important for understanding human diseases such as PPB.

column36: Solute transport in the innate immune response
column37: Cells are the smallest independent units of plants and animals. Virtually all human organs and tissues have specialized, sentinel cells (macrophages) that are dedicated to protecting the body from infection, damage, or toxins. When macrophages detect harmful stimuli, they cause inflammation, a protective response meant to eliminate the cause of the insult. The extent of this response needs to be measured by macrophages; too little inflammation enables the insult to persist and possibly worsen, while chronic inflammation is associated with multiple diseases including arthritis, atherosclerosis, and cancer. To detect signs of a threat, macrophages probe and survey their locale using sensors that distinguish harmful from healthy components. Second -and because some threats can be well-hidden- they internalize and digest massive quantities of their surroundings to expose such threats internally. Once swallowed, the ingested materials are sealed in a vacuole, digested, and probed for any signs of harm. These later steps require the evolution of the vacuole to acquire degradative enzymes, acidify, and distribute the contents to internal detectors. The consumption performed by macrophages is impressive; they take up their own body weight in just a matter of hours. An overlooked but essential part of the whole process is that the cells must expel these large volumes to maintain their appetite and surveillance. Excreting the remains of the ingested samples, a process termed resolution, is also essential to controlling infection/inflammation. I have obtained evidence that the resolution process is orchestrated by transporters: channels that expel the smallest components of the ingested medium out of the vacuole and cell. The objective of the proposed research is to now understand how the resolution process, orchestrated by our macrophages, is regulated, and why alterations in its regulation cause these cells to contribute to disease rather than correct it.

column36: Probing endocannabinoid tone in chronic pain patients with problematic opioid use: A PET study with [11C]CURB
column37: Approximately 20% of Canadian and U.S. adults live with chronic pain. Despite a downturn in the number of opioid prescriptions, U.S. data from 2017 suggests a significant number are dispensed. Long-term use of opioid medication can lead to loss of pain-relieving effectiveness and the development of dependence and withdrawal symptoms that make stopping administration difficult even when pain is poorly managed. Misuse of opioids prescribed for chronic pain occurs in up to 29% of patients with up to 12% developing opioid use disorder (OUD). Indeed, 80% of heroin users may have first misused prescription opioids. High rates of opioid prescribing, along with the emergence of strong synthetic opioids and the development of addiction has led to high overdose death rates and economic costs in North America. Research is needed to transform the way we identify, monitor and treat OUD. The proposed project aims to establish whether there are abnormalities in the brains endogenous cannabinoid (endocannabinoid) system (eCS) in chronic pain patients with OUD. There are well-established links between the brains opioid system (the site at which opioid medication works) and the eCS. For instance, these systems interact in pain and reward processing. There is also growing awareness that the eCS plays an important role in drug reward and addictive behaviours. Despite this, we still know very little about the eCS in those with OUD. Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) is an important enzyme within the eCS because it is responsible for the breakdown and inactivation of one of the main eCS neurotransmitters, anandamide. Reduced FAAH levels have previously been found in alcohol and cannabis use disorders. We will use positron emission tomography imaging, which uses small amounts of radioactive materials and specialized cameras, to investigate whether FAAH levels are lower in the brains of chronic pain patients with OUD compared to those without problem opioid use and healthy controls.

column36: Unplanned Hospital Readmission Following Critical Illness Survival: An Investigation of the Survivor-Family Dyad
column37: In Canada, the high (38-41%) unplanned hospital readmission rate in the year following intensive care unit (ICU) points to insufficient care of these vulnerable patients. Most individuals treated in an ICU will survive yet, up to half of these survivors suffer new or worsening physical, cognitive and psychiatric complications, termed post-intensive care syndrome. Family often become informal caregivers, but also suffer physical and mental health impairment, as well as loss of employment, financial difficulties and low quality of life. These complex, long-term complications often go unrecognized or untreated in the community, and result in survivor dependence on acute care services. While person-centred care entails addressing what matters most to survivors and families, there is limited understanding of what this even is, or how this influences health services use, eventually culminating in hospital readmission. The aim of this research is to describe the relationship between ICU survivors, their family caregivers and the healthcare system from the perspective of the survivor-family dyad, what matters to this dyad, and how this relationship influences unplanned hospital readmission. We will interview survivors, family caregivers and health care providers to develop an explanatory model, which will be extended and refined through focus groups across the Province of British Columbia. Study findings will inform the development of health services specific to ICU survivors.

column37: Starvation has always been a threat to people throughout evolution and to survive starvation specific gene products must step up and ensure that cells and organsims can adapt to a new state of low energy. Sometimes, when these gene products are faulty or missing the process doesn't occur correctly and results in maladaptation. We have shown that in a genetic model organism called C. elegans, this maladaptation results in a defect in reproductive capacity that is propagated through generations. This means that the descendants of the starved parent will eventually go extinct, although it may take few to several generations. We have tried to understand how this occurs and why starvation might lead ultimately to extinction of a family lineage. We show that a key mutagenic structure may be the culprit; one that causes significant DNA damage and thereby affecting future generations due to the mutations it can cause. We propose a series of experiments to better understand how this occurs and how we may be able to correct these defects through the use of transgenic approaches.

column36: How can health benefits of an effective, scaled-up, health promotion model for older adults be sustained?
column37: One-third of Canadians will be an older adult (>65y) by 2050. Thus, healthy aging is a public health priority. Many older adult health promoting interventions have been implemented, yet few were scaled-up and none were sustained. CTM is an effective, adaptable health promotion program for older adults. CTM improved healthy aging indicators-mobility, social connectedness, and decreased loneliness of older adults. We are now scaling-up Choose to Move (CTM) across British Columbia (BC) with support from BC Ministry of Health. Community partners and older adults identified three elements essential to CTM success: program flexibility, social interactions, and trusted relationships between participants and activity coaches (who deliver CTM). In this CTM sustainability (CTM-S) study we aim to determine if health benefits of CTM can be maintained. Therefore, we integrated the three essential elements into design of CTM-S and will assess three follow-up approaches: 1. activity coaches hold annual group meetings and call participants quarterly; 2. government service staff (HealthLinkBC) call participants quarterly; 3. we create a Facebook group for CTM-S participants and prompt participants daily. In a fourth group we will not actively follow-up. We will allocate 166 CTM programs (1743 participants) to follow-up arms. In our evaluation we will: 1) assess if during follow-up older adults' mobility, social connectedness/loneliness, physical activity and sedentary time across 12 and 24 months are maintained; 2) measure costs associated with each follow-up arm, program affordability and value to policy makers; 3) identify factors that support or inhibit implementation of CTM-S. We endeavour to generate strategies that can be used to implement and sustain effective health promotion strategies for older adults across Canada.

column36: Investigating the utility of markers of left atrial cardiopathy for the estimation of dementia risk in aging adults
column37: Two of the fastest growing conditions among aging adults are an irregular heartbeat, known as atrial fibrillation (AF), and dementia. AF is one of the most common heart conditions of aging. The chances of getting AF rise sharply after age 65. Having AF also increases the chance of developing dementia by 33%. Importantly, blood thinning medications lower the chance of getting dementia by almost half in people with AF. Doctors commonly use information about traditional cardiovascular risk factors (age, high blood pressure) in patients with AF to decide who might need blood thinners. But, AF often comes and goes or can be present with no symptoms at all. As a result, using symptoms of AF to identify people who need treatment might not capture everyone at high risk. New ways of identifying who is most likely to develop dementia caused by AF are urgently needed. Many changes in the heart's shape and function occur before the signs of AF appear and these changes can be seen on heart tests. These changes might also be related to the chances of developing dementia, as an early sign of increased risk. No research study has ever tested whether these changes might help improve doctors' ability to identify those likely to get dementia and determine who might benefit from blood thinning medications. In this study, we will use multiple computer databases that have information on heart tests and tests of cognitive ability from a large number of aging adults both in Canada and the US. We will identify people that have changes in their heart before the signs of AF start and test if these changes are related to the chances of developing cognitive decline and dementia. The results of this research will be very important for the development of screening programs to test aging adults for these heart changes and for clinical trials to test the best medications for aging adults with these heart changes to help reduce the risk of developing cognitive decline and dementia.

column36: Kidney and blood pressure disease burden and monitoring for chronic kidney disease in childhood cancer survivors
column37: Due to better cancer treatments in the last 30 years, more and more children with cancer are surviving. Yet, childhood cancer survivors (or CCS) get many health issues later in life, due to their cancer treatments. CCS often have kidney problems (Chronic Kidney Disease, or CKD) and high blood pressure (Hypertension, or HTN) later in life, which increase their chances for heart disease and many other serious health problems Ideally, CKD and HTN should be treated as soon as possible after cancer treatment, to prevent long-term kidney and heart issues. The first 5 years after cancer therapy is the best time to detect, prevent and treat CKD and HTN in childhood, before they worsen. Unfortunately, when CKD and HTN first appear after cancer therapy or if doctors are even testing for complications of CKD, isn't clear. Recommendations on testing for kidney and blood pressure issues after children finish cancer treatment are not very helpful to patients or doctors. This probably leads to missed opportunities to detect, prevent and treat CKD and HTN in these fragile patients. In the next 6 years, our team of doctors, researchers and patients want to understand kidney and blood pressure problems in the first few years after children finish their cancer treatments and whether doctors are testing for CKD and its complications. 1) We will study 500 CCS across Ontario, 3 and 5 years after they finish cancer treatment, to know how many have CKD and HTN early after cancer therapy and if they get worse over time. 2) In 5000 CCS treated for cancer from 2008-2018 we will find out if doctors have been testing for kidney problems and CKD complications. With this information, we will know what is needed to change recommendations on when and how to test for kidney and blood pressure issues after children finish cancer treatment, with the hopes that they get the CKD and HTN treatments they need, have less long-term kidney or heart disease and better overall health and well-being.

column36: The role of Parkinson's disease-related proteins in innate and adaptive immunity
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor impairment associated with the loss of dopaminergic neurones (DNs). Recent evidences indicate that the disease might be initiated away from the brain in peripheral tissues and involve autoimmune mechanisms. We have shown that two proteins associated with PD, PINK1 and Parkin, actively repress the immune system by limiting the presentation of mitochondrial antigens. In the absence of these proteins, or during a loss of function, stress conditions related to inflammation and fever triggers the presentation of mitochondrial proteins at the surface of a variety of cells of the immune system, as well as DNs. Our data indicate that this process engages autoimmune mechanisms leading the the establishment of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells able to recognize and attack DNs. In the next 5 years, we will characterize the role of PD-related proteins in mitochondrial antigen presentation (MitAP) and the engagement of autoimmune mechanisms. Understanding the molecular mechanisms regulating MitAP is of prime importance to develop therapies that would target the immune system.

column36: Uncovering the unexpected role of LTR promoter mutations in HIV-1 latency
column37: Viral latency currently constitutes one of the most formidable obstacles to curing HIV infection. Combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) is extremely effective at suppressing HIV infection and replication, but fails to eliminate long-lived immune cells infected with a dormant or latent virus. Latent viruses can persist indefinitely inside a cell until reactivated in periods of stress or when a patient interrupts cART. Several cellular mechanisms have been identified that can partially explain how HIV becomes latent, but the complete scheme of latency inducing factors has not yet been defined. Our research has recently revealed that certain types of mutations caused by the viral polymerase and by host immune proteins called APOBEC3 can contribute to create mutated viruses with a predisposition to become latent, thereby highlighting a potential new mechanism for latency. The research we propose will explore how these mutations cause HIV to become latent and in some instances resist the effects of various latency-reversing agents (LRAs). Our research will help to better understand HIV latency, contribute to the design of a new platform for testing the next generation of LRAs, and identify prognostic mutations in the viral DNA that will help predict the effectiveness of latency-reversal therapies.

column36: The Molecular Memory of Voltage-Gated Potassium Channels
column37: Neuronal activity is based on electrical signals in the cell wall of the neurons, leading to socalled action potentials. Small proteins in the cell wall, named ion channels, generate the electrical signals by letting sodium, calcium and potassium ions enter or leave the cells selectively and precisely timed. Learning and formation of memory is caused by repeatedly conditioning the electrical paths in the brain, reinforcing or abandoning neuronal connections. Upon this repeated or prolonged activation, the ion channels undergo an adaptation, which means that they develop a kind of short-term memory but on the scale of a single protein. The aim of this study is to understand how these molecular memories work. In principal, we are performing biomedical "reverse engineering" to unravel how the proteins work on the molecular level. To this end, we will use biophysical methods, in particular optical spectroscopy methods, (fluorescence) to directly follow movements of specific regions of the channels. These measurements are combined with functional measurements to correlate, in time, movement and function, and with molecular biology to manipulate the protein on an atomic level.

column36: Promoting Resolution of Acute Kidney Injury
column37: Acute kidney injury due to poor blood flow to the kidneys is among the most common causes of illness and death in hospitalized patients. Many patients who recover from initial injury are left with lasting kidney damage. Despite a better understanding, even at the level of the cell, of the events that cause progressive kidney damage, no treatments have emerged in the last few decades. The consequences of acute kidney injury are particularly devastating in kidney transplantation, and can greatly shorten the length of time in which transplanted kidneys continue to function. Progressive damage after acute kidney injury results from three main events, namely, excessive infiltration of white blood cells from the bloodstream into the injured kidney, formation of small blood clots within the kidney, and activation of cells that produce scar tissue. We discovered that Slit and Roundabout (Robo), molecules that block migration of brain cells during brain development before birth, can simultaneously block all three events, and prevent lasting kidney damage. Using a pig model, we also developed a new method of preservation of donor kidneys that allows even the most severely injured kidneys- kidneys that would never before have been deemed suitable for transplantation- to function after transplanting them. After acute kidney injury, some patients recover completely. The signals that favour resolution, rather than progression, of injury, are not well understood. The pro-resolving family of molecules enhance resolution of injury. The studies we propose will use molecular, cellular, and biochemical approaches, together with mouse models of acute kidney injury to determine how Slit and Robo act in concert with pro-resolvins to promote kidney recovery. Using our pig model of kidney transplant preservation, we will examine how Slit and pro-resolvins can be harnessed to reverse injury in transplanted kidneys exposed to extremely prolonged periods of impaired blood flow.

column36: Podocyte Remodeling in Hypertension and Diabetic Nephropathy: Role of CLIC5A
column37: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure in Canada, and Hypertension (high blood pressure) accelerates the loss of kidney function in patients with diabetic kidney disease. Both, Diabetes and Hypertension damage the filtering capillaries of the kidney. Normally, these delicate capillaries have to withstand a higher than normal blood pressure to help drive filtration to produce urine, but they also have to keep blood proteins from escaping into the urine. Specialized cells called Podocytes cover these capillaries with long tentacle-like projections, providing strength and preventing proteins from escaping. A number of studies, including studies from our laboratory, have shown that Podocytes react to a higher than normal blood pressure and diabetes by rearranging their shape. In the short term these responses are protective, but in the long run they are counterproductive causing podocytes to detach, protein to leak into the urine, along with progressive scarring the filtering capillaries and eventually kidney failure. Our laboratory studies a protein called CLIC5A, which is a major Podocyte protein involved in the remodeling response. We have worked out some of the molecular mechanisms by which CLIC5A produces the normal shape of Podocyte projections. We have also shown that CLIC5A is essential for the Podocyte remodeling response to Hypertension and when CLIC5A is absent Hypertension-induced damage to the filtering capillaries of the kidney is dramatically increased. More recent, as yet unpublished work indicates that CLIC5A also participates in the Podocyte response to Diabetes. Using cultured Podocytes and Mouse Models, the current project aims to work out how CLIC5A and its protein partners orchestrate the Podocyte remodeling response to Diabetes in the presence and absence of Hypertension. Our long-term aim is to develop approaches that modify the Podocyte remodeling response and prevent Diabetes- and Hypertension-induced Kidney Failure.

column36: Targeting a novel miR-185/PAK6 axis to overcome drug-resistance in human leukemia
column37: Blood cancer (leukemia) is common, with ~55,000 new cases expected in the United States and Canada in 2019. The National Cancer Institute (US) calculated an overall 5-year survival rate of 56% for various blood cancers. This is because drug resistance and relapse pose significant challenges. Life-long treatment is required, with potential side-effects and a high cost. Blood cancer cells generally respond to drug therapy at the onset, but the drugs lose their effectiveness after 6-12 months. We and others have discovered that this is mainly due to the inability of current therapies to eradicate blood cancer stem cells, which maintain the potential for relapse. There is thus an urgent need to develop new therapies that specifically target blood cancer stem cells, so that these cells can be eliminated, leading to a cure. However, there are currently no drugs that directly target blood cancer stem cells in a specific and potent way, nor any related drugs that are approved as therapeutics. Interestingly, we have recently discovered that PAK6, a novel drug target, displays abnormal activity in blood cancer stem cells, particularly in drug-resistant patients, compared to drug-sensitive patients. We have found that combining a PAK6 inhibitor with current anti-cancer drugs, to target abnormal activities of PAK6, more effectively inhibits blood cancer stem cell growth in culture than single drug treatment; this treatment strategy also doesn't have side-effects on normal blood stem cells, which provides a therapeutic window specifically for anti-cancer treatment. This study will investigate if this combination therapy will more effectively eradicate blood cancer stem cells obtained from drug-resistant patients and prevent blood cancer development, using our newly established animal cancer models. This work will provide ultimate proof-of-concept for the development of more effective therapies, with fewer side effects than currently used therapies.

column36: The impact of participation on body functions among youth with physical disabilities: A pragmatic individual-based study
column37: Youth with physical disabilities experience greater limitations to participation in community-based activities than do their average-developing peers, which can result in poor health outcomes. Emerging treatment approaches aimed at improving activity and participation have shifted from focusing only on impaired body functions towards the performance of functionally meaningful activities within the youth's natural environment. It is unclear; however, whether targeting intervention at the activity/participation level can simultaneously result in improvement of personal functional skills (e.g., reaching) and body functions (e.g., range of motion, balance) - components known to worsen with age and, thus, important to address and maintain within the rehabilitation process. Our team has partnered with key community-based stakeholders including youth, clinicians and policy-makers, and together we plan to examine whether engaging in an 8-week self-chosen community-based activity (e.g., sledge hockey, boccia, drawing, playing a musical instrument) can lead to a significant improvement in three key body functions: motor, cognitive and affective. Thirty youth with physical disabilities will take part in the study and engage in an activity program of their choice. Changes in their body functions (e.g., movement, attention, mood) will be measured multiple times before, during and after engagement in the chosen activity/program. Findings of this study can guide clinicians, families and policy-makers to select effective approaches that not only promote participation but also facilitate additional motor and mental benefits from one single intervention. Such treatment approaches may also reduce the burden on the healthcare system as well as on the youth and families. Moreover, findings can advance our understanding of methods for testing complex and unique 'real-life' individual-based interventions that are highly relevant to practice.

column36: Determining genetic and non-genetic risk for schizophrenia in a high risk group
column37: Schizophrenia is a serious and disabling illness that affects about 1 in 100 people. The cause is unknown for this brain disease that often affects youths, seemingly at random in a family. For babies born with a genetic deletion (missing piece of DNA) on one of the pair of chromosomes 22, the risk is very high: 1 in 4 will develop schizophrenia. By comparing people with the deletion who have and have not developed schizophrenia, we aim to identify additional genetic changes and non-genetic factors that will allow us to personalize risk estimates. Because the schizophrenia illness is the same, insights gained from studying this chromosome deletion can help us learn about schizophrenia more generally. An international collaboration has provided us with the opportunity to study the complete genetic codes of an unprecedented number of individuals with this high risk deletion. Our group has recently made this genetic information ready for analyzing the many types of DNA-level changes that could affect the risk of developing schizophrenia. We will obtain similar genetic data for 100 additional Canadians with this deletion where we know schizophrenia outcome. This will mean instead of just 435 people we will have 815 people with this deletion who also have outcome and detailed genetic information. For all 815, we will collect information on other possible risk factors for schizophrenia, such as premature birth. We will use this unique dataset to develop and test prediction algorithms for schizophrenia. Families, clinicians and researchers want to anticipate and ultimately prevent disabling outcomes like schizophrenia in at-risk individuals. Discovering the genetic and non-genetic factors that predict schizophrenia in people from a high risk group could help us predict risk for schizophrenia in the general population. This could help us intervene early to prevent major disabilities.

column36: The role of the lineage oncogene ASCL1 in treatment-induced neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: Prostate tumours are addicted to the androgen receptor (AR) for growth and survival. Capitalizing on this inherent weakness, potent drugs have been developed to "turn off" the AR and starve cancer cells of fuel. These therapies are widely used in the clinic and have undoubtedly benefited patient survival; however, they are merely palliative and no patients are cured. Alarmingly, nearly 25% of patients progress to a highly aggressive and deadly form of prostate cancer, called neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), where treatment remains decades old toxic chemotherapy and survival is measured in months. Our research is focused on uncovering how prostate tumours evolve into NEPC following AR targeted therapy. We discovered that the transition to NEPC is orchestrated by ASCL1, a pro-neural protein that changes the structure of DNA to allow a prostate cancer cell to turn on neuronal genes and take on the identity of a neuroendocrine cell. In the current proposal, we aim to decipher the role of ASCL1 in altering the structure of DNA and its impact on treatment resistance and the transformation to NEPC. This work will advance our understanding of how prostate tumours evade therapy by transitioning to NEPC, and inform future therapeutic strategies to benefit patients with aggressive prostate cancer.

column36: Targeting RNA Splicing for the Treatment of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a most common and devastating genetic disease. People with DMD usually die at 25 to 30 years of age from effects of muscle deterioration. A most promising strategy to treat DMD is a molecular therapy called exon skipping. Exon skipping uses a short DNA-like molecule that acts like a stitch in RNA, an important biological molecule that functions to convert the genetic information of DNA into proteins, to bypass the mutations that cause DMD. With this DNA stitch in place, people with DMD may be able to produce short working versions of their mutated protein in DMD. The first drug in this class of DNA-stitch molecules was approved in 2016. However, two problems have not been solved. First, people with DMD who were given this drug did not have their DMD symptoms improve. Second, this drug can only help around 13% of people with DMD-people with only some types of DNA mutations. Our research will first work to improve the effectiveness of exon skipping for DMD. We are creating the next generation of these DNA-like molecules to be more effective in humans. We will also work to expand number of people with DMD who can be helped by exon skipping therapy. We will experiment with a cocktail of DNA-like molecules that could help 63% people with DMD. Lastly, we will work to understand the mechanisms of how our DNA-like molecules affect the DMD gene. This will help us design a better cocktail of DNA-like molecules. Our DNA-stitching technology could create new therapies for DMD and improved quality of life for people with DMD.

column36: The SCF(FBXO11) - XAB2 axis mediates DNA repair and therapeutic resistance in small cell lung cancer
column37: In Canada, lung cancer is responsible for more deaths than colon, breast, and prostate cancer combined. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a particularly aggressive subtype that represents approximately 15% of all lung cancers. Despite an initial response of SCLC to therapy, disease recurrence often occurs, and cure is rare, with dismal 5-year overall survival rates of less than 8%. There is a critical need to understand the mechanisms of therapeutic resistance to develop more effective treatments for this disease. We have found that loss of a key component of a protein recycling complex leads to resistance to chemotherapy and a newer therapy, known as a PARP inhibitor, in SCLC. This key component is 1 of the 69 possible F-box components of a Skp1-Cul1-F-box (SCF) complex that targets various proteins for tagging with ubiquitin and leads to target protein degradation. Our preliminary results suggest that loss of this specific F-box leads to the lack of the ability to degrade a DNA repair protein known as XAB2. This results in an increase in DNA repair capacity in the cancer cell that can be responsible for treatment resistance as the cancer cell can more easily repair DNA damage caused by chemotherapy or PARP inhibitors. Here, we propose to understand more about how this F-box and SCF complex regulates DNA repair through experiments to precisely determine its impact on DNA damage and repair. In addition, we will determine how the SCF complex interacts physically and functionally with XAB2, its target DNA repair protein. Finally, we will conduct a high-throughput screen to identify potential drug targets that are specific to these treatment resistant cancer cells that have this F-box loss, while sparing normal cells. Through these efforts, we seek to further our understanding of how cancer cells repair, tolerate and become resistant to our current treatments while designing newer treatment approaches to improve outcomes for our patients.

column36: Long-term immune activation by a mucosal RSV subunit vaccine: mechanism of action and application to vaccination of elderly
column37: While previously underestimated, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) contributes to a significant proportion of severe respiratory disease and mortality in the elderly, similar to influenza. With a growing elderly population, a RSV vaccine is urgently needed, but not available. The elderly tend to respond more weakly or inconsistently to vaccination unless they receive vaccines that are specifically developed for them. Our overall objective is to develop and characterize a RSV vaccine for elderly. As RSV infects the respiratory tract, the presence of virus neutralizing antibodies at this site is critical. Boosting and maintaining high neutralizing activity of antibodies in the serum by intramuscular vaccine administration may be adequate as serum antibodies can penetrate and protect the lower airways and lungs. However, mucosal immunization is required to induce production of local IgA antibody and the correct type of T lymphocytes in the respiratory tract. We already have a safe, effective vaccine candidate consisting of a protective antigen of RSV and an immunostimulatory adjuvant. When administered either intramuscularly or intranasally, this RSV vaccine induces long-term, protective immunity in several neonatal and adult animal models, e.g. mice, cotton rats and lambs. We have evidence that this vaccine also elicits an immune response in old mice. We will evaluate the magnitude and longevity of this immune response, as well as protection from RSV infection in old animals, and if necessary optimize the RSV vaccine. Furthermore, we will fully characterize the properties of this vaccine, which will expedite human clinical trials and licensing. An effective RSV vaccine will decrease morbidity and mortality due to RSV infection, which will in the future, improve the health of the elderly and significantly reduce health care costs. In addition, our new adjuvant has applications in vaccines against other respiratory pathogens such as influenza virus as well.

column36: Development of a typology for patient navigation: Defining the essence of a complex intervention
column37: As the provision of health care becomes increasingly complicated, many complex interventions have been created to meet the needs of a diverse population. These interventions tend to contain many components that interact, and these components tend to be hard to define and describe. As a result, it is hard to know what these complex interventions really do, how they work, and ultimately how to replicate any successes seen. "Patient navigation" (PN) is one such example. Patients describe difficulty navigating their way through the health care system to access the right care provider or service in a timely manner. As a result, numerous PN programs have been developed to help facilitate and coordinate care in this fragmented system. These programs vary widely with no current definition or standards to guide them. Without such a foundation, there is great difficulty in developing, evaluating, and comparing PN programs. We propose an innovative way to study complex interventions-the creation of a typology, or a classification scheme, to characterize PN and how it works. Through a review of the literature, we will first explore how PN works, for whom, and in what circumstances. Then, we will elicit views from key stakeholders who are impacted by PN. These stakeholders include patients, health care providers, and health care administrators and decision-makers. A typology will be created based on these perspectives, outlining the key elements that form the core, or essence, of PN. We will then seek the input of patients and other stakeholders across the country to finalize this typology. The creation of a PN typology is an essential step to knowing how to develop these programs, where to implement them, and how to evaluate them. Patient involvement ensures that patient needs, perspectives, and values are incorporated into the very foundations of PN. This is a new approach to understanding a complex health intervention that can be applied to other interventions.

column36: Just Coverage Decisions: Including Legal Analysis into the Assessment of Health Technologies
column37: Governments make decisions about what technologies to include in public medicare and their decisions are heavily influenced by Health Technology Assessment (HTA) bodies across Canada. In their assessments, HTA bodies take into account how well a technology works (as examples, orphan drugs, personalized medicines, robotic surgeries, implantable devices) and how much they cost. Increasingly they also factor into their assessments ethics and larger social concerns. HTA bodies should also factor in legal issues. Examples include whether a failure to fund a new technology is likely be challenged under human rights law for discriminating on the grounds of disability, or whether an implantable device that collects personal health information from your body is in compliance with relevant privacy laws. Our multidisciplinary team of lawyers, ethicists and HTA researchers will work closely with representatives from HTA bodies. Our goal will be to equip non-lawyers working within HTA bodies so they can better identify and prioritize important legal issues that warrant professional legal advice before a positive or negative recommendation is made with respect to funding. To achieve our goal we will closely evaluate existing HTA decisions to see what legal issues they identify or fail to identify, and relevant court cases. We will use this as a basis to develop an Identification Framework, with categories of technologies with similar characteristics that we map to important legal issues with links to plain-language summaries and other supports. We will test this Framework out using a range of technology case-studies in workshops with HTA bodies. Building on this, we will develop a Prioritization Tool that will better help HTA bodies weigh the risks associated with different legal issues. Our ultimate goal is to improve how we decide what is and is not included within public medicare as pressures increase from patients and innovators to include more and more.

column36: Understanding the effect of adherence to system-level performance measures on outcomes for rheumatoid arthritis
column37: One in a hundred Canadians live with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and suffer daily joint swelling, stiffness and pain. RA causes disability and sometimes can lead to joint replacement surgery if not properly treated. Joint inflammation in RA also increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. These complications of chronic inflammation contribute to substantial disability, increased healthcare costs and premature deaths. Early and appropriate treatment of RA has been shown to improve patient pain, function, disability, and survival. The Arthritis Alliance of Canada (AAC), representing over 36 organizations including patient organizations, healthcare provider groups, researchers and funding agencies has developed a set of performance measures to measure whether patients with RA are getting timely care and treated appropriately. These measures have been tested across Canada and a number of gaps in care have been identified including long waiting times for rheumatology consultations, lower than expected rates of treatment with disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (the standard of care), and gaps in ongoing follow-up care. What is unknown is why these gaps occur and what this means for patients and the healthcare system. In the present study we will investigate in three Canadian provinces how better quality of care impacts patient outcomes and the healthcare system. While the measures have been nationally endorsed by the AAC, they are not routinely measured outside of a research context, as monitoring the quality of care in RA has not, to date, been a priority of provincial health organizations. The findings of our study will help solidify the importance of ongoing quality measurement for RA- one of the most expensive chronic diseases. Ultimately this work will instigate health systems to improve so that patients living with RA can get the best possible care and achieve the best possible health outcomes.

column36: Developing, Evaluating, Disseminating and Sustaining a School-Based Mental Health Literacy Intervention for Indigenous Youth
column37: Mental health challenges are common and substantial among youth, including Indigenous youth, which may lead to many negative life outcomes when unaddressed. This project will create a freely available evidence-based school mental health literacy resources for Indigenous youth in order to improve their understanding about mental health and wellness, reduce stigma against mental illness, enhance help-seeking behaviours and other outcomes.

column37: Zellweger Spectrum Disorder (ZSD) is commonly caused by mutations in the PEX1 gene, resulting in peroxisome dysfunction. column37: A high proportion of individuals hospitalized in the adult intensive care unit (ICU) experience significant pain. Although some are able to self-report their pain, others are unable to communicate due to their critical health condition or the use of medication that puts them to sleep. Pain that is left undetected and under-treated can lead to ICU longer stay, multiple complications, and can even cause death. Regular evaluations of pain using appropriate tools that are adapted to the individual's capacity to communicate are necessary to help provide suitable pain control. The main goal of this project is to implement an evidence-based pain management intervention for individuals in the ICU, to evaluate if it is applied by health professionals of the care team on a daily basis and if this practice sustains over time, and if it helps to reduce pain in these individuals. The order of implementation in each ICU will be pre-established at random, and each ICU will have received the intervention by the study end. Before and after intervention implementation in each ICU, frequency of pain assessments, administration of pain relievers and evaluation of their effectiveness will be documented from the medical charts and determine pain management practice indicators. Perceptions of ICU healthcare professionals on team collaboration and contextual factors will be assessed. Patient outcomes including incidence of significant pain, adverse events, ICU length of stay, mechanical ventilation duration, and mortality will be described. Key outcomes of this project are to improve pain control practices in the adult ICU, and to reduce the incidences of significant pain and their related negative outcomes.

column36: Exogenous signals that drive the Pseudomonas aeruginosa transition to pathogenesis
column37: To cause infection, free-living bacteria must sense the presence of a host and activate virulence mechanisms. Bacterial virulence relies on the ability to utilize host-derived nutrients as well as capacity to evade and suppress host immunity. column36: Effects of N-acetylcysteine on psychosis-like symptoms and a neurophysiological biomarker of the clinical high risk state for schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a chronic debilitating psychotic disorder. Identifying persons with "clinical high-risk" (CHR) symptoms which are like those of schizophrenia but less severe, and providing psychiatric care to these individuals has been shown to help prevent psychosis. Existing medications, however, have not been shown to reduce CHR patients' rates of developing psychosis and are associated with substantial side effect burden. Therefore, practice guidelines do not recommend current medications as routine treatment for the CHR state, and there is a need to identify new treatments for this condition. Research suggests that abnormal brain oxidative stress may contribute to schizophrenia, offering a potential novel treatment target in the CHR state. Oxidative stress is an excess of free radicals, which are generated from normal metabolism and environmental exposures, and can damage cells. Antioxidants in the body normally neutralize free radicals. Antioxidant deficiency could result in excess oxidative stress that damages brain cells, leading to schizophrenia. Recent studies suggest that N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a precursor of the most abundant brain antioxidant, glutathione, may be a safe, well-tolerated treatment for schizophrenia. In light of this, NAC may also reduce symptoms and brain abnormalities in CHR patients. We aim to examine whether, in CHR patients, NAC improves both psychosis-like symptoms and the mismatch negativity (MMN), a brain marker of schizophrenia and the CHR state. MMN is an EEG ("brainwave") response to rare sounds among frequent ones, which is reduced in both schizophrenia and the CHR state. Patients will take either NAC or placebo for 8 weeks in a randomized double-blind manner. We hypothesize that they will have symptom reductions and MMN increases after taking NAC vs. placebo. The ability of NAC to reverse symptoms and a biomarker of the CHR state would support further research on NAC as a preventive treatment against psychosis.

column36: The role of fibrosis signaling in adipose tissue regulation of insulin resistance
column37: We face a growing global epidemic of obesity and diabetes. About 9.3% of Canadians have diabetes, for an estimated economic cost of $12.2 billion. Fat or adipose tissue is increasingly recognized as an important and dynamic organ that grows massively when we gain weight. We also find that inhibiting another protein, focal adhesion kinase (FAK), seems to increase levels of YAP in fat cells. Thus, our goal is to identify the role of these signaling proteins in fat and fibrosis contributing to type 2 diabetes with obesity. First, we will measure if YAP is activated with adipose tissue fibrosis, obesity and diabetes. Then, we plan to test whether knocking out YAP can prevent adipose tissue fibrosis and diabetes. Finally, we will determine whether FAK regulates levels of YAP, contributing to fibrosis and disease. Together, these studies will help us better understand fat, fibrosis and the role they play in our metabolism. These discoveries will help us develop better treatments for obesity and diabetes in the future.

column36: Defining the molecular basis of regulation of PI3K gamma and its role in immune function and the tumour microenvironment
column37: One of the major developments in cancer treatment has been the use of cancer immunotherapy to utilise the immune system to target and destroy cancer cells. The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is at the crossroads of both cancer development and immune regulation, with mutations in this pathway being extremely frequent in the development and maintenance of multiple high mortality human cancers. Intriguingly, inhibition of the PI3K gamma isoform is able to act as a switch that can reprogram the tumour microenvironment to target cancer cells. This is a powerful approach to promote the immune system to generate an anti-cancer response. In addition, the PI3K gamma isoform is also frequently upregulated in many cancers, with the development of specific inhibitors being an excellent strategy for cancer therapeutics. This proposal focuses on studying the structural and dynamic basis of regulation of PI3K gamma, with a major focus on the development of specific small molecule inhibitors. One of our major goals will be in defining the molecular mechanisms that control how this enzyme is activated, and how it can be misregulated in human disease. This will be approached using a cutting-edge synergy of state of the art biochemical and biophysical methods including Cryo-Electron Microscopy, X-ray crystallography, and Hydrogen Deuterium Exchange mass spectrometry. A powerful team of collaborators including medicinal chemists, cell biologists, and clinical immunologists has been established to fully apply biophysical discoveries in both cellular and organism models of disease. PI3K gamma is an exceptionally important target for anti-cancer therapeutics. This proposal focusing on defining the molecular basis of how this enzyme is regulated will reveal novel insight into its role in immune regulation and cancer immunotherapy. The development of small molecule inhibitors in this proposal has the potential to act as therapeutics in cancer therapy.

column36: The molecular choreography of ion channel expression
column37: All signal processing depends on neurons correctly encoding input and transforming that into a series or pattern of spikes to convey the information to other cells in a circuit. We know that modulating the pattern of spike firing depends on calcium-dependent processes that create inhibitory feedback following spike discharge in the form of afterhyperpolarizations (AHPs). This process is so important that virtually every neuron generates a series of AHPs of increasing duration following a spike. In this way spike firing can be modulated over a timeframe of ~10 msec (fast AHP) to 10 sec (slow AHP). To understand how these responses are generated we need to identify the source of calcium increases and the calcium-gated potassium channels responsible for triggering the spike-AHP sequence. This study identifies a new level of interaction between calcium channels at the plasma membrane (PM) with an underlying cytoskeleton and even a deeper quilt-like membrane formed by the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Our work builds on recent findings that the slow AHP arises from the concerted action of a voltage-gated calcium channel at the PM with ryanodine receptors that release calcium from the ER, which together activate a class of IK potassium channels. These interactions are enabled at "ER-PM" junctions where the ER extends narrow columns of membrane to within 10 nm of the PM. We propose that these sites in fact act as "CaRyK hubs" where multiple calcium sources and potassium channels are coassembled to reliably trigger an all-or-none spike-AHP sequence. Moreover, CaRyK hubs are distributed across the soma with a high degree of organization in the form of a polygonal (honeycomb-like) matrix we have traced to interactions with the cytoskeleton and even the underlying ER. The work is thus important in effectively identifying a new node of ion channel expression to mediate the calcium-dependent control of spike output necessary for neural coding and information transfer.

We will use devices called actigraphs (which resemble wrist-watches) to objectively measure sleep timing, duration and quality in children and adolescents, including sons and daughters of parents with depression or with bipolar disorder. We will examine the relationships between sleep and mood disorders in parents, sleep duration and regularity in children and later development of mood symptoms in the children. We will compare the information from questionnaires and from actigraphs. Based on the results, we will develop a sleep monitoring procedure with feedback to the participants that can be used as part of preemptive early intervention to reduce the risk of mood disorders.

column36: Mucosal Associated Invariant T-cells (MAIT cells) as Key Mediators of Anti-Tumor Immune Responses and the Microbiome Effect in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC)
column37: The treatment of lung cancer has been recently revolutionized by the development of immunotherapies such as PD1 inhibitors. However, attempts to develop improved immunotherapies have been hampered by a limited understanding of the immune cell populations that modulate anti-tumor immune responses. Mucosal-associated invariant t-cells (MAIT cells) are a unique population of immune cells associated with mucosal surfaces including the lungs. MAIT cells have previously been demonstrated to be stimulated by the presence of specific types of bacteria. The presence of specific types of bacteria in the gastrointestinal tract have recently been associated with increased clinical benefit in metastatic lung cancer patients treated with a PD1 checkpoint inhibitor. Our group has recently identified the presence of activated MAIT cells within the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) of lung cancer tumors. MAIT cells may thus serve as key mediators of anti-tumor immune responses that are directly influenced by the type of bacteria present in the gastrointestinal tract (i.e. gut microbiome). This study will explore the relationship between the composition of the microbiome, the presence of MAIT cells in the tumor and the likelihood of response to a PD1 checkpoint inhibitor. Our overarching hypothesis is that MAIT cells serve as the key mechanistic link between the composition of the microbiome and the generation of an inflammatory tumor predisposed to respond to treatment with a PD1 inhibitor. We propose to characterize the frequency and activation state of MAIT cells in the tumor biopsies of 50 patients with metastatic lung cancer treated with a PD1 inhibitor and correlate this with the patient microbiome and likelihood of response to a PD1 inhibitor. The proposed study will be the first to demonstrate the presence of activated MAIT cells in lung cancer tumors as well as characterize their role as mediators of the microbiome's modulatory effect on response to PD1 inhibitors.

column36: Grappling with type IV pili: characterization of Nature's most powerful biological motor
column37: Many bacteria produce long thin hair-like filaments called type IV pili (T4P) on their surfaces. T4P are used by bacteria as grappling hooks to grab onto their hosts, where they colonize appropriate niches (in the case of good bacteria) or cause disease (bad bacteria). T4P filaments can be repeatedly extended and retracted, allowing the bacteria to crawl along surfaces or use them as fishing rods to capture free DNA from the environment, leading to acquisition of new antibiotic resistance genes. The T4P are made by a large multi-component nanomachine that assembles (extends) and disassembles (retracts) the filaments. It does this using highly-conserved molecular motors capable of generating some of the strongest retraction forces ever measured - up to 100,000 x the weight of the bacterial cell. The way in which the T4P motor functions is among the most important unresolved questions in the field. Mutation of critical motor components can cripple the bacteria, suggesting they are good therapeutic targets. In this proposal we will use multiple techniques to solve the three-dimensional structures of the motors from two evolutionarily-distinct types of T4P system to understand how they perform their extension and retraction functions. Combined with the expertise and tools for study of the T4P system we have built over the past 20 years, these structures will guide the generation of specific mutants that will allow us to test our predictions about motor function. As we reveal how the individual components work together, we will use that knowledge to understand how inhibitors of the motors, produced by natural predators of the bacteria, block their function, information that is valuable for the rational design of new therapeutics.

column36: Validation of a new multi-parameter technology to better diagnose pain in the adult intensive care population: The Nociception Level (NOL) Index
column37: Assessing pain in the adult intensive care unit (ICU) is challenging because many patients are unable to communicate due to mechanical ventilation and sedation. Therefore, it is necessary to have alternative methods to assess pain in this vulnerable patient population. In this project, we will test the use of a new technology (i.e., the Nociception Level (NOL) index) for pain assessment in ICU adults. The NOL index is a value from 0 to 100 obtained by calculating different parameters (e.g., pulse, skin temperature) captured through a small probe placed on the patient's finger. The NOL was initially developed for assessing pain and analgesia in anesthetized patients undergoing surgery, and its use in the ICU is new. We will test the NOL's use before, during and after usual care procedures known to be painful (e.g., tube or drain removal, suctioning of secretions through the endotracheal tube) and non-painful (e.g., cuff inflation to measure blood pressure) in ICU adults. We will monitor the NOL in three groups: a) patients able to communicate so they can self-report their pain (gold standard criterion), b) patients unable to communicate but express behaviors (reference criterion), and c) patients unable to communicate and to express behaviors. In the first group, patients will be asked to self-report their pain on a 0 to 10 numeric scale. In the second group, patients will be assessed for pain using a standardized behavioral scale which will be completed by trained research staff. In the third group, only the NOL will be monitored. Analgesic and sedative medication administered to patients will also be documented from medical charts. The ability of the NOL to diagnose pain based on self-reports of pain and behavioral scores, and its ability to discriminate between painful and non-painful procedures will be examined. If found to be useful, the NOL could be used as an alternative measure of pain and improve its diagnosis and treatment in vulnerable ICU patients.

column36: Pre-operative Risk Stratification in Endometrial Cancer to Inform Surgical Management
column37: There are approximately 70,000 new cases of endometrial cancer each year in North America; 7,300 new cases in Canada in 2017. Currently, it is difficult to reliably distinguish at the time of diagnosis, before surgery, which endometrial cancers are at high risk to progress to serious health events and even death; consequently, for example, we do not know which patients require a referral to a gynecological oncologist due to their increased risk and which can be treated in their community. Our team has recently developed a practical tool which helps categorize endometrial cancer patients, based on the genetic characteristics of their tumours, into four subtypes that are associated with patient outcome, such as recurrence and death from endometrial cancer. This practical tool uses methods that can be performed in the clinic and most importantly, can be performed at the time of diagnosis. We will use this tool with consideration of other risk factors (e.g., blood work, imaging and other disease) to develop models that can predict, from the time of initial diagnosis, which patients are likely to recur and consequently have an increased risk of dying. These models will help us improve guidelines for endometrial cancer management and determine the 'best' treatment (e.g. which patients should be referred to specialists which patient are candidates for ovary and fertility preservation) for every woman diagnosed with this disease, including those for whom current treatments may not work and would be best served through referral to clinical trials. This project will benefit both patients and the healthcare system as fewer endometrial cancer patients will be given expensive toxic cancer treatments that are not needed, or to which they are unlikely to respond.

column36: Elucidating the Role of Memory in the Transition from Acute to Chronic Pediatric Pain
column37: How children remember pain sets the stage for future pain experiences. These memories can easily become distorted. Negatively-biased pain memories (remembering pain as being worse than an earlier pain report) are associated with the development of pediatric chronic pain. Pediatric chronic pain is a growing epidemic, affecting 1 in 4 Canadian youth, and costing $19 billion/year. Treatments for pediatric chronic pain are largely ineffective, in part because we do not understand why acute pain transitions to chronic pain in the first place. We believe that children's pain memories are a key risk factor for the development of this growing child health problem. Children's memories of post-surgical pain can lead to chronic pain; however, it is not known how the brain is involved in pain memory biases or the development of chronic pain after surgery in youth. In adults, the hippocampus - a brain region critically involved in memory - underlies the development of negatively-biased pain memories and chronic pain. Our brain imaging data show abnormal hippocampal structure and function in youth with chronic pain versus healthy controls, suggesting that the hippocampus may undergo changes as pain transitions from an acute to chronic state. Therefore, it is likely that the hippocampus is involved in pain memory biases and the development of chronic pain in youth. In the proposed study, 160 youth undergoing spinal fusion surgery will be assessed at baseline, the acute recovery phase, and at the time that pain can transition to a chronic state. Pain memories will be assessed 2 months after surgery. Brain scans will be performed before and 4 months after surgery, when pain can transition to a chronic state. Given the key role of children's pain memories in the development of chronic pain, and the urgent need for prevention and treatment targets for these at-risk youth, this research will be critical in helping to understand and prevent this widespread child health issue.

column36: Stroke Metrics for quAlity, Reporting, and Translation in the implementation of EndoVascular Thrombectomy (SMART-EVT)
column37: Stroke happens when a blood vessel in the brain is blocked. Every 9 minutes, a Canadian has a stroke. Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) is a procedure to unblock blood vessels in the brain. With this treatment, fewer people die, more people are able to return home and go back to do activities they enjoy after stroke. Right now, not everyone has access to EVT. First, a special scan of the brain is needed to detect vessel blockage, but not all hospitals have this scanner. Second, even when a vessel blockage is found, not all hospitals offer this treatment and patients often have to travel to a different hospital to get it. Third, EVT must be done very quickly or it will not help the patient. We currently do not know if the right people with stroke are getting to the right hospital at the right time. Our study aims to identify ways to optimize access to EVT. We will collect information from all hospitals in Ontario to understand how people with stroke are being cared for now. Most research focuses on people who get EVT, but it does not study those who do not get it. We will find out how many people do not get the scan to look for blood vessel blockage, how many people with a blockage do not get EVT, and why not. Studying people with stroke who did not have the scan or the treatment is important because it will help us find out where we can improve care. For example, are there specific hospitals or regions in Ontario where resources are insufficient? Are there groups of people who are not being treated equitably? In particular, we want to study if women and men are equally likely to get EVT and whether this treatment is safe for both women and men. Our results will help understand where the needs of the people and hospitals are. We are working with CorHealth Ontario and the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada on this project. This study will inform provincial and national stroke systems of care to improve patient outcomes after stroke.

column36: Optic flow processing in midbrain-cerebellar circuits for the control of locomotion
column37: As we move through the world, we experience optic flow - the motions of surfaces and objects across our retina. Studies of human behaviour reveal that optic flow is used for controlling virtually all aspects of locomotion such as walking, navigating through cluttered environments like forests or airport terminals, and when driving motor vehicles. Despite the importance of optic flow, there is a major gap in our understanding of how these signals are processed in the brain to allow for complex locomotion. Thus, optic flow processing in the brain is one of the most important, but least understood aspects of locomotion control. Disruptions to optic flow processing in the brain are associated with common diseases including vertigo, oscillopsia, ataxias and Alzheimer's disease. For example, Alzheimer's patients require much stronger optic flow signals to be able to navigate through a series of hallways to find their rooms. For other patients, such as those with vestibular deficits and visual neglect, presentations of optic flow are effective rehabilitative tools. Improving our understanding of optic flow is therefore essential. The principal challenge to studying optic flow processing in the brain is that we lack an appropriate animal model for research. Mice and rats are often used for studies of vertebrate neurobiology, but they are crepuscular/nocturnal and use information from their whiskers to guide many aspects of their locomotion. We will investigate how optic flow is used to guide movement in different environments, how optic flow signals are processed along the pathway from the midbrain to the cerebellum, and how selective silencing of neurons in this pathway leads to deficits in locomotor ability. The experiments will be performed on the visually-guided flight of small birds, which can be easily studied in the lab. Because birds have the same optic flow pathways as humans, this research will identify specific neural connections as potential treatment targets.
