column36: Targeting Glioblastoma Heterogeneity through identification of subtype-specific genetic vulnerabilities
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. Current treatment for GBM (surgery, radiation and chemotherapy) extends survival but is ineffective at preventing disease recurrence due to the residual presence of tumor initiating "GBM stem cells" that evade therapy and patients will invariably succumb to the disease, on average, just 18 months after initial diagnosis. Genomics studies have identified a high degree of variability in the genetic make-up of GBM cells-both between patients and within the same patient-which has represented a major barrier to the efficacy of new therapies for this cancer. Recently, our group and others have identified two predominant subtypes of GBM stem cells that can both be isolated from patient tumor samples, indicating that curing a patient of all residual disease would require therapies that killed both subtypes. Herein, we propose to use cutting-edge CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology to determine which genes are required for the growth of each subtype, producing a roadmap of candidate therapeutic targets. By performing these genetic screens in a large panel of patient derived GBM stem cell lines generated by our collaborator, we will produce a powerful dataset highly reflective of the heterogeneity observed in the GBM patient population. Using this data, we will characterize the biological basis for subtype-specific gene dependencies, greatly increasing our understanding of the mechanisms of GBM progression. In addition, our screen data will allow us to nominate drugs and small molecules as potential new targeted therapeutic strategies which we will evaluate through both in vitro drug screening and in mouse models harboring human patient derived GBM tumors. In summary, our proposed study will strive to develop new therapeutic strategies that can be applied in combination to overcome tumor heterogeneity and successfully target both cell types and cure GBM.

column36: Adapting a Mindfulness-Based Intervention for Depression and Anxiety Symptoms for Use with Indigenous University Students
column37: There are several treatment options for non-Indigenous Canadians suffering from elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety. Unfortunately, the same cannot be said about treatment options for Indigenous people in Canada; despite comparable rates of depression and anxiety to those of non-Indigenous decent, there are very few sensitive and culturally appropriate treatment options for Indigenous Canadians who may be suffering from elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety, as most these existing interventions have almost exclusively been developed by or with individuals of the majority culture (White; middle class; Judeo-Christian). This is problematic, as this cultural mismatch between how the intervention is designed and traditional Indigenous elements and knowledge dissuades Indigenous patients from engaging with said treatments. Mindfulness-based interventions have gained tremendous popularity in the last two decades, and have been shown to improve mild-moderate symptoms of depression and anxiety. Fortunately, Eastern and holistic influences of mindfulness-based interventions make them more amenable for adaptation for Indigenous patients. In this investigation, the research team will use a community-oriented approach to a) adapt a preexisting mindfulness-based intervention for use among Indigenous university students, and b) pilot-test the initial efficacy of this intervention to reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety among a small sample of Indigenous students, and c) outline a model for adapting existing psychological interventions to make them culturally sensitive and specific for Indigenous peoples in Canada. column36: Accelerating Discoveries: The Employment Trajectory of Young Adults with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
column37: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus is a disease in which the body's immune system makes a mistake and attacks healthy tissue in many parts of the body. It is also called lupus or SLE. People with lupus are often very tired, feel pain all over their body and have mental health problems so it can be hard for them to find or keep a job. If young adults (18-30 years of age) cannot start work, they can run into problems later in life. That is why it is important for us to understand the details of how young Canadians with lupus work. We do know a bit about this, but we need more information so that we can help them in the future. Our research study has 3 parts. The first part of our research study will look at how young adults with lupus change in their work. For example, we will look at how they change from being a student to becoming employed or unemployed. We will compare this to how other people of same age and sex change in their work. Young adults can be hard to study. They move around a lot and they go through many changes in their lives. To deal with this problem, we want to collect this information in a new, quicker and better way (second part). We will use what we learn in the first part to test if we can use the new way to collect information so that we can design better research studies in the future. Finally, we will interview young adults with lupus to learn about their work and any problems they had in the past (third part). Our findings will be shared with young people living with lupus, their families, doctors and employers to raise awareness about how hard it can be to work when a person has lupus. column36: Artificial Placenta: A biomimetic approach to support neonates with respiratory distress
column37: Respiratory failure is the major cause of morbidity among low birth weight neonates. Mechanical ventilation has dramatically improved outcome in this condition but can have side-effects that lead to long-term impairment. Over the past few years we have developed a new approach known as the artificial placenta - a device that mimics the natural circulation before birth where the fetus obtains oxygen from the mother. The device is elegantly designed so that it can operate in a pumpless manner, much like the natural placenta. It is designed to use the baby's own heart to perfuse a significant fraction of the blood volume through a microfluidic extracorporeal device and exchange oxygen with the external ambient environment. Being a passive device, it does not require external pumps and has a small internal volume which eliminates the need for external blood transfusion when it is connected to the neonate. We have developed a series of devices with increasing capabilities and are at a stage where initial animal experiments on piglets with the same weight as human neonatal babies have shown that our devices can sustain them even when under respiratory distress like conditions. These initial experiments show the promise of our approach, but further experiments are needed to conclusively validate that they would be suitable to support the piglets over typical operational lifetime of this device (~ 3-4 days). Further research is also needed to confirm whether the internal coating that we provide to the device is active over the intended operational lifetime. In addition to the validation of the device using animal models, we will also simplify the manufacturing process for the device and evaluate new coating technologies to ensure highest reliability of the device operation as well as its manufacturing. The validation of the technology obtained in this project on animal models will be critical to move it to the next stage of human clinical trials.

column36: Neurobiomarkers of FASD for adolescents and adults in the Criminal Justice System: Portable eye tracking and EEG
column37: In Canada, an estimated 1M people live with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), a lifelong neurodevelopmental disability with wide ranging impacts on brain and behaviour that are linked with adverse outcomes. Studies suggest that over 60% of adults with FASD experience contact with the criminal justice system, and they are overrepresented in correctional and forensic settings at rates 30x that of the general population. They experience high rates of re-offending, health, and mental health problems, and have difficulty benefiting from traditional interventions in the justice system. Despite high numbers, there are currently no evidence-based ways of identifying adolescents or adults who could have FASD in the criminal justice system. Failure to identify people with FASD in this context can lead to increased risk of harm to self and others, recidivism, and high health, social, and economic costs. This study proposes to use novel neurotechnologies, including eye movement behaviour and EEG recordings, to better understand how to identify adolescents and adults with FASD, including those in the criminal justice system. Portable technologies such as these may be used to detect people at risk of having FASD with a high degree of accuracy. These tools are non-invasive, precise, cost effective, and portable, and may allow for early identification of individuals in need of more comprehensive and costly clinical assessment, diagnostic, and intervention services. Findings from this research will be used to develop and implement fast, non-invasive, and affordable screening protocols to aid in large-scale screening for FASD in criminal justice settings. Identifying people who may have FASD may lead to effective use of limited economic and health resources to best support their complex needs.

column37: Hip fractures are one of the most common causes of fall-related hospitalizations in adults over the age of 65. They are estimated to undergo many relocations or transfers within six months of incurring the injury. Unfortunately, many patients do not return to pre-injury functional status. Our goal in the proposed research is to fill a research gap through in-depth understanding of care journeys across the continuum for adults with hip fractures in urban and rural settings. We will conduct interviews with patients, caregivers, providers and decision-makers within urban and rural areas. We will also use quantitative health administrative data to gain a comprehensive view of care across the continuum. The research team will then summarize the findings and share with patients, caregivers, providers, managers and decision-makers and discuss how we can improve care transitions for person with hip fractures within Ontario and across Canada.

column36: Stepping-Up: Partnering with the Community to Prevent Early Mobility Decline
column37: Background: Older adults need to be able to walk around their community at a minimal speed in order to ensure their safety. Programs to improve mobility in people with preclinical disability need to encourage participants to be actively involved in managing their mobility (self-management), should be specifically developed for the individual and should include the practice of mobility tasks. This program will be compared to 2 control groups, either a 12-week telephone-based coaching walking program or a 12-week stretching program. We will also compare the cost associated with delivering each program. column36: Enabling Cellular Therapy Biomanufacturing through Integrated Modeling of Fluid Dynamics and Cellular Metabolism in Bioreactors
column37: Regenerative medicine is a rapidly growing billion-dollar multidisciplinary field at the intersection of medicine, engineering and science. It aims to create living, functional tissues that can repair or replace damaged, diseased or aging tissues or organs, as well as providing models for discovery and drug development. Stem cells are critical to the success of regenerative medicine therapies. Pluripotent stem cells are a unique adult-derived stem cell that can be used for both personalized and population therapies, but technologies are needed to bridge the gap between fundamental biology and clinical applications. One of the major obstacles preventing effective use of stem cells is the limited number of available donor cells, and the small-scale, labour-intensive methods for culturing and differentiating them. Stirred suspension bioreactors are emerging as a critical cornerstone of robust bioprocesses to generate sufficient numbers of stem cells and their differentiated progeny for multiple applications. However, there is a significant gap in our knowledge of how the dynamic environment in the bioreactor affects the quality of the final cell product. More specifically, cell metabolism, which can change greatly between stem cells and their differentiated daughter cells, can be modulated within the stirred suspension bioreactor environment. The overall goals of the research project are to a) develop a deeper understanding of the metabolic behaviour of human pluripotent stem cells in bioreactors, b) relate metabolism to the dynamic environment within the bioreactor through computer modeling approaches. The outputs of this research are essential for efficient, cost-effective, safe and reproducible cell manufacturing, which is a critical next step to precision treatments for conditions such as degenerative diseases, burns, fractures, and other ailments. This is an opportunity for Canada to be a leader in biomanufacturing for the regenerative medicine industry.

column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world, with 1 in every 250 Canadians affected. This translates into a considerable societal and economic burden ($1.6M per patient). At present, it is not possible to reverse the neuron damage in MS. Therefore, the best chance of curing this disease is to prevent it from starting in the first place. Thus understanding the risk factors for development of MS and the biology of how these risk factors initiate the disease process is an important area of research. Three times more women than men develop MS, and we still do not understand why this is the case. In addition, if men get this disease, they tend to exhibit more rapid progression. Our goal is to better understand the fundamental biological differences that account for the greater susceptibility of females to develop MS and for men to develop more rapid progression. Here, through studies in mice and in human MS patients, we are trying to better understand the nuts and bolts of why the immune response may be more vigorous in females and can lead to the initiation of autoimmunity. We are pursuing the novel hypothesis that the reason why females are more prone to develop MS is because they have more T cells that can recognize the myelin sheath. We have thus far found evidence of this in the peripheral blood of human patients and in a mouse model of this disease. Further studies are planned in mice to get to the underlying mechanisms for this sex difference in T cell numbers. We are also going to characterize the immune cells in men and women with MS in order to gain new insights into how the disease may be different between the sexes. Understanding this biology will improve our understanding of how MS gets started and may lead to new ways of preventing or treating this disease. .

column36: Targeting pericytes to restore sensorimotor function after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury disconnects the brain from parts of the body below the injury, resulting in paralysis, abnormal pain and bladder dysfunction. Unfortunately, treatments to repair the injured spinal cord are still lacking. However, we recently made the unexpected discovery that blood flow is permanently reduced in the entire spinal cord below an injury, suggesting that improving blood flow offers a new approach to treating injury. We found that this low blood flow is caused by an exaggerated activity in specialized cells called pericytes that act like valves on small blood vessels. This then leads to insufficient blood flow and ultimately loss of residual functions like walking. We find that transiently blocking this exaggerated pericyte activity, or supplying oxygen, temporarily promotes recovery of walking in animal models. This is the basis for our current proposal, where we ask three questions. First, how do we best apply treatments to more permanently restore blood flow and oxygen to the spinal cord, and are these treatments safe (e.g. does not enhance abnormal pain)? Second, what causes the excessive pericyte activity following spinal cord injury, and can it be prevented? We have convincing preliminary data that indicate that a lack of activity in the neurons below a spinal cord injury triggers the excessive pericyte activity, since daily nerve stimulation to excite the spinal cord over the first few weeks after spinal cord injury restores normal pericyte function, eliminates hypoxia and markedly improves residual movement. If proven correct, this idea opens up new clinically applicable treatments to restore blood flow, including electrical nerve stimulation and rehabilitation training that promote neuronal activity early after injury. Lastly, we explore whether humans with spinal cord injury also suffer from a lack of oxygen in the spinal cord below the injury and whether restoring blood flow promotes recovery in sensory and motor function.

column36: Using behavioural science to understand and improve participation in clinical trials: A theory-based research project.
column37: Participation in clinical research is an essential element of improving healthcare. Any change in treatment or management should be tested before it is put into practice, and this requires patients (and others) to participate in research, usually on a volunteer basis. Despite its importance, research participation is consistently low across almost all diseases and geographical regions. The costs of low participation are many and varied, including wasted money and other resources, inability to use those resources for other purposes, delayed new treatments, faulty findings, and unnecessary risks to those who do participate. While many studies have explored this problem, they have not been informed by theories from psychology that contain considerable knowledge about how to help people make difficult decisions, and how people change their behaviour. The overall goal for this project is to develop the knowledge and tools necessary to help patient groups, researchers, and trial sponsors optimize both the rate of participation and the experience of clinical trial recruitment. The work will proceed in four phases, including (1) reviewing the scientific literature to understand how recruitment is currently done from a theoretical perspective; (2) interviewing the range of different groups with expertise in these issues (e.g. participants, physicians, trial recruiters, and experts in the infrastructure underlying clinical research); (3) developing tools to help optimize trial recruitment (e.g. standard surveys that can identify problems before a trial begins; more participant-friendly consent forms); and (4) thinking and writing about the ethical challenges posed by these theories, to safeguard public trust in health research. Our international multidisciplinary team is uniquely qualified to do this work, which will help improve the health care system by optimizing the process of clinical trial recruitment.

This study proposes innovative approaches to better understand the regulation of antiviral signaling pathways. The results from each site will then be pooled together for an overall estimate of the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on bladder cancer. As patients with type 2 diabetes are already at an increased risk of bladder cancer, this large international study will provide concerned stakeholders with much needed information on the safety profile of these drugs in a timely and cost-effective fashion.

column36: Mechanisms of B cell-mediated immunity in human cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is a challenging disease with unacceptably high mortality. Despite this, about 30% of patients "beat the odds" and live for many years after treatment. Why do some patients do so well? In the past decade, it has become well established that many long-term survivors of ovarian cancer exhibit a strong immune response against their tumor, providing a plausible explanation for their favourable outcome. We have shown that the immune response against cancer involves collaboration between several types of white blood cells, including killer T cells and antibody-producing B cells. column36: Ultra-Low Tidal Volume Mechanical Ventilation in ARDS Through ECCO2R (ULTIMATE) Pilot Trial
column37: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a devastating form of sudden lung failure that can occur after common insults such as pneumonia, other severe infections, or trauma. Despite many advances over the past decades, mortality rates remain high and survivors experience significant and prolonged difficulties with physical and mental health. A key advance in the care of patients with ARDS was the recognition that although life-saving in some cases, mechanical ventilators (breathing machines) can worsen lung injury and contribute to death. Intensive care doctors now recognise that giving normal-to-small sized breaths (6 ml/kg) with the ventilator saves lives, compared with the larger breath sizes (12 ml/kg) that were used in the past. However, in a significant number of cases these smaller breaths are still big enough to cause further damage to the lung which is already injured. New technology is now available that may be able to help in this situation - extracorporeal carbon dioxide removal - is a device similar to kidney dialysis, where blood is pumped out of the body and through a type of artificial lung, removing carbon dioxide. This means that the patient's lungs have to do less work, and breath sizes and therefore stress and strain can be reduced further. This may reduce lung injury and reduce the risk of dying from ARDS, but this is also a new technology with costs and potential side effects, which needs careful evaluation. In this study we will randomly assign adults with ARDS to receive either best standard care or to this new technology allowing lower tidal volumes and will determine whether the new strategy is really better.

column37: The Long QT Syndrome (LQTS) is an electrical disorder of the heart, which is associated with abnormal cardiac rhythms and sudden death. The QT interval is determined by measuring the interval between the QRS complex and the T-wave on the electrocardiograph. One form of this syndrome, referred to as LQTS2, has been related to mutations of a protein called hERG (Human Ether-a-go-go Related Gene) that reduces the function of the hERG channel in the cell membrane. This channel also binds many drugs readily, which can cause sudden death, and therefore the U.S.A. Federal Drug Administration requires that new drugs are tested against hERG. However, the mechanisms that regulate the levels of hERG channels at the cell membrane are not well understood. The first mechanism is related to the removal of mutated and improperly folded hERG channels at the endoplasmic reticulum. A second mechanism involves the removal of hERG channels from the cell membrane that become destabilized. We discovered that there are two distinct cell membrane quality control systems, the more recent of which we have little information. Also, we screened a library of drugs and small molecules and found two compounds that can stabilize mutant hERG channels at the cell membrane, which could have potential therapeutic benefits. The nature of this mechanism also is not understood and will be the subject of further investigation. In our study, we will continue to evaluate the quality control and pharmacological modulation of hERG channels using a variety of techniques that involve electrophysiology, molecular biology and advanced microscopy. We believe that this quality control mechanism will provide a new explanation for the effects involved in clinically relevant cases of LQTS2.

column36: The Tumor Suppressor Function of CUX1
column37: Cancer develops following increased alterations within DNA, which are usually repaired by complex groups of proteins involved in DNA repair. Defects in one or more DNA repair mechanisms cause the accumulation of changes in DNA, called mutations, that increase the possibility that certain cells become tumorigenic. We work on a gene, called CUX1, that has been implicated in cancer. Normally, each gene has two copies or alleles, however, one allele of CUX1 is inactivated or lost in a fraction of human cancers. This finding suggests that the probability of developing cancer increases in cells that have only one copy of the CUX1 gene. This defines the CUX1 gene as a "tumor suppressor gene" and in our scientific jargon, we say that CUX1 is a "haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene". The goal of our research is to understand why having only one copy of the CUX1 gene increases the probability of cancer. We already know that less of the CUX1 proteins are expressed when one copy of the gene is inactivated or lost. We want to know and demonstrate what molecular function is affected when there is a lower number of CUX1 proteins. Since the CUX1 protein plays a role in DNA repair, our hypothesis is that cells with less CUX1 are not as efficient at repairing DNA damage and therefore they accumulate changes in DNA faster than normal cells. To make a bad analogy, cancer is like winning the lottery. Cells with less CUX1 accumulate more lottery tickets than other cells and therefore they have a higher probability of getting the bad ticket.

The premature failure of transplanted organ is related to both early rejection and chronic injury. Chronic rejection is the leading cause of late morbidity and mortality in transplant patients. Unfortunately, this long-term outcome has not improved over time. Furthermore, this inflammation is not affected by current anti-rejection drugs. In this grant, we will study how the form of cell death regulate transplant inflammation and rejection. column36: Investigating the regulation of ADAMTS13 in hemostasis and thrombosis
column37: Thrombosis is a pathological condition that occurs as a result of unregulated blood clotting that occludes blood vessels, and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Thrombosis can manifest in various organs and can lead to heart attacks or stroke. Despite the availability of drugs that either prevent blood clotting or encourage clot breakdown, thrombosis is responsible for 1 in 4 deaths in Canada and worldwide. Current therapies are limited by the need to balance their effectiveness at treating thrombosis with their risk of causing bleeding. As a result, more research is needed to explore the mechanisms of thrombosis in order to identify new targets for safe and effective therapy. A critical step in the progression to thrombosis is the recruitment of platelets to the injured blood vessel. This is accomplished in part by the protein Von Willebrand Factor (VWF). VWF is a long string-like protein that adheres to the site of vessel injury and captures platelets flowing in blood. Recruitment of too many platelets can lead to thrombosis. ADAMTS13 is a protease that cuts VWF strings, shortening them and reducing their platelet-capturing activity. Changes in ADAMTS13 activity can lead to dysfunctional VWF and cause either bleeding or thrombosis. However, there is currently very little that is known about the regulation of ADAMTS13. ADAMTS13 is known to remain in a folded compact form in circulation that becomes extended when it interacts with and cuts VWF. Whether this folded form of ADAMTS13 contributes to the regulation of its protease activity is currently not known. Therefore, the objective of this project is to explore the biochemical and structural mechanisms that contribute to the regulation of ADAMTS13. Because ADAMTS13 is an important regulator of blood clotting, investigating the mechanisms that control its activity may reveal novel targets for antithrombotic therapy development.

column36: Biophysical control of mesenchymal morphogenesis in the mammalian embryo
column37: The growth and formation of the mammalian embryo is an inherently physical process that is regulated by genes. Although the identity of genes responsible for development is relatively advanced, the physical principles that shape three dimensional embryonic structures such as solid organs including the face and limbs are not understood. It is also not known how genes regulate physical processes that underlie development. Consequences of these knowledge gaps are that we cannot fully explain how birth defects arise and current efforts at regenerating organs are based on trial-and-error methods rather than on recapitulating actual physical events that take place during natural development. The persistence of these knowledge gaps is attributable to the lack of tools to measure the physical properties of mammalian embryos. The Hopyan and Sun lab teams bring together developmental biologists and mechanical engineers with expertise in the manufacture of micro-scale devices to tackle the physical basis of development. Collaboratively, they generated multiple genetic and physical tools that allow precise measurements of the viscoelastic properties and forces of living tissues and cells in the mammalian embryo. Using those tools, they described how 3D tissues such as the developing face and limbs grow at the resolution of individual cells and measured cellular forces and tissue stiffness. They generated hypotheses about how cells move in response to the stiffness of their environment and about how three regulators (WNT5A, YAP and Piezo1) control that response. Mutations of those regulators cause human birth defects. Therefore, the experiments outlined in this proposal will define how molecular pathways regulate physical processes during development and more precisely explain how specific facial and limb defects arise. In the longterm, understanding the physical basis of organ development will accelerate strategies that are focused on organ regeneration.

column37: Recently, escape from tumor surveillance by the immune system has been identified as a critical mediator for cancer progression to lethal disease. Ultimately, results from this study can be used to inspire and guide clinical trials for the deployment of combination therapy in ILC patients. column37: Over 100,000 Canadians have type 1 diabetes. People with type 1 diabetes require lifelong insulin injections to replace insulin synthesized by specialized cells in their pancreas that have died due to an immune process. Currently there are few treatments to prevent or delay the underlying destruction of insulin producing cells. Studies have shown that many people with type 1 diabetes still produce small amounts of insulin. This is important because these people have less severe diabetes: they require lower doses of insulin; have better control of their blood sugar levels; are at lower risk for the development of low blood sugar; and also importantly at lower risk for long-term complications of diabetes, including eye, kidney and heart diseases which are major health problems. However, we have little understanding of the factors that result in differences in insulin production capacity between people with type 1 diabetes. Genetics provides a unique opportunity to identify causal factors for important biomedical measures, such as varying insulin production in people with type 1 diabetes. We already conducted a pilot study where we identified genetic variations at two different locations in the genome that are related to insulin production. In this project we will use data and samples from nine different studies, with a total of ~12,200 people with type 1 diabetes, to allow us to identify the genetic factors that influence residual insulin production. This would be the largest and most comprehensive study of this topic to date. Identifying the genetic factors is the first step to understanding the mechanisms, which could ultimately be used to develop new approaches to help preserve insulin production in people with type 1 diabetes. Since insulin production is also abnormal in many people with type 2 diabetes, which affects over 2 million Canadians, the findings from this work could also ultimately benefit some people with type 2 diabetes.

We will be able to determine if microinfarcts alter the amount of brain plasticity occurring following a major stroke. Unfortunately, certain bacteria now produce enzymes called carbapenemases that destroy these last- line-of-defense antibiotics. Thus bacterial infections that were once readily managed through the judicious use of carbapenems are now becoming life-threatening, especially for patients whose immune systems are compromised such as cystic fibrosis patients, burn victims, the elderly, AIDS patients, cancer patients and organ transplant patients. The goal of this project is to discover pharmaceuticals that inactivate the bacterial carbapenemases. Such drugs would be co-administered along with the carbapenems in order to block the bacterial resistance mechanism thus making the carbapenems effective against bacteria that are currently resistant.

column36: Hemodynamics of Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Using Accelerated and Motion-Compensated MRI
column37: Nearly 1% of babies born in Canada have heart disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential technology for evaluating this condition. In addition to showing the anatomy of the heart, MRI can also measure blood flow. This information helps doctors decide how serious the heart problem is, and how to treat the child. MRI can then be used again, to see how well the child responds to the treatment. A major challenge of MRI is that patients must remain motionless when pictures are being recorded, which is difficult for young children. In traditional MRI scans, motion will ruin the images. Medical staff must then repeat the scans, which prolongs the MRI examination. If a child is unable to remain still, sedation is necessary. Another significant challenge of traditional MRI scans of heart disease is the need to align the scan plane to the proper anatomy. This meticulous process further lengthens the scan and requires an expert in cardiac imaging. The goal of this proposal is to address these challenges by developing a fast (<5 minute), motion-insensitive MRI method to visualize three-dimensional (3D) anatomy and blood flow throughout the entire chest in children with heart disease. This proposal first focuses on developing new methods to speed up 3D MRI measurements of chest anatomy and blood flow, while also compensating for patient motions such as breathing and shifting within the MRI. Initially, development will be achieved by scanning adult volunteers. The resulting methods will then be applied to children with and without heart disease. This project will enable comprehensive evaluation of heart disease in a practical scan time and avoid the need for tailored scan prescriptions by an expert in cardiovascular anatomy. In addition to serving as a powerful tool for planning therapy, this work promises to transform our understanding and management of heart disease in kids.

column37: Senescent cells are induced during chronological aging and by a wide range of DNA damaging agents such as ionizing radiation (IR). column37: The Metis are post-contact Indigenous peoples of Canada with a unique combination of identity, values, language, and cultural traditions. They have been referred to as "hidden" Indigenous peoples because of the lack of health research and service policies specific to their needs and experiences. There are not many studies on Metis health and particularly about Metis children's health. Most research on this area groups the experiences of Metis, First Nations, and Inuit children together. Lii Zaanfaan means "the children" in Michif, the traditional language of the Metis. From a Metis perspective, the health of children is deeply linked to the health of their families, communities, and the land. This perspective is supportive of broader knowledge on social determinants of health and childhood development. This research results from a long-standing collaboration between the Metis Nation of Alberta and academic partners to develop community relevant knowledge to inform Metis-specific health initiatives. The project has three objectives: 1) evaluate health and well-being trajectories of Metis children during the first 10 years of life and the influences of maternal and social factors on these outcomes; 2) explore perspectives of Metis children and their families on social, environment and cultural factors that influence well-being and healthy development of children, and 3) identify community-led, culturally meaningful Metis initiatives to promote Metis children's health and well-being through cultural healing and self-determination. We will use a variety of quantitative and qualitative research methods that are culturally acceptable within a Metis context.

column36: Using MRI imaging to develop a personalized risk-based breast cancer screening strategy
column37: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can detect breast cancer earlier than mammography or ultrasound. However, because MRI is very expensive and more likely to mistake benign breast structures for cancer, MRI is usually only offered to women with the highest risk of developing breast cancer based on genetic testing, family history, or previous radiation to the chest. The High-Risk Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) is a unique screening program which provides annual screening with MRI to high-risk women. There is still a lot of variation in this high-risk group. At one extreme are young women with an inherited BRCA1 mutation who tend to develop aggressive, rapidly growing tumours. These women may benefit from more frequent screening or prophylactic mastectomy. At the other extreme are women with a strong family history associated with a currently unknown genetic abnormality who could actually be at average risk and who may not need annual screening. There is, therefore, a need for improved risk prediction methods. We propose to develop new artificial intelligence methods to extract information about breast tissue volume and texture from MRI. With MRI we can also measure how much contrast agent is taken up in normal breast tissue; this is known as background parenchymal enhancement, BPE, and it has been shown that there is a correlation between BPE and risk. We will assess whether a combination of these MRI properties can be used to predict cancer risk. We will also determine whether they are more strongly correlated with breast cancer risk than mammographic density which is already known to be useful in identifying patients at intermediate risk. Our methods will be tested on data from the OBSP which screens thousands of high-risk women each year at 30 different centres in Ontario. A more accurate assessment of risk could allow screening programs to be tailored to the needs of individual women and would also make better use of limited resources.

Ultimately the information generated in this grant application will help to better design clinical trials in terms of fatty acid formulation, expected level to reach in the plasma and the brain.

column37: Normal tissue turnover requires the clearance of dead and dying cells by special immune cells called macrophages. Without clearance, dead and dying cells can cause inflammation and damage to local tissues. We recently discovered that dead/dying cells accumulate in the lining of knee joints from patients with osteoarthritis (OA), suggesting that the process of clearing dead/dying cell clearance is defective. In this proposal, we will conduct experiments using animal models of knee OA and human tissues from patients with knee OA. Overall, our objective is to confirm and investigate why the process of dead/dying cell clearance is defective in OA to determine how best to treat OA. Specifically, we will: 1. Test the effects of a) blocking cell clearance, and b) stimulating cell clearance on important OA outcomes using a rat model of knee OA. We will look at joint tissue damage and pain outcomes in this model, which has been shown to mimic the symptoms and joint damage seen in human knee OA. 3. Identify the specific molecular mechanisms that cause cell clearance to be impaired. This step is needed to identify the key targets that will be the focus of new OA treatments. In the future, such treatments would be designed to improve the clearance of dead/dying cells as specifically as possible, without causing unwanted off-target side-effects. These studies are critical to understand the role of cell clearance in OA and to set the stage for new treatment targets to be tested. OA is a massive unmet clinical need because it causes significant disability for people with OA. OA also causes significant costs to our health care system in Canada. Currently, no approved disease-modifying OA treatment exists. Therefore, our proposal describes an exciting new way to look at OA treatments and hope for the future.

column36: Strategies to Relieve Suffering at End-of-Life (STRS-EOL): A longitudinal qualitative study of healthcare policy and nursing practice.
column37: Suffering at end-of-life is not new or uncommon. However, what is new in Canada are the options available to address this suffering and how those options are intersecting in end-of-life decision-making. In this grant, we are using the acronym STRS-EOL to refer to these options for relieving suffering at end-of-life and they include medical assistance in dying (MAiD), palliative care (PC), voluntary stopping eating and drinking (VSED), and palliative sedation (PS). Palliative patients often ask healthcare providers to hasten their death, particularly during moments of suffering. In past, however, no legal options were available to address this request. In 2016 that changed. Canadians who meet eligibility requirements can now have MAiD whereby medications are used to induce death. Persons who request MAiD must be given the option of palliative care; however, it is widely recognized that there is a need to improve access to palliative care in Canada. Further, not all clients meet the eligibility criteria for MAiD, and in those cases, patients may resort to VSED or PS. Patients stop eating until they qualify for MAiD or they are sedated. With these evolving changes, there is a need to understand how the interactions between these approaches, and how broader social and demographic factors, are influencing these end-of-life decisions. Building upon research we are currently conducting, our aim in this project is to gain a thorough understanding of the developmental trajectory over an eight year period of policy and practice related to STRS-EOL. We will gather and analyze longitudinal data from policy documents, key stakeholders, and nurses with the goal of creating unique and highly sought after data to track and compare the developmental trajectory of STRS-EOL across English-speaking Canadian health regions over time. Through this knowledge we will support wide-spread uptake of STRS-EOL best practices and improved practitioner well-being and moral development.

column37: Bed rest is a common feature of many clinical environments such as hospitals and long-term care facilities. However, the physical inactivity associated with bed rest results in reductions in muscle size, muscle strength, and physical performance (i.e. rising from a chair) that can lead to a reduced quality of life and a higher risk of disease and death. Eating protein-rich foods and exercising normally helps to maintain muscle size by building proteins found in muscle. However, during bed rest there is a reduction in the rate at which proteins found in muscle are made and this leads to smaller muscles. Bed rest leads to problems with blood glucose regulation and insulin resistance which can increase the risk for diabetes. Both the loss of muscle size and insulin resistance are linked to problems with components of our cells called mitochondria. Mitochondria do a lot of important things including keeping our cells full of energy. Bed rest occurs more frequently in older adults and also negatively impacts their health more than in younger adults. Sadly, there are limited options to prevent the problems associated with bed rest. Ketone bodies are molecules that come from fat that are normally produced in the body in response to reduced carbohydrate intake (i.e. a ketogenic diet). Recently ketone supplements have become available, which increase the amount of ketone bodies in the body without the need to limit carbohydrate intake from food. Elevated ketone bodies may help protect muscle size and health during bed rest by enhancing the process of building muscle proteins, improving blood glucose regulation, and helping mitochondria work optimally. The current research project will determine whether ketone supplements can prevent the typical decline in muscle size, protein synthesis, insulin sensitivity, and muscle mitochondrial function that occurs in response to bed rest. This may positively impact the heath of older adults and speed their recovery from bed rest.

column36: Low Dose Metronomic Chemotherapy as a Combination Strategy to Combat Innate or Acquired Resistance to Immune Checkpoint Therapy
column37: The most significant recent advance in oncology is the remarkable success of new drugs which harness the immune system to treat advanced metastatic disease of a number of different cancers. Foremost among these drugs are "immune checkpoint inhibitor" (ICI) antibodies. However, a dose of reality has set in to temper some of the initial euphoria about these drugs. First, they are enormously expensive, placing a likely unsustainable strain on health care system budgets. Second, only minor subsets of patient (an average of ~15%) benefit from receiving ICIs. Third, they can be very toxic causing a number of immune related adverse events (irAEs). Finally, tumors which initially respond to ICI therapy usually acquire resistance and relapse. A strategy being studied to improve the efficacy of ICIs is by combination with other types of drug. But this approach can exacerbate the problems of both overall toxicity and cost. This proposal is designed to evaluate a strategy to deal with both problems, and using it to combat ICI drug resistance, namely, evaluating the impact of using lower and hence less toxic doses of certain inexpensive off-patent oral chemotherapy drugs, but given in a close regular fashion - known as "metronomic" chemotherapy (MC) - which Dr. Kerbel's lab has helped pioneer; it has shown positive results in some recent phase III clinical trials, especially when used as maintenance therapies after initial induction chemotherapy. There is evidence that certain chemotherapy drugs given as MC can actually stimulate rather than suppress tumor immunity, the latter of which can occur when given at conventional 'maximum tolerated doses'. Finally, the research will involve use of a number of new mouse models that mimic the clinical treatment of metastatic disease, and new tumor models that are either minimally sensitive, or intrinsically resistant to an ICI, or which have acquired resistance after showing major durable tumor regressions.

As a consequence, the infection or cancer persists. Transcription factors, a class of molecules controlling gene expression, plays crucial roles in T cell response by inducing the proper gene expression program required for differentiation. Mutations in Tub and Tulp1, 2, 3 and 4 cause or are linked to human disorders. Loss of Tulp1, like Tub, leads to retinal degeneration in mice and humans, but not obesity. Loss of either Tulp3 or Tulp4 causes embryonic defects in mice. In humans variants in Tulp4 and Tulp2 are linked to orofacial clefting and morbid obesity, respectively. Despite their importance in embryonic and brain development, vision, and energy homeostasis, the mechanisms, by which TUB domain proteins act has remained a mystery. The fact that the TUB domain binds nucleic acids suggests that these proteins regulate critical gene networks. Here we propose to analyze how Tubby, the founding member of this gene family, functions, and thereby to gain new insights into how TUB domain proteins in general act, the programs they govern and the proteins with which they collaborate to regulate normal mammalian development and energy homeostasis.

column36: Holding Space for frontline Indigenous leadership in community-driven responses to the housing and overdose crises in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside
column37: Our research team supports frontline Indigenous community health organizers who are leading the public health response to the twin housing and overdose fatality crisis in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. There are over 5000 people who live in Single Room Occupancy (SRO) Hotels. Conditions in many SRO hotels are unlivable, yet they are the only option for people on low income, mental health survivors, sex workers, and people who use drugs. It is a colonial crisis of epic proportions: at least 35% of SRO tenants self-identify as Indigenous. But the twin crisis has also spurred a grassroots response led by Indigenous leaders in the DTES. While the crisis is predominantly affecting Indigenous men, the response is largely led by women and 2SLGBTQ+ leaders in the community, including among our team. Building on our previous research in support of housing and harm reduction organizing led by SRO tenants, we propose a project that strengthens our team by "holding space" for our Indigenous leaders, protecting them from harmful conditions of low pay and dangerous work, and supporting their ability to sustain themselves and their relations in a self-determined way. To do this, we will work with our partners and respected local Elders to organize five years of restorative Indigenous methodologies centred on land-based retreats and sharing circles that allow us to support each other, reflect on the trauma that surrounds us, and strengthen a wider coalition of Indigenous frontline organizations. This approach to research will ultimately tackle colonial processes in public health that have relied heavily on community-based Indigenous leaders to deliver culturally-appropriate care, while leaving them in short term, low wage contracts. Our partnership includes major grassroots organizations working in the DTES and to national Indigenous health organizations. Our project will make important contributions to the growing field of Indigenous public health in Canada.

column37: Preeclampsia, a condition characterized by high blood pressure and multiple organ impairment, affects 5-8% of pregnancies and leads to serious complications for both mother and baby. Unfortunately, there is currently no useful clinical tool for its early prediction.The stages of preeclampsia initiate early in the first trimester, but clinical symptoms appear only in the second half of pregnancy. Thus, there is a window of opportunity to predict preeclampsia early in pregnancy. Previous tools that have been proposed have been shown to inadequately predict preeclampsia. On the other hand, it has been increasingly realized that malfunction of the mother's arteries is associated with progression towards preeclampsia. Indeed, we have previously shown in a small group of pregnant women that this malfunction may be detected, in the first trimester, as hardened arteries. The evaluation of arterial hardening can be performed safely and non-invasively, and is thus a promising tool for early preeclampsia prediction.The present study aims to determine in a larger population whether the assessment of arterial hardening can be used to predict preeclampsia. To do so, we will recruit pregnant women at high risk for preeclampsia from 8 obstetrical centers across North America and Europe. We will measure the hardening of the arteries in the first trimester and compare its predictive performance for preeclampsia to that of known clinical risk factors as well as alternative tools (e.g. blood tests, ultrasound). We will also perform the same assessments in the second trimester to determine whether preeclampsia risk prediction could be improved. Effective prediction of preeclampsia would identify pregnant women who would benefit most from preventive measures in a timely manner. Moreover, it will allow for the concentration of limited health care resources towards those women who are truly at high-risk, and help in the long-term to accelerate the development of new preventive treatments.

column36: Relative effectiveness and safety of pharmacotherapeutic agents for treatment of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm infants: A National Comparative Effectiveness Research (CER) Project
column37: Patent ductus arteriosus is a common heart condition that develops in preterm infants. Left untreated, some of them may progress to cause severe lung disease, kidney failure, bleeding in the brain, cerebral palsy and even death. The primary modality of treatment is medical, using drugs such as indomethacin and ibuprofen, failing which some preterm infants may need to undergo heart surgery. Wide variation exists in the choice of medication and dosage for treatment of PDA across Canadian neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). Standard doses of ibuprofen (10 mg per kg body weight followed by 2 doses of 5 mg per kg at 24 hour intervals) is the most commonly used treatment option. However, based on recent research, many centers have started to use higher doses of ibuprofen as the first choice of treatment. In this project we intend to conduct a comparative effectiveness study across Canadian NICUs to compare the effectiveness and safety of the common medical treatment options in preterm infants requiring PDA treatment. We will also try to understand the relevance of PDA treatment in the real world by comparing their outcomes to those who were not treated for PDA. In this study, each participating site will self-select and adhere to one of the pre-defined treatment protocols for all their preterm babies who will be treated for PDA. Data will be collected through the Canadian Neonatal Network (CNN) platform. Twenty NICUs across Canada have agreed to participate in this study. It is expected to take approximately 3 years to enroll the projected sample size of 1100 infants. We will establish the safety and effectiveness of commonly used PDA treatment options in a large contemporary patient cohort in Canada. In addition, we will examine key outcomes in relation to PDA treatment practices in the real world. This will inform future practice, reduce variability and generate data on the best treatment method to improve outcomes in preterm neonates with PDA.

column37: Defining the problem. Ovarian Cancer (OVCA) ranks third in the number of new cases and is the leading cause of death in gynecologic cancer. Although combined surgical debulking and chemotherapy is an important treatment strategy, chemoresistance remains a major challenge to long term therapeutic success. There is currently no safe and successful therapy available once chemoresistance has developed. Recent studies indicate the tumour microenvironment as a strong contributing factor for chemoresistance. The microenvironment entails various cell types, including tumour cells and immune cells [e.g. T lymphocytes (T cells)], which communicate via cross-talks and local release of pro-cancer soluble factors. The overall objective of the proposed study is to determine if and how OVCA cells-T cells interactions regulate chemosensitivity and how deregulation of these interactions results in chemoresistance. The overall hypothesis is that OVCA cells-T cells interaction regulates OVCA CDDP responsiveness. A secreted protein called plasma gelsolin (pGSN) promotes cancer cell survival by down-regulating the anti-tumour functions of T cells. Clinical significance. Results from the proposed study could provide guidance to physicians on treatment strategies, particularly for platinum-based chemotherapy. The clinical management of OVCA patients may be individualized to achieve more benefits, especially avoiding treatment side effects in non-responders. In addition, the immune-modulatory role of pGSN may provide insight for future investigations on new immunotherapeutic for chemoresistant OVCA patients.

column36: Online Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Substance Use Disorder: The Impact of Peer Support
column37: Heavy alcohol and drug use is reported by a substantial number of Canadians, and incurs billions of dollars in costs to Canadian society each year. Yet, only a minority of those struggling with addiction receives specialized services. Numerous barriers to care exist, highlighting the need for scalable and engaging treatment alternatives. Online cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for addiction has exhibited promise in the reduction of substance use, although studies to date highlight the key importance of patient engagement to optimize clinical outcomes. Peer support may provide a way to engage patients using online interventions. The goal of this proposal is to evaluate the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of online CBT with and without peer support. The proposed research will specifically evaluate Breaking Free Online (BFO), which has demonstrated effectiveness in adults with substance use difficulties. BFO has developed peer support programming; however, the impact of peer support on patient engagement during the implementation has yet to be evaluated. We propose to randomize 225 outpatients receiving standard care to clinical monitoring (CM), BFO only, or BFO with peer support, in an eight-week trial with a three- and six-month follow-up. The primary outcome is substance use frequency; secondary outcomes include substance use problems, depression, anxiety, quality of life, treatment engagement, and cost-effectiveness. We hypothesize that BFO will be associated with greater reductions in substance use and other clinical outcomes, as well as more durable improvements and greater cost-effectiveness, compared to clinical monitoring alone. We further hypothesize that BFO with peer support will be associated with greater engagement in treatment, and that engagement will mediate improvements over treatment. Results will support the implementation of this innovative approach within adults with addiction, who face numerous risks for harm and barriers to services.

column36: Late preterm birth and cardiometabolic outcomes in children and young adults: Identifying opportunities for early life interventions
column37: Nearly 15 million babies worldwide are born premature each year and 75% of these babies are now born late preterm (between 34-36 weeks of pregnancy). Although it is well established that children born very premature (<34 weeks of pregnancy) are at increased risk of lifelong health problems, surprisingly little is known about the long-term health outcomes of children born late preterm. Cardiometabolic risk factors (i.e., factors known to be associated with heart disease and diabetes later in life), such as obesity, high blood pressure and elevated cholesterol, which can be measured in early childhood are known to track to adolescence and adulthood and are associated with increased risk of adult onset disease. Our study will evaluate the cardiometabolic health consequences of late preterm birth in children and young adults and will explore whether known interventions for preterm birth improve cardiometabolic outcomes. Our first aim is to evaluate the association between late preterm birth and both cardiometabolic risk and growth in children and young adults. Our second aim is to identify if World Health Organization recommended interventions at birth, such as corticosteroid use and breastfeeding, result in better outcomes for children born preterm to prevent poor cardiovascular outcomes later in life. We have the unique opportunity to address these aims by linking individual level data on children from three data sources ICES, BORN: Better Outcomes Registry & Network, and the TARGet Kids primary care cohort. This project will contribute to our understanding of the health consequences of late preterm birth and identify opportunities to intervene in early in life to reduce lifelong cardiovascular disease risk and improve health across the life-course.

column36: IRF1, IRF8 and partners: epigenetic regulators of normal and pathological inflammation
column37: Genetic variations and environmental factors influence host immune responses and can lead to susceptibility to pathogens and to inflammatory diseases. Two regulators of gene expression in immune cells, the transcription factors IRF1 and IRF8, have been implicated in life-threatening immunodeficiencies and with chronic inflammatory diseases. We and others have shown that both factors are essential in the development of acute neuroinflammation caused by malaria and for the defense against intracellular pathogens; highlighting their major implication in Th1 immunity. We have recently dissected the critical role of IRF1 and IRF8 in the epigenetic control of innate immune cells and revealed that their target genes are also associated with acute and chronic inflammatory conditions. In this work, we propose to investigate the intrinsic role of IRF1 and IRF8 in cells of the adaptive immune compartment (T lymphocytes) to better understand their involvement in human pathologies. Moreover, building on the IRF1 and IRF8 transcriptional networks that we have defined, we developed a bioinformatic prioritization method to identify genes that could be involved in chronic inflammatory diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease and multiple sclerosis. Amongst the strong candidates, some poorly studied transcriptional regulators were selected for functional validation. These will be investigated using genetically engineered animal and cell models, with a combination of functional genomics and immunological characterization methods. The project will further our understanding of the functional role of these important transcriptional regulators in inflammation and ascertain their role in immune cell biology; shedding light on the possible mechanisms behind their genetic association to chronic inflammatory diseases. A deep understanding of the genetic components and its translation into innovative therapeutic strategies is key to fight inflammatory diseases.

column36: Modelling the Impact of Government-Led Nutrient Profile Models on Preventable Mortality and Morbidity Burden, and Healthcare Use: A POpulation HEalth Model-Nutrition (POHEM-Nutrition) Microsimulation Study
column37: Chronic diseases are on the rise. They are the leading causes of early death and are common reasons for hospitalization. In Canada, unhealthy eating, mostly due to a food environment characterized by energy-dense packaged foods, is largely responsible for chronic diseases and early deaths. To address the rising rates of chronic diseases, international health organizations recommend a shift from policies focused on single nutrients to policies targeting multiple food components/nutrients using nutrient profile models (i.e., "ranking foods based on their nutritional composition for disease prevention"). This project will enable monitoring of health and healthcare impacts of adopting nutrient profile models for regulation of nutrition policies (e.g., front-of-package labelling)-an essential step for reducing diet-related health problems for Canadians. We will evaluate the impact of adopting the most promising nutrient profile models on health outcomes and examine the health and healthcare benefits of strategies to improve the nutritional quality of the food supply. A Canadian-specific nutrient profile model will also be "reverse engineered" to equitably reduce health and healthcare burden among Canadians. We will use Canadian national nutrition surveys conducted in 2004 (linked to health and healthcare outcomes) and 2015 (linked to food supply data) to develop a robust model for evaluating the future health and healthcare outcomes of adopting different nutrition policies. The infrastructure we will develop will be unique internationally, enabling timely and detailed evaluation of nutrition policies for reduction of diet-related diseases and healthcare use among different population groups (e.g., sex, age, ethnicity). These models will create a lasting infrastructure and will position Canada as a leader in population health and healthcare assessment of nutrition policies.

column36: Annotation and discovery of essential pathways in trypanosomatid pathogens
column37: Trypanosomatid species are parasitic unicellular organisms with insect and human infective life cycle stages that cause diseases in humans and livestock. They include the causal agents of human African sleeping sickness, Chagas' disease, and Leishmaniases (Trypanosoma brucei group, T. cruzi, and Leishmania species, respectively). Together they affect 20 million individuals worldwide including the industrialized world due to immigration and returning soldiers from the endemic areas. Most available drugs are increasingly ineffective, and new drugs are needed. Although the genome sequences of the most prominent trypanosomatid pathogens are available, more than half of their genes have no known function. This limitation has slowed the progress in drug discovery for these pathogens. This project proposes to expand the knowledge about the function of genes and their cellular roles in major trypanosomatid pathogens including conserved genes and pathways that are potentially responsible for survival and disease using our established experimental and computational approaches. This project will provide the first global view of protein functions in trypanosomatids, and will significantly advance our knowledge of the biology of these parasites and ability to predict new routes of disease intervention.

column36: Deafness Induced Brain Reorganization: a research program to examine how deafness modifies cortical functions and affects compensatory vision and auditory performance following cochlear implantation
column37: With this research program, we aim at understanding why cochlear implant (CI) is more efficient for some deaf individuals (DI). More specifically, we want to identify deafness induced brain changes that could impact sensory performances following auditory rehabilitation with CI. Indeed, previous research has established that deafness leads to brain changes at the structural (e.g. area volume) and functional (e.g. area response) levels. For example, in DI, an area typically dedicated to the processing of sounds might process visual information instead. The impact these changes have on rehabilitation is yet to be fully understood. The CI is the most effective method to re-establish audition. However, auditory performance with a CI can, in some cases, remain fairly poor. Thus, we want to study the brain changes in DI and predict performances with a CI. This way, patients and professionals could be better equipped to make decisions regarding eligibility to this surgery. In past projects, we have demonstrated that changes in visual and auditory areas during deafness can lead to better performances in visual tasks but reduced ones in auditory tasks. Today, we want to examine if the changes in the auditory areas of DI will influence auditory performance with CI in general or for voice and/or word recognition in particular. To answer these questions, we will combine behavioral, electrophysiological and brain imaging tasks. This array of techniques will allow us to 1) determine whether the anatomical differences in DI influence future rehabilitation with a CI; 2) examine the structural and functional connections between brain sensory areas, and 3) evaluate behavioral performances linked to modified brain activity before and after CI implantation. We believe the proposed project will permit a better understanding of the brain changes underlying the sensory performance variability with a CI and could allow professionals to offer better adapted rehabilitation strategies.

column36: Investigating the Dynamics of Thought using Brain Connectivity and Experience Sampling
column37: Our recent dynamic framework of thought (Christoff et al., 2016, Nat Neuro Rev) makes predictions about how we can differentiate forms of spontaneous thoughts. These dissociable thoughts (e.g., mind wandering, rumination, creativity) can be separated based on varying levels of deliberate and automatic constraints, which are predicted to align with specific brain networks' interactions, and which bear substantial implications for clinical conditions such as depression that are associated with systematic changes in spontaneous thought. The proposed research program will test the framework's predictions by combining functional connectivity approaches with experience sampling (e.g., periodic questioning about one's current mental state) during fMRI to investigate the neural basis of spontaneous thought and its alterations in healthy controls and participants with subclinical depression. This research will also examine the processes that underlie the conversion of subclinical depression into Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). This work has the potential to significantly contribute to improving the health and quality of life of Canadians. It could also help identify new opportunities for early intervention and prevention for depression. Overall, this research and its clinical applications have a strong potential to improve the wellbeing of Canadians and benefit our society as a whole.

column36: Strategy for understanding how expectations interfere with chronic pain management: a multi-modal neuroimaging study.
column37: Chronic pain is a societal problem that affects more than a quarter of Canadians. The suffering caused by debilitating pain is detrimental to proper functioning in day to day life. It is unclear why people with this condition suffer pain when there are no detectable signs of tissue injury. Pain medications that are generally effective for acute pain are ineffective for about half of chronic pain sufferers for unclear reasons. Failed pain treatments lead to need for higher doses of potentially addictive or risky pain medications. There are currently no tests for pre-identifying patients who are at risk of treatment failure. To improve the treatment selection process, we first need to understand why pain treatments are ineffective for so many people with chronic pains. Our previous studies have demonstrated that response to treatments may be linked with expectations. Negative expectations can reduce the effectiveness of a treatment or can even amplify pain in some but not all people with chronic pain. The brain systems through which the brain learns associations and uses cues to build expectations may be organized differently in people at risk of treatment failure. Most research on this topic has relied on experimentally evoked pain or on measuring responses to placebos (sham treatment). This study proposes to integrate mechanistic evidence garnered from an experimental study with clinical attributes of patients who suffer with chronic pain. These findings can be expected to lead to new evidence-based pain therapies and will contribute to new assessment tools for pre-screening people who are more likely to experience treatment failure. Clinicians should be able to select treatments that fit the patient's specific mental and biological makeup. In this way, we aim to help to make the treatment process more streamlined, cost effective and are determined to improve the lives of people with chronic pain.

column36: Gene Therapy for Alzheimer's Disease
column37: People with Alzheimer's disease have difficulties to learn and retain information. Toxic products are known to damage brain cells and prevent their function. New memories can no longer be formed, and old memories are lost. Alzheimer's disease is devastating, daily. This is particularly true for patients who live with an early-onset type, which is inherited through known genetic mutations and can impact people as young as 30. The efficacy of promising therapeutics is compromised because they cannot enter the brain. We propose to deliver genes to brain cells and make them capable of producing their own therapeutics. This is called gene therapy and will provide cells the ability to protect themselves against degeneration. Briefly, genes encoding for therapeutics are placed in carriers. Then, these carriers are injected in the blood, and they enter brain cells. These cells can now produce their own therapeutics to counter toxic molecules for years to come. This approach is refined with a technology pioneered by researchers at Sunnybrook called focused ultrasound which is guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI-guided focused ultrasound does not require any surgical procedure. Parts of the brain affected by disease are targeted by MRI. Then, focused ultrasound is used to facilitate the entry of gene carriers within the brain regions of interest. This research will be done in animal models of Alzheimer's disease. We propose that gene therapy will protect the brain against damage and loss of function. Our long-term goal is to treat and improve the quality of life of people with Alzheimer's disease. In 2018, the first clinical trial testing safety of MRI-guided focused ultrasound in patients with Alzheimer's was completed at Sunnybrook. Gene therapy combined with MRI-guided focused ultrasound is well-poised to offer non-invasive and lasting therapeutics in the fight against Alzheimer's disease, particularly those with heredity early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Machine Learning for Flow Cytometry Clinical Data and Trial Analysis
column37: Flow cytometry (FCM) is the predominant technique used to identify and quantify the widest variety of cell types. It plays critical roles in the characterization and diagnosis of cancer, blood diseases, and immune system disorders by basic researchers, clinicians and pharmaceutical companies as part of clinical trials. Recent technological progress on multicolour FCM results in the generation of vast amounts of high-dimensional data at the single cell level. However, manual analysis using commercial tools, is time consuming (an hour a file, with clinical trials having over 10,000 files) and the largest source of variation in results. As a result, manual data analysis is a critical bottleneck in the application of FCM. We have internationally recognized expertise addressing the challenges associated with FCM data processing, having developed and published a comprehensive suite bioinformatics algorithms for high throughput FCM analysis. column36: Treatment In Thoracic Aortic aNeurysm: Surgery vs. Surveillance (TITAN:SvS) - A Multi-center, Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Enlargement of the aorta (aneurysm) occurring close to the heart (ascending aorta) is typically a clinically silent disease until a catastrophic complication of rupture or tear (dissection) occurs, which leads to a high risk of death and complications. In contrast, preventive surgery for known aneurysms can be performed with a much lower risk of death or complications. The size of the aorta is the most important variable used to determine which patients should undergo preventive ascending aortic replacement surgery. However, the currently established size threshold of 5.5 cm is based on poor quality data from older studies. Recent studies have suggested that most patients who develop a tear in the ascending aorta have an aortic size less than 5.5 cm and would not be eligible for preventive aortic replacement surgery based on current guidelines. The proposed randomized controlled trial will aim to determine whether surgery or ongoing medical surveillance is the best treatment for patients with a moderately dilated aorta. Patients with aortic diameter between 5.0 and 5.5 cm will be assigned to receive either surgery or ongoing medical surveillance. They will be followed over a period of 5 years to determine the rate of death and aorta related complications as well as quality of life in each group. This study will be the first clinical trial to examine the impact of early surgery versus ongoing surveillance for patients with ascending aortic aneurysms and will provide important data to guide their care.

column37: Mosquito-borne diseases are thriving despite decades of large-scale control efforts. Aedes mosquitoes are responsible for transmitting arboviruses such as chikungunya, dengue, and Zika. The geographic distribution of these viruses has dramatically expanded in the last few decades and Colombia is one of the countries in the Americas most affected by these arboviral epidemics. The overall aim of this study is to use a multi-disease perspective to identify disease patterns, drivers, and accurate disease forecasting methods that allow clinical and public health services to proactively plan and implement control and prevention measures. Disease, sociodemographic, and environmental data will be used in this study, which will be available at the national and municipal level in Colombia. We will begin by exploring the individual and joint disease dependencies by quantifying the correlation and variation of reported cases over time and space with Poisson-lognormal mixture models. The Bayesian multivariate models will be extended to forecast weekly disease burdens for a period of one year. Machine learning algorithms such as support vector machine regressions and random forest regressions will be developed to forecast disease burden. Semi-mechanistic dynamic models will also be developed for burden forecasts and these models will capture disease transmission processes. All forecasting results will be compared using various metrics of evaluation. The findings have the potential to greatly add to our understanding of the epidemiological profiles of chikungunya, dengue, and Zika, which is necessary for their successful control. The identification of at-risk areas and time periods can be used to inform targeted, integrated Aedes control programs and education campaigns. The forecasts, if accurate, will provide clinical and public health systems in Colombia with the necessary lead time for informed, proactive decisions.
