column36: Calcium nanodomains and spindle assembly
column37: Cell division is the basic mechanism by which multicellular organisms reproduce, grow, and heal. Over the lifetime of a human, cell division will occur ~10^16 times, yielding perfect copies almost every time. The astonishingly low error rate is due to structures called spindles, which function to distribute genetic material evenly among the daughter cells. Yet despite their ubiquity and importance in biology and diseases, how these spindles self-assemble is not known. We recently hypothesize that spindle assembly requires the formation of focal hotspots of calcium called calcium nanodomains, which have so far escaped detection due to poor spatial resolution of traditional calcium imaging techniques. We have now developed a novel probe called TubeCamp which can localize calcium increase to 250nm. We are able to resolve, for the first time, the formation of nanodomains associated with spindle self-assembly in both vertebrate cells and cell-free cytoplasm aspirates. Furthermore, disruption of calcium nanodomains disrupts spindles. These results prove that calcium nanodomains are indeed a universal and essential feature of spindles in vertebrates. We propose to identify key components of calcium anodomains, and to provide insights on how they work together to regulate spindle ssembly. Microtubule-targeting agents are the most important cancer chemotherapy drugs. Loss of microtubules is thought to be an important contributing factor in neurodegenerative diseases; clinically approved microtubule stabilizing epothilones have shown promise in animal models of Alzheimer, Parkinson and spinal cord injuries. Our work has revealed a previously unsuspected mechanism of microtubule regulation. This mechanism is unlikely restricted to spindle microtubules, as calcium-storing membranes have been observed in close association with microtubules in neurons. Our work may thus have wide implications in human health and diseases including cancers and neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Investigating the role of the BH4 pathway in Parkinson's Disease (PD)
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects 1 in 500 people in Canada; over 100,000 Canadians are living with PD today and ~ 6,600 new cases of PD are diagnosed each year in Canada. PD is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's disease. It results from the loss of cells in the brain that produce dopamine, a chemical that controls the body's movements. As dopamine decreases, tremors can develop, muscle movements become slower and more rigid, and reflexes become impaired contributing to a loss of balance. Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is a molecule which is essential for the functioning of enzymes that produce dopamine and other brain chemicals. We recently uncovered another function of BH4 in the immune system by which it plays a role in T-cell activation by controlling mitochondria bioenergetics. This led us to ask whether BH4 might also have a role in controlling mitochondrial processes in the nervous system, as it is known that mitochondria play a role in the deterioration of nerve cells in neurodegenerative disease such as PD. Based on our first experiments, strongly supporting this hypothesis, we will investigate the role of BH4 in PD and examine whether increasing the production of BH4 can reduce the disease. Specifically, we will use genetic engineering to develop mouse models which either produce less or more GCH1, an enzyme that limits the production of BH4, specifically in their dopamine producing neurons. We will investigate if these mice indeed develop symptoms of PD, hence establishing a novel disease relevant model system, and whether known mouse models of PD show reduced PD due to increased BH4 production. Moreover, we will study the effects of BH4 in cells from PD patients to provide first evidence on the function of this pathway in human PD and demonstrate its therapeutic potential.

column36: Dissecting the Flow-induced Symmetry-Breaking of Animal Cell Division
column37: Cytokinesis is a critical step of cell division that separates a dividing cell into two daughter cells. In the animal body, cytokinesis does not only contribute to the multiplication of cells, but also to their arrangement within their space, by controlling the position and orientation of division (symmetry-breaking). Although defects in cell division orientation are also associated with cancer cells, the mechanisms underlying the symmetry-breaking of cytokinesis are not well studied. Emerging evidence suggests that cell surface flow of motor protein myosin-cortical flow-is a driving force of spatial control of cytokinesis. The direction of cortical flow is distinct among cell types, but how cortical flow is navigated in three-dimensional space remains largely unknown. Our goal is to elucidate the cortical flow navigation system that breaks symmetry of cytokinesis. Actin cytoskeleton and myosin motor protein are central players of cortical flow generation; thus, we will analyze and identify the molecules and mechanism that regulate them. For our experiments we will use the embryos of a powerful model organism, a roundworm called Caenorhabditis elegans that shares many molecular components involved in cell division and actin-myosin regulation with humans. We will capture the myosin dynamics in the living cells using state-of-the-art microscopy in different cell types and genetic backgrounds. By observing cortical flow control in multiple modes of spatially controlled cytokinesis, we will understand the molecular mechanisms that enable cortical flow navigation during embryogenesis. Our analysis of this fundamental cell division event in the context of animal development will expand the frontiers of cell division research and will provide a basis for curing cancers caused by abnormalities in cytokinesis.

column36: Defining the mechanisms of original antigenic sin to improve influenza virus vaccine effectiveness
column37: It has been well-documented that one's first influenza virus infection has a lasting influence on how one responds to future infections. This has concept has been termed "original antigenic sin (OAS)" or "antigenic imprinting". OAS/antigenic imprinting can have either beneficial or detrimental consequences, depending on the situation. Despite extensive descriptive data documenting occurrences of OAS/ antigenic imprinting, very little is known mechanistically about how these phenomena occur. Furthermore, most of what is known about OAS/imprinting in humans comes from historical studies wherein the first exposure to influenza was by acute infection. However, many children are now first exposed to influenza by vaccination. The number of influenza vaccine types continues to expand, and there is strong evidence that the specific nature one's first exposure (ie. infection, split vaccine, live-attenuated vaccine, etc.) has a strong influence on the extent to which OAS/imprinting occur. Using a unique longitudinal cohort of children, we will determine how the nature of a child's first exposure to influenza virus affects OAS/imprinting. We will then perform mechanistic investigations to define the factors that are responsible for the development of OAS/imprinting using mouse models. This information will inform which vaccine formulations should be administered to children, and those vaccine formulations that are most effective for eliciting strain-specific or cross-reactive responses.

PE is a common cause of preventable death in patients with broken bones that require surgery. Patients with broken femurs receive medication to help prevent blood clots. It is unknown how long this medication should be continued and whether patients who are more prone to forming clots should receive longer treatment. Thrombelastography (TEG) technology uses a small sample of blood to evaluate a person's risk for blood clots. Our study will test if TEG can also determine how long each patient should receive medication to minimize their clot risk, based on their individual risk. TEG technology is readily available, cost-effective, and provides valuable information to help doctors treat patients with abnormal blood clotting. Our multi-disciplinary research team includes doctors and surgeons with TEG experience. This study will use blood tests and imaging studies to look for blood clots and abnormal inflammation in patients with broken femurs, both before and after surgery. We will determine the length of time that patients are in danger of developing life-threatening blood clots after their injury. Our results will also help identify factors that increase clotting risk and will help develop protocols to minimize this risk. If our TEG study results help prevent blood clots, we will save the lives of trauma patients across Canada.

column37: Pediatric Low Grade Gliomas (PLGG) are the most common brain tumours in children. While PLGG usually have a good prognosis, their treatment can be challenging when the location of the tumour is not prone to complete surgical resection. Radiotherapy is increasingly used as a back-up or a last resort when the tumour progresses on chemotherapy. As a result most PLGG patients will require several lines of chemotherapy with a resulting impact on their quality of life. Long term data on PLGG patients show that for the majority cure comes at a cost. Recent advances in the knowledge of PLGG have brought new hope with the discovery of alterations of a pathway (the MAPK pathway) that can be targeted by non-chemotherapeutic agents, MEK and BRAF inhibitors. Data form the lab suggest that the combination of MEK inhibitors with chemotherapy is more powerful than each agent separately. The aim of the current project is to test this combination in children who have previously been treated with either agent and compare the long term efficacy of the combination. We will also try to identify in the tumour, in the cerebro-spinal fluid or in the blood, biomarkers that can predict the response to treatment.

column36: Development of Novel Type 1 Cannabinoid Receptor Positive Allosteric Modulators for Infantile Spasms
column37: The type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) is present throughout the brain and body. CB1R helps control appetite, mood, pain, and movement. Because CB1R helps control many important bodily processes, it is considered a potential drug target for the treatment of addiction, anxiety, pain, and epilepsy. Despite its potential as a drug target, very few drugs have been developed that work at this receptor to produce a medical benefit. Infantile Spasms syndrome is a newborn and paediatric epilepsy. High-dose corticosteroids or vigabatrin are typical treatments, but spasms persist in half of treated children and these drugs have significant side effects. New treatments are needed because early successful treatment may result in improved long-term developmental outcomes. Emerging clinical data suggest some cannabinoids have anti-seizure effects. CB1R is activated by d9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) found in Cannabis and the body's own cannabinoids. THC use produces intoxication and repeated use can result in tolerance and dependence. We are developing new compounds, called positive allosteric modulators, that increase CB1R's response to the body's own cannabinoids, but cannot activate CB1R alone. Our compounds will not produce the intoxication, tolerance, or dependence associated with other cannabinoids. We hypothesize that a CB1R positive allosteric modulator can be developed as a treatment for Infantile Spasms. The goals of our research are: (1) to develop allosteric modulators of CB1R that alter the body's response to its own cannabinoids, (2) test those modulators in animal models, and (3) to apply the knowledge gained from goals 1 and 2 to paediatric epilepsy in rodent models of Infantile Spasms. This research will improve our understanding of CB1R, inform our use of cannabinoids as medicine, and lead to the development of new drug compounds for a devastating childhood disease with an unmet clinical need.

One of the major characteristics of any kidney disease is a sustained and excess healing response, called fibrosis, that attempts to return the injured kidney back to health yet leads to serious and life-threatening complications. This proposal is designed to understand the biologically programmed healing machinery needed for adequate restoration of a damaged kidney. Our recent findings revealed SMOC2 to be highly produced during kidney injury and contributing to the development of fibrosis. We predict that our findings can be helpful in designing proper treatments and diagnosis for kidney fibrosis. Furthermore, understanding SMOC2 will provide new insights in kidney repair, giving it the potential to have multiple benefits (regulator and marker) to keep the kidney functional for a healthy lifestyle.

column36: The effects of smoking marijuana on lung cancer development: implications for screening and early detection.
column37: The poor prognosis for lung cancer patients is typically associated with a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis, highlighting the need for effective methods for early detection. It has recently been demonstrated that low-dose computed tomographic (LDCT) screening of patients at high-risk of developing lung cancer reduces improves survival outcomes, providing strong evidence that this approach may be useful for early cancer detection. With the coming legalization of marijuana in Canada, it is anticipated that more individuals will either increase or start smoking cannabis. However, very little is known about the effects associated with smoking marijuana and whether this influences lung cancer risk. We hypothesize that marijuana smoking induces mutations that promote lung cancer. We will test this through the treatment of mice with marijuana smoke and compare directly to tobacco smoke. We will also aim to determine what compounds contained in marijuana smoke might cause cancer and how it differs from tobacco smoke. Lastly, we will assess whether some patients might have developed cancer specifically from marijuana smoking. Together, this study will determine for the first time whether or not smoking marijuana is a significant health concern and how this information can be used to improve screening protocols aimed at the early detection of lung cancer.

column36: The critical role of the nuclear pore complex during the life cycle of RNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm
column37: RNA viruses are a major global concern for both human and animal health. HCV has infected approximately 130 million people and 71 million are chronic carriers. If left untreated, a significant number will develop cirrhosis and/or liver cancer. There are 50-100 million cases of Dengue fever annually, and the recent Zika virus outbreak emphasizes the human and economic cost of viral infections. This grant focuses on basic mechanisms that viruses use to replicate and assemble, and escape from the cells innate immune system. We first proposed and demonstrated that HCV steals a component of the cell nucleus, called the nuclear pore complex (NPC), to create a protected area in the cytoplasm where the virus replicates. This appears to be a general characteristic of positive strand RNA viruses as we have shown this for HCV, HAV, Dengue, and Zika viruses. We will study the details of how HCV uses its ability to move the NPC from nucleus to the cytoplasmic factory to replicate and assemble in a protected site. We plan to extend our studies to additional RNA viruses (Zika, Dengue and Rotavirus) to show that hijacking the NPC is a common mechanism used by many RNA viruses to escape the innate immune system. Finally, we plan to examine how viruses control host gene expression using HCV as an example. It is becoming clear that "junk DNA" in humans often has regulatory functions. Some "junk DNA" expresses specific RNAs that associate with the host cell DNA and lead to changes in gene expression. We will determine whether the association of HCV RNA with host DNA impacts the regulation of the innate immune response. How viruses regulate host gene expression is a key unanswered question in virology.

column36: Health System Learning from Knowledges and Evidence held within Indigenous Communities: A Multiple Case Study and Two-Eyed Seeing Review
column37: If you go to the doctor with a problem and the doctor tells you there is nothing wrong, you might feel rejected and misunderstood. Maybe in your community there is no other doctor to go to, so next time you are ill you decide not to go to the doctor at all, making things worse. Unfortunately, this situation is common in many parts of Canada. Our health care systems assume disease is the cause of illness. However, there is more than one way to understand health and health care. This study will help to build a health care system that learns from our different understandings, and constantly improves to provide better care. Many Indigenous peoples do not see health as an absence of disease, but as the result of good relationships with their family, community, environment, and spirit. The differences between these beliefs and the beliefs of our health care system mean that Indigenous patients often receive unhelpful, and even harmful, care. One idea is to build "learning health systems" that continuously improve care by learning from a variety of information sources, including patients. To improve care for Indigenous patients, learning health systems must know what to learn, how, and from whom. This research will take place over four years in Northwest Territories, where 51% of the population is Indigenous. Working with Indigenous and territorial governments, we will review literature and documents and speak with community members to answer three questions. First, how is health system learning understood from different cultural and academic perspectives? Second, how do health systems learn from the Indigenous communities they serve? Third, what should a comprehensive conception of health system learning look like? Our results will suggest what and how health systems must learn to improve care for Indigenous patients and all Canadians.

column36: Geriatric Intervention for Frail Heart Failure patients: The GIF-HF Trial
column37: It is estimated that 600,000 Canadians are living with heart failure - one of the most common causes of emergency department visits and hospital admissions nationwide. While in-hospital outcomes continue to improve with the advent of novel heart failure therapies, post-hospital transitions of care continue to be problematic, particularly for the frail older demographic. One in two older heart failure patients will be readmitted within 1 year of discharge, often within 30 days, leading to a cascade of disability and sometimes death, with the commensurate expenditures that have become unsustainable for the healthcare system. Avoiding preventable readmissions is a prioritized benchmark for quality of heart failure care and emergency department flow, yet there is little guidance on how to accomplish this. What is clear is that the cardiac and geriatric needs of frail heart failure patients must be addressed in tandem in order to yield meaningful benefits. Although much has been learned about drugs and devices to treat heart failure, this will be the first patient-centered trial to focus on the unmet need of optimizing post-hospitalization geriatric care for frail patients. The intervention has a high potential for sustainable clinical implementation due to our knowledge translation plan and the well-established roots of the comprehensive geriatric assessment as a clinical cornerstone of geriatric evaluation. If our hypothesis is correct, frail heart failure patients will be empowered to adopt self-care behaviors for effective transitions of care that maximize their survival and quality of life while minimizing their risk of unnecessary hospitalizations.

column36: Identification of novel antibiotic molecules by chemogenetic analysis and machine learning
column37: Antibiotic resistance is a serious threat to public health worldwide. The situation is that antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections are increasing while discoveries of new antibiotics are decreasing. One of the reasons for the lack of new antibiotics is that with existing methods of antibiotic discovery, the chance to find a new drug that kills bacteria is extremely low, which discourages pharmaceutical companies to pursue antibiotic discovery. Here we will show that we can increase the chance of finding new antibiotics if we use artificial intelligence to predict antibiotic activity among the millions of drugs available. While most of the known drugs do not have antibiotic activity, some of them can kill bacteria with mutations in antibiotic targets, revealing a potential antibiotic activity that can be chemically improved. We will then analyze the growth of a large collection of bacterial mutants in antibiotic targets against a library of chemical molecules, including antibiotics. This experiment will show characteristic mutant responses for each molecule (fingerprints) where different mutants may be killed, indicating potential antibiotic activity. Then we will describe the shape and charge of the chemical molecules (structure) using a language that computers can understand. With this information, we will train an artificial intelligence system to identify which are the molecule structures that produce fingerprints characteristic of potential antibiotic activity. Once the artificial intelligence tool is built, we will use it to predict the potential antibiotic activity of millions of "virtual" drugs, based on their structure. We will confirm the artificial intelligence predictions by analyzing the fingerprints and the antibiotic activity of the selected drugs in our laboratory. Our research will facilitate the discovery of new antibiotics alleviating the current crisis of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections.

column36: Complex genetics of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Towards an integration of polygenic risk in clinical care
column37: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the leading cause of sudden death in young apparently healthy individuals. It is a genetic disease where complications can be prevented with early diagnosis. Genetic testing using a blood sample is now routinely done in family members to assess the risk of developing disease. Current genetic testing techniques do not take into consideration the complex genetics of HCM. As such, current testing does not provide a proper estimation of risk of developing disease as well as risk of developing complications. Recent data identified common genetic variants called SNPs that are associated with HCM. We propose that assessing such variants can provide better estimation of disease risk in family members and complication risk in those who are affected by HCM. The proposed study is a collaboration between experts in genetics, heart imaging and cardiology from 16 cardiac genetics clinics in North America. A blood sample will be drawn from the ~1800 participants and evaluation of ~10 million different SNPs will be done using state of the art technology. The association of those SNPs with HCM and its complications will be assessed. Those SNPs associated with HCM and its complications can then be used in clinic to provide the patient and his doctor a precise estimation of disease risk. This approach will allow a personalization of treatment and preventive measures according to the patient's genetic code. Along the way, from study design to clinical implementation, the research group will involve patients with HCM as research partners.

column36: Long-lasting effects of oral contraceptive use during adolescence: An investigation of neural, endocrine, and cognitive systems
column37: Oral contraceptive pill (OCP) is a largely used contraceptive method that is often prescribed during adolescence, a time at which the brain is still developing. OCP is composed of synthetic sex hormones, which abolish the menstrual cycle and maintain very low levels of endogenous sex hormones. Various studies have shown that women using OCP perform differently on various cognitive tasks, have more difficulty to regulate their emotions, and exhibit a different pattern of stress hormone secretion relative to naturally-cycling women and men. It however remains to be determined whether these effects remain after OCP use cessation. Moreover, one aspect that has been neglected so far is to investigate the impact of timing, that is the age at which OCP use has been initiated. In fact, adolescence is a time at which brain development is important and the chronic use of synthetic hormones may influence its course of development. In this study, we will recruit healthy men and women. Women will differ based on their history of OCP use: current users, previous users, and never users. Participants will be exposed to various tasks in order to measure cognitive, emotional, hormonal, and neural outcomes. We hypothesize that OCP use will have long-lasting impact on these systems and that the effects will be more pronounced for women who have used OCP for a longer time and who have initiated its use at an earlier age. Our results will fill an important gap in the literature and will definitely provide women and clinicians with data that will guide a more informed decision about their choice of contraceptive methods.

column36: Towards Equitable Sexual Health Care in BC: Centring the Voices of Cis and Trans Feminine Youth and Young Women in Policy and Practice
column37: Equitable sexual health care access for cis and trans feminine youth and young women (15-29 years) outside major urban centres remains a pressing issue across Canada. In BC, rates of STIs, sexual violence, and unplanned pregnancies remain alarmingly high in a number of rural and mixed rural/urban centres, and are often a marker of a range of health and social inequities and gaps in sexual health care. Despite increasing attention to sexual health and calls to move away from a soley risk/ deficit-based model (eg. disease prevention) both in Canada and globally, there is a surprising dearth of research on uptake, barriers and facilitators for equitable sexual health care in Canada, or efforts to document and evaluate patient experiences with models of sexual health service provision. Drawing on mixed methods and feminist participatory-action research frameworks, we propose to conduct this community-based research project across rural and mixed urban/ rural communities on Vancouver Island. This 5-year study will address the following specific objectives to: Obj1: Characterize youth/ young women's sexual health service needs and experiences in interacting with sexual health services, across the sexual health domains, and variations by geographies and social identities; Obj 2: Document the lived experiences of evolving policy changes and socio-structural barriers and facilitators on access to equitable sexual health care among youth/ young women, and variations by sub-groups (e.g. Indigenous and other racialized youth/ young women, LGBTQ2S+ youth/ young women); Obj 3. Examine how different models of sexual health service provision (e.g. youth clinics; community clinics linked to secondary school clinics; or sexual health within primary care) are experienced by diverse youth and young women; Obj 4. Inform evidence-based development of community practice guidelines for equitable sexual health care for and with cis/trans feminine youth and young women in BC.

column37: In Canada, rates of tuberculosis (TB) are disproportionately high in Inuit Nunangat, the Inuit homeland. The Nunavik Regional Board of Health & Social Services (NRBHSS), the Inuit health authority in Nunavik, is creating a CHW role in its TB services. The goal of our project is to develop and pilot a training program for the formation of CHWs on TB prevention and care activities in Nunavik, that is informed by Nunavimmiut (Inuit of Nunavik) values and knowledge, including culturally-relevant and effective approaches to teaching. This will be achieved by working with Nunavimmiut to co-create a vision of what CHWs working on TB will do in Nunavik, and to co-develop the educational programme. We will work together then to pilot and evaluate the programme in two villages that are highly affected by TB, with the community and stakeholders deciding what to base the evaluation on. Our endeavour is a partnership between the NRBHSS and researchers and clinicians with expertise in community-based participatory-research with Indigenous populations, and in TB.

column36: Predicting antidepressant remission in late-life depression using polygenic risk scoring and machine learning models
column37: The absolute health care cost of depression currently equals $1.2 billion in Ontario alone. Treating older adults with the first onset of major depressive disorder (age 50 years or older, affecting up to 16% of older adults) results in a 30-50% increase in health care costs. The biology of late-life depression (LLD) is distinct from early-onset depression. LLD patients present with greater concurrent illness, in large part due to underlying cerebrovascular (e.g., stroke) and neurodegenerative (e.g., Alzheimer's disease, dementia) changes. Globally, more than 50% of LLD patients do not recover sufficiently after treatment with ongoing antidepressant medications, which further predisposes them to cognitive decline, representing an increased risk for dementia and stroke. Our proposed investigation will use Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) and genetic Machine Learning (ML) models, both of which use algorithms based on genetic patterns associated with the disease. The goal is to identify older adults who are likely to achieve antidepressant remission, prior to treatment selection. The genomic data for PRS is publicly available and will be applied to well-characterized clinical samples of older adults treated with antidepressants. By leveraging genomic data with ML, we aim to discover factors that differentiate and predict remission in LLD. We also hypothesize that comorbidities (e.g. neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease) and risk of such comorbidities may affect LLD patients' response to antidepressants. Ultimately, such models will aid in substantially reducing the functional, economic and social burden associated with poorly managed LLD. Within the next years, these findings will provide a platform that will allow us to develop a genetic test to personalize and optimize treatment of LLD.

column36: Long-read sequencing and bioinformatics analysis to identify cryptic genetic mutations in patients with undiagnosed intellectual disability
column37: Intellectual disability (ID) affects 2 to 3% of the population worldwide, and in Canada, 7,700 to 11,570 children with ID are born every year. ID places an enormous burden on affected individuals and their families, the health care system, and society. The lifetime costs to care for a person with ID is ~US$1,000,000. ID has many different causes, and optimal clinical management requires the identification of the specific cause in each affected individual. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS), an advanced genetic test that scans the entire DNA sequence of an individual, identifies mutations in more than half of patients with moderate to severe forms of ID. However, although WGS is an excellent test for some types of mutations, it cannot detect all of them, and the cause is not found in nearly one-third to one-half of the patients with a presumed genetic form of ID who undergo WGS. The goal of this project is to employ state-of-the-art genomic technology with an optimized data analysis framework to identify the genetic cause in at least 25% of the 60 families with moderate to severe ID who have strong clinical evidence of a genetic cause (e.g., similarly affected sibs or characteristic features of a recognized genetic syndrome) but in whom WGS has not revealed a causal mutation. All identified ID-causing mutations will be independently validated and returned to the patients and their families, and all computational tools developed through this project will be made freely available for use by scientists and physicians throughout the world. By developing methods to identify previously-unrecognized disease-causing mutations among patients with ID, we aim to improve our understanding of ID and enhance the care of affected patients and their families.

column36: Longitudinal impacts of violence and stigma on HIV care continuum and broader health care access among WLWH: the SHAWNA Project
column37: This study will characterize relationships between violence and stigma, and HIV and broader clinical care outcomes among women living with HIV (WLWH) over time. Persistent gaps exist in science and interventions to address gender disparities in HIV treatment and care continue to exist, with women falling behind men in all HIV clinical outcomes in BC. WLWH also experience high levels of violence and HIV stigma throughout their lifetimes, which has been linked to reduced HIV and broader healthcare access. There is limited data characterizing co-occurring harms of violence and stigma on HIV outcomes. Global calls exist to incorporate 'trauma- and violence-informed care' principles into HIV care and practice to address these barriers, but limited research exists to understand how this can be done, and how to tailor these programs to meet the needs of marginalized groups including Indigenous women and women identifying as gender and sexual minority people. Leveraging phase I cohort of 350 cis and trans WLWH in a Metro Vancouver, Canada (Sexual Health and HIV/AIDS: Women's Longitudinal Needs Assessment (SHAWNA)), funded by CIHR (2015-2019), we have the unique opportunity to refresh and extend this cohort to 500 WLWH to inform programs and interventions designed with and for WLWH. This study brings an established interdisciplinary team, including social scientists, epidemiologists and clinical researchers, together with knowledge users and collaborators, representing community experts, to examine how violence and HIV stigma shapes WLWH's access to HIV treatment and care. Our study offers an unprecedented opportunity to create an evidence base to understand how to mitigate violence and stigma impacts on HIV treatment and care outcomes. Knowledge translation and exchange will be conducted throughout the study, playing a key role in informing policy and programs that promote trauma- and violence-informed HIV practice for WLWH in BC, and can be replicated across Canada.

column36: Identification of molecular mechanisms involved in the biological response to implant wear and corrosion
column37: Estimates predict the number of 45- to 54-year-old people diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA) will double from 1991 to 2031. With an aging population and the steep rise in OA, the demand for total joint replacements will keep growing, as will the need to improve implant longevity. Importantly, patients are expected to return to an active lifestyle, which adds to the longevity requirements of joint replacements. Consequently, improving implant longevity has been an important focus of medical research and industrial R&D. Particles and metal ions from implant wear and corrosion are known to be a major contributing factor to adverse biological reactions and implant failures. It is therefore important to better understand and modulate the biological effects of implant wear particles and metal ions to prolong implant life. Our research focuses on the identification of the molecular mechanisms involved in the biological response to implant wear particles and metal ions. The proposed multidisciplinary research, at the interface of biology, medicine, materials science and engineering, will expand our knowledge of implant failure mechanisms and ultimately lead to the development of new therapeutic approaches to modulate the adverse effects of implant wear particles and metal ions, and thereby increase implant longevity. Therefore, this research has the potential to improve the quality of life for large patient groups and provide tangible benefits to the Canadian health care system.

column36: Remission of diabetes and improved diastolic function by combining structured exercise with meal replacement and food reintroducTion (Reset) Thomas Yates
column37: Eating more than we need and not being physically active enough can lead to a form of diabetes called type 2 diabetes (T2D). Now we have evidence that in people with T2D, with a very strict and strong approach to reducing how much we eat, we can even reverse T2D in some people. The approach involves a low calorie diet including special shakes for a few weeks, that usually leads to losing a lot of weight. Afterwards, normal foods are brought back, through a careful eating plan. In the weeks that follow, though, you go back to shakes, if you start gaining weight. In a British study, more than one third of people who started this approach no longer had diabetes. We plan to test what happens when we combine this diet approach with an equally strong exercise program. The exercise program will involve going to a gym three times a week to work with an exercise specialist. She will help participants learn to exercise on a treadmill and to work with weights, weight machines, and resistance bands to build up muscle. After some weeks, participants will exercise at the gym on their own or at home, but they will stay in contact with the exercise specialist who will track their activity and heart rate remotely. If the exercise amount goes down, they will be brought back to the gym for supervision. With the 'flip of a coin,' we will assign some participants to their usual care; others to the low calorie diet and their usual activity; and others to the low calorie diet and the exercise program. In this study, we will see if the low calorie diet group and the low calorie diet & exercise group both do better than the usual care group in terms of 'reversing' their diabetes at 24 weeks from starting. We will also look at other important aspects of health in study participants such as how stiff their hearts are, how fit they are, and what their mood is like. We will see if they like the different ways of trying to reverse diabetes.

column36: Bridging the gap to translation by understadning and preventing diabetic vascular complications using human organoid culture (MRC NPI: David Andrew Long)
column37: Diabetes affects 3.0 Million Canadians. Globally 8.8% of the population is affected by this disease and this number is rising due to an aging population and increasing obesity. In Canada, the cost of treating new cases of diabetes diagnosed from 2012-22 is estimated at $15.4 Billion, while in the UK 10% of the NHS budget is spent on treating diabetes and complications associated with it, such as kidney disease, blindness, heart attacks, and stroke. These complications are often caused by changes in the blood vessels, therefore, strategies which protect or repair blood vessels may provide new treatments for diabetic patients. Laboratory studies on mice and cells have identified several molecules that can protect blood vessels, but moving these findings from laboratories to humans has been difficult. Dr. Penninger has recently developed a novel method to create artificial human blood vessels from human stem cells. When exposed to diabetic conditions in the laboratory or in mice, these blood vessels show the same changes and features as seen in the blood vessels of diabetic patients. These artificial blood vessels allow scientists to examine promising laboratory findings in a human-like environment before conducting clinical trials with human patients. In this project Dr. Penninger will work with a team of U.K-based scientists, Drs. David Long, Luigi Gnudi, and Karen Price to assess the potential of two previously identified molecules angiopoietin-2 and apelin to reverse changes caused by high blood sugar levels in these artificial human blood vessels. Additionally, the team will examine why some diabetic patients do not develop blood vessel related complications, using blood samples from diabetic patients with or without albumin protein in their urine. Excessive albumin in the urine of a diabetic patient is an indication of diabetic kidney disease. Their findings will ultimately lead to the discovery of new treatments for blood vessel complications in diabetes.

column36: Precision medicine in diabetes: Pharmacogenetic studies of large randomised controlled trials of diabetes therapies. (MRC PA: Ewan Pearson)
column37: Diabetes is a chronic disease that affects how the body uses glucose which can lead to serious health problems including cardiovascular disease, neuropathy, nephropathy and eye disease. Type 2 diabetes is the most common type of diabetes, accounting for around 90% of all cases of diabetes. Treatment of type 2 diabetes typically proceeds with the drug metformin, followed by a range of new combination therapy options. The latest treatment guidelines offer treatment choices based upon risks, cost, and benefit, however there is considerable heterogeneity in who benefits and who is harmed from any of these treatments which are increasingly used in the UK and Canada. This UK-Canada collaboration brings together, for the first time, genetic data on randomised controlled trials of the newer diabetes medication, including SGLT2i trials (Dapagliflozin and Empagliflozin), GLP-1RA trials (Albiglutide, Lixisenatide), and DPP-4 inhibitor trials (Saxagliptin) in over 30,000 genetic samples. These unique resources are only available to the principal applicants and in combination provide great power to identify genetic variants that alter benefit to these medication, side effects and cardiovascular outcomes. Here, we will conduct a series of genetic studies making use of dense genomic data already available on all subjects which we will analyse using leading-edge bioinformatics and statistical approaches. We aim to identify genetic variants that alter response and outcomes of those new diabetes drugs (SGLT2i, GLP-1RA, DPP-4i) with the goal to enable the personalization of therapy for diabetes, such that we can one day prescribe the best anti-diabetes therapy suited to each individual patient. Thanks to the unique and extensive data collection from the joint UK-Canada teams and the outstanding combined expertise of the teams in precision medicine, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, this study has the potential to provide a major advance in precision medicine of diabetes.

column36: Mobile Health Biometrics to Enhance Exercise and Physical Activity Adherence in T2D
column37: Being physically active is really important for managing type 2 diabetes, but many people with type 2 diabetes find it hard to stick to an exercise program. Research is needed to try to find better ways to help people maintain a physically active life. The objective of this project is to examine how mobile technology can help men and women with type 2 diabetes exercise and maintain a physically active lifestyle. How will we do this? We will run an experiment with men and women with type 2 diabetes in Canada and the UK where we ask them to use mobile devices that monitor how active they are and the effect exercise has on their heart. Importantly we will see whether this information about the body motivates people to stick to their exercise plan and helps to manage their diabetes. What is unique about this project? Other people have looked at whether exercise helps manage diabetes, but usually the exercise is not continued long-term. Our project is trying to find a way to help those with type 2 diabetes continue to exercise. How will the outcomes of this project improve the health of people with diabetes? Most people use some form of mobile technology. Finding out whether we can use mobile technology to help maintain long-term increases in exercise in people with type 2 diabetes, and whether this leads to better management of diabetes, will help us to develop better ways of improving the health of those with type 2 diabetes.

column36: Supporting the trajectories of our spirit: Living Cree Pimatisiwin and Blackfoot Kiipaataapiisiinii (Our spiritual way of life)
column37: Indigenous knowledge states that we originate from the stars and that our life begins before conception (Buck, 2009). All Indigenous peoples have a creation story which details the instructions on how to live our spiritual way of life. This project will support the trajectory of our spirits by ensuring our children have access to their spiritual way of life from birth. The spiritual way of life includes speaking the language, connection to land and water and participating in ceremonies that support wellness across the lifespan. The long history of colonial practices in this country has disrupted the traditional lifeways of nations, including the transmission of birth knowledge and practices. The project will seek to answer the question, How do cultural, spiritual, land-based and community connections from the time of birth impact the health and wellness of our children as defined by our nations? The all Indigenous research team will work with three Cree communities in Manitoba and three Blackfoot communities in Alberta. The project will be governed by the Collaboration Circle and the Knowledge Keeper Circle. In addition each community will have a community-based research associate and an advisory circle that will oversee the implementation of the project activities in their community. The focus will be on examining what is working to promote wellness rather than measuring contributors to chronic illness. At the end of the two years the project will have (1) developed and refined nation based indicators of well-being, (2) have documented the existing culturally based activities that support living the good life, (3) will have a cohort of children that were born with the support of a culturally trained birth helper, (4) will have preliminary data on the impacts of culture as a foundation of wellness starting at birth for the Cree and Blackfoot nations and (5) key recommendations for biological sampling in research for the Cree and Blackfoot nations.

column37: Healthy families are the building blocks of Indigenous communities, and are pivotal to the well-being and survival of communities. They are the cornerstone through which infants and children develop, learn, grow, and flourish, and the basis for well-being for people across the lifespan. Our team brings together partners from across research disciplines and Indigenous communities with the overall goal of supporting optimal health during preconception, pregnancy and postpartum for diverse Indigenous populations through community-led and community-specific strategies that promote the best possible healthy life for families and children. Specifically, we aim to incorporate the strengths and resilience embedded in Indigenous knowledge, wise practices, and cultural teachings into appropriately designed and effectively evaluated strategies that help Indigenous communities move in the direction of rebuilding family and community systems that have been systematically dismantled. The Indigenous Healthy Life Trajectory Initiative (I-HeLTI) is an important and timely opportunity for Indigenous communities to identify strategies that are considered critical for optimizing health, beginning in early life (i.e. in pre-conception, pregnancy, infancy, and early childhood). column36: Listening to Children's Voices - Promoting Indigenous Mental Wellness (I aM Well)
column37: Indigenous children face serious health inequities in Canada. Suicide rates among youth, a marker of the devastating impact of intergenerational trauma, are higher in rural and remote communities where access to treatment is limited, and children are reluctant to seek help. There is currently an urgent need to address these inequities, a culturally-relevant screening tool to identify children-at-risk, and promising programs to support their healing (e.g., Journey to Wellness). This proposal focuses on the scale-up and national spread of the Aboriginal Children's Health and Well-being Measure (ACHWM); a tablet-based wellness measure, co-created with Indigenous children. It is remarkably efficient in screening for mental health challenges, connects children-at-risk to local supports, and provides locally relevant data to inform program planning and policy. Two factors are restricting the reach of the ACHWM: the structure of the existing sharing strategy has reached maximum capacity with 50 partners and is unable to meet the growing demand; and the children most in need of assessment and support are often not able to obtain parental consent. We propose to: (1) leverage technology to recreate our digital processes to redesign scale-up, spread nationally and create sustainability; and (2) study alternative consent options to respect the rights of parents and the needs of children, to develop culturally appropriate wise practices that extend the tool's reach and promote equitable access. Our team is strong, with years of respectful collaborative research with Indigenous communities across Canada. Our program will impact children by identifying needs and connecting them to healing services. It will reduce barriers to participation in community-based screening to enhance equitable access, and deliver a sustainable strategy to share the ACHWM. Together we will explore integration within local health systems, and develop community-to-community sharing of the approach.

column36: Utilisation de la retroaction virtuelle alteree comme outil d'evaluation et d'intervention aupres des personnes presentant des douleurs chroniques
column37: La douleur chronique est tres repandue dans la population adulte. Pourtant, a ce jour, peu d'interventions non pharmacologiques sont disponibles pour traiter les personnes qui en souffrent. De plus, ces personnes tendent a diminuer leurs activites et eviter certains mouvements, de peur d'aggraver leurs symptomes. L'utilisation de la realite virtuelle est une avenue de traitement prometteuse pour amener les personnes atteintes de douleur chronique a bouger davantage malgre la douleur et pour diminuer la douleur durant les exercices. Nous avons developpe une approche en realite virtuelle afin d'alterer la retroaction visuelle fournie lors de mouvements des bras, en presentant un mouvement plus petit ou plus grand que le mouvement reel. Le but est de determiner si les personnes presentant des douleurs chroniques sont en mesure de modifier leurs mouvements pour s'adapter a une alteration visuelle, comme c'est le cas chez des sujets sans douleur, et ce, malgre certains changements occasionnes par la douleur chronique sur diverses structures du cerveau. Nous souhaitons aussi verifier si les alterations visuelles influencent la douleur percue lors des exercices. Si ces hypotheses se confirment, nous pourrons developper et tester une intervention en realite virtuelle susceptible d'ameliorer la motricite et le controle de la douleur chez les personnes souffrant de douleur chronique.

column37: Indigenous peoples do not have the same level of health and wellness as non-Indigenous peoples. They have higher rates of chronic diseases, infection, suicide, poverty, and mental health issues. This is not surprising given the history of colonization in Canada- the epidemics, residential school, and the 60s scoop. The roots for these health inequalities is related to the historical and current relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. The Truth and Reconciliation Calls to Action recognizes and acknowledges the necessity of improving relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples as the foundation for reconciliation. The goal of this Research Program is to create the opportunity for personal, community, and collective healing, ultimately transform relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. This action oriented Program will be guided by an Indigenous Advisory Committee and Indigenous worldviews - The Seven Sacred Teachings and the Medicine Wheel. These Indigenous values and teachings will ensure a holistic approach throughout this Program. This Indigenous philosophy will guide the mentoring of nursing students and the foundation to address reconciliation in the College of Nursing, USask. By introducing and teaching Indigenous values, all Canadians will have the opportunity to learn how to live in harmony with each other and with Mother Earth. The Program will use both Indigenous and Western ways to address and evaluate the impact of mentorship with Indigenous students and will formalize an important first step towards collaborative reconciliation in the College of Nursing and on campus at the USask.

column36: Promoting Indigenous health equity and culturally safe health care through decolonizing nursing education and practice
column37: Health inequities still persist for Indigenous Peoples in Canada. One of the root causes of these inequities is systemic racism, resulting from ongoing effects of Canada's long history of colonialism. Ongoing colonial beliefs about and attitudes towards Indigenous people influence the ways in which they are treated in the health care system today. Consequently, many Indigenous people do not trust mainstream healthcare services and do not feel safe using them. Indigenous patients are more likely to be diagnosed at a later stage of disease, to discontinue or avoid treatment. Understanding how to create structural change through actively counteracting racism and racialized ways of interacting with Indigenous peoples at individual and organizational level within health care systems is essential for creating a more inclusive, equitable, and healthier society. This Indigenous Research Chair in Nursing will promote Indigenous health equity and culturally safe health care through decolonizing nursing education and practice. The objectives of the Chair are to, 1) advance knowledge on the development and evaluation of interventions aiming at decolonizing nursing education and practice, 2) mobilize knowledge on approaches and interventions to foster health equity and culturally safe health care for Indigenous Peoples, 3) build Indigenous research capacity of students, mentees, and researchers in culturally safe health care and Indigenous health equity. This Chair will enable Indigenous and non-Indigenous researchers, stakeholders and practitioners to co-construct knowledge on the best approaches for promoting Indigenous health equity and culturally safe nursing education and practice. It will contribute to building local capacity of Faculties, Schools, and Universities to decolonize their education programs, and will provide tools to decision makers and policy-makers working in regional health authorities to integrate a cultural safety approach to nursing and health care.

column36: Advancing Indigenous Wellness by Reconciling Parallel Pathways in Indigenous Health Nursing: Innovating Wise Practices for Education, Standards, Partnerships, and Research
column37: Nurses are the backbone of the healthcare system and pivotal in providing culturally safe and culturally secure health care across the lifespan for individuals, families, groups and communities. In 2016 the WHO projected significant shortfalls in nursing's labor force. Calls for an immediate responses to increasing the number of Indigenous health professionals and programs aimed at improving Indigenous health, both priorities outlined in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 94 Calls to Action (2015). The overall goal of my research program is to develop a framework for Indigenous Health Nursing that empowers nurses to provide access to traditional Indigenous wellness practices within culturally safe and secure health care environments. My 5-year research plan will focus on identifying current and best practices, understanding barriers to cultural safety in Indigenous health care, defining a Scope of Practice for Indigenous Health Nursing, and identifying the policy, regulatory and education changes required to move towards its implementation.

column36: Dissemination, Implementation, and Effectiveness of the Exercise Oncology Survivorship Partnership Model: Reaching Rural Cancer Survivors to Enhance Quality of Life
column37: Exercise is an evidence-based self-management strategy that benefits all cancer survivors (CS). However, the majority of research, and the limited development of evidence-based clinical or community programs in exercise and cancer, has been conducted almost exclusively in urban academic and clinical settings. Very limited implementation in "hard to reach" CS, such as those in rural or non-urban environments, has occurred. There are unique features of the rural environment that are significant barriers to cancer care in general, and to supportive cancer care resources in particular, such as: geographic diversity, isolation, limited access/travel distances to resources and facilities, and lack of trained personnel to implement survivorship services,. Rural CS (RCS), or those living in non-urban settings (defined as <100,000 in population), report higher cancer burden from diagnosis through treatment and into survivorship (i.e., greater symptom burden). This burden is associated with inequitable access to supportive cancer care resources, including exercise programs, resulting in RCS experiencing more negative effects after treatment than their urban counterparts and being overall less healthy. Objectives: To disseminate, implement, and assess the effectiveness of our Exercise Oncology Survivorship (EOS) partnership model to increase the reach and delivery of exercise programs to RCS. Reaching more RCS with an exercise program will enhance cancer survivorship, providing fitness, health, and psychosocial benefits. Significance: Given our previous implementation success, we will extend the reach of our EOS partnership model across rural Canada and change the exercise levels of RCS. Our impact will include a sustainable environment to support exercise as a supportive cancer care for RCS towards greater quality of life.

column36: Phase III randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of metformin for cognitive recovery and white matter growth in paediatric medulloblastoma patients
column37: Because of advances in treatment, survival rates for pediatric brain tumours have improved dramatically in the last 25 years: currently there are at least 30,000 survivors in North America. Unfortunately, the treatment used to cure paediatric brain tumours can result in permanent physical, psychological, and neurological problems. Currently, there are no effective medical therapies to help brain recovery and reduce disability in paediatric cancer. We hope to change this. The drug metformin can promote rescue of cognition and brain growth in animal models by activating stem cells in the brain: we have found that it is safe and feasible to use in children treated for a brain tumor and may improve cognition. We seek to ask if this is indeed true by using a multi-site clinical trial to test the efficacy of metformin treatment for cognitive recovery in children and adolescents treated for medulloblastoma which requires aggressive therapy leaving survivors with significant cognitive impairment. If we find that metformin promotes cognitive improvement and brain growth in pediatric survivors of medulloblastoma, then this may offer a viable therapeutic approach that may significantly improve the quality of life of these vulnerable patients - and provide a model for treatment of late effects in other pediatric cancers.

column36: Deciphering recurrence of glioblastoma for precision medicine using multi-omics data integration
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most lethal form of brain tumor. On average, patients survive only 15 months after diagnosis because most tumors inevitably recur after surgery. Intra-tumor heterogeneity is believed to cause this dismal outcome: GBMs are complex tumors that are made up of many different types of cells. Some of these cells likely escape surgery and chemotherapy and evolve into secondary tumors that ultimately kill patients. However, the mechanisms of recurrence remain unknown. In this project, we build genetic maps of primary and recurrent GBMs to understand tumor recurrence and to find novel target genes for further study. We will first perform genome sequencing of primary and recurrent GBMs from the same patients. We will build the largest dataset of this kind by also collecting and analyzing data from existing studies. We will then map distinct cell populations in the tumors and statistically predict which mutations in these cells likely caused tumor recurrence. Second, we will develop new computational algorithms that jointly analyze the genetic maps of primary and recurrent GBMs with additional molecular information of the same tumors already collected by the sponsoring TFRI team. Third, using these large and complex datasets with our new algorithms, we will find genes and molecular pathways that are involved in GBM recurrence, and distinguish those for which cancer drugs already exist. Our detailed catalogue of genes, pathways and networks serves as a resource of hypotheses that enable the sponsoring TFRI team to conduct molecular experiments with the ultimate goal of understanding and treating tumor recurrence. Our algorithms are useful to study metastasis in other cancer types and will be made freely available to the research community. If any predicted candidate genes are already known as targets of cancer drugs, these may be available to the specific GBM patients compassionately in collaboration with expert clinician-scientists.

column36: Canadian Cancer Rehabilitation (CanRehab) Team: Improving the systematic identification, management, and treatment of the adverse effects of cancer.
column37: The diagnosis and treatment of cancer can result in long-lasting side effects which interfere with a person's ability to work, engage socially, and perform daily activities. To optimize patient outcomes, the health care system must focus not only on controlling the disease (i.e. cancer) but also on improving functioning and quality of life for individuals. There is an urgent need for research that can help to inform care for cancer survivors, including the early identification of physical side effects and the development of effective and sustainable cancer rehabilitation programs that can be supported and maintained within our health care system. The CanRehab team will bring together a large group of survivors, researchers and clinicians at four cancer centres across Canada (BC, ON, NB, NFLD) to conduct three linked projects that are focused on improving equal access to timely, effective, and appropriate cancer rehabilitation.The CanRehab projects include people diagnosed with breast, colorectal, head and neck, and lymphoma cancers. In Project One we will develop and evaluate an online system to screen patients for cancer-related impairments and to link them to services and resources based on need. In Project Two will test an 8-week on-line cancer rehabilitation program and examine implementation factors. In Project Three will test the feasibility of a 8-week group rehabilitation program tailored for the growing number of survivors living long-term with incurable cancer. Through these projects, we seek to improve the systematic identification and management of cancer-related adverse effects in order to regain/maximize function, independence and quality of life.

column36: Preparing to survive: improving outcomes for young women with breast cancer
column37: Women aged 40 and under with breast cancer experience poorer outcomes, havea wide spectrum of supportive needs and face unique survivorship issues compared to their older counterparts. Comprising approximately 5.4% of all women diagnosed with breast cancer, research and supports are lacking for this population. To address this, we created RUBY (Reducing the bUrden of Breast cancer in Young women), one of the world's largest prospective cohorts of women with young-onset breast cancer. To date, we have enrolled over 1000 women from 32 sites across Canada at the time of cancer diagnosis following them through treatment and into the survivorship period. Through RUBY, we have identified a number of unique survivorship gaps, including high levels of anxiety at diagnosis and beyond especially given extended hormonal therapies, marital and motherhood challenges, and social isolation. Specific, accessible interventions are required, but are currently lacking. ICAN Survive, is a promising self-management, on-line intervention for patients with cancer designed to address global survivorship issues at diagnosis and beyond. Key areas of need include regaining balance/dealing with diagnosis, coping with treatment and side-effects, management of anxiety and depression, fatigue management, sexuality and relationships. The ICAN intervention aims to build self management skills through guided training and education, however does not focus on the specific needs of young women. Thus, we propose to modify the ICAN intervention in collaboration with young onset survivors and evaluate the modified tool (ICAN-RUBY) for effectiveness. We are uniquely positioned to develop this young women specific intervention given the direct knowledge of gaps identified to date from existing RUBY cohort. We will leverage established RUBY study infrastructure with a proven track record of recruitment, to evaluate the effectiveness of the ICAN-RUBY tool in an embedded randomized trial.

column36: Virtualizing survivorship: Implementing a more timely and comprehensive model of follow-up care
column37: Prostate and breast cancer are the most common cancers in Canadian men and women. Early diagnosis and effective treatment have increased survival rates However, cancer survivors are often left with unwanted physical and functional effects after treatment, as well as psychosocial and mental health challenges that decrease their quality of life. Recently, "virtual" cancer care has gained attention. Virtual cancer care models use technology to deliver personalized survivorship care to patients who are at low risk of recurrence. Building on the success of these virtual models, our research group was awarded a CCS/CIHR Innovation Grant in August 2018 to design, develop, and implement three virtual prostate cancer clinics - called the Ned Virtual Clinics - across Ontario to address survivor needs at scale, reduce the burden of care, improve the survivorship experience, and increase quality of life. We want to improve our current Ned Virtual Clinics and their impact on Canadian survivorship outcomes through completing five new projects: (1) spread our current virtual prostate cancer clinic model to two new sites in Halifax and Calgary; (2) develop and validate an algorithm to personalize prostate cancer care; (3) introduce a new Ned Nurse to review survivorship outcomes, triage patients to appropriate care providers and services, and provide care in between/in place of scheduled virtual visits; (4) adapt this virtual prostate cancer survivorship model to inform the concept and service design of a virtual breast cancer clinic, and (5) explore new models of funding in Ontario, Nova Scotia, and Alberta for virtual survivorship services.

column36: Access to precision therapies for young people with cancer: Developing a policy framework to guide technology assessment and public funding in Canada
column37: Cancer remains the leading cause of disease-related death in Canadian children, adolescents and young adults (CAYA). Advances in understanding the genetic causes of cancer have opened up new treatment possibilities tailored to individual patients. Canada is a leader in precision medicine for childhood cancer: PRecision Oncology For Young peopLE (PROFYLE), a unique national precision oncology initiative, will determine the entire genomic sequence of tumours in CAYA with hard-to-treat cancers in order to identify alterations that are potential targets for new drugs. All CAYA with high-risk cancers in Canada, regardless of where they live, are eligible to take part in this project. However, the potential health system impacts of PROFYLE, and precision oncology more broadly, are not well understood. Many countries are grappling with how best to incorporate precision medicine innovations, including new expensive cancer drugs, into existing health care budgets. If precision medicine initiatives are to achieve lasting impact in Canada's publicly funded health care system, sound knowledge to guide their implementation is required. The overall objective of this project is to understand the policy and regulatory challenges of access to precision cancer therapies for CAYA in Canada. We will achieve this objective through a rigorous program of qualitative research that: analyzes and compares policies, regulations and funding of precision therapies for CAYA in different international contexts, and generates a policy framework and options to guide access to precision therapies for Canadian CAYA with cancer. These data will provide policymakers with evidence-informed considerations for the design and implementation of policies to govern fair and sustainable access to precision cancer therapies for young people.

column36: Innate and adaptive immune regulation in human type 1 diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease caused by the immune system mistakenly killing the cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone, insulin. Without insulin, the body cannot regulate blood sugar and this can be life threatening. Insulin can be taken by injection (by syringe or insulin pump), but this cannot replace the natural ability of the pancreas to make insulin only when it is needed, and at the exact level needed. Hence, people with T1D face a lifetime of fluctuating blood sugar and run the risk of life-threatening highs and lows. A true cure for T1D requires the immune system to be re-set so it no longer attacks the pancreas, combined with regeneration of the insulin-producing cells. In this project we aim to assemble a unique cross-Canada team of experts in immune cell biology and diabetes, in order to study specific aspects of how the immune system kills insulin-producing cells (called beta cells) to cause T1D. First, we will collect blood samples from individuals with T1D, another autoimmune disease, or healthy controls. We will then use these blood samples to study how different aspects of the immune system change over time in T1D vs non-T1D subjects, to learn how immune changes correlate with beta cell changes. Results will also be analyzed to determine whether any observed changes are different in males versus females. Second, we will study how three promising types of immune cell therapies might be applied in T1D. We will study how these immune cell therapies might affect beta cell function/regeneration and develop new ways to apply such therapies as a treatment for T1D. Overall, this research will explore several never-before-investigated aspects of T1D biology and take existing therapeutic concepts a step closer to use in the clinic. We will also create synergy with other on-going international studies in T1D and further strengthen our research capacity in this domain.

column36: Prediction and prevention of rheumatoid arthritis in First Nations People
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common autoimmune disease that causes progressive damage to the joints. It is known that individuals destined to develop future RA have autoantibodies (Ab) in their blood that are detectable months to years before the disease actually starts. Our studies have shown that RA is very common in some First Nations families, and that this is based on complex and unique interactions between genetic and environmental factors. Since 2005, we have worked in partnership with several First Nations communities and followed more than 750 unaffected family members of RA patients to determine their risk of developing future RA. To date, 20 individuals have developed RA, indicating a rate of ~1% new cases per year in the family members. We found that the detection of RA Abs in the blood does increase the risk of future RA, but we also show that most individuals with these Abs do NOT develop RA. This compelled us to find ways of predicting future RA that are based on a better understanding the immune system abnormalities that occur during this preclinical stage, and how these changes advance over time in some individuals but not others. With this knowledge, our ultimate aim is to find effective and safe ways to reduce RA risk in these predisposed individuals. Based on existing human and animal model data, we think that a dietary supplement of the spice turmeric, which contains the active ingredient curcumin, has the potential to safely reduce RA risk by modifying the immune changes that lead to RA. Omega-3 fish oils and adequate vitamin D blood levels seem to help the curcumin even further to achieve this. We therefore propose a clinical study to test this in individuals who have RA Abs but have not developed RA. We will use state-of-the-art immune tests to let us know whether there has been some correction of the abnormalities in treated individuals. We also hope to understand how First Nations People view clinical trials that aim to prevent disease

column36: Deciphering the therapy-driven molecular evolution of glioblastoma stem cells
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive form of brain cancer with an expected survival of only 15 months. Traditional models of cancer that considered GBM to be comprised of identical tumour cells have not led to improved therapies. New research, however, now shows that cancer is instead comprised of a mixture of biologically distinct cell types. Importantly, one subpopulation of cancer cells shares many of the biological properties of "stem cells", primitive cells that facilitate the growth and cell diversity of our body during early life. These "cancer stem cells" have now shown to be the driving force in GBM growth and highly resistant to traditional therapy. This may explain why drugs developed to target the overall cancer biology eventually lead to recurrence and failure. To overcome this, Dr. Diamandis' team wants to better understand the biology of these rare cells and apply it to design cancer stem cell-specific therapies. Dr. Diamandis' team will first study the biology of cancer stem cells directly in GBM patient tissue before and after therapy. To achieve this, Dr. Diamandis' team will carefully cut out clusters of cells from the rest of the tumour using a laser and analyze them with a technology known as mass spectrometry. This has major therapeutic implications as this tool quantifies proteins, the same molecules that drugs are designed to target. To complement this, they will bioengineer artificial human-like brain tissue structures called "organoids" to model important aspects of how GBM interacts with normal brain tissue elements to evade therapy. Finally, will take advantage of a technology called "artificial intelligence" to study vast amounts of patient data to uncover subtle but critical interactions between the various cells found in cancer. Together, these activities hope to help develop cancer stem cell-specific therapies that debilitate cancer growth in its roots and holds promise to provide effective therapies for GBM patients.

column36: Neural Basis of Sickness Behaviour
column37: Most people who have experienced the flu will remember what it is like being sick. Sickness behaviour often involves fever, lack of appetite, reduced movement, sleep problems as well as mental depression. When germs get into our body, the immune system reacts by activating immune cells that fight against pathogens by releasing key immune chemicals which trigger inflammation. Evidence suggests that our nervous system can sense these chemicals to induce a constellation of sickness behaviour. However, it is unclear 1) which cell populations in the nervous system are sensing the chemicals and 2) how these neural cells orchestrate various aspects of sickness behaviour. Here, I propose to examine the neurobiological mechanism by which microbial infections can trigger behavioural changes using mouse models. I will identify key neural cells that sense immune chemicals during the acute viral and bacterial infection stage. I will also use genetic methods to map, image, and manipulate the activities of the neural cells responsible for various sickness behaviours. In addition, I will determine whether different types of pathogens engage common or distinct neural pathways, and whether different brain regions exhibit modular control of sickness responses. Together, this work should reveal basic mechanisms of neuro-immune communication and may offer new strategies to manage sickness symptoms.

column36: Analytic methods to identify important relationships between environmental exposures and health outcomes using epidemiologic and other large-scale observational data
column37: Randomized controlled trials represent the optimal design for investigating the health effects of medical interventions. They often pose significant challenges, however, for answering questions related to the health effects of nutritional and environmental exposures. Epidemiological studies can provide important information on the effects of exposures when randomized controlled trials are not practical. Such studies recruit tens of thousands of participants and collect information on a wide panel of exposures and health outcomes, typically by questionnaires, biomarkers, and linkage to disease registries and medical records. Current practices in epidemiology, however, have been criticized for producing a non-reproducible and misleading body of evidence, which limits scientific understanding of the determinants of health and disease, reduces our ability to make informed clinical and policy decisions, and potentially undermines the public's trust in research. The proposed program of research will develop novel analytic methods to address major issues that have limited epidemiology from yielding actionable insight on the causes of disease. The application of these methods has the potential to substantially improve the methodological rigor of epidemiology, accelerate our understanding of the environmental causes of disease, and increase the value of existing and future large-scale epidemiologic data sources for research.
