column36: Understanding spatial and population mixing variations in the transmission dynamics of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) to inform RSV vaccine delivery strategies which optimize population-level vaccine and reduce disparities: development and validation of a transmission (simulation) model, using administrative health data and cutting-edge spatio-temporal Bayesian methods
column37: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial illness in both infants and the elderly. Although there is currently no vaccine, several candidates are in clinical trial and are expected to soon become available. A variety of vaccination approaches are being considered and there is an urgent need to determine the optimal strategy. However, our current understanding of spatial and population variations in RSV transmission is lacking. Understanding these factors is imperative to accurately predict the impact of a new vaccine and identifying optimal delivery strategies that both maximize impact and reduce inequities. Routinely collected health data and cutting-edge analytical tools, which are commonly used to predict the impact of infectious disease prevention strategies, offer an efficient means of investigating these variations. This is particularly important, as comparison of these strategies in trial or field settings are not feasible or ethical. The goal of this project is to develop a rigorous simulation model that incorporates spatial variations in RSV transmission, including age-structure and population mixing. We will validate this model using routine health data to ensure our predictions accurately reflect the real-world. Next, we will investigate various proposed RSV vaccine strategies to identify which one(s) optimally reduce RSV burden across the entire population. Traditionally, these studies have characterized transmission dynamics and vaccine impact at aggregated levels. However, this ignores important local variability factors such as vaccine uptake and spatially structured contact networks. These variations can result in disparities in vaccine impact, as has been documented in recent measles outbreaks. Our research will enable a better understanding of RSV transmission mechanisms and can be used to inform the selection of optimal RSV vaccine strategies. Further, it will inform planning of current RSV prophylaxis programs and vaccine trials.

column37: For some women, their genes place them at a higher risk of breast cancer. Genetic testing for breast cancer risk is now common place among women with a family history of breast cancer. By knowing her genetic risk of breast cancer, a woman can make important choices regarding how to prevent breast cancer or how to detect it early. Having information specific to women at high genetic risk helps these women make these difficult decisions. For example, it is known that mammography and ultrasound are not as good at detecting breast cancer in women with high-risk versions of the BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 genes when compared to women who do not have these high-risk versions. Therefore, women who have these high-risk versions are advised to be screened for breast cancer using MRI additionally. Breast cancer risk can also be reduced through changes in health behaviours such as quitting smoking, drinking less alcohol or losing weight but there is no evidence tailored toward women who are at a high genetic risk of breast cancer to help them make these decisions. This project aims to produce exactly this type of information. For example, this project will look at whether quitting smoking might have a bigger impact on reducing breast cancer among women at high genetic risk of breast cancer than women at lower risk. This information, in combination with being at high genetic risk of breast cancer might make a woman choose to quit smoking. Without the information specific to women at high genetic risk, she may have made a different decision. This project will produce this type of information for smoking, alcohol and weight loss. It will also produce similar information but for policy makers about how much breast cancer rates might be reduced if, for example, the number of people smoking decreased by half. Finally, this project will lay the statistical groundwork so that other researchers can make the same type of information for people at higher genetic risks of other diseases.

column36: Mechanisms for assembly of membrane protein complexes in the endoplasmic reticulum
column37: Cells contain several nano-machines composed of protein molecules that perform most of the molecular functions required to keep a cell alive. For these nano-machines to function properly, their component protein molecules need to be synthesized and delivered to the right place at the right time. Human cells contain a billion different protein molecules and ensuring their correct localization creates a large logistical challenge for our cells. First, cells need to ensure that newly made proteins get to the right part of the cell and assemble into functional machines. Second, cells have to recognize errors in protein maturation and target the defective products for degradation. In this study, we propose assays and experiments by which we can identify the factors involved in assembly of GABA A receptors. Many of the assays proposed in this study were developed in our lab and have been made possible due to recent breakthroughs in gene editing and single-molecule technologies. With these tools, we aim to build a detailed map of cellular pathways involved in maturation of GABA A receptors present in our body. The data generated here can provide insights into the pathological basis of epilepsy-causing mutations and guide design of new therapeutics.

column36: Untangling the relationship ageing, frailty, and dementia.
column37: As the world's population ages, the number of people living with dementia is quickly growing. column36: Turning White Fat into Energy-burning Brown Fat: New hope in the fight against Obesity.
column37: Obesity, a condition characterized by excess fat accumulation and energy dis-balance, is skyrocketing and remains a major health concern worldwide. The study of white adipose tissue (WAT) 'browning' has become a 'hot topic' in obesity, based on the idea that WAT browning might be able to facilitate weight loss and improve metabolic health. Two types of body fat, white adipose tissue (WAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT), exist in humans. WAT acts as an energy reservoir to store excess calories and supplies stored lipid energy when the body is starved or has increased energy needs. An excessive accumulation of WAT over time results in obesity, a medical condition that has been linked to various life-threatening diseases such as cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes. In contrast, BAT burns excess calories to produce heat as a defense against cold temperatures. For a long time, the adipose tissue was categorized into these two distinct types (brown, white), but recently the lines have blurred with the discovery of beige fat. As the name suggests beige fat shares characteristics of both white (fat storage) and brown fat cells (fat breakdown). This unique bi-functional property in which white adipocytes cells store fat in the absence of stimulation, but burn fat in the form of heat production under-stimulation can potentially be exploited in obesity to induce weight loss. Therefore, this project first aims to elucidate the molecular pathways that regulate fat metabolism and remodeling (switch from white to brown fat) and to tease out the signaling pathways involved in macrophage-mediated WAT browning and energy expenditure. The results of this research project will also both characterize the lipidome associated with WAT browning and the associated effects of these lipids on organ and cellular function during obesity. Overall, this research project will allow us to uncover potential strategies for the treatment of obesity and its associated comorbidities.

column36: Mechanism of protein translocation across the parasitophorous vacuole membrane of the malaria parasite
column37: Malaria has caused widespread death tolls around the globe. According to the World Malaria Report released in November 2018, the number of malaria cases in 2017 spanned 90 countries and totaled 219 million worldwide. After infecting the human host, the malaria parasite remodels the cell by exporting hundreds of effector proteins that travel from the endoplasmic reticulum to the parasitophorous vacuole (PV). Upon arrival, these proteins are unfolded and cross the PV membrane with the aid of the Plasmodium translocon of exported proteins (PTEX), a membrane protein complex. Despite the progress in understanding the general protein export process, the molecular mechanism and dynamics of protein translocation across PTEX remain poorly understood. Recent crystal structures of the PTEX engaged and resetting states provide useful starting points for simulating and uncovering the translocation mechanism. By combining structural information with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, I aim to uncover the PTEX translocation mechanism in detail. Coarse-grained MD simulations will allow me to simulate the translocation process (including pre-translocation and post-translocation). I will also calculate the free-energy landscape from MD snapshots to identify distinct states and their associated timescales in the translocation processive phase. In turn, this can inform the design of inhibitors that target PTEX and other related parasitic translocons.

The first group, from Pakistan, will be recruited from the recently established Matiari Preconception and Pregnancy Supplementation Trial. The second group, from Canada, will be recruited from clinics in Toronto serving refugee communities. Both groups will provide direct access to samples that will reveal the composition and functions of the maternal microbiome over the course of their pregnancy. Computational analyses allied with unique mouse and swine models will allow us to associate microbial communities with pregnancy outcomes. Of particular interest are the abundance and diversity of gut parasites that we expect will influence other microbes in the gut to negatively impact nutritional status during pregnancy. Understanding these complex relationships and their impact on malnutrition and birth outcomes, will improve diagnoses and inform the development of novel targeted interventions that can significantly improve maternal health and child development. This project directly relates to CIHR's mandate to improve global child health.

column36: Examining the contribution of birth weight to mental health, cognitive, and socioeconomic outcomes: A two-sample Mendelian randomization
column37: Previous research reported an association between birth weight (a marker of fetal growth) and adverse mental health and socioeconomic outcomes. However, it is difficult to establish whether this association are causal, as associations between birth weight and adult outcomes can be better explained by a common factor (for example, maternal use of alcohol in pregnancy) that may cause a change in both birth weight and outcomes (confounding factor). To establish causality, the better research design would be a randomized trial. However, it is impossible and unethical to directly randomize birth weight. Therefore, to probe the causal role of birth weight, the most robust evidence would come from quasi-experimental design. In this study we used a quasi-experimental design called Mendelian randomization, which uses genetic variants robustly associated with birth weight as proxy of birth weight. Genetic variants are attributed randomly at birth and are not influenced by confounding factors (eg, maternal alcohol use cannot change the offspring genetic makeup), thus they are particularly suited to be used as proxy variables. Using dataset from international consortia who performed large scale genome-wide association studies, we found that we found evidence for a causal contribution of birth weight on attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and suicide attempt, as well as for socioeconomic outcomes, ie, educational attainment, income, and social deprivation. However, no evidence was found for a contribution of birth weight on the other mental health outcomes (including depression, autism, bipolar disorder) and for intelligence. Our findings support a causal role of birth weight in the pathway leading to ADHD, PTSD, and suicide attempt as well as socioeconomic outcomes, suggesting that early interventions targeting birth weight may therefore have a positive impact on promoting mental health and improving socioeconomic outcomes.

column36: Using acute exercise to boost the immune system of children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia
column37: Leukemia is the most common type of childhood cancer, accounting for 1/3 of diagnosed cancer cases. Side effects of leukemia and its treatment leave children with a very weak immune system. However, we don't know very much about the effects of exercise in children with a weak immune system, such as children with leukemia. Therefore, my study is looking at how safe and effective exercise can be for children with cancer. My study will help us understand how exercise triggers NK cells in children with leukemia as they receive treatment and recover from chemotherapy. The results of this study will help us learn how we can use exercise as a part of standard pediatric cancer treatment.

column36: Strength-based assessment in autism: toward more inclusive methods for the assessment of cognition across the whole spectrum
column37: Many subgroups of the autistic population, such as autistics who have behavioral challenges, or who have minimal or no verbal language abilities, have been overlooked in research. They do, however, represent an important proportion of the autistic population. In clinical or educational settings, many of these individuals are considered to be untestable and are therefore considered to be intellectually disabled. However, through my doctoral research project, we showed that when using tests that call upon autistics' strengths, by adapting them in ways to facilitate the administration process, it is indeed possible to evaluate young or minimally verbal autistic children. We also demonstrated that many of these children showed "unsuspected strengths", which we would not have been able to capture with usual tests. We called our method the Strength-Based Assessment (SBA). The objective of the current project is to test a new version of SBA that includes tests measuring attention, memory, etc. that were adapted using universal design principles, to make them accessible and feasible to all people regardless of their limitations. The goal is therefore to determine to what extend the adapted tests improve our ability to assess autistic individuals and their performance on these tests compared to standard assessment. Using the SBA method will allow a detailed description of strengths and weaknesses, which would have remained unknown with usual tests, and allow them to reach their highest potential. We hope the project will allow SBA to be implemented in clinical and educational settings and, in turn, will lead to intervention plans that are matched to the potential of each individual.

column36: Unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying cerebral blood flow deficits in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Reductions in blood flow within the brain has been identified as an early event in the development of Alzheimer's disease. It was recently discovered that the smallest blood vessels, capillaries, in the brain of Alzheimer's disease mice were being blocked by an immune cell, and this small blockage was responsible for large reductions in blood flow. Amazingly, when the immune cells were prevented from sticking to the inside of blood vessels, brain blood flow was returned to normal, and performance on memory tests also improved. There is a type of cellular stress that is increased in Alzheimer's disease that could initiate the pathway that leads to the adherence of these immune cells in the blood vessels. We hypothesize that there are two types of cells at the root of this problem: One cell found in close proximity to blood vessels that might be responsible for generating too much of this cellular stress, and another cell that lines the inside of blood vessels that is responding to it. We aim to investigate the role of this cellular stress in reducing brain blood flow by targeting molecular pathways in the brain that will remove this cellular stress and bolster the brain's defences against cellular stress, in hopes of restoring blood flow, and memory. We will use experimental methods that target our two cell types of interest so that we can change how the cells respond to certain molecules by adding or removing certain genes to test our hypothesis. We will also deliver drugs to these cells specifically and examine their effects on cellular stress, brain blood flow, and memory. The proposed project seeks to increase our understanding of how cellular stress can lead to immune cell adhesion in brain blood vessels, and thus reduced brain blood flow. Our work will allow us to identify more cell-specific molecular targets for future drug development efforts with reduced drug side effects, aimed at interfering with immune cell adhesion to blood vessels.

column36: Linking microstructure and macroscale function of affective brain networks in health and disease
column37: Emotional experience is a complex process involving the coordinated activity of a network of brain regions, with key contribution of limbic cortices. These regions are characterized by their unique microstructure (i.e. organization of neurons in the cortex), which can be directly related to functional networks underpinning emotion processing using advanced neuroimaging methods. Notably, microstructural changes in limbic areas are a core feature of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). These patients show connectivity alterations grounded in microstructural abnormalities of limbic structures, as well as increased prevalence of impaired mood and difficulties in emotional processing. This population thus offers a unique opportunity to study how altered limbic microstructure relates to changes in connectivity and affective processing. Our goal is to develop a novel framework integrating microstructure and connectivity of limbic regions to understand their role in affective functions. This approach will allow us to study how local microstructure constrains brain connectivity patterns, and how lesions in limbic systems impair affective functioning. Healthy participants and TLE patients will undergo high-resolution neuroimaging to probe cortical microstructure, functional networks, and brain activity associated with emotion processing. Electrophysiological data from intracranial electrodes recorded at rest and during emotion recognition tasks will also be collected in a subset of patients undergoing this procedure as part of their clinical workup. These investigations will extend neuroimaging findings with direct recordings of neural activity in task-free and affective state conditions. This research will shift our conceptualization of affective functioning, and promises to guide predictions of affective impairments. Our findings will also lead to better recognition of affective disruptions in TLE, facilitating access to treatment and improving well-being and quality of life.

column36: Call for Inclusive eHealth: Identification of Empirical Indicators to Achieve This
column37: Do you have access to your digital health record? What mobile applications do you use? eHealth, or any digital tool to take care of our health, is an integral part of our lives. column37: Background: The number of civilians forcibly displaced from their homes due to war and political violence reached over 60 million in 2015. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees estimates that older persons make up roughly 8.5% of the total population of displaced individuals. These individuals often receive limited attention from national and international aid providers although they are more likely to experience physical and psychological distress than younger refugees. After resettlement, older refugees experience challenges related to language barriers, family stress, social isolation, finding employment, and accessing health care. These experiences, in turn, are associated with poor mental health. Unfortunately, there are few evidence-based health-promotion interventions designed to meet the needs of older refugees. A collaborative partnership between refugee community stakeholders, researchers, and mental health providers will translate study findings into best practice guidelines for mental health care providers who work with older refugees. Implications and Public Health Significance: Findings from this proposal will increase our understanding of the impact of displacement on long-term mental health and inform clinical and policy interventions to improve mental health and successful aging of older refugees in Canada.

column36: The Predictive Value of Sensitivity to Physical Activity for Disability among People with Back Pain
column37: Back pain is the leading cause of disability in Canada. Although studies show that physical activity can help reduce disability in the long-term, this is hard to achieve in reality. A major challenge is that, for back pain, physical activity often causes increased pain or emotional distress. This is referred to as "sensitivity to physical activity" (SPA). Unaddressed, SPA often discourages patients from consistently doing physical activities for rehabilitation. SPA can also discourage participation in activities of daily living. I recently published an article showing that SPA is associated with disability. Past studies have also found this. However, no study has yet determined if SPA is able to predict disability in the future. Also, different studies tend to measure SPA differently. Therefore, I aim to determine if SPA predicts disability 3 months later, and if this depends on (1) how SPA is measured (by monitoring increases in pain or the emotional reaction) and on (2) how a person deals with physical activity and pain in their daily life. To test this, I will conduct a study on 100 adults with recent back pain (less than 6 months), who will be recruited from physiotherapy clinics. They will come in for an initial visit and for a follow-up visit (3 months later). They will answer questionnaires evaluating their disability and pain. They will also complete a lifting task and rate reactions (pain, emotional distress); the lifting task's difficulty is adapted to each participant, in order to provoke a painful response. Finally, a smartphone app will be used to complete a journal on pain and activity for 7 days to categorize how a person deals with physical activity and pain in their daily life. This data will be analyzed using statistical calculations. Our findings are expected to help improve success in using physical activity to reduce disability among people with back pain.

column36: Investigation of the function of de novo peroxisomal biogenesis
column37: A cell is a highly ordered and compartmentalized place with intracellular organelles that perform a large number of essential biochemical reactions. Mitochondria and peroxisomes are such examples. While, mitochondria are known as the "energy powerhouse" of the cell, there are many other reactions that rely on a second, smaller organelle called the peroxisome to complete the chain reaction to obtain the final product. For example, the breakdown of very long chain fatty acids occurs first in peroxisomes, and the resulting shorter chain lipids are then transferred to mitochondria to be burned as energy. Without peroxisomes this cannot occur and the accumulation of products are toxic, causing cell death and diseases. These include rare disease, with complete absence of peroxisome, such as Zellweger syndrome, associated with dramatic consequences for the patients. There is also more common diseases associated with dysfunction of a specific peroxisomal pathway like plasmalogen generation in Parkinson's disease. The formation of new peroxisome is poorly understood. Our team showed that small vesicles originating from mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum are involved in peroxisome biogenesis. This project aims to unravel the molecular machinery and the signals that carries this process. Understanding in physiology how peroxisome biogenesis is induced and regulated will allow to help design new therapies for diseases associated with dysfunctional peroxisome.

column36: Computer-Aided Discovery of Estrogen Receptor Activation Function 2 (AF2) Inhibitors as the First-In-Class Therapies for Drug Resistant Breast Cancers
column37: 26,000 Canadian women are diagnosed with breast cancer (BCa) and 5,000 die from it every year[1]. All current BCa drugs block estradiol binding to estrogen receptor alpha (ERa) directly or indirectly. While anti-estrogens are very effective in initially controlling advanced metastatic BCa, tumor cells eventually progress to a hormone-resistant state where they no longer respond to conventional treatments. The Activation Function-2 (AF2) site of ERa is a new promising therapeutic target for advanced BCas, as AF2 inhibitors would be effective in hormone-resistant forms, and mutations of the estradiol binding site should not affect their efficacy. We previously developed AF2 inhibitors able to suppress the growth of resistant BCa cells[2,3]. Herein we propose to expand on our preliminary results and identify better drug candidates for BCa. Despite the immense potential for drug discovery offered by this surge of chemicals, research has been lagging behind due to the unavailability of methods able to deal with such enormous amount of data. We developed progressive docking (PD), an artificial intelligence method capable to increase the speed of virtual screening by above 50X[4], allowing to evaluate for the first time billions of molecules. We will use PD to screen the entire ZINC15 database, containing 1.3 billion compounds, to discover new potent AF2 inhibitors with optimized drug-like profiles. We anticipate that this study will yeald a class of therapeutics with a novel mechanism of action to improve the outcome of resistant BCa for patients in Canada and worldwide. column36: A dissection of transmembrane signal transduction and downstream signaling response in cytokine receptors
column37: The immune system is of vital importance to maintenance of human health. There are two main branches of the immune system - the innate and adaptive immune systems. While both of these systems are required for proper defence against pathogens and other foreign challenges, it is truly the combined efforts of the two systems that provides the protection seen. At the intersection between the two systems, there are cytokines and cytokine receptors, which allow for intricate crosstalk between these systems. Many cytokine receptors are seen to have one transmembrane helix in their architecture and are thought to function by dimerizing or rearranging upon cytokine binding, resulting in signalling within the cell. Despite the vast efforts applied to the study of these receptors, the nature of how the signal is able to cross from outside the cell, with binding of the receptor, to inside the cell, where proteins will bind and downstream genes will be regulated, is poorly understood. One area of confusion is the notion that these receptors can have varied cellular responses to differential stimulus, which goes against the dogma that simple dimerization is a driving factor in these systems. I aim to fill this gap in knowledge by pursuing the structures of various full-length cytokine receptors with varying stimuli and resultant internal factors. In addition, I will use an existing toolkit of engineered ligands for a specific non-immunological cytokine receptor, EpoR, to modulate the receptor in a tunable way. In addition, we will expand this toolkit to immune cytokine receptors to decipher the differences between various receptor subtypes. Through this structural and protein engineering, we will provide vast insight into the mechanisms for cytokine signals being transduced across the membrane and provide a framework for the development of novel cytokine receptor targeted therapeutics.

column36: Investigating the impact of evolving cannabis access and use on substance use trajectories and drug-related harm in the context of an opioid overdose epidemic
column37: Cannabis is the most widely produced, distributed and consumed illicit drug worldwide. Canada and many other countries are introducing new regulatory approaches to cannabis, including legalization. Although most research has focused on the harms of cannabis use, recent evidence suggests that cannabis use may alter specific high-risk drug practices. This research indicates that cannabis is often used as a substitute for high-risk substances such as cocaine, heroin or prescription opioids. However, these studies have not examined the impact of cannabis use over time and it is uncertain how the legalization of recreational cannabis will influence rates of high-risk drug use, infectious disease risk and addiction treatment. Given the recent legalization of recreational cannabis in Canada and the current opioid overdose crisis, identifying the impacts of cannabis use on high-risk drug use will be important for informing clinical and public health practice, as well as policy. The purpose of this research program is to describe how changing cannabis access and use influences the development of high-risk drug use patterns and addiction treatment. To accomplish these objectives, we will use data from three long-running community-recruited cohort studies in Vancouver, Canada, which will be supplemented by linked administrative data on participation in addiction treatment. These cohorts are operated by the BC Centre on Substance Use and include over 3,700 individuals who use illicit drugs, including high rates of cannabis use (>40%). Importantly, these studies include participants at different points in their drug use career, including at-risk youth at early stages of illicit drug use and older adults who use illicit drugs and tend to be more involved in addiction services. The diverse composition of these cohorts provide the opportunity to study the effects of cannabis use on the trajectory of high-risk drug use across the lifespan of active illicit drug users.

column36: Genetic and epigenetic dysregulation caused by transposable elements in pediatric high-grade gliomas.
column37: Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are lethal brain tumours with no effective therapies. In most cases, the source of genetic damage leading to tumour formation remains unknown. One potential cause of pediatric DNA damage is specialized DNA sequences that can 'transpose' or move to different positions in the genome. Unlike most DNA, transposable elements (TEs) can mobilize by cutting or copying themselves and then reinserting elsewhere in the genome. Each TE reinsertion event may disturb the sequence or regulation of nearby genes. Although there are millions of TEs in the human genome, the vast majority cannot move around due to errors in reinsertion or DNA damage. Hundreds of TEs, however, remain capable of mobilization. TE mobility is normally prevented by various cellular defense mechanisms to limit further DNA damage, however, these defense mechanisms are weakened or disabled at specific times during development, allowing TEs an opportunity to cause damage. Considering that TEs mobilize more frequently in the brain than other tissues, we hypothesise that TEs could be a significant contributor to cancer-promoting genetic mutations in pHGG. We therefore propose to analyze TEs in pHGG by multiple molecular sequencing approaches: Whole genome sequencing to identify TE insertion sites, ATAC sequencing to identify open regions of DNA, RNA sequencing to measure gene expression, and proteomics to measure protein levels. Together, these approaches will allow us to identify genomic changes caused by TEs and their effects on gene regulation. Defining these genetic events will allow the development of targeted therapeutics or genetic screening approaches to identify individuals with increased risk of disease development. Additionally, this work could be extended to other pediatric brain tumour types with potentially similar developmental origins and elevated levels of TE mobilization.

column36: Quantifying Head Impact Biomechanics and Mechanisms of Sport-Related Concussion in Youth Athletes
column37: The immediate health effects of concussion can be catastrophic, but there can also be long-term cognitive consequences associated with the accumulation of sub-concussive impacts over time. An estimated one in ten youth sustain a sport-related concussion each year. Our current understanding of the mechanisms of concussion comes from studying adults. More work is clearly needed to understand the mechanisms of sport-related concussion in youth athletes, especially out in the field rather than lab-based tests. Recent developments in wearable technology have helped create impact monitoring mouthguards that are embedded with inertial measurement units. These mouthguards can directly measure head impact biomechanics in the field and can help us understand the mechanisms of concussion in youth athletes. Therefore, the main goal of this research project is to use the impact monitoring mouthguards to measure head impacts in high school football athletes and identify key features that characterize a sport-related concussion. A second objective is to determine which positions in youth football experience greater head impact exposure. High school football athletes will wear a validated impact monitoring mouthguard during practices and games. Key biomechanical features (i.e., acceleration and velocity) will be recorded for each head impact. Any incidence of concussion will be documented, and predictive analyses will reveal whether the incidence of concussion can be determined from key biomechanical features. A statistical test (Chi-square) will also be used to compare the head impact exposure between different positions. The results from this project will not only provide invaluable information on the concussion biomechanics for youth athletes, but they will also determine whether head impacts can be accurately measured in the field to monitor the risks of accumulated sub-concussive head impact in football and potentially other sports (e.g., rugby, hockey, lacrosse).

column36: Improving the quality of end-of-life care among cancer patients in Alberta, Canada through the development and assessment of a decision support tool for prognostication
column37: More Canadians die from cancer than from any other cause. It is therefore important to study and find ways to improve the delivery of healthcare to cancer patients who are close to death. Previous research has shown that approximately 20% of patients will experience unnecessary or inappropriate cancer treatment towards the end of life. For example, some patients will receive chemotherapy within two weeks of dying and some patients will die within a hospital without ever being referred to palliative care. Such end-of-life care is harmful because it reduces the quality of life of patients and represents a poor use of valuable healthcare resources. The purpose of our investigation is to: 1) determine how many individuals diagnosed with cancer in Alberta received unnecessary or inappropriate end-of-life care between 2004 and 2017; 2) develop a statistical model that will estimate the probability that a patient will die or experience serious adverse side effects within a short period of time if they decide to undergo or continue treatment versus if they decide to forego or stop treatment; and 3) use the statistical model developed in objective 2 to create a web- and mobile-based application that clinicians and patients can use to determine if additional treatment or referral to palliative services is appropriate for them and to assess the feasibility of this application within clinical practice. We plan to address objectives 1 to 2 using existing healthcare data collected by the Alberta government for the purposes of reimbursing physicians and hospitals. For objective 3, we plan to conduct a pilot study whereby we will give the decision support tool to a group of clinicians to obtain feedback about the perceived usefulness of this tool and to see if there were any changes in the way that the clinicians treated patients after they received the tool.

column36: The role of liver-secreted exosomes in linking non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and insulin resistance
column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) are common co-morbidities, with rates of fatty liver affecting ~20% of the general population and up to 70% of individuals with T2D. While the reasons underpinning the relationship between NAFLD and T2D remain poorly understood, fatty liver often precedes the onset of T2D. Therefore, it is possible that factors originating from the liver can negatively affect the ability for key metabolic tissues to control blood glucose levels. Interestingly, the liver secretes small vesicles known as 'exosomes' that carry biological cargo to other cells/tissues and can alter recipient cell function. We propose that NAFLD alters the exosome cargo secreted from the liver, and that these communicate with other tissues and promote the development of insulin resistance and glucose intolerance. To examine this, we will use a rodent model of NAFLD to characterize the exosome composition secreted from the liver relative to healthy control mice. We will then use these exosomes to identify their roles on whole body and tissue-specific insulin sensitivity and glucose control. Overall, these studies will determine the role of exosomes in NAFLD-driven impairments in blood glucose control, provide novel insights into the mechanisms linking NAFLD and T2D, and may identify new therapeutic targets for diabetes treatment.

column36: Novel measures to investigate listening effort with naturalistic, real-world auditory stimuli
column37: By age 60, around 50% of all adults will report hearing loss. As a result, listeners regularly fail to grasp what is being said. This is especially true in noisy environments, resulting in increased listening effort to understand speech and in extreme cases, anxiety and depression. Clinical tests of speech perception focus on intelligibility, and use brief, isolated sentences that are neither engaging nor meaningful. Two individuals can achieve the same word-report score, with one finding the task unpleasantly effortful, and the other finding it nearly effortless. Clinical measures of listening effort are urgently needed, and any solution to this problem requires a conscious transformation of both diagnostic content (i.e., in the form of engaging narratives that are true to the real world) and test methods. One solution involves the use of intersubject correlation (ISC). ISC captures shared information across brains by leveraging activity in one brain to model another. This approach becomes especially powerful when exploring dynamic, naturalistic scenarios - such as storytelling that occurs over several minutes. Here, I aim to validate a novel metric (ISC) to assess listening effort as people attend to real-world narratives using multimodal experimental methods of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and eye tracking. The advantage of using narratives is that they capture the dynamics of speech processing and can be used to differentiate between those who are struggling and those who are not - something current tests fail to do. fMRI will allow us to examine the simultaneous contributions of different networks in effortful listening. Whereas using eye tracking as a metric of spatial attention will enable us to calibrate more practical, non-invasive measures of listening effort. This will allow audiologists to measure effortful listening and implement individualised hearing-aid fitting, leading to better outcomes for those with hearing loss.

column36: Walk smarter not harder
column37: Knee arthritis commonly begins in the joint behind the kneecap, termed the patellofemoral joint (PF). It affects middle-aged and older adults, this impacts productivity and contribution to society and results in years of knee pain and disability across the lifespan. There is thus an urgent need for research aimed at understanding modifiable risk factors for PF arthritis that can guide treatment approaches. Cadence (i.e., number of steps taken per minute) during walking is one such risk factor. People with knee arthritis who take fewer steps per minute to cover the same distance (i.e., lower cadence) experience more severe PF arthritis in the future. Evidence suggests elevated knee joint loads contribute to development of PF arthritis and pain. Thus, research is needed to understand the relation of walking cadence to knee loading and pain, and whether cadence can be targeted to improve knee loading and pain in people with PF arthritis. Gait parameters such as cadence, joint angles and forces exerted on the ground can be measured very accurately in a research lab, but may not fully represent what happens outside that controlled environment. Wearable devices are relatively inexpensive and have the potential to monitor gait parameters in the 'real-world'. However, research to support the validity of these devices for measuring gait parameters is limited, especially at lower speeds typical of people with PF arthritis. The proposed study will address the following 3 research questions: 1) Is walking cadence related to knee loading and pain? 2) Does changing cadence (without changing waking speed) change knee loading and pain in people with PF arthritis? 3) Can wearable devices accurately monitor gait parameters (e.g. cadence, speed) in people with PF arthritis? My research will generate important new knowledge that will directly inform the development of a walking program for PF arthritis management that could aid in changing the trajectory of this disease.

column36: Central determinants of recovery from upper limb peripheral nerve injury
column37: Peripheral nerve injuries (PNI) affecting the hand can seriously degrade quality of life and self-efficacy. Following injury, peripheral nerves can regrow but successful regrowth does not guarantee the return of healthy hand function. The reasons for incomplete recovery are unknown. We will investigate the role of brain reorganization following peripheral nerve injury in successful and unsuccessful recovery using state-of-the-art brain imaging methods and carefully designed tests of real-world hand function. We will directly address three main shortcomings in previous research on this topic by (1) using imaging techniques with extremely high resolution, (2) using imaging analysis approaches that take into account individual differences in brain organization, and (3) using tests that reflect real-world hand use by incorporating natural sensory and motor functions. We will recruit individuals with peripheral nerve injuries who have been identified as candidates for nerve reconstruction surgery. These individuals will undergo brain imaging and hand function testing before surgery, as well as at 3, 6, and 12 month intervals post-surgery. We will track their functional recovery and its relation to changes in brain organization observed preceding and following surgery. We hypothesize that changes in brain organization improve hand function; however, because surgery also involves significant peripheral reorganization (like injury itself), brain reorganization before surgery could be counterproductive. The proposed study will yield important insights into the role of peripheral nerve regrowth and brain reorganization for recovery of hand function. It could also influence clinical practice such as the timing for surgery following peripheral nerve injury.

column36: Resisting Vascular Cognitive Impairment: The Effects of Resistance Training on Myelin and Blood-based Biomarkers of Neuroplasticity in Older Adults
column37: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) refers to the loss of cognitive and brain function due to blocked or narrowed arteries in the brain. Very often, these blockages are in the small arteries of the brain and are only diagnosed with brain scans. Another feature of VCI is myelin loss; myelin is critical for the proper transmission of signals within the brain. Thus, myelin loss is associated with impaired cognitive function and mobility. Importantly, VCI is the second most common cause of dementia in the world. Fortunately, VCI may be the most treatable form of cognitive impairment as many of its key risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol, can be reduced with lifestyle changes. While we know that exercise is effective in reducing these risk factors, little research has been done specifically in persons with VCI to determine whether exercise can slow down the disease progression. Specifically, despite evidence that shows strength training (i.e., lifting weights) can reduce the damage due to blocked small arteries, current VCI research focus solely on aerobic training (e.g., running, walking). Moreover, no study has examined whether exercise of any type can reduce myelin loss over time in persons with VCI. Based on our prior work, we propose that strength training is an effective treatment strategy for slowing down disease progression in persons with VCI. Using a special brain scan, we will evaluate the effects of twice-weekly strength training on myelin over a 12-month period in persons with VCI compared to an active control group. We will also examine how strength training may minimize myelin loss in VCI by examining levels of neurotrophic growth factors in the blood. Our proposal is very practical as exercise may be an effective, inexpensive, and accessible intervention strategy with minimal side effects. Our proposal is also timely as the prevalence and burden of VCI will only increase due to the world's aging population.

column36: Investigating the impacts of alcohol-sales deregulation on emergency department visits and hospitalizations due to alcohol in the province of Ontario
column37: Problematic alcohol use is responsible for a large and growing burden on the health of Canadians. Prior research has identified possible regulations that governments can put in place to reduce problematic alcohol use and associated health harms. We will then link this data into databases containing records of all emergency department visits and hospitalizations in Ontario and see whether individuals who live near a store selling alcohol are more likely to have an ED visit or hospitalization caused by alcohol. We will also examine this relationship for different demographic groups. We plan to work with health and government officials at the local, provincial, and national level to communicate the results of our research and help inform policy related to regulating how and where we sell alcohol.

column36: Health service use by lonely and socially isolated older adults in supportive living settings
column37: As people age, a spectrum of care is required including home care, retirement home, assisted/supportive living (SL), and nursing home (NH). These services are paid for by provincial health plans or privately. Historically in Canada's public health system, when advanced levels of care were required, support was provided in NHs. SL was envisioned as a homelike and less costly alternative to the healthcare system than NHs. It is a residential care setting where people access services through the provincial home care program. Alberta, has made major public investments in SL and consequently, has restricted investment in NHs. While this policy decision is meant to align with older adults' preferences and to reduce health system costs, there is little evidence that SL sector can achieve either goal. SL facilities have limited staff and no registered nurse on site. There is an expectation in SL facilities that residents have family or friends who can provide emotional or task-based support and this is not always the case. Furthermore, little is known about SL residents who are lonely and/or socially isolated. Poor social connections are associated with increased risk of hospitalization and transfer to NH, which SL is intended to avoid. Fewer staff, limited recreation services and an (unmet) expectation for family involvement raises concerns about the quality of care and quality of life for lonely and/or socially isolated SL residents. My postdoctoral research will address these issues by using provincial health administrative data to understand health and service use of residents who are socially isolated and/or are lonely compared to those who are not. I will compare lonely/isolated residents characteristics, number of hospital visits, and length of stay to those that are not lonely or isolated. Given this sector's tremendous growth, it is essential that we understand the impact of these models of care in order to optimize SL resident quality of life.

column36: Suicidality among youth with autism spectrum disorder
column37: Adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are nine times more likely to die by suicide and think about suicide 10 times more often than adults in the general population. Despite this knowledge about adults, little is known about suicidality (thoughts of taking one's life, creating a plan, attempts) among youth with ASD (15-30 years) as youth are significantly underrepresented in research. With little research that has examined suicidality in youth with ASD, it is unknown how they perceive, understand and experience suicidality. Furthermore, little is known about the factors that contribute to, and or protect youth with ASD from suicidality, and potential similarities/differences among young men and women. This limited knowledge is an urgent concern as it is unknown how to support suicidal youth with ASD, provide adequate health care, or best ways to prevent suicide in this population. Given these gaps in knowledge, the study aims to: 1)Explore the perspectives, perceptions and experiences of suicidality among youth with ASD. 2)Understand the factors that contribute to or protect youth from suicidality. 3)Work with youth with ASD, families, and stakeholders to share knowledge, and work to inform policy and practice. This research will generate new knowledge to inform how suicidality is identified, examine how suicidality may be similar or different among young men and women with ASD, uncover the individual/social factors which influence suicidality, and illuminate the factors that may protect youth with ASD from suicidality. column36: Neuromelanin Signals in the Substantia Nigra of Patients with Treatment Resistant Schizophrenia: A Cross-Sectional MRI Study
column37: Schizophrenia (Sz) is a chronic, progressive mental illness that affects 1% of the population. The current treatment for Sz includes the medications labelled 'antipsychotics (APs)' to block the action of dopamine. Unfortunately, APs do not work in 30% of patients (TRS: treatment-resistant schizophrenia). Clozapine (CLZ) is the only effective antipsychotic for TRS; its earlier introduction is recommended by the national guidelines. However, only 7% of patients with Sz are treated with CLZ and the average treatment duration before CLZ was 9.7 years in Canada. That could be attributable to the lack of biomarker of TRS. Recently, studies using positron emission tomography (PET) have suggested that those who respond to first-line AP treatment (TnRS: treatment non-resistant Sz) showed increased DA synthesis and release in the striatum compared to those with TRS. However, PET is not widely available in clinical practice and limited because of its high costs and the short half-life of radioligands. On the other hand, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more accessible, less costly, and is able to examine the dopaminergic function by measuring neuromelanin (NM), which is a byproduct of the synthesis of monoamine neurotransmitters, including noradrenaline and dopamine. This technique has already been investigated in Parkinson's disease, but not for any psychiatric disorders such as Sz. This study will measure NM signals using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) in the substantia nigra, which contains the majority of dopamine neurons, and compare among patients with TRS (n=23), TnRS (n=23), and healthy control participants (n=23). We hypothesize that NM-MRI signals will be increased in TnRS in comparison with controls and TRS. Our approach will validate a broadly available biomarker to predict antipsychotic treatment response. NM-MRI scanning can then be included in the criteria of TRS.

column36: Understanding patterns of healthcare utilization of Canadian Armed Forces Veterans living with chronic pain and their experiences, values, and perceived needs related to chronic pain management: A mixed methods study.

column36: Helping the Helpers: Examining the Mental Health and Support Needs of Direct Service Providers Working with People Experiencing Homelessness
column37: The health of service providers plays an important role in providing high quality and effective health and social care. Symptoms, such as burnout, among service providers are linked to lower satisfaction and poorer health outcomes for service users. The health of service providers is especially important in the homelessness sector, where negative experiences can contribute to avoidance of services and extended periods of homelessness. The rates of common mental health problems, such as depression, anxiety, burnout, and trauma, and the support needs of people working in the homeless service sector are largely unknown. This study aims to better understand the mental health and support needs of this population and learn how organizations are or can be supporting the positive mental health of their staff. This study will recruit service providers in three community settings in Canada: emergency shelters, supportive housing, and harm reduction services. Data will be collected in two ways: (1) an online survey of 430 service providers and (2) interviews with 30 service providers and 15 organizational directors. Data will be used to explore two research questions: (1) What are the rates of common mental health problems and the needs of service providers that are not being met? and (2) What factors are associated with common mental health problems among service providers? It is predicted that mental health problems will be more common among service providers who have less social support (colleagues, friends, and family); a higher workload; less supervision; and more experiences with traumatic events, such as violence and overdoses. To ensure that the study findings are easy to access and to facilitate future research, they will be shared publicly. An educational toolkit will also be made available for service providers and organizations in the homeless service sector.

column36: Attacking glioblastoma multiforme with chimeric antigen receptor Natural Killer cells: a novel therapeutic approach
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes narrowing and loss of blood vessels in the lungs, leading to increased stress on the heart and death by heart failure. Treatments for PAH are expensive and provide little benefit to the patient in terms of symptoms and survival. For many years, PAH has been associated with dysfunction in the immune system. Recently we have discovered that Natural Killer (NK) immune cells are reduced in number and impaired in function in PAH. Normally, IL-15 is needed for NK cell function and survival, while TGFb alters NK cell function and blocks the effects of IL-15. However, we and others have found that IL-15 and TGFb signaling is altered in PAH patients and in animal models of PAH. In the pregnant uterus and cancerous tumors, NK cells change their function to help form blood vessels that allow the fetus or tumor to grow. We believe that something similar occurs in PAH lungs, and NK cells are "tricked" into making the diseased lungs worse. To test this hypothesis, we have bred mice with NK cells that either can or cannot produce the main receptor for TGFb, called TGFbRII. These mice will be exposed to low oxygen levels, which will cause symptoms of PAH in normal mice. We will then test our mice for lung and heart function, as well as measure number and function of NK cells. We would expect the mice with NK cells that cannot produce TGFbRII will not develop PAH when exposed to low oxygen, and will have normal heart, lung and NK cell function. Furthermore, we will test a new treatment made by HCW Biologics which both stimulates IL-15 signaling and blocks the actions of TGFb (known as HCW9218). We will induce PAH in rats using two different methods and then treat the rats with HCW9218. We expect HCW9218 treatment will cure the rats of their PAH symptoms. These studies will help to better understand how NK cells contribute to PAH and will further develop a new treatment based on this idea.

column36: Investigating the relationship between apathy and tau burden in patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a brain disorder in which patients have more memory and thinking problems than healthy people their age, often progresses to Alzheimer's disease (AD) where memory abilities and daily tasks are severely impaired. Apathy, characterized by a state of reduced interest, motivation and activity is one of the most common non-memory related symptoms of MCI and AD occurring in about 50%, and 80% of patients, respectively. Furthermore, 60% of MCI patients with apathy progress to AD. Medications which have been studied for the treatment of apathy have shown that only 30% of patients benefit. Understanding the underlying brain changes that occur in patients with apathy may help identify new treatments and delay progression to AD. Apathy has been associated with changes in the frontal cortex; regions at the front of the brain. In patients with memory difficulties, changes in the frontal cortex have been associated with a build-up of AD-related harmful proteins such as tau. Tau is considered a primary biomarker of AD, and is linked to cell death in the brain. However the relationship between apathy and tau is unclear. Fortunately, tau can be measured easily using positron emission tomography, an imaging test that uses a radioactive molecule to detect disease before it shows up on other imaging tests. Understanding the relationship between apathy and tau would help identify which patients can be targeted for early treatment that may delay or prevent progression to AD, and may also identify a new treatment to improve apathy and AD. Specifically, drugs that target tau may be of interest. Therefore, I propose to study differences in tau accumulation in the frontal cortex between cognitively impaired (MCI or AD) individuals with and without apathy, and whether other important characteristics such as size of brain region, presence of other behavioural symptoms, and severity of memory difficulties, affect the severity of tau accumulation.

column36: Optical Coherence Tomography in Patients with Basilar Artery Ischemic Stroke
column37: Strokes are one of the leading causes of death and disease in the world. They occur due to blockages of blood vessels in the brain. These blockages are similar to a bathtub drain being clogged with debris. In this analogy, the bathtub drain would be the blood vessel, and the debris would be the blood clot. For a long time doctors used a clot-buster medication to help patients having a stroke, which is like using a liquid drain cleaner to unclog a drain. More recently, researchers have found that removing the blood clot from within the blood vessel works better than using clot-buster medication, and doctors now use a tool similar to a plumbers snake to remove the blood clot. An important step is checking if the blood clot is removed after the procedure, and making sure the blood vessel is open. This is done by injecting dye into the blood stream and taking pictures. Our research team recently started using a new device called optical coherence tomography in stroke patients. This device is just like a good camera that can take pictures from inside the blood vessel. What we found was very interesting. In three patients there was left-over blood clot even though the pictures with dye showed that the blood clot was completely gone. It was very eye-opening that what we once thought about complete blood clot removal may not actually be true. Just like many new scientific findings, the application of a new technology is what made this possible. Although naturally we would think that this left-over blood clot causes new/worse strokes, we don't know this for sure. Therefore, we propose a study at our regional stroke center to characterize the findings using our new device in a larger group of patients. Our objectives are to make sure that using this device is practical, safe, and compare patients with left-over blood to those without left-over blood clot.

column36: A Participatory Design Approach to Develop and Optimize Aquatic Therapy Practice for Stroke Survivors
column37: Stroke is a life-altering event that can leave a person with a significant physical and cognitive disability that affects their ability to be independent in the community. A promising therapy to help people with stroke recover their health and function is aquatic therapy. Aquatic therapy is where people with stroke undergo physical rehabilitation in a pool with a qualified therapist to help them regain their strength, balance, and ability to move independently. Although there are several accessible therapy pools and aquatic therapy instructors across Ontario, it is unknown how much stroke survivors are accessing aquatic therapy to help with their recovery. To help people with stroke get a better understanding about aquatic therapy and to support their ability to access it in the community, I am proposing to work with stroke survivors and clinical staff to develop a web-based tool-kit that will provide important information about aquatic therapy. To achieve this goal, I will first interview people with stroke and clinical staff about their thoughts and understanding of aquatic therapy, what might prevent them from using it, and what supports they need to be able to access it in the community (PHASE I). Using the interview data from Phase I, I will then partner with stroke survivors and clinical staff to develop a list of strategies and resources to help people with stroke become more aware of aquatic therapy and how to better access and use it (PHASE II). Finally, I will work with people with stroke and clinicians to develop and pilot test a web-based tool-kit that will help people be able to access information about aquatic therapy in their community (PHASE III). As a result of this work, people with stroke will be able to learn about aquatic therapy and how to better access it so they can optimize their recovery process.

column36: Understanding the interplay between cytosine demethylation and genome integrity
column37: Genes carry the information that determines human inherited characteristics, or traits. These genes are made up of mainly 4 types of building blocks, or nucleotides. Their order is what determines the shape and characteristics of the proteins, which will carry out the biological process in the body. However, not only the type of proteins, but also how and when these are produced is relevant for body functions. How genes are regulated without changing the nucleotide sequence in the genes is known as epigenetics. Importantly, alterations in epigenetics can lead to diseases such as cancer, neurodegeneration or failures during development. For this, is essential to understand the mechanisms by which human cells carry out this process. One of the key steps in epigenetics is the chemical labelling of one of the 4 building blocks of genes, the nucleotide cytosine. A subtle modification known as methylation in the nucleotides along a gene can dramatically change its activity, and therefore, the production of a certain protein. However, while we precisely understand how this labells are generated, the mechanism that erase these marks is not well-defined. This is highly relevant, since devastating diseases such as many blood cancers, are characterized by common alterations in the labelling of cytosines by methylation. Thus, understanding this alterations will open the possibility for the development of better clinical therapies. Through this project, I will dissect the mechanisms for the removal of these epigenetic marks. Moreover, I will find which components are essential for the growth of cells with alterations in this epigenetic process. This will allow the development of therapies to kill tumoral cells with alterations in this pathway. In summary, this project will allow us to understand better how human cells carry out epigenetic changes, and will find novel therapeutic approaches for the treatment of blood cancer.

column36: Dissecting hippocampal-amygdala circuit dynamics to predict depression vulnerability
column37: Depression is a major health issue, but we lack long-term effective treatment. This is partly due to our limited understanding of the disease biology. column37: Disordered weight control behaviours (DWCBs), such as self-induced vomiting, unhealthy calorie restriction, and the use of non-prescribed diet pills, are common among young Canadians. Promising policies will be evaluated using a modelling approach that allows us to estimate the impacts on rates of DWCBs, eating disorders, and obesity on youth as they age. Overall, the results of these studies will provide information on existing policies that can be used to evaluate progress on DWCBs prevention and inform concrete recommendations to address gaps. column36: Towards Precision Medicine for Violence and Aggression: Neuroimaging Biomarkers and Targeted Treatments
column37: Human violence is a common phenomenon that takes a large toll on individual lives and, indeed, Canadian society overall. Although the majority of individuals with psychiatric illness are not violent, some mental disorders are associated with increased risk of aggression toward oneself and others. Persistent violence may relate to underlying brain abnormalities or changes in brain chemistry that require specific treatment. Hence, research that strives to understand the brain differences of people who engage in repeated aggression could lead to new treatment tools and violence prevention strategies. We previously found using state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques that a brain chemical called fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) is increased in the brains of people with borderline personality disorder (BPD). BPD is a prevalent psychiatric condition that presents high rates of harm toward the self and others. FAAH is part of a chemical pathway in the brain that has been associated with increased aggression. Therefore, agents that block FAAH may be candidates for treating violence in BPD and other conditions. Continuing with this line of research, the current proposal evaluates whether talk therapies can affect brain FAAH levels in BPD and thus influence anger, hostility, and aggression. In addition, we will also look at FAAH levels in other psychiatric disorders, such as depression, which shares some commonalities with BPD and may also have high brain FAAH levels. The knowledge generated by these studies could stimulate new treatments for persistent violence and ultimately lead to improved health outcomes for both perpetrators and victims of violence. This research has the potential to reduce the economic burden of violence on the health care system, as well as the corrections system.

column36: Understanding the Ghost Core Phenomenon: Analysis of CT Perfusion Ischemic Core Overestimation in Acute Stroke:
column37: In an acute ischemic stroke, occlusion of cerebral blood vessels prevents the critical flow of oxygen to the brain. Without rapid revascularization, the death of brain tissue subsequently occurs. Computed tomography perfusion (CTP) can be used to visualize this process in real-time. Ischemic core, defined as tissue that is no longer salvageable, can be visualized alongside ischemic penumbra, tissue at risk of death that may be saved with blood flow restoration. Over the past 5 years, clinical trials have utilized CTP to select patients with severe stroke to undergo rapid revascularization via mechanical clot retrieval. Patients with a small core and large penumbra have been found to benefit the most from these interventions while, in contrast, patients possessing a large ischemic core benefit less and are at an increased risk of life-threatening bleeding. Patients with a large ischemic core are therefore less likely to be offered therapy. There is a growing recognition that in some cases, CTP may actually overestimate ischemic core. This phenomenon, termed Ghost Ischemic Core (GIC), carries the risk of precluding patients from undergoing necessary clot retrieval. Why GIC occurs in some patients, but not in others, is unclear. We aim to explore this particular question by analyzing the prevalence, topography, and natural history of GIC in relation to baseline clinical presentation, interventions utilized, and overall outcomes. In doing so, we hope to identify patients and/or clinical scenarios where ischemic core may be at risk of overestimation and shed further light into why this issue occurs in the first place. With the use of CTP becoming mainstream worldwide, the findings of this study will have the potential to launch new initiatives to improve ischemic core estimation and provide practical information for clinicians assessing patients at the bedside.

column36: Integrating Personalized Brain Simulation, Machine Learning, and Multimodal Neuroimaging for Early Detection of Alzheimer's Disease: A New Data-Driven Methodological Framework
column37: Maintaining a healthy brain through one's lifespan depends on the complex interaction between the brain, genetics, and lifestyle. With a rapidly aging population, the prevalence of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's Disease are significantly increasing, with a projected 107 million cases by 2050. This is now recognized as one of the major medical challenges facing the world in the 21st century. While treatment options are limited, early detection can allow prevention strategies to provide individuals with additional years of healthy living, significantly less burden on their loved ones, and a substantial reduction in healthcare costs. Current early detection methods mainly limited to inherited types of early-onset Alzheimer's Disease. Our goal is to greatly improve early detection of all types of Alzheimer's Disease. This project will, for the first time, integrate personalized brain simulation and the predictive power of artificial intelligence to improve our understanding of Alzheimer's Disease, to predict as early as possible who will develop the disease, and even to forecast what form it will take for each individual. Breakthroughs in personalized brain simulation, a type of mathematical brain modelling that is tuned to each individual, have already been used to show how and why the brain changes when inflicted with Alzheimer's Disease. We will use high-quality clinical databases that follow the development of thousands of individuals through the aging process in research that can lead to new clinical detection methods. We will use brain simulation to model the effects of Alzheimer's other dementias compared to healthy aging on each person's brain, and we will use artificial intelligence to discover changes in the brain that predict a diagnosis of Alzheimer's in later years. With this new data-driven approach, we aim to help add years of high quality of life for the millions of people who may be affected by Alzheimer's in the future, and their families.

column36: Precarious work and gender disparities in mental health
column37: Precarious work refers to working arrangements that include unfavourable conditions such as low wages, low job security, poor physical working conditions, low control, uncertain scheduling, and few benefits. Studies show that exposure to precarious work increases the risk of mental health problems including depression and suicidality. Because women make up a higher percentage of those in precarious work than men in both Canada and the US, the growth of precarious work in these countries has great implications for gender disparities in mental health. Few studies have linked the growth of precarious work and its associated gender-inequalities in mental health to the labour market and social policies that shape both how people work and its health effects. Evidence on the gendered experiences of precarious work and mental health for populations who face multiple adversities, such as poverty and substance use disorders, and who are commonly socioeconomically marginalized, is especially lacking. This research program has two aims: (1) compare the extent that precarious work contributes to gender-based inequalities in mental health in Canada and the US between 2000 and 2018, and (2) examine this relationship from the lived experiences of individuals who are socioeconomically marginalized. Aim 1 will be examined with comparable samples from the US Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the Canadian Community Health Survey. Aim 2 leverages survey and in-depth interview data from three ethno-epidemiological studies of socioeconomically marginalized individuals in Vancouver. Using quantitative, qualitative, and cross-national analyses, this research produces evidence on the gendered distribution of precarious work and its effect on mental health; the modifiable aspects of gender-based inequalities that can be linked to the policies shaping precarious work; and, the mechanisms driving gendered experiences of precarious work and mental health for marginalized individuals.

column36: Antimicrobial use and foodborne infections in humans from British Columbia: a multimodal approach to assessing associations and impacts.
column37: Each year, >4 million Canadians develop an illness from the food they eat. Commonly, people are given antibiotics to treat their illness. Sometimes the antibiotics are the appropriate treatment and sometimes they are used inappropriately. However, the impacts of taking antibiotics before and after the illness are not well understood. In order to investigate the link between antibiotic use and illnesses from food, my project has five AIMS: 1. Describe the relationship between antibiotic use and illness from food as you move through the stages of the illness; 2. Determine the chance of developing an illness from food after antibiotic use; 3. Determine whether the chance of developing long-term consequences (eg. reactive arthritis) following an illness from food is related to using antibiotics after illness (both appropriate and inappropriate use); 4. Determine whether the healthcare costs and chance of dying are related to using antibiotics after illness (both appropriate and inappropriate use); and 5. Identify specific ways antibiotics are used inappropriately to help inform future antibiotic use guidelines. For the entire ~4M population of British Columbia, for 2005-2014, I will look at information on all antibiotic prescriptions, healthcare costs, infections from food, long-term consequences, and other pertinent factors (eg. age, sex). I will conduct a review of the existing published literature and describe the types and amount of antibiotics used both before and after illness from food. I will test hypotheses to assess the relationships between antibiotic use, and developing illness, developing long-term consequences, healthcare costs and chance of dying. This novel assessment of existing health data from BC will advance our understanding of the link between antibiotic use and illness from food. The results of this project will inform and improve antibiotic prescribing guidelines in Canada and therefore will have a significant impact on the health of Canadians.

column36: Eye movements as a sensitive indicator of motion perception in healthy older adults and patients with ophthalmic diseases
column37: As our population ages, an increasing number of Canadians experience difficulties with their vision. Although it is well known that both normal aging and age-related eye disease can affect a person's ability to see fine detail (such as in reading), tests of visual acuity used in regular eye examinations do not provide a complete picture of a person's ability to see in everyday situations, such as exercising and driving, where moving objects are often involved. Our research will gather the scientific evidence that is needed to determine if this test is accurate, and whether it is practical to introduce it into clinical practice. This quick and non-verbal method of assessing vision provides a potentially cost-effective vision assessment strategy that addresses an important population health issue.
