column36: A pilot study for brain delivery of recombinant glucocerebrosidase in people with Parkinson's disease using MR-guided focused ultrasound induced opening of the blood-brain barrier
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 1-2 per 1000 people. There's a need for disease-modifying therapy in PD, but many potentially effective therapeutics are limited from the brain by the blood-brain barrier. Glucocerebrosidase is an enzyme that is the standard of care for Gaucher's disease, which recently has been shown to have shared pathophysiological features with PD. Animal studies suggest replacing brain levels of glucocerebrosidase can be restorative and improve motor symptoms in PD. However, glucocerebrosidase does not cross the blood-brain barrier into the brain. An emerging way to deliver drugs past the blood-brain barrier is by creating a temporary opening using MR-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS). MRgFUS effectively enhances the delivery of large molecules without open surgery such as previously through direct intracranial injection. Also, MRgFUS can explicitly target the blood-brain barrier of brain regions afflicted by PD pathologies. Sunnybrook Research Institute has the world's most extensive clinical experience in MRgFUS induced opening of the blood-brain barrier. Leveraging this experience, we are taking the first-in-human step to investigate the brain delivery of recombinant glucocerebrosidase using MRgFUS in six patients with PD. The primary outcome, safety, will be described by adverse events. The feasibility of blood-brain barrier disruption will be measured by MRI with contrast, and drug delivery by cerebrospinal fluid analysis, metabolic imaging, and clinical scores. Results of this pilot study will be vital in evaluating the safety and potential of MRgFUS drug delivery platform for recombinant glucocerebrosidase. This trial will open doors for future studies in PD, neuronopathic GD, and other alpha-synucleinopathies in urgent need of disease-modifying therapy.

column36: Cardiovascular stress testing in pregnancy and the prediction of preeclampsia
column37: Pregnancy is a unique period in which a woman's heart and blood vessels, also known as her cardiovascular system, change dramatically to allow her baby to grow. However, some women have unhealthy changes that lead to high blood pressure during pregnancy. This is a serious illness for mom, but it also increases the risk of giving birth early to a small baby. This means that later in life, both mom and baby are more likely to develop cardiovascular diseases. Blood pressure is controlled by the fight or flight part of the nervous system, known as the sympathetic system. We know that in healthy pregnant women, the sympathetic system is more active compared to non-pregnant women, but in pregnant women with high blood pressure, this is even greater. The causes of very high sympathetic activity are not well understood, but this could be identified before a pregnant woman actually develops a serious illness during pregnancy. Short-term stress tests are used in other non-pregnant groups to predict the development of high blood pressure. Short-term stress from placing a hand in cold water or maintaining a constant handgrip increase the demand placed on the heart and blood vessels. How well a mom adapts to this higher demand may allow us to predict the development of high blood pressure during pregnancy. Understanding how stress tests can be used to predict the development of high blood pressure during pregnancy is the aim of this research. We are recruiting ninety pregnant women (between 16-20 weeks of pregnancy) to complete a 2-hour study visit. Measurements of blood pressure and sympathetic system activity are completed at rest and during these short-term stress tests. The outcome of this research is to develop simple tools that can identify women at risk of high blood pressure during pregnancy. Early prediction of this complication could improve the diagnosis, treatment and outcomes for both mom and baby.

column37: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) catabolizes the breakdown of triglycerides in blood. We have previously developed a gene therapy treatment for the LPL deficiency and phase I-III clinical trials have demonstrated its long-term safety and effectiveness. column36: Childhood disruptive behavioural profiles - improving economic participation through early screening and prevention
column37: Childhood disruptive behaviours - including aggression, opposition, inattention and hyperactivity - underpin the most prevalent and costly psychiatric disorders in youth. They are associated with increased risk of unemployment, low earnings, welfare receipt and poor mental and physical health outcomes. Given the large costs of disruptive behaviors for individuals and society, it is important to identify children who are at risk as early as possible so that they can be monitored and supported. So far, few studies have identified high-risk behavioral profiles in the general population and examined the impact of these profiles on future economic outcomes. Furthermore, it is unclear what precise mechanisms explain the association between risk profiles in childhood and poor economic outcomes in adulthood (e.g. adolescent delinquency, education underachievement) or what factors in childhood protect against these harmful effects (e.g. consequential parenting, good peer relations). This study will use teacher-rated behavioural assessments from age 6-12 years drawn from the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Kindergarten Children (n=3017) and government tax return records from age 18 to 35 years obtained from Statistics Canada, to address four questions: (1) What are the risk profiles at age 6 years that are associated with poor economic outcomes? (2) What is the structure and stability of these risk profiles from age 6-12 years and are they associated with risk profiles at age 6 and with economic outcomes? (3) What social and psychological factors explain the association between risk behavioural profiles at age 6 and poor economic outcomes? (4) What factors protect against the harmful effects of risk profiles at age 6 and poor economic outcomes? Findings will inform the development of prevention programs and policy initiatives designed to reduce the harmful effects of disruptive behaviours on long-term economic and social participation.

column36: Engineering the design of regulatory T cell therapy in transplantation
column37: Solid organ transplantation (SOT) is a curative option for end stage organ failure; however, the success of this procedure depends on life-long use of immunosuppressive drugs which put patients at risk for infections and cancer. Regulatory T cells (Treg) are immune cells that favour the acceptance of the transplanted organ by the recipient's immune system. One way to increase the numbers of organ-protective Tregs is to isolate them, expand them in the lab, and then re-infuse them into patients. A limitation, however, is that it is difficult to isolate Tregs that are specifically able to suppress immune responses to a transplant. Recently, we developed a revolutionary way to overcome this limitation using a genetic engineering strategy in which organ-specific Tregs can be made by introducing a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This project aims to optimize the function of CAR-Tregs by studying how to best design the CAR and to find ways to reduce risks associated with this strategy. My first goal will be to modify the CAR structure trying to find ways so mimic how Tregs would be naturally activated so their function and lifespan are optimal. I will also aim to reduce the risk of using CAR-Treg therapies. We have recently identified that CAR-Tregs which do not express a protein called Helios are prone to lose their ability to favour organ acceptance. We thus aim to engineer CARs in a way that they would only be expressed in Tregs which continue to express Helios. I will carry out these aims using experimental systems that are well-established. Significance: by optimizing CAR structure I will improve the function and lifespan of CAR-Tregs and also reduce their associated risks. The results generated in this study will inform the design of future clinical studies and will also help to facilitate the use of CAR-Treg-based therapies as a new therapeutic tool to diminish transplant rejection.

column37: Children born very preterm are at high risk for behavior problems including inattention and social difficulties, placing enormous burdens on family, school and community. column36: Improving the utility of polygenic scores to predict and understand disease risk: a foundational resource.
column37: Many diseases are preventable by early detection and/or intervention if we knew who is most at risk. For diseases like coronary artery disease (CAD), risk predictions are made based on age and sex in combination with known risk factors (e.g. family history, cholesterol levels, body mass index, smoking habits). However, there is also a strong genetic component to the likelihood you will develop CAD (~50% of total). My research focuses on Polygenic Risk Scores (PGS), a method that can be used to predict genetic predisposition for a disease by aggregating the effects of variants across an individual's genome. Studies have shown that currently used risk prediction methods for multiple diseases can be improved by including PGS. Despite the benefits of PGS, there is both a lack of standardization and an incomplete understanding of their predictive ability (especially in people of non-European ancestry). This hinders PGS' adoption in clinical practice. To fill these gaps in our understanding, I am creating the PGS Catalog: a foundational resource to distribute the information necessary to apply and understand PGS for a wide range of diseases and traits. I will also perform a systematic comparison of PGS to measure PGS predictive ability and identify the best PGS for each trait (where multiple exist). Through this research I will identify any deficits in generalizability across ancestries and between sexes that need to be corrected. Finally, I will use the PGS to measure their ability to predict disease risk in rare disease patients, measuring how PGS combine with rare mutations. Together my research aims to establish the PGS Catalog as a foundational resource to advance our understanding of disease risk prediction using genetics, while also enabling new research and clinical uses of PGS.

column36: Exploring the actions of autoantibodies in fibromyalgia
column37: Fibromyalgia is characterized by widespread pain and tenderness. Between 1.5 and 10% of the population suffer from fibromyalgia, but despite this high prevalence no diagnostic tests exist and current therapies have limited effect. We know very little about the causes of fibromyalgia, which is partly why fibromyalgia is diagnosed with a list of criteria, rather than tests, and why current treatment strategies are so limited. We recently discovered that injecting antibodies from fibromyalgia patients into mice causes pain-like behaviour and increased activity of pain sensing neurons. These results suggest that some fibromyalgia patients' immune systems produce autoantibodies that attack their own bodies. Therefore, autoimmunity could underlie fibromyalgia in a subset of patients. Our findings have the potential to change how fibromyalgia is viewed and how it is treated. In this project we will build on our findings to better understand how fibromyalgia autoantibodies cause pain. First, we will search for the protein(s) fibromyalgia antibodies recognize. Identifying which proteins antibodies bind to will provide information about how they could drive pain. Additionally, these results can open the door to the creation of diagnostic tests based on the presence of specific antibodies, similar to the tests used in rheumatoid arthritis, rather than on a certain number of symptoms. Second, we will investigate how fibromyalgia antibodies increase the activity of pain sensing neurons. We have already found that fibromyalgia antibodies bind cells called satellite glial cells, which surround the cell bodies of pain sensing neurons. We will examine how fibromyalgia antibodies alter the activity of satellite cells, and how they then alter pain sensing neuron activity. Our expected results will provide the basis to develop diagnostic tests based on autoantibody presence and provide the rationale for using antibody targeting therapies to manage fibromyalgia.

column36: Understanding Pathways to Mental Health Care During and After the Psychotic Prodrome: A mixed methods study
column37: BACKGROUND: Multicomponent early intervention services have undoubtedly improved care for adolescents and young adults experiencing a first threshold-level episode of psychosis (FEP). However, access to such care remains challenging for many-especially since distress, symptoms and impairment begin long before the FEP, during a psychotic 'prodrome' consisting of non-specific and sub-threshold symptoms. Access can be operationalized by measuring 'pathways to care' (PTC) in the form of (a) treatment delays following onset of symptoms, and (b) subsequent attempts at help-seeking. PTC are well known in FEP, yet unstudied in the prodrome-even though most patients appear to seek help for mental health reasons prior to their FEP. METHODS/OBJECTIVES: Through mixed (qualitative and quantitative) methods, we will undertake the first direct examination of PTC during the psychotic prodrome in a well-established, catchment-based service for FEP based in Montreal, Quebec. We will utilize the Circumstances of Onset and Relapse Schedule in 148 consecutive patients, along with a series of smaller focus groups to better understand: 1) Treatment delays and help-seeking during the prodrome versus the FEP 2) When and why individuals, their families, and others delay decisions to seek help during the prodrome; 3) By whom, how, when and why help is eventually sought during the prodrome; 4) Reasons for and experiences of treatment delays and help-seeking before (versus after) the age of 18. SIGNIFICANCE: This study will be the first to fill the important knowledge gap of PTC during the psychotic prodrome; its KT strategy is designed to obtain multi-stakeholder input on how our findings are relevant to future research and service delivery. Finally, applying a mixed-methods lens to PTC during the prodrome permits us to identify which actors or agencies should be targeted in the next phase of our research: future early identification campaigns aimed at reducing treatment delays or simplifying help-seeking.

column36: Uncovering the synaptic and cellular basis of the persistence of long-term memory.
column37: Long-term memories can be highly unstable like in Alzheimer's disease patients or highly stable like in those suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, the development of clinical therapies for these and other debilitating memory disorders has failed because of a lack of a fundamental understanding of how memory persists. How does a memory change with time in the brain? Recently developed methods that can visualize those cells that store a memory, termed engram cells, have shown that engram cells in one brain region critical to memory storage, the hippocampus, are silenced over two weeks after mice acquired a memory whereas those in another brain region, the cortex, are unsilenced. Additionally, recalling memories at these remote time points is known to make the memory transiently labile by reinstating a hippocampal engram. Interventions that block the reconsolidation of this labile memory could erase memory in rodents but failed in human clinical trials. A significant and compelling amount of evidence has been gathered over many decades that the strength of electric signal transmission between brain cells across 'synapses' is adjustable and underlies learning and forgetting. Engram cells might be silenced because a) a fewer number or weakened synaptic connections from pre-synaptic engram cells fail to activate post-synaptic engram cells, or b) the engram cells are being inhibited by other nearby cells, or c) the responsiveness of the engram cells to inputs has decreased. The unsilencing of engram cells could be explained by these effects in the opposite direction. column36: Emerging roles of enteric glial cells in homeostasis and disease
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is an umbrella under which live a number of chronic inflammation disorders in the small or large intestine that induce symptoms like pain, weight loss and diarrhea. All of these make everyday life for patients difficult. Canada has one of the highest IBD incidence rates in the world (1/140 Canadians) and an alarmingly increasing prevalence, especially in infants and children. The intestine is the most highly regenerative organ in the human body as it undergoes constant wear and tear while breaking down food, absorbing nutrients, and eliminating waste. This repair is maintained by resident intestinal stem cells that generate all the different cells type of the gut. To function properly, stem cells need to receive appropriate signals from their environment. If those signals are altered, it can lead to disease, including IBD. My research focuses on glial cells, one of the most abundant cell types of the intestine. Glial cells are located in close physical proximity to stem cells, but their potential interactions are currently unknown. I investigate how glial cells can modulate stem cell behavior under normal conditions, during repair (after injury), and in chronic inflammation. Compiling analysis from a model of IBD created in mice, and from human glial cells from healthy and IBD patients, will reveal the role of glial cells in IBD and inform new targets for drug development and treatment. Improving stem cell response, through glial cells, in the early stage of the disease could enhance intestinal healing and thus prevent and/or alleviate the inflammation, especially in children, reducing or eliminating the human and healthcare costs of IBD in Canada and the world.

column36: Cognitive remediation for social cognitive deficits in schizophrenia: efficacy of the program RC2S and determinants of treatment outcomes
column37: Social cognitive deficits are one of the best predictors of functioning difficulties in schizophrenia. Social cognition refers to the mental processes underlying social interactions. Cognitive remediation therapy (CR) is a behavioural intervention that has shown its efficacy to improve social cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. Despite its efficacy, every patient does not benefit equally from CR, depending on individual characteristics. However, no study to date has systematically examined the role of these individual characteristics in CR efficacy for social cognition. Further, very few CR program targeting social cognition have used a personalized approach to tailor the treatment to individual difficulties. RC2S is an integrative and personalized CR program that targets several social cognitive functions and that uses virtual reality to emulate social interactions. However, no study has yet assessed its efficacy. The objectives of this project are to assess the efficacy of RC2S in terms of cognition, functioning and clinical symptoms in schizophrenia and to identify the personal characteristics that promote treatment outcomes. A total of 50 participants with schizophrenia aged between 18 and 65 years old, with a social cognitive deficit will be recruited. They will undergo an initial assessment of cognition, functioning and clinical symptoms and they will be randomized to the treatment group or to the waiting list. Participants in the treatment group will begin RC2S for 7 weeks. Participants in the waiting list will receive their treatment as usual during 7 weeks, will be reassessed and will then begin RC2S. Initial assessments will be repeated at post-test and 3-months post-test. This project will provide the first data regarding the efficacy of RC2S and the first assessment of individual characteristics that promote treatment outcomes in CR for social cognition. Ultimately, these results could help tailor CR and provide cost-effective interventions.

column37: Children born at a very low birth weight (VLBW; <1500g) are at high risk of early-onset obesity and cardiometabolic diseases. Causes are unknown, though poor nutrition is a likely contributor. Advances have been made to improve the nutritional status of VLBW infants in hospital, but we know very little about their diets post-discharge. Preliminary findings from our group suggest that poor diet quality at age 5 is associated with higher % fat mass among a cohort of children born VLBW. Eating habits are established early and track into adulthood; poor nutrition during childhood may exacerbate the consequences of VLBW. Research in term-born children has shown that food parenting practices (e.g., modelling and pressure to eat) influence children's dietary intake and weight status. Among those born VLBW, high rates of feeding problems and neurocognitive impairment may challenge the positive interactions necessary to develop healthy eating habits. Less desirable food parenting practices may also unintentionally contribute to or maintain problematic eating behaviours (e.g., using food as a reward). However, the feeding practices used by parents of VLBW children are unknown, and NICU follow-up is generally medical with little anticipatory guidance or support around feeding. This study will address these gaps by examining the association between directly observed food parenting practices and body composition and dietary intake among children born at a VLBW at 5 years of age in comparison to children born at term. Results will help to mitigate the consequences of preterm birth by helping to create anticipatory guidance and interventions to optimize nutrition throughout the early years.

column37: Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (cALL) is the most frequent pediatric cancer. column37: Recently, Dr. Richard Wilson's lab showed that small internal sensors in the neck - the carotid bodies - drive asthmatic attacks by activating the autonomic nervous system. His lab also found that the carotid bodies play an important role in lung inflammation. These observations suggest that the carotid body's influence over the autonomic nervous system may be a driving factor in common, costly and devastating allergy-associated inflammatory diseases such as asthma and irritable bowel syndrome. We know that the carotid body can active both the sympathetic and parasympathetic subdivisions of the autonomic nervous system. Since both of these systems can influence localized inflammation in select organs, they may therefore be crucial in initiating localized allergic responses. My current research has shown, in humans, that the autonomic nervous system can be controlled selectively to different targets throughout the body, a phenomenon known as differential control. Differential control has been shown to be drastically altered in many disease states, but how this mode of control is achieved, even in the healthy state, is unclear and whether it drives allergic disease is unknown. We suspect that the carotid body will have a strong involvement over differential control of the autonomic nervous system in the healthy state and will be responsible for the manifestation of organ-specific allergic responses and inflammation in asthma (lung) and irritable bowel syndrome (gut). We will also investigate whether we can halt the development of allergic disease by manipulating the activity of the autonomic neural pathways. We suspect these findings to be very translatable to other inflammatory disease states, such as hypertension, and will spark a new school-of-thought in how we treat allergy and chronic inflammatory conditions; that being through direct manipulation of dysfunctional neural circuits within the brain.

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a disease characterized by shortness of breath, cough and sputum production. COPD worsens over time leading to debilitating complications and frequent hospitalizations. In Canada, COPD affects over 2 million Canadians -the number is expected to rise in the coming years. In under a decade, the number of Canadians diagnosed with COPD increased by 82%, now affecting 1 / 116 Canadians. COPD is the 3rd leading cause of death in the United States, causing 120,000 deaths yearly. COPD is characterized by frequent exacerbations with life-threatening breathing problems requiring management in the emergency department (ED) or intensive care unit (ICU). Another non-invasive device provides a heated and humidified high flow of gas with controlled oxygen fraction through nasal cannula, avoiding the need for face mask. This promising alternative has not been tested yet in this situation. We recently showed that this technique has advantages compared to non-invasive ventilation in patients with cystic fibrosis which leads to similar problems with breathing. The aim of our program is 1) to assess the potential benefits of this technique compared to non-invasive ventilation, and 2) understand the mechanisms of action in order to adapt therapy to the degree of severity. We will compare the physiologic effects and tolerance of high-flow nasal oxygen and non-invasive ventilation in patients with COPD exacerbation admitted to the ED or ICU If high-flow nasal oxygen is at least as effective as non-invasive ventilation, this could be a major advance in the treatment of COPD, potentially reducing health-care resource burden, hospital admissions and optimizing symptom control for patients. column37: Epilepsy is a nervous system disorder that causes seizures from abnormal brain activity. It is a disease that affects nearly 1% of the population worldwide. While Retigabine is the most recognized drug in this category, several existing and emerging potassium channel targeting drugs, each with very different mechanisms of action, remain to be investigated or completely understood. column37: Rates of Type 2 Diabetes and cardiovascular disease are rapidly increasing in Canada. These conditions often occur together and evidence suggests that they should also be treated together. Together, these results will provide extremely important evidence on the development of Type 2 Diabetes and CVD and new therapeutic ways of predicting, preventing, and treating these conditions.

column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), that is commonly classified into Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease is the condition of inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. The incidence of the disease has shown a dramatic increase in the last decades in Canada and worldwide. Despite significant progress in developing improved therapies for IBD, many side effects with existing therapies indicate the need for the development of better therapeutic strategies. The Adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) consist of catalytic alpha-subunit and the regulatory beta-and gamma-subunits and is a key regulator of cellular and organismal metabolism, however, the importance of AMPK in the pathogenesis of IBD is not fully understood. In our lab, we have investigated the important role of AMPK in the pathogenesis of intestinal inflammation. Our data suggest that reductions in AMPK activity mediated through genetic deletion of AMPK beta1 in macrophages up-regulates the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and aggravates dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. We will further investigate the mechanism in the cellular level and investigate whether sodium salicylate, commonly used as anti-inflammatory and analgesic and recently an activator of AMPK targeting AMPK beta1, is effective in the amelioration of DSS-induced colitis in mice. The proposed study will prove to be very important in the development of safer and inexpensive therapy in the treatment and management of the condition of intestinal inflammation such as Inflammatory Bowel Disease which will benefit many Canadians and ultimately nations economy.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Recent statistics tell us that 90 percent of Canadians aged 65 and over live with at least one chronic condition including heart disease, respiratory conditions, diabetes, or arthritis. While the cause of chronic disease is complex and multifactorial, age-related changes to the immune system are a major contributor. Stem cells in the bone marrow give rise to two different lineages of immune cells: myeloid and lymphoid immune cells. As people age, these stem cells may acquire genetic mutations that skew the differentiation of immune cells towards the myeloid lineage at the expense of lymphoid cells. In addition to this "myeloid-skewing", the immune cells are often immature and have reduced function. Accumulating evidence suggests that this predisposes older adults to developing health complications, but the genetic changes that occur in the stem cells and the molecular events that underlie these changes remain unclear. The aim of my postdoctoral fellows is to determine the link between myeloid genetic mutations, myeloid-skewing, and immune impairment with age. We hypothesize that mutations in a specific gene called TET2 results in myeloid impairment. This is thought to be driven by the aging bone marrow environment, which has increased inflammatory mediators. To approach this, I will integrate my prior experience in machine learning with a custom next-generation sequencing platform to identify genetic biomarkers in blood of elderly patients. Concurrently, I will use transplantation studies in Tet2 knockout mice to determine if inflammatory mediators in the aging bone marrow results in myeloid-skewing and impairment. These experiments will determine whether modifying inflammatory mediators in the bone marrow is a viable option for reducing myeloid skewing, which we can pursue in subsequent experiments by administering inflammatory blockers. Ultimately, we believe the results of this research will provide avenues for new therapeutic interventions.

column36: Partnering with speech-language pathologists to improve interventions for children with language disorders
column37: Children with language disorders struggle to learn, make friends, and join activities in their neighbourhood and community. Speech-language pathologists provide treatments to help children develop language. For families of these children, the most important and meaningful treatment is one that targets all aspects of their child's life. In other words, families hope that treatments from speech-language pathologists not only improve the ways that children speak or understand certain words, but also improve how they join classroom activities and play with friends. The goal of this project is to improve preschool speech-language treatments. To do so, we will work with speech-language pathologists in the publicly-funded programs in Ontario. First, we will use award-winning tools to help speech-language pathologists design treatments to target all relevant aspects of children's lives. We will then check if these tools actually changed treatments. We will also ask speech-language pathologists and families to give feedback on how we can improve these tools. Aside from improving preschool speech-language treatments, this project will impact all Canadians. Learning from speech-language pathologists, we can improve the tools we have for designing treatments for children with other disabilities. For example, these tools can then be used to improve education and healthcare for children with all disabilities (e.g. to improve physiotherapy for children with cerebral palsy or classroom support for children with hearing loss). Families of children with disabilities can use these tools to advocate for better services for their child. Canadians can use these tools to understand the different ways they can help and engage children with disabilities.

column36: The role of NAD synthetase 1 in VACTERL syndrome
column37: VACTERL syndrome is a set of birth defects that affects multiple areas of the body, including the heart, limbs, kidneys, trachea/esophagus, and spinal cord. If a patient has any three of these defects, they can be diagnosed as having VACTERL syndrome. This syndrome occurs in 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 40,000 newborns. Treatment is specific to the type of symptoms but may include surgery along with long-term management. The exact cause of VACTERL association has yet to be identified, although in some people it appears to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors. At the Children's Hospital of Western Ontario, genetic testing of 2 patients diagnosed with VACTERL association and their parents identified a mutation in a gene called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) synthetase 1. NAD is an important molecule found in all living cells which regulates multiple different biological processes, such as metabolism, aging, and DNA repair. Past studies have shown that other defects in the NAD synthesis pathway have also resulted in VACTERL syndrome patients. My project will aim to understand the role of NAD synthetase 1 in early development and why defective activity of this enzyme results in a specific subset of developmental defects called VACTERL syndrome. I will be using stem cells with the same mutation in NAD synthetase 1 as was identified in the 2 patients in hopes of understanding what type of cell lineages are affected by this mutation and why. This work will be part of an international collaboration with Dr. Sally Dunwoodie at the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Sydney, Australia, who is developing mouse models to further understand the molecular basis of this association. Overall, our research will contribute to the identification and understanding of the genetic variants that may be associated with VACTERL syndrome in hopes of developing better treatment options and improving family counselling.

column36: Towards breaking the cycle of intimate partner violence in Canada: Technology-based healthcare screening and interventions for women
column37: Up to half of Canadian women experience sexual, physical, and/or psychological violence from their partners, referred to as intimate partner violence (IPV). IPV is a leading cause of death and impairment, and is estimated to cost Canadians >$6 billion each year. Most women do not disclose about IPV and have limited access to support. However, women affected by IPV visit their healthcare providers (HCPs) more often than other women. Therefore, HCPs are in a position to routinely screen for IPV. Routine screening for IPV is considered to be beneficial by patients and HCPs, and improve detection of IPV. My study tests the feasibility of implementing a technology-based IPV screening tool in different clinics across a large multidisciplinary hospital. I will also examine if screening is associated with increased rates of help-seeking behaviour and improved health for women experiencing IPV. Clinics are randomly assigned to use the screening tool or provide usual care. In clinics assigned to screening, HCPs provide women who screen positive for IPV with a "warm handoff" to a national IPV hotline for counselling. Each woman in each condition is called 3 months after their visit to assess help-seeking behaviours (how many times they contacted the hotline or other resources) and mental health symptoms. I hypothesize that the tool will be widely accepted by HCPs and non-burdensome (e.g., not add significant time to visits). I also hypothesize that screening will be significantly associated with improved help-seeking behaviours and mental and physical health outcomes for women who screen positive for IPV in the screening condition compared to women in usual care who endorse IPV. If found to be feasible and effective, my goal is to implement and test this tool across Canadian healthcare clinics, where no such IPV screening systems currently exists. Ultimately, my project will contribute to improving the health of women affected by IPV, a costly and deadly phenomenon in Canada.

column36: Investigating the role and impact of obesity and measures of adiposity on cognitive function
column37: Obesity is one of the most important unmet prevention and treatment health challenges. The high prevalence of overweight and obesity, which has more than tripled since the 1970s, is of serious public health concern since overweight and obesity are often concomitant with adverse complications, including diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Cognitive impairment and depression are also suggested to be associated with obesity and increased measures of adiposity. Given 50 million people worldwide are diagnosed with dementia and more than 300 million people of all ages suffer from depression, it is important to determine and address possible modifiable risk factors if we are ever to alleviate the overall global burden of these diseases. While obesity has been connected to cognitive health the evidence is still uncertain. Dietary factors have long been implicated in non-communicable disease risk. Consumption of specific dietary patterns may lead to decreases in adiposity and hence improve cognitive function and reduce the risk of neurodegenerative diseases. In order to address these concerns a comprehensive research program is proposed which conducts a series of studies investigating the relationship between obesity and changes to body weight with indicators of cognitive function as well as risk of dementia and depression. This will be done using data from the PREDIMED-Plus trial, one of the biggest milestone trials in nutrition research in Europe. Following this investigation a synthesis and comparison of dietary patterns in relation to body weight and risk of obesity will be conducted to determine potential strategies to reduce obesity, as well as potentially improve cognitive function. This research, specifically determining lifestyle related strategies, such as following a dietary pattern, has the potential to have significant local and global impact on health and our health care system.

column36: CRISPR-Cas9 genome-wide pooled screen for the identification of unknown glucocerebrosidase modulators
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, yet remarkably, no therapy exists that can slow the disease. The increasing incidence of PD makes improving our knowledge of the mechanisms and factors leading to PD of importance. Mutations in the gene GBA, which encodes the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase), are the greatest genetic risk factor for PD. In addition, it has been shown that augmenting GCase activity in mouse models can reduce disease progression of PD. Therefore, great efforts are made to identify enhancers of GCase activity. The link between GCase and PD however, remains poorly understood. We propose here the use of a novel chemical genetic screening approach to identify new genes that affect GCase activity. We will use a genome-wide pooled screen in order to evaluate the effect of each single gene on the activity of GCase. The readout will be achieved with our new GCase imaging substrates, that allow the measurement of GCase activity directly in living cells and fluorescence-assisted flow cytometry. The resulting hits, meaning genes having a significant effect on GCase activity, will be validated through downstream experiments and assessed in neuronal models in order to understand how they regulate GCase activity. We expect this project to have major outcomes. First, direct monitoring of enzyme activity in living cells has, to our knowledge, never been applied to genome-wide screening. This chemical biology approach would therefore be pioneering. Second, these findings could pinpoint upstream regulators of GCase activity, illuminating the molecular processes that lead to PD and opening new research directions. Third, as augmentation of GCase activity in PD patients is being pursued as a disease-modifying approach, the discovery of GCase regulators could lead to new targets that could be exploited to create small molecule or gene therapies for PD.

column36: The role of ketones in heart failure
column37: Although advancements in therapies to treat cardiovascular disease have reduced the number of deaths of cardiac patients, these treatments have ultimately increased the number of people who eventually go on to develop another clinical condition called heart failure. Simply stated, heart failure is a condition that is defined by poor heart function that prevents the heart from pumping enough blood to the rest of the body. For decades, it has been established that one of the contributing factors of the failing hearts poor performance is the heart's inability to generate enough energy to beat properly. Recent studies have shown that a major fuel for the heart is ketones. Ketones are molecules that are produced by the liver from fats and can be used in the heart to produce energy. Of importance, recent work has suggested that the failing heart increases the amount of ketones used to produce energy in what is thought to be an attempt to increase energy production. However, whether or not this increase in ketone use by the heart is beneficial or detrimental to the failing heart is still unknown. Using two mouse models of heart failure, we will investigate the role of ketones in heart failure and determine if they are good or bad for the heart. We hypothesize that increased ketone use by the failing heart is beneficial and propose that providing even more ketones to the heart can be used as a potential new therapeutic approach for the treatment of heart failure.

column36: Understanding counsellor-client interactions in spinal cord injury exercise counselling: a novel method to explain outcomes of randomized controlled trials by assessing intervention fidelity
column37: Behavioural interventions often consist of conversations between counsellors and clients and can be a successful way to promote a healthy lifestyle. However, these interventions are not always successfully translated to other real-world settings. A possible reason for this variation in outcomes, is that researchers do not always measure how counsellors and clients interact with each other. Recently, a new method, called state space grids, has been developed to study and visualize how a counsellor and client interact with each other over time. This study will use these state space girds to study conversations about health-enhancing exercise between exercise counsellors and clients with spinal cord injury (SCI) to better understand the frequency, sequence, and duration of behaviour change techniques used in the interaction between the counsellor and client. This study is part of a larger trial of the effects of exercise to reduce chronic pain in adults with SCI. Participants in the study will receive tailored exercise counselling from a trained counsellor. Audio recordings of the counselling sessions will be analysed line-by-line by two researchers. This study is the first to use state space grids methods in an exercise behaviour interventions trial. It will provide new insights into how counsellors and clients with SCI interact with each other. These findings will help us to better understand how, when, and why the counselling sessions are successful or not. The findings can be used to develop training guides for SCI exercise counsellors and can improve SCI exercise counselling. In turn, understanding and improving effective exercise counselling will enhance lives of many Canadians with SCI.

column36: Engaging spinal arm and leg networks to improve walking after spinal cord injury
column37: When we walk, we swing our arms in rhythm with our legs. This relationship between the arms and legs is needed to improve our balance and our ability to walk efficiently. This project aims to develop a novel, cost-effective, and widely translatable therapy to improve walking ability after spinal cord injury (SCI). Two thirds (67.3%) of all spinal cord injuries are incomplete (iSCI), leaving some neural connections intact across the lesion site. Nonetheless, the ability to walk is often lost after SCI, leading to multiple secondary complications that reduce quality of life and increase healthcare costs. Current rehabilitation interventions focus on restoring walking through intensive training of the legs, but ignore engaging the arms. We recently demonstrated that simultaneous arm and leg cycling assisted with functional electrical stimulation doubles the improvements in over-ground walking after iSCI compared to leg cycling only or other gait-specific training paradigms. These findings highlighted the importance of neuronal pathways between the arm and leg control regions in the spinal cord during locomotion, and emphasized the need for activating these pathways to improve walking after iSCI. This project will investigate the innovative use of non-invasive spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) to recruit previously inaccessible spinal circuits in conjunction with arm and leg cycling for improving walking capacity of persons with more severe iSCI than currently possible with conventional rehabilitation paradigms.The results of this pivotal study will be crucial for determining the importance of arm and leg networks in the rehabilitation of walking. If successful, arm and leg cycling coupled with spinal cord stimulation could become an intervention that can be readily translated to the clinic as an accessible, inexpensive and effective rehabilitation therapy, benefiting more persons with spinal cord injury than currently possible.

column36: A method to recapitulate early embryonic gut spatial patterning and morphogenesis in hESCs
column37: As an organism develops, simple homogenous tissues undergo successive patterning and morphogenetic events to produce structurally complex heterogenous organs. In vertebrates, these events are primarily driven by reciprocal morphogen and mechanical signals between two or more adjacent cell types. Despite extensive knowledge about the individual nature of the signals and cell types involved, however, less is known about how they come together to create large-scale patterns, sharp boundaries, and the final size and shape of tissues-especially in the context of human development. A marked example of this is the development of the human gut, where despite the ability to create and study human cell types for almost every region in vitro, we still lack basic knowledge about how the embryonic gut tube regionalizes and sets the sites of the future endodermal organs. Such knowledge is not only critical for understanding development, but also for understanding and potentially treating a variety of common congenital disorders. It would also be greatly beneficial for tissue engineers for deriving new strategies to create tissues and organs for regenerative medicine. With a Life Sciences Research Foundation Fellowship, I plan to build on recent progress combining tools from synthetic biology with human embryonic stem cells to create a novel model system for studying the patterning and morphogenesis of the human gut. The system will also be applicable more generally to studying other instances of tubular patterning during human development, and for experimenting with and creating synthetic organ systems for future clinical application.

column36: The use of machine learning and multi-omics to explore the role of diet in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Cirrhosis is the end stage for most liver diseases. It is caused by a build up of scar tissue and results in a gradual loss of liver function. A minority of patients are candidates for liver transplantation. As cirrhosis advances, most patients experience chronic decline, frequent complications, repeated hospitalizations and a high burden of symptoms. Nutrition and exercise have helped patients with other chronic diseases improve or maintain their overall health. This is particularly important in cirrhosis where 80% of patients have dietary issues and muscle loss contributing to physical and mental frailty. In turn, frail patients with cirrhosis have a higher risk of hospitalization and death. By taking in a liver-friendly diet and engaging in regular exercise, studies have demonstrated improvements in frailty, reduced symptom burden and higher health-related quality of life. The benefit of these treatments is not experienced by all patients however, and the reasons for this remain unclear. During my postdoctoral fellowship, I will have access to a large dataset collected across the length of a 6-month randomized controlled trial. The trial compares patients with cirrhosis receiving standard care (control group) versus those in a nutrition and exercise program (experimental group). Unique from anything else that is available, the dataset will contain a broad range of data including not only clinical features and laboratory tests but also gut bacteria (intestinal microbiome) profiles, and metabolomic profiles (small molecules) present in the urine and blood. I will use machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence to predict the response to nutrition and exercise therapy and understand the mechanisms that explain response. Findings will help medical teams and their patients determine how to personalize these treatments in the future to achieve the most benefit for each individual patient.

column36: Exploring RNA splicing regulation using direct sequencing of nascent RNA
column37: Messenger RNAs (mRNA) are copies of genes that contain the information necessary to produce proteins. The formation of the right cell type depends on the production of the correct mRNAs that contain the instructions to make this given cell type. This is achieved in part through RNA splicing, in which certain parts of the premature RNA called introns are removed to form the mature mRNA. Defects in RNA splicing are a common cause of many human disorders, including cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms that control splicing in human cells are not well understood, which is mainly due to a lack of tools to study splicing while it is occurring. We recently developed a new method, nanopore analysis of CO-transcriptional Processing (nano-COP), which relies on direct RNA sequencing and allows us to monitor splicing while new RNAs are being produced. For example, we gained insight into how fast splicing occurs and the order of intron removal in human leukemia cells. The objective of this project is to use nano-COP to better understand how these aspects of splicing are controlled in various cell types. We will first apply nano-COP to measure splicing in 10 different human cell lines, including normal and cancer cells, to determine how splicing dynamics vary across cell types and in cancer. Next, we will use white blood cells from 10 different individuals to examine how splicing kinetics and order are impacted by genetic variants in parts of the RNA that are known to cause abnormal splicing. Finally, we will remove three proteins that play a role in splicing to determine in which aspect of splicing they are most important. We will repeat this experiment in three different cell types to discover whether certain functions of these proteins are cell type-specific. This study will improve our understanding of the control of the splicing process, which is crucial in order to learn how it goes awry in various human diseases.

column36: Can a single bout of exercise improve clinical outcomes in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery? Investigating the effects of acute local (handgrip) exercise on attenuating cardiac and vascular injury to ischaemia-reperfusion
column37: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in Canada and worldwide. While coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery remains the preferred strategy to restore blood flow to the heart in CAD patients, this procedure is associated with peri- and post-surgery complications. The duration and/or severity of cardiovascular tissue exposed to ischaemia is strongly related to morbidity and mortality, hence the importance to minimize tissue injury to ischaemia during surgery. Novel cardioprotective strategies are needed to improve clinical outcomes in patients undergoing CABG surgery. This project will build on exciting research findings in both animal models and healthy participants demonstrating that an acute bout of exercise lowers tissue injury to ischaemia-reperfusion. The goal of the proposed research is to examine the hypothesis that a single bout of handgrip exercise can attenuate vascular and cardiac injury to ischaemia-reperfusion in participants with CAD. Moreover, I hypothesize that these effects can be enhanced through a short period (4-days) of daily handgrip exercise training. These effects of local handgrip exercise on mediating smaller vascular and cardiac injury to ischaemia will ultimately lead to lower post-surgery morbidity/mortality. The simplicity, low cost, and low risk of handgrip exercise makes it highly suitable to implement into clinical care to potentially reduce cardiac and vascular injury to ischaemia. Moreover, this work will contribute to informing and optimizing exercise guidelines prior to cardiac surgery.

column36: Moving past allergy: how histamine impacts infection by a multidrug resistant pathogen
column37: Histamine is a potent chemical mediator that is commonly known for its function in allergy, but also plays an important role in the immune response. Upon exposure to an allergen, injury, or foreign invader, immune cells such as mast cells and basophils are triggered to release histamine and other inflammatory molecules. Histamine has a number of diverse biological effects, many of which are associated with allergy symptoms, including enhancing mucus production and thickness, increasing blood vessel leakage, and inducing airway constriction. Increasing blood vessel leakage is a crucial early step in the immune response, as it allows immune cells to escape into the damaged tissue to directly engage the perceived threat. Interestingly, some bacteria are also capable of producing and releasing histamine during infection. Acinetobacter baumannii is an emerging hospital-associated pathogen that is not only often extensively resistant to antibiotics, but also has been shown to release histamine. In A. baumannii, histamine appears to be produced as a key precursor of acinetobactin, a small iron-binding molecule that helps the bacteria capture this essential growth-promoting metal. The goal of this project is to understand how histamine availability impacts the outcome of A. baumannii pneumonia and bloodstream infections. We hypothesize that histamine may actually worsen A. baumannii infection by enhancing the ability of the bacteria to obtain iron and by allowing them to hijack the local immune response, using congested airways and disrupted blood vessels to avoid clearance and promote spread within the body. column36: Identifying Early Biomarkers and Nutritional Correlates of Future Reproductive Disturbance in Adolescent Females
column37: Abnormal reproductive development in adolescent females may have long lasting consequences on health. Teens often wait two or more years after their first period (menarche) before being evaluated for reproductive disorders, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Early detection and intervention of abnormal reproductive development would help to reduce future health issues, but a major challenge relates to the lack of knowledge about the nature of the adolescent reproductive transition in the years immediately after menarche. In adults, features of the ovary on ultrasound are useful in detecting problems with reproduction. But, reliable data on how the ovary changes during adolescence are not available, limiting the ability of ultrasound to detect problems early in teens. We know that nutrition can impact the onset of puberty and contribute to reproductive problems later in life. However, what role nutrition may play in the years between menarche and the diagnosis of a reproductive disorder is unknown. This research will address these gaps by defining the changes in the ovaries that occur alongside the development of menstrual cyclicity during the first two years after menarche. We expect to see differences in the appearance of the ovary in teens that achieve regular periods versus those with irregular periods after two years. This research will also determine whether specific aspects of nutrition are related with the trajectory towards PCOS in teens. We predict that dietary intake, even at this early stage, impacts reproductive function. These studies will reveal changes in the ovary during adolescence that can be used to develop early diagnostic tools for clinicians when evaluating teens for risk of reproductive disorders. By identifying dietary factors that may influence reproductive development, this research will form the basis for future studies that can evaluate the impact of nutritional changes on reducing risk and progression of reproductive disorders.

column36: Solving unsolved neuromuscular diseases: harnessing the power of phenotype and data integration strategies to optimise diagnosis and discovery
column37: Rare diseases are an important issue in Canada and worldwide. They collectively affect 1 person in 17, or as many as 2 million Canadians. Neuromuscular diseases are rare inherited diseases that affect the muscles and nerves and cause significant disability in both children and adults. Even though we now know of over 500 genes causing neuromuscular disease, in around 50% of patients the precise genetic cause can't be pinpointed after the initial analysis. Recent therapy developments are for the first time showing tremendous promise, but if a patient does not have a precise genetic diagnosis they may not be able to receive the best treatment for their condition. New technologies that look across the patient's entire genome are resulting in more diagnoses, but even healthy individuals have many places where their genome differs from others in a way that doesn't cause disease. This means that when we look at a patient's genome, sometimes we don't have enough information to decide which of the many genetic changes we see is responsible for the disease. My research aims to show that by making better use of the data that we have already, we can often bring it together in a way that allows us to reach a diagnosis. This includes information specific to the patient, especially the "phenotype" - the precise characteristics and symptoms the disease causes in the patient - and also data from experiments done in animal models for the disease. By standardising the ways we capture this data and linking different data types, we can more easily establish which is the disease-causing change and also potentially find other patients in other parts of the world with the same condition. I also aim to develop strategies that optimise the way we use, link and share data in order to create a workflow for undiagnosed neuromuscular patients that results in patients receiving a diagnosis more quickly in future.

column36: Mechanisms underlying abnormal uteroplacental vascular adaptations in pregnancies complicated by advanced maternal age
column37: More women are having their first pregnancies at an older age. In Canada, 8% of women have their first child when they are over 35 years of age (also known as advanced maternal age). A woman's blood vessels need to go through large changes during pregnancy, so that the fetus can receive enough blood and nutrients to grow normally. If the blood vessels do not adapt well enough, this can cause problems during pregnancy such as poor fetal growth and preeclampsia. Advanced maternal age is a risk factor for both of these pregnancy problems. Unfortunately, advanced maternal age impacts on how well these blood vessels change in pregnant women. If we can find out exactly how advanced maternal age adversely affects these blood vessel changes in pregnancies in women at advanced maternal age, we can target these mechanisms for treatment. Our lab found that uterine arteries from aged pregnant rats did not function as well as the arteries from young pregnant rats. The differences that we found may explain the increased problems in advanced maternal age pregnancies. We thus need to know more about these poor functioning arteries and why they do not function well. To do this, we will assess the function of vessels from pregnant young (4 months old) and aged (9.5 months old, equivalent to ~35 years in humans) rats. We will test blood vessel function, and use specific drugs to identify how their function is different. We will also compare blood vessels from pregnant and non-pregnant young and old rats. This will allow us to test if the blood vessels from old rats adapt differently than in young rats. At the same time, we will assess this mechanism in vessels from human biopsies taken during caesarean deliveries from young and older pregnant women. Pregnancy affects the short- and long-term cardiovascular health of both mother and child. This will help develop new treatments for older pregnant women to improve pregnancy outcomes in this high-risk group.

column37: Heart failure is when the heart becomes injured and can no longer pump blood well. This can become severe enough such that a person may need a new heart called a transplant. However, the body will not see this new heart as a part of itself and the immune system will attack it in a process known as rejection. To stop this, these patients are given special pills to weaken their immune systems. Sadly, these pills are not perfect and after a few years, the new heart will also become injured. The pills can also have lots of side effects that make these people more likely to get sick from other things. When this happens, many of these people will die. To tackle this problem, our group is studying the use of new technologies to stop the body from attacking the new heart. This year, we have taken some big steps towards making this happen. We have made a new small particle that may be able to stop the immune system from attacking these hearts. Unlike the pills, these nanodots do not weaken the immune system but instead makes the new heart invisible to the immune system. To test this, our group has come up with some experiments to test how these particles work in an animal model as a necessary step before introducing the technology to humans. We know that one of the first parts of a new heart to be injured is its blood vessels. That's why we will be transplanting blood vessels treated with our material between animals. If the particles can stop rejection of these blood vessels, we may be able to stop the immune system from injuring these hearts entirely. These particles can then become a new treatment for these people to make their lives longer and better. We are hopeful that this will soon become a reality.

column36: Characterizing the role of ETFDH on cancer biology
column37: Cancer is a disease defined by uncontrollable proliferation. As part of cancer progression, cells undergo various molecular changes in how they metabolize nutrients and synthesize proteins in order to meet their high growth demands. Most neoplasms display an increased dependence on glucose metabolism and adapt to their surroundings by regulating the two energy pathways: glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Although the increased reliance of cancer cells on glycolysis is well documented, the role of oxidative phosphorylation in cancer progression is still unclear. Mining of numerous publically available datasets revealed that the electron transfer flavoprotein dehydrogenase (ETFDH) is consistently under-expressed across numerous cancer subtypes. Our preliminary studies identified ETFDH as playing an anti-neoplastic role, as ETFDH loss increased lymphoma cell proliferation, which was accompanied by increased glycolysis and mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) signaling. We propose to follow up on these exciting preliminary findings to determine the metabolic and translational mechanisms underlying neoplastic growth. These studies are anticipated to unravel metabolic and translational vulnerabilities that can be exploited to develop strategies that hinder the development of ETFDH-reduced cancers.

column36: Investigating the role of FAM72A in B cell antibody diversification
column37: Antibodies, also referred to as immunoglobulins (Ig), play fundamental roles in our immune system by providing protection against pathogens. Antibodies are "Y" shaped molecules produced by specialized immune cells called the B cells. The tips of the two arms of the "Y", named the variable regions, differ greatly among different antibodies, thus providing the antibodies with the specificity and diversity for binding pathogens. The stem of the "Y" is named the constant region and it determines the functional properties of the antibodies. Antibodies can be further divided into different classes, with different antibody classes adopting different modes of action, such as directly binding to microbes and neutralizing their effect, localizing antibodies to different tissues, and signalling other immune cells to kill the infecting microbes or microbe-infected host cells. Upon exposure to an antigen, antibodies undergo diversification process to strength their abilities to bind and neutralize antigens. Somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination, both initiated by an enzyme named AID, are two genetic mechanisms that enable B cells to produce antibodies with higher antigen binding affinities and different classes. Our current knowledge towards somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination is likely incomplete, as complex and multifaceted molecular events take place during these two processes. Through a genetic screen I have identified FAM72A as a novel gene that functions in antibody class switch recombination, and propose to fully characterize the role of this gene and its product during antibody diversification using mouse models and diverse biochemical and cellular experimentations. My proposed work will advance our understanding on how antibody diversity is achieved, and influence vaccine development or the generation of therapeutic agents that target specific B cell malignancies.

column36: Understanding and preventing serious bacterial and fungal infections among people who inject drugs
column37: People who inject drugs face extremely high rates of death and disability from severe and invasive bacterial and fungal infections (including infections of the bloodstream, heart valves, and bones) that require hospital admission for treatment with antibiotics and/or surgeries. These infections are devastating for individual patients, and also extremely costly for our health care system. So how can people who inject drugs, and health systems who care for them, prevent these serious infections from occurring? Unfortunately we don't have scientific evidence to inform us. One promising approach to reducing risk in opioid-injectors is medication treatment for opioid addiction (with methadone or buprenorphine) as this helps people to inject less frequency. However risk for serious infections likely reflects multiple factors, including homelessness, use of stimulants or alcohol, and individual injecting practices. Based at the Collaborative Centre for Inclusion Health (CCIH) at University College London, my Fellowship project aims to inform people who inject drugs, clinicians, and health systems on how to prevent serious bacterial and fungal infections. We will analyze a unique large dataset from South London that contains anonymous health records for anyone who has ever been to addiction treatment, linked to their hospital records. We'll assess whether methadone or buprenorphine treatment is associated with decreased risk of infection-related hospitalization or death in people who inject opioids. We'll also assess what other factors are associated with risk (including homelessness, sex work, injecting practices, stimulant or alcohol use), and see whether these change the effectiveness of methadone or buprenorphine. We'll collaborate with groups of people who use drugs in London, UK, and Halifax, Canada to help refine our analysis plan and determine what risk factors may be most important.

column36: Salt inducible kinases: novel therapeutic targets for chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)
column37: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is characterized by structural abnormalities and impaired kidney function. Inadequate filtration of wastes and minerals (including phosphate) leads to serious disruption in mineral metabolism and bone disorder (Mineral and Bone Disorder; MBD). In CKD-MBD patients, phosphate retention in blood triggers secretion of a hormone called fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) to promote renal phosphate excretion. However, FGF23 blocks the generation of the active form of vitamin D. As vitamin D is essential in calcium absorption, low vitamin D causes low blood calcium level, stimulating the production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by parathyroid glands. Elevated PTH levels restore blood calcium by bone breakdown, resulting in bone loss and fractures. Currently, no drugs can improve both vitamin D levels and renal phosphate excretion. Although PTH usually accomplishes these tasks, CKD-MBD patients do not show expected PTH effects on mineral metabolism, despite the high level of PTH. Therefore, we hypothesized that targeting the downstream mediator of PTH signaling pathway would bypass PTH resistance, yet still bring PTH-like effects to help CKD-MBD. Recently, a family of enzymes called salt-inducible kinases (SIKs) was reported to participate in the actions of PTH in bone. To test if SIKs participate in renal PTH actions, we will use cutting-edge genome editing and pharmacologic approaches in multiple cell lines, as well as two mouse models. The role of SIK deletion in kidney will be determined in mice using a genetic engineering technique known as Cre-lox system. column36: Molecular Dissection of MECP2 Protein Phase Separation in Rett Syndrome
column37: Lipid-lipid phase separation is a physical phenomenon characterized by molecules de-mixing into distinct lipid phases. This process is known to drive the formation of membrane-less compartments in cells that concentrate biochemical reactions. Increasing evidence points to the involvement of aberrant phase separation in neurodegenerative disorders through excessive protein aggregation. Rett syndrome (RTT) is a postnatal progressive neurodevelopmental disease associated with severe mental retardation that primarily affects females. The majority of the clinical cases have been traced to mutations of MECP2, a multi-talented protein that acts as a repressor or an activator of transcription. However, the mechanism underlying the complex role of MECP2 in cellular physiology and RTT particularly remains enigmatic. The Jaenisch laboratory has recently demonstrated that MECP2 can form phase-separated condensates in murine cells. On this basis, I aim to expand the role of phase separation in biological function and disease-causing malfunction of MECP2 to the human system. I will leverage the experimental paradigm established in the Jaenisch lab and use human embryonic stem (ES) cells to generate normal and RTT neurons in both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) culture systems, and explore the molecular properties of phase separation in these human models. The human ES cells will be engineered to carry relevant disease-causing mutations in the MECP2 gene. The goal of this project is to advance the mechanistic understanding of MECP2's function and pave the way for new therapeutic approaches for RTT.

column36: Canadian Study of Arterial Inflammation in Diabetes and the Evaluation of Colchicine Effectiveness (CADENCE)
column37: Diabetic patients are at high risk of suffering atherosclerotic disease related events (eg acute coronary syndromes (ACS), stroke, transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)) and have a higher recurrence rate than the general population. Inflammation has been extensively investigated as a promoter of atherosclerosis development and destabilization. Recent trials have revealed outcome benefit in patients with cardiovascular disease who are treated with anti-inflammatory therapy. The LoDoCo trial also showed a reduction in cardiovascular events in patients with known coronary artery disease who were treated with colchicine. Although the LoDoCo trial did show outcome benefit, colchicine's mechanism of action at the level of the atherosclerotic plaque in patients remains unknown. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging with 18F-fluordeoxyglucose (18-FDG) provides an opportunity to perform molecular imaging of specific components of the atherosclerotic plaque such as inflammation. 18-FDG has been validated and extensively used for this purpose, and it could potentially enable the prospective evaluation of inflammation targeted therapies and the identification of patients at high risk for vascular events. column36: Immune mechanisms of influenza A virus-induced susceptibility to myocardial infarction

column36: Fine-grained mapping of hippocampal subregions using 7T MRI
column37: Epilepsy is among the most common neurological conditions and affects 300,000 Canadians. Medial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common form. In many cases, seizures are thought to originate in the hippocampus, a brain structure critical for memory and a number of other cognitive functions. Removing parts of the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe is an established treatment that effectively relieves seizures. However, there are usually marked postoperative complications, such as memory deficits and psychiatric disturbances. To minimize postoperative cognitive deficits, we propose to develop a method that will localize, or map, subregions of the hippocampus. Such a map will enable us to determine which subregions are crucial for various functions. In doing so, we will be able to advise neurosurgeons in their surgical planning, to avoid removing subregions that would likely result in severe cognitive deficits. The hippocampus is a complex structure that mediate various brain functions. Different parts of the hippocampus display dissociable patterns of functional connectivity to the rest of the brain. We will leverage this varying connectivity to map hippocampal subregions. Importantly, we will use novel neuroimaging analysis techniques that will enable us to generate a hippocampal map that is unique to each individual. We will then assess the relationship between these subregions and several hippocampal functions, including memory, emotion, and topographical processing. Finally, we will validate the hippocampal maps in MTLE patients, in whom we will be able to directly measure hippocampal activity using intra-hippocampal electrodes. This project will significantly impact epilepsy research as it will enable us to identify hippocampal subregions that are functionally different. One day, these individual maps of hippocampal organization could be used to plan surgical procedures and minimize post-surgical cognitive deficits in patients with epilepsy.

column37: Despite their increased risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV, people who inject drugs (PID) are among those with the least access to HIV prevention and treatment. column36: Characterizing the role of stromal cells on hematopoietic stem cell division
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells supply all the blood cells required during life. During development stem cells migrate to vascular niches where they are enveloped by 'cuddling' endothelial cells and contacted by stromal cells. These stromal cells sustain the stem cells by releasing signals that encourage stem cell self-renewal. Contact with stromal cells also controls how the stem cells divide, ensuring that one of the dividing cells remains in the niche, while the other leaves to form mature blood cells. This makes stromal cells essential to the niche and if they are destroyed the stem cells can be lost leading to blood disorders. Despite the importance of these niche stromal cells no study has yet identified what makes them unique and what specific mechanisms they use to regulate stem cell division. This research will characterize stromal cells using zebrafish models which have many of the same cell types and signaling pathways as the mammalian bone marrow niche. Next generation sequencing technologies will be used to examine stromal cells at single cell resolution and identify the cell types that form the niche. Using this data, the genetic factors that specify niche stromal cells will be determined and used to build tools to target the niche. Stem cell divisions will be visualized within the optically clear zebrafish embryos using 4D microscopic imaging. Polarized proteins previously identified in isolated mammalian stem cells extracted from bone marrow will be fluorescently tagged and expressed in the zebrafish stem cells to visualize cell polarity and asymmetric divisions in context within the niche. Genetic ablation of stromal cells will then test the requirements for these cells in blood homeostasis. The results of this research will deepen our understanding of the stem niche and inform therapeutic strategies to improve the expansion of transplanted stem cells for the treatment of blood disorders.
