column36: Timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation during pregnancy and child growth and neurodevelopment: quantifying consequences and understanding mechanisms.
column37: The 2015 World Health Organization guidelines recommend all pregnant women who are positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) to initiate lifelong triple-drug antiretroviral therapy (ART) to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV and to improve maternal survival. While it is essential that HIV-positive pregnant women begin ART as soon as possible after learning about their diagnosis, recent evidence from multiple studies suggests that women who begin ART before pregnancy may have a higher risk of having babies that are born too soon (preterm birth) or too small (low birthweight). Such adverse birth outcomes can put these babies at a higher risk of poor physical growth and brain development in early life, which may have a lasting impact throughout the lifespan. Yet, no study has previously evaluated the direct impact of timing of ART initiation during pregnancy on child growth and neurodevelopment. To address this gap, the purpose of this research is: 1) to examine the role of timing of ART initiation on child growth and neurodevelopment in the first year of life; 2) to quantify the role of poor birth outcomes, as mediators, in the pathway between timing of ART initiation and infant growth and neurodevelopment; and 3) to investigate whether some subgroups of women have a higher risk than others (e.g. based on HIV disease stage or maternal nutritional status). To address these objectives, data from a recently completed longitudinal study of 2300 HIV-positive pregnant women in Tanzania will be used. In this study, 50% of women started ART before pregnancy and 50% at variable times during the second trimester of pregnancy. Using advanced epidemiologic methods in causal inference, which overcome common pitfalls of conventional statistical techniques, this research will provide new evidence to understand the potential unintended consequences of ART, and ways in which treatment of HIV during pregnancy may be optimized to ensure all children survive and thrive.

column36: The role of adipose tissue in host defenses to bacterial pneumonia
column37: A clinical entity termed the "obesity paradox" suggests that overweight individuals (BMI>25) are 20-30% more likely to survive hospitalized pneumonia. There are two ways to survive an infection. The first depends on resistance mechanisms that kill the pathogen creating an arms race between the host and pathogen that can lead to pathogen resistance, immunopathology, and mortality. The second is a distinct defense classification called the co-operative defense system. The co-operative defense system encodes disease tolerance mechanisms that prevent or alleviate pathology generated during infection without affecting pathogen number nor fitness. The role of tolerance in the obesity paradox is unknown. Legionella pneumophila (Lp) is a bacterial pathogen that infects and resides in immune cells of the lung. Preliminary data has identified that host utilization of fatty acids is critical for defenses and survival against Lp. These data suggest that an increased abundance of circulating fatty acids may improve host outcome to infection. I hypothesize that fat promotes host defenses during Lp infection through fatty acid release and availability for utilization by the host. This project will determine how host adipose composition and fatty acid availability effects tolerance defense mechanisms toward Lp lung infection. I will identify specific host immune or metabolic pathways that benefit from the increased abundance of fat and fatty acids that promote host health during infection. Discovering new disease tolerance mechanisms is critical for overcoming resistance in pathogens, creating new avenues to treat infectious diseases.

column36: Incorporating practical, high-intensity interval training (HIIT) into the workplace: Examining the impact on physiological and psychological health, absenteeism, and work productivity
column37: The workplace presents an environment where people tend to sit for prolonged periods of time and do not regularly engage in physical activity (PA), two factors that have negative health consequences, particularly related to obesity and diabetes. Traditionally prescribed, sustained aerobic exercise ("cardio") is impractical for many office employees who are unfit and low on time. Such barriers can be overcome by adopting high-intensity interval training (HIIT) - short-duration exercise that involves multiple brief, high-intensity efforts, separated by periods of rest. Stair climbing HIIT can benefit physiological health in less time than traditional exercise training. Further, recent studies show promising psychological implications of engaging in HIIT. Phase 1 of this research will involve office employees undergoing an 8-week HIIT program of either a) one short HIIT session completed during lunch break or b) brief exercise bouts performed throughout the workday as "exercise snacks." The exercise will consist of stair climbing, which is an effective, lifestyle-based form of HIIT. Phase 2 will deliver an 8-week optimized HIIT program designed to be sustainable. We will measure physical and psychological health, work productivity, sick days and PA behaviour during and up to 6-months following the program. This research will be the first to determine the health, work productivity, and PA behaviour benefits of practical HIIT programs delivered in the workplace. This research has important implications for employees who may be at risk for chronic diseases, employers seeking greater output from employees, and for Canadian society - which benefits from healthier and more productive workplaces.

column36: Uncovering the links between atrial stretch and inflammation in atrial fibrillation associated with cardiovascular disease
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained supraventricular arrhythmia worldwide and is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and socio-economic burden. AF affects 1-2% of the general population and with an incidence expected to double by 2060. While AF is tightly linked to aging and cardiovascular (CV) disease (i.e., heart failure, valve disease), its origins are complex, but are fundamentally linked to altered structural and/or electrical remodeling of the atria. Importantly, most conditions linked to AF are associated with elevated atrial pressures and atrial stretch, which is a powerful stimulus for adverse atrial remodeling. It is well-established that the pro-inflammatory and mechanosensitive cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa) is a critical factor in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, arrhythmias, and inflammation seen in heart disease as well as athletes with AF, and an enhanced inflammatory response is typically observed in AF patients. While previous work from our group established the requirement of TNFa in exercise-induced adverse atrial remodeling and AF vulnerability in mice, the overlap in pathways mediating arrhythmogenesis in exercise and CV disease is undeniable. My research seeks to translate our exercise findings to more clinically-relevant models of heart disease, including a mouse model of aortic regurgitation (AR), which is characterized by cardiac volume overload, dilatation, elevated atrial pressures, fibrosis, and AF. As AR patients have one of the highest risks of AF, AR offers a clinically-relevant model to study atrial stretch-dependent TNFa-mediated AF pathogenesis. This mechanistic link will be assessed by: 1) assessing the molecular and cellular basis for TNFa-mediated adverse atrial remodeling in CV disease; 2) identifying novel pathways involved in the TNFa-dependent differential effects of AR on the atria with a goal towards developing novel interventions; and 3) translating our findings to CV patients.

column36: Modeling blood-brain barrier dysfunctions using induced pluripotent stem cells: new insights into Huntington's disease pathology
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a strictly genetic disease which manifests with movement, cognitive and psychiatric problems. The dysfunctional protein that results from the genetic mutation, referred to as mutant huntingtin (mHtt), is found in all cells of the body, but it particularly affects the brain. Traditionally, it has been thought that the presence of the mutated gene is necessary for the disease to emerge. This view was radically changed by a recent discovery made by the Cicchetti group. When analysing fetal tissue that had been transplanted into patients with HD as an experimental therapy, they uncovered the presence of mHtt within the healthy cells of the graft. Since the fetal tissue did not express the mutant gene, the toxic form of the protein could only have come from the unhealthy tissue surrounding the transplant. This observation has many important implications, including the idea that the gene is not necessary for the initiation of disease. In association with mHtt in the fetal graft, they also found abnormalities in blood vessels. Normally blood vessels in the brain are surrounded by a barrier known as the blood brain barrier (BBB), which prevents toxins and other materials from reaching the brain. For my project, I will study the interactions between the protein associated with HD and changes in the function of the BBB. To do this, I will use a cell culture model of the BBB which closely resembles the BBB in the body in both cell composition and movement of fluids. Using this model, I will first measure how the presence of mHtt changes the function of the different parts of the BBB and second, determine if changes to the permeability of the BBB influences the negative effects that mHtt has on neurons. This project could shed light on new therapeutic targets for HD.

column36: Induction of Cortical Plasticity in Human using Theta Burst Ultrasound Stimulation
column37: Ultrasound is well known for making visible what is hidden, for example, when giving parents a glimpse of their child before birth. Conventional brain stimulation techniques use electric currents or magnetic fields to alter brain activity. These techniques, however, have limitations. They can only reach the surface of the brain and are not particularly precise. By contrast, beams of ultrasound can be focused at a millimetre scale, even deep within the brain. Ultrasound thus has the potential to provide new insights into how the brain works. Most studies of ultrasound stimulation have looked at what happens to the brain during the stimulation itself. But could ultrasound also induce longer-lasting changes in brain activity? Changes that persist after the stimulation has ended would be valuable for research. They would also make it more likely that we could use ultrasound to treat brain disorders by changing brain activity. This study is to establish a repetitive ultrasound pattern to induce long-lasting alterations in human brain activity. It can target areas deep within the brain, including those that are out of reach with other techniques. If this procedure shows longer-lasting effects in people, it could yield valuable insights into the links between brain and behaviour. It could also help us develop new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are a new class of drugs that unleash the immune system to combat cancer. Collectively, these efforts will enable us to understand how specific genetic mutations in cancer cells influence the immune microenvironment during cancer development and in response to therapy. column37: More than 10% of births are premature, and premature birth kills more Canadian children than any other cause. Babies delivered prematurely have increased risk for both short- and long-term negative health consequences. There is currently no screening method to identify which pregnancies will deliver early. A method to detect pregnancies with a high risk of premature birth is needed to improve health outcomes for both the mother and baby. During pregnancy, a fetus develops an organ called the placenta, which connects it to the mother and delivers nutrients from mother to fetus. DNA from the placenta circulates in the mother's blood, along with the mother's DNA. Many studies have used the sequence of circulating DNA to predict pregnancy complications. In this study, we will look at the chemical changes found between circulating DNA of healthy pregnancies and pregnancies involving premature birth. Specifically, we will look at DNA methylation, a kind of chemical change known to affect which genes are active in different human tissues. We will identify changes in DNA methylation that can determine pregnancies with a high risk of premature birth. Since the test only uses DNA in the mother's blood, we can do this with a non-invasive blood test with little additional risk to the pregnancy. As such, findings from this study can be easily applied to current pregnancy care. This study will result in a noninvasive blood test that can detect pregnancies with increased risk of premature delivery. Use of this test will lead to changes in pregnancy care to try to prevent premature birth. This will lead to better long-term health for both mother and child. It will also decrease the need for the extreme medical care often used on premature infants. Improved health outcomes with decreased interventions will reduce costs to the Canadian health care system.

This information can inform the development and implementation of interventions to alleviate depression and the DD in patients with advanced disease and to identify those most likely to benefit from such interventions. The results of this work will also provide an evidence base to inform decisions about eligibility and conditions for MAID and for the development of legislation and policy guidelines.

column36: Investigating the therapeutic potential of modulating lysosomal biogenesis in normal and leukemic human hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Currently, leukemia is treated by hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) and/or chemotherapies; however, there are challenges. Although 50,000 HSCT procedures are undertaken worldwide annually to treat blood disorders and cancers, two thirds of patients who need HSCT lack matched donor tissue. Although cord blood (CB) banks improve the search for matched tissue, hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) number is usually limiting. HSCs maintain lifelong blood production but they are very sensitive to stress and cannot be easily expanded in culture. Thus, expansion of functional HSCs in the laboratory from CB while maintaining their survival and self-renewal properties offers an avenue to increase the number of HSCs for transplant and tap an underused HSCT source. With respect to chemotherapy, in certain types of leukemias, the stress response of HSCs and leukemia stem cells (LSCs) appear to have some differences (although there are also similarities) and exploiting these differences could make LSCs sensitive to chemotherapy. We and others have shown that lysosomes-organelles that act like the janitors of the cell-play crucial roles in adult stem cell adaptation to stress and survival. Here, we propose that modulation of lysosome activity could be a novel two-prong therapeutic approach for treating leukemia patients: 1) Improving the expansion of CB curative hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Here, we propose to test chemical compounds to enhance lysosome activity and maintain survival of HSCs during expansion using our state-of-the-art xenograft models. 2) Targeting LSCs that are resistant to chemotherapy. We will investigate the role of lysosomes in LSC's survival and test the sensitivity of LSCs to treatment with different lysosome modulators. Collectively, we propose that uncovering the clinical applicability of compounds that can either enhance or inhibit lysosome functionality will selectively target LSCs in patients while sparing HSCs.

column36: Disturbances of neurogenic cardiovascular control in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: characterization and modulation
column37: When the heart pumps poorly, nerves in the body start to fire more often. At first, this improves heart function, but over time it increases heart rate, stores salt and water, tightens blood vessels, and makes it harder to exercise. If the heart weakens and no longer pumps blood well throughout the body, heart failure (HF) will occur. However, many Canadians develop another form of HF, with normal pumping function but a stiff heart that does not relax well or fill with blood properly. We know less about this form of HF even though it is an equally common cause of hospitalization and death. There is little we can do to treat this form of HF. Thus, our goal is to learn if the nerves that fire too often in HF due to poor pumping function also fire more in patients with HF due to poor heart relaxation, and if so, determine why and how to stop this. With a sterile electrode, we will record sympathetic nerve firing from a nerve in the leg, plus blood pressure and heart rate, at rest and during two conditions that we know causes the nerve to increase firing in patients with HF due to poor pumping function: 1) increasing the amount of blood in the heart's upper chambers; and 2) 1-leg cycling exercise. One experiment will help us learn what happens to nerve firing when we move blood suddenly from the legs to the heart, which increases the pressure in the heart. The second will teach us if exercise causes more nerve firing in these patients, if this increase is what makes it hard to exercise, and if this can be improved by exercise training. We will study healthy volunteers to learn the normal response, compare their responses to HF patients, and compare what we find in men and women because we know that more women get this form of HF. If we can identify reasons why patients develop HF because their heart does not relax well, even though it seems to squeeze normally, our findings should inspire new ways of treating it so that patients can live longer and more healthy lives.

column36: Achieving the WHO hepatitis C elimination goals: mapping existing gaps in care, determining the economic burden, and identifying areas of investment along the care-cascade that optimize health outcomes among immigrants living with hepatitis C in Canada
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment has been revolutionized by the introduction of extremely effective direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) in 2013. These drugs offer exciting opportunities to eliminate HCV as a public health concern. To this end, the WHO has set ambitious global elimination targets to be met by 2030. However, planning for HCV elimination requires an accurate understanding of the existing gaps along the "HCV care-cascade" (e.g., diagnosis, linkage-to-care, treatment, cure). Further, high-quality data on healthcare resource use and costs along this cascade is also necessary to optimize elimination efforts. HCV-infected patients are highly heterogeneous with a different set of challenges in accessing and remaining engaged in healthcare. For example, in Canada, 35% of HCV infections are among foreign-born individuals. These groups face long delays to diagnosis and are more likely to have advanced liver disease (i.e., cirrhosis and liver cancer). However, the current DAA-era care-cascade and resource use for this high-risk group remains unknown. This project will identify the strategies required to optimally meet the WHO's elimination targets in immigrants to Canada by 1) identifying the current gaps in the "HCV care-cascade", 2) estimating the healthcare costs attributable to HCV, and 3) using these data to identify investment opportunities along the "HCV care-cascade". We will use population-level administrative healthcare data held at ICES and immigration records at Immigration Refugees & Citizenship Canada, to map the "HCV care-cascade" and determine the mean healthcare cost attributable to HCV for immigrants in Ontario. This data will be used to parameterize an existing, validated economic model that projects the health and economic outcomes of various integrated elimination strategies. We will then use multi-objective optimization to determine areas of investment where policymakers should focus efforts to eliminate HCV among immigrants in Canada by 2030.

column36: Deciphering the Implementability of Epigenetic Reprogramming in Hematopoietic Stem Cells as a Novel Vaccination Strategy against Human Tuberculosis
column37: Ever since the German scientist Robert Koch discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) to be the infectious agent of tuberculosis in 1882, it has defied efforts by scientists to prevent or cure the disease. The presence of Mtb DNA in ancient Egyptian mummies (dated 1550-1080 BC) suggests a long-standing evolutionary relationship between this bacterium and humans. Despite the world-wide application of BCG vaccination and other anti-Mtb interventions, Mtb remains one of the deadliest human pathogens killing annually two million people. Eight to ten million new cases of active tuberculosis occur each year mainly due to asymptomatic people chronically infected with Mtb. The ability of Mtb to persist in individuals with apparently normal immune systems implies that Mtb has developed strategies to avoid, evade, and even subvert our host defense system. To date, BCG is the only licensed vaccine against tuberculosis (TB). It protects against disseminated forms of TB in children but not against pulmonary TB in adults. However, after 100 years of its discovery, the protective mechanism(s) of BCG is still unknown. Although initially it was thought that adaptive immunity is responsible for this protection, many studies suggested otherwise. We have recently demonstrated that the systemic administration of BCG expands and reprograms stem cells to generate protective innate immunity in pre-clinical mouse models of TB. In the current study, we aim to investigate the potential translation of this approach to humans.

column36: The role of adiponectin in cholesterol efflux and high-density lipoprotein biogenesis and functionality
column37: Atherosclerosis is responsible for more deaths in Canada than any other disease. This illness is described as a chronic condition that is characterized by cholesterol build-up inside the arteries, called plaques. However, cholesterol can be transported outside the cells (efflux) of the atherosclerotic plaque, which can be beneficial for the cells. There is a protein in the body called apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) that accepts this cholesterol from the cells and forms particles of the "good" cholesterol (HDL) in the blood that protects against atherosclerosis. Adiponectin, a protein secreted by fat tissue, has beneficial effects by preventing formation of plaques in the arteries. Studies have shown that adiponectin is strongly associated with the level of the HDL in the blood. However, it is not known if adiponectin can directly increase "good" cholesterol production and function, which would be very beneficial against atherosclerosis. Our preliminary evidence showed that adiponectin can interact with apoA-I and stimulate cholesterol efflux efficiently in a human cell model of macrophages. My project will focus on the study of the interaction between adiponectin and apoA-I. I will perform several advanced laboratory experiments to assess if this interaction increases the production HDL and its "good" cholesterol function. In other words, I will determine if and in which manner adiponectin can enhance the ability of apoA-I to accept cellular cholesterol and generate HDL particles. I will also study their interaction by examining where exactly adiponectin binds on apoA-I. Overall, these findings may support the therapeutic potential of combining adiponectin and apoA-I, to increase HDL, the" good" cholesterol. These may prove to be significant discoveries to reduce atherosclerosis and its related diseases, such as stroke and heart attacks, and save lives!

column36: Targeting and optimizing personalized pre-operative risk factors to achieve better colorectal surgery outcomes
column37: Colorectal surgery is a common surgery for the treatment of colon and rectal cancers as well as other bowel diseases. Recovery from colorectal surgery is difficult because of the many potential negative side effects. These side effects include surgical complications, long hospital stays, and slow recovery of pre-surgery fitness. It usually takes several months for colorectal surgery patients to recover the strength required to return to their typical daily activities. Prehabilitation is a new program for surgery designed to help patients experience better surgical recoveries by preparing them weeks before their operation with nutrition, anxiety reduction, and exercise advice to make better use of their waiting time for surgery. We think prehabilitation programs could be improved if targeted to patients' personalized risk factors for surgery. It might not be necessary for every patient to receive nutrition, exercise and anxiety-reduction advice. Some patients might benefit more from help with nutrition than help with exercise or vice versa. It is important that we figure out which patients benefit the most from the different aspects of prehabilitation programs so that we can use healthcare resources wisely, use patients' time wisely, and ensure the right patient receives the right care. We want to develop a tool that identifies patients who are at risk of having bad surgical recoveries and use this tool to develop a better prehabilitation program that truly meets patient needs and helps patients recover well.

column37: Sepsis is the life-threatening response to infection. It affects everybody, especially children, seniors and those with other health issues. Sepsis costs the Canadian healthcare system over $1.5 billion every year, and causes more deaths than breast, bowel and lung cancer put together. Survivors may end up with weak muscles and memory problems. They may lose an arm or leg, have to go on dialysis, and still be at risk for more infections. Yet most Canadians have never heard of sepsis. In 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared sepsis to be a world emergency. It asked countries to count their numbers of septic patients, educate the public and healthcare workers on how recognize and treat sepsis, and to develop new treatments. To meet the WHO's strategic plan, Sepsis Canada scientists, patients and families promise to do exactly that. By 2025, our goal is to ensure that every septic patient in Canada is identified and treated. Our slogan is: Suspect sepsis, save lives, support recovery! We will learn which Canadians are at greatest risk of sepsis and the impact on their families. We will create a bank of evidence-based tools to teach the public and health workers and we will study new sepsis treatments. As a result, more Canadians will be alive and well after sepsis, thanks to better and timely access to care. The healthcare system will save money (about $380 million dollars every year within the next 5 years). We will share our knowledge around the world so that every citizen of the planet will benefit.

column37: Les personnes ayant une lesion cerebrale acquise soit via un traumatisme a la tete soit via une tumeur, un anevrisme cerebral ou une autre atteinte intra-cerebrale non-traumatique peuvent consequemment avoir un etat de conscience alteree. Le plus connu est le coma, mais l'etat deveil non-repondant et l'etat de conscience minimal en sont aussi et font partie d'un continuum vers l'etat d'eveil. La periode de temps necessaire a une personne pour traverser ces stades et emerger de cette alteration est inconnue, meme que certains ne retrouveront jamais un etat de conscience normale. Jusqu'a maintenant, peu de moyens existent pour faire progresser quelqu'un d'un stade a l'autre. Par notre etude, nous esperons pouvoir moduler l'activite cerebrale par la stimulation du nerf vague afin d'ameliorer l'etat de conscience. Ce nerf a une influence sur l'activite des organes internes du corps dont le coeur et le cerveau. Nous esperons qu'en stimulant ce dernier, cela aura un effet positif sur l'activite cerebrale. Pour mesurer cette activite, nous utiliserons une evaluation clinique standardisee des alterations de l'etat de conscience, l'electroencephalogramme et l'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle. Toutes ces techniques utilisent des moyens differents pour mesurer l'activite des cellules du cerveau. Pour y arriver, nous voulons comparer un groupe avec stimulation placebo a un groupe avec une stimulation active afin d'eliminer l'effet de la progression naturelle d'une alteration de l'etat de conscience. Si notre hypothese est confirmee, cela permettrait d'utiliser cette technique non-invasive au chevet du patient, pendant le sejour hospitalier, afin de le faire progresser plus rapidement d'une phase a l'autre jusqu'a l'etat d'eveil.

column36: Aging into the 21st Century: A Longitudinal Evaluation of Facilitators and Barriers to Improved Care and Health Outcomes in those Aging with Disability
column37: As a result of medical and technological advancements, individuals with long-term disabilities are increasingly living to middle and older ages, resulting in a growing number of individuals who are aging with disability rather than aging into disability This population has the potential to be sizable, with 13% of Canadian youth and 20% of working age adults reporting at least one disability. The "normative" aging process is associated with higher disease burden, changing social roles, and more complex care needs. Individuals entering old age with a disability face additional difficulties including accessing regular health care, which can result in poor Continuity of Care (COC). COC is concerned with quality of care received over time and is strongly associated with health outcomes. This may be due, in part, to structural factors within and outside of the health care system (e.g., neighbourhood environment). However, this remains an understudied area and the limited evidence in this population precludes insight into how to support successful aging in this population. The overall aim of this project is to examine how features of the social, physical and built environment influence successful aging outcomes and care continuity for those aging with disabilities. To address this research question, we will identify a cohort of individuals with disability from Medicare & Medicaid data (2002-2016), which is the federal health insurance program that provides free health care to those with disabilities. In addition, we will link contextual measures generated from several data sources, indicators of health outcomes and trajectories of care continuity over follow-up. With this research, we aim to identify the contextual facilitators for positive health and care outcomes in this population. Through identifying potential areas of intervention, results can inform public health and clinical policies and prevention efforts to support successful aging for those with disabilities.

column36: Building Resilience through Integrated Knowledge Transfer in Police Organizations: A Case Study Series
column37: Resilience is an individual's capacity to effectively cope with extreme stress and persist through adversity, and is an important concept for police officers who are repeatedly exposed to potentially traumatic events and at increased risk for psychological injury. The consequences of these occupational exposures can include physical and mental illness, with significant direct and indirect costs. The current project will expand the definition of resilience to conceptualize it as an ecosystem comprising personal, family, and workplace factors, recognizing events in either of the three categories can impact individual officer resilience. Using an integrated knowledge translation case study design, this study will work with police agencies to develop and deliver training, examine organizational policy and procedure, and implement the Canadian Psychological Standards to build resilience. Individual data will be collected concerning shifts in knowledge, attitudes and behavior related to mental health and well-being. Police agencies will be the unit of analysis for case studies that will collect a comprehensive suite of data about each department, including organizational goals and work performed towards their achievement, aggregated information on disability and return to work rates, and mental health support mechanisms, policies and procedures. Machine learning analytics will identify similarities in case studies to determine enabling factors for a psychologically safe workplace. Sex and gender as biological and social determinants of health outcomes will also be analyzed. Development of an organizational culture supporting psychological health and reduced occupational stress are expected; individuals will enhance their resilience through increased knowledge and awareness of personal, family and workplace factors impacting psychological health and well-being. All resources and processes developed will be made open to other public safety agencies.

column36: The risk of multiple sclerosis among users of tumor necrosis factor inhibitors: A Canadian population-based study
column37: Thanks to better understanding of the inflammatory process, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) (i.e., a protein in our body that causes inflammation) and its inhibitors (i.e., drugs that suppress the effect of TNF) were discovered. TNF inhibitors (TNFi) are widely used in patients with moderate to severe inflammatory rheumatic diseases (RD, like rheumatoid arthritis) or inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD, like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease). RD and IBD affect approximately 1 million Canadians in total. Even though TNFi are able to improve patients' quality of life, a number of case reports have linked taking TNFi medication to a higher risk of developing multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is a disease that can cause problems with vision, balance, muscle control, and other basic body functions. MS is also associated with a very high healthcare burden in Canada, as it shortens Canadians' life by 6 years, incurs $2 billion in healthcare costs annually, and is most often diagnosed in young adults aged 20 to 49 during critical years of work life. Nevertheless, this issue has not been thoroughly studied. To fill this gap, I will do the following: 1. Find out how common MS is among RD or IBD patients who used TNFi compared to those who did not use TNFi. 2. Find out if RD and IBD patients with longer use and higher dose of TNFi have a higher risk of developing MS. I will use administrative datasets from British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan, with information routinely collected during clinic, hospital, and pharmacy records. The datasets include all RD and IBD patients (120,000 and 70,000, respectively) who received medical care between 2000 and 2015 from four Canadian provinces. I will conduct the studies for RD and IBD, separately. Findings from this work will identify MS risk factors, potentially prevent MS cases, and will positively impact Canadian public health, global health and new drug discovery.

column36: Engineering the HIV-1 gp41 pocket to increase rigidity and enable small-molecule drug discovery
column37: Since the start of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, over 77 million people have become infected with HIV and half of those infected have died of AIDS-related illnesses. The proposed research is focused on addressing the need for new classes of anti-HIV drugs that are resistant to the emergence of HIV-1 mutations. Gp41 is a HIV-1 surface protein that mediates fusion with host cells and contains a highly conserved cavity in its structure, referred to as the "gp41 pocket". Currently, there is only one drug that targets gp41 to inhibit viral entry into human cells. This peptide drug (T-20) has limited clinical utility because it has poor bioavailability and requires two daily injections. Literature reports indicate that efforts to identify a small-molecule drug against gp41 have hitherto been unsuccessful. A potential explanation for this is the observation that the gp41 pocket is highly malleable. Our hypothesis is that (1) it is more difficult to identify small-molecule drug leads for a target that is malleable compared to one that is rigid, and (2) a high-throughput screen (HTS) with a rigid target will yield better hit rates which will potentiate the discovery of a new small-molecule inhibitor of HIV-1 fusion. To test this hypothesis, the gp41 pocket will first be engineered to increase rigidity using protein engineering, and then the rigid pocket will be subjected to an HTS. An HTS will identify small-molecule chemicals, referred to as hits, that bind to the rigid gp41 pocket. By studying the binding mechanism of different hits to gp41 we hope to elucidate critical chemical interactions that are necessary for the design of a potent anti-HIV-1 drug. Since the gp41 pocket is highly conserved across HIV-1 strains, a drug that targets the pocket is likely to be resistant to the development of escape mutations. Thus, this research has the potential to improve the health of HIV infected individuals that develop resistance to the currently available antiretroviral medications.

column36: Understanding the cellular and molecular basis of Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell therapy resistance
column37: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has been a major breakthrough in cancer therapy, and recent clinical trials indicate that it is a potentially life-saving option for the most common form of pediatric leukemia. These clinical trials highlight one of the key questions in the field: why is this form of therapy so effective in some patients, yet ineffective in others? We hypothesize that early treatment failure to CAR T-cell therapy can be predicted by cellular pathways within the patient's T-cells, whereas treatment failure after initial response can be attributed to the clonal evolution of therapy-resistant cancer cells. To address this clinical challenge, we will use a systems immunology approach, leveraging modern high-throughput molecular assays on tumor and immune cells. We have collected T-cells from 71 patients prior to receiving CAR T-cell therapy and performed whole-transcriptome RNA-sequencing on their T-cell subtypes, providing a rich resource of gene expression profiles across patients. Using this data, we will develop a comprehensive atlas of T-cell pathways in therapy-responsive and therapy-resistant patients, allowing us to pinpoint the cellular pathways within these immune cells that allow for effective CAR T-cell therapy. In order to interrogate the mechanism of tumor evasion of CAR T-cell therapy, we have acquired tumor cells from patients prior to CAR T-cell therapy and at the time of relapse. Using whole-exome sequencing, RNA-Sequencing, and ultra-deep targeted Duplex sequencing, we will characterize the changes that occur within the tumor genomes and gene regulation that allow tumor cells to evade immune killing by CAR T-cells. Together, our approach will provide a comprehensive portrait of T-cell and tumor cell contributors to therapy response, and will inform the improvement of future cancer immunotherapies.

column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an incurable disease with a 50% 5-year mortality rate. In PAH, the walls of arteries in the lung become inflamed and thicken, which effectively means less blood can flow through to become oxygenated. The increased resistance to pulmonary blood flow creates back-pressure on the heart, which hinders its ability to pump blood effectively. Our understanding of what triggers the cascade of inflammation in PAH is limited, and because of this, there are no targeted treatments available. My doctoral work will investigate a new theory that dysfunctional immune cells found in the blood that flows through the arteries of the lung secrete factors that mediate inflammation in PAH. As we age, our cells divide and can acquire DNA mutations. In our white blood cells, the accumulation of certain mutations over time can lead to cancers like leukemia. However, since this is a progressive process, there are individuals whose immune cells have started to acquire DNA mutations but who have no overt cancer. That is not to say that these mutations are benign, however. We now know that some genetic mutations render white blood cells dysfunctional by making them secrete more pro-inflammatory molecules than healthy white blood cells. Our lab has found that it is common for PAH patients to have mutations in two key genes. These genes, dnmt3a and tet2, act as a lock and key, respectively, to control which parts of the DNA blueprint are accessible. With a broken lock-and-key system, DNA access, and therefore protein production, can be erratic - in the case of dnmt3a and tet2 mutations, for example, preliminary data suggests that pro-inflammatory proteins are overproduced. For my PhD research, I will characterize exactly how DNMT3A and TET2 mutations in our white blood cells mediate pulmonary hypertension. We may then be able to develop new targeted anti-inflammatory therapies (or re-purpose existing ones) to address the underlying problem in PAH.

column36: Elucidating the Impact of Allergen-Specific B Cell Frequency and Affinity on Allergic Reactivity Using Patient-Derived Antibody Sequences in Mouse Models of Peanut Allergy
column37: Peanut allergy is becoming increasingly common in Canada with serious consequences for Canadians' health. When a person with peanut (PN) allergy ingests PN, they can experience a range of symptoms from discomfort to anaphylaxis, a potentially deadly form of shock. PN allergy is among the most common and severe food allergies, yet it is unknown what drives its development or severity. Allergic symptoms in PN allergy are caused by antibodies. Antibodies are proteins that bind to specific targets with a particular binding strength. They then direct immune responses against their bound target. Antibodies that tightly bind to bacterial or viral proteins protect against infection. However, there are many types of antibodies, not all of which are beneficial. Allergic reactions occur when immunoglobulin E (IgE) type antibodies bind to allergens. Normally, antibody binding strength promotes immune responses, but we have observed the opposite effect for IgE responses. Antibodies are secreted by a type of immune cell called a B cell. Non-activated B cells have antibodies in a receptor form, but only when B cells are activated can they begin to secrete their antibodies. It is not known what activates PN-binding B cells to begin to secrete IgE-type antibodies. I hypothesize that PN-binding IgE responses are promoted when greater numbers of PN-binding B cells with lower PN-binding strength are present. To test this hypothesis, I will use the latest advances in CRISPR-Cas9 genetic editing technology and sequences of PN-binding IgE antibody genes from real PN-allergic patients to generate mice with different amounts and strengths of PN-binding B cells. These mice will then be put through a mouse model of food allergy and the impact of their B cells' PN-binding characteristics will be assessed. This research could reveal why some individuals develop PN allergy and not others and may one day predict the severity of an individual's PN allergy even before it develops.

column36: Brain imaging as a preclinical biomarker of chronic pain
column37: Chronic pain is a debilitating condition in which patients have ongoing pain and perceive normally innocuous stimuli (e.g. light touch) as painful. A major roadblock to progress in pain research and analgesic drug development is that conventional methods of assessing pain in animals are time-consuming and often monitor withdrawal reflexes. Reflexes are generated by spinal cord circuits and thus do not adequately represent the complex pain experience, which has both brain-mediated sensory and emotional features. Global monitoring of brain activity (fMRI, EEG) in humans has identified distinct brain regions that are critical to the pain experience and there have been efforts to adapt these for animal studies. However, these techniques lack the resolution necessary to probe the activity of distinct neural circuits within the brain, making it impossible to correlate activity patterns with behavioural measures of chronic pain. To address this problem, first, I will use powerful imaging techniques to record the activity of hundreds of individually identifiable nerve cells in the brains of awake and freely-moving mice, before, during and after a chronic pain develops. Second, I will correlate the neural activity of pain-processing regions in the brain with non-reflex-based measures of rodent pain using the Mouse Grimace Scale (MGS). The MGS, developed at McGill University, monitors pain and discomfort by scoring facial expression patterns and provides a more objective way to assay pain in mice. To induce chronic pain, I will use the spared nerve injury mouse model of neuropathic pain, which our lab developed. By combining these imaging and behavioural approaches, I expect to identify unique pain-related neural circuit activity patterns, which may serve as biomarkers for chronic pain. A reliable biomarker will allow us to accurately and objectively assess treatment efficacy in preclinical analgesic drug development studies.

vessel abnormalities to those who have no abnormalities, and test whether the number of EPCs is related to the development of memory or thinking problems over time.If we find that older adults with blood vessel abnormalities have more EPCs and that more EPCs are related to fewer memory and thinking problems, our study may explain why some people who have blood vessel abnormalities in their brain do not develop memory or thinking problems easily.This study will clarify how EPCs and memory or thinking problems are related and may indicate if EPCs could be used as a treatment to delay the column37: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the most common pancreatic cancer (~93%) and the most lethal solid tumor type in Canada, with a 5 year survival rate of 8%. The Canadian Cancer Society estimated 5800 new cases and 5300 deaths due to pancreatic cancer in 2019. Furthermore, pancreatic cancer incidence continues to rise and is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States by 2030. There remains no effective treatment or detection method for this devastating disease and new strategies are desperately needed. The refractory nature of PDAC has been attributed to its unique fibrotic tumor microenvironment (TME), which comprises 70-85% of tumor mass and is known to protect tumors from the effects of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. The PDAC TME is composed of a dense fibrotic matrix and an abundance of Cancer Associated Fibroblasts (CAFs) within a harsh environment. We believe that this harsh environment likely induces damage in the non-mutated CAFs and activates the stress response of senescence, which includes cell cycle arrest and the secretion of immune mediators. While senescent CAFs have been implicated in immunosuppression of skin cancer, their presence and role in PDAC remains unexplored. We have identified senescent CAFs in the PDAC TME of patient samples and mouse models. We hypothesize that these senescent CAFs contribute to immunosuppression and immunotherapy resistance in PDAC. To test this hypothesis, we will first assess the effects of senescent CAF depletion and co-implantation on the growth and biology of tumors in PDAC mouse models. Second, we will identify cellular, secreted, and transcriptional regulators of the senescent CAF phenotypes, to identify actionable molecular targets that can be targeted in PDAC combination immunotherapy strategies. Our work will provide novel insight into the PDAC TME and contribute to much needed progress in understanding and treating this lethal disease.

column36: L'impact de l'hypoglycemie neonatale sur le neurodeveloppement des nouveau-nes prematures
column37: Au Canada, 8% des bebes sont nes prematurement (avant la 37e semaine de grossesse). Ceux-ci sont particulierement a risque de developper des problemes visuels d'origine cerebrale (causes par des lesions au cerveau affectant le systeme visuel). L'une des principales causes de ces troubles visuels est l'hypoglycemie neonatale (taux de glucose sanguin trop faible). Bien que celle-ci affecte plus de 30% des nouveau-nes prematures, le lien entre l'hypoglycemie neonatale et les deficits visuels d'origine cerebrale n'a pas encore ete etudie dans cette population. L'objectif principal de notre etude est donc d'evaluer les effets de l'hypoglycemie neonatale sur le developpement du traitement cerebral visuel des nouveau-nes prematures a l'aide de l'electroencephalographie (EEG; technique utilisee pour mesurer l'activite electrique du cerveau). Nous croyons que plus l'hypoglycemie neonatale aura ete importante (en termes de severite, duree et nombre d'episodes), plus les reponses cerebrales associees au traitement visuel seront affectees chez les enfants nes prematurement. Afin de tester notre hypothese, 80 nouveau-nes a terme (apres 37 semaines de gestation) et 120 bebes nes prematurement (entre 28 et 36 semaines) seront evalues. Les taux de glucose seront collectes des la naissance. Puis, les participants seront vus pour des seances d'EEG a 3, 12, 24 et 36 mois. Les resultats de l'EEG seront compares entre les groupes (nouveau-nes prematures avec et sans hypoglycemie neonatale, nouveau-nes a terme) a chaque temps de mesure afin d'evaluer le developpement du systeme visuel des differents groupes durant l'enfance. Les analyses statistiques permettront d'evaluer le lien entre l'hypoglycemie neonatale, la prematurite et le developpement visuel. Cette etude permettra de mieux comprendre le role de l'hypoglycemie neonatale dans le developpement visuel des nouveau-nes prematures afin d'offrir les meilleurs soins aux bebes a risque de developper des atteintes visuelles importantes.

column36: Instrumented i-GRASP for the assessment and treatment of upper extremity function after neurological injury
column37: Neurological conditions such as stroke and traumatic brain injury can seriously impair one's ability to use their arm and hands for essential activities of daily living. We have previously developed the Graded Repetitive Arm Supplementary Program (GRASP) which has been shown in a multi-site randomized controlled trial to improve upper extremity function after stroke through hundreds of repetitions of the arm, hand and fingers, as well as strengthening exercises. It is utilized in over 3000 sites and is part of the Canadian Stroke Best Practice Recommendations. Under ideal supervisory conditions, the program is effective, but adherence is problematic as it is difficult to keep track of the many repetitions, can be challenging to know how to continually make the tasks harder, and lacks feedback to motivate individuals to do the exercise. I-GRASP will solve these issues by developing an instrumented platform derived from the evidence-based GRASP program where patients will be able to 1) measure their own upper extremity function, 2) improve their function through progressive exercises and 3) and receive feedback to help motivate their progress. Our team is a collaboration between engineer and health care researchers and our partners include a wearable sensor company, a public sector rehabilitation hospital, and a private rehabilitation clinic to ensure the relevance of our product. The proposed technology to measure, motivate and enhance hand function will improve the lives of individuals with stroke and will be applicable to other populations with hand problems. The project will also advance technologies related to smart materials and wearable sensors. Lastly, the research has great potential for commercialization by the industry partner Texavie and to potentially open new markets for rehabilitation technology that can be accessed by health providers and stroke survivors.

column36: Next Generation Micro-ultrasound Technology for Detection and Monitoring of Prostate Cancer
column37: In this project, we propose to combine three Canadian advancements in ultrasound imaging to implement a new and accurate solution for detection and monitoring of cancer. We will use prostate cancer (PCa) as a test case. This is the second most common cancer in Canadian men, with about 25,000 new cases per year, and the expected global market for diagnosis and monitoring of PCs is $27B CAD/year by 2021. Accurate detection of aggressive PCa enables effective treatment of patients through surgical excision of the prostate with minimal risk for recurrence of disease. It also allows continuous monitoring of cancer progression, which is key to improve quality of life, reduce morbidity and increase patient survival. However, current detection and monitoring methods are not robust: the established ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy is unable to accurately locate tumors, and recently developed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) approaches to visualize PCa have a very high rate of false positives and miss small and possibly aggressive cancer. Furthermore, MRI is very costly and not widely available in Canada except in large, urban centres, leading to delayed diagnosis with worse clinical outcomes. Our unique technology promises to capture changes in prostate tissue at high-resolution. We will validate this in patients with the help of our principal knowledge translation partner, Exact Imaging. In addition, we will bring together experts across natural sciences and clinical sciences with clinicians who will use the technology, at the Vancouver Prostate Centre. We will follow best practices in incorporation of sex and gender diversity in recruitment and research, and will train two PhD students, three undergraduate students, three urology fellows and one research engineer.

column36: Development of a near-care diagnostic test for Lyme disease
column37: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne illness in North America. New cases of Lyme disease are on the rise throughout Canada, which has prompted increased awareness of the disease and raised issues with the currently available tests used for diagnosis. The current tests rely on detection of antibodies found in the patient's blood that are produced in response to bacteria that cause Lyme disease. Because these antibody responses develop over time and vary with degree of infection, the test can be problematic for diagnosing early infection, which may delay antibiotic therapy. Recently, there has been a push to identify additional non-antibody Lyme disease markers for use in diagnosis. This research will use a sensitive and powerful protein discovery approach to mine blood samples for new markers of Lyme disease. The proteins identified will be used to develop an improved test for detecting Lyme disease.

column36: Clinical Advancement of an AAV Lung Gene Therapy Platform for the Treatment of Monogenic Lung Diseases
column37: Monogenic lung diseases (MLDs) include a variety of disorders that cause chronic lung disease. These diseases often begin in early childhood, lead to respiratory failure and early death, and have few targeted therapies. Surfactant protein deficiencies are a group of severe MLDs caused by mutations in the genes encoding for surfactant proteins A, B, C, and D as well as the ATP-binding cassette sub-family A member 3 (ABCA3). Surfactant protein B (SPB) deficiency is the most severe, leading to respiratory failure after full-term birth. Treatment with exogenous surfactant provides only transient improvement and without lung transplantation, SPB is lethal within the first year of life. MLDs are amenable to targeted delivery of viral vectors via intratracheal administration. Further, as SPB only affects the lungs, targeted delivery of gene therapy to the respiratory tract should be sufficient to treat this disease. We have engineered an innovative viral vector (AAV6.2FF) to treat SPB. AAV6.2FF selectively transduces alveolar type II cells (AT2) cells that produce surfactant and leads to rapid expression of SPB. Our compelling preliminary data in SPB-conditional knockout mice (Kang et al., in revision at Nat Commun) shows that AAV6.2FF efficiently transduces AT2 cells, delivers SPB to the lungs, and dramatically improves lung function and survival. These results demonstrate the promise of AAV6.2FF to treat, and potentially cure, SPB. Our goal is to advance AAV6.2FF gene therapy to clinical trials for the treatment of a variety of MLDs. We will expand our lung gene therapy platform to achieve the following objectives: 1.Evaluate safety and transducing efficiency of AAV6.2FF in neonatal lambs 2.Extend the therapeutic application of AAV6.2FF to other MLDs By combining our expertise in viral vectors, lung biology, and stem cells we aim to develop a variety of clinical trial-ready AAV6.2FF vectors that will transform the treatment of MLDs.

column36: Synthetic biology approaches to design living medicines to improve intestinal and metabolic health.
column37: The gut microbiota plays a key role in strengthening the gut barrier by stimulating protective responses from the human intestine. Loss of epithelial barrier integrity, also known as a "leaky gut" can lead to low-grade inflammation and is linked to the development of a number of chronic diseases in humans, from inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and metabolic syndrome/type 2 diabetes to Parkinson's disease, chronic kidney disease and even certain cancers. Because of its far-reaching impact on these chronic diseases, there is an unmet need to develop new strategies to counteract the detrimental systemic consequences of a leaky gut. In this project, we will design probiotic bacteria that will increase the levels of a microbial product, called MDP, which targets a host protein called NOD2. We have shown that NOD2 activation can fight against a leaky gut and promote healing of the intestinal lining after injury. At the same time, NOD2 triggering can also improve metabolic health. Consequently, these probiotics could be used to protect and treat individuals with gut-related problems as well as metabolic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes.

column36: Engineering healing: Combinatorial strategies to promote repair of the stroke injured brain
column37: In Canada, it is estimated that stroke costs the Canadian economy almost $3 billion per year. Stem cell based therapies hold great promise for the treatment of stroke. This research will lay the foundation for clinical approaches to treat stroke by addressing current challenges with cell based therapies. Our team of researchers and industry partner will take advantage of innovations in stem cell biology, cell transplantation, and bioengineering to promote both tissue and functional repair in preclinical models of stroke. Our measures of success are functional assays - undoubtedly the most relevant outcome for translation. We will perform our studies in chronic stroke models, as chronic stroke has been less well studied despite the serious impacts including premature death, poor quality of life and large adverse economic effects on families, communities and society in general. With the goal of developing clinically relevant strategies to treat the stroke-injured brain we will combine a novel, proprietary human cell source engineered by our industry partner, that permits patient specific cells to be used for cell transplantation. These cells are outside of ethical concerns and able to avoid rejection after transplantation. Importantly, the cells are designed to only make brain specific cells so will not form inappropriate cell types following transplantation. We will combine the cell transplantation with novel bioengineered tools to deliver drugs that promote brain plasticity and cell survival by reducing the negative environmental factors found in the injured brain. Further, to enhance cell survival - a significant challenge for cell based therapies - our preclinical studies will utilize a novel, patented drug that inhibits cell death. Together, these preclinical studies using combinatorial strategies will set the stage for clinical trials to treat stroke.

column36: Development and validation of a clinically feasible, novel therapy for improving standing balance and reducing falls
column37: Many Canadians who have experienced a stroke or spinal cord injury/disease (SCI/D) have lifelong physical impairments, such as paralysis. This makes standing and maintaining one's balance difficult. Poor balance is associated with falls. About 70% of people living with stroke or SCI/D fall at least once/year. Falls result in injuries, hospital admissions and reduced quality of life. Our objective is to create a therapy using functional electrical stimulation (FES) combined with video games that can effectively improve standing balance for people with a high fall risk. FES involves applying electrical currents to weak or paralyzed muscles. We have shown, in a small number of people with SCI/D, that FES combined with video games can improve standing balance. In the current project, we will develop a wireless FES system that can be easily used in hospitals and clinics. People with stroke or SCI/D, clinicians, researchers and representatives from industry will work together to develop the wireless system. Then we will test the system with twenty people living with stroke or SCI/D to study the system's effectiveness at improving balance ability. Participants will attend 18 training sessions over 6 weeks. Clinical and lab-based measures of balance ability will be collected before and after training. We will also ask ten physical therapists from three rehabilitation hospitals to learn how to use the wireless FES system and to try it with three of their clients. We will conduct interviews with the participants with stroke or SCI/D and physical therapists to collect their feedback on the usability of the wireless FES system. Our industry partner will be involved with the development and commercialization of the wireless FES system, ensuring the system becomes accessible to people with paralysis and clinicians. The outcomes will lead to fewer falls and injuries for those with SCI, resulting in greater participation in daily activities and increased quality of life.

column36: Integrating a low-barrier drug checking platform into public health responses to overdose
column37: Measures to ensure a safer drug supply are an essential component of reducing overdose deaths. Fentanyl test strips are fast, sensitive, and cheap, but cannot provide any information on potency, purity, or the existence of other harmful adulterants. There is an urgent need for technologies that can identify all components present and provide information on the concentration of active ingredients. British Columbia is the epicenter of Canada's overdose crisis and Vancouver Island experiences overdose deaths rates more than twice the national average. Researchers and student trainees at the University of Victoria are leaders in employing portable spectroscopy to drug checking as a public health response to overdose. In collaboration with Island Health Authority, we propose to expand on our current drug checking services to champion one technology which has the potential to meet all needs: highly sensitive to detect low concentrations, low cost to enable broad distribution, and ease of use to either eliminate, or significantly reduce the need for scientists to operate instruments and interpret results. We are a unique collaboration of Chemistry and Social Work supported by Computer Sciences working within a Patient Oriented Research framework that engages health care users, health care providers and health system decision makers. Our experience in operating a suite of the best portable spectrometers available in health and harm reduction settings informs this proposal to construct and implement an integrated platform that continues technological advances to improve portability, capability, speed and accuracy but also at a lower-cost and with a user interface that does not require employing highly trained technicians. Our project proposes a drug checking platform that has the potential to overcome the obstacles of instrument and staffing costs to facilitate public health to most fully integrate drug checking within the overdose strategies.

column36: Next Generation Platelet Storage Devices for Safe and Efficient Transfusion
column37: This research addresses serious challenges associated with blood transfusion: quality of stored platelets and the prevention of bacterial growth. Platelet transfusion is used for treating patients suffering e.g. from cancer and excessive blood loss (accident victims). In North America, approximately 4.5 million units of platelets are transfused every year. Currently platelets are stored in plastic containers which are originally not designed to store platelets at room temperature. There is very little innovation in platelet storage over the years. The quality of stored platelets decreases due to the surface induced damage by the current conventional storage bags. Transfusion of bacterial contaminated platelets is another longstanding serious complication. The incidence of bacterial contamination associated with platelet storage is as high as 1 per every 1500 units and represents a huge cost as every platelet unit is tested for contamination to avoid septic reactions in patients. Thus improving the quality of stored platelets, shelf-life and develop methods to prevent bacterial growth will significantly availability, reduce the wastage and increase transfusion efficiency. Our project seeks novel platelet storage devices based on latest breakthroughs at UBC on novel one-step universal antibiofilm coating and inhibitors that scavenge platelet activating molecules. The proposed device will improve the quality of stored platelets and increase the shelf-life by providing an environment that is highly cell compatible in comparison to the current storage bags. We anticipate that this will extend the storage life of platelets significantly compared to the current 5 days. Importantly this new device can be used in conjunction with the newly approved pathogen inactivation technologies by improve the platelet quality. The benefits over current methods will be substantial as it avoid wastage and increase safety and have significant cost savings to our health system.

column36: Determiner la qualite de la polypharmacie chez les aines : une approche basee sur l'intelligence artificielle
column37: La prise de plusieurs medicaments, la polypharmacie, est de plus en plus commune, surtout chez les personnes agees. Pour l'instant, il n'est pas possible de bien departager quelles polypharmacies apportent des benefices et quelles sont inappropriees. En effet, le nombre de combinaisons de medicaments possibles est imposant, et prendre en compte les caracteristiques individuelles de chacune des personnes rend la situation tres complexe. L'intelligence artificielle permettra de comprendre ces elements pour en degager des normes. Nous utiliserons les donnees du Systeme integre de surveillance des maladies chroniques du Quebec qui contiennent les informations sur les reclamations de medicaments pour l'ensemble des aines du Quebec depuis 1996, de meme que les informations sur les services medicaux, les hospitalisations et les deces. Ces donnees, decrivant l'exposition aux medicaments de chaque individu, permettront d'entrainer un systeme expert base sur l'intelligence artificielle pour etablir quelles combinaisons, sequences, durees de traitement sont associees a des effets negatifs (ex. hospitalisations, deces) et lesquelles les evitent en tenant compte des conditions medicales et sociodemographiques de la personne. L'analyse de ces donnees pourrait engendrer des enjeux ethiques, legaux et sociaux que nous explorerons afin d'assurer que les resultats ne conduisent pas a accroitre d'eventuelles inegalites dans les traitements que nous observons presentement entre differents sous-groupes de la population. Les resultats serviront a developper la surveillance de la polypharmacie dans la population et apporteront des connaissances nouvelles sur l'usage de medicaments qui pourraient changer la pratique clinique. De nouvelles avenues de recherche en intelligence artificielle seront egalement explorees, permettant le developpement de cette discipline en sante.

column36: Applying machine learning to 3D tumor histopathology for predicting patient outcomes
column37: The evaluation of biopsy samples from tumours has been used for decades by pathologists to assist in the diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis estimation for cancer patients. In order to improve outcomes for patients with cancer we need to develop improved and more accurate methods for histological analyses. We propose the development of techniques to enable three-dimensional (3D) histopathology of cancer biopsies powered by machine learning-based image analysis for prognosis prediction. We will develop a method to process human lung tumour biopsies that enable detailed sub-cellular 3D imaging, develop machine learning based algorithms to segment and quantify biological features from the 3D images, and use the features measured from the 3D images to train a model to predict patient outcomes (overall survival, treatment efficacy) from the information measured from the 3D imaging. This approach will allow us to measure key and new information about a patient's tumour that cannot be accurately measured using current methods. We have built a team of key interdisciplinary academic and industrial collaborators (Drs. Chan, Martel, Tsao, and Hwang, and Google Canada and Huron Digital Pathology) with expertise in imaging, machine learning, cancer pathology and bioengineering. Through these partnerships we have the ability to translate the technology generated into commercial products for the analysis of 3D histopathology images and tools to assist in predicting patient outcomes from the large amount of patient data generated from 3D imaging. Finally, we have developed a training plan that teaches researchers from different academic backgrounds to work together to solve pressing clinical issues and to translate the technological developments.

column36: Robotically assisted real-time metabolomic navigation of breast conserving surgery
column37: Breast cancer affects 1 in 8 women during their lives and is the second-leading cause of female cancer related deaths. The ideal treatment is breast-conservation surgery during its early stage to remove the cancer while conserving healthy parts of the breast. Wirth current resection methods, on average, one out of every three women undergoing breast-conservation surgery needs at least one additional surgery due incomplete tumor resection. Repeat surgery leads to increased risk of postoperative complications, impaired cosmetics, delayed radiation therapy, increased psychological distress, and increased costs and risks of undergoing a second general anesthesia. Repeat surgery often leads to full mastectomy, which is a traumatic experience for a patient who expected a curative treatment with breast-conservation. As early stage breast cancer is not palpable or visible, surgeons tend to apply generous "safety margins" around the target tumor and remove a great deal of healthy breast tissue. In current practice, up to 40% of patients who undergo breast-conservation surgery experience severe breast deformity that requires surgical reconstruction, but over half of these women do not get treated due to lack reconstructive surgical capacity. In this research, we aim to develop NaviKnife, a next-generation breast conserving surgery navigation system to achieve complete tumor resection with minimal tissue loss. NaviKnife builds on novel multiparametric ultrasound imaging to accurately target the cancer prior to resection and novel real-time metabolomic tissue typing to identify and trace the tumor boundary during resection while guided by a simple robotic arm. NaviKnife assists the surgeon in precise tumor resection and allows for systematic probing of the resection cavity for residual cancer and, if necessary, guides the surgeon in targeted shaving of the cavity wall with minimal loss of healthy tissue, thus guaranteeing complete tumor removal before the wound is closed.

column36: Automated placenta screening to improve maternal lifetime cardiovascular health
column37: The placenta is a critical organ of pregnancy, responsible for the exchange of all gases and nutrients between the mother and fetus. When the development or function of the placenta becomes compromised, common diseases of pregnancy can arise (e.g., hypertension in pregnancy, fetal growth restriction). It is now known that these diseases, which result from a damaged placenta, are significant risk factors for the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD) later in life. CVD is a leading cause of death for women. As such, several hospitals now run specialized follow up clinics for women following a pregnancy with placental disease, where their cardiovascular health is screened and prevention programs are offered. These clinics are a wonderful approach to tackle CVD in women, however, they are very expensive to run and are probably unnecessary for all women with placental disease, as ~50% of women referred to these clinics are later deemed to be at low risk for CVD. Our previous work has demonstrated that particular types of damage in the placenta, which can be seen under a microscope, are strongly associated with CVD risk at follow up. Unfortunately, visual screening by specialized pathologists is impractical as it is costly and unavailable in smaller hospitals and health care settings. The current research proposal will tackle this challenge, using machine learning methods to enable a computer to learn how to automatically detect these visual patterns in images of placentas from women who have high CVD risk. If successful, the developed technology will help streamline the identification and referral of high-priority women to cardiovascular screening and intervention programs in a cost- effective and timely fashion, ultimately improving the cardiovascular health of these women.

column36: Enhancing cell therapies using microfluidic encapsulation strategies
column37: Cell-based therapies hold tremendous potential to repair damaged tissue but the central problem confronting ALL cell-based therapeutics lies in promoting meaningful long-term engraftment of transplanted cells. Recently, we developed a novel microfluidic platform to encapsulate cardiovascular progenitor cells in protective hydrogel cocoons, promoting cell viability while improving engraftment within injured tissue and providing markedly improved therapeutic benefits. However, this therapeutic effect is ultimately ephemeral as transplanted egress their protective hydrogel microcapsules rapidly and typically fail to be retained for more than a few additional days in the targeted tissue, thus limiting their full therapeutic impact. Our vision is to overcome these limitations by exploiting the ability of cell-type specific biomaterials and by using novel microencapsulation strategies to extend cell viability, while ensuring tissue persistence upon engraftment, ultimately promoting therapeutic repair of injured tissue. With broad implications in cellular therapeutics, we have found that this is particularly relevant to chronic lung disease of prematurity, the main complication of preterm birth, to the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and to cardiac injury repair, in which we have shown the protective effects of MSCs, EPCs and EDCs in vivo. We are working with Northern Therapeutics, a Canadian biotechnology company, to ensure this research will be widely applicable to the field of regenerative medicine, be of marked benefit to chronically ill patients, aide in the global competitiveness of a Canadian company, and stimulate economic development in Canada in an emerging new market.

column36: Reducing vibrations to improve infant patient safety during transportation
column37: Each year, thousands of newborns in Canada are transported by air or ground ambulance to receive specialized medical care. These infants are often premature and especially vulnerable during transport. Vibration exposure during transport may contribute risk of serious long-term consequences including brain injury. To decease risk during transport, specialized equipment is used. However, vibration levels experienced by infants and contributing factors are not well understood. This lack of knowledge affects the ability to transport newborn patients in the safest manner possible. Our goal is to increase the safety of infant transport by reducing vibration exposure. We propose a research program which seeks to understand how vibrations caused by the road and air environments are transferred to the infant. This will allow us to propose novel methods to reduce vibration exposure and improve the equipment for transporting fragile infants. We will measure vibrations in many transport scenarios including within hospitals as well as in ground ambulances, helicopters, and airplanes. The results will be used to develop test equipment and procedures for evaluating the transport equipment. This research will enable better understanding of the problem and provide a reliable way to test the transport equipment and procedures. It will lead to new tools for planning routes that minimize vibration and for monitoring patient vibration. Our research brings together expertise in pediatrics and engineering to study novel solutions to this problem. The team includes engineers from Carleton University and physicians from large children's hospitals (CHEO in Ottawa, SickKids in Toronto). The physicians represent a provincial committee tasked with providing advice and recommendations to improve safety, quality of care, and the patient's and family's experience. This collaboration will ensure that the results are communicated to the clinicians who can impact positive change.
