column36: Optimization of an ex vivo heart perfusion device for pre-transplant preservation and evaluation of donor hearts
column37: Cardiac related diseases are a leading cause of death for Canadians. For definitive treatment of end-stage heart failure, cardiac transplantation remains the gold standard therapy. A short supply of donor organs however, limits the wider application of this life saving intervention. Compounding this problem is a high frequency of poor heart function observed in the multi-organ donor. This results in a low utilization rate of hearts that are offered. We are developing a device that will provide continuous warm blood-based perfusion of the donor heart, permitting optimal preservation of the organ. As well, functional assessment of the heart and potential treatment can be undertaken over a longer period of time, opening the window for an increase in the number of available hearts and the time available to carry out the transplant. The development, optimization and proving of this device is a collaboration between academics in Medicine and Engineering with the support of a company aimed at commercializing the device.

column36: Impacts of the new Reseau Express Metropolitain (REM) on mobility, health and equity: A pre-post intervention study
column37: In 2016, the Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec (CDPQ) announced plans to build the Reseau express metropolitain (REM), a state-of-the-art, $6.3 billion public transport project that will link numerous suburbs-and the airport-to downtown Montreal with frequent rail service. The undertaking is expected to impact all residents of the Montreal metropolitan region at various scales and in various ways. This research project will concentrate on measuring the impacts of such major infrastructure project on the health, social, environmental, economic, physical, and psychological wellbeing of all Montreal residents, before, during and after the construction. This is an unprecedented opportunity to study a major public transport project of this scale in the Canadian context. The last time a major public transport project of this size was built in the 1970s. The lessons it will teach are particularly timely. Even before the REM's completion, regional and provincial officials are already discussing expansions. At the same time, the federal government is pledging to support similar projects across Canada as part of its efforts to improve equity and combat the climate crisis. To our knowledge, no comprehensive study has been planned to fully assess the REM's possibly profound impacts on travel behaviour and public health. Several sections of the REM are already under construction and slated to open in 2021. Construction on others has yet to begin, giving us a brief window to conduct research to measure how the REM's impact is felt at various stages of development and operation. In the end, the research will help policymakers and planners make better-informed decisions about major public investments to improve Canadians health and welfare.

column36: Improved organ transplant across the ABO barrier through enzymatic removal of antigens
column37: Waitlists for organ transplants are often extremely lengthy due to the need to identify available donor organs that are a good "match" to the patient requiring the transplant. This process of "matching" involves identifying organs that have similar external "markers" known as antigens, to those on the patients own tissues. Amongst the antigens that have to be matched are those that distinguish A, B and O type blood from each other. The relevant antigens on red blood cells are in fact very simple sugar molecules. A,B and O red blood cells all share a common substructure of sugars, but A and B red blood cells differ in each having one extra sugar attached. The applicants have recently developed a way of removing that additional sugar with enzymes so that they can convert A or B red blood cells to O type red blood cells. They are currently testing the safety of the Universal" O type blood so developed. In this proposal the ability of these same enzymes to remove these antigens from the surface of donated human organs will be tested and the safety and use of the modified organs will be thoroughly tested. If successful this would allow the organs from A and B blood type individuals to be converted into O type organs. This would improve the odds of transplant patients obtaining matching organs, which would increase survival patient rates.

column36: Development of a non-invasive positron detector to measure the arterial input function for pharmacokinetic modelling in dynamic positron emission tomography imaging
column37: Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging has proven to be a useful tool in diagnosing cancer and cardiac diseases and has an increasingly important role in providing earlier diagnosis in several disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. PET studies evaluate the metabolism of a particular organ or tissue by using radioactive tracers made by attaching a radioactive atom to chemical substances that are naturally used by the particular organ or tissue during its metabolic process. This way. information about the functionality and anatomy of the organ or tissue is evaluated, as well as its biochemical properties. Thus, PET may detect biochemical changes in an organ or tissue that can identify the onset of a disease process before anatomical changes related to the disease can be seen with other imaging modalities. The radioactive tracer is administered into the patient before the PET scan. The measurement of the radioactive tracer concentration in blood, the input function (IF), is a necessary input for PET kinetic modelling to quantify tissue function. The IF is usually derived from multiple blood samples drawn from an arterial cannula and processed to obtain the radioactive tracer concentration in plasma. Unfortunately, the invasive withdrawal of arterial blood is a significant discomfort to the patient. The goal of this project is to develop and optimize a non-invasive, wrist detector that will be placed on the wrist of the patient, and subsequently measure the arterial IF through detection of passing emitted positrons.

column36: Epigenetic PowerBlade - DNA Precision Marks for Critical Illness
column37: Sepsis, whole body inflammation and organ failure triggered by an overwhelming and unbalanced response to infection, incurs enormous human and health care costs. Globally, over 30 million people are affected each year, at least a quarter of whom will die. The sequelae include physical, mental, and psychological disability. Currently, no specific treatments exist. For cancer patients, personalizing treatment on the basis of molecular characteristics of a tumor is simply 'good practice'. There is an urgent need to do the same for sepsis. We have identified 'tags' on DNA (DNA methylation marks) that can classify septic vs. non-septic patients, the likelihood of poor outcomes (death and organ failure) and response to therapy (blood pressure medications). In parallel, our partners have developed and patented a point-of-care device that uses an innovative microfluidic approach to isolate DNA from whole blood. We propose to adapt this technology to develop a prototype able to perform automated measurements of DNA marks from patients using whole blood; to test our device on banked DNA and whole blood samples; to use predictive modeling to integrate clinical and molecular data to validate outcome prediction and response to therapy in an independent cohort; and to test the performance of our prototype and precision marks prospectively in a real-world situation. Both the technology and biomarker detection approaches have never been tried for sepsis before. This proposal brings together bioengineers, health research scientists, bioinformaticians, physicians and clinical biochemists. Successful completion will provide a Lab-on-chip technology employing low-cost industrially manufacturable polymer microfluidic devices powered by an advanced patented centrifugal microfluidic technology that promises to be a disruptive innovation in the way to integrate and deploy genomic knowledge practical devices that will impact clinical practices and the care of the critically ill.

column36: Optimization and preclinical testing of a sclerosing and embolizing gel for embolization of varicose veins
column37: Varicose veins are a part of a spectrum of manifestations of chronic vein disorders that are characterized by the occurence of blood reflux in incompetent veins leading to vein dilatation. Varicose veins are often observed in lower legs due valve failure of the great saphenous vein (GSV). Beside aesthetic concern, edema and pain, varicosities can lead to serious complications such as leg ulcers. The recent estimates of the prevalence of varicosities in the United States range from 15% among men to 28% in women. Varicose veins are also observed in gonadal veins causing severe abdominal pain in women and testicular pain and infertility in men. Gastro-esophageal varices veins are often observed in cirrhosis patient with portal hypertension leading to life threatening bleeding. Different techniques were proposed to treat varicose veins. Mechanical techniques such as ligation, stripping, occlusion with mechanical devices are used to prevent reflux whereas chemical ablation with sclerosant or thermal ablation with laser or radiofrequency probes aim to destroy the wall of the vein. These therapies are often used in combination and the results can be suboptimal leading to recurrence of symptoms and redo procedures leading to increase cost and deterioration of the quality of life. We have developed and patented a sclerosing and embolizing gel at CRCHUM made of chitosan a bio-absorbable gel combined with a sclerosant agent (Sodium Tetradecyl Sulfate). This gel is also visible under X-ray and ultrasound which allows safe delivery under imaging guidance. The gel was licensed to Cook Medical (USA), a world leader company in the development of medical device for interventional radiology. We propose in partnership with Cook Medical and Chitolytic, a canadian company supplying pharmaceutical grade chitosan, to develop a formulation specifically adapted for venous sclerotherapy and test it in a porcine venous model.

column36: The Liquid Cornea as an alternative to corneal transplantation: Pathway to Clinical trials
column37: Going blind is a top fear of most people. Corneal blindness occurs when the transparent front of the eye loses it clarity due to injury or disease. We have developed a "Liquid Cornea", which is basically a new way to repair corneas. Instead of relying on transplantation with donor tissues, which are in severe short supply with Canadian in some provinces waiting 2-3 years for surgery, we propose to fill perforated corneas or corneas needing replacement of the front tissues by anterior lamellar grafting, with a biomaterials-based formulation made from collagen-like peptides. However, to make it practical for clinical use, we have to develop a syringe-like delivery system that would allow the surgeon to mix up the formulation and apply within minutes. Also, for patients with severe disease/damage, we need to block the inflammation and scarring in order to restore vision. Our research strategy is to incorporate an anti-scarring drug that is already successfully tested in clinical trials by our partner Birch Biomed into our Liquid Cornea and deliver this through our Rapid Reconstitution Delivery Device (R2D2) and test it in mini-pigs using optical equipment developed with our partner, WinTerra Global. Successful completion of this project will allow us to apply for regulatory approval for a first-in-human clinical trial. The use of the Liquid Cornea instead of current donor tissue transplants will potentially allow for treatment of a significant proportion of the current 12.7 million patients still awaiting cornea transplantation due to the donor tissue shortfall. The R2D2 system will potentially allow for treatment of ulcers or perforations in ophthalmologists' clinics instead of an operating room that is needed for donor transplantation, resulting in faster healing time for patients and healthcare savings.

column36: Personalized Contingent Neurostimulation for Epilepsy by Machine Learning in Organic Brain Interfaces
column37: Epilepsy is a chronic, neurological condition characterized by unpredictable, disabling seizures. This devastating disorder increases mortality by 4 times and depression by 2 times population rates. Unfortunately, epilepsy is extremely common, affecting 1 in 100 people, and in 33% of cases, medications do not prevent seizures. An emerging technology to aid such patients with drug-resistant epilepsy is contingent neurostimulation devices. These devices are implanted in a patient so that they can detect epileptiform activity and electrically stimulate the nervous system to prevent/abort seizures. Recently, two commercial contingent neurostimulators have been approved for treating epilepsy. These devices have proven successful at reducing seizure activity, however their efficacy is low. In particular, they are very unlikely to produce seizure freedom, which is necessary to restore patient independence and quality of life. The primary reasons why existing neurostimulation devices have had such limited success are that: (a) they use rudimentary (sparse and large) electrodes that poorly interface with the brain and (b) they are extremely simplistic in their seizure detection and abortion capabilities due to the use of basic electronics as constrained by energy limitations of an implant. We propose to combine (a) the far superior brain-interfacing electrode technology from our partner Panaxium and (b) our energy-efficient state-of-the-art implantable electronic circuits that employ artificial intelligence for optimal seizure prediction and prevention - to greatly improve the seizure-freedom efficacy of the neuromodulation therapy for intractable epilepsy. Our team is uniquely well qualified for this project. It is led by an expert in low-power biomedical and computational electronics (Genov), an epilepsy neurosurgeon and an expert in brain neurophysiology (Valiante), and Panaxium's Technology Commercialization Leader and a 20-year industry veteran (Weinroth).

column36: Conditionally-Reprogrammed Primary Prostate Cancer Cells as Novel Models for Patient Therapy Prediction
column37: There are an ever-increasing number of treatments available for prostate cancer, however they can have considerable side-effects. A significant clinical problem is predicting how a prostate cancer patient will respond to a treatment. Experimental models to study prostate cancer are extremely limited compared to other cancer types which limits research into how prostate cancer is able to resist anti-cancer treatments. My research tackles this problem by growing prostate cancer cells from patient biopsies, using a specialized growth technique. These patient-derived tumor cells (PDCs) represent a promising solution since they are quick to grow and retain the original genetic and biological characteristics of patient tumors. Additionally, their lower cost and ability to be used in a range of experiments, including anti-cancer sensitivity testing, makes them an attractive tool for the early prediction of treatment response. Using this innovative technique, I have successfully generated 25 novel PDCs from both early stage and advanced prostate cancers. The aims of my project are to continue deriving a large representative panel of PDCs and to use them to predict clinical response to various treatments. I will treat these cells with anti-cancer treatments used in the clinic (hormone therapies, chemotherapy, radiation treatment), measure their survival, and then determine if this can predict how a patient will respond to a given treatment in the clinic. PDCs which have an exceptional response or resistance to anti-cancer treatments will be of particular interest for additional study. I will search for changes in the genetic material or proteins in these PDCs that may explain the altered response to treatments. Ultimately, my research will determine if PDCs are a promising approach for predicting how a prostate cancer patient will respond to different treatments. It will also provide new insights into why certain prostate cancer patients respond differently to treatments.

column36: CSPG targeting for lesion regeneration in multiple sclerosis.
column37: Primary phases of multiple sclerosis (MS) are quite well controlled by anti-inflammatory drugs. However, these early stages are invariably followed with disease longevity by an uncontrolled progressive form of the disease mostly due to the lack of pro-regeneration therapies. Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) are one family of molecules known to exert inhibition of axonal regeneration in preclinical models of brain trauma. Recently, Dr Yong's group described that CSPGS are potent inhibitors of remyelination in mouse MS models, and that aging mice showed an increased deposition of CSPGs in their lesions. Concurrently, Dr Huard's group discovered a new natural ligand for CSPGs, expressed in MS lesions, A proliferation inducing ligand (APRIL). Drs Yong and Huard have thus combined their expertise in this project to test whether CSPG inhibition by APRIL may help induce regeneration in multiple sclerosis lesions. If so, this will have a considerable impact on regenerative biology in general and MS in particular.

column36: A randomized control trial of a novel approach to cognitive training in public safety personnel with post traumatic stress injuries
column37: Research concerning the effects of trauma exposure among public safety personnel (PSP) focuses primarily on its emotional consequences (e.g., increased irritability; hypervigilance) with little attention paid to the effects of trauma exposure on cognition. Critically, persistent cognitive difficulties (e.g., in concentration and planning) have been observed among PSP with post-traumatic stress injuries (PTSI), including those exposed to the 9/11 attacks. Difficulties with memory, concentration and planning reduce the ability to benefit from therapy and from medications available for treatment of PTSIs, and are associated with poor functional outcomes, including the ability to return to work and to function within a family. Despite this knowledge, very little attention has been paid to treatment approaches that seek to reduce cognitive difficulties among individuals with PTSIs, and, no work has addressed this issue among PSP. Not only is there an urgent need to identify evidence-based interventions for treatment of changes in cognitive functioning among PSP with PTSI, but it is also critical that research identify clearly any changes in brain structure and functioning that may occur as the result of participation in this cognitive intervention. Utilizing a highly experienced, multi-disciplinary team of clinicians, social and health scientists, and policy makers, we propose to examine the effectiveness of a well-established cognitive remediation strategy, Goal Management Therapy, aimed at improving cognitive functioning among PSP with PTSIs. In addition, we will examine expected changes in functioning (e.g., return to work) and in brain structure and brain functioning immediately following treatment and at three months post treatment. Working with the Public Services Health and Safety Association, we will widely disseminate our study findings in order to assist in reducing the tremendous burden of trauma-related illness among PSP in Canada and internationally.

column36: The Health and Economic burden of Cleft Lip/and or Palate (CLP) and the Cost-Effectiveness of Speech Care in Ethiopia
column37: Cleft lip and/or palate (CLP) is the most common craniofacial anomaly worldwide; however, speech therapy is often missing in low- and middle- income countries (LMICs). As normal speech is a primary goal of CLP management, speech therapy is crucial in helping correct CLP communication disorders. The estimated annual cost of untreated CLP communication disorders in an LMIC with a population comparable to Ethiopia is 17 million dollars. Speech therapy can help improve these communication deficiencies, thereby improving probability of employment and quality of life. In Ethiopia, there are an estimated 160,000 children born with CLP annually but only one center, Yekatit Hospital, providing speech care. The cost-effectiveness of interventions is an important consideration for clinicians and policy-makers in resource-limited settings. We performed a systematic review to summarize economic evaluations regarding CLP management in LMICs. All studies neglected speech care, reported only costs from the NGO perspective, and used outdated health values obtained in high-income countries. We are currently lacking evidence on the health and economic impact of CLP, and the value of different speech care models in an LMIC. Speech care will continue to be neglected by clinicians and policy-makers in Ethiopia and other LMICs without this data. First, we will measure health values and costs for pre- and post-primary cleft repair, with and without speech care from the perspective of Ethiopian patients and Ethiopian society. A pilot study was successfully conducted demonstrating the feasibility of carrying out this project. Using this data, we will conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis. We will then share the results with key stakeholders in Ethiopia to determine consensus on feasible interventions. This is the first study to provide evidence on the value of speech care for CLP in an LMIC, and thus has the potential to benefit children with CLP in many other low-resource settings.

column36: Patient Engagement in the Ethical Design of an Artificial-Intelligence-Based Heart Failure Remote Telemonitoring System
column37: Heart failure (HF) is a complex disease that occurs when the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the body's demands. HF affects over one million Canadians and is the most common reason for Canadians to be admitted to hospital. A multi-disciplinary group of researchers at the University Health Network (UHN) in Toronto developed 'Medly', a HF management mobile app. Patients can input their daily signs and symptoms into their phone and have their health care providers (HCPs) connected to the data to consistently care for and keep patients at home. While the use of Medly has improved patient quality of life and decreased hospital admissions by intervening early on HF concerns, there is a continuing unmet need for support of HF patients in the community. The UHN Medly team is partnering with the Vector Institute for artificial intelligence to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) might augment Medly's clinical capabilities and expand support to patients, including in more rural areas. 'AI Medly' would be the first AI-enabled mobile app in HF management in Canada. It is widely recognized that patient engagement is an essential component of the ethical design of AI-enabled applications in healthcare. However, patient engagement in AI research is a relatively new field, particularly in HF research. My doctoral research seeks to understand the unique perceptions and attitudes of patients and their caregivers about the use of remote monitoring and AI in HF care, engage their input in the design and implementation of 'AI Medly', and evaluate how 'AI Medly' affects their clinical care experience and health outcomes. My project aims to highlight the importance of the patient voice and will set a standard for AI-based research moving forward in Canada.

column36: Activity-based Therapy after Spinal Cord Injury or Disease: Development and Validation of a Tracking Tool Using the Delphi Method
column37: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) can be devastating to the person and very expensive for our health care system. Activity-based therapies (ABT) can help people with SCI recover some of their lost function, including legs, arms, hands, bowel, bladder and heart function. ABT are intensive requiring 1.5 to 3 hours a day, 3 to 5 times a week for several months. Even though ABT can reduce the strain on our healthcare system by helping people with SCI be healthier and more independent, it is rarely used in our rehabilitation centres. An ABT Summit meeting, held in March 2019 with over 40 experts, included people living with SCI. The members decided to focus on five goals for ABT research and practice. One of those goals was to develop a tool so people with SCI and health care workers could track participation in ABT, because this type of tool does not exist. The goal of this research study is to develop an ABT tracking tool. As a first step, we will do a library search of previous studies. Then we will run focus groups with people who have knowledge of ABT to find out what type of information they think we should include in an ABT tracking tool. For example, which types of activity-based movements to track and what details to include like duration and number of repetitions? We will then use this information to develop a survey for experts (people with SCI, physical and occupational therapists, community-based exercise trainers, hospital administrators, advocacy experts and ABT researchers) to rate the content to include in the ABT tool. The ABT tool we develop will be tested with 10 people with SCI and 10 therapists to see how well it works, how easy it is to use, how it could be improved and what challenges they had with the tool.The results from this study will be used to improve the tracking tool. An ABT tool will help us to collect important information in order to develop guidelines on how best to provide ABT to people with SCI, both in the hospital and community.

column36: Molecular and functional maturation of engrafted pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes
column37: Heart failure occurs when the heart loses its ability to pump blood; it is the second leading cause of death in Canada and kills more people than all cancers combined. There are specialized beating heart cells called cardiomyocytes that live in the heart muscle and are able to contract in synchrony with one another to push blood to every part of the body. When cardiomyocytes die or stop contracting as a result of a disease, the beating function of the heart is lost. Contrary to many cells in the human body, cardiomyocytes have a very low turn-over rate, therefore, the heart is unable to regenerate and recover its function after injury. My lab focuses on using stem cells, which are cells that can multiply and give rise to any cell type in the body, to generate cardiomyocytes that we transplant into failing hearts to evaluate their capacity to recover heart function. We have found that the electrical signals that coordinate heartbeats do not work properly until the third-week post-cell transplantation. We think this occurs because the cells we transplant are more similar to the cardiomyocytes found in fetal hearts rather than adult hearts and after spending some time in the adult heart, they begin to adapt and become more mature. However, the underlying processes that help these cells adjust to the heart are unknown. Therefore, the overarching aim of my project is to evaluate how the cardiomyocytes we transplant change over time and what kind of adaptations allow them to start beating in synchrony with the heart and recover its function. Ultimately, the results from these experiments will enable us to design strategies to trigger these adaptations in the cardiomyocytes we produce in the lab before transplantation. Consequently, this will help us determine if we can avoid the initial problems in electrical signalling. By solving this issue, the field will be able to overcome the main problem that is currently hindering the translation of this therapy into the clinic.

column36: Deregulation of Workplace Health and Safety: The Case of Occupational Health and Safety Law Reform in South Korea
column37: Work is integral to the health and well-being of individuals, their families and communities. This proposition, however, hinges on safe and healthy working environments for all workers. More than 2.8 million people across the world die at work every year due to poor occupational health and safety practices. South Korea (hereafter Korea), despite its high standard of living, has one of the highest rates of fatal occupational injuries among OECD countries, even after joining the ranks of "developed" nations. In the winter of 2018, the Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Act in Korea was revised after 28 years to reinforce corporate responsibility for ensuring a safe and healthy work environment for workers. This legislative reform, however, has been met with considerable opposition from victims' families, unions, and labour health activists, who have long envisaged more fundamental reform to address the root causes of serious work-related injuries and deaths, such as the outsourcing of dangerous work through elaborate networks of subcontracting. This research project aims to explore the ways in which the problem of work-related injuries and deaths is understood, problematized, and consequently addressed in Korea, especially throughout the recent legislative reform. I will conduct a critical discourse analysis of the law reform process, drawing on Foucault's notions of discourse and the power-knowledge nexus. Findings from this research will provide new insights into the ability of the revised OHS Act to protect workers' health and safety in Korea by explicating the concepts, assumptions and claims underlying the revised Act. It is my hope that this research will ultimately pave the way for implementing more adequate regulatory reforms that can promote safe and healthy working environments for all workers in Korea, and other emerging economies with similar problems so that 2.8 million workers across the world will no longer have to die for a living.

column36: Identifying Specific Receptor Mediated Mechanisms Underlying the Delivery of Nanoparticle Vehicles across the Blood Brain Barrier for the Treatment of Glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain tumor, accounting for 45% of malignant tumors in the central nervous system. First line treatment for glioblastoma is surgical resection followed by toxic doses of chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is used to shrink or eliminate cancer cells before and after surgery with the goal of reducing trauma from surgery and preventing cancer recurrence, respectively. Utilizing chemotherapy for these purposes in glioblastoma is difficult because chemotherapy delivers poorly to the brain. Chemotherapy delivery to the brain is limited by the blood brain barrier, a specialized network of blood vessels partitioning blood from the brain tissue environment. Nanotechnology provides an effective platform for enhancing chemotherapy delivery to the brain. Liposomes, nanoparticles composed of lipids, were first developed to exploit the passive transport of lipids across the blood brain barrier. This method enhances delivery to the brain relative to free drugs but overall delivery is low, numbering at 4% of the injected dose-a therapeutic quantity is 10% for solid tumors. This led to the addition of blood brain barrier receptor ligands to liposomes and other nanoparticles to increase delivery. The most effective ligands used to date are transferrin and insulin as their receptors are ubiquitous on the blood brain barrier. However, delivery only increases to 5% of the injected dose with these ligands. These approaches are deficient because they target receptors and transport mechanisms found widely across the body and not uniquely at the blood brain barrier. The objective of this project is to identify receptors specific to the blood brain barrier that transport nanoparticles with the goal of elucidating a blood brain barrier specific receptor and transport mechanism involved in nanoparticle uptake to guide brain targeted nanoengineering.

column36: Long-term outcomes after sepsis related critical illness in adult patients: time-trends, identification of high-risk subgroups and potential prevention strategies.
column37: The term sepsis is used to label severe infections that may produce widespread consequences. These are produced by the infection itself and the patient's response. Sepsis can result in the failure of everyday body functions, such as hypotension and injury to the kidneys, and up to 1 in 3 patients with severe infection may die within the first hospitalization. In addition, patients that survive severe infections may face long term consequences such as a decreased overall health condition and an increased risk of stroke and heart attacks. Elderly patients may be at higher risk of such consequences due to multiple factors including chronic diseases and the use of different medications to treat them. Moreover, the effect of sepsis on other related long term consequences such as the occurrence of clots in deep veins of legs or lungs remains unknown. Furthermore, there is not enough data on specific factors associated with these long term consequences in patients that survive a severe infection. Hence, the better delineation of both the burden and trends of long term effects of sepsis and the identification of subgroups of patients that may be at higher risk may aid in the clinical decision making process and the rational design of future studies. In addition, identifying potential therapies and ways to modify such risk may also prove relevant for clinical practice and patient centered treatment and outcomes. Hence, the present research proposal seeks to: 1) describe the occurrence and time trends of long term consequences (including stroke, heart attacks, kidney injury and venous clot formation) after severe infection in critically ill patients in Ontario, 2) identify factors that may help in the identification of patients at higher risk of these outcomes, with focus on baseline characteristics and the use of both chronic and new medications, 3) identify potential interventions that may reduce the overall long term consequences of severe infection among adult patients.

column36: Predicting psychiatric surgery outcomes using a machine learning approach to neuroimaging analysis
column37: Mental health illnesses like depression and obsessive compulsive disorder affects 1 in 4 worldwide. Nearly 20% of those affected do not improve, despite counselling and medications. In these treatment resistant patients, deep brain stimulation and other neurosurgical techniques allow for nearly 50% of patients to dramatically improve. Special types of neuroimaging, such a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), can be used to detect abnormalities in brain activity. Using fMRI and other imaging techniques, patterns can be determined which predict which patients are most likely to improve with treatment, and also which types of treatment a patient would most likely benefit from receiving. The data from patients who have already undergone these procedures will be used to create a formula which can be used to inform future patients about their likelihood of improving after each of the available treatments. column36: Robotic Surgery in Ontario: A Population-Based Retrospective Study of Outcomes and Costs
column37: Surgery of the abdomen and chest can be approached through either open or minimally invasive techniques. Open techniques are associated with longer patient recovery and more post-operative pain due to the length of the incision. Conversely, minimally invasive techniques use smaller incision and are therefore associated with less pain and faster recovery. Minimally invasive approaches include laparoscopic and robotic surgery. Laparoscopic surgery is affordable but uses straight instruments which at times can be ergonomically challenging. Robotic surgery is more expensive but uses articulating instruments that allow more degrees of freedom. Advocates of robotic surgery report improved range of motion and visibility with less surgeon fatigue and physiologic tremor. However, the benefits in patient-important outcomes after robotic surgery compared with laparoscopic or open procedures remain unclear and controversial. Preliminary analysis demonstrated that 5000 robotic procedures were performed in Ontario between 2006-2017; most frequently for management of prostate, uterus, kidney, rectum and lung conditions. Recently the Ontario Health Technology Advisory Committee recommended against publicly funding robotic prostate surgery due to minimal patient benefits and high cost. The goal of my project is to examine patient outcomes and costs after robotic surgery compared to laparoscopic and open surgery. This project will be the largest to date in Canada and will provide important information that would be critical in guiding funding decisions of robotic procedures in the future.

column36: Microglia Modulation to Protect the Developing Brain after Injury
column37: Cerebellar growth is highly vulnerable during the third trimester of pregnancy and could be affected by diverse insults leading to cerebellar growth failure and atrophy. Up to 19% of infants born extremely preterm will be affected by cerebellar injuries during their hospitalization. Despite a dramatic improvement of their survival and a major decrease in severe brain injury, almost 50% of infants born extremely preterm will suffer of long-term neurological impairments. We have developed the first animal model mimicking the most frequent type of cerebellar haemorrhage diagnosed in infant born extremely preterm. Combined with other stressors, such as inflammation, we can actually translate multiple cerebellar hits and further understand how these insults will alter cerebellar growth and impair neurological outcomes. The overall focus of this proposal is to examine the key role of microglial cell responses to perinatal insult, which may protect from damages induced to the cerebellum and means by which we may provide neuroprotection in the face of that damage. At first, we will examine the role of the brain innate immune system, microglial cells, in hindering the cerebellum's resilience to insult and prevent long-term cerebellar deficits. In second, we will describe changes in inflammatory expression pattern from microglial cells induced by perinatal cerebellar injury. In third, we will test the potential therapeutic benefit of FDA-approved drugs known to modulate brain inflammation. The focus has been so far on protecting cerebral injury in infants born prematurely; preventing cerebellar insults is as important and will result in significant neurodevelopmental improvement. Currently there is no therapeutic agent given routinely to prevent cerebellar injury affecting around 11 000 infants born extremely preterm in North America per year. Achievement of our goals will lead to expand the repertoire of potential therapies available to protect the developing brain.

column36: Epigenetic changes linking prenatal exposures to tobacco or cannabis smoke with asthma risk
column37: We know that the environment influences our health, and that babies are particularly sensitive to environmental exposures in the womb. When babies are exposed in the womb to pollutants like tobacco or cannabis smoke, health effects that can arise years or decades beyond the exposure itself. In 2018, over 11% of women of child-bearing age in Canada smoked cannabis, and nearly 20% of men. Both first- and second-hand tobacco smoke during pregnancy puts babies at risk of developing asthma, but much less is known about the risks of prenatal exposure to cannabis smoke. Research shows that many believe cannabis smoke to be less harmful than cigarette smoke to developing children. However, many of the inhaled products of combustion are similar between cannabis and tobacco smoke, and to date there is no evidence that cannabis smoke has different effects on developing offspring than tobacco smoke. This project uses epigenetics to try and understand what marks are being left behind in the cell by tobacco and cannabis smoke exposure. Epigenetics is a kind of cellular memory, that helps cells remember what kind of cells they are, but also what environments they have been exposed to. If we understand what cellular memories are left behind by specific environments, we may be able to reverse them, or even prevent them from being laid down in the first place, to ensure that every child in Canada gets the best possible start in life.

column36: The mental health impact and needs of those living with food allergy: Perceptions from children, parents and care providers to inform a needs-based multi-faceted support programs and policy
column37: For the 4-8% of Canadian children with food allergy, and thus their families, deciding what and where to eat can be challenging and costly. These decisions can also lead to acute and severe reactions which require emergency medicine. But, because food allergic reactions are potentially fatal, these decisions can also be a potential life-or-death choice. To prevent a reaction, allergic individuals must exclude the foods to which they are allergic. This can be challenging, socially limiting and costly. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms recognizes food allergy as a legal disability. Yet, at present, there are no national policies to support those living with food allergy. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a project that uses data from various sources to increase our understanding of these families' needs. Our group includes Canadian leaders in pediatric allergy, knowledge translation, mixed methods and child psychology. Manitoba is the ideal place to do this work because it is a leader in pediatric allergy patient education and engagement, and is home to the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy, which houses health administation data for nearly all registered residents in the province. The major goal of our work is to describe how food allergy impacts families. We will learn about this impact by talking to families, medical professionals and school staff, and by analysing healthcare records. Our other major goal is to create a needs-focused pediatric food allergy support programme for low-income Manitoba children and their families. We will use this information to develop the types of programs they believe would be most helpful. Our long term vision is to use the findings to help inform a national strategy for families with food allergic children, to help inform decisions for maximising available resources, to provide optimal care for those with food allergy, and to assist with future planning.

column36: Characterizing the mechanisms by which oncolytic viruses induce antitumour immunity
column37: Immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer care, in some cases generating cures in patients that have failed all other treatments. Our lab studies a new and exciting form of immunotherapy called oncolytic viruses (OVs). These are viruses that were originally designed to seek out and kill cancer cells in a patient while leaving normal cells unharmed. However, it's now become clear that these viruses work primarily by stimulating the patient's own immune system to fight his or her cancer. How this occurs is not well understood. Currently, the belief in the field is that OVs must first infect the patient's cancer cells to generate an immune response against the tumour. However, my research suggests a very different mechanism. I have found that in many cancer models, OVs can stimulate the immune system to eliminate tumours without first infecting cancer cells. Instead, the OVs infect immune cells in other organs such as the spleen and lymph nodes. These unexpected findings have prompted me to hypothesize that infection of immune cells is what causes tumour regression, and that cancer cell infection is not required. To test this hypothesis, I will do two things. First, I will engineer cancer cells to be resistant to infection by OVs. I will then treat mice bearing these "infection-resistant" tumours with OVs, to determine whether cancer cell infection is required for OV therapy to work. Second, I will identify which immune cells are infected by these viruses, and determine how these infections promote tumour regression. This research will greatly expand our understanding of how OVs work to promote cancer regression. Further, knowledge gained from these studies will allow for the development of new OVs that are better able to stimulate immune responses against tumours. Ultimately, this may result in improved outcomes for patients receiving OV therapy for the treatment of their cancer.

column36: Investigating the Translational Potential of Lubricin in Preventing Pericardial Adhesion Formation Post-Cardiac Surgery
column37: Scar formation following surgery is common. Post-surgical scars resulting from heart surgery are becoming more noteworthy as the number of repeat surgeries and subsequent scar-related complications increase. In repeat surgeries, these scars can cause major complications, such as ruptures, tears and excessive bleeding in the heart and lungs. They also extend the duration of surgeries and often result in longer hospital stays, thereby burdening the healthcare system's resources. There is currently no widely accepted therapy that has been shown to consistently and effectively prevent post-surgical scar formation. Discovering a natural solution to this major health problem is appealing since it will not have toxic side-effects. Lubricin is a protein that is native to different areas of the body, such as the joints. It is also found in the fluid that surrounds the heart. Lubricin has been shown to lubricate surfaces, and is known to have anti-inflammatory properties. Given its characteristics, there is great interest in investigating lubricin's potential use in preventing post-surgical scar formation in the space around the heart. Thus far, studies show that introducing lubricin into the space around a pig's heart significantly reduces scars. However, we have yet to fully understand how lubricin exerts its effects. The purpose of this study is to better understand how lubricin prevents the formation of scars around the heart after surgery so that we can optimize its application. We will use animal studies to investigate lubricin's effects in preventing long-term post-surgical scars. We will also consider how different heart diseases change the make-up and amount of lubricin that is present in the fluid surrounding the heart. Importantly, because scar formation is not unique to heart surgery, the findings of our study can also be applied to patients undergoing other surgeries. This will allow us to have a positive and wide-reaching impact on the healthcare system.

column36: The Impact and Treatment of Postural Tachycardia Syndrome.
column37: When a person stands up, gravity pulls blood from the chest down into the abdomen and legs. In a healthy person, the body adapts. In Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), the body does not adapt, leading to a racing heart and severe symptoms like dizziness and shaking. This happens every time one stands. The effects of POTS, however, extend beyond feeling unwell when upright. Patients have a reduced quality of life, comparable to other serious illnesses like congestive heart failure. Patients also experience economic, educational and social impacts. Over 70% of patients have lost income, and 21% have even lost a job. POTS is estimated to affect 1-3 million Americans, more than multiple sclerosis, a commonly recognized condition. Despite this, misdiagnosis is common, with patients seeing 7 different doctors, and waiting 5 years before diagnosis, on average. Once diagnosed, treating POTS is complex, as no one treatment works for everyone. My research consists of two aims: increasing awareness of the impact of POTS, and providing evidence for treatments to improve daily management. Through a large survey of over 9000 patients, I have investigated aspects of the patient experience. Next, I plan to develop and implement a follow up survey to understand changes in POTS over time, and develop an in-depth understanding of key impacts. To ensure my survey questions are relevant, I will interview patients about their experiences, and build from their responses. Compression garments are a commonly prescribed treatment for POTS, but their effectiveness has not been evaluated in an adult POTS population. I am currently conducting a clinical trial where I am testing this treatment to see if heart rate and symptoms improve when the garment is used. I am also interviewing patients to understand their experience with these garments. Following up on this work, I plan to conduct a longer-term trial with garments to evaluate effectiveness in "real life".

column36: Medication adherence for the secondary prevention of acute coronary syndrome: A randomized controlled trial of a motivational communication intervention in cardiac rehabilitation
column37: Over 60,000 Canadians will have a heart attack this year, and one person is hospitalized every 5 minutes because of a heart attack or chest pain. Patients who have a cardiac event are prescribed many types of new medication to prevent future complications such as a repeat heart attack, need for further hospitalization or surgery, or even death. It is also recommended that patients attend cardiac rehabilitation programs to make important changes to their lifestyle that will help improve their heart health, including helping people exercise safely, adopt a healthier diet and learn more about their medications. However, studies show that up to 46% of patients do not take their medications as prescribed, which increases their risk of complications. The aim of my project is to design a brief one-on-one intervention that can be added to currently-existing cardiac rehabilitation programs to help patients take their heart medications. Over 150 patients participating in a cardiac rehabilitation program in Alberta will be recruited for this study. Half will be randomly assigned to receive the one-on-one intervention in addition to regular cardiac rehabilitation, and the other half will only participate in regular cardiac rehabilitation. This will help us determine whether the intervention is effective at promoting adherence to heart medication. The intervention will consist of two confidential discussions with a doctoral student in clinical psychology, lasting up to 60 minutes each. These sessions will focus on providing information about heart medication, discussing internal motivations for taking medication, and supporting patients who are looking for concrete strategies to help take their medication. Following this study, I envision designing a training course to teach these techniques to healthcare professionals working in cardiac rehabilitation programs across the country. This project will contribute to the ongoing effort to improve the heart health of Canadians.

column36: Personalizing Pediatric Brain-Computer Interfaces: Establishing and Optimizing Performance for Children with Severe Neurological Disabilities
column37: Imagine being trapped inside your body: you are completely aware of your environment, but you cannot move or speak. Unfortunately, this is the case for many children with severe neurological disabilities such as quadriplegic cerebral palsy. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) represent a promising solution for restoring communication and independence for such individuals. BCIs non-invasively sample brain activity to allow users to voluntarily control external devices such as a computer. Unfortunately, nearly all BCI research has been done in adults, neglecting children who stand to benefit most. In order for severely disabled children to harness this potential, we must first establish how the young, developing brain can operate BCI systems. We will engage typically developing children, providing the opportunity to try six leading BCI systems and perform multiple tasks. First, we will evaluate their performance on standard systems that have been established in adults. While doing so, we will explore important potential differences between children and adults, including attention span and motivation, that are likely to influence BCI performance. Accordingly, we will explore how tailoring tasks to be more child-friendly can improve BCI performance. Another major goal of BCI research is to be able to predict performance before choosing devices and investing time in training. We will use novel, child-friendly methods to assess patterns of connectivity in the brain to try and predict children's performance on BCI tasks. Finally, we will translate the above findings to ongoing trials within our clinical pediatric BCI program, engaging and learning from severely disabled children and their families. Our research will contribute to the advancement of BCI systems for children with severe neurological disability, allowing them to realize new levels of independence and lifelong quality of life.

column36: Investigating the role of POLR3 in oligodendrocyte-lineage development and myelination in vivo: Translational disease models and proof-of-concept for using in vivo gene therapy to treat POLR3-related Hypomyelinating Leukodystrophy.
column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of rare genetic diseases affecting brain development that collectively occur in 1:7500 individuals. Children with leukodystrophy grow normally until they develop neurological signs, especially movement problems. Based on medical imaging, we know that leukodystrophies result from genetic alterations leading to abnormalities in the white matter of the brain. The main component of white matter called myelin is necessary for the correct function of the nervous system. Myelin is normally produced by a specialized cell lineage that itself grows and matures along with the brain. In different leukodystrophies, myelin may develop incorrectly or disappear. However, if myelin does not develop, it is called a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy (HLD). Functional decline is often drastic and fatal, and unfortunately no treatment is available for children with HLD. We discovered the recessive mutations that characterize patients with the most common HLD called RNA Polymerase III-related Hypomyelinating Leukodystrophy (POLR3-HLD). Patients inherit two affected copies of POLR3 genes leading to hypomyelination and decreased POLR3 expression and function, whereas carriers have one affected gene copy and no disease. The fact that hypomyelination is so pronounced in patients indicates an early deficit in the lineage of cells that produce myelin. These observations have led us to hypothesize that POLR3 gene defects lead to deficits in maturation and function of the myelin-producing cell lineage. This proposal aims to address two fundamental research problems for the first time. 1) We propose to implement an animal model to directly study the role of POLR3 in the maturation and function of myelinating cells during myelination in vivo. 2) In order to remediate POLR3-related hypomyelination, we propose to design and validate gene therapy techniques to target the myelinating cell lineage, which may also prove useful for other diseases affecting white matter.

column36: Identification of the algogenic toxin in lionfish venom and its mechanism of action
column37: The wealth of biodiversity in the world's library of venoms and their toxins represents an enormous untapped resource that could contain the scaffolds for a nearly infinite number of therapeutic drugs. Within the realm of venoms that have been studied, marine venoms represent only a small minority in comparison to those of insects and snakes. The red lionfish (Pterois volitans) is a venomous species of fish originating from the Indo-Pacific but now invasive in the Caribbean and Northwestern Atlantic, where it poses a significant stress on marine ecosystems. In addition to this stress, the lionfish is responsible for one of the most painful stings in the ocean. There exists no anti-venom for its stings because the venom and its mechanism of action remain unknown. By identifying the venom component responsible for the pain, I will uncover the molecular basis for the pain caused by the lionfish's venom. Furthermore, I will identify how resistance mechanisms developed through evolution in the fish's predators, such as the moray eel. This insight will allow me to identify pharmaceutical targets for the development of pain treatments. There is an enormous demand for the development of novel pain treatments, since most that exist are either inefficient or addictive. By studying lionfish venom and identifying how it causes pain, we can start to develop novel pharmaceutical agents for the specific and efficient treatment of pain conditions.

column37: Despite the long history of MS research, some components of the disease continue to elude scientists. Neurodegeneration is the best correlate to clinical disability, but there remains a lack of understanding of the mechanisms behind neurodegeneration. Therefore, my project aims to address this problem. There are two main levels that create a cell - DNA (the code), and RNA and proteins (the programs). Cells use this tiered system to regulate their internal responses to external stimuli. This means an external input - inflammation for example - may lead to changes in the code, enacting a degenerative program. Cells also have protective programs, but how or why one program prevails over another is not well understood. By characterizing changes in both DNA and RNA within neurons throughout the disease time course, I aim to identify how cells initiate degenerative or protective programs. This understanding will aid in identifying drugs that may promote a neuroprotective program and help identify new biomarkers specific to different stages of degeneration. It is essential to target treatment programs to a patient's specific disease stage. Identifying neuro-protective drugs specific for different stages of MS will create more effective therapies, bringing new hope for clinical improvement to people with MS.

column36: Assessing the Reproductive Healthcare Needs and Priorities of Women Living with HIV in Canada
column37: My doctoral research aims to produce much-needed evidence to support high-quality reproductive healthcare for women living with HIV. With advances in treatment, HIV is no longer a death sentence. People are living longer, healthier lives with HIV compared to the early years of the epidemic. This has led to a shift in the reproductive health needs of people living with HIV, particularly women. Women, who make up nearly a quarter of the people living with HIV in Canada today and over half of the people living with HIV around the world, have similar reproductive desires to HIV-negative women. Medical and scientific advancements have been made, but healthcare practices have lagged behind. Women living with HIV in most countries, including Canada, receive subpar reproductive healthcare. Healthcare providers often do not address the reproductive desires of women living with HIV, which include wanting to become pregnant, avoid or terminate a pregnancy and control the spacing between pregnancies. Women living with HIV are left to navigate reproductive health on their own, leading to higher rates of unwanted or unsafe pregnancies and stigmatizing experiences. To improve reproductive healthcare, we must understand the gaps in care and design strategies to address them. I will analyze data from 1,422 women living with HIV enrolled in a Canadian study designed by, for and with women living with HIV. Integrating women's perspectives throughout the analyses, I will examine whether women discuss their reproductive goals with their healthcare providers, and how they prioritize their reproductive healthcare among other aspects of their HIV care. Results will support evidence-based recommendations to deliver care that meets the needs and priorities of women living with HIV in Canada. Findings will also be relevant internationally where delivering reproductive healthcare to women living with HIV has been identified as central to supporting human rights and achieving gender equity.

column36: Identifying the differences in single-cell transcriptomes between schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and healthy individuals in the anterior cingulate cortex
column37: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are two chronic psychiatric disorders that greatly diminish the quality of life for affected individuals. Although these two disorders have high overlap, they differ between each other. To find the genetic differences between schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and a healthy population, we propose to use a method known as single-cell sequencing. Each cell activates different genes based on the signals they receive, and this powerful technique tries to understand which genes are more active between individual cells. Here, we aim to understand both disorders by single-cell sequencing relevant brain tissue from affected individuals, and determine how the bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and healthy patient cells differ from one another. After, we will combine those results with the entire genetic data from the patient brain tissue, to understand how genetic differences can lead to these single-cell differences. Currently, drug treatments for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder have many side effects, such as uncontrolled movements, sexual dysfunction, and memory impairment. This study could help identify novel target genes and cell types specifically altered in bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, which could lead to better targeted treatments. Additionally, this will help contribute to the research community by providing a rich resource for other researchers to build upon and integrate their datasets. Combined, both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are debilitating over one million Canadians and studying these disorders at a single-cell resolution can help understand each disease better.

column37: Brain injury is a common complication experienced by both infants born preterm and infants born with congenital heart disease (CHD), typically occurring in a characteristic pattern within the white matter of the brain. Additionally, both groups experience persistent neuropsychological impairments, including difficulties with cognition, behaviour, and daily functioning, throughout their lives. It has been proposed that the early-life white matter injuries seen in these populations may have long-term consequences on how white matter is organized at the cellular level. These possible long-term microscopic alterations, and their potential link to the neuropsychological impairments experienced by youth born preterm or with CHD, have remained unconfirmed due to the inability of traditional imaging techniques to detect precise cellular alterations in the white matter of living human patients. This study will use new and advanced magnetic resonance imaging techniques that are sensitive to specific cellular factors in order to detect alterations in the microscopic structure of white matter in youth born preterm or with CHD as compared to healthy peers. We will also explore the extent to which these precise alterations are associated with neuropsychological outcomes, including intelligence, executive function, behavioural regulation, and functional status. This will provide valuable insight into the role of specific white matter alterations in the impaired neurodevelopment of youth born preterm or with CHD. Identifying novel biomarkers of neuropsychological impairments in these clinical populations could facilitate the early diagnosis of these deficits and eventually promote the development of new therapeutic approaches to ameliorate the transition of these at-risk youth into successful and independent adult life.

column36: Studies of the therapeutic benefits of targeting neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) components in a mouse model of sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a type of blood poisoning that occurs when the body has an over reactive response to an infection. This can lead to tissue damage, organ failure, and death. Sepsis is recognized as a global health priority. The death rate from sepsis is high, suggesting that an improved understanding of how sepsis leads to death may develop into new therapies. Recently, it was discovered that high levels of free-floating DNA and histones in the blood can predict death in sepsis. This is likely released by white blood cells in response to trying to fight off the infection. In test tubes, free-floating DNA can trigger clotting in the blood. DNA often lives in blood together with histones. In test tubes, histones can kill blood vessels and make blood thicker. However, no one has confirmed that DNA and/or histones are harmful to mammals and contributes to death in sepsis. Some new studies show that getting rid of DNA with injections of DNase I minimally increases survival in mice. Other studies show that getting rid of histones with a treatment called heparin shows a small increase in survival in mice. Heparin is also a blood thinner and decreases inflammation. No one knows if these drugs used together can cure sepsis. Because both drugs on their own shows some survival improvement in sepsis, perhaps using them together will cure sepsis. This project has two objectives: (1) to find out if DNA and/or histones are just predictors of death or causes death and (2) if using a combination of DNase I and heparin can cure sepsis in a mouse model. As the Canadian population ages, sepsis is expected to continue to be a major contributor to mortality and an important health care issue. If we can find better therapies for sepsis, we will reduce the mortality and economic burden of sepsis.

column36: Creating a Positive Health Equity Action Plan: Exploring the impact of privilege on the clinical health outcomes of Canadians living with HIV and the creation of a community-informed positive health equity action plan
column37: The exploration of how the social sciences construct of privilege in public and clinical health impacts health outcomes is unique, timely, and fills an existing knowledge gap. Privilege occurs when specific groups possess rights or gains advantage over other groups causing social inequality (Mullaly, 2010). My proposed two-part mixed-methods study aims to explore the impact of privilege on the clinical health outcomes of people living with HIV within the CANOC dataset and the creation of a community-informed plan of action on health equity for Canadians living with HIV. As a community-informed research, an advisory group with members from socially less privileged groups will be formed to provide guidance. The privileged group within the CANOC cohort has been operationalized as White MSM (WMSM) living with HIV. This categorization is based on the literature on whiteness (DiAngelo, 2012; Kwate & Goodman, 2014) and the privilege in health access and health outcomes as experienced by WMSM (Moupali, 2010; Grace, Jollimore, MacPherson, Strang, & Tan, 2018; Raboud et al., 2010). Phase 1 of the study will explore if the social science construct of "privilege" (Du Bois,1903) correlates to clinical health outcomes of people living with HIV in Canada's largest HIV cohort dataset utilizing a critical epidemiology approach (Edelman, 2018). I hypothesize that "privilege" is correlated with clinical health outcomes of Canadians living with HIV whereby less privileged groups will have poorer clinical health outcomes. Phase 2 utilizes a community-informed approach to engage key stakeholders including people living with HIV from marginalized groups in an online critical health policy roundtable to develop policy recommendations and a sustainable health equity action plan. The study's findings will produce evidence-based recommendations on how Canada can meet the global targets to end HIV through realizing health equity among the diverse communities of Canadians living with HIV.

column36: Who Cares for the Dying Poor? Exploring the Experiences & Needs of Street Family in End-of-Life Care
column37: Vulnerable and marginalized populations - including those who are homeless, experience mental health and substance use issues and who are living in poverty - have higher rates of illnesses that will lead to their death and difficulty getting their needs met at end-of-life. While most people who are coming toward the end of their lives are cared for at home by family members, this is not the case for many people who are vulnerable and marginalized. Who supports these vulnerable and marginalized populations as their health is getting worse and they are approaching the end-of-life? Studies I have coordinated found that people who are vulnerable are cared for by many people that we would not traditionally think of as caregivers. These included people like "street family" rather than people's biological family. But there is little description of who these "street family" caregivers are, what they do, how caregiving affects them, and what supports they might need. As part of a larger study working with inner city palliative care teams in three Canadian cities to examine who "family" is in this context, I will focus on "street family" to understand what they do in relation to their roles. With these caregivers' consent, I plan to observe them in their community settings and interview them. I will explore what influences their capacity to give care and document what impact caregiving has on them. column36: Metabolic engineering of chimeric antigen receptor T cells for cancer immunotherapy
column37: Immunotherapy, a biological therapy that utilizes the immune system to fight disease, has emerged in the last few years as a major player in the field of oncology. The effect of immunotherapy is largely dependent on the action of white blood cells with powerful tumor-killing capabilities, called T cells. Novel approaches are currently being explored to enhance T cell function and improve responses to immunotherapy in hard-to-treat cancers. One such approach is the engineering of chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells, wherein patient T cells are extracted, modified with a receptor that enables them to better recognize tumor cells, and then re-infused in large numbers. CAR-T cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable success in blood-based cancers, but in solid tumors, physical and functional barriers pose a unique challenge. In particular, rapidly growing tumor cells produce toxic metabolites and consume large amounts of glucose and oxygen, creating a hostile environment that inhibits immune cells. The goal of my research is to overcome this metabolic suppression and improve CAR-T cell therapy for solid tumors. To achieve this goal I will use sophisticated gene-editing techniques to rewire metabolic pathways, thus producing supercharged CAR-T cells with enhanced metabolic and tumor-killing capabilities. Rigorous testing and optimization in the laboratory and in mouse models will enable me to develop a successful metabolic engineering pipeline with the potential to finally advance CAR-T cell therapy in solid cancers.

column36: Longitudinally evaluating the impact of traumatic brain injury on the brain structure and health of individuals who are homeless and precariously housed
column37: Homeless and precariously housed individuals (i.e., those living in housing that lacks security or stability) experience a higher burden of mental and physical illness, and higher mortality than the general population. Recent studies have suggested that traumatic brain injury (TBI) may be extremely common and associated with the significant health challenges faced by this population. The broad objective of my doctoral research is to characterize how the brain health and general health of homeless and precariously housed individuals is affected by TBI. My specific objectives are to (1) establish how common TBI is in this population and how TBI is related to the onset and duration of homelessness, (2) evaluate factors (e.g., TBI and drug use) that accelerate or are protective of brain health over time, and (3) evaluate how new TBIs affect brain structure and health outcomes of these individuals. I will use data from the Hotel Study, which has been working since 2008 with 515 homeless and precariously housed individuals living in the impoverished Downtown Eastside neighbourhood of Vancouver, BC. The Hotel Study collects monthly and yearly assessments of health and functioning (including psychiatric symptoms, drug use, neurocognitive functioning, and MRI scans). My thesis work will be the first comprehensive study on the potential for TBI to modify brain structure and health in homeless and precariously housed individuals. We expect to find that TBI will be far more common in homeless and precariously housed individuals than the general population, that TBI will predict a faster decline in brain health, and that new TBIs will lead to poorer brain health, poorer mental health and poorer functioning. These findings will immediately contribute to improved understanding and treatment for health consequences related to TBI in this population, and will contribute to improving the health of homeless and precariously housed individuals in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Smooth Muscle Cell Lysosomal Acid Lipase in Atherosclerosis
column37: BACKGROUND: Heart attack and stroke together are the leading cause of death in the world. They result from atherosclerosis, a disease in which cholesterol builds up in artery walls, causing arteries to become hardened and blocked. We discovered that smooth muscle cells (SMCs), the main type of cell in the artery wall, have low levels of Lysosomal Acid Lipase (LAL), a protein that is important to process and expel excess cholesterol. We therefore believe that SMCs are resistant to releasing excess cholesterol, and that this contributes to atherosclerosis even when blood cholesterol is lowered by diet and medications. Inducing SMCs to release their excess cholesterol, then, may be a very effective new means to treat atherosclerosis. GOAL: We have shown that feeding extra LAL to SMCs in a dish increases their cholesterol export. The goal of my project is to test if inducing mouse SMCs in arteries to produce more LAL will reverse atherosclerosis, by increasing cellular release of cholesterol. APPROACH: First, I will test if inducing mouse SMCs in a dish to produce more LAL increases their ability to export cholesterol. Second, I will genetically modify mice to produce more LAL in their artery SMCs, and test if these mice develop less atherosclerosis; I will also test if increasing LAL production in SMCs can reverse atherosclerosis in mice that already have the disease. This is possible using a genetic tool that triggers LAL production specifically in SMCs. Third, I will test if increasing LAL production in the livers of mice with atherosclerosis reverses the disease. This will increase the LAL that circulates in the blood, which may also increase LAL in artery SMCs. OUTCOMES: I expect that increasing LAL production in mouse SMCs will prevent the development of atherosclerosis, and that increasing LAL in mice with atherosclerosis will reverse the disease. This would support the development of new LAL-based treatments to prevent heart attack and stroke in humans.

column36: Characterizing Patterns of Hospital Healthcare Utilization Among Sexual Minority Populations with Substance Use Disorder: An Intersectional Population-Based Approach
column37: Substance use disorders (SUDs) are associated with a range of negative health outcomes and represent a significant cost to the Canadian healthcare system. Many of these costs are associated with repeat admissions to hospitals related to complications from substance use, which have been further exacerbated in the wake of the ongoing opioid epidemic. Beyond representing healthcare cost drivers, patterns of healthcare utilization may also be indicative of unmet service needs. Currently little is known about healthcare utilization among important sub-populations that may experience elevated rates of substance use and related harms. Specifically, research has repeatedly shown that sexual minorities, including lesbian, gay, and bisexual individuals, experience elevated rates of substance use, distinct substance-related harms, and population-specific barriers to treatment. Furthermore, there is evidence to suggest that other intersecting social identities (e.g., gender, race, and socioeconomic status) can play a critical role in how sexual minorities experience substance use and related health outcomes. Better understanding the impact of substance use on hospital utilization among sexual minorities could inform population-specific interventions to improve patient care, reduce healthcare costs, and address health inequities. This study will deploy an existing linked dataset of the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), a representative survey of the social determinants of health of the Canadian Population, and the Discharge Abstract Database (DAD), a national database containing information on hospital admissions and discharges. To ensure sufficient statistical power, multiple cycles of the CCHS and DAD will be used. Descriptive statistics and regression modelling will be used to identify differences in healthcare utilization outcomes among sexual minority sub-populations across intersecting social identities and in comparison to the heterosexual population.
