column37: People with long QT interval syndrome (LQTS), either congenital or drug-induced, can suffer serious arrhythmias and even sudden death. This research seeks to understand the underlying properties, and therapeutic drug modification of the proteins responsible for LQTS. The IKs current, generated by the pairing of a potassium channel protein called KCNQ1, with accessory subunit proteins, KCNE1 and calmodulin (CaM), together, play a vital role in maintaining normal heart rhythm. As such, drugs which enhance IKs activity have been proposed as a therapeutic strategy to treat LQTS. Mefenamic acid has been identified as one such IKs activator but, how this drug works on a molecular level - example, the drug's binding site(s) - are unknown. Presently, mutations in KCNQ1, KCNE1 and CaM have all been functionally linked to LQTS but whether mefenamic acid can rescue any of these LQTS-causing mutations in KCNQ1, KCNE1 and CaM has not been tested. In addition to examining these questions by electrical analysis using whole-cell patch-clamp and single channel recordings, the second part of our proposed project involves determining, for the first time, the channel's protein structure at a near atomic level using cryo-electron microscopy. By examining how mefenamic acid functions on a molecular level using electrical analysis will allow us to better understand how these channels activate. We can then use this information to help develop more specific and effective treatments for LQTS. In addition, once we uncover the channel's protein structure, computer simulations can then be run on the protein structure to predict important parts of the channel that should be targeted during drug development. Many of the people with LQTS presently have to wear implantable defibrillators. This work therefore represents the first step towards the development of more specific therapies that may eventually free them or their children from such necessities.

column36: Investigating the relationship between maternal diet and pregnancy hypertension in sub-Saharan Africa
column37: Background: Pre-eclampsia is the second leading direct cause of maternal deaths with associated with over 70,000 maternal deaths and 500,000 perinatal deaths annually. Nutrition has essential roles in placenta development during pregnancy and certain micronutrients have clinical anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory properties that may be important in the prevention of pre-eclampsia. However, current research into micronutrients to prevent pre-eclampsia remains inconclusive, suggesting a need to look broader at maternal dietary patterns, particularly in resource-constrained settings where many maternal deaths occur. Research objective: The purpose of the research is to map the pathways of risk between maternal dietary patterns and pregnancy hypertension for women in sub-Saharan Africa and investigate contextual risk factors. Methodology: This mixed-methods doctoral research is a part of the PRECISE network, which will recruit a cohort of 10,000 women across East, West and Southern Africa. First, a systematic review will be undertaken to evaluate current evidence on association between maternal dietary patterns and pregnancy hypertension for pregnant and postpartum women in low- and middle-income countries, followed by qualitative community-based research in Kenya, Mozambique and the Gambia. Third, PRECISE survey outcomes will undergo statistical modelling to ascertain the relationship between dietary diversity and pregnancy hypertension and map direct and indirect pathways of risk. Lastly, research findings will be summarized in context of relevant theories and current approaches. Potential contributions to knowledge: Little is currently known about dietary patterns in sub-Saharan Africa that may contribute to pre-eclampsia risk and this research will help build evidence towards understanding the associations between maternal diet and maternal outcomes, a step towards effective advocacy in international development and global health agendas.

column36: Narrative as a tool for knowledge translation with health policy makers
column37: It takes on average 17 years for research evidence to be adopted into healthcare systems. The gap between what the scientific literature recommends and what governments do in practice means that Canadians can wait almost two decades to benefit from new discoveries. My goal is to identify the best ways for scientists and governments to share new research evidence so that the Canadian healthcare system operates using the most up-to-date information. One of the reasons it takes years for new evidence to affect what governments do is that scientists and policy makers have different ways of thinking about health problems. Using real-life Canadian experiences to capture key research evidence may be a good approach for making research information more useful to policy makers. The overall goal of my work is to define the format, delivery, and mechanisms by which stories can achieve optimal impact. To do this, I will interview a group of provincial and federal policy makers about how stories affect their work on reproductive and sexual health. Next, I will use what I learn to help collect real-life experiences of Canadians accessing reproductive and sexual healthcare, and turn them into stories for policy makers. The last step will be to test what effect the stories have, which I will do by sharing them with policy makers who will give feedback on how they used the information. This study will provide a new set of methods to promote the use of research evidence in government. The methods will be created with and for policy makers and will be scientifically evaluated so that other scientists have tools to get research evidence into the hands of people who are responsible for the healthcare system. By closing the gap between science and government, this study will help ensure that the healthcare system provides the best possible care to all Canadians.

column36: The Effects of Low Cerebral Perfusion on Delirium and Long-Term Outcomes in Critically Ill Patients: A Multi-Centre Study
column37: Delirium is an abnormal state of consciousness that often occurs during critical illness. Significant behavioural changes can be seen when a patient is delirious, including confusion, inability to focus, emotional changes, and hallucinations. Up to 80% of patients develop this disorder in the intensive care unit (ICU), despite the fact that many are admitted for reasons unrelated to the brain. Most importantly, delirium's consequences can be long-term, including longer hospital stays, depression, higher mortality rates, and cognitive impairments as severe as mild Alzheimer's disease Unfortunately, there is currently no cure for delirium and the underlying cause is unknown. New research suggests that it is caused by the lack of oxygenated blood delivered to the brain. Without the critical oxygen that it needs, do patients develop delirium? Does a temporary reduction in blood supply lead to permanent changes that cause long-term cognitive impairments? To answer these questions, I will be studying 500 ICU patients across Canada, measuring the amount of oxygenated blood that is delivered to the brain. With this information, I will determine whether low brain oxygenation leads to delirium and cognitive impairments in ICU survivors. I anticipate that those with reduced blood supply will experience delirium more frequently and will have cognitive disturbances after ICU discharge. If true, we can conclude that low brain tissue oxygenation is a significant risk factor, and optimal levels can be targeted in these patients to treat delirium and prevent long-term consequences. Overall, the goal is to discover the underlying cause of delirium. With this knowledge, we will be able to develop treatment and prevention protocols for patients affected by delirium, both in and out of the ICU. This is especially important as treating delirium can significantly improve outcomes and ensure a full recovery to resume a healthy life.

column36: Fecal microbial transplantation and fiber supplementation in subjects with obesity and metabolic syndrome: a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial
column37: This study is looking at the safety and effectiveness of stool transplant, also known as Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) and fiber supplementation in obesity and metabolic syndrome. Obesity is one of the greatest health epidemics of the 21st century. In 2016 alone, over 650 million adults were diagnosed with obesity. Recent estimates place the total global cost of obesity at $2.0 trillion, almost greater than the combined costs of smoking, war, and terrorism. Current treatments have shown limited benefit, are expensive, and have major side effects with long-term use. Metabolic syndrome (MS) is a common progressive medical condition that is linked to obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. Much like obesity, metabolic syndrome is thought to be associated with abnormal changes in gut flora which lead to chronic intestinal inflammation. If this is true, restoring the abnormal gut flora may reverse the inflammation and provide a new therapy for obesity and MS. FMT is a one-time treatment that has been shown to replace abnormal gut flora and improve metabolic disease by increasing production of anti-inflammatory short-chain fatty acids (SCFA). However, the benefits of FMT are not permanent. A recent study has shown that abnormal gut flora can re-grow as early as six weeks after stool transplantation and reverse the changes of FMT. Fiber supplementation is one strategy that may help to extend the benefits of FMT by helping maintain high SCFA levels. At this point, we don't know how FMT and fiber work together to affect SCFA levels in patients with metabolic syndrome. Our study will look at this interaction and answer if fiber therapy is effective in prolonging the benefits of FMT in participants with metabolic syndrome. If we can show that a single FMT oral product combined with fiber as a maintenance therapy is beneficial, this will be a step forward in identifying a safe and effective alternative in combatting the obesity epidemic.

column37: Alberta has one of the highest rates of inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD, in the world. Yet it has received too little attention in our healthcare system. Unfortunately, care is typically provided reactively through emergency departments and hospitals. Diagnosing and providing treatment earlier can significantly improve an IBD patient's health outcomes and quality of life, while reducing costs to the healthcare system. How can we identify and diagnose patients earlier? One promising approach is a statistical technique called machine learning, or ML, which has been applied to healthcare data to detect tumors, diagnose eye and skin diseases. In IBD however, it is largely unexplored. One major limitation in successful ML research is attaining high quality data that contains huge numbers of patients. However, Alberta has rich province-wide clinical databases that follow a population of over 30,000 patients living with IBD. We aim to apply ML techniques to data from Alberta's provincial databases in order to classify IBD patients according to risk and to automatically identify features of the disease on diagnostic images and scans. We will collect demographic, clinical, laboratory, and imaging data. Then we will apply and test our algorithms using best practices. This research could demonstrate a new way to augment the precision of IBD care given by doctors and imaging experts. We hope the long-term result is the deployment of new systems to improve speed and accuracy of diagnostic testing and treatment, and ultimately, patient outcomes. Such systems could also be used as 'second observers', invaluable for trainees, and providers with suboptimal access to experts (such as in rural Alberta or Northern Canada).

column37: Coronary heart disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada, and results from the build-up of plaque in the coronary artery causing reduced blood flow to the heart. This can lead to a heart attack when the coronary artery is completely obstructed. A heart attack is usually treated by inserting a stent at the site of occlusion to restore blood flow and oxygen delivery to the heart. However, this sudden reintroduction of oxygen to previously deprived tissue can actually cause the heart cells to die in a process called ischemia reperfusion injury. Recent clinical trials of promising pharmaceuticals have failed to find any preventative therapies for this condition. Apelin is a mammalian peptide hormone that exerts a wide range of protective effects in the heart. Importantly, apelin has been shown to be protective against ischemia reperfusion injury, suggesting that targeting this hormone system may serve as a potential therapy for this deadly condition. There are three major types of apelin circulating in human plasma, each triggering slightly different protective physiological effects in the heart. However, apelin is degraded rapidly in the bloodstream. For apelins to be used as drugs to treat heart disease, the chemical structure of this hormone must be altered to achieve increased stability in the blood, while still maintaining potency and protective effects in the heart. My project proposes to study the way that the different types of apelin peptides direct differing effects in the heart, and will use the information learned to develop new analogues of apelin for use as drugs to treat ischemia reperfusion injury. This collaborative, interdisciplinary project combines chemistry, biology, and physiology in order to solve a major challenge to our healthcare system, and produce practical solutions to be used by both patients and physicians.

column36: On the Cusp of Planetary Health Equity: Adopting Watersheds as a Conceptual Framework for the study of SDGs Interactions and Health Outcomes.
column37: "This research respectfully involves Indigenous communities" My research uses watersheds - their ranks, sizes, boundaries, latitudes and spaces - as units of analysis to track difficult-to-detect human and environmental health outcomes and challenges arising from interactions among the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A watershed nests diverse human and biodiversity ecosystems (markets, industries, firms, farmlands, farmers, schools, regulations, government institutions, operating policies, species populations, etc.). Like its diverse ecosystems, a watershed crosses local, regional, national or international boundaries. It has characteristics such as size, area, rank, boundary, location, latitude, and space that help us to better understand nested communities, populations and interactions within the ecosystems. These include: how they exist, where they live, how they interact with one another, including nature, extent and scale of these interactions, and how to plan and distribute resources to support planetary ecosystems. I consider that watersheds can impart these characteristics to the SDGs, which were put together to make our world healthier. My research will use case studies of selected watersheds in Canada and Nigeria. Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and spatial analysis methods, I will adopt watersheds as natural boundaries to obtain denominator data that will reflect human and environmental health challenges in communities that often go un-reflected, unreported and monitored. Using watershed boundaries to show a side-by-side overlay of clusters of cases of specific SDGs interactions will help determine the geographical extent and scale at which these clusters occur in relation to populations at risk; while displaying multiple, rather than restricted, views of the distribution of health outcomes. This will facilitate inclusive monitoring of health outcomes and reduce health inequities that often abound in the least and farthest communities.

column36: Caracterisation in vivo des alterations cholinergiques dans le trouble cognitif leger de type amnesique a l'aide du [18F] fluoroethoxybenzovesamicol ([18F]-FEOBV).
column37: Dans la maladie d'Alzheimer il existe une atteinte des neurones produisant l'acetylcholine, un messager chimique du cerveau. Toutefois, il existe une controverse quant au moment precis ou apparait cette atteinte. Recemment, plusieurs evidences ont montre que les neurones cholinergiques sont touches bien avant les premiers signes cliniques de la maladie. Toutefois, les mesures utilisees pour caracteriser le systeme cholinergique tot dans la maladie sont imparfaite et peu sensibles. Notre equipe de recherche a recemment developpe une nouvelle molecule, le [18F]-FEOBV, permettant d'evaluer l'integrite des neurones cholinergiques du cerveau avec une precision sans precedent. Le [18F]-FEOBV est une molecule radioactive qui peut etre detectee par la technique de tomographie par emission de positrons. Son utilisation recente a montre qu'il est le marqueur le plus sensible pour identifier la maladie d'Alzheimer et en quantifier la severite. A l'aide du [18F]-FEOBV, je vais chercher a mieux comprendre si l'activite cholinergique est alteree ou non chez vingt personnes agees ayant un trouble cognitif leger de type amnesique. Ces personnes a tres haut risque de developper la maladie d'Alzheimer seront comparees a vingt personnes du meme age n'ayant aucun trouble cognitif, mais portant les stigmates de la maladie, puis a vingt autres personnes ayant un faible risque de developper la maladie. column36: Before Operational Stress: Evaluating Novel Psychosocial Interventions for Public Safety Personnel (PSP) and their Families
column37: Public safety personal (PSP) experience heightened operational stressors, including exposure to traumatic events, threats to personal safety, and witnessing acts of accidents, homicides, assaults, and suicide. The statistics regarding the physical, social, and psychological risks for members serving in PSP vocations are not encouraging; prevalence rates for posttraumatic stress injuries (PTSI) and posttraumatic stress disorders (PTSD) ranging from 8% to 32%. Children and spouses living in PSP-connected families also experience the effects of this operational stress, and too often programs and supports available to PSP are either unavailable to or noninclusive of family members. Given that many PSP report seeking informal support from family members, the study is guided by a superordinate query: Does providing intervention and support to youth and spouses in PSP-connected families in turn strengthen PSP mental health and wellbeing? The proposed study will address strategic awareness, prevention, and intervention strategies aimed at building on the strengths and resilience of PSP and their family members via a clinician-delivered Before Operational Stress (BOS) program. In addition to building capacity for professionals to deliver the BOS/BOS-Family programs, the study will also develop explore a new method of objectively measuring response-to-intervention via wearable technology. Strategic attention will be given to between-group differences, most notably exploring how PSP vocation and gender and sex interact with other demographic (e.g., age, family structure, region, PSP vocation) variables. The proposed research intends to support mental wellness among PSP by developing new knowledge pertaining to interventions and supports - delivered via targeted and intentional intervention programs - for PSP, youth, and spouses/partners related to their understanding the effects PSP occupational stress on the brain, emotional regulation, and relational development.

column36: An Augmented Training Program for Preventing Post-Traumatic Stress Injuries Among Diverse Public Safety Personnel
column37: Exposure to potentially traumatic events is a workplace reality for Canadian Public Safety Personnel (PSP), such as paramedics, firefighters, police, and emergency communications (e.g., 911 operators), who are at significant risk for post-traumatic stress injuries (PTSIs). Despite many groups offering interventions to build PSP resiliency, there is limited evidence that any are effective. A long-term study (www.rcmpstudy.ca) is underway with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) to test an evidence-based mental health training program provided during cadet training, coupled with psychological safety training for their leadership. The proposed study extends the RCMP Study to four other PSP groups-emergency communications, firefighters, municipal police, and paramedics-by tailoring the RCMP Study infrastructure for a broader PSP community. Participants from the four PSP groups will receive 13 hours of mental health skills training based on the well-supported Unified Protocol (UP) for cognitive behavioural therapy, but tailored specifically for diverse PSP. Second, the PSP participants' leaders will be provided with the same skills plus specialized training for building psychologically safe workplaces for high stress professions. Participants will be assessed with detailed self-report surveys and clinical interviews at pre-, post-, and 12-months after the training to assess the impact on their mental health. Participants will also complete short monthly surveys and very short daily surveys. The assessments provide ongoing mental health feedback so participants in need can get help faster. Participants can also evaluate their training experience during focus group discussions. Speciality technology will be pilot-tested to assess whether a PTSI can be identified using biological signals. Overall, the results will indicate whether the diverse assessments and tailored training can support the mental health needs of a more diverse community of frontline PSP and leaders.

column36: HomeBase: Enhancing mental wellness in public safety personnel families
column37: Public safety personnel (PSP), including police officers, fire fighters, paramedics, corrections personnel, and communications officers, are routinely exposed to potentially traumatic critical incidents that can have negative effects on their mental health and well-being. These negative effects can ripple into their family systems, which are already contending with PSP lifestyle dimensions like shiftwork and sleep disruption. Little is known about the specific experiences of PSP families. Much can be drawn from the experiences of military and veteran families, for whom there is a mature body of research on mental health and military lifestyle impacts. Working in close collaboration with representatives from family organizations, PSP, and PSP organizations, this study will take place in two phases. Phase 1 will involve two parallel research streams. We will identify and analyze existing PSP organizational and community-based supports for PSP families. We will also investigate the experiences and needs of PSP families regarding post-traumatic stress and PSP lifestyle dimensions like shiftwork. Findings will be synthesized and then priority statements will be created. In Phase 2, we will work with the PSP/family community to identify which priority statements are common and unique across the sectors, to problem solve barriers, and to embrace opportunities towards actioning these priorities. We will develop family-focused resources and tailor recommendations for PSP sectors to enhance the mental wellness of PSP and their families. Our established and multi-disciplinary research team consists of national and international researchers and experts to ensure that the complex and diverse lived experiences of Canadian PSP families are appropriately incorporated into the resources and recommendations. This research will be shared through traditional academic channels but also through rapid open science strategies with the community.

column36: Exploring Postpartum Sexual Health in Nova Scotia Using Feminist Poststructuralism
column37: After giving birth, postpartum individuals may experience many changes to their health, including sexual health. Despite being an essential component of health and wellbeing for postpartum individuals, sexual health is often discussed or defined in physically-focused ways, thus impeding health care support and services. As such, there is a need to move beyond the narrow approaches that currently dominate postpartum sexual health research, information, education, and clinical care to include emotional, social, and relational aspects of sexual health. No studies to date have explored the experiences of postpartum individuals with regards to their sexual health. Thus, the proposed study will address the significant knowledge gap by exploring how postpartum individuals experience their sexual health after birth. I will recruit eight to ten participants who are between one and six months postpartum and conduct interviews with them. Feminist poststructuralism and discourse analysis will be used to guide my research and analyze the interviews. This methodology will allow me to examine the meaning ascribed to sexual health in the postpartum period and to uncover how personal subjectivity, agency, and relations of power are experienced and negotiated. Findings will have important implications for informing how sexual health may be better supported and promoted during the postpartum period.

column36: The Impact of Cultural Connectedness on Mental Wellness in Indigenous Children and Youth
column37: This research respectfully involves Indigenous communities. Indigenous peoples face significant health inequities when compared with the rest of Canadians, which is evident even among children and youth. First Nations children and youth have higher rates of acute and chronic pain, mental illness, substance use disorders, and suicidal thoughts. One avenue that shows promise for addressing mental health concerns among Indigenous children and youth is cultural connectedness. In Indigenous communities, culture is foundational to healing and is nurtured through participation in cultural activities. The proposed project is based on a community-identified need for research surrounding how cultural connection promotes positive mental health for children and youth. This study uses multiple research methods to understand the impact of cultural connectedness and cultural identity on the mental health of Indigenous children and youth in both rural and urban areaas. A comprehensive review of the literature will be conducted to identify definitions of cultural identity and current strategies that use cultural connectedness in the context of mental health care. The second phase is a secondary analysis of national survey data, which will use statistical tests to determine the relationship between cultural connectedness and mental health outcomes. The third phase is a community-based project that will use arts-based qualitative methods to explore how Indigenous youth in Nova Scotia define and understand cultural identity and its connection with their mental health. The results of this study could allow health professionals to create culturally safe environments for Indigenous children and youth who are seeking mental health care.

column36: The role of mitophagy and extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness in the regulation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and subsequent metastasis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) model.
column37: Lung cancer is the main cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. A major risk for lung cancer deaths is when cancer cells escape the lung to invade other organs, causing new cancers to show up throughout the body. This process is called 'metastasis' and requires the cells to produce lots of extra energy. To supply the energy required for metastasis, cancer cells must first go through major changes in how they recycle old and damaged parts of the cell. A molecule called 'BCL2L13' helps control this recycling process in cancer cells. Importantly, we have found that less of this molecule is made in lung cancer patients whose cancer has spread to other organs. This means that BCL2L13 could help control lung cancer metastasis, and drugs that change BCL2L13 levels might be a good way to treat lung cancer. In my project, I will control the amount of BCL2L13 made in lung cancer cells and examine how it controls the escape of lung cancer cells to other organs. To confirm my results in a more realistic way, I will use an exciting new technology called '3D bioprinting' to build realistic lung cancers in a dish. By controlling the amount of BCL2L13 made in these realistic lung cancers, I can then see how energy production, recycling and metastasis change. Furthermore, we will extend our studies to live human tissue samples from patients with lung cancer. This provides us with extremely useful and first-hand clinical data about lung cancer metastasis and how we can harness BCL2L13 to combat metastasis in patients with lung cancer. Altogether, my project will give us a much better understanding of how BCL2L13 contributes to the spread of lung cancer cells to other organs. This is an important first step towards developing new cancer treatments that target BCL2L13, which will improve the lives of people living with lung cancer.

column36: Breastfeeding and child behaviour: Understanding the link through five different pathways in the Canadian CHILD birth cohort study
column37: Child behavioural problems are important to study because they are linked to lower academic performance, relationship problems, poor mental health and financial insecurity later in life. Understanding why some children have behaviour problems involves knowing which environmental and genetic factors lead to these behaviours. Breastfeeding is an important part of infancy that has been linked to better behavior in children when they get older. However, few studies have examined the pathways from breastfeeding to behaviour. This study will use information from a large, ongoing study of children (the CHILD study) to look at five possible pathways that help to explain the link between breastfeeding and better child behaviour at age 5 years, including: 1) specific substances in breast milk, 2) factors that show inflammation in the infant blood, 3) infant gut bacteria, 4) mother-child bonding, and 5) maternal mental health. The CHILD study is unique and powerful because it combines survey questions with lab work on human breastmilk, stool, and blood, which will help us to study these pathways. The latest techniques in statistics will be used to define how important each pathway is, while also including information about social status and income. Understanding how breastfeeding could protect against developing behaviour problems may encourage more mothers to breastfeed and may also point towards specific nutrients that could be provided as supplements for babies who cannot be breastfed. This research may also help support breastfeeding promotion and family support programs to help provide the best start to life for all infants.

column36: Immune system impairment and neuroinflammation in the pathogenesis of spinal muscular atrophy
column37: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetic neuromuscular disorder characterised by motor neuron loss, muscle wasting, and weakness. Despite SMA being traditionally considered a motor neuron disorder, accumulating evidence suggests that non-neuronal cell types also contribute to the disease. Abnormalities in certain immune organs like the spleen and thymus have been observed in different SMA mouse models. However, it is currently unknown whether such deficits could make SMA patients more susceptible to disease due to impaired immunity, resulting in exacerbation of disease progression and impacting survival. Additionally, it could also result in neuroinflammation, which is a well-established contributor in many neurodegenerative disorders. Nonetheless, neuroinflammation has yet to be studied in SMA. Consequently, we hypothesize that altered immune function and neuroinflammation contribute to SMA disease pathogenesis. We aim to investigate immune function in SMA mice when challenged with various pathogens. We will also perform experiments to understand whether the immune defects are intrinsic or extrinsic. Next, we will investigate whether immune organs in SMA have toxic properties, especially by neuroinflammation. To extract relevance, we aim to confirm that immune organ defects are present in SMA patients. Understanding the functional consequences of immune organ dysfunction will offer guidance in the development of combinatorial therapies and thus highlight new important considerations to be taken in SMA patient care.

column36: Delivering online cognitive behavioural therapy (iCBT) to address mental health challenges in correctional officers and other public safety personnel
column37: Public safety personnel (PSP) have regular and often intense exposure to potentially traumatic events at work and are at higher risk for developing mental health problems such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Studies have shown up to 4 times higher suicidal ideation, attempt and death among this population compared to general population. Despite the high rate of mental health problems among PSPs, their willingness to receive mental healthcare support is fairly low, mainly due to the stigma attached to these disorders. Those who are willing to seek help face unique barriers including their irregular shift hours, limiting their access to resources otherwise available to the public. Given these challenges and the critical contribution of PSPs to public safety, developing innovative solutions to address their mental health must be a healthcare priority. This proposal aims to study the efficacy of using an innovative approach in delivering mental health online, to address mental health problems among correctional workers (CW), who are especially prone to mental health problems given the high rate of workplace violence. We believe using an online platform to deliver cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), would lower the stigma of receiving care in a secure and confidential environment, easing CWs concerns about stigma from co-workers. The content is delivered through interactive and engaging therapy modules, designed for specific groups of CWs and customized by situational examples to make therapy more relatable. These online modules would provide CWs with 24/7 access to therapy content, solving the irregular work hour problem. The online iCBT modules developed in this study would provide a high quality and clinically validated resource to address mental health problems of CWs all across Canada. Knowledge acquired through this project could also be beneficial to using iCBT in general for addressing mental health challenges among other PSPs.

column36: AD_GRIDS - altered grid cell computations in entorhinal cortex as a unique window into preclinical Alzheimer's disease?
column37: Spatial navigation is a fundamental cognitive ability that is often impaired in advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease (AD). One central component of the brain's navigational system is the grid cell network in entorhinal cortex, whose discovery was awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine/Physiology in 2014. Given that entorhinal cortex is particularly vulnerable to neurodegenerative changes in the earliest stages of AD, deficits in grid cell function could provide a unique functional window into early AD pathology. This project will break new ground by investigating (i) the mechanisms that compromise the integrity of the grid cell network in mouse models of AD pathology and in patients with Subjective Cognitive Decline, and (ii) whether a behavioral readout of grid cell functioning can improve the detection of preclinical disease stages. To address these important questions, the team will employ an interdisciplinary methodological approach that combines advanced behavioral and neuroscientific approaches with innovative data analysis techniques. Moreover, we will employ cutting-edge user-interface design principles to establish a standardised test of grid cell functioning that fulfills the requirements of clinical settings. Together, AD_GRIDS has the potential to significantly advance the detection of early disease stages, the monitoring of disease progression and the assessment of treatment efficacy.

column37: La pleine conscience est une approche a la mode actuellement. Elle se definit en trois parties. D'abord, il s'agit de porter attention aux experiences internes, comme la sensation de la respiration, et externes, comme des bruits autour de nous. Ensuite, cette action se fait volontairement, deliberement. Finalement, ces actions se font dans une attitude sans jugement et avec bienveillance. Les effets de la pleine conscience sur le stress et la qualite de vie portent a croire qu'elle serait benefique aupres de personnes agees dont le fonctionnement de la cognition (ex. memoire, attention) diminue anormalement. La pleine conscience pourrait aider a diminuer les inquietudes et ameliorer le bien-etre de ces aines, tout en pronant des valeurs positives. Par contre, les resultats des recherches recentes sont non constants : il y a des benefices, mais ils ne semblent pas se distinguer de d'autres approches ou interventions. De plus, certains chercheurs trouvent des effets alors que d'autres n'en trouvent pas avec des etudes similaires. Le but de cette etude est de comprendre comment se deroule un programme d'introduction a la pleine conscience chez des personnes agees avec un declin de la cognition. L'etude s'interesse a comment s'integre la pleine conscience dans la vie de ces personnes et quelles caracteristiques (ex. personnalite) favorisent des resultats positifs. Pour ce faire, l'etude utilisera des methodes dites quantitatives, soit utilisant des questionnaires et des tests, mais aussi qualitatives, pour documenter directement, a l'aide d'entrevues individuelles, l'experience des participants. L'etude vise a faire la lumiere sur la pertinence de l'approche de pleine conscience chez ces aines qui presentent un declin cognitif.

column36: Weighing the Risks: Policies, Perceptions and Practices Influencing Healthcare Provider and Bariatric Surgery Recipient Decision Making, Experiences and Outcomes in Canada
column37: "Obesity" has recently been redefined by many in the medical community as a disease, with the goal of improving access to treatment and reducing "obesity" related stigma. Because of this increased medicalization of body weight, there has been an increased emphasis on treatments such as bariatric surgery and pharmaceuticals. Bariatric surgery can take several forms, with the goal of reducing food intake and therefore inducing weight loss. Little data is available on the long term success of bariatric surgery, but existing data suggests that these surgeries are risky, with possible outcomes including substance abuse, suicide, nutrition deficiencies, and death. Anecdotally, it is common for patients, and often specifically women and trans people, to be denied access to other medical treatments and ancillary care services until after they have undergone bariatric surgery and/or reduced their body weight, although policies and formalized guidelines tend to be unclear about when these surgeries are a necessary prerequisite to other procedures. What has yet to be explored is how patients and healthcare providers make decisions and make sense of their experiences related to bariatric surgery, and how these experiences match or are discrepant with relevant policy documents. The proposed research will focus on bariatric surgery clients and healthcare providers who work with individuals who have received surgery (pre- and post) in Canada, and will use qualitative interviews and thematic analysis to explore how participants make sense of their experiences. Additionally, participants will point me to relevant policy documents from healthcare authorities across Canada, to determine what risks are acknowledged, etc. Analysis will look for discrepancies and similarities across and between the interviews and the policy documents. This work has the potential to inform future research, policy and practice related to bariatric surgery and other medical "treatments" for "obesity."

column36: Trajectoires d'utilisation de services de sante mentale et physique dans la communaute par les personnes declarees non criminellement responsables pour cause de troubles mentaux
column37: Le systeme de justice criminelle est devenu une porte d'acces aux soins en sante mentale pour de nombreux individus ayant des troubles mentaux graves accompagnes de comportements perturbateurs. En plus d'etre onereux, ce phenomene entraine une stigmatisation plus lourde qui se traduit par des difficultes additionnelles a la reintegration dans la communaute. La vaste majorite des personnes declarees non criminellement responsables pour cause de troubles mentaux (NCRTM), qui forment la clientele principale des services psycho-legaux, etaient deja connus des services de sante mentale dans la communaute. Cela questionne la presente capacite des services dans la communaute a repondre aux comportements perturbateurs et fait ressortir la possibilite d'intervenir de facon precoce sur le potentiel passage a l'acte et sa judiciarisation. Ce projet de recherche novateur porte sur l'utilisation des services medicaux (sante mentale, physique, toxicologie) et des traitements pharmacologiques dans la communaute par des personnes ayant un trouble mental grave avant de commettre un delit NCRTM. Plus specifiquement, il decrira la nature, l'etendue et l'heterogeneite de l'utilisation des services; identifiera les facteurs psychosociaux et systemiques associes a la capacite des services a repondre adequatement aux besoins de differents types de patients; examinera l'impact des interruptions et modifications de traitements pharmacologiques sur le passage a l'acte; et mesurera l'importance de la proximite du lieu de residence aux points de services. Les resultats attendus mettront en lumiere les possibilites d'integrer les connaissances forensiques dans les services psychiatriques generaux et les services medicaux de proximite. Au bout du compte, cela ameliorera la qualite des soins offerts aux personnes ayant un trouble mental grave et presentant des comportements perturbateurs et reduira considerablement les couts lies a leur prise en charge.

column36: Examining the role of cannabis in the mental health of sexual minority youth: A community-based approach
column37: With the recent legalization of non-medical cannabis in Canada, much discussion has surrounded the relationship of this substance to mental health, especially in young people. To date, research on this association has produced mixed findings with respect to its direction, nature and magnitude. Moreover, there are specific groups for whom it is particularly important to better understand this relationship. This is the case for sexual minorities, who have higher rates of cannabis use and higher rates of concurrent mental health issues, which are both linked to difficulties in their environment related to their sexual orientation (e.g., discrimination, bullying). Previous research suggests that cannabis use occurs as a result of mental health issues. In fact, it is hypothesized that cannabis use is a coping tool in this marginalized group, which may importantly signal a lack of access to other coping resources. However, most of the literature has only examined these variables at one time point, and cannot determine the direction and nature of their relationship. Thus, it is still unclear why sexual minorities are turning to cannabis, and what other factors are important in the progression from mental health symptoms to later cannabis use. To answer these questions, this project will start by consulting sexual minority youth who use cannabis to better understand the reasons behind this practice, and to establish potentially important research questions. These questions will then be examined in a sample of participants followed from birth to early adulthood. Better understanding the nature of the relationship between cannabis use and mental health issues in sexual minority youth, while empowering these individuals by deeply involving them in the research process, uses research as a way to produce multifaceted impacts: involvement and validation of this group's lived experience, knowledge creation and dissemination, and establishment of key areas for intervention.

column36: Development of a harm reduction intervention for people with psychosis who use cannabis
column37: The Canadian legalization of cannabis exposed important knowledge gaps that needed prioritizing. While most cannabis users consume without experiencing any negative consequences, certain populations are more vulnerable to cannabis-related harms. For example, people with psychosis who use cannabis report worsened psychiatric symptoms and more hospitalizations than other people with mental health problems. Furthermore, problematic cannabis use is common in people with psychosis. However, few seek treatment, reporting that they want to avoid treatment-related stigma or continue using cannabis. It is thus crucial to put programs in place to reduce cannabis-related harms in young adults with psychosis. This project aims to develop an innovative intervention to reduce cannabis-related harms and which is tailored for people with psychosis who use cannabis. A review of the evidence has shown that no such interventions exist yet. Given the limited guiding literature, people with psychosis who use cannabis will first be surveyed on their preferences for cannabis-focused interventions. The intervention will then be developed, guided by the patient preference survey results. We will integrate a patient advisory committee into the intervention development process, to further ensure it is tailored to this population. The intervention will then be tested against standard care to see whether it is effective in reducing cannabis-related harms experienced by participants. Young people (aged 15 to 35) with psychosis who use cannabis and wish to modify their cannabis practices will be recruited to participate. My doctoral project will ensure the development and practical application of new knowledge that can directly improve practices to reduce the problems associated with cannabis among youth with psychosis. Various strategies will be employed to inform the clinical and research community of best practices for preventing cannabis-related harms in these young adults.

column36: Attachment & Child Health (ATTACH) Program: Promoting Vulnerable Children's Health At Scale
column37: Addressing the impact of toxic stressors (e.g. family violence, parental depression, low-income) on children can give children the best start in life and reduce entrenched societal health inequities. Toxic stress undermines parent-child relationship quality (including attachment) and puts children at risk for cognitive and motor developmental challenges, and health problems including alterations in immune function. Parents' reflective function (RF), i.e. capacity to understand their own and their child's mental states, can strengthen parent-child relationships, and buffer the impacts of toxic stress on children. We have developed and tested an intervention program called ATTACH for parents exposed to toxic stress and their vulnerable preschool-aged children, focusing on improving parents' RF. In extensive pilot work, we found the intervention not only improved RF, but also parent-child relationship quality and attachment, as well as children's cognitive and motor development. We recently adapted the program based on community partner feedback and developed a prototype e-learning platform to more rapidly train health care professionals to implement ATTACH. Using integrated knowledge transfer approaches, we will conduct an effectiveness-implementation hybrid study of ATTACH to evaluate real-world implementation: 1a) impacts on parent-child relationship quality (primary outcome), parental RF, and child development (cognitive and motor), 1b) for whom it works best/worst, 1c) impacts on immune biomarkers of inflammatory disease risk, 1d) health professionals' adherence to ATTACH program and (1e) longer-term impacts. We will also evaluate patients', health care professionals' and administrators' perspectives of 2a) intervention uptake and fidelity, 2b) implementation benefits, facilitators, barriers and challenges, and 2c) utility of the ATTACH e-learning platform.

column36: A Multi-Disciplinary, Patient-Partnered, Pan-Canadian, Comparative Effectiveness Evaluation of an Innovative Acute Pediatric Mental Health and Addiction Care Bundle
column37: For people suffering from an acute mental health or addictions crisis, emergency departments (EDs) serve as a vital settings for assessment, treatment and referral. The number of ED visits for such conditions is increasing rapidly. These crises are stressful and overwhelming, leaving the family vulnerable. In response, acute care must be evidence-based, family-centred, multidisciplinary, and lead to diagnosis and therapy while being integrated with community-based services. Current ED care is fragmented, system-centred and limits access to mental health services. Most families repeat their stories multiple times, and do not receive diagnostic assessments, therapy or clear follow-up instructions. Instead they find the 'door' they seek is closed and are left to navigate on their own. We will evaluate a patient and family-centred model of acute mental health care that is evidence-based. We will enroll 6,800 children and youth (<18 years of age) with visits to 8 pediatric EDs for mental health and substance use concerns. Using a cluster randomized trial design that integrates both comparative effectiveness and implementation science techniques, we will evaluate interventions that we believe will improve the care delivered leading to improved outcomes. These include: 1) Triage based evaluation of self-harm risk 2) Focused mental health team psychosocial evaluation to guide decision making 3) Choice And Partnership Approach (CAPA) to care These tools will be embedded into a model that removes the ED physician as the gatekeeper to mental health care and assures 24-48 hour community-based follow-up (booked before the child/family leave the ED). We believe this approach will provide the greatest value to children, youth and their families by matching resources and services to need while eliminating healthcare inefficiencies and closing care gaps. The model builds on existing services and committed investments, making it appropriate, feasible and highly likely to succeed.

column36: Innovative Pragmatic Cluster-Randomized Registry Trials to Improve Hemodialysis Care
column37: We are planning to conduct a trial that will compare different concentrations of magnesium in dialysis solutions that are currently used in Canadian hemodialysis centres. There is some early evidence to suggest that a higher concentration of magnesium in the dialysis solution may help patients live longer and experience less muscle cramping during dialysis treatments. We will use a new streamlined approach to do this large trial, which will be done in 160 Canadian hemodialysis centres (which during the 3-year trial period will care for 30,000 patients and provide over 8 million dialysis treatments). The streamlined approach includes analyzing information already collected in routine care that is stored in large healthcare databases. We will also train our community to use this trial approach, so that other treatments can be tested to help people on dialysis live well. If we can show that increasing the magnesium in the dialysis solution improves patient health, then it could become the standard of care for all dialysis patients worldwide. This simple adjustment to the dialysis procedure can be done at little to no cost and may even help reduce healthcare costs.

column36: Microbiome Regulation of Beta-Cell Autoimmunity and Type 1 Diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is caused by autoimmune inflammation of the pancreatic islets and destruction of beta cells, the only cell type that makes insulin. The incidence of this disease in developed countries has been rising at the rate of 3-5% per year over the past several decades. Similar trends have been observed for other autoimmune and allergic diseases. Our genes do not change this quickly suggesting the influence of changing environmental factors. The complex bacterial community in our intestines (the "microbiome") is essential for metabolism for development and function of our immune system. This project seeks to understand how environmental changes have influenced the gut microbiome in infants with defined genetic risk for T1D. There is also emerging evidence from observational studies in children at risk for T1D that the gut microbiome lacks the diversity of age-matched children who lack these genetic risk factors. However, we don't understand the mechanisms that link microbial activity and the human responses to gut microbes to this rise in T1D. Our project will use set of complementary approaches to determine how exposures to harmless intestinal bacteria can protect from or potentiate T1D, and to understand how the bacteria that confer these effects on the disease. Our project is focused on defining what these gut microbes do inside the developing infant, and to identify the immune responses in children at risk for diabetes that influence the development of the disease. The outcomes of this work will support new strategies for clinical trials to prevent and treat new onset T1D, identify microbes and their products with activity during early life and diabetes development, and advance the design and testing of new therapeutics.

column36: Nutrition Recommendation Intervention trialS in children's Healthcare
column37: Canada's children are falling behind. One in 4 are overweight or obese and more than 1 in 3 have factors that put them at risk for cardiovascular disease as adults. Children from low-income families are 70% more likely to be overweight or obese. Research across disciplines has shown that early life nutrition has profound effects on childhood obesity, development, mental health, and lifetime success. Optimizing early life nutrition to reduce inequalities in childhood obesity and its consequences is a promising approach. NuRISH is a suite of innovative clinical trials for children from low-income families which will determine whether primary healthcare prescription for: 1) Optimal breastfeeding with support from a mobile lactation consultant vs. usual care; 2) Appropriate introduction to solid food at 6 months with mobile support vs. usual care and 3) High-quality childcare starting at 1 year vs. usual care can prevent childhood obesity, and improve cardiovascular, developmental and mental health at 2 years of age. We will use new cohort trial methods leveraging Canada's largest childhood cohort study (TARGet Kids!) which will minimize cost and maximize feasibility. Parents and healthcare providers are involved in all aspects of this research. NuRISH holds promise to level inequalities in early life nutrition which will help prevent the next generation of Canadian children from experiencing childhood obesity and its long term physical and mental health consequences.

column36: An innovative registry-based trials platform to improve clinical care, outcomes, and health policy for children with treatable rare diseases
column37: New treatments for children with rare genetic diseases are appearing at a rapid pace. Many of these treatments have been found to improve outcomes in highly selected groups of patients under very specific conditions. In order to know how best to recommend, use, and pay for these treatments, patients and their families, health care providers, and policy-makers need more evidence about how the treatments work in all patients and settings. We also need to understand what additional supportive interventions are needed to get the best value from new rare disease drugs in order to improve functioning, quality of life, and other patient-centred outcomes. We are a group of patients, family members, health care providers, policy-makers, methodologists, and ethicists. We will work together to develop innovative registry-based randomized trials in order to rapidly develop comparative evidence about the effectiveness of treatments for rare genetic diseases in children. These high-quality trials will make use of comprehensive patient registries to enroll patients and measure outcomes. We will design and implement 3 inaugural trials to address priority questions for 3 rare diseases: spinal muscular atrophy, phenylketonuria, and mucopolysaccharidosis. Our methods are scalable so that we can also rapidly leverage the work to develop additional trials during and after the grant period for these and other rare diseases. We have a strong knowledge user engagement strategy that ensures we partner with patients and family members to co-design our research. We have also established partnerships with patient organizations, policy organizations, newborn screening programs, and other centres and networks. Our patient-partnered, equitable, and scalable approach to generating evidence will inform decisions about rare disease care and health policy, toward improved patient and system outcomes.

column36: Innovative Clinical Trials Program - Interdisciplinary Chronic Disease Collaboration
column37: Chronic diseases are associated with shorter lifespans, frequent contact with the health care system, and reduced quality of life. New ways of delivering health services are needed to promote health and ensure consistent, high quality care for Canadians living with chronic conditions. It is important, however, that new interventions and strategies are carefully studied to ensure they benefit patients and provide value. The Interdisciplinary Chronic Disease Collaboration (ICDC) is a team of health care leaders, researchers, patients, and care providers who work together to address health challenges. We research new ways of providing care for patients with chronic diseases and measure the impact of these changes on patient outcomes and experiences. We collect data and report our findings to the public and to health care decision makers. Over the next four years, the team plans to test health innovations and interventions that aim to improve care, safety and outcomes for people with three common and closely related chronic diseases: heart disease, diabetes and kidney disease. These studies will focus on: 1) the way patients' symptoms and experiences are recorded, communicated, and acted upon during doctors' visits, and whether these changes improve patient outcomes and experiences 2) the impact of using electronic health record systems (how doctors and hospitals collect health information and use it to deliver care) on patients'' experiences and outcomes in various settings across Alberta 3) strategies using pharmacists to improve safety in using common medications during times of illness to maximize benefits and minimize risks These research initiatives are each designed to produce new knowledge for patients, healthcare providers, and policy makers. The team is skilled in research design and rigorous evaluation, approaches that will allow rapid uptake of successful strategies into Alberta's health system.

column36: Applications of complexity science and network analysis to health behaviour change
column37: Four in five Canadian adults have at least one modifiable risk factor for chronic disease (e.g., smoking, inactivity, unhealthy eating). Additionally, the prevalence of Canadians with multiple preventable chronic diseases is increasing, which adds complexity to prevention and management. However, contemporary health and behavioural sciences tend to focus on health behaviours in isolation, failing to capture the dynamic interplay of psychological and environmental factors which influence the multiple behaviours contributing to health outcomes. There is an opportunity and a need to develop theory and methods to better understand how behaviour change is impacted by, and impacts upon, the rest of the activities in daily life, and how characteristics of an individual's behavioural patterns are related to their health and well-being. Despite calls in the literature for advancing our understanding of multiple behaviour change, there have not been major developments in theory or methods and efforts to date have been scattered across the literature. My PhD thesis aims to bring coherence to this literature by applying the principles of complexity science and network analysis to better understand and promote multiple health behaviour change.

column36: Examining the role of LRRK2 in peripheral immune modulation of brain health
column37: The Parkinson's disease-linked protein, LRRK2, has been linked by our lab and others, to an important role in innate immune response. Mutations in this protein can cause differential affects in the ability to fight pathogens. In our lab, we have begun to demonstrate that LRRK2 may be protecting the brain from infection primarily in the body-specific immune responses, rather than in the brain-specific immune responses. This would give important implication in the onset of Parkinson's disease if the disease-linked protein primarily has a function in the body rather than the brain. In three specific mouse-model experiments, we will investigate the role of Lrrk2 in the peripheral-specific and the brain-specific immune responses to determine where Lrrk2 is playing the biggest role. This will help identify the role of Lrrk2, and also where is best to target the protein in therapeutic approaches. We will use drug inhibitors, different viral and bacterial infections, and cellular signalling investigations to examine clearly the role of this protein. Through these distinct experiments, the role of LRRK2 in the immune system will be delineated between peripheral immune responses and brain-specific immune responses. This will provide insight into the origin and pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease. If we are correct, this will then inform potential new therapeutic targets (such as anti-inflammatory medication) and will directly inform ongoing clinical trials involving LRRK2-targetted drug therapies.

column36: Improving access to lung cancer screening in the underserved, and building capacity for future cancer patient oriented research in Canada
column37: Lung cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers in Canada, and is responsible for almost a quarter of all cancer related deaths nationwide. The use of low-dose CT as a screening tool to detect early stage and potentially curable lung cancers holds many promises in reducing mortality related to lung cancer. However, it is important to note, that lung cancer risk and mortality is closely linked to conditions of social disadvantage. People who are underserved are more likely to smoke, less likely to participate in cancer screening, and are more likely to die of their lung cancer. For a program such as lung cancer screening to be successful in reducing lung cancer death across the whole population, it will be important to understand and act upon patient identified priorities so that care can be provided to patients in a manner that meets their needs. In a recent study, patients at-risk of developing lung cancer and living with low income were asked to identify factors that influence their decision to participate in lung cancer screening. It was found that family physicians who were cognizant of the patients conditions of social disadvantage and provided care that was responsive to the social needs of the patients had a higher chance of referring patients to lung cancer screening. The proposed study therefore, seeks to fill this gap in the health delivery system by creating an online learning tool for family physicians together with patient partners. The purpose of this tool will be to impart learning on the social aspects of lung cancer, ways to navigate the clinical encounter, and provide patient-responsive care. The aim is to improve the uptake of lung cancer screening in people living with social disadvantage and potentially reduce lung cancer related mortality. The proposed project will also engage with cancer patient organizations across Canada to develop patient research committees, and build capacity for future cancer patient driven research.

column37: It is important that we do our best in Canada to make sure children are treated with tested and proven medicines and therapies. Child health research studies often need to be done in many hospitals or research institutes across Canada so that enough research participants can be found to finish the study in a timely way. In Canada, health research studies involving people must be reviewed and approved by a Research Ethics Board (REB). Often, when the same research study is being done in more than one hospital, the REB for each hospital must review and approve the same study. When a REB review must be done in each hospital it takes more time and work to start and finish a research study. As well, with different REBs reviewing the same study, how research participants are treated from hospital to hospital may differ. Our project will help will develop ways for all Canadian hospitals (and research institutes) involved in the same child health research study to have one REB review, instead of many. To do this we will build a web-based system that researchers and REBs across the country can use to manage a single REB review. We will also work with researchers and REBs to develop educational and other materials to ensure research involving children has the highest ethical standards. Clinical Trials Ontario (CTO) and the Maternal Infant Child & Youth Research Network (MICYRN) are the lead groups for this project. Our team involves over 35 experts in research ethics review and child health from across Canada. While our project focuses on child health research, we hope that this project will be a first step in developing a single research ethics review for any health research study done in more than one hospital or research institute in Canada.

column36: What's the secret sauce? Identifying effectiveness principles to enable the design, implementation and transferability of patient and community partnerships amongst marginalized populations using a developmental evaluation approach.
column37: The roles of patients and the public in the healthcare system are currently undergoing fundamental changes. No longer simply the passive recipients of care, patients and communities are increasingly seen as a transformative force in adapting healthcare services to the needs of today. This marked enthusiasm has translated to policy and funding initiatives for patient and public engagement in research, quality improvement, and healthcare governance. However, applying patient and community partnership principles requires researchers and decision-makers to more clearly understand how productive partnerships take shape for this promising, potentially transformative, approach to realize its potential. My research aims to evaluate the design, implementation and transferability of three partnership interventions in Montreal. As three distinct cases, with variations in team composition, origins of intervention models, funding sources, boroughs of implementation, and stages of realisation they provide a timely opportunity to evaluate partnership interventions as they occur in real-world settings. My research aims to answer the following questions: what key ingredients are needed for patients, care providers and researchers to work productively together to envision and create health interventions; are these same key ingredients applicable and useful to consider when implementing interventions; and finally, do these key ingredients transfer to other, emerging, partnership projects? The three partnership projects include: Caring Community (social isolation), Compassionate Communities (palliative care), and Community Links (HIV care). My research will be conducted using an internationally recognized developmental evaluation approach. In sum, this research aims to learn from the three interventions to strengthen our collective capacity to envision, plan, and conduct patient and community partnership projects with the ultimate goals of improving the care, and health of Canadians.

column37: L'isolement social est un probleme majeur chez les aines. Environ 20% des personnes de 65 ans et plus rapportent manquer de compagnie ou se sentir isolee. L'isolement social des aines est preoccupant puisqu'il est associe au declin cognitif, aux chutes, a l'institutionnalisation et a la mortalite. En multipliant et en rendant possible la participation des aines a des activites sociales signifiantes dans la communaute, il serait possible d'attenuer cet isolement. Plusieurs facteurs peuvent faciliter la participation sociale des aines dans leur communaute (ex. niveau de sante, amenagement des quartiers, presence d'organismes communautaires). A cet effet, le present projet vise a faire du quartier Cotes-des-Neiges a Montreal un quartier innovant ou les aines pourront plus facilement participer a des activites sociales signifiantes. Pour y parvenir, nous mobilisons toutes les parties prenantes (ex. aines du quartier, chercheurs, representant des organismes communautaires, du reseau de la sante et des services sociaux ainsi que des gens de l'industrie et du commerce). Ensemble, nous genererons des solutions innovantes basees, d'une part, sur la science et, d'autre part, sur les enjeux prioritaires en matiere de participation sociale exprimes par les aines du quartier. Nous travaillerons tous en synergie de facon a assurer que les innovations et changements crees via notre projet de recherche seront bien implantes de facon perenne et porteuse. Nos demarches seront documentees de facon detaillee afin qu'elles puissent etre reproduites dans differents quartiers a travers le Canada.

column36: Exploring sibling relationships of adolescents with disabilities during health care transition
column37: As children with disabilities grow up and become adults, they will move from their pediatric to adult health care providers. During this transition in health care, they need to learn how to make their own decisions about their health. This is not easy and they often need help from their family members. Siblings are part of the family who can support their brother or sister with a disability during transition. We developed the Sibling Youth Advisory Council (SibYAC), comprised of five young adults who have a brother or sister with a disability. We are collaborating with the SibYAC who identified this research project as important to raising awareness about siblings' roles. This research project includes three studies: 1) A review of information about current sibling programs 2) An interview with twenty young adults who have a brother or sister with a disability who can share how they have helped their brother or sister prepare for health care transition 3) The development and initial testing of a resource to help siblings better support their brother or sister prepare for health care transition Findings from this research can help young people with disabilities going through transition by promoting their siblings' role. Results will be shared with families and health care providers by: a) creating a summary of information, such as pamphlets, videos, or podcasts, to be posted on websites; b) publishing research papers; and c) presenting at health conferences and workshops. This information can encourage families and health care providers to use different ways to actively include siblings in health care transition. Successful transition to adult health care is important for young people with disabilities to live healthy and happy lives, be involved in the community, and have a good quality of life.

column37: L'itinerance est un phenomene complexe qui peut engendrer de nombreuses embuches pouvant etre difficile a surmonter en periode hivernale. Dans les faits, les personnes itinerantes sont considerees comme etant l'un des groupes de la population le plus a risque de subir des blessures dues au froid et de s'exposer a un risque de deces. Toutefois, bien que cela puisse entrainer des consequences irreversibles (ex: engelure, amputation, hypothermie) et voir meme aggraver leur sante souvent fragile, plusieurs personnes n'arrivent pas a trouver un endroit securitaire pour passer la nuit. En reponse a cette situation preoccupante, cette recherche vise, a partir du point de vue des personnes concernees par la problematique, a saisir les barrieres individuelles et structurelles qui engendrent ce non-recours, l'impact sur leur sante et leurs besoins en vue de cibler les pratiques pouvant faciliter l'acces a l'hebergement. Les enjeux lies a la consommation de substances psychoactives et la culture seront consideres afin de saisir les particularites qui peuvent faire obstacle, et ce, selon en tenant compte des enjeux lies a l'identite du genre. Par la suite, des approches innovatrices pour repondre aux besoins des personnes itinerantes qui n'accedent pas aux refuges d'urgence en periode hivernale seront mises en lumiere. Ce projet repose une approche qualitative pour mieux cibler les enjeux que vivent les personnes itinerantes qui n'ont pas recours aux refuges d'urgence et sur un devis de recherche participative afin que les personnes itinerantes soient parties prenantes dans cette etude a deux differents niveaux. Le premier sera d'avoir des presences-terrain dans un organisme frequente par les personnes itinerantes et la deuxieme sera de mettre en place un comite d'expert , la ou deux personnes qui ont deja vecues dans la rue en periode hivernale pourront prendre part avec d'autres professionnels ( gestionnaires, policiers, intervenants, politiciens).

column36: Lipogenetics of Dementia
column37: With a rapidly aging population, dementia is becoming a global crisis with no promising remedies. Presently, we still do not have either the prognostic or therapeutic arsenal to be able to halt or even significantly slow down dementia progression. Aberrant sphingolipid metabolism is linked to risk of dementia in a number of age-related neurodegenerative disorders, yet the critical metabolic pathways responsible for cognitive decline are unknown. Here, I propose to: 1) Determine how specific disruptions in sphingolipid metabolism act synergistically with pathological protein accumulation to cause cognitive decline; 2) Establish whether these metabolic changes are modulated by age and sex; and 3) Assess if targeting critical sphingolipid pathways can delay learning and memory impairment in experimental models of Lewy Body Dementia and mixed Alzheimer's Disease (AD)/Lewy Body Disease.

column36: Electrophysiological alarm signals of neurodevelopmental disorders.
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are diverse mental health conditions characterized by a delay or disturbance in the acquisition of skills in a variety of developmental domains (motor, social, language, cognition, etc.). In children, diagnoses include attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, global developmental delay, and intellectual disability. Specific interventions are necessary to promote social and school integration, academic success and employment. Yet, consistent and objective tools for NDD diagnosis are missing. Genetic risk factors have been identified but are not yet reconciled with behavioral and brain anatomy and activity phenotypes in individual patients, especially at the earliest stages of development. I propose to develop neurophysiological signal markers from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) that are predictive of neurocognitive outcomes in young children. The validation of these biomarkers and their alignment with genetic risks would significantly improve and augment the clinical toolkit for diagnosis and treatment response monitoring, in particular in remote or unprivileged regions of Canada and worldwide. I will thus propose EEG signal analytics in healthy controls and chosen groups of NDD patients. My project will use multi-omic datasets (including EEG) already collected from 400 infants, children and adults presenting genetic risk factors for cognitive impairments and autism disorders. Using cutting-edge statistical learning tools, I aim to identify "genomic-EEG dimensions" to dissect the phenotype heterogeneity in NDDs. I will clarify the relevance of EEG signal features to distinguish and anticipate atypical neurodevelopment trajectories. My research aims to contribute significantly to more systematic understanding of NDDs, associated genetic factors and to the development of cost-effective clinical markers that can assist with diagnosis, prognosis, and intervention.

column36: Identification of novel Pseudomonas aeruginosa metabolic regulators and characterization of their role in adaptive resistance and virulence
column37: Effective antimicrobial agents are essential for treatment of life-threatening bacterial infections. Although bacteria develop resistance to therapies naturally by mutagenesis, emergence of resistant strains is accelerating because of irresponsible antibiotic use. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a highly adaptable species of bacteria that is listed amongst the most threatening drug-resistant pathogens for which new antibiotics are urgently needed. The display of adaptive phenotypes, including biofilm formation and rapid surface propagation, are associated with increased resistance and are hallmarks of bacterial stress responses that allow coping with nutrient limitation and antibiotic exposure in the host. These adaptive lifestyles may be regulated by the expression of genes that are responsible for sensing and responding to environmental stimuli via central metabolism. Several metabolic regulators exist as substrate responsive proteins chromosomally encoded as components of larger regulatory networks. For example, NtrC is part of the NtrBC two-component system that is not only involved in nitrogen assimilation, but also activation of a bacterial virulence program known as the stringent stress response. Activation of the stringent stress response alters the transcriptome of bacteria at a global level via expression of genes involved in biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance. Whole genome analyses have revealed that NtrC contributes to the success of P. aeruginosa in acute and chronic wound infections. Here, we propose to examine the influence of NtrC as well as other metabolically important regulators on virulence-associated rapid surface motilities. Active motility allows migration toward preferred nutrient sources away from stressors, colonization of host tissue and formation of surface-associated biofilms. Consistent with these roles, motility is intrinsically associated with bacterial metabolism and often coupled with the expression of virulence factors.
