column36: Identification of molecular drivers and protein mediators of leptomeningeal metastasis in pediatric medulloblastoma for development of novel targeted therapeutics
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common type of primary brain tumour in children and a leading cause of pediatric cancer death. Currently, affected children are treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and aggressive radiotherapy, which leaves nearly all patients with lifelong health challenges and cognitive impairment. In a subset of these children, the tumours will spread from the cerebellum (a structure of the brain lying in the posterior base of the skull) where they first arise, and move through the bloodstream to the membranes which cover the brain (the leptomeninges). Once the leptomeninges are colonized, the cancer proliferates rapidly, progressively coating the surface of the brain and ultimately causing death of the affected child. The biological mechanism by which some tumours escape into the bloodstream and spread to the leptomeninges is unclear. Given that the metastatic disease carries mutations which are unique from the original disease in the cerebellum, we hypothesize that there exist specific genes or mutations which facilitate this metastatic process. Further, the very specific dissemination to the leptomeninges (but not other parts of the body) suggests the existence of unique proteins and receptors in the blood vessels in the leptomeninges which enable tumor cells to exist the blood stream uniquely in this location. By identifying the specific genes and cellular processes which drive metastasis, we hope to intelligently develop specific therapies which target these genes or the proteins they encode, and prevent medulloblastoma metastasis in affected children.

column36: Determining the role of endothelial activation on microRNA communication in atherosclerotic plaque: towards identifying of a novel therapeutic target in carotid disease
column37: Carotid artery stenosis (CAS) is a common cause of stroke, a devastating event that results in permanent neurological deficits. There are 400,000 people in Canada living with the disabilities of a stroke, resulting in major impairments to quality of life. The financial costs of stroke to the Canadian healthcare system amount to $2.5 billion a year. There is an urgent need to improve patient care and outcomes for carotid disease. The most effective way to prevent a stroke in patients with CAS is to perform an operation to remove the plaque. However, the surgery is not without risk. We have difficulty assessing this risk and managing these patients because we do not understand the molecular mechanisms of plaque progression. Here, I propose the development of a biomarker that predicts at-risk carotid stenosis and treatment to stabilize and decrease plaque size. The present project will outline the molecular mechanisms that cause plaque instability, rupture, and thus, stroke. I will delineate the mechanisms facilitating communication within carotid artery plaque that promote plaque instability. Specifically, microRNA - released by cells of the blood vessel wall - are prime candidates facilitating this communication within the plaque. Given their ability for systemic (blood) circulation, they are excellent biomarkers to help clinicians identify and treat patients prior to a stroke. Further, a mechanistic understanding of their local effects on plaque morphology will allow for design of therapeutics aimed at stabilizing plaque. The impact of this study to design biomarkers and therapeutics for stroke patients will allow improved patient selection and treatment. Such advancements in patient care will decrease stroke rates, thereby, reducing disability, mortality and overall cost of care.

column36: Determining the Role of Mitophagy in mtDNA Selection in Drosophila
column37: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of our cell due to their capacity for generating ATP, the energy currency of all cells in the body. Mitochondria can make ATP efficiently using instructions stored in DNA. A variety of neurological and metabolic diseases can arise when that DNA becomes mutated and our cells are unable to make ATP properly. To prevent the spread of mutated mitochondrial DNA from parents to children, cells monitor and remove any mitochondria with mutated DNA in a process called "mitochondrial DNA purifying selection". My project aims to understand the mechanism by which cells eliminate mutated mitochondrial DNA and keep that mitochondria healthy. Of particular importance is how a cell can distinguish between healthy and mutated mitochondria, and how the cell then targets and destroys those mutated mitochondria. This work has important impacts on medicine as well as our deepening understanding of how cells normally function.

column36: Family engagement in research: Evaluation, sustainability and scalability of an online training program for family and research partners in child health research
column37: Internationally, it is recognized that research benefits from meaningful stakeholder involvement. However, how stakeholders (e.g., patients and families) are engaged in research is not self-evident and the demand for such roles has not kept pace with the need for appropriate training. In 2018, researchers at McMaster University partnered with two parent advisors to develop and deliver an online training program in family engagement in research: 'Family Engagement in Research Certificate of Completion Program'. This program is unique in that it brings families of children with neurodevelopmental disabilities together with researchers from across Canada and internationally in a 10-week online course. The first two cohorts of the certificate program are now complete with an additional two cohorts in progress (~ 100 graduates). We are currently evaluating the feasibility and short-term impacts of the program. The aim of this research is to explore the longer-term impacts, as well as the sustainability and scalability of the program. Findings from this study will provide key insight into the impact of training in patient-oriented research and will have a transformative impact on the way child health research is conducted in Canada.

column36: Understanding the role of stigma for veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder and determining methods for better supporting the integration of service dogs in their lives
column37: Stigma refers to an attribute that is deeply discrediting (i.e., deviant) and experienced by individuals who are different from the norm in society or possess an undesirable attribute (Goffman, 1963). Many stigmatized individuals experience depression, anxiety, isolation, reduced social network, and limited social support. Several researchers have examined the concept of stigma related to veterans with mental health diagnoses like PTSD and with respect to veterans' concerns with accessing care for their illness. There are also a number of research teams examining the potential benefits of SDs as a compliment to other mental healthcare practices (i.e., pharmaceuticals, therapy). However, the examination of stigma in the context of Canadian veterans suffering from PTSD with SDs has not been undertaken yet. Results from a patient-oriented, community-based project with Canadian veterans with PTSD suggest that stigma is one barrier that can impede successful integration of service dogs in their lives. column36: Where do I belong? A participatory, mixed methods study examining citizenship among youth experiencing the onset of a mental illness
column37: Mental health problems typically begin during adolescence and young adulthood and can significantly disrupt the important trajectories that youth may be setting. In addition to negatively affecting these individual-level trajectories, mental health problems may disrupt young peoples' sense of being full citizens in their communities. Studies have shown that supporting people's capacities to live as full citizens can help people recovery from their mental health problems. However, all of this research has examined citizenship among adults with mental health problems. It is unclear if and how young people with mental health problems may suffer a lack of citizenship; what citizenship means for young people; nor is it clear what factors predict citizenship and if citizenship is related to recovery. Addressing these knowledge gaps may prevent or limit potential losses to young people's sense of citizenship; and may help young people remain or become more engaged in their communities. To address these knowledge gaps, I have worked with youth with mental health problems to identify three objectives to be evaluated through the use of participatory, mixed research methods. We will conduct interviews to discover the meaning of, and perceived facilitators and barriers to citizenship among youth with mental health problems, as well as the role citizenship plays in participants' recovery. Based on the qualitative findings, we will use questionnaires to examine rates and predictors of citizenship among a larger sample of youth with mental health problems, and the degree to which citizenship predicts recovery. We will then use qualitative methods to evaluate a pre-existing citizenship-based intervention. Results will be shared with youth, clinicians and policy makers throughout the world, and will help improve youth mental health services in Canada.

column36: A randomized clinical trial of an exercise intervention for older adults with mild cognitive impairment in residential care
column37: Many older adults experience changes in their thinking skills, such as having a hard time remembering new things. The good news is that scientists have discovered that exercise may actually help improve thinking skills - even in older adults! Research has shown that exercise can help your brain to grow new cells that can improve overall thinking skills. But, scientists still have more questions. What specific thinking skills improve with exercise? Could exercise also improve mood and quality of life? And can exercise actually help to delay or prevent thinking skills from getting worse? This study will test an exercise intervention in older adults living in a care home with "mild cognitive impairment", a term used to describe individuals who have some problems in their thinking skills that might get worse over time. People in the study will have their thinking skills, mood, and quality of life tested when they enroll in the study, after a 12-week exercise intervention, and 3-months after the exercise intervention has ended. The intervention will involve using a stationary virtual cycling device. It is really easy and fun for older people to use, as they can sit in a chair and use either foot or hand pedals to move their way through a virtual environment. Half of participants will use the virtual cycling device while the other half of participants will continue to do their normal activities. Everyone in the study will wear a watch-like device throughout the duration of the study to record daily physical activity and hours of sleep. This study will help us to determine the immediate and long-term effects of exercise on thinking skills, mood, and quality of life in older adults with some problems in their thinking skills. Importantly, this study is clinical, meaning the results can be used to inform treatment for older adults with thinking problems to help prevent, delay, and reduce the negative impacts of brain diseases on mood and quality of life in older adults.

column36: Turning up the heat: treating 'cold' tumors with combinatorial cancer immunotherapies.
column37: Cancer immunotherapy is a rapidly growing field of research which has led to several unprecedented advances in cancer treatment. Key to the success of immunotherapy are T cells, a type of white blood cell that can recognize and kill cancer cells. However, a major subset of solid tumors are immunologically 'cold', meaning they are resistant to T cell entry. One promising strategy shown to ignite immune activity within cold tumors has been the use of oncolytic viruses. These engineered viruses selectively infect and replicate within cancer cells, while leaving healthy cells unharmed. Yet, many cancers express inhibitory 'off switches' called immune checkpoints, which can prevent T cells from killing tumor cells. My thesis work will create a new therapeutic strategy that uses OVs in combination with blocking antibodies against immune checkpoints elevated in cold tumors. This strategy is designed to 'heat up' cold tumors, thereby enhancing the immune response against cancer. In Aim 1, I will use state of the art genomic and histological methods to profile tumor and immune cells following OV treatment. By discerning the landscape of checkpoints in OV treated tumors, I will design rational combination strategies to further enhance T cell activity. In Aim 2, I will assess the therapeutic efficacy of combining OV treatment with blockade of checkpoints in a cold murine cancer model. By targeting immune checkpoints found to be elevated in cold tumors, I expect to see enhanced immune cell infiltration and clearance of established tumors. Looking to the future, my research is part of the Canadian Oncolytic Virus Consortium, a national scientific network aimed at accelerating OV based treatments. This provides a unique opportunity for my innovative approach to quickly move from bench to bedside for the benefit of patients.

column36: An Investigation of the Earliest Changes in the Brain due to Mild Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects over 100000 Canadians, a number that is expected to rise as the population ages. While PD is typically characterized by motor symptoms, most people with PD will also experience cognitive impairments which can be more disabling than motor symptoms. Cognitive impairment in PD is progressive. It starts out as a decline in cognitive functioning that exceeds what would be expected in healthy aging but that does not interfere with daily functioning (mild cognitive impairment; PD-MCI). In the majority of cases, this cognitive impairment advances to dementia, which has a significant negative impact on daily functioning and quality of life. Treatment is most effective in early stages, thus timely identification of patients with PD who at risk for developing PD-MCI is imperative. Large databases such as the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) following newly diagnosed people with PD over many years using both cognitive and neuroimaging measures offer a unique opportunity to retrospectively identify the earliest changes in the brain before cognitive impairment is established and irreversible brain damage has occurred. Using the PPMI cohort, we will examine differences in brain structure in those who we know convert to PD-MCI compared to their counterparts with PD who remain cognitively stable. The ability to detect changes in brain structure prior to observable changes in cognition can inform the early identification of patients with PD who have the highest likelihood of developing PD-MCI, which is a risk factor for developing dementia. This has implications for patient management and prognosis, allowing for the implementation of early prevention or treatments methods that could improve long-term cognitive outcomes and quality of life, as well as allow for increased treatment options.

column36: Understanding the Impact of Patient Transfers on End-of-Life Patient Experience: The Effects of Institutional Abstinence from Medical Assistance in Dying
column37: Many healthcare institutions in Canada currently decline to provide medical assistance in dying (MAID) on-site for religious or moral reasons. If patients receiving medical care at such institutions request MAiD, they need to be transferred elsewhere in order to access this important medical service and Charter-protected legal right. The process places additional burdens-in terms of seeking information and support, navigating the health system, and communicating with health professionals-on vulnerable patients who are already battling grievous illness and psychological distress. While anecdotes relating to the issue occasionally appear in the press, there is very little systematic evidence on the experiences of patients and families who make this critical transition in care. This study aims to fill this vital knowledge gap by mapping the MAiD access trajectories of patients and families at MAiD-abstaining institutions. Through a combination of textual analysis (media sources and institutional grey literature) and in-depth interviews (with patients, families, policymakers, and health professionals), this project will generate evidence on how patients and families interact with healthcare institutions and professionals; where they seek information; who they turn to for support and decision-making; what alternative routes they choose when faced with barriers; and where key resources to support their transfer journeys are located. Utilizing the Patient Engagement Framework suggested by the Strategy for Patient-Oriented Research (SPOR), this study will involve patients and families-across all stages of its research design-for: (i) informing the socio-ethical debate on institutional MAiD-abstinence; (ii) identifying gaps in MAiD service delivery, and (iii) making policy recommendations for equitable access to MAiD.

column36: Transition Readiness and Experiences of Young Adults with Co-occurring Chronic Health and Mental Health Issues Exiting Pediatric Services: A Mixed Methods Study
column37: Transition from the pediatric to the adult health care system is challenging for adolescents and young adults (AYA) with chronic health conditions. AYA often feel inadequately prepared to manage their own health when they transfer into the adult system and are at risk of poor health outcomes. AYA with chronic health conditions are 2-3 times more likely to have mental health disorders than their healthy peers. The presence of mental health disorders in AYA with chronic conditions results in increased hospital admissions, decreased medication adherence, higher morbidity and higher health care costs. In addition, AYA with co-occurring issues (i.e. physical and mental health) may be exiting multiple pediatric services simultaneously, further complicating the transfer of care. Transition readiness, defined as AYA knowledge and self-management skills, contributes to successful health care transition. Transition readiness has not been explored for AYA with co-occurring health and mental health issues. The purpose of this patient-oriented, mixed methods study is to examine the transition readiness and transition experiences of 17-18 year olds with co-occurring chronic health and mental health issues exiting pediatric services in Alberta. First, Transition Readiness Assessment Questionnaire (TRAQ) scores will be compared among those with chronic health conditions, with and without mental health comorbidity. Next, interviews will be conducted with 10-15 AYA with co-occurring health and mental health issues to explore their experiences preparing for transition to adult services and analyzed using qualitative description. Integration will occur following analysis of the quantitative and qualitative data to allow for a deeper understanding of the transition needs of this group. Results of this study will inform the refinement of transition readiness practices in order to improve patient care for AYA with co-occurring health and mental health issues in Alberta.

column36: Patient-engaged development of standards for a reporting guideline for scaling studies of health interventions
column37: Health research generates evidence-based knowledge that need to be reported adequately to be translated effectively in decision making. Moreover, health interventions proven to be effective need to be scaled up to help improve health outcomes for the entire population in order to promote health equity. However, gap in the quality of reporting of health research are well documented in the literature, particularly for scaling studies, as documented in a systematic review. In addition, although the importance of sex and gender in the manifestation and management of health conditions and in health outcomes is well established, their considerations are rarely integrated into research design and reporting guidelines. To address this gap, the aim of this research project is to develop the standards for a reporting guideline for studies assessing the impact of scaling up of health interventions. The project will be guided by the steps recommended for developing health research reporting guidelines by EQUATOR, an international network that promotes transparent and accurate reporting of health research. As successful scaling up of health innovations is highly context-dependent, sex and gender considerations will be integrated into the development process. The whole process will involve national and international collaborators including two patient partners as members of the research team. As a result, the guidelines developed will be useful both in Canada and around the world to improving the quality of reporting of scaling studies and facilitate the replication and scaling of the health innovations studied.

column36: Examining the effect of Canada's unique medical abortion drug policy on patient abortion access and outcomes
column37: One third of women in Canada will have at least one abortion in their life. Until 2017, 96% of Canadian abortions were performed using surgery in fewer than 100 facilities, located primarily in large, urban centres. Under this model, access to abortion was markedly inequitable. Some patients traveled long distances to reach service locations, and experienced significant wait times, thus undergoing abortions at later (and thus less safe) gestational ages. Drawing attention to the urgency of this issue, in 2016, the UN Human Rights Commissioner called on the Canadian government to improve equitable access to abortion in Canada. The medical abortion drug mifepristone became available in Canada in January 2017. Canadian federal and provincial governments enacted policies that are unique globally to enable mifepristone abortion provision in primary care by family doctors or nurse practitioners, including those with no prior abortion practice. Within one year of its introduction, many provincial insurers fully subsidized the $350 mifepristone cost to reduce financial barriers to access. Health policymakers urgently need to understand whether their mifepristone policies were effective in improving abortion access and reducing inequities, and whether this change in abortion practice has impacted abortion outcomes. However, the effect of mifepristone policy on abortion access and outcomes have not yet been examined. The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of Canadian mifepristone medical abortion policy on abortion access and outcomes using comprehensive, high-quality, linked health administrative data from British Columbia and Ontario. This policy framework positioned Canada as an international leader for addressing reproductive health access inequity through innovative liberalization of abortion practice. Health policymakers eagerly await the findings of this study to inform policy changes in a wide range of international settings.

Par exemple, 41% des personnes ayant un probleme de toxicomanie ont aussi un probleme de sante mentale et 88,5% des personnes ayant un diabete de type 2 ont au moins deux autres problemes de sante (p. ex. obesite). Les personnes ayant des problemes complexes (PP) doivent y avoir un role central. Pourtant, les strategies proposees pour les integrer dans les approches de collaboration sont encore peu nombreuses, concretes et difficilement atteignables. Ce projet vise donc a identifier, selon la perspective des parties prenantes, les strategies qui favorisent l'integration des PP dans les approches de collaboration et les effets de cette integration, incluant ceux non desires. Pour ce faire, les strategies d'integration seront identifiees a partir de la litterature. Des entrevues seront faites aupres des parties prenants ayant participe a des approches de collaboration, dont deux au Quebec, une sur les troubles concomitants de sante mentale et de toxicomanie et une sur les maladies chroniques (diabete). Enfin, une activite collaborative sera organise pour identifier les elements importants qui devraient etre evalues a l'avenir. Cette etude permettra de mieux soutenir l'integration des PP dans les approches de collaboration.

column36: Relationship between brain cholinergic innervation and clinical manifestations of REM sleep behaviour disorder: a PET study using 18F-FEOBV
column37: A large initiative in Canadian health research at present is to develop tools that identify the early stages of neurodegenerative disease. This quest has been facilitated by the discovery that rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder is a significant early sign of a class of neurodegenerative diseases. People with REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) do not have enough muscle paralysis during REM sleep, which causes them to "act out" their dreams at night. More than 80% of these individuals go on to develop Parkinson's disease or a related neurodegenerative disease, such as Lewy body dementia. The neurotransmitter acetylcholine plays a role in REM sleep and in these neurodegenerative diseases, but it has not yet been sufficiently examined in people with RBD. Seeking to better understand this question, my doctoral project will look into the role of acetylcholine in RBD using a novel compound for PET imaging called 18F-FEOBV, which our laboratory has been developing over the last 15 years. This compound enables researchers to study acetylcholine systems in the brain in a more precise manner than the existing PET compounds. I will recruit thirty participants from the Montreal RBD study at the Sacre-Coeur Hospital and will guide them through an MRI scan and a PET scan using 18F-FEOBV at the Montreal Neurological Institute. The participants will also undergo a sleep recording, cognitive testing, and a neurological examination. My hypothesis is that the RBD individuals will show acetylcholine-related abnormalities in the brain, whereas the controls will not. Additionally, I expect to see a relationship between these abnormalities and muscle activity during REM sleep, lower cognitive scores, and other early signs of neurodegeneration. My ultimate goal in this project is, with the help of 18F-FEOBV, to shed light on the mechanisms involved in RBD, and in so doing, in the early stages of certain neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Transitional Care of Rural Older Adults: Understanding the Interplay between Older Adult Health Construction and the Influence of Multidimensional Contexts on the Transitional Care of Older Adults in Rural Communities
column37: Background: Providing health services for aging populations is the fundamental issue of modern Canadian health policy, yet ineffective models of service provision result in inadequate transitional support for the older demographic. Although numerous regional transitional care strategies exist, experts acknowledge that older adults in rural communities are still vulnerable during transfers between care settings, resulting in compromised patient safety and poor quality care. Objectives: Informed by inquiry in critical gerontology, health integration and rural health, the research will pursue the goal of better understanding the interplay between older adult health construction and the influence of multidimensional contexts on the transitional care of older adults. The study will pursue the following objectives: 1)To explore perceptions of how older adult health is constructed, 2)To understand the experiences of key stakeholders involved in the transitional care of older adults in rural communities, 3)To better understand the contexts in which older adult transitional care is provided and 4)To provide a foundation of information for a regional older adult care network. Method: The research will involve a case study of Haliburton County and use a multi-method approach that encompasses three phases: 1)A Community Inventory, 2)Go-Alongs and 3) Semi-Structured Interviews. Considering the influence of context and the perspectives of key informants, this study will focus on two types of transitions: 1)when an older adult is transferred from a hospital to a long-term care home and 2)when an older adult is transferred from a hospital to a home in the community. Significance: Establishing the first study of rural older adult transitional care that traverses multiple care settings, this research will prepare Canada for the impact of the aging population and transform transitional care of older adults to ensure health services meet the needs of Canadians in the 21st century.

column36: The effect of dioxin/dioxin-like pollutants on beta-cell development, function, and survival in mouse and human islets
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a global health issue, with an estimated 592 million adults diagnosed with diabetes by 2035. As such, understanding the cause of diabetes to reduce its prevalence is of upmost importance. Diabetes is a chronic disease associated with hyperglycemia due to inadequate insulin production by pancreatic beta cells. Mounting research suggests that the global increase in diabetes prevalence may be due to environmental factors. In fact, epidemiological studies have consistently shown a correlation between diabetes incidence and exposure to dioxins, a class of highly persistent environmental pollutants. Research in the Bruin lab has shown that exposure to dioxins suppresses glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in human and mouse adult beta cells, and causes beta cell loss in male mice. This suggests that dioxins may increase diabetes risk by altering beta cell function and survival. However, there is still a significant gap in knowledge on the mechanism responsible for dioxin-induced changes in beta cell physiology. My PhD will focus on establishing a potential mechanism by which dioxins increase diabetes risk by assessing effects of dioxins on beta cell development, function, and survival in mouse and humans. This research will inform the community about chemicals that are a concern for diabetes risk and will ultimately aid in altering our environment to reduce diabetes incidence.

column36: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cerebral organoid allografts of glioblastoma multiforme recapitulate patient disease phenotypes
column37: The brain tumour glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common malignant central nervous system tumour and is known for its extreme aggressiveness leading to a median patient survival of 15 months. GBM is highly resistant to therapy, with tumour cell and microenvironmental heterogeneity proposed as major contributing factors. Standard in vitro cell culture is limited in its ability to recapitulate this complex niche-tumour cell interaction, while genetic mouse-modelling and xenograft studies of GBM lack species-specificity. Collectively these limitations in pre-clinical models may contribute to the poor responses of patients in clinical trials observed particularly often with GBM. Alternatively, human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived cerebral organoids (COs) may provide a new platform for studying GBM that can overcome some of the current limitations in GBM models. These self-organized 3D-structures cultured in vitro recapitulate the structure and organization of a human brain. Our lab has optimized a CO-production protocol to limit intra-organoid variability and produce COs with high efficiency that mimicks the cellular physiology of a developing human cortex and its unique microenvironment. I hypothesize that the cellular landscape of hPSC-derived cerebral organoids creates a cortical microenvironment that when combined with human GBM better reflects the cellular and molecular behaviours of a GBM tumour-tissue niche in humans in vivo. Here I describe my work on establishing human GBM allografts (human COs engrafted with species-specific human GBM cell lines) where GBM cell marking, viability, and tumour progression will be explored, along with unique human patient-specific phenotypes observed not seen in xenografts. Allograft modelling of the GBM microenvironment will provide a new system to investigate oncogenic properties of GBM and identify new druggable targets that can be translated to the clinic.

column36: The EEG-Indexed Auditory Mismatch Negativity as a Biomarker to Predict Psychosis Onset
column37: Schizophrenia is a disorder that is often preceded by early symptoms of psychosis, however the accuracy of predicting conversion based on clinical symptoms is low. The healthy human brain is able to detect changes in our auditory environment, whether we are paying attention or not and even while we are sleeping. This function, originally thought to have developed so we could detect sounds indicating danger approaching, may seem simple but is an important part of our daily lives and is the result of complex computations within the brain. It has been long reported that schizophrenia patients show deficiencies in this auditory change detection mechanism, and that this might be an observable marker of greater dysfunction within the brain of those affected. Recent work has suggested that this deficit may be present in individuals at risk of developing a disorder of psychosis, such as schizophrenia, before psychosis emerges. What is unclear, however, is whether early-occurring deficits in auditory change detection can predict who will transition to psychosis and who will not. If we were able to identify an objective, accurate biological marker of psychosis risk, this would allow clinicians to initiate early treatment in those who will transition to psychosis, while avoiding unnecessary treatments in those who will not. This project aims to shine a light on this question by examining auditory change detection in individuals at risk of developing a psychotic disorder, whether it be due to a family history of schizophrenia or the presence of early symptoms that may or may not turn into psychosis. It is hoped that we might identify that elusive objective biological marker that would allow for accurate prediction of psychosis risk and early treatment, so as to change the course of this illness that the World Health Organization has called schizophrenia "youth's greatest disabler due to its typical emergence during young adulthood and the devastating impact on functioning".

column36: The cost of healthy eating: The development, pilot, and retail feasibility of two nutritious food basket assessment instruments
column37: Eating an unhealthy diet increases a person's risk of health problems and death. Most of the food that people buy are from food stores. Since the types and cost of foods available to customers in food stores can influence what they eat, it is important to understand the cost of a healthy diet and how food stores can offer healthy and affordable foods to customers. The Nutritious Food Basket is a tool made by the Canadian government and used by Canadian provinces to track the cost of healthy eating. The Food Basket is a list of the amounts and types of foods that make up a healthy diet for a family of four. The food items in the Food Basket are based on the most popular foods eaten by Canadians and that meet dietary recommendations from a 2004 Canadian survey which reported the amount of certain foods that Canadians ate. The provinces then go into a set number of food stores and price the items in the Food Basket to get the overall cost of the Food Basket. Recently, the Canadian government released the results of a new Canadian survey which reported on the foods Canadians ate and updated Canada's Food Guide. Based on this new information this project will look to update the foods in the Nutritious Food Basket and understand if less healthy foods that still meet Canadian healthy eating guidelines can be used to create a less expensive food basket. Two food baskets will be created; one that includes foods that make up a healthy diet and another based on what Canadians reported eating. Both baskets will be priced in 14 Nova Scotian food stores and be compared to see if there are any differences in the price and nutritional quality of food items between the two baskets. Management staff from 5-10 of the food stores studied will be interviewed to understand what makes it difficult for them to sell healthy and less expensive foods to customers. The project results will be used to create health policies to improve healthy eating and prevent disease in Canada.

column36: The Impact of Sex on Vascular Endothelial-Dependent Vasodilatory Adaptations to High-Intensity Interval Training in Older Adults
column37: Blood vessel disease remains a leading cause of death in Canada. Advanced age and a decrease in the ability of cells inside the arteries to make them relax are both risk factors. Regular moderate-intensity exercise can improve blood vessel health in older adults but the benefits of this type of training are less in older women than men. Perhaps older women need a greater exercise stimulus? High-intensity interval training (HIIT) has been shown to be a safe and better form of exercise for blood vessel health in older adults. It may provide improved results in older women but we do not know if older men and women respond the same (or differently) to this form of training. The aim of this project is to find out if HIIT improves artery health more in older women versus men. We have already finished a small pilot study in 12 older adults (7 women) who completed HIIT. We will now recruit another 18 older adults (8 women) to complete HIIT. Artery health in the upper arm and lower leg will be measured using an ultrasound machine. Our test of artery health involves briefly slowing blood flow to the hand or foot using a pressure cuff. Once the cuff pressure is released, blood flow will increase and cause the artery to get bigger. The larger it gets, the healthier it is. These tests will be made before and after HIIT. We will also repeat these tests in a group of older men and women who do not engage in HIIT as a control measure. We are still unclear about the best type of exercise training for improving blood vessel health in older men and women. Moderate-intensity training does not appear to be as helpful in older women. As such, we need to study other training protocols. If we know whether HIIT programs enhance artery health differently in older men and women then we can start to develop better targeted strategies to prevent blood vessel disease in older adults.

column36: Neurobiological markers for antidepressant response in major depressive disorder
column37: Depression is a serious and common condition that is poorly understood for its causes and brain features, and one that disproportionately affects women twice as often as men. The symptoms are diverse and wide-ranging, affecting emotional, cognitive and physical aspects. Although there are many medications that are available, the mechanisms for how they work are also not well-known and patients do not always respond to the first one they try. Multiple medication switches increase suffering and can increase the risk of suicide. A major challenge in psychiatry is to develop and incorporate "lab tests" in order to personalize the treatment for the patient based on their brain structure. One important structure is the hypothalamus, a small region that controls many unconscious processes in our body, including stress regulation. Stress is a major risk factor for developing depression, making the hypothalamus a region of interest. Additionally, the cerebral cortex (the large "bumpy" part of the brain) is also of interest, given that many of the more complex mental and cognitive functions affected in depression are processed primarily in cortical networks. Using MRI, we are interested in measuring the thickness of the cortex and the volume of the hypothalamus in depressed patients who participated in a 16-week clinical trial, and whether structural features that existed before they received treatment could predict their trial outcomes. We also believe it is important to study whether the brain features that are predictive of clinical improvement are different between male and female patients. This research might help us to further understand which structural brain features we can use to help patients with depression improve more quickly and reliably and shed light on whether sex makes a difference in this regard to further refine treatments.

column36: Older Adults Seeking Emergency Care: Investigating Patient Profiles and Health Service Exposures to Inform Geriatric Models of Care in the Emergency Department
column37: Population aging has resulted in an increase of older adults seeking health care, with emergency departments (ED) acting as a common access point for older people in search of medical attention. Older adults contribute a higher percentage of ED visits than younger patients, and are more likely to visit for an urgent reason and be admitted to the hospital. Unfortunately, traditional ED management strategies limit the department's ability to care for the complex needs of older adults. Diseases and assessments specific to older adults are commonly overlooked in the ED. ED health care providers report difficulty in assessing and treating older adults due to their atypical presentations and intricate medical and social histories. As a result, older adults experience high rates of hospitalization, repeated hospital use, functional decline, and death after ED discharge. Little is known about the patient characteristics associated with poor outcomes in older ED patients. Similarly, more data is needed on the post-discharge health services that can facilitate a successful transition back into the community. The aims of my doctoral research are to: (a) predict hospitalization, repeat hospital use, long-term care home admission, and death within 90 days of ED discharge, and (b) identify health services in the community that can be used after ED discharge to improve patient outcomes. The findings of this research can be used to create tools to identify older adults at risk for poor outcomes. Furthermore, this research can provide information to help supplement decision making for ED health care providers and policy makers surrounding discharge planning and referral services.

column36: Characterizing the Role of Profibrotic Monocytes/Macrophages in the Progression of Fibrotic Lung Disease
column37: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a disease of unknown cause that involves scarring of the lung. IPF patients normally die relatively shortly after diagnosis, and there are limited options for treatment. We do not know how to predict the timing of death of patients with IPF, and we have a poor understanding of what causes the progression of this disease. However, white blood cells in the circulation called monocytes have been correlated with progression. Monocytes originate in the bone marrow, and then enter the circulation from which they can be recruited into various tissue types in the body. It is believed that these monocytes enter the lung, transition into macrophages, and begin to cause fibrosis. Quantity of monocytes has previously been positively correlated with poor outcomes in IPF, suggesting that these cells may play a causal role in the development of fibrotic lung disease. Therefore, it makes sense to study these cells and their properties to potentially gain a better understanding of what causes progression of IPF. Here, we hypothesize that monocytes isolated from the blood of IPF patients are profibrotic and associated with progression of IPF. We also hypothesize that these monocytes enter the lung and contribute to fibrosis. To test this, we will collect blood from IPF patients and isolate monocytes. From there, we will examine the properties of these cells to identify "targets." We will then look for these targets in lung biopsies from patients with IPF to confirm that they are present in the lung. After determining viable targets present in both the blood and lungs of IPF patients, we will employ screening techniques to select an appropriate mouse model for studying these targets and their functions further. The results of this study may provide insight into better understanding what causes development of IPF, and potential routes for therapies for the disease.

column36: Teaching Trauma: Supporting Canadian Trainee Physicians in Responding to Survivors of Sexual Violence
column37: Over the course of their lives nearly 1 in 4 women living in Canada experience sexual violence. While these experiences can have significant effects on survivors' mental and physical wellbeing, sensitive and compassionate care from well-informed physicians can help to mitigate these negative health outcomes. Unfortunately, medical learners report receiving little by way of formal training around trauma; as a result of the lack of attention paid to training health care providers to respond to trauma, misinformation and stigma around sexual violence persists in health care. In order to begin addressing barriers that prevent survivors from seeking or receiving appropriate medical care, this project aims to take stock of what medical learners are thinking and learning about trauma related to sexual violence. To understand the scope and implications of the formal education students receive about trauma and sexual violence, I'll analyze academic curriculum and institutional policy documents at Canadian medical schools, including those that respond to recent research documenting the abuse of medical learners themselves. Next, I'll interview medical residents across the country to understand how their pre-existing beliefs, medical education, and professional experiences with sexual violence the informal aspects of their training once they begin practice. Finally, I'll interview community and institutional stakeholders with an interest in medical education to identify opportunities and barriers to developing and improving medical curricula around trauma and sexual violence. The knowledge that emerges from this research will spur the development of training about trauma for medical learners in all stages of their education, ultimately helping to better align medical practice with best practices identified in transdisciplinary trauma research.

column36: Engineering a universal oncolytic virus boost in adoptive T cell therapies for cancer
column37: Advances in cancer research have led to a field of research dedicated to using a patient's own immune system to target and treat their cancer. In general, these immunotherapies are more targeted and less toxic that traditional chemotherapies and radiation therapies. In order to "reprogram" immune cells to seek out and destroy tumour targets, we must teach these cells what to look for and how to respond when they come in contact with the tumour. A challenge in bringing these immunotherapies to the clinic is the diversity of tumour markers among and within individual patients, making it necessary for these treatments to be personalized. By using an oncolytic virus vaccine that infects only cancer cells, and engineered immune cells that target this virus, we may be able to improve the anti-tumour immune response without needing to analyze an individual's unique tumour markers first. In addition to this, the oncolytic virus has been shown to improve the immune response against the tumour which may lead to better tumour clearance. We think that this strategy may be a step towards a "universal" method of generating effective tumour-specific immune cells, and that this strategy could be used to improve immunotherapies by increasing the ability of immune cells to kill cancer cells while reducing the extent to which these therapies must be personalized on a patient-by-patient basis.

column37: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is a neurodegenerative disease caused by a mutation in the ATXN1 gene. Patients first begin to lose their balance and motor control, followed by difficulty speaking and swallowing food, and then cognitive decline. Symptoms begin in a person's thirties or forties, after which life expectancy is 10-15 years. There are no treatments available for SCA1. SCA1 is part of the polyglutamine expansion disease family, along with the more common Huntington's Disease (HD). This means that the mutation in the ATXN1 gene causes repetition of the amino acid glutamine in the ataxin-1 protein. We do not fully understand what function the ataxin-1 protein has in the body. We do know that these glutamine repeats cause problems which leads to SCA1. Recent studies have suggested that the proteins affected in HD and SCA1 may be involved in DNA damage repair. We have shown that that ataxin-1 goes to sites of DNA damage following stress events, and that the disease version of the protein is worse at going to damage. Our current project has three main goals. First, understanding what role ataxin-1 has at DNA damage. Second, figuring out how disruption of this function contributes to SCA1 disease symptoms. Third, identify how ataxin-1 travels to damage and how this is impacted by polyglutamine expansion. If we can identify a difference between the normal and disease protein during DNA repair, this would be the first step in developing a potential treatment for SCA1. We are figuring out what the function of the protein is, and how it is changed in disease. If we answer that question, we could then focus on how to fix the problem and make the disease protein act like the normal protein. That research is far in the future, but it will not happen unless we lay the groundwork with projects such as this one. Since HD and SCA1 are so similar, a discovery in SCA1 could help with HD research.

column36: A comprehensive investigation of bacterial nutrient biosynthesis as a novel source of antimicrobial targets
column37: The rise in antibiotic resistance coupled with the decline in novel antibiotic discovery threatens to create a public health crisis. Antibiotics function by inhibiting bacterial processes that are necessary for growth. Currently, antibiotics target a narrow range of all bacterial processes. To combat the rise in antibiotic resistance, it is fundamental to find new bacterial processes to target. Traditionally, when searching for new bacterial processes to target, bacteria are grown in a surplus of nutrients. However, this is not representative of the nutrient-limited environment of the human body. In nutrient-limited environments, bacteria must synthesize nutrients from scratch to survive. As such, it may be possible to find new antibiotics that inhibit the nutrient synthesis processes of bacteria. The goal of this research project is to identify nutrient synthesis processes that are critical for bacterial growth during infection and find chemicals to inhibit them. The study will first mutate bacteria to be incapable of synthesizing specific nutrients. The infective abilities of these bacteria will be tested in mice. If a particular bacteria cannot establish an infection, then the deactivated nutrient synthesis process of the bacteria is critical to its survival. All processes critical to survival are targets for antibiotic development. By establishing a wide range of antibiotic targets, it will be possible to direct searches for inhibitors of these processes in hopes of advancing antibiotic drug discovery.

column36: Development of novel in silico tools to predict pathogenicity of rare variants using post-translational modification data
column37: All humans have mutations that alter the product of their genes. In healthy individuals, these mutations are benign. In individuals with genetic disorders, such as familial hypercholesterolemia, one or more of these mutations are often the cause of their disease. For clinicians, identifying the disease-causing mutation is akin to finding a "needle-in-a-haystack". It is impossible to validate each mutation in a laboratory, so computational tools must be used to prioritize the list of suspected mutations. However, existing methods are too inaccurate for use in clinical settings. Post-translational modifications on proteins are an important source of regulation in cells. One such modification is the cleavage of proteins by protease enzymes based on recognition of patterns of amino acids on the target. This cleavage is necessary for proper functioning of the target protein. Therefore, it would be expected that a mutation that removes an existing protease cleavage site results in an inactive protein, while a mutation that inappropriately induces a protease cleavage site results in a truncated non-functional protein. Despite their regulatory importance, there are no computational tools that incorporate these enzymes into their predictions of disease-causing versus benign for mutations. Therefore, our project seeks to develop a novel tool that leverages machine learning and databases of known protease cleavage sites in humans to improve prediction of disease-causing mutations. Ultimately, this project will create a catalogue of human mutations involving altered protease sites. In the short-term, this will benefit clinicians and their patients with genetic disorders. In the long-term, it will improve understanding of the role of proteases in disease with potential for new drug therapies. Also, it will generally improve identification of disease-causing mutations, which is a precursor to emerging therapies in precision medicine, like CRISPR gene editing.

column36: Achieving equitable population-based lung cancer screening programs in Canada: An inquiry of social values and ethical considerations
column37: Over 20,000 Canadians are expected to die from lung cancer in 2019. Survival is less than 20% because most diagnoses are made at late stages when treatment effectiveness is limited. It is therefore a major advancement that low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) will soon be used to screen Canadians for lung cancer. Screening will help Canadians be diagnosed earlier, obtain timely treatment, and survive for longer and with a higher quality of life. Low-dose chest CT to screen for lung cancer is promising, but few individuals are correctly diagnosed from this lengthy process with a high false detection rate. Who should be screened for lung cancer? This is a dilemma for cancer system policymakers, who have turned to numerical models that predict individual lung cancer risk. Less is known about values Canadians hold towards screening and ethical issues related to screening some and not others. These knowledge gaps need to be addressed if future Canadian lung cancer screening programs are to be effective and fair. This research aims to uncover social values and ethical considerations that can help policymakers decide who to include in Canadian lung cancer screening programs. Cancer system policymakers, the general public, and communities affected by lung cancer will be asked about their values towards screening and benefits and harms of screening some and not and others. People will be interviewed from provinces with lung cancer screening-related activities. Specific values and ethical principles will be identified and analyzed with fairness in mind. When health care is oriented around patients, better individual health is often the result. Likewise, when health systems are oriented around what populations want, we can expect better health for all Canadians. By querying public and policymaker values, this research is anticipated to contribute to lung cancer screening programs that are effective, fair, and at the leading edge of socially relevant health systems.

column36: Uncovering a Cellular Pathway that is Associated with Human Amyloidosis
column37: A category of diseases called amyloidosis are caused by the irreversible formation of protein clumps (aggregates). The type of protein involved as well as its location in the body leads to different diseases, for example beta-amyloid protein accumulates in the brain in individuals suffering from Alzheimer's disease (a chronic disorder causing dementia in hundreds of thousands of Canadians), and amylin protein aggregates in the pancreas of patients with type 2 diabetes (a metabolic disorder affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide). Although the proteins involved may be different, the common factor to all amyloidosis diseases is the folding shape the proteins develop in the aggregates: the amyloid fold. While this shape has historically been associated with disease, the Audas laboratory recently discovered a protective cellular pathway that induces proteins to reversibly take on an amyloid fold during cell stress (i.e. high temperatures, low oxygen). Components of this pathway could be faulty in disease settings, leading to the irreversible aggregates observed in amyloidosis diseases. We aim to deplete, or "knock-out", a variety of different cellular factors to determine which ones are involved in the natural process, as these may be malfunctioning in amyloidosis disorders. Ultimately, this research could identify new therapeutic targets and uncover new avenues to pursue in the research of amyloidosis diseases.

column37: Injury is a major global health issue, leaving no country unaffected. However, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), the situation is especially dire with more than 70% of all deaths due to injury occurring here. Trauma registries-databases that systematically collect information concerning the injury event, process of care, and outcome of injured patients - have proven to be an effective tool for informing both injury prevention and mitigation efforts and improving quality of patient care. While they have been widely adopted in high income countries, their use in LMICs has remained limited, largely due to the high financial and resource demands of implementation and operation among other barriers. In recent years, a grassroots movement has taken hold with local stakeholders spearheading the development of trauma registries in lower resource settings by using innovative solutions to lower these barriers. Nonetheless, challenges to sustainable trauma registry implementation and operation in these settings remain and often vary across contexts. Furthermore, strategies that work for one trauma registry may not work for another. Research documenting these experiences however remains scarce. The purpose of this research project therefore is to better understand the barriers and facilitators to creating sustainable trauma registries in LMICs. This will be achieved through both a survey of trauma registry stewards in LMICs and a series of case studies that examine a select number of both successful and failed trauma registries in these settings. Findings from both of these components of the research project will be used to create an online narrative map that users can navigate and explore to learn how trauma registries in various low-resource contexts have been developed and implemented. Ultimately, the knowledge and resources generated from this research will help inform the development of more sustainable trauma registries in LMICs.

column36: Towards an HIV cure for all: increasing female representation in HIV latency research
column37: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy to treat HIV infection, these medications are not curative and need to be taken for life. This is because HIV integrates its genetic material into the genome of the infected human immune cells, and can persist in a dormant or "latent" state for many years. These dormant HIV copies are called the "latent HIV reservoir", and they persist in the body because they are invisible to the immune system and to antiretroviral drugs. But, these reservoirs can re-activate to produce infectious HIV at any time. To cure HIV therefore, scientists will need to develop strategies to eliminate the latent reservoir. Towards this goal, substantial efforts are being made to understand reservoir characteristics, composition, and longevity in individuals living with HIV whose infections are well-controlled with antiretroviral therapy. However, most participants of such research studies, particularly in North America, have been males. By contrast, females, who make up ~52% of people living with HIV worldwide, are significantly underrepresented in HIV latency research. As a result, fundamental questions around sex-based differences in latent HIV reservoir composition remain unanswered. To address this critical knowledge gap, I will combine cutting-edge laboratory and molecular evolutionary methods in my PhD research. I will study unique biospecimen repositories and data from established local and international cohorts, including the longest-running study exclusively comprising females living with HIV (the US-based Women's Interagency HIV Study). I will also perform a comparative study of latent HIV reservoir composition in females and males in a cohort established at St. Paul's Hospital in Vancouver. My PhD research will help understand latent HIV reservoir dynamics in females, towards the ultimate goal of developing a cure for HIV that will be effective in, and accessible by, all.

column36: Enabling Microbial Genome Analysis for Infectious Disease Outbreak Investigations
column37: Bacterial species, including pathogens, possess a remarkable ability to evolve rapidly and exchange genomic DNA with unrelated lineages in a process known as horizontal gene transfer. Clusters of these horizontally transferred genes, called genomic islands, are of high interest to computationally predict in pathogen genome sequences since they disproportionately encode genes that enable a pathogen to cause disease or resist treatment by some antibiotics. However, current genomic island analysis tools are limited to examining DNA from one bacterial isolate at a time, limiting the ability to rapidly investigate multiple isolates at once when tracking a disease outbreak. My project aims to enable the analysis of multiple isolates through the development of a new computational tool called IslandCompare, and apply this to analyze select datasets of pathogen genes. Ultimately, the goal of my project is to improve our understanding of the evolution of these genomic regions and their involvement in changes during a disease outbreak. IslandCompare will facilitate more rapid, integrated analysis of medically relevant gene mobility, which is of high interest for enabling public health investigations to more rapidly evaluate, and respond to, infectious disease outbreaks.

column36: Optimisation d'un modele pour evaluer l'impact de la direction des changements de pression arterielle sur l'autoregulation cerebrale dynamique
column37: La maladie vasculaire peripherique (MVP) atteint 5 a 18% de la population et est une pathologie des vaisseaux qui peut mener a leur obstruction complete. Elle peut survenir dans toutes les arteres, dont celles du cerveau. Son traitement repose sur divers facteurs dont le plus efficace est l'activite physique. La MVP entraine une rigidite arterielle qui augmente le risque de faire un accident vasculaire cerebral (AVC) et affecte la facon dont l'apport en sang est regule au cerveau. La fonction vasculaire cerebrale des patients avec une MVP est donc probablement anormale, particulierement a l'effort. L'entrainement par intervalles a haute intensite (HIIT) gagne en popularite pour son economie de temps et son efficacite par rapport a l'entrainement en continu. Il y a cependant peu de litterature sur les benefices et les impacts du HIIT sur les vaisseaux du cerveau. Un exercice court et intense comme le HIIT pourrait causer une augmentation trop prononcee du debit sanguin au cerveau. Cela pourrait augmenter certains risques tel que l'AVC. On sait toutefois que le HIIT entraine certaines ameliorations (ex. distance de marche) chez des patients avec une MVP. Cependant, nous ne savons pas si la vascularisation cerebrale des sujets avec une MVP est bien adaptee aux changements brusques de pression arterielle relies au HIIT. Il est donc primordial de connaitre la reponse vasculaire cerebrale des patients avec une MVP lors du HIIT avant de le recommander formellement. Cette etude apportera des connaissances sur les effets du HIIT sur la fonction vasculaire cerebrale a court et long terme. Ultimement, elle fournira aux cliniciens des recommandations objectives sur le HIIT et la MVP. Nous aurons ainsi une base solide de connaissances afin d'etablir une strategie optimale d'exercice pour le cerveau et pour optimiser le fonctionnement du cerveau tout au long de la vie des patients avec une MVP.

column36: The role of sexual functioning in a biopsychosocial model of disability in inflammatory bowel disease: From research to knowledge translation
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic illness with disabling repercussions. Sexual difficulties (SDs) are consistently reported by patients but are rarely addressed in disease management. Research on sexuality in IBD is limited. SDs are more prevalent among IBD patients compared to controls, and they relate to worse disease activity and disability. Yet, little is known about the progression from IBD disease activity to SDs to disability, or factors that may buffer this process. Objective 1 of my research is to empirically model this process in a large IBD sample. Another gap in the IBD literature is an examination of LGBTQ+ individuals' experiences, which is troubling given that minorities face health disparities and issues in the healthcare system. One study found that LGB IBD patients reported issues arising from the intersection of identities of being a sexual minority and having a chronic disease. Thus, LGBTQ+ individuals may face specific challenges related to SDs and accessing healthcare that warrant investigation. Objective 2 of my research is to query these issues using quantitative and qualitative methods in a diverse subsample. Objective 3 is to use the findings from above to implement a knowledge translation plan. Due to the lack of attention SDs and diversity receive in IBD disease management, educational resources will be created for patients and healthcare providers with information about such issues, tips on having respectful and inclusive conversations about sexuality, and resources for the management of SDs within the context of IBD. This educational program will be delivered online and through in-person workshops. This work will have important impacts on the IBD literature, healthcare services, providers, and patients by advancing knowledge and providing a framework for IBD disease management that considers SDs - a taboo albeit critical aspect of well-being - and diversity - an essential piece of effective and ethical patient care.

column36: Functional characterization of novel genes of immune evasion in Salmonella Typhimurium
column37: The bacterial pathogen Salmonella Typhimurium (ST) is one of the leading causes of foodborne illness in Canada and causes acute gastroenteritis, which often leads to hospitalizations in young children and elderly populations. The incidence of this bacterial infection represents a major health problem, and the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains that are difficult to treat has caused growing concern. It is, therefore, pressing to improve our understanding of how ST overcome the innate immune system of susceptible hosts in order to cause infection, as this knowledge can create opportunities for the development of new treatment strategies. Recently, six uncharacterized genes of ST have been identified. The expression of these genes being significantly inhibited under infection conditions, it is suspected that they render ST more susceptible to immune-based killing and are inhibited to evade the natural antimicrobial mechanisms of infected hosts, through potentially unknown resistance mechanisms. The objective of this project is to functionally characterize these six genes through structural biology, microbiology, and molecular biology approaches. The methodology that will be used to achieve this aim consists of three main steps: 1) predict the function of the gene products under study using bioinformatics tools, 2) characterize the immune pathways for which the inhibition of these genes is essential through cell culture infections and phenotypic assays, and 3) identify the mechanisms that control their expression. Overall, this project will provide a comprehensive portrait of the structure, function, and regulation of novel genes for which repression is essential during infection by ST. Thereby, this will improve our understanding of the mechanisms that ST can deploy to escape the immune system, and in the long term, this knowledge base will contribute to the development of new antimicrobial treatments with tangible impacts on public health in Canada.

column36: Developpement et evaluation de l'efficacite d'un programme d'autogestion de la douleur chronique chez les adultes en attente de services specialises : essai controle randomise
column37: Un adulte sur cinq au Canada souffre de douleur chronique. Les medecins de famille sont toutefois peu outilles pour soutenir ces patients, et le nombre d'individus atteints est trop eleve pour assurer a tous la disponibilite des services specialises. Pour soulager les individus en attente, des programmes d'autogestion, qui visent a developper une meilleure connaissance de la douleur chronique et a mieux la gerer, ont fait leurs preuves. Ces programmes peuvent ameliorer le fonctionnement au quotidien, les symptomes lies a la depression et a l'anxiete, ainsi que le niveau de douleur percu. Or, les programmes d'autogestion sont rares et peu accessibles. Ce projet visera donc a developper un programme d'autogestion de la douleur chronique, et a en evaluer les effets. Il sera base sur la litterature scientifique et sur les resultats de consultations aupres de patients et de cliniciens pour identifier les attentes et les besoins lies a un tel programme. Il presentera les methodes d'autogestion reconnues et soutiendra les patients dans leur application. Pour evaluer l'efficacite du programme, 100 adultes en attente de services dans l'un des trois centres de traitement de la douleur chronique participants seront recrutes et repartis entre un groupe temoin et un groupe d'intervention. Le groupe d'intervention completera le programme d'autogestion de la douleur chronique en ligne. Le groupe temoin continuera quant a lui de recevoir les soins usuels, soit les soins non specialises auxquels il a deja acces (par exemple, les soins d'un medecin de famille). Tous les participants rempliront des questionnaires au debut de l'etude, puis apres 3 et 6 mois. Des analyses statistiques seront realisees pour determiner si le programme developpe permet d'ameliorer le fonctionnement quotidien des participants et de diminuer l'intensite des symptomes lies a la douleur chronique.

column36: Le glutamate sanguin en contexte d'obesite: de la pathophysiologie a la clinique
column37: On sait depuis longtemps que le metabolisme des glucides et des lipides est altere dans l'obesite. Cependant, c'est seulement dans les 10 dernieres annees que nous avons decouvert que le metabolisme des acides amines est lui aussi affecte. En effet, certains acides amines comme la leucine, l'isoleucine, la valine et le glutamate sont plus eleves dans le sang des personnes obeses que des personnes minces. Le glutamate est particulierement un bon indicateur de l'emplacement ou le gras est accumule. Cela est important, parce qu'une grande quantite de gras au niveau de l'abdomen, est associe a un risque eleve de diabete et de maladies cardiovasculaires. L'hypothese globale de ce projet de recherche est que l'accumulation sanguine de glutamate en contexte d'obesite resulte d'un dysfonctionnement des tissus adipeux et hepatiques. Ces organes etant centraux dans le metabolisme, le glutamate sanguin pourrait representer une mesure accessible de la sante cardiometabolique. Il est essentiel de bien comprendre une maladie si on veut la prevenir et la traiter. Nos connaissances sur l'obesite sont nombreuses, mais encore incompletes. L'etude du metabolisme des acides amines pourrait eventuellement nous amener a trouver de nouveaux traitements pour l'obesite, le diabete ou les maladies cardiovasculaires. Mesurer la quantite de gras a l'interieur de la cavite abdominale necessite des techniques d'imagerie qui coutent tres cher et ne sont pas accessibles en clinique. Ainsi, il serait tres utile de pouvoir estimer l'accumulation de gras visceral en mesurant un acide amine dans le sang. Le fait d'etre capable d'identifier les personnes avec une obesite viscerale et un risque metabolique important, nous permettrait de mieux cibler nos efforts de prevention et de traitement.

column37: <<Une alimentation saine, c'est bien plus que les aliments que vous consommez>>, tel que cite par le nouveau Guide alimentaire canadien 2019, qui integre au premier plan des conseils tels que <<cuisinez plus souvent>> et <<prenez le temps de manger>>. D'ailleurs, ces comportements alimentaires ont ete associes a une meilleure qualite globale de l'alimentation. Toutefois, les parents de jeunes enfants peuvent etre confrontes a plusieurs barrieres qui les empechent d'adopter ces comportements. Le manque de temps, les contraintes du travail et la prise en compte des preferences et restrictions alimentaires de tous les membres de la famille peuvent faire en sorte que la planification des repas devienne un vrai casse-tete. De plus, les meres ayant vecu une grossesse compliquee par un diabete de grossesse sont encore plus vulnerables. Ces meres pourraient s'imposer une pression supplementaire a bien s'alimenter pour elles et leurs enfants, considerant leur risque eleve de developper des maladies chroniques plus tard dans leur vie. Dans le cadre de ce doctorat en nutrition, un portrait global des habitudes et comportements alimentaires (qualite de l'alimentation, temps de preparation des repas, duree des repas, etc.) des parents de jeunes enfants ages de 6 ans ou moins sera compare a celui des adultes n'ayant pas de jeune enfant, tout en tenant compte de l'antecedent de diabete de grossesse. L'impact sur la sante sera egalement documente. Les donnees d'un total de 234 parents (111 meres, 118 peres) de jeunes enfants seront analysees, de meme que celles de 442 meres avec ou sans antecedent de diabete de grossesse. Les resultats permettront de mieux comprendre les barrieres a l'adoption d'une saine alimentation chez les parents quebecois, l'impact sur leur sante et eventuellement d'adopter des strategies specifiques pour cette population.

column36: Air pollution and sentinel biologic health effects in Canada
column37: Outdoor air pollution is associated with increased lung cancer risk based on several epidemiologic studies over the past 20 years, and was recently classified as a carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). Additional studies link air pollution to other chronic diseases, as well as pregnancy related outcomes. However, the majority of these studies have been conducted in populations exposed to high levels of air pollution. Little is known about whether Canadians are exposed to levels high enough to lead to early detectable biological changes, or which specific components of outdoor air lead to these effects. The proposed study will be the first to study these relationships using a cohort of Canadian adults, as well as a vulnerable population of pregnant women who may experience higher doses of air pollution in the body due to pregnancy-related changes. The currently proposed epidemiology study will use a combination of satellite-based and ground monitor air pollution data to determine detailed exposure information for several components in outdoor air. Blood-samples from two national cohorts (Canadian Partnership for Tomorrow Project [CPTP] and Maternal-Infant Research on Environmental Chemicals [MIREC]) will be used to assess the relationship between the different components of outdoor air and oxidative stress - an early marker of cancer, chronic diseases, as well as pregnancy outcomes. We will also take into account individuals' genetic susceptibility to these exposures in terms of their ability to detoxify chemical exposures. Outdoor air pollution is an increasing concern, both in Canada and globally. This examination of air pollution in relation to an early marker of disease will inform on the early health effects of different air pollution components and levels, a necessary step in setting public health policy to reduce the burden of disease associated with Canadian air pollution.

Cela signifie que le personnel doit etre prealablement forme et disponible pour effectuer le suivi du patient. column36: Impact fonctionnel d'IDH1 sur le metabolisme des cellules de cancer de la prostate
column37: Le cancer de la prostate est le cancer le plus frequent chez les hommes au Canada. A ce jour, le seul traitement cible de cette maladie vise a bloquer le recepteur aux androgenes. Malgre le succes initial de cette approche pour la gestion du cancer de la prostate, l'evolution vers un cancer de la prostate resistant a la castration est virtuellement inevitable et letal, mettant l'emphase sur la necessite de developper de nouvelles approches therapeutiques. La prostate possede un programme metabolique unique, non observe dans les autres cellules du corps, et la reprogrammation de ce metabolisme a lieu dans tous les cas de cancer de la prostate. Notre objectif est de tirer parti de ce programme metabolique unique pour tuer les cellules cancereuses. Pour ce faire, nous etudierons une proteine essentielle au programme metabolique du cancer de la prostate. Nous utiliserons plusieurs modeles de cancer de la prostate pour etudier les fonctions de cette enzyme et ses liens moleculaires avec l'agressivite de la maladie. Par une meilleure comprehension de ses fonctions, nous pensons pouvoir bloquer la synthese de l'energie des cellules cancereuses et provoquer leur mort. Ces travaux ont le potentiel d'identifier et de caracteriser une nouvelle cible therapeutique innovante pour le traitement du cancer de la prostate. En cas de succes, cette approche sera la premiere du genre et revolutionnera le traitement du cancer de la prostate.
