column36: Clinical Applications of the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI): Exploring the Mechanisms Through Which the AAI Enhances Parental Engagement and Boosts Treatment Outcomes Following Brief Emotion-Focused Family Therapy
column37: Fee-for-service policies and long waitlists at many Canadian mental health agencies pose significant barriers for children, adolescents, and families in need of psychological support. In Ontario, approximately 36% of parents have sought mental health services for a child, but four in ten did not receive the help they needed. One way to improve access to mental health services in Canada is to develop and deliver brief and effective psychotherapy. Our group has been studying the impact of administering the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) before therapy. Originally developed for research, the AAI is now widely used as a clinical tool, and it has been suggested that using the interview can facilitate the therapy process and improve treatment outcomes. We conducted the first study to put this hypothesis to the test and found that administering the AAI before Emotion-Focused Family Therapy (EFFT) boosted treatment gains for parents and their children - unlike parents who did not receive the interview, those who did reported ongoing symptom improvement 12 months after treatment had ended. To advance our understanding of the clinical benefits of the AAI, this study will investigate how the interview leads to better outcomes; the process and mechanisms through which the AAI boosts treatment effectiveness. Two hundred and forty parents took part in an intensive 2-day EFFT intervention; about half completed an AAI before starting therapy and the other half did not. Using available video footage of therapy sessions, we will study parents' level of engagement with the EFFT process. Specifically, the level of emotional arousal experienced and the depth of emotional processing observed during therapy will be coded. It is expected that completing an AAI before therapy will lead to deeper levels of engagement during therapy, which will, in turn, lead to greater treatment outcomes. Our findings may point to a feasible way of enhancing therapy effectiveness and outcomes for families.

column36: Longitudinal Neurocognitive Outcomes and Trajectories of Brain Development in Pediatric Patients with Multiple Sclerosis and Relapsing Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein (MOG) Disease
column37: The immune system protects the body from intruders (e.g., viruses and bacteria). However, sometimes, healthy tissue might be accidentally mistaken for an intruder and become the target of immune system attack. This is associated with the onset of diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) disease. Researchers recently confirmed that pediatric patients with relapsing MOG disease represent a distinct population from those with MS; previously, patients with relapsing MOG may have been misdiagnosed with MS. MOG disease can either be relapsing or monophasic (i.e., a single demyelinating event), unlike pediatric MS which typically follows a relapsing course. MOG is produced exclusively in the brain and spinal cord. It is involved in the production of myelin, an insulating cover that permits electrical impulses to be conducted quickly along nerves for efficient communication between brain regions. Given that the myelin sheath is damaged in both MS and MOG disease, both conditions are called demyelinating diseases. Pediatric demyelinating diseases are diagnosed when the first attack is experienced before age 18. We have studied pediatric MS and identified challenges with organizing information and processing speed, among other cognitive deficits. What remains unclear is whether pediatric patients with MS and relapsing MOG disease have comparable patterns of cognitive function. The objective of our study is to understand the cognitive profile of patients with relapsing MOG disease. We will compare patient groups as well as patients with relapsing MOG and matched healthy participants. We will then examine patterns of brain growth in pediatric patients with MS and relapsing MOG disease. We will also evaluate whether brain changes due to these pediatric demyelinating diseases are associated with poorer cognitive performance in both patient groups. Methods include computerized cognitive testing and magnetic-resonance imaging (MRI).

column36: A brief mindfulness-based intervention to improve mental health among emerging adults: Evaluating a long-term follow-up randomized control clinical trial (RCT) and the mediating effects of self-compassion
column37: Post-secondary students between 18 to 29 years old (Emerging Adults; EAs) experience higher rates of depressive and anxious symptoms than other age groups. EAs are interested in mental health services, but there are limited available options and long-wait times on campuses. Brief mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) have been suggested as an efficacious method for reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression. MBI treatment effects (improved mental health and wellbeing) may also be explained by augmented self-compassion. Although, there is limited research to support the intervention efficacy and the mechanisms of change in EA populations. The proposed randomized control trial study will consider the efficacy of a brief MBI for EAs at York University, by comparing self-report mental health and wellbeing outcomes of the intervention (55 brief mindfulness participants) to a placebo-control group (55 mindfulness app participants). Based off my masters brief MBI research, this study hypothesizes (1) that a 5-week, brief MBI reduces mental health difficulties, and improves well-being in the short-term (immediately before session 3 and immediately after session 5) and in the long-term (3-, 6- and 12-months following the intervention completion) and (2) that the intervention effects (reduction in depression, anxiety, and improved wellbeing) are explained by augmented self-compassion. If an efficacious intervention, the proposed research study (1) could lead to a brief, evidence-based solution to improve the mental health and wellbeing of post-secondary EAs, that aligns with York Universities goal of Building Healthy Lives, Communities and Environment, (2) provide support for cultivating self-compassion in mental health-focused interventions for EA populations and 3) could result in dissemination of EA post-secondary student mental health knowledge nationally and internationally.

column36: Assessing caregiver influence on cortical, cardiac, and behavioural indicators of pain-related distress: New frontiers in neonatal pain assessment
column37: Infants hospitalized in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs) are exposed daily to painful procedures as part of their routine medical care. Due to these infants' inability to report their own pain, it is crucial that health care professionals have accurate pain assessment tools to enact optimal pain management. Unrelieved pain has been shown to alter brain structures and functioning, resulting in poorer long-term physical and psychological outcomes for the 8% of children who are born premature every year. Early in life, due to their developing ability to calm themselves down after distress, infants heavily rely on their caregivers to help regulate from distressing events, like needles. When infants are in pain, they are very sensitive to the way in which their caregivers respond to their distress, cognitively, behaviourally and physiologically, because they are learning from their caregivers how to react and regulate from distress. Caregivers also set the social-emotional context in which infants experience distress. Seminal longitudinal work from our lab showed that caregivers were the most influential factor predicting pain responses from infancy to preschool. By influencing the development of infants' pain responses, caregivers impact the way infant pain will be assessed and consequently managed. The proposed project takes this work and sets out to examine these relationships in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs). The present study will collect caregiver cognitive, behavioural, and physiological data during a routine blood sampling procedure in NICUs (a heel lance) and examine the relationships with infant brain responses (Electroencephalogram), heart responses (Electrocardiograms) and behaviour (facial activity). By furthering our understanding of how caregivers impact the way infants react and regulate from pain-related distress, this program of research seeks to improve the accuracy of current infant pain assessment practices used in NICUs.

column36: Longitudinal Tracking of Health Status Using Machine Learning Analysis of Wearable Sensors: A Framework for Non-Intrusively Detecting Deteriorating Health
column37: The average age of the Canadian population is increasing rapidly. As a result, health care costs are rising and the importance of maintaining a healthy, active lifestyle is becoming very clear. One way to promote healthy living and improve early detection of health problems is to monitor people's health over time. Health status tracking will provide people and their clinicians with useful information to guide their lifestyle and health care decisions. An important contributor to overall health is fitness. Poor fitness is associated with earlier onset of disease and even death. Traditional ways of testing fitness require access to expensive, specialized equipment. This is a barrier to monitoring fitness and health across the population. Wearable sensors, like those within "smart" clothing or watches, are a possible alternative to traditional fitness testing equipment because they are more affordable, more accessible, and can track body function over the course of an entire day. Despite these benefits, it is challenging to understand the complex data provided by wearable sensors. More work is needed to support individuals and clinicians in interpreting wearable sensor data. My research will translate these complex data into actionable knowledge that will inform health promotion and aid in disease detection. I will develop a new artificial intelligence system using data collected with a "smart" shirt from older adults during a two-week period of bed rest. This system will create models specific to older adults that use wearable sensor data to predict health and fitness. I will evaluate how well these models reflect changes in markers of health, aging, and frailty. This work will result in a personalized decision aid that gives people and clinicians new insights into human health. This non-intrusive smart monitoring system will improve population health and reduce health care costs in Canada.

column36: Investigating effects of ATRX ablation in embryonic excitatory neurons
column37: Intellectual disability affects 3.8 out of 1000 school aged children and poses a large social and medical challenge. Intellectual delays can occur during development when communication in neurons is disrupted. In neurons, the information in our DNA is regulated in structures called chromatin. In this study, we will examine the function of ATRX, a chromatin remodelling protein able to control how brain genes are turned "on" or "off". In children where the ATRX gene contains errors, the ATRX protein made in the brain is abnormal. We predict that this causes abnormal chromatin structure and gene expression, leading to intellectual disability. Understanding in detail the role that ATRX plays in the brain is crucial to identify possible points of therapeutic intervention. Mouse models are a valid method of studying intellectual disability, as they can be genetically modified, and their cognitive abilities can be assessed and related to molecular and cellular changes in the brain. We will study mice that lack ATRX expression only in the brain, and only in differentiated neurons. We propose to investigate how brain development is affected, what goes wrong at chromatin and with brain genes important for learning and memory. In addition, we will evaluate the effects of ATRX neuronal loss on different types of behaviours including learning and memory. Our end goal is to find a causative mechanism that can be reversed and identify therapeutic options for ATRX syndrome patients.

column36: The essential role of clathrin signalosomes in growth factor receptor signaling in cancer cells
column37: Cells communicate with each other through chemical cues, each of which can trigger a specific cell response. For instance, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a receptor on the cell surface that controls much of what cells can do such as growth, movement and survival. Therefore, EGFR must be tightly regulated by the cell. When this control fails, this can lead to cell growth, survival and metastasis of many tumors. Mutations in EGFR or an overexpression of the receptor is associated with multiple cancers, such as head and neck, glioblastoma, and breast cancer. We are specifically interested in a type of breast cancer called triple-negative because EGFR is overexpressed in a quarter of all patients. In this cancer the cells lacks the three conventional markers, which makes the cancer hard to diagnose and treat with conventional chemotherapeutic options. Our lab has identified a new function for the protein clathrin inside cells to control the function of EGFR. Clathrin was previously not known to control EGFR directly, and thus understanding how clathrin structures do so is critical to resolve how EGFR promotes breast cancer growth and survival. To resolve how clathrin controls the oncogene EGFR, I will use advanced microscopy that will image live cancer cells that have fluorescently-labelling of specific proteins, coupled to computer-based analysis methods. This research is significant because understanding this novel role of clathrin has the potential to reveal new weakness or drug targets within certain cancers, and may reveal new mechanisms to prevent resistance to current anti-EGFR therapies.

column36: The Contribution of Avolition to Apathy Symptomatology: Exploring the Sense of Agency in Frontotemporal Dementia using Intentional Binding
column37: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common type of dementia, following Alzheimer's disease, in individuals aged 65 years and younger. FTD is characterized by behavioural syndromes including apathy, disinhibition, loss of empathy/sympathy, and impulsivity. Apathy is one of the most striking behavioural outcomes of FTD. It often manifests a loss of motivation for work, hobbies, personal hygiene, and social interaction, compared to the affected individual's previous state. To date, there are no known treatments for symptoms of apathy. This is largely due to difficulties in conceptualizing the patient experience of apathy. Traditionally, apathy was understood as a general lack of motivation. However, recent studies have highlighted the importance of avolition in apathy. Avolition refers to the inability to perform self-directed behaviours. The cognitive and neural underpinnings of avolition is a topical area of research in cognitive neuroscience. Avolition is linked to the sense of agency (SoA), the feeling of control over voluntary actions and the outcomes of those actions. We can measure the SoA using a temporal compression effect, termed intentional binding, that occurs between our voluntary actions and the effects of those actions. The neurocognitive mechanisms and structures involved in producing the intentional binding effect coincide with structures and mechanisms invovled in FTD, such as the dopaminergic pathway. In the current study, we propose that intentional binding provides a promising avenue for better understanding symptoms of apathy in FTD patients. As such, we will explore the intentional binding effect in FTD patients. We predict that the intentional binding effect will be decreased in FTD patients compared to age-matched healthy controls, indicating a reduced SoA in FTD patients. Such a finding would have profound implications for future clinical and pharmacological techniques for managing symptoms of apathy in FTD and related diseases.

column36: Identifying the genetic determinants of neurodegenerative disease.
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases are conditions characterized by progressive deterioration of brain cells resulting in memory loss, behavioural changes, and lack of motor control. It was projected that, in 2016, over 500,000 Canadians were affected with these diseases. Currently, these conditions lack treatment options and diagnosis can be difficult, as individuals tend to present with varying disease features. To mitigate these issues, the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI) study is aiming to characterize five neurodegenerative diseases including: 1) Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment; 2) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; 3) frontotemporal dementia; 4) Parkinson's disease; and 5) vascular cognitive impairment. In total, 519 participants have been enrolled, each with one of the five neurodegenerative diseases. Each participant has undergone a variety of tests including brain imaging, cognitive evaluation, gait and balance analysis, eye assessment, and genetic sequencing; the last of which is the basis of my project. I aim to gain a greater understanding of the genetic factors that are contributing to neurodegenerative disease onset and the disease features. We are using a customized sequencing tool to analyze 80 genes in each participant's DNA that have each been previously associated with neurodegenerative disease. From these data, we will identify genetic variants-changes in the participant's DNA-that are contributing to their diagnoses. We are also collaborating with the other assessment teams within ONDRI to identify genetic variants that are associated with progression patterns and features of the neurodegenerative diseases, such as brain volumes and cognitive decline. The results of this study will provide further insight into what is causing the diseases on a molecular level and will allow for the development of new treatments and genetic-sequencing-based early diagnosis and risk assessment tools.

column36: Let's Talk About Sex....ual Health: Exploring Young Women's Sexual Health in the Canadian Context
column37: Sexual health is influenced by several different factors in a person's life, including issues related to gender and age. Women and girls have unique sexual health priorities/risks, particularly as they transition into adult roles. However young women's sexual health has focused on what adults want them to avoid and what is forgotten is that sexual health is normal. Understanding young women's perspective on sexual health is the first step to effective STBBI/HIV prevention in this critical population, and an important pathway to improved sexual health for all women. The purpose of this study is to understand how young women frame/experience sexual health within the context of their lives and, from that, to identify STBBI/HIV prevention strategies that align with their priorities. This study will make visible the priorities and experiences of young, diverse Canadian women related to sexual health and expand current evidence, theory, and frameworks for HIV/STBBI prevention in this population. The impact of this project lies in the opportunity to expose inequities in the sexual health of young women in Canada. Critical feminist theory will provide a framework for this three-phased qualitative, exploratory study. The study will include the use of one-on-one interviews with 25-30 women, aged 18 to 24 (phase 1), an arts-based method in which participants will take pictures related to the study's purpose (phase 2), and finally an action phase that addresses STBBI/HIV prevention (phase 3). This study aims to achieve actionable recommendations for inclusive sexual health promotion strategies. Establishing sexual health promotion opportunities in young women not only has immediate impact potential but can establish healthy patterns related to sexual health throughout their lives and at times when STBBI/HIV risk might increase. In the era of #MeToo, global leadership for women and girls, and the recent launch of Canada's Five Year Action Plan on STBBIs this research is timely.

column36: Investigating preclinical outcomes of intratumoral modulation therapy for diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma and glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) are categorized as high-grade gliomas (HGGs) and remain among the most malignant brain cancers in adults and children, respectively. This study will investigate a promising new treatment for HGG, termed Intratumoral Modulation Therapy (IMT) which uses low-intensity electric fields (e- fields) directly targeting tumor-affected brain regions. We hypothesize that IMT delivered via specially designed, implantable bioelectrodes within HGG tissue or resection cavity (where these tumors always recur in a short time after surgery) will slow HGG growth, kill tumor cells, and increase the sensitivity of HGG to standard chemotherapy and radiation. The present goals are to design and optimize IMT bioelectrodes using computational modeling, cell culture and HGG animal models. To date the benefits of IMT have been successfully assessed in cell culture conditions and in a robust rat GBM model using an early treatment system prototype. We will now test IMT using the newly designed hardware in these established models and also in new animal models that grow brain tumors from HGG cells obtained directly from patient tumor specimens. Advanced brain imaging techniques will be used to assess tumor and growth and survival alone and in combination with standard doses of chemotherapy and radiation. The clinical vision of IMT is to provide a concealed, anatomically guided, patient-specific therapy that can effectively fight these cancers and enhance the benefits of existing treatment options. The rationale behind IMT draws is supported by the proven clinical safety of numerous implantable neuromodulation systems presently used for non-cancerous conditions. The results of this project will provide key information needed to advance IMT towards clinical application. The successful development of IMT technology has the potential to markedly improve the survival and quality of life for patients facing these deadly cancers.

column36: Investigating brain mechanisms for social interaction and stress
column37: What keeps the brain and body healthy throughout our lives? It has become increasingly clear that strong social ties are an important predictor of longevity. Conversely, loneliness is a strong risk factor for mental illness, poorer disease outcomes and mortality. Despite the importance of this topic, how social interaction improves our health is largely unknown. One theory is that social interaction reduces stress, and thereby reduces the stress hormone, cortisol. Chronic exposure to cortisol is well-known to negatively affect mental and physical health. The stress response is chiefly mediated by the hypothalamus; a small area in the base of the brain that initiates a hormonal cascade leading to the rise of cortisol throughout the body. Here, I will investigate how positive social interaction reduces activation of the stress response. Specifically, I will identify brain mechanisms for social behaviours that reduce activity of the hypothalamic cells controlling cortisol release. I will focus on the neurotransmitter oxytocin, known to be important for social bonding and regulation of stress. The brain cells that produce oxytocin are closely located and intermingled with the cells that initiate the stress response within the hypothalamus, suggesting that the hypothalamus is a promising location for cross talk between social (oxytocin-mediated) responses and stress hormones. My research will reveal mechanisms for the protective effect of social interaction on stress. Such knowledge can be applied to develop social and medical approaches to delay and even reverse the decline of mental and physical health associated with life's stress and normal aging.

column36: Genetic Determinants of Atrial Fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation affects 200,000 Canadians and is on the rise worldwide. It is the most common form of arrhythmia or irregular heart rhythm. Patients with atrial fibrillation are at a higher risk for stroke and heart disease. Despite great advances in our understanding of the role of genetics in atrial fibrillation, most patients with atrial fibrillation have no known genetic cause. In a cohort of 255 atrial fibrillation patients, I am going to use DNA sequencing technologies to identify new mutations causing the disease. For aim 1, I will investigate for rare single base pair mutations in a set of atrial fibrillation-associated genes. Aim 2, I will focus in rare mutations that encompass thousands of base pairs occurring in the same set of genes as aim 1. Aim 3, I will calculate and test a polygenetic risk score to determine an individual's risk for atrial fibrillation. The score gives an indication of the number of common mutations occurring in the entire genome that increase the risk of disease in each patient. The score calculation along with my top findings from aims 1 and 2 will be available to the physician as a sequencing panel to use for patients suspected of atrial fibrillation. As a future clinician-scientist, I am determined to improve patients' health by pursuing bench-to-bedside research. My plan will not only improve the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation but also allow for early recognition, monitoring and treatment to avoid heart disease and stroke. Heart disease and stroke are the second and third leading causes of death in Canada, therefore the costs associated with these diseases amount to the millions. Indeed, the knowledge from this project would reduce the burden of this disease on our society, and ultimately improve the lives of many Canadians.

column36: Knee inflammation and post-operative outcomes after total knee arthroplasty
column37: For years, osteoarthritis (OA) has been thought of as a non-inflammatory, "wear and tear" arthritis; however, we now know that inflammation of the joint lining (synovium) occurs in many people. This inflammation largely contributes to joint damage and disease progression, and when OA of the knee becomes severe, many people require joint replacement surgery. Although most people have good outcomes, at least 1 in 4 people are unhappy with their outcomes after surgery. Studies show that knee joint inflammation can predict who will require joint replacement in the future, but we don't know if inflammation can predict or explain poor outcomes after surgery. This project will investigate if knee joint inflammation before joint replacement affects patient outcomes after surgery. A group of 100 people 40 years and older with severe knee OA going for joint replacement will be studied. Our unique approach will use clinical and basic science research techniques with a focus on inflammation, an under-recognized factor influencing patient symptoms and joint damage. The amount of inflammation in each patient's knees will be measured using ultrasound imaging specific for knee OA prior to and 1 year after surgery. During surgery, synovium will be collected to measure inflammatory cell types present in the knee and if these differ among patients. Our goal is to understand how inflammation impacts the patient's experience by collecting patient-reported symptom surveys, measures of physical performance, muscle strength, and 3-dimensional recordings of walking patterns. This work is highly novel since no information is available describing how knee inflammation impacts patient outcomes, even though knee replacement is the most common surgery performed for the most common type of arthritis in Canada and the world. This project will improve our understanding of inflammation in knee OA and provide information to improve the care/management of people undergoing joint replacement surgery.

column36: An Exploration of Child and Youth Mental Health Service Urgency and Intensity in Ontario
column37: In Canada, 20% of the children and youth experience a mental health concern. However, only a quarter of those identified as needing services are receiving them. Mental health services within Canada have been characterized as fragmented resulting in long waiting lists, duplication of services and inefficiencies within the service sector. A lack of standardized assessments for use in prioritizing children and youth based on the service urgency and complexity of their mental health concerns, has resulted in many children and youth going untreated and a paucity of information surrounding the effects of wait lists on mental health outcomes. This study aims to examine whether mental health service urgency and intensity in Ontario as measured by the interRAI Child and Youth Mental Health Assessment (ChYMH), changes over time and which subject-specific characteristics contribute to this change. The ChYMH is a comprehensive mental health needs assessment, being used in over 70 sites across Ontario, targeting psychiatric, social, environmental and medical issues for individuals between four and 18 years of age. The study will use secondary data collected from over 20, 000 children and youth who have completed the ChYMH. The tool provides the potential for a streamlined approach in assessment, prioritization and triaging of children and youth allowing for a more integrated network of services. In addition, the results from this study can be used to describe the current landscape of mental health services as they pertain to children and youth. This research is required to aid administrative leaders in the development of initiatives to target youth mental health concerns on an overburdened mental health care system.

column36: The Effect of Therapeutic Alliance on Treatment Dropout in Cognitive Processing Therapy
column37: Over 75% of Canadians will experience a traumatic event in their lifetime, and 10% will go on to be diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Left untreated, PTSD is a chronic condition associated with negative effects on emotional, occupational, and social functioning. Fortunately, there are short-term psychotherapies, such as Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), that improve PTSD and are recommended as the first choice in treatment for those with PTSD. One challenge with CPT is that a substantial number of patients drop out during the twelve sessions of treatment (28-80%) and generally continue to experience high levels of PTSD symptoms. This research will further understanding of a factor that could be modified to potentially decrease dropout: the therapist-patient relationship. This is defined as the working relationship between the therapist and patient that involves mutually agreed upon goals and collaboration on tasks during treatment. Although the therapist-patient relationship has been found to consistently predict dropout for other mental health issues, this association has not been explored for patients receiving CPT for PTSD. My study will examine the therapist-patient relationship in relation to dropout in a diverse sample of patients from North America. This will be the first study to explore the therapist-patient relationship in CPT. Findings from this study will help tailor CPT by training therapists to strengthen the therapist-patient relationship early on to prevent dropout from occuring. Decreasing dropout from CPT will increase the dose of CPT received, to ultimately provide better care and outcomes for Canadians with PTSD.

column36: An Integrated Evaluation of Surgical Techniques and Devices for Total Knee Arthroplasty using Imaging and Sensor Systems
column37: One of the most important procedures in our current Canadian health care system is total knee replacement (TKR). It is the only solution for treating arthritis of the knee joint, and while it has been a great success in reducing pain and returning function to the affected joint, one in five patients still report dissatisfaction following their operation. It is clear that new innovations are required to improve TKR, and the orthopaedic community has been very active in developing new concepts for both implant design and surgical technique. However, a history of failed orthopaedic technologies has highlighted the need for careful evaluation of new innovations before they are widely adopted in our health care system. Recently, there has been an increasing movement towards using more thorough approaches for assessing joint replacements. Radiostereometric analysis (RSA), an x-ray imaging technique commonly used for predicting implant failure and investigating joint motions, and wearable sensors are two tools available in our lab that can measure the success of new orthopaedic technologies. The goal of this project is to use both imaging and sensors in clinical studies to evaluate new orthopaedic innovations, including customized surgical cutting guides that are patient specific and a new implant that is designed to replicate normal knee structure and function. The results from these studies will help inform orthopaedic surgeons on which new innovations have the potential to help them improve the health of their patients following a TKR.

column36: The role of the striatum and dopamine in socioemotional dysfunction in Parkinson's disease
column37: Social behaviours, such as expressing emotions and telling jokes, are vital parts of the human experience. Although we often take them for granted, we engage in these behaviours every day. In fact, these social behaviours are exactly what gives humans the ability to work well in groups and form societies. The loss of these abilities can therefore be extremely devastating. Unfortunately, this sometimes occurs for patients with neurodegenerative diseases due to the brain deterioration they experience. Parkinson's disease (PD), which is known for its classic motor symptoms like tremor, is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the death of brain cells responsible for producing a chemical called dopamine. While PD is traditionally thought of as a movement disorder, we are now learning that the disease can produce other symptoms that interfere with thinking and social abilities. However, these symptoms have been overlooked for quite some time. My research aims to bring about a better understanding of the social symptoms of PD by investigating links between the brain and social behaviour. I am using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to look at changes in brain activity during social tasks like viewing emotional faces and hearing jokes. At the same time, I will be recording facial muscle activity to determine whether motor difficulties in PD affect emotional expression and whether this, in turn, affects social abilities such as emotion recognition or joke appreciation. This research is extremely important as over half of all Canadian PD patients have reported that the disease interferes with their interpersonal relationships (Wong et al., Health Reports, 2011). With Canada's ageing population, this burden is only expected to increase. By uncovering the mechanisms behind social behaviours and their dysfunction in PD, we will lay the foundation for future treatment approaches and ultimately improve quality of life for patients and families.

column36: Non-Invasive Electrical Stimulation of Cells Chemically Predisposed for Excitability as a Cell Type-Specific Treatment for Depression
column37: Depression is a serious condition that affects millions of Canadians each year. Although many options are available for treatment, many of them are associated with serious limitations, such as slow onset of relief and dangerous side effects. These problems highlight the need for new interventions that can effectively and safely relieve depressive symptoms. I will test a novel experimental technique to treat depression called EC stimulation, which will allow researchers to influence the activity of different types of brain cells without the need for invasive surgeries or complex genetic techniques. This will be done by combining non-invasive electrical brain stimulation with a drug that targets a specific kind of cell. These cells, known as interneurons, are located within the frontal lobe of the brain and have been found to influence depressive symptoms. By combining the effects of a weak dose of these two treatments, the activity of these interneurons can be increased, making them more likely to fire signals without affecting any other cell type. Using brain cell imaging techniques, I will locate markers for cell activity within the frontal lobe to verify that EC stimulation is successful in activating only these interneurons. I will also test whether this treatment can reverse depressive-like symptoms in a rat model of depression, and if this effect is related to chemical changes in other parts of the brain. My research will evaluate the effectiveness of EC stimulation as a method to selectively activate certain cell types. This will provide an important lead for determining the effects that different cell clusters have on mental health, while also promoting the development of better treatment options for difficult to treat disorders. Consequently, this project will guide further research towards the development of EC stimulation as a safe, simple, and accessible treatment for patients suffering from depression in both Canada and throughout the world.

column36: Evaluating Political Strategies for Achieving Global Collective Action on Antimicrobial Resistance
column37: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) is an evolutionary process whereby microbes like bacteria, fungi, and viruses become resistant to the antimicrobial medicines we depend upon to stop their spread such as antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals. The challenge is that every use of these medicines diminishes their future effectiveness, thereby accelerating AMR. Eighty years of unmanaged antimicrobial use has accelerated the development of AMR to a point of global crisis. AMR is now one of the greatest public health emergencies of our time. Some microbes have already developed resistance to all known antimicrobials, which means previously treatable infections are now untreatable. Many already die from AMR, and we risk losing countless more lives if nothing is done. The good news is there are national-level policies known to effectively curb AMR, but the world is so interconnected that almost all countries must implement these policies at the same time in order for the regulations to work. The challenge, therefore, is to craft effective tools to support international cooperation and to help countries act collectively to address AMR. This project identifies and evaluates the various political strategies that actors in the international community, like the United Nations, the World Health Organization, NGOs, and political leaders, can use to improve cooperation on the global collective action problem of AMR. It also looks at the role that countries with strong histories of global health leadership, like Canada, can play in leading the global response. Like many of today's greatest challenges, solving this problem depends on globally coordinated collective action. Achieving this will require strong global leadership, presenting an opportunity for global health oriented countries, like Canada, to rise to the occasion. The research seeks to generate and translate social scientific insights to tackle AMR and improve and protect population health around the world.

column36: Predictors and consequences of longitudinal recovery following moderate to severe traumatic brain injury.
column37: Substantial research implicates alcohol misuse as a risk factor for traumatic brain injury (TBI), but less is known about the inverse relationship - how TBI increases risk of alcohol misuse. It has been theorized that impairments in executive functioning following TBI, such as decreased impulse control and greater risky decision making, may contribute to alcohol misuse post-injury. Acute administration of alcohol has also been shown to decrease impulse control, which predicted greater laboratory alcohol consumption. Therefore, it is hypothesized that baseline executive dysfunction may make individuals with TBI more vulnerable to alcohol-induced impulsive behaviour, which could contribute to impaired control over drinking. The proposed study will investigate the relationship between impairments in decision making and impulse control and acute alcohol administration among individuals with and without a history of TBI. It is hypothesized that individuals with TBI will have decreased impulse control and increased risky decision making, both at baseline and following an acute dose of alcohol, compared to healthy controls. These alcohol-induced impairments in decision making and impulse control will predict greater difficulties limiting their drinking during a subsequent self-administration procedure. Findings will provide critical information to develop drinking guidelines for the TBI population and gain an understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms associated with alcohol misuse post-injury. This work will contribute greatly to the Canadian research ecosystem and foster impacts beyond the research environment, directly reaching individuals in the healthcare system.

column36: Emotional Reactivity and Reward Function in Concurrent Depression and Chronic Cannabis Use
column37: Depression causes significant burden on society and is a major health issue. Substance use, including the use of cannabis commonly co-occurs with depression and may be contributing to this burden. Indeed, some research suggests that compared to depressed individuals who do not use cannabis, depressed individuals who regularly use cannabis tend to report greater depressive symptoms and are less likely to improve during treatment; however, it is not yet clear how cannabis works to worsen depression in these individuals. Those who are depressed tend to experience greater emotional reactivity to stressors (i.e., react more negatively) and also tend to experience reduced reward function (i.e., decreased motivation to pursue rewards and decreased reward learning), which contribute to maintaining depressive symptoms. To better understand the role of cannabis on these two processes, we will explore whether the regular use of cannabis in depression is associated with greater dysfunctional reactivity to stress and greater impairment in reward function compared to what is seen in depression alone. We will also investigate whether reward dysfunction and/or emotional reactivity to stress predicts depression and functioning at a one-month and two-month follow-up in cannabis-using depressed individuals, and whether one process is more relevant than the other in predicting outcomes. Increasing legalization of cannabis and thereby easier access may lead to greater cannabis use in depression. As such, the results of this study have implications for how co-occurring cannabis use in and depression can be treated, informing the development of more targeted treatments or prioritizing existing treatments that either normalize reward function or emphasize stress management.

column36: Identifying Biotypes in Major Depressive disorder using Genomics, Sleep-EEG, Actigraphy and Neuroinformatics
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating condition that affects over 300 million individuals worldwide. Approximately 75% of these individuals experience sleep problems. These sleep problems are associated with a greater negative impact. Studies measuring the electrical activity of brain waves and body movements (actigraphy) during sleep have become valuable tools for studying sleep patterns in humans. There is even evidence to suggest that these sleep patterns are, at least partially, regulated by genes. Studies employing this technology have discovered several differences between the sleep patterns in MDD patients and healthy individuals ("sleep signatures"). Our biological target is the mitochondrial system because of prior evidence suggesting its involvement in MDD and sleep. In this proposal, we aim to combine genetics, electrical brain activity measures and actigraphy to identify sleep signatures in MDD individuals. We will also investigate whether any of the sleep signatures or genes studied can be used to predict which MDD individuals will respond to their antidepressant medication. In our approach, we will collect data from 100 MDD patients and 100 healthy individuals. First, we will examine whether there are alterations in the sleep patterns between our MDD patients and healthy individuals to identify which sleep signatures are present in our MDD sample. Next, we will perform association analyses to determine if any genetic markers from our susceptibility genes are associated with these sleep signatures, and whether any of the genetic markers or sleep signatures are associated with antidepressant response. Lastly, we will incorporate these results into a computational model that we can use to classify patient subgroups and predict at-risk populations in larger datasets. Overall, the results from this study will shed light on the genetics of problematic sleep in MDD and could provide evidence for a distinct subtype of MDD.

column36: A Data-Driven Approach to Identifying Therapeutic Targets for Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia
column37: With a prevalence rate of approximately 1%, schizophrenia affects a large proportion of Canadians and is associated with a tremendous burden for the individual, their family, and society at large. With increasing research suggesting the need for complementary psychotherapeutic interventions, this study aims to evaluate the specific psychological processes contributing to negative symptoms over time in order to uncover precise targets for these treatments. column36: Neural mechanisms of dual-task walking following cognitive training in late adulthood and Motoric Cognitive Risk syndrome
column37: A portion of the aging population has recently been identified as meeting criteria for Motoric Cognitive Risk syndrome (MCR), characterized by cognitive complaints (e.g., difficulty remembering) and slow walking speed, which places them at a greater risk for developing dementia. Early interventions are therefore needed to prevent or slow the progression of cognitive and physical decline in this at-risk population. Tests that assess cognitive task performance (e.g., subtracting) simultaneously with a motor task (e.g., walking; termed dual-tasking) are particularly challenging for those with MCR. We have recently shown that computerized cognitive training improves dual-task performance in healthy older adults. However, we do not yet know how brain activity changes during dual-task walking in older adults with MCR or in response to training. Therefore, the aim of this research is to examine brain activity during dual-task walking before and after cognitive training in healthy older adults and those with MCR. Evidence from neuroimaging shows greater activation in frontal brain regions during dual-tasking in older adults, compared to younger adults, which might represent a compensatory mechanism for declining brain structure. As such, we predict that prior to training, older adults with MCR will have greater frontal brain activation during dual-tasking compared to healthy older adults (suggesting less brain efficiency). However, following 12 weeks of cognitive training, we expect that the pattern of brain activity during dual-tasking will become more efficient due to enhanced cognitive capacity. The proposed research will shed light on how brain activity during dual-tasking changes after cognitive training in MCR, which will help optimize intervention strategies aimed at slowing the progression of cognitive and physical decline in older adults at risk of dementia.

column37: There is a growing body of research aimed at understanding the nature of mental contamination (i.e., feelings of internal dirtiness that arise in the absence of direct contact with a contaminant) in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Though recent studies suggest that this may exist in other anxiety disorders (e.g., post-traumatic stress disorder; PTSD), less is known about it in contexts outside of OCD. Similarly, the measurement tools for quantifying its severity, and treatment targets for alleviating its effects have been developed almost exclusively using OCD samples. There is, therefore, a knowledge gap with regard to how the nature, measurement, and treatment of mental contamination, differ and/or conform across anxiety disorders. The proposed program of study is aimed at understanding the experience mental contamination in PTSD, updating and validating the Vancouver Obsessional Compulsive Inventory - Mental Contamination Scale, and piloting an experiment to test a new possible treatment target for reducing mental contamination.

column36: Projet de recherche-action participative pour identifier et caracteriser les defis ethiques engendres par les maladies rares au quotidien et dans le milieu de la sante
column37: Etant mal comprises par la communaute medicale, les maladies rares sont complexes a diagnostiquer et a traiter adequatement. Les delais diagnostics et la deterioration de l'etat de sante qui en decoulent s'ajoutent au fardeau quotidien pose par les symptomes de ces maladies rares. Les maladies rares engendrent des defis ethiques pour les personnes qui en sont atteintes, leurs proches aidants et les cliniciens. Ces parties prenantes sont confrontees a des prises de decisions complexes qui opposent leurs valeurs, leurs besoins ou leurs preferences. Les sacrifices financiers familiaux en vue d'un traitement dispendieux, le recours a une intervention chirurgicale experimentale et la formation des cliniciens sur les maladies rares sont des exemples de ces defis ethiques qui emergent au quotidien et dans le milieu de la sante. Notre premier objectif est de bien comprendre les defis ethiques lies aux maladies rares pour pallier le manque de connaissances a ce sujet. Les defis ethiques qui nous interessent touchent precisement les personnes atteintes de maladies rares, leurs proches et des professionnels de la sante au quotidien ou dans le milieu de la sante. En analysant les connaissances scientifiques connexes a ce theme, ainsi qu'en realisant des entrevues, des observations, et un sondage aupres des parties prenantes, nous decrirons ces defis ethiques dans toute leur complexite globale. Notre deuxieme objectif est de proposer un plan d'action pour aider a resoudre deux a trois defis ethiques preoccupants parmi ceux precedemment identifies lies au milieu de la sante, pour les patients quebecois. Ce plan d'action ameliorera ainsi la qualite de la prise en charge clinique des personnes atteintes de maladies rares. Nous formerons un comite constitue de parties prenantes qui participera au developpement des etapes du projet, a l'analyse des resultats et au developpement de la proposition du plan d'action.

column36: Cell volume reduction after large intracerebral hemorrhage
column37: Intracerebral hemorrhage is a devastating stroke in which blood vessels rupture and there is bleeding in the brain tissue. This type of stroke has a high mortality rate and many complications as a result of the bleed. One of the complications is that the pressure inside the skull (intracranial pressure) becomes too high due to the injury. This high pressure can cause death due to the brain being forced out of the base of the skull. To compensate for high pressure, the brain can reduce the amount of blood and cerebrospinal fluid it produces, but this compensation mechanism often isn't enough after large bleeds. We recently found that in rats, this high pressure may be causing brain cells to decrease volume as another way to compensate. In this project, I will determine if human brain cells reduce volume after severe stroke when intracranial pressure is high. If they do, we may be able to augment this process or reduce any unwanted side effects. If they don't, further animal studies may determine a method for inducing these volume decreases to reduce pressure and save lives. Next, I will examine the effects of sex and age on cell volume decreases after inducing an intracerebral hemorrhage in rats, which will help us interpret clinical data and determine mechanisms. Finally, I will investigate the activation of ion channels and movement of ions, a potential mechanism of cell volume decreases. These studies will answer fundamental questions about a potentially life-saving mechanism of brain cells after intracerebral hemorrhage.

column36: Elucidating the factors dictating regulatory T cell function in immune-mediated glomerular diseases.
column37: Glomerular diseases are a group of autoimmune kidney disorders where the immune system destroys the kidney's glomeruli. Destruction of these structures that filter out wastes from the blood and into the urine leads to the buildup of waste in circulation. Consequently, patients with glomerular diseases often require dialysis for life or kidney transplantation for survival. Currently, there are no specific treatments for glomerular diseases, and instead, broadly immunosuppressive drugs are used to dampen immunity. However, this is associated with significant toxicity including recurrent infections, diabetes and infertility. Accordingly, we aim to better characterize the biological mechanisms involved in glomerular diseases to develop safer and targeted therapeutics. Regulatory T (Treg) cells are a class of immune cells that dampen inflammation and prevent autoimmunity in all body organs. Researchers recently demonstrated that in order for Treg cells to provide optimal regulation of kidney inflammation, they need to undergo a process referred to as functional adaptation. Here, Treg cells adopt a few characteristics of their inflammatory immune cell counterparts enabling them to migrate to and thrive in locations with heavy inflammation. However, this functional adaptation comes at a cost, as it may cause Treg cells to fully convert into pro-inflammatory, kidney-injuring immune cells. This is referred to as lineage instability. By identifying the factors controlling renal Treg cell functional adaptation and lineage instability, we can envision the development of targeted therapeutics that bolster Treg cell functions in glomerular diseases. Here, we propose to study two factors that we and others have previously observed to control Treg cell function in other inflammatory conditions, namely the IL-1 family of alarmins (IL-1 and IL-33) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAA), in the context of glomerular diseases.

column36: Investigating microglial contributions to inflammation in Parkinson's disease using brain-like organoids
column37: Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 100,000 Canadians. It is characterized by the loss of specific neurons in the brain, causing debilitating motor symptoms such as difficulty walking, postural instability and rigidity. Available treatments can alleviate the symptoms, but do not cure the disease. Microglia are the inflammatory cells that reside in the brain. They play an important role in maintaining neuronal health, but their aberrant inflammatory activities are thought to contribute to many neurodegenerative disorders. Genetic mutations of alpha-synuclein, a protein found in clumps in the brain of Parkinson's disease patient, have been associated with the risk of Parkinson's disease. Alpha-synuclein clumps provoke an excessive response of microglia. However, the impact of microglial expression of mutated alpha-synuclein on inflammatory processes, as well as the resulting harmful effects on the brain are not clearly understood. We propose to generate microglia from cells of patients harboring mutations in alpha-synuclein gene and integrate them into 3D "mini-brains" made in a dish. We will study the impact of these mutations on microglial function and neuronal health. Our study will allow us to better understand the contribution of microglial cells to the development of Parkinson's disease. The "mini-brains" containing microglia will serve as a model for drug development by other researchers.

column36: Deciphering the molecular routes by which an altered sperm epigenome elicits birth defects in the offspring
column37: In Canada, 1 in 25 babies are born with a birth defect. Craniofacial abnormalities (head and face abnormalities) are the most prevalent class of birth defects and are associated with high rates of infant mortality. Infants born with craniofacial abnormalities often require surgical, behavioral, and speech interventions which impose emotional and financial burdens for families and society. Although some craniofacial abnormalities are the result of a genetic mutation or an infectious disease, over half remain of unknown cause. Our research and that of others indicates that a previously overlooked origin of birth defects is the father's exposure to toxicants and poor diet. These paternal factors may be driven by the heritable non-genetic information in sperm known as the epigenome. The major focus of my doctoral research is to study how epigenetic information in sperm is transmitted to the embryo to influence fetal development. I have previously shown that a micronutrient folate deficiency in male mice alters the heritable epigenetic information in their sperm and is associated birth defects in their offspring. To further explore how a father's sperm epigenome can impact embryo development, I will next use a method of epigenetic manipulation in mice to identify the exact regions of the sperm epigenome that provoke craniofacial abnormalities in the offspring. This approach will permit me to map the developmental origins of a paternally-provoked birth defect. To date there exists little information about men's preconception health, resulting in missed opportunities for preventative health campaigns that would improve the rates of successful pregnancies and healthy children. This project will address a fundamental scientific question regarding the transmission of an altered sperm epigenome to the embryo and promote the development of better guidelines for men's reproductive health.

column36: Maintaining Cellular and Nuclear Integrity During Immune Cell Migration
column37: The human body is comprised of trillions of cells. The majority of our cells are structural, forming the building blocks of organs such as bones, muscle, and skin. However, protection from infection requires that one type of cell, our immune cells, is constantly moving throughout the body, searching for possible invasion and fighting it off when it occurs. T-cells are a specific type of immune cell that direct the actions of other immune cells and can directly kill infected cells to prevent infections from spreading further. To achieve this, T-cells must be highly mobile; they travel through a network of blood vessels to arrive at our various organs, whose structural cells form a complex maze. T-cells then squish and squeeze within the tight corridors of the maze as they find a path to their destination. This motion requires coordination between the cell body and the cell nucleus, which protects the cell's genetic material. The goal of my research is to understand how T-cells utilize physical cues from the maze to navigate within tissues and find the quickest path. I will use live imaging techniques to visualize in real-time how T-cells make decisions in different environments. I will focus on one particular inherited defect of immune cell migration that causes severe immunodeficiency disease in children to ask why in this case T-cell migration is ineffective. By studying what causes T-cell migration to fail, I will shed light on which molecular processes are critical to path-finding. This can inform treatments to improve T-cell navigation in tissues that are particularly challenging. For example, T-cells are often excluded from dense solid tumors. Both our body's own T-cells as well as engineered T-cell cancer therapies rely on T-cell infiltration deep into the tumor to destroy the cancer cells. Understanding how T-cells maneuver through tissue, such as these tumor environments, can help improve current treatment strategies which rely on immune cells to move.

column36: The intersection between innate and adaptive immunity in primary lung cancer
column37: Lung malignancies, including non-small cell lung cancer, are the most common cause of cancer-related death in Canada. Recent therapeutic advancements utilizing immunotherapy have yielded promising effects on overall survival compared to conventional cytotoxic therapies, suggesting an important role for the immune microenvironment in the lung. This PhD project, by bringing a detailed understanding of the immunological architecture underlying lung tumor expansion, will accelerate progress in treatment for a vast number of cancer patients. Neutrophils are first-responder inflammatory cells that have been associated with lung cancer progression. The objective of this proposal is to investigate the mechanisms by which neutrophils contribute to tumor immune escape by remodeling the lung microenvironment, with the long term aim of designing a novel neutrophil-targeting therapeutic strategy for lung malignancies. This study is based on the Quail and Spicer laboratories' previous observations and combines cutting-edge immune cell characterization technologies with in-depth analyses of patient-derived samples, bringing new and clinically relevant insights into the immunobiology of lung cancers. Given the building interest in immunotherapeutics for the treatment of various solid tumors, understanding how neutrophils orchestrate the host's response to lung malignancies will be critical to optimizing the development of personalized treatments targeting the tumor microenvironment.

column36: Elucidating the role of bacteriophage infection in ulcerative colitis
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) of the human gut that has a great impact on the health of patients and the overall costs of health care in Canada. Currently there is no cure for UC, however, it is thought that the trillions of bacteria that live in the human gut might contribute to the disease. During UC, there is an imbalance in the types of bacteria that exist in the gut. Viruses that infect these bacteria, known as bacteriophages (phages), are present at equal numbers to bacteria in the gut and also seem to be imbalanced during UC. In other ecosystems, phages have been shown to infect bacteria and change the types of bacteria that exist in these systems. It is possible that these phages could be used for therapy in UC by preventing the imbalance of bacteria that occurs in these diseases. However, we first need to understand how these viruses infect and interact with bacteria in the gut during UC. We plan to characterize how phages from UC patients infect bacteria in the gut. In order to investigate this question, we first plan to give phages from either healthy volunteers or UC patients to mice and follow how the number, and activity of bacteria changes in the gut of these mice. Using DNA sequencing of bacteria, we will determine how the addition of UC phages to these mice might change the composition of bacteria to a state that might promote inflammation and disease. Finally, we will characterize which specific phages infect which bacteria in UC patients and healthy volunteers by tracking phages with a fluorescent dye and then performing DNA sequencing on both the phages and bacteria. Collectively, our approach will provide insight into how phage infection of bacteria might be changed during UC. It is possible that our data could help develop future therapeutics focused on using phages to change bacterial communities in UC patients.

column36: The Role of Vps36 in Exosome Production and Infection by Leishmania Parasites
column37: Leishmaniasis is a widespread neglected infectious disease with 0.9-1.6million new cases every year, resulting in up to 40 000 deaths annually. This disease is caused by the Leishmania parasite, carried by the common sandfly whose habitat continues to grow due to climate change, making Leishmaniasis even more widespread. Research performed in our laboratory has led to the discovery that Leishmania secrete tiny particles called exosomes that are injected along with the parasite during a sandfly bite, and these exosomes enhance infection. Exosomes are key to cellular communication, and yet research on their role in infectious diseases is sorely lacking. Knowing their key role in Leishmania infection, we want to test whether inhibiting the release of exosomes by Leishmania will hinder infection and reduce the severity of Leishmaniasis. To accomplish this, we are disrupting a specific gene, Vps36, that has been shown to play a key role in exosome production. This will be done using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, which is capable of targeting specific DNA sequences. This will be used in our case to add an antibiotic resistance gene into the Vps36 gene, disrupting it and allowing for mutant Leishmania to be selected for using antibiotics. We will compare the wild type and mutant Leishmania to test if exosome production is altered. Continuing, we will infect mice with the WT and mutant Leishmania to examine whether Vps36 disruption is sufficient in reducing infection and Leishmaniasis symptoms. The results of this research will clarify the mechanisms of exosome production in Leishmania and potentially create an attenuated strain of Leishmania, which has implications for vaccine development. Additionally, Leishmania themselves may be useful for studying the mechanisms of exosome production present in all eukaryotes, which will be very helpful to cancer and immune cell research.

column36: Elucidating the mechanism of antibody-induced HIV-1 Env internalization
column37: Around the world, it is estimated that more than 37 million people are living with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In Canada alone, more than 65,000 individuals live with HIV/AIDS and there are thousands of new infections each year. In the absence of an efficient vaccine against HIV and with treatments still far away from eradicating the virus, there remains an urgent need to find new approaches to counteract this terrible virus. Recent studies have shown that our immune system already possesses a potentially effective protective mechanism against HIV infection, the 'antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity' (ADCC) response. However, for this response to be efficient, our immune system must be able to detect the infected cells first. These cells can be identified based on the presence of HIV envelope proteins at their surface. Our research group is currently studying the details of a biological mechanism, called 'antibody-induced envelope internalization', which limits the expression of envelope proteins on HIV-infected cells. Thus, by tracking these Envelope proteins, we can better understand how the immune system recognizes and clears these cells. The findings of this study will help us progress in finding a functional cure for HIV-infected patients by specifically eliminating HIV-infected cells.

column36: Characterising the effect of PM2.5 air pollution exposure on tuberculosis (TB) treatment outcomes and TB-associated mortality in a high TB burden setting
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is responsible for a greater number of deaths worldwide than any other single infectious disease. India shoulders a particularly high burden of TB, accounting for more than one quarter of global TB cases. Given the high levels of pollution in India's large cities, and the identification of air pollution as the most significant environmental cause of disease globally, India is a pertinent setting in which to investigate the association between air pollution and TB outcomes. Although past studies have identified smoking as a risk factor for progression to active TB as well as TB-related mortality, none have explored the effects of exposure to fine particulate (PM2.5) air pollution on TB outcomes. This study therefore aims to characterise personal-level exposures to PM2.5 among TB patients in India, comparing exposure in active TB patients in the highly polluted city of New Delhi to those in the less polluted town of Udupi, Karnataka. Personal-level exposure will be measured using small, lightweight personal aerosol monitors. Patients will be followed up over a period of 2 months, and outcomes measured will include treatment response and TB-associated mortality. Adequate treatment response will be defined by the absence of detectable viable TB bacteria in patients' sputum (mucus) samples at 2 months of treatment. Appropriate statistical methods, including logistic regression analyses, will be carried out to determine whether an association is likely to exist between PM2.5 air pollution exposure and poorer TB treatment outcomes. Being the first to investigate the effect of individual-level PM2.5 exposure in TB patients on TB treatment outcomes, this study addresses two significant and coinciding health concerns in India and globally: TB and air pollution. By providing an evidence base for TB treatment considerations in this context, the findings of this study may therefore contribute to improved TB control and prevention.

column36: The role of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis SigK regulon in infection and disease
column37: Globally, tuberculosis is the leading cause of death by infectious disease. In 2017, there were 10 million new cases of TB and 1.6 million deaths. Though Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), the cause of tuberculosis, has been investigated for over a century, mechanisms for how it subverts the human immune system to persist, replicate and spread remain poorly understood. In this project, I use novel techniques to investigate these unknown mechanisms. I will engineer variants ('mutants') of M.tb to specifically look at a set of genes present in all strains of M.tb, which spreads in humans, but are turned up in certain strains that spread in livestock. Previous work in the Behr lab has identified that strains of bacteria that cause disease in cattle have evolved these genetic differences, suggesting a role in adaptation to different host populations. By manipulating M.tb, I will be able to investigate how proteins that interact with the host are produced in different amounts, and how this affects the outcome of controlled experimental infections in the laboratory. Previously, methods to analyze this mutation were tedious, and ineffective. With new tools available, which I have already optimized in the lab, I will both conduct the proposed experiments, while also developing techniques that will be used to further study the biology of mycobacterial infections. Ultimately, this project aims to guide the management of tuberculosis and potentially contribute to a vaccine that prevents tuberculosis.

column36: Uncovering a novel role for a Neogenin-WAVE regulatory complex interaction in modulating synaptic inhibition in cortical circuitry
column37: Our studies have identified the protein Neogenin as a key regulator of the strength of inhibitory neuronal connections (synapses) in the brain. The mechanism through which Neogenin impinges on inhibitory synaptic function remains to be identified. Neogenin interacts with proteins of the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC) to regulate cytoskeletal dynamics. Several proteins of the WAVE complex, including CYFIP1, have been implicated in the regulation of synapse formation, maintenance, and function. In addition to interacting with the WRC, CYFIP1 can also interact with another protein, eIF4E, to regulate protein synthesis. These observations suggest that CYFIP1 can potentially regulate the balance of protein synthesis and actin polymerization required for inhibitory synapse formation and function. We hypothesize that Neogenin modulates inhibitory synaptic strength by regulating the equilibrium of CYFIP1-WRC and CYFIP1-eIF4E complexes formed, thereby modulating protein expression and cytoskeletal rearrangements at the synapse. To assess how Neogenin influences CYFIP1 complex interactions and inhibitory synapse function, we will define the effect of loss of Neogenin on CYFIP1 protein complexes and synaptic protein translation and demonstrate a requirement for Neogenin-WRC interactions in regulating inhibitory synaptic strength.

column36: Bridging the clinic and community: Implementing an integrated chronic pain management intervention
column37: Chronic pain is a devastating medical condition that impacts nearly 1 in 5 Canadian adults. There is a need to improve chronic pain management, to relieve the immense burden on the national health care system and improve the quality of life of individuals suffering from pain. This research aims to improve health care services for individuals with chronic pain by developing, implementing and evaluating a chronic pain management program that strategically integrates clinical care and community support. Specific objectives are to: 1) determine current community resources; 2) identify stakeholder needs and barriers; and 3) implement and evaluate an integrated pain management program with community resources. This work will be done in collaboration with individuals with chronic pain, to center the voices and needs of those directly impacted by the research.The first aim will be addressed by an online scan to determine the scope of existing local support resources for chronic pain (including educational resources, patient support groups and exercise programs). The second aim will be addressed through interviews with chronic pain patients, clinicians and community leaders, to determine their perspectives related to linking community and health care systems. These perspectives will be used to design an integrated evidence-based chronic pain management program, tailored to the local community. The final aim will be addressed by conducting a feasibility randomized clinical trial, to evaluate differences in patient outcomes between the integrated program and clinical pain management alone, in addition to evaluating the implementation process. This work is aligned with the current strategic effort to address the chronic pain crisis in Canada. By immediately assisting the community and adding to the growing literature related to pain management and delivery, this work strives to assist the Canadian initiative to improve the treatment of such common health concern.

column36: The impact of RNA Binding protein HuR on satellite cell commitment during myogenesis.

column36: Zika Virus Evolution and the Impact on Viral Fitness in Mosquito Cells
column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) is an emerging virus of public health concern. While the virus was historically limited to Africa and Asia and caused only mild illness, recent outbreaks in South and Central America have been linked to more severe symptoms such as fetal microcephaly and Guillain-Barre syndrome. The spread of ZIKV into these new regions has been linked to the spread of mosquitoes that transmit the virus between human hosts, but relatively little is known about the impact of recent evolution on viral growth in mosquito cells. column36: Clinical practice guidelines in psychosocial oncology: Usage by and attitudes of mental health professionals
column37: An estimated 1 in 2 Canadians will develop cancer at some point in their life. Individuals with this disease face a multitude of psychological struggles and their psychosocial needs are often reported as unmet. This reflects current trends in psychology: psychologists are often unaware of and fail to use evidence-based approaches in their practice. Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are commonly used as a means of promoting evidence-based practice in medicine and recent efforts have been made to increase their use in psychology in an attempt to bridge the science-practice gap. However, there are no currently available studies exploring psychosocial oncology-specific CPG use among mental health professionals. The purpose of this study is to explore mental health professionals' usage of and attitudes towards CPGs in psychosocial oncology. This will be accomplished through a mixed methods study divided into three distinct phases. In Phase 1, the directors of psychosocial oncology programs will be interviewed about the use of and attitudes towards CPGs within their programs. Qualitative interview data will be used to develop survey items. In Phase 2, the newly developed survey items will be pilot tested among a sample of researchers and practitioners in psychosocial oncology. Items deemed unessential will be dropped from the survey and remaining items will be finalized. In Phase 3, mental health professionals will be recruited to complete the final survey about their attitudes towards and usage of psychosocial oncology CPGs. Comparisons of all study variables within and across different mental health professions and work environments will be conducted through simple and multiple logistic regressions. This study will help address the gap between science and practice in the field of psychosocial oncology and contribute to efforts to promote evidence-based practice in psychology.
