column36: Investigating stalled polysome dysregulation as a shared feature of human intellectual disorders
column37: Intellectual disorders are often characterized by the inability of an individual to complete routine activities and interact with others. One cause of these disorders is the atypical development of the central nervous system. In the case of many intellectual disorders, atypical development results when specific sections of DNA, called genes, become mutated. Much like a 'typo' in an instruction manual, gene mutations can interfere with how a cell reads the instructions contained in DNA. The mutations involved in several intellectual disorders overlap in their tendency to cause a cell to receive faulty instructions for how to produce new proteins. This overlap may provide insight into what mechanisms cause the atypical development underlying these conditions. In the typically developing brain, new proteins are made at specific places and times. The brain accomplishes this by assembling the protein building machinery and then 'hitting the pause button'. Once the protein building machinery is paused, it can be shuttled throughout the cell and then turned back on when the time is right. We believe it may be this process of 'hitting pause' that goes wrong in intellectual disorders. Therefore, it is the goal of our research to understand how protein production is controlled in healthy, stem cell derived brain cells and whether the 'pause button' is missing or atypical in similar cells from patients with intellectual disorders. If the pause button is missing or atypical in these disorders, then drugs that restore the pause could be developed. In sum, this research will advance our understanding of fundamental brain pathways as well as provide insight into what causes atypical brain development in intellectual disorders.

column36: Should I tell my employer I have a disability? Understanding communication, decision making, support and accommodation processes in the workplace among adults living with chronic disabling conditions
column37: On average, Canadians spend over one-third of their lives at work. Employment has been found to provide a sense of purpose and well-being. Not having paid work has been found to be related to poorer health, social and financial disadvantages. In Canada, less than half of people with a disability are employed. The most common and costly health conditions resulting in disabilities are often invisible and unpredictable - depression, multiple sclerosis, arthritis, HIV, cancer, etc. Privacy legislation protects workers and prevents employers from asking for medical diagnoses or symptoms. Research also finds that workers are often unwilling to reveal their health and support needs at work due to fear of job or promotion loss or discrimination. The overall aim of this research is to enable individuals with a disability to remain working by seeking a better understanding of workplace communication decisions (to discuss a disability or not) and support. Objective 1: to examine worker and employers' perspectives of the challenges people living with a disability face at work, whether and how they communicate and seek support at work, and how these decisions may be shaped by different types of disability (e.g. physical and mental health), different job types, and personal factors like age and gender. Objective 2: to identify whether communication decisions, type of disability, and personal and job factors are related to outcomes at work such as job attendance, stress, productivity, and workplace relationships. This will be carried out in two studies 1) will use in-depth interviews with workers and employers and 2) will draw on the findings from the interviews to design a novel questionnaire that will be given to a larger group of people. Understanding how the nature of disability, communication decision making and support seeking in the workplace relate to gaining and maintaining employment can inform new workplace policies and practices to help people with disabilities.

column36: The Role of Autologous Mesenchymal Stem Cell Recellularization in Rescuing the Xenoreactive Immune Response
column37: Valve replacement surgery is one of the most common procedures performed by cardiac surgeons. Most patients undergoing valve replacement surgery receive either a tissue or mechanical valve. Mechanical valves are more durable than tissue valves, but require a daily blood thinner. Tissue valves are made from either cow or pig tissue, do not require blood thinners, but tend to fail over time requiring another operation. One reason these valves fail is due to a slow rejection of the animal tissue by the human immune system. Our ultimate goal is to create an artificial heart valve that does not require blood thinners and will last the lifetime of the patient. To do this, we will use autologous stem cells to repopulate animal tissue heart valves to prevent the immune system from recognizing this foreign tissue. We will achieve this goal with two experiments. First, we will use stem cells taken from human patients bone marrow and grow them on an animal tissue scaffold, analyzing the human immune response to this tissue in-vitro with donor human blood. These results will be used to inform the following experiment. Second, we have developed a rat aortic valve transplant model that closely resembles what happens in human patients. We will use rat stem cells to repopulate guinea pig aortic valves, then implant these valves back into rats to analyze the immune response to this tissue in-vivo. The proposed studies will contribute to our ultimate goal of creating an artificial heart valve that does not require blood thinners, is durable, available and leads to improved long-term patient outcomes.

column36: The use of patient derived gastric cancer organoids as a predictive tool to determine patient response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy
column37: Stomach cancer remains a deadly disease. In Canada, only 25% of patients diagnosed with stomach cancer survive five years after their diagnosis. Specific chemotherapy regimens established for stomach cancer have improved survival, however some cancers respond better to treatment than others. Unfortunately, there is no current way to predict which treatment is best for each individual patient. One way to personalize treatment for patients is to use cells from their own cancer and test how their cancer responds to various anti-cancer treatments in the laboratory. Due to new technological advancements we can now grow a patient's cancer cells in a three-dimensional space to form miniature organs, or "organoids", that resemble the patient's actual cancer. We hypothesize that organoids will respond similar to the patient's cancer when treated with the same anti-cancer therapy so that they may be used to predict treatment response. For our study we will enroll twenty stomach cancer patients and take a piece of their cancer prior to chemotherapy. We will then grow the cancer cells in the lab and treat them with the same anti-cancer drugs that the patient receives. Following surgery, we will compare the degree to which cells were killed in a patient's cancer to the number of cells killed in the lab to determine how similar they respond to treatment. The overall goal of our project is to develop tools that will allow for better prediction of stomach cancer response to chemotherapy so that each patient can receive the best treatment for their tumour. If successful, this study may provide evidence to apply these techniques to future studies with the purpose provide "precision medicine" to Canadian stomach cancer patients.

column36: Increasing Myocardial Ketone Oxidation as an Approach to Treat Heart Failure
column37: A growing number of Canadians (over 50,000) are diagnosed with heart failure each year. Heart failure is a chronic condition where the weakened cardiac muscle can no longer effectively pump blood to the rest of the body. Like a car engine, the healthy heart uses 'fuels' to meet its high energy demand and sustain its contractile function. However, the failing heart is akin to an engine out of fuel and is not only running low on fuels, but also running on the wrong type of fuels. While the healthy heart can tap into different 'grades/types of fuels', namely fats and carbohydrates, the failing heart loses its flexibility to use different fuels and becomes inefficient at fuel consumption, ultimately becoming energy-starved. Therefore, my research is focused on understanding a new 'grade of fuel' that is understudied - ketones. Ketones are produced by our livers during starvation and intense exercise. However, recent evidence suggests that the failing heart uses more ketones for energy compared to a healthy heart. Thus, are ketones a good or bad fuel for the failing heart? Answering this question will be the objective of my research project. To do this, mice with heart failure will have their hearts removed from their body and fixed to a system that can pump simulated blood through their isolated beating hearts. Ketones will then be added to the simulated blood and heart function will be assessed to see if ketones can improve how well the heart is working and using energy. Furthermore, we will also study the effects of ketones by feeding mice, with heart failure, a ketogenic diet. Heart function will then be monitored throughout the treatment to determine if this high-fat/low-carbohydrate diet can improve the failing heart's function. From these experiments and results, I hope to direct future therapeutic approaches for treating heart failure. If ketones are good for the failing heart, a ketone supplement or ketogenic diet could be used to treat heart failure patients.

column36: Fasted Exercise training in Type 2 Diabetes (FED)
column37: Diabetes is a major health concern worldwide. It is estimated that up to 30% of people in Canada are living with pre-diabetes or type 2 diabetes (T2D). Many people with T2D, also have fatty liver disease and this can worsen blood sugar control. It is recommended that people with diabetes increase their daily physical activity to manage their blood sugars. Sometimes, increasing the amount of exercise can be very difficult. In addition, many individuals who meet the recommended exercise guidelines experience minimal improvement in their blood sugar control, and minimal reductions in liver fat. This can be very discouraging. Improving the time of day that exercise is preformed (e.g., before or after breakfast) may be a simple method to improve blood sugar control and reduce fat stored in organs such as the liver, pancreas, and muscle. To date, only short-term studies have examined how modifying exercise time of day affects people with T2D. It is unknown which time of day is best in the long term. This study will examine 16 weeks of aerobic exercise training, performed before or after breakfast, on blood sugar control and fat stored in the liver, pancreas, and muscle. It could be very motivating for people with T2D to know that they can get more benefits from exercise by changing when exercise is performed, rather than increasing the amount. Ultimately, results from this study may help clinicians more optimally prescribe exercise to help patients achieve their clinical targets and improve their overall quality of life.

column36: Modelling Functional Recovery After Spinal Cord Injury Using Human Organoids
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) results in either temporary or permanent paralysis. Given that current therapies are ineffective in reversing paralysis, patients face drastically reduced life-expectancies and endure severe psychological, social and economic burdens. The goal of my project is to restore quality of life in SCI patients by promoting regeneration and functional recovery of their spinal cord. In mammals, each neuron from the brain communicates with neurons in other parts of the body using long projections called axons. These axons extend down the spinal column to form the spinal cord, ultimately making connections with skin and muscle tissue to coordinate sensory-motor function. Given that fully matured neurons are not able to repair themselves once injured, SCI disrupts information transfer through axons and causes an irreversible damage. In order to promote regeneration of axons, I plan to "trick" damaged neurons into thinking they are still in a growth-like-state using small-molecule drugs. To test these drugs, I will develop a model of SCI using a "mini-spinal cord" made of human tissue. "Mini-organs", known as human organoids, are tissues generated from embryonic stem cells that resemble human organs, both in morphology and function. As opposed to currently used animal models of SCI, a human organoid model is a far superior representative of human degeneration. After generating spinal cord organoids, I will induce injury to mimic SCI and treat the organoid with various small-molecule drugs. This way, a human spinal cord organoid will make the results of my drug testing far more reliable and speed up the drug discovery process. By developing a functional human spinal cord organoid and testing various growth-promoting small molecule drugs, my project serves to both promote functional regeneration of the central nervous system and provide a new drug discovery platform for spinal cord diseases.

column36: The role of Hedgehog signaling in basal-like breast cancer and the tumour microenvironment
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide and remains a leading cause of cancer death. One in 9 women will develop breast cancer at some point in their lifetime. Despite the success of current treatment, breast cancer remains a potentially deadly disease with multiple subtypes that respond very differently to treatment. Basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) is a specific subtype that comprises 15% of all breast cancers and primarily affects young women, people of African or Hispanic ancestry, and those with genetic mutations. Despite current treatments, BLBC often has a poor outcome. There is therefore an unmet need for improved treatments in this group of patients. Increasing evidence has shown that the Hedgehog signaling pathway is associated with BLBC. The Hedgehog pathway is a specific molecular pathway that is essential during development of the embryo and is critical for early breast development. My preliminary studies and those of others have shown a link between activated Hedgehog signaling and the growth of breast cancer cells, with more aggressive breast cancers harboring activated Hedgehog signaling. My project will aim to study exactly how the Hedgehog pathway promotes the growth of BLBC cells. My hypothesis is that Hedgehog is responsible for releasing specific molecules that promote inflammation, termed cytokines. These cytokines then recruit immune cells that help the cancer grow and mature. By identifying which cytokines are triggered by Hedgehog signaling and which immune cells are recruited, I will then begin to test different drugs to inhibit these cytokines, thereby changing the immune cell infiltration and inhibiting cancer growth. Many of these drugs are already approved and available to treat inflammatory diseases, such as Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ulcerative Colitis. My plan would therefore be to take these drugs that have already been shown to be safe with minimal side effects, and repurpose them for use in BLBC.

column36: Seeing Clearly: A Decision Analysis of Novel MRI, PSMA PET/CT, and Biomarker Testing in Early Prostate Cancer Detection
column37: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer amongst men in Canada, affecting 1 in 7 individuals. MRI, PSMA PET/CT, and biomarker testing have revolutionized the approach to early stage prostate cancer detection, identifying prostate pathology in a clinically useful and reliable manner. Given the prevalence of prostate cancer, these findings are remarkably salient to early stage and undiagnosed patients. In particular, when these are used in combination, studies have reported an excellent ability to discriminate patients who do not harbour clinically significant disease from those who do. This avoids potential overtreatment in low-risk individuals while properly risk stratifying high-risk patients. Despite demonstrating clinical efficacy however, an implementation gap exists in translating these outcomes within a publicly funded, resource limited system. Rigorous Health Technology Assessment must be completed to ascertain which test(s) and in which order will offer the most benefit per cost expenditure, while addressing patient, physician, and societal acceptability concerns in Canada. To date, no decision analyses have evaluated the effect of MRI, PSMA PET/CT, and biomarker testing in a head-to-head, staged, or combination approaches within our healthcare system. Methods: We plan to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of incorporating MRI, PSMA PET/CT, and biomarker testing in primary prostate cancer detection, compared to standard of care using a decision analytic model. We will assess the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer, avoidance of clinically insignificant prostate cancer, biopsies saved, cost, and corresponding quality of life impact. Our model will determine the most clinically and cost-effective initial diagnostic strategy across a wide variety of patient, physician, and societal scenarios to inform broad-based policy decisions as well as individualized patient-level decisions.

column36: Developing Population-Based Risk Tools to Predict and Reduce Premature Mortality in Canadian Cities
column37: Premature mortality, defined as deaths before 75 years of age, is considered avoidable through appropriate prevention or timely treatment. In Canada, premature mortality rates vary across sex, socioeconomic status, and geography. In this study, I will develop a tool to predict premature mortality, which will support policy and health system decision-making. First, I will identify social, environmental, and clinical risk factors for premature mortality. I will then use these risk factors to create the prediction tool using machine learning. This tool will be capable of predicting the effects of health policies that affect over 21-million people living in urban areas, 60% of the Canadian population. This prediction tool will be the first of its kind and will be built specifically for a Canadian context. This prediction tool is novel because it will be capable of incorporating information on people's social and physical environments as well as their clinical history and health-related behaviours. Incorporating social and environmental data has two benefits: it helps the model make more accurate predictions and it integrates a broader focus on the determinants of health. Including social and environmental perspectives emphasizes prevention and equity, and it incorporates these perspectives into machine learning applications for population health. Creating this prediction tool requires developing new predictive methods that combine the fields of epidemiology and machine learning. By leveraging the increasing availability of health data and growing computational power, this research helps meet the growing demand for analytic, decision-support health tools.

column36: Neural Mechanisms Underlying Changes in Internalizing and Externalizing Symptoms for Adolescents Undergoing a Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Skills Group
column37: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is a gold standard psychological intervention targeting self-harm, impulsive, and suicidal behaviours in individuals with borderline personality disorder, but multiple studies have found it to be efficacious for substance use disorders, eating disorders, and major depressive disorder. DBT consists of weekly individual therapy sessions, weekly 2-hour group skills training, weekly therapist consultation, and 24-hour coaching calls. However, dismantling studies have found that the skills group alone is as effective as standard DBT. There is a paucity of evidence about the effectiveness of the DBT skills group for adolescents, and in particular, adolescents with emotion dysregulation that do not engage in suicidal and self-injurious behaviours. Additionally, the physiological mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of the DBT skills group on emotion regulation has not yet been investigated and can provide objective indicators of change in emotional arousal and neural processing of emotions that can be reflective of DBT effectiveness. To our knowledge, the present study is the first to examine neurobiological substrates to treatment outcome in a DBT skills group intervention for adolescents with prominent symptoms of emotion dysregulation without suicidal and self-injurious behaviours. The study will investigate the neural mechanisms that underlie treatment-related improvements in emotion dysregulation, refining our understanding of the ways in which DBT skills may impact physiological arousal and brain circuits involved in emotion regulation. We will also examine correlations between changes in brain activation from pre-treatment to post-treatment and symptom rating scales across the same time frame. Together, this research will help to determine whether any baseline indications of brain function might be predictive of gains in treatment for adolescents with high levels of emotional dysregulation.

column36: Examining modifiable risk factors previously associated with breast cancer incidence on breast cancer survival among BRCA mutation carriers
column37: Those who inherit a deleterious BRCA mutation face a high lifetime risk of developing breast cancer compared to the general population. Modifiable risk factors such as physical activity, BMI, and dietary intake have previously been shown to increase or decrease the risk of developing breast cancer in BRCA mutation carriers; however, the effect of these modifiable risk factors have not been examined in survival after the diagnosis of breast cancer in this population. BRCA mutation carriers are typically associated with worse overall survival outcomes following the diagnosis of a breast cancer, compared to the general population. Since there is a role for modifiable risk factors in modifying breast cancer risk among BRCA mutation carriers, I hypothesize that these modifiable risk factors will also have a role in breast cancer survival after diagnosis of a breast cancer. Therefore the objectives of this study are to evaluate if the following modifiable risk factors impact breast cancer survival among BRCA mutation carriers: 1) energy balance (physical activity and BMI) 2) dietary intake (circulating vitamin D, folate, iron, and selenium levels) 3) lifestyle factors (smoking and alcohol). To our knowledge, this study will be the first to evaluate the effect of various lifestyle and dietary factors on breast cancer survival among BRCA mutation carriers. These findings will have the potential to compliment current treatment options, reduce breast cancer death attributed to a BRCA1/2 mutation, and ultimately help improve outcomes among those who develop the disease.

column36: Cholinergic prefrontal attention circuitry deficits in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Disruptions in attention occur early in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and can contribute to worsening memory and other cognitive declines. Improving early disruption in attention in AD is potentially a high-impact treatment goal. While we know of key neural networks necessary for attentional control, much remains unknown about cellular mechanisms causing attentional deficits in AD. Past work shows neurons in a key attention network have reduced activity in a mouse model of AD (Proulx, Power et al., 2019). Using electrophysiology, I am finding irregularities in neuron activity in the same attention network in an AD rat model. With the CIHR Award, I will continue investigating this network in rats, clarifying the causes of this irregular activity and measuring neuron activity at various ages to understand the time-course of disease development. In investigating this key attention network in mice, we applied neurotransmitter to the entire tissue, a process called exogenous stimulation (Proulx, Power et al., 2019). Revisiting the AD mouse, I will use a genetically modified version of this mouse where a specific population of neurons can be induced to release neurotransmitter, called endogenous stimulation. This activation more closely mimics stimulation in a living animal, giving better information about the cell signalling deficits in AD. Our previous work in the AD mouse shows that blocking a specific ion channel (SK channel) reverses the reduced AD neuron activity (Proulx, Power et al., 2019). I will test the efficiency of this SK channel blocker at reversing the dysfunction that arises from endogenous stimulation of AD mouse neurons. This would confirm the role of SK channels in causing deficits in this key attention network. I will also test the efficiency of the SK blocker on rescuing the neuron activity in the AD rat. If the SK channels seem to be contributing to dysfunction in both models, we would posit SK channels as a promising avenue for therapeutic development.

column36: Economic consequences of cancer in adolescents and young adults: a population-based Canadian national study
column37: Survival of cancer in adolescent and young adults (AYAs) has recently surpassed 80% resulting in a growing Canadian survivorship cohort; however, the economic outcomes of cancer in AYAs remain unexplored. A cancer diagnosis and its related treatment can result in psychosocial, occupational, and financial challenges in AYAs entering the workforce. Thus, it is hypothesized that cancer in AYAs is associated with immediate reductions in performance at work or school leading to financial impacts following diagnosis and throughout treatment, which may not recover during survivorship, compared to AYAs who do not develop cancer. The objective of this proposal is to determine the association between a cancer diagnosis and the economic trajectory of AYAs in Canada diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 29 years, from 1992 to 2015. We will obtain data from the Social Data Linkage Environment at Statistics Canada which links individuals' annual T1 tax records with population-based administrative databases. Cancer cases will be identified from the Canadian Cancer Registry and matched 1-to-10 on age, sex, index year, and postal code to population controls who do not develop cancer. Subjects will be followed from the index date (age at initial cancer diagnosis) until the earlier of a new cancer diagnosis, death, or December 31, 2017. Multivariable generalized estimating equations will be used to analyze the data and we will stratify the analysis by age group, sex, and neighbourhood income to identify potential risk factors of disparities in economic trajectory. Results from this project will address a current gap in knowledge on the financial hardship associated with a cancer diagnosis in AYAs. This study will deliver novel insight on the economic effects of cancer and will be used to inform future policy development and the potential need for tax incentives or other economic reform to ensure this growing population of AYA survivors has opportunities for a stable financial future.

column36: Reducing patient preoperative anxiety through an innovative translational simulation intervention targeting health professionals
column37: Preoperative anxiety is very common among surgical patients and can result in poorer surgical outcomes. Health professionals' ability to recognize when patients are anxious or fearful and respond reassuringly can reduce patients' anxiety. However, researchers have found that health professionals struggle to accurately recognize patients' emotions during preoperative clinical visits. This project aims to develop and test a virtual reality (VR) intervention to train health professionals to better recognize when patients are expressing anxiety and other emotions during the preoperative visit. They will also learn how to respond in a compassionate and reassuring manner. VR affords the opportunity to present health professionals with a range of realistic patient scenarios while tracking their nonverbal (e.g., eye gaze, vocal tone) and verbal responses to patients' emotional cues for feedback and learning. This intervention will be tested among health professionals who deliver preoperative care (e.g., anesthesiologists, nurses) working in a large hospital setting using a randomized controlled trial design. Health professionals will be randomized to either complete the intervention or not complete the intervention. Afterwards, a few of each health professionals' preoperative visits will be recorded and patients will report their level of anxiety after the visit. I expect that, compared to health professionals who do not complete the intervention, those who do will show more empathetic communication during the visits and their patients will report less preoperative anxiety. I will also explore the factors within and outside of the hospital that affect the extent to which the intervention is successfully implemented and sustained. By understanding these factors, the intervention can be more successfully implemented and sustained in other hospital settings. This will increase the impact my work has on the surgical care experiences and outcomes of patients in Canada.

column36: Enhancing sentinel lymph node mapping in lung cancer surgery using a novel liposome-based dual-modality nanoparticle
column37: Over 28 000 Canadians are diagnosed with lung cancer each year. Improved imaging and screening have increased the number of patients diagnosed with early stage disease, allowing treatment with surgery. However, key treatment decisions (e.g. providing chemotherapy after surgery, deciding the extent of surgery) are based on whether cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. Detecting the earliest evidence of cancer spread to lymph nodes remains a challenge in surgical patients. Clinical trials have shown that up to 20% of these patients may have lymph node disease that is missed by standard diagnostic approaches. We will evaluate a new 'dual-mode' dye that can be seen by both CT (a 3D X-ray image) and fluorescence camera. Once injected near a tumour, the dye drains to nearby lymph nodes. The first nodes to 'light up' are the first nodes cancer could spread to, making them key nodes to test for evidence of cancer spread. We will compare this new 'dual-mode' dye with current 'single-mode' dyes that can only be seen by CT or fluorescence camera. Our goal is to see if our new dye is more accurate and easier to use. The lymph node dyes will be studied in preclinical models. First, we will define dye performance with CT scan and fluorescence camera separately. Second, we will look at how injection technique can affect dye performance. Finally, we will compare the 'single-mode' and 'dual-mode' dyes using a combined CT-fluorescence technique in lung tumour models that spread to nearby lymph nodes. This model mirrors what we see in human patients. If we are successful, we will create a powerful new tool for finding key lymph nodes during lung cancer surgery. Information from these nodes would enable doctors and patients to make more informed, personalized treatment discussions with the goal of improving outcomes and quality of life. Given some similarities between cancers, success with lung cancer would suggest our new dye could be useful for other cancer surgery as well.

column36: Quality of care in people with lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: An overlooked population
column37: Lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are common health conditions that often co-exist. People who have both have worse survival than people with only lung cancer. They need supportive strategies and end-of-life care to manage their disease and discomfort. Despite similar symptoms, people with COPD do not receive the same end-of-life care as people with lung cancer or heart disease. There is little information about end-of-life care for people who suffer from both lung cancer and COPD. Research on the quality care in this vulnerable population would help to improve care and health outcomes. The ultimate goal of this research is to better understand the overlap of lung cancer and COPD and improve the quality of life for Canadians with both conditions. We will use health administrative data, patient surveys and other data that capture the Ontario population. This data includes visits to doctors, hospital admissions, diagnosis, other health conditions and medical testing. We will first determine how common lung cancer is in a population with COPD. Then we will examine whether people with both conditions use more healthcare resources than people with only COPD or lung cancer. Second, we will also examine which factors affect the care patients receive. We expect people who are older, have heart disease or live in rural areas are at risk for poor quality of care. Identifying these factors will help develop strategies to improve care and equity in healthcare. Finally, we will determine whether people with both conditions receive more end-of-life care measures than people with only one condition. This includes measures such as pain medication or home care. We will share the results of this research with clinical staff to directly help patients. We want to provide the best possible care to people with lung cancer and COPD. This will ensure they have the best possible health, and reduce unnecessary strain on the healthcare system.

column36: The association between current enrollment in opioid substitution therapy and risk of providing injection initiation assistance to others over time: a longitudinal cohort study of persons who inject drugs in Toronto, Ontario
column37: The ongoing national overdose crisis is driven, in part, by the increasing supply of illicit, synthetic opioids (including fentanyl and related analogues) and the transition of individuals from misuse of oral medications to injecting opioids (including synthetics and heroin). Correspondingly, experts have called for interventions to both reduce harms associated with opioid use and prevent the expansion of injection drug use practices within vulnerable communities. It is suspected that untreated opioid use disorder (OUD) -- a condition characterized by problematic opioid use resulting in significant impairment or distress -- is widespread and may be contributing to the increasing number of persons who inject drugs (PWID) by: 1) driving persons who have never injected before to seek more intense modes of drug use (i.e., via injection) and 2) increasing the likelihood that PWID (who assist in 90% of injection initiation events, i.e., the first time injection drug use of another) accept or initiate a request to provide injection initiation assistance. Therefore, it is hypothesized that enrolling PWID in opioid substitution therapy (OST) -- which can reduce the cycle of intoxication and withdrawal by blocking the effects of opioids -- will reduce the likelihood they share injection drug use practices with vulnerable individuals. This proposed research aims to: 1) estimate the prevalence of OST enrollment among PWID in Toronto, Ontario using prescription claims data; 2) determine the accuracy of self-reported OST enrollment versus prescription claims; and 3) assess whether PWID who are currently enrolled in OST are less likely to provide injection initiation assistance to others over time. In doing so, the intention is to provide evidence to support (or refute) the presumed protective effect of OST on injection initiation, while quantifying potential treatment gaps.

column36: Identifying rural-urban differences in access to treatment and harms associated with alcohol use disorder in Ontario, Canada
column37: Alcohol use is a leading cause of death and disease. In Canada, over 70,000 people are hospitalized yearly for alcohol-related reasons and alcohol-related emergency room visits in Ontario have increased by 82% since 2003. Rural communities have almost two times higher rates of alcohol-related hospitalization than urban centers. In turn, there is an urgent need to develop public health strategies to reduce the burden of alcohol-related harm in rural Canada. The development of these strategies has been limited by an incomplete understanding of rural alcohol use and its related harms. Limited access to addiction treatment for individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD, known colloquially as 'alcoholism') is thought to contribute to the increased burden of alcohol-related harm in rural communities. AUD is characterized by uncontrolled alcohol consumption and withdrawal symptoms during periods of abstinence. Treatment is provided by specialized healthcare workers and is effective at reducing the severity of AUD and risk of downstream harms, such as alcohol-related hospitalization or mortality. If rural communities face limited access to AUD treatment, which is likely given that rural communities have limited access to most specialist care, this would foreseeably increase both the prevalence of AUD and the risk of alcohol-related harm amongst those with AUD. No research has investigated rural-urban disparities in access to AUD treatment or the impact this has on downstream alcohol-related harm. The purpose of my research is to address this gap in knowledge. My specific aims are to evaluate the Ontario population for rural-urban differences in access to AUD treatment and the resulting effect on alcohol-related hospitalizations, emergency room visits and mortality. This research will lay a framework for similar studies to be conducted in other provinces and territories and will guide the formation of public health strategies to reduce alcohol-related harm in rural Canada.

column36: Symptom Burden as a Predictor of Emergency Room Visits and Unplanned Hospitalizations in Patients with Head and Neck Cancer
column37: Head and neck cancer can significantly impact the way a person looks, eats, breathes and swallows. In Canada, 1 in 10 cancers is diagnosed in the head and neck area. Unfortunately, unlike most other types of cancer, the number of new cases is rising each year. Of all types of cancer, patients with head and neck cancer report the highest symptom burden. Approximately half of all patients will end up in the emergency room or be unexpectedly hospitalized during the course of their treatment. Emergency room visits and unplanned hospitalizations are real concerns because they negatively impact the patient experience and can also lead to treatment interruptions. Treatment interruptions are a significant problem, as even a one-day interruption in radiation therapy has been shown to decrease a patient's chance of survival. Our study aims to use healthcare data collected from over 16,000 head and neck cancer patients in Ontario to understand why these patients are visiting the emergency room so frequently. We suspect that uncontrolled symptoms, like pain and depression, are leading patients to the emergency room and to be hospitalized. In Ontario, we routinely ask all cancer patients about their symptoms through a standardized survey that they complete each time they see their doctor. We will use this information to develop a tool to help identify vulnerable patients who are more likely to end up in the emergency room or hospitalized, paying particular attention to the elderly, those with a mental illness, recent immigrants to Canada and those living in rural communities. We will work closely with a group of patients, caregivers, healthcare providers, and policy makers during our study to get their feedback. Our hope is that this information will allow us to identify the patients most at risk of visiting the emergency room and help us to develop strategies to improve the quality of care provided to them.

column36: Expanding e-Mental Health Services: The Development and Randomized Clinical Trial of a Technology-based Psychological Intervention for Cannabis Use Disorder in Young Adults with Psychosis
column37: Cannabis ("pot") is the most widely used recreational drug among young adults (18-30 years) in Canada and frequent consumers are at higher risk of developing psychosis. In young adults with psychosis, cannabis use disorder (CUD, a medical term used to describe problematic cannabis use) is common (45%) and related to poorer symptomatic and functional recovery (e.g., working, studying, living independently) and increased use of healthcare services (e.g., hospitalizations). Psychological face-to-face interventions are effective in decreasing cannabis use and treating CUD, but many young adults do not benefit because of low accessibility, high treatment costs, stigma, and poorly adapted or unappealing treatments. Technology-based psychological interventions (TBPI), such as internet-based interventions, can eliminate these barriers and are efficient in decreasing cannabis use in individuals without psychosis. Research is needed to assess the efficacy of TBPI in reducing cannabis use in young adults with psychosis and CUD. My doctoral research project therefore aims to develop an efficient TBPI for reducing cannabis use in young adults with psychosis and CUD. My project consists of: 1) A review of published studies to acquire up-to-date knowledge about the efficacy of TBPI in young adults with psychosis and CUD; 2) Interviews with patients and clinicians to explore their preferences for a TBPI; 3) A survey with patients to elicit the facilitators for using a TBPI, and 4) a randomized controlled clinical trial comparing the efficacy of a TBPI in decreasing cannabis use in young adults with psychosis and a control group receiving usual treatment. I will be guided and supervised by a team of experts in the field of substance abuse disorders and mental health problems, who are passionate to find new efficient treatment modalities. I will disseminate the results through multiple channels to reach the general public, clinicians and healthcare policy makers throughout Canada.

column36: Cocreation et diffusion d'une formation pour ergotherapeutes portant sur la readaptation sexuelle suivant un accident vasculaire cerebral : une etude mixte quasi-experimentale.
column37: Les personnes qui subissent un accident vasculaire cerebral (AVC) sont fortement susceptibles de presenter des difficultes sexuelles (ex : dysfonctions erectiles, troubles de la lubrification vaginale, insatisfaction sexuelle). Pourtant, peu d'intervenants abordent la sexualite avec leurs clients au cours de la readaptation, souvent en lien avec un manque de connaissances. Considerant que les ergotherapeutes seraient des professionnels tout indiques pour entreprendre la readaptation sexuelle post-AVC, cette etude sera principalement consacree a la creation et a la diffusion d'une formation pour ergotherapeutes portant sur la readaptation sexuelle suivant un AVC. En utilisant un recensement des dernieres etudes portant sur le sujet, un comite d'experts compose de sexologues et d'ergotherapeutes (cliniciens et chercheurs ) mettra sur pied une formation destinee a ameliorer les connaissances et les competences des ergotherapeutes dans ce domaine. La formation sera testee aupres de 15 ergotherapeutes puis sera ensuite officiellement diffusee a 120 ergotherapeutes. L'influence de cette formation sur le niveau de connaissances et competences des participants sera mesuree par un questionnaire portant sur les connaissances, les attitudes et les pratiques cliniques liees a la sexualite des ergotherapeutes. Ce questionnaire sera complete avant et apres la formation puis 12 semaines suivant celle-ci. Un groupe de 120 ergotherapeutes n'ayant pas suivi la formation remplira le meme questionnaire pour agir comme comparatif. Des entrevues de groupe seront realisees avec environ 24 ergotherapeutes ayant suivi la formation pour mieux comprendre leur appreciation de la formation et son influence sur les participants. Cette formation, qui sera la premiere en la matiere repertoriee dans la litterature et creee de facon collaborative, devrait ameliorer le niveau de competences des ergotherapeutes, ce qui ameliorera ultimement la qualite des services transmis a la clientele post-AVC.

column36: Computational single-cell analysis of developmental programs disrupted in pediatric tumours
column37: Pediatric brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer-related death and the second most common diagnosed malignancy in children in Canada. Despite aggressive therapy, for many tumour types, outcomes have not changed in the last three decades. Survival is very low, and patients that do survive are left with severe lifelong side-effects. Current evidence suggests that in some childhood tumours, the initiating molecular event that causes the tumour occurs during development. During development, cells undergo a sequence of coordinated changes in gene expression that must be finely orchestrated, and alterations in this process often cause disease. Our goal is to identify the precise timing of these initial disease-causing events for several tumour types of uncertain origin, and understand why development does not proceed properly in these cells. For this, we propose to assemble a large collection of datasets at the single-cell resolution for both tumour samples and normal developing tissues. We will then develop the computational tools to analyze and integrate these large datasets. Finally, we will employ these novel strategies to characterize additional samples from patient cohorts. This project aims to address a critical gap in research on childhood cancers. Establishment of experimental models for specific tumour types and improving therapeutic strategies are both challenging because for many tumours, the origins of the tumour are unknown. Through generation and characterization of new datasets from normal tissues and patient samples, we will identify gene expression processes that may be altered in childhood brain tumours, which can provide therapeutic targets. This has the potential for major impact on the understanding and treatment of these cancers.

column36: Un essai clinique randomise et controle, a simple insu, comparant la Therapie Avatar a la Therapie Cognitivo-Comportementale pour les hallucinations auditives verbales chez les patients atteints de schizophrenie
column37: Plusieurs personnes atteintes de schizophrenie entendent des voix qui les persecutent, ce qui nuit a leur fonctionnement. Imaginez-vous essayer de vivre normalement alors que vous entendez des voix que personne d'autre ne semble remarquer: "Tu n'es bon a rien!", "Tu es laid!". Bien qu'il existe des medicaments pouvant aider a diminuer ou a arreter ces hallucinations, ils ne sont pas efficaces sur tout le monde. Malheureusement, il existe peu d'alternatives; en effet, la meilleure therapie qui existe actuellement n'a pas d'effet favorable sur plus de la moitie des patients qui la suivent. Par consequent, notre laboratoire a developpe une nouvelle therapie: la Therapie Avatar. Celle-ci a pour objectif d'aider ces patients a reguler leurs emotions, ce qui permet d'apprendre a mieux vivre avec leurs voix. En plus de diminuer l'impact negatif des hallucinations sur differents aspects de la vie des patients, cette therapie pourrait augmenter leur qualite, et meme diminuer la frequence des episodes hallucinatoires. Le principe est le suivant: le patient est invite a creer un avatar 3D en realite virtuelle et a personnaliser son apparence afin qu'il ressemble le plus possible a la representation qu'il se fait de sa voix la plus derangeante. Ensuite, en immersion, il entre en dialogue avec l'avatar, anime par le therapeute. Le patient sera d'abord confronte au personnage, pour ensuite se reconcilier avec celui-ci et travailler sur son estime de soi. column36: Application d'un protocole de stimulation magnetique transcranienne repetitive theta-burst multisessions dans la gestion de la douleur aigue et la prevention de la douleur chronique chez des patients victimes d'une fracture d'un membre superieur avec ou sans traumatisme craniocerebral leger concomitant.
column37: Le fracture des membres superieurs est la blessure la plus commune en milieu hospitalier. La douleur est le symptome le plus incapacitant a la suite d'une fracture et s'avere souvent le principal facteur retardant la reprise des activites pre-accidentelles, telles que le travail. Les patients avec fracture sont a risque de developper de la douleur chronique lorsque la douleur en phase aigue n'est pas prise en charge de maniere optimale. De plus, la fracture est frequemment accompagnee d'un traumatisme craniocerebral leger (TCCL), amplifiant le niveau de douleur rapporte. Malgre d'importants effets secondaires qui y sont associes, les traitements pharmacologiques conventionnels de la douleur demeurent l'approche preconisee par les professionnels de la sante. Des etudes suggerent que la stimulation magnetique transcranienne repetitive (rTMS) serait une avenue efficace dans la gestion de la douleur chez ce type de patient par son effet analgesique. Cette etude vise a examiner les effets d'un protocole de rTMS sur les marqueurs de recuperation fonctionnelle (douleur, reprise des activites quotidiennes, fonctions motrices et cognitives) chez les patients avec une fracture avec ou sans TCCL concomitant. Nous proposons que le protocole actif aura davantage d'effet sur la recuperation des patients avec fracture et TCCL concomitant, comparativement aux patients avec une fracture ou soumis au protocole controle. Les 80 patients seront recrutes et impliques dans une intervention d'une duree de 10 jours. Aucune etude a ce jour n'a explore la gestion de la douleur chez les patients victimes d'une blessure traumatique par le biais d'approches fondees sur la rTMS. En ciblant quatre obstacles majeurs nuisant a la recuperation suite a un trauma (douleur, detresse psychologique induite par la douleur, alteration des fonctions cognitives et motrices), le protocole rTMS est susceptible de reduire le temps de convalescence, mais egalement les pertes financieres qui l'accompagnent.

column36: Association between the concomitant use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and oral anticoagulants and the risk of major bleeding
column37: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most commonly used type of antidepressant medications in Canada. While these drugs have fewer side effects than other antidepressants, they can cause major bleeding in some people, which requires hospitalization and could be fatal. Patients with heart disease are often treated with oral anticoagulants (i.e. blood thinners), which can also cause major bleeding. Around 20-30% of people living with heart disease may also be diagnosed with depression and may need treatment with both SSRIs and anticoagulants. To date, we have not accurately measured the risk of major bleeding in patients taking both these drugs together. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to measure the risk of major bleeding in patients using SSRIs and anticoagulants together and compare it to those using anticoagulants only. We expect that this risk will be substantially higher in patients jointly using both medications. Furthermore, we will be studying novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs), a new group of anticoagulants that, unlike the older types, do not require regular blood test monitoring. To perform this study, we will use a database that has personal and medical information from over 15 million patients in the U.K. who visited a general practitioner. This data reflects the Canadian population well, since U.K. patients are similar when it comes to their patterns of SSRI and anticoagulant use. Also, we expect our results to be relevant to the general population, since the data is collected from real-life practices. Major bleeding is a severe and potentially fatal health issue. The findings of this study will be crucial for patients with heart disease who may need antidepressants and the doctors who are managing their care. In addition, NOACs are more convenient for patients than older anticoagulants. However, since we know very little about the safety of using NOACs and SSRIs together, this study will provide much needed evidence.

column36: Predicteurs precoces de l'evolution des difficultes d'anomie entre les phases precoce et chronique chez les aphasiques post-stroke
column37: L'aphasie post-stroke est un trouble du langage survenant a la suite d'un accident vasculaire cerebral. Le present projet de recherche vise a mieux comprendre les predicteurs precoces de la recuperation du langage chez les personnes atteintes d'aphasie post-stroke. Plus specifiquement, nous nous interessons a la mesure dans laquelle l'etendue des dommages qui touchent la matiere blanche du cerveau dans les jours qui suivent l'accident vasculaire cerebral permet de predire l'amelioration des difficultes d'anomie dans le temps. L'anomie, aussi appelee manque du mot, est un symptome tres frequent et handicapant observe chez les personnes atteintes d'aphasie post-stroke. Concretement, ces difficultes sont associees a une moins bonne qualite de vie, une perte d'autonomie et a plusieurs consequences psychosociales nefastes chez les personnes atteintes. Par ailleurs, l'age avance represente le principal facteur de risque pour la survenue d'un accident vasculaire cerebral. Ainsi, dans le contexte actuel du vieillissement de la population, on peut s'attendre a ce que les cas d'aphasie post-stroke soient de plus en plus frequents. Pour cette raison, mieux comprendre les facteurs qui permettent de predire la recuperation du langage a la suite d'un accident vasculaire cerebral devient un enjeu central afin d'ameliorer la prise en charge d'un nombre croissant de Canadiens. Entre autres, les avancees scientifiques dans ce domaine peuvent aider a mieux orienter les priorites de rehabilitation chez les patients atteints d'aphasie post-stroke et ce, dans les premiers jours suivants l'accident vasculaire cerebral.

column36: Organizational capacity needed by hospitals to optimize approaches and impacts of patient engagement in planning and improvement: a multi-method investigation
column37: Today, hospitals struggle to manage rising costs while at the same time improve the quality and efficiency of health care. Hospitals have implemented interventions for quality improvement that target clinicians and organizational processes. However, these interventions have shown to have low impact. On the other hand, some research has found that engaging patients in healthcare activities such as strategic planning and evaluation can have a moderate to high impact on care quality. Patient engagement (PE) has been used widely by hospitals around the world, and it has shown to improve clinician accountability, organizational performance, and relationships between patients and healthcare professionals. However, without organizational support, PE can be tokenistic, leading to poor experiences for patients and hospital staff involved in those efforts, and little or no service improvement. These barriers may prevent hospitals from realizing the potential beneficial outcomes associated with PE. The goal of this research is to identify which elements of organizational capacity for PE leads to health service improvement in hospitals and why. This investigation will map the impact of different organizational capacity elements to health service improvement through a systematic review of the literature on how hospital capacity influences PE methods and impacts, and a secondary analysis of survey data on different organizational capacity elements available in Ontario hospitals to support PE in planning and improvement activities. This investigation will then conduct interviews with patients, clinicians, and managers about the strategies they have used to strengthen organizational capacity for PE in different planning and improvement activities. The findings of this research will support patients and healthcare professionals to prioritize, evaluate, and improve PE in hospitals. This research may also aid hospitals to better fulfill the PE requirements of Accreditation Canada.

column36: Investigating the Effect of Hypoxia and Aryl Hydrocarbon Signalling on the Immune Response to Pancreatic Cancer
column37: The 5-year survival rate for pancreatic cancer is among the lowest of any cancer type and patients are resistant to most therapies. Interestingly, pancreatic cancer is characterized by a significant amount of immune cells infiltrating the tumour. This is encouraging since immune cells play a crucial role in fighting cancer. However, pancreatic cancer is able to subvert the immune response, resulting in a large population of macrophages (a specific type of immune cell) suppressing the good immune response. Macrophages are not always suppressive and they integrate many signals from their environment to decide between a suppressive state, which helps the cancer persist, and an inflammatory state, which is favourable for clearing tumours. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signalling plays a crucial role in determining which state a macrophage will take. Our lab has shown that AhR signalling is essential for the suppressive macrophage function that is undesirable in cancer. Thus, blocking AhR may relieve macrophage-driven suppression of the immune system and improve anti-tumour immune activity. Preliminary data supports this idea. However, macrophage signalling is complex; AhR signalling is closely intertwined with hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) signalling. HIF is relevant because it can also determine which state a macrophage will take, and importantly, HIF is also active in pancreatic cancer due to the low levels of oxygen (hypoxia) in the tumour. How AhR and HIF interact in pancreatic cancer is not known, but crucial to understanding the immune response to the disease. We aim to reveal the different roles hypoxia, HIF, and AhR play in polarizing macrophages towards either a positive inflammatory or negative suppressive state in pancreatic cancer. Being able to reprogram macrophages from one state to the other by drugging AhR and HIF will be useful not only in the treatment of cancer, but other diseases characterized by hypoxia, such as inflammatory bowel disease.

column36: Ephb4 signaling in pulmonary fibrosis development
column37: The wound healing response is a critical function for nearly all tissues and organs in the human body. When wound healing occurs, there is the formation of scar tissue which aids in wound closure and allows for the gradual recovery within the injured tissue. However, there are diseases in which wound healing and scar formation occurs in healthy tissue, which leads to the turnover of functional tissue into nonfunctional scar. In vital organs such as the lungs, scar formation can lead to death from loss of respiratory function. Lung scarring or lung fibrosis is a deadly outcome for multiple diseases, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and systemic sclerosis. Lung fibrosis is deadly, and a patient diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has a life expectancy of about 5 years. Further, treatment for lung fibrosis is severely limited, only slowing disease progression without capability of reversing scar formation. We have recently identified that a protein, ephB4, appears to play a significant role in lung fibrosis. We found that deletion of ephB4 was able to markedly protect against the development of lung fibrosis in mice. We aim to understand how ephB4 participates in lung fibrosis, in hopes of identifying a potential therapeutic mechanism of action for future drug development.

column36: Efficacy of a memory-reframing intervention for post-surgical pain in youth
column37: Millions of children undergo surgery every year, which places 22% of them at risk of developing chronic post-surgical pain. How children remember pain strongly predicts how they handle future pain experiences. Negatively-biased pain memories (e.g., remembering more pain as compared to initial/earlier reports) lead to worse future pain and have been shown to underlie the development of chronic post-surgical pain. Children's memories for pain can be reframed to be less negatively-biased to reduce the harmful effects of memories on future pain outcomes. Memory-reframing interventions can reduce negative biases in children's pain memories and pain at future needle procedures. However, these interventions have not been used in the context of post-surgical pain which, unlike needles, can lead to chronic pain. Moreover, previous memory-reframing interventions did not include parents, who are powerful agents of change in the context of children's pain experiences. Our recent research revealed that how parents and children talk about past painful experiences influences how children remember pain. Specifically, parents who reminisced with children in an elaborative way using emotion words had children who remembered past post-surgical pain in a less negatively-biased way. Drawing from existing and our emerging research on memory-reframing techniques and parent-child reminiscing, as well as feedback from parents and youth undergoing surgery, the proposed study will be the first to examine a parent-led memory-reframing intervention aimed at positively altering children's recall of post-surgical pain and preventing pain from becoming chronic. We will teach children and parents to talk in the most adaptive ways about their past surgery, which we hypothesize will lead to less negatively-biased pain memories. In doing so, this study will inform new pain management techniques that hold potential for preventing pediatric chronic pain, a rising child health epidemic.

column36: The BE-WEL in CR-AF Study: A BEhavioural WEight Loss INtervention delivered in Cardiac Rehabilitation for patients with Atrial Fibrillation and obesity
column37: One-in-four Canadians will be diagnosed with an abnormal heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation (AF) in their lifetime. People with AF have an increased chance of having serious medical problems like stroke and heart failure. Almost three-in-four people with AF also have obesity (excess body weight). According to research, people with obesity that lose approximately 10% of their body weight can experience relief from uncomfortable AF symptoms. Losing weight may even help people return to a normal heart rhythm. Cardiac rehabilitation is a proven way to help people with heart disease live longer, healthier lives. So far, research has not shown whether cardiac rehabilitation helps to improve the abnormal heart rhythms seen in AF. This may be because cardiac rehabilitation programs usually do not offer specific help with weight management. Behavioural weight-loss treatment (BWLT; group classes to change thoughts and behaviours such as eating and exercise habits to encourage weight-loss) has been shown to help people with obesity lose weight, and keep it off for up to two years. Therefore, adding BWLT to cardiac rehabilitation programs may help people with AF and obesity experience relief from their symptoms. This study will test whether people who receive BWLT during cardiac rehabilitation can lose weight and improve their AF symptoms. People who have AF and obesity will either attend a traditional cardiac rehabilitation program (12-weeks of exercise and medical help with reducing heart disease risk factors), or a cardiac rehabilitation program with added BWLT. We will then compare the two groups to see if people who received BWLT lost more weight and had greater improvement in AF symptoms compared to the traditional cardiac rehabilitation group. We believe this research will help efforts to provide effective treatment to patients with AF and obesity to help them lose weight and reduce or eliminate AF symptoms.

column36: The Role of Parenting Behaviours in the Intergenerational Transmission of Risk for Chronic Pain
column37: Chronic pain (pain lasting 3 months or more) is highly prevalent and costly. It affects 20-25% of Canadians, severely impacts individuals and their families, and costs society an estimated $7.2 billion per year. It is well-established that chronic pain tends to run in families, such that children of parents with (vs. without) chronic pain are at increased risk for developing their own chronic pain. New research suggests that parents transmit risk for chronic pain to their children. How this risk is transmitted is not well understood. The behaviour of mothers with chronic pain, specifically the consistency of their parenting, may play an important role. Indeed, research with community samples has shown that inconsistent parenting negatively impacts children's mental and physical health. While inconsistent parenting has yet to be examined in the context of maternal chronic pain, mothers with chronic pain may be particularly likely to be inconsistent in their parenting due to fluctuations in their pain, disability, and distress. This study will be the first to examine the role of inconsistent parenting behaviours in the transmission of risk for chronic pain from mother to child. Mothers with and without chronic pain and their children (aged 8-15) will participate. Mothers will complete questionnaires that assess their pain. Children will complete questionnaires that assess their pain and their mother's parenting behaviours (specifically her warmth, discipline, and responsiveness to distress). This study will examine (1) the difference between mothers with chronic pain and mothers without chronic pain on consistency of parenting behaviours and (2) the relation between inconsistent parenting behaviours and child pain. The results will improve our understanding of how risk for chronic pain is transmitted from mother to child and inform the development of interventions to prevent the continuation of chronic pain across generations.

column36: Does family history of type 2 diabetes influence fat oxidation and the source of oxidized fat during exercise in aging women?
column37: Aging and family history of diabetes are recognized as risk factors for type 2 diabetes. The accumulation of fat within the muscle and the inability to sufficiently utilize this fat source are amongst the proposed mechanisms to explain this increased risk. A potent intervention to prevent type 2 diabetes in various populations is aerobic exercise. However, individuals with a family history of diabetes are known to have reduced fat oxidation at rest and during submaximal exercise. Furthermore, recent results from our research group suggest that a greater proportion of fat-derived energy would be drawn from the blood at the expense of fat stored in the muscles. Together, these metabolic alterations could potentially limit the exercise-induced benefits on type 2 diabetes prevention. Our recent observations were however drawn from indirect methods and we thus wish to confirm our results with a more appropriate study design. Our objectives are to verify if : 1) Aging women with a family history of type2 diabetes utilize less fat stored in the muscle relative to fat in blood circulation, compared with aging women without a family history of diabetes. 2) To determine the exercise intensity at which the utilization of fat stored in the muscle is at its peak. Studies investigating exercise metabolism in individuals with family history fo type 2 diabetes are scarce and, to the best of or knowledge, inexistent in an aging population. Our study would thus be the first to investigate how different sources of fat are used during exercise in a population at high risk for type 2 diabetes. Results from this study will guide us in a future project assessing the impact of different exercise modalities on fat oxidation and their impact on glycemic control.

column36: Outlining the transition to precision performance feedback
column37: Feedback is an important part of learning and maintaining people's performance in healthcare. Data from electronic health records is increasingly being used to provide performance data to physicians through a process known as audit and feedback. In an audit and feedback process, an individual physician's performance is measured and then compared to professional standards or targets ("audited") and the results of this comparison are then fed back to the individual. Although the aim of audit and feedback is to encourage individuals to better follow professional practice standards, the effect of audit and feedback on professional behaviour and on patient outcomes ranges from little to no effect to a substantial effect. We are interested in understanding why there can be such variability in the effect of audit and feedback and whether there are ways to improve it. "How" the audited information is fed back to individuals has not been well studied. Research in other areas suggests that giving feedback can be influenced by many factors: how the feedback is provided, who is providing it, what the feedback relates to, and how specific it is. Our starting assumption is that feedback should not simply involve providing verbal or written information to practitioners but must involve a conversation that allows recipients to process and interpret the information and to formulate ways of improving their performance. We have called this feedback conversation "precision feedback" because it is targeted toward individual recipients in particular contexts. We are researching the role of precision feedback in physician performance improvement in the hopes that we can develop better strategies for audit and feedback that will have more consistently substantial effects on physician professional behaviour and patient outcomes.

column36: Three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound guidance for gynecologic high-dose-rate intracavitary/interstitial brachytherapy
column37: Brachytherapy is a radiation therapy technique that involves placing radioactive sources inside the body to deliver radiation dose to cancer. For gynecologic cancers, brachytherapy is the standard-of-care for advanced or recurrent cases since it has shown improved tumour control and reduced patient toxicities. For gynecologic intracavitary brachytherapy (ICBT), radioactive seeds are passed through channels within an inserted vaginal applicator to deliver radiation to the diseased area. At the Tom Baker Cancer Centre (TBCC, Calgary, AB), the patient receives a computed tomography (CT) scan then is transported to the brachytherapy suite for treatment. Though CT is required for treatment planning, this workflow is suboptimal since it introduces patient internal motion and applicator motion during patient transport (leading to increased treatment uncertainties), contributes significant end-to-end treatment time, and involves ionizing radiation. Interstitial brachytherapy (ISBT) is a different technique where needles are inserted directly into the patient using a rigid template. At TBCC, the needle insertion process is guided with conventional two dimensional ultrasound using a hand-held probe. This procedure is prone to needle clustering and organ perforation (such as the bladder), which may be avoided with more advanced imaging techniques. We intend to improve the quality of gynecologic brachytherapy treatments by incorporating transvaginal three dimensional ultrasound (3DUS) into the clinical workflow. Our collaborators at the University of Western Ontario have developed a 3DUS system that uses a custom stabilization system and cradle for 360-degree rotation of a conventional transvaginal ultrasound probe. We aim to show 3DUS can completely replace CT in the ICBT clinical workflow, saving time while avoiding imaging dose and patient motion. Also, we believe 3DUS guidance in ISBT will improve needle implant quality while reducing the risk of organ perforation.

column36: Treating chronic pain with pepducins derived from neurotensin receptor type 1 (NTS1)
column37: The treatment of chronic pain is an incredibly important medical issue. Nearly 20% of adults suffer from chronic pain on a daily basis, and unfortunately, most of the treatments available are not effective. Our team is now working on a novel strategy in pain relief called pepducins. Pepducins are small proteins that are designed to interact with receptors in a unique way. Rather than simply fitting into a receptor, like a key into a lock, they imbed themselves in the cell membrane, flip towards the inside of the cell, and interact with the receptor there, modifying the signals that it is sending. Although pepducins have been developed to tackle different diseases, they have not been studied much in the context of pain. This is precisely the aim of our project, and so, our team designed pepducins targeting a receptor involved in pain perception. column36: RecoverED: Centering the voices of those with lived experience when working towards a consensus definition of eating disorder recovery
column37: Eating disorders (EDs), mental illnesses characterized by abnormal eating habits, are associated with negative consequences, including risk of death. While most people agree that "recovery" is the goal of treatment, there is debate about what constitutes recovery. Researchers and clinicians suggest that recovery is defined by improvement in ED symptoms, such as more normal eating. Conversely, people with lived experience argue that recovery involves more than just improvements in ED symptoms, highlighting the importance of psychological growth. The goal of this project is to examine whether it is possible to develop a definition of recovery that comprises aspects deemed important by researchers, clinicians, and individuals with lived experience. Data will be collected in three waves. First, individuals with lived ED experience will be asked about their perceptions of recovery in a video interview. Qualitative data gathered from these interviews will be used to generate a tentative definition of recovery. In Wave 2, individuals with an ED history will be asked to complete quantitative measures online. Responses to these questionnaires will be used to test the definition generated in Wave 1. Finally, individuals with lived experience will be asked about the appropriateness of the proposed definition using open ended and forced response questions, in order to understand whether these individuals view this definition as having merit in healthcare settings. Findings from the three waves will be integrated to examine the feasibility and appropriateness of developing a definition of recovery from the perspective of those with lived experience, with the long-term goal of informing treatment. Whereas ED treatment in Canada is limited, costly, and often ineffective, integrating and communicating an understanding of recovery from the perspective of those with lived experience may instill hope and promote treatment adherence, thereby improving outcomes for Canadians with EDs.

column36: The Psychosocial Impact of Scars in Pediatric Patients Undergoing Scar-Directed Therapy
column37: Every scar tells a story. Beyond being just a permanent skin mark, a scar can influence quality of life, and alter a person's view of themselves. However, healthcare providers often only assess a scar's physical features and functional consequences - asking only if a patient's scar is tight, itchy, or painful; not if a patient is embarrassed, upset, or unhappy with their scar. In children particularly, without probing, such feelings may go unrecognized and therefore unaddressed. In fact, the psychosocial impact of scars, and a scar's effect on body image have not been investigated. Thus, with clinicians largely blind to the mental and emotional aspects of scars, scar patients are inadvertently denied holistic care. This proposal aims to rectify this knowledge gap to catalyze clinical change. This project measures the psychosocial impact of scars in children, determines factors affecting body image in children with scars, and evaluates the effect of scar therapy on body image and a scar's psychosocial imprint. Psychosocial impact is measured with the SCAR-Q - a new patient-reported outcome measure developed by our group to capture the patient perspective of scars. Body image is measured by the Body Esteem Scale for Adolescents & Adults (BESAA). Consented children with scars at The Hospital for Sick Children complete the SCAR-Q and BESAA before and after scar treatment (surgery, laser, compression) to uncover the psychosocial burden of scars, their body image, and the influence of scar therapy on these factors. Characterizing the psychosocial significance of scarring and identifying its relevance to the health status of people with scars, will inform clinical practice. Specifically, the need for evaluating the psychosocial scar, alongside the physical scar would be emphasized. Ultimately, by understanding the mental, emotional, and social weight of scars, healthcare providers may better deliver patient-centred care to improve the overall health of those with scars.

column36: Predicting health outcomes from hematopoietic evolution in large population cohorts
column37: Cancer and cardiovascular disease (CVD) are on the rise with the vast majority of disease occurring in low and middle income countries. Personalized medicine is emerging as a valuable approach to diagnose cancer and CVD at early stages when treatments are more likely to be associated with improved health outcomes. However, the vast majority of personalized medicine approaches are developed on a subset of the population and have limited utility in different ethnic groups and environmental contexts. Further, tools which do exist are impractical to implement in developing contexts. To address this, I will develop a non-invasive liquid biopsy-based approach to detect likelihood of progression to hematological cancers and CVD across a range of ethnic groups and environmental contexts using blood collected years prior to the diagnosis of disease. This work builds off recent studies which have linked the age-related mutation accumulation in blood to both diseases. While common in the healthy aging population, these mutations have been associated with subsequent cancer and CVD development. There is a clear need to understand the biology and develop biomarkers and tools that can distinguish benign and malignant patterns of mutation accumulation. To do so, I will capture and characterize the early evolutionary profiles of the mature blood cell pool in order to uncover the events causing an individual to shift from healthy to disease state. Through improving our understanding of early disease evolution, we will enable earlier diagnoses and identify novel therapeutic targets to prevent progression to disease. This study combines state-of-the-art machine learning techniques with classic population genetics to trace the evolution of disease in the aging blood cell pool. Our models will allow for clinical implementation and will lay the foundation for preventative medicine approaches for cancer and CVD in both Canadian and African contexts and improve health outcomes globally.
