column36: The role of gut-derived serotonin in intestinal fat absorption and chylomicron production.
column37: Type II diabetes is a major risk factor for heart disease and has been increasing at an alarming rate in both children and adults. The intestine plays an important role in absorbing dietary fat and packaging this fat into particles called chylomicrons for transport to other organs in the body. Chylomicrons become smaller chylomicrons remnants in the bloodstream and these particles contribute to the development of atherosclerosis and are associated with increased risk for heart disease. In diabetes the intestine overproduces these particles leading to the accumulation of pathogenic chylomicron remnants. We have identified important hormones produced by the intestine that can regulate dietary fat uptake. My research is focused on how dietary fat absorption and generation of chylomicrons by the intestine is regulated by the hormone serotonin, a hormone produced in the gut and in the brain. Using animal models, I aim to elucidate how serotonin will impact dietary fat absorption and chylomicron production. I will do this by administering serotonin to animals and determine if this increases or decreases fat absorption and chylomicron production. I will also administer a drug that prevents serotonin production to determine how the loss of serotonin impacts fat absorption and chylomicron production. Our preliminary results indicate that serotonin increases fat absorption and chylomicron production while preventing serotonin production produces the opposite effect. My next aim is to determine if serotonin plays a role in diabetic states where chylomicrons are overproduced. To do this, I will feed animals a high-fat/high-fructose diet which we have previously shown to induce diabetes. I will then determine how preventing serotonin production in these animals impacts chylomicron formation. This study will give us insight into how serotonin affects fat absorption and chylomicron production in order to find new therapeutic targets for diabetes and heart disease.

column36: Role of the sympathetic nervous system in mediating exaggerated blood pressure responses to exercise
column37: During exercise, blood pressure increases in order to supply muscle with an adequate supply of oxygen. However in some individuals, these increases in blood pressure are exaggerated, which has been shown to increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease. Currently, it is unknown if the sympathetic nervous system plays a role in causing this exaggerated blood pressure response. Therefore, this proposed research aims to measure sympathetic nerve activity during exercise in people with an exaggerated blood pressure response to exercise. Three groups (15 participants per group) will be recruited for this study: 1) participants with a normal resting blood pressure, but an exaggerated blood pressure response to exercise, 2) participants with both a normal resting and exercise blood pressure, and 3) participants with high resting blood pressure (hypertension). All participants will perform two different types of exercise, including cycling exercise and handgrip exercise. Cycling exercise and handgrip exercise will be performed in random order and separated by 15 minutes of rest. Before and during both exercise trials, sympathetic nerve activity will be directly recorded from the nerve in the upper arm using a technique called microneurography, and blood pressure and heart rate will be continuously measured. Lastly, changes in blood flow to the kidneys will also be indirectly measured using ultrasound.

column36: Exploiting natural products and their derivatives to identify novel antifungal strategies against human fungal pathogens
column37: Invasive fungal infections cause significant morbidity and mortality in vulnerable populations, especially individuals with weakened immune systems. The leading human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans, is one of the most frequently found hospital-borne infections and is rapidly becoming resistant to both first- and second-line antifungals. Furthermore, the number of clinically useful antifungal medications is limited due to toxic side effects and inadequate effectiveness. Current antifungals available in the clinic are limited to only three classes, all of which are vulnerable to resistance. A promising strategy to combat emerging drug-resistant fungi is through combination therapy, as combining drugs has the potential to increase drug effectiveness and can slow the evolution of drug resistance. The goal of my project is to identify and characterize antifungals that engage with new drug targets and enhance the effectiveness of the existing antifungals. To accomplish this, I screened ~20,000 chemicals for activity in the absence and presence of the azole antifungal, fluconazole, against C. albicans. To select compounds with favorable antifungal properties, I assessed each hit compounds' mammalian toxicity, activity against drug resistant isolates, and spectrum of activity across human fungal pathogens. Using this pipeline, I have prioritized one broad-spectrum compound that we discovered targets fatty acid synthesis, a key component of fungal membranes, and one azole-enhancing compound that induces cellular stress by modulating lipid homeostasis. Future experiments will include performing biochemical assays to verify drug mode-of-action. I will also investigate the effect of inhibiting these biological processes on fungal virulence traits and determining the therapeutic potential of these molecules. Overall, this research is poised to unveil novel antifungal targets and expand our knowledge of drug resistance to ultimately treat life-threatening fungal infections.

column36: Examining Mechanisms and Motives Driving Cannabis Use in Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder Features
column37: Drug use in individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD) represents a considerable health concern for Canadians. BPD is characterized by impulsivity, rapidly shifting emotions, and suicidal behaviour. Cannabis is frequently used among those with BPD, and is associated with greater symptom severity. Research suggests cannabis use is linked to difficulties regulating emotions and changes in emotional reactivity. Emotion dysregulation, a core feature of BPD, has been linked to motivation to use marijuana as a coping mechanism. It is likely that impulsive, emotionally dysregulated individuals with BPD use cannabis to avoid distressing emotions in place of more adaptive strategies, while also intensifying BPD symptoms. Given the increasing global burdens of problem cannabis use, understanding the relationships between cannabis use and BPD symptoms are of particular importance. This study seeks to explore the relationships between BPD symptoms, cannabis use, and emotion dysregulation, in 1) an adult community sample currently experiencing BPD symptoms and 2) a treatment seeking sample of college students reporting emotion dysregulation. Assessments will include diagnostic interviews for BPD, an evaluation of substance use severity, and questionnaires on BPD symptoms, motives for cannabis use, and emotion dysregulation. Biological measures of emotion sensitivity will also be used. Recruitment will be achieved through the use of an existing BPD research registry at the University of Toronto Scarborough, online advertisements, and flyers. It is expected that greater BPD symptom severity will predict more frequent cannabis use, and that this relationship will be driven by high emotion dysregulation. It is also expected cannabis use will be associated with blunted emotional sensitivity. These results will likely clarify consequences of cannabis use among individuals with BPD, and potentially identify skill deficits contributing to maladaptive substance use.

column36: The development of effective TNBC treatment through the co-inhibition of SCD1 and NF-kB pathways
column37: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive form of breast cancer, accounting for the majority of breast cancer related deaths. Chemotherapy remains the primary treatment option for patients with TNBC but leads to the enrichment of a subpopulation of cells with tumor initiating capacities called cancer stem cells (CSCs). Breast CSCs are responsible for chemotherapy resistance, metastasis and recurrence. Previous research has shown that lipid metabolism, specifically the enzyme stearoyl-CoA-desaturase (SCD1) is involved in the maintenance of CSCs. However, the inhibition of SCD1 alone is not effective as it is controlled by another signalling pathway known as the NF-kB pathway, which is also crucial for CSC survival. In this proposed work, I will show the need to inhibit both signalling pathways, SCD1 and NF-kB, as they activate each other and contribute to CSC survival and enrichment. I will use a clinically translatable and accurate tumor model where tumors extracted from actual patients will be implanted in mice to test the treatment success. In this way, I will accurately investigate the effect of the CSC pathway inhibition on reversing chemotherapy resistance and increasing treatment efficiency in TNBC. Our research is geared towards improving population health as it aims to combat this aggressive form of breast cancer by developing a therapeutic strategy to be used in the clinic while improving our understanding of breast cancer resistance.

column37: Epilepsy is a brain disorder characterized by frequent and recurrent seizures and affects approximately 1 in 50 children. Nearly one-third of patients with epilepsy do not respond to medical treatments, suffering from the medical and psychosocial burden of illness and consuming 80% of epilepsy-related health expenditures, highlighting the urgent need for the development of novel treatment strategies. During sleep, a slower pattern of brain rhythms emerges, and epileptic events become more pronounced. An intelligent algorithm that continuously monitors endogenous brain rhythms will deliver time-locked auditory stimulation to enhance the underlying slow waves. My project will be to develop and test the effect of closed-loop auditory stimulation during sleep and we hypothesize that it will result in the enhancement of cortical slow waves and (1) suppress epileptic discharges during sleep; and (2) improve overnight sleep-related memory consolidation, which is a significant comorbidity of epilepsy. My project brings together unique expertise in neurology, sleep medicine, neurosurgery, and biomedical engineering. It will be performed in the epilepsy monitoring unit at the Hospital for Sick Children, which houses Canada's largest comprehensive epilepsy surgery program for children. This work is enabled by new knowledge linking brain rhythms during sleep to the modulation of cortical excitability and vulnerability epileptic activity. It also builds on recent studies that found enhancement of slow wave activity during deep sleep using acoustic stimuli precisely timed to the brain's intrinsic rhythms improves memory function in healthy adults. My project represents an innovative paradigm shift in the treatment of epilepsy using non-invasive, intelligent and responsive neurostimulation. The results of this work are expected to yield novel treatments for an extremely vulnerable patient population with few therapeutic options.

column36: Modelling the developmental origins of human sonic hedgehog medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most frequently occurring malignant pediatric tumour, which usually arises in an area of the brain called the cerebellum. A large subset of MBs are driven by mutations that activate the sonic hedgehog (SHH) signalling pathway, a molecular circuit that regulates cell proliferation in the cerebellum and other organs. In genetically modified mouse models of SHH MB, the uncontrolled proliferation of a specific type of cerebellar neural precursor cell initiates tumour growth. It is unknown if this occurs in the human cancer, because human cerebellar development is poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, I am developing a model system to study human cerebellar development by differentiating human stem cells to cerebellar neurons and extensively characterizing intermediate cell populations that arise along this developmental arc. Using this system, I will activate the SHH pathway at specific points of differentiation, and transplant these activated cells into the mouse cerebellum to understand at which point of development cells are most vulnerable to cancerous transformation and why. The results of these experiments will further our knowledge of the developmental origins of human SHH MB, paving the way for the design of more effective detection and treatment strategies for SHH MB patients.

column36: Dopaminergic neuronal activity in the glioblastoma niche
column37: Brain cancer is a nasty disease and virtually all patients die within two years of developing its most aggressive tumour called glioblastoma. Surprisingly, despite decades of research into the nature of these tumours, we have largely overlooked the influence of their home: the brain. If we hope to intervene, we desperately need to understand how glioblastoma's home is nurturing its deviant growth. Therefore, I propose investigating a prime suspect of this bad influence: a brain chemical called dopamine. We now know that new glioblastoma treatments may only work if they target the cancer's stem cells. Early evidence suggests that these cells may exploit the brain's dopamine to grow the brain tumour. To provide novel therapeutic insights, I intend to figure out if this is the case. I will first investigate how these isolated stem cells (derived from human glioblastoma tumours) respond to precise dopamine-related manipulations. Then, adhering to Canada's animal care guidelines, I will move my studies into genetically-altered mice. These alterations will enable me to inject human glioblastoma stem cells into the mouse's brain and control dopamine release from its neurons using light. By repeatedly causing or inhibiting the release of dopamine into the human cells' surrounding environment, or inducing degeneration of dopamine-releasing neurons, I can unravel how dopamine inherently changes the growth of glioblastoma in the brain. Dopamine helps us think, feel pleasure, and move our limbs. So it makes sense that unusual levels of dopamine in the brain is linked to disorders like schizophrenia, addiction, and Parkinson's disease. Today, many successful dopamine-modifying drugs are approved to treat those disorders. If my theory is supported by my findings, drugs that decrease the brain's dopamine levels will weaken the growth of glioblastoma, thus enabling us to redirect these drugs and provide patients with new treatments to tackle the deadliest of all brain cancers.

column36: Investigating the roles of cell clearance and phagocytosis in planarian regeneration
column37: Tissue injury results in a buildup of dead and dying cells that must be cleared away before regeneration can occur. In humans, this process doesn't always happen perfectly, causing regeneration to fail. The planarian, a freshwater flatworm, doesn't have this problem: the worm can regenerate all of its tissues, even growing back its entire head, and always clears away dead cells perfectly. My research aims to answer the questions of how the planarian deals with all of its dying cells, and of whether this process is key to the planarian's amazing regeneration. In humans, immune cells called phagocytes eat the cell corpses and digest them. In planarians, I have identified a population of cells that might be phagocytes; I hope to find out if these cells are also responsible for eating dying cells. I plan to use a gene knockdown strategy known as RNAi to get rid of this cell population, and then determine whether the planarian is still capable of regenerating without these cells. These experiments will show if the planarian is better than humans at clearing away dead cells by phagocytosis, or if they use an entirely different mechanism to facilitate their regeneration. Ultimately, finding the answers to these questions will help in the development of new regenerative treatments for human patients.

column36: Investigating the role of recurrent hotspot mutations in U1 spliceosomal small nuclear RNA in medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour that affects children in Canada. Due to the location of the tumour within the brain and a propensity to spread throughout the nervous system, outcomes for children with medulloblastoma remain dismal. DNA encodes the complete instructions for how a cell functions, and these instructions are converted into RNA blueprints. From the RNA blueprints, a cell can make functional proteins, which are the building blocks of the cell. Cancers, such as medulloblastoma, result from mutations in the DNA of our cells that either affect the RNA blueprint or the functional proteins, and cause cells to grow uncontrollably. Recently, we discovered a novel set of mutations in medulloblastoma that arise from a single letter "typo". These mutations affect the way cells process the instructions from DNA, resulting in the creation of several new versions of the RNA blueprints and drastically changing how the cell behaves. With my project, I aim to understand exactly how these new mutations are driving the growth of medulloblastoma tumours. In particular, I will be investigating how the mutation transforms our normal brain cells into cancerous cells. Next, I will use our understanding of the changes in the RNA blueprints to develop targeted drugs against medulloblastoma. I will use three drugs which have been tested for other cancers with similar mutations, to determine their effect on medulloblastoma. Finally, I will examine whether the new versions of RNA blueprints can create novel proteins that do not exist elsewhere. Harnessing this information, I will generate drugs that specifically target cancer cells, but do not harm the normal brain cells. As a CIHR Canada Graduate Scholar, I will have the funding and support I need to identify and develop targeted therapies for medulloblastoma in hopes of treating this incurable disease.

column36: Health care utilization among adult survivors of childhood and adolescent cancer in Ontario
column37: With modern cancer therapies, most children and teenagers diagnosed with cancer will become long-term survivors. Unfortunately, the treatments used to cure the cancer can also cause long-term health problems years or decades later, called "late-effects". These include new cancers, heart disease, and poor psychosocial health. In fact, 3 out of 4 childhood cancer survivors will develop a chronic health condition by thirty years after their diagnosis. It is critical that all survivors of childhood cancer receive life-long risk-adapted medical care that optimizes the prevention, detection and treatment of late-effects. To address this need, the Ontario government funds a network of five specialized clinics for survivors of childhood cancer. The goals of our study are to examine the impact of these clinics on health care use among adult survivors of childhood or adolescent cancer, and to evaluate if specialized survivor clinics are cost-effective from a health care system perspective. To achieve our research goals, we will use Ontario's provincial pediatric cancer registry which contains information on demographic, diagnostic and treatment data from over 14,000 children and teenagers treated for cancer in the province since 1985. We will link patients in the cancer registry to a series of health care administration databases. We will determine their use of specialized survivors clinics and evaluate the relationship between clinic attendance with other healthcare use. These include rate of emergency department visits and hospitalizations, length of hospital stays, number of primary care and specialist visits, surgeries and outpatient imaging and laboratory tests. Findings from this research will measure the burden of late-effects on the health care system and examine the impact of specialized survivor clinics on health care use by survivors. Results will help the planning and distribution of resources to optimize care for this growing population of young Canadians.

column36: Investigating the role of oral bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum in human colorectal cancer
column37: In Canada, colorectal cancer (CRC) is among the commonly diagnosed cancers, and a leading cause of cancer-associated death. Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) is a pathogenic bacterium linked to CRC, but its exact pathogenesis remains elusive. Fn is commonly found in the human mouth, but it has been detected in various other body sites in cases of disease, such as in CRC. Colonic presence of Fn is associated with poorer cancer survival rates. Unfortunately, not all Fn strains are virulent, which prevents using Fn presence as a diagnostic tool. Colonic Fn infections may result from the bacterium-known to breach and invade human cells-crossing layers of human tissue to reach the bloodstream. Although there have been several studies of this infection route and CRC development in mouse models, the relevance to human disease is not clear. We have analyzed how an invasive strain of Fn, strain 7/1, adapts by changing its gene expression as it invades a human cancerous colonic cell line, Caco-2, as well as the Caco-2 cell's response to invasion by Fn 7/1. The goal of this research is to extend the previous work using CRC-derived Fn strains, and noncancerous gingival, vascular and colonic cells derived from both human and mouse sources. This is important because it will a) indicate relevance of the mouse model to human Fn infection; and b) detect host and pathogen genes consistently expressed during infection, which will become future targets for interventions and potentially biomarkers for CRC risk and/or complications. Future goals for this project include analyzing the role of Fn in multi-bacterial infection of human colonic cells. Additionally, the potential interactions between Fn and other cancer-promoting bacteria and a healthy gut microbial community will be examined using a bioreactor model of the human colon. This research is supported through an Innovation to Impact grant from the Canadian Cancer Society, and the Grant Challenge initiative through Cancer Research UK.

column36: Understanding Allergic Diseases: Insights from patients with monogenic primary atopic disorders
column37: Studying patients with disruptions in the immune system is one way of understanding how the human immune system works. Our lab studies patients with disrupted immune systems caused by single gene mutations. A genetic mutation is an alteration of a gene that changes the message carried by the gene (for example, the words quiz and quit only differ by one letter but have entirely different meanings). In this proposal we have identified three patients with severe allergic disease and abnormal immune function that we suspect is due to unique genetic mutations. These patients have alterations in two genes, STAT6 (2 patients) and OSMR (1 patient), previously reported to be have roles in allergy-like conditions. However, the exact alterations we see in these genes have never been reported before. This makes it hard for us to predict whether the messages carried out by these genes have changed. Therefore, for each case, I will investigate whether the messages carried out by the gene of interest have changed. I will do this by comparing patient cells with cells from healthy people. If indeed the patient's cells display allergy-like abnormalities, then it is likely that the identified mutations are disease-causing. This knowledge will help in better treatment of these affected patient, as drugs targeted to those genes might resolve the problem. It will also broadly inform the development of therapy for other related allergic diseases in the future. Furthermore, I also propose to develop a computer-based tool which will make it easier to distinguish a disease-causing gene alteration from a harmless one. Many software exist that do this, but recent research suggests that combining existing software might result in a better tool. I plan to collaborate with experts in artificial intelligence to make this tool. Once developed, I plan to make this tool publicly and freely available. This will greatly aid in more efficient diagnosis of genetic mutations across the world.

column36: Novel Protein Workflow to Discover Nanobodies Against Cell Surface Receptors for Biomedical and Therapeutic Applications
column37: Every cell is surrounded by a membrane that separates its contents from the environment and allows them to exist as stand-alone units. Embedded in this membrane are proteins that play crucial roles in the uptake of nutrients, cell communication and generally allow the cell to interact with its environment. Their importance in vital cellular processes, and easy accessibility on the outside of cells, make membrane proteins (MPs) the target of over half of all therapeutic drugs. Despite their fundamental and therapeutic importance, the study of MPs lags behind the study of proteins inside of the cell. The main barrier to MP study is their hydrophobic (water-hating) nature. Practically all methods biochemists have developed to investigate proteins require the protein to be first dissolved in water-based solutions. This proves difficult for MPs, as they tend to unfold and crash-out of these water solutions. Through my research I strive to overcome this incompatibility of MPs with water-based solutions to discover new research and therapeutic tools. Specifically, I will use the peptidisc technology - a new method for stabilizing MPs in water - to discover nanobodies (Nbs) against pathogenic bacterial outer membrane proteins (OMPs). Nbs are a type of antibody - molecules used by our own immune system to recognize and eliminate pathogens. Conventional antibodies have shown promise for their ability to tightly bind MPs, however due to their bulky size, they are not able to access the buried essential portions of pathogenic OMPs. Nbs are much smaller than Abs and can bind deep, hidden portions of bacterial OMPs, potentially upsetting their function. I hypothesize that Nbs will be able to access these hidden essential OMP portions and therefore kill bacterial pathogens. With the rise of antimicrobial resistance, these Nbs have the potential to offer new tools in the fight against pathogenic infections.

column36: Investigating the role of the orbitofrontal cortex in establishing inflexible patterns of risky behaviour on a rodent assay of cue-enhanced risky decision making
column37: The lights and sounds of a casino are exciting and increase enjoyment. However, these cues can cause intense cravings in those with pathological gambling, and there is increasing concern over their addictive nature. Previous research suggests that exposure to these cues contributes to the establishment of maladaptive addictive behaviours despite negative consequences. To investigate the influence of cues on brain functioning and cost/benefit decision making, our lab studies these behaviours in rats using the Rat Gambling Task. In this task, the majority of rats learn to favour options associated with low reward (1 or 2 sugar pellets on winning trials), and low risk (shorter time-out penalties that occur less frequently), which maximize reward earned over-time. However, some rats choose to go for the risky yet exciting high-reward options. Pairing lights and sounds with reward delivery results in a higher proportion of rats choosing the high-risk options, despite being disadvantageous in the long-run. Previous evidence from our lab suggests that adding these cues not only increases disadvantageous risky decision making, but also cements this behavioural pattern in stone. Rats become inflexible in their choice pattern, and it's difficult to shift their preferences. In my proposal, I outline four experiments which seek to uncover the neurobiological mechanisms of this effect. My research focuses on a key brain region - the orbitofrontal cortex. This region has been previously associated with managing cognitive flexibility and determining action-outcome contingencies. Experimental manipulation of activity in this region may reverse the negative effect of cues on risky decision making. If this is the case, our research could stimulate the development of medical and behavioural treatments that reduce the pervasive nature of habits associated with addiction and help to prevent relapse, by targeting the control of cues over behaviour.

column36: Frequency and etiology of ctDNA-positive metastatic prostate cancer with BRCA2, ATM, or CDK12 mutations
column37: Despite decades of clinical study, advanced prostate cancer remains a lethal disease. Research has shown that some prostate tumours are unable to properly repair changes (mutations) to their DNA; these cases are often particularly aggressive, and can rapidly develop resistance to most treatments. However, the inability to repair DNA also creates vulnerabilities to specific therapies, as seen by the dramatic response these tumours can have to platinum chemotherapy. Moreover, recent findings have shown the efficacy of a new therapy, poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, in treating tumours that have non-functional DNA repair. Unfortunately, the disruption of DNA repair in prostate cancer is poorly understood, and patients that could benefit from specific anticancer medications are often missed, and instead managed with conventional, but ultimately ineffective, therapy. My project aims to better characterize DNA repair-deficient prostate tumours, in order to help guide rational therapy selection. My preliminary research has identified three genes (BRCA2, ATM, and CDK12) that contribute to DNA repair, but are non-functional in ~15% of advanced prostate cancer cases. Initial findings suggest that tumours with a loss of one of these genes are unique, possessing specific mutations that set them apart from other prostate tumours. In this project, I will use DNA sequencing to determine the frequency of BRCA2, ATM, and CDK12 disruption in ~1800 prostate cancer samples. I will then employ computational tools to identify specific combinations of mutations unique to DNA repair-deficient prostate tumours. Given the poor response of these tumours to most standard therapies, there is an unmet need to determine which patients might benefit from anticancer treatments that exploit non-functional DNA repair. Findings from my research will readily translate to the clinic, facilitating a more personalized approach for the treatment of men with advanced prostate cancer.

column37: Rheumatic diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), are devastating conditions that strike more women than men, often during the childbearing years. Moreover, my own research to date has added to the current body of evidence showing that women with RA and SLE need information on medication use during pregnancy and that many pregnant women with rheumatic diseases stop taking their medications, even though these medications are known to be safe. Pharmacists are medication experts, trusted members of the healthcare team, and often the first point of access to the health care system for patients. As such, they are ideally positioned to close the information and care gaps for women with rheumatic diseases, particularly in supporting their medication decision-making. I propose to address the gap in pregnancy care among women with rheumatic disease by developing a collaborative care model supported by shared electronic medical records to integrate pharmacists with rheumatology practices. I will then study whether this collaborative care model is feasible, acceptable, and whether it improves care for women with rheumatic diseases.

column36: The role of B-1 B cells and natural antibodies in the lung tumor microenvironment
column37: The immune system plays a major role in lung cancer biology, and recently developed therapies that target or manipulate specific immune cells (i.e., immunotherapies) have revolutionized lung cancer treatment. Most immunotherapies have focused on improving the anti-tumor effects of T cells. However, B cells are also a major component of the immune system and the role of B cells in tumor control remains poorly understood. We have found that mice with elevated levels of a special type of B cell, called B-1 B cells, have dramatically decreased tumor growth in the lungs. B-1 B cells are immune cells that can destroy infectious microbes by producing a unique class of antibodies known as "natural IgM" antibodies. Natural IgM antibodies are found in the circulation and are the body's first defense against infection. Emerging evidence suggests that IgM antibodies secreted by B-1 B cells may be able to target certain cancer cells, representing an untapped resource for anti-tumor therapy. We will use a variety of pre-clinical tumor models to assess how B-1 B cells influence lung tumor growth, including the use of mice with elevated B-1 B cells and therapeutic transfer of B-1 B cells into normal mice. Additionally, we will test how IgM antibodies produced by B-1 B cells interact with tumor cells and determine whether IgM antibodies can be used as a new anti-cancer therapy. Therapeutic strategies that target the immune system are becoming increasingly common for treating lung cancer; however, we have just begun to harness the full power of the immune system for lung cancer treatment. Improving our understanding of the mechanisms by which B-1 B cells and their secreted antibodies can impact lung cancer growth will allow us to develop new and improved therapies to treat patients with lung cancer.

column36: Sex differences in epigenetic and gene expression profiles of the human placenta
column37: Whether a developing baby is male or female is associated with differences in growth and development throughout pregnancy, and with different risks of certain pregnancy complications. Male babies are typically born larger than female babies, but are also more likely to be born premature and to experience postnatal inflammation and infection. Currently, scientists do not have a good understanding of how and why the sex of a developing baby impacts prenatal development and the health of pregnancy. The placenta, the organ responsible for connecting mother and baby during pregnancy, is critical for development: it transfers nutrients needed for growth, removes fetal waste products, and regulates the developing baby's environment. The placenta likely plays an important role in mediating sex differences in development and pregnancy outcomes. My research project will investigate how male and female placentas differ on a molecular level, and how these differences might impact fetal health. Using samples from over 300 placentas from healthy pregnancies, I will ask 3 main questions: 1. Is there a difference in the chemical structures added to DNA that regulate the on/off status of genes between the placentas of male and female babies? 2. What genes are affected by these different chemical structures, and how much are they impacted? 3. Do placentas of male and female babies function differently because of the different on/off status of these genes? This research addresses a major gap in our knowledge; establishing how male and female placentas differ in healthy pregnancies will be a foundation from which we can begin to better understand the role sex plays in mediating adverse perinatal outcomes. In the future, we may be able to use this information to advance our diagnosis and treatment of certain pregnancy complications, as certain interventions may be more effective if tailored to the sex of the developing baby.

column36: An adaptive platform trial to assess the effectiveness of multi-component interventions for the linear growth of sub-Saharan African children during the complementary feeding period
column37: Prevention of stunting is critical to lower the child's mortality and neuro-impairment risks. Stunting occurs more often in sub-Saharan African nations such as Rwanda, where the fertility rates also happen to be high. In regions outside of the capital city, Rwanda has a high burden of stunting with rates varying from 24-41% among children aged 6-24 months, a period also known as complementary feeding period (CFP). Stunting has multiple causes with malnutrition, repeated infection, poor gut health and inadequate psychosocial stimulation all playing a role. Yet, the majority of trials studying this problem has only focused on a single intervention domain (e.g. micronutrients). Given multifaceted determinants of poor linear growth, there is a need to come up with multi-component intervention packages. There are multiple possible options of packages that can be formulated, so using an innovative approach in platform trials that offers flexibility and efficiency is more appropriate than conventional approaches that only allow for assessment of a fixed number of interventions after the last participant has completed their participation. My PhD project is to develop a master protocol for an adaptive platform trial that can test the effectiveness of multiple intervention packages for the CFP on child stunting in Rwanda. I plan to conduct a comprehensive review of platform trials and other master protocols for an overall landscape analysis. I plan to complement this with another review and network meta-analysis of published trials reporting on stunting prevention to identify a list of evidence-based and compelling interventions to be tested. These efforts will inform the development of the platform trial design for Rwanda's stunting problem. There is a need for further development of more innovative methods for global health research. This project will provide more effective evaluation options to inform policies that can be used to improve the health of young children.

column36: Uncovering political knowledge-to-action strategies to improve ecological determinants of health
column37: The World Health Organizations estimates that 12.6 million people die worldwide every year due to environmental factors such as climate change or air pollution. This is supported by research that provides extensive evidence on the health impacts of the so-called 'ecological determinants of health' - the air that we breathe, the water that we drink or the food that we eat. However, this evidence is often not considered sufficiently when political decisions about environmental regulations that would improve these health determinants are being made. This is partly because researchers mostly rely on ineffective knowledge translation strategies to influence decision makers such as politicians. This doctoral research program seeks to change the way we conduct knowledge translation in the health sciences with the goal to more successfully influence policy. More specifically, this research will draw on insights from the field of political science where more effective strategies have been developed and apply them to the issue of ecological determinants of health and environmental policies. The goal is to provide researchers and funding agencies with the tools to create and foster new and innovative political knowledge translation strategies in order to improve both the health of humans and the health of the planet.

column36: Determining the mechanism of action of cis-acting modifiers on the age of onset of Huntington Disease
column37: Huntington Disease (HD) is fatal genetic brain disorder whose symptoms include cognitive decline and uncontrollable movement. The disease occurs when part of the DNA sequence within a gene called huntingtin is repeated too many times. The larger the repeat expansion, the younger the age at which someone tends to start having disease symptoms. However, the size of the repeat does not fully explain the variation in age of onset. Someone with 39 repeats could become symptomatic as young as 30 years old or as late as their 80s or 90s. This means that even though we can genetically predict who will get HD, we cannot predict exactly when they will start showing symptoms. Recent studies have found some genetic differences in the repeat region in patients with unusually early or late disease onset. For example, patients with a particular variant in their huntingtin gene show symptoms on average 25 years earlier, while patients with a different variant show symptoms 4 years later. I want to understand why these variants cause differences in age of disease onset. Preliminary research suggests the variants may alter how much the repeated section of the huntingtin gene continues to expand in the brain during a patient's lifetime. To determine whether this causes the differences in disease onset, I will examine 1) the impact of these variants in brains of deceased patient, 2) differences in the clinical progression of patients with and without the variants, and 3) the effect of these variants in patient-derived cultured cells. A better understanding of how these variants affect onset will not only enable better disease onset predictions for HD patients, but could also suggest biological mechanisms that could be targeted to slow or prevent disease onset. Since many other diseases, collectively known as "trinucleotide repeat disorders," are caused by similar DNA repeat expansions in other genes, anything we learn may also benefit patients with these other diseases.

column36: Oral Dysplasia and Immune Cell Spatial Relationships: Potential Indicators of Malignant Progression
column37: Cancers of the mouth are a concern worldwide, and although the devastating impact of these cancers can be prevented or limited by early detection and treatment, long-term survival remains poor. Researchers aim to find ways to catch cancers at an early stage, or for lesions that are not yet cancers, to determine which ones have a greater risk of progression. Potentially cancerous lesions (PCL) that contain greater counts of abnormal cells are known to be at a greater risk of progression. However, predicting the outcome of PCL that contain a low amount of cellular abnormality is challenging, as many of these lesions will not progress, making clinical management difficult. As more is known about how cancer interacts with the immune system, the possibility of using immune factors to predict progression arises. Novel imaging techniques now allow for visualization of cell-to-cell interactions in tissues. This produces valuable information that has been used to predict survival and patient outcome in numerous cancers. No studies have investigated cell-cell spatial relationships between inflammatory cells and PCL in the mouth. Thus, the objective of this study is to apply this imaging technique to analyze the relationship of inflammatory cells and oral PCL to create a risk prediction model for subsequent progression to cancer. If lesions with a greater potential for transition to cancer can be identified, then treatment can be implemented at an earlier stage, ultimately improving patient outcome.

column36: A Genomic Epidemiology Investigation of Hepatitis C Virus Treatment Outcomes in the British Columbia Hepatitis Testers Cohort from 2017 to 2019: a Nested Case-Control Study
column37: Hepatitis C virus infects 71 million people worldwide causing complex liver disease, cancer and lifelong illness. Approximately half of those infected with Hepatitis C in Canada remain unaware, undiagnosed and untreated, presenting a real threat of continual transmission and long term burden on societal care systems. A medical breakthrough in the form of safe, effective and quick acting prescribed drugs to treat Hepatitis C infection prompted the Public Health Agency of Canada to prioritize elimination of the virus by 2030. Elimination requires increasing surveillance, detecting drug resistance and preventing re-infection. In partnership with the British Columbia Center for Disease Control, British Columbia Hepatitis Testers Cohort, Surveillance of Hepatitis-C Antiviral Resistance, Epidemiology and Methodology Network (SHARED) and the Public Health Agency of Canada, the nominated applicant (Aidan Nikiforuk) proposes to develop a new tool to identify and predict events of Hepatitis C virus re-infection in British Columbia. Research Outcomes: 1) measure how similar Hepatitis C viruses are between a patient's first infection and suspected reinfection. 2) monitor for known or suspected drug resistance in high risk populations. 3) apply sophisticated statistical equations to predict events of Hepatitis C re-infection in British Columbia. Support of this project will answer the important question, "What is the likelihood of Hepatitis C re-infection in British Columbia from 2017-2019?". In review: Hepatitis C virus causes a deadly but preventable epidemic in Canada, we possess new drugs to treat infection, treatment requires surveillance/diagnosis, knowledge of drug resistance and prevention of re-infections. This proposal aims to describe the likelihood of re-infection in British Columbia using new collaborations and tools. Funding support will directly benefit Hepatitis C elimination strategies in Canada and lead to successful elimination by the target year of 2030.

column36: Biomarker Discovery for Frontotemporal Dementia
column37: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a form of dementia that usually affects individuals under the age of 65. FTD symptoms overlap with other common forms of dementia like Alzheimer's disease, which makes it difficult for doctors to diagnose FTD. In addition to clinical care, the inability to confidently diagnose FTD hinders our ability to develop new treatments, as it is difficult to identify who should be receiving the new treatments as there is no simple test for FTD. A simple biofluid (e.g., blood) test for FTD is needed; however, we do not yet know what markers differentiate FTD from other forms of dementia. This study aims to accomplish this important step by identifying markers that are unique to FTD. To accomplish this aim, we will use brain tissue samples collected from individuals with FTD and compare them with samples from healthy individuals and individuals with other dementias. From this comparison, markers that are unique to FTD will be identified. We will then determine if these markers can be used to differentiate FTD from healthy individuals and individuals with other forms of dementia. This study is a critical first step toward developing a simple biofluid test for FTD.

column36: Granzyme K in the Pathogenesis of Psoriasis
column37: Psoriasis is a common skin disease that causes thick, itchy, red patches with a silvery white build-up of dead skin called 'plaques'. Around one million Canadians are currently living with psoriasis. This long-lasting condition can seriously impact a person's overall quality of life as it is linked to social humiliation, psychological distress, physical disability, pain and increased health risks. Unfortunately, current therapies often have negative side-effects and fail to provide long-term symptom relief. For these reasons, it is very important to further understand how psoriasis occurs. With this knowledge, we can develop more effective and better targeted treatments. A family of proteins called granzymes are found in drastically high levels in many inflammatory skin diseases. One granzyme, called Granzyme K (GzmK), has recently been shown to promote inflammation in diseases with characteristics similar to psoriasis. However, the role of GzmK in psoriasis is currently unknown. As our recent data suggest that amounts of GzmK are high in psoriasis, I believe this protein could play a key role in this condition. To better understand the role of GzmK in psoriasis, I will use a combination of human, mouse and human skin cell models of disease. First, I will determine what cells release GzmK in human psoriasis samples. Next, I will assess whether GzmK contributes to psoriasis using a mouse model in which GzmK is not present. Finally, I will use human skin cells to study how GzmK contributes to psoriasis. Overall, this study will improve our understanding of the role of GzmK in psoriasis which may help support the development of new drugs to treat this disease for the benefit of Canadians and the 125 million people worldwide currently living with psoriasis.

column36: Folic acid supplementation in Canadian children with sickle cell disease: Is it time to reassess current clinical practice?
column37: Sickle cell disease is a blood disorder that is passed down from parents to their children. People with sickle cell disease cannot make healthy red blood cells and have an increased risk of illness and death. Sickle cell disease also causes children to have higher folate needs than healthy children. Folate is a B-vitamin that is needed to help produce red blood cells. Currently, children with sickle cell disease take 1-5 milligrams (mg) per day of folic acid (the man-made form of folate). However, even the lowest recommended dose of 1 mg/d folic acid provides six times more folate than is recommended for healthy children aged 1-3 years. There is growing concern that high amounts of folic acid may be harmful in the long term, as it may interfere with how natural folate works in the body, and it is associated with an increased growth of some types of cancers. We will study the effectiveness and potential risk of folic acid supplementation in 36 children (2-19 years of age) with sickle cell disease who are attending BC Children's Hospital. Children will receive 1 mg/d folic acid, the current standard dose, or a placebo for 12 weeks. After a 12-week washout period (in which children receive no supplements), the treatments will be reversed. Blood samples will be collected at baseline and after 12 weeks of each treatment. We will measure several different forms of folate in the blood, hemoglobin, vitamins B12 and B6, and other clinical outcomes (anemia and pain crises) in children. Our study will be the first-step towards determining if the recommendation for high-dose folic acid supplementation in children with sickle cell disease requires re-evaluation. Our overall goal is to improve the nutritional status and clinical care of Canadian children with sickle cell disease.

column36: Enteroviral Infection in the Development of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
column37: Wouldn't it be wonderful if antiviral drugs could be used to treat or even prevent what is presently an incurable brain disease that affects 3,000 Canadians per year? We believe this may be possible for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), or Lou Gehrig's Disease, a condition where the death of muscle-controlling nerve cells in both the brain and the spinal cord leads to paralysis and eventually death. Currently, due to a lack of effective treatments, affected individuals have a life expectancy of only 3-5 years after their initial confirmed diagnosis. Our lab recently discovered that similar biological disease features seen in ALS patients are also seen in cells infected with a group of viruses known as enteroviruses. It has been proposed that enterovirus infection might contribute to ALS development, but this idea has never been fully studied. With the goal to gain a deeper understanding of this potential connection, I will first look into if virus infection in mice brain can result in similar ALS-related protein changes seen in ALS patients. In parallel, I will also use a mouse model of ALS that mimics the disease progression of ALS in human to test if a viral infection can intensify disease progression, and if so, what are the underlying relationships. Together, these results will provide evidence to support the association between viral infection and ALS development. Lastly, I will identify key interactions between the virus and human cells using computational and biological methods to potentially determine how viral infection is related to developing ALS and to select for potential therapeutic targets. The results from this project may open doors to using anti-viral drugs to treat and prevent ALS, providing hope for all those suffering from this devastating disease in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Investigating the role of ARID1A loss in cancer and its effects on R-loop accumulation and genome instability
column37: Every year in Canada, over 2800 women are diagnosed with ovarian cancer, and over 60% of these women die of the disease. In a particular type of ovarian cancer (ovarian clear cell carcinoma), as many as 55% of patients tumours contain a mutation (an error in normal DNA) in a protein called ARID1A. ARID1A is a subunit of a larger protein complex that functions in the regulation of DNA organization within the cell, which affects a variety of cellular processes including the expression of genes into proteins. Recent research has suggested that loss of ARID1A in cancer leads to an increased rate of mutations over the course of a cell division (referred to as "genome instability"), which contributes to the progression of the disease. However, the exact mechanism by which ARID1A loss results in genome instability remains unclear. One process by which genome instability can arise is through improper pairing of RNA and DNA during the expression of genes into proteins, resulting in a hybrid structure called an "R-loop". Importantly, my results show that ARID1A loss in cancer cell lines leads to an increase in these R-loop structures, which also results in more DNA damage accumulation, contributing to genome instability. Moving forward, my goal is to uncover the mechanisms underlying how R-loops cause genome instability in ARID1A-deficient cells to better understand how mutations in ARID1A contribute to cancer progression. In parallel, I have implemented a large-scale screening approach within our lab to identify genes that become essential for cell survival when ARID1A is mutated. This will allow me to identify new therapeutic targets to selectively kill cancer cells and improve current treatments of ovarian cancers. Ultimately, my research will provide new knowledge on how ARID1A loss promotes cancer development and may lead to improved therapies.

column36: Systematic evaluation and optimization of HIV transmission models for phylogenetic cluster identification
column37: Advancements in next-generation sequencing of human pathogens have catalyzed the generation of massive amounts of data well-suited to model their evolution and transmission. The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic is one of the best examples of how viral sequences routinely collected for drug resistant mutation surveillance have altered prioritization of public health service delivery. Comparisons of patients' HIV sequences, which are more similar when viruses are linked through recent transmission events, allow reconstruction of viruses' shared ancestry through the transmission network. In British Columbia (BC), HIV sequences are clustered according to thresholds of genetic similarity in order to identify subpopulations experiencing high transmission rates. Individuals in or associated with large or rapidly growing clusters receive prioritized treatment services, partner contact tracing, and HIV testing and pre-exposure prophylaxis for partners. While demonstrated to be an effective way to prioritize resources, clustering methods can be improved and optimized to best identify individuals with heightened transmission activity. Outside of BC, alternative clustering and transmission analysis methods have been applied, yet the comparative accuracy and sensitivity of these methods has not been explored. Therefore, I propose a systematic evaluation of HIV transmission modelling methods in regard to their thresholds, evolutionary tree models, and sensitivities to sampling biases. Using a combination of empirical data from the BC Drug Treatment Program and simulated epidemic data, we will identify and optimize the method that most accurately identifies clusters of individuals with high transmission rates. By pinpointing populations to whom public health resources should be prioritized, this research will improve the efficiency of HIV health service delivery and pave the way for prioritization schemes for other pathogens, such as hepatitis C virus, as well.

column36: Matrix Metalloproteinase cleavage of PCSK9 in Atherosclerosis
column37: Heart attacks and stroke are two of the leading causes of death in Canada every year. Both are affected by high levels of "bad cholesterol" in the blood, known as LDL-cholesterol. Through a process called atherosclerosis, excess LDL-cholesterol builds up in blood vessels, forming plaques that reduce blood flow to the heart or brain. White blood cells of the immune system enter these plaques and release a protein called MMP12 that destabilizes the plaque and could cause it to rupture, which in turn could result in heart attack or stroke. Therefore, reducing the amount of LDL-cholesterol is important to reduce the risk of heart attacks and stroke amongst Canadians. Newly developed drugs to reduce LDL-cholesterol in the blood work by blocking a protein called PCSK9, which normally increases LDL-cholesterol in the blood by preventing the liver from clearing it. These drugs are effective, but are expensive and difficult to produce on a large scale, and must be injected into the skin rather than simply swallowed as a pill. Therefore, more research is needed to understand how to develop better drugs to block PCSK9 or other proteins such as MMP12, which might be important for the effects of PCSK9 on LDL-cholesterol levels. We have discovered that PCSK9 can be cut and modified by MMP12 from white blood cells, and by a close relative called MMP14 that is produced by the same white blood cells and by cells in the liver that are important regulators of LDL-cholesterol levels. My PhD research focuses on understanding how PCSK9 is modified by MMP12 and MMP14, and on discovering the effects of these modifications on LDL-cholesterol levels and atherosclerosis. This research could contribute to developing the next generation of drugs that would help millions of Canadians with high LDL-cholesterol levels who are at risk of atherosclerosis, heart attacks and stroke.

column36: DNA methylation and cellular heterogeneity in the placenta
column37: Every cell in a person's body contains the same DNA. Yet, clearly there are differences between them. Cells that make up your skin, look and function differently than cells that float through your blood. These differences can be partly explained by many small chemical changes to the DNA that affect how DNA is organized and accessed. These are called epigenetic modifications, and are different for every cell type in the human body. Epigenetics can change over a person's lifetime, when individuals get sick, or are exposed to different environments. Understanding epigenetics is therefore important to better understand and predict health outcomes. My project aims to understand the epigenetics within major cell populations of the human placenta. This is challenging because placental tissue is difficult to obtain and separate into individual cells. However, understanding the epigenetics of placental cells is essential to understand how and why pregnancy complications occur. For example, many pregnancy-related conditions are connected to specific placental cell populations not functioning properly. But until we understand the epigenetics healthy pregnancies, it is difficult to fully understand the impacts of the changes seen in unhealthy ones. Building on this data, a secondary outcome is to create a computational tool to calculate the number of different placental cells in a whole placental sample, without needing to physically separate the cells. Having such a tool will allow researchers to determine which specific cell populations are responsible for the changes that we see a mother's pregnancy. For example, mothers with diabetes often have corresponding placental epigenetic changes. But it is unclear if these changes affect the whole placenta or only a sub population of cells. With our tool, we could determine exactly which cells are responsible, which will help understand the underlying causes of the condition, and to develop diagnostics/treatments.

column36: Genomic and clinical characteristics of the hyper-mutant molecular subtype of advanced metastatic prostate cancer studied using circulating tumor DNA
column37: When prostate cancer metastasizes beyond the prostate to bone and organs, it is invariably lethal and there is an urgent need for new therapeutic approaches. Immunotherapy has been a successful treatment avenue in other types of cancer, but similar success has not been replicated in prostate cancer. Genetically, prostate cancer is actually a collection of different diseases which are likely to require different treatments. One of these prostate cancer subtypes is referred to as "hyper-mutant", denoting the increased number of small genetic mutations distributed throughout the genome. These genomic scars occur as a result of the inactivation of one or more of a class of genes called mismatch repair genes, which in non-cancerous tissues act to correct errors that occur spontaneously during DNA replication. Importantly, in other cancers, high mutation rates and mutations in these genes indicate that the patients will respond to immunotherapy. Currently, there is no real-time method to identify (and therefore treat) these patients in a prospective fashion. This is especially true with metastatic prostate cancer, where the tumors that are actually killing the patients reside in the bone. I have developed techniques that analyze tumor DNA which is circulating in the blood. These "liquid biopsies" act as a real time indication of the genetics of metastatic tumors. My proposal is to use these methods to characterize the genomics of hyper-mutant prostate cancer. I will also develop methodology to detect currently used clinical biomarkers using blood instead of traditional biopsies. I will perform a retrospective analysis of collated clinical data to establish effects on response to conventional therapies. Finally, I will determine whether there is an association between somatic hyper-mutation and response to immunotherapy in two ongoing phase II clinical trials chaired by my co-supervisor Dr. Kim Chi.

column36: Looking past 'cure': refining our understanding of the long-term impacts of tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) survivors are at high risk of premature mortality following treatment. The mechanisms leading to the increased mortality seen in this population are incompletely characterized, but studies have shown that TB survivors experience chronic morbidity post-treatment, with high rates of respiratory and cardiovascular disease. This growing body of evidence indicates that supporting TB survivors post-treatment completion is a chance to mitigate other morbidity and mortality. To support the development and implementation of strategies aimed at improving the long-term health outcomes of TB survivors, we must first improve our understanding of the mechanisms leading to the increased morbidity and mortality in this population. This includes refining our understanding of the unique barriers and needs that face TB survivors and taking a holistic, person-centered approach to care. Collaborating with research partners from the University of British Columbia and the Woolcock Institute of Medical Research, an Australian medical research organisation that works in collaboration with the Vietnam National Tuberculosis Program, I will use social epidemiological methods to (1) identify patient and health system characteristics associated with morbidity and mortality in TB survivors in Vietnam, and (2) investigate how TB survivors in Vietnam view their post-treatment experience. My research project will advance our understanding of the long-term health impacts of TB and will begin to lay the groundwork for interventions that restore and preserve the health and well-being of TB survivors while maintaining a person-centered approach.

column36: Enhancing Transfusable Platelets Using mRNA Therapy to Produce Exogenous Proteins
column37: Platelets are small circulating blood cells that act as natural delivery vehicles for numerous biomolecules, and regulate many important processes such as blood clotting, immune function, and cancers. Platelets are regularly transfused to help stop severe bleeding, but can be ineffective in the most severe cases of hemorrhage. Furthermore, using them as a cell therapy for other diseases is limited by challenges to modify and enhance platelet function. For example, there are currently no methods to modify the protein content of transfusable platelets. This project therefore aims to develop novel approaches to directly engineer transfusable platelets by using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)-a recently FDA-approved drug delivery vehicle for nucleic acids-to deliver messenger RNA (mRNA) and alter the protein composition of platelets. Once successful, this strategy will create a platform technology to produce transfusable platelets with new and modified functions that current transfused platelets do not possess, and in the long term yield more effective platelet products, increase the efficacy of transfusions, and decrease the number of transfusion-related adverse effects. The technology will also enable transfused platelets to locally deliver therapeutics to injured tissues, such as sites of trauma, or potentially to diseased vasculature associated with atherosclerosis and Alzheimer's disease in the future. By controlling the expression of proteins in platelets, this technology will be an important tool for the field of platelet research.

column36: Identification of membrane-targeting factors for neurodegeneration-associated proteins VPS13C and VPS13D
column37: Inside each of our cells, we have a number of specialized compartments called organelles that perform different tasks. Recently we have learned that these compartments are not simply floating around in our cells but are in fact held together at places called "membrane contact sites". These contact sites have an important role in transporting nutrients, fats and proteins from one compartment to another. When this transport is disrupted, disease can occur. My proposed research focuses on VPS13C and VPS13D, related proteins found at membrane contact sites that are believed to transport fats between cellular compartments. Mutations in these proteins cause two different neurodegenerative diseases: early-onset Parkinson's disease and childhood-onset spastic ataxia, respectively. Evidence suggests that these human VPS13 proteins localize to different membrane contact sites which may explain why mutations in the two proteins result in distinct neurological disorders. My research is focused on determining how VPS13C and VPS13D are sent to contact sites and how mutations in these proteins can change their cellular locations resulting in neurodegeneration. We have been using yeast as a model system to study VPS13C and VPS13D, because yeast carries a single, related Vps13 protein which goes to many different cellular compartments. We have found that the yeast Vps13 is sent to different contact sites with the help of adaptors. These adaptors bind Vps13 at a site we have named the Vps13 Adaptor Binding (VAB) domain, which is conserved in human VPS13C/D proteins. My work will identify the adaptors needed for VPS13C/D recruitment and will examine the role of a secondary site in helping to send these proteins to the right compartments. Understanding how VPS13C and VPS13D are localized within the cell will give us a better understanding of the disease mechanisms associated with each disorder and give us insights into potential therapeutic interventions.

column36: A mixed-methods process evaluation of an eHealth intervention to improve tuberculosis patients' treatment adherence in Tibet, China
column37: This research respectfully involves Indigenous communities in Tibet, China and aims to evaluate the implementation of a program to support patients' in taking their tuberculosis (TB) medication. Tuberculosis is the number one infectious cause of death globally despite available treatment to cure the infection. Treatment for TB requires patients to take medications for many months, and the treatment may have side effects, which make it difficult for some to complete treatment. Not completing treatment increases mortality and leads to antibiotic resistance. To help patients take medication, healthcare workers watch patients take their medications, this is called Directly Observed Therapy (DOT). In rural settings, DOT is difficult to implement due to travel distances and limited human resources. The program we are evaluating uses Bluetooth pillboxes to monitor medication use, and an app to connect patients and their healthcare team. The program also involves a Treatment Supporter, a family member who helps the patient with treatment. As there is stigma towards TB, the role of family support is important. This study is a process evaluation, which aims to understand what worked and why in implementing the program. We also want to explore the perspectives of program participants to understand program acceptability. We will conduct interviews with patients, Treatment Supporters and other stakeholders to explore their views on the program. We will also use a survey to assess the program. This study will provide valuable information on using technology to support medication-taking, particularly in rural communities abroad and in Canada. This will help patients complete TB treatment, which will improve patient outcomes, help stop the spread of TB and reduce antibiotic resistance. The results of the study will identify barriers and facilitators to implementing the technology and help TB programs and health systems to better implement, scale up and sustain programs.

column36: The Longitudinal Association Between Anxiety and Restricted/Repetitive Behaviour in Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a disorder of brain development that affects 1-2% of children. It is usually diagnosed between 2 and 4 years of age and is a lifelong condition. A classic symptom of ASD is restricted and repetitive behaviour, like hand flapping and rigid adherence to routines. In addition, 40% of children with ASD will also meet criteria for an anxiety disorder during childhood or adolescence, which adds to existing impairments in functioning. A better understanding of which children with ASD develop anxiety disorders is greatly needed, to inform prevention strategies and treatments. Cross-sectional studies suggest that children with ASD with more severe restricted/repetitive behaviour also tend to have worse anxiety at the same time. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine which symptoms occur first, the different patterns of anxiety over time, and the underlying risk factors associated with high rates of anxiety in ASD. The Pathways in ASD study is the largest and longest-running longitudinal study in the world on how children with ASD grow and develop. A first project, as part of my master's thesis, found that children with ASD who had severe restricted/repetitive behaviour in preschool had more than three times greater odds of developing elevated anxiety between ages 8-11 years than those with mild restricted/repetitive behaviour. I have now transferred to a PhD program, where, based on these exciting results, two important follow up projects are planned: (1) to use a statistical approach called developmental cascade modelling to examine how multiple risk factors may together lead to increasing levels of anxiety in ASD; and (2) to examine the different trajectories of anxiety and restricted/repetitive behaviour in ASD, and how they relate to each other. The overall goal is to increase early recognition of anxiety disorders in ASD, to facilitate prevention and early intervention, and to ensure timely access to treatment.

column36: Myelofibrosis as a model to study the early evolution of stem cells that drive acute myeloid leukemia development.
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a dismal disease that results from the accumulation of genetic mutations in stem cells that normally work to maintain the blood system over an individual's lifespan. Although AML occurs with little clinical warning prior to diagnosis, recent advancements have clearly shown the presence of a pre-leukemic phase. While leukemic mutations are found in the blood of normal individuals, the high incidence of these mutations but low incidence of AML, argues that the vast majority people carrying "leukemic mutations" will never develop disease. Thus, the true preleukemic phase and the stem cells that drive its progression towards disease have been virtually inaccessible for study and early leukemia development remains a black box. While most AML cases are diagnosed de novo, some progress from a preceding blood disease, such as myelofibrosis (MF). MF is a high-risk malignancy, owing to its high transformation rate to AML, which is invariably fatal. Importantly, while AML onset is sudden and rapid, MF is a chronic disease. Thus, serial sampling over the entire course of MF pathogenesis represents a unique opportunity for unparalleled access to the preleukemic phase and the stem cells that drive it. I aim to study the entire arc of disease progression from the cell of origin to MF to AML. I will precisely study the stem cell populations that our group have previously found to be responsible for MPN initiation and leukemic progression. Using patient samples from biobanks and novel single cell approaches, I will track and characterize these stem cells at timepoints before diagnosis, during MF and at the time of progression to AML. A battery of computational approaches will be used to elucidate the key stem cell features responsible for disease initiation and progression. This approach will provide insights that facilitate early detection and intervention strategies that target pre-leukemic stem cells prior to their development of frank leukemia.

column36: "Nothing about us without us" - Development of a patient-centered digital health self-management program for marginalized, underserved populations with heart failure
column37: Heart failure (HF) is a global pandemic affecting over 26 million people worldwide. In high-income countries (HICs), the use of self-care models has led to a decline in HF prevalence. However, these improvements are less evident in low-and-middle-income countries (LMICs) and marginalized subgroup populations in HICs, like the Indigenous. HF is a complex condition and requires the combined expertise of specialists and primary care physicians, yet marginalized populations often live in remote areas with limited access to any source of care. To help minimize these health disparities, digital health has been offered as a tool to improve access to HF care. However, as the majority of digital tools have been designed for use in HICs, there is concern if they will be effective in these populations, since their health outcomes are strongly rooted with their cultural context. To support HF care in these populations, there is a need to understand the context-specific factors influencing their health outcomes. University Health Network has displayed the effectiveness of their Medly Program, which allows patients to manage their HF through their mobile phone. With this, my research aims to work in partnership with the Uganda Heart Institute in Kampala, and three Aboriginal Health Access Centres in Northern Ontario, to adapt Medly for the LMIC and Indigenous contexts. As the project lead, I will interview patients and clinicians to investigate their views on the factors affecting HF outcomes. This feedback will be used to adapt Medly for the LMIC and Indigenous contexts. Usability testing will then be held to evaluate the adapted systems effectiveness. Finally, results from all phases will be used to conduct a comparative case analysis to differentiate the impact of context between the LMIC and Indigenous systems. Ultimately, this study will support improved access to HF care in marginalized populations and will serve as model to design tools for settings with limited resources.

column36: Using concept mapping to create responsive cervical cancer screening knowledge translation and exchange for South Asian women who are under- or never screened in Ontario
column37: With regular screening, cervical cancer is preventable for women living in Canada. Organized programs exist at the provincial level to make this screening (i.e. Pap tests) available to women, and some groups have noticeably lower participation rates. In Ontario, around 60-65% of women get screened but this falls short of the province's aim of 85%. In particular, South Asian women have the lowest rates of cervical cancer screening among major ethnic groups and a suggested higher burden of cervical cancer, in Ontario. This is due to a number of reasons such as access to a physician, cultural barriers and indirect costs. Additionally, misconceptions and misinformation have also played a role and work in this area has shown the need for more tailored communication strategies. Understanding the knowledge and beliefs of these under- or never screened women, can allow us to create health education materials that speak to their information needs and communicate in different ways. This study will first review the available cervical cancer screening communications and research that exists in this area. Then we will work with women who identify as part of this group, to map out their ideas and opinions around cervical cancer screening to see how it differs from mainstream communications. Lastly, we will work in collaboration with the women in the study to create cervical cancer screening communications to reflect their input in the process. This work will contribute to an underexplored area and work in line with current priorities of Cancer Care Ontario (CCO) to increase screening rates for populations with low participation rates. It also responds to a research priority of CIHR's Institute of Cancer Research to support intervention research including knowledge translation into practice and policies in reponse to inequities in prevention services.
