column36: Does tau pathology propagate within human brain networks?
column37: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative condition that is defined by the aggregation of two specific pathologies in the brain: amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles. While amyloid-beta appears years before the onset of symptoms, tau tangles are very closely linked to the death of brain cells and to symptoms like memory problems. Correspondingly, it is important to understand how tau pathology appears in the brain and spreads from one brain region to another. In recent years, impressive strides have been made with animal models of Alzheimer's disease. Research has shown that when tau is injected into the mouse brain, we can observe tau at the injection site but also in anatomically connected brain regions. The goal of my project is to translate the research from mice (who do not naturally develop Alzheimer's disease) into humans to determine how the disease actually develops. Using recent advancements in molecular imaging, we can measure tau pathology in living individuals. This allows us to see where tau is located in the brain, and how it spreads with time - a critical advance, because in the past, doctors had to wait until a patient died to examine their brain for tau. My study will determine how tau pathology spreads in the brain. I am building on the hypothesis that tau spreads through the brain's anatomical connections. We first used data from over 130 elderly individuals who underwent MRI and fMRI to create a connection map of the brain. Next, we observed that tau in Alzheimer's disease patients mirrors the connection map of the brain. The final step is to test our hypothesis in several population-based cohort studies of Alzheimer's disease (over 500 individuals) to see if anatomical connections allow for tau to spread. Understanding how tau pathology spreads is critical to stopping it. Because tau pathology is closely linked to the death of brain cells, this research will have implications for the next generation of anti-tau therapies.

column36: Does physiotherapy plus brain stimulation enhance motor recovery? Evaluating the feasibility of transcranial direct current stimulation as an adjunct to physiotherapy intervention in children and youth with acquired brain injury
column37: A severe acquired brain injury (ABI) sustained in childhood results in the significant loss of motor skills, leaving some children without the ability to walk, run, or sit independently. Current treatment for motor skill recovery is intensive physiotherapy, which helps these children relearn the motor skills required for the mobility-based activities they want and need to do in everyday life. Unfortunately, even with intensive physiotherapy, children with ABI have persisting physical impairments that can seriously affect their development and ability to return to pre-injury activities. To improve upon current physiotherapy outcomes, there is an urgent need for new treatments that maximize motor recovery and minimize long-term physical complications. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a form of low-intensity brain stimulation that primes the brain for learning. It has been found to improve motor function in many adult neurological populations (e.g., stroke, Parkinson's) and in children with cerebral palsy, particularly when paired with practice of specific motor skills. However, it has yet to be studied in children with ABI. Our study will evaluate tDCS combined with the current physiotherapy intervention for children in the inpatient ABI program at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital (Toronto, Ontario). This feasibility randomized control trial will assign 30 participants (ages 5 to 18 years) to one of two treatment groups. One group will receive active tDCS before four physiotherapy sessions each week for a total of 16 sessions, while the other will receive placebo tDCS before their 16 physiotherapy sessions. Recovery of motor skills will be compared between groups by assessing abilities before, immediately after and three months after the tDCS treatments. Our study will elucidate the additive impact of tDCS and physiotherapy on recovery of gross motor skills.

column36: Maternal postpartum psychiatric emergencies: applying an intersectional feminist framework to understand outcomes and better identify groups of women whose care needs are not being met
column37: Mental illness is common in the first year after childbirth and impacts tens of thousands of Canadian women and their children. If treatment is delayed or inadequate, consequences can be devastating. Maternal suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in Canada, and there are likely missed opportunities to prevent this tragic outcome. Our team showed that the emergency department (ED) is the first point of post-childbirth mental health care contact for many women, particularly women from marginalized groups, including those living in poverty and living rurally. What happens to women after postpartum psychiatric emergencies is not known. High quality data about healthcare use and demographics are available for the entire Ontario population, presenting a unique opportunity to study postpartum psychiatric emergencies on a large scale. Using these data, my doctoral research will explore outcomes of all postpartum women who sought mental health care in an Ontario ED (2008-2016). I will study the nature and predictors of admission to hospital from the ED, timely outpatient mental health follow-up after the ED visit, and negative outcomes in the year following the ED visit (repeat psychiatric emergencies, psychiatric hospitalizations, self-harm, and suicide). I will look at how patterns may differ for women experiencing one or more forms of marginalization (e.g. poverty and rurality). I will apply advanced statistical methods to explore how experiencing multiple forms of marginalization could have a different effect than experiencing one form alone. I plan to disseminate my research among relevant policy makers to help inform the design, development, and delivery of equitable postpartum mental health services, and thus improve outcomes for new mothers with mental illness and their families. The methods used will also propose ways that psychiatric services research can better consider intersecting forms of marginalization so as to improve care for vulnerable patients.

column36: Identifying the genetic determinants of lipophagy using Saccharomyces cerevisiae
column37: Macrophages are specialized cells of the immune system that play a key role in the progression of atherosclerosis, a disease that is a major cause of cardiovascular disease - the most significant killer of Canadians each year. Atherosclerosis is characterized by cholesterol rich particles in the bloodstream that enter into artery walls and induce macrophages to follow and 'eat up' the cholesterol. These hungry macrophages become full of cholesterol, and unable to leave the artery. As the disease progresses complex accumulations of macrophages, known as plaques, increase in size. Eventually, plaques can rupture, block circulation and lead to heart attacks. Recently, macrophage lipophagy was discovered and has the potential to reverse the growth of plaques. In lipophagy, lipid droplets (cholesterol storage sites) are degraded by lysosomes and the free cholesterol is excreted from the cell. Put simply, lipophagy can reverse the accumulation of cholesterol in macrophages and thus the severity of plaques. However, little is known about the genes that control lipophagy. To adress this question we aim to conduct a comprehensive genetic analysis of lipophagy using yeast. The autophagic processes of yeast are remarkably similar to their mammalian counterparts and technology is available for efficient and large-scale genetic manipulation. Genetic screening to the same extent is not feasible in macrophages. For these reasons, it is viable to use yeast to answer questions about lipophagy. Presently, we have developed a library of several thousand single-gene deletion yeast and are now assessing methods to detect intact or defective lipophagy in these strains as well as screening the deletion yeast for lipophagy defects. We expect this analysis will identify novel lipophagy genes whose macrophage counterparts can then be targeted for future atherosclerosis therapies that specifically activate lipophagy.

column36: Estimating the risk of long-term cardiovascular outcomes in women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
column37: High blood pressure during pregnancy or 'hypertensive' disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are common, occurring in 5 to 10% of all pregnancies. Women with a history of HDP have a much higher risk of developing heart and blood vessel diseases (e.g. stroke, heart disease, heart failure) compared to women who do not experience HDP. These women are also at 4-times the risk of developing high blood pressure for the rest of their lives (i.e. chronic high blood pressure). This is important because high blood pressure is the number one cause of death and disability in the world and it is more dangerous for women than men. Currently, very little is known about whether the increased risk of heart and blood vessel diseases for women with HDP is due to chronic high blood pressure, or if this risk is increased even for women whose high blood pressure during pregnancy returns to normal after delivery. To address this question, we will analyze information from large computer databases on all women admitted to deliver in Ontario hospitals over the past 30 years. In our tests, we will account for several factors that might otherwise also affect a woman's risk. For example, in addition to conditions like diabetes, we will also consider gender-related characteristics (e.g. feminine and masculine personality traits) because we know these factors can increase people's risk of developing diseases of the heart. This research capitalizes on an important opportunity to improve our knowledge of factors that increase women's heart health risk. It will address a large knowledge gap for women's health and the results of this study will be an important first step in developing new ways for doctors to identify women at highest risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. It will also provide evidence for the importance of including information on a woman's pregnancy history when evaluating heart disease risk. Until these results are available, heart health outcomes for women with HDP will remain poor.

column36: Towards a pan-Canadian network for integrating research-evaluation and knowledge translation in youth mental health services
column37: Most mental illnesses have their onset during adolescence or young adulthood. This makes building youth mental health (YMH) services that identify and intervene during the earliest stages of mental illness critical to health system reform. Over the past 5 years, a resulting movement to transform YMH services in Canada has borne fruit: there are now multiple individual sites, provincial bodies, and a large-scale pan-Canadian national research-evaluation project underway. Supporting and integrating the evaluation and knowledge translation activities of these initiatives would synergistically improve YMH practices and outcomes, and disseminate the knowledge that results from their efforts. We therefore propose a 'network of networks' that brings together ACCESS Open Minds, like-minded provincial initiatives and individual sites (particularly those representing vulnerable populations and Indigenous contexts) to: 1) create a minimum evaluation protocol and low-cost database platform relevant to Canadian YMH services; 2) support data gathering and sharing by sites and provide reports for youth, families, clinicians and services that can prompt service improvement; and 3) share learnings, knowledge and best practices in this rapidly advancing area, beginning nationally and eventually extending to the international realm.

NMD4C will share expertise and resources, build capacity, and share knowledge to improve the care and treatment of NMD for all Canadians.

column36: Identification of Epigenomic Drivers and Predictors of Chordoma Development and Recurrence
column37: Chordomas represent 20% of primary spine and skull base tumours and median survival remains poor at 6-7 years despite standard treatment of surgery and post-operative radiotherapy. Patients that develop a recurrence of their chordoma experience poorer survival. Unfortunately there is no robust approach to predict which patients will have a recurrence and this significantly limits our ability to optimize patient treatment and survival. DNA modifications have been shown to predict patient-specific outcomes in other tumour types. Accordingly, the objective of this work is to identify DNA modifications, including methylation and histone marks, that can predict whether a patient's chordoma will recur in a cohort of 200 surgically resected chordomas. Drugs which target DNA modification signatures that we identify will be tested on established chordoma cell lines to assess for novel treatments to reduce the risk of recurrence. DNA modification signatures of recurrence will be combined with clinical factors to produce a nomogram for clinicians to obtain recurrence risk values for a specific patient. Overall, this work will provide clinicians with information that will allow them to balance the extent of a patient's treatment with their risk of having poor outcomes and may also identify new treatments for a tumour type with limited options currently.

column36: Does flavivirus infection trigger mitochondrial antigen presentation and autoreactive T-cell response in parkinsonism?
column37: The exact cause of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unknown and there is currently no cure for the disease. This is why there is a critical need for clinically-relevant biomarkers new therapeutic avenues. In this project, we will explore new research aspects of PD and atypical parkinsonism, related to autoimmunity (the immune attack of the self) triggered by flaviviruses. Indeed, these types of viruses are endemic in regions where atypical parkinsonism is highly frequent (such as Guadeloupe and Martinique) and are particularly associated with Parkinsonian features. Moreover, flavivirus infection is also associated with major mitochondrial disorders. Mitochondria was originally described as the powerhouse of the cell. However, the recent discoveries have highlighted the major role of this organelle in the regulation of the immune response. Particularly, our team have recently shown that the presentation of the proteins from the mitochondria leads to autoimmunity and to PD in a murine model. Therefore, we hypothesize that flavivirus infection trigger autoimmune attacks of dopaminergic neurons (target neurons in PD) through the induction of mitochondrial antigen presentation. Not only this would greatly impact the scientific community because of the first evidence of autoimmunity in PD and atypical parkinsonism patients, but it would generate several promising biomarkers.

column36: Role of microbes in the pathogenesis of PIBD: From discovery, through causation, to novel treatments
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic conditions that damage a person's intestines and cause lifelong pain. IBD is becoming more common in Canada, especially in children. Current treatments (drugs) suppress patient's immune systems and don't work all the time; even when they work they carry substantial risks. Therefore, we need to develop new treatments. While studying some of our patients, our Team of doctors and scientists has found several types of unusual bacteria in their intestines. These bacteria are able to attach to - or invade the cells lining the human gut, and trigger inflammation. These bacteria are also recognized by the patient's immune cells, suggesting these "pathobiont" bacteria are involved in either causing IBD, or making it worse, and thus removing these nasty bacteria could be a new treatment for IBD. Our Team is part of a national Network studying IBD in more than 1500 Canadian children. We plan to use the existing Network infrastructure to collect samples from these patients, including stool samples, intestinal washing, and tissues. We will use specialized techniques to identify potential "pathobionts" and grow them up in large numbers, allowing us to study them in great detail. We will test how they stick or invade human cells grown in the lab, as well as inject them into mice to see how they cause disease. As we gain a better understanding of how different "pathobiont" bacteria cause disease, we will develop new ways to target these bacteria and test these approaches in the lab, in mouse models, and ultimately in the patients themselves. For example, we will test if certain diets can starve these bacteria, if there are specific good bacteria we can give to patients in their food that can outcompete the pathobionts, or if we can use new drugs to kill, or flush away these harmful bacteria. Taken together, our studies will help develop new precise and personalized ways to treat children with IBD, and ultimately improve their lives.

column36: Accelerating Cervical Cancer Elimination in Canada: ACE-Canada
column37: Despite being almost entirely preventable, the World Health Organization estimates that one million women globally currently have cervical cancer. Although Canada is poised to be one of the first countries to eliminate cervical cancer (CC), in 2019, an estimated 1,350 Canadian women will be diagnosed and every day, a woman in Canada will die from this preventable cancer. CC is caused by long-term infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), and is largely preventable through effective vaccination and screening. Our research team will advance research on HPV vaccine and screening methods to reach the goal of eliminating CC in Canada. We aim to achieve this by focusing on improving uptake and delivery of HPV vaccination as well as cervical cancer screening in the general public including under-screened and under-served populations. Through five 'research projects', our team of researchers will evaluate the effectiveness of current HPV vaccine schedules and strategies for improving uptake of the vaccine in school based programs. Using the BC Cervix Screening Program and experience from our HPV FOCAL study, we will comprehensively examine the impact of population level recruitment strategies using self-collection and digital infrastructure to increase attendance at care and CC screening coverage. This evaluation will focus on examining how a population level strategy impacts CC screening coverage in under-screened women, particularly communities that face access inequities. In partnership with Indigenous communities, employing a strengths-based approach, we will examine ways to achieve equity in access to screening in First Nations and Metis communities adhering to OCAP and OCAS principles. We will strengthen and broaden our existing collaborative networks to ensure knowledge translation to other jurisdictions across Canada with the ultimate aim of will accelerate Canada's efforts to becoming the first country, globally, to eliminate of CC.

column36: Holistic Indigenous Mental Health and Wellness: Transforming Health Care Strengths and Solutions
column37: Indigenous peoples with serious mental illness face unique health care barriers due to racism, oppression, and intergenerational trauma of residential school and child welfare systems. Indigenous mental health is complex; research shows that challenges of cultural identity, food insecurity, environmental health, career, education, culture clash between biomedicine and Indigenous healing, and failure of Canada's health policy are mediating factors. Currently there are thousands of Indigenous youth and adults searching for healing, often stuck in cycles of mental health crisis that include lack of mental health service, extreme addictive behaviours, severe anxiety and depression, and chronic suicidality. Current mental health services focus on crisis and short term mental health programs; this network will move the focus to holistic culturally-based interventions that prevent illness and strengthen individuals' chances of successful wellness. There is a lack of national research networking among academics and communities in Indigenous health generally and specifically in holistic Indigenous mental health. The team will develop a cultural evidence-based Indigenous research network to improve mental wellness by generating data that shows that illness and crisis can be prevented with traditional knowledges, cultural safety, and Indigenous science, when applied to health systems. There are 6 research themes: Cultural safety; Indigenous holistic prevention and early intervention; Land based and planetary health solutions; Healing from trauma and reducing addictions; Enhancing wellbeing and eliminating suicide; and Translating Indigenous knowledges data to practice and policy. An Elders steering committees will govern the network. An Indigenous knowledges framework for mental health service and policy will be developed and results will have national and international impact for future generations toward ending Indigenous mental illness.

column37: Indigenous Peoples and communities have a long, often challenging relationship around research. In recent years, these relationships have healed and many communities and organizations have become leaders around self-determination in research. At the same time, Indigenous health researchers, many of whom are Indigenous women, have become emboldened and armored with ethical and effective approaches to Indigenous health research fostered by a growing network of scholars. Due in part to the success of the ACADRE/NEAHR programs, Indigenous health scholars are now flourishing across campuses and in Indigenous organizations as the leaders and the ones who "guard the lodge". In many of our Indigenous communities, we see the responsibilities of "guarding of the lodge" as also guarding our stories and knowledge, a role often undertaken by women. The Manitoba NEIHR will develop a pathway for existing and upcoming Indigenous scholars (both men and women) to work with Indigenous organizations to clear the path for self-determination over research resulting in meaningful engagement that is ethical and impactful. The Manitoba NEIHR grant develop research lodges at the Indigenous community level with four Indigenous organizations which includes the First Nations Health and Social Secretariat of Manitoba (FNHSSM), the Manitoba Association for Friendship Centres (MAC), the Manitoba Inuit Association (MIA), and Aboriginal Youth Opportunities (AYO). column36: A proposal for a Network Environment for Indigenous Health Research in Nunavut
column37: For almost 15 years our organizations have been implementing community-led research through Inuit-governed non-profit research centres, and we are ready to elevate our research models, methodological approaches, and mentorship capacity to the next level. The Qaujigiartiit Health Research Centre is putting forth this proposal on behalf of our collective of 4 Inuit-governed community-led independent Nunavut-based organizations that are leading research in various areas. Our unifying approach is that research should be used as a tool for action in our communities. Research for the sake of curiosity is not supported by our communities. Without action, there is no research. The Nunavut NEIHR will be a centre of excellence for Inuit methods, approaches, and tools, and provide training and support to the next generation of Inuit students and scholars in Nunavut. Each of the 4 'hubs' identified in this proposal are leaders in research and interventions that build on Inuit pathways to wellbeing. By coming together under the rubric of the NEIHR, we will elevate that research and these approaches to a national and international level. We will also formally coordinate and share our capacity and infrastructure to foster a learning environment for Inuit scholarship that will be unparalleled in Canada. With regard to feasibility: Since our inception, we have brought Inuit research methods into the forefront of discourse pertaining to Inuit health, and we have collectively brought more than 25 million dollars into the territory to strengthen the capacity of our communities to lead research. Qaujigiartiit, as the host institution, has a demonstrated record of excellence in the management of federal monies for the purposes of research and training, has an independent ethics review board, and has the administrative capacity to oversee the NEIHR.

column37: The First Nations and Metis Peoples' Health and Wellness Research, Training, and Knowledge Mobilization Centre (FMHRC) is a Saskatchewan-based consortium of First Nations, Metis and allied partners who have joined to apply for the CIHR Network Environment of Indigenous Health Research (NEIHR). The First Nations and Metis Centres will operate through a central NEIHR office in Saskatoon and three regional hubs (Regina, Prince Albert and La Ronge) to share NEIHR resources. The NEIHR Coordinating Centre will be co-located with the SK-NEIHR head office. Our network's Indigenous leaders are the Metis Nation-Saskatchewan, Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations, Saskatchewan Association of Friendship Centres, the Northern Inter-tribal Health Authority, the Office of the Treaty Commissioner, and Saskatchewan's Indigenous postsecondary institutes. The larger network includes First Nations and Metis communities and organizations, including established community-university partnered research teams. The structure of our NEIHR supports First Nations and Metis partnerships with university researchers to develop diverse and innovative health/wellness research, training and KM programs.

column36: Assessing the impact of residential care on the quality of life of autistic adults
column37: Research shows that approximately one third of the autism spectrum (AS) also has intellectual disability (ID) and important behavioural challenges. Once grown up, families are facing many challenges due to insufficient or inadequate services. Residential care is an important component of quality of life, yet there is still very few autistic-adapted residential programs and limited research on the evolution of autistic adults through these programs. The limitations related to their condition (e.g. language and communication impairment) make it even more challenging to evaluate their quality of life. In collaboration with the CISSS Monteregie-Ouest and the Vero & Louis Foundation, the aim of the current project is to assess the impact of an autistic-adapted residential program on the quality of life of adults with autism and complex comorbidities. In this longitudinal study, the goal is to explore whether autistic adults benefit from an autistic-adapted residential program in regards to 1) their quality of life; 2) the trajectories of their behavioral problems and 3) their socio-emotional wellbeing. To do so, 40 adults with AS-ID will be followed for 6 months before their entry in an adapted home and 18 months after their integration. Multiple biological/physiological, functional and subjective measures will be collected at multiple time points. Their evolution will be compared to 40 adults still waiting for autistic-adapted residential care (staying at home or in a traditional program). We hope that this project will give a deeper understanding of quality of life in adults with autism, and more specifically of the ways in which environmental and individual components might interact.

column36: Peer Support: Evaluating a pilot program among homeless shelter users
column37: Access to shelters can be a matter of death or life for individuals experiencing homelessness or population at risk of becoming homeless. This population includes women fleeing domestic violence, runaway youth or even people in economic hardship among others. These people generally have many and varied needs to be addressed, and also face many barriers to return to their normal life, including exit homelessness. Providing quality basic services, including availability of counseling services, can play a major role in supporting the affected individuals. In perspective to improve the quality of services in Toronto shelters, the City of Toronto wants to test a New Shelter Services Model (NSSM) program that integrates a peer support approach into shelter-based services for people experiencing homelessness. Based on their own past shelter experience and their pathway to recovery, individuals will be trained and hired to provide counseling services and support in shelters. This peer support service aims at facilitating transition to stable housing and improving the well-being of shelter users. Based on the partnership agreement between the City of Toronto and MAP Centre for Urban Health Solutions, this study aims to evaluate rigorously the effects of this Peer Support approach on improving housing outcomes and recovery among homeless individuals. Hence, this research will contribute to the elaboration of evaluation design and elaboration, supporting data collection, and rigorous analysis. In addition, it will include particularly a gender-based analysis. We hypothesize that women, men, and non-binary people intersecting with diversity factors will experience peer support differently, and this may lead to different results. In sum, this study can lead to important evidence for a new avenue for shelter programs.

column36: Using an implementation Science approach to design and evaluate an integrated service model for seniors social housing
column37: Housing an important determinant of health; however, a quarter of Canadian seniors have a core housing need, lacking access to affordable, suitable, or adequate housing. As a result of rising housing needs, more seniors have joined the waitlist for social housing. Seniors in social housing tend to live alone in poor health, experience high rates of loneliness, and have increased risk of hospital admission and nursing home placement. Toronto Community Housing (TCH) is home to 27,000 seniors, half of whom live in seniors' designated buildings; however, there is inadequate and inconsistent delivery of services in these buildings, negatively impacting tenants' ability to age in place. To better support senior tenants, the City of Toronto has been collaborating with TCH and the Toronto Central Local Health Integration Network to develop a new Integrated Service Model (ISM) to better integrate the delivery of housing and support services to senior tenants. Using an implementation science approach, the objective of this research project is to help the City of Toronto and its partners co-create and evaluate the ISM. To carry out this project, we will: a) help identify relevant stakeholders who should be involved in the implementation and evaluation of the ISM; b) employ a variety of methods (e.g., scoping review, qualitative interviews, environmental scan) to generate evidence on seniors social housing to support the policymakers; c) use consensus-building approaches to support the creation of an action plan to implement the ISM; and d) evaluate the impact of the ISM on tenancy stability and access to support services. As a result of this project, the City of Toronto will be better positioned to support senior tenant's physical, social, and housing needs. The lessons learned from this initiative will be packaged into a toolkit that other municipalities can use to develop their own social housing models for their senior residents.

column36: Second mitochondrial activator of caspases (SMAC) Mimetics as novel HIV Latency Reversal Agents for HIV eradication
column37: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV replication to undetectable levels. However, the persistence of latent viral reservoirs (VR) consisting majorly of CD4+ T cells and to some extent, macrophages allows for a rebound of viremia upon ART treatment interruption. Some of the most effective agents currently used in HIV treatment can reactivate cells that are latently infected with HIV by activating canonical/classical NF-kB pathway. But, these compounds are unable to clear out the reactivated cells and the effect is often associated with increased inflammation. Consequently, there is a need for novel therapeutics to eliminate/reduce the latent VR to achieve a stable remission of HIV. Cells that are latently infected with HIV are maintained in part by increased expression of inhibitors of apoptosis proteins, IAPs, these proteins are responsible for blocking caspase activities leading to prolonged cell survival. Second mitochondrial activator of caspases (SMAC) were shown to compromise cell survival by degrading IAPs. They further hijack host machinery and activate the non-canonical NF-kB pathway. This leads to the induction of cell death by activation of caspases. In this context, the current study is designed to investigate the effect of DIABLO/SMAC mimetic (SM) and particularly APG-1387, a novel SM developed primarily for cancer application as HIV latency reversing agent and to elucidate its mode of action and effect on viral reservoirs.

column36: The impact of loneliness on sexual behaviour among sexual minority men in Canada.
column37: Members of sexual minority groups, which include gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM), experience homophobic stigma. This can lead to internalized homophobia and identity related stress, which are closely linked with difficulty forming social connections and fewer social supports. This leads, in turn, to increased loneliness. Among GBM, loneliness is associated with behaviours that increase risk for STIs/HIV (e.g., substance use and compulsive partner seeking). This likely contributes to the fact that GBM remain at more than 71 times greater risk for HIV compared to other men. Maladaptive coping strategies for loneliness, like substance use and hypersexual behaviour, not only increase an individual's risk for STI/HIV infection, but can impair and interfere with the development and maintenance of positive social relationships, leading to only fleeting relief from the symptoms of loneliness and isolation. There are two types of loneliness: emotional loneliness (longing for a partner or a close confidant) and social loneliness (longing for a larger social network). However, the distinct impact of these two types is loneliness among GBM is not yet understood. It is also unknown whether GBM who experience loneliness may be using other means to protect themselves when engaging in ostensibly risky sex (i.e., condomless anal sex with multiple partners). Understanding more specifically how loneliness may be associated with risky sex, as well as with the uptake and adherence of biomedical HIV prevention (i.e., using HIV medications to prevent transmission) is another key component to developing effective STI/HIV prevention. Thus, the aims of my proposed project are to (1) understand which types of loneliness (emotional vs. social) are more important for STI/HIV risk and prevention behaviours among GBM. (2) Investigate whether biomedical HIV prevention plays a mitigating role in GBM's loneliness-related sexual risk taking.

column36: Polygenic variant patterns explain new pathway-based molecular models of inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has a major impact on the lives of many Canadians. Current estimates are that approximately 1 in 150 Canadians have IBD and this number is steadily increasing. It is estimated that within the next 10 years, IBD will affect 1% of all Canadians. This common disease can begin in childhood and burdens most individuals for their entire lives. The cause of IBD is unknown. However, it is known that genes play a crucial role in the development of this disease, especially in young children. To better understand the role of genes in IBD as a potential avenue to improve therapy, Dr. Aleixo Muise has established a database of the DNA sequences from over 1700 pediatric patients with IBD. More than two thirds of these individuals have had family members sequenced as well - both affected and unaffected kin. Thus far, this genomic data has been successfully mined to identify a small number of individual locations on specific genes that are disrupted that lead to IBD - so called monogenic-IBD. Specifically, our group has identified forms of IBD that have led to highly effective novel treatment strategies such as up-front curative hematopoietic stem cell transplant for XIAP deficiency and primary treatment of LRBA deficiency with the biologic drug abatacept. It is likely that in many more individuals there are multiple damaged genes that lead to disease. My project will broaden our established computational genomics pipeline approach to identify patients who have multiple damaging mutations within a specific molecular signalling pathway, not just a single gene. This could allow for personalization of therapy for more individuals. Similar approaches have been used successfully in analogous diseases, such as primary immunodeficiencies and cancer. Thus, the use of a computational genomics pipeline to identify polygenic mechanisms leading to IBD is both feasible and has the potential to directly impact patient care.

column36: The development of gene therapy as a cure for primary immune deficiencies
column37: Primary immune deficiencies (PIDs) are a group of life-threatening diseases that originate from abnormalities in genes that regulate cells of the immune system. If left untreated, most PIDs lead to premature death due to fulminant infections, autoimmunity, or cancer. In the most severe forms, bone marrow transplant (BMT) is needed for survival. Although BMT can be lifesaving, matched donors are not available for all patients. Moreover, BMT comes with the risk a devastating complication called graft-versus-host-disease (GvHD), which can lead to severe disease and even death. Gene therapy (GT) is a novel treatment which consists in collecting the blood stem cells of the affected patients and directly correcting the mutated gene by using a viral vector. The repaired cells are then reinfused into the patients, thus permanently restoring a functional immune system. This ingenious method eliminates both the need to find a donor and the risk of GvHD. My project proposes to study GT for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) and DOCK8 deficiency, two closely related PIDs that share many common clinical features including a susceptibility to deadly infections, severe allergies, recurrent autoimmunity, and early-onset cancers. Without treatment, survival is low. We first want study the efficacy of GT at curing autoimmunity in WAS, evaluating the kinetics of recovery of regulatory cells in patients currently enrolled in our GT clinical trial. We also plan develop GT for patients with DOCK8 deficiency by first showing safety and efficacy of GT in an animal model with Dock8 deficiency and show that the immune defects can be corrected, before moving on to clinical trials. This research will lead to improved treatment modalities for these two devastating diseases, and hopefully pave the way for future applications of GT in other similar diseases.

column36: Identification and mitigation of oxidized phospholipids as a novel mediator of neurodegeneration in the central nervous system.
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is currently an incurable autoimmune disease of the brain and spinal cord. Patients are afflicted with deteriorating MS for life. We aim to explore new mechanisms that cause nerve destruction during MS to provide better treatments for all MS patients. During MS, inflammation and myelin loss around neurons can result in the production of harmful molecules such as oxidized lipid molecules, which are reactive and can kill cells to cause permanent damage in the lesions. It is therefore important to understand the biology of these reactive lipid molecules in MS lesions, and if their removal by immune debris-removing cells such as the microglia may slow or stop disease progression. In addition, as MS is a life-long disease, it is important to evaluate if the ability of immune cells to remove oxidized lipid molecules becomes worse during disease progression, and if so, how this process may be rejuvenated. Thus, we propose new models to interrogate the harmful consequences of reactive lipid molecules in the central nervous system and the capacity of immune cells to help their clearance. We will also test for promising therapeutic targets and aim to repurpose cost-effective generic medications such as indapmide to promote neuroprotection from these oxidized lipid molecule.

column36: The fabric of the primate neocortex and the origin of mental representations. From transcriptomics to single neurons and neuronal networks.
column37: Mental representations are at the essence of high-level cognition. They allow us to memorize information for a matter of seconds and use it or are erased in the near future. Mental representations that are independent from sensory and motor signals are thought to arise in primates with the development of the prefrontal cortex. It has been speculated that the same features of the neocortex that allow mental representations to reach its high level of abstraction in humans are the key to our knowledge of mental diseases such as Schizophrenia and other psychosis where mental representations and reality become intermingled. This proposal studies the specializations that allow primates to generate mental representations with these qualities. We study primate brains across species at multiple levels, from molecules to single neurons to networks. Finally, we elaborate on a theoretical and computational model of the primate neocortex that explains at a mechanistic level how mental representations arise and have evolved across species. We pooled the efforts of an international team, USA, Germany and Canada, of experts in different disciplines organized into four International Research Groups (IRGs). IRG1 study mental representations in behaving primates and record the activity of hundreds of neurons during naturalistic tasks. It also manipulates the receptors and chemical systems of the brain to investigate essential mechanisms and their functioning during behavior. IRG2 investigates how neurons fire, their morphology, their connectivity profiles and their chemical regulation in brain slices providing a microscopic picture of brain circuits. IRG3 investigates mRNA and protein expression in different cell types across the brain of different species of primates. IRG4 uses modelling tools to synthesize the knowledge of all the other groups and produce a comprehensive picture with mechanistic insight into the functioning of mental representations in the primate brain.

It has been speculated that the same features of the neocortex that allow mental representations to reach its high level of abstraction in humans are the key to our knowledge of mental diseases such as Schizophrenia and other psychosis where mental representations and reality become intermingled. This proposal studies the specializations that allow primates to generate mental representations with these qualities. We study primate brains across species at multiple levels, from molecules to single neurons to networks. Finally, we elaborate on a theoretical and computational model of the primate neocortex that explains at a mechanistic level how mental representations arise and have evolved across species. We pooled the efforts of an international team, USA, Germany and Canada, of experts in different disciplines organized into four International Research Groups (IRGs). IRG1 study mental representations in behaving primates and record the activity of hundreds of neurons during naturalistic tasks. It also manipulates the receptors and chemical systems of the brain to investigate essential mechanisms and their functioning during behavior. IRG2 investigates how neurons fire, their morphology, their connectivity profiles and their chemical regulation in brain slices providing a microscopic picture of brain circuits. IRG3 investigates protein expression in different neuron types across the brain of different species of primates. IRG4 uses modelling tools to synthesize the knowledge of all the other groups and produce a comprehensive picture with mechanistic insight into the functioning of mental representations in the primate brain.

column36: Phylogenetically informed models of human immunodeficiency virus latent reservoirs in individuals on combination antiretroviral therapy
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus or HIV, the cause of acquired immune deficiency syndrome or AIDS, continues to contribute to a widespread epidemic in Canada and the world. Although HIV infection can be managed during the full normal lifespan of infected individuals with combination antiretroviral therapies, these therapies cannot cure HIV infection because of the presence of "latent" HIV integrated into the individual's cells that the drugs cannot target. Elimination of each copy of HIV in an individual is necessary for HIV cure, since latent HIV in the latent reservoir can "wake up" at any time to restart the infection. However, there are many gaps in the understanding of latent HIV; it is currently contested whether the latent reservoir is continuously added to throughout the course of infection or whether reservoir contribution is concentrated to a specific period of infection and whether HIV is truly latent on therapy or if there are low levels of replication is still unclear. HIV's fast mutation rate and short life cycle "stamp" the viruses with measurable signatures of evolution. I plan to exploit the virus' evolutionary patterns by developing methods to learn from the virus including: a computer simulation of the latent reservoir, a phylogenetic dating technique that uses the evolutionary relationships of the viruses to infer when the viruses entered the reservoir and an advanced statistical (Bayesian) method that models the migration of HIV throughout the body. With these methods I will glean information on the timing of HIV integration into the latent reservoir, locations and pathways used by latent HIV and whether or not there is ongoing replication in the presence of therapy. Since every copy of HIV must be eliminated to cure HIV including in the latent reservoir, it is important to accurately understand the dynamics of the reservoir. A cure for HIV will eliminate transmission of HIV from cured individuals and will be a significant asset to end the pandemic.

column36: The Cedar Project: Healing-centered care for urban Indigenous young people who use drugs in British Columbia
column37: Background: Colonialism weakened cultural buffers that traditionally helped Indigenous people cope with stress. Historical and intergenerational trauma (complex trauma) are passed down through generations of Indigenous families and communities and can lead to health challenges like higher chance of HIV and HCV transmission. Evidence suggests high numbers of Indigenous young people are impacted by complex trauma. The ways the mind, body and spirit react to trauma have been linked to negative health outcomes for people who use drugs, but traditional resources are known to help manage these challenges. There is a shortage of research in Canada that looks at complex trauma in urban Indigenous young people who use drugs, and positive action interventions that are built with culture. My research will support a land-based positive action intervention that is connected to culture and focused on healing complex trauma experienced by urban Indigenous young people who use drugs. Objectives: 1) Search the literature for important elements of interventions for complex trauma among urban Indigenous young people who use drugs; 2) find factors that protect against negative health outcomes among participants in the Cedar Project through survey data analysis; 3) map wise practices in response to complex trauma among health organizations in urban areas; 4) Engage with young people and elders through ceremony to explore Indigenous perspectives on harm reduction and positive action. Methods: An Indigenous approach is needed to help build an intervention for complex trauma among Indigenous young people who use drugs. The Cedar Project is an ongoing CIHR-funded cohort study that monitors HIV and HCV among 600-1000 Indigenous young people aged 14-30 who use drugs in Vancouver and Prince George, BC. I will co-design my study, including a protocol for integrated knowledge translation, in collaboration with participants, community members and knowledge keepers.

column36: Assessing the impact of bloodborne infections and treatment on non-communicable chronic diseases in a population-based cohort
column37: Despite advances in prevention, care and treatment, many people around the world and in Canada suffer from bloodborne infections (BBIs) caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). These infections are not only directly linked to detrimental health outcomes, but are also linked to chronic diseases such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular diseases. The advance in infection care and management has prolonged the life expectancy of people with chronic infections, and in turn, they are now at higher risk of other chronic diseases and complications. Social and health conditions can also accelerate disease progression in people living with BBIs. Currently, the knowledge on the impact of these infections on chronic diseases is limited. The evidence is especially scarce in population-based data accounting for other health, social and environmental factors. This project aims to study the impact of HBV, HCV and HIV mono- and co-infections on diabetes, chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular diseases, accounting for social and health conditions. Furthermore, new highly effective and well-tolerated drugs called direct-acting antiviral agents are expected to provide a protective effect in people living with chronic hepatitis C. The project will look at the real-world impact of this drug on reducing the risk of chronic diseases. This study will use a large population-based data including over 2 million individuals tested for HBV, HCV and HIV in British Columbia (BC), BC Hepatitis Testers Cohort. The cohort is linked with other databases such as chronic disease registry, medical visits, hospitalizations, drug prescriptions and vital statistics. Using this data will allow a comprehensive understanding of the impact of chronic HBV, HCV and HIV infections. Ultimately, the findings of this study will help to create targeted care and disease management strategies for people living with chronic infections.

column36: Addressing Communication Barriers in Clinical Encounters between Health Care Providers and Pregnant People with Obesity
column37: Physiological health risks often accompany obesity, in addition to psychosocial challenges due to weight-related stigma, including in the healthcare setting. Over 14 million people worldwide have obesity in pregnancy, which elevates the risk of a multitude of severe adverse outcomes for both mother and baby, in the short and long term. It is essential that these risks are communicated to patients, to ensure they are aware of any differences in care and the poor outcomes that may ensue. However, there is evidence suggesting a communication divide between providers and patients, as well as a distance between them in their understanding and approaches to obesity, complicated by stigmatizing attitudes amongst professionals. Given the health implications of unproductive clinical encounters and the difficulties facing this population, we seek to explore and improve the obesity-in-pregnancy clinical encounter through qualitative methodologies. Informed by narrative inquiry and stigma theory, we will conduct individual interviews to attain a greater understanding of stakeholder narratives that shape this clinical encounter, by elucidating patients' and providers' past experiences concerning communication of excess weight and associated risks. We then will implement the Brokered Dialogue to catalyze movement towards bridging the apparent divide between providers and patients in obesity-in-pregnancy care, in which we will provide a platform for stakeholders to share ideas and concerns with each other on the topic without in-person communication, using film as the arts-based research tool. We aim to devise strategies for clinicians to appropriately counsel on risks in obese pregnancies, and seek to enable stakeholders to understand the complex perspectives behind obesity in healthcare; both in management and the living with it. The final Brokered Dialogue film will be applied to a variety of settings namely for advocacy, clinical and research translational purposes.

column36: Translating milk pharmacokinetic data into infant plasma level prediction: an application of population pharmacokinetics and infant physiologically-based population pharmacokinetic models to predict drug exposure to breastfeeding infants
column37: Breastfeeding protects the mother and infant against a wide range of diseases and promotes infant development. A staggering 13.8% of all deaths of children <2 years old (823,000 deaths/year) could be prevented if all infants breastfed. Although the choice to breastfeed is clear, mothers taking medication often make a decision not to breastfeed and affect infant health, or to stop taking drug therapy and consequently affect maternal health. A main contributor to this mother-infant health problem is the lack of pharmacokinetic (movement of drugs in the body) information of drug secretion into breast milk and resultant levels of the drug in infant blood. This information is needed for risk assessments and clinical recommendations but is hard to attain as lactating women and infants are typically excluded from the drug development process. Mothers needing to give multiple milk samples on a strict timeline is a main barrier. To overcome this challenge, I am working with SickKids clinical collaborators to be the first to combine two mathematical modeling strategies: population milk-pharmacokinetic and infant physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, which we coin the "miPBPK approach". This approach allows mothers the flexibility to give milk samples at convenient times. My research is to develop the population milk-PK models to provide dose information for input into the infant PBPK models, and predict drug exposure to infants with the resulting miPBPK models for our study drugs. As such, the goal of my project is to predict how much of the drug may appear in infant blood to help inform breastfeeding decisions. As an impact, new knowledge predicting low risk of a drug to infants may support mothers to breastfeed and continue their therapy, leading to improved maternal and infant health outcomes. This new study framework has potential to guide the design of future mother and infant risk assessment studies in drug development and post-market settings.

column36: Transfer of Sinonasal Microbiota from a Healthy Donor to Treat Refractory Chronic Rhinosinusitis in Recipient Patient, A Prospective Safety and Efficacy Study
column37: Patients with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) have chronic inflammation located in the paranasal sinuses. This causes symptoms such as congestion, difficulty breathing, pain, pressure, and reduced sense of smell and taste. CRS can occur when the sinuses become blocked and filled with fluid and cause a sinus infection. Research has shown that persistent bacterial infection and bacterial biofilm formation, which is a collective of microorganisms that grow on surfaces, can be found in patients with reoccurring CRS. Current methods for treating CRS have been largely unsuccessful and could potentially lead to increased antimicrobial resistance. An imbalance in the bacteria, called dysbiosis, is linked to diseases like CRS. The community of bacteria in the sinuses, called the sinonasal microbiome, can become disrupted in patients. Sinonasal microbiota transplant (SNMT) is a new proposed therapy and the mechanism is not known. We hypothesize that SNMT, which is transferring healthy microorganisms from a healthy donor to the sinus cavity of a patient, could be a new and advanced form of therapy for CRS patients. It would work by re-colonising the diseased sinus cavities with healthy donor microbiota, thereby producing a newly intact and functional microbiota. We would like to investigate whether SNMT will change the microbiota of CRS patients, thereby preventing recurrence of sinus infections. We will assess clinical parameters of the patients to assess safety of SNMT and assess efficacy of SNMT by characterizing the microbiome. If this SNMT approach is successful, this could result in new treatment options for patients with CRS. CRS is known to be debilitating and patients suffer with chronic symptoms and complications. This could provide relief of symptoms, reduce disease burden, and help improve their quality of life.

column36: Roles of HcpE and DsbK in virulence of Helicobacter pylori.
column37: Helicobacter pylori (HP) is a bacterium that infects chronically up to 50% of the world's population and can cause gastric ulcers and cancers. It was estimated that HP colonization increases the risk of gastric cancer approximately 10-fold. In 2012, gastric cancer was the 5th most malignant cancer. Because of its high prevalence and the severity of the diseases, HP significantly burdens the health care system. Effectively treating HP infections is key to prevent these serious diseases but current treatments are cumbersome, poorly tolerated by patients, and jeopardized by antibiotic resistance. Thus, we are looking for alternatives. Upon detection of HP, the patient's immune system is activated and produces inflammatory molecules that are supposed to help eliminate the bacterium but also cause collateral damage to the surrounding gastric tissue. Unfortunately, HP can alter the normal function of the immune system so that, despite activation of the inflammatory response, the bacterium cannot be eliminated from the body. As the immune system persists in trying to eliminate the bacterium, the constant production of inflammatory compounds by the immune system damages the gastric tissue and favors ulcer formation or cancer development. Our approach is to study proteins produced by HP that trigger the inflammatory reaction in gastric and immune cells. Preventing the secretion or activity of these proteins should help the immune system regain control and clear the infection. Our study will determine the role of these proteins in inflammation using different types of cells, and will identify protein(s) from gastric cells that our proteins interacts with to perturb the normal function of gastric cells. This could be used to design new therapeutics that can inhibit the interaction between these bacterial proteins and their gastric cell targets. The inhibitors, used alone or in combination with existing treatments, should significantly improve outcomes of anti-HP therapies.

column36: Host response modulation results in altered Ebola virus replication and transcription kinetics in immune-privileged testis, which facilitates asymptomatic and persistent infections that may affect reproductive health and sexual transmission
column37: The current Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has resulted in more than 2,900 infections and 1,900 fatalities, with no end in sight. This outbreak is already the second largest in history; the largest only ended three years ago after causing 11,000 fatalities in West Africa. It appears that Ebola virus disease outbreaks are occurring more frequently and with increasing complexity, taking longer to resolve and affecting more people than ever before. Improved epidemiological surveillance, community outreach, and Ebola virus vaccines and therapeutics are being implemented to combat the current outbreak, yet new infections continue to occur. Efforts to respond to Ebola virus disease outbreaks are complicated because Ebola virus persists in the reproductive tracts of male disease survivors after recovery. Persistent Ebola virus disease infections can last for years, are not detectable in blood samples, and occur in the absence of disease symptoms. Critically, the virus can be transmitted sexually from these survivors, which leads to new chains of transmission and increases the duration and magnitude of outbreaks. In an era where globalization has enabled rapid mass movement of people over long distances, persistent and undetected Ebola virus infections could lead to global outbreaks. Despite the danger that persistent Ebola virus infections pose to public health, these infections are not well characterized; why are there no associated disease symptoms or abnormalities in the afflicted reproductive tract, how does the virus persist so long, and what danger does the virus pose during persistence? My goal is to determine how Ebola virus persists in the male reproductive tract, what effect this has on reproductive health, and how frequently sexual transmission occurs. This study will aid in development of therapeutics for persistent EVD infections and limit the risk that male survivors pose to their families and community.

column36: Cannabis for symptom management in children with cancer: a demonstration project by the Canadian Childhood Cannabinoid Clinical Trials (C4T) platform
column37: Unregulated cannabis products are currently being used by children with cancer for a variety of reasons including pain, sleep, nausea and as a cancer treatment. In Canada, no cannabis product has received Health Canada licensing approval for use in children. Without research evidence many doctors are hesitant to recommend cannabis products for children with cancer. Parents desperate for effective treatments and armed with anecdotal information from case reports and social media are obtaining cannabis products (e.g. online or storefront clinics). In order for doctors to feel confident in advising parents on the use and dose of cannabis they need better information on whether these products work and if they are safe. To address this goal, we established a national team of researchers, doctors, nurses, pharmacists, policy makers, youth and parents, called C4T. Our goal is to better understand the risks and potential benefits of medical cannabis use in children with cancer. Our diverse study team will determine how parents and youth are currently using cannabis products in cancer and what the reason for use is. C4T will review the literature and conduct a real-world study with children with cancer who are already using cannabis to try and establish a dose-response. C4T will use this information to create educational tools for doctors, youth and parents as well as to develop large scale studies to test the benefits and safety of medical cannabis products for children compared with existing treatments/standard of care. There is a large knowledge gap on if and when cannabis products can be used safely by children with cancer and other chronic health conditions. To ensure people can use our findings, we will create and update an online resource hut that is accessible to the public. Our research team is well equipped to fill this knowledge gap and continue to conduct high-quality research on cannabis for a variety of health conditions in children.

column37: Enteroviruses (EVs) are common human pathogens associated with a broad spectrum of diseases, including various neurological disorders, such as poliomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and non-polio flaccid paralysis, particularly in infants and children worldwide. Autophagy is a "self-eating" process in cells by which cells recycle damaged proteins and/or cell parts, called organelles. Autophagy is an important cellular response to limit viral growth and further infection. However, increasing evidence suggests that this pathway can be "hijacked" by EVs to ensure their successful infection of host cells. We discovered that EV infection disrupts the normal process of autophagy, resulting in enhanced viral replication/release and impaired clearance of damaged proteins that clump together and are toxic to the cells. We further showed that several proteins involved in the regulation of autophagy are broken down upon viral infection through the action of virus-encoded proteins. Despite the demonstrated importance of autophagy in EV infections, the exact mechanism by which EVs subvert this pathway and the functional significance of the resulting protein breakdown remain largely unclear. In addition, the possible value of autophagy-based anti-EV inhibitors has not been studied. In this project, we propose to: (1) investigate the mechanism by which EVs interfere with the process of autophagy; (2) determine the outcome of impaired function of lysosome (an organelle that contains digestive enzymes required for autophagy-mediated recycling); and (3) develop anti-viral inhibitors based on the mechanism identified in cells that prevent EV-mediated disruption of autophagy. These studies will provide new information and advance our understanding regarding the factors that govern successful viral infection and contribute to disease progression. Results generated from these studies also offer a potential to identify new strategies to prevent and treat EV infections.

column36: Canadian Users of Cannabis Smoke Study (CANUCKs): Impact on Lung Health via Clinical, Imaging, and Biologic Measures
column37: Almost 5 million Canadians smoke cannabis, but the effect that cannabis smoking has on their lungs is unclear. Some people think there is no harm caused by cannabis smoking, while others believe that cannabis smoking can significantly damage the lung like cigarette smoking does. Our study will look at a large population of around 1,200 Canadians to help settle the debate. We aim to describe what happens to the lung after cannabis smoking on multiple levels, looking at important health events and outcomes, breathing tests, imaging, and airway cells collected through a procedure called bronchoscopy. How all of these change in comparison to people who have never smoked and people who smoke cigarettes will be tested. The findings will help Canadians understand the long-term effects of cannabis smoking on their lungs. As well, they will help inform health care workers who will be counselling patients on cannabis smoking and potentially treating lung diseases that may be associated with cannabis smoking. Our analyses of the overall impact of cannabis smoking on the Canadian health care system from a cost and resource standpoint will also help to guide policy makers and health economists as to the burden of cannabis smoking on the Canadian health care system.

column36: Maternal-infant dyad health outcomes: infant neurodevelopment in the context of maternal cannabis use - a prospective cohort study
column37: In October 2018, recreational cannabis became legal in Canada; before then medical use was legal. Babies are exposed to cannabis their mothers use during pregnancy and through breastmilk. Research-informed information for parents and families is scarce and pregnant women receive mixed messages around the safety of cannabis. The Canadian government recommends avoiding it since there is no known safe level to use during pregnancy. Exposures have a higher risk of causing permanent health changes in growing and developing babies. Long term outcomes of cannabis exposure are not known. Some teens who use cannabis have permanent brain changes and an increased risk of mental health problems. Much less is known about second-hand cannabis exposure, especially in young children. We do not know whether cannabis smoke exposes children to biologically significant levels of cannabis. This study will follow women from early pregnancy until their babies are 18 months old. Mothers will report if, when and how they use cannabis. Their sleep, activity, mental and physical health and the baby's birth, development, behavior and health will be monitored, including a formal assessment at 18 months. The family will use an air quality monitor and passive environmental samplers for mothers and babies. They will also complete an environmental assessment. Breastmilk and urine will be tested for cannabis to see if babies absorb cannabis used by mothers. Passive sampler analyses will provide evidence of other exposures that could confuse the picture, like tobacco smoke and air pollution. Sleep and mood are related and impact development, so maternal and infant sleep will be monitored. Cannabis, used medically and for recreation, presents potential risks and benefits to expectant mothers and families. This study will provide valuable information to help families make informed choices about cannabis and set the stage for future research on the long term effects of cannabis exposure on children.

column36: Pan-Canadian network to investigate cannabis use in pregnancy and neurodevelopmental outcomes in children
column37: Even before legalization, cannabis use has been increasing in Canada, including among new and expectant parents. Cannabis use in pregnancy may harm fetal brain development and impact the long-term well-being of children and their families. The existing scientific literature is inconclusive and outdated. We are proposing a Pan-Canadian network of researchers, health care providers, decision-makers and families to lead a contemporary research program that will address knowledge gaps in our understanding of the risks of cannabis exposure to babies, mothers, and their families. Over the next five years, we aim to determine the likelihood of developmental impairments in children due to perinatal cannabis exposure. We will build a national database using existing Canadian pregnancy cohorts, perinatal registries, and novel data collection. Our research will identify "windows of susceptibility" to cannabis for the developing brain by analyzing biological samples collected from mothers and infants in the perinatal period. We will also seek the experiences and perspectives of new and expectant parents, and their care providers to develop reliable, accessible and easy-to-understand public resources that support informed decision-making about cannabis use in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Our proposed Network will be a sustainable platform for ongoing research on cannabis use in pregnancy in Canada. Our results will improve the transmission of knowledge around cannabis in pregnancy and contribute to better care and outcomes for infants, families and Canadian society.

column36: Impact of Cannabis Use on Indigenous Peoples' Oral Health
column37: The legalization of non-medical cannabis in 2018 has raised many questions about the health effects associated with the drug's use. For instance, emerging evidence associates smoking cannabis with several oral diseases, including oral cancers. However, the effects of cannabis use on the oral health of Indigenous youth and adults are unknown. This study addresses stakeholder priorities and the impact increased cannabis use has on the already disproportionate burden of illness borne by Indigenous Peoples. Self-identified cannabis users and non-users, ages 18 to 44 years, will be recruited from partnering Indigenous communities and neighboring non-Indigenous communities, with each group followed for three years. Baseline and yearly comprehensive oral health examinations will be conducted by calibrated dentists. Saliva samples will be collected to monitor salivary constituents. Saliva and urine analyses will assess cannabis exposure. Non-invasive sensory tests will measure pain sensitivity in the orofacial region. Oral health outcomes will include: oral mucosal lesions, periodontitis, dental caries, changes in oral microbial composition, and abnormal sensory function. We hypothesize cannabis use in Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations is associated with: 1) a shift in the oral inflammatory signature that promotes the progression of pre-malignant lesions to oral cancers; 2) a distinctive salivary bacterial fingerprint; 3) a shift in the proteins in saliva reflecting a higher incidence of periodontitis and early-stage oral cancers, and; 4) oral and facial somatosensory changes dependent on drug use. The Indigenous Learning Circle model will be used throughout to share knowledge around the oral health risks of cannabis consumption and the drug's impact on Indigenous communities. The Circles will also be used to evaluate the research outcomes through the lens of the community so as to inform policy and recommend measures that promote cessation and harm reduction.

column36: A prospective translational model of the therapeutic potential of cannabidiol in reducing acute pain symptoms and opioid usage following traumatic injury.
column37: Recreational cannabis is legal in Canada since October 2018. Based on Colorado's experience, the first U.S. state to have legalized recreational cannabis in 2014, effects on Canadians' health are to be expected including: 1) increased recreational cannabis use; and 2) increased risk of traumatic injuries. Traumatic injuries are associated with an increased risk of chronic pain especially when peripheral orthopedic injuries (i.e., bone fracture) are combined with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Following a traumatic injury, opioid therapy is common despite the high risk of addiction/misuse/diversion as there is no other alternative to relieve severe pain. In parallel, cannabidiol (CBD) is emerging as a potent anti-inflammatory agent extracted from the cannabis plant which could promote pain relief and reduce opioid use after traumatic injuries. However, the low quality of clinical evidence on the safety and action mechanisms of CBD along with the lack of knowledge on interactions with opioids contribute to physicians' hesitation to adopt CBD as a regular therapeutic tool to relieve pain symptoms. The ongoing opioid crisis coupled with cannabis legalization in Canada therefore calls for an intersectoral strategy aiming to determine the potential of cannabinoids as co-analgesic agents for the treatment of pain, especially in vulnerable multi-trauma patients. To this end, expertise from 5 Canadian universities and a patient-expert partnership have led to an action plan with 4 main deliverables providing: 1) The first clinical assessment of the therapeutic potential of CBD for acute pain alleviation after multi-trauma; 2) A long-term assessment of CBD treatment effects on pain symptoms and trauma outcomes; 3) Using animal models of multi-trauma, assessment of interaction between CBD treatment and factors contributing to pain symptoms; 4) Scientific & clinical knowledge transfer strategy tailored to the needs of patients, practitioners, and key stakeholders.

column36: Cannabis-based precision medicine for osteoarthritis therapy
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of disability, in part due to a lack of effective treatment options. Cannabis offers a potential treatment for OA, however, little research has been done on this topic. Cannabinoids are the main active components in cannabis. The most abundant cannabinoids are delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and cannabidiol (CBD). There are many causes and types of OA, so it is likely that any therapeutic (or harmful) effect of cannabis will vary based on characteristics of the patient, and levels of cannabinoids in the cannabis strain used. We propose to study the characteristics of the patient and of the cannabis that predict how well cannabis works for treating OA. First, we will do studies in mice that have OA to examine the effect of different cannabinoids on different types of OA. Specifically, we will measure the effect of THC, CBD, and THC+CBD on mice's pain, motor function and cognitive functions. Second, we will collect joint tissue and blood samples from patients undergoing knee surgery to measure whether the tissues respond to each type of cannabinoid. We will also identify traits in the patient's tissue and blood that predict whether their tissue will respond to cannabinoids. Third, we will carry out a study in patients with OA who use cannabis to manage their OA symptoms. We will measure each patient's daily pain scores, OA type, traits in their blood, and the concentration of CBD and THC from a sample of their cannabis. We will test whether each of these pieces of information predict a patient's pain scores. Our research could create evidence for or against using cannabinoids for treating OA symptoms. These results may help physicians and patients to decide whether a patient might benefit from cannabis and the type and dose of cannabis that might work best for the patient.

column36: Is cannabis a useful adjunct in the treatment of symptoms of persons with multiple sclerosis? A formal trial of CBD and THC for the control of spasticity and other symptoms: assessing the clinical effects and the basic mechanisms.
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease that manifests as relapses and/or progression. Multiple disease-modifying treatments (DMTs) are available to control the disease process. Lesser progress has been achieved to treat the multiple symptoms that MS can cause. Persons with MS PwMS, especially after 10 or more years of disease course, are frequently afflicted by a combination of leg weakness with spasticity, neuropathic pains, fatigue, sphincteric dysfunction, sleep disruption, and mood and cognition impairment. These are treated by muscle relaxants, neurotransmitter agents, tricyclics, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and CNS stimulants. The efficacy of these agents, which are fraught with side effects and drug-drug interactions, is often partial. Up to 49% of persons with MS (PwMS), have used cannabis, mostly for mood enhancing, to improve sleep, relieve pain and spasticity. A THC-CBD spray has been approved in Canada in 2005 for symptom improvement in adult PwMS with moderate to severe spasticity who have not responded adequately to other anti-spasticity medications. Now that the use of cannabis is legalized in Canada, the patient and medical communities expect the establishment of evidence-based guidelines for the proper use of cannabis. We are proposing to assess the clinical effects of THC and CBD positive and negative, in a carefully selected cohort of PwMS with single or multiple symptoms, enrolled in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, parallel groups trial of four weeks' duration. The main outcomes will be spasticity, with pain, sleep, mood and cognition, fatigue, and sphincteric function as secondary outcomes. The pharmacology of THC-CBD, as well as their effects on neuro-inflammation, will be explored. PwMS will be involved in all phases of the proposed study.

column37: The purpose of this research is to investigate the sexual health of Indigenous boys and men in the Atlantic region through a community-based intervention approach.
