Through creating spaces where respectful community-driven dialogue can lead to discussion related to manhood and sexuality, the findings of this project will help address social/structural factors that work against the gender and sexual health of Indigenous boys and men.

column36: Niikaniganaw (All My Relations) II: Continuing to Build Capacity for Stigma Free and Culturally Safe Care for Indigenous People Living with, Affected by, or at Increased Risk of HIV in Ottawa-Gatineau
column37: The proposed project, Niikaniganaw II, builds on the success of Niikaniganaw I, a 1-yr CIHR Catalyst Grant that brought together Indigenous People Living with HIV or AIDS (IPHAs), Knowledge Carriers, researchers, nursing students and staff members of six community organizations who provide health or related services to IPHAs. In a series of four full-day seasonal (spring, summer, fall, winter) land-based ceremonies and meetings that we called Niikaniganaw (All My Relations), we met to break down barriers, build relationships, and build capacity to provide HIV-stigma free and culturally safe care for IPHAs in Ottawa-Gatineau. We also pilot tested Niikaniganaw as a cultural safety intervention for non-Indigenous organizations who serve IPHAs. Results from this pilot test were overwhelmingly positive. One suggestion from participants was to expand our focus to include Indigenous people who are marginalized across multiple axes and are therefore at increased risk of HIV. In Niikaniganaw II, will partner with three academic departments and ten community organizations to achieve the following goals: (1) continue to build capacity to provide culturally safe and stigma-free care and services for Indigenous people living with, affected by or at increased risk of HIV, such as those who have lived or living experience of injection drug use, those with mental health issues, lived experience of incarceration, street involvement, and those who are 2SLGBTQ; (2) develop and test Niikaniganaw as a cultural safety intervention for non-Indigenous students and health and social service workers who provide services to Indigenous people living with, affected by, or at increased risk of HIV; and (3) document and learn from our experience through a collective reflexive practice that will result in a visual and written document that will guide others who wish to adapt Niikaniganaw to their local context. We will work with OLMCs in Ottawa and Gatineau, in both English and French.

column36: Connecting Health Assessments with INterventions for Healthy Aging with HIV (CHAIN Study): Advancing the Utility of a Short-Form HIV Disability Questionnaire (SF-HDQ) for use in Community-Based Settings
column37: Our goal is to establish a sustainable Community of Practice (CoP) - "HIV in Motion" to advance physical activity interventions with patient-reported outcomes (PROs) for people living with HIV (PLWH). It will include HIV+ persons, researchers, clinicians, representatives from community-based organizations, clinics and health centres, and community experts in Canada. Using the HIV Disability Questionnaire (HDQ) as our inaugural project, we will: 1) assess the use of a new short-form HDQ (SF-HDQ) across community-based settings; 2) assess SF-HDQ measurement properties; and 3) establish and sustain a CoP with PLWH, researchers, clinicians, representatives from community-based organizations, clinics and health centres, and community experts to advance PRO tools through integrated knowledge transfer and exchange (iKT) and capacity building. The formation and sustainability of "HIV in Motion" will overlap two technical phases of our inaugural project and lead a collaborative iKT work plan which includes online, in-person and blended capacity building and iKT activities. In Phase 1, we will assess the optimal use of the new SF-HDQ for patients and providers using a combination of interviews and questionnaires. In Phase 2, we will administer the SF-HDQ and assess it properties with PLWH in Canada. Standardized PROs that capture health and its fluctuation over time are critical to guide timely and appropriate HIV care. In earlier work, we developed a 69-item PRO, called the HDQ and demonstrated its reliability (consistency) and validity (accuracy) with PLWH in Canada, Ireland and the United Kingdom. As more adults age with HIV, there is a critical need for a brief yet comprehensive tools to inform interventions that can be equitably used by PLWH and providers. Findings will yield the first known short-form HIV-specific disability PRO developed through community collaborations while championing efforts to bridge PRO-use with interventions for healthy living with HIV.

column36: Hormones and Healthy Aging in Women Living with HIV: A Study By, With and For Community.
column37: In Canada, a woman's life expectancy is 4 years longer than a man's. However, for women living with HIV, not only is life expectancy 5-10 years shorter than for women without HIV of same age, but it is also 7 years less than that of men living with HIV. The reason for this remains unknown. This may relate to alterations in hormones normally protective of women's health and/or to social and structural factors that impact a woman's access to care. Women living with HIV more often have a history of amenorrhea/menstrual disturbance, and reach menopause earlier than women without HIV. Menopause and amenorrhea are associated with decreased sex steroid levels and accelerated progression of age-associated diseases. We herein leverage the expertise, experience, and infrastructure of the CIHR-funded BC CARMA-CHIWOS Collaboration (BCC3)- integrating established research cohorts of women living with HIV in British Columbia - CARMA (Children and Women:AntiRetroviral therapy and Markers of Aging Cohort) and CHIWOS (Canadian HIV Women's Sexual and Reproductive Health Cohort) to examine the relationship between the reproductive health of women with that of comorbidities in this population.

column36: A First Nations Community Response to Support Recovery from Opioids: Integrating Cultural and Land-based Practices with Clinical Approaches
column37: Wikwemikong Unceded Territory is one of the largest and fastest-growing First Nation communities. The community has many thriving Anishinabe people, pristine waters and lands, strong language, culture, and heritage; but the consequences of centuries of colonial oppression are also present. The most serious health issue is the opioid crisis. It has resulted in social problems, chronic drug-related illnesses, mental health issues, family violence, loss of children into foster care, trafficking of women, crime, vandalism, and breakdown of the social fabric and relationships in the community. Tribal police estimate that for each addicted person there are ten family members whose health and mental health is affected by drug-related consequences. The community is proactive in addressing opioid use and there is a strong commitment to move away from a punitive approach. The community offers opioid agonist therapy (OAT) to treat these addictions. In the clinic, patients are supported with culturally based therapies and counseling. Our pilot research shows documented promising results associated with this community-owned, culturally safe approach, but it also emphasizes that more research is needed to identify promising practices. column36: The role of the novel R2TP chaperone complex in ciliogenesis
column37: Protein folding and degradation are central to cell biology. An exquisite control of these processes is required to ensure the proper survival of the cell and the health of the organism. Protein misfolding and aggregation have been linked to many diseases including cancer, aging, and neurodegeneration. Maintaining protein homeostasis in the cell is mainly accomplished by a family of proteins termed molecular chaperones that assist in protein folding. My group identified a highly conserved protein complex, which we named the R2TP complex, that interacts with several other chaperones and adaptor proteins. R2TP acts as a scaffold for the assembly of other critical complexes in the cell. Hence, R2TP has a novel cellular activity dedicated to protein assembly. The aim of the proposed project is to determine the structure and mechanism of function of this complex using cell biological, biochemical, and structural approaches. Here, we will concentrate on the function of R2TP in the biogenesis of cilia, which is a critical sensory organelle of the cell. Understanding the function of R2TP should lead to new insights into the mechanisms that regulate cellular protein homeostasis. Importantly, the proposal will also lead to a better understanding of diseases caused by the loss of such regulatory mechanisms.

column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a deadly disease with few therapy options. Recent work has shown that leukemia cells are metabolically rewired such that compounds targeting mitochondria are able kill leukemia cells without killing normal cells. Mitochondria possess four complexes that are responsible for cell respiration and energy production. In leukemia cells, mitochondria complex II activity is higher than the other complexes. Indeed, our preliminary research shows that inhibiting mitochondria complex II selectively kills leukemia cells in vitro and in vivo. The end goal of this work is to develop new drugs aimed at extending the lives of leukemia patients.

column36: Prevalence, Burden and Reversal of Stringent Response-Mediated Antibiotic Tolerance
column37: Bacterial infections are a leading cause of hospitalization and death worldwide. Antibiotics are central to our ability to treat bacterial infections, but our capacity to cure these infections is jeopardized by increasing antibiotic resistance (where bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic). Added to this, very few new antibiotics with activity against resistant bacteria are being discovered. Therefore, it is essential that we preserve the effective use of the antibiotics we have. Antibiotic tolerance is emerging as a precursor to resistance that also contributes to antibiotic treatment failures in its own right. Tolerance occurs when bacteria are still killed by antibiotics, but die slower than usual. This means that live bacteria remain at the end of a typical course of antibiotics, resulting in infections that are persistent and recurrent. Persistent infections are associated with higher healthcare costs and death rates than resolving infections. While antibiotic resistance is routinely screened for in clinical laboratories, there are currently no appropriate tests that can detect tolerance. Therefore, the prevalence and consequences of antibiotic tolerance in terms of treatment failures are unknown and likely under-appreciated. We propose to develop a simple screen to detect tolerance and apply it to libraries of bacterial isolates derived from patients with persistent infections, thereby illuminating the true magnitude of this threat to effective antibiotic therapy. We will also investigate one of the mechanisms behind tolerance with a view to understanding how we can reverse it and preserve the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. Our research will improve the treatment of persistent infections by providing physicians with a tool to detect tolerance, as well as practical information on which types of antibiotic are most effective against tolerant bacteria. By targeting antibiotic tolerance, we aim to tackle it before it develops into resistance.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. Although significant efforts have been employed to understand the etiology of this cancer, the causes of this cancer is still unknown. Recent work has linked bacteria that reside in the gut to CRC, specifically, certain so-called "pathobionts", which are symbiotic members of the gut microbiota that can participate in disease under specific pathological conditions. Indeed, the list of pathobionts that cause CRC is growing, yet their oncogenic mechanisms are only beginning to be understood. To understand the role of the gut microbiota and pathobionts in CRC, we developed mice that harbor genetic mutations commonly associated with CRC. In addition, since inflammatory bowel diseases predispose to CRC, we have also developed mouse models of colitis-associated cancer. Using these mouse models, we show that certain pathobionts promote cancer by interacting with specific dietary factors, the immune system, or by exploiting mutations in specific genes involved in DNA repair. In short, our work is beginning to uncover the mechanisms by which pathobionts interact with specific etiologic factors to promote cancer. Using these animal models, we are now in position to dissect the mechanisms of how different factors promote CRC and develop protocols to reduce CRC incidence in pre-clinical models. We will leverage our expertise on DNA repair, microbiology, diet, and the immune system to explore the role of gut microbiota in CRC development. Our research has the potential to lead to the development of preventative protocols or therapeutics for CRC. In addition, our research has the capacity to develop diagnostics if certain pathobionts are identified to induce CRC under specific conditions. With this new knowledge, we will be in a good position to enable clinical trials to explore the use of antioxidants, or specific dietary interventions to prevent CRC.

column36: How the brain converts memory to knowledge during the resting state: a critical factor in age-related memory impairment
column37: According to a much investigated theory, most memories are initially stored as a set of synaptic links between a pattern of hippocampal (HC) activity (the 'index' code) and patterns of neocortical (NC) activity, which are distributed widely over NC modules that contain the actual 'attributes' of the memory. During quiet rest and slow-wave sleep (SWS), recently stored patterns are spontaneously reactivated in HC and this facilitates coherent reactivation of the NC attributes of the corresponding memory. In theory, during this coordinated 'replay' process, the NC extracts the gist of recent memories and modifies its connectivity weights to build up a knowledge representation structured to capture regularities in experience and to predict outcomes of situations and ones own actions within them. These internal representations subserve categorization of context-modulated inputs and the execution of, often arbitrary, motor acts that are mapped to these inputs. The foregoing provides a potential explanation for at least a considerable part of the effect of sleep deprivation and age-related sleep disturbance on memory function and the fact that disrupted resting state activity in amnesic mild cognitive impairment predicts more serious memory decline. The better the role of memory-related brain-dynamics during sleep is understood the more likely it will be that brain-interface related interventions can be developed to ameliorate learning and memory deficits. We propose to test a theoretically motivated hypothesis about how schema development and adjustment is furthered during sleep. Specifically, we will use closed-loop recording of brain activity and electrical stimulation in rodents to determine whether the association of HC and NC activation furthers encoding of new information, whereas similar activation of NC without HC reflects spontaneous refreshment of already acquired information, which may be necessary to prevent the old data from being overwritten by the new.

column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a respiratory disorder commonly caused by smoking, and is characterized by breathlessness and exercise intolerance. With this research, we will understand more about breathing efficiency, pulmonary vessel function and gas exchange in COPD patients, and find out whether improving pulmonary blood vessel function helps COPD patients breathe. column36: Understanding the Interaction of Acute Myeloid Leukemia with the Bone Marrow Microenvironment: Elucidating New Therapeutic Targets Through In Vivo Imaging
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a disease of the bone marrow (BM) that spreads throughout the bones of affected patients. Interactions between AML cells and its surroundings play important protective and promotive functions in leukemia growth, maintenance, and spread. Current laboratory experimental systems are not yet able to recapitulate this dynamic relationship outside of the body, and animal studies cannot visualize the changes in AML progression until death of the animal. Such methodologies are blind to important aspects of leukemia development and hinder the advancement of AML research. Our lab has developed a new technique, called the femur window chamber (FWC) model, that allows scientists to look directly into the bone of a living mouse and track the movements and/or changes of cells within the BM, over time. Our project will use this innovation to study AML cell biology and test the effect of various new anti-AML drugs. To do this, we will label AML cells with different colours and monitor their behaviour over time in the BM using the FWC. We seek to better understand the biological differences across AML subtypes and identify new treatments. We will also study the proteins that AML cells produce within the BM. If these proteins are found to be linked to certain disease subtypes or aggressiveness, this knowledge could help to better identify patients who would benefit from a specific 'personalized' treatment. Finally, we will use our unique FWC platform to study the effectiveness of various anti-AML drugs in real time and in the living mouse. Our goal is to uncover limitations in current therapies and find new treatment combinations that address vulnerabilities in AML biology to improve patient outcomes in the future. If successful, our project will establish an innovative new technique for leukemia research, uncover new knowledge surrounding AML biology, and help to develop new AML clinical trials.

Aims To conduct population-based cohort studies in British Columbia (BC), Canada and Sweden to examine if maternal chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, lung or heart disease) influence risks of neuro-developmental disorders (i.e., neurological and psychiatric disorders) in offspring. We also propose to investigate: -possible pathways linking maternal chronic diseases with the outcomes, using mediation analyses. -if maternal chronic illness in matched mother-sibling comparisons (i.e., analyses of mother-sister pairs) influence risks. This design accounts for familial (environmental and genetic) confounding factors. Methods We will carry out a longitudinal study of approximately 3.7 million births from 1992-2019 in Sweden and BC, with information on maternal chronic illness, pregnancy and neonatal complications, and long-term outcomes in children obtained from perinatal databases. In Sweden and BC we have access to longitudinal health data that are not available in Canada at the national level. Importance: In recent decades, the prevalence of advanced maternal age, obesity, and births to refugee mothers has more than doubled in Canada. Consequently, the prevalence of chronic diseases during pregnancy has also increased. Maternal diseases influence pregnancy and delivery complications, but little is known about impacts on long-term offspring morbidity. This will be the first study to use large birth cohorts with long term follow-up to examine neuro-developmental outcomes in offspring.

column36: Exploring the role of a mitochondrial protein prohibitin in Leydig cell steroidogenesis
column37: Steroid hormones are essential to life. They regulate critical phases of development, such as puberty, and are essential for a number of key physiological functions in our body. Inadequate levels of steroid hormones are associated with a variety of diseases including infertility, hormone-dependent cancers (prostate, breast, ovarian), osteoporosis, and autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. Thus, steroid hormone synthesis (steroidogenesis) in different steroidogenic tissues, such as adrenal glands, ovary, and testis, is finely regulated to ensure adequate amount are produced but also to avoid conditions of hormone insufficiency or excess. The fundamental framework of steroidogenesis across major steroidogenic tissues is very similar. For example, cholesterol is the common starting material for all steroid hormones. Moreover, its transport to mitochondria (a cell compartment where steroidogenesis begins) within different steroidogenic cells and subsequent utilization for the initiation of steroidogenesis, including the male sex steroid hormone (testosterone) production by the testis, is similar. However, our understanding of this essential step of steroidogenesis remains unknown. Unraveling this may open new therapeutic opportunities for a wide variety of diseases that involved impaired steroidogenesis. Recently, my team has found that a protein called prohibitin, plays an important role in testosterone production, including the functional coupling of the crucial steps across mitochondrial membrane for the initiation of steroidogenesis. However, the mechanisms involved remain to be determined, which is the focus of this international collaborative research project. Research outcomes will advance our understanding of testosterone production by the testis, particularly the role that prohibitin plays, which is entirely unknown. The knowledge gained may create new opportunities to treat testosterone deficiency and related comorbidities.

column36: Oxidative stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and its impact on liver inflammation in an aging mouse model
column37: A recurrent theme associated with aging processes is an increase cellular oxidative stress. In addition, a chronic low-grade systemic inflammation occurring in the absence of infection has been defined as "inflammaging" and represents a significant risk factor for mortality in the elderly. There are specific inherited mutations that appear to accelerate aging in humans and Werner syndrome (WS) is an interesting example of premature aging. To understand how oxidative stress causes liver diseases that affects 20% of Canadians with age, we generated a mouse model with a mutation of the mouse Werner gene that recapitulates WS including liver diseases. These mice produce a mutant protein that ends up in the wrong place in cells causing a distress in a cellular component called Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) in the liver tissue. Interestingly, treatments of such mice with vitamin C at weaning reverse all WS anomalies. The liver is an organ that plays a pivotal role in nutrient, drug, hormone, and metabolic waste product processing, thereby maintaining the normal function of other organs in the body. We found that the ER distress is caused by an abnormal increase in oxidative stress in this compartment. We thus hypothesize that a continuous oxidative ER stress causes a low but chronic inflammation in the liver of Werner mice. However, we do not know how exactly a mutation in the Wrn gene causes this oxidative stress in the ER. To answer this question, we propose the following 2 aims: 1) we will determine whether the mislocalized Wrn mutant protein affects the GRP78 interactome in the ER which is an important protein of the ER stress response and 2) we will determine how the Wrn mutant protein induces ER stress and an inflammatory signal. The results generated with our mice will allow us to identify molecular problems (and thus potential therapeutic targets) causing oxidative stress in the ER and inflammation during aging.

column36: Examining the long-term illness experiences of injured older adults to select patient-driven outcome measures in geriatric trauma
column37: Older adults (65 years and older) make up 51% of all injury hospitalizations in Canada. This number is expected to rise as the aging population surges in the coming years. The most common cause of unintentional physical injury in older adults is a fall, followed by motor vehicle collisions. The injuries resulting from these incidents include traumatic brain injury, fractures, broken bones and internal organ damage. Injured older adults receive specialized care in trauma centres that are equipped for injury management. Because of this organized care, many injured older adults will survive their injuries but their health status and quality of life will significantly change. Up to now, very little has been studied about the long-term illness experiences of older adult trauma survivors because most injury care in the past was tailored to a younger population. For this reason we know very little about the experiences of these survivors; we do not know what outcomes they consider to be most meaningful or if the way we currently deliver care to these patients will lead us to achieve these. Our study will examine the experiences of older adult trauma survivors over two years, so that we can, for the first time, describe and understand what a good quality of life after injury looks like from an older adult's perspective. Using interviews and observations, we will gather survivors' experiences from three Ontario trauma centres at 3-, 12- and 24 months after injury. We are especially interested in understanding how their survivorship experiences are influenced by sociocultural factors such as age and gender, and other social dimensions. Our study results will not only help us to understand what older adult trauma survivors experience and how they might want to receive care differently, but it will help in the selection of measures that healthcare providers and policymakers can use to evaluate and improve the overall quality of care to injured older adults in Canada and beyond.

column36: Novel mechanisms in diabetic cardiomyopathy
column37: As diabetes reaches epidemic magnitude worldwide, more diabetics face the problems of morbidity and mortality due to chronic complications. Diabetes causes scarring and damage to the heart and is one of the leading causes of heart disease in Canada. We plan to investigate the mechanisms leading to development of heart damage in diabetes. In diabetes, cells use its fuel differently and as such, causes damage to the cell nucleus. The cell's nucleus, in turn, sends signals to make additional proteins that cause tissue damage. If these processes continue, the cells ultimately fail to function. The signals sent out by the nucleus involve special types of molecules called lncRNAs. They are also known as the 'dark matter of the genome'. These molecules have been recently discovered and have a major role in regulating protein production. We plan to examine how lncRNAs can interact with other RNA molecules and other mechanisms that change the production of abnormal molecules. We will also determine whether by manipulating these mechanisms, we can prevent damage to the heart in diabetes. The proposed research is based on several aims, each of which will be investigated at multiple levels of complexities. Our experiments will include examinations of various types of cells from the heart and the cells of the blood vessels. We will also use animals with diabetes. As well, we will use several compounds to block these mechanisms to understand how this can be prevented. Some of our experiments will focus on specific lncRNAs that we have identified in our laboratory. We will further expand our studies to examine the heart tissues removed from patients and examine whether the abnormalities identified in the cells and in the animals also occur in humans. This proposal represents a comprehensive set of studies to investigate a specific process (i.e. heart damage) in diabetes. Understanding such mechanisms will help to develop preventive treatments for such conditions.

column36: The effects, costs, and cost-effectiveness of Montreal's harm reduction interventions for people who inject drugs
column37: Background: Montreal, Quebec has one of the largest populations of PWID in the country (n~4000), and despite offering a variety of harm reduction interventions (e.g. supervised injection facilities (SIFs), needle and syringe programs (NSPs), and opioid agonist treatment (OAT)) continues to grapple with the ramifications of injection drug use including HIV and HCV transmission, and drug-related overdoses and deaths. Methods: We will use patient-level data from administrative health data sets capturing inpatient, out-patient and publicly covered pharmaceutical dispensations; local cohort and surveillance data; and published literature to simulate the effects of SIFs, NSPS, and OAT on the population of PWID (18 years and older) living in Montreal. column36: Intranasal Vaccines for Pertussis and Influenza Using Novel Formulations of a Triple Adjuvant
column37: This research aims to further develop vaccines for flu and whooping cough. These diseases affect the very young, the elderly and anyone with a poor immune system most severely, even causing death. Yet those at most risk may not be able to take current vaccines. Changing the route of administration to intranasal, and avoiding live influenza virus will expand the range of those who can be vaccinated as well as generating a more effective immune response (both mucosal and systemic). Prior work shows the lipid-based adjuvant works well in animals using a model peptide intranasal vaccine. The proposed research will combine the new adjuvant formulations with either inactivated flu virus or with peptides from the whooping cough bacteria (antigens), followed by intranasal administration of the vaccine to mice and pigs. Cellular uptake, biodistribution and tissue gene expression responses will be measured to determine how the lipids improve the adjuvant's activity. Outcomes will include evaluating the immune response to the flu virus or to the whooping cough bacteria, such as antibodies raised and other immune responses. We will also look at how the animals respond to a challenge with the infectious agent after vaccination, such as whether they get sick and how much antibodies they make. The health of the nasal tissue and toxicity will be evaluated as well. In the case of whooping cough we will also evaluate the longer-term response to infection challenge after vaccination.

column37: Muscular dystrophies are genetic disorders that afflict more than 50,000 Canadians and for which there are currently no cures. The central hypothesis of our research project, which is based on our preliminary findings, is that PABPN1 functions in a specialized nuclear pathway of gene regulation. We propose to characterize this novel PABPN1 function using various cultured human cell lines, including muscle cells, which allow for detailed mechanistic studies of human PABPN1. In addition to shedding new, fundamental knowledge into the role of PABPN1 in gene regulation, our studies are expected to further the understanding into the molecular basis of OPMD. As such, our studies may ultimately address why OPMD is restricted to specific skeletal muscles, and therefore, lay the groundwork for developing much needed therapies.

column36: Deciphering the requirement for PIP5Ks in sperm head formation
column37: One in six couples is unable to conceive, and half of these cases are caused by problems in formation or viability of sperm. Thus, successful sperm development is a crucial aspect of reproductive success. During sperm development, male germ cells undergo dramatic cell shape changes, becoming long and thin, with compact sperm heads at one end and whip-like tails at the other. Together, these features allow the sperm to swim towards and fertilize an egg. Failures in sperm head or tail formation can lead to the production of defective sperm, resulting in infertility. Although formation of the sperm tail is fairly well studied, less is known about formation of the sperm head. To understand how sperm head formation occurs, we are studying male germ cells in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster). This allows us to take advantage of powerful genetic techniques and well-characterized stages of sperm development available in the fly. Using this system, we discovered that lipid molecules called PIPs are important for sperm head formation. Male flies with mutations in enzymes that affect formation of PIPs have abnormal sperm heads and are sterile. The main goal of our research is to understand how these enzymes and PIPs regulate sperm head formation. To do this, we will use advanced microscopy, proteomics, biochemistry and molecular genetic techniques in flies. Because human sperm form in a similar way, our discoveries will generate novel insights into human male fertility. Understanding this process will eventually lead to new treatments for male infertility as well as novel approaches to developing male contraceptives.

Although the enlargement of the heart can initially help in maintaining adequate blood flow to the body, excessive growth can lead to heart failure. However, fibrosis is essential for the heart to heal following myocardial infarction. Similar to a telephone network, information is transmitted into cells, including cells in the heart, by signalling networks. Information is also distributed within cells by signalling molecules, known as kinases, in a manner similar to a telephone operator directing a call to the intended person. When this information arrives, the cell responds. ERK3 and ERK4 are kinases in cells in the heart known as fibroblasts (ERK3) and myocytes (ERK4). These studies should reveal if ERK3 and or ERK4 are useful targets for the development of cardioprotective drugs. In addition to protecting the heart, it is also possible that such drugs may result in the regression of heart disease.

column37: Our bodies rely on 3 major fuel sources we obtain from the food we eat; fats, sugars, and protein. However, exciting data in our lab has shown that decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes. The major goal of our research project is to understand how decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control. In order to test our hypothesis, our lab has generated genetically modified mice that have reduced metabolism of ketone bodies only in their muscles. We have identified a number of potential factors that may explain the improved blood sugar control in these animals, which includes; (1) general increases in a protein modification known as succinylation, (2) activation of a global energy sensor protein, and (3) enhanced sugar metabolism. We will use both drugs and genetic approaches to independently reverse these 3 changes in our animals, in order to determine whether they counteract the improved blood sugar control we have observed during obesity/diabetes. column36: Reducing unsafe prescribing of prescription opioid medications to opioid naive patients
column37: Opioids are a complex issue. Prescription opioid addiction due to unsafe prescribing is associated with considerable harm and economic cost. If left untreated, the mortality rate is high. column36: Role of intracellular metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 in persistent nociception
column37: Normally the neurotransmitter glutamate acts at synapses on the cell surface of spinal cord neurons to signal pain. However, glutamate receptors are also found inside these neurons, including at the nucleus of the cell. We will use molecular biological techniques to show that glutamate receptors inside the cell are the key receptors underlying increases in pain sensitivity that occur after chronic inflammation or after nerve injury. We will also study whether changes in the activity of proteins which normally anchor glutamate receptors at the cell surface, which leads to the increase in the levels of these glutamate receptors at the nucleus of spinal cord neurons of animals with persistent pain, affects pain behaviour. Since it is likely that glutamate receptors inside spinal cord neurons are key in conditions of increased pain sensitivity, it may be possible, by targeting these receptors, to develop medications that specifically reduce chronic pain, without affecting other functions of glutamate receptors necessary for such processes as memory, normal pain reflexes, etc. Another approach would be to develop drugs which prevent the accumulation of glutamate at the nucleus of spinal cord neurons, by altering the function of proteins that affect their localization within the cell. Developing drugs that can specifically reduce increased pain sensitivity mediated by intracellular glutamate receptors should allow for more effective pain treatments, as well as reducing unwanted side-effects. This should improve the therapy of the nearly 20% of Canadians that suffer from chronic pain.

column36: When Pain Drives you N. U. T. S.: A mixed methods approach to investigating triggers of the stress response and multidimensional pain outcomes in a sample of individuals suffering from chronic low back pain
column37: One in five Canadian suffers from chronic pain. Psychological factors play an important role in the perception, development and maintenance of chronic pain. These factors however are often examined without considering the nature of the pain experience that could influence these psychological responses. In fact, someone experiencing pain that frequently shoots up to an intensity of 10/10 without any warnings (unpredictable) or ability to decrease its intensity (low control) might perceive this pain as more stressful compared to someone whose pain intensity is relatively stable even if on average both individuals' pain are of a similar intensity. From the general litterature, 4 characteristics of situations lead to a physiological stress response: Novelty, Unpredictability, Threat to ego, and Sense of low control (N.U.T.S.). The objective of this study is to examine the N.U.T.S. characteristics of pain-related and unrelated stressors, combined with individuals' vulnerability to these different characteristics and their associations with pain outcomes such as appraisal, interference, and disability. The study will recruit 300 patients with chronic low back pain from a provincial cohort of back pain patients. Participants will be asked to complete questionnaires at baseline and then fill out an electronic diary daily for 7 days and provide saliva samples to analyse basal cortisol levels. Finally, they will complete follow-up questionnaires 4-8 weeks later. A subgroup of patients will also be asked to participate in an individual interview to explore their experience of the stressful characteristics of pain. Study results will identify important dimensions of the stress experience that have been so far studied in isolation in the field of pain. Such knowledge could help improve the evaluation of pain and the treatment approaches that are proposed to patients. This study may thus potentially change the way we assess patients' psychological response to pain.

column36: Health-Related Quality of Life and Aging: Measuring what Matters to Older People
column37: This study addresses a measurement gap related to assessing those aspects of health that matter to the quality of life of older persons, termed health-related quality of life (HRQL). Measures exist for assessing the HRQL impact of illnesses and conditions but these measures are not best suited for older persons who may have many such illnesses and conditions but who are still interested and involved in aging actively. Some of the existing measures use many items to assess all the different illness aspects; others use very few items and capture only an illness snapshot. Often the items are not relevant to the experience of older persons and some of the items ask the same content in different ways, something that many find confusing, if not annoying. The intent here is to develop a brief measure of what matters to older persons as they attempt to get on with their life despite an illness burden. This study will also use modern statistical and measurement approaches to create a scoring method that produces a value that considers the preferences for different combinations of health circumstances from the perspective of the older person: "If I had to have that (pain) then I would also rather have this (many interesting distractions)". The gathering of evidence to support the interpretation of the scores across different groups of people (validation) will also be conducted through this project using a mix of in-person assessments and anonymous surveys using the internet. The methods proposed are consistent with the most up-to-date and rigorous guidelines for developing and testing measures and will result in a measure that can be used to evaluate seniors in their own communities.

column37: Entamoeba histolytica is a parasite that cause the disease amebiasis, which results in 100,000 deaths/year. The parasite colonizes and live in mucus and feeds on bacteria. To initiate disease, the parasite has to overcome the protective mucus barrier to invade intestinal cells that is not well characterized. Our recent studies have shown that mucus contains structural proteins that build and stabilize the mucus gel. This proposal examines the hypothesis that E. histolytica secreted enzymes degrade a major mucus associated protein allowing the parasite to gain access and cleave MUC2 mucin to abrogate mucus protective functions. This study will define the mechanism on how disease is initiated by E. histolytica to dissolve the mucus layer, which can aid in the identification and development of novel strategies to combat infection.

column37: Climate change is expected to result in an increase in hot temperatures (e.g., the number of hot days in the summer), and these changes can result in poorer health. As hot temperatures may affect people and communities differently, it is important to determine which groups are the most vulnerable, so appropriate steps can be taken to lower their risk of illness or death. column36: Redefining blood pressure: How novel views of the arterial tree can lead to better cardiovascular risk stratification.
column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and hypertension, one of its main determinants, are major health problems in Canada. Despite enormous progress in the treatment of hypertension, the principles of blood pressure (BP) measurement has remained largely unchanged in the past century. In recent years, the reliability of standard BP measurements (using a brachial cuff) has been questioned, raising doubts as to the best way to manage hypertension. This, in parallel with a better understanding of how the pressure travels in the blood vessels, results in a new enthusiasm to find improved ways to determine CVD risk using BP parameters. In this regard, the aim of this study is to determine if various novel arterial wave parameters (central BP, arterial wave reflection and reservoir, aortic stiffness) are better at determining the CVD risk compared to traditional brachial cuff BP and other known risk factors. To achieve these goals, we will use data from CARTaGENE, a large Canadian populational cohort with available arterial wave recordings, and follow-up data from governmental databases. Overall, data is available for 17,795 participants. Through a collaboration with the Austrian Institute of Technology, we will isolate and re-analyse each recording, which will provide the arterial wave parameter we wish to study. Then, using various statistical analyses, we will be able to determine if each arterial wave parameter is better at predicting CVD than traditional factors in the general population. This would by far the largest study to investigate the predictive power of these novel BP parameters, and should provide definitive answers as to their utility above and beyond standard cuff BP. This is the necessary first step to determine if we can improve hypertension management and reduce the burden of CVD. Given the recent technological advances, these innovative parameters can easily be incorporated into devices that could be used in clinical practice.

column36: Investigation of novel host-based approaches for the treatment of tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB), is a mycobacterial infection that is one of the world's most pressing health problems. Each day, 5,000 people die from TB globally. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that TB will infect 225 million and kill 75 million people between 2015-2050. TB spreads by aerosol through sneezing and coughing, and each person with TB infects ~15 more people/yr. The lack of an effective vaccine, the lengthy treatments with multiple drugs that have serious side effects, the prevalence of co-infection with HIV and the increasing number of cases of multi- and extensively- drug-resistant TB (MDR/XDR-TB), have made the control of TB highly challenging whether in developed or developing countries worldwide. Traditional antibiotics directly target and kill the mycobacteria after infection, but these have proven insufficient to curb this disease and have resulted in the emergence of incurable, totally drug resistant TB, (TDR-TB), putting this disease on high alert by WHO. There is a clear association between the immune status of an individual, the outcome of infection and reactivation of TB disease. It is crucial to find efficient host-based therapies if we are to conquer dreaded MDR, XDR and TDR-TB. Recently, we have discovered a novel immunotherapeutic that significantly reduces mycobacterial loads in mice. In the proposed work we will investigate its antimycobacterial potential in conjunction with modified Mtb antigens to enhance Mtb-specific host immunity, and in combination with the current anti-TB drugs. These studies will contribute significantly to the investigation of new approaches, and identification of new therapeutic regimens to treat active TB, MDR-, XDR- and TDR-TB infections, and will have major impact on the health of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: Does inflammation in brain cause hypoxia, which then exacerbates inflammation: a multimodal study using the EAE inflammation model of multiple sclerosis.
column37: We have discovered that many people with MS have low oxygen levels in the brain (hypoxia). We have also found brain hypoxia in the mouse EAE model, the most commonly used animal model of central nervous system inflammation. This supports the idea that both inflammation and hypoxia responses are linked in a cycle, where inflammation causes hypoxia and hypoxia stimulates inflammation. This grant proposal will use the EAE model and novel imaging tools that are only available in my lab to determine if inflammation can cause hypoxia, and whether that hypoxia can make MS worse. We can quantify hypoxia using unique implantable oxygen probes, which we helped design, MRI and NIRS. Hypoxia could be caused by inflammation, resulting in blockage of small vessels and reduction in local oxygen delivery. We will look for this with histology. The inflammation and the loss of myelin covering the axons could cause an increase in metabolic rate. With MRI, we can measure blood flow and assess myelin loss, and with a unique light based system (near-infrared spectroscopy or NIRS) we can quantify metabolic rate. Since the imaging methods have potential for translation to patients, this aspect of the proposal will demonstrate how MRI and NIRS might be used to monitor hypoxia in humans. After determining whether there is a correlation between hypoxia, brain damage and loss of function, we will further study the link by blocking either inflammation or increasing oxygen in parallel studies. We already know that there is inflammation in MS, but only recently did we discover that there is hypoxia. This project will be the only one in Canada to have our unique mouse NIRS system and the ability to combine this with MRI to study the link between hypoxia and inflammation. We will create new knowledge on how inflammation and hypoxia interrelate, and provide new evidence on how oxygen therapy can be helpful in a condition of inflammation induced hypoxia.

column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is the leading cause of disability in the world. In Canada, the lifetime prevalence of MDD is 12% and about 1.76 million Canadians suffer from MDD in any given year. Heart beat is controlled by the brain and is regular but flexible to change in response to environmental and internal stimuli. This is a healthy feature of the heart known as heart rate variability (HRV). MDD has been associated to diminished HRV (i.e. less flexible/adaptable heart rate), and this is believed to be a reflection of abnormal brain function cause by MDD. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a treatment that stimulates specific areas of the brain by means of small currents while the person is comfortably sitting in a chair. rTMS is associate to significant improvement in approximately 50% of MDD patients and is usually well tolerated. Studies have demonstrated that rTMS may be associated to changes in HRV, but there have been no studies providing direct evidence that brain changes induced by rTMS are responsible for those changes in HRV. The goal of this study is to test the hypothesis that rTMS induces changes in connectivity between the area of the brain stimulated with rTMS (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) and deeper areas in the brain associated to heart rate regulation (anterior cingulate cortex). The methodology to test his hypothesis directly is to use a complex method that obtains three sources of data at the same time to test for direct causality. This method consists of capturing both fMRI data and electrocardiogram data at the same time that TMS is stimulating the brain. Experiments will be conducted in a group of healthy volunteers as well as patients with depression. The results of this study may have profound implications in both our understanding of the causes of depression as well as the mechanism of action of rTMS and pave the way to the testing of reliable, feasible, and easy to access biomarkers of response in rTMS.

column36: Low frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) vs. intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation TMS effectiveness in depression and suicidal ideation: a randomized non-inferiority trial
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is the leading cause of disability in the world. In Canada, the lifetime prevalence of MDD is 12% and about 1.76 million Canadians suffer from MDD in any given year. MDD is associated with suicide, which is estimated to claim the lives of 800,000 people worldwide each year, accounting for 1-4% of deaths globally. It is estimated that 30-40% of patients with MDD do not improve with medications (treatment resistant depression-TRD). Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a treatment that stimulates specific areas of the brain by means of small currents while the person is comfortably sitting in a chair. rTMS is associated to significant improvement in approximately 50% of TRD patients and is usually well tolerated. Recent advances in rTMS have led to the approval of a brief rTMS protocol, intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS), that only takes three minutes to deliver. Low frequency rTMS (LFR) has also been shown to be an effective treatment for TRD in small studies, but has never been compared to iTBS and is currently not approved by the FDA. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that LFR works as well as the established iTBS treatment for TRD. In this multi-centre, triple-blinded, non-inferiority trial 420 patients with TRD will be recruited at three academic centres (UBC, CAMH and UHN). Patients will be randomised to receive either iTBS or LFR for 30 sessions. The primary outcome will be the improvement on a depression scale. Secondary outcome will be improvement of on suicidal ideation. A secondary aim is to test the predictive capacity of a novel, easy to implement heart rate based biomarkers (i.e. heart rate variability). The results of this study may lead to the approval of an alternative form of rTMS for depression and suicidal ideation available and ready for widespread use in clinical settings, including the possibility of exploring a home-based treatment with LFR.

column36: Organoids to guide Post-resistance Therapy In driver MutAted Lung cancers (OPTIMAL)
column37: Some types of lung cancer can be specifically targeted by "designer" drugs. Most patients initially respond very well to these targeted drugs with prolonged survival, but eventually they grow resistant and stop responding. Determining which drug to offer next is a major challenge. We have developed a novel model to study drug resistance: 3-dimensional Patient-Derived cancer cell clusters, or "Organoids" (PDOs). PDOs can be rapidly grown from patient biopsies, mimic important properties of patient tumours and are amenable to laboratory characterization. We hypothesize that extensive drug testing and molecular profiling of PDOs can help scientists identify new effective treatments and help doctors to make better treatment decisions for lung cancer patients. We have already shown that our PDO models successfully mirror their original tumours. Our first aim is to optimize PDO model generation and drug testing. Our second aim is to test our PDO model system in patients: we will biopsy patients when their tumours stop responding to a targeted drug and grow these biopsies as PDOs. We will then test a series of clinically-available drugs on these models to determine the most effective treatment for each patient. Tracking the molecular changes in these models will show us how these drugs are working (or not working). Our third aim will explore the use of experimental drug compounds on PDO models to discover new agents for lung cancer therapy. The results of this study have the potential to greatly impact the management of lung cancer: 15% of lung cancers (>4000/year in Canada) are targetable, mostly in younger patients who have never smoked. Targeted therapies have the potential to convert currently fatal cancer into chronic, controllable and manageable disease. The major barrier to this promise is drug resistance. Our research will identify novel resistance mechanisms and methods to overcome this resistance, providing a clinical pipeline to personalize cancer therapy.

column36: Indigenous Health Counts: Advancing Meta-analysis Methods for Respondent-Driven Sampling and Urban Indigenous Health
column37: The Our Health Counts studies are six urban Indigenous community-based research partnerships in the cities of Hamilton, Ottawa, Toronto, London, Thunder Bay and Kenora, Ontario. Each of these studies was done using an advanced statistical method, called respondent-driven sampling, which helps study hard-to-reach communities. Meta-analysis is a commonly used statistical technique that combines results from different studies to produce one single, overall summary of the available information. Traditionally used in the area of clinical trials, meta-analysis is considered the 'gold-standard' technique as it provides a complete picture of all available information and increases the reliability of our conclusions. Unfortunately, due to its statistical complexities, appropriate meta-analysis methods are not developed for studies using respondent-driven sampling. Using advanced statistical methods, we will develop and evaluate an appropriate meta-analysis method to combine data across all six Our Health Counts study sites and provide a more complete picture of urban Indigenous health information across Ontario. Of pressing interest, early evidence from the Toronto database shows a higher rate of diabetes and opioid use relative to the general Canadian population, and a high rate of experiencing discrimination from healthcare providers. However, this single study site lacks the precision to make strong conclusions. On a positive note, this database shows a strong desire for access to traditional Indigenous medicines, which we would like to investigate across study sites in more detail. In partnership with our six Indigenous Community partners, our research team will develop these advanced statistical methods and provide a more complete and accurate picture of the health of urban Indigenous adults. This more accurate, provincial-level information will inform local Indigenous community members, health and social support organizations, and various levels of government.

column37: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is the term used to describe children who struggle to learn tasks that require motor coordination. In Canada, about 1 to 2 children in every classroom have DCD. Parents and teachers tell us these children have problems learning to do everyday motor activities like tying shoelaces, playing ball, and climbing stairs. Some research has shown that these kids are more likely to be overweight, inactive, unfit, and to have more mental health problems by the time they are teenagers. Unfortunately, many of these children are not identified, and therefore do not get the help they need when they need it. To understand how to help kids with DCD, we need to be able to determine when they begin to be less active and less healthy, both physically and mentally. The goal of our study is to keep observing a large group of children with and without DCD who we have been following since they were 4 or 5 years old. We will continue following them once per year until they are 10 and 11 years old. At each visit, we will keep measuring their motor coordination, how much physical activity they do, how fit they are, their diet, and how much they weigh. We will also start to ask the children questions about how they feel about themselves and if they are feeling anxious or depressed. What makes our study new and exciting is that we will be able to find out when children with DCD start to become less active and less healthy. Working with doctors, teachers, and parents will help us make sure that we recognize kids with DCD as young as possible so that they are able to get the right type of support, at the right time, before they become inactive, obese, or depressed.

column37: Deficient blood supply to the central nervous system (CNS) leads to several debilitating diseases. Examples of such diseases include stroke which is a leading cause of brain injury affecting 800,000 individuals per year in the United States alone and causing upwards of 150,000 deaths. To study the molecular mechanisms of stroke, an easily accessible model system in which to investigate how blood vessels interact with nerve cells is the retina, the membrane of nerve cells at the back of the eye that relays visual information to the brain. The retina is biochemically analogous to the brain and its anatomical location allows for thorough investigation. In addition, findings that are obtained from studying stroke in the retina can be translated to better understand ischemic retinopathies, such as diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity which are the leading causes of blindness in the industrial world. These blinding diseases happen to also stem from compromised blood supply to the neurons of the retina. This proposal seeks to understand how blood vessels degenerate in ischemic diseases of the CNS by using the retina as a model. Furthermore, we propose to investigate the role of cholesterol metabolism in modulating inflammation upon ischemia. Ultimately, we hope to interfere with the disease process and promote regeneration of functional blood vessels.

column37: Cognitive decline in Parkinson's Disease (PD) may occur, anywhere from 20-60%, with an impairment in one or more cognitive domains. column37: GABAergic neurons, a particular subset of brain cells, powerfully control the function of brain circuits. column37: Pediatric high-grade gliomas are rare and always lethal brain cancers. Unlike other malignancies, they harbor few mutations in genes. Specifically, we hypothesize that DNA regions that that act as switches for genes could be aberrantly turned on or off to maximize the ability of the tumor to grow. Our studies will focus on rare pairs of diagnostic and relapse samples from the same patients, as well as on patient-derived models for functional validation. In the proposed studies, we will identify the transcription factors that are turning these switches on or off. The ultimate goal of our proposal is to understand how pediatric high-grade gliomas originate and evolve, and to identify strategies to prevent relapses through new and targeted therapeutic interventions.

column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive adult brain tumor with an expected survival of under 15 months despite aggressive treatment. In the past, traditional models of cancer biology have largely considered GBMs to be a uniform mass of cancer cells. Research, however, has now challenged this notion and instead supports the idea that cancer is "heterogenous" with important regional differences in the biological programs of cancer cells. This includes tumor areas with low oxygen (hypoxia) and regions where the tumor infiltrates through normal brain tissue. These differences appear to that play important roles in cancer growth and therapy resistance. In light of this, there is renewed interest in revisiting our theories and models of cancer and addressing how the different features of GBM, visible under the microscope, affect its regional biology. To answer this intriguing question, our team will use our expertise using a technology known as mass spectrometry to comprehensively survey the regional protein patterns ("proteomes") of well understood GBM compartments from different patients' tumors to understand how they differ from one another. Similarly, we will also use advanced laboratory tools to study these critical features. By growing cancer cells in various amounts of oxygen, we will be able to closely monitor how cancer cells dynamically change their biology in different environments. Similarly, we will use advances in tissue engineering to make three-dimensional artificial human brain tissue "cerebral organoids" to better simulate how GBM grows and interacts with human brain-like tissue elements. The small size of these structures also creates a convenient platform to test multiple agents and identify drugs that better target GBM and its ability to infiltrate through normal brain tissue. Together, this study looks to improve our understanding of the regionally variable biology of GBM, and use it to accelerate the development of new therapies for patients.

If successful, this new immune therapy approach will save millions of patients not only undergoing transplantation but also those undergoing surgeries to repair their damaged tissues. Importantly, the new therapy can be applied during the current clinical organ procurement and preservation protocols thus have significant translational potential. The new approach may also minimize or eliminate the use of immunosuppressants, thus increasing the health benefits.

column37: Oncolytic viruses (OVs) have emerged as a new class of cancer immunotherapeutics. Apart from their direct cancer-killing activity, OVs promote clinically desired immune attack on cancers from CD8 T cells. This OV-induced CD8 T cell attack on tumors can be further potentiated by immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) agents, and as such, OV+ICB combination therapies are becoming routine in clinical testing. Here, OV-induced, ICB-potentiated CD8 T cells can target existing cancer cells at local and metastatic sites, and maintain protection against possible relapse even after the discontinuation of the therapy. Thus, CD8 T cell response is clinically relevant and can be harnessed to enhance the efficacy of OV+ICB therapies. The harnessing of such CD8 T cell response requires information on the MHC-I ligands [MiLs] that drive their biological activity. Unfortunately, the identification of such MiLs, usually 8-11 amino acids long, has remained technologically challenging. We have addressed this challenge by developing the next-generation of applied immunomics and mass spectrometry-based platforms that now streamline the high-throughput discovery and biological validation of MiLs. Interestingly, OVs induce two types of CD8 T cell responses: antitumor and antiviral- which are defined by Mils arising from tumors (TuMiLs) and the virus (ViMiLs), respectively. These MiLs not only shape the clinically relevant biological features of underlying CD8 T cell responses, but also can be harnessed within novel CD8 T cell repurposing therapeutic strategies to attack cancers. In this context, this project is focused on comprehensively understanding the bio-therapeutic implications for TuMiL- and ViMiL-specific antitumor and antiviral CD8 T cell responses, respectively. Our proof-of-concept multi-disciplinary study promises to identify urgently needed information on establishing effective cancer immunotherapies aimed at promoting better outcomes from cancers in clinics.

column36: Bringing relief to caregivers: The effect of mindfulness training on psychosocial, biological and cognitive function in middle-aged and older adult informal caregivers of persons with dementia
column37: Approximately 25,000 Canadians receive a diagnosis of dementia each year. Within the context of an aging population and an emerging "aging at home" culture, the number of family caregivers who provide ongoing care and assistance to a loved on with a neurodegenerative disease is increasing. Caregivers who experience distress are at increased risk of developing stress-related disorders, including depression and cognitive impairment, which may compromise their ability to fulfill their caregiving duties. Existing caregiver programs have been characterized as uncoordinated and non-standardized. Mindfulness based interventions (MBIs) show promise in alleviating stress-related ailments including depression and chronic pain. Work by the NPA shows that MBI may be beneficial for older family caregivers of persons with dementia. The next phase in this research endeavor is to examine benefits associated with a tailored caregiver MBI program (C-MBI), and to determine whether C-MBI can enhance resilience, measured by improvements in psychological wellbeing, cognitive health, and biological indices of stress. The research team brings together expertise in the area of aging, stress physiology, mindfulness, cognitive aging, randomized controlled methodology and qualitative research. Family caregivers, aged 50+ years will be recruited and assigned to a C-MBI program, a psychoeducation program (PSY) or a respite-only group (RC). Compared with RC and PSY, C-MBI is expected to result in greater post-treatment improvements in self-reported distress, biological stress, and executive functioning. This study will contribute to improving the welfare of family caregivers who are considered a hidden patient population, and will contribute to the development of standardized programming targeted for family caregivers, to promote resilience while caring for a loved one.

column36: Signatures of protective immunity against HCV
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is still a public health priority as many remain undiagnosed and increased infections in association with the opioid epidemic. Direct acting antivirals offer complete cure in >95% of infected individuals but do not prevent reinfection. Furthermore, HCV disproportionately affects some populations with limited access to health services and who remain at high risk of HCV infection and reinfection like Indigenous peoples, people who use drugs (PWUD), newcomers to Canada, men who have sex with men and others. Hence, there is an urgent need for vaccines that can protect against this virus. Unfortunately, despite our knowledge about the immune response against HCV, we still do not have an effective vaccine. Recent results from the only vaccine candidate that made it into a large scale (Phase 2) clinical trial did not show any protection in PWUD at risk of HCV infection. This means that we have to understand better the immune factors that protect against HCV. This project will examine what constitutes such a good immune response by studying immunity in a group of PWUD who are constantly being exposed to the virus where some are able to clear it several times and others cannot. We will identify the differences in those who clear the viruses and those who cannot. We will also compare the immune response in individuals who clear the virus spontaneously versus those who clear it post treatment to determine if they are less protected against HCV if they are re-exposed to it. We will use the latest technology to examine the immune response at the functional and genomic level and identify cellular pathways and key molecules that are implicated in the development and maintenance of a protective immune response. We will attempt to use chemical compounds to correct the defects observed in those who are unable to clear the virus. Such compounds can be combined with different vaccine candidates to enhance their immunogenicity and protective capacity.

column36: The Impact of Funding Models on the Integration of Registered Nurses in Primary Health Care Teams
column37: Primary health reform in Canada have introduced various funding models designed to promote inter-professional teams. Despite the recognition that appropriate funding models are critical to support collaborative primary health care teams, few studies have described these funding models in relation to the roles and functions of non-physician health care providers. Family practice nurses are Registered Nurses (RNs) who practice in primary health care. Little is known about the impact of funding models on integration of family practice nurses in primary health care. The project consists of three studies: the funding model analysis, the case studies and the survey of family practice nurses. In the Funding Model Analysis, we will identify and classify funding models used to include family practice nurses in primary health care settings across Canada. In the Case Studies, we will conduct qualitative interviews with family practice nurses, family physicians and administrators; and administer a nurse activity survey in 32 practices funded by four funding models in Ontario, Quebec, and Nova Scotia: traditional fee-for-service, enhanced fee for service, capitation, and global funding. We will then conduct a cross-sectional, online survey of the 2000 family practice nurses in Canada to gather information about funding models, nurse work activities, and team functioning. Using the different methods of the Case Studies and the Family Practice Nurses Survey, we will study how the four funding models influence the activities performed by family practice nurses, the training and skills sets needed by family practice nurses, how the team functions, and the co-management of patient care. The research findings will help provincial governments in structuring funding models that best optimize the roles of family practice nurses and realize benefits from team-based care, and ultimately improve primary health care in Canada.

column37: An estimated 670,000 Canadians suffer from heart failure (HF) with the estimated direct cost of management >$2.8B annually throughout Canada. column36: The Development of Novel Neuroactive Compounds to Combat Parasitic Nematodes
column37: Over one quarter of the world's population is infected with a parasitic nematode. These infections result in over 130,000 deaths each year. The world health organization reports that disability caused by nematode infection is equivalent to that caused by malaria or tuberculosis. Resistance to molecules that kill parasitic nematodes is emerging in human infections. Public health experts warn that it is only a matter of time before resistance blooms in nematode parasites of humans. Consequently, public health experts are asking that new nematicidal drugs be developed now. To develop new molecules that kill parasitic nematodes, we screened for small molecules that paralyze and/or kill the tractable, but non-parasitic, nematode C. elegans. We re-screened lethal molecules in human cell culture to eliminate generally toxic molecules. We then screened the remaining molecules against several parasitic nematode species. We identified a small molecule family called 'wact-45' that inhibits the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT). VAChT functions to package the acetylcholine neurotransmitter within neurons so that they are able to properly communicate with one another. Our data suggests that wact-45 may preferentially inhibit nematode VAChT. We propose to: i) better understand VAChT structure and function, and ii) further develop the wact-45 small molecule structure to optimize its potency and nematode selectivity so that it is safe for use in humans who are infected with nematode parasites. Parasitic nematodes infect vast numbers of people, and especially in poor countries. Children are particularly vulnerable, and infections can lead to disability that lasts a lifetime. Given that resistance to existing anti-nematode drugs is emerging, our work has the potential to lead to new medicines that could have a tremendous global impact on the health of some of the most vulnerable people among us.

column36: How Unequal is Health Status Across Race/Ethnic Groups in Canada? Using Census-Linked Mortality Data to Answer the Government's Call for Rigorous Evidence
column37: A strong concern has been sweeping through Canada that we are falling behind other countries by underestimating inequities - unfair and systematic differences - in health status across race/ethnic groups. Research suggests that it isn't enough to only study how income and other forms of 'socioeconomic status' are related to health. Similarly, studying the health of immigrants as one big group, or even lumping all non-white immigrants together, as is done when we examine 'visible minorities' versus whites, is also inadequate for understanding inequities in the health of Canadians. We need to treat race/ethnicity and its relationship to health in far more nuanced ways. Currently, we have very little Canadian evidence on race/ethnic health inequities, and the Federal Government of Canada is clamouring for this evidence. This proposal will use Statistics Canada data to produce this evidence. We aim to: (a) determine the extent of inequities (differences) in chances of dying across race/ethnic groups in Canada; (b) determine whether inequities in chances of dying are further influenced by other social and economic characteristics, such as gender and income. We are a team that is diverse in terms of gender, race/ethnicity, and the intersections thereof. We bring a lot of scientific expertise and experience in engaging government and civil society organizations on matters of race/ethnicity and health. Public Health Agency of Canada and the National Collaborating Center on Determinants of Health has endorsed our project, and we will work with them and other organizations to communicate our findings to a wide audience. We will also produce a policy brief document for decision-makers, and will publish our findings in 'open access' journals.

column36: Bioenergetic control of plasticity by astrocytes in stress
column37: Adapting to external stress is essential for animal survival, but becomes problematic when the stress is intense or unrelenting. In humans, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorders and depressive disorders can all connect to previous stressful experiences. A fundamental aspect of the stress response involves altering body energy metabolism in response to stress hormones released by the adrenal glands. In the brain, support cells called astrocytes provide energy molecules to nerve cells, thereby helping to feed synapses - the communication points between nerve cells. This process is necessary for learning and memory and proper brain health. Importantly, stress interferes with the ability of synapses to store memories, yet a potential role for astrocytes in this well-appreciated phenomenon is not known. A central question driving our research forward is: how does the energetic support of nerve cells by astrocytes participate in the responses to external stress? Using advanced genetic and physiological techniques to study mouse brains after a bout of intense stress, our preliminary findings have discovered that the delivery of energy molecules from astrocytes to nerve cells is compromised, which prevents memory formation. This leads us to test the idea that astrocytes help regulate the brain's response to stress by gating synaptic memory via the supply of energy molecules to synapses. This proposal will reveal a new understanding for how intense or prolonged stress changes the brain. This is important because novel stress related mechanisms will be uncovered and potential therapeutic targets for stress-related disorders will be identified.

column37: Fracture healing is a complex biological process that fails in up to 10% of cases despite appropriate care and/or surgery. Fracture management results in significant financial expenditures by the Canadian healthcare system while also adversely affecting the patient's functionality and productivity during the lengthy healing period. An inexpensive, non-invasive strategy to increase bone healing would not only aim to reduce this burden but also improve quality of life for patients through earlier restoration of mobility and independence. Lithium is a safe and cost-effective drug that has been the standard treatment for bipolar disorder for over 60 years. Although reports in the past demonstrated a positive link between lithium and enhanced bone repair, the actual dose, duration and timing of lithium treatment was unknown. Our previous published work in animals assessing these precise parameters showed a 46% increase in strength of the healing bone compared to the untreated group. To translate this knowledge into clinical practice, we propose to conduct a double-blind, randomized control phase II clinical trial to evaluate the effect of an equivalent lithium treatment regimen in healthy patients presenting with fractures in the mid-section of the long bones in the thigh (femur), leg (tibia), arm (humerus) and collar bone (clavicle). The proposed low dose lithium intervention treatment represents an easily translatable pharmacological approach for managing long bone fractures in patients that could ultimately reduce the tremendous burden of such fractures on the individual as well as the healthcare system to accelerate and/or predictably heal fractures.
