column36: Maternal immune cells mediated endothelial activation in preeclampsia
column37: Preeclampsia (PE) is a syndrome specific to pregnancy and a leading cause of maternal mortality and morbidity affecting over 20,000 women across Canada yearly. Affected women are at higher risk of PE in subsequent pregnancies and have elevated incidence of cardiovascular diseases later in life. Hypertension is the main clinical symptom of PE and is strongly associated to inflammation, altered maternal immune system and activation of the vascular endothelium, namely the interior lining of every vessel in the body. However, the actual contribution of the maternal immune system to endothelium activation, hallmark of hypertension, is still poorly understood. This has hindered attempts to develop new therapeutic strategies. To develop efficient new therapeutic strategies for PE we need in-depth understanding of the mechanisms linking maternal immune changes with endothelial activation. We recently published strong evidences of the presence of inflammation and maternal immune system alteration in PE. We also have preliminary data supporting that women with PE have a pro-inflammatory bias in their immune profile, that their immune cells are potent activator of the vascular endothelium and that they respond differently following exposure to an inflammatory stimuli. Building on from this work, we want to further understand how does the maternal immune system is changed in PE-complicated pregnancies and how these changes contribute to the activation of the endothelium, leading to hypertension. Globally, this work will provide in-depth understanding of the mechanisms linking maternal immune changes with endothelium activation in PE as well as how immune cells are being programmed by pregnancy. This work is of high importance to develop new therapeutic target to minimize the impact PE on pregnancy and prevent the long-term impact negative on the mother. This work is also a needed first step towards the understanding of the changes induced by pregnancy on the maternal immune.

column36: Nurse-Led Model of Integrated Care Facilitated by Telemonitoring for Complex Patients at High-Risk for Hospitalization
column37: Caring for complex patients often with multiple chronic conditions is one of the biggest challenges facing our healthcare system. These patients are managed through siloed specialists and other providers, which can lead to suboptimal clinical management, poor outcomes, and poor patient experiences. While 75% of healthcare dollars are dedicated towards the management of chronic illnesses, more than 50% is consumed by complex patients, who make up only 5% of the population. The high costs are mainly due to patients repeatedly getting admitted to hospital after discharge. This project will explore how to best implement a Virtual Integrated Complex Care Clinic and the impact of the Clinic on patient outcomes including rehospitalizations. The Clinic will include a nurse-led model of integrated care, and telemonitoring. A nurse-led integrated care model means a nurse (or nurse practitioner) is the central point person to communicate with the patient and their care team to plan and execute a care plan that accounts for all of the patient's health conditions, thereby breaking down the current siloed care. However, even with a nurse-led integrated care model, the complex patients could get worse between visits to the clinic without the nurse knowing, and frequent visits to the clinic can be hard especially for these who are very sick. Telemonitoring enables patients to track important measurements (for example, blood pressure and weight) and symptoms at home, and to send this information to their clinicians so they know their patients' health status between clinic visits. The nurse can act on the information before patients are so sick that they need to be admitted to hospital again. This will be the first study to combine a nurse-led integrated care model and telemonitoring into a clinic to help complex patients as they transition from hospital to home. It may provide evidence to support a new scalable way to help complex patients stay out of the hospital.

column36: Novel therapeutic targets for Group 3 medulloblastoma stem cells
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Medulloblastoma is really made up of four diseases, of which one type, called Group 3 is highly aggressive and has a very poor outcome. The main tumor 'lump' in the brain is called the 'primary tumor'. The primary tumor can spread (metastasize) to cover other regions of the surface of the brain and spinal cord. When children die from medulloblastoma, it is mostly because the tumor has spread (metastasized). The most damaging therapies (radiation) for children with Group 3 medulloblastoma are necessary to treat the metastases. The dream of curing cancer through precision medicine has entailed sequencing cancers to identify tumor specific mutations, which could in turn be targeted by specific drugs that are lethal to the tumor but harmless to a child's normal cells. While this model is showing early success for some cancers, it holds limited promise for treatment of medulloblastoma. Recent results from the Ogilvie Lab have shown that Group 3 medulloblastomas appear to be driven by "control switches"-the factors that help choose which genes are turned on or off inside the cells. We want to know how one of these factors, called OTX2, controls other genes, interacts with other proteins, and regulates tumor growth both in a dish and when inside a patient. In addition, we also want to determine whether OTX2 plays different roles in medulloblastoma growth vs. normal development. Understanding how these control switches help make medulloblastomas grow, offers fresh opportunities to target Group 3 medulloblastoma, prevent the progression of metastases, and decrease the toxicity of therapy for children with this devastating disease.

column36: Harnessing exercise epigenomics to protect the brain from neurodegeneration
column37: Can exercise help heal the brain and protect it from degeneration? This is a critical question that not only applies to people who have a neurodegenerative condition like multiple sclerosis (MS) but anyone who wishes to maintain a healthy brain as they age. We think that participation in aerobic exercise can alter the immune system and shift the balance from a state of inflammation towards one that fosters brain repair. We can measure levels of inflammation and markers of brain repair, such as neurotrophins, in the blood. We detect changes to brain networks using a special device called transcranial magnetic stimulation, which provides a window on brain function and integrity. The chemical switch that makes the link between inflammation and restoration is likely a special molecule called a 'microRNA'. MicroRNAs help cross talk between the brain and the immune system. This field of 'exercise epigenomics' is new and could have important implications for MS as well as other diseases that involve neurodegeneration. Beginning in 2016, we created a unique longitudinal MS patient registry and biorepository which includes detailed demographic, clinical, immune, and exercise/rehabilitation profiles. Of the 220+ people recruited, we have complete data on 84 that are eligible for this project (have mild MS). We intend to gather three years of data on at least 100 people. In this project we will investigate potential links between aerobic fitness/physical activity and the balance of inflammation and brain repair on preservation of brain function, and sensorimotor and cognitive deficits in people with mild MS. People with MS, like anyone else, want to live long and productive lives. Using this unique and powerful dataset we will be able to probe the links between lifestyle and brain health like never before.

Addressing youth needs only during the crisis of homelessness is not sufficient. Providing housing in and of itself is not sufficient. There is increasing recognition of the need for well-timed, sequenced, and combined interventions - with a focus on preventing pathways into homelessness and supporting sustained exits from homelessness. This study examines an intervention that supports youth in their transition out of homelessness. The intervention involves the provision of transitional case management, peer and mental health supports to youth who have recently exited homelessness - provided for a period of 1 year in this critical time. The study is a randomized trial comparing the transitional support intervention as it compares with treatment as usual to determine if youth receiving the intervention have better outcomes with respect to sustaining housing and making gains in other important life domains. It is work that builds upon feasibility studies that have suggested that the intervention has the potential to make a difference and is well-received by youth and youth service providers. This work holds the potential to make a substantive contribution to a field in need of evidence-based interventions and to be a part of the larger systemic effort to ultimately prevent youth homelessness altogether.

column36: Characterizing and comparing sleep-related consolidation neurophysiological mechanisms for procedural and declarative memories
column37: Memories are a fundamental part of our identity, as they guide our behavior in everyday activities. For this reason, an abundance of studies using a large arsenal of neuroscience methods has been carried out, not only to understand how memories are formed and maintained overtime (through the process called 'memory consolidation'), but also to uncover factors and conditions that can enhance one's memory capacity. This research, including work conducted in my laboratory, has revealed that the consolidation of declarative (capacity to retain facts and events) and procedural (ability to acquire motor skills) memories can be enhanced by sleep, more precisely by specific oscillatory electrical brain activity that can be observed in deeper sleep stages. Despite significant progress in this field, however, we still do not know whether the consolidation of those two forms of memory on similar or different action mechanisms, and whether it depends on the oscillatory brain activity occurring in the same or different sleep stages. To answer these research questions, we plan to conduct three studies in which we will record the brain activity during task performance and sleep. In two of these studies we will also deliver auditory stimulation during precise sleep phases, in sync with specific oscillatory electrical brain activity, that are expected to enhance memory consolidation. These studies will allow us to compare directly the mechanisms underlying the consolidation of procedural and declarative memories. Moreover, the results and technical expertise developed therein will provide a basis for the development of non-invasive brain stimulation approaches that can improve memory consolidation when this capacity is impaired by aging or neurodegenerative disease, such as dementia.

column37: We study how animal tissues are built, focusing on sheets of cells called epithelia. Epithelia form our skin and internal organs, and act as regulated barriers to compartmentalize the body for its functions and protection (e.g. containing digestion inside the stomach). Epithelial structure can also be amazingly dynamic. Simple tissues of the early embryo must grow and reorganize to form the body and its organs. Even in adults, the maintenance of organs from resident stem cells requires continual epithelial remodeling. Similarly, these sheets of cells undergo dynamic movements to repair wounds. Moreover, >80% of human cancers originate from epithelial tissues, and cancers worsen with epithelial breakdown and invasive cell migration. Epithelial dynamics are dictated by the behaviors of cell-cell contacts (their constriction, growth, loss and gain). We are studying a molecular mechanism that regulates these cell-cell contacts. We are elucidating how a contact grows, and how contact growth is coupled with contact constriction. Our research relies on the experimental work-horse Drosophila melanogaster (the fruit fly). We visualize molecules, cells and tissues with advanced microscopy and manipulate specific components of the system with genetics. The molecules that organize cells and tissues in Drosophila have counterparts that perform similar functions in humans, and Drosophila has major experimental advantages. Drosophila research provides rapid advances that inform strategies for regenerative medicine and cancer therapies.

column36: Integrating Multi-Omics, Multi-Modal Neuroimaging and Artificial Intelligence for Biologically-defined Staging and Stratification in the Alzheimer's Disease spectrum
column37: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease (late-AD) is a complex neurodegenerative condition with abnormalities in protein accumulation (amyloid, tau), vascularization, inflammation and/or cerebral atrophy. Numerous clinical trials targeting only one of these components have failed to achieve significant clinical benefits, while the treatments have not accounted for the disease's clinical and pathophysiological heterogeneity. In keeping with the tenets of Personalized Medicine, treatments need to be tailored to individual therapeutic needs as opposed to treating all patients with the same approach. In neurodegeneration, however, we currently do not have appropriate methods for pathophysiological patient staging and stratification. Furthermore, because we continue to lack robust tools to characterize each patient's distinctive disease progression, evaluating the effectiveness of different therapies remains challenging. Prompted by the imperative for customized treatment of neurodegeneration, our goal is the implementation and validation of a biologically-defined staging and stratification of the AD spectrum using an artificial intelligence (AI) framework to integrate molecular, biological and neuroimaging data. Consequently, we are integrating a large amount of biological data (including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, neuroimaging) into a simplified and clinician-friendly personalized clinical profile reflecting both disease progression and variant. This framework aims to bridge the Molecular, Neuroimaging and AI fields in order to overcome the major limitations of traditional clinical diagnoses. We will validate its clinical applicability with five different populations in the AD spectrum. Critically, all resulting analytic tools will be shared with the international community via a user-friendly software and popular web-based code repositories, contributing to translate our research findings in daily clinical practice.

column36: Role of Hedgehog Interacting Protein (Hhip) in Diabetic Kidney Disease
column37: Diabetes is characterized by high blood sugar and is often associated with several complications as a result of poor blood sugar control, the most serious complications including heart disease and kidney failure. People with kidney failure may require treatment by artificial kidney (dialysis) or by kidney transplant to survive. Despite the use of currently available medications to lower blood sugar and blood pressure, kidney function continues to decline in most people with diabetic kidney disease (DKD). New alternative treatments are therefore urgently needed. A molecule called hedgehog interacting protein (Hhip) is a key regulatory component of Hedgehog signalling, which controls organ development during gestation (in the womb) and optimizes cell functions in adults. Our recent work led to the discovery that high blood sugar levels turn on the Hhip expression in diabetic kidney, causing kidney damage. Most importantly, we found that urinary Hhip (uHhip) appears to be elevated in early DKD before the development of microalbuminuria (a hallmark of onset of kidney disease) in diabetic mice and humans with type 2 diabetes, suggesting that uHhip might be a novel indicator that could be used for the early detection of DKD, possibly identifying patients who will benefit from more intensive renoprotective interventions at an earlier stage indicator in DKD. However, several key questions regarding Hhip gene regulation, secretion and cell-to cell communication in responding to elevated glucose levels are poorly understood. My research program is to perform studies in kidney cells grown in petri dishes and in diabetic mouse models to answer these questions. Our studies will provide new insights into the processes how does Hhip causing kidney injury in diabetes and should provide new treatment strategies to prevent kidney damage in patients with diabetes mellitus.

column36: Novel Approach to Peptide Therapy for Rheumatoid Arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a painful, chronic autoimmune disease that damages joints and causes disability. RA is the most common autoimmune inflammatory arthritis affecting >300,000 Canadians. There is no cure for RA and its cause is unknown. Currently, the only available treatments for RA are non-specific drugs that modify the immune system. These drugs may improve joint damage but can cause people to get infections or even cancer. Also, RA disease flares are common, requiring life-long treatment and frequent drug changes. New therapies are needed that target immune responses specific to RA. What is known about RA is that the immune system, which normally attacks bacteria and viruses, attacks specific molecules in the patient's own body. This attack leads to joint inflammation, damage and pain. We designed a new therapy for RA that alters these immune responses so that they do not attack the joints. This therapy is mixed with a new cream that penetrates deep into the skin so that injections are avoided. Preliminary tests in mice showed that this cream therapy prevents arthritis. The goal of this study is to test if this new RA cream therapy can reduce signs of arthritis in mice. We will apply the cream therapy onto the skin of arthritic mice and monitor for joint swelling and pain behaviours. Blood samples from the mice will be studied to see if this therapy alters immune responses. We will also collect immune cells from RA patients and compare them to the immune cells from mice to determine if they are similar. We expect that the RA patients with active disease will have similar immune cell characteristics to the arthritic mice. Similarities between mouse and human immune responses to the cream therapy would suggest that it can be tested in humans. This study will identify a new and specific treatment for RA without serious side effects. The RA cream therapy is easy to use, so expanding this study to human treatment trials is achievable.

column36: Running-induced urinary incontinence in females: pathomechanics and conservative options for prevention and intervention
column37: The experience of urinary incontinence when females exercise is very common, affecting between 15 and 80% of those who regularly participate in physical activities, depending on the frequency and intensity of training. This "exercise incontinence" may ultimately lead females to withdraw from their physical activities, and the resultant inactivity can lead to poor health and/or well-being later in life. Little is known about the mechanisms that cause exercise incontinence; damage to the pelvic floor muscles or their surrounding connective tissues and pelvic floor muscle fatigue are plausible explanations. Conservative management approaches such as pelvic floor muscle strengthening exercises and intravaginal support devices (pessaries) are effective for many females suffering from urinary incontinence induced by everyday activities such as coughing or sneezing, yet it is not known whether these approaches are effective specifically when leakage predominantly or only occurs during exercise. Through this study we will (i) investigate anatomical and mechanical properties of the pelvic floor muscles in female runners who do and who do not leak urine during running to determine whether differences are evident at baseline and/or after a single bout of running, (ii) determine whether abdominal pressures or impact forces experienced during running are different between females who do and do not leak urine when they run, and (iii) determine whether pelvic floor muscle training or an off-the-shelf pessary may effectively eliminate urine leakage during running among females who regularly experience exercise incontinence. The results of this study are essential to guide prevention strategies and conservative interventions that will allow females to continue to engage in physical activities without leaking urine, mitigating their ultimate withdrawal from physical activities because of urine leakage.

column37: Neural tube defects (NTD) are due to inadequate dietary folate. NTD rate has decreased via folic acid (FA) food fortification and consumption of FA-containing vitamins. A common genetic change is a 677C>T mutation in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), which generates the main circulatory folate, methyltetrahydrofolate (methylTHF). We had identified this change, present in ~ 10% of Canadians, as the first genetic risk factor for NTD and showed that it reduced activity and stability in the mutant enzyme. We also showed that methylTHF could stabilize the TT enzyme and improve function. FA reduces NTD incidence overall but it has never been shown that it reduces incidence for 677TT genotypes because clinical trials have not looked at MTHFR genotypes. Recent data suggest that methylTHF may also be useful, or even more useful than FA, to reduce NTD rate, but this has not been tested in any trial. Our goal is to determine if FA or methylTHF reduces NTD or other developmental anomalies in the 677TT genotype, using a new 677C>T mouse generated by our collaborator. We have just shown that the mutant TT mouse enzyme is similar to the human TT enzyme (reduced activity and stability, stabilized by methylTHF). We hypothesize that methylTHF will be more effective since it is the MTHFR product and can stabilize the mutant enzyme. Our aims are to first assess relevant metabolites in male and female mice of 3 genotypes (CC, CT and TT) fed diets with variable folate. We will then provide FA and methylTHF supplements to CC and TT females, mate them with CC males, and examine embryos for delays/defects; these studies will test impact of maternal TT genotype. We will perform the same experiments with CT females, mated with TT males, to examine impact of embryonic TT genotype. MTHFR activity will be measured in all aims. Our work will help to assess whether current strategies to reduce NTD are useful for 677TT women, and whether FA or methylTHF is more effective for all.

column36: The injured peripheral nervous system and aging
column37: Damage to nerves in limbs often results in motor and sensory problems because the fibers (axons) that form the nerves do not regrow in large numbers back to their targets. Some of the ensuing problems that occur, such as motor incoordination and neuropathic pain, disrupt the quality of life for millions of humans worldwide and create significant personal and economic burden. More concerning is that regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves declines with age. This deficit has become a pressing clinical issue with the growing maturing population and humans living longer because older individuals experience more peripheral injuries because of muscle weakness and slower reflexes. Since surgical interventions are limited in their efficacy, new and specific therapies are urgently needed. Schwann cells are the glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. They wrap axons with myelin, a fatty substance that acts like an insulator that allows electrical signals to pass rapidly from one nerve cell to another. After peripheral nerve damage, Schwann cells play a critical role in creating a favourable environment for damaged fibers to regrow. They accomplish this by secreting growth factors, remyelinating regrowing axons and removing inhibitory molecules. However, the functions of Schwann cells decline with age and this contributes to the impaired regeneration and thus poor functional recovery seen in older individuals. My lab is interested in understanding why regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves and functional recovery are worse with age. We will specifically investigate whether a protein called alphaB-crystallin (alphaBC) that is expressed by Schwann cells, and whose expression in peripheral nerves reduces as an animal ages, is responsible for the deficit in Schwann cell function and thus poorer regeneration in older injured animals. This grant will also inform us whether alphaBC is a possible therapeutic agent for improving functional recovery in older animals.

column36: Reducing ovarian cancer risk by regulating age-associated ovarian fibrosis
column37: For most women, the largest risk factor for ovarian cancer is the monthly ovulation. Oral contraceptives prevent ovulation and can reduce ovarian cancer risk by up to 35%, but how ovulation increases risk is not clear. In trying to find an explanation, our lab has found that ovaries from aged mice and post-menopausal women, which have had many ovulations, harbor a population of cells that are known to suppress the activity of the immune system. These cells were not found in young ovaries. We predict that these cells play a critical role in allowing both primary and metastatic cancers to grow in the ovary. The accumulation of immune suppressing cells in the aging ovary is associated with fibrosis. We have created a mouse model that develops ovarian fibrosis and the question we are asking is: Can this process be blocked or reversed? Metformin, a drug used mostly by diabetes patients, has been shown to reduce fibrosis in other tissues, and diabetic women who take metformin have a dramatic decrease in the incidence of ovarian cancer. We therefore propose to determine the contribution of fibrosis to the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells to the ovary, determine how the development of fibrosis is accelerated in women with BRCA mutations, and explore how metformin can prevent or reverse these changes. Our results would open the door to the possibility that metformin could be used for ovarian cancer prevention in women at high risk.

column36: Decoding gene & genome-regulatory functions of the RNA gene CISTR-ACT
column37: Three-dimensional genome organization in mammalian cells is important for gene regulation. Rewiring of gene-regulatory mechanisms can cause rare disease and cancer. Whilst interactions between genes and their regulators on the same chromosome are well characterized, mechanistic insights into contacts between different chromosomes (inter-chromosomal) remain mostly unknown. Moreover, non-coding RNAs are an important layer for gene regulation and genome organization, but their molecular mechanisms remain to be determined. We identified a long non-coding RNA involved in inter-chromosomal contacts which is biologically and clinically relevant. The RNA gene CISTR-ACT on human chromosome 12 interacts with SOX9 on chromosome 17 to regulate cartilage development. CISTR-ACT and SOX9 remain stably associated in normal cells, but disrupting this interaction leads to the rare disease brachydactyly (hand malformation syndrome) in patients with familial translocations. The results support the notion that CISTR-ACT facilitates developmental programs controlled by genes located on other chromosomes. Most importantly, CISTR-ACT is directly involved in the pathogenesis of brachydactyly, but how does defective inter-chromosomal communication cause brachydactyly? Here, we will use a multidisciplinary approach leveraging functional epigenomics, computational biology, and live-cell imaging to determine CISTR-ACT's function. We will show how CISTR-ACT impacts gene regulation and genome organization in brachydactyly to better understand spatial positioning of genes and RNA-mediated gene regulation. Our findings promise a better understanding of these novel epigenomic disease mechanisms and will establish a research discipline with clinical significance for other genomic rearrangements.

column36: Characterization of invadopodia formation in response to local cues and their role in orchestrating metastasis.
column37: The majority of breast cancer patients die from metastatic disease rather than the primary tumor. Metastasis, which is the spread of cancer cells from a primary tumor to other areas in the body, remains the main cause of patient related death, due to organ damage caused by the growing metastases. Awareness of the importance of metastasis and our basic scientific understanding of the metastatic process has improved substantially over the past few decades. However, many aspects of metastasis are still not well defined and our ability to prevent or treat metastasis is limited. In order to improve patient outcomes, a better understanding of metastasis is required. One way that cancer cells are thought to move around the body is by sprouting tiny 'feet-like' structures called invadopodia. We propose that these 'feet-like' structures respond to cues in their environment and this triggers cell movement and invasion at distant organs. Our work aims to study how these environmental cues promote the formation of invadopodia and how this changes the movements and actions of the cancer cells. Results from this work will identify proteins important for the formation and function of these 'feet'. This will help us understand the mechanisms by which cancer cells move throughout the body, seed and grow in distant organs. This could lead to the future development of therapies aimed at impairing the actions of these 'feet' to reduce metastatic spread and improve patient outcomes.

column37: Sports concussion is a major public health concern. Even more alarmingly, recent findings show that repeated subconcussive head impacts in sports may also lead to long-term brain changes. column36: Maternal Diabetes Induces Perinatal Programming of Chronic Kidney Disease: The Role of Hedgehog Interacting Protein (Hhip)
column37: Pregnancy with diabetes or gestational diabetes (i.e., maternal diabetes) creates elevated blood sugar levels in the womb, resulting in a variety of birth defects. In addition, there are lifelong consequences for the offspring-increased tendency to develop various disorders, such as metabolic syndrome, hypertension (HTN), obesity, cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease (CKD) in adulthood. The exact reasons for this phenomenon, called perinatal programming, are not well-defined. Moreover, this perinatal programming occurring in progeny of diabetic mothers could be further influenced after a 'second hit' during postnatal life-e.g., chronic exposure to factors including smoking, physiological stress, high-salt consumption or high fat diet, excessive alcohol consumption and a sedentary lifestyle, etc.. Therefore, knowledge of how HTN and CKD develop in at-risk people born to mothers with diabetes will lead to improved prevention/treatment strategies. We recently discovered that high blood sugar levels in the pregnant mother turn on the expression of a molecule called the hedgehog interacting protein (Hhip), which is associated with impaired kidney development in young offspring of diabetic dams. This proposal aims to understand the molecular bases of Hhip impact on maternal diabetes-induced renal programming of HTN and CKD in adult offspring. We will perform the studies using Hhip knock-out mouse model and kidney cells grown in petri dishes to define the physiological role of Hhip in maternal diabetes-induced renal programming. We expect the present project to generate a comprehensive understanding of Hhip impact on maternal diabetes-induced renal programming of CKD; facilitate the identification of novel drug targets to prevent/reduce the long-term risks of complications in the progeny of diabetic mothers; and reduce diabetic pregnancy-associated healthcare burdens in Canada and thereby improve the quality of life of Canadians.

column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic, debilitating illnesses. At present, the goal of treatment in IBD is complete healing of intestinal inflammation. Previous research has shown evidence of increased expression of the transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 receptor (TRPV1) in IBD patients with complete intestinal healing; TRPV1 is a key nerve receptor involved in abdominal pain sensation. There is early evidence that disruptions in gut microbes can also change TRPV1 on pain-sensing nerves. The goal of our research is to study the role of gut microbes in the development of chronic pain in IBD and the interaction between gut microbes and TRPV1 on pain-sensing nerves. We will examine this by performing stool transplants from IBD patients with/without chronic abdominal pain or healthy controls into a mouse model. We will characterize gut microbes and their metabolites in both patients and our mouse model. Finally, we will study how microbe-made short chain fatty acids, which are increased in our mouse model and change the activity of pain-sensing nerves, interact with TRPV1. Our research may have a broad impact on the health of patients suffering from IBD as it will give us a greater understanding into the role of gut microbes in pain sensation. This may in turn lead to new strategies, such as the use of stool transplants, targeted therapies against specific microbial products or microbes, and/or the use of pro-/pre-biotics to treat pain in IBD.

column36: The utilization, safety, and effectiveness of periconceptional high dose folic acid supplementation
column37: Neural tube defects are one of the most common congenital anomalies encountered in Canada. They can result in fetal deaths, newborn and child deaths, and life-long disability. Folic acid supplementation is an important intervention to prevent neural tube defects. While Health Canada has consistently recommended 0.4 mg per day (standard dose) for women at low risk, Canadian guidelines for high doses (5 mg per day) have varied considerably over time. These variations are due, in part, to a lack of strong evidence of additional benefits of 5 mg per day folic acid. Folic acid doses higher than 1.0 mg per day are only available by prescription and are therefore exclusively initiated by physicians. Following over seven years where high-dose folic acid was recommended widely for many potential risk factors, revised 2015 Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) guidelines considerably restricted the recommended indications for 5 mg per day folic acid. However, the impact of these more restrictive guidelines on physician prescribing practices is unclear. Furthermore, given that many women in Canada and around the world have taken high doses of folic acid, evidence is urgently required on any potential risks and benefits associated with the use of 5 mg per day folic acid. We will use prescription claims data from British Columbia and Manitoba to study the effect of revised 2015 guidelines on 5 mg per day folic acid use among pregnant women. We will use electronic health record data from the United Kingdom to compare women who receive high and standard dose folic acid with regards to their chances of developing breast cancer later in life or having a baby with neural tube defects. This study will provide information to help inform the public and the medical community about the use of high-dose folic acid to prevent neural tube defects in Canada and the risks and benefits of high-dose folic acid supplementation.

column36: Dissection of pathways regulating meiotic crossover formation
column37: Human reproduction requires the fusion of egg and sperm that each contains exactly half the number of parental chromosomes to form a healthy embryo containing a complete chromosome set. Inheriting an abnormal number of chromosomes is the most prevalent and documented cause of miscarriage, and is also associated with sterility and developmental defects. To produce egg and sperm, germ cells go through two specialized rounds of cell division called meiosis. Correct distribution of the parental chromosomes to these cells relies on meiotic processes which pair identical chromosomes along their lengths and physically anchor them to each other through DNA "crossovers" in preparation for segregation; failure to form crossovers results in germ cells containing abnormal chromosome numbers. While the events leading to crossover formation are highly conserved from fungi to humans, the study of meiotic processes in humans is difficult because of technical and ethical issues. In our laboratory, we use C. elegans, a small transparent roundworm that possesses many of the genetic counterparts found in vertebrates to study meiosis. Using the powerful genetic, molecular and biochemical tools of the nematode system, combined with the accessibility of the germline for detailed microscopy, we propose to identify and study new genes required for the critical processes regulating crossing over with the goal of understanding meiosis in humans.

column36: Characterization and treatment of a novel conditional mouse model of pyridoxine-dependent epileptic encephalopathy caused by antiquitin mutations.
column37: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (PDE) is a rare genetic form of epilepsy or seizure disorder that is also associated with abnormal brain development. PDE is caused by alterations (or mutations) in the antiquitin gene. These mutations lead to accumulation of toxic chemical compounds in the brain. PDE is characterized by recurrent fits or seizures that begin around the time of birth and are resistant to conventional seizure medications (anticonvulsant treatments), but show remarkable response to the administration of vitamin B6 or pyridoxine. The seizures usually begin again when pyridoxine is stopped either incidentally or for diagnostic purposes. Most PDE patients suffer also from developmental delay and moderate to severe intellectual disability along with variety of structural brain abnormalities. Progress in the development of effective treatments for PDE has been hampered by a lack of understanding of how the genetic mutation causes the brain disease and also by the absence of an appropriate animal model. We created a mouse model for PDE to fill the knowledge gaps about disease biology, and to use as a disease model in which we can test new treatments that can eventually be brought to human patients. The research plan of this project will be divided to three parts. In the first part, we will study the effects of modified diet on the PDE mouse model for the presence of various disease symptoms such as seizures and cognitive disturbances a well as testing the presence of disease associated chemical compounds in blood and brain tissue. In the second part, we will examine the effects of selective loss of the antiquitin gene in specific types of brain cells or selective loss at a specific ages. The third part of the project will be dedicated to treatment trials to improve the disease symptoms in these PDE mice. These will include manipulation of vitamin levels and administration of drugs that will minimize the toxic chemical compounds.

column37: Colorectal cancer is one of the common causes of cancer-related mortality. When detected at early stages, colorectal cancer can be cured with great success. The proteomics-based screening test for colorectal cancer is designed to detect colorectal lesions at early stages and reduce the number of unnecessary colonoscopies. The impact on the health of the Canadian population should be significant.

column36: Caregiving for vulnerable and marginalized older adults at the end of life
column37: Vulnerable and marginalized populations - including those who are homeless, experience mental health and substance use issues and who are living in poverty - experience "accelerated aging" compared to the general population. While most older people who are coming toward the end of their lives are cared for at home by family members, this is not the case for many seniors who are vulnerable and marginalized. Our recent research found that older adults who are vulnerable are cared for by many people that we would not traditionally think of as "family" caregivers. These included people like inner city housing workers, "street family" and sometimes biological family members. But there is little known about these caregivers - who they are and what they do and how caregiving affects them. In this study we will work with inner city palliative care teams in Victoria and Toronto to examine who the caregivers are of vulnerable and marginalized older adults. We will also explore factors that influence their capacity to give care and document what impact caregiving has on them. Our research will involve repeated observations over 2 years of inner city palliative care teams in Victoria and Toronto. We will also conduct interviews with these team members and other providers like housing and harm reduction workers, health care providers working in home and community care, and executive directors and clinical leaders in inner city agencies that support vulnerable and marginalized people. We will also interview caregivers of vulnerable and marginalized populations after asking them to take pictures that depict their caregiving work. Our goal is to provide a detailed description so that we can figure out how to best provide supports to these caregivers in order to reduce negative health outcomes including emotional distress, trauma, grief and burnout.

column36: Structural biology and biochemistry of PARP enzyme regulation in the DNA damage response and in cancer therapy
column37: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) are a diverse class of medically relevant human enzymes, with regulatory roles in virtually all aspects of cell biology. The enzyme PARP1 is a principal component of the cellular response to DNA damage. PARP1 rapidly detects DNA strand breaks and then creates the molecule poly(ADP-ribose) to signal the presence and location of the DNA break. Poly(ADP-ribose) recruits other cellular factors to the site of DNA breaks so that the damage can be repaired in a timely and efficient manner. Certain cancers have inherent deficiencies in the repair of DNA strand breaks, and the survival of these cancer cells is dependent on PARP1 activity. PARP inhibitor (PARPi) compounds block PARP1 activity and are thus toxic to these cancer cells with defective DNA repair, whereas normal cells are able to withstand PARPi treatment. The proposed research will provide fundamental insights into the control of PARP1 activity in cells that will improve our ability to regulate PARP1 activity for cancer treatment. PARP1 hyperactivity is associated with other diseases, such as cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, thus our findings will also impact our understanding of PARP1 regulation in other areas of biology that are important for human health.

column36: Assessment of renal function in adults born preterm: The HAPI-Kidney study
column37: Preterm birth can affect organ development with lasting impact on their structure and function. Over the last decade, accumulating evidence has shown that adults born preterm are at increased risk of high blood pressure and of cardiovascular diseases. The kidneys play a central role in the regulation of blood pressure. At the time of preterm birth, the kidneys are still forming and can be affected because of the adverse conditions associated with preterm birth. Very large population-based studies show that adults born preterm have an increased risk of chronic kidney diseases. However, studies have not been able to identify the causes of kidney disease in this population, which would be a first step towards prevention and treatment. Furthermore, kidney diseases most often do not cause pain or discomfort, and can therefore go unnoticed until late into the disease process. It is therefore essential to improve our understanding of the mechanisms leading to renal diseases in individuals born preterm, through more precise and fine measures of renal function, as we propose in the current project. To carry this project, we will evaluate adults (18-40 years) born preterm before 30 weeks of gestation, and a group of controls of same age, sex and reported race who were born full-term. Renal function will be measured precisely, with a scan in nuclear medicine. We will measure kidney size using magnetic resonance imaging, and we will perform analyses on blood and urine. Participants to our study will be recruited from of a cohort of young adults born preterm that we have constituted for a previous study conducted 5 years ago and with whom we have remained in contact. We will therefore also be able to assess kidney function change over time and identify early and predictive markers of kidney function decline in this population, that will allow implementation of preventative measures to protect kidney health and help identify the causes of kidney diseases in adults born preterm.

column36: Understanding the effectiveness and underlying mechanisms of interventions for socially frailty older adults: A systematic review alongside a realist review
column37: By the year 2050, two billion people worldwide will be 60 years of age and older. Global life expectancies are also on the rise, leading to an increased number of seniors who will develop chronic conditions and frailty. Given these projections, frailty is fast becoming a public health concern. Frailty is multidimensional (it affects biological, psychological, and social processes of a person's life), and therefore can lead to reduced functional ability, falls, disability, decreased quality of life, and death. Of the three types of frailty (physical, psychological, and social), social frailty is the least well understood. It is defined as "a continuum of being at risk of losing, or having lost, social and general resources, activities or abilities that are important for fulfilling one or more basic social needs during the life span". Although common among seniors, social frailty can be improved, reversed, and prevented, and therefore doesn't have to be considered as an inevitable part of aging. However, we know very little about the risk factors and interventions that may prevent or reverse social frailty. Therefore, our research goals are to better understand interventions addressing social frailty in older adults by conducting a systematic review and a realist review. The results of this work will help us to build a future intervention to prevent or lessen the negative consequences of social frailty affecting seniors.

column36: Cigarette taxes, prices and tax evasion in Canada: implications for tobacco control
column37: Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in Canada. There is overwhelming Canadian and international evidence that increases in tobacco taxes reduce tobacco use, save lives and increase government tax revenue. However, high taxes create an incentive for tobacco users, manufacturers and others, most notably criminal networks, to devise ways to avoid or evade tobacco taxes. From the mid-2000s, the effectiveness of tobacco tax policies in Canada has been hampered by the emergence of discount brands and the resurgence of contraband cigarettes, most notably in Ontario and Quebec. The illegal nature of cigarette tax evasion makes it intrinsically difficult to measure accurately. The scattered and at times conflicting estimates combined with the tobacco industry's narrative that cigarette contraband has been increasing in recent years and that any changes in policies such as tax increases or plain packaging will inevitably lead to large increases in cigarette tax evasion warrant a more systematic, transparent and timely approach to examine cigarette contraband in Canada. We have three research objectives. Our first objective is to estimate the magnitude of and temporal changes in cigarette tax evasion. Our second objective is to use the estimates of cigarette tax evasion constructed in objective 1 to study the relationship between cigarette tax evasion and cigarette prices (licit and illicit) and policy changes. Our third objective is to explore smokers' motivations for purchasing contraband cigarettes through an embedded qualitative study. Overall, this research has the potential to make important contributions to the evidence base on pricing and taxing policies to inform regulatory developments. Understanding the burden of cigarette tax evasion in Canada is critical for improving public health interventions and reducing the burden of tobacco-related disease in Canada.

When ER folding capacity is overwhelmed a stress management program called the unfolded protein response (UPR) is initiated in attempt to alleviate this potentially fatal stress. The UPR has evolved to sense the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER and deliver a signal to the nucleus to increase the expression of genes that (i) increase ER folding capacity and (ii) destroy terminally misfolded proteins. If stress cannot be resolved then the UPR initiates a cell death response. There is emerging evidence that the UPR is a node of control subverted by viruses to support viral replication and aspects of pathogenesis, but specific mechanistic details remain unclear. Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the causative agent of the AIDS defining cancer, Kaposi's sarcoma. We discovered that KSHV usurps host UPR processes to promote viral replication. Though this study, we will identify the viral genes responsible for controlling the host UPR system, and we will figure out how they work.

column36: The role of TOR kinase signaling and lipid metabolism in hypoxia tolerance
column37: Our cells and organs need oxygen from the air we breathe in order to survive. However, although air contains twenty percent oxygen, our cells are exposed to much lower levels. In addition, our cells are often deprived of oxygen in diseases such as stroke, heart disease and cancer. This lack of oxygen, known as hypoxia, leads to the tissue damage seen in these diseases. In important challenge in biomedical research is to understand how cells and organs can respond to, and cope, with low oxygen. We use the fruit fly as a model to address this question. Fruit flies naturally live in rotting fruit which is an environment characterized by low oxygen. Hence, they have evolved mechanisms to tolerate this hypoxia. Our work in the fly has identified the regulation of one enzyme - TOR kinase - as a mechanism by which cells adapt to low oxygen. The goal of this project grant is to use the ease and speed of fruit fly genetics to understand exactly how TOR controls the ability of tissues and organs to survive low oxygen. The fruit fly is proven as a 'lead' model system to discover new biological mechanisms that can guide work in other systems including human cells. For example, the TOR pathway is controlled the same way in human cells as in flies. In addition, TOR becomes deregulated in disorders such as cancer and heart disease. Hence our work will help identify how cells and organs can cope with hypoxia, and in doing so, will provide clues about the defects caused by disorders such as cancer and heart disease.

column36: In vivo roles of autophagy in gut homeostasis and impact on IBD
column37: The digestive system is complex, and it interacts directly with a large number of microbes. Consequently, small problems can lead to various types of digestive diseases. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, collectively named inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) affect 1 in 150 Canadians. Although these two diseases are etiologically different, they both are linked to a cellular mechanism called autophagy. Autophagy is the process by which cells degrade and recycle their own constituents. Autophagy can thus be compared to a recycling factory, where non-essential or damaged constituents can be destroyed and reused for other purposes. Autophagy is induced by different signals. In the intestine, autophagy (the recycling factory) also helps to destroy bad microbes and help to maintain the good ones. In an effort to understand how differences in our genes predispose individuals to develop IBD, differences in genes of affected and unaffected individuals were compared to identify mutations linked to an increasing susceptibility to develop IBD. These approaches have identified a large number of genes linked to IBD, and importantly a good proportion of those genes are regulators of autophagy. However, due to the lack of affordable and time-efficient systems to study the role of these genes in digestive health, their roles in the development or progression of IBD are for the most part unexplored. In this proposal, we will characterize, using Drosophila melanogaster (fruit flies) as an innovative in vivo model of gut health, the role of autophagy on gut function and gut/microbes interaction. Moreover, we will also quantify using a powerful new approach how autophagy is regulated in vivo under stress, and finally we will identify novel potential targets that could eventually help IBD patients with impaired autophagy. The identification of new regulators of intestinal health will generate new basic and translational research avenues and identify new targets for therapies.

column36: Characterization of Arrhythmia Substrate to Ablate Persistent Atrial Fibrillation (COAST-AF) Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major health problem that affects 350,000 Canadians. AF, an abnormal heart rhythm, increases the risk of heart failure, stroke and death. These risks increase when AF worsens to a level known as persistent AF. AF can be treated with catheter ablation, a treatment that aims to restore a normal heart rhythm. When successful AF catheter ablation improves quality of life, and decreases the risk of death or hospitalization for cardiac causes. Yet, only 50-60% of patients with persistent AF who undergo standard of care (pulmonary vein isolation catheter ablation alone) remain AF-free at one year. The optimal strategy for ablation of persistent AF is not yet known. We know that scar tissue in the atria (upper chamber of the heart) leads to AF. Recently, our group's pilot work demonstrated that catheter ablation of scarred regions in the atria in addition to pulmonary vein isolation has revealed promising results. Recent studies using a similar approach support our findings, yet a synthesis of current available research reveals that it is of variable quality with important limitations. To confirm the findings from these studies, experts in the field have called for a larger, more representative study. We are answering this call. We propose COAST-AF, a clinical trial to determine the safety and efficacy of atrial scar ablation in addition to pulmonary vein isolation versus pulmonary vein isolation alone (standard of care). COAST-AF is the only study that can provide a definitive answer to this crucial question in cardiac arrhythmia care. We anticipate this trial will directly impact the treatment of thousands of patients with persistent AF in Canada and Worldwide.

column36: Spinal interneuron subpopulations and modular circuits in normal locomotor control and after spinal cord injury
column37: Loss of locomotor activity due to accident or disease is devastating to patients and may lead to early death. Currently, we have limited understanding of the neural circuits that control movement, which hampers efforts to devise better therapeutics to treat loss of motor function. The fundamental goal of my laboratory is to reveal the organization of neural circuits that control normal locomotion in order to identify mechanisms that could be targeted when that behavior is disrupted by injuries and diseases. Currently, we focus on interneuron (IN) populations that form the locomotor circuits in the mouse spinal cord, and aim to reveal the organizational logic and functional roles of these circuits in locomotor control. More importantly, we hope to provide insight into the potential roles of spinal INs in neuroplasticity and recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI). Based on our previous and current studies of one specific IN population, designated V3 INs, as a model system, we predict that spinal IN subpopulations could serve as modular components in locomotor circuits, allowing for task-dependent selection of functionally distinct circuit outputs. These individual modules may function in different aspects of locomotor control and respond differently to SCI and subsequent rehabilitation regimens, knowledge that could be crucial for recovery from SCI. To address these issues, we will employ various genetic and molecular tools in combination with advanced anatomical, electrophysiological, optogenetic, behavioral and computational approaches to define functional V3 IN subpopulations; define task-dependent functional modules of V3 INs in locomotor circuits; and investigate their potential functions in normal locomotion and in SCI.

column36: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and social behavior. A translational study.
column37: Social behavior (SB) is a fundamental characteristic of human behavior and interaction. Several psychiatric diseases, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and social anxiety disorder (SAD), are accompanied by significant SB impairments. Several studies suggest that the psychedelic compound lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) may enhance SB in animals and humans via modulation of the serotonin and glutamate system, two major neurotransmitter systems. Moreover, increasing evidence suggests that LSD might enhance neuroplasticity (the growth of new neurons), and have antinflammatory effects (decrease over-activity of the immune system), and given that these processes are altered in conditions with impaired SB, these effects might also be involved in the prosocial effects of LSD The main hypothesis of this translational study is that LSD enhances SB via a) potentiating serotonin and glutamate neurotransmission in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and b) enhancing neuroplasticity and immune balance. We will reach our objectives firstly via studying LSD prosocial effects in rodents, and the effects of LSD on neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, and immune system balance. Secondly, we will determine whether the results obtained in rodents translate to humans, by administering LSD to healthy volunteers, and assessing resulting changes on SB, neurotransmission, mPFC function, neuroplasticity, and immune balance. This represents the first translational, proof-of-concept Canadian study investigating whether psychedelic compounds are useful for the treatment of psychiatric disorders accompanied by SB dysfunction.

column36: Developing a Patient-Specific Surgical Decision-Assistance Tool to Improve Reverse Shoulder Replacement Outcomes
column37: The human shoulder is a joint consisting of a ball on the arm side of the joint, and a cup on the shoulder blade side. When a person seriously injures their shoulder joint, they can be left unable to lift their arm. For these patients, the only way to regain function is to undergo a shoulder replacement called Reverse Total Shoulder Arthroplasty (RTSA), whereby the above-described joint geometry is flipped; a cup-shaped implant is placed on the arm side of the joint, and a ball-shaped implant is placed on the shoulder blade side. Because of this, the anatomical landmarks that surgeons use to determine the best implant configuration during a traditional shoulder replacement are not effective. Therefore, the goal of this research is to develop the biomechanical understanding necessary to provide surgeons with an objective and quantitative surgical decision-making assistance tool to aid in the optimal planning of RTSA. This objective will be achieved in a number of phases. First, we will systematically analyze how the shapes of RTSA patients' shoulder bones differ from those of other patient groups. We will then develop computer models that can inform us of how RTSA patients' anatomy influences how different RTSA implant configurations affect how well their joint functions after surgery. Results of these computer modelling studies will then be used to develop the desired decision making assistance tool using machine learning techniques that will help surgeons customize their surgical plans to each of their patients.

column37: Colorectal cancer is among the deadliest and most frequently diagnosed cancers in our country. Drugs currently used to treat colorectal tumors often fail to completely eradicate all types of cancer cell, giving an opportunity to the disease to come back (or relapse). Like many other cancers, colorectal tumors contain small reservoirs of malignant cells responsible for tumor initiation, relapse, and resistance to current treatments. Those are known as Cancer Stem Cells (CSC) and are recognized as "the root of cancer and seeds of metastasis". Previous research uncovered critical molecular mechanisms that are essential to CSCs development and maintenance. Importantly, those elements can be used as indicators in the quest to develop new medicines specifically eliminating CSCs from colon tumors. We have recently found clinically approved drugs with the capacity to alter CSCs biology while showing limited toxic effects in a normal cell model. These could represent new therapeutic avenues to safely eliminate cancer. In this project, we plan to demonstrate the capacity of those drugs to alter colon CSCs capacity to form tumors in mice, as well as in a unique culture system utilizing cells directly isolated from human patients. Moreover, we will use state-of-the-art techniques in biomedical research to understand how the candidate drugs can impact CSCs biology. Ultimately, the identification of molecules capable of suppressing colon CSC's activity would provide a new therapeutic option aimed at selectively targeting cancers, decreasing side effects and increasing patient survival rates.

column36: Central Mechanisms of Opioid Withdrawal
column37: Opioid medications provide potent pain relief in the short-term, but their long-term use can cause serious adverse effects. A major problem is that chronic opioid users experience debilitating withdrawal symptoms (e.g. tremors, anxiety, depression, insomnia, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal distress) when attempting to stop or reduce their opioid medications. Seeking relief, these individuals continue to use opioid drugs. A misconception is that only illicit opioid use or "opioid addicts" are susceptible to withdrawal. The careful use of prescription opioids can also lead to significant withdrawal symptoms. Optimal therapies for opioid withdrawal are unavailable. Our team recently discovered that immune cells (microglia) residing within the brain and spinal cord play an important role in opioid withdrawal. These immune cells communicate with other cells through specialized channels (pannexin-1), which are like gates that open and close to allow passage of chemical signals. Blocking these channels in the spinal cord alleviates withdrawal without diminishing the pain-relieving benefits of opioid medications. We have new data that pannexin-1 channels gate activity within the locus coeruleus, an area of the brain that communicates with the spinal cord by sending specialized projections containing a chemical (norepinephrine). This proposal addresses exciting new questions about how pannexin-1 channels modulate specific circuitry in the brain and spinal cord that are important for opioid withdrawal. Using advanced cellular imaging, biochemical, and behavioural approaches, experiments will also deconstruct the machinery by which norepinephrine enhances pannexin-1 activity and its impact on microglia signaling. Finally, we will translate our findings into the development of next generation, more potent pannexin-1 targeted drugs for treating opioid withdrawal.

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disease that results in the progressive loss of cells in the brain, in particular in an area important for the formation of new memories, called the hippocampus. This project aims to characterize the aging female brain and how is affected by reproductive experience (pregnancy) and genetics (APOEe4 status) under hormone therapy, immune, and metabolic (diet) challenges. Menopause is associated with dramatic changes in hormone levels and with cognitive decline and certain hormone therapies (HTs) positively affect cognition depending on timing and genotype. Our research shows that the sensitivity of the female brain to estrogens is altered with past parity to affect neuroplasticity and immune signalling. The goal of this proposal is to study the effects of parity and genetics on aging in the female brain exposed to hormone therapies, immune and metabolic challenges in preclinical models. This work will determine how physiological challenges faced by females during aging interact with motherhood and genetics can affect brain aging. It is clear that tailored treatment based on sex, genetics, and possibly reproductive history need to be developed to best treat individuals at risk to develop AD.

column36: Improving clinical practice recommendations for late preterm antenatal corticosteroids: incorporating a decision support tool to tackle the uncertain balance of risks and benefits
column37: Antenatal corticosteroids are a medication given to women who are at risk of an early delivery to help reduce the chance of breathing problems for their baby after birth. Current guidelines recommend giving antenatal corticosteroids to pregnant women who might have their baby before 34 weeks of pregnancy. This medication may also help those at risk of an early delivery at 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy but the balance between the benefits and harms of this treatment is less clear at these ages. Clinical guidelines for giving this medication at 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy are also unclear, making it difficult for doctors and patients to decide whether to use it. We previously found that many doctors are not talking about this decision with patients, or when they do talk about it, different doctors discuss different risks and benefits. Decision support tools that clearly state risks and benefits can sometimes help doctors and patients make decisions about whether a treatment is right for them. Our goal is to find out if including a decision support tool in clinical guidelines will improve how doctors discuss antenatal corticosteroids with patients who might deliver at 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy. We will ask patients who delivered at these preterm ages whether their doctor discussed antenatal corticosteroids with them, and see if they report having had better discussions with their doctor about this treatment decision after their doctor had access to the decision support tool within the clinical guideline. We will also ask doctors if and how this decision support tool impacts their counselling. By helping doctors and patients communicate about the risks and benefits of antenatal corticosteroids, this project could promote fully-informed and optimal use of a drug that can reduce breathing problems in newborns. Our results could also serve as a model for other clinical guidelines when there is no clear answer about whether the benefits of a treatment outweigh its harms.

column36: Prediction of multiple sclerosis disability worsening scores using multi-stream deep learning
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a common neurological disease that disables young Canadians. There are 14 approved therapies now for many who have a relapsing remitting form of MS (RRMS). Yet within 10-15 years of disease onset, >50% of RRMS patients develop secondary progressive MS (SPMS), which remains untreatable. While many factors may cause this poor outcome, the inability to optimize therapy based on an individual's risk of worsening is crucial. There is no reliable way to identify the risks but if there is, early aggressive treatment would be possible for those with a greater risk of worsening, which is critical to save the tissue before irreversible damage accumulates. This project will establish a novel deep machine learning method to predict the 5-year risk of disability score worsening in RRMS patients. We will take a unique approach by simultaneously evaluating patient outcomes from brain pathology, clinical measures, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Deep learning has shown enormous progress recently in disease prediction, especially when combing pathology-directed outcomes, and multiple types of patient data. Using standard brain MRI, our pilot deep learning data is 83% accurate in predicting RRMS and SPMS. By assessing the pixel pattern (texture) of MRI, our pioneer work also discover that the scale and direction of MRI texture detects specific elements of MS pathology. We have now built new deep learning methods using 3 types of outcomes from MRI texture pathology, clinical data, and brain MRI, and cutting-edge techniques to unveil how deep learning works. Built on these solid data and large cohorts of MS patients, this project will establish a novel objective method to identify the high and low risks of disability worsening for individual RRMS patients so that each can receive the best treatment regimen to improve prognosis. This personalized medicine approach will directly benefit MS patients and families, the health care system, and society.

column36: Understanding and quantifying the impact of stroke and other brain structural disconnections
column37: Stroke affects an increasingly large number of individuals in Canada and around the world. Brain damage as a result of stroke can often lead to difficulties in mobility, language production and understanding, and other functions such as memory and reasoning. Though these difficulties lead to serious reductions in quality of life, we still do not know how damage in one location of the brain is related to specific difficulties. This is in part because we do not yet fully understand how the brain is connected and how its connections support our everyday behaviours. Brain damage is typically described based on its location and size, but this completely ignores how the damage may have interrupted some connections between different regions of the brain. For example, damage to the front of the brain will result in different functional deficits depending exactly where it is: if it is more towards the top the patient may experience difficulties with memory (e.g., phone numbers) but if it is lower the patient may experience emotional issues (e.g., understanding facial expressions). We have a fairly good idea of what the processing regions of the brain do (grey matter, made up of cells that do the "thinking") but we know very little about how they are connected through the white matter of the brain (i.e., the "wires" that connect different processing regions together). Without this knowledge, damage to the "wires" is difficult to predict the effects of or, ultimately, treat with clinical intervention.

column36: Placental contributions to maternal and fetal health outcomes: Lipid signatures in diabetes mellitus in pregnancy
column37: Globally, an increasing number of pregnancies are complicated by diabetes, paralleling the obesity trends in women of child-bearing age. These pregnancies carry a significant risk of complications for the mother and the baby, both during and after pregnancy. In fact, later in life, women with a history of diabetes during pregnancy and their offspring, are at higher risk of developing cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. The placenta, strategically positioned between the mother and the fetus, likely mediates these feto-maternal complications, but the mechanisms involved remain elusive. Lipids, classically thought to be purely structural elements of the cell membrane, are now recognized as key mediators in normal processes and in the development of a variety of diseases. However, global lipid profiles across gestation in pregnant women with diabetes of varying severity have never been characterized. This proposal builds upon a series of novel experiments in which we will define lipid changes across gestation in vesicles, called exosomes that are released from the placenta and travel in the maternal and fetal circulations to target a variety of organs. These vesicles can act as messengers that modify the well-being of target cells like those of blood vessels. Hence, in addition, we will investigate the effect of these vesicles on cellular events linked to cell-death in blood vessel cells.

column36: Primary Care for Individuals with Serious Mental Illness (PriSMI)
column37: Even more than the general public, people living with serious mental illness also live with chronic health conditions like heart disease or diabetes. For this population, health care providers tend to ignore these other chronic health conditions and focus primarily on their mental illness. As a result, these other health conditions are often poorly managed, which leads to hospitalizations and death (not including suicide or accident) that could have been avoided. Our research looks to understand how primary care providers (e.g., family doctors, nurse practitioners) can better care for the physical health of people living with serious mental illness. We will focus on people who have been hospitalized due to a mental illness and who have a primary care provider in either Ontario or British Columbia. We will interview primary care providers as well as people living with serious mental illness who have experience with a hospitalization. These interviews will shed light on the experiences of getting help with preventing and treating chronic illnesses. Using large data sets, we will also look to understand the types of primary care services people with serious mental illness use and how these services might be different based on the type of primary care practice they go to (for example, doctors who work alone versus doctors who work with groups of professionals). Lastly, we plan to explore how recent policy changes (for example, Ontario Health Teams) may have impacted primary care service use and patterns for this population.

column36: Vitrified cartilage chips from allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells for one-step off-the-shelf joint cartilage repair - proof of concept in a preferred pre-clinical model, the Horse.
column37: Ten percent of Canadian adults suffer from joint cartilage damage and osteoarthritis (OA) with an estimated cost to society of more than 33 billion dollars a year and incalculable suffering for affected individuals and their families. Sixty percent of OA patients are of typical working age (20-64 years). Cartilage defects larger than 4 centimeter-square are a clinical challenge to treat, but joint cartilage chips, sometimes referred to as particulate or morselized cartilage, has shown significant clinical promise, regardless of whether the cartilage was sourced from juvenile human cadavers, unrelated adult cadavers or the patients themselves. Current cartilage chips methods are hampered by limited supply of human donor material, risk of disease transmission, suboptimal graft tissue, donor site morbidity in case of autologous cartilage, and cost of human allograft material in some cases. Donor age, co-morbidities, and harvest site may all negatively influence the biological potency of the cartilage graft. We propose to solve these issues by using cartilage generated in the laboratory from neonatal allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC). We will vitrify (freeze) the cartilage tissue for indefinite storage and availability as an off-the-shelf live-cell cartilage graft that can be implanted using standard surgical methods. Aims for this 3-year proof-of-principle project: A1) In vitro generation of vitrified equine MSC-derived cartilage chips. A2) In vitro generation of vitrified human MSC-derived cartilage chips. A3) In vivo assessment of non-vitrified (fresh) and vitrified equine MSC-derived cartilage-chips for large induced cartilage defects in research horses. Fully implemented, this therapy would provide a safe, efficacious, cost-effective and technically simple treatment for Canadians as well as provide an opportunity for a Canadian biotechnology business to bank and distribute vitrified cartilage tissue in unlimited quantities to the world market.

column36: Survival and Cardiac Recovery In Pediatric Cardiomyopathy (SCRIPT study)
column37: Heart failure can be described as a state when the heart cannot function in its role to supply oxygen rich blood to the rest of the body and if severe, can ultimately lead to death. Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle and a leading cause of pediatric heart failure. Pediatric heart failure is an important public health problem associated with high mortality and multiple heart and non-heart complications. Risk factors for these complications, including for death, are poorly understood in children. With this project, our main objective is to find out what happens to children with cardiomyopathy outside our hospital and after they transition to adulthood. We want to determine the chances of these patients living without the need for a heart transplant and the risks for other important heart and non-heart complications even well into adulthood. We also want to describe how much healthcare usage is required to care for these patients to understand better the burden on their families. As the largest pediatric heart failure program in Canada, SickKids is well positioned to study this problem by combining pediatric data from our patients seen at SickKids hospital with information from ICES databases. Over the past 2 years, we have been building a detailed cohort of all children cared for at SickKids with a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy from 2001 to 2017. ICES is a provincial database that includes administrative information on health care usage and outcomes for everyone living in the province of Ontario. It is a unique collection of databases with strong quality data which has not been reproduced anywhere in the world. With the help of mentors from ICES, this project will link our database to ICES to find out what happens to our patients throughout their lifetime. This project represents the first study where a pediatric cardiology group is linked to ICES and will create a study that will span pediatrics into adulthood.
