column36: Identifying sex differences in the molecular mechanisms of socially-mediated pubertal suppression
column37: Puberty is an essential developmental process in mammals. Puberty marks the onset of sexual maturation and is associated with increased incidence of depression and anxiety. Two risk factors for the development of depression are psychosocial stress and pubertal timing. Importantly, psychosocial stress can itself shift pubertal timing. Puberty onset, susceptibility to stress, and risk of depression all differ between males and females. For these reasons understanding sex specific mechanisms underlying how social stress influences pubertal timing has tremendous importance for human health. The naked mole-rat (NMR) is a unique rodent exhibiting extreme socially-mediated reproductive suppression. NMRs reside in large colonies of adults who remain in a pre-pubertal state due to the presence of a dominant breeding female known as the queen. In addition to the queen, a dominant breeding male (known as a consort) has also gone through puberty. Most NMRs will never go through puberty unless they are removed from the suppressive cues of their colony. By studying NMRs, we have an exceptional opportunity to learn how social cues influence pubertal timing. Here we will identify genome-wide gene expression patterns as well as modifications to the DNA that turn genes on and off (known as epigenetic changes) in the brain, adrenal glands, and gonads of NMRs. We will also manipulate stress-relevant genes to examine how they influence puberty and gene expression in brain. The goal of our research is to discover sex specific genes that are involved in suppressing puberty in NMRs, which may explain associations between age of pubertal onset, stress reactivity, and risk for psychopathology in humans.

column36: SUMOylation Pathways in Alzheimer Disease and Their Therapeutic Implications
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a common, progressive and ultimately lethal disease affecting ~5% of adults over 65 years of age and ~30% of adults over the age of 85 years in most Western societies. Both the prevalence and the annual expenditures on AD are expected to increase as the proportion of the population at risk increases over the next 20 years. The currently available treatments are of limited effectiveness as they target the symptoms of the disease but not the root cause. The major features of AD are accumulations of abnormal proteins called amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles within the brain. Amyloid plaques appear as densely packed thread-like fibers that form around nerve cells and blood vessels. Evidence suggests that amyloid is highly toxic and is the primary cause of nerve cell death. Loss of these cells is the underlying event in AD and results in the clinical features of cognitive dysfunction and memory impairments. We have recently discovered a link between AD pathology and a family of proteins called, small ubiquitin-like modifiers (SUMOs). Our initial investigations have uncovered links between SUMO-related pathways and the development of Alzheimer disease plaques and tangles. This was made possible by the generation of novel animal models that combine SUMO and the key amyloid and tangle proteins. The ultimate objective of this research is to understand the cellular processes which cause AD and to use that information for the development of safe and effective treatments.

column36: Towards the non-invasive, most accurate radiotherapy of mobile tumours in a hybrid linac-MR system
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada and nearly half of the patients receive radiotherapy (RT). RT uses strong radiation to kill tumour cells, and the radiation is typically delivered by a device called linear accelerator (linac). If a tumour is static during irradiation, e.g. brain tumour, modern RT can deliver highly accurate radiation to the tumour without much damage to the adjacent normal cells. Unfortunately, most tumours are mobile and can deform due to respiratory and cardiac motions (e.g. lung tumour), and such accurate RT is difficult due to the lack of sufficient soft-tissue imaging. Most tumours reside in soft-tissue, and soft-tissue is best seen in MRI. However, current imaging devices on linacs are typically X-ray based, which provide poor soft-tissue imaging. Thus, small metal markers that can be seen in X-ray image must be surgically implanted near the tumour to estimate its shape and location during RT. Our laboratory built the first radiotherapy-MRI hybrid device (linac-MR) in 2008, and a human whole-body system in 2014. This MRI on-board linac allows continuous MR imaging during irradiation, providing clear image of moving tumours. Using linac-MR, our objective is to enhance the geometric accuracy of RT treating mobile tumours without the need of invasive surgery. To achieve the objective, we have established a framework of novel RT method, non-invasive intra-fractional tumour-tracked RadioTherapy (nifteRT). The feasibility of nifteRT was verified in 2013 using our prototype linac-MR system. We were able to deliver accurate radiation to a moving target reproducing 1D lung tumour motion in linac-MR. In this proposal, we aim to further improve our nifteRT research to the level of clinically usable technology. We expect < 3 mm error in radiation delivery to mobile tumours in nifteRT. This will allow the escalation of radiation dose only to the tumours without excessive damage to the adjacent normal cells, which is the ultimate goal of RT.

column36: Contribution of endothelial fatty acid metabolism to diabetes-associated heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a leading contributor to cardiovascular death, having damaging effects on organs such as the heart as well as blood vessels. One such disease associated with diabetes is 'heart failure with preserved ejection fraction', also known as HFpEF. In this type of heart disease, the heart stiffens resulting in defective relaxation of the heart between beats, meaning the heart has less blood inside it to pump out to the rest of the body. People are often diagnosed at very late, and untreatable, stages of disease as there are no diagnostic tests that can detect early disease warning signs. The reasons why this disease develops are not understood, but recent evidence has suggested that the function of small blood vessels in the heart is defective. Therefore, dysfunction of blood vessels in the heart may be an early warning sign of disease and may also be a target for therapy. We have been seeking for markers in the blood that indicate defective blood vessel function in the heart. Using animal models of HFpEF we found a small RNA molecule, microRNA-30, is increased in the blood at the same time as blood vessels become dysfunctional. It appears that this microRNA is secreted by dysfunctional endothelial cells (the cells that line blood vessels) in the diabetic heart. We found that in the endothelial cells of the heart, microRNA-30 regulates proteins that are involved in fatty acid metabolism. When microRNA-30 is elevated, endothelial cells use more fatty acids, which causes oxidative stress and defective endothelial cell function. We believe this may be an early defect in HFpEF since fatty acids are highly elevated in the blood of diabetics. Our proposal will determine whether the utilization of fatty acids by the endothelium is involved in diabetic HFpEF and whether targeting microRNA-30 can be a potential therapy. We will also test whether measuring microRNA-30 in the blood of human patients with diabetes can be used to detect the earliest stages of HFpEF.

column36: Targeting TSLP - Novel anti-inflammatory compounds for the treatment and prevention of atopic diseases
column37: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is one of the most common inflammatory skin diseases and up to 17% of the Canadian population is affected at some point in their lives. Furthermore, AD often is an entry point for further allergies such as food allergies, hay fever or allergic asthma. As such, AD has a significant socioeconomic impact. Since AD is a highly complex and heterogenic disease, its pathophysiology is still not fully understood. Over the past years, however, the keratinocyte-derived cytokine thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) has been identified as a key player in skin inflammation and a trigger for the development of further allergies. This has sparked the interest of pharmaceutical companies to develop inhibitors of TSLP. Tezepelumab is the most advanced drug showing promising results, however it is a protein which means that it must be administered systemically and cannot be applied locally, for example as a cream. However, drugs which can be applied locally offer several advantages such as reduced side effects, targeted drug delivery at the site of action as well higher acceptance rates among the patients. Hence, this project aims to develop effective blockers of TSLP which can be applied topically. To achieve this goal, we combine our expertise in drug development and skin research. First, we will develop and synthesize potent low molecular weight TSLP inhibitors which will then be tested with regard to efficacy and tolerability in 2D and 3D cell cultures. Finally, the most promising compounds will be tested in animal models of atopic dermatitis. The overall goal are new topical treatment options for AD and the prevention of the development of further allergic diseases such as asthma.

column36: Tau pathology and circuit vulnerability in the hippocampal memory system
column37: Alzheimer's disease is the primary form of dementia in old age and rates are increasing due to longer human lifespan and the aging population of baby boomers. It is estimated that prevalence will quadruple between 2006 and 2050, at which point 1% of the worldwide population will have the disease. Despite these bleak figures, it is important to note that patients typically only live with the severest form of Alzheimer's for 1-2 years. Thus, treatments that can delay disease progression have tremendous potential to reduce the burden of Alzheimer's disease. Here, we will identify exactly which brain cells and circuits are initially most vulnerable to the tau pathology that is observed in aging and Alzheimer's disease. Tau is a toxic protein that is first observed in the memory centers of the brain, before spreading and causing irreversible damage. More specifically, the neurons that first harbor tau also connect with another region that produces newborn neurons throughout life. These newborn neurons have an enhanced ability to integrate into neural circuits, suggesting they may be better at forming connections in disease states. However, no one has ever examined whether they less vulnerable to tau, or more capable at repairing circuits that are damaged by tau. Here we will therefore mimic the human pattern of tau pathology in mice, and examine whether new vs. old neurons are more likely to be damaged. We will then use various therapeutic strategies to enhance new cell growth, with the goal of repairing the damaged circuits. Whereas we currently know, at a general level, which brain regions are sensitive to tau pathology and Alzheimer's disease, these experiments will reveal the precise subpopulations of neurons that are vulnerable and capable of being exploited to delay the progress of disease.

RSV has been listed as a public health priority and there are several vaccines and antivirals currently in development, including those targeted for older adults, who are at high risk for RSV hospitalization, severe outcomes, and death. Given the changing landscape of RSV prevention, efforts need to focus on better understanding the epidemiology of RSV infections in this critical, pre-vaccine era, including disease burden in high-risk populations and factoring in consequences of severe RSV. We propose a series of studies of laboratory-confirmed severe RSV infections (i.e.,hospitalizations) in adults that will inform our understanding of disease burden and long-term impact of infection, and identify priority populations as vaccines are developed. We will estimate the burden of disease across Ontario in important subgroups, including by age group and comorbidity status, such as in immunocompromised adults. We will also examine risk factors for severe outcomes, such as admission to an intensive care unit, need for higher level of care following hospital discharge, and death. The results of these studies will help inform decision making as future vaccine strategies are evaluated and as antivirals become available and will build awareness about the impact of RSV infections in adults.

column36: Abinoonjees Nikanenim: Delivering Mental Health Services to Youth Living in Island Lake Anishininew Nations
column37: In Canada, approximately 20% of youth experience mental health issues that impact their daily lives. The rate of mental illness and need for access to mental healthcare is especially troubling for First Nations (FN) youth. As a result of colonial processes, FN youth are at higher risk for developing a mental illness, misusing drugs and alcohol, and dying by suicide compared to non-FN youth. Despite this, there remains a lack of mental healthcare services that are both readily available within FN communities and are culturally appropriate. The goal of this mixed-methods study is to conduct an evaluation of an enhanced telemental health services (ETHS) model to examine its impact in delivering mental health services to FN youth living in the four Island Lake Anishininew communities in Manitoba. Telemental health involves the provision of health information and services over a distance via information and communication technologies such as patient-provider videoconferencing. The ETHS model is rooted in Jordan's Principle-a child first principle developed to eliminate barriers to health and social services, including mental healthcare services for FN youth. The ETHS model takes an innovative approach, using both traditional clinical methods of service delivery (e.g., direct intervention and face-to-face interactions with clinicians) as well as novel strategies (e.g., delivery of services using telehealth) to provide care for youth in their FN communities. The model includes building community capacity as well as educating community service providers to develop sustainable mental healthcare services that are rooted in FN communities and responds to the needs of FN youth and their families. The evaluation of the ETHS model will adopt a child/family-centred approach and integrate multiple methods such as a review of available data, qualitative exploration across multiple levels (e.g., youth, family, community), and arts-based methods.

column36: The common haptoglobin phenotype as a predictor of cardiovascular disease and mortality: a re-analysis of four randomized controlled trials of glycemic control
column37: Nobody knows yet why strict blood sugar control (aiming for lower blood sugar levels) prevents heart disease in some people with type 2 diabetes but can cause harm in others. It makes it hard for patients with type 2 diabetes and their doctors to plan their blood sugar goals. Our team has been working to fill this gap, and we think that the answer may include the form of the blood protein 'haptoglobin' that a person has. Everyone's body makes one of two major haptoglobin forms, and the form can be measured by an inexpensive blood test. We just published a major study in which we used this blood test in participants from a large completed study that had tested strict blood sugar control. We re-analyzed the data in the two haptoglobin groups separately and found that strict blood sugar control prevented heart disease in people with one haptoglobin type, but people with the other type had no heart disease benefit and even had an increased risk of death. We now plan to expand our work to include more: (1) diversity in the people we study (more women, ethnicities, ages, and lengths of time having diabetes), (2) variety in the types of blood sugar control (different blood sugar goals, medications, and lifestyle actions like diet and exercise), and (3) different methods to analyze the data. This research unites us with skilled researchers from four different existing studies of blood sugar control to run the blood test in their studies and re-analyze their data. This is a cost-effective and ethical way to learn whether the haptoglobin type blood test can consistently tell which people will benefit from strict blood sugar control and who will not. It will tell us whether we should further study the blood test with doctors and patients in clinics to personalize their blood sugar control goals. Type 2 diabetes is very common in Canada and worldwide, and so research like ours that aims to better prevent heart disease in people with diabetes could impact millions of people.

column36: Role of early childhood viral infection on the development of childhood sleep disordered breathing
column37: Children with sleep disordered breathing (SDB), from habitual snoring to sleep apnea, are more likely to have ADHD symptoms and poor school performance. There are limited resources to identify and treat children with SDB. Canadian children can wait up to 2 years for a sleep study. SDB treatment often includes surgical removal of enlarged tonsils or adenoids. In Edmonton, children wait up to 1 year to see a surgeon and an additional 6 months on the surgical wait-list. Taken together, children with SDB may wait several years for treatment. Our research program will address 2 of the major questions in pediatric SDB: -Can we predict which children will develop SDB? -Can we prevent childhood SDB? Why some children develop SDB is not known. Viral infections of the respiratory tract in the preschool age group are extremely common. We hypothesize that children with SDB are more likely to have a history of a viral infection compared to children without SDB. This research will leverage data from the CHILD Study Edmonton site; the first study with assessments of SDB symptoms from infancy through to 8-years of age. We will use a comprehensive antibody detection method to determine whether the child has had a prior infection from any of over 1000 strains of 206 human viral species at ages 1, 5 and 8-years. Advantages of our proposal are the broad assessment of viral infection, a very large pediatric study population (over 800 children), our ability to determine if the viral infection came before the child developed SDB symptoms, and testing for many other factors that may cause children to develop SDB. Understanding the role of viral infection on the development of SDB will help spur vaccine development and inform vaccine scheduling. Early identification and ultimately preventing childhood SDB will improve childhood neurobehavioral development while optimizing limited sleep testing and surgical resources.

column36: Pragmatic Pediatric Trial of Balanced Versus Normal Saline Fluid in Sepsis (PRoMPT BOLUS)
column37: Sepsis is a medical emergency caused by severe infection. Septic shock is the most severe form. More than 25 million children worldwide are diagnosed with sepsis/septic shock every year. Sepsis is the most expensive hospital condition in North America and for critically ill children is the most common cause of hospital death. The World Health Organization has called for optimized treatments in sepsis. Crystalloid fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of initial treatment of sepsis. However, there is currently no research that clearly shows which is the most effective and safest type of crystalloid fluid in children. Two types of crystalloids are used for resuscitation in sepsis: balanced fluids (BF) and 0.9% "normal" saline (NS). In the absence of high quality, pediatric-specific data, NS resuscitation remains the overwhelming preference among pediatric emergency clinicians. The objective of this large, pragmatic, randomized study is to test the comparative effectiveness of the two most common types of crystalloid (BF vs NS) to improve clinical outcomes in children treated for septic shock. Thirteen pediatric emergency departments in the Pediatric Emergency Research Canada (PERC) network will collaborate with sites in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand to enroll 8,800 children with suspected septic shock. Children will be randomized to receive fluid resuscitation and maintenance fluids with either NS or BF for 24-48 hours, with all other aspects of care (other than fluid type) at the discretion of the managing health care team. Our primary outcome is major adverse kidney events within 30 days from randomization (MAKE30), a patient-centered endpoint that includes persistent kidney dysfunction, initiation of dialysis, or death. An economic analysis will be completed. The PRoMPT BOLUS study will be the largest trial of pediatric-specific, ED-initiated sepsis management to address the important clinical question of efficacy and safety of crystalloid fluids.

column36: Identifying low bone turnover disease in chronic kidney disease in order to guide anti-fracture therapy
column37: It is now well recognized that people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have weak bones. However, in contrast to people with osteoporosis, those with CKD have specific types of bone disease that could contraindicate the use of common anti-osteoporotic therapy. Indeed, up to 50% of people with CKD have what we call low bone turnover (LBT) disease (extremely low bone formation and resorption), in which anti-resorptive therapy is not recommended. In those patients, anabolic therapy (to stimulate bone formation) could be given. Identifying LBT disease is therefore of extreme importance if we want to propose adequate bone therapy in CKD patients. Until today, doing a bone biopsy at the iliac crest (anterior part of the hip) remains the only way to diagnose low bone turnover in CKD but is rarely done. Based on our prior works, we hypothesize that non-invasive markers could be used to identify CKD patients with LBT. Our global objective is to identify non-invasive biomarkers that will help in identifying patients with low vs non-LBT so that adequate anti-fracture therapy coud be offered. Methods We will recruit patients with CKD for iliac crest biopsy. We will compare CKD patients with low vs non-LBT. We will evaluate non-invasive biomarkers in the skin (AGEs) and in blood (AGEs, sclerostin, micro-ARNs) that may differentiate CKD patients with low vs non-LBT. Their predictive capacity will be evaluated alone or in combination. Then, Iliac crest biopsy specimens will be evaluated for bone quality parameters (microarchitecture, bone material composition) to evaluate the effects of LBT on bone strength. Significance Bone fragility is a major health issue in patients with CKD. We have a unique opportunity to conduct a bone biopsy study in this population to identify non-invasive markers that may predict LBT disease. Our results have the potential to change clinical practice so that personnalized bone therapy could be offered to CKD population.

column36: Sublingual Fentanyl for acute relief of breathlessness in patients with advanced COPD : A randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design trial.
column37: According to Health Canada, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) affects over 2 millions of Canadian adults and,with an ageing population , the prevalence of the disease has increased. Breathlessness is the main manifestation of COPD and is often an invalidating symptom for patients with severe disease despite being on optimal inhaled treatment. In fact, the presence of dyspnea is recognized as a major determinant of health-related quality of life and it often leads to unplanned hospitalizations, which result in significant cost on the healthcare system. Breakthrough COPD dyspnea represents an important element in the spectrum of managing breathlessness in COPD patients. Breakthrough COPD dyspnea are acute episodes of breathlessness that could peak in intensity within a few minutes and for which the speed of medication onset is crucial for proper control beyond the use of existing short acting inhaled therapy. Recently, oral morphine was demonstrated as an effective and safe option for the control of refractory breathlessness and is now recommended by clinical guidelines in this context. However, this approach might not always offer optimal onset of action to match the rapid nature of an episode of breakthrough COPD dyspnea. Novel approach that includes the use of small dose sublingual liquid fentanyl might be more effective while remaining safe to treat breakthrough COPD dyspnea. This approach has been shown to be effective for pain control but it has never been tested to treat breakthrough COPD dyspnea. We propose a multicenter randomized trial to evaluate the effect of sublingual fentanyl on breathlessness control in severe to very-severe COPD patients with persistent shortness of breath despite optimal therapy. This study is a crucial step toward appropriate treatment selection for breakthrough COPD dyspnea and it will also pave the way to future research for control of acute refractory breathlessness in other severe respiratory diseases.

column36: Participation in aerobic exercise during stroke rehabilitation: a mixed-methods study
column37: People are often physically unfit early after stroke, which can make participating in therapy and daily activities difficult. Aerobic exercise improves physical fitness and general health, which reduces the risk of another stroke, and also promotes stroke recovery. Aerobic exercise is beneficial and safe even early after stroke. Clinical guidelines recommend completing aerobic exercise within stroke rehabilitation. Most physiotherapists say that they prescribe aerobic exercise to their stroke patients. However, the number of people with stroke who participate in aerobic exercise during rehabilitation is low. We need to understand the barriers to exercise from patient and clinician perspectives so that we can develop interventions to promote exercise participation during stroke rehabilitation. The purpose of this study is to understand what stops or helps people with stroke participating in aerobic exercise during rehabilitation. This study will collect information about patients with stroke who are undergoing rehabilitation at one of four different hospitals. Information collected will include medical history, social supports, physical and cognitive function, and exercise preferences. We will compare characteristics of those who participate in exercise to those who do not. We will also interview patients and their physiotherapists to find out how they feel about exercise during rehabilitation. We will combine the quantitative (statistics) and qualitative information (interviews) to get a complete idea of the problem of exercise participation in stroke rehabilitation. Knowing what prevents or helps people with stroke to participate in exercise during rehabilitation will allow us to create strategies to increase the number of people who participate. These strategies will increase the number of people with stroke who can benefit from this important therapy (aerobic exercise), and can in turn improve recovery and health of those with stroke in the future.

column36: The impact of amyloid-induced neurodegeneration on sleep features and memory processes
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an age-related neurodegenerative disease that primarily impairs memory for recent facts and events (explicit memory). Loss of connections (synapses) between cells (neurons) in specific brain regions involved in explicit memory, such as the hippocampus, gradually leads to neuronal cell death and induced the progressive cognitive decline that characterises the disease. Since the hippocampus is also involved in other functions such a sleep, some features of sleep are also affected at the onset of the disease, including poor sleep quality, insomnia and early morning wakening. Given the importance of sleep on memory performance, these sleep disturbances have in return a deleterious impact on memory function of AD patients. The main objective of this project is to determine how hippocampal neurodegeneration and sleep disturbances influence each other to impair memory function in the development of AD. We also propose to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying this bidirectional interaction at the onset of the disease. To achieve our goal, we will perform chronic hippocampal injections of amyloid-beta oligomers in animals to mimic cell death and cognitive deficits observed in AD. Electroencephalographic measurements will be performed to determine sleep alterations in these animals. The impact of neurodegeneration and sleep perturbations will be tested on the acquisition and consolidation phases of memory. Identifying the specific signature of hippocampal neurodegeneration on sleep features might serve as a non-invasive marker to refine the diagnosis of AD. A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underpinning the effects of neurodegeneration and sleep disturbances on cognitive decline in AD could be of great interest to develop new therapeutic targets effective at the onset of the illness before neurodegeneration induces severe memory loss that prevents patients from functioning independently.

column36: What works for whom? Individual participant data network meta-analysis of exercise for persistent low back pain
column37: Low back pain is a leading cause of disability in Canada and globally. Almost every Canadian suffers from low back pain at some point in their life. Most of the cost associated with low back pain is generated by a small percentage of individuals with persistent symptoms. Exercise therapy is a commonly recommended treatment strategy. However, there is no evidence to support the use of one type of exercise over another and very limited evidence about individual patient characteristics associated with effectiveness of specific treatments. There are two specific directions of research evidence that are needed to answer, 'what works for whom?' for patients with persistent low back pain. Neither of these directions can be pursued with more randomized controlled trials or traditional evidence synthesis projects: 1.Determine what types of exercise therapy, design or delivery characteristics improve its effectiveness for patients with persistent low back pain, and 2.Determine the persistent low back pain patient characteristics and patient subgroups that have better or worse outcomes with exercise therapy. To identify different types and characteristics of exercise programs that may be more effective we will use an approach called network meta-analyses. To identify patient characteristics and subgroups of individual patients who may benefit more from exercise therapy compared to no treatment, non-exercise usual care, and other conservative treatments, we will conduct an analysis using individual patient data from the best available trials. There are currently more than 350 randomized controlled trials of exercise therapy for persistent low back pain. Individually, these trials provide limited evidence and have not advanced decision-making for back pain patients. This team will advance the low back pain field by combining and re-analyzing trial data using best-practice statistical methods.

column37: In Canada, 2% of the population lives with a traumatic brain injury (TBI), and there are 18,000 hospitalizations for TBI each year. We will also examine the risks of maternal and newborn medical complications associated with having both TBI and perinatal mental illness. Evidence of an association between TBI and mental illness around the time of pregnancy will lead to the development of health care services that address the unique mental health needs of women with TBI. Given that TBI is a leading cause of disability worldwide, these efforts will result in better outcomes for mothers, infants, and families by providing more responsive support to women with TBI.

column36: CARE NT: Caring and Responding in the Northwest Territories
column37: A major priority of three communities in the Northwest Territories (NT) (Inuvik, Fort Good Hope, and Yellowknife) is improving the experience of patients and access to healthcare services. The team has worked with the three communities for almost twenty years, and, having very well established, trusted, and respectful relationships, has been asked to address the communities' concerns. For residents of remote NT communities, basic health services are provided through a nurse-based primary care model, supported by visiting doctors and telehealth services. Residents who require more than basic primary care must travel to services that are only available in regional centres, or in southern provinces. Accessing these services can involve lengthy wait times, as well as long distance travel and time away from home communities, family, and social support networks for weeks at a time. In this project, the communities of Yellowknife, Inuvik, and Fort Good Hope with a Community Advisory Board and the team plan to: 1) Gather community members' perspectives via sharing circles using Two-Eyed Seeing to improve access and availability of healthcare services; 2) Develop, implement, and evaluate a community-driven and community-led program to improve access to and experience with health services that will take place on-the-land and alongside Elders, traditional knowledge holders, and healers; and 3) Share materials and all findings with community, territorial, and national organizations, as well as healthcare providers and policymakers to ensure culturally appropriate health service delivery. This project will generate new knowledge on the impact of community-led, locally-designed health promotion programs and the importance of utilizing Indigenous methods for implementation, documentation, and dissemination to improve healthcare access and experience with NT communities.

column36: Molecular and Mechanistic Investigations of the Role of Prolactin in Women's Health: A Focus on Breast Morphogenesis and Suppression of Tumorigenesis
column37: The mammary gland undergoes complex molecular and morphological changes during the pregnancy/lactation cycle. These developmental changes within the mammary gland allow the differentiation of mammary cells to properly synthesize and secret milk components into the mammary duct ready for breastfeeding. Breast cancer is a major disease affecting women worldwide. Breast cancer progression to a metastatic disease is still a clinical challenge as there are no treatments once metastasis has occurred. Indeed, our incomplete understanding of the molecular mechanism(s) that promote tumorigenesis of the breast underlies the lack of effective therapeutic options for patients stricken by this disease. Importantly, extensive research has shown that the lactation hormone prolactin is indispensable in mammary gland development and lactation. Interestingly, we have previously found that prolactin plays a direct role of in mammary morphogenesis and differentiation of the mammary cells. Moreover, we have also recently shown that prolactin receptor gene expression is associated with tumor differentiation status, that it is lost during tumor progression and in more aggressive disease. Whereas, high expression of prolactin pathway is associated with prolonged and better patient survival outcomes. We postulate here that deciphering the role of prolactin in breast cancer and its role in mammary morphogenesis and differentiation and will enhance our understanding breast cancer development and progression and will provide new avenues for therapy against breast cancer.

column36: The Impact of Nutrient Excess and Neuroinflammation on Hypothalamic Reproductive Neurons.
column37: Reproductive dysfunction is a major health concern, where it is estimated that 16% of the Canadian couples affected. Reproduction is controlled by a number of external factors, which include nutritional status. It is well known that reproductive success is linked to nutritional and metabolic health. Yet the mechanisms by which nutritional status, whether through obesity or anorexia, directly influences the hypothalamic neurons that are responsible for reproduction are not yet studied. Our society has evolved to the state where obesity is prevalent, particularly in women and men of childbearing age. Obesity, mostly due to the ingestion of diets high in saturated fats, has reached epidemic levels in North America. Whether high-fat diet has a direct effect on the neurons responsible for reproductive function can be studied at a number of levels in my laboratory, from the cell to the whole animal, and from rodent models to humans. Exactly how the brain senses nutrients is not yet understood, but it is now recognized that the brain can sense fat and carbohydrates through specific neurons. Interestingly, it has been found that the brain produces an inflammatory response when exposed to high levels of fat. Therefore major efforts are currently underway in my laboratory to dissect the brain pathways involved in sensing nutrients and the development of a low grade chronic inflammatory response in specific reproductive neurons. Whether there is an effect of neuroinflammation on reproductive function will be studied. We are also testing novel therapeutics to try to rescue the function of these neurons at the brain level using anti-inflammatory agents. Our research to explore how excess nutrients contributes to the development of inflammation leading to reproductive disorders is an essential step for development of improved treatment regimens for infertility, obesity, and other related disorders, such as polycystic ovarian syndrome.

column36: Mechanisms of Arterial Stiffening in Calcification
column37: Calcification of arteries occurs in more than 1/2 of the population over the age of 60, and causes significant morbidity and mortality in diseases like atherosclerosis, diabetes, hypertension and in chronic kidney disease. Smooth muscle cells within the arteries deposit minerals in the extracellular matrix, in a process similar to the mineralization and hardening of bones, and this causes thickening, stiffening and sometimes rupture of these vessels. At present, there are no effective medical treatments to prevent or reverse calcification. Furthermore, calcified vessels cannot be angioplastied or stented, the two most common and successful treatments for atherosclerosis and peripheral vascular disease. We have recently discovered that a receptor protein which is expressed on arterial smooth muscle cells is responsible for calcification. This receptor, DDR1, causes a switch in the smooth muscle cells so that they start to behave like bone cells, and deposit minerals (calcifications) in the tissue. We seek to better understand the role of DDR1 in these processes during atherosclerosis and diabetes, and the consequences for normal function of blood vessels. Importantly, we will test a new inhibitor for DDR1 in a mouse model of atherosclerosis, to see if we can inhibit calcification. Most or our work to date has been performed in tissue culture and mouse models. We will now for the first time investigate the expression and function of DDR1 in human diseased arteries. Our hope is that the work will lead to the development of new therapies designed to inactivate DDR1 and therefore prevent the calcification of arteries.

column36: Working together to implement novel, culturally informed early childhood oral health interventions for young First Nations and Metis children in Manitoba
column37: First Nations and Metis Canadians face significant oral health challenges, especially children. This proposal is submitted to continue to work with First Nations and Metis communities in the spirit of Reconciliation to deal with the problem of early childhood caries (ECC) (tooth decay). Past funding from CIHR allowed us to work with four Manitoba communities to tailor the Healthy Smile Happy Child (HSHC) initiative so that it was culturally appropriate. The aims of this application are to: i) add in traditional oral health teaching to the HSHC initiative in new partnering First Nations and Metis communities in Manitoba and ii) introduce the practice of caries risk assessment (CRA) (judging a child's risk for tooth decay) by non-dental healthcare staff as a way to improve access to dental care. HSHC has had success in promoting good early childhood oral health, improving knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours, and preventing ECC. CRA is a promising way to increase access to early childhood dental health assessments and to create dental homes (i.e. clinics where children get ongoing dental care) for children. The main goal of this project is to deal with the problem of ECC experienced by Indigenous children in Manitoba. This will be done in two ways. Objective 1 will add traditional oral health teaching to improve and strengthen the HSHC initiative. We will study changes in parents' attitudes, knowledge and behaviours about ECC and changes in young children's dental health. Objective 2 will study the practice of CRA by non-dental healthcare staff as a way to improve access to dental care. We will study if CRA leads to the successful uptake of this practice, more children receiving dental health assessments, improved access to dental care, and increased the number of children being referred to dental offices to create dental homes for them.

column36: Genetic Determinants of Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a heterogeneous group of disorders that result in irreversible scarring over time. CKD affects more than 750 million people globally, and results in more than 1 million deaths each year. Large, granular datasets have now been gathered from world leading cohorts in Canada and the United States, with growing expertise to apply novel biomarker combinations collected at different disease time points with clinical traits. In this proposal, we will focus on a leading cause of CKD called Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and genomics, which is emerging as one tool to identify disease subtypes according to mechanism and treatment outcomes. We have recently reported that a series of rare genetic variations account for ~11% of adults with FSGS, but in the majority of patients, the causes are unknown. We also find that within these genetic cases, different gene categories influence disease progression. However, the cumulative effects of common, subtle variations (called single nucleotide polymorphisms or SNPs) in many genes that are important for normal kidney function have not been explored in FSGS. We will address this critical knowledge gap. By bringing together leading investigators in Canada and the US, we aim to uncover the effects of common genetic determinants, in isolation and cumulatively, important for disease progression in a large cohort of FSGS patients (n=6500). There is a large unmet clinical need for mechanism-based therapy and to achieve this goal, precise definitions of FSGS subtypes are required. Genomics has emerged as one tool to successfully stratify patients with heterogeneous diseases like major depressive disorder, coronary artery disease and cancers such as breast cancer that have, like FSGS, been historically heavily reliant on pathology. We intend to apply these same genomic approaches to identify clinically meaningful FSGS subtypes to inform management.

column36: HIP fracture Accelerated surgical TreaTment And Care tracK (HIP ATTACK) trial - 2
column37: Worldwide millions of adults (>35,000 Canadians) suffer a hip fracture every year. Hip fractures result in bleeding, inflammation, and stress states that can cause complications and death. There is evidence that early surgical treatment of a hip fracture may improve patients' outcomes, however, standard care in Canada is that most patients wait more than 24 hours to have surgery. Some patients may benefit more from the early surgery than others. Results from the HIP ATTACK-1 trial suggest that patients suffering heart injury (measured by a serum protein called troponin) at the time of a hip fracture have a higher risk of dying within 90 days. Standard care has been to medically manage these patients and postpone surgery; however, the HIP ATTACK-1 trial results suggested that hip fracture patients with heart injury had a lower risk of dying from early surgery as compared to standard care (i.e., surgery typically 24 hours later). Patients with a heart injury just after their hip fracture may reflect patients who are not tolerating the physiological stress of the fracture, and therefore accelerated surgery may reduce the time of heart injury and the risk of mortality. We plan to perform a new study (HIP ATTACK-2) to assess the impact of accelerated surgery (goal of surgery within 6 hours of diagnosis) versus usual timing of surgery on the 90-day risk of death in adults with a hip fracture that have elevated troponin levels after the fracture. We will randomize 1100 patients to receive accelerated surgery or standard care. We will include patients =45 years, with a hip fracture that requires surgery, and have elevated troponin levels on Emergency Room arrival. We will follow patients in hospital, and at 90 days after surgery. This trial will determine if a specific high-risk population should be prioritized with expedited surgical care. This is the first large trial that may change the paradigm to postpone surgery in patients suffering heart injuries before surgery.

column36: Role of trained immunity in the response to BCG immunotherapy of bladder cancer
column37: Bladder cancer is one of the most common cancers worldwide. It is a very serious cancer because it is not easily cured and it substantially lowers the quality of life of those affected. Most patients with higher-risk bladder cancer are treated with surgery followed by a form of immunotherapy. This immunotherapy involves introducing into the bladder of patients the same bacteria that are used to vaccinate people against tuberculosis (TB). For reasons that we do not fully understand, patients given these bacteria mount an immune response that fights the bladder cancer cells and prevents the cancer from coming back. Unfortunately, up to half of the patients do not respond fully to this therapy, and the cancer comes back. Our research aims to better understand how this immunotherapy of bladder cancer works and, in doing so we also hope to determine why some patients don't respond well to it. Knowing which patients will not respond to this treatment is important because such patients could then be offered an alternative therapy that could potentially save their lives and also spare them from the undesirable side effects of the TB immunotherapy. We have obtained results showing that giving the TB vaccine to bladder cancer patients primes and activates some of the more primitive cells of the immune system. Interestingly, these immune cells are found circulating in the blood of these patients, and their activation appears to occur to a larger extent in cancer patients that respond better to the TB vaccine than in poorly responsive or unresponsive patients. We plan to do experiments to investigate how these 'primed and activated' circulating immune cells can lead to rejection of tumour cells in the bladder. Another potential benefit of our proposed research is that it could lead to the development of new ways to treat bladder cancer patients. It could also help us determine whether similar immunotherapies can be used to treat patients with other types of cancer.

column36: Targeting brain cholesterol homeostasis to counteract prion diseases
column37: Many diseases of the brain are caused by proteins that change their three-dimensional shape, and as a consequence form 'clumps' or aggregates in brain cells, eventually destroying the brain. Prion diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are the prototype group for such disorders. They are always fatal and cannot be treated to date. We found that cholesterol, an important component of cellular membranes, is elevated in prion-infected neurons, which favors the aggregation of the disease-causing protein. We propose to elucidate the consequences of elevated cholesterol levels and use a re-purposed pharmaceutical as a new approach for treatment of prion diseases.

column36: Safe places for aging and care? A site-specific analysis of features influencing violence in care for older adults
column37: There is an urgent need to address different forms of violence and strengthen violence prevention strategies across the long term care continuum for older adults and carers. Violence can lead to physical and psychological harm, emotional exhaustion, and burnout for carers while being labelled as violent, aggressive, or difficult can have a direct impact on older adults' sense of self, care relationships, and quality of care. Although some research indicates environmental causes of violence, we still know little about the specific ways that social, physical and organizational features of care environments produce violent actions across the long term care continuum. The proposed study explores this question through a comparative case study of violence and responses to violence in home care and residential long-term care settings in two provinces (Manitoba and Nova Scotia). By integrating findings from document analysis, interviews, digital diaries, and ethnographic observations in these care settings, this research will ultimately strengthen existing violence prevention strategies, which sometimes fall short of protecting the safety and long-term well-being of older adults and carers.

column36: Stress and loss of ovarian function: novel insights into the origins and treatment of respiratory control disorders in females
column37: Sleep apnea (SA) affects ~25% of the Canadian population. Respiratory instability and prolonged apneas during sleep indicate that parts of the nervous system regulating breathing are dysfunctional in SA patients. This is clinically important because SA increases the risk of disease, including cardiovascular problems. SA is ~2 times more frequent in men than women, thus indicating that ovarian hormones "protect" against respiratory problems. However, this ratio changes as women age and it is estimated that SA affects nearly half of post-menopausal women. Since loss of ovarian function is a normal part of life, this project aims to explain why menopause results in respiratory problems and hypertension in some women but not others. Because experiencing stress during early life affects brain development and increases vulnerability to disease, we propose that the consequences of menopause on respiratory function are aggravated by neonatal stress. Thus, the impact of early life stress on the cardiorespiratory system becomes apparent with loss of ovarian function. We will address this fundamental issue in female rats exposed to stress during early life. This model reproduces abnormalities in respiratory function and hypertension; in females, SA-related symptoms become apparent following loss of ovarian function. Experiments will be performed in the intact, naturally sleeping rats. We will then delve into the underlying mechanisms by quantifying the consequences of loss of ovarian function on the sensory, central, and neuroendocrine components of the respiratory control system of rats raised under normal conditions or subjected to neonatal stress in the form of neonatal maternal separation. As the Canadian population is aging, understanding the basic principles explaining such divergences in the aging trajectory of women is becoming urgent. This proposal offers a novel and comprehensive approach to an important health issue that affects a growing proportion of Canadians.

column36: Sleep and Circadian Misalignment and their Relation to Cardiometabolic Health during Adolescence
column37: Humans have a built-in circadian rhythm (body clock) that repeats every 24-hrs. It tells our bodies when we should be awake or asleep and it stays on time by using information from the environment around us, like light, regularly timed meals, and activity. The body clock controls the rhythms of most functions including body temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and hormone release. Sometimes the timing of these bodily functions gets disrupted and out of sync with the rhythm of the body clock, which is called circadian misalignment (e.g., bed/wake times shifts later). Teenagers experience many changes in the timing of their sleep. Teens commonly go to bed later and sleep in on the weekends. Our 24hr society promotes this later sleep delay. Using gadgets late at night, staying up late on weekends, and having inconsistent routines across the week can contribute to this shift toward later sleep timing. Shifts in sleep times often happen during puberty. Girls start going to bed later before boys, which coincides with their earlier puberty onset than boys. In fact, compared to adults, teenagers have a body clock slightly longer than 24 hours. Our project tracks the evolution of the circadian timing system changes across puberty. We will investigate if circadian misalignment might be a culprit in child obesity and cardiometabolic health. Wearable gadgets will be worn by teens to monitor their sleep, activity, temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure. The information we learn from this project will help parents, schools, and policy makers develop better prevention programs to improve childhood health. We also help science make technology smarter so wearable gadgets can give more accurate information about bodily rhythms.

column36: Predicting and Evaluating Anal Cancer in HIV with novel biomarkers: The PEACH Study
column37: Though there have been many improvements in the health of those living with HIV since the mid 1990s when effective therapies first emerged including reductions in AIDS-associated cancers, there have been increases in other types of cancer since that time. One category of these is cancers caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is the main cause of anal cancer, and gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) have rates of anal cancer up to 100 times higher than the general population. Despite this, there are currently no clear guidelines for anal cancer screening in gbMSM living with HIV, the currently available screening tools do not perform particularly well, and there are very few clinics and health care providers trained in providing these services. As such, there is an urgent need to investigate ways to better provide anal cancer screening to this at-risk population. One of the ways to do this is to develop and examine different tests that can predict the presence of lesions in the anal canal that may lead to cancer (called high-grade dysplasia, or anal precancers). These are called biomarkers, and there are several that have not been adequately examined as possible predictors of anal cancers and pre-cancers in gbMSM living with HIV. The proposed study will recruit participants from an existing set of Canadian studies to examine these novel biomarkers as predictors of anal pre-cancers.

column36: Characterization of oncogenic splicing pathways driven by RNA-binding proteins
column37: Genes can produce multiple distinct products through a process called "RNA splicing". The normal splicing pattern of genes is often disrupted in cancer, and many of the molecules that result from this abnormal splicing have been functionally implicated in cancer malignancy. However, the underlying cellular mechanisms that govern RNA splicing and the extent to which they play a role in cancer progression remain largely unknown. To address this challenge, we have developed new computational frameworks that, in combination with large-scale genomics data, can identify novel factors that are involved in RNA splicing. Using this approach, we have discovered and partly characterized a previously unknown RNA element that drives abnormal splicing in highly metastatic breast cancer. We have also identified the associated protein that interacts with this novel RNA element - through this interaction, this protein can change the splicing of gene products and lead to metastasis. Our studies also indicate that the role of this protein is not limited to breast cancer, and it may in fact be involved in multiple other cancer types. In this project, we will build on these recent developments to perform a detailed dissection of RNA splicing programs across different cancers, identify the genes that are modified as a result of abnormal splicing, cellular and molecular deficits that drive abnormal splicing, and their contribution to cancer development, progression, and metastasis. This study will enable us to obtain a better understanding of how the cellular behaviour and function changes in cancer and how tumour cells become metastatic, and may lead to new avenues for development of therapeutic strategies.

column36: The impact of Monte Carlo dose calculations on prostate and breast low-dose rate brachytherapy dose-outcome relationships and radiobiological modeling.
column37: Prostate and breast cancer are the most common cancers for Canadians, at 20.7% and 25.5% of men's and women's cancers, respectively. Radiation therapy (RT) is a preferred treatment modality, either alone or combined, for 50% of cancer patients. In recent years, technological developments have enabled RT to accomplish significant advances in the local control of various cancer sites; 40% of cancers are cured by RT, compared to 49% by surgery and 11% by chemotherapy (2010 IAEA report). As such, RT remains a formidable, and very affordable, weapon in the fight against cancer. One RT approach is low-dose-rate brachytherapy that using permanently implanted mm-size sources. These radioactive sources are implanted directly in the tumour, enabling higher local dose and greater protection to organs-at-risk. These procedures are usually performed as a 1-day outpatient procedures. It provides a well-tolerated treatment with a good therapeutic ratio. Accurate knowledge of dose-outcome relationships is critical to success in radiation therapy. Despite the overall good results clinically, a critical barrier to progress in further advancing brachytherapy treatments is the inaccuracy of dose evaluations which lead to a major disconnect between clinically-measured outcomes and "accurate" dose distributions. The assembled team comprised of world-experts in state-of-the-art dose calculations as well as world-leading brachytherapy physicians from all major programs across Canada comes together to tackle this problem. The proposed research will provide more accurate knowledge of prescription doses needed for relapse-free survival as well as a better understanding of radiation toxicity thresholds. It has the potential to further improve tumour control while reducing the incidence and severity of complications, thus enhancing patient quality of life and reducing healthcare costs: simply put improving the therapeutic ratio of BT treatments of prostate and breast cancer.

column36: A randomized trial of doxycycline chemoprophylaxis for the prevention of sexually transmitted infections in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM)
column37: Globally, syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhea are three of the most common sexually transmitted infections (STI). Over the last decade, these STIs have seen a resurgence in many parts of the world, including Canada, with the bulk of infections seen in major urban centres. More recently, these increases have been even more significant, with a 150% increase in these infections in Canada between 2014-2018. These infections have primarily affected gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM). Further, HIV-positive gbMSM are disproportionately affected by many STIs. In addition to playing a role in the enhanced transmission of HIV, STIs also place individuals living with HIV at higher risk of complications and more severe disease. A few years ago, a small pilot study found that doxycycline - an inexpensive, well-tolerated antibiotic - given daily may prevent new STIs in HIV-positive gbMSM. More recently, another study looked at the use of one dose of doxycycline given after a sexual encounter for prevention of STIs, and the results of this study demonstrated protection against STIs as well. Based on these promising data, along with the concerning increases in these STIs, the current study will examine the use of doxycycline as either a daily preventative therapy (preexposure prophylaxis, or PrEP) or an 'after sex' prevention tool (postexposure prophylaxis, or PEP) for STIs in gbMSM living with HIV. While examining for efficacy as its primary goal, this study will also do a thorough examination of some of the potential challenges and concerns associated with the use of a daily antibiotic: drug resistance, tolerability and side effects, and how acceptable this drug is for people to take regularly.

column36: Manipulating mast cells to modify the interferon and inflammatory responses to viral infection
column37: Viral infections are a major cause of illness and death. This is especially true of respiratory viruses such as Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) which is a major cause of hospital admissions in young children. The devastating impact of such diseases have been further confirmed by the recent COVID-19 outbreak. In each of these diseases, some people respond effectively to infection with little damage to their airways or development of difficulty in breathing while others can develop problems due to inflammation and tissue damage in the lungs, leading to difficulties breathing due to bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Individuals with asthma are often most vulnerable to becoming seriously ill as a result of such infections. In this project we will be examining how to better control such damaging inflammatory responses by understanding how they are regulated and exploring potential new therapeutic targets. In order to complete this work we will focus on a resident immune cell found in the airways and other sites of infection, known as the mast cell. This cell initiates and controls early immune responses to infection and produces many factors that can enhance inflammation and tissue damage as well as factors that can regulate inflammation and combat viral infection. By learning more about these cells and how to control them, we aim to identify new treatments that will substantially reduce the lung damage and deaths caused by such respiratory infections.

column36: A novel mechanism for GPCR-dependent activation of BRD4
column37: Cells are constantly responding to signals from their surrounding environment. These signals influence cellular behavior in many ways: they can promote or arrest growth and division, stimulate migration, alter electrical properties, or lead to programmed cell death. Cells respond to these signals by virtue of receptors on their surface, which, when engaged, trigger cascades of molecular events inside the cell; in disease these pathways are abnormally wired or abnormally active. In many cases these pathways culminate in changes in gene expression, but we still do not fully understand the molecular events that translate signals into effects on genes. In this project we will characterize a novel mechanism we have discovered for signal-dependent regulation of a protein called BRD4. BRD4 is a key regulator of gene expression and is abnormally active in a wide range of diseases including cancer and heart disease. By learning more about how BRD4 activity is turned on and off, we hope to uncover new therapeutic strategies for modulating BRD4 activity in disease states, as well as new clinical settings in which BRD4 inhibition may be beneficial.

column36: The role of TNF in stress-induced synaptic and behavioural change
column37: Acute stress causes a number of changes to brain circuits, resulting in changes in behaviour. But the stress response can also become unbalanced; it is a contributing factor in the development of several psychiatric disorders, including anxiety disorders. A detailed understanding of the mechanisms driving stress-induced changes in brain circuitry may allow mitigation of stress-induced dysfunction. These changes were thought to directly result from the elevation in stress hormones. However, we have evidence that many of these changes require inflammatory signaling. Here we will define how stress results in inflammation, the cell types involved, and how inflammation changes brain circuitry. We will then test if blocking the inflammatory signaling can reverse stress-induced changes. This could be a potential therapy for stress-associated pathologies, including posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

column36: Identifying Critical RNA-RNA Interactions during Ribosome Biogenesis
column37: All cancer types share a need for increased protein production to enable rapid cell divisions and tumor growth. Accordingly, all cancer cells are characterized by an enhanced production of protein factories called ribosomes and by an enlarged cellular compartment, where ribosomes are assembled, which is used as a diagnostic marker. Therefore, inhibiting ribosome formation is a promising therapeutic strategy in cancer treatment. However, we are lacking a good understanding of ribosome formation which renders it difficult to target this pathway. Here, we strive to open a new avenue for impairing assembly of protein factories in cancer. Ribosomes consist predominantly of RNA, a sister molecule of DNA. Critical steps during ribosome formation constitute the chemical modification and three-dimensional folding of ribosomal RNA. Interestingly, these steps are mediated by other small RNAs in the cell. Our long-term goal is to inhibit these interactions between small RNAs and ribosomal RNAs thereby depriving cancer cells of protein factories. Here, we will combine functional, structural and cellular studies to enhance our understanding on how small RNAs promote modification and folding of ribosomal RNA. Thereby, we will provide detailed insight into the early stages of ribosome biogenesis which are currently only poorly understood. Importantly, our multi-disciplinary approach will allow us to identify critical interactions between RNAs that are needed for ribosome formation. The generated knowledge will enable us to suggest promising small RNAs to be inhibited in future cancer therapies by so-called antisense drugs that target a specific RNA. In conclusion, this research will increase our knowledge on ribosome formation as fundamental process in life and will also provide critical information for the design of antisense drugs to eventually inhibit ribosome assembly in cancer cells.

column36: Resident-to-Resident Abuse in Long-Term Care: Reporting for Change
column37: Mounting anecdotal evidence suggests that sexual, material and physical conflict between long-term care (LTC) residents is a large and pervasive problem that can often be fatal. This proposed project examines resident-to-resident abuse (RRA) in long-term care (LTC). Despite projections that over half a million Canadians will require LTC by 2031, there is a conspicuous lack of research on the extent and types of RRA in LTC (physical, verbal sexual, material), that often contributes to the challenges of prevention and intervention. In Canada, preliminary estimates of reported abuse cases in LTC indicated that the total number of incidents was 6,455 in 2011 representing 28% of all abuse cases. In the same study, 56% of cases of abuse in Ontario LTC were attributable to RRA. Because there is no real prevalence for RRA in Ontario, the overarching goal of this research is to establish the occurrence for RRA in LTC. Furthermore, a major provincial task force in Ontario found that of the 2,773 elder abuse critical incidents reported to the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-term Care, 57% of the events represented RRA while 33% of incidents were staff abuse or neglect of residents. Media coverage regularly documents serious assaults and even homicides of LTC residents sustained at the hands of other residents. Although some data across all of the provinces exists, a national picture with respect to RRA in LTC has yet to be established. Multiple methods will include a pilot study as a precursor to a prospective, observational study, an assessment of the cost of RRA, and an evaluation of models of patient-centred care based on behavioural support and the use of technology. Evidence-based digital and pocket tools that describe the most vulnerable for abuse, the perpetrator, the location of the abuse, the type of abuse and the most helpful approaches to prevention and intervention will be made available to all stakeholders through knowledge translation activities.

column36: A realist evaluation of the implementation of a health information system in a large community hospital.
column37: The 21st century is an age of digitization of health information. Hospitals and health systems around the world are implementing Health Information Systems (HIS). These systems provide a comprehensive electronic data capture of patient personal information, diagnostic results, clinical treatments and outcomes gathered as part of treatment and care. Digitizing health information is meant to improve patient safety, reduce errors, speed information transfer and hopefully lead to better patient outcomes and more effective and efficient care processes. Past evaluations have found some of these outcomes, but there have been no robust Canadian evaluations, and none seem to have considered patient and provider experience as a core measure of implementation success. Trillium Health Partners is one of Canada's largest community hospitals and they are currently implementing a new health information system to replace some 22 other legacy systems. We propose to use this large-scale transformation to rigorously study the impact of implementing an HIS on patient experience, health outcomes, provider experience and total cost of care. We will study this with the purpose of both improving the local implementation success and creating new knowledge for others about the causes for successes and failures so that future implementations will have a higher likelihood of early success.

column36: Identification of HOXB13 inhibitors to treat castrate-resistant prostate cancer
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) affects an estimated one out of every seven Canadian men in their lifetime. The standard of care to treat recurrent or metastatic disease is designed to inhibit androgen receptor activation. While treatment is initially successful, almost all patients eventually develop resistance and progress to an aggressive "castrate-resistant" state. Even with the introduction of more potent therapeutics the median survival for these patients is less than 3 years. There is therefore a critical need for drugs that target novel molecular drivers of prostate cancer. HOXB13 is a prostate-specific protein that is essential to the growth of almost all prostate cancers experimental models. Importantly, it does not affect any other tissue. Given this critical role, HOXB13 represents a promising target to treat prostate cancer. The proposed project will first characterize the role of HOXB13 in PCa. Using these results we will identify small molecule inhibitors that directly inhibit HOXB13. From this study, a new class of inhibitors will be created which could lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat lethal prostate cancer

column36: Probing molecular mechanisms of epithelial ovarian cancer therapy-induced senescence to find biomarkers and drug targets
column37: This project aims to develop new strategies to improve the efficacy of treatment options for human ovarian cancer, one of the most lethal malignancies affecting women. Currently, in order to achieve the best treatment, the cancer is removed surgically and the inevitable cancer cells that escape surgery are targeted with therapeutic agents causing DNA damage to tumour cells. Surprisingly, while general non-cancer-specific health risks in response to treatment are well documented (side-effects), very little is known about the cellular biology behind the actual tumour regression. ln other words, the exact response of cancer cells in the tumour reacting to the damage initiated by chemotherapy remains unknown. Damaged cells have many options: they can repair themselves but risk accumulating more DNA damage; they can die; or they can enter a state of permanent growth arrest termed cellular senescence (cellular aging). ln previous research, we unexpectedly found that human ovarian cancer cells strongly undergo therapy-induced senescence, but how this occurs and whether "accelerated cancer aging" influences patient survival remains unknown. Our hypothesis is that therapy-induced cancer senescence during treatment will impact long-term patient survival. Here we propose to extensively characterize ovarian cancer cell senescence at a molecular level (how it works), and to define whether it has a clinical impact on patient survival. This knowledge could help us predict before the start of treatment whether a cancer will respond appropriately, and should help evaluate early, after treatment initiation, whether a cancer is indeed responding. This could also improve our ability to generate new pharmacological targets to manipulate therapy-induced cancer senescence toward beneficial outcomes in ovarian cancer patients

column36: Evaluating the palliative and end-of-life care of older Canadians living and dying with dementia
column37: Dementia is associated with a limited life expectancy and has become the leading cause of death of females in many Western countries. Among Canadians who are diagnosed with dementia, the average life expectancy is just 3.3 years. Despite these trends, clinicians rarely have discussions about the impact of dementia on life expectancy with their patients. This lack of discussion is partly because there are no tools that provide personalized and easy to understand information on how long a person with dementia has left to life. As a result, less than one in three Canadians dying of dementia receive palliative care before death. This gap is also partly a result of how we have designed the delivery of end-of-life care; its focus is on patients with terminal diseases, such as cancer, which have a clear pathway of often quick decline. Dementia, on the other hand, has the trajectory of gradual cognitive and physical functioning decline which makes the task of identifying a terminal phase difficult. Consequently, clinicians are often faced with the difficulty of deciding when to introduce palliative care. In this project, we propose to look at the survival trajectory of those with dementia, capturing patients at various points of healthcare contact-including at diagnosis, home care start, long-term care (i.e., nursing home) entry. We will focus on the delivery of palliative care to identify gaps in care and assess the impact of palliative care on the dying experience at various points of the disease progression. Finally, we will create user-friendly online calculators that will be hosted on our team's web platform, www.projectbiglife.ca, which will allow patients, families, and caregivers to answer personalized questions, such as "how long can this person be expected to live?" or "what typical healthcare experience and outcomes can be expected for this person?". Our ultimate goal is to enable better care planning and delivery for people with dementia.

column36: Delineating between pathophysiologic phenotypes of hypoxic ischemic brain injury after cardiac arrest
column37: Cardiac arrest, an entity where the heart stops beating, results in a brain insult called hypoxic ischemic brain injury (HIBI). HIBI occurs from a lack of blood and oxygen supply to the brain when the heart has stopped. beating. HIBI is the main determinant of clinical outcome in patients who have been resuscitated from cardiac arrest. After returning function of the heart, HIBI can continue to occur from insufficient supply of oxygen to the brain, namely from post-resuscitation low blood pressure and low blood oxygen levels. Conventionally, management guidelines have recommended increasing post-resuscitation blood pressure and blood oxygen levels; however, the clinical neurological outcomes in HIBI survivors remain poor. This discrepancy suggests there are gaps in our understanding of this complex disease. Recently, our research group has demonstrated that there appear to be distinct patterns of HIBI patients with respect to how well their brains utilize oxygen. For example, half of HIBI patients are dependent upon increasing blood pressure to achieve improved brain oxygenation and function. The other half of HIBI patients do not appear to be able utilize oxygen normally no matter how much clinicians increase blood pressure or blood oxygen levels. Differentiating between these types of HIBI patients in real time is imperative to identify patients who may especially benefit from interventions aimed at increasing blood pressure and blood oxygen levels. As such, we are proposing a prospective study of HIBI patients using brain monitoring techniques to differentiate these phenotypes in real time. We are attempting to link non-invasive methods of assessing the brain to predict these two patient groups. These non-invasive methods include MRIs of the brain, blood tests that reflect dysfunction in the brain and ultrasound techniques aimed at measuring the brain's blood flow.

column36: Understanding age at first autism health claim and acute health service use in girls and women relative to boys and men
column37: It is harder to recognize autism in girls and women, compared to boys and men. In practice, this can mean that autism goes undiagnosed for longer and as a consequence is unsupported for longer in girls and women compared to boys and men. Girls and women on the autism spectrum have described many social and mental health challenges associated with delayed diagnosis of autism. However, no research has looked at how often this happens and what the impact is at a population level. This study aims to use anonymized health data for all Ontarians to understand more about the age when autism is first diagnosed in girls and women versus boys and men, as well as how potential sociodemographic (e.g., measures of poverty), medical (e.g., other diagnoses like epilepsy), and psychiatric (e.g., anxiety disorder) correlates of the recognition of autism may differ in girls and women versus boys and men. We will also explore how the timing of autism diagnosis relates to how people use health care and how such patterns differ in girls and women versus boys and men. This study is the first of its kind, using data for the entire province of Ontario to understand sex-related and gender-related health inequities in autistic people. The new knowledge learned from this study may help us to improve the recognition and care for autistic people, especially girls and women, in the Canadian population.
