column36: The molecular basis of Muller cell dedifferentiation during retinal regeneration
column37: Humans exhibit a poor ability to regenerate photoreceptors in response to injury or disease. In contrast, other animals, like zebrafish, are capable of regenerating photoreceptors. The regenerative response in zebrafish is mediated by Muller glial cells, which are normally quiescent cells (i.e., they do not divide) and are thought to acquire stem cell characteristics by reprogramming their genome in a process called dedifferentiation in order to replace the lost photoreceptors and ultimately restore vision. However, not all Muller cells participate in the regenerative response and those that do have very limited cell division, and this is presumably to control the numbers of new cells that are produced. In general, the behaviour of Muller cells during dedifferentiation in zebrafish, arguably the best model system to study retinal regeneration, is poorly understood. We aim to capitalize on the natural regenerative ability of Muller cells in zebrafish in order to gain insight into how dedifferentiation is regulated. Specifically, we aim to: (1) Test if genes related to wound repair affect Muller cell shape changes and function in response to a lesion; and (2) Characterize the role of gene networks that control how Muller cells make the decision to divide. Although some regenerative properties are evident in human Muller cells, these cells do not produce new photoreceptors in vivo. Our research will allow us to discover new methods for overcoming the barriers to human Muller cell reprogramming into an active stem cell state. In the long term, this could facilitate the development of new pre-clinical models of human retinal regeneration and bring us closer to an endogenous repair strategy for treating blindness.

column36: Regulation of chromatin and transcription by a Cdk9-Spt5-Rtf1 pathway
column37: The flow of information from DNA to RNA to protein is fundamental to all cells in every living organism. The first step in this process-the synthesis of messenger RNA from a DNA template-is called transcription and is carried out by the enzyme RNA polymerase. Transcription occurs in multiple steps, each of which can be regulated by a diverse array of proteins. Defective regulation of transcription underlies many complex human diseases. The elongation phase of transcription, in which the RNA polymerase enzyme travels along the DNA template synthesizing RNA, is an important point of control that is abnormally regulated in heart disease and in a variety of cancers. How elongation is controlled at a molecular level remains poorly understood, and the central goal of the proposed research is to gain further knowledge of these molecular details so that they can be exploited for therapeutic benefit in human disease. Since the elongation process is fundamental to gene activation and is highly conserved in evolution, we use a simple unicellular organism (fission yeast) to model the elongation process and its control in human disease. The research focuses in particular on proteins that are functionally related to Cdk9, a master regulator protein for transcription elongation. Our research has uncovered novel functions for these proteins at unexpected locations on chromosomal DNA, as well as mechanisms that dynamically link elongation to other steps in the transcription process. Given the recent development of drugs that target elongation, further study of the molecular basis for these effects will provide important knowledge that may have important clinical implications.

column36: Towards an improved understanding of myometrial quiescence and contraction: Differential regulation via G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) and control by regulator of G-protein signaling 2 (RGS2)
column37: Preterm labour and delivery before 37 weeks of pregnancy is a serious health problem. Babies, born too soon, may face difficulties breathing, suffer with brain injury or long-term disability. Unfortunately, current clinical treatments to stop preterm labour do not work. To improve this, we must gain a better understanding of the labour process. The key to addressing the problem may be the uterus itself. Questions to ask include; how does the uterus expand throughout pregnancy to house the growing baby yet still stay inactive (quiescent), how does this change at term when contractions begin and the baby is delivered, and, what factors affect this balance that shift the uterus to the onset of preterm labour. Specialised cells within the uterus, called myometrial smooth muscle cells, provide the contractile machinery of the uterus. Located on these cells are receptors, regulated by biochemical and hormonal signals to cause either contractions or to enhance relaxation. The response of each myometrial cell is dependent on the type of signal and the specific receptor at which it acts. The aim of this project is to better understand the role of receptors present in the pregnant uterus, those important for maintaining quiescence in pregnancy, and those that stimulate contractions during labour. To this end we recently identified receptors, from the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family, present and previously unidentified in the pregnant uterus, and some of which show differential localisation and regulation with pregnancy and labour. We will use myometrial tissue and myometrial cell culture models to investigate GPCR function within the pregnant uterus, and how this may be regulated with labour, term and preterm. Knowledge generated will be clinically relevant in the management of labour, especially pre-term labour, where pharmacological strategies aimed to promote or maintain quiescence may be beneficial in delaying labour onset.

column36: Simultaneous targeting of multiple domains of HER2 and EGFR using domain-specific alpha particle labeled radioimmunoconjugates
column37: Epidermal growth factor receptor I (EGFR) and II (HER2) are two proteins that are overexpressed in most solid tumors, making them prime therapeutic and imaging targets. In particular, 25 - 30% of all breast cancers overexpress HER2. EGFR is overexpressed in up to 90% of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). About 15 - 20% of all breast cancers is TNBC. TNBC is very aggressive and is prevalent in younger women < 50 years of age. EGFR and HER2 consist of extracellular ligand binding and intracellular binding parts. The extracellular binding part consists of four sub-parts (termed domains 1 - IV) to which different molecules can specifically be bound. A combination of trastuzumab (targets domain IV) and pertuzumab (targets domain II) is approved for treating HER2 positive breast cancer but these only offer a small albeit significant improvement in outcome in patients. No approved therapies exists for EGFR positive TNBC. Our overall goal is to develop new radioactive drugs that simultaneously target different unique domains of EGFR and HER2 proteins. Radioimmunotherapy (radiolabeled antibodies) has shown promise in treating other cancers and many clinical trials are ongoing. Most radioimmunotherapy strategies have often given suboptimal results since these studies have focused on beta emitting radiation, which is less potent and tends to be toxic to adjacent healthy cells. In contrast, radioimmunotherapy based on alpha particles, such as actinium-225 (225Ac), are up to 1000-fold more effective. In this project, we will develop and test new compounds consisting of 225Ac-radiolabeled antibodies that target domains IV and II of HER2, and domains II and III of EGFR. These compounds will be tested in mouse models of HER2 and EGFR positive breast cancers. We anticipate that these strategies will be more effective than current treatment approaches in more than 50% of all BC. This work will support a potential clinical trial application for this population.

column36: The role of TRPML1 in Helicobacter pylori infection and disease
column37: Helicobacter pylori is a very common infection worldwide. Infection is usually acquired in childhood and persists for life unless specific treatment is given. H. pylori infects the stomach lining causing a chronic infection. Most people don't experience any symptoms or complications. However, about 10 percent of infected people will develop stomach ulcers and about 1 percent will develop stomach cancer. My laboratory is trying to understand how this bacteria causes disease so we can develop better treatments. We do not know exactly how infection with the bacteria causes disease. However, certain toxins that the bacteria produce can cause more severe disease. One of these toxins is called VacA. My laboratory has recently shown that bacteria that have VacA can survive in a special protected niche inside gastric cells. In contrast, H. pylori that do not have the toxin can not survive inside cells. We showed this in stomach cells grown in petri dishes, in stomach biopsies obtained from patients and during infection in mice. We then looked for H. pylori inside of stomach cells in a small number of stomach biopsies that were taken from people infected with the bacteria. When we tried to cure the infection in mice with antibiotics treatment, all mice that were infected with H. pylori that did not have the toxin were cured. In contrast, the majority of mice that were infected with H. pylori that had the toxin were not cured of infection. Therefore we now want to understand how VacA causes the formation of this protected niche so we can develop new treatments to help cure infection and prevent disease.

column36: Tuberculosis in Canada: Modeling to Inform Elimination
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) causes more deaths worldwide than any other infectious agent: 1.5 million deaths in 2018. The World Health Organization has set key targets for TB reduction and elimination. For countries like Canada, with higher income and lower TB incidence, the targets are to reduce incidence to 1 case per 100,000 population by 2035, and to 1 per million by 2050. However, Canadian TB rates have not changed for over a decade, and have reached a plateau just under 5 cases per 100,000. Over 70% of these cases occur in foreign-born persons. Progress toward elimination will not be possible without better approaches to prevention in this group. This proposal uses computer simulation of tuberculosis epidemiology and trends to examine the potential impact and cost of potential new approaches, over the period between 2020 and 2050. Specifically, we will: 1.Predict the long-term epidemiologic and economic impact of broadened pre- and post-migration screening for dormant TB infection among migrants to Canada. 2.Predict the impact of shorter, more effective, and safer treatment regimens for dormant TB infection, as well as the impact of new technologies, such as better tests for dormant infection, and a new TB vaccine, among migrants. 3.Consider the impact of investment in specific elements of TB prevention and care in high-incidence countries, with respect to their downstream implications for Canada and other countries which receive large numbers of migrants. 4. Consider the ethical implications of these new approaches, including potential stigmatization and treatment risks. This work will provide relevant information to decision makers, including public health and immigration medical authorities. It will also pave the way for better information sharing and input from affected communities. Findings will also be highly relevant to other low-incidence, higher-income, migrant receiving countries.

column36: Role of Inositol 1, 4, 5-trisphosphate Receptor Type 1 in Cardiac Arrhythmias
column37: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death, claiming more lives than all forms of cancer combined. A major cause of cardiovascular death is cardiac arrhythmia. Unfortunately, most existing anti-arrhythmic drugs provide little or no survival benefit. Therefore, a better understanding of the molecular basis of cardiac arrhythmia is urgently needed. One of the most lethal cardiac arrhythmias is catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT), which is characterized by stress-induced syncope and sudden death. CPVT is primarily linked to mutations in the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), which account for ~65% of the CPVT cases. However, the genetic basis of a significant portion of CPVT cases (~30%) remains unknown. Recent studies have implicated that hyperactivity in the type 1 inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (ITPR1) may contribute to the genesis of CPVT. However, direct evidence for the role of ITPR1 in CPVT is lacking. We have recently identified a number of hyperactive human ITPR1 mutations, indicating that ITPR1 hyperactivity exist in humans. The overall objective of this project is to define the role of ITPR1 hyperactivity in cardiac arrhythmias. To achieve this goal, we will exploit our unique and novel animal models to determine whether ITPR1 hyperactivity alters calcium handling and membrane excitability, and whether ITPR1 hyperactivity increases the propensity for CPVT in mice. We will also determine whether ITPR1 hyperactivity is associated with CPVT and other cardiac arrhythmias in humans. We expect to identify ITPR1 as a novel risk gene for CPVT and other cardiac arrhythmias. We have substantial experience and expertise in the cardiac electrophysiology and calcium handling research. We expect to provide novel insights into the mechanisms underlying irregular heartbeats and sudden death, thereby advancing the knowledge, diagnosis, and treatment of life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

column36: The gut-liver axis in host defense against bacterial infections and sepsis
column37: Our gut is home to trillions of microbes, called the microbiota, that engage in a synergistic relationship with our body's immune system to maintain health. Disruption of the gut microbiota, or "dysbiosis," is linked to the development of immune system dysfunction and disease, including susceptibility to infections. Nowhere is this more relevant than in the intensive care unit (ICU), where many critically ill patients battle life-threatening infections and sepsis as a result of impaired immune defenses. Recent research has revealed that critically ill patients harbour extreme dysbiosis of their gut microbiota, but how this dysbiosis contributes to the breakdown of immune defense during sepsis is unknown. A crucial site of immune defense against the spread of infections in the bloodstream is the liver, as it is home to specialized anti-bacterial immune cells that are responsible for capturing and clearing pathogens from the blood. Positioned between the gut and the systemic circulation, these liver immune cells are constantly exposed to molecules released by the gut microbiota. We hypothesize that communication between the microbiota and liver immune cells is required to maintain this immune firewall against the spread of infections in the bloodstream, whereas dysbiosis causes a breakdown of liver immune cell function resulting in uncontrolled pathogen dissemination and sepsis. Our research will test this hypothesis using cutting-edge mouse models with "designer microbiota", combined with sophisticated imaging that allows us to directly visualize the function of immune cells in the liver as they combat infections. The overall goal of this research is to discover how the microbiota regulates the liver immune firewall, and use this new knowledge to create precision-guided therapies that restore host defense for the prevention and treatment of infections and sepsis in the ICU.

column37: HIV-1 remains a major global health problem, with 38 million people living with the virus worldwide. To date scientists have not developed a successful vaccine to prevent HIV-1 infection. The virus enters human cells using a viral surface glycoprotein termed gp160. HIV-1 gp160 is commonly known for its central role in host attachment and fusion of the viral envelope with the host membrane, thus allowing for the deposition of infectious materials into the host. However, the fusion subunit of HIV-1 gp160 has also been implicated in contributing to disease progression through immune evasion, misdirection, and confrontation. A better understanding of the mechanisms employed by HIV-1 to escape immune responses is key to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. We aim to understand the mechanisms of how HIV-1 modulates the immune system. We will characterize interactions of HIV-1 with the immune system using an integrative approach that combines structural virology, immunology, biochemistry and computation. Our results will identify new fundamental model principles to explain immunosuppression and immunodominance, to better understand the virus-host conflict. The proposed work has the potential to both impact the design of vaccines as well as provide new therapeutic strategies aimed at activating the host immune system against HIV.

column36: The NeurO2 study: optimal brain oxygenation in neurocritically ill patients
column37: Acute brain injury from trauma (TBI) or a burst artery in the brain (aSAH) often affects young people (40-60 years), nearly half of whom will die, and a third will have permanent disability. A particular challenge in managing these patients is that the recovering brain is very sensitive to low oxygen delivery and at great risk of further injury (like new strokes). Oxygen delivery is dependent on blood flow and oxygen attached to the red cells within it. Low blood levels (anemia), is very common in these patients, and leads to worse outcomes. It is unclear if giving blood (transfusion) to treat anemia improves otherwise terrible outcomes in acute brain injury because it has never been properly studied. The few studies that exist do not help clinicians with the decisions they must make every day in these patients. The NeurO2 study, is a nested study within two large trials in TBI and aSAH patients respectively (HEMOTION and SAHaRA Trials). These trials are designed to guide clinicians to better understand if maintaining a higher blood level will improve outcomes. In the NeurO2 study, we will monitor (using Near-Infrared Spectroscopy - NIRS) the effects of our intervention on the measure of brain oxygen delivery. We believe that, in adult patients suffering from anemia, a low blood oxygen delivery (as measured by NIRS) is associated with a poor outcome, but could be affected by blood transfusion and may serve as a trigger for when to give blood. The NeurO2 study is a unique opportunity to clarify the clinical use of this technology as a potential tool to guide therapy in the acute brain-injured vulnerable population.

column36: Magnetic resonance navigation of drug eluting beads for liver cancer therapy: in-vitro optimization and preclinical safety efficacy study
column37: Liver cancer, or hepatocellular carcinoma, is a major health concern as it is one of the most common cancers in the world and the third most lethal. For advanced stages of the disease, the preferred treatment consist in the injection thought the liver arteries of chemotherapeutic drugs, designed to kill cancerous cells, and eventually embolization agent, which deprive the tumors from oxygen and nutriments by blocking their feeding vessels, thus causing their death. However, current techniques that are able to efficiently target the tumor areas, and spare healthy tissues, require the use of x-ray images and the navigation of a catheter from an artery in the leg, the femoral artery, or in the left arm, the radial artery, to the desired position in the liver. This procedure is time consuming and cannot be repeated too often for patient comfort and safety. We propose a non-invasive treatment that use a catheter implanted directly in the proper hepatic artery to deliver microbeads loaded with magnetic nanoparticles and chemotherapeutic drug, whose size is chosen to embolize the small arteries of the liver. These microbeads will be steered to the tumors using the magnetic force of a MRI scanner. Once in the feeding vessels of the tumor, they start to desegregate, progressively liberating the chemotherapeutic drug. This new method will allow for repeated targeted treatments that are a key element in the regression of liver tumors and the prolongation of the patient life.

column36: Social adjustment in survivors of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
column37: Background: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a cancer that affects the white blood cells and is the most common cancer affecting children. Thanks to many advances in treatment, most children diagnosed with ALL will survive. The treatments needed to cure ALL, however, are toxic because they are directed at the brain and therefore negatively impact survivor's health and psychological well-being. Survivors of ALL experience social difficulties. As children, these survivors do not have as many friends because they are more withdrawn. As adults, these survivors are less likely to go as far in school, have a job or be married compared to others who have not had ALL. In recent years there have been efforts to reduce the toxicity of treatment for ALL. We do not yet understand how less toxic treatments might effect the social difficulties of survivors. We need to understand this in order to find the best way to treat these problems. Social difficulties are a serious health risk that may be comparable to the health risks associated with drinking and smoking. The goal of the current study is to better understand the social difficulties in survivors of pediatric ALL treated with less toxic treatments. Methods: One hundred and twenty survivors of pediatric ALL and 120 survivors of solid tumours who have not received brain-directed therapy will be invited to participate and complete tests that will assess aspects of their social function. Their parents, teachers and classroom peers will also complete measures designed to assess social function. We will assess other factors that might be related to social function such as mental health. Expected Results: This study will increase our knowledge about the social functioning of survivors of pediatric ALL as well as to identify factors that might be related to their social function. This will help us identify which survivors may be at greatest risk of social difficulties and design better treatments to help these survivors.

column36: The physiological, molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying lateralization of motor control
column37: Lateralization of motor control refers to the ability to perform movements on only one side of the body and is essential for activities such as coordinated hand movements and walking. Lateralization of motor control depends on the correct communication between the right and left sides of the nervous system through crossing nerve fibres. Defective lateralized motor control can result in mirror movements (MM), involuntary movements that mirror voluntary ones on the opposite side of the body. In 2010, we reported that MM can result from mutations in DCC, a gene critical in guiding developing axons (long extensions of nerve cells) to the nervous system midline. We have assembled the world's largest cohort of MM individuals (n=94). 58% carry mutations in DCC and 42% are genetically unexplained, suggesting that many more MM genes remain to be discovered. Furthermore, though DCC deficits in animals result in locomotion deficits, the role of DCC in human gait circuitry and motor control of legs has not yet been explored. Our unique MM cohort provides an exceptional opportunity to study the physiological, molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying lateralization of motor control. We will: 1-Identify novel genes important for lateralization of motor control by genetically studying our MM cohort. 2-Functionally assess the role of novel MM gene mutations using in vitro and mouse experiments. We hypothesize that the majority of novel genes will have a role in midline axon guidance and DCC signaling. 3-Investigate the role of DCC in human gait patterning. We will use biomechanical and electrophysiological approaches to investigate left-right coordination and motor tract lateralization abnormalities in DCC individuals. This study will (1) identify novel MM genes, (2) expand our understanding of the physiological and molecular basis of lateralization of motor control, axon guidance and circuit formation, (3) decipher the effects of DCC deficits on human gait circuitry.

column36: An autobiographical memory prosthetic to treat memory loss
column37: Millions of Canadians live with brain damage that affects their memory. Acquired brain injury (e.g., from viral infection, tumor removal, epilepsy, or stroke) and Alzheimer's disease cause profound memory problems that make it hard to remember life's daily events. These memory problems can diminish one's autonomy and sense of identity, leading to a vicious cycle of social isolation and depression, which in turn hurts memory. Digital Memory Augmentation (DMA) is a new and promising approach to lessen memory loss by harnessing advances in digital technology. Here, portable devices capture information about everyday events, allowing for later recall. DMA can produce memory benefits - more so than common strategies such as keeping a diary. However, prior DMA approaches have not been informed by our understanding of brain function and often neglect basic principles from cognitive science about how best to learn and retain information. We have created a simple and effective DMA tool that is based on our understanding of how the brain optimally stores and retains memories. This smartphone-based app uses principles from cognitive science and neuroscience to create powerful memory cues that trigger memory for the original event. It then replays these memory cues in a manner known to optimize learning and long-term retention. Our prototype has dramatically improved memory for real-life events in healthy older adults. These memory gains lasted up to 3 months, they were superior to the gains from typical smartphone event recording, and they were accompanied by enhanced brain function. Toward our goal of aiding memory, we will therefore (i) disseminate this new memory tool to people with severe memory impairments; (ii) measure the benefits for event memory and overall wellbeing; (iii) measure the brain reorganization associated with the app's use; and (iv) make the app publicly available on any modern smartphone so that its benefits can be enjoyed on a large scale.

column36: Molecular basis of and preclinical approaches to overcome therapy-resistant cystic fibrosis mutations
column37: The cystic fibrosis (CF) protein (CFTR) resides at the cell surface and ensures normal water and ion content of the airway surface liquid layer. Disease causing mutations in CF impair the structure and function of CFTR and alter the composition of the airway surface liquid layer. This leads to recurrent lung infection and uncontrolled inflammation, the primary cause of mortality in CF. Although effective drug combinations have been recently identified to rescue the basic defects of the most common mutants (folding and gating mutants), the long-term decay of the CF lung function can only be delayed but not prevented by available drugs. Other mutations either have not been tested, remained partially or fully therapy resistant towards the presently available drugs. Furthermore, a unique class of mutations, represented by "premature termination codons", which introduce and early termination signal for protein synthesis, manifests in variable truncation of CFTR. We propose a variety of biochemical, biophysical and cellular assay to a) unravel the molecular bases of those mutations that mechanism is presently not known, b) deepen our understanding of the channel opening mechanism, a prerequisite stimulate this process for mutants that lead to functional defect and c) identify the binding sites of the available gating and folding correctors drugs, the foundation for rationally improving their efficacy. Finally, we propose innovative experiments to rescue the functional expression defect of premature truncation mutants that presently lack any therapy. Our program with interdependent basic and translational components will help to identify improve therapeutic interventions in CF and may serve as a framework for other genetic diseases caused by mutations in ABC transporter family.

column37: The prevalence of chronic disease represents a significant burden for the Canadian health care system. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a chronic condition that effects lung function and reduces the quality of life for nearly 5% Canadians. Care for patients living with COPD can be improved through the use of integrated models of team-based care. These models involve coordination of services across providers to deliver better care for patients, caregivers and families. Integrated models of team-based care involve multiple healthcare professionals working together to provide appropriate care for patients. The aim of this research is to gain a better understanding of how successful integrated models team-based care are spread to new contexts and how these models are sustained over time, to ensure benefits are maintained. The objectives of this research are: (1) explore the spread of integrated models of team-based care for COPD, (2) explore the sustainability of these models, and (3) create a framework to support future efforts to spread and sustain these models. The study will be conducted in three years and will use mixed methods (surveys, observations, and focus groups). The expected outcomes of this study will be a description of how integrated models of team-based care are spread and sustained in different contexts along with an in-depth understanding of the barriers and facilitators to these processes. Our research will provide guidance of policymakers wanting to improve in chronic disease management. We will also offer a common language for research and practice, and support the best care for patients and caregivers.

column36: Oncofertility among adolescent and young adult cancer survivors in Alberta: a mixed methods study
column37: Each year, approximately 7,600 adolescents and young adults (AYAs; aged 15-39 years) are diagnosed with cancer in Canada. Since people are having children later in life now, more AYA cancer patients have not started a family at the time of diagnosis. As a result, fertility is the second biggest concern among AYA cancer patients because previous research has found that radiotherapy and chemotherapy treatments can cause infertility. Although fertility counseling before cancer treatment is recommended as a part of standard AYA cancer care, it is unclear how often it is being used. Also, no one has explored how many AYA cancer patients have cancer-related fertility appointments or use fertility services before or after cancer treatment. Thus, this proposal's aim is to understand the impact of cancer and its treatment during adolescence and young adulthood on fertility by using a mixed methods study to explore cancer-related fertility care in Alberta. Specifically, among AYA cancer patients from Alberta that were diagnosed from 2010-2019, our first objective is to assess: -referrals to fertility services; -appointment attendance at a fertility clinic; -fertility procedures (and what kind); and -fertility-related financial costs. For Objective 2, we will use a mail-out to invite AYA cancer survivors to complete an electronic questionnaire that will collect information on fertility and sexual health factors, as well as demographics. This questionnaire will then be used to identify participants for focus groups (Objective 3) that will explore psychological and social factors that influence reproductive experiences and choices, as well as the impact of cancer on family building among survivors and their partners. The results of this study will help us understand how AYA cancer patients' fertility is impacted by cancer, and may lead to clinical or policy recommendations in Alberta and beyond.

column36: Interrogation of novel B cell pathways in chronic lung allograft rejection
column37: Lung transplantation is lifesaving for people with terminal lung diseases and improves quality of life. Unfortunately, the long-term outcome of lung transplantation is poor compared with transplantation of other organs - only about half of patients survive 6 years. This poor survival rate is due to lung scarring, a process called chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), which causes severe breathing difficulty. CLAD occurs because the recipient's immune system recognizes the lung as foreign and initiates a powerful rejection response against it, which is only partly controlled by current anti-rejection drugs. We recently developed a unique mouse lung transplant model in which we can induce CLAD-like lung scarring by causing damage called "ischemia-reperfusion injury" (IRI). Just like in lung transplant patients, IRI increases CLAD-like disease in this model. Importantly, we have found that this process is highly dependent on a specific type of white blood cells called "B cells." B cells are responsible for making proteins called antibodies that protect us from infection but can also damage transplanted organs. In our research project, we will use this mouse model and samples from our lung transplant patients to study how B cells contribute to CLAD-like disease in the animals and in humans. We will test this question directly with the following interventions: 1) studying how B cells are distributed in human CLAD lungs and in samples from lung transplant patients before the onset of CLAD, 2) removing B cells or giving B cells back to the animals at specific times to assess their contributions, 3) using genetically modified mice that lack B cells or have dysfunctional B cells that cannot make antibodies, to assess their role in CLAD-like disease after IRI. By identifying new pathways involved in CLAD development, we will be able to find new treatment targets that will improve the outcome of lung transplantation in the future.

column36: Automatic Palliative Care Referrals: Acceptability and Uptake by Patients with Advanced Lung Cancer
column37: People living with advanced (incurable) cancer are not routinely provided with timely access to a therapy that is proven to help them feel better, reduce depression and anxiety, and support their quality of life. That therapy is palliative care. Patients, and those close to them, experience high levels of distress when faced with a life-limiting diagnosis, and often don't know that palliative care can be received at the same time as cancer treatments as an added layer of support. Other barriers to timely access to palliative care include cancer clinic time constraints, healthcare provider concerns that referring patients to palliative care might increase their distress, and cost of having a palliative care provider in every clinic. To overcome these barriers, our study asks "Can we develop a process so that everyone recently diagnosed with advanced cancer is automatically phoned by a palliative care provider and offered a consultation? Would patients find this phone call acceptable and how many would take up the offer of a comprehensive palliative care consultation?" What will the study do? We will work with patients and healthcare providers to design the process and appropriate language for these automatic referrals. We will then test the process, starting with people recently diagnosed with advanced (stage IV) lung cancer. We will interview patients about the acceptability of being called directly by a palliative care provider shortly after their advanced cancer diagnosis, and will measure how many patients attend a palliative care consultation. Why do this? If acceptable, automatic referral will overcome existing barriers to palliative care referral and guarantee EVERY patient is offered early access to palliative care. If we find that direct phone contact is acceptable and leads to more people receiving timely palliative care, this will provide a routine, effective way to enhance the lives of all Canadians living with advanced cancers.

column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is generally dependent on the male sex hormone (androgen) for survival and progression; therefore, the primary treatment strategy for advanced and metastatic PCa is androgen deprivation therapy. column36: Characterization of Frailty in Older Men
column37: Frailty is a common issue facing older men. This syndrome predicts poor health outcomes. We need to understand more about how to prevent frailty, but also about how frailty affects our general well-being. However, there are some gaps in our understanding of frailty. First, frailty seen through the eyes of older men may seem different than when seen through the eyes of researchers and health care providers. This different viewpoint needs further study. Second, we need to understand how frailty changes over time. Third, we need to understand what factors about a person in early life predict frailty in late life. We propose an analysis of a long term study of 3983 men who qualified for air crew in the Royal Canadian Air Force during the Second World War. Since 1948, the health of these men has been documented over time. We will study how frailty changes over the period of 1996 - 2019; how the mens' own rating of frailty is related to a commonly used clinical measure of frailty, and how frailty affects the mental health of older men. Finally, we will find out factors in early and mid-life which predict late life frailty. These study results will give important information for health care providers, and for those who plan health care services. Most importantly, the results will be useful for older men and their families.

column37: At least 1 in 5 women in university will be sexually assaulted. Sexual assault has many immediate and long-term health consequences, including injuries, sexually transmitted infections, pregnancy, depression, substance use, post-traumatic stress, and suicide. Some experts have begun to address this problem by using intensive skill-building programs to help women avoid and resist sexual assault. Some of these programs have been quite successful, but with so many potential victims, such an intensive approach is difficult to fully implement. Furthermore, women should not bear this onus, as sexual assault is ultimately a male responsibility-98% of reported sexual assaults are committed by men. However, because a minority of men commits the majority of sexual assaults, prevention and treatment efforts will be most effective and appropriate when they focus on high-risk men in high-risk situations. Unfortunately, little is known about risk factors for future perpetration of sexual assault on campus. In this multisite study of university men, we seek to identify risk factors related to the perpetration of campus sexual assault, including first-time and repeated assaults. Here, we compare five major risk factors, including (1) deviant sexual interests, (2) psychopathic traits, (3) hostile attitudes towards women, (4) having peers who support sexually aggressive behaviour, and (5) alcohol use in sexual situations. Risk factors that most strongly predict sexual assault will be identified as future targets for prevention and early intervention. Our findings will be published in open access journals and a summary of our findings will be provided to all Canadian universities, sexual assault centres, and Provincial/Territorial Ministries of Education and Health.

column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability in adolescents and a potent risk factor for adolescent suicide. Evidence-based treatments are available; however many clinics do not provide guidelines-based treatments. Integrated Care Pathways (ICPs) are treatment algorithms based on the highest quality practice guidelines intended to facilitate the implementation of evidence-based treatment at the clinic level. Our group has already tested the feasibility of ICP for adolescent depression at an academic setting. Whether or not ICPs actually lead to improved outcomes in adolescent depression is still unknown and testing this approach is a complex undertaking. The aim of this project is to test the feasibility of multi-centre randomized control trial of an ICP for adolescent depression versus treatment-as-usual (TAU) in community settings. We also wish to see if the ICP can be implemented with fidelity in the community. Two of the Hubs will be randomized to the ICP intervention; two of the Hubs will continue with treatment as usual. Research feasibility outcomes will include: (1) 1-year recruitment rate, and (2) data collection efficiency. Clinical outcomes include: (1) rate of decrease in depressive symptoms and (2) rate of change of functional improvement. Implementation outcomes include: (1) fidelity to the planned implementation process and (2) fidelity to the ICP. Knowledge Translation Strategy: We intend to use the knowledge gained in this trial to later conduct a definitive multicentre randomized control. Should the definitive trial show improved outcomes and "implementability", scaling up the model to other Hubs provincially, nationally and internationally would be indicated.

column36: Improving physician competency in communication skills for behavior change counselling: The validation of a new digital assessment tool
column37: Poor health behaviors such as smoking, being physically inactive, eating an unhealthy diet, and not taking medication as prescribed are important risk factors for the development and/or worsening of chronic diseases (like heart and lung diseases, obesity, diabetes and cancer). In order to get people to engage in good health behaviors, doctors typically give people advice about what they should (and should not) be doing in order to improve their health. However, people often resent getting advice when it is perceived as being "told what to do" - which tends to make people resistant to changing their behavior. This indicates that 'advice-giving' is not a useful strategy. Motivational communication (MC) is a communication style used to motivate people to adopt a healthy lifestyle by exploring how having good health behaviors can help them achieve their personal life goals. It is very personalized so it can be used in people of all ages, races, cultures and languages. It has been very effective in helping people quit smoking, lose weight, and be more active. As a result, more and more doctors are getting trained to use MC with their patients. However, there are no really good tests for assessing how well doctors are using MC, which is important for ensuring the quality of training programs but also for ensuring patients benefit from the approach. This project focuses on the development a new test to measure MC skills in doctors that is scientifically valid, fun, easy and quick to use. Then we want to verify that it tests what it is supposed to test (MC skills), so that we can use it to assess how well our training programs are able to improve doctors' MC skills. Helping doctors learn more effective methods for supporting patients to adopt a healthier lifestyle and engage in good health behaviors is critical for improving health outcomes in those with or at risk for chronic disease.

column36: The role of depression in the intergenerational transmission of type 2 diabetes
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a prevalent disease in Canada. Family history of T2D is one of the major risk factors for T2D. Familial aggregation studies estimate that genetic variants explain less than 10% of the disease's heritability, suggesting that that a substantial proportion of the remaining heritability comes from shared behaviours and shared environmental factors. Parental depression might play an important role in the intergenerational transmission of T2D. The combination of parental T2D with parental depression might increase the risk of T2D in offspring. Stress resilience, the ability to adapt successfully to stress and adversity and flourishing (social, emotional, physical and psychological well-being) might decrease the risk of T2D onset in individuals with parental T2D/depression history. Using a two-generation sample of adults without T2D and their parents, the main objectives are to identify a) if the combination of parental T2D and parental depression history increases the risk of T2D in their offspring; b) if parental T2D and parental depression increase the risk of depression and chronic stress in offspring, which, in turn, increases the risk of T2D in offspring; c) if high stress resilience in offspring of parents with T2D/depression decreases the risk of developing T2D; and d) if flourishing in offspring of parents with T2D/depression decreases the risk of developing T2D. We propose to recruit 9,000 participants without T2D aged 40 years and older and their parents from the Lifelines Cohort Study in the Netherlands. Incidence of T2D will be assessed at two additional bi-annual follow-up assessment. The Lifelines study offers a unique opportunity to study the role of parental depression in the intergenerational transmission of T2D due to its large sample size (167,729 participants), its open protocol and its intergenerational design. column36: The role of the kinetochore in age-related oocyte aneuploidy
column37: A major cause of the decline in fertility experienced by women in their 30s and 40s is a decrease in the quality of the egg. Specifically, it is known that eggs of older women are more likely to contain the wrong number of chromosomes - a state known as aneuploidy. These aneuploid eggs rarely give rise to a healthy offspring. To understand how aneuploidy arises in oocytes, we need to understand a process known as chromosome segregation, which determines which chromosomes are delivered to the egg as it develops. Here we will study this process, focussing on a key structure termed the 'kinetochore'. column37: Heart failure afflicts 350,000 Canadians and contributes to 10% of deaths in Canada. Despite significant research and treatment advances, heart failure morbidity and mortality will increase 3-fold by 2050. Our pilot studies show decreasing CapZ with our peptides stops heart muscle dysfunction associated with heart attacks. We have also identified changes in CapZ proteins in samples from human and veterinary heart failure patients. Our objectives are: 1. determine how altered CapZ affects hearts under stress; and 2. develop a clinically viable approach to target CapZ to protect hearts. To address these objectives we will test the ability of our unique CapZ interfering peptides to protect against injury associated with heart attacks and heart failure. These innovative ideas can only be tested in our laboratory as we are the only group to possess both the TG mice and CapZ interfering peptides, as well as the expertise to cover the full range of studies. column37: Screening for hazardous and harmful drinking is rarely done in clinical practice. column36: Social environment and functioning of adolescents born pre-term
column37: Most pregnancies last 40 weeks. Babies born before the 37th week are known as preterm (or premature) babies; in Canada, about 8% children are born preterm. Preterm birth is associated with a number of adverse outcomes varying in severity and onset, such as cerebral palsy (manifesting shortly after birth), autism (developing in early childhood) or bipolar disorder (presenting by early adulthood). On average, individuals who were born preterm function less well than their term-born peers across many cognitive domains, achieve lower levels of education and have lower employment rates. As with other adversities, however, many preterm-born individuals function very well despite the presence of a long-term disability, lower cognitive functioning or behavioural problems. These inter-individual variations may arise at many levels (biological. psychological, social) and developmental periods. Here we focus on identifying features of social environment that may change long-term outcomes of preterm birth with regards to brain maturation, cognition and mental health of adolescents & youth (~12 to 22 yrs). We chose this period of development because of its dynamics with regards to biology (growth, sex hormones) and sociology (friends, romantic partners). We are interested in how psychosocial stress combines with puberty to shape the brain and mental health. To address our questions, we will use two approaches: (Aim 1) A population-based aggregate-level analysis linking "exposures" (preterm birth) and "outcomes" (health) across neighbourhoods; and (Aim 2) A targeted individual-level analysis linking exposures (preterm birth) and outcomes (cognition, brain structure) of adolescents living in a selected subset of neighbourhoods (n=600). The project will be carried out in the City of Toronto that consists of 140 neighbourhoods, with ~275,000 individuals of the target age (~22,000 born preterm). Both approaches build on our previous research in typically developing children.

column36: Regulation of neuronal pacemaker channels by cannabinoids
column37: Cannabinoids are a broad class of molecules that act on nerve cells, affecting pain sensation, appetite, mood, learning and memory. There are 3 classes of cannabinoids: (1) endocannabinoids produced naturally by the body, (2) phytocannabinoids from some plants, and (3) synthetic cannabinoids. Cannabinoids may provide effective treatments for addiction, pain, epilepsy, major mood disorders, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, spasticity in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease. However, to use them, without negative effects on learning and memory, we must understand exactly how they affect nerve function. Cannabinoids bind to Cannabinoid receptors (CBRs). However, activating CBRs cannot directly change the firing of nerve cells, since CBRs do not generate electrical signals on their own. Instead, electrical signals are controlled by ion channels, which allow for the movement of charged "ions" from one side of a membrane to the other. My lab focuses on hyperpolarization-activated cyclic-nucleotide gated (HCN) channels. HCNs are important for nerve function, learning and memory, pain sensation, and vision. The endocannabinoid WIN55,212-2 effects memory by activating CB1R, which leads to changes in electrical currents through HCNs. However, cannabinoids can also bind ion channels directly, or alter their membrane environment. In addition, different cannabinoids (for example, THC and cannabidiol from marijuana) have different effects on people's mood, pain sensations, and memory. Since HCN channels are involved in all of these processes, we are asking, do cannabinoids have a direct effect on HCNs, independent of CBRs? If so, are these effects specific to the type of cannabinoid? These findings will help us to develop therapeutic approaches to the treatment of numerous neuronal disorders. Also, our results will also help in the development of novel nootropics or "smart drugs" that can enhance memory, creativity, or motivation.

column37: Lung transplantation is the primary life-saving treatment for patients with end-stage lung disease. Since the first successful clinical lung transplant in the world was performed at Toronto General Hospital (UHN) in 1983, we have led a global effort to improve outcomes, ultimately resulting in more lungs being transplanted each year. However, despite this success, median recipient survival has reached only 6.8 years-largely due to detrimental immune responses that result in lung injury and negative early and late effects on the transplanted lung and the recipient. We have developed key innovations in lung transplantation, including the gold standard preservation solution (LPD, Perfadex(R)) and the Toronto EVLP (Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion) System. With EVLP, surgeons worldwide can now perform advanced assessments and treatment of donor lungs, providing the unprecedented ability to determine donor lung function and quality prior to transplant. EVLP also allows surgeons to treat and control the host immune response to the transplanted lung. We will develop EVLP-based advanced gene regulation of the donor lung to improve the immune response. This technique will better manage harmful inflammation, reduce short-term lung injury and prevent long-term transplant rejection. We will use engineered stem cells and a method to change how genes work in the body, called CRISPR/Cas9, to make better therapies and improve the immune response. As a continuation of our successful track record in gene therapy for transplantation, including a planned first-in-human clinical trial as a result of our past CIHR-funded projects, we will work with our established partners to help achieve our goals. Globally, we aim to improve the quality of life for all transplant recipients. Project outcomes match CIHR's goal to strengthen Canada's health care system and serve as world leaders in scientific excellence, as well as CIHR's goal to maximize transformational impacts on the health of Canadians.

column36: Optimizing HIV testing services in sub-Saharan Africa to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030
column37: Ending the AIDS epidemic begins by building efficient HIV testing services. HIV testing has, and remains, a cornerstone of HIV prevention efforts. A positive diagnosis entails that people living with HIV can receive life-saving antiretroviral therapy and, if the test is negative, people vulnerable to HIV acquisition can be identified and linked to prevention services. The Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) put forward the objective of ending the AIDS epidemic by 2030 by strengthening the HIV care cascade. The proportion of people living with HIV aware of their status is a key progress indicator and common bottleneck in the cascade. Tracking this indicator in sub-Saharan Africa is difficult, however, as surveillance systems are often incomplete. Our team has recently developed tailored tools that specifically address these challenges. Yet, current models are agnostic about testing modalities (e.g., opt-in, HIV self-tests, mobile campaigns) and cannot stratify coverage metrics by key populations (e.g., female sex workers and men who have sex with men). Members of these populations represent close to 50% of global new HIV infections and, if the goal of ending AIDS is to be achieved, they need explicit consideration. To fill these knowledge gaps, we will develop methods, build tools, and validate models to inform, strengthen, and optimize HIV testing services. Specifically, we will 1) improve estimates by integrating new data sources, 2) adapt current frameworks to consider key populations, and 3) optimize national HIV testing strategies considering affordability and cost-effectiveness. By drawing on the expertise of an international team of HIV researchers, biostatisticians, economists, modelers, and knowledge users, our project will guide global recommendations on how best to sustainably close gaps in diagnosis coverage among some of sub-Saharan Africa's most vulnerable groups.

Prevailing dogma is that IgA protein is released into the blood from cells within tissue along mucosal surfaces. We have recently identified that individuals with IgAN have higher levels of IgA targeted against tonsil bacteria (Neisseria) than healthy counterparts. Using a mouse model, we confirmed that infection with Neisseria causes IgAN in mice. This is a radical change in our understanding about the origins of IgAN. Our goal is to explore these transformative findings further in both our mouse model and human subjects. By understanding exactly what type of cell is establishing a niche in the kidney, and what is triggering the cells to move there, we can develop new treatments for IgAN.

column36: The impact of cannabis legalization on the illicit cannabis market in Canada
column37: On October 2018, Canada became only the second country to legalize non-medical cannabis. Reducing the illicit market is critical to achieving the public health objectives under the Cannabis Act; however, the extent to which consumers will transition to the legal cannabis market is unknown. The proposed study will examine how cannabis legalization impacts cannabis purchasing and the illegal cannabis market in Canada. First, an environmental scan of cannabis retail sources will be conducted in each province annually, over a 4-year period. The scan will identify the location of legal and illegal cannabis stores, and collect objective measures of cannabis prices and potency. Second, data from the scan will be linked with data from the International Cannabis Policy Study, a CIHR-funded prospective cohort survey of 10,000 Canadians (1,000 per province, 16-65 years of age) conducted over the same 4-year period. The survey includes comprehensive assessments of cannabis consumption and purchasing-including product types, quantities, price paid, and purchase source-as well as household postal code to enable geographic analyses. Analyses will address five primary objectives: 1) to estimate changes in the retail availability and price of illegal cannabis in Canada following legalization; 2) to examine changes in legal and illegal cannabis purchases, including the overall size of the cannabis market in Canada; 3) to examine the impact of provincial retail policies, such as the number of retail stores, on cannabis purchases and market size; 4) to examine individual-level predictors of purchasing illicit cannabis, including geographic proximity to legal and illegal retail outlets; and 5) to examine changes in THC and CBD levels of cannabis products. Overall, the proposed study represents the most comprehensive assessment of the cannabis market to date. The data has the potential to directly inform cannabis policy in Canada and other jurisdictions.

We will then use our hydrogel delivery system in a GBM mouse model to quantify tumor killing. column36: Activating the piRNA pathway to prevent heart disease
column37: Heart disease (HD) is a leading cause of death worldwide. 1.3 million Canadians are living with HD, and more than 400,000 are living with long-term disability due to HD. When the heart is sick stress stimulates profound changes in the heart's structure and function. Changes in structure include enlargement of heart muscle cells, which cause the whole heart to enlarge. If the heart remains sick for a longer time, the muscle cells start dying and are replaced by cells that make the heart stiff. Loss of muscle cells results in the thinning of the walls of the heart chambers, causing a significant reduction in the heart's capacity to push blood to the body. These alterations eventually cause the heart to fail. Stopping the progressive changes induced by stress to the heart is required for preventing it to fail. Recent studies have found a family of small messengers that protect the heart against the negative effects of stress. This is very promising and prompted researchers to find ways of controlling the production of such messengers in the heart. However, researchers haven't been able to harness their protective properties. My lab has discovered that inactivating a single gene in the mouse heart activates the machinery that produces such small messengers. Moreover, we found that the machinery producing small messengers is depleted in human failing hearts, indicating that our findings are relevant for human disease. Furthermore, we have identified novel small messengers in the heart. To harness the protective properties of small messengers, we have three objectives. 1) We will find the processes that regulate the production of small messengers in the heart. 2) We will test the protective properties of the machinery that produces the small messengers, and 3) Test the protective properties of our newly discovered small messengers in muscle cells of failing human hearts. These studies will provide much needed new strategies to prevent heart failure.

column37: Heart transplantation is a life-saving treatment for end stage heart disease. After transplant, narrowing in the heart arteries can cause the new heart to fail and shorten lifespan. This condition is known as cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV). It is very common and affects about half of all transplant patients. There are few treatments to prevent or treat CAV. Platelets are cells in the bloodstream involved in clotting and inflammation. Both mechanisms are involved in the development of CAV. Studies have shown that platelets are more active in heart transplant patients. Medications that interfere with platelets are commonly used to treat patients having heart attacks due to heart artery blockages. Aspirin and clopidogrel are examples of drugs that work differently to block platelets.These drugs may be able to reduce CAV in heart transplant patients. The aim of our research is to determine if drugs that block platelets can be used to prevent CAV after heart transplant. A large clinical trial is needed to answer this question. We will first perform a trial in 3 Canadian transplant centres, and if shown to be feasible, continue to a larger international trial. We will randomly assign patients early after transplant to receive aspirin, clopidogrel or placebo (non-active sugar pill). Neither the patient or the medical team will know which drug the patient is receiving. We will assess if patients have developed CAV by performing an angiogram at 1 and 2 years post transplant and 1-2 years thereafter. An angiogram involves taking x-ray pictures after dye is injected into the heart arteries. Patients will also have special tests to look for early signs of CAV including thickening of the heart artery wall and abnormal blood flow. Blood tests will be used to measure platelet clumping function and assess the response to aspirin and clopidogrel. New treatments for CAV will improve the lives of heart transplant patients and increase life expectancy.

column37: Tinnitus is a bothersome noise or ringing in the ears occurring in the absence of external auditory stimulation. Furthermore, we will also make use of novel chemogenetic approaches that allow us to manipulate plasticity-regulating neurons to determine whether they are dysfunctional in tinnitus. The chosen methods, all mastered by at least one member of our team, were selected to best answer our research questions and maximize the quality and quantity of the data obtained. The proposed research will shed light on some of the neural mechanisms that underlie the emergence of tinnitus. We furthermore expect that our findings will significantly enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the emergence of tinnitus and will also hopefully provide new therapeutic targets for future research.

column36: Functional analysis of mitochondrial-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites
column37: All cells in the body require chemical energy to carry out their normal physiological functions. The majority of this energy is packaged as a compound called ATP and is produced by the oxidation of carbohydrate and fat in a biochemical process called oxidative phosphorylation. This process takes place in a compartment of the cell called the mitochondrion, and is carried out by several large protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Respiratory chain dysfunction interferes with the normal supply of energy, and this produces a wide variety of different diseases, such as neurodegenerative and heart disease, the nature and severity of which depend on the exact genetic defect. The genetics of respiratory chain diseases is complicated by the fact that some components of the system are encoded in nuclear genes, others in a small genome that is contained within the mitochondria themselves. Mitochondria also rely on intimate contacts with other organelles in the cell, most notably a structure called the endoplasmic reticulum, which, among other things, supplies mitochondria with the lipids required for mitochondrial growth and division, and acts as a reservoir for calcium, which in part regulates mitochondrial metabolism. Several neurological diseases result from disturbances in the contacts between mitochondria and the ER. The proteins that interact across the mitochondrial-ER contact site are referred to as tethers, but the nature of these proteins remains incompletely characterized. Likewise, their roles in neurological disease and in the physiological regulation of contact sites remains relatively unknown. This project is aimed at identifying and characterizing the proteins at ER-mitochondrial contact sites, and investigating their precise molecular functions in healthy cells and in cells from patients with mitochondrial disease.

column36: Anatomically relevant brachytherapy implants by a 3D printing and radiosensitizing approach
column37: In brachytherapy (internal radiotherapy), millimeter-sized radioactive implants are used to treat different types of cancers. Usually very effective, brachytherapy requires precise calculations for the positioning of radioactive seeds, prior to their insertion. Unfortunately, the size, shape, and radiation per seed, allow very limited flexibility to the implants, and this is a strong limitation for further improvement of brachytherapy and more personalised approaches in the field. In this research project, an integrated 3D-priting (additive manufacturing) approach will be developed to allow the fabrication of anatomically-relevant radioactive implants that could be used in the most geometrically and precision-challenging brachytherapy application: eye cancer. First, a "radioactive polymer ink" will be developed, and used as the base material for a high-performance polymer 3D printer. Then, "radioactive eye plates" will be printed, as potential substitutes for eye cancer plates currently used in radiation therapy. The geometrical models for these plates will be provided by the imaging scans of real patients. The personalised 3D-printed radioactive implants will be evaluated through a dosimetric study based on a combination of numerical simulation and 3D radiographic dosimetry with hydrogels. Finally, a new "radiosensitization" approach based on coatings of gold nanoparticles at the surface of the implants, will be demonstrated as a possibility to decrease the overall amount of radioactivity necessary per implant. Overall, this new brachytherapy approach could open the door to a whole generation of 3D-printed high efficacy radioactive implants that could be fabricated directly in hospitals, and perfectly adapted to the anatomy of patients. An increased number of brachytherapy treatments could therefore become a reality, in particular in the case where geometrical precision and radioactivity concentration per volume of radioactive implant, are challenging.

column36: Overcoming suppressive micro-environments in early breast cancer progression
column37: Drs. McCaffrey, and Muller will investigate how breast cancer cells disrupt tissue barriers to escape the local environment, and how they subsequently evade elimination by the immune system. Project description Breast cancer develops from early stages that are localized and pose little immediate risk tothe patient. However, up to 50% can progress to potentially lethal forms of invasive breast cancer that move into surrounding normal tissue. Some cells in localized cancers are poised to become invasive, and additional mutations are not required. However, the surrounding normal tissue functions as a barrier and represses invasion of these cells. There are currently no tests that can predict which localized cancers will progress and there is concern of overtreatment. We predict that signals from localized breast cancers reprogram the initially repressive adjacent normal tissue to permit the transition to invasive breast cancer. To test this we will characterize how cancer cells alter the behavior of adjacent normal cells as they progress from localized to invasive cancer. We will test if these changes are functionally relevant by modifying cancer cells or normal cells to promote or suppress the invasive transition using animal models that accurately reproduce cancer progression in patients. We will also elucidate how cancer cells promote suppression of the immune system by looking at the types and activities of immune cells present and whether they function in an anti-cancer or pro-cancer capacity. Finally, we will explore approaches that reactivate the immune system to target and eliminate localized cancer cells that try to escape and invade surrounding tissue. Impact and Relevance A better understanding of how cancers initiate and progress is crucial to develop tests that can guide doctors and patients for treatment decisions, as well as to identify new disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets for preventative treatment.

column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult neurological disability with most survivors suffering moderate to severe long-term sensorimotor deficits. These studies will lay the foundation for development of personalized noninvasive transcranial current stimulation for targeting functional deficits following ischemic stroke.

column37: Cancer and heart disease are responsible for almost 50 % of all deaths in Canada annually. In the past ten years these leading causes of mortality in both sexes have accounted for more than 1,250,000 Canadian deaths. Mitochondria are small compartments in our cells that manufacture a chemical store of energy essential for countless physiological processes. Calcium (Ca2+) uptake into mitochondria not only influences this energy production, but can also trigger cell death. Indeed, a high level of mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake drives the tissue damage caused by heart attacks and a low level of Ca2+ uptake permits the uncontrollable cell growth associated with cancer. Thus, the ability to control mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake with drugs rationally designed to modulate MCU activity is hampered. To increase our understanding of how MCU functions, we plan to map the atoms that promote interactions between MCU proteins and reveal how their relative orientation control these interactions. We will also elucidate atomic level details of MCU regulating protein-1 (MCUR1), a protein that acts as scaffold for MCU assembly, alone and in complex with MCU. Finally, we will study the role these protein interactions play in opening the MCU channel and causing damage to heart cells. The proposed work is an imperative first step toward developing novel modulators of MCU function, ultimately helping to manage the staggering and undiscriminating Canadian mortality associated with heart disease and cancer.

column36: New Drug and Technology Assessment in Bladder Cancer: Creation of a Novel Canadian Policy Model for Bladder Cancer
column37: Introduction Bladder cancer (BCa) treatment is rapidly evolving, with hundreds of new therapies and drug combinations in development or being tested. While revolutionizing BCa management and providing new hope to patients, they are expected to result in considerable discussion for policy-makers, administrators, physicians and patients. Already one of the most expensive cancers to treat, new therapies will increase BCa costs. Research that assesses how to effectively distribute health care resources for BCa will be essential for patients and funders. With patient input at every step, we aim to develop a Canadian Policy Model (CPM) that will provide a novel methodology to evaluate the benefits, effects, and costs of new BCa treatments. Methods We will delineate the phases of BCa care (called health states) to simulate all possible paths of patients' journeys through BCa. We will then obtain (i) costs; (ii) health outcomes; and (iii) quality of life (QOL), for each health state. These data will serve as inputs for our CPM. For population-level, health state-specific costs, we will identify health care services and drug use, using administrative databases in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec, thus capturing 75% of the Canadian population. Health outcomes data (e.g., probabilities of complications, recurrence, progression, etc.) will be collected by reviewing the published literature. To measure BCa QOL, we will prospectively administer BCa-specific, cancer-specific and generic QOL questionnaires (Bladder Utility Symptom Scale (BUSS), EORTC QLQ-C30 and EQ5D, respectively) to BCa patients at 3 large BCa centres in the 3 provinces. Impact Our final CPM will prioritize the new and emerging BCa therapies that should be selected for funding while balancing effectiveness, cost, ease of administration, and side effects. The CPM will lead to informed, evidence-based best practices in BCa treatment, resulting in better patient management, and lower healthcare costs.

column36: Sleep, Circadian Rhythms, and Dementia-Related Changes in the Human Brain - An Integrated Physiological, Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Cognitive, and Genomic Study of Adult Ontarians
column37: Common forms of sleep and circadian rhythm disruption such sleep deprivation, repeated awakenings at night, sleep apnea, shift work, and irregular sleep patterns, affect millions of Canadians and may be contributing to the growing number of adults with Alzheimer's disease and other dementias. This study of three thousand adult Ontarians will combine wearable technologies for comprehensive sleep and circadian assessment with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain to identify dementia-associated brain changes, analysis of regions of participants' DNA related to sleep and circadian rhythms, and detailed cognitive testing, to fill important gaps in our knowledge about the impact of sleep and circadian disruption on Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, and associated brain changes. This study will facilitate efforts to use sleep and circadian screening to identify adults at high risk for Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, support clinical trials of existing and emerging sleep and circadian interventions to decrease the growing burden of dementia, and may lead to targeted therapies that improve brain health for the millions of Canadians who experience sleep or circadian rhythm disruption.

column36: Integrated discovery studies and commercialization for a preterm birth diagnostic and a therapeutic
column37: This commercialization project addresses the unmet medical need to diagnose and treat preterm birth (PTB, birth <37 weeks) and to commercialize relevant new products. PTB is the #1 health problem of pregnancy. There are no reliable products available to diagnose or treat it. New breakthrough discoveries provide the first-ever opportunity to combine a PTB diagnostic and therapeutic within one new company, Maternica. The Olson lab developed a new test, the leukocyte migration assay, or LMA, that predicts delivery within 7 days with 96% accuracy. The Chemtob lab developed an anti-inflammatory therapeutic that blocks the action of interleukin-1, rytvela. They share a common mechanism; hence the LMA is the perfect tool to indicate the need to treat with rytvela for PTB risk and improved fetal outcome. Our primary objective is to complete the pre-clinical and regulatory requirements to advance our commercialization program towards FDA/Health Canada 510 K (device) and Investigational New Drug (IND) approval of LMA and rytvela for clinical prediction and prevention of PTB. We will test the LMA and rytvela together in a non-human primate (monkey) model and how responsive the LMA and rytvela are to each other. We will also test promising analogs to rytvela to confirm that the present formulation is the most efficacious, expand our intellectual property profile and provide backups. Once we clear these hurdles, new investors for clinical trial phases will be attracted. In the first 1.5 years we will complete our pre-clinical testing of the products, and in the second 1.5 years will prepare the data and presentation materials for discussions with FDA/Health Canada. Then Maternica will proceed to the necessary clinical trials. Maternica will seek permission for orphan drug designation and a breakthrough designation for accelerated approval. column36: A wearable technology approach to managing challenging behaviours in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
column37: An estimated 68% of children with autism may have challenging behaviours like aggression and self-injurious behaviours. These can negatively affect the safety, and the emotional and physical well-being of these children and their care-givers. Many children with ASD may not be able to effectively communicate the emotional states that are precursors to these behaviours, making it difficult to prevent and intervene before these behaviours escalate. To solve this challenge, we have developed the Anxiety Meter, a software application that uses heart rate measurements from smart watches to detect changes that can be warning signs of challenging behaviours. This can help care providers recognize early signs of challenging behaviours so that de-escalation strategies can be applied in a timely manner. Over the past seven years, our team has developed and tested the Anxiety Meter in laboratory settings. The goal of this project is work on two areas that can help the move the Anxiety Meter closer to clinical settings. Our objectives are to: 1) improve the usability of the Anxiety Meter for care providers in clinical and education settings, and 2) improve the accuracy of the Anxiety Meter for detecting challenging behaviours. The results of this project will help move our technology closer to real-world implementation, ultimately improving the safety and quality of life for children with ASD and their care-givers.
