column36: An analysis of the food environment in Canada: INFORMAS Canada
column37: The food environment has a major influence on dietary choices and is a critical factor in efforts to reduce rates of obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases. In Canada, the Healthy Eating Strategy contains a broad suite of policies that have potential to majorly influence the Canadian food environment. Monitoring the impact of such a strategy is essential. The proposed research builds on international efforts to monitor, benchmark and support polices and actions related to the food environment using an internationally-adopted monitoring framework with 12 'modules' (public sector policies, private sector policies, food composition, labelling, marketing, provision, retail, prices, trade and investment, population diet, physiological/metabolic risk factors, and health outcomes), to understand policy processes and monitor the food environment and downstream outcomes. The current study aims to prepare a comprehensive national report on the current food environment in Canada to evaluate changes in the food environment since the implementation of the Healthy Eating Strategy. This research project will collate and analyze existing data from the PAs/Co-As and collect additional data, as required, to apply established methods for each of the 12 modules. The project will apply a health equity lens to all modules to examine how environments may differentially impact disadvantaged populations. The results of this research will be a comprehensive national report that identifies the strengths, weaknesses and gaps in the food environment in Canada. This research will support policy evaluation, and serve as a marker of accountability for forthcoming changes to the food environment as the Healthy Eating Strategy policies, regulations and programs unfold over the next 3 years. The study will contribute to a national evaluation in a critical policy area, and will further global efforts to improve food environments.

column36: Monocyte activation by energy sensing pathways in atherosclerosis
column37: Healthier nutrition and lifestyle, along with cholesterol-lowering drugs (statins) have lowered the rates of heart disease in Canada, yet it is still a major health concern and the second leading cause of death. Our research is focused on understanding how the metabolism of cells important for CVD might be controlling its onset. The job of a protein called HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR for short, which is the protein that is shut down by statin drugs) is to make cholesterol, but also something called isoprenoid groups, which are small attachments that are added to proteins to help or control how they work. Since HMGCR is such an important protein, it has many layers of control. One of these layers of control is called phosphorylation (which acts very quickly) and we know that a master regulator of cell metabolism (a protein called AMPK) can switch off HMGCR using this type of control. What we don't fully understand is the importance of this control step in cholesterol and isoprenoid production. We have genetically engineered mice so that they have a very specific and small mutation that makes their HMGCR completely resistant to the control that AMPK would usually have. Using these mice, we saw that when the HMGCR protein (cholesterol and isoprenoid production) was not controlled by AMPK, atherosclerosis (what leads to heart disease) is much worse. The current proposal is focused on understanding HOW and WHY this happens. We will build on our early results and experiments to see if having more heart disease is because of something to do with cholesterol or the use of isoprenoids, and also whether this metabolic pathway is important for making the cells that, in the end, form the plaque found in heart disease. It is our hope that by understanding how this pathway controls the early stages of heart disease, and how this might be different in males and females, we can potentially fine-tune or make new drugs that will further help Canadians affected by this disease.

column36: Self-Management for Amputee Rehabilitation using Technology (SMART) program: A peer supported mHealth approach for rehabilitation after lower limb amputation
column37: Lower Limb Amputations (LLAs) are a substantial burden on the Canadian health services with nearly 50,000 cases reported between 2006 and 2011. To address the challenging nature of a LLA (e.g., decreased mobility, pain, depression), patients need to go through extensive rehabilitation programs. Effective self-management programs can help those with LLA to monitor their own condition and improve their quality of life. However, a lack of self-management programs, a limited healthcare budget, and a decrease in quality of services (e.g. shorter lengths of stay for inpatients and rapid movement to outpatient services) pose further challenges for patients with LLA. Self-management programs can be provided to clients through online mobile technologies (e.g., tablet) and offer accessible, low-cost, and potentially augmentative rehabilitation after discharge, in both urban and rural areas. To address these needs, we designed and developed an online educational and training platform for individuals with LLA called, Self-Management for Amputee Rehabilitation using Technology (SMART). SMART focuses on LLA education, prosthetic limb management, and weekly support of peers. It is monitored by a trainer through a website. We aim to evaluate SMART in men and women with LLA aged 50 years and over, admitted to prosthetic rehabilitation throughout Vancouver, BC and London, ON. SMART has the potential to influence a client's post-LLA needs with direct (e.g., individual's health) and indirect (e.g., healthcare utilization) benefits. The purpose of our randomized controlled trial is to evaluate the effect of SMART in community dwelling older adults with unilateral, above or below, knee amputation.

column36: Establishing the epigenetic drivers of aggressive behaviour in meningiomas
column37: Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumor and will become even more prevalent in the future in the face of an aging population. Surgical removal of the tumor followed by possible radiation therapy is the first line treatment for meningiomas. However, even with maximal treatment, nearly a quarter of meningiomas have aggressive behavior with fast tumor regrowth and a mortality rate that is similar to other well recognized brain cancers. The standard clinical systems that are used to determine the risk associated with tumor regrowth only modestly reflect the degree of aggressive behavior in the tumor, and therefore patients are not being appropriately selected for radiation therapy to prevent tumor regrowth. In addition to this, chemotherapy or other medical therapy options are non-existent for patients with meningiomas, and therefore patients often need to multiple high-risk surgeries and rounds of radiation to try and control disease, and this is often unsuccessful. Recent studies from our research team has found that changes to the tumor genes that do not involve the DNA sequence (i.e. epigenetics) are linked to aggressive behavior in meningiomas. We therefore hypothesize that the drivers of aggressive behaviour in meningioma are a combination of epigenetic changes in the tumour that have yet to be fully characterized. We propose to use high-resolution state-of-the-art scientific approaches to comprehensively study the epigenetic changes that are characteristic of aggressive meningiomas in order to accurately identify which patients are at risk for fast tumor regrowth and to develop novel medical treatment options.

column36: Evaluating the Wiiji app to improve Indigenous workplace mental health: a mixed-methods approach
column37: There is a need to tailor mental health interventions to the needs of Canadian Indigenous people. Indigenous individuals are less likely to seek help for mental health and accordingly, have rates of suicide at least twice as high as non-Indigenous counterparts. E-health interventions have shown success for several mental health related conditions, including anxiety, depression, sleeping disorders and feelings associated with low self-worth. Yet, only one Australian study has started to explore the acceptability of e-mental health approaches among remote health service providers working with Indigenous populations, and no study has explored the possibility of e-mental health approaches for individual workers and managers within workplaces. So, we developed an e-mental health application (app) for Indigenous workplaces titled 'Wiiji' to improve Indigenous workplace mental health through a CIHR Catalyst Grant: Work Stress and Wellbeing Hackathon. Wiiji provides information on work-related mental health and mental health resources that Indigenous workers can access, and provides a mechanism to connect with a peer-support who can assist the worker in times of stress.The primary goal of this application is to evaluate the app for improvement in Indigenous workplace mental health. We will use a mixed-methods approach to conduct this study. This work will be done in partnership with the Nokiiwin Tribal council, which consists of 5 communities. Results of this project will help us understand the impact of the app and will help us to better understand mechanisms for scale-up. These contributions have the potential to increase Indigenous participation in employment, reduce work disability, and improve the mental health of the Indigenous population. This will return economic and health benefits to Indigenous employers, communities, families, and individuals.

column37: Clostridioides difficile (or C. diff) is a bacterium that causes life-threatening intestinal infections and diarrhea. This strategy could provide much needed alternatives to antibiotics for the treatment of C. diff infection.

column36: Use of antimicrobial peptides, LL-37/17BIPHE2, as vaginal spermicides/microbicides as part of multipurpose prevention technology (MPT)
column37: The increasing world population and escalating rates of sexually transmitted infections (STI) have prompted the WHO to promote the development of MPT (multipurpose prevention technology), which involves applying into the vagina single compounds/devices that simultaneously inhibit pregnancy and kill the bacteria and viruses that cause STI. Recently, we have shown that a human antimicrobial peptide, LL-37, which is secreted as part of innate immunity to fight against microbial pathogens, can act as a spermicide against both human and mouse sperm and by injecting LL-37 along with sperm into the mouse uterus, these mice fail to become pregnant. A shorter form of LL-37, GF-17 (half the size of LL-37 and thus less expensive to be made), also exerts the same spermicidal and microbicidal activities as LL-37. Our pilot study also shows anti-HIV effects of LL-37. However, LL-37 and GF-17 are prone to be broken down by enzymes in cervical-vaginal fluids (CVF). Therefore, we have started to work with a modified form of GF-17, called 17BIPHE2, which is much more resistant to CVF-induced degradation. Our results indicate the same contraceptive efficacy of 17BIPHE2 as LL-37/GF-17. Herein we propose to determine whether 1) multiple administration of LL-37/17BIPHE2 does not cause injury to the female reproductive tract (FRT) or decrease good microbes in the vagina, and the treated females can resume fecundity after cessation of the peptide treatments; 2) LL-37/17BIPHE2 inhibits HIV infection on host target cells in the FRT. 3) We will develop "nanoparticle (NP)" forms containing LL-37/17BIPHE2 for optimal delivery with a controlled rate of peptide release, following placement of these NPs into the vagina. The MPT efficacy of LL-37/17BIPHE2 will provide women with empowerment to protect themselves against unwanted pregnancies and STI.

column36: Advancing and Mobilizing Indigenous Tuberculosis Knowledge: Impacts of Racially-Segregated Tuberculosis Treatment in Manitoba
column37: The Indigenous history of health care in Canada deserves rigorous, dedicated, and collaborative research that centres Indigenous experiences. "Advancing and Mobilizing Indigenous Tuberculosis Knowledge: Impacts of Racially-Segregated Tuberculosis Treatment in Manitoba" deploys assesses and repatriates newly-accessible historical photographs of mid-twentieth-century Indigenous tuberculosis (TB) patients. The project unites former Indigenous TB patients, their descendants, historians, archivists, health researchers, and museum curators to repatriate these historic photos, record survivor testimonies, and disseminate Indigenous TB histories. The objectives are: 1) identify unnamed individuals in the photographs 2) repatriate copies of the photos to survivors, descendants, and communities 3) record survivor testimonies about experiences as patients and staff of TB hospitals 4) preserve the currently photos 5) disseminate these histories through commemorative public projects. The approach is to repatriate previously-inaccessible archival photographs to Indigenous community partners. Participants are asked to identify individuals in the photos and share personal testimonies about TB histories in community-based workshops and through a social media campaign. We provide physical or digital copies of the photos on request and will preserve the fragile original photos for future generations. We will collect information drawn from the research to create a major exhibit and symposium, a medical and professional health education module. This project is in service to now-elderly Indigenous TB survivors, descendants, and communities; the research outcomes of this project benefit Indigenous stakeholders and their health first. We will also train undergraduate and graduate students and in the handling of Indigenous archives and present and publish our work in peer-reviewed venues.

column36: COMPLETE-2: A prospective, randomized, multi-centre trial of physiology-guided versus angiography-guided complete revascularization to treat multivessel disease after early percutaneous coronary intervention for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.
column37: Patients suffering a heart attack undergo a life-saving procedure called angioplasty, by which the blockage in the artery that caused the heart attack is opened and a stent is placed. In about half of the patients, additional blockages are found in other arteries. These are incidental findings and doctors have debated for years whether they should be treated with angioplasty or medications. We recently answered this question in a large multinational study called the COMPLETE trial. We showed that opening additional blockages reduced patient deaths or repeating heart attacks. A major concern is that not all of these angioplasties are necessary, but doctors do not know which arteries should be opened and which should be left alone. In the COMPLETE trial, the severity of blockages was estimated by visual inspection which is not a reliable method. Recently, new technique involving a special wire was proposed. It measures the blood pressure before and after a narrowing to estimate its severity. The advantage of this method is it can reduce the number of angioplasties by opening only the most important blockages thereby improving safety and costs. The main problem with using this method today is that doctors do not know of it. We are proposing a first large-scale trial to address this important issue. COMPLETE-2 trial will enroll 5100 patients at 140 sites worldwide. We aim to test whether the use of a pressure wire is as good as visually estimating the degree of narrowing when deciding which additional blockages found during the heart attack need to be treated with stents. We will test the usefulness of both methods and if it will improve patient safety by reducing unnecessary procedures, thereby decreasing bleeding, strokes and kidney injury. This study question is important in Canada because we have an unique health care system and the collaboration of doctors across the country will allow for efficient performance of randomized trials of heart attack patients.

column36: Traumatic stress symptoms in family caregivers of patients with acute leukemia: a longitudinal observational study
column37: Acute leukemia (AL) is a life-threatening cancer of the blood with sudden onset that occurs in individuals of all ages. The diagnosis of this disease typically requires urgent hospitalization for a course of intensive treatment, often for long periods of time. The disease and the treatment are likely to cause substantial distress in those affected and in their family caregivers (FCs). Research has demonstrated that FCs of individuals with solid tumours are equally or even more distressed than patients. However, little is known about the experience of FCs of patients with AL (who may be partners, adult children, or parents), despite the likelihood that they will be highly distressed and have a central role in supporting their family member with the disease. This lack of knowledge about their experience has limited our ability to help FCs to manage their distress and better support their ill family member. The present study aims to reduce this knowledge gap by assessing psychological distress and risk factors for its occurrence in the FCs of patients with AL across the life course. Consenting FCs of newly-diagnosed AL patients will complete questionnaires at the time of admission to the hospital and at 1-, 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-months thereafter. Statistical tests will be used to evaluate distress in FCs, the severity of this distress, its fluctuation over time, and the risk factors for its occurrence. We will also conduct interviews with a diverse group of FCs at 3-, 6-, and 12-months to learn more about their experience of distress over time, and their views about what help is needed for it to be best managed. This research study will help us understand more about distress in FCs of patients with AL and what approaches are needed to help them best manage this problem. Our results will be shared widely, including with FCs, patients, clinicians, and policy makers.

column36: Exploiting genetic vulnerabilities to improve outcomes in small cell carcinoma of the ovary
column37: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) is a rare but very aggressive type of ovarian cancer affecting young women. Its rarity has hampered the development of effective treatments. In 2014, several groups, including ours, discovered that SCCOHT is almost always caused by mutations in the gene SMARCA4. Our goal is to improve outcomes for women affected by this devastating cancer by providing new potential treatment strategies to treat SCCOHT. Part of our research strategy focuses on repurposing drugs already approved for other cancer types to treat SCCOHT. This approach can greatly facilitate clinical studies by bypassing drug development and safety testing. We recently found that SCCOHT cells are highly sensitive to a type of chemotherapy agents called CDK4/6 inhibitors, which are currently approved to treat breast cancer. This already led to a clinical study testing these inhibitors to treat SMARCA4-mutated cancers. Our research results suggest that SCCOHT cells are also sensitive to PARP inhibitors, also approved in Canada to treat another ovarian cancer subtype. In this project, we will fully validate PARP inhibitors as potential treatment for SCCOHT using a variety of model systems, including cell culture, mouse preclinical models, and patient tumor samples. As with all single-agent cancer therapies, drug resistance is expected to eventually arise in patients. To pre-empt this, we will use powerful genetic tools to identify the mechanisms at work in resistance development as well as identify novel drug targets in SCCOHT to develop secondary treatments or combination therapies to overcome resistance.

column36: Improving social justice in observational studies
column37: Population and public health is concerned not just with overall health but also the distribution of health in the population. Observational studies are conducted in real-world settings. Thus, they are ideal to understand the distribution of health inequity and monitor changes in response to policies over time. Observational studies often do not report/analyze sufficient details related to social determinants of health, thus undermining their ability to inform decisions with implications for social justice. This project aims to develop a reporting guideline on health equity in observational studies using an evidence and consensus-driven integrated knowledge translation process. This will extend the well-known STROBE (STrengthening Reporting of Observational studies in Epidemiology) reporting guideline. The project is novel in co-producing knowledge with Indigenous people, people in low and middle income countries and socially excluded people with diverse stakeholders including patients/public, researchers and decision-makers. We will apply an equity and sex/gender lens throughout. Data will be collected on analysis and reporting of health equity and sex/gender in observational studies. Existing journal and funding guidance will be reviewed. We will use an online global survey to seek broad feedback. We will hold a consensus meeting with researchers, patients/public and knowledge users to draft a global reporting guideline on health equity in observational studies. We will assess the applicability of this guideline to Indigenous research in Canada using a parallel process and consensus meeting. We will develop, implement and evaluate an end of grant knowledge translation strategy which will include pragmatic tools for authors and journal editors. Trainees will co-lead studies with mentorship from senior coinvestigators. The long-term vision is to improve transparent reporting of equity to inform policy and practice in reducing health inequities.

column36: Identifying cancer intrinsic immune evasion mechanism for target discovery
column37: Cancer cells can acquire features that allow them to evade recognition and destruction by effector cells of the immune system known as cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). These features or phenotypic changes not only facilitate progressive expansion and dissemination of cancer cells from within the tumor, but also promote resistance to currently employed immunotherapies that harness the potent cytotoxic properties of CTLs, including checkpoint inhibitors and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. The use of traditional genomic approaches (especially genome sequencing) to characterize patient cohorts treated with immunotherapy has provided fundamental insight into several mechanisms that promote immune evasion. Central to these genetic alterations that allow cancer cells to directly escape CTL killing, a form of immune evasion, includes loss of antigen presentation machinery and defects in cytokine signaling (e.g. interferon, TNF). While these landmark studies underscore the need to understand cancer intrinsic CTL evasion, they are limited to detecting only frequently occurring genetic alterations that contribute to this hallmark of cancer. As such, there remains a paucity of data systematically cataloging how individual cancer cell genetic elements act in a coordinated fashion to facilitate cancer intrinsic CTL evasion. Our research proposal aims to chart genetic dependencies that contribute to cancer intrinsic CTL evasion; to understand how core genetic dependencies that contribute to tumor heterogeneity in vivo and the tumor immune microenvironment, including in the presence of immune checkpoint blockade; to determine how our murine results translate to human cancer models; and to map genes that can overcome mutations that promote resistance to CTL toxicity using a combinatorial CRISPR targeting system recently developed in the lab.

column36: Preventing blindness by going to where you are: Culturally-competent tele-retina programs to support newcomers to attend diabetic retinopathy screening
column37: Retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness in Canada affecting people with diabetes. Yearly eye screening is recommended and there are treatments that limit vision loss. However, most people with diabetes in Canada don't get their eyes screened annually, and over 30% never have. Newcomers to Canada with diabetes are at greater risk and are even less likely to get screened. We conducted studies to understand why this may be and what can help. We looked into all other previous studies to summarize what is known about barriers to screening and which strategies work for addressing those barriers. We conducted interviews in Mandarin and French with immigrants to Canada with diabetes from China, Africa and the Caribbean about barriers for them getting eye screening. Access is a key barrier, and a promising solution is tele-retina screening, involving bringing portable screening equipment to a community location rather than requiring people to wait for specialist clinic appointments. However, there are many other barriers: language, knowledge, concerns about harms to eyes, misinformation about cost of screening, family influences and remembering. This project will involve two steps: First, we will work with newcomers from China, Africa and the Caribbean and community centres in Ontario and Quebec to co-develop strategies to support eye screening using tele-retina screening. Next we will launch screening programs in community centres on a small scale to test if the strategies we co-develop are acceptable and feasible to community centres and patients, how many patients attend and whether the screening is delivered as we expect. Results will give us the evidence needed to justify a larger study that would randomly allocate people to receive the intervention and then check if more people get their eyes screened. If that works, this may be a way of making sure groups at greater risk of blindness get their eyes screened to reduce the chance of vision loss.

column36: Discovering the transcription regulatory networks that control uterine contractions
column37: The contractile activity of the smooth muscle component of the uterus, the myometrium, generates the force needed to expel the fetus at birth. To initiate contractions, individual smooth muscle cells within the myometrium turn on a group of genes in response to hormonal, mechanical and inflammatory signals. In many patient cases this cell-coordinated contractile response occurs prior to term; women can consequently enter labour too early, which results in the delivery of underdeveloped infants at high risk of death or complications later in life. There is currently no effective treatment for preterm labour. Recent research has identified activated genes in the myometrium at term and preterm labour; however, the mechanisms that stimulate expression of these genes remain unclear. To understand the basis of preterm labour and develop new preterm labour therapies, we need to find the components involved in activating genes in both term labour and preterm labour. Inside cell nuclei the DNA that makes up our genome is highly organised into three dimensional structures so that regions of the genome that turn genes on or off can contact the genes they regulate. This genome organisation is specific to each cell type which ensures genes are expressed in the correct context. Currently, genome organisation in the myometrium as well as the parts of the genome that regulate gene expression changes during pregnancy and labour are unknown. Out team will identify the three dimensional genome structures specific to myometrial cells and the labour process. In addition, we will identify the proteins that bind to the genome to regulate gene expression during preterm or term labour. Uncovering the suite of genomic regions and regulatory proteins that underlie the labour process will provide new targets for the development of therapeutic treatments for preterm labour, preventing complications that occur when babies are born preterm.

column37: Platelets are small cells in the blood that help control bleeding. Heparin is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used in heart surgery and to manage heart attacks and strokes. Patients receiving heparin may have an allergic-type reaction called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia resulting in low platelets (thrombocytopenia) and can also develop severe clotting causing loss of limbs, heart attacks, stroke and death. So this drug (heparin) that usually helps patients can actually cause more strokes and heart attacks in some patients. In HIT, some patients develop attack proteins (antibodies) once they are given heparin which attack platelets. However, other antibodies appear similar but do not attack platelets. Testing if people have HIT is a major problem because most tests cannot tell the difference between the dangerous antibodies and the antibodies that do not cause HIT. Our first goal is to study the antibodies that cause the disease in HIT patients and what separates them from other antibodies who do not get the disease. Our second goal is to use the information regarding specific characteristics of antibodies to make tests more efficient and accurate. In addition, we will identify drugs that can interfere with the disease-causing proteins and stop them from causing HIT due to the use of heparin. Our group has hundreds of frozen blood samples from patients who received heparin since we are a test centre for many hospitals across Canada. Once we understand why some patients get HIT and others do not, we will be able to provide better tests, resulting in better patient care for many Canadians at risk of getting this disorder.

column36: Human Cytomegalovirus as a Driver of Adverse Health Outcomes among Children Exposed to HIV in Utero
column37: Every year, nearly 1.5 million HIV infected women give birth around the world. Due to the development and use of antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy, the majority of their children will be born HIV free (1.3 million). These HIV exposed but uninfected children, referred to commonly as "CHEU" children, now make up nearly 30% of the newborn population in some countries where there is a very high prevalence of HIV. While these children are not infected by HIV, they remain affected by it, and have a much higher rate of mortality when compared to children who have never been exposed to HIV, are more likely to be hospitalized, and get sick from infectious diseases. Among children living with HIV (CLWH), antiretroviral therapy works well in suppressing the virus, but is not curative due to the immune system's limited ability to attack the remaining HIV viral particles what is known as the viral reservoir. We suspect that co-infection with another common childhood virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV) may play a role in explaining to poor health outcomes of CHEU infants and maintain the HIV viral reservoir in infected children. CMV is a virus also transmitted from mother to child and is even more common than HIV, affecting nearly 1 in every 100 births worldwide. Because the HIV virus facilitates/enables the replication of the CMV virus, women living with HIV are at much higher risk of transmitted the virus to their newborns, However, at the moment, there are no recommendations for routine CMV testing in HIV exposed and infected children. The objective of our study is to assess the impact of CMV infection on HIV exposed, and HIV infected children. This is important because CMV is a treatable virus. If we find that CMV is contributing to their poor health outcomes, as a team, we will advocate for testing of all HIV exposed children.

column36: Epigenetic mechanisms of gastric cancer associated with ARID1A mutations and H. pylori
column37: Gastric cancer (GC) is the third most deadly cancer in the world, ranked within the top ten fatal cancers in Canada. It is known to be highly influenced by environmental factors. Indeed, Helicobacter (H) pylori is a human gastric pathogen that infects half of the world's population and is associated with 70% of invasive gastric tumors, making it the most significant risk factor for GC. However, how H. pylori promotes gastric cancer initiation and progression is still unclear. During cancer initiation and progression, the chromatin structure, a massive protein complex, organizes DNA available for changes in gene expression. Altered chromatin structures are associated with abnormal expression changes in genes that play critical roles in cancer. Consequently, new therapies targeting these chromatin structures in cancer have emerged recently. Notably, mutations identified in a number of chromatin modifier genes appear consistently in GC, implying that chromatin regulation is central to the disease pathogenesis. Among chromatin modifiers highly mutated in gastric cancer, ARID1A is one component of the key chromatin remodeling complex, and it is the second most frequently mutated gene after TP53. However, its role in GC is still unclear. Utilizing our novel mouse models mutated for Arid1a and infected with H. pylori, as well as mini-gut (organ-on-chip and organoid culture) systems, we will define GC-specific chromatin structures and gene expression profiles, and examine novel, chromatin-based therapeutic strategies targeting a key initiating phase of gastric cancer. This work will not only define how H. pylori interacts with altered chromatin structures to promote GC but also form a key foundation for highly innovative GC therapies.

column36: Remodeling of cerebral plasticity by early-life adversity: cellular and molecular mechanisms in the human brain
column37: Child abuse, defined as childhood sexual, physical or emotional abuse or neglect by a parent or caregiver, causes lasting pain and hardship for millions of Canadians. The aim of this research is to understand the nature of lasting changes in the organization of brain circuits in people having suffered from child abuse. We will examine the consequences of early-life adversity on perineuronal nets (PNNs) which are molecular structures embedding certain types of neurons in the brain. PNNs arise as brain regions mature and, as suggested by animal studies, stabilize brain circuitries while limiting their plasticity. Alterations of PNNs by early-life stress could be associated with the rise of maladaptive emotions and behaviors that can predispose to mental illness. Currently, very little is known about PNNs in the human brain. Here, we hypothesize that a history of child abuse associates with a remodeling of cerebral plasticity through the modification of PNNs in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region that has been implicated in depression and found to be vulnerable to early-life adversity. Having a unique combination of expertise and direct access to the well-characterized post-mortem brain samples (Douglas-Bell Canada Brain Bank), we propose to conduct this research by comparing brain tissues from individuals having suffered from severe child abuse to matched controls with cutting-edge microscopy and molecular approaches. This research will provide novel insights regarding the cellular and molecular nature of altered brain plasticity associated with child abuse and may in turn help identify novel therapeutic targets and better inform public policies aimed at preventing child abuse or minimizing its impact on mental health.

column36: To define the role of primary cilia in long-range axon tract formation
column37: Primary cilia are hair-like, signaling antenna protruding from the cell body on virtually all cell types, including neurons. In the past decade, primary cilia have sparked enormous interest due to the discoveries that mutations in over 100 genes that encode ciliary proteins can lead to 30+ human rare disorders collectively termed "ciliopathies". The brain is particularly vulnerable to impaired primary cilia as reflected in a large group of ciliopathies that are characterized by severe axonal defects associated with intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorder. However, we know little of how primary cilia function in the brain. Using our ciliopathies disease models and cilia-specific experimental tools, we are uniquely poised to systematically investigate the primary cilia-dependent mechanisms in axonal development. We recently made exciting progress: We found that impaired cilia in neurons result in malformations of major axon tracts such as corticospinal tract (the longest) and corpus callosum (the biggest). Mutant neurons show defects in axonal growth and guidance, as well as dysregulated cilia-PI3K (Phosphoinositide 3-kinase) signaling. These data are important in beginning to unravel the undefined signaling mechanism linking primary cilia to the control of axonal development. Based on our preliminary work, we will test the intriguing notion that primary cilia function as essential signaling centers to convey environmental signals to neurons for axonal development and circuit formation.

Medications like methadone are the best available treatment for opioid use disorder and have been shown to lower the risk of death from opioid overdose. The study will last for 12 weeks and compare safety, tolerability, between people who received cannabis and those who received placebo. At the end of 12 weeks, participants adherent to the study protocol will be offered another 12 weeks on cannabis. There will be no cost for participating in this trial. This pilot study is an innovative proposal to try and improve treatment for people with opioid use disorder at high risk of overdose. It will not only help patients and care providers better understand cannabis use during methadone treatment, but also advance efforts to address Canada's overdose crisis.

Several reports indicate that autophagy under normal conditions is important for the maintenance of skeletal muscle size and that autophagy is enhanced and promotes muscle wasting under pathological conditions such as fasting, loss of innervation and sepsis sepsis. Despite major progress in our understanding of how autophagosomes (double membrane vesicles) are formed inside skeletal muscles, many of the proteins involved in autophagy remain unclear. We performed preliminary experiments in mouse skeletal muscles to identify novel genes that are involved in autophagy. These experiments revealed the presence of an uncharacterized gene that we named MYTHO (Macroautophagy and YouTH Optimizer). We named as such because our preliminary experiments revealed that this gene is critical for longevity in worms. These experiments also revealed that MYTHO protein is present in skeletal muscles of humans and mice and that deletion of this gene in cultured cells inhibits autophagy. In this proposal, we will conduct several experiments designed to identify the importance of MYTHO in the autophagy of intact skeletal muscles in humans and mice and to identify the mechanisms through which MYTHO regulates autophagosome formation in skeletal muscles. These objectives will be achieved by using molecular biology tools to visualize MYTHO protein inside skeletal muscle fibers and to either increase its expression or reduce it and measure its contribution to the formation of autophagosomes and recycling of proteins and organelles in normal skeletal muscles and in muscles of mice in which autophagy is induced and contributes to muscle wasting. These conditions include acute fasting, denervation and severe sepsis elicited by bacterial products.

column36: Investigating risk factors for cognitive impairment using precision neuropsychological and neuroimaging measures in a Canadian multi-ethnic cohort
column37: Cognitive impairment (problems with memory and thinking) is on the rise and so is the proportion of visible minority groups in Canada. Risk factors for cognitive impairment have mostly been studied in Caucasians, with much less research carried out in visible minority groups. This is a problem because some ethnic groups may be at higher risk for cognitive impairment. Furthermore risk factors may differ across ethnic groups. Because visible minorities represent 20% of Canada's population, there is an urgent need to study risk factors for cognitive impairment in these understudied groups. Cardiovascular risk factors, like high blood pressure and obesity, negatively affect the blood vessels of the brain. We call these harmful changes vascular brain injury (VBI). Both cardiovascular risk factors and VBI can lead to cognitive impairment. Interestingly, there are striking differences in the vascular health of Canada's two major visible minority groups: South Asian and Chinese individuals. That is, Canadian South Asians are more prone to cardiovascular risk factors, as reflected by earlier disease onset and more severe risk factors. By contrast, Chinese individuals have less severe cardiovascular risk factors, but are at greater risk for brain hemorrhage (bleeding). An important, but unanswered, question is whether Canadian South Asians and/or Chinese individuals are at heightened risk for cognitive impairment due to cardiovascular conditions and/or VBI. This is the first study to use sophisticated brain imaging and comprehensive cognitive testing to investigate risk factors for cognitive impairment among Canadian ethnic groups. Such knowledge is critical for developing and implementing appropriate prevention and intervention strategies for Canada's diverse communities. Our study will also yield a model for calculating a person's risk of cognitive impairment that takes ethnicity into account. This model could ultimately be used in primary care settings.

column36: Patterns of mortality and cancer incidence among adults who live near Canadian nuclear power plants: A population-based longitudinal study of CanCHEC participants between 1991 and 2016.
column37: Nuclear power is used in Canada to provide electricity, with its greatest use in Ontario where 61% of the province's electrical generation is from 18 CANDU reactors. Barriers to increased production of nuclear energy include public concern over the intractable nuclear waste disposal problem and about the possible health impacts of low levels of exposure to ionizing radiation. In Canada, 7% of the population lives within 25km from a nuclear power plant. Ionizing radiation is a carcinogen, and has been associated with other health conditions such as cardiovascular disease. There are uncertainties about the health risks at low levels of exposure. While previous reports support the conclusion there are no adverse health effects from living near nuclear power plants (NPPs), these studies have many weaknesses. These include: small study populations, lack of lengthy follow-up, the inability to account for residential mobility, and to control for other disease risk factors. Our study overcomes these limitations. We propose to examine patterns of cancer incidence and mortality among adults who live close the 5 NPPs in Canada. The study population is drawn from those who completed a mandatory long form Canadian Census between 1991 and 2011. The cohort contains data for 13.4 million adults whose place of residence is tracked annually. Cancer diagnoses and cause of death information for each of these individuals through 2015/16 has been determined by linkage to national registry data. We will investigate differences in mortality and cancer rates between those who live near NPPs to those who don't while accounting for other determinants of health. We will also create exposure surfaces that map differences in ionizing radiation around the NPPs, and we will estimate how health risks vary by these exposures. Our findings will provide important evidence about the population health impacts of exposure to ionizing radiation for both the public, and regulatory agencies.

column36: A Web-Based Peer Navigation Program for Men with Prostate Cancer: A Hybrid Effectiveness-Implementation Trial
column37: One in nine Canadian men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer (PC) in their lifetime. Although all treatment options can be effective in controlling the disease, treatment side effects such as problems with erections and controlling the bladder can significantly affect men's quality of life. Many men with PC say they do not get relevant information and emotional support, and experience gaps in care when dealing with these difficult issues. Previous studies have shown that cancer patient navigation improves access to care and support, and reduces healthcare costs. We developed TrueNTH Peer Navigation - a peer navigation program for men with PC and a peer navigator training course. Men are matched online with a trained peer navigator who provides practical information and emotional support through the cancer journey. A pilot evaluation showed that it is highly acceptable to patients and peer navigators, and improves patient quality of life, social support and ability to manage their health. In this study, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial of the TrueNTH Peer Navigation program in cancer centres in Ontario, British Columbia and Nova Scotia. Patients will be randomly assigned to receive TrueNTH Peer Navigation or usual care with access to information on the TrueNTH Peer Navigation website. We will evaluate the effect of the TrueNTH Peer Navigation program on patient outcomes such as their ability to take a more active role in their health, quality of life, social support and use of health care services. In addition, we will evaluate how TrueNTH Peer Navigation was implemented, the factors that make it easier or harder for people to deliver the program to patients in different settings, as well as the cost of delivering the program, which will help us learn how to spread the program across the country. This research will help to improve the quality of life and health outcomes of men with PC in Canada.

column36: The impact of preterm birth on socioeconomic and educational outcomes of children and families
column37: One in every 12 children in Canada are born preterm (< 37 weeks gestation). Nevertheless, it is unclear what impact preterm birth has on the long and short-term socioeconomic outcomes of the individual and family. This data linkage includes, among others, tax, birth and death, healthcare, and postsecondary education registration records. Given our expertise in statistical and simulation modeling and, we are going to employ methods, such as multistate models and mediation analysi, that will allow us to account for the complexities of longitudinal, cohort data. column36: COLCOT-T2D : Colchicine for Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Events in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Inflammation appears to play an important role in atherosclerosis. Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory medication and is one of the oldest remedies still in use today as a treatment for gout and for Familial Mediterranean Fever. Recently, we have shown in the COLCOT-1 study (COLchicine Cardiovascular Outcomes Trial) that a low dose of colchicine reduced the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with a recent heart attack. Patients using colchicine had 23% fewer events compared to those receiving an inactive substance (placebo) in a study including 4745 patients with a recent heart attack. We now want to study the possible benefits of colchicine in other high-risk patients, such as those with diabetes. The primary objective of the new COLCOT-T2D study is to determine if long-term treatment with colchicine will reduce major cardiovascular events in patients with diabetes. We will also assess the effects of colchicine on the development and progression of cognitive impairment. Additionally, cost-effectiveness and quality of life will be assessed. COLCOT-T2D is a study comparing colchicine 0.5 mg/day and placebo in 10,000 patients aged 60 years and up with type 2 diabetes and at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor. The main criterion of efficacy will be the development of unfavorable events such as death, heart attack, stroke or urgent hospitalization for angina requiring invasive intervention. Cognitive function will also be evaluated. The study will be overseen by an independent monitoring committee. We hope to demonstrate that low-dose colchicine safely reduces the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with diabetes who were initially not known to suffer from heart disease.

column36: Structural characterization of lysosomal enzyme trafficking
column37: The lysosome is a compartment in the cell that acts as the waste disposal system. It degrades proteins, fats, carbohydrates and other molecules so that their components parts can be reused. This is accomplished by numerous enzymes in the lysosome that break up the unwanted molecules. The task of directing these enzymes into the lysosome is a critical step that is currently not well understood at the molecular level. It involves the recognition of numerous unrelated enzymes by a series of protein complexes in the endoplasmic reticulum that tags the enzymes with a marker called M6P. This marker guides the enzymes to the lysosome. This proposal is aimed at understand the molecular basis for the process of marking lysosomal enzymes using structure imaging techniques. Specifically, we are interested in how the protein complex called GNPT manages to mark lysosomal destined enzymes with M6P. Deficiency of GNPT prevents enzymes from reaching the lysosome in many cell types and organs, and mutations in the GNPT gene cause several severe lysosomal storage diseases, for which there are no cures. The results from this proposal will help understand how this process works in great detail, which will be important for designing strategies to help treat diseases.

column36: A population-based assessment of pharmacological treatments for gestational diabetes
column37: Gestational diabetes (a type of diabetes that occurs during pregnancy) is one of the most common pregnancy complications. It can lead to harmful short-term (e.g., preterm birth) and long-term outcomes (e.g., heart disease) for both the mother and child. Proper control of a woman' blood sugar level is crucial in preventing these complications. Drugs are given to women who are not able to meet their target blood sugar levels through lifestyle interventions. Although insulin is the recommended treatment for gestational diabetes, it is inconvenient because it requires increased medical visits, injections, and intensive self-monitoring of one's blood sugar level. Insulin also is known to cause hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Metformin, a drug used to treat diabetes that is taken orally, may represent an alternative treatment. However, there are safety concerns surrounding its use during pregnancy that require further investigation. There is currently no clear consensus regarding the effectiveness and safety of using metformin for gestational diabetes due to the limitations of the available evidence in this area. We will address this knowledge gap by conducting a study using the electronic health records of pregnant women with gestational diabetes in the United Kingdom using a database called the Clinical Practice Research Datalink. We will compare the occurrence of pregnancy outcomes with metformin to that with insulin. We will also study outcomes among the offspring. We will use rigorous statistical techniques to obtain valid treatment effects. This study will generate real-world evidence to help inform decisions made by government agencies, guideline writing committees, clinicians, and pregnant women. In doing so, it will improve the health of pregnant women with gestational diabetes and their offspring. With a growing number of women with gestational diabetes worldwide, this study will have important clinical and population health implications.

column36: Unravelling regulatory networks of stem cell states using single cell analysis
column37: Cells continuously sense their external and internal environments to both adapt and perform specific functions. They process such information through intracellular networks of proteins, which are often organized into specific structures or circuits, to induce specific responses. One such biological response involves conversion one cell fate (or type) to another. Conversion of cell fate is fundamental to development of an organism - progenitor cells such as pluripotent cells go through series of cell fate decisions to give rise to variety of adult cell types, and is often misrelated in disease. The differences among individual genetically identical cells response to a condition often also generates both molecular as well as cellular heterogeneity allowing them to exhibit diverse cell states. For instance, pluripotent stem cells exhibit such heterogeneous cell states: Totipotent, Pluripotent and differentiation-Primed, each with distinct differentiation capacity. Pluripotent stem cells are increasingly used for disease modelling and regenerative medicine. By introducing multiple sources of differentiation bias, such multiple cell states compromise the effective use of pluripotent cells. Thus, it is highly important to understand the molecular basis of pluripotent stem cell states. What are their potential cell states? What are the key regulatory mechanisms governing their transitions? Can we control and reverse-engineer such mechanisms to modulate the cell states? We propose to address these in the current grant. We will study the cell states of pluripotent stem cells at the single-cell level using our expertise in the interdisciplinary systems biology approach - combining quantitative single-cell experiments in proteomics and genomics with computational biology.

column36: The novel combinatorial role of Irx3 and Irx4 in ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy
column37: Left ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy (LVNC) is a rare but distinctive heart disease that affects both children and adults. column37: Lay summary. While the failure of several clinical trials has led to an energetic debate as to the importance of Abeta, many labs agree that accumulation of abnormal tau in the brain leads to irrevocable cell loss and that tau can be considered as an executioner molecule. Moreover, beyond AD there are a number of other dementias that also feature abnormal tau deposits, speaking to its importance. column36: Neuro-immune control of postoperative pain via CCL22:CCR4 signaling
column37: Pain is one of the major complaints of patients suffering from various neurological and non- neurological conditions, such as autoimmune diseases, tissue infection, and injury. Current therapies for pain caused by inflammation, such as after surgical wound or bacterial infection, include NSAIDs and acetaminophen. These drugs often provide inadequate pain relief and are accompanied by serious gastrointestinal and cardiovascular side effects. Opioids are more effective pain-killers but carry a heavy burden to both the patient and society. While treatments targeting the spinal cord or brain can be challenging and carry risks of unwanted side effects, modulating the inflammation that occurs at the site of injury may be more amenable to treatment. Recent work from our lab has found that dendritic cells in the skin, which act as sentinels to injury and infection, secrete specific immune mediators after injury that can directly activate sensory neurons to cause pain. In preliminary studies, we discovered that tissue injury activates a specific molecule (the chemokine CCL22) in dendritic cells located at the site of tissue injury. We also discovered that blocking its receptor, CCR4, substantially reduces pain. Our work also suggests that pain-sensing neurons control the activation state of dendritic cells in response to injury, and may function in a feedback loop. This proposal will examine how these immune cells communicate with pain-sensing neurons to mediate pain, and whether the neurons themselves can alter the dendritic cell response. Understanding why and how pain occurs during inflammation will enable us to develop new health care strategies to prevent or treat pain in patients with bacterial infection and tissue injury.

column36: Prospective Evaluation of Breast-Conserving Surgery Alone in Low Risk Ductal Carcinoma in Situ Defined by a Molecular Expression Assay Combined with Clinico-Pathological Features
column37: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast cancer that represents over 25% of all new breast cancers in North America. Treatment is recommended given the potential of DCIS to progress to invasive cancer. Most women are treated with breast-conserving surgery followed by breast radiation which can lower the risk of breast cancer recurring. Breast radiotherapy carries a risk of toxicity and has no impact on survival. Therefore, there is great interest to reduce over-treatment by identifying the subgroup of individuals with DCIS who have a very low risk of recurrence after local excision for whom it is safe to omit radiation. Currently, clinicians use clinical and pathological criteria to estimate an individual's risk of local recurrence after breast-conserving surgery such as age at diagnosis older than 45 years, tumor size 2.5 cm or less, low/intermediate grade and clear margins, but these features at best identify women whose risk of local recurrence 10 years after breast-conserving surgery is 11-15%. Given that most women with DCIS receive radiation suggests that this risk is considered too high to omit radiation. The Oncotype DCIS Score is the first genomic test for DCIS. Integration of the DCIS Score with clinicopathological features can more accurately estimate local recurrence risks after surgery and may help identify a subgroup of women with a lower risk of recurrence where there would be greater consensus and patient satisfaction to omit radiotherapy. column36: Ubiquitin-Dependent Regulation of DNA Replication during Stress
column37: Our cells need to make perfect copies of their genetic material (DNA) in order to divide and proliferate thereby allowing our bodies to stay fit and healthy. Cancer cells often have defects in these protective systems and therefore accumulate genetic abnormalities more readily than healthy cells. This is leveraged by doctors to destroy tumors through the use of chemo- and radio-therapy which cause unsustainable levels of damage to the genetic material of cancer cells. We have evidence that RFWD3 enables many important pathways that allow accurate and complete genome duplication. Our work will help us understand how RFWD3 allows our cells to fully and accurately replicate their DNA thereby avoiding potential mutations that may lead to cancer. This new information will improve our understanding of the complex pathways that protect our DNA, and guide us in the elaboration of novel strategies that will improve the efficiency of current anti-cancer treatments.

column36: High-Throughput Analysis of Low Dose, Repetitive Alpha Particle Irradiation as a source of Radon-Induced Lung Cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the highest lethality Canadian cancer. It is overwhelmingly caused by tobacco smoke and/or inhalation of radioactive radon gas. Radon emits ionizing radiation that can cause serious health effects depending on dose and type. Relative to photon radiation (such as x-rays), the alpha particles emitted by radon produces much more disease-causing, complex DNA damage. Radon is very prevalent in our environment and is the main cause of lung cancer in the ~20% of patients who are never-smokers, encompassing >25,000 North Americans per year. Despite this, technological limitations to conveniently deliver alpha particles repetitively, in low doses and in an affordable, high throughput manner have constrained research on this topic. Consequently, our knowledge of why some people, tissues and cell types are susceptible to radiation is mainly derived from high dose, acute exposure photon research. This is problematic, as health protection risk models are being built on data derived from photon studies that have an ambiguous relevance to what we are most exposed to in life, which are alpha particles via radon inhalation. To resolve this, our lab has developed a next-generation, high throughput alpha particle irradiator able to deliver adjustable, low doses that reflects what is happening to Canadians in our environment. We will use this to define - in exquisite molecular detail - alpha particle effects on the stability of our DNA and changes that can lead to cancer. This project will be the first to employ a high-throughput approach to systematically solve key alpha particle biology questions. This is important as, while radon causes thousands of lung cancer diagnoses annually, knowledge to meaningfully intervene before clinical manifestation is unacceptably low. We will be impactful by building the essential knowledge to identify those at risk of radon-induced cancer based on novel, next-generation methods fuelled by expert knowledge of DNA damage repair biology.

column36: Axonal swellings in the cerebellum in health and disease
column37: In many diseases, post-mortem analysis of the brain reveals an abundance of swellings on axons - the wire-like structures that carry information across the brain - in the cerebellum, a brain region involved in motor coordination. This has led scientists to hypothesize that these axonal swellings contribute to the pathology that causes motor coordination deficits. Our results, however, suggest that this may not be true. The overall goal of this grant is to understand how these axonal swellings function in health and disease. We have surprising results from healthy brain tissue showing that axon swellings improve, not impair, the function of axons, and that this causes mice to learn better. Now we want to determine if axonal swellings do the same thing in disease. We hypothesize that axon swellings are something that the brain produces to repair axonal dysfunction. We will study the function of axonal swellings in two different diseases: one, a mouse model of ataxia, and the second a mouse model of Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Both display prominent axonal swellings, and in MS mice especially, axons eventually degenerate profoundly. We will test whether axonal swellings contribute to axonal dysfunction or work to counteract it. We will also unravel the mechanisms by which axonal swellings form, what role they serve in the developing brain, and where they are located and how long they persist in the intact brain. By studying the role of axonal swellings in health and disease, we hope to deeper our understanding of the brain's mechanisms of healing, which may lead to new understanding about disease mechanisms, and perhaps new treatment strategies.

column37: Finding the genes that are essential for a tumor cell to survive is one of the oldest goals of cancer research. Genes that are essential and fall into classes, which allow drug development to suppress their function, lie at the heart of finding novel therapies to combat cancer. Conventional experiments use cells grown in a plastic dish and switch off one gene at a time followed by analysis of a cell's ability to divide and grow. While we have learned a great deal from those studies, cells grown on a plastic dish do not mimic the situation of a tumor within a patient where dozens of cell types interact in a very intricate and sophisticated way. As such, the genes that might be necessary for a tumor cell to grow on plastic might be very different than the genes required for growth in an organ within a living organism. Our first proof-of-concept experiment shows that lung cancer cells grown on plastic behave very differently compared to the same cells grown in an organism such as an experimental mouse. This experiment has taught us that the mouse experiment indeed appears to be physiologically more relevant. As such, we are proposing to establish several physiologically-relevant models of lung cancer in mice and test every gene, for which drugs and therapeutic strategies can conceivably be generated with the goal of finding novel and more potent drug targets to combat lung cancer.

column37: Advances in screening and management have improved the lifespan of those diagnosed with breast cancer. However, since patients are living longer, complications of breast cancer management have become increasingly apparent. Chronic pain is a devastating complication of breast cancer surgery and can affect up to half of patients undergoing surgical resection of their disease. It can last for years and is associated with decreased function and quality of life. To make matters worse, there are not many ways to treat this pain disorder and we are not sure how to prevent it. Fortunately, recent studies indicate that infusing a medication called lidocaine to patients while they undergo breast cancer surgery can prevent chronic pain from developing. Two small studies, including one by our own research team, have shown that administering lidocaine during the procedure can prevent chronic pain 3-months after surgery. Intravenous lidocaine is the most promising intervention to potentially prevent chronic pain in breast cancer patients. However, results from these studies are limited by their small sample sizes. We plan to conduct a large randomized controlled trial (highest quality study) of 1,144 patients to definitively identify whether lidocaine during breast cancer surgery can prevent the development of chronic pain. Each patient in the study will be randomly assigned to receive either intravenous lidocaine or a placebo (salt water) during surgery. Patients will be contacted in-hospital, for the first 3 days after surgery, and at 3 and 12 months after surgery. We expect that patients who received lidocaine will experience less pain, improved function, less opioid use, and improved quality of life. This study could reduce long-term pain and suffering in patients with breast cancer. Since intravenous lidocaine is low-cost and easy to deliver, results of this study have the potential to impact breast cancer treatment around the globe.

column37: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are designed to be used by patients to describe their health, including their quality of life, pain, fatigue, and functional abilities. PROMs can also be used by clinicians, health professionals, and healthcare decision makers to describe the outcomes of care from the patient's point of view. In order to contribute to improving patient care, PROMs must be valid (i.e., measure what they are supposed to measure) and reliable (i.e., measure the same thing over time and for patients with different characteristics). Sometimes, patient responses on PROMs are not consistent with what was expected. These inconsistencies may occur because patients with different characteristics may not understand or interpret questions about their health in the same way (differential item functioning), or their interpretations may change over time (response shift). While these differential interpretations and response shifts in PROMs data could be a result of positive adaptations to health challenges, such as a chronic illness or a healthcare treatment, they are often difficult to detect and, if ignored, could lead to incorrect conclusions about the outcomes of care. Our research focuses on data-driven machine-learning methods to efficiently cluster (i.e., group) patients with similar patterns of differential item functioning or response shifts. We will develop and apply machine-learning item response methods and compare them to model-based item response methods using computer simulation. We will apply the proposed machine-based methods to existing data for patients with specific health conditions to predict healthcare use. The research will be shared with healthcare providers, PROMs developers, and researchers. The overall goal of our study is to improve the ability to accurately interpret patient-reported information when measuring the effectiveness and responsiveness of the healthcare system.

column36: Characterization of typical and atypical brain development
column37: Neuroimaging-based characterization of typical brain development is of utmost importance to form a baseline for understanding cognitive development and its deviations in neurodevelopmental disorders. Many groups including ours have addressed this question by building prediction models of brain development. However, previous studies focused on 'static' brain measures although there is a need for considering trajectories as opposed to static 'final' brain measures. We need to leverage the availability of large-scale open longitudinal datasets to build prediction models of individual variations in brain and cognitive development. Our first aim is to explore whether developmental changes in individual brains can be used to predict future cognition. Using longitudinal data, we will use within-subject developmental changes in brain in prediction models of cognitive outcomes. Although generative models have been proposed for developmental changes in the brain. However, previous studies lack one important component: they have modeled developmental changes in brain connections, but not brain structure. Brain structure also changes during development; as such generative models need to take into account both brain structure as well as connections. Our second aim is to explore models used in complex systems, particularly co-evolving network models that consider changes in both nodes and edges with time. Furthermore, although previous studies indicate the utility of studying brain trajectories, little is known whether social factors such as the socioeconomic conditions influence these brain trajectories. By studying the epigenetic mechanisms behind the influence of children's environment on their neurodevelopmental trajectories, we can gain insights into the biological processes. In collaboration with Dr. Linda Booij, our third aim is to investigate epigenetic mechanisms underlying socioeconomic conditions and deviant neurodevelopmental trajectories in children.

column36: HPV vaccination effectiveness in a Canadian setting, 12 years after implementation: are we on the road to eliminate cervical cancer?
column37: In Canada, screening has helped to reduce the number of cervical cancer cases. However, there were still 1350 women diagnosed with cancer and 410 deaths in 2019. Persistent infections of high-risk HPV types can lead to the development of precancerous lesions that may slowly transform into cervical cancer. Because cervical cancer usually takes several decades to develop, there is time to identify precancers by screening and thus prevent cancer. Vaccination against high-risk HPVs, especially if done through school programs, can lead to more effective and equitable prevention, with less adverse effects. Our research team will evaluate the effectiveness of HPV vaccination against cervical pre-cancers and cancers, to determine if vaccine effectiveness is as good "in real life" as what was found in initial studies. Some studies have attempted to answer this question, with very mixed results, partly because the methods used led to some errors in the estimation of effectiveness in "real life". Between 2020 and 2023 we will contact women aged between 21 and 32 who will receive a diagnosis of cervical precancer or cancer. With their agreement, we will determine which HPV types are present in the lesions. This information will enable us to calculate the effectiveness of HPV vaccination. We will also check whether the effectiveness varies according to the age at vaccination, the number of doses of vaccine received, whether vaccination was started before or after the beginning of sexual activity and by the severity of the lesions. Vaccination against HPV offers the possibility to improve the prevention of cervical precancers and cancers, while using resources efficiently and few adverse effects. The demonstration, in Canada, of a high effectiveness of vaccination "in real life" could foster greater acceptance of vaccination and help plan future screening activities.

column36: Mitochondrial dynamics and metabolism in muscle stem cell maintenance and muscle regeneration
column37: An estimated 4 million Canadians currently suffer from muscle wasting conditions, manifesting as loss of muscle mass and function. Muscle wasting is the most significant cause of disability in the aging population and individuals with muscle degenerative diseases, including muscular dystrophies, myopathies and cancer cachexia. The decline in muscle function affects mobility, voluntary function and quality of life, often leading to institutionalization and mortality4. This imposes a dramatic burden on individuals and society, costing Canadians several billions of dollars per year. Thus, there is a pressing need for the development of preventative and therapeutic strategies targeting muscle wasting. For many years, muscle wasting was thought to be only a problem of the myofibers, yet recent evidence shows that muscle stem cell (MuSC) dysfunction plays a significant role. Adult skeletal muscle normally has a high regenerative capacity, however, within the context of muscle wasting MuSCs are depleted and muscle regeneration is impaired. Currently, the reason for MuSC depletion is unclear and thus there are no therapies targeting their restoration. Understanding the underlying etiological factors leading to MuSC depletion is instrumental in identifying novel approaches to restore muscle repair and function. The overarching goal of this proposal is to restore MuSC number and function and promote muscle repair in aging and muscle wasting diseases.

column36: vCHAT-HF: a Virtual Community promoting Health literacy, self-cAre, and peer supporT for Heart Failure
column37: International heart health societies advocate lifestyle counseling for chronic heart failure (CHF) to improve quality of life and self-care behavior (exercise, diet, medications, smoke-free living), and to decrease medical events such as hospitalization, emergency department (ED) visits, and death. Current counseling programs require moderate-to-high contact between the health care team and patients, which is a barrier to delivering self-care counseling to the wider population of persons with CHF. This 2-year pilot trial will evaluate the clinical benefit and usability of a new program of digital counseling + social network support (vCHAT-HF). We will randomly assign 162 CHF patients to vCHAT-HF or to a Control group that receives conventional CHF self-care education through our website. All patients will be contacted bi-weekly by email over 12 months. The vCHAT-HF group will have unlimited home access to CHF self-care chat rooms, and they will be invited to join bi-weekly internet presentations by health professionals and patient representatives. Each presentation will have a 30-minute talk, 30-minute question-answer period, and 30 minutes for free discussion. We hypothesize that over 2 years vCHAT will reduce the combined risk of death, an ED visit, or hospitalization due to HF. We also hypothesize that the vCHAT group (vs. Control) will spend more time engaged with online self-care resources and that they'll have improved quality of life. This trial builds on our previous clinical trials for telehealth and digital counseling. It provides a novel program that promotes CHF self-care, quality of life, and heart health through the synergy of natural peer support that is informed by best evidence information. We will present our findings to key stakeholders (patients, researchers, health care professionals). These findings will be applied to support a Canada-wide trial to promote CHF self-care and quality of life, using this patient-centered approach.

column36: The Montfort Postnatal Care at Home Program: How do health outcomes, costs, patient and provider experiences compare with usual hospital-based postnatal care?
column37: Childbirth is the most common reason for hospitalization in Canada. Although most mothers and newborns are healthy, they stay in hospital for an average of two days after birth. A main purpose of the hospital stay is to assist mothers with breastfeeding and newborn care. However, exclusive breastfeeding rates remain very low and many mothers report not feeling adequately prepared to care for their newborns. Therefore, there is a need to improve postnatal care. Our team designed the Montfort Postnatal Care at Home Program (MPCHP) that aims to be more effective in supporting mothers, and at less cost than the usual care. The MPCHP gives low-risk mother-baby pairs the option of early hospital discharge (at 6-24 hours after childbirth) and midwifery care at home during the first postnatal week. In April 2018 we received funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to offer the MPCHP at Hopital Montfort in Ottawa, Ontario. Therefore, we have an important opportunity to study whether the MPCHP increases the quality of postnatal care, including improving health outcomes (e.g. exclusive breastfeeding, parental readiness to care for newborn) and reducing the health care system costs. We will collect and compare data between mothers in the MPCHP and those who receive the usual care. We will also conduct interviews with parents and health care providers to learn from their experiences with the MPCHP. This research will provide evidence regarding the quality of an innovative program that moves postnatal care for healthy mother-baby pairs from hospital to home and extends it over seven days after childbirth. Findings will be highly relevant to Ontario's Ministry of Health and Long- Term Care and other policy makers, administrators and clinicians across Canada who endeavor to provide the right care, in the right place at the right time.
