column36: Kaiso, Triple Negative Breast Cancer and Women of African Ancestry.
column37: Despite increased awareness, early detection and novel therapies in the past 20 years, breast cancer (BCa) remains the most common cause of female cancer deaths worldwide. Triple negative BCa (TNBC) is a very aggressive type of BCa that spreads rapidly to vital body organs and for which there are no specific treatments. Thus women diagnosed with TNBC are more likely to die than those diagnosed with other types of BCa. Notably, TNBC is most common in young Black women who although less likely to develop BCa, are more likely to die from BCa than Caucasian women. This difference in TNBC prevalence and mortality seems unrelated to socio-economic status and hints at unknown genetic factors or an ancestral genetic predisposition as the cause. Recently our lab found that a protein named Kaiso was highly expressed in TNBC tissues from Black women compared to Caucasian women, and these Black women with high Kaiso expression were less likely to survive. In mouse models of BCa, low Kaiso expression prevented the spread of TNBC cells to the lungs and liver, suggesting that Kaiso plays a role in the spread of BCa. To learn more about Kaiso's role in TNBC, we seek to determine how Kaiso promotes BCa spread and how Kaiso contributes to the racial difference in BCa outcomes. By clarifying Kaiso's role in TNBC features and outcomes, and identifying genetic differences in Black women, we will better understand TNBC and contribute to the development of better tests and therapies for TNBC. Our findings will help decrease the racial differences in BCa outcomes, and help millions of women diagnosed with TNBC worldwide regardless of ethnicity.

column36: Single turnover covalent chaperones for disease related lysosomal enzymes
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a worldwide health problem that has been linked to deficiencies in an enzyme called glucocerebrosidase (GCase). This enzyme plays a critical role in the body by breaking down a particular large molecule into two smaller, more easily metabolized components, a sugar (glucose) and a fat (ceramide). Without a properly functioning GCase, these large molecules are not recycled normally. Genetic mutations associated with GCase often result in an unstable enzyme structure that is easily damaged within the cell. In the case of PD, loss of function of this enzyme may contribute to disease progression. We plan to stabilize various enzyme's structure by using small molecular mimics of the sugar that form a bond to the enzyme. This event allows the enzyme to fold around our molecule. This can be thought of as using a mannequin to make a suit, once made the suit has a function that the cloth did not. However, one must be able to remove the mannequin for normal use of the suit. Our molecules were designed so that the bond to the enzyme breaks the resulting molecule doesn't properly fit the enzyme and so it departs. The analogy would be an inflatable mannequin that can be deflated to allow the suit to be used normally. This type of strategy has been tried before but with a major difference, the chemical mannequin does not change any of its interactions with the enzyme over time. Thus, it is often difficult for it to be removed (mannequin) efficiently from the enzyme (suit) to liberate free enzyme.

column36: Improving epilepsy surgery outcome by mapping high frequency oscillations.
column37: More than 54,000 Canadians have epilepsy with seizures that often occur daily and are poorly controlled by medication. In these cases, surgical removal of seizure generating tissue (which contains the critical seizure onset zone) is their best chance of seizure freedom and relief from psychiatric and cognitive problems associated with epilepsy. Currently, the clinical gold standard for identifying the seizure onset zone is EEG recordings during seizures. Unfortunately, the surgical success rate is <50%, mostly due to imprecise identification and removal of the seizure onset zone. We propose here a strategy to correct this. Mounting evidence indicates that high frequency oscillations (HFOs), detected between seizures using electrodes implanted into the brain (intracranial electrodes), better localizes the seizure onset zone than seizure recordings. However, intracranial EEG only samples a few brain areas. By combining intracranial EEG with functional MRI, which can measure responses across the entire brain, we have observed HFO-associated brain activity both at the conventionally measured seizure onset zone and in nearby regions. We propose that these additional regions are critical parts of the full seizure onset zone. As a result, we predict better surgical outcomes when they are also resected. We also postulate that the degree to which the seizure onset zone is connected to the rest of the brain (measured by functional MRI) predicts clinical outcome: fewer connections, better outcome. We will study 120 patients with uncontrolled epilepsy. We will determine if a better surgical cure rate is associated with i) the extent of surgical removal of the seizure onset zone as defined by intracranial EEG-functional MRI, and ii) fewer pre-operative functional connections of the seizure onset zone. Our study will offer an unprecedented ability to accurately identify the seizure onset zone and improve surgical and neurocognitive outcomes in persons with epilepsy.

column36: Life beyond vulnerability: Using developmental neuroscience to inform child health, life-course well-being and resilience to chronic disease
column37: Early life adversity, such as stress or malnutrition, exerts a sustained influence on health, increasing the risk for common diseases (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression). For this reason, we are unable to effectively identify high-risk children solely on the basis of environmental conditions. We aim to characterize children using several biological markers (genetics, salivary cytokine measures, brain function) that in concert with environmental exposures will define vulnerability in early life, when interventions are most effective. This integrative approach to the study of the developmental origins of common disorders will serve to more effectively identify high-risk children and thus contribute to improved intervention/prevention research designs. Such advances in 'Precision Pediatrics' would also enhance our ability to evaluate the efficacy of intervention programs by focusing exclusively on high-risk individuals. These same analyses will inform on the basis of resilience to early life adversity. This research has the objective of informing the best Canadian scenario for healthy growth and development, long-term well-being, and improved human capital.

column36: A behavioural and neural analysis of secondary fear triggers
column37: Tackling fear behaviourally and in the brain holds the key to developing successful clinical interventions for fear and anxiety-related disorders. One way to do this is through exposure therapy, that is, exposure to fear-eliciting cues or triggers with the aim of decoupling them from fear. This approach has been successful for some but many relapse or fail to respond at all. The key to providing a better treatment to sufferers from anxiety is to look beyond the standard approach of targeting primary triggers for fear, that is, triggers have a direct association with a traumatic or aversive event. Our proposal does this. We will understand how fear spreads across a memory network, how it links with cues were never part of the original traumatic memory, thereby proliferating secondary triggers with fear. The present proposal will utilize a multifaceted approach to examine the behavioural and neural profile of secondary fear. Specifically, we will establish how secondary triggers lose their fear eliciting properties, and whether these properties can be restored under specific conditions. We will also examine whether secondary triggers depend on the original fear memory for retrieval by tackling the integrity of the original fear memory behaviourally (through extinction) and neutrally (through deletion of function-specific cells). Finally, we will uncover the neural circuits that support fear triggered by secondary cues. Our ultimate goal is to provide the basic science platform of fear triggered by secondary cues which will serve as a springboard for the development novel behavioural and pharmacological routes for the treatment of fear- and anxiety-related disorders.

column36: The role of the cholinergic system in cognitive deficits in schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe mental health disorder that affects about 1% of the Canadian population. Cognitive problems, such as difficulties in remembering, focusing and planning, are among the most disabling symptoms of the illness. For instance, cognitive problems make it more difficult for individuals with schizophrenia to finish school and retain stable employment. Consequently, these symptoms cause most of the economic burden associated with schizophrenia. Yet, there are no medications to treat these symptoms. Development of drug treatments for cognitive deficits in schizophrenia has been hindered by the lack of understanding of the underlying neurobiology. The cholinergic system of the brain is important for normal cognitive abilities. Research has shown that, in dementias, a dysfunction of this system is related to impaired cognition. It has been proposed that dysfunctions in the cholinergic system would also underlie cognitive problems in schizophrenia. However, this hypothesis has not been tested. Therefore, the current study is designed to investigate if people with schizophrenia have a dysfunction in the cholinergic system of the brain. We will also test if this dysfunction is related to the degree of cognitive deficits in individuals with schizophrenia. This research will produce fundamental new knowledge about the neurobiology of schizophrenia. Ultimately, our findings will help design more effective treatments for cognitive deficits in people with schizophrenia.

First, we will look at whether patients had a higher or lower risk of prostate cancer when using GSK3Is and second, we will look at whether patients had a higher or lower risk of dying from the disease when using GSK3Is. If we find a protective effect from GSK3Is being used in treatment, we can design follow-up studies to determine which drugs work best and how to use them to improve patient care. If we find these drugs worsen prostate cancer, we could recommend the use of other drugs. In the event there is no effect, this would still be reassuring to those who take these drugs on a regular basis.

column37: Increased tissue stiffness has previously been implicated as an important driver of cancer metastasis in primary and secondary tumors. However, the biological mechanisms by which tissues stiffen during cancer progression remain unclear. Neutrophils have emerged as important elements of the immune system that regulate metastatic disease progression, and we have recently discovered that under cancer-related conditions, neutrophils spray out sticky molecular webs called 'extracellular traps' that can stiffen the surrounding tissue. In this work, we propose defining the interconnected relationships between neutrophils present in breast cancer-related conditions, their capacity to stiffen the surrounding tissue, and metastatic progression of the disease into the liver. Specifically, we will examine cancer-related neutrophil subpopulations to evaluate their distinct potential to stiffen tissues and promote metastasis. Furthermore, we propose proteomic-based strategies to understand how neutrophil extracellular traps induce mechanical stiffening of the tissue matrix; and anticipate that these experiments will provide us with strategies that reduce or eliminate immune-driven tissue stiffening. Finally, we believe that certain neutrophil subtypes are primed to produce extracellular traps by incorporating tumor-derived extracellular vesicles. We will therefore define the role of these circulating particles in promoting metastasis, which will ultimately provide prophylactic approaches to disrupt this pro-metastatic disease mechanism. Together, these studies will make fundamental and interdisciplinary advances in our understanding of metastatic disease progression, while providing insight into potential therapeutic avenues to target this process and reduce metastatic disease burden.

column36: Signaling mechanisms in axonal degeneration
column37: Nerve damage is a common adverse side-effect of cancer chemotherapy. Chemotherapy-induced neuropathy (CTIN) can cause severe pain and reduce ability to walk, write, button a shirt, or pick up coins. CTIN can last for weeks, months, or even years after treatment is done. Severe CTIN can cause more serious problems, including dangerous falls, changes in heart rate and blood pressure and trouble breathing. Despite the widespread incidence of CTIN, the specific mechanisms that cause it are not well understood and there are currently no treatments available to prevent or recover from CTIN. During development, more neurons are made than can be used and for the nervous system to function properly, excess neurons must be destroyed. The initial step in this process is the loss of neuronal axons which are destroyed through an active signaling process. The overarching hypothesis in this proposal is that chemotherapeutic agents destroy axons by activating the signaling processes that exist to destroy sensory axons during normal development. Our goals are identify the signaling processes that drive DRG axon destruction, and determine which of these are activated in CTIN.

column36: Precision Medicine for Myeloid Malignancies with 5-Azacitidine
column37: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are common and deadly blood cancers. MDS/AML develop from DNA mutations and abnormal regulation by DNA methylation. Changes to DNA methylation also can change the 3-dimensional (3D) structure of bundles of DNA (chromatin) through proteins such as the CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) protein. Another important factor affecting the survival of blood cancers is dysregulation of normal cell death programs, such as the B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) pathway. New drugs, such as one called venetoclax, can turn on this pathway and treat blood cancers. Many patients receive 5-azacitidine (5-aza) with or without novel drugs (e.g. venetoclax). 5-aza affects methylation, but only 60% respond. Our preliminary data suggests 5-aza resistance arises from the level of maturity (cell of origin) of the MDS/AML leukemia cell, rather than being associated with specific genetic mutations. We will confirm this is the case by examining DNA methylation on a single-cell level in specific sub-populations of cells to prove these cells are either more or less mature in 5-aza responders or non-responders. We will also prove these cells are different by directly assessing the 3D structure of their chromatin, which is unique to specific cells. We will then examine where the CTCF protein is in these cells, to show that it is mediating these changes. We will also develop and utilise an assay (pyrosequencing) for targeted measurement of DNA methylation in these cells that could potentially be used as a clinical biomarker. Finally, we will examine what role cell death pathways (BCL-2) play in the mechanism of action of 5-aza either as a single-agent or combined with venetoclax. Our findings, including biomarkers, will be poised for clinical translation. This could both prevent patients from getting chemotherapy that is ineffective by predicting whether they will respond, and pave the way for novel, rational 5-aza combination regimens.

column36: Precision-guided editing of the gut microbiota to protect against bacterial infections during critical illness.
column37: Our gut is home to trillions of microbes, called the microbiota, that engage in a symbiotic relationship with our body's immune system to maintain health. Disruption of the gut microbiota, or "dysbiosis," is linked to the development of immune system dysfunction and diseases, including susceptibility to infections. Nowhere is this more relevant than in the intensive care unit (ICU), where critically ill patients develop extreme dysbiosis of their gut microbiota, which is linked to the development of hospital-acquired infections. This represents a major clinical problem in the care of critically-ill patients, because hospital-acquired infections are unacceptably common (affecting up to 40% of patients), and exceedingly deadly in the ICU (20-25% mortality rate). The ability to therapeutically modify the gut microbiota holds great promise to reduce the burden of infections in the ICU, but we are currently limited by a lack of understanding about how the microbiota regulates immune function during critical illness. Therefore, we will directly address this problem by performing a comprehensive study to discover how dysbiosis of the gut microbiota induces immune dysfunction in critical illness. Our research will investigate this important clinical question in both critically-ill patients, as well as cutting-edge animal models with "designer microbiota." Furthermore, we will translate our findings into innovative treatment strategies that use precision-editing of the gut microbiota to correct dysbiosis-induced immune dysfunction to restore host defense against infections. Together, this research will advance our understanding of microbiota-immune interactions in critical illness, and deliver novel therapeutic innovations to combat the scourge of infection-related morbidity and mortality in the intensive care unit.

column37: Pericytes are cells that wrap around the smallest blood vessels known as capillaries. Recently, pericytes in the brain were shown to regulate blood flow and help maintain the blood-brain-barrier, the protective border that separates the brain from the blood. This suggests that pericytes are very important for conserving a healthy brain, but there is still much we do not know about these cells. My work uses advanced fluorescence microscopes and genetic tools to observe pericyte calcium signaling and blood flow in intact animal models. We will then build on our work in healthy brain tissue and follow the same pericytes and blood vessels through adulthood to old age. This will be compared to a mouse model of AD. My work is important because it will provide new knowledge of pericyte signaling and communication. We will also show how pericytes regulate blood flow or the blood brain barrier and how these change with aging or during AD. Our work may ultimately result in new therapies to target pericytes and slow the progression of aging or Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Mechanisms of opioid-induced respiratory depression
column37: Opioid medications are widely used in pain management, but present the side-effect of respiratory depression that can be lethal with overdose. Opioid drugs induce sedation, i.e. loss of consciousness, and considerably reduce breathing. When overdosed, opioids can shut down the nervous system, completely stop breathing, induce severe hypoxemia and patients may eventually die. The current epidemic of opioid overdoses is resulting in over 2,500 in Canada according to the Public Health Agency of Canada. Opioid drugs are responsible for thousands of emergency visits every year, causing a severe health and financial burden. Nevertheless, opioids remain the pharmacological cornerstone of modern pain therapy and there are currently no treatments to prevent respiratory depression by opioids without reducing their analgesic properties. The current opioid antagonist naloxone is very effective at blocking mu -opioid receptors, i.e. the receptors that mediate respiratory depression by opioid drugs, but it also blocks opioid analgesia so it cannot be used as a preventive treatment. The development of new therapies has been hindered by a lack of knowledge about how opioid medications alter brain activity and what mechanisms underlie respiratory depression by opioids. This research program proposes to identify the mechanisms underlying respiratory depression by opioids and to find new therapeutic solutions to prevent it. Without a preventive treatment to reduce the severity of respiratory depression, opioid medications will continue to present severe health issues and the death toll associated with opioid drugs will continue to rise.

column37: Glioblastoma (GB) is the most aggressive primary cancer in the adult brain. Two major cancer-causing proteins in GB are STAT3 and EGFRvIII. In order to identify new drug targets for GB, we aimed to better understand how EGFRvIII/STAT3 functions to promote GB growth. Here, we will establish the molecular details of LGALS1 regulation of GB and its therapeutic value for GB patients alone or in combination with present standards of care. These studies advance our understanding of GB pathogenesis and have the potential to lead to establishing a new approach for treatment of EGFRvIII subtype of GB.

column36: A Longitudinal Study of Correctional Services Canada Correctional Officers' Mental Health and Well-being: The Role of Prison Work and Prisons in Shaping Correctional Staff Health and Self over Time
column37: Correctional work is challenging, stressful, and can be traumatic, so researchers have tried to understand what makes a correctional officer (CO) more or less likely to develop mental health problems. To date, no researchers have considered if COs feel prepared for their job and the associated challenges that will arise at recruitment and during training. Or how their experiences on the job shape their mental health and well-being over time. With the support of Correctional Services Canada, the employer of federal COs, and their unions, we will first learn about correctional officer recruits (CORs) mental health status, coping skills, views, and experiences when they are first hired during their training. Next, we will follow these officers through deployment to the prison they will work in, and across their career for three years, doing qualitative and psychological interviews each year as well as surveys, to see if we can identify CORs that develop mental disorders or have poor well-being versus those who do not, and work toward preventing negative mental health outcome for all staff. We hope our study can help improve COR training and CO experiences; resulting in a healthier correctional service labour force. Our research team come from many backgrounds, this helps us use lots of tools to holistically understand staff mental health needs and experiences. We will conduct face-to-face interviews and clinical assessment interviews with at least 300 CORs/COs each year. The information will help us understand what CORs/COs need in their job, a job that leaves them exposed to potentially traumatic events and adversity. The proposed project also represents a central priority of the Public Safety Stakeholder Committee (PSSC) of the Canadian Institute of Public Safety Research and Treatment. Our study will help frame the needs of COs before and during their jobs in correctional services and generate training to support COs mental health resiliency.

column36: Autonomic Modulation Training: A Biological Approach to Building Resilience and Wellness Capacity Among Police Exposed to Post-Traumatic Stress Injuries (PTSI)
column37: Police officers are exposed to hazardous, disturbing events, resulting in severe stress and trauma. Accumulated stress results in physical and mental health conditions, of which post-traumatic-stress-injuries (PTSI) are central. PTSI is related to reduced occupational performance, absenteeism, and risky behavior, health problems, suffering, and even suicide (Austin-Ketch et al., 2012; Ruotsalainen, et al., 2015). Existing interventions to prevent and treat PTSI show limited clinical effectiveness (Carleton et al., 2018). Traditional interventions to build resilience or relieve symptoms of PTSI are focused on addressing cognitive, emotional and behavioural components without addressing underlying neurological and physiological mechanisms that erode resilience, maintain pathology, and cause symptoms to resurface following treatment (LeDoux & Pine, 2016; Minassian et al., 2015). The objectives of this proposal are to 1) reduce mental health symptoms of PTSI through a biopsychosocial intervention 2) to build wellness capacity (i.e., strengthen biological resilience) among police officers to manage accumulated stress and future exposures to trauma (Arpaia & Andersen, 2019; Andersen et al., 2018). 3) To examine how sex and gender are related to both baseline biological differences PTSI symptomatology and in response to the intervention. AMT is an 8 week intervention using real-time biological heart-rate-variability biofeedback (HRVB) to rewire physiological reflexes while individuals process current psychological and physical symptoms (Arpaia & Andersen, 2019; Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014). We will provide personalized, training and education, tailored for police officers, delivered using leading edge research tools and methods (interactive online engagement) and innovative technology (biometrics to assess changes in wellness and resilience). AMT training is compatible with learning management systems and can be distributed to all police services across Canada if effective.

column36: Exploring sex differences in the etiology of cancers: a critical look at endocrine disrupting agents (EDCs) in the workplace
column37: Colorectal, lung, breast and prostate cancers represent more than half of all cancers diagnoses and deaths among Canadians. Men are more likely to develop colorectal cancer and lung cancer than women. Different environmental, lifestyle and biologic factors may explain this risk difference. However, sex hormones, an obvious difference between men and women, have been shown to affect the development of various cancers. Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that interferes with the proper functioning of sex hormones. We are exposed to these chemicals in the environment and in diet; however, workers in certain sectors are highly exposed to endocrine disruptors. In this research program, we will examine whether exposure to endocrine disruptors in the workplace increases the risk of cancers. Three projects are proposed to use data collected as part of ongoing studies in Canada and abroad. In Project 1, we determine whether workers exposed to endocrine disruptors are at an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer and prostate cancer. Project 2 focuses specifically on breast cancer to examine whether workplace exposure to endocrine disruptors and genetic factors that predispose individuals to the effects of these chemicals may mutually increase risk. Finally, Project 3 undertakes a more mechanistic approach to relate workplace exposures to endocrine disruptors and sex hormone levels measured in the blood. Given that this research program is based on using existing data, this program offers a valuable opportunity to examine, in a short time frame and at low cost, whether endocrine disruptors play an important role in cancer risk.

column36: Sex and Asthma: Immunomodulatory mechanisms in airway inflammation
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic respiratory disease, resulting in lung inflammation and narrowing of airways making it difficult to breathe. Nearly 3 million Canadians suffer from asthma, and more than 10% of patients do not respond to available steroid therapies. These non-responders represent the major burden of asthma and account for annual healthcare costs of around $2B. Also, common steroid therapies can increase the risk of lung infections, which can make asthma worse. Adult females experience greater disease severity and are more likely to develop steroid-resistance, and thus are more likely to have uncontrolled asthma than males. These sex-related differences are largely ignored during drug development. New therapies are urgently needed that can alleviate steroid-unresponsive disease without compromising the ability to resolve infections. However, effective development of new treatments must consider the differences in disease and response to therapy between females and males. This study focuses on new molecules known as innate defence regulator (IDR) peptides, which can control both inflammation and infection. We have shown that IDR peptides improve breathing capacity in an animal model of asthma, and control cellular processes linked to steroid unresponsiveness. This project aims to develop IDR peptides as a new therapy for asthma, by examining the effects in both females and males concurrently. Our recent research has identified specific molecular differences following allergen exposure, which will be used to examine the biological effects of IDR peptides in females and males, in animal models of asthma and in human lung cells. This research will directly support the development of a new IDR peptide-based therapy for asthma, by taking into consideration how the treatment affects females and males. It is entirely possible that we will need to develop sex-specific treatment protocols to provide the most efficient care for asthma sufferers.

column36: Negotiating Care and Navigating Health Services: The Experiences of Community-dwelling People Living with Dementia and their Family Caregivers
column37: Gender is widely recognized as a key factor in the experience of living with dementia and caring for a person living with dementia. With the rising number of people living with dementia, accompanied by growing demands on family caregivers, it is timely and important to focus greater attention on examining gender in the context of these experiences. Most people with dementia understandably have a desire to live in their homes until the end of their lives. However, this desire requires a myriad of supports - in the form of health and social care services, as well as family caregiver support. Examples of health and social care services includes: adult day programs, home care, and respite, as well as primary care, emergency department visits, and hospitalizations. As dementia progresses, the need for health and social care and family caregiving becomes more complex. To date, there has been limited attention to the role of gender in shaping these experiences. In this program of research, I will examine the gendered experience of people with living with moderate-to-advanced dementia and their family caregivers as they negotiate care (e.g. decision-making, allocation of care work) and navigate services in the community. This program of research will generate new knowledge about the complex journey of people living with dementia and their family caregivers, including how men, women, and gender diverse individuals experience this journey in similar or different ways. Knowledge translation activities will focus on sharing findings with policy/decision-makers, healthcare planners and providers, and, importantly, people living with dementia and their family caregivers to improve the processes of negotiating care and navigating health and social care in the community.

column36: Developing a Patient-Reported Outcome Measure for Children and Youth Seeking Gender-Affirming Health Care (GENDER-Q Kids)
column37: Children and youth who are gender-affirming are increasingly seeking acces to transgender health services. Hormone blockers, gender-affirming hormones and transgender surgery can help pediatric patients reduce gender dysphoria. A critical barrier to measuring outcomes for such gender-affirming healthcare is the lack of a patient reported outcome measure (PROM). This Chair Award would be used to cover the development of a PROM for gender-affirming treatment for children and youth. This new PROM (GENDER-Q Kids) will provide a comprehensive set of independently functioning scales that cover concepts such as appearance and health-related quality of life for children aged as young as 8 years. Phase 1 consists of an qualitative study to elicit information about outcomes important to patients. From the analysis, a conceptual framework will be formally defined that covers outcomes of importance. We will also create a pool of items that will inform the development of scales. Scales will be refined through cognitive patient interviews and expert input. In Phase 2, preliminary scales will be administered to a large international sample of children and youth. The modern psychometric method of Rasch analysis will be used to shorten and define the measurement properties for each scale. At this stage the GENDER-Q Kids will be ready for use and made available to researchers, providers, administrators and payers to collect meaningful, valid and reliable data on important patient-centered outcomes.

column36: Discovery of genes and mechanisms underlying sex differences in insulin pathway function using Drosophila as a model
column37: Millions of Canadians suffer from diseases linked with abnormal insulin pathway function (e.g. type 2 diabetes). One important risk factor for diseases caused by abnormal insulin pathway function is whether you are a man or a woman: men have a higher risk of developing diseases such as type 2 diabetes. While scientists know the insulin pathway is different in men and women, and that these differences are one reason men have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, we know very few genes that cause insulin pathway differences in men and women due to the widespread neglect of female animals in research. Since the number of Canadians suffering from insulin-associated diseases like type 2 diabetes is rising rapidly, finding genes that control the insulin pathway in each sex will lead to better therapies for insulin-associated diseases. In my lab, we use the fruit fly as an innovative model to find genes that control the insulin pathway in males and females. Flies have two sexes, like humans, and all the genes in the human insulin pathway are also found in flies. In fact, many important discoveries about how the insulin pathway works have been made in flies. Our study will use flies to find all the genes that control insulin pathway function in each sex - this large-scale genetic analysis is not feasible in mice or humans. These genes will guide pre-clinical and clinical studies in finding new treatments to correct abnormal insulin pathway function in each sex. By completing these studies, we will also build capacity in Canada to study the insulin pathway in male and female animals. This involves training the next generation of researchers studying the insulin pathway in both sexes by providing funding for students, by promoting awareness of sex differences in the insulin pathway by presenting at conferences and public events, and by forming strategic partnerships to enhance funding in this critical area.

column37: La programmation de cette Chaire vise a mieux comprendre l'influence du sexe et du genre sur les trajectoires d'usage de substances psychoactives (SPA) et risques associees en vue d'ameliorer des interventions, programmes et politiques de sante tout au long du continuum de services (intervention precoce, reduction des mefaits, traitement specialise). Guide par un cadre theorique de promotion de la sante basee sur le genre (Pederson et al., 2014), le programme de recherche s'interesse aux individus qui qui s'identifient comme hommes ou femmes (cis ou trans) ou autrement (ex. non-binaire, queer), au-dela du sexe qui leur a ete attribue a la naissance. L'influence du sexe et du genre sur les dependances est encore peu documentee, les programmes et services en ce domaine qui sont deployes etant largement peu adaptes aux enjeux de genre, contribuant a maintenir ou meme accentuer certaines iniquites. Le besoin de recherche et de mobilisation pour augmenter les connaissances en matiere du sexe et du genre et les appliquer aux interventions afin de reduire les iniquites et ameliorer les resultats de sante de tous les sous-groupes touches par des problematiques de dependance est a l'origine de ce projet. Cette programmation repose sur d'etroits partenariats entre chercheurs et decideurs du systeme de sante afin de guider l'amelioration de pratiques en continu, processus guide par des recherches basees sur des devis participatifs. Une amelioration et une meilleure integration des pratiques et services en dependance adaptes au sexe et au genre et a la diversite sexuelle et de genre pourraient combler des manques d'equite en matiere d'acces aux soins et augmenter l'efficacite et l'adequation des services et du systeme de sante. Ultimement, le projet pourrait contribuer a prevenir l'aggravation et a reduire les consequences associees aux dependances et ameliorer la qualite de vie et les resultats de sante des personnes ayant une consommation de SPA a risque ou problematique.

column36: Investigating the effects of sex and gonadal function on immunity and the sex disparity in multiple sclerosis incidence and progression
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of MS in the world. At present, it is not possible to reverse the neuron damage in MS. Therefore, the best chance of curing this disease is to prevent it from starting in the first place. Thus understanding the risk factors for development of MS and the biology of how these risk factors initiate the disease process is an important area of research. Age of puberty has an impact on one's risk of getting MS. This is surprising since most MS patients do not experience their first clinical attack until aged 30. This suggests that there is a large disconnect between when the disease may get started and when it manifests into a clinical entity. Because of this, animal models of MS are critical to understanding and modeling how puberty and other factors including sex impact the initiation of this disease. The first goal of this Chair is to understand how puberty or ovarian function enhances immunity and initiation and autoimmunity. Being female is another MS risk factor. Women outnumber men with MS by 3-fold, and we still do not understand why this is the case. This higher female to male sex ratio in MS emerges with puberty, indicating that sex hormones produced by the gonads are responsible for the sex difference in MS incidence. A second goal of this Chair is to better understand the nuts and bolts of why the immune response is more vigorous in females through studies in an animal model of MS. We are pursuing the novel hypothesis that females are more prone to develop MS because they have more T cells that can recognize the myelin sheath. The final goal of this Chair is to explore how immune cells are different in men and women with established MS. This will be important to understanding another enigma in this disease, that men who develop MS are more prone to more disease progression. Altogether this research program has the high potential to increase our understanding of the role of sex and gender on the immune system and MS.

column36: Advancing Gender-Transformative Sexual Health Policy and Practice
column37: Gender transformative sexual health care for youth (15-29 years) remains a pressing issue across Canada. In BC, rates of STIs, sexual violence, and unplanned pregnancies among youth remain alarmingly high, and represent a marker of a range of gender and social inequities and gaps in effective sexual health care. However our understanding of gender-transformative policies and practices that promote or mitigate youth's engagement in sexual health care, and experiences in interacting with sexual health providers remain largely absent. Despite increasing attention to sexual health and calls to move away from a solely individual-level and risk/ deficit-based models both in Canada and globally, there is a surprising dearth of research on gender and intersecting socio-structural factors shaping access and uptake of sexual health care in Canada, or efforts to document and evaluate gender transformative interventions both within and outside health sector on reducting or promoting sexual health inequities. To address these gaps, the Sex and Gender Science Chair in Advancing Gender Transformative Sexual Health Policy & Practice will undertake participatory program of research, integrated knowledge translation and exchange (iKTE), and capacity-building to: 1.Develop novel methodologies, theories, and tools to advance research on gender transformative sexual health policy and practice; 2.Develop novel and integrated KTE strategies to promote gender-transformative sexual health policy and practice; and 3.Foster training and mentorship opportunities for sexual health practitioners, policy makers, researchers, and youth.

column36: Epidemiological Methods in Sex- and Gender-Based Analysis Plus (SGBA+): Advancing Intersectional Approaches to Sex and Gender Science
column37: Epidemiologists design and conduct quantitative studies that measure health outcomes and use complex statistics for analysis. The overarching goal of the proposed program is to strengthen the methods that epidemiologists and other researchers use to study health, by better incorporating a sex- and gender-based analysis plus (SGBA+) approach. SGBA+ means we always consider not just sex/gender differences in health or the factors that promote or hinder good health, but that we do two additional things: 1) clearly incorporate diversity of biological sex characteristics and social gender characteristics that can affect health through very different pathways (the "SG" part of SGBA+), and 2) use methods that allow for sex and gender to have different effects or impacts among groups of people of varying identities or social positions, e.g., ages, socioeconomic statuses, ethnoracial backgrounds, sexual orientations (the "+" part of SGBA+). As researchers, we have not been very good at doing these two things in our work. The proposed program of research and knowledge translation provides vital information that researchers need to improve their capacity for SGBA+, including: 1) understanding dimensions of sex or gender and their perform as substitutes (proxies) for the dimension(s) researchers believe are most relevant for particular health issues; 2) identifying the statistical methods currently used in intersectional research, how well they reflect intersectionality theoretical frameworks, and how best practices might be applied in Canadian data. This research will inform development of academic research papers, an Online SGBA+ Methods Toolkit, SGBA+ Methods Workshops at conferences. It will also inform curriculum for a Summer Training Intensive in Intersectionality Research in conjunction with the recently-chartered Intersectionality Training Institute in Washington DC. Together, these research and training initiatives serve to build capacity for SGBA+ in epidemiology.

column36: Focusing on Sex and Gender in Neurodevelopmental Disorders
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), characterized by early-onset atypical behaviour and brain development, are relatively common and constitute a critical, but often overlooked, developmental background that affects health and wellbeing. NDD have a male-predominant prevalence. The accumulated male-focused research to date, particularly due to male-bias lens and sex/gender-ignorance, has led to ungrounded assumptions that findings about NDD learned from a male-sex-lens can be generalized to people of all sexes and genders. To mitigate these sex and gender biases, this Chair program will establish an integrated clinical-research program that clarifies how sex and gender affect and intersect with the most common NDD (i.e. autism, ADHD, intellectual disability, genetic syndromes). The research will unveil sex and gender related subtleties of behavioural presentations of NDD to aid clinical recognition (by an innovative research approach working with individuals with "subthreshold" NDD), and explore the brain and cognitive mechanisms of the "female-protective effect" of NDD (by utilizing three innovative designs studying subthreshold individuals, infants carrying risk genes for NDD, and families with multiple members with autism). The program will support next generation health researchers and clinicians by bringing sex and gender science perspectives and methodologies into NDD research and practice. The knowledge translation activities will improve sex- and gender-sensitive assessment and care for individuals with NDD, especially girls, women, and gender-diverse individuals, who have been underserved in the past, and even currently. The ultimate goal is to achieve and ensure sex and gender equity across all domains of research and clinical practice related to NDD.

column36: LGBTQI2S Wellness and Resilience
column37: This CIHR Chair on LGBTQI2S Wellness and Resilience aims to study stress biology, mental health, and resilience of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ+) people across adulthood. To better understand how stigma makes us sick, we will measure a comprehensive index of chronic stress called allostatic load. Allostatic load indexes hormonal, immune, metabolic, and cardiovascular health. Previous work by our group has pioneered the study of allostatic load among the LGBTQ+ community and found very mixed findings that point to distinct risk and resilience profiles. We expect that lifelong stigma exposure contributes to unique patterns of allostatic load and mental health among LGBTQ+ sub-groups, but also unique resilience buffers like health behaviours and social support. This Chair will allow us to identify modifiable resilience factors. First, we leverage existing data collected from a past study that recruited 217 heterosexual and cisgender people - that is, people whose gender identity matches with their birth-assigned sex. This Chair will recruit 480 LGBTQ+ new people to provide comparison of allostatic load to that of heterosexual/cisgender people of different ages. Next, we will identify individual differences that boost or buffer the negative effects of stigma on allostatic load and mental health. Lastly, changes in risk and resilience pathways among LGBTQ+ sub-groups (e.g., older, transgender) will be explored in a 2-year follow-up of 120 younger LGBTQ+ participants. In our knowledge translation plan, we will adapt Collaborator Isabelle Ouellet-Morin's +Fort (C) mobile app designed to fight victimization. The new app will be piloted by LGBTQ+ participants ages 18-25 to create an LGBTQ+ version called +Fier in French or +Proud in English. Studying LGBTQ+ health provides better understanding of stress mechanisms. This can help us unravel the ways in which stigma 'gets under the skin and skull' of Canadians from diverse minority populations.

column36: Studying Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Fatigue in a Semi-Naturalistic Environment in the Mouse
column37: A large literature in mice and rats documents the existence of sex differences in pain, which parallels known sex differences in humans. The existing animal studies are flawed, however, in a number of ways, and especially because of the practical realities of behavioural testing in animals. In pain experiments--like those in other fields--animals are removed from their home cages for testing, often for the first time ever, and thus experience very high levels of stress, which is well known to affect pain. To avoid this problem, we will house and test mice within a semi-naturalistic enclosure (an Eco-HAB), in which their position is automatically recorded and video cameras capture behaviours without any direct experimenter involvement. This setup will be used to test a number of hypotheses regarding sex differences in pain, including: 1) the frequency and duration of chronic pain behaviours in male and female mice, 2) the social impact of chronic pain in male and female mice, 3) pain-related huddling and allogrooming in mice of both sexes lacking a newly found type of sensory fiber mediating rewarding touch, and 4) the effect of chronic pain on lifespan in male and female mice. The data to be collected may have broad impact not only on our understanding of sex differences in pain and fatigue, but on preclinical research more generally.

column36: Sex differences in the effect of age on episodic memory-related brain function across the adult lifespan
column37: Memory for our past experiences (episodic memory) declines in healthy aging. Age-related episodic memory decline negatively impacts older adult's quality of life and can be an early sign of Alzheimer's disease. Studies show that women are more at risk of developing AD, compared to men. This suggests that there may be sex differences in how ageing effects memory and brain function. Using functional MRI, we have found that age-related memory decline starts at midlife and worsens with age. It is related to deficits in a distributed set of brain regions, including the right lateral prefrontal cortex, ventral occipito-temporal cortices and the medial temporal cortex. We also found that the aging brain attempts to compensate for these deficits by activating left fronto-parietal cortices during memory encoding, and that this may be a marker of successful neural compensation in the aging brain. In our recent preliminary analysis of sex differences, we found that women and men show different detrimental patterns of brain aging. Intriguingly, we also found that left fronto-parietal compensation was only observed in women with increasing age. This provides preliminary support that there are sex differences in memory-related brain function. We will expand upon these findings in the current brain imaging study. We will test healthy women and men aged 21 - 75 yrs of age to investigate if there are sex differences in neural compensation, and whether neural compensatory responses generalize across memory tasks and stimulus types in women and men. This will provide evidence that there may be consistent patterns of brain decline and compensation in women, compared to men, across a variety of memory tasks. Such information can be leveraged to develop precise, sex-specific neurocognitive therapies to support successful aging in both women and men.

column36: Sex-differences in placental and fetal development
column37: Many differences between males and females arise between conception and birth. As the main regulator of fetal growth and development is the placenta, many of these differences arise because male and female placentas are not equivalent. Male and female placentas differ in their sex chromosome complement, XX vs XY; This leads to sex-chromosome gene expression differences that cause downstream effects on the remainder of the genome. The degree to which male and female placentas differ from each other can also be affected by exposures to fetal and maternal androgens and by genetic variation affecting the expression of key hormones. As such, the effects of sex on the non-sex chromosomes is not discrete, but exists on more of a continuum. Data from DNA methylation, a chemical modification to DNA that is associated with gene expression, has been collected on over 1000 placentas. Our goal is to identify sex-influenced DNA methylation within the placenta, identify the factors that affect this measurement, link this to functional changes in gene expression and determine if the sexual differentiation of the placenta is associated with perinatal outcomes, such and fetal birth weight and gestational age at birth. Ultimately this data could be linked to longer term outcomes in neonates, infants and children. This work is important to understand the early events that set males and females on different health trajectories.

column36: CD4 T cell-mediated roles in protective immune responses during viral myocarditis
column37: Heart failure and cardiomyopathy are diseases that cause great mortality in Canada. These are caused by a progressive worsening of heart function, due to several causes that are not always well understood. Virus infection is thought to be a major cause of heart disease development. Virus infections of the heart are not too uncommon among the population, as they are often confused by a simple viral process, such as a cold. However, in some individuals infections of the heart can be much severe and cause hospitalization. Whether a person has had a heart infection with clears signs or not, there exists an important chance that they will slowly progress to heart disease. The reason for that is unknown. In some cases, the damage caused by the virus is too big for the heart to adapt and keep functioning well. In other cases, the virus cannot be completely removed and causes the immune system to keep fighting it in the heart, causing important collateral damage. Finally, sometimes, a virus infection of the heart is accompanied by the wrongful activation of protective cells of the body that learn to attack the heart instead of the virus. In the studies proposed here, we will investigate the functions of a specific subset of protective cells, referred to as CD4 T cells because they express a protein called CD4. These CD4 T cells are the major designers of the fights against infections, by deciding which other defensive cells and mechanisms will be used to fight. Unfortunately, we know very little of how these cells behave during viral infection of the heart and what determines a good strategy against the virus. We believe that studying these cells we can better understand why some people are unable to beat the virus and limit heart injury, which otherwise can lead to a lethal heart disease.

column36: Understanding Sex and Gender Influences on Self-Management Practices of Indigenous Men, Women and Two-Spirited Individuals Living with Type 2 Diabetes: A Strengths-Based, Patient-Oriented Approach.
column37: Indigenous Peoples have a much higher rate of type 2 diabetes compared to non-Indigenous Peoples. Of interest, more non-Indigenous men have type 2 diabetes compared to non-Indigenous women. However, this is different in Indigenous People where more Indigenous women have type 2 diabetes compared to Indigenous men. Reasons for this difference is unclear. This program of research will use a patient-oriented, strength-based approach to learn how sex and gender influence the self-management of type 2 diabetes in Indigenous men, women and two-spirited (2S) people. We have collaborated with patients and community partners to identify research priorities and outcomes, ways to collect/analyze/interpret data, disseminate results, and integrate our results into practice. Our program of research consists of 3 phases: Phases 1a, b and c. Phase 1a is a scoping review and has already been completed in Year 1 of the NPA's PhD studies. Differences between western and traditional Indigenous worldviews of the self-management of T2DM were found, and although studies collected data on sex and/or gender, these terms were often used interchangeably. Also, there was only one study that included 2S people. Phase 1b will be a secondary data analysis of the Regional Health Survey conducted by the First Nations Information Governance Centre in 2015. This secondary data analysis will help us learn how sex and gender influence the self-management practices of Indigenous Peoples living with T2DM in Northern Ontario. We will use a strength-based approach in Phase 1c to explore type 2 diabetes self-management experiences of Indigenous men, women and two-spirited people using storytelling and a gender-based lens. We will collaborate with Indigenous artists to make patient journey maps to visualize the lived experiences of Indigenous People living with T2DM. Gender will be included into the journey maps and a separate journey map will be made for men, women and 2S people.

column36: Community health workers and cultural safety training in tuberculosis prevention & care in Nunavik: a patient-oriented, participatory research program
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is a public health crisis among Inuit in Canada. The Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK) and the Canadian government are committed to eliminating TB by 2030 and have laid out Inuit-specific priority actions, one of which is to strengthen TB care and prevention capacity. This proposed research, which is co-led by the Nunavik Regional Board of Health & Social Services (NRBHSS), contributes to that priority action. The overarching goal is to develop, implement and evaluate an Inuit-specific community health worker pilot program in TB, and a video-based training programme on cultural safety for all health care workers in TB prevention and care, in the communities of Salluit and Kangiqsualujjuaq, Nunavik. The specific research objectives are to: 1) Understand patient, community, and health care provider perspectives on TB and TB-related care needs and priorities, including on issues of cultural competency and cultural safety; 2) Produce and evaluate a video-based training module on cultural safety for TB health care providers; and 3) Identify and evaluate community and patient-oriented outcomes for a pilot local CHW training program. This research is a collaborative effort between non-Inuit and Inuit researchers and community leaders, and follows a Two-eyed Seeing approach, which can be understood as the synthesis of Indigenous ways of knowing with non-Indigenous methodologies and participatory action research. The output of this research includes Inuit-specific training programs for CHW and health care workers in TB in Nunavik, and local research and health capacity development.

column36: Healing practices and paradigms: a study of Indigenous and biomedical healthcare at Yellowknife's Stanton Territorial Hospital
column37: To improve the quality of care for Indigenous patients, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) has called for greater collaboration between Indigenous and biomedical healing practices. In the Northwest Territories (NWT), where over 50% of residents are First Nations, Inuit and Metis, the need is particularly great. My PhD research builds on a project I conducted with the Stanton Territorial Hospital Elders Council in Yellowknife, NWT. During our work together, the Elders emphasized that Indigenous and biomedical health services may be understood and experienced differently by patients and health providers and that these different understandings can greatly impact the quality of hospital care. Using an Indigenous storytelling methodology that is grounded in two-eyed seeing and postcolonial theory, my research asks: How do Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients, health providers and traditional healers experience and understand Indigenous and biomedical healing practices at Stanton Territorial Hospital? This project will (1) describe participants' stories and experiences of hospital care and the extent to which their stories and experiences are shaped by their understandings of Indigenous and biomedical healing practices; (2) illuminate the extent to which colonial practices and representations shape participant experiences of hospital care; and (3) provide clear recommendations to improve patient care experiences at Stanton Hospital. This project has been created in partnership with Elders, patients, community leaders and health authority officials and will be guided throughout by a Community Advisory Committee to ensure that the project is patient-oriented and abides by ethical practices and community protocols. Ultimately, this research seeks to address the TRC's calls for action and improve health services for Indigenous patients in the NWT by providing clear direction on how to enhance Indigenous and biomedical health service provision at Stanton Hospital.

column36: Decolonizing childbirth with Nunavik Inuit women transferred to high-risk hospitals for childbirth: a co-designed pilot intervention
column37: BACKGROUND Inuit women in Canada carry a disproportionate burden of poor health, with higher rates of maternal mortality and negative birth outcomes. Some 14% of Inuit women in Nunavik (Inuit territory in Quebec) travel to tertiary southern hospitals for specialized obstetric care (a process known as fly-out births). Fly-out births are linked to adverse health outcomes for Inuit women, their families and communities. This participatory research supports culturally safe Inuit childbirth, and will co-design pilot interventions with Inuit stakeholders and their care providers, to inform the decolonization of obstetric care in Quebec tertiary hospitals. METHODS The study engages Nunavik-based Inuit women, their families and community members, as well as perinatal healthcare providers and policy makers in Nunavik and Montreal. With each group, a series of group fuzzy cognitive mapping sessions will explore experiences with fly-out childbirth and perspectives of decolonization in obstetric care. Individual and household questionnaires will document the frequency of these findings. Stakeholders will co-design an intervention through deliberative dialogue and community meetings. Recommendations will be shared with obstetrical staff of a Montreal tertiary hospital. A follow-up survey will measure quantitative changes in birth outcomes, patient satisfaction, and decolonizing care practices. An integrated knowledge translation and exchange strategy engages stakeholders in cognitive mapping sessions, and co-design interventions in deliberative dialogue. DISCUSSION Evacuation for childbirth aims to reduce health disparities faced by Inuit women, yet it is inadvertently associated with adverse health outcomes. Affirming Inuit values of childbirth and engaging Inuit voices in service delivery improvement can support culturally safe care. The protocol and instruments developed may have wider relevance for rural Inuit across Canada.

column36: Identity as Visibility: gathering knowledge around the collection of racial and ethnic identifiers from the perspectives of Indigenous patients and health data collectors in Manitoba.
column37: Within Canada, significant information gaps exist regarding the collection of racial and ethnic identifiers within the healthcare system leaving a large data void around the collection of Indigenous identity information. This creates barriers to understanding health and healthcare issues among Indigenous peoples and impacts the ability to achieve health equity for Indigenous populations by preventing the analysis of critical health data related to race-based health disparities and outcomes. The collection of racial and ethnic identifiers through systemic and mandatory policy and practice will result in a first attempt to make visible racism and racial discrimination in the healthcare system. While the collection of this data holds importance for western-based research driven by large data sets, an equally important and more meaningful outcome for Indigenous peoples is also possible. That is, a return of personal and collective agency within healthcare, along with an ability to gain control over what happens regarding health and healthcare; an act of resistance by disrupting ongoing silencing and marginalization with health care and systems. The inclusion of Indigenous perspectives is a critical initial step to inform the larger implementation plan. As well, success will require understanding the perspectives of those collecting the data within the system. Therefore, in this study for my doctoral dissertation research, using Indigenous methodologies, I will gather knowledge of the perspectives and understandings from both Indigenous patients and those who will be collecting the data within healthcare systems. This baseline data will inform the larger implementation project within the Manitoba healthcare system by addressing the gap in knowledge around Indigenous patient and data collector perspective and understanding around the collection of racial and ethnic identifiers, how to do this work better/differently, and the desired outcomes of this policy and practice.

column36: Sex, Drugs & Chronic Pain after Pelvic Organ Prolapse Surgery: investigating patient and clinician priorities related to pelvic floor surgery in Canada
column37: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a medical condition in females where pelvic organs, such as the uterus or intestines, fall out of normal position and press into the vagina. column37: The current Problem: The incidence of keratinocyte carcinoma (cutaneous basal and squamous cell carcinoma) is increasing and the estimated patient care and economic burden of the disease is significant. Capturing keratinocytes carcinoma is not mandated by most cancer registry associations including the Canadian Association of Cancer Agencies. As a result, keratinocyte carcinomas are not part of most cancer registries in Canada, including the Ontario Cancer Registry. With an estimated 40,000-keratinocyte carcinoma cases in Ontario per year, the standard approach to capturing cancer cases using manual review by cancer registrars is not feasible. Therefore, alternative methods are needed. Objectives: Develop and implement a robust, sustainable methodology to identify and characterize keratinocyte carcinomas from electronic pathology reports obtained from Ontario's public and private laboratories in near real-time. 1. Create a population-based data repository of keratinocyte carcinomas for analytics and reporting of incidence, health services utilization, and outcomes in Ontario to enable sustainable disease surveillance, patient care, system planning, quality improvement, and performance management, as well as evaluation and research. Methods: The pathology reports we require to identify keratinocyte carcinomas typically consist of unstructured blocks of narrative text. Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a process by which a computer converts a string of text into analytic data. We will use an iterative approach to develop a methodology based on NLP and other data science techniques to create case-finding algorithms to capture cases of suspected keratinocyte carcinomas (develop > test > refine > test). Once cases are ascertained, an analysis-ready data repository will be created and linked to other databases held at CCO to enrich the data with patient demographic information, health service utilization, outcomes, as well as relevant pathology information (e.g. histology and behaviour) obtained using NLP. Using this cohort, we will address the current information gap on skin cancers by building a comprehensive knowledge base on keratinocyte carcinoma. We will assess whether sociodemographic characteristics, geography, and clinical factors are associated with incidence, health care utilization along the care continuum, and patient outcomes using Poisson regression, logistic regression, and Cox proportional hazards regression, and other statistical methods where appropriate. Anticipated knowledge translation activities will include disseminating methods and analytic results to researchers, healthcare providers, government (e.g. health and labour ministries), clinical and population health programs, and the general public through openaccess academic journals, conference presentations, cancer prevention messaging, and other media. Significance of the research: The development of a keratinocyte carcinoma data repository will fill a significant knowledge gap in the Ontario and broader Canadian cancer system. The results from our analyses will enable data-informed decision-making and guide the identification and prioritization of future initiatives in health care quality planning, improvement, and performance management. We anticipate health care providers and provincial, national, and international policy makers to be the key audiences for this new knowledge and expect an impact on clinical decision-making and policy development. The data repository will also be available to health services researchers who have an interest in keratinocyte carcinoma. In the future, we anticipate that we and others will be able to extend the approach to capture other diseases requiring a pathology diagnosis, including but not limited to cancer, to enable broader health monitoring. Furthermore, our NLP methodology could be leveraged to automate the extraction of data from other narrative texts, such as radiology and surgical reports.

column37: Impaired cardiovascular health is predictive of cognitive impairment as a consequence of cerebrovascular defects. Despite being a high medical need, assessment of cerebrovascular health is inexistant in general pratice. The retinal microcirculation in the eye, however, offers a window to the brain to acquire both structural and functional parameters. Dysfunctions of small blood vessels preceeds symptomatic cardiovascular vascular diseases. Retinal microvascular function has been shown to be impaired with increasing age and sedentariness, and in patients with glaucoma (group of eye conditions that damage the optic nerve) as well as vascular and metabolic diseases. Importantly, retinal vascular function can be improved by physical exercise in patients with risk factors for cardiovascular diseases, suggesting that monitoring the capacity of retinal blood vessels to dilate could permit identifying patients at risk of developping cognitive (learning and memory) impairment of vascular origin and perform follow-up efficacy studies. In this project we will explore the potential of state-of-the art retinal imaging to detect and monitor microvascular dysfunction, and its association with cognitive decline (Aims 1 and 2). To better understand the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms and identify novel therapeutic targets, we will study the role of vascular aging, vascular permeability and vascular cells function as determinant of microvascular dysfunction (Aim 3). The overarching goal of this project is to develop a reliable and standardized method to assess retinal vascular function as a biomarker of cerebrovascular health. This simple ocular exam would enable timely interventions aiming at preventing vascular-related neurodegeneration.

column37: Recently, our 24-hour culture has been identified as a factor that can cause type 2 diabetes. Technological and societal advances such as electric lighting and digital screens, shift work, time zone transfers, and round-the-clock food availability disrupt our intrinsic and evolutionarily preserved 24-hour rhythms resulting in a desynchronization between light cues and behavior cues to our circadian system. The proposed Dutch-Canadian research consortium objectives are to elucidate the mechanisms and the impact of differentially timed life style throughout the 24-hour period on the development of type 2 diabetes to develop more effective interventions to prevent this disease. The proposed consortium will regroup some of the world best experts in integrative physiology, epidemiology, lifestyle interventions, patient engagement, and scientific networking to optimize interventions based on circadian metabolic rhythmicity to prevent type 2 diabetes, train the future generation of health researchers in the field, and develop patient partners' engagement at the international level.

column37: Hypertension is widely recognized as one of the most impacting risk factors for cognitive impairment. While epidemiological associations strengthened this observation during years, mechanistic investigations that may unravel the pathophysiological basis of this detrimental relationship are just at dawn. In the last years, we became aware that immune system participates to onset of hypertension and related target organ damage. Several studies demonstrated that various players of innate and adaptive immunity shape the effect induced by hypertension in target organs. Despite protected by a unique vascular system, the brain is not an exception, suggesting that the crosstalk between peripheral and resident immune components may play a decisive role in the evolution of cognitive impairment in hypertension. The complexity of vascular and immune interactions in the brain are further enriched by cells lining the vasculature, like pericytes, and the neuronal network itself. Here we have combined the complementary expertise of our groups to investigate the cerebrovascular-immune interface in experimental hypertension, with unprecedented details. Transgenic animal models, advanced in vivo imaging, fate mapping studies and an innovative experimental system to reproduce and study ex vivo the interface established by immune and vascular cells in the cerebrovascular system will be merged in our ImmuneHypertCog Strategy. In the end, we conceived a translational aim dedicated to investigating the correlation between the immune landscape and early markers of brain damage at MRI in patients.

column36: Optimizing the Ageing Brain? Situating Ethical Aspects of Dementia Prevention (BEAD)
column37: Background: Dementia (the most common form is Alzheimer's disease) has for a long time been conceived of as an unpreventable process of mental deterioration. Now, however, researchers claim that one out of three dementia cases can be prevented if at least nine risk factors are man-aged. These risk factors include some that have not been traditionally linked to Alzheimer's, such as diabetes, hypertension, social isolation, and hearing loss, and which require management over the life course, making prevention a lifelong endeavor. Early detection through biomarkers and digital tracking technologies have also become a central feature of what we call 'the new dementia'. This raises a number of ethical questions, such as: should individuals be considered personal-ly responsible for their own dementia prevention? Should we accept extensive monitoring of our cognitive functions through digital technologies? What does dementia prevention entail for our healthcare systems and cultures of care? And, do national or local contexts play a role in how prevention is articulated and lived? Objectives: We propose a research project that studies in three countries the way the 'new de-mentia' is being articulated, and asks what ethical problems are arising, what the impacts are on health-related and everyday practices, and what solutions might be envisioned. Methodologies: We will study the 'new dementia' through complementary disciplinary approaches. We will adopt a comparative perspective looking at differences and similarities between three countries: Germany, Canada and Switzerland. Expected outcomes: Our results aim to make people more aware that preventing dementia is a highly complex issue that needs to be seen in context through an extensive knowledge transfer on multiple levels.

column36: HYBRID MINDS: Experiential, Ethical and Legal Exploration of Intelligent Neuroprostheses
column37: Intelligent neuroprostheses represent the next phase in the evolution of devices integrated with the nervous system to assist, replace or alter human sensory, motor, cognitive, and affective functions. These devices include "read out" or output systems that detect, interpret and translate neural signals for various applications such as to allow a paralyzed person to move a robotic arm or cursor. They also include "write in" or input systems that deliver signals or stimulation to the brain, to alter thinking, emotions, and the ability to move, among other things. The technology is increasingly incorporating Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create neuroprostheses that adapt automatically without voluntary user input. The current rate of development of AI-based neurotechnology systems is outpacing ethical reflections and is challenging regulatory systems. The current technological departure lies in the complexity, unpredictability, and psychological impact of the integration of AI with human brains and minds. Such hybrid minds are characterized by mutual adaptation, in which both user and self-learning algorithm change over time to optimize system output. Such interactions become even more intricate when "write-into" devices generate stimuli that directly influence mental contents and cognitive processes of users. Our project attempts to lay the foundations for a unified theoretical approach to the ethical-legal assessment of intelligent neuroprostheses, informed by the experiences and perspectives of users, and in dialogue with the neuroengineering community and other key stakeholders, culminating in the central questions: Which AI-elements should future neuroprostheses incorporate, or rather leave out? What technical design choices or legal/regulatory measures are required? How can we support patients in clinical decision-making to avoid overblown hopes and to know, to borrow Thomas Nagel's famous phrase, "what it's like to have a hybrid mind"?

column36: High Frequency- Heart Rate Variability (HF-HRV) as a Risk Factor for Stress-Related Insomnia Among Older Adults
column37: "Insomnia is common among older adults, and studies indicate that exposure to stressful life events is one factor associated with increased risk for insomnia. However, there is substantial variability in vulnerability to stress-related insomnia. A biomarker of parasympathetic system (High Frequency-Heart Rate Variability) is also considered a biomarker of vulnerability to stress-related insomnia. Individuals with low parasympathetic functioning experience greater physiological and emotional arousal in response to stress, which may promote a state of hyperarousal that interferes with sleep initiation and maintenance. Moreover, High Frequency- Heart Rate Variability decreases with age. The goal of this study is to examine whether the biomarker is related to stress-related insomnia among older adults with chronic insomnia. Older adults aged 65+ with chronic insomnia will be recruited and will partake in two overnight studies; the first one ruling out other sleep disorders. The second one will evaluate sleep features, and in the following morning, the biomarker will be measured. In between the two overnight sleep studies, participants will be asked to complete a stress diary before going to bed at the end of each day and other questionnaires that measure subjective measures of insomnia severity. This study will contribute to the understanding of etiology of insomnia and the identification of vulnerable older adults."
