column36: Age Effects of Cognitive Impairment in Major Depressive Disorder
column37: "Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is the leading cause of disability worldwide. It manifests as a variety of psychological, physical and cognitive impairments. Cognitive impairments may include poor memory, slow reaction time and struggling to focus on a task. Cognitive dysfunction plays a large role in daily psychosocial functioning and productivity, both of which impact life satisfaction. MDD can trigger cognitive impairments in anyone, regardless of age. Although we know depression can cause cognitive impairments, what is not understood is how these impairments differ across the lifespan.The purpose of this study is to determine: (i) the association between age and different types of cognitive impairments triggered by MDD and (ii) the association between age and the severity of these cognitive impairments.To conduct this study, I will use the THINC-it test - a new assessment tool specifically designed to identify and classify cognitive impairment in patients with MDD. Four groups will complete the test: young and old adults with MDD, and young and old adults with no mental illness. Participants will be tested in the areas of memory, executive function, attention and processing speed, all of which can be impaired by MDD. Comparisons made between the MDD groups will identify the types of cognitive impairment experienced by each age group. Additional comparisons between the MDD and the non-MDD groups will identify the effects of age on the severity of cognitive impairments. This information will contribute to our understanding of the symptoms triggered by MDD and will improve diagnostic assessments and treatment therapies. Ultimately, the knowledge gained will benefit individuals suffering with depression and diminish the negative effects MDD has on our society."

column36: Evaluating the role of electro-mechanical integration of human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte graft in the treatment of myocardial infarction
column37: "Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Because the human heart has a limited capacity to regenerate, stem cell-based therapies have emerged as exciting treatment avenues. We can generate new cardiac cells from stem cells that mediate an improvement in heart function when injected after a heart attack in animal models. It is unclear, however, whether this improvement is due to new, functionally integrated heart muscle or due to indirect effects such as the release of growth factors or improved heart geometry. This mechanistic uncertainty remains a source of controversy in the field, and hampers progress towards clinical trials (as it, for example, remains unclear what cell dose, type and delivery mode are ideal). This project aims to investigate the roles of the direct and indirect mechanisms underpinning the improved heart function observed after injecting new cardiac cells into an infarct scar. First, we will genetically engineer stem cells such that they have non-functioning channels called gap junctions (GJ). Without GJs, cardiac cells cannot communicate electrically or contract in a coordinated fashion. We will use a variety of lab techniques to confirm that our engineered cells have lost these functions. Second, we will use a pig heart attack model to compare outcomes after the transplantation of normal cardiac cells, our engineered cardiac cells (incapable of synchronous contraction), or placebo. If we find that the normal cells improve heart function (as we have shown in prior work) but that the engineered cells do not, this would provide compelling evidence that the beneficial effects of our cell therapy are direct and are mediated by the formation of electrically integrated new muscle."

column37: An integrated approach to surveillance spanning different sectors has been promoted by international organisations for more than a decade and constitutes a central recommendation of the WHO action plan on AMR. Two scientific workshops will be held to build on researchers' experience and expertise, and consolidated guidance will be developed and made publicly available through the existing online websites. column36: The JPIAMR Primary Care Antibiotic Audit and Feedback Network (PAAN): An international collaboration on best practices for the delivery of antibiotic prescribing feedback to community clinicians using behavioural science
column37: Antibiotic overuse is an important contributor to antimicrobial resistance. Over 90% of antibiotic use is in the community, with estimates of unnecessary use ranging from 25%-50%. Audit and feedback (A&F) can be effective in improving prescribing behaviour. Jurisdictions implementing community antibiotic A&F programs will benefit from tools and resources to optimize effectiveness. Research that builds on existing knowledge to advance the field of A&F is needed. Important questions remain surrounding the optimal data to use and methods of data delivery to clinicians, tools to incorporate data into practice, and ensure sustainability over time. We propose assembling an international network of antimicrobial stewardship, primary care, and implementation science (with A&F expertise) experts, which will bring diversity in expertise, geographical locations, career stages, and genders. The network will be coordinated by three co-leads; antimicrobial stewardship (Schwartz), primary care (Lindbeak), and implementation science (Ivers). With overall objectives to provide best practice resources on conducting A&F interventions on antibiotic use in primary care and define research priorities to advance this field. We will employ a modified Delphi method to solicit input, while minimizing bias, from subgroups of experts via video conferencing and 2 multi-day in-person meetings over two years. There is also a contingency plan to host virtual meetings due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. We will leverage existing international collaboration with the A&F MetaLab, to facilitate ongoing knowledge translation. Multiple outputs from this network, including a systematic review, best practice resources and toolkits, and a paper outlining research priorities, will be organized into publishable peer-reviewed manuscripts as part of a broader dissemination and knowledge translation plan that leverages existing stakeholder networks among this diverse network.

column36: BRAIN STIMULATION RECONSIDERED - PARTICIPATIVE DEVELOPMENT OF A CODE OF CONDUCT FOR THE EUROPEAN UNION Acronym: TIMCODE Coordinator: Prof. Dr. Martina Schraudner (CERRI)
column37: Nerve cells communicate via electrical processes. Therefore, these can also be influenced by electrical or magnetic impulses or by other physical stimuli (e.g. ultrasound and lights). Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) uses this ability. The most commonly used methods are repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). In recent years, these very effective instruments have been approved in numerous countries for the treatment of various diseases. In this context, the scientific community has developed safety guidelines for the treatment of patients. However, in recent years, in addition to clinical research, a large market has developed in which people buy devices for cognitive enhancement or for selftreatment of neuropsychiatric conditions, and use them at home without medical supervision. This development, inter alia, raises questions that are currently difficult for researchers and governments to answer as the extend beyond their respective communities to larger spectrum of society. For example, where exactly is the border between enhancement (when NIBS is used to perform better in a given task or sport) or recreational (when NIBS is used because itself produces pleasure, e.g. lucid dreaming) and treatment (when NIBS is used to correct a given disease or to ameliorate symptoms)? Should the procedures also be used to treat children? In order to address questions like this in a reflective manner, this project aims to develop a participatory code of conduct for NIBS. To this end, actors from various scientific disciplines, society, business and governments will be involved. The involvement of laypersons and various expert perspectives will provide scientists with a tool to reflect on their own research and governments will be able to use the Code of Conduct for NIBS to create long-term guidelines that are valid EU-wide.

column36: Development and preclinical testing in human cell models and transgenic mice of a novel treatment for Schinzel-Giedion Syndrome
column37: Schinzel-Giedion Syndrome (SGS) is a rare disease usually leading to death in the first decade of life. SGS is caused by mutations in a gene called SETBP1, which increases the stability of the SETBP1 protein allowing it to continue carrying out its function when it might otherwise be degraded. While SGS is a multi-system disorder, a major burden on affected children and their families are the intractable seizures (ie seizures that do not respond to any known medication) that occur frequently in any given day. In collaboration with the SGS Foundation which is run by and for families of people with SGS, we have developed stem cell models derived from six children with SGS and their healthy parents, as well as four mouse models of SGS. We have re-purposed an internationally approved drug currently used to treat Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and that is being investigated in other non-MS clinical trials related to brain health. We have discovered that this drug can reverse molecular signatures of SGS in human brain-like cells. The purpose of this proposal is to perform preclinical proof-of-principle studies to develop this drug and to understand its mechanism of action to create a viable treatment for SGS to reduce seizure intensity and frequency. These studies include investigating: 1) protein and lipid turnover in single cells from mouse and human before and after drug treatment; 2) changes in synaptic vesicle release to understand if this is rescued by drug treatment, which is especially relevant for seizure control; 3) drug effects on mouse brain structure and behaviour, as well as bioavailability of the drug in mouse SGS models; 4) the transcriptional effects of the drug in different types of human brain cells and mouse SGS models with the idea of understanding downstream effects on all human genes; and 5) machine learning approaches using data across all research modalities to aid in determining the validity of the drug as a future treatment for SGS children.

column36: Designing a toolbox of paradigmatic treatments for a targeted molecular medicine approach to autosomal-recessive ataxias
column37: Autosomal-recessive cerebellar ataxia (ARCA) is a heterogeneous group of rare neurodegenerative genetic diseases that share the common hallmark of progressive damage to parts of the nervous system that coordinate movement, such as the cerebellum. Despite its devastating consequences in daily life on mobility and communication and reduced life span, no disease-modifying treatment is available for these disabling disorders. TREAT-ARCA aims at designing and testing new complementary treatment strategies, including both repurposed and newly identified molecules, as well as gene therapies in two exemplary multisystemic flagship ARCAS: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) and COQ8Aataxia (ARCA2). In addition, TREAT-ARCA aims at identifying and validating biomarkers that will enable to follow treatment. This will directly complement our consortium's prior clinical trial readiness work on these ARCAs (see PREPARE consortium; www.prepare-ataxia.com), thus now attaining all prerequisites required for directly facilitating clinical treatment trials in these two ARCAs

column36: Novel therapeutic approaches to target GNE Myopathy
column37: GNE myopathy (GNEM) is a rare severely debilitating muscle disease which affects 1 to 9:1,000,000 people among all ethnicities, with elevated carrier rates in populations of Eastern Europe and Asian heritage, including Jewish, Persian, East Indian, Arab and Japanese. GNEM is characterized by hypo-sialylation of muscle glycoproteins, degeneration and weakness of skeletal muscles, causing severe impairment of function and quality of life. It is caused by mutations in the GNE gene which encodes synthesis of the sialic acid enzyme. There are no approved therapies and research efforts on sialylation-increasing therapies are difficult because of drug absorption and the absence of biomarkers in clinical development. These challenges are the main focus of our project. ProDGNE aims to overcome these obstacles through a unique joint collaboration among European and Canadian experts in clinical GNEM and basic research in sialic acid, organic synthesis, and -OMICS. Our developed prodrug when processed within cells becomes an active therapy, highly increasing sialic acid in GNEM patient cells and demonstrating a higher stability when compared to clinically tested drugs. The ProDGNE consortium will develop proof of principle studies fostering early stage development for innovative therapeutic strategies tested in vitro in patient derived cells and in vivo in GNE animal models that mimic the pathological mechanism in patients. Moreover, post-translational modifications will be explored and the newly identified biomarkers, will be utilized to monitor efficacy.

column36: SMILE: Optimising SMarter Inclusive Living Environments for ageing people within their circles of care.
column37: The SMILE project is an international effort where European countries and Canada are coming together to provide digital solutions that can help people aged 65 - 80 years with brain disorders (dementia), lung disease (COPD) or other complex health conditions. Working together, SMILE will put the seniors and their caregivers at the center of design by understanding their needs and preferences. This feedback will be used to make smart living environments with artificial intelligence solutions to support ageing people by addressing their specific problems and needs. The Canadian study will specifically use a device called Vitaliti (TM)-a light weight device worn around the neck that can monitor seniors' vital signs and heart beat continually, while they go about their day. This observational study (VISION-2) will be conducted with 900 patients who have surgery and are at risk for serious complications. We will use a type of artificial intelligence called machine learning to study these readings. We will look for slight changes in vital signs that may lead to heart muscle injury, bleeding and infection. Once we know what these signs are, we can then develop an alert system to warn us so we can stop the complications before they happen. We will then look at how effective this alert system can be in 100 patients who will be assigned at random to wear the Vitaliti (TM) device or not for the first 30 days after surgery. At present, seniors die from infection and other serious complications after surgery- this work is an opportunity to make a real difference. Currently, few structures in current healthcare systems across the EU and Canada support seniors in dealing with unfavorable outcomes related to the ageing process. With SMILE, the hope is to develop age-friendly innovations that are accepted by the ageing population and their care teams. This work is an opportunity to empower older adults and maintain independence and wellbeing to overall improve the quality of life.

column37: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is the most prevalent muscle disease that afflicts both children and adults regardless of their gender. FSHD is caused by aberrant gain of expression of the double homeobox 4 (DUX4) gene causing toxic effects in muscle cells. Despite the consensus on the pivotal role of DUX4 and several clinical trials, there is currently no cure or an effective therapeutic approach for FSHD patients. In our studies, we identified a novel regulator of DUX4 expression. Targeting this factor allows to block DUX4 expression and rescues the pathogenic behavior of muscle cells from FSHD patients. The treatment is safe to healthy muscle cells. Based on our results, we will use cellular and animal models of the disease to investigate a novel pharmacological approach that could represent a promising therapeutic option for FSHD patients.

column36: CHAnging Rare disorders of LysInE metabolism
column37: Rare inborn errors of lysine metabolism such as pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (PDE) and glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1) cause debilitating, often progressive neurologic symptoms with chronic care dependency. Medical needs are unmet as current dietary therapy is burdensome and often ineffective, with negative impact on quality of life and socio economics. Our international CHARLIE project synergizes the expertise of patient representatives, basic and clinical scientists, to collaboratively develop and validate new therapies and biomarkers. We pursue different strategies to avoid brain damage: inhibition of the enzyme upstream to GA1 and PDE with the potential to prevent build up of highly reactive metabolites as well as gene therapy to replace the missing GA1 enzyme. We will first apply these in PDE and GA1 model systems, such as neuronal stem cells, mouse and zebrafish models. To evaluate and compare the efficacy of these different treatment approaches, we will perform biochemical, morphological, neurobehavioural analyses. We will develop tools for monitoring therapeutic effect, enabling personalized medicine. With our patient advocacy organizations, we will prioritize the most promising treatment strategy/-ies and enhance trial readiness. To inform families, professionals, and stakeholders, we will organize regular meetings and create digital platforms. For successful exploitation we engage industry and policymakers. Together our CHARLIE consortium will translate knowledge from bench to bedside, with drug access for improved outcomes for PDE and GA1 patients and families.

column36: Treating inherited blinding disease with a slow released form of the rod-derived cone viability factor protein
column37: Vision relies on two types of photoreceptors in the retina at the back of the eye: rod photoreceptors, which are responsible for night vision, and cone photoreceptors, which are responsible for daylight vision. Rods and cones have an intimate relationship, with rod photoreceptors producing a factor, rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF), which is critical to cone viability. When rod photoreceptors die, cone photoreceptors die and all vision is lost; however, if we could find a way to preserve cone photoreceptors, then we could overcome vision loss associated with blinding diseases. Geneticists have shown that one of the most common forms of inherited blinding diseases is caused by mutations in large numbers of genes, some of which are only active in rod photoreceptors. The death of these rods results in the loss of a protein, rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF), which then results in the loss of cone photoreceptors and ultimately blindness. In order to stop the progression of this disease, we propose to save cone photoreceptors, and hence daylight vision, by replacing the lost RdCVF with newly delivered RdCVF. Specifically, we propose to deliver a novel slow-release formulation of RdCVF directly to the eyes of patients using a strategy already shown to be safe for patients with age-related macular degeneration. We will study the benefit of our treatment strategy in three models of blinding diseases, starting from the mouse and rat to a novel model in a minipig, a species in which the eyes are similar those of humans. DrEYE is a preclinical study of an innovative treatment that, with success, will restore vision to the two million patients worldwide suffering from inherited blinding diseases and for which there are no other options.

column36: Targeting Sensory Dysfunctions in Autism Spectrum Disorders
column37: Autism and sensory processing challenges often occurred together, and affected individuals might experience 'hyper or hypo' reactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment. These sensory differences can affect behavior and learning. Sensory function is regulated by the sensory nervous system, which is a part of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) in the body. Over the past decades, independent lines of clinical and basic research have supported the hypothesis that dysregulation of the sensory system is part of the core symptomatology of ASD. For a long time, it was thought that sensory issues in autism were due to disruption of the central nervous system. However, there is emerging evidence that sensory processing disorders in autism arise due to the abnormal function of the sensory nervous system. In our study, our team is studying whether 3 established high risk genetic factors for autism cause sensory dysfunction. We believe that mutations FMRP, CYFIP1 and TAOK2 impair sensory nerve cell development by disrupting the production of important proteins required for electrical communication. To study this, our team will utilize a combination of model systems, including genetically engineered flies, mice, and stem cell-derived human sensory neurons. We will perform behavioral experiments to identify the sensory defects (eg. smell and touch). Further, we will test whether the production of proteins in neural cells is abnormal. Finally, we will test whether specific drugs and gene therapies that correct the abnormal protein production defects, will lead to a reversal of the sensory behavioral deficits in our animal models. Together, these studies will reveal a new line of scientific evidence that genetic mutations impair protein production in sensory neural cells, which ultimately leads to sensory deficits. Our study would open up new possibilities for treating sensory abnormalities related to ASD.

column36: Ion channel modulators to treat itch
column37: Chronic itch can be devastating to such an extent that patients may be willing to accept a shorter lifespan in return for an alleviating treatment. Itch, or pruritis, is commonly associated with a primary skin disorder; however, in a substantial subset of patients, pruritis originates from an unknown origin. Even though pruritus occurs in nearly 20% of adults, treatment options are typically limited to over-the-counter drugs or not effective. To efficiently address itch disorders with safe therapeutics, it is vital that we are able to pharmacologically manipulate the relevant sensory neuron pathways, which is the essence of the project that we propose here. We will build on our previous work in which we reported a clinical case of debilitating itch resulting from a mutation in SCN11A, a gene that encodes for NaV1.9 which is involved in transmitting sensory signals from the skin to the brain. To further investigate the role of NaV1.9 in itch, we propose to establish a discovery platform to help identify molecules capable of tackling the clinical problem of chronic itch and dramatically expand our understanding of its working mechanism. The results of this project will ultimately lead to new, more effective and safe itch treatments.

column36: Restoring Motor Functions in Parkinson's Disease with Noninvasive Hybrid Transcranial Neuromodulation

column36: Developing BBB-ASL as non-invasive early biomarker of Alzheimer's disease (DEBBIE)
column37: One of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's Disease is the loss of the Blood-Brain-Barrier (BBB) integrity in the brain's vascular system, which can be imaged with positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). While most methods require contrast agents, arterial spin labeling (ASL) is an MRI technique for non-invasive measurement of perfusion and change in the vascular permeability or BBB integrity. ASL is currently the only technique for mapping local changes in BBB integrity without the use of contrast-enhancing agents or radioactive tracers. However, for BBB integrity measurement it cannot be used reliably in a clinical setting due to often rather long scan times and sensitivity to patient-specific dynamic changes in blood flow. We propose to develop a robust ASL BBB integrity mapping technique by using novel innovative concepts to automatically adapt relevant MRI scan parameters to the patient's dynamic blood flow status at scan time. Combined with standardized image processing, this will provide a sensitive non-invasive biomarker/predictor of cognitive decline. The newly developed imaging technology will be validated against established BBB invasive technique (PET) and evaluated on patients at four clinical sites.

column36: NEURofeedback for self-stimulation of the brain as therapy for ParkInson DisEaSe (NEURIPIDES)
column37: We will develop a new type of treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD) based on neurofeedback. Neurofeedback is a type of treatment that allows people to see their own brain activity in real time, so that they can learn how to control and self-regulate it. Existing PD treatments are not effective for certain symptoms, and can also require brain surgery. Therefore, new treatments that address these problems are needed. Our project will take place over 3 stages: In stage 1, we will find out what the brain activity of people with PD looks like when their symptoms are well controlled. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a type of brain surgery that is able to give many people with PD good symptom relief. Using an imaging tool called functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we will see what the brain activity of people with PD who have successfully received DBS looks like. We will find patterns of brain activity associated with PD patients who have improved their i) motor symptoms (such as tremor, slowness, or stiffness), and ii) non-motor symptoms (such as their mood, memory, or attention). In stage 2, we will develop a neurofeedback system for people with PD. They will be able to see their own brain activity in real time, and will try to match it to the patterns of good brain activity we find in stage 1 in order to improve their symptoms. In stage 3, we will perform a trial - taking place at multiple hospitals in different countries - of our neurofeedback system to see whether it can help improve the symptoms of people with PD. Our hope is that we will develop a new type of treatment for PD that does not require brain surgery. We believe that it will be able to help patients who have never received DBS, and patients who have had DBS but could benefit from more symptom relief.

column36: Stepped care solutions to reduce impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on youth living with chronic pain, their families, and health care providers: A pan-Canadian study.
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic is one of the greatest threats to youth mental health in generations. Similar to past disasters, youth today report increased pain complaints. Without treatment, this pain will become chronic (CP; pain lasting >3 months), which already affects 1 in 5 youth and has devastating impacts on whole families. CP in childhood can trigger a wave of mental health and substance misuse issues that carry forward into adulthood. In 2019, our team revealed that "access to pain care" is a priority for youth with CP and families. Unfortunately, COVID-19 has only made access more difficult. CP clinics cannot see patients in person and only some can offer virtual care. Meanwhile, youth have lost access to school counselors, and physical distancing has likely worsened their mental health. The pandemic offers a once-in-a-lifetime chance to improve access to CP care moving foward. "Stepped care" is a promising way to do this. A good thing about stepped care is that it tailors care based on how bad a person's symptoms are. Like a ladder, a person may start with one type of care and then "step up" or "step down" to more or less intense care depending on need. We want to hear from youth, families, and healthcare professionals (HCPs) in the CP community about COVID-19 impacts. We will then create a "stepped care" program called Kids Pain Portal. This online Portal will increase access to CP care and ensure youth get the right treatment at the right time. Our study has four phases. In Phase 1, youth, families, and HCPs from across Canada will complete online surveys. In Phase 2, we will interview some patients, families, and HCPs from Phase 1. These surveys and interviews will tell us about COVID-19 impacts on CP care. In Phase 3, we will meet with HCPs, researchers, and family partners. There, we will create best practice recommendations for virtual "stepped care" in Canada. In Phase 4, we will co-design the Kids Pain Portal and ensure it is easy and satisfying to use.

column36: EXERGETIC: An innovative digital solution to individually improve physical and cognitive functions using an exergame (video game-based) training in an ecologically valid and safe setting for the geriatric population
column37: People live longer, and when they grow older, their brains and bodies do not function as well as they used to. We need training options for a person's mind and body to help older adults stay healthy. Staying healthy will let them remain independent and mobile longer, and reduce their risk of falling (which can have particularly harmful side effects and long-lasting health consequences for older people's lives). Research shows much promise in using video games to help older adults train their bodies and brains via so-called exergames (game-based exercise training). In the EXERGETIC project that we are proposing, we will develop an exergame (the "ExerG") to help older adults train their brains and bodies. The prototype will be based on an already existing exergame: the ExerCube fitness game from Sphery AG. The existing ExerCube is currently designed as a training tool for young, healthy adults. In the EXERGETIC project, we will redesign the ExerCube to work for older adults: we will invite older adults to interviews and ask them what they would prefer or need from the ExerG. We will focus on designing the ExerG's graphics and audio, and whether or how to include their therapists to make sure older adults have a good experience when they use the ExerG. We will also make sure that the ExerG is easy and fun to use for anyone. The ExerCube will also be remodelled to include hardware like a harness that is mounted from the ceiling - with this safety harness; older adults will not be able to fall over during training in the ExerG. The final goal is to create a working prototype that older adults enjoy and test it in user studies. The result can then be turned into a certified product for the market of tools that help keep older adults fit and healthy. We will communicate our study results-focused on the design of this training tool for older adults-to the public through web sites, social media, research publications, and exhibitions.

column36: (MiTy Tykes) A multi-centre follow up study of the effect of in-utero exposure to metformin in 5-11 year old offspring of mothers in the MiTy Trial
column37: Background and Importance The incidence of diabetes in pregnancy is rising, with rates of 1 in 7 pregnancies globally. Metformin is used for type 2 diabetes (T2DM) outside of pregnancy and is now increasingly prescribed during pregnancy. There are some concerns as metformin crosses the placenta and effects on offspring exposed during pregnancy are unknown. Animal and human evidence indicate that metformin may create an atypical in-utero environment similar to under-nutrition which has been associated with adult obesity. This is supported by studies in children of mothers treated with metformin in other populations where an increase in childhood obesity was found at 4-9 years of age. We now have evidence from the MiTy trial, that offspring of metformin-exposed women with T2DM have less large infants and are less adipose at birth, but are also more likely to be small for gestational age (SGA). These effects could lead to benefit or harm in the long-term. Offspring of MiTy mothers are currently being followed up to 2 years. Given that long-term effects may not be evident until 5 years of age, it is imperative to follow these children longer. Goals/Research Aims: To determine whether in-utero exposure to metformin, in offspring of women with T2DM, is beneficial or harmful in the long-term. Research Questions: 1. In offspring of women with T2DM, how does treatment with metformin during pregnancy affect a) adiposity b) growth over time c) metabolic syndrome 2. What factors predict altered childhood adiposity and insulin resistance in these offspring? Methods/Approaches/Expertise Primary Outcome: Body mass index (BMI) z-score Secondary Outcomes: 1) other measures of adiposity ie skinfolds, 2) growth over time 3) measures of insulin resistance 4) adipocytokines Expected Outcomes Given these increasing concerns, this study will inform the best treatment for pregnant mothers with diabetes by studying the long-term outcomes of children exposed to metformin during pregnancy.

column36: Characterization of novel type VI secretion system effectors in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
column37: One of the ways harmful bacteria make us sick is by secreting protein toxins that damage nearby cells. Many bacteria secrete these toxins using a needle-like nanomachine called a 'bacterial type VI secretion system'. Bacteria use this molecular needle to secrete toxins that not only damage human cells but also kill the good bacteria that reside in healthy individuals. The human disease-causing bacteria known as Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses the type VI secretion nanomachine to wipe out other bacteria, damage our healthy cells and establish life-threatening infections in susceptible individuals, such as people with cystic fibrosis or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The goal of the proposed research is to fully understand how the toxins secreted by this bacterial nanomachine function at a molecular level so that we can one day disable them, thereby giving our immune system and our beneficial microbes a much better chance of warding off the deadly Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria.

column36: Synthetic Biomaterials to Package and Deliver siRNA Nanoparticles in order to Curb Uncontrolled Growth of Leukemic Cells
column37: Leukemias are a significant cause of death among cancer patients. Great strides have been made in understanding the factors causing leukemia and numerous new types of drugs are being continuously explored for therapy. However, the traditional chemotherapy is still the treatment of choice for most leukemias, but it is rarely curative and it loses its effectiveness on the long-term therapy. The main reason for this is that the leukemic cells adopt and become resistant to chemotherapy. This project is intended to develop a new approach for therapy of leukemia by developing a new type of drug for therapy. We plan to achieve this by silencing (or eradicating) the molecules responsible for uncontrolled growth of cancerous cells. Engineered biomaterials effective for silencing will be paramount to accomplish the desired goal. The biomaterials are intended to deliver the silencer molecules into leukemic cells without harming the healthy cells. Animal models will be utilized to determine the effectiveness of the proposed biomaterials. If successful, our approach will introduce a new treatment modality for leukemia.

column36: Identifying patient-specific behaviors to understand illness trajectories and to predict relapses in bipolar disorder using passive sensing and pattern recognition
column37: What do we want to do? The overall objective of this study is to characterize illness trajectories and to predict relapses in stable adult patients with Bipolar Disorder (BD). Specifically, we aim to develop new data modeling that will enable more tailored signal detection to examine changes within each individual over time, to predict a future episode of illness. Our preliminary studies relevant to this proposal include those related to using nonlinear techniques (time-series analysis and entropy) to understand how mood is regulated in healthy controls, bipolar patients and their relatives; as well as our ongoing study analyzing heart rate variability and clinical characteristics in BD patients during different phases of their illness (stable, depressed, hypomanic or mixed). How are we going to do it? We will collect data using passive sensing (Oura ring), including sleep, activity and heart rate variability, in 200 BD patients. This ring measures these variables continuously, so we will have a large amount of data. These data will be combined with a detailed description of the clinical course of illness in each patient. Then, we will use nonlinear techniques to obtain an individualized measure of variability (entropy levels) in each participant. Finally, we will feed these entropy levels for each participant into a machine-learning technique called Markov Brains to distinguish those at a higher risk of relapse. Why is this important? Because BD is a complex and heterogeneous illness. This means that we cannot assume that all depressive episodes or all manic episodes will look the same in all patients diagnosed with BD. Thus, we need to incorporate each patient's variability (e.g., the unique way in which each patient's mood or sleep change) to extract individual patterns suggestive of a future episode of illness. The long-term benefits of our studies include reducing rates of relapse and related complications, including substance abuse and suicide.

column36: Refining the molecular endotypes for precision medicine of osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA), the most common form of arthritis, is expected to affect 130 million people symptomatically worldwide and 40 million will be severely disabled by 2050. However, there is no cure for it yet. The biggest challenge to develop OA drugs is the wide heterogeneity of the disease. It is now recognized that OA is a nebula of several diseases, but we do not have markers to differentiate them yet. Several clinical classifications of OA have been proposed based on the OA risk factors and joint magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment. These classifications improved our knowledge in the etiologies of OA but failed to subset the disease which results in inconsistent response to treatments. We performed metabolomic studies (study of small chemical compounds present in body fluids) on plasma and joint fluid samples obtained from OA patients and healthy controls and found at least three subtypes of OA characterized by different markers, implicating different metabolic pathways involved in OA. These markers have potential to be used to better stratify OA patients for clinical trials and developing personalized medicine tools. We now propose to confirm the findings and refine the markers and related pathways for each of the subtypes of OA by integrating genomics (study of all the genes) and metabolomics in three existing cohorts - the Newfoundland Osteoarthritis Study (NFOAS) as the discovery cohort (n=1113), the Longitudinal Evaluation in the Arthritis Program, Osteoarthritis Study (LEAP OA; n=900) and the Tasmania Older Adult Cohort Study (TASOAC; n=568) as the validation cohorts. The study will identify molecular subtypes of OA. It will help inform a better understanding of the etiologies of OA, provide tools to better stratify OA patients for clinical trials, and develop personalized medicine tools for OA management.

column37: The section of a peripheral nerve over a distance of several centimeters causes severe motor and sensory impairments of hands, arms or legs compromising the quality of life of the patients. The purpose of this project is to repair this type of injury by interposing between the two nerve stumps a tissue-engineered nerve tube prepared with the patient's own cells. In addition, the conduit will be prevascularized with endothelial cells to promote the development of a network of capillaries inside the tube leading to a rapid connection to the host's blood circulation after graft. This project is expected to greatly enhance the repair of severed nerves following trauma, surgery, or ablation of tumors.

column36: Role of vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation in beta cell and diabetes
column37: Vitamin K is an essential micronutrient known to regulate blood coagulation and bones. Recent clinical observations in humans suggest that partial vitamin K deficiency might be linked to the development of diabetes. However, the biological mechanism by which vitamin K may influence diabetes remains unknown. Beta cell is a unique cell type of the pancreas responsible for the production of insulin. Diabetes is caused by a reduction in the number of beta cells or by a decrease in their capacity to secrete insulin. This research project aims at understanding the function of vitamin K-dependent proteins in pancreatic beta cells and its potential link with the development of diabetes. Our approach includes the use of genetically modified mice lacking the components of the vitamin K cycle in pancreatic beta cells. We will analyze these animals to determine the role of vitamin K in protecting beta cells from cell death, and in promoting their proliferation and function. We will also study the interaction between vitamin K and the capacity of human and mouse beta cells to respond to stress. Finally, we will test if vitamin K can improve or prevent diabetes in pre-clinical mouse models. Altogether, these studies will allow us to understand how vitamin K is implicated in the biology of beta cell and how partial vitamin K deficiency contributes to the development of diabetes.

column36: Hematopoietic stem cell sequelae in fetuses and offspring exposed to in utero Zika infection
column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) emerged in the Americas in 2015 and posed ongoing public health concerns. The outcomes of ZIKV infection are fetal death, brain lesions, and life-long impairment in children. Alarmingly, the majority of fetal infections are mild with no easily identifiable birth defects; however, later health complications in initially asymptomatic ZIKV-affected offspring were demonstrated in our animal model studies and studies in humans. It is not known, however, how abnormalities acquired during fetal infection are sustained and endure in offspring. Our preliminary studies suggest that mild ZIKV infection in fetuses causes systemic inflammation deteriorating fetal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)-long-living cells that maintain the immune system for the life span. Fetal HSCs affected during a developmental period in the maternal womb may sustain acquired pathology after birth causing long-term HSC abnormalities and enduring dysfunction of immunity in offspring. We will use state-of-the-art molecular techniques and advanced large animal models to understand better how ZIKV affects HSCs and their ability to maintain the immune system. A better understanding of long-term effects caused by mild in utero infection will support the development of therapeutic strategies. Importantly, in addition to ZIKV infection, the new knowledge may be applied to other viruses that are known to cause mild fetal infections. Our studies may help to reduce health sequelae in offspring and treatment required after birth. It will be highly-rewarding for patients, families, and society and will decrease the social and economic burden associated with congenital infections.

column36: Role of Female Sex Hormones on Aging in Women Living with HIV.
column37: In Canada as of 2019, a woman's life expectancy is 4 years longer than a man's. However, when a woman is HIV-positive, not only is her life expectancy 5-10 years shorter than other women her age who do not live with HIV, but it is also 7 years less than that of a man who is HIV-positive. This may be related to changes in levels of sex and stress hormones that when normal would protect a woman's bones, heart and other organs. Women who live with HIV more often have a history of having menstrual periods that are not regular or went away entirely for a while. They also reach menopause earlier than women without HIV. These changes are associated with women having more difficulty with kidney, bone and liver disease, and with abnormal cholesterol and blood sugar levels. Thus, women who have HIV and have a history of abnormal menstrual periods may have an increased risk of several diseases of aging and at an earlier age. Here we aim to determine how abnormal menstrual periods and hormone levels affect and are affected by social factors and gender inequity to have an effect on diseases of aging and the reproductive health of women living with HIV. With this information we can improve care for women and in so doing prevent disease, and promote healthy aging.

column36: Investigating the role of cognitive brain networks in human motor learning
column37: The human brain's capacity to learn new motor commands is fundamental to almost all activities we engage in. Indeed, it is not only essential when we acquire novel skills, such as learning to play a musical instrument, but it is also required on a daily basis as we adapt to changes in our environment, interact with new objects, and refine existing skills. As such, impairments in sensorimotor learning, which often occur following stroke and neurological disease, can be particularly devastating. Gaining a better understanding of the neural bases of sensorimotor learning is essential for characterizing these impairments and for developing more effective therapies for rehabilitation. The broad goal of the proposed research is to better understand, at the level of interacting whole-brain networks, the role of cognitive brain systems in driving human sensorimotor learning. The proposed work will employ a combination of behavioural, neuroimaging and computational approaches to characterize how brain regions change their interactions during learning, and how these changes relate to individual differences in learning ability. This work will produce important new knowledge that can be leveraged in characterizing and treating many of the core sensorimotor and cognitive deficits that result from brain disorders and disease.

column36: Epigenomic changes trigger a decline in uterine function and reproductive health in females of advanced maternal age
column37: The first most acute sign of advancing age experienced by women is a decline in fertility. Maternal age not only affects the risk of having a baby with chromosomal abnormalities (such as Down's syndrome), but also increases the frequency of suffering from various pregnancy complications such as pre-eclampsia or preterm birth. The reason why these latter complications are more prevalent in older women is not well understood, as they are not commonly associated with chromosomal defects of the baby. Advanced maternal age is an immense societal challenge as many women delay child bearing until later in their lives, with now well over 20% of babies born to women over 35 in Canada. Therefore it is extremely important to gain better insights into why these complications increase with age, and explore potential therapeutic avenues that may help mitigate this risk. Using the mouse as a model to study how age affects pregnancy outcome, we have found that the cells lining the womb (the so-called endometrium) undergo a significant decline in their ability to support pregnancy with age. Similar changes likely affect pregnancy in older women. These defects correlate with widespread changes to the regulatory layer of information that is imposed onto DNA (known as the epigenome) that controls which genes can be switched on and off. In aged cells many important genes have an altered epigenetic signature, which prevents them from being activated at the right time. In this proposal, we are aiming to gain fundamental novel insights into the precise nature and progression of these epigenetic alterations and how they affect endometrial cell function. Our goal is to discover new pathologic and genetic markers that can more accurately stratify risk of progression in newly diagnosed prostate cancer so that a greater number can be monitored safely with active surveillance, including a subset that would be considered intermediate risk by current criteria, while higher risk cases can be selected for definitive treatment. Novel biomarkers will be extremely valuable to patients, caregivers and physicians in deciding on best treatment. This could dramatically decrease the risks of undesirable and unexpected cancer progression, and anxieties related to being on a cancer surveillance program. column37: One in five Canadians lives with chronic pain, which is pain that is persistent or recurring for three or more months. Caring for patients with chronic pain costs more than cardiovascular disease, cancer or diabetes. The recent opioid crisis has highlighted a need to improve the care of people with chronic pain; chronic pain is now being recognized as a public health crisis and comprehensive, population-based strategies are being developed to improve the care these patients need. Two sources of data, electronic medical records (EMR) and administrative health data, provide opportunities to facilitate improvements for chronic pain sufferers in Canada. An EMR is essentially a digital version of the traditional, paper-based medical record for a patient and these data, particularly from primary care, provide rich insight into a patient's health. Administrative health data captures all visits to the healthcare system that are covered by publicly funded health insurance (i.e. the Ontario Health Insurance Program [OHIP]). Currently there is no reliable method to identify chronic pain patients in these types of data. To date, research has relied on patient self-report of pain. We will develop accurate methods to identify patients with chronic pain in both primary care EMR data and administrative health data. We know that chronic pain affects men and women differently, so we will ensure that the methods we develop work equally well to identify pain in both men and women. Using these methods, we will study the healthcare needs of patients with chronic pain. This project will provide valuable information about the burden of chronic pain and help to inform an evolving national pain strategy. The development of valid methods to identify chronic pain in EHR and administrative health data has implications for clinical research, patient care and health policy.

column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (aLL) is a devastating cancer of immature white blood cells called lymphoblasts. It largely affects children, representing more than a quarter of all childhood cancers, and causing most of the death from cancer among children. L-asparaginase (ASNase) is a key component of aLL chemotherapy, but how ASNase kills aLL cells remains undefined. Our recent studies point to proteins designated as PAR2 and OPRM1 as cell signaling pathways through which ASNase causes aLL cell death. PAR2 and OPRM1 have been separately implicated to trigger an increase in cell calcium, which at overwhelming levels cause cell death. column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is an obesity-linked metabolic disorder that affects >25% of adults in Canada. Most people with NAFLD have a benign case of simple steatosis (excess fat storage in liver) but an estimated 1 million Canadians will progress to a more severe pathology called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which is characterized by steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis of the liver. NASH is the leading cause of liver failure and liver cancer and also contributes to cardiovascular complications such as heart failure and stroke. In obesity, a key determinant underlying NASH and its detrimental impact on health is the capacity of the liver to resist the metabolic stress imposed by excess levels of cholesterol and its metabolic product bile, which promote liver cell damage and inflammation. Hence, there is an important role for therapeutics that are specifically designed to enhance the capacity of liver to manage elevated metabolism of cholesterol and bile. In our proposed research, we will investigate the mechanisms by which a pair of evolutionarily conserved stress-adaptive transcription factors named NRF1 & NRF2 regulate metabolic, stress, and inflammatory processes to promote resistance to the stress of elevated cholesterol and bile in liver during obesity. Our goal is to determine whether NRF1 & NRF2 work independently or in a coordinated manner to engage adaptive countermeasures and whether these actions are capable of resolving liver cell damage and inflammation caused by excess cholesterol & bile. We will also test whether stimulating these transcription factors may be an effective strategy to treat NASH in obesity. We anticipate these findings will be relevant for the large & growing population of Canadians with obesity who are at risk for NASH and its consequential impact on liver failure, liver cancer, heart failure and stroke.

column36: Neuroimaging of disease progression and tauopathy in temporal lobe epilepsy
column37: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological disorders. While antiepileptic drugs can control the seizures in many patients, 30-40% of patients are drug-resistant. Furthermore, many patients present with cognitive deficits, affecting functioning and wellbeing. Epilepsy surgery is currently the most effective treatment to control the seizures and to improve quality of life in drug-resistant patients. However, many do not undergo this procedure (as they are not offered surgery, or decide against it), and some only do so after decades. While epilepsy is still widely considered a 'static' disorder, mounting evidence indicates that the adverse clinical and cognitive effects of the disease aggravate over time. Our project will examine disease progression in temporal lobe epilepsy, the most common drug-resistant epilepsy in adults. Building on findings in brain tissue of patients that underwent epilepsy surgery, we will test the role of misfolded tau protein in disease progression. Accumulation of tau is commonly seen in Alzheimer's Disease, and closely associated with neurodegeneration and dementia. Our project will capitalize on novel neuroimaging techniques to measure tau in the brain. We will examine whether tau is elevated in epileptic patients compared to controls and assess relations to brain atrophy and cognitive decline. Patients and controls will be longitudinally re-assessed with the same protocols, and we will test whether increases in tau and atrophy in patients relate to cognitive trajectories. We will enroll drug-resistant and well-controlled patients, to ascertain the potential modulation of progression by seizures. Finally, we will assess whether tau measures predict future cognitive function in patients undergoing and not undergoing epilepsy surgery. Our project will provide novel insights into progressive brain changes in epilepsy, their contribution to cognitive decline, and the modulation of this process through seizures and tau accumulation.

column37: There are several lines of evidence to suggest that silicon (Si) is important for the proper functioning of many tissues. In particular, Si is believed to provide resiliency to bone and prevent the premature aging of arteries, that is, of atherosclerosis. We have recently identified Si transporters in human for the first time and feel that this discovery should enable us to study the biological role of Si in much greater detail than before. One group of transporters is called the aquaglyceroporins. These proteins are also specialized in the facilitated movement of water and alternative substrates such as urea into and/or out of cells. We should also be able to show that the changes observed translate into deleterious abnormalities in vivo. column37: Background: There is a need for adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer research because the number of new cancers in young people is increasing and the survivor population is growing. Aim: Given the many positive effects of physical activity (e.g. improved fitness and quality of life), our study aims to encourage AYA cancer survivors to be more physically active as they shift from treatment to survivorship care. At the start of the study, participants will complete fitness testing and questionnaires. Participants will then be randomly put into either a control or intervention group. The control group will receive educational information only. The intervention group will also receive a personalized physical activity plan, an activity tracker watch, access to a private, online survivor community, motivational text messages and check-in calls/e-mails. Fitness testing and questionnaires will be repeated at 6 and 12 months to see if the intervention increased physical activity levels and improved health outcomes among the participants in the intervention group compared to controls. A final measurement at 24 months will test long-term use. Impact: This study could provide AYA cancer survivors with a simple and affordable mHealth intervention that benefits their physical and mental health. If our intervention works in Alberta, we aim to test its effectiveness nationally.

column36: Fundamental Lysosome Membrane Biology in Health and Disease
column37: Clear relationships exist between lysosome activity, cancers and age-related diseases but many fundamental aspects of lysosome biology remain enigmatic preventing development of effective therapies: Lysosomes are membrane-encapsulated organelles responsible for recycling biomaterials within all eukaryotic cells, like the trillions that make up you and I. As important sources of nutrients, growing and dividing cells rely on lysosomes especially when starved, as is the case for cancer cells in tumor environments. But lysosomes generate molecules called reactive oxygen species that damage their membranes, causing them to rupture and kill cells. However, for reasons unknown, lysosome membranes within cancer cells are resistant to rupture. Aging brain cells also depend on lysosomes to clear toxic protein aggregates. Loss of this function leads to premature cell death underlying many age-related diseases, like Alzheimer's disease. Often this correlates with abnormal accumulation of lipids called diacylglycerol, ceramide and sphingosine on lysosome membranes that promote dysfunction and rupture. But it is unclear how lysosomes handle these lipids to function and remain intact. Furthermore, enhanced lysosome activity in both cases relies on inhibition of TOR signaling, an important mediator of cell metabolism - but the molecular basis of how this occurs is not entirely understood. The aim of this project is to better understand the basis of these three aspects of lysosome biology relevant to cancer and age-related diseases by studying baker's yeast as a model organism. I suspect that a process that my lab discovered called the IntraLumenal Fragment (ILF) pathway is responsible and will test this hypothesis using microscopy, genetic and biochemical techniques. Knowing the basis of lysosome activation and rupture will facilitate the development new therapies for these devastating diseases that affect millions of Canadians.

column37: Human cells take on a large range of shapes that are important for fulfilling specific biological functions. Cells can change their shape based on particular stimuli by altering components of the cell's inner skeleton, called the cytoskeleton. column36: Characterizing Cardiovascular Outcomes in Subclinical Primary Aldosteronism
column37: Background: Hypertension (high blood pressure) management generally involves a 'one size fits all' approach. Employing a more personalized approach targeting the cause of an individual patient's hypertension provides the opportunity to improve long-term health. Primary aldosteronism (PA) is a common hormonal cause of hypertension that leads to disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease. Importantly, the adverse health consequences of PA are preventable with early targeted treatments which are distinct from other forms of hypertension. Recently, a growing body of evidence has demonstrated that milder forms of PA ('Subclinical PA') are exceedingly common in the general population yet go undetected in modern-day clinical practice. Whether Subclinical PA increases the risk for long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes remains unknown. Purpose: To study the long-term effects of Subclinical PA on cardiovascular disease. Procedure: We will investigate Subclinical PA using CARTaGENE - a study which enrolled over 20,000 Quebec residents in 2009-2010. These participants had blood samples stored at the date of enrollment, and follow-up data regarding their health has been collected since that time. We will use the stored blood samples to perform hormonal profiling and identify participants with Subclinical PA at the time of enrollment to determine their long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Outcome: We anticipate that participants with Subclinical PA will develop higher rates of cardiovascular disease compared to participants without Subclinical PA. Relevance to Patients: If indeed patients with Subclinical PA experience worse cardiovascular outcomes, the logical next step will be to study whether using medications that specifically target Subclinical PA (and are not used routinely as first-line hypertension therapy) will improve cardiovascular outcomes. This study will provide a much-needed step toward a more individualized approach to hypertension management.

column36: Impact of copy number imbalances in mutant KRAS on pancreatic cancer chemoresistance and metastases
column37: Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence that can transform the normal behaviour of a cell. Mutations that lead to cancer cause the cell to grow uncontrollably. Cancer is the product of many mutations that have accumulated in the DNA of a cell. KRAS is one of the genes that is often mutated in cancer. In pancreatic cancer, KRAS mutations are present in 90% of patients. When KRAS is mutated experimentally in a mouse model, the cells develop cancer. Hence, it is a well-known "driver" gene, which means that it can initiate cancer. However, our research group have found a strong clinical correlation with a less known effect of KRAS. We have found a link between KRAS, therapy resistance and the spread of the cancer (also known as metastases). We found that when the tumour spreads to other organs (usually liver for pancreatic cancers), the cells make more copies of mutated KRAS, resulting in more repeats of this gene. Each cell has two copies of a gene (one inherited from the mother and one from the father), but in cancer, when the cell divides, it makes more copies. Our findings showed that when a tumour have more copies of the KRAS gene, it does not respond to chemotherapy and usually spreads to the liver. We have developed a human model that recapitulates different copies of mutated KRAS. We will use this model to study the changes that occur in the cell when it has more copies of mutated KRAS, and to look for a drug that can kill tumour cells with elevated copies of mutated KRAS or make it respond better to the standard treatment. Although KRAS is a well-studied gene and is under investigation by many other research teams, our question and experimental strategy are novel. Our main aim is to better understand the role of mutant KRAS gene copies in therapy resistance and metastasis in order to contribute to finding new treatment options for metastatic pancreatic cancer patients.

column37: HIV continues to be a major Global Health threat and curbing the epidemic will require several concurrent approaches, including a focus on preventing new HIV infections. The two major HIV prevention strategies (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis [PrEP] - a proactive approach; Post Exposure Prophylaxis [PEP] - a retroactive approach) are effective, however major gaps continue to exist with these HIV prevention modalities. Patients are counselled to fill the prescription and, in the event of a possible HIV exposure, to initiate their 28 days of medication as soon as possible (and within 72 hours). PIP is likely to prevent HIV infection while addressing the many barriers and drawbacks of conventional PEP and PrEP; PIP enables immediate access to HIV preventative care, may reduce patient attrition, and eliminates the need for costly and inconvenient emergency department visits. column36: Neural control of sequential action: controlling the present while planning the future
column37: While we go about our everyday activities, our brain constantly looks ahead and plans our next actions. Being able to multi-task - controlling current actions, while planning the next ones - is important in many skills, from cooking dinner to driving a car to playing the piano. Our ability to do so declines with age and is severely impaired after brain damage. Despite its importance and ubiquity, we know very little about how the human brain accomplishes this task. In our experiments, we will study humans and non-human primates performing sequences of finger or arm movements. We will use a combination of behavioral experiments, functional magnetic resonance imaging, and electrophysiological recordings to decipher the mechanisms by which the brain plans for the future while simultaneously controlling ongoing actions. We will investigate which parts of the brain are involved in solving this task, how they communicate, and how their interactions change with learning. To further our theoretical understanding, we also investigate how artificial intelligence algorithms, specifically recurrent neuronal networks, solve this task. Together these lines of basic research will provide a new understanding of how the brain solves complex sequential tasks and provides the basis for novel clinical interventions that improve the brain's ability to multi-task after damage or degeneration.

column36: Mechanisms of heart rhythm disorders and therapeutic interventions in myotonic dystrophy type 1
column37: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a form of muscular dystrophy, it is characterized by multiorgan impairments including the heart. Eighty percent (80%) of patients with DM1 have abnormal heart beats known as cardiac arrhythmias and can die suddenly. Cardiac arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death are major health concern as it is estimated that every day >1000 sudden cardiac deaths occur in North America in general and in particular for DM1 affected individuals. Problems with heart rhythm and conduction will arise first and can cause shortness of breath, discomfort, palpitations, loss of consciousness and in severe cases, sudden cardiac death. The only available treatment for more severely affected DM1 patients is the implantation of a pacemaker or a defibrillator. These are small devices that are placed in the chest or abdomen of most vulnerable patients. Overall, the goal of this research is to identify the causes of heart electrical abnormalities in DM1 patients and come up with ways for interventions that will correct these abnormalities. column36: The S. aureus Network Adaptive Platform Trial (SNAP) Canada: A Randomized Controlled Trial for Penicillin-susceptible, Methicillin-susceptible, and Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus Bloodstream Infections in Hospitalized Patients
column37: Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection (bacteremia) is a major public health problem and one of the most common and deadly bacterial infections in the world. There are over 15,000 episodes per year in Canada, resulting in more than 3,500 deaths with an estimated treatment cost exceeding $120,000,000. Despite the high morbidity and mortality of S. aureus bacteremia, there are no international guidelines for its treatment. Despite being such a common disease, to date, there have been only five high quality randomized controlled trials involving fewer than 3,000 patients for a disease which kills an estimated 22,000 per year in the United States and Canada alone. Therefore there remains considerable uncertainty as to the best choice of antibiotics to fight this infection, providing an excellent opportunity to improve the current standard of care We will address three crucial questions surrounding treatment that will allow us to study every combination of subtypes of S. aureus bacteremia in Canada. Firstly, we will compare the antibiotics penicillin vs. cloxacillin for penicillin-susceptible S. aureus. Secondly, we will determine if cefazolin or cloxacillin should be preferred for methicillin-susceptible strains of S. aureus. Finally, we will determine if the addition of cefazolin to vancomycin improves outcomes for patients with methicillin-resistant S. aureus. We propose a pragmatic clinical trial embedded within the current standard of care for S. aureus bacteremia. Our Canadian team will be key partners in an international collaboration which revolutionizes our capacity to study this infection. By refining the optimal treatments for all types of S. aureus bacteremia, our team will help establish best practices to be deployed worldwide. Since this intervention requires no new technology, any findings from our research program will offer immediate benefits to all patients and the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: SPECT-CT Guided ELEctive Contralateral Neck Treatment (SELECT) for Patients with Lateralized Oropharyngeal Cancer: A Phase III Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Oropharyngeal carcinoma (OPC) is the most common type of head and neck cancer and ninth most common cancer in Canadian men. Most OPCs are associated with the human papilloma virus (HPV) and have a good prognosis. The primary treatment is usually radiation therapy (RT). Although less than 15% have obviously involved lymph nodes on the opposite side of the neck, most patients receive RT to both sides of the neck because of the concern that microscopic cancer cells could spread to the opposite side. This approach increases the risk of swallowing impairment, dry mouth, and temporary feeding tube insertion, as compared to treatment of only one side of the neck. Lymphatic mapping with Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT-CT) imaging may help to identify whether an OPC is at risk for spread to the opposite side of the neck and, if so, the specific areas that are at risk for nodal disease. Lymphatic mapping is performed by injecting a radioactive tracer around the tumour, followed by capturing the distribution of the tracer to the lymph nodes of the neck. Patients will be randomized to either lymphatic mapping-guided RT or to standard bilateral neck RT. In patients randomized to the lymphatic mapping-guided treatment and in whom the radiotracer only migrates to the same side of the neck, RT will be limited to that side. In those patients in whom the radiotracer migrates to the opposite side of the neck, only the regions of the neck to which the radiotracer migrates will receive radiotherapy. We anticipate that this personalized treatment based on lymphatic mapping will provide similar cancer control, but will reduce side effects and improve quality of life compared to routinely treating both sides of the neck. We will evaluate the cost-effectiveness of this new approach and expect that it will offer a safe, effective, and cost-effective standard of care to patients in Canada and across the world.

column36: Integrative Medicine in North America: Paradigm Shift or New Physician Specialty?
column37: Over half of Canadians and 1/3 of Americans use complementary medicine (CM) therapies that are not fully integrated into mainstream healthcare. While medical schools offer little CM-related training, increasing numbers of medical doctors (MDs) are incorporating CM therapies into clinical practice. In 2014, 'integrative medicine' (IM) - a movement to include CM in mainstream care - was formally recognized as a new medical specialty for Canadian and American doctors. Does IM represent a paradigm shift in medicine? Alternately, does IM being siloed as a new specialty limit CM's influence within medicine; or, are IM doctors co-opting CM therapies into the dominant medical paradigm? Little is known to date about the IM field, which raises major questions for sociologists, medical educators and policy makers. This is especially important in Canada, where institutional, educational and policy responses to IM lag behind the United States. This study aims to: 1. Assemble a critical sociological account of IM's emergence in North America; 2. Characterize the workforce, practices and worldviews of IM physicians in Canada and the United States; and 3. To critically interrogate the policies, pedagogies and professionalization strategies that have accompanied IM's recent ascent to legitimacy. Four primary data types will be analysed: a) a survey of integrative MDs in Canada and the US (n=4000); and b) key informant interviews (n=40) with IM physician leaders; c) policies governing MDs' use of CM therapies; and d) curricula from established IM fellowship trainings. The proposed project will culminate in a book for scholars and the public; while providing usable findings for policy makers, physicians, medical educators. Close attention will be paid to Canadian vs. US distinctions, as well as issues of gender, ethnicity/race, financial accessibility and worldview.

column37: COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2 has caused a worldwide pandemic. Male patients have a worse outcome compared to the females. column36: Bringing focus to the invisible injury: Defining a role for microbleeds and microglia in mild traumatic brain injury.
column37: Concussions are a form of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), often called the "unseen injury", because of the lack of obvious damage. As a result, many individuals suffer repeated concussions, often in short time spans. In some sports, like hockey and football, awareness is growing that repeated sub-concussive blows to the head are routinely incurred in practices and games. Although many of these impacts do not result in a diagnosis of concussion, there is a growing appreciation that both concussions and sub-concussive impacts can negatively impact cognitive function in the developing brain, and that repeated concussions (r-mTBI) can have long-term detrimental effects for cognition in elderly populations. Despite these concerns, few laboratories have systematically studied r-mTBI in a preclinical model that properly mimics the human condition. We have recently developed a model that enables us to accurately examine r-mTBI and understand how the brain responds to repeated mTBI. Because significant structural damage does not occur in mTBI, our focus is on whether there is damage to small blood vessels in the brain. These vessels are below the threshold of resolution for magnetic resonance imaging, but can be resolved using high resolution microscopy. When damaged, these vessels can release a compound in the blood called fibrinogen. Fibrinogen is normally important for clotting, but can also initiate an inflammatory process involving brain microglia that negatively impacts neurons, and impairs learning and memory processes. The results of the proposed work will help us to better understand the mechanisms involved in mTBI; how they directly impact brain function, and increase our understanding of how r-mTBI early in life could negatively impact individuals as they age. More importantly, this work will enable us to determine the therapeutic value of modulating fibrinogen's effects in the brain to help reduce the negative impact of r-mTBI on cognition.

column36: Mobilizing the Antiviral Capacities of MAIT Cells to Combat COVID-19: From Fundamental Immunology to Vaccine Optimization and Immunotherapy
column37: In December 2019, a pneumonia associated with a novel coronavirus, now called severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), emerged in Wuhan, China. To date, the ongoing pandemic has resulted in over 36 million infections worldwide, and nearly 1.1 million people have succumbed to coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19). There are currently no approved vaccines or effective treatments for COVID-19. The ultimate goal of vaccination is to elicit antibody and T cell responses that will specifically detect and destroy SARS-CoV-2. However, the quality of these responses often varies at the population level. In addition, conventional vaccination strategies have encountered serious obstacles, and SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies may not be always protective. The goal of this proposal is to reveal the potentials of a specialized subset of unconventional innate-like T lymphocytes, called mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, in COVID-19. MAIT cells are enriched in mucosal layers and in the lungs, SARS-CoV-2's main ports of entry. Also importantly, MAIT cell responses are rapid, robust and consistent in human subjects irrespective of their genetic HLA (human leukocyte antigen) makeup. Inspired by recent preliminary data, we will investigate MAIT cell roles in host response to SARS-CoV-2 and also test the efficacy of a MAIT cell-activating molecule both as an adjuvant (vaccine-enhancing agent) and as a fast-acting treatment. To do so, we will establish a unique and clinically relevant mouse model harboring the human pulmonary receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and an abundance of MAIT cells. Simulating human subjects, this model will enable studies on the prophylactic and therapeutic potentials of MAIT cells and their stimuli. These studies will be complemented by a comprehensive and longitudinal analysis of MAIT cell frequencies and functions in COVID-19 patients, which may help predict the severity of illness and inform important clinical decisions in its management.
