column37: Drug discovery was historically based in animal models of disease- which while being a slow process, was fairly successful In the modern era, we have move away from experiments in animals, because of technologies that have allowed us to screen many more drug candidates in cell systems that express the target of interest. These gains in speed have not led reliably to more successful drug discovery programs- to a large extent because they rely on what are called generic or "heterologous" cultured cells that most probably do not accurately reflect the tissue or cell type affected in the disease we are trying to treat such as Parkinson's Disease or chronic neuropathic pain. However, in recent years a whole new set of technological improvements has allowed us to use primary cells from animal (or even stem cells from patients) to screen for drugs in this more relevant physiological and pathological context. Further, we and others have been able to adapt these screening technologies to live animals making it possible now to compare the effects of potential therapeutic drugs in cultured heterologous cells, cells derived from animals or patients, and whole animals. We propose here to test a key concept in modern drug development which aims to make drugs with fewer side effects by biasing them toward the required effects of a drug and away from the adverse effects. These concepts were developed in cell models but have not be rigorously been tested in animals. If we can establish whether these convenient cell culture-based models predict drug effects in living animals, this will greatly facilitate our ability to design and test better drugs.

column36: Structural and functional changes in the brain of early and late blind individuals
column37: For human and non-human primates, vision is one of the most privileged sensory channels used to interact with the environment. The importance of vision is strongly embedded in the organization of the brain as about one-third of its cortical surface is involved in visual functions. It is therefore not surprising that the absence of vision from birth, or the loss of vision later in life, has huge consequences, both anatomically and functionally. We have shown in previous studies that, although the visual system undergoes some atrophic changes following the loss of vision at birth, it is nonetheless present and can be activated by a variety of non-visual stimuli such as touch, audition and even smell. In this project, we will address a number of critical and timely questions on the effects of late-onset blindness on the organization of the brain connectome and its associated compensatory behavioral changes. The specific and novel goals of this project are 1) to investigate the pathways through which non-visual information is conveyed to the occipital cortex in late blind individuals 2) to investigate the role of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA in the occipital cortex in cross-modal neuroplastic responses in blind individuals, and 3) to clarify the brain microstructural and functional organization in late-onset blindness via the dynamics of neuroplastic adaptations, following the loss of vision in adult life. Our results will further our understanding of the capacity of the blind brain for plastic changes. With the advent of novel methods for restoring vision in blind individuals, this will be instrumental in defining the optimal window to help them "see".

column37: We previously discovered pathologic changes in gene expression that appear to trigger the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and showed that they were mediated by "epigenetic changes" in gene function. Epigenetic means that the changes in DNA function occur without changes in DNA sequence. The changes we identified were caused by increased DNA methylation (addition of methyl groups) of certain genes. We have identified two new gene mutations which may regulate these same DNA methylation epigenetic pathways. If confirmed this would show for the first time that mutations of genes or environmental factors can both result in epigenetic changes that promote development of PAH. Two crucial genes which regulate DNA methylation are DNMT3A and TET2. Mutations which impair their function promote the development of vascular disease, such as coronary disease. We hypothesize that mutations in DNMT3A and TET2 genes contribute to PAH development and represent new therapeutic targets. Our research is uniquely supported by our established access to the genetic material and clinical information from 2500 patients in the PAH Biobank (US) and two large biobanks in the United Kingdom and at Johns Hopkins University, as well as the expertise available at our state of the art translational research facility at Queen's University, the Queen's CardioPulmonary Unit (QCPU). We will test new anti-inflammatory therapies for PAH in these novel mouse models as a step to translating this knowledge into therapy for human PAH patients.

column36: Brain cell volume reduction in animal models and people with intracerebral hemorrhagic stroke.
column37: An intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke caused by a bleed into the brain. Almost 40% of ICH patients die, many in days. The bleed destroys brain tissue, alters the delicate balance of important ions and water, and takes up valuable space within the skull. This causes pressure to rise. High intracranial pressure (ICP) impairs blood flow to the brain, causing more damage and sometimes death. The body has several natural ways to compensate and help lower ICP. Our animal research has found an additional mechanism. We discovered that cell shrinkage (CS) occurs in areas located away from the damaged tissue. Some cell bodies shrink by up to 50%. This means that those parts of the brain become a bit smaller. This frees up space within the skull and limits the rise in ICP. While this helps reduce the risk of death, it still commonly occurs after very large ICHs. Thus, we need to do more to treat high ICP. Our research will study patients who died from a large ICH. Using their brain tissue, we will look for whether CS occurs in humans, if there are any harmful effects, and we will examine how CS occurs. Concurrently, we will use rat models of severe ICH to determine how age, hypertension and ICP control therapies affect CS in male and female rats. These are clinically important factors that we will incorporate into our research to improve the validity of our animal studies (e.g., to explain the negative impact of hypertension). We will also look to better document how CS affects neuronal health and function. Finally, we will examine rat and human tissue to determine the mechanisms underlying CS. For example, we know that movement of potassium, chloride and water across a cell membrane is very important to cell size, and so we will study these and other mechanisms. Eventually, we hope to safely manipulate CS to improve the medical management of high ICP after large strokes and other brain injuries, thereby improving survival and recovery.

column36: Impact of transient neonatal hyperoxia on skeletal muscle development: Relevance for impaired exercise capacity after preterm birth.
column37: In Canada, it is estimated that 8% of children and young adults were born preterm (<37 weeks of gestation), a condition that is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Thanks to the advancements in medical care, the survival rate of the infants born preterm has strongly increased in the last few decades. However, long-term studies showed that the development of different organs, such as the lungs, heart and central nervous system is affected in preterm born individuals, which results in higher risk of developing different disorders. Moreover, accumulating evidence also indicates that preterm born individuals have a reduced exercise capacity. While skeletal muscles constitute about 35-40% of total body weight and play crucial roles in movement and exercise, it is unknown how they are affected by preterm birth. The current project proposes to use an animal model that mimics the harmful conditions associated with preterm birth (newborn rats transiently exposed to high levels of oxygen) to characterize its impact on skeletal muscle development, growth, and regeneration. Furthermore, we propose to investigate the potential of physical exercise to mitigate the detrimental effects of preterm-birth related conditions on skeletal muscle. Considering the growing number of young adults who were born preterm, who are at higher risk for different disorders, it is important to understand how skeletal muscles are affected in this condition, and which aberrant mechanism can be targeted to prevent or treat these skeletal muscle disorders.

column36: The development of a risk of bias assessment tool for network meta-analysis
column37: Being able to critically appraise the findings of studies is central to informed decision-making in patient care. Patients, healthcare providers and policy makers (i.e. knowledge users [KUs]) need the highest quality studies to make decisions about which treatments should be used in healthcare practice. The most reliable way to answer questions using research is a systematic review, which is the most common type of knowledge synthesis used to summarize all existing medical literature on a topic. These reviews are needed to support patient care, develop policies, and assess new drugs and devices. Currently there are many different types of systematic reviews, such as scoping reviews, reviews with meta-analysis, and reviews with network meta-analysis (NMA). Reviews with NMA can rank and order medicines used for the same medical condition by their safety and effectiveness. Many tools are used to assess the potential biases in these different reviews. For example, the AMSTAR checklist assesses whether a review with pairwise meta-analysis (MA) has been well conducted. The ROBIS tool assesses whether a MA is at risk of containing dangerous biases that may distort the findings. However, no tool currently exists specifically to assess the risk of bias in a review with NMA. Our project has 4 objectives. First we will identify biases that are found in NMAs through a methodological review (a type of knowledge synthesis where all the evidence on a given methods topic is identified and described). Second, we will select the most important biases to be included in the tool through an agreement-building process (Delphi) and finalise the tool. Third, we will use 3 examples to test the usability of the tool through an evaluative pilot study, and four, develop a KT strategy. Our outputs will be 4 journal articles, presentations, video, webinar and plain language products. Our newly developed tool will help KUs choose the highest quality NMA, which will improve evidenced-based care.

column36: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT): arrhythmogenic mechanisms and personalized intervention
column37: Certain heritable arrhythmias, like catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) have a high risk of triggering sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) in some afflicted individuals. Most cases of CPVT are related to inherited mutations in a large protein in the cardiac cells (cardiomyocytes) called the ryanodine receptor (RyR). We propose to develop means of better understanding the risk of SCA in specific individuals by understanding how the mutation affects the structure of the RyR and developing highly sensitive and personalized means of assessing the risk of SCA using a sophisticated human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hiPSC-CM) approach to reduce mortality rates. This is important to patients' treatment because: 1) Different patients react differently to drug treatments. In some cases, beta-adrenergic receptor blockers do not work; in other cases, flecainide may be used, but not without risk. The hiPSC-CMs can be used directly to test the effect of various types of beta-blockers (including carvedilol, which has multiple effects) without having to pre-screen them in patients. In particular, this study will allow us to test whether there is a correlation between drug response in patients and drug response in the CMs which will help one derive more informed decisions on treatment regime in the future. 2) The hiPSC-CMs will be used to establish causality. It is crucial to know whether these inherited mutations cause this often lethal arrhythmia, as this informs family members with the same mutation and who are thus at risk.

column36: Prebiotic supplementation in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a serious autoimmune disease where the body destroys its' own insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. T1D incidence in Canada has grown faster than the global average. The changing environment in which we live is likely driving this increase. Disruptions in our gut microbiota, or all of the microorganisms that live in our intestinal tract, has been identified as one factor that could cause our intestines to become more leaky and lead to inflammation and the development of T1D. Prebiotic fibre on the other hand is a type of fibre that promotes the growth of healthy bacteria in the gut, reduces inflammation and improves the intestinal barrier so it is less leaky. Prebiotic fibre has also been shown to improve glucose control which is important in preventing complications of T1D. At the time that a person is diagnosed with T1D, they have some remaining beta cell function which is important because it is associated with lower risk of hypoglycemia, better glycemic control and lower risk of long-term complications. We recently showed that prebiotic fibre could increase C-peptide, a marker of residual beta cell function, and reduce the frequency of hypoglycemia in children who had T1D for at least 1 year. Starting the prebiotic fibre earlier could improve outcomes even further. The goal of this randomized clinical trial is to examine the ability of prebiotic fibre supplementation to reduce blood glucose fluctuation (less hypoglycemia and better overall glucose control) as well as improve residual beta cell function, inflammation and intestinal barrier function in patients newly diagnosed with T1D. Since prebiotic fibre is known to alter the gut microbiota and the metabolites they produce, we will measure these outcomes as well. Our ultimate goal is to identify new therapies that could be given to newly diagnosed patients with T1D to improve their immediate and long-term health.

column36: Novel Infection Resistant Coating in an Era of Drug Resistant Bacteria for the Treatment and Prevention of Medical Device Infection
column37: Urinary catheters are plastic (polymer) tubes inserted into the bladder to drain urine. Over 25% of hospitalized patients are catheterized during their stay. These tubes are a major cause of infection in hospitalized patients result in prolonged hospital stays with skyrocketing health care costs and may result in death. Currently, antibiotics are our only method of attempting to deal with these infections, but they do not work well due to the fact that bacteria can form special communities on the surface of the catheter-known as biofilms-which render the antibiotics ineffective. In addition, bacteria can activate specialized mechanisms that inactivate antibiotics-to form antibiotics resistant bacteria-making them difficult to kill. The technology in our grant is the latest breakthrough at UBC based on the development of a special coating. Our coating is utilizing a special mechanism to prevent infection- by killing and preventing the bacterial adhesion- to impart long-term activity (>90 days) unlike competing technologies. Our technique both PREVENT and TREAT catheter associated urinary tract infections unlike any other catheter technology available. Our preliminary studies show that the new coating prevents the biofilm on catheters for extended periods in both test tubes and in a mouse model. However, we need to further test how effective the coating is against different types of bacteria using large animal models that is similar to human anatomy. Furthermore, we need to ensure that the coating can be easily and safely produced and have good storage stability, and can be sterilized. The overall goal is to attract investment and prove that we can transfer this technology to other industries for use in the medical field. Although the current project is specifically looking at catheter infections, the data from this project will also provide a general method for preventing infections associated with other medical devices which is a major problem in our hospitals.

column36: Protein phase separation: A new mechanism of protein function regulation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
column37: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) causes the devastating lung disease tuberculosis (TB). Nearly two million people die from TB annually. Mtb infects and grows inside macrophages, a type of white blood cell present in the lungs of patients. Within these host cells, the bacteria are hidden from the human immune response and are protected from drug therapy, thus creating challenges for anti-TB drug discovery. With the increasing prevalence of multi-drug and extensively drug resistant tuberculosis worldwide, there is a pressing need for new approaches to combat TB. In this research project, we will study how a very exciting, recently discovered phenomenon, called "protein phase separation", helps Mtb survive within human macrophages. Phase separation is a localized clustering of a protein into a microscopic liquid- like "droplet". More specifically, we will investigate how intracellular signaling processes control the phase separation of a transporter protein that is used by Mtb to build its protective cell wall. These processes, which lead to the chemical modification of the transporter with phosphate groups, allow Mtb to sense environmental stimuli and mount appropriate responses for survival in human cells. We will also investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms by which phase separation occurs and how it changes the function of the transporter protein. Our research will yield new fundamental information about protein regulation in bacteria such as Mtb. This may also lead to the discovery of previously unrecognized cellular processes amenable for anti-TB drug intervention.

column36: Materials and Technologies for Highly Sensitive Biomarker Analysis of Extracellular Vesicles Toward Cancer Diagnostics
column37: Cells in body release nanoscale particles called extracellular vesicles (EVs). These particles are 10 000-times smaller than a grain of sand and contain proteins and other biological molecules that can indicate the health or disease status of the cell that released them. EVs are constantly being released by cells and we, and others, have shown that they can be readily found in the blood. Just like healthy cells, diseased cells (e.g. cancer cells) also release EVs. The EVs released by diseased cells are different than those released from healthy cells, having their own unique 'barcode.' If there were a way to scan this barcode, we would be able to identify diseases such as cancer by simply scanning through the EVs in the blood. Cancer and other diseases could thus be diagnosed from a simple blood test. We have been working towards detecting diseased EVs by identifying a protein signature that gives them a unique barcode. We scan for this barcode using fluorescent antibodies that bind to the EVs and cause them to 'light up.' A challenge is that EVs may only have 20-30 copies of the proteins of interest, giving a dim signal that is difficult to detect. What is needed is new super- bright fluorescent materials that can bind the proteins of interest and give an easily detectable signal. At present, such methods are lacking. We propose to address this challenge in two ways: (1) the use of advanced fluorescent materials, called "quantum dots" and "polymer dots," to provide larger signals when analyzing EVs via current standard methods; and (2) the novel use of advanced microscopy technology and methods to enable analyses down to the level of just one biological molecule of interest per EV. By developing tools to detect as little as one molecule per EV, we will be able to maximize our ability to find EVs from diseased cells, and use them to diagnose and monitor different diseases from a simple blood test.

column36: Using super-resolution microscopy to define the role of caveolin-1 in cancer
column37: Caveolin-1 (CAV1) expression is associated with poor outcomes in aggressive breast and prostate cancer. CAV1 is found in caveolae, small invaginations in the plasma membrane of cells and also in flat domains called scaffolds. Understanding the contribution of CAV1 to cancer malignancy requires defining its role in these two domains. However, caveolae and scaffolds are both smaller than the diffraction limit of light, making them difficult to visualize by standard microscopy. We have developed super-resolution microscopy and artificial intelligence-based computational approaches to study this protein in each of these membrane domains and will now apply them to study CAV1 function in tumor progression and more particularly in tumor cell metabolism. Cancer cells switch their metabolism from mitochondrial respiration, that generates high energy for each molecule of glucose consumed by the cell, to a fermentation like process that does not produce high energy levels but does produce the building blocks (sugars, nucleic acids, amino acids, fats) required to build the cellular macromolecules (proteins, DNA, membranes) that are necessary for cell growth and division. A critical protein that promotes the metabolic switch of cancer cells is pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), whose expression in place of the more ubiquitously expressed PKM1, slows metabolic supply to mitochondria. We have found that CAV1 interacts with PKM2 and will now study which CAV1 domain (caveolae or scaffolds) interacts with PKM2. We will test how CAV1 regulates tumor cell metabolism and impacts tumor cell survival and migration and assess whether available clinical inhibitors of metabolism may be useful for the treatment of aggressive CAV1-positive cancers. This work will advance our understanding of highly aggressive breast and prostate cancers and will help us identify new mechanisms and molecules that can be targeted to treat these cancers.

column36: Evaluating the impact of a mandatory switching policy for biosimilars
column37: Biologic drugs have revolutionized the care of patients with many chronic diseases including inflammatory diseases (including rheumatic and bowel diseases). Biologic drugs are extremely expensive, and three of the most costly drugs to the Canadian health care system are biologics used in inflammatory diseases. Now that patents are expiring on the oldest biologic drugs, it is possible to make cheaper copies of these products, known as biosimilars. However, because biologics are complex drugs with a complicated manufacturing process, it is not possible to make sure that biosimilars are exact replicas of biologics. Despite small differences, biosimilars are expected to be as safe and effective as biologics, and offer the chance to save millions of dollars to the health care system. This money could be spent treating other patients, with no impact to the outcomes of patients using biosimilars. British Columbia introduced a policy which mandated the use biosimilars instead of biologics in 2019. This project aims to study the outcomes of patients in British Columbia who are using biosimilars. Our findings will provide valuable and timely information to people with chronic diseases using biosimilars and biologics, as well as to health care professionals and health care policy makers who are seeking to deliver the best possible health care to their populations.

column36: Using imaging to understand how parental diet programs offspring brain structure
column37: Many people suffer from disorders such as anxiety, depression, ADHD, and autism. Eating a high fat diet and being overweight during pregnancy and while breast feeding increases the risk of these disorders in offspring. What dads eat may increase risk as well. column36: The role of CK2 in translational reprogramming in cancer
column37: Signaling pathways convey information from the environment to regulate fundamental cellular processes including the synthesis of proteins. Cancer cells are characterized by abnormal function of signaling pathways and protein synthesis machinery. This distinguishes malignant and normal cells thus providing sufficient therapeutic window to target abnormal activity of signaling pathways and/or translational machinery to selectively eradicate cancer cells while causing minimal damage in normal tissue. Such therapeutic efforts are underexploited largely because of the incomplete understanding of the "nuts and bolts" that underpin dysregulation of signaling pathways and protein synthesis in neoplasia. Our labs have uncovered that CK2 which is a pivotal component of cellular signaling circuitry, may play a major role in translational reprogramming in cancer. We will follow up on these studies and investigate the role of CK2 signaling to protein synthesis machinery in breast cancer. Our motivation to focus on neoplasia of the breast comes from well-documented aberrant function of CK2 and translational machinery in this type of cancer. In addition, our team possesses the expertise and state-of-the-art models to study this disease. Collectively, our proposed studies promise to reveal unprecedented insights into orchestration of signaling and protein synthesis programs in breast cancer that could ultimately guide the development of new therapeutic approaches. Finally, since dysregulation of CK2 and protein synthesis apparatus is observed over a broad range of cancers, these data may be applicable to malignancies arising from tissues other than the breast.

column36: Simplifying and improving the pre-surgical evaluation of epilepsy
column37: Epilepsy can strike anyone at any time. It is therefore time to offer more effective treatment options for the 70.000 Canadians suffering from drug-resistant seizures. Surgery is the only hope to cure focal epilepsy. However, only 500-1000 epilepsy surgeries are performed each year across Canada. Reasons for this immense gap include the complexity and availability of pre-surgical evaluation. It requires a 1-2 week hospitalization for seizure recording. Developing a shorter 24-hr evaluation that does not require capturing seizures, avoiding seizure-related complications, and that can outperform the current approach (only 50% of patients are postsurgically seizure-free) would be a game changer: It will significantly increase its accessibility, reduce costs drastically, and improve surgical outcomes. This project aims for a time efficient, accurate, and minimally invasive presurgical evaluation. (i) Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) is the ideal technique to establish seizure-independent markers, as it is the most direct tool to define the epileptogenic zone. We will develop for patients requiring iEEG new seizure-independent markers to identify the epileptogenic zone within 24 hrs, thus making recording of seizures unnecessary resulting in shorter hospitalization. (ii) Intracranial EEG has major limitations: it is invasive, costly, and has limited coverage of the brain. A translational approach to non-invasive techniques is necessary. We will develop non-invasive markers based on the combination of 256-channel EEG (in clinical routine 19 channels are used) and multimodal magnetic resonance imaging to identify the epileptogenic zone within 24 hrs. Our new approaches will be compared to localization accuracy and surgical outcome obtained with the standard 1-2 week evaluation including prolonged EEG monitoring. This research is timely and will be of benefit for the many patients with focal epilepsy who need epilepsy surgery to cure their seizures.

column36: Interrogation of cell surface antigens on B lineage cells using structurally unique variable lymphocyte receptor antibodies of the evolutionarily distant sea lamprey
column37: Cell surface receptors function as sensors that receive signals from the environment and transmit these signals to allow for appropriate cellular responses. These responses range from cell activation or inhibition to proliferation, differentiation and cell death. The cell surface receptor composition reflects the biological and functional requirements of various cell lineages of the immune system and aberrant receptor expression can interfere with a correctly functioning immune system. Additionally, cell surface receptors can be modified by various protein modifications that alter their functional characteristics. We identified one such protein modification - tyrosine sulfation - that is of particular relevance to human memory B cells and plasma cells using the variable lymphocyte receptor (VLR) antibody system of the evolutionarily distant sea lamprey as novel biomedical research reagent. The radically different protein architecture and the unique origins of VLR antibodies allow these reagents to bind to targets, which cannot be readily recognized by conventional antibodies. In our research proposal, we aim to (i) investigate tyrosine sulfation as novel regulatory mechanism controlling human memory B cells and plasma cells and to (ii) explore memory B cell and plasma cell specific cell surface structures identified using monoclonal VLR antibodies, determine the molecular identity of these structures and define their functional properties. The proposed study is a structure-based approach to identify and functionally characterize unique epitopes on B cells, particularly those generated by modified cell surface proteins. The distinct binding characteristics with which VLR antibodies recognize their targets will establish a new line of investigation in addressing B cell function in health and disease.

column37: Food allergy impacts 1-in-2 Canadian households, and up to 80% of severe allergic reactions in children are triggered by food. In Canada, approximately every 10 minutes, there is an Emergency Room (ER) visit for food-induced allergic reaction. In the event of an allergic reaction, treatment guidelines recommend that children be transported by an ambulance to an ER for observation, even if symptoms are mild or have stopped. The rationale behind the need for observation in the ER is that some patients are at risk of delayed reactions which can be life-threatening. The delayed allergic reaction consists of a return of symptoms after a period in which patients seem to recover from the first reaction successfully. Unfortunately, research data on the frequency, timing, severity, and predictors of delayed allergic reactions are very limited. As a result, many children are also admitted to the hospital or observed in the ER for long hours to increase the chance of detecting delayed reactions. The unpredictability of reactions and anticipation of ER visits can have a significant psychosocial impact on children and their caregivers. In fact, surveys of Canadian families showed that almost half of respondents described their anxiety level as 8 out of 10 or higher. The main objective of this study is to determine which combination of risk factors identify children with allergic reactions who are at risk of developing delayed reactions. From this knowledge, we can develop appropriate guidelines so that children at high risk are monitored appropriately, whereas those at no or low risk can be discharged from the ER once they became asymptomatic. These guidelines will be highly beneficial to our community and to the healthcare system.

column36: Making training better: Error augmentation motor learning in stroke.
column37: Many Canadians each year suffer stroke, and this number is increasing as the population ages. Although many people survive stroke, they still have significant problems recovering movement in their affected arm. We know that intensive exercise is important for the recovery of movement in people who have had a stroke. However, we do not fully understand what type of exercise and how much exercise is needed to get the best results. We also do not know whether people with different types of brain damage need the same type of exercise. We will address these questions in a study combining high intensity exercise tailored to the individual together with personalized feedback. Our objectives are to determine 1) the effectiveness of the new personalized treatment approach, 2) whether the amount of training affects the outcome, and 3) whether the amount of damage to brain regions that control movements can tell us about how well a person will recover arm movement using this approach. With technology experts in Israel, we designed a state-of-the-art training device using an arm support and virtual reality. The training uses a special type of error feedback to help the learner automatically use more elbow movement when reaching for objects. This is done by changing the type of feedback the learner receives. We will compare the effect of reaching training in three groups of people who have finished their rehabilitation but are within 12 months of their stroke. After evaluating the person's arm function and scanning their brain to measure how much damage there is from the stroke, individuals will be assigned to different practice groups. Exercise will be done 3 times/wk for 9 wk. We will measure progress after 3, 6 and 9 wk of practice to find out which exercise dose have the best results. We will also measure progress again 4 wks after the end of the training (wk 13) to see if improvements last. Research outcomes are important for guiding treatments for motor recovery.

column36: Experiences of care aides in long-term care with residents having psychological trauma
column37: Estimates of posttraumatic stress disorder are 9.2% in the general population and as high as 22% in long-term care (LTC) homes. Residents with past trauma have more agitation and aggressive behaviours in response to triggers that may be mistaken for responsive behaviours of dementia. Care aides frequently experience the resultant responsive behaviours (e.g., being yelled at, hit), that are a significant contributor to care aide burnout. These challenges for care aides and residents have been sharply exacerbated by the pandemic. We located no studies in the literature focused on how care aides manage these residents. Therefore, we recently completed a short trauma assessment administered to over 4000 care aides. The responses revealed that care aides frequently encounter residents with traumatic histories and that they struggle to find strategies with which to assist them. Our objective is to explore the impact of residents' past and present psychological trauma on quality of worklife for frontline staff in long-term care. We will conduct interviews with care aides to understand some of the complex ways that responsive behaviours affect the quality of work life when caring those with dementia and a history of trauma. We will uncover their unique challenges and how they cope and use this information to explore what support care aides would find most valuable and how managers could assist them and ultimately contribute to improving quality of care for residents with a history of psychological trauma. The results of this study will guide intervention development to assist care aides to care for these residents. We will share our study findings with nursing homes managers and directors of care. Together, we will discuss our results and generate recommendations on how best to assist care aides working with this population to improve quality of care and life for nursing home residents with dementia and a history of past trauma.

column36: Treating multiple forms of age-related cognitive decline with cannabinoid compounds: efficacy and potential mechanisms
column37: Canada is facing a health care crisis of epic proportions because of the large aging cohort of baby boomers. One area of particular concern is the numbers of individuals that will descend into various forms of age-related cognitive decline including the most common Alzheimer's disease (AD). As of today, there are no particularly effective treatments on the horizon, insufficient long-term care facilities available, and no clear plan to deal with this emerging problem. For example, Alzheimer's disease is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder that currently affects approximately 500,000 individuals in Canada. This number is expected to increase to 937,000 by 2031. This means that the prevalence of dementia in Canada will almost double in 10 years with the costs increasing 10-fold. The financial costs associated with dementia are predicted to reach $16 billion a year by 2038. More importantly, AD has devastating effects on the quality of life of the afflicted individual, and caregivers bear a heavy financial and emotional load. This research program will focus on compounds found in marijuana as potential treatments for age-related cognitive decline. There is preliminary evidence, in animal models of AD, that cannabinoid compounds can dramatically slow or even reverse brain pathology and cognitive impairments. This treatment approach is exciting because these compounds appear to modulate multiple mechanisms of neural dysfunction and they are currently available, inexpensive, and relatively safe for human consumption. We will use various animal models of age-related cognitive decline and advanced techniques to assess functional, representational, and biochemical changes in brain areas implicated in learning and memory functions in subjects treated with cannabinoid compounds. These treatments are predicted to reverse brain pathology and prevent the descent into dementia.

column36: Identification and prediction of sex-specific cardiovascular causes of death and outcomes in people with diabetes mellitus post myocardial infarction (SCD-DM-MI)
column37: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major public health crisis in Canada: by 2030, over 1 in 5 individuals are projected to develop DM resulting in total costs to the Canadian healthcare system of $336 billion over the next 10 years. The presence of DM is one of the strongest risk factors for the development of cardiovascular (CV) diseases including heart failure (HF), myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and CV death. Despite nearly half of all people with type 2 DM in Canada are biologically female, there has been surprisingly little evaluation of the sex specific distribution of clinical predictors for cardiovascular outcomes. As highlighted by consensus guidelines, the distribution, predictors, and mechanisms associated with sex differences relating to cardiovascular outcomes among people with DM has historically neglected. This knowledge gap is even more apparent in people with DM who have had a recent heart attack, where the risk of recurrent cardiovascular events is significantly increased. Clinical variables combined with blood-based proteins (biomarkers) allow us to create models that can more precisely predict clinical outcomes. Furthermore, using multiple biomarkers, we can create 'biomarker profiles' that allow us to determine how and why certain people develop adverse outcomes. We propose the 'Identification and prediction of sex-specific cardiovascular causes of death and outcomes in people with Diabetes Mellitus post Myocardial Infarction' (SCD-DM-MI) study to address these knowledge gaps. We will use several large clinical trial databases with large number of biomarkers that have been measured to identify the clinical factors and biomarker profiles associated with specific cardiovascular outcomes. This will lay the foundation to allow us to target health services interventions and therapies to those who need it the most and identify new possible drug targets.

column36: Single-cell approaches to characterize and target the cellular reservoirs of HIV infection
column37: Antiretroviral therapy blocks HIV replication and extends the life of people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, it does not eliminate the virus and should be taken for life. In addition to persistent stigma, lifelong treatment entails both health risks to PLHIV and a significant economic burden to society. As such, there is a desperate need to develop a cure for HIV infection. HIV persists in cells called "HIV reservoirs" for the lifetime of PLHIV. Reservoirs are the reason why antiretroviral therapy should be taken for life. In our quest to find a cure for HIV infection, there is a need to either completely eliminate these reservoirs, or reduce their size to allow the immune system to control them naturally (like herpes viruses). From more than 20 years of research on HIV reservoirs, it is now clear that the size of the HIV reservoir slowly decays with time on therapy, but this decay is too slow to eliminate the virus during a lifetime: HIV hides in cells that have the ability to proliferate or to persist in deep tissues such as lymph nodes and bone marrow. In this project, we propose to use novel state-of-the-art technologies developed in our laboratory to characterize and eliminate HIV reservoirs. We developed a novel assay that allows us to visualize and characterize single infected cells in blood and tissues from PLHIV. Our goal is to identify the immunological and virological features of these cells. In particular, we will focus on 1) the nature of the cells in which HIV persists to identify mechanisms that lead to their persistence and proliferation and 2) the nature of the virus to understand how it escapes recognition from the immune system. We will then functionally validate our findings by testing strategies to target these vulnerabilities in test tubes. By performing these studies, we believe we will have a better understanding of the cellular and viral factors that should be targeted to eliminate HIV reservoirs.

column36: High Resolution Structure of Human ABCA4, an ATP-binding Cassette (ABC) Lipid Importer Associated with Inherited Retinal Degenerative Diseases
column37: Inherited retinal degenerative diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders that are a major cause of blindness in the world population. They typically result in progressive loss in vision due to mutations in genes encoding proteins essential for the function and survival of rod and cone photoreceptor cells. Mutations in the gene encoding the membrane transporter ABCA4 are known to cause Stargardt disease and related retinal degenerative diseases with a prevalence of about 1 in 8000 individuals worldwide. Affected individuals typically experience loss in central vision in their first or second decade of life followed by progressive loss in peripheral vision in later stages of the disease. Currently, there are no treatments for ABCA4-related diseases. We have previously shown that ABCA4 is present in rod and cone photoreceptors where it functions as an ATP-dependent membrane transporter - facilitating the removal of a retinoid compound that is produced as part of the visual process. The loss in ABCA4 retinoid transport activity leads to the accumulation of toxic retinoids that cause rod and cone photoreceptor cell death and a loss in vision. Although the role of ABCA4 in vision and retinal degeneration is generally understood, currently we know little about the molecular structure of ABCA4, the mechanism by which ABCA4 transports its substrate across membranes, and how disease-causing mutations affect the structure of ABCA4. The goal of this project is to determine the high resolution structure of ABCA4 in the presence and absence of its substrates using 'state-of-the art' cryoelectron microscopy, define how ABCA4 transports it substrate across membranes using biochemical and biophysical techniques, identify and characterize regions that are important in function of ABCA4. This information will serve as a basis for developing novel drug and gene based therapeutic strategies to prevent or slow vision loss in affected individuals.

column36: How Can Facilitation be Used as an Implementation Science Strategy? An Exploratory study on the "Lived Experience" of Facilitation in implementing Canada's Mental Health Recovery Guidelines
column37: The goal of this project is to understand the role of facilitation or coaching in implementing Canada's mental health recovery guidelines. We will conduct qualitative individual interviews (in-person or online) with members of the Implementation Teams (n=56) and current and former members of the research team who were facilitators/coaches (n=10). Nine focus groups with Implementation Teams and with facilitators will be conducted to explore topics emerging from the interviews. A direct output of this research will be the production of a Guide for Facilitators that will be added to the Recovery-Guideline Implementation Toolkit website. Our model for implementing the Canadian Recovery Guidelines is unique and if more widely adopted stands to make an important contribution to the scaling up of the Recovery Guidelines into housing services.

column36: Opioid Overdose-Related Cardiac Arrest: What are the Best Interventions?
column37: Opioid overdoses have resulted in over 8000 deaths in Canada in last two years. Unfortunately, the COVID-19 pandemic has only increased the mortality rate. An opioid overdose causes an individual to stop breathing, which can be effectively treated with rescue breaths and naloxone (the opioid antidote). However, if these initial treatments are not quickly performed or ineffective, the lack of oxygen will result in patient's heart to stop-a "cardiac arrest". Thus, every single opioid-related death has experienced a cardiac arrest. Knowledge of how rescuers can best respond to cardiac arrests due to opioid overdoses is urgently needed. Unfortunately, there is a paucity of studies examining opioid-related cardiac arrest; therefore, there is a lack of evidence to guide bystanders or professional rescuers on how best to intervene. Specifically, there is controversy regarding the benefits of bystander-performed rescue breaths (in addition to chest compressions) and paramedic-delivered naloxone. The goal of this project is to determine the best resuscitative strategies for opioid-related cardiac arrest to inform national and international guidelines. Within this project we will create the largest and most comprehensive dataset of cardiac arrest cases due to opioid overdose in the world, complete with detailed data on bystander and professional interventions, and patient-oriented outcomes. We will build on the existing British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry and link to other administrative data sources. We will analyze this data to determine the optimal bystander interventions, as well as the therapies paramedics should offer. We will determine how rescuers can identify that a cardiac arrest is due to an opioid-overdose. In addition, we will examine the benefit of public access opioid overdose kits and their optimal locations. Finally, we will implement a knowledge translation and dissemination plan in collaboration with key knowledge-users.

column36: Developing a Measure of Resiliency-related Adaptive Self-Capacities for Rehabilitation Intervention
column37: Resiliency, defined as a critical process of adaptation to changing life circumstances, is a relatively new area of interest in rehabilitation. Rehabilitation interventions typically aim to reduce impairments and enhance functioning, although some programs aim to prepare people with disabilities for life situations, and thus may promote resiliency. No measures of resiliency exist that are geared to the types of adversities commonly experienced by individuals with disabilities. As a result, research on resiliency in the rehabilitation context has been greatly hampered. We have developed a preliminary version of a measure of four resiliency-related adaptive self-capacities: Activity Self-efficacy, Marshaling Resources and Supports, Life Situation Adaptability, and Envisioning a Positive Future. In the proposed research we will pursue three objectives. First, we will ask clients with disabilities, caregivers, and service providers to describe factors and processes that affect the development of these capacities. Second, we will finalize the development of a reliable and valid measure of these capacities. Third, we will conduct a longitudinal study to investigate the ability of the measure to capture change across three types of interventions differing in their ability to enhance these capacities: (1) participation-oriented and transition programs, which are hypothesized to have the greatest effects, (2) arts- or activity-based programs, and (3) standard therapy services, which may have lesser effects as they focus on impairment or function rather than on preparing people for life situations. This practice-based research will inform and potentially change service providers' perspectives and practice with respect to understanding, measuring, and optimizing resiliency-related adaptive self-capacities in rehabilitation interventions. Further, this research has the potential to enhance client outcomes by informing the design and delivery of rehabilitation interventions.

column36: Impact of an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker in Aortic Stenosis - a Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: With aging, the aortic valve calcifies, thus the opening of the valve decreases, blocking the ejection of the blood in the body: this is aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis is the most common cardiovascular disease in developed countries after coronary artery disease and systemic arterial hypertension. When the stenosis progresses, the heart needs to work harder to eject the blood into the body. This increase in workload leads to heart failure and death without treatment. The only available treatment is to replace the stenosed valve by a prosthesis. There is no medical treatment to slow down the progression of the aortic stenosis. Despite aortic stenosis is perceived as a "men disease", 50% of patients are women. Unfortunately, the vast majority of studies have been performed in men or male animals. Women are often referred later for valve replacement, with more symptoms and worse heart function. We recently demonstrate that, for the same severity of the disease, women have less calcification in their valve but more fibrosis. We also demonstrated that for the same valve disease, women have more fibrosis in the heart. In our mouse model, we also demonstrated that angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) was effective to slow down aortic stenosis progression in female but not in male. This finding was expected given that ARBs protect against fibrotic deposition. This may explain why some previous studies were not able to find an impact of ARBs in aortic stenosis progression. Indeed, studies enroll a vast majority of men. We believe that ARBs will be able to 1) slow down aortic stenosis progression, with more impact in women than in men and 2) reduce fibrosis deposition in the myocardium which will protect heart function. Thus, we propose to realize a randomized control trial comparing ARBs and placebo, in patients with aortic stenosis, to document the impact of the medication on aortic stenosis progression and heart fibrosis and dysfunction.

column36: The Role of BRIL in the Pathogenesis of Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
column37: Brittle bone disease, or osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), is a heritable disease that is mainly haracterized by bone fragility and short stature. In the large majority of patients, OI is caused by mutations in the two genes that encode collagen, the primary building block of bones. Other rare types of OI are caused by mutations in at least 10 other genes, all directly involved in the proper production and assembly of collagen. Two 'unique' types of OI are caused by mutation in a gene called BRIL (Bone-Restricted Ifitm-Like). The patients carrying such mutations in BRIL resemble other OI forms caused by collagen mutations with regard to many skeletal characteristics, such as fracture incidence, long-bone deformities, vertebral fractures and abnormal spine curvature. However, these 2 types have their own peculiar clinical and radiographic features not seen in other types of OI. The first shows uncontrolled bone masses growing on shafts of long bones like tibia and femurs, and fusion of the forearm bones. The second shows signs of bone that is very poorly mineralized. All patients identified have moderate to severe skeletal problems. However, it is still totally unknown how the mutant BRIL protein causes such variable and marked defects in the affected patients. The present project is aimed at elucidating some of these questions. We propose in part to characterize mouse models we have generated and which mimic symptoms observed in the patients. These will represent unique and valuable tools to study the mechanisms by which the mutant BRIL is detrimental to the skeleton. Furthermore, the outcome of our studies may be exploited to devise effective pharmacological treatments for OI, and be tested pre-clinically in the current mouse models.

column36: Making the most of Canada's "natural laboratory": advancing difference-in-differences methods for unpoolable data
column37: Canadian provincial health systems have been called a "policy laboratory" where variations in health policies and health care system structure can be used to inform learning health systems and improve population health. Capitalizing on innovation and experimentation across Canadian health systems generates valuable opportunities for natural experiments and cross-jurisdictional comparative analyses to better understand what works - and what doesn't. One analytic approach that can be used to learn from policy variation in Canada is difference-in-differences (DiD) estimation, which is a simple and effective way to identify causal effects in the absence of randomization. This approach allows us to move beyond quantifying the basic difference in two units to quantifying the effect of the exposure itself, a crucially important parameter in policy analysis. Given its ease of use and interpretability, DiD is an increasingly common analytic strategy in Canadian health economics and health services and policy research. However, Canadian administrative health data are largely siloed by province and cannot be combined into a single data set, which is a significant barrier to DiD estimation. Despite the indispensability of DiD for health services and policy research, no "best practices" currently exist for conducting DiD analyses in the absence of pooled data. The goal of this proposal is to develop strategies to overcome this barrier. Our team, which consists of experts in econometrics, biostatistics, and health services and policy research, will consider methods to generate DiD estimates using econometric/statistical theory, simulated data, and real Canadian data that is not siloed across provinces (e.g., the CCHS). The methods developed by this project will be relevant for both Canadian interprovincial comparisons and international comparisons.

column36: Imaging microvascular dysfunction: a new paradigm for early detection of heart failure
column37: Heart failure is not simply a condition that results from the classical "heart attack" due to blocked arteries. Many other conditions, such as diabetes and hypertension, damage heart muscle in ways that are poorly understood and not as well recognized. In fact, 50% of heart failure patients have hearts that pump out normal volumes of blood but are nonetheless functionally diseased. These patients have what cardiologists refer to as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). The condition develops silently and slowly and is not diagnosed until the late stages when irreversible heart damage has set in, at which time the 5-year death rate is on par with that of heart attack survivors at over 50%. The grim reality for this growing HFpEF population is that, unlike heart attack survivors, there is no defined diagnostic or proven therapy from which they can benefit. In this project, we propose a paradigm-shifting concept for early detection of HFpEF: detect microvascular dysfunction (mvD) throughout the body. The known comorbid conditions in HFpEF all involve damage to the small blood vessels early in HFpEF development. Our pilot data revealed mvD in skeletal muscle of diabetic rats when the heart was still structurally and functionally normal on ultrasound imaging. In other words, microvessel damage is an early biomarker of HFpEF. The objective of this project is to develop a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) biomarker of mvD in key organs, including the heart and skeletal muscle, with the long-term goal of using this biomarker for early detection and intervention before the HFpEF heart becomes stiff and dysfunctional. Through a transformative approach to the currently intractable task of early HFpEF diagnosis, we are taking the first critical step in detection technology development towards solving the dilemma of managing the HFpEF epidemic.

column36: Understanding Nuclear Envelope Reformation after Mitosis using Drosophila
column37: Cancer is caused by cells that divide excessively. Errors in cell division lead to genomic alterations that contribute to a further loss of control over cell division. Chromosomes are contained in a nucleus delineated by a nuclear envelope comprising several important proteins that ensure structural integrity and intracellular communication. When a cell enters mitosis, the nuclear envelope breaks down to allow the sorting and partitioning of two identical sets of chromosomes in mitosis. After mitosis, the nuclear envelope must reassemble around chromosomes in an orderly manner. Defects in nuclear envelope reformation can lead to fragmented nuclei and DNA damage, which can accelerate cancer progression. However, the immune system is capable of detecting and destroying cells with defective nuclei. The molecular mechanisms by which the nuclear envelope reassembles and can become defective are not completely understood. As genes and mechanisms controlling cell division have been strongly conserved in evolution, we will take advantage of the powerful and versatile model that is the fruit fly Drosophila. We will use flies and fly cells in culture to dissect in details the mechanisms of nuclear envelope reformation after mitosis. We will also determine the biological consequences of defects in this process in different tissue types of the developing animal. The new knowledge will serve as a basis to understand how nuclear envelope reformation defects can impact cancer progression in humans. It may also suggest potential new therapeutic avenues. In particular, interfering with nuclear envelope reformation in dividing cancer cells could enhance their destruction of by the patient's immune system.

column37: BACKGROUND: Cancer can spread from its original site of origin, most commonly the lung, breast or skin, to the brain in a process called brain metastasis. Brain metastasis occurs in approximately 20% of patients with solid cancers and comes with a devastating prognosis. Our research has established two distinct types of brain metastases, one that exhibits extensive cancer cell invasion deep into the distant brain and another that is non-invasive and remains localized in one area of the brain. Our results show that patients with abundant invasion have poor outcomes compared to those with minimal invasion. The reasons why some brain metastases exhibit invasion and others do not remain unknown and is an important area of study. We will focus our efforts on: 1) identifying factors present in the cancer cells themselves that promote invasion, 2) understanding how reactive astrocytes, a specific type of brain cell that interacts with tumor cells, can enhance cancer cell invasion and 3) determine the nature of the immune microenvironment that surrounds minimally invasive versus highly invasive brain metastases. These approaches will uncover a number of mechanisms that may explain why some brain metastases exhibit invasion and others do not. SIGNIFICANCE: Understanding why some brain metastases are invasive, and others are not, has important implications for patients. We have already begun to use this information to guide changes to local treatment of brain metastases, such as surgery or radiation treatment. However, diving deeper into the underlying biology of this invasive process will allow us to find new drivers that might represent attractive targets for intervention. The long-term goals of this work are to generate knowledge that can be used to develop new therapeutic strategies for better clinical management of patients with brain metastases.

column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious lung disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). This unique combination of methods overcomes the challenges that the heterogeneity and the size of proteasome machinery represent and enables discovering allosteric hotspots that regulate the proteasome function in vivo. column37: The cellular DNA damage repair response protects us from genotoxins and maintains the stability of our genome. When errors accumulate in the repair machinery, we are prone to both cancer and age-associated diseases. A functioning response is essential even for cancer cells, so a standard therapeutic approach is to overwhelm the repair response using "blunt instruments" such as ionizing radiation and genotoxic drugs. This level of targeting is crude by any measure, leading to unwanted toxicities and an incomplete response. The applied goal of our project is to better understand how mechanisms of DNA repair work, in order to sensitize cancer cells to existing therapies. While DNA damage takes many forms, Double Strand Breaks (DSBs) are particularly dangerous and their repair machinery is a compelling target for anticancer therapy. The response to a DSB involves interacting mechanisms that generate different repair outcomes. Our proposal seeks to establish the structural and functional properties of a master end-sensing complex that ultimately determines how the repair program unfolds. The key protein involved in this end-sensing complex is a massive kinase called DNA-PKcs. One of our major goals is to determine how this protein responds to the damage event itself, not just the signalling events that initiate them. They must work together to determine repair outcomes. To do this, we will use cutting-edge structural techniques, including Cryo-Electron Microscopy, Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange Mass Spectrometry and Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry. We have assembled an excellent team of collaborators to assist in translating molecular/structural insights into mechanistic validations at the cellular level, in order to define new strategies for targeting cancer.

column36: Decreasing Postoperative Blood Loss by Topical vs. Intravenous Tranexamic Acid in Open Cardiac Surgery (DEPOSITION) Trial
column37: During open heart surgery patients are at high risk of bleeding due to the extensive tissue damage required in gaining access to and fixing the heart. After surgery, excessive bleeding may be due to the inhibition of normal blood clot formation (coagulation system) or over-active break down of blood clotting (fibrinolytic system). Tranexamic acid (TxA) is a generic medication that blocks the fibrinolytic system, so called anti-fibrinolytics, and is used around the world during heart surgeries to stop or prevent excessive bleeding. TxA is usually given intravenously without issue but a serious side effect-seizures, occurs in about 1% of heart surgery patients-. Patients experiencing a seizure are more likely to have a stroke and stay longer in hospital. The risk of seizures increases with the intravenous TxA dose. Thus seizures can be reduced by lowering the TxA dose but at a lower dose the drug is less effective in preventing bleeding, putting patients at a higher risk for bleeding. In theory, applying TxA more directly to sites of tissue damage (local) rather than broadly to the circulatory system (systemic) should decrease side effects from intravenous TxA (seizures) by decreasing the ability of TxA to reach the brain and decrease the need for RBC transfusions by enhancing the blood-sparing effects of TxA. Results from our previous trial (DEPOSITION pilot) suggest that when TxA is poured over the heart (topical) rather than given intravenously fewer seizures and red blood cell (RBC) transfusions are observed. column36: MR-Linac guided adaptive radiotherapy in glioblastoma multiforme
column37: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary brain cancer. The treatment for GBM involves involves surgery, chemotherapy, and 6 weeks of radiation therapy. A major obstacle is that once radiation therapy begins, patients will receive the same radiation dose each day, even if the tumour changes. This may mean that the tumour may not be fully treated, or too much normal brain tissue is irradiated, leading to side effects. Clinicians currently do not adjust the radiation dose, because tumour sizes do not typically change until months after the treatment is complete. If there was a more sensitive tool that could be used earlier to determine how well the treatment is working, then we might be able to improve treatment outcomes and quality of life for GBM patients by adjusting the radiation dose for each individual, during the course of their treatment. We are developing advanced MRI scans in our lab. These scans have potential in determining how well the radiation treatment is working, before any change in tumour size happens. The scans are non-invasive and can be used repeatedly during treatment. The scans can be used to predict, early in the treatment process, which tumours will shrink after being treated. Our study will combine these advanced MRI scans with a new state-of-the-art MR-Linac treatment device that takes images while the patient is receiving their daily radiation dose. In our study, we will evaluate the MRI scans in GBM patients receiving radiation treatment to predict which part of the tumour will require more, the same, or less radiation dose. If the study is successful, the radiation dose will be delivered to the tumour more accurately, with less radiation given to surrounding healthy tissues. Increasing the dose to specific parts of the tumour may reduce the chances of a recurrence and improve outcomes. These methods are not limited to the brain, and can eventually be applied to other cancer types.

column37: Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreaks continue to increase in frequency. Recently, we have witnessed the largest EVD outbreak in recorded history in West Africa, and the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the second largest. Asymptomatic persistent Ebola virus (EBOV) infections in survivors could result in the initiation of new chains of transmission. This raises important public health concerns. Virus has been found in semen from EVD survivors >500 days following recovery and in the absence of clinical symptoms. Further, sexual transmission of EBOV from survivors resulted in new disease transmission events in multiple EVD outbreaks and represents a major public health and containment concern. Clinical trials with antivirals have suggested that drug treatment has no effect on reducing EBOV persistence within the male reproductive tract. Thus, it is imperative to identify how and when EBOV is transmitted to the male reproductive tract in order to identify treatment and care strategies for patients, as well as help guide containment efforts. The aim of this proposal is to characterize EBOV transmission to the testes and spread of the virus through sexual intercourse. Here, we will identify the mechanisms that help the virus enter into the reproductive tract and the interactions between host cells and the virus that allows for persistence in the testes. We will also examine how these factors relate to sexual transmission using a small animal model of infection. Further, we will also assess the long-term reproductive health complications that are encountered by both male and female EVD survivors in West Africa through questionnaires and analysis of historical samples. This investigation will address critical knowledge gaps in our understanding of this public health concern and will have important impacts for future outbreaks, including informing patient care strategies, outbreak containment and the long-term health of disease survivors.

column37: Our research is focused on improving the efficacy of oncolytic viruses for breast cancer treatment. Oncolytic viruses are viruses that infect and kill cancers without damaging normal organs. They can be administered to cancer patients intravenously to kill both the primary tumor mass as well as the metastases. Oncolytic viruses are considered a promising treatment for breast cancer, the most common cancer amongst women. Breast cancers are often disseminated to several organs and there is an urgent need for new therapeutic options for the most advanced and aggressive forms of the disease. Our findings will allow for a better selection of the patients to treat with oncolytic viruses and determine if some drugs that are commonly used for the treatment of breast cancer and that interfere with estrogen should be avoided during the time of the virus treatment. column36: The influence of sex-related differences in cognitive-motor integration on brain injury recovery in working-aged adults
column37: A prominent health issues facing Canadians is the impact of concussion on working aged adults. The effect of mild brain insult on one's functional abilities is not well understood. Our research has documented that "cognitive-motor integration" (CMI), or tasks which rely on rules to plan a movement, is impaired following concussion. The ability to think and act simultaneously is something crucial for safe performance at work, in the sport arena, and in activities of daily living. Our work has produced an effective assessment tool which sensitively detects functional impairment in working-aged adults at risk for dementia, and youth recovering from concussion. We have also demonstrated the neural underpinnings to this functional impairment. Separately, we have documented that different types of skilled movements are processed in separate brain networks, networks that are not the same for females and males. The goals of the present research are twofold. First, we will extend our CMI assessment research to middle-aged adults, a group not studied to date yet one in which individuals may have both concussion history and a known dementia risk. Second, we will characterize sex- and age-related differences in CMI in working aged adults, a time that spans nearly 50 years and passes into the post-menopausal age for women. Our methodological approaches will include integrated sensory, motor, and cognitive behavioural assessment as well as a neurophysiological (MRI) and hormonal measures. On a fundamental level, this project will provide a basic understanding of how our brains process rule- based information to make accurate movements in our everyday lives. Clinically, this research will provide insight into the effects of brain injury on rule-based movement control, particularly in those who are experiencing extended recovery times, and characterize sex and age-related differences in this functional behaviour.

column37: Fragile-X syndrome (FXS) is the primary hereditary cause of intellectual disability and the first monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder. There is currently no cure for FXS, and the few therapeutic options available focus solely on the management of behavioural and cognitive symptoms, with limited efficacy. Recent advances now allows investigating interventions that target the mechanisms causally involved in the disorder, and potentially modify its natural course. In that regard, the endocannabinoid system (eCB) emerges as a particularly appealing therapeutic target for FXS. The overarching goal of the proposed project is to measure the eCB system in FXS, and assess the behavioural and neurophysiological effects of cannabidiol (CBD) in patients with FXS. The project is divided into three main aims: 1) To measure the abnormalities affecting the eCB in humans with FXS; 2) To quantify the effects of CBD administration on the main neurotransmitter systems in the brain of FXS patients; and 3) To establish the effects of CBD on behavioural, emotional, and cognitive difficulties of patients with FXS. Design: To achieve these aims, 60 participants with FXS will take part in a cross-over study for a total duration of 36 weeks. Sixty (60) healthy controls will also take part in the study to provide reference ranges. Techniques: (Aim 1) the eCB system will be measured using biochemical analyses performed on blood samples; (Aim 2) neurotransmitter concentration levels and their functional impacts will be assessed with neuroimaging tools, namely magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). (Aim 3) The efficacy of CBD on behaviour, emotion, and cognition of patients with FXS will be measured with well-validated questionnaires and psychometric tests. Results from this study will provide important information regarding the mechanisms of action of CBD and its efficacy as a treatment for FXS.

column37: Social networks are sophisticated structures involving multiple relationships between individuals and other members to create a complex web of interactions. Each individual makes multiple contacts with other members of the network to establish communication channels. Typically, individuals will be connected to keep in touch, share interests or reach a common goal. In the era of social media, networks are expanding and accessible worldwide. The sum of these interactions creates complex network topologies which allow the dissemination of information beyond the confines of individual peer-to-peer interactions. In addition, social networks topologies are constantly adapting, adding and shedding individuals and connections in response to environmental changes. Similar to individuals, our genes are using networking strategies to exchange information. Indeed, each cell type in the human body plays specific roles or functions which require the presence of a unique operating system, a gene program. Each individual gene can be accessed following a precise number of commands that need to be executed in an orderly fashion. Similar to traffic lights which are coordinated through sophisticated hidden control modules, our genes talk to regulatory regions dispersed throughout the genetic material. The result is a complex network of control modules and genes physically connected in the three-dimensional environment through an extended web of relationships. This network defines which gene program will be used in a designated cell type. Our goal is to emphasize that hormonal stimulations or a genetic event in a regulatory region trigger the global response of connected genes. We hypothesize that these mechanisms are central to understand and treat diseases where gene misregulation is causative.

column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a life-threatening event associated with a major socioeconomic burden. In addition to neurological deficits, it can lead to long-term neuropsychiatric co-morbidity, cognitive impairment, and be a risk factor for the development of Alzheimer's disease. There is currently a paucity of effective treatments to improve memory deficits, neuropsychiatric disorders and mitigate neuropathological hallmarks of TBI. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) involves the delivery of electrical current to the brain through implanted wires called electrodes. It is an established therapy to treat movement disorders, such as Parkinson's disease and tremor, and has been recently approved for the treatment of epilepsy and obsessive-compulsive disorder. To date, DBS has been mainly used as a symptomatic treatment and not to halt the progression of disease states. We have recently found that DBS may reduce brain inflammation and increase levels of substances called trophic factors. These aspects suggest that DBS may have the potential of mitigating memory deficits, neuropsychiatric problems and neuropathology after traumatic brain injury. Another recently proposed treatment for neurological and psychiatric disorders is focused ultrasound (FUS). This consists of the emission of multiple ultrasonic beams to a single point to create brain lesions or to focally deliver drugs into the brain. The latter can be done when drugs are loaded into small particles called droplets, which burst and release their content when in contact with the ultrasound. In this study we will test whether DBS or drug-loaded droplets administered during FUS improve memory performance, anxiety and are neuroprotective in a rodent model of TBI. This work will be quite novel, as it will be the first to test whether treatments that alter brain function (DBS and FUS) may be used to improve TBI-induced neurodegeneration and memory deficits.

column36: Characterization of Dyskerin in DNA double-strand break repair
column37: A genome can be damaged in many different ways. One type of damage cuts through both strands of the double helix and this is called a DNA double-strand break (DSB). DSBs are very dangerous because DNA ends are generated at internal sites in the genome, which makes the genome unstable, promoting cancer formation. Luckily mechanisms have evolved to repair DSBs, and this involves many factors being recruited to the site of damage.
