column36: Characterizing Chronic Opioid Use in Cancer Patients
column37: The opioid crisis is a major public health problem. With the recent increase in overdose-related deaths from prescription opioids in the general population, the potential dangers of these medications are further underscored. In 2017, over 10 million adults in the United States reported misusing prescription opioids and close to 2 million met the diagnostic criteria for an opioid use disorder. Patients with cancer represent a particularly vulnerable population that may be at high risk for chronic opioid use because of distress from their illness, multiple invasive procedures, pain from their underlying cancer or treatment, and poor coordination in prescribing due to the large number of healthcare providers involved in their care. Patients with no prior opioid use are at risk of becoming chronic opioid users, and chronic opioid users are at risk of misusing opioids, both of which can result in substantial morbidity and mortality. Little is known about the patterns of chronic opioid use in the cancer setting. There is also a lack of information on the experiences and attitudes of patients and prescribers about the risks of opioids. Policies have been proposed to guide safer prescribing of opioids to cancer patients, but little evidence is available to support the implementation of these policies. Our aim is to better understand the risk of chronic opioid use in the cancer population, its associated outcomes, physicians' decision-making process when prescribing, and specific patient factors. We will conduct a retrospective cohort study of non-metastatic cancer patients undergoing cancer therapy in Alberta. We aim to describe the burden of chronic opioid use, identify patients who are at high risk of chronic opioid use, and estimate the effects of preventing chronic opioid use on hospitalizations and survival. We will also explore prescribers' and patients' views and experiences with opioids. This information can be used to inform safer opioid prescribing practices.

column37: Genome instability is the loss or rearrangement of genetic material. A major source of genomic instability is DNA damage that is not properly repaired. Genome instability drives tumor formation and develops before cancer can even detected. A double strand break (DSB) is one of the most dangerous type of DNA damage because DNA ends are generated at internal genomic regions. Normally, cells have the ability to detect damage, protect the broken ends, and activate repair machinery that puts the DNA double helix back together without the loss of important genetic material. However, if there are defects in these repair factors then the DNA ends can interact with other regions of the genome. When this happens, deletions and rearrangements in the genetic material develop and a cell does not function properly and can convert to a cancer cell. Understanding how DNA repair factors function at the molecular level has therapeutic implications. For example, novel and more sophisticated cancer treatments can be designed to target cells with defective repair machinery.

column37: IL-17 is a molecule involved in inflammation and abundant in the plasma of Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients and animal models of AD. A key role for cerebrovascular dysfunction in the onset and progression of AD is increasingly recognized and we recently demonstrated that IL-17 exerts detrimental effects on cerebral circulation. However, the mechanisms by which IL-17 alters cerebral blood flow and whether IL-17 is involved in impaired cerebral blood flow regulation in AD remains to be investigated. More precisely, IL17 impairs the increase in cerebral blood flow produced by neural activity (neurovascular coupling), a critical mechanism that matches substrate delivery with energy demands in brain. Because impaired neurovascular coupling increases the vulnerability of the brain to stroke and neurodegenerative diseases, it is important to understand how changes in vascular tone in response to neural activity may be altered. Our preliminary data showed that antiinflammatory therapy, including immune cell therapy, normalizes neurovascular coupling in a model of hypertension. These data are very exciting since there are very few studies that aimed at studying the effects of the immune system on cerebral blood flow. Accordingly, the major objective of this research program is to study the role of inflammation on neurovascular coupling impairment observed in AD. We will test therapies targeting IL17 on cerebral blood flow, molecular characteristics of AD and cognition in a murine model of AD. These studies will be conducted in mice in vivo and in vitro using genetic, biochemical, anatomical and pharmacological approaches. These studies will improve our understanding of the mechanisms underlying linking vascular risk factors, neuroinflammation and AD. This may provide further therapeutic targets to reduce premature disability and death from dysfunctional cerebral blood flow.

column37: Universal access to comprehensive primary care reduces preventable mortality and morbidity. But even countries with 'universal' health care systems struggle with the equitable utilization of basic primary care across socioeconomic groups. In the early 2000s, Canada's primary care system performed poorly compared to many developed countries when it comes to access to primary care among socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Specifically, individuals with higher socioeconomic status used more primary care and specialist services compared to those with lower socioeconomic status; but individuals with lower socioeconomic status used more services provided in emergency departments and hospitals. We will use a concentration index approach to quantify income-related inequalities in healthcare utilization and health status and decompose the indices to identify the sources of important modifiable factors. Our findings will provide guidance to policy makers for targeting modifiable factors to reduce disparities in health.

column36: Tissue-resident mesenchymal progenitors and aging
column37: Adult stem and progenitor cells play fundamental roles in tissue homeostasis, renewal and regeneration. When these cells become dysfunctional, these processes are negatively impacted and contribute to faster aging. My laboratory is particularly focused on one type of adult stem/progenitor cell termed a mesenchymal progenitor (MP), and their role in tissue restoration and aging. In a newly generated mouse model, we have shown that expression of progerin exclusively in MPs is sufficient to cause an accelerated aging phenotype and the resulting mice exhibit many of the symptoms observed in human HGPS. These results demonstrate that MPs play a fundamental role in aging. In this grant, we will use a variety of models to explore the cellular and molecular consequences of MP dysfunction and its impact on tissue restoration. This information will lead to a better understanding of the processes underlying normal and accelerated aging, and also provide a foundation to support therapeutic strategies aimed at improving MP function and promoting healthy aging.

column37: Anxiety and anxiety-related disorders (AD) are the most common of all mental health conditions. The majority of screening studies have used poor quality research methodology or have assessed measures which appear to perform too poorly to be recommended for widespread use. This research is in response to an urgent global demand for evidence-based perinatal AD screening tools. AD among perinatal people typically go unidentified and untreated, resulting in continued suffering and life impairment. This research will provide important information to inform healthcare providers, policymakers and scientists, about the most effective approach to screening for anxiety and related disorders in pregnancy in the postpartum period.

column37: Pancreatic cancers are highly lethal with most patients succumbing to disease within a year of diagnosis even with the use of harsh chemotherapy treatments. We will then use CRISPR gene editing to control the DNA mutations that form chemotherapy resistant tumours in mice and study how the immune system helps or hinders the tumour. To see if our findings can be used to help human patients, we will partner with the ongoing NeoPancOne clinical trial to identify the same changes in patients as they receive treatment. column36: A lactate trap that lowers blood glucose and liver fat
column37: Many Canadians are overweight or obese and have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. Sticking to a diet to prevent or reverse obesity is hard. Bariatric surgery is effective because it stops some of the nutrients from being absorbed through the gut. Surgery is not possible for many overweight people and surgery is not selective for nutrients that are worse for diabetes or fatty liver disease. We found a new way to trap a source of fuel that comes from gut bacteria. There are 2 forms of lactate. L-lactate is made by us. D-lactate is mainly made by bacteria. We discovered that D-lactate fuels the liver to store fat and increases blood glucose. Nearly all metabolism research is on L-lactate. There is more L-lactate in the blood, but D-lactate is a better fuel for the liver to store fat and make glucose. Usually, we think of blood glucose and liver fat coming from nutrients after eating food. However, gut microbes are always producing D-lactate, which may be one reason that is so hard to lower blood glucose and liver fat by dieting. D-lactate from bacteria also promotes liver inflammation. Our "first-generation" D-lactate trap is a long string (or polymer), which keeps D-lactate in the feces and removes it from the body. This prevents D-lactate entering the blood. This trap is safe since it is biodegradable and does not to cross the gut barrier. We already know that our "trap" lowers blood glucose and insulin in obese mice. We will now build a better trap by blocking D-lactate production from all bacteria and by forcing bacteria to eat D-lactate transforming it into beneficial bacterial factors. There are lots of associations between the microbiome, obesity, diabetes or fatty liver disease. This work is new because we have found a bacterial metabolite that fuels higher blood glucose, liver fat and inflammation. Safely trapping D-lactate or stopping its production from bacteria can help lower blood glucose and liver fat without changes in diet.

column36: Transcriptional programs of synapse maturation
column37: Neurons communicate via synapses. During development, synapses must grow and establish correct levels of communication. Failure to do so has major implications for neurological and psychiatric disorders during development and maturation. In adulthood, degeneration of synapses underlies many progressive degenerative disorders. Synapses are high energy places that need a constant supply of parts (or proteins) to make build themselves up and them carry out repairs and make adjustments. To get the right parts, synpases send requests back to the nucleus, which converts the request into the parts list that the synapse needs. Our project aims to figure out how the nucleus converts requests into the right type and number of parts, and to determine what some of these parts do at the synapse. We study this question during the developmental growth of motor neurons, which contact muscles to allow us to move and breath. Our work is directly relevant to motor neuron diseases, but we expect our work to provide fundamental understanding of this critical process that occurs in all other neurons. Failure of any part of this process is devastating to neuronal health, and underlies many disorders. This is because during early embryonic and childhood development, these parts sent by the nucleus are needed to help the synapse grow, establish communication and respond to developmental changes in brain function. In adulthood, these parts keep synapses in good repair and make necessary adjustments to keep the synapse working optimally. The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported that neurological conditions affect 3.6 million Canadians (~1/10th of the population), at a cost of billions in direct healthcare and family care costs. Given these devastating statistics, and our inability to effectively treat the majority of these disorders, it is critical that we make headway in understanding such basic processes as studied here that are required for basic neuronal function

column37: Antimicrobial resistance is one of the biggest health, economic and security threats to mankind. We, and others, have recently revealed that clinical drugs for conditions such as heart disease and diabetes can be repurposed as antibiotics due to their effects on bacterial energetics. Furthermore, we will examine the antibiotic efficacy of these drugs in in vitro and in vivo infection models to validate their potential as effective clinical therapies. With promising preliminary results to date, our proposal provides a realistic and feasible path toward the development of new therapeutic options for bacterial infections. The FDA-approved status of these drugs, the protection of intellectual property, and current negotiations with commercial partners, offers promise for rapid progression into the clinic, which is urgently needed to combat this global emergency.

Current medical management of MSKD is associated with high rates of opioids prescriptions with the majority of patients presenting to the ED for painful MSKD being discharged with an opioid prescription, even though opioids should not be the first-line treatment for the management of MSKD and while recommended non-pharmacological approaches, such as physiotherapy, are scarcely utilized. New collaborative models of care have been emerging in various settings, such as EDs, and physiotherapists (PT) have been identified as expert clinicians to care for patients with MSKD. Their involvement in these models in EDs allows for collaborative practice with physicians and nursing that is aimed to benefit ED performance, patient care and health care resource usage. In these roles, PTs can triage patients and, in some jurisdictions, order medical imaging or prescribe medications, in addition to providing recommended non-pharmacologic interventions for the management of MSKD. ED physiotherapy has emerged as a promising new ED care pathway, but evidence is still limited. Only a few RCTs have been conducted and no studies have assessed the efficacy or cost-utility of physiotherapy models of care for patients with MSKD in Canadian EDs. Evaluation of the benefits of such models is highly context-dependent and systematic evaluation of these models is warranted to support further implementation in Canada. The aim of this multicenter cluster RCT to evaluate the impact of this PT-led model of care compared to usual physician ED care for persons presenting with MSKD, in terms patients-related outcomes, healthcare resources utilization and healthcare costs.

column37: Hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable death both for civilians and for military personnel. Internal bleeding within the torso is particularly lethal, as it cannot be controlled by compressing the wound and requires surgery. Surgery can be delayed for a few hours using non-surgical treatments, but these cannot definitively stop bleeding. Medications that stop external bleeding cannot be effectively delivered into the torso to stop bleeding. We will create a technology for managing torso bleeding with CounterFlow, a powder that we developed which is highly effective at delivering medications into bleeding wounds. CounterFlow will enable physicians to stop massive bleeding in sites without surgical capabilities using routine emergency room bedside procedures, and it will also be used by highly trained military combat medics in the field. It could prevent death from blood loss before surgery, and some injuries could be managed using CounterFlow entirely without surgery. We have already shown that CounterFlow stops several types of severe bleeds, including preliminary studies in torso bleeds. The Surgeon General of Canada has approved funding to advance CounterFlow for torso bleeds in the military setting, which would match funding from CIHR and enable future clinical testing. Here, we will create and develop this technology by (i) building a hand-held spray device to deliver CounterFlow into the torso, and fine-tuning the powder formulation; (ii) verifying in pigs that it can stop severe abdominal bleeding that cannot be treated with compression, and (iii) verifying in rabbits that it does not damage tissues or cause adverse systemic effects. This work will help decrease pre-hospital death due to bleeding. Once developed, CounterFlow is expected to be used first by the Canadian Armed Forces, and will then be transitioned to the civilian sector where it could especially impact the 20% of Canadians in rural communities that may not reside close to hospitals.

column36: Role of inflammation in recovery after spinal cord injury
column37: Inflammation after injuries of the brain or spinal cord is generally viewed as negative as it potentially adds to tissue damage. We have however shown that inflammation seems to also play an important role in rewiring the nervous system after injuries and thus contributing to recovery, especially when it is combined with rehabilitative training. Thus, inflammation is a double edged sword that has to be applied carefully when used as a treatment. In this proposal we will explore whether and how the beneficial aspects of inflammation can be harnessed without causing detrimental effects. For this we will first investigate at what time points after injury is beneficial for training induced recovery in rats and how reducing inflammation can potentially affect recovery. Furthermore we will explore a promising cellular messaging pathway (i.e., histamine release) that translates inflammation to rewiring of the nervous system. We will start the experiments using cells and then a rat model of spinal cord injury to test whether inhibiting this pathway (for example by giving antihistamine drugs) reduces recovery and the effects of training and activating the pathway promotes recovery. Lastly, we will investigate a second mechanism how histamine can affect motor recovery as it potentially directly influences neuronal function.

column36: Functional micro-ultrasound imaging of the neurovascular response to focal ischemia
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of brain impairment, affecting more than 7% of Canadians over 65. Stroke occurs when blood stops flowing to a region of the brain, such as when a clot blocks a vessel, preventing oxygen and nutrients from reaching the region, and resulting in the death of brain cells. In some cases, physicians can intervene early to remove the blockage, minimizing the effects of the stroke and maximizing opportunities for recovery. Yet, many patients still have sensory, motor, or cognitive impairments, requiring significant long-term support. The cause of these lasting disabilities is likely that the blood flow does not fully return to normal in the network of small vessels that supply the brain tissue. However, we have not hitherto had a technology to observe how the small vessel flow is affected by the blockage and removal of occlusion. To meet this need, we are developing micro-ultrasound imaging tools that can visualise the tissue in and around the stroke region while also measuring blood velocity in individual larger and smaller vessels. Our method uses injected ultrasound contrast agents that are made to vibrate at low frequency , with much higher vibration harmonics detected by another transducer. With this method, not only is resolution dramatically improved compared to clinical ultrasound imaging, but "background" signal from tissue is virtually eliminated, resulting in high contrast images of the small vessels. We will optimise the ultrasound probes and imaging techniques for imaging the brain vessels in a rodent model of stroke, then investigate the changes in blood flow patterns across the network of blood vessels as stroke progresses. Through this work, we will establish the first model of the vascular network response to stroke and provide an imaging platform that can be used in future studies to assess effectiveness of new stroke treatments in re-establishing flow through smallest brain vessels.

column36: Elucidating brain inhibition and excitation in pediatric migraine
column37: Migraine is the second most prevalent and disabling disorder across the lifespan worldwide. Research suggests early treatment results in better long-term outcomes. However, migraine in children appears different than in adults, specifically treatments used for adult migraine are ineffective in children. In order to develop specific, evidence-based treatments, we need to better understand what is different about the brain in children and adolescents with migraine. Data suggests that there are imbalances in brain activity states in migraine. Activity states are based on brain chemistry and electrical activity. 'Excitation' reflects the active and reactive state. 'Inhibition' acts as the controlling state. Using three complimentary approaches/methods, this study will measure and compare inhibition and excitation in children and adolescents with and without migraine (aged 7-18 years). We will measure: (1) brain chemicals using a method called magnetic resonance spectroscopy; (2) the electrical responsivity of the brain using transcranial magnetic stimulation; and (3) inhibition and excitation in the brain indirectly through behavioral tasks. We expect the inhibition/excitation brain states to be different in migraine compared to age-matched controls. Secondly, we will perform follow-up measurements for 2 years to determine brain changes over time, comparing developmental differences in migraine to controls as well as changes in migraine severity. We expect there will be changes in brain state related to development and to changes in migraine burden. Finally, we will perform repeated measurements in children with migraine over a short period of time (2 weeks) to see how brain chemistry fluctuates throughout the migraine cycle. We expected the brain to become more excited as time to the next migraine approaches. The results of this project will provide foundational knowledge to improve therapies with the ultimate goal of reducing migraine burden across the lifespan.

column36: Mineralization mechanisms and osteopontin in bones and teeth
column37: Bones and teeth undergo a process called mineralization where small calcium- and phosphate-containing crystals are deposited into a scaffolding of proteins called the extracellular matrix. Protein-mineral interactions define properties of the mineral phase making the tissues strong and hard. Our work is relevant to understanding the decreased mineralization that occurs in the osteomalacia and odontomalacia diseases where bones and teeth are incompletely mineralized, soft and deformable, and prone to buckling called pseudofracturing. The research is also relevant to calcification diseases of normally "soft" tissues (such as the mineralization of blood vessels and heart valves). Compelling evidence indicates that a protein called osteopontin (OPN) controls mineralization in most tissues. Also important is that processing of OPN by enzymes leads to mineralization-inhibiting protein fragments (peptides) with different inhibitory potencies. We investigate how processing of OPN defines a control mechanism affecting biomineralization. Here we propose to examine this possible regulation, guided by the general hypothesis that OPN in bones and teeth, and peptides derived from enzymatic processing of OPN, control mineralization by binding to mineral precursor phases and crystal surfaces in a way that influences the hardening process. We will investigate these mechanisms in cell-free systems in which calcium-phosphate crystals are grown in the presence of OPN/peptides, in cell culture and mouse models of disease, and in humans from small bone biopsy samples and extracted teeth. We will use biochemical measurements, bioimaging microscopies including high-resolution electron and atomic force microscopy and X-ray approaches, and various biophysical methods to characterize tissues, mineral and mineral-protein complexes. Such work should provide insight into keeping bones and teeth strong and healthy, and may suggest ways to treat patients where these tissues are defective.

column36: Vascular events in patients undergoing same-day noncardiac surgery (VALIANCE) - a prospective cohort and nested biobank study
column37: More than 1.8 million Canadians have same-day surgery every year. Same-day surgery used to be offered only to healthy patients having minor surgery, like cataract surgery. But in recent decades, more complex surgeries are performed as same-day procedures, often on older and sicker patients. In patients who have surgery and stay overnight in the hospital, studies have shown that cardiac complications are frequent and that most patients do not show any symptoms. Without routine blood work and follow-up after surgery, these events would go undetected. This raises the question: do patients who have surgery and are discharged home on the same day also suffer cardiac complications that are not recognized? Currently, clinicians do not have the tools to identify the frequency of cardiac complications or which patients are at higher risk. Routine blood tests done before and after surgery might be able to detect cardiac complications in patients undergoing same-day surgery. We propose to enroll adults from Canadian hospitals who are undergoing same-day surgery and will be monitored at 1 month and 3 months for the occurrence of cardiovascular complications. We aim to identify risk factors for a cardiovascular complication following a same-day surgery, and examine the impact on a patient's long-term health. We will also collect blood samples before and after surgery in a subgroup of patients with cardiovascular risk factors to determine if cardiac blood tests (i.e., NT-proBNP and troponin) can help identify those at higher risk of having a cardiac event and allow for early detection of these events. This study will enable us to develop tools allowing for better selection of patients eligible for a same-day surgery and improve management and surveillance of these patients in the future.

column36: Development of Interdisciplinary Strategies to Prevent Chronic Opioid Use in Adult Trauma Patients
column37: Long-term opioid use has recently been associated with many deaths as well as a substantial decrease in psychological well-being and daily functioning while significantly increasing healthcare costs. Persistent pain is an issue affecting many of the 3.5 million Canadians who sustained traumatic injuries every year. Considering the pain intensity induced by traumatic injuries and the needed surgeries to treat them, opioids are often considered as a first-line therapy in the trauma population. However, opioid use persisting beyond 3 months has been linked to negative individual and social outcomes. Alarmingly, up to 20% of trauma patients treated with opioids were shown to still use opioids a long time after their injury. Limited strategies are available to prevent opioid long-term use in the trauma population. These patients received treatments from multiple professionals, such as physicians, pharmacists, nurses and physiotherapists in hospitals, rehabilitation centers and in the community (family medicine clinics and pain clinics). Hence, this research program aims to develop multi-professional strategies to be integrated in trauma patients' continuum of care in order to reduce long-term opioid use while managing pain appropriately. To do so, a survey will be completed by professionals in three Canadian provinces to evaluate their perceptions with regard to their actual practices in terms of opioid prescriptions and strategies that should be implemented in the trauma population. Patient partners and healthcare professionals working in these provinces will then be met to make the final selection of strategies to be used. Finally, patient partners and clinical experts will design the preventive strategies to be implemented along trauma patients care trajectories. This program has a great potential to improve the access to care and the health of people who have sustained traumatic injuries and to reduce the social burden associated with opioid long-term use.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of host shutoff by respiratory viruses and their contribution to viral pathogenesis
column37: Viral respiratory disease burden remains high despite continuous efforts to limit virus infection and spread through vaccination, surveillance, and quarantine measures. Now the world is in the middle of a pandemic caused by a novel respiratory virus - severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Despite unprecedented efforts by researchers worldwide to develop vaccines against SARS-CoV-2, there is still uncertainty as to whether and when they will become available. Even if vaccines are deployed, people with underlying health conditions will remain under threat. This is true in the case of another respiratory virus, influenza, to which vaccines were developed decades ago, and which continues to cause seasonal epidemics. In Canada, influenza infections peak each year in the late fall and winter months resulting in over 12,000 hospitalizations and over 3,000 deaths annually. This underscores the need for better treatment options for those who develop severe respiratory disease. The long-term goal of our research program is the development of new antiviral treatments based on detailed understanding of virus-host interactions. Specifically, we are interested in the mechanisms used by respiratory viruses like influenza and SARS-CoV-2 to overcome antiviral immune responses. One such mechanism is host shutoff - the blockade of new protein synthesis in infected cells. Both influenza A viruses and coronaviruses produce dedicated host shutoff factors: polymerase acidic X (PA-X) and non-structural protein 1 (Nsp1), respectively. These viral genes interfere with cells ability to synthesise new proteins, including those that are involved in immune responses. In the proposed research, we will determine how PA-X and Nsp1 work at the molecular level and how their function disrupt immune responses to these respiratory viruses.

column37: Major depressive disorder is a debilitating condition resulting from a combination of alterations affecting the activity of the brain. We also propose to investigate the gene programs modified by chronic stress and test how these genes modulate stress responses by altering the activity of both pathways in males and females. Overall, our research program will allow us to identify the molecular and functional mechanisms by which chronic stress induces behavioral stress responses in order to develop better therapeutic strategies for the treatment of mood disorders in males and females.

column36: Spinal Neuromodulation for Restoring Function after Neural Injury or Disease
column37: Nearly 1.6 million people live with paralysis resulting from traumatic or non-traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) in North America, of whom >50% never recover the ability to walk. Electrical stimulation of nerves and muscles has been one of the few interventions to date to provide functional improvements after SCI; however, restoring functional walking has remained an unresolved challenge. An alternative electrical stimulation approach for restoring walking focuses on stimulating the spinal cord. Two paradigms of spinal cord stimulation have shown great potential: epidural spinal cord stimulation (ESCS) and intraspinal microstimulation (ISMS). Both activate spinal networks in the same small region of the spinal cord, but through different pathways. Exciting new results suggest that ESCS, coupled with extensive physical therapy, may restore some ability to walk (up to 100 m) for people experiencing severe SCI. Also exciting are results from ISMS work done in animals that show that ISMS can restore long distances of walking (close to 1 kilometer)! However, despite the compelling findings, it remains unknown how ESCS or ISMS work, and which neural networks in the spinal cord they activate. It is also unknown how long-term use of ESCS or ISMS can change the neural networks in the spinal cord, how much they are dependent on extensive physical therapy to produce good functional outcomes, and how effective they are in restoring stable and sustained walking. This proposal will systematically address these unknowns in the adult Yucatan pigs. This strain of pigs has spine and spinal cord anatomies that best resemble those of humans. Therefore, the findings from this project can be readily translated to humans. Very importantly, the results of this pivotal study will be crucial for determining the suitability of ESCS and ISMS for restoring meaningful distances of walking after severe SCI, and will guide the use of these stimulation strategies in persons experiencing SCI.

column36: Role of neutrophils in liver fibrosis
column37: Chronic inflammation and fibrosis or scarring are the first triggers of cancer in the liver. Liver fibrosis occurs in response to injury like inflammation due to infection or fatty liver disease where high levels of collagen deposits in the liver leading to stiffness or fibrosis and gradual loss of liver function. The immune system, specifically different subsets of white blood cells produce immune mediators (cytokines) that may increase or decrease the inflammation in the liver and the progression of liver fibrosis. We and other groups have identified a cytokine known as IL17 as a key accelerator of liver fibrosis. We have also identified a subset of white blood cells known as "neutrophils" that produce IL17 and that are increased in advanced fibrosis. In this proposal we are interested in understanding how these neutrophils go to the liver during different types of injury and whether different subsets or types of neutrophils can have different functions or play different roles during early versus late stages of liver injury and fibrosis. We would also like to know where these neutrophils are located in the injured liver and how they interact with the different liver cells. Finally, we would like to see if blocking the activity of these neutrophils and/or IL17 can stop or delay liver fibrosis. To achieve these goals, we will use a combination of imaging techniques and assays to examine these cells in liver tissues from patients at different fibrosis stages as well as mice. We will also use genetically modified mice where cells that produce IL17 at any time during their life will become permanently fluorescent. This will allow us to monitor how these cells travel or change their function in the liver at different stages of liver injury. We will also block the action of IL17 or neutrophils to monitor how this influences fibrosis. The results obtained will guide the development of new treatments to stop liver fibrosis and prevent cancer.

If XeI and X5in can predict clinical deterioration, doctors will have better information about when to start treatment or referral to lung transplant. The condition is due to mutations in a gene known as STING (that stands for STimulator of INterferon Genes), that trigger the constant activation of the STING protein. STING is normally involved in the production of interferons and other inflammatory proteins as a way to deal with infections by viruses and bacteria. Although STING helps protect the host from the effects of viral or bacteria attack, if it is over-active it can lead to excess inflammation. Therefore, the continuous activation of STING due to the activating mutations in SAVI lead to tissue damage. Thus, children with SAVI become ill, develop rashes, severe lung inflammation, and gangrene of fingers and toes, as well as ears and nose. Hand and foot amputations can be required. Thus far, drug treatments have not been completely effective. The gangrene is due to blood vessel damage and blockages that starve tissues for oxygen and nutrients. The vessel damage, known as vasculopathy, accounts for the 'V' in SAVI. To study this condition we developed a mouse model, based on introducing one of the mutant human STING genes (identified in children), into mice via genetic engineering (a.k.a.transgenic technology). Our model is unique in that the mice, much like the children, develop blood vessel damage, leading to paw damage and inflammation as well as damage to other extremities, including ears and tail. With the advanced imaging methods we have, we have been able to see the blood vessel blockages. Our plan is now to define how different cells and other factors (including cold exposure) are responsible for blood vessel damage in our mice. Importantly, we will also evaluate a variety of therapies in using the mice, that are potentially applicable to this devastating disease of children.

column36: Multimodal Sensing Guidewire with Random Optical Gratings by Ultraviolet laser Exposure for Peripheral Vascular Interventions
column37: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) revascularization is a minimally invasive treatment to remedy occlusions in femoral arteries, but it's success in long occlusions has been limited by the technical challenges associated with crossing occluded vessels with guidewires. Revascularization needs to be planned and guided closely using ionizing imaging modalities such as fluoroscopy, while intra-vascular catheters lack the capability of measuring non-invasively blood flow or estimate plaque or occlusion stiffness at the blockage site. In recent years, our team has developed new optical sensing technologies measuring light deflections within optical fibers for biomedical applications, surpassing the accuracy of traditional sensors based on Bragg gratings. These continuous random sensors were tested in-vivo to measure 3D shapes of medical devices such as needles, guidewire and surgical robots, and enabled the visualization of catheters to monitor the therapeutic response during intra-vascular procedures. The primary objective of this project is to fabricate a biocompatible multi-modal sensing guidewire integrating a optical fibers with random optical gratings. The device will be able to simultaneously measure: 1) 3D shape and location, 2) blood flow in peripheral arteries and 3) the pressure applied by the guidewire on surrounding tissue. Clinical proof of concept will be performed in 20 patients with occlusive peripheral artery diseases undergoing PTA. A recently developed real-time deep learning motion prediction tool will continuously adjust the fusion of the tracked guidewire with diagnostic imaging, facilitating translation toward effective clinical utilization for targeted treatments. The long-term research goal is to allow a more effective utilization and integration of guidewire devices combined with non-invasive imaging modalities, in order to improve true lumen re-entry, and ultimately, a better outcome for patients requiring catheterization procedures.

column36: Innate immune activity, the aging brain, Alzheimer's disease pathology and symptoms: a novel approach to prevention.
column37: "Inflammation" of the brain is a process that involves activation of many different cytokines, chemokines, and other signalling molecules in a process is known as "innate immunity". The innate immune system goes far back on the evolutionary tree and is found even in sponges. While the brain does not harbour more advanced types of immune activity, innate immune changes are prominent in both aging of the brain and development of Alzheimer's disease (AD). It is not clear, however, which particular elements of the innate immune system are present during these unwanted changes. Furthermore, we don't know whether they aggravate ongoing brain damage (the usual interpretation) or may instead represent the body's attempt to avoid it. In fact, innate immune activity may even delay or prevent adverse brain changes, i.e., inability to mount such a response might even foster the development of amyloid deposits and other aspects of brain aging or development of AD. This project will use advanced methods to identify the precise pattern of innate immune molecules found in brain aging and AD. It will analyze >650 samples of spinal fluid collected over 10 years from 200 participants in a cohort of aging Canadians at high risk of AD, revealing whether specific innate immune changes precede, accompany, or follow brain changes of aging and AD. Furthermore, it will tell us whether these innate immune mechanisms foster or deter such changes. As well, some innate immune activities appear either to aggravate or -- importantly -- to reduce the severity of cognitive symptoms that accompany age- or AD-related brain changes. We will discover more about harm or possible benefits from innate immune activity. Our findings will pinpoint specific hypotheses regarding innate immunity that aggravate or help prevent age- or AD-related brain changes. These hypotheses will help guide the development of strategies for the prevention of Alzheimer's disease and age-related cognitive decline.

column37: Major affective or non-affective disorders such as schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder(BP) affect around 2% of the population. Heredity plays a major role in the development of SCZ and BP which means that, when variations occur in groups of genes, the likelihood of developing the disease increases. Indeed, no single gene is responsible for the disease but variations in multiple genes will act together and increase the global risk of illness. The complexity of identifying specific genes involved is further complicated by the clinical manifestations of these disorders which differ from one individual to the other. For almost 30 years, our research team have gathered a sample of nearly 1300 members from 48 well-characterized multigenerational families from Eastern Quebec that are densely affected by SCZ or BP. This cohort include individuals affected with SCZ and BP, nonaffected adult relatives and high-risk offspring that have been followed through the years. New technologies are now available that allow us to draw a more precise portrait of the genetic variations of an individual. Using these technologies, we will compare small genetic variations between affected, non-affected and high-risk individuals. The results obtained through this first set of analyses will be confirmed in another cohort of children born to an affected parent. If successful, this project will allow a better understanding of the genetic causes of SCZ and BP, a genetic-based indicator for early detection and management of high-risk offspring and an improved classification of patients based on genetic variations in order to personalize and optimise treatments.

column37: Children with sickle cell anemia (SCA) have trouble providing sufficient oxygen to their brain, leading to problems in blood flow and vessel function in the brain, small brain insults and thinking problems. Hydroxyurea (HU), a drug taken by mouth, is now the standard of care for SCA patients. However, despite aggressive use of HU, the rate of brain insults and thinking problems are still increasing. Using brain imaging, we have recently shown that children with SCA have abnormal blood flow and small injuries in the brain. Furthermore, we have obtained tests showing that thinking processes, especially thinking speed is compromised in these children. Finally, using functional brain imaging we have shown that brain injury distributes brain activation important for thinking. Brain activation is an important function for quickly processing information. Based on these findings, we believe that in children with SCA compromised blood flow and vessel function predicts impaired speed of thinking via its disruptive effect on brain activation. The goal of this project is to characterize the function of blood vessels in the brain and the burden of brain injury in children with SCA. We also want to test if these brain anomalies are related to impaired thinking speed. Furthermore, we would like to know if this is influenced by disruptive brain activation. We will examine children with SCA on HU at 2 timepoints to measure various aspects of brain and vascular health using brain imaging, and assess how they relate to the problems in thinking in these children. Our study will help to understand the relationship between abnormal blood vessel function in the brain and brain activation and how this may relate to problems in thinking. This will help with assessing risk of thinking problems in children with SCA and provide guidance for potential treatments with the goal to halt or reverse thinking problems in these patients and ultimately mitigate the lifelong burden of disease.

column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating condition resulting from a combination of alterations affecting the activity of the brain differently in men and women. When modified, these genes change neuronal activity resulting in inadequate responses to chronic stress and ultimately to the expression of depressive-like behavior. To do so, we will combine the use of micro-endoscopic devices, advanced molecular techniques and cutting edge functional approaches in a mouse model of chronic variable stress known to reproduce the behavioral and molecular impact of chronic stress in males and females with MDD. Overall, our analyses will provide exciting new insights into the sexual differences underlying cellular activity in response to chronic stress, identify neuronal populations more significantly involved in stress responses, reveal the critical time windows during which stress induces its impact and define the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects in order to develop better therapeutic strategies for the treatment of mood disorders in males and females.

column36: Control of invariant Natural Killer T cell helper and cytotoxic functions in cancer
column37: T cells constitute one arm of the mammalian adaptive immune system. They originate in the thymus, and thereafter patrol the body until they encounter their specific antigen in peripheral lymphoid organs. Upon activation, various signals trigger antigen-specific T cells to expand and differentiate into discrete effector subsets that perform functions tailored to the type of ongoing threat, such as infection or tumour development. Different functional T cell subsets have been characterized and the signals driving their differentiation are well known. invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells are unconventional T cells that respond faster than conventional T cells and to a different class of antigens. iNKT cells respond to lipid antigens and regulate the magnitude and quality of immune responses during numerous diseases. Notably they provide immunity to pathogens and tumours. iNKT cells develop in the thymus. They can also differentiate into various functional subsets, but unlike conventional T cells, this process happens in the thymus, and may be refined in peripheral tissues. The mechanisms and signals that control iNKT cell development and differentiation remain ill-defined. Using advanced genomics and more traditional immunology approaches, we have recently generated data that challenge our current understanding of the events and signals that govern iNKT cell development and differentiation. Therefore, our goal is to establish the pathways of iNKT cell development and functional differentiation, determine how they are regulated, and characterize their function in cancer immunity. This project builds on our recent observations and long-standing interest in iNKT cell biology. Our team combines expertise in developmental and cancer immunology, advanced genomics and bioinformatics. These innovative and exciting experiments will foster our understanding of iNKT cell biology and may lead to novel ways to selectively manipulate these cells in disease.

column37: Children have been called an indicator species for cities. The visible presence of children and youth of different ages and backgrounds, with and without their parents, outside in city streets, sidewalks, yards, and open spaces is a sign of the health of human habitats. Indeed, the extent to which a neighbourhood supports children's outdoor play - ie. its playability - can be directly linked not only to children's health, levels of obesity and psychological well-being, but also to the population's well-being as a whole. Research concerns about stranger-danger, traffic accidents and a general lack of safe, enticing places for children and youth to play outdoors, have been partially responsible for children and youth becoming more sedentary and remaining indoors to play. Concomitantly there has been an increasing interest in promoting children and youth's outdoor play due to the myriad of benefits it is shown to provide. This proposal takes children and youth's outdoor play as a critical public health issue that can help municipal policy makers, public health practitioners, active transport advocates, urban designers, child advocates and society in general join the dots between complex issues like pollution and global warming, active transport planning and community cohesion on the one hand, and concerns regarding the physical and mental health of both children and adults on the other.

column36: Impacts of human and bacterial natural genomic diversity on cholera disease severity
column37: Cholera is a diarrheal disease caused by the waterborne bacterium Vibrio cholerae that has caused devastating pandemics and mortality throughout human history. Today, cholera causes over 100,000 deaths every year. Despite extensive study, it is still difficult to predict cholera outbreaks or virulence within individuals. Cholera vaccines exist, but are less than 60% effective, and do not confer long-term immunity. Remarkably, some people exposed to V. cholerae do not become ill and instead become asymptomatic carriers, capable of transmitting the infection. My team will study cholera patients and their household contacts in Bangladesh, where cholera is endemic. Cholera patients are treated by doctors, and most recover. Their contacts have a high risk (~20%) of being infected with V. cholerae, and ~75% of those infected go on to develop symptomatic cholera. By prospectively sampling both cholera patients and their at-risk contacts, we can follow the transition from asymptomatic to symptomatic cholera and identify risk factors. The risk factors measured in our study include mutations in the human or V. cholerae genome, human immune responses, and potentially protective bacteria in the gut microbiome. V. cholerae mutations can occur during an infection, and may help V. cholerae evade the human immune system, or allow it to cause more severe disease. However, even if mutations can benefit V. cholerae on the short term (within one patient), they might be "evolutionary dead-ends" if they hinder its ability to transmit to new patients. Our study will allow us to identify such dead-ends, which could eventually be exploited to reduce cholera transmission. V. cholerae mutations associated with desired outcomes (e.g. strong immune responses, less severe disease and less transmission) could eventually be used in new vaccines.

column36: Metabolism of dietary tryptophan by intestinal microbiota in chronic intestinal inflammation
column37: Our gut is regularly exposed to foods that need to be processed and digested ("metabolism") to provide nutrients necessary for life. The gut also harbors a vast number of microbes, collectively called "microbiota", that are in constant interaction with its host and the ingested food, to maintain the balance between health and disease. Many food components are metabolized by gut bacteria, producing molecules or "metabolites" that affect human health. In this sense, the microbiota behaves as a key additional metabolic organ, degrading and producing essential nutrients for the host. There is growing evidence that when food-microbe interactions are broken, chronic conditions such as inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) can develop. However, the factors that contribute to break this equilibrium remain unclear. Tryptophan is an essential amino acid, contained in most protein-based foods, that when ingested in the diet can become a source of energy for gut bacteria. Beneficial bacteria, such as certain Lactobacillus, produce tryptophan-derived metabolites called "indoles" that activate protective immune responses in the gut. Patients with IBD have both altered gut microbiota and abnormal tryptophan metabolism, raising the possibility that dysregulated gut bacterial metabolism of tryptophan plays a role in IBD. The general aim of this project is thus, (i) to understand the precise metabolic interactions between gut microbiota and dietary tryptophan and, (ii) to determine whether and how when disrupted, they contribute to inflammation. Our long-term goal is to provide evidence-based dietary recommendations and discover specific probiotic formulations that through indole production can prevent, or help treat, IBD.

column36: Axon Guidance by Extracellular Gradients: Mechanisms Regulating Neural Circuit Formation
column37: During development nerve cells must form appropriate connections for the nervous system to function properly. A developing nerve cell extends a thin process called an axon that may grow past thousands of other cells before it reaches its target. We aim to identify the mechanisms that axons use to navigate in the embryo. Netrins are a family of proteins secreted by axonal targets during development. Without netrins, many types of axons become lost and the nervous system develops abnormally. Secreted proteins, like netrins, are thought to form gradients that direct axon growth in the early embryo. Our past findings and ongoing studies reveal gradients of netrin protein in the early embryo. In specific aim one, we address how these gradients are formed and maintained in the early embryo. The second aim proposes to investigate how cells read the distribution of netrin to move in a particular direction. This aim takes advantage of powerful new tools that we have developed to study neurons through collaborations with laboratories in the departments of Physics and Biomedical Engineering. We propose to use these tools to identify how a gradient of netrin causes molecular changes in the axon and how this results in directed axon growth. These studies will provide insight into fundamental mechanisms that regulate cell movement in the embryo. Importantly, mutations in netrins and netrin receptors are associated with developmental disorders in humans, and these proteins are also present in the mature nervous system. Obtaining a better understanding of how the nervous system develops is critical to generate strategies that aim to recover nervous system function that has been lost due to injury, aging, or neurodegenerative disease.

column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) affects up to 1 in 5 mothers and can have profound effects on both mothers and their families. Even though the cost of one untreated case of PPD is estimated to exceed $150,000, just 10% of women receive evidence-based care. Access to PPD treatment has not only worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic, but women's concerns about exposing themselves and their infants to the virus has profoundly affect their preferences around securing care for their mental health needs in both the short- and long-term. At present time, the healthcare system is not well-equipped to deal with common, time-sensitive conditions like PPD that require talking therapy. Innovative new approaches to providing safe and acceptable treatments to mothers struggling with PPD are urgently needed. The purpose of this study is to test the effectiveness of an Online 9-Week Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT; a type of talking therapy) program delivered by women who have recovered from PPD. We will randomize 224 women with current PPD to receive Online Peer-Delivered CBT plus treatment as usual from their other care providers (treatment group) or treatment as usual alone (control group). We will compare how effective Online Peer-Delivered CBT is at improving maternal depression and anxiety, social isolation, parenting stress, mother-infant attachment, and offspring behaviour immediately after treatment, and three and six months later. We will also assess its cost-effectiveness. It is vitally important that we help overcome the barriers that keep mothers with PPD from receiving treatment. Given the large supply of potential peer therapists, women's desire to help other mothes, and evidence that peers may be able to deliver talking treatments as effectively as trained professionals, task-shifting the treatment of PPD online and from professionals to trained peers offers a potentially safe, effective, appealing, and cost-effective way to improve PPD in Canada and globally.

column36: Contact-force controller to eliminate the effects of motion during cardiac radiofrequency ablation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a severe electrophysiological heart disease with an ever-increasing incidence rate. A large portion of AF patients are treated with an invasive procedure called cardiac ablation, where catheters are inserted into the heart and used to burn specific parts of the heart wall in order to disrupt the electrical signals that cause AF; following a successful ablation procedure patients are free from AF. Unfortunately the success rate of first-time ablations is as low as 50%, requiring the patients to return for at least one repeat procedure. One of the main reasons for ablation failure is insufficient burning of the cardiac tissue. The motion of the beating heart periodically minimizes contact with the ablation catheter, resulting in insufficient burning of the tissue. Out team has invented and developed a small device that removes the effects of heart motion and stabilizes the force between the tip of the catheter and the moving heart wall. The device adds on to routinely used catheters with minimal impact to regular procedure workflow. Based on the success of our lab prototype, which has been shown to work effectively in preclinical studies and to remove the effects of motion on lesion size in the lab, we are designing and manufacturing a second-generation prototype of the catheter contact-force controller and aim to perform first-in-human testing within the tenure of this grant.

column36: Improving Care for Knee Osteoarthritis by Predicting Who Will Get Worse: Exploring the Interactions of Joint Biomechanics, Inflammation and Immunity
column37: IMPORTANCE By 2041, over 10 million Canadians will have osteoarthritis (OA), with the knee most often affected. Knee OA causes long-term pain and immobility. It damages all tissues in and around a joint. About half of people with knee OA will decline toward disability, some very rapidly. At diagnosis, we cannot predict who will experience steady disease, versus those on a fast path to disability. Our goal is to predict knee OA worsening so that we target treatment to those who need it the most. In-depth movement analysis shows that the torque rotating the lower leg into a bow-legged position at the knee (called the knee adduction moment (KAM)) predicts worsening knee OA - but only people who are obese. The reason why obesity heightened the effect of KAM is unknown. We believe obesity creates inflammation and changes the way our immune system fights off disease. OBJECTIVES To figure out how KAM and obesity work together to worsen knee OA, we will determine if: 1) Obesity-related alterations in tissue quality, inflammation and immunity relate to tissue function for cartilage and muscle. 2) The combination of KAM with poor cartilage function predicts cartilage loss over 3 y. 3) Pain, mobility and function are related with obesity-related inflammation and immune responses. METHOD In 135 people with knee OA, at baseline and 3 y we will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure the quantity and quality of cartilage and muscle. We will use MRI to assess cartilage function (changes in cartilage thickness after walking) and a strength-testing machine to assess muscle function. Every 9 months for 3 y, we will collect blood to measure inflammation and immune function; analyze walking; and measure pain, mobility and function. OUTCOMES By examining how KAM and obesity work together to worsen knee OA, we will understand why some with knee OA remain stable, while others get worse. This work is essential to targeting treatment for those facing rapid decline.

column37: Background: Over 60% of extremely low gestational age neonates (ELGANs, defined as gestational age < 28 weeks) suffer from patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and they are the neonates at highest risk for mortality and severe morbidity, including life-limiting neurodevelopmental impairments. PDA management is highly controversial, mostly due to a lack of improvement in neonatal outcomes reported in clinical trials of treatment, though studies have failed to properly define which PDAs are 'hemodynamically significant' through validation against major clinical outcomes. Objective: The objective of this study is to define 'significant PDA' by comprehensively examining clinical and echocardiography characteristics early in the disease process and developing prediction models for mortality and severe neonatal morbidity in a large, prospective, multicentre, national cohort of ELGANs. Setting and Methods: This study will be a collaboration of the Canadian Neonatal Network (CNN, a comprehensive neonatal database) and the Canadian Targeted Neonatal Echocardiography Collaborative (a collaborative of neonatologists with expertise in echocardiography and hemodynamics, representing nearly all institutions in Canada which care for ELGANs). Together the already comprehensive clinical data in CNN will be augmented with clinical and echocardiography parameters of PDA evaluation and treatment. Models will be derived for four postnatal-age specific periods after birth (Day 1-3, Day 4-7, Day 8-14, and Day 15-28) using evaluations conducted during the respective time periods. Partial least square discriminate analysis will be used to derive the prediction models and all models will undergo internal and external validation. Impact: This study will provide valuable information for clinicians by identifying which infants with PDA are at risk for mortality and severe morbidity and by defining and validating patient inclusion criteria for future trials of PDA treatment.

column36: Evaluating the potential of blood biomarkers to improve Alzheimer's Disease risk stratification
column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia and causes symptoms such as memory loss and problems with language and thinking that eventually limit everyday activities of life. In Canada, over 1 in 3 seniors die from AD and over 25,000 new cases are diagnosed each year, 65% of which are women. Although clinical onset and diagnosis of AD typically occurs after age 65 years, we now know that brain changes including build-up of amyloid plaques, spreading of neurofibrillary tangles, and loss of neurons, begin ~20 years before the emergence of memory problems. The challenge is that current methods to detect these early brain changes require very expensive brain scans or very invasive collection of cerebrospinal fluid through a lumbar puncture. Fortunately, new technologies now raise the possibility of using blood tests to measure these brain changes. This project will evaluate 5 candidate proteins that can now be measured in blood as candidate biomarkers that improve our ability to predict a person's risk of AD at least a decade before memory problems start. The candidate proteins we will test are called p-tau-181, NF-L, Ab40, Ab42 and GFAP. First, we will work with a large collection of 5,200 blood samples already collected by Statistics Canada from the Canadian population to define what the normal levels are for these proteins across the life span, from age 3-79 years, as it is important to define what "normal levels" are so that abnormal levels can be recognized. Second, we will measure these proteins in three Canadian cohorts including the Canadian Consortium for Neurodegeneration in Aging (CCNA, 1,400 specimens), the UBC AD clinic (2,000 specimens) and disease-free "Super-Seniors" (500 specimens). As each cohort already has a wealth of clinical, genetic and brain scan data, we will be able to determine whether blood tests improve our ability to predict a person's risk of AD.

column37: Over 37 million people are infected by HIV-1 worldwide and up to 50% of these patients can develop HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders that highly impair their quality of life. It is well established that antiretroviral drugs are not as effective in the treatment of HIV-1 brain infection and equally well established that the brain concentrations of several antiretroviral drugs are much less than those seen in the peripheral blood. Ample evidence suggests that HIV-1 can induce an inflammatory response in brain cellular compartments that in turn can promote neuronal loss and contribute to the development of neurocognitive disorders. Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors (PPARs) are cellular receptors known to play a major role in fat and sugar metabolism. We have recently demonstrated that once activated by specific compounds, these receptors can reverse HIV-associated inflammation both in isolated brain cells, known to be a target or HIV-1, and in animal models of HIV-brain infection and inflammation. Furthermore, PPAR activation has also been shown to inhibit HIV-1 replication. Using various human and animal cell culture systems of the brain or brain tissues isolated from humans and macaques (healthy or HIV-1 infected or SIV infected) as well as animal models of HIV-1 brain inflammation, we plan to investigate the protective role of these receptors in reversing HIV-associated brain inflammation, once activated by specific novel compounds. This work is clinically important since identifying novel compounds that can effectively permeate into the brain and exhibit anti-inflammatory properties may provide a treatment option in preventing/treating HIV-1 brain inflammation and associated neurocognitive deficits which ultimately will improve the health of HIV-1 infected populations in Canada and worldwide.

column36: The impact of sex and gender in occupational disease prevention
column37: Workplace exposure to hazardous substances (such as asbestos, radiation, and some chemicals) is an important and preventable cause of disease in Canada. Exposure to occupational carcinogens alone leads to an estimated 9,700 to 10,400 new cancers each year in Canada. However, we do not know how the effects of these exposures might differ between men and women for two reasons. First, occupational studies have generally focused on male-dominated occupations and industries. As a result, women were not included in most of the available research studies until quite recently. Second, researchers did not anticipate that biological differences (physical size, hormonal differences, or how quickly a chemical can be cleared from the body) and sociocultural differences (which jobs and tasks we do, and which exposures were considered important) between men and women would have a large impact on occupational disease. Recent evidence tells us that both these factors (sex and gender) are very important to consider in occupational health research. In this timely, innovative project, we will develop tools to assess how sex and gender influence exposure to hazardous chemicals at work. Then, we will use these tools to examine differences in risk of three major occupational diseases (cancer, asthma, and dermatitis) between men and women in two existing Canadian disease surveillance studies. These novel results will help answer key questions about where men or women might be at different risk of disease from exposures they experience at work. We will generate new research questions that will contribute to efforts to reduce the burden of occupational disease among men and women in Canada.

column37: Fatty liver disease affects one third of people in North America. The disease has few symptoms, but over time causes irreversible damage to the liver. We are also investigating whether a common gene variant in PGC-1alpha is associated with the incidence or severity of the disease in humans. Identifying the cause of fatty liver disease will help to discover ways to diagnosis patients early and to design more effective treatments.

column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a severe and debilitating anxiety disorder afflicting about 2% of the population. Untreated, OCD runs a chronic and deteriorating course. According to the World Health Organization, OCD is among the top 10 leading causes of disability worldwide. Examination of non-medicinal treatments for OCD has focused on two distinct treatments: exposure and response prevention (ERP) and cognitive therapy (CT), often combined into an integrated cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT). However, there are a significant number of treatment non-responders and the majority of responders are still left with impairing residual symptoms. One area of investigation that has shown potential benefit for general mood and anxiety disorders has been mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), yet the potential benefits of MBIs in OCD has been largely unexamined, except for several small preliminary studies that show clinical promise. The purpose of this study is to examine the clinical benefits of a standardized MBI treatment for OCD in a large-scale, multi-site randomized controlled trial. The results of this study will directly determine whether Mindfulness can be considered an effective treatment for OCD. If this study can demonstrate that a short-term mindfulness intervention can significantly reduce the suffering associated with OCD, then the findings could easily be translated into routine clinical care in and out of hospital settings. Results of this study will also potentially add to our understanding of the mechanisms that drive OCD symptoms, improve our knowledge of psychological treatment mechanisms, and elucidate how biological factors influence psychological treatment outcomes.

column37: The objective of the BRAIN AF trial is to find a preventive treatment against cognitive decline in young patients suffering from atrial fibrillation. Cognitive impairment refers to a disturbance affecting cognitive functions, such as reasoning or memory. There is a progression in cognitive impairment that could be mild, moderate or severe (this is referred to as dementia). Unfortunately, no treatment has yet been shown to be effective for dementia. Therefore, prevention therapies are prioritized. Research has shown that the brain could be affected by multiple factors, internal (i.e., family history) or external (i.e., obesity and lack of exercise). In recent years, growing evidence has shown that atrial fibrillation (the most frequent arrhythmia in Canada) increases the risk of developing cognitive impairment especially in patients <75 years old. The main hypothesis is that the accumulation of tiny blood clots in the brain could affect cognition. Indeed, in atrial fibrillation, contractions of the upper parts of the heart (the atria) are irregular and rapid and can induce the formation of blood clots. If the blood enters the brain, it can cause a stroke (large blood clot) or silent cerebral ischemia (tiny blood clots). In the absence of risk factors other than atrial fibrillation, the medication to prevent clot formation (blood thinners) is recommended after the age of 65 years. We are performing a randomized clinical trial where patients are randomly assigned to receive either an anticoagulation therapy or standard of care (placebo in most of the patients or aspirin in patients with vascular disease). Our goal is determine whether this therapy improves cognitive functions. Yearly cognitive testing (by questionnaires) are planned. The BRAIN-AF study seeks to demonstrate whether anticoagulation therapy, started earlier in patients with atrial fibrillation, produces a protective effect and decreases brain damage and cognitive decline.

column36: A Mindfulness-Based Intervention to Improve CPAP Adherence in Adolescents with Obstructive Sleep Apnea - A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is very common in adolescents with co-existing medical conditions and in those who are obese. OSA is associated with snoring and disrupted, unrefreshing sleep leading to daytime sleepiness. The current treatment for OSA is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), which is very effective, but adolescents do not feel comfortable wearing it and approximately 50% of adolescents with OSA will not use CPAP regularly. Untreated OSA can negatively impact physical and mental health. Since surgical treatment and weight loss strategies are largely unsuccessful for treating OSA, different strategies are necessary to improve adherence to CPAP. This is especially important for adolescents, who may be overwhelmed with using CPAP while adapting to an independent lifestyle and transitioning into adulthood. There is supporting evidence showing that mindfulness-based interventions can improve adherence to treatment by re-directing attention and avoiding negative thoughts and behaviours. We want to see whether mindfulness training can be beneficial with increasing CPAP adherence especially in adolescents who have severe OSA but rarely use CPAP. The main purpose of this randomized controlled study is to assess the effectiveness of a mindfulness-based intervention in improving CPAP adherence when compared to regular peer support activities. In this study, in addition to standard of care in-clinic CPAP support, adolescents will be randomized to either an online mindfulness-based intervention or a peer support group. There will be a total of 8 sessions and each session will last 60 minutes. We will measure adherence to CPAP therapy, daytime sleepiness, quality of life and psychosocial functioning before and after the interventions. We believe that mindfulness training compared to peer support will increase CPAP adherence, and improved CPAP adherence will be associated with reduced daytime sleepiness, improved quality of life and overall better health.

column36: Identification of novel therapeutic targets for SOX2-driven lung squamous cell carcinoma
column37: Lung cancer causes the greatest number of cancer deaths. Squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) is the second most common form of lung cancer and patients with this disease have limited treatment options. Immunotherapy and chemotherapy are standard of care, but most patients will not derive longterm benefits from these therapies. Development of new treatment strategies has been hindered by a poor understanding of what causes LUSC cancer cells to grow and a shortage of potential drug targets. In ~90% of LUSC patients, too much of a protein called SOX2 is made. These abnormally high levels of SOX2 are essential for growth of the cancer cells, but unfortunately, due to its small size and structure, SOX2 is not easy to target with drugs that block its function. Furthermore, because our understanding of how SOX2 works is limited, it is not clear whether designing drugs to other proteins might somehow interfere with SOX2 function. Here, we propose to use a new biochemical technique to identify proteins that physically associate with SOX2 to promote growth of LUSC cancer cells. We also propose to do in depth studies on the changes SOX2 and its closely associated partner proteins make in the cancer cells to cause them to grow. These studies will be facilitated by new LUSC models we have created that can either be grown in Petri dishes or as tumors in mice, which closely resemble the disease in patients. We believe that by identifying partners of SOX2 and the key changes SOX2 and its partners make in the cancer cells, we will discover new proteins that can be more easily targeted with drugs, which will ultimately have the same effect as blocking SOX2 function. We have already discovered hundreds of SOX2 partners and are currently investigating which of these proteins are essential for SOX2 to promote cancer cell growth. Given the widespread role of SOX2 in LUSC, this work has the potential to be broadly relevant to the second most common form of lung cancer.

column36: Caring Over the Lifecycle: the Roles of Families and Welfare States Today and Into the Future (WELLCARE)
column37: With ageing populations, there is growing concern about how societies can best meet their caring responsibilities, which are highest for children and the elderly. They are met by combinations of informal care provided by family member, and formal care either privately purchased or from publicly-funded government programs. This research proposal compares the ways formal and informal care are provided in four countries - Spain, Austria, UK, and Canada. With careful cross-national comparative analysis, we can learn about alternative approaches to meeting caring responsibilities. A 2019 analysis for Canada showed that the increasing share of the population at higher ages combined with continuing increases in life expectancy and declines in fertility rates could create major tensions by 2050 for meeting their care needs. Still, the complement of population ageing is a decline in the proportion of children, giving rise to a what some are calling a "demographic dividend". But will a decline in caring responsibilities for children be able to offset increasing needs for formal and informal care for the elderly? The core of the research will build on detailed population surveys in each country, and extend current computer simulation models to project scenarios by which each country can meet its caring needs. Phrases like the "gray tsunami" and "demodoom" paint a very negative picture where the baby boom cohort impose heavy burdens on future working age cohorts. Thus, a central aspect of the analysis of both formal and informal care services will be an assessment of inter-generational equity. However, there is tremendous variation across individuals within each generation, so the analysis will also draw on the survey data and simulation models to assess intra-generational patterns of caring from a full life course perspective. The results will include new insights and actionable policy ideas on how best to meet Canada's caring responsibilities.
