column37: Undernutrition accounts for at least half of all childhood deaths worldwide. Those who survive are at an increased risk for repeated infections, chronic diseases, poor physical and mental development, and poor economic prosperity later in life. Infants and children between 0-23 months of age are particularly vulnerable to the detrimental effects of undernutrition. This formative period therefore offers a window of opportunity for promoting healthy growth and improving child survival. Child undernutrition remains a devastating problem in Pakistan, with one in three children reported to be underweight, four in 10 too short for one's age, and almost one in five dangerously thin for one's height. The study team will engage the community to identify uncommon but successful behaviors practiced by local mothers of well-nourished children from economically disadvantaged homes, and transfer these to mothers with undernourished children who are equally disadvantaged in the wider study community. We will collect pre-intervention data to learn about the uncommon practices and design the intervention. Mothers and interested family will come together in a home-like setting to rehabilitate their malnourished child and learn new behaviors to sustain growth in their home. Home visits, print information and community events will reinforce key messages. Data will be collected during and post-intervention, and findings will be shared with the local and global community.

column36: Toward a paradigm shift in the promotion of healthy eating: Systematic development and feasibility testing of an intervention integrating pleasure to improve diet quality
column37: A high proportion of Canadians do not meet dietary guidelines. This suggests that there is room for improvement in the way we intervene to promote healthy eating. Traditionally, interventions that are used to improve dietary habits are mainly focusing on health attributes of foods. Unfortunately, one downside to these approaches is that what is thought as "being good for your health" is often considered as being less tasty and less rewarding than "unhealthy" food. In that context, innovative approaches that consider the obvious importance of eating pleasure in everyday food choices and food-related contexts could be of great interest. However, no systematically developed evidence-based intervention is currently available to test the efficacy of such a strategy. Accordingly, the general objective of this project is to develop an intervention that integrates the different dimensions of pleasure to promote healthy eating. This intervention will be developed for both men and women, aged between 18-65 years, living with obesity. We want to make sure that the intervention is well aligned with evidence in the literature as well as with the needs of our population and perspectives of intervention providers. In order to do so, we will use strategies consistent with Intervention Mapping which is a flexible framework that is used for effective decision making at each step in the intervention development process. In conclusion, although it can seem as being a laborious and time-consuming process, a comprehensive and systematic approach is needed to develop effective interventions. Not doing so can dramatically reduce the efficacy of the intervention, leading to waste of time and money. The development of the first comprehensive intervention that integrates the different dimensions of pleasure to promote healthy eating in people living with obesity will be eventually followed by a randomized controlled trial conducted to evaluate the efficacy of our intervention.

column36: Development, validation, and implementation of a knowledge synthesis reporting guideline for outcome measurement instruments in health research
column37: Healthcare providers rely on information collected from research studies to decide which treatments work best for patients. Central in these studies are health outcome measurement tools for any given health condition, such as lab tests, questionnaires that the patient completes, or rating scales that a physician completes. Outcome measurements are only as good as the tools used to make them and deciding which tool to use is an important research decision. Not all tools are created equally; some are better than others, either overall or when used in specific settings or populations. A comprehensive research process that helps researchers and doctors decide which tool to choose is available. It provides set criteria to evaluate possible tools, and guidance on how to decide which tool is best for the purpose at hand. However, there is no consensus on what core information is needed to describe this process in published reports. Currently, these reports often do not provide enough detail on how well this process was conducted, impairing the choice of the right tool. To address this issue, we assembled an international group of experts to develop and evaluate a checklist for researchers to use for publishing the results of their studies on tools, which will ensure all necessary information is included. Our team includes measurement tool developers, tool users such as doctors and researchers, checklist developers, and users of knowledge generated by tools including patients. The new checklist, developed using cutting edge research methods, will be tested across mental health, rheumatology, neurology, surgery, and child health specialities. It will be freely available worldwide to use, and have a global impact by teaching researchers how to describe their studies on tools appropriately, so that measurements made are useful, correct, and meaningful. Our work will improve the quality of research studies that inform health decisions, ultimately improving health outcomes.

column36: Impact of Emergency Department Opioid Prescribing on Health Outcomes
column37: During the last 20 years, emergency department (ED) doctors have prescribed more opioid (narcotic) painkillers for pain. Some experts believe that many patients became addicted to these opioids and that this has contributed to the opioid epidemic, causing thousands of deaths. One solution is for doctors to reduce or stop prescribing opioids, and some health leaders suggest that emergency departments should become opioid free and not use or prescribe opioids. Many doctors have done this. Eliminating opioid prescriptions might reduce the chance of addiction and overdose, but it also means that patients with injuries and other painful conditions might not receive good pain control. Public health experts also worry that, if doctors refuse to prescribe opioids, patients who need them may be forced to buy impure replacement drugs on the street, putting themselves at risk of overdose. No one knows how often patients become addicted or have health problems because of painkillers prescribed in the ED, and no one knows what type of patients are at highest risk. We plan to study patients who receive an opioid prescription after their ED visit, to see how many become addicted or have a bad outcome, like death, an overdose or hospitalization. If these bad outcomes are common, then perhaps emergency doctors should stop prescribing opioids. If bad outcomes are rare, then it may be safe to prescribe opioids to selected types of patients who are unlikely to suffer harm. We will also study whether patients who regularly use opioids are safer if they get an opioid prescription (or don't get one), and what types of patients are more likely to have problems because of their prescription (for example, older patients or patients with specific types of illnesses or injuries). This research will help doctors and patients decide how risky an opioid prescription is, and whether, depending on the circumstances, it is reasonable and safe to take these drugs after an emergency visit.

column36: Glucocorticoid signalling in regenerating muscle: Mechanisms behind wasting side effects in healthy muscle and paradoxical benefit in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy treatment.
column37: Glucocorticoids are one of the most widely prescribed classes of drugs in both children and adults due to their potent anti-inflammatory action. However, one of the major side effects of glucocorticoid treatment is muscle atrophy, a condition where muscle mass is lost. Despite the side effects, for boys suffering from Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a muscle wasting disease, glucocorticoids are the first line of treatment, preventing disease worsening for up to three years. While glucocorticoids remain the best treatment for many conditions, little is known about how glucocorticoids cause muscle atrophy as a side effect or paradoxically improve the disease course of DMD. Since the maintenance of muscle mass is dependent on the activity of muscle stem cells, which are essential for muscle regeneration, it is critical to understand how glucocorticoids affect these cells and their activity. To understand how glucocorticoids act on muscle stem cells, we made a mouse model where muscle stem cells cannot respond to glucocorticoids. We found that glucocorticoids are important during muscle repair as they act to organize the muscle fiber's contraction machinery and to correctly position cell nuclei. We predict that glucocorticoids alter the structure of the cytoskeleton, a fibrous protein latticework inside the muscle cell that gives it its shape and ability to resist mechanical stress. In diseased muscle, like in DMD patients, we think glucocorticoids improve the cytoskeleton by making the connections more square and less random, which protects the cell from contraction-induced injury. In healthy muscle, we think glucocorticoids make the cytoskeleton too rigid and inflexible, and this causes the damage we see as atrophy. To study this, we will use molecular and cell biology techniques to determine how glucocorticoids exert their actions in newly formed muscle fibers and their effects on normal and wasting muscle.

What's more, LLD is hard to treat, as many people will not respond to treatment and many will stop taking antidepressant medication due to negative side-effects. We will recruit 213 patients who will be randomly assigned to 8-weeks of either MBCT or HEP. We will observe whether these treatments improve symptoms of depression. In addition, we will investigate the impact of this intervention on cognitive functioning and explore the underlying changes in brain structure/function. If successful, MBCT may be a potential solution to this gap in treatment options, as it is easily given in groups and is well-tolerated by older adults with LLD. This study will pave the road to a more scientific understanding of depression treatment for vulnerable older adults.

column36: Acting at a distance: How pediatric brain tumors perturb neural stem cell function
column37: One of the success stories in the cancer field is that most children with brain tumors survive. Aggressive treatment of these tumors, however, results in "late effects" that include long-term neurological and psychosocial disabilities. For example, up to 97 per cent of survivors of the childhood brain tumor medulloblastoma that receive radiation treatment exhibit learning and memory deficits that prevents them from holding jobs or succeeding academically. Radiation is not the only predictor of cognitive deficits, since up to 50% of children who do not receive radiation treatment also show deficits. We ask here whether brain tumors secrete substances that cause the stem cells that build the brain and are responsible for optimal cognition to misfunction. Indeed, our initial studies in mice show that brain tumor cells and the substances they secrete can decrease by half the numbers of stem cells and the cells they produce during brain development. This finding suggests that brain tumors can "act at a distance" by producing substances that travel throughout the brain and directly affect the function of stem cells. Stem cells depend upon receiving signals from their environment to make the precise numbers of cells that refine the connections and circuitry required for optimal cognition. We think that brain tumors disturb this communication, causing perturbations in stem cell function. Here, we will identify the substances produced by brain tumors, ask how they perturb stem cell function and discover how to block the action of the substances on stem cells. If we achieve our goals, we will identify potential treatments for the many survivors of brain tumors with cognitive deficits.

column36: PEITHO-3. Reduced-dose thrombolytic treatment for patients with higher-intermediate risk acute pulmonary embolism.
column37: When a patient is diagnosed with blood clots in the lung (pulmonary embolism or 'PE'), the treatment is blood thinners. Additional treatment they receive is guided by how severe the blood clots are. Around a third of people diagnosed with PE can be categorized as intermediate risk and these patients have double the risk of dying within the next month. Currently these people are treated with injectable blood thinners. Very few patients have high risk PE and they are all given a powerful medication called thrombolysis. Thrombolysis breaks down the clot but can also cause bleeding (which may lead to death or stroke). Only one study has looked at using thrombolysis for intermediate risk patients with PE. This study found that the benefits of thrombolysis were offset by a higher rate of serious bleeding. column37: Learning something new is easier if we already have knowledge on that topic, but how this happens in the brain is only beginning to be understood. Most studies of how the brain makes new memories use stimuli, such as a list of unrelated words, that separate information from its broader context. However, this approach cannot explain how memory formation in the brain works in the real world. Only recently have groundbreaking animal studies discovered that prior knowledge promotes new memory by transforming the way the cortex (the brain's outer surface) learns. Prior knowledge transforms the brain from being a "slow learner" to a "fast integrator" of new knowledge related to old knowledge. Still, little is known about how this transformation happens, whether and how rapid cortical learning works in humans, and the extent to which this process continues into old age. In a series of experiments, we will test old and young bird experts and non-experts to see whether degrees of prior knowledge speed new learning and offset age-related memory decline. By measuring electromagnetic brain signals in participants, we will test whether intentionally activating prior knowledge of birds leads to increased cross-talk between cortical regions, and whether this promotes integration of new knowledge into networks of old knowledge. Using magnetic resonance imaging, we will examine how specific cortical activity that is active when learning new birds differs between experts and non-experts. Our research is also testing the theory that too much inhibition of the cortex might prevent older adults from fully benefitting from their often-superior prior knowledge. We predict that removing that inhibition using non-invasive mild electric current would particularly benefit experts who have more extensive prior knowledge. These studies will pave the way for optimizing the use of prior knowledge to improve memory in older adults, impacting both their rehabilitation and quality of life.

column36: Effect of Hypoxia and Nitric Oxide Therapy on Adenylyl Cyclase Activity in Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn
column37: After a baby is born, air rushes into the lungs with its first breath - but to pick up oxygen from that breath, blood urgently has to flow to the lungs too. Newborn lung blood flow is normally triggered by the presence of oxygen. Babies who have difficult deliveries, or who don't get enough oxygen during their birth, sometimes can't get enough blood flowing to their lungs. So even when they try to breathe, they can't pick up oxygen from their breaths - and they stay blue. This disease is called newborn pulmonary hypertension. It accounts for 10% of admissions to the newborn ICU, and these blue babies are the sickest in the newborn ICU. We have some drugs to treat them, but they don't always work. Heart muscle and lung blood vessel muscles have opposite jobs at birth. The heart needs to contract harder, and lung blood vessels need to relax to let blood flow. These opposite events happen through a single system of signals inside the cell, called the adenylyl cyclase pathway. We studied effects of low oxygen levels on the function of the heart, and on muscle lining the blood vessels of the newborn lung. In low oxygen, muscles in the heart and blood vessels don't respond properly to medications. We found that adenylyl cyclase doesn't work in low oxygen. Exposure to a low oxygen level makes this enzyme slow down, like a foot on the brake of a car. That means lung blood vessels can't relax, and blood won't flow into the baby's lungs. Even after oxygen levels normalize, this enzyme doesn't resume its normal function. Many important drugs use the adenylyl cyclase system, including those we use in the ICU to make a baby's heart pump better. These drugs also stop working in low oxygen. We hope to help these babies' lungs relax to allow blood flow, and help their hearts pump against the burden, by testing the switches that turn the adenylyl cyclase molecule on and off, in animal and cell models of pulmonary hypertension, and in models of the adenylyl cyclase molecule.

column36: Role of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) in intestinal homeostasis
column37: Advances in treatment of Cystic Fibrosis (CF) has led to an increased life expectancy of CF patients. As more patients survive for longer, more of them are suffering from intestinal symptoms of the disease. These patients suffer from intestinal inflammation, obstruction and the overgrowth of intestinal bacteria but the mechanisms underlying these effects are not well understood. We analyzed the intestines of several mouse models for CF and found that CF mouse intestines were also inflamed. To understand better how the handling of intestinal bacteria may be altered in CF, we infected the CF mice with Citrobacter rodentium, a natural mouse pathogen that infects the intestinal tract and is widely used to study intestinal responses to bacteria. CF mice had striking defects in their handling of this bacterial infection, with uncontrolled growth of bacteria and defective immune responses, leading to high mortality. Further experiments unexpectedly showed that the cells lining the intestinal tract, which many have proposed are the cause of intestinal defects in CF, were not responsible for these effects. Investigating further we found that specific immune cells were altered in the CF mice, and we found defects in certain processes within these cells that could potentially explain the results. In this grant proposal we are proposing experiments that we anticipate will definitively identify the cell types responsible for the effects we see in the intestine in CF mice and in CF patients and will help us understand better the processes that are altered to cause these effects. Since there are already drugs available that target these processes, we will also test if these drugs can improve the defects we have described in the CF cells and mouse intestines. These studies would be a first step towards potentially repurposing these drugs to treat gastrointestinal symptoms of CF patients.

column36: Uncovering the mechanisms of stress granule disassembly and their role in neurodegeneration
column37: Cells are constantly exposed to various stresses that cause deleterious damages to essential molecules, such as proteins. To deal with this, cells stop the production of proteins from RNA and store these molecules in a compartment called stress granules. Once stress is resolved, stress granules are rapidly disassembled and protein production resumes. Blocking this process promotes cell death, indicating that effective stress granule disassembly is crucial for cells to survive post-stress. In neurodegenerative diseases, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Frontotemporal Dementia, stress granule proteins are frequently mutated and aggregate into rigid clumps that are toxic to cells. In this project, we are testing the hypothesis that in disease, the combination of mutations in stress granule proteins and defects in stress granule disassembly of stress granules causes protein aggregation that promotes neurodegeneration. As such, the goal of this project is to determine how stress granule disassembly is regulated normally and how defects in this process contributes to protein aggregation and neurodegeneration. We will study this problem in the cell type that degenerates in disease, called neurons, using state of the art microscopy and biochemistry methods. The majority of the neurons are made early in our development and age with us. Consequently, these cell types accumulate damages from repeated exposure to stressors. By identifying the cellular processes that deal with stress-induced damages, our goal is to develop new strategies to promote their actions and aid in treatments for neurodegeneration.

column36: Molecular mechanisms and functional contributions of long-term memory decay
column37: Forgetting is commonly perceived as a failure of normal memory. Yet, in the last decade it has become increasingly clear that much of everyday forgetting results from dedicated forgetting processes that are built into the brain, which seem necessary for the brain to function normally. We have shown that one of these forgetting processes systematically reduces the strength of connections between neurons over time. This "active decay" process gradually disassembles the neuronal structures supporting memory, leading to memory loss. We now wish to learn more about active decay, which seems responsible for a significant amount of everyday forgetting: (1) It is known that programmed, controlled cell death involves the disassembly of the connections between neurons. We therefore will to test whether the same molecular events that trigger the disassembly of connections during cell death could also be involved in normal, everyday forgetting without causing cell death. (2) We aim to better understand how exactly decay reduces the strength of connections between neurons, and how this process is regulated. (3) Finally, we will explore whether dysfunction of this forgetting process contributes to certain cognitive problems. In autism spectrum disorder, for example, inflexibility in adjusting behavior might reflect a problem in forgetting inadequate responses, which can persist and disrupt normal functioning. We will try to restore normal forgetting in rat strains that carry genetic modifications found in neurodevelopmental intellectual disorders. Better understanding forgetting will provide us with vital knowledge about the normal functioning of the healthy brain. This will also help us understand how dysfunctional forgetting contributes to disorders of the brain in which individuals forget too little or too much, which is the case in some neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism spectrum disorders, and neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease.

column37: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system where a tumour develops from the abnormal growth of white blood cells. Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas (NHL) are the fifth most common cancers diagnosed in Canada. Our group and others have provided numerous genetic studies which resulted in a better understanding of the internal chemical mechanisms of communication (signaling pathways) altered in malignant cells. However, the cross-talk between different signaling pathways as well as their role in affecting lymphoma cell survival is still unknown. The tumour is not only composed of cancer cells; these cells, in fact, are surrounded by a milieu of other cells and molecules (also known as the tumour microenvironment) that contribute to the development and survival of the tumour. Although some improvements have been made in the treatment of lymphoma, current standard of care therapies still fail to cure a significant proportion of patients who are then very likely to succumb to their disease. With this proposal we aim to significantly improve our knowledge about how gene mutation combinations contribute to lymphoma growth and survival. In particular, we will explore the influence of mutations (alone and in cooperation) in the so-called Janus kinase-signal transducer and activation of transcription (JAK-STAT) (such as IL4R) and interferon (such as IRF4) signaling pathways on tumour growth and on the tumour microenvironment. Our studies will be very important for the generation of data that will guide physicians to select patients for future clinical trials. We hope that our research will guide physicians to deliver "personalized treatments" to lymphoma patients that will lead to better cure rates and fewer treatment-related side effects.

column36: Neurobiology of fructose-induced obesity
column37: Fructose is a simple sugar found in natural foods like fruits and honey, but it is used excessively in the Western diet via sweeteners like high fructose corn syrup and added sugar in processed foods or baked goods. This is a concern because excessive fructose intake can lead to metabolic syndrome, which increases the risk for fatal health diseases, including obesity, diabetes, heart and liver disease, and cancer. We have shown that a high fructose diet leads to overeating, weight gain, more body fat. The brain is the vital organ that drives food intake, and in particular, specialized brain cells that produce Neuropeptide Y (NPY) become more active, such as after fasting, to increase food intake. We recorded the activity of NPY neurons to learn how they respond when eating a high fructose diet, and we found that NPY neurons receive more excitatory input after eating a high fructose diet. This response is acute and develops within one week, and it is remarkably adaptable, so it can be dialed back down to a normal state when terminating the fructose diet. Our proposal will determine whether prolonged periods of fructose feeding, as seen in the human diet, would sustain the stimulation of NPY neurons long after fructose feeding stops. Importantly, we plan to shut off this excitatory input to NPY neurons to see if it would prevent weight gain while continuing to eat a high fructose diet. This proposal will provide answers that help us identify what goes wrong at key players like NPY neurons after fructose feeding. It is important because these answers will guide the development of treatment targets or interventions to alleviate the effects of prolonged fructose feeding that is pervasive in our diet. Our research strives to contribute strong scientific evidence to fuel food policy changes and healthful food practices backed by science. In effect, our research will improve the nutritional health of all Canadians.

column36: Validation of the Canadian Prehospital Syncope Risk Score
column37: Background: Syncope is defined as a sudden, brief loss of consciousness (LOC) followed by a rapid complete recovery. It accounts for 160,000 emergency department (ED) visits each year in Canada. Despite this, few people are hospitalized (~15%) and even fewer will die (~1%). Two-thirds of patients with syncope arrive to the ED by calling 911. There are many causes of syncope. Identifying patients at low risk for bad outcome would allow paramedics to safely determine which patients need care in the ED from those who can remain home. We recently developed the Canadian Prehospital Syncope Risk Score (CPSRS) which accurately identified patients at low risk for 30-day serious outcomes. Objective: The goal of this study is to validate the accuracy of the CPSRS in the prehospital setting to predict the risk of 30-day serious outcome for patients with syncope. Methods: We will enrol patients with syncope from five paramedic services across Canada (British Columbia - Vancouver and Kelowna areas only, London-Middlesex, York Region, Frontenac, and Ottawa). We will exclude patients <18 years old, LOC >5 minutes, changes in mental status from baseline, alcohol or drug intoxication, or language barrier. Paramedics will fill out a study data collection form with the CPSRS items and additional data should the tool need refinement. The data will be entered into a secure database and will assess patient outcomes (death and potentially life-threatening medical conditions) at 30 days. We will examine model accuracy using standard prediction measures and look to improve model accuracy if needed. We expect to enrol 4875 patients over a 1-year recruitment period based on annual call volumes. Expected Outcomes: Once validated, the tool could reduce the number of patients transported to hospital by identifying those at low risk. This would improve patient-oriented care, while at the same time saving valuable paramedic and ED resources.

column36: Repurposing Metformin to Target TET2 Mutation Driven Clonal Hematopoiesis and Malignant Transformation
column37: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) refers to the expansion of blood cells carrying mutations associated with leukemia in individuals without evidence of a blood disorder. One of the most common CHIP mutations is in the gene TET2. Individuals with CHIP are at a substantially higher risk of developing blood cancers than non-carriers. The time period from CHIP to a diagnosis of blood cancer can be many years. This finding opens up the intriguing possibility of intervening to prevent blood cancers from developing in the first place. To achieve this goal, safe and effective interventions are needed. Here, we will explore the preventive potential of metformin, a safe and commonly-used diabetic medication, in suppressing TET2 mutation-driven CHIP. Mutations in TET2 reduce the activity of TET2, which in turn causes the expansion of mutated blood cells. We recently discovered that metformin is able to restore TET2 expression and activity and suppress the growth of TET2-mutated cells. In this proposal, we will build on these findings by exploring how metformin works. We will study the role of a protein called AMPK and determine how metformin changes the genetic code in TET2-mutated cells. Finally, we will determine if metformin treatment can prevent or delay the development of leukemia in a mouse model of CHIP. Our proposed studies, if successful, will establish a novel approach for preventing blood cancers.

column37: Microglia are the immune cells residing in the brain and play key roles in its development maintenance of proper functioning, and immune response against infections and injuries. Work by us and others recently demonstrated that discrete regions of the genome called enhancers are critical to ensure that genes are correctly expressed in microglia. However, how enhancers, in the number of 40,000 in microglia, are regulated in the brain under both under healthy and pathological conditions remains largely unknown. To investigate how these genomic regions contribute to gene regulation, we will characterize the interactions between proteins involved in gene regulation and enhancers. To do so, we will isolate microglia from the mouse brain and perform assays with next-generation sequencing technologies to reveal how enhancers are involved in specifying microglia gene expression in a given context. Collectively, this research program will enable a much greater understanding of the signalling and epigenetic mechanisms that are responsible for gene regulation microglia, and by extension, the mechanisms that underlie the cellular functions of microglia. Thus, precisely defining the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate microglia gene expression in mice as proposed by this research program represents a critical step towards the development of more efficient therapies to treat neuropsychiatric disorders and neurodegenerative diseases.

column37: Pregnant women are on daily injectable blood thinners if they are at risk of a blood clot in their legs (deep vein thrombosis) or lungs (pulmonary embolism) during pregnancy. We will collect information about the amount of blood lost at the time of delivery and other delivery details. We will see or call participants at 6 weeks and 90 days postpartum to assess for complications of bleeding, blood clots, and wound complications. Because the patient experience is very important, we will also ask participants about the choices they made and satisfaction with their delivery experience. We will also collect information about hospital resources used with each of the different management strategies. By better understanding what practices are happening around the world and collecting outcome information in a similar way at all participating centres, we can provide doctors and patients with more information about the risks and benefits of the different options of blood thinner management around delivery.

column36: Navigating the Valley of Death: How Evidence is Evaluated in Phase 2 Trial Initiation
column37: The vast majority of new drugs tested in patients fail to demonstrate enough safety and efficacy to receive approval. Most of this failure occurs in "phase 2" clinical trials- a stage of testing aimed at showing drug efficacy in patients for the first time. Every time a drug fails in phase 2 trials, patients are exposed to a drug that is either unsafe or ineffective, and healthcare and research systems expend scarce resources pursuing blind alleys. The aim of this grant is to improve the way we make decisions about which phase 2 trials to pursue. Previous studies suggest that ethics committees and other decision-makers find it difficult to form judgments about risk, benefit and the clinical promise of new treatments tested in phase 2 trials. Moreover, the documentation used to support such evaluations often lacks critical information to help reviewers form judgments. Our study will proceed in four steps. First, we will examine what kind of information is presented to scientists and others who make decisions about whether to launch phase 2 trials. Second, we will observe how ethics and scientific committees make decisions about starting phase 2 trials. Third, we will interview experts to find out what sorts of information experts seek out when evaluating proposed phase 2 trials. Fourth, we will perform a series of experiments to test whether information formats used in trial documentation sometimes results in biased decisions. Once our four studies are complete, we will synthesize our findings into a series of recommendations for improving the information and processes used to make decisions about which phase 2 trials to pursue. We have lined up numerous partners to help ensure our findings translate into better protections for human volunteers in phase 2 trials, and more impactful drug development efforts.

column36: Defining and measuring the value of genetic testing from patients' perspectives: Developing the Patient-reported Genetic testing Utility InDEx (P-GUIDE)

column36: The maternal gut microbiome as a target to prevent fetal spina bifida
column37: Spina bifida, one of the most common birth defects, occurs when the spine does not close properly before birth. It is associated with poor development of the baby before birth, and after birth, babies born with spina bifida have paralysed limbs and developmental delay. Key risk factors for spina bifida are low levels of folic acid and vitamin B12 in the mother's blood in early pregnancy. Currently, the primary prevention strategy is to increase a woman's intake of folic acid through food or vitamins. Yet, 1 in 4 women still have low vitamin levels and only ~50% of cases of spina bifida are prevented. An important contributor to healthy nutrient levels are the bacteria (microbiome) in the gut. A healthy gut microbiome can produce up to 30% of the daily required folic acid and vitamin B12, supports nutrient absorption, and produces molecules that can affect transport of these and other nutrients by the placenta to influence development of the baby. We think the gut microbiome plays a critical role in vitamin regulation in pregnancy and an abnormal gut microbiome may cause some cases of spina bifida. To test our hypotheses, we will compare the gut microbiomes of pregnant women carrying a baby with spina bifida with the microbiomes of women carrying a healthy baby. We will examine how specific changes in the microbiome correlate with vitamin levels in the maternal blood and the development and function of the placenta, including nutrient transport. We will use a mouse model of spina bifida to test if modifying the maternal microbiome using dietary interventions like probiotics can potentially reduce the rate of spina bifida and improve placental function. Lastly, we will administer probiotics to non-pregnant women to determine if it improves their vitamin levels and is a safe, acceptable, and feasible intervention. Findings from our study will help us understand how spina bifida occurs and, ultimately, find new ways to prevent spina bifida and improve development.

column36: Prevention of anastomotic leak in colorectal surgery through microbiome mediation of intestinal healing
column37: Gastrointestinal resections are surgical procedures where a part of the bowel is surgically resected and reconnected. These procedures are common in several pathologies, especially in colorectal cancer. In some patients, the reconnection site, or "anastomosis", may not heal properly and leak, a major complication called anastomotic leak (AL). Despite major efforts in the last decades to prevent AL, this complication still occurs in many patients, and continues to be a major cause of morbidity and mortality in colorectal surgery. Some recent evidence has suggested the gut microbiota, or the collection of bacteria in the gut, may influence healing and cause, or prevent, AL. We propose to investigate which bacterial species may be associated with anastomotic healing by conducting animal experiments where microbiota transplant is performed in mice undergoing colonic surgery. We will also test microbiota-targeted interventions to improve anastomotic healing and prevent AL. These interventions will include prebiotics, namely the fiber inulin, and the probiotic Akkermansia muciniphila. We propose to evaluate by which mechanisms these interventions may improve colonic recovery after surgery. This project aims at characterizing how the gut microbiota may be associated with intestinal healing after surgery, and at assessing how the proposed nutritional interventions may enhance recovery and prevent leakage. The findings that this proposal may lead to will improve surgical care and pave the way toward clinical interventions that may greatly improve patients quality of life.

column37: Fabry disease is an inherited disorder that affects many organs in the body, including the heart. Men and women are both affected, with average life expectancy reduced by 10-20 years. The heart muscle can become thick and scarred in over half of patients, eventually resulting in heart failure, abnormal heart rhythm and death. We are focused on improving the detection of early heart disease before irreversible damage has occurred in order to improve patient outcomes. The techniques that have traditionally been used to look for disease in the heart are inadequate, as they often identify abnormalities once permanent scarring has already developed. Patients with heart damage have poor outcomes even with treatment. Therefore, it is critical to develop an earlier and reliable way to identify subtle disease in the heart, so that treatment can be initiated early when patients will benefit the most. We have previously shown that cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can identify changes in the heart muscle in patients with Fabry disease. We hypothesize that new cardiac MRI techniques called T1 and T2 mapping will improve our ability to detect early abnormalities in the heart. Early detection of cardiac disease may enable a personalized treatment approach, potentially improving patient outcomes. The results of this study will help identify which patients might benefit from early initiation of treatment to prevent bad outcomes in the future by using cardiac MRI to identify those at higher risk.

column36: Investigating the Impact of Cannabis Retail Policies on Health Harms and Benefits
column37: In October 2018, the Cannabis Act legalized recreational cannabis in Canada. The Act had two goals: to eliminate the illegal cannabis market and to reduce the use of cannabis by young Canadians. There are benefits to legalization such as eliminating harms from the criminalization of cannabis possession and increasing government revenue. However, cannabis use has been linked to health harms including addiction, mental health problems like psychosis, and poisonings. Policy makers wanting to minimize cannabis harms can draw on decades of research looking at the best way to regulate the sale of legal substances such as alcohol and tobacco. This research has found that when more stores sell alcohol and tobacco, people tend to use more of these substances, resulting in more health harms. Determining whether a similar relationship exists for cannabis has important implications for the goal of reducing use of cannabis by youth. To investigate this relationship, our research team will collect the location and hours of operation of all stores selling cannabis in Canada over a four-year period. We will track the evolving cannabis retail environment for important measures such as density of stores and concentration in low-income areas. In Ontario, cannabis retail stores were chosen by a random lottery, allowing us to compare people who live close to a store that was chosen vs. those that live close to a lottery applicant that was not chosen. We will then use databases containing records of all emergency department visits and hospitalizations in Ontario to see whether individuals who live near a store selling cannabis are more likely to have a health care visit caused by cannabis compared to those who do not. We will work with health and government officials at the local, provincial, and national level to communicate the results of our research and help design stronger policy related to regulating how and where we sell cannabis.

column36: Could mitotic senescence in NG2-glia explain the remyelination deficit in MS?
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the fatty sheaths that are wrapped around neuronal processes and that aid communication between brain cells become damaged. During the initial phase of the disease, the brain is able to repair those damages but this ability is frequently lost as MS progresses. So far the exact cause of this failure has not been pinpointed. Much of the sheath repair is reliant on new sheath-forming cells (called oligodendrocytes) produced by brain cells known as NG2-glia. We propose that the status of these NG2-glia is key to effective repair. Evidence suggest that these cells need to divide to ensure effective remyelination. We aim to determine whether the need of continuous brain repair as in case of progressive MS, eventually wears out the NG2-glia, rendering them successively less effective at restoring brain function after each period of damage. The proposed research may critically contribute to our understanding of the exact causes that lead to the transition to progressive MS disease stages. Based on our findings, future treatment strategies may focus on preventing or slowing down the decline of the repair capacity of NG2- glia thereby helping to prevent or delay disease progression.

column36: Therapeutic approach to preserve Tfh cells and improve B cell immunity in simian immunodeficiency virus infected rhesus macaques
column37: The depletion of CD4 T cells is a hallmark of HIV infection. A newly characterized population of CD4 T cells (T follicular helper, Tfh), which is essential for maintaining an efficient B cell immunity and for the maturation of HIV-specific antibodies, is depleted in different anatomical immune tissues after HIV infection. Despite early antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV persists in sanctuaries that permit viral rebound after ART interruption. Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) is closely related to HIV, and it causes a disease in rhesus macaques that is similar to AIDS in people, including the depletion of CD4 T and Tfh cells, and the constitution of ART-resistant reservoirs. We have tested a new compound that prevent SIV-induced CD4 T cell depletion in the absence of ART. We have also demonstrated that this protective effect was associated with both a reduction in the size of the SIV reservoirs and a delay in disease progression to simian AIDS. The main objective of this proposal is to test if combining this new anti-apoptotic agent with ART can both reduce the SIV reservoirs and improve the immune response against SIV. We hypothesize that combining this anti-apoptotic compound with ART will restore Tfh cells, improve B-cell immunity compared to ART alone, and help produce better antibodies capable of controlling viremia and broadening the immune response against SIV reservoirs. Thus, we also expect this beneficial effect to last beyond ART interruption. The project will include treatment-naive and ART-treated SIV-infected macaques that will receive this anti-apoptotic compound. We will analyze extensively T and B cell dynamics, tissue distribution, and antibody production in relation to the size of viral reservoirs. Overall, our main objective is to contribute to the improvement of cure strategies for people living with HIV.

Testing the xacqanal itkinil approach was the first step along the pathway toward a long-term working relationship between Ktunaxa Nation and Interior Health Authority. The goal of the next step is to use the xacqanal itkinil approach to look at how the health care system can learn from Ktunaxa understandings of wellness to improve health services in Ktunaxa communities.

column36: ACCELERATE: Partnering with ICU patients and family caregivers toward early transitions in care
column37: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are very sick and receive vital supportive care for all kinds of illnesses such as trauma, infections and stroke. Once a patient begins to recover, they leave the ICU and usually move to another part of the hospital or go directly home. This is part of the journey to recovery. For patients who have been very sick this is a big change in their care environment. There are new doctors and nurses in charge of their care (or maybe even no one when they go home) and their everyday looks very different from when they were in the ICU. This can cause a lot of confusion and stress for patients and their families (who often play key support roles for patients). Only the patient and their family stay the same as they move through the healthcare system. This makes it very important for the patient and their family to be informed and involved in their care. Starting an early discussion with patients and their families about their return home can help make the discharge process a lot smoother and less stressful. The goal of this study is to create a tool for early discharge planning that helps patients and their families become involved in their care as soon as they are admitted to the ICU. To do this we will work together with patients, families, doctors and nurses to create a tool that is easy to use and that meets their needs. We will help patients and families learn about their ICU care and learn what they need after the ICU. Patients and their families will be more informed and have more control over their care. We will improve communication between patients, families, doctors and nurses. Our goal is to have patients as the leaders of their own care, informed and in control.

column36: Developing a value framework for the assessment of precision cancer technologies for children
column37: Cancer remains the leading cause of disease-related death in Canadian children, adolescents and young adults (CAYA). Advances in understanding the genetic causes of cancer have opened up new treatment possibilities tailored to individual patients. However, these 'precision medicine' advances have created challenges for drug funding. There is lack of consensus about how to assess the value of precision cancer therapies (PCTs) to guide decision-making about which drugs to publicly cover. The result is inadequate evaluation and reimbursement of PCTs for CAYA, creating access barriers to innovative high-value therapies for young Canadians with cancer. If precision medicine advances are to achieve a lasting impact in Canada's publicly-funded health system, sound knowledge to guide their adoption is required. The overarching goal of this research is to develop a value framework to guide the evaluation and reimbursement of PCTs for CAYA in Canada. We will achieve this objective through a rigorous program of research that: elicits expert, patient and public input on the principles that should guide the evaluation and reimbursement of PCTs for CAYA; and generates and evaluates an assessment framework to guide PCT coverage decisions in Canada. These findings will equip national and provincial policymakers with evidence to guide fair and sustainable access to innovative therapies for young Canadians with cancer.

Ongoing colonialism and intergenerational family separation among Indigenous peoples may be experienced differently by First Nation and Metis families. Therefore, we will look at each research question separately for three groups of parents: First Nation, Metis, and all other Manitoban parents. Questions will be answered using population-based administrative data for all parents who had a child born in Manitoba from 1998 to 2020. column36: Pax2 Mediates Glomerular Repair
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a heterogeneous group of disorders that result in gradual loss of kidney tissue. We have reported that mutations in a gene named Pax2 account for ~4% of adults with a form of CKD called Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). There are reports that suggest Pax2 may play a role in kidney repair during aging or after injury. Stem cell marker studies show that Pax2 expressing cells could retain a capacity to regenerate some cells of the kidney. Other studies suggest that Pax2 cells remain closely related to other cell types, potentially to facilitate regeneration. However, studies performed in mouse models where Pax2 cells are labeled and tracked after injury have been conflicting in terms of supporting these conclusions. To study the function of Pax2 in the adult kidney, we obtained a Pax2 mutant mouse model which mimics the disease we observed in patients with FSGS. We find that mutant mice are more susceptible to injury and that more Pax2 cells die compared to wildtype mice. We thus postulate that kidney cells expressing mutant Pax2 are compromised in their ability to repair and enter cell death pathways after injury. To explore this hypothesis, we will integrate recently available technology called single-nucleus RNA sequencing to precisely map which cells of the human and mouse kidney express Pax2. We will take isolated Pax2 expressing cells from mutant and wildtype mice and compare their function and ability to repair after injury. Parallel experiments will also be performed in mice wherein Pax2 expressing cells are genetically labeled and tracked, an approach called lineage fate mapping. Our interest in Pax2 began with our report of mutations leading to FSGS in adults. We focus this proposal on exploring the role of Pax2 in inherent glomerular repair mechanisms, with the potential that exploiting these will lead to the development of novel therapeutics not only in FSGS but to all CKD.

column36: Investigating the unique experiences and needs of youth and young adults who use drugs during the dual crises of overdose and COVID-19
column37: Public health measures taken to respond to the COVID-19 crisis have been expected to negatively impact the health and well-being of youth and young adults who use drugs and challenge responses to the overdose crisis. Early in the pandemic, BC has been praised for having managed to contain the outbreak of the novel coronavirus. However, May, June and July 2020, saw record numbers of overdose deaths in BC with young people age 19-29 years consistently accounting for approximately one-in-five of all decedents from an overdose in BC. In this context, the impact of the pandemic and COVID-19 mitigation measures on street-involved youth who use drugs is largely unknown. To address this knowledge gap, we propose to build on the At-Risk Youth Study (ARYS), an established open prospective cohort of more than 1,200 street-involved youth (age 14-26) who use drugs in Vancouver, BC. At baseline and biannually participants complete a questionnaire which elicits information pertaining to behaviours and exposures occurring throughout the lifespan and in the previous six months. Using the infrastructure of the ARYS cohort, and in collaboration with Indigenous partners including the First Nations Health Authority, we propose to expand the ARYS questionnaire to include COVID-19 specific measures. Our specific objectives are to: (1) evaluate the impact of COVID-19 on the illicit drug supply and associated overdose risks; (2) investigate the impact of COVID-19 on access and engagement with overdose prevention interventions; and (3) evaluate the influence of COVID-19 clinical risk mitigation interventions on long-term trajectories of addiction treatment engagement and subsequent drug use patterns. Our aim is to generate evidence to inform interventions that prevent drug overdoses, promote engagement with health and social services, and support the overall health and wellness of street-involve youth in Vancouver and beyond as they contend with the duel crises of drug overdose and COVID-19.

column36: Endoscopic ultrasound-guided biliary drainage (EUS-BD) of first intent with a lumen apposing metal stent vs. endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) in the management of patients with malignant distal biliary obstruction: a multi-centre randomized controlled trial (ELEMENT trial)
column37: Pancreatic cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer related deaths in Canada. It has the propensity to invade or compress the bile duct, which is the conduit that allows bile to flow from the liver to the small intestines. Bile duct obstruction leads to symptoms of jaundice (yellowing of the skin), itching of the skin, malnutrition (bile is necessary for fat digestion/absorption), bile duct infection, and liver dysfunction. Without adequate bile flow patients cannot start chemotherapy treatments, which requires adequate liver function. The standard treatment for bile duct obstruction is through an endoscopic procedure called ERCP where a camera is advanced through the patient's mouth to the natural opening of the bile duct. A metal stent (metal tube) can then be inserted to re-establish bile flow. Although effective this procedure is associated with up to 30% need for re-intervention due to stent blockage from tumor growing through the stent. Stent blockage is associated with risk of bile duct infection, re-hospitalization, re-intervention, interruption in chemotherapy treatment, decreased in quality of life, and cost to our health care system. A new modality using endoscopic ultrasound (another type of camera with ultrasound capability) and a novel metal stent allows the placement of the stent above the tumor creating a new tract between the bile duct and gastrointestinal lumen. This "bypass" stent is postulated to minimize the risk for stent obstruction from tumor ingrowth. The goal of our proposed study is to compare this new modality with ERCP. This is a randomized controlled trial (patients will receive one of the treatments at random similar to a "flip of a coin") involving 10 Canadian centres. We believe that the "bypass" stent is more effective with better stent patency leading to better oncological care for patients with pancreatic cancer. The results of our study could potential change our approach to cancer related bile duct obstruction.

column36: Repeated Ketamine Infusions for Treatment-Resistant Bipolar Depression: A Randomized, Midazolam-Controlled Phase II Clinical Trial
column37: New treatments are urgently needed for bipolar depression (BD). Low doses of intravenous (IV) ketamine (an anesthetic medications) have been shown to have rapid antidepressant effects and reduce suicidal thoughts in major depressive disorder (MDD; unipolar depression); however, there is minimal research on the use of ketamine for BD. No completed or ongoing randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have evaluated the effects of repeated doses of IV ketamine for BD. Our group has treated 47 BD patients with repeated ketamine infusions and observed large decreases in depression symptoms and suicidal thoughts. Our primary research goal is to determine the antidepressant effects and side effect of repeated doses of IV ketamine for BD. We will also evaluate the impact of ketamine on suicidal thoughts and quality of life. We propose a two-site (University Health Network and the Canadian Rapid Treatment Centre of Excellence), double-blinded, two-week RCT evaluating the antidepressant effects, safety and tolerability of four flexibly-dosed ketamine infusions for moderate to severe BD, as compared to a control group. Active psychosis, mania, substance use and significant medical conditions will be exclusion criteria. 100 participants will be recruited (50 per group). The primary outcome will be changes in Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS; a validated depression severity scale) scores during the two-week trial. Response and remission rates will also be evaluated. Secondary outcomes include evaluating safety, side effects, and effects on suicidal thoughts, anxiety, quality of life and functional improvements. This study will be the first to evaluate the antidepressant effects and side effects of repeated doses of IV ketamine for BD. As the first RCT of its kind, our trial will add essential knowledge to either support or refute the use of IV ketamine in BD, informing Canadian and international treatment guidelines.

column36: Fostering healthy aging in naturally occurring retirement communities: a mixed methods explanatory case study
column37: Seniors are the fastest growing age group in Canada. By 2041, older adults will represent an estimated 25% of the population. The vast majority (>92%) of older adults live in the community and want to continue to live at home and independently for as long as possible. Unfortunately older adults are also at risk of becoming socially isolated and experience loneliness as they age. Inadequate nutrition, difficulty with mobility and decreased physical activity can also lead to poor overall health. The Oasis Seniors Supportive Living (Oasis) Program is a low-cost seniors-driven program aimed at supporting older adults who live in naturally occurring retirement communities such as an apartment building. The three core elements of the Oasis Program are social engagement, physical activity, and nutrition. An Onsite Oasis Coordinator facilitates activities and programs that address the self-identified needs and wants of the members, including connecting them to existing services in their community. Since April 2018, our research group has partnered with older adults and landlords in four cities in Ontario to develop seven Oasis Communities. The aim of this project is to understand how the Oasis Program promotes healthy aging in older adults living in these naturally occurring retirement communities. We will monitor the health of Oasis community members over four years. We will also measure the impact of this program on use of health care services, such as hospitalizations and transitions to long term care. Finally, we will hold focus group discussions with the participants over the 4 years to help us understand the strengths and limitations of the Oasis program, and how these communities develop and evolve over time. Throughout the entire project, we will be comparing these seven Oasis Communities to seven matched, non-Oasis communities. This project will inform aging-in-place strategies across the country and internationally.

column36: Phototherapy to modulate regulatory T cells and prevent autoimmune disease
column37: Sunlight therapy (phototherapy) is commonly used by dermatologists to treat inflammatory skin disease. It is known that this treatment works in part in the skin by inducing the death of disease-causing immune cells. This treatment also improves the function and number of immune protective cells called regulatory T cells. We have shown in an animal model that sunlight treatment of mice destined to get autoimmune diabetes prevents the development of diabetes in these animals. We will determine the characteristics of ultraviolet light (a portion of sunlight) that is required to prevent disease such as dosing, timing and wavelength. We will determine how the light affects regulatory T cells in the animal model. This work will lay the groundwork for the prevention of autoimmune diabetes in at risk humans through the use of sunlight therapy.

column36: Sante psychologique du personnel infirmier en periode d'insertion professionnelle: Predicteurs et consequences sur la retention dans la profession, l'etablissement et l'unite de soins
column37: Le personnel infirmier est confronte a d'importantes difficultes d'adaptation au travail en debut de carriere, ces dernieres se manifestant par le biais d'une diversite de formes de desengagement. Au Quebec, on estime que 12% du personnel infirmier abandonne la profession durant les cinq premieres annees de travail, une augmentation de 4%, soit un sommet, depuis cinq ans. Ces donnees sont particulierement alarmantes en raison de la penurie de personnel observee. Si plusieurs facteurs, a la fois psychologiques et sociaux, ont ete associes aux problemes entourant la retention du personnel, la sante psychologique, qui englobe tant l'absence de manifestations negatives que la presence de manifestations positives, tarde a etre etudiee en contexte d'insertion professionnelle, specialement lors de la periode de transition entre la fin de la formation initiale et l'entree en carriere. Le projet vise precisement a eclairer les questions suivantes: a) Quelles trajectoires de developpement de la sante psychologique presente les membres du personnel infirmier en contexte d'insertion professionnelle? b) Comment l'environnement de travail et les facteurs individuels influencent-ils la trajectoire de developpement de leur sante psychologique? c) Comment les differentes trajectoires influencent-elles la retention dans la profession, l'etablissement et l'unite de soins? Outre l'identification des facteurs susceptibles d'expliquer la fidelisation et la retention du personnel infirmier, nos resultats ouvriront sur le developpement de moyens favorisant l'harmonisation entre les imperatifs des etablissements de soins de sante et les besoins du personnel infirmier.

column36: High-Flow Nasal Oxygen with or without Helmet Non-invasive Ventilation for Oxygenation Support in Acute Respiratory Failure (HONOUR) Pilot RCT
column37: Patients with severe respiratory failure (including due to COVID-19) are at high risk of dying and will often require invasive mechanical ventilation. These patients typically require supplemental oxygen. However, the best way to deliver supplemental oxygen to these patients - in order to reduce their risk of dying or requiring invasive ventilation - is not known. This pilot study will determine if it is feasible to conduct a large definitive randomized controlled trial that directly compares two different approaches to delivering supplemental oxygen, each of which has potential benefits and risks: providing oxygen at very high flow rates using nasal cannulas, or supplementing this approach by also providing oxygen using a specially designed helmet interface connected to a ventilator. The results of this work will directly inform the design of the large trial comparing these two approaches, which in turn should identify the strategy that saves more lives of patients with acute respiratory failure, including those with COVID-19.

column36: Low dose ColchicinE in pAtients with peripheral Artery DiseasE to address residual vascular Risk (LEADER-PAD): A randomized trial (Vanguard Phase)
column37: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is caused by fatty deposit build-up (atherosclerotic plaques) within an inflamed arterial wall that obstructs blood flow in leg arteries. The reduced blood flow to the legs can cause disabling leg pain and limit walking. Other arteries, such as those supplying the heart and brain, are commonly affected too. Inflamed arteries are more prone to the sudden formation of blood clots. These clots can completely obstruct blood flow and lead to acute complications such as leg gangrene, heart attack and stroke. Surgery to open up arteries, blood thinning medications, blood pressure control and cholesterol lowering therapies can help prevent and treat these complications but about one-third of patients still end up with these complications. None of the existing therapies target inflammation. Because a major driver of plaque build-up and clotting is inflammation in the blood vessel wall, we believe that it makes sense to develop anti-inflammatory medicines to heal the arteries to reduce the risk of long term complications. The main aim of the LEADER-PAD research program is to examine whether an anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, will reduce complications in patients with PAD. This medication lowers complication rates by about 25% in patients with angina or heart attack, but has not been studied in patients with PAD, who would likely derive an even greater benefit because of the widespread atherosclerosis. As a first step, we will evaluate the feasibility of conducting such a definitive multicenter randomized trial in this (vanguard) proposal.

column36: Development of a tumour-targeted RAS-specific protease for pancreatic cancer therapy
column37: Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest of all human cancers, with less than 10% of patients surviving 5 years after initial diagnosis. What's more, our ability to treat pancreatic cancer has only marginally improved despite numerous advances in therapies for other cancers. In the case of pancreatic cancer, the vast majority of patients have tumors that are driven by mutations in a protein called KRAS. As such, KRAS is one of the most sought-after drug targets in oncology, and yet despite almost 40 years of effort, there are no approved drugs targeting KRAS. Recently, a protein called RRSP was discovered in bacteria that specifically cleaves and inactivates KRAS. RRSP - like all proteins - is unable to cross cell membranes to access mutant KRAS inside the cell. Without a way to enter cells, RRSP is ineffective as a therapeutic. Our lab has recently developed a protein delivery platform that uses the remarkable properties of bacterial toxins that can transport proteins into cells. Recently, we engineered a fusion protein where we fused RRSP to a fragment of diphtheria toxin, that delivers RRSP into cells. We demonstrated that this new protein potently inactivated KRAS and shrunk tumors in a mouse model of cancer. In this proposal, we are asking for funding from CIHR to modify RRSP-DTB to treat pancreatic cancer, where the need for a KRAS-targeted drug is most dire. We propose to re-target RRSP to bind to receptors that are enriched on pancreatic cancer cells relative to "healthy cells" to improve its safety by sparing healthy cells. We will test targeted RRSP chimeras against a panel of ~70 patient-derived pancreatic tumour cells (organoids) before testing the best candidate for testing in mouse models of pancreatic cancer. These studies represent a major step on the path towards understanding the potential of this molecule and this concept in developing urgently needed anti-RAS therapies.

column36: An umbrella review of prehabilitation interventions in surgery to inform policy and practice
column37: Over half a million Canadians have major surgery (like joint replacements, heart or cancer surgery) yearly. Surgery stresses people's bodies, much like running a marathon. Unlike runners, who train for their race, most Canadians are not actively preparing for surgery. This means that they may not be in the best possible shape for surgery and may suffer from complications, long hospital stay, or even die. Effective strategies to better prepare people for major surgery are needed. Prehabilitation means preparing for surgery through exercise, nutrition and/or stress management. People are very interested in prehabilitation because it makes sense that preparing people's minds and bodies for surgery will lead to better outcomes. Unfortunately, research has not always shown these benefits; we think this is because different types of patients need different types of prehabilitation. If we can understand what patient characteristics and what types of prehabilitation programs work best, we can use healthcare resources wisely, use patients' time wisely, and make sure the right patient receives the right care before surgery. We can also direct new research efforts toward the most promising programs and under-served patients. When research studies have conflicting findings, systematic reviews are important to sort out the reasons why. These studies summarize what is currently known in an area. Many systematic reviews of prehabilitation exist, but each focuses on a different aspect of prehabilitation or subsection of patients. Therefore, we will do a systematic review o systematic reviews to bring all existing prehabilitation evidence together. This type of overview will let us describe in detail what is known to work or not work in prehabilitation programs, as well as to identify the type of patients who may benefit most. Our review will be used to inform policy around how we prepare people for the stress of surgery and identify key areas of research that must be addressed.

column36: Dynamic Ultrasound Localization Pulsatility Imaging
column37: There were an estimated 46.8 million people worldwide living with dementia in 2015, and this number is expected to double every 20 years, at enormous cost to patients, caregivers, and healthcare systems. Dementia is a major manifestation of cerebrovascular disease. For instance, as we age, our blood vessels stiffen and enable the propagation of pulse waves (i.e., pulsatility) into deeper structures of the brain. We think that this pulsatility could cause damage in the brain and eventually lead to dementia. However, mapping pulsatility in small vessels in the brain remains a major technological challenge in small animals and in humans. Blood vessel imaging using ultrasound has undergone multiple breakthrough innovations over the past 10 years. In particular, a recent novel technique drastically improved spatial resolution of blood vessels images, by the detection of millions of individual microbubbles (approved for human use) injected in the blood stream. In recent work, we introduced two critical innovations to this technique: the capability to perform imaging in vivo in 1) three dimensions and 2) dynamically (in other words, movies). Together, these innovations have enabled Dynamic Ultrasound Localization Pulsatility Imaging (DULPI) in entire rodent brains in vessels as small as 20 microns in diameter. The long-term objective of this proposal is to further develop and optimize DULPI to 1) enable the robust and validated imaging of the angioarchitecture and pulsatility of the microvasculature in entire dementia animal model brains and 2) apply it clinically for the development of novel biomarkers of dementia. Should the results of this study indicate high reliability of the DULPI findings, this novel imaging system could be readily applied in pre-clinical settings for fundamental studies, and in a clinical setting for the detection of abnormality and, potentially, treatment guidance.

column36: Understanding inevitable relapse of multiple myeloma following highly-effective anti-BCMA treatment
column37: Multiple myeloma, a cancer of the bone marrow, remains difficult to treat due to the presence of numerous cancer cell subpopulations that can be resistant to treatment. We have also found that while many immune cells within the bone marrow actively combat cancer cells, there are subpopulations that appear to have a cancer-supportive role. To understand how cancer and non-cancerous subpopulations change when patients undergo cancer treatment, we will use a new technology to sequence all genes used by cells that inhabit the bone marrow from patients with multiple myeloma. This measurement will again be repeated after 2 weeks of treatment with a targeted therapy directed against myeloma cells (anti-BCMA) as well as drugs that boost the immune system, pomalidomide and dexamethasone. This will allow us to understand why some myeloma cells are resistant to treatment and to observe the effect of this combination treatment on the bone marrow microenvironment. To enable longitudinal tracking of cancer and immune systems, we will test the blood of these patients every month using a blood test we pioneered in patients with myeloma. This technology enables, from a single blood sample, measurement of cancer-causing mutations as well as rearrangements of the T- and B-cell receptor indicative of clonal immune response and the malignant myeloma clone. Together, single cell and circulating tumour DNA sequencing technology will enable us to 1) better understand the effect of drugs on myeloma and myeloma-supporting cells, 2) nominate new treatments to attack cancer cells or to activate anti-cancer immune cells, and 3) enable early detection of ineffective treatment so that patients can be moved to more effective drugs.

column36: Caspase 3 stimulation of dystrophic muscle stem cell differentiation
column37: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is a fatal genetic disease caused by mutations in dystrophin, the largest gene in humans. This gene produces a protein called dystrophin, which is critical to maintain long term structure and function of muscle fibers. Loss of dystrophin leads to the development of very weak muscle fibers, which cannot sustain the forces of contraction, leading to loss of muscle function and and death in early adulthood. Over the preceding two decades the investigation of new treatment options for DMD has primarily focused on two objectives. The foremost effort has focused on replacing the defective dystrophin gene, while other strategies have been developed to protect or reduce DMD muscle fiber fragility. However, recent investigations suggest that dystrophic muscle also suffers from an inherent loss in muscle regeneration capacity. Specifically, DMD muscle stem cells are incapable of initiating the maturation process and the production of new muscle fibers. In this proposal, we highlight our efforts to identify mechanisms that can be used to over-ride this stem cell defect in DMD and promote robust production of new muscle fibers. We have identified a protein that is critical to this process (caspase 3) and we propose to test a new drug/small molecule that stimulates this factor to engage stem cell maturation in DMD muscle. We anticipate that our studies will provide a first in class therapeutic to improve muscle regeneration and reduce DMD disease progression.

column36: Preventing Injecting and Overdose by Disrupting Injection Drug Use Transitions: The PRIMER II Study
column37: Injection drug use is a key risk factor for overdose death, so preventing people from initiating injection drug use would reduce the unacceptably high death toll due to the opioid overdose epidemic. At present, though, there are no effective and scalable approaches to preventing people from starting to inject drugs. However, research does indicate that people who already inject drugs play a critical role in facilitating the entry of others into injecting. Emerging evidence also suggests that enrolling people who inject drugs into medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder (e.g., methadone or buprenorphine) may reduce their risk of initiating others into drug injecting. The overall goal of this project is therefore to investigate whether enrolling people who inject drugs in medication-assisted treatment can help them reduce their risk of assisting others into drug injecting, and to determine how effective, adaptable and scalable this approach to preventing injection drug use can be across different settings. This study -- known as PRIMER II (Preventing Injecting by Modifying Existing Responses) -- achieves this goal by pooling data from 5 cohort studies of people who inject drugs across North America in 6 different settings. These include cohort studies in Vancouver and Toronto; Baltimore, Rural Kentucky, and San Diego (USA); and Tijuana, Mexico, which collectively provide data from approximately 5,000 participants, making this the largest study of injection initiation to date.

column36: Oligonucleotide-bioconjugate mediated repression of the HOXA9 gene to treat mixed-lineage leukemia
column37: DNA is the language of life written in 20,000 blueprints or genes. The amount of a gene made is as important as the DNA sequence of the gene, and changes in the amount of a gene that is produced can cause disease. Some cancers are caused by over-production of certain genes. Inherited, small chemical modifications to the proteins associated with DNA, control gene production. This field is known as epigenetics. The types and positions of chemical modifications constitute an epigenetic code controlling production of the gene. Some types of leukemia result from misprinting of this epigenetic code causing inappropriate changes in the production of specific genes. Current therapies that target misprinted modifications do so at every gene even though a cancer may only be caused by one of those genes. Therefore this type of cancer therapy needs to be made gene specific. The objectives of this research are to make new cancer therapies that are directed to particular gene, altering the small chemical modifications to the proteins associated with that gene. This will be done by making drug carriers that target only the specific genes involved in a particular type of leukemia. This will target the effect of the drug only to the gene involved in that type of leukemia. This project will result in the creation of a totally new series of cancer treatments that are directed to the particular genes involved in disease. These treatments will have increased efficacy and specificity while reducing side effects when compared to current cancer therapies. Moreover, the strategy employed could potentially be expanded to produce treatments for many different cancers. This will result in a reduction of cancer mortality rates and enhanced quality of life.
