column36: Computational assays for individual treatment predictions in first episode psychosis.
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness characterized by psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusions. A key challenge is the treatment response heterogeneity across patients: despite similar initial symptoms, patients often show divergent disease trajectories over time, and some symptoms persist in spite of treatment. Neuroleptic medication that targets either dopamine or acetylcholine receptors or both neuromodulatory systems is used to treat schizophrenia. However, there are no clinical tests to guide treatment and predict which individual patient will benefit from which type of pharmacological intervention. Consequently, treatment decisions rely on a trial-and-error process, which places a severe burden on patients. To overcome this impasse, this project introduces a neurocomputational approach for understanding the emergence of psychosis symptoms focusing on key pathologies of dopaminergic and cholinergic systems using reward and contextual learning paradigms combined with validated mathematical models of cortical computation. To examine the clinical validity of this approach, we propose a study with mixed cross-sectional and prospective design in first episode psychosis (FEP) patients. As this is a purely prospective study, we do not assign FEP patients to any treatment or diagnostic procedure. Instead, we use a cross-sectional comparison, contrasting two groups of FEP patients for whom the treating psychiatrist has decided that pharmacological intervention is necessary: Patients who respond (R+ group) and do not respond (R- group) to first-line neuroleptic medication will be recruited and assessed using noninvasive brain imaging between 96 hours before and 120 hours after medication is initiated. As this computational approach is a mechanistic model embedded in neurophysiology, it characterises the key cognitive and neurobiological causes of psychosis, in order to inform treatment intervention strategies.

column36: Tuberculosis Whole Genome Sequencing for Disease Control in Madagascar - A Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial to Evaluate Different Community-Level Strategies to Reduce the Burden of Disease
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) whole genome sequencing (WGS) allows outbreak identification and disease transmission tracking. We hypothesize that prospective WGS-guided epidemiological investigations improve case detection compared to current best practices by adapting contact tracing strategies to local transmission patterns. A cluster randomized controlled trial (cRCT) will be performed in high TB incidence villages of Haute Matsiatra region in Madagascar. Communities will be randomized in three separate TB control strategies comparing standard of care, WHO recommended best practices and a novel intervention involving TB WGS cluster-guided epidemiologic investigations. The incremental value of TB WGS on case notifications and reduction of TB burden will be measured. Secondary studies will be nested within this cRCT. Qualitative approaches will increase the understanding of the factors facilitating and hindering implementation of WGS-based diagnostics within health systems. A cost analysis will measure the cost effectiveness of newly implemented laboratory methods. Field and genomic epidemiology data from this project will inform future work on the design of community-level TB elimination strategies in collaboration with Madagascar National TB program.

column36: A neuropathic-like component in arthritis pain: characterization and therapeutic possibilities
column37: Arthritis pain is a serious clinical issue in Canada. Its relief is often unsatisfactory, and it is often increased by movement. Our understanding of its mechanisms is poor, which makes developing more efficacious therapies difficult. There are two major arthritis subtypes, osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis, depending on whether joint damage or inflammation prevail. However, they have something in common: the level of degeneration and inflammation seen does not correlate with the pain experienced. These disconnects between pain and inflammation, or degeneration, suggest other factors contribute to arthritis pain. We strongly believe that this disconnect is caused by a component in arthritis pain which is neuropathic-like, i.e. like pain following nerve damage, but this is still poorly characterized. In this grant, we will characterize the neuropathic-like pain component in both osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis and assess how it is influenced by movement (forced walking). Our research will be done in both male and female rats, to account for possible sex differences in pain mechanisms. We will use pain-related behaviour testing, drugs and anatomical tools to investigate: a) what peripheral and central changes drive this hypersensitivity in freely moving rats after induction of inflammatory arthritis or osteoarthritis; and b) investigate how drug treatments affect these changes. This project will 1) give a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying arthritis pain, 2) identify appropriate targets for the treatment of arthritis pain.

column36: Natural and artificial evolution of toxin-receptor interactions
column37: Large Clostridial toxins (LCTs) are a family of extraordinarily potent bacterial toxins. For example, the most common hospital-acquired diarrhea in developing countries is caused by Clostridioides difficile and its two LCTs TcdA and TcdB. These toxins cause tissue damage by modulating host cell function and behavior in order to promote tissue invasion and proliferation of pathogens. But before doing so, LCTs must gain entry into the cell. They enter human cells by exploiting cell-surface molecules normally present in healthy tissues and use these for docking onto the cell. However, in most cases it is not clear which receptors these toxins use to gain entry. Although recent studies have started to identify receptors for C. difficile toxins, there are many other LCTs whose receptors are not known. In this project, we will use modern genome engineering tools to identify human receptors for multiple LCTs from several different pathogens. We will then characterize at the structural level how LCTs engage their receptors. Finally, we will engineer toxins to bind new receptors on the cell surface in order to develop next-generation therapies for human diseases.

column36: Systematic functional characterization of transcriptional repressors
column37: Although almost every cell in the human body contains the same genome, cells from different tissues express different sets of genes. This difference in gene expression patterns explains how heart cells but not brain cells beat in rhythm and how white blood cells fight invaders but muscle cells do not. At the center of gene expression patterns is the ability to turn genes on and off. Accurate control of gene expression is important for human health, as failure to turn genes on or off properly can lead to development defects, autoimmune disorders, and cancer. At the same time, modifying gene expression can be to our advantage: forced changes in gene expression is behind reprogramming, i.e. turning somatic cells into stem cells. Gene expression is regulated by proteins called transcription factors (TFs) that bind other genes' regulatory regions and instruct other proteins to activate or silence expression of these genes. However, although we know how to identify TFs and where in the genome many of them bind, we generally do not know if they activate transcription, repress transcription, or do both. In this proposal we will take a systematic approach to test all human proteins, including all TFs, for their ability to repress transcription. This will allow us to understand how TFs and other proteins in the human genome regulate the expression of other genes, and how they keep genes and larger genomic regions silent. Moreover, this research can help design better tools for cellular reprogramming in therapeutic applications.

column36: Deciphering the impact of genetic and microenvironmental variation on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell phenotype and response to therapy
column37: Survival rates for many cancer types, in particular pancreatic cancer, are poor and there is a need for new therapies to be developed. Developing effective cancer therapies is difficult because cells in different locations within a tumour do not respond equally well to treatment. This is because tumour cell properties are influenced by their genetic profiles and the environmental conditions they experience. Tumours are complex environments containing multiple cell types and variable chemical conditions that affect each cell's response to therapy. In particular, immune cells in the tumour environment strongly influence tumour cell properties and how well the tumour cells respond to therapies. A better understanding of how tumour cells with different genetic properties and immune cells interact and talk to each other in different locations within tumours could provide a basis for developing new drugs that modify these interactions to make current tumour-killing therapies more effective. Understanding these interactions is challenging in animal models however. Here we propose to use tissue engineered culture models to characterize the molecular interactions between immune and tumour cells in different tumour environments to identify interactions that can be modified to improve pancreatic tumour cell response to therapy.

column36: Identifying a novel neuromuscular biomarker signature of chronic temporomandibular disorders
column37: Pain is the primary cause of long-term disability, and it poses the most significant health-related burden on Canadian society. Temporomandibular disorders (TMD), a set of conditions affecting the jaw muscles and the temporomandibular joint (the jaw joint), are the most common cause of chronic (persistent) pain relating to the mouth and face. The causes of muscular TMD, the most common TMD, are still poorly understood, and a definite cause of this condition has yet to be identified. This uncertainty contributes to misdiagnosis, delays accurate diagnoses, and leads to inappropriate treatments. For these reasons, more than 30% of patients with TMD have recurrent or persistent pain after 5 years regardless of the treatment they had received. Currently, patients' self-reported pain is the main way that TMD severity is diagnosed, but the experience of pain is influenced by other factors, including cultural context and coping strategies, so this may not be the most accurate way to determine a case of TMD's severity. Therefore, in order to improve diagnosis and treatment of TMD, this project aims to identify and characterize the muscular and neural abnormalities associated with chronic muscular TMD. This will allow us to determine whether biological severity - in other words, the extent of changes in the jaw muscles and neurological systems of people with TMD - predicts the extent of the disability caused by a given patient's TMD. To accomplish this, we will use multiple methods to characterize the structure and function of the jaw muscles in patients with chronic TMD, as well as the structure of their nerves and brains. In the long term, our project will allow us to classify the extent and spread of TMD, leading to increased understanding of biological severity, improved diagnosis, more efficient and specific treatments, and a reduced burden on patients and the healthcare system.

column36: Repair in Transplant Vasculopathy
column37: Heart transplantation is the best treatment for individuals with end stage heart failure. However, the endothelial cells that line the blood vessels of the heart transplant are attacked by the recipient's immune system. Despite modern immunosuppression drugs, the injury to the blood vessels accumulates resulting in narrowing of the major arteries that supply blood and nutrients to the heart, and loss of the small feeder blood vessels of the heart muscle. In time, the heart muscle of the transplant fails, in part because of the lack of blood supply. We seek to understand the repair response undertaken by the endothelial cells that line the blood vessels of a heart transplant. We will focus on one repair molecule, Apelin, that we recently identified to play a critical role in the development of transplant vascular disease in both mice and humans. We will determine if administration of the candidate molecule (drug), Apelin, blunts narrowing of the major arteries in a heart transplant model. Currently, little is known about the repair response mounted by the blood vessel cells in the transplant organ. Since mouse models of heart transplantation faithfully replicate the key features of injury to blood vessels of human heart transplants, we will study the vascular repair response in these mouse models in detail. We will exploit mutant mice that lack endothelial cell expression of specific genes-of-interest as heart donors to determine if the genes are required to mount the repair response. Our group has identified a major role for Apelin to protect against transplant vascular disease, and is the first group to find a potential treatment. We have assembled a unique set of mutant mice to further test and extend our findings, and collaborators with specialized expertise in genetics, aging, and apelin-like drug development. These collaborations aim to bring advances in diagnostics and therapeutics arising from the work into the clinic.

column36: Establishing strategies to preserve donor lungs for multiple days: Cyclic Normothermic Ex vivo Lung Perfusion and Mitochondrial Transplantation .
column37: Currently, lungs donated for clinical transplantation are preserved in an ice cooler where the organ rests at a temperature of around 4C. Due to the potential injuries manifested during the preservation period, transplant surgeons adopt a conservative approach of only 4-6h of total preservation time. Recently, we have shown that by preserving the lungs at 10C (rather than 4C), the preservation window can be significantly extended without comprising organ quality. However, even under these conditions, organ viability eventually deteriorates, and the lungs are no longer suitable for transplantation. Therefore, novel approaches are required in order to extend further organ preservation periods, which would, in turn, have several important implications in the field of lung transplantation. Longer preservation times will allow for the opportunity to match donors and recipients better, overcome geographical hurdles faced in organ donation, and, importantly, the progression of lung transplantation towards a scheduled- instead of an urgent - procedure. Another advantage in safely prolonging organ preservation will be the ability for many patients to stay at their home city while waiting for an organ rather than re-locating to the city of the transplant hospital with many social and financial advantages. To achieve this, we will combine the 10 C storage with cycles of normothermic ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP). EVLP is a revolutionary technology that allows for the simulation of physiological conditions outside of the body. During EVLP, lungs are brought back to human body temperature, provided with oxygen and nutrition, and metabolism is restored. To understand the benefit of this approach, we aim to fully characterize cell metabolism and mitochondrial health, thus elucidating mechanisms and pathways of lung damage and recovery.

column36: Machine M.D.: How Should We Regulate AI in Health Care?
column37: Advocates argue that artificial intelligence (AI) technologies will transform health care for the better by, e.g., reducing high levels of medical error that occur within hospitals. However, there are also many concerns. For example, can a surgeon obtain "informed" consent from a patient if the surgeon does not understand how AI makes its decision? Who should be held to account, and for what, when injury arises from the use of AI? How can we prevent "algorithmic bias," which is when AI products discriminate because the data they are built upon are under-representative of, e.g., women, Indigenous Peoples or Black Canadians? And will patient privacy be jeopardized as AI tools process huge quantities of personal health information and share that data with others? We do not yet know whether Canada's complex web of uncoordinated laws and regulations will adequately protect patients and other users against potential problems with AI in health care. Our multidisciplinary research team will rigorously assess 10-12 AI case studies in different care settings, representative of the potential risks of AI in health care. We will use a case study method to scrutinize the sufficiency of legal governance of current and emerging AI technologies in the Canadian system and in selected foreign jurisdictions. This will enable us to clearly identify where there are gaps in existing legal protections and if law reform is required, whether that be changes to existing laws or ethical codes, or entirely new laws. To generate the best advice on law reform options, we will work closely not only with AI innovators and health care providers that are part of our research team, but also with key decision-makers, like Health Canada, and with patient representatives. Our goal is for Canadian patients and society to truly benefit from the revolutionary potential of AI in health. This will require optimal regulation of heath care, which is as important as the health innovation itself.

column36: Optimization of cell culture media and substrates to mature pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyoctyes for improved cardiac cell therapy
column37: Heart attacks damage heart muscle, replacing it with non-beating scar tissue. Damaged hearts can be repaired by injecting heart muscle cells called cardiomyocytes. Cardiomyocytes made from induced pluripotent stem cells show the best results, but only a portion of the injected cells survive. Furthermore, cells that survive often interfere with electrical function of the heart. A solution to these problems is to mature stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes in the lab beforehand, as more mature cells do better once transplanted. However, existing technologies do not produce highly mature stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes in the quantities needed to repair a heart, which has stifled progress towards cell therapy. We will address this need using engineered screening systems and artificial intelligence (AI) approaches developed by our team. As proof-of-principle, we used these approaches to invent a cocktail to nourish stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes that makes them more mature than the best cocktails available currently. We also engineered materials that promote stem cell growth better than standard materials. In this project, we will build on our previous work to find cocktails and materials that improve cardiomyocyte maturation assessed in multiple ways that are important for function, including their structure, gene expression, contraction, and electrical properties. Guided by AI, hundreds of possible recipes will be assessed for the best overall performance in advancing cardiomyocyte maturity. Finally, the best combinations of cocktails and materials will be used to produce highly-mature cardiomyocytes for injection into damaged guinea pig hearts, an excellent model to test the survival and function of the transplanted cells using state-of-the-art medical imaging and functional testing. The knowledge and technologies developed here will provide new insights and strategies to generate cardiomyocytes towards the treatment of heart failure, a growing epidemic in Canada.

column36: Chronic non-cancer pain, substance use, and related harms: Towards an optimal treatment pathway for people who inject drugs in the context of the opioid crisis
column37: One in five Canadians lives with chronic pain, an invisible but debilitating, distressing, and costly condition that is complex and difficult to treat. Meanwhile, from January 2016 to June 2019, 13,900 opioid-related deaths were recorded in Canada, with contamination of the illicit drug supply a major driver of overdose mortality. People who inject drugs (PWID) are disproportionately affected by both epidemics. Chronic pain is estimated to be 1.5 to 3.0 times more common among PWID compared with the general population, and these individuals may face particular difficulties obtaining adequate pain treatment. There is concern that some might turn to illicit substances (particularly opioids) to manage their pain, inadvertently exposing them to a greater risk of adverse events such as overdose. Nonetheless, little data exists to describe the effects of chronic pain on substance use and related harms in this population. Building on our current work, this study aims to build knowledge of the relationships between chronic pain, substance use, and the risk of adverse events (fatal and non-fatal overdose, hepatitis C infection) and to investigate how use of health services and mental health status influence outcomes. To achieve this, we will continue to follow a cohort of active PWID in Montreal at 3-month intervals, collecting data via questionnaires and blood samples at each visit. Data will be analysed by statistical techniques examining the relations between pain, substance use, and adverse events over time. We will also conduct in-depth interviews with a subset of the cohort (individuals who have chronic pain and have recently experienced an adverse event) to explore their perceptions of living with chronic pain, its relationship to their use of substances and their experiences with health services, and how this has evolved since the event.

column36: Intraplaque Composition Combined with Stress Echo for Cardiac Risk Stratification
column37: The root cause of heart attacks and strokes is atherosclerosis, the hardening and thickening of blood vessels due to the presence of "plaque" which is a build-up of fat and cholesterol in the walls of vessels. To diagnose heart disease, patients receive a stress test to find out if they require a procedure known as an angiogram. Up to 52% of patients receiving an angiogram are found to have no significant heart disease. On the other hand, a stress test can also miss patients that should be referred for an angiogram (false negative). In Ontario alone, 90% of stress tests are found to be normal and these patients are sent home with little follow-up. Of these 3-5% (~4,000 patients/year) will have a major cardiovascular event (heart attack, surgery, or death) within 3 years. Thus we need to improve the accuracy of stress testing to better decide who needs procedures, and to better identify which patients are at risk of heart disease earlier. We propose improving this by using ultrasound at the time of stress testing to look for plaque blockages within the neck arteries of patients. If the ultrasound shows that these plaques have additional leaky blood vessels within them, then this could indicate that the patients are at higher risk of having a major cardiovascular event in the future, even if the stress test does not show an abnormal result. To prove this, we propose a study looking at the combination of stress testing and the neck ultrasound (to assess plaque composition), to identify patients at risk for cardiovascular events (heart attacks and death). It is easy to combine these tests because they use the same ultrasound technology and so additional important information can be obtained during the same test to help better identify patients that may be at risk of disease in the future, and would benefit from earlier prevention.

column36: Signalling and regulation of antigenic variation in trypanosomes
column37: Kinetoplastid parasites affect millions of people each year worldwide, with an increasing number of cases in North America and Europe. These parasites are transmitted by insect bites and affect humans and animals. They include three main species of medical importance: Trypanosoma brucei, T. cruzi, and Leishmania sp., which cause Sleeping sickness in Africa, Chagas disease in the Americas, and Leishmaniasis in multiple countries, respectively. These parasites cause fatal chronic illnesses that affect numerous organs, including the brain, heart, spleen, and skin, depending on parasite species. It remains unknown how these parasites escape the human immune response during infection. This project focuses on how T. brucei avoid host antibody recognition during infection. T. brucei express a surface coat made by a protein called variant surface glycoprotein (VSG), which they periodically change to escape host antibody recognition in a process known as antigenic variation. The processes that control the periodic change in the VSG surface coat are poorly understood. We have discovered that T. brucei use a signalling system to control changes in the VSG coat. This proposal will investigate the protein composition of this signalling system, its organization within the parasite, and how it controls the periodic changes in VSG proteins. Understanding this system will help to identify drugs that can disrupt the parasite's ability to change the VSG coat, which will result in parasite elimination by the host immune system during infection. Many other parasites use similar processes to escape the host immune system, such as Plasmodium spp., which cause malaria and Giardia spp., which cause intestinal infections. Hence, understanding the processes that control antigenic variation in T. brucei may also help to fight other pathogen infections.

column36: Elucidating conformational transitions in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor to enable drug discovery
column37: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are signaling proteins that play a central role in the communication between nerves and muscle. At the neuromuscular junction, the nAChR converts the chemical signal received from the nerve, acetylcholine, into an electric impulse leading to muscle contraction. Altered nAChR function at the neuromuscular junction leads to a disease known as Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome or CMS. CMS is characterized by muscle weakness, respiratory difficulties, reduced mobility and delayed motor milestones. Genetic mutations leading to CMS ultimately impair how the body controls muscle contraction. To date, over 350 CMS-causing mutations have been identified, with approximately half of these located in genes encoding for the nAChR. Some CMS-causing mutations alter the expression levels, the amount of nAChRs at the muscle surface, to impair neuromuscular function. Others alter how the nAChR responds to its stimulus, acetylcholine, to impair neuromuscular communication. In this research project, we will study the structure of the nAChR and will learn how disease-causing mutations alter nAChR function in order to pinpoint "sites" that can be targeted by small molecule drugs to correct the disease-causing behavior. By understanding the pathological basis for the disease, we will devise new treatments to ameliorate or cure CMS.

column36: Adoption and enhancement of a primary care management pathway for obstructive sleep apnea: an implementation evaluation project
column37: Over 6% of Canadians have obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a disease in which individuals do not breathe normally because of airway narrowing or collapse during sleep. People with OSA are at increased risk of motor vehicle collisions, cardiovascular disease and lower quality of life compared to the general population. The complications of untreated OSA are also costly to the healthcare system. The diagnosis and treatment of OSA usually involves patient referral by a primary care doctor to a sleep specialist, which can lead to very long wait times for care. Research studies have shown that primary care doctors can provide high quality care for patients with OSA. However, there are many barriers preventing primary care doctors from managing OSA effectively. In 2018, an online clinical care pathway was created to help Calgary primary care doctors to diagnose and treat most patients with OSA, and to identify more complex patients who should be referred to a specialist. In this study, we will determine if the pathway has achieved this goal. We have three aims: 1) Measure visits to the pathway website and the number and characteristics of patients who are referred to sleep doctors before and after the pathway was launched. This information will help us describe how the pathway is being used and how it affects decisions that primary care doctors make about referring patients with OSA to specialists 2) Survey and interview primary care doctors to determine whether they find the pathway useful and how it could be improved 3) Enhance the pathway based on this feedback and re-evaluate its use and referrals from primary care doctors to determine if the enhanced pathway achieves its goal Our results will improve the use of the pathway by primary care doctors, to help them diagnose and treat most patients with OSA without specialist referral. We will also increase the understanding of how clinical care pathways can be used to improve patient care for other conditions.

column36: Enabling liver cryopreservation by controlling ice recrystallization with small molecule inhibitors
column37: As stated by the Organ Preservation Alliance in their recent call to action, "the ability to replace organs and tissues on demand could save or improve millions of lives each year globally and create public health benefits on par with curing cancer" (Nat Biotech 2017: 35: 530-42). Storage at subzero temperatures has long been pursued as a strategy to improve the availability of the liver for transplantation. However, the successful cryopreservation of liver remains a formidable challenge as ice crystal formation and growth can cause cell damage and disrupt important structures within the tissue or organ resulting in poor post-thaw function. Our group has developed synthetic, small molecule ice recrystallization inhibitors which function to control both extra- and intracellular ice crystal growth and can be used to improve the recovery of many different cell-based therapeutic products. As this approach of controlling ice crystals is similar to strategies used in nature by freeze tolerant organisms to survive winter, we are interested in testing if these ice control agents can protect liver tissue and whole liver from freezing and thawing damage. Through this work, we will develop new insights into how these ice control agents function to protect cells, tissues and organs from freezing injury and we will explore their use in the low temperature preservation of cell-based products that are needed in biomedical research, drug testing, and transplantation.

column36: Molecular drivers of the drug tolerant persister state in patient-derived colorectal cancer models
column37: Colorectal Cancer (CRC) is the 3rd highest cause of cancer-related deaths in North America. In total, 40% of CRC patients will develop metastatic disease and the majority of these patients will die of their disease. Thus despite being one of the best understood cancers from a genetic perspective, there remains significant opportunity to improve outcomes in CRC. We have developed in vivo models using patient-derived CRC samples injected into immunocompromised mice. We treat the mice with the same chemotherapy agents used in CRC patients and can demonstrate tumour regression, however, upon stopping chemotherapy the tumours regrow. Furthermore, we show that in response to chemotherapy, cancer cells are entering a drug tolerant persister (DTP) state which allows them to avoid the toxic effects of chemotherapy and yet continue to divide once the chemotherapy is stopped. This DTP state differs from classical chemoresistance because the state is reversible and not driven by genetic mutations. Therefore the DTP state represents a therapeutic opportunity to target cancer cells prior to the development of classical irreversible genetic clone driven resistance. We have characterized our DTP models and shown that they significantly downregulate genes important in cholesterol metabolism. The DTPs also significantly upregulate autophagy pathways, which is process that allows cells to survive under stressful conditions. Understanding the roles cholesterol metabolism and autophagy are playing in the context of the DTP state forms the basis of this grant. We want to determine why cancer cells in the DTP state appear to be dependent on downregulating cholesterol metabolism and upregulating autophagy. These are important questions because both the cholesterol and autophagy pathways are druggable with existing FDA approved drugs. Therefore the work we do in this grant could lead to novel therapeutic strategies designed to target DTPs.

column37: Contexte: Ameliorer l'efficacite du systeme de sante est devenu un enjeu cle dans le contexte actuel ou les besoins sont en croissance, et les services pour y repondre evalues non optimaux. Les troubles mentaux (TM) representent un enjeu majeur de sante publique. Au Quebec, la prevalence des TM est evaluee a 12% annuellement et a 33% a vie. Les TM engendrent des couts de sante et des pertes de productivite importants. Ils contribuent substantiellement a l'engorgement des urgences et aux hospitalisations. Ces derniers dispositifs de soins ne sont cependant pas adequats pour le suivi de ces patients, rapportant de nombreux besoins non combles. Objectifs: L'etude vise a mesurer les trajectoires de soins des patients avec des TM, traduites en indicateurs de qualite des soins, et a y associer des profils de patients et des resultats de sante. Methode: Les donnees seront extraites de la Cohorte TorSaDE, ou les donnees des individus ayant repondu a cinq enquetes generales sur la sante dans les collectivites canadiennes (ESCC) de Statistique Canada ont ete jumelees aux donnees de la Regie de l'assurance maladie du Quebec de 1996 a 2016. Representative de la population du Quebec, la cohorte rassemble des donnees riches. Une sous-cohorte de patients avec des TM sera constituee (n=3 200 patients). Des le diagnostic d'un TM, les trajectoires de soins de ces patients seront investiguees sur 6 mois, et traduites en indicateurs de qualite (acces, continuite, integration), qui seront relies a des profils de patients (ex.: sexe, groupe d'age, type de TM), et associes a des resultats de sante (visites a l'urgence et hospitalisations) sur 12 mois. Retombees: L'etude permettra d'identifier les inegalites socioeconomiques ou d'acces aux soins, les profils de patients moins bien suivis, et ceux utilisant plus les urgences et plus hospitalises, contribuant a des recommandations solides pour ameliorer l'adequation des soins aux patients avec des TM, clientele parmi les plus vulnerables.

column36: Using Precision Medicine to Study Maternal Inflammation in Pregnancy as a Cause of Early Childhood Depression
column37: While a large body of research suggests that inflammation and depression are closely related, there is an urgent need to refine our understanding of this association if more targeted interventions are to be developed. One methodological issue that has limited progress in this area is that most studies have been done in adult populations with various co-morbidities and complexities. As a result, the inflammatory changes reported in many studies could relate more to chronic stress, medical co-morbidities and long term medication exposures than to depressive pathology per se. To address this, our research group is exploring possible links between maternal inflammation in pregnancy and depressive symptoms in young children in a prospective birth cohort called the Ontario Birth Study. Initial pilot data are highly promising, including significant associations between a key maternal inflammatory marker in pregnancy (C-reactive protein) and both the presence of sad mood and lack of positive mood in the respective children assessed at age 4 years. The specific findings are dependent on when in pregnancy the maternal samples are collected, and on the sex of the child. The current proposal is to extend this initial work into a much larger sample of mother-child dyads, and to extend the follow-up period for the participating children into later childhood. If successful, this work will shed significant new light on how inflammatory processes change brain circuitry in general, and in early life in particular. This in turn will inform the design and implementation of more targeted preventative strategies for a disorder that is now the single greatest contributor to disability across the lifespan worldwide.

column36: Trial of Intradialytic Cycling as Kidney Exercise Rehabilitation for cardiac Stunning in Hemodialysis (TICKERS_HD)
column37: Most people with kidney failure require hemodialysis treatment three times per week to clear toxins from the blood. Even though hemodialysis helps to remove waste from the body, it can cause low blood flow to vital organs during dialysis which decreases the travel of oxygen and nutrients to the heart and other organs. The low blood flow causes parts of the heart to pump poorly (called "stunning") and is associated with troublesome symptoms that are difficult to treat such as fatigue, cramping and poor cognition. Heart stunning also leads to more heart damage over time and higher rates of heart disease and death. In our previous studies, exercise during hemodialysis decreased the amount of heart stunning that occurred with treatment. In this study, we will look at the effect of cycling during hemodialysis on heart stunning over a longer time and see whether decreases in heart stunning with exercise improve fatigue after dialysis, symptom burden (the number and severity of symptoms) and other outcomes over 3 months. Since the treatment of heart disease and managing symptoms in individuals on dialysis has been identified as a research priority in Canada, we hope to address an important knowledge gap with this study. We will enrol 160 volunteers who are receiving hemodialysis in 7 centres in Canada, the US and Australia. Half will be randomized to receive usual care. The other half will be randomized to receive usual care plus 3 months of cycling 3 times per week during dialysis. We will assess heart function, fatigue after dialysis and symptom burden between groups over time. The information provided by this study will help us better treat people on dialysis and improve their well-being. Results will also help us plan and design a future study looking at the effect of exercise on longer term outcomes such as cardiac disease and death. Improvements in such outcomes are important for individual health and could also reduce burden and costs to the health care system.

column36: Characterizing immune evasion in pancreatic adenocarcinoma: an integrative computational and experimental approach to understanding aberrant antigen presentation
column37: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer with a median 5 year survival of 8%. While its poor outcomes are often attributed to late detection, there are few effective targeted therapies and novel immunotherapies that have shown promise across multiple cancers have failed in clinical trials. Key to understanding both tumour progression and therapy resistance is how tumour cells undergo immune escape, effectively hiding themselves from the immune system. While a myriad of such mechanisms exist, downregulation of antigen presentation (AP) pathways - those that display mutated peptides -- has received surprisingly little attention in the context of PDAC. In particular, the frequency, interaction with established subtypes, utility as a biomarker, and functional origins remain largely uncharacterized. To address this significant knowledge gap, we will take an integrative computational and experimental approach. Firstly, we will perform a large-scale genomic analysis of whole genome and transcriptome sequencing of resectable and advanced PDAC cases to assess the frequency of loss of antigen presentation and relate this to the dynamics of PDAC progression, elucidating its relationship to existing subtypes and clinical outcomes. Secondly, we will uncover the spatial architecture of PDAC tumours using highly multiplexed imaging applied to resected tissue from an immunotherapy trial. We will design novel computational methodology to identify cells with aberrant subcellular localization of key proteins and evaluate this as a biomarker of clinical course and immunotherapy response. Finally, we will use in-vivo CRISPR screens to study the functional origins and phenotypic consequences of knocking out key components of the AP pathway through the generation of single-cell transcriptomic and multiplexed imaging data. Together, this establishes cutting-edge computational and experimental methods to map a hugely important but understudied process in a deadly cancer.

column36: Post-Bleed Management of Antithrombotic Therapy after Gastrointestinal Bleeding (PANTHER-GI): A Mixed-Methods Study of Patient Values and Preferences
column37: Blood thinners (anticoagulants) are used to prevent and treat blood clots (thrombosis). The main side effect of blood thinners is bleeding, the majority of which is from the stomach or intestines (gastrointestinal). After bleeding, anticoagulants are stopped permanently in about half of patients even though they are still needed to prevent thrombosis. Patients who restart blood thinners seem to have less blood clotting and death, but more bleeding. No one knows when it is safe to restart anticoagulants after a gastrointestinal bleed and there is no published information about patient values and preferences about restarting blood thinners after bleeding, which is critical for shared decision-making. Our goal is to understand patient values and preferences after gastrointestinal bleeding while on anticoagulants. We will determine the issues that are important to patients when they are considering restarting anticoagulants after gastrointestinal bleeding. The results of this study will (1) help doctors make shared decisions with patients, (2) help experts make recommendations that take patient values and preferences into account, (3) help plan a definitive study to find out whether, when and how blood thinners can be restarted safely. We will start by determining the main themes of patient experiences and preferences in individual interviews. We will then use a survey method called discrete choice experiments to determine the importance of different factors that affect decisions about blood thinners. The survey will be distributed in clinics using tablet computers and online through the National Blood Clot Alliance and Thrombosis Canada. The National Blood Clot Alliance is a non-profit patient advocacy organization with more than 5,400 online support group members and a total annual website viewership of more than 3 million individuals, including nearly 180,000 Canadians.

column36: Evaluating CFTR-function and response to new CFTR modulator drugs in non-cystic fibrosis patients with CFTR-related lung disease
column37: Defects in the Cystic Fibrosis gene (CFTR) cause Cystic Fibrosis (CF), a multi-organ disease with progressive lung disease as the main cause for early mortality. Next to classic CF, there are patients presenting later in life with chronic lung disease. Extensive diagnostic work-up often times finds CFTR gene defects and abnormal CFTR function. Those who do not fit the strict criteria for a CF diagnosis are diagnosed with a CFTR-related disease. Patients with CFTR-related lung disease benefit from CF therapies, but have no access to a new class of drugs, which targets the basic CFTR defect. These CFTR-modulator drugs dramatically improve lung disease in CF patients, but come at a high cost. There is no knowledge whether these drugs improve lung disease in non-CF patients with a CFTR-related lung disease. We also do not know how much CFTR dysfunction these patients have and what other factors are contributing to lung disease. Similarly, newborns who are screened positive in CF newborn screening programs have similar CFTR gene defects and also do not fit the diagnostic criteria of CF (CFSPID). While these newborns have not yet developed any symptoms, we believe that a subset of these children is at risk for developing lung disease. With this study proposal we want to study the degree of CFTR dysfunction in nasal cells collected from individual patients with a CFTR-related lung disease and CFSPID children and test for response to CFTR modulator drugs in laboratory measurements. Nasal cells are particularly suited for this study as they closely reflect airway tissue, but can be obtained easily by nasal brush from individual patients. Results from our study will help to identify those non-CF patients with CFTR-related lung disease for whom CFTR dysfunction is substantial and who therefore benefit from CFTR-modulator therapy. This will help organizing clinical studies testing CFTR modulator drugs in these patients aiming to improve long-term health outcome in the future.

column36: The Power of Linked Data: Investigating Social Determinants of Child Health and their Implications in Reducing Pediatric Traumatic Injury.
column37: Traumatic physical injuries are the number one cause of hospitalization and death among children in Canada. These injuries have a significant impact on mental, physical, and social health for the remainder of the child's life. The Canadian Pediatric Society has identified that ninety percent of these unintentional injuries are preventable. The burden from injury can be reduced through prevention programs tailored to at-risk groups. Thus, it is important to understand what social factors place some children at greater risk for traumatic physical injury. Existing research does not provide a strong explanation of how these factors influence a child's risk of injury. We propose to better understand the association between social factors and traumatic physical injury in children using information based on large population-wide data. We will examine a 17-year group of 11,000 children hospitalized for traumatic physical injury and 55,000 matched uninjured children by linking longitudinal administrative and clinical data contained at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy. We will examine 14 social factors including: Use of income assistance, rural/urban status, socioeconomic status, children in care, child mental disorder, and parental factors (involved with criminal justice system, education, social housing, immigration status, high residential mobility, mother's age at first birth, parental Axis I mental disorder, parental Axis II mental disorder, and parental physical disorder) to identify groups and periods of time when children are at greatest risk for traumatic physical injury. Knowing these at-risk factors will guide decision-makers and health policy makers to improve injury prevention efforts by targeting children that are most vulnerable.

column36: Targeting TMPRSS6 to treat hepcidin-deficiency disorders.
column37: Hepcidin is a hormone that is produced in the liver and circulates in the blood. Although hepcidin has numerous physiological roles (and has antibacterial properties), it is mostly known as the major regulator of iron levels in the body. Interestingly, diseases such as beta-thalassemia, hemochromatosis, liver fibrosis and liver cirrhosis have been associated with low levels of circulating hepcidin suggesting that hepcidin itself might have a direct role in these diseases. Therefore, it is logical to assume that elevating hepcidin levels could be beneficial in these conditions. Our group has been focusing on an enzyme called matriptase-2 (also known as TMPRSS6), which is found only in liver and which controls hepcidin production. Our project begins by initially focusing on our findings that the human liver expresses four distinct forms of TMPRSS6. Some of the forms are enzymatically active, some are not but how one form is expressed in comparison to other forms remains unclear. Our proposal will study the different forms of TMPRSS6 found in liver, will focus on their functionality and the consequence of the presence of these different isoforms on the production of hepcidin. Conversely, we also propose two different approaches to reduce the enzymatic activity of TMPRSS6 thereby increasing hepcidin levels. One of these involves the synthesis of small molecule inhibitors to abolish the enzymatic activity of the enzyme. Another is a completely novel pharmacological approach based on the use of small sequences of DNA to control which TMPRSS6 isoform is expressed. Knowing that certain isoforms are enzymatically inactive, this 'switch' of expression could have profound effects on the production of hepcidin. Therefore, our studies are meant to shed light into the role of TMPRSS6 in hepcidin production and to propose novel ways at increasing hepcidin levels in hepcidin-deficiency disorders.

column36: The impact of the publicly-funded health insurance on social inequalities in use of sexual, reproductive, and maternal health services, and on maternal, newborn, and infant health: an evaluation of the Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana scheme in India
column37: India accounts for more than one-fifth of global maternal and neonatal mortality and there are substantial inequalities across states and regions, urban and rural areas, and across various dimensions of socioeconomic status. Promoting access to quality sexual, reproductive, and maternal health services is an important mechanism for accelerating progress toward Sustainable Development Goal targets for reductions in maternal and newborn death. Out-of- pocket costs represent a substantial barrier to access to maternal and reproductive health services, particularly among poorer households, in India. In 2008, the Government of India launched the Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY) health insurance scheme to improve access to health services for families below the poverty line, and later expanded to cover unorganized workers. The program provides eligible families with cashless healthcare for inpatient health services, capped at INR 30,000 (USD 500) annually. This includes certain sexual and reproductive health services, such as insertion of an intrauterine device; a maternal care package including antenatal care, diagnostics, and delivery; and neonatal care for newborns admitted with complications. In this study, we will use information collected from three district-representative household surveys to evaluate the impact of expanded access to RSBY on social inequalities in the use of recommended sexual, reproductive, and maternal health services, maternal health, and neonatal health. The findings from this study will help to inform interventions for reducing overall levels and inequalities in maternal and neonatal mortality. More generally, these results will have the potential to influence the design of universal health coverage systems through a better understanding of how to improve equitable access to quality health services and reduce social inequalities in maternal and newborn health.

column36: Genetic Frontotemporal Dementia Initiative (GENFI) in Canada: Combined Investigation of Clinical, MRI, Genomic, and Epigenomic Biomarkers
column37: There have been three major genes discovered that cause familial forms of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), a devastating group of disorders associated with personality and behavioural changes and/or language difficulties in those suffering. These cognitive and behavioural deficits prevent affected individuals from being able to function in society. Specifically, they are no longer able to work, communicate and may get into trouble with the law as a result of their aberrant behaviours. The impact to individuals and their families is huge because FTD affects those in the prime of their lives, often between the ages of 45 to 55. The gene abnormality predicts that an individual who harbours it will be at high risk of developing symptoms, but does not predict when this will occur and what clinical features they will have. Therefore, it is critical that research studies concentrate on developing powerful biomarkers of FTD that can identify the earliest stages of disease before symptoms develop and that can be used to monitor disease progression in those already affected. We will use brain imaging, genetics, and epigenetics to identify signatures of the FTD disease process and modifiers of FTD course. The development of such biomarkers will substantially aid in the design of novel clinical trials of new drugs. It is hoped that novel drugs being developed can be used to eventually prevent the disease from starting in those at risk and modify the course in those already affected.

column36: Neuro-developmental Disorders in Canadian Children: Burdens of Conditions and Effects of Maternal Morbidity
column37: Globally, neurological disorders are the leading cause of disability and the second leading cause of death, and its health and economic tolls are expected to increase. Neurological disorders with early onset in life such as cerebral palsy, autism, and epilepsy have multiple lifelong comorbidities in developmental outcomes including sensory-motor and cognitive impairments and poor behaviour control. Although damage to the developing brain is identified as a cause, the cause of the brain damage is poorly understood. The functional architecture of the brain is formed during gestation, prenatal exposures to maternal illnesses would have adverse effects on the brain development. Two of the most common maternal illnesses during pregnancy are diabetes and severe maternal morbidity (SMM) defined by the presence of multiple life-threatening and disabling diseases and conditions (e.g., eclampsia, thromboembolism, and hemorrhagic disorders). Nevertheless, evidence on the effects of maternal morbidity during pregnancy on offspring neuro-developmental outcomes are scarce and inconclusive. In this study, we propose to systematically examine burdens of major childhood neuro-developmental disorders and effects of maternal diabetes and severe maternal morbidity on neuro-developmental disorders in Canadian children born between 2002-2020 in Ontario. Our research will provide evidence that is needed to assess the current and future burdens of neuro-developmental health in children, to understand their causal mechanisms, and to plan further research on management and preventive interventions.

column36: Adverse Drug Events and Medication Errors in adult Intensive Care Units
column37: In Intensive Care Units (ICU), one in every four to five patients is harmed by healthcare. Nearly half of harm is judged to be preventable. Drugs are the most common cause of this harm. There are data suggesting that the healthcare landscape has changed: pharmacists have been better integrated into ICU teams, and computerized tools are more widely used. Our goal is to better understand the amount of drug-associated harm affecting critically ill patients, as well as factors that put certain patients more at risk, in order to build safer healthcare systems. These systems will enable healthcare workers to provide safer care to Canada's sickest patients. This study will be added to a large ongoing study looking at harm in adult ICU. The study we propose in this application will focus specifically on harm and errors related to medications. Research nurses trained in detecting errors and harm will evaluate every patients' chart daily, and describe the medication errors and/or harm that lead to ICU admission or occurs in the ICU. For every event, expert pharmacists and ICU doctors will then help in deciding whether the harm is related to the medication, whether it was preventable, and how serious the harm is. The study statistician will look for characteristics of patients, prescribers or the hospital system, that increase the chances a patient will have a drug error or drug-associated harm. This study will help us identify the current extent of drug-related harm in Canada's ICU, the patients who are most at risk, and the health systems that reduce risk. column36: Uncovering early mediators of lineage plasticity and validation of a metabolic vulnerability in neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: It is estimated that in 2020 adenocarcinoma of the prostate will be diagnosed in 23,300 Canadian men and 4200 will die from it. New potent therapies such as abiraterone, enzalutamide, and apalutamide are effective at controlling the disease but ultimately progression to castrate-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is universal. It is now known that these potent drugs can cause normal CRPC to turn into a lethal neuroendocrine cancer (NEPC) in 15-25% of patients. This is called neuroendocrine transdifferentiation (NEtD) and there are no effective therapies to prevent it or treat the subsequent neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC). At the Vancouver Prostate Centre, we transplanted a patient's tumor into mice making a so-called patient-derived xenograft (PDX). This PDX turned out to be a particularly valuable and clinically relevant model of the neuroendocrine transdifferentiation (NEtD) for identifying mechanisms of NEtD and drug targets. Recently we applied a powerful new technology called single-cell RNAseq to this PDX model. All expressed genes are sequenced in thousands of individual tumour cells simultaneously. This allowed us to monitor NEtD at single-cell resolution and to identify the very first NE-like cells to emerge. Importantly, in these cells, we identified genes that act very early in NEtD and we confirmed them to be present in multiple NEPC patient cohorts. We will inactivate these in our PDX model to try and block NEtD. If this works the genes will form the basis of novel therapeutic targets for abrogating NEtD. In addition, we found that the emerging LTL331 NEPC has a metabolic weakness - dependence on an external supply of arginine - an important amino acid. We propose to test if this can be exploited to block NEtD. If successful, it will open a radically novel approach to NEPC prevention and/or treatment via dietary changes.

column36: Harnessing STING activation for the treatment of sarcoma
column37: Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are connective tissue (fat, muscle, tendon, ligament) derived malignancies that affect both children and adults. Apart from a few select subtypes, there are no effective systemic therapies against STS. There have been no meaningful therapeutic advances for these cancers in decades. Present treatment involves a combination of morbid surgical resections and high-dose radiation. Unfortunately, in patients who develop metastatic disease, there are very limited treatment options. The average survival in patients with metastatic STS is 14 months. There is a desperate need to discover new systemic therapies for these aggressive cancers. Our group has developed an immune-competent mouse model of one of the most common STS subtypes: undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS). Using this model we have demonstrated that intra-tumoural activation of an immune pathway (STING pathway), can lead to immune-mediated tumour destruction and the development of protective immunologic memory against further UPS tumours. In this proposal, using multiple different immune-competent mouse models of sarcoma, our goal is to evaluate different clinically relevant therapeutic strategies to activate the STING pathway in STS. These include, small molecular activators of STING, engineering specific immune populations to over-express activated STING within tumours, and using viruses to infect tumour cells with activated STING. We will also combine STING therapy with standard clinical practice (radiation and surgery) to determine if pre-treating STS with STING therapy prior to surgical resection can shrink tumours pre-operatively and protect against tumour relapse and metastatic spread after surgery. The results stemming from this work will expand the scientific rationale and justification for pursuing clinical applications of STING agonist therapy for sarcoma patients.

column36: Effects of Reducing Social Media Use on Emotional Distress in Youth
column37: Anxiety and depression affect large numbers of youth. Social media use (SMU) is also prevalent among youth. This is concerning given high SMU is related to feelings of anxiety, depression, and loneliness, which may be due to unfavorable social comparisons that arise with SMU. A study done in adults found reducing SMU resulted in less emotional distress, but no studies have been done in youth. This study will test whether reducing SMU is an effective way to reduce feelings of anxiety, depression, and other symptoms in youth who are already experiencing emotional distress. We will also explore whether sex, gender or social comparisons influence the impact that the intervention has on emotional distress. We plan to recruit 216 youth aged 12-17 years who are on the waiting list for outpatient mental health services at a local children's hospital. Each participant will have an equal chance (like flipping a coin) of being assigned to the intervention group (108 youth) or to the control group (108 youth). The intervention group will receive an educational handout on tips for reducing SMU and will be required to limit SMU to 1-hour per day. Participants in the control group will receive the same educational handout but will have no limits put on their SMU. All participants will monitor their SMU daily on their smartphones and send us screenshots of their daily use. We will measure participants' symptoms of emotional distress using questionnaires that will be completed before the program, after 4 weeks of intervention, and again after 8 and 12-weeks to see if youth in the intervention group show greater reductions in emotional distress compared to those in the control group. This study may be the first to show that reducing SMU is an effective way to reduce emotional distress in a vulnerable group of youth waiting for mental health services. If this study is successful, findings would suggest that reducing SMU should be included in the treatment of distressed youth.

column36: The Amino Acid Requirements of Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) Fed Human Neonates.
column37: Worldwide, 13 million babies are born premature. In Canada, premature births have increased 20% over the last two decades. Premature babies have high nutritional needs but immature intestines and inability to suck and swallow, making them dependent on intravenous nutrition called total parenteral nutrition (TPN). As part of the TPN, the infants receive amino acids (AAs); the building blocks of proteins for growth and bodily processes. However, preterm babies are not able to use AAs the same way as full term babies. Excess AAs damage organs like the brain leading to decreased intelligence, while low intakes can lead to poor intestine and lung health in early life. Using the piglet model and 4 studies in human babies, our group showed that the AAs in current TPN solutions are not appropriate for the neonate, and need urgent attention. The goal of the current project therefore is to determine the requirements for 8 AAs in the TPN fed preterm baby. We developed the minimally invasive indictor amino acid oxidation method to determine AA requirements in vulnerable populations. The project will be conducted at three sites, two in Brazil and at SickKids in Toronto, Canada. The requirements for 3 AAs will be determined at SickKids and 5 between the two sites in Brazil. Twenty TPN fed, 32 weeks gestation (or older), appropriate for gestational age babies will be recruited to estimate each AA requirement. All resources are available in our lab at SickKids and will be shared to conduct the experiments in Brazil. Methods and operating procedures will be standardized between sites and all samples analyzed at SickKids. We expect the requirements for all AAs will be different than commercial TPN solutions. These results will allow the design of a TPN solution with optimal protein quality for the TPN fed neonate, likely among the most important contribution to nutritional management of these patients. It could improve survival and long term outcomes of infants born prematurely.

column36: Generating EMR-Based Algorithms to Identify Hospital Adverse Events for Health System Performance Evaluation and Improvement
column37: In healthcare, patient safety is often quantified by the occurrence of adverse and unintended events that may befall them. Capturing adverse events is a critical component of understanding the quality of health care and has been widely studied in many countries. These events are used to create patient safety indicators, which are specific safety- related adverse events. Adverse events are largely under-reported in hospital data and health surveillance systems. Thus, despite various efforts to identify hundreds of patient safety indicators, multi-specialty panels recommended only 26 indicators as the 'accepted' set of patient safety indicators. Electronic medical records (EMRs) contain detailed information regarding various aspects of patient care and have been widely implemented across Canada. As such, EMRs have become a valuable resource for the timely detection of various adverse events. However, the implementation of EMRs has not yet been coupled with powerful computational tools that automatically detect adverse events. To bridge this gap, we propose the current study, which aims to create EMR-based algorithms that detect adverse events for defining patient safety indicators. We will use artificial intelligence techniques (i.e. natural language processing) to automate the detection of a comprehensive list of adverse events using linked EMR and discharge abstract data from Alberta. We will then assess the validity of the developed algorithms by comparing them with clinical expert reviews conducted on a dataset of 10,000 EMR charts from Calgary. The developed EMR-based algorithms can be used to routinely detect adverse events for patient safety surveillance and monitoring and facilitate decision-making.

(2) To perform a preliminary assessment of how measures of aortic health may predict future TAA complications, such aortic tears or ruptures, death, or the need for aortic surgery. Our innovative research has significant potential to advance the field and improve the health of people with TAA, which is our long-term goal.

column36: Stamsh Slhanay Llawat II (Warrior Women Healing II): Continuing the Wellness Journey for Urban Indigenous Women and their Families
column37: There is an urgent need to support urban Indigenous women in using land and culture to promote healing and to restore and maintain wholistic wellness. Now, however, Indigenous women are overrepresented among mental illness diagnoses, addictions and chronic diseases. In the Canadian context, urban Indigenous women are subject to high rates of poverty, violent victimization, gender and racial oppression, and discrimination when seeking health services. Colonization, enacted through diverse policies and tactics, was driven by the goal of separating Indigenous people from their land and culture, and resulted in isolation, marginalization and reduced coping mechanisms for Indigenous people. The women participated in our study, some self-assuredly and some with great apprehension, but all came bravely, with the hope of healing. Findings revealed improved wellness and the necessity for sustained, low-barrier, trauma-informed, land- and culture-based healing activities that include the family to begin the healing process. Building on success of SSL-I, the goal of this study is to support Indigenous women in the DTES with diverse lived and living experience achieve improved wellness. Land- and culture-based healing, reinforced by family involvement, will be privileged, with expressive therapies interwoven, where appropriate, for wholistic healing and wellness. A multi-disciplinary, Indigenous-led research team will work with community partners to create a "two-worlds doing" approach. Knowledge generated will inform the development of Indigenous, gender-specific wellness care system with urban Indigenous populations.

column36: Comparative Effectiveness and Safety of Long-acting Insulins and Neutral Protamine Hagedorn (NPH) Insulin among Patients with Type 2 Diabetes

Treatments include lifestyle modification (e.g., diet, exercise), use of oral drugs, and then insulin when other treatments fail to control blood sugar levels. However, insulin can cause potential side effects, including severe low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Newer insulins that have a more gradual effect and control blood sugar levels for a longer time entered the market over the last two decades (long-acting insulins). These insulins are believed to have a lower risk of hypoglycemia compared to the older insulin types that stay in the body for a shorter time (intermediate-acting insulins). Benefits of long-acting insulins were observed in clinical trials with respect to hypoglycemia. However, these trials were conducted in highly-selected patients that are different from those seen in everyday clinical practice. Some studies have examined the effect of these newer insulins on the occurrence of heart-related events and hypoglycemia using data from patients seen in routine clinical practice, but they had important flaws and did not compare all available long-acting insulins. Higher quality studies that use real-world clinical data are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of long-acting insulins. To do this, we will use data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD). We will first compare the effectiveness of long-acting insulins and intermediate-acting insulins (called NPH insulin) at preventing heart attacks, strokes, and dying of heart problems. We will then compare the risk of severe low blood sugar in patients using these different types of insulin. This study will provide regulatory agencies, clinicians, and patients with important information on the use of these insulins for the management of type 2 diabetes.

column36: Immunophenotyping Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma: Identifying Predictive and Prognostic Biomarkers for Combinatorial Immunotherapy
column37: Although the immune system is thought of as a defense against infections, immune cells can also recognize and kill cancer cells. The immune system has safeguards to prevent immune cells from attacking healthy tissues. Unfortunately, cancer cells take advantage of these safeguards to effectively "turn off" the anticancer immune response. Fortunately, immunotherapy is a new way of treating cancer that "turns on" the anticancer immune response. Despite long cancer remissions and some cures in a small percentage of patients, most patients do not respond. As a pathologist and immunologist, I study immune responses in human tumour tissues using a microscope. I label each cell or molecule of interest with a differently colored (fluorescent) marker and generate a digital image of all of the cells in the tumour (a technology called multiplex immunofluorescence). Using digital image analysis software, I convert these images into large databases that include each cell's position and measurement of each molecule. By comparing these "cellular maps" from tumours that do and do not respond to therapy, key cell types and molecules can be identified that predict how a patient will respond to treatment. I am teaming up with the Canadian Cancer Trials Group to study tumours from patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma who are receiving immunotherapy in a large clinical trial. The large number of patients and well-documented clinical data collected for the trial make this an amazing resource for researching the best way to predict who will respond to therapy. Pretreatment tumour tissue collected in the trial will be studied to develop clinical tests that will help doctors decide which immunotherapy drug is most likely to "turn on" a patient's immune response to treat and, hopefully, cure their mesothelioma. This research bridges a critical gap in converting exciting scientific discoveries into improvements in clinical care for patients.

column36: Is stretching superior to walking for reducing blood pressure?
column37: High blood pressure is a leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Traditionally, one of the ways to treat or prevent high blood pressure is to prescribe aerobic exercise training (i.e. brisk walking). In a small study of 35 participants with moderate elevated blood pressure, we showed an exercise program that involves stretching may be superior to aerobic training for reducing blood pressure. We are excited about this finding because, if stretching is more effective, it would change the way we prescribe exercise to people with elevated blood pressure. Our proposed study will now assess a larger group of individuals (i.e. 96) participating in a supervised stretching or walking program five days per week for six months to determine for certain whether stretching is superior for reducing blood pressure. This research will contribute to recommendations about the most effective exercise programs for reducing blood pressure and risk of cardiovascular disease.

column36: Amplifying Treatment Response in Early Intervention 'Minimal Responders' with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Virtual Parent-Coaching Intervention
column37: Increasing numbers of children receive diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This brain-based condition affects children's communication and social development, and their play and interests may differ from those of typical peers. Canadians have made large investments to provide specialized early intervention programs for this growing group of children. These programs can greatly improve the lives of children with ASD and their families. However, not all children benefit equally. Nova Scotia's Early Intensive Behavioural Intervention (NS EIBI) program is unlike the early intervention programs in other provinces. Although it provides fewer hours of intervention than most other programs, results are comparable with some children making large gains. We must learn more about how to make a difference for all children with ASD, including those with the greatest learning challenges. Our research team designed a brief intervention to boost children's response to treatment. We identified children who were likely 'minimal responders' to NS EIBI, then showed that the intervention built the skills that should improve response to the EIBI program. We are ready to take the next steps in refine and test this intervention. When in-person treatment was halted by the pandemic in 2020, we learned that 'virtual' interventions provided online to parents may reduce barriers for families seeking help. In our new study, parents will receive live on-line coaching to build their children's skills before starting the EIBI program. We will monitor children's progress and compare the gains made in EIBI to those of similar children whose parents do not receive coaching. We will also talk to parents about their experiences to learn about the positive aspects of the intervention and what we could improve. We want to determine whether the on-line coaching intervention is effective in helping parents to promote their children's development, and how acceptable the program is for families.

column36: Treating Children with Arthritis According to their Individual Probability of Outcomes and Response to Treatments - The PERSON-JIA Trial
column37: When arthritis strikes a child, families face tough questions. Will their child suffer? Will they outgrow arthritis? Will they respond to treatment? Will there be side effects? The answers to these questions are crucial to choosing the best treatment for their child. Using information provided by thousands of families, we have developed a way of providing answers to these questions that are specific for the child and accessible right on the doctor's smartphone. The answers are generated automatically based on the child's circumstances using "personalized prediction algorithms" and presented in an app. In this study, we will test whether a structured discussion between families and doctors (guided by a graphical report produced by our personalized prediction algorithms and presented in the doctor's smart phone or computer) improves the tailoring of treatment to the child and control of the disease. The report is called the PERSON-JIA report and it presents the expected severity of disease for the child, the likelihood that the child will be arthritis-free as an adult, and the chance that treatments will be effective and/or have side effects. We will randomize (like flipping a coin) all willing Canadian pediatric rheumatologists to either (a) review the PERSON-JIA report in clinic with the family, or (b) continue to provide standard care. We will then check the decisions made and how well the children are doing six months later. We expect that using our personalized prediction algorithms in a frank and thoughtful discussion will help physicians and families make better decisions for managing the child's disease. This in turn will result in better disease control, greater family engagement and satisfaction with care and better-tailored treatment. If so, we will have a ground-breaking way to use information provided by families to improve the care provided to and the outcomes of children with arthritis in Canada, and establish a world-leading approach for JIA care.
