column36: Developing and validating biomarkers for chronic pain
column37: The cause of chronic pain remains elusive and the development of better diagnostic tools is among the most promising targets for improving pain management. This proposal means to leverage recent advances in artificial intelligence applied to brain imaging data to develop objective biomarkers for chronic pain. Magnetic resonance imaging is a brain imaging method that has been successfully used for decoding thoughts, feelings, and dreams from brain activity. Despite its potential for capturing pain, brain imaging has yet provided clinically useful tools for diagnosis, prognostication, and prediction of chronic pain. The advent of openly available very large datasets provides new opportunities to use artificial intelligence to develop biomarkers for chronic pain. The main objective of this proposal is to develop and validate brain-based biomarkers using data from a large number of individuals and to test the generalization of this marker to another data set. The secondary objective is to test the stability of the biomarkers across contexts and imaging sessions across time. More precisely, we will test if the expression of the biomarker is changing in patients receiving placebo or pharmacological treatment. This will help us determining if our biomarker can predict and/or track pain analgesia following treatments. Furthermore, we will test if our biomarkers can predict the prognostic of chronic pain in subacute back pain individuals one year later. A biomarker for chronic pain would represent an objective measurement of the pathology that can be used for both clinical and research contexts. This would ultimately represent an important advancement for prevention strategies and may ultimately lead to improved chronic pain management as well as a reduction of harms for patients.

column36: CMV Dynamics and Transmission in Pregnancy: Comparison Between Women Living with and without HIV
column37: There are very little recent data on cytomegalovirus (CMV) among the 20 million women living with HIV (WLWH) globally, who are at increased risk of CMV manifestations and transmission to their infants during pregnancy and shortly after delivery. Up-to-date data are critical as recommendations have changed such that all WLWH should now be receiving HIV treatment for life and this may change the risks associated with CMV. Improved understanding of the dynamics of CMV infection in the context of pregnancy in WLWH compared to women without HIV will inform optimal clinical care and infant outcomes through the use of available and novel interventions. This study will use existing samples and the ongoing recruitment infrastructure of an existing CIHR-funded cohort to comprehensively study CMV dynamics in HIV-affected pregnancies compared to HIV-unaffected pregnancies. We will examine the association between CMV transmission to infants and CMV viral replication, diversity, and shedding in different bodily compartments in pregnancy and the postnatal period, compare the dynamics of CMV shedding during pregnancy between women with and without CMV reinfections during pregnancy, and compare the genotypic features of transmitted CMV strains acquired during pregnancy and after delivery to those of non-transmitted CMV viruses, as well as to determine the overall CMV viral diversity in infants infected during pregnancy. These data will inform what genotypes should be included in candidate vaccines and may result in recommendations for targeted CMV screening in infants based on maternal viral shedding during pregnancy. Ultimately, our findings will help to reduce the enormous global health burden of CMV infection, which is the leading infant infection during pregnancy and is the leading cause of non-genetic childhood hearing loss and neurodevelopmental delay.

column36: A non-restrictive approach to facilitate appetite control and long-term body weight loss in individuals with obesity: can we do better?
column37: Calorie-restricted diets (i.e. low calorie diets) can lead to weight loss, but this method has not been found to be effective because of weight regain and negative effects such as an increase in appetite. Our group has shown that a non-restrictive highly satiating diet, that includes satiating (i.e. filling) foods and ingredients, reduces body fat and improves satiety and compliance without a negative impact on eating behaviours compared to a standard healthy diet over 16 weeks in men with obesity. We do not know the effects of this approach on appetite and long-term body weight loss and if the negative effects can be counteracted with this diet in both men and women with obesity. Our goal is to investigate the effect of a non-restrictive satiating intervention on appetite, body weight loss and maintenance and its potential to minimize the negative effects that usually happen with weight loss caused by caloric restriction in men and women with obesity. This is an 18-month weight loss (phase 1: P1, 6 months) and maintenance (phase 2: P2, 1 year) study with three groups: 1) non-restrictive satiating intervention (P1) followed by a continuation of this intervention (P2); 2) calorie-restricted diet (500 kcal/d deficit) (P1) followed by the non-restrictive satiating intervention (P2) and 3) control diet that includes minimal healthy guidelines (P1) followed by weight maintenance strategies (P2). This study will look at the effect of these interventions on body weight and composition, the appetite, physiological, psychobehavioural and other health-related factors. We expect that the non-restrictive satiating diet will improve the appetite and lead to more sustainable body weight loss and prevent the negative health effects of a calorie-restricted diet, therefore, leading to better maintenance of body weight.

column36: Development of Antisense Oligonucleotide-Based Therapy for Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is one of the most common kinds of muscular dystrophy in adults. It is a genetic problem that results in slow weakening and wasting of muscle in the face, shoulders, and limbs. FSHD is equally common in women and men. It can start at different ages, but most people with FSHD begin to show symptoms as teenagers. A childhood form of FSHD starts as early as 10 years of age-this type of FSHD is much more severe, with a high risk of patients developing problems with hearing and vision. Once FSHD starts, people with it experience a lifetime of disability. There is currently no cure for FSHD. Our proposed research aims to develop a new treatment for FSHD. FSHD is caused by abnormal production of a protein called DUX4 in muscle cells. Healthy muscle cells do not have DUX4. We plan on using small-DNA like molecules called gapmers to decrease the amount of DUX4 protein in muscle cells. Gapmers are able to do this by specifically finding and destroying the gene products responsible for making DUX4. In our research, we will use muscle cells to test the effectiveness and safety of gapmers that specifically target DUX4. We will also assess our gapmers in a mouse model of FSHD. In those mice, we can directly observe how our gapmers improve muscle function. The ultimate result of this work will be to identify a possible gapmer that can be tested in clinical trials for treating FSHD. Developing a new therapy for FSHD will positively impact the lives of people with the disease.

column36: A multigenerational study of the atopic march for deciphering the epigenetic heritability of allergic respiratory diseases and contribution to the elaboration of a predictive tool
column37: Eczema precedes food allergies, asthma, and allergic rhinitis in what is known as the atopic march. An infant with eczema has a weakened skin barrier, allowing allergens to enter the body and cause sensitization, meaning that the immune system recognizes harmless substances as hazardous, leading to a higher risk of developing other allergies. Although simple treatments for preventing these allergic diseases are available, their prevalence is still increasing. This inspired the development of a predictive tool that will help identify newborns at higher risk and motivate parents to adopt those treatments. Efforts have been made to determine genes that increase the risk of developing these diseases; however, knowledge of epigenetic heritability, changes caused by the environment on DNA that do not modify its sequence, is lacking. Epigenetic marks change throughout life, but can also be transmitted to the next generation. The aims of this project are 1) to identify epigenetic marks associated with diseases of the atopic march in the Canadian population; 2) to select marks that contribute to the epigenetic heritability of the atopic march; and 3) to validate the best hits by evaluating their biological impact using measures of gene activity and a replication in a European cohort. Ultimately, validated inherited marks will be added to a genetic predictive tool presently in development for the identification of at-risk newborns. This project will be possible thanks to the expertise of a geneticist and four biostatisticians.

column36: Development of TCR-engineered T cells against novel NY-ESO-1 epitopes for the treatment of triple negative breast cancer
column37: Triple negative breast cancer is an aggressive cancer type with limited treatment options. Immunotherapy, which utilizes the immune system to find and attack cancer is a promising treatment approach. One type of immunotherapy, called adoptive cellular therapy, uses T cells that are genetically-modified to express an anti-cancer T cell receptor (TCR). This TCR helps the T cells specifically seek and kill cancer but not healthy organs. These geneticallymodified T cells have been successfully used in clinical settings against other cancer types, but are limited in their availability to only patients expressing a certain type of human leukocyte antigen (HLA, which varies between individuals, like blood type). Our group has developed technologies that allow us to find anti-cancer TCRs available to patients who have different HLA, thus making this type of immunotherapy more widely available. From this technology, we have found additional anti-cancer TCRs that can detect cancer cells with different HLA. This proposal seeks to utilize this technology and test anti-cancer TCRs for use in adoptive cellular therapy to treat triple-negative breast cancer. Using breast cancer models derived from patients with different HLA, we will determine the effectiveness of the anti-cancer TCRs and optimize the therapy in laboratory settings. With genetic tools, we will determine how anti-cancer TCRs see tumors and whether we can safely boost the anti-cancer response by combining this adoptive cell therapy with different drugs. It is hoped that upon completion of this proposal, we will have developed safe and effective anti-cancer TCRs for adoptive cellular therapy that will make this potentially transformative treatment available to more patients with triple-negative breast cancer.

column36: Assessing the broad impacts of neighbourhood crime on the mental health of marginalized and vulnerable populations
column37: The numerous social and health disparities faced by marginalized and vulnerable populations (MVPs) in Canada require an intersectoral approach to find innovative and applicable interventions. This research focuses on crime, victimization, safety and criminal justice responses as social environmental exposures that are detrimental for mental health. The first objective is to assess the impact of crime in the broad sense on the mental health of MVPs. A secondary objective is to identify modifiable neighbourhood-level features associated with crime and safety, and related inequities in mental health. Neighbourhood crime may impact mental health through three key processes: direct exposure (i.e., as a victim), indirect exposure (i.e., witnessing neighbourhood crime and disorder), and through contact with the criminal justice process as a victim, criminalized person, or their family member (i.e., procedurally). This research integrates socioepidemiological, sociological and criminological theories, and adopts an intersectional approach (i.e., assessing impacts by age, gender and racioethnic group). Measures of mental health will be obtained from the Canadian Community Health Survey (2015-2017) and the Social and Psychiatric Epidemiology Catchment Area of the South West of Montreal (ZEPSOM) study (2014). Ego-centered measures of neighbourhood exposures will be derived using data from CANUE, Statistics Canada and Donnees Ouvertes Montreal. Novel measures of neighbourhood hostility and policing will be developed by combining these data sources. Advanced quantitative methods will be used to adjust for clustering of data, assess direct and indirect effects, and differential effects at the individual and neighbourhood-level. The results will provide the first comprehensive assessment of the impacts of exposure to crime, in the broad sense, on mental health, speak to the differential impacts for MVPs, and identify modifiable features to reduce mental health inequities.

column37: Youth onset type 2 diabetes (T2D) is increasing in children worldwide and especially in First Nation children in Canada. These youth develop early onset kidney disease that can lead to kidney failure in young adulthood despite receiving lifestyle and diabetes drugs. Current treatment approaches are failing. Youth have identified stress and lack of supports as critical barriers to managing their disease. We are proposing an extension of the iCARE cohort study to further evaluate the most relevant risk factors for worsening kidney disease using a wholistic approach in 350 existing and 150 new participants age 10-18 years with T2D from centres across Canada. Embedded within the study we will recruit 30 Manitoba children to study a new skills-based mental health intervention called Dialectical Behavioural Therapy (DBT) to help youth understand, manage and cope with their emotions. The program is 16 weeks long and runs once weekly for 2 hours/session (in person or virtual). We will evaluate DBT success (participation rates, retention and participation) and acceptability utilizing traditional and Indigenous Worldview interview techniques. In parallel, we will work with our Patient Advisory Group and Indigenous partners to determine how best to incorporate Traditional Medicine components into a modified DBT curriculum. We will then refine the DBT program and recruit an additional 30 Canadian children to evaluate the modified intervention. Our team has expertise in diabetes, kidney disease, Indigenous health, mental health, trials and interviewing. We are hopeful this study will provide new knowledge about how mental health and social factors impact kidney complication development and progression. At the same time, we are evaluating a new approach to help youth with T2D learn skills to manage their emotions and their disease. If our findings are promising this study will lead to a multi-centre International study to test DBT benefit more broadly.

column37: Roseola is a familiar disease to most parents, affecting virtually all children in infancy. While it usually only results in a high fever and a spectacular red rash, there are complications for 15% of patients, requiring a visit to an emergency department. The more frequent are febrile seizures, which may predispose to epilepsy. It can also lead to very severe inflammation of the brain, resulting in death or leaving patients with profound disability. Roseola is caused by a virus in the herpes family. Herpes viruses can infect the brain, where they usually become dormant. How the virus infects the brain, and occasionally damages cells, is currently unknown. These viruses are notoriously difficult to study in animals. Fortunately, there have been recent advances in tissue engineering that can help us. We can reprogram patient skin cells into stem cells, and then force them to become brain cells in the dish. The brain contains four major cell types. Neurons are the electrical cells: if they are damaged or die, this can cause seizures or lasting disability. Other cells play various roles in support of neurons. One type of immune cells, called microglia, specializes in responding to microbes. We devised methods to generate all these cells, and will investigate how Roseola infects each of them, and how each reacts. We will grow them together, as tissue, to mimic what happens in the brain: infection of one cell may indirectly damage another. We think microglia play a big role in harboring the virus, occasionally amplifying the damage. Our work will allow us to understand how the virus enters specific cells, what reaction this triggers, and how some cells may die. Altogether, this work will provide readily applicable knowledge to understand rare but grave complications from infection by one of the most common viruses affecting young children. This work will also inform our knowledge of adult disorders linked to this virus.

column36: Discovery and validation of vulnerabilities and therapeutic strategies for cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitor-resistant hormone receptor positive breast cancer
column37: CDK4/6-inhibitors are a new form of targeted therapy that have been approved for the treatment of hormone receptor positive breast cancer - the most common form of this disease. These drugs, when added to standard hormone-based therapies, substantially improve disease control and survival for people with metastatic cancer. However, eventually these cancers evolve and develop resistance to these therapies enabling their further growth and spread. Thus, effective treatment of this resistance disease is necessary to maximize the survival and quality of life for affected individuals. Using state of the art laboratory techniques, we have developed a strategy to identify new opportunities to attack these resistant cancer cells. In this program we will build on our existing platform of sophisticated laboratory models of drug resistant breast cancer. We will further characterize and expand on our initial discoveries to study the most promising drug candidates that can be rapidly developed into new treatment strategies. Importantly, our work takes advantage of emerging clinical data in order to ensure that our laboratory results are most relevant to patients in the real world, and to identify the specific markers of an individuals' resistant cancer that would enable us to most precisely "match" a new treatment strategy to deliver effective and personalized breast cancer treatment in the near future.

column36: Air pollution, climate and COPD: acute and long-term impacts in Canadian populations
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a long-term condition in which respiratory symptoms, in particular chronic breathlessness, and flare ups (acute exacerbations) lead to morbidity and disability, with subsequent reduction in health status. COPD is the number one cause of hospital admissions among chronic illnesses in Canada and the fourth leading cause of death globally. COPD is also an extremely costly disease: yearly costs of COPD in Canada are expected to increase from $4 billion in 2010 to $9.5 billion by 2030. While tobacco smoke is recognized as the single most important risk factor for the development and progression of COPD, 25% to 45% of individuals with COPD have never smoked. To decrease the burden of disease, we must therefore better understand the contribution of environmental factors beyond cigarette smoking to COPD development and exacerbation. While past studies have shown associations between COPD and air pollution and weather, the consequences of climate change on COPD and respiratory health are not well understood. Climate projections show that Canadian cities can expect an increase in abnormal weather events such as heat waves and extreme cold events, more wildfires leading to poor air quality episodes, and overall higher levels of air pollution over the next decades. This project will make use of data collected by three large pan-Canadian studies linked to short and long-term air pollution and climate data as well administrative health information on COPD hospital admissions and medication use to explore how environmental factors stemming from climate change will impact the burden of COPD in Canada. Results from this project will help develop public health and clinical management guidelines for COPD and respiratory heath, thereby allowing clinicians and policy makers to adapt to a changing climate. This study will also help communicate the respiratory health risks of climate change to the public and decision makers.

column36: Genome-wide tandem repeat expansions in neurological disorders
column37: Rapid development of technologies has allowed detection of a wide range of genetic contributing factors in neurological disorders. It has improved diagnosis and gene discovery for numerous human disorders. However, the casual contributing factors identified so far can only explain a portion of many disorders. For example, genetic contributing factors have so far been identified only in ~20% of the cases in autism spectrum disorder. Such missing cases can be due to the technical hurdle of the current sequencing technology and limitation of available analytic tools for repetitive regions of DNA. In particular, gene-specific repeats have been linked to over 50 known genetic disorders. Most of them are caused by increased length of the repeats (repeat expansions). Notably, currently available analytic tools cannot detect most of these factors from sequencing data. We have recently developed a comprehensive repeat calling strategy that allows us to unbiasedly detect thousands of repeat expansions per person from sequencing data. In this project, we will apply our pioneered repeat expansion analytic strategy to enable identification of relevant expanded tandem repeat loci and their modifying factors in neurological disorders.

column36: Proteinase-Activated Receptor-2 Agonists as Adjuvants for Mucosal Vaccination
column37: The flu is a lung disease caused by infection with the influenza virus. Flu infections are very common during the winter months and can cause death in vulnerable people such as the very young, the very old, and those with chronic diseases. One way to decrease deaths from the flu is to vaccinate people. Most vaccines are given by injection into muscles. The cost of these vaccines is high because they are expensive to produce and require medical personnel to administer. There is a lot of interest to develop vaccines that we can give into the nose because they are less painful, less expensive, easier to administer, and also more effective. The main problem with this approach is that the vaccines we give into the nose need to have an "adjuvant", a compound that will help stimulate our immune system to respond to the vaccine. Unfortunately, we do not have good adjuvants for nasal vaccines. We have identified a compound that has the potential to work as an adjuvant for a nasal flu vaccine. This compound is a small molecule that triggers a cell surface structure called Proteinase-Activated Receptor-2 (PAR-2). When we trigger PAR-2 the body produces chemicals that can activate our immune system. Our objective is to study the ability of this molecule (we call it PAR-2AP) to function as adjuvant for flu vaccination using mice. We will give mice a vaccine against flu alone or together with PAR-2AP. We will then measure the ability of their immune system to protect the mice in case they develop a flu infection. We will identify the best approach to give the vaccine with PAR-2AP to induce the highest level of protection and we will study the mechanisms that lead to protection from infection. This is the first time that this compound is studied for this ability as an adjuvant. The benefit of our approach is that this compound is easy to produce and inexpensive, and can be delivered into the nose so it will be easy to produce vaccines using this compound.

column36: Extracellular vesicles derived from amniotic fluid stem cells as a novel treatment strategy to rescue fetal lung underdevelopment
column37: Some babies are born with such underdeveloped lungs that they either die or survive with very poor quality of life. Underdeveloped lungs caused the deaths of more than 300,000 North American babies in the last 20 years. Right now, we can diagnose underdeveloped lungs early in pregnancy, but do not yet have an effective way to treat them. We discovered that stem cells from the amniotic fluid release droplets, called EVs, which make the lungs of fetal rodents bigger and more mature. Now, we want to find out if EVs that we isolate from donated human amniotic fluid can improve the underdeveloped lung tissue of human fetuses. We will measure the ability of EVs to improve lung development in three areas: growth, maturation, and blood vessel formation. Our results will provide the evidence needed to bring us a step closer to using this treatment in babies with underdeveloped lungs.

column36: Beyond survival: examining health of mothers after severe maternal morbidity in Canada (the BEYOND project)
column37: Pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a window into a woman's future state of health and well-being, and complications occurring in pregnancy can identify women at risk for chronic health conditions. Severe maternal morbidity (SMM) refer to serious unexpected outcomes during pregnancy, or around delivery that increase a woman`s risk of dying. Even for women who survive the delivery period, SMM has significant short-term health consequences to a woman. For example, women with SMM often have increased length of hospital stay, and a greater need for admission to an intensive care unit, compared with women without SMM. However, we do not know enough about a woman's long-term health after SMM, that is, her health status after 42 days of delivery (immediate postpartum period). Some SMM, e.g. severe pre-eclampsia and obstetric hemorrhage, have been reported to increase the risk of heart disease in the mother months to years after delivery. Therefore, it is possible that SMM has long-term effects on a woman's physical and mental health. As SMM rates are rising, including in Canada, it is pertinent to understand how these conditions may impact a woman's future health. This study aims to find out if women who survive after experiencing SMM in pregnancy become ill and require more health service use, compared with women who did not have SMM in pregnancy. We will find out the most common reasons for health service use e.g. recurrent pregnancy complications, mental health and other health issues. We will also examine how these health outcomes vary by province and year. This will be the first known study to explore these issues using Canadian databases. The results from this project will help health care providers understand the risk of future health outcomes in women with SMM, and plan necessary interventions, procedures, follow-ups and resources. Overall, this research will provide information that will help to improve the health of women in Canada.

column36: Use of an automated prospective clinical surveillance tool to drive screening for unmet palliative needs among patients in the final year of life
column37: One of the most important obstacles to improving end-of-life care is the inability of clinicians to reliably identify those who are approaching the end-of-life. Every aspect of a palliative approach to care - screening for unmet needs, treating symptoms, discussing goals of care, and developing a palliative management plan - depends on the reliable and accurate identification of patients with palliative needs. We developed an accurate and reliable mortality prediction tool that automatically identifies patients in hospital at elevated risk of death in the coming year. We have shown in previous studies that these patients also frequently have unmet palliative care needs at the time they are identified by the tool. We have successfully implemented this tool in 4 Ontario hospitals, and have shown that it is feasible, acceptable to patients and providers, and effective for changing physician behaviour in an inpatient clinical context. Recently, an additional 13 Ontario hospitals have started to implement the tool using site-specific, comprehensive implementation plans, including stakeholder engagement, education, electronic medical record integration, and peer-peer collaboration and learning. In this project, we propose to evaluate this tool in the 13 hospitals that have started implementation to facilitate reliable and timely identification of unmet palliative needs and improve the quality of palliative and end-of-life care provided to patients and families. The goal of this proposal is to systematically evaluate the barriers and facilitators to implementation given different clinical settings and contexts, and assess whether the tool was effective for promoting the identification and documentation of unmet palliative needs. We will also follow patients who were identified by the tool over time to collect outcome and impact measures to see if their end-of-life care was affected by the intervention.

column36: The PREVENT trial: a pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial of a multicomponent fracture prevention model for long-term care
column37: Hip fractures occur nearly twice as often for older adults residing in long-term care as they do in older adults of a similar age still living in other settings. Hip fractures are the leading cause of hospitalization and often result in loss of independence, problems with walking and sometimes death. To address this problem our team has designed the PREVENT program for use in long-term care homes. PREVENT uses a tool ("fracture risk calculator") based on a residents electronic health record to capture who is most at risk of fracture due to osteoporosis and falls. The program then trains the health care team including doctors, pharmacists and nurses on the latest recommendations on how to best assist residents and their families in making treatment decisions. The healthcare teams are also given tools that help them stay on track such as templates for ordering medications, strategies to reduce falls and fractures and making care plans. Our study will examine if this program is effective for decreasing hip fractures by assigning some homes to receive the PREVENT program (intervention group) and some homes to usual care (control group) and comparing the results. Our study team includes scientists, health care providers and family and resident councils who will also consult with front-line long-term care workers to design and carry out the study. If successful, the strategies from the PREVENT trial can be widely implemented across Canada and internationally with potential life saving and health care cost-saving implications.

column36: Aggressive Smoking Cessation Therapy Post-Acute Coronary Syndrome: The ASAP Trial
column37: Patients who continue to smoke after an acute coronary syndrome (ACS), including a heart attack or recurrent chest pain at rest, have a 35% increased risk of another heart attack or death compared with those who quit. Quitting smoking is therefore key to improving the health of patients with ACS, with benefits that exceed other cardiovascular disease prevention strategies (e.g., blood pressure and cholesterol control). Our previous smoking cessation trials in patients post-ACS have established varenicline (Champix) as the most effective smoking cessation therapy in these patients. However, more than 50% of motivated quitters who receive 12 weeks of varenicline immediately post-ACS will return to smoking within 6 months. Based on new data which suggest that nicotine e-cigarettes increase smoking abstinence more than conventional nicotine replacement therapies (e.g., the patch, gum) and counselling, we proposed to combine varenicline and nicotine e-cigarettes. The proposed combination therapy is a novel approach needed now to increase abstinence in patients with ACS. We will randomize (like the flip of a coin) 798 participants to one of two treatment arms: (1) varenicline and nicotine e-cigarettes for 12 weeks or (2) varenicline alone for 12 weeks. Both arms will receive individual smoking cessation counselling at all follow-up telephone calls and visits. Participants will begin varenicline and counselling in-hospital, and e-cigarette use (if applicable) upon discharge. Eligible patients will be hospitalized for ACS, self-identify as regular smokers (>/=10 cigarettes/day), and be motivated to quit. They will complete telephone follow-ups at weeks 1, 2, 8, and 18, and clinic visits at weeks 4, 12, 24, and 52. At follow-up calls and visits, we will collect information about self-reported smoking, treatment adherence, and adverse events. The ASAP trial will provide important new information about the efficacy and safety of combination smoking cessation therapy post-ACS.

column36: Understanding Delirium Pathophysiology using Urine Metabolomics from Older People with Hip Fractures
column37: Delirium is a state of acute confusion or "brain failure" that robs people of their ability to think clearly. Delirium was thought to be reversible, but we now know it can cause permanent damage. It affects up to 62% of older people treated for a hip fracture and doubles their risk of death and the chances of admission to a nursing home. Delirium is difficult for busy doctors and nurses to diagnose and they currently miss up to 75% of cases. When hospital staff fail to recognize delirium, care worsens further, and their risk of death is tripled. Unfortunately, there are no lab tests that can accurately diagnose delirium and no effective treatments to reverse it. Delirium is especially challenging to study because it is difficult to predict which patients will develop delirium, and to know when it will occur because it has so many different causes. As a result we still don't understand the underlying steps that lead to delirium and exactly how or why people get delirium. We propose to take advantage of a "natural experiment" to better understand the underlying changes that lead to delirium and then develop lab tests to diagnose delirium. We will do this by obtaining daily urine samples from 608 older people who come to the Emergency with a hip fracture. Experience shows that about 1/3 of these people will develop delirium within 5 days. By comparing samples taken before and after delirium develops, we can use a new technique called "metabolomics" to search for thousands of chemicals at the same time. Studying this large number of different chemical patterns will ultimately allow us to develop an accurate lab test to diagnose delirium as well as to better understand the changes that occur in people that lead to delirium. We have already obtained promising results in a pilot study. While the test will be used for the 30,000 Canadians with hip fracture initially, we expect the test to be useful in a much larger range of people affected by delirium in the future.

column36: The WHEAT International Trial: WithHolding Enteral feeds Around red cell Transfusion to prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm neonates: an international, multi-centre, randomized controlled trial.
column37: WHEAT stands for Witholding Enteral feeds Around packed red cell Transfusion to prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm neonates. It is an international, multi-centre, randomized controlled trial that will examine whether withholding milk feeds before, during and after blood transfusion in preterm infants reduces the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). NEC is a serious gut disease that affects about 1 in 20 very premature babies; about 1 in 3 will die of the disease and survivors are at high risk of long-term health and developmental problems. Premature babies receive frequent feeds (every 1-3 hours) and often need blood transfusions because they become anemic (not enough red blood cells). Some doctors worry that feeding babies during a blood transfusion may increase the risk of NEC but others think that it is more dangerous to stop feeds. Feeding approaches around blood transfusions therefore vary between sites and different professionals. The purpose of WHEAT is to determine which approach is best by comparing two groups of babies randomly chosen by computer to either have milk feeds stopped or continued around blood transfusions. WHEAT will compare standard practices and involves nothing new or additional to standard care. We aim to enrol over 4,000 babies and will collaborate with co-applicants undertaking an identical study in Australia to identify the best approach. Preventing necrotizing enterocolitis has been identified by parents, patients and professionals as the third most important research priority in the field of preterm birth. If simply stopping feeds when giving a blood transfusion can reduce the risk of NEC, we could quickly and easily start to prevent this devastating disease. On the other hand, because breast milk has so many beneficial effects for premature babies, stopping it might be harmful. A clinical trial like WHEAT is the only way to resolve this uncertainty.

column36: Investigating a New Biomarker for the Inherited Arrhythmia Condition: Brugada Syndrome
column37: Brugada Syndrome (BrS) is a heart disorder causing sudden death at night, particularly in young men. BrS affects 1 in 2000 persons and is causes for 28% of sudden deaths people under age 65 with normal hearts. This results in many lost years of life. BrS is hard to detect because the ECG pattern comes and goes. Genetic testing misses 80% of patients. There are similarities between BrS and a heart muscle disorder where we recently found an antibody. We looked for antibodies in BrS, and found four. These antibodies now very accurately identify BrS. The antibodies are against proteins that form clumps in heart cells. So this clumping can also help identify BrS after someone has died. Our objectives are: 1. To confirm that these antibodies accurately diagnose BrS, identify those who will later get disease, and identify those who will have dangerous arrhythmias. 2. To determine if the clumping proteins can identify victims who have died from BrS. 3. To find out if the antibodies cause disease, or are just a marker for it. To achieve these objectives, we will collect data, blood samples and (where available) tissue from BrS patients, by working with large groups including from Toronto General Hospital, Ottawa Heart Institute, a Canadian Registry, Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, Zurich, Poland, Germany, UK and China. These will provide us with over 3600 samples and data, allowing us to answer each of the questions above. We will measure antibody using standard research and clinical methods. For comparison, we have blood samples from many normal individuals of different ages, sex & ethnicities. Our study is unique in that it will provide an easy test to diagnose Brugada Syndrome before and during disease, and also after death.

column36: Assessing attitudes, barriers, and opportunities for human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination (HPVV) to inform, develop, implement, and evaluate a culturally appropriate program for increasing utilization and addressing vaccination hesitancy in Arctic Canadian Indigenous communities
column37: Northwest Territories (NT) Indigenous communities have expressed concerns for the number of people affected by cancer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted infection that can lead to cervical and other types of cancer. HPV vaccination is a safe and effective way to prevent cervical cancer caused by HPV. Yet, NT school-based vaccination rates are among the lowest in Canada for reasons that are not well-known. There is an urgent need for community-specific, culturally-relevant strategies that are appropriate and effective to increase knowledge and willingness for HPV vaccination in the NT. Given the current pandemic, communities have also asked us to address concerns regarding vaccination for when a COVID-19 vaccine is developed. Furthermore, COVID-19 is likely further reducing HPV vaccination coverage and utilization of other cancer screening services in NT. This project will work closely with 2 NT communities using Indigenous methodologies and Two-Eyed Seeing to listen to peoples' experiences and concerns surrounding HPV, HPV vaccination, and vaccine hesitancy within the context of COVID-19. Working collaboratively with community members and healthcare providers, this project will develop, implement and evaluate a culturally safe, community-based program, designed and delivered by local staff, utilizing on-the-land and traditional activities, to understand and address concerns related to cervical cancer, and HPV/COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy; increase HPV vaccination; and ultimately reduce the burden of HPV-related cancers. This project could greatly reduce the burden of cervical and other related cancers by increasing HPV vaccination in remote Arctic Indigenous communities while providing salient knowledge regarding HPV vaccination, as well as community member willingness towards a potential COVID-19 vaccine.

column36: ESCAPE-MeVO trial (EndovaSCular TreAtment to imProve outcomEs for Medium Vessel Occlusions)
column37: The most common cause of stroke is when a clot blocks an artery that supplies blood to the brain. Every second lost in removing that clot results in more damage to the brain. There are two established treatments to remove the clot. A clot busting drug can be given as an injection through the veins. This drug however only works in a minority of patients. Alternatively, thin tubes and wires can be inserted through the groin and taken up to the brain to remove the clot (endovascular treatment). This latter treatment works 80 to 90% of the time with clots blocking big arteries. For every three patients treated this way, one extra patient lives a functionally independent life - making this treatment one of the most effective treatments in all of medicine. At least two out of every five patients with strokes due to clots however have clots in smaller arteries. The clot busting drug works, at best, around 50% of the time. Until now, tubes and wires that can safely reach these smaller arteries and remove clots were not available. Moreover, newer imaging techniques are helping physicians identify these clots better. These advances in technology mean that physicians can now reliably and safely treat patients with these smaller clots using miniaturized tubes and wires. If we prove that endovascular treatment with tubes and wires is safe and effective in removing clots in these smaller arteries in the brain, we could offer patients with such strokes a better chance at improving. We therefore need a study that randomizes subjects to the new treatment vs. what they currently receive as standard care. The ESCAPE-MeVO study seeks to do this. This study will recruit around 600 subjects across centres in Canada, US, and Europe and will follow the highest standards of ethical conduct of research, patient confidentiality and data collection.

column36: It takes two to tango: Parental obesity and sex-specific impacts on placental development
column37: Maternal factors, including obesity, increase the risk of obesity in her offspring - independent of postnatal diet and lifestyle - in a sex-specific manner where males and females show different metabolic outcomes. Some of this risk is due to poor placental function, and whether placenta is associated to a male or female fetus ("placental sex"). While decades of work have focused on the impact of maternal obesity on sex -specific placental function and offspring disease risk, the father has been largely overlooked. The father contributes not only genes to the embryo and fetus, but also contributes to the formation of the placenta and might even control how the placenta functions. We now have data that paternal obesity, like maternal obesity, impacts placental development and influences the way in which the fetus develops and increases the risk of metabolic complications in his offspring (not unlike maternal impacts). Importantly these outcomes are sex specific - where female placenta and female fetuses appear more vulnerable than males. These sex-specific risk factors depend on whether the mother or the father is obese. In our study we will investigate how the father and mother independently and together, affect the placenta of male and female fetuses and offspring and determine if daughters or sons are more or less affected. We will also for the first time determine whether these sex-specific outcomes are magnified if both parents are obese. We will also determine if we can improve outcomes by using a readily available nutritional intervention.

column36: Exploiting minor histocompatibility antigens for personalized cancer immunotherapy
column37: Blood cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related death in young adults and the sixth in adult. In 2016, more than 22,000 Canadians were diagnosed with lymphoma, leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome or other blood cancers. Although extensive research in the field has led to improved survival, leukemia relapse remains the most important cause of treatment failure. A large part of the curative potential stem cell transplantation, one of the most intensive therapies for blood cancers, resides in the ability of donor cells to recognize minor histocompatibility antigens (MiHA) found on the surface of malignant cells. Alternatively, cell therapy in the form of chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells allows to coax our immune system to recognize specific targets, such as CD20, present on B-cell cancers. However, current CAR-T approaches are only applicable to a very limited number of blood cancers (i.e. B cell lineage blood cancers). Hence, there is a need to develop novel treatment options that can target wider lineages of hematologic cancers while demonstrating low toxicity. We propose to develop a personalized cancer immunotherapy modality that builds on our recent identification of novel germ-line derived minor histocompatibility antigens (MiHA) expressed specifically on the surface of blood cancer cells. Our large library of target antigens enables targeting of 99.8% of European-Americans population. We have demonstrated in a Phase I study that we can generate anti-MiHA T cells ex vivo that can be administered safely to patients in order to generate anti-leukemia activity. We intend to improve this process by characterizing those MiHA-specific T cells and subsequently generate engineered T cells with the ability to recognize these antigens that are specifically expressed on blood cancer cells, therefore preventing complications associated with non-specific binding to healthy tissues. This strategy should allow treatment of the wide variety of blood cancers.

column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common pediatric cancer and the most frequent cause of death from cancer before age 20 in North America. The main focus of this application is T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), a high-risk leukemia affecting children and young adults. Current T-ALL treatments entail high-dose multi-agent chemotherapy, leading to cure rates of 80% in children and 60% in adults. However, a large number of patients still relapse, and refractory or relapsed patients remain very difficult to treat. Another limitation of current therapies is the severity of secondary effects resulting from chemotherapy treatments, that can lead to stunted growth and reduced quality of life. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop precision therapies that are both more efficient and less toxic to target specifically the oncogenic proteins responsible for disease while preserving healthy cells. Recently, we have obtained results suggesting a new mechanism through which the oncogenic protein TLX1 induces and maintains leukemia. Specifically, we found that TLX1 perturbs interactions between genes in leukemic cells. Such disruption leads to rearrangement of the gene expression program, block in differentiation and development of leukemia. In this application, we will use state of the art molecular approaches to resolve the mechanism through which TLX1 rearranges the topological organization of the genome. We will also use in vivo models of disease to test for new therapeutic approaches based on targeting TLX1-mediated aberrant loop formation in the genome. Thus, successful completion of this proposal is expected to identify new therapeutic targets that could be used to treat leukemia patients while having fewer side effects.

column36: In silico Design of Precision Electrical Stimuli for Electrical Vestibular Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease.
column37: Stimulating the balance organ, by applying a mild electrical current via electrodes behind the ears (at a level so low that people can't even feel) is an exciting potential treatment for Parkinson's disease. It is safe, non-invasive, inexpensive, and portable, but the effects of this therapy are relatively mild, and depend upon the exact sequence of electrical pulses delivered. We believe that if we tailor the sequence of pulses to the individual, we can dramatically improve the effectiveness of this potential therapy. However, if we were to apply many, many different sequences of pulses and then check how much this improved their Parkinson's symptoms, it would take far too long, and we wouldn't be able to check very many sequences to determine the best one before people got tired. We get around this problem by stimulating while measuring both the brain waves and brain activation in an MRI scanner. We then use Artificial Intelligence to predict what the brain's response would be to any sequence of pulses. This allows us to use a computer to check millions and millions of potential sequences to determine the best one for that individual. We will then take this best sequence, as predicted by the computer, and test it in actual subjects to verify that this results in substantial improvement in their motor symptoms. To achieve these goals, we have assembled an expert team of a Parkinson's doctor, engineers and artificial intelligence experts. Success of this project would demonstrate a way to significantly improve the effectiveness of this novel treatment for Parkinson's disease.

column37: End-stage organ failure presents complex issues and challenges for Canadian patients, clinicians and the health care system. Patients with end stage organ failure often require a transplant to save their lives. Survival rates of recipients have improved over the past several years because of drugs given that suppress the immune system and prevent rejection. These drugs are routinely used in transplantation, and we are proposing to study the effect of one of these commonly used medications (tacrolimus) in deceased donors for organ donation. This small study will investigate the use of tacrolimus in deceased kidney donors to see if it is possible to obtain the information needed to prove that use of this drug during deceased donor management is beneficial for organ recipients in a larger study. Results of this study will inform researchers for the design of a future clinical trial on organ donor management; and final results will hopefully change practice, and improve the rate and success of transplant surgery in Canada.

column37: Endometrial cancer (EC) is diagnosed in >60,000 North American women each year. Unlike other cancers where advanced tumors can be reliably distinguished pathologically based on their appearance under the microscope, ECs are very difficult to tell apart. column36: The leptin receptor expressing pericyte links obesity to neuroinflammation
column37: Maintenance of body weight chiefly depends on a thermostat-like control system that measures fat mass and reports this measure to the brain centers that drive appetite. Fat mass is communicated to the brain by the hormone leptin which is produced by fat cells in proportion to the amount of fat: more fat leads to more leptin which in turn leads to less appetite, which thus allows for maintaining a set body weight much like a thermostat controls room temperature. The proposed research is aimed at elucidating the precise mechanism by which the hormone leptin enters the brain to act on the appetite regulating brain centers. We want to investigate if as we suspect circulating leptin makes blood vessels leaky in order to gain access to the brain. We want to further study if this leakiness depends on a specific brain cell type, the pericyte, which tightly enwraps brain vessels and is known to constrict the vessels they enwrap when engaged. If we indeed observe that leptin leads to vessel constriction and subsequent leakiness, we would have found a possible explanation why obesity is so strongly associated with neuroinflammation: it is due to increased vessel constriction and leakiness caused by the chronically high leptin levels of the obese state.

column36: Development of a Novel Therapy to Prevent Breast Cancer Metastasis: Modulation of TAFI, a Master Regulator of Extracellular Proteolysis
column37: Over 90% of cancer deaths are caused by metastasis, the spreading of cancer from the primary tumor site to other parts of the body. Dr. Boffa and his team have discovered a new way to potentially prevent this process. Metastasis depends in part on a group of enzymes called proteases that sever the protein connections between tumor cells and allow cancer cells to chew their way through tissues. Previous attempts to develop a drug to prevent metastasis have not been successful. The best known example is drugs meant to inhibit the proteases on which metastasis depends. However, these drugs proved in some cases to be toxic and in other cases not effective because they inhibited many proteases, not just the ones important for metastasis. Dr. Boffa has found that two proteins, TAFI and thrombomodulin (TM), work together to prevent these proteases from becoming active, thereby preventing metastasis. His team has designed a new protein drug based on thrombomodulin, and they are proposing to test whether this new drug is effective against metastasis of breast cancer cells in animal models of the disease. Dr. Boffa's project encompasses three major aims. First, he will use isolated cells to examine particular aspects of the mechanisms that TAFI and TM may use to prevent metastasis. Next, he will use mouse models of breast cancer metastasis and angiogenesis to determine if TAFI and TM inhibit these processes in an intact animal in the way they do in isolated cells in the laboratory. Finally, he will develop a form of TM that has lost all of its normal functions except its ability to help activate TAFI. Dr. Boffa will test this potential new drug in mouse models of breast cancer cell metastasis. The novel anti-metastasis drug to be developed by Dr. Boffa's team, if proven to be effective in animal models in the proposed research, could then be further developed for use in human patients and entered into clinical trials to prevent metastasis.

column36: Machine Learning Based Craniosynostosis Triaging System
column37: Infant skull deformations have become increasingly common since the introduction of the Back to Sleep Campaign, occurring at least once in every 60 live births. The majority of these abnormalities are related to plagiocephaly-a relatively benign condition-and can be treated with simple interventions such as changing sleep positions. Conversely, craniosynostosis (synostosis) is a more severe condition in which one or more of the sutures in an infant's skull fuse prematurely, causing debilitating abnormalities in skull growth and potential impacts on brain development. SickKids receives thousands of new consultations for infant skull assessments per year, with the majority being benign cases. This volume of patient referrals results in prolonged consult visit wait-times and diagnostic delays for those who need surgery. This is of particular concern, as infants who are diagnosed prior to 4 months of age can be treated with a relatively minimal invasive endoscopic surgical intervention. Our institution will consider treating all subtypes of synostosis endoscopically. Those diagnosed after this window of time require an extremely invasive high-cost higher-risk procedure in which the skull is removed from the head, reshaped, and applied back on. We currently miss 71% of all synostosis cases beyond the 4 month age window of opportunity. This equates to an estimated $760,000 dollars per year in healthcare costs. We have successfully built high-performing machine learning models to predict which infants have synostosis early using 3D images. To build on this success we aim to complete the following: 1. develop a model to predict synostosis using 3D images captured on mobile devices and 2. validate our model and triaging system with a clinical trial. The use of 3D images captured with mobile devices will enable us to deploy our system outside of SickKids at scale creating a foundation for sustainable impact and deployment to community providers and parents directly.

column37: Although emotional "ups" and "downs" are a natural part of life, major depression results in a significant deviation from our normal patterns of thoughts, feelings and behaviors. Ranging from mild to severe, major depression robs its victims of the natural emotional "coloring" of life and creates a mental state that can best be described as "lifeless". It is estimated that about 8- 12% of Canadians will suffer from an episode of major depression during their lives. The emotional, societal and economic burden of the disease for the Canadian society is enormous. Feelings of hopelessness and guilt may pervade, along with significant disturbances in thought patterns, energy/motivation, sleep and appetite, in the pleasure in previously enjoyable activities, lack of concentration, and others. Despite the existence of pharmaceutical interventions for depression, their lack of clinical efficacy in approximately 30% of patients and delay in action (up to 3 weeks) points to a pressing need for research. It's often said that depression results from a chemical imbalance, notably of the neurotransmitter serotonin. However, that figure of speech dramatically falls short of providing a satisfactory explanation of how the activity of serotonin-secreting neurons in the brain operate. Indeed, mood-related networks in the brain constantly talk to one another to ultimately control key aspects of our behaviors such as motivation and decision-making process. We currently have a poor understanding of how these networks communicate and the nature of the signals that are being communicated. In this proposal, we propose to take advantage of recent technical developments to gain a better understanding of how brain networks involved in depression are functioning. These studies will significantly improve our current understanding and provide a rich framework that will contribute to the development of new and novel therapeutic strategies.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the fourth cause of cancer death, and breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women, worldwide. The tumour microenvironment consists of tumour cells and immune cells, and it has become clear that immune cells must be functional for long-term control of tumour development. However tumours secrete factors that inhibit immune cells, and promote the accumulation of dysfunctional immune cells termed immunosuppressive myeloid cells, which support tumour growth and spread. To address this, new immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) immunotherapies have been developed. However, for most cancer types ICB responses are limited, with the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid cells being a key barrier to success. The vast heterogeneity of immunosuppressive myeloid cells renders their identification and classification, and identification of the tumour-associated factors controlling their development, challenging. We have identified a cytokine - granulocyte colony stimulating factor (GCSF) - as a key factor driving the development of immunosuppressive cells, and found that inhibition of GCSF normalizes myeloid lineage composition, reduces tumour growth, and improves immunotherapy. Importantly we have also identified a novel myeloid subset present in both mice and humans, which develops in cancer. We have termed these cells "patrolling tumour enriched monocytes" (pTEMs). Our research plan is to comprehensively characterize tumour-induced alterations in myeloid subsets, and identify GCSF-gene regulatory networks underlying immunosuppressive myeloid cell developmental patterns. To do this, we will utilize mouse models of CRC and breast cancer. We will determine the spatial locations of immune cells within tumours. In addition, we will remove pTEMs from tumour bearing mice, and further characterize them with respect to their ability to regulate CD8+ T cells and NK cells (types of immune cells that kill tumours), to determine their role cancer.

column37: The COVID-19 pandemic is having devastating effects on the mental health and well-being of Canadians, particularly, for those living with chronic mental health conditions such as schizophrenia. Psychological interventions have been proven to be effective to support recovery in this population, however, access to these interventions has historically been limited (e.g., due to factors such as limited availability of trained professionals). The restricting measures due to COVID-19 (e.g., no non-essential health visits and guidelines for physical distancing), have made it even more difficult for these patients to access psychosocial therapies. This, in turn, increases the risk for hospitalizations and suicide, in a group where such risks are already high. To address this issue, our team will implement and evaluate an innovative, online psychological and social therapy intervention called "HoryzonsCa." HoryzonsCa consists of web-based resources to build strength and resilience, social connectedness, and access to peer support and mental health professionals. We will recruit 100 English and French-speaking adults diagnosed with schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders from: University of Montreal Hospital Centre and the Douglas Mental Health University Institute. We will study the issues that are important to consider when adapting and implementing HoryzonsCa, and its potential benefits. The results will provide health care professionals, hospital administrators, policymakers, patients, and families with important and timely information on the use of technology to improve access to psychosocial therapies for individuals living with chronic mental health conditions, during and after COVID-19. We will communicate results through our well- established and extensive local, national, and international networks within the field of psychosis; and, through online media to accelerate the impact of this study during an important time in Canadian history.

column36: Personalized seizure forecasting to improve epilepsy management
column37: Epilepsy, one of the most prevalent and stigmatized neurological conditions, affects 1% of Canadians of all ages and is characterized by recurrent seizures as a result of excessive neuronal brain activity. Unfortunately, more than a third of people living with epilepsy are not adequately controlled with currently available medical or surgical treatment options. The most disabling aspect of living with epilepsy is the unpredictable nature of seizures, which creates a constant source of worriment and danger for patients and their caretakers. This has motivated researchers to investigate the possibility of forecasting seizures. Similar to meteorologists who use equations of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics with measures provided by weather stations to forecast the weather, we propose to predict seizures using a) equations measuring particular nonlinear correlations across the different frequencies of the brain's electrical activity provided by implanted EEG electrodes; and b) new approaches based on artificial neural networks, a form of artificial intelligence capable of learning to perform a task, in our case automatically detecting the pre-seizure state, by seeing many training examples. Our algorithm would then be implemented into a personalized framework which would continuously forecasting the probability of being in a pre-seizure state. Real-time seizure forecasting would offer a life-changing solution to patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. Simple devices such as automated triggered alarms (to warn patients to lie down, take a rapid-acting antiseizure drug, or to alert caretakers) can realistically be implemented on a short-term basis with high impact (improved quality of life and reduction of seizure-related injuries and deaths).

column36: Investigating Use of Prescription Opioids and Multiple Psychotropic Medications During Pregnancy: Impact on the Mother and Developing Child
column37: Canada is in the midst of an opioid crisis. With more women taking prescription opioids during pregnancy now than at any time in the past, it is important to understand how these drugs are used during pregnancy and how they affect the development of children. This information is critical to policymakers working to reduce negative effects related to prescription opioids, and to women faced with the decision of whether to take these medications during pregnancy or not. Increasing the complexity of the issue is the fact that prescription opioids are often taken together with other psychotropic medications, such as anti-depressants. The risks to mothers who use these drugs and to their infants are largely unknown. We will use powerful, comprehensive administrative data from two Canadian provinces and sophisticated statistical analysis techniques to investigate the effect of prescription opioid and psychotropic medication use during pregnancy. We will include women from the full spectrum of income, generating insight into how these medications affect mothers and their developing children over time. The project will: 1) describe patterns of prescription opioid use during pregnancy, including the specific opioid (e.g., codeine, hydromorphone), the intensity of use (total days supply and morphine equivalent), the demographics of users (age, socioeconomic status, morbidity), and information about the prescribers (e.g. specialty, location of training); and compare women who use prescription opioids to non-users to examine 2) short term outcomes (e.g., neonatal abstinence syndrome), and 3) long term outcomes (e.g., ADHD, autism) for children exposed in the womb. 4) We will also use education data to assess impacts on school readiness and test performance.

column36: A Pragmatic Randomized Clinical Trial on Immersive Virtual Reality Compared to Non-Immersive Distraction Using a Tablet for Pain and Anxiety Management of Children During Bone Pins and Sutures Removal in Orthopedic Clinics
column37: Children presenting with a fracture to a limb or fingers will often require the insertion of bone pins to maintain the fracture in place while it heals. Afterwards, they require a followup with an orthopedist about a month after the insertion of the pins in their fractured bone. The withdrawal of these pins is done in an outpatient orthopedic clinic by an orthopedist. This procedure generates pain, apprehension and anxiety in most children. Further, there is actually no intervention done before or during the withdrawal of the bone pins to help children cope with their pain and anxiety. This study aims at improving pediatric pain care while they are consulting for the withdrawal of their bone pins during their visit to an orthopedic outpatient clinic. We propose to verify if virtual reality through the use of goggles would provide enough distraction to children while they are undergoing painful and stressful procedures such as removal of metal pins that were inserted into their bones to help heal a fracture. We hope that by providing a total immersive distraction experience we will allow children to undergo the procedure with less pain and stress and overall providing a more humanistic approach to children's care.

column36: Novel Biologic Therapies and Delayed Release Scaffolds for Tissue Fibrosis
column37: Tissue stiffening (fibrosis) can occur after damage to any organ, produced by the activation of fibroblast cells near the site of injury. Fibrosis is more problematic in organs that require movement, like the heart that must continue to beat and squeeze to provide blood to the body. There are no treatments that target fibrosis, or can stop the process once it starts to occur. We have studied how small molecules (proteins) released from fibroblasts in the heart can either propagate this damage, leading to organ failure, or prevent the fibrosis, depending on the characteristics of the fibroblast. In the project, we will create a 3-dimensional model (organoid) of the human heart and model fibrosis, testing the ability of the identified beneficial small molecules to improve heart function. After determining which of the molecules is the most beneficial, we will test how well they can treat heart fibrosis in a pig model of disease. Fibrosis is a slow, progressive process, and ideally any therapy would be released over time. We will develop a dissolvable scaffold to provide a slow-release of the therapeutic molecules, inducing organ repair over a longer time course. Through these experiments, we will develop the first targeted therapy for fibrosis.

column36: Defining clinically important bleeding outcomes for clinical trials in hematological malignancies: perceptions of patients and health care providers
column37: Patients with acute leukemia bleed more easily due to the disease and its treatments. Researchers use bleeding as an outcome in clinical trials to test new products and better ways to prevent bleeding in these patients. Currently there are four categories of bleeding: levels 1 and 2 represent more mild types of bleeding and levels 3 and 4 are more severe types of bleeding (transfusion needed, vision loss or bleeding into the brain which could cause death). Outcomes used in clinical studies usually combine levels 2, 3 and 4 bleeding, but this is problematic because: the majority of bleeds are mild grade 2 bleeding events, which may not be related to more severe bleeding and may not be important to doctors or concerning to patients. We will explore 3 objectives to define bleeding in patients with acute leukemia that is important to patients and physicians: 1) Information from 3 international studies of 2300 patients will be used to determine whether our recent finding that the symptom of blood in urine predicts more severe bleeding is correct; 2) We will conduct interviews with patients who have received treatment for acute leukemia and physicians and nurses who care for patients with acute leukemia to understand what kind of bleeding is important to them 3) Using interview results and previous work that identified medically important bleeding, a smaller group of interview participants will rate and score the most important bleed items. This information will be used to develop a utility bleeding score (UBS) for use as an outcome in clinical studies. We will send a survey to physicians in different countries who treat leukemia to obtain their input about the UBS and to see if they would accept the use of this new bleeding outcome in future research studies. The findings from this project will help medical researchers to use an outcome that will be important and meaningful for patients and health care providers when performing studies in the acute leukemia population.

column36: Brain Energy Supply in Alzheimer's disease
column37: The principal energy fuel of the brain is sugar. From the bloodstream, sugars are taken up by the cells of the blood vessels and are then further provided to cells in the brain. Specialized transport proteins are needed for the sugar uptake, the most important transporter in the brain is glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1). In the most common neurodegenerative disorder, Alzheimer's disease, the amount of GLUT1 transporters is much lower and the affected brains utilize less glucose as compared to healthy controls. Consequently, the restriction of energy to the brain itself may contribute to neurodegeneration. It is therefore imperative to understand how GLUT1 is regulated at the molecular level. My laboratory discovered a novel GLUT1-regulating mechanism inside the cell. We aim to understand this mechanism in detail to learn if this molecular pathway could be used to ameliorate Alzheimer's disease symptoms.

column36: Lentiviral infusion as a universal approach for genetically modified immune effector cell therapies.
column37: Ordinarily, a cancer patient's immune system can recognize cancer cells as being altered, and mount a natural immune response. The immune cells that directly attack the cancer are called T lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, but sometimes they are ineffective - they may fail to recognize tumour cells, fail to activate, or fail to be maintained long enough to have an impact. Recent clinical research has shown that it is possible for these limitations to be overcome by isolating a sample of a patient's T lymphocytes from their blood, genetically modifying and activating the cells in the lab, and then re-administering them to the same patient. The genetic modification step involves introducing into the T cells an extra gene for a new cell surface molecule called a "Chimeric Antigen Receptor" or "CAR" that confers precise and powerful recognition and killing of tumor cells. These therapies are called CAR-T therapies and currently they are very personalized (they require genetically engineering the patient's own cells) and there is considerable laboratory and hospital infrastructure and expertise required to manufacture and deliver treatment. This adds logistical complexity and cost to an already overburdened health care system. We will test (in mice) the feasibility of a radically different approach that would allow CAR-T therapy to be administered in the same manner as a vaccine. Specifically, the approach involves injecting a gene transfer vector (a type of genetically modified, non-infectious virus) into the bloodstream to deliver the CAR gene to directly to T cells, rather than first extracting T cells, processing them outside of the body in the lab, and re-administering them. Additional testing, genetic engineering and virus development is required to evaluate this direct method, and this work is the basis of the current proposal.

column36: Implication of early embryonic epigenetic dysregulation in fetal alcohol spectrum disorders-associated outcomes
column37: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD), a widespread yet under-recognized condition found in all socioeconomic groups in Canada, results from maternal consumption of alcohol during pregnancy. The severity and presentation of FASD symptoms are highly variable and heterogeneous. Across lifespan, patients with FASD may experience a multitude of conditions related to physical, cognitive, emotional, behavioral and/or social functioning. Additionally, patients may develop secondary disabilities including psychiatric and personality disorders, problems with drugs and alcohol, and difficulties with the law, affecting everyday functioning or adaptive behavior and impeding achievement of adult independence. In Canada, 40% of pregnancies are unintended. Consequently, a proportion of women that are unaware of their pregnancy inadvertently expose their early embryos to alcohol. However, we do not know how maternal consumption of alcohol during such an early life stage may lead to FASD. During early embryonic development, cells divide and grow under a specific program, dictated by major changes in chemical modifications (epigenetic marks). We predict that irregularities occurring via alcohol exposure during the organization of this program may disrupt normal gene expression and increase the vulnerability of the central nervous system to neurodevelopmental disorders later in life. The goal of this project is to understand the dysregulation initiated by alcohol on the early embryo and on the evolution of the disturbances during brain development that lead to FASD-associated conditions in children. This project could lead to novel information and tools to promote earlier diagnosis, better treatment, and health outcomes for these children.

column36: Investigating the Adamts19-dependent mechanisms that regulate valve maturation
column37: Heart valves allow blood to flow in only one direction through the heart. They consist of small leaflets, which are pushed open to allow unidirectional blood flow and then close together to seal and prevent backflow. The valves form during early development of the embryo, but continue to mature later during development and after birth. The individual valve leaflets contain cells that are supported by specialized building blocks around them. This building material provides structural support, analogous to the scaffold of a building, and helps to ensure proper valve function. We have recently discovered that a specific form of valve disease, in which valves become malformed, is caused by the mutation of a gene called ADAMTS19. We think that the function of this gene is to rearrange cells and building materials in the valve. When this gene is lost, valves become destabilized and dysfunctional. We have made a mouse line that has the same type of mutation and which develops valve disease as well. In this grant, we will first use this mouse to see how valve cells become disturbed during disease. We will focus almost entirely on the type of cells that make up the inner three layers of the valves and compare how they mature under normal versus disease conditions. We will use a combination of experimental and computational methods to investigate in more detail how Adamts19 regulates valve formation. We will study relevant signaling pathways in control Adamts19 mutant mice, investigate which building materials are altered by Adamts19, and compare our data to large human datasets to link mouse and human valve maturation. Taken together, our study will help to understand how valves are built in space and time, how they mature into fully functional structures, and how this process is disturbed in disease. Our contributions will also feed into an international initiative called the Human Cell Atlas, which aims to provide a map for all cells in the human body.
