column36: Improving surgical safety: Understanding and aligning interventions for safety threats and resilience supports
column37: Surgical errors are a leading contributor to patient harm and death. Safety threats leading to such errors (e.g. surgical instrument left in body) result from the many system factors (e.g. technology and environment design, interruptions) that impact health care providers ability to work safely. We must identify these safety threats so that we can design interventions to address them. In addition to studying the conditions surrounding surgical threats, it is equally important that we identify the factors that support resilience in the system. Resilience supports (e.g. access to back-up equipment) enable workers to respond to unexpected disturbances to resume safe operations with a minimum negative impact. By studying what we do right and wrong, we can find opportunities to improve performance. The main goal of this study is to improve surgical safety in our Canadian hospitals. First, we will identify safety threats and resilience supports across multiple sites by analyzing operating room (OR) video recordings of surgeries in 4 Canadian hospitals. This is made possible thanks to an innovative technology, called OR Black Box, that extracts information from surgical procedures through audio-visual data, physiological data and data from devices and sensors. Experts then analyze this data and make suggestions for improvements. Second, we will design and distribute an online pan-Canadian risk-assessment survey, to be completed by operating room clinicians, to assess their perceptions of safety threats and resilience supports in their operating rooms. This will provide a national data source about the type, range, and amount of safety threats and resilience supports. Third, we will provide a quick reference guide (QRG) containing evidence-based intervention recommendations. Finally, we will engage key health system stakeholders to strategize how best to implement the intervention recommendations to improve surgical safety.

column36: Linking preclinical mechanisms of neurodegeneration to individual risk profiles of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is one of the largest impending healthcare policy crises worldwide. An estimated 564,000 Canadians currently live with dementia. By 2031, this figure will increase by 66%. For many diseases with age as a primary risk factor, such as heart disease and cancer, the medical field has shifted to a strategy of early detection and individualized preventative care. Yet for AD, palliative care remains the sole option for patients. There are two major obstacles for developing individualized preventative care for AD. The first obstacle concerns when the disease is studied in its progression. Most AD research in living humans focuses on patients who are already exhibiting cognitive deficits. However, cognitive deficits only emerge after a long clinically 'silent' period during which extensive neuronal damage occurs in the brain. We are therefore studying AD at stages which are too advanced for prevention. The second obstacle concerns who is studied in AD research. Most studies in living humans do not account for the contribution of individual risk factors. Yet epidemiological research shows that there are three primary risk factors for AD: age, sex and specific genes which regulate the brain's ability to repair itself. These three factors predict disease onset, severity and patient responsiveness to treatment. This project will address both the when and who of preclinical AD. We will examine when vulnerable neurons begin to show signs of damage in cognitively normal older adults. We will examine who is most vulnerable to this early neuronal damage as a function of age, sex and specific genes. We will also bridge our studies in humans with studies using mouse models of AD to more precisely link neuronal vulnerability to individual risk profiles. In sum, our project will fill key gaps in our understanding of the earliest stages of AD and provide novel methodological tools to advance preventative individualized treatment strategies.

column36: Predicting Risk and Identifying Mechanisms of Cardiotoxicity in Breast Cancer Patients - Application of Novel Biomarkers
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in Canadian women and a leading cause of cancer related death. As a result of improved screening and treatment, a majority of those diagnosed will have curable early stage disease. A Subgroup with an aggressive subtype (called HER2 positive breast cancer) require combined treatment with anthracycline and trastuzumab. Unfortunately, ~1 in 4 women receiving this treatment develop early stage heart failure (HF). HF results when your heart muscle is injured and therefore unable to pump enough blood to the rest of the body. The development of HF increases the overall risk of death and can prevent completion of cancer therapy. To better identify patients at an increased risk of HF and initiate preventive strategies we need to understand which patients are at the greatest risk and why chemotherapy causes HF in some patients and not others. Unfortunately, there are currently no reliable early indicator that could be measured in patients with breast cancer to identify those at elevated risk. Recently, extracellular vesicles (EVs), which are small particles that circulate in the blood have been explored as predictors for heart diseases. Importantly, the content of EVs have been shown to change very early in the course of diseases, making them prime candidates as markers of risk for HF. Of interest, by interacting with different cells throughout the body, EVs can directly alter cell function. Our preliminary work suggests that EVs and their content can in fact identify women with breast cancer at high risk of HF even before starting cancer therapy. This has not been shown before. In this study we will validate these preliminary findings in a large cohort of women with breast cancer receiving cancer treatment and will assess how EVs may be involved in the development of HF. This will lead to a novel approach to identify women with breast cancer at risk of HF and to institute personalized cardiovascular care of women with breast cancer.

column36: Characterization of a novel anti-fibrotic peptide for the treatment of scleroderma
column37: Scleroderma or systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is a complex rheumatoid disease that is characterized by defective immune system function, blood vessel damage and scarring (fibrosis) of the skin and internal organs. Fibrosis is a prominent feature of scleroderma and involves excessive production of extracellular matrix proteins, such as collagen and fibronectin, leading to disruption of normal tissue structure and eventually organ failure. Fibrosis has a significant impact on the quality of life of scleroderma patients and much research effort has been put towards developing therapies that can block or reverse fibrosis. Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) is a protein produced by cells of the body that is important for the development and maintenance of healthy tissues. Abnormal stimulation of TGF-beta action is thought to be involved in many fibrotic disorders including scleroderma. We have identified a protein named CD109 that binds to TGF-beta and neutralizes its biological activity in human skin cells. We have generated a shorter version of the CD109 protein (a CD109-based peptide) and found that this shorter version or peptide can reduce fibrosis in skin and lung cells. Our research goal is to characterize the above peptide molecule to determine its potential to reduce experimental fibrosis in human skin and lung tissue donated by scleroderma patients and in animal models of scleroderma, and to understand how (mechanism by which) this molecule reduces fibrosis. The proposed research will allow us to assess the potential this molecule to decrease or block fibrosis in scleroderma patients. The results from the proposed work may also have application to reduce fibrosis in other organs such as the kidney and liver.

column36: Life course body fatness and physical activity, and ovarian cancer etiology
column37: Ovarian cancer is the most deadly of the cancers that occur only in women. It has proven difficult to diagnose disease early when treatment may be more effective, as symptoms are not easy to recognize and screening techniques are not efficient at a general population level. Thus, identifying factors that may help prevent ovarian cancer from occurring in the first place is the most promising approach. Hormones are involved in ovarian cancer. Past studies of lifestyle factors that affect hormone levels, including body fatness and physical activity, are not clear. In these past studies, body fatness and physical activity were measured among the women when they participated in the study, which was generally in late adulthood. Some research suggests that body fatness in early life may be more strongly associated with ovarian cancer risk, and thus suggests that exposures during different times in life may be more important. In this research, we will use data from an epidemiological study in Montreal to (1) estimate patterns of body fatness and physical activity from early to late adulthood, (2) examine how the timing of high body fatness and physical activity levels over the adult lifetime may differently affect the development of ovarian cancer, and (3) examine to what extent physical activity is associated with risk because of its relation to body fatness. Ovarian cancer is a cancer of critical importance to women's health, given its high fatality. This project will help in understanding if body fatness and physical activity at certain moments in a person's life is particularly important in ovarian cancer. The results will also generate knowledge important for defining important time points for cancer prevention efforts. column36: The Long-Term Effects of War on Biological Aging: The Case of Vietnam
column37: War punctuates the lives of millions throughout the world. Most live in lower- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where health infrastructure is underdeveloped and living conditions are often substandard. The numbers that endured conflict in these parts of the world are increasing. Despite this, systematic knowledge about how traumatic war experiences affect health and aging in LMICs is inadequate. Given the numbers, this knowledge is essential for advancing global population health. Our study analyzes data from a sample of about 2,500 in late-middle and early-old age differentially exposed to conflict during wars in Vietnam (1955-1975). Many were directly engaged in battle; others had family members engaged; and many lived in or near communities targeted by bombing. Linking blood samples to comprehensive survey responses, a global multidisciplinary team, that bridges social, medical and biological sciences, will analyze how exposure to war associates with long-term health by connecting wartime exposure with rates of biological aging. Outcomes are based on integrative indicators of aging including allostatic load, dysregulation, metabolic syndrome and inflammaging. We also integrate contemporary measures of epigenetic aging using methylation. Further, qualitative data collection is used to develop a deeper understanding of the mechanisms linking exposure to health. We test hypotheses about how war exposure and biological aging are connected and the degree to which current stressors and social support modify these trajectories. Associations are compared across men and women considering effects of biological sex and socially constructed gender. The Vietnamese people were exposed to one of history's most brutal wars. They live in a country challenged by population aging and under- diagnosed, noncommunicable chronic diseases. These factors present a time- sensitive and unique opportunity to learn much about how war impacts on the long-term health of populations.

column36: Challenging the dogmas of monocistronic genes and pseudogenes using proteogenomics and systems biology approaches to better define the human proteome in health and diseases
column37: Proteins are the workers of every cell and thus affect all aspects of human health and disease. Hence, deciphering all the proteins produced by an organism is a crucial challenge for biologists. Our genes contain instructions to make proteins, but they must first be copied into molecules called genetic messengers (or RNAs). The region of a genetic messenger that codes for a protein is called an open reading frame (or abbreviated ORF). For many years, scientists have assumed that every human genetic messenger carries only one functional ORF -usually the longest possible ORF. Many also presumed that RNAs copied from genes labeled as "non-coding" or "pseudogenes" did not contain any functional ORFs. Our laboratory has demonstrated that genetic messengers carry several ORFs and thus allow the production of several completely different proteins. The goal of this research project is to create a catalog of the true coding potential of genes and their genetic messengers. This project will not only generate new knowledge on molecular mechanisms, but also new tools. These will be necessary to better understand fundamental molecular and genetic errors linked to diseases, and to develop adequate molecular interventions to correct them.

column36: Towards a future optimising quality of life in bipolar disorder: A focus on digital health
column37: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic, severe mood disorder. Worldwide, it affects 2.4% of people, and has been ranked as the fifth a leading cause of disease burden among mental disorders. BD is linked to significant negative impacts on relationships, physical health, cognition, educational achievement and workforce participation. It is therefore increasingly recognised that recovery in mood disorders involves not only reducing symptoms, but also improvements in a person's quality of life (QoL). While it had been previously assumed that these two goals would be synonymous, there is growing evidence to suggest that the trajectories of mood and QoL improvements are not always parallel. Interventions known to improve mood may not improve QoL to the same degree, and changes to QoL may be delayed relative to changes to mood symptoms. Not only this, but QoL may be have unique mechanisms for improvement that are not fully addressed in treatments targeting mood symptoms, and people with BD report receiving limited support for their QoL goals in the context of usual healthcare. This suggests a significant unmet needs for QoL-focused treatments in BD. The overarching aim of this postdoctoral research program will be to address critical gaps in the science of QoL in people with BD. Firstly, novel machine learning methods will be used to develop a sophisticated understanding of factors which predict QoL in BD, in order to improve the design and ability to individualise future interventions. Secondly, the potential of a mobile phone app intervention for QoL in BD will be explored. A mixed-methods approach will explore the feasibility, engagement, and impacts of this app. Together, this program of research will create a foundation for next-generation interventions optimising health and wellbeing in one of the most serious mood disorders affecting Canadians.

column36: Blood-brain-barrier dynamics in healthy aging and Alzheimer's disease
column37: During the normal aging process, about 40% of people >65 years old experience memory loss unattributable to disease, classified as aging-related memory-loss. However, Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other dementias pathologically affect our brains. Over 500K Canadians are currently living with AD or other dementias, and this number is projected to double to 1M in 2031. In 2019, the Canadian government released the country's first dementia strategy with 3 objectives: (1) prevent dementia, (2) advance therapies and find a cure, and (3) improve the quality of life of people living with dementia and their caregivers. In order to follow through on these objectives, more research needs to be done in order to understand the underlying cause of AD in the aging population. We hypothesize that the breakdown of the blood-brain-barrier (BBB) plays a key role in the progression of AD. This proposal, through the use of high-dimensional neuroimaging, aims to find key differences between aging-AD-BBB dynamics. Neuroimaging is critical to understand the cellular and structural landscape of the brain. We aim to understand the spatial landscape of the BBB to understand the interplay between physiology, metabolism, pathology, and immunology in aging and AD, which can: (1) identify risk factors for AD, (2) uncover therapeutic targets to manage the disease, and (3) aid in understanding of the disease progression mechanisms - concordant with Canada's dementia strategy. We will use multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBIscope) to characterize and spatially localize BBB features contributing to disease in donor brains. Unlike current technologies, MIBIscope will allow us to look at >40 proteins simultaneously, which have a role in AD, and examine how they interact with one another. This approach will allow us to understand the role the BBB dynamics play in healthy aging and AD pathology, and potentially identify therapeutic targets for the development of novel drugs to manage AD.

column36: Microenvironmental determinants of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) progression to invasive breast cancer
column37: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a precursor to breast cancer, however, only ~50% of women with DCIS develop breast cancer. With the introduction of early screening for breast cancer, more and more women are being diagnosed with DCIS and aggressively treated with surgery regardless if their condition would have developed into breast cancer or not. In other words, ~50% of women may be receiving treatment they do not need, reducing their quality of life. There is a need to better understand how DCIS develops into breast cancer and identify characteristics, also known as biomarkers, that indicate if treatment is needed. Previous efforts to identify biomarkers have focused on tumour cells. However, a tumour is not only made up of tumour cells but instead also includes normal cells and immune cells, among others. The accumulation of cells can restrict access to important nutrients, like oxygen. My research focuses on understanding how the environment of a tumour - the nearby immune cells and the ability of the tumour to access oxygen - can dictate if DCIS will progress to breast cancer. I will use the knowledge acquired in this study to build biomarkers that can predict which women with DCIS should be treated and which would be better off being actively monitored.

column36: Identifying spatial patterns and neighborhood-level risks of opioid-related overdoses to guide implementation of overdose prevention interventions
column37: North America is in the midst of a drug overdose epidemic, and the number of drug overdose deaths (ODs) has surpassed motor vehicle incidents and homicide deaths combined. This study will be conducted in collaboration with Rhode Island's Department of Health, the Governor's overdose task force, and representatives from treatment programs and community-based agencies. column36: Cyp46A1 as a novel therapeutic target in prion diseases
column37: Prion diseases are a group of infectious and incurable neurodegenerative disorders that affect humans and animals. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is the most common human prion disease. Animal prion diseases include scrapie in sheep/goat and mad cow disease which has been transmitted to humans from cattle. There is no treatment available for prion diseases, therefore, in this study we will apply a novel therapeutic strategy to treat prion diseases. Brain locally synthesizes cholesterol which is a major component of brain cells; however, its excess amount is harmful as it cannot exit the brain. In prion diseases, we know that cholesterol is required for the formation of prions, and that the build-up of prions in the brain further increases cholesterol levels in the brain, subsequently facilitating prion formation. Therefore, regulating brain cholesterol levels during prion infection could prevent prion disease. The primary pathway for brain cholesterol elimination is achieved by the brain-specific enzyme, cholesterol 24-hydroxylase (CYP46A1). Cyp46A1 converts cholesterol into 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol, a molecule that exits the brain. It is of utmost importance to determine the role of Cyp461 in prion diseases. We have collected preliminary data which demonstrate for the first time that the brains of prion infected mice and CJD patients have reduced Cyp46A1 levels. This project will be the first to determine the therapeutic efficacy of the Cyp46A1 activator, Efavirenz (EFV) in prion diseases. EFV is an FDA approved drug which reaches the brain and is currently used for the treatment of HIV patients. Our goal is to test if this drug could be repurposed for treatment of prion diseases. Mice overexpressing human prion will be infected with CJD patients brain homogenates, which will be treated with EFV. Thus, Cyp46A1 is a novel therapeutic target, and its activation through repurposed medications such as EFV is a valuable approach for the treatment of prion diseases.

column36: Solve-Mosaicism: Using deep-DNA and single-cell sequencing to investigate the contribution of mosaicism to unsolved rare genetic disease
column37: Rare genetic diseases affect approximately 1 in 40 people, therefore representing a significant societal burden. The genetic cause of thousands of rare diseases remains unsolved. Mosaicism occurs when a cell acquires a genetic mutation at some stage during the development of the embryo, which is then passed on to the offspring of that cell. The result is an individual with two populations of cells with different genetic makeups; some cells will harbour the mutation and others will not. Because the mutation is not present in all cells, it can be difficult to detect using standard diagnostic test. In this project, we will use advanced technological approaches to investigate whether some unsolved rare diseases are caused by mosaic mutations. Deep-DNA sequencing and single-cell sequencing are specialised techniques capable of detecting mosaic mutations. For a group of patients with suspected mosaic disease, I will leverage these techniques to identify the genetic cause and provide an accurate diagnosis. This study will have important implications for affected families, as receiving a genetic diagnosis is imperative for determining the best treatment strategy and supports the psychological and financial well-being of families. Successful outcome of this research will identify new approaches for detecting mosaicism that can be translated into everyday clinical testing of rare disease patients, which will help all affected families receive a genetic diagnosis. In the longer term, understanding the underlying defect of these diseases may lead to the development of targeted therapies.

column36: Characterization of neuroimmune interactions in the tumour microenvironment
column37: Most of the time, the immune cells in your body do a great job of killing cancer cells. Unfortunately, a tumour has the ability to suppress the immune system, sometimes turning anti-tumour immune cells into pro-tumour immune cells. In fact, over 50% of a tumour's mass can be made up of immune cells alone! This is why some of the best cancer therapies to date work by turning the immune system back on. Unfortunately, for breast cancer patients, and especially those with the particularly aggressive "triple-negative" form of breast cancer, current immune targeting therapies are not very effective. Interestingly, breast cancer prognosis is related to the density of neurons in tissues, and there is evidence that by removing neurons, cancer growth is reduced. In non-cancer settings, such as infection, it has been shown that neurons can control the immune system. In this project, we propose to test the hypothesis that neurons in breast cancer tumours can suppress the immune system. This will lead to the development of novel therapies that activate the immune system by targeting neurons. To study this, we will model breast cancer growth in mice and then block the sensory neurons from firing. Then, we will look at changes in immune cells from the tumour using an advanced technique called time-of-flight mass cytometry, which allows us to measure over 20 different cell types at once. Next, intravital microscopy will be carried out on tumour sites, before and after blocking neurons, to look at immune cell behaviour. Finally, we will design an in vitro culture system where neurons and cancer mini-organs will be grown together in a dish. This will allow us to use single cell RNA sequencing to see if the tumours are secreting something that changes the expression of genes by neurons. All of this data together will provide new information on therapeutic avenues for breast cancer.

column37: Cancers of the lower digestive tract are called Colorectal Cancers (CRC). They are the 2nd most common form of non-skin cancers and will kill 5 times more Canadians this year compared to motor vehicle collisions. Alarmingly, today's young adults are 2-4 times more vulnerable to CRC compared to their parents which may be the first indication that CRC may become an even larger public health burden in the coming years. The human genome was "completed" in 2001, yet several difficult to study areas of our DNA were excluded from this reference genome and remain under-explored. In a pioneering study on rRNA, Dr. Babaian discovered that almost half of CRC patients contain a cancer-specific "onco-ribosome" with a variant rRNA. Normally, ribosomes create proteins in a tightly controlled and regulated manner. These onco-ribosomes are associated with the most rapidly growing tumors, differing from their normal counterparts by a modification of the rRNA. Normally, this RNA modification is found in the ribosomes of all animals and plants, except for cancer tissues, yet its role in protein synthesis is unknown. The objective of this proposal is to use cancer cells genetically modified to produce only onco-ribosomes to understand how these cancer ribosomes translate proteins differently. Significantly, onco-ribosomes differ enough from the healthy ribosome that they could be targeted with precision drugs. Fortunately, there already are dozens of common and approved antibiotics which target the ribosome for treating bacterial or parasitic infections. This proposal will also evaluate if it's feasible to re-purpose antibiotic-like compounds for the treatment of colorectal cancers. This would establish an entirely new class of chemotherapies based on a medicine we have used safely for over 60 years.

column37: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive and lethal type of brain cancer accounting for 50% of all brain tumors. Despite extensive research aiming to improve GBM treatment, treatment efficacy is still extremely poor and the current 5-year survival rate is only 5.5%. A fast and effective workflow for tumor delineation based on molecular and quantitative imaging will be developed and assessed on a cohort of patients with Glioblastoma. If successful, this technique can not only change the current clinical practice in RT treatment planning, but also enable many new applications in the clinical management of glioblastoma, including diagnostics, grading, and assessment of response to therapy.

column36: Dissecting mechanisms of mammalian gene regulation by the essential histone acetyltransferases p300 and CBP
column37: Every cell in a human body has the same DNA sequence. However, different segments of DNA, called genes, are read out in each distinct cell type to produce the specific set of proteins needed for cellular function. As such, activating the wrong gene at the wrong time can lead to developmental defects and disease, and many human diseases stem from mutations in regulators of gene activity. Two such regulators are p300 and CBP, which have largely redundant functions and for simplicity will be referred to as p300. p300 stimulates gene activity by chemically modifying proteins in an enzymatic reaction called acetylation. Acetylation alters protein charge, affecting binding partners and enzymatic activities of numerous factors, with pervasive effects on gene activity. Accordingly, p300 frequently works together with other regulatory factors and this cooperation is crucial for gene activation. Aberrant levels or activity of p300 and collaborating factors are implicated in numerous human diseases, including Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome, diabetes, and multiple types of cancer. However, accurately targeting p300 and its co-regulators in disease is challenging because we don't fully understand how these factors work, or work together, to control gene expression. To address this important question, I have used powerful small molecule inhibitors and genomic methods to define genes at which p300 directly stimulates activity at particular steps in the transcription process. Further, this work has revealed distinct sets of genes where p300 collaborates with other factors, providing opportunities to understand co-regulation. Here, I propose to leverage this information to test specific models for p300 activity in gene control. These experiments are anticipated to clarify the basis for gene dysregulation in cells with mutations or perturbations in p300 and suggest new therapeutic avenues to target this factor in disease.

column36: Investigating the Effect of the Ageing Astrocyte Secretome on Regeneration in the Central Nervous System
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world. In MS, the accumulation of nerve damage results in progressive disability. This progression is thought to be due in part to the effect of age on the repair of damaged nerves. As an individual ages, the ability to repair damaged nerves becomes slower. There is a lack of available treatments designed to increase the speed of repair. This project is seeking to understand why repair slows down with ageing and to potentially discover new treatments that can speed up repair. This study may provide a new treatment for patients with multiple sclerosis that will help slow down or potentially reverse the buildup of disability. This will be accomplished by studying a cell type involved in nerve repair that has not been thoroughly studied before. There is strong reason to think that this cell type, which is called an astrocyte, slows down the repair process during ageing. In this study, some of the molecules produced by ageing astrocytes will be investigated. These molecules will then be targeted to increase nerve repair. This strategy will provide new knowledge as to why repair slows down with ageing and may identify a new treatment for the thousands of Canadians suffering from the progressive form of MS.

column36: Upregulation of immune response to reduce tumor progression and metastasis of melanoma using photodynamic therapy
column37: Melanoma is an aggressive and highly lethal form of skin cancer. The main treatment is surgery, possibly in combination with radiation, chemotherapy and, more recently, immunotherapy. However, there is a significant incidence of local recurrence and metastatic spread. Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) is an approved treatment modality for a range of malignancies that relies on light activation of non-toxic molecules (photosensitizers) to induce tumor cell death. The applicant has recently shown in a mouse model that primary melanoma can be eradicated using a novel form of PDT, using clinically-approved photosensitizers combined with applying a non-toxic "optical clearing agent" to the tumor to overcome the high light absorption by melanin that has previously limited the treatment efficacy. It has also been shown in many other tumors that PDT can upregulate the immune system and so reduce tumor progression and metastatic spread that are responsible for reduced survival and quality of life. Conversely, there is increasing evidence that surgery-induced stress has the opposite effect. The concept to be tested here for the first time is that PDT can be used, either as an alternative to surgery (e.g. in difficult sites such as eyelids, nose, ears) or together with surgery, to counteract this negative immune response, reducing tumor progression and metastasis. This will be evaluated in the mouse melanoma model. Tumor growth and metastasis will l be monitored by multiple imaging techniques. Blood analysis will be carried out before and at times after treatment to directly measure the immune response. Tumor response to PDT, surgery, and surgery plus PDT will be measured. These studies will provide the first proof-of-principle of the use of PDT to modulate the immunological system in melanoma. If successful, it should be possible to translate this approach into a minimally-invasive, safe and effective new treatment option for patients with this highly aggressive cancer.

column36: The Relationship Between Overt Visual Attention and Constructive Episodic Simulation in Older Adults
column37: One of the most frequently reported and debilitating signs of cognitive aging is difficulty recalling details from one's past (episodic memory). Consequentially, older adults not only have trouble reconstructing past events, but also simulating future events (episodic simulation) by drawing on information from past experiences. Despite the significant health, social, and economic outcomes of cognitive aging, relatively little is known about the cognitive and neural processes underlying age-related changes in episodic memory and simulation, and particularly, how they interact with other cognitive processes. Recent work indicates that aging is accompanied by significant declines in visual attention and perception. In short, older adults see the world differently than younger adults. Given that where we look determines what we can encode into memory and subsequently remember, understanding how older adults orient visual attention is critical for understanding age-related changes in memory. Accordingly, the proposed research program will use converging eye movement monitoring and neuroimaging techniques to investigate the relationship between episodic memory and simulation and overt visual attention, indexed via eye movements, in older adults. Specifically, the proposed studies will aim to: (i) characterize the role of overt attentional shifts in episodic memory and simulation in older adults, (ii) investigate age-related changes in the brain areas supporting these processes, and (iii) identify potential strategies for improving episodic memory and simulation by manipulating overt visual attention (i.e., where older adults look). Together, the proposed studies will significantly improve our understanding of age-related memory declines by probing the cognitive and neural links between mnemonic and attentional processes, and will advance new methods for investigating, and potentially mitigating such declines by directly manipulating visual attention.

column36: Leveraging genomic, metabolomic, and proteomic data to identify clinically-relevant subtypes and new pathways driving risk of coronary artery disease
column37: Heart disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada and affects millions of individuals each year. Despite efforts to reduce disease risk with healthy lifestyles and medications, these strategies are not always successful. The variation in effectiveness may be linked to differences in an individual's genetic make-up (i.e. DNA), resulting in different biological mechanisms that drive heart disease. Here, I propose to uncover new disease-driving mechanisms and develop methods to stratify individuals by their main biological driver for heart disease. To do so, we can leverage 'genetic risk scores'-a method to aggregate information from many sites of DNA variation into a single measure of disease risk-along with information obtained by studying circulating blood molecules or 'biomarkers' (ex. fats and proteins) to reveal new insights. For example, abnormal biomarker measurements in individuals with a high genetic risk score, indicating a high inherited risk for heart disease, can highlight dysfunctional biological pathways. Therefore, by aggregating genetic and biomarker information, we can develop new genetic risk scores specific to these pathways, and use them to identify individuals likely to have heart disease because of a particular biological mechanism. Canadians will greatly benefit from this work because: 1) the new genetic risk scores to stratify individuals by biological driver for heart disease will empower clinicians to prescribe personalized risk-reduction strategies; and 2) the discovery of new dysfunctional disease-causing mechanisms provide researchers an opportunity to develop new drugs to target those pathways and continue to reduce risk of heart disease.

column36: Investigating the role of trained immunity on protection against acute cardiac injury.
column37: Heart failure (HF) arises after an injury to the heart causes it to pump less effectively. There are about 23 million HF cases worldwide, ~660,000 of which are in Canada, with the number steadily increasing. Standard HF therapies enhance heart pumping and improve clinical outcomes. Although patients initially stabilize on these therapies, recent studies show that HF recurs after this initial phase. Why some become stable (termed "remission") and why some "relapse" and have recurrent HF despite having optimal therapy is unknown, but represents a significant unmet clinical need. To begin to address this problem, a clinically relevant mouse model of HF recovery was developed. Importantly, HF redevelops in these mice when stressed a second time. A striking observation from this model is that the level of inflammation in HF-recovered hearts is the same as in failing hearts, raising the possibility that persistent inflammation may contribute to relapsing HF. The proposed work examines the role of immune cells called macrophages in HF recovery, as they are primary mediators of tissue repair and inflammation in the heart. The healthy heart typically harbors two macrophage types: one population that everyone is born with (embryonic) and is responsible for tissue repair, and one derived when blood cells from the bone marrow enter the heart after tissue injury, which is inherently more inflammatory. In this work, the applicant will first examine how these macrophage populations are affected in the course of HF recovery using the HF recovery mouse model. Using genetic methods, the applicant will then selectively alter the abundance of each macrophage population when the hearts are stressed a second time. These studies will allow us to determine the contributions of each macrophage group to the stability of HF recovery, and relapse. Results from this work may lead to new therapies that help lengthen the time HF patients remain in remission, free from costly hospital admissions.

column36: Novel approaches to understand and enhance gray matter remyelination during aging
column37: Myelin is an insulating sheath that is important for sending strong and fast impulses from one place to another in the brain and spinal cord. The brain and spinal cord can be segmented into white matter, which is heavily myelinated, and gray matter, which has less myelin. Loss of myelin (demyelination) in the white and gray matter of the brain and spinal cord is a hallmark of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and understanding the mechanisms of myelin repair (remyelination) is a major focus of MS research. Loss of myelin within the gray matter is associated with motor and cognitive symptoms making researching gray matter demyelination and remyelination a high priority. I strive to understand the dynamics of gray matter remyelination, how this remyelination is affected by aging, and hypothesize that a drug shown to speed up remyelination in white matter might also be effective in gray matter. Here, I will use a genetic approach that allows me to visualize directly the new generation of myelin-forming cells (oligodendrocytes) and their new myelin sheaths in both the demyelinated lesions of mice and in a culture dish. These tools will allow me to look at how gray matter's myelin properties change with remyelination in the context of aging. Better understanding of the mechanisms that underlie remyelination in the gray matter will help me to identify potential new drug targets that could improve motor and cognitive symptoms in people living with MS.

column36: The circadian clock and Alzheimer's disease pathology
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common dementia, in which afflicted patients progressively lose their cognitive and functional abilities, starting with memory. AD is incurable and a colossal burden to patients and caregivers' lives, and to society overall, with billions spent annually in Canada. Although we know that AD is caused by the accumulation of specific proteins in the brain (amyloid-beta and phosphorylated tau), we still do not completely understand how these accumulate and progress. Studying the circadian clock is a promising research avenue to better understand how AD develops: The circadian clock is composed of neuronal networks, genes and proteins in all cells of the body, which together regulates physiological functions (sleep-wake cycle, energy expenditure, inflammation) in phase with the 24 h light-dark cycle. Preliminary findings show that AD patients have disturbed circadian function, and that changes to the circadian clock may be associated with higher AD risk. Therefore, because the circadian clock regulates so many physiological functions, understanding the role of the circadian clock in the occurrence of AD might prove to be a key therapeutic target to prevent or even slow down the disease. In this project, we will use four different cohorts to investigate AD at all stages (healthy, people at risk, AD patients) to establish a causal model between the circadian clock (genes, proteins levels in brain tissue, circadian sleep markers) and AD (genes, AD diagnosis, cognition, amyloid and tau pathology, inflammation). Understanding the role of the circadian clock in the development of AD is imperative since circadian dysfunctions are treatable. Findings from this project will further our understanding of how people develop AD, and has the potential to result in possible circadian therapeutic strategies to prevent or delay AD, which remains a main cause of death and suffering in the elderly of Canada.

column36: Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging biomarkers of disease progression in multiple sclerosis
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world. More than half of the MS population will develop a progressive form of the disease (gradual accumulation of disability independent of MS attacks). At this time, however, there is only limited treatment available for progressive MS in Canada. This lack of effective treatment is largely due to an inadequate understanding of underlying biological mechanisms of the disease that is responsible for MS progression. Furthermore, clinical measures of progression change slowly and require a large number of study participants, who are monitored over a long period to detect treatment effects. Effective markers of progression thus represent an urgent and unmet need in the development of progressive MS treatment. We aim to use non-invasive, quantitative imaging techniques to study brain and spinal cord pathology (biology resulting in disease) and its relationship to global disability (e.g. ambulation, dexterity, visual acuity and cognition) annually over 4 years. CanProCo is led by my supervisor, Dr. Jiwon Oh. We expect to establish biologically relevant imaging markers for MS progression that can 1) be used as outcome measures in shorter and less costly drug therapy trials in the future, which will accelerate the development of effective therapies, 2) monitor disease activity or tissue repair over time, and 3) evaluate the effectiveness of treatment or predict therapeutic outcomes to enable optimal clinical management. Our findings would be important for scientists, doctors, policymakers, people with MS and their caregivers by providing informational evidence to improve health policies and quality of life for people affected by MS.

column36: Exploration de la microarchitecture du sommeil pour expliquer la physiopathologie et l'heterogeneite des phenotypes dans l'hypersomnie idiopathique
column37: L'hypersomnie idiopathique (HI) est un trouble du sommeil chronique se caracterisant pas une somnolence excessive pendant le jour. Le fonctionnement de cette maladie est encore peu connu et il existe une grande variabilite de symptomes entre les patients. En effet, les cliniciens et les travaux de recherche rapportent des manifestations tres heterogenes, possiblement expliquees par la presence de sous-types dans l'HI. De plus, le diagnostic des patients avec l'HI represente un defi de taille puisque certains individus vont rapporter des symptomes importants sans rencontrer les criteres diagnostiques aux tests standardises. Afin de mieux comprendre les mecanismes biologiques derriere l'HI, de nouveaux marqueurs objectifs doivent etre trouves. La microarchitecture du sommeil, soit l'ensemble des evenements electriques du cerveau uniques au sommeil de l'etre humain, aurait le potentiel d'expliquer en partie les mecanismes de la maladie et les dissimilitudes entre les differents cas d'HI. Grace a des analyses avancees du signal EEG, il est possible de mesurer l'efficacite de la regulation du sommeil, la synchronisation neuronale pendant le sommeil et la qualite du sommeil. Le premier objectif de ce projet est de caracteriser la microarchitecture du sommeil des patients avec l'HI afin de trouver de potentiels biomarqueurs objectifs. Le second objectif est de determiner la presence de sous-types dans l'HI en se basant sur la microarchitecture du sommeil. Pour atteindre ces objectifs, 284 patients avec l'HI, dont la moitie ne rencontrent pas les criteres objectifs aux tests d'hypersomnie ont ete recrutes dans les dernieres annees ainsi que 94 sujets controles sains. Les participants ont rempli un journal de sommeil de 2 semaines avant de faire l'enregistrement d'une nuit de polysomnographie. column36: Investigating the role of senescence during age- and disuse-related bone loss.
column37: Over 1.5 million of Canadians are affected by osteoporosis, a disease that is caused by weak bones and leads to increased risk of fracture. As the Canadian population ages, the burden of osteoporotic fractures is predicted to increase. One of the hallmarks of age-related bone loss is cellular senescence; a process characterized by cells that can no longer divide. In bone, there is normally a balance between building bone (i.e. bone formation) and destroying bone (i.e. bone resorption). When bone cells senesce, the mechanisms that destroy bone overwhelm the mechanisms that build bone and there is a decrease in bone strength. Like age-related bone loss, there is a decrease in bone strength when bones are not being used, this is called disuse-related bone loss. Whenever we walk or stand, our bones experience pressure (a load) and this helps them to stay strong. In patients who are bedridden or have limited mobility, however, these forces are no longer present and bone strength decreases. When the bone is no longer experiencing these forces, it is said to be unloaded. Age-related bone loss and disuse-related bone loss share many similarities, and the combination of the two can lead to even worse outcomes for elderly patients. Hence, finding ways to prevent either or both types of bone loss is imperative. Senolytic drugs, such as dasatinib and quercetin, are compounds that will selectively kill senescent cells. When administered to aged mice, they are found to be protective of bone strength. To date, the role of senescence on the skeletal system in response to unloading has not been examined. Since, age- and disuse-related bone loss share many similarities, it is possible that senolytics may exert a similar protective effect on disuse-induced bone loss in young and aged mice. The relationship between senescence, disuse and age-related bone loss has the potential to elucidate mechanisms of osteoporosis and identify novel therapeutic targets.

column36: EVEP: Investigating the role of extracellular vesicles in endometriosis-associated pain
column37: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory condition, affecting an estimated 190 million women globally. It is characterised by the presence of endometrial- (uterine lining) like tissue outside of the uterus, mainly within the pelvis. While endometriosis can cause infertility and other comorbidities, endometriosis-associated pain (EAP) is the predominant symptom affecting these women. One of the enigmas of endometriosis is how the disease causes pain and why this differs between women. This is further complicated by the fact that disease severity does not correlate with pain symptoms. Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is often the central problem for women with endometriosis, as many seek a diagnosis to more effectively manage their pain. However, recent data which I have generated has shown that women with widespread pain (WP) compared to those with CPP have distinct comorbidities, psychological profiles, and reproductive outcomes. Moreover, women with endometriosis are more likely to have an autoimmune inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Therefore, there is an urgent need to better understand the physiological underpinnings of the distinction between those with CPP and WP. This project will investigate the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), small nanoparticles found in many bodily fluids, from blood samples to better understand EAP. I will investigate medium-large (m/l) EVs (> 200nm) derived from cells known to be implicated and well characterised in other chronic inflammatory, pain associated diseases, such as RA. This pilot study aims to characterise m/lEVs in endometriosis patients with different pain phenotypes and will determine if they can serve as indicators of EAP, in a way that questionnaires alone cannot. This highly novel project will provide the first data on m/lEVs and EAP, and may provide a biologically relevant assessment of pain that can one day inform personalized treatment for women with EAP.

column36: Understanding adolescent mental health in American Samoa: The role of family-related intergenerational factors.
column37: Suicide rates are alarming among adolescents in remote Indigenous populations worldwide. Indigenous health leaders call to incorporate Indigenous traditional healing models into existing mental health systems. However, no randomized controlled trials have evaluated this approach in remote contexts for adolescent mental health. My doctoral thesis will explore how mental health trials in remote Indigenous communities can incorporate decolonizing frameworks while maintaining epidemiological rigour. My dissertation will be composed of three incremental aims: (1) a systematic scoping review to identify and synthesize barriers and facilitators to the conduct of trials in remote Indigenous contexts; (2) a qualitative study in American Samoa to identify best practices for the development and conduct of a mental health trial for adolescents in this context; and (3) an Indigenous-partnered pilot trial in American Samoa evaluating a community-developed intervention to improve adolescent mental wellness. These projects will be feasible given that Yale University has a history of community partnership, trial implementation, and established infrastructure in American Samoa (a high-risk setting, with parallels to Indigenous communities in Canada). The results of this dissertation will produce the first Indigenous-led adolescent mental health trial in a remote Indigenous community. Our results will not only inform Indigenous-partnered health system change in American Samoa, but will also produce a model that can inform design and adaptation of equitable mental health trials in other settings. This dissertation will: (1) provide Indigenous communities with scientific methods to empower rigorous evaluation of future innovations to improve the health of their communities; and (2) produce knowledge to advocate for the incorporation of Indigenous ways of healing into existing mental health systems, ultimately improving the resiliency of Indigenous youth worldwide.

The ultimate goal is to make genetic counselling and testing more accessible and equitable to all patients and families who may need it.

column36: A mixed methods exploration of young peoples' experiences of climate anxiety and its impacts in British Columbia, Canada
column37: Extreme weather events, negative impacts on agricultural production and the liveability of human settlements, as well as potential for mass migration and conflict have all been linked to climate change. This is increasingly being linked to mental health challenges such as PTSD, suicidality, depression, and substance use. At the same time, new concepts such as climate anxiety and eco-anxiety have emerged. Concerns about the mental health consequences of climate change have focused on youth, with the issue gaining attention through the activism of young people such as Greta Thunberg and Isra Hirsi. However, there is debate as to whether climate anxiety is always unhealthy or if it can instead be a healthy response to the current crisis. Furthermore, there is limited research on the role that adults and mental health professionals should play in helping young people with climate anxiety. This study will explore the impacts of climate anxiety among youth on British Columbia (BC), Canada, making use of both interviews and surveys. Twenty youth aged 13-17 will be recruited to participate in interviews. These interviews will explore young people's experiences of climate anxiety, ask how they cope, and elicit their expertise on how adults and mental health professionals can support them. Information from the interviews will then be used to create survey questions specifically about youth climate anxiety, which will be used in surveys given to 200 youth. The surveys will also have questions about overall anxiety, wellbeing, and young peoples' actions and knowledge about climate change. This will make it possible to explore the connection between climate anxiety and overall mental health, as well as whether engaging in environmental activities can be helpful, as some have suggested. This research will add needed evidence on the impacts of climate change on youth mental health in Canada as well as provide information on how to best support young people.

column36: Profiling T cell cross-reactivity in elite HIV controllers
column37: 'Elite controllers' are individuals infected with HIV who develop natural immunity that delays or prevents disease altogether. Elite controller immune responses seem to be resistant to frequent mutations of the virus. Prior studies suggest a reason: key immune cells known as T cells may recognize multiple parts of the HIV virus rather than one. Existing technology is unable to find these 'cross-reactive' T cells and match them to parts of the HIV virus. My project proposes a new method to determine the targets and cross-reactivity of T cells on a significantly larger scale than previously possible. Using this tool, I will examine the T cells of HIV elite controllers and patients who require treatment. If successful, this project will help to resolve a long-standing debate: do T cells in elite controllers target parts of the HIV virus in meaningfully different ways? If so, this information could be applied to vaccines and therapeutics to generate 'elite controller'-type immune responses in other HIV-infected individuals.

column36: B. fragilis genetic variants differentially modulate the immune response in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, damages the digestive tract and causes painful symptoms. Although the number of cases in the world are increasing, we still do not understand the exact cause of the disease, nor do we have a cure. Aside from our genetics and environment, scientists have identified bacteria that normally live in the gut as important players that can aggravate or ameliorate disease. We have limited understanding of how these bacteria interact with our cells. Of note are a particular species of bacteria that appear to vary between healthy individuals and inflammatory bowel disease patients in their contribution to disease pathology. In healthy individuals, these bacteria appear to have the ability to direct our cells to maintain a healthy gut environment; in diseased patients, bacteria seem to have limited ability to do so. We thus aim to understand what the differences between these bacterial "strains" are, and how they link to health and disease. Pinpointing the basis for these strain differences gives us a better understanding of our symbiotic relationship with bacteria in the gut. We can leverage our results for advancing future scientific studies, and importantly, for improving therapies in development and proposing therapeutic interventions to come.

column36: Understanding the role of 17beta-estradiol signaling in induced regulatory T cell induction, activity, and stability
column37: Immune responses vary based on biological sex and tend to be more robust in females compared to males. In fact, males are generally more at risk of infectious diseases, while many autoimmune conditions have a higher prevalence in females. While many factors contribute to these differences, the sex hormone estrogen is a major driver of biological sex-based variations in immunity. Estrogen was orignially characterized as a female sex hormone, but it is also produced in lower concentrations in males. It plays important roles in many physiological processes including reproductive development and function, metabolism, cognition, and immune system regulation. Although its role in these processes is well established, its mechanism of action remains poorly understood. Our goal is to deepen our understanding of how estrogen interacts with regulatory T cells, which are a specific type of immune cell. Regulatory T cells dampen the immune response and help prevent autoimmunity. Estrogen has been shown to enhance the regulatory activity of these cells, as well as to promote their development outside of immune organs. Our research project focuses on understanding the mechanism by which estrogen carries out these functions both in healthy women and men, as well as in individuals with Crohn's disease, an autoimmune condition affecting the gut. We aim to understand how estrogen signaling affects the development of Treg cells outside of immune organs, and how it affects their stability and regulatory activity. We will also determine how changes in estrogen signaling affects Treg cells in individuals with Crohn's disease, and assess whether manipulating the estrogen signaling pathways in these cells can enhance their regulatory activity. Our project will contribute to our understanding of the role of estrogen and biological sex on the immune response, and will help lay a groundwork for advances in cell therapies against Crohn's disease and potentially other autoimmune conditions.

column36: Exploring Perceptions and Experiences of Structural Violence, Mental Health, and Positive Adaptation Among Emerging Adults who have 'Aged Out' of Foster Care in Canada: An Explanatory-Sequential Mixed Methods Research Study
column37: Of the estimated 78,000 youth in the Canadian foster care system, nearly half will 'age out' of care on their 18th birthday. Forced to grow up almost overnight, these youth are left to navigate complex social services with minimal guidance and structured supports. This abrupt transition to independence is associated with poor physical, social, and mental health; however, the chronic effects of such adversities remain under-explored. Further information is needed to uncover how challenges and barriers experienced by this population affect longterm development and success. The purpose of this mixed-methods study is to understand how youth aging out of foster care navigate the transition to adulthood, and how adversities faced during this period may influence mental health and resilience. Approximately 100-150 youth ages 18-25 from across Canada will be recruited for this study. All participants will receive an electronic questionnaire capturing demographic information, foster care experiences, and transition outcomes. This quantitative data will be compared and analyzed to determine associations among participant characteristics. A subsample of 20-30 youth will then be selected to take part in virtual interviews exploring subjective transition experiences using a qualitative interpretive description approach. Integration of quantitative and qualitative data will aid in the identification of participants who have demonstrated resilience in response to adversity, leading to the discovery of internal and external factors that serve as barriers and facilitators to resilience in this population. Study findings may also reveal opportunities for tailored and proactive mental health care that reflects the unique psychosocial needs of these vulnerable youth. Future research in this area may lead to clinical, policy, and legislative reform that improves mental health outcomes and reduces barriers to societal participation among youth aging out of foster care in Canada.

column36: Risk for disordered eating among North American Asian emerging adults: Examination of the roles of ethnic identity, parenting, and satisfaction of basic psychological needs
column37: Eating disorders can result in serious medical consequences, including electrolyte disturbance and cardiac arrhythmias, and have the highest mortality rates among any psychiatric disorders. Asians constitute the largest group of visible minorities in Canada and, compared to White Canadians, have similar or higher rates of eating disorders, yet they are less likely to receive treatment. Emerging adulthood (18-25 years of age) is a developmental period when individuals are at particularly high risk for developing eating disorders. During this period, many parents continue to play a significant role in emerging adults' development. However, the impact of particular parenting practices on the children may vary across cultures. For example, parental control is perceived negatively in Western cultures, but may be perceived as well-meaning in Asian cultures. Therefore, strong ethnic identity in Asian emerging adults may buffer them against the negative impact of parental control. That is, for Asian emerging adults who identify strongly with their ethnic culture, parental control may not pose as much risk for psychological adjustment, including eating disorders, as for those who have a weaker ethnic identity. The proposed research examines this possibility and contributes to understanding how various individual, familial and cultural factors may explain Asian emerging adults' risk for eating disorders. Findings will inform theories regarding psychosocial risks for eating disorders in Asians living in North America by clarifying the role of ethnic identification in their mental health. These findings could also inform the development of more family-oriented, culturally-sensitive intervention and prevention programs attending to the needs of Asian emerging adults at risk. We note that causes of eating disorders are multifaced and cannot be solely attributed to one's familial environment. Instead, families usually play an important role in one's treatment and recovery.

column36: Single-cell probing of epigenetic memory in immunity
column37: The rapid development of sequencing-based techniques has revolutionized our comprehension of the genome, paving the way for gene identification, analysis of genetic diversity, determination of the epigenetic code, and study of the 3D genome structure. These techniques have allowed the identification of a limited number of transcription factors, the pioneers, that can initiate a series of events to reshape the epigenome and modify the regulatory chromosomal contacts in response to developmental or stress signals. In innate immune cells, the chromatin reprogramming initiated by a primary insult has been recently shown to induce a stable epigenetic 'memory' that influences the response to further infections, a process named 'trained immunity'. Nevertheless, due to technical limitations, it is unclear how heterogeneous is this epigenetic encryption and how individual cellular functions are affected? Our overarching objective is to develop methods to overcome these technological and knowledge gaps to render possible the detection of chromatin conformation and long-range interactions at single-cell and single-molecule resolution. Big data and the development of accompanying algorithms will elucidate the dynamics of epigenetic states and heterogeneity during trained immunity. We aim to develop bulk and single-cell Single-Molecule chromatin Capture (SM-C) to analyze the genome-wide allele-specific interactions and reveal epigenetic heterogeneity. We will also develop a targeted SM-C method to evaluate how the recruitment of a novel pioneer factor reprograms the transcriptional networks and contributes to the establishment of the epigenetic memory. This joint effort between Canada and Japan research teams will deliver techniques that will be a major advancement in the field of epigenetics, allowing us to understand how epigenetic diversity is established and which should guide the development of novel preventive diagnostics and treatments for infectious and immune diseases.

column36: Examining the Role of Online Discussion Forums in Unguided ICBT for Canadian Public Safety Personnel: A Randomized Trial
column37: Public safety personnel (PSP) are police officers, firefighters, paramedics, and others who work hard to keep Canadians safe. They frequently encounter traumatic events and have high rates of mental health problems. Many PSP face barriers to traditional mental health treatments related to location, busy schedules, cost of treatment, and concerns about privacy and stigma. Internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy (ICBT) can help overcome these barriers. It allows users to learn the same coping skills as they would learn in face-to-face cognitive behavioural therapy-a gold standard treatment for common mental health problems-but it tends to be cheaper and easier to access. ICBT is typically offered with therapist guidance, which generally makes it more effective, or in a purely self-help format, which generally makes it easier to provide to a larger number of people. A recent study found that most PSP report a preference for a therapist-guided format, but some said they would prefer a self-help format. Both formats have advantages, and it is important that researchers explore new ways to improve them. Some research suggests that adding an online discussion forum to self-help ICBT makes it more effective, but more research is needed to confirm this. My colleagues and I have developed a therapist-guided ICBT course for PSP, which is being offered in Saskatchewan and Quebec. I am proposing to develop a self-help version of this course and deliver it to PSP across Canada. I will then randomly assign 315 users to receive access to (a) a forum in which a therapist is involved in the discussion, (b) a forum without a therapist involved, or (c) no forum. I will measure each user's symptom change through questionnaires and use statistics to test whether forums lead to better improvement in symptoms. This study is expected to help PSP across the country with mental health problems and test whether two kinds of online discussion forums are helpful in self-help ICBT.

column36: Artificial Intelligence based adaptive and interpretable models for analyzing multi-track epigenomic sequential data
column37: In this project we will take a fresh approach to harness the great potential of AI in the big data-analyses of epigenomic sequences. Epigenetics is the study of molecules and mechanisms that can perpetuate alternative gene activity states in the context of the same DNA sequence. Key factors in epigenetic control are chemical modifications to DNA and histones, which establish a complex regulatory network that controls genome function. Although epigenetic marks are established early during development and differentiation, adaptations occur throughout life in response to intrinsic (e.g. oncogenes) and environmental stimuli (e.g. diet) and may lead to disease late in life. Moreover, epigenomes react to environmental influence (e.g. maternal care, diet, exposure to toxins) with possibly long-term consequences. Thus, the life of an individual is not only defined by their genome, but also by their epigenome, which is flexible and changeable throughout the lifetime. The research team has two epigeneticists (Yamanaka, Davie) and two artificial intelligence (AI) experts (Ashraf, Khan). Working as a collaborative team, the four research groups will develop new tools to analyze DNA sequence data that will be able to predict 3D organization and functional aspects of these interactions in vertebrate epigenomes, which would be transformative in epigenetics research. We also propose the paradigm of iteratively refining the AI models through wet-experiments. In cancer, resistance to specific treatments often results in worse outcomes. It is now known that the 3D organization of the genome gets modified in these cancers. These sequence changes affect genome interactions and predispose some individuals to disease or an inadequate response to a virus attack as in COVID-19. Our studies have the potential to exploit the genome-wide data to predict the changes in the 3D organization of an individual's genome and gene activity, adding a new dimension to personalized medicine.

Thus, investigating alternate coping strategies, such as mindfulness and self-compassion, may afford a unique opportunity to address coping-motivated alcohol and marijuana use and the associated problems on Canadian university campuses. The purpose of the interview will be to gather detailed information about their experience using mindfulness and self-compassion as alternate coping strategies, as well as their impressions of the program. Using the results of Part One and Part Two to improve the program, I plan to pilot the program at the host university and subsequently implement it across interested Canadian universities in Part Three. Teaching mindfulness and self-compassion as alternate coping strategies to alcohol and/or marijuana use may help reduce coping-motivated use and the associated problems on Canadian university campuses. column36: Neuromodulation with cognitive training to enhance working memory
column37: Memory loss is a normal part of getting older; but for people with dementia, this process is severe and disabling. What if we could strengthen aspects of our memory and reverse cognitive decline? Brain training has the potential to rehabilitate people with cognitive deficits, but research in this area has made little progress over the past decades and there is ongoing debate on the efficacy of brain training programs. We aim to accelerate the development of cognitive enhancement therapies by combining training on a musical memory task with a type of individualized brain stimulation that is known to boost brain function. By asking people to reorder musical notes in their mind, our training program targets auditory working memory, which is the ability to remember and manipulate sounds. Neurologically healthy participants will come to the lab for several days to practice this task, while receiving either real or sham transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). A TMS machine generates a small magnetic field, which can be directed at a person's head to transiently alter the electric signal within their brain. When we apply rhythmic pulses of TMS at the same frequency, timing, and location of brain waves that are naturally generated during auditory working memory, we are able to improve people's performance on the memory task. The more their brain waves synchronize with the stimulation, the better they do. We will now investigate whether performance enhancement can outlast the period of stimulation and generalize to other cognitive tasks. The results will shed light on the mechanisms of brain wave entrainment, and potentially open a new avenue for treatment of neurocognitive deficits. In the future, people who have impaired working memory could undergo a form of rehabilitation using our combined training and stimulation protocol, with the goal of restoring their brain to a normal level of functioning.

column36: Multi-ethnic polygenic risk scores to improve risk screening of complex diseases for populations of non-European ancestries
column37: Genetic predisposition to disease is an important risk factor for many complex diseases. Advances in human genetics have enabled the development of efficient genetic scores, named polygenic risk scores, that aggregate information across millions of genetic features to predict disease risks. In combination with effective application of high-dimensional statistics, machine learning and artificial intelligence, the predictive power of recently developed polygenic risk scores is increasing and indicating high clinical utility. However, nearly all of these advances have occurred using data from individuals of European ancestry. The effectiveness of polygenic risk scores in individuals of non-European ancestries is still largely unknown. But in the cases where it has been evaluated, the predictive performance of polygenic risk scores is substantially attenuated. This is likely due to differences in the underlying genetic basis of disease in different populations, together with varying environmental exposures. To date, there are no clinically-acceptable polygenic risk scores available to people of non-European ancestries, though these populations, including minorities and aboriginals, who support the health care system and its patients, make up very important proportions of the population of Canada and of many other countries. Therefore, having gathered several large population-based cohorts of different ethnic background, we aim to develop novel machine learning methods, together with open source software packages to improve the accuracy of polygenic risk scores for complex diseases, such as various types of cancer, coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and osteoporosis, for individuals of non-European ancestries. We anticipate that these polygenic risk scores applicable to multiple ethnic groups will help not only realize the goals of generalizability and clinical utility, but also mitigate long-standing health care disparities.

column36: Neighbourhood environmental exposures and their associated health risks: evidence and policy implications for urban health and health equity from Accra, Ghana
column37: As low- and middle-income countries develop, their populations move increasingly into cities. While urban populations are healthier overall than their rural counterparts, the benefits of urbanization are not experienced equally. The gap between rich and poor is large in many cities, and may be growing, resulting in unequal health outcomes in all age groups. Governments in those cities, such as Accra, Ghana, rely on scientific evidence to ensure that they can plan their development in a way that is healthy and equitable for all residents. For my proposed research, I will study characteristics of areas in Accra to understand what neighbourhoods look like across the city, how risk factors in the neighbourhood environment influence health outcomes, and how environmental factors can be targeted with well-planned policies to improve the health and well-being of people living in the city. I will use methods from epidemiology and geography to create data and evidence about neighbourhoods and their role in health. In partnership with city planners and other policymakers in Accra, I will also identify policies with the potential to improve the neighbourhood environment and reduce health inequalities in low- and middle-income urban settings. My work will be supported by the Pathways to Equitable Healthy Cities program (PEHC), a global consortium funded by the Wellcome Trust. Through PEHC, I will have access to technical and scientific expertise from world-class faculty at several global universities, and policy expertise from stakeholders in five cities around the world. I will use these resources and opportunities to conduct research that will impact human health on a local and international scale. By working with motivated policymakers and diverse international project partners, I will advance our collective knowledge about neighbourhoods and urban health and co-create viable, innovative policy solutions to build healthier and more equitable cities around the world.
