column36: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Dysanapsis
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. It is a leading cause of death and disability in the world and in Canada. Although smoking is the main risk factor, only a minority of smokers develop COPD. Besides, people who had never smoked can also develop COPD, suggesting that other risk factors must exist. Air is transported into the lung via airways that resemble the branches of a tree and they filter inhaled particles. 50 years ago, scientists using simple tests that measure lung function, speculated that some people have undersized airways relative to the volume of their lungs. The size mismatch between airway and lung volume was termed dysanapsis and is believed to develop early in life when airway branches grow more slowly than lung volume. Recently, by measuring airway tree size using medical imaging called computed tomography (CT), our team showed that people with dysanapsis are eight times more likely to develop COPD. Thus, dysanapsis is a major COPD risk factor on par with cigarette smoking. In this project, by analyzing airway trees of thousands of adults aged 20-97 years old, I will assess how the airway tree grows across different ages and if there is a difference between males and females. In addition, I will discover the genes that play a role in dysanapsis development and assess if children having those genes would manifest low lung function. Finally, I will investigate if dysanapsis involves all airways in the lung and will explore if it leads to more absorption of cigarette smoke in the body and consequently more limitation in breathing. The results of this project could help us prevent dysanapsis by interventions targeting the early years in life. This would promote healthy and resilient lung development, explain the variability in individual susceptibility to inhaled particles like cigarette smoke, and ultimately promote healthy lungs for life.

column36: Fabrication of a vascularized bioartificial pancreas using macroencapsulation of stem cell-derived pancreatic islet cells for the treatment of type 1 Diabetes.
column37: Type 1 diabetes affects more than 300 000 Canadians and its impact continues to rise in Canada and the world. Transplantation of pancreatic islets, the tissue regulating insulin and blood sugar, is a promising strategy to treat diabetic patients because it can eliminate their dependence on external insulin sources for many months. There are however severe disadvantages with this approach. One of the most critical problem is graft rejection, a process where your own immune system attacks the newly transplanted tissue and destroys it. To protect the islets, scientists are encapsulating them in selectively permeable materials. These are biocompatible materials that create a physical barrier to prevent the immune cells to reach the graft while allowing nutrients to go through to keep the islets alive. Unfortunately, the large quantity of islets needed to treat human diabetic patients make it difficult to have enough nutrients for all the graft, leading to significant cell death and failure of the therapy. To address these issues, we are fabricating a small device that can encapsulate several hundred thousand islets and protect them from immune destruction. To optimize survival of the graft, our device contains many blood vessel-like channels that can be directly irrigated by the patient's own blood after transplantation. With our approach, the islets inside the device will take on the function of the patient's failing pancreas, producing the insulin needed to regulate blood sugar level for several years. This strategy will allow patients suffering from type 1 diabetes to be treated by islet transplant without suffering from the difficult complications related to immunosuppression or insulin management. It thus represents an important advance in cellular therapy for diabetic patients.

column36: Episodic memory and theory-of-mind in children with autism
column37: We use memory of our past experiences to imagine what other people are thinking. Being aware of other's mental states is crucial for successful social interactions. In autism, detailed recollection of past events and experiences is commonly impaired, along with the ability to imagine what others are thinking. Together, these challenges may create difficulty when conversing with others, providing a potential explanation for the social impairments commonly seen in autism. The detailed memory deficit may be due to the fact that people with autism have difficulty relating experiences to themselves, a phenomenon which normally boosts detailed memory. We aim to see how the effect of relating memories to oneself differs in children with autism compared to typically developing children. Children will complete a memory task where they will relate some objects to themselves by answering the question: "Do you like this object?". We will test them on their detailed memory for the objects and look at their brain activity while they are resting and while they are performing this activity. Additionally, participants will be assessed on how they can think about others' states of mind. We expect that children with autism will not show improved memory when making a self-relation and will show less engagement of brain areas related to detailed memory, understanding others' perspectives, and social processing. This research will tell us if the difficulty in relating memories to oneself is related to difficulties in imagining others' mindsets and how the brain behaves differently in this scenario in the presence of autism. This will help us to understand the roots of social impairments as they exist in the brain and behavior in autism and will inform future interventions to improve day-to-day interactions for these individuals.

column36: Acute effects of non-invasive repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in the management of chronic orofacial pain and problematic opioid use.
column37: Temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) are common chronic pain conditions of the face and jaw that impact significantly the well-being and quality of life of people suffering from them. Chronic TMD pain is challenging to treat and many patients do not respond well to usual treatments. Moreover, medications such as opioids are associated with different risks and side-effects. Hence, the investigation of newer and safer treatments becomes highly relevant. "Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation" (rTMS) is a safe and non-invasive technique used to stimulate the brain and potentially change neurons. rTMS has proven to improve pain and addiction, but its use in TMD has not been tested yet. Thus, we aim to assess if rTMS can improve pain and opioid problems in TMD participants. This thesis project is divided in two studies. One study is focused on pain, where 30 TMD participants not taking opioids will be recruited, and the other is focused on opioids, where another 30 TMD participants taking opioids will be recruited. In both studies, each participant will have two separate treatment sessions, one where they will receive active rTMS, and one where they will receive a "sham" (i.e., fake) treatment with an identical device but with limited power. The order of the sessions will be random and neither the participant nor the staff will know when the patients receive one or the other. Following each treatment session (rTMS or sham), participants will complete electronic diaries at home, twice daily, for one week. These diaries will ask questions about pain intensity and pain interference with daily activities. Patients who use opioids will also answer diary questions about opioid use. We expect that rTMS decreases pain intensity, pain interference, and opioid problems in TMD participants. This project is novel and important, as its findings could support the use of a new and safe treatment for improving pain, opioid problems, and suffering associated to TMD.

column36: Co-Developing & Piloting a New Model of Care Delivery for Migrant People Living with HIV in Montreal
column37: As of June 2019, immigrants accounted for 82.8% of Canada's annual population growth. Immigrants represent an increasing proportion of people living with HIV (PLWH) in Canada. In fact, a Canadian surveillance report indicated that immigrants accounted for 40% of all new HIV diagnoses reported in 2018. Efficient access to HIV care for new immigrants has significant individual-level health benefits (e.g. reducing the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV infection), which can translate into major society-level benefits (e.g. prevention of HIV transmission to others). However, immigrant PLWH face longstanding and complex barriers that prevent them from accessing and adhering to HIV care compared to native-born citizens. For example, immigrants often lack medical coverage and have limited financial resources to access HIV medications. Furthermore, immigrants are often unable to fluently speak English or French, making medical terminology harder to understand for them and hindering their ability to navigate the Canadian healthcare system. Also, personal barriers such as fear of being stigmatized when accessing HIV care, and organizational barriers such as scheduling appointments at HIV clinics, have both intensified with the COVID-19 pandemic. A possible solution to mitigating or eliminating a number of the barriers immigrants face is to conceive and implement a new model of HIV care specific to this population. This likely means giving healthcare providers a set of specific guidelines to follow when working with this population and integrating clinical care with social programs from community-based organizations that serve immigrants. My research program seeks to do the following: (1) co-design a model of care with patients, clinicians, community organizations, and hospital administrative decision-makers; (2) co-design an efficient implementation strategy with all stakeholders; and (3) test this new model of care at two major HIV care centres in Montreal.

column36: Developing Glycan-Based Antiviral Prophylactics to Prevent the Spread of COVID-19 and Other Respiratory Infections
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has now surpassed 34 million confirmed cases. No vaccine or antiviral drug has yet been approved to prevent the spread of SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19. Moreover, the most vulnerable people are also at risk of severe infection from seasonal circulating respiratory viruses, such as influenza. In the absence of effective vaccines against COVID-19 and most strains of common respiratory viruses, new approaches guided by interdisciplinary research are required. Most viruses initiate attachment to the surface of human cells by interacting with complex carbohydrates called glycans. I aim to identify which subtypes of glycans are used by SARS-CoV-2 and other respiratory viruses for entry and infection of human airway cells. Through collaboration with an expert carbohydrate chemist, we will design and test glycan-mimicking antiviral molecules that block the interaction with glycans to prevent viral infection. With this project, I will rapidly identify prototype antiviral prophylactics to help limit the spread of COVID-19 and other common or emerging viral respiratory infections.

column36: Detecting eating disorder biomarkers in youth via video-based eye tracking
column37: Generally starting in adolescence, eating disorders are among the most burdensome mental health problems, with some of the longest recovery times and highest mortality rates. Eating disorders, such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, have one of the highest hospitalization costs in comparison to other disorders, thus there is an urgent need to increase our scientific understanding of these disorders and to increase early detection. Early detection gives patients and at-risk populations the best chance of recovery. The present research project aims to discover measurable markers in youth that are unique to eating disorders. To do that, we will study eye movements in youth with and without eating disorders. The study will be conducted at two research sites- Hotel Dieu Hospital (Kingston) and McMaster Children's Hospital (Hamilton)- where participants will complete a series of eye tracking tasks and questionnaires assessing thoughts, behaviour and personality. Eye tracking technology, used to record eye movements, is a low-cost and portable tool used in the study of various conditions. The biological mechanisms that guide eye movements are scientifically well understood. By examining differences in eye movements made during complex tasks, variations in cognition and frontal cortex activation can be discovered. Therefore, by comparing eye movement data with measurements of personality traits (e.g. impulsivity) and patient clinical information, we expect to detect typical markers of eating disorders. Our results have the potential to yield new insight on the biology of eating disorders. Identifying these markers could allow clinicians to diagnose eating disorders faster and more impartially, potentially fostering early diagnosis and prevention. By identifying eating disorders earlier, the costs to the health care system incurred due to lengthy eating disorder treatment may be minimized and eye tracking equipment can integrate within Canadian treatment clinics.

column36: Improving diagnostic accuracy in early psychosis: Differentiating the neuropsychological profiles of cannabis-induced and primary psychotic disorders in a 12-month follow-up study
column37: Cannabis use is common in psychotic disorders, especially among young people experiencing a first episode of psychosis. Cannabis is linked to the development of temporary, 'induced' psychotic symptoms, which are caused by cannabis use and diminish with abstinence (cannabis-induced psychosis), while individuals with primary psychosis who also frequently use cannabis (cannabis-comorbid psychosis) have a distinct mental illness requiring a different treatment approach. However, the similarity of the symptoms of these disorders often renders them indistinguishable, creating barriers to intervention and treatment. Previous attempts to identify differentiating features have been unsuccessful at reliably distinguishing between diagnoses. As such, there is an urgent need to refine the diagnostic tools available to psychosis clinics. Despite the abundance of research identifying cognitive deficits, eye movement abnormalities, and speech deficits as core neuropsychological symptoms of primary psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia), limited research has examined these well-established markers as potential methods to improve diagnosis in first-episode psychosis. The proposed novel line of research will assess first-episode psychosis patients upon entry to a psychosis clinic using cognitive, visual, and speech tasks. Participants will be re-assessed at 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-up time points to evaluate if assessments at baseline can predict diagnostic classification reliably over time. These objective, well-replicated methods are hypothesized to increase accurate diagnosis above and beyond traditionally used measures. The ability to reliably differentiate these disorders is crucial to early intervention in psychosis and holds promise to reduce the diagnostic load on mental health care workers. This research will facilitate more rapid and successful intervention, promote individualized treatment plans, and lead to widespread benefits for patients.

column36: Women Empowerment-Cancer Awareness Nexus (WE-CAN): An Implementation Research of Cervical Cancer Prevention through HPV Self-Sampling and Education
column37: With appropriate screening cervical cancer is highly preventable. However, some vulnerable groups of women in India, like those living in rural or impoverished urban areas, continue to be victims of premature deaths. Presently, cervical cancer screening is performed via the Pap test, which requires a visit to a clinician's office. Self-sampling for HPV, the virus that causes cervical cancer, is an innovative and useful method of screening that allows a woman to test in a space and at a time of her choosing and could overcome many of the barriers to the Pap test like transportation, child care, and cultural modesty. Our goals are to provide sexual health education and to determine the acceptability, uptake and impact of HPV self-sampling on women's health. We will recruit 600 never/under screened women age 25-69 in rural and low income urban areas. We will provide sexual health education sessions to both women and their male partners. The cultural sensitivity and appropriateness of the content of educational materials will be determined through extensive consultation and collaboration with the local communities. To overcome issues related to low literacy we will rely heavily on audiovisual, info graphs, story boards and locally developed plays and videos. We will use a combination of surveys, focus group and interviews to assess the feasibility and impact of the HPV self-sampling and explore barriers and facilitators to cervical cancer screening uptake. The implementation of this proposed novel strategy of HPV self-sampling has the potential to lead to a new screening standard for hard-to-reach women by removing known barriers and offering it as a primary screening test for subsequent Pap testing. Furthermore, HPV self-sampling can be adapted and scaled up to other regions in India and other low- and middle- income countries to advance cancer prevention, community health literacy, public health policies, and enable women to make healthful and personalized decisions.

column36: Evaluating the enhanced Community-based Health Education and Communication (eCHEC) model in improving the knowledge and behaviours of community residents on known risk factors and protective factors for preventing Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) in Khon Kaen Thailand
column37: Liver Cancer caused by liver flukes is very common in Khon Kaen Thailand. People get infected with the liver fluke when they eat raw fish that is infected with the fluke. There have been many programs that have tried to prevent this type of cancer. However, it remains a common problem especially in the Northern parts of Thailand. Researchers from Khon Kaen University have created a Community-Based Health Education and Communication (CHEC) program to prevent intake of raw fish in the communities in Khon Kaen. They have found that this program has improved the knowledge and behaviour of community residents regarding eating raw fish which is part of how the liver fluke infects humans. In our research we plan to improve the CHEC program and test it in communities in Khon Kaen Thailand. We intend to do an experiment to give the program in some communities in Khon Kaen. We will compare the knowledge and behaviours regarding liver cancer among residents living in communities that received the program and those who live in communities that did not receive the program. We also intend to compare the quality of life of residents living in communities with the program versus the residents in communities without the program. We believe that an enhanced Community-Based Health Education and Communication (eCHEC) Model can improve the knowledge and behavior of people living the communities regarding prevention of liver flukes and liver cancer. The new eCHEC model will include ways to reduce the key aggravating factors (raw fish consumption, liquor consumption, and praziquantel intake) as well as to improve the protective factors (fresh vegetable consumption). If the program is effective, we will share our results with local health leaders and politicians so that this program can be spread out to more communities that have many cases of liver fluke and liver cancer.

column36: Establishing predictive factors of success for non-operative management of femoroacetabular impingement syndrome in a prospective cohort
column37: Background: Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS) is a painful hip condition caused by abnormal bone structure of the hip joint affecting young patients, most commonly 20-45 years old. Previous research studies would suggest that both surgery and physiotherapy can lead to a significant improvement in patients' pain and quality of life. Despite this, very little research has been done to determine which patients will benefit most from non-operative care. Purpose: The primary aim of this study is to determine which patient characteristics are able to predict success of a 3-month physiotherapy program, as measured by patient reported outcome scores. Secondarily we will also assess the association of baseline core-strength with hip related disability scores, and the association between treatment adherence and treatment success. Methods: A cohort of FAIS patients will be assembled. A combination of demographic, clinical and radiographic data would be collected at the patients' initial visit. All study subjects will then enter a 3 month treatment program with a core-focused, home physiotherapy regimen. Repeat patient related outcomes, clinical and radiographic data will be collected and compared with the initial scores.

column37: Indigenous peoples living in urban areas are more likely to experience homelessness compared to non-Indigenous peoples. Colonial definitions of homelessness do not consider Indigenous perspectives and understandings of homelessness and therefore likely underestimates homelessness in urban Indigenous communities and its' impact on connection to self, culture, and community and use of drugs and alcohol. An indicator that measures Indigenous homelessness will provide a quantitative 'evidence-base' for the many direct and indirect structural and social factors that contribute to homelessness among Indigenous peoples. The information generated from this research is important to understand Indigenous homelessness in an appropriate context that will inform the current gaps in urban Indigenous social and health services dedicated to supporting Indigenous peoples experiencing homelessness.

column36: Understanding the Impact of Osteoarthritis on Depression in the Canadian Population
column37: In Canada, a major public health concern is that osteoarthritis (OA) and depression affects millions of Canadians, and both conditions co-occur in about 20% of adults. Most people know a friend or loved one whose quality of life has been negatively affected by either of these two chronic conditions. OA pain symptoms and depressive symptoms are two of the leading causes of disability in adults. The double burden of having both OA and depression further compromises a person's quality of life and severely limits activity. There has been inconclusive evidence regarding the assertion that OA can lead to subsequent depressive symptoms facilitated through pain. In addition, there has been a lack of available Canadian data sources to examine the relationship between OA and subsequent depression in a population of adults where variables are measured across different time points (also known as a longitudinal study). There is a great opportunity to better understand the relationship between OA and depression, by using recent data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA). The CLSA provides pan-Canadian data that has information on OA, depression, pain, and other key variables. I will study the temporal relationship between OA and subsequent depressed mood using statistical methods appropriate for longitudinal data. A cure for OA does not exist at present, but it is possible to minimize the impacts of this debilitating health condition. Current OA treatment is focused on pain management, but it is not clear whether pain management is effective at dealing with the psychological consequences of OA. The study results will help to clarify the risk of developing depressive symptoms among people with OA, in order to improve the lives of people with OA, by informing OA clinical management (e.g., screening tools for depression) and supporting health services planning (e.g., social support programs).

column36: Predicting invasive ventilation and its effect on mortality for patients with pneumonia: an observational study using machine learning and a target trial approach
column37: Pneumonia is a common, dangerous, and treatable cause of mortality and morbidity. More than 2 million people worldwide die from pneumonia each year, not including the accumulating mortality from the COVID-19 pandemic. The burden of pneumonia falls disproportionately on people made vulnerable by poverty, insecure housing, or malnutrition. Treatments focus on antibiotics and supportive care, with severe cases frequently placed on ventilatory life support also known as invasive ventilation. However, invasive ventilation comes with significant side effects including the danger of the procedure to start invasive ventilation, the risks of weakness, hospital-acquired infection, and delirium that are common during invasive ventilation, and the difficulties in communication that come from having a breathing tube prevent speech. The decision to start invasive ventilation requires careful weighing of the risks and benefits, but there is almost no data available to assist physicians and patients in making this decision. Our project will investigate the risks and benefits of invasive ventilation in patients with pneumonia according to practical clinical characteristics. We will use data from three large, detailed databases of critically ill patients featuring minute-by-minute clinical data, and we will use the innovative "target trial" method which has improved our ability to gain helpful information from observational research. This research will help motivate clinical trials to help improve our care for patients with pneumonia and it will guide patients and clinicians who are faced with the difficult decision of whether or not to start invasive ventilation when a patient is very sick with pneumonia.

column36: Characterizing the mechanisms of glutamate-mediated activation of spinal cord neural stem/progenitor cells to reveal therapeutic targets for spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating condition with currently no available treatment options. A number of stem cell-based therapies have been examined to promote regeneration and recovery after SCI but all have been limited by minimal neuronal differentiation and a lack of functional connectivity. Overcoming these barriers is essential in translating effective stem cell therapies to patients. The adult spinal cord contains a population of endogenous neural stem/progenitor cells (NSPCs) that proliferate after injury thus providing a promising source of endogenous repair potential. However, the mechanisms that activate spinal cord NSPCs previously remained unknown and strategies to promote their functional integration into neural networks have been limited. Recently, I demonstrated that the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate plays a key role in the activation and neuronal differentiation of this population of stem cells by way of the AMPA receptor. The downstream mechanisms of this effect have yet to be characterized. In the proposed project, I will characterize the mechanisms involved in glutamate-mediated activation of adult human spinal cord NSPCs. I will determine the changes in glutamate receptor expression induced in NSPCs after injury. Furthermore, I will test the therapeutic potential of positive AMPA receptor modulator drugs in promoting NSPC survival and neuronal differentiation after SCI. This work will uncover important mechanisms to enhance stem cell neurogenesis and integration into functional neural networks in order to ultimately advance the clinical translation of stem cell therapies to SCI patients.

column36: The dura mater as a reservoir and entry point for IgA+ plasma cells into the brain during inflammation
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease of the brain and spinal cord in which the protective covering of nerves is destroyed by immune cells that cause inflammation. We have found that anti-inflammatory cells that originate in the small intestine can migrate to the brain during MS attacks, where they secrete an anti-inflammatory protein and decrease MS symptoms. As of yet, it is unknown how these anti-inflammatory cells access the brain or what signals bring them there. The healthy brain has been considered to lack immune cells. However, recent literature has established that the lining of the brain is a rich reservoir of immune cells. The outermost layer of this lining, the dura, is particularly capable of supporting immune cell populations. As a result, I hypothesize that the dura acts as a reservoir for anti-inflammatory immune cells that rapidly migrate into the brain during inflammation. In order to investigate this, my project will (1) characterize dural immune cells and the structural cells that provide support to these immune cells in healthy and MS post-mortem human and mouse dural tissues, (2) visualize the movement of anti-inflammatory immune cells in an animal model of MS and (3) identify the signals that attract anti-inflammatory immune cells into the brain during MS. By identifying how anti-inflammatory immune cells migrate into the brain, we can design new therapeutic approaches that harness this protective immune response to quiet inflammation in MS, a disease that has remained without a cure despite its prevalence in Canada.

column36: Characterizing Cytokine Biomarker Profiles as a Novel Means of Predicting Sight-Threatening Complications of Retinal Detachment
column37: Retinal detachment is an ophthalmic emergency affecting approximately 1 in every 10,000 people per year that may lead to blindness if left untreated. Although ophthalmologists are able to repair and restore vision with new advances in surgery, half of all patients will go on to develop complications and subsequent long-term vision loss. Currently, there is very little evidence on how to best detect and prevent these complications. This study aims to develop a new tool to help healthcare providers identify patients with retinal detachment who are at high risk of becoming blind. The tool includes small fluid samples from the eye that are routinely collected during surgery. An analysis of the biomarkers in the eye fluid can show important early signs of any complications. Technologically advanced ophthalmic imaging machines that evaluate microstructural pathologies inside the eye will also be used to assist in determining which eyes have disease and how the disease is progressing over time. This will mean that vision loss can be detected and prevented sooner than was previously possible. Ultimately, this more tailored approach to patient care will improve vision outcomes and reduce disability. A pilot study has been successfully conducted demonstrating the feasibility of carrying out this project. This research will also analyze the direct and indirect healthcare costs of caring for patients with retinal detachment. It will be determined if the use of biomarkers for predicting eye disease have good value for money spent when used by health care providers. A better understanding of the biomarkers and outcomes of patients with retinal detachment will enable researchers and clinicians to develop improved treatment options that target those affected and ultimately decrease the burden of vision loss. Additionally, the findings from this study will help future studies in developing tools that use biomarkers for preventing and treating a variety of other medical conditions.

column36: Developing an Adaptive Intracranial Neurostimulation Procedure to Rescue Attention Deficits in Children with Epilepsy.
column37: Have you ever daydreamed or lost your focus? If so, you've experienced what doctors call a momentary lapse in attention. Children suffering from epilepsy can experience hundreds of these lapses every day, unable to regain focus. Through advances in treatment, we can control seizures for many of these children; however, behavioural issues and impaired attention remain incurable. Without treatment, thousands of Canadian children continue to suffer from blunted academic performance, impaired social functioning, and lost opportunities. My research is aimed at restoring function to brain regions impaired by epilepsy. Using a novel technology called stereoencephalography, our team has been studying attentional networks in the human brain with a precision that was impossible just a few years ago. The anterior cingulate region of the brain is one of the most critical for attention. Our lab has discovered that precise timing of brainwaves (neural oscillations) in this area controls maintenance and shifting of attention with millisecond precision. We have shown that epilepsy repetitively disrupts this finely tuned activity to cause recurrent lapses of attention. These brainwaves are specific to each child and remain impaired even after seizures stop. As a neurosurgeon-in-training, I am developing an implanted device that learns the specific brainwave pattern each child needs to sharpen their focus. When this pattern is disrupted, the device will recognize the change and deliver a precisely timed electrical pulse to restore optimal rhythms. This personalized, next-generation, treatment relies on a multidisciplinary team of neuroscientists, neurosurgeons, psychologists, and engineers at SickKids with the decades of experience required to develop such a groundbreaking treatment. Together, we are driven to improve treatments for children, their parents, and their families. Because every child deserves to thrive, be a kid, and one day achieve their dreams.

column36: Interrogating the Differences in Memory Engram Function in Young and Aged Mice
column37: Memory is essential to who we are as individuals - it is the mental representation of our past and it is central to our ability to learn and imagine the future. Unfortunately, diseases of the brain often damage the ability to recall past memories and to form new ones. However, even in the absence of disease, memory function declines during the normal aging process. Indeed, the single greatest risk factor for disorders of memory is advanced age. As the average age of the Canadian population continues to increase, it is imperative that we advance of understanding of how the fundamental mechanisms of memory are altered in aging in order to identify strategies to prevent, diagnose, and treat memory disorders. At the most basic level, the brain represents memories through patterns of connections between neurons, termed engrams. Recent advancements have been made in our understanding of how engrams function, however, these studies have all been conducted in youthful animal models, and little is known about how engrams change with age. To address this gap, my study will investigate how engram formation, storage, and retrieval are altered with age. To achieve this, I will use genetically engineered mouse models that allow me to identify and manipulate engrams. Using these models, I will investigate differences in the structure and efficiency of brain-wide networks of engrams that are formed during learning in young and old mice. I will then investigate if memory deficits in old mice are due to failures of memory formation or retrieval. Finally, I will investigate if brain stimulation using optogenetics, a technique that allows neurons to be directly activated by laser light, can reverse memory deficits in old mice. The results from this study will contribute to our understanding of memory and to the development of rational targets for the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of memory disorders.

column36: Pilot Trial of Deep Brain Stimulation for Children with Autism and Refractory Self-Injurious Behaviour
column37: Children with autism and severe self-injurious behaviour (SIB) have limited treatment options. This can severely impact daily functioning for patients and caregivers. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established treatment involving the surgical implantation of stimulators in the brain, similar to a cardiac pacemaker for the brain. It has been used for decades for the treatment of Parkinson's in adults. Recently, DBS has been utilized to treat pediatric epilepsy, Tourette's syndrome and other new indications. Children (< 18 years) with autism have inadequate treatment options for self-injurious behaviours, I hypothesize that DBS will reduce the severity and frequency of self-harm events in children with refractory SIB. My doctoral work has three main objectives with a mixed-methods approach. First, I am performing a systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data on the effect of DBS for patients displaying SIB. This comprehensive summary will provide important information for the planned pilot trial. Second, in my qualitative analysis, I will construct and conduct semi-structured and iterative interviews of patients, and caregivers, and clinicians to identify limitations of current treatment. Last, for the clinical trial itself, I am running a prospective, single institution, pilot study using pre-post measurements of self-injurious behaviour in children. I am comparing behaviour before DBS surgery and behaviour after 12 months of DBS. Children with autism and self-injurious behaviour and their families face a severely decreased quality of life, with consequences on healthcare resource utilization. My proposed research will find the efficacy and safety profile of DBS for children with self-injurious behaviours and autism. The results will enhance the knowledge of anatomic neural networks associated with autism, improve current clinical measurement tools, as well as explore a new treatment option for this vulnerable population.

column36: Opioid Agonist Therapy Amidst the Overdose Crisis and the Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19) Pandemic: Attitudes and Access
column37: Thousands of Canadians continue to die each year from the overdose crisis, which is largely caused by the presence of fentanyl in the street drug supply. The COVID-19 pandemic seems to have further worsened the overdose crisis, with rates of overdose deaths increasing since the pandemic began. As a result, people who use opioids (PWUO) are now facing two life-threatening crises. The primary medical treatment used to help people stop using non-prescribed opioids is medication, also referred to as opioid agonist therapy (OAT), to help reduce cravings and prevent overdose. However, some PWUO have difficulty accessing or prefer not to use these medications. It is important to get the opinion of PWUO as to why some are choosing not to use or stay on OAT; however, those opinions are often neglected by researchers. This PhD project aims to incorporate the views and preferences of PWUO to examine three important aspects of how the overdose crisis and COVID-19 may be impacting medication treatment. First, we will use data collected from a large group of PWUO to analyze whether fentanyl use is associated with lower satisfaction for methadone, the most commonly used form of OAT. Second, we will ask PWUO to make choices between different aspects of medication treatment and use that information to determine what is preferred; this research method is called a discrete choice experiment. Finally, we will use a large Ontario-based database to see how the COVID-19 pandemic is impacting access to OAT. The results of this PhD thesis will be used to decide how to best provide medications for opioid use in order to reduce overdose death and improve care for PWUO during the overdose crisis, COVID-19 pandemic, and beyond.

column36: Rational Design and Characterization of a Conformationally Stabilized Next-Generation Immunogen Against Malaria
column37: Malaria is a global health concern and increasing resistance to current interventions has amplified the need for a potent vaccine. Antibodies (Abs) targeting circumsporozoite protein (CSP), a protein coating the surface of malaria parasites that mediates infection, facilitate protection in animal models against malaria. In fact, the current leading malaria vaccine candidate induces protective human Abs against CSP upon vaccination. However, this vaccine provided only 30-50% short-lived protection against malaria in children. Thus, a better vaccine is needed. One strategy to improve the potency of the antibody response elicited by a vaccine is to computationally design proteins that will display antibody-binding targets such that these segments are readily accessible for the immune system to mount an antibody response against them. This strategy has been used and tested against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) whereby monkeys were protected from infection by protective Abs induced by computationally designed proteins presenting a site of vulnerability from the viral particle. To improve the duration of the antibody response, these molecules can be linked to the surface of a spherical delivery platform such that numerous copies are readily presented to the immune system. I plan to apply these techniques to malaria by developing proteins that display the protective antibody-binding targets of CSP to the immune system and linking them to a spherical delivery platform. This will be achieved using Rosetta, a robust computational software that was also used to design the aforementioned RSV-targeted proteins. Based on computer-generated scores and manual inspection, I will then select promising candidates to be produced and tested in the lab to ensure that antibody binding occurs as intended during the design. Finally, our international team will evaluate our top designed proteins in immunization experiments and an in-depth study of the immune response elicited in mice.

column36: Exploiting a novel role for BRCA1 in the regulation of Pol II-dependent ribosome biogenesis
column37: Increased risk of breast and ovarian cancer is associated with mutations in the breast cancer protein (BRCA1), which is one of the proteins that protects the genome from damage. BRCA1 has been shown to prevent the accumulation of potentially DNA damaging structures known as R-loops. R-loops are highly enriched in the DNA region that encodes the protein synthesizing machineries known as ribosomes (rDNA). Recently we have shown that moderate levels of R-loops at the rDNA is critical for proper ribosome synthesis and cell survival. Objective 1 is to study whether BRCA1 protects the genome from damage by preventing R-loop buildup at the rDNA. To study this, I will use breast cancer cells that have the normal BRCA1 protein and examine the level of R-loops in presence and absence of BRCA1. To assess if the genome is being protected from damage, I will examine the level of DNA damage, problems with DNA replication and defects in ribosome synthesis. Objective 2 is to study whether increasing R-loop accumulation at rDNA in BRCA1-mutated breast cancer cells will increase DNA damage, stop cell growth and increase cell death. I will increase R-loop accumulation in the cells by getting rid of two proteins, and I will examine if the cells exhibit increased R-loop levels, DNA damage, disrupted ribosome synthesis, increased problems with DNA replication, and increased cell death. For Objectives 3 and 4 I will study wither increasing R-loop accumulation at rDNA will decrease tumor potential of BRCA1-mutant cells, both in a dish (objective 3) or in mouse models (objective 4). I will increase R-loop accumulation in the cells similar to objective 2 and assess whether there is decreased number of cancer cells, tumor growth and size, and increased cancer cell death. Overall, my work may point to novel therapeutic strategies that exploit the partly elevated R-loop levels of BRCA1-deficient cancer cells to further increase R-loop accumulation and selectively kill cancer cells.

column36: Targeted therapy of meningiomas: establishing the therapeutic role and molecular mechanisms of epigenetic modification in clinically aggressive meningiomas in vivo and in vitro
column37: Meningiomas are most common brain tumour in adults but are severely understudied compared to other tumours. Most meningiomas are benign and can be successfully treated with surgery. However, there are a significant cohort of meningiomas (20-30%) that are clinically aggressive and recur rapidly and repeatedly despite maximal standard of care therapy with surgery and radiation. The genomic changes underlying meningiomas have been well investigated but none have led to the development of any effective therapeutics. Our group has focused on DNA methylation in meningiomas, a reversible epigenetic change to DNA that turns specific genes on and off. We identified specific methylation markers that are predictive of tumour aggressiveness and tumour recurrence. Based on these epigenetic changes, we have identified a panel of pharmacologic compounds that act as specific and non-specific epigenetic modifiers. We isolated and cultured benign and clinically aggressive meningioma cell lines from patients in which to test these compounds for their ability to inhibit tumour cell growth and proliferation. We will perform genomic and epigenomic analysis of these cell lines before and after treatment to assess for drug effects on a molecular level. Compounds that demonstrate inhibition of tumour cell growth and proliferation will be translated into our mice model. As part of this model, we will implant meningioma tumour cells into the mouse cranium and monitor for tumour growth with interval neurological imaging. Once tumours grow to a specific, standardized size, we will treat these mice with the candidate compounds identified above, delivered systemically, and monitor for tumour growth, stability, or shrinkage. We will harvest these tumours for staining and molecular analysis as above. Compounds that demonstrate efficacy and safety have the potential to be translated into future clinical trials, particularly for aggressive, treatment-refractory meningiomas.

column36: Dismantling Dominant Discourse surrounding Complex Death with Urban Indigenous Youth Experience
column37: Suicide is commonly described as an urgent health concern and tragedy. Indigenous peoples' in Canada are familiar with this devastating reality, whereby Indigenous youth are five to seven times more likely to die by suicide than non-Indigenous youth in Canada. Additionally, while health data related to suicide and suicidality (suicide attempts, thoughts, and plans) are slightly documented in on-reserve First Nations populations, instances of suicide, and inquiries into mental health more broadly, in urban-based Indigenous youth groups are vastly understudied and underreported. This gap is alarming given that the highest percentage of First Nations, and Metis youth who died by suicide, did so in an urban area. As a result of these gaps and inequities, this research aims to 1) develop a more contextual and nuanced understanding of complex death, specifically Indigenous deaths by suicide that considers social, economic, historical, ecological and political factors, and 2) this research aims to challenge dominant discourses of complex death by providing a space for a critically situated and experienced informed investigation that centers the voices of urban Indigenous youth. This work will employ youth-engaged qualitative methods comprised of semi-structured interviews with urban-based Indigenous youth wellness facilitators in British Columbia. This research is aligned with critical suicide studies in that it critiques mainstream Western conceptualizations of suicide prevention and mental health intervention efforts as being largely inapplicable within Indigenous contexts (e.g. due to not incorporating decolonization frameworks). This work will contribute to an unexplored research area and provide empirical evidence for much-needed change in urban-based Indigenous youth's material, political and colonial realities. This timely research will have applied value in informing innovations in Indigenous mental health, educational and social service practice.

column37: This work builds on a novel treatment that uses a special immune cell called a regulatory T cell, which suppresses immune responses. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are the policemen of the immune system. They shut the party down before it gets too rowdy, thus inhibiting immune attacks from getting out of control. An autoimmune disease is a condition in which your immune system mistakenly attacks your body. The exact cause of autoimmune disease is unknown, they often are caused or exacerbated by ineffective Tregs. The reason is unclear: sometimes they have a genetic deficit, or they might resist activation because of something in their environment. Many autoimmune diseases such as diabetes, lupus, multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel diseases are often associated with an abnormally low number or defective Tregs. Fueled by successes of immunotherapy in cancer, promising new ways to modulate the immune system to treat immune mediated diseases are currently being developed. Genetically engineered Tregs are promising given that they are able to maintain their policeman nature of regulatory functions, with preferentially relocation to the target sites of autoimmune disease. We plan to apply this concept in a disease model of Multiple sclerosis, an auto-immune disease of the nervous system using artificially engineered Tregs to test out their suppressive capacity in helping curb the inflammation. If successful this strategy can be rapidly used for other auto-immune diseases and may also help in protection against transplant rejections.

column36: Developing a Guideline Methodology for Rare Diseases: Bleeding Emergencies in Patients with Immune Thrombocytopenia.
column37: Right now, guidelines for rare diseases can be hard to develop because sometimes there is not enough information to help create them. A group of doctors and researchers normally make decisions on the best treatment for a rare disease based on their opinions and relevant experience, which can be biased. Since rare diseases impact approximately 250-450 million people around the world, guiding the treatment of people with rare diseases is important. Blood platelets are needed to prevent bleeding in the body. One of the main causes of low blood platelets is a rare disease called immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Children and adults with ITP are at high risk of bleeding and when serious bleeds occur, they need to go to the Emergency Department immediately. The problem is that there is no standard way for emergency doctors to treat these ITP bleeding emergencies, and they are often unprepared to deal with them. This can cause delays in treatment and people can end up bleeding more, or even dying. My PhD thesis project project will fill an important gap for emergency treatment in a particularly vulnerable group of people. We will develop a standard guideline for treating ITP bleeding emergencies using the best available information. We will bring together a group of ITP doctors, emergency doctors and nurses, and researchers as well as ITP patients and caregivers of patients to create a guideline for ITP bleeding emergencies. This will be an important first step towards improving the health of people with low blood platelets, by making sure bleeding emergencies are handled quickly and properly, and restricting expensive treatments to those who need it most. We will also develop a new strategy for creating guidelines that can be applied to all rare diseases. We will overcome the challenge of having not enough information by collecting new information from experts in the field where necessary.

column36: Investigating the Influence of the Human Gut Microbiota in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Our bodies are inhabited by thousands of bacteria, collectively referred to as the microbiota. These bacteria are not passive inhabitants, but instead play important roles in metabolism, protection against pathogens and immune system development. In addition to these functions, alterations in the bacterial makeup of the microbiota have been observed in several diseases including Parkinson's Disease (PD). PD is a movement disorder resulting from the loss (neurodegeneration) of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain. The causes of PD are not completely understood though it is thought to be the result of both of genetic and environmental factors. In recent years, the microbiota has been investigated as one of these important environmental factors. However, many of the current studies are correlative, demonstrating that alterations in bacterial makeup of the microbiota are present in PD patients, but do not demonstrate a causal role in disease development. My project focuses on determining if, and how, alterations in the microbiota contribute to the development of PD with the goal of identifying possible interventions that will slow or stop neurodegeneration. This goal requires deciphering which specific bacterial factors influence the disease state and how these factors work. To accomplish this, an experimental system is needed that allows for manipulation of the microbiota and where there are no genetic differences between individuals. We use a small nematode (worm), C. elegans for this purpose. Using these animals, we can easily generate large populations (millions) of genetically identical animals for analysis. We will determine the influence of hundreds of bacterial strains isolated from humans, on neurodegeneration using C. elegans models of PD. Using the bacteria that differentially influence neurodegeneration, we will identify specific molecules produced by these bacteria and examine changes in the expression of genes that occur in response to these factors.

column37: Ovarian cancer is known as the silent killer because patients often have the disease for a long time before it is detected, making it hard to treat. At diagnosis treatment is often to surgically remove as much as possible. This has to be followed by chemotherapy and radiation to target any remaining cancer. Unfortunately, the cancer returns in 70% of these patients and fewer than half of these patients live to 5 years after their diagnosis. New treatments called immunotherapies that aim to strengthen or activate a person's immune system are being developed. While immunotherapy is treating some cancers, they haven't had much success in ovarian cancer. To understand why these immunotherapies aren't working we need to understand how the tumour interacts with the immune system. Natural killer (NK) cells are an important component of the immune system that identify and kill cancer cells. We don't yet understand how NK cells are interacting with ovarian tumours and how this impacts response to therapy. My PhD project aims to improve the effects of therapies by answering this question. We will use slides of ovarian cancer tissues that have been removed from patients to look for NK cells in and around the tumour. This is important because it will tell us whether NK cells in the tumour correspond with better or worse outcome for patients. It will be important knowledge that scientists can use when developing future immunotherapies or combining the ones we already have.

column36: Evaluation of the Cardiovascular Actions of Succinyl CoA:3-Ketoacid CoA Transferase Inhibition in Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Diabetes, a disease defined by high blood sugar, affects 463 million people globally. It is well-established that diabetes increases one's risk of developing heart disease, even when blood sugar levels are under control. Given the strong link between diabetes and heart disease, health agencies (e.g. Health Canada) now require that all drugs in development for diabetes undergo rigorous testing to determine their impact on heart health. Recently, we have identified that a clinically available drug for treating psychoses, pimozide, can improve blood sugar control in diabetic animals. We identified that pimozide improves blood sugar levels by preventing the body's muscle from metabolizing ketone bodies, a fuel source produced by the liver. Although the link between ketone body metabolism and blood sugar control requires further study, pimozide represents an exciting new drug for potentially treating diabetes. However, before pimozide can be approved as a drug for diabetes, it is critical that it is deemed safe for the heart. Therefore, the goal of our research will be to study the effects of pimozide on heart function in order to validate its potential as a new drug for diabetes. Although the exact cause of diabetes-induced heart disease is unknown, there is evidence that the heart of a diabetic individual is unable to produce enough energy to effectively pump blood throughout the body. Specifically, the ability of the heart affected by diabetes to use sugar for energy is reduced. Our previous data suggests that pimozide improves blood sugar control in diabetes by increasing sugar metabolism in the muscle. Interventions that increase heart sugar metabolism improve heart function in animal models of diabetes. Therefore, we hypothesize that pimozide will improve the health of the heart in diabetes. If our hypothesis is correct, our research will identify a new approach for both the improvement of blood sugar control and heart function in individuals with diabetes.

column36: Engineering an in vitro arterial niche for the development of lymphoid-competent hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Immune cells are a subset of blood cells that function to prevent and fix illnesses. Researchers are trying to control immune cells to more effectively combat cancer, infection and other diseases. Recently, one type of immune cell, a T-cell, has been successfully modified to target and clear cancer cells at levels never before seen. However, technical limitations make this therapy prohibitively expensive, and it is currently not feasible for countries with single-payer healthcare systems. These treatments, called CAR-T, require that T-cells are removed from a patient with cancer, modified to target cancer cells and then returned into the body of that same patient. My work focuses on generating new, affordable and broadly applicable sources for these treatments by allowing for production of T-cells outside of the body in mass quantities. To do this, we mimic where immune cells come from in the body. They develop from a type of stem cell, called blood stem cells, which arise from a specific blood vessel cell called hemogenic endothelium (HE). We now know that not all blood stem cells are created equal, and so far, we have been unable to produce blood stem cells that efficiently develop into immune cells. Similar to how when something changes in someone's environment - if they're at work or home, for example - it changes the way that person acts, the external environment changes how cells behave. My work is deciphering how the environment around the HE can direct the development of blood stem cells, with the intention of producing immune cells. I am focused on what types of cells are around the HE and how they will change the production and behaviour of blood stem cells. I am also investigating the physical environment: are there external forces that alter blood stem cell production and behaviour? I am using state-of-the-art two- and three-dimensional cell culture systems to understand how to change the HE environment to control the types of blood stem cells produced.

column37: The human genome encodes ~21,300 proteins, over 95% of which are subjected to reversible phosphorylation at nearly a million sites by at least 568 protein kinases (PK) and about 156 protein phosphatases (PP). Many phosphorylation sites act as on/off switches in proteins to control their diverse functions. Transcription factors (TFs) represent one of the largest families of targets for PK and PP, and may include over 1600 different proteins that bind to DNA. TFs bind immediately upstream of genes to regulate their abilities to produce their protein products. Only a relatively small number of transcription factors have been well studied and shown to be controlled by phosphorylation. Knowledge of the regulation of the vast majority of TFs remains very limited, because it has been extremely difficult to track the activation or inhibition of specific TFs in response to diverse treatments. Our aim in this project will be to develop and apply methods that will permit tracking of TFs in high-throughput, and establishment of their interactions with PK and PP and target genes in regulatory networks by wet lab and predictive bioinformatics approaches. Dr. Steven Pelech's lab has access to purified preparations of over 360 different PK and over 30 PP. The combination of the microarray technology with the subcellular fractionation of treated human cancer cells will be used to monitor TFs locations and phosphorylation states following treatments with diverse factors, mediators, and (PK/PP) inhibitors. I will also use purified preparations of PK and PP to try to phosphorylate and dephosphorylate TFs. Altered phosphorylation of these TFs will be tracked by differential binding of the phosphorylated TFs to the phosphosite-specific antibodies printed on the antibody microarrays. Immunohistochemistry and subcellular fractionation will be applied to confirm that potential PK-TF and PP-TF pairs of interacting proteins reside in the same locations inside of cells.

column36: Discovery and characterization of novel monogenic causes of allergic diseases in humans
column37: The immune system plays critical roles in protecting us against a wide range of diseases. However, the dysregulation of the immune system not only makes us more susceptible to infections, but it can also lead to the development of allergic diseases. My research aims to identify and understand the genetic changes which cause the immune system to become dysregulated and result in severe and rare allergic diseases in humans. By collaborating with clinicians across Western Canada, I will be recruiting individuals with severe and early onset allergic disorders into our study and sequencing their DNA to look for genetic changes (mutations) that could explain their allergic symptoms. I will also look for and test existing treatments which can restore proper immune system functioning and alleviate their allergic symptoms. Lastly, I will determine if milder forms of these genetic changes are associated with less-severe, more common allergic diseases in the greater population. Understanding the genetic causes of these severe and rare allergic diseases will not only be life changing for the affected individuals and their families, but it also has the potential to help other similarly affected individuals worldwide. Additionally, with a better understanding of how these allergic diseases are caused, we can develop new treatments that can precisely target the affected parts of the immune system, resulting in significantly better outcomes for the patients.

column37: The human brain contains nearly 700km of blood vessels, so it is no surprise that brain health and vascular health are closely related. One of the biggest threats to brain health as we age is Alzheimer disease, a type of dementia that currently affects over half a million Canadians. The main genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease is a version of a gene called "APOE", which makes a protein that acts as the FedEx of the body - transporting fats and other proteins in the brain and through the blood vessels. Most work trying to figure out how APOE connects to Alzheimer disease has looked at how it works in the brain, largely overlooking what it does in the blood vessels. One way that the APOE protein transports its cargo through the blood vessels is by sticking to high-density lipoproteins (HDL) - commonly known as the "good cholesterol". HDL supports blood vessels in many ways, and the proteins stuck to the particles dictate their function. HDL carrying the APOE protein has been shown to have extra protective functions in the context of heart disease but has not yet been studied in the context of Alzheimer disease and dementia. This project will take a new approach to understand how APOE and Alzheimer disease are connected by looking outside of the brain, and focusing on HDL carrying the APOE protein in the blood. The first goal is to discover exactly how these particles protect brain-specific blood vessels, and this will be done by modeling vessels using human cells in a dish and treating them with HDL from human blood. It will also explore whether the amount of the particles in someone's blood can help diagnose or predict their risk of developing Alzheimer disease, by measuring the particles in blood banked from a nation-wide aging study. This research could lead to prevention and treatment avenues for Alzheimer disease that wouldn't need to enter the brain to be effective, and advance the international search for an Alzheimer disease blood test.

column36: Investigating the role of reproductive hormones in healthy aging for women living with HIV: A community-collaborative cohort study
column37: BACKGROUND: Globally, more than half of all people with HIV are women. With effective treatment, people are now living with, rather than dying from, HIV. However, women living with HIV experience higher rates of chronic diseases and live 5-10 years shorter than their HIV-negative peers, suggesting they may be aging faster than the general population. Aging leads to the gradual decline of bodily functions and may be impacted by cellular, clinical, socio-demographic, and psychosocial factors - and, for those with HIV, the virus itself. Women living with HIV exhibit an increased burden of illness and shorter life expectancy compared to their male counterparts, in contrast to what is seen in the HIV negative population. A possible explanation for this is that women with HIV are more likely to have periods of prolonged amenorrhea and may be at increased risk of early menopause, predisposing them to comorbidities that are worsened by low estrogen states. In addition to HIV infection, social stressors like gender-based violence, substance use, and lack of supports increase women's risk for chronic disease and accelerated aging. I will investigate how hormonal abnormalities and social stressors affect health and aging in women living with HIV. METHODS: This study will enroll 700 women with and without HIV in British Columbia. I will collect blood samples, measure anthropometric variables, and ask participants about health diagnoses, reproductive history, and social factors. Markers of cellular aging, hormone levels, number of diseases, and social stressors will be compared between women with and without HIV. To ensure this research is in line with community priorities, women with HIV will be hired as key members of the research team. SIGNIFICANCE: This study has the potential to elucidate how HIV infection, hormones, and social conditions contribute to aging in women. This could significantly impact the health care of the 16,000 women with HIV across Canada.

column36: Examining the impact of dietary diversity/food variety on type 2 Diabetes
column37: Diversity in a diet has long been considered essential to healthy eating and many dietary guidelines have incorporated recommendations on dietary diversity to reduce the risk of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, some dietary guidelines have minimized and potentially undermined the importance of dietary diversity by reducing the number of food groups relevant to a healthy diet. Moreover, most of the diet quality measures do not capture dietary diversity, while quality and diversity are not completely alike despite a positive correlation, and diversity may be linked to disease prevention independent of quality. To date, most of the existing knowledge on dietary diversity comes from developing countries, where dietary diversity is an approach to address nutritional inadequacy, and thus is not a measure of diet quality in the context of a sufficient amount of food. And, in higher-income settings, research on dietary diversity rarely looks at the risk of T2D. Even less is known about diversity within food groups separate from the diversity of total diet. Moreover, although we know from previous studies that gender/sex, socio-economic status, and obesity can affect both dietary intakes and development of diabetes, it is still unclear whether mentioned factors can alter the degree of a potential association between dietary diversity and T2D. The underlying mechanism linking dietary diversity to T2D also remained to be elucidated, despite some studies separately showing the beneficial effect of dietary diversity on gut microbes and the protective effect of gut microbes against T2D. Therefore, this project aims to use data from multiple European countries to answer three main questions: (1) Do greater diversity across total foods and within food groups (e.g. vegetables) reduce the risk of T2D?; (2) Is this relationship altered by gender/sex, socio-economic status, and obesity?; and (3) Do gut microbes have a role in linking diversity to diabetes?.

column37: Childhood obesity is a major health concern in Canada. In 2017, 30% of Canadian children between 5 and 17 years of age and 64% of adults were overweight or obese. This study aims to improve the ability to identify children at risk of obesity and explore opportunities and barriers for effective communication of growth information between healthcare providers and parents. column36: Parental and family functioning as predictors of longitudinal trajectories of post-concussive symptoms following pediatric concussion
column37: Concussions are a pressing public health concern, occurring in 1-2 million children in North America annually. Concussions often result in physical, cognitive, and emotional problems, known as post-concussive symptoms. Although most children who sustain a concussion recover in weeks to months, a subset of children are hindered by persistent symptoms that reduce their quality of life. Recovery from concussion can be influenced by both injury-related and noninjury-related factors. Noninjury-related factors may be more modifiable than injury-related factors and, for that reason, may make better targets for treatment. Previous research has identified a variety of noninjury-related factors that are related to outcomes following traumatic brain injury, including parental and family functioning. However, these factors have not been examined in detail in pediatric concussion, so their importance to concussion recovery remains unclear. Additionally, much of the existing research on concussion in children employs conventional statistical analyses that are not likely to capture the significant variations in symptom trajectories displayed by children with concussion. Group-based multi-trajectory modeling, a statistical technique which identifies groups of individuals following similar symptom trajectories, should provide a more accurate characterization of the outcomes of concussion. The first aim of the proposed study is to identify trajectories of symptoms after concussion. The second aim is to determine whether symptom trajectories are predicted by parental and family functioning. Data will be drawn from a larger parent study involving children/adolescents aged 8-17 years with either concussion or orthopedic injury, recruited during emergency department visits at five children's hospitals across Canada. The study findings will provide guidance in developing family-based treatments and enabling the targeting of those treatments to children at risk for poor recovery.

column36: Exercise and anti-diabetic drugs to restore brain function in obesity
column37: With two-thirds of the adult Canadian population obese or overweight, obesity is a public health crisis. Excess weight and poor "obesogenic" diets increase the risk of dementia more than three-fold - we are faced with a huge burden of disease. Obesity affects brain functions by reducing the numbers of stem cells residing in the hippocampus, which are vital for memory and mood regulation. Numbers of these stem cells decline with age, and pathologically in neurodegenerative diseases - putting the brain at risk of dementia. In a population with high numbers of obese and overweight individuals there is a critical need for interventions that encourage weight loss and protect the brain. A two-pronged approach to combat obesity involves modifiable lifestyle factors, such as exercise, as well as pharmacological interventions, such as the anti-diabetes drugs metformin and liraglutide. Research shows that these drugs can increase the brain's stem cell niche in laboratory animals. But do these interventions functionally improve memory and mood? I will study the efficacy of exercise, metformin, and liraglutide in reversing the negative brain effects of dietary obesity in mice. I will take a translational approach - using diet manipulations in mice that mirror the modern "obesogenic" diet and cognitive tasks that parallel human clinical tests. I will define the benefits of exercise on metabolic factors alone and in synergy with anti-diabetic drugs. By combining my clinical trial experience in anti-diabetic therapies with my preclinical work characterizing behavioral changes in mouse models of obesity, I will elucidate how frontline diabetes treatments can restore memory and improve mood in obesity. column36: Grabbing head and neck cancer by the throat: understanding recurrence to improve treatments
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada. In recent years, Canada is experiencing an epidemic of head and neck cancer caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV), best known as a cause of cervical cancer. HPV head and neck cancer is the fastest growing cancer type in Canada and often deprives patients the ability to talk and swallow. Unfortunately, current treatments are too intense for most patients. As a result, there is significant interest to decrease their intensity and reduce their toxicity. However, even with the current intense treatments, 20% of patients suffer a return of cancer. These recurrent patients often only live 6 - 15 months. Thus, there is an urgent need to reduce the toxicities of current treatments, prevent recurrence, and find new therapies for those who suffer recurrence. In the current project, I will comprehensively tackle these three challenging issues by studying the characteristics of all three levels of the central dogma: DNA, RNA, and protein in tumours before and after-treatment. The insights generated from analyzing the tumours before treatment will allow us to predict a patient's response to treatment and tailor the treatment for each patient. By studying post-treatment recurrent tumours, we can better understand why some patients suffer recurrence. We can then identify drugs for treating these patients. HPV head and neck cancer before and after-treatment tumour samples are rare. At Western University, we have collected over 175 HPV head and neck cancer samples in which 56 are recurrent samples. These samples provide a window of opportunity to tackle the pressing problems associated with this cancer. We have further garnered the support of our clinical colleagues to rapidly test and translate our bench-side findings to the patient's bedside. Our results will be an invaluable resource for further studies and can potentially transform the management of HPV head and neck cancer patients.

column36: Clinical, echocardiographic and magnetic resonance evaluation of the pulmonary autograft.
column37: Aortic stenosis, a valve disease which limits the ability of the heart to pump blood to the rest of the body, is the most common valve disease in Europe and North America. Left untreated, this condition is associated with a mortality of >50% at 3 years following the onset of symptoms. Aortic valve replacement (AVR) has improved the natural history of patients suffering from this disease. Current surgical options all have advantages and drawbacks. Mechanical prostheses are durable but require lifelong anticoagulation with an associated risk of bleeding and stroke. Biologic prostheses do not require anticoagulation but have an increased risk of failure. More importantly, both prostheses are associated with suboptimal long-term survival. In patients <65 at the time of surgery, survival is reduced by more than 10 years compared with the general population. A third option, known as the Ross procedure puts a living valve in the aortic position. The Ross procedure consists of replacing the aortic valve with the patient's own pulmonary valve (pulmonary autograft). A valve from a deceased donor is used to replace the pulmonary valve. The Ross procedure is associated with better survival. However, it is a more complex operation. To date, no study has adequately compared the outcomes patients undergoing prosthetic AVR or a Ross procedure. Patients <65 years old represent 25% of all patients requiring AVR. It is thus pressing to determine which valve substitute offers them the best long-term outcomes. We hypothesize that the characteristics of the pulmonary autograft result in lower heart workload, which leads to better long-term survival. To test this hypothesis, we will use imaging studies to assess the heart workload at rest and during exercise in patients who have received a mechanical prosthesis, a pulmonary autograft and in healthy volunteers. We will also assess the clinical outcomes (ex: survival) of patients undergoing a mechanical AVR and a Ross procedure.
