column36: Mieux-etre physique et psychologique d'adolescents suite a une pathologie du genou: Une etude longitudinale sur le soutien a l'autodetermination et le role de la motivation et de l'observance de la reeducation
column37: Le genou est le plus touche par les problemes articulaires et les blessures a l'adolescence, pouvant causer plusieurs complications. Une reeducation est donc necessaire pour tenter de retrouver la pleine capacite du genou. Par contre, le taux d'adherence a la reeducation est peu eleve, tout comme celui de la recuperation des capacites physiques du genou. Selon la theorie de l'autodetermination, ce qui favorise l'adoption et le maintien d'un comportement est le sentiment d'etre a l'origine et a la source de ses actions ; c'est ce qu'on appelle le besoin d'autodetermination. Un environnement soutenant l'autodetermination d'un individu est lie a son mieux-etre et a une motivation plus optimale, dite autodeterminee, aux traitements proposes. Toutefois, la plupart des etudes dans le domaine ont ete menees aupres d'adultes et n'incluent donc pas la perception du soutien a l'autodetermination (SA) des parents, qui, pourtant, jouent un role essentiel dans la reeducation du jeune. Dans cette etude, 107 patients, ayant une pathologie du genou, comprenant le francais ou l'anglais et etant ages entre 10 et 19 ans, seront recrutes a un hopital orthopedique pediatrique. A tous les moins pendant trois mois, les patients recevront des questionnaires en ligne pour evaluer leur perception du SA de la part des parents, du medecin et du physiotherapeute ainsi que leur bien-etre, leur motivation autodeterminee, leur adherence et les capacites physiques de leur genou. Les objectifs de l'etude sont de savoir de quelle facon la perception du SA contribue a ameliorer la sante psychologique et physique des jeunes patients et si les bienfaits du SA sur la recuperation des capacites physiques passent par la motivation autodeterminee et l'adherence a la physiotherapie. Identifier des determinants sociaux et motivationnels contribuant a reduire les repercussions negatives (psychologiques que physiques) d'une pathologie du genou chez les adolescents permettrait d'ameliorer leur qualite de vie.

column36: Sexualized drug use among HIV sero-positive gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men using crystal methamphetamine: Exploring the intersection between sero-status, substance use, addictions, and mental health issues
column37: In Canada, gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) are among the individuals most affected by HIV. While HIV is now considered to be a chronic, manageable illness, among gbMSM, HIV care can often be impeded by HIV-related traumas, mental health, substance use, addictions issues, and other intersectional factors. Recently, sexualized drug use (or "chemsex") with crystal methamphetamine has re-emerged as a topic of concern in health and nursing research due to increasing rates among gbMSM living with HIV. Not only can crystal methamphetamine cause neurologic damage (e.g., changes in mood, cognition, and thoughts), it can also act as a catalyst for negative health outcomes while living with HIV, such as decreased immune function, exacerbation of underlying mental health conditions, and long-term substance dependency and addictions issues. Presently, little is known about the sub-culture of gbMSM living with HIV, mental health, substance use, and addictions issues who are engaging in chemsex. As a result, nurses and other clinicians can only provide "patch-work" solutions to manage care for this group. The focus of this doctoral research will to undertake a qualitative research study to understand (1) the sub-cultural norms of gbMSM living with HIV, mental health, substance use, and addictions issues engaging in sexualized drug use and (2) how group values affect health and risk-taking practices. This research could yield promising findings in health and nursing research to help support the development of prevention interventions for gbMSM living with HIV who are engaging in sexualized drug use. Indeed, in the absence of concrete solutions on how to support this sub-group of gbMSM, it is extremely possible that their health and social outcomes will continue to decline, and that this already vulnerable group will become increasingly isolated.

column36: Uncovering the role of lipophagy during atherosclerosis regression
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Atherosclerosis, the underlying cause of heart disease, is characterized by an accumulation of fat within the arteries that supply blood to the heart, narrowing these blood vessels and impairing blood flow. The accumulation of fat within artery walls, called 'plaque', is also associated with the buildup of different cell types filled with fat called 'foam cells'. Over time, the plaques grow and can become vulnerable to rupture, creating a blood clot which obstructs the blood vessels and leads to a heart attack or stroke. A major risk factor for atherosclerosis is high levels of circulating blood cholesterol. Current therapies to treat atherosclerosis consist of cholesterol-lowering therapies which prevent the progression of plaques, but these therapies do not cure the disease nor drive plaque shrinking. Discovery of drugs which could reduce plaque size and reverse atherosclerosis would prove to be a breakthrough. All the cells in our bodies possess an intrinsic ability to degrade defective or excess of cellular components through a recycling system named autophagy. This process is key to maintaining balance in cells. During heart disease development, autophagy becomes dysfunctional. Autophagy can mediate fat degradation and export excess fat out of foam cells for excretion through the feces. Our project aims to investigate the mechanism of fat degradation through autophagy for plaque shrinkage and the enhancement fat degradation via autophagy to promote plaque size reduction. For these studies, we will engineer a mouse that will allow us to track autophagy in real time and a small compound that can selectively enhance the degradation of fat through autophagy. Gaining a better understanding of the role of autophagy in foam cells may identify new therapeutic intervention and new targets to shrink atherosclerotic plaques, bypassing the need for lifelong therapies or invasive surgical procedures.

column36: Personalized Resistant Starch as an Adjuvant Therapy for Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a category of chronic, incurable illnesses that affect over 270,000 Canadians. People with IBD suffer from nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bloody stool throughout their life. Among the many ways IBD can affect a person's quality of life, diet is always a concern. Doctors have limited evidence to suggest one diet over another, and the consensus among people with IBD is that the best diet is "different for everyone". A healthy person's intestines harbour a community of trillions of beneficial bacteria. However, people with IBD often have fewer beneficial bacteria that produce butyrate - a molecule that helps to keep our gut healthy. Beneficial bacteria produce butyrate by fermenting dietary fibres that we cannot digest. One type of fibre is resistant starch - a natural component of starchy foods. Unfortunately, restoring one's gut health is not as simple as eating starch. Everyone's gut bacteria community is as unique as their fingerprint, and the bacteria they harbour are able to digest some starches but not others. My goal is to determine which type of resistant starch someone ought to eat prior to actually eating it. We will collect stool from children recently diagnosed with IBD and feed their gut bacteria with nine different powdered resistant starches. We will determine if these resistant starches restore their gut bacterial balance and butyrate levels. We predict that children will respond to one resistant starch better than others. They will be prescribed this "optimal" resistant starch (or regular starch placebo) along with standard IBD medications for 6 months. We will monitor their gut bacteria, butyrate levels, and disease activity for an additional 6 months to determine if the therapy is effective. Our plan capitalizes on diet being "different for everyone" with IBD, and could potentially lead to a revolutionary, safe, economical, and personalized therapy for IBD based entirely on a common food ingredient.

column37: With childbirth being the top reason for hospitalization in Canada, it is important that the care provided in maternal-newborn hospital settings is safe and aligned with best practice recommendations. Across Ontario, there is wide variability in maternal-newborn care practices and outcomes for mothers and infants; this shows that room for improvement exists. All Ontario maternal-newborn hospitals have access to a novel online audit and feedback system, a "dashboard", which shows how they are performing on selected key performance indicators. This dashboard is an important first step to show maternal-newborn units where there is need for practice improvements in their setting. However, previous work with Ontario maternal-newborn units has shown that seeing an evidence-practice gap on the dashboard is not enough for all teams to commit to making a change, nor does it provide any guidance on how to actually implement or sustain improvements. Using an established implementation science framework, my study will develop and field-test an implementation guide to help maternal-newborn hospital teams to develop an action plan to most effectively create practice change on key performance indicators. I will first create a working group with experts in implementation science and stakeholders from maternal-newborn care. Together, we will work to create an implementation guide based on information from the literature and previously collected data on user experiences with the dashboard. The implementation guide will then be reviewed by maternal-newborn stakeholders. I will then follow 3-5 maternal-newborn units for six months as they use the implementation guide in real-time to plan for practice improvements on one or more key performance indicators. The findings of this study will contribute to developing a resource that can facilitate implementation of priority practice changes in maternal-newborn units, which can ultimately improve the care and outcomes for mothers and infants.

column36: The Cholinergic System and Cognitive Impairments in Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia affects about 1% of Canadians. Cognitive impairments are a core feature of schizophrenia that drives functional disability and socio-economic burden in this illness. Currently, there are no medications that significantly improve cognition in schizophrenia. A better understanding of the neurobiology of cognitive deficits in schizophrenia could guide the development of new pharmacological treatments. The cholinergic system of the brain is important for cognitive abilities and it has been proposed that dysfunctions in this system would underlie cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. However, this has not been tested yet. Here, we propose to study the cholinergic system with a positron emission tomography tracer that allows to quantify cholinergic innervation in the brain. The goals of the proposed study are to (1) establish whether individuals with schizophrenia show reduced cholinergic innervation compared to healthy individuals, (2) determine if reduced cholinergic innervation is related to less brain activation in schizophrenia and (3) to greater cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. We hypothesize that, in schizophrenia, cholinergic innervation is lower (goal 1) than in healthy individuals, that this is related to general cognitive dysfunction (goal 2) and abnormal brain activity (goal 3). We will also explore the effect of sex on cholinergic innervation. We will inform patients and family, clinicians, and pharmaceutical firms of our findings to have them translated into clinical practice. Results will be presented in international conferences and published in high-impact journals. As there are no drugs that alleviate cognitive impairments in schizophrenia, it is imperative to better understand the underlying neurobiology. This project will increase our understanding of the cholinergic system in schizophrenia and opens doors for breakthroughs in the development of new treatments.

column36: Nutrient sensing pathways direct hematopoietic inflammatory rewiring in atherosclerosis
column37: Heart disease remains one of the most devastating diseases in Canada. When blood vessels become clogged with plaque buildup it becomes difficult for the heart to pump efficiently. Plaque is a complex mixture of much more than cholesterol and fat. It also contains cells from the immune system that become trapped and produce inflammation. Before these immune cells reach the plaque, they must first mature through a process called hematopoiesis. All immune cells receive characteristics from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) just as children receive genes passed down from their parents. Metabolism, which is the collection of biochemical reactions that convert the foods we eat into energy, occurs on many levels within our bodies. At the smallest scale, our cells manage nutrients by using tools that recognize when nutrients are low or high. These tools are proteins called AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) and mTORC1 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1). These proteins balance each other to make sure the cell uses its nutrients in the most efficient way. Taking all of this together, we aim to understand how an unhealthy diet alters HSC metabolism and how these changes affect immune cells downstream. We ask: "does HSC metabolism affect plaque buildup?" and for therapeutic purposes, "can exercise reverse these changes at the cellular level?". To investigate this process, we will feed mice a high fat and high cholesterol diet that produces plaque. The unique mice in this study have mutations that prevent AMPK and mTORC1 from stopping each other. Using a technique that separates individual cells, we will closely examine HSCs and immune cells from mice that have been exercised or not to evaluate how metabolic signals alter plaque buildup, and whether exercise can reverse these changes in HSCs. Together, this work will highlight important considerations to be taken when treating heart disease and lay the foundation for new and exciting therapeutic strategies.

column36: Short- and long-term effects of adolescent e-cigarette vapour exposure: reward, withdrawal, and neural correlates.
column37: Adolescent e-cigarette use has seen a dramatic increase in recent years with past year nicotine vaping among Ontario grade 7-12 students growing from 10.7% to 22.7% between 2017 and 2019. JUUL is currently the most popular e-cigarette, with 78% of the Canadian e-cigarette market share. It is also unique in its higher nicotine concentrations through the use of nicotine salts which allows for smoother inhalation and higher absorption, all potentially contributing to its high uptake among adolescents. Currently, the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying the high uptake of JUUL e-cigarettes in youth, as well as the long-term causal consequences of this use, are not known. Therefore, there is a critical need for establishing the short- and long-term effects of nicotine vapour on the adolescent brain. There is a substantial body of literature that suggests that adolescents are especially vulnerable to the addictive effects of nicotine. There are also longitudinal studies that associate adolescent e-cigarette use with a greater risk for future initiation of cigarette smoking. This may suggest that adolescent nicotine vapour exposure produces behavioural and neural effects that are distinct from those in adults, and may impact the neurodevelopmental trajectories in adolescents that lead to future addiction vulnerability. No studies to date have studied the causal impacts of adolescent nicotine vapour exposure on future nicotine addiction liability and related neural circuitry. The proposed research intends to contribute to our understanding of the vulnerability of the adolescent brain to the rewarding effects of e-cigarette vapour. This research has the potential to have a high impact through improving our knowledge of nicotine's short- and long-term effects on brain circuitry, apprising the public of the potential neurodevelopmental ramifications of adolescent nicotine exposure, and through future research aimed at preventing or reversing these effects.

column36: The metabolomics of frailty and cardiovascular health in older females
column37: Thirty percent of Canadians are 55 years of age or older, and are living longer than ever. Health declines with age; however, the declines are not experienced uniformly between individuals; rather, some people are more vulnerable to stressors and experience more rapid reductions that lead to poor health, which is a condition called frailty. Increases in frailty predict poor health outcomes, such as cardiovascular disease (CVD).The standard approach for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk screening in Canada is the Framingham Risk Score (FRS). column36: Technologies for Home Medication Vigilance and Protection (TEC4Home MVP)
column37: Many patients with one or more chronic diseases, such as heart failure or weakness, need to take multiple medications for their condition. These patients face daily difficulty in following a complicated schedule in taking many medications at different times and dosages. For older patients, especially those with memory loss, taking medications as directed can be very hard if not impossible. One common but avoidable outcome for these patients can be the worsening of symptoms, which requires visiting the emergency department (ED) or being admitted to hospital for treatment. Home-based digital technologies can unobtrusively help patients taking medications regularly, monitor vital signs such as blood pressure and heartrate, and allow patients to connect with health professionals by video. In this project, we will put together the Medication Vigilance and Protection (MVP) platform, combining technologies that patients can use at home to manage their illness. We will: 1) use Spencer, a digital tool to remind patients when to take medications and get refills; 2) use devices for patients to easily measure their vital signs and share results with their doctors, nurses and pharmacists; and 3) analyze their data automatically to forecast their future health condition. We will work with scientific, medical, and technology experts and patient advisors to develop the MVP platform and ensure it meets the needs and preferences of older adults with heart failure. We will test the MVP platform in different communities in BC and Ontario to determine if it improves patients' health. We expect this project will help older adults with heart failure avoid unnecessarily visiting the hospital/ED, better manage their medications at home, and improve their quality of life. We also expect the platform to lower healthcare costs and be useful to caregivers and health professionals managing these patients.

column36: Outcomes Associated with Direct Rapid Genetic Testing at Time of Breast Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Approximately 11% of all breast cancers are due to a mutation in a cancer predisposition gene, most frequently BRCA1 or BRCA2. These breast cancers should receive different treatments to increase the chance that a woman will survive, including bilateral mastectomy. However, women must know if they have a genetic mutation in a cancer causing gene at the time of diagnosis when treatment decisions are being made (rapid genetic testing). A new model of genetic testing at time of cancer diagnosis is needed to ensure equitable access to genetic testing for Canadian patients. Direct genetic testing offers patients limited to no pre-test discussion with a genetic counsellor, and written documents or other resources are provided. Our overall objective is to evaluate the impact of Direct Rapid Genetic Testing (DRGT) for breast cancer susceptibility genes in newly-diagnosed breast cancer patients on treatment and psychosocial outcomes, compared to women who received rapid genetic testing (RGT) with standard pre and post-test genetic counselling. We will recruit from 1000 women from hospitals throughout Canada, including those which do not have genetic counselling programs. Sequencing will be done on BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, PALB2, PTEN, STK11, TP53, ATM, and CHEK2 genes. We will have one central genetic counsellor (Women's College Hospital) who will provide post-test counselling. Genetic test results will available in 7 days. Outcomes will be compared between those who received RGT with standard genetic counselling to those who received Direct Rapid Genetic Testing. The traditional cancer genetics model is not sustainable with the current volumes of genetic testing. This proposed delivery of RGT at the time of breast cancer diagnosis is responsive to the need for new models. This research has the potential to lead to the development of a sustainable and accessible model of genetic testing at the time of cancer diagnosis, which has a very high potential to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Every maternal death counts: understanding driving safety in pregnant and post-partum women
column37: Motor vehicle crashes are a common reason why Canadian women die in pregnancy or shortly after delivery. Yet, these deaths aren't counted in most efforts to track and prevent maternal deaths, because the conventional definition of "maternal death" excludes deaths due to accidents. We propose to do this by linking British Columbia motor vehicle collision claims records with the province's population health databases, including the British Columbia Perinatal Data Registry, which will provide us with pregnancy-related information. column36: Advancing virtual care in stroke rehabilitation: TeleRehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery Post-Stroke (TRAIL)
column37: Leg weakness is very common after stroke. It affects the ability to walk and balance among people who have had a stroke. The first year after stroke is an important time for rehabilitation because it is the best time for recovery. Unfortunately, many people who have had a stroke often feel that they do not receive enough rehabilitation to restore their ability to use their legs. This is especially true for people who live in smaller communities where there are few health services, and more recently due to the COVID-19 pandemic where physical distancing between patients and clinicians has limited the amount of in-person rehabilitation. It is therefore important to develop innovative leg rehabilitation programs that are both cost-effective and accessible. Our team of stroke survivors, clinicians and research scientists from across Canada has recently developed TeleRehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery Post-Stroke (TRAIL). TRAIL is a 4-week program that focuses on exercise to improve leg function. It is delivered using the Internet and computer/tablet by a physical therapist. In this study, we will examine if TRAIL improves walking, balance, leg strength, and quality of life to a greater extent than a 4-week lifestyle coaching program (LIFESTYLE), that focuses on improving physical activity, diet, and stress management. Ninety-two volunteers who have had a stroke in the past year will be randomly assigned to participate in either TRAIL or LIFESTYLE. Volunteers will be asked to complete assessments and questionnaires before and after the programs. Assessments will be conducted using videoconferencing so that volunteers will not need to travel to a hospital to participate in the study. We are working with 5 cities across Canada (Halifax, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Vancouver). We anticipate that TRAIL is an accessible program that will help improve leg function within the important early window of recovery after stroke.

column36: Gestational weight loss in obese women and risk for adverse perinatal outcomes: a population-based retrospective cohort study
column37: Currently almost 20% of Canadian women enter pregnancy with a BMI in the obese range. Appropriate weight gain during pregnancy helps to improve outcomes for both mothers and their babies in women of all weights, including obese women. Due to limited and controversial findings of current studies, there is no tailoring of weight gain recommendations during pregnancy by severity of obesity. Although weight loss during pregnancy is not recommended, it has been shown that 5-8% of obese women in general, and up to 15% of women with extreme obesity, reported intentional weight loss during pregnancy. Given that a clinical trial of weight loss during pregnancy is not ethical, a high-quality observational study is greatly needed to explore potential harms of intentional weight loss during pregnancy for mothers and their babies. Our study will use Ontario birth registry data to examine the impact of weight loss during pregnancy on a wide range of adverse maternal and infant outcomes among obese women, divided into more precise obesity classes. Our study will overcome limitations of previous studies and fill research gaps by investigating dose-response effects of weight loss during pregnancy on perinatal outcomes. The study findings will inform prenatal counseling and help guide weight management during pregnancy and improve the quality of care for obese women. The current study will provide relevant, contemporary evidence of short-term perinatal outcomes of intentional gestational weight loss among obese women. Future research is needed to create optimal weight gain trajectories specific to obese women, based on their severity of obesity.

column36: Understanding the Role of Social-Economic Inequality on Deaths Due to Drug Overdose, Suicide, and Alcoholic Liver Disease in Canada
column37: Life expectancy is a key measure of the health of a population and is a reflection of a nation's social and economic conditions. Among high income countries, increases in life expectancy have been observed during the 20th and 21st centuries. However, recent trends point to a majority of high income countries experiencing declines in life expectancy, causing concern. Researchers have attributed these trends to increases in rates of deaths of despair, defined as deaths caused by fatal opioid-related overdoses, suicide, and cirrhosis of the liver due to excessive alcohol consumption. Preliminary research points to increases in societal inequality as a cause for these trends. This study will identify trends over time of the relationship between social-economic inequality and rates of deaths of despair over time. We will determine if social economic indicators of inequality within residential areas, in particular income inequality and labour force participation rates, are risk factors for deaths of despair risk among Canadians over and above other area and individual level characteristics over time. Also, we will study the mechanisms involved. We will use large administrative population-based datasets that have been linked with the mortality records. With recent declines in life expectancy, there is an urgent need to study the role of social-economic inequality on the risk for deaths of despair. This study will be among the first to investigate the role of social-economic inequality on the risk for deaths of despair at the individual level and will determine if findings within a Canadian context are consistent with those in other high income countries.

column36: Illuminating deficits in engram synapse structure and function in Alzheimer's disease
column37: When we form a memory, it becomes stored in our brains in small connections between brain cells called synapses. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), it is thought that these connections become dysfunctional. As they break down, memories that were previously formed become harder to remember and new memories no longer form successfully. There is therefore a pressing need to understand how exactly these connections become impaired in AD in order to design therapies to target them. This is an especially urgent goal given that current treatments for AD are not effective. However, up to now it has not been possible to directly visualize and study these connections, limiting our understanding of how they become faulty in AD. My project aims to address this issue. Using newly developed technology, I will for the first time directly visualize the connections that store memories in a mouse model of AD. First, I will investigate how the structure of these connections is altered as memory becomes disrupted. Next, I will determine whether these synapses show impaired activity relative to those in healthy brains. Finally, I will use brain stimulation to alter the function of these synapses and determine whether this corrects their deficits and alleviates memory impairment. Alzheimer's disease places a devastating burden on individuals, families, and society, and this challenge is unfortunately met with inadequate treatments at the moment. With CIHR support, I believe my project will make a significant contribution to the overall effort to better understand this disease and develop promising therapies to treat it.

column36: Identifying novel interacting partners and signalling complexes coupled to adapter protein CCM3
column37: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are defects that affect the blood vessels of the brain and are found in approximately 1/200 people. Unfortunately, the only treatment for bleeding lesions is surgery, which carries a high risk of complications. And so, to develop therapeutics for CCMs, we require a better understanding of the events that take place under normal circumstances. Some CCMs are a result of inherited mutations in one of three genes. Mutations in genes CCM1 or CCM2 typically result in fewer lesions and milder symptoms, but CCM3 mutations result in dozens of lesions that can bleed and cause strokes or seizures. A cell communicates with other cells via signals passed along by proteins called kinases. These kinases add a small chemical tag onto other proteins thereby changing their activity. CCM3 shuttles a specific group of kinases to proteins found in different locations within the cell. In this context, proper signalling results in the maintenance of a sturdy blood vessel wall, and a cell that loses CCM3 cannot properly assemble into a functional blood vessel. I use an instrument called a mass spectrometer that is capable of identifying proteins accurately, based on the "fingerprints" that they produce. This instrument can also detect which proteins have received chemical tags from the kinases. My project will define, in the cells that form blood vessels, all the proteins that are chemically tagged by the kinases associated with CCM3 and where they are located inside the cells. Knowing which lines of communication CCM3 and its associated kinases participate in may aid in understanding what cellular processes are important and go awry in a disease state. By understanding the network of events that are associated with CCM3 and its kinases, my research should assist in developing alternative, non-invasive treatments for patients affected by CCMs.

column36: Development of imaging tools for simultaneous PET-MRI imaging of acute inflammation and fibrosis associated with inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a lifelong, chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract. It affects 1 in 150 Canadians, one of the highest rates in the world. A common and serious complication of Crohn's disease is narrowing in the bowel, which stops movement of bowel contents out of the body. The cause of this is often buildup of scar tissue (or fibrosis) due to uncontrolled bowel inflammation. Once a section of bowel becomes fibrotic and non-functional, surgery is the only treatment available. Despite advances in treating bowel inflammation to prevent fibrosis, over 50% of IBD patients require surgery in their lifetime. This is often due to mild/moderate inflammation that goes unnoticed and untreated, due to a lack of serious symptoms. As such, there is a critical need to not only identify active disease (regions of inflammation) within the bowel, but also measure disease progression (degree of fibrosis present). Molecular imaging allows us to see the biology of tissues, and not just their physical appearance. This approach takes advantage of protein-based markers of disease present in blood vessels during the early stages of disease progression. We aim to design an approach for detecting and measuring active inflammation and fibrosis in a single session using positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Our objectives are: 1) to test and refine a PET contrast agent that we have previously constructed, which attaches to and identifies inflamed blood vessels; 2) to validate an advanced, quantitative MRI sequence to measure fibrosis in humans with IBD; 3) to combine our PET contrast agent and MRI sequence to image active inflammation and fibrosis simultaneously using PET-MRI. This novel imaging approach has the potential to help clinicians detect inflammation early and assess the degree of fibrosis present, giving them the information required to personalize treatment and reduce the need for surgery.

column37: Canada has among the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world and studies suggest rates may be highest in Saskatchewan. In progressive MS, the nerve cells of the brain and spinal cord are damaged in a process called neurodegeneration, a well-known feature of MS. Many researchers believe this is the reason why people living with MS get worse. The cause of this nerve damage is unknown and treatments that halt or prevent it are currently unavailable. Our team discovered that autoantibodies, molecules made by the body that attack itself, to a specific nerve cell protein called 'heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A1' (or 'A1' for short) may lead to neurodegeneration in people living with MS. In healthy individuals, 'A1' performs a number of functions to help cells stay alive. However, in people with MS, 'A1' becomes misplaced within the nerve cell leading to its malfunction and damage to the brain and spinal cord. We have shown that the addition of 'A1' autoantibodies (similar to those found in people with MS) to mice with MS-like symptoms makes the mice sicker. Additionally, giving 'A1' autoantibodies to these mice leads to 'A1' malfunction and significantly increased death and damage to nerve cells compared to mice injected with non-specific antibodies, which do not enter nerve cells. The next step is to test treatments that minimalize the harmful effects of 'A1' autoantibodies on nerve cells. This work suggests a new theory about how nerve cells are damaged in MS. By understanding how 'A1' autoantibodies and 'A1' malfunction cause nerve cell damage or death, we will be able to design new medications to treat neurodegeneration in MS, reduce the disability associated with neurodegeneration and improve the lives of persons living with MS.

column36: A Biophysical Mechanism of Vaping Toxicants in E-Cigarette/Vaping Associated Lung Injury
column37: Use of e-cigarettes and vaping devices are often touted as safer alternatives to traditional smoking. As more users transition to modern inhalation devices, a health crisis has quietly developed. E-cigarette/vaping associated lung injury (EVALI) can range from shortness of breath to severe lung damage requiring intensive care. Little is known about what causes EVALI, but evidence suggests that it may stem from an interaction between toxicants in the vape and the pulmonary surfactant - a thin layer inside the lungs that helps with the expansion and contraction of breathing. Through a partnership with the Canadian Centre for Alternatives to Animal Methods, we will use novel 3D bioprinted lung tissue models to ethically collect pulmonary surfactant that has been exposed to various components of vape. A range of biophysical experiments on extracted pulmonary surfactant, including a multidimensional suite of neutron scattering studies, will reveal sub-molecular level changes to the properties of pulmonary surfactant. These small changes can have very serious large-scale effects that may define the lung dysfunction observed in EVALI. Together, the knowledge gained from this study will offer new insights that can benefit the prognosis of EVALI victims and identify potential complications associated with long-term use. More immediately, the results will serve to promote the importance of informed use and to guide appropriate regulatory policies. On a wider scale, we intend to pioneer a biophysical perspective on health research and will explore a modern, animal-free method to connect fundamental research to medical solutions for acceleration of future discoveries.

column37: Canada lacks information on the oral health and dental care of our population and how these outcomes and services are distributed and evolving over time. Only two national surveys have been conducted in Canada, the last in 2007-2009. To address knowledge gaps and provide present-day information, we propose a collaboration with Statistics Canada through their Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) platform. The CHMS is a regularly repeated survey of the health of Canadians gathering detailed self-report, physical and biological data from a representative sample of people living in Canada. Our proposal is to add relevant and essential oral health clinical and self-report data in Cycle 7 of the CHMS. The project will use Statistics Canada's existing research infrastructure and expertise to address oral health-related knowledge gaps, to explore links between oral and systemic health, and establish a modern, world-class, research platform that will provide numerous opportunities for new research discovery and research training. This project aims to: a) Address research objectives and questions beyond those identified in the call for applications, focusing particularly on: social determinants and inequalities in oral health, oral health care and associated impacts; potential adverse effects of common dental treatments; and the relationships between oral and systemic health. b) Provide capacity building opportunities to a wide range of trainees and early career researchers in oral health-related research and beyond. c) Partner and collaborate with other large, national databank projects such as Health Data Research Network Canada and the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging, as well as with international peers running similar national oral health surveys in the UK and USA. d) Create multiple knowledge translation, exchange and mobilization opportunities with a range of stakeholders to ensure findings are widely diffused and used in policy and intervention development.

column36: Professional regulation in healthcare: Exploring trends, predictors, and the disciplinary action process for health professionals in Canada
column37: Independent regulatory bodies oversee and regulate health professionals. Disciplinary action by these bodies is one way to protect the public from clinicians who provide poor care or from those who abuse their position of power (e.g., sexual abuse or financial gain). Knowledge about current processes, practices, and outcomes of these disciplinary actions is needed to ensure that the public remains protected and has access to safe and effective care from health professionals. However, these processes, practices, and outcomes have never been summarized before in Canada. My project will determine the causes and consequences of discipline for health professionals (physicians, pharmacists, dentists, and nurse practitioners) across ten Canadian provinces to describe current processes and inform future changes. My research will fill a critical gap in understanding disciplinary action by characterizing what Canadian health professionals are disciplined for, what penalties are applied, and describing different regulatory body approaches to how health professionals are disciplined. With changes to regulatory processes pending in some provinces, this research will identify strengths and limitations of current processes, which will help regulators and governments implement evidence-based policy changes to ensure public safety. For example, comparing Canadian processes and outcomes to other countries and identifying international best practices will support the development of more efficient and effective regulation here. Universities that train health professionals can use this knowledge to improve curriculum related to professionalism, and regulatory bodies can create materials to educate clinicians about discipline. Ultimately, this research will identify potential areas of concern that may impact the safety and effectiveness of healthcare services in Canada.

column36: Waning Measles Immunity in Ontario: A Population-Based Cohort Study
column37: Immunity derived from the measles vaccine has been shown to decrease over time in countries where measles has been eliminated. This phenomenon is called waning immunity. Canada eliminated measles in 1998 and with increasing measles cases reported globally, waning immunity puts Canada at risk for future outbreaks. Although children are recommended to be vaccinated at 12 months of age, vaccination at older age has been associated with higher long-term immunity. This has been shown in Canada through studies resulting from measles outbreaks, albeit with small sample sizes. We aim to use a large population-based cohort study to examine the effect of age at and time since first dose of measles vaccine on measles immunity using antibody test results from Public Health Ontario (PHO) linked to health administrative data from 2010 to 2019. Results from this study may inform changes to the measles vaccine schedule to optimize measles immunity and ensure that future generations maintain measles elimination status.

column36: Investigating the Underlying Molecular Mechanisms of Brain Arteriovenous Malformations to Identify Novel Therapeutic Targets
column37: Brain arteriovenous malformation (bAVM) is a vascular disease with the development of abnormal blood vessel connections in the brain. The sites of abnormal connections are constantly under high-pressure blood flow, which makes them prone to rupture and leakage. Patients with bAVM often experience a wide range of neurological symptoms, such as seizure and impaired brain functions. Current treatment for bAVM is limited to surgical procedures, which are highly invasive and carry inherent risks of disabilities or even death. Due to these risks, the surgical procedures are not suitable for a significant portion of the patient population. The lack of a therapeutic drug product for bAVM is largely due to our insufficient understanding about the disease. As such, our group aims to investigate the biology of bAVM development and progression in the search for an effective pharmaceutical treatment option. Previously, our group had identified genetic mutations in the KRAS gene from clinical bAVM samples. These mutations were present specifically in the endothelial cells (ECs), which are cells that line the inner surface of blood vessels. KRAS is a protein that regulates multiple cellular functions, including cell growth, movement and metabolism. Mutations in the KRAS gene alter normal protein activities and disrupt the regulation of important cellular functions. In the present study, we aim to use a human brain EC model to characterize the effects of mutant KRAS on EC growth, movement, metabolism and barrier function. Then, we will use a technique, named phosphoproteomics, to examine changes in the regulation of cellular functions. Separately, we will perform a small molecule screen to search for novel compounds that can rescue the KRAS-induced cellular abnormalities, which will be followed by validations in animal studies. Together, this project contributes to our cumulative understanding of bAVM development and sheds light on novel therapeutic directions for the disease.

column36: System-level impact of antimicrobial-resistant Neisseria Gonorrhea in Canada: an equity-informed economic analysis
column37: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when organisms that cause infections, like bacteria or parasites, become immune or unaffected to medications. With time, these organisms slowly evolve and adapt, becoming strong against drugs. Therefore, some diseases that were previously under control are now more common and difficult to treat. Neisseria Gonorrhea is an example of a sexually transmitted infection that has become resistant to different types of antibiotics. Health issues associated with gonorrhea have become more frequent as some strains are now incurable. Furthermore, this issue represents high costs to the healthcare system, as infected patients get sicker and must be treated for longer periods. However, the impact of resistant gonorrhea usually affects vulnerable populations the most. As such, AMR has been identified as a global health threat and its mitigation is a priority in Canada. My research has three main objectives: first, I will estimate the health care costs attributed to resistant gonorrhea using clinical data. This will allow me to quantify the amount of money spent by the health care system to treat and cure infected patients. Second, I will conduct surveys to understand how society values the benefits associated with preventing resistant infections across high-risk and vulnerable population groups. This will allow me to consider the equity-informed impact of specific mitigation strategies. Lastly, I will use mathematical tools to predict the capacity of different mitigation strategies to save costs and lives. My study will provide decision-makers with high-quality evidence on the health impact and costs related to resistant gonorrhea in the next years and the value of implementing preventive interventions. It will also be the first of its kind to consider equity and different at-risk populations. These results will provide evidence to help reduce the already alarming scale of AMR.

column36: The mental health consequences of COVID-19 stress on children and parents: A multinational, longitudinal cohort study
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in significant changes for families that include heightened risk of job loss and financial insecurity, changes to schedule, interpersonal disconnection, and related confusion, fear, and anger. These experiences pose a clear risk to the well-being of children, as they are still in development and sensitive to stressful experiences. Despite international calls for research on the mental health consequences of COVID-19 for vulnerable groups, few studies have been designed to determine the extent of mental health difficulties among children during this period. As such, the proposed study plans to carry out a series of investigations into the mental health ramifications of COVID-19 on both parents and children. To achieve these objectives, data will be collected from two sources that include: the international Child Resilience and Managing Pandemic Emotional Distress in Families (CRAMPED) longitudinal cohort study and the national COVID-19 Adjustment, Resilience, and Experience (CARE) cohort study. Data will be collected on COVID-19 related stress, family functioning, parental childhood experiences, and parent/child mental health. The proposed project will explore the relationship between COVID-19 stress and mental health, as well as how parental COVID-19 stress influences child mental health. In addition, the way in which early-life adversity and positive experiences influence respective risk and resiliency in the relationship between COVID-19 stress and parental mental health, will be explored. Given the substantial social disruptions that COVID-19 presents to children and families, the proposed research is paramount for better understanding the impact, as well as identifying public health targets to intervene and deter substantial individual and social burden.

column36: Digital Epidemiology Applications for Promoting Resilient Health Systems Response to Pandemics
column37: In the face of health emergencies such as pandemics and natural disasters, researchers, clinicians, and public health professionals have been working to promote 'resiliency' in health systems. Resilient health systems can prepare for and respond to crises while maintaining core functions (e.g. offer elective surgical care). There is a wealth of data collected outside of our health system (e.g. global airline traffic, location data from cellphones, social media interactions, etc.) that can be used to help health systems prepare for and respond to emergencies. This work will explore how this digital data and a branch of computer science known as artificial intelligence can be used to guide public health response to an infectious disease emergency, using COVID-19 as an example. The first aim will involve creating guidelines for ethical collaborations with private technology companies to build and use software products to help health systems respond to emergencies. The second aim will create an infectious disease simulation model to help guide decision-making on international border closures (i.e. how risky is leaving a border open in the context of a pandemic?). The last aim will create a model to forecast COVID-19 burden in small geographical areas (roughly the postal code level) across Ontario. COVID-19 is among a series of infectious diseases that have emerged or re-emerged in the last twenty years along with SARS, H1N1, MERS, Ebola, and Zika. There will be emergencies to come, in the form of infectious diseases or otherwise, and COVID-19 offers a vital opportunity to prepare our health systems accordingly.

column36: Identifying areas for quality improvement of pediatric emergency and critical care in Pakistan
column37: Over 6 million children and adolescents die each year, largely in low- and middle-income countries, due to preventable causes. Pakistan is a middle-income country with among the highest number of child and adolescent deaths worldwide. Community prevention strategies, such as sanitation and vaccination campaigns, have dramatically improved child health and survival in Pakistan. However, children continue to develop severe illness due to infectious diseases, injuries and chronic conditions. High-quality emergency hospital services are needed to improve survival for children with these conditions. Challenges to providing essential care include poorly functioning triage systems, insufficient trained personnel, and lack of functional medical equipment and medications. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic may place additional strain on the health status of children in Pakistan due to threats to food security, increased poverty, lack of access to primary healthcare and fear of contracting the virus by visiting the hospital. Hospital resources may be overwhelmed by the number of sick adults, detracting from routine and emergency care for children. This project aims to describe causes and rates of death among children and adolescents (0 to 14 years) presenting to district healthcare services prior to and following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020. We will use patient registry data and routine community follow-up to identify risk factors for child death that may be mitigated by improved quality of hospital care. This research will inform subsequent hospital-based care improvement initiatives in Pakistan that are contextualized to the current conditions of the COVID-19 pandemic.

column36: Investigating Sex and Gender Effects on the Neurobiology of Autism
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) that affects social communication and behaviour. ASD can be presented categorically as a clinical diagnosis and dimensionally as autistic traits that can be presented continuously in the population. Our understanding of ASD is largely based on males as this condition affects males three times more than females. This male-based understanding leads to significant gaps in our knowledge about how biological sex and gender can play a role in mechanisms and risks that may lead to ASD. Previous studies have shown that difficulties of social communication in ASD may result from abnormal brain development affecting the coordinated activities of white matter tracts; however, the effects of sex and gender remain largely unclear. Thus, the proposed study will investigate the effects of sex and gender on structural connectivity of the brain in ASD. We will measure biological sex based on their genetic characteristics and their sex assigned at birth. Gender will be measured using parental reports of the Gender Identity Questionnaire for Children. Using available neuroimaging data from the POND Network, an integrated discovery program across Ontario, I will use both a categorical approach to compare ASD and control participants and a dimensional approach where I will be comparing all POND NDD and control participants based on their autistic traits measured by the Social Communication Questionnaire. We aim to test two models that may coexist: males and females with autism differ by 1) regions of the brain that are affected and 2) extent of the brain regions that are affected. Findings from this study will give direction for future investigations of how changes in the brain are related to differences in behaviour between males and females with ASD and autistic traits and help determine possible sex/gender-specific targets for intervention and support.

column36: Exploration of Epigenetic Profiles in Circulating Tumor DNA to Identify Predictive Cancer Biomarkers
column37: Current methods of tumor assessment through direct analysis of tumor tissue are invasive, painful, costly, and risky. Fortunately, much of the important information used for tumor assessment can be obtained from a cancer patient's blood, where material from dying tumor cells can be captured and analyzed. New non-invasive technologies using small amounts of blood are enabling extraction of tumor information for cancer diagnosis and monitoring response to treatment. In some instances, this information has also been used to select the optimal drug for treating a cancer patient in a process termed 'precision medicine'. One of the components extracted from cancer patient's blood is DNA from the tumor itself. Tumor-derived DNA fragments floating in the circulation hold a wealth of information that can be used to guide treatments. Specifically, new classes of drugs which act to change how genes in the tumor are controlled are moving into clinical settings. Unfortunately, tumor tissue is currently required to evaluate whether these drugs are having their intended effect in the tumor. Patterns of biological markers in the blood-derived DNA may hold information that will help guide clinicians on this new class of drugs, and evaluating these patterns is the goal of my project. In addition to guiding treatments, these markers may eventually be used to predict tumor growth without having to see the tumor itself in the patient. Our method, if successful, may be employed in the clinic for early cancer detection, monitoring of tumor recurrence, and prediction of patient tumor drug response on an individualized basis. Our method fills a crucial space in the health care industry for non-invasive evaluation of cancer patients.

column36: Evaluating Duchenne muscular dystrophy treatments with a 3D innervated skeletal muscle model
column37: Motor neurons are cells that transmit electrical signals from the brain to skeletal muscle cells and evoke contractions that assist in human functions such as walking, swallowing and breathing. The position on muscle fibers where motor neurons attach is referred to as the neuromuscular junction. Although it is well accepted that neuromuscular junction activity is vital to skeletal muscle function and health, it is difficult to study the role of neuromuscular junction activity on healthy or diseased human skeletal muscle in part due to a lack of appropriate culture methods. To overcome this technical hurdle, we created and characterized a three-dimensional model of human skeletal muscle tissue containing motor neurons that can produce skeletal muscle cell contractions when treated with the biologically relevant stimuli. Furthermore, we miniaturized our innervated human skeletal muscle tissue platform allowing us to create many replicate tissues. Miniaturization is particularly important when performing research studies with precious human biopsy samples. In the current application, our goal is to use our pre-clinical tool to study the human neuromuscular junction in the context of the genetic disorder, Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy harbor a mutation in a gene that contains the instructions to produce a protein called dystrophin. Dystrophin is situated near the neuromuscular junction in skeletal muscle cells, but an involvement in regulating neuromuscular junction activity is not clear. The goal of our study is to uncover new roles of the neuromuscular junction in Duchenne muscular dystrophy disease progression and to evaluate the impact of clinically approved drugs that modify neuromuscular junction activity as a possible treatment for Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients.

column36: Novel Cholinergic Biomarkers in Dementia: An Imaging Study Using Brain Quantitative Structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Eye Optical Coherence Tomography
column37: Dementia is one of ten leading causes of death in Canada. Dementia is a syndrome that leads to loss of cognitive function and independence. Delaying its onset by just 2 years can decrease its incidence by 19% and its economic burden by $218 billion in the next 30 years in Canada. While there is no cure for dementia, investigational interventions appear most effective in early stages of the disease. As such, detecting dementia's underlying disease process early is important. A major contributor to loss in cognitive function in the commonest diseases leading to dementia is degeneration of the brain's cholinergic system, which regulates attention and memory. I intend to make early detection of this system's degeneration quicker and less expensive by proposing a novel eye biomarker. To test this eye biomarker, I will investigate whether the volume of certain cholinergic-rich layers of an eye structure called the retina correlate with the volume of the brain's cholinergic-rich center and certain indicators of cognition in individuals with common diseases leading to dementia, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. These individuals will mostly be in the early stages of the disease. Both the brain's and retina's cholinergic rich-centers have been shown to undergo changes in their volume in dementia, but their correlation has not been investigated to date. For this investigation I will consider factors that may impact my analysis, for example the type of dementia the individual has, as well as their age and sex. Should eye biomarkers correlate with brain biomarkers, this can be a potential screening tool that is both more time and cost effective than brain imaging or neuropsychiatric tests for the detection of dementia in the early disease stage when investigational interventions appear to be most effective. I hope my work in early detection of dementia will help advance the cause of Canada's national strategy to better understand dementia and decrease its burden.

column36: Determining the therapeutic potential of HLA-deficient human pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-like cells
column37: Diabetes affects 10% of Canadians and increases blood sugar levels, which causes kidney failure, blindness, and other diseases. Patients with diabetes must therefore take medications to control blood sugar levels, but many of these, like insulin injections, do not fully normalize blood sugar levels and negatively affect quality of life. Transplantation of the pancreas or pancreatic islets - the part of the pancreas that makes insulin- can restore normal blood sugar levels without monitoring or input from patients, and in this way is superior to common diabetes drugs. However, there are two major problems with transplantation: 1) there are not enough organs for all patients, and 2) patients must take immune suppressing drugs to prevent organ rejection. These drugs have many side effects, such as increasing the risk of heart disease, infections, and cancer. Using human pluripotent stem cells, which can develop into any organ in the body, we can now make islet-like cells in vitro. Like islets, these mini-organs produce insulin and can restore normal blood sugar levels in diabetic animals. However, unlike organs used for transplantation, stem cells can multiply endlessly in vitro and are not in limited supply. Therefore, islet-like cells could be a superior, widely accessible therapy for diabetes. However, immune suppressing drugs would still be needed to prevent rejection, which would increase the risk of dangerous side effects. Scientists have engineered modified stem cells that can potentially avoid immune rejection by genetically editing a group of proteins known as "HLA", transforming them into universal donor stem cells. This proposal will study whether these stem cells can be used to generate safer islet-like organs in vitro. I will focus on whether these HLA-deficient islet-like organs can effectively control blood sugar levels, and how well they can avoid rejection without immunosuppression. This work could lead to a novel and superior therapy for diabetes.

column36: Short-term Cognitive Effects of Hearing Aids and Personal Sound Amplification Products in Older Adults with Mild to Moderate Hearing Loss: A Longitudinal Comparative Study
column37: According to Speech-Language & Audiology Canada, hearing loss is the third most common chronic disability among older adults. Hearing loss has also been associated with accelerated cognitive decline and an increased risk of being diagnosed with dementia. Yet, mild to moderate hearing loss remains under-treated, notably due to the high cost of conventional hearing aids. It is therefore important to investigate the potential of low-cost alternatives to protect the cognition of older adults with hearing loss. One alternative is the use of personal sound amplification products, which are inexpensive and widely available devices that amplify sounds. Studies have shown that these devices help understand speech better and improve the quality of life of older adults with mild to moderate hearing loss. However, there is no evidence that the use of these devices can efficiently address cognitive decline associated with hearing loss. The objective of my project is to compare the cognition of older adults with mild to moderate hearing loss before and after using either conventional hearing aids, personal sound amplification products or no device for three months, and to study the changes in the brain related to each intervention. For this purpose, 150 older adults with mild to moderate hearing loss will be recruited and divided into three groups: 50 adults who will receive conventional hearing aids; 50 adults who will receive personal sound amplification products; and 50 adults who will receive no device. All participants will complete cognitive tasks and brain imaging before the interventions and three months later. After the three-month period, I expect both groups receiving devices to show a better cognition due to similar changes in cognitive regions of the brain. The results will provide new information to protect the cognition of older adults with hearing loss who cannot afford conventional hearing aids, and even more so for those at risk of cognitive decline or dementia.

column36: Preclinical assessment of endovascular hydrogel embolization for the treatment of vascular disorders
column37: Recent advances in technology has furthered our ability to treat various blood vessel diseases through minimally invasive procedures, as opposed to open surgery. One such treatment is endovascular embolization, where through a blood vessel puncture, catheters can be navigated to various parts of the body, and embolic material can be delivered to seal the diseased blood vessels. This is used to treat cerebral aneurysms, bleeding, or abnormal vessels. However, there are still limitations in terms of the safety and efficacy of this treatment, and those usually relate to limitations of the embolic material used. Current materials such as coils or liquids may not fully seal the blood vessel abnormality, leading to incomplete treatment, or be difficult to fully control, causing off target embolization leading to stroke. Finding better embolization materials and methods would improve the ability to treat a wide range of diseases safely and effectively without requiring open surgery. One possibility is through hydrogels, a class of materials which may be modified to meet the needs of an ideal embolization agent. We are investigating the use of hydrogels as an embolization agent, using biologically inert, light sensitive, liquid formulas. Once injected through the catheter, it fills the blood vessel and then solidifies through a crosslinking process. The crosslinking process is driven by a light source embedded within the catheter, which can be adjusted to give varying degrees of hydrogel viscosity. This allows for better control and improved filling of the target vessel, hopefully leading to better treatment outcomes. The goal of our study is to test and finetune this technology, through 3D printed models and animal models of various diseases, including aneurysms, blood vessels, and tumors.

column36: Functional characterization of circular RNAs in neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: Prostate cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers in men worldwide. Localized prostate cancer can be highly curable, however, the overall survival rate for metastatic prostate cancer is only around 30%. Metastatic prostate cancer is a heterogenous disease consisting of different subtypes such castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC). NEPC, in particular, is lethal with most patients survive less than two years after diagnosis. Research is needed to further dissect the progression of NEPC in order to identify therapeutic targets and biomarkers to improve clinical outcome. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are noncoding RNAs with unique circular structure and have been shown to play important roles in various cellular processes as well as cancer development. Our group and others demonstrated that they can promote the progression of localized prostate cancer. However, how circRNAs affect metastatic prostate cancer development has not been explored. We aim to investigate the function of circRNAs in metastatic prostate cancer with a focus on NEPC due to its poor clinical outcome. We performed RNA sequencing of 5 CRPC and 5 NEPC patient tumours and identified circRNAs that are associated with NEPC. We aim to investigate the potential function of these circRNAs and how they may contribute to the development of aggressive prostate cancer phenotype. Our study will provide the first functional characterization of circRNAs in metastatic prostate cancer which remains largely incurable at this moment. We aim to impact disease management by revealing novel therapeutic targets and biomarkers.

column36: Improving Food Purchasing Behaviours of Canadians at-risk for Type 2 Diabetes Using Front-of-Pack 'High-in' Warning Labels and the FoodFlip(C) Smartphone Application
column37: Grocery stores are filled with many food choices and confusing marketing messages. The Canadian government recently introduced regulations that will require front-of-pack warning labels that can help consumers easily identify foods high in nutrients to limit: total sugars, saturated fat, and sodium. My research will look at how these warning labels can help individuals at high risk for type 2 diabetes grocery shop for healthy foods. First, I will use a packaged food database to identify foods that will carry the warning labels and foods that are not consistent with the guidelines for individuals at high risk for diabetes. By comparing these two categories of foods, I can see how the front-of-pack warning labels match the dietary guidelines for individuals at high risk for diabetes. Second, I will assess if a mobile app with warning labels can help consumers make decisions about which foods to buy while grocery shopping. Researchers in my training lab have developed a mobile app called FoopFlip(C) that shows the Nutrition Facts table and warning labels with healthier alternatives when users scan barcodes of foods or search foods by name. In this study, participants will be randomized to see different features of the App (Nutrition Facts table only or all the features) or not receive any App. I will look at purchased groceries for 6 weeks to see how the information on the App helped participants make healthy food choices. I will also send an online survey to participants to see how the App affected their nutritional knowledge and purchasing behaviours. My research will show whether user-friendly mobile apps can be developed to help Canadians make healthier food choices and change purchasing behaviours in relation to their health conditions.

column36: Vasopressor Selection and Administration in Septic Shock
column37: Septic shock is infection that overwhelms the body with low blood pressure and is associated with a very high possibility of death in the hospital (40-50%). These patients receive fluids and antibiotics for treatment. As well, they receive medications called vasopressors (such as norepinephrine) that are infusions into the vein to keep the blood pressure up. But vasopressors themselves carry risks, such as causing abnormal heart rhythms and lack of oxygen to parts of the body that can result in death. Guidelines for the use of vasopressors recommend norepinephrine as the first one to use for care of patients with septic shock. However, it is unknown how often norepinephrine is used as the first choice in Canada and what factors might be associated with failure to use it as recommended by guidelines. Additionally, there is uncertainty about whether special catheters called central venous catheters are needed to deliver norepinephrine. On the one hand, these catheters remove risk of damage to veins in the arms and surrounding tissues, however, they have their own risks including bloodstream infection, bleeding and damage to the lungs during placement. To address these concerns, I will use detailed data from Alberta that includes information on vasopressor use and other information about patients and their care. I will look at variation in use of norepinephrine for patients with septic shock and will determine whether the presence of a central venous catheter influences vasopressor choice. I will also perform a decision analysis examining whether doctors should place central venous catheters for use of norepinephrine, weighing the risks and benefits. This work will 1) identify variation in what medication for blood pressure doctors choose and 2) identify the best way for norepinephrine to be given. Since many people get septic shock every year and there is a high death rate, this study is important, and may have a large impact on patients' care in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Use and effectiveness of zoledronic acid as a second-line treatment for osteoporosis
column37: Osteoporosis is a brittle bone disease that can result in debilitating fractures. Osteoporosis is a major health problem in Canada with over 2 million people affected, an estimated 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men will experience an osteoporotic fracture. The spine and hip are common fracture sites in older adults. Spine fractures reduce quality of life and are often accompanied by difficulty breathing. Hip fractures are deadly: up to one third of patients die within the year after hip fracture. In addition, up to a quarter of patients enter a nursing home for the first time following hip fracture. Thankfully, medications are available to strengthen bones and reduce fracture risk. In Ontario, residents over the age of 65 receive drug coverage through the Ontario Drug Benefit program. Weekly doses of oral bisphosphonates are the first-choice therapy, which are taken by mouth and can be hard on the stomach. However, some patients stop taking their medications because they are not working, are difficult to swallow and then cause digestive issues. As a result, patients need to switch to more potent therapy, such as an annual infusion of zoledronic acid. Zoledronic acid is very effective in preventing fractures and recently, questions about how often patients need an infusion of zoledronic acid and when it is appropriate to stop therapy have arisen. Uncertainty about the relationship between dosing frequency and the benefits and harms of zoledronic acid are important clinical questions identified by Osteoporosis Canada. We are working directly with Osteoporosis Canada to answer questions about zoledronic acid therapy for osteoporosis. Results will inform clinical practice guidelines currently in development.

column36: Access to post-discharge mental health care for transgender people in Ontario: a mixed methods study
column37: Transgender (trans) people are people whose gender identity is different than the sex they were assigned at birth. A trans person may be female, male, non-binary, or another gender identity. Trans people are at least 1% of the population. They face significant discrimination, violence, and marginalization in society for being who they are. They experience high rates of homelessness, unemployment, and lack of access to needed health care due to this discrimination. These experiences can lead to depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts and behaviour. Trans people have five times the rates of depression and anxiety compared to the general population, and ten times the rate of suicide attempts. For some trans people, these mental health symptoms may require a mental health hospitalization to treat. After they are discharged from the hospital, follow up care with a mental health professional can further improve symptoms and reduce risks of suicide and readmission to hospital. However, many trans people have experienced discrimination within the health care system so many may avoid care after discharge. No one has studied the mental health care trans people need and use after discharge. My study will use health record data from trans patients to understand what diagnoses and other factors may lead to needing a hospitalization in the first place. I will also look at how many trans people are able to access timely mental health care after discharge, i.e. within a month of discharge. I will use these results to design interview questions so I can ask trans people directly about their experiences of hospitalization and seeking care after discharge. Together, the health record data and interviews will be used to create a model of what mental health care trans people need after discharge, and what can facilitate or prevent trans people from accessing the care they need. This model will allow us to build a better mental health care system for and with trans people.

column36: Measuring uptake and effectiveness of direct-acting antiviral treatment for hepatitis C among key populations in Ontario: a population-based retrospective cohort study
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HepC) targets the liver and, if left untreated, can lead to cirrhosis, liver cancer, and death. HepC is a major public health problem in Canada, affecting an estimated 250,000 Canadians and leading to more years of life lost than any other infectious disease. However, with the advent of a HepC cure (direct-acting antiviral treatment) in 2015, public health efforts have shifted towards the elimination of HepC. Achieving elimination will require reaching key populations - including people who inject drugs and immigrants from HepC-endemic countries - that are disproportionately burdened by HepC and who may also experience unique challenges in accessing healthcare. To date, there is a lack of research assessing the uptake and effectiveness of direct-acting antiviral treatment for HepC in Ontario at a population-level, both overall and within key populations - my proposed research project aims to fill this knowledge gap. This proposed research will use data from a population-based cohort of people living with chronic HepC in Ontario to address the following objectives: 1) measure direct-acting antiviral treatment uptake in Ontario; 2) identify potential disparities in direct-acting antiviral treatment uptake among key populations; 3) estimate the effect of direct-acting antiviral treatment on health outcomes including liver-related and all-cause mortality and explore whether treatment effectiveness differs meaningfully between members of key populations and other Ontarians. This research will provide evidence on the uptake and effectiveness direct-acting antiviral treatment among all Ontarians with chronic HepC. Planned comparisons of treatment uptake and effectiveness between members of key populations and other Ontarians may inform future provincial (or national) interventions to reduce HepC-related disparities and work towards HepC elimination.
