column36: Improving the management of patients with diabetes and coronary artery disease using large clinical and administrative registries from Ontario
column37: Approximately 7% of the Canadian population is living with diabetes. Diabetes increases the blood sugar levels, which may cause severe and diffuse obstructions in the heart vessels. If left untreated, these obstructions may lead to heart attacks and death. Many are the challenges when dealing with heart disease in patients with diabetes. Drugs commonly used to treat heart conditions in the general population, such as beta-blockers, may have a detrimental effect on diabetes control. Procedures that are frequently used to fix the heart vessels in the general population, such as angioplasty with stent, cannot fix the complex lesions caused by diabetes. We will study better approaches to treat heart disease in patients with diabetes, aiming to prevent heart attacks, hospitalizations, and ultimately death. In the first part of this project, we will evaluate the role of beta-blockers in patients with diabetes and heart disease, using large populational registries from Ontario. This project will establish if these pills have any effect in preventing heart attacks and death, which will help doctors to decide if they should prescribe this medication to patients with diabetes. The second part of this project will focus on the procedures used to fix the lesions in the heart vessels during a heart attack in patients with diabetes. Open-heart bypass surgery can repair the complex lesions caused by diabetes better than angioplasty with stent, but angioplasty is a less invasive procedure, allowing patients to recover faster. We will determine which of these procedures have better long-term results after years following the heart attack, using data from the Ontario registries. We are particularly interested if open-heart surgery, compared to angioplasty with stent, can prevent the occurrence of new heart attacks and death. Taken together, our results will improve the cardiovascular health of patients with diabetes.

column36: Associations between the physiological consequences of sleep apnea and cerebral small vessel disease in community dwelling adults
column37: Over half a million Canadians currently live with dementia, and the rising prevalence of dementia is a pressing public health concern. With no effective cures for dementia, there is a need to identify treatable risk factors. Dementia can result from many brain changes, one of the most important being small vessel disease (SVD) of the brain, or damage to brain's blood vessels. SVD is seen in one third of all dementia patients and half of patients with Alzheimer's disease. However, we only partly understand its causes. A possible risk factor for SVD is sleep apnea, a condition caused by collapse of the airway in sleep that affects over 5 million Canadians. It has several negative consequences for the body, including sleep disruption, low blood oxygen, high blood pressure, and a "fight or flight" stress response, which can all lead to SVD in animal studies. There are discrepancies in recent research about the effect of sleep apnea on SVD. Thus, my project aims to identify how each consequence of sleep apnea is specifically related to each form of brain SVD, and to investigate the potential underlying mechanisms. I will analyze sleep and brain scan data from over 1000 adults in four studies coordinated by our lab spanning a wide range of age, and sleep apnea and dementia severity. I will relate SVD measures measured by brain scans and after-death specimens to measures of sleep disruption, low blood oxygen, and activation of the "fight or flight" stress response obtained from wearable devices. I predict that sleep apnea and its consequences are related to SVD burden measured by brain scans and after-death specimens, and that they may, alone or in combination, drive the associations between SVD and decreased memory and cognition. Results from this study will support clinical trials of treatment for sleep apnea or its physiological effects to prevent or even reverse SVD, which may potentially improve the health of millions of Canadians who are at risk for dementia.

column36: Modulation of a Candida albicans Virulence Trait by Lactobacillus-Secreted Beta-Carbolines
column37: In humans, the fungus Candida albicans naturally colonizes mucosal sites such as the mouth and vagina. As a member of the commensal microbial community, C. albicans is an opportunistic pathogen that can cause superficial infections in healthy people and life-threatening systemic disease in immunocompromised individuals. Approximately 75% of people with a vagina will experience vaginal candidiasis, commonly known as a yeast infection, at least once in their lifetime. Previous work demonstrated that a decrease in the abundance of commensal bacteria, due to factors including antibiotic treatment, allows for the overgrowth of fungi and the development of fungal infections. Current research is therefore focused on exploiting probiotic bacteria, such as Lactobacillus species, to promote a healthy vaginal microbiome and prevent the development of vaginal yeast infections. To identify the mechanism by which probiotics affect the ability of C. albicans to cause disease, I examined the effects of several Lactobacillus species on a key virulence trait in C. albicans. I observed that several species of Lactobacillus produce a factor that represses this virulence trait and may reduce the ability of C. albicans to cause disease. I identified and characterized this secreted factor, which was a single small molecule. Through selection-based experiments, I was then able to identify C. albicans mutants which are resistant to the effects of the molecule. Whole genome sequencing and follow-up genetic analyses identified a resistance-conferring mutation in a protein that regulates C. albicans virulence. Currently, I am characterizing the ability of this molecule to treat vaginal candidiasis using a mouse model of infection. Collectively, this research will provide a novel strategy to treat recurrent fungal infections that affect millions of people worldwide.

column36: Extracellular DNA in cancer: implications for the anti-tumour immune response
column37: The human body is equipped with a stellar army - the immune system - that protects us from disease. Occasionally, dangerous invaders sneak past the immune system and wreak havoc on the body. Cancer is one such invader. Every year, cancer kills tens of thousands of Canadians. While new treatments have emerged that aim to bolster our natural defences, we still do not fully understand how cancer can evade the immune system and spread throughout the body. Without this knowledge, we rely heavily on chemotherapy and radiation therapy to eliminate cancer; unfortunately, these treatments can hurt healthy tissue. Most cancers develop from a few rogue cells that multiply rapidly within normal body tissue. These cancer cells produce toxic by-products that cause structural damage to their DNA - the molecular instructions that determine what a cell is made of and how it works. Damaged DNA can actually slow a tumour's growth, so tumour cells get rid of their damaged DNA by releasing it into the surrounding space and the bloodstream. Remarkably, cells from the immune system can capture and ingest this damaged DNA. In my doctoral work, I seek to demonstrate that the immune system recognizes damaged DNA from cancer cells as a harmful invader, similar to how it identifies bacteria, viruses, and other foreign invaders that harm healthy tissue. I also aim to show that when damaged DNA alerts the immune system to a cancerous invader, immune cells seek out and destroy tumour cells to protect healthy tissues from cancer. By understanding how the immune system recognizes and reacts to damaged tumour DNA, we can harness the power of our bodies' natural defenses and develop new treatments that help the body fight cancer on its own.

column36: Functional Genomic Analysis of Protein Kinases in the Human Fungal Pathogen Candida albicans
column37: Invasive fungal infections exert a devastating impact on human health worldwide, resulting in an estimated 1.5 million deaths per year. Candida albicans is a leading fungal pathogen of humans, with a crude mortality rate of 40% despite antifungal intervention. Poor patient outcomes are a result of the limited number of antifungal drug classes available to treat fungal infections, as well as the unprecedented increase in drug resistance. Thus, it is undeniable that there is a pressing need for the development of novel antifungal therapeutic strategies. Protein kinases have served as one of the largest protein classes targeted in pharmaceutical development, particularly in the field of cancer therapy, given their impact on diverse cellular functions and the fact that their activity is readily inhibited by small molecules. Few studies suggest that targeting kinases may be effective at combatting candidiasis however, a systematic exploration of kinases in the pathogenic fungus C. albicans is lacking. The goal of my project is to investigate the roles of protein kinases in C. albicans pathobiology in a systematic manner. To that end, I will complete the construction of a collection of C. albicans conditional expression mutants that will enable transcriptional repression of every kinase present in the C. albicans genome. Thus far, I have expanded this resource to 96% coverage, representing 141 out of 147 kinases. Using this expanded kinase collection, I conducted systematic phenotypic screens to identify genes required for fungal growth, antifungal drug tolerance and virulence in vitro, which led to the discovery of several kinases with previously undescribed roles in these processes. Future work will identify kinases required for in vivo infectivity using a murine model of invasive candiasis. Overall, this project will advance our understanding of protein kinases in C. albicans pathobiology and will expand our repertoire of fungal targets for therapeutic intervention.

column36: Elucidating the mechanisms governing interactions between the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans and macrophages
column37: Candida albicans is a leading cause of human fungal infections, which collectively result in as many deaths as the pathogens that cause tuberculosis and malaria, with more than 1.5 million deaths per year. There are a limited number of antifungal drugs available and even those are troubled by issues of both patient toxicity and the emergence of drug-resistant fungi. Developing a deeper understanding of how the human immune system interacts with C. albicans could lead to new avenues for antifungal drug discovery. The first line of defence against fungal infections are cells of the human immune system called macrophages, that engulf C. albicans but are ineffective at killing them. Engulfment triggers a physical change in C. albicans from circular yeast to elongated filaments - a transition important for the fungus' ability to cause disease. Although the mechanisms governing filamentation in macrophages could be exploited for antifungal drug development, they remain largely unknown. I recently identified that the macrophage-derived protein, prothymosin alpha (PTMA), triggers C. albicans filamentation. Building on this discovery, the goal of my research is to elucidate the mechanisms by which PTMA induces C. albicans filamentation and identify the genes used by the fungus to activate this transition. I will visualize the location of PTMA within the macrophage and how it interacts with the engulfed C. albicans using fluorescence microscopy. I will also use a biochemical approach to identify C. albicans proteins that interact with PTMA. Finally, using a genetic approach, I will identify the genes that C. albicans uses to initiate filamentation in macrophages. Altogether, my project is poised to determine the mechanisms underlying C. albicans filamentation in macrophages and reveal new therapeutic strategies to combat life-threatening fungal infections.

column36: Sex Differences in the Cardiometabolic Profiles and their Impact on Cardiovascular Diseases
column37: In Canada, the first cause of mortality in women is cardiac diseases. Risk factors for cardiac diseases differ between sexes; some of them being more frequent, having a worse impact or being specific to women. Compared to men, women are less physically active and more obese. As they get older, they have more rigid arteries, which can have a negative impact on cardiac health. Women are also exposed to pregnancy-related risk factors like pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure associated with damage to other organs). Women who suffer from pre-eclampsia develop more rigid arteries and are at increased risk of cardiac diseases in the rest of their life. These differences between sexes in risk factors suggest that different mechanisms may be involved in the development of cardiac diseases. For example, aortic stenosis (stiffening of a cardiac valve which becomes more difficult to open) in women leads to different complications on the heart when compared to men. We will thus compare sex differences in three separate settings: 1) obese patients with cardiac risk factors, 2) women who suffered from different pre-eclampsia subtypes during pregnancy, and 3) patients with aortic stenosis. Our hypothesis is that cardiac risk factors, related to blood cholesterol and blood sugar abnormalities, obesity, and pregnancy complications, will lead to accelerated development of rigid arteries, earlier and worse development of silent cardiac dysfunction, accelerated aortic stenosis progression and worse consequences of the aortic stenosis on the heart muscle in women. We will compare blood tests results, physical examinations, non-invasive evaluation of arterial rigidity, cardiac echocardiography and magnetic resonance imaging studies. Our project will help us better understand why cardiac diseases evolve differently between sexes. It may also help us improve the prediction of the risk of cardiac diseases and tailor preventive and therapeutic strategies for women.

column36: Identification de cibles therapeutiques pour le lupus erythemateux dissemine
column37: Le lupus est une maladie grave et imprevisible qui affecte majoritairement les femmes en age de procreer. La fameuse lesion cutanee en <<masque de loup>> est la manifestation la plus caracteristique du lupus, mais plusieurs autres parties du corps sont aussi endommagees par l'inflammation chronique, notamment les reins, les articulations et les poumons. Puisqu'il n'existe actuellement aucun moyen de guerir du lupus, le developpement de traitements plus efficaces est crucial. C'est pour cette raison que nous cherchons a mieux comprendre les mecanismes de cette maladie. L'une des principales caracteristiques du lupus est la presence abondante de structures appelees <<complexes immuns>>. Un trop grand nombre de complexes immuns en circulation peut mener a la formation de depots dans les tissus des patients atteints de lupus, et entrainer des dommages inflammatoires. Les neutrophiles, les cellules immunitaires les plus nombreuses en circulation, participent a l'elimination des complexes immuns et assurent habituellement la protection de l'hote contre les envahisseurs microbiens. Cependant, en contexte de lupus, les neutrophiles semblent reagir aux complexes immuns en attaquant les organes de l'hote et en causant des dommages qui menent a une inflammation incontrolee. Ils agissent donc, par erreur, comme s'ils avaient rencontre un microbe dangereux a eliminer. Dans ce projet, nous voulons etablir les facteurs qui menent a l'activation inadaptee des neutrophiles en reponse aux complexes immuns chez les patients atteints de lupus. De plus, nous etudierons les recepteurs des complexes immuns (recepteurs Fc) presents sur les neutrophiles, plus precisement le recepteur FcgRI, afin d'identifier la maniere par laquelle il contribue aux activites pro-inflammatoires des neutrophiles. A notre humble avis, ce projet est tres innovant car il se concentre sur la comprehension des mecanismes du lupus et tend a identifier, chez le neutrophile, une nouvelle cible therapeutique prometteuse.

column36: Identification des fonctions genomiques des recepteurs aux estrogenes dans le cancer de la prostate
column37: La prostate est une glande accessoire faisant partie de l'appareil reproducteur masculin. De maniere generale, sa biologie est dependante de l'action des hormones << males >>, soit les androgenes. Ces hormones se lient au recepteur aux androgenes, qui possede plusieurs roles cles dans les cellules de prostate comme le controle de la production de l'energie. Dans le cancer de la prostate, les cellules composant les tumeurs restent sensibles a ces hormones, et les therapies pharmacologiques utilisees pour traiter cette maladie visent donc a bloquer l'action du recepteur aux androgenes. Cependant, il arrive que les cellules cancereuses de prostate finissent par developper une resistance a cette << castration chimique >> et continuent de se multiplier malgre tout. Le besoin de trouver de nouveaux traitements contre le cancer de la prostate nous pousse a envisager de bloquer d'autres recepteurs hormonaux afin d'empecher la proliferation des cellules et le developpement de tumeurs. Les estrogenes et leurs deux recepteurs (alpha et beta) sont envisages comme nouvelles cibles d'interet, puisque ces derniers sont egalement localises au niveau de la prostate et sont necessaires a son bon developpement. Etant traditionnellement decrits comme les hormones << femelles >>, les estrogenes sont en fait tout aussi essentiels a la biologie de la prostate, et il est clair maintenant que des niveaux eleves d'estrogenes rendent le cancer de la prostate plus agressif. Cependant, leurs roles dans le cancer de la prostate ne sont toujours pas bien connus. Mon projet de recherche de doctorat consiste donc a combler cette lacune en etudiant les fonctions de ces recepteurs au niveau cellulaire, ce qui permettra d'ouvrir la voie a un nouveau traitement hormonal contre le cancer de la prostate qui sera capable de prolonger la vie des patients.

column36: Des mini-anticorps a chaine unique comme agent therapeutique pour prevenir la propagation de l'alpha-synucleine dans un modele murin de la maladie de Parkinson
column37: La maladie de Parkinson est caracterisee par des symptomes moteurs tels que des tremblements et une instabilite posturale. Ces derniers sont causes par la degenerescence d'un type specifique de neurones dans le cerveau. Ces neurones, appeles dopaminergiques, presentent des agregats intracellulaires majoritairement composes de la proteine alpha-synucleine. Les formes nocives d'alpha-synucleine ont la capacite de migrer d'une cellule a une autre et de declencher l'agregation dans les cellules saines. Son accumulation interfere ensuite avec une multitude de processus cellulaires, ce qui affecte le fonctionnement et la survie des cellules. Nous souhaitons stopper la propagation de l'alpha-synucleine dans le cerveau par l'utilisation de mini-anticorps de type << fragments variables a chaine unique >> (scFvs). Les scFvs sont plus petits que les anticorps traditionnels, ce qui leur confere une meilleure penetration des tissus. Ils font egalement moins reagir le systeme immunitaire et peuvent entrer a l'interieur des cellules pour cibler l'alpha-synucleine intracellulaire. Nous testerons l'efficacite de notre approche dans un modele pre-clinique. Nous utiliserons des souris auxquelles nous administrerons une forme d'alpha-synucleine qui a la caracteristique de se propager facilement d'une cellule a une autre. Nous injecterons le scFv a differentes etapes du developpement de la pathologie et etudierons le cerveau des souris. Nous croyons que nos mini-anticorps se montreront efficaces pour reduire la proliferation des formes nocives d'alpha-synucleine et par consequent la degenerescence des neurones dopaminergiques. Nous nous attendons donc a observer des symptomes moteurs moins importants chez les souris ayant recu le scFv. Si notre approche s'avere efficace, elle pourrait facilement etre adaptee a une utilisation chez l'humain. Notre projet pourrait donc progresser vers une etude clinique avec comme objectif de stopper la progression de la maladie de Parkinson.

column36: Etude de la contribution de l'adiposite viscerale et des lipides ectopiques en tant que mediateurs de l'association entre la condition cardiorespiratoire et la sante cardiometabolique
column37: Les consequences de l'obesite sur la sante et l'economie temoignent de l'urgence de sa prise en charge et de sa prevention. Cependant, l'evaluation de l'obesite en tant que facteur de risque pour la sante est difficile en pratique clinique en raison de son heterogeneite. En effet, malgre le fait qu'elle soit definie comme << une accumulation anormale ou excessive de graisse corporelle qui peut nuire a la sante >>, sa mesure en clinique repose sur l'indice de masse corporelle (IMC), un indicateur base sur la taille et le poids. Bien que son utilisation soit appropriee au niveau populationnel, l'IMC ne permet pas d'identifier l'obesite a risque pour la sante a l'echelle individuelle. En effet, cet indice ne tient pas compte de la quantite de graisse corporelle ni de sa repartition. Plusieurs travaux ont montre que l'accumulation de graisse a l'interieur de l'abdomen (obesite abdominale dite viscerale) est plus fortement associee aux problemes de sante que la quantite de graisse ou l'IMC. Les etudes suggerent que l'obesite abdominale reflete une incapacite du corps a entreposer le surplus d'energie sous forme de graisse sous la peau. Cette incapacite entraine un debordement de lipides (gras) qui s'accumulent pour former des depots de graisse a l'interieur de l'abdomen (au foie, entre autres) qui sont associes a un risque accru pour la sante. Par ailleurs, un facteur important a considerer dans la relation entre l'obesite abdominale et la sante est l'activite physique. En effet, une bonne condition physique est associee a un risque moindre de problemes de sante meme en presence d'obesite. Cependant, le role que joue l'obesite abdominale dans l'association entre la condition physique et la sante demeure meconnu. Cette etude vise a comprendre ce role afin de mettre en evidence, au-dela de l'IMC et de la perte de poids, l'importance d'evaluer et de prendre en charge l'obesite abdominale et d'ameliorer la condition physique pour mieux traiter/prevenir l'obesite en clinique.

column36: La depense energetique, les apports nutritionnels et le gain de poids durant la grossesse - Projet quebecois DEPENSE
column37: Problematique: En plus d'etre prevalant chez plus d'une femme sur deux, le gain de poids gestationnel (GPG) excessif engendre plusieurs complications pour la sante de la mere et de son futur enfant. Deux determinants importants du GPG est possiblement les apports et la depense en energie. Une meilleure comprehension des determinants du GPG excessif est necessaire afin d'identifier plus precocement les femmes a risque de GPG eleve et prevenir ainsi ses consequences indesirables sur la sante maternelle et neonatale. Objectifs: chaque trimestre de la grossesse, 1) quantifier les apports et la depense en energie et leurs principales composantes et evaluer leur evolution durant la grossesse; 2) comparer les apports et la depense en energie entre les groupes de GPG (excessif, adequat, insuffisant) et 3) determiner les variables maternelles qui predisent un changement accentue dans les apports et la depense en energie et/ou un GPG excessif. Methodologie: L'etude DEPENSE sera menee aupres de 40 femmes enceintes. Chaque trimestre de la grossesse, diverses variables maternelles seront evaluees par des questionnaires valides completes en ligne ou sur place au Centre de recherche du CHU de Quebec - Universite Laval. Les informations collectees portent sur les comportements sedentaires et alimentaires, la prise de supplements, les attitudes envers le gain de poids, la presence et la severite des douleurs lombaires et pelviennes, la qualite de sommeil et l'usage de tabac. La depense en energie au repos sera aussi mesuree a l'aide d'un appareil de calorimetrie indirecte. Les niveaux d'activite physique seront evalues par le port d'un accelerometre au poignet non dominant durant sept jours consecutifs, alors que les apports nutritionnels seront evalues par trois rappels de 24h web valides. Perspectives: Les resultats issus du projet permettront de mieux comprendre le GPG et ses determinants et ainsi favoriser l'optimisation des approches liees a la prevention du GPG excessif.

column36: New Risk-Stratification Tools in Organic Mitral Regurgitation: Best Approach for An Enlightened Clinical Decision-Making Process
column37: The mitral valve is a cardiac valve that ensures the right direction of the blood flow. Sometimes this valve is leaking (blood goes back in the wrong way) because the valve is distorted, this is Organic Mitral Regurgitation (OMR). When severe, this disease has serious consequences on the cardiac function. OMR is one of the most prevalent valvular heart diseases and it is associated with high rates of mortality. The only treatments are to repair or replace the valve surgically. When symptoms occur, patients must undergo surgery right away. Before the onset of symptoms, sending patients to surgery for OMR is controversial: physicians must balance the risk of surgery versus the risk of irrecoverable damage to the heart. Unfortunately, markers of heart damage are scarce and often lead towards sequels after intervention. Moreover, most triggers for surgery are not defined according to the sex of the patient (women have smaller cavities). The objective of this project is to develop and validate novel sex-specific imaging and blood markers to improve risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making process in asymptomatic patients with OMR. To achieve this objective, patients with OMR are recruited in the prospective PROGRAM study (NCT01835054; CIHR funded). These patients are followed 10 years and each year they undergo several clinical exams (i.e. echocardiography) in order to find good predictive parameters. There are currently over 195 participants and recruitment is still ongoing (objective of 330). This doctoral project will contribute to 1) obtain a better representation of the impact of valve leaking on the functional ability of these patients, 2) establish a better risk stratification, and 3) discriminate the patients who benefit from early ''prophylactic'' surgery from those who can wait without risk before surgery. Finally, differences between men and women in the pathophysiology, diagnosis, management, and treatment of OMR will be investigated by this study.

column36: Definition et validation d'indicateurs de qualite de soins pour les personnes agees victimes de traumatisme hospitalisees en soins aigus.
column37: Les aines sont a risque eleve de traumatismes dont les consequences sont souvent plus importantes que chez les adultes plus jeunes. Depuis 1991, le Continuum de soins en traumatologie (CST) est implante au Quebec dans le but de garantir l'accessibilite et la continuite des soins aux victimes de traumatismes, de la prevention des blessures jusqu'aux soins hospitaliers, de readaptation & de reintegration sociale post-traumatique. Le CST, qui s'appuie sur des criteres precis de qualite des soins dans ses etablissements (hopitaux et centres de readaptation), a permis de diminuer de facon importante la mortalite suite aux traumatismes. Toutefois, on constate qu'il n'y a aucun critere sur l'adaptation des soins aux personnes agees qui representent plus de 52% des patients admis dans les etablissements du CST. Ce projet vise donc a definir des indicateurs de qualite de soins hospitaliers adaptes aux personnes agees admises suite a un traumatisme et a les valider. Pour atteindre ces objectifs, une recension de la litterature scientifique sur le sujet sera realisee pour identifier une liste d'indicateurs potentiels. Par la suite, ces criteres seront soumis a un groupe d'experts en traumatologie et en geriatrie pour obtenir un consensus. Finalement, l'application des indicateurs sera evaluee avec les donnees du registre des traumatismes du Quebec qui regroupent tous les patients admis dans les centres de traumatologie du Quebec. La conformite a chacun des indicateurs sera evaluee pour chaque patient. Nous analyserons si la conformite a chacun de ces indicateurs permet de predire la survenue de trois issues de sante : le deces, les complications, le retour a domicile aupres l'hospitalisation et la readmission a l'hopital. Les connaissances issues de ce projet permettront d'identifier des criteres pour adapter les soins a la personne agee hospitalisee suite a traumatisme et permettront d'ameliorer les soins hospitaliers a cette clientele grandissante.

column36: Personalized prediction of Alzheimer's dementia development in at-risk individuals with mild cognitive impairment
column37: Since pathology from Alzheimer's disease (AD) can develop in the brain up to 20 years before symptoms appear, early diagnosis is needed to ensure treatment is started before significant brain damage develops. People with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may present measurable cognitive decline and are at high risk for dementia. These individuals are also important candidates for pharmaceutical trials of new AD treatments. However, it is very difficult to identify which individuals with MCI will go on to develop AD dementia. Existing methods of detecting AD pathology are either too costly to be used widely (e.g., positron emission tomography), or are not accurate enough on their own to be reliable prognostic tools in the clinic (e.g., magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or cognitive testing). In my project, I will develop the DaMoCLES score (Decline prediction using MRI, Cognition, and LifEStyle data). DaMoCLES will predict MCI conversion to AD dementia using (1) results of standard cognitive tests, (2) results of advanced MRI analyses detecting AD brain damage, (3) demographics, and (4) cardiovascular lifestyle risk factors (e.g., smoking, obesity, physical activity). I will use baseline and followup data (cognitive, clinical, and MRI) on over 900 MCI subjects in three existing studies to develop and test DaMoCLES. I will validate DaMoCLES prospectively in an independent dataset by predicting MCI conversion to AD in 400 MCI subjects from the Canada-wide COMPASS-ND study. DaMoCLES will identify key predictors for AD dementia and highlight new directions for research and intervention in early AD. Clinicians will use DaMoCLES to identify which MCI patients will develop AD dementia, aiding the design of personalized treatments to slow its progression. DaMoCLES will help optimize clinical trials for new treatments by enriching with MCI patients having AD-related cognitive decline. Optimized recruiting will shorten trial times and accelerate new treatment development.

column36: Understanding Inequalities in Lung Cancer Care and Outcomes in Canada
column37: Lung cancer is the most common and deadly cancer in Canada. The chances of survival beyond five years for individuals diagnosed with an advanced stage of lung cancer is extremely low. Previous studies have also shown that patients living in low socioeconomically deprived areas have higher chances of getting advanced lung cancer and dying from it. It has been shown that being diagnosed with advanced lung cancer is not the main reason why people are dying faster in these groups. Other potential reasons for observing lower survival in these groups are worse health or lower quality of care in comparison to those living in socioeconomically advantaged areas. My research focuses on examining inequalities in lung cancer care and survival in Canada, with a particular interest in understanding what drives these inequalities. I will be using a novel and unique dataset developed by Statistics Canada that links self-reported information from national-level health surveys to hospitalization, emergency department visit, and cancer diagnosis information obtained from health administrative databases. I will be estimating socioeconomic-based inequalities that exist at an individual-level, which is lacking in the evidence to date. The answers from my study will be useful inputs to inform the development of targeted interventions to deliver cancer care in a timely, effective, and equitable manner in Canada.

column36: Turning a new leaf: Examining referral pathways, service engagement, and mental health outcomes following discharge from an early intervention for psychosis
column37: Schizophrenia and related psychoses are debilitating conditions that emerge primarily in adolescence or young adulthood and are a leading cause of years lived with disability in Canada. Early intervention services aim to provide rapid and specialized care to improve outcomes in individuals with a first episode of psychosis. Most early intervention programs provide follow-up for two years. However, evidence suggests that there is a need for continued support following early intervention. As a result, research has begun to investigate the impact of transferring from early intervention services to primary, secondary, and tertiary care. However, comparatively little work has been done exploring service use and mental health outcome trajectories following early intervention longitudinally, as well as the predictors of these trajectories. Therefore, the proposed project will first describe referral pathways (transfers between primary, secondary, and tertiary care services), service engagement, and mental health outcomes two years following discharge using Quebec health administrative data (study 1). Using predictive modeling, patient factors that can predict these trajectories will be identified (study 2). Finally, interviews will be conducted with patients who were recently discharged out of an early intervention program (study 3). Interviews will discuss transfer experiences, barriers and facilitators to accessing and receiving new care, service engagement, and met and unmet needs. Ultimately, the proposed project will examine the critical issues in identifying the needs of patients who are no longer in an early intervention program; how primary, secondary and tertiary services can meet these needs; and which sorts of resources and supports could help maintain better outcomes after early intervention.

column36: Socioeconomic disparities in colorectal cancer diagnostic pathways and diagnostic interval
column37: Within the cancer system, socioeconomic factors influence screening, stage at diagnosis and cancer survival. Less is known about how socioeconomic factors affect initial access to the cancer system through diagnostic pathways. Diagnostic pathways represent the route a patient takes from initial presentation of symptoms or screening to diagnostic tests and the final cancer diagnosis. The diagnostic interval is the time between initial presentation of symptoms to final diagnosis. A longer diagnostic interval is associated with later stage at diagnosis, increased patient anxiety and potentially shorter survival. Policies and interventions, such as rapid diagnostic assessment programs, exist to clearly describe diagnostic pathways, shorten the diagnostic interval and improve cancer care. Contact continuity with a primary care physician (PCP), defined as repeated interactions with the same PCP, increases participation in cancer screening and could facilitate quicker referral to specialists. A consistent relationship with a PCP may result in better understand of the patients' health history and social situation, which could result in increased awareness of cancer symptoms and decreased time to diagnosis, however, little is known if having a consistent family doctor shortens the diagnostic interval. This thesis will use routinely collect data to determine differences in the diagnostic pathways and intervals by socioeconomic deprivation and understand if contact continuity with a regular PCP mediates these relationships for patients with a diagnosis of colorectal cancer in Ontario. Diagnostic pathways and intervals are modifiable factors at the system-level that policy makers can act upon to improve equitable access, quality of care, and health outcomes for cancer patients. This proposal lays the groundwork for future studies using routinely collected data to examine the impacts of policies and interventions that outline clear diagnostic pathways on inequalities.

column36: Resolving the cis-regulatory role of the histone post-translational modification H3K36me2 in driving tumorigenesis
column37: Changes to the DNA sequence -- genetic mutations -- have long been recognized to play a critical role in causing crippling afflictions. In addition to directly hampering the function of a single gene with known functions and a straightforward link to disease, indirect but potentially more damaging paths also exist. For example, the process of reading DNA itself is non-trivial, as they are wrapped around structural proteins called histones to form compact fibres, which, through multiple levels of organization, ultimately adopt complex 3D shapes in order to fit 2 meter long strands within our tiny cells. As a result, modifications to DNA that do not alter its sequence and those to histones, altogether known as epigenetic marks, can dictate how much a gene is read and consequently the amount of its biologically functional products -- proteins. We and others have discovered that certain epigenetic marks can stratify a number of heterogenous cancers into finer clinically distinct subtypes. Subsequently, we unveiled that some tumour subgroups are characterized by mutations to particular histone genes themselves or to epigenetic writers, demonstrating a convergence of downstream impacts. To do so, we applied gene editing and other techniques to mimic tumours in a dish, after which we subjected these models to a variety of epigenetic assays. Based on recent findings, we believe that perturbation of enhancer function can link epigenetic changes to eventual disease, with enhancers being DNA sequences that do not necessarily code for genes but can be brought in close proximity to activate genes for reading. We thus aim to supplement our previous epigenetic data with assays of 3D DNA organization to determine how enhancers' epigenetic marks and the way they fold onto other elements in 3D space contributes to cancer with specific epigenetic defects. These mechanistic insights will be crucial to improve our understanding of basic biology and inform therapeutic development.

column36: Neural tracking and neuroplasticity of social motor synchronization of children with autism spectrum disorder.
column37: One core symptom of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is social challenges, and a specific example of that is difficulty in synchronizing movements with a social partner. Neuroimaging techniques like electroencephalography (EEG) allow us to measure electrical activity in the brains of children with ASD and measure how much they engage in a synchronizing task at a specific brain wave frequency. Comparing the neural electrical activity of children with ASD or typical development (TD) allows us to show how brain activity could explain social motor challenges (Study 1). While children with ASD have social challenges, they have strong musical abilities and preferences. Music has also been shown to produce improvements to social and motor functioning and strengthens connections in motor regions in the brain. Therefore, we predict that the ability to synchronize movements and the associated brain electrical signals will improve after 16 weeks of music intervention (Study 2). Findings from Study 1 may reveal associations between brain electrical activity and ASD characteristics. These neural markers could explain some symptoms in ASD and EEG techniques can contribute to a cost-efficient diagnostic method of ASD. Findings from Study 2 may show that music programs can improve social motor functioning by changing brain activity, which would enhance the overall health and well-being of children with ASD.

column36: Apoptotic cell signaling regulates tissue morphogenesis and cancer progression
column37: In the Bouchard Lab, we study transitions that cells undergo during development and how these processes relate to disease and cancer. Specifically, I study cell suicide, a natural process called apoptosis. This phenomenon plays a role in shaping tissues and organs. Take for instance the cells in a tadpole tail, which die off as the tadpole matures into a frog. We study a similar process in the developing mammalian urinary tract. Here, a small piece of tissue is removed by apoptosis allowing the ureter, which transports urine from the kidneys, to connect to the bladder. During cancer therapies as well, where chemo or radiation therapy lead to massive amounts of cancer cell death, the remaining carcasses must be removed from the tissue to prevent inflammation. Specialized cells called phagocytes devour dying cells by cell engulfment. Phagocytes have detectors that recognize "eat me" signals exhibited on the dying cell surface and begin the process of engulfment. A molecule engineered by scientists at Osaka University in Japan efficiently binds and blocks the "eat me" signal. I genetically modified a mouse to produce this molecule, where it will block the "eat me" signal of dying cells in the developing urinary tract of the mouse embryo. By looking at how this effects the other cells/phagocytes in the tissue, we can deduce how this signal is working and what genes are involved in the process. I will also be using this molecule in cancer mouse models, to block the phagocytes from clearing dying cancer cells, and compare my observations to those I find in the developing urinary tract. Our ultimate goal is to understand how the body manages apoptosis which will help scientists and doctors develop improved cancer therapies.

column36: Internal and external mechanisms of 'feeling fat': The roles of negative affect, thought-shape fusion, and social comparison in eating disorder maintenance
column37: 'Feeling' fat is a sense of physically gaining weight when no real change in size has occurred. This is common in people with eating disorders and makes it difficult to overcome symptoms. Our first goal is understanding if negative emotions, atypical thought patterns about eating "fattening" food, or both cause feeling fat. To do this, women with and without eating disorders will complete one of two tasks: imagining experiencing negative emotion or imagining eating a "fattening food." They will rate how fat they feel, and sensors will record their bodies' reactions. Changes in heartbeat and sweat gland activity can indicate levels of emotion regulation and stimulation. We will compare the levels of feeling fat, heart, and sweat gland activity to see if women with eating disorders feel fatter after the negative emotion and fattening food tasks compared to their normal level of feeling fat. We expect the imagination tasks to cause feeling fat and that our measures will reflect this. Our second goal is to clarify the role of social comparison - contrasting one's shape with another person's - in feeling fat. Participants will view a series of images, including women who are thin and obese and neutral objects, while sweat response (i.e., stimulation level) is recorded. We will compare firsthand reports of feeling fat and sweat responses to see if women with eating disorders feel fatter and are more stimulated when viewing thin and obese versus neutral images. All results will be compared in women with and without eating disorders to see if these findings are only true in eating disorders. Results may improve treatments for eating disorders, which focus only on negative emotions causing 'feeling fat.' If food-related thought patterns influence this experience, we must address such thoughts. Further, since biofeedback treatments use technology to track bodily functions and reduce associated symptoms, monitoring heartbeat and sweat response may help treat feeling fat.

column36: Deconstructing cancer evolution using population genetic inference and ecological understanding
column37: Cancer is an evolving disease. The evolutionary trajectory of cancer is defined by the selective pressure within the tissue microenvironment, or ecological niche, of origin. As new mutations arise, the potential for new cellular phenotypes, or subclones, with varying degrees of fitness also increases. This intratumor heterogeneity, or clonality, is known to be an important factor in predicting cancer progression, survival, therapeutic response, and drug resistance. Currently, there are issues with quantifying and detecting clonality in cancer. Existing methods utilize short-read sequencing to reconstruct subclonal populations through either single-nucleotide variant (SNV) analysis or copy number aberration (CNA) analysis. SNV methods use variant allele frequencies to calculate cancer cell fractions, but they require statistical correction because copy number changes and variable whole-genome duplication events impact allele frequencies and mask linkage information. As well, CNA approaches for subclonal reconstruction face issues with statistical variation and sequence coverage noise across SNVs. These limitations constrain the accuracy of subclonal reconstruction as we cannot assign specific groups of sequences to specific subclones. Accurately quantifying clonality is critical for making evolutionary inferences about mutation rate and selection both temporally and spatially within tumours. Therefore, methodological improvements are needed to produce evolutionary biomarkers that are clinically relevant for patients. Overall this research will improve on subclonal reconstruction and haplotype assignment methods. This will enable better analysis of tumour's past while simultaneously generating evolutionary biomarkers that inform on survival, optimal therapy, and drug resistance. Ultimately our methods will help understand the evolvability of an individual's cancer with the goal of improving clinical outcomes, and, most importantly, saving patients' lives.

column36: Investigating the structure and mechanism of beta-catenin dependent gene transcription
column37: Transcription regulators are proteins that control the rate at which DNA is read to make proteins, which carry out specific roles in the body. beta-catenin is a particularly important transcription regulator that is essential for proper cell growth, development and survival. Mutations that influence the ability of beta-catenin to carry out its function are associated with a wide variety of cancers, but most notably in skin and colon cancer. Blocking beta-catenin activity makes these cancer cells more susceptible to chemotherapies and can cause tumor regression. In order to carry out its activity, preliminary studies suggest that beta-catenin associates with another protein named CREB-binding protein (CBP), making this interaction a potential drug target. Despite the therapeutic potential of controlling beta-catenin function, the specific details of how beta-catenin associates with CBP still remains unclear. This research aims to understand both the biological function and mechanistic details of how these proteins interact with one another. I will first determine the atomic-resolution molecular structure of beta-catenin bound to CBP and probe where and how tightly they bind. Using this knowledge, I will then design molecules to disrupt these interactions and examine the biological effects in melanoma and colon cancer cell lines. This multidisciplinary project will help us understand the fundamental molecular mechanisms of gene regulation and may provide new targeted strategies to treat cancer.

column36: Exploring Attitudes and Anticipated Uptake of a COVID-19 Vaccine among Patients with Chronic Illnesses in the Canadian Maritimes
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has changed the world we live in. Until a vaccine is developed, strict public health measures will need to be in place to prevent transmission of this infectious disease. As we wait for a COVID-19 vaccine, there is a need to identify attitudes and beliefs about a future vaccine to ensure uptake once it is available to the public. Uptake will be vital in patients with chronic illnesses, as they are a high-risk group who have received little attention during pandemic planning to date. Vaccine hesitancy, or concerns around vaccination, is a significant threat to global health and may affect uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine. The proposed project aims to understand the attitudes and barriers to anticipated uptake of the future COVID-19 vaccine among patients living with chronic conditions in the Maritimes. A three-phase study will address this research question. First, a survey will be conducted with patients across the Maritimes to explore attitudes, beliefs and anticipated uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine. These findings will be used to develop an interview guide to conduct in-depth interviews with patients and stakeholders, including physicians, pharmacists and nurse practitioners, to investigate barriers and enablers to vaccine uptake. Evidence from these two phases will be used to co-design an intervention with patients and stakeholders to help maximize uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine in high-risk patients. Understanding barriers to vaccinating against COVID-19 is necessary for improving quality of life and health outcomes in patients at high-risk for COVID-19 living in the Maritimes.

column36: Opportunities with a capital "O": Understanding the school environment and its impact on children's health behaviours
column37: We live in an environment where it is more accessible to drive than to walk, where foods high in fat and sugar are more available than healthy options, and now more than ever have interactions through our phones rather than face-to-face conversations. This problem is most concerning for children who are being brought into an environment that promotes rather than hinders unhealthy opportunities; therefore having damaging effects on their health and well-being. In Nova Scotia, we have some of the highest rates of childhood obesity and poor mental health in the country. It is recognized that the school environment is an important place for children to develop, learn and reinforce health behaviours. An intervention called Health Promoting Schools has been put in place across Nova Scotia schools to help create opportunities that support the health and well-being of children (e.g. availability of health food options, increased time for physical activity). However, there is a lack of understanding of how the different parts of the school environment impact children's health behaviours. This research project will focus on examining what components of Health Promoting Schools impact children's health behaviours across Nova Scotia. The project will administer an established health promoting research tool to examine differences in school environments across Nova Scotia. Further, discussions groups will be held with teachers, principals and children to understand what parts of the school environment they think increase or decrease children's health behaviours. Participants will also have the option to photograph different parts of the school environment to provide more input. The collection of information will be used to develop potential ways Health Promoting Schools could improve upon the strategies and policies used to create opportunities in schools that positively impact children's health behaviours across in Nova Scotia.

column36: Exploring the Demographics, Culturally Appropriate Health Services, and Experiences of Indigenous Older Adults Residing in Long-Term Care Facilities in Canada
column37: The aging population in Canada has garnered considerable attention; however, this focus has not been distributed equitably among all Canadian demographics. Indigenous Elders and older adults are integral to cultural revitalization, building intergenerational connections, and sharing knowledges. They are living longer lives than ever before, yet still do not have equitable access to healthcare that promotes wellbeing, especially into later life. Indigenous older adults are more likely to have chronic health conditions compared to non-Indigenous Canadians, and when intensive health services are needed, moving to a long term care (LTC) facility may be necessary. These relocations separate Indigenous older adults from family, friends, community, and culture. Research on Indigenous older adults residing in LTC homes in Canada is sparse. This program of research comprises of three separate but related studies which will contribute to a foundation of knowledge on the topic and answer the following research questions: 1) What culturally appropriate supports and services do Indigenous older adults identify to be important for aging well in LTC? 2) What are the current demographics of the Indigenous older adult population living in LTC in Canada? 3) What are the experiences of Indigenous older adults who move from their communities to a LTC home? The studies use a range of research methods: Question 1 conducts a comprehensive systematic review; Question 2 performs a secondary data analysis on Indigenous LTC resident data from a Canadian LTC database; and Question 3 applies narrative and Storywork methods to explore Indigenous older adult residents' experiences of living in LTC and their perceptions on the necessities for aging well. Findings from these studies have a wide range of applications and can be used to inform healthcare providers, policymakers, and LTC facilities about supporting and promoting the health and wellbeing of Indigenous older adult residents.

column36: Investigating the role of dietary tryptophan metabolism by intestinal microbiota in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Our gut is exposed to a vast number of bacteria and microorganisms, called microbiota, which in combination with food, are important for maintaining good health. There is growing evidence suggesting that when food-bacterial interactions are broken, conditions like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can develop. IBD is a chronic relapsing disease that is increasing in prevalence worldwide, has no cure, and is characterized by severe inflammation in the digestive tract. I propose to study how certain bacteria from the human gut metabolize dietary proteins like tryptophan, to produce molecules which activate a receptor called the (A)ryl (H)ydrocarbon (R)eceptor (AhR). Recent studies have shown that AhR function is abnormal in patients with IBD. This is likely explained by changes in gut microbiota, resulting in a decrease of molecules which activate AhR ("agonists"). What is not known is which bacteria are responsible for the defective production of AhR agonists from foods, and the metabolic pathways involved. In this project I will study and isolate bacteria involved in tryptophan metabolism from IBD patients and healthy people. I will assess their ability to metabolize tryptophan and create AhR agonists using germ-free mice colonized with the selected bacteria. Finally, I will use models of colitis to study the ability of these bacteria to restore AhR function and decrease inflammation and injury in models of colitis. About 1% of the Canadian population could be affected by IBD by 2030. Additionally, current therapies to induce and maintain remission are dominated by drugs that lose effectiveness over time. This suggests the need for complementary therapies. My long-term goal is to develop combinations of bacteria or probiotics, which act on tryptophan in foods to restore AhR function and prevent and treat IBD.

column36: Exploring novel combinatorial therapies for personalized management of Cystic Fibrosis using primary human airway epithelial cells
column37: Cystic Fibrosis is the most common genetic condition affecting Canadian newborns (1 in 3600), and is caused by the inheritance of a mutation, from each parent, in the gene for the Cystic Fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. People with Cystic Fibrosis, due to their mutations, experience several problems with their lungs including shortness of breath, increased mucus production, and susceptibility to infections. Collectively, these problems can lead to damage of the lungs and early death. There have been great strides in the development of drugs that can treat many patients that have Cystic Fibrosis, with combinations of several drugs more effective than a single drug. However, some Cystic Fibrosis patients remain unresponsive to existing drug combinations and continue to experience symptoms and damage to their lungs. It is therefore important to find new combinations of drugs that can improve the quality of life for all Cystic Fibrosis patients. In this project, I investigate the effectiveness of new drugs, which can be added on top of existing drugs, that target proteins that interact with the Cystic Fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. This study will use human airway epithelial cells from Cystic Fibrosis patient donors covering a diverse range of the Cystic Fibrosis population. These drugs will be given in combination with currently approved drugs to cells from Cystic Fibrosis patients and we aim to identify potential Cystic Fibrosis patient populations that will benefit from our novel treatment strategy. Our research provides an alternative and complementary strategy to increase the function of the Cystic Fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. This has the potential to help all Canadians living with Cystic Fibrosis and may reveal distinct populations that may benefit from our proposed drug combination. In addition, this will provide a rationale for the development of new drugs for personalized therapy in Cystic Fibrosis.

column36: Understanding Resilience in Child Mental Health for Children and Families Experiencing Poverty and Poverty-Related Risks: A Mixed-Methods Study Using Population-Based Survey and Clinical Cohort Data
column37: It is well-established that poverty is a cause of poorer health outcomes for children. However, even in the setting of poverty, many children have positive outcomes. This may be because children, families and neighbourhoods are able to adapt positively in the setting of adversity, a concept known as resilience. The goal of this research is to identify characteristics at the child, family and neighbourhood levels which act as buffers to enhance resilience for children facing poverty, leading to better mental health outcomes and fewer mental health concerns. This research will use two data sources: the Ontario Child Health Study (OCHS), a survey of more than 10,000 Ontario children, and the TARGet Kids! Research Network, a primary care practice-based research network in Toronto, Canada of more than 11,000 children, to conduct a mixed-methods study to comprehensively assess buffers that may reduce child mental health concerns. The overall goal of this research program is to systematically identify existing strengths which are potentially modifiable and are already associated with better outcomes. This knowledge can be used to design effective and scalable clinical and public health interventions to optimize child mental health in the setting of poverty. Important strengths of this proposal include a large and representative data source (OCHS) and a clinical platform for immediately knowledge translation, dissemination, and intervention implementation (TARGet Kids!). This project will contribute meaningfully to our knowledge of potential buffers of poverty-related risks for child mental health and lay the groundwork for the candidate's career as a clinician-scientist.

column36: A Tale of Two Receptors: Antibiotics Bypassing the Outer Membrane
column37: We have taken antibiotics to treat potentially life-threatening infections at some point in our lives. However, mismanagement and misuse of antibiotics have reduced the number of treatment options as bacteria acquire resistance. One of the ways pathogenic bacteria, like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, resist killing by antibiotics is through the outer membrane. The outer membrane acts as a barrier that prevents antibiotics from getting into the cell. Our team is addressing this problem using a novel approach. We have identified two antibiotics, thiostrepton and thiocillin, that bypass the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa using iron uptake pathways. When P. aeruginosa encounters iron-limited environments, such as at sites of infections, they release molecules that scavenge iron. The iron-bound molecules return to the cell using specific receptors on the outer membrane. Thiostrepton and thiocillin use the same receptors and P. aeruginosa is tricked into taking up the antibiotics. We have shown that there is a low level of resistance to the two antibiotics in clinical isolates and thiostrepton improved survival in a mice model of infection. This research addresses antimicrobial resistance. It will also have positive implications for the treatment of P. aeruginosa infections using a novel strategy to bypass the outer membrane and improve health outcomes.

column36: The Role of Family Adaptation in the Transition to Adulthood for Youth With Medical Complexity: A Qualitative Case Study
column37: Youth with "medical complexity" have a combination of chronic health conditions and severe disabilities that profoundly impact their lives and those of their families. They rely on their families and machines to help them eat, breathe, and move. They also need the support of many health care and other service workers in order to thrive. The extreme needs of this group can be seen in the high costs to health care systems. They account for one third of all child health care costs in Ontario ($419 million per year). These costs do not include family wages lost to provide unpaid caregiving. In over half of these families, one family member has to stop work to care for their child. Recent advances have helped extend the lifespan of many of these youth, leading to a new generation who are surviving into adulthood. As they become adults, they face many big changes. Their families are now forced to transition abruptly from child to adult health care, education, and social services. It is very far from a smooth and seamless transition. Instead, families experience an abrupt change or ending of services. They report feeling overwhelmed, abandoned, and unsupported-as if they had been "pushed off a cliff." Yet family function and support are critical for these youth to successfully transition into adulthood. It is clear that these families need help during transition. In this study, I aim to learn how to best support families of youth with medical complexity during transition. I will ask families what works for them, what does not, and what support they need most at this time. I will focus on how they manage the change from child to adult health care, education, and social services. Study findings will identify approaches that boost family strengths and support them where they need it most.

column36: Development of a 'friends & family' fall prevention screening tool for community-dwelling older adults and their caregivers
column37: With an aging population, there are increasing concerns over health system capacity. A key reason for hospitalization among older adults is falls. Falls contribute to over $2billion in healthcare costs and lead to lasting physical and emotional injuries that can be challenging to recover from. Although falls are costly, they are preventable. Screening for risk of falling and programs designed to prevent falls have been shown to be effective. However, these screenings are largely conducted by a primary care clinician or after a patient is already admitted to the emergency room, which places a high burden on the healthcare system. To help alleviate this burden on the healthcare system and improve patient outcomes, public health has focused on promoting patient engagement and empowerment in their healthcare. Older adults themselves and their friends and family may be the first to notice a change in their health and mobility that might increase their risk of a fall before being seen by a clinician. To this end, our goal is to identify the most important and easy to measure risk factors for falls among community-dwelling older adults and then develop a tool for patients and caregivers to use independently in the community. In doing so, we can empower older adults and their caregivers to detect and reduce the risk of falling as early as possible.

column36: Alcohol-related Social Network Density and Alcohol Misuse: Examination of Clinical Utility and Predictive Validity
column37: Alcohol misuse is a major public health concern that leads to serious financial, mental, and physical health consequences. One possible factor related to alcohol misuse is a person's social network, and specifically how many people in the network also have problematic alcohol use. Measures of alcohol use in a person's social network may be relevant to clinical settings, by helping clinicians understand where the problematic use may be occurring in the social network, and allowing helpful social changes that could reduce the negative consequences of problematic alcohol use. However, the use and possible benefits of these social network measures in clinical settings have not been established. The goal of this current project is to explore whether measures of alcohol use within a person's social network may be helpful in clinical settings in two ways: first, to examine whether these measures may be used as diagnostic screening tools, and second, to determine whether these measures can predict positive changes in alcohol misuse over time. If these measures are found to be clinically meaningful, this may support the development of specific social network interventions.

column36: Dietary triggers of gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome
column37: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. It affects over 5 million Canadians, producing an economic burden of over $6.5 billion per year. Gluten is the protein found in wheat, rye, and barley responsible for the elastic properties and texture of flour. It is commonly believed to trigger IBS symptoms; however, the mechanism is not yet understood. Also found in wheat, rye, and barley, amylase trypsin inhibitors (ATIs) may contribute to IBS symptoms by activating the innate immune system. ATIs are present in higher quantities in modern wheat, which may explain the greater reported levels of gluten and wheat sensitivity than in the past. Current research suggests that ATIs and gluten interact to trigger more severe symptoms. However, there are no studies in IBS patients investigating the effects of pure gluten versus gluten with ATIs. We designed a placebo-controlled study to investigate the effects of pure gluten compared to gluten with ATIs. IBS patients (n=35) whose symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet will be randomly assigned to consume granola bars containing either pure gluten, gluten with ATIs, or placebo (gluten-free flour). Participants will receive the three different interventions in a period of 10 weeks separated by 2-week washout periods. We will study the underlying mechanisms, including the effects on the immune system and gut bacteria. This research is the first to test the effects of pure gluten against gluten with ATIs in IBS patients. If some patients are sensitive to ATIs instead of gluten, this research would allow for the development of ATI-free foods using pure gluten so that ATI-sensitive individuals can consume gluten-containing breads, pastas, and pastries. The results will also improve our understanding of the potential mechanisms and effects of gluten and ATIs on IBS, leading to better diagnosis and personalized dietary recommendations in the future.

column36: Brain white matter microstructure following SARS-CoV2 infection
column37: In the Spring of 2020, the lives of people worldwide have changed in unimaginable ways. Activities that were once deemed normal everyday activities now require careful consideration, weighing the potential risks against the benefits. Decisions are now made in regards to what is deemed safe, or of an acceptable level of risk, on a daily basis. In order to make these decisions, it is important to be fully aware of the impact that contracting the SARS-CoV2 virus can have on overall health. Importantly, several cases have been reported where SARS-CoV2 infection led to neurological symptoms including severe headache, nausea, loss of smell and taste, and even stroke. A large amount of evidence now shows that the virus can not only enter but also damage the brain, and, in some cases, this damage can prove to be fatal. Although there are known neurological complications to Covid-19, much remains unknown concerning the mechanisms at play. In this project, we will study the impact of Covid-19 on the brain, especially on white matter (the connective pathways between neurons) and cognition, using brain imaging techniques (MRI) and cognitive tests. We will also explore how risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, and smoking, influence the impact that Covid-19 has on white matter and cognition, as the presence of these risk factors has been shown to increase the risk of neurological complications with Covid-19. Neurological pathologies have a high incidence in Covid-19 patients, occurring in over one third of patients. These neurological complications lead to severe symptoms and high mortality rates. Our goal is to uncover the type of damage that can occur within the brain following SARS-CoV2 infection. We hope this study will be the first step in designing effective prevention and intervention programs to reduce the incidence and severity of neurological complications with Covid-19 in future research.

column36: Identifying the Role of Protease PrpL in the Virulence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Pathology of Cystic Fibrosis
column37: Cystic fibrosis is a common, inherited disorder that mostly affects a person's respiratory and digestive systems. Complications from frequent and prolonged lung infections often result in the need for double lung transplants in individuals with CF. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterium that frequently contributes to respiratory failure in children and adolescents suffering from CF. How P. aeruginosa has such a profound affect on the health of CF patients over other bacteria species is not fully understood. It is known that P. aeruginosa capable of producing a protein called PrpL cause longer and more intense infections than those that don't. Our lab has discovered that PrpL likely intensifies infections by altering the ability of the patient's immune system to clear P. aeruginosa from the lungs. Through my research I will confirm how PrpL is able to manipulate the immune system and identify other ways that PrpL leads to severe and prolonged infections. In doing so I will uncover valuable information regarding how PrpL contributes to infections caused by P. aeruginosa and potential treatment options to prevent the bacteria from destroying the lungs of CF patients.

column36: Sport-related Concussion in Youth: Are Symptoms and Recovery Informed by Inflammatory or Endocrine Biomarkers?
column37: Concussion has been described as a "silent epidemic", affecting 250,000 Canadians and 40 million worldwide each year. Youth are at high risk of sport-related concussion (SRC). To date, diagnosis of concussion has been based on clinical assessment which can lead to misdiagnosis and unknown trajectory of recovery. Research into objective blood tests for SRC is underway, but has thus far been largely focused on adults, leaving a substantial gap in the context of pediatric SRC. Changes in inflammation and hormone levels are commonly seen after more severe traumatic brain injury, but recent studies show they may be altered after SRC. Blood tests examining changes in inflammation, hormones, and various markers of brain injury hold promise for the future of SRC diagnosis in youth. This study will include 700 high school students (male and female, ages 13-16 years) with an expected 70 SRCs per year based on established injury rates. After students sustain a SRC, blood tests will be performed within 72 hours, 1 week, and every following 2 weeks thereafter until medical clearance to return to play. Serial blood tests will allow us to determine the physiological consequences of SRC and optimal timing for effective testing and diagnosis. Additionally, results from blood tests will be examined in relation to symptom burden to help clinicians predict who will have a normal or prolonged recovery. With growing public health concerns for youth following SRC, there is an urgent need to provide clinicians with an accurate method to aid in diagnosing and predicting outcomes. Analysis of multiple blood biomarkers of brain injury has the potential to contribute to a better understanding of the pathological changes following concussion and fill a largely ignored gap in pediatric SRC research.

column36: Protective equipment in Canadian high school athletes: Can mouthguards and optimal helmet fit prevent sport-related concussions in youth collision sport?
column37: Concussions (e.g., including sport-related concussions) are brain injuries sustained by over 1.5 million North American youth each year. Over 60% of concussions in youth result from sport participation, with contact from another player being a common mechanism. Unfortunately, concussion can lead to physical (e.g., headaches), emotional (e.g., depression), and social (e.g., isolation) disruptions to a youth's wellbeing. Therefore, sport-related concussion prevention strategies for youth must be explored. Equipment-based strategies are simple, cost-effective, innovative and may be effective in reducing sport-related concussions. Specifically, mouthguard use and optimal helmet fit may protect against sport-related concussion; however, evidence is lacking. The current International Sport Concussion Consensus suggested a 19% reduction in concussion when athletes wear a mouthguard and a recent study demonstrated a 64% reduction in concussions when youth ice hockey players wear a mouthguard. Moreover, helmet use is effective for reducing head injury in recreational activities (e.g., bicycling). For concussion prevention, helmet fit may be an important consideration. Preliminary data in youth ice hockey evaluating helmet mobility, chin-strap fit and other criteria suggests that proper fit is protective against sport-related concussion. Unfortunately, the current literature lacks high quality studies with large sample sizes that assess equipment-based SRC prevention strategies across multiple collision sports. Therefore, this study will examine mouthguard use and helmet fit (where applicable) at time of injury between players with a concussion (cases) and musculoskeletal injured (controls) in grade 10-12 high school students participating in collision sport (e.g., ice hockey, football, rugby) in five Canadian provinces. Understanding the protective effect of equipment will inform concussion prevention equipment strategies and policies to promote lifelong sport participation.

column36: Expanding Capacity in Alberta to Deliver Contingency Patient Management in Outpatient Addiction Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial for Methamphetamine Use
column37: Alberta is facing a methamphetamine (MET) crisis. MET-related hospitalizations have increased by 800% between 2010-2015 in Alberta. Promising data indicates that Albertans are increasingly seeking help for their MET use, with treatment enrolments being three times higher in 2018 compared to 2012. Yet, individuals who use MET in Alberta are having significant difficulty remaining in treatment, with a retention rate nearly six times lower than what has been found in other studies with this population. This suggests that the interventions that are currently provided have been ineffective at retaining, and ultimately treating those seeking help for their MET use. Thus, it is important to find a treatment that can improve retention in this population. Contingency management (CM) is an extensively studied treatment for addictions. This intervention provides prizes, like canned goods, when someone meets a behavioural goal, such as attendance. Current findings from the United States have shown that CM improves various outcomes, including retention. Despite research findings, CM is rarely used in Canadian clinical settings. Therefore, this study will implement CM in Alberta (Calgary and Edmonton) for individuals seeking treatment for their MET use. One CM program will incentivize participants for their treatment attendance and the other for MET abstinence. 300 participants will be randomly assigned to one of the CM programs for 12-weeks and a 3, 6, and 12-month follow-up. Prize CM will be used-participants who meet their goal will draw from a prize bowl with a 50% chance of winning. We will evaluate whether CM improves retention, attendance, abstinence, substance use, quality of life, and impacts on the health system. Current efforts to treat MET use in Alberta have been ineffective, leaving this population without the proper care for their addiction. It is hoped the use of CM will increase retention and therefore result in better outcomes in this population.
