column36: The kaposin gene cluster drives KSHV latent and lytic infection cycles and viral tumourigenesis
column37: Viruses are estimated to account for 12-20% of cancer cases worldwide. As a cancer-causing virus replicates, it co-opts cellular machinery that would normally be used to detect and resolve dangerous pre-cancerous events. Without the use of this machinery, cells can divide unchecked and cancer may develop. My project addresses a major knowledge gap for one of the seven human cancer-causing viruses, Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV). KSHV is the cause of Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS), an unusual skin cancer which develops from the unrestricted growth of cells that line our blood vessels. When KSHV infects these cells, it can adopt either a dormant (latent) or active (lytic) life cycle, both of which are important for cancer development. During these lifecycles, a set of three proteins, known as kaposin proteins, are produced by virus-infected cells. Very atypically for a herpesvirus, the kaposin proteins are made in both the dormant and active viral lifecycles. The role of these proteins however, and the cellular machinery they may co-opt, is not fully understood. My goal is to determine what role(s) the kaposins have in viral infection and in cancer development. To achieve my goal, I have developed an important set of tools for the KSHV field that will now permit us to study these poorly characterized kaposins: a set of KSHV viruses deficient in kaposin protein production yet otherwise, normal. By studying KSHV using my toolbox of kaposin-deficient viruses, I will learn how these proteins are important to both lifecycles of the virus and how they contribute to tumour development. In doing so, we expect KSHV to act as a homing beacon to help us identify key molecules involved in tumour development. Completion of this project will therefore lead to novel therapeutic targets for KS, and cancer therapy in general.

column36: Modeling Human Glioblastoma in the Context of the Extracellular Environment
column37: "I always like to have a glimmer of hopefulness, even in collapse" - Gordon Downie, Canadian singer-songwriter, activist, glioma patient. Approximately 1000 Canadians a year are diagnosed with brain tumors, and those diagnosed with the most aggressive and fatal form of brain tumors called gliomas have an average survival of 18 months. Research in the past has primarily focused on identifying and targeting specific genetic mutations in the tumor. However, it is apparent that the environment surrounding the tumor can influence tumor growth, tumor spread into the brain, and drug resistance. The brain presents many challenges to glioma treatment, one of which is the unique environment in which gliomas grow, which contributes to poor patient outcomes. The interaction between tumor cells, surrounding normal brain tissue, immune cells, and the structural support of the tumor, the extracellular matrix (ECM) provides an environment that supports the progression and aggressiveness of glioma. The ECM, a 3-dimensional network of proteins, provides tissue-specific molecular and mechanical cues to the tumor. By isolating the ECM, we will determine the components of the glioma environment, study how cells grow and move within this environment, and how the ECM contributes to therapeutic failure. In addition, we will look at the influence of the ECM on immune cells located within the tumor environment. It has become abundantly clear through the failed use of the primary glioma chemotherapy, that directly targeting the tumor is insufficient. Therefore, targeting the glioma environment in addition to the tumor may be considered a better therapeutic strategy. Treating the environment may result in a switch from a tumor-promoting environment to a tumor-suppressing environment. Understanding and characterizing the glioma ECM, may provide unique opportunities to target the glioma environment in addition to targeting the tumor, leading to more successful patient outcomes.

column36: Facilitating Successful Transitions to Home Dialysis: Identifying Support Needs and Care Priorities of Patients and Families
column37: An increasing number of Canadians are getting end stage kidney failure and will start on dialysis treatment to replace their kidney function. There are many dialysis options, one of which is home dialysis. Home dialysis is being promoted by our healthcare system as it has many benefits. However, high levels of support are required for it to be successful as the patient or family sets up and performs the dialysis themselves at home. Without this support, patients experience overwhelming responsibility, and many find it hard to do home dialysis. This is especially true during the transition to home dialysis, which patients describe as a particular difficult time. Little is known about the support needs and priorities in care for patients and families during this time, which makes it hard for programs to put successful interventions in place. This leads to a need for research to be done in this area. We will identify care priorities and support needs for people transitioning onto home dialysis in Canada. This project will be guided by input from patient and family partners, national and international home dialysis clinician leaders, front-line staff and health system administrators. This will be done in three parts. In part one we will perform a literature review to identify other studies that have done similar work. In part two we will follow home dialysis patients during their transition and perform in-depth interviews with them at key times to help us identify what is important at different stages. In part three we will engage with a group of national stakeholders to identify care priorities during this transition. This work will provide valuable information that will help us develop an intervention for use in clinical settings. It is our hope that by creating a more supportive transition experience that patients will have better outcomes on this type of dialysis and that kidney programs will have a better idea of how to address patient and family needs.

column36: Child Bicyclist Injuries and the Built Environment: A Case-Crossover Study
column37: Traffic related injuries are one of the leading causes of injury and death in Canadian children. Collisions involving vehicles and child bicyclists contribute significantly to these injuries and are a cause for concern for the safety of our children. While bicycling and other forms of active transportation improve the physical and mental health of children, there is a decline in participation in part due to the safety concerns of traffic related injury. Child bicyclists experience and interact with traffic and traffic infrastructure differently than adults, which can increase risk of injury. Strategies to prevent these injuries must continue to be explored by both government and non-government organizations across municipalities. By examining the traffic infrastructure/built environment and its link to injury risk in child bicyclists in multiple cities across Canada we can determine the relation between the built environment and child bicycling safety. The case-crossover design of this study uses participants as their own controls and will be used to compare the location a child was injured to two other locations on their route where they were not injured (i.e., control locations). We will examine child bicyclist injury and the built environment through child interviews and site observations. Interviews will allow for additional understanding of the child's perspective of bicycling safety. Using these approaches will allow for us to determine the built environment features such as traffic infrastructure that influence child bicyclist safety and perceptions of safety.

column36: Causal role of intestinal fungi on host immunity and susceptibility to airway inflammation
column37: The intestines are colonized by a large community of microbes, called the microbiome. Research shows that the microbiome provides signals that are important for immunological development of infants, with early-life microbiome alterations (dysbiosis) changing immune responses and increasing the infant susceptibility to allergic diseases, such as asthma. During the first years of life, the immature microbiome undergoes fast developmental changes, and is more susceptible to environmental stressors, which can cause dysbiosis and permanent immune changes to infants. For example, birth via C-section, exclusive formula feeding, and use of antibiotics, which are known to directly alter the gut microbiome, are associated with an increased risk of asthma in young children. Most studies on this area have only investigated bacterial members in the microbiome, ignoring other microorganisms that colonize the infant gut, such as fungi. It was recently shown that fungal dysbiosis is strongly associated with antibiotic use and risk of asthma in infants, however, it is still not known how fungi are involved in asthma development. My research project aims to determine the impact of early-life gut fungal colonization and antibiotic-induced fungal overgrowth on immune development and asthma susceptibility. In my experiments, I will use a model with mice completely lacking microbes (germ-free). These germ-free mice will be colonized with defined mixtures of bacteria only, fungi only, or both. Additionally, I will colonize mice with fungus specifically expanded in young babies receiving antibiotics. I will determine different immune measurements and apply a model of allergic asthma in these colonized mice. These experiments will allow me to determine if fungi alter immune development and increase airway inflammation in mice. This work also has great potential to reveal novel approaches to prevent immune dysregulation and allergic diseases in children.

column36: How does parenting interact with genetic differential susceptibility in predicting attachment patterns in preschool-aged children?
column37: Attachment represents a brain-based biological evolutionary system that helps to ensure the survival of the human infant (Bakermans-Kranenburg, 2015). A secure attachment is when a child feels secure, safe, and protected while exploring the world around them (Ainsworth, 1978). Secure attachment to a caregiver is critical to healthy brain and organ-system development, optimal child behaviour, and adult mental and physical health. Caregiving qualities, such as how sensitive caregivers are in responding to their infants' needs (i.e., sensitivity), were thought to be the most significant influence on whether an infant develops a secure attachment pattern (Ainsworth, 1978; Feeney, 2016). However, there is an increasing debate on how much caregiver sensitivity alone influences attachment pattern development, leading to the exploration of other contributing factors such as genetics (Belsky, 2015). Gene by environment studies look at how the environment can influence early childhood development, disease, and health overall (McAllister, 2017). However, there are few studies examining gene-environment interaction and the influence this has on developing attachment patterns (Golds, 2020). This research will examine how children's genetics interact with the caregiving environment in predicting attachment patterns. We plan to examine these factors in a sample of 176 participants who were a part of the larger Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) study. This research will show the degree to which children's genetics contribute to their attachment pattern, with implications for deepening our understanding of the developmental origins of health and disease. This knowledge will advance our ability to target programs and nursing interventions to specific populations based on children's genetics and caregiving environments and therefore contribute to improving the health of Canadians.

column36: The Feasibility and Acceptability of Dialectical Behavior Therapy for Treating Non-Suicidal Self-Injury and Suicidal Behavior in Women With Autism
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition occurring in 1% of the population. While we used to think (ASD) occurred more frequently in males, we now know that the ratio is closer to 1.8:1 (males:females). Females with ASD without intellectual disability (ASD-WID) experience high rates of self-harm and suicide. Indeed, rates of suicide in this population are close to 50 times higher than in the general population. Despite this, there are currently no evidence-based treatments available for treating self-harm and suicidal behavior in females with ASD-WID. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT; a type of cognitive behavioral therapy) is an evidence-based treatment designed to treat self-injury and suicidal behavior in females. That said, DBT is a very time and resource intensive treatment, and might not be readily accessible to females with ASD-WID. One component of DBT, skills training groups, has been found to reduce suicidal behavior and self-harm. As such, it is possible that DBT skills groups could be used to treat self-injury and suicidal behavior in females with ASD-WID. In this research, I will look at whether DBT skills trainings is an acceptable, feasible, and effective treatment for self-injury and suicidal behavior in females with ASD-WID. Participants will complete 26 weekly 2-hour DBT skills groups. They will be asked to complete weekly measures regarding the acceptability, feasibility and effectiveness of the treatment. I will also ask participants to take part in focus groups to discuss their experiences of treatment, and to suggest modifications for adapting the treatment for future use. The results of this study could have significant health impacts. Suicide is a serious public health problem, but no evidence-based treatments exist for individuals with ASD. I hope to use the findings to refine the DBT treatment protocol as appropriate and to conduct a larger research study.

column36: Intersectional determinants of im/migrant women's sexual and reproductive health access: Informing interventions during COVID-19 and beyond
column37: British Columbia(BC) is a key destination setting for immigrant women, who make up over 25% of residents. Immigrant women in Canada may face critical sexual and reproductive health(SRH) issues, potentially from health system challenges, negative experiences with providers, and a lack of culturally sensitive and language-specific care. There is a need to examine how factors such as gender, age, discrimination, migration experiences, and temporary immigration status shape immigrant women's healthcare and SRH experiences in BC. There is also a need to understand impacts of racism on immigrant women's health access given ongoing health issues highlighted by COVID-19 among immigrants in Canada and globally. My study will describe how factors such as gender and race, as well as immigration factors (e.g. status, time in Canada, migration experiences) shape immigrant women's SRH needs and access in BC; evaluate any changes during COVID-19; and explore potential differences among immigrant sub-groups (e.g. youth, undocumented). I anticipate that the findings will highlight deeply rooted barriers to SRH access, including racism, insecure status, and strict gender norms, which may be more severe during COVID-19 and for recent and younger immigrants of colour. My study will use interviews from 'IRIS', a study of immigrant women's SRH access in BC housed at the Centre for Gender & Sexual Health Equity. Interview data will be collected during and beyond COVID-19 to examine potential variations, and analyses will examine potential differences by age, time in Canada, immigration status, and country of origin. This study aims to advance knowledge of immigrant women's SRH access in BC, calling for improved healthcare access for immigrants during COVID-19 and beyond. It will build understandings of how gender, migration experiences, and other changes shape SRH needs and access, and will contribute urgently needed evidence of strategies to best improve healthcare during COVID-19.

column36: Effect of neurovascular defects on brain metabolism in 16p11.2 deletion mouse model of autism spectrum disorders
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are neurodevelopmental disorders associated with social interaction deficits, communication impairments, repetitive behaviors and restricted interests. Causes are still enigmatic, but ASD-associated mutations have been identified, one of them corresponding to a loss of DNA known as the 16p11.2 deletion. The brain's high metabolic demands and negligible intrinsic energy reserves makes it continuously dependent on the adequate influx of oxygen and nutrients from the blood stream to ensure proper brain development and function. Although the neuronal underpinnings of ASD are being extensively studied, very little is known about the vascular contributions to these conditions. Recently, we revealed that 16p11.2 deletion was linked to functional and structural abnormalities in brain vascular networks. My project will focus on thoroughly examining the impact of these abnormalities on brain metabolism at a cellular level using a genetically-engineered mouse model of ASD harboring the 16p11.2 deletion. My goal is to investigate key regulators of brain metabolism in order to identify target pathways to modulate. The research program that we proposed will provide novel insight into the involvement of brain metabolism in ASD while further pinpointing biomarkers which could lead to selective therapeutic approaches that can address core symptoms of ASD.

column36: A Healthy People Initiative: Improving the Socio-Economic Circumstances and Recovery Outcomes of the Homeless and At-Risk for Homelessness Populations in Ottawa and Toronto (Canada)
column37: Tobacco is the most preventable cause of disease and death in Canada. Although the tobacco use rate has substantially gone down in the general population, significant differences exist between sub-populations in Canada, where for example Ottawa's highly vulnerable People Who Use Drugs (PWUD), homeless or at-risk for homelessness population has a 96% tobacco smoking rate relative to 9-18% in the rest of Ottawa. This stark inequity in tobacco use translates into devastating healthcare outcomes such as a disproportionate amount of cancer, stroke, heart disease and death. In order to tackle tobacco related health disparities, a novel approach to smoking cessation in vulnerable populations is required. Despite commonly held dogma that the PWUD and homeless populations does not want to quit smoking, many studies have demonstrated that in fact they are very interested in quitting. Pragmatic peer-led community-based approaches have demonstrated that tobacco dependence strategies can be implemented with great success in this population. The Healthy People Initiative (HPI) aims to compare two tobacco dependence management strategies in the homeless (or at-risk for homelessness) multi-drug use population in two large Canadian cities, Ottawa and Toronto.

column36: A tailored viro-immunotherapy combination approach for the treatment of BRCA1/2 mutated breast and ovarian cancers
column37: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are known as tumour suppressor genes, both playing essential roles in the DNA repair pathway. Loss of function in either may lead to genetic instability of cells, ultimately leading to malignancy. Alterations (mutations) in either BRCA1 or BRCA2 pose the greatest risk factor for developing breast or ovarian cancer. With 1 in 300 to 500 people in the general population carrying mutations in either BRCA1 or BRCA2, the development of effective treatment for these cancers is an important topic in the field of cancer research. The treatment of BRCA1/2 mutated breast and ovarian cancers with certain specific DNA repair inhibitors (commonly known as PARPi) has initially led to promising outcomes. Oral PARPi treatment can selectively kill BRCA1/2 mutated cancer cells through a combination effect targeting the DNA repair pathway. Unfortunately, this treatment is not successful in all patients. Various mechanisms for PARPi resistance have been shown, including restoration of BRCA1/2 function due to differences in the genetic make-up of tumour cells or additional alternations in the BRCA1/2 genes. Oncolytic or "cancer-killing" viruses are an innovative approach to treating even the most complex cancers. Oncolytic viruses target and destroy cancer cells, leaving normal cells unharmed, all while activating a patient's own immune system to fight the cancer. The aim of this project is (1) to engineer cancer specific viruses targeting the BRCA1/2 genes, (2) evaluate the combination effect of these engineered BRCA1/2 targeting viruses with PARPi, and finally (3) complete a pre-clinical evaluation of BRCA1/2 targeting viruses with PARPi therapy including safety and efficacy by treating a panel of non-malignant cells, malignant cells and various mouse models. The overarching goal of this project is to develop a combination therapy using oncolytic viruses and PARPi that could overcome resistance and lead to curative treatment for patients with BRCA1/2 mutated cancers.

column36: Engineering and characterization of a novel immunomodulatory oncolytic virus via modification of cellular phosphorylation homeostasis
column37: A cure for cancer, the leading cause of death in Canada, has yet to be found. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are modified viruses that selectively infect and kill cancer cells. Although they have shown promise, its success has been limited by the cancer's natural anti-virus response. Our lab has recently shown that drugs containing the metal vanadium can increase the virus' cancer killing effect. Vanadium does this by lowering the anti-virus defence while strengthening the patient's immune system against the tumour. Unfortunately, vanadium is not easily delivered to the human body; therefore, our project aims to create a new virus product that imitates vanadium's beneficial effects. To do this, we will first identify how vanadium boosts the effect of the virus by screening for its different targets within the cell. We will then code genetic instructions to block these identified targets into the virus. By looking at measures like the amount of virus infection and cancer cell death, we can assess how effective our designer virus is in human and mouse cancer cells. Next, we will assess how well our virus works in mouse models. After identifying a safe dose and no dangerous side effects, mice bearing tumours will be injected with our virus. We will monitor how quickly the tumours shrink with treatment and whether their survival is improved. The ability for the mouse to produce long-term tumour protection will then be measured by looking at their immune response and monitoring whether mice recover when given a second tumour. If successful, this strategy that combines the advantages of both oncolytic viruses and vanadium while overcoming their disadvantages represents a promising treatment option for cancer patients. We hope to eventually have the product ready for health and safety testing in human clinical trials. This work will also lead to a better understanding of how the body reacts to viral infection and provide insight into new treatment strategies.

column36: Role of DUSP4 in diabetic nephropathy and end-stage renal disease
column37: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a renal complication affecting many diabetic patients and is one of the preeminent causes of renal insufficiency leading to dialysis or renal transplant. Our project is based on podocytes, important cells for blood filtration in the kidneys. Their loss of function and death is an early event in the development of diabetic nephropathy. Ultimately, structural changes will get worse and lead to complete renal decline (ESRD). DUSP4, a molecule that regulates proteins involved in cell death, is important for renal function. We have observed a decrease in DUSP4 levels in diabetic kidneys. Previous results have emphasized the importance of DUSP4 in the kidney since whole-body removal of DUSP4 worsens characteristics of diabetic nephropathy. To this day, the kidneys of diabetic patients suffering from ESRD are said to have reached the point of no return. Thus, it is critical to find treatments that could stop/slow down the progression of kidney problems. With the use of mice that have elevated levels of DUSP4 specifically in podocytes, our objective is to determine the clinical significance of DUSP4 in the prevention of diabetic nephropathy. Our hypothesis is that increased levels of DUSP4 in podocytes will prevent the onset of kidney problems in diabetic mice and will also re-establish renal function once the disease has already started. Secondly, with the use of a mouse model of ESRD (adenine-rich food), our 2nd objective is to investigate the role of DUSP4 in the progression towards complete renal insufficiency, an area that lacks research. We hypothesize that DUSP4 deletion will accelerate the progression and onset of complete renal insufficiency. My projects will help us better understand the mechanisms leading to DN and ESRD as well as the importance of DUSP4 in the kidney while ultimately contributing to support patients affected by these conditions to potentially give them a better quality of life.

column36: Attitudes and outcomes associated with weight related intentions from adolescence to adulthood
column37: Introduction: Lifestyle-based weight management strategies are essential to reduce the prevalence of obesity in children. About 50% of young people report having intention to lose weight and 20% of them are concerned about their weight. Weight-related intention may be a determinant of behavioral weight-related actions. Objectives: This study aims to assess the influence of a change in body image on weight-related intentions and the influence of weight-related intentions on lifestyle and adiposity. Methodology: The data for this study will be drawn from the MATCH study, a prospective study of 937 young people from New Brunswick followed 3 times a year for 8 years (aged 10 to 18) and the NDIT study, a longitudinal study of 1,293 young people from Montreal followed for 17 years (13 to 30 years old). Relevance: This doctoral project is unique in that it will provide a broad and longitudinal understanding of the influence of weight-related intentions on lifestyle and health of adolescents and young adults. More research is needed to improve interventions promoting healthy lifestyles and weight considering that current weight management strategies have modest long-term effects. There is an urgent need to act to decrease obesity in young people.

column36: Trajectoire, prevalence et gestion du risque de maladie cardiovasculaire chez les canadiens ayant un diabete de type 2 : implication de l'entrainement par intervalle de haute intensite
column37: Afin de reduire le risque de maladie cardiovasculaire chez les personnes ayant le diabete de type 2, il est recommande d'atteindre la triple cible therapeutique, visant l'amelioration du controle glycemique, de la pression arterielle et des niveaux de cholesterol LDL. Cependant, aucune donnee recente n'existe sur l'atteinte de cette cible, ni sur le role de differents facteurs environnementaux influencant celle-ci chez les Canadiens ayant un diabete de type 2. Diabete Canada suggere de faire 150 min d'exercice aerobie d'intensite moderee (ECM) ou 75 min semaine d'entrainement par intervalles a haute intensite (HIIT) afin de diminuer le risque de maladie cardiovasculaire et la variabilite de la glycemie. De plus, pour mieux aider les canadiens ayant un diabete, il est essentiel de comparer l'effet les deux modalites d'exercice suggerees sur l'atteinte de la triple cible therapeutique. Ainsi, des premiers travaux viseront a determiner la proportion de canadiens atteignant la triple cible therapeutique et son evolution entre 2007 et 2019 grace aux donnees de l'Enquete canadienne sur les mesures de la sante de Statistique Canada. De plus, cette etude tentera de determiner les principaux facteurs environnementaux qui peuvent expliquer l'atteinte de cette cible. Dans un deuxieme temps, les donnees de 30 femmes agees ayant un diabete de type 2 et ayant participe a une etude portant sur l'effet de 12 semaines d'entrainement (HIIT vs ECM) seront analysees pour tenter d'etablir si les differentes modalites d'exercice actuellement recommandees par Diabete Canada permettent, de facon similaire, d'ameliorer l'atteinte de la triple cible therapeutique et de reduire la variabilite de la glycemie. Ces etudes permettront de mieux comprendre comment les Canadiens gerent leur diabete et l'effet de differentes modalites d'entrainement sur le risque de maladie cardiovasculaire ce qui ultimement, permettra d'ameliorer la prise en charge des personnes ayant le diabete de type 2.

column36: Assessing the safety and efficacy of intra-arterial chilled saline infusion following focal ischemic stroke
column37: With ~55,000 new cases each year in Canada, the social, individual, and economic costs of this ischemic stroke are unparalleled. Despite advances in treating this disabling disease, not all patients benefit. This proposal aims to improve outcomes for all patients, but especially those that do not benefit from current therapies by investigating whether intra-arterial chilled saline (IACS) infusion is a safe and effective treatment. IACS treatment involves flushing the injured tissue with cold saline. Previous research has shown that IACS is beneficial. However, previous research is homogenous and not aligned with clinical reality (e.g., only studied in young, healthy, male rats, creating a mismatch with reality). In Year 1, we will develop our stroke model using hypertensive rats, a key risk factor. We will vary the stroke duration, and assess brain injury at 48 hours post-stroke. Our brain injury severity measurements in Year 1 will inform groups for Year 2 and 3. In Year 2, we will randomly assign male AND female rats to moderate, severe, and very-severe stroke, and either treat them with IACS or sham IACS. HYPOTHESIS: moderate and severe injuries will benefit from IACS treatment, but very-severe brain injuries may require more prolonged cooling. Our outcome measures are behavioural impairment (using established tests) and brain injury volume. Year 3 will be like Year 2, except rats will survive for 28 days, rather than 48 hours, and the treatment will be prolonged with a skull cooling device. Long-term studies are lacking in current literature. As before, we will assess behavioural deficits and brain injury. HYPOTHESIS: the combined hypothermia groups will have better outcomes than controls. Altogether, my research proposal will inform whether IACS is a safe and effective treatment for ischemic stroke by carefully considering clinical reality and addressing the limitations of current research (e.g., using multiple injury sizes, both sexes, hypertensive animals).

column36: Population genomic, bioinformatic, and molecular parasitological assessment of diversity and function of the membrane-trafficking machinery in Giardia intestinalis, a common Canadian enteric pathogen.
column37: Infectious organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites are an immense burden on the healthcare system in Canada. One such parasite is the diarrhea-causing Giardia intestinalis that is transmitted through contaminated food and water and is prevalent in young children. Previous studies have shown that this parasite is missing many important features in its cargo transport system that is necessary for uptake of nutrients, disposing waste, and protecting itself from the host's immune system. Instead, it has modified its existing compartments and protein machinery and uses it to establish infection in human and animal hosts. Unfortunately, the specific process and the protein parts involved are still not entirely known. Using a combination of cutting-edge computational methods, we will first aim to identify molecular switches in Giardia that normally turn on and off cargo movement processes in our cells. We will then follow it up with molecular testing to determine exactly where and how they are functioning in Giardia's existing transport system. We will also assemble DNA from strains of Giardia from patients, beavers, and water samples collected during outbreaks in British Columbia and examine whether there are differences between them. We have previously used this combinatorial approach to study other proteins in the system which allowed us to uncover new functions that have never been described before. Therefore, we can expect similar findings that will ultimately help us piece together the puzzle of what parts are present and exactly how are they functioning together for this parasite to be causing disease in us.

column36: Helpful or Harmful? Consequences of Cellular Volume Changes following Stroke
column37: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke subtype that is fatal for over 40% of patients. ICH occurs when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures, causing blood to spill into the surrounding tissues and form a clot. The skull is a closed compartment, so a large blood clot takes up essential space in the brain and drives up pressure within the skull, with often fatal outcomes. Interestingly, we recently discovered a novel phenomenon in which brain cells experience a dramatic reduction in volume (up to 60%) in the days following a moderate to large ICH. We believe that this is a regulated process, in which brain cells get rid of compounds called osmolytes, which are low-weight organic molecules that influence properties of cells, such as protein stability, cell size regulation, and cellular health. By doing this, cells are able to reduce their size in attempt to equalize deadly pressure elevations and prevent death. However, by getting rid of osmolytes to reduce their size, cells are ridding themselves of an important protective mechanism essential for survival in a stroke setting. Therefore, we assert that the loss of protective osmolytes in order to maintain cell size reductions is detrimental to the health of brain cells, resulting in the global functional impairments that we observe in ICH patients, rather than local reductions in blood flow as previously thought. We aim to assess whether these cell size reductions occur across multiple brain cell types, examine the impact of stroke severity, and quantitatively determine how extreme cell size reductions impact cellular health and function through gold standard techniques such as electron microscopy and Fourier Transform Infrared Imaging.

column36: Elevating circulating ketones as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of heart failure
column37: Although treatments for cardiovascular diseases have reduced the number of deaths, they have increased the number of patients who develop a condition known as heart failure. Simply put, heart failure is the inability of the heart to pump enough blood that is required by the rest of the body. For decades, it has been shown that the poor function of the failing heart is due to its inability to make enough energy to pump properly. While fats and sugars are the main energy sources for the heart, recent evidence suggests that the failing heart relies on ketones, potentially to increase energy production. Ketones are molecules that are produced by the liver from fats and can be used to provide energy in the heart. Yet, ketones also have many non-energetic properties such as reducing inflammation, which often occurs with heart failure. Currently, it is not understood if and/or how ketones may help the failing heart and if giving more ketones can be a useful therapy. Thus, using mouse models of heart failure, my project will investigate the role of ketones in heart failure and determine if and how they are good for the heart. Although ketogenic diets are commonly known to increase ketones, they reduce sugars, which are known to be an important source of energy for the failing heart. Therefore, our new approach will use a safe, commercially sold ketone water which increases blood ketone levels. We hypothesize that increased ketone use is beneficial for the failing heart and propose that providing even more ketones to the heart will improve heart function by reducing inflammation and increasing energy production. Together, our studies will increase our knowledge of heart failure and may create a new, more practical therapy to help the patients affected by this debilitating condition.

column36: Modulation of responses to insulin in white adipose tissue by egg white bioactive peptides
column37: The number of type 2 diabetes cases is increasing worldwide and is largely attributed to changes in dietary patterns and lack of physical activity. Currently, management of metabolic conditions relies mainly on drug therapy but is limited by low adherence and undesired side-effects of long-life treatment, thus unveiling a need to explore non-pharmaceutical approaches, such as the use of functional foods or nutraceuticals. Food-derived peptides are generated from food sources and have potential to be used for the development of alternative approaches to treat patients with obesity and diabetes. Egg proteins are a well-known source of bioactive peptides with multiple biological effects, exerting nutritional and physiological benefits. In cell culture, we observed that egg white (EW) peptides improved the response of fat tissue to insulin. Studies in rats further showed that EW peptides improved glucose metabolism. However, the exact mechanism of action on glucose metabolism, and the interaction between peptides and their molecular targets remain unclear. Based on our previous results, I hypothesized that EW peptides cause those effects by acting on fat tissue. I intend to study their mechanisms of action in the fat tissue of mice with pre-diabetes. The findings from this project will contribute to our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of EW peptides towards glucose metabolism, providing the scientific basis for future applications in clinical studies and potential expansion of the functional food market.

column36: Optimizing Opioid Agonist Therapies for Pregnant Women in British Columbia
column37: Opioid use disorder (OUD) during pregnancy is associated with multiple negative maternal and fetal outcomes. Although evidence suggests that opioid agonist therapies (OAT) may result in better health outcomes for mother and infant, many pregnant women enrolled in OAT are prescribed treatments that are of insufficient dose or duration. These issues may contribute to challenges with adherence or relapse, which can have negative maternal and fetal health consequences, including heightened risk of overdose. Our research will seek to: 1) Compare pregnancy outcomes between women living with OUD who are prescribed different types of OAT or no OAT during pregnancy; 2) Evaluate factors associated with adherence to and retention in different types of OAT during pregnancy and postpartum; 3) Examine changes in risk of non-fatal and fatal overdose during pregnancy and postpartum, and whether this differs by OAT dosage and retention. We will rely on a province-wide linked retrospective cohort of people living with opioid use disorder using linked data from the BC Perinatal Data Registry, prescription dispensations, and other databases held by the Ministry of Health. We will analyse the impact of different OAT regimens on pregnancy outcomes, the role of sociodemographic, clinical, and geographic factors in adherence to different types of OAT, and changes in overdose risk during pregnancy and postpartum. These findings can be used to inform evidence-based harm reduction policies and clinical practice guidelines that will connect pregnant women with safe and effective therapies, reduce stigma around OAT for pregnant women, promote uptake of prenatal care, and result in healthier and safer pregnancies for both mother and child.

column36: A multimodal neuroimaging approach to identifying subgroups of children with neurodevelopmental disorders with shared brain characteristics
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) are common neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) that are diagnosed separately yet share causes and symptoms. The overlap between disorders and variable behavioural presentations within disorder has made finding effective treatments difficult. To better understand the heterogeneity and symptom overlap, it is critical that subgroups of NDDs who share similar patterns of neural pathophysiology are discovered. Despite evidence that NDDs are caused by atypicalities in both brain structure and function, existing studies have only considered subgroups based on structure. Identifying subgroups utilizing both types features may identify groupings of children with a higher degree of shared biology, and thus provide more precise targets for treatments. I aim to discover whether measures of brain structure and function can be integrated to discover subgroups of NDDs. My objectives are 1) to use functional neuroimaging to identify subgroups of children with ASD, ADHD and OCD, and 2) to investigate the effects of combining measures of brain function with structure on the groupings. I hypothesize that subgroups identified via brain function will differ from those identified with structure, yet their combination will lead to more distinct groupings. Magnetic resonance imaging and magnetoencephalography will be used to measure brain function and structure using data from the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental Disorders network. Measures of brain structure and function will be used to identify clusters of participants which may better differentiate on their clinical and cognitive characteristics than the current diagnostic labels, and thus support using interventions designed for one diagnosis for children with other diagnoses. Furthermore, the decreased variability within the subgroups would provide more precise targets for treatments and interventions.

column36: Beyond the binary: Measuring gender diversity in cancer research
column37: Gender diverse people, or more commonly transgender, nonbinary, and gender nonconforming people, may be at risk of receiving worse cancer care and having worse outcomes when compared to other groups. Although there is some research supporting this belief, it is difficult to identify gender diverse people in data that are regularly used for cancer research. Without this information, leaders and health care providers cannot make helpful changes to their organizations or to how they provide cancer care. The goal of this project is to create a guide for researchers to help them understand what gender diversity means and different ways they can include it in their own projects. The first part of this project will explore ways gender is included in other cancer research. The information gathered in this step will be used to guide conversations with gender diverse people to find out what they think is important for other researchers to know about gender diversity and how researchers should be including them in their projects. Based on these conversations and what is currently done in other research, I will see if gender is being included the way it should be in the data often used in cancer research. I will combine the results from all of these steps to create a guide for researchers. Creating this guide will allow gender diverse people to say, in their own terms, how they want to be included in cancer research. Ultimately, this guide will help us better understand the challenges gender diverse people face through their cancer journey. It will also help decision-makers make changes so that gender diverse people receive the best possible care.

column36: Developing a comprehensive set of quality measures for the prevention and management of delirium in older adults in the emergency department
column37: There is no doubt that Canada's population is ageing. Many older adults use the emergency department (ED) as their first point of contact with the healthcare system. As the number of older adults increases, so too will the number who visit EDs for care. Many of these patients will have some form of cognitive impairment, such as, delirium. Science shows that these ED patients tend to have poorer outcomes (e.g., longer hospital stays and risk of death), partly because traditional ED care strategies are not appropriate for these patients. To address this issue, my research will create measures to evaluate the quality of care provided to older ED patients with delirium. I will first review the current literature that describes best care practices for older adults with delirium in general. I will then work with ED stakeholders (practitioners, administrators, and patients) from across Canada to determine which of these care practices best apply to the ED to create a set of quality measures for ED care. I will present my research findings at conferences and to ED planners and providers. My study results are a first step in helping to improve the quality of care for older ED patients with delirium. In future research I will pilot test these measures to examine their impact on quality care. My longer term career goal is to expand successful ED care improvement strategies across Canada and internationally.

column36: Investigating the role of lysosomal exocytosis in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a cruel disease that gradually worsens over time. Afflicted individuals experience progressive memory loss and personality changes that negatively impact both themselves and their loved ones. As there is no cure for AD, therapeutic approaches rely on medication that only alleviate symptoms. AD is associated with abnormal accumulation of two major toxic proteins, called tau and beta-amyloid (AB), in the brain. The mechanism controlling the build-up and release of these proteins from one cell to another is poorly understood. A specialized compartment in the cell, termed lysosomes, are known for their ability breakdown of material, but also function in the discharge of material from a cell. It has been previously shown that not only are tau and AB made within lysosomes, they also accumulate and become resistant to breakdown at this site. Taken together, there is evidence to suggest that the pathway in which material is released from lysosomes also plays an important role in the spread of toxic proteins from cell-to-cell. The proposed study aims to investigate the pathway that controls lysosomal release of material in cells of the brain. We will test the hypothesis that lysosomes play an important role in the clearance of toxic tau and AB from brain cells through this pathway. In this study, cells will be configured to express a marker for lysosomes and treated with toxic tau and AB. A specialized microscope will be used to capture nanoscopic events occurring at the cell surface when lysosomes are stimulated to discharge. This will allow for live analysis of these events, including number and timing. With an ageing population and the prevalence of AD on the rise, there is a need to better understand how tau and AB accumulate and can spread from one cell to another. This project would advance the development of targeted therapeutics for AD, which is vital in preventing future disease progression.

column36: Early neuromuscular stimulation and motor imagery interventions during immobilization of distal radius fracture to reduce the resulting motor impairments and improve rehabilitation outcomes.
column37: Fracturing the wrist usually requires a brace/cast to be worn for at least six weeks to keep the wrist inactive for fracture healing. The inactivity leads to loss of motor function (i.e. reduced strength and movement), which may require extensive rehabilitation and often leaves lasting impairments. Stimulating the nerves of the arm and mental rehearsal of movements, without physically performing the movement, have shown to be beneficial in recovering from the resulting loss of motor function. This research project aims to use these strategies, with some changes so they can be used during the time the wrist in casted/splinted, with the aim of reducing the loss of motor function from the inactivity. For the nerve stimulation a brace/cast will be designed and developed to deliver the stimulation to the underlying tissue while in the cast. The project consists of 6-week in-home programs for two groups. One to stimulate the nerves of the arm and the other to encourage mental rehearsal of movements both in hopes of improving recovery and shortening the time needed to heal. These two groups, and a third comparison group, will all take part in standard rehabilitation programs after immobilization. The in-home program will be assessed for ease of use. Motor function and pain will be measured at various time points up to 2.5 months after the intervention to see if the interventions speed up recovery at a functional level. This study will provide innovative cast for early rehabilitation for wrist fractures and sustainable new interventions to improve care for the large volume of people who incur wrist fractures.

column36: Surpassing Symptomatology: Exploring Posttraumatic Growth in MDMA-Facilitated Cognitive Behavioral Conjoint Therapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
column37: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a debilitating illness that impacts almost 1 in 10 Canadians in their lifetime. Individuals suffering from PTSD are at risk for suicide, other mental illnesses, and poor health outcomes. Yet, PTSD is not a solitary disorder. PTSD also impacts the mental health of loved ones. For this reason, Cognitive Behavioral Conjoint Therapy (CBCT) treats the patient and their partner. After this therapy, a majority of patients no longer meet diagnostic criteria for PTSD. However, symptom reduction is not the only measure of treatment success. Positive changes matter. Posttraumatic growth (or improvements in multiple areas of life following a trauma) can occur as stronger interpersonal relationships, personal strength, appreciation of life, seeing new possibilities, and spiritual change. It has been shown that CBCT can lead to posttraumatic growth. Yet, not all patients respond to treatment or show positive changes, and ways to improve therapies are needed. The drug 3,4 methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has shown remarkable promise when combined with psychotherapy; and MDMA has been named a breakthrough therapy for PTSD. However, no study has examined if posttraumatic growth occurs in MDMA-assisted couples therapy for PTSD. In this study, 40 couples will receive either MDMA-assisted CBCT or CBCT. We hope to uncover if posttraumatic growth increases for patients and partners in MDMA-assisted CBCT compared to CBCT, when posttraumatic growth occurs in therapy sessions, and to understand the lived experience for patients and partners longer term. To answer these questions, we will measure posttraumatic growth before and after therapy, examine therapy session tapes, and interview patients and partners 6 months after therapy. This will be the first study to examine posttraumatic growth in MDMA-facilitated couples therapy for PTSD. Given that the FDA has scheduled MDMA to become a medicine by 2021, this research is necessary and timely.

column36: Cortical responses to median nerve stimulation as a prognostic tool in acute severe brain injury: a functional neuroimaging study
column37: One of the greatest challenges doctors face in the intensive care unit (ICU) is accurately predicting if a patient will wake up from a coma and make a meaningful recovery. Currently, there are no accepted methods to determine the likelihood of good outcome for patients with severe brain injury. There are reliable tests to determine if a patient will have a poor outcome. One such test is called a median nerve stimulation task. This test records brain activity while stimulating the median nerve at a patient's wrist to determine if the brain perceives the stimuli. When no response is detected, an individual will not survive their injury. However, when the response is present, the patient's outcome remains unknown. This is likely because the device used to measure the response does not provide information about brain areas beyond the somatosensory cortex (SI), which is the part of the brain that is the first step in the pathway for perceiving sensations. It remains unknown if other areas that receive signals from the SI would give more information about sensory processing that would be relevant to regaining consciousness. Functional neuroimaging, a method that measures activity across the entire brain, holds promise in this regard. I will use this method to assess the brain's activity in response to nerve stimulation at the wrist. I plan to recruit 30 comatose patients and correlate the strength of brain activity to clinical outcome following coma. I predict that patients with widespread brain activity in response to nerve stimulation will be more likely to wake up from coma and make a meaningful recovery, whereas patients with minimal activation will likely not regain consciousness. Identifying accurate predictors of good outcome will have significant impacts on the assessment and care of patients in the ICU, inform medical decision making, and provide answers to loved ones of patients in coma.

column36: Investigating the effects of inflammation on breast cancer cell dormancy in the brain
column37: Breast cancer is the second leading cancer-related cause of death among women. Death from breast cancer is most often caused by the spread of cancer from the original tumour to other locations in the body. This often happens many years after a patient was thought to be cancer free. When this happens in the brain, the outlook is devastating. It is thought that this recurrence of cancer happens because some cancer cells hide in the body in a state where they are not forming tumours and are unable to be detected. This is called cancer cell dormancy. The need to understand what causes these cells to awaken and grow into tumours later is alarmingly clear. Inflammatory diseases and various lifestyle factors causing chronic inflammation are associated with higher rates of breast cancer recurrence. This has inspired recent preclinical studies, which identified chronic inflammation as a condition that can 'awaken' dormant cancer cells. Our lab is developing new ways to study dormancy after breast cancer cells have spread to the brain. We use dormant cells and radiation treatment along with special magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques that allow us to see when cancer cells spread to the brain, when cells form tumours, and cells that remain dormant. My research will use a chemical called lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to cause brain inflammation in mouse models to see if inflammation will trigger the dormant cancer cells to begin dividing and forming tumours. This work will provide valuable information to doctors and patients on the effects of inflammation and the increased risk of recurrence that inflammatory diseases and lifestyle factors may present.

column36: Improving the efficiency and accuracy of acute stroke computed tomography imaging to better treatment outcome
column37: Stroke is mainly caused by a blood clot that limits blood flow to the brain and can result in serious brain injury if not treated quickly. For every minute a stroke remains untreated, almost two million neurons die, which is equal to three weeks of normal brain aging. Early treatment with clot-dissolving drugs or by pulling out the clot with a catheter can greatly reduce subsequent disability. The key challenge is to select patients who will benefit from treatment without causing harm. Head CT scans can show how much of the brain is already dead or only injured and can be saved with treatment. Currently, three consecutive CT scans are used to qualify stroke patients for treatment. The first scan makes sure that the patient's symptoms are not caused by a bleed, which requires other forms of treatment. The second scan requires x-ray dye injection, which lights up the blood vessels to help find the clot. The third scan also uses x-ray dye and scans the patient many times to see the dye passing through the brain. Computer programs then analyze the movement of the dye through the brain to measure blood flow. Brain blood flow can find how much brain tissue is already dead or still surviving and can be saved with treatment. Each of these CT scans has an important role in assessing a stroke patient but performing them sequentially can delay treatment, which increases the chance of disability. My research aims to develop new ways to scan stroke patients so that only one CT scan is needed rather than three. This can speed up diagnosis time, reduce CT x-ray radiation exposure, and reduce the amount of x-ray dye needed to assess a stroke patient. Our technique will simplify CT scanning at less-experienced community hospitals while still providing thorough diagnostic information. My work will result in an all-inclusive CT scan that is quick, easy, and ready to use at all hospitals and will improve the care and outcome of stroke patients.

column36: Investigating Perfusion Responses and the Development of Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Oncology Patients Using Laser Perfusion Imaging
column37: Advancements in cancer treatments have improved patient outcomes with a wide range of malignancies such that treatment is now often given with the intent to cure the cancer. The extended survival of cancer patients has given time for the negative effects of these cancer treatments to manifest in the form of cardiovascular disease (CVD) including heart disease, stroke,and others. This means that from the point of cancer diagnosis onward cancer patients are at elevated risk of dying from CVD compared to the general population. Examining the change in blood flow of the skin in response to heat non-invasively using lasers may provide an early indicator of declining regulatory mechanisms and signal the onset and progression of cardiovascular disease. The goal of this project is to determine skin blood flow responses under resting conditions, during and following increased blood flow from heat, in healthy subjects and in cancer patients prior to, and following completion of their cancer treatment. As well as, to evaluate the utility of the specific markers in the blood flow response as a predictive marker for cardiovascular disease in patients following completion of cancer treatment. The proposed work has the potential to be of clinical use in the assessment and diagnosis of conditions related to the impairment of blood vessels and can provide insight into how to effectively target these impairments. Although this study is examining the effect of cancer treatments on cardiovascular disease risk this research has the potential to be applied to many other conditions affecting the cardiovascular system.

column36: The role of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use and bacterial vitamin B6 metabolism in kidney stone formation
column37: Kidney stone disease affects approximately 10% of North Americans, and the prevalence of this disease is increasing throughout the world. Stone disease is characterized by a buildup of crystalline minerals in the kidney, which can cause immense pain that is typically managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). While there are many types of kidney stones, the vast majority of stones are made up of calcium oxalate. Oxalate concentration, being a causal factor in stone formation, can be regulated by vitamin B6. While it is known that NSAID use decreases circulating levels of vitamin B6, it is unknown if this affects kidney stone formation. Moreover, the gut microbiota is another key player in B6 production; however, bacteria that produce vitamin B6 have been found to be diminished in stone formers. Thus, we hypothesize that the use of these pain management drugs depletes vitamin B6 production from the gut microbiota, which causes an increase in oxalate that leads to a higher risk of stone formation. The objectives are three-fold: i) Understand how NSAIDs and vitamin B6 affect kidney stone formation using a fruit fly model. ii) Investigate if NSAIDs directly interact with the gut microbiota in a host-free model. iii) Assess the effects of gut microbial reconditioning on stone burden in stone formers taking NSAIDs. These studies are important because they will improve our collective understanding of how resident bacteria in the gut influence stone formation in humans. The project also elucidates if a common management strategy for the symptoms of stone disease (NSAID use), could further increase the prevalence of stones. Ultimately, this study could lead to changes in management practices for the use of NSAIDs or a potential therapeutic for kidney stone disease. Given that the incidence of kidney stone disease is increasing, this project should be of importance to both the general public and academic and clinical communities.

column36: Dementia and hearing loss: Using preclinical models to uncover the mechanisms that accelerate cognitive decline in aging and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Dementia affects ~50 million people worldwide; a daunting statistic that highlights the need to limit its risk factors. Numerous studies have identified that hearing loss increases one's risk for developing dementia, including Alzheimer's disease. This is highly concerning given the prevalence of hearing disorders amongst Canadians (~35% of those aged 20-70). Although a clear link has been established, the brain mechanisms that cause hearing loss to accelerate the brain pathology associated with dementia remain poorly understood; a gap in knowledge that has ultimately impaired our ability to clinically intervene. While inflammation in the brain has been seen in both hearing loss and dementia separately, it has not been investigated as a potential common link when both disorders co-occur. To that end, I will use rodent models of hearing loss and dementia for this study. Rats will be exposed to noise during young adulthood, and then at given times throughout their lifespan, will undergo a novel combination of non-invasive neuroimaging, behavioural testing of learning and memory, blood biomarker testing, and microscopic analysis of brain tissue. Looking forward, once the underlying brain mechanisms linking hearing loss and dementia have been uncovered, I will be in a unique position to use our animal models to investigate novel therapeutic strategies. In 2050, the global prevalence of dementia is expected to increase to ~130 people; however, if an intervention were to delay its onset by only one year, this number would decrease by 10%. Thus, considering the millions of people suffering from dementia and/or hearing loss, this work could lead to profound clinical implications.

column36: Preoperative patient education program for a total shoulder arthroplasty surgery: a randomized control trial
column37: Issue: Shoulder problems affect many Canadians yearly. While surgery is one of the best treatments for shoulder problems, patients are unaware about shoulder replacement surgeries, the exercises needed after surgery and how to safely recover from the surgery without having another injury. Uncertainties about the surgery and recovery process can further cause post-surgery problems such as: pain, anxiety and re-injury. While some healthcare centers offer an in- class program to educate patients before surgery, some patients face issues with distance or transportation, and cannot regularly meet their doctor to address all their concerns. Solution: Our project aims to create an online educational program that will teach patients through online videos and educational materials before they go into shoulder replacement surgery. By creating online modules, we can increase the accessibility for home use, and prepare patients on topics such as: their concerns about the surgery and proper exercises they can expect after surgery for a safe recovery. column36: Uncovering preclinical biomarkers of Parkinson's disease using iron imaging
column37: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) is a substantial risk factor for Parkinson's disease (PD). RBD can appear years before PD allowing the unique opportunity to study disease markers before diagnosis. Discovery of early disease markers would improve diagnosis and treatment options for millions of PD patients worldwide. RBD showed similar structural changes to the brain as those seen in PD, providing evidence that RBD resembles an early form of PD. Fittingly, the conversion of RBD to PD can be predicted by these structural changes. An increase in brain iron is a consistent structural change in PD that indicates neurodegeneration. We anticipate elevated brain iron will also be present in RBD and will be the first to test this using iron imaging techniques. If successful, an increase in brain iron could be the earliest marker of PD. We will scan RBD patients, early-stage PD patients, and healthy controls in a state-of-the art magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner to measure iron levels in the brain. Using various imaging techniques, we will assess differences in the brain iron levels across the three groups. We predict that the brains of RBD patients will resemble early-stage PD patients and be different from healthy controls. This study will seek to uncover early markers of PD, which is a clinical and research priority. The findings will have major implications for earlier diagnosis and treatment of PD, ultimately improving patient quality of life in our ageing population.

column36: Investigation of the Interplay between Stress and Genetics in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
column37: Given that 90% of ALS cases are without obvious genetic etiology (sporadic), environmental components have long been suspected as contributing factors in ALS pathogenesis. The design and development of effective therapies for ALS requires a deeper understanding of how the environment impacts the cell biology governing disease initiation and progression. We hypothesize that compromised stress granule dynamics, an important protection mechanism for cells, are central to motor neuron vulnerability in ALS. To study how the environment plays a role in stress granule dynamics in vivo, we will subject healthy and TDP-43 mutant mice to chronic hyperthermic shock at different ages and examine ALS pathobiology. We believe that this non-invasive stress will provide insight on how the environment affects ALS disease progression in the context of pathogenic TDP-43. To complement this, we will use proteomics to deepen our understanding of the regulation governing the mRNA encoding G3BP1, a fundamental player in stress granule formation which we view as a potential therapeutic target in ALS. Taken together, this project will greatly expand our knowledge on the interplay between stress and genetics in relation to ALS and help identify a new therapeutic target to mitigate impaired stress granule formation.

column36: Allostatic load as a predictor of pharmacological treatment response in patients with major depressive disorder
column37: According to the World Health Organization, depression is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Approximately 15% of people will experience depression at some point in their life. Less than half of people diagnosed with depression respond to current treatments, including antidepressant medication. Future research must better understand factors that predispose individuals to depression, but also be able to find ways to predict who will respond to antidepressant medication or not. One reason that could explain poor antidepressant treatment response rates is the popular belief that depression is a 'disease of the mind'. This has shaped how we screen/diagnose depression in clinical practice - that is, by assessing the presence of at least 5 of 9 symptoms of depression listed in a diagnostic manual in a standardized interview. As such, two patients could receive a same depression diagnosis, while only sharing one symptom. Importantly, this suggests that distinct types of depression exist, that may in turn respond differently to a similar antidepressant treatment. Contrary to popular beliefs, depression is a 'full-body disease' that emerges from complex interactions of repeated exposure to stressful life events, like unemployment or divorce, along with biological factors that increase a person's risk of developing depression. As such, research must identify markers of biological functioning that will help predict health trajectories and treatment responses. Our project aims to measure biological markers of allostatic load - a comprehensive measure of biological wear and tear that chronic stress exerts on hormonal, immune, cardiovascular and metabolic systems - in a large sample of patients who have consulted psychiatric emergency services, and were seen again 1 month later at an outpatient clinic. This will allow us to measure how multiple markers of biological functioning can help predict antidepressant treatment responses and help guide novel drug discoveries.

column36: The origin of the Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor and its isoforms in platelets
column37: The Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) is a naturally occurring substance that has been discovered in the brain. It is responsible for neuron growth and healing of the brain blood vessels. When insufficiently produced, BDNF leads to depression, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. BDNF had also been found in platelets at much higher concentrations than in the brain. Most cells have a nucleus which is an important structure that stores DNA and allows cells to produce different proteins and hormones they need to function. Platelets are exceptions to that rule, as they do not contain a nucleus which makes them unable to produce their own different proteins. This fact raises the question about the origin of BDNF in platelets. Do platelets inherit it from their mother cells, megakaryocytes, or do they capture it from the bloodstream? My PhD project aims to answer these two questions. Megakaryocytes will be isolated from the bone marrow of patients. A blood sample will also be collected, and platelets will be isolated. We will compare the BDNF content/pattern of platelets with megakaryocytes. To check if BDNF in platelets is acquired from the bloodstream, we will mimic this in the lab by exposing platelets to BDNF in a test tube. We will then measure how much BDNF crosses over into platelets, to see if they acquire it from their surroundings. The project will thus help us understand how BDNF makes its way into platelets. Ultimately, we want to use this information to make platelets into BDNF transporters to sites of injury, either in blood vessels of the heart or of the brain, to help heal after a heart attack or stroke.

column36: Traduction, adaptation et validation d'un instrument de mesure de la resilience familiale aupres de parents de nouveau-nes prematures francophones
column37: Introduction. La resilience familiale a ete identifiee comme un facteur protecteur contre la detresse psychologique lors d'experiences familiales difficiles. Elle peut etre definie comme << la capacite du systeme familial a s'adapter a une periode d'adversite pour en ressortir plus fort et mieux outille >>. Ce concept semble prometteur dans le contexte neonatal, ou il est reconnu que l'hospitalisation d'un nouveau-ne premature a l'unite des soins intensifs neonatals (USIN) engendre chez les parents plusieurs sentiments negatifs se rapportant au deuil, a la detresse et a l'isolement. Afin d'evaluer adequatement la resilience familiale, un instrument de mesure valide et fidele est imperatif. Cependant, peu d'instruments de mesure de la resilience familiale ayant des qualites psychometriques adequates sont disponibles. La Family Resilience Assessment Scale (FRAS), se demarque neanmoins pour les populations requerant des soins de sante, mais cet instrument n'est pas disponible en francais et n'est pas valide pour les parents de nouveau-nes prematures. Le but de ce projet doctoral est donc de traduire en francais, adapter et valider un instrument de mesure de la resilience familiale, la FRAS, aupres de parents de nouveau-nes prematures francophones. Methodologie. Un devis methodologique de cinq phases est prevu : (I) la traduction en langue francaise (II) la validation de contenu des items traduits par un groupe d'infirmieres et de parents de prematures, (III) l'administration en ligne de la FRAS aupres de 330 parents de prematures recrutes sur une base volontaire (IV) l'adaptation de la FRAS en une version courte et (V) l'estimation de ses proprietes psychometriques (coherence interne, structure interne, fidelite inter-juges). Retombees attendues. La traduction, l'adaptation et la validation de cet instrument de mesure offrira aux chercheurs une mesure fidele et valide de la resilience familiale a utiliser dans des etudes ulterieures en sciences infirmieres.

column36: The effects of TCR affinity on the quality and persistence of peripheral T cell tolerance
column37: T cells are specialized immune cells that protect us against infection and cancer. These cells express a molecule (known as the T cell receptor) that recognizes pieces of foreign or abnormal proteins that are displayed on the surface of infected or cancerous cells. If a T cell recognizes these protein fragments, it can eliminate the abnormal cell. Therefore, during the development of T cells, our immune system ensures the generation of a massive number of different T cells that will be able to recognize any pathogen we encounter during our lifetime. Unfortunately, this process also leads to the generation of T cells that can recognize our own native proteins (self). A mechanism called tolerance ensures that T cells that can interact with 'self' protein fragments are either deleted or become unresponsive, preventing the establishment of autoimmune diseases. Although most studies focus on understanding how tolerance occurs when a T cell binds strongly to 'self' protein fragments, some T cells that bind only weakly to 'self' protein fragments actually do the most damage to our own organs in autoimmune diseases. Therefore, we hypothesize that T cell tolerance is induced and maintained differently based on how strongly a T cell binds to 'self' protein fragments. In the cancer setting, different therapeutic approaches have been used to try to reinvigorate T cell function to fight cancer. However, such procedures can lead to the activation of T cells specific to 'self' protein pieces, causing autoimmunity. My research will help us understand the impact of these therapeutic approaches on T cells that interact with 'self' proteins and how they can be improved to limit the unwanted autoimmune side-effects of these drugs.

column36: A neuromagnetic investigation of the nonlinear brain dynamics of mental health: Depression and schizophrenia as departures from criticality
column37: Complex systems such as earthquakes, flocking birds, highway traffic and the stock market have all been found to operate at the delicate boundary between the orderly and the chaotic, a dynamic state known as criticality. At this middle ground, an optimal balance of stability and flexibility gives the system the remarkable ability to sense, process and remember information from its environment. The trick is to keep this fine balance, and not topple over into frozen order or destructive chaos. There is now mounting evidence that the healthy brain also operates at this critical boundary, which raises the possibility that some forms of mental illness may be due to a difficulty in maintaining criticality. Depression and schizophrenia are two of the most common and least understood mental illnesses, and their symptoms bear a striking resemblance to the behaviour of critical systems out of balance. Depression languishes in excessively ordered black-and-white thinking and poor behavioural flexibility, while schizophrenia is plagued by chaotic thinking and unstable behaviour. In this project, we will test the hypothesis that depression and schizophrenia are both explained by a deviation from criticality into excessive order or chaos, respectively. Patients with depression or schizophrenia, as well as mentally healthy volunteers, will undergo recording of their ongoing brain activity in a MEG scanner. From each participant's signals, we will estimate the distance from criticality and its direction (order or chaos), and test whether these can predict diagnosis and symptom severity. A benefit of the criticality model is that it can point the way to new, more targeted therapeutic treatments. Thus, in a second phase, we will synthesize audiovisual signals that can boost criticality and test them on volunteers to see whether we can also boost their mood. We are hopeful that this project will usher in real advances in the understanding, treatment and prevention of mental illness.

column36: Physiopathologie et traitement du somnambulisme chez l'adulte
column37: Le somnambulisme est un trouble du sommeil qui se caracterise par des comportements moteurs, une desorientation cognitive relative au temps et a l'espace, une perception erronee de l'environnement immediat ainsi qu'une absence de reaction face aux stimuli externes. Les episodes de somnambulisme surviennent principalement lors d'eveils soudains mais incomplets, principalement en sommeil lent profond. Cependant, malgre ce lien etroit entre le somnambulisme et le sommeil lent profond et pres de cinq decennies d'investigations cliniques et en laboratoire, la physiopathologie du somnambulisme demeure peu documentee a ce jour. De plus, considerant qu'il n'existe actuellement aucune etude prospective menee de maniere appropriee pour evaluer le traitement du somnambulisme, les preuves appuyant les recommandations et les effets des traitements sont limitees. Les observations cliniques suggerent que l'hypnose est un traitement efficace du somnambulisme, mais les mecanismes par lesquels l'hypnose reduit les episodes sont inconnus. L'objectif de ce projet de recherche est donc de clarifier la physiopathologie du somnambulisme en etudiant les caracteristiques du sommeil lent profond avant et apres un programme d'intervention base sur l'hypnose en comparant trois groupes de participants : des patients somnambules recevant un traitement par hypnose, des patients somnambules ne recevant pas un tel traitement et un groupe de sujets temoins. Elucider la physiopathologie du somnambulisme et explorer l'impact de l'hypnose sur les mecanismes physiologiques sous-jacents au somnambulisme sont des etapes necessaires qui contribueront a l'elaboration d'essais controles randomises sur l'hypnose et le somnambulisme.
