column36: Effects of an overground walking program with a robotic exoskeleton in long-term manual wheelchair users with a chronic spinal cord injury
column37: Many individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI) use a wheelchair as their primary mode of locomotion. The prolonged inactive sitting time associated with this mode of locomotion contributes to the development or worsening of numerous adverse health effects. To counter this vicious circle, engaging in a walking program with a wearable robotic exoskeleton (WRE) is a promising physical activity intervention. In fact, walking with a WRE promotes, among other things, lower limb weight-bearing and mobility while engaging the trunk and upper limb muscles and the cardiorespiratory system. Our novel pilot project allowed us to measure beneficial effects on bones, muscle and body fat after participation in the program, in addition to physical, physiological, and psychological benefits reported. This project aims to strengthen this evidence by measuring the effects of an overground walking program with a WRE on cardiorespiratory health, body composition and wheelchair functional capacity. Wheelchair users with a chronic SCI (>18 months) will enroll in a 16-week overground walking program with a WRE. They will complete 1-to-3 training sessions/week supervised by a physiotherapist. Data will be collected 1 month preceding and immediately before and after the intervention, as well as 2 months after the program. Clinical and laboratory assessments, as well as questionnaires, will be completed. Interviews will be conducted to measure participant satisfaction and perspectives at the end of the program. The new knowledge will inform the development of novel community-based and home-based adapted physical activity programs and may facilitate the prescription and uptake of WRE by wheelchair users with a chronic SCI.

column36: The 13-item Pain Stages of Change Questionnaire (PSOCQ-13): An evaluation of its psychometric properties and ability to predict strategy use and treatment satisfaction in adolescents undergoing an active, interdisciplinary intervention for chronic pain self-management
column37: The complex nature of pediatric chronic pain poses many challenges for youth, families, and healthcare providers. Poorly managed chronic pain in youth can have debilitating effects, including psychological and academic difficulties, increased healthcare utilization, and adult chronic pain. Research suggests that a multidisciplinary approach to care is most effective, which includes psychological interventions aimed at teaching patients how to manage their pain independently. However, waitlists for such treatments are long and their success is highly reliant on patients' willingness to learn and use self-management strategies. A brief, established measure that can help determine which treatments components will benefit whom is needed. In the context of the Pediatric Chronic Pain Program at the McMaster Children's Hospital ("clinic"), which offers a 10-week manualized adolescent program (MAP) targetting pain self-management, my doctoral research aims to evaluate the shortened Adolescent Pain Stages of Change Questionnaire (PSOCQ-13A) and assess its ability to predict changes in strategy use and treatment satisfaction in adolescents. First, the PSOCQ-13A and related measures are completed at the clinic intake will be used to assess the reliability, validity, and factor structure of the PSOCQ-13A. Second, in a sample of patients completing MAP, the number of self-management strategies endorsed at weeks 1 and 10 and their ratings of the usefulness of skills learned and overall treatment satisfaction at week 10 will be assessed. Comparisons will be made across participants in three different stages in their willingness to self-manage pain at intake (i.e, precontemplation, contemplation, action/maintenance). This research will determine the efficacy of the PSOCQ-13A. Ultimately, this work will aid in developing idiosyncratic treatment plans, enhance treatment success, and reduce the negative social, emotional, physical, and economic sequelae of pediatric chronic pain.

column36: Examining Neuropsychological Outcomes of Preterm Neonates with Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease
column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is one of the most common congenital defects worldwide, affecting ~1 in 80-100 newborns in Canada. Advancements in surgical techniques and perioperative care have improved survival; yet, children remain at risk for adverse neuropsychological outcomes, such as cognitive, academic, motor, behavioural, and social outcomes. Past research has shown that newborns with CHD and preterm newborns without CHD have similar brain anomalies. To date, there is little research examining neuropsychological outcomes and brain anomalies in preterm neonates with CHD. The proposed research program will examine the neuropsychological profiles of children born preterm with CHD during infancy and at 4-years of age and will examine the brain-behaviour relationships that are associated with neuropsychological outcomes. Using a clinical sample of preterm infants with CHD (N=75), I will conduct a series of 4 studies that will examine preterm infants with CHD's cognitive, language, and motor abilities in infancy (18 and 36 months), as well as compare these outcomes with those of children born term with CHD and children born preterm without CHD. Further, I will examine the neuropsychological profiles of a subset of these children that received an assessment at 4 years (n=40) and identify brain characteristics from the neonatal period that may be predictors of neuropsychological functioning at 4 years of age. This program of research will provide critical knowledge about short and long-term neuropsychological outcomes of preterm neonates with CHD and associated neurological and medical characteristics. This will help inform clinical practice and direct intervention planning initiatives associated with neuropsychological outcome with this unique, understudied population.

column36: Meeting the Challenge: Comprehensive Neurodevelopmental Profiles of Vulnerable Infants and Young Children
column37: Infant and early childhood neurodevelopment unfolds within contexts of risk and protection. Cumulative risks exacerbate neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities; however, the accumulation of protective factors can ameliorate such effects and promote positive neurodevelopment. Brain development from 0-6 years is foundational for lifelong neurodevelopment. There is a substantial gap in knowledge around early neurodevelopmental profiles and trajectories. The field is hampered by limited assessment measures available for use with children under age 6 years, with minimal consideration of contexts of risk and protection. My proposed research will address this gap in knowledge by 1) establishing a method of assessing the neurodevelopment of vulnerable infants and young children which encompasses contexts of cumulative risk and protection to 2) identify comprehensive neurodevelopmental profiles. In Study 1, I will conduct a systematic literature review of neurodevelopmental assessment measures available for infants and young children. Measures will be organized by age and neurodevelopmental capacity to establish comprehensive assessment batteries. In Study 2, I will conduct neurodevelopmental assessments using the batteries established in Study 1. Contexts of risk and protection will be captured using the cumulative risk and protection measures developed in my Master's research. Such assessments will enable comprehensive neurodevelopmental profiles to be identified across age ranges (0-2, 3-4, 5-6 years) and compared across clinical and control samples with differential social-emotional and neurological vulnerability (N=54). This research will catalyze the field as advancements in early assessment methods are essential to evaluate and understand comprehensive neurodevelopmental profiles. Findings will have policy implications around advocacy and the cost benefits of targeted early interventions to maximize the neurodevelopmental trajectory of vulnerable young children.

column36: The role of the alpha-11 integrin in pressure overload-induced right ventricular remodeling
column37: Heart failure is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, costing the Canadian healthcare system more than 2.8 billion dollars annually. Right-sided heart disease is a poorly-researched, major contributor to heart failure and is a consequence of factors such as high-blood pressure within the lungs and left-sided heart disease. During the development of right-sided heart disease, the landscape of scar tissue within the heart changes significantly. Specifically, fibroblasts (scar tissue-producing cells) malfunction and produce profuse amounts of scar tissue, ultimately stiffening the heart and impairing function - a process known as fibrosis. Although fibrosis is exceedingly common, there remains no effective treatments to halt its progression in the heart, especially in the right ventricle. The aim of this project is to understand how an environment-sensing protein in fibroblasts, the alpha-11 integrin, impacts the development of fibrosis in the right ventricle of the heart. Our group discovered that in response to Diabetes, a common cause of cardiac fibrosis in humans and rodents, the absence of alpha-11 significantly reduced fibrosis in mice. Additional work by our group demonstrated that alpha-11 is also upregulated during right-sided heart disease, making this protein a promising and potentially new way to treat fibrosis in the right ventricle. We will use our current techniques to understand the mechanism by which the alpha-11 integrin promotes fibrosis, with a focus on the right side of the heart. We will test these mechanisms on a scale ranging from the whole heart down to an individual cell. This project will be the first to define the role of the alpha-11 integrin, in right-sided heart disease where there is a scarcity of therapeutic knowledge. This work will be crucial in developing new drug treatments not only against fibrosis in the heart, but also for other organs where fibrosis leads to death, such as the lungs, liver, and kidney.

column36: Determining a safe way to increase physical activity in children
column37: Physical activity prolongs life, reduces disability, and improves mental health. In children, regular activity strengthens muscles and bones, increases fitness, and prevents obesity. Many children, especially those who play competitive sports, consistently increase their levels of activity. However, increased physical activity can increase risk of injury. Injuries can result in time lost from school, work, or hobbies, and lead to chronic conditions like osteoarthritis. Previous research suggests that injury risk increases if activity increases suddenly by more than 30%. However, these studies used flawed techniques and focused on adults. My project will determine the relationship between physical activity and injury risk in children. I will use more novel and advanced statistical methods than previous studies to analyze datasets that include activity and injury information for 1500+ Danish schoolchildren and 6000+ Canadian high school athletes. I will determine the maximum amount of physical activity that should be performed to avoid injury. My results will help generate guidelines on how children can safely increase physical activity without injury.

column36: Investigating the relationship between externalizing and internalizing behaviours, executive functioning and brain networks in children with and without mental health disorders
column37: In Canada, 20% of children and youth are diagnosed with mental health disorders, and yet, there is limited understanding of the underlying biology of these disorders. The traditional approach of understanding biology of mental health disorders compares patients with a disorder to those without one. However, this approach has limitations including investigating a small number of participants and using statistical approaches which do not leverage the different ways a disorder can be presented. Treatment innovations would benefit from increased knowledge of the different manifestations within a single disorder and the overlap between mental health disorders. Mental health disorders feature problems with behavioural regulation (such as aggression and anxiety), impairments in executive functioning (such has a poor self-control), and alterations in the brain activation patterns. However, it is unclear how these three components are linked to one another in a given disorder or across disorders. My project aims to understand the relationships between these three components using: 1) a large dataset comprising of children who have mental health disorders and those who do not, 2) measures of brain activation, behaviour and executive functioning, and 3) innovative statistics. By exploring these relationships, we hope this could be the first step towards understanding whether certain combinations of these three components lead to higher risk of a mental health diagnosis or greater everyday life impairment. From there, this research may be able to inform early preventative and/or intervention treatment strategies.

column36: Pre-Clinical PET Imaging of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
column37: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a medical technique that creates an image of biochemical processes occurring in a human, by injecting radioactive compounds (radiotracers) that bind to specific target and their distribution in the body is then detected by a PET camera. With the high burden of neurodegenerative disease in Canada, and worldwide, new PET radiotracers must be developed to image illness-related processes in the brain. This work will develop radiotracers designed to advance scientific understanding of a brain enzyme known as glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3), along with related molecules involved in neuroinflammation, all characteristics highly involved in chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). CTE is a neurodegenerative disease, associated with brain injuries where affected individuals may experience diverse symptoms including cognitive impairment, mood disorders, self-medication, substance use disorders, aggression and memory loss. At present, diagnosis of CTE occurs after death, upon autopsy. Despite the extensive efforts in biomarker development, PET imaging is not widely utilized for CTE diagnosis, partially due the lack of radiotracers for detecting early stages of cognitive impairment and pathology. Through this research, we aim to better understand the interactions that occur between our imaging tools and other biological targets in the brain, as well as differences in target expression throughout CTE progression. Through the development of new imaging biomarkers for GSK-3, misfolded proteins and neuroinflammation molecules, the opportunity arises for earlier detection of disease pathology and potential for advancing therapeutic intervention. By completion of the proposed project, the goal is to have translated the first PET radiotracer to image GSK-3 in the living human brain and transform how physicians diagnose millions of patients suffering from neurological disorders, CTE and related dementias.

column36: Investigation into molecular pathway dynamics underlying sensory processing and habituation learning impairments in Autism Spectrum Disorders using C. elegans
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) are a group of neurodevelopmental disorders that affects roughly 1 in 59 children, and is characterized by a range of behavioural and communication impairments. This variation in symptoms, along with the more than 100 genes thought to contribute to ASD, makes identifying effective therapies extremely challenging. Impairments in sensory processing and habituation learning (a type of learning where one learns to stop responding to repetitive stimuli) are reported in up to 90 percent of ASD cases. The high presence of sensory processing and habituation learning impairments suggests that ASD-associated genes may be acting together in common pathways to control these behaviours. Identifying these common pathways provides a unique opportunity to investigate why sensory and learning impairments occur when different ASD-associated genes are affected and inform us of new therapeutic targets to help individuals with these behavioural and learning difficulties. I will use the established Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) model system to investigate if ASD risk genes function together to regulate sensory processing and learning. I propose to 1) define common molecular pathways affected in ASD that contribute to sensory and learning impairments, 2) identify where in the nervous system and when in development ASD risk genes function together, and 3) determine whether behavioural impairments caused by the inactivity of one gene can be rescued by targeting the activity of another gene. I believe this research will significantly improve our understanding of the function of ASD-associated genes, the mechanisms of ASD pathology, and progress our ability to identify new therapies for the individuals with ASD who experience sensory and habituation learning impairments.

column36: Sex Differences in the Pharmacology of Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, THC; The Primary Psychoactive Component of Cannabis.
column37: Cannabis is one of the most commonly used addictive drugs, with an estimated 192 million users worldwide. With the recent legalization of non-medical cannabis in Canada, regulators, policy makers, law enforcement and health care professionals lack adequate scientific guidance to effectively regulate cannabis use and educate the public. Robust research is required to minimize harm, leverage the benefits of legalization and protect individuals. The primary psychoactive component of cannabis, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) affects men and women differently. Previous research has demonstrated sex related differences in cannabis use, abuse, methods of consumption and reasons for therapeutic use. Additionally, THC has differential effects in men and women in terms of pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, subjective effects, abuse liability and therapeutic potential. The mechanisms of these underlying sex differences are unclear and narrowly researched. I hope to examine pharmacological sex differences in how men and women use and abuse cannabis. In order to examine these differences, various doses, potencies, and routes of administration will be utilized in healthy volunteers to better understand how sex differences in THC pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics underlie behavioural differences produced by cannabis in men and women. With the recent legalization of cannabis and the rapid emergence of new cannabis products (e.g., edibles, drinkables, oils, concentrates), cannabis use and abuse are expected to increase across Canadian society, particularly among vulnerable populations such as youth. This research can help to proactively create sex-dependent guidelines for use, better individualized treatment options for cannabis use disorder, and mitigate risk factors associated with cannabis use that differ for males and females, in order to protect the health of our population.

column36: Iitsim'kaatsita: Enhancing relations between Indigenous women and registered nurses. Journeying toward transformative reconciliation to foster maternal health equity.
column37: There are unique forms of relationships between Indigenous women and the Canadian health care system. These relationships are informed by historical and contemporary forms of structural violence, racism and discrimination. Many Indigenous women face multiple barriers accessing health care and are often reluctant to utilize services based on past negative experiences. Additionally, Indigenous women have been relegated to the periphery of Indigenous life and politics. More specifically, colonial states such as, Canada and United States, attempted to wipe out Indigenous communities by radically altering the roles and responsibilities of Indigenous women to be submissive and domesticated. These settler colonial processes have permeated Indigenous Nations, leading to internalization of gendered violence. To more fully capture issues from the perspectives of Indigenous women, is important for inquiries, especially those concerned with maternal healthcare services, to consider the impacts of gendered violence. While these health care barriers have been described, how these dynamics can be mitigated has not been studied. This study seeks to understand the relationships between registered nurses and Indigenous women during a time of reconciliation, with the goal of improving maternal health experiences and outcomes for Blackfoot women. A theoretical framework of Critical Indigenous Feminism and a Blackfoot Indigenous research methodology will guide this exploratory sequential Indigenous mixed-methods research study. It will include the perspectives of RNs and Blackfoot women about maternal-child community- and hospital-based care across prenatal and postnatal periods. Shedding light on the current challenges in maternal health practices and co-designing an innovative study with Blackfoot women and RNs will identify what matters most to Blackfoot women living in Blackfoot territory and help present solutions for culturally safe maternal health practices.

column36: The Multiple Sclerosis Prodrome
column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a disease of the brain and spinal cord. Common symptoms include fatigue, vision problems, numbness, weakness and unsteady gait. Canada has one of the highest rates of MS globally. The causes of MS are still not well understood. Many people with MS recall subtle symptoms before the start of typical MS symptoms. These earliest signs of MS are called prodromal symptoms. Much of the research on prodromal symptoms has focused on people who developed MS in adulthood. Recently, researchers have found that adults with MS were more likely to seek health care (i.e. visit a physician, have a hospitalization and fill out prescriptions) for certain conditions (e.g. fatigue and pain) in the 5 years before their first typical MS symptom. However, there are many questions that are still unanswered. During my PhD I will determine (i) what the most common groups of prodromal symptoms among adults with MS are and (ii) whether men and women with MS experience different prodromal symptoms. Five to ten percent of people with MS develop the condition in childhood. Less is known about prodromal symptoms among children with MS. During my PhD I will determine (i) whether children with MS are more likely to seek healthcare for certain conditions in the years before their first typical MS symptom and (ii) whether children with MS are more likely to have lower education scores before their first typical MS symptom. These findings will be important as they may help doctors diagnose MS earlier, allowing people with MS to start MS therapies more promptly. Moreover, once researchers have a better understanding of how far back in time people with MS can experience symptoms, they will be able to investigate the causes of MS better. Lastly, in the future, new therapies will likely be developed that protect the brain and spinal cord. People with prodromal symptoms can then be identified and prescribed these protective therapies.

column36: The effects of running on arthritic knee cartilage: A biomechanical and imaging analysis
column37: Knee osteoarthritis is an incurable disease characterized by the breakdown of cartilage which cushions the ends of bones in your knee joint. This condition is an expensive cause of disability in Canada, with annual costs of more than $27.5 billion. Experts recommend regular exercise to self-manage knee osteoarthritis through improving pain and function while slowing disease progression. While running is a cheap and popular physical activity across Canada, many people with osteoarthritis stop running or hesitate to start because they are unsure if it is safe to participate in an activity which involves high impacts. However, current scientific evidence does not support the wide-spread belief that running can lead to or aggravate knee osteoarthritis, and stopping running could have a bad impact on a person's quality of life. My research will compare how healthy and arthritic knee cartilage respond to running. In people with and without knee osteoarthritis, I will use medical imaging to look at cartilage inside their knee joints, and assess the movement patterns of their legs while they run. I will also test out ways to change their running technique to help reduce their pain. My findings will allow us to understand how the knee joints of people with osteoarthritis react to the heavy loads experienced by the body during running. Using this information, we can eventually make recommendations about the safety of running with respect to knee joint health.

column36: Digital health equity in online sexually transmitted and blood borne infection testing in British Columbia
column37: The consensus among public health practitioners is that digital interventions can potentially be used to equitably improve access to healthcare especially among people who experience marginalization including gay, bisexual men and minority language populations. This is crucial in sexual health where stigma and discrimination still constitute significant barriers to healthcare. Yet, many digital interventions have not given deliberate attention to health equity and some may inadvertently reinforced existing inequities in society in this situation. In this study, I will study people's behavior as they use an online sexually transmitted infections (STI) testing platform called GetCheckOnline to understand how aspects of the platform affect adoption and utilization of care. I will then interview the website visitors who start the process of requesting an STI test but do not complete it to identify their issues with the website and how to improve the experience. I will pay specific attention to ways in which gender and sexual orientation play into peoples' experience and their outcomes. I will use research methods that are specifically adapted to identifying what works, for whom and under what conditions. This research will improve the delivery of online STI services, especially for people who experience marginalization in Canada. Through this work, we may identify aspects of online STI interventions that may be adapted to promote equitable access to health services. In addition, by understanding user characteristics, behaviors and experiences at various steps of the service cascade on the online STI testing platform, we may learn how to best tailor digital interventions to meet the unique needs of various categories of people who experience marginalization.

column36: Out on the street: A critical ethnography with homeless 2SLGBTQ+ youth who use drugs
column37: Two-Spirit, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and other queer (2SLGBTQ+) youth are known to face many social challenges, including bullying, rejection from family and friends, homophobia, and transphobia. These social determinants place 2SLGBTQ+ youth at much higher risk of homelessness and substance use. Alarmingly, 2SLGBTQ+ people are estimated to make up as much as 40% of the overall homeless youth population in Canada. Of further concern, those who use drugs experience inequitably high rates of drug-related harms, including overdose, sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections, and criminalization. In British Columbia, these negative outcomes are poised to be exacerbated by intersecting public health crises related to opioid overdoses, housing affordability, and COVID-19. In response to these crises, innovative health policy and programming interventions in BC are now underway, including the provision of a safer drug supply, the scale-up of outreach-based harm reduction services, and expansion of housing shelters and subsidies. Yet, it remains unclear how these services can be tailored to best serve homeless 2SLGBTQ+ youth who use drugs - a critical research gap, given inequities and public health challenges faced. This study addresses this gap by using community-based, critical ethnographic approaches to examine the drug-, housing-, and broader health-related experiences of homeless 2SLGBTQ+ youth who use drugs, with particular attention to how these experiences are influenced by features of healthcare services and broader socio-structural environments. Set in Vancouver, British Columbia, this study will include intensive qualitative interviews and arts-based photovoice methods with 40 homeless 2SLGBTQ+ youth who use drugs. Findings from this study will identify how interventions (e.g., clinical, programming, structural policies) can best be used to reduce drug-related harms and improve health and social outcomes for this priority population.

column36: The impact of residential displacement on health among people who use drugs living with HIV in Vancouver, Canada
column37: While effective treatment for HIV is available, people who use drugs (PWUD) living with HIV continue to experience poor HIV-related health and other unfair and avoidable health outcomes. While housing status (e.g., homelessness) has previously been identified as a factor that influence the health of PWUD living with HIV and other vulnerable populations, little is known about the health consequences of residential displacement. Residential displacement is defined as the involuntary move of households from residence, such as when eviction or rent increase forces tenants out of housing. The ongoing affordable housing crisis alongside social distancing orders (e.g., no-guest policies in low-income housing) and a looming eviction crisis brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic is expected to further displace low-income, marginalized groups across North America. The proposed study based in Vancouver, Canada will be among the first to examine how residential displacement influences health. Using innovative research methods that involve interviews, observations, and mapping, this study will follow 40 PWUD living with HIV for a period of one year to explore the impact of residential displacement on health among this population. The proposed study will involve meaningful participation of community partners (e.g., HIV service organizations, drug user-led organizations) and peer research assistants in the research process to ensure that findings are useful to the affected community. column36: Temporal transcriptomic and epigenetic analysis of leukocytes in sepsis and COVID-19 patients
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition caused by the body's severe response to infection. Those who survive sepsis can develop long-term symptoms such as a persistent impairment of the immune system. This weakens the ability of sepsis survivors to fight infections and increases their risk of rehospitalization and death. Post-sepsis care is still poorly researched despite scientists predicting that rehospitalizations due to sepsis are increasing, especially with the COVID-19 pandemic. Sepsis is the most common life-threatening complication of COVID-19 and COVID-19 survivors can have similar long-term symptoms as sepsis survivors. It is not well understood why the immune system remains dysfunctional months after sepsis. To answer this question, we need to track how the immune system of a sepsis patient changes over time. My project will examine changes in gene expression (what genes turn on or off) in patients during and after sepsis, as well as in COVID-19 patients with sepsis, to determine what immune pathways are malfunctioning. At the same time, I will investigate changes in DNA methylation, which is an epigenetic process where methyl group molecules are added to areas of DNA to turn genes off for long periods of time. I hypothesize that DNA methylation is "locking in" the changes in gene expression to cause long-term immune dysfunction. I will then test if targeting the genes and pathways identified from these patient studies can prevent immune dysfunction in a cell model. The results from this project will identify the processes that cause long-term immune dysfunction, which is the first step for developing treatments that prevent sepsis survivors from falling sick again. Another potential outcome is the discovery of new biomarkers to diagnose sepsis patients earlier or predict patient survival. Overall, this project will help address a devastating but under-researched consequence of sepsis that affects many sepsis survivors.

column36: Deciphering and harnessing the role of tumor-infiltrating B cells in anti-tumor immunity
column37: The goal of cancer immunotherapy is to stimulate the immune system to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Ovarian cancer has remained largely resistant to today's immunotherapies, demonstrating that more work is needed to devise the optimal strategy to properly activate the immune system in this disease. Among the white blood cells, B cells are uniquely responsible for producing antibodies, proteins that specifically bind to foreign substances, pathogens, or other dangerous materials to neutralize them or flag them for destruction by other immune cells. The presence of B cells in tumors is associated with prolonged patient survival, yet we do not fully understand how B cells mediate this effect. To fill this knowledge gap and develop better immunotherapies, we will define the different types of B cells found in patient-derived ovarian tumor samples and determine what proteins their antibodies bind to enable recognition and killing of cancer cells. In Aim 1, we will employ sophisticated sequencing techniques to "read" molecular information from individual B cells and infer their functions based on the genes they express. This technique will also allow us to identify the antibodies that B cells use to recognize cancer cells. In Aim 2, we will determine which proteins B cells are recognizing on the surface of cancer cells, which may reveal new targets for immunotherapy. In Aim 3, we will determine the functions of B cell-derived antibodies by assessing their effects on immune cell activity and tumor cell death when added to cultures with these cells. By studying tumor-associated B cells at this high level of resolution, we will reveal for the first time how these cells facilitate the immune response against cancer. We may also identify new targets to incorporate into the next generation of immunotherapies relevant to ovarian cancer and other malignancies, leading to better outcomes for future cancer patients.

column36: Implementing a Frailty Severity Scale using Primary Care Electronic Medical Record Data in Canada
column37: Frailty is a worldwide problem. Over 1.5 million older adults in Canada are frail and in 10 years this number is expected to reach 2 million. Frailty is a state of increased vulnerability from physical, social, and cognitive factors. It results in greater risk of negative health outcomes such as immobility, falls, and hospitalization. Frailty is best thought of as being on a continuum and can be reversed if caught early. Currently there is no standard way to identify frailty severity. The purpose of this research is to identify the severity of frailty on a continuum in older adults using primary care electronic medical record (EMR) data. This research will address two questions: 1) What is the validity of implementing a frailty severity scale using primary care EMR data? and 2) How is frailty understood from physicians', nurses', and patients' perspectives? This study builds on work completed in the United Kingdom using their electronic frailty index. I will translate electronic terms, called codes, that represent frailty to a coding system used in Canada. I will interview physicians, nurses, and patients to explore their experiences with and thoughts about frailty to determine whether there is agreement on the codes representing frailty. I will then develop a revised electronic frailty index within EMR systems and explore primary care clinicians' experiences with it and its usefulness. This would be the first study in Canada to examine frailty severity using primary care EMR data. This work would be available to more than 1,500 clinicians. The frailty index will support clinicians in helping older adults remain independent and prevent unnecessary hospitalizations associated with frailty. This research aligns with the goals of the Canadian Frailty Network, and with policy directions from the British Columbia Ministry of Health, where early detection of frailty and intervention are prioritized to enhance quality of care and reduce healthcare system spending.

column36: Virtual Reality Exposure for the Treatment of Vaginismus: A Pilot Study
column37: Background: Vaginismus is a female sexual dysfunction characterized by interference with intercourse, and is conceptualized as a specific phobia of vaginal penetration. The treatment literature reveals that many women with vaginismus do not respond to conventional interventions. However, therapist-guided gradual exposure therapy - an evidence-based intervention for phobias - has proven successful in the treatment of vaginismus. Despite this progress, institutional restrictions pose significant barriers to therapist-guided exposure. Alternative exposure-based treatments for vaginismus are therefore needed. Aim: We aim to identify components of virtual reality (VR) erotic stimuli that elicit phobic responses (fear/anxiety) in women with vaginismus, and apply these findings to develop and pilot test VR exposure therapy for vaginismus. Procedure: Women with vaginismus and controls (n = 25 per group) will use a VR headset to view 3D sexual encounters showing penetrative or non-penetrative activities either from a 1st or 3rd person point of view. Participants will provide ratings of anxiety, distress, and fear of vaginal penetration after each video. Erotic video characteristics that evoke negative affect will be identified, and these findings will inform the development of a VR intervention for vaginismus. Two groups of women with vaginismus (n = 25 per group) will be randomized to either a 3-week VR exposure therapy or an active control group involving imaginal exposure. Women will complete questionnaires assessing fear of vaginal intercourse, avoidance of sexual activity, and sexual distress before treatment, 1 week-, and 6-months following treatment. Implications: This study will be the first to examine the therapeutic potential of VR exposure therapy for vaginismus, and is likely to innovate clinical practice and improve the quality of life of women affected by this distressing health concern.

column36: Hypoxia promotes treatment-resistance and lineage transformation of EGFR-driven non-small cell lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer related death in Canada. There are 2 major subtypes of lung cancer: the more common non-small cell lung cancer and the rarer, but deadlier, small cell lung cancer. Recent advances in lung cancer therapy has led to drugs that are not only effective in non-small cell lung cancer patients, but also well-tolerated, thus improving patient outcomes and well-being. However, after initial treatment with these drugs, a small but significant fraction of patients' tumours become more aggressive, resistant to treatment, and ultimately lethal. A closer look at these non-responsive tumours shows that some have morphed into the more deadly small cell lung cancer. This process is known as small cell transformation and we are interested in understanding how this transformation takes place in order to develop new strategies to treat or prevent this phenomenon. Cells in tumours often experience low levels of oxygen (hypoxia), even in tumours developing in the lungs. Cancer cells are able to adapt to hypoxia, which tends to morph them to be more aggressive and resistant to treatments. This project aims to clarify the role of hypoxia in small cell transformation by exposing cell lines created to mimic patient lung cancers to hypoxia and then evaluating their molecular similarity to small cell lung cancer cells. Our lab also possesses a unique experimental mouse model that naturally develops lung cancer, which we will use to investigate the natural progression towards small cell transformation. Understanding the mechanism underlying the deadly small cell transformation will provide critical information that can lead to the development of new treatment and prevention strategies against a deadly form of lung cancer where all current therapies fail.

column36: Fine-tuning drug-polymer conjugate chemistry for enhanced drug delivery to breast cancer
column37: Over 40% of marketed drugs are poorly water-soluble, which reduces the drugs' potency and can cause severe side effects. Attaching a highly water-soluble compound to these drugs is a simple way to improve their water solubility. Although this approach is frequently used, a majority of reports in the literature only disclose one compound without exploring other potential structures. This reported compound may not be the optimal candidate to reach and eradicate its target. Because each drug has its own unique chemical profile, I hypothesize that the method used to incorporate the water-soluble compound needs to be fine-tuned to obtain the best version of the drug. Very few reports in the literature explore other versions of the drug before performing expensive experiments on cell lines and animals. Unfortunately, resources are invested on likely a subpar drug candidate. In my thesis project, I have developed a chemical method that allows for easy attachment of water-soluble compounds to existing chemotherapy drugs used for breast cancer treatment. First, attaching these water-soluble compounds to the drug will increase drug solubility. Second, these water-soluble derivatives of the drug self-assemble into particles that are approximately 1000 times smaller than the diameter of a single strand of hair. Because of its shape and size, these particles display prolonged blood circulation, selective accumulation in tumors, and can release the drug once at its target site. Breast cancer is an ever-prevalent disease, as it makes up approximately 25% of new cases of cancer and 13% of all cancer deaths in Canadian women. Those undergoing chemotherapy treatment often experience side effects that are a direct result of off-targeting effects. My research offers a way to improve the delivery and increase the chances of the drug reaching its target. This method can also be used to modify a wide variety of drugs that are used to treat other diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis.

column36: A mixed methods evaluation of lived experience, adaptation, and identity development in adolescents with genetic conditions
column37: Genome-wide sequencing (GWS) is a sophisticated technology that looks at all of a person's genetic information in a single test. GWS is being used more often and growing numbers of people are receiving genetic diagnoses, including adolescents. It is important to understand what the experience of receiving and living with a genetic diagnosis is like, so we can improve health services to make sure patients have the best possible outcomes. Studies have explored the experiences of adults who receive a genetic diagnosis and parents who receive a genetic diagnosis for their newborn or young child. But we know very little about experiences of adolescents in these circumstances. We do not know what impact a genetic diagnosis has on their identity development or how they adapt to their genetic conditions. Little is known about what adolescents with genetic diagnoses need from healthcare services to help them cope with their diagnosis. We will study the experiences of adolescents with genetic diagnoses made by GWS with regards to receiving, understanding, and living with a genetic diagnosis. We will explore what these adolescents need from healthcare services in order to adapt to their conditions, so that we can modify care to improve outcomes. To do this, we will interview adolescents with genetic diagnoses who agree to participate and ask them to complete questionnaires about how they adapt to the diagnosis, what impact it has on their identity, and whether they regret being tested. We will use the data we collect to develop a model to understand how adolescents adapt to genetic conditions. This model can be used to inform clinical services in British Columbia so that this group of patients has what they need from their healthcare services.

column36: Using a novel anti-FXIII agent as an effective and safe antithrombotic for ECMO
column37: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a form of mechanical circulation of blood, used to bypass the hearts and/or lungs of very sick patients. Blood is pumped through a series of medical devices that act as an artificial lung. When blood comes into contact with these devices, however, it can become activated and trigger blood coagulation, leading to pathogenic clots that can cause these machines to fail, and put patients at risk of deadly pulmonary embolism or ischemic stroke. Anticoagulation is the treatment currently used to stop these clots from forming; unfortunately, bleeding is also a common complication of ECMO, and the risk of bleeding events, such as intracerebral or pulmonary hemorrhage is exacerbated by anticoagulants. A new therapeutic option must be developed to stop these clots from forming, without adding to the risk of bleeding. Coagulation factor XIII (FXIII) has long been considered a promising target to prevent thrombosis while avoiding bleeding risks. I recently published findings that a novel agent, the first to be effective for long-term inhibition of FXIII in vivo, reduced the burden of pathological clots while maintaining hemostasis, in vivo (Strilchuk, et al. Blood, 2020). The current project seeks to build upon these findings, testing the hypothesis that this novel agent will limit unwanted clotting during ECMO, while not increasing the risk of bleeding or pulmonary embolism. Well established in vivo models of ECMO and thromboembolism will be used to assess the efficacy of this novel agent at preventing clots from forming, while bleeding events are monitored. These experiments will be supported with ex vivo characterization of clot structure, an indicator of clot severity. If successful, this project will point to a new mechanism that can be used to prevent the deadly complications associated with ECMO, and provide valuable information on the efficacy and safety of this novel agent as a potential therapeutic.

column36: Determining biomarkers of response to docetaxel chemotherapy in men with metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer.
column37: The primary chemotherapy for late-stage prostate cancer is only effective in 45% of patients. However, there is currently no way of knowing in advance which patients will benefit from treatment, and which patients could avoid the side-effects of chemotherapy through receiving a different therapy instead. Herein lies an urgent clinical need for tests that can predict patient response to chemotherapy, thereby helping clinicians select the best cancer treatment for an individual patient. Our aim is to identify molecular markers capable of predicting whether a patient will respond to the chemotherapy docetaxel. Our assay relies on the fact that cancerous tissues shed a small amount of their DNA into the bloodstream, creating an opportunity to examine the tumour by analyzing DNA isolated from a patient's blood sample. This DNA, termed 'circulating tumor DNA' (ctDNA), provides a molecular snapshot of the tumor. CtDNA profiling is a novel technique that enables us to extract information about a cancer via a routine blood test, where it can be quickly translated to the clinic to inform treatment decisions, eliminating the need for invasive tissue biopsies. Over the next three years we will have obtained blood samples from 216 patients with advanced prostate cancer beginning treatment with docetaxel chemotherapy. In this project we will extract the ctDNA from the blood samples, and perform DNA sequencing to detect changes present in each patient's cancer. We can correlate the DNA changes that we find with the patient's clinical outcome, and find the changes that would have predicted how the patient responded to treatment. Finally we will confirm that our predictive 'biomarkers' indeed work, by testing them in blood samples collected from an independent cohort of patients receiving chemotherapy at our cancer centre. This will help us understand why some cancers are resistant, and we will have developed a test to help select the best treatment for an individual patient.

column37: A spinal cord injury (SCI) occurs from damage to the spinal cord and is associated with adverse health and social implications. Traditionally, health promotion has focused on the prevention of disease and disability, resulting in limited health promotion interventions for persons with SCI. Compared to the general population, persons with SCI are more likely to smoke, experience more significant tobacco-related health disparities, and encounter unique circumstances to treatment. Despite these inequities, smoking cessation interventions have yet to be developed to support persons with SCI to stop smoking. Interventions developed using theory, systematic processes, and engagement of knowledge users are often more useful and relevant to those who may benefit from it. The ORBIT model was developed to improve the real-world impact of behavioural interventions by ensuring that interventions are carefully crafted and developed incrementally over time. The objective of this research is to use behaviour change theory and meaningful partnership with an SCI organization to develop and conduct preliminary testing of a smoking cessation intervention for persons with SCI. First, in a small sample of persons with SCI, we will test whether a tailored smoking cessation intervention helps persons with SCI stop smoking. Second, using gold-standard video recording methodology, we will determine whether peers with SCI can be trained to deliver the intervention as intended. Third, using a randomized design, we will determine whether the peer-delivered smoking cessation intervention can demonstrate greater smoking cessation rates compared to a care-as-usual control group. column36: Understanding the mechanisms of primary 5-Azacytidine resistance in the treatment of MDS
column37: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are cancers originating from the blood-forming cells present in the bone marrow. In MDS, the disease either results in a failure to produce enough blood cells to survive or in 20% - 40% of the patients, the disease progresses to a very aggressive leukemia. Currently, only a bone marrow transplant can cure a patient. However, not all patients are eligible for a marrow transplant. For such patients, the only standard therapy is the use of a drug called Azacitidine (AZA). In MDS, chemical changes to the DNA called DNA methylation, is commonly observed. AZA reverses this DNA methylation changes. However, 50% of the patients do not respond to the AZA. It is yet unknown why some patients respond to AZA while others don't, in other words are resistant to AZA. Currently, there are no further treatment options for such patients, raising the pressing need to understand how AZA resistance develops. In the bone marrow of an MDS patient, certain rare cells are responsible for the initiation and progression of MDS. These rare cells also known as the MDS-stem cells can give rise to more MDS-stem cells as well as mature cancerous cells which then fill up the patient's bone marrow. Previous studies have shown that treatment with AZA only kills the more mature cancerous cells but not the MDS-stem cells themselves . Thus, to understand how resistance to AZA develops, we need to understand the nature of these MDS-stem cells. This project focusses on studying these rare MDS-stem cells from patients who are responsive and non-responsive to AZA. Through this project I want to identify which type of blood cell becomes the MDS-stem cell and examine if the nature of the identified MDS-stem cells in AZA responders is different from the non-responders. Understanding the nature of these stem cells will help identify new therapies that can be used along with AZA to target these stem cells and improve the outcomes of AZA non-responsive patients.

column36: Is 5-methyltetrahydrofolate as effective as folic acid in increasing serum and red blood cell folate during pregnancy and lactation, while resulting in reduced unmetabolized folic acid in maternal blood and breastmilk?
column37: Nutrition during pregnancy has an important impact on infant development and pregnancy outcomes. Folic acid (the man-made form of the B-vitamin folate) is recommended during pregnancy and while breastfeeding because it is important for healthy development, but there is growing concern that Canadian women are getting too much. Our bodies are only able to process small amounts of folic acid, and when we eat too much, our bodies cannot use folic acid properly. Unused folic acid has been found in nearly all (>90%) blood and breastmilk samples of Canadian women while pregnant and breastfeeding. The effects of unused folic acid are not fully understood, but have been associated with cancer, concerning infant health outcomes, and it may interfere with folate's role in growth and development. Also, unused folic acid in breastmilk is concerning because babies are not able to absorb it as well as natural folate, which could cause low folate levels. Natural folate may be better for women to take while pregnant and breastfeeding than folic acid. Some prenatal vitamins in Canada contain natural folate instead of folic acid (as it is approved by Health Canada), but natural folate has never been tested during pregnancy. Therefore, a study is needed to help address this gap. We will recruit 60 healthy pregnant women and give them prenatal vitamins with either natural folate or folic acid starting at 8-21 weeks gestation until 1 week after birth. We have three goals for this study: 1) To measure serum folate, red blood cell folate, and unused folic acid after supplementing with natural folate or folic acid for 16 weeks of pregnancy; 2) To learn about recruiting pregnant women to this type of study, to help design a larger follow-up trial; 3) To compare breastmilk folate levels (total folate and unused folic acid) in each group. This study will provide needed information to determine the safest and most effective form of folate supplements for Canadian women and their babies.

column37: In recent years, the significance of genetic information in the diagnosis, screening, and treatment of myeloid (blood) cancers has become highly evident. The increasing impact of identifying genes associated with these cancers necessitates more comprehensive screening techniques. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a tool that permits the identification of many genes in one efficient test that can be applied for patients using blood or bone marrow. NGS works by assessing a patient's DNA (obtained from these blood or bone marrow samples) to determine whether there are any variations in the sequence (mutations) that may be contributing to their disease. Targeted NGS refers specifically to the assessment of a group of genes known to play a role in blood cancers. NGS allows the simultaneous assessment of many genes in a single, efficient, comprehensive test. The results of this test (showing whether there is variation in a patient's DNA) can inform clinicians about this patient's disease based on current research surrounding affected genes. This tool will not only complement current techniques but may in fact replace them. We performed sequencing of DNA from patient samples using the Thermo Fisher Ion Chef and Ion S5 sequencer. We analyzed the sequencing results and classified variants (changes in genes/DNA) based on their potential to impact patient care. To date, we have performed sequencing of 187 samples from 168 unique patients with a variety of myeloid cancers. Of the variants (abnormalities) detected, 77% were potentially actionable (impacted patient care). In the majority of patients, we were able to identify variants that may aid clinicians in achieving/clarifying diagnoses, informing follow-up/prognosis, and guiding treatment decisions. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating NGS into clinical testing for patients with myeloid cancers.

column36: Identifying neurocognitive outcomes and cerebral oxygenation in critically ill adults on acute kidney replacement therapy in the intensive care unit: The INCOGNITO-AKI study
column37: Adults admitted to hospital intensive care units (ICUs) are more likely to develop problems with cognition. Cognition affects how people think, feel, and react. Problems with cognition can cause poorer quality of life, difficulties doing daily activities and caring for oneself, and strain the Canadian healthcare system. Patients who need dialysis for kidney issues during their ICU stay are at an even higher risk for these problems. Over half of critically ill patients develop kidney problems, and up to 13% need dialysis to replace the function of their kidneys. Patients who need long-term dialysis outside the ICU have worse cognitive function. We do not know the effect of short-term dialysis during an ICU admission on cognition. We expect the effect to be similar to long-term dialysis. Brain oxygen levels are linked to cognitive function and can be an early warning sign for cognitive problems. To understand how dialysis affects the brain in adults admitted to the ICU, we will a) measure the level of oxygen in the brain while patients are on dialysis; and b) see if these levels are associated with cognition and patient safety at 3- and 12-months after they have been discharged from the ICU. To understand any differences in brain effects, we will also compare the brain oxygen levels of patients when they are treated with two kinds of dialysis: intermittent hemodialysis (patients are treated for hours at a time with breaks in between), and continuous kidney replacement therapy (patients may be treated continuously for days with no breaks). Cognitive function is important for good quality of life. To support patients and the healthcare system, we need to know how treating patients with dialysis in the ICU impacts their cognition. This will help providers and patients make more informed decisions about both the type and the impact of dialysis. This study may inform future interventions to help prevent cognitive problems for patients treated with dialysis in the ICU.

column36: Uncovering a role for gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids in the anti-Factor VIII immune response
column37: Hemophilia A (HA), an inherited bleeding disorder that is characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction in the coagulation protein Factor VIII (FVIII), can result in major bleeding events that can lead to serious health complications if not properly managed. The most effective treatment for these patients is intravenous injections of the FVIII protein. However, up to 30% of patients develop an adverse immune response towards the therapeutic FVIII that results in inhibitors, antibodies that bind to and neutralize the FVIII protein. FVIII inhibitors render treatment ineffective and complicates the management of bleeding in people with HA. Although several risk factors have been identified, no significant progress has been made to prevent inhibitors from forming. Interestingly, bacteria throughout our gastrointestinal tract are critical for the healthy functioning of our immune system. Evidence suggests that a loss of certain healthy bacteria, termed dysbiosis, can predispose you to immune-related disease. Thus, gut dysbiosis may be a potential risk factor for FVIII inhibitor development. Research published by us shows that dysbiosis in HA mice results in enhanced FVIII inhibitor production but how this occurs is not understood. We hypothesize that a specific class of metabolite healthy bacteria produce, short-chain fatty acids, are responsible. This study aims to elucidate the way gut bacteria and their metabolites regulate FVIII inhibitor production and will give insight into what an ideal gut composition may look like to prevent inhibitor occurrence. Results generated here may also provide rationale for clinical translation, whereby bacteria in the gut of people with HA is screened prior to their first FVIII injection. Ultimately, knowledge contributed to the field by this study may benefit research in rheumatoid arthritis, whereby anti-drug antibodies can also develop, and other diseases characterized by autoimmunity to self-proteins.

column36: Improving epilepsy diagnosis through machine learning-based interpretation of routine electroencephalography recordings
column37: Epilepsy is a common and debilitating disease, characterized by recurrent seizures as the result of abnormal and excessive neuronal discharges. Its diagnosis frequently relies on the electroencephalogram (EEG). During an EEG, electrodes on the patient's scalp record the brain's electrical activity, typically for 30 minutes. Neurologists then visually examine these recordings looking for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), i.e. "spiky" discharges sometimes occurring between seizures in epileptic patients. Unfortunately, a routine EEG will manage to capture these spikes in less than half of epileptic patients. In absence of IEDs, neurologists have no other means to distinguish an EEG of an epileptic patients from that of a non-epileptic patient. Recently, researchers have turned towards computers to interpret EEGs more objectively, and possibly extract subtle patterns that may be missed by the human eye. Deep learning (DL), a type of artificial intelligence, is revolutionizing our modern society. Inspired by the organization of neurons in the brain, DL allow computers to capture hidden patterns in images and other signals. Applied to EEG, DL is capable of automatically identifying seizures. Could DL detect hidden, abnormal patterns in the brain signal of epileptic patients? The objectives of the project are: 1) To extract thousands of anonymized EEG recordings from the CHUM database and review the medical files to identify which EEG are from epileptic patients and which are not; and 2) To implement a DL algorithm and train it to recognize epilepsy in seemingly normal EEGs. The impact of this project is important. Identifying new patterns of epilepsy could increase the sensitivity of the EEG in epilepsy, potentially automate its interpretation, and improve its availability to a larger percentage of the population.

column36: The therapeutic potential of miR-486-5p in ischemic acute kidney injury
column37: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a condition where patients experience a rapid decline in kidney function. AKI is a common complication of hospitalization with a high prevalence in intensive care units and has a high mortality rate. Recovery from AKI has long-term consequences including an increased risk of death and new or progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD). In Canada, the annual cost attributed to AKI is estimated at approximately $200 million; more severe episodes of AKI are associated with incremental increases in hospital length of stay and cost (Collister D, et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2017). Despite these health and economic consequences, no effective intervention for AKI exists. One common cause of AKI is ischemia reperfusion injury, where the kidneys experience a period of reduced blood flow and lack of oxygen, followed by the return of blood supply. Damage to kidney endothelial cells further compromises blood supply throughout the kidneys, which can impair recovery and lead to chronic kidney disease (CKD). MicroRNAs (miRs) are small molecules that regulate the expression of proteins. The administration of microRNAs has been shown to protect against AKI in mice. Our lab has shown that the administration of miR-486-5p reduces ischemic AKI in mice. We will further characterize the mechanisms by which miR-486-5p protects against AKI, with a focus on endothelial function. We will increase our understanding of microRNA in human AKI by (i) studying the effects of miR-486-5p in ischemic AKI using a mouse model with chronic high blood pressure, which can affect susceptibility to AKI and CKD and (ii) conducting a systematic literature review of microRNA in human AKI. These studies will provide an important step towards the development of therapies for patients with AKI.

column36: Developing a clinically accessible decision rule for return to activity following a paediatric anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
column37: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is the most frequently damaged knee ligament, with rates continuing to rise among active paediatric athletes. Moreover, the risk of ACL re-injury after surgical reconstruction (ACLR) is significantly higher than the initial injury. Despite the high risk for re-injury, and the lifelong associated health implications, there is minimal evidence available to guide return-to-activity (RTA) timing following a paediatric ACLR. One of the barriers restricting the development of RTA criteria are limitations on what can be collected in a clinical setting, as many factors associated with ACL re-injury risk require access to specialized laboratories. To address this issue, my thesis will achieve the following objectives: i) validate a novel suite of mobile technologies, ii) use the technology and a multidisciplinary approach to develop a decision rule for RTA timing, and iii) implement the decision rule into clinical practice. Through an established collaboration with orthopaedic surgeons at the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO), we will recruit paediatric patients who have undergone an ACLR. Data will be collected following the patient's ACLR during a series of dynamic tasks (ex. side-cuts) using clinically accessible mobile technologies. We will use this data to identify variables that predict positive clinical outcomes (ex. re-injury). Based on these measurements, cut-off thresholds can be identified to determine whether a paediatric patient is ready to RTA. The final phase of the project will focus on implementing the decision rule into clinical practice at CHEO. This project will create the first clinically accessible paediatric-specific RTA decision rule, reducing the risk for premature RTA and subsequent ACL re-injury. Furthermore, by ensuring our suite of technologies is transferable to other institutions, this project has the potential to improve the quality of care for all young Canadians recovering from an ACLR.

column36: Verbal memory impairments in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder: A transdiagnostic investigation of neural correlates and the effects of cognitive remediation therapy
column37: Schizophrenia (SZ) and depression (also called major depressive disorder [MDD]) are mental health conditions that involve problems memorizing information. Research has shown that individuals with SZ and MDD have abnormal activity in specific brain regions responsible for memory, but it remains unknown whether these abnormalities are the same in SZ and MDD. Researchers have begun looking at the effects of cognitive remediation therapy (CRT) on improving these memory problems. CRT is a type of treatment that involves computer-based training to improve certain types of cognition, like memory. It is unclear, however, if the effects of CRT are the same in individuals with SZ and MDD, or if CRT can improve the abnormal brain activity in SZ and MDD. The goals of the current research are to determine: (1) the specific brain abnormalities linked to memory problems in SZ and MDD; and (2) if CRT can improve the memory problems in SZ and MDD. Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we will measure brain activity in individuals with SZ, MDD, and healthy volunteers during a memory test. We will also measure memory using questionnaires. Next, we will give the individuals with SZ and MDD either 6 weeks of CRT or 6 weeks of unrelated control tasks. Then, we will remeasure their memory using the questionnaires and MRI tests to see if CRT improved their memory compared to the unrelated control tasks. The outcomes of this research will show if the abnormalities in brain activity in SZ and MDD are the same or different, and if CRT can help improve these abnormalities. This will help individuals with SZ and MDD because it may offer an additional treatment option that will help improve their memory and quality of life. Therefore, this research has the potential to help improve the lives of many Canadians. This research will also move the field forward by revealing brain abnormalities specific to SZ and MDD, and will inspire new treatment approaches using CRT.

column36: Effect of a professional development intervention on psychotherapists' skill in increasing reflective functioning in patients during psychotherapy sessions: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Psychotherapy is one of the most effective treatments for mental illnesses, but not all patients improve. Researchers are now becoming interested in the mechanisms by which psychotherapy works in order to improve patients' mental health, and reflective functioning may be one of those mechanisms. Reflective functioning refers to a person's ability to understand their own and others' actions in terms of thoughts and emotions. Reflective functioning is essential for forming relationships, and a lack of reflective functioning has been associated with many psychiatric disorders. My research will be a new study within a project that is currently underway. I plan to evaluate the impact of a training intervention on psychotherapists' skills in increasing reflective functioning in their patients during psychotherapy sessions. Sixty community-based psychotherapists will be recruited, and psychotherapists will then recruit patients who recently started psychotherapy (120 patients total). Half of the psychotherapists will receive evidence-based training on how to increase reflective functioning in patients. The other half of the psychotherapists will not receive training. All psychotherapists will then video-record six psychotherapy sessions with their patient participants. Using those videos, I will count the number of times that psychotherapists encourage reflective functioning in their patients during each session, and assess whether patients demonstrate increased reflective functioning as a result. I will also evaluate the patients' level of distress at the end of each session. This will allow me to compare trained versus non-trained therapists on their abilities to encourage patient reflective functioning during sessions, and whether these therapist interventions have an impact on patient distress. In addition to publishing my results in peer-reviewed journals, I will share the results of this study directly with over 1900 Canadian psychotherapists.

column36: Control of circulating levels of dietary fat by glucagon-like peptide-1
column37: Over time, inflamed, cholesterol-rich plaques build up in the arteries of the heart. As these plaques continue to grow, they can cause a blockage in blood flow, leading to a heart attack or a stroke. Drugs that lower blood cholesterol levels decrease the occurrence of these devastating events; however, they do not completely stop plaques from growing particularly in patients with diabetes, suggesting that other fundamental drivers must exist. Studies in humans have shown that high levels of fat in the bloodstream contribute to plaque growth. In patients with diabetes, this contribution is increased as they have higher amounts of fat in their blood even after the same meal as a healthy person. We do not understand why this happens. In response to a meal, our bodies release a molecule called glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) into the bloodstream. Drugs modelled after GLP-1 are currently used in the clinic to control blood sugar levels in patients with diabetes. Importantly, these drugs also decrease blood fats and death from heart disease but how this happens is unclear. We hypothesize that GLP-1 instructs the intestine to burn fat from the diet so that it does not enter the bloodstream and arteries. Using a mouse model that cannot perform this fat-burning process specifically in the intestine, we are going to test if GLP-1 can still work to lower blood fat levels. We will use high-resolution microscopes to see what cell type burns it. Overall, this project aims to understand how a drug for diabetes uses the intestine to lower death by heart disease.

column36: Investigation of chromosome 1q gain in pediatric posterior fossa ependymoma
column37: Brain cancer is the most prevalent cause of cancer associated deaths in children and adolescents. Ependymoma is the third most common pediatric brain tumour. The most aggressive and frequent subgroup of ependymoma is known as group A (PFA) arising in the cerebellum of infants with a median age of 3 years old. The current standard of care for children with these tumours includes surgery and radiation, which often results in long-term disabilities. Further, chemotherapy has been shown to be ineffective emphasizing the urgent need to find new therapeutics. A recent discovery from our lab has demonstrated the unique conditions required to grow patient derived ependymoma cancer cell lines, positioning us as the first research group in the world to routinely grow these tumours for experimentation. Approximately 25% of PFA tumours have been shown to exhibit an extra copy of a segment of DNA known as 1q. The presence of this additional copy is associated with a very poor prognosis despite aggressive treatment. Using a diverse set of emerging molecular technologies and our unique cell lines, this study aims to identify the key molecular pathways that are altered in tumours harboring this copy gain. Our discovery-based approach will help find genetic weaknesses that can be leveraged to inform drug screening using our cancer cell lines, to be further validated in mouse models of ependymoma for pre-clinical testing. Findings from this project have the potential to immediately improve the standard of care for this vulnerable patient population.

column37: The heart is an electrical organ. Once electrical signal is generated by the heart's pacemaker cells, it travels through the specialized electrical wiring network of the heart to stimulate muscle cells to beat synchronously. Therefore, maldevelopment or dysfunction of these biological wires can result in abnormal beating of the heart, and even lethal arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The anatomical structure of this wiring network was originally discovered in the 19th century by Drs. His and Purkinje; however, it is still not fully understood what they are made up of and how they are developed even until today. For example, are all these conduction cells in this network identical or unique depending on location within the heart? (e.g. top or bottom) In my study, I will address this question by utilizing the state-of-the-art techniques which enable the examination of the cellular and genetic identities of each single cell, and therefore generate a genetic blueprint of this conduction system. Furthermore, I will explore how the identities of these individual cells transform as the conduction system develops and matures to ultimately understand how it adapts to the meet the needs of a growing heart. My study will be the first to clearly track the genetic profiles of every cell in a maturing conduction system and identify key molecules regulating this process. This discovery will not only be foundational to scientists studying the electrical function of the heart, but also be valuable to discover treatments for patients with abnormal heart rhythms.

My proposed PhD research will be embedded within a larger funded study called Synbiotics for the Early Prevention of Severe Infections in Infants (SEPSIS), which aims to test interventions (probiotics, prebiotics and synbiotics) for the prevention of severe infections during early infancy in Bangladesh. My proposed doctoral research aims to explore whether the bacteria that are naturally found in the gut of newborns has an impact on their risk of developing a severe infection such as sepsis, pneumonia or meningitis. I will explore whether maternal and infant factors, such as mode of delivery and breastfeeding practices, affect the presence of these naturally occurring bacteria and the resulting risk of severe infection; in addition to whether the amount of bacteria influences the severity of infections. The burden of severe infections and neonatal mortality is high in South Asia; however, most of the promising research on interventions that affect infants' gut bacteria is conducted in high-income countries and among preterm newborns only. My research is important because it will contribute to the development of innovative prevention and treatment tools in settings where simple and inexpensive interventions can have the largest impact on a child's chance for a healthy life and ultimately towards global health equity.
