column36: Development and Interrogation of a Therapeutic Modality for STAT1 Gain-of-Function using CRISPR/Cas9 Base-Editing
column37: STAT1 Gain-of-Function (GOF) is a disease caused by mutations (genetic "spelling mistakes") in the STAT1 gene, which is important in regulating the immune system. Patients usually start becoming sick as infants with repeated infections, and can later develop auto-immunity, blood vessel disease, and cancer. Most people with STAT1 GOF depend on life-long medications (like antibiotics and immune-suppressive drugs), and many die young. The only cure available for STAT1 GOF patients is a stem cell transplant, where cells from a healthy donor are used to replace the diseased bone marrow cells of the patient. This treatment is used in other diseases with great success. Unfortunately, in patients with STAT1 GOF the survival and cure rates are much lower, and their bodies frequently reject the donated stem cells. A recent study showed that of all STAT1 GOF patients who received a transplant, more than half died. Because rejection of donor cells is a big barrier to treatment success in STAT1 GOF patients, we want to develop a system that directly treats patient bone marrow cells, a process which we call autologous (self) transplant. Our team wants to develop and test such a strategy in cells and mice that have STAT1 GOF, with a tool called 'base-editor' (genetic "spell-editor"). Using a guide molecule, we can direct the base-editor to the "spelling mistake" in the gene, where it swaps-out the mis-spelled "letter" ('base') with the correct one. We will test whether we are able to use this system correct a "spelling mistake" causing STAT1 GOF in cells. We will then test if giving corrected bone marrow cells back to mice can cure them of the disease. If we are successful, we will have a treatment for STAT1 GOF that can improve survival and cure-rates of patients, giving hope to both children and families affected by this devastating disease. We may also be able to use this method to treat people with other diseases which are caused by similar kinds of "spelling mistakes".

column36: Barriers and enablers to quality implementation of clinical genome sequencing in Canada: A comparative case study
column37: Background: Patients with rare diseases suffer from long delays in diagnosis. They also suffer from emotional and financial burdens associated with their disease. Objectives: This study will explore how four Canadian provinces are implementing clinical genome sequencing within their health system across Canada. Four Canadian provinces that are preparing to implement clinical genome sequencing will be studied: Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. Data collected for each province will include documents about genetic service delivery and interviews with four key groups of stakeholders involved in providing genetic services (i.e., clinics, laboratories, provincial government, and funding organizations). A comparison of stakeholder views and experiences within and across the provinces will inform recommendations for optimizing genome sequencing delivery in other Canadian provinces and territories. Significance: Study findings will guide the effective implementation of a delivery system for clinical genome sequencing in Canada to transform the care of patients with rare diseases.

column36: Autophagy regulation in spinal dorsal horn neurons and its role in pain signalling
column37: Chronic pain is a debilitating condition that affects around 20% of Canadians yet effective treatments are lacking. To develop treatments, we must understand the mechanisms underlying chronic pain at the initial pain processing site of the central nervous system - the spinal cord. Recent studies have identified that autophagy, a protein degradation process, is inhibited in spinal cord neurons during chronic pain. I have also discovered that autophagy affects pain behaviour in males but not females. However, little is known about the molecular signals that inhibit autophagy during pain nor the function of autophagy in pain sensation, which is the focus of my research. My plan of study will address three key gaps in knowledge. I will identify the sex-specific signals that lead to autophagy inhibition in the spinal cord during chronic pain. I will characterize how the proteins that mediate autophagy change during chronic pain and whether these changes differ between sexes. Lastly, I will address how autophagy affects the firing of spinal cord neurons, leading to increased sensitivity to pain. Altogether, my research will provide a greater understanding of the mechanisms by which autophagy regulates pain and how this differs between sexes. The results of these experiments may identify specific molecular targets for treating chronic pain. Since autophagy-modulating drugs are already used clinically to treat a variety of conditions, my findings could lead to the reassessment of such drugs as potential treatment for chronic pain.

column36: Intranasal Delivery of a S. mansoni Cathepsin B expressing Adenovirus Provides Sterilizing Immunity from Schistosomiasis
column37: Schistosomiasis (schisto) is one of the most important helminthic parasitic diseases in the world. Over 700 million people are at risk of infection. Schisto is acquired by fresh-water parasites and causes debilitating illnesses that can last over 30 years leading to death. Praziquantel is an effective treatment, however drug resistance is emerging, and it does not protect from reinfection. To solve this problem, the formulation of an effective vaccine is pertinent. In recent clinical trials human adenovirus 5 (hAdV-5) has been used as an effective vector to deliver various vaccines for malaria and SARS-CoV-2. It is the hope of this project to develop a vaccine using the same hAdV-5 technology which has moved to clinical trials in previous years. When tested, this vaccine provided 90% protection from parasite infection. We plan to increase this protection by delivering our vaccine intranasally to stimulate immune responses in the lung where the parasite is most vulnerable and prevent infection 100%. The study will be run in both male and female animals to determine sex differences caused by our vaccine. It will also determine the vaccine's ability to harness the immune response by assessing antibody production, and response by immune cells in the blood and lungs. The reality of a schistosomiasis vaccine would not only prove useful to stop transmission of the parasite within tropical and sub-tropical regions (where it is commonly found), but also to travelling Canadians. Additionally, with increased immigration a vaccine which provides sterilizing immunity would reduce the burden of schistosomiasis on the Canadian public health system.

column36: Netrin-1 is a novel regulator of inflammation in diet-induced non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
column37: More than 1.9 billion people worldwide suffer from obesity, which is associated with accumulation of fat in the liver known as steatosis. It is estimated that 35% of people with liver steatosis will develop non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), an inflammatory complication associated with higher risk of liver failure and cardiovascular complications leading to death. Projection models suggest that by 2030, more than 2.6 million Canadians will suffer from NASH. Notably, there is currently no standard of care treatment to treat this disease. An important event in the development of NASH is the infiltration of immune cells like macrophages into the liver. These cells contribute to the inflammatory and fibrotic responses that characterize NASH and lead to hepatic dysfunction. Thus, it is critical to understand the mechanisms by which macrophages infiltrate the liver and how this impacts inflammation and subsequent liver dysfunction. Netrin-1 (NTN1) is a protein that induces macrophage retention and allows for their survival in tissues, although its role in the liver is unclear. Preliminary studies from our laboratory suggest that loss of NTN1 in macrophages protects mice fed a high-fat diet from developing NASH, despite the development of obesity. To do this, we have developed various strategies to modulate NTN1 expression in macrophages in mice fed a diet specifically designed to induce NASH. These studies will be the first to determine if NTN1 is a valid drug target to halt or possibly even induce regression of NASH.

column36: Sex and age difference in the immune response to viral myocarditis
column37: Heart failure is a growing burden on patients and healthcare systems with a 5-year survival of less than 50%. column36: Characterizing the role of the endothelial transcription factor ERG in the development of abdominal aortic aneurysms: Towards novel therapeutic targets
column37: The aorta is the largest blood vessel in the human body and is responsible for carrying high pressure blood away from the heart and towards the abdomen. In approximately 1 in 100 older adults, the wall of the aorta weakens and expands over time, producing a blood vessel enlargement or aneurysm. Continual expansion of the aorta can lead to rupture, with an 80% total rate of death and a 50% rate of death for those that make it to hospital. Surgical repair before rupture has major risks (e.g., heart attack and stroke), with the highest risk occurring in older patients. Furthermore, there is currently no medical treatment available to slow the growth of aneurysms before surgical repair is required. Our research seeks to discover how the cells of the aorta interact during aneurysm formation. We are particularly interested in the protein ERG, which has been identified as a master regulator of healthy function in the cells that line the aorta (i.e., endothelial cells), but has not been studied in aneurysms. ERG will be investigated in cells isolated from the aorta, as well as in mice and humans who have developed aneurysms. We expect that the amount of ERG will be reduced during aneurysm development, which will then cause these cells to weaken the blood vessel wall and contribute to aortic expansion. We aim to identify molecules secreted by these cells that can be used as novel targets for creating new medical therapies. For example, molecules that promote aneurysm formation can be reduced by these therapies, while those that prevent aneurysm formation can be increased. In summary, our research will determine how ERG regulates cells of the aorta to contribute to aneurysms and identify new targets for the medical treatment of this disease. Importantly, these targets may also be used for the treatment of aneurysms in other blood vessels, including those supplying the brain or kidneys.

column36: Developing porphysome nanomedicines for applications in colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is common and deadly, with approximately 1 million new cases in 2018 and accounting for nearly 6% of all cancer deaths. There are several key problems that currently exist in the management of CRC that offer opportunities for improvement through emerging nanomedicine technology. The current mainstay of treatment consists of surgical removal of the tumour and the lymph nodes downstream from the tumour (which may harbour tumour cells); however, not all lymph nodes that are potentially affected may be removed. Up to 22% of patients may have malignant lymph nodes left behind. Another problem arises from the fact that in up to 39% of patients with rectal cancer, removal of the anus is required, which means that patients must live with a permanent colostomy (when the bowel are reconstructed such that feces drains through a hole in the abdomen). This can be avoided if the tumour is shrunk before surgery. Porphysome nanomedicines offer a solution to these problems: these are spheres composed of the porphyrin dye that fluoresce and can be used to kill tumours through a process called photodynamic therapy (PDT). Additionally, porphysomes naturally accumulate in tumours, which makes them particularly effective for targeting tumour and minimizing side effects. These porphysomes have shown promise in guiding surgery through fluorescence in other cancers and in destroying tumours; however, their effectiveness in CRC has not been established. My project will examine the effectiveness of porphysomes for fluorescence-guided surgery and photodynamic therapy to improve the management of CRC. I will also test an emerging relative of the porphysome, called the EDTA-porphysome, which appears to hold promise for more effective fluorescence-guided surgery and PDT. My project will develop these porphysome nanomedicines with the goal of using this emerging technology in patient care to improve the length and quality of life for people with colorectal cancer.

column36: Efficacy, mechanisms, and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients
column37: Kidney transplantation improves survival and quality of life. Diabetes in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) increases the risk of losing their transplant, developing cardiac disease, and/or dying. However, there are no diabetes treatments in KTR with proven cardiac and kidney benefits. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are a new class of drugs for diabetes. In a first among diabetes therapies, this class of drugs was demonstrated to have major cardiac and kidney protective effects in patients with diabetes. What differentiates SGLT2i from other diabetes therapies is that they act directly on the kidneys independent of improvements in blood sugar levels. This may occur in several ways, including salt removal via the kidney leading to lower blood pressure (BP). Considerations when using SGLT2i in KTR include the risk of infections as SGLT2i may increase the risk of certain genital infections and drug interactions with anti-rejection medications. We believe that the kidney protective effects of SGLT2i including BP lowering and salt removal are preserved in KTR with diabetes. We propose a study where 52 adult KTR with diabetes will be randomly assigned to a SGLT2i called dapagliflozin or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary objective is to determine whether dapagliflozin lowers BP in KTR. Secondary objectives include identifying potential mechanisms for BP lowering and kidney protection, as well as the safety of dapagliflozin and its ability to lower blood sugar in KTR. To accomplish this, we will simultaneously measure several variables in our kidney physiology laboratory including kidney function and blood flow, urine sodium and protein, blood vessel stiffness, blood sugar control, and safety measures including infection or transplant rejection. Results from this study could help confirm protective mechanisms of SGLT2i in KTR, potentially leading to larger studies in a patient population in need of new cardiac and kidney protective therapies.

column36: Investigating the role of ATF3 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma pathology
column37: Pancreatic cancer is a devastating cancer with only 8% of those diagnosed surviving past 5 years. Two major contributors to this low survival rate are lack of early detection and resistance to treatment. To address these factors, we need to understand (1) initiating events in pancreatic cancer and (2) mechanisms that underlie chemotherapy resistance. The purpose of my project is to understand how the unfolded protein response (UPR), a cellular stress response, contributes to initiation and maintenance pancreatic cancer. Research from our lab has shown that one molecule within the UPR pathway, Activating Transcription Factor 3 (ATF3), plays an important role in pancreatic cancer formation. Additionally, our evidence suggests ATF3 functions in more than the tumor cell type of pancreatic cancer, implicating immune cells and fibroblasts. The goal of my project is to determine if the role of Atf3 in cancer initiation is acinar cell specifc. To do this I will delete Atf3 only in pancreatic acinar cells of mice and compare to mice with a global deletion. In addition, this project will determine how ATF3 and the UPR stress response contributes to chemotherapy resistance of pancreatic cancer. I predict tumor cells with a greater stress response will have greater chemotherapy resistance. To address this, I will treat pancreatic cancer patient-derived tumor cell lines with a combination of UPR inhibitors and chemotherapy and compare their surival to cells treated with chemotherapy alone. This study will identify pathways in initiation of pancreatic cancer and mechanistic understanding gained through this study will offer potential therapeutic targets for preventing pancreatic cancer development and chemotherapy resistance.

column36: Temporality of bone loss on long-duration spaceflight using three-dimensional high-resolution imaging
column37: Physical activity is essential for bone health. Everyday activities, like walking, dancing and other forms of exercise force our bodies to work against gravity to carry our body weight, making our skeleton stronger. When we are less active, our bones get weaker. This can pose a serious health risk for elderly individuals who are less mobile, patients confined to their beds for long periods of time, and for astronauts in space who spend most of their time floating. Astronauts typically launch to the International Space Station for 6-month missions at a time. Average loss over 6-months is similar to what we would expect to see over two decades on Earth. The purpose of this study is to understand the time-course of bone loss in space. Astronauts will participate in either 2-, 6- or 12-month space missions. Astronauts will undergo high resolution bone imaging on their leg and forearm before and after spaceflight to investigate how long it takes for bone loss to stabilize in space. Results will help us understand the risks and feasibility of longer-duration spaceflights in the future (e.g., to Mars) and how to ensure astronauts remain healthy on long-duration missions. The applicability of this research extends beyond long-term spaceflight, since bone loss due to spaceflight is an accelerated model for bone loss due to immobilization, aging, or decreased physical activity on Earth. Findings from this project will be used to understand the time-course of bone loss on Earth, such as bone loss in individuals with spinal cord injuries and individuals who are immobilized. This research will also be used to identify individuals who are predisposed to bone loss and lead to individualized treatment strategies in terrestrial and spaceflight populations. The first phase of this project was recently completed (N=17 astronauts), and this next exciting phase is part of an international effort by NASA to study the effects of the human body on long-duration missions in space.

This reality highlights the importance of considering sleep as a determinant of health and well-being, and the need to further our knowledge of the underlying mechanisms. Compared to the existing indexes, these new indexes will help to better characterize sex and gender and inter-individual differences in sleep quality. Many of the existing indexes have indeed been shown to not be sensitive to detect sex differences for example. This targeted approach will contribute to the development of personalized medicine and treatments that are closer to patients' needs.

column36: Investigating functional Optical Coherence Tomography and hypercapnia to diagnose and treat neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
column37: The Autonomic (or "automatic") Nervous System (ANS) regulates internal processes, including control of heart rate and blood pressure (BP). When someone stands, and gravity tries to pull blood away from the brain, the ANS works to maintain BP and brain blood flow. Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (NOH) occurs when our "fight-or-flight" part ("sympathetic") of the ANS fails. BP can drop a lot when upright, reducing blood flow and oxygen delivery to the brain, and this can cause symptoms of lightheadedness, nausea, and fainting. column36: Drip and Ship vs. Mothership in the Era of Neuroprotection and the RACE-CAT Trial: Validation and Iteration of a Predictive Model for Most Optimal Transport and Treatment Strategy for Acute Ischemic Stroke Patients with Suspected Large Vessel Occlusion
column37: An ischemic stroke occurs when a blood clot blocks blood flow to an area of the brain, similar to a clog in a pipe. When this happens, the brain becomes deprived of oxygen and irreversible damage begins to occur. Patients need to be treated quickly after signs of a stroke begin to improve their chance of survival and prevent disability. There are two treatment options for stroke patients: medication to dissolve the blood clot, or surgery to remove the clot. These treatment options can be combined. The clot-dissolving drug can be administered at many hospitals across the country but is only effective 30% of the time. The surgical procedure is > 80% effective, but it requires specialized equipment and specially trained physicians so it can only be performed at a few large urban hospitals. This means there are two options for patients who are far away from large hospitals: 1) go to the closest hospital for quick but less effective treatment (clot-dissolving drug) and then be transferred to a large hospital for more effective treatment later (surgical procedure); or 2) spend extra time upfront being transported to the larger hospital for more effective treatment (surgical procedure). Previously, I developed an algorithm that predicts which option is best based on distances travelled and the length of time it takes to administer treatments. Stroke care has improved in the past few years and now it is time to improve the algorithm. The algorithm needs to be validated. This will be done using data from a recent clinical trial that tested the two transport options listed above. Second, there are new medical treatments available for ischemic stroke now (neuroprotective agents which temporarily "freeze" cell death) and we need to put this option in the algorithm too. This updated algorithm will ensure that all stroke patients, regardless of where they live, receive the best possible care.

column36: Structural basis and mechanism of BAP1 ubiquitination and tumor suppressor regulation by the E2/E3 hybrid enzyme UBE2O
column37: The well-orchestrated functioning of our cells is under the control of a multitude of devices called proteins. In our body, our cells destroy damaged or unwanted proteins using a highly complex protein degradation process called the Ubiquitin Proteasome System (UPS). The UPS is composed of molecules called ubiquitin ligases (E3s) that mediate the attachment of a marker called ubiquitin to unwanted proteins to direct them for destruction. On the other hand, deubiquitinases (DUBs) remove ubiquitin from proteins to prevent their destruction. Working together, E3s and DUBs tightly regulate almost all biological processes in the cell. The breakdown of this finely tuned process, resulting from improper functioning of E3s or DUBs, frequently leads to human disease including cancers and auto-immune disorders. Among the different E3s in the cell, the incorrect functioning of UBE2O is associated with 20% of breast, liver and lung cancers. Among the different DUB family members, BAP1 is the most frequently mutated in human cancers. E3s and DUBs have become very appealing targets for the development of new therapeutics to treat human disease. However, these proteins are difficult to exploit as drug target because we lack detailed knowledge of what many of them they look like at an atomic level. My postdoctoral project carried out in the laboratory of Dr. Sicheri at Mount Sinai Hospital, will involve visualizing the atomic structure of UBE2O and BAP1 using powerful X-ray based and electron based microscopes. In the long term, these approaches will facilitate the discovery, characterization, and development of highly specific and potent drugs to correct their function and treat human disease.

column37: The loss of spinal cord function due to injury or disease in humans results in lifelong disability for individuals and associated annual health care costs in the billions of dollars. This work will provide the foundation for establishing the Mexican cavefish as a new model for spinal cord regeneration in a clinically relevant context.

column37: The synucleinopathies are a group of neurodegenerative diseases that arise from the abnormal accumulation of the alpha-synuclein protein in the brain and include Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies. Multiple system atrophy presents with autonomic failure and variable degree of parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and pyramidal dysfunction, while dementia with Lewy bodies is characterized by early dementia, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism. The underlying factors driving the development of these disorders remain largely unknown and, as such, there exists no disease-modifying treatment available to halt disease progression. Nonetheless, little is still known about the genetic determinants of these two disorders. Recent advances in genetic technologies offer an unprecedented opportunity to bridge this gap. The main objective of this research project is to gain further understanding of the genetic underpinnings of these diseases by leveraging new genetic techniques. This will be accomplished through a three-step approach. Firstly, cases of multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies will be studied using cutting-edge genome sequencing technologies and bioinformatic tools to identify disease-causing mutations. Secondly, similar techniques will be used to study specific cell populations in the brain of deceased multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies cases. Finally, genome-wide association studies will be performed on large cohorts of patients to look for genetic risk factors of these two disorders. This project is expected to provide new insights into the complex genetic architecture of multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies, which may pave the way for the development of disease-modifying therapies for these yet incurable diseases.

column36: Discovering the origins of trachea-esophageal birth defects
column37: Trachea-esophageal birth defects (TEDs) occur when the trachea and esophagus do not completely separate from a common gut tube during fetal development. Occurring in about one out of every 3,000 live births, these life-threatening birth defects prevent proper breathing or feeding in newborn infants. It is not yet well understood how these birth defects happen. There is compelling evidence of a genetic cause, but specific genetic mutations are only known in 15% of TED cases worldwide, moreover it is unclear how these mutations disrupt fetal development. The goal of my research project is to determine the genetic and cellular causes of TEDs using an innovative combination of animal models and bioengineered human esophageal tissue from patient stem cells. As part of CLEARconsortium.org, our human geneticist colleagues have found a number of genetic variations (mutations) from genome sequencing over 300 TED patients, but we do not know which mutations cause disease. My goal is to identity the causative mutations and investigate how they cause TEDs. By making similar mutations in frogs and mouse embryos I have screened over 20 variants and found several that cause defects similar to patients, and thus are likely to be causative, including the gene ITSN1. Excitingly this has revealed a novel cellular pathway known as endosome-mediated epithelial remodeling. I propose to 1) continue screening patient variants, 2) determine the molecular mechanism by which ITSN1 regulates trachea-esophageal development and 3) test the hypothesis that other genes in this pathway may be disrupted in patients. My proposed research will discover the origin of TEDs, which will provide new fundamental knowledge of the genetic and cellular networks regulating normal and disrupted trachea-esophageal development, ultimately improving the diagnosis and treatment of children born with these life-threatening conditions.

column37: My research program at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center will be focused on understanding the molecular abnormalities in lung cancer cells in order to discover novel therapeutic avenues in patients with lung cancer. I will be supervised by Dr. Marc Ladanyi, who is a world expert in this field. Dr. Ladanyi developed a new clinical tool to diagnose mutations in lung cancer called MSK-IMPACT, which is now approved by the Federal Drug Association (FDA). This tool allows doctors to identify a "driver mutation" associated with a patient's cancer. This "driver mutation"-an abnormal modification in the cancer cells' DNA -is responsible for uncontrolled cancer growth for the patient's specific cancer. Personalized medicine has allowed for physicians and scientists to specifically target this driver mutation, thereby blocking cellular replication and the growth of cancer. Despite these significant advances, patients with advanced lung cancer are rarely cured, and drugs that target these driver mutations only work for a short period of time. column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by impairments in social behavior and emotional processing. To date, no therapies exist that specifically target ASD. column36: Dissecting the effects of mutation order and timing on lung tumourigenesis
column37: Lung cancer results from mutations in tumour suppressor genes and oncogenes. DNA sequencing of patient tumours indicates that cancer-causing mutations arise with defined sequential orders, where specific mutations mostly occur early during tumour development, while other mutations tend to occur later. Why mutations follow these defined orders is unknown, and their impacts on tumour behaviour have not been explored. To better understand the role of mutation order in lung tumour development, I will combine an innovative DNA barcoding approach with mouse models that closely represent human lung cancer. This approach labels each tumour and its associated genetic mutation with a unique DNA barcode, allowing the growth of thousands of tumours with different mutations to be tracked and measured simultaneously. To understand the effect of mutation timing, genes that suppress tumour growth will be inactivated at different time points after tumors start growing. This will reveal the impact each genetic mutation has on tumour growth at different time points along a tumour's developmental trajectory. Next, I will introduce cancer-causing mutations sequentially into normal lung cells. By analyzing the impact each mutation has on normal cells' growth, I will uncover mutations capable of initiating lung tumours. To gain insights into the molecular mechanism of mutation order on tumour development, I will determine the effect of mutation order on gene accessibility using single-cell sequencing. Overall, this study will provide a better understanding of how mutation order and timing drive cancer which could inform prevention, detection, and early intervention strategies.

column36: Individualized prognosis and prediction of cognitive decline in individuals with subjective cognitive decline
column37: Worldwide, Alzheimer's disease (AD) is one of the largest health care costs. In Canada, approximately one million cases of AD are expected by 2030, costing the health care system over $20 billion annually. AD can be present in the brain more than a decade before clinical symptoms start, making it impossible to treat the important early damage caused by the disease. In addition to these pre-clinical brain changes, subtle cognitive changes detectable by the individual may also occur years before meeting the criteria for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD. However, accurately identifying people at risk of AD before symptoms appear is extremely difficult. Nevertheless, this pre-clinical period is the earliest phase of progressive AD where disease-modifying treatments are likely to be most effective. To identify individuals at risk of AD, we propose to study those with subjective cognitive decline (SCD). These are individuals with perceived cognitive deficits but they do not show objective cognitive decline on standardized tests. Individuals who report SCD have a 3-5x increased risk of progressing to dementia and therefore make ideal candidates for prevention strategies with lifestyle changes or as subjects in clinical trials. The goal of the current project is to develop and validate a tool that combines MRI, clinical risk factors, and cognitive testing to be used in clinical settings to determine 1) which patients will develop cognitive decline, 2) determine their rate of decline, and 3) determine who will progress to MCI. This prognostic tool will help clinicians develop individualized prevention/treatment strategies. This method will also help optimize clinical trials by including people who are likely to progress to AD. Overall, this research will make clinical trials more powerful, allowing new drugs to be properly tested with fewer participants over shorter durations, bringing new treatments to patients sooner.

column37: Our immune system is the arsenal providing weapons to fight infection. When the macrophages cannot perform their job, many many immune cells race into the lungs to try to kill the bacteria. A famous scientist once described this as a bunch of hunters with grenade launchers trying to kill a duck. The likelihood of collateral damage is 100%. It is our hypothesis that this is what is happening but how to prove it. We will see if it works in SARS-Cov2 infected mice and we have been given approval by the FDA to test it in COVID-19 patients. column36: Later-life attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder as a possible risk factor for the development of Lewy body diseases
column37: Older adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) commonly show cognitive deficits similar to adults in the early stages of neurodegenerative disease (e.g., forgetfulness, distractibility). It is, however, still unclear whether older adults with ADHD have an increased risk of developing a neurodegenerative disease, or if there is simply an overlap of symptoms. Previous research suggests a possible link between ADHD and Lewy body diseases (LBD, which include Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia). Older adults with ADHD have a higher risk of developing LBD than healthy eldery, and many LBD patients report having features of ADHD early in life. It is therefore possible that ADHD may be a risk factor for LBD; discovering whether they are truly linked would provide significant opportunities to learn more about LBD. We aim to examine the possibility that ADHD is a risk factor for developing LBD, by looking at specific symptoms that have been consistently shown to be very early indicators of LBD, including loss of smell, autonomic dysfunction, or sleep disorders. This project will look at 55 healthy older adults, 55 older adults with ADHD, and 55 older adults with LBD (all over the age of 50). A smell test, self-reported questionnaires, and an actigraphy monitor will be used to measure sense of smell, autonomic dysfunction, as well as the presence of sleep disorders. ADHD symptoms in both childhood and older age will be assessed using a questionnaire completed by the participants and corroborated by someone close to them (for example, a sibling). We expect to find that patients with LBD more commonly report having childhood ADHD symptoms than controls, and that early features of LBD are often present in older adults who have ADHD. If the findings do not support these hypotheses, this could mean that ADHD is not a risk factor for LBD and the two simply share common symptoms, or both are unrelated to each other.

column37: Atherosclerosis, or the hardening of arteries, is the major cause of death worldwide, mainly due to heart attacks and strokes, and is the leading cause of heart failure that more than 600,000 people in Canada live with. Atherosclerosis is characterized by the build-up of low-density-lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C, also known as "bad cholesterol") and inflammatory cells in the arteries. This leads to the formation of atherosclerotic plaques that can potentially break, resulting in a blood clot that causes a heart attack or stroke. The Francis laboratory studies changes in the structure and cell composition of blood vessels like the coronary arteries that lead to plaque formation. They have made the ground-breaking discovery that the main place fats like cholesterol build up in arteries to form plaque are smooth muscle cells that line the arteries, not the white blood cells called macrophages that have long been believed to be the main site of cholesterol build-up. The purpose of this project is to study the genetic and phenotypic differences in smooth muscle cells and macrophages grown in dishes and collected from human coronary arteries of hearts. This will allow us (i) to elucidate how these cells contribute to the development and progression of atherosclerosis, (ii) to identify new pro- and anti-atherogenic cell markers, and (iii) to develop novel treatments to reduce the build-up of cholesterol in these cells. We hypothesize that foamy smooth muscle cells that contain cholesterol will further promote the development of atherosclerosis compared with macrophages. This is because smooth muscle cells do not easily release cholesterol from within the cell, and therefore are more likely to be resistant to current lipid-lowering treatments. This research is expected to lead to better comprehension of plaque formation in arteries and new ways to reduce heart attack, stroke, and heart failure in Canadians and throughout the world.

column36: Live two-photon calcium imaging in retinal ganglion cells: characterization of pathological changes and mechanisms in glaucoma.
column37: Glaucoma, characterized by the death of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Our recent data suggest that the microtubule stabilizing protein tau accumulates in RGCs soon after the onset of glaucoma. Tau has been shown to inhibit calcium efflux making neurons vulnerable to stress-induced cell death. However, a clear molecular link between calcium dysregulation pathways and early RGC dysfunction and damage in glaucoma has been lacking. In addition, our current understanding of calcium dynamics in RGCs and how they are altered in glaucoma is poorly understood due to lack of reliable calcium imaging techniques in living RGC. To address this knowledge gap, we will optimize a novel two-photon laser scanning microscopy to characterize intracellular calcium dynamics in living RGCs in early stage glaucoma. Additionally, using this powerful technique, we will investigate the molecular mechanisms leading to loss of calcium homeostasis in RGCs. Furthermore, we will address the fundamental question of whether calcium pathway modulation serves as a therapeutic target for vulnerable RGCs in glaucoma. The outcome of this project will provide important insights into the role of pathways that regulate calcium influx and efflux in RGCs and their effect on structural and functional neuronal damage in glaucoma. Importantly, this study will identify strategies to regulate calcium homeostasis in RGCs and might validate new therapeutic approaches to counter neurodegeneration and loss of visual function in glaucoma.

column36: Identifying and leveraging metabolic vulnerabilities to treat clonal hematopoiesis
column37: The hematopoietic system populates the cellular components of the blood throughout the lifespan from a limited number of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) and failure of this system manifests in a variety of blood disorders including cancer. A major consequence of aging is the random accumulation of genetic mutations in somatic cells; it is established that specific mutations occur at high frequencies in the blood of individuals >50 years old indicating that the hematopoietic system is relying on fewer HSPCs, or clones, resulting in a condition termed clonal hematopoiesis (CH). This is problematic as the most common mutations in CH are also implicated in the development of blood cancers and cardiovascular disease. Because the accumulation of genetic mutations is progressive, starting early in life, traditional interventions that have accompanying side effects when taken for long periods, such as pharmaceuticals, are not feasible. The most successful interventions for restoring HSPC function in old animals have been metabolic in nature. The proposed research will build upon tools built in our laboratory that model CH by replicating CH driving mutations in the zebrafish. Furthermore, these tools allow for the quantification of CH and isolation of clonally dominant and non-dominant HSPCs using fluorescent proteins and DNA barcoding. Using these tools, we will explore how the metabolic state of clonally dominant and nondominant HSPCs differ and use this information to identify vulnerabilities that can be targeted with metabolic interventions to slow CH development. Furthermore, we will explore which dietary supplements, with known safety profiles, may be leveraged to abate the progression of CH. The results of this research will give us an unprecedented insight into how CH affects metabolism and how we can develop sustainable, long-term interventions to prevent aging-associated blood disorders.

column36: Imagerie de la propagation de l'alpha-synucleine dans les phases prodromale et clinique des synucleinopathies
column37: Les synucleinopathies sont un groupe de maladies caracterisees par l'accumulation anormale d'alpha-synucleine dans le cerveau. Ces maladies incluent la maladie de Parkinson et la demence a corps de Lewy, une demence severe associee a du parkinsonisme et des hallucinations visuelles. Ces maladies n'apparaissent pas spontanement et sont precedees d'une periode de plusieurs annees lors desquelles les caracteristiques pathologiques et cliniques apparaissent progressivement. On en sait encore tres peu sur les mecanismes et les changements cerebraux qui menent au developpement d'une synucleinopathie. Une facon de mieux comprendre ces changements est par l'etude d'un trouble de sommeil appele le trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxal idiopathique (TCSPi). Il s'agit d'un trouble de sommeil au cours duquel la personne perd l'atonie musculaire du sommeil paradoxal et se met a agir ses reves par des mouvements souvent agressifs et violents. Il s'agit d'un facteur de risque majeur du developpement d'une synucleinopathie. Au cours de ce postdoctorat, j'etudierai plusieurs des plus grandes cohortes multicentriques internationales de scans IRM de patients avec un TCSPi, avec une maladie de Parkinson et avec une demence a corps de Lewy. L'objectif sera d'utiliser plusieurs techniques sophistiquees de neuroimagerie et d'analyses computationnelles afin de comprendre les mecanismes expliquant les changements cerebraux chez ces patients. Specifiquement, j'utiliserai un modele computationnel qui simule la propagation de l'alpha-synucleine dans le cerveau a partir de l'expression genetique et des connexions anatomiques entre les regions afin de tester si la propagation simulee replique l'atrophie retrouvee chez les patients avec un TCSPi, une maladie de Parkinson ou une demence a corps de Lewy. De plus, je profiterai de l'acces a ces cohortes internationales pour conduire un ensemble d'analyses cerebrales morphologiques allant du volume a la surface corticale et sous-corticale.

column36: Sex-differences in the cardiovascular consequences of spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating condition that critically impairs the nervous system's regulation of the heart and blood vessels. Individuals with higher-level injuries (i.e. the midback or higher) live with a number of adverse cardiovascular complications, including frequent episodes of excessively low and high blood pressure (called orthostatic hypotension and autonomic dysreflexia, respectively), all of which drastically impact the individual's quality of life and likely predisopose them to future cardiovascular complications or disease. To that point, cardiovascular disease has been identified as a leading cause of death in individuals with SCI, who have 3-5 fold greater odds of heart disease compared to able-bodied individuals. Recently, our group completed a large-scale review and found that individuals with SCI have much smaller hearts and notable changes in heart function; yet, of the data available, only 5% represented females with SCI. In Canada, females comprise over 25% of the SCI population, as such it is clear that females are largely underrepresented in SCI research to date. So far, researchers have characterized key differences between the male and female hearts in healthy, able-bodied populations; yet, whether such sex differences exist in the SCI population is not known. What's more, we currently do not know whether the frequency or intensity of extreme blood pressure swings (i.e. orthostatic hypotension, autonomic dysreflexia) differs in females versus males with SCI, and how SCI impacts the heart's ability to respond to daily physiological stressors, like changing posture. Therefore, the primary objective of this work is to assess the impacts of high-level SCI on sex differences in the heart's function and structure i) at rest and ii) in response to orthostatic (postural) stress. The secondary objective is to assess the frequency and intensity of extreme blood pressure swings in females and males with SCI.

column36: A mixed-method examination of physical activity and its correlates among children with co-occurring physical and mental health illness
column37: Physical activity (PA) promotes positive physical and mental health and reduces the risk of disease among children. However, there is an alarming trend of physical inactivity among children and youth across the globe and this is particularly concerning because PA habits formed during childhood track consistently into adolescence and adulthood. Physical inactivity burdens children and society with a myriad of negative health consequences and increases their future risk of developing physical and mental health illnesses. Children with already existing physical and mental health illnesses, known as multimorbidity, are at a higher risk than their typically developing peers to experience physical inactivity due to their unique health care needs. To support the PA needs of children with multimorbidity, information on their levels of PA and what factors promote or prevent them from engaging in PA is needed; currently this information is unknown. Therefore, the purpose of this project is to evaluate the PA behaviours of children with multimorbidity and identify what variables are correlated to their PA. A quantitative analysis of a cohort study of children ages 2 to 16 years with multimorbidity will first be used to measure PA and variables associated with PA. A qualitative study will follow in which semi-structured interviews will be used to explore novel barriers and facilitators of PA engagement among children with multimorbidity and their caregivers. This information will both contribute new knowledge on the health consequences of multimorbidity and be used to inform PA interventions directly targeting children with increased risk of inactivity.

column36: Reducing the risk of osteoarthritis after a sport knee injury: Proof-of Concept of the SOAR (Stop OsteoARthritis) program
column37: North America has the highest rates of osteoarthritis (OA) in the world. OA is a joint disease that causes pain, physical disability, and reduced quality of life. By 2040, 25% of Canadians will have OA. This number will be as high as 50% for those who hurt their knee playing youth sport. Currently, the treatment of youth sport knee injuries focuses on the initial injury and return to sport. Few patients receive follow-up or care beyond their injury, and despite being a priority for patients, limited effort is made to prevent OA. Stop OsteoARthritis (SOAR) is a novel online physiotherapy guided program that aims to reduce the risk of OA after a youth sport knee injury. Designed with a team of patients, clinicians and researchers, SOAR teaches active youth how to self-manage their OA risk, and improve knee muscle strength and physical activity levels. SOAR consists of a knee education camp, personalized exercises, wrist-worn activity-tracker and weekly counselling. This research will assess the experiences of youth with a sport knee injury while participating in the SOAR program and how well SOAR works to reduce muscle weakness and inactivity - proven risk factors for knee OA. We will also develop a plan to assess how well SOAR works in the real world. The SOAR team will continue to include patient and clinician partners to make sure that SOAR is practical and relevant. To date, no other research group has taken this unique 'patient-orientated' approach to tackling the problem of OA. This research represents a critical step toward the goal of reducing the long-term consequences of youth sport knee injuries and will deliver an intervention that is capable of improving the health and reducing the risk of OA for the ~2 million young Canadians who have a sport knee injury annually.

column36: Characterizing the divergent functions of IL-23 in the induction of encephalitogenic T cells.
column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a devastating autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) caused by the progressive deterioration of myelin, a substance that coats nerve cells. The development and progression of MS results from pathogenic immune effector T cells that harbor specificity for myelin antigens. A key mediator that potentiates pathogenic responses in MS is the cytokine, IL-23, which skews myelin-specific T cells towards an inflammatory phenotype. Recently however, we have found that a subunit of IL-23, p40, forms a novel complex with a soluble protein, CD5L, and acts to suppress the activity of pathogenic T cells and inhibits the development of MS in mice. Therefore, the opposing functions of IL-23 signaling on auto-reactive T cells in MS is poorly understood. My research will focus on delineating the exact process by which the p40:CD5L complex acts on auto-reactive T cells to suppress inflammation while clarifying its opposing contribution in IL-23-mediated pathogenic responses. I will use a combination of cutting-edge techniques including genetic engineering, single-cell transcriptomics, and high dimensional immune profiling to address these goals. This investigation will deepen our understanding of the mechanism that drives MS pathology and provide important insight into the development of new therapeutics that can selectively inhibit pathogenic auto-reactive T cells.

column36: Physical exercise to mitigate the effects of bed rest on brain health in older adults.
column37: Physical inactivity is associated with many negative health outcomes, including impaired thinking abilities and increased dementia risk. Older adults become inactive for many reasons. They may become inactive over time due to chronic conditions (e.g., arthritis, lung disease), or acutely due to bed rest resulting from injury, surgery, or hospitalization. Bed rest is a reality for many older adults and often is a "tipping point" for functional and cognitive decline and loss of independence. Exercise is beneficial for both cognitive and brain health. But it is currently unknown whether exercise training during periods of bed rest can reduce the negative impact of inactivity on older adults' cognitive and brain health during physical inactivity periods. Thus, maximizing on an opportunity provided by CIHR and the Canadian Space Agency, we will determine: 1) effects of daily physical exercise sessions in counteracting the effects of experimental bed rest on cognitive function (i.e., thinking abilities); 2) how both bed rest and sessions of exercise impact cognitive function in adults aged 55 to 65 years old; and 3) factors that moderate the effects of bed rest and exercise on cognitive function. Twenty to 24 healthy male and female middle-aged and older adults aged 55 to 65 will be randomized to 14 days of bed rest with three physical exercise daily sessions (60 minutes total) or a control group (bed rest only). The protocol also includes five days of adaptation and seven days of recovery. Results will help to understand how to prevent the acceleration of cognitive decline due to bed rest. A better understanding of how both physical inactivity and exercise impacts cognitive function will guide future strategies to shape cognitive aging during transitions in care positively. Also, it will provide us more evidence to prescribe individualized physical activity recommendations for healthy cognitive aging.

column36: Metabolic and epigenetic regulation of cancer associated fibroblasts by angiotensin II
column37: Hypoxia, or low oxygen, occurs in tumours with disrupted blood vessels. Cancer cells in hypoxic tumours are resistant to both radiation and chemotherapy, and increase risk for cancer progression. To improve cancer therapy, it is therefore important to develop strategies that prevent blood vessel disruption in tumours and eliminate hypoxia. A group of drugs named "Angiotensin Receptor Blockers", or ARBs for short, are widely prescribed to treat high blood pressure. Interestingly, we found that that ARBs may be repurposed to prevent blood vessel disruption in tumours. This research project will investigate which cells in tumours are targeted by ARBs in order to identify which patients can benefit from ARBs, if there are any treatments that may act similar to ARBs but more effectively, and if the benefits of ARBs may be applied to other diseases. We are studying how ARBs affect cells called "fibroblasts". Fibroblasts respond to injuries by attempting to rebuild the basic structure of the body, such as creating a scar to heal a cut. Similarly, fibroblasts respond to a cancerous growth by modifying the structure of a tumour. We believe that fibroblasts are critical in causing disruption of tumour blood vessels, leading to hypoxia. We will apply techniques that assess how ARBs alter the DNA of fibroblasts, and whether the changes to fibroblast DNA affect tumour structure. These experiments will advance the fundamental understanding of fibroblast biology and determine how ARBs control tumour structure to alter the effectiveness of cancer therapy as well as other fibrotic conditions. As ARBs are already approved drugs and many cancer patients are already taking ARBs to treat high blood pressure, this research project will connect laboratory studies on fibroblasts with clinical data. Doing so will allow the findings from our proposed research to be applied towards improving clinical care relatively soon.

column36: Concussion and injury prevention in youth rugby: Targeting rule changes, equipment recommendations and training strategies.
column37: Rugby Union is one of the most popular team sports globally, with increasing popularity in Canada. It is also a high injury risk team sport, with the rate of injury as high as 77 injuries every 25 matches and a concussion rate as high as 20 concussions every 25 matches. Several strategies have previously been used to reduce injury risk, including the use of a sport-specific neuromuscular training warm up program. Other promising approaches for reducing concussion risk include rule changes (e.g., greater penalization of head contact, height of the tackle) and tackle training for improved technique. To date, a large number of the rugby studies have been conducted outside of Canada, where rugby is a well-established sport played from a young age. This is not currently the case in Canada. As such, it is unclear whether similar injury prevention strategies will be effective in reducing concussion and injury more broadly. This research project will therefore investigate whether introducing a targeted rugby-specific neuromuscular training warm-up program, potential rule change and/or tackle training would be beneficial in reducing injury risk in the context of the Canadian youth. If successful, these strategies would have significant impact on the personal health of players as well as the health care system on which they rely on for care. Injury and concussion rates present a significant concern for rugby as it grows throughout Canada and despite improved understanding of the injury, there are still significant health related consequences for the injured player, including financial cost of treatment, inability to participate in physical activity and importantly in the context of concussion, potential absence from academic pursuits. We anticipate that participation rates will continue to rise and therefore, significant emphasis needs to be placed on prevention strategies to ensure the increased participation does not result in a corresponding rise in injury and concussion.

column36: Improving young adults' experiences with and access to digital health interventions in the context of COVID-19 and beyond
column37: In response to the COVID-19 directives that have limited in-person health care interactions, many health services have pivoted towards the provision of digital health interventions (DHIs) (e.g., web-based platforms). Concurrently, emerging evidence indicates that COVID-19 and associated measures are negatively impacting mental health problems (e.g., depression, anxiety) and substance use-related harms (e.g., substance use disorder) among young adults (ages 18-29). New evidence is needed to inform DHIs that can best address the mental health and substance use-related health needs of youth. The proposed international mixed-methods study will investigate youths' experiences with and access of DHIs in Canada and France in the context of COVID-19 pandemic and beyond. The objectives are to: 1. Document and inventory the 'state' of existing, emerging and evolving DHIs that seek to address the mental health and substance use-related health needs of youth. 2. Characterize the experiences and perspectives of youth and health providers to understand how various individual, social, and structural factors influence experiences with and access to DHIs for youth. 3. Identify how DHIs can best be adapted to optimize positive health outcomes and reduce health inequities among youth. The proposed study will begin with a scoping review to inventory existing DHIs regarding mental health and substance use for youth in Canada and France (Objective 1). A series of online surveys and qualitative interviews will be conducted in each country to characterize the experiences of youth and providers with DHIs (Objective 2). Two World Cafes in each country will be organized with youth, providers and policy makers to identify recommendations for DHIs (Objective 3). This study will generate context-sensitive and population-specific data to identify strategies to reduce negative health outcomes and health inequities among young adults within and after the COVID-19 pandemic.

column36: The role of interferon-gamma in controlling Cryptosporidium infection in intestinal epithelial cells
column37: Cryptosporidium parasites infect epithelial cells (ECs) in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and can cause severe diarrhea. This infection can be fatal in individuals with a compromised immune system, such as organ transplant recipients, while infections in children are associated with growth defects, reduced cognitive development and death. Current research indicates that long-term, protective immunity against Cryptosporidium is possible, suggesting that vaccine development is an important strategy to prevent infection. However, current small animal models fail to replicate important aspects of human infection and this has limited our ability to study the immune response to Cryptosporidium, thereby hampering vaccine development. To address this knowledge gap, my research will use a recently identified murine strain of Cryptosporidium that is highly similar to human strains genetically and in terms of pathogenesis. This strain was used to demonstrate that an immune molecule called interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) is crucial for controlling Cryptosporidium infection. My research project will aim to determine how ECs responding to IFN-gamma become resistant to Cryptosporidium. I hypothesize that IFN-gamma has this effect by activating anti-parasitic responses within ECs, and by increasing the rate of EC turnover to help shed infected cells. Within the intestine, EC precursors begin at the base of the intestinal villi, and as they develop and mature, they "ride the elevator" to the villus tip, where they die and are released into the intestinal lumen. By speeding up the EC elevator, infected cells may be released before they are able to spread the infection to healthy cells. Together, my work will improve our understanding of how IFN-gamma contributes to protective immunity against Cryptosporidium infection and provide new insights into how normal, physiological processes like the EC elevator can be used to combat this and other intestinal infections.

column36: Contribution des professionnels non-educateurs au developpement des enfants en milieu de garde : entre l'offre de services actuelle et ideale.
column37: Au Quebec, 27% des enfants a la maternelle sont a risque de retard de developpement. Afin de soutenir ces enfants, le Gouvernement du Quebec a mis en place diverses strategies, dont l'augmentation de ressources pour depister et accompagner les enfants avec des difficultes dans les milieux de garde. Cependant peu d'informations sont disponibles pour guider l'offre de services. Le projet vise a decrire l'offre de services actuelle et souhaitee, ainsi qu'a identifier des recommandations quant a l'offre de services a privilegier au Quebec. Il vise plus particulierement les services offerts par les professionnels non-educateur pour soutenir le developpement des enfants dans les milieux de garde. Le projet se deroulera en 3 phases : un sondage, des entrevues et un processus de consensus d'experts. Les directions des Centre de la petite enfance et bureaux coordonnateurs completeront un sondage en ligne visant a decrire les differentes dimensions de l'offre de service en place et souhaitee. Des entrevues seront realisees avec 10 a 15 participants au sondage afin d'approfondir la description des services et le contexte du milieu de garde. Des ebauches de recommandations obtenues par l'analyse des resultats seront utilisees dans le cadre d'un processus de consensus d'experts afin de fournir des recommandations quant a l'offre de services a privilegier en milieu de garde au Quebec. Le processus inclura 15 a 20 experts cibles qui auront une expertise de contenu ou terrain et une bonne connaissance du systeme educatif et de sante au Quebec. Ils participeront a trois tours de consultation en ligne afin d'exprimer leur accord quant aux recommandations (0-10/10), jusqu'a l'obtention d'un consensus. Ce projet permettra de faire murir la reflexion sur ce que le Quebec a et souhaite avoir comme offre de service en milieu de garde. Il permettra aussi de soutenir les decisions politiques et cliniques, notamment pour le deploiement de nouveaux services.

column36: Overdose and recidivism among people with criminal justice system involvement and substance use disorders: Identifying longitudinal trends during dual public health emergencies in British Columbia
column37: People with criminal justice system involvement (e.g. incarceration, criminal charge or conviction) are more likely to use illicit substances (e.g. heroin, methamphetamine) compared to the general population. Those who do, are at higher risk of negative outcomes including overdose and more rapid and/or frequent return to custody. Efforts to address overdose, both in prisons and in the community, have been focused on treatment for people with opioid use disorder, by prescribing opioid agonist treatment. This alone may not be sufficient to reduce illicit opioid use, particularly among people who also use other substances. In March 2020, in the context of COVID-19, British Columbia's Ministry of Health took a significant step to expand access to prescription alternatives to the toxic drug supply and provided doctors with new guidelines and permissions for prescribing opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and alcohol withdrawal management medications to people at risk of overdose. The goal of this study is to evaluate whether these guidelines, which account for coexisting substance use disorder diagnoses, are effective at reducing overdose and criminal justice system involvement. Provincial health and criminal justice records will be examined to identify how many people with and without criminal justice system involvement have substance use disorder diagnoses (and which type of diagnosis) in British Columbia. Trends of overdose and criminal justice system involvement will then be examined, to identify whether there were any changes after opioid agonist treatment expansion efforts, or after the new treatment guidelines introduced in March 2020. Findings will highlight gaps in substance use services in British Columbia, and will inform policies and services intended to reduce overdose in both criminal justice and community health systems.

column36: What predisposes women to Alzheimer's Disease? A study to determine the role of G-protein coupled receptors in this phenomenon.
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease which is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly. The cause of AD remains disputed, resulting in the lack of successful therapeutics. This is a grave concern, given the increase in life expectancy and the large number of baby boomers entering the age at which AD tends to manifest. AD is confirmed by aggregates of the protein beta-amyloid (Abeta), which are toxic to neurons. Glutamate is the major excitatory brain neurotransmitter which plays a critical role in learning and memory formation; the dysregulation of its receptor, mGluR5 has been implicated in AD. Abeta binding to mGluR5, can stimulate the release of calcium inside neurons, and inhibits autophagy, the process of removal of misfolded, damaged, or toxic proteins. This can result in neuronal death and subsequent cognitive decline. Women are more predisposed to developing AD when compared to age and risk-matched men, but the cause of this predisposition remains unclear. Our lab has shown that inhibiting mGluR5 can improve AD symptoms in male AD mice, but not in female mice. Similarly, we have also observed that Abeta does not bind to mGluR5 in female AD mice, like they do in males. Therefore, we plan to determine whether other proteins bind differently in male vs female mice. We will also examine whether calcium release from internal stores are altered differentially in male vs female AD mice. Excessive calcium release from the internal stores is buffered by the mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell. Mitochondria are critical to cells with high energy demand like the neurons, and mitochondrial damage has been observed in AD. Here, we will determine if there is a sex-difference in mitochondrial health and whether this is due to a change in autophagy and/or calcium signaling. This will provide us a better understanding of the sex-differences in the progression of AD, allowing for better drug development and clinical trial design

column36: L'embolie pulmonaire en exacerbation aigue de la maladie pulmonaire obstructive chronique
column37: La maladie pulmonaire obstructive chronique (MPOC) est la 4e cause de mortalite dans le monde. L'exacerbation aigue de la MPOC (EAMPOC), definie comme une aggravation soudaine des symptomes respiratoires, est associee a une augmentation de la mortalite. Les EAMPOC resultent parfois d'un caillot dans les arteres du poumon (embolie pulmonaire (EP)) mais sont aussi associees a un plus grand risque d'embolie. Faire le diagnostic d'embolie chez les patients MPOC demeure difficile parce que les symptomes sont souvent les memes. L'objectif general du programme de recherche propose est d'ameliorer la prise en charge des patients avec EAMPOC quant au diagnostic d'une eventuelle embolie sous-jacente. La vraie frequence et les consequences reelles de l'EP en EAMPOC ne sont pas bien connues. La premiere etude sera une revue systematique avec meta-analyse qui permettra de mieux caracteriser la prevalence d'EP parmi les patients avec EAMPOC. Les patients avec EAMPOC presentent des symptomes similaires a ceux de l'EP et les outils de prediction d'EP n'ont pas ete valides dans cette population. Optimiser la prise en charge de ces patients permettrait de limiter l'investigation par imagerie qui engendre couts et irradiation. Le deuxieme projet consistera en une meta-analyse de donnees individuelles des participants d'etudes ayant permis d'etablir les outils de prediction dans la population generale afin de determiner, chez les patients MPOC, les parametres cliniques et paracliniques permettant de discriminer les patients avec et sans EP lors d'une exacerbation. Le but est d'elaborer un outil de prediction diagnostique specifique a leur condition. Le troisieme projet consistera en une analyse groupee des patients MPOC inclus dans des etudes historiques afin d'evaluer le nouvel outil MPOC-specifique comparativement aux outils de prediction disponibles. column36: A Public Health Surveillance System of Mental-Ill Health among Young People in Canada
column37: Mental illness is the largest contributor to adolescent disability worldwide. Over the past decade, there have been increases in mental illness among adolescents and young adults aged 12 to 25, which have disproportionately impacted females. Despite these alarming trends, Canada lacks a coordinated and systematic approach for monitoring mental illness in youth at a national level. As such, we plan on filling this urgent need by developing a national public health surveillance system of mental-ill health among youth in Canada, which systematically collects, analyzes, and reports data on mental-ill health among youth. This system will provide more accurate and representative estimates of mental illness among youth by using all available data sources across Canada. Furthermore, it will provide the opportunity to compare and contrast estimates of mental illness in youth across time, space, and population sub-groups, including differences by sex, gender, race/ethnicity, and poverty. The goal of this work is to inform policy makers of trends in mental illness in youth using the best possible evidence available in Canada. The objectives of this fellowship are to fill current evidence gaps required to inform the development of a surveillance system. This will include collecting available evidence on mental illness in youth across Canada and testing and evaluating the quality of various common measures of mental health in youth. Furthermore, we will begin developing a model to estimate the prevalence of mental illness using information from multiple data sources simultaneously. There is an urgent need to develop the infrastructure required to monitor trends in mental illness among young people in our country. By leveraging existing Canadian data, our goal is to establish the necessary pre-requisites for a public health surveillance system of mental ill-health among young people in Canada that can inform equitable mental health policy.

column36: A dose-response of protein intake on integrated and individual protein turnover and the associated mechanistic underpinnings in healthy and sarcopenic older men and women
column37: The aim of this research project is to determine, using novel and innovative scientific methods, whether consuming greater protein in older individuals with sufficient and diminished muscle mass will provide a greater stimulus for muscle growth. As we age, our muscles become much smaller, weaker, and less able to use the nutrients that we consume, specifically proteins, to rebuild/repair our muscles. Given that muscle makes up a significant amount of our body mass, muscle loss increases the risk of developing frailty, disability, and a host of chronic diseases. Muscle is continuously being built and broken down, and the protein we consume as food provides the building blocks for muscle maintenance and repair. One of the leading causes of muscle mass loss with aging is the reduced ability of dietary proteins to renew damaged aged skeletal muscle proteins, which means that older individuals require greater amounts of protein to stimulate the same muscle maintaining) response as younger counterparts. Interestingly, it appears that older women display a more pronounced reduction in their sensitivity to protein feeding, suggesting that biological sex may play an important role in the maintenance of muscle mass in older individuals. Evidence is accumulating to suggest that consuming a greater amount of protein may be a feasible strategy to overcome the blunted response to protein nutrition, and older individuals that consume more protein may be better at maintaining their muscle mass. Our idea is that by consuming a greater amount of protein older individuals may may improve - or at least preserve - muscle strength and functional capacity and subsequently reduce the risk of developing frailty and disability.

column36: Methodological issues in the design and analysis of cluster randomized controlled trials in hemodialysis
column37: The cluster-randomized trial is an important design for evaluating health service interventions in the outpatient hemodialysis (HD) setting. Cluster-randomized trials randomize intact groups of people (such as patients being treated in HD centres) rather than individuals. In the HD setting, a cluster-randomized trial design is a logical choice when the intervention is delivered at the centre-level, where nurses in each centre are trained to follow similar protocols for all patients. Also, when study outcomes are available from routinely collected sources (called "registries"), cluster randomization gives researchers an efficient way for following patients during the trial. This design and registries can reduce trial costs, time, and patient loss to follow-up. Moreover, this design can help avoid treatment contamination when patients in the same HD centre are on the same intervention compared to a setting where multiple interventions are in place at one centre (e.g., evaluating different advertising strategies to encourage smoking cessation). However, there are some challenges to conducting cluster-randomized trials. This fellowship addresses three methodological gaps in the existing literature to design, conduct, and analyze CRTs unique to the HD setting. The three proposed projects are embedded within a CIHR-funded platform with the primary objective of conducting large-scale, pragmatic, registry-based CRTs in the HD setting. Our results will directly inform the design and analysis of Canadian HD trials within our funded SPOR Innovative Clinical Trial Multi-Year Grant.

column36: Adherence to the Portfolio Diet and cardiometabolic disease risk in 3 large U.S. cohorts: A transformative approach using metabolomics and mendelian randomization
column37: Diet remains an important contributor to heart disease and diabetes prevention in Canada and globally. The evidence to support specific dietary strategies is limited, and current dietary advice relies largely on evidence from small randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of risk factors, and prospective cohort studies that are based on self-reported diet and cannot provide cause-and-effect relationships. Innovative nutrition research is needed that can replace the evidence from traditional large clinical outcomes trials at a much lower cost. Metabolomics is an emerging field in nutrition and chronic disease epidemiology. This approach uses the products of overall metabolism to develop an objective metabolic signature for a dietary pattern, which is not subject to the same measurement and reporting errors of traditional self-report dietary tools. This approach can also be used to produce an inferred genetic signature for Mendelian randomization, which allows for the assessment of causal relations. Through this project, I will work with the Portfolio Diet, a plant-based dietary portfolio of cholesterol-lowering foods (nuts, plant-protein, sticky fibre, plant sterols, and heart-healthy oils), to include this new transformative approach. The primary aim of this project is to determine a metabolic signature of the Portfolio Diet from past and ongoing RCTs of the diet. The secondary objective is to apply and compare this metabolic signature to 3 large U.S. cohorts (the Nurses' Health Study and Health Professional Follow-up Study) and assess the relation of the Portfolio Diet, its metabolic signature, and inferred genetic signature with heart disease and diabetes. This approach will be an innovative technique that will advance the field of nutrition epidemiology. Heart disease and diabetes are very common in Canada and worldwide, therefore, research like this project that aims to identify dietary patterns to prevent these diseases could impact millions of people.
