column36: Ultra-high field functional mapping of the brain circuits serving understanding social interactions and actions in common marmosets
column37: A crucial component of social cognition is to observe and understand the social interactions of other individuals. Recognizing these interactions and their meanings helps the 'observer" to understand the feelings, thoughts or the consequences of some actions, e.g. play or fight. This process is performed quickly and effortlessly. Individuals with autism spectrums disorder often exhibit deficits in social cognition including social recognition or social interaction. To identify the pathological processes and potential pharmacological interventions, we need to understand how these processes are implemented at the whole-brain level. To accomplish this, the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a New World primate, is an ideal animal model. First, unlike rodents, marmosets have functional brain networks similar to humans and exhibited complex prosocial behaviors. Second, compared to the traditional primate model-the macaque monkey, the marmoset is more practical as a model species given its small size, fertility and rapid development. The aim of the present research project is to identify the brain networks involved in social interaction and action observation. To do this, we will use functional magnetic resonance imaging on marmosets while they are viewing videos of marmosets interacting with each other or performing specific actions, or on two marmosets facing each other to see the relationship impact. In the short-term, this project will provide insights into a) how social interaction and action are processed in marmosets and b) how these mechanisms compare between marmosets and humans. Once established, experimental manipulations can be applied to this monkey model to simulate social interaction deficits observed in psychiatric disorders. This model will facilitate the search for potential neuropharmacological treatments for individuals with social interaction deficits and help Canada gain a competitive edge in research and treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders.

column36: Evaluating embedding-based representations of multidimensional clinical datasets: Examining their utility for detecting suicidal ideation in patients with Major Depression
column37: Suicide is preceded by suicidal thinking, which people are often hesitant to disclose. This can lead to missed opportunities for closer monitoring and intervention. To address this issue, the proposed project examines predictors of suicidal thinking that do not rely on self-report. Various predictors have been identified, such as age, sex, mental health status, genetic susceptibility, and sleep disturbances. As information on these predictors is increasingly captured in the clinic (e.g., with questionnaires, psychiatric notes, DNA sampling, actigraphy), clinical datasets are becoming larger and more complicated to analyze. One way to deal with diverse datasets is by converting them into smaller, more manageable representations, called embeddings. We will evaluate whether embeddings can represent data for 500 depressed patients over 3000 visits to The Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH). To do this, we will examine how well embeddings contribute to predictions of suicidal thinking, measured with a depression questionnaire. We will compile four datasets for each patient visit containing varying numbers of predictors of suicidal thinking. The smallest dataset will contain demographic predictors, whereas the largest dataset will contain these predictors, as well as predictors from clinical assessments, psychiatric notes, genetic susceptibility, and daily activity and sleep. From these datasets, we will generate four sets of embeddings and examine how well each set predicts suicidal thinking. If the embeddings are good representations of the datasets, prediction based on embeddings of larger datasets (with more predictors) should outperform embeddings of smaller datasets (with less predictors). Our findings have potential to inform the development of a suicide risk estimate, to complement clinical judgment when self-reported suicidal thinking is unavailable or unreliable. Improved detection may lead to opportunities for early intervention and prevention.

column36: Targeting CD38 in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL): A Phase I trial with correlative biology to evaluate a novel chimeric antigen receptor T-cell against CD38 (CART38) in paediatric patients with relapsed or refractory T-ALL
column37: The immune system is the part of the body that fights infection. Recently, new treatments that use parts of the immune system to fight cancer have been made. One example is chimeric antigen receptor T-cells (CART). With CART, immune cells from a patient are collected. The cells are modified in a laboratory to fight cancer cells. The modified cells are then given back to the patient. CART is very effective at curing some cancers. The most common cancer in children is called acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). ALL has two types: B-cell (B-ALL) and T-cell (T-ALL). CART works well in B-ALL. CART has not yet been used for T-ALL. Children with T-ALL who relapse are very hard to cure. CART could help them. We have tested a CART that targets something on the outside of T-ALL cells called CD38. We call this CART38. CD38 is found at high levels on T-ALL cancer cells but not usually on healthy cells. I have tested CART38 in mice with T-ALL and found it works very well. We will test CART38 in children with T-ALL who received chemotherapy that did not work for them. We will see if CART38 works and if it causes side effects. In some patients, other CART make the immune system overactive. This is called cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Different CART may cause different types of CRS. If we understand CRS after CART38, we can treat it. Understanding CRS is important to make sure that we can use CART38 in children with T-ALL safely. We hope that CART38 will work and cure children with T-ALL. We know with other CART that not all children are cured. We want to make CART38 work even better. In the lab, I will study why T-ALL cells have CD38. I will also study how CART38 kills T-ALL cells. I will look for other medicines that that we can give with CART38 to make the CART38 better at killing T-ALL cells. I hope these studies will lead to better cures for children with T-ALL.

column36: Mental Disorders Risk Prediction using Objectively Measured Family Health Histories: a Multigenerational Linkage Study
column37: Mental disorders affect one in five Canadians and influence employment, education, and relationships. The origin of mental disorders is unknown, but both genes and the environment are believed to play a role. Family members share part of their genes and environmental exposures. Therefore, it is expected that individuals are more likely to have a mental disorder if they have a family history of the disorder. This study aims to test if individuals are more likely to have a mental disorder if they have a family history of the disorder. The study also aims to test if mental disorder risk prediction can be improved using the entire family history of mental and physical health conditions. We will conduct a large study using claims healthcare databases in Manitoba; one of a few sites in the world with family linkage across the generations at the population level spanning 50 years. We will include all adult offspring residing in Manitoba between 1974 and 2020 and who can be linked to at least one parent. We will identify diagnoses of mental disorders and physical health conditions in these individuals and their family members (i.e., parents, grandparents, and siblings). Mental disorders will include mood and anxiety disorders, schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, or substance abuse disorders. We will use machine-learning techniques to identify specific risk factors from these detailed health histories to predict mental disorders in the adult offspring. This innovative study will be the first of its kind; constructing thorough, objectively-measured health histories from existing databases to predict the likelihood of mental disorders. Identifying individuals at risk of mental disorders will help develop early support programs and inform healthcare resource decisions. Investigating the influence of family health histories with different degrees of relativeness will provide important information about mental disorders' developmental origins.

column36: The Pocket Skills Project: A digital health solution delivering dialectical behaviour therapy to adults with concurrent disorders.
column37: People with concurrent disorders (CD) commonly present with depressive or anxiety and alcohol or substance use disorders at the same time. 81% of people with CD are aged 18-44. People with CD often experience emotion dysregulation, defined as challenges in applying effective strategies to regulate negative emotions, leading to maladaptive coping (e.g., substance use) and poorer quality of life. The only psychological treatment that targets emotion dysregulation is dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), but availability is limited, making access to this intervention difficult. Web-based DBT skills training (DBTST) is effective for CD in as little as 8 weeks and may be of substantial therapeutic benefit. This project seeks to leverage technology to expand treatment options for people with CD, where stigma and engagement are barriers to receiving evidence-based care. This project will implement an existing, not-for-profit, web-based DBTST intervention called PocketSkills to evaluate its efficacy against clinical monitoring (CM) in 82 adults seeking treatment for CD. CD outpatients aged 18-44, who have no history of psychotic-spectrum disorders or intravenous substance use, will be randomized to two treatment conditions: CM alone or DBTST+CM, with the latter group receiving an 8 week augmentation of PocketSkills with online exercises. Participants will be followed for 8 weeks of acute treatment with a 3-month follow-up using validated measures. Results seek to evaluate a web-based DBTST intervention in adults with CD, for whom available services are limited and treatment alternatives are sparse. PocketSkills is a promising and innovative digital health solution, co-developed by the founder of DBT and supported by initial research. Results will inform the efficacy of this intervention in CD beyond standard treatment. This project could also support the creation of standalone digital programs and other combination interventions to improve access to psychological services.

column36: In situ structural characterization of nature's strongest nano-motor by cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging
column37: Many pathogenic bacteria (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Vibrio cholerae, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Legionella pneumophila, etc) use long cell-surface filaments called the type IV pili (T4P) to sense contact with surfaces and to initiate infections. Using the strongest biological motor, T4P can undergo rapid cycles of extension and retraction. This repeated assembly (extension) and disassembly (retraction) of the grappling-hook-like T4P filaments helps bacteria crawl along surfaces towards various niches for colonisation and to capture free DNA that can include antibiotic resistance genes. The T4P motor is a multi-protein complex within a larger nanomachine that spans the bacterial cell envelope. Although individual components of the T4P nanomachine have been intensively studied, how they work together to assemble and disassemble the T4P filaments remains one of the most important unresolved questions in the field. One major technical limitation is that no one has been able to isolate intact T4P nanomachines from the bacterial envelope. I will use an advanced imaging technique called cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) to reveal the intact architectures of two evolutionarily distinct types of T4P nano-machines directly within the cell envelopes of a significant human pathogen, P. aeruginosa, and the model species Caulobacter crescentus. By comparing structures of the wild-type T4P nanomachines, and those of informative deletion and point mutants, I will visualize the T4P motor complexes in their extension and retraction states at unprecedented resolution. These data will not only reveal the exact positions and roles of individual T4P components but also answer the key question: how does the T4P filament extend and retract? Since mutations in the T4P motor components impair the virulence of bacterial pathogens, results from this work may serve as a guide for the rational design of new therapeutics that can combat infections without encouraging the development of resistance.

column36: Functional connectivity as a potential neural mechanism linking personality traits with risk for Alzheimer's disease
column37: People with certain personality traits, such as high neuroticism, and low conscientiousness and openness, are at higher risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD), but we don't yet know why this is the case. Other research has shown that AD is caused by the spread of toxic proteins, amyloid and tau, through connections in the brain. It is possible that people with certain personality traits have a brain wiring system that makes them more vulnerable to the spread of AD proteins, but no previous studies have looked at this. The current study aims to explore this question using a sample of 386 older adults who do not have AD dementia, but are at increased risk of developing it. Participants completed a personality questionnaire, functional MRI (fMRI) scans of brain connections, and PET scans measuring the amount of amyloid and tau the brain. We will look at how an individual's personality is related to their brain connections on the fMRI scan, then examine whether these neural connections are also related to the amount of amyloid and tau in the brain on the PET scans. Finally, we will look at whether neural connectivity is a factor that links personality traits with the amount of amyloid and tau in the brain. We will also check for sex differences in these relationships. Our early results suggest that personality traits such as neuroticism, extraversion, and openness are related to different patterns of brain wiring. Also, low levels of extraversion, openness, and conscientiousness, and high levels of neuroticism, are related to high levels of toxic AD proteins in the brain. We will next explore these relationships in more detail. The good news is that personality is a 'modifiable' risk factor, that can be modified with therapy. This means that findings from our study may lead to new interventions to slow down the progression of AD. Looking at sex differences in the relationships between personality and brain connectivity and AD will also help to personalise these interventions.

column36: Identification of Bacterial Genotoxins in the Human Microbiome
column37: Microbial communities within humans are thought to impart considerable environmental influence on health and diseases. Molecules derived from bacteria are key to deciphering the roles microbes have in this relationship. Colibactin, is a cancer-linked, DNA-damaging agent made by certain gut bacteria, including many gut commensal E. coli. Bacteria that produce colibactin can damage DNA in human cells and are linked to colorectal cancer. This raises questions whether other gut bacteria make yet-uncharacterized DNA damaging agents or mediate other interactions within the community affecting cancer development. Here, I propose to uncover novel bacterial genotoxins in the human microbiome and investigate their DNA damage capability. Aim 1 describes how I curate the collection of genes encoding the assembly bioactive molecules. I use the presence of DNA repair and maintenance enzymes that protect the organism from its own cytotoxic compounds to identify potential genotoxins. Aim 2 outlines multiple approaches that will be used to rapidly access and synthesize these molecules, while Aim 3 determines potential toxic activity of the molecules in human cells. Molecules damaging either DNA or block the normal cell cycle are candidates for future animal studies to determine the contributions the producing gut bacteria have in cancer development.

column36: Oral Sildenafil therapy for mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: targeted therapy for pulmonary vascular remodeling to improve dyspnea and exercise tolerance.
column37: Lay Abstract: The goal of this project is to examine how lung blood vessel dysfunction contributes to exercise intolerance in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is a condition characterized by airway obstruction and is currently the 4th leading cause of death in Canada. Patients with COPD experience significant shortness of breath, which has been shown to reduce quality of life and physical activity, and increase risk of mortality. Much work has examined breathlessness in moderate and severe COPD, but the reasons for breathlessness in patients with mild COPD are not well understood. Mild COPD patients show an exaggerated breathing response to exercise. Recent work suggests that the increased breathing response during exercise in mild COPD is because of poor matching of regional lung air and blood flow. Researchers have proposed that this imbalance is because of dysfunction of blood vessels in the lungs. Recently the Stickland Laboratory has shown that inhaled nitric oxide dilates blood vessels in the lungs, and therefore reduces shortness of breath, the breathing response to exercise, and improves exercise capacity in mild COPD. These findings suggest that dysfunction of blood vessels in the lungs is an important contributor to exercise intolerance in mild COPD. Building on this previous work, we aim to determine whether oral sildenafil (a pill given clinical to improve blood vessel function in the lungs) improves exercise tolerance in mild COPD patients.

column36: Characterizing neuronal circuit assembly of the pharyngeal nervous system during C. elegans embryogenesis
column37: A functional nervous system requires neurons to be connected in very specific ways to allow animals to move, sense the environment, and form memories. Here, we use a transparent microscopic round worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, as a model organism to study the nervous system. While the nervous system of other organisms, such as mammals are far more complex, many of the fundamental aspects their molecular and cellular mechanisms are conserved. The entire nervous system of C. elegans is simple and well-characterized: a hermaphrodite worm has a total of 302 neurons, and how they connect to each other has been mapped out. In particular, 20 neurons are precisely interconnected to form a small but functional nervous system in the C. elegans pharynx to coordinate pumping of the organ and allow the animal to take in food. Our project aims to studying how this simple nervous system is assembled in the embryo. column36: A Multi-Modal Imaging Approach To Study and Predict Early Inflammatory Arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), the most common form of inflammatory arthritis, is a chronic joint disease that results in joint pain, swelling, and stiffness, all of which can reduce the quality-of-life, as affected individuals are unable to perform daily routine tasks (e.g. cooking, cleaning, dressing themselves, etc.). The debilitating effects of RA are related to the degradation and loss of bone as a result of swelling. While treatments for RA have improved, the bone damage progression still occurs and is rarely repaired to pre-diseased states. The absence of a "total RA treatment solution" is due to our lack of knowledge about the exact mechanisms by which inflammation promotes bone degeneration. Current research points to two possible hypotheses, inflammation arising from (1) outside the bone or (2) inside the bone. However, testing these hypotheses has proven challenging for any single imaging modality due to the inability to simultaneously image inflammation and bone. Thus, I propose combining imaging techniques that are optimized for each; with the collected data achieving a simultaneous visualization of the progression of inflammation and bone degradation. To understand these changes as a function of time, I will perform imaging experiments to monitor and follow early-RA participants for up to 6 months. This study will provide critically important information on where inflammation first arises, and how it relates to bone erosions within RA-affected joints.

column36: Pre-clinical development of small-molecule catalytic pocket inhibitors that block AID/APOBEC-driven mutations in cancer development, aggression and resistance.
column37: Our lab studies AID/APOBEC, a family of DNA mutating enzymes involved in immunity and antiviral defense. AID's job is to mutate a few specific genes in B-cells (antibody-producing cells) to boost immune function, while APOBECs mutate viruses, such as HIV, to deactivate them. Unfortunately, AID/APOBECs frequently makes mistakes and targets thousands of other genes which are not its intended targets. These undesired mutations are a leading mechanism by which healthy cells turn cancerous (e.g. leukemia, lymphoma, breast cancer). To make matters worse, these cancers often maintain, turn on or drastically increase AID/APOBEC expression. This continued AID/APOBEC expression serves as a "mutational fuel" for cancer cells, promoting more aggressive and treatment-resistant cancers. AID/APOBECs are extremely difficult molecules to purify and study. As a result, their molecular shape was unknown until recently. With knowledge of AID/APOBECs shape, our lab has begun to develop small-molecule drug-like compounds that specifically bind and inhibit AID/APOBEC activity. The goal of this proposal is to 1) Identify inhibitors and refine them, such that they are more effective, 2) test our hypothesis that these inhibitors can block AID/APOBEC-driven cancers, aggressiveness and chemotherapy drug-resistance and 3) test whether these inhibitors can block AID/APOBEC-mediated cancers in mouse models that mimic human cancers. The outcome of this work will generate effective inhibitors against AID/APOBEC-expressing cancers that can be further tested in clinical trials.

column36: Multiphasic prehabilitation compared to usual care for patients undergoing surgery for head and neck cancer: a randomized controlled trial
column37: Head and neck cancer (HNC) is the 7th most common type of cancer worldwide. Treatment for HNC usually requires major surgery. This is a complex and intensive medical procedure that often results in complications and impaired function. Recovery is difficult for patients, and their quality of life can be reduced. Helping patients prepare before surgery may help improve outcomes after surgery. This type of preparation is called "prehabilitation," and it can be delivered virtually. Patients who have surgery for HNC often then have radiation and chemotherapy, so prehabilitation can also be used to help prepare for these additional treatments. Prehabilitation focuses on helping patients to move more and eat well to help the body to prepare for cancer treatment (similar to a runner preparing for a marathon by training, and eating to fuel their body before the big day). Research in patients undergoing other types of surgery shows that prehabilitation has the potential to help patients recover faster, move more and feel better after surgery. However, we do not know if this will also be beneficial for people with HNC because this type of surgery is very different. In this research, we will randomize patients into two groups: one group who will receive standard care and another who will receive exercise and nutritional prehabilitation that starts before surgery and continues after surgery. Patients in the prehabilitation group will receive education and guidance to move more while in hospital (this is called early mobility) because this reduces complications and helps patients return home sooner. We will test the effectiveness of prehabilitation by measuring mobility, function and quality of life in both groups in the weeks and months after surgery. If effective, prehabilitation can be introduced for all patients having HNC surgery in Calgary, and other hospitals will have a model to copy to help improve care for HNC patients across Canada.

column36: Investigating the role of intestinal commensal bacteria in innate memory induction
column37: The intestinal microbiota encompasses a community of commensal bacteria that live in a mutually beneficial relationship with their host. The profound importance of microbiota-host interactions in regulating the host immune system has been demonstrated in multiple illnesses, including cancer, diabetes and infectious diseases. Humanity has constantly faced the challenge of overcoming infectious diseases and, despite massive advancements in medicine, they continue to represent significant threats to health. Following infection with a pathogen, cells of the adaptive immune system display long-term changes in their function leading to the development of immunological memory. For a long time, immunological memory was considered an exclusive hallmark of the adaptive arm of the immune system. Yet emerging evidence has shown that innate immune cells can also adapt their function after previous insults and thereby also showing the ability to be 'trained'. However, unlike adaptive immune memory, innate memory is not pathogen-specific. For example, epidemiologic data suggests that some existing vaccines, such as Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG), have beneficial effects against later infections unrelated to the target infectious agent. The underlying mechanisms involved in such innate memory are only beginning to be elucidated. The ability to successfully eliminate a pathogen has been associated with continuous cross-talk between the microbiota and the host immune system. However, whether the gut microbiota can induce such innate memory has not yet been studied. I propose to investigate the role of intestinal microbiota in the induction of innate memory and determine the impact on protective immunity. Understanding the mechanisms involved in 'training' innate cells will be critical for the design of new therapies and vaccines and allow us to better harness the power of the intestinal microbiota to boost immune responses to infections or modulate inflammation in chronic diseases.

column36: Elucidating the Determinants and Mechanisms of Tau Liquid - Liquid Phase Separation In Situ at Multiple Length Scales from mu m to A: Exploring the Role of Membraneless Compartments in Alzheimer's Disease
column37: The build-up of pathological aggregates in the brain comprised of the tau protein is a clinical hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD). The progression of AD is closely associated with the spreading of tau aggregates i.e. neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), through anatomically connected regions of the brain, suggesting that tau is a major driver of AD pathology. A notable discrepancy with the clinical presentation of NFTs is that tau is a highly soluble protein in solution and exhibits very low tendency to aggregate. Recent studies have proposed an unconventional pathway through which tau overwhelms its native high solubility. It has been demonstrated that in the presence of RNA, tau undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming liquid droplets that condense high concentrations of tau into a relatively confined space. The supersaturation of tau in turn promotes its conversion into solid-like toxic aggregates. However, LLPS is also involved in the regulation of normal biology, such as the translation of genes into proteins. Therefore, it remains unclear how the phase separated systems involved in gene regulation differ from those promoting the formation of pathological aggregates. Critical to distinguishing these two opposing cases is determining the arrangement of protein building blocks i.e. amino acids, involved in phase separation vs. transition from liquid droplets into solid fibers. Such maps are essential for the development of therapeutics selectively targeting abnormal condensates, with minimal off-target effects. Here we propose to uncover these amino acids networks using a combination of Nuclear Magnetic Resonance spectroscopy and light microscopy techniques that break the resolution barrier for the description of abnormal phase separated systems. Importantly, these studies will be performed in the presence of age-related stress factors to gain an understanding of how aging contributes to the disease process and how we can prevent it.

column37: Many reports have established a correlation between obesity and diabetes with cardiovascular complications such as heart failure. This occurs due to changes in the structure and function of the heart, yet the precise mechanisms responsible for regulating these changes in diabetes remain to be determined. This project will focus on the role played by a substance (adiponectin) which is released from fat cells. Upon release, adiponectin can travel in the bloodstream to have effects in the heart. Interestingly, the amount of adiponectin circulating in the blood decreases in obese and diabetic individuals. We intend to determine how too much or too little adiponectin alters the structure and function of the heart. Research has shown cardioprotective effects of adiponectin and this has generated tremendous interest in recent years about its therapeutic potential. Yet we still need to understand more details about how the effects mediated by adiponectin on the heart occur to facilitate development of new treatments.

column36: Equity in the intersection of scientific publishing and academic reward
column37: Inequities exist in research publishing; researchers typically publish their research in journals to share the results of their research. The number of research publications and where they are published are important academic measures. Researchers who cannot afford to publish their research and whose research is not considered interesting and relevant by peer reviewers may not be valued highly in their institutions. Those with less publishing experience may make or be left with suboptimal journal choices for submitting their research. The process for selecting research for publication (i.e., peer review) is dominated by men in high income countries who tend to select articles from researchers of similar profiles for publication. As a result, published research is dominated by male researchers from high-income, English-speaking countries. Researchers in high-income countries tend to cite (i.e., reference in their research) domestic research more often, potentially incentivizing journals, whose reputations are formed on the basis of citations, to accept more research from such countries. This research aims to understand the inequities researchers face in publishing. A review of the literature followed by interviews with researchers will identify potential strategies for achieving equity in scholarly publishing. This research will also explore the use of preprint servers. Preprint servers allow research to be freely posted online, without undergoing peer review. They may provide a more equitable publishing option than scholarly journals. We will compare the characteristics of authors of preprints to those of journal publications. The trustworthiness of preprints, which have been included in some systematic reviews during the 2019 novel coronavirus pandemic, will additionally be compared to research published in scholarly journals. This research will provide evidence to facilitate improved equity in scholarly publishing and publishing-dependent academic evaluation.

column36: Granzyme B: A novel therapeutic target in cutaneous leishmaniasis
column37: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is an infectious skin disease caused by Leishmania parasites and is transmitted by the bite of a sandfly. The skin lesion of CL begins as a small papule at the site of inoculation, usually at an exposed body part such as the face or extremities, which slowly grows and becomes ulcerated. Without treatment, the ulcer ultimately heals over 3 to 18 months and leaves a permanent disfiguring scar with psychosocial sequelae. Up to 10% of CL cases will progress, become chronic, and exhibit more severe clinical features. Unfortunately, there is no effective vaccine for prevention of CL and currently available therapeutic options are invasive, have toxic systemic side effects, and show varied efficacy. Although, CL is endemic in over 70 countries, including United States, and is diagnosed in up to one million new cases annually, this devastating disease is a World Health Organization top neglected tropical disease. Granzyme B (GzmB) is a protein that is aberrantly elevated in CL lesions and other inflammatory skin conditions. GzmB activity has been demonstrated to cleave important proteins in the skin, aggravating tissue damage, delayed wound healing, and scarring in human skin specimens and experimental models. Importantly, inhibition of GzmB have shown efficacy in impeding these disease phenotypes. In recent years, accumulating reports have linked GzmB expression and activity to disease severity measures of CL but GzmB's functional role is unexplored. Herein, we hypothesize that in CL lesions, GzmB contributes to inflammation, impaired wound healing, and scarring that can be averted by a GzmB inhibitor. To test this hypothesis, our 3-pronged approach will include lesional specimens from CL patients, a well-established experimental model to study GzmB function, and a GzmB inhibitor, Serpina3n. Together, the proposed study findings will provide key rationale to pursue GzmB as a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of CL.

column36: The influence of multimorbidity on dementia, neuroanatomy and cognition
column37: 50 million individuals suffering from dementia worldwide have difficulty with memory, emotion, and problem solving abilities, and struggle with daily tasks such as planning and preparing meals. This impacts family members and caregivers of dementia patients, who dedicate time and energy to meet the needs of their loved ones. The goal of this project is to better understand dementia risk, so those at risk can be identified before symptoms appear in hopes of preventing dementia from affecting them and their families. An important risk factor for dementia is multimorbidity, defined as the coexistence of multiple chronic conditions. Multimorbidity leads to difficulties in cognitive performance in the elderly and up to 80% of individuals with dementia are multimorbid. However, key gaps in our understanding of multimorbidity remain. It is unknown how multimorbidity affects the brain. As dementia is caused by damage to brain cells, this information is key to understanding the role of multimorbidity. Also, previous studies commonly define multimorbidity by a simple disease count, or by the presence of any two diseases. However, this perspective does not account for different impacts of specific diseases, their combinations, or the order in which they develop. An individual with hypertension and depression may have different brain structure and risk of dementia, and require different treatment than an individual with cardiovascular disease and osteoporosis. I aim to investigate how specific patterns of multimorbidity impact the brain and dementia. Using population level datasets, I will identify groups of diseases which coexist. Then, using magnetic resonance imaging to measure brain health, I will describe the structural brain features of these multimorbidity groups. The proposed work will help understand how multimorbidity impacts dementia, and help better identify those at risk of developing dementia before symptoms develop.

column36: Using placental transcriptomics to understand the impact of maternal BMI on placental function and fetal growth
column37: The placenta (afterbirth) is important for a healthy pregnancy. When the placenta does not work properly (called placental insufficiency), the developing fetus (unborn baby) may not grow properly and can be born small and sick. Right now, we do not know what exactly causes placental insufficiency. In order to help these babies, it is very important to learn what causes placental insufficiency so new treatments can be developed. In this project, I will study a special type of cell in the placenta called "trophoblast stem cells" (TS cells). Like other stem cells found in the body, TS cells respond to damage and may act to help repair the placenta. We do not know the role of TS cells in placental insufficiency. In my project, I will use a mouse model of placental insufficiency to study these cells. In part one of my project, I will use special mice that have TS cells tagged with coloured markers. Mice will either undergo surgery to cause placental insufficiency (we place a small tie around the blood vessels feeding the uterus), surgery with no tie or no surgery. Afterwards, I will collect the placentas and look for coloured cells in the placenta under the microscope. I will be able to count the number of TS cells as well as look at their location in the placenta and compare them between the groups. The results will tell us if TS cells respond to placental insufficiency. Next, I will use a special virus to kill all the TS cells and look to see if removing TS cells causes the pregnancies to be healthy or unhealthy in the same 3 groups. If removal of the TS cells leads to poor health in the fetuses, this would tell us TS cells play an important role in helping the placenta when there is placental insufficiency. My project will confirm the role of TS cells in placenta insufficiency. If TS cells help repair the placenta, we may be able to target them for treatment in human pregnancies in future studies.

column36: Probing the conformational dynamics of the frameshift-stimulatory pseudoknot of SARS-CoV-2 at the single-molecule level.
column37: The virus causing the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2, uses a process called -1 programmed ribosomal frameshifting (-1 PRF) to express proteins essential for viral replication. -1 PRF involves a change in the way the viral genome is read that is triggered by a specific structure in the viral genome: a pseudoknot. Changing the level of -1 PRF in viruses can suppress infectivity, suggesting that the SARS-CoV-2 pseudoknot may be a good target for developing new drugs against the coronavirus. It is therefore essential to understand what features of the pseudoknot are important for its ability to stimulate -1 PRF. Work on other viruses has shown that specific interactions within pseudoknots play a key role, as do the dynamics of the structure under tension during -1 PRF. I will build on my previous published work on -1 PRF in SARS-CoV-2 showing that it can be inhibited by small-molecule drugs, aiming to study systematically the mechanisms by which the pseudoknot stimulates -1 PRF. Making mutations that knock out specific interactions within the pseudoknot, one, by one, I will measure both the functional effects these mutations have on -1 PRF, using enzymatic assays, and also the changes they cause in the structural dynamics of the pseudoknot under tension, using high-precision optical tweezers to apply force to single molecules. These studies will allow me to relate specific changes in the structure and dynamics of the RNA to their functional outcomes, and thereby map out the features of the pseudoknot that are essential to -1 PRF. I will also repeat these measurements in the presence of small molecules that inhibit -1 PRF, to deduce the modes of action by which different inhibitors act to change the -1 PRF level and determine which are most effective functionally. This work will provide crucial insights that can be used to target RNA pseudoknots for developing drugs against COVID-19 and possibly other viral diseases involving -1 PRF.

column36: The microbiota-immune-brain axis in glioblastoma initiation
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the deadliest and most aggressive malignant brain tumour. Virtually all patients die within two years of developing this disease, despite current therapies. In order to develop more effective treatment, it is crucial to better understand the mechanisms involved in its initiation and progression. Brain tumours are not only comprised of cancer cells, but also normal brain components such as brain resident immune cells called microglia. One of the roles of microglia is to maintain homeostasis by protecting the brain from infection and injury. Our ongoing research suggests that GBMs exist in a state reminiscent of an inflammation/injury-response, suggesting that microglia may play a role in tumourigenesis. The brain-gut axis is an emerging field that is largely unexplored in the context of brain tumours. The gut microbiota-the collection of bacteria living in our guts that can communicate with the brain-has been shown to regulate microglia maturation and activity. I hypothesize that the gut microbiota plays a role in GBM initiation through modulation of microglia activity. I will investigate whether gut bacterial infections can signal to the brain to create an adverse inflammatory environment that subsequently promotes GBM tumour initiation in mice that are primed with genetic mutations that predispose them to spontaneously develop GBM. By modifying these mice to be completely devoid of gut bacteria, I will study whether and how tumour initiation is affected. This work will drive novel therapeutical strategies targeting the gut that could bypass the challenge of developing drugs that reach the brain. It will also explore how environmental influences synergize with underlying genetic mutations and drive brain cancer development. Finally, it will develop a framework for identifying higher risk behaviours/circumstances that may enable earlier detection or preventative measures that can mitigate the risk of developing GBM.

column36: Investigating the impact of a CAPRIN1 condensate solvent on the conformational equilibrium and activity of the CNOT7 deadenylase
column37: Understanding how machines such as cars work requires us to know the components that comprise them and how they interact with each other to ultimately perform the desired function, which in the case of cars is transportation. In an analogous manner, our bodies are made up of tiny units called cells, which together perform tasks that are integral for life. Cells themselves are made up of different types of biological molecules, or biomolecules, which interact with each other to give rise to the cell's activities. This process typically involves changes in the shapes of the biomolecules themselves, particularly of molecules called enzymes that perform chemical reactions in the cell, in a manner analogous to how pistons in an engine move to power a car. Recent studies over the past decade have uncovered a novel mode of interaction of biomolecules in which they self-associate with one another to form liquid-like droplets, in a manner analogous to how oil droplets in water coalesce with each other. These liquid-like droplets are implicated in mediating many cellular activities, and aberrant droplet function results in cellular dysfunction and consequently disease. Thus, understanding the functional consequences of droplet formation is important. In this project, we hypothesize that formation of liquid-like droplets of the CAPRIN1 molecule can cause changes in the shape of the enzyme CNOT7, thereby activating the enzyme's function of mRNA deadenylation. We propose to test this hypothesis by monitoring how droplet formation affects CNOT7 function and correlating this to changes in its shape inside CAPRIN1 droplets using a technique called Nuclear Magnetic Resonance spectroscopy. column36: Exploring the role of lipid transfer at the mitochondria-lysosome contact sites in the regulation of mitochondrial shape and function
column37: Mitochondria are essential cellular organelles that are often defined as the powerhouse of the cell. Their morphology is strongly linked to their functions and can be modulated through fission or fusion. Notably, it was shown that intricate contact with other organelles are involved in these processes. However, the exact roles of such contacts are poorly understood. These intimate contacts were shown to be enriched for proteins able to transfer lipids and that are thus capable of regulating the lipid composition of the contacting membranes. This raises the hypothesis that the transfer of these lipids could be involved in the fission or fusion of mitochondria. As their role is vital for the cell, it is not surprising that dysfunctions of mitochondria lead to numerous diseases, among which neurological diseases, as Parkinson's disease or Friedrich's ataxia disease. It is therefore crucial to decipher the mechanisms involved in the regulation of the shape and function of mitochondria. I recently identified two lipid transfer proteins as important regulators of mitochondrial morphology. I hypothesize that these proteins regulate the lipid composition of mitochondria at contact with other organelles, influencing fusion and/or fission processes. I will test this hypothesis by characterizing their role in the regulation of mitochondrial shape and functions and determine the lipid composition of mitochondria when the expression of these two proteins is modulated. Additionally, we will establish how these proteins are carrying out their functions at mitochondria by exploring their partners using a powerful proteomic technique. This research will provide important insight on the mechanisms that are used to regulate the shape of mitochondria and their functions. As mitochondrial dysfunctions and lipid metabolism alteration are associated with numerous diseases, we expect that this research will help to understand various diseases pertaining to mitochondria.

column36: Association between thyrotropin (TSH) levels and cancer recurrence among patients with well differentiated thyroid cancer: A retrospective cohort study

Currently, the ideal thyroid hormone target level is unclear among thyroid cancer patients who have had surgery. This lack of clarity can subject patients to risks of over and/or under treatment, and may cause significant anxiety for both patients and physicians alike. A better understanding of optimal thyroid hormone target levels is urgently needed to help improve patient outcomes in thyroid cancer. Thyroid hormone levels of these individuals will be obtained from the Ontario Laboratories Information System. We will evaluate the relationship between thyroid hormone levels and outcomes after surgery, including cancer recurrence and treatment complications such as fractures and heart disease. We will determine the ideal thyroid hormone level that reduces cancer recurrence while minimizing the harms of excess thyroid hormone replacement. The results of this study will be informative to all clinicians who manage this common condition and improve the lives of thyroid cancer survivors.

column36: Uncovering the transcriptional regulatory networks that control uterine contraction to identify novel therapeutic targets in preventing pre-term birth
column37: One in ten babies are born early (pre-term), underdeveloped and at high risk of complications or death. The impact of being born prematurely can continue to effect individuals much later in life, costing Canada ~$2 billion annually and imposing emotional and physical burdens on those involved. Term and pre-term delivery of infants occurs in the same manner, the smooth muscle component of the uterus (myometrium) contracts to generate a force that expels the fetus. This contraction is controlled at the cellular level with individual muscle cells of the myometrium activating a group of genes that promote this contraction. How exactly these genes are regulated to induce contractile forces at term or pre-term is unknown. There are currently no treatments for pre-term labour. Therefore, understanding how these genes are regulated will be essential in providing new treatments to prevent pre-term birth. Genes can be regulated by proteins that interact with regions of DNA in the genome to turn on/off expression. We will be the first to identify differences between proteins binding in pre-term and term labour, with these proteins providing potential therapeutic targets. Another manner in which genes can be regulated is the result of how the genome is folded three-dimensionally in the nucleus. This three-dimensional structure enables different regions of the genome to come into contact with one another, regulating if a gene is on or off. This organization is cell-type specific and contributes to a cells specific function. Genome organization of the myometrium and regulation of genes in pregnancy and labour is also unknown. By determining this organization, alongside identification of regulatory proteins, it will be possible to construct a model by which pre-term labour occurs, and provide novel targets for the development of treatments to prevent preterm labour.

column36: Understanding the role of local environments in supporting community belonging and population health
column37: Research shows that life satisfaction influences how much we use health care, our risk of chronic illness, and even our life expectancy. Among many ingredients that contribute to our life satisfaction, the sense of belonging we have to our communities has been linked with many health benefits, but also depends on where we live. Some neighbourhoods are designed to promote social activities and active public lives, while others are less focused on community connectedness. Many neighbourhoods are structured around other needs, such as automobile transport or industry. More and more Canadians live in cities than ever before. We also tend to spend more time in our neighbourhoods as we get older. Our neighbourhood environments are likely to impact our ability to build and grow our communities. My goal is to identify which aspects of our neighbourhoods impact our sense of community belonging and determine how much neighbourhoods influence the relationship between community belonging and the health of Canadians. I am conducting a large-scale study using data on participants that have been linked with their hospital records and death records for whom we have postal code information. From there, I will map participants to their neighbourhoods and explore their environmental conditions, such as active living friendliness (i.e. walkability), air pollution, and heat. Then, I will examine the relationship between these environmental factors, community belonging, and health outcomes such as hospital visits and premature death. I will also be focusing on specific groups of interest, such as older adults. This project will give us new insight into whether neighbourhood-related interventions to encourage community belonging might help prevent illness and premature death.

column36: Identifying cortical network properties that underpin obsessive-compulsive disorder symptoms and brain stimulation treatment outcomes
column37: Obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours are disabling symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) that can persist for decades despite traditional treatments. A promising treatment alternative for OCD is non-invasive brain stimulation. It is not well understood, however, why some patients improve with brain stimulation treatment, while others do not. The brain circuits that give rise to OCD symptoms and are modified by successful treatment might be key to understanding individual differences in treatment outcomes. In this project, we will combine single pulses of brain stimulation (transcranial magnetic stimulation) with brain activity recordings (electroencephalography) to measure the interactions between brain regions in brain circuits that have been implicated in OCD. We will collect these measurements of brain functional connectivity in 400 OCD patients and 135 healthy control participants. OCD patients will then repeat these measurements after 2 weeks of accelerated brain stimulation treatment targeting the brain circuits under study. Using this data, we aim to identify subgroups of OCD patients that show similar brain profiles. We will examine how these distinct brain profiles differ from the brain profiles of controls. We will also assess whether pre-treatment measures of functional connectivity can be used to predict which patients will benefit from accelerated brain stimulation treatment. Lastly, we will examine the changes in functional connectivity that occur when symptoms improve during treatment. From this work, we aim to discover the interactions between brain regions that perpetuate obsessions and compulsions, and how individual differences in these brain circuits translate to accelerated brain stimulation treatment outcomes in OCD. This project therefore stands to improve brain stimulation treatment for OCD, and our fundamental understanding of the brain mechanisms underlying obsessive-compulsive symptoms.

column36: Structural dynamics of nucleosome core particles upon DNA methylation and MeCP2 binding
column37: In humans DNA is organized into basic units in which it is wrapped around a protein core to form a structure called a nucleosome core particle (NCP). NCPs are subject to a variety of chemical modifications, affecting both their DNA and protein components, which in turn regulate their interactions with other protein partners to favor or inhibit the expression of specific genes. Misregulation of gene expression can lead to a variety of different diseases, including cancer. One way of controlling gene expression is through the addition of chemical moieties to the DNA components of NCPs, in particular methyl groups. Molecular players are then recruited to the methyl groups where they can prevent gene expression. One such player is methylated-CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2). A number of mutations ("errors") in MeCP2 cause Rett syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder specifically affecting females, but other mutations lead to diverse neurological pathologies as well as to breast cancer. A three-dimensional picture of how DNA methylation affects the NCP is not available, and a detailed understanding of how methylation, in turn, regulates binding of MeCP2 to the NCP has not been established. I will use a combination of different powerful biophysical techniques, including Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and Electron Cryo-Microscopy (cryo-EM) to address these questions, and to understand how Rett syndrome mutations in MeCP2 lead to impaired interactions with methylated NCPs. The combined NMR and cryo-EM approach will provide novel insights into how the methyl mark changes the shape and properties of the NCP, and controls interactions with other molecules that regulate gene expression. The identified key regions of MeCP2 that will emerge from this study will inform the development of new therapeutic agents for mitigating Rett syndrome.

column36: Redefining Population health research agendas in Canada: A multilevel analysis of the COVID-19-related global health governance architecture
column37: Health equity and social justice for improving population health at national and global levels are the main objectives of population health and global health efforts, respectively. Since the declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic by the World Health Organization (WHO) in March 2020, the promotion of health equity and the health of marginalised or vulnerable groups have been hampered by both global health governance processes and decisions, and public health measures taken to control the pandemic. These have not only exacerbated underlying social and health inequities, but they have also led to massively redirecting financial, technical and human resources of existing research to address the COVID-19 pandemic. The research objective is to explore how the COVID-19 pandemic related global health governance is redefining population health research agendas in Canada from the perspectives of different actors. Global health governance refers to "governance arrangements needed to further agreed global health goals" such as health equity. We will conduct a multilevel analysis of the COVID-19 global health governance on population health research in Canada. Intersectionality, highlighting social, gender, and health inequities experienced by vulnerable populations, and the Kingdon Multiple-Streams Approach in agenda setting, will be used as conceptual and analytical frameworks. We will deploy various qualitative methods to triangulate information obtained from four levels of actors: researchers, research institutes and universities, research funders, and WHO. The study findings will enable us to better understand both the impacts of the pandemic related global health governance architecture on population health research agendas in Canada, and the potential unintended consequences on health equity and vulnerable populations. Research analyses will further help Canadian researchers and funders to improve accountability in terms of research intent, content, reach and outputs.

column36: Therapies to Promote Neuroplasticity in Disease
column37: Neurological disorders are among the most serious health problems facing modern society. As the average human lifespan increases, a concomitant increase in the incidence of disability due to neurological dysfunction has devastated the lives of many. This project will develop a therapeutic approach that can be broadly applicable across a large spectrum of neurological disorders, to benefit human health.

column36: HIV-1 glycoprotein gp41's roles in both immune misdirection and suppression
column37: Viruses need access to the inside of a host's cells in order to proliferate and launch an effective infection. They have therefore developed protein molecules to fuse with the outside of human cells and subsequently transfer themselves (or at least the portions required for duplication) within. These fusion proteins are called viral glycoproteins (GPs). However, viruses produce few types of proteins, meaning that many viral proteins must pull double or triple duty and take on additional roles. This is true of a GP from HIV (gp41), which - besides its role in viral entry -also interacts with and negatively impacts the host's immune system. This is done in two ways: 1) Immunodominance - gp41 contains two unique segments that draw the production of host-made antibodies to them, misdirecting these protective molecules away from areas that prevent infection; and 2) Immunosuppression - gp41 contains a segment that interacts directly with immune cells and suppresses their activity. Our goal is to understand how the different segments of gp41 achieve these two processes, providing a comprehensive overview of how viruses like HIV avoid the immune system. We will determine the shape and chemical properties of the gp41 immunodominant regions to elucidate why these segments are bound preferentially by human antibodies. Preliminary results have shown that the two segments use different mechanisms, one taking up many different shapes to be easily recognized by different antibodies, with the other binding with a single shape but with exceptional strength. We will also determine how the immunosuppressive region is able to interact with human immune cells. Initial data suggests that this region of gp41 binds to only certain types of immune cells, implying a preference for molecular components on these cells' surfaces. Our studies will impact the future production of HIV vaccines and antivirals, bringing further weapons to bear on a virus infamous for its debilitating infections.

column36: Characterizing the Role of VAPB as a Novel Regulator of Cardiac Structure and Function
column37: Cardiovascular disease remains one of the leading causes of death in Canada and there is a continued need to find new strategies to improve patient outcomes and mitigate the progression to heart failure. Although the molecular pathways driving heart failure pathophysiology are not fully characterized, the role of dysregulated sarco/endoplasmic reticulum (SR/ER) and mitochondrial function in the development and progression of heart failure is well-established. The SR/ER and mitochondria have largely been studied as structurally separate organelles with independent functions. However, increasing evidence suggests that close proximity between these intracellular organelle membranes can create ER-mitochondrial contact sites which facilitate inter-organelle crosstalk and alter cell function. Importantly, the key protein interactions at these contact sites as well as the role of organelle crosstalk in the pathophysiology of heart failure are still poorly understood. In order to identify novel membrane proteins which may participate in these intracellular signaling complexes in the cardiac muscle, we performed in-depth cardiomyocyte membrane proteomics and bioinformatics analyses of human and mouse heart failure samples. From these analyses, we identified an ER membrane protein, vesicle-associated membrane protein-associated protein B/C (VAPB), which has been shown to participate in ER membrane tethering with the mitochondria in non-myocyte cells, but has not been studied in the heart. This project will investigate 1) the role of VAPB in in vivo cardiac structure and function, 2) how VAPB regulates SR/ER-mitochondrial interactions in the cardiomyocyte, and 3) whether VAPB can be targeted to improve outcomes in heart disease. Collectively, these studies will have important translational applications as we will establish a novel role for VAPB in regulating healthy cardiac structure and function and establish a new therapeutic target to improve outcomes in heart disease.

column36: High dimensional protein characterization of glial tumor tissues and relevance to outcomes in immunotherapy clinical trials
column37: Gliomas account for ~80% of all malignant brain tumors. Glioblastoma (GBM) is a high-grade glioma and is the most common and lethal primary malignant central nervous system tumor. Despite an aggressive standard of care regimen of surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy, 3-year survival rate for GBM patients are just 10%. New therapies are desperately needed for patients diagnosed with gliomas. Harnessing the immune system to combat tumors have been increasingly successful in the last decade. However, more insights into the tumor immunology are needed to develop effective immunotherapies for glial tumors. Majority of the current research on developing immunotherapies depend on genomic analysis of bulk cell populations from tissue biopsies, which precludes distinguishing the role of different components (tumor-vs-immune cells) of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Single-cell methods have been instrumental in resolving some of these complexities. However, a major limitation of these studies is that they require tissue dissociation to isolate single cells, resulting in the loss of spatial information. Tumor/immune spatial relationships, as they pertain to immune infiltration and/or exclusion from the tumor, provide insights into disease stage and overall prognosis. Therefore, novel methodologies need to be developed to study tumor immunobiology while preserving spatial information to comprehensively understand the TME and interpret the data in the context of patient outcome and other clinical characteristics. In this study, I will be using a revolutionary imaging instrument "MIBI" for quantitative, high-resolution, simultaneous imaging of protein markers in glial tumor clinical biopsy tissues without disrupting spatial information. The data from this study will provide insights on tumor immunobiology at a single cell level while preserving spatial information and will provide unique/broad rationale the development of targeted immunotherapy.

column36: Identifying microglial-derived factors mediating tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease
column37: As the aging demographic grows, Alzheimer's disease has become the most common form of dementia in the elderly, occurring in 1 in 3 individuals over the age of 85 and affecting almost 50 million people worldwide. With longer life expectancies and an aging baby-boom generation, the number of Canadians living with Alzheimer's disease is expected to double to almost 1 million with an annual economic burden of over CAD$16.6 billion annually by the year 2031. The urgent need for improved diagnostic and treatment methods cannot be overstated given the profound social and economic impact of a surging Alzheimer's population. One of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease is the presence of thread-like structures within the brain, called tau tangles. While it is still unknown exactly why these lesions develop in the first place, scientists believe that tangles clog the brain's communication highways and prevent cells from carrying out normal and necessary functions, causing them to degenerate. New research suggests that the brain's immune system may be to blame. Under normal circumstances, specialized inflammatory cells, called microglia, are deployed to surveil the brain for foreign cells, like viruses and bacteria. It is thought that, during Alzheimer's disease, these microglia begin to engage in 'friendly fire', inadvertently exposing healthy brain cells to toxic substances meant for unknown intruders. The purpose of our research is to identify exactly which of these toxic substances causes tau tangles to form in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease. The results of our study will contribute to the development of novel drugs that can protect healthy cells from this bombardment of toxic molecules and prevent the assembly of tau tangles.

column36: A randomized controlled trial to test the effects of a maternal high-fat diet in pregnancy on the infant gut, inflammatory milieu, and adiposity
column37: The gut influences our risk for developing obesity. Studies completed in animals show that diets high in fat during pregnancy negatively impact the offspring gut. We hypothesize that mothers eating a high-fat diet will have increased inflammation which changes the infant gut and increases fat absorption and storage. We will collect an infant stool sample when the baby is 1-2 weeks old and maternal blood at ~28 and 25 weeks of pregnancy. We will then test whether the diversity of bacteria and inflammation in the infant gut are related to how much fat an infant has, and how much the amount of fat is due to inflammation in the mother. column36: Disparities in Reproductive Health Profiles between Black and White Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: Discovering Novel Roles for Nutritional and Genetic Factors
column37: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a highly common and complex hormonal disorder affecting women of all ethnicities. Women with PCOS (1) make excess male hormones called androgens (testosterone); (2) have absent/irregular menstrual periods and (3) have enlarged ovaries that contain an abundance of small follicles ("polycystic" appearance), all of which contribute to an increased risk for several adverse health outcomes such as infertility, obesity, diabetes, depression and certain cancers. Most research to date has focused on White women with PCOS, and it is unclear whether health risks are similar for women of other ethnicities. We recently showed that among women with PCOS in the US, non-Hispanic Black (NHB) women have higher cardio-metabolic issues (insulin and blood pressure) vs. non-Hispanic White (NHW) women. Whether these cardiometabolic abnormalities in NHB women contribute to an increased burden of reproductive health problems could not be addressed as reliable data were not available for NHB women. This proposed research will directly address this important knowledge gap for NHB women with PCOS and reveal any role of genes and nutrition to impact the relationship between cardiometabolic health and reproduction as part of working toward health equity in women with PCOS. We expect to show that increases in cardio-metabolic problems are associated with worse reproductive issues in NHB vs. NHW women with PCOS, given their interconnected disease pathways. Further, we predict that unique variations in genetic makeup together with aspects of nutritional status will relate to increases in reproductive problems in NHB women. By identifying genetic and nutritional factors that may work in concert to influence disparities in reproductive health, this research will form the basis for future studies that integrate nutrition into precision medicine to establish population-specific prevention and treatment strategies to improve the life-long health of women with PCOS.

column36: Collagen-like peptide-based implants as an alternative to donor corneal transplantation in high-risk corneal blindness
column37: The cornea is the transparent window that covers the anterior part of the eye and lets light rays in. Diseased corneas become opacified and lead to visual impairment, affecting over 27 million people globally. Corneal transplantation using cadaveric tissue is the only currently available treatment but is at high risk of immune rejection and failure in patients affected by severe pathologies, such as infection and trauma. Artificial corneal prostheses have higher success rates in these cases but often lead to vision-threatening complications, such as glaucoma. Most patients with high risk corneas are not prioritized for corneal grafting due to donor tissue shortage, have limited access to expensive prostheses, and remain untreated. Accessible effective alternatives are urgently needed. Our team developed corneal implants made from short collagen-like peptides that serve as scaffolds to be repopulated by patients' own cells, thus regenerating the cornea. Fully synthetic, cell-free, and incorporating an anti-inflammatory agent, these implants carry virtually no risk of immune rejection. Preclinical studies have confirmed their efficacy in recovering corneal transparency. We aim to test these implants in a first-in-human clinical trial. Implants will be manufactured and undergo quality control in a certified environment. After Health Canada approval, we will recruit ten patients with unilateral high-risk corneal blindness. Those receiving the implant will be compared to those undergoing traditional donor corneal transplantation. Patients will be followed over two years to determine implant safety and preliminary efficacy in rehabilitating vision. The study will allow to determine whether a larger clinical trial is justified. Collagen-peptide based implants may represent a solution for high-risk patients currently deemed untreatable. Their large-scale manufacturing could reduce the societal cost of blindness and alleviate the cornea donor tissue shortage worldwide.

column37: L'intelligence artificielle et les sciences omiques dans le combat contre l'infarctus du myocarde L'infarctus du myocarde (IM) resulte du blocage d'une artere du coeur, ce qui provoque la destruction d'une partie du muscle cardiaque. Les sciences omiques, qui etudient l'ensemble complexe des molecules qui composent le corps, ont permis de mieux comprendre les maladies, dont l'IM (1). Par ailleurs, des modeles issus de l'intelligence artificielle (IA) ont le potentiel de predire le risque de certaines maladies, dont l'IM. Toutefois, ces modeles sont difficiles a interpreter puisqu'ils fonctionnent comme des << boites noires >> : ils generent des predictions ou des recommandations, sans fournir d'explications ni de justifications (2). Or, l'interpretabilite biologique du modele est essentielle pour le developpement de ses applications cliniques. Quelques etudes font etat de l'interpretabilite biologique de methodes d'IA, mais tres peu concernent la sante. L'objectif de ce projet novateur est d'evaluer l'interpretabilite biologique d'une nouvelle methode d'IA qui utilise des donnees omiques pour predire le risque d'IM. Le projet compte 2000 participants, dont 1000 avec des antecedents d'IM et 1000 sans antecedents d'IM. Les donnees omiques et cliniques sont disponibles via la Biobanque de l'Institut de cardiologie de Montreal. La methode d'IA permettra d'integrer plusieurs donnees omiques afin de predire le risque d'IM. Des analyses seront realisees pour verifier que la methode est interpretable d'un point de vue biologique en lien avec le risque d'IM. Ce projet permettra de mieux predire le risque d'IM et, ultimement, d'aider au developpement de programmes de prevention et de traitement tout en ciblant les populations les plus a risque d'IM. L'interpretabilite biologique de la methode renforcera la confiance de la communaute medicale face a l'IA et favorisera son application en clinique. 1) Dehghan et al. PLoS ONE 2016. 2) Tobore et al. column36: Local protein synthesis at presynaptic terminals in learning and memory
column37: Long-term memory formation requires synthesis of new proteins, which are the basic biological building blocks and function executors. Perplexingly, the tiny connections between brain cells, known as synapses, are often located far away from the cell body where proteins are thought to be made. Recent findings, however, show that hundreds of proteins are produced on-demand locally at synapses, but precisely how this local source relates to information storage in health and disease is unknown. I aim to reveal how this local protein synthesis determines memory formation specifically at some synapse types but not others. Synapse dysregulation is a hallmark of disorders such as Alzheimer's, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Fragile X syndrome, which have increasingly been associated with abnormal activity in protein synthesis globally or even locally at synapses. For example, human clinical trials are already underway to treat Fragile X by targeting global protein synthesis, which would be the first-ever therapy of this disease. There is similarly the potential to treat Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and epilepsy. However, non-discriminatory targeting of global protein synthesis can disrupt normal cellular processes and result in serious side effects. This has prompted me to examine how highly localized protein synthesis at synapses underlies information storage, which is key to facilitate rational drug design to treat major neurological disorders with high specificity and efficacy. Because synapses are micrometer sized and difficult to study, this area is presently a blank on the map. To answer what local translation does and how it acts at synapses, I will combine multidisciplinary strategies such as electrophysiological, molecular, and optical approaches. The study I propose here will greatly expand our understanding of how local protein synthesis determines learning and memory in health as well as disease.

column36: Investigation of the utility of transcriptome sequencing for the resolution of unsolved rare genetic diseases
column37: Rare diseases (RDs) are typically genetic conditions caused by mutations in genes essential for one of the many complex reactions within our cells. Although by definition RDs affect less than 1 in 2000 individuals, cumulatively, they affect an estimated 1 in 12 Canadians. Numerous individuals affected by RDs have been evaluated by multiple medical professionals, but do not have a diagnosis. In addition to mutations that directly alter genes, RDs can be caused by mutations in an individual's DNA which result in changing the activity of that gene - this type of mutation is difficult to identify with DNA sequencing. This project will use a new technology to evaluate gene activity directly in patient cells compared to healthy cells, to determine which genes are impacted. It is anticipated that this approach will provide a diagnosis for many RD patients who have not been able to obtain a diagnosis from DNA-sequencing. This research is significant because the pace of novel RD gene discovery is slowing and new methods are needed to identify the remaining, yet undiscovered, RD mutations. By enabling accurate molecular diagnoses and guiding the identification of therapies, this will ultimately enhance patient care. Within the healthcare system, accurate diagnoses removes the need for further testing and unnecessary surveillance, thereby creating healthcare efficiencies. For patients, an accurate genetic diagnosis informs care and counseling, and facilitates targeted and effective treatments.

column37: Calcific aortic valve degeneration (CAVD) is the most common heart valve disease worldwide and is increasing exponentially in our aging population. Over time and with aging, the normal aortic valve undergoes structural changes leading to its thickening while maintaining normal function as assessed by echocardiography. This condition is known as aortic valve sclerosis (ASc). Epidemiologically and clinically, we know that within the population of patients with ASc, two clearly differentiated groups exist: one that will progress towards CAVD and another that will remain stable over time. Aortic Stenosis (AS) is the late-stage manifestation of CAVD, characterized by severe thickening and calcification of the aortic valve leading to pressure and flow changes measured by echocardiography. ASc is highly prevalent in the population; however, it remains unclear which ASc patients will progress towards the development of AS. The following proposal will provide the possibility of creating a new window for clinical observation to study CAVD. The currently available tools are unable to detect early, sub-clinical phases of the disease, or stratify patients, segregating the ones that will remain stable throughout time versus the ones that will progress to more severe stages of the disease. This project will help restage the early phase of aortic valve degeneration, ASc, providing the framework necessary, using novel imaging and molecular biology tools, to open the way for the potential development of non-invasive therapies to alter the progression of CAVD in the future.
