column36: Assessing Balance post-Concussion with Dual-Task Evaluation (ABCDE study): Derivation of a clinical biomarker to identify balance deficits in concussed adolescents
column37: Every year in Canadian emergency departments, 46,000 Canadian children are diagnosed with a concussion, constituting a significant public health concern. Determining when it is safe for children with concussion to return to sport is critical to prevent prolonged recovery or reinjury and international guidelines recommend balance testing as an essential part of concussion assessment and recovery tracking. Balance problems persist weeks beyond the initial injury when measured using advanced pressure sensor technology, however, balance tests available at the bedside often appear normal within days following a concussion. Clinicians relying on these tests might miss balance deficits and misclassify concussed children as uninjured or recovered and return them to sport prematurely, exposing them to serious consequences. Normal activities of living and sport require the simultaneous coordination of thinking and vision to maintain balance control. Combined skill testing is effective at detecting balance problems, but is unfeasible as a screening tool as it relies on expensive laboratory equipment and specialized training. My project will address this problem by combining existing clinical tests of thinking, vision, and balance to develop a novel, simple, no-cost, clinical test that better identifies balance deficits in concussed adolescents than the current standard. If balance deficits can be identified sooner, clinicians can target early interventions to improve prognosis and track recovery. By including this new balance measure into future editions of national and international guidelines, this research will have wide reach and improve the health of outcomes of children by enabling safe return-to-sport decisions following concussion.

column36: Bioinspired virus-like particles which cross the intestinal epithelia to deliver therapeutic cargo
column37: Oral delivery is the easiest way for patients to take drugs. Other routes, like intravenous injections, can be useful because they ensure that 100% of the drug is absorbed into the body. However, injections are painful and can require visits to the clinic and trained healthcare personnel to administer them. This decreases quality of life and decreases the likelihood that patients will stay committed to their treatment. Oral dosage forms, such as pills and drinkable liquids, are much easier and more comfortable for patients to take by themselves. Taking drugs orally is limited though since, for multiple reasons, the body does not easily absorb drugs through the stomach and intestines. This makes it difficult to design drugs which can be taken orally since it would require ingesting large amounts of drug, which can be toxic and expensive. One particularly difficult barrier to absorption is that drugs do not easily pass through the walls of the intestines. Cells of the intestinal wall have evolved to specifically uptake nutrients but exclude foreign substances. Some pathogens - such as cholera, HIV, and norovirus - can either disrupt the intestinal walls or travel through cells and escape the intestines. Particles that could mimic this ability and be loaded with drugs could enable orally administered drugs to be absorbed at levels high enough to sustainably treat disease. The proposed research will design particles, inspired by norovirus, which can pass through the cells of the intestinal wall and deliver their cargo. We will test these particles in human epithelial cells that we culture outside the body, and determine what kind of particles increase absorption the most. If successful, these particles could potentially be loaded with many kinds of drugs and enable their formulation into oral dosage forms which are easier for patients to take, which will increase their health and happiness.

column36: Electrophysiological Signature of Pediatric Concussion: A Pathway to Improving Clinical Diagnosis, Prognosis, and Management
column37: Concussions are a common brain injury in teenagers that can have negative effects on physical and mental health. There is no test or biological maker to clearly determine when a concussion has occurred or when a person has fully recovered after concussion, making it difficult for doctors to identify and treat concussions. Electroencephalography (EEG) is a tool that records electrical signals generated by the brain. EEG may be able to uncover a biological marker of concussion. Research shows that the brain's electrical signals change after a concussion, but these studies were mainly completed with adults in laboratories at a single test session. In order to determine if EEG may be helpful in identifying and managing youth concussion, researchers must study EEG in teenagers with concussion at important medical time points and compare EEG findings to results on common concussions tests used by medical professionals. We will have teenagers with concussion and healthy teenagers complete an EEG and common concussion tests three times over 6-months. Our goals in this study are to: 1) determine which EEG outcomes can accurately separate between teenagers with concussion and healthy teenagers; 2) describe the changes in EEG outcomes in healthy and concussed teenagers over the 6-month testing period; and 3) assess if EEG outcomes collected in teenagers early following concussion can predict who will have on-going symptoms one month after injury. These findings are the first step to improving the ways that medical professionals identify and treat concussion. This can keep teenagers with concussion safe by helping them avoid activities where there is a high-risk of sustaining a second concussion, creating better guidelines for returning to school and sporting activities, and providing individualized rehabilitation sooner after injury to reduce the negative effects of concussion.

column36: Role of the immune system in the transition from acute to chronic pain
column37: Chronic pain is a public health concern affecting over 20% of the world population, leading to physical and emotional distress, and to the loss of patients' autonomy and quality of life. Over the past decades, tremendous efforts have been made in the discovery of new pain targets and in the development of novel analgesics. Yet, the number of pharmacological treatment options for chronic pain management remains limited, and too often ineffective. In light of the ongoing opioid crisis, the need for novel pain medication is particularly urgent. Given the recurrent failures in drug development, we clearly need to delve deeper into the pathophysiology of chronic pain, to better understand the transition from acute to chronic pain and to identify new therapeutic targets. Our previous studies identified a population of immune cells infiltrating the peripheral nervous system responsible for the development of chronic pain. The aim of this project is therefore 1) to investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in the transition from acute pain to chronic pain within the immune system in order to 2) identify new therapeutic targets in the treatment of pain. The study is based on an animal model of neuropathic pain through which we wish to identify the molecular dynamics within different immune populations in the transition from acute pain to chronic neuropathic pain. We will also identify the impact of different peripheral immune populations on the molecular deregulation of sensory neurons following nerve injury. Finally, we wish to identify specifically the cell populations responsible for nervous hyperexcitability by inhibiting each of them and by measuring their impact on the development of chronic pain using behavioral pain tests.

column36: Evidence-based policy to help increase data sharing and improve hereditary cancer risk assessment
column37: Many aspects of our daily lives depend on vast amounts of data getting into the right hands, but we lack the evidence needed to create policies that actually result in data getting in the right hands. Many companies who produce data on cancer gene variants treat that data as their own property and therefore do not share it, but still benefit from also accessing public data despite not contributing any. The communities of users (scientists, clinicians, counselors, and the people contributing genomic variants) are diverse but share a common interest in using the best possible information to make very high stakes decisions, and to formulate policies to produce and govern a robust resource. Using multiple data sources, I will examine the data sharing and use over time and work with experts to develop polices based on this evidence. First, semi-structured interviews will be conducted with local senior surgical trainees and faculty who perform MIGS. Second, results from the first stage will be used to develop a web-based survey that will be disseminated nationally. Third, based on the survey results, second set of interviews will be conducted, to explain the findings of the survey. Significance: Results of this project will inform RC and residency programs on how to optimize the implementation of MIGS assessments.

column36: Assessing the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of artificial intelligence in lung cancer screening
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in Canada, resulting in more cancer-related deaths than breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer combined. Lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (CT) has been demonstrated in multiple large scale clinical trials to reduce mortality. However, due to the non-specific appearance of lung nodules on CT imaging, current lung cancer screening approaches have a high proportion of false positives resulting in many unnecessary investigations, increased patient anxiety, and significant healthcare costs. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been shown to have high accuracy for classifying lung nodules as malignant or benign on lung cancer screening CT exams, with strong potential to decrease the number of false positives. However, it is unclear how output from AI algorithms can be used to direct clinical decision making. Additionally, health outcomes and downstream costs relating to the use of AI have not been assessed, limiting clinical translation of this technology. This research will address these knowledge gaps by using a well-validated simulation model to assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of lung nodule management strategies using AI to guide lung nodule management in lung cancer screening programs. This research will provide key evidence for health system leaders and policy makers to potentially support the implementation of AI in lung cancer screening, leading to earlier diagnoses of lung cancer, reduced lung cancer mortality, and reduced healthcare costs. Reducing costs associated with lung cancer screening with the use of AI may enable additional lung cancer screening programs to be developed in Canada, increasing access to screening for Canadians. The research methodology developed through this work, uniquely at the intersection of AI and health services research, will provide a framework for investigating effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of AI in other important clinical domains.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer in the world. In spite of detailed understanding of its mutational progression and established therapies, the average 5-year survival rate of all CRC patients is 65% in Canada. The mechanisms that control the fate of cells at normal levels are known to be very complex and still poorly understood. However, it is clear that colorectal cancer (CRC) in humans involves a perturbation of this control system that results in the production of too many cells that cannot function properly. A key player in this control system is the DNA inside each cell and certain proteins that are bound to it to form a complex referred to as chromatin. The goal of this proposal is to understand how the composition of the chromatin of normal intestinal stem cell alters in CRC. column36: Evaluation de l'utilisation des membres superieurs et de l'influence des deficits somatosensoriels sur la performance motrice chez l'adulte ayant une paralysie cerebrale
column37: Les personnes ayant la paralysie cerebrale presentent des difficultes motrices (ex. diminution de la force) et sensorielles (ex. diminution de la sensibilite au toucher) qui limitent leur participation dans les activites de la vie de tous les jours. Ces difficultes s'expliquent par des atteintes predominantes d'un cote du corps, mais egalement par des deficits dans l'utilisation coordonnee des deux bras. Les interventions effectuees avec la clientele ciblent autant l'utilisation d'un bras que les deux en simultane afin de maximiser l'autonomie. Cependant, l'evaluation objective de l'utilisation reelle du bras atteint demeure un defi. Les mesures effectuees recueillent la perception des patients de leur capacite a realiser les taches de la vie quotidiennes ou encore la capacite de chacun des bras individuellement ce qui n'est pas representatif de l'utilisation coordonnee des deux bras. De plus, ces mesures ne considerent pas l'apport d'autres difficultes, telles que les deficits sensoriels, dans les difficultes observees au quotidien. Le developpement de technologies dans les dernieres annees (systeme robotise et capteurs sans-fil) est prometteur afin de pouvoir pallier ce manque. L'objectif du present projet est d'evaluer la pertinence de taches robotisees pour evaluer la performance des deux bras en les comparant a des mesures cliniques existantes et des mesures en milieu reel. Deux seances d'evaluation sont prevues pour realiser ce projet. Lors de la premiere, des taches motrices seront effectuees a l'aide d'un systeme robotise, en plus d'evaluations cliniques des deux bras. Lors de la seconde, un systeme de capteurs sera utilise pour quantifier l'utilisation du membre atteint dans des taches de la vie de tous les jours (ex. cuisiner). Ces donnees seront comparees afin de mieux comprendre le fonctionnement moteur et sensoriel des personnes presentant une paralysie cerebrale, permettant ainsi d'offrir des interventions de readaptation plus adaptees a leurs besoins.

column36: The role of motherhood on neural stem cells physiology
column37: Motherhood is a period of women's life covering both pregnancy and postnatal period. This period is accompanied by several adjustments, both at the hormonal and structural levels in the brain. These changes will ultimately prepare the mother to care for her newborn infant(s). Although clearly identified, it remains for now impossible to investigate the impact of such functional modifications at the single cell level. During adulthood, the brain preserves a plastic ability and can partly regenerate, although at some specific brain locations, through a process of adult neurogenesis. The adult neurogenesis, which results in the production of new neuronal cells from stem cells, is particularly widespread in the olfactory bulb of rodents. Notably, the subventricular zone, located at the border of the lateral ventricles, gives rise daily to thousands of new cells. Previous studies have correlated adult neurogenesis levels in the SVZ, with maternal behavior and motherhood. However, the underlying mechanisms linking these processes are unclear. It is also not known if and how motherhood directly affects stem cells' activation and dynamics of their division. Here, using advanced in vivo imaging tools allowing to monitor stem cells division in freely behaving mice, I will first investigate the impact of motherhood on the regulation of neural stem cells activation and division. I will then study the impact of different brain regions on stem cells physiology through viral tools and light-induced modulation of these regions in vivo. Overall, this project will allow to understand the role of maternal behavior on stem cells physiology.

column36: High-Throughput Heart-on-a-Chip Platform for Studies of SARS-CoV-2 Induced Myocardial Injury
column37: Recent study reported that 78% of the patients recovered from COVID-19 have cardiac involvement and 60% of the patients have ongoing myocardial inflammation based on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. However, the direct contribution of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the beating cells types of the heart, cardiomyocytes, versus supporting cells that makeup the blood vessels and the matrix as well as immune cells homing to the heart after the infection are not well understood. Human stem cell derived heart-on-a-chip models afford the most direct and efficient route for answering these questions. My preliminary data collected in the CL3 facility demonstrate profound and progressive loss of contractile ability in my heart-on-a-chip platform upon SARS-CoV-2 infection. Stem cell based heart-on-a-chip model is additionally unique as it enables us to systematically study infection on different cell types that make up the heart, an experiment that is not possible in vivo. I will first scale up the production of the heart-on-a-chip platform using 3D printing. I will situate this platform in a 24 well plate, a setting that is suitable for working in biohazard level 3 facility. After infecting the human heart tissue with SARS-CoV-2, I will non-invasively measure how the contractile force changes with time. At the same time, I can collect culture media and determine the extent of inflammation. Through electron microscopy, I will visualize the virus in the human heart tissue. Therapies for covid19 infected heart currently do not exist. I hypothesize that extracellular vesicles derived from healthy cells could represent a viable biological therapy. These consist of a rich mixture of micro RNAs and proteins that are known to be able to protect the heart in other settings, such as loss of oxygen. I will isolate these EVs from healthy cells and apply them to the infected heart-on-a-chip to study preservation of beating function and subsequent improvement.

column36: The mechanism of ADAR1 in regulating cancer immune evasion
column37: The immune system protects the body against infectious diseases, as well as inherent diseases such as cancer. The immune system is the first line of defense charged to eliminate cancer cells from the body. However, cancer has evolved mechanisms to evade the immune system, some of which have been exposed and leveraged with powerful immunotherapies. Despite the incredible advances made with new immunotherapies in the past two decades, the majority of cancers remain refractory to immunotherapy through intrinsic and acquired genetic and/or epigenetic mechanisms of resistance. Our understanding of the genes and pathways that program cancer cells to evade the immune system is very limited. In other words, the inventory of secret weapons that cancer cells harbour against the immune system still needs to be fully catalogued. Identifying cancer intrinsic immune invasion genes and the mechanism of action by which these genes help cancer cells evade the immune system will uncover the Achilles heel of cancer and find new ways to weaken cancers against the immune system and immunotherapy. Using state-of-the-art technologies in genetics including systematic genome-wide CRISPR screening, as well as a cutting edge cost-effective single-cell sequencing approach, our lab has identified key genes that help cancer cells evade tumor infiltrating immune cells. One such gene is Adar, which helps cancer cells resist the immune system. It is currently not known how the Adar gene contributes to resistance to immunotherapy; however, preliminary results by our group and others suggest that Adar is involved in innate immunity. The goal of my project is to study how ADAR regulates cancer immune evasion and which molecular pathways synergize with ADAR activity to enhance immunotherapy. In this project, in collaboration with Agios pharmaceuticals company, we also aim to translate our findings to clinical medicine by developing new anti-cancer treatments based on targeting ADAR-mediated pathways.

column36: The association between COVID-19-related attitudes, concerns and behaviours in relation to Government policies (the iCARE Study): Optimising policy and communication strategies to improve health, economic and quality of life outcomes throughout the pandemic.
column37: COVID-19 has caused a global public health emergency. While waiting for a vaccine, governments are using a number of policies that focus on changing people behaviour to stop the spread of the virus. However, for these policies to work and stop the spread of COVID-19 and improve the economy, people need to actually do (adhere to) the recommendations. For people to adhere to these policies they need: 1) to be aware of the policies; 2) see the policies as important; and 3) feel able to actually do the things they are being asked to do. All of these 3 things are influenced by where people are from, who they are, their current health, and the environment around them. Unfortunately, policies have changed over time and the exact polices and how people are told about the policies (messaging) varies greatly between and within countries. This has led to uncertainty among people about what is behind the government decisions and confusion about which policies to follow. The iCARE Study is a global survey that captures data on peoples' awareness, attitudes, and behaviours in relation to COVID-19 policies. We also ask how the pandemic is impacting peoples' physical and mental health, economic situation, and quality of life. In addition to over 70,000 survey responses, we collect data on number of cases and deaths, information about policies across different countries, and how people are moving about in their countries. These data will be linked and analysed together to understand which government policies are (or are not) influencing population behaviour, and in whom these policies are most or least effective. Of note, iCARE study has significant impact, and has been working directly with the government of Canada (supervisor Lavoie is on federal COVID-19 advisory board), as well as the governments of Ireland and Australia.

column36: Non-intrusive monitoring of fluid congestion and exercise capacity for predicting heart failure outcomes
column37: Heart failure is the fastest growing cardiovascular disease, affecting 1 in 5 Canadians over the age of 40, with an average life expectancy of only 2 years. Heart failure describes a heart that no longer effectively pumps blood, which causes fluid buildup in the lungs and body (such as arms and legs), making it difficult to take in and deliver oxygen at the cellular level. Common symptoms are breathlessness and gradual decrease in exercise ability, making it difficult to engage in daily activities and maintain independence. An important part of individualized treatment plans is clinically managing fluid levels, but this requires careful monitoring that is invasive. Assessing pressure in the lungs for remote daily monitoring can help reduce hospital readmission by over 30%, but requires surgically inserting a probe into the central lung arteries. Recently, new wearable technologies powered by artificial intelligence have been developed to monitor fluid levels and the body's response to activity, providing new non-intrusive ways to monitor physiological changes inside and out of the clinic. This study seeks to determine if (1) non-invasive fluid monitoring will provide indications of treatment efficacy in critical care; and (2) remote monitoring of fluid and activity levels provide early warning signs and predict hospital readmission. This study will take place at University Health Network in the healthcare research hub of Toronto. Heart failure participants will be recruited with cardiologists at Peter Munk Cardiac Centre and Mount Sinai Hospital. The non-intrusive wearable technologies will be compared against invasive gold standard monitoring performed by partnering cardiologists. The proposed study will be one of the first to assess new wearable technology innovations for heart failure management, and will seek to further explore the role between physiological monitoring and early interventions for reducing hospital stay duration and readmission.

column36: Development of evidence-based reference intervals (RIs) for variety of clinical biomarkers in older adults
column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is one of the most common and deadly hematologic malignancies. AML treatment results in very poor outcomes, even with aggressive therapy such as intensive induction chemotherapy. There is therefore a dire need for new and more effective treatments. In this project, I will explore blocking two mitochondrial genes (PNPT1 and SUV3) as new therapeutic strategies. These genes are involved in multiple RNA processing functions in the mitochondria. My preliminary data shows that the encoded proteins are highly expressed in most AML cell lines and patient samples, but expressed at very low levels in normal blood cells. I have also shown that blocking their expression using genetic approaches preferentially kills leukemia cells over normal cells. I now intend to determine the specific mechanism(s) by which PNPT1 and SUV3 inhibition kills leukemia cells. I will also investigate the impact of inhibiting these proteins on mitochondrial structure and function. Finally, I will determine the impact of PNPT1 and SUV3 inhibition on immune recognition of AML cells. In summary, this project will validate and mechanistically elucidate a potential novel therapeutic strategy for a subset of AML.

column36: Discerning cell types and intercellular communication in the normal and atherosclerotic mouse artery intima.
column37: Atherosclerosis is a condition defined by unresolved inflammation in the major arteries. A primary indicator for cardiovascular disease is high cholesterol, but despite effective cholesterol-lowering therapies it remains the principal cause of death in our society. Atherosclerosis develops silently for decades before causing heart attacks and strokes. My research focuses on cells and genes that participate in atherosclerosis. Currently, there are no therapies targeting cells in the artery wall to inhibit the formation and progression of atherosclerosis. These therapies would benefit patients with risk factors (ie/ high cholesterol). Myeloid cells (MCs) are white blood cells and important components of the immune system. MCs are found in the inner artery wall of healthy humans and animals, under a barrier of cells called endothelial cells (ECs). MCs are found specifically in areas where atherosclerosis develops. MCs in mice with high cholesterol engulf lipid and become "foam cells". This is the first step in the formation of atherosclerosis, and is followed by significant accumulation of foam cells within the artery wall. Recently, our group discovered a novel protective process by which MCs will leave the artery wall in response to inflammation. However, engulfed lipid blocks MC exit. We have also found new cells in artery which require investigation, as their role is disease is unknown. We believe that the MCs and ECs communicate with each other within the artery wall and that elevated cholesterol is disrupting this communication and preventing MCs from leaving the artery. My goal is to understand how cells communicate with each other under normal conditions and how cholesterol, foam cells, and novel cells can alter the normal signals. This is an important endeavor since we believe that in the future we can overcome these inhibitory mechanisms so that accumulated lipid can be removed from the artery wall by exiting lipid-loaded foam cells.

column36: Facilitating Communication Through a Multisensory Virtual Reality Intervention for Persons with Dementia
column37: According to the World Health Organization, approximately 50 million people around the globe are currently living with dementia, and this number is expected to rise in the coming years. In Canada, the majority of these individuals still live at home and are cared for by their family members. Despite extensive research revealing that dementia negatively affects the physical and mental health of the person diagnosed and their family caregivers, little is known about the value of interventions that are focused on both parties. The goal of the proposed research is to improve interpersonal interaction through a Virtual Reality (VR) intervention. In recent years, VR systems have become increasingly popular for persons with dementia as they allow the individual to escape to alternative realities, helping to improve physical health, mood, and reduce social isolation. The proposed study will design and implement a multisensory VR intervention that utilizes immersive visual scenes and auditory sounds with the goal to facilitate communication between persons with dementia and those who care for them. This could result in better quality of life and well-being for both the persons diagnosed and their family caregivers. Further, I will explore various ways that this technology can be improved to enhance the immersive experience for this population. This will be accomplished by presenting different scenarios and by monitoring both the quality of communication and real time reactions to the VR experience during the course of the entire intervention. The findings will provide valuable insight into the effectiveness of VR interventions and will also inform the design of future technologies for persons with dementia. Importantly, this work will contribute to efforts aimed at reducing the negative consequences of dementia for the persons diagnosed, their family caregivers, the Canadian health care system, and the national economy.

column36: Directional neural network connectivity in multiple sclerosis pain: a dynamic causal modelling approach using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging and magnetoencephalography
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the nervous system. Chronic pain is a debilitating symptom that occurs in approximately 50% of MS patients and has a severe impact on quality of life. It is important to understand the brain mechanisms underlying MS pain so that better treatments can be developed. There have been recent advancements in our understanding of how the brain functions in patients with MS pain. Researchers have used functional neuroimaging technologies to identify that MS pain is associated with changes in the functioning of a network of brain regions known as the "dynamic pain connectome". It is likely that altered communication throughout this network contributes to MS pain. However, analysis techniques used in these studies are unable to determine causality - that is, how individual regions within the dynamic pain connectome influence one another to ultimately generate pain. Recently, a new technique has been developed allowing researchers to model causal relationships within brain networks. The current project aims to employ this technique and functional neuroimaging to model causal relationships throughout the dynamic pain connectome in MS pain patients. We will explore whether MS pain patients differ from healthy individuals in the strength of causal connections throughout the pain network. We also aim to extend the study to patients with other forms of chronic pain, such as pain resulting from nerve injury, to explore if the findings in MS pain are generalizable to other pain conditions. We propose that MS pain, and chronic pain in general, will be associated with altered connections between specific brain regions that drive abnormal communication throughout the dynamic pain connectome. If we determine the causal nature of communication throughout the brain, and its deficits in chronic pain, this may allow for a region- or connection-specific targeted approach to the treatment of pain - both in MS and in other pain conditions.

column37: Diabetes is a major issue in Canada. Metformin is the most widely used prescribed medication for people with type II diabetes and obesity. Metformin lowers blood glucose levels and body weight in humans and animals with diabetes and obesity, but the molecular target(s) of metformin action in the body remains unclear. Both the small intestine and the liver have been implicated to mediate metformin to lower blood glucose levels and body weight. Using rodent models of obesity and type II diabetes, we will characterize novel mechanism in the small intestine, liver, and brain that is necessary for metformin to lower weight and blood glucose levels. Additionally, we will evaluate whether activating these pathways will lower food intake and body weight as well as blood glucose levels. Our results may help to uncover novel therapeutic targets in the small intestine, liver, and brain for obesity and type II diabetes.

column36: Deconvolving the cistrome of colon cancer metastasis using deep learning to integrate multi-modal single-cell genomics data
column37: Introduction: Colon cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canada. Metastatic recurrence remains the greatest cause of death for colon cancer patients. The heterogeneous nature of these tumours complicates identifying biological pathways of recurrence. Only recent advances in genomics have allowed us to study tumour transcriptome at the single-cell resolution and unravel tumour heterogeneity. The long but incomplete list of signature transcripts, however, fails to provide plausible upstream regulators. We propose a novel algorithm using deep learning to integrate single cell transcriptome with epigenome measurements and identify targetable upstream regulators of metastatic colon cancer. Methods: The Goodarzi lab has developed an experimental setup that effectively models colon cancer metastasis in mouse models. They injected poorly metastatic parental cells into immunocompromised mice and selected for highly metastatic derivatives. They performed single-cell RNA-seq to identify the transcripts at each of the cells within these tumours. They also performed ATAC-seq to assess the chromatin accessibility of these tumours. I developed a deep-learning based algorithm to integrate these two modalities and identify epigenomic signatures of metastatic tumour cells. I will perform regulatory network analysis to identify the upstream regulators which regulate these metastatic programs. Using publicly available epigenomics and pharmacogenomics datasets, I will investigate the relevance of these targetable regulators to metastatic pathways. I will also perform gene activation and silencing experiments to validate the role of these factors in mouse models. Conclusion: This project brings together the state-of-the-art from experimental models, single-cell genomics, and machine learning to identify potential therapeutic targets for a devastating disease; the metastatic colon cancer.

column36: Chemotherapy, nutrition, and intestinal microbiota: deciphering the interplay underlying inflammation, cardiometabolic disease and gastrointestinal complications in pediatric cancers
column37: Approximately 4,715 new cases of childhood cancers are diagnosed each year in Canada. The treatment of these patients with chemotherapy often causes significant side effects. These include vomiting, diarrhea, and severe infections. Bacteria colonizing the gut, also known as intestinal microbiota, play a major role in the health of individuals. The modification of the gut microbiota profile (by nutrition, antibiotics, or other chemical agents) can lead to beneficial or adverse effects on health status, especially on metabolic status (obesity, diabetes) depending on the bacteria that survive the treatment. It has been proposed that chemotherapy changes the gut microbiota which in turn may modulate the response to therapy and side effects of cancer treatments. However, clinical studies are lacking to prove this concept in children. We propose that chemotherapy can alter gut bacteria in children, and that specific profiles are associated with negative side effects of treatments, response to therapy, and metabolic complications. To explore this new line of research, we have developed an innovative study that will be conducted at the Sainte-Justine UHC, in Montreal, and will combine clinical and fundamental research. We will document the diet and treatments of 40 patients undergoing cancer therapy and will collect blood and stool samples. We will use advanced molecular and bioinformatic technologies to study the impact of chemotherapeutic treatments on the composition of the gut microbiota in relation to markers of health. Based on our experience in clinical studies in pediatric cancers, the renowned Sainte-Justine UHC infrastructure, and fruitful collaborations with many quality partners, we believe that the results generated will bring unprecedented insights to this field of research. We hope the resulting discoveries will contribute to improve patient care, counter the adverse side effects of chemotherapy, and reduce the suffering of children with cancers.

column36: Predictors of the development of substance use disorders in young people
column37: One in five Canadians will experience a substance use disorder in their lifetime, resulting in significant personal, social, and economic costs. Research is needed to identify factors that contribute to and protect against the development of such disorders. Once risk and protective factors are identified, they can be used to inform effective prevention and early intervention programs for at-risk youth. Early onset substance use (<16 years of age) is a significant risk factor for the development of substance use disorders later in life. However, not all individuals who initiate substance use early will develop a substance use disorder. Instead, the relationship between early onset substance use and the development of substance use disorders is likely affected by other personal, social, and environmental factors. However, research is yet to examine how these factors combine with early onset substance use in the development of substance use patterns across adolescence and into early adulthood, a vital time for the development of substance use disorders. The present project will use data collected across two cohorts of the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development (QLSCD) followed from birth to early adulthood (21+ years of data), to examine trajectories of substance use across youth and their association with problem substance use in early adulthood. Further, this project will examine how behavioural problems, mental health symptoms, familial history of substance use, family conflict, and personality combine with early onset substance use in the development of problematic substance use in early adulthood. Identifying the combination of risk factors most likely to contribute to problematic substance use will aid the development and refinement of existing prevention and early intervention programs for at-risk young people, with the ultimate goal of decreasing the likelihood that these individuals go on to develop a substance use disorder.

column37: The development of the fetal brain during pregnancy is a carefully regulated but highly vulnerable process. Maternal infections during the second trimester of pregnancy are strongly associated with increased risk of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders in offspring. The work proposed in this application seeks to understand the mechanisms by which maternal inflammation during pregnancy rewires fetal brain development, and specifically to investigate why there are differences in susceptibility between male and female offspring. To date, I have discovered that maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy is associated with autism-like behavior selectively in male mice. I found that MIA triggers the activation of a signaling cascade - the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) - only in the male fetal brain, which profoundly alters the process of translating genes into proteins (mRNA translation). However, we do not understand why female offspring are resilient to intrauterine inflammation, and conversely, why male offspring are more vulnerable. The proposed work will expand on our earlier findings in two ways: (1) I will characterize changes in neural stem cell (NSC) pools in response to MIA in male and female offspring. Disruption of NSC proliferation and differentiation could contribute to abnormal cortical development and circuit mis-wiring. (2) I will investigate how modifications to RNA molecules - the 'epitranscriptome' - may contribute to sex-specific vulnerability to maternal inflammation. I have already discovered changes in many of the molecules that regulate the epitranscriptome in the fetal brain exposed to MIA. Therefore, I hypothesize that the stress-mediated modification of RNA in the fetal brain is critical to the disruption in RNA translation and fetal neurodevelopment. In total, the proposed work will characterize novel mechanisms by which adverse early life experience re-programs neurodevelopment in a sex-dependent manner.

column36: Abnormal persistence of Cajal-Retzius cells and seizure susceptibility
column37: Epilepsy affects about 1 in 200 children and adolescents in Canada. Treatment of epilepsy presents a complex challenge because it is caused by vastly different mechanisms that perturb the brain circuitry. As a result, 30%-40% of epilepsy patients do not respond to drug treatments. Children and youth with uncontrollable epilepsy are not only at a higher risk of mortality but also more likely to have learning disabilities, depression, and anxiety, leading to reduction in quality of life. Further insight into the etiology of treatment-resistant epilepsy is needed to develop effective therapies for children and youth suffering from this devastating neurological condition. An abnormally large number of Cajal-Retzius cells-a type nerve cells that are mostly found in the brain during embryonic development-have been reported in cut-out brain tissues from patients undergoing epilepsy surgery. This suggests a role of Cajal-Retzius cells in difficult-to-treat epilepsy. But how Cajal-Retzius cells constitute an important element in the pathogenic cascade of epilepsy is unknown. Addressing this question has proven challenging, partly due to the lack of animal models that mimic the human pathology of abnormal Cajal-Retzius cell persistence. Here, we have developed a unique mouse model with an abnormally high number of Cajal-Retzius cells. Armed with this mouse model, we ask: 1)What causes Cajal-Retzius cell to abnormally persist in the postnatal/juvenile brain? 2)How does abnormal Cajal-Retzius cell persistence contribute to seizure susceptibility? We design a set of experiments to investigate how Cajal-Retzius cell death is regulated. We will determine whether abnormal Cajal-Retzius cell persistence, and therefore their abnormal activity, contributes to increased seizure susceptibility.

column36: A proposal to evaluate safer supply pilot programs in Canada
column37: Safer (or 'safe') supply is defined as a legal and regulated supply of drugs with mind/body altering properties that traditionally have been accessible only through the illicit drug market. Safer supply programs have been established in Canada primarily to reduce overdose caused by the unregulated ("street") drug supply, which is saturated with high-potency opioids (e.g., fentanyl) and potentially toxic adulterants (e.g., etizolam). Beginning in 2019, Health Canada has been funding a growing number of safer supply pilot projects (SSPPs). SSPPs provide standard dose pharmaceutical-grade opioid formulations via dispensation to individuals. These programs appear beneficial but have yet to be subject to systematic evaluation. Understanding how they are organized, the makeup of their clients, and their impact on overdose and other drug-related outcomes is critical to developing an effective response to the opioid overdose epidemic. We propose an implementation science approach that will a) assess SSPP organizational structures, delivery models, and the contexts in which they are being implemented; b) identify the makeup of their clients and assess how SSPPs are impacting client health across distinct settings, and c) track how these programs evolve, particularly in light of the impact of disruptions from COVID-19.

column36: Therapeutic Targeting a Shared Inflammation Pathway in the Lung and Kidney
column37: Patients that are very sick and in the intensive care unit (critical illness) often develop problems with their lungs and kidneys. These problems are frequently due to excessive inflammation which can damage these organs in the short term leading to lung and kidney failure. These patients often require supportive treatments such as dialysis or mechanical ventilation. In patients who survive their illness, lung and kidney injury experienced in the intensive care unit can often result in long term (chronic) lung and kidney disease.Thus, the consequences of surviving a critical illness can remain with patients for their lifetime, resulting in disability, reduced quality of life and an increased burden on the healthcare system. This proposal will test whether a new class of drugs developed at the University of Calgary can limit short term lung and kidney injury during critical illness by blocking a new mechanism of inflammation in these organs. Studies will also assess the best way to introduce these new drugs into patients in the intensive care unit. Research in this proposal will help advance these new drugs into clinical trials in humans aimed at preventing short term lung and kidney injury during critical illness to reduce the risk of long term disability from chronic lung and kidney disease.

column36: Allogeneic thymus-derived Tregs to prevent chronic inflammation in transplantation.
column37: A process called immune tolerance allows the immune system to fend off dangerous foreign substances yet leave the body's own tissues untouched. When immune tolerance fails, autoimmune diseases and/or chronic inflammation occur. There are no medications that promote or replicate immune tolerance. This is particularly problematic for transplant recipients, whose immune systems must be suppressed with medications to prevent rejection. As a result, transplant recipients must live with impaired immune tolerance and chronic inflammation. Our goal is to move beyond symptom management and find long-term solutions. We have been working towards this goal by developing a therapy that takes advantage of a specialized type of white blood cell, called regulatory T cells, or Tregs, which suppress undesired immune responses and promote the formation of an appropriately balanced immune system. Tregs are rare in circulating blood, but we have shown that an organ called the thymus (which is routinely removed and discarded during heart surgery) is an abundant source of easily-isolated, pure Tregs. We have shown that thymus Tregs have beneficial effects in mouse models of transplantation, and now, we aim to conduct a clinical trial to determine if thymus Tregs are a safe and effective way to prevent immune complications after bone marrow transplantation. Data from this proposal will show how to best design the trial and how to best match donor thymus Tregs to the patient. Once we establish safety and effectiveness of thymus Tregs in the context of transplantation, we will be able to extend off-the-shelf Treg therapy to many other inflammatory diseases.

column36: Regulatory Natural Killer Cell Treatment in Chronic Graft-versus-Host Disease and Solid Organ Transplantation Chronic Rejection
column37: Bone marrow and organ transplantation is often the only cure for a number of life threatening diseases. Unfortunately, chronic rejection is a possible outcome for 10-70% of transplants. Patients that receive a bone marrow transplant can develop life-long rejection of many organs in their body by the immune system that is part of the transplanted bone marrow. This chronic immune rejection by the transplanted bone marrow is called chronic graft-versus-host-disease (cGvHD). In our work with patients, who have received bone marrow transplants, we found that cGvHD is far less likely to develop in patients that have a higher number of a specific type of immune cells called a regulatory natural killer cells (NKregs). Our goal is to determine whether NKregs can be isolated from either healthy bone marrow transplant donors or kidney transplant recipients and grown in a lab to increase their numbers, and then used as a therapy to prevent transplant rejection. In this research, we will develop protocols to isolate and grow human NKregs in the lab, and test whether administering NKregs, alone or in combination with a new engineered drug that can cause them to expand in the blood, can prevent transplant rejection. If successful, we will have developed a new understanding of how NKregs extend the life of transplanted tissue and improve the long term quality of life and learn the best way to expand NKregs for patient use, leaving us well-poised for clinical trials.

column36: Pro-Resolving Inflammatory Mediators in Neurovascular Gains in Aerobic Training (PRIMiNG-AT)
column37: Exercise holds potential to reduce inflammation and slow brain aging; however, these effects are highly variable in people with age related inflammatory comorbidities like cardiovascular disease or diabetes. With aging, we have identified changes in the way the body processes good fats from diet, limiting their anti-inflammatory benefits. This is due to an enzyme, soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH), that breaks down good fats. Excess sEH renders fat metabolism less effective at controlling inflammation. Normally, this enzyme pathway is involved in the body's response to exercise, but in older people with chronic low-grade inflammation, it might become a problem. We will follow people with diabetes or heart disease over 6 months of exercise and measure sEH metabolites in their blood before beginning and after 3 and 6 months. We hypothesize that people who have more sEH metabolites in their blood will have smaller cognitive benefits of exercise over time. Furthermore, we hypothesize that sEH metabolites will be related to damage of the brain's smallest blood vessels, their ability to regulate blood flow, and less blood supply to the brain and peripheral tissues. If this is true, the benefits of exercise might be optimized for people with heart disease or diabetes in future studies by combining exercise interventions with a drug that blocks sEH to protect the brain's small vessels. This study will determine for which of these populations that drug might be beneficial.

column36: IMplementing Predictive Analytics towards efficient COPD Treatments (IMPACT)
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) affects the lives of millions of Canadians. Patients with COPD often experience 'lung attacks' (worsening of symptoms, also known as exacerbations). Besides childbirth, a COPD lung attack is the number one reason for being hospitalized in Canada. Current COPD treatment guidelines are based on treating the "average patient". Previous research has shown that clinical prediction tools that consider each patient's unique characteristics can significantly improve the accuracy of treatment decisions. It is also known that proper communication of risks and benefits of treatments can help patients make better decisions about their health. The use of sophisticated clinical prediction tools has become easier with the availability of Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which now routinely collect a lot of relevant information about each patient. We propose to tap into the power EHR to improve the prediction of lung attacks and communication of risk to patients. This is a timely project because major health providers in British Columbia will soon be using a linked EHR system. In this project, we will validate a recently developed lung attack prediction tool for integration within EHRs. We will work with patients, doctors, and health administrators to integrate the tool into clinical practice such that it is easy to use for doctors and is understandable to patients. We will conduct a randomized clinical trial of the resulting shared decision-making tool at two major hospitals, to examine how it impacts prescription patterns and patient-reported and clinical outcomes. We will perform an economic evaluation to explore the 'value for money' potential of this tool. This research has the potential to significantly improve the care for COPD patients. By connecting researchers, patients, care providers, and health administrators, this team project can open the door for the use of clinical prediction tools for many other health conditions.

column36: Integrated Precision Medicine Technology and Approach for Optimal Drug Therapy for Canadians
column37: Patients who are diagnosed with cancer face a daunting journey that starts with anxiety and uncertainty associated with the diagnosis as well as having to deal with important but sometime painful and grueling treatments including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. There is a need for reducing patient suffering by individualizing medication dosing and selection for the treatment of pain, depression, and cancer treatment side-effects. After a decade of treating thousands of patients, we have garnered unique insights relating to what works and does not work when implementing Precision Medicine-based patient care. Our team recently created an advanced eHealth solution that can directly interact with an existing hospital electronic medical record (EMR) system to generate clinically meaningful and actionable drug dosing and selection information in real- time. A unique feature of our system is it includes not only pharmacogenetic information, but also drug-drug interactions risk. In this application, we will provide drug dosing and selection recommendations for pain medications, antidepressants, and certain chemotherapy drugs used for cancer patients, from the beginning of their diagnosis until the end of treatment period. We will engage patients and include patient perspectives and empower patients to participate in their care. Patient perspectives will be captured using the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System. We will also conduct health economic evaluation. Importantly, we will implement our eHealth solution in partnership with treating oncologists, cancer patients, our hospital, The Medical Letter, an internationally recognized source for drug interactions risk assessment, as well as Ivey School of Business at Western.

column36: The Genetics Navigator: A novel digital platform for delivering personalized genetic services
column37: Genomic sequencing (GS) is a test that scans a person's genetic code to identify changes that may be disease-causing. GS is increasingly being used for patient care as it improves diagnosis and health outcomes. In spite of these benefits, GS is a complex and costly health service. This results in unequal access, increased wait times and inconsistencies in care. The use of eHealth tools to support GS delivery can result in a better patient experience and reduced distress associated with waiting for results and empower patients to receive and act on medical results. Our study will develop a patient centred eHealth platform to deliver GS services and then evaluate its effectiveness compared to usual care. The platform will include a conversational chatbot and innovative strategies for pre-and post-test genetic counselling and result reporting. First, we will identify the key components of this novel platform with end-users and build the chatbot to provide educational, decisional and emotional support to patients. We will then conduct usability testing with a pan-Canadian sample of patients and health care providers to ensure the platform is patient-centred and optimized for a range of contexts. Next, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial, to understand if our eHealth platform is better than usual care. Patients undergoing GS will be randomly assigned to receive either our eHealth platform or usual care that consists of meeting with genetics providers in-person or over the phone. The outcomes include patients' distress, experience, satisfaction, empowerment, knowledge, perceived utility, behaviour change, and cost effectiveness. This study represents a significant advance in personalized health by developing a novel, comprehensive eHealth platform to improve genetic service delivery, accessibility, patient experiences, and patient outcomes. The shift to virtual care during the COVID-19 pandemic underscores the critical importance of this platform.

column36: The Canadian Collaboration for Complex Care: Innovations for optimal and appropriate care for all
column37: By the age of 65, half of all Canadians will be living with multiple chronic conditions. These conditions are common, but they require people to monitor their health, take medications, attend appointments and sometimes, experience side effects of the condition or it's treatment. The more conditions people have, the more work it is to look after oneself as medication and appointment schedules get increasingly complicated. When people are able to engage in fair and balanced discussions with the doctors about what medications and investigations make sense for them-a process called Shared Decision-Making- they are often happier with their care and more successful in keeping healthy. Unfortunately, Black, Indigenous and older people are all less likely to experience Shared Decision Making. This is a problem as Black, Indigenous and older adults are also more likely to have several chronic conditions. Even more concerning, Black, Indigenous and older adults want to be involved in their care and are simply not getting the chance to be. The Canadian Collaboration for Complex Care is focused on creating a more fair and balanced approach to care for people living with complex health and social situations. We will work to create tools and strategies that will promote comfortable, safe discussions about what care should look like for each person.

column37: When approaching end-of-life, most Canadians want to spend their last days at home with their loved ones. Unfortunately, that often does not happen-most Canadians die in hospital. Both have the potential to help make sure that the right decisions and supports are in place to improve the quality of end-of-life of all Canadians. With this grant, our team of patients, researchers and health professionals will combine, validate and enhance these algorithms to form RESPECT Now!. We will test and validate it with New Zealand collaborators. We will make sure that health professionals, patients and families are supported when discussing personalized life expectancy by integrating RESPECT Now! into patient decision aids to identify decision-making needs, plan next steps of care, and share preferences. We will also evaluate whether RESPECT Now! improves care at end-of-life and integrates into the health system. We will foster an international network of patients and researchers collaborating to develop, evaluate and disseminate personal health algorithms and decision tools for end-of-life.

column36: Integration of artificial intelligence with surface topography for managing scoliosis
column37: Scoliosis is an orthopaedic condition resulting in curvature and rotation of the spine. It typically first appears during adolescence, and affects females more than males. Deformity of the torso is one of the symptoms. Cosmetic improvement of the torso resulting in better symmetry is appreciated by patients, especially in adolescent females. Scoliosis is diagnosed and monitored using x-rays. Unfortunately, x-rays expose young patients to the effects of radiation including a documented increase in cancer risk. Surface topography (ST) is a non-invasive three dimensional (3D) assessment of the torso shape. Using a laser scanner, 3D images of the torso are acquired and the deformity of the torso is measured. The severity of scoliosis is then quantified using indices reflecting the symmetry of the torso. Previous studies using surface topography with 2D measurements instead of the available 3D data were not able to accurately predict the severity of the spinal deformity. In our recent work, we introduced a novel 3D asymmetry technique that does not rely on markers placed on the torso or on simple 2D measurements. Our St measures were able to quantify the severity and progression of scoliosis. In the current proposal, we will develop artificial intelligence techniques to better use the surface topography parameters to estimate the actual shape of the underlying spinal curvature. The developed methods will be designed to ensure that no moderate/severe curves are missed and that all progressing curves are detected to make sure that patients are not missing important treatment opportunities, while dramatically reducing the x-ray radiation exposure to patients.

column37: Background Among preterm infants, those born at a gestational age less than 26 weeks are considered the most vulnerable with a high risk of short- and long-term health problems that include chronic lung disease, brain bleeds, gut injury, kidney failure and death. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most common heart condition with almost 70% preterm infants in this gestational age group being diagnosed with a PDA. Though many PDAs spontaneously resolve on their own, research suggests that if the PDA persists, it may contribute to a number of these short- and long-term health problems. Given the wide variation in PDA treatment approaches in this age group, a randomized trial design, where extremely preterm infants with a symptomatic PDA are randomly assigned to early treatment or no early treatment, is essential to address this question. Purpose of the study The overall purpose of this pilot study is to assess the feasibility of conducting a large study to explore the following research question: In preterm infants born <26 weeks' gestation, is a strategy of selective early medical treatment of a symptomatic PDA better than no treatment at all in the first week of life? column36: Development and Pilot Evaluation of a Mindfulness Smartphone App for Adolescents with Dysmenorrhea
column37: One in four girls experiences dysmenorrhea, or menstrual pain, that is severe in nature and interferes with their daily activities. There is a significant need for non-pharmacological and easily accessible intervention options for this population. Despite the demonstrated effectiveness of psychological interventions such as mindfulness in effectively relieving pain and decreasing activity interference, psychological interventions for menstrual pain among adolescents have not been examined. Additionally, digital interventions, such as smartphone apps, which have the potential to be easily accessible and designed to meet the needs of adolescents, have not been researched in this population. The goal of this project is to develop, conduct usability testing, and examine the acceptability and preliminary efficacy of a mindfulness app for adolescents with menstrual pain. We will use a user-centred design and a three-phased approach. In phase one we will conduct a needs assessment using a survey and focus groups to identify menstrual pain management needs and preferences, and mindfulness preferences and knowledge among adolescents. This will inform the development of an app prototype. In phase two, we will conduct iterative cycles of usability testing to refine the mindfulness app prototype. In phase three, we will recruit adolescents to use the app over a 4-month timeframe. The acceptability and satisfaction with the app will be evaluated and preliminary efficacy of the app on improving pain and mindfulness outcomes will be assessed. This will be the first study to investigate the use of mindfulness in adolescents with menstrual pain and the use of an app targeting menstrual pain among adolescents. This research has the potential for widespread impact on the wellbeing of adolescents who menstruate.

column36: Conversation Cards for Moms: A mixed methods study to create and evaluate a new clinical tool for use in maternity care settings
column37: It is estimated that 50% of Canadian women who give birth every year will gain more weight than recommended during pregnancy. Starting discussions about certain topics, especially those about body weight, can be difficult. Previous research has shown that conversation cards are a great way to help patients and healthcare providers start talking about sensitive topics; however, none have been created for pregnant women. This 3-phase, person-centered study will create and evaluate Conversation Cards for Moms (MomCards) with the goal of empowering women to discuss sensitive topics with their providers. Step 1: This phase includes recruiting pregnant women living with different pre-pregnancy body mass indices (BMIs) and maternity care providers to participate in virtual focus groups designed to determine topics (e.g., lifestyle behaviours and weight gain) that are important to women and maternity care providers. An analysis of the results will help create the first draft of the topic statements for the MomCards. Step 2: Next, the first iteration of the MomCards statements will be sent out to a large sample of Canadian pregnant women and maternity care providers as a survey to refine the statements and rank the most important card statements to have a deck of ~45 MomCards. Step 3: Finally, we will test the use of the MomCards with a diverse sample of pregnant women who have different pre-pregnancy BMIs to determine their confidence, acceptability, and feasibility of using the cards as a way to initiate discussions with maternity care providers. Each step is critical in helping to create and refine the MomCards in preparation for a clinical trial. In collaboration with key maternal health stakeholders and exchange partners, our goal is to disseminate the cards to inform clinical practices in prenatal maternity care settings. Ultimately, we hope to empower women to discuss topics that matter to them which will in turn improve health outcomes for mom and baby.

column36: The use of genomics-driven drug repurposing to prevent cisplatin-induced ototoxicity in pediatric oncology patients
column37: Cisplatin is a chemotherapeutic which is used in the treatment of several cancers. Unfortunately, this cancer treatment also causes severe and debilitating adverse drug reactions such as hearing loss, which occurs in approximately 60% of children receiving this treatment. Once cisplatin is administered, it can change how much of a gene is expressed in specific tissues, the effects of which are mediated by genetic variants. These cisplatin-induced changes in gene expression are likely to result in adverse drug reactions in tissues where these changes are observed. However, no studies have examined the effect of cisplatin on gene expression in inner ear hair cells - the most important cells for hearing. This can be attributed to the difficulty in examining gene expression in these cells, which represent only approximately 3% of the cells found in the inner ear. Recent technological advances have allowed for the investigation of genes in single cells, providing the opportunity to examine gene expression patterns in the low abundance inner ear hair cells. My research aims to use these technologies to investigate the effect of cisplatin treatment on gene expression levels in inner ear samples obtained from mice. Using these data, in combination with data from genome-wide association studies of cisplatin-induced ototoxicity and publicly available gene expression databases, we will uncover small molecules that induce gene expression profiles that are highly dissimilar to the cisplatin-induced gene expression profiles. The potential of these small molecules to prevent hearing loss, without impacting the antitumor activity of cisplatin, will be investigated using mouse models.

column36: Maternal outcomes and mode of delivery following pregnancy in women with inflammatory bowel disease
column37: A significant proportion of female patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are diagnosed before or during their childbearing years. One of the difficulties faced by young women with IBD is a lack of information about how their disease will affect their pregnancy, delivery, and post-pregnancy outcomes, and how pregnancy and delivery may affect their IBD outcomes in the long-term. These fears may be magnified in women who have had prior major abdominal surgery to improve IBD control. There are a number of studies evaluating outcomes for the baby, but little data on how pregnancy and mode of delivery (vaginal vs. cesarean delivery) can affect outcomes in mothers with IBD. In this study, we will use large administrative databases from Ontario, which contain important clinical information on a substantial number of young women with IBD, to improve an understanding of maternal outcomes in women with IBD. Specifically, we will gain a detailed appreciation of the management of women with IBD in pregnancy in Ontario with respect to where care is delivered, mode of delivery, and complications after delivery. We will then determine whether maternal outcomes differ from the general population (women without IBD), and if this is influenced by mode of delivery. The proposed research is very timely in an era when IBD patients are striving to be active participants in decision making around their IBD care. This research is hugely important in allowing young women with IBD and their partners better prepare and plan for pregnancy and delivery as an important, life altering event. Our findings will be shared with relevant healthcare providers (obstetricians, family physicians, midwives, gastroenterologists, and colorectal surgeons) at conferences and published in peer-reviewed journals. We will also share our findings with patients through education materials.

column36: The Building Regulation in Dual Generations Program (BRIDGE); Preventing the intergenerational transmission of mental illness in at-risk preschool children
column37: One in five children experiences mental illness, which contributes to poor health and development outcomes. Exposure to maternal mental illness during the preschool years is an important risk factor for child mental illness, but there are limited programs that specifically target both parent and child mental health needs. The BRIDGE program aims to fill these gaps by treating maternal mental illness and teaching parenting techniques to improve children's mental health resilience. The program is built on best-practice approaches for improving self-regulation, the effortful control of emotions and behaviours, a critical factor implicated in a range of mental health problems. We will use an innovative experimental design to inform how mothers with mental illness struggles to manage their own emotions are linked to risk for poor child health and development outcomes. Knowledge gained will be used to improve the utility of the program by understanding how, why, and for whom the program is most effective. Factors expected to promote success include pilot data, an engaged Patient Advisory Board, and alignment of program goals with multiple health services agencies. The long-term goal is to develop targeted programs that can be used worldwide to improve health outcomes across the lifespan for at-risk families.

column36: Investigating racism in youth mental health care: A mixed-methods youth-engaged study
column37: Youth mental health is a national priority in Canada, with estimates of up to one in four young people affected by a mental health condition. While progress is being made to improve youth mental health services, there continue to be significant knowledge gaps in what diverse youth identify as facilitators and barriers to safe, inclusive mental health services and systems. To date, there is limited research on the associations between mental health and perceived racial discrimination among youth, or the extent to which existing youth mental health care contexts are accessible, safe, and inclusive. The proposed research will contribute new information about the associations between mental health and racial discrimination among youth in Canada; youth perspectives on their experiences related to racism and mental health services; and the factors that facilitate or create barriers to inclusive youth mental health services. This project will gather evidence through a combination of surveys, interviews, and concept mapping workshops. The information from the study will be used to inform action plans that address systemic barriers in youth mental health care and improve mental health outcomes for all youth in Canada.

column36: Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC) 2021-2025
column37: The Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC) is a truly innovative and Canadian approach to the ethical care and use of animals in science. Since 1968, the CCAC has provided the only independent oversight of animal-based scientific activities in Canada through a rigorous process of assessment, certification, and standards development. In the absence of a national regulatory framework, the CCAC's programs are some of the most powerful instruments available for setting national standards and ensuring the ethical treatment of animals in Canadian science. The CCAC has, since its inception, fulfilled the Government of Canada's national and international responsibility "to provide high standards for experimental animal care and use through the development of relevant standards and a code of ethics, and through education and the certification of institutional programs" (Guillen, 2018). The CCAC plays an essential role within the scientific community by supporting robust and valid scientific findings built upon ethical animal practices, such as the Three Rs of replacement, reduction, and refinement (see the Three Rs and Ethics section of the CCAC website for more details). This framework is also essential to an overwhelming majority of Canadians (95%), who, while supportive of animal-based science, believe that the welfare and ethical treatment of the animals involved are of the utmost importance (Nanos, 2019; see Appendix 5).

column36: The Impact of Early Childhood Education and Care Policies on Health Outcomes in Adolescence
column37: Background: Early childhood education and care (ECEC) programs are part of large-scale social policy reforms in high-income countries, however surprisingly few studies having evaluated their impact, particularly regarding inequalities and non-academic outcomes (e.g., health and behavioural outcomes) in adolescence. Objectives: 1) To evaluate the impact of reforms which increased assess to ECEC between 1995-2008 on health and behavioural outcomes in adolescence, as well as socioeconomic inequalities within these endpoints; and 2) To inform the optimal design of ECEC policies by examining how impacts on adolescent health and behavioural outcomes are related to other policy domains, including the quality and governance of the ECEC program. Methods: A database containing systematically-cataloged ECEC policies will be used to identify natural experiments which expanded ECEC participation in high-income countries between 1995 and 2008. We will estimate the impact of these reforms on adolescent health and behavioural outcomes, using linked microdata from the World Health Organization's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey. We will then assess the impact of indicators of ECEC quality and governance on these outcomes. Significance: Evidence concerning the impact of large-scale ECEC reforms is severely limited. This research will address this gap and enable the identification of policy characteristics that have the potential to improve adolescent health and well-being, as well as to reduce social inequalities in health outcomes.

column36: Burden of HIV and chronic comorbidities in BC's aging populations: A population-based cohort study
column37: The advances of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in the past three decades have allowed the transformation of HIV from a deadly infection to a manageable chronic condition. As life expectancy of people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWH) increases and the number of HIV-related deaths decreases, a rise in premature illness and deaths from non-AIDS chronic diseases associated with old age has been simultaneously observed, presenting novel challenges to patients and health providers. In British Columbia (BC), these challenges are augmented by the growing public concerns about the sustainability of its healthcare system as the overall population ages. As such, this study intends to examine, at a population level, the impact of growing older while living with HIV. In particular, this study will utilize advanced statistical models to assess the disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), a measure of disease burden considering both early death and disability (i.e., states other than good health), associated with experiencing age-associated and mental health conditions in PLWH and in HIV-negative control population in BC. Ultimately, this study seeks to provide unprecedented data-driven evidence that will identify existing gaps in care for this aging population and an approach that best addresses the future healthcare needs of PLWH.

column36: Lii kaansayr kipihtinaant (Cancer Prevention): HPV immunization among Alberta Metis families.
column37: First Nations, Metis, and Inuit (FNMI) young people should have free and easy access to human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines to prevent cancer, but rates of cancer caused by HPV remain higher in FNMI people than the general population. Therefore, it is important that we figure out whether Metis people are getting vaccinated for HPV, and if not, why not, and what would be helpful? The study will happen in three phases, starting with an online community survey to Metis Albertans. Phase two will analyze government health data to learn how many Metis people were vaccinated for HPV in the past. This information, in connection with the survey information, will help inform the final study. Phase three will use a Metis research method of keeoukaywin or 'visiting' with different Metis people in communities across Alberta, to try to understand the reasons people do, or do not, get vaccinated for HPV. All parts of the study will consider whether age, gender, sex, sexuality, disability, and Metis identity have an impact on vaccination and experiences of getting vaccinated. Throughout the process, Metis Nation of Alberta community members will help make decisions about how the study is conducted, how the data are analyzed and shared, and what is done with the information. We hope that through the process, community members become engaged and support HPV related cancer prevention activities for Metis Albertans. The ultimate goal of this study is to inform future development of intervention strategies, policy decisions, and community action supporting HPV vaccination in Metis youth.
