We will determine if this latter approach can lead to disease correction and extension of lifespan in the mouse model of SMA. Together, these studies will uncover novel approaches to disease management in patients with SMA.

column36: Analyzing the central role of Zasp family proteins in muscle architecture and function
column37: Muscles contain a highly regular, subcellular assembly of proteins that enable contractility. These huge molecular machines are called myofibrils and we aim to understand how they are built during development, and how different proteins are arranged withing myofibrils to contribute to a fully functional muscle. Contractility is mediated by two different filaments, actin and myosin, that slide past each other. Myosin filaments are anchored at the M-line and actin filaments are anchored at the Z-disc. And finally, how does Zasp self-interaction initiate and terminate Z-disc and thereby muscle growth? This will help us to better understand Z-disc, but also pathological aggregate formation, which is an important aspect of muscle disorders. This work is done in the Drosophila model system, but human Zasp proteins are closely related, and we will confirm our results with human Zasp proteins.

column36: ATF3+ tumor-innervating neurons control anti-cancer immunity
column37: Itch is a common feature of various cancers, while cancer cells actively secrete factors promoting neuronal infiltration of tumors. Experimentally stopping the electrical signals of tumor infiltrating neurons helps decrease tumor growth, but the specific means by which neurons regulate cancer cells survival is yet to be uncovered. Given that we discovered that cancer cells drive major changes in the gene expression profiles of tumor-infiltrating noxious detecting neurons, we hypothesize that cancer cells exploit nociceptors interplay with the immune system to sustain their growth and survival. To investigate this, we aim to study: 1) whether cancer cells directly activate these nociceptors, 2) nociceptor-induced expression of immune checkpoint receptors on NK cells, and 3) the role of nociceptors in cancer immunosurveillance. Studying the biology of cancer, by simultaneously embracing the disease's nervous and immune aspects, as well as their reciprocal interplay, will likely lead to the discovery of unexpected biology and novel therapeutic avenues. As such, this proposal represents the first attempt to amplify the immune system's capacity to fight cancer cells by harnessing the nervous and immune system's interplay.

column36: 'Real-time' measures of anxiety and physical activity in 15-18 year olds with prenatal antidepressant exposure
column37: A mother's depressed mood during pregnancy and the antidepressant medicines used to treat this common disorder affect her child's developing brain and may be associated with anxious behaviors in early adolescence. For over 20 years, we have studied the development and behavior in children of mothers who were depressed and treated with antidepressants called serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs) when they were pregnant. We have observed great variations in child behavior such as anxiety and not all outcomes are associated with prenatal antidepressant exposure. A mother's prenatal mood has emerged as one of the strongest predictors of child behavior. Even among children of depressed mothers treated with an SRI in pregnancy, children can experience negative behavioral outcomes and we wonder why some children are affected. To address this question, we will investigate whether everyday patterns of distressing symptoms (anxiety, somatic symptoms) in youths (15-18 yrs) of depressed mothers treated with an SRI during pregnancy and youth of healthy mothers are more anxious, are less physically active and have lower stress-related factors found in saliva. We have followed a cohort of mothers and their children since the second trimester of pregnancy (n= 110). We now propose to investigate behavior (anxiety) in our youth and determine whether everyday patterns of behavior at early ages 'predicts' similar behaviors at mid-late adolescence. Now in light of in person restrictions of COVID-19, we will use using a smartphone app and a wearable accelerometer to study whether 14-day 'real time' measures of anxiety, somatic symptoms and physical activity are related to two stress biomarkers found in saliva (cortisol, alpha amylase), prenatal maternal depressed mood and SRI exposure. We believe that our work will help us understand how a mother's depressed mood and treatment with a SRI antidepressant in pregnancy influences her child's well-being during a critical time of development.

column36: Deciphering the immunopeptidomic landscape of COVID-19 disease
column37: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the causative agent of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Between December 2019 and September 2020, SARS-CoV-2 had infected more than 30M people and killed more than 1M. Ease of transmission combined with disease severity have led leaders around the world to restrict individual movements and promote physical distancing measures to limit the spread. Therefore, rapid delivery of safe and efficient vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 is the top priority. Importantly, the development of efficient vaccines can be accelerated by a clear understanding of the SARS-CoV-2 targets that are recognized by the human immune system. Until now, very limited information is available about those targets. In addition, SARS-CoV-2 is mutating as the pandemic persists, but it is unclear how those mutations influence the ability of the immune system to eliminate the virus. Here, we propose to deploy an innovative viral epitope discovery platform to identify those mutated and non-mutated targets in a rapid, systematic and unbiased manner. The proposed research will therefore assist vaccine design and will facilitate the evaluation of vaccine candidates as they advance in the clinic.

column36: Design a Double-Bolt Lock to Control Cancer Cell Growth
column37: Cancer cells differ from normal cells in many ways that allow them to grow out of control and become invasive. That is why one major goal of anticancer therapy is to suppress cancer cell growth. DNA topoisomerase II (TOP2) genes, TOP2A and TOP2B, are two key genes to control cancer cell growth/division. TOP2A is essential for a parent cell to divide into two daughter cells, while TOP2B is important for cancer cells to increase oncogenes that promote cell division. Blocking both TOP2A and TOP2B would create a double-bolt lock to inhibit cancer cell growth. Although several TOP2 blockers are used as drugs to treat cancer patients, they are also toxic to normal cells and in some cases can transform normal cells into tumors. These limitations urge researchers to discover new inhibitors that block TOP2 activity through different mechanisms so that there will be less toxic effects on normal cells. In this study, we will build complex software incorporated with computer clusters to screen millions of chemicals from a chemical bank and then test these chemicals for their inhibitory effects on TOP2 activity. We will decipher how these chemicals inhibit TOP2 activity at the molecular level and determine whether these chemicals block cancer cell growth. This study will lead to the discovery of new TOP2 inhibitors as potential anticancer drugs.

column36: Preserving microcirculation and function in the diabetic brain
column37: A growing number of Canadians have some form of diabetes which costs the Canadian healthcare system 15.6 billion dollars a year. Although diabetes related disease is well appreciated in the heart, kidney and eye, the brain appears to be particularly sensitive given that diabetics are at significantly greater risk for developing cognitive impairment and suffer more severe disability after stroke. Unfortunately no cure exists as insulin therapy cannot completely prevent these problems. Making matters worse, current stroke therapies such as clot busting drugs are not recommended for some diabetics. One common explanation for the diverse array of brain disturbances is that diabetes perturbs brain circulation in the smallest blood vessels (micro-circulation). Here, our working hypothesis is that blood flow in the microcirculatory networks of the diabetic brain are prone to stalling. These microcirculatory traffic jams can accumulate over time, which in tandem with capillary pruning (a common outcome of stalling), lead to progressive deterioration of vascular, neuronal and cognitive function. Since diabetes is a major risk factor for stroke and poor outcome, we suspect that diabetes worsens capillary stalling after stroke, thereby limiting the return of blood flow in vulnerable, but salvageable brain regions. The goal of our research will be to determine how diabetes affects brain micro-circulation. Since we have preliminary data showing there are problems, we will then explore ways to improve brain microcirculation by targeting a specific protein (called IL-10) that modulates inflammation. And finally, by altering IL-10 signaling after stroke, we believe we can better protect brain tissue from stroke damage and improve recovery in an experimental model of diabetes. Ultimately, this project will shed new light on the effects of diabetes on brain circulation and function, which will stimulate new treatment options for those Canadians suffering from diabetes.

column36: Connective Tissue Growth Factor (CTGF): A key player in Fibrosis and Cancer
column37: CTGF is a cysteine-rich matricellular protein involved in the control of biological processes, such as cell proliferation, differentiation, adhesion and angiogenesis, as well as multiple pathologies, such as tumor development and tissue fibrosis. This research proposal aims to define the molecular basis of CTGF-TGF beta and CTGF-IGF complex interactions and to unravel the structural basis for relevant signaling pathways. In these studies we will seek to develop new therapeutic targets with the overall goal to interrupt CTGF-mediated receptor complexes and thereby causing apoptosis in tumor cells.

column36: Regulation of transcription by SUMO
column37: Sumoylation is the process by which specific proteins in eukaryotic cells become modified through attachment of the SUMO peptide, which has various possible effects on the functions of the targeted proteins. When cells encounter environmental stress conditions, the number of SUMO modifications increases dramatically and rapidly, but it is not fully understood why this occurs. SUMO-targeted proteins, which number in the hundreds or thousands, are involved in multiple processes in the cell, but proteins that control gene expression are particularly subject to this type of modification. This suggests that the elevated sumoylation levels that occur in response to stress may promote changes to gene expression that allow cells to adapt to the stress condition. To explore this, we will identify specific proteins involved in gene expression that are targets of sumoylation to characterize how SUMO modification controls their functions at the molecular level. Additionally, we will examine how changes to cellular sumoylation levels affect gene expression by determining which genes are regulated this way and through what mechanisms this regulation takes place. In cancer, tumour cells frequently show abnormal sumoylation levels, which often correlates with poor prognosis and metastasis. In the long term, our work is important for understanding whether these abnormal sumoylation levels promote the expression of genes that favour tumour growth.

column36: Evaluating Microdosing in Emergency Departments: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing the Effectiveness of Buprenorphine/Naloxone Microdosing vs. Standard Dosing (EMED Study)
column37: Buprenorphine/naloxone (commonly known as Suboxone) is a life-saving medication for people with opioid addiction. Studies show that Suboxone works when started from emergency departments (EDs), which is important because many people make ED visits before they overdose. However, Suboxone is hard to start, because it can cause people to experience bad withdrawal symptoms (vomiting, sweating, pain) if it is started too soon after a person has used other opioids like heroin or morphine. This is called precipitated withdrawal and makes many people afraid of starting Suboxone at all. To prevent this complication, doctors tell patients to wait for 12-24 hours since they last used other opioids and to already be in withdrawal before starting, which is very uncomfortable for patients. A new method, called microdosing, tries to improve patient comfort by avoiding precipitated withdrawal and withdrawal altogether. This method starts people on very small Suboxone doses that gradually increase while they continue to use other opioids. Microdosing has never been evaluated in a formal study. This study will identify adult patients with opioid addiction in EDs in BC and Alberta. We will provide them with either take-home Suboxone microdosing or standard dosing packages to start after they are discharged. We will look at whether patients who receive microdosing are more likely to stay on Suboxone than those who receive a standard dosing package. We will also look at whether people who receive microdosing are more likely to take any opioid agonist therapy in the future, and we will compare deaths, overdoses, and healthcare use between the groups. We are working with health regions, provincial policy makers, public health, and people with lived experience with opioid use to make sure that we share our findings with EDs and patients across Canada. We hope that EDs will use our study results to develop Suboxone programs that are most likely to help patients at risk for overdose.

column36: Smart Discharges for Mom+Baby: Saving mother-newborn dyads by developing a predictive risk model to identify vulnerable dyads and guide delivery of evidence-based, locally-informed interventions for targeted post-discharge care.
column37: Mothers and babies are at higher risk of dying in the first six weeks after birth. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends regular follow-up visits for all mothers and their newborns. However, follow-up visits are not possible in many poor countries. The lack of money and nurses at hospitals and limited time and money at home stop mothers from seeking care for themselves and their babies. In our study we identify mother-baby pairs that are most at-risk of getting sick or dying using the Smart Mom+Baby risk score at the time of birth. A baby is more likely to get sick if its mother is sick. The mother is more likely to get sick if the baby is sick. Our risk score looks at both the mother's and baby's risk. The combined risk for the mother and baby can then be used by a nurse to guide the number of follow-up visits recommended for the pair, with mothers and babies at higher risks receiving the most number of visits. This allows mothers and babies at high risk to get good care when they need it. Our approach is ideally suited to poor countries where nurses and money are limited. In this study we will build our risk score, working at different types of hospitals across Uganda. We will also talk to mothers, grandmothers, fathers, midwives, nurses, and doctors to determine what stops mothers and newborns from receiving a follow-up visit. We will find ways to remove these barriers and ensure that improvements in care are long-lasting. To do this, we will use more than 10 years of experience making risk scores that help nurses and doctors make better choices about treating patients in poor countries.

column36: Investigation into RAS GTPase control of cell adhesion and proliferation through alternative downstream effectors
column37: Abnormal changes to the genetic material of various cell types in the human body can lead to cancer, or more specifically the uncontrolled proliferation of cells. When this occurs, the affected genes create proteins that cannot be turned off in a normal fashion. It is remarkable that mutations to one set of proteins, called RAS, are responsible for at least a quarter of all human cancers. A lack of effective therapies for RAS-driven cancers is the major reason why lung, colon, and pancreatic cancers remain the most refractory to available treatments. Of course, normal cells require these same proteins during development or in the process of healing a wound, to guide proliferation and such basic functions as attachment to other cells. To improve outcomes for patients we require significantly more research to understand all of the proteins connected to RAS in the cell, how they work in both normal and cancer cells, and to identify vulnerabilities that may be targeted by therapeutics. My team has developed new methods to study RAS function and its involvement with other proteins. Targeting these associations is finally proving effective in treating some cancers, yet important connections between RAS and many protein partners remain understudied. This includes proteins that regulate the ability of cells to attach or move, linked to metastasis, and proteins that lead to self-directed cell death. We use leading-edge techniques to gain insight to the three-dimensional shape of these proteins and complement our data with studies in cultured human cells or mice to observe how changes to these genes lead to cancer formation. We propose to identify and characterize new therapeutic targets in the vicinity of mutant RAS proteins, and these efforts will be complemented by the drug discovery capabilities at our institute. Our study has significance for many patients, particularly those with untreatable cancers such as pancreatic adenocarcinomas and lung NSCLCs.

column36: Improving adherence to controller medication in children with asthma - the unexplored contribution of behavioural sciences
column37: Asthma is one of the most common chronic diseases affecting children. Low adherence to medication is a modifiable cause of preventable asthma attacks and poor asthma control. One reason for lower adherence to medication may be cognitive factors. Concerns and worries that tax the brain as well as focus on the present at the expense of the future may lead to low adherence. Children living in poverty have worse asthma control due to a variety of factors, including lower adherence to medications. Families living in poverty may be particularly affected by stress taxing the brain, and may have to focus on more immediate concerns rather than distant ones. Whether cognitive factors are linked to adherence to medications in childhood asthma is not currently known. It is also not known whether these factors differ between families living in poverty and those who are not. We will study 200 families (from a range of socioeconomic status) followed in asthma clinic to determine 1) if children of parents who focus more on the present, and have less cognitive space to make decisions have lower adherence to asthma medication, 2) whether families from lower socioeconomic status have more cognitive tax and/or focus more on the present, and 3) whether the effect of cognitive tax and focus on the present explain in part the effect of socioeconomic status on adherence to asthma medication. This research will allow us to determine whether cognitive factors represent potential targets for interventions, especially for lower income families. The development of such interventions could help improve asthma control for vulnerable children, and ultimately reduce health disparities. This research also has important potential implications for other common diseases where medications need to be taken regularly.

column36: Moving beyond blood glucose with continuous multiplexed hormone measurement
column37: Over half of the Canadian population is either overweight or obese. Obesity leads to higher levels of blood insulin and glucose. These are features of prediabetes and most people with prediabetes progress to type 2 diabetes (T2D). We use blood glucose as the key indicator of T2D progression. Higher blood glucose is associated with over 2 million annual deaths. Continuous glucose monitoring is changing the way we think about what foods and other factors alter risk of T2D and its complications. However, we don't know as much about blood insulin and other hormones/peptides connected to diabetes. Current methods can only measure insulin or other hormones/peptides a few times after a meal. Obesity contributes to prediabetes, but we do not understand the triggers of higher blood glucose or blood insulin. We do not know if certain foods cause unique blood glucose and blood insulin responses in certain individuals that may be at risk for T2D. This is important because only some individuals with obesity develop prediabetes. So far, we have not been able to measure how certain foods change blood insulin every second after a meal. We have been limited to taking blood ~every half hour to measure insulin or other hormones. We have built a new biosensor for continuous insulin monitoring. Our biosensor operates with ultra-fast sampling and will measure blood insulin and other related hormones and peptides (glucagon and C-peptide) and glucose in real-time. We can use this biosensor to make new discoveries about why certain people and risk factors, such as obesity, diet, stress and genetics alter how key hormones can promote the progression from prediabetes to T2D. This biosensor can also help with personalized nutrition approaches to obesity and T2D by uncovering how certain foods alter the levels and location of insulin and other hormones, which is a key addition to the current methods that use continuous glucose monitoring.

column36: The Role of Alternative Gene Splicing in Psychiatric Disorders
column37: Psychiatric disorders are major health problem that can severely impact affected individuals' quality of life. The majority of associated DNA variants found through genetic studies of psychiatric disorders are expected to change the expression of the risk genes. Gene expression is regulated by multiple mechanisms including alternative splicing. Splicing is the process by which different parts of the gene are linked together to create a functional protein and alterations in this process allow diversity in the proteins that can be expressed from a single gene in different tissues. Deregulation of this tightly controlled process however can result in disease. We mined large datasets of DNA variants predicted to alter, or are correlated with, gene splicing changes and identified those that were also associated with psychiatric disorders. Using those datasets we identified candidates, and confirmed alternatively spliced genes for 6 of the 13 tested thus far, 4 of which were correlated with genetic risk. Three of these are involved in mitochondrial function (APOPT1, AS3MT, NEK4), implicated in psychiatric disorder by multiple lines of evidence. column36: Predicting fragility fractures by non-invasive high-resolution imaging and advanced morphometrics
column37: Osteoporosis is a condition where bones become fragile and more likely to break due to a decrease in bone mineral density and concurrent structural changes, leading to decreased bone strength. Unfortunately, fragility fractures, especially at the hip, are devastating for patients and place enormous burden on our healthcare system. Over a quarter of patients who suffer a hip fracture will die within a year. Assessing who is at risk of having a fracture is challenging because current clinical tools only account for bone density, not structure. Recent advances in medical imaging allow us to measure bone structure, also known as microarchitecture, in vivo, which has greatly advanced our understanding of human bone health. Our state-of-the-art imaging approach is based on high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography, and we are international leaders in this technology. Through over a decade of research, we have established that there are recurring patterns of bone microarchitecture, and believe that using these patterns, we can advance our ability to develop personalized fracture risk screening tools. Current clinical tools are successful at identifying patients at high or low risk of fracture based on bone density and clinical risk factors. However, the majority of fractures occur in patients who fall between those limits. We have chosen to focus on patients whose bone density and clinical risk factors place them at moderate risk. We will develop a novel approach to quantify characteristics of bone microarchitecture that have been elusive to measure until now and use artificial intelligence techniques to classify bone phenotypes associated with fracture in the population. Our research will employ a fresh look at how we assess bone health using cutting-edge technology to establish the characteristics that underpin bone fragility. We aim to improve the stratification of fracture risk towards management and prevention of fragility fractures.

column36: Molecular analysis of Herpes simplex virus type I egress
column37: Cold sores are a medical and recurring issue for about a third of the population that is caused by a virus called Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). This virus belongs to a family of human infectious agents associated with several other clinical conditions (for example genital herpes, blindness, newborn infections, mononucleosis, varicella, Zona, encephalitis and some cancers). Unfortunately, while the propagation of the virus is treatable with current medicines, these viruses hide in our cells and persist forever once contracted. Moreover, they can be awakened under certain conditions and asymptomatic people can even shed infectious viruses. Finally, drug resistance is becoming an issue, pinpointing the need for novel therapeutics. To succeed, however, we need to understand how the virus spreads. All viruses are parasitic in nature and intimately depend on our cells to replicate, using many of their proteins and functions. However, it is not always clear which of those proteins each virus employs. This is certainly true for the aforementioned HSV-1 human pathogen. Our laboratory consequently examines the intimate interactions between HSV-1 and our cells. More specifically, our research program sets out to identify the viral and cellular proteins that help HSV-1 replicate and to explore their mechanisms of action with the ultimate goal of designing novel therapeutic approaches. Such therapeutics may be useful not only against this virus but also against the entire herpes family of viruses, with which it shares many properties. Finally, viruses represent excellent tools to explore how our own cells function. Studying viruses may thus reveal unexpected findings on these cellular mechanisms and address a number of diseases associated with these processes.

column36: Specialized Cellular Functions of Human Ribosomal Proteins
column37: The general view of ribosomal proteins (RPs) is one of generic cellular proteins that function exclusively to maintain the integrity of the ribosome, the cellular machine responsible for protein synthesis. column36: Role of circadian rhythms in bone adaptation to the mechanical environment
column37: Physical forces are critical for successful function of many organs including bone. Bone is formed or removed to meet changes in the local mechanical environment. Exercise is the most efficient and cost-effective intervention to improve bone health. column36: Understanding Human Primary Atopic Disorders
column37: Nearly 1-in-3 Canadians suffer from an allergic disease, such as asthma, food allergy and eczema. Globally, asthma alone affects an estimated 300 million people, with annual costs over $20 billion dollars worldwide. Solutions to this allergy health crisis are urgently needed. Understanding how and why allergies occur can help us find answers to prevent and treat these burdensome conditions. In our research we use new and innovative ways to understand how the immune system causes allergic disease. We begin by studying people who have severe allergic conditions caused by changes in genes that control how their immune system works. These conditions are called primary atopic disorders (or PADs). We work with clinicians across Canada and the world to identify patients who may be suffering from a PAD. With the full consent of the patient, we use new gene sequencing technologies to read their genetic material or DNA and look for troublesome changes ("mutations"). If mutations are identified in genes that have not been reported in PADs, we then perform experiments to prove that these mutations are responsible for the patient's symptoms. In this project, our initial focus is to study changes in three genes that we have identified in patients with PADs. This is the first time changes in these genes have been reported in other patients with PADs, so they are an exciting and important starting place. Finally, we will work with a large study (the CHILD cohort) that has data and samples for over 3000 Canadian children to determine if changes in the PAD genes are also associated with common allergic diseases. This research is important and timely. Understanding what causes PADs is life-changing for the affected people and families. It means we can find better treatments for them. Our work also provides a unique opportunity to discover how changes in the human immune system cause or contribute to allergic diseases.

column37: The sinus node controls heart rate, and is considered the natural pacemaker of the heart. Electrical impulses from the sinus node travel throughout the four chambers of the heart: the two upper chambers, called atria, and the lower two ventricles. Inappropriate electrical activity in the upper part of the heart (sinus node or atria), results in abnormal heart rhythms referred to as supraventricular arrhythmias. During pregnancy, there is a significant increase in the risk of cardiac arrhythmia. The increased incidence of these arrhythmias may have significant consequences on the health of the mother and the fetus. However, the mechanisms by which pregnancy increases the risk of arrhythmias have been largely unexplored. Thus, the first objective of this project is to explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms responsible for the increased incidence of arrhythmias during pregnancy. Additionally, considering that hormonal status has emerged as an important factor in the development of some types of cardiac arrhythmias, a second objective is to determine whether the major increase in estrogen levels that occur during pregnancy are implicated in these changes. The proposed studies will be realized using a combination of electrophysiological and biochemical techniques in mouse and human-derived cells. This work will provide important information related to the understanding of the influence of pregnancy on cardiac arrhythmia, and on the influence of estrogen on the electrical activity of the sinus node and atria. As comorbidity and the number of pregnancies at an advanced maternal age continue to rise, this issue is becoming even more pertinent. Ultimately, with further understanding, management of pregnancy-induced arrhythmias, and/or arrhythmias correlated with estrogen fluctuation could be significantly improved.

column36: ING1a mechanisms of cell senescence
column37: Cell aging, also called senescence, is largely controlled by stress signals of different types including those generated internally in the cell and by external agents like chemicals and radiation that damage DNA. We have identified a protein we called ING1a that is only found in humans and non-human primates (apes and monkeys), which is induced by stress and very rapidly causes cells to age. We previously found that it does this through a role in the nucleus of cells and now we have discovered another role at the mitochondria that function as the powerhouse of the cell. In our project we propose to determine exactly how ING1a can so rapidly make cells age via this unique mitochondrial mechanism and we will also determine what causes cells to make this protein normally as human cells age. Our observations in human cells are timely since it was recently discovered in yeast, that both a mechanism operating in the nucleus of yeast cells and a mitochondrial energy-based pathway serve as two distinct major mechanisms to lead to their senescence. This is exciting since it suggests that cell aging may have clear parallels between the yeast that is used as a model organism to study aging, and human cells. We propose to use a series of ING1a protein fragments tagged with a molecule that is fluorescent so we can see it in cells under the microscope, to see exactly what piece of ING1a causes cells to rapidly age. After that we will determine what other proteins this fragment binds to so we can understand how it causes rapid cell aging. Once we determine the pathway(s) in the cell that are used to make the cell produce ING1a, and the pathways used by ING1a to cause rapid cell aging, we will plan strategies to block ING1a production and/or block its effect in cells to allow cells to grow for longer periods of time. There is good evidence that increasing cell lifespan will improve human healthspan by delaying the onset of many different age-related ailments.

column36: Intergenerational transmission of vulnerability to PTSD : When children learn fear from their parent
column37: The brain processes underlying fear learning have been well documented. Most of the protocols that have been used to examine these questions have paired a neutral cue with an aversive stimulus (for example, an electrical shock) to create a fear association. However, one can be afraid without directly experiencing the negative stimulus. Observational fear learning refers to the ability to learn a fear association without being directly exposed to the aversive stimulus. What if a child learns from a parent who has a dysregulated fear system, as it is the case for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)? Our project aims to disentangle the mechanisms of observational fear learning in children of mothers with PTSD and to assess if these fear learning patterns could predict subsequent symptoms of mental illness. At Time 1 and Time 3 (which will occur 4 years later), children will watch their mother and a stranger adult woman going through a fear conditioning procedure while psychophysiological measures and subjective ratings of fear will be measured. Children's symptoms of mental illness will be assessed at Time 1, as well as 2 years (Time 2) and 4 years (Time 3) later. Given that high fear levels and low emotional regulation abilities are key characteristics of PTSD and that children of parents suffering from PTSD have an increased risk of developing various psychopathologies, it is important to define the mechanisms of observational fear learning in children and to assess how they predict subsequent mental health problems. The results from this application could play a critical role in developing and implementing interventions in at-risk families.

column36: Characterizing and monitoring the healthfulness of the food supply: a fundamental step towards creating healthier food environments
column37: Improving the quality of the food supply is one of the cornerstones for healthier food environments. A critical first step toward this goal consists in getting a clear picture of the nutritional quality of the food supply, i.e. foods and beverages that are offered to consumers on the market. While analyzing the food supply on a per-nutrient basis (e.g. sugar or salt content) remains informative, it does not provide a complete picture of the overall nutritional quality (healthfulness) of foods. Nutrient profiling (NP) is an objective method that characterizes the healthfulness of foods. Indeed, NP models evaluate the quality of a food based on its content in multiple nutrients (e.g. sugars, sodium, fibre), as opposed to relying only on the content in a single nutrient (e.g. sodium only). The proposed project, conducted in collaboration with key organizations such as the ULaval Food Quality Observatory and the INFORMAS-Canada group, aims to characterize and monitor the healthfulness of the food supply using the most reliable NP model in the Canadian context. Because very few existing NP models have been validated, the first objective is to validate three models potentially relevant for use in Canada in different adult populations, to determine which one is the most reliable indicator of the healthfulness of foods. Second, the healthfulness of foods commonly purchased by the population (e.g. breakfast cereals, sliced bread), and its associations with characteristics influencing food-purchasing decisions (e.g. food prices), will be evaluated using the most reliable model. Third, a follow-up evaluation of the same foods will be conducted after 5 years to monitor potential changes in their healthfulness. Taken together, the results of this innovative and essential project will provide useful information about which actions could be undertaken to improve the nutritional quality of the food supply, and ultimately contribute to better diet quality and health in Canadians.

column36: Elucidating the roles of miRNAs and Hippo signaling on lineage specification in the human and mouse embryo
column37: Subfertility affects 1 in 6 couples and despite advances in assisted reproductive medicine (ART), our understanding of human embryo health and infertility is limited. Embryonic development during the first week post-fertilization is arguably the most critical window. During this time, the first lineages are formed which give rise to the placenta and embryo proper. Successful formation of the first lineages is a developmental milestone required to ensure healthy embryo development. Currently, our knowledge pertaining to the mechanism(s) that control lineage segregation during human preimplantation development is lacking. Most of what we know about preimplantation development is extrapolated from studies using animal models and though they have provided a wealth of information, with recent advancements, it is clear that species differences exist. Therefore, findings must be carefully extrapolated to human development, highlighting the need for more studies directly in the human embryo. Further, miRNAs can regulate gene expression, and our recent work suggests that miRNAs are driving lineage specification in the embryo and that this is, at least in part, mediated by Hippo signaling. Hippo signaling is the current leading model for trophectoderm-inner cell mass specification. In the cancer field, miRNA-Hippo crosstalk is an emerging area of interest that remains to be explored in development. This proposal will determine, for the first time, the regulatory role of miRNAs and miRNA-Hippo crosstalk on lineage specification using a parallel model of human and mouse embryos. Further, this work will help us better understand the role of miRNA in embryo competence and their potential as predictive biomarkers in clinic. Overall, results from these studies are expected to make significant contributions to our understanding of early embryogenesis. I envision broad utility of this data in the fields of developmental, stem cells, and ART.

column36: Colonic Goblet Cells and Mucus: Defining Their Roles in Host Defense and Mucosal Protection
column37: Intestinal mucus is a mix of proteins and sugars. It coats the inner surface of mammalian intestines, lubricating the passage of food and stool along the length of the gut. In addition, mucus acts as a barrier, keeping the vast community of resident, and largely peaceful bacteria from escaping the intestine and causing damage. My group has been exploring if mucus has other functions, by infecting mice with disease causing bacteria called Citrobacter, relatives of the bacteria that cause "hamburger disease". We have been comparing how well Citrobacter infects mice that produce mucus, with mice that are lacking mucus, or mice that lack key mucus sugars. We know that when Citrobacter enters the gut, it has to compete with resident bacteria for space and food. Normally it can take up to 1 week for Citrobacter to outcompete the resident bacteria, expand in number and cause disease. Interestingly, when Citrobacter infects mice lacking mucus, or key mucus sugars, it bypasses the resident bacteria, spreading through the gut and causing disease almost immediately. We found that the resident bacteria in these susceptible mice are very poor at producing a fatty acid called butyrate, but when we add butyrate back, the mice showed improved protection against Citrobacter. We will explore how resident bacteria use mucus sugars to produce butyrate, and define how loss of mucus impacts Citrobacter-host interactions. In addition, we know that as Citrobacter infection progresses in normal mice, some of the cells that line the gut produce significantly more mucus, presumably to thicken the protective mucus barrier and further protect the gut, as well as flush away some of the Citrobacter. It is unclear however, to what degree this mucus response actually protects the host, which cells participate in the response, and finally, whether this release of mucus reflects the direct actions of the cells that make mucus, or if they need to be activated by cells of the immune system.

column36: Neuronal demise in the developing brain shapes the adult brain
column37: In the developing brain, the birth of neurons is followed by the death of 20-40% of these neurons, raising the question of the importance of such demise for the adult brain. Cajal-Retzius cells (CRs) - pioneer neurons of the embryonic brain but then almost completely disappear - present a unique system to address this question. CRs are organizers of early brain development. They secrete protein factors to regulate the migration of other neurons to build proper architecture of the brain. They also act as "placeholders" that form transient neuron-neuron connections to ensure functional assembly of the brain network. Despite their important roles in brain development, the vast majority of CRs are destined to die during early postnatal life in mice as well as in humans. Incomplete CR cell removal has been described in human brain pathologies including epilepsy, opening the intriguing possibility that CR cell death plays a constructive role in sculpting the mature cerebral cortex. Here, we propose a series of experiments to probe the mechanism that drives CR cell death in the developing brain and investigate how abnormal CR cell survival impinges on adult brain function and contributes to seizure susceptibility. Our work will not only provide novel insight into CR cell biology but will also address the role of CR death and persistence in different brain regions. As abnormal CR cell survival is linked to epilepsy, our study will also shed light on the pathogenic mechanisms of epileptic disorders.

column37: Cardiovascular disease such as heart attack and stroke is the leading cause of death worldwide. The drugs that are most often prescribed to lower lipids in blood are the statins. They can reduce cardiovascular events by 20% to 40%. A new second type of drug, the PCSK9 inhibitors, can be prescribed together with statins and reduce cardiovascular events by 15% more. Therefore, the risk of cardiovascular disease is still high, though, even with these current drugs. Considering that more than 50,000 strokes and 75,000 heart attacks occur in Canada every year, the need for new cardiovascular therapies is clear and urgent. In our research, we are looking for alternative ways to reduce levels of cholesterol in blood and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

column36: Oral microbiome and caries risk in young First Nations and Metis children in Manitoba
column37: Many First Nations and Metis children develop Early Childhood Caries (ECC), which is tooth decay involving baby teeth in children < 6 years of age. Several will suffer from an aggressive form of ECC, called severe ECC (S-ECC). S-ECC often requires treatment under general anesthesia. A recent joint position statement on "ECC in Indigenous Communities" recommends research on the microbiology of ECC. The dental microbiome, which includes the tooth microorganisms, their genomes and the surrounding environmental conditions is the major risk factor for tooth decay. There is an urgent need to identify all of the various risk factors, like sex of the child, access to care, diet, and dental microbiome, and how these interact, to understand why many First Nations and Metis children develop ECC. This led to our hypothesis that because of limited access to oral health care, poverty and lack of clean water, food insecurity, and a lack of traditional diets, "First Nations and Metis children with ECC have higher levels of harmful microbial strains that increase their risk for tooth decay". We will: 1) Determine the composition of the dental microbiome and its role in severe tooth decay risk in First Nations and Metis children. The focus in this aim is to identify the strain or type of bacteria and fungi strains that are associated with S-ECC. In keeping with our established distinction-based practices, this information will be reported separately for First Nations and Metis children. 2) Physiologically characterize the bacterial strains that increase risk for S-ECC and healthy strains associated with caries-free children. The idea behind these experiments is to understand why only some dental microorganisms cause tooth decay and the local environmental factors that might influence them. This research on the dental microbiome associated with severe tooth decay will assist with new lines of possible tooth decay prevention strategies for young First Nations and Metis children.

column36: Cellular characterization of a novel putative immune biomarker of MS progression.
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease of the brain and spinal cord that affects close to 1 in 300 Canadians. MS is believed to result from the immune system mistakenly attacking myelin, which is the protective insulating material that surrounds nerve cells. Losing myelin ultimately results in nerve cell death and in disability for the individual. A number of drugs are available to treat the early, relapsing/remitting form of the disease. However, at least half of all MS patients will develop chronic progressive symptoms during their disease course, and treatment options for this form of the disease are limited. It is therefore crucial that we identify genes that could predict progressive MS and that could be potential targets for therapy. Using data mining approaches, we have identified a gene, Gpr160, whose expression is increased in white blood cells taken from people with progressive MS. In this grant application, we propose to identify the specific types of white blood cells in which Gpr160 is expressed during progressive MS. We will also study multiple blood samples taken over several years from the same patients (a "longitudinal" study) to see if Gpr160 can predict MS progression. In the second part of the study, we will use well-established mouse model of MS to study the role of GPR160 in disease processes. We will generate GPR160-knockout mice using cutting-edge CRISPR technology, and will study whether they develop less or more severe progressive disease.

column37: Sleep loss is a hallmark of modern life. Poor sleep has many consequences including impairments in attention and memory, and chronic sleep disturbances are associated with most brain disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia). Although sleep is essential for proper brain function, major issues have not been addressed in the field of sleep research. For example, it remains to be defined whether alterations in the shape of brain cells directly impact sleep quality, and whether sleep loss affects the shape of cells in various brain areas, which is inherently related to their function. Here, we propose addressing these two precise questions, together with studying sex differences, by locally manipulating specific structure of neuronal cells (i.e., spines) in distinct brain regions and assessing the impact of such manipulations on sleep and behavior. Furthermore, we will examine whether the number and shape of spines in defined brain regions, including some critical for memory and information processing, is susceptible to sleep loss and what mechanisms underlie these changes. This will be done by studying male and female mice and making use of genetic engineering, pharmacology, sleep measurements, and behavioral and biochemical approaches. Through these studies, we will define the direct bidirectional relationship between wake/sleep quality and the structure of brain cells. In addition, we will identify brain regions in which cell shape is directly affected by sleep loss, and elucidate the molecular underpinnings of these changes. Together, our research will greatly improve the knowledge about the role of sleep in brain functioning and, importantly, about negative impacts of dysregulation of brain cell structure on sleep quality and behavioral outputs. As such, the project will contribute to novel treatments to combat adverse consequences of sleep loss and poor sleep quality that are hallmarks of, for instance, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia and autism.

column36: Targeted delivery of novel inhibitors of DNA repair and combination treatments for the modulation of therapeutic response against metastatic colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related death. It is often diagnosed at the advanced stages where metastasis in nearby or distant organs is seen in patients. Patients with metastatic disease make up over 60% of CRC patients. Conventional chemotherapy treatments such as oxaliplatin and irinotecan used in the treatment of metastatic CRC, function by damaging the DNA of cancer cells. Many patients do not benefit from this treatment because their tumors have strong DNA repair systems. Our aim in this project is to develop new drugs that can block DNA repair in CRC, but do not affect normal cells, so that the toxic effects of DNA repair inhibition is not observed in normal cells. We have already found "hit" molecules that block specific DNA repair pathways in human CRC cells as well as in CRC tumors inoculated in animals. In addition, the "hit" inhibitors of DNA repair were found to sensitize CRC cells to DNA damaging chemo and radio therapy. We have also developed nano-carriers of these inhibitors of DNA repair that can direct the inhibitors of DNA repair to CRC tumors. The nano-carries of DNA repair inhibitors have shown to increase the anticancer activity of radiation therapy in CRC tumors in mice. In this project, we would develop second generation of these nanocarriers modified on their surface with molecules that can target CRC cells in metastatic sites and evaluate the activity of these systems in specific sensitization of metastatic CRC to DNA damaging chemo and radiotherapy. The toxicity of combination on normal tissues will also be evaluated. Unrepaired DNA damage can lead to the development of immunogenic tumors by several mechanisms. In this context, we will also investigate the potential of developed nanocarriers of DNA repair inhibitors in the induction of immune response against metastatic CRC. This project can generate knowledge and potentially lead to the development of new therapeutics for the treatment of advanced CRC.

column36: Coronary angiocrine control of heart regeneration
column37: Cardiovascular diseases, particularly myocardial infarction, are the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Myocardial infarction occurs when a cardiac artery is occluded, preventing the supply of blood to a portion of the cardiac muscle and causing tissue damage. After an infarct, patients cannot regenerate the lost heart muscle, developing a permanent scar that leads to heart failure. Recent studies showed that the adult human cardiac muscle retains some capacity to proliferate, indicating that stimulation of heart regeneration might be possible. This observation motivated the design of new therapies to stimulate cardiac regeneration in humans. Efficient restoration of the cardiac vasculature is critical to reduce the infarct size. Several molecules that promote vascular growth play a role in cardiac repair in non-regenerative animal models, but all failed in clinical trials revealing an urgent need to understand regenerative vascularization. Contrary to humans, zebrafish possess a unique capacity to regenerate their adult hearts after injury. As part of this regenerative response, different cell types and tissues get activated and proliferative. We found that zebrafish cardiac vessels pioneer the regenerative response. Importantly, we showed that cardiac vessels serve as a scaffold for the regenerating cardiac muscle, which follows their track towards the injury. It is increasingly clear that the vasculature can regulate processes in other tissues producing secreted (angiocrine) factors. In the heart, cardiac vessels have been classically perceived as a supply network of oxygen and nutrients, but the role of cardiac angiocrine factors during heart regeneration remains largely unexplored. The main goal of this research program is to find how vascular angiocrine factors regulate heart regeneration. Using the regenerative zebrafish model, we will learn how these factors stimulate the formation of new heart muscle after an infarct.

column36: Cortical mechanisms of visual perceptual plasticity
column37: Sensory perception allows us to interact with the world around us, and all of us are capable of learning to perceive new stimuli. How the brain implements this learning is an active area of study, but there are, broadly speaking, two possible mechanisms. The first mechanism involves changing the way neurons in the brain respond to sensory signals, and the second entails changing the connections between neurons in different brain regions. For visual perception, evidence suggests that the first method is how children learn, but that it is far less effective in adults. In this research project, we will attempt to understand the rules that govern the second kind of learning: How does the brain decide which connections to change? How much can they be changed and how quickly do the changes take place? This knowledge will allow us to design new approaches for improving visual function in normally-sighted individuals, and for restoring vision in patients who suffer from stroke or other brain injuries.

column37: Schizophrenia is a psychiatric illness with a huge burden for patients, their families, and the society. However, the reasons why some people develop Schizophrenia remain poorly understood. This proposal is anticipated to provide the first proof for a reduction of brain MAO-B levels in Schizophrenia and particularly in those who use cannabis and do not respond to current treatments. Our study, if funded, can provide a novel strategy in treating a devastating illness that affects a quarter million Canadians and their families. Our study also has the potential to identify a new treatment target in cannabis using patients.

column36: The ASSET Study: Assessing economic transitions and their impacts on health and well-being
column37: Unemployment, poverty and material insecurity (e.g. housing insecurity) are key drivers of health and well-being. This is particularly the case for inner-city, drug-using populations in the context of the ongoing and conjoined overdose and COVID- 19 health emergencies, which disproportionately impact this population. The ASSET study leverages and expands an existing pilot study, seeking to examine the dynamics and impacts of innovative economic participation in the context of multiple intersecting health challenges, with a view to identifying programmatic and policy responses to improve individual health and socioeconomic well-being. The study's objectives are to: (1) identify relationships between economic activities and individual health and socioeconomic well-being; (2) examine the impacts of the pandemic and associated government responses on participants; (3) explore how participants navigate, perceive and experience economic participation; and (4) identify modifiable barriers to and facilitators of economic participation. An ongoing cohort-based evaluation with a nested qualitative component, this study employs innovative, pandemic-appropriate remote data collection techniques, drawing on quarterly surveys and annual semi-structured interviews to assess whether and how economic participation impacts the health and well- being of inner-city, drug using populations. The study will pay specific attention to naturally occurring changes in the health, service provision and policy environment. The ASSET study works with a range of community and government partners to optimize impact, will provide data for economic-opportunity-providing organizations for internal evaluations and will inform policy and programmatic responses to ongoing health emergencies. Understanding the effectiveness of strategies to disrupt the poverty-drug use-poor health nexus in times of formidable public health crises, as this study proposes, is critical to addressing health inequity.

column37: Pain in the genital and/or pelvic regions ("genitopelvic pain") affects between 14-27% of people and can have a significant impact on one's mood, relationship, and quality of life. Addressing the unmet sexual health needs of people of all sexual orientations, sexes, and genders with genitopelvic pain is essential for the health of Canadians.

column36: Discovery and Development of Brain-Sparing Inhibitors of Succinyl-CoA:3-Ketoacid CoA Transferase
column37: Our bodies rely on 3 major fuel sources we obtain from the food we eat; fats, sugars, and protein. However, during starvation our livers make a 4th fuel source that our organs (brain, heart, and muscle are the main users) can use to make energy, the ketone body. Past research has heavily focused on understanding the regulation of fat, sugar, and protein metabolism in health, and how they malfunction in various diseases such as obesity and diabetes. The regulation of ketone body metabolism in health and disease has received much less attention. However, exciting data in our lab has shown that decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes. In addition, we have identified an old-group of drugs previously used to treat psychoses, which are able to decrease the ability of the muscle to burn ketone bodies for energy. Unfortunately, this old group of drugs is used less frequently for treating psychoses, due to the development of next generation anti-psychotic drugs, despite this old group of drugs being significantly cheaper. Importantly, this old group of drugs also appears to improve blood sugar control in obesity, but does have some brain-related side effects (e.g. drowsiness, dizziness, etc.) that may hinder its use as a therapy for diabetes. Thus, the goal of our research is to use both pharmaceutical science and chemistry methods to develop new drugs that are similar to these old group of drugs for psychoses, but are modified in a manner where they cannot reach the brain. We believe these new drugs may represent an exciting new treatment option to lower blood sugar levels in people with diabetes.

column36: Evaluating the intended and unintended consequences of opioid prescribing interventions on primary care
column37: British Columbia (BC) has been hit particularly hard by the ongoing opioid overdose epidemic. In response, the province mobilized a variety of policy levers to encourage physicians to expand access to opioid agonist treatment (OAT) including adding variants of OAT to public benefits formularies, investing in physician training, and implementing two new fees to compensate physicians who provide treatment for opioid use disorder (OUD). Meanwhile, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia (henceforth, 'the College') released the Safe Prescribing of Drugs with Potential for Misuse/Diversion practice standard which set enforceable thresholds for prescribing. Physicians found non-compliant with the new standard could be disciplined or fined. Policies aimed at expanding the provision of OAT may have positive spillover effects by expanding access to primary care physicians, thereby improving continuity and comprehensiveness of care. Meanwhile, for patients on opioid analgesics, the College's practice standard may have inadvertently restricted access to quality primary care. Given the magnitude of the opioid crisis, it is imperative to understand the consequences of changes to opioid prescribing on patients' access to quality health services. Our objective is to conduct a comprehensive investigation of the intended and unintended consequences of the changes to OAT prescribing and the College's practice standard for patients and physicians. This is a population-level, retrospective cohort study of all BC primary care physicians and their patients. Although the project uses BC data, many jurisdictions have implemented changes to prescribing in the context of the opioid epidemic, and we expect findings will be of international relevance.

One third of patients with ID are prescribed antipsychotic medications, which are known to cause significant weight gain, leading to obesity and other related diseases like diabetes. Weight gain is associated with poorer quality of life, decreased social engagement, worse medication adherence, and poorer brain function. Unfortunately, current treatments for managing obesity and other related risk factors for heart disease are inadequately studied in individuals with ID. Research has shown that the drug metformin helps to reduce the weight gain associated with antipsychotic drugs, but this has not yet been tested in adults with ID. Our preliminary findings show that metformin may be quite effective in reducing the weight gain associated with taking antipsychotic medication in adults with ID. We plan to study patients with ID who are overweight or obese and are taking antipsychotic medication to test metformin's ability to reduce body weight, and improve cardiovascular health. Participants will be randomly assigned to take either metformin or a placebo ("dummy") for 6 months. Neither patients nor study personnel know if placebo or metformin is being given. All participants will receive diet and lifestyle advice, and have their weight, blood pressure, and waist circumference measured at each visit. Participants will also do two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans, one at the start of the study and one at the end, to measure abdominal fat. After the trial is over, all participants will be given the choice to continue taking metformin for an additional 6 months. We believe that the patients taking metformin will lose a greater percentage of body weight than those who were given the placebo, leading to improvements in other heart disease risk factors, physical health and quality of life.

column36: Regenerative approaches to treat back-pain in mice and men
column37: Painful degeneration of the spine is one of the most common disabilities in young and middleaged professionals. However, very little is known about the cause of this pain and no early treatment options are currently available. In the body, all normal cells have a limited number of cell divisions where after they permanently stop dividing, they become "senescent". Senescent cells therefore build up in our tissues as we age. The number of senescent cells can drastically increase prematurely following DNA damaged, injury, cytokine exposure or cellular stress. This is called "premature stress induced senescence". Senescent cells were long thought to be inactive bystanders, however more recent discoveries have shown that they actively contribute to illnesses such as cancer, arthritis, and diabetes. Ageing and degenerating discs in the spine accumulate senescent cells where they act as small factories spewing out factors causing pain and inflammation along with enzymes that degrade the tissue. They also create an environment that prevents the heathy cells from building new tissue, and they may directly contribute to back pain. Recent studies in mice have shown that clearing of senescent cells slows many age-related problems which has a marked positive effect on spine health in older animals. There are several emerging drugs that remove senescent cells or that interfere with the effects of senescent cells coming close to clinical studies. Here we will test two drugs in intact human IVDs from organ donors as well as in a validated mouse model of back pain.

column36: Targeting bone morphogenetic protein-9 as an angioproliferative switch in pulmonary arterial hypertension
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a fatal disease that preferentially targets young women in their 30s and 40s. PAH involves the disordered and uncontrolled growth of blood vessels in the lung. This overgrowth leads to obstruction of these vessels, increased stress on the right side of the heart and eventual death due to heart failure. PAH is strongly linked to mutations in a gene called BMPR2, which encodes a protein on the surface of lung vascular cells. Interactions of this protein with a circulating factor, known as bone morphogenetic protein-9, or BMP9, has been shown to restrain the growth of lung vascular cells in healthy people. However, our previous research has shown that when the BMPR2 gene is mutated or lost, as it is in some PAH patients, BMP9 instead promotes the excessive growth of these same vascular cells. Based on this information, we hypothesize that BMP9 can serve as a "switch" that either promotes or prevents vascular growth, depending on the expression level of the BMPR2 gene. The current project will use genetically modified mice, which lack BMPR2 selectively in their blood vessels, to study the effect of BMP9 on mouse models of PAH. Additional studies will aim to understand the molecular changes within vascular cells that drive the altered BMP9 response in disease. This information will ultimately be used to develop and test candidate drugs that restore the normal growth-limiting response to BMP9, even in disease states where BMPR2 is lost. Despite the approval of several new treatments, the annual mortality rate for PAH remains high (~15%/year). The proposed work will help to clarify a completely original phenomenon that drives disease progression, with the goal of developing new treatments that are grounded in the genetics of the human disease.

column36: Overcoming Dihydrofolate Reductase Inhibitor Resistance Using Pyrimethamine-inspired Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras
column37: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is an important enzyme for folate metabolism and is a prominent anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory drug target. Commonly used DHFR therapies can effectively block folate metabolism, which impairs the production of building blocks needed for DNA synthesis. Despite their widespread use as cancer therapies, clinically used DHFR inhibitors frequently encounter resistance mechanisms that limit their efficacy. Resistance to classic DHFR inhibitors typically results from their similarity to dihydrofolate or due to overexpression of DHFR protein. To overcome DHFR inhibitor resistance, the proposed work uses an alternative DHFR inhibitor scaffold based on the anti-malaria drug Pyrimethamine (Pyr). As an anti-parasitic agent, Pyr binds to parasitic DHFR to halt replication of the parasite. We have recently shown that Pyr has promising anti-cancer activity, primarily through its ability to inhibit human DHFR. Using Pyr as a focal point, we will produce novel compounds that will not just inhibit DHFR, but will remove DHFR from cancer cells. This will be done using an approach known as Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras (PROTACs). PROTACs are bifunctional molecules, where one part will bind to DHFR and the other part will recruit proteins that tag DHFR for cellular destruction. We have recently demonstrated that Pyr-inspired PROTACs can block DHFR accumulation in cancer cells, which is a hallmark of DHFR inhibitor resistance. Specifically, this project aims to develop and optimize Pyr-inspired PROTACs. We will assess their ability to degrade DHFR in cancer cells and overcome DHFR inhibitor resistance. To accomplish these ambitious goals we have assembled a team with broad expertise in cancer biology, enzymology and drug discovery. We share the common aim to identify novel cancer therapies that can be used in the fight against cancer.

column36: Stigma and the Brain Disease Model of Chronic Pain: An Empirical Bioethics Investigation
column37: Chronic pain is highly stigmatized. People living with chronic pain frequently experience doubt, skepticism, and distrust about their experiences, resulting in poor health outcomes. These harms arise largely because pain is an invisible and subjective experience. There is no clinical test that can confirm objectively that someone is experiencing chronic pain. Some neuroscientists and clinicians suggest that advances in the brain imaging of pain demonstrates that chronic pain is a brain disease. Some researchers argue that brain disease explanations of conditions such as addiction will eliminate the stigma associated with them and improve access to treatment. However, research suggests that brain disease explanations of addiction may unintentionally increase stigma and social distance. With chronic pain neuroscience following a similar trajectory, It is unknown whether brain disease explanations of chronic pain will reduce stigma. This research builds on the findings from a CIHR SPOR grant that examined perspectives from patients and healthcare professionals about the relationship between clinical brain imaging and chronic pain. The goal of the current research is to determine the pervasiveness and influence of a brain disease explanation of chronic pain on stigma specifically. We aim to: 1) Investigate the effects of a brain disease explanation of chronic pain on the degree to which adults without chronic pain stigmatize others who live with chronic pain; and 2) Explore the influence of a brain disease explanation on stigma with members of the public, chronic pain sufferers, and healthcare professionals. A secondary aim is to explore intersectional relationships between gender, brain disease explanations, stigma, racism, and pain diagnosis. Our study will contribute an evidence-informed understanding of how a brain disease explanation influences chronic pain stigma that can guide the development of anti-stigma interventions focused on chronic pain contexts.

column36: Variation in Men's Health by Cumulative Lifetime Violence Severity and Social Determinants of Health: A Longitudinal Exploratory Study
column37: Violence is a major public health problem. Men experience and commit many forms of violence across their lifetime at home, in workplaces, and in public, yet we know little about the health effects of lifetime violence for men. Health can be linked to violence through direct injury, stress effects, or behaviours such as substance use. Social determinants of health such as gender (beliefs about what it means to be a man), income, food security, and education intersect to influence health effects of violence over time. In this study, we will conduct an online survey with a national sample of 1400 English-speaking Canadian men 3 times at 12-month intervals. We will ask about their current physical and mental health, health behaviours, social factors that affect their health, and the nature and extent of violence they have experienced in their lifetime. We will evaluate a new measure of cumulative lifetime violence severity (CLVS) that reflects how men define and sustain violence as target and perpetrator across the lifespan. We will explore differences in patterns of men's experiences of CLVS as a target and/or perpetrator in childhood through adulthood and social determinants of health that are associated with health over time. Expected outcomes of this research include: 1) increased knowledge of sub-groups of violence-affected men most at-risk for negative health outcomes; 2) validation of a new measure of CLVS for men's health research; 3) insights into variation in men's health over time according to CLVS and social determinants of health; and 4) evidence of ways in which different patterns of violence are associated with health outcomes. Together, the findings of this study will help health providers, policy makers, and other stakeholders develop programs and policies to assist men most at-risk for violence-related health problems, such as depression, chronic pain and cannabis use, to promote and manage their health.

column36: Improving Patient Mental Health With Psychotherapist Virtual Training: A Practice-Research Network Study
column37: Several types of psychotherapy are equally effective to treat mental disorders. However, many patients remain symptomatic after treatment. Our team demonstrated that a professional development training program to improve psychotherapists' skills at identifying and repairing therapeutic alliance tensions resulted in improved therapeutic alliance (an important therapeutic ingredient) and patient mental health outcomes. However, we delivered this training program by conventional in-person workshops which limited access by psychotherapists living outside large urban centres. Further, post-study interviews with therapists suggested that cultural/diversity factors complicated the therapeutic alliance. We propose to test the effectiveness and acceptability of a virtually-delivered training program to psychotherapists in urban, rural, and remote areas to improve their capacity to identify and repair problems in the therapeutic alliance, including tensions related to patient diversity. We will also examine how acceptable the virtually-delivered training is to psychotherapists, and whether they would use such training in their practice. Participants in the study will be community-based licensed psychotherapists and their patients. Patient mental health outcomes, therapeutic alliance, and diversity issues will be assessed. Our team developed Canada's largest psychotherapy practice-research network and has expertise in clinical trials, diversity, and education research of virtual training. State of the art training is often out of the reach of therapists who live outside of urban centres, and the effectiveness and acceptability of providing training virtually is not well-studied in mental health care. This study will improve psychotherapists' effectiveness at managing the therapeutic alliance and issues related to diversity, and will improve patient mental health outcomes thus promising to reduce the burden of mental illness among Canadians.

column36: Post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms of host gene expression during Leishmania infection
column37: The leishmaniases are a group of infections caused by Leishmania parasites. Globally, 12 million people are infected and 1-2 million new cases occur annually. Clinical symptoms range from cutaneous lesions to visceral pathologies that can lead to death if untreated. Unfortunately, no efficient vaccine has been developed yet and the emergence of drug resistance is a growing concern. Leishmania lives inside immune cells named macrophages, one of the most potent lines of defense against microbial invasion. To survive in such a harsh environment, Leishmania has evolved numerous mechanisms that inactivate macrophages. At the molecular level, the parasite modulates many intracellular signals required for the activation of DNA transcription into mRNA, which is the first step towards gene expression. As a result, numerous functions of the macrophage are affected. We recently demonstrated that in addition to altering transcription, Leishmania dysregulates macrophage protein synthesis, also known as mRNA translation. Our computational analyses identified subsets of host mRNAs that are differentially translated during infection which encode proteins related to mRNA metabolism and microbicidal activity. These findings led us to develop the current proposal, which is designed to explore in greater depth the mechanisms and functional consequences of altered mRNA metabolism in the progression of leishmaniasis. To this end, biochemical and genetic experimental approaches will be carried out using cellular and experimental in vivo models of Leishmania infection, and parasite strains isolated from patients living in endemic regions. The long-term goal of this study is to identify regulatory nodes implicated during leishmaniasis. Ultimately, we wish to provide insight into the pathogenesis of clinically relevant infectious organisms and to pave the way to novel therapies.

column36: Identifying a Novel Role for GDF15 during Exercise
column37: Exercise has profound effects on virtually every organ and tissue y and profoundly influences how the body utilizes carbohydrate and fats. The wide-ranging effects of exercise are mediated, at least in part, by signaling factors secreted from different tissues, such as muscle, liver and fat tissue. A recently identified signaling factor that increases with exercise is GDF15. This molecule signals to the brain and regulates food intake. In addition, we have found that GDF15 also increases the utilization of fat in the liver and the production of molecules called ketone bodies that can be taken up and used as a fuel source by other tissues like the heart and muscle. The purpose of the current project is to determine how GDF15 increases the production of ketone bodies, and then investigate if GDF15 regulates the effects of exercise on these processes. It is our hope that identifying how GDF15 controls sugar and fat metabolism and the role that it plays in exercise, will lend insight into potential new avenues to treat conditions of altered sugar metabolism such as those seen in type 2 diabetes.
