column37: Public and healthcare provider trust is the cornerstone of deceased organ donation. It is important to ensure that donors are dead and cannot suffer during the organ donation process. In donation after brain death, this is done by confirming that brain function has stopped permanently before organ retrieval. Because brain death is rare, donation after circulatory determination of death (DCDD) has become an important strategy for increasing donation opportunities. However, in contrast to donation after brain death, current DCDD protocol does not mandate confirmation of permanent cessation of brain function prior to organ retrieval. Instead, the medical community assumes-based on scientific principals-that brain function stops within 5 minutes of when the heart stops. However, some animal-based research suggests that brain function: (1) may persist beyond when the heart stops; and (2) can be restarted hours after the time of death. Without research in people regarding when brain function stops compared to when the heart stops, these reports may reduce public and healthcare provider trust in DCDD. Research in people is needed to maintain and promote stakeholder trust in the DCDD process, and to ensure that DCDD protocol protects donors from harm. We will determine when brain function stops relative to when the heart stops by monitoring electrical brain activity in patients who are taken off life support and progress to death in the intensive care unit. Our findings will increase trust in DCDD and help to protect donors from harm by providing data from people that will inform the best time for organ procurement in DCDD. This data will be critical for preserving and promoting public and healthcare provider trust in the DCDD process. This will also help address current shortages of organs in Canada, and save the lives of people urgently awaiting transplant.

column37: Combined antiretroviral therapies (ART) are highly efficient in controlling HIV replication at undetectable plasma levels, therefore improving the life quality of people living with HIV (PLWH). However, ART does not eradicate HIV and treatment interruption results in rapid viral rebound, due to the persistence of proviral HIV-DNA integrated in the genome of long-lived memory CD4+ T-cells. Therefore, a life-long treatment is recommended. In addition, ART does not prevent the multiplication of the virus inside reservoirs cells (residual transcription), a process controlled mainly by host cell molecules. This residual HIV transcription maintains a state of chronic inflammation leading to the occurrence of non-AIDS co-morbidities in ART-treated PLWH. In the past years, our group identified the helper 17 (Th17) cells, a subset of CD4+ T-cells localized at mucosal sites, as being preferential sites of HIV infection/persistence during ART and we discovered a molecular signature associated with HIV multiplication in these cells. Among these potential therapeutic targets, the master regulator transcription factor RORC2 controls the differentiation and functionality of Th17 cells. This knowledge prompted the pharmaceutical company GlaxoSmithKlein (GSK) to design selective RORC2 inhibitors (antagonists, reverse agonists) for the treatment of autoimmunity, a conditions associated with exacerbated Th17 responses. Our preliminary results demonstrate that RORC2 also regulates HIV transcription in Th17 cells. Therefore, in collaboration with internationally renowned experts in Virology/Immunology and GSK, the purpose of this proposal is to determine whether RORC2 inhibitors can be used in immune therapy strategies to reduce the deleterious consequences of residual viral transcription during ART in men and women living with HIV.

column36: Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Long-term Health Consequences
column37: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is the most common respiratory disorder of sleep and affects hundreds of millions of people globally. It is characterized by recurrent upper airway collapse leading to asphyxia and low oxygen levels. The recurrent low oxygen levels leads to oxidative stress and inflammation and this in turn can lead to many adverse health complications (e.g., vascular disease, dementia, kidney damage). We believe that oxidative stress/inflammation contribute to OSA-related outcomes, and therefore, blood markers of these processes will help us predict them. We also hypothesize that adhering to CPAP treatment will be beneficial in improving long-term health (i.e., improving brain function, kidney function, and reducing risks of cardiovascular disease). This work will help us predict (and eventually prevent) these complications in sleep apnea patients. Goals: 1. To determine whether oxidative stress/inflammatory biomarkers can help predict long-term health complications in OSA 2. To determine whether CPAP adherence improves outcomes Methods: This proposal will use an ongoing project that is establishing a large group of patients with suspected OSA who receive a sleep study at one of six sleep centres. They have blood, extensive survey, and cognitive performance information collected at baseline. Patients will return for follow up 4-5 years after initial assessment for repeat blood collection, brain function, and detailed survey data. Detailed OSA treatment information (e.g., CPAP adherence from machine downloads) will also be obtained. Baseline and follow-up samples will be processed for inflammatory markers. For the first goal, we will determine whether baseline markers are associated with future adverse outcomes. For the second aim, the impact of CPAP adherence on outcomes will be assessed by comparing those who use and don't use CPAP using complex statistical matching.

column37: The epidemic of diabetes continues to grow across the world and our country. Currently, 1 in 3 Canadians lives with prediabetes or diabetes. In some communities that rate soars above 60%. For Indigenous Canadians, that risk is 80%. Canadians under 20 years of age now face a 50% chance of developing the disease in their lifetime. Diabetes has cost our healthcare system $16 B/y in 2020 representing 30.7% of the total health care system cost. Without prompt action, diabetes threatens not only an increasing number of Canadians but also the viability of our healthcare system. A small cluster of cells known as the islets of Langerhans are responsible for the release of insulin to regulate blood sugar levels. The loss of these cells ability to produce insulin is the origin of diabetes. Patients are treated with a lifetime administration of exogenous insulin to achieve normoglycemia. Other alternative is the islet transplantation as a viable treatment option for Type 1 diabetes (T1D). However, islet transplantation suffers from immunogenicity which leads to the dysfunction and eventual loss of the graft. To overcome this reaction, one strategy involves forming a protective barrier that can maintain the function of the cells while shielding them from immune attacks. A key feature of such barrier its thickness and the transplant volume to make sure cells can have adequate circulation of nutrients/waste as well as glucose and oxygen. As such, the aim is developing a conformal coating to provide a nanoscale barrier between islets and their environment with adequate stability and immunoprotection, while regulating the circulation of materials into and out of the cells. To achieve this goal, the nanocoating on islets will be developed using polysaccharide-based polyelectrolytes. The coated islet will be fully characterized in vitro and in proper mice model to assess the coated islet functionality and the absence of immunogenicity for their transplantation and treatment of T1D.

column36: The role of myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF) in polycystic kidney disease
column37: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is the most common inherited disorder of the kidney, affecting 1 in every 500 people. The vast majority of PKD cases are caused by a mutation or loss of one of two proteins, polycytsin 1 or 2. These proteins are located in the mechanical and chemical antenna of the cells, the so called primary cilium. The loss of polycystin function leads to the formation of large fluid-filled cysts, because it disturbs normal cell division in the renal tubules, the system responsible for resorbing nutrients and secreting waste products. Beside cyst formation, the other major feature of PKD is progressive organ scarring or fibrosis. This is a key problem because fibrosis completely disrupts the normal tissue architecture and leads to end-stage renal disease. The mechanism of how PKD leads to fibrosis is not understood, and currently there is no cure for the disease. Our previous studies showed that tubular cells play a major role in fibrosis because they can secrete scar-inducing chemical mediators (cytokines). We showed that myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF), a protein regulating gene expression, is a central inducer of this process. Our preliminary data show that the level of MRTF is highly increased in mouse and human PKD tissue samples, and MRTF relocates into the nuclei of tubular cells. Based on these intriguing findings we surmise that MRTF is a key mediator in PKD, and a major contributor to the ensuing fibrosis. We will test this hypothesis by using a variety of cellular models, stem cell-derived kidney tissue (organoids), animal models and human samples. Utilizing a set of sophisticated molecular approaches we will examine whether genetic or pharmacological inhibition of MRTF ameliorates PKD. These studies may lead to completely new therapeutic approaches to treat this common and incurable kidney disease.

column36: Manipulating methionine metabolism to shape immune responses and modify disease progression in both sexes in MS
column37: Western diet and obesity are risk factors for multiple sclerosis (MS), an inflammatory neurological disorder affecting 1 in 500 Canadians. Diet and obesity influence the activation of the immune system, a key player in MS. Immune cells are indeed considered to orchestrate an aberrant 'attack' of the immune system against the brain and spinal cord in MS. Immune cells use available nutrients to proliferate and to produce proinflammatory factors that lead to injury of the brain and spinal cord. By limiting the presence of the essential amino acid methionine in the culture medium of immune cells, we were able to decrease their activation and to limit their production of pro-inflammatory factors. Importantly, restriction of methionine in the diet of the mouse model of MS resulted in a significant delay of onset of MS-like symptoms. Based on these results, we propose to investigate the role that methionine metabolism has on the activation of the immune system and its capacity to infiltrate the brain and spinal cord in animal models of MS. Since methionine metabolism can differ between men and women, and as MS frequency and evolution are influenced by biological sex, we will specifically assess the impact of dietary methionine intake on the risk to develop MS-like symptoms in males versus in females in an active and a spontaneous mouse model of MS, as the latter mimics the course of MS in humans. We will use these pre-clinical models to identify the mechanisms by which manipulating methionine influences the activation and function of the immune cells, including through regulation of the expression of genes for immune-related factors. We will also investigate if methionine metabolism is different in MS patients according to sex and versus healthy controls. This proposal will assess whether we can use specific dietary and pharmacological interventions modulating immune cell methionine metabolism as a therapeutic intervention to improve MS in women and men.

column36: Options for Increasing Plasma Supply in Canada: A Health Economic Preference and Modelling Study (HEMO-CAN)
column37: Plasma is the liquid component of blood and is collected from donors. It is used for transfusions in hospitals, and for the manufacture of treatments that are used for patients with various chronic and life-threatening conditions. But we currently do not receive enough plasma from donors in Canada, and this will only get worse as the demand for plasma is increasing. The Canadian Blood Service is considering how to best invest in new donor centres that will increase plasma donations. There are a number of different options to consider - from where to geographically place the centres, to what hours the centres should be open, to what incentives to provide such as free meals. All these options have different costs- from rents and material costs to staff salaries, and it can be hard to predict how impactful these different options will be on overall volume of plasma donated. This project will survey existing blood donors and non donors to understand the impact of these different options on their willingness to donate. This will enable us to predict what locations, and features will result in the most plasma being donated. We expect people will say they will donate more than they actually do, but because people tend to do this in a predictable way, we will be able to adjust for this. The results of the surveys will be combined with costs in a model. For example, one option (e.g. a centre in a downtown) might be expected to obtain a 20% higher volume of donated plasma, but if this comes at an additional 50% cost, it might not be the best investment. The model will inform which options and locations are expected to provide the most plasma donation for the CBS investment budget.

column36: Mechanisms of Endosomal Acid-Base Imbalance linked to Interneuron Circuit Dysfunction in Christianson Syndrome
column37: Neuronal networks consist of different types of neurons that all play their own role in order to maintain proper network function. The two main types of neurons segregate in excitatory and inhibitory neurons, which together regulate the flow of information through the network. It has been proposed that changes in the relative strength in these two opposing forces underlie the symptoms observed in many psychiatric disorders, including autism and schizophrenia. Recently downregulation of NHE6 has been associated with with a rare and severe autism-related condition known as Christianson syndrome, generalized autism and Alzheimer's disease. NHE6 regulates the pH of intracellular membrane vesicles called 'recycling endosomes' that play important roles in the targeted delivery of growth factor and neurotransmitter receptors to synapses. Inappropriate trafficking of such cargo inside the synapse results in malformation of the neuronal circuitry in the brain, which can lead to progressive motor impairment (called ataxia), epilepsy (imbalance between excitation and inhibition in the brain), and intellectual disability, all of which have a devastating effect on the wellbeing of the individual. In this grant we build on our previous published work and extensive preliminary data. We will investigate the mechanisms of how lack of NHE6 leads to defects in excitatory inhibitory synapse maturation, and neural circuit formation in the hippocampus an area of the brain involved in learning and memory. We have developed novel tools and assembled a multidisciplined team putting us in a unique position to make groundbreaking discoveries. This work will result in important findings that could directly contribute to our better understanding of neurocircruitry development and shed new insights into the contributions of NHE6 to human health and disease, and identification of efficacious strategies for disease treatment.

column36: How Missed Care Occurs in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of Care Aides' Perspectives
column37: Care aides (also called personal support workers or nursing assistants) give most of the hands-on care for older adults who live in nursing homes. For example, care aides help these nursing home residents with eating, taking baths and other daily activities. However, care aides often leave some of these tasks undone. This is partly because nursing homes do not have enough care aides to finish all the tasks each day. Yet lack of staff alone does not explain why some tasks are left undone. Researchers found that care aides in nursing homes with good staffing also reported care tasks left undone. Besides having too few care aides to help nursing home residents each day, what other factors can cause care aides to leave tasks undone? How these factors cause tasks to be left undone? What changes can be made to prevent tasks from being left undone? Our study will answer these questions by asking care aides themselves. We will have detailed conversations with about 48 care aides who work in nursing homes in Alberta and British Columbia. We will ask them questions such as: What happened when you left tasks undone? What could have helped you to complete the tasks? We will use the knowledge that we learn from this study to help care aides reduce tasks left undone. We will apply the new knowledge to co-design, with care aides, strategies that they can use at work to avoid leaving tasks undone in daily care for residents. Our long-term goal is to improve the quality of care and quality of life for residents in nursing homes.

column36: The REM-Spike Project: A Set Theoretic Concordance Evaluation of Rapid Eye Movement Sleep in Localizing the Epileptogenic Zone
column37: Around 65 million people worldwide have epilepsy, which is the tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures. Everyone's lifetime risk is 1 in 26, which translates into over 1.4 million Canadians. While medications can often control seizures, just under half a million Canadians will still have unrelenting epilepsy with devastating everyday consequences on driving, working, quality of life, and even survival. Though medications can control seizures, they often come at the cost of debilitating side effects. In such cases, epilepsy neurosurgery is the preferred treatment; however, many individuals cannot qualify for surgery because the part of the brain giving rise to seizures - the "epileptogenic zone" (EZ) - cannot be identified, or cannot be narrowed down enough for surgery to be safe enough to avoid severe neurological deficits. To identify the EZ, brainwaves are recorded on a test known as the electroencephalogram (EEG) that records the electrical signature of epileptic activity. This signature varies widely depending on whether the patient is asleep or awake. In rapid eye movement (REM) sleep when most dreaming occurs, the EEG footprint of epileptic activity in the brain is thought to be smaller. Using actual EEG and magnetic resonance imaging data from patients with epilepsy, this project aims to rigorously quantify the size and location of epileptic activity to determine whether the EZ really is smaller in REM sleep. This project will also compare how much the EZ in REM sleep overlaps with the EZ recorded while awake or in other stages of sleep. These comparisons will determine whether REM sleep is the best state of consciousness to find the EZ. This project holds the promise of one day safely offering life-changing epilepsy neurosurgery to more patients than currently possible by using dreams to map out where seizures arise within the human brain.

column36: Infection Control in ERCP using a Duodenoscope with a Disposable Cap (ICECAP)
column37: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is an important procedure used to diagnose and treat conditions of the pancreas or bile ducts. ERCP is universally performed using a specialized instrument called a duodenoscope. Due to their specific design, duodenoscopes are among the most complicated medical devices to sterilize. This is mainly due to an inaccessible area in the scope tip that makes manual and automated disinfection very difficult, meaning that bacteria can remain in the scope even after intensive cleaning processes. A contaminated scope can then pass on the bacteria to the next patient(s) who have a procedure with that scope, which could result in a serious infection. There has been a sharp recent rise in rates of duodenoscope-related infections and outbreaks. A large proportion of these outbreaks have been unrelated to any identifiable breaches in disinfection protocols. This has led doctors and scientists to question whether we need to improve on traditional duodenoscope designs. More alarmingly, these outbreaks are increasingly involving multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs). These organisms are much more difficult to treat with available antibiotics, and mean significantly higher rates of worse outcomes for patients, including death. Newer duodenoscopes with disposable caps have been approved for use in Canada. These devices could significantly reduce the primary source of persistent duodenoscope contamination, and therefore also lower the risk of transmission and illness for other patients. However, it has not yet been proven whether this design actually results in lower bacterial contamination after cleaning processes. Also, it has not yet been proven whether these scopes perform as well at the ERCP procedure, which is also crucial before hospitals decide to use them. This study aims to compare this newer scope design to the traditional scope design in terms of bacterial contamination rates and performance characteristics.

column37: In patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), the decision to initiate dialysis is based on the degree of kidney dysfunction as well as the presence of any acute indications including high acid levels, high potassium and fluid overload. In patients without any acute indications, the decision to initiate dialysis is subjective and based on a constellation of "uremic" symptoms, nutrition, and physical factors. Examples of "uremic" symptoms include anxiety, depression, difficulty sleeping, nausea and vomiting, poor appetite, fatigue, itchiness and restless legs. These symptoms are thought to be due to the accumulation of "uremic toxins" normally cleared by the kidney which may or may not be removed by dialysis. How individual uremic symptoms respond to dialysis is unknown. If clinicians were able toaccurately predict which uremic symptoms are responsive to dialysis, this could improve decision-making regarding starting long term dialysis. Patients with uremic symptoms responsive to dialysis might be able to start dialysis earlier with improved quality of life and patients with uremic symptoms unresponsive to dialysis might be able to continue to defer dialysis and avoid its potential harms (e.g. infection, heart problems). Our study will evaluate the trajectory of uremic symptoms in adults with advanced CKD followed by kidney doctors in ten or more clinics across Canada. It will identify which symptoms are responsive to dialysis as well as determine which specific uremic toxins are responsible for individual symptoms including restless legs, mood, itchiness, fatigue and nausea/vomiting. The study will be used to inform dialysis decision-making based on uremic symptoms and help us understand why some symptoms occur in some patients while other do not.

column37: Cancer immunotherapy uses a patient's immune system to fight cancer. Unfortunately, until recently, most cancer immunotherapies did not work for most patients, or caused severe side effects, and almost all failed. The dream of a successful cancer immunotherapy treatment only came to life in the last few years. This breakthrough approach targets a recently discovered way to jump-start the immune system, using immune checkpoints' inhibitors. The discovery of these immune checkpoints pathways was recognized by a Nobel Prize in 2018. Drugs targeting these pathways activate a patient's immune system and allow it to recognize and kill tumors. They are game-changers for cancer. For example, combining two of them helped 88% of metastatic melanoma patients to live for two years. Traditional treatment results only in 10% of patients with this disease to live for two years. Current available drugs targeting the immune checkpoints are limited to monoclonal antibodies. While yielding impressive clinical response rates, they still have many limitations. For example, they require intravenous route of administration and stay active for weeks in the body, making side effects hard to control. They are also very expensive, making them inaccessible to many cancer patients. Our proposal seeks to develop an alternative therapy to these antibodies. Our alternative therapy is a small molecule immune checkpoint inhibitor. Once developed, our treatment can be much cheaper to manufacture, can be taken orally, taken each day and is only active for a short time (less than one day) in the body. This allows precise dose adjustments, which should reduce serious side effects of current immune checkpoints' antibody-based therapies.

column36: Blocking the metastatic spread of uveal melanoma
column37: Metastasis is the dissemination of cancer cells from their birthplace in the body to distant organs. As it turns out, this is an inefficient process. Of the millions of cells in the primary tumor, only a small subset manage to gain access to the lymphatic or circulatory systems and an even smaller fraction ever colonize a distant site or grow into a clinically relevant tumor. Unfortunately, the inefficiency of the process does not lessen its devastating effects: metastatic stage cancer is very difficult to treat and remains a critical problem in medicine. In this grant proposal, we describe how we will study the ways in which cancer cells become metastatic. There are three key potential mechanisms that have previously been linked to metastatic behavior. The first involves changes to the physical characteristics of the tumor cells, in a way that promotes cell invasion and migration. The second mechanism involves the regulation of gene expression through reversible marks left on the genome, called epigenetic alterations. The third mechanism involves immune cell infiltration into the tumor, which generates inflammation and immune suppression. We have developed a new model system to study the metastasis of melanoma, an aggressive cancer of the pigment cells. What is unique about our model is that the melanoma begins within the eyes and then spreads to the liver and lungs. This type of cancer is called uveal melanoma. It is the most common eye cancer and it is deadly. Uveal melanoma metastasizes in half of all patients, after which there is no effective treatment. A better understanding of the ways that cancer cells escape the primary tumor and adapt to survive in different parts of the body will help us develop more effective therapies for late stage cancers.

column37: The intestine is under constant assault by infectious and physical insults. To counter these environmental challenges, this barrier organ has evolved various defensive measures to counter invasive pathogens and quickly repair itself after injury. The remarkable regenerative capacity of the gut relies on dynamic interactions between the immune system and stem cells that give rise to the epithelium, a thin layer of cells that protect our tissues from the outside world. However, the ways in which immune cells and stem cells coordinate tissue regeneration remains poorly understood. To discover new pathways that promote tissue healing, our group has turned to intestinal helminths, one of the most prevalent parasites of the animal kingdom. Helminths are multicellular worms that migrate through tissues leaving significant damage in their wake. Resistance to helminths requires striking changes to the intestinal epithelium that not only repair the damaged tissue, but also lead to parasite expulsion. Thus, parasitic helminth infection provides a powerful model system to investigate how immune-stem cell interactions orchestrate tissue regeneration. Using animal models of helminth infection to track how the immune response shapes the fate and function of intestinal stem cells, our studies will uncover previously unrecognized mechanisms of tissue repair that may lead to new therapies for regenerative medicine.

column36: Targeting mRNA translation to effectively treat uveal melanoma.
column37: There is no cure for metastatic uveal melanoma. Although there has been considerable progress made on other types of melanoma, such as cutaneous melanoma, we have made very little progress on metastatic uveal melanoma. This is why our team is dedicated to exploring the possibility of a new treatment strategy for this disease, by using inhibitors of mRNA translation. column37: Canada is entering its second year of a public health emergency, with each province/territory employing varying containment policies given differences in the extent and intensity of the pandemic across the country. As the pandemic continues, Canadian children, youth (hereafter, children) and their families face major economic, social and psychosocial stressors. The impact of these stressors on health and well-being will likely be unequal, disproportionately affecting families living in adverse socio-economic circumstances, as well as those with pre-existing physical, mental and neurodevelopmental conditions. The magnitude and distribution of these impacts for Canadian children and their families, however, remains largely unknown. To understand impact and inform policy responses and practice, reliable evidence collected at the population level, with comparable pre-pandemic data, is required. We propose to leverage the 2019 Canadian Health Survey of Children and Youth (CHSCY) - a nationally-representative sample of 26,870 children aged 1-17 years with data collected by Statistics Canada immediately prior to the pandemic - and conduct a follow-up survey with this sample in 2022, when they are 4-20 years of age. In doing so, we will: (a) examine longitudinal changes in health and functioning, before versus after the pandemic; and (b) examine the extent to which changes in health and functioning are more pronounced for specific population subgroups and communities. By documenting the scale of change in population health over time (pre- vs. post-pandemic) and by identifying sub-groups most vulnerable to ill-health, we will provide policymakers and service provides with reliable, high-quality evidence to inform resource allocation, universal and targeted intervention strategies, and mitigation strategies for future pandemic preparedness.

column36: The Implementation Playbook: e-health technology for effective implementation of evidence-based interventions
column37: Evidence-based interventions are necessary for improving health outcomes; however, their implementation is complex, often disorganized, subject to high rates of failure, and can take years to navigate, making it costly and resource-intensive. International consensus argues there is an urgent need to improve implementation. Effective implementation is best guided by implementation science (IS), the study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of evidence-based practices. However, healthcare organizations lack know-how in evidence-based implementation processes. They are not aware of the evidence, and when they are, they have difficulty putting it to use. To address this gap, we propose to develop an innovative software platform (The Implementation Playbook) that will help stakeholders to apply a systematic approach to implementation guided by prevailing IS evidence. Based on pilot work, we will i) develop a testable minimum viable software prototype; and ii) evaluate its' feasibility in six healthcare organizations. The team are experts in implementation science and practice, e-health and user-centred design, knowledge users/implementers of evidence, and patients/consumers. The Implementation Playbook will facilitate effective implementation and optimal outcomes by transcending limitations of existing implementation supports that are passive, text-based, variably informed by evidence, and resource-intensive. We will explore whether The Playbook can be used autonomously, thereby circumventing reliance on costly in-person implementation assistance that is not widely available to healthcare organizations. We will also explore if the software platform is useful for different organizations and interventions being implemented, as it will be based on the universal core components of effective implementation. The Playbook's external validity will make it exceedingly usable and scalable beyond healthcare.

An estimated 30-60% of all patients treated in these services belong to this category, which some analysts regard as a source of emergency department overuse or misuse. The debate has been complicated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which has shifted primary care practices and walk-in clinics significantly towards telemedicine (remote or virtual consultation by phone or videoconferencing), presumably a more convenient and efficient consultation modality under the circumstances. As healthcare expenditures continue to rise, the most efficient care pathways must be identified and strengthened in order to ensure sustainable healthcare systems for all Canadians. column36: Demystifying the role of esophageal stem cells in esophageal diseases
column37: What are stem cells? They are the "orchestra conductor" in an organism. First, they are a rare population of cells that can self-renew. That means that when it will divide, it will produce two daughter cells: one of which is identical to the "mother" cell assuring the prosperity of its descendants. Second, stem cells have the capacities to give rise to all the cell types from an organ. The best stem cell example is the zygote formed when the spermatozoid fused with the egg, it will later form a baby comprising a multitude of different cell types. Stem cells are highly active in embryos but also in adult tissues. On a daily basis, they produce new cells to compensate for all the cells that are lost. They are also key players in tissue healing upon injury like bone fracture, gut inflammation or skin burns. Unfortunately, they have two faces: the Good and the Bad. Indeed, in cancer by example, they are linked to tumor formation and resistance to treatment. Since they divide frequently, they are more prone to form a tumor if they acquire sufficient number of mutations. Also, through several mechanisms they are able to survive to anti-cancer treatments such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy. They would then be "hiding" or "sleeping" at the tumor site ready to divide again and form a new tumor leading to cancer relapse. They are therefore a major issue in oncology. Our goal? Specifically target stem cells to improve tissue repair and cure cancer. Our lab particularly focuses on the esophagus because it is covered by an actively dividing epithelium. Also, it is an organ severely affected by inflammation due to acid reflux by example, which affects roughly 15% of Canadians. Furthermore, esophageal cancer is also a deadly cancer with only 15% of patients surviving 5 year following their diagnosis due to high rate of cancer relapse. Thus, we are studying the role of esophageal stem cells in these diseases to find new therapeutic approaches to improve the life of patients.

column36: Distributed Machine Learning for Diagnosis and Treatment Decision Support of Pediatric Brain Tumors
column37: In an increasingly data-driven world, artificial intelligence is expected to be a key tool for converting the big data into tangible benefits. Machine learning, a sub-field of artificial intelligence, aims to identify complex patterns in multi-dimensional data and use these uncovered patterns to classify or make predictions on new unseen cases. However, many datasets are typically needed for training of the advanced machine learning models to produce highly accurate results. This is also the main limiting factor why these advanced machine learning models cannot unfold their full potential in health care applications if personal or other sensitive data is used that data owners cannot or will not share for training of a machine learning model at a central location. The main goal of the distributed learning architecture is that the individual patient data does not leave the contributing clinical centers but are only used locally to train the machine learning models, which do not contain any patient data at the individual level anymore. In this research project, we will invent, develop, implement, and evaluate multiple approaches for distributed machine learning model training that have the potential to improve diagnosis and treatment of children with brain tumors.

Yet, many have developmental disabilities that become apparent over time and include challenges in thinking, socializing, language, and behaviour. Our work has shown that brain injury and disrupted brain growth are common in these babies. Yet, we do not know why some children with these brain changes have developmental challenges while others do not. We focus on the two most common types of heart defects cared for in the newborn period. Newborns with these heart conditions require early surgery, but their brain oxygen supplies differ after heart surgery. Studying children with these heart conditions can help us understand how better heart function improves brain growth and function. A new measure of brain function will now be used to study brain information exchange and processing when children are doing tasks important for thinking skills. We will: 1. Determine how a child's heart function modifies the relationship between newborn brain injury and the child's functions and behaviour at age 5 years. 2. Determine how the way the brain processes information at age 5 years is linked to specific thinking skills, and how this is modified by (a) newborn brain injury and (b) a child's heart function. Through this work, we hope to identify specific opportunities to promote optimal child development.

Altogether, with this project, our team will aim at improving our knowledge of NAFLD and at finding new and safe drugs to help patients living with NAFLD.

column36: Study of the Innate Immune Response to Drugs that Cause IDRs
column37: Adverse drug reactions are a significant problem. One type, called idiosyncratic drug reactions (IDRs), do not occur in most patients but can be life threatening when they do occur. Their unpredictable nature makes them a major problem for patients, drug development, and for regulatory agencies. Because they are very unpredictable, they are very difficult to study. There is a large amount of evidence that they are mediated by the immune system. This is analogous to how most people are not allergic to peanuts, but the allergy can be fatal for people who are allergic. Although most patients do not have a serious reaction when they take drugs that can cause IDRs, there is evidence that most patients and animals do have an immune response, called an innate immune response. This innate response happens early, causes no symptoms, and usually resolves on its own. It is only when the innate immune response leads to an adaptive immune response that a serious IDR occurs. The adaptive immune response is dependent on genetics and previous exposure to other agents, which is why, like other allergies, it is idiosyncratic. It is this initial asymptomatic innate immune response to drugs that can cause serious IDRs that we will study, first in animals and then in humans. With a better understanding of this innate immune response we should be able to predict which drug candidates are likely to cause serious IDRs and which patients may be at risk. In addition, a better mechanistic understanding may lead to ways to treat patients experiencing IDRs, or even prevent them altogether. Ultimately, these studies are likely to lead to increased drug safety and decreased health care costs. Already our mechanistic studies have led to a method to prevent severe adverse reactions to a new anti-seizure medication, which led to its approval by the US Food and Drug Administration. I am also consulting for another company to improve the safety of another drug.

column36: The role of glia plasticity in salt-dependent hypertension
column37: Hypertension is the leading cause of death and disability in industrialized countries, accounting for 9.4 million deaths each year. In 2010, the estimated cost of hypertension treatment across Canada was ~ $13.9 billion, and the number is projected to rise to over $20 billion by 2020. While numerous effective antihypertensive drugs are available, up to 30% of patients are resistant to these treatments and do not respond to any available medication nor their combinations. In Canada, over 6 million are hypertensive, and in ~30% of these individuals, hypertension remains uncontrolled. Thus, additional therapeutics are needed to target this population of hypertensive individuals. Excessive dietary salt is strongly correlated with cardiovascular diseases and is regarded as a major contributing factor to hypertension. While the link between salt and hypertension is well established, the mechanisms by which high dietary salt intake leads to increased blood pressure remain unclear. Increases in plasma sodium are detected by specialized brain centers, causing an activation of neurons that secrete vasopressin (VP). VP is antidiuretic hormone that mediates water retention in the kidney and causes the constriction of blood vessels, contributing to the elevation of blood pressure. We propose to study the molecular mechanisms by which high salt intake leads to excessive secretion of VP, leading to hypertension. Our hypothesis is that high salt intake provokes inflammatory processes in specialized brain centers controlling VP neuron activity, leading to exaggerated activation of VP neurons. This, in turn, leads to enhanced VP secretion, fluid retention and vasoconstriction and thereby increases blood pressure. The proposed research program will elucidate the mechanisms modulating VP release in hypertension. A better understanding of how high salt intake alters mechanisms controlling VP secretion may therefore lead to novel approaches for treating hypertension.

column36: Alpha-Particle Radioimmunotherapy of Brain Metastases from HER2-Positive Breast Cancer
column37: Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is an effective drug for treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer that has spread to other organs in the body. However, this drug is not effective for treatment of breast cancer that has spread to the brain because it penetrates the brain in only limited amounts that are not sufficient for eradicating tumours. This is due to the blood-brain-barrier (BBB) which prevents trastuzumab from being taken up into the brain. In the proposed research, we plan to develop a more potent form of trastuzumab by linking the drug to a radioisotope, actinium-225 that emits a type of radiation called alpha particles that is very powerful for killing cancer cells. column36: Impact of tandem repeat expansions in schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a serious and disabling illness that affects about 1 in 100 people. The causes are mostly unknown for this brain disease that often affects youths, seemingly at random in a family. Recent studies have however identified relevant genetic changes in some cases. By applying the latest technologies, we aim to identify previously undiscovered genetic changes. Because the schizophrenia illness itself appears the same, regardless of the high-impact genetic changes identified, insights gained can help us learn about schizophrenia more generally. Using a highly detailed method called whole genome sequencing, our group has recently found that in some individuals with schizophrenia there are genetic changes called tandem repeat expansions known to cause neurological diseases. Also, we have discovered new types of tandem repeat expansions that increase risk of autism. We will now apply advanced genetic methods to a Canadian community-based sample of 640 individuals with schizophrenia where we already have DNA available for study. We will identify these special genetic changes, determine where they are in the human genome, and whether and to what degree they expand within families, as they do in other diseases. We will assess genetic changes with respect to important clinical features relevant to schizophrenia. Discovering new types of genetic changes involved in causing schizophrenia is important for learning about the biological pathways that lead to illness expression - as it has been for other illnesses like cancer and heart disease, leading to new treatment possibilities and clinical diagnostic testing.

column36: Co-Creating a Rehabilitation Strategy to Support the Psychosocial Recovery of Individuals with Long COVID
column37: About 35% of COVID-19 patients experience 'long COVID' (LC), which means they face at least one long-lasting COVID symptom (e.g. fatigue) 28 days or longer since they first became ill. Persons with LC (PWLC) feel left behind by the healthcare system (because we don't know a lot about LC yet) and socially excluded (because people are afraid that they are still infectious). Since PWLC also face physical and mental health challenges, this can all make it very hard for them to return to work and participate in social and community activities the way they used to. Rehabilitation (rehab) care is known to improve patients' physical and social functioning. However, most rehab for PWLC has been very focused on the physical aspects of recovery, while the psychological and social aspects of care have not receive a lot of attention. For our project, we want to learn more about PWLC's experiences with LC and how it affects their quality of life and ability to participate in activities that are important to them (e.g. employment). We also want to learn about family caregivers' experiences and needs since they play an important role in supporting PWLC. To do this, we will first ask PWLC to complete a survey asking them about their symptoms and how LC affects their quality of life. We will then interview LC patients, family caregivers, and healthcare providers (HCPs) to gain more detailed information about their experiences with LC, what kinds of support they need, and how rehab can help them to participate in the community and other social activities. The second stage of our project will bring together PWLC, caregivers, and HCPs to create a plan for how rehab can help imrpove community participation and quality of life for PWLC and their caregivers. Finally, we will bring together PWLC, caregivers, HCPs, and decision makers in a series of meetings to further improve the rehab plan and make it relevant for different places in Canada.

column36: Identifications and functional characterization of proteins involved in Listeria monocytogenes cell-to-cell spreading during pregnancy
column37: Listeria infections are a constant concern to pregnant women as these bacteria can cause premature delivery and death of the baby. During these infections, the bacteria enter cells and hide from the immune system as they move from one cell to another within the placenta to infect the fetus. To move from cell-to-cell, rocket-like structures form behind the bacteria that push Listeria against the border of the cells that they have already infected. This forms finger-like protrusions (that are led by the bacteria) in the infected cells called listeriopods that press into the borders of the neighbouring cells making corresponding invaginations that suck the listeriopods into the cells using a process requiring an internalization protein called caveolin-1. To initiate our study we will examine the role of a caveolin-1 associated protein called EphB1 and its binding partner, Ephrin B1, during the cell-to-cell movement of Listeria. We are certain that there are also many undiscovered proteins required for Listeria to move from one cell to another. To identify those proteins we will use 2 unbiased strategies. First, we will isolate listeriopods and use proteomics to identify the proteins at the structures. Then we will pre-infect cells with Listeria, mix those infected cells with uninfected cells that have had 1 gene (and thus the corresponding protein) removed from each cell and examine the genetically altered cells that have blocked Listeria entry. By studying all genes in the human genome we will identify genes/proteins that are involved in the cell-to-cell movement of the bacteria. Confirmation and characterization of the identified proteins will then be pursued in detail in cultured placental cells then in the placentas of infected mice. Through this work we will identify and functionally characterize proteins used for the cell-to-cell movement of Listeria in the placenta and will provide targets for future work aimed at developing molecules to block the infections.

column36: Patient and Family Perspectives on Operationalized Assent in Canadian Pediatric Intensive Care Research: A Survey and Interview Study
column37: In pediatric research, permission for a child to participate is usually obtained from the child's legal guardian. When possible, the child also participates in the decision making and gets to voice whether or not they would like to be part of the study. This important process is referred to as "assent". Children in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) are suffering from critical illness, and often have high levels of distress. Most PICU studies require time-sensitive enrollment within the first 24-48 hours after the child has been admitted. As a result, obtaining assent for research in the PICU is very challenging, especially because there are no clear guidelines on the best assent processes to use in this unique population. Our long-term goal is to develop guidelines for assent in Canadian pediatric critical care research. However, it is very important that these guidelines are based on patient and family preferences. The goal of this proposal is to explore the perspectives of PICU patients and their parents/caregivers towards assent in the PICU, including how they would like the assent process to be carried out and their perceived barriers to the assent process in this environment. To do this, we will perform two studies, a survey study and an interview study, in four Canadian PICUs. Twenty PICU patients and 20 parents/caregivers of PICU patients will be invited to participate in the interview study, and 100 families will be invited to participate in the survey study. We will aim to recruit a diverse study cohort, with specific attention paid to underrepresented minorities. The results of these studies will represent the initial step towards creating guidelines for assent in Canadian PICU research. Clear guidance will address the challenges associated with obtaining assent for research in the PICU, and increase the frequency of involving PICU patients in the decision-making process around research participation.

column36: Circadian clock regulatory mechanisms and the etiology of behavioural disorders
column37: Approximately one in three Canadians experience a mental illness like depression in their lifetime, which costs Canadian society $51 billion every year. Current drugs are not always effective and can have unwanted side effects. We need better treatments with fewer side effects. To develop these treatments, we first need to understand how mental illnesses happen. We use fruit flies to study the effects of mental illness on the brain. Sleep-wake cycles, or circadian rhythms, are controlled by coordinating functions of different parts of the brain. Some people with mental illnesses have mutations in genes controlling these sleep-wake cycles. We plan to learn how these mutations cause mental illness. We discovered that mutations in some sleep-wake cycle genes disrupt some parts of the brain, but not other parts. This causes different parts of the brain to cycle at different rates, disrupting the whole brain. We believe that this may be one way in which mental illnesses develop. We will study this problem three ways. (1) We will study how gene mutations change the function of the gene, and how other proteins in brain cells act on the gene. (2) We will then study how these mutations affect the function of different brain cells. (3) We will use what we have learned to understand why so many mutations in genes that are connected with mental illnesses cause changes in behaviours, like sleep, fighting, eating and memory. (4) We will artificially change different parts of the brain to see if we can cause the same change in behaviours as mutations. Overall, we will study the molecules, the brain cells and the behaviours to gain a complete picture of how mutations in circadian genes cause mental illnesses.

column36: A mixed methods study to evaluate functional recovery, care needs, and caregiver needs in older adults undergoing surgery: The Frail sub-study of the Fit After Surgery study
column37: In developed countries around the world, about 190 million people have surgery every year. Many of them are older and have pre-existing health problems such as heart disease. A study already underway (called the Fit After Surgery study) funded by CIHR is looking at how well patients who are over 65 recover after surgery. For example, are they more disabled after surgery than they were before? What kinds of things might happen after surgery that makes life more difficult? We plan to build on this study to find out more information. We will specifically look at those older adults who are over 65 and are frail. That is, they are more likely to have many health issues that affect how well they can do their daily activities compared to other older adults. What happens when they leave the hospital? Do they need more care from their caregivers? Do they function as well as they did before surgery? A very important but unanswered question is whether their caregivers are able to provide all the care they need. This can be difficult when caregivers also have health issues. To answer these questions, we plan to do an in-depth sub-study of the main Fit After Surgery study. We will invite older adults living with frailty and their caregivers in multiple Canadian cities to answer more detailed questions about their health and function on 2 occasions over the course of a year. We will ask them what their care needs are. We will also ask them what resources they need at home and whether there is anything - at home, at hospital, getting to and from places, or cost - that makes it difficult for them to get the care they need. Our study will help patients make better-informed decisions about having surgery. It will also help identify patients who need extra help to recover after surgery. Lastly, it will identify what caregivers need, and how to make sure they stay healthy and well.

column36: Unravelling the role of ARHGEF3 during skin development and hair follicle regeneration
column37: Dissecting the molecular events sustaining organogenesis is essential to comprehend the cause of developmental disorders, and to contemplate cures using regenerative medicine approaches. Yet, our understanding of the mechanisms that coordinate cytoskeletal dynamics required for tissue morphogenesis remains rudimentary. Due to their ability to orchestrate cytoskeletal rearrangements, Rho GTPases are key regulators of tissue morphogenesis. In mammals, there are 20 Rho GTPases and nearly 150 regulators that are part of the RhoGEFs, RhoGAPs and RhoGDIs families. However, only a few molecules from these networks have been studied in depth. The mouse skin is an ideal system to study morphogenesis processes since it develops through a succession of sophisticated cellular rearrangements, but the molecular details of these processes remain poorly comprehended. Moreover, it is amenable to in utero lentiviral injections, a method that dramatically improved our ability to genetically modify this tissue. Using this technology, we developed a high throughput screening methodology that allowed the identification of new regulators of skin morphogenesis among the Rho GTPase signaling networks. Strikingly, we discovered that depletion of the understudied RhoGEF ARHGEF3 reduced the number of hair follicle that formed during embryonic development. Remaining hair follicles are misoriented and form lesions that are associated with the expansion hair follicle stem cells. Using state-of-the-art multidisciplinary approaches such as lentiviral injection, cell imaging and proteomic, this CIHR program focus on understanding the role of ARHGEF3 during skin development and regeneration. This work will provide fundamental insights into the molecular mechanisms that regulate skin development and it will be the first analysis of the function of ARHGEF3 in this tissue. Additionally, this work will contribute to our knowledge of how Rho GTPase signaling regulates tissue stem cells activity.

column36: Online Public Health Nurse-Delivered 1-Day Cognitive Behavioural Therapy-Based Workshops for Postpartum Depression
column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) affects up to 1 in 5 mothers and is associated with costs of $150,000 per case over the lifespan. The COVID-19 pandemic has fundamentally altered the ways in which mothers access postpartum mental health care, with most now preferring to receive treatment online or by telephone. Under normal conditions, just 1 in 10 mothers with PPD get evidence-based treatment, a situation that has worsened substantially during COVID-19. As a result, innovative interventions capable of overcoming barriers and reaching large numbers of women safely are urgently needed to reduce the adverse effects of PPD on mothers, their families, the healthcare system, and society as a whole. The purpose of this study is to test the effectiveness of a Public Health Nurse-Delivered Online 1-Day CBT-Based Workshop for PPD. We will conduct an Ontario-wide randomized controlled trial where 406 women will be recruited to receive either the Nurse-Delivered Online Workshop plus treatment as usual from their healthcare providers (treatment group), or treatment as usual plus three online information sessions (control group). We will compare the effect of the Public Health Nurse-Delivered Online 1-Day Workshop on levels of maternal depression, anxiety, and parenting stress, their relationship with their partners and infants, as well as the behaviour of their offspring in the treatment and control groups at three, six, and twelve months. We will also assess the cost-effectiveness of the intervention. Only treatments that are safe and that can be rolled out on a large scale can have a significant impact on PPD at the population level. To achieve this, a shift is needed toward treatments that can reach large numbers of mothers safely and efficiently. Public Health Nurse-Delivered Online 1-Day CBT-Based Workshops reduce many of the barriers to treatment that currently exist, and can help women and families both in Canada and around the world during the pandemic and beyond.

column36: Mechanism and Treatment for Neuronal Hyperexcitability in Smith-Magenis Syndrome
column37: Neural hyperexcitability is a common feature of autism spectrum disorders (ASDs), a collection of neurodevelopmental disorders affecting 1 in 66 children in Canada. ASD is genetically heterogeneous, making it difficult to study the pathogenic mechanism. Smith-Magenis Syndrome (SMS) is a type of ASD caused by genetic deletions of chromosome 17p11.2. Importantly, the dosage-sensitive gene has been identified as Retinoic acid induced-1 (Rai1), a chromatin-binding protein. SMS patients exhibit prominent neurologic symptoms, including seizures, learning deficits, obesity, and autistic features. How Rai1 loss causes neuronal dysfunction is unknown. My recent work found that Rai1 regulates expression of ion channels and growth factors. Our preliminary data found that loss of Rai1 causes the over-excitation of several cell types in the brain, including hippocampal dentate gyrus granule cells (dGCs) that play an important role in epilepsy and cognitive function. We also found that Rai1 loss results in hyper-activation of a key pathway involved in regulating neuronal activity. Our collective work to date has led us to hypothesize that loss of Rai1 causes altered neuronal signaling pathways and ion channel expression, thus driving neuronal hyperexcitability and behavioral symptoms. Therefore, we will determine the mechanism by which Rai1 regulates neuronal excitability at molecular, cellular, and synaptic levels. We will also test if targeting the hyperactivated neuronal signaling pathway rescues hyperexcitability and SMS-like neurobehavioral phenotypes. The proposed studies will create new knowledge of how Rai1 regulates brain excitability and uncover potential therapeutic strategies for treating brain hyperexcitability and behavioral deficits in SMS.

column36: Central control of energy homeostasis by neuronal adipose triglyceride lipase
column37: Obesity affects nearly 14 million Canadians and is a major risk factor for diabetes (type 2). The hypothalamus is a brain region that plays a critical role in controlling body weight by regulating food intake and amount of calories burned. The activity of hypothalamic neurons is strongly regulated by metabolic hormones and nutrients circulating in the blood. In turn, these neurons activate appropriate physiological responses to maintain proper body weight. Our preliminary findings suggest that the activity of hypothalamic neurons is regulated by an enzyme called Adipose Triglyceride Lipase (ATGL) that degrades lipid stores inside these neurons. Indeed, gene invalidation of neuronal ATGL leads to fat deposition in worms and flies, and affect calorie intake and expenditure in mice. Together, these results support a conserved mechanism throughout evolution by which neuronal ATGL acts as a regulator of body fat and energy balance. The overall goal of our research is to determine the role and the mechanisms by which neuronal ATGL modulates the activity of hypothalamic neurons to regulate energy balance. In addition, we will examine if neuronal ATGL is involved in the etiology of obesity and diabetes. We propose to explore our goals using a combination of pharmacological and genetic strategies to precisely modulate hypothalamic ATGL and its signaling in flies and rodents. With growing health concerns regarding obesity and diabetes, it is critical to understand the mechanisms underlying these diseases. We believe the novel contribution of neuronal lipid stores and ATGL in the hypothalamus are key to controlling energy balance and the underlying cause to these pathologies. Identifying a causative and druggable target for obesity and diabetes that could be challenged with prospective therapies remains an unmet clinical need.

column36: Evaluating and Informing Canada's Proposed Pharmaceutical Price Regulations
column37: Canadians pay some of the highest prescription drug prices globally. This translates to high and unsustainable costs for patients and our healthcare system. The Patented Medicine Prices Review Board (PMPRB), the federal agency charged with preventing the excessive pricing of patented prescription drugs, is modernizing its pricing rules in an effort to reduce drug prices. These changes include updating the set of reference countries against which the Canadian prices will be assessed, and introducing new criteria for determining if an expensive and top-selling drug is over-priced. To do so, it will assess each new drug's health impact relative to its cost ("value for money") and its overall budgetary impact. The modernized PMPRB regulations, which will come into effect in July 2021, have raised questions and concerns as to whether they will deliver the desired reduction in drug prices and not delay Canada's access to essential medicines, given historical trends and predictable responses by drug companies. Our research goal is to assess the impact of the new PMPRB drug pricing rules. Our approach will investigate how the new rules would have impacted drug pricing in previous years (as if they were already in effect) compared to the actual prices under the current rules. First, we will calculate how changing benchmark countries affects drug prices. Next, we will analyze factors that determine how expensive, top-selling drugs are valued and how these factors impact the price cap for drugs in this category. We will also estimate how drug companies will respond to the new regulations in terms of their decisions to launch new drugs in Canada and their investments on research and development. Finally, we will use models to predict the price cap for future drugs launched in Canada. Our work is timely and provides an important opportunity to independently evaluate and inform this new policy that will affect Canada's drug spending and access to new drugs.

column37: Two bacteria, called E. coli and K. pneumoniae, are among the most common causes of blood infection in Canada. Overuse of meropenem comes at a cost as it represents one of the last lines of defense against many other drug-resistant bacteria. Use of drugs like meropenem increases the risk of acquiring carbapenem-resistant bacteria in the future. Meropenem may also have a higher risk of C. difficile. Therefore, keeping an option like PTZ available is important to protect meropenem (and similar drugs) for the future. Along with international partners, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial which addresses the flaws in the previous trial and seeks to demonstrate whether piperacillin-tazobactam is non-inferior to meropenem for the treatment of blood infections due to ESBL E.coli and K. pneumoniae. Our Canadian team will make an important contribution to this international study.

column36: The impact of opioid and cannabis use during pregnancy on placental and fetal development
column37: Drug use during pregnancy is increasing in Canada. This trend is concerning for healthcare providers because it is known that drug use in pregnancy can cause babies to be born small and underdeveloped. Currently, we do not know exactly how this outcome happens. One possible explanation is these drugs such as marijuana and opioids (heroine, morphine) may affect the function of the placenta (afterbirth). The placenta is important for a healthy pregnancy and changes to how it works can prevent babies from developing properly. Previous research in laboratory animals suggests that drugs may change how the placenta works and transports nutrients to the developing baby. Drug use may also cause the cells of the placenta to become unhealthy but this work has yet to be confirmed in humans. Also, we do not know if using opioids and marijuana at the same time during pregnancy has a greater effect on the placenta than using only one drug. In this project, we will examine the effect of marijuana and opioids on placental health using different scientific technologies and experiments. First, we will compare the tissue from placentas from pregnancies with different drug exposures to see how unhealthy the placenta becomes. Next, we will look gene expression in the placentas from these pregnancies to determine the effects of these drugs on nutrient transport and placental cell health. Finally, to understand the effects of these gene changes on how the placenta works, we will use a mouse model of drug use to uncover the pathways that lead to these changes. We have assembled an experienced team of scientists, doctors and midwives to perform this work and ensure its success. At the end of this project, we will know if certain drugs are more harmful to the placenta than others or if using more than one drug during pregnancy causes more placental damage. This information can help pregnant individuals make informed choices about drug use during pregnancy.

column36: Brain development and the onset of depression in youth
column37: Depression is one of the most common and disabling human health problems worldwide. Depression most often starts in adolescence or in early adulthood, at a time when a rapid phase of brain development is culminating. Mapping brain development through adolescence may help predict which youth are at risk. Pinpointing the timing and nature of the brain characteristics preceding depression will help us understand how and why depression develops. We have completed accurate brain scans in 200 youth at increased risk for depression. We will follow these youth for three years to find out which aspects of the developing brain predict depression. It is important to confirm that brain findings can be reproduced. Therefore, we will also scan a second group of 200 youth and follow them for three years. We will test each finding from the first group in the second group. Analysis of repeat brain scans across the two groups will help us map the areas of the brain that are important and pinpoint the age when the brain development in those who are going to get depression diverges from those who are going to remain healthy. The results will be used to develop a model of depression development and framework for early identification of youth who may benefit from preventive interventions.

column36: Impact of 18F-FDG-PET/CT on Management of Patients with Suspected Native Valve Infective Endocarditis
column37: Infection of heart valve, called infective endocarditis (IE), occurs when bacteria circulating in the bloodstream attach and multiply on a cardiac valve. This infection can lead to serious complications, including destruction of the valve, spreading of the infection, and in some cases, death. Symptoms of patients with IE are highly variable, making the diagnosis challenging. To help physicians, a set of criteria called the Duke criteria were developed. The Duke criteria are composed of 2 major and 5 minor criteria representing various symptoms and examination findings. Based on the number of major and minor criteria, patients are classified into 3 groups: definite IE, possible IE, and IE excluded. In patients classified with possible IE, infection is neither confirmed nor excluded and further investigations are required. Approximately a third of patients are classified as having possible IE. In those cases, there are often delays in diagnosis and initiation of treatment, which leads to more disease progression, more complications, and death in some cases. Positron emission tomography (PET scan) is an imaging tool that allow us to see diseases with a high degree of precision. PET scans were initially used for cancer detection and have since become extremely useful for imaging many infectious diseases. To image infections with a PET scanner, a tracer called FDG is injected in a patient vein and pictures are then taken with the PET scanner. FDG is a radioactive sugar that accumulated in the cells found at infection sites. Whether PET scan can improve detection of IE on patients without valve prosthesis remains unknown. The purpose of this proposal is to assess if PET scan can improve the Duke criteria performance by reducing the number of patients classified with possible IE. The results of the proposed research could have a direct and immediate impact on the management of patients with suspected IE.

Although the proposed studies are mainly focused on an understanding of drug action and to demonstrate their beneficial effect in animal models of the disease, the knowledge to be gained is mandatory to better position the drugs for their future development by pharma. column37: Canada was the second country to legalize cannabis at the Federal level, and, with increased access, it is imperative to understand best practices around cannabis use. Despite the prevalence of co-use of these substances, laboratory studies into the impact of tobacco on cannabis-related harms, such as impaired driving, is lacking. An understanding of the interactions between tobacco and cannabis on the experience of cannabis may help to provide evidence-based guidance on the safest use of cannabis. Participants will be regular users of cannabis and will be invited to the lab for four test sessions. In these test sessions they will drive the simulator and undergo cognitive tests before and after smoking: 1) cannabis; 2) tobacco; 3) cannabis + tobacco; or 4) placebo. Outcomes will be measured at several time points after smoking the product. Participants will also give blood for determination of levels of THC, and will complete subjective effects questionnaires both before and after smoking the cigarette. This study will be one of the first experimental laboratory studies of the reasons behind co-administration of tobacco and cannabis. This study will provide important insights into the best use of cannabis, and we will work closely with advisors on developing campaigns to inform the public about the relative benefits and risks of mixing cannabis with tobacco.

column36: Identification of therapeutically relevant targets in telomerase overexpressing prostate cancers
column37: Prostate cancer arises as an androgen driven disease and androgen deprivation therapies (ADTs) are the mainstay of systemic therapies for patients with advanced disease. Although ADTs offers remission, this is temporary, as the cancer resurfaces as castration-resistant PC (CRPC) and in a small percentage of cases, cells trans-differentiate into neuro-endocrine PC (NEPC). While there is a biologic continuum with prostate adenocarcinoma evolving from a hormone naive state (HNPC) to CRPC to NEPC, we found the enzyme telomerase is overexpressed all these states. By upregulating telomerase, these prostate cancer cells overcome the finite replicative life span and gain potential for unlimited growth. In fact, targeting the enzyme telomerase with inhibitors is pursued as a potential avenue for treating cancer patients. Unfortunately, despite several efforts, such inhibitors were so far ineffective in clinical trials. Here we propose to identify and validate alternative druggable targets, that are essential for the survival of telomerase overexpressing HNPC, CRPC and NEPC. This way, normal cells that do not express telomerase remain unaffected. The targets identified and validated in this study can eventually lead to effective prostate cancer therapies.

column36: Anticoagulation for stroke prevention in patients with recent episodes of perioperative atrial fibrillation after noncardiac surgery - The ASPIRE-AF study
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an arrhythmia of the heart, and occurs in approximately 3% of patients within 30 days of a surgical procedure not including open heart surgery (i.e. perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery). For patients who develop AF outside of the surgical setting, there is strong evidence that blood thinners prevent the occurrence of stroke. Patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery also have an increased risk of stroke and other adverse outcomes. This suggests that these patients may benefit from blood thinners as well. However, it is currently unclear whether these medications are effective and safe in this patient population. The aim of this proposal is to assess in a randomized clinical study whether an anticoagulant compared with usual clinical care reduces the risk of stroke and other adverse outcomes in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. For this purpose, we will perform a randomized clinical study of 2800 patients comparing a blood thinner with usual care not involving a blood thinner in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. Patients will be assigned by chance (randomized) to one of the two groups. To be eligible for the study, patients need to have at least 1 confirmed episode of perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery, they have to be in normal (sinus) rhythm at the time of randomization, and they need to have some additional risk factors for stroke. Patients will be followed up for up to 24 months. There will be two main study outcomes: 1. stroke/systemic embolism (i.e., blood clot occluding a major blood vessel), 2. a combination of adverse vascular events (e.g. heart attack, stroke and others). The main safety outcome will be bleeding. In summary, this proposal will assess the efficacy and safety of using a blood thinner for up to 24 months in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. Such a trial has the potential to inform and change clinical practice.

column37: Mutations in KRAS gene are found in deadly forms of cancer like colorectal, lung and pancreatic cancers. Mutant KRAS gene produces a protein, which has the capacity to enhance the proliferation of cells and promote tumor growth. Also, mutant KRAS rewires cellular metabolism to increase the production of building blocks of cells and energy to sustain tumor growth. Knowing how mutant KRAS makes cells addicted to metabolic alterations is important for the design of therapies that deprive cancers from the essential metabolites required for their growth. Herein, we investigate how STAT1 stimulates lipid metabolism and how essential this is for the growth of mutant KRAS cancers. In normal cells without mutant KRAS, a well-defined property of STAT1 is its ability to boost the immune system against tumor growth. However, this property of STAT1 is not possible in mutant KRAS cancers. We investigate the mechanisms employed by mutant KRAS to disarm the ability of STAT1 to stimulate the immune system in fighting cancer growth. Our work not only lead us to the discovery of novel mechanisms implicated in mutant KRAS cancer growth, but also allows us to evaluate STAT1 as an important player in biological processes that render mutant KRAS cancers vulnerable to metabolic therapeutic interventions.
