column37: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disease worldwide and the most common human movement disorder, affecting over 100,000 Canadians. Characterized by a progressive decline in voluntary movement, motor function eventually dissipates, and patients lose the ability to move. To date, there is no effective treatment capable of halting or reversing disease pathology. While many brain regions are affected in PD, dopamine producing neurons in the midbrain are most susceptible to degeneration. As the disease progresses, evidence suggests that pathology spreads from this area through anatomically linked regions of the brain. Our work has shown that PD patient derived brain cells can transmit pathology in a cell to cell manner, triggering disease in previously healthy cells. The current project will focus on determining how pathogenic material can move from diseased cells into a healthy brain. The protein, alpha-synuclein, accumulates in the brain of PD patients and is the primary component of Lewy Bodies, which are the primary hallmark of the disease. For disease to spread, alpha-synuclein must move between cells and trigger formation of Lewy Bodies in new areas of the brain. We believe this results from dysfunction in a cell survival process called autophagy, that functions to clean the cell of dysfunctional components and debris. We find that alpha-synuclein interacts with and perturbs components of the autophagy pathway. As result of the cell being unable to clean debris, the cell releases it into the surrounding area where is can affect neighboring cells. We will therefore determine if alpha-synuclein inhibits autophagy in PD and if stopping the release of alpha-synuclein slows the spread of disease. If successful, this study will yield a target drug development against PD.

column36: Reimagining O2 Demand-to-O2 Supply Coupling In the Microcirculation: Cellular Mechanisms to Disease Application
column37: The microcirculation is an intricate web of vessels, guiding blood flow delivery and the matching of oxygen supply with oxygen demand. When this key process breaks down, there is a marked drop in blood flow and organ failure ensues. Mechanistic explanations of demand-supply coupling have many shortcomings, thus scientists continue to search for new paradigms. One we champion states that red blood cells (RBC) sense oxygen demand and when they desaturate of oxygen, key molecules are released, triggering ion channels to send electrical signals along blood vessels. Work herein will test this provocative idea and then use this new knowledge to explain microvascular failure in sepsis, a life-threatening systemic infection that kills 1-in-5 patients. In detail, our three aims will: 1) Define RBCs as a dynamic regulator of microvascular blood flow. 2) Define the signaling process linking RBCs to microvascular flow regulation. 3) Define the relationship between sepsis, RBC signaling, and microvascular failure. We will first test our ideas in rodent models using state-of-the-art imaging and then translate findings into humans. Computer models will help inform our experiments as will biochemical assays. Our blended approach aligns with our strengths in imaging, signal analysis, device engineering, computational biology, and vascular signaling. Impact: This proposal rewrites the foundation of blood flow control and the concept of demand-supply coupling. We argue that RBCs, rather than tissue, "sense" oxygen demand, with oxygen desaturation triggering blood flow responses through electrical signaling. Our studies will also show that demand-supply decoupling occurs early in sepsis and leads to a defined pattern of microvascular breakdown that we can diagnostically monitor in humans with portable, low-cost, noninvasive tools.

column37: Cell therapies are changing medicine. Cell therapy refers to the use of immune cells or stem cells to treat disease. Although very promising, there are many questions remaining about cell therapy that can only be answered using imaging. For example, where do cells go after implanted? how long do they last? and has there been an immune response against the implanted cells. We will develop a new imaging method called magnetic particle imaging, or MPI. MPI detects cells that are labeled with iron particles. MPI detects only iron so the signal is very specific. MPI is also very sensitive, current estimates say as few as hundreds of cells can be detected. For these reasons it may be superior to other imaging methods, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The type of iron particle is important in MPI. We will make new particles designed specifically for imaging cells with MPI. We will evaluate these to determine which lead to high MPI signal and the ability to detect small numbers of cells for periods of time after their implantation. We will also test different features on the MPI system for improving cell detection. To add functionality to MPI we will develop a new method called multicolour MPI. This method aims to allow us to image two different kinds of cells that are labeled with two different kinds of iron particle. This could allow us to detect the therapeutic cells and the cells that infiltrate the transplant and lead to rejection, at the same time. Our overall goal is to improve on the ability to track cells used in therapies. Human MPI scanners are under development and this project will advance the limits of therapeutic cell tracking and give researchers and clinicians a new tool for developing and refining cellular therapies.

column36: Developing Culturally Appropriate and Community Informed Virtual Healthcare for Pediatric Specialized Acute Care Services in Saskatchewan's Rural and Remote Indigenous Communities
column37: Indigenous children in remote Canadian communities are at risk, as access to specialized medical resources is challenging. In the absence of direct paediatric specialist care, children are often transported unnecessarily to distant care centres, separating them from their families and communities. As sick Indigenous children from these remote communities are presenting to their health centre, a solution that is culturally appropriate, community informed, and enables an early diagnosis, intervention and refined transport triaging must be sought. Virtual care has the potential to address these challenges. Building on lessons learned from our virtual care pilot platform in a remote Northern Indigenous community, the goal of our study is to introduce virtual technology to at least 13 other rural and remote Indigenous communities. Consistent with The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's Calls to Action, Indigenous children will receive timely and culturally safe paediatric healthcare. With 24/7 access to a paediatric intensivist, all sick children < 17 years will be virtually assessed, managed, triaged, and if necessary, receive virtual follow-up. Data from our pilot suggests that this should result in a decreased need for children to be transported out of their communities, and when necessary, expedited to tertiary care. Unfortunately the cultural appropriateness of virtual care in Indigenous communities is unknown, as they have been largely implemented without considering Indigenous notions of wellbeing. A community based participatory research approach will guide the creation of the platform, with subsequent modifications facilitated through perspectives from local care providers and family members post virtual encounter. Ultimately, recommendations will be suggested to guide future virtual healthcare initiatives in Indigenous communities.

column36: Sustainable health technology regulation: Mobilizing regulation to improve the environmental performance of health technologies
column37: Though they aim to improve health, drugs and medical devices contribute to the climate crisis and environmental degradation. The agencies that regulate which technologies become available for patients, and that inform how those technologies will be used, have an important influence on these environmental impacts. Three sets of agencies are especially important: (i) Market access agencies, such as Health Canada, which regulate which health technologies can be sold within a country; (ii) Health Technology Assessment agencies, such as the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health, which advise on what technologies should be paid for by health systems; and (iii) National and provincial procurement agencies, which determine which technologies will be bought and used in hospitals and other care settings. Globally and in Canada, several of these agencies have developed ways to include some information about environmental impact into their decisions. As well, a number of research groups are developing methods to support them. Yet these efforts are not sufficient to identify policy options. First, we need to know more about how agencies can use different approaches to incorporate environmental considerations into decision-making. Second, we need to understand how agencies influence environmental performance even when that is not their aim, for example, through unintended effects and interaction effects. Finally, research needs to account for the many organizations that influence regulatory decisions about environmental performance by setting standards for evidence and evaluation, even though they have no regulatory authority. Our multidisciplinary research team, advised by an Expert Advisory Committee of regulators, plan a multiple case study to fill these knowledge gaps, to inform policy makers and agencies about options to support the adoption and use of environmentally preferable health technologies.

column36: Implementing an mHealth App to Manage Depression in Vietnam (ImHAMD)
column37: The purpose of the study is to examine whether a supported self-management (SSM) intervention for depression adapted for delivery using mobile technology is feasible in Vietnam. The World Health Organization and the Government of Canada have identified global mental health as a priority area requiring immediate action, particularly in response to COVID-19. Up to 75% of people in low- and middle-income countries like Vietnam do not have access to mental health care (WHO, 2019). Services for depression offered in the community and using mobile technology, such as smartphones, may be an effective way to provide mental health services in Vietnam and globally. Yet, challenges including individuals' familiarity with and acceptability of the technology must be explored, along with ensuring the correct adaptation of existing in-person interventions to mobile technology. This study will build on work led by an international team of researchers that showed SSM's effectiveness in Vietnam in a randomized controlled trial (RCT) and follow-up study. SSM, consisting of an Antidepressant Skills Workbook and supportive coaching, is delivered using task-sharing, where non-specialist health workers provide the intervention. The Government of Vietnam has requested SSM to be adapted and tested using a smartphone app to help with sustainability. An app will be developed and tested with patients and non-specialist health workers in Vietnam to see whether it is easy to use and helpful with depression symptoms in a mixed-methods study involving surveys and in-depth interviews. This study will be supported by strong commitments from the Vietnamese Government. If the study produces promising results, the team will apply for funding to scale-up SSM in an RCT. Findings would be applicable to other countries, including Canada, which also experiences gaps in mental health treatment.

column36: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are major actors in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
column37: Heart failure (HF) is a cardiovascular (CV) condition caused by the inability of the cardiac muscle to provide enough blood flow and oxygen to muscles and organs. There are two types of HF, first, the classical form taking place mainly following a partial cardiac muscle death after a heart attack, reducing the capacity of the heart to pump blood, termed HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF); second, there is a rapid rising form of HF, mainly caused by population aging, characterized by a stiff, yet almost normally contracting heart, and termed HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). HFpEF is characterized by chronic inflammation and mounting evidence suggest that neutrophils which are the most abundant circulating white blood cells might play a major role in the development of the pathology. Neutrophils have the capacity to release a meshwork of filaments termed NETs, which are linked to inflammatory proteins. The presence of those NETs in the circulation might lead to microvascular occlusion and exacerbate the progression of HFpEF. This is a novel observation from our group. Since all pharmacological approaches, have so far, not provided successful results to treat HFpEF adverse events, we are aiming to address the role of NETs in the progression of HFpEF both in animal models (mice) and HFpEF patients. In addition, we will be using an anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine which has a potent blocking effect on neutrophils. Consequently, we will be able to assess if colchicine can block the release of NETs by the neutrophils, and if it can contribute to stop or delay the progression of HFpEF disease both in mice and humans.

column36: Targeting molecular pathways that influence aging as a novel therapeutic strategy for Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease affecting as many as 10 million individuals worldwide. While aging is the greatest risk factor for PD, the role of aging in the disease is poorly understood. In the inherited forms of PD, the disease-causing mutations are present from birth and yet disease onset occurs multiple decades later. This indicates that these mutations are well-tolerated in younger individuals. Based on this observation, we wondered whether changes that take place during normal aging contribute to the development of PD. If so, then delaying some of these changes may be beneficial in PD. To test this idea, we used a simple model organism, the worm C. elegans, which has been used extensively to identify genes that modulate aging. We treated worm models of PD with genes that have been previously shown to increase lifespan, and measured the extent to which these genes could prevent the loss of brain cells. We found that all five aging-associated genes that we tested protected the brain cells from death and preserved their function. This experiment provides support for our idea that delaying changes that take place during aging will be beneficial in treating PD. The current proposal will build upon these exciting preliminary studies to answer two important questions: (1) Which genes that have been shown to influence aging will be the most beneficial in the treatment of PD?; and (2) How do these genes protect against PD? Importantly, these studies will serve to prioritize therapeutic targets to be validated in mammalian models in subsequent studies. This work has the potential to improve human health through the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of PD.

column36: Determining the mechanism underlying selective neuronal vulnerability in ALS
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease without effective treatment. ALS affects neurons that control voluntary movement in the central nervous system, leading to muscle weakness and paralysis. However, our understanding of the disease mechanism is limited. The critical questions that we ask are: How do these motor-controlling neurons undergo degeneration? Can we define disease-initiating events? Why motor-controlling neurons are selectively vulnerable compared to other neurons? Our proposal explores these questions. Recently, we created and established a new ALS mouse model, MATR3 S85C knock-in mouse line, that expresses the disease-causing protein at the physiological level and closely mimics human disease features of ALS, including motor deficits and degeneration of neuronal groups that control motor function. This new ALS mouse model provides an unprecedented opportunity to dissect the natural disease course at early disease stage and to address the question of selective neuronal vulnerability in ALS. Using this unique ALS model, we will characterize and study the mutant mice at pre-symptomatic and early disease stages to identify key disease-initiating events and investigate how and why these specific neuronal groups are more susceptible to degeneration. Identification of the disease-initiating events will provide important clues to the development of effective strategies for early disease prevention and therapeutic intervention for ALS. In addition, our studies will advance knowledge in our understanding of selective neuronal vulnerability in ALS and provide a cellular and molecular map that pinpoint which cells and molecular pathways need to be targeted for therapeutic intervention. Our findings will provide invaluable insights into other neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Randomized, Prospective, Placebo-Controlled, Crossover Study of Atomoxetine in the Prevention of Vasovagal Syncope: The Seventh Prevention of Syncope Trial (POST7)
column37: Background and aim: We think we have found a drug, atomoxetine, that should work based on a human laboratory model of fainting. However, this needs testing in lots of people who faint. We have already shown that it works in carefully controlled test environments, using doses widely used for treating attention deficit disorders. The study: We will ask 180 people who faint distressingly often to help us with the study. If they agree each one will get both the atomoxetine and dummy pill for up to 6 months each for comparison. Whether they get atomoxetine or dummy will be by chance, and no-one will know which one until the study ends. When finished, we will compare the effectiveness of the two, look at their costs, see how people feel about them, and at how we can quickly teach other doctors about using it. Patient engagement: We will be working together - patients, doctors, researchers, pharmaceutical industry - in some really new ways. Patients on the Steering Committee have provided advice on the study design and conduct to focus on issues important to the patients. Patients are involved right from the start. We will also do "exit interviews" to better understand the patient experience with both the randomized trial and atomoxetine that may inform future knowledge translation and dissemination efforts. Importance of the project: This interesting project could help many Canadians who faint repeatedly. Unfortunately, even after decades of research, we have no good treatment for frequent fainting. Atomoxetine, a drug already approved for attention deficit disorder, shows high promise to address this problem. Expected impact: By the time we are finished, we may have at least one treatment that we know works, and a new use for an old drug for a common problem, and which is made by the Canadian drug manufacturer (Apotex).

column36: Genetic control of postnatal hypothalamic neurogenesis and energy homeostasis
column37: Obesity, which will be affecting a third of global population in 2025, is a major health problem with increased risk for various chronic diseases. Recent studies from my lab identified the IRX3 and IRX5 genes as two major risk factors involved in human obesity. The hypothalamus of our brain controls appetite (and the food intake we consume) as well as metabolic rate (and how we burn excess energy intake). Our data suggest that IRX3 and IRX5 regulate food intake by modulating the formation of new leptin-sensing neurons in the hypothalamus (After meals, leptin is a hormone secreted by adipocytes to signal satiety). Importantly, we found that IRX3 and IRX5 appear to control the activities of a novel population of neural stem cells in postnatal mouse hypothalamus. In this proposal, we propose molecular genetic experiments using various mouse models to investigate the molecular actions of IRX3 and IRX5 in these hypothalamic neural stem cells. The proposed research could provide useful knowledge for potential intervention of eating disorder, obesity and related metabolic diseases.

column36: Ribosome impairments, translation and bone marrow failure
column37: Bone marrow (BM) makes millions of blood cells per day via a complex multistep process. White blood cells fight infections, platelets prevent bleeding and red cells deliver oxygen; all are crucial to sustain life. Reduced blood formation is a common problem. It can be caused by infections, toxins, cancer therapy, among others. Inherited BM failure syndromes (IBMFSs) are rare life threatening genetic diseases in which BM cells are lost or impaired. Current therapies for BM failure (e.g. transfusions or transplant) often cause serious side effects in IBMFS patients or have low efficacy. The goal of this study is to discover how BM cells develop and function, while learning why blood cell formation is disrupted in an IBMFS called Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS). SDS affect patients from infancy causing low blood cell counts and a risk of leukemia. We discovered that the DNAJC21 gene is mutated in a portion of SDS patients. This gene is required for making proteins in the cells. We will use BM samples from SDS patients with DNAJC21 mutations that were collected during periodic clinical testing to detect early signs of leukemia. We have already generated SDS-cell models that can be used when patient cells are insufficient. We will quantify each BM cell type and its ability to make blood cells. We will test whether patient blood stem cells can be repaired by adding a healthy copy of DNAJC21 to their DNA. This can be a basis for future gene therapy. Next, we will identify proteins that patient cells don't make; thus are missing in their BM, which impairs blood cell formation. Our research will reveal why the protein making process in SDS is flawed and results in blood cell loss. Since DNAJC21 is crucial for making many other body tissues besides BM (e.g. pancreas) and since several other diseases are caused by defects in the protein making process (e.g. cancer) the results from our study will be relevant to diseases in other organs and to many other health conditions.

column36: Decisions to Seek Emergency Medical Care Among People with Kidney Failure: Implications for Optimal Care Delivery
column37: Kidney failure is the most advanced stage of chronic kidney disease, where dialysis is often needed as a life-sustaining therapy. Adults with kidney failure have complex health care needs and are at increased risk of developing urgent health complications. People with kidney failure visit the emergency department 8 times more often than people without kidney failure for a variety of health issues. Research tells us about the patient characteristics and medical reasons for emergency department visits among people with kidney failure. However, we know very little about how or why someone with kidney failure decides to seek care (or not) in the emergency department. These decisions are complex and require a person to consider his or her past experiences, values, and preferences. It is important to understand how people's need for dialysis and the availability of kidney care services might influence their decision making, so that care can be provided in a way that meets their needs and preferences. In this research study, we will examine the medical and non-medical factors that contribute to the decisions of people with kidney failure to seek emergency care for a variety of health issues. This is a qualitative study, which means that we will interview patients and their loved ones about their experiences with urgent health issues and the medical care they received. We will ask them about the circumstances leading up to their emergency department visit, and what or who may have influenced their decision to seek emergency care. We will analyze transcripts of our discussions and present patterns that summarize and explain the decision-making process. Findings from this study will provide direction for future research by our team to develop and test novel ways of providing urgent care for people with kidney failure.

column36: Mitochondrial signaling plays an important role in the regulation of sperm motility and fertilizing ability.
column37: The role of spermatozoa is to bring the paternal genetic content in close proximity to the maternal genetic content during fertilization. Sperm flagellar motility is required to bring themselves close to the egg, and their head must interact with the egg surface, bind and fuse with the egg membranes to finally deliver their nucleus inside the egg. Defects in any of these sperm events jeopardize the success of fertilization and might lead to male infertility. Spermatozoa are highly differentiated cells that are unable to multiply, to transcribe their genes and to synthetize new proteins. They must therefore rely on their own set of proteins, which they can modify through intracellular biochemical reactions, in order to successfully achieve their roles. Sperm motility and interaction with the egg are regulated by intracellular biochemical events. Intracellular agents like cyclic AMP, Ca2+, reactive oxygen species, trigger a cascade of signalling and biochemical events that will ultimately lead to the phosphorylation of proteins involved in sperm motility or in sperm interaction with the egg. Like every living cell, spermatozoa possess mitochondria, known as powerhouses generating the ATP necessary to various enzymatic activities and cell functions. In spermatozoa however, although motility requires a huge amount of ATP, the role of mitochondria in this cellular activity remains debatable. Extra-mitochondrial production of ATP through glucose metabolism is recognized as a significant player. It has been recently shown that STAT proteins positively affect cell mitochondria independently of their gene transcription activity. When sperm are incubated with STAT inhibitors, they lose their motility within 4 hours. Therefore, our goal is to better understand the regulatory mechanisms of mitochondria on sperm function and the importance of STAT proteins in sperm mitochondria. This study will help to determine the importance of sperm mitochondrial function in male fertility.

column36: Statistical Methodology for Prediction Modelling to Improve Depression Screening with Individualized Risk Estimates in the Context of Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis
column37: Depression is a chronic and disabling condition that is the leading global cause of life-years lived with disability. However, most Canadians with depression do not receive adequate care. Thus, the development and implementation of effective depression management programs is urgent. Depression screening has been recommended as a solution. However, when trials have been conducted, they have failed to show benefit from depression screening. One reason is that screening tools have not been accurately calibrated for use with individual patients. The CTFPHC has emphasized the need for high-quality research that generates unbiased estimates of depression screening tool accuracy and considers individual patient risk factors. Individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA), which uses actual patient data from primary studies, can address existing problems and incorporate important depression risk factors. Our team has built four large IPD databases including individual and study level characteristics. However, best practices for developing prediction models in the context of IPDMA are unknown because of a number of statistical challenges. Particularly, accounting for study specific intercepts and slopes, dealing with study level variables, and accounting for missing data have not been studied. The proposed research will advance and validate statistical prediction models in the context of IPDMA and apply the advanced models to generate personalized risk probabilities for MDD based on individual screening scores and depression risk factors in actual individual participant datasets, which has not been done previously. Results will be used to improve individualized depression screening and management programs and to make better decision for individual patients in primary, perinatal, and hospital care.

column36: Regulation of Antigen-Specific Memory CD4+ T Cell Responses in Cutaneous Leishmaniasis
column37: Leishmaniasis are complex spectrum of diseases that affect over 12 million people globally with an estimated 350 million people at risk of becoming infected. Depending on the species of Leishmania and host genetics, the disease manifestation ranges from small self-healing skin ulcers to large disfiguring scars and involvement of the liver, spleen and bone marrow that results in death. Despite this significant health and societal burden, there is currently no effective vaccine against the disease. Worse still, the existing treatments either cause major side effects or are only minimally effective. The lack of effective vaccine is mainly due to poor understanding of how a special type of immune cells, called memory cells work. Humans and animals that recover from infection remain immune for life, suggesting that memory cells able to protect against reinfection develop following recovery. My laboratory identified a conserved protein (expressed in all Leishmania species) that is critical for causing disease in mice. With the help of collaborators worldwide, we showed that this protein also induces strong immune response in human patients and dogs. These studies led to the development of first Leishmania reagent called tetramers, which is capable of identifying T cells that only respond to Leishmania at single cell level over the entire course of infection. It also allowed us to show that majority of the host immune response is directed against this protein. This unique reagent, which is now being used around the world, helped us to generate genetically engineered (transgenic) mice whose T cells only recognize this particular protein. We are now poised to use these animals to address fundamental questions regarding the factors that regulate the development, maintenance and loss of antigen-specific memory response in leishmaniasis. Understanding these factors is critical for development of effective vaccine and vaccination strategies against leishmaniasis.

column36: The characterization and therapeutic targeting of aberrant metabolic and inflammatory signaling in chronic lymphedema
column37: The lymphatics are one of two essential circulatory systems present throughout the human body. When the lymphatic vessel system is blocked, fluid accumulates in tissues causing swelling and tissue scarring. Up to 1 in 5 cancer patients have lymphedema as a side effect of cancer treatment because surgery and radiotherapy often unavoidably damages lymph nodes or lymphatic vessels. This condition is chronic, progressive, incurable, and leads to a high risk of infection and an additional risk of developing a lethal cancer. This research will develop the first effective drug treatment for lymphedema to improve the health and quality of life for patients with this chronic condition. Lymphedema is characterized by progressive accumulation of fibrotic tissue. Until recently, scarring disorders have been assumed to be irreversible. Our group, however, has successfully identified a new strategy that can potentially reverse tissue fibrosis. During scarring, cells accumulate and break down fat abnormally; restoring normal fat metabolism can reduce fibrosis. In lymphedema, we believe that: i) the excess accumulation of fluid and nutrients in tissues may exacerbate the metabolic and inflammatory defects in this condition, which lead to fibrosis; and ii) repairing these defects will reduce chronic lymphedema. This research will investigate the metabolic and inflammatory causes of lymphedema (Aim 1); evaluate metabolic and inflammatory targets for lymphedema therapy (Aim 2); and optimize drugs to normalize multiple disease processes in lymphedema simultaneously (Aim 3). Our research team consists of scientists in metabolism, inflammation, bioinformatics, and chemistry as well as clinicians in oncology and lymphedema surgery. Based on our expertise, we will deliver new knowledge regarding the causes of tissue scarring in lymphedema. We will also identify and test new drugs to treat lymphedema, an incurable chronic condition affecting up to 1 in 5 Canadian cancer survivors.

column36: REVIVe: Frailty, Rehabilitation, and Hospitalization Outcomes in Adult and Pediatric Survivors of COVID-19
column37: Background: Many adults and some children with COVID-19 become critically ill and need advanced life support in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Frailty is a medical condition of reduced function and health. Adults with frailty have a lower chance of surviving critical illness. We are still learning about critically ill adults with COVID-19, and we do not have much information on how frailty affects outcomes in critically ill children, with or without COVID-19. Rehabilitation can help survivors of COVID-19 by improving strength and improve quality of life (QOL). Objectives: The main goal of this research study is to see if patients with frailty have a lower chance of surviving COVID-19 critical illness and more health problems after survivival than patients without frailty. We will also study the types of rehabilitation received by patients with COVID-19. Methods: We will include adults and children with COVID-19 who are admitted to the ICUs that participate in our study. We will gather data about each patient, including before and during their illness. Outcomes: We will collect level of frailty, function, and types of therapy, or rehabilitation received by patients. In adults, we are most interested in learning if frailty influences mortality, or death. In children, we are most interested in whether children with COVID-19 critical illness are more likely to develop frailty. We will also study post-hospital discharge location in survivors (e.g., home, rehabilitation). Relevance: The COVID-19 pandemic is a global public health crisis. We need to understand how COVID-19 critical illness affects groups of people who are at higher risk, and the impact on outcomes that are important to patients, like functioning and QOL. The results will help policy makers plan post-hospital services for survivors, help healthcare workers understand the importance of rehabilitation practice for patients with COVID-19, and researchers develop treatments to improve QOL after COVID-19.

column36: Deciphering the molecular & cellular basis of aggressive basal-like breast cancer
column37: Despite remarkable strides made by the research community, 1 in 8 Canadian women are expected to develop breast cancer in her lifetime. The most aggressive type of breast cancer is called basal-like breast cancer (BLBC), which affects commonly pre-menopausal women under the age of 40 and is associated with high risk of metastasis, chronic pain, organ failure, wasting and death. Current treatments for BLBC are poor and broadly toxic, killing the dividing cells not only of the tumor but also of healthy tissues. A major impediment to developing more selective therapies is the incomplete knowledge of the constellation of genes that fuels tumor growth. Comprehensive sequencing techniques have elucidated the genetic alterations associated with BLBC. Now, the biggest challenge is to weed out circumstantial 'bystander' mutations and identify the 'driver' mutations that trigger tumor growth and metastasis. However, conventional methods to achieve these goals are tedious, too costly and take several years. We have therefore developed a unique technique to analyze the role of hundreds of genes in BLBC development within a single mouse within a couple of weeks. We produce highly concentrated viruses specifically designed to destroy or activate candidate cancer genes. We then inject these viruses directly into the mammary gland, where the viruses infect the mammary epithelial cells. This enables us to manipulate hundreds of potential 'driver' genes in the mammary tissue and to analyze whether these genes alter tumor development. The overreaching goal is to conduct a series of comprehensive screens to identify the genes that cause BLBC initiation, progression and metastasis, and to elucidate the genes required for tumor growth - the quest for a tumor's Achilles' heel.

column36: A Mixed Methods Social Network Analysis Approach to Understand Knowledge Translation in Child Development and Rehabilitation
column37: Children receiving healthcare to support their development and rehabilitation needs deserve treatment based on the best available knowledge. Unfortunately, this care does not always happen because people are not aware of current research or the best treatments to use. Connections between people and across groups can help in sharing this type of knowledge. We aim to understand how these connections work to help or hinder knowledge sharing and use among researchers, clinicians, knowledge brokers, and families across Canada. Methods: This study builds on a CIHR bridge-funded Canada-wide social network analysis (SNA) survey. We will interview participants about their connections (i.e., networks) with others related to child development and rehabilitation, and develop recommendations to improve knowledge sharing and use. Objective 1: Interview participants from each of four stakeholder groups (researchers, clinicians, knowledge brokers, families). We will recruit people who differ in how connected they are with others, and who are diverse in gender, ethnicity, (dis)ability level, age, and other factors. Interviews will ask what is working well and what can be improved for knowledge sharing. Objective 2: Develop recommendations to improve knowledge sharing on a local and national scale, which build on what is working well, and address barriers. Participants from each stakeholder group and select study team members will take part in a series of anonymous surveys to develop these recommendations. In the future, these recommendations can be used to design and test strategies to improve knowledge sharing. Conclusion: We want to develop a deep understanding of the strengths and gaps of knowledge sharing networks in child development and rehabilitation in Canada so we can make recommendations to improve them. Ultimately, our goal is to enhance knowledge sharing and use, which is required to enhance care and outcomes for children with development and rehabilitation needs.

column36: Accurate classification of NPC1 variants with saturational genome editing
column37: As we enter an age where we understand more about genetic disease we are beginning to regularly implement genome sequencing and personalized medicine in clinical practice. These efforts are hampered by a lack of knowledge about how mutations contribute to disease. This is particularly the case for diseases like Niemann Pick disease type C (NPC), a rare genetic disease in which most patients present with a mutation that has not previously been reported. This leads to long wait times between presentation and definitive diagnosis, as specialized laboratories are required to biochemically diagnose each potential patient. Here, we propose a new method to quickly and easily create every possible mutation in each DNA base in the NPC1 gene using next-generation gene editing technologies. Once we have generated a group of these mutant cells, we will perform a functional test to rapidly ascertain if each would likely lead to developing Niemann Pick or not. Once identifying which mutations are disease-causing, we plan to test various drugs that are currently in clinical or preclinical trials for NPC to further classify a mutation into categories based on drug-response.

column36: Effects of Parenting Programs on Trajectories of Medical Service Utilization among Boys and Girls receiving Child Protective Services
column37: Maltreated children are heavy medical service users; however, no study has investigated the trajectories of medical service use among maltreated children or the effects of parenting programs on these trajectories. This study has three objectives. The first is to establish trajectories of medical service use between birth and adolescence of maltreated children in comparison to children from the general population. The second and third are to verify if the reception of parenting programs (objective 2) or components of parenting programs (objective 3) can alter trajectories of later medical service use among maltreated children. These questions will be examined using data from three administrative datasets. Data regarding doctor's visits and hospital stays will be provided by the Regie de l'assurance maladie du Quebec (the public single-payer medicare provider in Quebec), and the Ministere de la sante et des services sociaux. Data on services received by maltreated children within the two largest urban child protection agencies in Quebec will be provided from the Projet integration jeunesse. Four groups of participants will be used. Group 1 will be all maltreated children whose parents received a parenting program from 2007-2017, when the child was 5 to 10 years (n=1104). Groups 2 and 3 will be maltreated children of the same ages, but whose parents either received the services of a psychosocial clinician but no parenting program (group 2), or no parenting support (group 3). Group 4 will be children from the general population. The total sample will be 4416 children (4 groups x 1104 children/group). Knowledge from this project will help clinicians anticipate maltreated children's medical needs to provide preventative interventions. Understanding the impact of parenting programs or their components on trajectories of medical service use will assist clinicians when choosing programs to implement, and may provide guidance in the modification of clinical practices.

column36: Artificial Intelligence to Support Preoperative Grading of Perforated Appendicitis in Children
column37: Acute appendicitis is a very common surgical condition in children. While treatment for simple appendicitis is straightforward, once the appendix bursts there are several ways to manage the problem, and the hospital stay can be long and complicated. The burden on the child, family, and the hospital depends on how severe the condition is found during the surgery. Being able to identify the grade of perforation before the surgery - right in the emergency room - would be very useful, helping families in the counseling process, the surgical team in choosing the best way to manage the child, and the hospital in allocating resources for the patient. In order to achieve this, we plan to use artificial intelligence (AI) to identify the grading of the appendicitis based on child's symptoms, blood tests in the emergency room, and ultrasound examination before surgery. We will collect data from children who have been operated for appendicitis at the Montreal Children's Hospital over the past decade. We will then use this data to create several AI algorithms, by first training them on part of the data, then testing them on the remaining data. We will then compare the different algorithms, to find the one which best predicts the perforation severity in children with appendicitis. Finally, we will use the winning algorithm on a new group of children presenting with acute appendicitis, and evaluate the accuracy and usefulness of the algorithm in their care. In keeping with the interdisciplinary nature of this study, our team includes pediatric surgeons, emergency pediatricians, AI engineers, and patient collaborators. The study fits in and is supported through McGill's CommiSur Lab, which explores the connections between clinical communication and technology. The resulting diagnostic tool will be used to guide the future management of perforated appendicitis in children and the discussions between patients, families, and the surgical team.

column36: Role of COP 9 signalosome subunit 5 in preserving immunoprivilege of allogeneic mesenchymal stem cells in the ischemic heart
column37: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Canada. Currently available treatments offer effective relief of symptoms but unfortunately cannot provide a permanent cure. Therefore, new research is needed to find a permanent solution for this disease. Therapies using adult stem cells have recently come up as a new option for the treatment of heart disease. These stem cells are found in the body and participate in the normal healing process after an injury. They also have the ability to help repair the heart after a heart attack. In particular, allogeneic (donor-derived) mesenchymal stem cells (allo-MSCs) from the bone marrow of young and healthy donors are considered to be the favourite cell type for heart repair. These cells are easy to collect in large numbers from consenting adult donors and often perform better than cells from older patients suffering from heart disease. Furthermore, these cells have been shown to evade the immune system, meaning no medications are needed to prevent the body from rejecting these cells. However, outcomes of recent animal studies and clinical trials have been disappointing. Many have reported that although allo-MSCs therapy was initially effective in repairing the heart after transplantation, these cells are still eventually rejected by the host immune system, ultimately reducing the benefits of these therapies. Therefore, new strategies are needed to prevent rejection of transplanted allo-MSCs and bring its benefits to patients living with heart disease. The research proposed here will focus on understanding the reasons why transplanted stem cells are rejected in the heart and how that can be prevented. Results from this research will lead to development of new stem cell treatments for repairing the heart, by preventing rejection and improving survival of transplanted stem cells in heart. In the long-term, this research will help improve the quality of life of patients with heart disease using stem cell therapy.

column36: Auditory Cortex Plasticity Following Cochlear Implant
column37: In Canada, hearing impairment is the most common sensory disability in adults (affecting 26% of those >45 years old) and deafness is the most common birth defect. Cochlear implants are extremely useful tools in providing auditory sensations to the profoundly deaf and have restored hearing to over 1 million people worldwide. The use of cochlear implants in the profoundly deaf makes human speech comprehension possible. In hearing subjects, acoustic input shapes the development of auditory cortex of the brain. However, in deaf individuals the auditory cortex has no acoustic input. Other senses, such as vision and touch, exploit the unused "deaf" region of cortex for their own purposes. This commonly results in enhanced visual or tactile abilities reported in the deaf. However, if the dormant auditory system is then activated by a cochlear implant, how does "deaf" auditory cortex respond? Does all of "deaf" auditory cortex begin to process sound? Does the visual or tactile processing that invaded "deaf" auditory cortex retreat? Does each auditory cortical area begin to perform the same functions identified in a hearing subject? By better understanding the plastic properties of the brain following cochlear implant, it will be possible to develop implantation strategies to better exploit the plasticity of the brain and improve cochlear implant efficacy and hearing restoration success. The greatest benefit of cochlear prosthetics has been found in young children. Therefore, in the proposed studies, cochlear prosthetics will be implanted in young subjects. We will examine auditory cortical function in the congenitally-deaf cat (the only natural model for human congenital deafness) following cochlear implant. The results from these studies will be directly applicable to clinical studies investigating functional outcomes of cochlear implants in children.

column36: Unravelling the Impact of Diet on Cardiovascular Health in Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia: a Metabolomic Approach.
column37: High blood cholesterol (HBC) increases heart disease risk. In most cases, HBC outcomes from suboptimal lifestyle habits. However, more than 150,000 individuals in Canada and 34 million worldwide have HBC from birth due to inherited genetic disorders. People with inherited HBC (iHBC) face a very high risk of premature heart attack, which usually occurs before reaching 55 years old, if they are not adequately treated. Canada's Food Guide (CFG) emphasizes diets low in red and processed meats and high in plant foods as these are recognized to reduce heart disease risk in the general population. However, among individuals with iHBC, the impact of diet on heart health remains misunderstood. Over time, this has led to a misleading perception that diet, relative to cholesterol-lowering medication, is of little or no help in controlling blood cholesterol and preventing heart disease in people with iHBC. In fact, people with iHBC even report engaging in unhealthy dietary behaviors because of this perception. The objective of the proposed research is to document the impact of a diet reflecting CFG principles on heart health in adults with iHBC. We will conduct a feeding intervention in which adults with iHBC will consume a diet low in red and processed meats and high in plant foods, as recommended in CFG, and a diet reflecting current dietary habits of Canadians in a random order for 4 weeks separated by a 4-week break. Blood samples will be collected at the end of each diet from which we will first measure blood cholesterol levels. We will also use cutting-edge biochemistry techniques to measure a broad spectrum of small molecules in the blood to identify the blood signature of the healthy diet. Lastly, we will evaluate how the blood signature of the healthy diet is associated with heart disease risk in a separate cohort of nearly 1,000 adults with iHBC. With this research, we will demonstrate the crucial importance of diet for heart health among individuals with iHBC.

column36: Investigation of centrosome amplification as a therapeutic vulnerability in non-small cell lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is a deadly disease and new therapies to target the biology supporting tumour growth are needed. Centrosomes are multi-protein complexes involved in cell division. One of their functions is to help cells distribute two copies of the genome equally into the cells produced during cell division. Normal cells have two centrosomes during mitosis and this is tightly regulated to ensure the genome is divided evenly. Lung cancer cells often have several centrosomes, a feature called centrosome amplification. This increase in centrosome number makes it more difficult for cells to carry out cell division, and can cause major DNA abnormalities and mutations that help tumours grow. Because centrosome amplification is specific to cancer cells and it can promote their growth, it is an attractive target for lung cancer therapy. The goal of this research program is to understand how centrosome amplification could be targeted to treat lung cancer. We will determine how frequently centrosome amplification occurs and identify strategies that lung cancers use to cope with the stress that it causes during cell division. Knowledge gained from these studies will inform how centrosome amplification could be targeted to treat lung tumours. We will then evaluate how well treatments designed to target centrosome amplification inhibit the growth of lung cancer models. Finally, we will investigate whether this new therapeutic approach can be combined with standard lung cancer treatments to enhance their abilities to kill tumours. The new discoveries from our research program will improve our understanding of lung cancer biology and specifically, how lung cancers cope with centrosome amplification. They will also provide insights about how we can take advantage of this cancer-specific feature to treat patients. Thus, our work has great potential to lead to the development of new therapies and drug combination strategies for treating lung cancer that could improve patient outcomes.

column36: Judiciarisation des personnes souffrant de troubles mentaux : une recherche en theorisation ancree sur la perception des patients judiciarises et le personnel soignant
column37: L'insertion des personnes qui souffrent de troubles mentaux (PSTM) dans le systeme de justice (criminelle et civile) est une realite omnipresente au Canada. Plusieurs enjeux sont associes a cette surrepresentation des personnes vivant avec des problemes de sante mentale a l'interieur du systeme de justice, dont la forte stigmatisation qui affecte ces personnes. La judiciarisation s'effectue dans une optique de protection de la securite du public et, par le fait meme, dans un objectif plus large de controle social. Les professionnels de la sante qui pratiquent aupres de ces personnes, bien qu'ils agissent a titre de soignants, s'inscrivent dans ce mandat de controle social. Cette realite peut affecter significativement la relation therapeutique entre les soignants et les patients, et, par le fait meme, le retablissement des PSTM. Ce projet vise a mieux comprendre comment la judiciarisation affecte les PSTM et les soignants (infirmiers.eres et educateurs specialises) qui travaillent avec ces personnes. Nous voulons aussi explorer comment la judiciarisation influence la relation therapeutique entre soignants et soignes. La theorisation ancree sera utilisee comme methodologie de recherche. Des PSTM, hommes (n=15) et femmes (n=15), ayant ete en contact avec le systeme judiciaire seront rencontres lors d'entretiens semi-structures. De plus, des membres du personnel soignant (n=30) qui pratiquent aupres de ces personnes judiciarisees seront aussi interviewes (60 participants en tout). Ce projet s'avere des plus pertinent afin d'etudier comment le phenomene de la judiciarisation affecte la relation therapeutique entre les patients judiciarises et le personnel soignant. Cette recherche permettra de mieux informer les cliniciens sur les impacts de la judiciarisation a l'endroit des PSTM, et comment les pratiques cliniques peuvent etre mieux adaptees a cette population.

column36: Gendered Social Determinants of Health and Adverse Clinical Outcomes in Atrial Fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common irregular heart rhythm and is associated with significant increased risk of stroke, and overall mortality. To improve of survival and quality of life, risk scores have been tested for their ability to also predict all-cause mortality. Clinical factors and biomarkers have been tested for improving the predictive ability of scores with limited results and have not been tested in males and females separately. While biological sex has been reported to play an important role in clinical outcomes of AF, the role of gendered social determinants of health in the assessment of adverse outcomes have not been fully explored. The factors including gender roles, relations and institutional policy must be taken into consideration in males and females to better understand the risk of overall adverse events and to support the move towards a patient-centered approach in AF care. The overall aim of this study is to improve our understanding of the relationship between gendered social determinants of health and adverse outcomes in AF patients and to determine sex specific risks. We will analyze a large cohort of AF patients that has collected the necessary information on clinical factors, social determinants, and relevant outcomes to test different models and arrive at identifying the best predictors of outcome to develop sex specific interventions to improve the care of AF patients. Despite major improvements in treatments, patients with AF still face a high risk of mortality. The role of gendered social determinants in predicting risks of stroke, major bleeding, cardiovascular adverse events, and all-cause mortality has yet to be evaluated. Sex specific models for adverse clinical outcomes in AF have not been developed. The current project will fill these knowledge gaps and provide a platform for the integrated interdisciplinary management of AF patients.

column36: Gender in Focus: A Photo Elicitation Study of Gender, Self-management, and Care with Emerging Adults with Type 1 Diabetes
column37: Early emerging adulthood (18 to 24 years) is a time of emotional, psychological and social change, and for those living with type 1 diabetes, represents a period of life that is often associated with loss to follow-up, the emergence of long-term complications and increased risk of adverse health outcomes. Gender - known to impact health behaviours, needs, and opportunities for health - is thought to be particularly influential in shaping health-related experiences during emerging adulthood. However, little is known about the relationship between gender and experiences of type 1 diabetes and diabetes self-management as well as how gender might affect the delivery of care to this group. This study aims to provide a theory-informed understanding of the ways in which gender frames individuals' perspectives of type 1 diabetes, impacts self-management practices, and informs delivery of care. To achieve this aim, we will employ critical and arts-based qualitative methods as well as Bourdieu's Theory of Practice. In phase 1, we will conduct focus groups and individual photo elicitation interviews with 30 emerging adults living with type 1 diabetes. Leveraging results from phase 1, we will construct a photographic exhibit that will be shared with formal (e.g. physician, nurse) and informal (e.g. family/friends) care providers in phase 2. Twenty individuals will be recruited from each group (total n=40) to participate in an interview to discuss their perceptions of the exhibit. These interviews are intended to capture the relevance/impact of the exhibit and how it may inform delivery of care and support. Results from this study will provide a deeper understanding of the ways that gender frames illness experiences for emerging adults living with type 1 diabetes and enhance the personalization of care for this group as a result. Findings will also be used to help build a community of emerging adults living with type 1 diabetes and foster opportunities for greater peer support.

column36: Agir ensemble sur la resilience d'equipe au travail en cancerologie pour optimiser la capacite de faire face aux situations difficiles: une etude de cas multiples selon l'evaluation realiste dans le reseau de cancerologie du Quebec
column37: Les equipes de soins aupres des personnes touchees par le cancer font face a des situations difficiles au quotidien: annonce du diagnostic de cancer et de mauvaises nouvelles sur l'evolution de la maladie, detresse des patients et de leurs proches, rarete des ressources. Ces situations sont amplifiees avec la COVID-19. Les equipes sont a risque de fatigue de compassion, d'epuisement et d'etre a bout de moyens. Ces risques affectent le fonctionnement des equipes, la sante et la qualite de vie au travail; et au final impactent l'offre de soins. Bien qu'il existe des interventions prometteuses, les recherches pour soutenir la resilience et en apprecier les effets aupres des equipes specialisees en cancerologie sont quasi inexistantes. L'etude vise a mieux comprendre comment intervenir en soutien a la resilience d'equipe oeuvrant aupres des personnes touchees par le cancer. Pour etre utile et faisable, l'intervention s'appuie sur une approche de partenariat etroit avec les professionnels des equipes cliniques et les membres des equipes de gestion afin qu'elles puissent offrir des soins de qualite et securitaires. Nous analyserons les facilitants et obstacles a la resilience et evaluerons les effets de l'intervention a l'aide d'entrevues, d'observations et de questionnaires. Quatre etablissements de sante au Quebec ayant plusieurs equipes en cancerologie se sont engages a participer. L'etude fournira des donnees inedites sur les meilleures pratiques pour mieux soutenir la resilience d'equipe au travail dans un secteur de soins specialises. column36: Heterogeneity of interprofessional primary care teams and its effect on quality of care and health service use in older adults
column37: Experts agree that primary care clinics where family doctors work in teams with other health professionals like nurses and social workers are an effective way to give older patients the care that they need. Teams, however, come in different shapes and sizes and it is not clear how these differences might affect patients' quality of care or their need for hospital services. Given the large health policy investments promoting primary care for the aging population, it is important that we better understand the ways in which team-based clinics can best support the care of older persons. This project will breakdown the complex links between primary care teams, quality of primary care, such as access, continuity and coordination of care, and hospital use in older persons. We will use data from one of Statistics Canada's health surveys and Quebec government data on patient's use of hospital and other medical services and focus on persons 65 years old and older with health conditions that are considered best managed through high-quality primary care. Our team will use advanced methods in statistics to describe the different types of teams and which might perform better in improving quality of care and hospital use in older patients. Overall, this project will help health professionals and policy makers understand what features of team-based primary care gives the best outcomes in terms of access, continuity and coordination while also avoiding the ED and hospital when not necessary. This will help implement solutions to better organize and plan the services needed to best care for our growing aging population.

column36: Understanding the Common CHILDhood Inflammatory Origins of Asthma and Atherosclerosis
column37: Chronic respiratory disease, CRD (asthma and COPD) and cardiovascular disease, CVD (heart attack, stroke and heart failure) often occur together and are the leading cause of illness and death in adults. Although CRD and CVD may not appear until a person is older, risk factors for these conditions begin in early life. Low lung function and high blood pressure are risk factors that may develop together and might be related to how our immune system responds to colds and chest infections when we are very young. The CHILD Cohort Study is following 3,400 children (born in 2009-12) who have answered questions on their health, come in for medical visits and given blood samples many times from birth until 8 years of age. We will ask the same children to repeat these measures at age 13. We will analyze their lung function and blood pressure to see if these measures are related to asthma and changes (stiffness) in blood vessels. We will also study their blood samples for signs of inflammation and determine if this is connected to early life colds and chest infections. With this information, we hope to better understand how CRD and CVD develop in early life, which will help scientists develop new and earlier ways to prevent these important chronic disorders.

column36: Electric Field Modeling to Optimize Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation and Engage Neurophysiological Therapeutic Targets in Treatment Resistant Depression
column37: About 2.5% of Canadians are diagnosed with treatment resistant depression (TRD) yearly. Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is an efficient form of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation that is an effective, evidence based treatment for TRD. However, iTBS, like all brain stimulation, is implemented via trial and error, as, to date, there are no predictive methods to assess the likelihood of patient response to iTBS. Work from our centre focused on TRD has previously established changes in cortical activity indexed via TMS-EEG after brain stimulation, but not with placebo, indicating the promise of TMS-EEG markers of cortical activity as markers of brain stimulation response. In contrast to other forms of rTMS, iTBS is known to result in enhanced plasticity, or cortical excitation. Even with these advances, response rates with iTBS remain at 30-40%. The optimization of electric field (E-field) delivery may improve treatment response by accounting for the individual differences in head structure and brain regional anatomy. We will examine if iTBS combined with E-field modeling (iTBSe) better engages TMS-EEG markers of cortical excitation and improves clinical response when compared to conventional iTBS in patients with TRD.

column36: Training Intervention and Program of Support (TIPS) for fostering the adoption of family-centred telehealth interventions in pediatric rehabilitation: A pan-Canadian implementation-effectiveness study.
column37: One in five Canadians care for someone with a disability, and nearly 50% of them are parents of a child with a disability. Many felt their rehabilitation needs were not being met, even before the disruptions to healthcare and education systems caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Telehealth, or healthcare services provided through technologies (mostly online), offers therapists an effective means of providing parents with timely information, education, counselling and training to meet their child's needs. Numerous pediatric rehabilitation organizations 'adopted' telehealth in response to the pandemic, but many therapists lacked the appropriate training and voiced a need for support to ensure telehealth practices were effective and led to meaningful results for their patients. This study aims to address this need. Our team has developed a telehealth intervention for parents of children with a disability living in Quebec, for which a training and support program (TIPS) was provided to therapists. The present study is an extension of this work, to implement and assess the impact of TIPS on a broader scale. Twenty centres from across Canada that provide pediatric rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy or speech and language pathology) to children with a disability ages 0-12 and their families have committed to participate. The TIPS program will first be adapted to meet the training and support needs of each participating centre and will then be offered to their therapists for one year. Before, during and after the support period, the study will monitor a number of indicators to track how TIPS was implemented and what effect it may have had on the therapists, on the participating centers and on how families perceived their services. This study will provide important insight into how best to support pediatric therapists so that telehealth becomes a sustainable option used by therapists to meet the needs of children with a disability and their families.

column36: A novel mechanism of antibiotic tolerance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
column37: Pseudomonas aeruginosa can cause devastating chronic infections that are nearly impossible to clear with antibiotics. During chronic infections, bacteria grows slowly or as aggregates called biofilms, and this physiological state leads bacteria to become "indifferent" (also termed tolerant) to the toxic effects of antibiotics. Tolerant bacteria thus cause antibiotic treatments to fail and infections to persist or relapse. Unfortunately, current antibiotics are not effective against tolerant bacteria and our understanding of the mechanisms of tolerance is still very limited. The goal of our project is to understand the mechanism of tolerance and to advance the discovery of new antibacterial therapies effective against tolerant bacteria in order to treat chronic infections. We have recently discovered that a bacterial enzyme (called cyclopropane fatty acid synthase CFAS) that modifies the Pseudomonas membrane lipids, making its envelope less permeable when they are in a slow-growing state, and thus shielding it from antibiotics. Conversely, when CFAS is disrupted, Pseudomonas become highly sensitive to antibiotic killing, leading to more effective antibiotic treatments. This suggests that CFAS could be a promising target to discover new drugs that will enhance the efficacy of existing antibiotics. For this project, we propose 1) to study how CFAS makes the Pseudomonas envelope less permeable and renders bacteria more susceptible to antibiotics; 2) to define the importance of CFAS in chronic infections using lab models of biofilms, mouse infection models and human samples of chronic infections; 3) to assess whether CFAS can be a drug target for the discovery of CFAS inhibitors as new drugs that can enhance the efficacy of antibiotics in the treatment of chronic infections.

column36: Traditional Indigenous Land-Based Diet and Chronic Inflammation: Does Adherence to the Traditional First Nations Diet Decrease the Severity of Chronic Inflammatory Diseases?

column36: Reducing bleeding with DOACs in breast cancer patients: The STOP-Bleed Cancer Study
column37: Cancer patients are particularly prone to have blood clots and/or irregular heart beats, and blood thinners are medications used to treat and prevent blood clots that may lead to stroke, death and other complications. There is a new class of blood thinners called "direct oral anticoagulants" that are used more and more often in cancer patients. This new class of blood thinners has the advantage of being able to be taken by mouth and no need for frequent monitoring. However, these drugs could still thin patients' blood too much and cause bleeding problems, especially when they interact with other drugs including cancer therapies. A worrying interaction between this new class of blood thinners and several different classes of cancer drugs is suspected to lead to dangerous blood thinning and internal bleeding, but there have not been studies to investigate this. We are proposing this study that will examine the risk of bleeding in older patients who were prescribed direct oral anticoagulants and certain breast cancer therapies that could have interactions from large healthcare databases in Ontario. Our study will be the first and largest of its kind ever done and the results will immediately provide information for patients and their doctors.

column36: Alberta (AB) Collaborative Quality Improvement Strategies to Improve Outcomes of Preterm Infants 32 - 36 Weeks' Gestation: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial (ABC-QI Trial)
column37: Every year in Canada 1 in 12 infants is born preterm, before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Of these preterm infants 85% are born between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy. Infants born before 32 weeks are at the highest risk of death or complications from prematurity. This has resulted in a significant amount of research and quality improvement initiatives focusing on improving outcomes for this patient group. On the other hand there is very limited research or quality improvement activities focusing on infants 32-36 weeks. This group composes a larger proportion of infants admitted to Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). These infants require intensive care for temperature control, nutrition support, breathing support, and infection management. Information available on infants 32-36 weeks demonstrates significant variability between units in treatment approaches and length of stay. Our diverse research team aims to implement collaborative quality improvement strategies in a step-wise fashion targeting standardization of care for 32-36 week infants in Level 2 NICUs across the province of Alberta. This will be achieved by using validated quality improvement method and evidence based care bundles. These bundles will target two common issues, breathing support and nutrition support. Once trained, NICUs will benefit from collaborative networking to share information and maintain engagement. Decreasing duration of hospital stay and getting the babies home as quickly as possible is the primary objective of the study. Other objectives include reducing healthcare costs, reducing duration of breathing support, supporting infant feeding, and reducing transfer to higher level of care and emergency room visits. This study will provide evidence of the benefit of collaborative QI strategies in infants born at 32-36 weeks. This will help policy makers and government agencies in directing resources to support collaborative quality improvement in this patient group across Canada.

column36: Dissecting the origins and microenvironment of replication repair deficient hypermutant gliomas for novel immune based therapies
column37: Gliomas are the most common brain tumours in children, adolescents, and young adults (CAYA, 0-40 years) and are a leading cause of cancer death in this population. We discovered that some of these gliomas contain the highest number of DNA mutations (hypermutation) in all cancers. Hypermutation is caused by the cell's inability to repair mistakes when it replicates its DNA. Although these hypermutant gliomas are resistant to chemotherapy and radiation they are remarkably sensitive to immunotherapy. We have established an international consortium focusing on these tumours in CAYA. As a first step we found that in Canada, many of these gliomas are missed due to lack of awareness and appropriate testing. Then, through an international clinical trial, we saw that, for the first time, a third of patients with hypermutant gliomas treated with immunotherapy are long-term survivors. Recently, we discovered that these gliomas can be divided into 3 groups. Each group has different mutational spectrums and respond differently to immunotherapy. We have also established mouse models which are similar to the human glioma groups. These will be used to test new immunotherapy combinations for each glioma group. In this project we will define the impact of hypermutant glioma in Canada and find new therapies for these tumours through the following aims: In aim 1 we will use a new genomic tool to screen >1500 CAYA gliomas from 3 Canadian provinces to determine how common these gliomas are and if we can treat them differently. In aim 2 we will discover the cell of origin and how these glioma groups develop. In aim 3 we will find which immune cells are specific to each glioma group and how this can explain why they respond differently to immunotherapy. In aim 4 we will use genome editing to uncover specific gene targets, revealing weaknesses of these aggressive gliomas. We will then combine these targets with immunotherapy to improve survival for these deadly hypermutant tumours.

column36: Bridging the divide between acute medical care and housing: A comprehensive evaluation of a "medical respite program" for the homeless
column37: People with lived experience of homelessness (PWLEH) have poor health and complex medical and social needs. They frequently present to hospital to meet these needs. Unfortunately, while hospitals can treat acute medical conditions, they are not well-equipped to address social barriers (such as housing) that are frequently the root causes of ill-health. PWLEH are therefore discharged back to the street, with no real change in either their long-term trajectory in health or social conditions. Medical respite programs (MRPs) are an innovation that bridges hospital-based medical care with shelter-based housing and social support. They are designed for patients too well for acute care, but too sick to be discharged to the street. In Calgary, an MRP was recently created as a transitional unit (based within a homeless shelter) that provides nursing care, while simultaneously focusing on expediting housing. There are only three other MRPs in Canada. It is unknown how effective they are in improving health and well-being. We will conduct a mixed methods evaluation to assess the effectiveness of the Calgary MRP. Our study will follow a group of PWLEH before and after attending the MRP, to determine whether the MRP reduces rates of hospital admission, hospital length of stay, and visits to the emergency department. We will also explore whether the MRP changes patterns of drug and alcohol use, and whether it improves quality of life and time to stable housing. Lastly, in-depth interviews with MRP patients will be conducted to better understand how the MRP has (or has not) affected their social circumstances, support network, engagement with the health system and ultimately their well-being. Our findings will inform other jurisdictions on the effect of this innovation for a particularly underserved population.

column36: The "Atrial FIBrillation in Pregnancy: assessing seveRe matErnal morbidity and anticoagulation strateGies" (AFIB-PREG) Study
column37: Cardiac problems have become the first cause of maternal mortality in Canada. Transformations to the cardiovascular system during pregnancy may explain why some women experience new or sudden worsening of their cardiac problems in pregnancy. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most frequent type of heartbeat abnormality to occur in pregnancy. AF can be associated with serious maternal complications, such as heart failure and strokes. What we do not know is what proportion of women with AF in pregnancy will experience serious complications. In addition, blood thinners are a kind of medication that may be given to pregnant women with AF to prevent strokes. However, blood thinners can also lead to bleeding problems. Information is currently lacking about the safety and efficacy of these medications when given for AF in pregnancy. The objective of our study is to gain more knowledge on how best to care for pregnant women with AF. First, we will measure the proportion of women with AF with serious complications. We will also evaluate whether blood thinners are effective and safe medications to prevent strokes during pregnancy and the 6 weeks following delivery. To do so, we will analyse the anonymous information of patients in Canada and the United States with AF during pregnancy. The results of the proposed study will provide information about the specific healthcare needs of pregnant women with AF. In turn, this study will help to improve the care of pregnant and postpartum women with cardiovascular diseases.
