column36: Modulating attentional circuitry in the anterior cingulate cortex using adaptive intracranial stimulation
column37: Attention is an incompletely understood, complex process that requires precise coordination of brain rhythms within the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Children with epilepsy are disproportionately affected by attention deficits and intracranial electrodes implanted for surgical treatment of epilepsy in this population provide a unique opportunity to safely study and modulate the neural underpinnings of attention in vivo. In the current study, we will first study the association between brain rhythms in the ACC and behaviour during a task of shifting attention performed while intracranial electrodes are implanted within the ACC. Second, we will characterize how the ACC interacts with large-scale brain networks known to subserve attention while the children perform the task. Finally, we will develop and test a novel, intelligent brain stimulation algorithm that will identify disruptions in brain rhythms within the ACC in real-time. When these disruptions are detected, precisely time-locked electrical stimulation will be administered to the ACC to improve attentional performance. This work will lead to a better understanding of the fundamental mechanisms of human attention and facilitate the development of innovative avenues for the treatment of attention deficits in children with epilepsy. The novel methodologies that we will develop and test can be leveraged to understand numerous cognitive functions facilitated by the organized coordination of brain rhythms.

column36: Elucidating the cellular and network mechanisms for stress sensitivity control in the hypothalamus
column37: How do our brains determine whether something is stressful or not? Responding to threats is essential for survival (ex. escape from predator), but how we perceive certain situations as stressful is highly dynamic and variable among individuals. Clinically, high stress sensitivity is a key symptom for major depression and other mental illnesses that impose profound health and financial burden. Understanding the neural mechanisms of stress sensitivity will facilitate new prevention, diagnosis and treatments for mental illnesses. In this grant proposal, we reveal the circuit and cellular mechanisms that integrate signals at a key node of stress information processing in the brain - neurons classically known as the output neurons that drive the neuroendocrine response. Newly emerging data indicate that these neurons play more complex roles, by bidirectionally responding to competing (e.g.stressful and pleasurable) stimuli and triggering rapid behavioral changes besides the slow hormone output. Currently, we know very little about the activity patterns of these neurons in living animals, and how they process stress information. By combining cutting-edge neuroscience techniques for recording and manipulating activities of specific neuron-types inside of living animals and advanced computational simulations, we will understand how our brain perceives certain information as stressful and how their sensitivity to stress changes due to past history of stressful experiences as well as biological sex. For basic neuroscience, this study will reveal mechanisms for how our brains encode stress. For clinical translation, this work will reveal neural mechanisms controlling stress sensitivity and offers potential targets leveraged to diagnose and treat heightened stress sensitivity prevalent in mental illnesses.

column36: Defining how a common food dye affects microbiota and serotonin signalling to promote colitis
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are the most common chronic intestinal conditions and their incidence and prevalence have shown a dramatic increase in the last decades. Emerging evidence suggests linkages between IBD and diet, based on both epidemiological and experimental studies. One factor by which the diet may impact colitis involves the presence of food additives in the food supply. Among various food additives that are commonly used, artificial food dyes play a key role in enhancing the appearance of food and attracting consumers. Allura red, is one of the most widely used artificial dyes in food products, and its consumption is increasing. However, we still don't know whether allura red plays a role in pathogenesis of colitis. Serotonin is a key molecule in the human body that controls many normal and disease processes, and recently we demonstrated a novel role of serotonin in shaping gut microbiota composition and in increasing susceptibility to colitis. We hypothesize that the allura red in food enhances the susceptibility to colitis. We plan to pin down three key points: (1) Does allura red alters intestinal barrier function to increase susceptibility to colitis? (2) Does allura red influences susceptibility of colitis by affecting microbiota? and (3) Does allura red influences serotonin signaling in relation to severity of colitis. This study will not only provide us important information on the effects of allura red in pathogenesis of colitis but will also help in increasing awareness in IBD sufferers to avoid such additives as well in planning preventive programs for subjects at high risk to develop IBD.

column36: Achieving Healing and Wellness through Cultural Continuity Approaches: Strengthening Promising Practices for Addictions Treatments in an Indigenous Community in Saskatchewan
column37: Contemporary literature affirms that colonization explicitly sought to disconnect First Nations, Metis and Inuit peoples across Canada from their land and culture. Our histories of colonization and colonialism differ, but many of us are rediscovering Indigenous Ways of Knowing, Being and Doing. Within these knowledge systems, wellness is more wholistic than mere health, encompassing physical, mental, emotional and spiritual wellbeing. Forced disconnection exacerbated by a number of other socioeconomic and structural determinants is recognized as a critical factor in the current health inequities experienced by many Indigenous communities. Substance and alcohol use is a problem in northern Saskatchewan, with the rate of hospitalizations for alcohol-related issues and injuries suffered while intoxicated more than five times the national average. To address these health inequities, the adoption of community-based initiatives entrenched in decolonizing philosophies and strengths-based approaches is strongly recommended. The proposed project will be based in the Northern Village of Pinehouse, Saskatchewan. Following a needs assessment using community-based participatory methods, the Recovery Lake Program (RLP) emerged as a research priority for the community. The community has identified the need to improve RLP and develop a culturally responsive model that can be adapted and contextualized across the region. This research project will explore improving service delivery by incorporating additional land- and culture-based activities as part of the program, conduct process and outcome evaluations. column36: Use of Wearable Sensors for Early Detection and Tracking of Viral Respiratory Tract Infections: The WE SENSE study
column37: Viral respiratory tract infections (VRTI) like the flu and COVID-19 are among the most common human illnesses, impacting billions globally. There is an unmet need to identify novel ways to detect, treat and prevent their spread. A new technology harnessing wearable biosensors (wearables) worn by people could address this need. We will assess the potential of wearables to detect small changes in vital sign patterns (e.g., breathing, heart rate variability, oxygen saturation, skin temperature, sweat level, blood pressure) and activity levels that can accompany VRTIs. METHODS: A clinical study of 60 healthy adults aged 18-59 years. Participants' vital signs and activity levels will be monitored continuously using wearable biosensors for 7-days prior to and 7-days following receipt of live attenuated influenza virus (FluMist vaccine), along with symptom tracking and blood tests to measure immune responses. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms will be used to analyze the data and develop a detection model for low grade influenza infection. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: This multidisciplinary study will assess a new indication for wearable biosensor technologies. AI and ML will identify subtle changes in vital signs and activity levels from the immune response to respiratory viruses. These data will help design future studies to address important public health questions related to respiratory virus detection, containment and management.

column36: A Tale of Two Resident Lung Macrophages and Their Biology In Health and Disease
column37: The lung is exposed to the external environment so we breath in some bacteria and noxious molecules with every breath. Most of these bacteria never reach the little sacs (alveoli) where oxygen is taken up but some bacteria always do. We use a special microscope to image the alveoli of mice and we have uncovered some critical functions of the immune cells. The immune cells that live in these sacs are called alveolar macrophages and they run from alveolus to alveolus through little tunnels between alveoli and vacuum up all bacteria. If the alveolar macrophages cannot crawl between alveoli than problems arise. When you get a viral infection like the flu, then macrophages cannot crawl very well and now bacteria take advantage of the situation and grow in the alveoli causing infection. The lung is surrounded by a really large sac called the pleural space and we have macrophages inside that sac as well that may oversee the role of the alveolar macrophages New macrophages come into the lung and need training to be lung macrophages. This will happen through epigenetic changes ie., environmental changes that affect the way your genes work (not changes in gene sequence though) and this will lead to better vacuuming of bacteria. In other words if our macrophages see a bacterium and have to kill it, through epigenetic changes the macrophages will kill bacteria much better the next time. We think that the more robust the microbiome is and the more we are exposed to environment the better our macrophages will be at vacuuming bacteria. However, this may make our macrophages worse at doing other chores. As mentioned, sometimes noxious stimuli enter the lungs and cause some damage and repair is required. If our macrophages are trained to do that they may not be as good at vacuuming bacteria. We will investigate how these macrophages manage to clear bacteria and repair.

column36: Leveraging Trans-Canada Expertise and Resources to Design and Evaluate Novel Auger Electron-Emitting Radioimmunotherapies (RIT) for Metastatic Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC)
column37: In this project, a team of researchers from across Canada with unique and complementary expertise and resources will work together to develop and study new targeted radiation treatments for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), a form of the disease which has a poor outcome. The radiation treatments will consist of radioisotopes that emit short-range electrons (Auger electrons) that are very damaging and lethal to cancer cells, linked to a pharmaceutical quality antibody, panitumumab that is already used to treat certain types of cancer, in order to target these radioisotopes to tumours. The radioisotopes will be made at TRIUMF, which is Canada's world-leading facility for producing radioisotopes. Bifunctional chelators, which are molecules that strongly bind the radioisotopes and which can be attached to panitumumab will be synthesized at Simon Fraser University. The radiation treatments will be constructed from the radioisotopes, bifunctional chelators and panitumumab at the University of Toronto. They will then also be studied at the University of Toronto for treatment of metastases from TNBC in a mouse tumour model that has been established. The effectiveness and normal tissue toxicity of these new radiation treatments for TNBC will be assessed in the mouse model. The proposed project may lead to new methods to produce these radioisotopes, to stably attach them to antibodies, as well as new treatments for metastatic TNBC. Ultimately, if successful, the proposed research could be advanced to a Phase 1 clinical trial in patients with metastatic TNBC, which is a poor prognosis form of breast cancer for which there are currently very few effective treatments.

column36: Harnessing predictive analytics for personalized high-value health: nesting clinical decision support for cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a provincial lung cancer screening program
column37: Background: Quebec is implementing a provincial lung cancer screening program which will screen 3,000 high risk smokers between 55-74 years of age with two annual low dose CTs over two years. The three main causes of death in participants screened for LC are cardiovascular disease (CVD 25%), LC (24%), or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, 10%). Participants enrolled in lung cancer screening have been shown to have high rates of untreated cardiovascular disease, identified on imaging of the heart on low dose CT of the chest, and untreated COPD, identified on imaging and history documented by lung cancer screening navigators. Methods: We will perform a randomized clinical trial of comprehensive personalized health intervention provided to physicians and patients. Exploiting data already extracted by nurse navigators for lung cancer screening, and data from imaging by low dose CT as part of clinical care, we will implement a clinical decision support for primary care providers, and educational resources for patients. This will empower patients and their providers to engage with proven effective treatments for cardiovascular disease and COPD. Primary outcomes, determined at one year, are guideline concordant statin therapy in participants with moderate to severe coronary calcifications (objective 1), and guideline concordant inhaler therapy in symptomatic COPD (objective 2). Conclusions: If our hypotheses are confirmed, this patient-centered low cost approach will prove effective in mitigating health disparities among high risk men and women who have shown significant barriers in access to evidence-based care. It will also provide added value to lung cancer screening programs at low cost.

column36: Improving Maternity Outcomes by Engaging Stakeholders in a Holistic Assessment of the Social and Clinical Determinants of Severe Maternal Morbidity in Canada - a Feasibility Study
column37: Serious complications during pregnancy can impact the birth experience, mother-baby bonding, and short-term maternal health as well as have long-term effects on families. National health databases can describe total numbers of women experiencing serious pregnancy complications, also known as severe maternal morbidity (SMM), but current Canadian databases are not able to provide detailed information about the sequence of events during pregnancy that could lead to SMM. Information about maternal health, social considerations and care prior to SMM will help identify techniques and processes to target, in order to reduce SMM. Canada is a vast country with many birthing units led by obstetricians, midwives and family doctors. When a SMM occurs, often it is reviewed and shared confidentially with the birthing unit to determine what events led to it and prevent similar events in the future. However, there is no local, provincial or national mechanism for sharing lessons learned, examining trends or collecting data about SMM. We believe that lessons learned in individual units could be relevant to other units as well. Sharing and summarizing anonymous SMM information at the local, provincial and, eventually, national level will help us understand the similarities and differences between units, identify preventable factors that lead to SMM and make recommendations to reduce SMM. Other countries, such as the United Kingdom, have started sharing SMM information and the information sharing has resulted in a considerable improvement in the health of mothers. We will assess the feasibility of collecting and collating information from individual birthing units in four Canadian provinces in order to build a robust SMM surveillance system that provides ongoing information on SMM, identifies prevention strategies, and results in improved maternal health.

column36: AcT-Cog: Online cognitive assessment in the Alteplase compared to Tenecteplase (AcT) trial.
column37: When a clot stops blood flow to the brain it causes injury, called a stroke. Strokes cause problems with key functions like movement or cognition (memory and thinking skills). Three-quarters of people can have cognition problems after stroke, and this is among the most feared complications of stroke. Even before 2020, but especially in the COVID-19 pandemic, we need new ways to measure thinking that are easier for people to do. We also need to understand what the cognitive test scores really mean - how to they relate to people's quality of life, or to costs to care for people? We are doing a large study comparing two emergency stroke treatments (Alteplase compared to Tenecteplase, AcT). Using this platform, we propose a new study (AcT-Cog), in which people will complete 6 proven cognitive tasks (www.cambridgebrainsciences.com) on computer at home. The tests will be done 3-6 months after their stroke. This type of study, with easy-to-use tests that people can do at home, has not been tried before as an outcome in studies of new stroke treatments. The first goal of our study will be to see how useable it is (i.e. can people access and complete the tasks?) and understand what makes it easier or harder for people to complete the tasks. The second goal will be to see if cognitive test scores relate to important outcomes like quality of life or future need for health care. The third goal of our study will be to see if the scores from this assessment are different between the groups who get alteplase or tenecteplase. The results of this trial will help us understand when and how computer testing can be used to measure cognition after stroke and will help us understand the importance of changes in the scores. If scores differ between treatment groups, that will help inform treatment for stroke patients around the world and could help to improve cognitive outcomes after stroke.

column36: Targeting obesity-associated monocytosis in colorectal cancer liver metastasis
column37: Obesity is associated with an elevated risk of developing 13 cancer types, and an elevated risk of dying from 14 cancer types. In Canada, 24% of adults are obese and another 36% are overweight. In addition, 20% of people with a normal body weight are 'metabolically obese', meaning they have similar health risks as obese people, even though they appear healthy. Consequentially, obesity now rivals smoking tobacco as the leading preventable risk factor for cancer mortality, estimated to be responsible for up to 20% of all cancer-related deaths in adults. Most cancer deaths are caused by metastasis (cancer spread), yet we lack a strong understanding of how obesity regulates cancer metastasis. In previously published work, we discovered that obesity enhances cancer metastasis to the lungs through its effects on immune cells. We observed similar effects on immune cells in the liver, suggesting that obesity may also enhance liver metastasis. The biggest source of liver metastasis is colorectal cancer (CRC), which is the 2nd leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. Obesity increases the risk of death from CRC by >40% in men and >30% in women, and we suspect it does this by enhancing liver metastasis. In new experiments, we have found that CRC liver metastasis is enhanced in mouse models of obesity. This occurs in part through the effects of obesity on specific cells of the immune system (monocytes and T cells). The objective of this proposal is to determine how monocytes and T cells regulate obesity-associated liver metastasis. We hypothesize that therapies that target these immune cells will reduce cancer progression in obese hosts. Given the prevalence of obesity and its association with cancer mortality, our research will uncover therapeutic opportunities for patients predisposed to have poorer outcomes.

column36: Tracing the Cellular and Molecular Origins of Mouse and Human Medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma is a common childhood malignant brain tumour that has a 70% 5 year survival but only with therapy that is toxic to the developing nervous system and with a significant risk of secondary cancers. My lab discovered that medulloblastoma growth is driven by rare populations of cancer cells that have stem cell properties. These specialized cancer cells divide very slowly and are called quiescent, but they give rise to daughter cells that divide very quickly. The medulloblastoma stem cells are also resistant to therapy. These findings strongly suggest that to have safer and more effective treatments, we need to first understand the growth properties of the medulloblastoma stem cells and then we need to devise treatments that kill them. In particular, we think that targeting the transition from quiescent cells to rapidly dividing cells is a pivotal treatment opportunity. In this project we will deeply study the mechanisms of how medulloblastoma stem cells transition from a quiescent state to a rapidly dividing state. We will study how internal factors regulate of this transition and how external factors may wake up the quiescent stem cells, with an aim of blocking these factors. Blocking this transition may also be preventative for medulloblastoma initiation in some circumstances. In our studies, we will use mouse models of medulloblastoma and a new human cell culture model that we developed in our lab to develop new understanding and treatment approaches. We predict that in targeting this tranistion, we will uncover new important new features of medulloblastoma growth that will lead to more effective and less toxic therapies.

column36: Predictive modeling in multiple sclerosis: using real world data to inform practice, policy, and research
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease of the brain and spinal cord, affecting over 2.3 million people worldwide and 93,500 people in Canada. Canada has one of the highest rates of MS globally and it is estimated that the number of people living with MS in Canada will increase to approximately 33,600 in 2031. MS mainly affects people between 15 and 40 years of age, placing a significant strain not only on patients in the prime of their life, but also on the healthcare system. Although there is no cure for MS, there are treatments available to help manage episodes of increased disability (relapses), reduce relapses, and control symptoms. Treatment with drugs known as interferon-betas were the first medications for MS and being the only promising therapeutic option initially for many years, treatment selection was limited. An increasing number of new treatments have emerged since then, however, there are limited evidence based guidelines concerning the use and selection of treatments for the various disease states of MS. Additionally, while there have been many studies that have identified specific independent risk factors for patient health outcomes, no study to date has attempted to combine these patient, disease, and treatment-related factors into a complete model to enhance the prediction of how patients will respond to treatment and whether or not they will improve. The objective of this study is to use patient data from provincial healthcare records as well as clinical data collected over an extended time period to develop and test of a series of predictive models in MS, and make these models freely available on a web-based platform. Ultimately, these models will help guide the selection of the best therapeutic approach for each individual, which will improve decision-making at the patient level. In addition, these predictions should result in better patient care as well as a more efficient and cost-effective use of healthcare resources.

column36: Combination Antithrombotic Thrombotic therapy for prevention of recurrent Ischemic Stroke in patients with IntraCranial Atherosclerotic Disease (CATIS-ICAD)
column37: Stroke is the 3rd leading cause of death and primary cause of disability in Canada and globally. Stroke caused by narrowing of the brain arteries from cholesterol plaques is the commonest cause of stroke. Many patients with narrowing of brain arteries suffer "silent" strokes, that are only picked up by MRI scans of the brain, in addition to the diagnosed symptomatic stroke. "Silent" strokes are about four times common as symptomatic stroke and overtime lead to significant memory and gait difficulties. Currently when someone has a stroke due to narrowed arteries they are treated with aspirin, blood pressure and cholesterol-lowering medications to prevent another stroke. However even with these treatments, there is a high risk of recurrent stroke (1 in 20 chance in 30 days and 1 in 10 chance at one year) A recent study in patients with narrowing of arteries in heart and limbs that added low-dose rivaroxaban (blood thinner) to aspirin showed a 50% reduction of stroke without an increase in bleeding into the brain or fatal bleeding. We plan to assess if use of low-dose rivaroxaban and aspirin is safe (no increase bleeding into brain) in patients with stroke due to narrowing of brain arteries. The ultimate goal of this pilot study is to gather necessary information to plan for a larger study to assess for effectiveness of this combination in preventing recurrent symptomatic and "silent" strokes. If this combination is eventually confirmed to reduce stroke by 50%, it would be the biggest advance in secondary stroke prevention in the past 30 years. We will enrol 100 patients from 10 Canadian sites and randomly assign to the combination treatment (50) or aspirin (50). Patients will qualify to be in the study if they are over 40 years and has a stroke or transient ischemic attack (warning stroke) due to narrowing of the brain arteries by plaque. Patients will be followed for 2 years and have an MRI scan at the beginning and end of the study to look for "silent" strokes.

column36: A comprehensive study on bone quality for the prediction of second hip fractures
column37: Hip fracture is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality; it happens easier in older people especially females. A question here is: what makes bone fragile as we become older? Current consensus is that our femoral bone becomes weaker and brittle because of the loss in bone mineral density. However, there are some unique aging related structural changes to femoral bone. These include increased porosity and decreased thickness in cortical shell. Additionally, we recently discovered that the femoral cortical bone has a layer of highly mineralized tissue covering the surface of human femoral neck, which is extremely brittle. We hypothesized that the presence of these weak structures directly increases hip fragility. In this project, a biomedical engineer with expertise in bone fracture, a bone imaging specialist, an experienced bone biologist and an orthopaedic surgeon teamed up to study the impact of decreased bone quality on hip fragility fracture. By using various advanced microscopy techniques, we aimed to answer the following three questions: Why is femoral bone fragile in older people? Are there any differences between older male adults and female adults? What are the roles of bone quality in second hip fractures? Answers to these questions will advance our knowledge on bone biology and mechanics, help to develop new techniques of bone diagnoses and lead to new measures of preventing second hip fractures.

column36: Age-associated B cells in viral infection and autoimmune diseases
column37: Our research is focused on uncovering the mechanisms in which autoimmune diseases are initiated and influenced by virus infection. In our youth, we are infected with a number of viruses that remain with us for the remainder of our lives. For its part, the virus can live forever with us and with those we come in contact with through re-infection. In our body, a cold war exists between the virus and our immune system that takes a toll on us by creating a system with strong hyper-reactive immune cells. One of these cell types, age-associated B cells (ABCs), increase in numbers as we age and engage strong immune responses capable of attacking invading pathogens and causing autoimmune responses. The relative success of generalized anti-B cell therapies for autoimmune diseases such as MS and RA is a strong piece of evidence of a common but rare B cell component to disease pathology. In this project, we aim to link these ABCs that are generated during maintenance of a common virus infection (EBV-people, and MHV68 for rodents) with increased and enhanced autoimmune diseases such as MS and RA. Identifying this common immunopathogenic cell type during the onset of disease will create an obvious target for common autoimmune therapies.

column37: Opioid-related overdose and death is one of the greatest public health crises in Canadian history, with approximately 3,800 deaths occurring nationally in 2019 alone. column36: FLASH radiotherapy - mechanisms and translational studies
column37: The effectiveness of radiotherapy is determined by normal tissue tolerance. In other words, the dose of radiation administered to the tumour is determined by how well the 'normal' tissue within the irradiated beam can tolerate the dose. Over decades the maximum dose and the optimal fractionation regime that produces the maximum anticancer effect whilst minimizing normal tissue complications has been determined for different cancer types and locations. Most often this radiotherapy treatment is fractionated, for example a prescribed dose of 60 Gy last 6 weeks with 30 fractions of ~2 Gy each. FLASH radiotherapy is a new investigational approach that can administer the total 60 Gy dose in one burst, typically lasting less than a second. This FLASH technique has emerged very recently when it was observed that in some situations radiation delivered at this high rate has less effect on normal tissues than on cancers. To advance this technique for eventual benefit to patients it is crucial to understand the precise circumstances where this differential effect on normal vs cancer tissue occurs. We will use our custom-developed laboratory techniques and experience in radiation biology to elucidate the mechanism for FLASH radiation activity, adding unique and significant insight to the building science surrounding FLASH. Ultimately, application of FLASH would significantly improve patient quality of life and treatment experience, on top of improving cancer cure rates.

column37: Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer (CAR-NK) cell therapy involves modifying NK cells to in the lab with a CAR to redirect them to interact with and kill cancer cells once infused into a cancer patient. We will then build tools to allow us to safely insert these reporter genes at defined locations in the NK cell DNA so that safety is maximized. Finally, we will build tools to allow one to visualize when the CAR-NK cells interact with their target cancer cells. These state-of-the- art technologies will allow us to measure CAR-NK cells numbers, survival over time, and communication with cancer cells throughout the body. This collection of important information can inform on treatment effectiveness, potential toxicity, as well as determine if the cells stay alive long enough to keep killing any residual or new cancer cells long after the patient is considered cured. In doing this, it will be possible to better assess CAR-NK cell therapies in individual patients, leading to safer and more precise treatment of cancer.

column36: An unexpected role for type I Interferon underlies cardiac adaptation to stress and prevents heart failure
column37: Hypertension (HTN) can leads to detrimental changes the structure and function of the heart, a process termed hypertensive heart disease (HTN-HD). The immune system directs the sterile inflammatory response triggered during HTN-HD; however, it is unclear what components prevent or exacerbate the development of HTN-HD. Type I interferons (IFN)s are cytokines secreted by cells upon sensing of nucleic acids normally found within a cell, but released upon cell stress or cell death. IFNs bind the IFN receptor (IFNAR), required for clearance of viral pathogens. Interestingly, recent studies have shown that following a heart attack, IFNs play pathological role, are triggered by DNA released from dying cells, worsening inflammation and impairing tissue repair. Despite its well characterized role in immunity, the role of type I IFN in HTN-HD is essentially unknown. We have new, surprising evidence that rather than participating in heart damage, type I IFNs protect heart function during high hypertension and prevent HTN-HD. Our preliminary data in animal models of hypertension show mice that lack signaling through the type I IFN pathway have worse cardiac function and increased tissue fibrosis. We localize separate protective roles to immune and non-immune cell type I IFN activity, opening a new area of investigation into a previously unknown cardioprotective role of type I IFN in HTN-HD.

column37: A major cause of sudden death is the development of a sustained very rapid heart rate associated with damage to cardiac muscle due to reduced blood supply. Specifically, we will directly characterize targeting accuracy, tissue destruction and subsequent healing with MRI and relate these results to procedure success. Results will inform further development of methods for MRI tissue characterization and more effective integration of MRI information into procedures for use in patient studies, yielding better outcomes.

column36: Timing in the cerebellum: from plasticity to behavior
column37: A remarkable feature of our brains is their ability to support learning. It is widely accepted that the connections between neurons, or synapses, are capable of plastic changes. Synaptic plasticity adapts neural circuits to encode learning. However, there are thousands of synapses in a circuit, and we do not know why specific synapses are chosen to undergo plasticity. As a consequence, we cannot predict how exactly neural circuits are changed by learning, either in health or in disease. We address this fundamental problem by investigating a brain region called the cerebellum in mice, which supports the learning of precise and well-calibrated movements. Thus, forms of cerebellum-dependent motor learning can be reliably induced and measured with a high degree of accuracy. Moreover, it is particularly important to understand the cerebellum because it is strongly implicated in mental health disorders such as autism, but remains understudied. In this project, we propose to identify how plasticity serves to support learning, at multiple levels of analysis - from molecules and synapses, to neural circuits and behavior. Our preliminary results identify that plasticity is shaped by experience so that it is optimized for different behaviors. Our overall goal is to identify how and why this occurs. This knowledge is critical to understand how the brain itself can be modified, in response to injury, disease or aging. Both in Canada and worldwide, mental health disorders remain a major contributor to human suffering and economic burden - partly because effective therapies are lacking. In turn, the lack of therapies stems from a lack of knowledge about how the brain works. The proposed research into the mechanisms of learning and how these learning mechanisms can be disrupted, shaped or regulated, is thus essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies for the broad spectrum of disorders where learning is perturbed.

column37: Gabapentinoids (GABAs) are drugs that are approved for the treatment of seizure and certain types of pain. COPD is a severe chronic respiratory condition that impairs breathing and leads to symptoms of breathlessness, cough, chest tightness, and fatigue. Patients frequently require hospitalizations due to acute exacerbations of symptoms that can be life-threatening. However, warnings from these health agencies are based on limited evidence and no large studies have been conducted to date in COPD patients. Thus, we aim to conduct a study that will assess whether the use of GABAs increases the risk of severe exacerbations in patients with COPD, when used alone and in combination with opioids. To perform this study, we will use a database that has medical information from over 50 million patients in the United Kingdom who visited a general practitioner. We will then identify patients with COPD and determine whether those using GABAs were hospitalized with a COPD exacerbation more frequently than those who did not. We will also assess whether COPD patients using GABAs in combination with opioids were hospitalized more frequently than those using GABAs or opioids alone. The use of GABAs may potentially increase risk of exacerbations and related death in COPD patients. Thus, the findings of our project will provide important information to guide prescription choices for COPD patients and to update safety guidelines for GABAs.

column37: The benefits and risks of fluoride exposure have been debated for decades. The Centers for Disease Control hails water fluoridation as one of the greatest public health achievements while others argue that fluoride exposure causes adverse health effects. While it is undisputed that fluoride is toxic at high levels (e.g. >5 mg/L), studies examining neurodevelopmental outcomes in populations exposed to optimal levels of fluoride are disputed. Existing human studies are limited in their ability to examine dose-response relations due to the restricted range of fluoride typically found in areas with fluoridation. Only a few studies have measured biomarkers of fluoride exposure across critical periods of development. Moreover, given the widespread sources of fluoride, few studies have directly linked sources of exposure when studying fluoride neurotoxicity. This study capitalizes on the New Hampshire Birth Cohort Study (NHBCS), a large, prospective cohort designed to examine how contaminants in drinking water and food affect the health of pregnant women and their children. We will leverage existing data from this cohort to assess the association between early-life exposure to fluoride (pregnancy and infancy) and children's IQ and behavioral problems in 578 mother-child pairs. Novel to our work is the measurement of fluoride in biospecimens (urine samples and toenails) as well as in tap water samples that are known to vary in fluoride concentration from approximately 0.1 to 2.0 mg/L. We will use detailed dietary intake information to understand sources of fluoride exposure in pregnant women and their infants. Finally, we will determine whether there is an increased risk of lower IQ scores or behavioral difficulties in children resulting from the use of fluoridated water to reconstitute infant formula. Results of this study will directly impact decision making on the safety of fluoride exposure during early brain development at levels relevant to the U.S. and Canada.

column36: Indispensable Amino Acid Requirements in Pregnancy and Lactation
column37: Protein is important in diet to help growth and maintain health. All body proteins are made up of 20 amino acids. Among these 20 amino acids there are 9 amino acids, which our body cannot make, and therefore must come from food sources, and are called essential amino acids. We are in now in a position to study this further and also find out the how much essential amino acids our body needs during different stages of pregnancy and lactation. Our study results will help in making improved diet recommendations to make sure both mother and baby are actively growing, and have a healthy, successful pregnancy and lactation.

column36: T cell immunity in tissues: maintaining mobility and adapting to external forces
column37: In our globally interconnected world, many of us travel to and from work, fly between cities, or even set up residence somewhere entirely different. Establishing residence in a new place involves adapting to new circumstances, and impediments either to our travels or our adaptation to new environments can have a dramatic impact on our lives. T lymphocytes have a similarly cosmopolitan lifestyle within our bodies. The job of T cells in the immune system - to find and stop the replication of a pathogen or cancer cell as quickly as possible - requires them to commute continuously between the blood and secondary lymphoid organs. During infection T cells become able to enter other tissues and even set up residence there, establishing long-term tissue resident memory which protects the body from reinfection. We are only beginning to understand the processes that allow T cells to adapt to their new environmental circumstances and to retain their mobile behaviour even within tissues that are far more dense than the lymphoid organs they came from. From other work on heart cells and connective tissue cells, we know that cells have to protect their genomic material from external forces. The denser the tissue environment a cell finds itself in, the greater the external forces on the cell. Cells adapt by increasing the rigidity of their nucleus in which the DNA of a cell is kept. However, we also know that a very rigid nucleus can prevent the motion of cells through dense tissue. Here, we are investigating how T cells balance the need to protect their DNA from damage, and survive long-term in dense tissues, with their need to move around and search for possible pathogen invasion. If we figure this out, we may be able to selectively target the survival of T cells in tissue where they are doing damage (as is the case in autoimmune disease) or improve their ability to move into dense tissue to fight tumour cells.

Migration of cancer cells, in particular, depends heavily on mechanical properties, e.g. stiffness, of the microenvironment. The project we propose seeks to identify the specific mechanisms and key players that control cell response to tissue stiffness. We propose changing force dynamics suppresses cell migration towards stiffer tissue, a specific type of cell migration that drives cancer metastasis. This project will shed light on how healthy mammalian cells and cancer cells sense the mechanical properties of the environment. Our results will improve the understanding of how cells migrate in response to mechanical cues. In the long-term, this information will be important to developing drugs that target cell migration in human diseases.

column36: Prediction of Cognitive and Motor Symptom Progression in Multiple Sclerosis Using Myelin Imaging
column37: At least 50% of people living with multiple sclerosis (MS) have a progressive form of the disease, meaning that disability increases steadily. This can include physical progression, e.g. difficulty walking, and cognitive progression, meaning that people experience problems with memory, attention and problem solving. Cognitive impairment has a negative impact on quality of life, making it difficult to perform everyday tasks, and is the leading cause of unemployment for people with MS. It is difficult to determine if treatments for MS will help slow or reverse progression because symptoms worsen gradually, so clinical trials require a large number of participants and take many years. If we can understand the cause of progression in MS, we can find better ways to figure out if a treatment is working. Our goal is to show that we can use new magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques to predict progression. MS damages myelin, a fatty substance that covers and protects nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. We have developed an advanced MRI technique that can measure the amount of myelin present. We looked at the relationship between the amount of myelin and how well people performed on physical and cognitive tests. We found that myelin and test scores are closely linked, which tells us myelin damage plays a role in progression. In this study, we will ask our previous volunteers with MS to return 4 years after their original visit so we can collect additional physical, cognitive and myelin MRI data. We will explore whether the amount of myelin at the beginning of the study can predict changes in disability. column36: Investigating the Regulation of RET Receptor-Mediated Perineural Invasion and Metastasis
column37: Cells require signals from their surroundings in order to grow, to move, or just to survive. These processes are essential for normal development, but they can be hijacked in cancer cells, allowing the disease to grow and spread. We are interested in a cell surface molecule called RET that helps convey messages (signals) from outside the cell as part of its normal roles in tissue development. However, in some cancers, such as tumours of the pancreas, RET can also help tumour cells to spread by following a trail of signals that leads them to move toward and along nerves that lie close to the tumour (perineural invasion). In response to these signals, RET can cause cancer cells to detach from the main tumour, move through surrounding tissues and invade the nerve, making the disease hard to treat and causing the patient much pain. These roles make RET an attractive target for therapies to reduce cancer spread. Here, we aim to elucidate mechanisms that contribute to RET's roles in cancer invasion and spread. We will do this using a panel of human pancreatic cancer cell lines, and well established visualization methods and molecular tools that we have developed to identify the key protein interactions and signals RET requires to promote invasion. Once we have identified these, we will evaluate their contributions to RET's roles in in vivo pancreatic cancer growth, nerve invasion and spread to other distant sites. We will also determine whether blocking or reducing these signals can prevent cancer invasion and reduce the pain it causes when these cells are grown in vivo. Finally, we are designing a new kind of virus therapy that can specifically attack RET-expressing tumours as a way to address these processes. Our studies will establish the mechanisms of RET-mediated tumour cell dissemination and provide additional tools and therapeutic opportunities to address this complicated problem and combat human cancer spread.

column36: Investigating the regulation of the Hsp90 functional cycle by ATP, co-chaperones, and post-translational modifications
column37: All proteins must fold into a functional 3 dimensional structure in order to function in cells. However, extremely high protein concentrations in cells can lead to aggregation and loss of function before proper folding can occur. Molecular chaperones aid in the acquisition of the correct 3 dimensional structure by preventing inappropriate interactions between proteins that can lead to misfolding and aggregation. There are dozens of chaperone systems that each act in different ways to help proteins to fold. They can act as protective chambers, clamps, and even exert forces on vulnerable surfaces of the proteins they act on. The Hsp90 chaperone is critical for the folding of a large but specific set of substrate proteins that include important players in diseases like cystic fibrosis and cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. The mechanical basis for how Hsp90 acts on its substrates is not known but is linked to discrete physical states or 'poses' that the Hsp90 dimer can acquire. The complete set of poses that the Hsp90 dimer can assume collectively define the Hsp90 functional cycle. The rate at which Hsp90 progresses through all of the poses must be finely tuned in order to help individual substrate proteins to fold correctly. This tuning is carried out by a family of proteins called co-chaperones that are transiently recruited to Hsp90 under the influence of ATP and post-translational modifications. My lab is concerned in defining the relationship between the different poses of Hsp90 and specific co-chaperones and post-translational modifications. We employ a blend of biological (cell based), enzymatic, and structural assays to investigate the mechanics and biology of the Hsp90 system in yeast and mammalian systems.

column36: Application of Magnetically Actuated Robotic System for Minimally Invasive Epilepsy Surgery
column37: Epilepsy is a type of brain disorder which affects nearly 1% of children where 30-40% do not respond to medical treatment for seizure control. Patients who have a seizure will experience a disruption to the sensory and motor control. The seizures can range from several seconds to a few minutes. For patients with medically resistant epilepsy, surgical treatment has been shown to be a cost effective method to stop the seizure activity. Current surgical treatment is an invasive open procedure that involves exposing the brain and performing 3 core steps to disconnect and isolate the seizure zones. In this project, we are proposing to apply a magnetically controlled robotic system for performing minimally invasive epilepsy surgery. The system will use external magnets and sensors on the tools to allow the surgeons to perform the various parts of the surgery through a single incision. The surgeon will be able to insert and deploy a steerable robotic system into specific seizure areas and use a magnetically controlled wrist to cut and isolate the target areas. The tools are also equipped with sensors such the surgeons will be able to detect any forces and collisions on the tool to help avoid causing un-intended damage. The system will be first validated on an existing brain model to confirm the robotic system's reach and visibility. After model testing, the project will conduct a pre-clinical study with a piglet model to allow surgeons to assess the efficacy and viability with live tissue. This study will have a significant impact on epilepsy care as it will improve patient care by reducing the trauma from an open procedure while decreasing the operation and patient recovery time required.

column36: Attrition in pediatric obesity management: A randomized feasibility study
column37: In the past 20 years, Canada's healthcare system set up many clinics to treat childhood obesity. We will form a Steering Committee with children, caregivers, clinicians, and researchers to design and refine our Family Navigation intervention. By having better access to care, children and their families working with navigators may be less likely to drop out and more likely to attend more treatment appointments. Ultimately, they may be more likely to achieve success in managing obesity.

column36: B cell intrinsic mechanisms of the germinal centre reaction
column37: Production of high affinity antibodies after virus such as COVID-19 infections or vaccination is the linchpin of the protective immunity. However, the molecular mechanism regulating high affinity antibody production is not fully understood. High affinity antibodies are produced in the germinal center (GC) in which antigen-specific B cells modify and select their antibody encoding genes in order to become high affinity antibody producing plasma cells (PCs). Abnormal regulation of molecules in B cells may lead to immune deficiency, autoimmune diseases, and even B lymphomas. In this regard, it is important to elucidate B cell intrinsic mechanisms that control the GC reaction under physiological and pathological conditions. In our previous CIHR supported studies, we have demonstrated that CBL and CBL-B (CBLs)-mediated ubiquitination plays a critical role in high affinity antibody production. CBLs do so by enabling B cells to get help from T cells and controlling GC B cells to differentiate into PCs only after they acquired a high affinity antibody. Our recent experiments further reveal that CBLs themselves are temporally regulated at different stages of the GC reaction and may involve the degradation of CBLs by the lysosomes regulated by TFEB, a master regulator for lysosome biogenesis. Interestingly, removal of CBLs from B cells leads to development of B cell lymphomas, indicating that CBLs are tumor suppressors preventing B lymphomas. Here, we propose to explore molecular mechanisms how GC B cells temporally control the expression of CBLs during the dynamic GC reaction. In addition, we will explore the role of TFEB in generating high affinity antibody producing PCs. Moreover, we will elucidate how CBLs prevent B lymphomagenesis and whether they also contribute to human B lymphomas. Completion of this project will not only bring new insight into our understanding of the antibody production but also help to treat various immune system disorders and cancer.

column36: Measuring What Matters: Development and Dissemination of a Core Outcome Set (COS) for Clinical Trials in Pediatric Anxiety Disorders
column37: Anxiety disorders are common in children and adolescents and cause significant impairment in all aspects of a child's life. Based on the available evidence, no treatment can be recommended as "optimal". The main problem is the wide variability of health outcomes measured across studies making it difficult to compare study results with each other, "pool" data across studies, and make decisions about what is the most effective treatment for various mental health concerns. A "core outcome set (COS)" is an agreed, standardized minimum set of outcomes that should be measured in all trials in specific areas of health. COS development outside of mental health care has resulted in greater standardization across research studies, which has led to enhanced research quality, and ultimately a better understanding of what treatments are best for which patients. This project plans to develop, an evidence- and consensus-based COS for pediatric anxiety disorder trials with active engagement of youth and family members and other stakeholders. We will identify outcomes used in the literature and engage with youth and family through virtual workshops, to understand what they view as important outcomes. With a list of outcomes, we will use a consensus process to help us develop decisions on what to measure across future trials. Once the outcomes of the COS have been established, we will define "how" to measure these outcomes using measurement instruments that are reliable, valid and responsive to measure changes that are important to youth and families. This project will ensure that outcomes that are important to youth and families are part of the final COS. With greater standardization, and more patient-centric outcomes measured across trials in pediatric anxiety disorders, this project and the developed COS will lead to improved research quality and ultimately better mental health outcomes and better health utilization.

column36: MYCBP2 as a pleiotropic effector of developmental EphB tyrosine kinase signalling
column37: Cells respond to their environment by special protein signals binding cell surface receptors, which then relay this binding to other proteins inside the cell. Various disease states may change or subvert such signalling events such that, for example, cancerous cells may become unresponsive to signals that tell them to stop dividing, or tissues that normally remain separated may become aberrantly intermingled. Eph receptors mediate many such signalling events and have been implicated in diseases such as cancer and neurodegeneration, but the precise details of Eph signalling are still unknown. External signal binding to Eph receptors causes them to bind to other proteins inside the cell, and to activate their function, which in turn causes them to bind other proteins and so on, causing the activation of a signalling cascade. Such a chain of events eventually reaches some key cellular compartments like for example the cellular skeleton, which may change its shape and result in cell movement. We propose to study a protein that may participate in such a chain originating from Eph receptors. This protein, called MYCBP2, has been involved in diseases and developmental malformations suggesting that its function is critical for normal cellular signalling in humans.

column37: More than two hundred thousand people suffer from heart attack or stroke every year in Canada. This number continues to grow despite drug developments to treat diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol and obesity. Vascular diseases that affect arteries in the heart and brain are, in fact, the advanced stage of a progressive vessel alteration that begins by silently affecting the very small vessels of the body. A better understanding of mechanisms altering the small vessels would provide earlier and improved risk prediction for heart attacks and strokes, and would help identify new drug targets for these diseases. Retinal images can be used to assess an individual's overall small vessel condition for three reasons: (1) retinal vessel images are an easily observable part of an individual's small vessel abnormalities using ocular fundus photographs; (2) retinal vessel architecture is affected by diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, obesity, and smoking; and (3) retinal vessel changes can predict the occurrence of heart attacks and strokes. By combining advanced method to analyze genes and blood proteins with artificial intelligence programs to read retina images, in large populations (Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, UK Biobank, Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology study), we will identify genes and proteins involved in small vessel diseases. Those findings will help discover new biological mechanisms and druggable targets to maintain small vessels healthy, and thus early prevent the occurrence of cardiovascular diseases. We will also test whether automated retinal screening can be used to improve the prediction of heart attacks and strokes. Our findings will improve risk assessment, prevention strategies, and will guide future clinical trials for cardiovascular diseases. This study will also provide targets for effective lifestyle and pharmacological interventions for small vessel changes, and in fine, to decrease heart attacks and strokes.

column36: Parsing heterogeneity in the autism spectrum through a developmental cognitive and brain perspective
column37: Approximately 1 in 66 Canadians receives a diagnosis on the autism spectrum, which represents more than 500 000 Canadians, a number constantly on the rise and challenging health services. Individuals with an autism spectrum diagnosis are very different from one another in terms of development, cognitive strengths and weaknesses, as well as underlying brain mechanisms. It makes intervention using a one-size-fits-all approach ineffective. There is an emerging consensus that we need to delineate subgroups among the autism spectrum to overcome the heterogeneity challenge. The subgrouping approach currently most supported is the age of speech onset, as autistic individuals who experienced speech onset delay have distinct cognitive, reasoning and cerebral profiles from those who did not experience a delay in speech onset. We propose to incorporate both the characteristic autistic reasoning profiles and the development of brain mechanisms into the subgrouping process to parse the heterogeneity of the autism spectrum. We will employ computerized tasks and brain imaging techniques to investigate reasoning development and brain mechanisms from 7 to 15 years old in autism spectrum children versus typical children. We aim to understand: 1) the developmental trajectory of reasoning mechanisms in autistic children; 2) whether speech onset helps to define subgroups; 3) how the brain mechanisms supporting reasoning evolve from childhood to adulthood; 4) develop a reasoning signature (abilities combined with brain mechanisms) to optimise subgroupings on the autism spectrum. Combining methods for defining meaningful subgroups among the autism spectrum appears as the most promising way to make significant progress in genetic and neuroimaging models, as well as to develop targeted tools for clinical diagnosis and intervention suitable to autism spectrum children.

column36: Prone positioning in neurologically deceased potential lung donors to improve donor lung function and lung transplant recipient outcomes
column37: Lung transplantation is the only effective life-saving therapy for patients with end stage lung diseases. However, due to the susceptibility of the donor lung to damage, only about 30% of potential donor lungs can be transplanted as many lungs are ultimately discarded due to injury or uncertain function. Damaged donor lungs can lead to the development of severe failure of the transplanted lung, so-called primary graft dysfunction, which is a major cause of early morbidity and mortality. Reducing donor lung damage by improving the management of lung donors before transplantation could be an important intervention to address this problem. One promising method for protecting the lungs is caring for the lung donors in the prone position. There is substantial evidence that use of prone position in patients with severe respiratory failure improves oxygenation and reduces lung injury. The goal of our study is to test whether prone positioning will significantly improve lung function of potential lung donors, which may result in the improvement of outcomes of lung transplant recipients and an increase in the number of actual lung donors.

column36: Advancing methods and analyses to support evidence-informed decision-making on the coordinated use of travel-related measures during public health emergencies of international concern: Lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic
column37: During public health emergencies of international concern (PHEICs), effective global responses require coordinated action across jurisdictions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries have used travel measures to an unprecedented degree and in an uncoordinated way. Our Pandemics and Borders Project is analysing a global dataset on travel measures; systematically reviewing evidence of their impacts; and conducting case studies of decision making in Canada, USA and Hong Kong. Our findings suggest limited scientific evidence and principles to guide complex decisions on using travel measures. Poorly coordinated border management contributes to underreporting of cases, increased disease transmission, and unnecessary economic and social impacts. The proposed project will build on these findings to support evidence-informed decision making on whether, when, what and how travel measures should be used. Our aims are to: 1) comparatively review and apply new methods to assess public health risks from travel during COVID-19; 2) evaluate the effectiveness of mitigating public health risks during COVID-19 of specific travel measures under different conditions; and 3) use findings to develop scenarios and pilot training exercises that simulate decision making on managing borders during PHEICs. We will use systematic reviews, various types of modelling, and viral genomic analyses to newly available datasets. We will focus on our three current case studies, with potential extension to other jurisdictions. Our interdisciplinary team, composed of 5 internationally recognized scholars and 6 outstanding trainees, will work collaboratively with knowledge users in senior national and international positions. We will produce open access datasets, methods and analyses to inform decision makers in government and key international organizations. The primary outcome will be strengthened capacity to make evidence-informed choices that enhance coordinated use of travel measures during PHEICs.

column36: Does menthol affect nicotine's impact on brain reinforcement mechanisms in dependent and nondependent users of electronic nicotine delivery systems?
column37: The use of Electronic Nicotine DeliverySystems (ENDS) is increasing significantly in Canada. Evidence suggests that the presence of flavouring is associated with both the initiation of ENDS use and their continued use. Although several jurisdictions have initiated bans on certain flavourings of ENDS, menthol, a common flavour additive in ENDS, is often exempt from such bans. Nicotine, the primary active ingredient in ENDS, is widely assumed to be responsible for their addictive potential; however, there is growing evidence that nicotine addiction can be impacted by menthol. For example, in animal studies menthol has been demonstrated to modulate the actions of nicotine receptors in the brain areas that are known to be involved in addiction. Our group recently reported that menthol-containing flavoured nicotine inhalers significantly altered neural responses in brain regions known to be involved in nicotine addiction. However, this study did not include unflavoured inhaler conditions. In the proposed research, we aim to determine the separate and combined effects of nicotine and menthol on subjective and neural responses, in two sex-balanced samples of ENDS users, occasional non- dependent users (ONUs) and daily dependent users (DDUs). It is expected that menthol will increase the magnitude of nicotine related effects on neural responses in each sample, but that for DDUs this will primarily involve areas linked to the expression of withdrawal and for ONUs these effects will be related to brain regions involved in reward. We plan to conduct a four-session experiment that will include male and female ENDS users. Participants will receive nicotine inhalers during two conditions, and nicotine-free inhalers during the others. For each type of inhaler, half the sessions will involve the co-administration of menthol and half will not. Across conditions, brain responses will be measured using magnetic resonance imaging before and after inhaler administration.

column36: Journey to the Center of the Cell: Reprogramming intracellular transport to the nucleus enhances HER2+ tumor killing for trastuzumab conjugated to payloads active in the nucleus
column37: The nucleus is the organelle controlling the expression of gene products, with functions necessary for cellular survival. Nuclear targeting is a potential tool for improving the efficacy of chemotherapy, vaccines, and gene therapy. Research focused on understanding and harnessing nuclear targeting is a topic of intense research interest. Unfortunately, nuclear-targeting agents suffer from poor nuclear localization efficiency and, as a result, this approach has yet to become a broadly effective therapeutic standard of care for cancer. Understanding and implementing nuclear targeting strategies as well as increasing knowledge of relevant fundamental principles in nuclear transport provide paths forward for biopharmaceuticals to the nucleus, increasing their efficacy, and applications beyond cancer. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) utilize antibody selectivity to deliver a conjugated cytotoxin to receptors abundantly present on tumor cells, while sparing healthy cells and, thereby, are an improvement over traditional chemotherapy. However, tumor killing can often be modest due to the inability to accumulate the cytotoxin inside tumor cells to evoke effective cytotoxicity. This is because ADCs are reliant on delivering their cytotoxin using small intracellular vesicles named endosomes. The proposed research describes our developed technology (Accum) that couples endosome escape to nuclear localization. Accum-modified ADCs are able to maintain receptor-specific tumor targeting. Once internalized into tumor cells, Accum enables ADCs to escape endosomes and efficiently localize and accumulate in the nucleus. This results in significant improvement in therapeutic efficacy. The proposed research will develop novel Accum-modified ADCs conjugated to nuclear-active cytotoxins to enhance therapeutic efficacy for breast cancer. We will also determine dominant nuclear transport pathways for breast tumor cells in order to fine-tune localization and further enhance efficacy.

column36: Peer Support and Type 1 Diabetes: Incorporating Experiential Knowledge into Service Design with Adolescents and Their Caregivers
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a lifelong disease that impacts the everyday lives of adolescents with T1D and their families. Research shows that adolescents with T1D and their caregivers can benefit when learning from other adolescents and caregivers who share similar experiences. We will work with adolescents with T1D and their caregivers to understand how peer support is helpful for improving disease self-management. This 4-phase project uses a participatory research approach by working in partnership with adolescents with T1D and their caregivers. Phase 1 will establish a Community Advisory Board made up of adolescents, caregivers, clinicians, community partners, and researchers to guide all stages of the project. Adolescents with T1D and caregivers will be recruited and formally trained as Peer Co-Researchers to help with all project activities. In Phase 2, adolescents and caregivers will make digital stories to share their perspectives about peer support in T1D. In Phase 3, adolescents with T1D and their caregivers will attend an event to view the digital stories, generate ideas, and prioritize what should be included in peer support interventions. In Phase 4, the adolescents and caregivers will participate in a 'Hackathon' to co-design accessible, inclusive, and equitable peer support interventions and ideas for research studies to test the interventions. The phased evaluation findings of this project will support the development of a Toolkit, with comprehensive learnings, that will be shared with diabetes clinicians, researchers, people with lived experience, and community partners provincially, nationally, and internationally across various research, clinical, and lived experience networks. This project will demonstrate that T1D services can be more meaningful, accessible, and inclusive if they are intentionally co-designed with service users and align with community needs and values.

column36: Disturbances of neurogenic cardiovascular control in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
column37: When the heart pumps poorly, the brain releases into the bloodstream more noradrenaline (NA). At first, more NA improves heart function but it also increases heart rate, stores salt and water and tightens blood vessels. If the heart weakens and no longer can pump blood efficiently throughout the body, heart failure (HF) will ensue. However, many older Canadians develop another form of HF, caused by a stiff heart but normal pumping action that is an equally common cause of hospitalization and death. Their heart muscle fails to relax normally between heart beats, resulting in more fluid pressure in its pumping and reservoir chambers and in the lungs. There is little we can do in 2021 to treat this particular form of HF aside from giving pills to encourage urination to make breathing easier. Our goal is to learn if the nerves that release NA are firing at high frequency in such patients and if so, to determine why and how to prevent this. With a sterile electrode, we will record from a calf sympathetic nerve before and during 2 conditions that we know stimulates it to fire and release NA more in people with poor heart pumping. These are: increasing the volume of the heart's upper chambers and 1-leg cycling. One experiment will discover what happens to nerve firing when we apply lower body positive pressure to move blood suddenly from the legs to the heart. A second series will teach us if leg exercise stimulates more nerve firing in HF with normal pumping action, if this increase makes it hard to exercise, and if this can be improved by exercise training. We will study healthy volunteers to learn the normal response, compare their responses to HF patients, and compare what we find in men and women, as women are more likely than men to have this form of HF. If we can identify reasons why women and men develop HF because their heart does not relax well, even though it seems to squeeze normally, our findings should inspire new ways of treating this unhealthy condition.

column36: Characterizing the Effects of Immune Activity on Intestinal Epithelial Regeneration During a Vibrio cholerae Infection.
column37: The aquatic pathogen Vibrio cholerae is responsible for the severe, and potentially deadly disease, cholera, that claims roughly 100,000 lives each year. Vibrio passes through the host stomach, and enters the intestine where it encounters a dense community of gut-resident bacteria that form a natural barrier to infection. To dismantle the bacterial barrier, Vibrio injects toxic molecules into susceptible prey. By eliminating competitor bacteria Vibrio has access to host cells, where Vibrio grows, and causes the severe, rice-water diarrhea that hallmarks cholera disease. Despite the importance of bacterial competition for infection, we know very little about the effects of interbacterial warfare on the host. Researchers in my group use zebrafish and fruit flies as animal models to address this important question. Flies and fish are ideal for this work, as they develop diarrheal disease upon Vibrio infection, and have similar gut architecture to mammals. Importantly, we have access to a large number of tools for genetic experiments with fish and flies. Thus, studying disease in the fly and fish models has considerable potential to help us understand how Vibrio causes disease in humans. Recently, we showed that Vibrio-dependent killing of gut bacteria activates evolutionarily conserved immune responses in the fly host. Remarkably, immune activation is not protective for the host. Instead, immune activation blocks the repair of intestinal cells damaged by Vibrio, greatly enhancing disease severity. In this project, we will use our expertise in genetics and live models of Vibrio infection to understand how an immune response is detrimental to host recovery from infection. We believe this work represents a significant step towards identifying actionable therapies for a global health and economic burden.

column36: Developing An Indigenous Value-Based Approach to Environmental Health Risk Assessment
column37: Indigenous communities (ICs) experience detrimental health impacts living near industrial development. Pictou Landing First Nation (PLFN) was exposed to effluent from a pulp and paper mill for over 50 years, until the mill was forced to close in 2020. Government reported that PLFN's health was not impacted by exposures, but their concerns would not go away. In 2010, we (PLFN and NPA) co-designed a project to assess the health status of PLFN using Statistics Canada data and other quantitative data. We used oral histories from Knowledge Holders in PLFN which highlighted their unique relationship to land and developed a Mi'kmaw environmental health framework to analyze the data which revealed governments' failures. PLFNs experience underscores the need for community centered/controlled approaches to environmental health risk assessment, governance and data. Our proposed research will examine health impacts of living near oil and gas extraction (Cree, Chipewyan (Dene), and Metis) and a landfill site (Haudenosaunee), and work with each of the four ICs to co-develop their own environmental health frameworks to show how community-led/locally relevant/culturally safe governance frameworks and cultural protocols ensure the highest ethical standards are followed and promote community health decisions that respect Indigenous values and traditions. We will support community-led environmental health literacy efforts to build capacity and learning for ICs and address impacts of current/proposed development affecting the four ICs. Finally, we will critique existing state-led environmental health risk assessment (EHRA) methodologies. Guided by Etuaptmumk (Two-Eyed Seeing), using a community-based participatory approach and the Mi'kmaw framework as a starting point we will advance the capacity of ICs to develop Indigenous EHRA to assess their own health and environmental status and share our research widely to show how Indigenous-led assessments result in more effective decisions.

column37: A congenital anomaly is a birth defect. Some babies are born with a congenital anomaly that requires surgery immediately after birth. We currently do not know how these babies do later in life when they grow up. Until a few decades ago, most of these babies died. We created a database of more than 750 congenital surgical anomaly patients recording birth and surgery details. column36: Regulation of the epigenome by replication stress in vascular disease and aging
column37: The epigenome is the layer of protein modifications to DNA and the proteins that assemble DNA into the nucleus known as histones. Together, these epigenetic modifications to the DNA and histones as well as proteins that anchor the DNA to the nucleus organize DNA into a 3-dimensional (3D) structure that allows some genes to be expressed and others to be silent, depending on the cell type. Thus, the epigenome is responsible for a heart muscle cell to express genes and proteins important to the heart muscle rather than genes and proteins expressed by bone cells. Aged and diseased cells lose their epigenetic modifications, leading to an altered epigenome, loss of cell identity, and cellular function. Thus, vascular cells of the heart can begin expressing bone proteins leading to "hardening of the arteries", also known as atherosclerosis. Importantly, many epigenetic modifications are reversible using drugs. In this project, we generated stem cells from patients with a rare disorder known as Progeria, in which the vasculature and other organs age very fast and the patients suffer heart attacks and stroke in their teen years due to hardening of the arteries. Underlying this vascular degeneration are DNA damage, rapid cellular aging and loss of the epigenetic modifications to the vascular cells, which we also find in the vascular cells grown from the Progeria patient stem cells. We will piece together the molecular mechanisms driving these defects using the Progeria patient stem cell-derived vascular cells. We will then test these mechanisms in tissue isolated from organ donors and patients with heart disease following surgical intervention to determine whether the Progeria patient cells model normative vascular aging and pathogenesis. We will also test the abnormal cellular behaviour using drugs that target the epigenome, thereby potentially identifying a new drug to treat vascular and heart disease.
