column36: Understanding the effects of ERK hyperactivation in cancer: implications for therapy
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Canada and worldwide, suffering from a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis and a paucity of effective drugs available to treat advanced tumours. Despite a greater understanding of the genetic basis of lung cancer development, discovery of new therapeutics has been slow as the activities of genes implicated in this disease are difficult to inhibit while new agents targeting lung cancer cells have been ineffective due to drug resistance. Therefore, new strategies are urgently needed to develop effective therapeutic strategies for lung cancer patients that yield robust responses and improve long-term survival rates. Currently, drug discovery is based on identifying mutated genes in lung tumours, determining if its modulation impacts growth, and then screening or designing drugs to inhibit gene function. In this manner, therapies are aimed at "putting the breaks" on the signals that promote tumor growth. Unexpectedly, we have recently found that lung cancer cells also cannot tolerate increases in signaling, akin to "flooring the gas pedal". However, we still do not know why this hyperactive signaling is toxic to cancer cells and whether or not we can use this information to treat cancer patients. The goal of this proposal is to understand why too much signaling kills cancer cells and determine whether drugs that can mimic this scenario offer an effective way of inhibiting lung tumour growth. We aim to test candidate drugs that target the "regulators" in lung cancer cells which act as a fail safe to prevent hyperactivation from occurring. By disrupting these key regulators, we predict that cancer cells will "overheat" from too much signaling, causing their death, and we will assess their effectiveness in model systems for the first time. Thus, this work will offer true progress towards developing new agents for the treatment of lung cancer, ultimately leading to improved survival rates for patients.

column36: Role of the mitochondrial carrier family protein SLC25A46 in mitochondrial dynamics and early onset neurodegenerative diseases
column37: All cells in the body require chemical energy to carry out their normal physiological functions. The majority of this energy is packaged as a compound called ATP and is produced by the oxidation of carbohydrate and fat in a biochemical process called oxidative phosphorylation. This process takes place in a compartment of the cell called the mitochondrion, and is carried out by several large protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Respiratory chain dysfunction interferes with the normal supply of energy, and this produces a wide variety of different diseases, such as neurodegenerative and heart disease, the nature and severity of which depend on the exact genetic defect. The genetics of respiratory chain diseases is complicated by the fact that some components of the system are encoded in nuclear genes, others in a small genome that is contained within the mitochondria themselves. Mitochondria also rely on intimate contacts with other organelles in the cell, most notably a structure called the endoplasmic reticulum, which, among other things, supplies mitochondria with the lipids required for mitochondrial growth and division, and acts as a reservoir for calcium, which in part regulates mitochondrial metabolism. Several neurological diseases result from disturbances in the contacts between mitochondria and the ER. We have identified mutations in a gene coding protein of the mitochondrial metabolite carrier family, that seems to be involved in communication between the mitochondrial outer membrane and the endoplasmic reticulum, which result in an astonishingly large spectrum of neurological diseases and this project is aimed at investigating its precise molecular functions in healthy cells and in cells from patients with mitochondrial disease.

column36: Immunomodulatory Gene Therapy Strategies for Post-Traumatic and Metabolic Forms of Osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a disease that occurs when joint structures, including the articular cartilage that protects the ends of bones, degenerate following trauma or due to conditions such as obesity. OA leads to chronic pain and disability and places a significant burden on the Canadian healthcare system and economy. However, there are no therapies available that can slow or reverse disease progression. Our previous studies have shown that gene therapy vectors can be used to deliver therapeutics directly to affected OA joints for an extended period. Using this approach, we have shown that a gene therapy vector expressing IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) - an anti-inflammatory molecule - can slow disease progression in small and large animal models of injury-induced OA. Thus, broader inhibition of inflammation may be necessary to curb OA progression, or other factors that drive inflammatory resolution may be required for tissue repair. This proposal will examine whether blocking multiple inflammatory factors simultaneously during active inflammation can better slow OA progression in mouse models of injury-induced disease. We will also explore inflammation-responsive switches to activate the delivery of regenerative factors to promote tissue repair only in the context of injury. In parallel, since little research has examined gene therapies for obesity-induced OA, we will investigate whether these anti-inflammatory strategies can slow disease progression in diet-induced mouse models of early-onset disease. Importantly, this will reveal the role of inflammation in the pathogenesis of OA resulting from various causes, including trauma and obesity.

column36: Identifying Metabolomic Markers of Disease Activity in Psoriatic Disease using Solid Phase Microextraction - Liquid Chromatography - High Resolution Mass Spectrometry
column37: Psoriasis is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease that affects more than a million Canadians. Many patients with psoriasis also have involvement of the joints and develop a specific form of arthritis called psoriatic arthritis. Patients with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis have flaky, red, itchy skin, joint destruction, limitation of function and poor quality of life. It is important to accurately determine how active psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis is so that appropriate treatment is initiated and further damage to joints reduced. However, current methods of assessing disease activity are imprecise, subjective and labour intensive. We do not have a good understanding of pathways of metabolism underlying active disease. Our purpose is to confirm whether small molecules (metabolites) and pathways that we have previously identified reliably measure disease activity. To achieve our objectives, we will test blood samples collected from patients with psoriatic arthritis who have undergone careful assessment of disease activity by ultrasound scan of their joints. We will also collect blood samples from patients with PsA who have the full range of severity of skin psoriasis. We will then subject the samples to novel laboratory methods to identify metabolites associated with active skin and joint disease. We will also determine if these blood metabolites are able to identify patients with psoriatic arthritis who have mild, moderate, and severe disease as measured by routine clinical methods. The study will confirm previously identified small molecules and pathways driving inflammation in the skin and joints in patients with psoriasis. In future we will confirm that biomarker-based assessment is better than currently used clinical methods. Once confirmed we will have better means of measuring disease activity and will help make treatment decision making easier and better informed, thus leading to better outcomes for patients with psoriatic disease.

column36: Cumulative effects of contact sport participation: a multi-parameter brain imaging investigation
column37: There is growing concern about the risks involved with playing contact sports, as there is evidence that repeated head impacts may lead to long-term problems with brain health, including difficulties with thinking and mood and potentially an increased risk of conditions such as Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease. column37: The cystic fibrosis (CF) protein (CFTR) ensures the normal water and ion composition of the liquid that lines the airway. To capture the variability of cellular responses to CFTR modulators and innate immune signaling among CF patients, HNE and HBE collected from 20 patients homozygous for the F508del mutation will be used in the proposed model. column36: Translation initiation via factorless internal ribosome entry site mechanisms
column37: All viruses go through an important stage during their life cycle called translation where viral proteins are expressed from a viral RNA. Some viruses such as poliovirus and Hepatitis C use a translation mechanism called an Internal Ribosome Entry Site or IRES for expressing their proteins. This IRES mechanism is not only important for viruses but also for cellular genes, including those involved in cancer. Therefore, elucidating IRES mechanisms is crucial for understanding a fundamental process of gene expression. Currently, IRES mechanisms are poorly understood. To gain insight, we will characterize a novel IRES mechanism found in an insect virus, called dicistrovirus. Using biochemical techniques, we will identify how this IRES interacts with and hijacks the host cell machinery. This insect IRES is functional in many systems including yeast and human cells, indicating that this unprecedented mechanism is conserved and that specialized cellular genes may also use this mechanism. Using biochemical methods, we will elucidate key elements that govern IRES mechanisms. Moreover, we will identify key viral proteins that promote IRES gene expression. Finally, using this knowledge, we can search for cellular genes that also use this mechanism for gene expression. This proposal will not only shed light into the biological significance of this novel viral IRES mechanism but also provide a framework for understanding other viral and cellular IRES mechanisms in general.

column37: Risk factors such as high blood pressure [BP], also known as hypertension, lead to changes in blood vessel structure and function, which can damage vital organs such as heart, kidney and brain. We will isolate labelled Sca1 cells, test their function, and look at gene changes as in Aim-1A. We suspect genes changed in Aim-1B cause disease. So, in Aim 2A, we test if healthy Sca1 cells become diseased by changing these genes, and if diseased cells can be cured by reversing these changes. Lastly, in Aim-3, we will use mice genetically modified to not have Sca1, to see how their stem cells and blood vessels respond to high-BP. Together, these studies will help us understand what is happening to stem cells and blood vessels after high-BP, and help us find which genes cause high-BP-related vessel disease.

column36: Expediting the drug approval process in oncology through access with evidence development schemes
column37: The process of approving new drugs to treat cancer can be time-consuming and expensive, which prevents universal access to life-extending/life-saving treatments. Researchers have proposed a process for approving drugs that reduces the time between their initial development and their widespread use in Canada. This process is known as an Access with Evidence Development scheme (AEDs). An AED gives approval for an innovative drug to be used in Canada whilst further evidence, usually on the real-world effects of the drug, is collected. Once this evidence has been collected, the approval can be removed if the new evidence indicates that the drug is less effective than we hoped. Data collected routinely as part of clinical care can be vital source of data to reassess these drugs. It can be difficult to determine what evidence should be collected and when it should be analysed to reassess the drug. A method known as "Value of Information" has been suggested to support these decisions, but several barriers have previously prevented its use. The advantage of the Value of Information method is that it ensures that the evidence collected during the AED would help policymakers decide whether a novel cancer therapy can improve patient outcomes. This project aims to tackle the barriers to its implementation by developing an example AED for a drug to treat colorectal cancer. The project will also develop new methods that allow us to determine the best time to reassess a new drug and create guidance and statistical code to support the use of the Value of Information method in practice. This project will improve the development of AEDs to ensure that effective, safe and efficient treatments are approved in a timely manner. This will reduce the time taken for Canadian patients to access innovative drugs for treating cancer while also ensuring that patients are not exposed to ineffective or harmful treatments.

column36: Unifying Molecular Omics, Multi-Modal Neuroimaging and Artificial Intelligence for Biologically-defined Patient Stratification in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating heterogeneous neurodegenerative condition with abnormalities in protein accumulation (TDP-43, SOD1), vascularization, inflammation, neuronal activity and cerebral atrophy. In keeping with the tenets of Personalized Medicine, treatments should be tailored to individual therapeutic needs as opposed to treating all patients with the same approach. In ALS, however, we currently do not have appropriate methods for pathophysiological patient staging and stratification. Furthermore, because we continue to lack robust tools to characterize each patient's distinctive disease progression, evaluating the effectiveness of different therapies remains challenging. Prompted by the imperative for customized treatment of ALS, our goal is the implementation and clinical validation of a biologically-defined staging and stratification of the ALS spectrum using an artificial intelligence (AI) framework to integrate massive amounts of molecular and neuroimaging data. Consequently, we are integrating a large amount of biological data (including transcriptomics and neuroimaging) into a simplified and clinician-friendly personalized clinical profile reflecting both disease progression and variants. This framework aims to bridge the Molecular, Neuroimaging and AI fields to overcome the major limitations of traditional clinical diagnoses and eventually provide patients with true Personalized Medicine. In this project, the clinical applicability of our already developed model will be validated with two large-scale populations in the ALS spectrum. Critically, all resulting analytic tools will be shared with the international community via user-friendly multitool software, contributing to translate our research findings into daily clinical practice.

column36: Genomic dissection of de novo metastatic prostate cancer prior to treatment
column37: In its most aggressive form, prostate cancer has already spread to the bone and/or lymph nodes at the time of first diagnosis. These sites of cancer outside the prostate are called metastases, and cause most cancer-related deaths. People with metastases at first diagnosis have what is termed 'de novo' metastatic prostate cancer, and have a very poor prognosis. This is not currently the case in prostate cancer management: patients receive treatments that are not personalised against their cancer. The major barrier to improved patient stratification is that we do not understand the relationship and composition of the prostate and metastatic cancers in de novo metastatic disease. This is because affected patients do not undergo surgery to remove their prostate or metastases, so historically there has been little cancerous tissue to study. We have compiled the first standardized cohort of surgically-removed tumours from people at first diagnosis with de novo metastatic prostate cancer, before they begin other treatment. This includes the whole prostate, individual metastases, and also tumour DNA shed into the blood (a 'liquid biopsy'). We plan to use custom DNA sequencing approaches and novel computational algorithms to understand how these coexisting primary and metastatic cancers are related to each other. We will identify the precise regions of the primary cancer that gave rise to lethal metastatic disease. Our work will establish a framework for identifying the molecular features of metastatic prostate cancer at first diagnosis. This framework can then be used in clinical trials to implement therapeutic strategies that are more tailored to patient-specific disease biology, reducing the mortality and morbidity of aggressive prostate cancer.

column36: Devices for Image-Guided Biopsy of Peripheral Lung Nodules
column37: Lung cancer continues to be the leading cause of cancer death in Canada, accounting for nearly 1 in 4 of cancer deaths. Low-dose spiral computed tomography (CT) scanning can identify potentially cancerous lung nodules earlier than ever before. However, for definitive diagnosis, these lung nodules must be biopsied - a difficult task since these nodules are often located in the lung periphery and are inaccessible using standard video bronchoscopy. Radial endobronchial ultrasound probes can be used with bronchoscopes to extend imaging into smaller airways, but this technique suffers from low diagnostic yield (~70%). Patients with nodules that cannot be endoscopically sampled often undergo CT-guided needle biopsy through the chest wall, but this method has a higher rate of serious complications such as collapsed lung and internal bleeding. column36: Disease-modifying effects of osteotomy and exercise for knee osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a growing cause of pain and disability that already affects over 4 million Canadians. OA of the knee is especially common and disabling. OA is not just a natural part of aging, but is a disease with serious effects on our health. While we have treatments that help with symptoms for the short-term, none stop the process of joint damage and long-term pain and decreased function. The need for treatments to slow OA progression has been identified by patients and researchers around the world as a top priority. One of the reasons why this has been so difficult is that the mechanisms involved in OA are complex. We know that excessive knee loading (mechanics) and the knee tissues' responses (biology) to loading are important, but we have not yet learned how to change them in a long-lasting way. Our team has some early positive findings from prior studies on a surgery called High Tibial Osteotomy (HTO). HTO straightens the lower limb of patients with varus (bowed) knees (present in over half of patients with knee OA). The goal of the surgery is to improve how our knees are loaded during walking. This should result in less joint damage and long-term improvements in pain and function. We plan to test patients from our earlier studies comparing HTO to standard care (exercise, weight-loss, pain medications) to see if the surgery provides benefits 5 years after treatment. This is important since OA progresses over long periods of time in most people. Since this is such a different approach than standard treatments, it also allows us test disease processes. We will use state-of-the-art gait analysis, imaging techniques, and tests on blood and fluid removed from the patients' knees. We will look for different patterns of OA progression for men and women with and without this surgery. Understanding the factors that determine these different patterns of disease progression will help us understand the mechanisms, target existing treatments or create new ones.

column37: Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease of unknown cause and it can be estimated that currently there are between 19,000 and 22,500 Canadians living with sarcoidosis. The disease can be very serious if it affects the heart, when it is called cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) and most CS occurs in patients aged 25-60 years. Patients with CS have a much higher risk of dying than sarcoidosis patients without heart involvement. In addition, it is becoming clear that CS is much more common than once thought. The three main ways that CS can affect the heart are: (1) blockage of electrical conduction from the upper to the bottom heart chamber, (heart block), (2) very rapid heartbeats (arrhythmias) and (3) weakening of the heart muscle, (heart failure). The disease has been largely neglected by researchers and the current science is of modest quality. Hence, there is a lack of evidence to guide doctors in treating patients The current standard of care treatment for CS is with steroids which can be very effective but have lots of side effects and negatively impact patient's quality of life in a major way. Hence there is interest in trying alternative agents and in this trial, we will be comparing two treatment regimes. Patients will be allocated to treatment group by random chance (electronic 'toss of the coin'). We hypothesize that the experimental treatment will have similar efficacy to standard treatment with steroids and that experimental treatment will result in significantly better quality of life and fewer side effects than standard dose steroids. We plan to recruit 194 patients over 4 years in 32 major hospitals in Canada/US/Japan/UK The University of Ottawa Heart Institute will manage the study and will be responsible for managing information generated in this study. Our study is unique and innovative as it is the first trial involving multiple centers in the world evaluating patients with CS. This study will produce the highest quality information in the medical field.

column37: Childhood is marked by constant learning. Despite their more limited knowledge bases and functionally immature brains, children acquire a vast amount of information about the world. What supports this rapid new learning, and how is the child's learning brain different from that of an adult? In the current project, we aim to answer these questions by characterizing how children differ from adults in (1) their knowledge of real-world concepts and (2) the specific brain structures and pathways that guide the creation of new concepts. We focus on the hippocampus, a brain region known to support concept learning in adults by connecting elements of experience across time and space. Emerging evidence suggests children learn differently: unable to flexibly connect multiple pieces of experience, children instead learn about inherent properties of concepts like their appearance. Here, we test the prediction that these developmental differences in concept learning arise due to maturation of the hippocampus. We combine behavioural, brain imaging, and neural network modelling methods to investigate the structural development of the hippocampus and the emergence of specific learning operations that support the formation of rich, real-world knowledge in children, adolescents, and adults. Our multifaceted approach will provide novel insight into how the brain's memory system supports learning and inform our understanding of developmental disorders (autism, schizophrenia) known to impact memory.

column37: Hemorrhagic strokes happen when weakened blood vessels rupture and cause bleeding into the brain. Patients with recent hemorrhagic stroke are at high risk for clot formation. These clots can cause damage to organs, such as in the case of heart attacks. Due to their risk of bleeding, patients with hemorrhagic stroke often have their blood thinners stopped and never restarted. This further increases their risk of clotting. An alternative treatment option is needed that can reduce the risk of clotting without increasing the risk of another bleed. Colchicine is a drug that has been used for more than 50 years in various medical conditions. It is well tolerated and safe. Recently colchicine was found to reduce clotting by reducing inflammation, in a manner that does not increase bleeding. These properties make colchicine an attractive drug for patients with hemorrhagic stroke. We are hoping to test whether colchicine can reduce the risk of clotting without increasing the risk of re-bleeding in patients with hemorrhagic stroke. A very large study at many hospitals is needed to answer this question. We are starting with a smaller study to gain information on whether it is possible to perform a larger definitive one, and if so, how best to plan for it. We will study 100 patients with a hemorrhagic stroke within 48 hours. These patients will be assigned randomly (like flipping a coin) to either receive a daily low-dose of colchicine or a daily dose of placebo. All patients will be followed for at least 6 months. We will monitor how many patients are included in the study per year at each hospital and how many continue treatment for the duration of the study. We will also monitor patients for new clotting events, bleeding in the brain and deaths, amongst other clinical outcomes. These results will provide important information to plan our larger study with the goal of reducing heart disease and stroke in this vulnerable population.

column37: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2)-the causative agent for the ongoing coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19) pandemic-is a major global health threat. In severe cases, SARS-CoV-2 infections lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome, multi-organ failure, and cardiac injury. Strikingly, those with a history of cardiovascular diseases (such as hypertension [HTN] and coronary artery disease [CAD]) are at much higher risk of cardiac injury and adverse clinical outcomes when infected with SARS-CoV-2. In this proposal, we will determine how cardiovascular co-morbidity exacerbates viral-induced cardiac injury. Deciphering the specific mechanisms by which cardiovascular risk factors affect outcomes in SARS-CoV-2 infection is incredibly challenging in humans. To address this unmet clinical need, we will utilize a novel small animal model of natural SARS-CoV-2 infection. Specifically, we will induce HTN and CAD in Golden Syrian hamsters prior to infection with SARS-CoV-2 and study organ injury (cardiac injury, as well as lung, brain and kidney - organs known to be affected by the virus) and the inflammatory response to the virus in detail. Our preliminary data demonstrates that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces significant cardiac injury. While an overall goal of this proposal is to determine the mechanisms by which HTN and CAD exacerbate viral pathology, in doing so, we will develop a cardiovascular-focused SARS-CoV-2 animal modeling system that can be used to test vaccine candidates and other therapeutic agents as we work toward ending the pandemic. Without properly determining how clinical risk factors alter therapeutic outcomes, there is a high risk for failure.

column37: Despite remarkable progress in treatment, hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains an enormous global public health problem with over 70 million people infected including 250,000 Canadians. One of the major barriers to HCV control is the lack of a protective vaccine. Vaccine development has proven difficult due the extreme diversity of the virus - even in a single infected individual, millions of closely related but distinct HCV strains circulate. Finding a single vaccine that can protect against all of these strains is very difficult. However, it is possible that a vaccine may only need to be effective against specific strains of HCV that are more efficient at infecting new individuals. By taking advantage of samples from a recent clinical trial, we have a unique opportunity to observe intentional HCV infections that will hopefully provide critical insights to help develop a vaccine. In a recent study, we showed that we could safely transplant lungs from HCV-infected donors to uninfected recipients with prompt treatment of HCV after transplant. In the current proposal, we will use the samples from the days immediately following transplant to identify the specific strains of HCV, out of the billions in the donor, that established infection in the recipients - the so-called founder variants. We will compare sequences from strains that did and did not establish infection in the trial to see if we can identify specific patterns that are associated with successful infection. We will then generate pseudoviruses and replicons, from founder and non-founder variants to determine if founder variants have an advantage at entering or replicating in liver cells over non-founder variants. Finally, we will infect mice with human livers with founders and non-founders to confirm the founder advantages. Using these unique samples, we will determine whether a vaccine must cover all HCV strains or only a subset - knowledge critical to vaccine development.

column37: Asthma affects over 339 million people worldwide and 14% of Canadian children, making it the most common chronic disease in childhood. Specifically, we will identify genetic factors inherited from parents to children that are associated with lung health and asthma risk. Our innovative study leverages existing data and resources from the largest population-based birth cohort in Canada that recruited over 3000 families to study early-life determinants of chronic diseases such as asthma. In addition, we have established collaborations with international childhood cohorts to replicate identified risk factors. The knowledge gained from this proposed study will inform on mitigation strategies to reduce the burden of asthma and other chronic respiratory diseases through public policy and educating the public as well as health care providers.

column36: Determining the mechanisms underlying disease pathology in Kabuki syndrome
column37: Our proposal focuses on understanding Kabuki syndrome, a genetic condition characterized by specific facial features, intellectual disability and growth deficiency. Kabuki syndrome occurs due to a change (mutation) in a gene that functions as an epigenetic regulator. Epigenetic regulators control the activity of other genes by adding or removing chemical marks and informing each cell about which genes need to be turned on or turned off. The pattern and timing of epigenetic mark placement are critical for healthy development. To date, there are ~70 genetic conditions caused by mutations in different epigenetic regulators characterized by intellectual disability. We have found that for each condition, a unique pattern of epigenetic marks can be identified that furthers our understanding of the disorder. This grant outlines a plan to better understand the genetic and epigenetic changes that lead to Kabuki syndrome as a starting point for studying the broader group of conditions caused by deficiencies in epigenetic regulators. We will study the pattern of epigenetic marks in human blood and neural cells (generated from blood) from individuals with Kabuki syndrome. We will compare these marks in different types of cells to understand how they lead to the characteristic features of Kabuki syndrome. We will also compare a Kabuki mouse model to control mice to identify changes in epigenetic marks between blood and brain tissues. Then we will investigate if epigenetic changes due to Kabuki syndrome can be reversed in mice that show improved memory and learning following drug treatment. If we find that epigenetic marks are normalized in response to drug treatments that improve brain function, this could speed up the process of identifying drugs for human clinical trials. We anticipate that findings from this study will be of tremendous value in advancing our understanding of Kabuki syndrome, its molecular causes, and potential treatments.

column37: Heavy bleeding is common after open-heart surgery (occurs in 1 in 5 patients). Bleeding often requires the transfusion of blood and can lead to major complications. One cause of bleeding is the loss of clotting factors to levels that are too low to form strong blood clots. To replace clotting factors, doctors administer plasma, which is the liquid part of blood that contains clotting factors. While plasma is usually safe, in some patients it causes complications such as infections, injury to the lungs, heart failure, and even death. In addition, plasma does not always work and can lead to more transfusions. Studies suggest that a newer blood product called prothrombin complex concentrate, which is made from plasma and contains most of the clotting factors, may be better for replacing clotting factors. In some countries, this newer product is already being used instead of plasma. The risks and benefits of these two treatments have not been studied very well. Our study will compare these two treatments (at multiple hospitals across Canada) in 750 adults who need clotting factors because of bleeding during open-heart surgery. Patients will be randomly (by chance) assigned to get either plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate. We will compare how well the two treatments control bleeding (e.g., the number of patients needing blood product transfusions, amount of blood lost, etc.) and their side effects. If the results of this study show that use of prothrombin complex concentrate is more effective than plasma and is safe, it will improve the way we manage bleeding during open-heart surgery, leading to less bleeding and transfusions, better outcomes for patients, and more efficient use of healthcare resources.

column36: Targeting cortical integrative mechanisms to treat cognitive impairment
column37: The cognitive deficits of developmental disorders carry life-long personal, familial, and societal costs. Domains of cognition mediated by the prefrontal and other associative cortical regions appear especially vulnerable to disruption. Independence in education and the workplace relies on the ability to synthesize information from multiple external and internal sources in order to direct behaviour. Deficits in such integrative cognition carry a disproportionate burden of disease and have been thought to be immutable. However, recent work suggests the window of opportunity to treat cognitive symptoms remains unexpectedly open into adulthood. The proposed experiments characterize high-impact cellular mechanisms of cortical integration with respect to their vulnerability to perturbation. We focus on a subset of neurodevelopmental disorders associated with genetic disruption of one essential subtype of excitatory receptor. The properties of this receptor make it essential for the synthesis and processing of information. We use molecular, electrophysiological, and pharmacological tools - together with extensive behavioural investigation - to interrogate and quantify the impact of treatments to restore this receptor population critical for normal cognitive function.

column36: Identifying mechanisms of cell size sensing with implications in normal and malignant populations
column37: Healthy epithelial tissues display an elegant regularity in the size and shape of individual cells. In contrast, deregulation of cell size is a common signature of malignancy. Despite the clear importance of the subject, both the mechanisms responsible for the increased cell size variability in cancer and the links associating this variability with tumor pathology remain unclear. The mTORC1 pathway is recognized as the fundamental regulator of macromolecular biosynthesis and cell growth. Yet, how can a common set of signals (including mTORC1) specify a different and distinct size for each of the different animal cell types? In 1975, Nurse and Hartwell showed that the size of animal cells is determined by cell size checkpoints - molecular mechanisms that sense cell size to selectively promote the growth of cells that are smaller than their target size. Recently, our research has identified the first molecular mechanism of size sensing to have ever been reported in animal cells. In a series of three publications, we demonstrate that the homeostasis of cell size is maintained by a molecular circuitry involving mTORC1, p38MAPK, and CDK4. Just as a thermostat maintains room temperature - our data shows that p38 functions to selectively promote the growth of cells that are smaller than their target size. Further building on the thermostat analogy, if p38 functions downstream to a cell size sensor (or thermometer), and mTORC1 is the furnace that promotes cellular growth, our data shows that CDK4 plays the role of the thermostat 'dial' that sets the critical target size (setpoint temperature). In this proposal, we address the process of cell size homeostasis in the specific context of cancer to pose two questions. (1) What are the molecular mechanisms that 'sense' and communicate information on cell size to selectively activate p38 in small but not larger cells? (2) What are the mechanisms that link the loss of cell size homeostasis with a more aggressive cancer phenotype?

column36: Targeting the Metabolic Mevalonate Pathway as an Actionable Prostate Cancer Vulnerability
column37: There is an urgent need for new effective anti-prostate cancer treatment strategies, and our recent research suggests the statin family of drugs will help to fill that gap. Statins have been safely used for decades in the control of cholesterol and men taking statins have a lower incidence of cancer. The basic metabolic pathway that statins block produces many products that are essential to the growth and survival of prostate tumor cells. This tumor cell dependence makes the prostate cancer cell particularly vulnerable to the inhibition of the metabolic mevalonate pathway. Indeed, we have recently completed a Phase I/II clinical trial with cholesterol-lowering doses of Fluvastatin in men diagnosed with prostate cancer and shown for the first time that Fluvastatin can reach the tumor and trigger prostate cancer cell death. These results warrant further investigation focused on how to best use statins as prostate cancer therapeutics. To maximize the pro-apoptotic activity of statins we aim to identify statin-drug combinations that increase the efficacy of statins to kill prostate cancer cells. We will build on our recent results showing another drug approved for use in humans, called dipyridamole, augments statin-induced tumor-specific cell death by blocking the feedback loop that restores the mevalonate pathway activity after statin exposure. We will also conduct discovery research to better understand the role and regulation of SREBP2, the master-regulator of the restorative feedback response. With this knowledge we will unveil novel strategies to inhibit SREBP2. In addition, we will identify additional FDA-approved drugs that maximize statin tumor cell death by novel feedback-independent mechanisms. The outcome of this grant is to mobilize statin-drug combinations for the treatment of prostate cancer in a timely manner using Health Canada-approved agents that are readily available for immediate evaluation in future Clinical Trials of prostate cancer.

column36: Investigation of the sexual dimorphic role of DDX3X in melanoma
column37: More men develop melanoma than women. Once male patients have melanoma, they have a worse prognosis than female patients. In the past, this has been attributed to differences in behaviour. Our research will provide a better understanding of the differences in the biology of melanomas between male and female patients, which will have important implications for future drug development.

column36: Uptake and gaps in HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use among HIV-negative gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) in Metro Vancouver, Canada before, during and following COVID-19
column37: Antiretroviral medication taken prior to HIV exposure to prevent infection is known as pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. Men who have sex with men (MSM) are the most affected HIV risk-group in Canada. In randomized trials, PrEP has been shown to be about 90% effective in preventing HIV infection when taken regularly. In 2018, the BC Ministry of Health, through the BC Centre for Excellence (BC-CfE) in HIV/AIDS, began full public funding for PrEP for individuals at high risk of getting HIV. The initial uptake of PrEP through this program has been very high -- more than 5500 individuals have accessed PrEP through the program as of December 2019. Nearly all (99%) PrEP users through this program are male and most (70%) live in Greater Vancouver. However, the impact of PrEP on the HIV epidemic among MSM will depend on uptake by those most at-risk. Further, behavioural risk compensation (e.g., decreased condom use) may result in higher incidence of other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The covid-19 pandemic has likely also affected MSM in terms of sexual behaviour and access to essential health services, including PrEP. This study aims to evaluate determinants and trends of initiation of PrEP among of HIV-negative MSM over a four-year period and to compare in incidence of new STIs, including syphilis, chlamydia, and gonorrhea, prior to and after starting PrEP, We also want to understand what are the common characteristics of factors of MSM who meet clinical eligibility criteria for PrEP but whom have never initiated its use. Lastly we wish to examine the impact of Covid-19 on sexual behaviour and PrEP use among MSM in BC. Through our study team's position within the BC-CfE and existing collaborations with government and community agencies, these results will directly influence provincial and national policies regarding PrEP access. Our results will inform health promotion and clinical interventions to support PrEP uptake and adherence among Canadian MSM.

column37: Asthma is the most commonly experienced chronic illness in children. Recently, our group published work that supports the notion that a decline in the use of antibiotics in babies may account for some of the observed decline in asthma rates in children and that this occurs because children who get antibiotics may be missing bacteria in the gut that help tune a baby's immune responses away from allergy. We aim to see if this effect is demonstrable in children born in BC and Manitoba at the patient-level over 10 years of recruitment, following the children up to age 7. We have determined that comparable data to assess this relationship already exist in data sets held within both jurisdictions. Hence this proposal is for funds to allow the access, linkage and analysis of such data in both provinces. We want to test the idea that children who are not exposed to antibiotics in infancy are at lower risk for asthma and other allergic diseases later in childhood. In doing so we must also take into account other important factors linked to asthma, such as air pollution exposure and have identified sources of information that will allow us to do so. If we show that the risk of asthma falls when unnecessary antibiotic use is avoided, this would point the way to a new tool for those working to prevent this troubling illness. When combined with existing knowledge about smoke avoidance, the importance of breastfeeding and other factors, we believe that acting on this knowledge could help to substantially reduce the burden of illness from allergic asthma and related conditions for future generations.

column36: Characterising brain network dynamics in very young children with autism using OPM-based MEG
column37: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental disorder that causes difficulties for these children in their academic and social interactions. Interventions can reduce some problems and are most effective when started early in life. Two related models of the development of autism propose a) an imbalance in brain rhythms and b) abnormal communication among brain regions (called functional connectivity). Functional brain imaging with magnetoencephalography (MEG) is the most sensitive way to measure brain rhythms and connectivity but is rarely possible in toddlers. We will use newly developed 'wearable' MEG sensors (optically pumped magnetometers (OPM)) that for the first time allow us to study brain function with MEG in very young children. To test if abnormalities in brain rhythms or connectivity are seen before or at diagnosis of autism, we will use OPM-MEG in 330 toddlers, grouped as follows: 1) diagnosed with autism 2) at a very high risk of autism due to having an older sibling with autism, 3) without autism. The OPM-MEG studies will be repeated yearly to track early-life developmental changes in brain rhythms and connectivity to see how and which of these metrics relate to autism onset and symptom severity. MEG protocols will include emotional faces and speech stimuli, areas of difficulty for children with autism. These data will be the first of their kind and will provide scientific information that was previously unavailable due to technological limitations. Leveraging our extensive experience with young children and our access to children with autism, this proposal will allow us to measure the early presence and trajectory of brain rhythm imbalances and brain connectivity abnormalities and relate them to autism onset and behavioural presentation. Collecting these data this early in life will open the possibility of identifying early markers of autism and future targets for early life behavioural and pharmaceutical interventions.

column36: Architecture and metabolic modulation of genetic networks in human cells
column37: Recent breakthroughs in gene editing technologies have transformed mammalian cell genetics and disease research. In particular, genome-scale screens employing CRISPR-Cas nucleases have already started delivering unprecedented insight into genotype-to-phenotype relationships. For example, such screens have defined genes required for human cell line proliferation that share functional, evolutionary, and physiological properties with essential genes in other organisms. These studies have ushered in a new era of functional genomics by enabling the systematic perturbation and characterization of genes in human cells that underlie biological processes and phenotypes. During the last funding stage, our team has made pioneering contributions to the development of world class genome-wide CRISPR resources for screening all human and mouse protein coding genes. The complexity of genome-wide CRISPR-Cas screening data led to the development of databases, computational models and machine learning to quantify gene perturbation effects in cancer cell models and under different environmental conditions. In one recent study we performed genetic screens on biological processes that impinged on lipid metabolism and were able to identify an uncharacterized gene that is required for regulation of lipid uptake, which we named LUR1. This study also highlighted how cellular metabolic reprogramming can be dissected by studying genetic interactions. Importantly, deregulated cellular energetics is a hallmark of cancer and we are interested in understanding how cancer cells adapt to changing environmental and metabolic conditions in order to reprogram their metabolism for robust tumor growth. We propose to take a systematic approach to identify and validate targets that can be modulated by drugs and impact cancer outcomes.

column36: Interactions between cortical stimulation and prefrontal population dynamics
column37: Cortical stimulation could be a powerful way to treat mental illnesses and restore brain functions lost to stroke or brain injury. In theory, techniques like electrical, magnetic, or light stimulation could someday allow clinicians to directly change neural activity into some desired, therapeutic pattern. However, there is at least one substantial obstacle to the tremendous clinical promise of cortical stimulation: the technique is notoriously unreliable. Stimulation can produce unexpected effects, different effects at different times, or it can fail to produce any effect at all. We do not understand why this occurs. If we did, we could develop methods to increase the precision and reliability of stimulation and clear a path towards realizing the promise of cortical stimulation in the clinic. This proposal will first test a novel idea about how the state of the brain at the time of stimulation may alter how stimulation affects neurons and behavior. Next, it will determine whether we can improve stimulation by using knowledge about the state of the brain before stimulation. We will do this by measuring neural activity while we stimulate a part of the prefrontal cortex in which we can also measure the behavioral effects of stimulation. To make sense out of the data, we will use mathematical techniques, including tools from machine learning and a computational model of brain activity. One outcome will be tools for ensuring precise stimulation outcomes in this part of the prefrontal cortex. These tools could have applications in treating hemineglect (a common consequence of stroke and brain injury). If our central hypothesis is correct, this work also has the potential to identify a general set of tools that could be used to improve our ability to control populations of neurons across the cortex, with broad applications in the next generation of stimulation-based treatments for psychological and neurological conditions.

column36: Localization of epileptic spike generators using combined EEG and MRI
column37: Knowing where epileptic activity is generated in the brain is vital for epilepsy patients who need surgery to remove these areas and become free from seizures. The analysis of regional functional magnetic resonance (MRI) time courses, given the epileptic spike timing from electroencephalography (EEG) recording, can suggest the target areas to be removed if both data sets are collected simultaneously. However, EEG data are very contaminated by noise when recorded during functional MRI. Here, we propose to combine a fast MRI method (one brain volume in 0.1 seconds) and EEG (fast MRI-EEG) to sensitively and accurately detect the brain areas generating epileptic activity. Without compromising functional MRI spatial resolution and sensitivity, the EEG in fast MRI-EEG has much less noise contamination than conventional MRI-EEG. Using a method of modeling the dynamics of a patient's heartbeats can further reduce the EEG noise. The combination of both novel methods will greatly improve the EEG data for detecting epileptic activity. We will pursue two aims in this project. First, fast MRI-EEG will be tested and validated in simulations and simple experiments that produce brief intervals of brain activity called "evoked potentials," then translated to a clinical protocol. Second, the brain areas generating epileptic activity from fast MRI-EEG will be validated by invasive stereotactic EEG (sEEG) recordings and the outcome of brain surgery in epilepsy patients. This project will show that fast MRI-EEG can better suggest the site of electrode implantation and the brain volume to be removed to minimize further risk of seizure. These are important steps forward to help neurosurgeons provide better surgical planning and patient management to improve the lives of many Canadians with epilepsy.

column36: HIF1-alpha interacts with MIF to drive inflammation and new bone formation in spondyloarthritis
column37: Background: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a common form of arthritis characterized by inflammation and new bone formation (NBF) in the spine and joint. Patients experience severe pain and restriction in mobility. Currently available treatment provides relief of symptoms in only 60% of patients and there is no definitive treatment to control NBF. Preliminary data: We discovered that macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) plays a critical role on inflammation and NBF in SpA patients and animal models. We further explored the molecule that interact with MIF and found that hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF1a) promotes inflammation and NBF in the SpA mouse model. We observed that blocking MIF or HIF1a substantially suppresses inflammation and NBF in the animal model. Furthermore, we found common genes that regulate both MIF and HIF1a. These results indicate that the MIF/HIF axis is a potential therapeutic target in SpA. Research approach: We will confirm that HIF1a expression in SpA animal model and SpA patients' tissues is higher than in controls. Using functional assays, we will confirm how MIF and HIF interplay during inflammation and NBF. We will then test if conditional genetic deletion of HIF could prevent NBF in the SpA mouse model. Next, we will use a HIF blocker in the SpA mouse model to assess prophylactic and therapeutic effects on NBF. Finally, we will test whether modification of the identified common target genes could also be potential novel therapeutics to stop both inflammation and NBF in SpA. Research Impact: Our pilot study suggests that blocking MIF/HIF axis is a new therapeutic strategy to stop both inflammation and NBF in SpA. Given there is no currently available drug that stops both inflammation and NBF, the potential impact of this research is significant.

column36: A Randomized Trial of Partial Breast Irradiation
column37: Most women with node negative breast cancer are treated with breast conserving surgery (BCS) followed by radiotherapy (RT) to reduce the risk of local recurrence. Maintaining the cosmetic appearance of the breast is key to this local therapy. Usually RT is given as a daily treatment to the whole breast for 3-5 weeks called whole breast irradiation (WBI). Recently based on the results of a single trial from the UK and the COVID-19 pandemic, radiation oncologists including those in Canada have switched to larger daily treatments of WBI for only 5 days. However, in the past 4-5 treatments of WBI has been associated with increased breast toxicity and worse long-term cosmetic results. Poor breast cosmesis can have a devastating impact on a woman's quality of life (QOL). Short course RT is very attractive to patients and physicians. There is an alternative for WBI called partial breast irradiation (PBI) where RT is delivered just to the tumour bed area and not the whole breast. The recent experience with PBI is that it does not result in poor cosmesis. The objective of the study is to determine if PBI compared to WBI both given once-a-day over 1 week following BCS results in non-inferior rates of local recurrence and improved cosmesis. The primary outcomes are local recurrence and patient assessed cosmetic appearance of the breast at 3 years. Secondary outcomes are overall survival, toxicity and QOL. A multicentered randomized trial will be performed. The planned sample size is 910 patients (455 per arm) to determine if local recurrence with PBI is not inferior to that with WBI, and if cosmesis is improved with PBI compared to WBI. Short course WBI is increasingly used in women with early breast cancer, but concerns remain about the potential toxicity of this approach. If we are able to show PBI is not inferior to WBI with respect to local recurrence and results in improved cosmesis, women will have a convenient therapy with limited toxicity, which will be widely adopted.

column36: Exploiting the synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities of stem cells and cancer cells with eroded telomeres
column37: Stem cells are the cells that can replenish themselves or differentiate, and they generate and maintain all tissue-specific functions in adults. Stem cells share certain properties in common with tumor cells, including shortened chromosome ends (telomeres) with age, and age-associated non-genetic changes (called the epigenetic state). We recently discovered that stem cells or cancer cells with short telomeres are also hypersensitive to DNA damage and to proper DNA replication progression. Our data suggest these properties are linked, and can be modified to improve cell function during aging, or to target cancer cells with short telomeres. We will pursue these ideas with 3 aims: 1) We will investigate the genes and gene networks that lead to the defective ability of stem cells with eroded telomeres to differentiate, and probe how modulations of these networks may restore stable cell fate commitment. 2) We will determine whether an elevated response to DNA damage leads to increased lethality in tumor cells with short telomeres, and how these genetic alterations affect the genome-wide epigenetic state. We will also test if reducing this enhanced DNA damage response in tumor cells might alter their epigenetic state and improve their response to differentiation therapy. 3) Using vivo cell-tracing and cell clearance strategies, we will test if we can remediate the defects that arise due to eroded telomeres to reduce tumor formation and improve tissue health. We have uncovered that cells with short telomeres are more sensitive to disruptions in DNA integrity and replication. Building on these new results, we will undertake a comprehensive investigation of this vulnerability in stem cells and cancer cells with short telomeres. Since cancer cells and stem cells rely on telomerase for their proliferation and function, the ability to manipulate these vulnerabilities may provide means to improve tissue function, or to impair cancer cell survival and tumor formation.

column36: Defining the Impact of Socio-Structural Determinants of Health on Immune Activation and Inflammation in Adolescents and Youth Adults in a Vulnerable Environment
column37: Excessive immune activation and inflammation contribute to poor health outcomes. Chronic inflammation and associated diseases cause 60% of deaths globally, and are cited by the WHO as the greatest threat to human health. Complex processes that trigger chronic inflammation, including infection, injury, and psychological distress, alter our health trajectories, especially if they occur in our youth. While biological factors associated with inflammation (infection, stress) have been reasonably well studied, less is known about how markers of socio-structural inequity (poverty, food insecurity, gender-based violence, gender inequity) contribute to inflammation or whether pathways differ by sex and gender. We will use existing biological specimens and linked survey data from 425 adolescents and young adults (16-24yrs; 60% female) enrolled in the AYAZAZI cohort study (South Africa) to answer new questions about the pathways through which the socio-structural determinants of health (SDoH) affect chronic immune activation, inflammation, and youth health. This study includes three exploratory aims examined for the overall sample and stratified by sex and gender: (1) Characterize inflammation profiles of youth; (2) Determine if key SDoHs are associated with immune profiles of youth; and (3) Examine pathways from SDoHs to inflammation among youth. Directed acyclic graphs and structural equation models will be used to identify direct and indirect pathways from key SDoH to inflammation, through indicators of health risks and recent stressors. This research will provide novel data to help explain the mechanisms through which socio-structural inequities experienced by youth lead to chronic inflammatory conditions that compromise health during adolescence and in later adulthood. Characterizing the SDoH foundations of inflammation will inform equity-oriented population health interventions for youth in Canada and globally.

column36: Integrating Trauma-Informed Evaluation and Treatment of Adverse Childhood Experiences with a First Nations Treatment Seeking Population
column37: Indigenous peoples in Canada experience more health difficulties compared to non-Indigenous populations and are more likely to have poorer access to factors that may reduce the impact of these disparities, such as continuous health services in remote or rural settings. Further, Indigenous peoples in Canada have unique experiences of historical oppression and colonization, resulting in subsequent marginalization, discrimination, and loss of culture. Decades of research across non-Indigenous populations has identified that ten specific adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with poor health outcomes and the presence of chronic diseases. These ACEs describe experiences such as abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction (such as having a parent incarcerated). However, the relationship between intergenerational trauma, ACEs, and health outcomes among Indigenous peoples is not well documented. There is also a lack of research that examines how factors such as cultural connectedness, community support, and resilience protect Indigenous adults who have a history of ACEs. The proposed community-based participatory research project aims to examine the relationship between ACEs and various aspects of wellbeing, in order to have a knowledge base that Indigenous community-based organizations can use to better support their community members facing difficulties with mental health and addictions. To that end, the proposed project also aims to evaluate the use of pilot data to inform three therapy groups offered to Indigenous adults with chronic substance use difficulties at the partnering organization. Ultimately, results can be used by Indigenous organizations to tailor substance use treatment for their clients to adequately address potential origins of substance use, in a trauma-informed and culturally relevant way.

column36: Circular RNAs and their role in congenital diaphragmatic hernia
column37: Every day, 150 babies are born worldwide with a hole in the diaphragm and abnormal lung development. This disease is called congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Almost one-third of these babies die because they have abnormally developed lungs which makes it hard for them to breathe. It is currently not possible to predict how these babies will do after birth when the diagnosis is made in a pregnant mother. We have discovered that a particular class of biomolecules - circular pieces of genetic code called circular RNAs - can be used to predict the outcome in CDH babies when the diagnosis is made. We will study profiles of circular RNAs in CDH biofluids such as amniotic fluid and compare them with profiles from control patients. We will use a rat model of CDH and human lung CDH lung samples to determine where these circular RNAs are localized. Finally, we will remove the most abundant circular RNAs from lung cells and explanted control and CDH rat lungs to determine the role of circular RNAs in normal and abnormal lung development. Our research team consists of an international team of experts in CDH and circular RNAs. Results from our studies will help to better predict outcomes in mothers who are pregnant from a CDH baby. We will also learn more about how abnormal lung development occurs in CDH.

column36: Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy to Improve Quality of Life in Patients Undergoing Pancreatoduodenectomy: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial (PERQ-UP Pilot)
column37: In up to 80% of patients, surgery of the pancreas (most commonly for pancreatic cancer) leads to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI), a disease where the pancreas no longer makes sufficient digestive enzymes. Tests to diagnose PEI are difficult to perform and have limited availability, therefore most patients only receive treatment for severe, symptomatic PEI, leaving up to 75% of patients untreated. Treatment of mild to moderate PEI with pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) may improve quality of life, reduce weight loss and improve overall survival in patients with PEI as a result of cancer. Given the minimal side effects of PERT and serious problems that may occur in untreated PEI, there is a need for well-conducted studies examining this. Findings from this pilot trial randomizing patients to receive PERT or standard of care (PERT only upon presentation of severe symptoms) at the time of discharge following surgery and continuing for 3-months will be used to establish the feasibility of proceeding with a larger trial in Canada to determine if treating all patients with PERT after surgery can decrease weight loss and improve quality of life. Approximately 1200 patients undergo pancreatic surgery each year in Canada and could potentially benefit from this low-risk intervention.

column36: Periacetabular Osteotomy with or without arthroscopic management in patients with hip dysplasia: A multicenter randomized controlled trial
column37: Hip dysplasia is one of the most common causes of hip arthritis. Many patients with hip dysplasia experience years of painful hip symptoms that interfere with activity and quality of life before arthritis develops. The Bernese periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is a procedure that reorients the acetabulum (hip socket) and has been used successfully for over 30 years to treat the symptoms of hip dysplasia and delay the onset of arthritis. Unfortunately, some patients have symptoms that persist after PAO surgery for problems inside the hip joint that could not be corrected with a PAO alone. Hip arthroscopy is a surgical procedure performed using a small camera that allows surgeons to see and address problems like cartilage and labral tears inside the hip joint. Although both procedures are considered standard of care treatment options, it is unknown whether or not the addition of the hip arthroscopy to PAO surgery adds value to the patient and the healthcare institution when compared to a PAO alone. Furthermore, the association between hip arthroscopy outcomes and cartilage quality is not well elucidated in the literature. The quality of the cartilage can be assessed by a noninvasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique called T1rho that enables the evaluation of early cartilage changes. As such, this study will recruit 126 participants undergoing a PAO for hip dysplasia across two sites in Canada and two sites in the United States. Patients will be randomized to receive a PAO alone or a PAO and a hip arthroscopy simultaneously. Both groups will be compared in terms of quality of life and health system costs. Furthermore, a sub-group of patients (18 in each group) will receive a T1rho MRI before and after surgery to study changes in cartilage quality over time.

column36: Integrated Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (i-CBT) and Intravenous Ketamine for Suicidality in Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized, Midazolam-Controlled Clinical Trial
column37: Approximately four thousand Canadians die by suicide every year, and suicide is the second leading cause of death in youth and young adults (15-34 years). Most people with depression experience thoughts of suicide and many will also plan and/or attempt suicide at some time in their life. There is an urgent need for new scalable treatments that can effectively reduce suicidality in people with depression. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) reduces suicidal behaviours and thoughts, and can be delivered through internet-based modalities (i.e., i-CBT), allowing for increased scalability and accessibility. However, CBT has not demonstrated a robust rapid-onset effect. Emerging evidence suggests that intravenous (IV) ketamine rapidly reduces thoughts of suicide. Integrating i-CBT with IV ketamine may be more effective in rapidly reducing suicidality than i-CBT treatment alone. No randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have evaluated the efficacy of integrated i-CBT and IV ketamine for the treatment of suicidality. We propose a 12-week, multi-site, double-blinded RCT to evaluate the efficacy of integrated i-CBT and IV ketamine treatment for suicidality. Individuals with depression who have recently experienced suicidal thoughts or behaviours will be included. All 140 participants will receive 12 weeks of i-CBT, and will be randomly assigned to also receive six IV ketamine treatments or the placebo treatment over the initial 30 days. We will measure suicidality using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale before treatment and at the primary endpoint (i.e., day 30), and will evaluate change in suicidality between the i-CBT + IV ketamine group compared to the i-CBT + placebo group. This will be the first RCT to examine the effects of combined i-CBT and IV ketamine on suicidality. The findings will provide the foundation for a scalable intervention to reduce suicide risk and provides a requisite first step towards reducing suicide mortality.

column36: Improving access to family planning services for Indigenous peoples through storytelling
column37: The right to have children, not have children, and parent with dignity is central to the health and well-being of individuals, families, and communities. Respectfully supporting Indigenous peoples to plan and space their pregnancies is crucial to protecting this right in Canada. Indigenous communities are the holders of knowledge about what it means to have safe, culturally appropriate, and accessible family planning care. Data indicates that Indigenous clients routinely experience inequitable access, coercion, stigma, and reproductive violence when engaging with family planning care. Developing family planning programs and services that meet the physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual needs of Indigenous peoples first requires an understanding of their experiences with existing services. This research is a collaboration between Indigenous communities, researchers at the University of British Columbia, the BC First Nations Health Authority, Vancouver Coastal Health Authority, the ekw'i7tl doula collective, and health care professional organizations. We aim to understand a) Indigenous peoples' experiences accessing family planning care and b) what approaches to family planning care are best-suited to Indigenous communities, contexts, priorities, and needs. We will explore what "family planning" means to communities, what are clients' experiences of accessing family planning health services, how racism and stereotypes influence access to care, and what are the characteristics of good access to family planning for Indigenous clients. The results of this research will help fill the gap in knowledge about Indigenous experiences of current family planning care in Canada and will highlight opportunities for improved service delivery.

column37: Some women with breast cancer confined to the breast are treated with chemotherapy before undergoing surgery. For many of these patients, chemotherapy works so well that there will be no more cancer cells left in the lumpectomy specimen removed at surgery. The current standard approach is to give radiation to the breast after surgery even if there are no cancer cells left. The purpose of the radiation treatment is to decrease the risk of the cancer coming back within the breast. The radiation treatment does not decrease the chance of the cancer coming back in other places. However, previous studies have shown that women with no cancer cells left in the breast after chemotherapy have a very low chance of breast cancer coming back in the breast. Based on this information, the radiation treatment may not be needed. Radiation treatment can have negative effects including tiredness, breast pain, and skin and lung damage. Women with no cancer cells left after being treated with chemotherapy and lumpectomy, and interested in avoiding radiation will be followed in this study to see if they have the same risk of the cancer coming back as women who are treated with radiation. The side effects of radiation will also be measured, including local side effects to the breast and effects on quality of life. Women treated in health care centers across Canada will be asked to participate and will be followed for 5-years or until the cancer comes back.

column37: The 9 months in the womb is the most dramatic period of growth and development that ultimately shapes our long-term health. Prenatal care and promotion of healthful behaviours during pregnancy have been identified as key intervention strategies for supporting optimal long-term health. Poor diet and sleep, high stress and low physical activity levels can lead to pregnancy complications such as gestational diabetes and hypertension, depression and inappropriate/excessive gestational weight gain (GWG). A new approach to prenatal health care delivery is urgently needed and we believe that intervention via mobile technology is the answer to better outcomes for mom and baby. We will evaluate recruitment and adherence to SmartMoms Canada, data collection/outcome measures and intervention procedures. Our study aims to evaluate user experience, measured by adherence to the program via app software metrics (e.g., number of logins, app use, 'counts' on specific pages [i.e., nutrition, exercise]); overall study completion rate of greater than or equal to 75% of participants (at delivery); and score of greater than 2 on a Participant Satisfaction Questionnaire. We intend to revolutionize the existing prenatal health care delivery model by launching a personalized, real-time technology that is accessible to all Canadian pregnant women and therefore, supporting all women with improving health behaviours throughout gestation and downstream maternal and child health.

column36: A multi-site population health study evaluating the physical activity levels of patients with atrial fibrillation (CANSURVEY-AF)
column37: This project is concerned with a serious heart-beat condition known as atrial fibrillation (AF), a major health problem in Canada. AF sufferers have poor exercise tolerance and bothersome symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness, fatigue), with increased risks of stroke and death. Unfortunately, most AF patients report debilitating ongoing symptoms with current treatments (i.e. medications and surgery). Regular physical activity (PA) has been shown to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life (QoL), and reduced symptoms and time spent in AF. The 2020 clinical guidelines for AF patients include exercise targets, but patients may not be receiving this information. Research in other countries shows low PA levels among AF patients, but high-quality data are lacking for the PA levels of Canadians living with AF. AF patients' knowledge, outcome expectations and self-efficacy that influence their decision to engage in PA have also yet to be researched. Our project aims to measure the PA levels of AF patients across Canada. We will also examine their knowledge, outcome expectations and self-efficacy regarding PA, and how this relates to their PA levels, time in AF, symptoms and QoL. We will use monitors to measure the PA levels and time in AF, and questionnaires to examine their knowledge, outcome expectations and self-efficacy regarding PA as well as symptoms and QoL. We will recruit 1,136 people with AF from five sites across Canada (Ottawa, Halifax, Laval, Toronto, Vancouver). If our project shows that AF patients have low PA levels and these levels relate to their time in AF, symptoms and QoL, then doctors will have important information to convey to AF patients as they consider their treatment options. Understanding the knowledge, outcome expectations and self-efficacy of AF patients regarding PA will also help to improve strategies that can increase PA and QoL, and reduce bothersome symptoms for the management of this serious medical condition.

column36: Personality-Targeted Interventions for Addressing Polysubstance Use among Opioid-Addicted Clients Undergoing Opioid Substitution Therapy: A Feasibility Study
column37: We are amid a severe opioid crisis, worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic. In Canada, prescription opioid use and opioid overdoses/mortality were soaring pre-pandemic, reaching epidemic levels, with opioid-related deaths only increasing since the pandemic. Powerful and dangerous synthetic opioids (e.g., Fentanyl) are increasingly being used to cut street drugs given disruptions to the drug supply chain with pandemic border closures. More effective interventions for addressing opioid use disorder are sorely needed. An effective mainstay treatment for opioid use disorder in Canada is opioid substitution therapy (OST; e.g., methadone, buprenorphine). However, OST clients frequently have other problems that are not well served by OST alone such as high OST drop-out and continued polysubstance use during OST. The latter can include "topping up" with opioids, using substances that are dangerous when combined with OST (e.g., sedatives), and risky administration routes (e.g., injection). We have recently shown that personality traits that predict risk for mental health/behavioral problems also predict risky forms and routes of substance use in OST clients. We will use our expertise in brief cognitive-behavioral interventions and clinical research methods to test the feasibility of personality-targeted substance use interventions in OST clients. We are currently using our existing personality model along with interviews already collected from OST clients and service providers to adapt our personality-targeted interventions. For the proposed grant, in collaboration with our knowledge user partners, we will aim to try 4 personality-targeted interventions with clients across 4 OST clinics, evaluate feasibility, and provide a first test of their impacts on clients' polysubstance use and OST retention. We will examine feasibility from the perspectives of clients, therapists, and clinic directors to see if the personality targeted approach should be pursued further in this population.
