column36: The Effects of repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation on Performance, Fatigue, and Pain
column37: Fatigue and pain are often considered to be limiting factors of performance, especially in endurance sports. Central fatigue is not fully understood yet, but parts of the brain have been identified as main contributors. First, the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is the brain region responsible for perception of fatigue and pain. Second, the primary motor cortex (M1) is the part of the brain sending a direct output for muscle contraction. As a means to maintain homeostasis and protect the body during exercise, the brain perceives pain and fatigue, and then decreases the output of the M1 to the muscles. This protection imposes a limitation on the body's ability to perform. Being able to overcome this protection through brain stimulation would allow to improve performance in endurance sports. Neuromodulation strategies like repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) enable the stimulation of specific areas of the brain. It is thus possible to inhibit the PFC, reducing perceived pain and fatigue, and to excite the M1 area, increasing the brain output to the muscles. This technique has never been used on runners to measure performance, which will be the main outcome of this study. We expect to see an improved performance following excitatory stimulation on the M1 area, as well as following inhibitory stimulation on the PFC. 20 elite long-distance runners will undergo four different stimulation sessions, presented in a random order: real rTMS on both areas targeted by this study, sham stimulation on both areas, real rTMS on the PFC and sham stimulation on M1, as well as real rTMS on M1 and sham stimulation on the PFC. After the stimulation, participants will perform a time to exhaustion treadmill test, which allows to quantify the improvement in performance levels.

column36: The Role of Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase in Humans with Comorbid Borderline Personality Disorder and Depression
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious mental health condition that influences the way people think about themselves and others. Anger, mood swings, poor self-image, and suicide attempts are all common symptoms of BPD that negatively impact one's relationships and ability to function in everyday life. BPD commonly occurs alongside major depressive disorder (MDD), which causes persistent feelings of sadness, worthlessness and disinterest. MDD affects many individuals worldwide, but it is more severe and persistent in those also diagnosed with BPD. Currently, psychotherapy is the primary treatment for BPD, but this option is both costly and time-consuming, which creates a barrier for individuals to access or adhere to treatment. A pharmacological alternative is necessary to ensure equitable access to care. Antidepressant medication is currently the first-line treatment for MDD, but only about half of individuals experience an improvement in their symptoms. The most widely prescribed antidepressants target two important brain chemicals, serotonin and norepinephrine; however, another brain system might play a key role in the development of both MDD and BPD symptoms. This project will focus on the endocannabinoid system (ECS) to investigate potential markers in BPD and MDD. There is evidence to suggest that the enzyme fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) is altered in BPD and MDD, but no study has investigated FAAH in individuals with both diagnoses. We hypothesize that the levels of FAAH will be elevated in adults with BPD and MDD compared to healthy controls and MDD alone. The results from this research may reveal FAAH to be a potential target for the development of more effective treatment options for both disorders.

column36: Linking Cell Function and Gene Expression to Define Maturation of Stem-Cell Derived beta-Cells for the Treatment of Type 1 Diabetes
column37: In July 2000, a type 1 diabetes treatment named the ""Edmonton protocol<sup>1</sup>"" was developed and has subsequently been used to treat thousands of patients worldwide, including ~400 in Canada. The Edmonton protocol uses insulin-producing islet cells from organ donors for transplantation into those with severe diabetes. Although significant progress has been made, new cell sources are needed to treat the millions living with the disease, since access to tissue from organ donors remains limited. Stem-cell derived β-cells (SCβ-cells) offer a promising alternative for cell replacement therapy since these can be grown in large amounts; however, key characteristics displayed by mature human β-cells, such as insulin secretion and cell excitability, remain blunted in SCβ-cells, reflecting immaturity after cellular differentiation. My project aims to understand the gene expression changes that underlie the mature functioning of primary human β-cells and the in vitro maturation of stem-cell derived β-cells to produce improved cell-based therapies for type 1 diabetes. I will use single-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology combined with RNA sequencing (Patch-Seq), in conjunction with a machine learning platform, to identify genes whose expression correlates with functional maturation of SCβ-cells. Identified targets will be validated, and the mechanism of function will be assessed using gene knockdown methods. Advances in this field will be critical for the development of cell replacement therapies for type 1 diabetes and will transform the lives of those in need of insulin producing cells to reduce the tremendous burden on Canada's health care system.

column36: Genetic and non-genetic factors of pre-eclampsia
column37: Pre-eclampsia (PE) is a pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and protein in the urine, and it affects 2-10% of pregnancies world-wide. A form of severe PE with Hemolysis (rupturing of red blood cells), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets is termed HELLP syndrome. Currently, it's unclear what causes PE and how it manifests, so the only definitive treatment is to deliver the fetus. Thus, much research attention has been given to the prediction and prevention of PE through studying genetic and environmental risk factors. Abnormal immune processes in the placenta, an organ that supports fetal life, has been proposed as a mechanism of PE. I hypothesize that genetic variants that influence the innate immune response in the placenta will be associated with placental inflammation associated with PE. I will test this hypothesis by first identifying immune-related genes that are expressed in the placenta. Then, I will identify genetic variants associated with the expression and methylation of these genes. Lastly, I will test for associations between these genetic variants and PE and summarize the results into a polygenic risk score (PRS). In addition to genetic factors, I will examine non-genetic factors such as obesity, in another dataset. Prior studies suggest that obesity increases the risk of HELLP, but this association remains to be better examined in a larger cohort. By developing a PRS for PE, I hope to identify key pathways involved in placental immune dysregulation in PE. By clarifying the association between obesity and HELLP, I hope to provide better information for pre-pregnancy counselling and maternity care. These two conceptually complementary studies will prepare me to build a gene-environment interaction model for PE in the future.

column36: Comparative Health and Economic Effects of Universal Hepatitis B Vaccination in Infants Versus Adolescents in Canada: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
column37: Hepatitis B, one of three most common forms of viral hepatitis, is a potentially life-threatening infection that can cause acute and chronic disease. In Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland and Labrador, hepatitis B vaccines are administered in Grades 6 or 7, despite the World Health Organization's recommendation of vaccinating within the first 24 hours of life. The benefits of vaccinating as soon as possible after birth is largely driven by the fact that the likelihood of developing chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is the highest for the younger population. Infants infected with hepatitis B virus in the first year of life have 80 – 90% likelihood of developing CHB, while the likelihood for adults is less than 5%. The age-associated chronic infection incidence suggests that the current vaccination schedule in many of the Canadian provinces does not align with best practices in preventing the occurrence of CHB. To address this issue, our proposed research aims to assess the cost-effectiveness of providing hepatitis B vaccines during infancy in Canada. We hypothesize that by proactively vaccinating the highest risk group for developing CHB, the incidence of CHB will decrease and prove to be a cost-saving intervention. The decrease in CHB incidence may potentially lead to massive savings for the government, allowing for better utilization of healthcare funds. To our knowledge, there is no research to demonstrate the cost-effectiveness of hepatitis B vaccination during infancy versus adolescence. The results of this research are expected to delineate the clinical and economic impact of providing hepatitis B vaccines earlier than the current Canadian vaccine schedule. This novel model will provide crucial data to advise policy changes in Canada.

column36: Blood Biomarkers to Improve the Diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis Pulmonary Exacerbations
column37: Pulmonary exacerbations (PEx) are common events for cystic fibrosis (CF) patients that cause difficulty breathing, worsening cough and mucus production due to uncontrolled inflammation and infection. Timely treatment of PEx with antibiotics is important to minimize irreversible airway damage. Currently, CF patients have quarterly routine appointments to assess any change in symptoms and lung function, to ensure that they can be quickly diagnosed and treated for PEx. When patients experience increased respiratory symptoms and a drop in lung function, the clinical decision to treat with antibiotics is clear. However, deciding whether to treat with antibiotics is unclear when only an increase in symptoms or a decrease in lung function is seen, weighing the consequences of antibiotic overuse with permanent loss of lung function. Developing a blood test for PEx could help improve diagnosis and treatment of PEx. Our group has found that C-reactive protein (CRP) and calprotectin could be used in a blood test to differentiate PEx from stable status. We hypothesize that a blood test for CRP and calprotectin will help identify patients that will do poorly without antibiotics when showing only a change in symptoms or a decline in lung function. My specific objectives are to compare the respiratory outcomes of patients with versus without high levels of CRP and calprotectin. I will use blood samples from CF patients who experienced either an increase in respiratory symptoms or a decline in lung function and evaluate if the blood test can predict worse respiratory outcomes at clinical follow up without antibiotic treatment. If this blood test is found to be useful, it will improve outcomes for many CF patients allowing PEx to be better diagnosed and treated.

column36: Population-based analysis of major lower extremity trauma in Ontario: the role of interdisciplinary management in outcomes
column37: Open lower extremity fractures from high-energy traumas are a significant management challenge, and frequently requires a concomitant approach by both orthopedic and plastic surgeons for early fixation and soft tissue coverage by microsurgery. This project aims to elucidate the impact of a prompt transfer to Level I TC and early coordinated intervention by orthopedic and plastic surgery teams on the outcome of patients who had open tibial fractures. We hypothesize that those who received early evaluations by both surgical teams and pertinent surgeries in a TC will have improved outcome. Patients who were transferred to an Ontario Level I TC from peripheral centers between the years 2009-2015 will be included in this study. Utilizing the ICES database, data pertaining to patient demographics and management, such as admission location, hospital transfers, and time from initial injury to procedure will be obtained. Outcome parameters including amputation, infection, and death will also be analyzed. The results of this research will help instigate discussions for alternative care delivery models for those with severe open fracture traumas, and ultimately lead to initiatives such as development of an ""orthoplastic"" team in TCs to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Evaluer le potentiel anti-psoriasique des polyphenols sur les substituts cutanes psoriasiques enrichis en lymphocytes T

La qualite de vie des patients souffrant de psoriasis est grandement affectee par l'inconfort cutane, la douleur et m eme la stigmatisation sociale. Recemment, de nouvelles molecules polyphenoliques issues de la for et boreale ont montre une forte activite anti-psoriasique. Parallelement, les microaiguilles (MNs) sur timbre representent une option interessante pour la liberation transdermique de medicaments. Leur petite taille leur permet de traverser la couche cornee sans toutefois affecter les neurones cutanes, constituant ainsi un systeme indolore. column36: A Quantitative Intersectional Approach to Studying Inequalities in Intimate Partner Violence in Canada
column37: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a recognized public health concern in Canada. It is known that there are certain groups who are at higher risk of IPV, including younger women, sexual and gender minority men and women, Indigenous women, and disabled women. Although past research has identified specific groups that are at higher risk of IPV, it may have left out people who are at the intersection of these identities, meaning that they identify with more than one of these groups. Intersectionality is a theoretical framework that explains how people at multiple intersections of identity have unique experiences that cannot be understood by studying each identity individually. In order to get a more accurate picture of who is at risk of IPV in Canada and include groups that may have been missed in previous research, this study will use two new statistical methods to analyze a very large Statistics Canada dataset called the Survey of Safety in Public and Private Spaces. The goal of this study is to find out new information on which intersectional groups are experiencing the greatest amount of IPV in Canada, and what types of IPV (i.e. sexual, emotional, physical) these high-risk groups are experiencing. The findings from this study can then be used to better inform public health interventions and improve knowledge on IPV. This study will also provide an example of how these new methods can be used to incorporate intersectionality into population health research.

column36: Improving the Continuity of Mental Health Care Through Professional Collaboration
column37: The Canadian government recognizes the need to improve support for the mental health system as demand for mental health services grows. Facilitators and barriers of processes or other factors should be identified; this data can inform future collaborative programs that aim to provide continuity. Results can encourage prioritization of mental health and continuity of care in policies to reduce rising costs and inequities. The case is contained to the program of a tertiary mental health hospital (The Royal) in Ottawa, Ontario that aims to improve collaboration between registered nurses and family physicians. I will conduct semi-structured in-depth interviews with 3-4 registered nurses working in the program, 3 program managers or coordinators at The Royal, and 8-10 community physicians caring for patients enrolled in the program. Program documents will be provided by The Royal and I will analyze documents to corroborate interviews, minimize bias, and enhance credibility. column36: Investigating NK cell dysfunction in the aftermath of surgical intervention
column37: For patients with solid tumours, the best course of action is undoubtedly tumour removal surgery, however, in the immediate post-operative window, and sometimes lasting months after surgery, the immune system is significantly suppressed. The Auer Lab has identified this dysfunction in a subset of immune cells, known as natural killer (NK) cells, as a decrease in the ability to directly kill target tumour cells as well as a decreased secretion of signalling proteins that help coordinate the anti-tumour response from other immune cells. Previously, the Auer Lab has identified multiple signalling factors bringing about change in the NK cells similar, but not identical, to that seen in the post-surgical environment. In following one of these candidates, the changes in gene expression after surgery compared to the gene expression of NK cells prior to surgery were quantified, showing that the NK cells from the post-operative period demonstrate a significantly different gene expression program than the NK cells from the screening time point. Among these genes that seem to be decreased in the postoperative window, are the genes responsible for the killing function of NK cells, thus partially explaining a defect in the post-surgical NK cells. Additionally, a significant increase in remodelling enzymes of the genome was seen, suggesting that there are changes in the way the NK cells are able to express genes. For this project, we aim to further investigate the exact mechanism by which the NK cells are forced to change the expression of their genes on and off. In identifying the events that lead to differential gene expression, we can propose candidate therapeutic interventions to prevent NK cell dysfunction through surgery.

column36: Relating structural and functional connectivity in subcortical-cortical networks across psychopathology
column37: Psychiatric disorders affect around 20% of children, causing great burden to families and society. Yet, our understanding of how they develop and can be treated has been stalled by psychiatry's continued focus on traditional diagnostic categories (e.g. 'schizophrenia'). These categories, based only on subjective symptoms, do not reflect the reality that symptoms ascribed to different diagnoses often coexist, and different diagnoses show overlapping patterns of brain abnormalities. Instead, psychiatric symptoms may be better understood as the results of different mixtures of deficits in the brain, which give rise to dimensions of symptoms that across current diagnoses and exist in individuals to varying degrees. Understanding the biology of these symptom dimensions may thus produce markers of illness that can better predict the course of disease. To this end, brain imaging provides two related indices of abnormal brain development: structural connectivity (SC), measuring the strength of the physical connections between brain regions, and functional connectivity (FC), describing the coordinated activity of different regions. Disruptions in the normal coordination of SC and FC (structure-function coupling) represent a potential marker of psychiatric illness. Yet, how this coupling relates to dimensions of psychiatric symptoms in the dynamic, developing brain remains unclear. Thus, this study will examine patterns of brain structure-function coupling in ~900 youth of a range of mental health, focusing on brain regions vulnerable to disease, and how variation in this coupling is linked to symptom dimensions. The findings may aid earlier detection of mental illness, and offer a novel, biology-based way to stratify youth with psychiatric symptoms to inform improved treatments.

column36: An environmental scan of follow-up practices after discharge from pediatric intensive care units
column37: Advances in intensive care have resulted in a decrease in deaths in children admitted to pediatric intensive care units (PICU). Improved survival has led to increased physical, cognitive and mental health challenges in survivors and their families, which has raised the question of whether we are trading death for other long-term health consequences in this population. There are important knowledge gaps of the causes of these impairments, including which children are at highest risk and what factors affect these outcomes. Outpatient follow-up of children after admission to the PICU has been proposed as one way of monitoring health outcomes and managing impairments. New research suggests that PICU-led follow-up programs, where follow-up is initiated and organized by members of the PICU team and specifically target PICU-acquired complications, would be beneficial. Although such programs exist, there is little information describing existing practices, and less is known about their impact. Our project aims to conduct a survey of PICUs in Canada and the United States to outline the frequency of follow-up of pediatric patients following critical illness, both in specialized multidisciplinary and PICU-led programs, describe the follow-up practices of such programs and examine whether there is an association between the existence of follow-up programs and PICU size, complexity and re-admission rates. This research will describe the landscape of current follow-up practices and serve as an important first step in creating a North American consensus on best practices for post PICU care. Information from this study may inform hospital and health system planning, namely in terms of resource allocation and financial investment in such programs in the future.

column36: Immunomagnetic separation (IMS) followed by viability PCR (vPCR) as a tool to determine "real" clinical cases of bacterial gastroenteritis in the culture-independent diagnostic era.
column37: As laboratories embrace culture-independent diagnostic tests (CIDTs), microbiologists can be left to ask: are live bacteria present? When a patient is suspected of having bacterial gastroenteritis (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), their specimen is genetically screened for pathogens. By reducing turnaround time and lowering the limit of detection, CIDTs have increased diagnostic efficiency and sensitivity. However, CIDT results can be discordant with the gold standard: despite genetic detection, culture can be unsuccessful. Some bacteria are difficult to culture and free-DNA (released from dead cells) can cause false-positive CIDT results leading to incorrect diagnoses. To resolve these issues, I propose a novel combination of immunomagnetic separation (IMS) and viability PCR (vPCR) as a way to exclusively detect intact cells directly from specimens. IMS involves antibody-coated magnetic beads, which bind organisms of interest before being recovered (with the bound-cells) by a magnet. I will then use vPCR to address non-specific binding. When activated by light, propidium monoazide (PMA) can irreversibly bind any free-DNA carried by the beads, ensuring that subsequent real-time PCR only detects DNA from intact cells. Though I will use shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC), a common cause of gastroenteritis, this protocol will be compatible with most bacteria. Culture is used to characterize bacteria for surveillance purposes. In an outbreak, non-culturable specimens can delay investigations and worsen patient outcomes. The method proposed can be implemented to help confirm if live bacteria are present in cases of CIDT and culture discordance. This will help guide clinicians' decisions regarding patient therapy based on whether live bacteria are present or not.

column36: Sedentary Behaviour and Health Risk: Is excessive "screen time" the real culprit?
column37: Time spent sitting or reclining while awake is called sedentary behaviour, and large amounts of time spent in sedentary behaviours is associated with increased health risks even if the individual also participates in regular physical activity. Additionally, time spent in certain activities such as watching TV in a seated or reclined position may result in greater health risks compared to other activities such as reading or socializing in a seated or reclined position. However, the current methods of measuring sedentary behaviour do not take into account the different types of activities that can be completed while sedentary, therefore a new method of measuring sedentary behaviour is needed. In this project, I will develop and test a new method tentatively called the Index of Sedentary Screen Time (ISST), which will be a weighted measure incorporating both an individual's amount of sedentary ""screen time"" (leisure time spent using a smartphone, TV, or tablet) and their total amount of sedentary time. Additionally, I will determine if this new ISST score is related to cardiovascular and metabolic health by measuring blood pressure, inflammation, blood glucose, body mass index, and waist circumference in addition to ISST score in a volunteer sample of adults. Overall, this project will benefit future research in this field by providing a more accurate way to measure the health risks associated with sedentary behaviour by incorporating both the type of activity completed and the total amount of sedentary time. This project may also assist with the development and modification of the current recommendations for limiting daily sedentary screen time in order to promote overall long-term health.

column36: Elucidating Geographic Clustering and Environmental Triggers of Systemic Sclerosis in Canada
column37: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe, fibrosing, autoimmune disease affecting the skin and the internal organs of middle-aged adults and is chronic and irreversible. There is significant extracutaneous involvement with considerable morbidity and mortality and the ten-year survival is estimated to be 65%. The pathogenesis of SSc, while not fully understood, is believed to be induced by an environmental trigger in a genetically predisposed host. The aim of this study is to evaluate geographic disease clustering in Canadian provinces to understand the epidemiology of this disease and identify novel putative triggers, using provincial administrative databases. Incident cases will then be mapped and correlated to maps of identified exposures. Specifically, we will use existing maps from Enhanced Points of Interest files for industrial presence and the Canadian Urban Environmental Health Research Consortium data for information on air quality, solar radiation, vegetation index, transportation intensity which might be impacting disease as triggers or exacerbating factors. We will analyze the environmental exposures, disease comorbidities, severity, and outcomes between areas with high and low incidence to strengthen our findings and understand the burden of SSc in Canada. This work will serve as the first, and the most comprehensive study, investigating the impact of environmental triggers on this devastating autoimmune skin disease. This will enable us to build a foundation for future research regarding modifiable environmental factors in autoimmune skin diseases, help inform patient counselling, provide grounds for advocacy for environmental and workplace protection from dangerous pollutants, and help inform the distribution of medical resources for SSc patients.

column36: Self-management, lifestyle and cardiovascular risk in First Nations with cardiometabolic multimorbidity
column37: First Nations people are at increased risk of cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CM). CM is the diagnosis of at least two of stroke, heart disease, or diabetes. Evidence indicates that people with CM have a drastically increased risk of premature mortality compared to healthy individuals and that majority of Canadians with CM have poor management of their lifestyle behaviours. Healthy lifestyle behaviours are protective against premature mortality, and therefore, improving self-management to promote and sustain participation in healthy lifestyle behaviours after CM may prevent further health complications. Our primary objective is to quantify the association between self-management and lifestyle behaviour in First Nations people with CM. As a secondary objective, we will explore the association between self-management and cardiovascular risk. We will recruit 55 participants with CM into this observational, cross-sectional study. Kleinbaum's 3-stage multiple regression-modeling strategy will be used to establish valid and precise estimates of the associations between self-management, lifestyle behaviour, and cardiovascular risk. This study will develop important knowledge on an imminent health issue among a high-risk population. The results will be used to leverage larger funding opportunities to develop and evaluate culturally relevant self-management interventions for First Nations populations that will ensure optimal management of CM to prevent health complications.

column36: Components of the COPD Assessment Test Associated with Cardiopulmonary Exercise Test Outcomes in the Canadian Cohort Obstructive Lung Disease (CanCOLD) Study
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common disease that is characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms, most significantly dyspnea. The COPD assessment test (CAT) is an eight-item questionnaire focused on respiratory and non-respiratory symptoms commonly used to assess COPD patients. It remains unknown whether individual CAT items and clusters – particularly dyspnea and the respiratory items– carry useful information regarding the existence of pathophysiological abnormalities in cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) outcomes in people with or at-risk of developing COPD. Therefore, the objective of the proposed research is to perform an evaluation of CAT items in a large population-based cohort to reveal, to which extent single and clustered CAT items, as opposed to the CAT total score, carry additional information regarding pathophysiological abnormalities in physiological and perceptual responses to CPET. From a clinical management perspective, the results of this study may facilitate early identification of people with or at-risk of developing COPD with impaired health status due to exertional dyspnea or respiratory symptoms and who may respond most favorably to currently available respiratory drug therapies.

column36: Effects of a physical training program on physical and functional capacity in chronic low back pain patients
column37: Chronic low back pain (CLPB) is increasingly recognized as a major public health issue. In Canada, it is the most common form of chronic pain. Pain levels will be monitored during each training sessions as well as after the completion of each physical and functional tests. column36: Does interferon-gamma influence LDL transcytosis, the earliest stage of atherosclerosis?
column37: Every blood vessel in the body is lined by a layer of specialized cells known as the endothelium. The accumulation of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (i.e. the ""bad cholesterol"") underneath that endothelial lining is one of the key and earliest steps in the initiation of heart disease (atherosclerosis)^3. For LDL in the blood to accumulate under the endothelium, it must first cross the layer of endothelial cells through a process called transcytosis. However, the mechanisms of LDL transcytosis and how it is affected during disease remain largely unknown. The objective of the present study is to determine the effect of a well-known inflammatory protein, interferon gamma (IFN-γ) on LDL transcytosis. IFN-γ is a cytokine that can be detected in the earliest lesions of heart disease. Hence, we hypothesize that IFN-γ stimulates LDL transcytosis and accelerates atherosclerosis. To quantify LDL transcytosis in the presence of IFN-γ, a live cell imaging assay using total internal fluorescence microscopy was developed by our lab and will be performed using human endothelial cells. Next, western blot and immunofluorescence will be performed to assess the mechanism of any effect. To validate our findings from cells in culture, a mouse model for atherosclerosis will be used. Immunohistochemistry will be conducted to quantify and visualize the localization of LDL and mediators of LDL transcytosis under the influence of IFN-γ. Overall, this will allow us to better understand the pathophysiological basis of atherosclerosis and has the potential to reveal novel preventative and therapeutic approaches for atherosclerosis.

column36: Modelling the interactome of Diphtheria Toxin with the promiscuous biotinylating enzyme TurboID
column37: Toxins secreted by bacterial pathogens cause the tissue damage observed in many infectious diseases. Multi-domain protein toxins bind to host cell receptors and enter the cell through a process that is poorly understood, ultimately inactivating key host factors. I aim to identify the array of host-toxin interactions that mediate intoxication through a novel application of enzyme-catalyzed proximity labelling. By using Diphtheria Toxin (DT) as a model, I can confirm host targets of this well-characterized toxin to validate the protein-protein interaction screen. DT is a three-domain toxin that inactivates a ribosomal factor, arresting protein synthesis. To map the toxin's transit into the cell, I will express various fusion constructs of the promiscuous biotin ligase TurboID and DT and intoxicate cells with these chimeras. Previous work in the Melnyk lab has demonstrated that DT can co-deliver numerous and diverse protein cargo; therefore, I hypothesize that TurboID will be a ""silent passenger"" permitting detection of the full range of DT-host protein-protein interactions from receptor binding through to translocation of the catalytic domain and interaction with the toxins intracellular target(s). TurboID covalently binds biotin to adjacent proteins, which are then recovered through a streptavidin pull down. Mass spectrometry reveals a list of candidate proteins from which I can identify known host targets and novel interactions. Ultimately, this work will deliver the first comprehensive map of toxin-host protein-protein interactions and demonstrate a novel, efficient discovery tool for new therapeutic targets of other toxins.

column36: Identification d'un biomarqueur cerebral de la modulation de la douleur par l'hypnose

Afin de preciser les mecanismes neurologiques sous-jacents a l'hypnose, il importe de decrire les reseaux neuronaux dont l'activite est modulee par les suggestions hypnotiques d'analgesie. Il existe des signatures cerebrales de la douleur. Elles constituent un patron d'activation neuronal nous permettant de reconnaitre l'activite du cerveau liee a la douleur, a l'intensite du stimulus la provoquant et a l'analgesie pharmacologique (la NPS), mais aussi aux fluctuations spontanees de la perception de la douleur, peu importe l'intensite reelle du stimulus (la SIPPS). Ces signatures cerebrales sont telles qu'on peut, a la seule observation des activations du cerveau, decrire la condition experimentale qui a induit cette activite. L'hypnose est generalement decrite par des echelles comportementales. a ce jour, on ne connait pas de signature cerebrale pour l'effet de suggestions hypnotique de modulation de la douleur. Notre etude vise donc a la recherche d'une signature cerebrale de l'hypnoanalgesie avec une approche en apprentissage automatique. Cela nous permettra de verifier si cette intervention module l'activite du cerveau comme le font la NPS et la SIPPS, mais aussi de tenter de developper une signature cerebrale distinctive et potentiellement plus specifique a la modulation de la douleur par l'hypnose.

column36: Investigation of Facial Affect Processing Following Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Patients with Schizophrenia: An Event-Related Potential (ERP) Study
column37: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a disorder that results in symptoms like hallucinations, delusions, and deficits in cognition. These symptoms impair the ability of those affected to engage in processes like interpreting the emotions of others. This is thought to reflect deficits in mental processes like recognizing facial expressions of emotion, which is a critical component of social cognition. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for SZ that has been proven to mitigate information processing difficulties and improve social cognition. Half of the SZ group will receive a 5-month CBT treatment and the remaining half will be waitlisted for 5 months. Patients will be asked standardized and validated questions about their symptoms, daily functioning, and social skills, as well as being tested for brain activity in response to emotive faces via an EEG test battery. This will be done at baseline and after 5 months. This study will provide important evidence regarding the efficacy of CBT in improving face and emotion recognition, reducing symptoms of SZ, and improving daily social functioning. column36: Evaluating the effects of tumor discordance on metastatic lesion formation in a model of synchronous bilateral breast cancer using molecular imaging
column37: Synchronous bilateral breast cancer (SBBC) is defined as the detection of cancer in both breasts at the time of diagnosis or within a short interval of 3-12 months. Clinical studies have found that SBBC patients have higher rates of metastasis and lower overall survival compared to patients with unilateral breast cancer. I recently led the establishment of the first preclinical model of SBBC in mice, revealing a high degree of cross-seeding of spontaneous metastases from each tumor and high intratumoral cellular heterogeneity. This model involved two primary tumors of the same tumor biology (triple-negative in estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2). However, in the clinic, SBBC patients also may have discordant primary tumor phenotypes, but the effects of this on metastatic patterns and potential response to treatment are currently unknown. I propose to model intertumoral discordance of SBBC by implanting cells of different breast tumor biology into contralateral mammary fat pads of mice. By pre-engineering these cells to express different sets of bioluminescence and fluorescence reporter genes, we will track the formation of spontaneous metastases arising from each primary tumor using in vivo bioluminescence imaging. At endpoint, mice will be sacrificed, and tissues will be removed for ex vivo fluorescence microscopy of metastatic tumors. This will enable us to visualize the cellular makeup of each metastasis and whether they are composed of cells from only one or both primary tumors. The findings of this study will provide insight into the degree of metastatic cross-seeding in SBBC patients with intertumoral discordance, and help understand treatment resistance and optimal planning of treatment for SBBC patients.

column36: Statistical and Ethical Implications of Pimavanserin Drug Trials Published with Unexplained or Missing Datasets on Parkinson's Disease
column37: Pimavanserin is a drug that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to offset Parkinson's Disease Psychosis (PDP), a side effect of common Parkinson's Disease (PD) medications. However, it has not been approved in Canada. It was originally proposed as an alternative to traditional antipsychotic medications, which have been documented to worsen the motor symptoms of PD. Pimavanserin initially performed well in clinical drug trials. However, since being approved by the FDA in 2016, the Institute of Safe Medicine Practices (ISMP) has published a report raising concerns as to Pimavanserin's safety and efficacy, citing hallucinations, confusion, and death as common adverse side effects. Drug trials in the past have been published with missing datasets and without proper statistical adjustments, which are a cause for statistical and ethical concern. This retrospective study will examine the Pimavanserin drug trials published in PubMed and the US National Library of Medicine between 2006 to the present (i.e. commencing a decade prior to FDA approval). The reported trial data, alongside the statistical adjustments made by the authors will be examined. The percentage of missing data, statistical methods employed by the authors, and the subsequent trial outcomes will be compared to determine if there were possible inaccurate inferences based on missing or incomplete datasets. Clinical drug trials are critical in determining whether pharmacotherapies are approved for public use. As such, the statistical strength of these studies must be carefully examined as to reaffirm the public's trust towards the drug regulatory process, provide evidence informed recommendations to Health Canada, and to protect PD patients who may be looking for alternative medications.

column36: Exosome MicroRNA Evaluation for Biomarker Development in Patients with Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Treated with Immunotherapy
column37: Renal cell carcinoma is the most common type of cancer affecting the kidneys and its incidence is increasing. It is frequently diagnosed in advanced stages and upon diagnosis of metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC), systemic treatment is initiated. The standard of care for mRCC is now immunotherapy in the form of dual immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) or in combination with targeted therapy. These drugs work by activating the immune system to target cancer cells. Though overall response rates are excellent, unfortunately many patients do not respond to these treatments. Therefore an important unmet need in the treatment of mRCC is the development of biomarkers to predict who will best respond to ICI. Exosomes are small vesicles which are released from cancer cells and carry a variety of components, including microRNAs (miRNAs). MiRNAs are small non-coding RNA which impact gene expression and can modulate the tumour cells' environment. Exosome miRNAs have been isolated from blood of patients with mRCC and have been shown to have prognostic value and associated with worse clinical outcomes. As proof of concept, we have successfully isolated exosomes from 4 blood samples of patients with mRCC and found a differential expression of at least 3 key miRNAs. MiRNAs have not been studied for use as predictive biomarkers in this new era of mRCC treatment with ICI. Based on this rationale and promising preliminary results, we propose the first study of its kind, to our knowledge, to utilize exosome miRNAs from blood samples of patients with mRCC for full characterization and clinical correlation of outcomes with ICI. This information can help physicians identify the best treatment, amongst multiple options, for each patient thus improving outcomes.

column36: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions Following Outpatient Antibiotic Therapy: A Population-based Study
column37: Drug allergy can affect up to 6% of the general population. It is unpredictable and can develop in anyone at any age after exposure. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) are rare type of drug allergy that has a reported death rate up to 50%. Antibiotics are the most common cause of both drug allergy and SCARs. One in four patients who develop an adverse drug reaction that needs an emergency department (ED) visit can be due to drug allergy. However, the incidence of SCARs following outpatient antibiotic use is unknown. Our study aims to estimate the incidence of SCARs, describe the clinical outcomes of SCARs, and compare the relative risk of SCARs associated with different antibiotics. In this retrospective population-based cohort study, we will include Ontario residents who received an outpatient antibiotic prescription and subsequently presented to ED within 60 days between April 1, 2002 to December 31, 2020. We will use various administrative databases to collect information on antibiotics, date of ED visit and/or hospital admission and discharge, diagnosis and patient demographics. While outpatient antibiotic use is common, severe allergic reaction can happen and increases the risk of death. No previous studies have established the incidence of SCARs following antibiotic use or examined hospital-based outcomes at a large scale. A better understanding in the epidemiology of SCARs following outpatient antibiotic therapy will raise awareness among physicians about this potentially lethal adverse reaction. Our study will highlight the importance of appropriate antibiotic use, drug allergy prevention and early diagnosis in order to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with SCARs.

column36: Emotion Regulation in Children with Autism: The Role of Ethnicity
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by social communication deficits, repetitive habits, and challenging behaviours. Challenging behaviours in children with ASD are believed to be linked to impaired emotion regulation (ER), the ability to control one's emotional experience. In neurotypical (NT) populations, ER ability is influenced by ethnicity as ethnicities differ in value systems, social status, emotional socialization, and emotional expression. In children with ASD, the ER-ethnicity interaction has yet to be studied. Thus, the objective of this investigation is to (1) determine if individual differences in ER ability and physiological arousal (an indicator of ER) are associated with ethnicity in children with ASD; and (2) determine if the effect of ethnicity on ER ability and physiological arousal are different in children with ASD compared to children with anxiety or NT controls. To explore these objectives, this study will recruit children with a diagnosis of ASD, children with an anxiety disorder (but no ASD), and NT children from six different ethnic categories. ER will be characterized by the Emotion Dysregulation Inventory (EDI), and challenging behaviours will be characterized by the Child Behaviour Checklist (CBCL). Physiological arousal will be measured during the participant's completion of a frustrating situation task. Following the study, multiple regression analysis will be used to analyze the data and determine the influence of ethnicity on ER. The results of this study will inform ER interventions for children with ASD, and may promote an ethnically-sensitive approach to improve ER abilities in this population.

column36: Predicting disease progression in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with machine learning using wearable sensor measurements
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative motor neuron disease with an estimated incidence of 2 per 100,000 per year in Canada. Progressive disability due to weakness inevitably leads to death in an average of 3 years from symptom onset. There is currently no cure. Patients make significant sacrifices to participate in research, but differences in the way individuals progress and difficulty monitoring disease are two reasons for the failure of over 50 clinical trials in ALS. Our objective is to use smart watches to monitor the way patients move and develop a more accurate measure of disease progression that can optimize clinical trials. We will collect data in patients across Canada over a 12-month period. We will use machine learning to identify unique features in each patient and train algorithms to accurately predict disease progression in real time. This technology would allow patients to participate in clinical research without frequent in-person visits, while improving the quality of clinical trial data. Our objective is to develop a new precise and cost-effective digital biomarker of ALS disease progression for use in future clinical trials and clinical practice.

column36: Exploring the role of Striated-muscle Preferentially Expressed Kinase (SPEG) in Zebrafish
column37: Centronuclear myopathies (CNM) are a group of congenital neuromuscular disorders characterized by hypotonia and diffuse muscle weakness. The pathobiology of these disorders has been linked to mutations in genes encoding proteins essential for excitation-contraction coupling (ECC) in muscle. Striated muscle Preferentially Expressed Kinase (SPEG) is the most recent gene found to be mutated in CNM. SPEG has two Ser/Thr kinase domains, and several immunoglobin (Ig) and Fibronectin (Fb) repeats, and has been found to co-localize with proteins critical for ECC. While the implication is that SPEG is somehow required for formation and/or function of the ECC machinery, its actual function in this process is unknown, and its role in muscle development not yet established. Zebrafish is an emerging model organism for the study muscle development and disease. Our lab has generated a speg knockout zebrafish model to better under-stand SPEG's role in skeletal muscle. This model was found to recapitulate phenotypes observed in mouse models and human patients, including loss of speg expression, structural defects in the triad (the location of the ECC machinery), altered calcium dynamics, reduced survival and impaired swimming performance. My project will utilize this model to investigate SPEG's function as a protein kinase, in hopes of understanding its role ECC. Through a multi modal approach including liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectroscopy, we will elucidate SPEG's kinase substrates. Moreover, we will validate these targets in the con-text of kinase-dead speg zebrafish in order to define the role of Speg's two kinase domains. By defining SPEG's kinase activity, we will gain critical insight(s) into its roles in ECC and muscle development.

column36: Effects of Age-Related Macrophage Dysfunctions on Atherosclerosis Regression
column37: Atherosclerosis is a disease characterised by the build-up of plaque in blood vessels. These plaques, comprised of cholesterol, fibrous material, and cells of muscle and immune origin, arise in conditions of high blood cholesterol, where cholesterol can deposit in the lining of blood vessels. While patrolling the circulation, immune cells known as monocytes recognise and migrate to the deposit site. Once there, these cells become macrophages that start ""eating up"" the lipids and produce inflammatory factors. Additional monocytes can recognise these inflammatory markers and migrate to the developing plaque. Increased lipid deposition, immune cell recruitment and inflammation mediate atherosclerosis progression, defined as the growth in the size of atherosclerotic plaques. Conversely, through a mechanism known as reverse cholesterol transport, these macrophages can process the deposited lipids and unload excess cholesterol. The excess cholesterol is then brought to the liver or intestines for excretion in the bile and feces. These events contribute to atherosclerosis regression, defined as the reduction in size of the atherosclerotic plaques. Interestingly, aging has been identified as the strongest risk factor for atherosclerosis. This is likely the result of a myriad of age-related conditions that promote atherosclerosis development, including increased base levels of inflammation, metabolic dysregulation, and immune cell dysfunctions, to name a few. Here, we seek to understand how age-related dysfunctions in macrophages affect the regression of atherosclerosis. This research aims to bring forth new knowledge that could be leveraged into novel therapeutics for atherosclerotic disease, which remains the leading cause of death worldwide.

column37: Periodontitis is the second most prevalent disease in Canada. column36: Les effets du stress chronique sur la sante neurovasculaire et les implications pour la depression post-accident vasculaire cerebral
column37: Selon l'Organisation mondiale de la sante, la depression est la premiere cause d'incapacite dans le monde. Parallelement, 33% des individus ayant souffert d'un accident vasculaire cerebral (AVC) developpent une depression dans les cinq annees suivant l'accident. Ce pourcentage tres eleve suggere que les AVC contribuent au developpement de la depression. Un AVC est un evenement dans lequel le tissu cerebral meurt en raison d'une perte d'apport en sang par une obstruction ou une rupture d'un vaisseau sanguin cerebral. Les mecanismes impliques dans le developpement de la depression a la suite d'un AVC sont peu connus. Il est actuellement accepte que des elements psychosociaux et des elements biologiques y contribuent. Ainsi, les incapacites causees par l'AVC et le dommage cerebral en lui-m eme contribueraient au developpement de cette maladie. Le present projet de recherche propose d'etudier le dommage d'une region cerebrale precise : le noyau accumbens, qui est implique dans la gestion des emotions. Sur un modele animal de souris, il sera etabli si un AVC du noyau accumbens est suffisant pour engendrer des symptomes depressifs. Les cerveaux seront ensuite collectes et le dommage cerebral sera etudie. Specifiquement, les alterations de la barriere hemato-encephalique (BHE) seront evaluees au niveau anatomique, cellulaire et moleculaire, puisqu'il a ete decouvert par notre laboratoire qu'une perte d'integrite de cette barriere peut mener a des symptomes depressifs chez les souris dans un contexte de stress chronique. La BHE est la barriere entre le sang et le cerveau protegeant celui-ci. Une perte d'integrite de la BHE due a un AVC dans une region centrale de regulation des emotions pourrait faire partie des mecanismes biologiques menant a la depression post-AVC.

column36: Effects of Social Skills Group Interventions on the Emotional Wellbeing of Youth with Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Feeling accepted by others is an important source of socio-emotional health, especially during adolescence. This benefit extends to youth with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), yet social difficulties – a core diagnostic component of ASD – can make it difficult to form and maintain social interactions and relationships. Targeting social skills deficits is an increasingly common intervention for youth with ASD, typically delivered in a group setting. While studies show some evidence of efficacy of group social skills programs to improve social competence for adolescents with ASD, the results are inconsistent, and there is little information regarding generalizability of the knowledge gained into real life benefits such as feeling accepted by others and forming meaningful relationships. Importantly, the effect on emotional wellbeing, or how youths ""feel"" about themselves, is largely unknown. The uncertainty about how the self-perception of youth with ASD may shift upon completing a social skills program is particularly important as they navigate the mostly neurotypical social landscape with greater awareness of their differences. Taking lessons learned from adult self-advocates with ASD who voice harmful effects of interventions that aim to 'normalize' their behaviour, and who call to celebrate autistic pride, it is imperative that therapeutic approaches such as social skills training are health-promoting. This is particularly salient given the prevalent mental health comorbidities in this group. This study will examine the effects of group social skills programs on the emotional well-being of youth with ASD who engage in this commonly used intervention.

column36: Density of hydraulic fracturing wells and concentrations of trace elements in urine, hair, nail and drinking water samples from pregnant women living in Northeastern British Columbia
column37: Abstract: Exposure to toxic contaminants (i.e. pollutants) in the population is a major concern in public health, especially for the pregnant woman and the developing fetus. Northeastern British Columbia, and more precisely, the Peace River Valley, is an area of unconventional natural gas exploitation by hydraulic fracturing which can release contaminants that can have potential deleterious health effects on fetal development. To date, there is limited data on exposure of pregnant women to contaminants associated with hydraulic fracturing. My project aims to evaluate exposure among pregnant women to trace elements (e.g. lead, arsenic, manganese) and their association with density of hydraulic fracturing wells in Northeastern British Columbia. As part of the EXPERIVA study, hair, nails, urine and drinking water samples have been collected from 85 pregnant women from this region in 2019. The concentrations of trace elements measured in these samples will allow statistical analyses to be carried out to 1) compare concentrations with those measured in the general population; 2) assess the correlation between the levels measured across hair, urine, nail and drinking water samples; and 3) evaluate the association between the density of hydraulic fracturing wells and trace element concentrations. The results of my project will provide a portrait of gestational exposure to trace elements in this region and will allow determining if the density of hydraulic fracturing wells influences exposure levels. Such results will help regulatory bodies assessing the health risks associated with gas extraction by hydraulic fracturing.

column36: A comparative analysis of the ethical weight assigned to individual rights and collective good in the context of the COVID-19 response by socialist and democratic nations
column37: The field of global health and its work is generally conceived of in terms of a human rights framework, rooted in the United Nations 1948 Declaration of Human Rights. Few dispute the human rights framework's strong commitment to individual rights; however, individual rights are sometimes defended at the expense of a collective right to public health. In the current context of the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries are facing challenging decisions with regards to the balance between individual freedom and public health. Countries are each approaching the pandemic differently, responding to the individual rights and collective good calculus in varying ways. I seek to understand the relationship between a political context and the weight given to individual rights and collective good – and how that weighing shapes and is shaped by public health crises. To understand this relationship, I propose to study the response to and outcomes of the COVID-19 pandemic in the socialist (collective-minded) context of Cuba and the democratic liberal (individual-minded) context of Canada. A qualitative content analysis of news sources in Canada and Cuba will be conducted to identify the countries' relative weighing of individual rights and collective good during a public health crisis. The outcomes of this analysis will be used to answer the research question: how do the respective political structures of Cuba and Canada, specifically the ethical weight of individual rights and collective good, affect their responses to COVID-19 and public health outcomes? This work will contribute both to the ongoing conversations on the COVID-19 response, as well as the broader conversations on how the work of global health orientates itself to the balancing of individual and collective good.

column36: Perfusion Recellularization of Rat Hindlimb for Vascular Composite Allotransplantation
column37: Patients with severe limb trauma and soft tissue loss require reconstruction. Vascular composite allotransplantation (VCA) allows multiple tissue types to be surgically transplanted to restore limb form and function. VCA requires immunosuppression therapy to suppress adverse immune reactions from transplants which pose several health risks. Decellularization and recellularization of these transplants are emerging techniques for VCA where immune reaction inducing content is removed from grafts while their structure is preserved. Grafts are repopulated with tissue-specific cells to restore function. Repopulating with relevant cell types and regenerating transplant grafts to functionality are current challenges in recellularization. In this study, we hypothesize that recellularization of a decellularized rat hindlimb graft with tissue-specific cells and maturation in a bioreactor will form a regenerated bio-artificial rat hindlimb. The bioreactor will be specifically adjusted for its design to accommodate the rat hindlimb. Due to their preservation of native endothelial cell features, human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) will be used with primary rat myoblasts (for skeletal muscle development) and primary rat fibroblasts (for cellular structure development) during recellularization. Native, decellularized and recellularized grafts will be comparatively evaluated for structural and muscle integrity using histological and fluorescence staining. Recellularized grafts will be assessed for live and dead cells, and for regenerated muscle functionality using an isometric force measurement test. Altogether, this initial proof-of-concept study will act as a first step towards regeneration of a functional bioartificial hindlimb using de- and recellularization.

column36: Participatory Arts as Social Determinants of Mental Health in Pandemic-Era University Populations
column37: Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, mental health issues among university students are on the rise - resulting in an urgent need for research and creative solutions in this area. My research will assess how arts-based participatory action research (PAR) workshops can: 1) improve mental health outcomes and provide self-care strategies for university students; 2) create 'safer spaces' for neuro-diverse students to respond to mental health issues through collaborative discussion and art-making; and 3) inform and disrupt the societal stigma around mental health issues. Students will develop a foundational understanding of critical disabilities studies and mad studies through the lens of intersectionality - disciplines that move away from bio-medical models emphasizing individual pathology, to look at the greater socio-political context as a determinant of mental health and well-being. My series of arts-based workshops will involve a group of 8-10 university students and will provide creative outlets for self-expression, personal narrative, and identity-building, culminating in an online exhibition. The workshops will also foster participant awareness of accessibility, equity, inclusion and diversity, and help to develop resilience, creative coping strategies, and a sense of community during this stressful and isolating time. My research will evaluate the use of participatory arts as a social determinant of positive mental health and well-being outcomes, serve as groundwork for further research and therapeutic solutions, and help establish a complementary model to traditional bio-medical approaches. Finally, it will address the systemic deficit in awareness concerning mental health issues and take meaningful steps toward changing societal misperceptions about mental disability.

column36: Investigating the impact of arginine metabolism on Salmonella virulence
column37: Globally, we are seeing a rise in bacterial infections that cannot be treated with conventional antibiotics. These bacteria have developed resistance mechanisms that allow them to evade antibiotic killing. One major cause of antibiotic-resistant infections is the intestinal pathogen Salmonella, which is able to survive inside human immune cells and infect the entire body. Within these cells, Salmonella produces a protein called SsrB. This protein helps Salmonella replicate by controlling genes that protect it from immune-based killing. In our lab, we have determined that SsrB controls arginine production in Salmonella by reducing the expression of arginine-producing genes. Arginine is an amino acid that can be used by immune cells to protect against bacterial infections, but it can also be used by bacteria for survival; in this way, it is a double-edged sword. We hypothesize that instead of producing its own arginine, Salmonella takes arginine away from the infected immune cells in order to protect itself. In this project, we will research how SsrB reduces arginine production during infection, and if this helps protect Salmonella from immune-based killing. This research will provide valuable insight into how Salmonella resists killing by immune cells, which may be used for the discovery of antibiotic alternatives.

column36: Exploring the diagnostic journey of individuals and families with mitochondrial disease
column37: Mitochondrial diseases are a complex group of inherited metabolic disorders that affect 1 in 5000 people. Diagnosis of mitochondrial disease (MID) is complicated and typically involves visits with various specialists, undergoing many tests, and often being misdiagnosed. As a result, individuals and families navigating this diagnostic journey experience psychological, emotional, and social difficulties. However, no previous research has used in-depth interviews to understand this underserved patient population's specific needs. Therefore, this study seeks to (1) explore the experiences of patients with a known MID diagnosis, (2) determine factors that positively and negatively impact the diagnostic experience, and (3) develop recommendations for healthcare providers providing care for MID patients. Participants will be recruited in partnership with the Pediatric Neurology Clinic at the Winnipeg Children's Hospital and the Shared Health Program of Genetics & Metabolism in Winnipeg. Individuals with a confirmed MID diagnosis or parents of a child with a confirmed MID diagnosis will be invited to participate in this study. Interviews will be completed with participants to explore their experiences of receiving a MID diagnosis and factors that influenced this experience. These factors could include the type of diagnosis, connection to support groups, and encounters with healthcare providers like genetic counsellors. Interviews will then be transcribed, coded, and analyzed for emerging themes. This research will lead to participant-driven recommendations that we hope will be shared with MID support organizations and healthcare providers to improve the care of MID patients in Manitoba and across Canada.

column36: A new generation of GAL-9-specific inhibitors.
column37: Given the critical role of galectins in many diseases and their immunosuppressive functions that antagonize the success of cancer immunotherapy, considerable efforts have been directed towards the development of galectin inhibitors. Building on our recent success with GAL-7, the general objective of our research program is to develop a novel galectin inhibitor for the treatment of triple-negative breast cancer, a very aggressive form of cancer for which there are few effective treatments. Alyssa's project will focus on GAL-9, a galectin expressed by cancer cells that plays a central in the development of the anti-tumoral immune response. She will develop, generate and characterize GAL-9-specific recombinant camelid antibodies (nanobodies, Nbs). More specifically, she will (1) generate Nbs against GAL-9; and (2) identify lead Nbs with neutralizing potential. Galectin-specific Nbs will be obtained following in vitro screening of a non-immune recombinant antibody synthetic library. The selection of our lead GAL-9-specific Nbs will be carried out by prioritizing those that can inhibit GAL-9-mediated immunosuppressive functions and have the best pharmacological properties, including high affinity for GAL-9, high selectivity, and stability. These Nbs will then be fused to a human Fc framework for therapeutical purposes. Therapeutically, we can envisage that GAL-9-specific Nbs can be utilized as neutralizing agents, as receptor-ligand antagonists and as vehicles for effector delivery or targeted vehicle-based drug therapy. Overall, this project will allow Miss Dumoulin to acquire cutting-edge expertise in the field of immunotherapy, which represents a radical paradigm shift in oncology for the management of patients with aggressive subtypes of breast cancer.

column36: The effect of a 12-week home-based exercise program on muscle-mass, strength and quality of life in children with sarcopenia who have undergone liver transplantation.
column37: We have recently identified that children with end-stage liver disease (ESLD) have sarcopenia (reduced muscle mass) pre-and-post liver transplantation (LTx) and that this is associated with adverse pre and post-operative outcomes (e.g. increased infection risk, delayed growth and gross motor skill development, longer length of stay/re-hospitalization). We have shown that sarcopenia lasts up to 8-10 years post LTx and that reduced muscle strength, along with reductions in lean body mass, directly influence physical performance and participation in daily physical activity in children post-LTx. All of this can severely impact the health-related quality (HRQOL) of life for a child living with liver disease. Hence, development of effective rehabilitation strategies for the treatment of sarcopenia in children with liver disease is important because the potential for adverse long-term outcomes into adulthood related to sarcopenia is high. The goal of this project is to develop an effective treatment for this condition and to understand the underlying physiological determinants of sarcopenia in children with ESLD. This study aims to develop a 12-week, home-based, exercise program comprised of progressive resistance training using video-based technology. This is especially important during the COVID-19 pandemic, as virtual technology provides access for Canadians living in remote areas where rehabilitation services may be limited. We aim to study whether this home-based exercise program results in improvements in muscle mass, muscle strength and overall ability to participate in routine physical activity resulting in significant improvements in HRQOL. Results from study findings have direct translation effects to disease progression from childhood into early adulthood.

column36: Altered emotional regulation in chronic primary insomnia: Neural correlates and responses to cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia
column37: Chronic insomnia is a sleep disorder that is defined as difficulty falling or staying asleep for at least 3 months. Some individuals with insomnia may also have trouble regulating their emotions, especially in response to sleep-related stimuli. They may experience intense emotions toward these stimuli, which can persist for a while before returning to baseline. Cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBTi) – the gold standard treatment for chronic insomnia – includes strategies to alter maladaptive thoughts or actions that can negatively affect sleep, and techniques to improve sleep. But, some patients still experience sleep problems or associated issues after receiving the therapy. Researchers have used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure how active the amygdala – a brain region involved in emotion processing – is in response to sleep-related stimuli. They found that patients with insomnia had greater amygdala activity while viewing negative images related to insomnia compared to good sleepers. But, not much is known about the effectiveness of CBTi for emotion regulation among patients with insomnia. Thus, this project seeks to examine brain responses, using fMRI, of adults with insomnia and good sleepers while they perform an emotion task. We will examine the impact that CBTi has on how these patients regulate their emotions by assessing subjective ratings and brain responses. We will examine if brain activity while rating how much the sleep-related images elicits a negative emotion, prior to receiving CBTi, can allow us to predict whether or not they will respond to CBTi. Overall, we hope that this research will help us better understand if CBTi is helpful for patients to regulate their emotions when they encounter sleep-related stimuli.

column36: Pseudomonas intracellular niche in chronic rhinosinusitis
column37: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is an inflammatory condition of the nasal and sinus mucosa lasting 12 weeks or longer despite medical treatment. Rhinosinusitis affects about 1 in 8 adults in the United States and is associated with significant socioeconomic costs, loss of productivity, and impaired quality of life. The gram-negative bacteria Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P.a.) is known for being hard to treat and often antibiotic-resistant. Studies have noted a shift toward gram-negative organisms in patients who have been repeatedly treated with antibiotics or have undergone sinus surgery. The objective of our research is to learn more about P.a.'s behaviour in CRS. We hypothesize that, like in some case reports in bronchial epithelial cells, P.a. could be present intracellularly in the sinuses' epithelial cells of infected patients suffering from CRS. This finding could shine some light towards future research surrounding P.a.'s treatment in CRS. The approach we will be using is collecting sinus tissue and mucus swabs from P.a.-infected CRS patients and control patients (skull-base and CRS) during their surgery. The goal is to use mass spectrometry to identify which bacteria is found in the patients' sinuses and to use immunofluorescence to try to identify intracellular P.a.. We will also collect clinical data in the patient's files, including but not restricted to cortisone usage, previous antibiotic courses, previous sinus surgeries, and sinuses computed tomography scores. The research plan includes a written research protocol and ethic's board review, a systematic literature review, the patient's recruitment, preliminary experiments, method refinement, updated experiments, and validation and analysis.

column36: Health care networks for children with inherited metabolic diseases: a mixed methods study of family perceptions of relational continuity and care coordination
column37: Background: Delivery of high-quality family-centred care for children with IMD is challenging. To inform the development of interventions tailored to the needs of children with IMD, we first need to better understand current health care needs and gaps in care specific to this population. Objectives: To describe, for children with IMD and their families: (i) child and family well-being and home health care needs; (ii) children's networks of care providers and services; and (iii) families' perceptions about relational continuity with key providers and care coordination. Methods: A 4-month prospective cohort study is currently underway. Participants are parents or guardians of children 12 years of age with IMD, enrolled from one of 10 participating Canadian centres; the target sample size is 100. During follow-up, respondents report on their child's health care experiences using real-time quantitative surveys, free-text narratives, and interviews. My thesis will encompass the analysis of the baseline survey and care map data using a mixed methods explanatory sequential design. I will analyze the survey data descriptively. I will analyze the care maps using social network analysis to describe the numbers and types of children's care providers and relationships among providers. I will analyze the qualitative data (the narrative baseline data and a subset of the prospective interview data) thematically to gain further insight into families' perceptions and experiences. Contributions: This thesis project will yield a rigorous and thorough summary of the care networks of children with IMD, emphasizing parental perceptions of relational continuity and care coordination, which will contribute to a better understanding of gaps in family-centred care for this population.

column36: Relation of honey and its constituent rare sugars on cardiometabolic health - epidemiological and compositional analysis
column37: Rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes in Canada are rising and excess intake of sugars has become an area of intense concern. While honey is categorized as a free sugar by the World Health Organization, it has a complex composition of proteins, organic acids, and bioactive compounds, providing benefits to glycemic responses, lipid levels, and weight loss. Honey is also host to numerous rare sugars which, with subtle differences in their chemical structure compared to traditional sugars, have shown benefit to glycemic responses and cardiometabolic outcomes in human trials. As such, both honey and its constituent rare sugars offer potential benefits as alternative sweeteners. Currently, however, guidelines offer no distinction between consumption of traditional sugars and honey or rare sugars. My research will be completed in three parts. The first part will consist of a systematic review and meta-analysis (SRMA) on the effect of longer-term oral honey intake on lipid levels, glycemic outcomes, inflammatory markers, and adiposity markers. The second part will consist of a SRMA on the effect of acute and longer-term rare sugar intake on glycemic outcomes. Part 3 will consist of a compositional analysis of four honey varieties to determine its nutrient composition, its bioactive compounds and their potential health effects. The sum of these projects will synthesize the literature on honey, rare sugars, and their cardiometabolic effects while examining the possible bioactive compounds that contribute to these benefits seen. This research can be used to determine guidelines for the use of honey and rare sugars as alternative sweeteners.

column36: Perturbations to exercise hemodynamics and outcomes in patients with chronic thromboembolic disease
column37: Our study is a retrospective hemodynamic cohort study of patients in our CTEPH/D program who underwent right heart catheterization (RHC) with exercise. We have two broad objectives in our study. The first objective is to conduct a detailed analysis of the integrated exercise physiology in this cohort with a focus on resistive and pulsatile measures of RV afterload. Currently, in the clinical setting, the leading measures of RV afterload employed in the evaluation of CTEPH/D are mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) measures by RHC at rest. However, patients are not typically symptomatic at rest and provocation such as exercise is thought to be required to fully reveal abnormalities of the RV afterload. Moreover, relying only on mPAP and PVR provides an incomplete assessment of RV afterload. The specific goals of this objective are to (1) examine the relationship between pulmonary resistance and compliance at rest and during exercise, (2) conduct a beat-by-beat analysis of pulmonary waveform morphology, and (3) evaluate the relationship of these physiologic measures to anatomic disease burden as measured by quantitative V/Q scanning and to exertional limitation as measured by 6-minute walk distance. We hypothesize that exercise-associated impairment of pulmonary compliance (or pulsatile load) will be directly related to evidence of anatomic disease burden and 6-minute walk distance. The second broad objective is to examine the relationship between physiologic endpoints measured from the first objective and clinical improvement after pulmonary endarterectomy surgery.
