column36: Navigation par resonance magnetique de particules ferromagnetiques porteuses de chimiotherapie pour traiter le cancer du foie: optimisation in-vitro et guidage au niveau lobaire dans le porc
column37: Les tumeurs du foie sont la troisieme cause de deces par cancer au monde. Les tumeurs non resecables sont traitees par injection de chimiotherapie et de petites particules dans l'artere de la tumeur. Cette therapie bloque l'artere pour priver la tumeur d'oxygene et de nutriments et tuer les cellules cancereuses avec la chimiotherapie. Un mince tube appele << catheter >> est introduit dans une artere de l'aine ou du poignet, puis dirige sous rayons X a l'artere de la tumeur dans le foie. Parfois, la visualisation imparfaite par rayons X mene a des injections mal-ciblees qui detruisent du foie sain. Ce traitement invasif necessite plusieurs seances et expose le patient et le personnel a beaucoup de rayons X. Pour eviter l'irradiation du patient et les seances invasives repetees, nous proposons de guider des particules metalliques porteuses de chimiotherapie a travers le sang avec la force magnetique d'un appareil IRM. Nous guiderons les particules a partir d'un catheter dans l'artere principale du foie jusqu'aux tumeurs. Cette technologie s'appelle navigation par resonance magnetique (NRM). Dans ce projet, nous allons utiliser des images d'arteres de porcs pour fabriquer des maquettes realistes avec une imprimante 3D et y faire circuler du fluide. Avec ces maquettes nous allons tester le guidage de particules par NRM. Par la suite, nous guiderons des particules dans les arteres de 12 porcs. Nous visons de guider precisement vers un des deux lobes du foie sans que les particules aillent dans le lobe non-cible. Ces resultats augmenteront la precision de notre technique. Dans peu de temps, ces experiences produiront des traitements de pointe. Cette technologie pourrait augmenter la duree et la qualite de vie des patients, diminuer les coûts et augmenter l'acces au traitement.

column36: Investigating the role of Eosinophils in the Thymus during Neonatal Development
column37: Eosinophils are a type of immune cell present in the body of mice and humans. Under normal, healthy conditions they are present in many organs and tissues but their role is unknown. The thymus is an organ in the body where critical immune cells called T cells develop. Eosinophils have been found in the thymus and their numbers increase at developmental stages of mice and humans. I hypothesize, that eosinophils are important in guiding normal development of T cells which in turn, aides normal immune system functioning. I will be investigating this question by dividing it into three parts: 1. To determine what is causing the increase of eosinophils in the thymus of developing mice. Proteins can send messages to cells and attract them to different tissues. I will identify which proteins are causing eosinophils to increase in numbers in the thymus. 2. To uncover which proteins eosinophils are producing in the thymus of developing mice. Eosinophils have the ability to produce protein which might influence the development of T cells. My goal is to determine which proteins eosinophils are producing in the thymus. 3. To find out specifically, where eosinophils are located within the thymus of developing mice. It is our intention to identify which part of the thymus the eosinophils are located in. This will help us determine which other cells eosinophils are interacting and communicating with, such as T cells. Mice are ideal animals to use to model the human immune system, because they have similar immune cells and proteins. With these three aims we expect to gain insight as to how immune systems should function normally and draw conclusions as to why sometimes these processes fail. Failure of T cell development can lead to diseases such as autoimmune disorders.

column36: Pathophysiology and Preclinical Endpoints of Retinopathy in a Murine Model of Zellweger Spectrum Disorder
column37: Peroxisomes are ubiquitous sub-cellular structures and are required for many vital metabolic processes. Zellweger Spectrum Disorder (ZSD) is a genetic disease in which peroxisome formation and function is impaired. ZSD patients suffer from progressive retinopathy leading to vision loss, impacting their quality of life. Our laboratory developed a mouse model with a genetic mutation in the PEX1 gene, equivalent to the most common ZSD-causing mutation in humans. Despite having dramatically reduced retinal function and visual acuity, retinal cell structure is relatively well preserved in these mice. This suggests that peroxisome dysfunction affects retinal cell function more than structure, but the mechanism(s) for this remain(s) unknown. I aim to study the pathophysiology of ZSD using our mouse model to define the mechanism by which peroxisome dysfunction leads to retinopathy. I hypothesize that by assessing the retina electrophysiological and histological response to various functional challenges, I can elucidate how PEX1 deficiency disrupts retinal function. The experiments I will complete have never been performed on any peroxisome deficient animal model, and will provide a more in-depth understanding of the role of peroxisomes in retinal health. This work will define which cell types and retinal processes are most affected by peroxisome dysfunction, thereby identifying therapeutic targets for ZSD and other peroxisome-mediated vision loss. Currently, our lab is developing gene and drug-based therapies to improve vision in ZSD. My studies will complement these efforts by ensuring the correct cell types are targeted, and identifying additional electrophysiological outcome measures to assess functional retinal improvement in response to therapy.

column36: Investigating Intratumoral Modulation Therapy as a Novel Treatment Modality for Brain Metastases
column37: Brain metastases, also known as secondary brain tumours, most commonly arise from lung and breast cancer and are 10 times more common than primary brain tumours, occurring in 10 to 30 percent of cancer patients. With the median survival being 3 to 6 months despite treatment, new therapeutic approaches are needed to tackle these deadly tumours. Cancer cells are innately vulnerable to low-intensity electric fields, whereas healthy brain cells are unaffected. Our research group is focused on developing Intratumoral Modulation Therapy (IMT), a promising new treatment that uses bioelectrodes to deliver electric fields directly to brain tumours to slow growth, promote cell death, and increase sensitivity to other treatments such as chemotherapy. These effects of IMT have been observed when treating glioblastoma, a primary brain tumour, that has been grown in culture dishes and in rodent brains. However, the impact of this therapy on brain metastases has not yet been investigated. This study will test the effects of IMT alone and in combination with chemotherapy and radiation on metastatic cancer cells grown in cell culture dishes. The cells will be obtained from patient brain tumour specimens of lung and breast origin. We predict that metastatic tumour cells will be sensitive to IMT as evidenced by less expansion and more cell death compared to untreated populations and that there will be an additive effect when combined with chemotherapy or radiation. Several implantable neuromodulation systems used for non-cancerous conditions have proven to be safe and provide support for potential clinical use of IMT. The results of this project will yield key information needed to advance the development of IMT towards clinical application for metastatic central nervous system disease.

column36: Study of the olfactory system in the preclinical stage of Alzheimer's disease (AD)
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis is only made very late, at the stage of dementia, where cognitive disorders resonate in the activities of daily living. Faced with this situation, the category of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) has been introduced to characterize people at risk of developing AD. Even further upstream, Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD) is characterized by the presence of non-objectified cognitive complaints. However, although SCD constitutes a sensitive marker for the development of AD, it is not very specific. In order to use it as an early marker of AD, one could combine it with smell tests. Indeed, altered olfactory abilities have been demonstrated in MCI and more recently in SCD. A few recent studies report abnormal brain activity patterns in patients with AD using olfactory evoked potentials (OEP). Thus, this project aims to assess the olfactory functions of individuals with an SCD and to compare them with those of a control group using behavioral and electrophysiological measures. We hypothesize that (1) individuals with SCD have lower behavioral olfactory scores than controls; (2) individuals with SCD have longer OEP latencies and smaller OEP amplitudes than controls; (3) behavioral olfactory tests scores and OEP latencies/amplitudes are correlated. To test these hypotheses, 80 individuals with SCD and 80 control participants matched by gender and age will be recruited and invited to the laboratory for evaluation. We will test olfaction (1) by behavioral and (2) electrophysiological measurements. Other measures assessing cognition will complement this assessment. This research will allow the development of new tools for early detection of AD and will help to initiate rapid action before the onset of cognitive symptoms.

column36: Caracterisation de la physiologie du systeme moteur primaire en phase aigu en lien avec les forces biomecaniques suite a un match de football
column37: Au Canada comme aux etats-Unis, les commotions cerebrales liees a la pratique sportive representent un probleme majeur de sante publique. Considerant les limites importantes decoulant des decisions medicales basees sur des informations majoritairement auto-rapportees, le recours a des mesures objectives est fondamental afin de mieux cerner les sequelles associees a ces blessures et d'assurer un retour au jeu securitaire. Des etudes suggerent que l'analyse du profil biomecanique des coups a la t ete survenus durant un match peut predire la severite des sequelles. De plus, d'autres etudes demontrent que la stimulation magnetique transcranienne (SMT) s'avere un outil utile permettant d'objectiver des perturbations neurophysiologiques des neurones stimules causees par une commotion cerebrale ainsi que par des chocs sous-commotionnels repetes. Pertinemment, ces perturbations ont ete associees a des symptomes cliniques persistants, dont un ralentissement d'execution motrice et des perturbations de l'equilibre. L'objectif principal de cette etude est de caracteriser les modifications neurophysiologiques, fonctionnelles et cliniques engendrees par les forces cinematiques impliquees lors du cumul de coups a la t ete au cours d'un match chez des joueurs de football universitaire. Cette etude vise aussi a investiguer si le delai d'une semaine entre deux matchs de football est suffisant afin de permettre un retour a la normale des mesures neurophysiologiques, fonctionnelles et cliniques. Ce projet de recherche pourrait permettre d'ameliorer la prise de decisions quant au retrait du jeu d'un joueur en se basant sur des donnees objectives refletant le risque d'alterations du cerveau, plutot que sur des symptomes subjectifs, auto-rapportes par l'athlete.

column36: Investigating the effect of the microbiome on Alzheimer's Disease
column37: The aim of this project will be to study the impact of bioactive ginger extract (GE) on the GI flora and on an Alzheimer's lined microbiome using a computer controlled human dynamic gastrointestinal model. Recent studies have emphasized the benefits of the components of ginger for treating Alzheimer's disease, however, limited information is available on the possible mechanism through which it renders anti-Alzheimer's activity. Data confirms that systemic inflammation triggered by GI tract bacteria plays a pivotal role in Alzheimer's and other neurological disorders. However, the impact of ginger extract (GE) on GI bacterial flora and Alzheimer's is yet to be established which is goal of this project. The compositions of the gut microbiota have an important role in human health and are known to be disturbed in various diseases such as neurological disorders through gut brain axis and have a direct impact in colon cancer, IBD, IBS, and other diseases. I plan to investigate the GE formulation's effect on the composition of the microbiota using a computer-controlled simulation of a gastrointestinal model. The GI model consists of a series of bioreactors: the stomach, the small intestine, the ascending colon, the transverse colon and the descending colon. Human fecal slurries containing the contents of the gut microbiota are inoculated into the colon sections and the whole system is maintained at 37°C in an anaerobic state using nitrogen gas flushing. I expect that the most-active GE fraction will affect GI inflammation-causing bacterial cells. The part of the gastrointestinal system in which GE extract phytochemicals get metabolized will be identified which will be very useful in designing GE extract based prostate chemotherapy, and dietary health benefit formulations.

column36: Impact of cultural influences on health: An exploration of maternal food taboos in Cambodia
column37: Food taboos are defined as avoidances that go beyond personal taste or preference. They are prevalent in many cultures throughout pregnancy and lactation, yet they may put the mother and baby at risk of nutritional inadequacy. The purpose of this study will be to characterise the food taboos of pregnant and lactating women in Cambodia and to evaluate their potential nutritional and health impacts. We believe that dietary restrictions stemming from food taboos contribute to poor energy, protein, and micronutrient intake in women, and as such taboos are a contributing factor to poor health status amongst women and children. The proposed research project is a mixed-method, secondary analysis of data collected in the central Cambodian province of Kampong Thom between September 2018 and May 2019. Interviewer-administered questionnaires were used to gather open-ended data on the dietary practices of 320 women at 2, 12, and 24 weeks postnatal. Open, thematic coding using MAXQDA software will be employed to analyze food taboos in pregnancy and lactation. This will be complemented by demographic and socioeconomic data to evaluate potential differences in adherence to various food taboos. The nutritional value of each identified food be assessed via SQL software, and compared to the nutritional requirements of this life stage and deficiencies known to be prevalent in Cambodia. Dissemination of the results of this study will use a community-based participatory research approach to draw on the expertise of local stakeholders, ensuring that the information reaching the wider community is adapted for their needs. The findings of this study will also serve health professionals in Canada by enhancing their knowledge of cultural influences on the nutritional practices of the population.

column36: Functional characterization of METTL7B, a biomarker in KMT2A-MLLT3 translocated acute myeloid leukemia
column37: METTL7B (a putative methyltransferase) has been found to be highly expressed in AML cells with the KMT2A-MLLT3 gene fusion (KM3 known hereafter) but not expressed in other blood cell types, and therefore represents a novel biomarker. The METTL7B protein remains uncharacterized and therefore it is unclear whether it has a functional role in the development of leukemia. Previous research in other cell types has suggested it may interact with mitochondria associated proteins or in pathways regulating cell proliferation. Our preliminary data suggest that METTL7B expression is essential for KM3-AML and that it may influence RNA processing. To further define its biological importance, we will: 1. Determine the intracellular localization METTL7B in HeLa cells (as a control), and then in KM3-AML cells by using an EGFP-tagged METTL7B and confocal fluorescence microscopy. 2. Identify METTL7B interacting proteins in HeLa cells (as a control), and then in KM3-AML cells by completing co-immunoprecipitation assays with EGFP-METT7B followed by LC-MS/MS analysis. 3. Perform modified RNA-seq studies to elucidate putative METTL7B methylation targets in leukemic cells. This will be followed by an analysis of the surrounding sequence of the methylation site to determine if METTL7B targets contain a specific recognition motif. Since METTL7B is a biomarker for KM3-AML, analysis of its targets and localization should identify the changes in cellular properties associated within the translocation. Therefore, from the results of the methods proposed, I should be able to determine the potential functions of METTL7B and its role in KM3-AML.

column36: NMDA receptor subunit GluN1 isoforms in dendritic spine structure and synaptic plasticity
column37: Learning and memory are thought to be supported by long-term changes in the strength of synaptic connections between neurons. The hippocampus is an important brain region for many forms of learning and memory. N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) play integral roles in mediating changes to synaptic strength in the hippocampus. This synaptic plasticity is dysfunctional in many neuropsychiatric disorders that manifest cognitive impairments, including Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder. There are many NMDAR subtypes with roles in synaptic plasticity that are largely unknown. It was recently found that expression of GluN1b-containing NMDARs was reduced in favour of GluN1a-containing NMDARs in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. Thus, we are interested in understanding the role of GluN1a- and GluN1b-NMDARs in synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. To address this, we generated mice expressing only GluN1a- or GluN1b-NMDARs. We found that compared to wild-type mice, synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory were enhanced in mice expressing GluN1a-NMDARs and impaired in mice expressing GluN1b-NMDARs. However, the mechanisms underlying these functional changes are unclear. I will investigate how GluN1a- and GluN1b-NMDARs affect 1) the structural changes at hippocampal synapses proposed to support long-term memory and 2) NMDAR diversity at hippocampal synapses, which has important functional consequences for plasticity processes. This proposed study will break new ground in understanding the role of NMDAR subtypes in learning and memory. Findings from this study will open the future possibility of using pharmacology to target specific NMDAR subtypes as a therapeutic intervention for neuropsychiatric disorders.

column36: Gene-Environment Interaction Underlying Childhood Aggression: The Effects of Monoamine Oxidase A Genotype and Methylation
column37: Childhood aggression is one of the leading causes of youth deaths world-wide and accounts for 200,000 homicides each year. There is strong evidence that both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the risk for aggressive behaviours. One of the genes that has been highly linked to childhood aggression is the monoamine oxidase A gene (MAOA). A region within the MAOA gene can exist in low and high repeats, and the number of repeats in this region can influence a child's predisposition to aggression. Meanwhile, environmental stressors can also affect childhood aggression through an environmentally sensitive mechanism known as epigenetics. Epigenetics can externally modify and alter the functionality of the MAOA gene by turning the gene on or off. Therefore, the MAOA gene may influence the levels of aggression with both the numbers of repeats as well as the epigenetic modifications it has. The aim of this research is to analyze how childhood aggression is influenced by the interaction between the number of repeats and epigenetic modifications of the MAOA gene. I will examine three diverse populations: 10,627 socioeconomically diverse children, 300 clinically aggressive children and 226 children who experienced developmental adversity. Analyzing two diverse datasets and a unique high aggression sample will provide an unparalleled opportunity to identify the genetic and environmental risk factors for aggression. Furthermore, understanding these risk factors may allow for the discovery of early detection, prevention and intervention strategies for youth violence. For example, these results could open up new avenues of exploration for novel and personalized medications for children with high aggression, significantly reducing youth violence rates.

column36: A population-based cohort study of outcomes in kidney transplant patients with emergency general surgery conditions
column37: Kidney transplantation is the most common solid organ transplant in Canadian adults and helps to improve and prolong life in many patients with severe kidney disease. Patients that have undergone kidney transplants are living longer because of modern improvements in treatment and surgery. As a result, they may be more likely to develop common surgical diseases that affect the general population. Emergency general surgery conditions, which typically involve inflammation of intra-abdominal organs such as the appendix or gall bladder, are thought to occur frequently and be especially dangerous in this group. Despite these concerns, there are few studies that examine this problem and most involve only a small number of patients. We will use existing large databases of transplant and non-transplant patients seen in the emergency department or admitted to hospital in Ontario to further investigate this problem. By doing so, we will determine if patients with a previous kidney transplant are more likely to die of these disorders. We will also investigate how often these patients suffer life-changing complications such as a heart attack or blood clot, how long they remain in hospital, what factors are associated with an increased risk of death, and how their treatment is different from those who have never had a kidney transplant. This study will examine a larger number of kidney transplant patients with these conditions than any other published work and will therefore provide us with valuable information on the outcomes and treatment of these life-threatening diseases. By gaining a greater understanding of these disorders within this population, we can plan methods for reducing their risk and improving their survival and quality of life in the future.

column36: Service Engagement in Early Psychosis Intervention Following the Transition to Virtual Care
column37: Repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic are expected to be particularly detrimental for youth with serious mental illness, especially persons with psychosis. Access to services is critical for this population, as early identification and treatment in the form of specialized early psychosis intervention (EPI) can significantly improve illness trajectories. The pandemic has disrupted service delivery, urging EPI programs to rapidly adopt models of virtual care; however, little is known of the quality or effectiveness of psychosis services delivered virtually. Historically, one-third of early psychosis patients dropout from services prematurely, though the effect of a transition to virtual care on disengagement is unknown. The present study aims to investigate factors associated with disengagement from a virtual model of EPI as compared to traditional, in-person services. To meet this objective, this project will leverage data collected on an evaluation of the implementation effectiveness of e-NAVIGATE, a structured, virtually-delivered EPI program at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, funded by CIHR, the Ontario Ministry of Health, and the University of Toronto. Routinely collected demographic, clinical and service use information will be extracted from electronic health records. Using prior data on in-person EPI, time to disengagement will be compared between the virtual and in-person models, examining factors that predict traditional service disengagement (namely, substance use and lack of family involvement), as well as additional health equity factors thought to impact the uptake of virtual care. Findings from this study may help to inform further development of virtual models, facilitating ongoing delivery of high-quality EPI during the pandemic and beyond.

column36: Targeting thymic stromal lymphopoietin - Novel anti-inflammatory compounds for the treatment and prevention of atopic diseases
column37: The most common inflammatory skin disease worldwide is atopic dermatitis (AD) and up to 17% of Canadians are affected during their lifetime. AD impairs the quality of life as patients suffer from very dry skin, as well as social stigmatism. Additionally, AD often results in development of further allergies such as food allergies, hay fever or allergic asthma. Thus, AD has a significant socioeconomic impact. Because AD is a highly complex, multifactorial disease, its underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. However, over the past years, the keratinocyte-derived cytokine thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) has been identified as a key player in skin inflammation and a trigger for the development of further allergies. Pharmaceutical companies have developed inhibitors of TSLP, such as tezepelumab, the most advanced drug showing promising results. However, tezepelumab is a protein that must be administered systemically and cannot be applied locally, for example as a cream. Drugs that can be applied locally offer several advantages such as reduced side effects, targeted drug delivery at the site of action, and higher acceptance rates among patients. Moreover, current treatment options for AD are subpar due to treatment-limiting side effects which prevents their continuous use. This interdisciplinary project aims to address both issues by developing blockers of TSLP that can be applied topically. To achieve this, we will first develop potent low molecular weight TSLP inhibitors. These will then be tested for efficacy and tolerability in 2D and 3D cell cultures. The most promising compounds will be tested in animal models of AD. The goal is to develop new topical treatment options for AD, and the prevention of the development of further allergic diseases such as asthma.

column36: Impact of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps and Low Density Neutrophils in Primary Graft Dysfunction following Human Lung Transplantation
column37: Neutrophils, which are the main immune cells in the blood, play a significant role in complications associated to human lung transplant. These cells, classified in two subtypes as high-density (HDNs) and low-density neutrophils (LDNs), can be activated by various factors both in donors and recipients. About 30% of lung recipients develop life-threatening complications due to dysregulation of their freshly transplanted lungs. Recently, neutrophils were found to produce web-like structures in blood, termed Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs), leading to the blockage of blood vessels and inflammation. Thus, we hypothesize that NETs, primarily produced by LDNs, are responsible of blood vessels blockage in grafted lungs, leading to severe pulmonary inflammation, dysfunction and subsequent recipient death. In order to explore the role of NETs and LDNs in complications following lung transplant, blood samples are taken from the donors and recipients prior, during and after surgery. With the blood samples, isolation of neutrophil subtypes followed by quantification of NETs and associated inflammatory mediators is done to follow the dynamics of NETs production and inflammation within the patients. When possible, we also sample lung tissue to be grafted for the visualization of NETs and vascular blockage. Our preliminary data are highly supportive of a major role of NETs in postoperative complications. The potential benefits of our research can be significant considering that a treatment exists to degrade NETs. This treatment (DNase I, also termed Pulmozyme) is already used for cystic fibrosis and could readily be available for lung transplant. In short term, we may have a life-saving and low-cost therapeutic approach to help a great number of heavily harmed lung recipients.

column36: Investigating the Impact of the Great Recession (2007-2009) on Socioeconomic Inequalities in Blood Pressure in Canada using Distributional Decomposition.
column37: The Great Recession of 2007 to 2009 led to widespread unemployment and financial losses for families. Since income is a crucial determinant of health, the crisis may have led to adverse health outcomes. However, despite the abundance of research on the health impacts of the Great Recession, few studies have been conducted in the Canadian context and there appear to be inconsistent conclusions across disciplines. This inconsistency may exist because most studies use extreme measures of health (e.g., hypertension) which do not capture less severe but more pervasive health impacts. These subtle albeit widespread impacts can be examined by studying a population's distribution of a health outcome, such as blood pressure. However, a distributional approach has been absent in population health literature due to longstanding methodological challenges, until now. My proposed master's thesis will use a novel method known as distributional decomposition (DD) to evaluate changes in the blood pressure distributions of Canadians pre- and post-recession. I will use DD to quantify how much variation in income contributed to variation in blood pressure between 2007 and 2010. Quantifying the impact of income on variations in blood pressure distributions pre- and post-recession can inform effective policymaking to mitigate widening socioeconomic and health inequalities in Canada. This research is pertinent to the current socioeconomic climate as COVID-19 may lead Canada into another recession. My study is the first to use a distributional approach to investigate the health impacts of the Great Recession and will enhance our understanding of how economic crises impact socioeconomic disparities in health.

column36: L'influence de l'alexithymie sur l'empathie et la theorie de l'esprit en autisme
column37: L'autisme est souvent associe a des difficultes d'empathie et de theorie de l'esprit. L'empathie refere a la capacite a comprendre et partager les emotions des autres alors que la theorie de l'esprit est la capacite a comprendre les pensees, les croyances et les emotions des autres. Puisque les definitions de l'empathie et de la theorie de l'esprit se chevauchent beaucoup, il serait interessant de mieux comprendre les relations entre ces deux construits. De plus, l'alexithymie, une condition caracterisee par, entre autres, des difficultes a identifier et a verbaliser ses propres emotions, aurait aussi un impact sur l'empathie et la theorie de l'esprit. Or, pres de la moitie des personnes autistes seraient alexithymiques, contre seulement 5% des personnes neurotypiques. Mon etude vise donc 1) a comparer l'empathie et la theorie de l'esprit entre les personnes autistes et neurotypiques, 2) a examiner les relations entre l'empathie et la theorie de l'esprit et 3) a evaluer l'influence de l'alexithymie sur l'empathie et la theorie de l'esprit. Pour ce faire, je vais administrer un test d'empathie, le Multifaceted Empathy Test, un test de theorie de l'esprit, le Theory of Mind Assessment Scale et un questionnaire d'alexithymie, le Bermond-Vorst Alexithymia Questionnaire, a 90 adultes autistes et 90 adultes neurotypiques. Ainsi, mon projet de recherche permettra d'etudier l'influence de l'autisme et de l'alexithymie sur l'empathie et la theorie de l'esprit. Il pourra aussi mener au developpement d'interventions ciblant plus precisement les difficultes d'empathie et/ou de theorie de l'esprit des personnes autistes et facilitera l'etude du developpement de l'empathie et de la theorie de l'esprit chez les enfants autistes.

column36: The Effect of Maternal Height and Body Mass Index on Perinatal Outcomes
column37: The proportion of Canadian women of reproductive age who are obese have increased from 16% in 1997 to 23.9% in 2009, and this trend correlates with an increase in medical complications during pregnancy. Obesity is defined by body mass index (BMI) derived from an individual's mass and height, BMI > 30 kg/m2 indicates obesity. Maternal obesity is a known risk factor for pregnancy complications and contributes to a variety of adverse birth outcomes. However, little is known about the association between maternal stature and perinatal health, even though short and tall women may differ widely in their risks. My study will use data about all singleton births in British Columbia, Canada, between 2004 and 2018, to examine the effects of maternal height on adverse birth outcomes in women who had low, normal and high BMI before or early in pregnancy. The outcomes will include, for instance, cesarean delivery, preterm birth, stillbirth, infant death and severe maternal complications. Pre-pregnancy counseling utilizes information about the factors contributing to elevated risks, and emphasizes the importance of optimal bodyweight. However, this information can be more specific with respect to maternal height and BMI. My research will help to create pre-pregnancy counseling guidelines specifically tailored to women with various statures, including individualized advice about particular risks, preventive screening, and beneficial lifestyle changes. My results can also optimize maternity care, obstetric interventions and pregnancy outcomes for both the mother and the baby.

column36: Role of the Hippo signalling effector Yap in the metaplastic response and regeneration of the gastric epithelium.
column37: The gastric epithelium is continuously exposed to various microbial and chemical insults. Consequently, the stomach has evolved various mechanisms to ensure barrier function in response to injury, while also maintaining nutrient digestion and immune defense strategies. One of the most important threats to epithelial integrity is brought upon by the bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, which upon chronic infection leads to the elimination of acid secreting parietal cells. In this inflammatory setting, the glandular epithelium triggers a metaplastic process whereby fully mature cell types adopt alternative cellular fates. This regenerative response is driven by trans-differentiation of post-mitotic chief cells of the stomach into highly proliferative metaplastic cells through mechanisms that are still poorly understood. Previous work in our laboratory has shown that Hippo signaling plays an essential role in controlling cell fate decisions during tissue regeneration. In this research project, we will examine the role played by the Hippo transcriptional effector, Yap, in driving gastric metaplasia and uncover the transcriptional changes and biological responses that are controlled by Yap. This research project will provide much needed insight into one of the earliest lesions associated with gastric cancer, a major contributor to cancer-related deaths worldwide. column36: Behavioural Addictions and the Lived Experiences of Self-Directed Recovery
column37: Behavioural addictions are one of the most prevalent psychological problems. Yet, treatment strategies for behavioural addictions are lacking. Although previous research has found self-directed recovery to be beneficial for gambling addiction, little is known regarding self-directed recoveries of other common behavioural addictions (e.g., problematic internet use, compulsive shopping) despite their harmful consequences. Therefore, the objective of this proposed research is to investigate recovery processes and self-directed strategies from the lived experiences of those with a behavioural addiction. Through identifying personal resources from individuals who have recovered, self-help programs can be developed for those still suffering from significant distress caused by their behavioural addiction. A mixed methods approach will be used to investigate these recovery processes using questionnaires and a semi-structured interview. Specifically, participants will be asked to reflect on their resolution goals, stages of change, and the benefits of different recovery strategies. Given the need for more resources in helping those experiencing problems with behavioural addiction, the results from the proposed study will be helpful in addressing the treatment opportunities necessary in committing to long-term abstinence.

column36: Does Subjective or Objective Cognitive Impairment Best Predict Functioning in Depression?
column37: Lay title: Does Subjective or Objective Cognitive Impairment Better Predict Daily Life Functioning in Individuals with Depression? Major depressive disorder (MDD) is currently a leading cause of disability worldwide. Individuals with depression commonly experience a pronounced change in mood and/or have difficulties feeling pleasure. Other common symptoms include changes in appetite, disturbed sleep, fatigue and a diminished ability to think or concentrate. Importantly, up to two-thirds of individuals with MDD experience cognitive impairment which encompasses deficits in attention, learning, memory and other cognitive domains important for daily functioning. However, individuals' subjective and objective cognitive functioning often differ from one another, and it is not entirely known which type of cognitive impairment (subjective or objective) better predicts daily life functioning in individuals with depression. Therefore, the goal of the present study is to determine which type of cognitive impairment predicts overall functioning in patients with MDD. To do this, participants with MDD will complete a series of questionnaires and cognitive tasks to assess their subjective and objective cognitive functioning, respectively. They will then complete a questionnaire to assess overall daily life functioning. Performance on these questionnaires and tasks will allow us to determine which cognitive impairments lead to problems in daily functioning. In turn, this will provide practical information regarding the need for treatments that are specifically directed at improving subjective or objective cognitive impairment.

column36: Investigation of the Influence of Pretangle Tau on Cellular Properties in Different Brain Regions involved in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Tau neurofibrillary tangles are one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's Disease. Evidence suggests that different neurons throughout the brain are affected differently by tauopathy so we would like to observe the effects of pre-tangle tau on various brain areas and their associated behavioural functions. To do so, we will use an animal model where Sprague Dawley rats will be infused with a pretangle pseudophosphorylated human tau (htauE14) and these animals will then receive an infusion of AAVdj-PRSx8-htauE14- EGFP in the LC or AAVdj-CaMKII-htauE14-EGFP in the PC or hippocampus. We hypothesize that htauE14 will alter neuronal excitability over time and these deficits will correlate with behavioural data. In order to test this hypothesis, animals will undergo olfactory behavioural tests including a go/no-go odor discrimination task and spatial behavioural tests such as the spontaneous spatial pattern discrimination task. Behavioural deficits are expected to be specific to the site of infusion. In parallel with these behavioural experiments, we will also conduct in vitro electrophysiology at various time points post-infusion. Synaptic deficits are likely the primary signs of neurodegeneration caused by htauE14 so we expect to see decreased excitability and synaptic properties in htauE14 animals prior to the onset of behavioural deficits. Observing more than one brain area will allow us to understand the rate of tauopathy progression and correlated behavioural and electrophysiological deficits specific to those areas. These experiments in parallel will allow us to better understand pretangle stages that occur prior to the onset of clinical symptoms and the knowledge gained from this study could lead to the development of effective AD treatment strategies.

column36: Developing a polygenic score to aid in the prediction of cisplatin-induced ototoxicity
column37: Cisplatin is a common and effective chemotherapy drug which is used to treat many different types of cancer, and as with many chemotherapeutics, it harms both tumour and healthy cells. One of the most frequent adverse drug reactions seen with cisplatin is ototoxicity (hearing loss). Up to 80% of patients experience this adverse drug reaction and hearing loss is more commonly seen in pediatric cancer patients. As hearing loss impacts children's ability to develop critical language skills, this puts the patients at a disadvantage in educational and social settings. One method that can be used to predict who is most likely to suffer from cisplatin-induced ototoxicity (CIO) is the development of polygenic scores (PGS). Studies have shown that CIO has a genetic component that can be traced to multiple genetic variants. PGS would account for the genetic risks attributed to each of these genetic variants, to create a single risk prediction score for each patient. As the genetic architecture of CIO is similar to other forms of hearing loss, genetic variants that are significantly associated with heritable forms of hearing loss can be harnessed to develop a PGS for CIO. The relevance of this PGS for CIO will be increased by only including variants occurring in genes that are expressed in the inner ear, or which display a relationship with cisplatin-induced cell death. This project will be novel as it is the first study to use PGS to predict adverse drug reactions and will provide a way to improve the prediction of who is most likely to suffer from CIO. As cancer rates are steadily increasing, this project will allow for personalized treatment strategies to be developed which will help to reduce health care burdens in cancer survivors, especially in pediatric cancer patients.

column36: The Role of Galectin-1 in Glomerular Basement Membrane Injury due to Antibody Mediated Rejection
column37: Kidney transplantation is the best treatment for end stage kidney disease. Unfortunately, transplanted kidneys fail prematurely. The main reason for premature kidney loss is antibody mediated rejection (AMR). AMR occurs when the immune system of the recipient recognizes the transplanted organ as foreign. The recipient's immune system then attacks the graft leading to damage to all the compartments in the transplant, including the basement membranes that form scaffold for cells. This scaffold is very important as it helps cells to communicate with each other and limits the entry of immune cells. However, the mechanisms leading to injury to this scaffold in AMR are not well understood, due to the lack of good models to study it. There are also no effective treatments for AMR. In our previous study, we analyzed the distinct compartments in kidney biopsies (including the filters, called glomeruli, and the tubes which absorb fluid, called tubules) with AMR. Among multiple basement membrane molecular actors decreased in the AMR glomeruli, we found galectin-1, which was significantly increased. This is interesting because galectin-1 modifies the immune cells and binds to the basement membrane. Galectin-1 may play an important role in transplantation. My goal is to investigate the link between galectin-1 and basement membrane injury, and to test a new model of AMR. This new model is made in collaboration with biomedical engineers, and it consists of artificial glomerulus on a dish (""glomerulus-on-chip""). I will study galectin-1 in cell culture to test its effect on cells and scaffold in a simulated AMR using the glomerulus-on-chip. Galectin-1 may be a new therapeutic target for AMR. As well, our glomerulus-on-chip may address the lack of effective models to study AMR.

column36: The Band-Frail Pilot Study: Intervention to Outweigh Diabetes and Frailty in Fredericton
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a disease in which your body does not properly use the insulin it makes or cannot make enough insulin, which results in high blood sugar. This long-terms high blood sugar has detrimental health consequences. Frailty is a health issue where the person is less able to manage physical and mental stressors, which also leads to health issues. As people are getting older, they often get both conditions, which makes them more vulnerable. Therefore, the objective of the current study will be to look at the effects of an elastic band strength training program along with education about diabetes on people living with type 2 diabetes and frailty. This study is a pilot project at the University of New Brunswick and will be the first location for this multisite study. The program will be 16 weeks and be given by a diabetes educator. Before and after the program, the participants will have their physical function and blood sugar tested to see what effect the program has on people with type 2 diabetes and frailty. The elastic band exercise program as well as the education session to be used were created by Diabetes Canada in 2012. This program is important since the proportion of individuals with Type 2 diabetes and frailty is constantly increasing as well as their associated health issues.

column36: Identifying Pathogens in Ulcerative Colitis using Bioinformatics and Phenotypic-Assays
column37: The prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in Canada is among the highest in the world and is estimated to affect approximately 1 in 100 Canadians by 2030. IBD can negatively impact an individual's quality of life and result in substantial costs on the health care system and society. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a type of IBD that is characterized by inflammation of the inner lining of the large intestine. UC is thought to arise through a complex interplay of host genetics, environmental factors, the immune system, and the gut microbial community (microbiota); however, the cause of the disease remains poorly understood. There is evidence that at least in some patients, pathogenic or disease-causing bacteria may contribute to UC and the bacterial family Enterobacteriaceae are prime suspects. We hypothesize that strains of many species in the Enterobacteriaceae family, which have common virulence genes, contribute to disease activity in some patients with UC. The Surette lab is involved in randomized control trials of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) for adult UC and microbiome studies in early onset pediatric UC. We will use targeted culture of Enterobacteriaceae combined with metagenomic sequencing and phenotypic characterization of patient fecal samples before and after treatment. Bacterial genes and corresponding phenotypes that are important for colonization in the gut and the disruption of the gut lining will be investigated. We are particularly interested in detecting phenotypes that were lost in patients who responded to treatments and phenotypes that were constantly present in non-responder patients. Identifying an infectious role in even a subset of pediatric and adult UC patients will allow for more targeted diagnosis and treatment approaches.

column36: Perspectives and practices of medical professionals when assessing pain in maltreated children
column37: A variety of factors can influence a child's developmental trajectory. Positive childhood experiences are associated with more positive trajectories while adverse childhood experiences are associated with more negative trajectories. Two types of adverse experiences a child may encounter are maltreatment, often known as child abuse, and painful experiences. As such, in medical settings, adequately managing a child's pain is critical to reducing the risk of negative life outcomes. Both children who have been maltreated and experience frequent, or severe, pain are more vulnerable to adverse life outcomes. There is also evidence to suggest that maltreated children may conceal their emotional expressions and limit their communication about abusive experiences, which is salient given that emotional cues and self-reports are frequently used to assess pain in children. However, there is very little research about how children who have been maltreated experience pain or communicate their pain, yet the tendencies to limit verbal and non-verbal communication cues may extend to painful experiences, as they are often intrusive experiences similar to abuse. As such, maltreated children may be at risk for inadequate pain management in medical settings. The proposed research project will examine how medical professionals assess pain in children who have been maltreated and if they consider how a history of maltreatment may influence a child's pain experience and communication about their pain. Results of this study will enhance the scientific and medical community's knowledge about how pain is assessed in children who have been maltreated and inform subsequent studies which will aim to enhance how children, particularly those who have been maltreated, should have their pain assessed.

column36: Preventing Postoperative Immunosuppression by Inhibition of PI3K in Surgery-Induced Myeloid Derived Suppressor Cells
column37: Surgery is a necessary treatment for patients with solid tumors. However, data shows that surgery leads to a weakened immune system which can contribute to the worst-case scenario of the tumour reappearing and spreading throughout the patient's body. Natural killer (NK) cells can act as defenders against cancer as they survey the body and destroy any cancer cells that appear before they can develop into solid tumours. Although the importance of NK cells in controlling tumour growth is well known, our research has shown that surgery dramatically hinder their ability to recognize and eradicate tumour cells. Unfortunately, there is no current therapy for treating the suppression in NK cell activity which occurs following surgery and new approaches targeting this critical stage may hold the potential for reversing this immune suppression. We have shown that following surgery, a large number of cells that contain the ability to suppress NK cells are produced by the body, called myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Targeting these MDSCs in patients may provide an effective treatment against the immune suppressive effects of surgery. To accomplish this goal, we have attempted to identify ways of shutting down MDSC activity without harming beneficial cells in the body. We have found a distinct identifier present only on MDSCs which we have used to deliver a drug to inhibit their suppressive activity to restore the NK cells' tumour-fighting ability. The current goal is to answer whether this strategy would be safe and effective before using it on cancer surgery patients. We hope that our efforts will one day help eliminate the risk of cancer recurrence for patients who undergo surgery for tumour removal.

column36: Evaluating the diversity of values in a decision support tool
column37: Racial and ethnic disparities in attitudes towards genetics services risk exacerbating existing health inequities. Research has identified values of health literacy, family history of cancer, mistrust in healthcare systems and genetics, and varying levels of genetics awareness to influence attitudes towards genetics services in diverse populations. Decision aids have been demonstrated to align informed values with the available care choices to achieve high quality decisions and efficient healthcare use. There is a paucity of data evaluating how decision aids in genetics support the range of values important to a diversity of patients. The Genomics ADvISER 2.0 (GA) digital decision aid was developed to guide users through categories of incidental findings that may be detected during genome sequencing. I will evaluate how inclusive of values the GA 2.0 is and if it is sufficiently supportive of values that have been identified as important for decision-making in diverse users of this tool in an RCT. Participants in this trial will complete survey scales at baseline and after a genetic counselling consult (control) or use of the GA 2.0 (intervention). I will measure health literacy, concern for family, mistrust, and genetics knowledge at baseline. Outcomes of decisional conflict (primary outcome), and knowledge, preparation for and satisfaction with decision making and anxiety (secondary outcomes) will be measured post-intervention. From baseline scores, I will build subgroups of low trust, health literacy, genetics exposure, and high concern for family to represent diverse values. I will analyze the subgroups across the two arms of the trial to evaluate how they associate with outcomes. This research could inform how digital support tools are constructed in genomics.

column36: Developpement de nouveaux inhibiteurs pour l'immunotherapie contre le cancer
column37: Parmi tous les sous-types de cancer du sein, le cancer du sein triple negatif (TNBC) offre le moins d'options therapeutiques en raison du manque de cibles moleculaires bien definies. Les TNBC representent 10 a 20 % de tous les cas de cancer du sein et ont un taux de mortalite a 5 ans de 30 %. C'est une maladie biologiquement agressive et particulierement difficile a traiter. Le developpement d'un microenvironnement tumoral immunosuppresseur par les galectines est d'ailleurs un obstacle majeur a la restauration d'une reponse immunitaire antitumorale efficace. Les galectines produites par les cellules cancereuses exercent leur action immunosuppressive en se liant aux glycorecepteurs de surface cellulaire exprimes sur les cellules immunitaires. Sur les lymphocytes T, la liaison de la galectine a leur surface cellulaire declenche une cascade d'evenements de signalisation qui conduisent a l'apoptose des lymphocytes T qui tuent le cancer. Dans les TNBC, la galectine-7 (GAL-7) est la principale galectine produite par les cellules cancereuses du sein. Le developpement d'inhibiteurs de la galectine a partir de ligands naturels, cependant, fait face a un certain nombre de defis importants, y compris leur synthese difficile, la sensibilite a l'hydrolyse de leurs liaisons glycosidiques, leur polarite elevee et leur faible affinite. Le plus grand defi en utilisant de tels medicaments est d'atteindre une selectivite elevee. Dans ce projet, nous proposons de proceder a des etudes precliniques visant a valider le potentiel des premiers anticorps camelides capables d'inhiber l'activite immunosuppressive de GAL-7 et ce de facon specifique.

column36: International Food Policy Study: Evaluating the impact of food marketing policies on children
column37: In Canada, the prevalence of childhood obesity has tripled over the past three decades, with more than 150 million children obese globally. This rise in obesity has resulted in part from an increased exposure to highly-processed, caloric and nutrient-poor foods. To help limit this rise, several countries have enforced policies aimed at reducing the influence of food marketing in children, such as advertising restrictions and food labelling. However, there is relatively little data on the impact of national-level food marketing regulations on dietary patterns in young people. This study will determine the effects of food marketing policies on exposure to food marketing and dietary behaviours among children across six countries (Canada, United States of America, Australia, United Kingdom, Mexico and Chile) using a rigorous 'quasi-experimental' design. We will expand upon the International Food Policy Study (IFPS), an established prospective cohort study involving adults 18 and over that assesses the impact of food policies on dietary behaviour. The proposed research will enhance our understanding of food marketing policies in children and establish a consistent method for evaluating its role on dietary behaviour. By collecting data across six countries, this study will provide a global perspective to help shape healthy food environments, while acting as a baseline for evaluating future policy changes. This study's research team includes worldwide experts in food policy and marketing, who have direct links to policy makers in each country. Therefore, this project will also prioritize knowledge translation and career development opportunities among researchers in each partner country.

column36: A Longitudinal Evaluation of High-resolution Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Hippocampus in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy
column37: Temporal lobe seizures originate from the brain temporal lobes that are located behind the ears. Only 10% of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) patients can control their seizures with medications, necessitating surgical removal of part of the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. Human hippocampus is a tubular complex brain structure made of smaller portions. Notably, seizures reoccur in 50% of the patients that undergo this epilepsy surgery. This poor success rate may be linked to injury in specific regions of the hippocampus. It would be better if one could see which smaller regions of the hippocampus are damaged prior to the surgery to improve patient selection to those most likely cured. While standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can detect overall damage in the hippocampus, it can not identify injury in specific portions of the hippocampus. Our lab has developed an advanced diffusion MRI technique that enables acquisition of higher resolution (8x) images of the hippocampus compared to the standard MRI. In this project, I will use high-resolution diffusion MRI in a cohort of TLE patients to assess whether this tool can detect the consistency or change in the hippocampus structure over time. Next, I will assess the relationship between the MRI findings and clinical outcomes (seizure freedom) after the surgery. Finally, to validate the imaging findings, I will assess the molecular architecture of the hippocampus tissues that are obtained after the TLE surgery. These results will help establish high-resolution diffusion MRI as a surgery selection tool for epilepsy surgery. Ultimately, this tool may enable prediction of surgery success in epilepsy patients and allow physicians and patients to make informed decisions about whether surgery is the right choice for them.

column36: Effect of obstructive sleep apnea on sleep depth and architecture in Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that affects movement, but also sleep and cognition (e.g. memory, attention). Sleep disturbances in PD heavily affect quality of life, and can be caused by sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is a common disorder in the general population that causes breathing pauses during sleep. If untreated, patients with OSA can develop problems with memory and attention, which are likely related to their sleep disturbances. However, we do not know how these sleep disturbances affect cognition in patients with both PD and OSA, and whether treating OSA is helpful in improving sleep and cognition. This project will examine how sleep disturbances affect cognition in patients with PD and OSA, and whether treating OSA improves sleep and cognition. We will study brain waves during sleep using a new, automated sleep analysis tool, which provides more information beyond traditional sleep analyses. This tool allows us to measure the odds ratio product (ORP), which is a continuous sleep depth score related to how likely someone is to wake up. This tool also allows us to measure other sleep features such as sleep spindles, which are short brain waves that are linked with memory formation during sleep. We will study how brain waves are affected by OSA, and how this is related to cognition in patients with PD and OSA. We will also study changes in brain waves when we treat OSA. This will help us identify the impact of sleep and sleep disorders on cognition in patients with PD. These findings may have the potential to guide the development of strategies to improve cognitive function and quality of life for people with PD.

column36: Cultural adaptation of family psychoeducation for West African families of patients with First Episode Psychosis: A qualitative process evaluation
column37: First Episode Psychosis (FEP) is a term that describes the first time anyone experiences psychotic symptoms or a psychotic episode. FEP is a treatable condition with many well-established psychiatric treatments and interventions available to those in need. One such intervention is family psychoeducation, which involves conducting educational seminars with families of patients with FEP, and is known to reduce relapse and re-hospitalization rates of patients, decrease familial stress and burden, and lessen symptoms of psychosis. One issue regarding these family psychoeducation programs, is that the specific needs of family members from various cultural, religious, and linguistic backgrounds are rarely considered when creating and delivering this type of programming. Therefore, there is a need to culturally adapt these programs, to ensure that family psychoeducation remains accessible and culturally safe for all participating families. An understudied and underserved population in Montreal is the West African community. Thus, this project will examine what West African patients with FEP, their families, and their mental health care providers believe to be necessary components of a family psychoeducation program. By conducting semi-structured interviews with these three groups, I will explore the cultural understandings of mental health and psychosis in West African communities, uncover how patients, families and providers perceive family psychoeducation programming, and assess what adaptations are required to meet the needs of families of patients with FEP. Results will help inform the cultural adaptation process of family psychoeducation for West African families and ensure that the programming is culturally safe and addresses the population's specific needs.

column36: Elucidating the function of the Argonaute family of proteins in human hematopoietic stem cells.
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are rare regenerative cells that can replenish all blood cells in our bodies over lifetime. These cells are tightly regulated on many molecular levels to ensure the proper stoichiometric numbers and types of cells that are produced. One level of control occurs during gene expression when genomic information stored in DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA) that serves as a template for protein production. mRNA levels are further regulated by small microRNA (miRNA) molecules to modulate the amount of proteins that carry out diverse cellular functions. miRNA is, thus, a key regulator of cellular properties and function. miRNAs bind to Argonaute (AGO) proteins to carry out their function. In humans, there are four AGO proteins. However, the function of each AGO in HSCs remains unclear. Previously, these four AGO proteins were thought to perform the same function and be redundant. However, when we quantify individual AGO protein in different types of blood cells, each AGO protein has its unique abundance pattern across all blood cell types. Since some types of cells only contain certain AGO proteins, I hypothesize that each AGO protein has a unique function in the blood system. This is supported by our early data that the depletion of individual AGO in HSCs results in different outcomes, including differentiation into different cell types and their ability to self-maintain. The main objective of my project is to determine the function of AGO1-4 in HSCs and identify their unique functions in the blood system. Overall, this project will uncover the role and mechanism of each AGO during blood cell development and how HSC are governed. This knowledge is essential to better harness HSCs for regenerative medicine and stem cell therapeutics.

column36: Mitochondrial Metabolism as a Therapeutic Target for Relapsed B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
column37: Acute Lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a cancer of the blood characterized by an increase in white blood cells in the blood and bone marrow. This malignancy affects one to five per 100,000 persons per year, worldwide. B-cell ALL (B-ALL) is the most common type of ALL. Relapse- a return of cancer after a cancer free period, will occur in 15-20% of pediatric and 40-70% of adult patients. Upon relapse survival is poor. Relapse B-ALL cells are more dependent upon metabolism of mitochondria, the energy factory of the cell, than diagnosis cells. This suggests that targeting mitochondrial metabolism could provide a means of targeting therapy resistant relapse cells and diagnosis cells which are destined to become therapy resistant. To test this, I will carry out three aims. Aim one, profile the mitochondrial metabolism of diagnosis, relapse-fated, and relapse samples, with the SeaHorse metabolism assay. Aim two, utilize a variety of computational approaches to identify unique properties of relapse and relapse-fated cells, which will identify the unique vulnerabilities of these cells. Aim three, target the vulnerabilities of relapse and relapse-fated cells, identified in aims one and two, and assess their sensitivity to standard chemotherapy treatment. I will use the gene editing technique, CRISPR, to eliminate the function of important genes in chemotherapy resistance, following which, I will assess sensitivity to standard chemotherapy treatment. I will identify candidate drugs by treating relapse cells with drugs targeting their vulnerabilities and assess their sensitivity to standard chemotherapy treatment. Significance: By targeting mitochondrial metabolism, my project will identify new therapeutic targets for B-ALL and potentially improve the cure rates of relapsed B-ALL.

column36: Evaluation des Changements de Preferences Alimentaires apres une Chirurgie Bariatrique
column37: La prevalence de l'obesite a augmente drastiquement au cours des dernieres decennies au Canada. La chirurgie bariatrique, dont la gastrectomie parietale, est actuellement un traitement efficace pour entrainer une perte de poids significative et une resolution des comorbidites chez les individus souffrant d'obesite severe. La perte de poids resulte principalement d'une diminution des apports alimentaires causee par la restriction calorique et la baisse de production de ghreline, une hormone qui stimule l'appetit. Quelques etudes ont montre une diminution de la consommation et de la preference pour les aliments riches en gras et en sucres post-chirurgie, qui pourrait etre causee par des changements dans les processus centraux impliques dans le systeme de la recompense (systeme hedonique). Le Leeds Food Preference Questionnaire (LFPQ) permet d'evaluer les preferences alimentaires en mesurant separement et simultanement differentes composantes de la recompense alimentaire (le plaisir et la motivation). a notre connaissance, aucune etude n'a utilise le LFPQ pour examiner les effets de la gastrectomie parietale sur la regulation hedonique de la prise alimentaire. Nos objectifs sont: (i) d'examiner les changements de preferences alimentaires en lien avec la regulation hedonique de la prise alimentaire apres la gastrectomie parietale; et (ii) d'examiner comment ces changements sont associees aux apports et aux comportements alimentaires, ainsi qu'aux niveaux plasmatiques de ghreline. Ce projet permettra une meilleure comprehension des changements de preferences alimentaires observes apres la chirurgie bariatrique, ce qui permettra de developper de nouvelles strategies therapeutiques nutritionnelles et psychologiques afin de prevenir la reprise de poids apres la chirurgie.

column36: Explorations into the mechanism and potential of BOLD-100 as a treatment for COVID-19
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread morbidity and mortality worldwide, and threatens many more lives in the months to come. There is an urgent need to discover and test new therapeutics to treat patients with COVID-19. BOLD-100 is a promising new drug that has been shown to potently inhibit SARS-CoV-2 (the cause of COVID-19) in initial cell culture experiments. Although the mechanism of BOLD-100 is still under study, it appears to work by reducing the levels of certain host proteins that help viruses replicate. The proposed research will help advance our understanding of BOLD-100 as an antiviral agent, and help determine whether it is a promising therapeutic candidate for treating COVID-19. We will use a variety of molecular biology techniques to determine the ways in which BOLD-100 inhibits SARS-CoV-2 replication in human cells. Additionally, we will use a hamster model of COVID-19 to evaluate the therapeutic potential of BOLD-100 in a living organism. This information will support the further development of BOLD-100, and inform future clinical trials in humans. Identification of new antiviral drugs will provide additional treatment options for vulnerable patients and may alleviate the burden of future pandemics.

column36: Effets du cannabidiol sur les marqueurs inflammatoires de personnes ayant un trouble de l'usage de la cocaine: un essai clinique randomise controle
column37: L'inflammation chronique entraine des dommages aux cellules et tissus du corps humain favorisant l'apparition notamment de cancers, de maladies cardiovasculaires et de depression. Plus de 50% de la mortalite dans le monde est causee par des maladies reliees a l'inflammation. Mais d'où provient cette inflammation? Elle est induite entre autres par l'exposition a des substances toxiques dont la cocaine fait partie. En effet, l'utilisation repetee de cocaine entraine une forte reponse inflammatoire, qui elle-m eme peut mener au developpement de differents problemes de sante. Cibler l'inflammation chez les personnes ayant un trouble de l'usage de la cocaine (TUC) pourrait permettre d'en eviter les consequences nefastes a long terme. Le cannabidiol (CBD) a gagne en inter et pour ses proprietes anti-inflammatoires dans les etudes precliniques ainsi que pour son profil securitaire. Cette analyse secondaire d'un essai clinique randomise controle souhaite evaluer l'efficacite du CBD a diminuer les marqueurs inflammatoires de personnes ayant un TUC. 79 adultes avec un TUC ont ete randomises (1:1) au traitement quotidien de CBD ou de placebo (800 mg) durant 12 semaines. column36: Correcting Age-Related Overactive Bladder Syndrome by Inhibiting Matrix Metallopeptidase-9 Overexpression
column37: Overactive bladder syndrome (OAB) is characterized by the loss of bladder control and the frequent urge to urinate, interfering with daily life activities, such as sleep, work and leisure, which reduces the quality of life. OAB affects around 20% of the Canadian adults and increases in prevalence with age. Although the underlying causes of OAB are unknown, a recent study has shown that aging females with OAB exhibit lower levels of a protein, Nerve Growth Factor (NGF), in their urine. NGF is essential for nervous system health. Since the bladder is under strict control of the nervous system, the decrease in NGF reduces the neurological control of the bladder and poor control of urine storage and release. Decreased NGF may be explained by an increased activity of Matrix Metallopeptidase-9 (MMP-9), an enzyme responsible for degrading NGF. MMP-9 activity is regulated by microRNAs, biological molecules that play a role in controlling gene expression. The microRNA, miR-491-5p, inhibits MMP-9 gene expression to prevent NGF degradation. In the urine of aging females with OAB, MMP-9 activity is increased and miR-491-5p levels are reduced, likely explaining the reduced NGF levels. Thus, controlling MMP-9 may restore NGF levels and reverse OAB. Our study aims to inhibit the activity of MMP-9 to correct OAB through administration of miR-491-5p mimics in mouse models of age-related OAB. We hypothesize that miR-591-5p mimics will prevent the synthesis of MMP-9, restoring adequate NGF levels to correct OAB in aging mice. Most of our preliminary data are derived from a cohort of human patients. The clinical implication of this study lies in our assessment of the functional benefit of restoring bladder NGF in aging mice with OAB, which may enable future treatments for age-related OAB.

column36: Neurodevelopmental Trajectories of Metis Children in Alberta
column37: Neurodevelopmental Health of Metis Children in Alberta The first decade of life is an important period for the influence of biological, social, cultural and intergenerational factors on growth and brain development. At a time when world economies and responses to societal challenges depend on critical thinking and emotional intelligence, the impact of neurodevelopmental problems starting in early childhood have negative consequences on long-term health and well-being. Canadian Indigenous children face a disproportionate burden of disease and neurodevelopmental problems compared to their non-Indigenous counterparts. Currently, there is a lack of studies informing the neurodevelopmental health of Metis Children in Canada. As Metis children's health is intimately linked to the health of their families, communities, and the land, a Metis-specific lens to research is needed to inform policies aimed at improving their health and well-being. This research engages the Metis Nation of Alberta (MNA) as knowledge users and research partners. Using quantitative research methods that are culturally appropriate within a Metis context, we will evaluate the trajectories of neurodevelopmental health of Metis children in Alberta and explore the influence of maternal and social factors on these outcomes. Results from this research will help to inform and plan culturally-competent actions supportive of Metis Children's health and wellbeing in Alberta and other jurisdictions across Canada.

column36: Functional Somatic Disorders: Understanding the patients experience of patient-physician communication
column37: Conditions such as Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, Fibromyalgia, Post-Viral Illness and Medically Unexplained Symptoms cause high rates of disability and impact the lives of millions of Canadians. Many doctors find it difficult to explain these conditions to patients and this can lead to misunderstandings and frustrations for patients and doctors. There is little guidance for doctors on how to best explain these conditions because there is relatively little research in the area. Particularly, there is a lack of focus on understanding the patient point of view when studying these communication breakdowns. Better understanding of the patients' experiences will help to identify the best ways for doctors to discuss these conditions with their patients. This project has three parts, each of which will help doctors better understand the patient experience of communicating about these conditions. First, I will create a review article covering the research that has been done so far. Review articles help doctors understand what is known so far and highlights questions not already answered in previous studies, which can then be studied. Second, I will do a survey of patients with post-COVID-19 symptoms, a type of post-viral illness, looking to help doctors understand how these symptoms impact patients' lives. Third, I will do interviews with patients to explore the patients' experience and what influences communication between doctors and patients. These interviews will help provide support for guidelines to help doctors improve the way they discuss these conditions with patients. Altogether, it is expected that the results of this project will help improve communication between doctors and patients with these type of conditions.

column36: Intersectional Artificial Intelligence: An Empirical Ethics Investigation for Decision Support Tools in Healthcare
column37: Artificial intelligence empowered decision support systems (DSS) are increasingly encouraged for use in Canadian healthcare. Current existing ethical guidelines for AI-DSS are not specific for use in the context of healthcare. To build these guidelines, how intersecting identities of race, gender, ability, socioeconomic status, and structural discrimination factor into the development of AI-DSS needs to be better understood. In this study, I aim to identify the ethical considerations in the design and implementation of AI-DSS in healthcare. In the first phase, I will conduct a scoping review of the AI-DSS ethics texts to present the current field and relevant considerations for healthcare. In the second phase, I will hold unstructured observations at the Goldman Herlz Family Practice Centre to define the institutional setting in which discussions on AI-DSS take place. To understand how social inequalities and complex identities are conceptualized, experienced, and accounted for in the design and use of AI-DSS in healthcare, I will conduct in-depth interviews with developers, patients, and physicians. In the final phase, I will analyze the findings in collaboration with AI experts, patient representatives, and clinicians to identify the ethical considerations emerging from the fieldwork. This study locates the context-specific ethical considerations for AI-DSS in healthcare at the institutional, clinical, and individual levels. The findings will translate into a set of practical tools to ensure AI-DSS accounts for intersecting social advantages and disadvantages of its design and implementation. The collaborative focus of the study will ensure the development of pluralistic ethical guidelines that facilitate trust, quality of care, and healthcare systems efficiency.
