column36: Using a multidimensional model of impulsivity to investigate the relationship between social anxiety and alcohol consumption
column37: Previous research has shown a relationship between social anxiety-the fear of being negatively evaluated in social situations-and alcohol use. Further, impulsivity plays an important role in this relationship. Specifically, socially anxious people with impulsive personalities are more likely to use alcohol to deal with their anxiety than those who are less impulsive. However, these studies have not taken into account the different dimensions of impulsivity. For instance, impulsivity can manifest itself as failing to plan ahead or lacking the ability to persevere. These studies also typically rely on alcohol craving measures rather than actual alcohol consumption. The proposed research project will investigate which dimensions of impulsivity are most likely to lead people to self-medicate with alcohol when they are socially anxious. To do so, we will measure how much alcohol participants drink after facing a stressful social event. First, we will measure how socially anxious and impulsive participants are using questionnaires. Impulsivity will be measured according to its various dimensions. In one condition, participants will then complete a public speaking task to induce social anxiety. In the other condition, participants will complete a task that does not induce any anxiety. After these tasks, all participants will rate their levels of anxiety and alcohol cravings in a laboratory bar while alcoholic beverages are prepared in front of them. They will be permitted to drink as much alcohol as they want. This study will enable us to see which dimension of impulsivity best predicts the quantity of alcohol participants consume when they feel socially anxious. This information will help shape treatments for alcohol dependence in socially anxious people.

column36: The role of innate immunity in melanoma
column37: Cutaneous melanoma is the most lethal form of skin cancer, and its incidence is increasing. In 2020, approximately 8,000 Canadians will have been diagnosed with cutaneous melanoma and 1,300 will have died from it. The current mainstay of treatment for advanced disease, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), have revolutionized patient outcomes. ICIs work by harnessing the patient's own immune system to recognize and kill tumour cells. However, adverse events related to this immune activation, including colitis, pneumonitis, and dermatitis, as well as resistance can limit use of ICIs. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are newly identified cells in humans with roles in cancer immunity. However, their specific pro- or anti-tumour effects in patients with melanoma, and their role in response to ICIs are unknown. This is the first-in-human study to determine the effects of ICIs on ILC2s and the role of ILC2s in response to ICIs and development of adverse events. This study will also demonstrate that the ILC2 immune response and ILC populations can be monitored using peripheral blood mononuclear cells isolated from patients with cancer. To assess the ILC2 response to ICIs, multi-parameter flow cytometry will be used to determine the levels of ILC2s in the blood of melanoma patients on ICIs at defined time intervals. Following extraction from the blood using cell sorting and ex vivo expansion, the functional properties of the ILC2s will be assessed. Statistical analyses will be performed to identify correlations between the presence of ILC2s and response rates and toxicities to ICIs. Ultimately, this innovative research will provide evidence for novel melanoma therapies that may offer greater efficacy and overcome the concerns associated with current treatments.

column36: The role of regulatory T cells in blood during acute heart transplant rejection
column37: Acute cellular rejection poses a significant challenge in fully realizing the potential of heart transplantation to cure end-stage heart failure. In order to prevent organ rejection, patients receive maintenance immunosuppression, and are prescribed even higher doses or additional immunosuppressants when rejection is diagnosed. However, these drugs produce a myriad of serious side effects, including cardiovascular complications, infection and cancer. Therefore, a radically different and more specific approach to treating and preventing acute rejection is needed to allow heart transplantation to become a true cure. Therapies based on immune-modulating regulatory T cells (Treg) can protect the allograft from the host's immune system while still allowing for normal immune function. However, the activity of Tregs during acute rejection is unknown and thus their therapeutic applicability in the context of heart transplantation has not been explored. In this proposal, I will investigate the changes in Treg activities during acute cellular rejection by quantifying 46 genes in blood that track acute cellular rejection trajectory and Treg activities. These biomarkers have been developed and validated in a large cohorts of patient samples; in the case of the rejection panel, the discovery work alone included more than 160 heart transplant patients from 7 hospitals across Canada. Results from this work will provide insights into Treg biology during acute cellular rejection, and may provide a complementary diagnostic platform for future investigations of using Treg-based therapies for creating personalized, longer-term immune management strategies for heart transplant patients.

column36: Effet de la vitamine K sur la cognition de patients presentant une maladie cardiovasculaire : une etude pilot d'intervention de 12 semaines.
column37: Les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) touchent un nombre important de Canadiens et augmentent le risque de problemes cognitifs au grand age. La nutrition possede la capacite d'influencer le developpement de maladies. Decouverte pour son role dans la coagulation, la vitamine K (VK) possede des actions importantes au niveau des systemes vasculaire et nerveux. La VK se trouve en quantites importantes dans les legumes verts feuillus (epinards, brocoli) ainsi que certaines huiles (canola, soya). Dans differents groupes de participants ages, des apports eleves de VK ont ete associes a de meilleures performances au niveau de la memoire, des fonctions executives, de la cognition globale, et a une prevalence reduite de plaintes cognitives subjectives. a la lumiere de ces resultats, nous proposons une etude pilote de 12 semaines visant a determiner l'impact d'un supplement de VK sur la cognition de participants presentant une MCV. La moitie des participants recevra un supplement quotidien de VK et l'autre moitie un placebo. La cognition sera evaluee au debut et a la fin de l'etude et comprendra la memoire episodique, les fonctions executives et la rapidite de traitement de l'information. Ces domaines cognitifs sont connus pour etre affectes dans les MCV et se sont averes sensibles au statut vitaminique K. Le maintien des fonctions cognitives est central a la capacite de mener une vie independante et epanouie. Les individus presentant une MCV sont davantage a risque de declin cognitif et de demence avec l'age. La VK a potentiellement un role significatif a jouer sur la cognition dans un contexte de MCV. Le projet propose fournira des informations uniques et novatrices et servira a planifier des etudes de plus grande envergure au sein de ce groupe de patients a risque.

column36: Permeabilisation de la barriere hemato-encephalique en situation d'inflammation post-irradiation pour l'optimisation de la distribution des traitements adjuvants a la radiotherapie
column37: Les tumeurs cerebrales secondaires necessitent des traitements agressifs qui incluent generalement de la radiotherapie. Malgre les avancees faites pour le traitement de ce type de cancer, on observe souvent des recidives locales qui contribuent au taux de survie de moins de deux ans. L'utilisation d'un traitement complementaire a la radiotherapie pourrait ameliorer ce pronostic. Malheureusement, la chimiotherapie standard montre peu d'efficacite et la distribution des medicaments au cerveau est limitee par la barriere hemato-encephalique (BHE). Cependant, la radiotherapie entraine une inflammation des tissus cerebraux sains qui augmente le niveau du recepteur β2 de la bradykinine. Dans ce contexte inflammatoire, l'activation du recepteur par une molecule injectee (agoniste) induit l'ouverture de la BHE. Notre hypothese est qu'il serait possible d'utiliser l'inflammation cerebrale causee par la radiotherapie pour ouvrir cette barriere et permettre l'entree de molecules (p. ex. chimiotherapie) dans le cerveau afin d'ameliorer le traitement des tumeurs cerebrales. Pour ce faire, nous allons determiner les niveaux du recepteur β2 de la bradykinine dans les cerveaux d'animaux vivants avec des techniques d'imagerie par resonance magnetique en utilisant un nouveau type d'agent d'imagerie qui cree des regions sombres a l'endroit où ces recepteurs sont presents. Nous allons par la suite evaluer si la BHE peut etre ouverte avec une molecule injectee (agoniste) et si cela ameliore l'efficacite de la therapie dans un modele de cancer cerebral chez la souris. Ceci devrait etre confirme par une diminution de la taille de la tumeur au fil du temps. Cette technique pourrait eventuellement etre utilisee pour ameliorer le traitement des tumeurs cerebrales chez l'humain.

column36: Evaluation of Human Endogenous Retrovirus Proteins as Cancer Biomarkers using Immunoaffinity-Mass Spectrometry
column37: Millions of years ago, viruses infected and integrated into our germline genome and have been passed down. These viruses are known as Human Endogenous Retroviruses (HERVs) and currently there are limited studies to assess whether these genes encode for proteins and to study their function. There has been an interest in assessing the potential role of a specific group of HERVs, called HERV-K envelope (env) proteins in cancer development. As such, I hypothesize that HERV-K env proteins are a promising class of cancer biomarkers that can be detected and quantified using a highly sensitive and specific tool called immunoaffinity-mass spectrometry (IA-MS) assays. Different HERV-K env proteins have very similar protein sequences which hinders commonly used tools such as immunoassays from being able to differentiate between them. IA-MS takes the best of two worlds by using immunoassays' high sensitivity which uses specific antibodies to capture only our proteins of interest from the entire sample. Following this, our concentrated sample with our proteins of interest will be analyzed by mass spectrometry where its high level of specificity can tell us each individual amino acid (building block) of the captured proteins. Notably, due to our lab's expertise, resources, and collaborations, I will first assess HERV-K env protein expression in prostate cancer cell lines. Concurrently, I will develop IA-MS assays to detect and quantify these proteins. Lastly, I will evaluate the expression of these proteins in clinical samples (prostate tissue biopsies, seminal plasma, and blood serum). The successful implementation of this project will further our knowledge on a fairly unstudied area of the human genome and aid in finding novel biomarkers for prostate cancer diagnosis.

column36: Investigating the Roles of microRNAs miR655 and miR526b in Cellular Senescence using a Breast Cancer Model
column37: By 2030, 23% of Canadians will be 65 years of age or older, and the average life expectancy will increase to over 82 years for both men and women. Age increases the risk for developing chronic diseases. According to 2019 Canadian Cancer Statistics, 90% of cancer diagnosis occur in Canadians 50 years of age or older. MicroRNAs (miRNA) are small, non¬coding RNAs that function to regulate gene expression and functions of the cell. We have recently shown that two miRNAs, miR526b and miR655, promote oxidative stress and down¬regulate multiple tumor suppressor genes in breast cancer. Cellular senescence is characterized by permanent cell cycle arrest and is important for tissue development, healing and tumor suppression, but can also attribute to decline in tissue function and disease as senescent cells accumulate with age. Senescence can be caused by several factors, including damage to cells and DNA and also by repetitive cell divisions as many cells in our body have a limit to how many times they can divide. During cancer treatment, senescence can occur in both normal and cancerous cells. The role and effects of senescence in cancer treatment varies. Some studies indicate that intentionally promoting senescence in cancer cells could be beneficial. Other studies indicate that promoting senescence in normal and diseased tissue could attribute to relapse, as it has been shown that senescent cells release many inflammatory secretions. The roles of microRNAs in the case of senescence and, more broadly aging, have not been fully explored. Understanding cellular senescence in breast cancer will contribute to understanding its significance as an outcome of conventional cancer therapies and could subsequently aid in understanding other chronic age-related disorders in Canada.

column36: The (pro)renin receptor: an emerging player in tumorigenesis
column37: According to the Canadian Cancer Society, 1 out of 4 Canadians is expected to die from cancer. Studying emerging players in cancer allows us to identify novel therapeutic targets. This research slowly, but surely, paves the way to a cancer-less world. The (pro)renin receptor (PRR) is an emerging player in tumorigenesis, or tumor formation, as it engages cell signaling pathways central to cancer biology. However, how PRR contributes to tumorigenesis remains elusive. The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is highly activated in cancer. PRR is essential in Wnt/β-catenin signaling because it is needed for assembling the vacuolar H+-adenosine triphosphatase (V-ATPase) complex. The V-ATPase complex is required for Wnt ligand binding to the Wnt receptor complex and for the cellular internalization of the Wnt receptor complex, which are key processes in Wnt/β-catenin signaling. The PRR can be processed into two fragments: soluble PRR (sPRR) and the M8.9 fragment. When measured clinically, levels of sPRR were elevated in cancer patients of several cancer types. The M8.9 fragment is the predominant PRR structure associated with the V-ATPase complex. This data suggests a pertinent role of PRR processing in tumorigenesis, possibly through Wnt/β-catenin signaling. To test this hypothesis, our lab generated a mouse model with aberrant PRR processing, as suggested by reduced plasma sPRR levels, through introducing mutations in the PRR gene processing sites. Mating these mice with a cancer mouse model will allow assessing whether aberrant PRR processing decreases cancer susceptibility in living organisms. Using cellular models derived from these mice, experiments will be performed to elucidate the effect of aberrant PRR processing on V-ATPase function, Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and tumorigenesis.

column37: Survivors of adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer, aged 15-39 years, may experience a higher risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. We aim to identify factors associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes in female AYA cancer survivors versus no-cancer women. column36: Measuring biological activity during compound accumulation in Escherichia coli using time-course gene expression profiles
column37: Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria are a cause of infections worldwide and have few effective treatment options. In Gram-negative bacteria, the presence of the outer membrane (OM) is a barrier to antibiotic activity. The OM is a selectively permeably, complex lipid bilayer of polysaccharides, phospholipids, and proteins that reduces access to intracellular antibiotic targets. By exploring the biological responses to intracellular accumulation of antibacterial compounds we can identify unique compound-target interactions and resistance mechanisms of the cell crucial for developing novel treatment strategies. The OM barrier of Gram-negative bacteria limits our available knowledge of biological responses to only the antibacterial compounds that can bypass the membrane. The goal of this research project is to explore the cellular response phenotypes of Gram-negative bacteria to compounds that are limited by the membrane. Using a fluorescent reporter genetic library of the Gram-negative bacterium, Escherichia coli, and a unique fluorescence imaging platform we can collect promoter expression phenotypes to a variety of antibacterial compounds. Disruption of the OM with a known OM perturbant will facilitate compound entry into the cell and we can report on the transcriptional responses to a variety of chemical probes that are traditionally inactive in E. coli. These responses will be used to inform on susceptible genetic pathways for combination therapy and the novel treatment of Gram-negative bacteria.

column36: Sex Differences in Participation in Structured Exercise Programming from the Acute Stroke Event to 6 months Later: Access, Motivators, Barriers and Facilitators
column37: In a Canadian study, women with stroke were twice as likely to not participate in exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programs compared to men. This is concerning as there is strong evidence showing that taking part in structured exercise programming (SEP) is related to increased muscular strength, walking ability, and lifespan, as well as a reduced risk of having a repeat stroke. The proposed research study will promote women's health by addressing a knowledge gap in the factors that influence lower proportions of women taking part in SEP along the continuum of care. Therefore, this study's main goal is to determine sex differences in SEP participation along the continuum of care in patients with stroke and to determine factors that influence these sex differences. Sex differences in SEP participation and factors influencing SEP participation will be tracked and monitored at three stages during stroke recovery within the first six months of stroke. These study outcomes will be measured using a series of questionnaires that will ask about factors that prevent, discourage, enable, and motivate participation in SEP, and a wearable monitor that will track the amount of physical activity completed. Bivariate analyses and a logistical regression will be conducted to determine the predictors of SEP participation between sexes. Study findings will inform clinical practice guidelines and education tools for doctors and clinicians involved in stroke recovery to better reflect the needs of women with stroke. These findings will also inform the redesign of how SEP is delivered along the continuum of care to allow for more equitable access for women with stroke. It is through these channels that stroke recovery and quality of life for women with stroke will improve.

column36: Structural elucidation of IKs activators bound to ion channel complexes
column37: Irregular heartbeat disorders, known as arrhythmias, present a severe strain on the healthcare system, can greatly lower patient quality of life and may result in sudden death. KCNQ1 is a voltage-gated potassium ion channel that serves an essential function in the maintenance of cardiac rhythm through the repolarizing action of the slow-delayed rectifier potassium current (I<sub>Ks</sub>). Mutations of the KCNQ1 gene that cause a loss-of-function of I<sub>Ks</sub> are implicated in a wide array of arrhythmias, including long QT-interval syndrome (LQTS). Thus, I<sub>Ks</sub> activator drugs which bind KCNQ1 are a potential therapeutic option for LQTS, and while a number of these have been reported, their mechanisms of action are poorly understood. Here we propose using cryogenic-Electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to probe the actions of the archetypal agonists, ML277 and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) on the I<sub>Ks</sub> ion channel complex. Cryo-EM is a revolutionary advancement in protein structure determination, capable of achieving high resolution 3D images of protein-drug interactions by bombarding a frozen solution of purified protein with electrons. We have already begun to use cryo-EM to visualize KCNQ1-protein complexes, and so we are equipped with an optimized protocol to achieve our goals. We will also perform functional studies of the KCNQ1-ML277 complex to understand the relationship between drug binding and subsequent channel effects. The determination of a structural model of this complex will facilitate a better understanding of how I<sub>Ks</sub> activators change the kinetic properties of KCNQ1, paving the way for the development of new drugs to treat LQTS, and improve our understanding of mechanisms that modulate I<sub>Ks</sub> through binding to KCNQ1.

column36: Pharmacists' Role in Mental Health: Exploring the Current State and Understanding Barriers to Enhanced Care
column37: Pharmacists' Role in Mental Health: Exploring the Current State and Understanding Barriers to Enhanced Care Mental illness is a rapidly growing issue – far-reaching in the number of people it affects and complex in each individual characterization. In any given year, one in five people living in Canada experience mental health problem(s). Saskatchewan residents suffering from mental illness face many barriers to care and would benefit greatly from improvement in timely access, safe and effective comprehensive medication management, and mental health education. Involvement of pharmacists in mental health care has been shown to improve safe and effective medication use, reduce hospitalization, and increase patient satisfaction. However, in Saskatchewan, limited resources are available for pharmacists to provide mental health related care, and there is currently no financial reimbursement model focused specifically on community pharmacists providing mental health care. Although pharmacists can play a critical role in addressing the mental health crisis in our province, there are gaps in our understanding of the current extent of pharmacist involvement in caring for patients with mental illness and of barriers to effectively providing this care. This study will describe and quantify the current practices, experiences, and challenges of Saskatchewan pharmacists in the provision of mental health care. Ultimately, data collected from pharmacist surveys and patient interviews will be analyzed and utilized to inform future mental health pharmacy related research and education initiatives in ways that guide practice change and enhance the care of individuals living with mental illness.

column36: Blood Transfusion in Major Non-Cardiac Surgery
column37: Blood transfusions are commonly administered in patients undergoing surgery. Although potentially lifesaving, blood transfusions are known to be associated with various side effects. Furthermore, transfusions are expensive, costing up to $761 USD per unit. There is significant variability in how physicians decide to transfuse blood products to surgical patients. Guidelines for blood transfusion in this patient population are limited and may not be based on adequate evidence from the operative period. The goal of this research program is to form the groundwork for a future trial that will test strategies to minimize unnecessary blood transfusions in patients undergoing surgery. This will be accomplished using two study designs. Firstly, we will review the charts of 500 patients who received a blood transfusion during surgery in the last year. We will assess whether these transfusions were appropriate and explore the different variables that were associated with receiving an unnecessary blood transfusion. We will also assess the financial burden of these unnecessary blood transfusions on the healthcare system. Secondly, we will assemble an expert panel of 30 anesthesiologists and surgeons to obtain a consensus regarding various elements that will be important to incorporate in the previously mentioned trial. For example, we would ask questions about the lowest acceptable hemoglobin level that they would tolerate before initiating a blood transfusion. We hope that conducting these two studies will help define the scope of our research question and inform a future trial aimed at evaluating safety of implementing strategies that reduce blood transfusion in the operating room.

column36: Efficacite d'un traitement cognitif-comportemental transdiagnostique pour troubles anxieux sur l'insomnie
column37: Cadre theorique: Les troubles du sommeil sont frequemment concomitants avec les troubles anxieux. Pourtant, seulement 2% des articles portant sur les traitements de therapie cognitive-comportementale d'anxiete se sont attardes sur les difficultes de sommeil comorbides. La TCC transdiagnostique (TCC-T) est une therapie de groupe qui cible les processus cognitifs et comportementaux communs des differents troubles d'anxiete. Une seule etude a mesure les effets de la TCC-T sur des symptomes d'insomnie concomitants. Objectifs et hypotheses: Le 1er objectif est d'etudier l'efficacite clinique d'une TCC-T de groupe pour les troubles anxieux sur les symptomes d'insomnie comorbides aupres d'une clientele adulte. Le 2e objectif est d'evaluer l'effet des symptomes d'insomnie comorbides sur l'efficacite de la TCC-T sur des symptomes d'anxiete. Le 3e objectif est de verifier si le sexe des participants est une variable moderatrice importante dans les deux premieres hypotheses. Methode: Ce projet s'insere dans une etude plus large qui a recrute 231 participants qui ont participe a 12 seances hebdomadaires de groupe de deux heures. Les criteres d'inclusion comprennent de rencontrer les criteres diagnostiques du DSM-5 pour au moins un trouble anxieux. L'Anxiety and Related Disorders Interview Schedule for DSM-5 et l'Index de Severite de l'Insomnie sont utilises. Des mesures seront prises en pretraitement, post-traitement et en suivi apres 4, 8 et 12 mois suivant la fin du traitement. Retombees: Une comprehension plus approfondie de l'interaction entre l'insomnie et l'efficacite de la TCC-T permettrait de reviser le protocole de traitement pour une clientele affectee par ces deux troubles. Un usager presentant ces deux troubles pourrait beneficier d'un seul traitement efficace.

column36: SARS-CoV2 Proteins Alter the Mitochondria-Associated Membrane, a Structure that Controls Neuroinflammation
column37: The 2019 coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is an infectious disease, where severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV2) infects cells of the airways. Additionally, coronaviruses are known to activate inflammatory signaling pathways and cause dysfunction of the brain (neuroinflammation). To address brain defects within COVID-19 patients, a better understanding of the consequences of SARS-CoV2 would be beneficial. The Simmen Lab has previously identified an intracellular structure known as the mitochondria-associated membrane (MAM) as a key control station of neuroinflammation. This structure controls the energy output of mitochondria, but also promotes inflammation. We hypothesized that COVID-19 could trigger the same effect, because several SARS-CoV2 proteins, including ORF8, are known to colocalize with MAM proteins. Indeed, preliminary results from the lab have indicated that SARS-CoV2-infected human cells show changes to the mitochondrial structures and have hallmarks of cell stress. I therefore hypothesize that a subset of SARS-CoV2 proteins compromise the control of mitochondria through the disruption of MAM proteins. To test this hypothesis, I will express SARS-CoV2 proteins in different human cells systems and observe the structure of MAM. Next, I will monitor cellular energy, stress levels, and inflammatory levels. Using different brain cell types, I will test whether response also occurs in these cells and whether it can be transmitted from one cell type to another, a frequent event during neuroinflammation.

column36: Impacts vasculaires des inhibiteurs de point de controle immunitaire
column37: Au cours de la derniere decennie, l'immunotherapie est devenue le point central de la therapie contre le cancer. Les inhibiteurs du point de controle immunitaire (ICI), un type d'immunotherapie, sont utilises pour stimuler la reponse immunitaire contre les cellules cancereuses. Cependant, il ne s'agit pas d'une therapie ciblee et l'activation diffuse de la reponse immunitaire peut egalement conduire a des maladies de type auto-immunes ou des reactions inflammatoires generalisees qui peuvent donner differents symptomes selon les systemes touches. Les resultats de plusieurs etudes ont demontre que la reponse inflammatoire chronique joue un role important dans le remodelage vasculaire en contexte de maladies chroniques. a notre connaissance, la reponse vasculaire aux ICI reste a ce jour inconnue et pourrait avoir des implications cliniques pour les patients atteints de cancer. Dans ce contexte, nous proposons que les ICI conduisent a une inflammation vasculaire generalisee qui peut etre evaluee en mesurant l'epaisseur intima-media de l'artere carotide et en evaluant la rigidite des grandes et petites arteres. Ainsi, dans cette etude longitudinale, nous allons etudier l'impact cumulatif de l'immunotherapie sur la rigidite arterielle et les fonctions vasculaires. Cette etude nous permettra de comprendre les effets vasculaires des ICI et d'examiner si les changements dans la reponse vasculaire se traduisent par une reponse au traitement. a long terme, nous souhaitons que cette etude permette le developpement d'une therapie personnalisee pour les patients atteints de cancer et ainsi favoriser leur sante et leur qualite de vie.

column36: Investigating the role of dead-box helicase 6 in acute myeloid leukemia
column37: Over the years, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), such as the DEAD-box helicase 6 (DDX6), have been reported to alter the expression of cancer driver genes. Notably, DDX6 has been shown to be highly expressed in multiple cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Previous work done by our research group suggests that the reduction of DDX6 levels impedes the growth of AML cells. Therefore, we hypothesize that DDX6 is functionally required for AML cell survival due to its control of leukemia-specific expression programs. To address this hypothesis, our first aim will be to characterize the effects of differential DDX6 expression levels in AML cells. This will be done by reducing or elevating DDX6 levels in AML cells. Our second aim will address DDX6s mode of action. We will be using an ascorbate peroxidase (APEX) proximity labeling method to identify unique protein interactions of DDX6, as well as mRNA targets of DDX6 in AML cells. This project will further our knowledge on how post-transcriptional processes, such as those performed by RBPs, influence AML disease development and progression. Furthermore, it will aid in the search for novel therapeutic targets for AML patients, especially for those lacking suitable therapies due to disease relapse.

column36: Sport Concussion Mechanics
column37: There is growing concern that soccer headers may cause long-term neurological damage. Intentionally redirecting the ball with the unprotected head may cause minor traumatic brain injury (mTBI). These repetitive minor injuries are believed to cause cumulative damage. Despite this there remains a deficit in literature regarding the exact biomechanics and the complications that arise from purposeful heading. One factor that has been shown to decrease concussion incidence in soccer is neck strength. Therefore the objectives proposed study are two fold: 1) Assess the short term effects of soccer heading on electrophysiological brain responses using electroencephalography (EEG) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). 2) Evaluate the relationship between neck strength, head accelerations and electrophysiological activity. Twenty five healthy amateur soccer players will be recruited for this study. The participants will be will be equipped with a previously tested and validated instrumented mouth guard that contains a triaxial accelerometer and a triaxial gyroscope to measure linear and rotational head accelerations in six degrees of freedom. Neck strength will be measure using a digital handheld dynamometer, and short term electrophysiological changes will be measured using EEG and TMS immediately after heading session. Heading is expected to alter brain function. This impact on brain function is expected to be correlated with the magnitude head of accelerations. Stronger necks are expected to accelerate less decreasing short term electrophysiological changes.

column36: Positional Therapy for the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children: A Randomized Crossover Trial
column37: Sleep apnea is common in Canadian children and is diagnosed on an overnight sleep study test. It is caused by a temporary blockage of the airway that leads to sleep disturbance and a fall in oxygen levels. This airway collapse is worse in up to half of children with sleep apnea when they lie on their back. This results in daytime sleepiness, difficulties in learning and memory, and increased risk for diabetes and heart issues. The primary treatment for persistent sleep apnea is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). CPAP delivers pressured air through a tight-fitting mask to keep the airway open and must be worn on a nightly basis to be effective. However, many children will never wear CPAP because they find it uncomfortable. New treatments for sleep apnea that are comfortable and acceptable are urgently needed. One new treatment is a body positional belt that is worn around the chest and has built-in cushions to prevent a child from sleeping on their back. The main goal of this study is to compare a body positional belt with CPAP therapy for treating sleep apnea. Children who have worse sleep apnea on their back based on a sleep study test will be included in our study. This group of children will have two sleep study tests on separate nights, one with CPAP and one with a body positional belt, which will be done in random order. We will compare the results of the body positional belt with CPAP to see if the body positional belt is just as effective in treating sleep apnea. Body positional belts could be an affordable, comfortable, and easy to use alternative therapy to CPAP for treating sleep apnea in children. If positional belts are an effective treatment for sleep apnea, they may help improve the overall health of Canadian children with sleep apnea.

column36: Health Care Costs Associated with Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Bariatric Surgery Patients: A Population-Based Study
column37: One of the main risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is obesity; and, therefore, OSA is a common disorder in patients being evaluated for bariatric surgery. One study reported that 70% of bariatric surgery patients have OSA. Untreated OSA has been associated with an increased risk of post-operative complications. Patients being evaluated for bariatric surgery are screened for OSA symptoms and signs prior to undergoing surgery. Because of limited resources, polysomnogram, the diagnostic test for OSA, is recommended only for patients who screen positive. However, there is evidence that this screening approach does not accurately identify all patients with OSA. Under-recognized OSA in this population may lead to increased health care utilization and costs. In this study, we will use population-based data from the Ontario Bariatric Registry and the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences to measure the rate of OSA in patients who underwent bariatric surgery in Ontario between 2010 and 2015. We will compare this rate to the rate reported in the bariatric surgery literature to determine whether current OSA screening practices are adequate. We will stratify results by individual Ontario bariatric centre to identify possible differences in OSA screening practices and areas for improvement. Secondly, we will compare post-bariatric surgery health care costs between patients with and without OSA in order to inform whether current OSA screening practices are reducing health care utilization and costs. Thirdly, in bariatric surgery patients with OSA, we will compare health care costs in the 1-year prior to vs. the 1-year post OSA diagnosis to inform whether identification and treatment of OSA leads to decreased health care utilization and costs.

column36: Etude du mecanisme d'action de l'ozanimod dans le contexte de la COVID-19
column37: En date du 23 novembre, 57 millions de personnes atteintes de la COVID-19 ont ete repertories, dont 1,3 millions qui en sont decedees. Dans les cas severes, on remarque une inflammation pulmonaire prolongee qui mene au developpement de detresse respiratoire et souvent, a la mort. Pour le moment, aucun medicament efficace n'est present pour soigner les patients gravement atteints de la maladie. Mon projet s'inscrit dans l'etude clinique COZI, où l'ozanimod, un medicament tout recemment approuve dans le traitement de la sclerose en plaque, est teste pour contrer les cas severes de la COVID-19. En effet, en plus de ses effets benefiques dans le contexte de la sclerose en plaques, ce medicament est egalement reconnu comme etant capable de reduire la detresse respiratoire causee par une infection a un virus de l'influenza. Nous pensons que l'ozanimod permettra de reduire, dans le contexte de la COVID-19, le nombre et le niveau d'activation des globules blancs tout en reduisant les molecules inflammatoires dans les poumons et le corps. On comparera donc les populations de globules blancs des patients qui recevront l'ozanimod versus ceux qui ne la recevront pas et on analysera la modulation de differentes molecules inflammatoires qui sont normalement augmentees dans la maladie. On mesurera egalement l'impact de l'ozanimod sur les niveaux d'anticorps contre le virus de la COVID-19, qui sont necessaires pour une immunisation a moyen/long terme, afin de s'assurer que le medicament ne nuit pas a ce processus. Les donnees de ce projet pourront nous permettre de mieux comprendre l'evolution de la COVID-19 chez les patients hospitalises et a potentiellement ameliorer les traitements offerts a ces derniers.

column36: Evaluating the Role of Parents/Guardians as a Determinant of Treatment Outcomes in Children and Adolescents with a History of Sexual Abuse
column37: The Applicant will conduct research in the context of a multimodal residential mental health program for children who have a history of sexual abuse. This program has demonstrated significant reductions in anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms. However, less is known about the long-term outcomes about what happens when a child returns back home and continues their relationship(s) with their parent(s)/guardian(s). The role of parents/guardian is therefore not well understood in treatment outcomes, so the current study seeks to fill the gap by evaluating this multimodal treatment in children and the effects on parents/guardians in terms of health outcomes and their lived experience. Since there is limited evidence for treatment outcomes in relation to parents/guardians, this research project will use surveys, interviews and focus groups to understand the role of the family environment on outcomes in children who have a history of sexual abuse. This 4-week residential treatment program will look at 50 children to evaluate various treatment outcomes at a residential treatment centre. We hypothesize that the children who have parents/guardians that actively participate in treatment will show significant improvements in anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms compared to baseline ratings. The results of this study will inform the Patient/Family/Guardian lived experience and be useful for Real World considerations for effective program improvement and informing patient and family stakeholders and public policy. Knowledge Translation and Dissemination will be facilitated by Little Warriors and by the Women & Childrens' Research Institute.

column36: Sociodemographic Analysis of the Incidence and Survival from Paediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Ontario
column37: Background: Paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (POHCA) is associated with significant neurological morbidity and mortality. Interventions such as bystander CPR and shorter EMS response times have been shown to increase the likelihood of survival with neurologically favourable outcomes, yet recent research from the U.S. reports racial and neighbourhood-level inequities in the provision of these services. In Canada, there are known disparities in health care access among remote and rural communities, and some Indigenous communities are at an increased risk of experiencing an OHCA. However, the impact of sociodemographic factors on POHCA incidence and survival has not been examined, even though their impact is potentially modifiable. The proposed study would describe the population of children who have experienced an OHCA in Ontario to identify potential sociodemographic disparities in incidence and outcomes. Methods: We will conduct our analysis at ICES where patient records are linked across administrative databases. Eligible patients will include those who have experienced a POHCA in Ontario within the last 15 years. Incidence rates will be calculated using census data for the study period and for each study year. The primary outcome will be survival to hospital discharge. To identify sociodemographic disparities in POHCA incidence and outcomes, we will link patient data to available social descriptors from the Ontario Marginalization Index, Census, and Immigration, Refugees, and Citizenship Canada datasets (available within ICES). Implications: This research will likely identify at-risk communities or groups, and work to reduce disparities through mobilizing resources and informing local interventions which could include CPR training or improved access to EMS.

column36: Cell Shrinkage as a Result of Raised Intracranial Pressure after Intracerebral Hemorrhage
column37: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke subtype in which a blood vessel ruptures in the brain. Normally, the skull has three components: brain, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which must remain in equilibrium to maintain brain health. However, ICH results in bleeding and swelling in the brain. To maintain equilibrium after ICH, blood and CSF can be ""pushed"" out of the skull, reducing the amount of pressure. These ""compliance mechanisms"" help maintain normal intracranial pressure (ICP). When these mechanisms fail, ICP elevations can worsen outcome and increase the risk of death. Previously, brain tissue was not thought to play a role in ICP compensation. However, we have recently shown cell shrinkage (a decrease in the size of brain cells) following ICH, and we hypothesize that this is a previously uncharacterized compliance mechanism to blunt rises in ICP. Importantly, we have found evidence that this cell shrinkage can harm brain cells. Our goal is to test whether two clinically used methods of ICP reduction after stroke still result in cell shrinkage, and their impact on cellular health. First, we will reduce ICP with one clinical treatment. Since reducing ICP will reduce the pressure on shrinking cells, we expect to see less cell shrinkage after this treatment, and perhaps lessen or prevent injury to brain cells. Second, we will use a clinical treatment that reduces brain swelling. We expect that this will lessen swelling, and since cell volume is related to water content, perhaps facilitate cell shrinkage throughout the brain. We additionally expect any cell damage associated with CS will be amplified with this treatment. Overall, this project provides exciting and novel insight into the mechanism of cellular shrinkage and its benefit and harm.

column36: Investigating Immune Responses to HIV/TB Co-infection in Humanized Mice
column37: The bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis that causes latent or active tuberculosis (TB) disease has infected 1/4 to 1/3 of the human population. Unfortunately, the risk of latent TB developing into the contagious and deadly active TB can be increased by over 20 times if the person is also infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Even though therapeutics are available, HIV/TB co-infection reduces quality of life, and globally it causes 300,000 deaths each year. From this information, it is clear that further research investigating HIV/TB co-infection in the body is urgently needed. One main issue is that much of HIV research has been conducted using isolated human cells or tissues, but these models are not an accurate representation of what actually happens inside the human body. Therefore, it is necessary to use animal models to further our understanding of these diseases. Until recently, this has been challenging as HIV only infects human cells, so the commonly used animal models for infectious disease research such as lab mice or primates would not be properly infected to accurately represent the disease in humans. Humanized mice address these issues. When human stem cells are given to mice lacking their own immune system, they begin to grow and support human immune cells that are able to be infected by HIV. This project will be using a new generation of humanized mice with well-established human immune cells to investigate HIV/TB co-infection in organs known to be greatly impacted by the disease such as the lungs, liver, and spleen. Understanding how co-infection behaves in a host and how the body's immune defence responds will allow for more effective vaccines, therapies, and treatments to be developed in an effort to reduce disease burden around the world.

column36: The Impact of a Remotely-Delivered Yoga Intervention on Cognitive Function in Breast Cancer Patients Receiving Chemotherapy: A Feasibility Study
column37: Background: Cancer-related cognitive impairment – or chemobrain – is a common and persistent quality of life complaint among breast cancer survivors. Exercise has been shown to improve attention and memory impairments, however the optimal exercise type and timing of delivery is still unknown. Research on the effects of yoga on cognitive impairments in breast cancer patients has been inconclusive. No studies to date have measured changes in cognitive function as a primary study outcome following a yoga intervention, highlighting the need for a feasibility study. Objectives: This study will explore the feasibility of a 12-week, virtual yoga intervention on cognitive function in breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy. It is hypothesized that the intervention will improve memory in breast cancer patients. Methods: The Hatha yoga intervention will consist of one 90-minute live yoga class delivered virtually via Zoom and one 60-minute pre-recorded yoga class each week. The primary study outcome is feasibility measured by enrollment rates, adherence to and completion of the yoga program, and patient satisfaction scores. Secondary outcomes include objective and self-reported cognitive function and self-reported physical activity levels. All measures will be taken at baseline and post-intervention (12 weeks). Significance: This study will provide evidence on whether a virtual yoga intervention improves cognitive impairments and is feasible for breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy. It will inform future, larger-scale yoga interventions aimed at improving cognitive impairments and long-term quality of life for breast cancer survivors.

column36: Investigating CYM as a target for the treatment of MYC-driven group 3 medulloblastoma
column37: Investigating CYM as a target for the treatment of MYC-driven medulloblastoma Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumour in children. An increased amount of a protein named MYC in some MB tumours is strongly associated with an increased likelihood of metastasis and poor outcome. Unfortunately, MYC is a difficult protein to target with drugs. However, data from our lab show that targeting and inhibiting another protein named CYM indirectly affects MYC, causing human MB cells to stop growing. Furthermore, we believe CYM is a much more easily druggable target than MYC. There is still a lot we do not know about CYM. This project has two main aims: to determine the localisation of CYM (i.e. where it is in the cell), and to determine whether inhibition of CYM reduces tumour growth and increases survival. If it does, that would indicate that it can be targeted to treat cancer. The localisation of CYM will be investigated by looking for its presence in human MB cells as well as in the cell media. Thin sections from MB tumours will be stained to reveal CYM under the microscope. MB tumour growth and survival will be assessed in mice, comparing animals that have been treated with antibodies against CYM to those which have received an inactive control. Using gene editing CYM will then be deleted from human MB cells and these cells will be used to compare tumour growth and survival to unedited MB tumours. MYC is one of the most frequently upregulated proteins in cancer. Beyond MB, the ability to target MYC through the inhibition of CYM could improve the prognoses of a wide range of deadly cancers including lymphoma, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma.

column36: Developing a viral tool for bidirectional control of neuronal activity in the mouse spinal cord
column37: Neuropathic pain is a chronic, debilitating disease with unmet medical needs. Lack of proper pain management in patients is due to our incomplete understanding of changes in pain processing pathways under health and disease conditions. One of the trademark symptoms of neuropathic pain is called mechanical allodynia, where gentle touch is perceived as painful. Specifically, the dorsal horn of the spinal cord contains a complex network of interneurons that processes touch and pain inputs from the periphery. The function and connectivity of these interneurons remain poorly understood. In this project, I designed a novel tool that allows me to activate or silence these neurons in an awake mouse and determine the impact of activation or silencing on pain sensitivity. Based off the behaviour of these mice, we can deduce the physiological role those neurons play in the transmission of pain and touch signals. We anticipate finding neurons whose activation produces analgesia, and others whose silencing will reduce mechanical allodynia. The outcome of these experiments will be to identify target neurons whose modulation will be beneficial in the treatment of chronic pain.

column36: Thrombelastography-Defined Duration of Hypercoagulability Following Pelvic and Acetabular Fractures
column37: The development of blood clots, known as venous thromboembolism, are serious and common complications following broken bones that require surgical treatment. The body responds to injuries, such as a broken bone by triggering a coagulation cascade, where the imbalance in blood factors causes the blood to change from a liquid to a gel-like consistency, leading to clot formation. Pelvic and acetabular fractures are considered major broken bones, which are reported to have the highest incidence of pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs) and deep vein thrombosis (blood clots in the legs). Pulmonary embolism carries a significant mortality risk on its own; however, even less severe, non-life threatening blood clots can still result in physical activity limitations and a decrease in functional abilities. It is unknown how long after pelvic and acetabular fractures a patient remains at increased risk for blood clots. There are currently no guidelines to direct which medication is best and for how long it is required to prevent blood clots. In order to address these knowledge gaps, we will use thrombelastography (TEG). TEG analysis uses a small amount of blood to provide an accurate and almost immediate picture of the change in clotting ability of the patient's blood. Therefore, TEG can be used to help identify which patients are at greater risk of abnormal clotting, when the risk is highest, and for how long after their injury. Using TEG analysis to define the duration and extent of increased risk for blood clots in this vulnerable population will help inform clinical practice guidelines for future prevention of blood clots after major injury.

La litterature propose une implication du faisceau longitudinal superieur, inferieur et du faisceau occipito-frontal inferieur. Nous proposons ainsi une etude visant notamment a determiner l'implication de ces faisceaux dans la fonction visuospatiale et de mettre en correlation cette fonction a la qualite de vie des patients. Des tests visuospatiaux, cognitif ainsi qu'un questionnaire portant sur la qualite de vie seront egalement administres. Les resultats aux differents tests seront ensuite correles a l'etat des faisceaux observes a la tractographie. De plus, la chirurgie de resection devrait pouvoir corriger les deficits causes par un deplacement des fibres, mais pas ceux dus a une rupture des faisceaux. Finalement, une alteration de la fonction visuospatiale devrait etre associee a une baisse de la qualite de vie. Bref, cette etude permettra d'ameliorer la pratique chirurgicale afin de preserver ces faisceaux durant l'operation ainsi que de modifier le counseling preoperatoire puisque nous pourrons mieux expliquer les symptomes potentiellement reversibles et les consequences relies a la rupture d'un faisceau.

column36: Associations Between Supported Housing and Health Outcomes of Adults with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder in Canada
column37: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is the leading cause of birth defects and developmental disabilities in North America. Without effective supports, adults with FASD to face exceptional challenges with independent living and housing stability. Despite the well-established fact that housing stability is a critical social determinant of health, very little is known about supported housing and associated health outcomes of adults with FASD, and no best practices for supporting this population have been determined. To answer these important questions, the proposed study will conduct video interviews with adult participants living with FASD who use supported housing. Participants will be recruited by the committed developmental and housing service partners who are collaborating on this project. Interviews will include quantitative questions from the RAND Health Survey and the World Health Organization's Quality of Life assessment to measure health and wellbeing, and qualitative questions to explore participant needs and experiences with supported housing. As supported housing varies greatly across locations, representatives from participants' housing providers will also complete questionnaires regarding characteristics of each supported housing location (e.g. conditions for tenancy, whether an FASD-informed approach is used, etc.). Results from this study will clarify critical unknowns concerning how characteristics of supported housing are associated with the health and wellbeing of adults living with FASD. Further, the nuanced and specific supported housing needs of this population will be revealed to guide future directions for this work. This study will establish the necessary foundation for creating best practices in supported housing for adults living with FASD.

column36: A regenerative therapy for Alzheimer's pathology using non-invasive gene delivery
column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) affects more than 30 million people worldwide and there is no effective treatment capable of modifying disease progression. With age being the main risk factor for the development of AD, increasingly aged populations across the globe poses a major threat to economies, healthcare infrastructures, and the well-being of patients and caretakers. A recent Canadian estimate suggests that the cost of the disease totals more than $10.4 billion annually, and national disease prevalence is expected to double by 2030. Given the urgent need for therapeutic advancement, the proposed project aims to develop an effective and long-lasting treatment for AD. Specifically, this project aims to develop a gene therapy that activates a receptor which prevents degeneration by promoting cell survival and function. A novel and non-invasive method that uses harmless ultrasound waves to access the brain will be used to ensure safe therapeutic delivery. Promoting brain health using ultrasound-mediated therapeutic delivery has shown promising results in animal models of AD; however, to date, this treatment requires frequent ultrasound applications for repeated therapeutic delivery which poses safety, feasibility, and efficacy concerns. The proposed approach eliminates this issue through its ability to deliver a gene which, after a single administration, allows for the production of a therapeutic compound for 10 or more years. Specifically, this therapy modifies brain cells and enables them to produce the therapy they need for their own survival, regeneration, and function. I hypothesize that this approach will slow disease progression in AD. This will be tested experimentally in an animal model of AD to bring us one step closer to clinical therapies.

column36: Mecanismes de la maintenance a long terme de l'architecture du systeme nerveux chez C. elegans.
column37: Un assemblage initial du systeme nerveux est etabli tot dans le developpement, et son integrite structurelle et fonctionnelle est ensuite mise a l'epreuve par des processus de maturation, plasticite, stress mecanique lie aux mouvements et croissance de l'organisme. Des mecanismes moleculaires post-developpementaux assurent la protection a long terme de l'architecture neuronale. Par exemple, la proteine d'adhesion cellulaire SAX-7/L1CAM est requise apres la naissance pour maintenir le systeme nerveux chez le ver et la souris. Par ailleurs, les cellules gliales possedent des roles cles dans le developpement et le fonctionnement neuronal, mais leur implication dans la maintenance de l'organisation neuronale a long terme reste inexplore. Mon projet de maitrise vise donc a approfondir ce sujet grace a la simplicite du nematode C. elegans. Son court cycle de vie, sa petite taille et sa transparence permettent des manipulations genetiques et moleculaires efficaces, avec une resolution unicellulaire. Je caracteriserai l'importance des molecules de maintenance pour les cellules gliales, puis je testerai le role des cellules gliales dans le maintien des structures neuronales par ablation post-developpementale pour en evaluer les consequences. Ces travaux permettront de mieux comprendre les mecanismes preservant l'integrite du systeme nerveux a long terme. Une deregulation de ces mecanismes de maintenance pourrait etre impliquee dans l'apparition de maladies neurodegeneratives, dont les premiers symptomes apparaissent parfois a un stade avance de la maladie. Ainsi, le developpement d'outils diagnostiques plus performants et de traitements preventifs sont necessaires et constituent des retombees possibles de la caracterisation de tels mecanismes.

column36: Developpement d'une approche therapeutique pour les maladies hereditaires avec le << prime editing >> : une etude sur l'Alzheimer et la dystrophie musculaire de Duchenne
column37: Le domaine de la genetique permet dorenavant de guerir des maladies qui etaient autrefois considerees comme incurables avec les therapies geniques. Celles-ci sont composees d'un vehicule transportant les composants et de l'outil biologique generant une reparation de l'ADN. Des problemes surviennent lors de la selection de ces outils, car certains phenomenes appeles <<off-target>> se produisent lors de l'edition, causant des modifications non desirees. Il est donc necessaire de prendre en compte le pourcentage d'efficacite de l'edition therapeutique et les mutations hors cible. Il faut savoir que l'ADN, le materiel hereditaire chez l'humain, est compose de deux brins et inclut les informations sous forme de code compose de quatre bases chimiques. Un nouvel outil biologique propose recemment a le potentiel de contourner bien des inconvenients. Le <<prime editing>>, compose d'un guide pour l'edition, d'une proteine synthetiseur de brins et d'une proteine servant a couper l'ADN, est capable d'editer le genome en changeant les bases chimiques sans necessiter de couper l'ADN de chaque cote. Cette technologie semble etre un candidat ideal pour les therapies geniques futures en raison de sa capacite a corriger specifiquement les mutations tout en diminuant les mutations hors cible en raison des etapes supplementaires requises pour l'edition. Notre objectif est d'evaluer le pourcentage de correction et d'evenements hors cible en definissant et en optimisant une methode de <<prime editing>> pour inserer des corrections pour la dystrophie musculaire de Duchenne et une mutation protectrice pour l'Alzheimer. Selon nous, cet outil peut atteindre des taux d'edition d'ADN suffisants dans les cellules humaines pour fournir un avantage clinique dans d'eventuels traitements de therapie genique.

column36: Identifying the Hematopoietic Precursors Immortalized by Enforced Homeobox Expression
column37: Adult hematopoiesis is a process that results in the formation of blood cells in the bone marrow and is organized as a hierarchy, with hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) at the top and red and white blood cells at the bottom. Long-term (LT)-HSCs have the greatest self-renewal capacity, which means that they are able to divide and generate clones for a long time (immortalization) and this ability diminishes going down the hierarchy. In fact, the first mutation to initiate blood cancers is thought to be one that immortalizes hematopoietic cells. The Homeobox (Hox) proteins are considered to be involved in regulating self-renewal. One particular Hox protein, Hoxb4, has been shown to immortalize hematopoietic cells when forced to be continuously expressed. These immortalized cells are able to reconstitute red and white blood cell populations in irradiated mice that have no bone marrow cells and sustain this reconstitution for a long time. But which hematopoietic cells are immortalized and how Hoxb4 regulates self-renewal is unknown. To address this, the purpose of my project is to identify and characterize cell types in the hematopoietic hierarchy that are immortalized by enforced HOXB4 transgene expression in order to study the molecular mechanisms behind self-renewal. I will first identify what cell type has long-term reconstitution in HOXB4-expressing bone marrow. Next, I will examine if this same cell type in normal bone marrow can still give rise to long-term reconstitution without HOXB4. Once the cell type that is immortalized by HOXB4 is discovered, the final aim is to then analyze this cell type and uncover which genes HOXB4 interacts with. This project will reveal how self-renewal is controlled and render potential targets for new therapies to treat blood cancers.

column36: Macrophage Contributions Towards the Sarcoma Immune Architecture and Response to Stimulator of Interferon Genes Agonist Therapies
column37: Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) is an aggressive, highly metastatic malignant tumour of muscle. UPS is resistant to all available systemic therapies and metastatic disease is rapidly fatal. New UPS therapies are desperately needed. The STING (STimulator of INterferon Genes) immune pathway is a promising new therapeutic target for cancer immunotherapy. Using a small molecule STING agonist (SMSA), we have recently demonstrated very promising anti-sarcoma effects and durable survival following intra-tumoural STING activation in a mouse model of UPS. To pursue clinical application of SMSA therapy, it is important to further understand how STING activation works in sarcoma. The precise intra-tumoural cell populations activated by SMSAs are poorly characterized. Macrophages are the most abundant immune cell in UPS tumours and are sensitive to SMSAs. We therefore hypothesize that intra-tumoural macrophages are essential for the initiation of anti-sarcoma immune responses following SMSA therapy. To test this hypothesis, we have developed the following aims: (Aim1) To evaluate the therapeutic effects of STING activation in the context of macrophage deficiency; (Aim 2) To determine if STING pathway activation restricted to intra-tumoural macrophages can recapitulate the therapeutic effects of SMSAs. Liposomal clodronate will be used to deplete intra-tumoural macrophages before SMSA therapy. A novel transgenic mouse line engineered to express inducible, activated STING exclusively in macrophages will also be evaluated. This study will provide insight into the role of UPS tumour macrophages in the therapeutic mechanisms of STING activation in UPS tumours. This study will also generate new knowledge of how the UPS tumour immune microenvironment is shaped by macrophages.

column36: Combining Multiplexed Immunohistochemistry and Deep Learning to Spatially Map the Tumour Microenvironment
column37: The tumour microenvironment(TME) is a highly complex mixture containing, epithelium, stroma and a diverse network of immune cells and the spatial organization of these immune cells within the TME reflects a crucial process in anti-tumor immunity. Different components of the TME play various roles in promoting tumor growth or suppressing it and thus, in determining the optimal treatment strategy, the heterogeneous tumor microenvironment must be fully considered for treatment planning. The usual standard of care for assessing if a patient has cancer, its stage and its likely future biological behaviour is visual examination of one or more stained sections. Immunohistochemistry(IHC) has changed the paradigm of digital pathology, moving from single-marker IHC towards multiplexed labeling, increasing the need for more advanced techniques that can be easily integrated in routine clinical pathology. To address the clinical need for high-dimensional analysis of tissue sections in clinical pathology, we propose to develop an automated multiplexed IHC technology combined with a deep learning cell segmentation method that would enable analysis of complex immune cell population's on a single slide through consecutive cycles of staining, destaining, hyperspectral imaging and spectral unmixing. Using deep learning to recognize/segment individual cell nuclei in multiplexed stained tissue sections, we can improve the accuracy of tissue classification based upon the measured characteristics of these cells and their spatial organization. The combination of the two would be transformative to multiple areas of clinical research, improving our understanding of the biological aggressiveness of specific cancers and enabling an accurate spatial cell level representation of the tissue.

column36: Evaluating the function of covalent immune recruiter molecules in an in vivo murine model
column37: A promising targeted approach to treat cancer is to use the body's own immune system to attack cancer cells. Antibodies possess a unique ability to redirect immune function against cancer cells and form the basis of a large class of FDA approved tumour immunotherapeutic antibodies. However, these therapeutics have limitations with regards to tissue accessibility, inadequate dosage, and weak interactions with the immune/cancer cells. A possible solution is to use the antibodies already present in the body. Synthetic small molecule therapeutics are a way to reprogram antibodies naturally present within the body to recognize and mark malignant cells for destruction. One such approach is the use of covalent immune recruiters (CIR) as an adapter or bridge between antibodies and the cancer cell. My project looks at a CIR molecule that specifically targets a prostate cancer protein. After binding to pre-existing antibodies in the body, the CIR molecule can then bind to the cancer cells. By binding both the antibody and the cancer cell, the CIR targets the antibodies towards the cancer cell and triggers an immune response to kill the aberrant cells. My project will evaluate the CIR's ability to treat a tumour in a mouse model with a fully intact immune system. Following the cancer cell transplantation into mice, I can treat the tumour using the CIR. I can determine the efficacy of the CIR by examining the extent of cancer cell death, tumour reduction and immune cell recruitment/activation. My project will not only validate the existing CIR molecule as a potential therapeutic for prostate cancer but will also provide a firm foundation for future CIR research since CIRs may be synthesized to target a variety of cancer cells.

column36: Neurofunctional Signature of Copy Number Variants
column37: In spite of considerable efforts, the neurobiology underlying psychiatric disorders remains poorly understood. In the past decade, disruptions within and between network connections in the brain subserving cognitive functions have been proposed as factors explaining clinical symptoms. Until now, research investigating brain connectivity has primarily focused on case-control studies using symptom-based diagnosis to define patient groups. These efforts proved to be unsuccessful as no robust biomarker could be identified. Recently, new technologies in genetics and the access to large patient cohorts are allowing us to adopt genetic-first approaches. Copy number variants (CNVs), defined as mutations of large DNA segments are associated with a higher risk for neuropsychiatric conditions, such a schizophrenia and autism, and are routinely identified in patients referred to the neurodevelopmental clinic. As opposed to studies investigating heterogeneous groups of individuals with the behaviorally defined diagnosis, group of patients with the same CNVs can be leveraged to study the effect of a specific molecular pathway irrespective of symptomatology. In line with this, our study will investigate the effects of CNVs most frequently diagnosed in the clinic on brain connectivity as intermediate phenotype. We will also investigate the effects of CNVs by bringing additionnal information on the nature and function of genes they disrupt. We hypothesise that CNVs as well as gene function will predict functional connectivity alterations.

column36: Restoring endogenous muscle stem cell function as a treatment for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a lethal neuromuscular disorder caused by the loss or malfunction of a protein named dystrophin, which stabilizes muscle fibers during contraction. Muscle stem cells (MuSCs) are a type of adult stem cell that can repair and regenerate damaged muscle tissue through a process known as differentiation. However, without dystrophin, MuSCs do not differentiate properly and exhibit signs of biological aging, thus reducing their regenerative potential and contributing to the muscle degeneration in DMD. DMD therapeutics currently aim towards improving patient care, hoping to prolong survival by targeting all muscles in the body. However, none specifically target MuSCs. Intriguingly, in studies of cachexia, a muscle-wasting syndrome, treatment with low doses of drugs that inhibit the process of protein synthesis were found to improve muscle differentiation and function in mice. At low doses, these drugs eliminated factors that induce cachexia by sequestering them into aggregates within the cytoplasm of the cell, known as stress granules. Given that DMD MuSCs exhibit impaired differentiation, we reasoned that treating DMD MuSCs with low doses of these drugs may improve their ability to differentiate and hence their regenerative function. Indeed, our experiments show enhanced differentiation following treatment of healthy and DMD mouse muscle precursor cells. The goal of this research project is to continue investigating how these drugs improve muscle differentiation at the cellular level. These findings will enhance our understanding of the pathways that control muscle differentiation in healthy and DMD contexts. Our goal is to provide proof of concept for a new therapeutic approach to enhance muscle stem cell function in DMD.

column36: The role of mechanosensing of tissue stiffness by dendritic cells and macrophages in promoting inflammation and obesity-associated insulin resistance
column37: Obesity and associated insulin resistance (IR) predispose individuals to develop chronic metabolic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. These disorders affect a significant proportion of the global population, but their underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In many chronic diseases, inflammation is often accompanied by processes that alter tissue stiffness. Excessive chronic inflammation during obesity can lead to scarring and stiffening of organs such as the liver, potentially activating pathways that sense mechanical cues. Immune cells in the body experience a variety of mechanical environments, and accumulating evidence suggests that physical cues coming from tissue stiffness promotes immune cell recruitment, activation, and inflammatory function. Our lab has identified a potential pathway in which immune cells sense mechanical signals that includes two protein mediators, YAP and TAZ. This project will examine the role of YAP/TAZ in regulating immune cell function by using genetically manipulated mice lacking YAP and/or TAZ in two types of immune cells, macrophages and dendritic cells. These mice will be given either a normal-chow diet or high-fat diet to induce obesity, and we will analyze and characterize cell populations residing in tissues directly affected by obesity-mediated inflammation, such as fat, liver and heart. Differences in immune cell function and the molecular pathways by which YAP/TAZ regulate these differences will also investigated. These studies will advance our knowledge on how mechanical cues regulate immune function during metabolic diseases, and may lead to the exploration of novel therapeutics for diseases associated with excessive chronic inflammation such as type 2 diabetes.

column36: How ROS modulate the oncogenic Ras signaling pathway to promote longevity
column37: For decades, antioxidants have been believed to be a key to anti-aging. Yet, several studies have shown that reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are antagonized by antioxidants, may in fact help combat aging. In roundworms, lifespan can be increased by treatments with chemical compounds that increase ROS generation. Similarly, genetically mutated worms in which ROS levels are elevated are long-lived. Strikingly, the long lifespan of these mutants is suppressed when treated with antioxidants. Similar observations were made in flies and mice, suggesting that the pro-longevity effect of ROS might be universal. Because worms share many genes with mammals, much of what we learn from them can likely be applied to human health. Among the genes that are shared, many function in cellular information processing, that is, signaling pathways. A recent study has shown that ROS targets an important signaling molecule called Ras. Ras is crucial for animal development and growth as well as in the deregulated growth that characterizes cancer. It is unknown, however, whether the targeting of Ras by ROS affects lifespan. I aim to use a variety of molecular genetics techniques to 1) uncover the details of how ROS can alter the function of Ras and 2) identify how Ras affects lifespan when its function is modulated by ROS. The proposed research will further our understanding of the aging process and have potential for the development of therapies that could slow down aging and, consequently, the severity of age-related diseases.

column36: Doxorubicin and Paclitaxel-Loaded Nanoparticle Bone Cement for the Treatment of Metastatic Spine Disease
column37: In advanced stage cancers, metastasis to the bones is common, that is, when the original cancer spreads to the bones. Among the bones, the spine is the most common site where metastases occur. The primary cancers responsible are mainly breast, prostate, lung, and kidney cancers. Spinal metastases cause severe pain, impair mobility, lead to paralysis, increase the risk of fractures, and significantly reduce quality of life. Only 10-20% of patients with spinal metastases survive 2 years beyond the diagnosis. When cancer cells migrate to the spine, they cause bone degeneration. Current medical therapy involves drugs to prevent bone loss, and chemotherapy to treat the cancer. The problem is that chemotherapy drugs are often given systemically through an intravenous route, and have significant negative side effects. Surgical treatment involves removing the cancerous tumor and using bone cement to fill the void created by the resection. The problem with this technique is that bone cement is not bioactive and it does not lead to adequate healing of the bone. Additionally, some cancer cells remain hidden and can be the source for the recurrence of the tumors. Doxorubicin and paclitaxel are two commonly used anticancer drugs. They are administered intravenously. Doxorubicin can cause heart damage, while paclitaxel can lead to nerve degeneration. Delivering these drugs locally at the cancer site would bypass these negative side effects. Since bone cement is used to fill the void created by surgery, loading these drugs into the cement would provide a local and sustained release of these drugs to treat the cancer and prevent recurrence. This research projects aims to develop such a bone cement and test it in rats to determine its viability as a treatment option for cancer patients.
