column36: Deciphering the Role of Microbiome-Immune Interactions in Host Neurobiology and Behaviour
column37: The human microbiome is a complex ecosystem known to shape a range of host physiological processes, from gastrointestinal function to higher-order cognition. However, despite a well-documented relationship between microbiome dynamics and behavioural outcomes, the mechanisms underlying microbiome-brain communication remain largely undefined. The adaptive immune system is one intermediate pathway of strong interest, given the congruencies in anxiety-like behaviour and stunted immune development seen in both germ-free mice lacking a commensal microbiota and various immunodeficient mouse models. Furthermore, previous work in our lab has shown that mice lacking functional T lymphocytes display altered microbial composition and reduced anxiety-like behaviour, highlighting the codependence of microbes, host immunity and host brain function. The current proposal outlines a novel exploration of adaptive immunity as a key mediator of gut-brain communication, and looks to elucidate the role of bidirectional signaling between T-cells and gut microbes in host neurodevelopment. This will involve a longitudinal comparison between wild type and T-cell receptor knockout mice, that will assess the impact of removing functional T cells on neuroanatomy, microbiome composition and metabolomic profile. It is expected that interrupting gut-brain-microbiome communication at the level of T-cell mediated processes will produce neuroanatomical differences at both the cellular and structural level, as well as alterations to functional microbiome characteristics. The results of this experiment will shed light on specific bacterial strains and metabolites that participate in immunomodulatory gut-brain signaling, and direct future research targeting the microbiome to improve behavioural outcomes.

column36: On the other side of depression: How competitive athletes develop personal identity
column37: Perfectionism is becoming a more prevalent personality trait that is traditionally considered to be a transdiagnostic precursor for psychopathology (Gaudreau, Louvet, & Kljajic, 2018). A core factor leading to these poor psychological outcomes is a faulty and overly critical thinking process that results in biased interpretations of one's experiences (Rozental et al., 2017). Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) addresses this core factor and attempts to alter the interpretative process of perfectionists, such that self-evaluations in light of failing to meet one's expectations will have fewer negative consequences (Dodd et al., 2019). Recently, researchers have been interested in assessing the efficacy of a highly accessible, online treatment intervention, known as an internet-based Cognitive Bias Modification intervention (CBM-I; Dodd et al., 2019). CBM-I interventions are a form of CBT that directly addresses this defective interpretation process by repeatedly exposing participants to scenarios in which they must learn how to interpret the information in a more positive manner (Salemink, Wolters, & de Haan, 2015). This study aims to understand the relationship between adverse psychological outcomes and dimensions of perfectionism (adaptive vs maladaptive), as well as to assess the efficacy of an online treatment intervention in reducing maladaptive perfectionist tendencies. It is imperative that we deepen our understanding of this multidimensional construct and to further address preventative treatment options for maladaptive dimensions of perfectionism. The current global pandemic urges research assessing the efficacy of highly accessible and online interventions, such as this CBM-I intervention used for maladaptive perfectionism, and some psychological disorders.

column36: Examining distress and quality of life of cancer patients and caregivers during the cancer process.
column37: Purpose: There is a growing number of cancer survivors and family members who care for them, but not nearly enough research addressing the mental health concerns and needs for these populations during the cancer process. A common concern reported by survivors and caregivers is fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), which has the ability to impact communication with the oncology team and one's overall quality of life (QOL). Cancer patients' mental well-being is often overlooked during the cancer process due to the focus that is placed on physical health. There is a need to examine patient experiences in order to determine their primary mental health needs. Method: Through a mixed-methods study using questionnaires and interviews, adult cancer patients will be recruited from various hospitals in Ontario, Canada based on a list of eligibility criteria. We will assess patient FCR, attachment security, QOL, and interactions with healthcare providers (HCP). Analyses will be conducted in order to understand how the mentioned variables impact one another and ultimately impact the patients' well-being during the cancer process. Results: We will use various methods of analyses in order to assess which variables may be impacting the patient's well-being. We will be discussing the relationship of attachment in patient QOL and FCR as these variables are not deeply understood in the existing literature. Conclusions: The findings of the study will be used to develop psychosocial interventions aimed to continuously assess and meet the needs of patients during the cancer process. The research will help to improve the health of Canadians through the implementation of evidence-based interventions for cancer patients.

column36: Pandemie et acces aux ressources alimentaires a Montreal: quels impacts sur les populations vulnerables en insecurite alimentaire ?

Les resultats seront utilises afin d'ameliorer les interventions en sante publique de la Direction regionale de la sante publique de Montreal et par d'autres instances, permettant de favoriser l'acces et l'approvisionnement alimentaire des personnes vulnerables sur l'ile de Montreal.

column36: Development of Novel Therapies for Focal Control of Angiogenesis
column37: In all animals, oxygenated blood is transported from the heart throughout the body by arteries, then smaller arterioles and eventually by capillaries, the smallest of blood vessels. Although this blood circulatory system is very stable, should one or more of these vessels become blocked or damaged as a result of disease, the vessels can respond by promoting the formation of new blood vessels from those already in existence. This process is called angiogenesis. Endothelial cells, which line all parts of this circulatory system that is in contact with blood, are critical cells in this growth of new vessels. Indeed, as a result of research into the role of endothelial cells in angiogenesis, several therapies to control angiogenesis have been developed and tested. Regrettably, despite these findings, focused control of angiogenesis in health and disease remains lacking. As a result, it is vital to further understand how endothelial cells drive angiogenesis and to use this knowledge to develop better more focused approaches to control this important process. It is hoped that such studies would allow angiogenesis to be increased when therapeutically advantageous, such as in cardiac ischemia when there is decreased blood flow to heart. Or therapeutically reduced when this was required, such as when trying to prevent blood flow to tumours in cancer development. Specifically, we aim to define the roles of critical inner-endothelial cell signalling molecules in angiogenesis. More precisely, we aim to study a process that we identified in conventional two-dimensional cell culture systems and compare the importance of our findings in tests using a three-dimensional cell culture system. Studying in this physiological context, we will be able to uncover more accurate therapeutics.

column36: Oxytocin Promotes Interpersonal Behaviours During Cognitive Behavioural Therapy
column37: Oxytocin (OT) is associated with cooperation, pro-social communication, and empathy. As such, research has investigated OT's clinical efficacy in treating disorders of social dysfunction, such as Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). However, no studies have examined how OT affects behaviours during psychotherapy. The present study examines the effects of OT, relative to placebo, on psychotherapist-client interactions during cognitive behavioural therapy. Data from an ongoing CIHR-funded Randomized Control Trial studying the effects of OT vs placebo during therapy will be used. One hundred and sixty participants diagnosed with MDD will be administered OT or placebo prior to video-recorded psychotherapy sessions. Behavioural coders will assess the therapist-client alliances and positive and negative behaviours following a validated coding scheme. We hypothesize that 1) participants in the OT condition will display more positive social behaviours within therapy, relative to placebo; 2) participants in the OT condition will display less negative social behaviours within therapy, relative to placebo ; 3) participants in the OT condition will rate their therapist-client alliances as stronger, relative to participants in the placebo condition; and 4) objective raters will rate the therapist-client alliances of participants in the OT condition as stronger, relative to the therapist-client alliances of participants in the placebo condition. If our hypotheses are confirmed, our findings will illustrate a novel treatment for depression. Specifically, OT in conjunction with psychotherapy may improve various clinical outcomes by changing relational behaviours. Future research might want to see if this is true in other dyads besides the psychotherapeutic context (e.g., romantic couples).

column36: Efficacite de rytvela et/ou peptide HSJ633 a prevenir les dommages aux tissus foetaux et maternels lies a la pre-eclampsie
column37: La pre-eclampsie est une complication survenant dans 5% a 8% des grossesses et peut mener a des morbidites severes et a la mortalite foeto-maternelle. Cette condition est generalement caracterisee par de l'hypertension et de la proteinurie maternelle se manifestant a partir de la 20e semaine de grossesse. Il est suppose qu'un apport reduit de sang au placenta induit une inflammation locale et systemique chez la mere gestante. La liberation de messagers pro-inflammatoires et antiangiogeniques dans la circulation maternelle jouerait un role cle dans le developpement de l'hypertension gestationnelle causant d'autres dommages majeurs chez la mere et le fœtus. Des agents anti-hypertenseurs sont frequemment administres chez la mere afin d'attenuer l'hypertension maternelle. Par contre, cette therapie s'avere comme etant peu efficace pour contrer les repercussions engendrees par la pre-eclampsie. a ce jour, le seul traitement connu est le retrait du placenta de la mere gestante. En consequence, ceci causera la naissance prematuree du fœtus qui sera generalement accompagnee de complications tout au long de sa vie, d'où l'importance de developper de nouvelles therapies. L'objectif de ce projet est de caracteriser les repercussions engendrees par la pre-eclampsie sur la mere et le nouveau-ne et d'etudier l'efficacite de trois traitements potentiels inhibant l'inflammation. Ce projet contribuera a elucider le role de l'inflammation dans la preeclampsie afin de developper des therapies freinant sa progression.

column36: The Anti-Inflammatory Effects of INSL5
column37: Hyperglycemia & diabetes cause chronic inflammation. Insulin (INS) lowers glucose levels, reducing hyperglycemia. INS counters hyperglycemic inflammation and activates the P13K/Akt and MAP kinase pathways, inducing an anti-inflammatory response. This results in glucose homeostasis, down-regulation of pro-inflammatory regulators, and up-regulation of anti-inflammatory regulators. INSL5 is secreted by enteroendocrine epithelial cells (EECs) in the colon. It binds to a relaxin family peptide 4 (RXFP4), found in many cells. Hypothesis: INSL5 induces anti-inflammatory effects by altering the immune response in macrophages. H1: Hyperglycemic mice will exhibit high levels of inflammatory markers after 30 days. H2: ISL5 treatment of macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) will release altered LPS-induced cytokine levels in non-diabetic mice. H3: The anti-inflammatory effect of INSL5 is mediated by the ERK1/2, MAPK, or mTOR pathways. Objective 1: To compare markers of inflammation and gut microbial diversity in C57/B16 mice. Objective 2: To identify if INSL5 affects LPS-induced cytokine release in DCs and macrophages. Objective 3: To identify signalling pathways initiated by ISL5-RXFP4. Methods: Diabetes will be induced in mice. Mice will be euthanized, and blood, intestine, feces, spleen, and bone marrow will be collected. Macrophages and DCs will be cultured and either pre-treated with INSL5 followed by LPS, INSL5 and LPS co-treatment, solely LPS, or vehicle. RT-PCR will be used to compare cytokine levels in cells without inhibitors. Immunoblotting of proteins will be assessed via t-tests or ANOVA to identify INSL5-RXFP4-initiated signalling pathways. Significance: If INSL5 has anti-inflammatory effects in the gut, it could result in health related funding.

column36: The genetic landscape of early-stage breast cancers with lymph node involvement
column37: The management of lymph nodes within axilla in breast cancer has evolved significantly over the past two decades, with a shift towards less invasive surgery. Sentinel lymph node biospy, which is the sampling of the few first lymph nodes that the breast tissue drains into, has largely replaced the highly morbid removal of the entire axillary lymph node base for staging of the clinically negative axilla. Yet, sentinel lymph biopsy is still associated with significant risks for our patients. Up to 75% of sentinel lymph node biopsies in patients early-stage breast cancer are negative, emphasizing a deficit in our medical ability to distinguish patients who would most benefit from these operations. To date, there has not been a focused study in differentiating early-stage breast cancers by lymph node involvement using a combination clinical, histopathologic and multi-platform molecular analyses. We propose to conduct a detailed investigation of these early-stage breast cancers using available datasets such as The Cancer Genome Atlas, and to validate our findings in local cohorts. Ultimately, our objective is aimed at expanding our knowledge of early-stage breast cancer, and the identification of factors increasing the risk of metastasis to local lymph nodes. We hope to develop a predictive tool that allows us to avoid unnecessary axillary surgery in most patients with early-stage breast cancer along with the risks and health-care costs associated with these operations.

column36: Move&Connect-Caregivers: A feasibility study of a group-based online intervention for caregivers of youth with prolonged concussion symptoms
column37: Pediatric concussion is a common injury in Canada. Almost 30% of youth experience prolonged concussion symptoms (PCS) which continue four weeks post injury. In addition to impacting youth health, pediatric concussion has been found to affect caregivers' mental health. For example, distress and burden levels are higher in parents of children with PCS. Despite the important role the caregivers play in youth recovery post-injury, there are no interventions tailored to the specific needs of caregivers of youth with PCS. Hence, this study introduces a novel, online and group-based intervention to address caregivers' health challenges. Intervention topics will include mental health management, concussion education and self-care strategies. The proposed program 'Move&Connect-Caregivers' will run for six weeks total with one-hour session per week. The study objective is to explore the feasibility of this virtual intervention in order to suggest improvements and enhance its utility. Study methods will include conducting interviews with caregiver participants to explore their experiences with the proposed intervention. I will also collect measures pre- and post-intervention to examine changes related to mental health and family functioning. It is well-known that health of youth and caregivers are dynamically interconnected. Hence, this study will shed light on supportive strategies that will improve the well-being of families dealing with concussion.

column36: Prevalence and correlates of perceived stigma and access to medical care, employment and housing among people who use drugs in British Columbia (BC)
column37: People who use drugs are more vulnerable to stigma and its health consequences. Perceived stigma can make patients more reluctant to use services, and can lead to an increased number of emergent cases, due to a higher tendency to use drugs alone, hide drug use and an unwillingness to report stigmatized practices. It is therefore necessary to assess and inform healthcare providers and policymakers about the factors that are associated with increased perceived stigma among people who use drugs, in order to better adapt services that are patient-centred and appropriate for this population's needs. This project aims to assess the prevalence and correlates of perceived stigma, as they relate to access and use of medical care, employment and housing facilities among people who use drugs, across five health authorities in BC. Cross-sectional data from the 2020 British Columbia (BC) Harm Reduction Client Survey (HRCS) will be used to collect province-wide information on the participants' demographics, parenting/guardianship status, housing situation, drug use patterns, as well as access and barriers to harm reduction and treatment programs. The factors will be analyzed in relation to perceived stigma outcomes using predictive multivariable regression models. Moreover, a literature review will be conducted to assess previous studies on perceived stigma among people who use drugs and identify associated factors with accessing healthcare, employment and housing opportunities. This project can help inform healthcare providers and policymakers across BC regarding factors that may impact perceived stigma among people who use drugs and help identify those who are most vulnerable in the system, by comparing urban and rural locations across the province, through a quantitative analysis.

column36: L'immunogenetique et la production d'anticorps de haute affinite
column37: The immune system is complex and consists of several white blood cells that provide defense against microorganisms foreign to our body such as parasites, fungi, viruses, and bacteria. To eliminate these foreign bodies, the immune system sets up responses involving the production of antibodies. These antibodies can recognize and facilitate the elimination of the intruder, as well as protect us from a secondary infection to the same foreign body. As we know, each of us responds differently to an infection explaining why, for a given disease, some are more ill than others. Variations in the genetic code of each individual partly contribute to this divergence. Dr. Lesage's group has shown that the genetic variability driving immune differences in humans can be paralleled by studying the immune system in multiple genetically divergent mouse strains. We hypothesize that the induction of immune responses leading to effective antibody production will differ for each mouse strain. To define the genetic underpinnings driving this difference, we will vaccinate various types of mice with different foreign bodies such as sheep red blood cells. The efficacy of the immune response generated to these foreign bodies will be quantified in each mouse. This project will allow us to determine the impact of genetic variability on the immune response and to identify genes that facilitate better immune responses. The information gained during this project will enable us to improve vaccination protocols, anti-cancer responses, production of antibodies for therapeutic purposes, and more, consequently improving the health of Canadians.

column36: Lived Experiences with Symptomatic Degenerative Cervical Radiculopathy: The Patients' Perspectives
column37: Degenerative cervical radiculopathy (DCR) is a condition causing irritation to branches of the spinal cord in the neck region, leading to severe neck and arm pain, numbness, tingling and weakness. These symptoms can result in significant disability, leading to a negative impact on a person's quality of life. Non-surgical management is the first-line of treatment, with the majority of patients recovering and not requiring surgery. However, high quality research examining these non-surgical management options is lacking. One important step for the development of useful interventions involves understanding the physical, psychological and functional impact a condition has on an individual's life. Intervention mapping is a 6-step process that develops an intervention based on input from patients, clinicians, and researchers. The first step is gaining a more in-depth understanding of the health problem to understand the impact that it has on the daily lives of those affected. This information is then used to guide the development of treatment objectives and outcomes. Therefore, the aim of this project will be to understand the physical, psychological, and functional experiences of individuals with DCR. Participants with DCR will be recruited from multiple clinical settings, such as neurosurgery and chiropractic clinics in order to study a wide range of symptom severity. Participants will be categorized into low and high disability focus groups with interview questions exploring the physical, psychological and functional impact of DCR on participants' lives. The results of this work will provide the basis for future intervention mapping steps, in order to ensure that the intervention developed will be effective, useful, and importantly, meet patients' needs and expectations.

column36: Impact of novel anti-CD11d neurotrauma therapy on leukocyte function via outside-in signalling
column37: Impact of novel neurotrauma therapy on white blood cell function. A novel CD11d antibody therapy has been developed at the Robarts Research Institute that improves recovery following neurotrauma. Neurotrauma includes traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries which damage the central nervous system (CNS). The early immune response to neurotrauma induces a harmful migration of inflammatory white blood cells into the CNS and exacerbates the injury. The late immune response, however, induces the migration of beneficial white blood cells into the CNS and aids in recovery. The CD11d antibody therapy functions by reducing the early migration of inflammatory white blood cells into the CNS but allows for the beneficial pro-recovery migration. Exciting previous studies from our lab have shown that CD11d therapy improves neurological recovery in both rat and mouse neurotrauma models. We know that the promising neurological recovery is a result of CD11d therapy altering the ability of white blood cells to migrate into the CNS, but we do not know if the therapy also affects the normal cellular function of white blood cells in the body. My project is designed to determine how CD11d antibody therapy binds white blood cells and potentially alters their function. Significance: Neurotrauma is a devasting injury that has serious complications and debilitating long term consequences. The fact that no current neurotrauma treatment can improve neurological recovery makes developing an effective neurotrauma therapy a serious unmet global medical need. Understanding the impact of CD11d antibody binding on white blood cells is necessary to ensure the safety of the exciting CD11d antibody therapy. Additionally, my project may produce the potency tests required for future clinical trials.

column36: Investigating the Mechanisms Driving Fluoroquinolone-Associated Aortic Remodelling
column37: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are amongst the most prescribed in the world. These drugs provide an invaluable resource to physicians against respiratory and urinary tract infections. Recent clinical studies have shown, however, that these antibiotics increase the risk of rupture and dissection of the aorta – the main artery that carries blood from the heart. Aortic rupture and dissection are catastrophic events and often results in death, and frequently do not have symptoms until it is already too late. The high usage rates of fluoroquinolones coupled with the devastating consequences of aortic rupture and dissection present a major health problem. The way in which fluoroquinolones increase risk of aortic rupture and dissection remains unclear. Thus far, studies examining fluoroquinolones and aortic disease have only focused on one specific fluoroquinolone called ciprofloxacin. These studies have found possible ways in which ciprofloxacin may break down the walls of the aorta. However, there are tens of fluoroquinolone antibiotics and ciprofloxacin is only one of these. We must then ask the question: are all fluoroquinolones harmful to the aorta? My study uses cell and animal studies to investigate if differences exist between fluoroquinolones, and their effect on the aorta. We will also study how these antibiotics cause aortic damage. By determining if some fluoroquinolones are less harmful than others, this study can optimize how physicians treat infections with this life saving class of antibiotics.

column36: The relationship between maternal dietary patterns with maternal iron and Vitamin D status and their impact on maternal, infant and child health
column37: Deficiencies of important nutrients, including iron and Vitamin D, during pregnancy are commonly associated with poor health outcomes, including altered brain development in infants and impaired mental health in mothers. Despite this, very little is currently known about how very high nutrient statuses and very low nutrient statuses, which can occur during different pregnancy timepoints, impact specific health outcomes. In response, this project will explore if the dietary intakes and nutrient statuses of mothers, during different pregnancy and postpartum periods, are associated with the health of mothers, infants and children. Specifically, the objectives involve determining how maternal blood iron markers, including iron stores, change at all three trimesters and at 3 months post-birth. The impact of iron statuses, Vitamin D status, and dietary patterns, with an emphasis on milk and dairy intake, on maternal mental health, infant growth and brain development, and child brain development and behaviour will also be explored. Data will be used from the Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) study, which recruited 2,200 pregnant Albertan women from 2009-2012. Dietary and mental health data was collected from mothers, and growth and neurodevelopmental data was collected from their infants and children up to 8 years old. This data will be extracted from our APrON databases and dietary patterns will be determined using our dietary records. Iron markers and Vitamin D will be measured in the blood. Analysis will involve the use of multiple statistical tests. Results will provide new evidence regarding the potential health implications of a mother's nutritional intake across pregnancy and postpartum, which may guide future dietary and clinical recommendations.

column36: Effets durables de la prise de la pilule contraceptive sur les fonctions cognitives
column37: Au Canada, la pilule contraceptive constitue la methode contraceptive reversible la plus utilisee chez les femmes de 15 a 49 ans. La pilule contraceptive est composee d'hormones sexuelles synthetiques. Le corps etant expose a ces hormones synthetiques, il en diminue sa production naturelle. Les recepteurs d'hormones sexuelles sont situes dans des regions du cerveau qui sous-tendent certaines fonctions cognitives pour lesquelles la performance differe selon le sexe, notamment les habiletes visuospatiales et les habiletes verbales. Les resultats de recentes etudes suggerent qu'au-dela d'une difference due au sexe, les modulations hormonales causees par la prise de la pilule contraceptive influenceraient ces fonctions cognitives. a ce jour, les etudes ont grandement etudie le phenomene chez les femmes qui prennent actuellement la pilule contraceptive, sans s'attarder a ses effets potentiellement durables. En effet, des etudes recentes suggerent qu'une prise d'hormones sexuelles synthetiques peut induire des effets a long terme sur le cerveau qui persisteraient m eme apres l'arr et de l'utilisation de la pilule. Ce projet vise donc a examiner les effets a long terme de la prise de la pilule contraceptive sur des fonctions cognitives pour lesquelles les hommes et les femmes performent differemment. etant donne le lien entre les hormones sexuelles et la performance a certaines taches cognitives, il importe de documenter la persistance des effets de variations hormonales sur la cognition. Une meilleure connaissance de la durabilite de ces effets fournirait davantage d'informations aux cliniciens sur les consequences de la pilule contraceptive, ce qui permettrait aux jeunes femmes de faire un choix plus eclaire quant a la contraception qu'elles souhaitent utiliser.

column36: Measuring Mitochondrial Protein Turnover Rates in an Organoid Model of Parkinson's Disease
column37: Parkinson's Disease is a devastating brain disorder that affects movement, leading to shaking and stiffness. As the disease progresses, patients may have difficulty walking or talking and can develop behavioral changes such as depression. Medication can improve the symptoms but cannot cure the disease as we do not fully understand the root cause of the disorder. The goal of this project is to investigate potential underlying causes of this illness. One of our interests includes studying a protein called alpha synuclein which is associated with Parkinson's Disease. The abnormal form of this protein is not degraded properly by the body and could potentially interfere with the creation, breakdown and recycling (turnover) of other proteins in the body. This can be harmful as it could disrupt a cell's ability to communicate, produce energy…etc. The cells in the brain responsible for Parkinson's Disease require a lot of energy and could be vulnerable to any imbalances. Hence, our project plans to create a model of these cells and study the effect that abnormal alpha synuclein has on the turnover of other proteins. Currently, protein turnover has never been studied in mammals and this project could lead to exciting treatment methods for Parkinson's Disease.

column36: Cannabidiolic acid methyl ester as preventive treatment in a preclinical model of schizophrenia risk
column37: The objective of this study is to uncover the role of the endocannabinoid system, its interaction with the serotonergic/dopaminergic and neuro-immune systems in neural inflammation, neural development, and schizophrenia-related cognitive and social impairments. Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental disorders with multiple symptom presentations that typically emerge in late adolescence and early adulthood. Schizophrenia remains incurable, and an alternative approach to treatment is the development of drug interventions that could prevent the conversion of early prodromal symptoms to schizophrenia in clinically-at-risk individuals. Of recent interest for neuropsychiatric therapeutics is cannabis' non-intoxicating component, cannabidiol (CBD). CBD acts on CB1/CB2, likely to mediate its ant-inflammatory effects, but also modulates the serotonin system as agonist on serotonin-1A receptors, which are implicated in cognitive-emotional behavior, and in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Cannabidiolic acid (CBDA) methyl ester (HU-580), a more stable derivative of the precursor of CBD, has been reported to be more potent for its serotonergic effects, and therefore a promising alternative for therapeutic development. By uncovering the role of the endocannabinoid system and the effects of cannabis in neural inflammation and serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission resulting from prenatal viral infection, we will be able to determine new avenues of developing preventive treatments for schizophrenia when a cure remains elusive. This has clinical implications not only for schizophrenia but also for neuropsychiatric conditions that may arise from abnormal immune activation, including those that could be related to covid-19

column36: Non-Opioid Prescriptions after Arthroscopic Surgery in Canada (NO PAin): A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Orthopaedic surgeons prescribe more opioids than any other type of surgeon. Opioids have the potential to be highly addictive and can cause serious harm or even death if taken in excess. They are routinely prescribed after surgical operations even though there is little evidence to suggest that they are needed. Knee and shoulder arthroscopy are the most common orthopaedic surgeries and the majority of Canadian surgeons prescribe opioids after arthroscopic surgery. Previous research has shown that non-opioid pain medications, including anti-inflammatories, may provide adequate pain relief after these operations. We don't know if opioids are required for pain control after arthroscopic surgery. The aim of our study is to determine whether a standardized prescription of non-opioid pain medications and a patient education infographic reduces opioid consumption while still effectively managing patients pain and function after shoulder or knee arthroscopy. Patients will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group 1 will receive a non-opioid medication, a patient education infographic and small ""rescue"" opioid prescription. Group 2 will receive the current standard of care, an opioid. We will ask patients if, and how many opioids they took, how much pain they have, and how satisfied they are with their pain control. We will also collect data on how many patients requested a refill of their meds, and any adverse events that happen during the study. The two groups will be statistically compared postoperatively. We will determine if this standardized approach to pain management after surgery reduces opioid medication use without negatively affecting pain and satisfaction.

column36: Mechanisms of change in CBTp: comparing the effects of cognitive restructuring, cognitive defusion, and belief monitoring on distress about voices
column37: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for psychosis (CBTp) is an effective treatment for individuals with schizophrenia. However, it has considerable room for improvement. To improve the efficacy of CBTp, it is important to determine the components of the therapy that lead to therapeutic change. For the majority of individuals with schizophrenia, therapeutic change means reducing distress from psychotic symptoms, such as hearing voices. Changing one's beliefs about psychotic symptoms is a CBTp technique called cognitive restructuring and is thought to reduce distress. Another cognitive technique is called cognitive defusion, which involves creating distance from the literal meaning of a distressing thought. The current study will determine which one of these techniques is best at reducing distress around voices in psychosis. Furthermore, the mechanisms through which cognitive restructuring and cognitive defusion effect change may overlap. Therefore, this study will inform what mechanisms are involved in cognitive restructuring and cognitive defusion. In this study, participants will practice cognitive restructuring or cognitive defusion exercises when they hear distressing voices throughout a period of one week. The technique that leads to the greatest reduction in distress will be evaluated. Participants will also report which strategies in the exercises helped reduce distress. The results will inform which technique is best at reducing distress around voices and why one or both of these techniques are effective. Overall, this study will help improve the efficacy of CBTp and recovery from psychosis.

column36: A chemogenetic approach to recovering breathing after opioid-induced respiratory depression
column37: The use of both prescription and non-prescription opioids has led to over 16 000 deaths in Canada over the past 4 years. When opioid overdose occurs, there is a decrease in respiratory rate and potentially total respiratory failure. Currently, Naloxone is effectively used to counteract opioid overdoses but, in recovering breathing, the pain-relieving effects of the opioid is also lost. The pre-Bötzinger complex is known to be a crucial area within the brain for inducing respiration. We believe that selectively activating cells in this region of the brain will allow for recovery of breathing without impacting the pain-relieving effects of opioid treatment. Through viral vectors, we are able to introduce designer receptors into the pre-Bötzinger complex that are not responsive to any naturally occurring substances in the body. After these receptors are incorporated into the cells, we can inject clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) which is known to bind exclusively to these receptors. In theory, only the cells containing the designer receptors will be activated by the injected CNO. Since we only insert these receptors into the pre-Bötzinger complex, CNO injection should cause an increase in respiration. If the system works as we expect, the decrease in breathing caused by opioids can be recovered through subsequent receptor activation with CNO. Ultimately, the goal of this study is to determine whether the pre-Bötzinger complex is an available target for more selective interventions for the recovery of breathing after opioid treatment. Since opioids are crucial in the treatment of pain, there is a need for recovery from respiratory depression without diminishing pain-relief.

column36: Neuronal Protection Following Spinal Cord Injury Through Inhibition Of The Mitochondrial Calcium Uniporter
column37: Traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) is a devastating condition where patients lose sensation and locomotion, making them dependent on lifelong support. tSCI causes direct damage to nerve cells (neurons) and also initiates a cascade of destructive events termed 'secondary' spinal cord injury (SSCI). These events last for days to weeks and cause further loss of function, mainly as a result of additional neurons dying. If the early causes for the various destructive events are targeted, it should be possible to effectively treat SSCI. Each neuron contains about 1000 mitochondria which are small structures providing its energy. The mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) is an opening in the mitochondrial membrane that allows calcium and iron into mitochondria. After tSCI, calcium and iron levels rise excessively, damaging the mitochondria and ultimately killing the nerve cell. We propose that blocking the MCU early after tSCI will safeguard mice from SSCI by protecting mitochondria. This will be tested as follows. First, we will study if genetically altered mice with MCU selectively inactivated in neurons are resistant to SSCI. Next, we will test the protective effects of injecting normal mice with a newly developed, potent MCU blocker called Ru265, following tSCI. The ability of Ru265 to improve mobility after tSCI will also be studied. These findings would encourage the development of drugs to block the MCU for the prevention of SSCI.

column36: The impact of frailty on long-term adverse outcomes of cardiac rehabilitation patients
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) involve problems of the heart or blood vessels. They affect one in three older adults, making it a leading cause of death in Canada. Often, those living with CVD also have a number of other health problems which impact their health. People with many health problems can be described as frail. Research has estimated that frailty is present in up to half of patients living with CVD; this is concerning because frailty can worsen the problems of CVD. Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) programs help patients recover from CVD and related events, such as a heart attack. These programs support patients with exercise, education, and counselling. Research shows that these programs improve quality of life, unplanned hospital visits, and premature death. Our research group has shown that many CR patients are frail, and completion of the program reduced their frailty levels. However, we do not know if reducing frailty improves the long-term health outcomes of patients. Our work will determine if reducing frailty levels with CR can reduce the risk of dying prematurely or being re-admitted to the hospital. My study will investigate the change in frailty of 4000 people in a Nova Scotian CR program. These frailty changes will be linked with health data which keep records of deaths and hospital admissions. We will analyse this data to determine if frailty improvements from completing CR leads to better patient health outcomes. If improving patient frailty improves their long-term health, then frailty screening and management could be additional goals of care in CR programs. These results will be useful to organizations such as the Canadian Association of Cardiovascular Prevention and Rehabilitation to address frailty in CR programs as to benefit future patients.

column36: Combined Assessment of Cognitive Load & Situation Awareness in Resuscitation Medicine: Understanding how the Novice becomes the Expert
column37: In the high stakes field of resuscitation medicine, successful patient outcomes rely on expertise in crisis resource management (CRM) skills, including situation awareness (SA) and cognitive load (CL) management. In order to understand the cognitive processes of expert physicians and novice medical students, quantitative and qualitative methods have been developed to assess CL and SA. These methods include Artificial Intelligence-driven adaptive simulation, cognitive task analysis, and measurement of SA using the Situation Awareness Global Assessment Technique (SAGAT). Despite the known importance of the development of these skills in resuscitation medicine, there is a lack of research that integrates adaptive simulation based on real-time physiological measurements of CL, assessment of SA, and post-simulation cognitive task analysis, and validates these tools across the expertise spectrum. This mixed-methods study will compare 4th-year medical students (MS4) and critical care (CCM) and emergency medicine (EP) physicians' performance on two adaptive resuscitation simulations. The study will provide a binary classification of expertise and real-time assessment of CL based on measurements of heart rate variability, galvanic skin response, and eye-tracking metrics. It is hypothesized that for a given set of responses, CCM and EPs will demonstrate more efficient utilization of CL, reduced overall CL, rapid return to baseline after CL peaking, and increased SA compared to MS4s. The results of this study will further our understanding of the quantitative and qualitative measures that separate novice and expert performance in resuscitation medicine. This will help form the foundation for future work in improving the quality of care delivered to critically ill patients.

column36: Investigating the Molecular Mechanisms Underlying Wnt-ROR2 Signalling in Human Mesoderm Cells
column37: In multicellular organisms such as humans, cells communicate with one another by sending and receiving signals. Signalling pathways regulate cell behaviours during embryonic development and throughout the lifespan to maintain tissue homeostasis. Wnt proteins are signalling molecules that bind to a variety of different receptor complexes on the surface of cells to activate multiple distinct signalling pathways inside the cell. Previously, the study of the molecular mechanisms underlying individual Wnt pathways has been limited because there have not been any laboratory techniques that can selectively activate one Wnt pathway independently from other Wnt pathways in cultured cells. The Angers lab has recently developed novel synthetic antibody molecules that can be engineered to selectively bind to a specific Wnt receptor complex and activate its corresponding signalling pathway inside the cell. For my project, I aim to utilize these antibodies to selectively activate the Wnt-ROR2 signalling pathway in human mesoderm cells. This will enable me to study the molecular mechanisms underlying this signalling pathway by analyzing changes in gene expression and protein modifications in the cells following pathway activation. The Wnt-ROR2 pathway is important in human biology because it is required to achieve normal embryonic development. Consequently, mutations in this pathway contribute to developmental defects such as Robinow Syndrome and Brachydactyly type B, which are characterized by skeletal abnormalities. This pathway also promotes the metastasis of many human cancers. Therefore, studying the Wnt-ROR2 pathway will provide insight into the molecular basis of these developmental defects and may inform new therapeutic approaches to treat cancer.

column36: Prenatal and postnatal maternal depression and child brain development
column37: The effects of the COVID-19 pandemic have led to increased symptoms of depression in pregnant individuals, with 37% of individuals experiencing elevated symptoms during the pandemic, compared to 12% before the pandemic. Depressive symptoms during pregnancy and after pregnancy can lead to behavioural problems in children and altered brain structure in regions of the brain that control emotions. The relationship between maternal depressive symptoms during different time points in pregnancy/postpartum and growth of the child brain over time remains unclear. The objective of this work is to identify how a pregnant mother's depressive symptoms during and after pregnancy might influence child brain growth in infants and in preschool-aged children. Maternal depressive symptoms were measured during pregnancy and after birth. Structural brain data were collected at multiple time points in preschool-aged children between 2.5 and 8 years of age using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before the pandemic. Brain images from infants born to mothers during the pandemic will be obtained at 3 months and 12 months of age. Volume and thickness of brain regions involved in emotional control such as the amygdala and hippocampus will be measured, and connections between these regions and frontal areas of the brain will be quantified and observed. Relationships between maternal depressive symptoms in pregnancy and the postnatal period and child brain structure will then be investigated. Through this work we will identify when in pregnancy screening and interventions may be most effective in order to improve outcomes for children and their mothers. This will be one of the first studies to observe the developing brains of infant children born during the pandemic.

column36: COVID-19 and Spinal cord injury: The impact of societal lockdown on healthcare utilization and costs for individuals with lived experience
column37: Over 85,000 in Canada have a spinal cord injury. Individuals with spinal cord injury require additional health care services, involving substantial out-of-pocket payments for these services. These health care accessibility issues may have been exacerbated by the social distancing, lockdowns, and reduction in rehabilitation clinic services during the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. column36: Gene Therapy as Treatment for Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase Primary Immune Deficiency
column37: Patients born with purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiencies suffer from recurrent infections, autoimmunity, and cognitive and developmental delays since infancy. Many of the symptoms and complications that arise from the weakened immune system in PNP deficiency can be mitigated with early diagnosis, in addition to the use of antibiotics preventatively and therapeutically, protein replacement and immune suppression medications. However, these therapies require life-long adherence to medication schedules, and are often associated with significant burdens on the patient's quality-of-life, their families and society. Currently, the only option for long-term correction of the immune abnormalities for these patients is a stem cell transplant from a healthy matched patient. This option, however, is not available for most patients while using unmatched or parent donors is associated with higher chances of complications and death from the immune reaction of the donor cells against the patient recipient following the transplant. To combat these challenges, we have produced a virus that can deliver the corrected PNP gene into the patient's cells that will be used to repair the deficiency in human patients. We will ensure that the virus is both effective in its ability to reconstitute activity of the missing or non-functional enzyme, and that it is safe for use in patients. This novel gene therapy will provide a one-time, safe and effective long-term solution for these patients thereby significantly enhancing the quality-of-life for these individuals.

column36: Identifying Drugs that Suppress Childhood Liver Diseases
column37: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis is a rare childhood disease where dysfunctional proteins in liver cells cannot support bile flow from the liver to the duodenum. Consequently, a build-up of bile acids occurs within the liver, leading to nutrition deficiencies, and other serious adverse effects including biliary stones, ductal fibrosis and liver scarring. Mild cases are treated with therapeutic agents; however, the majority of patients do not respond, and liver transplants are almost always required. Our goal is to discover a superior pharmacologic treatment resulting in restoration of bile composition facilitating proper liver function and nutrient processing. Work in our collaborator's lab has established 14 FDA-approved drugs that successfully reverse this disease in a nematode model. We propose to test these drugs in vitro using a cell culture model expressing human proteins and in a mouse model of the disease. We hypothesize that these drugs will restore the composition of bile by altering phospholipid composition, restore bile flow and alleviate the disease phenotype. To model the disease in cells, we will over-express the proteins required for bile formation and determine whether the 14 drugs impact the integrity of the plasma membrane. Furthermore, transgenic mice with dysfunctional transport proteins required to make bile will be treated with the drugs, and blood and bile will be collected to assess the effects of the drugs on the composition of bile when compared to vehicle treatment. This project aims to determine whether these drugs can inhibit dysfunctional transport proteins, thereby suppressing the cholestatic phenotype of the disease. Although this disease is rare, the development of an effective therapeutic will be life-altering.

column36: Using nanopore sequencing in CNS tumour diagnosis and characterization
column37: Every year thousands of people get diagnosed with brain tumour in North America and only about a third of all malignant (type of cancer that can spread to other parts of the body) brain tumour patients survive five years after diagnosis. Fast and accurate diagnosis of brain tumours is extremely crucial to improve patients' survival rate with timely intervention. Current diagnosis methods for brain tumour involves assessment of tissue structure and detection of DNA abnormalities known as markers. Detection protocol for these markers involves multiple testing methods requiring huge infrastructure and long turnaround times further adding to the emotional toll on patients. We want to use a new tool called MinION to overcome these challenges. MinION is a pocket-sized device known to accurately sequence DNA and detect DNA abnormalities in shorter time (hours to days) using relatively simple procedures. We aim to develop and optimize protocols to simultaneously detect the most common markers of brain tumours on a single MinION device to diagnose and characterize types of brain tumour. One of the markers we want to detect is methylation status on a gene called MGMT. Patients with methylated MGMT react better to chemotherapy and have greater survival rate. By assessing methylation status of MGMT in brain tumour patients, physicians can provide personalized treatments. We will be using brain tumour samples from patients with known tumour type and DNA abnormalities to detect the markers using MinION. We will assess validity of our developed testing methods by comparing our results with the known marker statuses of the tumour samples. In the future, this tool can also be implemented in diagnosing other types of tumours to acquire faster and easier results.

column36: Effects of Acute, High Dose Nitrate on repeated 1000m time-trial performance in Elite Cross-Country Skiers.
column37: BACKGROUND: Nitrate (NO-3) supplementation may elicit performance benefits in endurance athletes; however, few studies have looked at the effects of NO-3 supplementation on exercise relying predominantly on Type II muscle fibers found in the upper body (e.g., cross-country skiing). Type II fibers rely on nonoxidative metabolism and therefore, may have an enhanced response to NO-3 supplementation when compared to Type I fibres. The effects of dietary NO-3 have been attributed to its reduction to nitrite (NO-2) by oral bacteria, which in turn enters the circulation after swallowing, and is further reduced to nitric oxide (NO). NO has proved significant for increased mitochondrial cellular respiration, blood vessel vasodilation and muscular contraction, all of which positively effect endurance sport. For these reasons, NO-3 rich supplements, such as beetroot juice, and foods, such as leafy green vegetable, currently receive considerable attention as ergogenic aids. PURPOSE: Determine if an acute, high dose of NO-3 (8.4mmol) has a positive effect on repeated 1000m cross-country sprint races. Furthermore, our research will determine if NO-3 supplementation decreases Heart Rate (HR), decrease blood lactate levels, increases VO2 max, and decreases Rate of Perceived exertion (RPE). During each visit, participants will perform four 1000m sprints on a ski ergometer with 15-minute breaks between each sprit. HYPOTHESIS: Supplementation of acute, high dose NO3 has a positive effect on repeated 1000m sprint race times.

column37: Adverse childhood experiences, such as physical, psychological, and sexual abuse, can promote chronic stress and pain development. This proposal is for a study designed to test the nervous system's activity in individuals who have experienced at least one adverse childhood experience and now have a chronic pain condition and whether mediation is an effective treatment for these individuals. The experiment used to test these questions uses heart rate variability. Heart rate variability is the measurement of the difference in time between successive heartbeats and can be used to understand activity patterns associated with stress. Participants are monitored through a rest phase, a reactivity phase, and a recovery phase of the experiment. Electrocardiogram electrodes are attached to the participants throughout the experiment to collect their heart rate variability data. To test the participants' stress response, the experiments reactivity phase if five minutes of a Stroop task. In the Stroop task, participants are shown words that are coloured; the goal is to say the letters' colour, not the word itself. The Stroop task induces stress within the participant, which can be measured with heart rate variability. The final portion of the experiment is a guided meditation; the participant is given instructions on attending to their breath, and returning to it attentively when distracted over the 15 minute recovery phase. The goal of the meditation is to promote a relaxation response than can be measured by assessing the participants' heart rate variability.

column36: An investigation of constructs related to self-concept as mediators in the relationship between self-compassion and Generalized Anxiety Disorder symptoms in a clinical sample: A longitudinal mediation analysis
column37: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a chronic illness characterized by excessive worry, resulting in significant social and occupational impairment. GAD affects approximately 8.7% of Canadians over their lifetime, and is associated with reduced work productivity, economic loss, and elevated use of health services. As the least successfully treated anxiety disorder, more efficacious treatments that lead to full and sustained recovery are needed in order to relieve personal and societal burdens of GAD. Self-compassion (SC), defined as a kind, understanding, and non-judgemental attitude toward oneself, has been identified as a potential ameliorative factors for GAD. SC is inversely related to pathological worry and GAD symptom severity; however, little is known about how SC may lead to improvements in worry and GAD symptoms. Inflated sense of responsibility, perfectionism, and self-efficacy are self-concept constructs implicated in GAD that perpetuate worry and self-criticism, and that a self-compassionate attitude may improve. The proposed study is a longitudinal mediation analysis that will examine these constructs as mediators in the relationships between SC and worry/GAD severity. Individuals with GAD will receive a 3-week intervention intended to increase SC. It is predicted that changes in SC will inversely relate to changes in sense of responsibility and perfectionism, and positively relate to changes in self-efficacy. It is also predicted that changes in these constructs will mediate the relationships between SC and worry/GAD severity. This study is an important step in solidifying SC as a therapeutic variable in GAD. Findings could inform greater focus on SC or implementation of adjunct treatments that foster SC in order to improve treatment outcomes for GAD.

column36: Experiences of Food Sovereignty in Northern BC
column37: Compared to urban populations, northern and Indigenous communities experience the highest rates of food insecurity in Canada. Prior to colonization, which violently disrupted Indigenous food systems, Indigenous food sovereignty was a living reality. Directly related to coloniality, food insecurity is central to the disproportionately high burdens of poor health that Indigenous peoples face. Barriers to Indigenous food sovereignty is a pressing issue in Canada today as illustrated by the recent attacks on the Mi'kmaq fishery. Scholars identify food sovereignty as a valuable focus of health-related research and practice. Little research to date, however, has focused on food sovereignty in northern BC. My research addresses a gap in academic health literature by focusing on health-related experiences of Indigenous and settler food sovereignty leaders in northern BC. My research asks specifically: How does practicing food sovereignty affect peoples' health and what are the sociopolitical, environmental and cultural factors that foster (or limit) peoples' food sovereignty practices? This 2-year long, qualitative, social justice informed, health master's project (1-year CIHR funding sought) is driven by anti-colonial theory: it is sensitive to present and ongoing (neo)colonial and paternalistic research histories and approaches. The research enacts a community-based participatory process where research is conducted with and for those involved. My research is timely and significant: highlighting the experiences of those practicing food sovereignty can inform policy that supports the resilience and self-determination of those doing this work, and can translate to better physical, emotional, social, environmental and spiritual health for Indigenous and northern communities.

column36: Predictive Aspect of Optimized Bone Marrow Dosimetry on Hematological Toxicity Induced by Personalized PRRT for Neuroendocrine Tumors
column37: Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are a family of tumors originating in the diffuse neuroendocrine system. Even though most patients develop a generalized form of this condition, the presence of somatostatin receptors on their surface allows the use of treatments specifically targeting it. One such approach, the peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT), can reduce its symptoms and its progression. The most used drug for PRRT is <sup>177</sup>Lu-octreotate. It is a molecule targeting neuroendocrine tumors, namely the somatostatin analogue Octreotate, to which a Lutetium-177 atom is added. This atom is radioactive and damages tumor cells. To limit treatment toxicity, the same activity is administered for every patient every 2 months for 4 cycles. However, most recent studies have shown that severe toxicity occurs in only 10% of patients. In this context, an innovative research protocol aimed at personalizing injected activities (P-PRRT) was developed at the CHU de Quebec-Universite Laval. This protocol aims to adjust the drug dosage according to the images acquired after each treatment. These images allow the medication to be properly adjusted according to renal toxicity. However, the adjustment of doses to consider blood toxicity is not optimal. Indeed, the current method is imprecise and does not allow to predict this toxicity from imaging. We believe that we will improve the prediction of blood cells toxicity by improving the accuracy of the method currently used. This improvement will allow the adjustment of doses according to the patient's blood sensitivity. Another part of the research project is to make P-PRRT more accessible. Our automated algorithm will make it easier for clinicians to use images, which could lead to a widespread use of P-PRRT in clinical settings.

column36: Oral probiotics mediate the host innate immunity response to tackle periodontal biofilms
column37: Microorganisms residing in our oral cavity, collectively known as the oral microbiome, play major roles in systemic health and diseases. Gum disease, such as periodontitis, is a chronic inflammatory condition and the causative factor of adult tooth loss worldwide. Periodontitis significantly affects our quality of life, burdening us with deteriorating ability to eat, speak, or even smile, along with significant financial and psychological consequences, including feelings of pain, stress, and self-consciousness. In the past several years, scientists have discovered human-friendly bacteria called ""probiotics"", which have the potential to limit disease-causing bacteria. This project aims to investigate how oral probiotics can help fight periodontitis-associated bacteria, and alter our body's immune response to this disease for the better. Probiotics have attracted much attention as a potential alternative to widely used antibiotics, which carry issues such as antibiotic resistance and negative side effects. Our study will be the first-of-its-kind to use a complex multi-species biofilm model to test the effects of well-established, commercially available probiotics on the behaviour of pathogenic bacteria associated with periodontitis and the innate immune system. These findings could shape an exciting and promising new treatment for oral diseases and infections, thereby improving our oral health status and wellbeing.

column36: Optimizing an Online Couples PTSD Self-Help Treatment
column37: Cognitive-Behavioural Conjoint Therapy (CBCT) is an efficacious couples therapy that targets posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and relationship satisfaction. However, there are significant barriers to accessing CBCT, including additional barrier from the COVID-19 pandemic. To increase accessibility an online, therapist-assisted couples self-help intervention was modelled after CBCT, Couple HOPES (CH). Generic couples therapy and CBCT literature suggest that initial relationship satisfaction may moderate treatment outcomes and predict dropout. Determining if preintervention relationship satisfaction moderates outcomes in CH is imperative to ascertain if it is an effective treatment alternative for couples with both high and low relationship satisfaction. The proposed study aims to examine the effects of preintervention relationship satisfaction on PTSD, relationship satisfaction and dropout in CH. The proposed project will utilize data from a larger funded trial. Military members, veterans, first responders, and healthcare workers exposed to COVID-19 with PTSD and their significant other (N = 140) will be receive access to 7 CH modules and 4 brief therapist calls. Self-report measures will be administered at pre, mid, post, and follow up. PTSD will be assessed with the PTSD Checklist for the identified patient and the PTSD Checklist Collateral version for the partner. The Couples Satisfaction Index will assess each partners' relationship satisfaction. PTSD and relationship satisfaction outcomes will be analyzed using growth curve modelling. Dropout will be analyzed with a continuous time survival analysis. These findings have clinical implications for maximizing outcomes by paring couples with the most suitable intervention based on their relationship satisfaction.

column36: Personal factors affecting community participation for adults with acquired aphasia.
column37: Acquired aphasia is a language disorder that affects speaking, understanding, reading, and writing. Participation is often severely affected in people with aphasia due to their difficulties in communication, and this lowers quality of life. Personal factors, such as confidence or motivation, are important considerations in clinical practice, but more research is needed to understand how these personal factors interact with community participation for people with aphasia. Recent qualitative research has provided a framework of personal factors perceived by people with aphasia as being important to their community participation; however, it is unclear how this framework may be applied to people with aphasia accessing their community. Adult participants with aphasia will be interviewed about their community participation and asked to complete two relevant and comprehensive quality of life scales. Themes will be extracted from the interviews through content analysis and will summarize the influence of personal factors on community participation for our participants. These themes will be compared to their quality of life scale scores and a previous framework of personal factors in community participation to evaluate the pattern of consistencies and differences. This comparison will aid our understanding of why people with aphasia may perceive certain personal factors as important and provide an example of how to apply previous research in this area to a series of cases. The results from this study will increase clinician's understanding how to apply previous frameworks to specific patients, how the personal factors of their patients may be influencing their participation, and additionally how these personal factors may be used to increase community participation.

column36: Skeletal muscle structural and functional adaptations to training- versus immobilization-induced sarcomerogenesis in rats
column37: Immobilization of a muscle at a long length and exercise training biased to eccentric contractions both induce hypertrophy by addition of sarcomeres in series. column36: Investigating the Role of Lymphocyte Activating Gene-3 (LAG-3) in HIV Susceptibility
column37: Over 38 million people are still infected with HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) to this day, despite the use of antiretroviral therapy to combat HIV infection. Like a lock and key, the virus uses CD4 on human T-cells to attach and enter cells, for infection. Specifically, HIV's envelope protein, gp120, binds to its main receptor, CD4, and then to a host chemokine receptor enabling viral and host membranes to fuse, which allows the virus to enter cells. Lymphocyte activation gene-3 (LAG3) is a strong candidate as a surface receptor for HIV due to its high structural similarity to CD4, based on DNA sequence and function in binding shared molecules. Therefore, LAG3 can be thought of as CD4's evil twin serving as an alternative lock for HIV entry. LAG3 is an immune checkpoint (IC) molecule which inhibits the activation and functions of immune cells so the cell doesn't over react and cause harm to the host. Thus, such IC molecules serve as the breaks of immune system. Compared to other ICs, LAG3 is highly expressed on HIV-infected cells. So, is LAG3 enhancing viral entry, given its high similarity to CD4? If we block the LAG3 receptors used for entry of virus, could this be used to decrease, if not prevent, HIV infection? Hence, we aim to understand LAG3's role in HIV viral entry and discover ways to block these surface molecules to limit the HIV susceptibility of cells. Doing so would collectively reduce disease severity by not only blocking viral entry, but also reinvigorating the function of these immune cells to help the immune system in clearing HIV when HIV therapy is administered to patients. Thus, the ability to alleviate HIV susceptibility by blocking LAG3 could inform and augment current cure strategies and ultimately relieve the burden of HIV/AIDs globally.

column36: Cumulative impact of social and health disparities on pregnancy outcomes in women with disabilities
column37: Around 12% of women of childbearing age in Canada have some form of disability. In recent years, more of these women are becoming pregnant. Few research studies have looked at the ways in which these barriers come together to affect pregnancy and newborn health in women with disabilities. Therefore, the purpose of this study will be to look at the ways in which these social and health barriers combine to affect pregnancy outcomes in mothers with disabilities and their newborns. This will be done by looking at data from the health care system in Ontario, which is collected by ICES in Toronto. Mothers with disabilities will be compared to mothers without disabilities on pregnancy outcomes like gestational diabetes, high blood pressure conditions, blood clots and newborn weight and gestational age at birth, and also on how these pregnancy outcomes change for mothers based on interactions between low income, health conditions before pregnancy, or poor access to health care. It is hoped that the results of this study will improve scientific knowledge on how social and health barriers affect pregnancy and health in women with disabilities. column36: Tolerogenic RNA nanoparticles to treat autoimmunity
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by the dysregulation of multiple immunity-related genes, which results in the body's inability to tolerate the myelin proteins sheathing its nerves. The outcome is an immune system attack on the nerves and patient debilitation. A potential treatment for MS and other autoimmune diseases is to replenish regulatory T cells (Tregs), a subset of lymphocytes that maintain immune tolerance to self-proteins. Adoptive transfer of Tregs is promising to treat MS, but cell therapies have significant manufacturing and regulatory challenges, hence the importance of developing therapeutic options to induce Tregs in vivo. Current tolerogenic therapies fall short of successfully treating this autoimmune disease. Since each patient has a distinct disease signature, the lasting induction of Tregs requires a personalized therapy that can re-engineer the immune response and restore tolerance. We propose a ribonucleic acid (RNA)-based nanotechnology to treat this complex disorder. Our objective is to develop a non-immunogenic nanoparticle capable of delivering RNA combinations that expand antigen-specific Tregs. The payload includes the genetic code of the antigen requiring tolerance along with instructions to modulate the phenotype of immune cells. We hope to determine whether this unique nanotechnology can treat MS, thus paving the way for new curative treatments against MS and other autoimmune diseases.

column36: The Role of Attachment in Predicting Borderline Personality Disorder and Non-Suicidal Self-Injury
column37: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) and Non-suicidal Self-injury (NSSI) are pertinent to both psychological and healthcare areas of research. Both BPD and NSSI place individuals at an increased risk for suicidal behaviour and result in those with BPD or NSSI eliciting heavy utilization of healthcare resources. Previous research has indicated a combination of risk factors that uniquely increases risk for both BPD and NSSI. These risk factors are childhood maltreatment or an invalidating childhood environment, trait impulsivity, and emotion dysregulation(ED). Attachment has been found to be independently related to both NSSI and BPD as well as childhood maltreatment, and ED, however research has yet to combine these areas in order to clarify the role attachment may play in this complex pathway of development. Given the risk of suicide that is increased by these factors, it is an urgent area of research. The current project aims to examine the nature of this relationship by using data from a larger, multi-site study of young adults between the ages of 18-35. These young adults completed a series of self-report, diagnostic interview, and physiological measures at baseline and over a series of follow ups. The self-report and diagnostic interview measures will allow researchers to examine the role attachment plays in affecting risk factors and predicting BPD and NSSI. The current study will also examine the resulting changes in BPD symptoms and NSSI severity over the 12-month period of study that relate to the three specified risk factors as well as attachment. The findings will contribute to our understanding of BPD and NSSI development, and can inform future treatment and prevention in order to streamline treatments to suit all areas of risk.

column36: Deciphering the role of FOXA1 in diet-induced, obesity-dependent prostate cancer progression
column37: In Canada, prostate cancer remains a significant health burden, as it is the most common cancer among Canadian men. Notably, there is evidence that obesity, which can be driven by the consumption of high-fat foods, is associated with advanced prostate cancer. Understanding the molecular mechanism behind this association is of key importance, as it will help us to identify patients who are at risk for advanced prostate cancer, and it will help us to develop precision medicines for prostate cancer patients who are obese or who have these aggressive molecular profiles. Alterations in the tumour epigenome have been proposed as a potential mechanism linking diet-induced obesity and aggressive prostate cancer. Specifically, we are interested in the pioneer transcription factor forkhead box A1 protein (FOXA1) which is capable of eliciting epigenetic reprogramming and is frequently mutated in prostate cancer. Notably, preliminary data suggests that the epigenome of the cancer cells is modified during prostate cancer progression, particularly in areas associated with FOXA1 activity. These modifications are further exaggerated under conditions of diet-induced obesity. Therefore, we hypothesize that FOXA1 mediates diet-induced, obesity-dependent prostate cancer progression by inducing epigenetic reprogramming to favour cancer progression. To determine the role of FOXA1 in prostate cancer development, we will use a combination of in vitro and in vivo experiments, which will offer us insight into the role of epigenetic remodeling in the evolution of prostate cancer. This opens up the exciting possibility of leveraging epigenetic profiling in predicting patient responses to cancer treatment and in developing personalized, epigenome-based medicines.

By evaluating these targets in a mouse model of ASD, we can gain insight into the mechanism of probiotic action and further advance the process of developing probiotic treatments for this disorder.

column36: Long-term consequences of delirium among immigrant older adults: Using administrative data to explore outcomes after hospital discharge
column37: Older Canadians represent over 40% of hospital admissions and are at increased risk for experiencing hospital related harms. One of these harms is delirium, a severe neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by an acute onset of confusion. Delirium affects up to 50% of hospitalized older patients and is associated with serious consequences including functional decline, dementia and mortality. Despite this, delirium is still largely viewed as a temporary condition and there are inadequate hospital and community-based interventions to support older adults and their caregivers after discharge. Immigrant older adults, in particular women and those experiencing low income, may be at greater risk of poor outcomes after discharge due to insufficient measures to support them. In the case of delirium, there may not be equitable access to home supports and clinical follow-up, measures that help prevent further cognitive decline and long-term care home admission. There is a lack of research exploring the health inequities that may exist for immigrant populations after discharge from hospital with delirium. Our proposed study will use administrative health databases in Ontario to describe women and men 65 years and older with delirium in hospital and investigate post-discharge outcomes, such as the development of dementia. We will compare outcomes between recently immigrated and long-term residents, as well as explore key factors such as sex, age and income. We anticipate that immigrant older adults, women and those with low income will be at increased risk for developing dementia after discharge and will receive less community supports. This is a health equity issue that would be important for patients and families, and of interest to clinicians, researchers and policy makers.

column36: The role of cadherin cell adhesion molecules in postnatal porcine islet cell function.
column37: Islet transplantation is an attractive treatment for patients with type 1 diabetes, and could allow for millions of diabetics worldwide to live without insulin injections. Islet cells, found in the pancreas, secrete insulin and other hormones critical for glucose control. Clinical islet transplantation is currently limited by the finite number of human islet donors. A proposed solution to this is pig to human islet transplantation, known as pig islet xenotransplantation. This has been proven effective in various pre-clinical animal models; however, multiple immunological barriers still exist, preventing the clinical success of pig islet xenotransplantation. Many current limitations stem from an inadequate understanding of pig islet biology. Our project is focused on understanding the development of pig islets in the early postnatal period, a key time point in endocrine cell development.
