column36: Sex-Related Alterations in Joint-Specific Health and Overall Health Responses to Walking
column37: Women have a higher prevalence of osteoarthritis (OA), a common joint disease that causes breakdown in joint tissue, than men. The knee, the most common joint affected by OA results in mobility decline directly linked to poor health. There is no cure for OA and treatment focuses on symptom (i.e., pain) management. There is strong evidence for heart health benefits of physical activity (PA) like walking, but less evidence to support how long, how fast or how often someone with knee OA should walk. Baseline muscle function and walking mechanics can impact how quickly OA pain and joint damage worsens. Differences between sexes exist in baseline walking mechanics, and in pain, muscle strength, blood biomarkers, and joint structure. New research in OA populations show changes in pain, blood biomarkers, walking mechanics, and muscle function after short bouts of walking, but whether sex affects these changes is unclear. Preliminary work from our laboratory looked at changes after walking but the sample was too small to do a proper sex analysis. Women with OA have lower PA levels and more do not meet current walking recommendations than men. This study will look at whether there are differences between sexes in pain intensity and sensitization, blood biomarker, walking pattern, muscle function, and heart rate changes after 30 minutes of walking. Data will be collected in 40 men and 40 women over the age of 40 years diagnosed with OA before and after a 30-minute walk. Our findings will help us understand if women have similar or different changes in joint and heart health measures compared to men. Thus, our findings can lead to developing better walking guidelines for people with knee OA that consider differences between sexes.

column36: Integrated time-series visualization tool to facilitate AMR surveillance and outbreak investigations
column37: Understanding the transmission of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes found on mobile genetic elements by integrating genomics data with epidemiological and other contextual data is crucial to formulating policies and strategies for infection control and antimicrobial stewardship. To facilitate this understanding, I will develop an application that visualizes AMR transmission events and contextual attributes in a dynamically-generated, interactive, and compact time series diagram. I will begin the development of my application by exploring the visualization of two specific scenarios for which our lab already has data, requiring me to integrate large amounts of genotypic, phenotypic, specimen, strain, host, and geographic information. To ultimately assess the merit of my work, I will conduct a validation study on infection control healthcare workers, where I will assess the ability of participants to investigate AMR outbreaks and conduct AMR surveillance using my application. I believe my visualization solution will provide healthcare workers a more intuitive way to examine AMR transmission data than simply poring over raw tabular data.

column36: Neurophysiological and Respiratory Mechanical Mechanisms of Exertional Dyspnoea
column37: During outbreaks of respiratory diseases, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, health officials have widely encouraged the use of face masks to prevent the spread of infection. In the current COVID-19 climate, the use of face masks during exercise is being strongly encouraged, which has led some to raise concern over the potentially detrimental effects of face masks on their health. However, a recent compilation of data demonstrated that there are no abnormal physiological effects of face masks during exercise in healthy individuals. Despite this, there is consistent evidence that face masks increase the sensation of breathlessness during exercise, which may lead to decreased face mask compliance. Unfortunately, the quality of research in this area appears to be lacking with no studies having systematically examined the physiological mechanisms of breathlessness while wearing a face mask. Accordingly, this study aims to delve deeper into the relationship between face masks and the known mechanism's of breathlessness during exercise through a detailed evaluation of breathing mechanics, respiratory muscle function, and the subjective perception of breathlessness. Additionally, we aim to identify possible sex-based differences in the physiological responses to mask-wearing. Therefore, we hypothesize that face mask-induced breathlessness will be linked to increases in respiratory muscle load and activation during exercise. This study will provide the most comprehensive exploration into the physiological effects of mask-wearing on breathing mechanics and breathlessness, as well as insight into whether alterations in breathing mechanics contribute to exercise intolerance while wearing a mask.

column36: L-asparaginase-induced apoptotic pathway in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (aLL)
column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (aLL), a malignancy characterized by rapid expansion of immature lymphocytes in the blood and bone marrow, is the most common paediatric cancer and the principal cause of cancer death among children. L-asparaginase (ASNase) is a central component of current combination chemotherapy for aLL but it comes with the risk of resistance. While newer targeted therapies have been developed, their effectiveness is enhanced when used in combination with chemotherapy, which remains to be the major treatment for aLL. Patients treated with ASNase-containing regimens show greater remission induction compared to those treated with ASNase-free regimens. However, the mechanisms by which ASNase causes aLL cell apoptosis remain elusive. The proposed project is primarily based on our lab's recent discovery of the ASNase resistance biomarker that serves as a critical element of the putative PAR2 signalling pathways stimulated by ASNase to induce aLL cell apoptosis. This is the very first attempt to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which ASNase induces aLL cell apoptosis. Thus, our lab is in a unique and excellent position to address the above goal. My detailed and innovative combinatorial experimental approaches are expected to unambiguously define the involvement of the PAR2 signalling pathways in ASNase-induced aLL cell apoptosis. Results from my studies will, therefore, reveal new paths for advancing aLL research and for developing new strategies to treat aLL. Potential creation of modified forms of ASNase that cause enhanced PAR2 activation, and development of targeted therapy such as small molecular activators of PAR2 and activators/inhibitors of their downstream apoptotic mediators could prevent or stop the progression of aLL.

column36: High-affinity HLA-DP4/WT1 cognate T cell receptor screening using a novel reporter system
column37: Adoptive cell therapy is an immunotherapeutic strategy that engineers the natural human immune system to target cancers. T cell, a type of immune cell, recognizes peptide fragments (antigens) presented in complex with a molecule called major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on host cells, through surface molecules T cell receptors (TCR). In adoptive T cell therapy, tumour-responsive TCR are incorporated in natural T cells to redirect their specificity toward specific tumours. This strategy has elicited promising results targeting various diseases and provides perspectives for future tumour therapies. However, one obstacle underway is that most identified cancer-targeting T cells exhibit insufficient affinity for effective recognition of tumour antigens. One approach to tackle this challenge is to artificially enhance the affinity of the TCR while minimizing any toxicities. Here, we aim to engineer TCR responsive for Wilm's Tumour 1 (WT1), a tumour antigen expressed on various leukemia, such as acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), and solid tumours. Through manipulating the TCR gene sequence, TCR molecular structures will ultimately be altered and can elicit optimal targeting effects. In addition, unlike the current T cell therapeutic approach that primarily utilizes TCR targeting MHC-I restricted antigens, we will investigate TCR targeting MHC-II, which have been hypothesized to elicit a longer-lasting and broader anti-tumour response. This project will bring more insight into the future trajectory of adoptive T cell therapy and potentially contribute to therapeutics for patients who cannot benefit from the current immunotherapeutic strategies.

column36: Investigation of Sphingolipid Synthesis Pathway in Leukemic Stem Cells
column37: Leukemic stem cells (LSC) in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) often cause relapse, decreasing long-term survival rates among patients and raising the need for effective therapeutic strategies. We first identified essential genes for AML cell growth and viability by conducting a genome-wide CRISPR screen in a human AML cell line. The results of this screen revealed 3-dehydrosphinganine reductase (KDSR), a protein in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, as a top hit. Furthermore, analysis of LSC gene expression dataset showed high KDSR levels in LSC+ fractions of AML patient samples. KDSR is a component of de novo sphingolipid synthesis pathway, which produces key bioactive lipids such as ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P). Ceramide and S1P are indeed critical regulators of cancer progression; while ceramide levels induce cancer cell death, S1P activates signalling pathways to promote cell proliferation. Based on this evidence, I hypothesize that LSCs have increased reliance on sphingolipid synthesis pathway to increase production of S1P which promotes LSC function. I will test this hypothesis by comparing sphingolipid profiles of LSCs versus non-LSCs, characterizing the effect of KDSR inhibition on downstream sphingolipid levels, and determining the importance of KDSR for general LSC function.

column36: Investigating fatty acid metabolites in the serum of psoriatic arthritis patients using solid-phase microextraction - liquid chromatography - high-resolution mass spectrometry
column37: Psoriasis is a common inflammatory skin disease that affects more than 1.25 million Canadians. Many patients with psoriasis also develop an inflammatory arthritis called psoriatic arthritis (PsA) that affects their joints. These patients suffer from flaky, red, itchy skin and joint damage leading to reduced quality of life and functional capacity. It is important that clinicians are able to accurately assess the activity of a patient's psoriatic arthritis so that appropriate treatment can be initiated quickly to prevent joint damage. It is very difficult to assess PsA disease activity because each patient presents with a wide array of symptoms. Current methods of assessing disease activity are subjective and imprecise. A previous study looking at small molecules (metabolites) in PsA patients found that certain lipids may be able to differentiate patients based on mild, moderate and severe disease activity. The purpose of this study is to validate these potential biomarkers and determine if they correlate well with joint, skin and overall disease activity. We will test blood samples collected from patients with psoriatic arthritis who have been assessed using three separate activity measurements: ultrasound scan of their joints, severity of skin psoriasis and overall patient and physician scores. We will determine if the lipids in the blood are associated with these three clinical scores. This study will confirm previously identified small molecules and will further our understanding of metabolic pathways in PsA patients. Our future goal is to be able to translate the biomarkers we find into a clinical assessment that can be used to accurately measure disease activity and give clinicians the insight to make better treatment decisions.

column36: Exercise Intervention for Perinatal Women with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
column37: Research studies have shown exercise to be effective in decreasing the severity of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) symptoms in the general population, but no research studies to date have investigated the effect of exercise on perinatal women with a diagnosis of GAD. The objective of this study is to examine if 150 minutes of weekly moderate intensity exercise for a duration of 6 weeks effectively decreases symptoms of anxiety in perinatal women diagnosed with GAD. It is hypothesized that women who complete this exercise program will have a decrease in anxiety symptoms compared to a control group. Participants in this study will be screened to ensure they are 1) within one year postpartum or pregnant, 2) have a primary diagnosis of GAD, 3) do not have any contraindications to exercise. The weekly exercise intervention will occur over six weeks, three times a week virtually for 50 minutes. Baseline measures will be redistributed to participants after the 6 week-exercise intervention to measure changes in anxiety symptoms, or six weeks after the baseline for the control group. The results on the post-group questionnaires will be compared to the pre-group questionnaires to determine if the exercise intervention effectively decreased anxiety symptoms in perinatal women diagnosed with GAD. This will be the first study to determine if exercise decreases anxiety symptoms in perinatal women who have a diagnosis of GAD. This study will have implications for healthcare providers who have perinatal patients with GAD and for the perinatal population by providing an accessible alternative to medication and therapy to manage anxiety symptoms.

column36: How does physiological arousal in response to perception of challenge impact the rate of re-learning of walking balance post-stroke
column37: Following stroke, one key goal of rehabilitation is retraining walking ability. In fact, walking balance confidence post-stoke is a strong predictor of community re-engagement. However, how level of walking balance confidence interacts with the rate of motor learning during training of walking post-stroke remains unknown. Physiologically, perception of increased challenge to walking balance can be captured by measurement of the sweat response and skin conductance. As physiological arousal increases, skin conductance increases. This provides an objective measurement associated with balance confidence during a task that challenges walking abilities. The goal of this project is to determine how physiological arousal associated with perception of task challenge interacts with the rate of motor learning of a walking task in people with stroke. Split belt treadmill walking paradigms are used as a method to challenge walking patterns. Individuals must adapt their walking pattern to successfully walk with different belt speeds for each leg. To conduct this study 20 people with stroke and 20 age matched controls will be taken through a walking protocol consisting of walking with each side of the treadmill's split belt at different speeds. This will create greater step length asymmetry between legs. Previously, it has been shown that motor learning has occurred when both people with stroke and older adults begin to show greater symmetry between the step length of each leg. We will measure the relationship between the rate of adaptation of step length symmetry and the level of physiological arousal over time of a single training session. We will compare the strength and nature of this relationship between groups to understand how stroke impacts this aspect of motor learning.

column36: Deciphering the role of Campylobacter jejuni morphology determinants, 1291 and AmiA, in cell shape and pathogenesis
column37: Campylobacter jejuni is often the leading cause of food-borne bacterial diarrheal disease in humans in the developed world. Infection with C. jejuni, known as campylobacteriosis, commonly causes mild to severe watery or bloody diarrhea and can lead to hospitalization and death in old, young or immunocompromised patients. Even though C. jejuni can cause acute gastrointestinal disease in humans, it lacks common virulence mechanisms found in other gastrointestinal pathogens like Escherichia coli or Salmonella spp. The helical cell shape of C. jejuni has recently been found to be critical for human pathogenesis. Loss of function in enzymes that modulate peptidoglycan, a rigid structural component of the bacterial cell wall, can lead to changes in cell shape and therefore, a reduction in virulence. This research aims to further understand the connection between C. jejuni cell shape and pathogenesis by characterizing a potential peptidoglycan enzyme, 1291, and investigating its interaction with a known peptidoglycan modifying enzyme, AmiA. The role of 1291 in C. jejuni will be characterized by examining changes in the overall shape of the cell as well as motility and the ability to form biofilms in C. jejuni mutants that lack functional 1291. The interaction between 1291 and AmiA will be investigated by isolating both enzymes and performing protein binding assays as well as observing their localization in the cell. The results of this project will contribute significantly to a growing database of C. jejuni morphology factors which could be utilized for the future development of campylobacteriosis control strategies.

column36: Implementing a Quantified Intentional Binding Procedure to Assess Sense of Agency in Upper-Limb Myoelectric Prosthesis Users
column37: Many persons with limb amputation use myoelectric prostheses to perform activities of daily living. These devices are advanced technological systems that use the electrical activity from muscles within the remainder of the amputated limb to direct the movement of a robotic limb. Still, prosthesis users struggle with developing a sense of embodiment over these systems. Difficulties may be due in part to individuals lacking a Sense of Agency over their devices, which refers to a feeling of control over one's actions. This subjective experience has many implications for movement initiation and task performance; however, it is difficult to study in a quantified and objective manner. A phenomenon called Intentional Binding, which describes a subconscious compression of the time interval between a voluntary action and its sensory effects, may serve as a quantifiable measure of the Sense of Agency. Intentional Binding has been studied in previous research, but the majority of existing strategies face difficulties such as bias and variability in results. Furthermore, many studies do not address Intentional Binding in non-able-bodied individuals such as persons with amputation. In previous research, we found that an adaptive procedure was able to serve as an Intentional Binding tool in a computer-based task. Here, we aim to use this tool to quantify Intentional Binding while participants operate a myoelectric device. This experimental paradigm will allow future researchers to objectively study Intentional Binding and address its effects on myoelectric control. Results will lead to a better understanding of myoelectric control and action initiation, which may contribute to improvements in functional assessment tools and training protocols for myoelectric prosthesis users.

column36: The association between childcare attendance in early childhood and adiposity in later childhood
column37: Early childhood is a critical period for the development of healthy eating behaviours and the prevention of childhood obesity. Childhood obesity impacts children's physical health, social skills and emotional well-being. Overweight and obesity in childhood often tracks into adulthood, increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and stroke. Childcare is an important early childhood environment for an increasing proportion of Canadian children. Childcare settings can be licensed government-regulated centres or unlicensed care provided by grandparents, relatives or informal caregivers. Quality childcare has the potential to promote the development of healthy food preferences and eating behaviours, which may be related to the development of childhood obesity. Surprisingly little is known about the influence of childcare attendance on obesity, eating behaviour and dietary intake in later childhood. Our goal is to determine if children who attend childcare prior to 2 years of age have a lower likelihood of being overweight or obese and have healthier eating behaviours from 2-10 years of age. Further, we will explore how childcare setting (licensed versus unlicensed), family income and maternal employment modify obesity and nutritional outcomes. We will do this by conducting a longitudinal cohort study using data from Canada's largest children's cohort called TARGet Kids! in Toronto, which has included over 11,000 children since 2009. This research will lead to an understanding of how the childcare environment influences obesity and eating behaviours in later childhood. It will also address a knowledge gap for supporting licensed childcare as a policy relevant intervention to prevent childhood obesity and promote the health of Canadian children.

column36: Neural Biomarkers of Response Inhibition in Borderline Personality Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder and Associations with Disinhibited Personality Traits
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) and major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently co-occur and both diagnoses are associated with impairments in everyday functioning and well-being. A central impairment in these disorders is the ability to exert control over one's behaviours, commonly referred to as response inhibition. Using brain imaging, researchers have identified brain regions underlying response inhibition that are disrupted in people with BPD and MDD. Separately, neural activation during response inhibition has been linked to personality traits related to disinhibition (e.g., impulsivity, risk-taking), a pathological personality trait dimension that cuts across traditional diagnostic boundaries and is featured in proposed alternative dimensional diagnoses of personality disorder. To date, no research has examined whether activity in brain regions involved in response inhibition is more substantially disrupted in people with both BPD and MDD compared to MDD alone, and whether individual differences in disinhibition are related to such brain activity regardless of diagnosis. The proposed study will analyze an existing brain imaging dataset of individuals with these diagnoses, as well as controls with neither diagnosis, to compare brain activation differences and associations this activation with disinhibited personality traits. The findings from this research have potential to clarify whether disruptions in neural activation underlying response inhibition in MDD are further impacted by BPD, and perhaps more crucially, to identify how such brain activation relates to a cross-cutting pathological personality trait dimension, which would ultimately support the validity of proposed alternative dimensional personality disorder conceptualizations.

column36: Imaging Synaptic Function in Mouse Models of Autism
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a diverse group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by social and cognitive deficits that affect up to 2% of the population. There currently exist no effective diagnostics or treatments for these conditions, demonstrating the need for the further study of ASD. Synaptic dysfunction has been identified as a common pathology of ASD. This proposal aims to study synaptic function through imaging of synaptic formation and transmission in rodent models of ASD using three positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers. [<sup>18</sup>F]SynVesT-2 will be used to image synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) in order to approximate synaptic density to study impaired synapse formation and vesicle-mediated neurotransmitter release in these conditions. Hyper-glutamatergic signaling is often observed in patients with ASD, so excitatory signaling will be indirectly imaged by targeting metabotropic glutamate receptor subtype-5 (mGluR5) using [<sup>18</sup>F]FPEB. Lastly, gamma amino butyric acid receptor A (GABA-A) expression will be visualized using [<sup>11</sup>C]RO6899880 to study potential suppression of inhibitory signaling in ASD. All three radiotracers will be used in novel and well-characterized murine models of ASD, as well as healthy controls, as a method of evaluating novel murine models, investigating shared synaptic dysfunctions, and performing a preclinical validation of the proposed radiotracers. Successful completion of the proposed work will provide novel insight into synaptic function in rodent models of ASD to guide new diagnostics and treatment strategies. Preclinical validation of the proposed radiotracers would permit for their clinical translation, and provide a significant clinical impact in the form of a potential diagnostic tool in human patients.

column36: Development of a computational pathology toolbox for advanced cancer diagnostics using artificial intelligence
column37: In 2020, approximately 225,000 Canadians are expected to be diagnosed with cancer. In each case, experienced pathologists analyze tumour slides and molecular data to reach a final diagnosis. Recently, advances in artificial intelligence (AI), specifically deep learning, have allowed AI-based programs to perform at an expert-level in medical image analyses, including classification of tumour slides. Most studies to date, however, have mainly shown proof-of-concepts rather than developing tangible platforms for widespread adoption by the research and medical communities. This project aims to address this issue by developing an online repository of computational tools that can begin refining many traditionally manual tasks in pathology. Ultimately, we aim to integrate several deep learning classifiers on this easily accessible website to generate pathologist-like reports. To do this, we will first develop a classifier that classifies common brain tumors based on their size and shape. Then we will develop molecular classifiers to subclassify the common brain tumor types and resolve challenging cases based on the presence of molecular markers. Both types of classifiers will be developed by training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) using images of different brain tumours. The tools will also be validated using test images for diagnosis accuracy. By the completion of this award, we will have developed the first AI-driven interface that integrates both molecular and histomorphologic information to automatically generate standardized expert-level neuropathology reports. By making these decision support tools widely available, this project is expected to accelerate the eventual routine adoption of deep learning in cancer research and clinical care.

column36: Improving radical cystectomy outcomes by developing a surgical guideline
column37: Radical cystectomy is a complex surgical procedure which includes removal of the bladder, adjacent organs and lymph nodes and creation of an new urine reservoir with intestine. This is considered the gold standard curative surgical therapy for treating aggressive bladder cancer. Radical cystectomy is among the most morbid surgical procedures and many patients experience complications during their recovery. These complications and overall outcomes have been found to be quite varied between surgeons. While clinical practice guidelines help clinicians treat medical conditions in a standardized way, there are no procedural guidelines that exist that attempt to summarize optimal surgical care. We aim to use radical cystectomy as a prototype procedure to generate a surgically oriented guideline to help surgeons provide standardized care for bladder cancer patients and improve clinical outcomes. Our hope is that this will be translatable to other surgical procedures across various surgical specialties.

column36: MicroRNA targets, genetic variation and schizophrenia expression in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
column37: About 1 in 3000 people are born with a piece of genetic information (DNA) missing from one copy of their chromosome 22. Individuals with this disorder, called 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11.2DS), are about 20 times more likely to develop schizophrenia (SCZ), a severe psychiatric illness. Having a 22q11.2 deletion leads to a reduction in a class of small molecules called microRNAs (miRNAs), which help turn off other genes. Multiple genetic factors are believed to be important in causing SCZ, and changes to miRNA levels may be a critical link in the cascade of events that lead to SCZ. Genetic variation includes structural changes (copy number variants or CNVs) and changes at a single building block of DNA (single nucleotide variants or SNVs). Scientists have proposed that a reduction in miRNAs may cause genetic variants that are normally tolerated to increase risk for expressing an illness. We think that the lower levels of miRNAs in 22q11.2DS could therefore increase the potential for expression of SCZ. We will use DNA sequencing data from people with 22q11.2DS to study this. We predict that in those with SCZ, compared to those with no SCZ, there will be a higher proportion of CNVs and SNVs that affect the gene targets of the miRNAs that are reduced in 22q11.2DS. We will assess the significant findings using data from general population SCZ samples from international repositories. Identifying genetic changes that lead to SCZ and are involved in a miRNA mechanism in 22q11.2DS may help explain why individuals with 22q11.2DS are at such a high risk to develop SCZ. Most importantly, a miRNA mechanism could lead to a better understanding about SCZ in general, and could lay the foundation for developing new therapies.

column36: Transitions in Care from Hospital to Community for People Who Use Drugs: An Investigation of Predictors of Engagement in Outpatient Addiction Care after Hospital Discharge
column37: Despite increased vulnerability following hospital discharge, little is known about transitions in care from hospital to community and associated outcomes for people who use drugs (PWUD) in a Canadian context. Addressing the existing knowledge gap is essential to improving hospital-based care for PWUD, preventing morbidity and mortality, and addressing the ongoing opioid crisis in British Columbia. This proposal describes a Master's project conducting an analysis of sociodemographic and linked administrative health data from the ongoing longitudinal cohort Tracking Health Outcomes & Health Care Utilization among Patients Evaluated for Addiction Care (OPAC) Study (PI: Dr. Seonaid Nolan). This study contains sociodemographic, clinical, behavioural, and health service utilization data for a sample of patients accessing specialized addiction care in hospital. I will use the OPAC study data to: 1) investigate proportions of patients engaged in outpatient addiction care at 30 days, six months, and one year; 2) compare overdose mortality for patients who access outpatient addiction care following hospital discharge compared to those who do not; and 3) identify sociodemographic factors, substance use patterns, clinical, and structural predictors associated with engagement in outpatient addiction care at 30 days, six months, and one year. Findings from this research will contribute to the continued development of evidence-based interventions for addressing the critical transition from acute to outpatient addiction care. Overall, this research will serve to contribute to addressing the absence of research on transitions in care for PWUD in order to improve care, prevent associated morbidity and mortality, and address the ongoing opioid crisis.

column36: The role of the RNA-binding protein G3BP1 in senescence-associated neurodegeneration.
column37: As the global life expectancy increases, the prevalence of age-related neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases rises steadily. Developing therapeutics for these disease requires a greater understanding of aging at the molecular and cellular level. A well-established hallmark of aging organisms is cellular senescence, a complex cellular program by which olders cells cease to replicate. Although senescence is a tumor-protective mechanism in young individuals, the accumulation of senescent cells throughout life is thought to be at the root of many age-related diseases. The deleterious effects of senescence are mediated by the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP): pro-inflammatory molecules secreted by senescent cells, known to promote disease in otherwise healthy cells. Astrocytes are brain cells known to undergo senescence. We wish to study the effect of astrocyte SASP on the onset of neurodegenerative diseases.Our laboratory has shown that impairing senescent cells' ability to make a protein called G3BP1 prevents the SASP. We generated astrocytes depleted of G3BP1, which can become senescent but cannot secrete SASP. We will co-culture these astrocytes with neurons to determine whether SASP is indeed involved in neurodegenerescence. Then, we will identify the mechanism by which G3BP1 promotes the SASP when it is present. G3BP1 is a protein that binds messenger RNAs (mRNA), an intermediate molecule between a DNA gene and the functional protein product of that gene. When G3BP1 binds mRNAs, it is thought to protect them and to promote protein production from this mRNA. We will identify the specific mRNAs to which G3BP1 binds, and exactly how it impacts these mRNAs.This will lay the groundwork for further therapeutic research.

column36: Understanding and controlling mouse embryonic stem cell competition
column37: Due to their ability to continuously divide and produce all the cell types in our bodies, pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) represent a powerful tool for understanding development and for generating therapeutic cells. Recently, research unexpectedly has shown that these cells are constantly competing with one another, driving out their unhealthy neighbours. This process, cell competition (CC), has been shown both with cells in a dish and during embryonic development across several species, indicating its importance. While our knowledge of what causes a cell to be unhealthy has been growing, how these cells communicate and compare their health remains unknown. Using mouse embryonic stem cells (mECSs), a type of PSC, I first aim to define a consistent and reproducible way to measure the competition between cells. With my standardized test, I can investigate how previously ignored culture conditions affect competition and better understand what happens to cells that lose in competition. I will use this new testing approach to allow mESCs to compete and measure the proteins found on the surface of winner and loser cells. In doing so, I will be able to identify these cell surface proteins that allow cells to communicate with each other as they compete, labeling themselves as winners or losers for their neighbours to see. Finally, by finding these proteins, we can control competition by either removing a cell's ability to communicate its winner or loser state, or by masking a weaker cell as a winner by allowing it to display winner proteins on its surface. By controlling CC in this way, we can gain further insight into the role of competition during development and can better control the production of next-generation cell-based therapies.

column36: Development of a Patient-Reported Outcome Measure for Genito-Pelvic Pain Associated with Vaginal Penetration
column37: Painful sex (dyspareunia) is a common phenomenon, a contributor to infertility concerns, and is associated with reduced quality of life and decreased sexual satisfaction. Diagnosis of the cause(s) underlying dyspareunia rely on a clinician's understanding of a patient's location of pain. Therefore, if pain location is not clearly characterized, this may prevent adequate treatment of the dyspareunia. Patients commonly report sexual pain at more than one anatomic location, presenting a challenge in patient-clinician communication pertaining to location and other dyspareunia features. Current measures used to characterize dyspareunia inadequately account for diversity in sexual experiences, were not developed with patient partners, are specific to a single gynecological condition, and/or are not validated to differentiate between locations of pain. This project's objective is to develop a patient reported outcome measure that characterizes personal experience of dyspareunia with respect to location and impact: The Deep vs Superficial Pain Questionnaire (DSPQ). In aim one, a comprehensive item list will be established for the DSPQ via item identification and subsequent review by a panel of patient partners, psychologists, researchers, and physicians. In aim two, the DSPQ will undergo focus group, cognitive interview and pilot psychometric testing in patients to qualitatively assess content validity and inform DSPQ modifications. The DSPQ will validly assess patient report of pain location and descriptors resulting from penetrative sexual activity to decipher probable cause(s) of dyspareunia, outline a targeted patient oriented approach to treatment, and provide a sensitive and standardized method to examine changes in dyspareunia outcomes in clinical and research settings.

column36: Estimating prognosis among advanced heart failure patients referred for advanced heart failure therapies
column37: This single-center retrospective cohort study aims to evaluate the accuracy and potential clinical impact of existing and newly derived risk prediction models to estimate 1-year mortality risk in patients undergoing assessment for advanced heart failure (HF) therapies. In light of the increasing prevalence of HF, and high associated mortality rate, advanced HF patients are often considered for advanced therapies, namely ventricular assist device or heart transplant. These therapies aim to improve quality of life and patient survival but are costly and associated with serious risk. Given the clinical complexity of this patient population, evaluating prognosis for advanced HF patients is very challenging. Predictive models may offer important advantages to help physicians when evaluating the risk of mortality and candidacy for advanced HF therapies. I plan to conduct a retrospective analysis to 1) evaluate the accuracy of existing risk models for predicting risk of mortality among adults with advanced HF; 2) determine if a new risk model, developed using a larger scope of clinical data results in more accurate prognostic estimates; (3) evaluate the impact of using the best performing model among HF patients deemed adequate and inadequate candidates for advanced HF therapies; and (4) evaluate the clinical benefit of these therapies for patients considered appropriate candidates. This study will inform future guidelines and practices for assessing risk in advanced HF patients. By developing a more powerful risk prediction model, we hope to improve prognostic accuracy in this high-risk population, better identify who should receive advanced therapies, and optimize donor organ allocation and healthcare resources in Canada.

column36: Follow-Up and Patient Expectations for Thyroid Cancer Survivors Transitioning From Cancer Treatment Teams to Primary Care
column37: The number of new thyroid cancer cases has been rising in Canada, and it is now the fifth most common cancer in women. This is partly due to earlier detection of small, low-risk tumours. Consequently, there are more people with successfully treated thyroid cancer, referred to as thyroid cancer survivors. Currently, more than 1,500 thyroid cancer survivors in Nova Scotia are followed by one specialized hospital-based cancer care team, as they need lifelong monitoring and follow-up. Due to increasing strain on limited healthcare resources and recent research showing similar patient outcomes with lower healthcare related costs, there is serious interest in transitioning the long-term follow up of low-risk thyroid cancer survivors to primary care. However, the optimal approach to do so remains unclear. Recently, a national study from the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer using the comprehensive ""Cancer Transition Survey"" showed that cancer survivors consistently report unmet physical and emotional needs in the transition to community care. However, as thyroid cancer survivors were not included in this study their experiences and concerns specific to this vulnerable transition period are not yet known. I plan to administer the ""Cancer Transition Survey"" in adult patients with low-risk thyroid cancer transitioning to primary care within Nova Scotia to assess their unmet needs and compare this to existing provincial data from other cancer survivors. With this key understanding on the patient-perspectives of thyroid cancer survivorship we hope to empower cancer-care and primary care teams to better support and advocate on behalf of thyroid cancer survivors and their families.

column36: Passing the buck? Impact on caregiver burden when shifting to outpatient surgery
column37: With recent advancements in surgical care and anaesthetics, there is a rising interest in shifting typical short-stay inpatient surgeries (e.g. knee replacement, total hip replacement) to outpatient pathways, allowing patients to return home on the same day of surgery. Prior studies have demonstrated outpatient surgery to improve patient satisfaction and reduce the caregiving responsibilities of the hospital. However, a large portion of the caregiving responsibilities saved by the hospital is now being passed onto the caregiver of the patient. Caregiver burden is the stress perceived by the caregiver when looking after a family member. While most studies have focused on the benefits of outpatient pathways, the impact on the burden of care placed on caregivers has not been investigated. This is a critical knowledge gap that greatly affects the caregiver's quality of life and slows down the progress of modernizing surgical care. In this study, we aim to create an understanding and ideally quantify, the various dimensions contributing to caregiver burden in the outpatient setting. Through a scoping review, our team will develop a framework aimed at identifying the various dimensions of caregiver burden. Using our framework, we will interview caregivers of patients undergoing outpatient total hip and knee replacement at Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Ontario to determine and rank the most important factors contributing to the burden of care. With the increasing number of outpatient procedures being performed, caregiver burden has the potential to become its own healthcare problem. Therefore, our framework aims to understand and identify the most important factors contributing to caregiver burden in order to make meaningful improvements in the future.

column36: Molecular Characterization of Premalignant Lesions in Pancreatic Cancer
column37: Pancreatic cancer is a lethal disease with only 9% of patients surviving past 5 years. Patients are often diagnosed late and have rapidly deteriorating conditions. Early detection has the potential to increase survival by 30-40%, though efforts are hindered by the lack of understanding of how certain premalignant lesions can initiate and progress to pancreatic cancer. The most common precursor lesions, referred to as PanINs, are currently thought to be initiated by the mutation of the gene KRAS alone; however, recent evidence suggests otherwise. Thus, to study the evolutionary progression of pancreatic cancer, I aim to determine the dysregulated pathways responsible for PanIN lesions by profiling their transcriptomic signatures. I hypothesize that KRAS mutations occur in conjunction with secondary pathway alterations to form PanINs. First, I will model the effects of KRAS activation in patient-derived, normal pancreatic cells in vitro. Then, I will verify the results and identify other altered pathways in PanINs from patient-derived tissue sections. To do this, I will use spatial transcriptomics, a novel technology that allows sequences to be mapped back onto a location in the original sample. This will allow for the identification of signatures specific to PanIN lesions, without losing precision from a decrease in resolution, or losing accuracy if confused with signatures of contaminating invasive tumors. Overall, this work will aid to inform the diagnosis and treatment of pancreatic cancer precursor lesions.

column36: Investigating the role of Ankyrin-B in heart and brain development
column37: Ankyrin-B (ANKB) is a protein that holds other proteins in place, like a scaffold. ANKB's job is to support other proteins that regulate the beating of heart cells and firing of nerve cells, a phenomenon called cellular 'excitability'. Our group discovered a version of the ANKB protein that is not able to properly support the proteins it normally does, which causes adverse effects for people, including heart malformations, sudden death, and seizures. The regulation of excitability is important for proper functioning of fully mature heart and brain cells and, importantly, also plays an earlier role in their differentiation, a process where new cells mature from newborn, partially functioning cells to fully-functioning cells. As ANKB regulates excitability, we have good reason to believe it also plays a role in the differentiation of heart and brain cells. Our lab has identified a new ANKB-interacting protein partner, called spinophilin, which is known to regulate heart and brain cell development. I hypothesize that ANKB regulates heart and brain development, and that this in part through an interaction with the spinophilin protein. I will examine the role of ANKB in the differentiation of heart and brain cells by measuring the levels of proteins that indicate differentiation and of proteins that normally interact with ANKB. I will also use microscopy to see how changes in ANKB impact the cell structure. I will then confirm the interaction between ANKB and spinophilin and determine what happens to heart and brain cell development when we prevent this interaction. Improved understanding of ANKB's role in heart and brain cell development, and its interaction with spinophilin, will provide critical insight into the impact of ANKB in heart and brain health, and disease.

column36: BPA substitutes and endothelial function: role of estrogen signalling
column37: After the common plasticizing agent bisphenol A (BPA) was declared toxic by regulatory agencies, bisphenol S (BPS) has become an increasingly prevalent substitute that is now detectable in the urine of over 80% of adults in the US and Asian countries. BPA interferes with the normal operation of estrogen in the body. The safety of BPS was not fully investigated before its implementation, and studies suggest that BPS also interferes with estrogen function. BPS also poses a particular risk to fetal development; BPS has been shown to cross the placenta and accumulate in the fetal compartment to a greater extent than BPA, potentially compromising fetal development. The Thompson lab is interested in understanding how exposure to BPS during pregnancy influences later-life blood vessel function. We will examine the impact of BPS on nitric oxide (NO) production, a key promoter of blood vessel health that is rapidly induced by estrogen. NO causes blood vessels to relax, which is essential for regulating blood pressure. We therefore hypothesize that prenatal BPS exposure influences blood vessel health through modulating NO production via interaction with estrogen receptors. We will explore this hypothesis by using a human umbilical vein cell model to mimic the effects of BPS during pregnancy and determine the mechanism by which BPS interferes with estrogen function. We will furthermore determine the sex-dependent effects of prenatal BPS exposure on blood vessel relaxation by examining the NO-dependent relaxation of blood vessels from male and female mice exposed to BPS during pregnancy. This study will uncover the mechanisms underlying the effects of BPS on the cardiovascular system and explore a potential risk to maternal and fetal health.

column36: Analyzing the SLX4-ATRX-DAXX complex and its roles in genome stability
column37: Every living organism needs to be able to accurately transmit genetic information to progeny cells and thus maintain genome stability. However, genome stability is constantly challenged by sources of DNA damage, such as chemicals and UV radiation. In turn, damaged DNA can lead to mutations and cell death. This can be detrimental to both the cell and the organism, since genome instability is a known hallmark of cancer cells. Therefore, the cell has several systems in place to maintain genome stability. A key player in genome stability maintenance is SLX4, a scaffold protein that binds and controls other proteins that function in DNA repair and cell homeostasis. Although the role of SLX4 in genome stability is well-studied, little is known about how these complexes are recruited to chromatin. Recent work from the Wyatt lab suggests that SLX4 and ATRX, a chromatin remodelling protein, interact in human cells. I hypothesize that the SLX4-ATRX interaction is needed for accurate DNA repair and genome stability. My research aims to characterize and determine the functional significance of the SLX4-ATRX complex. This research has implications in both genome stability and disease development. Indeed, SLX4 mutations can cause Fanconi anemia, a genetic disorder distinguished by a strong disposition in patients for developing cancer. Similarly, ATRX mutations are found in several human cancers and can result in ATRX syndrome. Revealing the biological functions of the SLX4-ATRX complex will thus uncover clinically important insights into the role this complex plays in genome stability maintenance and DNA repair

column36: The effect of anxiety severity on cardiovascular health
column37: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health disorder in Canada, affecting ~10% of individuals. Exaggerated fear and stress responses to everyday events are two defining features of anxiety disorders. In addition, anxiety disorders are correlated with many health risks and they have been independently associated with increased risk for developing cardiovascular diseases (CVD), the second leading cause of death in Canada. While the specific mechanisms responsible for this link remain unclear, it has been suggested that elevated resting sympathetic nervous system (SNS; i.e. the fight or flight system) activity may be a direct mechanism through which anxiety increases CVD risk. Thus, this study aims to evaluate the effect of anxiety severity on SNS activity at rest, and in response to protocols designed to cause acute stress. Additionally, this study will assess if the relationship between SNS activity and anxiety severity differs between the sexes. If there exists a relationship between anxiety severity and SNS activity, then this will support the hypothesis that anxiety directly increases one's CVD risk through altered SNS activity. Consequently, this would improve our knowledge regarding the physiological effects of anxiety and would allow for better informed treatment options, such as interventions that target the SNS, to reduce the risk of CVD for individuals with anxiety.

column36: Effect of Psilocybin Treatment on Addiction in Rat Models.
column37: As the chemical basis of addiction has become clearer over recent years, treatments for addiction have not reflected that understanding and have remained relatively stagnant. Psilocybin is the main psychoactive ingredient present in most species of psychoactive mushrooms, particularly Psilocybe cubensis. Research surrounding psilocybin has increased due to recent breakthrough studies demonstrating anti-depressive and anti-anxiety effects and improvement in quality of life of participants. While the results are hopeful, most of these studies had low participant numbers and more vigorous clinical trials and greater scientific understanding of the therapeutic effects of psilocybin are required to establish psilocybin as an effective and safe therapeutic approach to addiction. The presence or absence of addictive behaviours will be measured by conditioned lever presses and will be statistically analyzed using a factorial ANOVA. Due to the limited amount of research in this area, the results of this study will be impactful whether any significant effects are found or not.

column36: A multi-level integrative approach to autism subtyping
column37: A multi-level integrative approach to autism subtyping Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly complex neurological condition that is not only characterized by a diverse set of conventional diagnostic symptoms such as impaired social and communication skills, but is also often coupled with other symptoms including medical conditions and intellectual disabilities. Due to the complex nature of autism, rather than grouping all autism cases into a general spectrum as is done by current diagnostic measures, categorizing autism into distinct groups may provide better opportunities for targeted treatments and therapies. Previous work on ASD subtyping has often been hindered by limited data focusing on either brain imaging or genomics alone, which fails to fully encompass autism heterogeneity. This project plans to address this issue through the development of a multiscale data-driven framework that stratifies ASD individuals into distinct subtypes based on their genomic, neuroimaging, and phenotypic data. Structural and functional brain imaging measurements and genomic measures of the same individuals will be integrated as features in this framework and machine learning and dimensionality reduction algorithms will be employed to identify ASD subtypes and important properties that distinguish these subtypes. The results of this research are significant for understanding the neuroanatomical and genetic mechanisms underlying ASD heterogeneity. The determination of ASD subgroups with distinct imaging and genomic features will provide prospective directions for precision medicine through targeted treatment and support methods.

column36: Mindfulness-Based Intervention for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury

column36: Weaving Wellness: Indicators of Social and Emotional Well-being in Metis Children in Alberta
column37: Indigenous children in Canada carry an unequal burden of health inequalities, as compared to non-Indigenous children in Canada. These inequalities are largely shaped by colonialism and historical experiences that continue to impact health and well-being through disrupting important connections to place, identity, culture, and community. Public health policies and programs that aim to address health inequalities among Indigenous children must consider the historical experiences and reflect the current realities of Indigenous communities to be effective. The Metis are one of Canada's constitutionally recognized Indigenous populations and have a unique combination of identity, language, cultural traditions, and historical experiences that distinguish them from the other two Indigenous populations of Canada (First Nations and Inuit). The objective of this research is to develop indicators of social and emotional well-being that reflect the historical experiences and current realities of Metis children in Alberta. This study will use consensus methods that incorporate community perspectives and existing evidence to reach agreement among a group of Metis knowledge holders. This research is important to inform public health programs and policies directed at improving the health and well-being of Metis children.

column36: Untethering audiology from the clinic: Evaluation of a new technology as a publicly accessible hearing screening tool
column37: Millions of people across the world live with preventable and treatable hearing loss. It has been estimated that 1 in 3 people over 65 struggle with disabling hearing loss causing decreased quality of life, emotional, social, and communication dysfunction, and in increased risk of isolation and depression. A diagnostic audiometric assessment is considered the most effective means to diagnose hearing loss. However, conventional audiometry is not always readily accessible due to cost constraints, availability of trained audiological professionals, and social stigmatization. It is thus estimated that only 17% of adults who require hearing aids have pursued hearing loss treatment. It has become clear, particularly in light of the COVID-19 pandemic, that efficient, affordable, and accessible hearing screening tools are needed for use outside of clinical audiology settings. The goal of this project is to create a publicly accessible hearing screening test for little or no cost, allowing for ease of access to valid hearing health screening for remote self-assessment and in a wide range of healthcare and community settings. This study will modify the Digit Triplets Test (DTT) to improve sensitivity to specific types of hearing loss using a novel auditory modelling framework. We will use this model to predict audiometric assessment data based on results of the DTT and to determine how best to modify speech sounds to improve predictions. This test would enable non-clinical identification of communication barriers and suggest appropriate referrals in order to prevent further hearing loss and promote hearing health care. A widely accessible hearing screening tool would be an important step in improving the hearing health and related quality of life for millions of Canadians.

column36: Adaptation et validation d'une version francophone du programme <<Facing your Fears>> pour le traitement de l'anxiete aupres des jeunes avec un trouble du spectre de l'autisme
column37: Parmi les jeunes qui vivent avec un trouble du spectre de l'autisme (TSA), pres de 40% presentent egalement un trouble anxieux (TA). Ceux-ci engendrent des consequences pour les jeunes vivant avec un TSA comme plus de symptomes depressifs et de problemes de comportements. La therapie cognitive-comportementale (TCC) est le traitement psychologique de premiere instance pour traiter les TA chez les jeunes. Cependant, il existe peu de programmes de TCC des TA adaptes aux jeunes qui ont un TSA et ceux-ci presentent des resultats mitiges. Parmi les rares programmes existants, il a ete demontre que l'intervention << Facing your Fears >> (FYF) permet d'ameliorer significativement les symptomes d'anxiete chez seulement 50% des jeunes vivant avec un TSA. Le present projet vise donc a : 1) offrir une version bonifiee du programme FYF (p.ex., en ajoutant un module sur les emotions) a des jeunes qui presentent la comorbidite TSA et TA et 2) evaluer son efficacite sur les symptomes anxieux et depressifs, ainsi que sur les problemes de comportements. Cette etude portera aussi une attention quant a l'influence du sexe sur la reponse au traitement, car la litterature propose que les filles aient un profil clinique different des garcons sur le plan du TSA. Le devis de la recherche consiste en une serie de cas uniques, qui permet d'evaluer les donnees des participants de maniere individuelle. Deux groupes de 7 participants equilibres selon le sexe suivront le programme. Les symptomes anxieux et depressifs seront mesures a trois reprises par le jeune et ses parents a l'aide de questionnaires et de maniere continue avec un journal de bord. Ce programme permettrait d'ameliorer le traitement des TA chez ces jeunes. a notre connaissance, il serait le premier du genre a etre concu en francais.

column36: Impact of Nusinersen on Public Health Service Utilization and Associated Costs in Children with Spinal Muscular Atrophy
column37: The aim of my proposed Master's research project is to evaluate the impact of nusinersen on public health service utilization and associated costs in children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) using ICES data.SMA is a rare neurodegenerative disorder affecting anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, leading to progressive muscle weakness and atrophy. It is the leading cause of infant mortality in developed countries. Nusinersen is a novel disease-modifying medication that can improve motor function and overall survival, but comes with a price tag of almost 1 million dollars for the first year of therapy. There are currently no provincial or national data on public healthcare utilization and costs of patients treated with nusinersen. For patients with SMA, however, these data are paramount because of the extraordinary cost of treatment. We hypothesize that both utilization and costs are diminished in children with SMA treated with nusinersen compared to those who were not. We will carry out a retrospective cohort study using linked population-based, health administrative data housed at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES). We will import a provincial cohort of children receiving nusinersen in Ontario. Not only will our study help inform allocation of limited resources, but it will also help us understand the impact of new policies and emerging therapies, such as the recent approval for SMA newborn screening in Ontario and novel therapies awaiting Health Canada approval (eg. gene therapy, slice modifier therapy). As the clinical landscape of SMA evolves, we hope that our study will help guide evidence-based policy-making to ensure high quality care of children with SMA.

column36: Functional characterization of Anti- and Pro-tumorigenic Immune Cell States in Glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma is one of the most deadly human cancers, with very few examples of long term survivors. Despite modern sophisticated treatment regimens, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, survival outcomes for glioma patients remains at a dismal 14.6 months. In recent years, immunotherapies, which reprogram the immune system to recognize and target malignant tumors, have made a breakthrough as a curative therapy for many cancers. Yet, these therapies have been unsuccessful in glioblastoma, due to the unique immune repertoire in the brain and a poor understanding of how current treatments affect this environment. In our previous study of the brain tumor microenvironment, we identified the cytokine interleukin 33 (IL33) as a driver of inflammatory gliomas that recruits and reprograms innate immune cells in the brain to promote rapid and ultimately fatal tumor growth. Furthermore, we found that by crippling the ability of IL33 to enter the nucleus of glioma cells, tumors were no longer capable of developing in mice. We therefore hypothesize that the immune system in brain tumors can be in pro- or anti-tumorigenic states, and an understanding of how to exploit these states will be key in the development of effective immunotherapeutic drugs to treat glioma. To this end, our proposal has two major aims: (i) to understand how current standard-of-care therapies program innate immune cells and (ii) to ascertain the underlying regulation of pro- and anti- tumorigenic environments that promote and suppress tumor progression. With this information, clinical practice for current therapeutics can be modified to maximize the efficacy of immunotherapies and future studies will have immunotherapeutic targets to validate for clinical application.

column36: Les manifestations cognitives et comportementale de l'intolerance a l'incertitude predisent-elles la severite du trouble d'anxiete generalisee?
column37: Le trouble d'anxiete generalisee (TAG) se caracterise par des inquietudes excessives et incontrolables. Les croyances negatives face a l'incertitude (ex : << l'incertitude est injuste et gache tout >>) constituent un facteur de risque important pour le TAG. Ces croyances negatives produisent un biais negatif d'interpretation de l'ambiguite (ex: penser qu'il y a une catastrophe parce qu'un ami laisse un message disant qu'il veut nous parler de quelque chose d'important) et menent a l'utilisation de comportements securisants (ex: demander a l'ami de nous rassurer sur la solidite de notre relation). Il a ete demontre qu'il a y un lien entre les croyances negatives face a l'incertitude et la severite du TAG. La presente etude a pour objectif de repliquer ce resultat a partir d'un grand echantillon de 160 participants ayant un diagnostic principal de TAG. L'etude vise aussi a approfondir les connaissances en determinant si le biais negatif d'interpretation de l'ambiguite et les comportements securisants peuvent aussi predire la severite du TAG. Par la suite nous analyserons lequel sera le principal predicteur de la severite du TAG. En plus d'offrir une replication d'une etude precedente, ce projet sera le premier a s'interesser aux manifestations cognitives et comportementales des croyances negatives face a l'incertitude. Ultimement, une meilleure comprehension des facteurs de risque du TAG menera au developpement de traitements psychologiques plus efficaces pour ce trouble anxieux tres prevalent et eprouvant.

column36: Investigating the role of dendritic cells in the development of Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases.
column37: Systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs), including Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and Sjogren's disease (SjD), are chronic conditions characterized by recurring flares of disease activity and a variety of clinical symptoms. Often, when people first develop symptoms of SARD, there is already irreversible organ damage. The bloodwork changes (anti-nuclear antibodies; ANA) associated with these conditions can be found many years before the development of symptoms. While this would suggest that these changes could be used to predict development of disease, they are also frequently found in healthy women (~20%), of whom >90% will never develop SARD. There is still much to be understood regarding the cause of SARDs and the immune changes that are associated with the development of these diseases. To study the immune changes that lead to the development of SARD, our laboratory is following a large number of individuals who have some of the bloodwork changes of SARD but who have no clinical symptoms. Some of these individuals have developed disease and our preliminary data suggests that these progressors have altered function of a subset of immune cells, known as dendritic cells (DCs). These cells have previously been shown to play an important role in the activation of the immune subsets that lead to ANAs. By using advanced research techniques, we will further characterize the functional differences between DCs from SARD patients and ANA+ individuals who have no symptoms. Additionally, we will elucidate the immune changes that distinguish the ANA+ individuals who progress, from those who do not. Ultimately, this study will define the immune mechanisms that result in the development of SARD and potentially lead to novel treatments that can be used to prevent disease.

column36: Med15 function in pancreatic beta cells
column37: When the insulin secreting ß-cells of the pancreas are unable to secrete enough insulin to maintain normal blood sugar (glucose) levels, type 2 diabetes (T2D) develops. Making insulin secreting ß-cells in the lab for transplantation is a promising therapy for T2D, but we need more knowledge of ß-cell function and maturation to do this. Transcription factors (TFs), are important proteins for ß-cell maturation and interact with coregulators such as the Mediator complex. Mediator subunit 15 (MED15) has a role in glucose and lipid metabolism in worms and in human cells. Previous data from our lab show that mice without Med15 (aka Med15 knockouts) at an early age have dysfunctional ß-cell maturation and insulin secretion. However, we do not know if Med15 is also required to maintain a matured state in adult mice. I hypothesize that Med15 is consistently required to maintain maturity of pancreatic ß-cells. Using mouse models, I will knockout Med15 after ß-cells are fully matured, to test if Med15 is required in already mature ß-cells. I will then test if insulin secretion in response to glucose levels is affected by the loss of Med15. Expression of maturity markers in the pancreas will be measured. To examine how Med15 helps the ß-cells cope with molecular stress, I will place mice on a high fat diet (HFD), which is similar to the processed food diet of the Western world, to induce T2D, and then undergo similar assessments. These experiments will reveal if Med15 is required to maintain functionally mature ß-cells, and if Med15 could be used to defend ß-cells against HFD-induced stress. Both are important insights for the successful in vitro generation of pancreatic ß-cells, which will produce a much-needed supply of human insulin-secreting cells for T2D patients.

column36: Using Transient Hypoxia to Quantitatively Map Blood Flow in the Brain
column37: The ability to visualize blood flow (perfusion) in the brain has been pivotal in the diagnosis, prognosis, and surgical mapping of various neurological disorders. These disorders include, but are not limited to, cancer, neurovascular disease, and neurodegenerative disease. Dynamic susceptibility contrast is an effective magnetic resonance technique for gaining qualitative and quantitative insight into perfusion. A current limitation to this method is the use of an exogenous contrast agent, known as gadolinium, which is known to cause an array of side effects and conditions. A further limitation to using gadolinium is the inability to image multiple times within a relatively short time frame; successive imaging is critical for characterizing certain perfusion characteristics. A possible approach to circumvent gadolinium's limitations involves the induction of hypoxic conditions using an inert gas challenge. This gas challenge aims to provide contrast through briefly, and safely, increasing the concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin, a substance capable of strengthening the magnetic field in the blood vessels; in turn, the hypoxia is thought to generate the necessary contrast for perfusion imaging. Therefore, the primary goal of this clinical work is to elucidate the efficacy of the gas challenge in yielding quantitative and qualitative perfusion metrics which agree with those obtained from gadolinium contrast. A simultaneous goal involves the optimization of perfusion equations to account for physiological differences in contrast induced by gadolinium versus deoxygenated hemoglobin. To the best of our knowledge, this will be the first study to compare the efficacy of a gas challenge to gadolinium, in turn validating a safer clinical alternative for perfusion imaging.

column36: Direct-to-consumer genetic tests: Is there a role for Canadian genetic counsellors?
column37: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) genetic testing for health purposes, one of the latest iterations of commercialized personalized medicine, presents a challenge for Canada's genetic counsellors. The Canadian Medical Association, Canadian Association of Genetic Counsellors and many academics have called for genetic counselling pre- and post-DTC testing, but no framework currently exists for how the service ought to be provided. Without counselling, Canadians receive minimal support through the return of information linking their genetic profile to risk scores for disease, which could easily be misunderstood by the average consumer. Furthermore, due to the population bias of DTC test datasets, results may also be vague or inaccurate for people of colour. For my Master's thesis, I will examine the following research question: as academic discourse moves toward requiring pre-and-post counselling for DTC tests, is there a role for genetic counsellors and how are their traditional duties challenged? I will complete a literature review of the communication practices of all the DTC testing companies that operate within Canada, including internal policies and consent forms. I will then conduct a voluntary response, semi-structured survey of at least 20 Canadian genetic counsellors to seek their opinion on how various models of intervention could aid in DTC test counselling, the feasibility of pre-/post- DTC test counselling, and how this model challenges the traditional duties of Canadian genetic counsellors. The research will have implications for informing future legislation of DTC testing communication standards in Canada and is closely aligned with the CIHR's objective to embrace the scientific opportunity of emerging technologies while considering the health needs of Canadians.

column36: Evaluating a mindfulness-informed intervention for eating disorder symptoms in adults seeking weight loss surgery: A pilot feasibility trial
column37: BACKGROUND: Bariatric (weight-loss) surgery is an effective intervention for treatment-resistant severe obesity (ie., BMI>=40 kg/m<sup>2</sup> or 35 kg/m<sup>2</sup> with comorbidities). At least one-in-two patients seeking bariatric surgery experience eating disorder (ED) symptoms (e.g., binge eating, emotional eating), which may interfere with outcomes following surgery, including sustained weight-loss and quality of life. Mindfulness-informed interventions (MIIs) have been shown to reduce ED symptoms in bariatric patients via mechanisms of change that include mindful eating, self-efficacy for healthy eating behaviors, and emotion self-regulation. AIMS: This proposal represents Part III of the 3-part BE-EMPOWERED Study to evaluate a MII for ED symptoms pre-bariatric surgery. The primary aim of the present study is to evaluate feasibility of a large scale randomized efficacy trial of the MII. METHODS: 40 pre-surgical, adult (18+) patients with ED symptoms will be recruited from a Calgary bariatric surgery clinic and randomized to the MII or wait-list condition. The MII consists of four 2-hour group sessions, held weekly in a virtual format (Zoom video-conferencing) with homework assignments. The MII includes mindfulness (e.g., mindful eating practice, mindful breathing), behavioural (e.g.,meal tracking), cognitive (e.g., identifying maladaptive thoughts, addressing unrealistic expectations), and psychoeducation (e.g., principles of learning) components. Measures to assess recruitment, retention and drop out rates will be used to assess feasibility of the study and design methods. IMPLICATIONS: Results from the present study will be used to inform a large scale RCT of the MII. Feasability results will support an application to Tri-Council funding for a large scale, efficacy trial.

column36: Opioid Prescribing Preferences and Risk Mitigation Strategies of Ontario Dentists and Dental Specialists Prior to and During the COVID-19 Pandemic
column37: In dentistry, the primary indication for opioid use is in the management of moderate to severe pain. If used appropriately, opioid analgesia can benefit patients who are unable to use alternative analgesics. However, opioids have other effects that can cause harm. Often a patient's initial exposure to opioids is from the dental practitioner. Research indicates that opioid toxicity over the past 10 years in Canada was highest among people aged 15-24 years, with a 62% increase in hospital admissions in 2014-2015. The steep increase in incidents of toxicity and death has prompted public health officials in Canada to term it the 'opioid crisis'. In Ontario, dentists are the second largest group of opioid prescribers after family physicians and therefore contribute to the opioid crisis. This study will use a survey to investigate the opioid prescribing preferences and risk mitigation practices of Ontario dentists and dental specialists prior to and during the imposed COVID-19 shutdown of Ontario dental practices during March 17-June 12, 2020. We hypothesize that limitations on in-person dental care had an impact on opioid prescribing preferences for emergency and non-emergency dental procedures. The study aims are 1) Describe opioid prescribing preferences for dental emergencies associated with acute pain. 2) Identify non-emergency dental procedures associated with a higher rate of opioid prescription. 3) Learn if dentists use a risk mitigation plan to prevent opioid abuse, addiction and overdose. All aims are investigated both prior to and during the COVID-19 pandemic shutdown. The results of this study will impact delivery of patient care by providing foundational knowledge to target interventions to reduce or mitigate risks associated with opioid use in dentistry.

column36: Postprandial lipids in adolescents with obesity and insulin resistance
column37: Adolescents with obesity have an increased risk for developing cardiovascular disease (CVD) and Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), where postprandial dyslipidemia is an important risk factor. Postprandial dyslipidemia refers to abnormal lipid metabolism in the non-fasted state. This primarily occurs due to the overproduction of lipid carriers, termed lipoproteins, from the liver. The accumulation of certain lipoproteins is associated with both obesity and insulin resistance (IR) and facilitates the formation of plaque on arterial walls, a risk factor for CVD, in part by promoting an inflammatory state. Indeed, the state of systemic inflammation induced by obesity is associated with the development of IR and other obesity-related morbidities. Furthermore, the regulation of lipid metabolism involves critical hormones, known as glucagon-like peptides, and bile acids. A recent study from our group uncovered the postprandial dysregulation of these metabolites in adolescents with obesity and IR. Specifically, blood samples were taken at baseline and for several hours post-ingestion of a high-fat meal in adolescents with normal weight and with obesity and IR. Through further analysis of these samples, the proposed research aims to understand the postprandial dysregulation of inflammatory and metabolic markers in adolescents with obesity and IR, and their potential role in the development of postprandial dyslipidemia. In addition, we seek to determine the clinical utility of these novel biomarkers in predicting the subclinical progression to T2D. Postprandial dyslipidemia is a common complication of obesity and IR, and the proposed work will assist in uncovering the contributing role that inflammatory and metabolic markers may play in the dysregulation of lipid and lipoprotein metabolism.
