column36: Internet-based Small Changes for young Adults' life Longevity and wEight health: The iSCALE Trial
column37: An increasing number of Canadians are struggling to manage their weight. Unfortunately, as one's weight increases so to do their risk for other health conditions such as diabetes and cancer, and a shorter lifespan. Weight gain in young adulthood (ages 18-35) is common through experiences such as ""the freshman 15"" or parenthood, in addition to the 1-2lbs gained annually. This weight gain is troubling given that the reduction in life expectancy associated with overweight or obesity is greatest among young adults. Traditional weight management programs advise large changes to diet and physical activity that do seem to help people lose weight initially, but these changes are challenging to maintain long-term resulting in weight regain. This can result in people giving up or dropping out of these types of weight management programs, which is especially frequent among young adults. An alternative program exists called Small Changes. The Small Changes program advises changes to diet and physical activity that are small, sustainable, and self-selected. In this approach, weight loss is slower but more maintainable long-term. This approach has been successful in a number of populations but has not yet been tested among young adults in Canada. The proposed study aims to evaluate the impact of an online version of Small Changes on weight management (i.e., preventing weight gain, and producing sustainable weight loss) among a group of young adults. Measures of height, weight, and waist circumference, as well as, a healthy behaviours checklist will be taken at three time points across 6 months. This study has the potential to improve weight health, life longevity, and reduce healthcare costs associated with the treatment of overweight and obesity and its related health conditions.

column36: Design and Evaluation of Therapeutic Oligonucleotides for Acute Myeloid Leukemia
column37: 11 000 individuals this year alone will die from Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). AML is a rapidly progressing and ruthless blood cancer. In AML, the bone marrow produces immature blood cells that cannot carry out the function of healthy cells, leading to symptoms such as anemia, infection, and bleeding. Even with contemporary therapies, only ~ 30% of cases are cured. The goal of this project is to develop and validate a novel strategy for the treatment of AML using a new class of drugs: therapeutic oligonucleotides (TOs). TOs work by directly altering the expression of currently ""undruggable"" genes. Two different TO strategies will be tested: 1) decreasing gene expression using duplex small-interfering RNA (siRNA); 2) increasing gene expression using small-activating RNA (saRNA). A prime target of TOs in AML is PU.1, an essential factor in the production of specific blood cell types. Over half of AML patients have low PU.1 levels. It would be advantageous to increase the expression of PU.1 in such AML patients. Therefore, PU.1-targeted TOs will be designed, optimized, and tested in such cases. Developing saRNA and siRNA therapies can allow for the improved treatment of currently extremely difficult to cure AMLs, moving towards a future with more survivors.

column36: Double Negative T Cell: "Off-the-Shelf" Allogeneic CAR T Cell Platform for T Cell Malignancies
column37: Using double negative T cells in immunotherapy for T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive cancer of the immune cells. Current treatment involves combination chemotherapy; however, 20-40% of patients relapse with limited recourse. Recently, a form of immunotherapy, called chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy, has shown clinical success in certain leukemias. In current CAR-T cell therapy, T cells from patients are genetically modified to target and kill cancer cells. However, its application to T-ALL is currently limited due to several challenges. Since leukemic and CAR-T cells share the many targetable molecules, CAR-T cells that target leukemic cells also kill other CAR-T cells. Moreover, it is difficult to isolate enough number of healthy cells from T-ALL patients for CAR-T cell manufacturing. Alternatively, T cells from healthy donors can be used, but the donor's immune cells can mistakenly attack the recipient's normal cells. This study aims to circumvent these challenges by employing a type of unconventional T cells, called double negative T (DNT) cells. Unlike conventional T cells, DNT cells do not express certain surface molecules typically found on T-ALL, meaning that they can be modified to target leukemic T cells without the risk of self-killing. Further, donor-derived DNT cells have shown not to attack normal cells of recipients. Importantly, our preliminary data show that DNT cells can undergo genetic modifications to target T-ALL and increase their anti-cancer function. This study will examine the specificity, safety, and efficacy of CAR-DNT cells against T-ALL in cell culture and animal models. The findings may provide a feasible approach to CAR-T cell therapy for relapsing T-ALL patients.

column36: Development of a provincial inpatient diabetes database to study and improve quality of care for patients with diabetes using pharmacoepidemiologic and machine learning methods
column37: Diabetes is among the most prevalent chronic medical conditions, affecting roughly 30% of adults by age 65. Patients with diabetes are frequently hospitalized, both for complications directly related to their diabetes control, and secondary problems associated with diabetes such as heart attack and stroke. There is currently an absence of data on patients with diabetes while they are hospitalized. This presents a barrier to completing high quality studies of inpatient diabetes care and presents an opportunity to improve the inpatient management of adults with diabetes. Our study involves three components: 1. First, we will create a database of adults hospitalized with diabetes across the 30 hospitals in Ontario using the GEMINI (GEneral Medicine INpatient Initiative) database. Preliminary analyses have shown that this cohort will consist of rougly 200,000 patients with diabetes. 2. Second, we will conduct a pharmacoepidemiologic study to assess the use SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP1 agonists among patients who are eligible for these medications and risk of cardiovascular outcomes and mortality in the year after hospitalization. These agents have been shown to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, and death, and the identification of barriers to their use is essential for improving care for patients with diabetes. Studies in the United States have suggested that less than 5% of eligible patients receive these medications. 3. Third, we will develop a machine learning tool to predict and prevent inpatient hypoglycemia. This is among the most serious adverse events occurring in patients with diabetes and can result in seizure, coma and death.

column36: Collaborating with Indigenous Stakeholders Towards a Paradigm Shift for Neurotechnology
column37: Interventions to the brain using modern neurotechnologies offer hope, dignity, remediation of unbearable symptoms and, in some cases, a cure for many people living with treatment-resistant disorders such as Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, and chronic physical pain. While access to the benefits of such advances in healthcare is codified in Canada's Health Act, the voices of Indigenous peoples have been largely excluded from relevant research and translational progress. Drawing upon preliminary results that ground the proposed research in both the imperative and real likelihood of the beneficial possibilities of such interventions for Indigenous peoples living in urban and rural communities, I will bring together experts in Indigenous health, clinical neuroscience, and biomedical and neuro ethics for three successive, virtual half-day collaborative working sessions. We will explore meanings and values for brain wellness in Indigenous communities, alongside priorities and partnerships for clinical applications of rapidly evolving invasive and noninvasive neurotechnologies. The 12-member working group will include Knowledge Keepers and healthcare providers from diverse communities, including major cities and rural areas where telehealth is currently in place or imminent. We will apply research methods that facilitate the centering of Indigenous knowledge, focus on sustainable actions and long-term relationships, and are alert to power differentials. Through collaborative reporting and writings, we will deliver recommendations for strategic approaches to community-based and systems-based prioritization of neurotechnology for brain health, education, and consultation.

column36: A Phase I Qualitative Study to Develop a Patient-Reported Experience Measure for Adolescents and Adults Receiving Gender-Affirming Treatments
column37: Transgender and gender diverse individuals often face stigma within healthcare settings and represent an underserved patient population within Canada and abroad. For those able to access care, existing treatments can dramatically alter appearance as well as function to allow transgender patients to feel more comfortable within their own bodies. However, the impact of known financial, cultural, and systemic barriers on the transgender patient care experience remains unclear and underreported in the existing literature. To address this limitation, patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) can be developed to identify and evaluate factors that interfere with optimal healthcare delivery from the patient perspective. As such, the primary objective of this international, multicenter, qualitative study is to identify concepts of interest to transgender individuals seeking gender-affirming treatment(s) (GATs) to inform the development of a treatment-specific PREM. This PREM for GATs will comprise of independently functioning scales and will be developed over 3 phases. In phase 1 (focus of this proposal), we will conduct a series of interviews to elicit concepts related to the patient experience seeking GATs. Transgender men and women aged 16 and older, at participating institutions in Canada, USA, Denmark, and the Netherlands will be invited to participate. Patient interviews will be digitally recorded, transcribed, and coded. The outcome of this phase 1 study will be the development of preliminary patient experience scales. In phase 2 and 3, the measurement properties of these scales will be established. Once completed, a GAT-specific PREM will enable clinicians to better recognize healthcare barriers and guide quality improvement initiatives for transgender patients.

column36: The impact of spinal cord injury on cardiorespiratory interactions
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is well known to cause paralysis and loss of sensation, but high-level SCI may also affect nerves that regulate the heart and blood vessels, resulting in impaired control of heart rate and blood pressure. The muscles responsible for breathing are also affected: individuals with SCI tend to breathe in rapid and shallow breaths. This breathing style is thought to contribute to impaired cardiovascular control. Of note, SCI patients are 5 times more likely than the general population to experience obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). OSA is a breathing problem that occurs during sleep, with prolonged periods without breathing during sleep, and is associated with harmful cardiovascular consequences. Thus, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases are the leading causes of death among individuals with SCI. However, it is unknown how SCI interferes with the relationships between breathing patterns and cardiovascular function. As such, I will test and compare these cardiorespiratory interactions in individuals with and without SCI. Specifically, I will examine the effect of breathing rate on cardiovascular control in individuals with SCI. I will compare heart rate and blood pressure responses during periods of natural breathing and paced breathing. Additionally, I will characterize the relationships between OSA and breathing-related cardiovascular regulation. I will correlate blood pressure and heart rate data collected during sleep with questionnaire data assessing daytime sleepiness and risk of OSA. By revealing the impact of breathing rate and sleep-disordered breathing on cardiovascular control, this study will provide a better understanding of the SCI-associated risks of developing devastating cardiorespiratory complications.

column36: Rate versus Rhythm Control for the Acute Management of Uncontrolled Perioperative Atrial Fibrillation
column37: Perioperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is a common complication after non-cardiac surgery. Acute POAF can induce adverse hemodynamic changes, leading to increased length of stay and hospital costs. The optimal acute management strategy for POAF is unclear. A safe and effective strategy for arrhythmia control has the potential to reduce hospital length of stay and costs of patient care. I hypothesize that a pharmacological treatment strategy using rhythm control for acute management of POAF reduces the number of days patients remain alive and out of hospital compared to rate control. To test this hypothesis, I propose a pilot randomized control trial (RCT) assessing the feasibility of a larger study evaluating whether rhythm control is superior to rate control for POAF after non-cardiac surgery. I will lead this pilot RCT. The study will be a prospective, randomized, open-label clinical trial with blinded outcome assessment, with a planned enrollment of 100 patients. Patients will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either a rate or rhythm control strategy. The primary endpoints of the pilot trial will be recruitment rate, completeness of follow-up and protocol adherence. Patients will be followed for 30 days post-randomization. We will collect data on the proposed endpoint of the main study (days alive and out of hospital) and our safety outcomes. Patients who have undergone non-cardiac surgery within the same admission, have sustained POAF with a heart rate >100 beats per minute at the time of randomization, and are hemodynamically stable will be included. I will be responsible for leading the development of the study protocol, obtaining funding, as well as leading project operations, data analysis, and manuscript preparation under the supervision of Dr. David Conen.

column37: Inhaled tiotropium (Spiriva Respimat®) is a medication used to treat respiratory conditions including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma. Technically, tiotropium is referred to as a long acting muscarinic antagonist or ""LAMA"". The term long acting suggests the drug is used once a day. Muscarinic refers to a type of receptor on airway smooth muscle involved in causing bronchoconstriction or a tightening of the airway which makes breathing more difficult. Antagonist means it blocks or inhibits the effect. Therefore, tiotropium blocks muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle and prevents bronchoconstriction. Recent non-human research suggests tiotropium may also have anti-inflammatory effects. The potential anti-inflammatory effect of tiotropium is relevant to individuals with asthma, allergic asthma in particular, since allergen exposure not only causes acute bronchoconstriction (i.e. asthma symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest tightness and wheezing) but also leads to airway inflammation. The purpose of this study is to investigate the protective effects of tiotropium on the response to allergen exposure in individuals with mild allergic asthma in terms of both acute bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation.

column36: Validation de l'equation metabolique pour la course a pied sur tapis roulant de l'American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM)
column37: Chez la population generale, une augmentation de la VO<sub>2</sub>max diminue les risques de mortalite et de morbidite de types cardiaques et coronariennes. La capacite aerobie maximale (VO<sub>2</sub>max) est consideree comme la meilleure mesure de l'endurance cardiorespiratoire et de l'aptitude aerobie. C'est la plus grande quantite d'oxygene pouvant etre utilisee par le corps a l'effort. Malheureusement, l'accessibilite a sa mesure directe est limitee et c'est pourquoi de nombreuses equations permettant de l'estimer existent. L'equation de l'American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) pour la course a pied est l'une des plus largement utilisees mondialement pour mesurer indirectement la VO<sub>2</sub>max lors d'evaluations a la course a pied. Cliniquement, il fut observe des differences majeures entre les resultats obtenus indirectement et ceux mesures directement, alors que des etudes abondent dans le m eme sens. Malheureusement, peu d'etudes s'interessent a la validite de cette equation pour determiner la VO<sub>2</sub>max. Plus encore, aucune etude, a notre connaissance, n'a ete developpee aupres de coureurs reguliers durant un protocole d'evaluation a la course a pied. Dans ce projet, nous nous interesserons aussi a l'estimation de la VO<sub>2</sub>max par extrapolation de donnees sous-maximales et aux differences interindividuelles de la consommation d'oxygene. L'etude consiste a comparer les resultats de VO<sub>2</sub>max reelles et estimees chez 180 coureurs reguliers de 18 a 65 ans afin d'evaluer sa fiabilite d'estimation. Ils realiseront un test a l'effort maximal sur tapis roulant lors duquel leurs echanges respiratoires seront mesures. Cette etude possede de nombreuses applications theoriques et cliniques permettant a de nombreux intervenants du milieu sportif et medical d'ameliorer la qualite de leurs interventions.

column37: The proposed project aims to study the impact of employment transitions (i.e. remaining employed, becoming unemployed, entering retirement) on weight change among the Canadian aging population. Studies have linked job-loss with poorer physical health and changes in lifestyle factors. The changes in lifestyle factors have also been independently shown to impact weight status. The research objective is to create Canadian evidence on the direct and indirect impact of employment transitions on weight change. column36: Assessing the feasibility of nanopore clinical metagenomics in the context of the Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic and ensuing public health emergency that has highlighted the need for new rapid, cost-effective, and comprehensive viral screening techniques. The current RT-qPCR method, despite its relatively low-cost and reliability, still requires many hours of lab time and is only useful for detecting targeted pathogens. There is an urgent need to explore alternative diagnostic strategies to aid in the fight against COVID-19, as well as future pandemics. Metagenomic whole genome sequencing (MWGS) allows researchers to characterize all genetic material of a biospecimen, allowing the detection of multiple pathogens or co-infections not captured by standard diagnostic panels. This approach to testing can also assess the contribution of one or more pathogens to patient clinical outcomes. Sequencing technologies have been historically expensive and logistically challenging for diagnostic laboratories. However, the Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) MinION device has reduced the cost and increased the portability and speed of MWGS, opening the door for future clinical applications. This project will optimize and assess the performance of a MWGS diagnostic assay using the ONT sequencing platform to detect SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses in oropharyngeal swab specimens. We will non selectively amplify viral RNA into cDNA to obtain sufficient genetic material for MWGS, an approach that has been applied previously to both influenza and SARS-CoV-2. Test performance metrics will be estimated. We will work with the Public Health Laboratory at the BCCDC to ensure technological and knowledge translation. This study will determine the feasibility and performance of clinical metagenomics as a diagnostic tool for viral infection in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic and beyond.

column36: Characterizing Intratumor Heterogeneity with Spatially Aware Clustering
column37: Cancers are complex organs not simply masses of malignant cells, but a mixture of cell types. In the course of tumor progression, normal and malignant cells form complex patterns of cell-cell interactions which creates the tumor microenvironment (TME). The dynamics within the TME fosters intra-tumour heterogeneity. Intra-tumour heterogeneity describes the presence of cellular subpopulations each with a specific sensitivity to treatment. Investigating cell-cell interactions that characterizes heterogeneity in the TME can potentially elucidate mechanisms of tumour cell invasion, tumour growth, and metastases. Current analyses use analysis of single cells in suspension to advance our understanding of tumor heterogeneity. However, the data generated by this approach are disaggregated and do not retain information about the spatial structure of tumours. We propose to perform analysis using emerging technologies like imaging mass cytometry (IMC), which provides spatial relationships between cells. We will be addressing the following question: Does spatially aware clustering characterize heterogeneity more accurately than current methods which ignore spatial information? To answer this, we will develop a computational approach to identify the cell type of each cell using protein expression and spatial structure and to infer the cell-cell interactions of the TME. Through our method of spatially aware clustering of cells, the inferred cell-cell interaction data can potentially characterize patient-specific phenotypic heterogeneity better than our current methods. As heterogeneity promotes therapeutic resistance, the cell-cell interaction profiles can potentially provide prognosis for lymphoma and breast cancer in hundreds of patients at BC Cancer.

column36: Exploring the diabetes self-care experiences of patients with food insecurity and type 2 in a subsidized healthy food prescription program
column37: Type 2 Diabetes (T2DM) is a demanding chronic disease for patients. Self-management activities, such as healthy eating and taking prescribed medications, are essential to manage blood glucose levels and avoid adverse outcomes. Yet, many patients with T2DM in Canada face financial barriers to self-management, including an inability to access sufficient quantity and quality of food (also known as food insecurity), which can result in uncontrolled blood glucose levels. The result of poorly managed T2DM is detrimental to patients and is costly to the healthcare system: T2DM is estimated to have an economic burden of $1.5 billion/year in Canada. Researchers are investigating the impact of a potential solution for food insecurity in people with T2DM: a subsidized healthy food prescription. Currently, there is limited knowledge of how food subsidies impact diabetes self-management from the patient's perspective. Without knowing this, research evaluating the effectiveness of food subsidies on patient blood glucose levels can produce results that are less actionable for key stakeholders interested in implementing these programs in other settings. We aim to conduct a study to better understand the mechanisms by which a healthy food subsidy impacts self-management of T2DM. This project will complement a randomized control trial providing a subsidized healthy food prescription to Albertans experiencing T2DM and food insecurity. Our focus will be on the patient's experience, using both quantitative patient-reported measures and qualitative interviews, to gain an in-depth understanding of the subsidy's role in self-management. The study will allow us to generate findings that help explain the results of the broader RCT, optimizing future program delivery and provincial scale-up.

column36: Assessing the Effect of Hemodynamic Management and Thromboembolic Prophylaxis on Spinal Cord Hemorrhage After Traumatic Injury in a Porcine Model
column37: This proposal is focused on understanding the severe, and poorly understood, hemorrhage within the spinal cord after traumatic injury. The severity of this bleeding is associated with worsened neurologic outcome in spinal cord injury (SCI) patients where the blood itself can be toxic to the injured cord and have negative downstream consequences. SCI patients receive two routine clinical therapies, which may lead to increased hemorrhage within the injured cord. The goal of the first intervention is to increase their mean arterial pressure to maintain adequate blood flow to the cord and prevent further damage. However, this increase in blood flow may also unintentionally worsen bleeding within the injured cord. SCI patients are also prone to developing blood clots due to their immobility after injury. As a result, the second routine clinical therapy is the use of blood thinners to prevent the formation of blood clots. However, these blood thinners inherently increase the severity of any bleeding. Therefore, the goal of this study is to determine whether the combination of these two routine clinical therapies worsen spinal cord hemorrhage after SCI in a pig model. We have developed the techniques to evaluate the extent of hemorrhage using ultrasound imaging, magnetic resonance imaging and histology of the cord. The amount of hemorrhage after injury will be measured and compared between groups that either received one or both of these routine therapies and the group that did not receive any treatment after SCI. The results from this proposed study have the prospect of informing clinical approaches for SCI patients and may potentially improve neurologic recovery.

column36: Rewiring tumour cell-macrophage communication to elicit de novo anti-cancer immunity
column37: The human immune system, specialized in removing harmful or foreign material from the body, can easily fight off the common cold yet fails to eliminate many cancers. This is because tumor cells have evolved mechanisms to suppress or evade recognition by the immune system. For example, tumor cells display cell-surface proteins which act as ""don't-eat-me"" signals to inhibit clearance by immune cells that normally ingest dying or diseased cells. This in turn stops the full recruitment and activation of downstream immune responses against the tumor cells. To combat this mechanism, I will synthesize a therapeutic molecule that combines an inhibitor of the ""don't-eat-me"" signal with a pathogen-associated molecule. Binding of this therapeutic to the tumor cell will block its ""don't-eat-me"" signals and simultaneously display the pathogen-associated molecule on the tumor cell surface, providing ""danger signals"" to promote ingestion by immune cells. In this proposal, I aim to evaluate the extent to which this strategy will enhance tumor cell clearance by immune cells and its impacts on downstream immune activation. I hypothesize that enhancing the ability of certain immune cells to ingest tumor cells can lead to the development of a ""cancer vaccine"". Compared to similar approaches for cancer vaccination, I believe that my strategy will improve therapeutic benefit due to an increase in the perceived ""danger-level"" by the immune system via the ""danger signal"". My research lays the foundation for future investigations in animal models and will deepen our understanding for the impacts of modulating ""danger-levels"" in immune cell ingestion and activation processes. Looking forward, I hope this research will improve patient outcomes and culminate in an off-the-shelf cancer vaccine.

Puisque la vision est le sens principal utilise lors des deplacements, ces individus eprouvent de nombreuses difficultes pour la mobilite, l'orientation et la comprehension de l'espace. Bien qu'ils beneficient d'outils (comme la canne blanche, les chiens guides, les telephones cellulaires et les systemes GPS) afin d'augmenter leur autonomie, ils eprouvent toujours plusieurs limites pour la navigation dans les milieux interieurs non-familiers. En effet, l'inefficacite des systemes GPS a l'interieur et l'absence de signalisation interieure accessible les emp echent d'acceder aux services offerts de facon autonome et simultanee au reste de la population. Ce projet a pour but de verifier le potentiel de l'impression 3D afin de creer un systeme de carte tactile standardise et durable pouvant etre adapte a tout batiment. En effet, puisque les cartes tactiles constituent un moyen efficace pour les personnes en DV d'obtenir de l'information spatiale et de demeurer orientes, un tel systeme pourrait resoudre ce probleme stigmatisant de l'orientation interieure. Ainsi, nous determinerons l'avantage que peut avoir l'impression 3D sur la memorisation de symboles, sur la capacite de se construire une carte mentale et sur la facilite des deplacements autonomes aupres d'individus vivant avec une cecite totale. Ainsi, avec la participation active de sujets DV dans ce projet, il sera possible d'obtenir une meilleure comprehension de l'effet du 3D sur l'apprentissage spatial tout en promouvant un systeme de cartographie 3D qui aura le potentiel d' etre adapte a tout type de batiment afin d'augmenter leur autonomie et leur participation sociale.

column36: Associations entre la distribution des graisses au 1er trimestre, la resistance a l'insuline et l'alimentation chez la femme enceinte
column37: L'alimentation est un element determinant de la sante des femmes enceintes et de leur progeniture. Cependant, plus du tiers des femmes canadiennes en age de procreer presentent un embonpoint et ainsi, plusieurs femmes entament leur grossesse dans un tel etat. Pendant la grossesse, bon nombre de femmes outrepassent les apports energetiques recommandes, ont une alimentation de qualite sous-optimale et ne respectent pas les directives de gain de poids. Enfin, l'accumulation excessive des graisses a l'interieur de la cavite abdominale est un determinant des complications de grossesse, dont le diabete gestationnel. Il est donc primordial d'identifier les femmes enceintes a risque nutritionnel. Les echographies de routine permettent d'obtenir des mesures fiables, reproductibles et precises de l'epaisseur et de la distribution des depots de tissu adipeux visceral et peuvent faciliter l'identification des femmes a risque nutritionnel. Ce projet a comme objectif d'examiner les associations entre l'accumulation de graisse abdominale mesuree au 1er trimestre, la resistance a l'insuline, les apports nutritionnels et la qualite alimentaire. Cent-cinq femmes ont ete recrutees et ont effectue, a chaque trimestre, 3 rappels alimentaires de 24 heures Web, desquels les apports nutritionnels seront evalues et un indice de qualite alimentaire sera calcule. Des variables metaboliques comme le glucose et l'insuline ont ete mesurees par prelevements sanguins et la distribution abdominale de tissu adipeux visceral a ete evaluee par echographie. Ce projet pourra faciliter l'identification et la prise en charge des femmes a risque de complications gestationnelles et, par la mesure echographique de la distribution des graisses, modifier les recommandations de depistage du risque nutritionnel.

column36: Uncovering the molecular mechanism underlying lysine-specific demethylase 6A in Kabuki Syndrome
column37: Kabuki Syndrome is a rare genetic disease that affects 1 in 32,000 individuals and is characterized by intellectual disability, abnormal development of the brain and heart, and malformations of the face and skull. Genetic diseases involve errors in patients' DNA and in Kabuki Syndrome, these errors can occur in a specific DNA segment that codes for the KDM6A protein. This protein modifies complexes around which DNA is wrapped, called histones. By modifying histones, KDM6A can signal to the cell to turn on the production of certain proteins. My preliminary data in stem cell models show that when KDM6A is lost, genes involved in making the cell's respiratory organelle, the mitochondria, are reduced. This proposed research thus aims to understand the molecular mechanism that involves KDM6A, KDM6A-associated histone modifications, and mitochondria biogenesis. Our goal is to understand why the loss of KDM6A causes Kabuki Syndrome. We will be using genetically engineered stem cells and stem cells derived from a patient and the patient's sex-matched parent's blood samples to investigate our question. We expect to see an increase in a specific kind of histone modification mark when KDM6A is lost, which will block mitochondria production and function. By uncovering the molecular mechanism underlying Kabuki Syndrome caused by KDM6A loss-of-function, we hope to help clinicians better understand a subgroup of patients who present with developmental abnormalities, and to open doors to the development of potential treatments for this disorder.

column36: Reprogrammation de la voie metabolique de AMPK dans les cellules du cancer de la prostate
column37: Le cancer de la prostate (CaP) est le cancer le plus frequent chez l'homme. Diagnostique tot, il peut etre traite par chirurgie ou radiotherapie. Toutefois, de 25 a 30% des patients auront une recidive, et la deprivation aux androgenes est le traitement standard pour lutter contre cette maladie a ce stade. Malgre une reponse positive a cette therapie, l'effet sera en general temporaire et la majorite des CaP y developpe une resistance. Afin d'identifier de nouvelles cibles therapeutiques, le laboratoire etudie la facon dont le recepteur aux androgenes (AR) reprogramme le metabolisme energetique des cellules de CaP. Notamment, il a ete demontre que ce recepteur peut moduler l'expression des genes metaboliques et controler certaines voies de signalisation cellulaires. Dans le cadre de mon projet, je m'interesse plus particulierement a la facon dont AR regule la voie de signalisation de la AMP-activated kinase (AMPK), impliquee dans le metabolisme cellulaire. Les resultats preliminaires du laboratoire montrent que AR active la voie AMPK ce qui augmenterait la production d'energie par respiration mitochondriale. Notre hypothese est que l'activation de AMPK est requise pour que les cellules tumorales qui dependent des androgenes proliferent, etant donne son role majeur dans le controle de la respiration mitochondriale. Nous pensons qu'inhiber AMPK permettrait de bloquer la proliferation des cellules du CaP et d'induire leur degenerescence. L'objectif principal de mon projet est donc d'etudier dans differents modeles cellulaires de CaP comment la modulation de l'activite de AMPK influence la proliferation, la survie et le metabolisme. Ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre les vulnerabilites metaboliques de ce cancer et d'identifier de nouvelles avenues therapeutiques.

column36: Health Inequity and Late-Life Orphancy
column37: Canada's aging landscape is shifting. Increased longevity, declines in marriage, and rises in divorce, childlessness, and family mobility are upending traditions of family-based elder care, and heightening the prevalence of isolated and unsupported older adults known as elder orphans. Despite the significant vulnerability associated with elder orphancy, including cognitive and functional impairment and risk of early institutionalization, this subset of the elderly population remains relatively unexamined within Canada. This masters-doctoral transition research project will address this gap in four phases. In phases 1 and 2, an exploratory review of peer-reviewed literature will be conducted to examine what is currently known regarding the barriers and facilitators impacting elder orphans' access to health and social care services and navigation of care systems. In phase 3, a stakeholder consultation will be performed through interviews with individuals identified as key informants on the topic of care access for elder orphans in order to confirm or refute the findings from phases 1 and 2. In phase 4, a statistical analysis will be conducted using the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging to identify key characteristics of older Canadians at risk of elder orphancy, the prevalence of unmet care needs among this population, and the relationships between their unmet needs and health status. This research will contribute to a direly neglected area of inquiry in seeking to identify and address this population's challenges in accessing needed services, highlight areas of care policy in need of reform, and facilitate the development of responsive strategies to promote Canadian elder orphans' wellbeing, independence, and engagement within their communities as long as possible.

column36: The Characterization of Pain in Youth with FASD
column37: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is common, debilitating, and poses a large economic burden. Functional deficits in youth with FASD are thought to only be caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, when there are many other contributing factors. Pain is a universal experience that can lead to mental health issues, academic and social challenges, and a reduced quality of life. These are issues that children with FASD often experience. Despite the increasing amount of research on FASD, there has been no examination to date into the rates and impact of pain in this population. Given the fact that FASD impacts more Canadian youth than other neurodevelopment disorders, pain may play a key role in the already complex neurobehavioral profiles of youth with FASD. This study will be the first to characterize pain in youth with FASD. Youth and their parents will be recruited from an ongoing longitudinal study at UCalgary. They will be asked to complete a questionnaire assessing youth pain outcomes (i.e., frequency, intensity, and interference). They will also come to UCalgary for a laboratory visit where youth will participate in an experimental pain task (cold pressor task). Acute pain and distress behaviours will be assessed by coding various aspects of the video-recorded pain task. The proposed study will be the first to examine pain in youth with FASD. Findings will directly inform treatment-tailoring approaches to improve outcomes for youth with FASD and offset a path of increased mental health issues and disability into adulthood.

column37: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory disorder characterized by painful nodules, abscess and sinus tracts in apocrine gland bearing regions. Patients affected by HS not only experience debilitating physical symptoms including pain and recurrent infections, but also under severe psychological stress secondary to their disease. Moreover, as HS is now recognized as a systemic inflammatory disease and patients with HS are also at a higher risk for developing metabolic syndrome, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Treatment options for HS are generally limited and focus on treating the primary skin lesions. Of all the approved treatment options for HS, metformin is the only medication that has the additional benefit of also treating the cardiovascular risk factors associated with HS. Although metformin is a recommended treatment options for HS, current studies are limited to only one case report and one case series. Given the benefit of metformin on HS and its comorbidities, it is an important medication that warrants further investigation and hence the purpose of our study is to establish the first province wide HS database, which will be used to determine the impact of metformin as a treatment option in our patient population.

column36: Subacute Speech and Language Rehabilitation Outcomes in Paediatric Stroke Patients
column37: Background: Paediatric stroke is among the top ten causes of mortality in children, with devastating impairments in speech and language functioning. A critical period for speech and language recovery is the subacute rehabilitative stage, which aims to mitigate these potential chronic impairments. The neural mechanisms that drive speech and language recovery in response to rehabilitation in the subacute stages post childhood stroke need to be elucidated in order to innovate efficacious new treatments. Aims: 1. Prospectively document the clinical and neural outcomes of speech and language rehabilitation in the subacute phase of recovery from paediatric stroke. 2. Identify brain-behaviour associations of speech and language at the times of admission, discharge and 3-month follow-up. 3. Determine the neural mechanisms of recovery from post-stroke speech and language disorders. Hypotheses: 1. Clinical speech and language functioning will improve throughout admission and maintain or improve at 3-month follow-up. 2. Speech and language impairment will positively track with the number of grey matter regions and white matter tracts lesioned in either hemisphere. 3. In the subacute stage of recovery, improved clinical outcomes will be associated with normalization of brain microstructure and function. Methods: Prospectively assess speech and language outcomes of 50 paediatric stroke patients at admission, discharge, and 3-month post-discharge. At each time point, T1-MPRAGE, resting state fMRI, and Diffusion Kurtosis Imaging will be collected. Children will complete a speech perception task-based fMRI paradigm. Significance: My vital research will inform innovative and personalized clinical treatments for paediatric speech and language post-stroke care recovery in patients.

column36: The Role of Microglial-Mediated Synaptic Loss in Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy
column37: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is an umbrella term that encompasses several age-related degenerative conditions that cause a compression of the cervical spinal cord. DCM is the most common cause of spinal cord injury (SCI) and is associated with debilitating functional deficits such as impaired upper limb function. This condition is prevalent in adults over the age of 65, which causes a burden for our increasingly ageing global population. Recent research in a traumatic animal model of SCI has shown that deletion of the fractalkine receptor (CX3CR1) is associated with improved upper limb function and increased synapse formation. The CX3CR1 receptor is a part of the fractalkine signalling pathway (CX3CR1-CX3CL1), which can regulate synaptic pruning in the central nervous system. However, the relationship between fractalkine-mediated synaptic loss and impaired upper limb function in a non-traumatic model of SCI (e.g. DCM) is not well-understood. Based on past research, I hypothesize that the forelimb deficits observed after DCM are in part due to fractalkine-mediated synaptic loss. Either Cx3cr1 or Cx3cl1 deletion should increase the number of synaptic connections and improve functional outcomes. The proposed study aims to: 1) determine the effects of Cx3cr1 and Cx3cl1 deletion on synaptic plasticity and forelimb function following DCM, and 2) examine if re-introduction of CX3CL1 (the fractalkine ligand) via viral vectors will exacerbate deficits. This study is the first to investigate the relationship between fractalkine-mediated synaptic loss and forelimb function in the context of DCM and will reveal novel therapeutic targets for this increasingly prevalent and devastating condition.

column36: Implications of Coronavirus Disease 2019-related worry and isolation for the mental health of cancer patients: The effect of a 24-week mobile health exercise intervention on depressive symptoms, anxiety, and exercise engagement
column37: Cancer patients have a greater risk for more severe health outcomes if infected with the novel coronavirus (COVID-19), and COVID-19-related worry and isolation may inadvertently increase depression and anxiety among this population. Past research reveals that exercise improves depression levels of people with cancer. Further, mobile health (mHealth) exercise programs have improved patients' physical activity levels and quality of life. As a result of the pandemic, research is needed to determine whether mHealth exercise programs can be used to address the mental health concerns amongst cancer patients. The proposed research will evaluate whether a) greater COVID-19-related worry and isolation predict greater depressive symptoms and anxiety, and less engagement in exercise; and b) depressive symptoms, anxiety, and exercise engagement show greater improvement following participation in a mHealth exercise intervention. To assess how COVID-19-related worry and social isolation relate to mental health and exercise engagement, Canadian cancer patients will complete an online survey assessing self-reported worry, isolation, depression and anxiety symptoms, and physical activity. Participants will then be randomly assigned to either a 24-week mHealth intervention or to a control group (no intervention). Subsequently, all participants will re-complete the online survey to determine whether intervention (vs. control) results in greater improvement in mental health and exercise engagement. Results will inform cancer care and advance exercise delivery as an approach to supporting the mental health of those diagnosed with cancer. Further, results may introduce an accessible and feasible online exercise counselling tool that can be prescribed by oncologists to improve mental health.

column36: Investigating mechanisms responsible for the pro-regenerative effects of conditioning electrical stimulation
column37: Peripheral nerve injuries are widespread and often result in disabling symptoms in patients that can reduce quality of life. Following a nerve injury, It can take up to two years for the nerve to reach its target tissue after which time the muscles are atrophied and unable to be reinnervated (Grinsell and Keating, 2014). Despite surgical advancements in treating these injuries, only approximately half of patients achieve a satisfactory outcome after nerve repair, suggesting that these patients have lifelong sensory and motor deficits (Ruijs et al., 2005). This demonstrates the need for methods to promote successful nerve regeneration. Forty years ago, the conditioning crush lesion (CCL) in which a nerve was intentionally crushed one week prior to a nerve repair surgery, was discovered as a promising solution to this problem as it can accelerate the rate of nerve regrowth 2-4 times the normal rate of regrowth (Richardson and Issa, 1984; Senger et al., 2018b). However, this invasive strategy is not appropriate for patients as it requires an intentional nerve injury. Conditioning electrical stimulation (CES) has been shown to accelerate nerve regeneration and promote functional recovery comparable to CCL by increasing the same pro-regenerative genes, known as regeneration-associated genes (RAGs) (Senger et al., 2018; Senger et al., 2019). The mechanism behind these beneficial effects remains unknown; therefore, the Webber laboratory's ongoing research is seeking to identify the unique pathways associated with CES, as well as confirm that it involves a non-inflammatory and non-injurious process that is safe for patients.

column36: Geographic and socioeconomic differences in mechanical thrombectomy - is everyone reaping the same reward?
column37: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has revolutionized acute stroke care over the past half-decade. Unfortunately, it is a resource intensive therapy and tends to be centralized at specialized stroke centers. As such, there may exist a discrepancy between access to MT between different populations based on socioeconomic status (SES) and rurality. This may actually worsen pre-existing inequalities in healthcare and make disadvantaged populations comparatively worse off. Our project will aim to assess whether access to MT varies based on the aforementioned population characteristics and evaluate whether increased investment in this intervention is associated with an opportunity cost in the form of worsening healthcare inequality. We will use government and institutional databases to evaluate the rates of MT per acute stroke admission. We will then compare these rates based on established location-specific deprivation indices across Alberta, Canada. Any worsening of inequality from increased investment in MT should spur healthcare organizations and governments to take steps to address this finding.

column36: The Impact of the Provincial Regulatory Environment on Canadian Nurse Entrepreneurs
column37: The Impact of the Provincial Regulatory Environment on Canadian Nurse Entrepreneurs Nurse entrepreneurship or self-employed registered nursing represents an important role that advances the profession of nursing by seizing the independence needed to care for patients according to professional values rather than institutional efficiency goals. Current provincial nurse regulation has been identified as the most significant barrier to Canadian nurse entrepreneurship, therefore this qualitative case study is focused on identifying how the provincial regulatory context and processes impact Canadian nurse entrepreneurship. Each Canadian province has a separate nurse regulatory organization with a unique combination of contextual features including traditional or umbrella regulation legislation and single or dual mandate regulatory model. This case study includes four purposely chosen distinctive cases each made up of a provincial regulatory organization with a unique combination of contextual features and its respective regulation of nurse entrepreneurs. Evidence including documents, application forms, multi-media sources, and interviews with regulators will be collected and analyzed within and across the cases to gain insight into how the regulatory context, stakeholders, content, and processes impact the regulation of Canadian nurse entrepreneurs. This research will address significant gaps in the existing literature and will have practice implications for provincial health authorities, policymakers, regulatory bodies, as well as entrepreneurial nurses and their advocates by informing efficient and effective regulatory practices for nurse entrepreneurs, thereby improving access to care and the health and wellbeing of Canadians who utilize their services.

column36: Investigating the role of glutamate in mitogen-activated protein kinase inhibitor-resistant melanoma and its effects on CD8+ T cell subsets and response to anti-PD1 immunotherapy
column37: Melanoma skin cancer is easily treatable on early detection, but less than half of patients with metastatic disease survive past two years. About 50% of melanoma patients have an alteration in the protein BRAF that increases cell growth and replication. These patients can be treated with BRAF inhibitors (BRAFi), but relapse occurs after 9-10 months. Relapse on BRAFi has been associated with tumour cells increasing export of glutamate, a molecule involved in cell metabolism. Glutamate can decrease the efficiency of T cells – warriors of the immune system that identify and kill invaders and cancer cells. Therefore, BRAFi may decrease the immune response to cancer. This is supported by evidence that patients treated with BRAFi become more resistant to subsequent immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy that increases immune response to cancer. It is therefore hypothesized that BRAFi increase tumour glutamate export which decreases effectiveness of immune therapy by lessening T cell killing ability. To test this, BRAFi-treated melanoma patients will be tested for increased tumour glutamate. Further investigation of glutamate effects will use mice. Mice will be injected with tumour cells that have increased, or normal, glutamate export and will be given immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment. If glutamate decreases immune system efficiency, mice with increased glutamate export will have less tumour shrinkage compared to those with normal glutamate export. Finally, to test the role of T cells, glutamate will be given to mouse T cells to assess changes in killing efficiency as measured by cell metabolism and proteins/signals given off by the cells. This result is important for improved treatment of many cancers as glutamate export is a common indicator of metastatic disease.

column36: Investigating the Effects of Electronically Delivered Cognitive Behavioural Therapy on Brain Activation Levels in Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder Using Functional MRI
column37: Background: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a debilitating and prevalent anxiety disorder. While the basal ganglia and frontal cortex are the most commonly hypothesized brain regions involved, the exact pathophysiology is unknown. By observing the effects of treatment on brain structure, the etiology of OCD can be better understood. Currently, the gold standard treatment for OCD is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) with exposure and ritual prevention (ERP). However, this is often temporally and geographically inaccessible, time-consuming, and costly. Fortunately, the electronic delivery of CBT (e-CBT) has presented a promising solution to these barriers. Objectives and Hypothesis: This study will implement an e-CBT program for OCD and observe its effects on brain activation levels using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). It is hypothesized that brain activation levels in the basal ganglia and frontal cortex will decrease following treatment. Methods: Individuals with OCD will be offered a 16-week e-CBT program with ERP mirroring in-person CBT content that will be administered through a secure online platform. Efficacy will be evaluated using clinically validated symptomology questionnaires at baseline, week 8, week 16, and at a 6-month follow-up. Using fMRI at baseline and post-treatment, brain activation levels will be assessed at resting state, and while exposed to an anxiety-induced image (i.e., dirty dishes if cleanliness is an obsession). The effects of treatment on brain activation levels and the correlation between symptom changes and activation levels will be analyzed. Significance: The findings from this study can further our understanding of the etiology of OCD, helping to develop more effective treatments for this disorder.

column36: Resilience and coping mechanisms among children during COVID-19: A mixed-methods study grounded in attachment theory
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic is an adverse experience for many, especially children. It is imperative that we strive to increase knowledge surrounding resiliency and healthy coping mechanisms of children, abilities that if used amidst stressful experiences, are attributed to favourable maternal attachment styles. Data analysis conducted in RStudio will compute measures of central tendency, dispersion, and correlational relationships between variables. Interpretive description will be performed on qualitative data. Findings from this study aim to inform how educators and parents can best support and understand children's resiliency amidst adverse circumstances, including the eventuality of future pandemics.

column36: Using the Perfectionism Social Disconnection Model to Predict Disordered Eating Behaviours in an Undergraduate Sample
column37: Physical distancing regulations implemented to limit the spread of the novel coronavirus during the COVID-19 pandemic have increased feelings of social isolation globally. Unfortunately, this presents another public health concern as social isolation has been linked to depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. Previous research has shown that people with perfectionistic personality types are more likely to experience adverse mental health outcomes in response to social isolation. This is concerning when considering that, similar to social isolation, perfectionism increases individuals' risk of developing depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. The Perfectionism Social Disconnection Model (PSDM; Hewitt et al., 2006) can be used to understand the relationship between perfectionism, social isolation, and adverse mental health outcomes. The PSDM states that perfectionism creates social disconnection, which increases the risk of experiencing mental health concerns. To the best of my knowledge, this model has not yet been applied to the understanding of eating disorders in adults. This is an important population to study as eating disorders have devastating effects both at the individual level and for society. Further, perfectionism has been found to maintain these disorders. The goal of my Master's research will be to apply the PSDM to a sample of undergraduate students to determine if this model can be used to predict disordered eating behaviours. Understanding this relationship has powerful implications for the prevention and treatment of eating disorders in adults. By addressing underlying contributing factors i.e. perfectionism and social disconnection rather than the specific symptoms, we can uncover treatment targets that can be used to prevent multiple disorders.

column37: All prescribers (physicians, pharmacists, nurse practitioners, and others) rely on drug benefit/risk information when working with patients to make important decisions regarding their use. My drug information tool will have a unique advantage compared to classic drug information sources (such as drug monographs), as it will include both text and visual components that appeal to a wide range of prescriber learning styles. column37: Lutter contre la resistance a la chimiotherapie dans le cancer de l'ovaire. Selon les statistiques de l'annee derniere faites par de la Societe canadienne du Cancer, 3000 femmes ont recu un diagnostic de cancer de l'ovaire et 1900 sont mortes des suites de cette maladie. Les medicaments de chimiotherapie utilises pour le traitement du cancer de l'ovaire sont initialement tres efficaces et permettent a une grande proportion des patientes d'entrer en remission. Malheureusement, la majorite de ces patientes vont subir une rechute et generalement, a ce moment, leur cancer aura acquis une forte resistance a la chimiotherapie. Pour reduire le taux de mortalite associe a cette maladie, il est primordial de mieux comprendre comment les cellules de cancer de l'ovaire acquierent cette resistance. Recemment, notre laboratoire a decouvert un nouveau mecanisme par lequel les cellules de cancer de l'ovaire dejouent les effets de la chimiotherapie. Ce mecanisme de resistance permet aux cellules cancereuses non seulement d'eviter la mort par la chimiotherapie, mais aussi de mieux croitre et se multiplier en sa presence. Notre objectif est de comprendre les details moleculaires de ce mecanisme, de facon a pouvoir l'exploiter pour ameliorer les traitements. Nos recherches pourrait donc, a terme, permettre une meilleure survie et des therapies mieux adaptees aux femmes atteintes du cancer de l'ovaire.

column36: A Mixed-Methods Feasibility Trial of an Adapted Novel Psychoeducational Intervention for People Affected by Advanced Cancer
column37: The diagnosis of advanced cancer significantly challenges psychosocial wellbeing for patients and their families. The uncertainty and distress associated with a new diagnosis can be further amplified by insufficient information and preparedness. The informational and psychosocial needs of people affected by advanced cancer are high. However, there is a lack of standardized and sustainable psychosocial support for patients and families at time of diagnosis. I propose an adaptation of my previously developed early, group psychoeducational intervention for patients and families facing a new diagnosis of pancreatic cancer to other cancer types. The intervention will address disease management, decision-making, engagement in life, and access to palliative care and end-of-life care. I will aim to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and preliminary efficacy of the psychoeducational intervention in oncology clinics. Findings will inform the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention and inform methodological refinements for the conduct of a future randomized controlled trial. My program of research presents an innovative approach to operationalize supportive care and inform sustainable, standardized support for patients and their families at a particularly symptomatic and distressing time in the disease course. The goals of my research are consistent with the holistic goals of integrating early supportive care with oncology care to improve quality of life for patients and families.

column36: Modulation of p300 to protect against doxorubicin-mediated cardiotoxicity
column37: Doxorubicin (Dox) is a widely prescribed and highly effective chemotherapy drug that is used to treat a wide variety of cancers. However, it is also known to have adverse effects on cardiac function, and can cause arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, left ventricular dysfunction, and congestive heart failure. Dox acts through a variety of molecular mechanisms, including free radical production, induction of apoptosis, and extracellular matrix remodelling. The major mechanism by which Dox induces apoptosis involves increasing the activity of the tumour suppressor protein p53, which activates apoptotic pathways in the cell. Dox increases p53 activity through the production of reactive oxygen species, direct activation of p53, and decreased degradation of the lysine acetyltransferase p300, which activates p53. Epigenetic modifications such as acetylation are important in the heart because cardiac muscle cells do not have a high turnover rate. Consequently, preventing post-translational acetylation of p53 by p300 may be an important strategy to limit Dox cardiotoxicity. Curcumin, a natural product found in turmeric has been shown to inhibit p300 by promoting its degradation by proteasomes. In addition, curcumin has been shown to have its own anti-cancer properties. However, a drawback of curcumin is its low bioavailability and low half life, resulting in poor absorption through oral consumption. Recently, a new formulation of curcumin, named theracurmin, was developed that is 27x more bioavailable than curcumin alone. We believe that through its effects on p300, theracurmin will protect Dox-treated mice from Dox-mediated cardiotoxicity.

column36: Auto-traitement en ligne pour promouvoir la resilience chez les victimes masculines d'agression sexuelle
column37: L'agression sexuelle (AS) porte atteinte a l'integrite des victimes, et comporte des sequelles severes et recurrentes (ex. anxiete, depression, stress post-traumatique, insomnie, etc.). Le devoilement est determinant dans l'obtention d'un traitement psychologique. Cependant, seulement 5% des AS sont devoilees. Pour les victimes masculines, le devoilement serait encore plus difficile, puisqu'elles sont confrontees aux stereotypes de genre (ex. virilite, role de l'agresseur, etc.) et aux pressions sociales. Des interventions en ligne existent pour favoriser la resilience suite a une AS. Toutefois, aucune intervention ne cible specifiquement le genre masculin ainsi que le devoilement, alors qu'un homme sur 10 est victime d'AS. L'objectif de ce projet est d'adapter un programme d'auto-traitement en ligne visant a promouvoir la resilience en fonction de facteurs entourant le devoilement de l'AS au masculin. Nous posons l'hypothese qu'une version (V) adaptee du programme d'auto-traitement RESILIENT reduira significativement la symptomatologie (symptomes post-traumatiques, anxieux, depressifs et d'insomnie) des victimes masculines d'AS, et qu'une meilleure qualite d'experience utilisatrice sera rapportee. RESILIENT est une plateforme en ligne d'auto-intervention cognitive-comportementale de 12 semaines qui cible la resilience post-traumatique. Afin de comparer l'efficacite des 2 traitements, un essai clinique randomise sera conduit aupres de 2 groupes de participants (1: V<sub>adaptee</sub>, N=15; 2: V<sub>non-adaptee</sub>, N=15; N<sub>total</sub>=30), sur 12 semaines. Une analyse de variance par modele mixte testera l'efficacite des 2 versions sur les symptomes et l'experience utilisatrice. Des tests t a deux echantillons independants compareront la satisfaction des utilisateurs pour chaque version.

column36: Sexual Function and Markers of Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Young Women with End-Stage Kidney Disease
column37: BACKGROUND: Heart disease is the leading cause of premature death for women in Canada. Kidney disease, particularly end-stage kidney disease, which is the most severe form where the patient needs a dialysis machine to survive, affects a rapidly growing number of women each year. Consequently, women with kidney disease are at highest risk of heart disease. In addition, sexual dysfunction is a common risk factor for heart disease among men; however, the association between sexual dysfunction and risk of heart disease has previously not been studied in the high-risk population of young women with end-stage kidney disease. OBJECTIVE: To determine the association between sexual function and risk of heart disease in young women with end-stage kidney disease. METHODS: Women aged 18-50 with end-stage kidney disease on dialysis will be recruited and interviewed in Calgary, Alberta. Sex hormone levels in participants' blood will be collected and assessed and a modified version of the validated Female Sexual Function Index tool will evaluate sexual function separately from sexual activity. Heart disease risk will be measured using pulse-wave velocity and the aortic augmentation index to determine arterial stiffness. First, pulse-wave velocity will be obtained by measuring pressure waveforms from the forearm or thigh and compared to the R-wave that will also be recorded on an electrocardiogram. Next, the aortic augmentation index will be determined from the forearm to ascertain arterial stiffness, which is an indicator of heart disease. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Among young women with end-stage kidney disease, sexual dysfunction will be associated with a higher risk of heart disease.

column36: Characterizing a possible cellular and animal model of clear cell renal cell carcinoma
column37: In 2019, kidney cancer represented approximately 3% of all cancer cases and 2% of cancer deaths in Canada. Most patients are diagnosed with a type called clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), which is often aggressive and resistant to conventional cancer therapies such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Once it becomes metastatic, which is when the cancer has spread beyond its original site, ccRCC is associated with low survival rates. However, in current research on ccRCC, cells that are used to model this disease often do not look similar to what is seen in ccRCC tumours. Furthermore, there is a lack of models for metastatic ccRCC, which limits our ability to understand the mechanisms involved in cancer growth and metastasis. Recently, our collaborators have established ccRCC cells that look more similar to those seen in tumours, which may represent a more relevant model to conduct kidney cancer research. As a result, we want to investigate this possible cellular and animal model of ccRCC that can allow us to have a better understanding of the disease process. To do this, we aim to identify possible differences between cancer cells grown on a plate and cells that are grown in the kidneys of mice, in order to see if this will affect the testing of cancer drugs, which is often performed on cells that are grown on plates. Furthermore, we want to create a model with metastatic cells, which remains elusive, in order to perform experiments to investigate mechanisms within the cell and test therapeutics. By investigating these aims, we want to understand if these cells are more relevant for ccRCC, which can potentially allow for its use as a more widespread model that can assist in identifying mechanisms in ccRCC and in the development of cancer therapeutics.

column36: Risk Factors for Progression of Mild Cognitive Impairment
column37: There are more than 500,000 Canadians living with dementia, and by 2031, that number is expected to increase by 66 percent. This burden on our healthcare system is unsustainable, and there is an urgent need for effective solutions that will allow seniors to maintain cognitive integrity and continue to live independently for longer, limiting the number of care transitions. Cognitive decline encompasses difficulty remembering, learning new things, concentrating or making decisions in everyday life. While some amount of age-related cognitive decline is normal and expected, higher amounts of cognitive decline is considered pathological (termed mild cognitive impairment [MCI]) and may lead to dementia. There is currently minimal understanding of the factors that may lead from MCI to dementia. Although risk factors have been identified (including genetic, psychological and social), it is unclear how they might interact. The proposed study seeks to further characterize individuals with MCI by examining interactions among risk factors. We will use data from UK Biobank. We will examine data from two time points, baseline assessment and follow-up 5-7 years later. We will examine cognitive function, level of physical activity at baseline, level of social support at baseline, and genetic risk status. We expect that individuals who report high levels of physical activity and social support at baseline will be less likely to show decreased cognitive function at follow-up. Furthermore, we predict that those with high genetic risk will benefit less from high levels of physical activity and social support. This study will help to elucidate how risk factors interact and contribute to MCI progression, which will help to inform public health interventions and policies.

column36: Investigating the interplay between endometriosis, polycystic ovarian syndrome, infertility, gynaecological cancer, and their shared risk factors.
column37: Gynaecological disorders such as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), endometriosis and infertility are all associated with endometrial cancer (EC), the most common gynaecological malignancy. These disorders share many risk factors, including obesity, diabetes and hormone imbalance, making it difficult to discern the true aetiology of the diseases or the causal relationships among them. This study aims to elucidate the interplay between these disorders by developing an explanatory model to determine the causal relationships among PCOS, infertility, endometriosis, endometrial cancers and their risk factors. This population-based retrospective cohort study will be carried out in two phases. During phase 1, a hypothesized causal network will be generated based on a thorough literature search. In phase 2, data will be retrieved from the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation database, a multi-site longitudinal study and from CanPath, a prospective cohort of over 300,000 Canadians. All female participants at risk for EC, i.e. women with an intact uterus who were disease-free at the time of recruitment will be considered. The data will be analyzed using machine learning techniques, causal inference methods and traditional epidemiological methods to uncover the underlying causal mechanisms. It is hypothesized that the causal relationships between gynaecological diseases and common risk factors, such as hormonal imbalance and obesity, can explain some of the associations observed between the different disorders. By determining etiologic factors, we can better understand the evolution of different diseases and propose appropriate targets for preventative strategies to reduce the prevalence of common disorders affecting women.

column36: Evaluating WHO infant 'danger' signs and other clinical signs during routine postnatal assessments as predictors of hospitalization and mortality in Dhaka, Bangladesh
column37: Evaluating WHO infant 'danger' signs and other clinical signs during routine postnatal assessments as predictors of hospitalization and death in Dhaka, Bangladesh Background: Current World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend routine home visits to assess infants and urgently refer to hospital if any of eight 'danger' signs (e.g., fever) are present. However, these 'danger' signs were derived from studies in which infants presented to hospital due to caregiver concern, placing them at higher baseline risk for poor outcomes. The 'danger' signs may therefore not be accurate when applied to routine home assessments of usually well infants. In addition to 'danger' signs, other clinical signs detected over time during routine home visits may better predict poor outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the predictive accuracy of WHO 'danger' signs and other clinical signs detected during routine home visits for hospitalization and death among infants in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Methods: Data will be analyzed from a previous clinical trial in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Weekly home visits were conducted with 1164 infants and data were collected on 35 clinical signs (including WHO 'danger' signs), hospitalizations and deaths. Using these data, we will create a model that predicts hospitalization and death based on the values of a range of infant clinical signs. Study significance: Per WHO guidelines, the presence of any infant 'danger' sign on a single home visit signals the need for hospital referral which may lead to over-referral and overburden low-resource health systems. This study can help to improve WHO guidelines by establishing patterns of concerning clinical signs detected over time that can be used to identify at-risk infants early and prevent severe illness and death.

column36: Young Women with Chronic Pain: A Narrative Inquiry
column37: Chronic pain remains a stigmatized and invalidated condition despite global recognition as the third-largest health problem (Finley et al., 2018). Approximately one in five Canadians live with chronic pain, and the estimated cost of chronic pain in Canada is between 56 and 60 billion dollars per year (Canadian Pain Task Force, 2019). In 2019, one-third of Canadians with chronic pain surveyed knew someone who took their own life because of uncontrolled pain (Chronic Pain Association of Canada, 2019). Chronic pain rates are higher among women when compared to men and women are more likely to experience dismissal, delayed diagnosis, misdiagnosis, and inadequate pain management (Ballweg et al., 2010; Schäfer et al., 2016). An increasing prevalence in chronic pain has been observed across all age groups in Canada, most notably among those aged 20 to 29 (Schopflocher et al., 2011). Pain in young adulthood can have negative effects on development and increases risk for substance and psychological disorders (Groenewald & Palermo, 2019). In women of child-bearing age, unmanaged chronic pain can incur long-term consequences on infant and childhood development (Wilson & Fales, 2015). My proposed research will examine the experiences of women aged 18 to 29 living with chronic pain. Using narrative inquiry, I will conduct in-depth semi-structured and unstructured interviews with young women to understand their unique experiences, needs, and challenges faced. By first understanding the lived experience of a demographic that has traditionally been marginalized (Hirsch, 2018), my findings will increase awareness and inform tailored interventions, potentially altering the lifetime trajectory of chronic pain and reducing the individual and societal burden of chronic pain.

column36: Developing an Off the Shelf TAC-T Cell Therapy using Covalent Immune Reprogramming Molecules
column37: Immunotherapy is the use of the immune system to target and fight disease. In the field of cancer research, the immune system has proven to be an extremely effective tool. Adoptive T cell transfer (ATCT) uses immune cells (T-cells) taken out of a patient and engineered to target and kill cancer cells. These have proven to be effective with two clinically approved treatments, however, there still exists production difficulty, time, and cost issues associated with these therapies. T-cell antigen coupler (TAC) receptor T-cells are a new advancement in the field and are engineered to target cancer cells, killing them using the natural signalling pathway of the immune cell. In this project we plan to overcome the current time and accessibility issues faced by ATCT therapies by developing TAC T-cells targeted toward small covalent immune reprogramming molecules (CIR's). These CIR's will be used to permanently link the T-Cells with a molecule that can guide them to cancer cells. The advantage of using these CIR's is that they can be easily made and modified to create a library of molecules that can target different cancer types. The goal of this project is to create a universal T-cell therapy where one set of T-cells can be manufactured and modified using the library of CIR's to go after various different types of cancer. This combination of technologies is hypothesized to overcome some of the largest current limitations in the field as it removes the need to re-engineer cells for each new target and person, in turn lowering both production time and cost. This would bring to the field a new accessible treatment option that can be tailored easily for each patient.

column36: Developpement et evaluation preliminaire d'une formation interdisciplinaire concernant la gestion optimale des symptomes comportementaux et psychologiques de la demence sur le sentiment de detresse des equipes soignantes en CHSLD: une etude pilote
column37: Les symptomes comportementaux et psychologiques de la demence (SCPD) sont un groupe de comportements perturbateurs pouvant etre presents chez les usagers atteints de troubles neurocognitifs (TNC), tels que l'agitation verbale, l'errance, les comportements agressifs et la resistance aux soins. Ces comportements peuvent engendrer de la frustration, du stress et de la peur chez l'usager, ses proches et le personnel soignant. Consequemment, l'evaluation de l'infirmiere, ainsi que la mise en place d'interventions interdisciplinaires par celle-ci, sont des elements primordiaux lors de la prise en charge d'un usager avec des SCPD. Bien que plusieurs lignes directrices sur la gestion optimale de ces symptomes aient ete publiees dans les dernieres annees, la majorite des soignants en CHSLD n'ont pas les connaissances et les habiletes leur permettant d'evaluer adequatement et d'intervenir efficacement aupres de cette clientele. Ce projet de recherche vise a remedier a cette situation. Cette etude de maitrise resultera vraisemblablement en la creation d'une intervention de formation interdisciplinaire validee, laquelle s'adressera au personnel soignant œuvrant aupres des personnes atteintes de TNC en CHSLD.
