column36: Canadian Self-Employed Experience in Returning to Work Following Cancer
column37: Nearly one in two Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer at some point in their lifetime, but due to advances in early detection and treatment, mortality of cancers is on the decline with over 60% of those diagnosed with cancer surviving. Self-employed cancer survivors remain an understudied group with the majority of the literature focusing on salaried cancer survivors, despite self-employed workers accounting for 15% of the Canadian workforce. The lack of research on self-employed survivors means that the barriers and facilitators of remaining or returning to work following cancer remain relatively unknown. The study will be completed by interviewing 25 Canadian self-employed cancer survivors who have remained or returned to work following a cancer diagnosis. Data will be collected during semi-structured phone or zoom interviews of 45 to 60 minutes will be conducted guided by the Vocational Rehabilitation Model for cancer survivors. Interviews will be transcribed verbatim and a continuous, comparative method will be used to code and analyze data of the 25 interviews. The goal of the study is to describe the unique experiences and strategies of self-employed Canadian cancer survivors with remaining or returning to work following cancer. Interviews will explore (1) the overall experiences while remaining at or returning to work; (2) work-related barriers and facilitating factors while remaining at or returning to work; (3) work accommodations employed to address the barriers; and (4) the impact of COVID-19 on cancer survivors ability to remain or return to work. The analyzed data will be used to develop future interventions to support self-employed cancer survivors with remaining or returning to work following cancer.

column36: Identifying the mechanism of adverse inflammatory events induced by red blood cell antibody therapy in immune thrombocytopenia
column37: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is the most common bleeding disorder in children and the case number is continuously rising. This disease is characterized by an abnormally low level of platelets, a cell type that prevents blood loss by forming clots. Thus, patients experience symptoms of easy or excessive bleeding. Currently, the treatment for a significant proportion of patients is either IVIg or anti-D, both of which are specific proteins isolated from blood donations. Unfortunately, these medications have considerable side effects, notably severe inflammation throughout the body. Our lab possesses molecules, called RBC antibodies, that are very similar to anti-D in function. These show therapeutic effects in a mouse model of ITP, but likewise cause inflammation. Understanding how RBC antibodies induce inflammation is a crucial step in uncovering potential ways to prevent it. In the human body, inflammation is caused in various ways, but researchers have identified a relationship between thrombocytopenia and a specific protein involved in inflammation, known as PAF. Interestingly, our lab also discovered that PAF and RBC antibodies stimulate the immune system in similar manners. Therefore, we theorize that PAF is the key protein causing the inflammation associated with RBC antibodies. We will study this by analyzing changes in PAF levels in mice that have been given RBC antibodies. In addition, there are compounds that block the activity of PAF. Thus, our subsequent focus will be to examine whether these inflammatory effects can be reduced or avoided by blocking PAF activity. By providing insight into how these therapies cause inflammation, we can work towards preventing it, and ultimately deliver a safer treatment option to patients.

column36: Investigating Connectivity Changes with Theta Burst Stimulation in Youth Depression
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability in Canadian youth ages 15-24. MDD has devastating social, economic, and personal consequences, as well as carries the serious risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and death by suicide. Failure to respond to the first line of treatment (i.e. psychotherapy and/or antidepressants) is common in youth and some antidepressants can cause serious side effects (e.g. increased suicidal thoughts). As such, novel treatments for youth MDD are being investigated. A treatment involving non-invasive brain stimulation (called theta burst stimulation or TBS) is a promising alternative. In youth, recent research suggests that TBS was feasible, well tolerated, and significantly reduced depressive symptoms. However, the specific mechanisms underlying this protocol's therapeutic effects in youth MDD have yet to be fully determined. Therefore, the objective of this project is to investigate the effects of a TBS protocol on brain connectivity (i.e. the communication amongst distinct brain regions) by means of a randomized clinical trial. This is important as previous research suggests that the development of MDD may implicate an abnormality in the connectivity of certain brain regions. Connectivity will be assessed by measuring the electrical activity of the brain through electrodes placed on the scalp combined with non-invasive brain stimulation (TMS-EEG). Participants will include youth (16-24 years old) with MDD. The results of the proposed project could assist in designing future treatments for youth MDD that focus on correcting the abnormal connectivity of certain brain regions. Altogether, the findings of this project could have a clinical benefit for youth depression.

column37: Indigenous Peoples experience health disparities at a disproportionately high rate. The goal of this research is to understand how health sovereignty might address issues of health inequalities and environmental disparities Indigenous Peoples experience. The specific objectives are to i) determine how health and wellness are defined from an Indigenous perspective; ii) work with communities to collect and analyze community health data, with a particular focus on the current COVID-19 pandemic; and iii) identify solutions with communities to address the issues with health and health care access. Important themes reflected in the questionnaire include general health and wellbeing, access to health services and information, mental health, access to and control over food, access to land, ceremony, and demographics. This research is an opportunity to look at how health sovereignty might close the health gap that exists between Indigenous and non-Indigenous people and will play a crucial role in understanding how Indigenous communities are changing and overcoming barriers. The holistic nature of this research will allow for better understanding of mental, physical, social, and cultural health in Indigenous communities in Canada. column36: Evaluation of strategies to enhance intervention fidelity of a multi-component intervention to reduce non-indicated imaging for low back pain
column37: For most patients with low back pain (LBP), imaging tests such as x-ray, MRI, and CT scans have limited use in diagnosis and treatment, and are not recommended by research. However, these tests are still commonly used in clinical practice. While several interventions have been developed to reduce imaging, the effectiveness has been variable. This could be due simply to ineffectiveness of the intervention, or it could be due to poor implementation of the intervention during the study period. For example, if the intervention was delivered inappropriately or not at all, it may not be that the intervention was ineffective, but instead, we are unsure if the intervention was ineffective because it was not used properly. The latter case describes the concept of intervention fidelity, which is how well intervention components were delivered; this was not assessed in many of the previous studies. Assessing intervention fidelity during a study can help us better interpret the study's findings on intervention effectiveness. However, assessing intervention fidelity before a main study starts, for example, in a pilot study or by asking a sample of the target population to identify barriers to using the proposed intervention, can help us understand how to optimise the intervention to be more feasible and pragmatic, thereby reducing research waste. The proposed research will use interviews to explore strategies to ensure intervention fidelity of a multi-component intervention designed to reduce imaging for LBP by general practitioners and chiropractors in Newfoundland and Labrador. The findings will play a role in improving interventions aimed at reducing imaging for LBP in several Canadian provinces, improving care for patients and the sustainability of the healthcare system.

column36: PET-MRI Framework for Response Monitoring and Therapeutics in Myocardial Infarctions
column37: About 2.4 million Canadians aged 20 years and older live with diagnosed ischemic heart disease, and 578,000 with a history of a heart attack, or myocardial infarction. The adverse effects of a heart attack contribute to death of heart cells, or cardiomyocytes. This can lead to poor pump function, affecting circulation of oxygenated blood to the body. This eventually leads to heart failure conditions. Several treatments have held promise for the repair and replacement of damaged heart tissue; In particular, cardiomyocytes derived from stem cells have been shown to be a promising therapy after a heart attack. However, the mechanisms of structural and functional integration of the transplanted cells with host tissue and their impact on cardiac function are less understood; the metabolism of transplanted cells has also never been studied in live animal models. The primary objective of this project is to establish a hybrid Positron Emission Tomography and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (PET-MRI) framework to reveal non-invasively the underlying evolving structural and metabolic alterations impacting heart tissue following cell therapy. MRI is the gold standard imaging method to study heart function and detect scar tissue. Complementing this, PET provides the metabolic state of cells as reflected by their glucose uptake. With well-established imaging protocols, this project will provide the first in-depth look into the maturation and integration of stem cell derived cardiomyocytes in the clinically relevant large animal model. Developing the PET-MRI framework opens the possibility of its widespread use as a non-invasive imaging modality for any regenerative therapy, with clinical implications for response monitoring in patients suffering from heart failure.

column36: The role of IL-1beta in regulating adseverin expression, chondrocyte phenotype and cartilage formation
column37: Osteoarthritis is an irreversible, degenerative joint disorder with limited treatment options. Recently, the loss of chondrogenic phenotype and subsequent production of degradative enzymes within articular cartilage have been theorized to contribute to OA pathogenesis. Studies have shown that chondrocyte phenotype is regulated by the actin cytoskeleton, which is in turn regulated by actin remodeling proteins such as adseverin. Adseverin protein has been shown to depolymerize filamentous actin within the cytoskeleton, resulting in the decrease of stress fibres and increased expression of chondrogenic genes, thereby maintaining the biomechanically superior chondrogenic phenotype. In contrast, interleukin-1β, a proinflammatory cytokine upregulated in osteoarthritis, is known to increase the amount of filamentous actin and stimulate the release of various catabolic enzymes, representing a departure from the chondrogenic phenotype. Interestingly, preliminary data from the Kandel Lab has shown that interleukin-1β treatment results in premature loss of adseverin in primary chondrocytes. Thus, this study aims to characterize the effects of interleukin-1β on adseverin expression and chondrocyte phenotype, as well as identify the mechanisms behind interleukin-1β-induced downregulation of adseverin. This work will further our current understanding of osteoarthritis development and may help to identify potential drug targets.

column36: The Effects of Empagliflozin in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction
column37: The treatment of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is perhaps the most pressing unmet need in clinical cardiology. Despite accounting for approximately half of all heart failure patients, there remains no reliably effective treatment for HFpEF. Empagliflozin (EMPA) is an emerging therapy with promise in treating HFpEF. While large scale clinical trials are on-going to establish high-level effects, a fine grained understanding of how EMPA interacts with HFpEF is yet to be brought forward. Some existing research suggests EMPA protects the heart through a beneficial shift in cardiac metabolism. This mechanism is of particular interest in HFpEF, which often presents with metabolic dysfunction that may be improved by EMPA. Thus, my work aims to uncover the magnitude and nature of EMPA's effects in an animal model of HFpEF, with a particular focus upon metabolic alterations. By examining improvements in HFpEF symptoms in live animals, while simultaneously interrogating the driving mechanisms, this research will connect specific effects of EMPA to specific causes. This work promises to optimize the use of EMPA clinically, while enhancing our foundational understanding of HFpEF itself.

column36: GM-CSF autoantibodies: a novel diagnostic marker and personalized therapeutic for Crohn's disease
column37: Crohn's disease (CD) is a severe and chronic inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract. Affecting almost 400 per 100,000 Canadians, CD currently has no cure. Research suggests that CD results from a combination of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors, leading to dysregulated immune activation in the gut. Mononuclear phagocytes (MNPs) are crucial cells that balance intestinal immune activity and are dependent on granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF), a key protein that supports growth and function of MNPs. Interestingly, our study of two retrospective cohorts of CD patients revealed that a large proportion of patients display increased levels of autoantibodies in their blood that specifically bind to GM-CSF up to 7 years prior to disease diagnosis. Characterization of these antibodies demonstrated that they specifically neutralize the function of GM-CSF through binding sugar chains on the protein, dampening MNP activity. In line with our results, mutations in genes involved in GM-CSF signaling have been identified as strong risk factors for CD, emphasizing the importance of GM-CSF in intestinal health. In this proposal, we aim to genetically engineer GM-CSF variants that can escape neutralization by autoantibodies in CD patients. These variants will be used to develop a diagnostic assay to identify CD patients and classify them based on their reactivity against GM-CSF. Collectively, this proposal opens an avenue towards a predictive diagnostic and personalized treatment strategy for CD.

column36: Deep Learning Approaches to Deciphering Intra-Tumoural Heterogeneity for Precision Medicine
column37: Cancer therapeutics for aggressive cancers such as glioblastoma (GBM) based on traditional models of cancer have failed to yield durable and improved outcomes in clinical trials. One recent explanation for these previous failures is that while we often think of a patient's tumour as being a homogenous mass of identical cancer cells, there are in fact a number of tumour subclones within each cancer tumour that respond differently to our conventional and traditional therapies. This means that existing treatments may not equally target all tumour cells and allow resistant subclones to survive and drive disease recurrence and progression. To address this, this project will aim to harness expertise in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and molecular profiling to explore if AI technology can help automate the detection of biologically distinct tumour subregions and understand the biological significance of these computer defined regions. First, previously trained AI tools and dissection technology will be used to determine if computer defined regions of variability do indeed show unique biological activity that may be driving partial responses to therapy. Secondly, the degree of morphological variation within selected tumours will be examined to determine if AI-defined variation predicts therapeutic response and/or success within our dataset. If successful, this project will help to define areas within cancer tumours that should be distinctly targeted therapeutically. Routine use of this tool will help define and characterize distinct tumour subpopulations, as well as aid in designing personalized drug cocktails to target a larger fraction of the tumours' true biology. Ultimately, this could provide more durable responses for patients.

column36: Prehabilitation in adolescent and young adult extremity sarcoma patients: a mixed methods study
column37: Prehabilitation (prehab)before cancer surgery represents a shift from reactive to proactive cancercare, providing immediate action steps down a path to recovery followingdiagnosis. The concept is analogous marathon training, where structuredexercise over time builds the physical and psychological capacity necessary forsuccess at a taxing event. column36: Impact of a stromal 16p11.2 microdeletion on tumor progression, angiogenesis, and pro-oncogenic transcriptional networks

column36: Inhibitors of the Nef-Src Family Kinase Interaction: Small Molecules to Enable an HIV-1 Cure
column37: Despite many tried approaches, there is no practical cure for Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV-1) infection. Indeed, many candidate cures rely on the host immune response to clear persisting virus, but HIV-1's ability to evade immune clearance effectively compromises cure success in vivo. In this light, HIV-1 immune evasion translates to cure evasion and thus strategies to block HIV-1 immune evasion are required for cure success. A majority of the HIV-1 immune evasion phenotype is encoded by the HIV-1 Nef protein. Specifically, Nef facilitates immune evasion by driving HIV-1 escape from Cytotoxic T Lymphocyte (CTL)-mediated killing. To do so, Nef binds and activates a Src Family Kinase (SFK) to induce the endocytosis of cell surface Major Histocompatibility Complex Class I (MHC-I), thereby halting HIV-1 antigen presentation to CTLs. Previous studies have demonstrated that blockade of the Nef-SFK interaction rescues cell surface MHC-I and promotes CTL-mediated HIV-1 killing. As such, inhibitors targeting the Nef-SFK interaction could restore HIV-1 clearance to functionalize otherwise failed curative strategies. Previously, our group identified a small molecule inhibitor of the Nef-SFK interaction through an in silico drug library screen against Nef. Subsequent in vitro work determined that the inhibitor, H3-1, rescues MHC-I in a Nef-dependant manner and is minimally cytotoxic. However, H3-1 demonstrates suboptimal efficacy in cell culture and is rapidly cleared in vivo. Thus, we aim to expand upon H3-1 in order to develop second generation Nef-SFK inhibitors with improved biostability and target affinity. We anticipate that inhibitors of Nef-mediated immune evasion will play an essential role in functionalizing a practical HIV-1 cure.

column36: The impact of oxytocin on stress-induced hyperalgesia
column37: Chronic pain affects approximately 20% of the population and, compared to other chronic conditions, results in the lowest quality of life. As a chronic pain patient, I have personal understanding of the factors that affect chronic pain. One such factor is the impact stress has on pain symptoms. Research has extensively confirmed the connection between stress and pain, both clinically and experimentally. In my thesis, I propose to research the underlying mechanisms behind the impact of stress on pain. I will measure how stress affects both subjective experiences and neurobiological responses to pain, as measured by self-reported pain and electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. I will compare two methods of experimental stress induction and their impacts on pain. Pain tests will be performed before and after stress induction while an EEG records brain activity. The impact of stress will be measured by changes in pain scores and EEG responses before and after stress induction. Additionally, I will explore whether oxytocin inhalation mitigates the stress induced pain sensitivity compared to placebo inhalation. Oxytocin is a hormone released during positive social interactions and has been shown to inhibit cortisol responses in experimental stress. My thesis has strong clinical implications; by isolating a potential mechanism behind the stress-pain relationship, new insights may be provided to support pain interventions focused on stress reduction. Additionally, exploring the therapeutic approach of oxytocin on pain exacerbation provides a new therapeutic possibility for chronic pain patients. Oxytocin has a strong therapeutic potential because it has few side effects and can be strategically taken by the patient before stressful events (e.g. before writing a final exam).

column36: Modeling Human Robinow Syndrome Mutations in Drosophila
column37: Fruit flies are ideal for studying the underlying mechanisms and potential therapies for human genetic disorders since they share up to 75% of disease-causing genes with humans. Humans and flies have many common developmental processes, but the fly is much simpler. Flies are also much easier, cheaper, and quicker to raise than other vertebrate models. Using flies, we can precisely manipulate genetics to study human mutations within cells in developing tissues, yielding much more dynamic information than 2D cell culture and more efficiently than other vertebrate models like mice. In my project, I study mutations in a gene called Dishevelled1 (DVL1) that were obtained from patients with Robinow Syndrome (RS). RS is a rare genetic disorder that is associated with craniofacial abnormalities and shortened stature. Many of the mutations associated with this disorder affect components of the same signaling pathway, referred to as non-canonical Wnt signaling, which guides neighbouring cells to orient in the same direction. Much about this pathway is still not well understood and needs further research. I manipulate flies to express normal or mutated versions of DVL1 in specific regions of their bodies. I can then compare the resulting phenotypes, such as misaligned hairs, vein abnormalities and cell death, to well-characterized mutations in flies to identify which components or pathways are being disrupted by the variants. By learning which signals are being heightened or squashed by the presence of the mutation, we gain insight into the underlying mechanisms of non-canonical Wnt signaling and more broadly, how development in individuals with RS is altered. This information may guide future therapeutics for RS patients.

Le gardiennage, quant a lui, vise a repondre aux besoins des familles desirant vivre leur quotidien tout en compensant la charge additionnelle de responsabilites qu'amenent les incapacites de la personne. Pour les familles de personnes en situation de handicap, l'offre de ces services est nettement insuffisante. En effet, on reconnait le manque de ressources financieres et humaines pour offrir un service de qualite. En plus, les criteres d'admissibilite pour les services sont tres precis limitant l'accessibilite aux services. Donc, est-ce que certaines familles s'en sortent? Quels sont leurs moyens? Qui leur offre ces services? C'est ce que ce projet documentera, soit les moyens utilises par les familles ayant a charge une personne en situation de handicap pour obtenir du repit, du gardiennage ou du depannage. Un questionnaire en ligne sera envoye aux familles ayant a charge une personne en situation de handicap a travers le Quebec afin de recueillir ces informations. Par la suite, des entrevues seront menees avec une douzaine de familles dans le but de mieux comprendre les strategies innovantes mises en place. column37: Obesity is a growing issue in our society, especially during childhood where the effects can persist long-term, as well as predispose children to other health concerns. column36: Sex as a biological variable: Immunomodulatory mechanisms of Innate Defence Regulator (IDR) peptides in asthma

Steroid-unresponsive patients with uncontrolled asthma represent the major burden of disease, and account for annual healthcare costs of around $2B in Canada. Steroid therapies can also increase the risk of lung infections, which makes asthma worse. Thus, there is urgent need to develop new therapies that can control steroid-unresponsive asthma without compromising patient's ability to resolve infections. Adult females experience greater disease severity, are more likely to develop steroid-unresponsiveness and have uncontrolled asthma than males. Such Sex-bias is largely ignored during drug development. It is necessary to consider sex-differences in response during development of new treatments. This study will focus on new molecules known as Innate Defence Regulator (IDR) peptides, which can control both inflammation and infection. We have shown that IDR peptides improve breathing capacity and control lung inflammation in an animal model of asthma. This project will comprehensively examine the effects of our lead IDR peptide in both females and males concurrently, to define sex-related differences, using an animal model and human lung cells. This research will directly support the development of a new IDR peptide-based therapy for asthma. It is entirely possible that we will need to develop sex-specific treatment protocols to provide the most efficient care for asthma sufferers.

column36: Investigation into the structure and function of Junctophilin, an important protein in the skeletal and cardiac systems
column37: Heartbeats and muscle contractions are essential to life. A small molecule plays a key role in both processes: the calcium ion. Although generally known as a building block for healthy bones, calcium ions are crucial for the function of almost all the cells in our bodies. In cardiac and skeletal muscles, calcium is a messenger for muscle contraction. Muscle cells are separated into many compartments by membranes. When muscles contract, calcium ions move from one compartment to another, which is achieved by a special pathway embedded in the cell membranes. This calcium transport system is regulated by a wide variety of proteins, all of which must function properly for muscle contraction. I will study a crucial protein in this system known as junctophilin. Mutations in this protein lead to the disorder hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which causes irregular heartbeats and may be fatal. In order to study how this protein normally behaves and how it misbehaves in patients with mutations, I will study the 3D structures of junctophilin proteins in both the normal and diseased forms. Because proteins are too small to be viewed under light microscopes, I will utilize X-rays to analyze the proteins' structure in a crystal. In addition, I will measure how the normal and diseased junctophilins interact with other protein players in the calcium transport system. Comparing the differences between normal and mutant proteins will lead to a deeper understanding of the mechanism behind heartbeats and muscle contractions. The insights gained from 3D structures of junctophilin and the protein's interactions with other components of calcium transport can pave the way for new therapeutic strategies aimed at correcting the mistakes of faulty proteins in patients.

column36: Gene expression regulation in recurrent paediatric acute myeloid leukaemia by characterization of non-coding ribonucleic acids
column37: Despite research advances leading to better treatments, paediatric cancers continue to claim the lives of children year after year. Cancer recurrence or relapse occurs after treatment initially appears to be successful, but later the cancer returns. In the case of paediatric acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), children who relapse are known to have poorer clinical outcomes than those that stay in remission. Like other cancers, paediatric AML is partly caused by mutations in genes in certain human cells. In addition, how these genes are regulated and how they become dysregulated in cancer, is partially due to the activity of certain ribonucleic acids (RNAs), collectively called non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). There are many kinds of ncRNAs and a number have been found to have varied roles in maintaining cells in non-cancerous states. Logically, when certain ncRNAs do not function in the way they are supposed to, cancer may develop. Hence, by characterizing ncRNAs in paediatric AML, a better understanding of why some children relapse and others do not, may emerge. Most importantly, it is hoped that this understanding may facilitate the development of better treatments that improve the outcomes for kids with paediatric AML.

column36: The role of astrocytes in stress-induced behavioural dysfunction
column37: Stress is essential for survival however, prolonged and repeated exposure to stress often precedes the development of mental health disorders such as depression and anxiety. As such, a deeper investigation of stress will permit a better understanding of mental health and related pathology. Non-neuronal brain cells comprise of 50% the brain, yet previous research has neglected the role of these cells in stress-induced behavioural dysfunction. Our study aims to determine how astrocytes, a sub-set of non-neuronal brain cells, are influenced by stress and how this interaction impacts behaviour. Prior research has revealed stress-related structural and functional impairments of astrocytes. Despite these observations, the downstream consequences for behaviour remain ill-determined. To determine the effects of stress on astrocyte activity and how this influences behaviour, we will use a combination of advanced imaging, behavioural and chemogenetic techniques. By investigating the involvement of non-neuronal brain cells, we hope to provide better understanding of the mechanisms by which stress contributes to the development of behavioural dysfunction. Together, these data have the potential to reveal novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of stress-related disorders such as anxiety and depression.

column36: Suivi longitudinal intensif au moyen d'une application mobile pour predire les changements de symptomes en psychiatrie
column37: Les troubles de sante mentale varient en severite dans le temps, alternant entre des phases de stabilite et de crise. Un des principaux defis pour les professionnels en sante mentale est de pouvoir predire ces changements sur la base de donnees suffisamment objectives. Malheureusement, les entretiens cliniques menes dans le cabinet medical sont souvent rares et l'information fournie par le patient est empreinte de subjectivite (difficulte de rappel, etc.). Il apparait donc necessaire de developper des outils permettant de quantifier l'evolution d'un trouble a l'aide de mesures objectives, obtenues de facon continue dans le milieu de vie du patient. Dans le cadre de ce projet, nous explorerons l'utilite de donnees dites de phenotypage digital, c'est-a-dire des donnees de questionnaires d'auto-evaluation des symptomes ainsi que des donnees d'utilisation (p. ex., nombre de deverrouillage) et des capteurs (p. ex., Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, accelerometre) du telephone intelligent, recueillies en continu par une application mobile dediee. Les donnees utilisees sont obtenues tant chez des personnes en bonne sante mentale pour evaluer le stress et l'humeur que chez des personnes souffrant de troubles mentaux pour evaluer des symptomes plus severes. Les donnees sont d'abord transformees en indicateurs interpretables pour les cliniciens (sommeil, isolement social, etc.). Puis, l'apprentissage (automatique) profond est ensuite utilise pour creer des modeles personnalises qui formulent des predictions de l'etat futur de l'utilisateur du telephone intelligent. Le phenotypage digital combine a l'apprentissage automatique a le potentiel d'ameliorer les soins en sante mentale en rendant possibles des suivis personnalises bases sur des donnees objectives.

column36: Probing multimodal hippocampal connectivity and memory in psychosis using ultra-high-field neuroimaging
column37: Schizophrenia and related psychoses (SZ) are debilitating psychiatric disorders affecting around 3 % of the Canadian population and are characterized by positive (e.g., hallucinations, delusions), negative (e.g., reduced motivation, flattened affect), and cognitive (e.g., memory, attention deficits) symptoms. Verbal memory is one of the most affected cognitive functions in SZ and predicts poor clinical and functional outcomes. Studies have shown abnormalities in the structural and functional connections between the hippocampus, a deep brain region, and other brain regions, especially frontal areas, which may drive verbal memory impairments in SZ and first-episode psychosis (FEP). However, previous research has been unable to reliably distinguish the effects of different regions of the hippocampus due to limitations with brain imaging techniques and study design. The goal of our study is to investigate the relationship between cortical-hippocampal connectivity, verbal memory, symptoms and functional outcomes in 30 FEP patients and 30 healthy controls. Our study will leverage the advantages of multimodal (structural and functional MRI) and ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging (7T MRI) as well as multivariate statistical techniques to better understand the neurobiological substrates of symptoms and functioning in psychosis. We hypothesize that patients will show decreased hippocampal connectivity in key regions and that these will be differentially associated with decreased verbal memory, more severe symptoms and poor outcomes of FEP patients. This study will provide a clearer understanding of the role of distinct areas of the hippocampus and their connectivity profiles in relation to cognitive and negative symptoms and functioning in SZ.

column36: Linking phosphatidylcholine to basal forebrain degeneration in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disorder that results in extensive cell death in the brain. The brain contains many different types of cells, but certain brain cells are more susceptible to death during AD than others. Cholinergic neurons are a type of brain cell located mainly in a region called the basal forebrain. Research indicates that cholinergic neurons are among the first cells to die in AD, but why this occurs is unknown. One emerging explanation for the early death of cholinergic neurons in AD points to the high demand of these neurons for a fat called phosphatidylcholine (PC). Cholinergic neurons are the only cells in the brain that use PC for two purposes: to maintain their cell structure and to make the chemical they use to communicate. Therefore, cholinergic neurons require large amounts of PC. If levels of PC are low in AD, this deficiency may increase the susceptibility of cholinergic neurons to death in AD. To test this hypothesis, we will use data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP). ADNI and ROSMAP contain data from healthy older adults and individuals with AD. We will use structural brain imaging data from ADNI to measure the volume of the basal forebrain across time within individuals and examine if this relates to blood levels of PC. Next, we will use data from ROSMAP which contains blood PC measurements before death, and brain PC measured after death in the same individuals. This will be used to ensure blood PC levels are strongly related to brain PC levels. ROSMAP will also act as a second test sample to validate any relationships found in ADNI. Overall, our findings may reveal a novel mechanism underlying the early death of cholinergic neurons in AD.

column36: Determining the Ability of Optical Coherence Tomography to Discriminate Middle Ear Pathologies
column37: The middle ear is a mechanical system which carries sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear. Approximately 4% of the general population experiences issues where middle ear function is impaired causing hearing loss. Middle ear disorders can often be treated with surgery, but because it is difficult to distinguish different causes of middle ear disease, surgeons often go into the operating room not knowing exactly what they will be dealing with. This uncertainty results in the frequent need for exploratory surgery, creates difficulties around informed consent for middle ear procedures and introduces costs and delays due to the inability to adequately plan surgeries. Previous studies have shown that rich diagnostic information can be obtained by optically measuring the motion of middle ear structures in response to sound. However, these measurements cannot currently be obtained in the clinic without removing the ear drum. We have developed an imaging and vibrometry system using Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) technology that can non-invasively image through the ear drum to obtain structural and functional information about the middle ear. My research will show that OCT imaging and vibrometry of the middle ear can be used to differentiate and diagnose various middle ear diseases in a cadaveric temporal bone model. I will identify those features and measurements visible in the OCT data that distinguish a set of middle ear diseases that are not readily distinguishable using current diagnostics and that have different surgical treatments. Successful completion of this experiment will allow us to translate the findings to the clinic where those same measurements can be used to improve the differential diagnosis of middle ear diseases and plan surgeries.

column36: Non-coding RNA regulation of RIPK1 in necroptosis
column37: Background: Atherosclerosis is a common cardiovascular condition where blood flow can be restricted by lipid and immune cell buildup inside arteries. Necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death, is activated during atherosclerosis. As a critical mediator of the necroptotic pathway, receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) helps to determine whether a cell survives or dies. These pathological processes can be controlled by microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), which show dysregulation in diseases including atherosclerosis. Rationale: While existing research reveals elevated RIPK1 activity in atherosclerotic plaques, it remains unclear how RIPK1 is regulated at the RNA level. Our project aims to fill this gap by highlighting key non-coding (ncRNAs) that interact with Ripk1 messenger RNA (mRNA). Hypothesis: Distinct miRNAs and lncRNAs regulate RIPK1 expression in macrophages, which in turn influences RIPK1 activity in necroptosis during atherosclerosis. Methods: We will be using mouse macrophages and adding specific stimuli to create a necroptotic environment. Pull-down assays will be performed to identify miRNAs and lncRNAs binding Ripk1 mRNA, and RNA sequencing will allow us to analyze their expression. With miRNA mimics and lncRNA vectors, we will overexpress sequences of interest in treated cells. Other molecular biology techniques will also be used to examine the presence of inflammatory and cell death markers. Significance: This research will broaden our knowledge of mechanisms that drive macrophage necroptosis in vulnerable plaques, paving the way for future analyses and applications in vivo. Our findings may potentially lead to the development of targeted therapies for advanced atherosclerosis, reducing the global burden of disease.

column36: Epidemiology and surveillance methods of non-traumatic spinal cord injury: shedding light on an ignored disease burden
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a major cause of morbidity and socioeconomic burden in Canada. Indirect, public health costs associated with SCI have been estimated as the highest of any neurological disease. SCI can be divided broadly into two categories: traumatic (tSCI) and non-traumatic (ntSCI). In Canada, ntSCI is associated with an overall greater disease burden. Unfortunately, there is a lack of epidemiological research on ntSCI; specifically, there is a lack of consensus defining ntSCI and a lack of methodological tools for ntSCI surveillance, from onset of injury to recovery. To optimize health care, and thus eventually improve disease burden associated with ntSCI, we must first analyze the shortcomings of available literature describing ntSCI and its surveillance. The current research will address these limitations, paving the way for future high-quality research aimed at optimizing care of patients suffering from ntSCI. Specifically, the current research focuses on two systematic reviews and meta-analysis. The first will seek to 1) estimate the incidence of ntSCI in the general population, 2) identify widely-used case definitions to identify SCI across multiple surveillance data sources, and 3) quantify the association between study-level methodological characteristics of ntSCI surveillance studies and incidence estimates. The second systematic review will analyze the evaluation of the accuracy of several different surveillance data sources and algorithms identifying ntSCI. Eventually, we aim to assess the interventions used for treatment of ntSCI. Ultimately, this leads to optimized health care resource allocation for patients with ntSCI, which can contribute to decreased societal costs, disease burden, and improved individual patient quality of life.

column36: Social cognition in youth who have a first-degree relative with schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a heritable and disabling mental health disorder that affects approximately 1% of the population. A symptom of schizophrenia is impaired social cognition, the ability to understand and respond appropriately to the intentions and behaviours of others. The resulting social dysfunction is a major barrier to recovery and significantly impacts quality of life. As schizophrenia is highly heritable, individuals who have a first-degree relative (i.e., parent, sibling) with schizophrenia are at increased risk of developing the disorder themselves. These individuals also tend to show reduced social-cognitive performance and reduced functioning in their interpersonal relationships, school, and work. Although social cognition has been well-studied in adults who are at familial high-risk for developing schizophrenia, it has been under-investigated in younger populations. This is an important group to study because the onset of schizophrenia tends to occur in adolescence and young adulthood. Impairments in social cognition experienced by youth who have a first-degree with schizophrenia may predict the later emergence of the disorder and the related social dysfunction. In addition, little is known about how impairments in social cognition in these youth are associated with their ability to function in various areas, such as maintaining relationships and performing well at school or work. This research will therefore provide novel information on the social-cognitive profiles and functional outcomes of youth with a first-degree relative with schizophrenia. Findings from this research can be used to guide the development of innovative treatments that could prevent or delay the onset of schizophrenia and the resulting social dysfunction.

column36: Etude du role des plaquettes activees par les complexes immuns dans le recrutement des neutrophiles aux reins dans le lupus erythemateux dissemine
column37: Le lupus erythemateux dissemine est une maladie immunitaire qui touche 1 personne sur 1000 et les femmes dans 90% des cas. Le systeme immunitaire se compose de globules blancs qui patrouillent le corps et qui reconnaissent et tolerent les cellules et ses composantes. La nephrite lupique est une complication du lupus durant laquelle les globules blancs attaquent les composantes des reins. Elle touche 60% des patients lupiques et represente une cause majeure de mortalite. Les globules blancs s'accumulent aux reins et accentuent les dommages tissulaires durant la nephrite lupique. Lors de saignements, les globules blancs requierent une interaction avec les plaquettes, un petit element du sang connu pour arr eter les saignements, pour entrer dans le tissu. Nous ne savons pas dans le contexte du lupus si ce m eme mecanisme est implique dans le recrutement des globules blancs aux reins. L'hypothese est que les plaquettes interagissent avec les globules blancs et accelerent leur recrutement aux reins dans le lupus. Dans un premier temps, nous etudierons les interactions plaquette-globule blanc dans un appareil mimant ce qui se produit aux reins durant la nephrite lupique. Cela permettra d'etudier par quel mecanisme les plaquettes recrutent les globules blancs aux reins. Ensuite, la presence des plaquettes et des globules blancs sera caracterisee en microscopie dans les reins de souris a differents stades de la maladie. Le mecanisme responsable de l'arrivee des globules blancs aux reins sera bloque chez ces souris et l'effet sur leur recrutement sera evalue. Ce projet pourrait mener a l'identification de nouvelles cibles pour des medicaments permettant de limiter la severite de la nephrite lupique en bloquant l'arrivee des globules blancs aux reins.

column36: Measuring the Impact of the COVID-19 Pandemic on all Persons with Dementia
column37: Persons living with dementia in Canada are most at risk of experiencing severe outcomes of the COVID-19 pandemic. This population accounts for the majority of deaths, and faces inherently higher risk due to advanced age, presence of chronic conditions, and cognitive and functional declines associated with more challenges in implementing social distancing. Furthermore, there is growing evidence that COVID-19 has a more severe impact on racialized persons and persons of lower socioeconomic status, especially in populations where these two social determinants intersect. To date, we do not know how the pandemic impacts diverse populations of persons living with dementia. In order to understand the impact of the pandemic on these diverse populations, we will (1) describe the diversity of persons living with dementia, and (2) measure the extent to which the intersection of racialization and socioeconomic status modifies this impact. This project will use health administrative databases to conduct the first description of the diversity of persons living with dementia in Canada. We will then measure the diverse impact of the pandemic on persons living with dementia in comparing mortality, care, and health service use of two cohorts, one exposed to the pandemic and one not exposed to the pandemic, using advanced statistical methods, strengthening causal inference from observational data. Results will be presented to key stakeholders including persons living with dementia, caregivers, decision makers, managers, and clinicians in four provinces (ON, SK, AB, QB) to generate recommendations through deliberative dialogue in order to decrease the inequitable impacts of the pandemic, and improve the care of all persons with dementia.

column36: Investigating signalling changes leading to recurrence in matched primary and recurrent pairs of glioblastoma brain tumour stem cells
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common primary brain tumour in adults. High invasiveness, aggressive growth, and recurrence make GBM difficult to treat. Despite the current standard of care, GBM has a median overall survival of a mere 15 months after diagnosis. Based on the poor prognosis, there is a dire need for new treatments for GBM. Cancer stem cells, a sub-population of cells found in many different cancers, have the ability to self-renew and differentiate into the heterogeneous population of cells that make up the bulk of a tumour. In GBM, brain tumour stem cells (BTSCs) are considered one of the primary causes for treatment resistance and high rates of recurrence. The process of tumour recurrence is vastly understudied in BTSCs and has never been fully examined in matching primary and recurrent pairs of BTSCs from the same patients. Only a few matching BTSC primary/recurrent pairs exist in North America. Our lab has BTSCs generated from single patient's primary tumour and the matching recurrent tumours. We will use the BTSCs from matched sets in order to examine signalling changes that occur in recurrent BTSCs. We will further investigate how those changes can be targeted or modulated in order to reduce the aggressive phenotype associated with recurrent tumours and revert it back to a more primary (less aggressive) phenotype. Modulating the matching primary and recurrent BTSCs to change their growth, migratory, and tumour producing phenotypes into each other using genetic or pharmacological means has never been done before. This project will help identify important mechanisms in BTSCs that contribute to GBM recurrence. This, in turn, could lead to new treatments for recurrent GBM and hopefully improve the overall survival for this devastating disease.

column36: A Randomized Controlled Trial of MomsInMind: A Mobile Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Application for Postpartum Depression
column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) is one of the most common complications of childbirth, affecting up to one in five women. Left untreated, it increases the risk of future mental health problems in mothers and can have significant negative effects on children. Mothers with PPD breastfeed less often and struggle more with parenting, and the children of women with PPD have more difficulties in school and higher rates of mental health problems. Indeed, every single case of PPD costs Canada around $150,000 over a mother's lifetime. The lack of social support from friends, family, and other mothers during COVID-19 has worsened feelings of loneliness and isolation, increasing symptoms of PPD and worsening outcomes for families. In order to treat PPD, experts recommend talk therapy (i.e., psychotherapy) for most mothers. Talk therapy techniques have been used in mobile applications previously; however, it is unclear how effective these techniques will be in reducing symptoms of PPD when delivered by a mobile application without the guidance of an expert. In this research study, we wish to determine if MomsInMind, a new mobile application created in collaboration with women's health experts, reduces symptoms of PPD. We will conduct a study of 340 Canadian mothers to see if the mothers who use MomsInMind in addition to treatment as usual from their healthcare providers can improve PPD more than mothers who get treatment as usual alone. If the MomsInMind intervention can improve the mental health of mothers during the postpartum period, it will provide the scope for the reduction of problems related to PPD and lead to brighter futures for Canadian mothers and their families.

column36: Does repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) preserve muscle mass and strength during limb immobilization?
column37: Throughout the lifespan, a person may require a period of limb immobilization to heal from an injury, surgery, or illness. Because muscles in the immobilized limb do not get used, they rapidly decrease in strength and size, decreasing physical performance or quality of life after immobilization. The decrease in muscle strength with immobilization is primarily due to changes that occur in the neuromuscular system rather than changes in muscle size. Interestingly, there are a few immobilization studies suggesting that the relative decrease in muscle size is similar between men and women, but neuromuscular function decreases up to four times more in women. To counteract the negative effects of immobilization, we propose the use of an electrical brain stimulation method known as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). rTMS sends an electrical current through a metal coil above the head to stimulate a targeted area of the brain. By stimulating the region of the brain that is usually less active during immobilization, we hope to minimize decreases in muscle strength. Our study will investigate the effects of rTMS on muscle strength, muscle size, and neuromuscular function after 14 days of arm immobilization. We will recruit 20 healthy women aged 18-29 years old and randomize them into either a group receiving daily rTMS or a group receiving a sham treatment. All volunteers will receive the immobilization. We will measure the strength and size of the biceps muscle before and after the study. Neuromuscular function before and after will be measured by looking at the person's ability to stimulate the biceps using electrodes on the muscle. Compared to sham, we expect rTMS to preserve more muscle strength and size, as well as neuromuscular function.

column36: Photochemically-activated Protein Signaling in a Hydrogel
column37: A physically and chemically similar environment to the human body is needed for cells to grow into complex tissues. Protein-embedded hydrogels offer this similar environment but are unable to control the spatial and temporal presentation of proteins in a similar fashion to how the human body does during the development of organized tissues. I propose to design a photocage which will block cells from interacting with the signaling protein attached to the hydrogel until the photocage is removed. Using a multi-photon caging chemistry and multi-photon laser, I will have precise temporal and spatial control of signaling protein presentation. Jagged1 (Jag1) is a protein presented to liver cells in the body to induce the formation of bile ducts. I will use photocaged Jag1 along with liver cells called cholangiocytes to control bile duct formation in a hyaluronan hydrogel. Successful chemical modification of the hydrogel will be measured through <sup>1</sup>HNMR and rheology. Biological interactions between Jag1 and cholangiocytes will be measured through cellular genetic expression and seen via the formation of organized cellular structures. By designing a temporally and spatially-controlled Jag1 signaling hydrogel, my research will enable a controlled process to model bile duct formation. This can serve as a framework for developing pathophysiology or drug models for bile duct diseases which are currently lacking. The same process of photocaging proteins to a hydrogel may serve as a platform strategy and extended to other proteins for differentiating stem cells or killing cancer cells. Thus, the temporal and spatial photo-uncaging of proteins in a hydrogel offers a method to explore various protein-cell interactions for tissue modeling, drug testing, and developmental studies.

column36: The Relationship Between Chronic Pain and Suicidality in Adolescents
column37: One in five children and adolescents experiences chronic pain (i.e., pain that lasts longer than 3 months). They also often experience other problems, such as family conflict, depression, and thoughts about suicide. These thoughts of suicide can be influenced by factors such as loneliness, poor relationships with family and friends, feelings that others would be better off without you, hurting oneself without intent of death, and not being afraid of pain or death. This study uses data from 190 adolescents (10-18 years old) who have been diagnosed with chronic pain. Adolescents were interviewed about their experiences with suicide and pain and were asked to complete questionnaires about their thoughts of suicide, family life, relationships with peers, depression and pain. This study will explore how chronic pain in adolescents and thoughts of suicide may be related to each other, and how other factors, like depression and poor relationships with family and friends, might change this relationship. The results of the project will help health researchers to learn more about how chronic pain relates to adolescents' thoughts of suicide. This is important because it will help health professionals to design treatments for chronic pain that focus on not only managing that pain, but also on managing depression, loneliness and other thoughts and feelings that may contribute to suicidality. This research will promote the wellbeing of youth with chronic pain in the present and into adulthood.

column36: Delineation of HuR function during muscle development, regeneration and fibre type switch
column37: Skeletal muscle is composed of slow¬-twitch (Type I) and fast-¬twitch fibers (Type II). The fiber type composition of skeletal muscle directly impacts muscle function. For example, in muscle-related diseases, such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), Type I fibers have been shown to be resistant to degeneration. Proteins, such as SIRT1 and PGC1? regulate the production of these fiber types. Proteins are expressed from messenger RNA (mRNA) which is transcribed from our DNA. mRNA stability is controlled by binding partners, such as RNA binding proteins (RBP). Our laboratory has previously shown that HuR, an RBP, modulates the expression of the mRNA of these fiber type determinants. We have also shown that if HuR is not present, mice will have an increase in Type I fibers. We hypothesize that HuR binds to these mRNAs, which destabilizes them such that the proteins are not expressed. The objective of my project is to determine where HuR binds to these mRNAs to better understand the mechanism by which it can regulate their stability. My experiments will identify specifically where these interactions take place. By identifying these binding sites, an inhibitor of HuR could be designed to prevent it from destabilizing the mRNAs. This inhibitor could treat muscular degeneration in DMD by promoting the expression of the proteins that lead to Type I fiber formation.

column36: Dysregulating the mitochondrial caseinolytic protease P (hClpP) for combating acute myeloid leukaemia
column37: Proteins are large biological molecules that perform many of the critical functions in cells. Often these proteins are organized as molecular machines and, like their macroscopic counterparts, these machines work through a series of moving parts. Only through an understanding of how these parts move and how their motion is related to function can these molecular machines be manipulated to potentially cure disease. One critically important molecular machine, called human mitochondrial caseinolytic protease P, or hClpP, is involved in maintaining the health of mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell. Previous studies have shown that hClpP is essential for the survival of leukaemia cells and have established that hClpP is an important target in the fight against blood cancers. I propose to study hClpP using a number of different biophysical techniques, including NMR spectroscopy and cryo-electron microscopy, which will allow me to obtain movies of how this molecule works in solution and how it interacts with existing small-molecule activators and inhibitors. column36: Interactions between milk microbiota and human genetics in childhood asthma susceptibility
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children in Canada, resulting in an annual healthcare cost of $2.1 billion. Breastfeeding is known to benefit the health of children but the impact on asthma susceptibility remains poorly understood. Previous work in our laboratory suggested that specific sugars that are variably secreted in the breastmilk of lactating mothers protect their children against asthma. Since microorganisms in human breastmilk are known to feed on these sugars, our study aims to determine how variable sugar concentrations affect the microbial composition of breastmilk and risk of childhood asthma. Then, we will determine which microbes are correlated with increased prevalence of asthma among the breastfed children. This study will provide a better understanding of how breastfeeding impacts asthma risk, and in particular, how milk sugars shape the microbial composition of the breastmilk and infants' gut microbes to modify asthma susceptibility. column36: COVID-19 Immunologic Antiviral therapy with Omalizumab (CIAO trial)
column37: The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) has affected over 35,000,000 people across 216 countries, resulting in the death of at least 1,000,000 individuals and the numbers continue to climb exponentially. Despite these staggering numbers, there is currently no standard treatment for COVID-19. Omalizumab is a humanized anti-IgE antibody approved by Health Canada for the treatment of moderate to severe asthma and chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU). Omalizumab has an excellent safety profile and has been effectively used in children, pregnant women, and patients with severe lung diseases (e.g. asthma, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) and bronchopulmonary aspergillosis). Preclinical and clinical data indicates that omalizumab decreases the duration of hospitalization and need for mechanical ventilation in virally-induced respiratory exacerbations in patients with the aforementioned comorbidities. Additionally, omalizumab has been shown to attenuate inflammatory and pro-coagulable responses, similar to what is found in the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), the leading cause of mortality due to COVID-19. Although omalizumab demonstrates anti-viral and anti-inflammatory properties, it has not yet been tested for use against the coronavirus species. We therefore hypothesize that omalizumab may have therapeutic potential to treat COVID-19. To test this hypothesis, we propose to to conduct a Phase II, adaptive, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial to evaluate if omalizumab improves survival in hospitalized COVID-19 patients with a history of atopy, CSU or asthma relative to the current of standard care. Confirming the efficacy of omalizumab in COVID-19 may help improve patient outcomes and reduce the burden on the health care system.

column36: Does Inferential Confusion Moderate the Relationship Between Fear-of-self and OCD Symptoms?
column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a disorder in which people have recurring, unwanted thoughts, ideas or sensations (obsessions) that make them feel driven to do something repetitively (compulsions). OCD significantly lowers the quality of life of sufferers. It is important to better our understanding of OCD in order to improve treatment approaches and, as a result, the quality of life of sufferers. Theories of OCD have recently focused on the potential causal role of vulnerable self-themes, suggesting that the fear of who one could be or become (fear-of-self) may specifically cause OCD symptoms. It has been proposed that intrusive doubts take on obsessional qualities in relation to how much these thoughts differ from an individual's beliefs and/or morals, as well as threaten core perceptions of the self. With fear-of-self, obsessions become more believable when they originate from a distrust of the self, where the individual overinvests in a possible feared self rather than their actual self. In this study, virtual reality and deception will be used to induce fear-of-self in one third of the participants. Individuals who have trouble separating imagination from reality might also be more influenced by the virtual reality task. The idea that individuals with OCD confuse imagination with reality is referred to as inferential confusion. Individuals who tend to experience inferential confusion might be more prone to believe the false feedback given by the actor in the study. It is expected that inferential confusion will affect the strength of the relationship between feared self-perceptions and OCD symptoms, and that this effect will be stronger in those with higher levels of inferential confusion.

column36: Investigation of the Genetic Factors Underlying Severe Adverse Drug Reactions in Paediatric Cancer Patients
column37: Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) represent the 5th leading cause of death in North America and cost between $30-130 billion healthcare dollars each year. Certain genetic differences can make a person more or less likely to suffer from an ADR. My research team at the Canadian Pharmacogenomics Network for Drug Safety (CPNDS) works to reduce the occurrence of permanent disability and deaths related to ADRs as well as develop predictive genetic tests for children who may be at higher risk. Second is to replicate any significant genetic findings in a different cohort of patients, these genetic findings are also known as genetic variants. Finally, is where my research comes in-functionally validating the genetic variants by elucidating the mechanism by which they confer an increased risk for an ADR. Currently, I am working on a project to discover how the presence of a specific genetic variant for a drug metabolizing enzyme-known as UGT1A6-increases a child's susceptibility for an unfortunately common ADR known as anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity. I use novel techniques developed to express the variant in cells grown in our lab and then treat them with an anthracycline known as doxorubicin-a widely used chemotherapy drug. When I confirm this specific genetic variant makes a patient more susceptible to the cardiotoxic effects of doxorubicin, it would allow us to integrate this knowledge into the Canadian healthcare system. Genetic testing prior to drug treatment would significantly decrease the prevalence of ADRs to both save healthcare dollars and most importantly, alleviate suffering amongst paediatric cancer patients.

column36: Quantifying the impact of childhood-onset lupus on the developing brain
column37: Childhood-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (cSLE) is a wildly unpredictable autoimmune disease that can affect any organ in the human body, including the brain. When it damages the brain, cSLE leads to the expression of neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as psychosis, seizures and mood disorders. On top of that, children displaying brain damage due to cSLE may suffer life-long health consequences if their normal neurological development is hindered. However, the specific biological traits that describe how exactly cSLE affects the brain remain poorly understood. For this reason, there are currently no accurate diagnostic tools nor highly effective treatments for this disease. With this in mind, the main goal of our current project is to discover unknown biological disease markers of neuropsychiatric cSLE. In order to do so, we will analyze brain scans from 70 cSLE patients and 70 healthy controls using cutting-edge brain imaging technologies. These scans will allow us to extract crucial measures of brain structure, function and development. Given the significant size of the resulting data, we will build a parallelized computational pipeline on a supercomputer to run our analyses. This pipeline will be entirely dedicated to (1) processing the imaging scans, (2) extracting biological features of interest and (3) using these acquired measures to perform statistical comparisons. We expect our pipeline to successfully quantify the most significant biological differences found between the brains of cSLE patients and those of healthy controls. We hope that the results of our project will inspire the development of new clinical tools that could drastically improve the lives of children suffering from this disease.

column36: Characterization of the single-cell expression profile and immune status of replication repair deficient glioma
column37: Cells must replicate their DNA to divide and grow. To protect the integrity of the genome, the cell has two systems which prevent mutations during each replication cycle. The first is the ability of proteins that replicate DNA (POLD/E) to recognize when they have made a mistake and repair it. The second is a complex of mismatch repair (MMR) proteins which correct mistakes that have been missed by the first system. A significant portion of pediatric gliomas have replication repair deficiency (RRD) caused by errors in these systems. RRD gliomas are aggressive and respond poorly to conventional treatments. Recent work has shown that immunotherapy, drugs which activate the patient's immune system to attack their own tumour, is effective in more than 30% of RRD gliomas. However, tumour response to immunotherapy is variable and depends on the specific mutations which cause RRD. Our lab has identified three subtypes of RRD glioma which are associated with high, variable and low response to immunotherapy: MMR and POLE mutation, MMR and IDH1 mutation, and MMR mutation alone. This project aims to discover how these subtypes of RRD gliomas develop and how they interact with immune cells. We will use single cell RNA sequencing, a technique which tells us which genes are being expressed by each cell inside the tumor. We will compare the expression profile of tumour cells to the profile of normal cells during brain development to determine the type of cell that led to this cancer. We will also probe the types, quantities and activation states of immune cells to understand why some are able to kill the tumour and others are not. This work will allow us to create more accurate mouse models to study these cancers and develop better combination treatments for RRD glioma.

column36: Investigating the Role of Janus Kinase 2 in Intestinal Homeostasis and Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), which groups together Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, will become exponentially more prevalent in Western countries. Currently, treatment aims to reduce inflammation to improve symptoms. Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) are critical to gut health and form a protective physical and chemical barrier against gut contents. While the cause of IBD is unknown, dysfunction of this barrier is widely observed in IBD. Genetic evidence has linked variation in Janus Kinase 2 (JAK2), a protein that mediates cells' responses to various stimuli, to IBD. This suggests abnormal JAK2 may have a role in the development or progression of IBD. Our research will address the questions: what role does IEC JAK2 play in gut health and how does its status affect susceptibility to IBD and its severity? To do so, we will delete JAK2 from IECs in mice and compare their gut barrier function, levels of inflammation and tissue damage, and overall disease severity in models of IBD to normal mice. Early data shows that JAK2 deficient mice have less barrier function, higher levels of tissue damage and the pro-inflammatory molecule, IL-6, and more severe disease in a chemical model of IBD. This suggests an essential role for JAK2 in gut health. To determine if IL-6 causes the observed gut defects, IL-6 or its receptor in IECs will be genetically deleted in JAK2 deficient mice to assess whether this prevents abnormalities. Given mixed results of co-inhibiting multiple JAKs to treat IBD, differentiating between the JAKs that protect gut health and those which impact it is important and timely. Our research will clarify JAK2's role in gut health and help refine approaches to better target inflammation and protect any health-promoting, JAK-based processes in the gut.

column36: Investigating microexon function during neurodifferentiation
column37: Alternative splicing (AS) is a process whereby cells generate multiple protein products from a single gene. AS functions by modifying precursor messenger RNA transcripts that encode proteins by differentially including coding regions, known as exons, in the final message. This process is near ubiquitous in humans, where more than 95% of genes with multiple exons are alternatively spliced. AS has important roles in brain development. For example, a program of AS, common to all vertebrates, results in the inclusion of short exons known as ""microexons"" into protein coding messages. Microexons are required for neurogenesis and cognitive functions, and their dysregulation is common in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. However, the function of the vast majority of microexons is unknown. To systematically investigate the functions of microexons in neuron development, I will employ a new CRISPR-based screening strategy to delete them in stem cells that will then be induced to differentiate into neurons in vitro. By monitoring the ability of these stem cells to divide and differentiate, I will be able to determine which microexons are important for neuronal development. In addition to assessing their impact on neurogenesis, I will monitor the consequence of microexon deletion on gene expression patterns to determine their roles in intracellular signaling and transcriptional programs associated with neuronal development. I will next perform a series of molecular assays on selected examples with the largest impact to elucidate mechanisms by which individual microexons affect neuron development. Collectively, these studies will significantly advance our knowledge of how a conserved AS microexon program linked to autism impacts nervous system development.

column36: Development of "Covalent Antibody Recruiting Molecules" Tumor Immunotherapeutics
column37: A person's immune system is excellent at recognizing and killing diseases, but sometimes diseases are able to hide or block the immune system from killing it. Immunotherapy uses a person's immune system to better recognize and fight diseases such as cancer. A growing strategy in immunotherapy is to use Antibody Recruiting Molecules (ARMs). These work by directing natural antibodies in the blood to the surface of cancer cells. Antibodies coating the cancer cell acts as a molecular ""flag"" helping the immune system find and destroy the cancer. ARM function depends on their ability to contact antibodies and the surface of cancer cells simultaneously. While promising ARMs have 2 major problems. The first is since they are small, the body clears them in a few hours, limiting the amount in the body. The second is for an ARM to work, the immune system, antibody, ARM, and cancer all have to be associated simultaneously for long enough time for the immune system to kill the cancer. Both these problems limit how well they can work. To solve these problems, I propose creating Covalent Antibody Recruiting Molecules (cARMs). These are identical to ARMs, but have one extra part. This extra part enables ARMs to permanently link to the antibody, resulting in more efficient coating of the cancer cell with antibodies to enhance immune recognition. Additionally, the ARM cannot be cleared from the body as quickly. Because of these changes we can learn more about the mechanisms behind how the immune system kills cancer by comparing cARMs to ARMs. In addition, cARMs may work as a new immunotherapy.

column36: Golgi versus endocytic trafficking in the delivery of major histocompatibility complex II molecules to antigen-loading compartments
column37: Antigen presentation on MHC II is crucial for generating immune responses against pathogens. Unfortunately, many pathogens-including SARS-CoV-2-can suppress immune responses by impairing this process. While the mechanisms for this immune evasion is known for some pathogens, it remains unclear how SARS-CoV-2 limits antigen presentation. During antigen presentation MHC II is loaded with pathogen-derived peptides inside of a lysosome-derived MHC II-loading compartment (MIIC). However, how MHC II is delivered here is controversial, but occurs either via export to the cell surface followed by reinternalization and trafficking to the MIIC, or direct Golgi-to-MIIC transport. We previously identified Erc1 and Rab6-regulators of Golgi-to-lysosome transport-on MIICs. We also demonstrated that Erc1 accumulates on the MIIC and is required for MHC II delivery, supporting the direct trafficking route. Additionally, several components of this trafficking pathway, including Erc1, have been identified as SARS-CoV-2 interacting proteins, suggesting that antigen presentation is manipulated via the direct route. Thus, we hypothesize that Erc1 mediates the direct Golgi-to-MIIC transport of MHC II, and that SARS-CoV-2 targets Erc1 to block this route. Time-lapse microscopy will be used to determine the definitive MHC transport route, and knockdowns of trafficking regulators will be performed to elucidate their role in MHC II delivery. Host proteins found to interact with SARS-CoV-2 proteins through immunoprecipitation and mass spectrophotometry will also be knocked down to determine whether these interactions are necessary for immune evasion. Understanding the mechanisms by which SARS-CoV-2 inhibits antigen presentation will be essential for developing vaccines and therapeutics for COVID-19.

column36: Studying Depression in a Homeless and Precariously Housed Sample
column37: BACKGROUND: Clinical depression is a major cause of disability in groups that experience homelessness and precarious housing (i.e. housing that lacks security or stability). Given its immense burden, the accurate assessment of depressive symptoms is a crucial first step in facilitating diagnosis and treatment in this population. The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) is a self-report questionnaire commonly used to measure depressive symptom severity. However, the BDI's ability to measure depressive symptom severity accurately and consistently (i.e. its psychometric properties) has not been studied in those who are homeless or precariously housed. GOALS AND HYPOTHESIS: I will determine the psychometric properties of the BDI in a homeless and precariously housed sample. Specifically, I will evaluate the BDI using classical test theory (CTT) and the Rasch analysis, which are two different statistical methods. I will then compare the results of the CTT and Rasch analyses. I hypothesize that CTT will show that the BDI effectively assesses depression symptom severity, and that the Rasch analysis will provide helpful information for diagnosing clinical depression. METHODS: I will use data collected from the ""Hotel Study"", which works with 475 participants living in an impoverished neighbourhood in Vancouver, Canada. The study is ongoing, and participants complete monthly assessments that evaluate mental health (e.g. the BDI), medical conditions, and quality of life. OUTCOMES: This work will help us understand how to interpret BDI scores in individuals who are homeless or precariously housed. Ultimately, through well-informed measurement, we hope to accurately identify and subsequently treat the many underprivileged Canadians who suffer from depression.
