column36: Anticoagulant use and associated outcomes in palliative care
column37: Background Blood thinners (anticoagulants) are commonly prescribed to prevent recurrent blood clots or to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (the most common abnormal heart rhythm) but come with the risk of serious bleeding. Patients with advanced illness, often seen in palliative care settings, will have reasons for anticoagulant treatment, but the benefit of such treatment in this group-known to be at high risk of bleeding-is uncertain. Goals Our overall goal is to help patients with terminal illness and their healthcare providers make better informed decisions about anticoagulant treatment by performing a comprehensive assessment of anticoagulant use in patients receiving palliative care. This will include describing the prevalence and reasons for anticoagulant prescription, and characterizing the risks and benefits of treatment (focused on survival, blood clots/strokes, and bleeding). Methods Using routinely collected administrative data, we will describe anticoagulant use and its associated characteristics for all Ontarians >65 years old with advanced cancer and/or non-cancer terminal illness receiving palliative care. We will study the relationship between stopping (vs. continuing) long-term anticoagulant treatment and survival, subsequent strokes or recurrent blood clots, and bleeding episodes. Impact For individuals receiving palliative care, a patient-centred approach requires an understanding of the risks, benefits of anticoagulant treatment. We will, for the first time, describe how frequently such patients receive anticoagulants, and how these medications impact survival and the risks of future blood clots/bleeding. Our findings have the potential to change clinical practices and improve patient-centred palliative care.

column36: Probiotic bifidobacteria as a promising therapy to mitigate uremic toxin accumulation in chronic kidney disease
column37: The accumulation of uremic toxins in the blood of chronic kidney disease patients is a common occurrence and enhances the severity of the disease. Dialysis is the gold standard therapy to filter these toxins from the body. However, the procedure is ineffective against protein bound toxins, like p-cresyl sulfate (PCS), allowing them to remain in circulation. Thus, novel therapeutic strategies to mitigate the accumulation of these toxins are needed. PCS is formed by the sulphation of its microbial derived precursor, p-cresol (PC). Increased serum PCS is associated with poor gut health, atherosclerosis, and mortality. In addition, elevated serum PCS has also been linked to a reduction of bifidobacteria in the gut. Interestingly, probiotic bifidobacteria can limit toxin absorption in the intestinal tract and reduce atherosclerosis risk. After testing commercial products, we discovered four Bifidobacterium spp. strains from Seed<sup>®</sup> synbiotic that depleted PC in a relevant bacteriological growth medium. This led us to hypothesize that a probiotic product containing toxin-clearing bifidobacteria can remove PC from the gut and limit PCS accumulation in CKD patients. To address this, we plan to: 1) Supplement Drosophila melanogaster with individual strains of toxin-clearing bifidobacteria to mitigate PC toxicity; 2). To identify prebiotic compounds, such as acetate and butyrate, that will improve toxin clearance in the intestinal environment; and 3) To determine how the multi-strain Seed<sup>®</sup> synbiotic, containing toxin-clearing bifidobacteria, alters PCS abundance in serum of healthy adults. Ultimately, this project uncovers a novel metabolic pathway and will assess if a probiotic can reduce PCS burden and improve management of chronic kidney disease.

column36: Is underweight in the first 2 years of life associated with growth in later childhood?
column37: The first 2 years of life are important for children to achieve their full growth and development potential. Underweight, which means having a low weight for the child's height, is a frequently used measure by healthcare providers to indicate sub-optimal nutrition. Underweight in otherwise healthy children can be due to problems such as affording food, abnormal eating behaviours, and/or parenting. There is a lack of research on the relationship between underweight in the first 2 years of life and growth in later childhood. This has led to unclear expectations by parents and healthcare providers alike. This study will evaluate the relationship between underweight in the first 2 years of life and weight gain in later childhood. It will also explore the relationship between underweight in the first 2 years of life and height in later childhood. I hypothesize that underweight in the first 2 years of life will be associated with lower weight and height in later childhood. This study will use data from Canada's largest children's cohort study - TARGet Kids!. Healthy children from 0 to 10 years of age will be included, except children with a health condition affecting growth, born premature and/or with low birthweight. Children's growth measurements will be measured during the first 2 years of life, and between 2 to 10 years of age to determine the relationship between underweight in the first 2 years of life and growth in later childhood. Results from this study will provide important evidence for healthcare providers and parents about the potential risks of underweight within the first 2 years of life for healthy Canadian children. This knowledge will help healthcare providers and policy makers to maximize children's growth and developmental potential.

column36: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: circulating tumor DNA as a novel translational clinicopathologic and molecular biomarker
column37: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) is the second most common cause of primary liver cancer with a dismal survival rate of 10% over five years. The main challenge in delivering the optimal treatment lies in: 1) obtaining gene mutational information of the iCCA tumor 2) reliably detecting cancer recurrence after surgical cure. Harvesting circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from the bloodstream and studying them might provide a solution to these issues. ctDNA or so-called ""liquid biopsies"" are DNA fragments released in the bloodstream from the tumor cells undergoing programmed cell death. ctDNA is hypothesized to carry the same genetic altercations of the main tumor. Potential ctDNA application includes: 1) monitoring for cancer recurrence 2) delivering tailored therapies based on mutations discovered 3) serving as a biomarker to detect cancer recurrence after surgery. However, there is very few data available for patients with iCCA diagnosis. One iCCA study highlights up to 92% concordance rate between the mutations of the cancer tissue and ctDNA after analyzing 15 cancer genes of interest. As this study only includes patients with metastatic cancer, the utility of ctDNA in patients undergoing curative surgery remains unknown. Hence, this research proposal seeks to study adult patients who undergo curative-intent surgery for iCCA by: 1) assess whether the mutations of peri-operative (before and after surgery) ctDNA in the bloodstream matches to those of the resected primary tumor 2) assess whether peri-operative ctDNA concentration in the bloodstream is a predictor of recurrence and overall survival for resected iCCA. We hypothesize that the bloodstream ctDNA is a surrogate for mutations in the main tumor and associated with natural history in resected iCCA.

column36: Understanding cross-talk between macrophages and smooth muscle cells in foam cell development.
column37: Atherosclerosis, the major cause of heart attack or stroke, is a leading cause of death worldwide. Atherosclerosis causes a progressive narrowing of blood vessels due to the build-up of fat-containing cells, known as ""foam cells."" Although foam cells were previously thought to originate primarily from a type of white blood cell called macrophages, research has shown that foam cells can also originate from smooth muscle cells (SMCs) that line the walls of arteries. Evidence also suggests that mixing SMCs and macrophages, as occurs in the artery wall, can promote cells to take up fat, leading to foam cell development. To further understand these mechanisms, the proposed research project focuses on how direct and indirect interactions between macrophages and SMCs can affect foam cell formation and development. We hypothesize that inflammation causes macrophages or SMCs to release signaling molecules that promote the other cell type to form foam cells. To test this hypothesis, we will grow SMCs with macrophages in laboratory cultures, either with indirect contact (separated by a permeable membrane), or with direct cell-cell contact, to determine the effect of each cell type on foam cell formation. We will also assess the key genes driving this process in both SMCs and macrophages. Key markers found in laboratory cultures will be confirmed in human samples to determine the physiological relevance of our findings. Ultimately, a better understanding of SMC and macrophage foam cell development will contribute to our understanding of how atherosclerosis progresses, and will allow us to develop new ways to treat and prevent this leading cause of death worldwide.

column36: Modulation of substrate utilization can improve myocardial function during ex situ heart perfusion
column37: Heart failure (HF) is one of the most rapidly rising diseases in Canada with 1.4 million people hospitalized annually with this diagnosis. For patients with end-stage HF, transplantation remains the gold standard. Unfortunately, there has been a widening gap between the number of donors and recipients, which led to death on the waiting list. Currently, we cannot procure more hearts for transplant due to our basic organ storage solution, where a heart is simply stored on ice. Without the ability to evaluate and preserve hearts during transport, we are limited to donors who have suffered brain death, where we can evaluate the heart's function before procurement. This precludes us from donors who have suffered circulatory arrest because we cannot assess their heart before procurement. Ex situ heart perfusion (ESHP) has been developed to reanimate hearts outside of the body on a machine where it can be assessed for function. This technology will allow us to procure hearts from circulatory arrest donors and increase donation rates by 30%. However, these reanimated hearts deteriorate after the first hour. It is known that the dysregulation in the heart's metabolism is causing this decline. However, there is a knowledge gap on how this dysregulation occurs. We will close this gap by studying the entire metabolome of the heart during ESHP. Using microextraction fibers, we will analyze the heart's metabolome using a machine learning algorithm that will output the most disturbed metabolites. We will then design a cocktail using this information to prevent the heart's decline. Preventing decline during ESHP can be impactful by allowing hearts to endure longer transport times; thus, providing more options and more hearts for the long list of patients waiting for a transplant.

column36: Impact of traffic-related air pollution on the cardiovascular response to exercise in adults with hypertension
column37: Abnormally high blood pressure (BP), also known as hypertension, is currently the greatest risk factor for premature death worldwide. In 2019 alone, high BP was responsible for more than 10 million deaths. Regular exercise is widely accepted as a cornerstone therapy in the primary prevention and treatment of hypertension. Conversely, traffic-related air pollution (TRAP) is an important environmental risk factor for hypertension. Even short-term exposures to TRAP have been shown to increase BP, as well as hypertension-related emergency department visits. However, engaging in exercise transiently increases the volume of air one breathes in. This in turn causes an increased intake of air pollution, potentially exacerbating the adverse health effects caused by TRAP. Recent studies have demonstrated reductions in BP following short exercise bouts, even when performed in high-TRAP environments; this implies exercise may confer a protective effect against TRAP-induced increases in BP. Unfortunately, these studies have only been performed in healthy participants, limiting their clinical relevance to unhealthy populations. The primary objective of this real-world, randomized crossover study is to determine whether TRAP modifies the acute cardiovascular responses to exercise in adults with hypertension. Participants will complete four 30-min exposures, consisting of either exercise or rest in a high- (located beside a busy road) or low-TRAP environment (located in a forested park). BP and other markers of cardiovascular health will be quantified before, during, and after exposures. Ultimately, this study will aid in the development of practical, evidence-based recommendations that can be used by clinicians and patients to optimize the health benefits of exercise.

column37: Physical distancing restrictions posed by the current pandemic are associated with adverse physical and mental health outcomes, such as sedentary lifestyles and increased levels of stress and anxiety, which may contribute to the exacerbation and maintenance of pain among individuals living with chronic pain conditions. Evidence from previous epidemics further suggest that individuals with pre-existing chronic pain conditions are particularly susceptible to developing posttraumatic stress symptoms, and consequently, may experience long-term functional impairments. Despite evidence that individuals living with chronic pain will be disproportionately impacted during the current COVID-19 pandemic, researchers have not yet extensively explored psychological responses to COVID-19 among individuals living with chronic pain. The proposed study will examine psychological responses to the pandemic among population representative samples of individuals living with (n = 500) or without (n = 750) chronic pain. Participants will complete online measures of COVID-19-related stress and anxiety, levels of pain and impairment, and posttraumatic stress symptoms, among others. It is hypothesized that COVID-19-related stress and anxiety response profiles will differ among individuals living with chronic pain and the general population. Levels and predictors of posttraumatic stress symptoms, as well as associated functional impairments among individuals living with chronic pain will also be explored. Identifying how COVID-19-related stress and anxiety responses differ among individuals living with chronic pain and the general population may help to inform psychological interventions for this vulnerable group, thereby having the potential to reduce the exacerbation and maintenance of pain.

column36: Determining how Pseudomonas aeruginosa PilS distinguishes between minor and major pilins
column37: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a multidrug resistance pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a critical pathogen for the discovery of new, and alternative antibiotics. Type IV pili (T4P) in P. aeruginosa are hair-like protein filaments involved in motility and pathogenicity. T4P allow for bacterial pathogen attachment to solid surfaces such as medical devices and host tissues, leading to increased risk of hospital acquired infections. Surface attachment triggers upregulation of virulence factors through processes that remain poorly understood. T4P are comprised of the major pilin, PilA, and a set of minor pilin subunits. pilA expression is regulated by the PilSR two component system (TCS). The sensor kinase of this TCS, PilS, interacts with PilA as well as minor pilins. When a pilus attaches to a solid surface, PilA levels decrease and the TCS upregulates genes implicated in pathogenicity. The role of T4P in pathogenicity makes it an attractive target for novel therapeutics. We hypothesize that disruption of PilSR-mediated signaling will impair the ability of P. aeruginosa to sense and respond to surface attachment and thus reduce virulence In this study, I will compare PilS interaction between PilA, and minor pilin subunits, respectively, to determine how PilS distinguishes between the types of substrates. I will also investigate the genes regulated by these respective protein-protein interactions. Findings will aid future strategies to disrupt PilSR-mediated signalling. Investigating this TCS is an important step in development of new treatments and combatting antibiotic resistance.

column37: Asthma is a common respiratory disease in Canada where patients have difficulty in breathing with flare-ups that require hospitalizations and healthcare utilization, all mounting to a significant economic burden. Corticosteroids are used to treat the inflammation, yet 60% of asthmatics remain uncontrolled. Our research has shown that in some asthmatics, airway autoantibodies are generated causing severe inflammation that is unresponsive to current treatments. Autoantibodies are produced by B cells mistakenly against the body's own cells. In a healthy individual a type of B cell, known as a regulatory B cell, would suppress the autoantibody-producing B cells. We believe that in severe asthmatics there is a decrease in factors that normally support regulatory B cells and there is a corresponding increase in autoantibody-producing B cell activity. As a part of my Master's thesis, I will investigate this theory and understand what is contributing to autoantibody production in asthmatics, so that we can find ways of better treating these patients.

column36: Examining Mental Health and HIV Risk in Middle Eastern-Immigrant Men Who Have Sex With Men in Canada
column37: Members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) community are more at-risk for negative mental and physical health outcomes compared to heterosexual individuals. Particularly, gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are at-risk for health issues such as depression, anxiety, and sexually transmitted infections (e.g., HIV). Studies have shown that these risks worsen in multiple-minority populations, such as racial/ethnic minorities who identify as LGBT. Another example of a multiple-minority population are LGBT immigrants, who are relatively understudied. This study will focus on the unique sociocultural risk factors (e.g., discriminatory laws in home country, religious-based sexual stigma) experienced by MSM immigrants from the Middle East, and whether their experiences place them at higher risk for contracting HIV and having negative mental health than Canadian-born MSM. I hypothesize that Middle Eastern MSM immigrants will demonstrate unique risk factors that place them at higher risk for contracting HIV and experiencing mental health issues than Canadian-born MSM. I will use online self-report surveys to collect data on demographics (e.g., age, birth country, number of years living in Canada), sociocultural experiences (e.g., experiences of racism, discriminatory laws in birth country, English-language fluency), and high-risk sexual behaviours (e.g., frequency of condom use). column36: Neural Correlates of Socioeconomic Status in the Human Brain: A Population Neuroscience Analysis
column37: Socioeconomic status is linked to critical determinants of life quality which makes it an important predictor of health outcomes. Recent work connected socioeconomic status to common-variant genetic profiles. The identified genes, preferentially expressed in the central nervous system, have well-documented associations with intellectual disabilities, schizophrenia, and synaptic plasticity. The neural mechanisms through which socioeconomic determinants impact the architecture of the central nervous system remain obscure. We are interested in investigating the long-term biological footprints of socioeconomic status in the brain. We aim to use the UK Biobank imaging resources and cutting-edge machine learning techniques to derive brain patterns associated with several important indicators of socioeconomic status. We will look at how brain measures concurrently vary with respect to these distinct socioeconomic measures by building a supervised pattern extraction algorithm. This multi-outcome learning algorithm will allow us to derive individual-level predictors that could be used to design targeted medical and psychosocial interventions in vulnerable patients. Investigating the long-term consequences of socioeconomic status in the human brain is especially relevant in times of global pandemic, where social isolation accentuates the disparity in health outcomes between low- and high-status individuals.

column36: Randomized Controlled Trial on the Effect of Palatal Brushing in Patients with the Denture Stomatitis
column37: Denture stomatitis (DS) is inflammation of oral mucosal areas covered by a denture. It is the most prevalent oral mucosal disease in edentulous individuals with a prevalence rate up to 75%. Despite the high prevalence and significant burden of DS, its etiology is still not well understood. Most of the time, the treatment of this recurrent condition has challenged clinicians. It has led to the over-prescription of medications and unwanted side effects due to the lack of evidence-based clinical guidelines for managing this disease. Recently, impaired salivary flow has been suggested to potentially play a role in DS. In addition, the chance of remission of denture stomatitis was shown in a recent study to be 3.9 times higher in participants who brushed their palate. Hence, this research is proposed to conduct a randomized controlled trial with the following objectives: 1- To assess if palatal brushing can affect the palatal salivary flow rate among patients with DS, and 2- To assess if palatal brushing can change palatal mucosa's cytology towards the reduction of inflammatory cells, bacteria, and fungal organisms among patients with DS. Participants will be selected based on inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data will be gathered in a blinded fashion using a self-administered questionnaire and clinical examination (during which biological specimens will also be collected). Follow-up data collections will be conducted at 3- and 6-months post-randomization. This trial will help provide practice guidelines and improve the standard of care for millions of edentate people wearing dentures. It will also help in clinical decision-making and protect edentate patients from the harm caused by over-diagnosis and over-treatment, such as an antifungal and antibiotic prescription.

column36: Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Canadian Pediatric Emergency Departments
column37: The novel corona virus SAR-CoV-2, which emerged during the later part of 2019, has since infected over 34 million people and has been tied to more than 1 million deaths worldwide. While most research being done on SAR-CoV-2 has focused on its direct health consequences, it is becoming clear that the virus has health impacts beyond the disease itself. Recent studies from other countries found a considerable reduction in pediatric emergency department visits since the start of the pandemic. This decrease in hospital visits may be due to social distancing measures, which result in a general reduction in common childhood illness, or alternatively, parental fear of visiting hospitals. The short and long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on pediatric emergency departments in Quebec remain unstudied. This project aims to investigate the differences in number and pattern of visits to the pediatric emergency department visits since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic compared to a pre-COVID. Specifically, we will compare trends in the number of visits that resulted in admission to the medical ward, the severity of admissions, the reason of hospital visits, and the socio-demographic characteristics of children visiting the pediatric emergency department. This large-scale pediatric study will provide insight on the possible unintended consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic and associated confinement measures in Quebec on child health. In doing so, we aim to inform future decision and policy making throughout the remainder of the COVID-19 pandemic and also in possible future pandemics. This study will also serve to learn about the current structure of pediatric emergency departments in Quebec, which in turn may help inform their improvement beyond the COVID-19 pandemic.

column36: Caregiver-child relationship consistency and controlling behaviour in high school: A focus for family-based violence prevention?
column37: Insecure attachment is associated with violence perpetration (Adam et al., 2004). One predictor of insecure attachment is inconsistent caregiver-child relationships (Szepsenwol & Simpson, 2019); children who have inconsistent relationships with their caregiver(s) may seek predictability by controlling external relationships, potentially through violence. Indeed, a desire for control has been shown to underlie various forms of violence (e.g., Humphrey & Vaillancourt, 2020). Improving family dynamics would thus be an ideal approach to preventing the development of a desire for control and subsequent violence in children. However, there is scant research indicating concrete aspects of the caregiver-child relationship to be changed when a child is deemed at-risk. Additionally, many children at risk of perpetrating violence are not identified prior to the emergence of problem behaviour. To this end, identifying specific mechanisms associated with controlling behaviour is a critical step in recognizing risk for violence perpetration and promoting prosocial behaviour through family-based approaches. The proposed study will examine whether inconsistent caregiver-child relationships are associated with controlling behaviour in high schoolers, specifically bullying, sexual violence, and discrimination (racism and homophobia). The results of this study could help identify a tangible point of risk assessment and intervention to encourage prosocial behaviour and prevent violence, beginning early in life.

column36: Circulating tumour DNA analysis to predict and monitor minimal residual disease in breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant treatment
column37: Breast cancer is the second most diagnosed cancer in Canada, with 27,700 Canadians expected to be diagnosed in 2020. Despite recent progress in breast cancer survival rates, about 20 percent of patients relapse and die from metastatic disease. Many of these deaths are caused by undetectable metastases present at diagnosis that persist following therapy, over time leading to incurable metastatic relapse. Therefore, further advances in reducing breast cancer mortality require better methods to identify which patients have minimal residual disease (MRD) following standard therapy. This would allow for stratification of high-risk patients who may benefit from additional treatment while sparing low-risk patients from unnecessary side effects of overtreatment. Many studies have shown that the detection of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) may be used to detect MRD in early breast cancer patients. ctDNA are cell-free DNA fragments released into circulation when tumour cells die. ctDNA contains cancer-specific genetic and epigenetic alterations, enabling its use as a minimally invasive biomarker through liquid biopsy. Our research will characterize an optimal ctDNA test to detect and monitor MRD in high-risk early breast cancer patients following therapy, with the ultimate goal of finding accurate predictors of relapse and treatment response. We will assess the tests in serial samples from patients with high-risk early breast cancer collected throughout therapy and follow-up. This research will help precise risk assessment and development of intervention strategies to enable more effective treatment decisions and prevent relapse in breast cancer patients. Overall, our work has the potential to directly impact the care of breast cancer patients and improve their survival outcomes.

column36: Neural correlates of connected speech in Parkinson's disease and vascular cognitive impairment
column37: Communication disorders are a common symptom across neurodegenerative diseases. Looking at connected speech – speech that involves whole phrases rather than individual words – provides a thorough way to evaluate communication. However, the link between different patterns of neurodegeneration and deficits in connected speech has yet to be investigated. The Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI) is an Ontario-wide study that was launched in 2013 to characterize five neurodegenerative disease cohorts across a wide range of clinical, biological, and functional assessments. These assessments include connected speech analyses and neuroimaging – namely, diffusion tractography imaging (DTI). In this project, we aim to correlate various measures of connected speech and DTI in the Parkinson's disease and vascular cognitive impairment cohorts of ONDRI to determine which white matter tracts are associated with disease-specific changes in connected speech, as well as to characterize the sensitivity of each DTI measure in detecting these changes. We anticipate that careful characterization of the link between connected speech deficits and different patterns of neurodegeneration will provide more accurate detection of these diseases in the future.

column36: Consequences and repair of mitochondrial protein import defects in mammals
column37: Known as the ""powerhouses of the cell"", mitochondria are essential organelles involved in energy production, metabolism, and signaling. Since the vast majority of mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus and synthesized in the cytosol, the constant import of proteins into the organelle is necessary for mitochondrial function. Defective mitochondrial protein import is a feature of aged cells and many human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. Recent studies have revealed that when mitochondria become overwhelmed with a traffic jam of proteins, these proteins cannot fully enter, and lead to clogging of the mitochondrial protein entry sites. Two pathways can alleviate this stress by removing clogged proteins from the gates and promoting their destruction: the mitochondrial compromised protein import response (mitoCPR) and mitochondrial protein translocation-associated degradation (mitoTAD), both discovered in budding yeast. However, in mammals, the consequences of protein import defects and existence of similar pathways remain unknown. This project seeks to address this deficit by first developing methods to disrupt and detect mitochondrial protein import in human cells. Such methods will allow us to study the consequences of impaired protein import on mitochondrial homeostasis at both the cellular and molecular levels. I will further shed light on how cells repair damage caused by import defects by focusing on the mammalian homologs of mitoCPR and mitoTAD factors. This will be done using genome editing, biochemical and cell biology methods. Overall, this work will yield valuable insight into the discovery of new cellular protein quality control mechanisms and facilitate the discovery of potential therapeutic targets.

column36: Telemedicine in the care of older people in primary care: a systematic mixed studies review
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has substantially changed the delivery of primary care health services. Most primary care doctors had to adapt to virtual remote care without training. Telemedicine has the potential to improve the quality of primary health care and increase accessibility to the population, however it presents a challenge to older people (e.g. hearing and visual impairment, cognitive impairment, access to the Internet, telephone and video devices). Our research will therefore focus on describing the effects of telemedicine on the quality of primary care for older people compared to in-person care. Our objectives are to identify the different types of telemedicine, describe the various barriers and facilitators to the use of telemedicine by older people and health professionals, and provide our recommendations. We will conduct a mixed systematic review to describe the experience of older people living in the community when using telemedicine in primary care. Our mixed-method approach will combine qualitative data and research techniques (descriptive), quantitative methods (including effect size calculations) and an explanatory approach to mixed methods. A narrative approach (content synthesis and thematic synthesis) will be applied to describe the types of telemedicine, identify barriers and facilitators and draft recommendations on the use of telemedicine by elderly people and health professionals in primary care. Our review will be particularly needed in this period of pandemic during which telemedicine is widely used.

column37: Arthritis in children and youth is a group of rare and ultra-rare diseases. Children of all ages suffer from joint pain, stiffness and swelling slowly destroying they joints and resulting in life-long disability. Pain, decreased mobility and fatigue dramatically impact the child's everyday quality of life and the life of the family. The burden of arthritis is far larger than medication costs. Children miss school days and when at school face lack of proper accommodation. They miss out on sports, play dates and other childhood milestones. Often families face a lack of understanding, since "children don't have arthritis, only elderly people do". The results are often devastating: failed education, a future of low paying jobs or unemployment due to disability, and for many poor mental health. Parents face regular loss of working hours, frequent hospital visits, sometimes resulting in unemployment. Parents become health care providers, have to make up for interrupted schooling providing home tutoring and face their own anxieties, depression and mental health struggles as the child's primary caregiver. Siblings suffer and not infrequently marriages fall apart. There is a dramatic hidden burden of arthritis. The PAVE team is a strong international partnership of 6 countries including clinical leaders, researchers, social scientists and strong engagement with patient organizations. Our team will focus on the unmet needs of children and families and empower them with new ways to address the hidden burden of arthritis. The PAVE team will build a first-of-its kind value framework that will unite the voices of children and families with data-informed calls to action to measure and ultimately reduce the cost and burden of childhood arthritis. Together, we will improve the lives of children living with arthritis, reduce inequities and pave the way for improved lives for people of all ages living with rare diseases. Children with arthritis and their families need a voice.

column37: Indigenous gender and identity are deeply rooted in cultural practices. Gender affects identities, choice of occupation, and participation in ceremony and cultural activities. Through Indigenous cosmologies, gender is viewed wholistically, with people of many genders holding important roles in families and communities. Gender and identity are overlooked in research, especially action-oriented, Indigenous-led, community-based participatory wellness projects. The purpose of this study is to bring together Indigenous youth, young adults, Elders, and Knowledge Keepers to share/create knowledge, raise awareness and improve understanding of Indigenous concepts of gender and identity to co-develop strengths-based Indigenous-led culturally safe and gendered approaches for self-determination and improved wellness. Friendship and Metis Centres, local Community Research Liaisons, Advisory Teams, Elders, Knowledge Keepers, youth/young adults, and the research team will work to support knowledge creation/sharing of Indigenous-led priorities, and action-oriented community-based projects related to gender and identity to improve wellness among urban Indigenous Peoples. Knowledge creation will occur through Talking/Healing/Learning Circles, Community Gatherings, Cultural Safety Education & Resilience Gatherings, site-specific interventions, and surveys. Multi-site, multi-sectoral partnerships will be developed for knowledge mobilization, and collaboration/communication strategies. The project will explore (intersections) what gender, identity and wellness mean to urban Indigenous youth/young adults (wellness indicators) in a life-long connection to the land, their culture, and one another. Indigenous ways of understanding will guide the co-development of adaptable wholistic pathways/models of gender, identity and wellness for programs/activities, and regional/community-specific wellness indicators, that can be shared with other urban Indigenous communities and organizations.

column36: Exploring 9Genders Within the Life Cycle "We Will Always Love"
column37: The Exploring 9Genders within the lifecycle "We Will Always Love" proposal is in direct alignment with the Indigenous Gender and Wellness Team Grant in its emphasis on generating new knowledge to raise awareness and improve understanding of Indigenous concepts of gender in wellness and healing contexts. Our project activities are designed to support individuals, organizations and communities through events and ceremonies on the land that will improve wellness and support healing among Indigenous communities from gender-diverse perspectives. Our national research team of Indigenous and allied knowledge users, investigators and collaborators unite experience with opportunity for meaningful engagement of those new(er) to research. Together our goal is to examine the concept of 9Genders and the impact of gender on wellness and healing for First Nations, Inuit and Metis (Indigenous) Peoples in Canada. The teaching of 9Genders offers a new way of organizing gender, acknowledging a person's gender as determined by the spirit or spirits they are born into the world with. Expanding upon a one-year development grant (THE NINE GENDERS A Traditionalist way of organizing Indigenous gender, interpreting gender through an Indigenous worldview), the purpose of this community-based participatory project is to connect gender diverse people in examining the 9Genders' role in organizing gender, strengthening wellness and creating opportunities for on-the-land healing through ceremonies in Indigenous communities across Canada. Through the facilitation of sharing circles (Lavallee, 2009), research is woven into the ceremonies, serving to document experiences and insights related to wellness for gender diverse people. These circles will allow people to participate in developing a research question, identifying possible community wellness indicators relevant to 9Genders, and looking at ways we will move forward by exploring the grant objectives and future activities (Lavallee, 2009).

column36: Risk factors and markers for early detection of Alzheimer's Disease: focus on early-life stress, inflammation and lipid mediators
column37: Finding suitable and easily measurable early biomarkers for neurodegeneration and cognitive dysfunctions represents the next frontier for prevention and early intervention strategies. A key may rely on identifying very early environmental risk factors and understanding the temporal and causal relationships between the central alterations and peripheral changes. As part of these early factors, neuroinflammation has been increasingly acknowledged as an important player in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) pathology and early-life adversity primes microglia rendering them more sensitive to subsequent challenges. In addition, polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and their derivatives play a key role in modulating microglia. Importantly, these PUFA can be modified by the diet. We thus propose a translational project on neuroimmunology, lipid mediators and metabolic sensors that will leverage human data and biosamples as well as established mouse and rat models to identify early biomarkers of neurodegeneration. Candidates generated in human cohorts will be to back-translate into validated animal models of cognitive decline. We will use several innovative approaches including microglial functional assays, microglia depletion, PUFA/SPM assessment, organotypic slice cultures, and animal models of early-life adversity, AD, omega-3 fatty acid deficiency and microglial defects. On completion of this proposal, we will have identified i) early biomarkers (PUFA/SPM and metabolic sensors) predictive of cognitive dysfunction and neurodegeneration ii) the causal role of early-life adversity on central neuroinflammatory and peripheral alterations associated with neurodegeneration; and iii) a PUFA/SPM dietary intervention strategy for alleviating these effects.

column36: The psychosocial, economic, and patient-reported impact of Friedreich's Ataxia
column37: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is the most common hereditary ataxia in Europe characterized by imbalance, poor coordination, speech problems, muscle weakness, sensory loss, cardiomyopathy, skeletal abnormalities, and diabetes mellitus with typical onset before the age of 25 years. FRDA is associated with impaired health-related quality of life, reduced social inclusion, and an increasing need for care, resulting in a psychosocial and economic burden. Therefore, in the light of new therapeutic interventions, we aim to assess patient-reported outcomes, specifically including dysarthria, as well as the health economic impact of FRDA. Data will be acquired in real-time in members of a large prospective clinical cohort of FRDA patients (European Friedreich's Ataxia Consortium for Translational Studies (EFACTS) cohort by using a patient-centric, remote monitoring e-health app. Within the e-health app, ataxia severity, daily activity, health-related quality of life (patient-reported outcomes), medication and health services used (health economic outcomes), and specific events that affect patients' health will be monitored in real-time on a daily to monthly basis. We will assess (1) the acceptability, feasibility, and usability of the app, (2) the total societal costs (medical care cost and indirect costs, including productivity losses and cost of informal care) as well as the association between treatment patterns that adhere to evidence-based guidelines and costs, (3) the health-related quality of life in FRDA, its associated factors and the fluctuation of health as well as (4) the psychosocial impact of the communication handicap caused by dysarthria.

column36: Engendering a Healthy Indigenous Identity: Focusing on Who We Are, Not What We Are
column37: A healthy Coast Salish identity avoids restrictive categorizations and envelopes rather than foregrounds gender. A holistic Indigenous worldview shapes the process of creating that identity. Transmotion and the Peoplehood Matrix provide theoretical and methodological points of reference for studying this process. In "transmotion" Indigenous people work through and across the events of life, and live life as change. The Peoplehood Matrix, comprised of four interactive elements-language, sacred history, place/territory, ceremonial cycle-constitutes a group identity and ensures the persistence of a people. Community-based, action-oriented activities aspire to revive, reorient and renew the expression of the Matrix where a healthy Coast Salish identity, including gender, can be re-imagined. Wellness indicators focus on improving identification and recognition of, respect for and access to culturally relevant and holistic pathways to creating a healthy identity. In an Indigenous planning process, Indigenous people hold their proper governance position. Consensus decision making and community capacity building (spiritual, sovereign, linguistic, skills oriented, administrative)-especially for youth-are central. The proposed action plan is rooted in three basics: personal, local, small. Identity in an Indigenous community context is rooted in personal, local and small activities that engage substantively with elements of the Peoplehood Matrix. Some proposed activities include a cross-community Elders Gathering, production and community premiering of short documentaries of community Elders teaching Coast Salish values, and language immersion day camps for youth. Later possibilities include an herbal medicine Family Camp, ceremonial transfer of salmon fry, and rebuilding of the community Pit House used for life stage ceremonies.

column36: Lil'wat Medicine Shed: Supporting Traditional Medicine Usage and Traditional Knowings of Gender
column37: The traditional medicines of the Lil'wat Nation have a gendered aspect, with traditional roles, ceremonies and medicines being associated with gender identities and roles. However, there is an increasing awareness amongst Lil'wat community members that binary gender is a legacy of colonialism. Moreover, Lil'wat community members have identified a need to support community learning and education about gender and sexuality to build knowledge and acceptance for members of the community who identify as Two Spirit or LGBTQIA+. This initiative proposes to build support, education and awareness about gender and sexuality into traditional medicine practices, as part of the Lil'wat Cultural Re-Connection Classroom. This proposed work that has been identified by the project Elder and Elder-in-Training, both of whom are Lil'wat community members. During this 3-year long initiative, Lil'wat and UBC Researchers, will pilot a new community institution that envisioned to be a place where Lil'wat youth can come together to engage in topics related to culture, gender, sexuality, and take part in traditional medicine harvest and processing and other culturally based activities that promote health and wellness. This research will work to generate indicators to gauge Lil'wat youth health and wellness, particularly in protective factors related to cultural continuity. We are requesting support for the hiring of Lil'wat Nation members as researchers and consultants to initiate the design of activities and services that will be offered from Years 1-3, along with support for materials and to invite Two Spirit leaders from other Indigenous communities to visit the Lil'wat Cultural Re-Connection Classroom as guest speakers and presenters and Lil'wat Elders to lead traditional medicine activities. This initiative is anticipated to bring significant long-term gains for the Lil'wat Nation to enhance knowledge and capacity around the intersections of gender, sexuality and wellness.

column36: Maternity Experiences Behind Bars: Exploring Incarcerated Indigenous Women's Reproductive and Maternal Health and Wellness
column37: Indigenous womxn now account for 41.4% of all federally incarcerated womxn in Canada (OCI, 2019). Many incarcerated womxn are mothers, however prison pregnancy, and reproductive health statistics and health indicators are currently unavailable. In addition, previous public health research on maternity experiences has excluded incarcerated Indigenous womxn (Leason, 2017; PHAC, 2009). Given the over-incarceration of Indigenous womxn, the exclusion and limited research, this research aims to explore the current state of incarcerated womxns sexual, reproductive and maternal child health. Through interdisciplinary, Indigenous, and mixed methods research, this research will examine the available Correctional Service of Canada's Indigenous sexual, reproductive, and maternal child health data. To compliment this data and fill in the gaps, we will hold arts-based workshops with incarcerated womxn at 5 federal prisons and one Healing Lodge to gather their sexual, reproductive, and maternal child health experiences, needs and gaps prior to or during incarceration. This research will generate new knowledge and provide evidence to inform advocacy, policy, and action-oriented programming to improve the health and wellbeing of incarcerated Indigenous womxn.

column36: Land-Based Learning, Healing Lodges, and Reintegration for Previously Incarcerated Indigenous Women, Men and Two Spirited People in Ontario
column37: Despite making up only 5% of the general population, over 30% of people incarcerated in Canada's federal prisons identify as First Nations, Metis, or Inuit (Zinger, 2020). This project aims to take an action-oriented, community-based approach to understanding the perspectives of previously incarcerated Indigenous women, men, and 2SLGBTQQIA+ people, as well as service providers at Indigenous and criminal justice advocacy organizations. Using Indigenous research methods, this project will establish an Ontario-wide Indigenous guidance council to inform the design and delivery of research activities to ensure balanced power dynamics, increased trust, and a sense of project ownership. To facilitate reciprocal relationships and rapport building, care packages that were created with community input will be given to partners to distribute to previously incarcerated clients. We will host talking circles (Brown & Di Lallo, 2020) with council members throughout the project's duration. Additionally, we will conduct one-on-one interviews with both Indigenous and non-Indigenous criminal justice-related service providers as well as individuals with experiences with incarceration who have used healing or re-entry programs since their release to gain knowledge about interconnectedness of incarceration, gender, family relations, and reintegration into their community(s). This will be done with an intersectional lens that incorporates the Medicine Wheel teachings and accompanying knowledge from an Algonquin perspective (PI and Elders contributing). We are interested in learning if there are differences in gender and family-inclusive policies for those who were previously incarcerated and how to assist with reintegration and healing after their release.

column36: Knowing Ourselves, Re-Membering Our Roles and Responsibilities: Pathways to the Health and Wellness of Cree Boys and Men
column37: The negative implications of Euro-Western gender systems on the health and wellness of Indigenous peoples is widely recognized. Notwithstanding the disruptive impact of colonialism on diverse Indigenous gender formations, tribally-specific gender values, roles and responsibilities continue to exist in the stories, places, and practices of the community. This project employs an Indigenous-centred, community-first design to explore the relationship between Cree values and practices, identity, healing, and wellness as a pathway for re-membering and reclaiming Cree roles and responsibilities of boys and men. The project will centre Cree Elders and knowledge holders in addressing three research questions: how has colonialism impacted Cree gender formations, specifically the values, roles and responsibilities of boys and men; what is the relationship between Cree values, practices, identities and wellness; how can Cree values and embodied practices be re-membered and reclaimed in fostering the resurgence of tribally-specific roles and responsibilities of boys and men. This project focuses on cisgendered Cree boys and men, not to the exclusion of diverse genders, but as part of a relational ecology. It is our contention that Cree ways of life represent a critical pathway to re-balancing the relationships between boys and men, diverse genders, communities, and the Cree Nation, all of which lead to holistic, Indigenous-centred, health and wellness. The project is significant in that it draws upon tribally-specific (that is, Cree) ways of life and gender formations in addressing Cree health and wellness.

column36: Cognitive propagation in prodromal Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) has a long pre-symptomatic phase, in which cerebral changes can manifest as prodromal symptoms, for example sleep disorder, loss of smell, and cognitive or affective symptoms (e.g. anxiety and depression). Increasing evidence suggests that the propagation of brain dysfunction in PD may take different routes in the brain, and that it may affect focal versus diffuse brain systems. Here we aim to link these different neurobiological routes of PD propagation to distinct mechanisms of cognitive or affective dysfunction. By leveraging computational model-based analyses of cognition, we will localize specific cognitive deficits to brain systems. These data will be linked to brain imaging, computational models of brain dysfunction, and genetic risk factors. We will take advantage of existing longitudinal patient cohorts where brain imaging and genotyping is available. These data will be enriched by online cognitive and mood testing. Our work may help to further prediction of disease progression, and it may offer a mechanism-based approach to treatment in prodromal PD.

column36: Remembering "Right Relationships": Traditional and Land-Based Indigenous Knowledge and Practices as Intervention for Gender-Based Violence
column37: "Remember Right Relationships" is a three-year mix methods Indigenous, community-based participatory research (CBPR) project that seeks to reduce gender-based violence (GBV) experienced by Indigenous women and gender diverse people in Edmonton by developing, implementing, and measuring the effectiveness of Indigenous culture and land based interventions designed to strengthen cultural connectedness. Our diverse team of researchers, in collaboration with Elders and community advisors, will engage with participants to co-create urban (during the winter) and land-based (spring/summer/fall) GBV interventions including three land-based ceremonial and teaching culture camps led by invited traditional knowledge keepers. Winter activities will include traditional teaching and knowledge translation gatherings, participant digital storytelling, and peer support group development. We hypothesize that by enhancing cultural knowledge and connectedness through rich culture based activities, participants will experience improved wellness, thereby mitigating the role of GBV in their lives. We will invite everyone to engage with several Indigenous measures of cultural connectedness and holistic wellness to investigate the relationship holistic well-being and cultural connectedness; analyzing the data using hierarchical multiple linear (HML) regression analysis. AtlasTi software will aid our analysis of qualitative data. We anticipate outcomes to include a statistically significant increase in cultural connectedness and well-being among participants, and validation through robust qualitative analysis. Knowledge mobilization will include journal articles, webinars, website and social media updates, and community dissemination events. We anticipate the findings will lead to GBV wise practices service delivery recommendations and shifts in our own service provision towards wise Indigenous practices, which we will share with others through presentations, reports, and journal articles.

column36: Iligiingniq: Inuit Perinatal Health & Wellness Project in Arviat, Nunavut
column37: Colonialism continues to have lasting effects on gender and childbirth within Inuit communities, creating ongoing challenges and barriers that can impact wellbeing. For example, women must leave their families and communities to give birth. They receive limited perinatal care, support, and access to resources/information in their first language. These circumstances are inherently stressful, and create isolating contexts for women at a time when they are most vulnerable. The role of gender within Inuit perinatal wellbeing is often overlooked. Wellness studies have also typically involved an evaluative framework developed by non-Indigenous researchers and has not focused on gender. Inuit in Arviat, Nunavut, perceive perinatal wellbeing as a priority, yet issues continue to go unaddressed in policy and program delivery. Co-designed with Arviarmiut and aimed at improving perinatal wellness, the Ilagiingniq project involves a pilot program of support and study that aim to strengthen the relationship between gender, wellness, and cultural traditions/activities. Rooted within Inuit values and knowledge, this three-year project aims to create knowledge concerning gender and perinatal wellness, and facilitate knowledge sharing activities that amplify Inuit voices, and build upon existing capacity within the community. Ilagiingniq will be developed within/underpinned by Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (IQ) (Inuit traditional knowledge) and involve the hiring and training of community-based perinatal support workers. Research will focus on Inuit-specific wellness indicators and follow the Aajiiqatigiingniq research methodology developed by the Aqqiumavvik Wellness Society, which outlines four stages to research according to Inuit cultural systems: 1) relationship-building, 2) reach shared understanding, 3) share lived experiences, and 4) relational consensus-building. column36: Strengthening Kinship Relations Through Inclusive Rites of Passage for Indigenous Gender and Sexuality-Diverse Youth and Their Support Systems

column36: Supporting the Journey to Fatherhood: A Community-led and Father Driven Approach
column37: Early childhood development is critical for a healthy life trajectory, and supporting parents during this time is critical to healthy parenting and promoting the healthy development of children. In particular, the impact of fathers on their infants has been demonstrated to lower infant mortality rates, decrease risks of cognitive delay, improve parent-infant attachment and reduce parental depression. The role of Indigenous fathers in the lives of their infants is less understood. Colonization has disrupted traditional parenting roles leaving few resources to conceptualize fatherhood and its associated responsibilities. Additionally, parent programs are typically Euro-centric and focus on mothers. In a scoping study on the role of Indigenous fathers in meeting the health needs of their infants, we found that Indigenous men take a journey to becoming fathers, and that supportive parenting programs developed for and by fathers are severely lacking globally yet an important way to support healthy parenting and early childhood development. This 3-phased project takes an Indigenous community-led and gender-focused approach. While the literature suggests that Indigenous fathers are adopting contemporary parenting styles, they long to regain traditional roles and value integrating culture and spiritual wellbeing into their parenting. Phase 1 involves gaining a thorough understanding of fathers' needs during their journey to fatherhood. Phase 2 is a community-led development of a Parenting Program for Fathers. Phase 3 will see the implementation of a pilot Program and its evaluation. This project will fill a current gap in services for Indigenous men and Two Spirit folks by supporting fathers in their parenting and promoting the healthy development of children. In future, the Program can be adapted for use by other Indigenous communities, having a national and global impact on the wellbeing of Indigenous families.

column36: Proclaiming our Stories for Indigenous-Black Community Mental Health
column37: The histories of mixed Indigenous-Black (IB) Peoples have been erased in Canada's collective memory and consciousness. Indigenous People's cultures, contributions, and legacies have been systematically expunged as part of the colonial cultural genocide and assimilation project. Meanwhile, Black Peoples are imagined having always "just arrived" as newcomers to Canada, rather than recognizing the hundreds of years of Black presence on these territories. Thus, the process of gathering, archiving, documenting, and creatively sharing cultures, stories and truths is one way to speak back to these injustices. Our team will organize five powwows in communities across Northern Turtle Island that are known to have IB presence, as an important traditional ceremony representing Indigenous knowledge sharing and community wellbeing. Our goals, through this community-based participatory-action research project are to: a) Engage IB communities in participatory storytelling at cultural events such as powwows to share their histories, stories of survival, culture, and reflect on the impact of culturally-relevant activities on mental health and wellbeing; b) Cultivate space at community-organized powwows for the engagement and narratives of diverse IB folks including Elders, youth, Two-spirit and Indigiqueer IB folks, etc.; c) Foster a space for networking, land-based learning, and intergenerational knowledge sharing between young adults, Elders, community leaders, activists, service providers, and interdisciplinary scholars who identify as being mixed with Indigenous and African diasporic ancestry; d) Contribute to the growing body of work in Canada on the histories, geographies and realities of people of both African diasporic and Indigenous ancestry in Canada; e) Develop reports, resources and tools that capture the mental health impact of the aforementioned activities and interventions to inform health service delivery to IB communities.

column36: Youth-centered development and evaluation of a gender wellness toolkit promoting healthy relationships in Indigenous communities across Canada
column37: Persistent health inequities experienced by Indigenous youth (11-15 years old) in Canada, are at least in part, due to the failure to include Indigenous youth in the development, implementation, and evaluation of programs and interventions directed at them. A focus on youth-led approaches to the development of community-based health and social programs underscoring the formation of healthy relationships and gender wellness is particularly imperative to better meet the needs of youth who use these programs. In partnership with two Access-OM sites (Eskasoni & Puvirnituq) and a youth advisory committee made up of Access-OM participants, the Access team will develop and evaluate a culturally grounded, healthy relationships toolkit aimed at addressing gaps related to issues of gendered violence among youth of all genders and stigma faced by 2SLGBTQIA+ youth. The toolkit will provide support for families, increase health awareness of gender-based issues, and an evaluation framework will be developed that communities can use to gauge program impact. The participating ACCESS-OM teams will lead the project and utilize participatory methodologies to work with new and existing community organizations across Canada that serve Indigenous youth, as well as youth themselves to facilitate the co-development, implementation, and evaluation of the toolkit. First, we will work to develop content for the toolkit and culturally adapt it with community partners and youth through discussion groups and talking circles. Second, we will collaborate with community organizations delivering youth programs to understand how they use and integrate the toolkit in their programming. Finally, we will work with youth and community organizations to co-develop an evaluation framework that can be used to assess whether the toolkit is doing what it is intended to do, and to capture the experiences of service users. Our team will then use this feedback to revise the toolkit.

column36: Does level of social engagement mediate the relationship between conflicted shyness and substance use?
column37: Individual differences in shyness and sociability have been implicated in the development of substance use problems. Individuals who are high on shyness and sociability (i.e., conflicted shyness) are at an elevated risk for developing substance use difficulties. Researchers speculate that individuals with conflicted shyness likely rely on substances to cope with their anxiety created in social situations, although this has never been directly tested. The COVID-19 pandemic provides the opportunity to examine the mechanism through which conflicted shyness is related to substance use because there have likely been significant changes in individuals' levels of social engagement. The proposed study will use a mediated regression analysis to examine whether changes in levels of social engagement during the COVID-19 pandemic mediate the relation between conflicted shyness and substance use. An independent sample of undergraduate students will be asked to complete an online survey and retrospectively report their level of social engagement and their degree of substance use at two different time points: before the COVID-19 shut down and during the height of wave 1 of the pandemic. The online survey will also measure shyness and sociability to index conflicted shyness. We predict that conflicted shyness would be related to reductions in substance use in the context of decreasing levels of social engagement. The findings of this study will provide important insight into specific risk factors of substance use, which can inform prevention techniques and treatment interventions for substance use problems. Moreover, the results will empirically evaluate a longstanding hypothesis related to the mechanism underlying the relation between conflicted shyness and substance use.

column36: Investigating the Social Determinant and Developmental Risk Patterns in Childhood and Adolescence Associated with Adult Asthma and Diabetes Onset
column37: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are the leading global causes of death and its impact on annual deaths is expected to rise (World Health Organization, 2011). Research has found that NCDs often originate in early life during childhood and adolescence where certain risk factors and patterns for disease outcomes based in developmental experiences, social determinants and sociodemographics are present (Kelishadi, 2019). This research aims to address the identification of the social determinant and developmental risk factor patterns found in the pediatric age range for the NCDs of asthma and diabetes in older adolescents and early adults. The proposed project will focus on analyzing data linkages between multiple data sets on a cohort of approximately 40,000+ children in BC from birth to 19 years of age. Data sets will include the Early Development Instrument (EDI) and the Middle Years Development Instrument (MDI) to measure children and adolescents' wellbeing and development, health insurance subsidy status records supplied from the BC Ministries of Health and Education to provide sociodemographic information such as gender, ESL level and relative household poverty level, and MSP administrative data to provide asthma and diabetes prevalence data in later adolescents and early adults. This research provides a unique opportunity to examine the combination of health, education, teacher-rating, self-rating and social context data for an entire population linkage to look at specific joint risk patterns for asthma and diabetes in the pediatric age range. This research will inform our understanding of early risk patterns to predict disease onset for asthma and diabetes that can be targeted earlier in the life course to help mitigate future health problems and promote wellbeing.

column36: Etude des mecanismes sous-tendant une forme de deficience intellectuelle associee au gene TBC1D7
column37: La deficience intellectuelle (DI) est un desordre neuro-developpemental affectant environ 2-3% de la population. Plusieurs genes associes a la DI agissent le long de la voie biochimique mTOR qui favorise la croissance des cellules et la synthese des proteines. Cette voie est regulee negativement par le complexe proteique TSC1-TSC2-TBC1D7. Des mutations des genes TSC1 et TSC2 ont ete impliquees dans une forme de DI, la sclerose tubereuse. Recemment, des mutations du gene TBC1D7 ont ete identifiees chez des patients presentant une DI et un cerveau de grand volume (megalencephalie), ainsi qu'une augmentation de l'activite de mTOR dans les cellules de la peau. Notre hypothese est que la DI et la megalencephalie de ces patients sont causees par une activite excessive de mTOR liee a une diminution de l'inhibition par le complexe TSC1-TSC2-TBC1D7. Notre hypothese secondaire est que l'on peut corriger les deficits cognitifs des patients par l'administration d'un inhibiteur pharmacologique de mTOR. Afin d'explorer ces hypotheses, nous introduisons une mutation dans le gene Tbc1d7 chez la souris afin de repliquer l'impact fonctionnel des mutations retrouvees chez les patients. Nous procederons a une caracterisation du profil comportemental des souris mutantes. En parallele, nous etudierons l'activite de la voie mTOR et nous caracteriserons la morphologie des reseaux neuronaux chez ces souris. Si nous observons des deficits cognitifs et une hyperactivation de mTOR chez les souris mutantes, nous chercherons a les corriger par l'administration d'un inhibiteur de la voie mTOR. Ces etudes nous permettront d'evaluer une strategie therapeutique dans un modele animal qui a le potentiel d'ameliorer les deficits cognitifs et comportementaux des patients porteurs de mutations de TBC1D7.

column36: Investigating the Molecular Processes Behind Motor Learning
column37: Stroke remains to be one of the most debilitating disease in North America. Stroke induced damages in brain motor regions lead to problems in motor execution. One hypothesis that would allow movement recovery is to reinitiate motor learning and reestablish new neural connections among surviving cells. Therefore, our research focuses on understanding the mechanisms behind motor learning in order to treat diseases such as stroke. It has been shown that motor learning induces reorganization in neuronal connectivity as a way to encode memory. This is regulated by a specific type of neurons called somatostatin-expressing interneurons (SOM-INs). Our previous findings show that a transcription factor called Npas4, becomes highly expressed in SOM-INs during motor learning. Furthermore, when Npas4 is ablated in SOM-INs, motor learning and neuronal connectivity reorganization is impaired. As a transcription factor, Npas4 regulates numerous genes. Therefore, my project aims to identify genes that are up- or down- regulated by Npas4 in SOM-INs during motor learning. For this, we plan to isolate Npas4-expressing and non-Npas4-expressing SOM-INs in brain motor regions of mice subjected to a motor learning task. Once separated, the cells will undergo RNA-sequencing, which would identify differentially expressed genes in SOM-INs upon the absence/presence of Npas4. From this, we would be able to identify a molecular mechanism regulated by Npas4 in SOM-INs that allows this interneuron to regulate the learning-induced neuronal connectivity reorganization. Lastly, this proposal has the potential to provide a new repertoire of cell-type specific molecular candidates that may have critical roles in promoting other mechanisms underlying learning in normal and potentially, diseased brains.

column36: Development of an inducible gene editing system to efficiently knock out PTPN12 phosphatase in mammary cells
column37: Genetic knockout is an indispensable tool for studying cellular functions. Recent genomic engineering advancements have led to the gene-editing technology called CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat). This system utilizes a single guided RNAs (sgRNAs) to target a specific gene of interest and effectively induce knockout in nearly all organisms. While CRISPR has been widely applied, it faces limitations such as inconsistent knockout efficiency, effective knockout of only a single gene, and off-target effects. Thus, modification of the CRISPR system is required to solve these issues. The Hippo signaling pathway is a multifaceted gene network that regulates cell proliferation and apoptosis. Signaling is most heavily reliant on phosphorylation and dephosphorylation by kinases and phosphatases respectively, where mutations can lead to tissue overgrowth and cancer. Dr. Yang's lab has recently identified novel regulators of the Hippo pathway in initiating tumorigenesis, notably PTPN12. We hypothesize that PTPN12 downregulation contributes oncogenic responses in mammalian cells through dysregulation of the Hippo pathway. To elucidate the role of PTPN12, we will develop an inducible Cas9 (iCas9) using Doxycycline (Dox)-inducible system established in Yang lab. Constructs expressing sgRNAs targeting PTPN12 will be made to induce knockout in non-tumorigenic mammary breast cells before quantitative assessment. Enhanced cancer cell proliferation is expected in PTPN12 knockout cells in comparison to wild-type cells. The proposed research will establish the first inducible gene-editing system to study the role of PTPN12 involved in tumorigenesis and will have a significant impact for effective cancer therapy.

column36: GA4GH Genomic Data Sharing Tools Against COVID-19
column37: The COVID-19 outbreak has highlighted the need for genomic data standards in order to enable the rapid sharing of high quality genomic and health data. Researchers have shared viral and host sequence data at an unprecedented pace, a first step in creating vaccines in record time. Simultaneously, the cost of genome sequencing continues to decrease, yielding millions of samples in the coming years from both research and healthcare. Sharing of this data is necessary to understand human diseases and eventually help patients. Strengthening international standards over time will prepare us to more effectively respond to future outbreaks as well as advance basic biology and inform clinical care across a range of disease areas. Doing so requires the community to agree on common methods for collecting, storing, transferring, accessing, and analyzing data. The Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) was established in 2013 to accelerate progress in genomic research and human health by cultivating a common framework of standards and harmonized approaches for effective and responsible data sharing. GA4GH brings together 1,000+ individual contributors and 660+ organizational members across 35+ countries working in the areas of healthcare, research, patient advocacy, life science, and information technology to deliver genomic data sharing standards and frameworks. This proposal will provide support for the GA4GH to bring in additional personnel, support the existing team, and drive engagement with the Canadian COVID research community. GA4GH will develop, refine, and adapt GA4GH standards and open-source tools to facilitate research data sharing for COVID applications and the greater infection disease community. Collectively, these efforts will ensure the rapid and timely research response to the current phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in Canada and around the globe, which will be heavily impacted by emerging variants of concern.

column36: Enhancing vaccine development via comprehensive evaluation of humoral immunity: COVID-19 as a paradigm
column37: As of July 2021, four COVID-19 vaccines are available in Canada. Approval of new vaccines will require a better understanding of how COVID-19 vaccines work and protect against infection. Our overall objective is to compare (i) antibody responses to these 4 COVID-19 vaccines and (ii) peoples' immune responses after vaccination or natural infection by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Natural infection is usually considered the 'best' immune response to protect against future infection. We will recruit child and adult volunteers in two groups: those who were vaccinated (total 400 people) and those who had COVID-19 (total 158 people). For those who were vaccinated, we will collect blood samples in before and after vaccination. In those who were infected, we will collect samples up to 12 months after infection. We will also collect information to see if there are other factors (eg, age, sex, gender, other health issues) that affect the person's responses. We will measure responses after vaccination and infection by analysis of how much antibody there is and what the antibody is doing, and of changes in genes that are switched 'on' or 'off'. To analyze the data, we will use sophisticated methods we developed and used to understand how hepatitis B virus vaccines work. We predict to be able to identify similarities and differences, at a molecular level, in immune responses among the different vaccines and between vaccination and natural infection. These head-to-head comparisons will help us to make more effective vaccines in Canada and around the world.

column37: The University of Calgary Brenda Strafford Centre on Aging is both extremely interested and well-positioned to host the 2022 CIHR Summer Program in Aging (SPA) on the topic of "Neurodegeneration and Cerebrovascular Disease in Aging" using a completely virtual platform. While we will be focusing on major neurocognitive disorders (dementias), using neurodegeneration (progressive loss of structure or function of neurons and/or glial cells in specific region or functional system of brain and/or spinal cord) and cerebrovascular disease as the organizing theme would allow us to incorporate conditions such as Parkinson's disease where appropriate and deal with the situation where more than one condition is present, which is common among older adults. A commonality of all these conditions is that aging is the greatest risk factor. The scope and focus of SPA 2022 will be tailored to the objectives of the program and the particular needs of the participants. This would include exploring underlying mechanisms, approaches to prevention, management across the continuum, and addressing social issues such as stigma and the role of caregivers as well as developing and practicing the skills required to achieve success in graduate science training. Inter-disciplinarity, novelty and effectiveness in both 2022 SPA content and format, attention to equity/diversity/inclusivity in all aspects, and excellence in delivery will be the cornerstones of the program. The University of Calgary is home to a wide range of recognized experts in neurodegeneration and/or cerebrovascular disease, representing several faculties and research institutes. While we will marshal local experts, our plan is to also recruit faculty nationally through, for example, our links with the Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging (CCNA). Delivering the 2022 SPA with a virtual platform rather than in-person will allow for greater national faculty representation. Through the experience of the 2021 SPA, we are confident that we can address the challenges that have arisen from the move to a virtual format. As part of our pre-planning for the 2022 SPA we have compiled a list of potential faculty members (some of whom are listed below) with the required core expertise needed to develop the curriculum and oversee meeting logistics. Our Centre on Aging is closely linked to local advocacy groups and people with lived experience, including family care partners and people living with neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases.
