column36: Developing a COVID-19 Vaccination Strategy that Addresses the Needs of People Who Use Drugs in Canada
column37: Background: People Who Use Drugs (PWUD) have intersecting health and social vulnerabilities that elevate their risk for COVID-19 infection, complications and mortality. It is therefore critical that PWUD are vaccinated to reduce their risks. However, research has suggested that vaccine acceptability ratings are lower than the general population (Iverson et al., 2021) with safety concerns being the most common reason for vaccine hesitancy (Dietze et al., 2021). Objectives: The purpose of this study is to: (1) identify drivers of vaccine hesitancy and approaches to improve vaccine confidence and; (2) to develop national tailored knowledge mobilization and translation products that are for and by PWUD to promote vaccination based on the findings from Objective 1. We will work closely with PWUD and service providers who work with this population to develop these materials. Methods: The study will recruit 100 participants from an existing national sample of PWUD who previously participated in telephone/video interviews about the impact of COVID-19 in May-June 2020. Semi-structured interviews will be used to identify barriers to receiving vaccinations and ways to address barriers. An advisory committee of PWUD, service providers working with PWUD, and the research team will use responses from the interviews to co-create a multi-pronged approach to address vaccine hesitancy among PWUD. The strategy will include the following components: (1) Developing and disseminating vaccine information resources for PWUD; and (2) Providing training tools to service providers working with PWUD to improve conversations about vaccinations.

column37: The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) is Canada's first, population-based, comprehensive, national, sustainably funded research platform. The CLSA includes 51,338 participants, aged 45-85 at enrolment (2011-2015) who are being followed every three years until 2033 with a goal of providing important information on the health and well-being of Canadians as they age. In the next two follow-ups of data collection, additional information will be collected in several areas including sexual health, how people experience health care services and changes in mobility and vision. The CLSA team has developed modified methods of data collection to accommodate challenges that participants may face in physical health, mobility, and cognitive health to allow them to participate if they wish to continue in the study.

column36: Predicting Response to Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment Using the Addictions Neuroclinical Assessment
column37: Alcohol use is a leading cause of death and disability in Canada. However, treatment of alcohol addiction, also known as alcohol use disorder (AUD), is challenging, with high rates of relapse to heavy drinking following treatment. At present, we do not know which individuals are most likely to benefit from existing treatment for AUD. This study proposes using a framework known as the Addictions Neuroclinical Assessment (ANA) to determine whether it can be used to better understand who responds to a standardized intervention for AUD. ANA consists of measures that assess three neurobiological domains that are thought to affect substance use: executive function, negative emotionality, and incentive salience. In this study, we will recruit 64 individuals with AUD and assess each of these domains prior to treatment. Following assessment, each participant will undergo a 12-week treatment program in which they receive weekly manualized group psychotherapy in addition to anticraving medication (prescribed using a standardized algorithm). We will collect preliminary data on whether differences in each domain predict treatment outcomes over the 12-week program. Results from this project will help healthcare decision makers and clinicians determine which patients are likely to benefit most from existing treatments and stimulate the development of new targeted treatments for those who do not respond to current evidence-based care.

column36: The effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of population-level policies to reduce alcohol use: a systematic review
column37: Alcohol consumption is currently the world's third-largest risk factor for disease, attributable for about 5% of the global burden of disease, with clear links to conditions such as neuropsychiatric disorders, gastrointestinal diseases, cancer, intentional injuries, unintentional injuries, cardiovascular diseases and diabetes. In youth, heavy episodic drinking (HED), such as binge drinking, has been associated with long-term consequences such as cognitive, structural and functional brain changes and liver disease. Canadians are among the largest consumers of alcohol in the world. The most recent cross-country data indicate that Canadians (15+ years) consumed 10 litres of alcohol per capita as compared to the global average of 6 litres per capita. In addition, almost one fifth of Canadians over the age of 12 were classified as heavy drinkers in 2018 and 2019. Since the COVID-19 pandemic started, alcohol use has dramatically increased, highlighting alcohol consumption as a chief area of concern for population health. Given the clear risks associated with alcohol use and the levels of alcohol consumption in Canada, federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments have an important role in developing and implementing evidence-informed policies to reduce the consumption of alcohol. These policies may include decreasing access and availability of alcohol (e.g., via taxation, minimum pricing, outlet density, minimum age for sale, hours of sale), and regulating marketing and advertising of alcohol (e.g., plain packaging and volume of advertising). Our aim is to systematically review and synthesize evidence about the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of population-level policies to reduce alcohol use. We will draw upon literature from several disciplines - health economics, health policy, political science, psychology - to present comprehensive findings.

column36: The Power of Social Determinants of Health and their Implications for Reducing Alcohol-related Trauma.
column37: Alcohol-related deaths have been referred to as a silent epidemic in Canada, with 250 alcohol-related hospitalizations daily. Alcohol is a risk factor for traumatic physical injury. Traumatic physical injuries are the primary cause of death and a leading cause of hospitalizations worldwide. Injuries have significant impact on mental, physical, and social health for the rest of the person's life. While burden from injury can be reduced through prevention programs, the programs are more effective if targeted to at risk groups. Social determinants of child health (SDOH) can help us understand which factors place young adults at greater risk for alcohol-related traumatic injury, guiding the development of targeted prevention strategies that engage participants from at-risk groups. We propose to better understand the association between SDOH and alcohol-related traumatic physical injury in young adults by using information based on large population-wide data. We will examine a longitudinal group of over 2800 young adults hospitalized for alcohol-related traumatic physical injury and over 2000 young adults with injury but no alcohol, by linking longitudinal administrative and clinical data contained at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy. We will examine 13 SDOH over childhood including: Use of income assistance, rural/urban status, socioeconomic status, children in care, child mental disorder, parental factors (involved with criminal justice system, education, social housing, immigration status, high residential mobility, mother's age at first birth, parental mental disorder, and parental physical disorder) to identify groups and periods of time which identify females and males at greatest risk for alcohol-related traumatic injury. Knowing these evidence-based at-risk factors will guide decision-makers/health policy makers to improve injury prevention efforts by targeting individuals that are most vulnerable.

column36: Piloting of an intervention to reduce problematic alcohol use in Early Phase Psychosis patients
column37: A focus of research for youth and Emerging Adults with early phase psychosis (EPP) has been cannabis use. However, this focus has led to overlooking the possible negative influence of another legal recreational drug, alcohol. Previous studies we have done demonstrated that over use of alcohol reduces the effectiveness of early intervention in psychosis treatment services. These treatment services are wrap around services that address medical, and social needs of young people with psychosis. Individuals with alcohol use disorder and EPP have fewer positive symptoms such as hallucinations which are the aspects of psychotic disorders that respond most readily to medication but have greater levels of depressive symptoms. Biologically, we can see the negative impact of alcohol on brain structure in our MRI studies. Our aim presented in this grant is to pilot a psychosocial intervention using cognitive enhancement therapy to reduce alcohol consumption in individuals with early phase psychosis. This intervention has shown promise in reducing alcohol use in individuals with long standing schizophrenia and compare it to treatment as usual which involves brief (1 session) psychoeducation. We hope to reduce substance use in young people in the early stages of a psychotic disorder and improve their odds of a full recovery. In addition to measuring symptoms and hospitalizations, we plan to measure what are called social determinants of health such as return to school or work and resumption of relationships. These variables have not been measured previously in alcohol use interventions in this population but in our experience are the best indicators of long term recovery from psychosis. The symptoms will generally improve with antipsychotic drug treatment but reach a threshold after 6 months in most individuals who engage with our 5 year program. Further functional and social recovery seem to be the best determinants of a full return to health in this population.

column36: Immunosurveillance of breast cancer by innate immune cells
column37: Although treatment of patients with non small cell lung carcinoma has improved over the last decade - most notably with checkpoint-based immunotherapies - the majority of patients relapse with resistant and disseminated disease. This highlights that current treatments likely incite incomplete clearance, and may allow outgrowth of escape mutants. The success of cancer therapies, especially checkpoint blockade, relies on collaboration with the immune system. Complete and durable control of NSCLC will require continued activation and activity of the immune system, in a way that is sufficiently dynamic to recognize and control evolving tumors. Anti-PD1/PD-L1 immunotherapy is thought to function by relieving immunosuppression of lymphocytes; in addition to T cells, NK cells can be inhibited through PD-1/PD-L1 interactions and rescued by checkpoint inhibition. PD-1/PD-L1 therapy does not universally result in complete control of NSCLC, and tumor genomic analyses have revealed that relapsing tumors lack HLA expression, owing to alterations in the genes and/or expression of members of the HLA processing and presentation pathways. We find that both PD-L1 and HLA expression on NSCLC are highly dynamic, suggesting that the role of NK cells in controlling NSCLC might vary over the course of treatment and evolution of the tumor. Natural killer (NK) cells are important mediators of cancer surveillance and contributors to treatment efficacy, but understudied as targets to maximize the impact of immunotherapy. NK cells' anticancer functions are various and include direct lysis of transformed cells, graft-versus- leukemia effects following hematopoietic cell transplantation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), in response to delivery of therapeutic antibodies. Targeting NK cells in situ, or delivery of ex vivo expanded NK cells are therapies underway that are safe, feasible and scalable because NK cells can be transplanted across allogeneic barriers without graft-versus-host complications. The function of NK cells varies within and between individuals as a result of variegated expression of germline-encoded ligands and a functional process called "education", based on interactions with "self" human leukocyte antigens (HLA). Unlike T cells, NK cell killing is not HLA-restricted. The "educated" population of NK cells actually responds to cells that have lost HLA expression in a process called "missing self" reactivity. The "uneducated" population of NK cells functions to recognize stressed cells, but does not interact with "self" HLA molecules. Hence, NK cells may be ideal effectors against NSCLC because they can target both the HLA-sufficient and HLA-deficient phenotypes, but establishment of the functional roles of each of the educated and uneducated NK cell subsets will be important toward balancing their efficacy in NSCLC. In this operating grant, we will explore the conditions that enable NK-mediated recognition of NSCLC, with a focus on the educated and uneducated NK cell subsets. Using high parameter flow cytometry, we can identify additional features of both populations that may predict their function and become next-generation targets for immunotherapy. We will pursue the following specific aims: Aim 1: Determine how loss of HLA expression influences recognition of NSCLC by NK cells. Aim 2: Determine how recruitment of NK cell subsets influences the ultimate outcome of NSCLC. Significance: Our studies will demonstrate how NK cells may contribute to control of NSCLC, and highlight opportunities for intervention to maximize NK cells' contribution to cancer control. By leveraging the multifaceted mechanisms of target cell recognition of which different NK cell subsets are capable, it will become possible to more completely and durably control NSCLC.

column36: Overcoming inactivation of oncolytic reovirus by proteases in breast tumor microenvironments.
column37: BACKGROUND: Reovirus (T3wt) is in phase 3 clinical trials for treatment of breast and other cancers. My laboratory seeks to further adapt reovirus towards breast tumor cells and environments, with hopes to improve the potency of reovirus therapy. Using expired project grant funding from CRS, we discovered that breast tumor microenvironments are enriched in zinc-dependent metalloproteases (MP) that cleave the T3wt cell attachment protein s1 and reduce reovirus infectivity towards many BC cell types by 100-fold. Moreover, we introduced a T249I mutation in s1 to withstand inactivation by BC MPs, which lead to improved tumor regression and prolonged survival in a syngeneic ErbB2+ BC (TuBO) immunocompotent mouse model, relative to T3wt. Aim 1 will conduct a comprehensive pre-clinical study of BC MP-resistant reovirus relative to T3wt in two BC models: the TuBo syngeneic model and the aggressive human MDA-MB-231 orthotopic xenograft model. We will use large sample sizes to monitor for survival and tumor regression benefits, and also to monitor reovirus s1 cleavage and virus replication kinetics within the tumors. If BC MPs reproducibly restrict reovirus oncolysis, then BC MP-resistant reovirus will show higher tumor clearance and infectious virus relative to ReoWT in multiple BC models, and prove itself worthwhile of clinical testing. Aim 2. We observed reovirus-inactivation and s1-cleavage by extracellular extracts of three mouse BC tumor types and five BC human cell lines. Triple negative breast cancers (TNBCs) are hardest to treat, so in aim 2, we will establish the repertoire of TNBC models that inactivate reovirus through MPs in their microenvironment. Secretion of MPs will first be evaluated in 17 human TNBC cell lines, and then confirmed in mouse xenograft tumors for 3 of these models. We will also evaluate reovirus-inactivating MP levels in the E0771 and EMT6 syngeneic orthotopic mouse TNBC models. The findings will not only reveal the prevalence of MPs as barriers to reovirus oncolysis, but will enable future efficacy trials in a variation of aggressive, metastatic TNBC models with different mouse genetic backgrounds and tumor immunities. Aim 3 will create reovirus variants with highly divergent s1 proteins that resist BC MPs, retain utmost infectivity in breast cancer cells, and avoid antibody cross-neutralization. The T249I mutation in s1 brought benefits to oncolytic activity but also costs to virus fitness that if overcome, may further enhance oncolytic activity. We therefore plan to switch s1 of ReoWT with s1 proteins from diverse reoviruses with as little as 22% amino acid similarity and that can withstand proteolytic cleavage. Some of these recombinant viruses that withstand cleavage will also ideally retain high infectivity in BC cells. Moreover, s1 is the immunodominant protein during antibody neutralization. By replacing s1 of ReoWT with s1 from other reovirus serotypes that do not cross-neutralize, we will create antigenically-distinct versions of oncolytic reovirus. In future, these recombinants will create the first tools to test the extent of oncolytic impairment imposed by host neutralizing antibodies against subsequent injections of the same oncolytic virus. OVERALL SIGNIFICANCE: This proposed project will provide detailed understanding of the obstacle created by BC MPs to reovirus therapy of breast cancers, and best-strategies to overcome this obstacle to maximize therapeutic efficacy. Note that other oncolytic viruses, antibodies, and protein-based therapies are proteinaceous as well and could be vulnerable to proteolysis; our novel findings on proteolysis as an obstacle to therapeutic activity in BC might therefore extend to other proteinaceous therapies as well.

column36: Development of molecular imaging probes targeting Nectin4 (PVRL4) expression in cancer
column37: Background: Nectin-4 is a cell adhesion molecule that is expressed during embryonic development and is absent in normal adult tissues. However, high expression of Nectin-4 is seen in several cancers including ~62% of triple-negative breast cancers (TNBC). Nectin-4 expression is tumorigenic and it plays in important role in cell proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, and metastasis through PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. Therefore Nectin-4 is an excellent target for anticancer therapy. In this proposal, our goal is to develop molecular imaging probes targeting Nectin-4, for non-invasive imaging of TNBC. Monoclonal antibodies that bind to cancer cell-surface markers are traditionally used for both therapy and non-invasive imaging of tumors, in a "theranostics" approach. However, long half-life of monoclonal antibodies in patient serum, is not ideal for molecular imaging applications. Recent advances have led to the development of alternative binding proteins that are ~20 times smaller than antibodies. The small size (~20 times smaller than antibodies) enables better tumor penetration and rapid clearance from the bloodstream. High contrast PET/CT images can be generated in a much shorter time frame when compared to full-length antibodies. Hypothesis and Objectives: We hypothesize that small protein-based imaging probes will be more effective in tumor penetration due to small size and monomeric binding capacity compared to bivalent monoclonal antibodies. Our goal for this proposal is to develop and evaluate small protein-based imaging probes targeting Nectin-4 and compare their efficacy with antibody-based imaging probes for molecular imaging of TNBC. Research Methodology: We have recently developed human origin antibodies (N4mAb) and alternative scaffold based binders (N4bp) to proximal IgV domain of Nectin-4. In this proposal, our plan is to further develop and compare antibody and small protein-based imaging probes; Our specific aims are: 1. Optimize site-specific labeling of lead small protein binder, N4bp, to minimize loss of affinity 2. Develop and optimize genetically fused dimers of N4bp for studying the effect of bivalent binding 3. Develop 89Zr derivatives of N4bp, N4bp-dimer and N4mAb and evaluate their potential as non-invasive PET/CT imaging agents in TNBC cell xenograft models. Expected Outcomes: The imaging probes developed from this study will be useful for diagnosis, stratification personalized treatment and monitoring progression of TNBC. This study will enable the pre-clinical development of optimal probes that can be translated for non-invasive imaging of primary and metastatic tumors in TNBC patients.

column36: Identifying changes in cancer risk factors during the COVID-19 pandemic and predicting population risk
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic had a profound impact on the daily life of Canadians. Public health measures to slow the spread of COVID-19 (e.g., physical distancing), have resulted in unprecedented changes in behaviors and activities of daily life. Smoking, alcohol, poor diet, and lack of physical activity are well established factors that increase a person's risk for cancer and unintended changes in these risk factors during the COVID-19 pandemic may have led to increased cancer risk. The overall goals of this study are to measure changes in cancer risk factors, identify populations at greatest risk, and predict how these changes may impact the future incidence of cancer. We will use a multi-pronged approach to evaluate the changes in cancer risk factors. First, a traditional research approach will be used by evaluating national data from repeated surveys collected through the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. Second, we will apply novel artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning approaches to non-traditional electronic sources of data (e.g., social media, websites) to evaluate changes in cancer risk factors in real-time. The resulting measures of the change in risk factors during the pandemic will then be applied to existing cancer prediction models to estimate the potential increase in cancer burden due to risk factor changes during the pandemic. The results of this study will inform population and public health interventions for cancer prevention.

column36: The role of prolactin-inducible protein (PIP) in promoting breast cancer metastasis in the lung
column37: Despite many advances in the treatment of breast cancer, the recurrence of disease in other parts of the body (called metastasis) remains a significant threat to survival of the patient. A particularly aggressive type, called triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), accounts for 15-20% of all breast cancer diagnoses and has the lowest survival rate, largely due to metastasis. Our lab has developed a way to study this cancer in mice by transplanting a mouse version of TNBC cancer cells into the mammary glands of mice and observing the development of both the primary tumor and its metastasis. Using this model of the human disease, we can study the role of a molecule called prolactin-inducible protein (PIP). We have studied PIP in breast cancer over many years and have shown that it can be used in the clinic to determine that cancer cells in other parts of the body came from a primary tumor in the breast. In our animal model of human disease, we have recently discovered that the presence of PIP in the primary tumor correlates strongly with metastasis to the lung. We now wish to determine any causal relationship in this correlation, that is, to know what it is about PIP that makes it have this effect. We will study this from the perspective of PIP's action in the primary tumor and metastatic lung as well as the response of other lung cells to the arrival of PIP in their environment. We expect this work will help point to more effective ways to treat TNBC.

column36: The Role of Microbiota and Immune Microenvironment in Breast Cancer Metastasis
column37: Metastasis is the major cause of death for cancer patients and treatment options for patients with aggressive, highly metastatic forms of breast cancer, such as triple negative breast cancer, remain limited. The microenvironment of metastatic breast tumours is associated with poor oxygenation (hypoxia), acidic conditions and inflammation that promote disease progression. Bacteria are also present in breast tumors, but it is currently unknown whether specific types of bacteria are present in the hypoxic, acidic conditions common to aggressive breast cancer and how such bacteria may contribute to metastasis. Drs Dedhar and Finlay, together with their research teams, are studying the role that host bacteria, or microbiome, play in driving the process of metastasis in breast cancer. A major objective this research proposal is to identify and characterize the microbiome specifically associated with aggressive, metastatic disease, and to understand how these bacteria regulate the function of immune cells and inflammatory cells such as neutrophils to drive metastatic cancer. These studies aim to identify the micobiome specific to metastatic cancer and determine the functional consequences of the microbiome in regulating metastasis, with the long term goal ofestablishing the microbiome as a predictor of development of metastatic disease that could be targeted therapeutically to effectively treat patients with aggressive breast cancer.

column36: Bonifier l'offre d'intervention en dependance destinees aux personnes frequentant des dispositifs de stabilite residentielle et vivant des enjeux lies a leur consommation d'alcool, au vieillissement et a l'itinerance : des besoins complexes a considerer
column37: Ce projet vise a soutenir l'amelioration de l'offre de services en dependance pour les personnes presentant des enjeux lies a l'usage d'alcool, au vieillissement et a l'instabilite residentielle, frequentant des dispositifs de stabilite residentielle pour populations en situation de precarite sociale du reseau communautaire. Les impacts croises du vieillissement, de la consommation d'alcool et de l'instabilite residentielle fragilisent davantage les personnes sur le plan social et de la sante, et font emerger des besoins complexes. Le reseau communautaire offre diverses modalites d'hebergement, associees a un soutien psychosocial et en sante individualise appuye par le reseau public de la sante et des services sociaux. Neanmoins, la transition des personnes vers des dispositifs d'hebergement plus autonome fragilise l'accompagnement en dependance, alors que ce suivi reste essentiel. Une demarche de recherche descriptive et interpretative permettra de mieux comprendre le parcours au sein des services de sante et sociaux des personnes presentant des problematiques liees au vieillissement, a l'usage d'alcool, a l'instabilite residentielle, et frequentant des dispositifs de stabilite residentielle, ainsi que leurs besoins specifiques de prise en charge. Des entrevues individuelles de 60 minutes seront realisees aupres d'usagers (n = 15) de ces dispositifs, ainsi qu'aupres d'intervenants et de gestionnaires (n = 15) au contact de ceux-ci. Une revue de portee de la litterature sera menee afin d'identifier les pratiques en dependance efficaces aupres de cette population. Ces donnees seront discutees avec les milieux concernes afin de faire emerger des pistes d'innovations en matiere d'intervention et d'organisation de services. Ce projet contribuera a renforcer les liens entre les reseaux communautaire et public, et le milieu academique, et soutiendra le developpement d'une offre de soin integree repondant mieux aux besoins et objectifs des personnes les plus vulnerables.

column36: Quels sont les significations de la consommation d'alcool parmi les personnes de la diversite sexuelle et de genre ?
column37: Les jeunes LGBTQ+ consomment plus d'alcool que les jeunes de la population generale. La discrimination et la stigmatisation dont ces jeunes sont l'objet, peuvent expliquer cette situation. Malgre les avancees concernant la reconnaissance des droits civiques des personnes LGBTQ+, la consommation d'alcool n'a pas diminue dans ces communautes. Le parcours de vie des personnes LGBTQ+ est teinte par une serie d'evenements dont : l'acceptation de sa propre orientation sexuelle ou son identite de genre, le processus de coming out, la socialisation, etc. Or, les etudes sur la consommation d'alcool parmi les personnes LGBTQ+ n'abordent pas, a notre connaissance, les liens entre ces parcours de vie et les trajectoires de consommation d'alcool. Ainsi, notre etude a pour objectifs de : 1) comprendre les significations de la consommation d'alcool parmi les personnes de la diversite sexuelle et de genre; 2) examiner s'il existe des liens entre les trajectoires d'utilisation d'alcool et le parcours de vie en tant que personne de la diversite sexuelle ou de genre; 3) identifier les besoins en termes de services associes a la consommation d'alcool. Pour repondre a ces objectifs, des entrevues semi-dirigees d'une duree d'environ 90 minutes seront menees. Le projet suivra les principes de la recherche communautaire, c'est-a-dire l'implication des personnes concernees dans toutes les etapes du processus de recherche. Les resultats de cette etude permettront le developpement des interventions preventives ciblees concernant la consommation d'alcool ainsi que le developpement des services adaptes pour les jeunes LGBTQ+ ayant une consommation problematique d'alcool.

column36: Microbial modification of the cervicovaginal glycome as a risk factor for chlamydia
column37: Chlamydia is the most common sexually transmitted infection in Canada and worldwide, contributing to serious consequences for women's reproductive health such as infection of the uterus and infertility. Chlamydia disproportionately affects adolescent girls and young women, with 15-24 year old Canadian females exhibiting 2-3X higher rates of chlamydia than their male peers. Though important, social/behavioural factors do not fully explain the excess burden of chlamydia experienced by adolescents. Consequently, several biological explanations have been put forward, including physiological differences in cervical tissue and mucus. However, these are difficult features of a woman's body to clinically evaluate or manipulate with therapy. Thus, we are investigating a more easily diagnosed and therapeutically tractable factor that could influence STI susceptibility in adolescents, the vaginal microbiome. Microbial communities in the vagina obtain the nutrients needed sustain themselves by degrading sugars and proteins in vaginal fluid and on human cells. The nature of these activities is poorly understood, but if proteins that defend against infection are degraded, they may weaken a woman's natural immune defenses. This project will apply advanced methods in sugar profiling to learn if the microbiota in adolescents sometimes modifies the sugars that decorate vaginal cells, making them more susceptible to chlamydia infection. This could identify new avenues of inhibiting these activities to prevent chlamydia to improve adolescent health.

column36: Estimating chronic hepatitis B prevalence and the undiagnosed proportion in Canada using health administrative data
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is one of the most burdensome infectious diseases and one of the most expensive infectious diseases to prevent and treat. HBV infection can cause chronic infection of the liver (i.e. chronic hepatitis B (CHB)), that is silent for 20-30 years before about one in five infected people develop liver failure or liver cancer. The Government of Canada has endorsed and committed to the World Health Organization (WHO)'s strategy on viral hepatitis, which has called for a 90% reduction in new HBV cases, a 65% reduction in HBV-related deaths, and treatment of 80% of eligible patients by 2030. To achieve these targets, the government has to understand the geographic and demographic distribution of the disease, in terms of the number of infections (e.g. prevalence), and, the number of patients who remain unaware of their infections. We propose to 1) measure the number of complications associated with the disease and their corresponding time to diagnosis in both the general population and immigrant populations using data from British Columbia and Ontario that describe almost every interaction with the health system; and 2) develop a computer simulation model that can estimate the current CHB prevalence and proportion of undiagnosed individuals infected with the disease. Together, this will provide needed evidence to help decision makers to improve HBV care and help Canada achieve the WHO targets.

column36: Mechanisms of immunity and protection against Chlamydia of RNA and protein vaccines
column37: Chlamydia is the most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) in Canada, occurring in 346 in every 100,000 people. While the majority of infected individuals have no symptoms, untreated chlamydia in women can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility and ectopic pregnancies. Although testing and treatment are available, the increasing prevalence of chlamydia in the population motivates the development of a vaccine. A recent human clinical trial for a protein chlamydia vaccine showed a good safety profile and immune responses in humans, but the vaccine immunization schedule requires five doses, which makes implementation challenging. Furthermore, the vaccines tested in animal models to-date do not completely prevent infection. We propose to test three types of chlamydia vaccines to identify how well they work for preventing infection, including a protein vaccine (similar to the one used in the human clinical trial), a messenger RNA vaccine (similar to the approved COVID-19 vaccines) and a self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine. Self-amplifying RNA is a type of messenger RNA that is able to replicate itself in a patient's cells, which increases the total amount and duration of the vaccine protein expression. We hypothesize that using self-amplifying RNA will allow us to use a lower dose of RNA than mRNA and fewer doses compared to the state-of-the protein chlamydia vaccine. We will characterize the immune responses with the protein, mRNA and saRNA vaccines and determine how well each of them protects against chlamydia infection. The results of this research will inform the design of future chlamydia vaccine candidates and seed a collaboration with the goal of developing and rolling out an effective chlamydia vaccine. Furthermore, the knowledge regarding the immune mechanisms of protein, mRNA and saRNA vaccines generated from these studies may be useful for development of vaccines against other STIs or infectious diseases.

column36: Characterizing the disease burden from hepatitis B virus in British Columbia, Canada
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a significant source of morbidity and mortality in Canada and globally. In 2015, HBV-related complications accounted for 66% of viral hepatitis-related deaths worldwide. Large proportions of people living with chronic HBV may be unaware of their infections due to the asymptomatic nature of the early phases of the disease, and may get diagnosed once they develop symptoms during advanced stages of the illness. Thus, screening is essential for early diagnosis of HBV infection, and for timely linkage with care and treatment initiation to slow disease progression. Groups facing the greatest burden of disease from HBV in Canada include persons immigrating from HBV-endemic countries in East Asia, Southeast Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa, where HBV is highly prevalent (HBsAg: ~6.2%-10.5%), unimmunized people who inject drugs, gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men, and Indigenous Peoples. Immigrants in Canada may be diagnosed and linked with care late in the course of their infections and, consequently, have an increased risk of hospitalization for complications related to HBV. Canada has committed to reducing HBV incidence and HBV-related mortality by 95% and 65%, respectively, by 2030 but is lacking national and provincial action plans for HBV elimination. These action plans would require measurable indicators of hepatitis-related services for progress tracking and program evaluation. Comprehensive population-level HBV data are necessary for the creation of care cascades and other tools for program planning and evaluation but are currently unavailable for HBV in British Columbia. This project aims to provide a detailed understanding of the epidemiology of HBV in British Columbia by developing a comprehensive, dynamic, population-level integrated dataset comprised of linked laboratory and administrative data to support the mapping of a current HBV care cascade and to highlight areas for improvement in the continuum of care in BC.

column36: Paving a path to improved access: The STBBI-CARE study [community/access/respect/equity]
column37: Sexually transmitted infections (STI) are rising dramatically despite many measures taken by public health agencies to slow the spread. Some individuals and groups are much more at risk of becoming infected, these are the same people that face greater challenges in accessing care; and this issue has only been made worse by the COVID-19 pandemic. Mail-out STI programs where people do their own sample collections have been tried in some regions across the world and found to improve access and be acceptable both for people to use and for test accuracy. However, these programs are not available in the majority of Canada and, therefore, not a part of public health care. Our team of experts will work with the Center for Sexuality that works with at-risk persons to provide STI care; partnering with them to develop a web-based program where persons 14 years of age and older can access the website and complete a questionnaire about sexual health and history. Depending on the answers, the appropriate testing kit will be mailed direct to them to do the tests in their own home and mail it back. People will also have the chance to speak about barriers to accessing STI care and provide feedback on this program. Based on the responses, we will also work together with patient advisors to develop an improved pathway of care for STIs with a focus on persons most at risk of becoming infected. During this study, we will also be implementing a novel dried urine spot test which can be used to test for two of the most common STIs. If this test performs as well as the current standard of swab or urine testing, then this represents a very non-invasive and easy way to test for STIs and use can be rapidly expanded to other clinics and regions in Canada and elsewhere. Similarly, we will apply our pathway of care by partnering with other sexual health clinics in the region and expand to other Canadian regions over time to improve care standards for and access to high-quality STI care.

column36: Development of a Canadian Hepatitis B Virtual Centre of Excellence
column37: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) is the leading global cause of end-stage liver disease, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC or primary liver cancer). The management of hepatitis B is often complex and depends upon identifying patients at risk, appropriate diagnostic workup, treatment and follow-up. CHB affects ~260,000 Canadians but disease prevalence and the burden of associated liver disease is expected to increase due to the impact of immigration and an aging population. Despite the availability of potent oral antiviral therapy, persons living with HBV remain at risk for progressive liver disease due to suboptimum linkage to care and low treatment uptake. There is an urgent need for systematic research to identify gaps in the HBV care continuum, improve access to therapy and reduce the risk of HBV-related end-stage liver disease. The Canadian HBV Network is well-established with key infrastructure to help improve the HBV care continuum in Canada. This catalyst grant funding will spearhead an initiative to determine barriers in the linkage to HBV care and access to treatment in patients followed by the Canadian HBV Network. We will (i) conduct a pilot study to describe diagnostic workup, referral patterns, the proportion referred to tertiary care, and those who receive HBV antiviral treatment, (ii) conduct survey studies and focus groups of patients, primary care providers and hepatitis B specialists to inform development of strategies that facilitate access to care and treatment and (iii) develop working groups to inform a larger team grant to enhance collaborations on HBV research, training and improve access to care for hepatitis B in Canada. The PI and co-PIs can engage patients and stakeholders through established collaborations, and have expertise in hepatitis B and/or required research methodology. Our studies will help understand and predict the risk of liver disease related to hepatitis B an often devastating liver disease.

column36: Preventing Breast Cancer Metastasis by Disrupting MT1-MMP Trafficking
column37: The ability of malignant tumour cells to degrade extracellular matrix (ECM) and invade neighboring tissue is crucial to the metastatic spread of tumours, ultimately contributing to the vast majority of cancer-caused deaths. Degradation of ECM proteins is mediated by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and evidence indicates that membrane type 1-matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP) is a central regulator of invasion in aggressive tumours, including breast cancers. Herein, we propose to define the molecular mechanisms that control the trafficking of MT1-MMP to sites of ECM degradation in breast cancer cells, and how this contributes to tumour progression in vivo. Using the human mammary tumour cell line MDA-MB-231, we have determined that Syntaxin4 (Stx4), a t-SNARE, is required for MT1-MMP trafficking, and the metastatic spread of tumour cells in a murine xenograft model. [SNARE: soluble NSF attachment protein receptors; NSF: N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor.] We also found that perturbing the interaction between Stx4 and Munc18c, an S/M protein family member that regulates Stx4, impairs trafficking of MT1-MMP and tumour cell invasion in vitro. These findings are the first to indicate that tumour cell invasion can be regulated by the interaction of Stx4-Munc18c, and suggest this interaction may be a regulatory point in the process of cell invasion. We now plan to define how the Stx4-Munc18c interaction regulates trafficking of MT1-MMP and metastatic spread of MDA-MB-231 cells in vivo, and the role of this interaction in other types of breast cancer cells and tissue samples. We will also identify amino acids in the N-terminal region of Stx4 that are required for its interaction with Munc18c, to spur future efforts aimed at targeting this interaction therapeutically. The specific goal of the research proposed here is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms through which Stx4 and Munc18c regulate MT1-MMP-mediated cell invasion and mammary tumour progression in vivo. Three aims are proposed: (1) Define Stx4-Munc18c function in MT1-MMP trafficking and metastasis, (2) Identify amino acids required for interaction of Stx4 and Munc18c, and (3) Analysis of Stx4-Munc18c interaction in different breast cancer types. In aim #1, Stx4-Munc18c interaction will be disrupted in MDA-MB-231 cells, and changes to trafficking of MT1-MMP will be examined in vitro, and effects on tumour progression will studied using a mouse xenograft model. In aim #2, mutations in the N-terminal region of Stx4 will be generated and used to assess binding to Munc18c. In aim #3, the interaction of Stx4 and Munc18c will examined in panels of breast cancer cell lines and tumour tissues.

column36: Therapeutic Exploitation of Metabolic Rewiring in Tumor Heterogeneity
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common type of primary brain cancer in adults and is characterized by its highly aggressive nature. The average survival rate for patients with GBM is approximately 15 months with treatment. Therefore, it is extremely important to find new therapies to improve the prognosis for GBM patients. It may be possible to treat GBM by starving the tumor of the nutrients and energy that it needs to grow by targeting cancer metabolism. In order to do so, we need to better understand the metabolic requirements of the different cancer cell populations which make up GBM tumors. This project aims to comprehensively characterize the metabolic pathways that are used by different types of GBM cell populations and understand how these cells change their energy metabolism in response to treatment with metabolic inhibitors. The findings from this project will aid in the development of new therapies for the treatment of GBM to help improve patient survival.

column37: Infectious syphilis is a potentially devastating sexually transmitted infection that has recently had a resurgence in North America. In the Canadian prairies (Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba), syphilis mainly impacts young, urban, heterosexual, highly marginalized young adult populations. The prairie provinces have the highest syphilis rates in Canada, and also the highest number of congenital syphilis, or infants born with syphilis. Any occurence of congenital syphilis is thought to be a public health failure in high-income countries. There has been a lack of published studies examining syphilis in the Canadian prairies; thus, at a time when evidence is most needed to inform public health efforts to control syphilis, a dearth existis in the literature. At the same time, new technologies, such as molecular epidemiology and data science offer never-before-seen potential to unlock the epidemiology of syphilis, and why it appears in certain groups. Moreover, community perspectives towards syphilis, and new technologies has not been integrated into research and practice. Partnering with public health from the 3 prairie provinces, and researchers from Canada, US, and Europe, the projects in this proposal seek to address this gap in the literature, while also building a multilevel, action-oriented embedded research agenda on syphilis. The study aims include: 1) engage impacted communities to inform ongoing and future syphilis research; 2) describe and compare the epidemiology of syphilis in Alberta and Manitoba; 3) understand the healthcare utilization patterns of individuals diagnosed with syphilis in Manitoba; 4) establish molecular epidemiology capacity for syphilis. We anticipate generating novel and innovative insights into syphilis epidemiology, providing new data and knowledge that can be used to address current syphilis epidemics, and establishing an infrastructure for future STBBI research

column36: Oral Administration of Reoviruses for the Treatment, Prevention and Early Diagnosis of Colorectal Cancer.
column37: Could ingesting a virus help clear malignant cells in the digestive tract? Could this virus prevent cancer progression in the colon? Or could the virus be used to diagnose colon tumours in the form of polyps? We believe that the gastroenteric virus Reovirus can do all that. REOvirus (Respiratory Enteric Orphan) was originally isolated from the respiratory and enteric tract of humans, but is classified as an orphan virus because it is associated with any known disease. The natural cycle of Reovirus is to spread through the oral-fecal route of mammals; this is how this virus has evolved for perhaps millions of years. Reovirus has been shown to preferentially replicate in and destroy cancer cells with high efficiency (a process called oncolysis). There have been numerous clinical trials using Reovirus injected intravenously or within tumors to test its ability to eradicate cancer. While colon cancer cells are known to be very sensitive to Reovirus oncolysis, most surprisingly the oral administration route of oncolytic Reovirus has never been investigated. We propose that ingesting Reoviruses can be used as a treatment or preventive measure for colorectal cancer. Furthermore, we will modify the virus to expose colon cancer antigens to improve its potential to stimulate the immune system to eradicate the cancer cells. We will also the potential to of Reoviruses to be used as a diagnostic tool by measuring the levels of Reoviruses in feces in models of advanced colon cancer.

column36: Investigating the role of ShcD signaling in metastatic breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer worldwide and it is responsible for more female deaths than any other cancer. It is a heterogeneous disease, so tumours can have different molecular features and clinical behaviours. Highly metastatic tumours, such as those of the triple-negative subtype, are associated with the worst prognoses. There are limited treatment options for triple negative tumours as they lack the cell surface receptors that are recognized by current therapies, thus there is intense interest in identifying new molecular targets to assess and treat disease. We are studying the ShcD adaptor protein, which functions as a relay within the cell to transmit signals for growth, movement and invasion. We have found increased levels of ShcD in human triple-negative breast cancer, and our preliminary data shows that overexpression of ShcD can promote breast cancer cell invasion and activate signalling pathways that allow tumour cells to migrate, invade and form metastases. This project will investigate how altered ShcD signalling promotes breast tumorigenesis. Our overall goal is to determine whether ShcD could serve as a prognostic indicator and/or target of metastatic disease, and ultimately provide a more precise therapeutic entry point.

column36: Understanding the role of adipose tissue and fat cells in cancer virotherapy resistance
column37: I. BACKGROUND. Increasing global incidence of obesity has highlighted the role of fat cells in cancer progression. Obese breast and ovarian cancer patients exhibit more aggressive tumors and disease progression is markedly faster. In breast cancer, fat cells are the most abundant and active component of the breast tumour microenvironment (TME). Recently, numerous studies have shown that adipocytes and their progenitor cells promote breast cancer aggressiveness by stimulating proliferation and invasion. Ovarian cancers are largely detected in advanced stages when the tumour has already preferentially metastasized to the omentum, a major site of abdominal fat. Adipocytes are well known for maintaining tissue architecture, providing a source of energy, and participating in endocrine processes; however their involvement in cancer development, progression, metastasis, and response to therapy is just beginning to unfold. Moreover, the effect of fat cells on cancer cell responses to therapeutic treatment remains poorly explored. Recent reports indicate that human adipose tissue may contribute to resistance of cancer cells to various chemotherapeutic and anti-angiogenic drugs. These studies provide accumulating evidence for the activation of survival mechanisms in tumor cells due to crosstalk with surrounding adipose tissue and it is conceivable that such TME also modulates the effects of other anti-cancer therapeutics like immunotherapies. Oncolytic viro-immunotherapy (OV) has emerged as a novel therapeutic for the treatment of cancer. Our laboratory is currently investigating how the TME, which contains a diverse population of cells including cancer-associated fibroblasts, cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs), vascular endothelial cells, immune cells and the extracellular matrix that binds them together, impact virus-based immunotherapies. The project proposed herein builds upon preliminary studies performed in our laboratory that have evaluated the efficacy of OV therapy in breast cancer tumour models where the tumour is grown subcutaneously or in the fat-pad of high-fat diet-induced obesity or normal diet mice. This work showed that tumours developed in "fatty" environments are significantly less sensitive and responsive to virotherapy. In vitro, ovarian or breast cancer cell culture in adipocyte conditioned media led to a decrease in virus replication and OV-induced cell death in a panel of diverse OV platforms. The overarching goal of this project is to unveil and dissect how the interplay of cancer-associated adipocytes and cancer cells influence OV responses in the tumour niche. II. RATIONALE: We propose that CAAs not only modulate tumour development, progression, metastasis, but also induce resistance to virus-based anti-cancer therapies in tumours enriched in fat cells, such as breast and ovarian cancers. Adipocyte-released bioactive molecules (i.e. lipids) can confer OV-resistance. We will test this model by addressing two aims: AIM 1. Characterize the nature of the crosstalk between CAAs and cancer cells that inhibits virotherapy. AIM 2. Determine the role of CAA on OV resistance in-vivo. Orthotopic syngeneic breast and ovarian cancer mouse models will be used to evaluate the role of adipocytes and their secreted products in virotherapy resistance. III. RELEVANCE: Understanding and harnessing the crosstalk between cancer cells in CAAs would allow the optimization of the next generation of OV therapy for tumous grown in "fatty" microenvironments.

column36: Unlocking new options for patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
column37: Lung cancer is the greatest cause of cancer related death. Yet funding for lung cancer remains poor. While treatment for primary lung cancer can be intermittently effective, the vast majority of patients recur which ultimately leads to lung cancer related death. Immunotherapy has shown great promise with improved outcomes and prolonged survival in a wide variety of cancers, including lung cancer. However, approximately 60% of lung cancer patients treated with immunotherapy will fail to respond and an even larger proportion will fail to respond to chemotherapy. Therefore, this research proposal is aimed at improving these outcomes to reduce the incidence of recurrence in lung cancer patients. We have identified a new therapeutic target for squamous cell lung cancer, a type of lung cancer that affects nearly a quarter of all lung cancers. This target is currently being tested in clinical trials for breast cancer, therefore, this research proposal sets the stage for early translation to clinical trial implementation for squamous cell lung cancer. If successful, this proposal would offer the first available molecular precision medicine therapy for patients with squamous cell lung cancer, which could dramatically improve overall outcomes for these patients as well as reduce toxicity-related to treatment. Indeed, to date, unlike in adenocarcinoma, the other major type of lung cancer that accounts for 30% of all lung cancers, squamous cell carcinoma has no targeted therapies.

column36: Investigating the role of the immunoproteasome in the efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy against breast cancer
column37: Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are viruses that specifically kill cancer cells while leaving normal tissues unharmed. Our recent research has focused on breast cancer: we developed several OV-therapies that greatly improved outcomes and were able to uncover the crucial role of anti-tumor immunity induced by OV-therapy, but the mechanisms by which OVs trigger cancer-specific immunity remain to be fully understood. The recognition and elimination of cancer cells by T cells require the presentation of tumor antigens at the cell surface. The first step of this process is the generation of antigenic peptides, a process that requires the optimal function of the immunoproteasome (ImP): a modified form of the proteasome for which 3 alternative subunits are incorporated. The processing of proteins by the ImP generates peptides that have higher affinity for MHC molecules compared to the ones produced by the constitutive proteasome. The ImP-generated peptides are therefore optimal for antigen presentation. The ImP is induced by pro-inflammatory stimuli such as interferons, which are produced in substantial amounts in response to OVs such as the Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), our model OV for this study. We therefore hypothesize that the mechanism by which OVs like VSV trigger anti-tumor immunity is by inducing the ImP and modifying the peptidic repertoire of infected cancer cells. Focusing on breast cancer, our specific objectives are to: 1) Measure ImP levels and function in breast cancer cells in response to VSV infection 2) Determine the importance of the ImP for the efficacy of oncolytic VSV using murine breast cancer models 3) Characterize the peptide repertoire of VSV-infected vs non-infected breast cancer cells Scientific approach: The E0771, 4T1 and EMT6 murine breast cancer cells lines will be used for both in vitro and in vivo studies. We have extensive experience using these tumor models. ImP-/- variants of the cell lines will be generated using the CRISPR-Cas9 system. The MCF7, T-47D, MDA-MB-231, BT-549, ZR-75 and Hs 578T human breast cancer cell lines will be used in key in vitro validation experiments to confirm the relevance of our findings to the human disease. The constitutive proteasome and ImP expression from infected and non-infected tumor lysates will be quantified by western blot analysis. The incorporation of the different ImP subunits into the proteasome (assembly of the ImP) and ImP function will be measured after proteasome isolation followed by western blot analysis. In addition, commercially available colorimetric assays will be used to characterize the cleavage activity of the isolated proteasomes (chymotryspine-like, caspase-like and trypsine-like cleavage). Finally, the peptide repertoires with and without VSV treatment will be compared by mass spectrometry. For immune response analysis, spleens, blood and lymph nodes will be collected at different time points for IFN-gamma ELISPOT assays and flow cytometry analysis. For efficacy studies, tumor growth and Kaplan-Meier survival curves will be generated. Expected outcome: Overall, this proposal will not only elucidate a mechanism by which VSV induces anti-tumor immunity, but it will also point to improvements in this treatment platform. The understanding of the role of the ImP for OV-therapy and the generation of new improved OV variants could provide a new therapy and dramatically improve the long-term protection breast cancer patients.

column36: Rab32 Promotes Autophagic Elimination of a Metabolism Control Center in Breast Cancer
column37: The investigation of tumor tissue weaknesses over the past 20 years has identified their energy and biomass production as a characteristic. During the transformation of normal into cancer tissue, the cells change their metabolic properties drastically. They first interweave sugar and oxygen consumption reactions to increase the production of cellular building blocks and when a tumor reaches critical mass, they are able to completely eliminate oxygen consumption, while still allowing growth. Our research aims to understand the mechanisms that change these key properties of cancer cells. We have identified the protein Rab32 behind such changes. Rab32 is specifically induced in aggressive breast cancer cells. Patients with high levels of this protein have a poor prognosis. We have scanned all known biological pathways controlled by Rab32 and have identified a mechanism called autophagy that cooperates with Rab32 to decrease patient survival. The autophagy type triggered by Rab32 specifically alters how cells use sugar and oxygen. Therefore, we postulate that Rab32 is a protein that gives cancer cells the ability to switch their metabolism. With the present proposal we will investigate how Rab32 achieves this goal. The information generated by our research will be used in the future to attack metabolic changes of tumor tissue therapeutically.

column36: Exploring the role and therapeutic potential of hypoxia-driven AKAP12 expression in glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumour with an expected survival of 15 months despite treatments. While traditional GBM models have considered tumours to be a uniform mass of cancer cells, current research suggests that GBM show significant region-to-region biological differences that contribute to cancer growth and therapy resistance. For example, areas of low oxygen promote increased tumour aggressiveness and infiltration into surrounding brain tissue. Our work aims to investigate the role of AKAP12, a protein enriched in areas of low oxygen, in GBM aggressiveness and infiltration. First, we will use innovations in artificial intelligence to map AKAP12 distribution across different GBM subtypes and following treatment. Then, using a gene editing tool known as the CRISPR, we will interfere with AKAP12 expression in GBM cells to study the effects on aggressiveness and infiltration. We will grow AKAP12-deficient GBM cells in various oxygen levels to evaluate their ability to grow. We will also introduce these cells into three-dimensional artificial brain tissue we engineer in the lab to define the role of AKAP12 in GBM infiltration. Lastly, in combination with these models, we will use a technology known as mass spectrometry, which surveys global changes in protein expression patterns, to determine pathways activated by AKAP12. Together, this study looks to improve our understanding of AKAP12 in GBM biology to develop new therapies to overcome previous limitations.

column36: Tracing the Origin of Kidney Cancer from Renal Stem Cells, Understanding Tumour Pathogenesis for Effective Cancer Prevention
column37: Background: Renal cell carcinomas (RCC) are tumours that arise from the renal tubules. Due the nature of the disease it is often discovered late and about 1/4th of the cases have a very poor prognosis. Yearly 7500 Canadians will be diagnosed with kidney cancer, and 1950 Canadians would die of the disease. Hence, it is essential to manage early, localized, renal cancer before it progresses into late or metastatic stages. Early renal cancer disease is identified clinically as pathological stage pT1a < 4cm in size and designated as "small renal masses", SRM. On the other hand, many SRMs remain indolent for years and don't progress. The current available treatment modalities of renal cancer can all be associated with co-morbidities such as surgical complications and an increased risk of chronic kidney disease. A more conservative active surveillance approach would be ideal for these indolent masses and particularly for patients that are at risk for treatment complications. Thus, it is important to identify the early lesions that have the potential to progress to aggressive disease, from the more indolent lesions, and selectively treat them with definitive modalities. Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) have an increased risk of developing RCCs that tends to be also bilateral and multifocal. A field effect in ESRD that promote tumour development has been proposed. In our previous work on RCC we investigated a possible progenitor/regenerative cell population in the renal tubular epithelial cells that is increased upon kidney injury and was found to be biologically similar to RCC subtypes. Consequently, ESRD and established renal cancer precursor lesions can be assessed in the time-line progression of renal cancer to establish the mechanism of disease evolution. This proposal attempts to discover biomarkers that can aid in the clinical management decisions of early renal cancer disease, through studying the stepwise tumour's progression from precancer lesions. Hypothesis: Understanding the stepwise pathogenesis of renal cell carcinoma would allow for the detection of biomarkers that can be tested in early renal cancer disease to predict its progression Aims: 1. To investigate the progression in time of molecular events that lead to the development of renal cell carcinoma as in our proposed model of tumour progression Normal kidney to end stage renal disease kidneys (with enriched precancer cells) to precursor cancer lesions to renal cell carcinoma lesions The different disease stages will be assessed with comprehensive molecular platforms to generate a disease evolution map and to identify key molecular events that cause the transition to each of the subsequent disease stages 2. To identify prognostic biomarkers that can be tested for in small renal masses to predict the potential of renal cell carcinoma progression Significant molecular markers that are identified as part of the disease progression from early lesions will be validated in an in silico renal cancer cohorts using univariate and multivariate survival analysis. The purpose is to identify biomarkers that can predict renal cancer progression Expected outcome and Significance: The aim of this proposal is to understand early events that lead to renal cell carcinoma development and detect biomarkers of early disease progression. The findings would translate to prediction of early tumour behaviour and guide the management strategies of early renal cancer disease for better patient care.

column36: Role of ARF1 as a key GTPAse regulating immune surveillance in breast cancer
column37: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer with an overall poor clinical outcome. Reports have demonstrated that the unique microenvironment in which tumor cells grow (suppressive immune cells, altered extracellular matrix and soluble mitogenic factors) contributes to further promote cancer progression. In our effort to identify key molecular switch that control progression of TNBC, we have uncovered that the small G protein ARF1 (ADP-ribosylation factor) is overexpressed and act as a key regulator of the signaling cascades that control cell migration, invasion and proliferation. When ARF1 is knocked down, the ability of triple-negative tumor cells to proliferate and form metastasis in animal models is markedly impaired. Our most recent findings supporting this project grant suggest that ARF1 regulates the ability of TNBC cells to release factors such as pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6, but also expression of immune checkpoint ligands such as PD-L1, to control immune cell infiltration and ultimately immune bypass. Together, these results suggest that ARF may be a key protein, expressed in TNBC cells, that not only contribute to tumorigenesis and metastasis by regulating alterations of signaling cascades regulating key physiological features of tumor cells, but other factors that are known to control the nature of the unique microenvironment that support tumor cells growth and cancer progression. HYPOTHESIS & AIMS Our main hypothesis is that high ARF1 expression confers tumor cells advantages by modulating the signals they send to the immune system to escape surveillance. We therefore propose: 1) Define the role of ARF1 on the secretion of cytokines associated with the modulation of the immune response and the expression of checkpoint molecule ligands important for immune bypass. We will assess whether modulation of ARF1 expression or activity affect secretion of IL-6 and other cytokines, by TNBC cells, known to regulate tumor growth. We will also define the underlying molecular mechanisms by examining signaling events and activation of transcription factors. We will determine whether ARF1 expression or activation control transcription of the PD-L1 gene (cd274) in TNBC cells, and test if this GTPase can act to control stability of PD-L1 protein knowing that post-translational modifications are important for function. 2) Define the role of ARF1 in the recruitment of tumor growth promoting immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. We will use in vitro assays (cell culture and co-culture) and pre-clinical animal models (syngeneic and humanized) to examine the role high ARF1 expression plays on the ability of TNBC cells to regulate the recruitment of Tumor Infiltrating Macrophages and lymphocytes. The sygeneic murine model will provide key information regarding the context of an intact immune system, while the human TNBC cells transplanted in humanized mice will allow extrapolating our findings to the clinical context of breast cancer progression in patients. Insights gained from the proposed research project will greatly contribute to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of ARF1, on the immune system, to promote tumor growth and cancer progression. Because current TNBC therapies are only partially effective, we must continue to search for new molecular targets in order to improve current immunotherapies or find new one so we can optimize treatment strategies for TNBC patients. All our work suggest that ARF1 is a potential new pharmacological target because of its central role in invasive breast tumor progression.

column36: Single-cell analysis of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in pancreatic cancer
column37: Pancreatic cancer is a highly lethal disease with a dismal 5-year survival of 9%. Major limitations to improving the prognosis of pancreatic cancer have been the lack of its early diagnosis and efficient treatment options. Overcoming these limitations requires us to first gain precise and in-depth knowledge of pancreatic cancer, such as its establishment, invasiveness through metastasis and drug resistance. Facilitating tumor progression and metastasis is a process in which individual cells of primary tumor loose epithelial but acquire mesenchymal properties, referred to as "epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)". The EMT process involves mosaic of cell states including the 'stem-like' state often associated with drug resistance and cancer recurrence. Yet, most of our current understanding of the EMT comes from bulk population measurements, which mask individual cell beahavior, thus undermining both the resolution and precision of our knowledge. In this project, we propose to address this by systematically studying the pancreatic cancer EMT at single-cell resolution. To this end, we will use an interdisciplinary approach by combining quantitative single-cell measurements, computational biology, biochemistry and cancer cell biology. Our single-cell study of EMT cell states, and their cell signalling and genome-wide gene-expression patterns will provide precise and deeper mechanistic understanding of pancreatic cancer, and will reveal novel biomarkers for its diagnosis.

column36: Leveraging community-based surveillance data to explore the development of tailored and evidence-based syphilis prevention strategies for 2SGBTQ people living in syphilis hotspots
column37: An estimated 85% of syphilis cases occur among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (including trans, queer, non-binary, and Two-Spirit peoples; 2SGBTQ). Within this population, only a small proportion have ever acquired syphilis. Further analyses suggest that syphilis risk is driven by individuals with larger sexual networks. Consequently, syphilis infections among 2SGBTQ people are clustered in large urban centres across Canada, within so-called geographic "hotspots." It is apparent that the education and uptake of syphilis prevention strategies have not been sufficient to eradicate syphilis. The aim of this catalyst grant proposal is to leverage community-based surveillance data to explore the development of tailored and evidence-based syphilis prevention strategies within hotspot neighbourhoods across Canada. To accomplish this aim, we will (1) Identify syphilis hotspots by calculating syphilis infection rates using community-based survey data and validating the identified hotspots using public health surveillance data, (2) Identify and compare the prevalence of the risk management practices associated with the greatest reduction in syphilis risk for 2SGBTQ people within hotspot and non-hotspot regions; and (3) Assess the acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness of under-utilized community and public health risk management strategies that could reduce syphilis risk within hotspot and non-hotspot regions. To accomplish these aims, we will use serial cross-sectional data from the 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2022 Sex Now Survey, Canada's largest and longest running enhanced surveillance study of 2SGBTQ. Sex Now employs a community-based design, recruits large samples of 2SGBTQ in each cycle, and collects survey data and biological specimens (e.g., dried blood spots). Survey data includes a wide variety of behavioural, social, and structural variables that play an important role in syphilis transmission.

column36: Cellular Systems Design
column37: Many physiological traits and disease states are caused by genetic determinants that act as modifiers. Whole genome sequencing projects have revealed the prevalence of sequence variants and copy number variants in human population. However, knowledge about how such variants interact to generate phenotypic outcomes is lacking. Since multiple modifiers often act to modulate phenotypic variation in natural populations and impact disease onset and progression by generating unexpected phenotypic outcomes, which cannot be predicted from those of individual mutations, it is important to study such complex genetic interactions. The overreaching goal of Dr. Kuzmin's CRC program is to investigate how multiple modifiers act to modulate phenotypic variation in natural populations and impact disease onset and progression by interrogating complex genetic interaction networks. Her vision is to build a unified, translational approach for studying complex genetic interactions in yeast and human cells. To reach this goal, her research in the next 5 years will address the following central questions in complex genetic interaction networks (a) what is the extent of genetic interaction network rewiring between distantly related yeast species, such as fission yeast, S. pombe, and budding yeast, S. cerevisiae, (b) what are complex genetic interaction network dynamics of duplicated genes in response to environmental changes, (c) what are the genetic vulnerabilities of cancer-associated large chromosomal aberrations and (d) what is the genetic interaction wiring diagram of genes residing within large chromosomal aberrations and the genetic network connecting these aberrations thereby providing valuable knowledge for understanding genetic events that modulate tumorigenesis. Dr. Kuzmin's research program utilizes an integrative approach combining systematic genetic screens using trigenic Synthetic Genetic Array in yeast and CRISPR-Cas9 in cell and organoid models of TNBC. Dr. Kuzmin's research program aims to provide insight into complex genetic interaction network conservation, dynamics in response to environmental changes, and their therapeutic potential in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) with an ultimate goal to improve our understanding of the genotype-to-phenotype relationship and improve outcomes for TNBC patients.

column37: Dr. Ayeni has dedicated his research career to advancing the field of evidence-based joint preservation by establishing a research program that evaluates both pragmatic and cutting-edge interventions. The main objective of Dr. Ayeni's research program is to advance joint preservation care across the human lifespan, including protection and prevention of joint injuries in childhood and adolescence; minimally invasive treatments to curb the development of joint disease in the young adult; and new treatments for older patients with cartilage defects and early onset osteoarthritis to significantly delay or even avoid total joint replacement. column36: Translational Immuno-Cardiology
column37: Heart disease is among the leading causes of death worldwide. In Canada, 2.4 million currently live with this condition and every minute 12 Canadians die as a result of this disease. As the disease progresses it often leads to a heart attack that can contribute to sudden death. For patients that able to survive this event, they are left with a damaged heart that over time will fail, preventing many from living a normal life. Roughly 700 thousand Canadians currently live with a failing heart and this number is continually growing with 50 thousand new cases every year. In many cases, a heart transplant becomes one of the only treatment options. Alternatively, what if we could stop the heart from failing in the first place? There is growing attention to understanding how the body tries to repair the heart after the initial damage caused by a heart attack and how this process may influence how the heart fails and the speed with which this happens. Our objective is to determine how specific components of the immune system contribute to the healing process after a heart attack. We will utilize high powered microscopes to track how specific cells from the blood or that live in the cavity surrounding the heart can be attracted to the heart after a heart attack and visualize which cells they talk and play with in that local environment. Our ability to directly visualize cells of the immune system in a beating heart makes us one of four groups in the world, and the only one in Canada to use this type of tool. To test how specific immune cells affect the ability of the heart to pump blood to the rest of the body after a heart attack we will use two approaches 1) we will selectively block certain cells from getting to the heart after injury, 2) we will block the molecules specific cells make to influence their local environment. Understanding how specific immune cells behave following a heart attack will generate new information about repair in the heart. Regardless of whether these components are beneficial or harmful to the healing process, knowing their roles in or around the heart can provide new treatments to try preventing the damaged heart from eventually failing. Considering that 1 in 12 Canadians live with heart disease, this can have an enormous impact on increasing survival and maintaining a better quality of life for patients that have suffered a heart attack.
