column36: Public Health `Omics for Heart and Lung Health
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a systemic disease. CVD events such as myocardial infarction (MI) dysregulate numerous systemic regulatory networks, including inflammation and immunity. While such dysregulation increases subsequent CVD risk, many MI patients also present with, or subsequently develop, other diseases (comorbidities), and numbers are increasing. This is a major public health concern as emerging evidence suggests that cross-disease communication can occur, resulting in worse outcomes for patients. Thus, MI poses risk to not only CVD-specific, but also non-CVD-specific morbidity and mortality. Insights into the mechanisms that mediate cross-disease communication, as well as therapeutic interventions to improve multi-disease outcomes in CVD remain largely unexplored. Dr. Koelwyn's research has begun to define the mechanisms that enable cross-disease communication between CVD and its comorbidities, including cancer and infection, as well as how exercise may be a viable therapeutic strategy to mitigate such deleterious interactions. The primary objective of his proposed research program is to apply a translational, 'omics-based approach to specifically define how MI induces, and exercise protects from, inflammatory and immune dysregulation, which impact CVD patients' comorbidity risk and progression. His overarching hypothesis is that exercise enhances innate immune responses and attenuates MI-induced innate immune dysfunction, leading to improved outcomes to concurrent (e.g. cancer) and subsequent (e.g. infection) comorbidities. It is expected that this research will bring foundational insights into the mediators of cross-disease communication in the setting of CVD. Such findings will inform clinical validation studies of identified MI- and exercise-induced factors and/or phenotypes that can be used for discovering biomarkers, identifying high-risk patients, and unveiling new therapeutic targets. Further, defining the biological plausibility of exercise to improve multi-disease outcomes in CVD will provide valuable insights for future studies to inform public health strategies (e.g. relevant health guidelines) and patient-oriented (e.g. cardiac rehabilitation) approaches.

Developing a culturally relevant framework that will guide academic and community researchers in the gathering of baseline data within individual Indigenous communities is a major objective of the proposed CRC. Stream 2: Share stories of Indigenous environmental health governance . Dr. Lewis and her research team will develop a process to adapt the cultural framework developed for PLFN to be flexible enough to reflect the Creation Story and Indigenous worldview in the local context of individual communities. Stream 3: Build a cadre of practitioners in Indigenous environmental health governance. Dr. Lewis will develop a cadre of trainees in quantitative skills to analyze data using statistical analysis software such as Stata/SE 16.0, qualitative skills using qualitative software such as NVivo 1.0, and Indigenous methodologies/methods using, for example, land-based learning techniques or talking circles. Stream 4: Implement Indigenous environmental health governance in policy. Indigenous environmental health governance - What does this mean in practice? This research program is intended to make a meaningful contribution to the assertion of Indigenous sovereignty over the health of Indigenous community members and their lands and environment, by providing communities with the data that is required to make informed decisions, by mobilizing their knowledge in meaningful ways, and by working together to influence policy in environment and health.

column36: Viral Pandemics
column37: Despite a substantial increase in the frequency of major viral epidemics/pandemics during the 21st century, the global response to these outbreaks has remained largely reactive. However, as we have learned during the 2009 H1N1 "Swine Flu" pandemic, and the current COVID-19 pandemic, our ability to respond when an outbreak emerges is greatly outpaced by the rate of which viral pathogens can spread globally. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop proactive solutions capable of protecting the global population from potentially high-consequence viral pathogens before they emerge. The research program supported by this CRC in Viral Pandemics will advance the development of broadly-protective vaccines and antivirals against influenza viruses and coronaviruses, two viral families that will continue to pose significant pandemic risk. This program will build off of cutting-edge strategies that have led to the development of vaccine platforms and approaches that maximize breadth of protection by focusing immune responses on conserved antigenic epitopes and mechanisms of immunological protection that favor broad and durable responses. Significant focus will also be given to the design of excipient formulations that facilitate equitable distribution of these vaccines to remote and underserviced communities in Canada and worldwide. In parallel, the program will exploit state-of-the-art genomic/chemogenomic techniques to identify drugs and druggable pathways capable of providing broad and efficacious protection. Special consideration will be given to ensure that drug candidates can be feasibly administered in settings that maximize therapeutic benefit. Combinatorial drug strategies designed to reduce the emergence of antiviral resistance will also be prioritized. Altogether, this program will generate and apply innovative strategies to advance the development of preventative measures needed to protect the Canadian and global populations from future viral pandemics.

column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI), Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have an extremely high occurrence and a dizzying array of associated biological changes that arguably make them the most important cause of neurodegeneration and impairment requiring rehabilitation. Sleep disorders (SD) often occur in conjunction with TBI and ADRD and have long been connected to adverse cognitive outcomes. The predisposition to these adverse outcomes depends on age, concomitant disorders (i.e., comorbidities), and a variety of social equity parameters including gender, which makes it difficult to treat these diseases. Dr. Tatyana Mollayeva's Canada Research Chair (CRC) program aims to address this challenge by focusing on how SD and TBI, among other factors, affect newly developed dementia, cognitive rehabilitation and disability. Her research will use various analytical methods, including data mining, to capture the risk and protective factors that interact across an individual's lifespan to impact functional outcomes for these diseases. The relationships uncovered through this research will be used to develop gender-transformative frameworks to prevent and treat sleep disorders, traumatic brain injury, and dementia

column36: Cell Therapies for Diabetes
column37: Dr. Pepper's research pursues innovative strategies to manage and treat type 1 diabetes. These new strategies may also be applied in the future to preventing type 1 diabetes and to shifting people with type 1 diabetes into disease reversal. His research program can shed light on the factors controlling cells that are key to diabetes. His results will improve quality of life for people with diabetes, eliminate the need for insulin injections, reduce diabetes complications, and lessen the economic strain on Canada's health care system. More than 3 million Canadians live with diabetes. Each year, it costs our health care system more than $17 billion. Since insulin was discovered in Canada a century ago, it has been the go-to treatment for people with type 1 diabetes. Insulin sustains life for these people, but insulin injections cannot accurately mimic the natural control of blood glucose by islet cells of the pancreas. We can now replace islet cells and restore glucose control with islet transplantation, but this option is currently useful only for a small number of people with type 1 diabetes. In his research, Dr. Pepper is mapping how help islet cells best survive and function after they are transplanted into people with type 1 diabetes. For example, what are the elements that islets need to survive when they are transplanted outside the pancreas? Where can we transplant islet cells in the body to prevent the immune system from rejecting them? How can we minimize the need for anti-rejection drugs? By leveraging his expertise in islet biology and transplantation, Dr. Pepper has already developed a new and effective way to place islets under the skin and shield them from the body's immune system. Dr. Pepper's research program is also examining why islet cells die after transplant, which causes disease recurrence. What molecular pathways are part of this cell death, and can we target those pathways with potential new drugs? Preventing islet cell death may lead to the development of therapies that preserve transplant function indefinitely. The third strand of his research is to identify and apply new sources of islet cells for transplants. These alternative sources, such as animal cells or stem cells, could reduce or eliminate the need for scarce human donors. Together, these new options from Dr. Pepper's research have great potential for extending the benefits of islet transplants to many more people with type 1 diabetes.

column36: Global Health Intervention Justice
column37: The field of global health faces a critical challenge. Interventions that test therapeutic prevention technologies promise solutions to some of the world's most pressing health challenges (e.g., HIV, COVID-19). However, global health research to develop and test these interventions, as well as their roll-out and introduction into health systems, can produce and exacerbate inequity and injustice experienced by the marginalized communities they target, in both resource-limited and resource-rich countries. This fuels lack of trust in intervention science and contributes to treatment hesitancy, often among those who could most benefit from these interventions. Addressing the 2020 World Health Organization's urgent health challenge of `Earning public trust,' Dr. Perez-Brumer's unique CRC in Global Health Intervention Justice will build on her existing international and national research through the systematic and multilevel analysis of the way global infectious disease prevention interventions and clinical trials are executed and their impact on marginalized communities. Dr. Perez-Brumer's focus on justice offers a novel framework through which to advance equity and trustworthiness within clinical trial designs. This justice-driven framework builds on approaches championed by bioethics by recognizing that global health research stakeholders are nested within systems that produce and reproduce harms. Further, this program of research, located at the intersection of critical global health and implementation science, actively intercedes on how health research is conducted and promotes trustworthiness by advancing novel data-driven tools to promote more equitable design, adaptation, and evaluation of interventions targeting marginalized communities. This will be achieved through three interrelated aims: (1) Identify multi-level sociopolitical and technical factors that undermine equity and justice in how global prevention interventions are designed and implemented; (2) advance methods and policy to promote trustworthiness in global intervention design, practice, monitoring, and scale-up; and (3) create a global network to support justice-driven global health practice. This timely and groundbreaking research delves into the conceptual and methodological aspects of justice that have been underexplored and is critical to fostering public trust in global health interventions.

column36: Glial Neuroimmunology
column37: Dr. Plemel studies how the immune system develops and functions in the brain and spinal cord (our central nervous system). This central nervous system is protected from the actions of our body's immune system in the other parts of our body. It has its own immune cells called microglia, which are the key initiators of any immune process in the brain. Dr. Plemel studies these remarkable cells. Microglia constantly survey their local surroundings looking for signs of damage, dysfunction, or subtle changes in the activity of other nerve cells. Microglia are the brain's "canary in the coal mine." Researchers can use microglia to understand dysfunction in the brain, because they can observe how microglia respond to damage and disease. Microglia are part of a larger family of cells in the central nervous system, called glia. Glia are named after glue, because they were thought to hold brain structures together. We now know that glia are diverse and vitally important to the health and wellness of the central nervous system. When injury or disease damages the central nervous system, microglia and other glial cells respond to protect the brain, restore normal function, and even promote repair of the damage. However, in some situations, the immune response in the brain can damage healthy cells that are close to the site of damage. Dr. Plemel's goal is to find ways to direct the immune response in the central nervous system to maximize repair and minimize further damage. As Canada Research Chair in Glial Neuroimmunology, Dr. Plemel will lead research on how glial cells-particularly microglia-develop and behave in diseases like multiple sclerosis. In multiple sclerosis, our immune system attacks the central nervous system. The role of microglia in multiple sclerosis is confusing because microglia can help to damage the brain tissue, but they are also needed to repair that damage. Dr. Plemel's research is untangling these complex roles of microglia in multiple sclerosis. First, he will identify how microglia change and respond during the different stages of multiple sclerosis. His goal is to find new ways to promote a more favourable response of microglia for brain health. Because microglia are a critical part of how the central nervous system stays healthy, Dr. Plemel's research could also help people with other diseases of the central nervous system.

column36: Indigenous Health Systems Safety
column37: There is irrefutable evidence that Indigenous people living in Canada experience racism in the healthcare system associated with direct impacts to health outcomes, including brain health and dementia. The need for health care services and models of care designed and determined by Indigenous people is outlined in the Truth and Reconciliation of Canada's final report and aligns with refined definitions of person-centred and relationship-centred dementia care provision. This research program integrates anti-racist and decolonial approaches to develop culturally congruent dementia services and improve health systems safety for Indigenous people. Objective 1 (systems) is to co-create Indigenous measures of dementia healthcare quality. Participatory social justice research methods grounded in Indigenous ethics will be used to design, implement, and evaluate new patient experience measures with Indigenous people and families navigating the healthcare system. Objective 2 (services) is to co-design culturally safe family-centered treatments for Indigenous dementia care. Through use of sequential focus groups and modified nominal group techniques with Indigenous communities and Elders we will design content and mechanisms of new culturally congruent dementia care interventions for families and communities. Objective 3 (individuals) is to develop performance indicators for the measurement and monitoring of Indigenous health and antiracism medical education in order to improve health systems safety. Using systems-mapping exercises, consensus-based approaches and qualitative research methods a model of longitudinal Indigenous health medical education and a knowledge base of measurable indicators will be developed by which to internally and externally measure medical school performance in the domains of Indigenous health and anti-racism education. Large-scale systemic action is needed to create accountability structures to improve equitable, safe, and anti-racist educational and health care systems and services. Transformative Indigenous medical education that is closely linked to community needs and health care service provision to enhance social accountability is critical to improving population-level Indigenous health outcomes. This research program addresses systemic barriers to improving population level brain health and dementia care for Indigenous people by targeting research at the health systems, services, and individual levels.

column36: Implementing Digital Health Innovation
column37: It is widely recognized that digital health (or eHealth) technologies hold significant potential to transform and revolutionize the delivery of health care. While digital transformation in Canada has been relatively slow, rapid shifts in health and social care service delivery in response to COVID-19 has resulted in an unprecedented surge in the adoption of digital health tools globally. While promising, these innovations are often difficult to develop and scale, and adoption of these technologies can have wide ranging implications for the nature and structure of care delivery to individuals and populations. These challenges require a deeper understanding of the implementation of these technologies to understand what technologies work for whom under which circumstances. The Canada Research Chair in Implementing Digital Health Innovation will address this challenge, through the generation of high-quality evidence regarding the impact of these novel technologies and the factors that drive their adoption. To achieve this core objective, three streams of work will be pursued to: 1) produce a better understanding of factors that influence technology implementation; 2) create tools and frameworks to inform implementation; and 3) advance innovative research methods needed to study these complex systems. An implementation science lens will be applied to the three streams of work, adopting multiple methods to answer research questions, including co-design, pragmatic trials, qualitative ethnography, and comparative case study designs. Through the application of relevant social science and critical theory, findings build on and challenge existing knowledge regarding the implementation of digital health tools and the methods we use to study them. Developments in the three research streams will inform each other over time and provides a rich environment for development of trainees and highly qualified personnel. Trainees will be given the opportunity to advance objectives and develop new lines of inquiry within and across streams. This program of work applies an integrated Knowledge Translation approach (iKT), in which all projects partner with knowledge users (including patients and communities) and system leaders, to ensure the outputs provide high value knowledge and tools that address pressing health system challenges. An iKT approach additionally supports the scale and spread of promising findings.

column36: Cardio-Oncology and Molecular Medicine
column37: Chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity (CIC) is an emerging clinical problem, whereby commonly used cancer therapies cause heart failure. This generally results in early termination of cancer therapies, despite responsive tumors to chemotherapeutics. Unfortunately, while an increasing number of patients survive cancer, they end up dying from heart failure. Currently, there are no therapies to prevent or limit CIC. In addition, there no biomarkers that predict which cancer patients are susceptible to CIC. Dr. Sutendra's research program aims to, a) discover novel mechanisms and therapeutic targets that would prevent CIC, but enhance chemotherapy-mediated tumor regression and, b) identify novel serum biomarkers that would predict which cancer patients will be susceptible to heart failure due to their cancer therapy. The outcomes from this research (and training) program will benefit heart failure and/or cancer patients (the two most common conditions leading to death of Canadians). To do this, Dr. Sutendra will first focus on novel pathways (identified in his laboratory) that are selective to the heart (a tissue that is exposed to high levels of oxygen), compared to the tumor (a tissue that is exposed to low levels of oxygen). Dr. Sutendra has discovered that proteins that can initiate cell death that are also preferentially oxidized (tagged by oxygen) in the heart, compared to the tumor, could be a novel therapeutic approach to selectively inhibit death in the heart, but not the tumor. In fact Dr. Sutendra has shown that these proteins (i.e. tagged by oxygen) can be therapeutically targeted with drugs to inhibit CIC, but (at the same time) enhance chemotherapy-mediated tumor regression. This is important because it provides a better and "more focused" cancer therapy, but at the same time completely protects the heart from any negative effects (i.e. death) from chemotherapeutics. Secondly, Dr. Sutendra has identified specific tumor-secreted factors (TSFs) as novel biomarkers that predict CIC susceptibility. It also appears that these TSFs directly suppress a unique survival pathway in the heart (making the heart susceptible to death from chemotherapeutics), identifying additional therapeutic targets. This work is highly novel and translational with the outcomes of this research program providing new therapeutic targets (and potential biomarkers) against CIC, which are desperately needed.

column36: Translational Sarcoma Research
column37: Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are a rare, aggressive type of cancer that arise from connective tissue. New discoveries have significantly improved survival in other types of cancers but similar success has not been had in sarcoma and novel approaches are urgently needed. Nanoparticles are a new technology with enormous promise in oncology as they can be designed to target specific sites in the body and when there act as imaging and/or therapeutic agents. My research is focusing on two particular challenges negatively impacting survival in STS patients for which nanotechnology can offer unique solutions: poor survival in STS patients with lung metastases and high rates of relapse in infiltrative subtypes of STS. Even when the primary tumour is successfully treated, nearly half of patients develop metastases and are then incurable. Sarcomas are unique as most metastases occur in the lung but there is no effective treatment for this situation. One promising avenue is to focus on targeting immune cells that support cancer growth. We are examining which immune cells are present in lung metastases and contribute to disease. Next, we will use nanotechnology, in particular liposomes, to develop and test a therapy to target these cells. Ultimately, this study will improve our understanding of metastatic STS and introduce a novel approach for its treatment. Myxofibrosarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma are two kinds of STS that have higher than normal rates of local recurrence and are termed infiltrative. They are different as they often have large areas of abnormal signal (edema) surrounding the main tumour. In some patients these abnormal areas contain tumour cells but in others reflect only benign tissue swelling. There is no way of predicting which abnormal areas contain tumour cells and it is difficult for surgeons to know how much tissue to take. To address this problem, we are first investigating whether we can use genetic mutations to identify areas that contain tumour cells. We will then use these findings to design a fluorescent nanoparticle-based tool that can be used by the surgeon to ensure that all the cancer is removed. Together, we will present a new strategy to both determine and improve margin assessment in infiltrative STS. This innovative research program is unique in Canada and is poised to make a strong impact in the fields of sarcoma and nanomedicine.

column36: Critical Care Outcomes and Systems Evaluation
column37: The intensive care unit (ICU), vital to modern acute care hospitals, is a busy and complex environment, providing 24-hour monitoring and organ support for patients at-risk of or who have developed life-threatening critical illness. ICU care is also resource-intensive and expensive; and the short-term efficiency, long-term effectiveness and overall cost-benefit for much of ICU care is uncertain. There is urgent need to improve our understanding for how to best respond to evolving trends in critical illness, how best to deliver critical care, and how to optimally facilitate the timely adoption of innovations and new evidence into dailyl ICU practice. Dr. Bagshaw is Professor of Critical Care Medicine and a Clinician-Scientist in the Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry at the University of Alberta. He has led several novel, innovative and high-impact research programs. He co-led the largest international collaborative randomized clinical trial focused on acute dialysis therapies in critical illness, was first to describe the concept of frailty and its relative importance in critical illness, and has led a large program of work focused on ICU organization that has provided insights into the health systems impact of strained capacity in ICU care. His work has fostered international collaborations and has leveraged global research networks to influence and realize health systems change. Dr. Bagshaw's proposed research program aims to identify and characterize the health care inequities, evidence-to-care gaps, and health systems inefficiencies in critical care. He proposes to realize this by leveraging existing health data assets to describe and respond to the evolving changes in the epidemiology of critically ill patients (e.g., burdens, care processes, outcomes) and ICU practice. He will use these learnings to develop, test and implement innovative and pragmatic clinical trials aimed to improved patient outcomes, quality of care, and health systems efficiency. The program represents a fertile landscape for training the next generation of clinician-scientists in critical care medicine. Dr. Bagshaw proposes to vertically integrate highly qualified trainees and embed an equitable, diverse and inclusive scientific learning environment within his research program. He further proposes to embed research experience and directly engage with the stakeholders to invest in and build a learning healthcare system supported by high-quality and rigorous research.

column36: Medications and Pregnancy
column37: The thalidomide disaster has thought us that medications used during pregnancy need to be continuously studied. At present, evidence suggests that >75% of women take at least one medication during pregnancy. Yet, data on the safety and effectiveness of medications used during pregnancy is lacking due to Health Canada's and the FDA's routine exclusion of pregnant women from clinical trials because of concerns about potential harm to the developing fetus. Observational studies on large longitudinal cohorts on the risks and potential benefits of medication use during pregnancy are the only way to bridge the knowledge gap Canada and the US healthcare systems, which are mostly administered by provinces (Can) or by private insurers (US), result in the accumulation of a wealth of data representing real-life diagnoses, hospitalisations and medication use. These real world evidences (RWE) can be used for the development of policies/guidelines to increase patient wellbeing and decrease risks; they can also allow for the detection of infrequent events and long-term infrequent outcomes. Although such cohorts are essential for prescribing practice or policy making, it remains that some important variables are sometimes missing from these large RWE databases such as standardized mental health variables. Field studies with in-person recruitment are best suited in these situations, and should be complementary to RWE. Finally, given the wealth of health data collected in various forms, artificial intelligence (AI) modelling has the potential to generate global risk estimates that can be directly applicable to the clinic. The proposed Research Program of this CRC1 is based on data from the multi-provincial Canadian Mother-Child Cohort Active Surveillance Initiative (CAMCCO; 4 million mother-child pairs, 6 provinces; 20 years of follow-up; largest pregnancy cohort in World; A Berard et al.), and the US AM-PREGNANT cohort (3 million mother-child); and includes AI methodology. The Medications and Pregnancy CRC1 will gather evidence to: Axis 1: Quantify the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with gestational use of antidepressants and anti-migraines using RWE cohorts (CAMCCO, AM-PREGNANT) and AI methodology; and, Axis 2: Address the mental health impact of pandemics such as COVID-19 on pregnant women using innovative recruitment/analytical and AI strategies. This CRC1 is timely, and will be a catalyst for worldwide perinatal pharmacoepidemiology leadership.

column36: Microbe-Surface Interactions
column37: All infections start with physical contact between a pathogen and host, and thwarting these interactions can prevent disease. Disrupting microbial interactions with surfaces also reduces formation of biofilms, adherent communities of bacteria that are highly resistant to antibiotics. Biofilms are responsible for up to 65% of infections; thus, preventing biofilm formation has the potential to mitigate disease and antibiotic resistance, a serious and evolving global crisis. Burrows' fundamental research program focuses on understanding the physical and chemical cues that modulate biofilm formation. Bacteria use thin, hairlike, mechanosensory filaments called pili to gather physical information during establishment of biofilms. Pili act as attachment factors and retractable grappling hooks for rapid spread after attachment. Using the model pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burrows studies the expression and function of pili, and their interactions with bacteria-specific viruses called bacteriophages (phages) that use pili as receptors and have potential as therapeutics to kill antibiotic-resistant variants. She will a) use a novel and diverse pilin library to compare the specificity of pilin-specific antibodies (relevant to vaccine development) with pilus-specific phages isolated from environmental, clinical, and wastewater samples to assess their potential as therapeutics; and b) study the ability of diverse phages to `steer' bacteria towards reduced infectivity by selecting for phage-resistant mutants and defining the repertoire of mutations that lead to loss of piliation in response to phage pressure. These data are important to predict potential outcomes of phage therapy. Her second focus addresses chemical cues, studying how antibiotics influence biofilm formation. Her group found that exposure to low levels of antibiotics increases biofilm formation, and showed that this phenotype can be exploited in innovative screening assays for identification of new antibiotics. Objective 2 aims to a) characterize the pathways linking sub-inhibitory antibiotic exposure to corresponding increases in biofilm formation, using new genetic and microbiological tools; and b) identify and develop new antimicrobial candidates using the biofilm stimulation phenotype. The results of this research will provide novel insights into ways to manipulate biofilm development, and lead to the discovery of new and desperately-needed antimicrobial treatments for resistant infections.

column36: Stem Cell Models of Childhood Disease
column37: Dr. James Ellis is a leader in using stem cell models to discover disease mechanisms that cause childhood neurodevelopmental disorders and cardiomyopathies (CMP). Major gaps remain in our understanding of how regulation of gene and protein levels are changed in these disorders and cause disease. For example, in the neurodevelopmental disorder Rett syndrome (RTT), thousands of genes make abnormal levels of RNA, but how this affects the final protein levels that actually define whether a cell is healthy or not is poorly defined. In CMP, the importance of mutations (known as "variants") found in patients at DNA regions (called "promoters") that control RNA production by genes is unknown. Dr. Ellis is a global pioneer in reprograming patient blood or skin cells into induced pluripotent stem cells to produce the affected nerve or heart cells to study childhood genetic diseases. His research objectives are to: 1) explore the mechanisms that cause incorrect RNA and protein levels in RTT nerve cells and reduce their activity, and 2) demonstrate that variants in DNA promoters alter the RNA levels of CMP genes and compromise the activity of beating heart cells. In Objective 1, patient-derived RTT nerve cells will be used to investigate changes in RNA production and RNA stability controlled by microRNAs using a method called RATESeq. Next the importance of newly discovered micropeptides and how changes in protein modifications called ubiquitin affect protein stability will be determined, and their role in altering nerve function evaluated. The discrepancy between RNA and protein levels can only be explained by a comprehensive understanding of these processes and will uncover biological targets that point to novel potential therapies. In Objective 2, patient-derived CMP heart cells will be used to show that DNA promoter variants reduce the RNA levels of important cardiac genes when compared to control heart cells where the variant is corrected by gene editing. Effects on beating activity of the patient heart cells will be defined and used to test rescue by drugs targeted to the affected gene pathways. The discovery of DNA promoter variants in CMP will establish a functional genomics roadmap that uses stem cell models to show effects on regulation of other disease-causing genes. These findings will validate genetic screening for DNA promoter variants in CMP patients and identify affected pathways for targeted precision medicines.

column36: Multiomics of Lipids and Innate Immunity
column37: The health consequences of unwanted inflammation have been known for many years in both academic and public settings. Greater awareness of the impact of inflammation was brought to light in the early 2000s as illustrated by the 2004 TIME magazine cover story entitled "Inflammation: The Secret Killer". Inflammation is a complex human response to harmful stimuli such as pathogens and damaged tissue. It is a coordinated response involving immune cells, blood vessels, and mediators (including cytokines). Ideally, inflammation aids in the rapid clearance of pathogens and damaged tissue and is resolved to allow the tissue to return to its previous state. However, many Canadians have excess or unnecessary inflammation that significantly impacts their health. Unwanted inflammation can range from prolonged low-level inflammation as seen in inflammatory bowel disease, heart disease, or arthritis to hyper-inflammatory conditions such as "cytokine storm" seen in septic and some COVID19 patients. This program will investigate how cellular lipid metabolism and the cells of the innate immune system promote human health and how dysregulation contributes to human disease. This program will use state-of-the-art `omics platforms including proteomics, lipidomics, metabolomics, and functional genomics, together with advanced imaging techniques and machine learning to improve our understanding of the underlying pathology and to identify novel therapeutic targets. Specifically, Dr. Fairn will lead a group focused on studying the role of inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease, bacterial infections, heart disease, and cancer. Collectively these conditions cost Canadians >$50 billion/year. Thus, a better understanding of the drivers of inflammation in these cases and identifying new treatments is imperative.

column36: Applied Child Health Services and Policy
column37: Despite a universal health insurance system, Canada ranks 30th out of 38 high income countries on measures of child well being, including physical health and mental well-being. Within Canada there are important socio-economic inequities in these outcomes. While there are multiple levels of influence on child well-being, high quality and accessible primary healthcare is a major determinant. The goal of Dr. Guttmann's program of health system research is to investigate how health services and policy can reduce these inequities. Using population-based health, demographic and education data in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia and a variety of analyses, her CRC research will focus on three key areas. These include the impact of a universal developmental screening program in primary care on children's readiness for school; the role of innovative primary care models in meeting the healthcare needs of resettled refugee children and families in the context of Canada's first-in-class refugee private sponsorship model; and the long term impact of COVID-19 restrictions on important primary care outcomes for children. Building on existing partnerships with policymakers and a strong training program, this program of research will inform health care delivery for Canadian children and increase capacity for evidence-based decision-making.

column36: Genome Cell Biology and Dynamics
column37: Dr. Hendzel's research aims to understand what properties the packaging of DNA imparts to the genome of cells. 2 meters of DNA are packaged into each cell nucleus, with diameters of only a few micrometres, while maintaining the ability to read, write, and repair it. Dr. Hendzel's recent work has found that the genome forms a gel, similar to Jell-O. This gel is decorated with binding sites that attract proteins that have a particular property-they can cause the water in the cell to separate, similar to oil separating from water. This could create a microenvironment that prevents the inappropriate expression of genes. This is important because some genes, such as endogenous retrovirus sequences which mutate our genome, must be shut down. Additionally, this gel state provides the DNA with an additional unexpected function-it can be used as structural support. This may be important in tissues that undergo significant strain, such as the contracting cells of a beating heart. Dr. Hendzel will use state-of-the-art microscopes to determine if and how specialized microenvironments are assembled in the cell nucleus. In collaboration with a mathematician, who will develop molecular models to explain what we observe in living cells, they will determine how molecules move through the nucleus and how they are prevented from entering these dense gels containing unused and potentially harmful sequences. In collaboration with a polymer physicist, they will apply concepts derived from polymer chemistry to interpret the DNA polymer organization, its dynamics, and its response to cellular forces. They will accomplish this by tracking individual molecules' movements as they move through the nucleus and encounter these different environments. Tracking changes in shape as the cell applies forces to the nucleus's surface will be used to inform us on how the DNA responds to these forces. In particular, they will address whether gel formation is used to adapt to changes in the forces that the DNA experiences. Our understanding of the genome is dominated by results from experiments done outside of cells. Dr. Hendzel's research focuses on the emergent properties that arise in the concentrated and complex environment of the cell. A gel state to chromatin and the creation of local microenvironments are examples of such properties. These introduce new and potentially transformational ways of thinking about these reactions, their mechanisms, and their control.

column36: Epigenomics, reproduction and development
column37: Globally the prevalence of diabetes, obesity, infertility and other chronic diseases are on the rise. These increases have occurred at rates that cannot be due to changes to the DNA. Instead it is likely that rising rates of chronic disease are instead caused by environmental exposures such as diet and toxicants that modify can how our genes are used. The environment and other factors such as body weight can alter what is known as epigenetic information. The epigenetic layer associated with DNA is made up of heritable molecules in sperm that are transmitted at fertilization to the embryo. This information impacts how the embryo develops and the health of that child. The overarching goal of my research is to understand how environmental exposures alter the heritable epigenetic information to impact health across generations. These studies will create new knowledge that will allow for the development of intervention strategies to improve the health of men, babies and children.

column36: White matter plasticity and cognitive development
column37: In Canada, over 140,000 children and teenagers suffer a brain injury each year due to trauma, stroke, cerebral palsy, and brain cancer. Children are often left with permanent thinking and learning problems. Currently, there are no effective medical therapies to help brain recovery and reduce disability following an acquired brain injury. Dr. Mabbott hopes to change this by understanding the innate plasticity of the brain; how the brain can grow and adapt - with a focus on white matter. Our brain connections are insulated with a fatty white substance called myelin. Across the entire brain this insulation is called white matter. White matter helps in sending messages and the growth of new white matter - or white matter plasticity - is thought to be very important in brain communication. Disrupted white matter plasticity occurs in many brain disorders and can cause difficulties in thinking. Despite this problem, it is not yet known how white matter plasticity has an impact on the brain communication that produces thinking. It is important to know this because understanding these links can help us in creating and testing new treatments for brain injuries. Dr. Mabbott's work will focus on children and teenagers who survive a malignant brain tumour. These children often sustain a brain injury as a consequence of the cranial radiation therapy used to cure them and are left with devastating learning problems. Dr. Mabbott will: (a) use network neuroscience to discover whether white matter plasticity helps support thinking through fine-tuning brain communication; (b) examine whether a novel radiation modality, proton radiation, spares thinking skills compared to the current standard of treatment; and (c) conduct clinical trials focused on treatments that harness white matter plasticity for recovery of thinking skills. To accomplish these goals, he will use novel neuroimaging to measure the growth of white matter and brain activation. Standardized psychological tests will be used to study thinking skills. Dr. Mabbott's research provides a model that can be applied to other types of brain injury and disease. He has expanded the scope of his work to include other injuries to white matter, including multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy, and sickle cell disease. Dr. Mabbott's work has the potential to reduce devastating neurological morbidity and bring new hope to families dealing with the effects of brain injury in children and teenagers.

column36: Biomedical Imaging
column37: Biomedical imaging technologies provide a window onto biological organisms as well as the human body, revealing the spatial patterns of growth and development, the structure of tissue and their chemical composition, as well as the function of organs and body systems. The focus of Dr. Sled's research program is the development of new biomedical imaging technologies and applications with the goal of improving human health through better diagnostic methods and improved understanding of the mechanisms by which diseases arise and progress. Dr. Sled has an extensive track record in developing imaging technologies for assessing fetal and placental health. This proposal builds from recent progress by his group in identifying fetuses at risk for brain injury. Inadequate supply of oxygen or nutrients while in the womb, premature delivery, congenital conditions, acquired infections or diseases, toxicants in the environment, and drug exposures are all known to affect brain development and can have persistent consequences for cognitive abilities, mental health, and quality of life. Under this proposal, he will develop two diagnostic technologies, BOLD MRI and wave reflection ultrasound, that will aid in identifying fetuses most at risk for these injuries. BOLD MRI is a non-invasive imaging method that is sensitive to the availability of oxygen to the developing fetus. A program of research is proposed that leverages the strengths of mouse models of fetal distress to overcome the current gaps in knowledge for interpreting BOLD MRI in the fetus and identifying risk of brain injury. This work will combine non-invasive MRI measurements similar to those made in human fetuses with advanced 3D optical imaging that is only feasible using invasive methods and genetically engineered mice. In parallel to this work, an advanced form of wave reflection ultrasound will be developed for detecting placental disease that can cause brain injury or stillbirth. This will build upon a new diagnostic approach developed in Dr. Sled's lab, and will leverage an emerging technology called ultrafast ultrasound that is 100-fold times faster than conventional ultrasound imaging. Together these proposed technologies address an unmet need for more sensitive and specific monitoring of fetal development. Translated to humans, these approaches could identify individuals at risk and guide interventions to promote healthy brain development.

column36: Palliative Approaches to Care in Aging & Community Health
column37: Several population-based studies report that most people prefer an out-of-hospital death. Yet, ~85% of Canadians die in inpatient settings. Many of these admissions could be prevented if patients and their caregivers had equitable access to palliative approaches to care in the community. The overarching aim of the proposed Canada Research Chair (CRC) - Tier 1 in Palliative Approaches to Care in Aging & Community Health is to improve equitable access to, and quality of, palliative approaches to home and community-based care for people with chronic life-limiting illness and their caregivers. This will be accomplished by studying three major issues: (1) Formal (paid) and informal (unpaid) caregiving; (2) Palliative approaches to care for vulnerable populations; and (3) Optimizing home and community-based care. This aim will be achieved through two objectives: (1) build upon my existing research program to generate new knowledge and to design, implement and formally evaluate community-based interventions; and (2) scale and sustain training opportunities (graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, clinician scientists and new investigators) to build capacity in research and practice and to inform policy and health system decision-making. My research addresses inequities in vulnerable sub-groups, pays attention to gendered dimensions of care, and is framed by social justice and health equity theories. The knowledge generated will guide design, implementation and evaluation of community-based interventions, while directing clinical practice improvements and informing health and social policies. Building on my deep practice roots as a nurse and clinician scientist before taking up an academic position in 2004, I bring strong leadership skills as a clinician, teacher, researcher, and collaborator, the sum of which equips me well for the CRC. The research that I lead is critically-oriented and pragmatically focused toward `real world' impact. My research has positioned me as a leader in palliative approaches to care for older adults and their caregivers, equity-oriented care, integrated knowledge translation, and mobilizing research findings for health system transformation, both nationally and internationally.

column36: Improving Infectious Disease Innovation Governance
column37: Although the threat posed by coronaviruses has been known for a long time, the world was ill-prepared for Covid19. Prior to the pandemic significant amounts of funding had been allocated to research related to coronaviruses. But progress toward a drug therapy or vaccine was limited before the pandemic began because the systems we rely upon to encourage innovation are tied closely to financial rewards. Unless the financial rewards are predictable, in other words, the interest in developing a drug or vaccine to address an infectious disease like Covid19 will be weak outside of a public health emergency. To improve the world's preparedness against infectious diseases, we therefore need to rethink how we develop drugs and vaccines-we need to change the laws, policies, and practices that we use to drive innovation in order to make the world less vulnerable to future public health emergencies. And we also need to ensure that there are no barriers to sharing knowledge and producing an important intervention like a vaccine in quantities sufficient to meet the world's needs when an infectious disease outbreak occurs. Building upon ten years of research about important public health interventions like the Ebola vaccine that was developed in a Canadian government laboratory, as a Chair in Applied Public Health my goal is to improve the system of infectious disease innovation. I will study how drug and vaccine innovations are developed in the real world, identify practical solutions that can sustain infectious disease research outside of outbreaks, and train the next generation of infectious disease scientists to ensure that their research improves our security and remains broadly accessible to people who are in need, both within Canada and beyond its borders.

column36: Still I Rise: Indigenous youth-led strategies as a pathway to wholistic health and health equity
column37: Indigenous youth are disproportionately affected by poor health. The root causes are broad and directly linked to the lasting effects of colonization. To improve wholistic health, we need to acknowledge these generational and structural challenges. Accordingly, population health interventions aimed at reducing disparities must recognize the historical and contemporary adversity Indigenous youth face, and be grounded in decolonizing approaches which prioritize Indigenous resurgence and self-determination. This program of research will determine how an exemplar, evidence-based culturally affirming population health intervention (the Indigenous Youth Mentorship Program, IYMP) serves as a pathway to wholistic health and health equity. IYMP is an after-school healthy living program delivered by Indigenous high school (youth) mentors for younger elementary students. The core components are: 1) healthy eating, 2) physical activity, and 3) relationship building and mentorship. While children are the intended beneficiaries, we now understand the tremendous impact IYMP has on youth mentors. Mentors have experienced positive benefits related to the social determinants of health including their education, employability, and social networks. We have started to document these benefits; however, efforts have been piecemeal. This research will build on IYMP's success, to determine how IYMP serves as a pathway to address two critical determinants of health: educational attainment and pathways to employment. This work will generate innovative methods and will rely on implementation science adapted for relevance within Indigenous communities prioritizing youth voice and ways of knowing. The proposed program of research will, in partnership with Indigenous youth examine if and how a school-based, communal culturally affirming intervention (i.e., IYMP) serves as a pathway to educational attainment and employability - ultimately improving wholistic health and health equity.

column36: Hesitation a la vaccination : Comprendre pour mieux agir
column37: La vaccination est une mesure de sante publique tres efficace pour prevenir des maladies. Toutefois, de plus en plus de personnes ont des craintes et doutes importants par rapport aux vaccins. On estime ainsi qu'une personne sur trois hesiterait a se faire vacciner ou a faire vacciner son enfant. On nomme ce phenomene <<hesitation a la vaccination>>. Les personnes hesitantes peuvent refuser certains vaccins ou retarder la vaccination et ces comportements ont ete associes a des eclosions de maladies evitables par la vaccination, comme la rougeole. Cette situation est particulierement preoccupante dans le contexte de la vaccination contre la COVID-19, car l'hesitation a la vaccination pourrait nuire au succes de la campagne de vaccination. Ce programme vise donc a mieux comprendre pourquoi des personnes hesitent a se faire vacciner ou a faire vacciner leur(s) enfant(s) ainsi qu'a examiner pourquoi certains professionnels de la sante ont des reticences face a la vaccination. De plus, des travaux seront menes afin de developper et evaluer des solutions pour diminuer les craintes et les doutes par rapport a la vaccination et favoriser des decisions vaccinales informees. Differents projets de recherche de nature qualitative (entrevues, recherches ethnographiques) et quantitative (sondages) seront realises pour ce faire.

column36: Healthy environments through learning from and enhancing community capacity for climate change and food system action in northern Canada
column37: The food systems of Indigenous Peoples in the Northwest Territories (NWT) and other communities in northern Canada are based on the harvesting of country foods, and form the foundation of spiritual, cultural, physical, and mental well-being for individuals and communities. There is a dual food system in communities in the NWT, with country foods as a preferred way of life, complemented by market foods. The lack of fresh and affordable market foods compounded by changes in country food access and availability fuels alarming rates of food insecurity throughout the NWT. There are documented impacts of climate change for Indigenous Peoples' food systems, including: access to, and availability of traditional food species and, changes in harvesting practices (including harvester safety concerns), as well as food safety. Understanding climate change impacts and identifying local adaptations in the food systems of Indigenous communities in the NWT is critical for the health and sustainability of communities, the environment and land. The proposed research program aims to learn from and enhance community capacity to address place-based priorities to inform climate change and food security action locally, regionally, and territorially. Through supporting and evaluating community-led initiatives, this research will promote community action and self-determination of local food systems in communities in the NWT and ultimately improve health outcomes. The knowledge gathered, and shared across multiples levels (locally, regionally, territorially, government decision-makers/ knowledge users) will facilitate development of more effective programs and policies, including communication and knowledge sharing strategies, to address food security and climate change in the NWT, other northern regions in Canada, and globally, the circumpolar north, and remote communities in other countries.

column36: REsearch and ACtion for Healthy Cities (REACH-Cities)
column37: The REsearch and ACtion for Healthy Cities (REACH-Cities) program is focused on how cities can welcome and support people of all genders -especially those of age, racial, income, or ability groups who have historically been overlooked within city planning. The research spans the implementation and impacts of population health interventions (e.g., municipal transportation and community planning policies, to on-the-ground changes to the built environment such as new rapid transit and bicycle facilities, to programs to support social connections and physical activity) and focuses on the health-related outcomes that pattern by gender and other intersectional identities. There are three connected themes of work: A.Generate new knowledge on the implementation and impacts of healthy cities interventions, using a gender-based intersectional lens (Population Health Intervention Research) B.Develop and apply novel approaches for integrating gender equity into decision-making in local, national, and international settings (Methods and Tools for Intersectoral Action) C.Foster a generation of changemakers, equipped with the expertise to catalyze action toward cities that promote health and health equity for all people. (Training for Healthy Cities) REACH-Cities is designed as a responsive program, adopting community-engaged research methods to ensure it reflects both urgent needs and timely opportunities. My primary partners are local government decision-makers: those responsible for designing and building healthy cities. Outputs will empower partners with relevant evidence on their pressing needs around gender equity; embed change in how equity is considered within city planning processes and actions; and train the next generation of healthy cities researchers and practitioners to advance action on gender equity. Collectively, these impacts will shape a host of future interventions that serve to improve urban environments for all genders.

column36: Upstream action at the individual-, organizational- and policy-level to improve health and reduce inequities
column37: Upstream prevention means addressing the root causes of illness and disability, such as the social determinants of health, and often engages diverse sectors in a coordinated effort to improve health and reduce inequities. Upstream prevention in primary healthcare is a central focus of my research. As a family physician, public health specialist and scientist, and as founder and director of the Upstream Lab, I have built a strong foundation for this Applied Public Health Chair. Over the 6 year term, I will work closely with decision makers, primary care organizations and communities to: 1) establish a system of ongoing evidence syntheses to identify the most effective upstream interventions and support scale-up in primary care organizations; 2) use implementation science methods to study change in primary care organizations as they engage in upstream prevention, and provide this to knowledge users to inform health system reform; 3) identify gaps in the evidence, and work with patients, providers and policymakers to identify future research priorities and obtain funding to develop and evaluate new upstream interventions; 4) link upstream efforts in primary healthcare to rapid responses to future health threats and opportunities for policy change in collaboration with public health. Throughout, I will build capacity among research trainees and early career researchers, share methodological lessons learned with an Upstream Summer Institute, and extend our impact through Upstream Lab International Fellows. This work is in close collaboration with decision makers such as Anna Greenberg (Chief of Strategy and Planning, Ontario Health), and a National Advisory Council involving patient partners, primary care organizations, public health organizations and funders from across Canada. Collectively, my activities proposed for this Chair will significantly advance upstream prevention in primary healthcare to promote health and health equity nationally and internationally.

column36: Improving the equity, appropriateness and sustainability of sexually-transmitted and blood-borne infection testing systems through implementation science research
column37: As an Applied Public Health Chair, my focus will be on developing and evaluating programs for getting tested for sexually-transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBI), focusing on programs that make it easier to get tested, and reduce the strain on the health care system. People living in rural and remote communities face many barriers to getting tested, including limited laboratory services or greater concerns about privacy, in addition to barriers such as concerns about being judged by healthcare providers faced by many people at risk for STBBI. In order to reduce these barriers, my program of research will continue to focus on the impacts of GetCheckedOnline (GCO), BC's internet-based testing system for STBBI. I have shown GCO to be an effective way to reach people with these barriers and health agencies in BC are keen to continue rolling out the service in different communities. However rising costs are becoming increasingly difficult to manage and I will conduct research that more closely looks at the factors affecting the sustainability of GCO (that is, how we can continue scaling up the service in BC). I will also look at what is needed to develop two new testing programs in BC, the use of testing kits that provide instructions for collecting your own specimens, and how non-health care providers such as staff in community based organizations can take a greater role in providing testing. My goal of this Chair is to conduct research that has an impact on reducing testing barriers, improving access, and ultimately reducing the spread of STBBI. I will also use the funding available through the chair to develop stronger relationships with stakeholders to ensure my research is useful in meeting new public health challenges over the course of the chair. Finally through my Chair I will develop a hub for applied public health research on STBBI, and provide support and mentorship for junior researchers starting their careers in the area of STBBI research.

column36: To assess the impact of COVID-19 on prenatal education and pregnancy outcomes in mothers and children in remote First Nations communities in Manitoba
column37: COVID-19 pandemic seriously affected the prenatal education for pregnant women and potentially has long lasting adverse effects on the pregnancy outcome and health of mothers and their children. First Nations (FN) pregnant women and children particularly those living in remote communities, may be more severely affected. We propose to determine the impact of COVID-19 on the interruption of prenatal education and resultant consequences including GDM, cesarean section, infant growth and breastfeeding initiation in FN women and their offspring in Manitoba via a database study, and on prenatal education, food intake, physical activities, spousal support, breastfeeding initiation and duration to pregnant FN women in remote Island Lake communities compared to those in rural FN communities in Manitoba, and FN and non-FN pregnant women and children living in Winnipeg via online or hardcopy survey with the support from regional health authority, communities, health workers and community Elders. The results of the proposed study will demonstrate the negative consequences of COVID-19 on prenatal education, lifestyle, family support, child growth and pregnancy outcomes in FN and non-FN mothers and their children in urban, rural and remote communities. The findings from the project may help to understand and mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on the health of FN pregnant women and their children to identify the areas in pregnancy and postpartum programs, which are required to be improved in remote and rural FN communities and to protect the health and wellness of Indigenous women, children and their families.

column36: Indigenous People's response to the Covid-19 pandemic: Conceptualizing concepts of risk and health through an Indigenous midwifery-led approach
column37: How do pregnant Indigenous Peoples in Ontario conceptualize health and risk before and during the COVID-19 pandemic in the context of maternity care? Using Indigenous feminist theory, Indigenous feminist methodology, qualitative interviewing using an open-ended questionnaire with Indigenous participants who have or will experience evacuation for birth before or during the COVID-19 pandemic, we will: 1) Investigate how Indigenous Peoples who are pregnant conceptualize pregnancy related health and risk and how this informs their navigation of public health measures before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. 2) Document the strategies employed by Indigenous Peoples to maintain their spiritual, emotional, physical, and mental health and wellness when facing evacuation for birth and how this has been affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. 3) Explore the effects of the COVID-19 restrictions in relation to evacuation for birth and their impacts on the cultural webbing of Indigenous communities in Ontario during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Our research team, comprised of scholars, Indigenous midwives, and health policy analysts will address a gap in our knowledge about the weighing of risk Indigenous Peoples undertake when accessing healthcare systems and how this affects both their cultural fabric and health-related decision-making process. This proposal builds on research conducted in the spring of 2021 regarding the impact of the pandemic on evacuation for birth in Ontario, that concluded Indigenous Peoples in Ontario receive substandard care, care that is jeopardized by complicated, disconnected healthcare systems. The research will be led by an Indigenous NPA with strong Indigenous leadership and will contribute knowledge to further the meaningful development of maternity care policies and programming that is reflective of the experiences of Indigenous Peoples who live in and access maternity care in Ontario during the COVID-19 pandemic.

column36: Inuit Youth and Families During COVID-19: A Strengths-Based Focus on Resources Needed to Optimize Post-Pandemic Resilience.
column37: How the COVID-19 pandemic has affected Inuit youth in Nunavut is not yet well understood. Enduring effects of colonialism, infrastructure inequalities, geographic isolation, and loss of cultural identity may make Inuit youth more vulnerable to the psychological effects of COVID-19. In this research, we are hoping to support Inuit youth in sharing what the impact of this pandemic has been on their own and their families' mental wellness. We are further hoping to invite youth to identify the culturally specific personal and community resources they relied on to get through the many restrictions that were imposed in the pandemic. This information, as well as the youth's reports on COVID-19 related challenges and needs, would provide input on useful tools and services that could be offered to communities in post-pandemic efforts to best support resilience. The proposed study builds on recommendations provided by youth who participated in a recent small pilot study which identified multiple facets of youth and community resilience. In that preliminary study, youth highlighted the notion of connection as being an important concept leading to resilience when physically isolated. This study would 1) Add to our limited understanding of the psychosocial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic 2) Design, together with youth leaders, a way to identify a comprehensive list of cultural and community aspects of connection believed to contribute to resilience: several culturally sanctioned research approaches will be considered in consultation with the youth. 3) Investigate additional and alternative ways of creating connection in a technological age. 4) Identify, together with youth, existing as well as wished-for social structures and systems that may further support connection and resilience during a pandemic. 5) Situate resulting findings in a culturally-embedded philosophical framework-Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (IQ)-to allow for a richer and more accurate understanding of resilience.

column37: Dietary fibres are fermented by microbes, typically promoting gut health; however, patients with inflammatory bowel diseases, describe worsening symptoms following fibre consumption. Our novel findings demonstrate that select unfermented fibres induce pro-inflammatory, and cancer-promoting pathways mediated by microbes, and are associated with microbe function, luminal metabolites, barrier integrity, and patient dietary fibre avoidance. The objectives of this program are to define the molecular mechanisms underlying the link between diet, microbes, microenvironment, and inflammatory responses and to further utilize our readily available national patient cohorts to develop safe and affordable tailored dietary and microbe-altering interventions to mitigate these detrimental health effects.

column36: Brain Cancer Epigenomics
column37: As CRC in Brain Cancer Epigenomics, I have set up a diverse research group that includes trainees and staff with expertise in genomics, informatics and functional studies with patient-derived models. This integrated team is contributing new knowledge on epigenetic principles underpinning childhood and adult brain cancers. Renewal of my CRC will enable continuity in our search for targetable epigenetic entities that characterize these lethal malignancies. I propose a program that builds on our recent discoveries, incorporates new technologies, and integrates dry and wet lab activities to delve into unexplored contributions of the non-coding genome to cancer initiation and progression. We will use clinical samples to perform bulk and single-cell (epi)genomic techniques to identify new mechanisms that lead to aggressive cancer behavior. We will deploy our patient-derived primary cultures and xenografts to test hypotheses generated from our -omics data. We will leverage our national and international networks to foster collaborative efforts that benefit from the best expertise and models. And we will pursue translational opportunities through established and new partnerships with industry and clinicians. My research program will focus on two main problems: (1) Investigating the epigenetic determinants of cancer stem cell fate in adult glioblastoma. Cancer stem cells are crucial populations of cells that escape treatment and seed relapses. Targeting them is an immediate and unmet clinical need. (2) Understanding how the epigenomes of childhood brain cancers evolve following treatment. Finding ways to predict the evolutionary trajectories of these tumors could put us "one step ahead" of cancer and give us a real chance at preventing relapses. The complexity of these problems requires the seamless integration of orthogonal approaches, which we will execute by integrating the complementary skills and expertise we have in the lab.

column36: Pain Research
column37: It is estimated that 25% of Canadians suffer from chronic pain; a large proportion of whom have non-specific chronic back pain (CBP) which is not related to specific tissue damage. Unfortunately, more than 50% of patients with non-specific CBP do not benefit from pharmacological treatment (refractory CBP). While some can benefit from cognitive therapies, in the absence of valid pre-screening methodologies, identifying those most likely to benefit is an ongoing challenge. Contributing to this challenge is our limited understanding of the mechanisms behind refractory CBP. While many patients can experience pain relief from the expectations generated during a health care encounter, how variability in brain mechanisms of expectation interferes with CBP recovery and reduces the efficacy of administered treatments is unclear. Hence, we aim to establish the neurobiological features through which expectations and negative ideation lead to refractory CBP, with the goal of improving outcomes in this population. Our lab is investigating the variability in the extent to which negative expectations can amplify perceived pain and reduce the effectiveness of treatment in people with CBP. We are testing whether the variability is due to underlying differences in structure and function of associative-learning-circuitry of the brain. People with non-specific CBP conditions will be recruited from clinics. MRI data will be acquired with a 3T GE MRI located at the Biomedical Translational Imaging Center, Halifax. Functional MRI scans will be acquired while participants perform an expectation task that uses visual cues and heat evoked pain. The experimental data will be used to predict changes in clinical pain measured after two weeks of placebo treatment in one group of people while an additional group will serve as a control group for the placebo effect. The analysis plan will include mapping of task data to identify activations in associative learning circuitry. A connectomics approach will determine how functional and structural brain connections underpin affects of expectation on pain modulation in resting-functional and diffusion MRI brain scans respectively. Strengths of our proposal include a unique multidimensional approach that is novel and clinically relevant. By demonstrating a clear neurobiological basis for refractory CBP, we will facilitate the development of valid pre-screening tools and improve treatment strategies and outcomes in this population.

column36: Molecular Pathogenesis of Emerging Viruses
column37: Background and Importance: Emerging infectious diseases are a global health threat with outbreaks often resulting in complex patterns of severe illness that are either unknown or poorly understood. Infectious diseases are responsible for at least 10 million deaths worldwide per year, or approximately 25% of all global deaths. Zoonotic diseases, which result from the spread of pathogens between human and animals, comprise ~60% of these infections. Thus, emerging zoonotic viruses are a critical concern for human and non-human animal health. Further, emerging virus spillovers have been increasing in frequency and disproportionately affect low- and middle-income regions of the world. Given the public health and economic impact of emerging virus outbreaks, there is a critical need to expand our understanding of the mechanisms that contribute to disease during infection, the long-term impacts of these infections following disease recovery and increase preparedness and capacity in regions where emerging viruses are overrepresented. Program Goals: The overall goal of this program is to identify, characterize and increase responsiveness for emerging viruses that have the potential to impact global human and non-human animal health and disrupt regional economies. The primary objectives of this program are: i) Characterization of emerging virus pathogenesis at physiological barriers; ii) Assessments of long-term sequelae following recovery from emerging virus infections; and iii) Identification of emerging virus threats through international One Health surveillance studies in Africa. Novelty and Expected Impact: This research program will combine traditional laboratory investigations with field-based surveillance and patient studies to study how emerging viruses move from animals to humans, the mechanisms underlying severe disease following spillover and long-term health complications in recovered patients. Given the increasing frequency of emerging virus spillovers, there is a definitive need to better understand where and how emerging viruses are circulating in Nature and better prepare for spillovers by enhancing our understanding of the complex diseases they often result in. These activities will increase preparedness and response capacity at the focal points of emerging virus spillovers and will help reduce the overall health and economic tolls of these outbreaks.

column36: Molecular Genetics and Neurodegenerative Diseases
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease with no cure. ALS affects motor neurons in the central nervous system (CNS) that control the voluntary movement of muscles. Neuroinflammation and abnormal accumulation of microglia, which are the primary innate immune cells in the CNS, are further characteristic disease phenotypes in the affected brain regions. Together, ALS leads to muscle weakness, paralysis, and death within 2-5 years of diagnosis. Several fundamental questions in the ALS field remain unanswered: (1) How do these motor-controlling neurons undergo degeneration? (2) Do these disease-associated microglia protect neurons from dying or damage the neurons? Understanding the molecular basis of the disease process is pivotal to facilitate effective strategies for disease prevention and therapeutic intervention. Many transgenic mouse models of ALS have provided insights into the disease process; however, showed limitations as these transgenic mice exhibit accelerated end-stage phenotypes and rapid death, rendering difficult to dissect the natural disease course, particularly at early-stage ALS. During the last five years, Dr. Park pioneered a new mouse model that addresses these limitations: The MATR3 S85C knock-in mouse line expresses the disease-causing protein at the physiological level and closely mimics features of early-stage ALS, including progressive motor deficits, degeneration of motor-controlling neuronal groups and neuroinflammation. This new ALS mouse model thus provides an unprecedented opportunity to dissect the disease process at early disease stage. In the next five years, Dr. Park will characterize and study MATR3 S85C knock-in mice at presymptomatic and early disease stages to (1) identify the key disease-initiating events leading to neurodegeneration and (2) determine how microglia contribute to ALS pathogenesis particularly during early disease stage. Identification of early disease events and elucidation of the role of microglia will enhance our understanding of the disease mechanism and provide important clues to the development of effective strategies for disease prevention and therapeutic intervention for early-stage ALS. More broadly, her findings will illuminate valuable insights into other neurodegenerative diseases.
