column36: Cognitive Neuroscience of Memory
column37: The ability to retrieve autobiographical memories lies at the center of many aspects of our daily life, from thinking about who we are to helping us solving problems, however the underlying brain mechanisms are not fully understood. Reaching this understanding is important because declining autobiographical memory can reveal differences between healthy and pathological aging, such as older adults at risk for dementia. Dr. Sheldon's innovative research program will discover the neurocognitive processes that support autobiographical memory, how these processes contribute to non-memory functions, and are affected by age. Her research focuses on the understanding the contributions of the hippocampus to construct autobiographical memories as this brain region is a neural target of both normal and pathological aging. Her objective is to first use behavioural studies and cutting-edge neuroimaging technology to determine how the hippocampus can be recruited for constructing different types of autobiographical memories as well as imagined future events that guide everyday tasks like problem solving. Equipped with a new understanding of how the hippocampus works for autobiographical memory, Dr. Sheldon will then determine how hippocampal processes are affected by normal cognitive aging and pathological aging, and the behavioural consequences to memory. Dr. Sheldon's anticipated discoveries about autobiographical memory have the potential to provide a richer and more accurate portrayal of how human memory works in the real world. In addition, by situating her studies in the context of aging, her work has major implications for understanding age-related memory decline, which is urgently needed given the rise in Canada's aging population.

column36: Critical Care Neurology and Trauma
column37: Finding Better Ways to Treat Neurocritically Ill Trauma Patients Traumatic brain injuries from road traffic accidents, contact sports and falls cause millions of deaths around the world every year. They also represent an enormous economic burden, as they can result in severe permanent impairments that cost the health care system billions of dollars. Despite clinical advances, we still face important knowledge gaps when it comes to managing the care of survivors. As Canada Research Chair in Critical Care Neurology and Trauma, Dr. Alexis Turgeon is looking to fill these gaps. The goal of his research is to improve bedside practices and outcomes in critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury by using evidence-based, patient-centered decision making. Dr. Turgeon and his research team are working on ways to improve prognostic assessment and level-of-care decisions as well as on how to better manage care by conducting patient-oriented research on current interventions used in neurocritically ill trauma patients. The chairholder is also looking at brain resuscitation strategies and intervention to improve long-term outcomes in this population through large-scale multicenter collaborative research and trials. Dr. Turgeon is looking for developing and implementing tools to guide decision-making processes in bedside care. Dr. Turgeon's research is informed by his years of experience in caring for neurocritically ill and trauma patients as a specialist in anesthesiology and critical care medicine. His previous research looked at how long-term outcomes following traumatic brain injury vary greatly across treatment centres, as do decisions to withdraw life support. Dr. Turgeon hopes his latest research will lead to substantive changes in the way health care workers care for critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury and, ultimately, improve their health outcomes.

column36: Surgical Innovation
column37: Dr. Bhandari's research program will advance the identification of innovative treatments using high quality collaborative research practices to improve the lives of persons with musculoskeletal injury and disease. Key objectives include the identification of optimal approaches to improve the lives people experiencing musculoskeletal trauma and intimate partner violence, as well as therapies to reduce major adverse events after surgery. Three core themes are the focus of the research program: 1) Advancing Surgical Innovations in Musculoskeletal Trauma 2) Uncovering Novel Insights about Intimate Partner Violence in Surgical Patients 3) Preventing Adverse Outcomes in Surgery The above core research themes are operationalized primarily by the conduct of multi-national large randomized trials and large observational cohort studies. This program of research advances results from prior research and informs treatments across a broader population of persons-those with both acute conditions (fractures) and chronic conditions (arthritis). By conducting 3 large randomized trials, 3 large observational studies, and 1 national knowledge translation program, this research program will transform patient care and deliver new treatments and insights for improving the health outcomes after musculoskeletal injury and disease. This research program will also expand over the next 7 years to include pilot trials in opioid reduction interventions in surgery. The rationale for the three major themes, each with their unique foci, are driven by the increasing global burden of orthopaedic trauma injuries worldwide and the need to identify low cost-effective treatments, the crisis of intentional injuries in women from domestic violence, and the need to identify and reduce adverse outcomes towards safer surgery worldwide.

column36: Cellules Souches et Genie Tissulaire
column37: Cette Chaire de recherche du Canada vise a reconstruire des tissus humains par genie tissulaire a partir de cellules souches qui sont presentes dans les tissus apres la naissance. Le programme s'articule autour de 3 principaux domaines de reconstruction d'organes, soit la peau, la cornee, et les valves cardiaques. L'objectif principal vise a reconstruire, a partir de cellules humaines, des organes humains vivants dont les proprietes histologiques, physiologiques et fonctionnelles se rapprochent le plus possible de celles des tissus d'origine afin d'utiliser ces substituts pour ameliorer la guerison des plaies. Ces tissus reconstruits nous procurent des modeles pour mieux comprendre des phenomenes physiopathologiques (e.g. guerison des plaies ou epidermolyse bulleuse). L'approche experimentale mise sur la methode de genie tissulaire (auto-assemblage) que nous avons decouverte pour reconstruire des tissus vivants sans ajouter de biomateriaux. Le potentiel de ces tissus humains reconstruits comme modeles sophistiques de recherche fondamentale et pre-clinique sera exploite afin d'ameliorer nos connaissances en biologie cellulaire, communications intercellulaires, et developpement de nouveaux traitements. Un des defis consiste a ameliorer la pigmentation des peaux reconstruites. En recherche appliquee, la combinaison du genie tissulaire et de la therapie genique est prometteuse pour la correction de deficits resultant de maladies genetiques. Il s'agit de corriger le gene non fonctionnel par le transfert du gene fonctionnel dans les cellules malades in vitro avant la production des tissus puis leur implantation autologue in vivo. VISION Le point culminant se trouve dans les applications cliniques qui favoriseront le traitement plus rapide des grands brules grace a des peaux reconstruites bilamellaires(PRB, derme et epiderme) autologues; l'amelioration de la surface oculaire des patients atteints de deficiences en cellules souches limbiques par la greffe de culture d'epithelium corneen autologue; le soulagement des patients atteints d'epidermolyse bulleuse dystrophique par la greffe de PRB combinees a la therapie genique. Le besoin grandissant pour les organes de remplacement et les applications du genie tissulaire pour ameliorer la guerison des plaies permettent de predire que cette technologie deviendra un element important pour l'economie de la region. Cette Chaire contribuera a l'excellence et a la renommee de l'Universite Laval en medecine regeneratrice.

column36: genomique de l'asthme et des maladies allergiques
column37: Des millions de personnes au Canada sont asthmatiques et 7% a 9% des enfants souffrent d'allergies alimentaires ou d'eczema. Il est reconnu que certaines maladies allergiques sont interreliees et s'inscrivent dans un continuum debutant par de l'eczema chez les nourrissons. Ceux-ci presentent par la suite 35% a 75% plus de risque de developper des allergies alimentaires, de l'asthme ou de la rhinite. Il est capital de mieux comprendre leurs bases biologiques afin de mieux predire, diagnostiquer ou traiter ces maladies. C'est tourne vers ces objectifs, repartis suivant quatre axes de recherche, que se deploiera le programme de recherche de la Chaire en genomique de l'asthme et des maladies allergiques. L'axe 1 vise a poursuivre l'identification des regions du genome associees a ces maladies par l'etude des variations dans le code genetique, de l'expression des genes ainsi que des mecanismes qui l'influencent. Cet axe permettra de mieux comprendre les mecanismes biologiques impliques. L'axe 2 vise l'etude de la diversite microbienne afin d'identifier des profils de risque ou de protection pour le developpement de maladies ou l'application de traitements. Ainsi, la diversite microbienne intestinale, nasale, orale et cutanee des enfants souffrant d'allergies alimentaires et repondant adequatement au traitement de desensibilisation de meme que ceux des individus asthmatiques et non asthmatiques ayant developpe la COVID-19 seront analyses. L'axe 3 vise l'integration des donnees multiples obtenues par les travaux des axes 1 et 2 et permettra par le biais de modeles statistiques complexes le developpement d'outils predictifs, diagnostiques et therapeutiques. Par exemple, la combinaison de plusieurs facteurs genetiques pourrait permettre de detecter quels sont les enfants a risque de presenter des maladies allergiques pour prevenir leur developpement ou reduire leur severite par une intervention precoce. column36: Evidence-Informed Health Systems
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has shown us both how well and how poorly: 1) governments are equipped to find and use research evidence to inform their decision-making; 2) evidence groups are equipped to: a) create the right evidence product at the right time; b) engage stakeholders who can help to understand what the evidence means for a particular decision; and c) use evidence products and work with stakeholders as part of a broader approach to support decision-making; and 3) networks of individuals and groups are equipped to work together and in innovative ways to support decision-making. The proposed program of research will address three objectives: 1) evaluate how government policymakers organize themselves to make decisions based on the best available research evidence; 2) create and evaluate innovative ways that evidence groups can summarize evidence, work with stakeholders and more generally support decision-making; and 3) create and evaluate networks that can support decision-making in more coordinated and innovative ways. For each objective, the focus will include efforts to address both urgent issues (like COVID-19 response) and long-standing issues (like improving care experiences and health outcomes in our health system). The research methods will capture descriptions of, views about, experiences with and the impacts of the approaches being used to inform decision-making. The data will come from existing datasets (e.g., evidence products that have been created) and from interviews, surveys, available documents, and directly observing what individuals and groups do. The governments, evidence groups and networks will be drawn from Canada and internationally, including governments with which I work directly (like the Canadian federal government and many provincial governments) and evidence groups and networks that I lead or co-lead (like the McMaster Health Forum, RISE and COVID-END). Returning to more everyday policy challenges after the worst of the pandemic is over will provide an opportunity to build on what went well in the evidence response to the pandemic, as well as to previous challenges in our health system, and learn from and address what didn't. The research will capitalize on the attention being given to evidence as a result of COVID-19, make significant contributions to the science of supporting decision-making, and shape future efforts to address policy challenges based on the best available research evidence.

Can we use genomic, chemical genomic, and genome architecture data to infer evolutionary relationships? 4. Finally, how can we apply the tools we develop for model organisms to human biology? column36: Valvular Heart Disease
column37: Approximately 1,100,000 Canadians (~3.5% of the population) have valvular heart disease (VHD). Aortic valve stenosis (AS) is among the 2 most frequent VHD. If left untreated, severe AS is inevitably fatal and the only available option for the treatment of this disease is the aortic valve replacement (AVR) by a prosthetic valve using surgery (SAVR) or transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVR). AS represents a major public-health and socio-economic burden, which is expected to increase exponentially in the next decades due to population aging. The overarching goal of the proposed research program on the Canada Research Chair (CRC) in VHD is to perform multi-disciplinary, patient-oriented, research to advance the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of VHD, and particularly of AS. The Chairholder has brought together a consortium of clinicians, scientists, and engineers from academia and industry to achieve a large magnitude and impactful research program that includes 5 main work-packages: WP#1: Develop and validate a novel tool based on capacitive electrocardiography and artificial intelligence (AI) for universal screening of AS in the general population. WP#2: Develop and validate AI-based algorithms: i) to determine the different aortic valve disease phenotype clusters; ii) to identify patients with AS who are at risk for rapid disease progression. WP#3: Undertake a randomized controlled trial (RCT) (EARLY-TAVR) to assess the timing of AVR in asymptomatic severe AS; WP#4: Undertake two RCTs (TAVR-UNLOAD and PROGRESS) to assess the timing of AVR in at-risk moderate AS. WP#5: Undertake a pharmacotherapy RCT that will assess the effect of aggressive lipoprotein(a) lowering to slow stenosis progression in mild to moderate AS. The innovative research program proposed by the Chair for the next 7 years will transform the screening, diagnosis, and treatment of AS. The new technology proposed in WP#1 has the potential of greatly enhancing the efficacy and generalizability of AS screening in the population. The AI-based algorithms developed in WP# 2 will allow the determination of the aortic valve disease phenotypes and of the risk of rapid disease progression in each individual patient, which is key to enable personalized therapeutic management of AS. The RCTs conducted in WPs # 3, 4 5 will constitute major advances for the optimization and individualization of the timing and type (pharmacotherapy vs. SAVR vs. TAVR) of treatment in patients with AS.

column36: Chemical Genetics
column37: Exploiting the Nematode C. elegans as a Platform for Drug Discovery Dr. Roy has pioneered the use of the nematode C. elegans to discover small molecule tools and potential drug leads. Here, he describe his vision for his next seven years of exploration. Parasitic Prodrugs: Dr. Roy's group has discovered a suite of small molecule scaffolds that are bioactivated within nematodes into lethal products. Focusing on 'nemactivin', they have shown its bioactivation is restricted to nematodes and that it has real-world utility against plant parasitic nematodes. They are: i) further developing nemactivin as a nematicide with industrial partners; ii) developing additional nematicide prodrugs, and iii) building a system to identify otherwise innocuous small molecules that can be metabolically converted into lethal products within any targeted organism. Novel Neuromodulators: Dr. Roy's group has developed a pipeline to identify small molecule disruptors of motor behaviour in nematodes. They discovered a scaffold called 'nementin' that induces convulsions, paralysis and death though massive synaptic vesicle release. They are: i) further developing nementin with industrial partners; and ii) characterizing a second neuromodulatory molecule called wact-45 that inhibits a neurotransmitter transporter. Wact-45 has anthelmintic potential and is a candidate drug for Myasthenic Syndrome, a rare human disease caused by excess neurotransmitter release. Liver Disease Drugs: Dr. Roy's group discovered that select small molecules form crystals within the C. elegans alimentary cuticle. At least two cuticle components are required for this phenomenon; intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs- see below) and polar lipids. The group found that the PGP-14 worm homolog of the ABCB4 polar lipid pump, which is mutated in the liver disease PFIC3, is required for cuticle lipid accumulation. They identified 30 FDA drugs that suppress the pgp-14 mutant's lipid deficit and are exploring these as candidate drugs to treat PFIC3. Amyloid Disruptors: As introduced above, Dr. Roy's group discovered small molecules that crystallize in the alimentary cuticle through interactions with amyloid-like IDPs. Molecules that prevent human amyloid formation disrupt crystal formation in the IDP-rich cuticle. Dr. Roy's group is exploiting this system to identify novel small molecule that disrupt amyloid formation and develop them as candidate treatments of amyloid-based diseases such as Alzheimer's.

column36: Neuroimaging of Aging
column37: Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) is a uniquely non-invasive and versatile neuroimaging method that provides both neuronal and vascular readouts and was the focus of Dr. Chen's first CRC term. Specifically, the rs-fMRI technique can be used to obtain maps of intrinsic brain networks, which are believed to sustain cognitive function. Moreover, it inadvertently provides vascular information, which can, in turn, be capitalized in the study of vascular aging. Dr. Chen and her team were the first in the world to elucidate the vascular and physiological contributions to rs-fMRI by showing the contribution of CVR, cerebral blood flow, blood oxygenation saturation, vasomotion, and respiratory cycles to rs-fMRI measurements. Dr. Chen's team also demonstrated how rs-fMRI could become a method for mapping cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR). CVR is a measure of vascular health that is highly valued clinically, given its reliable prediction of cerebrovascular disease. Since establishing the only existing rs-fMRI-based CVR quantification technique, Dr. Chen and her collaborators have validated the resting-state CVR mapping technique in varying clinical scenarios. The publications resulting from her first CRC term have helped propel me into a recognized world leader in rs-fMRI of brain physiology. In her second CRC term, Dr. Chen will innovate methods for extracting neurovascular information from rs-fMRI data. Specifically, she will probe the relationship between whole-body vascular health and neurovascular health, and clarify the association between vascular and microstructural changes in the brain, which can clarify the neurodegenerative process and help identify new treatment targets. She will also, through industry and clinical collaborations, translate her research findings into new therapeutic tools and practices. Specifically, she will expand on her research program with 4 research themes. ? Theme 1. Mapping neurovascular physiology in brain aging. ? Theme 2. Understanding the brain-body connection in aging and age-related disease. ? Theme 3. Clarify the vascular contribution to early microstructural brain changes in aging. ? Theme 4. Applying neurovascular mapping to age-related diseases and therapies. The proposed research will be important for advancing health screening and care and will be critical for enhancing collaborations across the Baycrest and University of Toronto network across Ontario, Canada, and abroad.

column36: A deep phenotyping network for understanding human islet variation in health and diabetes
column37: Insulin is secreted from cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans into the blood after a meal to control blood sugar levels. In type 1 diabetes (T1D) islet cells are destroyed by an auto-immune reaction. In type 2 diabetes (T2D), islet cells fail to produce enough insulin to meet the body's needs. Thus, understanding the factors that control insulin production by islet cells is an important step towards determining the causes of diabetes, the potential for diabetes reversal, an ultimately prevention of the disease. Even in people without diabetes insulin levels in the blood are extremely variable and is impacted by factors that include nutrition, genetics, and exposure to environmental chemicals. This variation can also be seen in insulin secreted by pancreatic islets isolated from the pancreas of organ donors. Led by the Alberta Diabetes Institute IsletCore, one of the world's top pancreas tissue biobanks, our team of experts will catalog the variability in human insulin secretion, islet cell functions, and molecular profiles across many pancreas organ donors with and without diabetes. The result will be a comprehensive 'encyclopedia' and web portal that links genetics, gene expression, environmental chemical exposures, metabolites, islet proteins, and more with detailed cellular functions of insulin-producing islet cells. Our Team will also answer key questions about how genetic-risk for diabetes acts to impair insulin secretion; about personalized insulin responses to different nutrients; and about the links between environmental pollution and reductions in insulin secretion. We will also make this 'encyclopedia' available to researchers around the world, supporting a better understanding of human insulin secretion and diabetes.

column36: A First-in-human Trial of Autologous Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSC)-Derived Islets: Developing a Personalized Diabetes Therapy
column37: Diabetes is caused by the lack of insulin, a hormone produced by the islet Beta-cells in the pancreas that regulates blood sugar. Chronically high blood sugar can cause complications such as blindness, amputations, stroke, heart disease, kidney failure and shortened lifespan. Insulin injection is lifesaving but is not a cure. Islet transplant has been successful in regulating blood sugar levels in some patients with T1D; however, it requires life-long anti-rejection (immunosuppression) drugs and is limited by the scarcity of organ donors. Building on our 21 years of experience in islet transplant, our team will address these challenges by developing a stem-cell based therapy to replace or supplement damaged Beta-cells in people with various forms of diabetes, including T1D, T2D, and surgical diabetes after total pancreatectomy. We propose to manufacture new islet beta cells from patients' own blood cells, so that the cells will be accepted by the immune system and no anti-rejection drugs will be needed. In this project, we will generate 'self'-islets from people with diabetes and implant these cells under the patient's skin. In parallel, we will transplant these cells into rats. We will also test whether these cells function similarly to human islets. We anticipate that this project will establish safety of the manufactured 'self'-islets and that they can produce insulin. This will pave the way to our next step - Health Canada approval for a clinical trial with therapeutic doses to be infused in the liver to assess efficacy of this cell therapy. Being able to transplant an unlimited supply of self-derived islet cells without immunosuppressants is a novel approach to treat various forms of diabetes and could be the world's first functional cure.

column36: Designing Stem Cell Derived Islets for Diabetes Therapy
column37: Diabetes is a debilitating disorder of high blood sugar that afflicts millions of Canadians. People living with type 1 diabetes lack the cells that release the hormone insulin, so multiple daily insulin injections remain the conventional way to control blood sugar levels and survive. Scientists in Edmonton made breakthroughs for the transplant of clusters of insulin-producing cells, called islets. The "Edmonton Protocol" is quick and works remarkably well, such that many islet recipients are able to reduce or even eliminate insulin injections. Unfortunately, the only source of islets for transplant is recently deceased donors and only a tiny fraction of those in need can receive them. There have been remarkable breakthroughs in unraveling the process by which islet cells develop naturally in the body. As a result, it is now possible to replicate this process in the lab with cultured stem cells, culminating in insulin producing cells. Exciting clinical trials are now underway in which islet precursor cells generated from stem cells are loaded into thin devices and implanted under the skin. While initial assessments in patients are encouraging, insulin production from the transplanted cells is currently inadequate to reverse diabetes. Our goal is to utilize our broad expertise and a new lab-based model of human islet development to significantly improve upon the manufacturing of the islets to obtain more robust insulin delivery. To achieve this, we have assembled a team of leading experts who will apply their diverse and complementary skills to develop novel strategies to improve the generation of fully functional stem cell derived islets. In particular, we will engineer new cell culture methods to selectively control islet architecture and enhance cell fitness. Collectively our work may form the basis for new clinical trials in patients with type 1 diabetes, and ultimately generate an effective therapy that will free Canadians from insulin injections.

column36: Immunometabolism in diabetes: harnessing metabolic crosstalk between islets and immune cells for therapy
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease that occurs when the immune system mistakenly kills the beta cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone, insulin. A true cure for T1D requires the immune system to be reset, so that it no longer attacks the pancreas, and for the insulin-producing beta cells to be replaced or regenerated. We have assembled a unique team of experts in the biology of immune cells and insulin-producing beta cells in diabetes, to study how these cells interact in diabetes, and understand why the immune system becomes over-activated and kills the insulin-producing beta cells and causes T1D. We will focus on a growing area of research known as immunometabolism, which is the study of how metabolic pathways inside cells affect their ability to divide and function. We propose that changes in metabolic pathways within beta cells and immune cells may enhance the immune attack on the pancreas. We will study metabolic pathways in immune cells in health and in T1D. Through this work we hope to gain a better understanding of how changes in metabolism in immune cells may influence autoimmunity, and to design ways to alter these metabolic pathways in immune cells to prevent or slow T1D.

column37: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure in Canada, and requires either dialysis or a kidney transplant. Kidney failure leads to persistent unpleasant symptoms that reduce quality of life to levels seen in certain types of advanced cancers. In addition, kidney failure increases the likelihood of cardiovascular disease and premature death. Fortunately, new therapies called "SGLT2 inhibitors" have been discovered that reduce the risk of kidney failure and cardiovascular diseases in people with a kind of diabetes linked with being overweight, called "type 2 diabetes". These drugs may delay the need for dialysis by as much as 15 years, or prevent it entirely. Unfortunately, it is not known if these medicines are also beneficial for people with type 1 diabetes ("juvenile diabetes"), and these medicines are not approved in North America for use in this condition. In our research program, we will perform a series of studies in people with type 1 diabetes. First, we will study kidney effects of SGLT2 inhibition in people with type 1 diabetes over a two year treatment period, including routine blood and urine tests that reflect kidney protection. We will also perform research-based blood and urine tests to understand how these medications may reduce kidney damage over the long term. We will also examine ways to avoid side effects. As part of this study, we will study how patients feel about taking these medications, in terms of both benefits and side effects. Next, we will use Danish health records (where SGLT2 inhibitors can be used for type 1 diabetes) to determine if these therapies reduce the risk of kidney disease when used as part of routine care in type 1 diabetes. Finally, we will study the effectiveness of these medications as a long-term kidney protective therapy using mathematical models. Overall, this program has the potential to reduce the risk of diabetes complications and improve the quality of life in people living with this serious condition.

column37: For individuals living with diabetes, one of the major complications of the disease is diabetic retinopathy (DR), which, if not treated, can lead to blindness. Unfortunately, not everyone living with diabetes sees an eye care professional regularly. Screening rates are lowest in the populations most vulnerable to adverse health outcomes in Canada, including younger individuals, individuals located in large cities in low-income communities, newer immigrants, in rural, remote and Indigenous communities. Depending on where a person lives in Canada, up to 60% of individuals living with diabetes have not had their eyes examined within 1 year. Knowing who has not had their eyes checked is not always possible for community-based doctors and nurses by looking at their electronic health records. This information, however, is found in provincial healthcare data. Giving this information to doctors and nurses would help to improve DR screening (DRS) rates across the country. This project proposes to support primary healthcare DRS activities by using provincial administrative data in Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia and New Foundland and Labrador to determine who needs to have their eyes examined according to clinical practice guidelines. The generated lists of individuals will be provided to community care setting to arrange an eye appointment using existing optometry, ophthalmology and tele-ophthalmology services. Coordination and capacity of care within the four provinces will also be examined. We will use various research methods to evaluate the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, implementation challenges, sex and gender-related differences in care provision, and critical factors to success. The broader goal of this public health initiative is to identify unmet care needs and begin the pathway towards the creation of a Canadian DRS programme, similar to that in the United Kingdom, and consequently eliminate DR as the leading cause of blindness in working-age individuals.

Blood samples will be collected by patients themselves, by using a special self-collection device, and we will use proteomics to measure the levels of over 3000 circulating proteins. We will also measure the concentration of colchicine and of other commonly used diabetes medications used by study participants. By combining these data with the genomic data and the detailed information collected during the clinical study, the research team will study the biological pathways underlying differences in treatment benefits between diabetes patients. The study will also allow for the validation of the previous findings made in COLCOT to determine whether some patients may benefit more from colchicine. We will also study the role of sex and gender on diabetes and drug response and on study participation. Precision medicine has the potential to identify who benefits more from diabetes medications. Such risk stratification is important as there are increasing treatment options for patients with diabetes. Our Team Grant will provide valuable evidence toward better prevention strategies and treatment options for women and men living with diabetes.

column36: The Developmental Origins of Pediatric Type 2 Diabetes and Early Renal Dysfunction
column37: T2D in childhood continues to increase worldwide and affects Indigenous children and families more than non-Indigenous populations. Childhood onset T2D is associated with high rates of early onset rapidly progressive kidney disease. As more children are diagnosed with T2D, more babies are being born having been exposed to diabetes in the womb (in utero). Consequently, we now know that diabetes exposure in utero is a potent risk factor for the exposed child to develop childhood-onset T2D; however, it is not yet known how diabetes exposure increases the risk or if it increases risk of associated renal complications. Recent scientific advances have revealed that the environment in the womb can alter the expression of genes in the offspring via a process called "epigenetic regulation", which can impact important metabolic pathways needed to maintain health. In addition, a specific change in the DNA sequence (HNF1a gene variant) also imparts a risk of T2D development in the offspring. In this study, we aim to define the epigenetic signature of babies born to mothers with diabetes so that we can determine which genes and pathways are affected by this exposure. Subsequently, we aim to use mouse and cell models to examine how these epigenetic changes impact function of important metabolic tissues, including the pancreas. Finally, we will examine how the HNF1a variant results in T2D risk for children and if it also impacts renal development, function and risk. Upon completion of this study, we hope to better understand how maternal diabetes exposure and the HNF1a gene variant impacts offspring health, to identify biomarkers at birth that can be used to determine which children are at highest risk of developing T2D, and to inform the development of new treatments to prevent T2D and renal complications in exposed children.

column36: Central role of muscle autophagy in metabolism and musculoskeletal health
column37: Diabetes and osteoarthritis (OA) are two of the most common diseases affecting approximately 11 million and 4 million Canadians, respectively. Diabetes is associated with several serious complications, including eye disease, nerve damage, foot ulcers, kidney disease, heart attack, and stroke. OA can cause chronic pain, making it challenging for individuals to exercise, walk, and carry out daily activities such as getting dressed or bathing. Furthermore, both diabetes and OA are associated with depression and can significantly impact a person's quality of life. Despite how common and debilitating these conditions are, there is no cure for either. Therefore, we need to understand their underlying causes better to identify more effective treatment targets and earlier detection. Diabetes (specifically type 2 diabetes (T2D)) and OA often occur together, and both are associated with a condition called sarcopenia. Sarcopenia refers to the loss of muscle mass and strength that occurs with aging. We, therefore, thought that sarcopenia and changes within the muscle might provide a common link between T2D and OA. Autophagy is a process that basically "cleans out" damaged components of cells. When autophagy is reduced or not working properly in muscle, damaged cell components accumulate, and this contributes to sarcopenia. This team project aims to determine how problems with muscle autophagy contribute to T2D and OA. To do this, we will study mouse models in which genes regulating autophagy have been altered in muscle. We will also test if we can treat or reverse T2D and OA using gene therapy to correct the defect in autophagy in muscle. Finally, we will take samples of muscle and blood from individuals suffering from these conditions and analyze them to identify common genetic links between T2D and OA to identify new drug targets.

column36: Bringing An Evidence-Based Community Physical Activity Program to Francophone Minorities in New Brunswick: Can We Fit the Brain with Physical Activity
column37: Compared to Anglophones, more Francophones living in NB are over 65 years, present low levels of education, are considered physically inactivity, have a low socio-economic status, and have poor access to primary healthcare. As such, it has been documented that older adult living in mainly Francophone regions of New-Brunswick have worse general health profiles (physical and cognitive) than those of people in mostly English-speaking regions. Sustainable prevention and management strategies delivered in rural settings, where Francophone seniors live, are therefore needed to address health disparities between French older adults and their Anglophone counterparts. Improvements in healthy living behaviours, such as uptake of a regular physical activity program is generally associated with improvements in physical function, mental health and improvements in cognition in older adults. In New Brunswick, access to such physical activity programs is of particular concern for seniors who are Francophone as they are more likely to live in rural settings and to cumulate multiple chronic conditions. A logical target for addressing these inequities is to facilitate an uptake of physical activity among Francophone seniors living in rural regions of New Brunswick. Targeting this behaviour therefore has the potential to help overcome the physical and cognitive challenges faced by Francophones living in a rural setting. The objectives of this project are to:1)Engage partners and community members in the development and delivery of a 16-weeks 'community-tailored' physical activity program in underserved rural francophone regions (Village de Memramcook), 2)Adopt an inclusive approach to encourage and facilitate engagement of community members from underserved groups, who can take part in a physical activity program and 3) Understand the role of a community physical activity program on physical and cognitive well-being in francophones (males and females) living in rural NB.

column36: Understanding healthcare access barriers and health and community resource information needs of Official Language Minority Communities across Canada, exploring the interaction of minority language status, and cultural and community contexts.
column37: When health services and health information are not available in an individual's preferred language, access to care and health promotion services can be compromised. Understanding the nuances which distinguish the healthcare needs of a recent Francophone immigrant from West Africa living in Winnipeg, Manitoba from a fifth-generation Francophone farmer living in Cornwall, Ontario and the interaction of language and other socioeconomic factors, is essential to diminish barriers to accessing healthcare and health information. This study will conduct a secondary analysis of patient reported data to examine self reported healthcare access barriers, as well as health and community resource information needs of Official Language Minority Community members (OLMC) across Canada, considering the intersectionality of minority language status, as well as cultural and community contexts. We will conduct mixed methods analyses on data combined from two ongoing repeated cross-sectional evaluation studies enrolling 340 primary care providers caring for an estimated 450,000 patients. We will compare results from OLMC Canadians to English or French speaking Canadians not in minority status. We expect a sample 10800 OLMC members compared to 61200 non OLMC members. Multivariable logistic regression analysis will be used to assess associations between reported access barriers and patient OLMC status and sociodemographic charactiersistics. We will also use a machine learning clustering algorithm approach to identify groups with similar characteristics and then conduct a qualitative exploration of OLMC members' free-text reported health and community resource information needs across and within these groups. Our interdisciplinary, bilingual and multicultural team leverages a network of communications experts, primary and public health care researchers, leaders and teachers, who can ensure the results of our project drive better health services for, and research on, OLMCs.

column36: Sante mentale, comportements a risque et acces aux services de soutien: l'experience des etudiants postsecondaires des CLOSM au Manitoba et au Nouveau Brunswick
column37: Les jeunes adultes en milieu postsecondaire vivent une transition de vie importante; plusieurs sont susceptibles de developper des troubles de sante mentale, des comportements a risque et de connaitre des difficultes academiques. La pandemie liee a la COVID-19 a exacerbe les difficultes liees a la formation d'un reseau social, ayant un impact negatif sur leur sante mentale. Les jeunes n'ont pas souvent recours aux services de soutien professionnel en raison d'une meconnaissance de la disponibilite des services et de barrieres a l'acces. Par le biais d'un sondage en ligne, cette etude vise donc a decrire l'experience de la population etudiante de premier cycle de deux universites francophones canadiennes de communautes de langue officielle en situation minoritaire (CLOSM) (Universite de Saint-Boniface et de Moncton) quant a la sante mentale et l'acces aux services de soutien psychosocial, la consommation de substances, la securite routiere, la violence, les pratiques sexuelles et la dependance aux appareils electroniques personnels. Les donnees seront analysees selon l'age, le genre, le profil identitaire ethnolinguistique (francophones de langue premiere et de langue seconde; francophones de l'international) et le site (contexte rural/urbain et densite de francophones), car ces facteurs peuvent influencer la sante et le bien-etre. Des entretiens de groupes serviront a diffuser et valider les resultats du sondage aupres de la population etudiante et a identifier les obstacles auxquels sont confrontes ces jeunes en ce qui concerne l'acces aux services de soutien sur le campus et dans la communaute dans la langue officielle de leur choix. Les donnees recueillies sous-tendront la formulation de recommandations quant aux moyens de favoriser leur acces aux services de soutien disponibles. Ces recommandations seront partagees avec les collaborateurs et les decideurs politiques afin de soutenir l'epanouissement de ces jeunes, essentiels au maintien de la vitalite des CLOSM.

column36: Remedier a la penurie de ressources professionnelles au sein des CLOSM : renforcement des strategies de recrutement et de retention au profit des communautes francophones et acadiennes du Nouveau-Brunswick
column37: Au pays et ailleurs, la COVID-19 a mis en evidence les lacunes en ressources humaines deja bien ressenties dans les systemes de sante. L'offre de services et soins de sante au Nouveau-Brunswick est fragilisee par une penurie d'infirmieres immatriculees et de medecins, laquelle touche plus particulierement les milieux ruraux, ou sont concentrees des communautes de langue officielle en situation minoritaire (CLOSM). Depuis 2008, le Reseau de sante Vitalite (Reseau), dont la langue de fonctionnement est le francais, dessert des CLOSM reparties dans quatre zones geographiques. Or, une centaine de postes de medecins et environ deux cents postes d'infirmieres immatriculees sont a pourvoir sur le territoire administre par le Reseau. Devant cette realite, cumulee a la crise sanitaire actuelle, il est imperatif de renforcer les strategies de recrutement et de retention du Reseau pour assurer sa viabilite et maintenir des services et soins de sante qui repondent aux besoins des CLOSM. Dans une dynamique de co-creation de connaissances, nous avons ainsi etabli un partenariat aupres du Reseau. Les resultats de cette etude permettront a notre partenaire d'identifier et de mettre en oeuvre des solutions concretes qui emanent de son contexte afin d'augmenter le taux de recrutement et de favoriser le maintien des professionnels en poste. En dressant un bilan des postes vacants et en examinant le taux de roulement, il sera possible, d'une part, de determiner si les defis les plus importants se situent sur le plan du recrutement ou de la retention. D'autre part, il s'agira d'examiner les facteurs qui rendent attrayants les environnements interne, telles les conditions de travail, et externe (ou communautaire), comme le milieu de vie des professionnels. La methodologie est basee sur un devis mixte qui combine des approches quantitatives et qualitatives.

column37: Given the Official Languages Act and the impact of language barriers on health treatment outcomes, it is imperative to understand and address the needs of the Francophone Official Language Minority Communities (OLMCs) across Ontario. Ensuring optimal substance use disorder treatment across communities, including in Francophone OLMCs, should be a top research priority. The proposed project will explore the needs of addiction providers in Francophone OLMCs through a survey and develop an Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes (ECHO) model in collaboration with these practitioners to address knowledge gaps and create a community of practice. The ECHO model utilizes videoconferencing technology to connect with primary care providers and support them in the management of chronic diseases, thereby reducing geographical barriers and improving access to specialized care within the community. Previous research shows that the ECHO model is effective in building capacity and improving patient outcomes. The results of this project will therefore serve to optimize addiction care for Francophones living in OLMCs across Ontario.

column36: Effet de la langue utilisee lors de l'evaluation cognitive aupres de francophones en situation minoritaire presentant divers niveaux de bilinguisme: vers l'elaboration de lignes directrices pour le depistage securitaire des troubles cognitifs a l'aide du Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
column37: Les francophones vivant dans des communautes ou l'anglais est la langue majoritaire ont souvent des difficultes a avoir des services de sante dans leur langue, une situation qui peut apporter plusieurs defis dont des erreurs de diagnostic. Des membres de notre equipe ont observe que leurs clients francophones ne semblaient pas avoir les memes resultats si leur evaluation de fonctions cognitives etait faite en francais ou en anglais. Ils ont aussi observe que certains qui s'identifient comme etant bilingues (francais/anglais) ne savent pas dans quelle langue ils devraient passer l'evaluation cognitive. De fait, peu d'etudes ont examine les consequences de passer des evaluations cognitives dans sa langue seconde, l'influence du degre de bilinguisme sur les resultats et quels facteurs aideraient le client et clinicien a choisir la langue d'evaluation. Le MoCA est une evaluation utilisee frequemment pour depister des difficultes cognitives. Malgre que des etudes pilotes ont montrees que passer le MoCA dans sa langue maternelle entraine des meilleurs resultats que dans sa langue seconde, les preuves sont encore insuffisantes. Ce projet de recherche vise a identifier l'effet de la langue utilisee lors d'une evaluation cognitive (MoCA) avec des participants bilingues. Specifiquement, le projet cherche a evaluer si les resultats au MoCA passe en francais different de ceux passe en anglais pour des francophone en milieu linguistique minoritaire, en fonction du degre de bilinguisme du participant et de son niveau de fonctionnement cognitif. L'etude recrutera 200 participants de plus de 55 ans qui repondront a des questions au sujet de leur profil de bilinguisme (age d'acquisition, utilisation et competence dans chacune des deux langues), passeront le MoCA dans les deux langues et des evaluations objectives de leur competence linguistique dans les deux langues. Les resultats serviront a suggerer des lignes directrices pour l'evaluation des personnes bilingues.

column36: Effet d'une intervention de coaching sur le bien-etre et la detresse des medecins francophones dans les communautes de langue officielle: un essai controle randomise
column37: Les patients ont besoin de medecins en bonne sante. La detresse et l'epuisement des medecins ont des repercussions sur le bien-etre des medecins et de leurs patients. Il est prouve que les medecins francophones travaillant dans des communautes francophones en situation minoritaire sont plus exposes au risque de detresse et d'epuisement professionnel, du aux defis uniques que represente le fait de servir une population en situation minoritaire. Le coaching de vie est un outil de developpement personnel qui aide les individus a maximiser leurs forces et leurs competences et les aide a reprendre le controle de leur vie selon leurs valeurs personnelles. Le coaching de vie, dispense par des coachs certifies, reduit la vulnerabilite a la detresse et a l'epuisement. Malgre son potentiel, le coaching de vie n'a pas encore ete teste pour les medecins au Canada. Notre but est d'evaluer le coaching de vie sur la qualite de vie, la detresse et l'epuisement professionnel chez les medecins francophones des communautes francophones en situation minoritaire au Canada. Nous menerons une etude dans laquelle les medecins francophones au service des patients francophones en situation minoritaire seront repartis au hasard en deux groupes: soit ils recevront du coaching par un coach professionnel (groupe intervention), soit aucune intervention (groupe temoin). column36: Canada's COVID-19 Vaccine Confidence in Indigenous Populations: A Mixed Method Study
column37: Vaccines are important public health invention to curb many lethal diseases like smallpox. Vaccines are not always accepted by the people and there is a lot of hesitancy. People are misinformed on vaccine related research and hence reluctant to receive vaccines. Such vaccine hesitancy is found to be more common in the Canadian Indigenous populations than in the non-Indigenous populations. Thus, we are proposing an in-depth learning of the reasons of vaccine hesitancy in the First Nations (FN), Metis, and Inuit people. We are building this project on the ongoing CIHR-funded COVID Impact project at the Bridge Engagement Center, a community-based research center in Ottawa, Canada. Thus far, the COVID Impact project has successfully recruited 397 participants, collected detailed data around all objectives via a survey administered by peers with lived experience. A preliminary analysis of the COVID Impact project (N=397; Indigenous=138 (FN=46, Inuit=61, Metis=9, Mixed=10 and Did not mention any specific tribe=12)) demonstrated significantly more vaccine hesitancy in the FN and Inuit participants. The proposed study will follow a community based participatory action research approach, designed, and operationalized in previous Bridge studies. We will conduct 3 peer-led Focus Groups (1 each with FN, Metis, and Inuit) and 25-30 semi-structured interviews to learn vaccine hesitancy in the Indigenous populations. The short-term outcome of the study will benefit Indigenous populations, as their unique needs and challenges will be identified to inform Ottawa specific COVID-19 vaccine insecurities and strategies for implementing public health responses to strengthen vaccine confidence. We will co-create Grade-6 reading level material around vaccine hesitancy, barriers, and facilitators of vaccine confidence, specific for Indigenous populations. In the long-term, findings from this project will help guide vaccine strategies for Indigenous communities with a people first approach.

column36: Interactions between hippocampal vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) loss and amyloid pathology in circuit and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease is thought to be caused by abnormal accumulation of amyloid beta proteins in the brain, which lead to neurodegeneration and dementia. However, most people over the age of 70 have amyloid in their brains, but the majority do not develop dementia. In addition, treatments developed to decrease amyloid have not been beneficial in Alzheimer's. This suggests that other critical factors must interact with amyloid to increase the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. One strong possibility is that a protein named the vesicular acetylcholine transporter is this critical factor interacting with amyloid. This protein-which regulates how effectively a type of brain cell called a cholinergic neuron can communicate with other brain cells-is decreased early in Alzheimer's. We propose that the degree to which this protein changes in cholinergic neurons helps to drive the development of Alzheimer's disease. We will address how disruptions in the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, combined with amyloid pathology, contribute with cognitive dysfunction and degeneration related to the hippocampus, a critical brain region involved in memory and affected early in Alzheimer's disease. In mice which present both amyloid pathology and reductions in the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, we will use novel tools to investigate rapid chemical changes in, and activity of, cells in the hippocampus, while the mice solve touchscreen tests of learning and memory that are the same as those used in human patients. We will also chemically restore function to the vesicular acetylcholine transporter in these same animals to potentially slow or stop the course of hippocampal dysfunction and memory loss. Our research will provide a deeper understanding of how chemical changes in the hippocampus contribute to the earliest cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, as well as how next generation therapies might target these changes to prevent disease onset and progression

column36: Methylphenidate-primed rTMS for apathy in neurocognitive disorders
column37: Apathy is a common, early, and disabling symptom in dementias such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is characterized by reduced self-initiated behavior. Attempts to treat apathy include methylphenidate, a dopamine releasing agent, and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a non-invasive brain stimulation method. Both treatments were only modestly effective in reducing apathy in patients with AD and its precursor state, mild cognitive impairment. Emerging evidence suggests that rTMS may also partly act by releasing dopamine, indicating that both treatments share a common mechanism of action. Here, we hypothesize that providing methylphenidate prior to rTMS (or "priming") will be an effective treatment for apathy. By increasing dopamine availability, priming is expected to improve the ability of rTMS to stimulate apathy-specific circuits while minimizing possible adverse effects of higher doses of each treatment. Sixty dementia patients with apathy will receive either methylphenidate (20 mg/day for 2 weeks) and active rTMS (10 sessions over two weeks), methylphenidate and sham rTMS, placebo and rTMS, or placebo and sham rTMS. Our primary aim is to determine if apathy is reduced to a greater degree in patients receiving methylphenidate-primed rTMS compared to those receiving other treatment combinations. Stability of treatment benefits will be determined after 12 weeks. We will also explore blood-based biomarkers of treatment response that will enable novel hypothesis-generating analyses.

column36: Novel mechanisms and therapeutic approach for aging-related pruritus
column37: ITCH: Itch is a debilitating symptom experienced by 40% of the elderly. Itch can have severe impact on quality of life, cause extreme stress and depression, and is the most common skin complaint in the elderly. Currently, many of the current therapeutic interventions for itch are not suitable for the elderly due to their adverse effects, pointing to an urgent medical need. GRANZYME B: Granzyme B is a protein that plays a key role in the body's normal immune response and is present at low levels in healthy individuals. However, our team has shown that high levels of active Granzyme B are found in the skin of the elderly and in patients with itchy, inflammatory skin diseases. Further, it has been demonstrated that Granzyme B levels in the blood are linked to multiple measures of itch severity. In an experimental model of aging skin, we have early evidence that suggests that inhibiting Granzyme B will prevent itch and inflammatory skin. Our team has also recently developed a new topical medication that can inhibit Granzyme B activity and reduce disease severity in experimental models of itchy skin diseases. PROPOSED PROJECT AND IMPACT: We will comprehensively investigate the relationship between Granzyme B levels and measures of itch using aging human skin specimens (collected with full informed consent). We will also use a newly-developed technology to discover unknown functions of Granzyme B in aging itchy skin. Finally, we will use experimental models of aging itchy skin to test the efficacy of our new topical medication in alleviating itch. Taken together, our findings will advance the development of our Granzyme B-targeting medication towards clinical approval and improving patient outcomes.

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible, progressive brain condition that affects memory and intellectual skills. People suffering from AD eventually lose their autonomy and are not able to carry out the simplest tasks. AD is characterized by the progressive accumulation of protein aggregates (amyloid and tau) in the brain and cell death. It is now known that the accumulation of these proteins starts before any cognitive symptoms appear. The major deliverable of this project is the 36-month follow up, large-scale, biomarker study describing tau progression using a second-generation tau imaging agent, CSF and plasma measures of tau and the modulation of brain amyloid on these outcomes. These deliverables will: provide better ways to select patients for clinical trials and permit to better estimate sample sizes necessary for estimating the effects of AD therapeutic interventions.

column36: Platform of synthetic specific promoters for immunotherapies and regenerative medicine
column37: Targeted expression of a gene exclusively in a given cell type or tissue is not currently available. To address this gap, we have developed a technological platform that allows to design specific promoters, that target and limit gene expression to a specific cell type. Building on this technological platform, a start-up company, Immugenia, was created with the goal of bringing this technology to the clinic. The first potential application is cancer immunotherapy with Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). In this strategy, T cells (that are immune cells) are engineered to express at their surface the CAR molecule that recognize tumor cells and induce their killing. However, CAR-T cells are efficient in leukemia, but not in solid cancer. Here, instead of T cells, we propose to engineer hematopoietic stem cells (HSC). Our specific promoters will allow the CAR to be expressed only on T and NK cells (another immune cells), to get CAR-T and CAR-NK cells that will work together against the cancer. We will test this strategy in a model of breast cancer. In regenerative medicine, induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) are seen as a potential therapeutic tool since they can give rise to any cell type when cultured in specific condition. Our specific promoters would allow induce the expression of the gene only in the cell subtype of our choice. In gene therapy, our specific promoters would allow to target the expression of a therapeutic gene with a specificity that is lacking today with the current methods of gene delivery. Through this financial support, we will perform key proof-of-concept experiments in cancer immunotherapy and will broaden and strengthen our intellectual proprietary (IP) portfolio to expand the utility of this platform to a large array of indication. column36: Targeting BMP signaling in the tumor endothelium to improve cancer immunotherapy
column37: Cancer immunotherapy is a type of therapy to treat tumours that aims to use the immune cells of the patient (white blood cells) to kill cancer cells. While this type of strategy has produced encouraging results, numerous hurdles still need to be overcome. One of the main problems facing immunotherapy is the poor functionality of the blood vessels present in tumours, which impedes the recruitment of immune cells to cancers. In addition, tumour blood vessels are highly abnormal, and this leads to poor perfusion, resulting in poor delivery of oxygen to the tumour. This has profound consequences for immunotherapy, as white blood cells used for immunotherapy cannot reach the tumour. Furthermore, the lack of oxygen in the tumours impedes the tumour-killing functions of immune cells. Our project aims to develop strategies to make better tumour blood vessels, so that they will facilitate the infiltration of immune cells in tumours. We hypothesize that this will improve the delivery of immune cells to cancers and improve their tumour-targeting activities, thereby improving the effectiveness of immunotherapy.

column36: Development and preclinical validation of first-in-class dual inhibitors of the atypical MAP kinases ERK3 and ERK4
column37: The development of selective chemical inhibitors of protein kinases is of key importance for understanding kinase mechanisms and exploring their roles in physiology and disease. These chemical tools are also essential to validate potential drug targets and to spur the development of new medicines. Protein kinases are considered highly druggable given the extensive know-how and successful record in kinase drug discovery. MAP kinases are a subfamily of protein kinases that play important roles in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation and immune response. These enzymes have attracted considerable attention as their aberrant regulation has been linked to several human diseases including many cancers. Our laboratory has recently unveiled novel roles of the MAP kinases ERK3 and ERK4 in the pathogenesis of cancer. However, no chemical inhibitor of ERK3 or ERK4 has been available, which hampers the study of their functions and their validation as potential drug targets. In an effort to identify novel chemical inhibitors of ERK3/ERK4, we have recently screened a collection of small molecules and identified a series of compounds that potently inhibit ERK3 and ERK4 kinase activity. This project aims to improve the potency and pharmaceutical properties of the molecules and test their activity in preclinical models of cancer. Our proposal has the potential to lead to the identification of first-in-class dual ERK3/ERK4 inhibitors for cancer therapy.

column36: Erythroid progenitors and precursors impair tumor immunogenicity and promote tumour progression in breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer type and is the leading cause of female mortality worldwide. Unfortunately, the incidence of breast cancer is still increasing in North America. The use of immunotherapy that reinvigorates the immune system against cancer has witnessed an unprecedented revolution in cancer treatment. There is tremendous interest in using immunotherapy to treat breast cancer. However, breast cancer patients do not respond well to such treatments. Therefore, there is an urgent need to better understand how the immune system fights breast cancer in particular in the tumor microenvironment. We have found that immature red blood cells are expanded in the blood of breast cancer patients and also in their tumors. These cells suppress the immune system against cancer and at the same time secrete a protein that binds to the breast tumors and expands them. We have shown that tumor spread can be prevented by stopping the interaction of this protein with the cancer cells. Therefore, this project will allow us to better understand how these immature red blood cells affect tumor progression and how this can be prevented. We believe our novel approach will answer some fundamental questions in the breast cancer field and assist us to develop an immunotherapy approach to prevent breast cancer metastasis. Alternatively, this knowledge can be applied to other cancers.

column36: Engineering injectable cold atmospheric plasma-preserved hydrogel to treat breast cancer
column37: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy is an emerging cancer therapy that reactivates the immune system and has greatly transformed the landscape of human cancer therapeutics. ICB uses immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) to block negative immune regulators so that anti-tumor immune systems are strengthened to fight cancer. Several ICIs have been approved for treating solid multiple cancers and have shown encouraging outcomes in some cancer patients. However, challenges associated with ICB still exist, including low response rates in patients and severe side effects. Therefore, engineering strategies to address these unmet clinical challenges to improve impact of current and future immunotherapies are highly needed. We will engineer a novel injectable therapeutic hydrogel, namely cold atmospheric plasma (CAP)-preserved hydrogel, to deliver ICIs for enhanced ICB therapy with minimized side effects. CAP, a unique type of ionized gas that is preserved in gels, can augment efficacy of ICB therapy. Injectable gels offer local and sustainable drug release to reduce systemic toxicities associated with ICB. We will investigate this strategy for treating triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), an aggressive type of breast cancer that has a high mortality rate among breast cancer patients. While ICB shows some positive effects in a small number of TNBC patients, the overall efficacy requires improvement and unwanted side effects need to be eliminated. In summary, we aim to engineer an injectable hydrogel containing both CAP and ICI to treat TNBC. We will investigate the engineered gels in treating primary TNBC and metastatic TNBC. We will also evaluate the engineered gels in preventing tumor relapse. We anticipate that this treatment strategy can be easily modified and further extended to treat other solid cancers, advancing research and translation of biomaterials-mediated cancer immunotherapies, which could ultimately bring immense clinical benefits for cancer patients.

column37: Despite significant improvements in our ability to treat some breast cancers, a significant subset of women retain a poor likelihood of survival when diagnosed with this disease. For many of these women, chemotherapy remains the only treatment option and often is palliative as opposed to curative. Our research addresses this unmet clinical need. Our research has uncovered a molecular basis for this resistance. We showed that simultaneously decreasing the ability of cancer cells to neutralize a class of toxic molecules, called free radicals, profoundly sensitizes breast cancers to the tumoricidal properties of complex I inhibitors. column36: Toward elucidating the interplay between cell contractility state, mechanotransduction and alternative splicing during tumor progression
column37: The physical properties of biological tissue, including its stiffness, can drastically change over a lifetime, be it during regenerative processes or the evolution of a disease. An abnormally high tissue stiffness is an important risk factor of developing a cancer and is linked its progression. However, we don't know how exactly the stiffness of the tumor contribute to the progression of the disease, or if it can be leveraged to identify those aggressive cells. In this research project, we will use a multidisciplinary approach based on tissue engineering, cell biology and high throughput genomics to identify a genomic signature characteristic of the response of aggressive cells to tumor stiffness. First, we will use a combination of engineered scaffolds to identify a stiffness signature based on the presence of alternative versions of specific proteins. Then, we will validate this in an animal model. Finally, we will investigate whether expression of such a protein variant can influence how a cell interacts with the stiffness of the tumor and if it can influence the metastatic outcome. We will focus on the focal adhesion kinase, a prototypical mechanical sensor of tissue stiffness, as a model of the contribution of protein variant to cell response to stiffness. Overall, this multidisciplinary project at the interface of physical science, biology and medicine will provide new biomarkers that identify aggressive cells based on a signature linked to the tumor stiffness. In addition, we will gain new understanding on the processes that link the tumor stiffness with the progression of the disease. This project will ultimately open the way for more personalized prognostics and treatments.

column36: Targeting metastatic breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer affects one in nine Canadian women and those with metastatic breast cancer have a disheartening five-year survival rate of only 28%. Triple negative breast cancers lack the receptors for estrogen, progesterone and HER2 that are present in other types of breast cancer. Those receptors allow them to be targeted by specific therapies. Thus, the main treatment for triple negative breast cancer is chemotherapy which often has serious side effects. Having a targeted treatment option for triple negative breast cancer that is both effective and has reduced side effects is a current unmet clinical need. We have been studying a protein called CREB3L1. It is present in normal breast cells, but it is missing in highly metastatic breast cancers, including ~75% of triple negative breast cancers. The function of CREB3L1 is to block cells from making genes that increase cancer cell growth and metastasis. Therefore, when CREB3L1 is missing, these cancer promoting genes are present at higher levels and these can be targets for new treatments. We validated one of these genes as an excellent new target for metastatic breast cancer. Since there are no known inhibitors for this target gene product, we used computer modelling to identify a panel of likely inhibitors and successfully identified four hit compounds that are good inhibitors. In this project, we will generate, and test compounds closely related to these four hit compounds to find the most suitable drug-like compound that is not toxic to healthy cells. The most promising inhibitor will then be tested for its effectiveness at reducing cancer cell growth and metastasis in models of breast cancer. Our goal is to provide a new and more effective treatment for metastatic breast cancer with a focus on triple negative breast cancer. This novel therapy would have a significant positive impact on patient survival and will improve the health of Canadians diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer.

column36: Defining the role of CDK6 and DNA repair pathways in tumorigenesis and identify CDK4/6-dependent synthetic lethal vulnerabilities in triple negative breast cancer.
column37: Metastatic cancers are the most aggressive cancers, accounting for 90% of all cancer-related deaths. Radiation as well as chemotherapy are not effective enough to fight against these types of cancers. Our lab is studying triple-negative breast cancers (TNBCs), the most aggressive and the deadliest of all breast cancer molecular subtypes. Patients with TNBCs have limited treatment options and their life-threatening condition is most often clinically unfavorable. TNBC have poor prognosis, high metastasis rates, tumor recurrence and show resistance to conventional therapy. To date, there are no approved treatments or effective or approved targeted therapy against TNBC, highlighting a clear medical gap and unmet clinical need for these deadly tumors. The goal of this project is to develop an effective "targeted therapy" for these breast tumors. Our team has recently found that a protein called CDK6 could the DNA repair processes and lead to tumor progression in TNBC. We further found that blocking CDK6 and its downstream DNA repair target genes could efficiently block both the formation and the progression of TNBC tumors. Our objectives are to understand how CDK6 DNA repair functions affect cancer progression with the long-term goal of developing novel drugs that will help combat local and distant relapse and provide improved clinical benefits and outcome for TNBC patients.

column36: Hepatitis C prenatal and postpartum linkage to care and treatment desires
column37: Over the last five years, hepatitis C virus treatment has led to the possibility of elimination in Canada. With highly effective, all-oral therapies of 8-12 weeks that are widely available, the major barrier to elimination is engaging those who have acquired hepatitis C. Typically men have higher rates of hepatitis C as compared to women, however Canadian studies have demonstrated that women of childbearing age now have higher rates than men and are less likely to be treated. These increased rates are related to the power imbalance in injecting practices, and survival sex, and put women at higher risk. Prenatal care is a time where women are often engaged with the healthcare system, and thus may also be an opportune time to link women to hepatitis C care. At present it is not known whether women receive hepatitis C care postpartum prior to their next pregnancy. We propose a formal analysis using Ontario data to better understand at which point women can be better supported to receive treatment. At present, there are two treatments that work against hepatitis C; and it will be important that both are considered in the treatment of pregnant women. As small safety studies have been completed, with larger studies underway, better understanding women's desires regarding both screening and treatment is imperative. We propose to complete a survey of women's desires to be treated in pregnancy, as well as to better understand the stigma they may have faced in healthcare settings by enrolling 100 women who are pregnant with hepatitis C from practices in Ontario, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia. The finding of the Ontario data, paired with the prenatal desires of women from the survey, will provide better understanding of how women with hepatitis C can be better supported to be tested and treated for hepatitis C in pregnancy or postpartum.

column36: Characterization of a novel family of epigenetic readers.
column37: Akin to a novel written by Margaret Atwood wherein words are elegantly placed to narrate a fascinating story, DNA is the book of life enabling complex organisms to live. One can easily see that if someone hides or remove specific words from a novel, the story would change dramatically. The work proposed in this grant aims at identifying novel mechanisms hiding DNA sequences to change the story of life. If genetics is the area of research interested in studying the impact of gene sequences and their mutations in cancers, epigenetics relate to the study of mechanisms that changes the structure of DNA to hide its DNA sequences from being read by the cell; a novel and emerging area of innovation for the cure of cancers and degenerative diseases. Using a combination of several biophysical approaches, the Couture laboratory proposes to study the protein TONSL; a protein linked to developmental diseases. Considering that epigenetic errors are common in diseases such as cancer and aging, the findings stemming from this grant will bring new insights into how epigenetics is regulated and define novel paradigms underlying the sheltering of specific DNA sequences to control life. Consistent with the fundamental roles of epigenetics in human biology, these studies have great potential for new therapeutics avenues for the treatment of aggressive cancers.

column36: Metabolic control of vascular regeneration in retinopathy of prematurity
column37: Retinopathy of prematurity is one of the leading causes of blindness in children. Loss of blood vessels in the immature retina of premature infants decreases energy delivery to neurons, leading to visual impairment. Finding ways to regenerate blood vessels rapidly may help improve vision. In humans and mice, retinal vessels stop growing and degenerate upon exposure to high oxygen concentration. Soon after that initial insult, however, new blood vessels begin to regenerate. Both healthy and diseased (tufts) vessels form simultaneously to reinstate fuel delivery to retinal neurons. What drives the formation of healthy and diseased vessels remains ill-understood. Nutrients and oxygen fuel the energy requirements of the retina. We, therefore, hypothesize that a change in energy signals may dictate healthy vessel growth to reinstate nutrient supply. Our preliminary findings suggest that Sirtuin-3 (SIRT3), a key regulator of energy signals in mitochondria, governs how blood vessels use various fuels. New blood vessels regenerate faster in Sirt3-deficient mice because glucose becomes the preferred nutrient, conferring growth advantage. Hence, changes in energy metabolism in mitochondria may trigger a regenerative vascular signal. Sirtuin-3, through changes in metabolism, sculpts the vasculature to ensure adequate nutrient supply to the retina. Energy signals may, therefore, also drive angiogenesis, besides oxygen, and are promising targets to discover new therapies that will improve vision for patients with retinopathies.

column36: Transcriptional Control of Glioma Stem Cells by a Novel LGALS1/HOXA5 Signalling Pathway
column37: Glioblastoma (GB) is the most malignant primary brain tumor in adults. The present standard of care includes maximal surgical removal of the tumors followed by treatment with Temozolomide (TMZ) and ionizing radiation (IR). Despite these intense efforts, the median survival rate for GB patients remains less than ~18 months following diagnosis. Multiple mechanisms may underlie the resistance of GB to therapy. Brain tumor stem cells (BTSCs) are a rare population of self-renewing stem cells in GB tumors that are highly proliferative. At the same time, they also have the capacity to give rise to all the cellular subpopulation within a tumor. BTSC play important roles in GB resistance to therapy and tumor relapse. We have discovered that two molecules, LGALS1 and HOXA5 function on the same pathway to control BTSC and glioblastoma resistance to IR. In this proposal, we will investigate how LGALS1/HOXA5 signalling pathway regulates BTSCs and glioblastoma tumors. Importantly, we will determine the mechanism of action of drugs that can suppress LGALS1/HOXA5 axis. This work will generate important knowledge for better understanding and treatment of GB.
